en: Now begins the first quarter of the first chapter of the *Padamañjarī*:
"Vṛddhi is āt and aiC. (1.1.1)

This sūtra consists of three words: *vṛddhiḥ*, *ād*, and *aij*. Here, the letter *a* [of *ād*] is meaningful because it stands for the long vowels (*ākāra*) found in actual usage. The singular number is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*). The word *aij*, however, represents both the diphthongs *aikāra* and *aukāra*. Although the two things designated (*saṃjñin*) are dual, the dual number is not employed; for both are expressed as if they had attained unity, being colored by the single form of the word [the compound]. In this way, the singular number should be understood in all pratyāhāras. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a collective dvandva compound: *ād-aij*.

The compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) prescribed by the rule "after a *dvandva* ending in *cu*, *da*, or *ṣa-ha*, when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*)" does not apply here; for the application of compound-ending suffixes is non-universal (*anitya*). This non-universality is understood from the citation of the word *mūrdhan* in the rule "after *dvi* and *tri*, [the suffix *ṭac* is added] before *pād*, *dan*, and *mūrdhan*. Otherwise, since [the word *mūrdhan* would end in the suffix *ṣa* according to the rule] "after *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *ṣa* is added to *mūrdhan*," the citation would have had to be *mūrdheṣu*.

Because of the word *ādaic*, because it is a compound, or because it possesses meaning, when a case-ending arises, the substitution of *ku* for *ca*—as prescribed by the rule "for *cauḥ*, *kuḥ* [occurs] at the end of a *pada*"—would have been applicable; however, since it is treated as a *bha*-stem due to its inclusion in the *ayasmayādi* group, it will not occur. Furthermore, the Sūtras are like Vedic verses (*chandas*). According to the view that the term *vṛddhi* applies to the three types of vowels, the derivation is from the root *vṛdh* (meaning "to increase") with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); and through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the term is applied to the *ādaic* sounds which possess such growth.

Nor is the Sūtra rendered purposeless because the application of the term *vṛddhi* to vowels beginning with *ā* is already established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for it serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatvāt*). Otherwise, it would apply to *ik*-vowels and the like when they are associated with the action of increasing (*vardhana*), as well as to protracted vowels (*pluta*). The restriction is intended so that it may not apply there, but rather apply only to vowels beginning with *ā*.

But how is this so in the view that there are four categories? For when [the term *vṛddhi*] has been assigned as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it is more logical that the word *vṛddhi* should first apply to the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* in another rule such as "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), rather than here at the very time it is being assigned as a technical name? It is replied: according to the view that "the relationship between word and meaning is eternal," a word does not become expressive through human activity after already being expressive prior to any human activity. [Rather, its expressive power is manifested by human convention.]

Therefore, all words are capable of conveying all objects by way of technical designations (*saṃjñā*). In that regard, since linguistic usage cannot be established through an unrestricted meaning, the human effort [of rule-making] is for the sake of restriction—[namely], "The word *vṛddhi* employed by me has the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* as its referent. Thus, the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) has been explained.

Furthermore, there are eight types of alternative explanations regarding the subject matter of the sentences [of the grammatical treatise]: (1) the useless, (2) the instruction on correct forms, (3) for the sake of restricting usage, (4) for the sake of substitution, (5) for the sake of augmentation, (6) for the sake of qualification, (7) for the sake of superimposing its qualities, and (8) for the sake of technical designation (*saṃjñā*). Among these, the statement of something being useless arises from negligence, reliance on error, lack of attention, or incapacity. However, this fourfold set is not possible in the case of the Blessed One.

For the Teacher, with *darbha* grass as a purifier in his hand, seated facing east in a clean place, composed the *Sūtras* preceded by auspicious rites and with great concentration. In that regard, it would be impossible for even a single meaningless syllable to exist, let alone such an entire *Sūtra*! Furthermore, [the objection that] this is not a good instruction (*sādhvanuśāsana*) is also invalid; for the word *vṛddhi* is already established [as a technical term], being formed with the suffix *ktin*, and the word *ādaic* is likewise meaningful.

[Objection: Surely, by virtue of being treated as *chandas* (Vedic), the usage is established within the Sūtra itself; this must therefore be an exceptional rule (*nipātana*) intended to prevent the occurrence of *kutva* even outside the Sūtra. [Response: It is said in reply: in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word *vṛddhi* not being syntactically connected [to the rest of the sentence], and moreover, the fact that words function collectively is established through linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, this position is not tenable. Nor is it for the purpose of restricting usage, for a restriction must be applied only where there is the possibility of simultaneous usage.

Nor does it follow that there would be the undesirable consequence of using both *vṛddhi* and *ādi* together, because they are unrelated prior to their specific application (*viniyoga*), and because the meaning is already conveyed by the word *vṛddhi* alone at a later time. Furthermore, no rule regarding usage is being initiated here. [Objection: But is it not initiated by the rule "and what follows" (*paraśca*)? [Reply: No, it is not initiated with respect to a *pada*. [Objection: Is it not initiated even for a *pada* by the rule "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first"? [Reply: It is not initiated for those two words between which there is no single-word status (*aikapadya*).

Is it not the case that for those two [roots] as well, the rules "before the verbal root" (*te prāgdhātoḥ*) and "the root *kṛ* is employed subsequently in the periphrastic perfect" (*kṛñcānuprayujyate liṭi*) are initiated? No, it is not initiated by such an enunciation. Even so, is it not initiated by the rule "let them know" (*vidāṅkurvantu*) optionally? No; here it is not merely the employment [of the root] that is being regulated, but rather the suffix *ām* and so forth are also prescribed. Therefore, since there is no instance anywhere where a restriction on employment alone is directly enunciated, this is not a restriction on employment. Nor does it serve the purpose of an *ādeśa* (substitute).

For substitution (*ādeśatva*) belongs only to that which is capable of expressing the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*). Now, the word *vṛddhi* does not denote the sounds *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, nor do those [sounds] have the capacity to express its meaning. This is also known from the specific formulation [of the rules]; for when [Pāṇini] says "vṛddhi occurs in place of [the root vowel] before *sic*" (*sici vṛddhiḥ*), or "in *yāti*, *vāti*, *drāti*," or "*rāyaḥ*", "*nāvaḥ*," and so on, it is understood from this that "the word *vṛddhi* does not denote *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, nor are those the substitutes for it. [Objection: Why then is the word *vṛddhi* not the substitute for the word *ādaic*? For there is no such indicative mark (*liṅga*) here. [Reply: True.

This position, however, is simply not possible. For the rule *ādirantyena* (P. 1.1.71) has already assigned the word *aC* as a technical name (*saṃjñā*); how then could there be a reference to its own form? This is because of the prohibition: "not when it is a technical name of a word" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*). By these very same indicative marks, it cannot have the status of an augment (*āgama*). Furthermore, due to the absence of the genitive case, whereas in the rule *pūrvau tu tābhyām* (P. 6.1.84) the meaning of the genitive is understood from the ablative case. Also, because of the absence of indicative marks such as *ṭit*-ness, for no augment devoid of such marks is ever observed.

Nor can it function as a qualifier, because such a relation is impossible and serves no purpose. For it is not possible for the word *vṛddhi* to be identical with the expression *āT-aiC*, nor is it possible for the action of increasing (*vardhana-kriyā*) to be identical with *āT-aiC*. Likewise, there is no purpose served by treating it as a qualifier. By this, the superimposition of its qualities (*tad-guṇādhyāropa*) is also refuted. Just as in the case of "the boy is a lion," the qualities of a lion are superimposed upon the boy, such a possibility or purpose does not exist here.

Therefore, considering that by process of elimination it must be the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), he says: "The word *vṛddhi*," and so forth. The reverse—that the word *vṛddhi* is the named and *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the names—is not the case. For that [reverse] would be threefold: either the word *ādaij* itself, the aggregate *ā ai au*, or those [sounds] individually. Among these, the term *ādaij* cannot be the name; because *aij* is already a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), it is impossible for it to denote its own form (*svarūpa*), it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and it would not apply repeatedly (*anāvṛtti*).

For designations (*saṃjñā*) are indeed subject to repetition; thus, the term *vṛddhi* and the word [itself] recur. [But] the word does not recur from the sound (*nāda*). Nor can it be the aggregate (*samudāya*), because that would involve prolixity (*gaurava*) and because there is no repetition [of the aggregate]. Well then, let it be for each individual [element], because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of repetition—as in "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau," "pūtakratoraica," and "manorau vā"? No; for it is improper to assign multiple designations to a single thing without a specific purpose, for this word *vṛddhi* is not to be praised by a thousand names.

The term "word" (*śabda*) is included so that the object (*artha*) might not be understood as the name; this is established because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is impossible with respect to an object. Thus, here, by stating that the word *vṛddhi* is prescribed as a name, the position that [the technical terms] are meaningless as a whole is refuted. By the phrase "the word *vṛddhi*," the opposite view is refuted. Through the specific formulation—"the word *vṛddhi* is the name, and not the word *āT* etc."—the inclusion of the object is excluded by the mention of "word": namely, that the word *vṛddhi* is the name, and not the object.

Where one desires an operation upon a collection, one exerts effort there—as in the rule "both [are called] *abhyasta*. For in that case, the mention of "both" is for the purpose of understanding them as a combined unit. Alternatively, one creates a significant technical term (*saṃjñā*) based on its etymological meaning, as in "consonants not separated by vowels are *saṃyoga* (conjunction). But here, the creation of a major technical term is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). This is precisely why it is uttered first; otherwise, since an operation must apply to something already existing, it would have been formulated like "aṭ-eguṇaḥ" and so forth.

Therefore, because there is an absence of effort [to apply them collectively], the designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to each individual [vowel]. Furthermore, since the *ā*, *ai*, and *au* vowels are established in common usage, they ought to be subject to this designation. Yet, there is no usage of the entire group [as a single unit] anywhere; thus, due to impossibility as well, the designation applies only to each individual. And there is evidence from an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the evidence? It is the rules: "In *prastha*, [the vowel] is *vṛddha* for *makarka* and so on," and "and for *mālā* and so on. For this is a statement made when the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of what is not *vṛddha* would otherwise apply in cases such as "*mālāprasthaḥ*"; therefore, the designation applies only to each individual. Thus he says: "each individually" (*pratyekam*).

In that regard, there are three possibilities: [the designation applies] only to those elements transformed by the rule, like the technical term *luk* and others; or only to those not so transformed, like the technical term *ṭi*; or to both, like the technical terms *anunāsika* and others. If it were only for those transformed by the rule—namely, those which are to be designated as *vṛddhi*—then [the suffix] *cha* would not apply in *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*; the suffix *mayaṅ* conditioned by *vṛddhi* would not apply in *āmramayam* and *raikulamayam*; and the suffix *phiñ* [conditioned by the rule] "udīcāṃ vṛddhāt" would not apply in *āmraguptāyaniḥ*.

Now, [if it were not for this rule], the suffix -cha would not occur in the forms *gārgīyaḥ*, *aitikāyaniyaḥ*, and *aupagavīyaḥ*—which are derived from bases that have not been modified by that [suffix]. Therefore, because he perceives this fault and because no distinction [between the two types of bases] is being apprehended, he states "by way of generality" (*sāmānyena*) to indicate that the designation applies to both. Since the vowel *ā* is not short (*anaṇ*), it cannot be the grasper of vowels of different durations; thus, the addition of *t* (as in *āt*) is neither for the purpose of excluding those [long vowels] nor for the purpose of including those endowed with other qualities (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, because qualities (*guṇa*) do not cause differentiation: in common worldly experience, even when a theft is committed by a bald man, one who has grown hair is recognized and apprehended as the same person. Similarly, the mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) in the rule "aḍudāttaḥ" serves as an indicator (*liṅga*); otherwise, one would simply pronounce the *aṭ* with its inherent acute quality. Therefore, the inclusion of the letter *t* (in *tapara*) would be purposeless; to this he says: "The inclusion of *tapara*. Here, *taḥ* (the letter *t*) and *paraḥ* (subsequent) form *taparaḥ*; its "inclusion" (*karaṇam*) means its pronunciation. The meaning is: the pronunciation of the letter *t* subsequent to the vowel *ā*.

Alternatively, the compound *taḥ paraḥ* (followed by *t*) is a *bahuvrīhi* with *saṃvijñāna* of its own qualities (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), meaning that the vowel *a* is uttered together with the letter *t*. Regarding the phrase *aij-artham*: that for which the purpose or motive is the vowels *ai* and *au* is so described. In the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, a *bahuvrīhi* was adopted where "that followed by *t*" is the meaning. Anticipating the objection—"How then can the addition of *t* (*tapara*) be for the sake of *ai* and *au*?"—the author shows that a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is also resorted to there, stating: *tād api paraḥ*. The particle *iti* indicates the reason.

"Because that [long vowel] also [is included], it is for the sake of *ai* and *au*. He clarifies the very purpose of being for the sake of *ai* and *au*: "In the case of *khaṭvailaka*, etc. If the marker *t* (in *tapara*) were not present, then by the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*), even the diphthongs (*aic*) consisting of three or four morae (*mātra*) would be grasped; consequently, in forms such as *vṛkṣailakaḥ*, *vṛkṣaudanaḥ*, *khaṭvailakā*, and *khaṭvaudanaḥ*, the substitutes for the three- or four-moraic original bases (*sthānin*) would themselves be three- or four-moraic *e* and *o*. Therefore, the marker *t* is employed to prevent that.

*Āśvalāyana* and so forth are examples of forms (*rūpa*) of those [names] derived from *ākāra*, etc., presented in their respective order. The words *aśvala* and *itika* belong to the *naḍādi* group; the word *upamanyu* belongs to the *bidādi* group. The fourth example is introduced to indicate that the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) has a wide range of application. He states an example of the effect (*kārya*) of an *ākāra* that is not derived from such [a name]: *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*.

As for the examples of *aikāra* and *aukāra* when they are not derived from such [names], they are *raikulamayaṃ* and *naukulamayaṃ*; here the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs by virtue of the rule concerning "vṛddhi" [vowels].
The vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* are termed *guṇa*. Pāṇini 1.1.2.

This is the same as the previous case. However, the purpose of including *ta* (the *tapara* marker) here is for all purposes (*sarvārtham*), whereas in the previous case it was for one of the two purposes; such is the meaning of the word *tu*. For if that [marker] were absent, the designation *guṇa* would apply even to long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels; consequently, in the word *tarati*, sometimes the vowel *a* would be used and sometimes *ā*, because once *raparatva* (the substitution of *r*) has been applied, one [vowel] would be one and a half *mātrās* while the other would be two and a half *mātrās*. Nor does the designation *vṛddhi* override [the application of] the *guṇa* designation.

Because the governing rule concerns a single designation (*ekasaṃjñā*), there is no simultaneous application of multiple designations elsewhere. Furthermore, regarding the designation *guṇa* for *eṅ* (the vowels *e* and *o*) when they consist of three or four morae (*trimātra-caturmātra*), [if that were the case], forms such as *ratheṣā*, *khaṭveṣā*, *aśvoḍhaḥ*, and *vaḍavoḍhaḥ* would result in having three or four morae. Forms such as *taritā* and so on are examples of the phonetic forms of those *adeṅ* sounds (*a*, *e*, *o*) which have been produced by grammatical operations (*tadbhāvita*). *Pacanti* and *jayanti* are examples of the operation (*kārya*) affecting the vowel *a*; here, when the vowel *a* follows [the final *i* of *pac-* and *ji-*], the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by the rule "ato guṇe. An example of the vowel *e* not being produced by an operation (*atadbhāvita*) is *ahaṃ pace*. However, such an example is not possible for the vowel *o*.
The *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions apply in place of *iK*.

This is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule), not an *adhikāra* (a governing heading); for it lacks the *svarita* accent and because it is not stated in conjunction with another rule. For if it were an *adhikāra*, one would have stated it in conjunction [with the following], as in: "In place of *ik*, there are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, except when there is elision of a verbal root. Nor is it an injunction (*vidhi*), because *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* will be enjoined by other rules in the form: "In place of *ik*, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* occur."

[Objection: But surely, when this is an independent injunction (*vidhi*), then since there would be no basis for the application of the term *it* (the augment *it*) to those [roots], an injunction of *it* would apply even to roots ending in *i*, such as *yāti*; and here, even in the absence of the designation *sārvadhātuka* and so on, let there be an injunction [of *guṇa*] in cases like *dadhi* and *madhu*. [Response: If that were so, then because of the re-mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for guṇa and vṛddhi, this is not an injunction. Although the mention of "guṇa" and "vṛddhi" under discussion refers to the technical names (*saṃjñā*), here, by the force of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), it will refer to the things named (*saṃjñin*).

In the rule *adeṅ guṇaḥ*, even though the term *vṛddhi* is being carried over [from a previous context], it is not connected here, because a different statement is made and because the particle *ca* ("and") is not employed. For in that [previous] case, a distinct technical name (*saṃjñā*) for *guṇa* was stated and the particle *ca* was not used; therefore, under the view that this is an original injunction (*vidhi*), the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* need not be mentioned again. For this very reason, it is also not a governing heading (*adhikāra*). However, we shall explain later that in the case of a *paribhāṣā* (a general interpretive rule), those terms must be included in order to establish its specific scope. Therefore, this is a *paribhāṣā*.

Whether this be designated as a *yoga* (rule) or a *sūtra*, how can there be a feminine designation as "this" (*iyam*)? It is said in reply: Just as this is a *yoga*, or as this is a *sūtra*, so too is it a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule); because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [term *paribhāṣā*], there is the designation "this. But surely, it is the status of being a *paribhāṣā* that is intended to be enjoined (*vidhitsita*), whereas the word "this" (*idaṃ-śabda*) is a demonstrative indicator (*uddeśaka*). Furthermore, an indicator refers to something already established (*siddha-rūpa*), and since the status of being a *sūtra* or the status of being a *yoga* is already established, the feminine gender of the indicator remains unaccounted for once again.

If someone were to say, "Having restated here that 'this is a paribhāṣā,' its status as a restrictive rule regarding the substituendum (*sthānin*) is enjoined—meaning, 'this which is a paribhāṣā serves to restrict the substituendum,' and its nature as a paribhāṣā is not being enjoined"—then he must be asked: "How can the status of being a paribhāṣā, which is itself unestablished (*asiddha*), be restated? Furthermore, this solution is not comprehensive; for in rules such as *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*, only this much is heard: "this is a paribhāṣā," but not "it is for this purpose."

We, however, say this: pronouns bring about identity between that which is being pointed out (the *nirdiśyamāna*) and that which is being referred back to (the *pratinirdiśyamāna*), and they assume the gender of the latter in turn. In this regard, just as in the rule "that which is the object (*karman*) in the case of the root (*aṇ*), if it is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the case of the causative (*ṇi*)," the word *tat*—though referring to the form of the object—takes on the gender of the agent which is being enjoined; likewise here too, since the sūtra itself is the subject being pointed out, the word *idam* will take on the gender of the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) which is being enjoined.

"Having the purpose of restricting the locus (*sthāninīyamārthā*). This means that its purpose—its *prayojana*—is the restriction of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* when the locus is designated as *ig*. Although, according to the rule "in a *dvandva*, the *ghi* [term] comes first," the word *vṛddhi* would have been expected to appear first, it is permanently superseded by the specific mention in the sūtra. Indicating this by stating "both [terms are used] in cases such as *dharma* etc.," he says "vṛddhi-guṇau," and so forth. What, then, is expressed by this passage? Is it not the case that this sūtra functions by way of restriction (*niyama*), just as in the rule "for *ec*, there is *ig* in place of a short vowel," where a short vowel being prescribed must be an *ig* specifically?

If this were the case, then in the event of the contingency of non-restriction, the restriction [stated] as "for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes" and "vṛddhi before *sic*" would apply only there; for if this rule did not exist, since the augment *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would apply to the final letter of the base (*alo'ntyasya*), and because no specific [final letter] is distinguished, both the first vowel (*ika*) and any other vowel (*anika*) would result. However, in rules such as "mid, mṛj, roots ending in *pu*, light penultimate vowels, *chid*, *dṛś*, *kṣip*, and *kṣudra*," the application of "the final letter" (*alo'ntyasya*) would result only in the case of an *anika* vowel, and not in the case of *mid* and so forth.

Now, since all sentences possess a restrictive force (*avadhāraṇa*), the restriction already implied is expressed by the word *eva* as "only one" (*eka eva*); however, a formal rule (*niyama*) is not being demonstrated here. This is just as in the case of the statement, "Austerity (*tapas*) is [the substitute] for that which has the root *tapa-* as its object. Therefore, its function is intended solely in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, because it is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, this is another preparatory injunction (*saṃskāraka-vidhi*), just as the rule "of the final *al*" (*alo'ntyasya*) is [relative to] the rule "of *i* and *u* in *goṇī*" (*idgoṇyāḥ*), and so forth—this is the position.

Therefore, since this [rule] is being introduced while the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (the rule stating that a grammatical operation applies to the final letter) has not yet been reached, it would subvert that [paribhāṣā]. Consequently, wherever this [new rule] applies, the former would not operate. Thus, just as the *guṇa* substitution occurs here in *abibhayuḥ* and *abibharuḥ* by virtue of the rule *jusi ca*, so too would it apply here in *anenijuḥ* and *paryaveviṣuḥ*. And just as the rule *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* applies here in *cetā* and *stotā*, so too would it apply here in *īhitā*, *ūhitā*, and *umbhitā*.

However, the relationship of sublation (bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva) occurs only when both the general rule (*sāmānya*) and the specific rule (*viśeṣa*) cannot simultaneously apply. But here, such a possibility does exist: that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions might occur for the final vowel (*alo’ntyasya*) as well as for an *ik* vowel. Consequently, in rules such as "jusi ca," the *paribhāṣā* regarding *ik* vowels also presents itself, because the term "of the base" (*aṅgasya*) is specified with a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), and the rule "of the final [vowel]" (*alo’ntyasya*) is likewise present. In that case, there is no conjunction (*samuccaya*)—namely, that a *guṇa* substitution occurs for the final *an* vowel of the base and also for an *ik* vowel that is not final, which is a part of that base.

Nor is there an option; for sometimes the final element of a *aṅga* may have more than one substitute, and sometimes a single substitute may belong to a non-final part of it. Since the meaning of the genitive case is unitary, the meaning of the genitive in the expression "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*)—heard only once—is indeed one: either its connection with the *sthāna* (the position to be replaced) or its connection with a part, but not both simultaneously nor as an option.

In this context, if the term *aṅgasya* were first connected with *ikaḥ* through grammatical apposition—as "the *guṇa* [substitution] of that *ik* which belongs to the *aṅga*"—then the rule *alo 'ntyasya* would become inapplicable. Therefore, it is first connected with *alo 'ntyasya*, and by that, the final *ik* is specified: "the *guṇa* [substitution] of the final *ik* of the *aṅga*. Alternatively, the *aṅga* is qualified by *ik*, and by means of that qualification, the principle of *tadantavidhi* applies: "of an *aṅga* ending in *ik*."

For even so, since the status of being the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī) as denoting position remains unchanged, the rule "of that which is not final" (*al-antyasya*) would have its application unimpeded; thus, in every respect, there would be no fault regarding the *guṇa* substitution for the final vowel of the stem before the suffix *jus*, whether it be a *sārvadhātuka* or an *ārdhadhātuka*. However, in the case of *mid* and the others, because it is impossible for both [the stem-final and the suffix-initial] to apply simultaneously according to the method previously stated, one or the other must be abandoned. In that situation, since there is no distinction, both might be discarded; yet, since *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* are prescribed by the rules "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" (*mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*) and "guṇa for *mid*" (*mider guṇaḥ*), those two would consequently become substitutions for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*).

Therefore, the operation of this sūtra should not be accepted as being either prescriptive (vidhi) or restrictive (niyama); what then? By this [sūtra], the presentation of a word-form is effected: where one might say "guṇa occurs" or "vṛddhi occurs," let this word "ika," ending in the genitive case, be presented there. However, the status of [the sūtra] "alo 'ntyasya" is that of a syntactical sentence (vākya).

For when this is understood, in rules such as "asaci vṛddhiḥ" (P. 7.2.1), where the final phoneme *i* is possible, the term *ika*—which has been brought to mind [by the previous rule]—qualifies the *aṅga* (base). When the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to that which ends in it) applies, the operation of the sentence is finalized as "there is *guṇa* for an *aṅga* ending in *i*. Subsequently, the rule "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52), which would have applied to the *guṇa* of that which ends in *i*, is drawn away from there and enjoins it instead for the final phoneme of the *aṅga*. However, it does not apply at the time when the term *ika* is brought to mind.

In cases such as "miderguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.82), however, where the final *iṅ* is not possible, the operation of the sentence—"the *guṇa* of the *ik* of the *aṅga*"—is completed with the *ik* qualified by the *aṅga*. Since there is no genitive of relation (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) [between the *ik* and the *aṅga*], the rule does not apply to the *aṅga* itself; nor does it stand together with the term "*ik*" [as a qualifier of the *aṅga*], whereby both would be excluded without distinction. Thus, the desired conclusion is established.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, has demonstrated the purpose of this sūtra by summarizing it as follows: "In every respect, whether [the original element] is final or not final, only *ika* undergoes *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; there is no operation upon the phoneme (*akṣara*) itself. For this very reason, he says "they are to be understood" (*veditavyau*). If, on the other hand, the operation upon the phoneme were being demonstrated, it would have been sufficient merely to say that they occur in place of *ika*. The phrase "being taught by their own technical names" (*svasaṃjñayā śiṣyamāṇau*) means "being enjoined in such a manner as 'let there be *vṛddhi*', 'let there be *guṇa*'."

"What is the purpose of [specifying] *ika*?"—the meaning is: by implying the primary components, there is an implication of the whole collection; thus, the question is, "What is the purpose of this *sūtra*? [The answer begins with] "ātsandhyakṣare," etc. Now, one might object: since the *kit* designation of the suffix *ṭak* in the rule *gāpoṣṭak* would ensure that the *āl*-elision occurs in forms such as *sāmaga*, the form *sāmaga* would already be established. Likewise, in cases like *glāyati*, even for diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), a *guṇa* substitution will not occur due to the force of their being taught [in the *upadeśa*]; otherwise, for the sake of brevity in the process of derivation, one would have taught only the vowel *e*.

Because of the marking with the *ḍi*-sign in the rule "janerḍaḥ," there will be no *guṇa* substitution even for consonants. For if that were the case, when a *guṇa* were applied to the half-mora vowel in the one-mora *akāra*, the form *upasarajaḥ* would be established. If this were so, however, the *guṇa* prescribed for the root *mid* would be excluded from the final letter and would instead become a substitute for the whole stem. Furthermore, this *ḍa* also applies to the root *gam*, and by virtue of positional proximity (*sthānata āntarya*), its *guṇa* would be *o*.

Furthermore, if there is actual usage, then in forms such as *rāyaṇau* and *glāvaṇau*—derived from the denominative roots *rāya-ṇic* and *glāya-ṇic* followed by *kvip*—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of Guṇa substitution before suffixes beginning with *tṛ*. Likewise, in cases such as *citaḥ*, *cinutaḥ*, *bhinnaḥ*, and *bebhidya-te*, the Guṇa must be accepted as being characterized by the letter *i* (i.e., having *i* as its cause) for the purpose of applying the prohibition "before *k* and *ṅ*" (*kṅiti ca*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *vṛddhi*? It is so that the *vṛddhi* [prescribed by] "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ" may apply to the *ik* [vowels], and not to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*). This is established through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): "mṛjer vṛddhiracaḥ. The *vṛddhi* occurs for the *ac* [vowel] of the root *mṛj*. Since the suffix, implied by the term "aṅga," serves as the qualifier for the *ac*, there will be no *vṛddhi* for the augment *aṭ* in the form *nyāmārṭ*. [Objection: In that case, let there be no *vṛddhi* for the vowel *a* in the case of the *sic* [augment] in *acikīrṣīt*.

Therefore, the elision will occur by virtue of the statement: "The rules for *ṇi*-elision, *al*-elision, *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening take precedence over each other in the order mentioned" (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*). For example, as in *cikīrṣakaḥ*. There is no distinction regarding the vowel *ā*; because its prescription [as *āt*] exists, its occurrence [as *ai*] is impossible. Furthermore, a stem ending in *ej* is also impossible, because the rule for *āt* has been prescribed.

In the case of the words *rai*, *nao*, and *go* when followed by *kvip* in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), there is no distinction; for the word *dhātuḥ* (root) is understood from the rule "for the root vowel *ṛ*, *it* is substituted" (*ṝta iddhātoḥ*) due to its recurrence, and since it is understood that "only that which is a root" is meant, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* in the *sic* augment.

In examples such as *abhaitsīt*, when the rule "vṛddhi in the presence of *sic*" (*saci vṛddhiḥ*) is applicable, the vṛddhi prescribed by the rule for roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā vṛddhiḥ*) is a sublater (*bādhikā*). Furthermore, the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) is understood to apply to all vṛddhi of a root ending in a consonant—whether that vṛddhi be the one prescribed by "vṛddhi in the presence of *sic*" or the one prescribed for a root ending in a consonant. Consequently, in forms such as *anardīt*, there will be no vṛddhi of the final letter.

Thus, for the purpose that "the *vṛddhi* [substitution] should apply to *ik*, but not to *adeṅ* or *vyaṅjanas*," the mention of *vṛddhi* need not be made at all. If that were so, then in forms such as *mṛjyate* and *mṛṣṭaḥ*, the fact that the *vṛddhi* of *mṛj* is characterized by an *ik* vowel would be necessary for the sake of the prohibition [stated in Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.5], namely, "and when a *kṅit* [suffix follows]. This too is established through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): immediately after the rule "the *vṛddhi* of *mṛj*," one should add "or [the *vṛddhi* applies] before a *kṅit* suffix beginning with a vowel."

It must be stated: [the rule] "they polish" (*parimṛjanti*) means they cleanse (*parimārjjanti*), and likewise *parimamṛjatuh* and *parimamārjatuḥ*. In this regard, there is a separation of the *yoga*: "In the presence of an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that has the markers *k* or *ṅ*, there is *vṛddhi* for the vowel of the root *mṛj*. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtham*): "If [the *vṛddhi*] occurs in the presence of an affix marked by *k* or *ṅ*, it occurs only when that affix begins with a vowel. Consequently, it will not occur in forms such as *mṛjyate* and *mṛṣṭaḥ*. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as] "even in the presence of an affix beginning with a vowel, [the *vṛddhi*] is optional. Therefore, the status of being characterized by the letter *i* is for the purpose of prohibiting the *vṛddhi* in the case of the *sic* suffix.

In the case of the roots *ṇu* (in the sense of praise) and *dhū* (in the sense of shaking), which belong to the *kuṭādi* class—as in *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*—the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs because it is *antaraṅga*, depending only on the inclusion of the *sic* suffix. Consequently, since the root ends in a consonant (*halanta*), the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) applies. If *sic* were *antaraṅga*, then in forms such as *acaṣīt*, *ahauṣīt*, and *ahauṣīt*, the *guṇa* substitution would have occurred.

Let it be so; shall the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) be applied to that very [root] alone? In forms such as *akārṣīt*, the *vṛddhi* is governed by the rule for roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*). In forms such as *atārīt*, when the prohibition "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) blocks the *vṛddhi* prescribed for roots ending in a consonant, the rule "of a root beginning with a consonant and ending in *a*" (*ato halādeḥ*) is set aside, and the *vṛddhi* is obligatory by the rule "of a root ending in *lṛ* or *r*" (*ato lrāntasya*). In forms such as *alāvīt* and others ending in *u*, even though the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitutions of *guṇa* and *avādeśa* have already taken place before the *sic* suffix with *iṭ*, the *vṛddhi* is still obligatory because, in the rule "of a root ending in *lṛ* or *r*" (*ato lrāntasya*), the letter *v* is also indicated as elided (*luptanirdiṣṭa*).

If this is so, then in cases such as *mā bhavānavīt* and *amavīt*, there would also be a prohibition of *vṛddhi* due to the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *v*. Furthermore, since it has been stated that [the substitution] in *sic* is *antaraṅga*, the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* in the rule *ahmyantakṣaṇ* need not be made; for in cases such as *aunayīt* and *aśvayīt*, once *guṇa* and *av-ādeśa* have been applied by virtue of being *antaraṅga*, the desired result is already established by the rule itself: "there is no [prohibition] for those ending in *yānt*."

In its place, we shall introduce the term *avimavi*: by including the letter *va* within the rule "ato lrāntasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.2), the resulting *vṛddhi* [augment] will not apply to *avi* and *mavi*. Thus, is this mention of *vṛddhi* purposeless? It is not purposeless; for the mention of *vṛddhi* is rejected only on the assumption that an *antaraṅga* [operation] applies before the *sic* suffix. And if an *antaraṅga* operation were to apply before the *sic*, then from roots such as *cinī* with *yaṅ*-luṅ, and from *ciriṇoti* and *jiriṇoti*, in the *luṅ* tense with *sic*, one would have *acecāyīt*; [but this is not desired].

Otherwise, forms such as *acirāyīt*, *acirāyīt*, and *ajirājīt* would not be possible; for once the substitution of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* have been applied, there would arise the prohibition "not for those ending in *y*" (*yāntānām na*). However, when the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is conditioned by *sic* and characterized by an *ik* vowel, it sublates that [prohibition] because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). If this were not the case, no stem (*aṅga*) would ever end in *y* after *sic*; consequently, forms such as *acirāyīt* are established. Just as that [vṛddhi] sublates the substitutions of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*, so too would it sublate the *uvaṅ* substitution in forms such as *nyanuvīt*.

Therefore, even for the sake of this prohibition, it must be accepted that *vṛddhi* is characterized by the vowel *i*; thus, everything is clear. Because there is so much to be said, the author of the *Vṛtti* has not demonstrated the purpose of the mention of *vṛddhi*.

Now, how is this distinction—that "those being taught by their own technical names" (*svasaṃjñayā śiṣyamāṇau*)—obtained? To this he says: "The mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, etc. Here, the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* from the two preceding rules (*pūrvasūtra*) is carried over (*anuvartate*). Since the inclusion of *adeṅ* and *ādaic* is already established by that alone, the fact that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are mentioned again is for the purpose of restricting the rule to those [elements] taught by their own technical names (*svasaṃjñayā vidhāna-niyamārtham*). Otherwise, the current mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would become a detached, merely indicative mark (*taṭastham upalakṣaṇam*), meaning: "whenever there is an injunction of what are in reality *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*."

However, that rule would not have relied on the distinction that "the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [denote] by means of another mode [of reference]," because the force of the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* implies that the operation of the word itself is also relied upon—namely, that *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are those very things designated as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Thus, one of the two mentions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* results in having the word-form (*svarūpa*) as its primary referent. By this, the intended distinction is obtained; such is the meaning.

Otherwise, if the rule *acaśca* were applied by its own technical name (*saṃjñā*), then that restriction would apply only to those rules such as *diva ut* where no *iṅ* (the vowel *i*) is possible—both among those designated as "guṇa" or "vṛddhi" and among those that possess those names, such as *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*. Since the restriction would have found its scope (*caritārthatva*) there, it would fail to apply to rules like *diva aut* where *iṅ* is possible, such as in the forms *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*, and *imam*. As for *saḥ*, it is not an example [of this failure], because *iṅ* does not exist here.
Thus has our profound acquaintance with the *Bhāṣya* been made manifest by us.
I believe that even its full realization is difficult to attain.
There is no elision of a root-vowel before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

Regarding the rule *durīṇo lopaśca*: when the word *duḥ* is used as an upapada (governing word), the suffix *ap* is applied to the root *iṇ*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the root. In the formation of *dūram*—meaning "that which is reached or attained with difficulty"—although the elision of the entire root is possible, nevertheless, because there is no possibility of the occurrence of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* in such cases, he says "a portion of the root" (*dhātvekadeśa*), meaning that the term "root" (*dhātu*) applies here to a single part [of the root].

Regarding the expression "dhātulopa" (loss of a verbal root), since it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there are three possible interpretations for the term *ārddhadhātuka*: it may qualify the elision (*lopa*), it may qualify the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions], or it may qualify both. Among these, if it were to qualify the elision, the meaning would be: "when there is an elision of a verbal root caused by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, then *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur, regardless of whatever cause they might otherwise have."

Furthermore, in the case of *preddham*, when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *indh* preceded by *pra*, and the *na*-elision (*nalopa*) occurs by virtue of that suffix, there would also be a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution (which would otherwise result from Pāṇini 6.1.87). Even though the term *ika* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], nevertheless, since a single substitute takes the designation of either of two elements specified in the genitive case, the *guṇa* would indeed occur. Moreover, there is no evidence within this sūtra itself that the word *ika* refers to a specific form; however, we shall state the evidence for this in the subsequent sūtra.

Now, one might object: "In the view that 'the root is first joined with its suffix' (*pūrvaṃ dhātuḥ sādhanena yujyate*), since the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) depends on the suffix which presents itself first, it is *antaranga*; and thus the prohibition [of that elision] which depends upon it is also *antaranga*. However, in the view that 'the root is first joined with a prefix' (*pūrvaṃ dhāturupasargeṇa yujyate*), the *guṇa* substitution is *antaranga* because it depends on the prefix which presents itself first. Consequently, by the rule 'what is *bahiranga* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what is *antaranga*', the prohibition will not apply. This is not so.

This is because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 1.1.5]: "not when there is no subsequent element" (*nājānantarye*). Now, if the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* were a qualifier for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, then the meaning would be this: "whenever a cause exists for the elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*), provided that the cause is an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur. In that case, there would be no fault in the word *preddham*, since the *guṇa* there is not caused by that [suffix]. However, in the word *kranopayati*—derived from the root *vanūyī* (meaning "to sound") with the addition of *ṇic* and *puk*, followed by the elision of *ya*—there would be a prohibition of the *guṇa* conditioned by the *puk* suffix.

Therefore, there is a dual qualification: when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu-lopa*) caused by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions caused by that same *ārddhadhātuka* suffix do not take place.

In this regard, it is first of all difficult to establish that what is heard only once can serve as a dual qualifier. Even if it were possible, even so, the fact that the elision, *guṇa*, and *vṛddhi* would share a single cause in the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix would not be obtained.

Furthermore, in the view that [the suffix] is explained by splitting [the compound], in the case of *bhedyate*—where, after adding the causative marker *ṇic*, we have *bhid-ṇic*, and then the *yak* affix in the passive sense, resulting in *bhid-e-ya*—the *ṇilopa* (elision of *ṇi*) would take effect first because it is mandatory (*nitya*). Consequently, since the prohibition of *guṇa* would apply by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule with respect to the *ṇic* (which remains even after its elision) as viewed from the perspective of the *yak* affix, there would be a fault; for both [the elision and the *guṇa*-prohibition] are conditioned by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. Having seen this fault in the case of the *tatpuruṣa* compound, he says: "The elision of that [suffix] occurs in which [the *yak*]."

In this view, the phrase "in which there is the elision of the root" (*dhātorlopo yasmin*) qualifies the elision (*lopa*) by means of the *ardhadhātuka* suffix, which serves as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), while the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions themselves are directly [qualified]. Thus, the meaning is: "in that [suffix] where there is the elision of the root. Consequently, it is established that the elision, *guṇa*, and *vṛddhi* are all caused by the same single *ardhadhātuka* suffix; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. By this, he demonstrates that this prohibition applies to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, but not to the operation of the preceding rule. For the operation of the preceding rule consists in the introduction of the word-base (*pada*).

Nor does such a [substitution] apply to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; otherwise, the rule "for *dīdhī*, *vevī*, and *iṭ*" would be irrelevant regarding the prohibition of their presence. [The examples are] *loluva* and so forth. From the roots *lup* and *pū*, there is *yaṅ*, reduplication, and by the rule "guṇa in *yaṅ* and *yaṅluk*," when *guṇa* is prohibited, *upadhā-vṛddhi* occurs. [The example is] *marīmṛja*. [This is formed] by the rule "also for that which has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel" (*rīgṛdupadhasya ca*). By the phrase "from *lolūyā* and so forth," he demonstrates the meaning of the sūtra through these examples.

But surely, once the *yaṅ* suffix has been elided by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), neither guna nor vṛddhi will occur simply because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*sthānivadbhāva*). For example, in *pāpacaka*, there is vṛddhi by the rule "vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel when *at* follows" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*); for here, a prohibition is not established by this [present rule]. Why? Because it is not characterized by *it*. Nor can the elision of *at* be obtained, because it is superseded by the specific (pratipada) elision of the entire complex [the *yaṅ* suffix] prescribed by the rule "elision of *yaṅ* before a vowel" (*yaṅo 'ci ca*).

This is established through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): first, there is the elision of *at* (the *at* of *ataḥ*) before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix; then, for the entire expression "of *ay*"—that is, of the *ya* in *ayaḥ*—there is also the elision of the vowel *a*. For what purpose is this? It is so that the elision of the entire complex (*samudāyaluk*), which is prescribed as a specific rule, does not subvert the elision of *at*. Consequently, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* will occur.

In that case, just as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* do not occur, so too would *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*—as in *kṣetriyaḥ*, *cekriyaḥ*, *loluvaḥ*, *toṣṭuvaḥ*, and *suśruvaḥ*—not occur, since they depend upon an *ac* suffix. Let them not occur when there is an *ac*; however, they will take their support from that very *akāra* which is the *sthānin*. For when the *yakāra* is elided, that [original *akāra*] retains the designation of a suffix (*pratyaya*).

Now, one might object: in the case of *toṣṭuvaḥ* from *tuṣ*, since the external elision (*luk*) supersedes even internal rules, the elision of the *yaṅ* would occur first—before the rule "lengthening before non-*kṛt* or *sārvadhātuka* suffixes" (P. 7.3.84). Thus, we would have *cekṣi-a-a* and *toṣṭu-a-a*. Even though the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies here, the base (*aṅga*) would have a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) due to the original *a*, and consequently, there would necessarily be *guṇa* substitution when the *ac*-pratyaya (*a*) follows, just as in *aśiśriyat* and *adudruvat*. Therefore, the internal *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions should not occur. [Response: This is not so. Internal *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* will indeed take effect, just as in the examples *aśiśriyat* and *adudruvat*. This is because the elision of the *yaṅ* is considered to have taken place at the very moment the *yaṅ* was introduced; thus, the condition for the application of *guṇa* does not arise. Furthermore, the elision of the *yaṅ* is not subject to the rule of "asiddha" (non-existent) with respect to the subsequent *guṇa*, because the elision is based on the presence of the suffix (*pratyaya*), whereas *guṇa* is based on the presence of the suffix beginning with a vowel (*ac*). Since they are based on different causes, the elision is not "asiddha" for the purpose of *guṇa*. Consequently, the *guṇa* rule does not apply, and the internal *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* proceed unimpeded. Thus, the forms *toṣṭuvāḥ* and *cekṣivāḥ* are correctly derived.

Therefore, since this is already established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), is there no purpose for this [rule]? It is said: in all cases where *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* have been applied to bases ending in long vowels as well as short vowels, the *guṇa* substitution characterized by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) would again apply. Furthermore, the status of *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply here again, because [the *guṇa*] would precede the original vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*). Moreover, if the elision of *ataḥ* were performed, then in the word *jaṅgama*, the elision of the *u*-vowel [of the root] by the rule *gamahana...* would occur. If, on the other hand, there is a prohibition here by the term *anaṅī*, then in the word *darīdṛśa*, the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛdṛśoḥ* would occur.

In the case of *dedya*, the augment *yuṭ* would apply by the rule "the augment *yuṭ* [is added] after *dīṅ* before a vowel-initial suffix"; in *sanīsraṃsaḥ* and *danīdhvaṃsaḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) would apply by the rule "of roots not having *i* or *t* as it" (*aniditām*); and in *yāyāvara* and similar forms, the elision of the long *ā* would apply. However, when—without performing a division of the sūtra—the elision of the entire complex (*samudāyaluk*) is prescribed as a specific rule, then, because the substitute for the *hal* and *ac* [of the complex] lacks the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of the penultimate vowel and other such operations do not occur; therefore, the elision of the entire complex must necessarily be accepted.

In this way, even in cases such as *loluva*, both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would occur; therefore, the rule must also be formulated. Regarding *lūñ* [in the form] *lavita*: since the elision of the *anubandha* occurs even before the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "root" has taken effect, it does not constitute an "elision of a root. Regarding *reḍasi*: from the roots *ruṣa* and *riṣa* in the sense of "injury," the suffix *vic* is applied by the rule "it is seen after others as well"; then, by the rule "there is elision of *vi* when it is not followed by a vowel," the elision occurs—yet this does not constitute an "elision of a root."

[Objection: Even if the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) were not present, there would be no [application of the rule] in the case of the elision of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) or an affix (*pratyaya*), because the word *lopa* is understood as having the sense of a locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), meaning "that in which something is elided. [Response: In that context, the word *lopa* is indeed a technical name (*saṃjñāśabda*). How can its status as a locative derivation be obtained? [Consider the example: *roravīti*. This is the form derived from the root *ru* ("to sound") with *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*) and the suffix *tip*.

Now, even if the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* were absent, it would be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is an elision (*lopa*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*)," and in the case of *roravīti*, the *yaṅ*-luṅ would be non-contingent (*anaimittika*). For the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* is not a proof for the status of a *bahuvrīhi*; even if that [mention] were present, a *tatpuruṣa* compound is possible.

In that case, this is the purpose: the roots *turvī*, *thurvī*, and *dharvī* have the meaning "to injure," and *mūrchā* has the meanings "to faint" and "to rise up. From these, when followed by a sārvadhātuka suffix such as *tiP* in the yaṅ-luk formation, there would indeed be a prohibition [of the elision of *ch* and *v*] in forms such as *totorti* and *momorti*, because the elision of *ch* and *v* and the subsequent *guṇa* substitution would share a single cause. The word *eva* (only) in the rule *ikaḥ* means that one should not entertain any doubt regarding the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ikaḥ*.
Therefore, in the forms *abhāji* and *rāgaḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) occurs by the rules *bhañjeśca ciṇi* and *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*.
Who can restrain Haradatta Hari as he wanders at will, his mind delighted, having entered the depths of the logic of grammatical derivation?
And [the substitution of guṇa and vṛddhi] does not take place before an affix marked with the indicatory letters *k* or *ṅ*.

If the mention of *kṅit* were a qualifier of the prohibition being enjoined—meaning "guṇa and vṛddhi do not occur when a *kṅit* [suffix] follows"—then, because of the contact with the injunction, the rule "when that is specified, it refers to what precedes" would apply, and the prohibition would occur only immediately after a *kṅit* suffix. Even though, at the time of the formulation of the prohibition, no temporal sequence is possible between the suffix and the prohibition itself, nor between the suffix and the guṇa and vṛddhi that are being prohibited; [nevertheless, the rule would still apply].

Nevertheless, there would be a prohibition of the *sthānin* (the original element) *iK* when followed by a *kṅit* suffix. For even after the rule has been formulated, such a prohibition—consisting in the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—is possible when a *kṅit* follows; this same sequence of priority and posteriority applies even in rules such as "iKo yaṇ aci," where the *sthānin* exists at the time of formulation, while the element to be substituted (*vidheya*) exists at a subsequent time.

But when *kṅit* is a qualifier of the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* being restated—meaning that those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which would otherwise apply when a *kṅit* follows do not take place—then, because it is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), the paribhāṣā "in that [which has *at*, etc. does not apply. For when it is said, "those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which [apply] when a *kṅit* follows," there is no contact with the *kṅit* through the operation of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Furthermore, *paribhāṣās* (metarules) that function as auxiliary elements (*vidhyaṅga*) apply only to a specific injunction (*vidhi*), not to a restatement (*anuvāda*), because even the latter is for the sake of another, and there can be no mutual connection between two things that are each for the sake of another. Otherwise, in the rule "That [word] whose first vowel among its vowels is *vṛddha* is called *vṛddha*" (*vṛddhir yasyācām ādis tad vṛddham*), when the *ik-paribhāṣā* were to apply, the designation *vṛddha* would not exist for the word *śālīya*, and consequently, the substitution of *cha* prescribed by that definition would not occur. Thus, [the rule] "In place of *āt* of the Northerners... (*udīcām ātaḥ sthāne...*)...

Thus, the mention of *sthāne* (in place of) has been made; because [the rule] "of the *a* that is in place of *āt*" is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), the application of the term *sthāna* according to the principle "the genitive denotes the relation of being in place of" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) would not be obtained. Therefore, in this view, the phrase *kṅiti* is a locative absolute (*sati-saptamī*) according to the rule "and [that which occurs] by the existence of which... (*yasya ca bhāvena*).

For here, by means of the state (*bhāva*) characterized by existence (*sattā*) [denoted by] *kṅit*, the state characterized by the attainment of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is indicated; and by the existence of the cause (*nimitta*), the attainment of that which possesses the cause (*nimittin*) is indicated. Thus, the meaning of the phrase "when *kṅit* is present, those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which would otherwise obtain" becomes: "those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which would obtain when there is a cause consisting of *kṅit* do not take place."

Considering that in forms such as *bhinnaḥ* and *mṛṣṭaḥ*, both guṇa and vṛddhi would apply to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), yet they also apply by depending on *kṅit* as the cause, [the author] says: "This is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). A locative of cause means a locative based on a cause; since the sense of the ablative is intended as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). By saying "when *kṅit* is the cause," he shows that the mention of *kṅit* is an adjective qualifying guṇa and vṛddhi.

But surely, because it is being enjoined and thus possesses primacy, this qualification ought to belong to the negation itself? This is not so; for when a subordinate element (*guṇa*), having undergone its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), is capable of rendering great assistance to the principal element (*pradhāna*), it connects with the principal after first undergoing refinement itself—just as water refined by cardamom and other ingredients is used by a person. And it has been said: "A subordinate element, having undergone its own refinement, serves the principal;
for in this way, it functions more extensively toward the benefit of the principal."

And here, by qualifying *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* with the mention of *kṅit*, there is great benefit for the primary prohibition, since it is established even for that which is separated [from the cause]. In *bhinnaḥ*, there is *natva* (the substitution of *n*) by the rule "radābhyām". In *mṛṣṭaḥ*, there is *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) by the rule "vraścādi". In *cinvanti*, [there is the substitution of *i*] by the rules "sārvadhātukamapit" and "huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke". If this were a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*), there would be a fault regarding forms ending in *śapa* and *caṅ*.

In the case of the roots *dhṛ* (meaning "to hold") and *ṛ* (meaning "to go"), when followed by the suffix *tip* from the *tudādi* class, the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ* applies, yielding *dharati*. Then, by the rule *ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ kartari caṅ*, the *caṅ* suffix is applied for the agentive voice, resulting in the forms *dhi-a-ti*, *ri-a-ti*, *śri-a-t*, *dru-a-t*. At this stage, two operations would apply to the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *ś* and *caṅ*: first, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the *laghu* (light) penultimate vowel due to the suffix *tip*; and second, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes following *ś* and *caṅ*. In that situation, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] would apply only to that caused by *ś* and *caṅ*, but not to that caused by the *tiṅ* suffix.

In the alternative view, however, a prohibition is obtained even for the *guṇa* substitution which is conditioned by a *tiṅ* affix when followed by *śapa* or *śaṅ*. Or rather, because it is characterized as *bahiraṅga*, the *guṇa*—which depends on an external *tiṅ*—is *bahiraṅga* and will be superseded by the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions, which depend on the internal *śapa* and *śaṅ*. Regarding this, he will state under the rule *glājisthaśca snuḥ*: "This suffix is *giṭ* and not *kiṭ*; therefore, the *īkāra* does not occur for *sthā*," and also: "Because of the *giṭ*-nature of *snus*, there is no *īkāra* for *sthā*."

Furthermore, since there would otherwise be no prohibition in the case of *bhūṣṇu*, he says: "The letter *ga* also [is included] here," and so forth. It has undergone *cartva*—that is, it has attained the state of *cartva*. Precisely because of this elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *ga*, there is no application of the rule of correspondence by number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*); otherwise, since *ki* and *ṅi* are two, and *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are also two, a correspondence by number would result—namely, that *guṇa* applies before *kit* and *vṛddhi* applies before *ṅit*.

Or rather, it is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): namely, that the Teacher teaches the *guṇa* substitution for the root *mid* in the presence of the affix *śyan* and an affix marked with *ṅ*, thereby indicating that "in this case, there is no application of the rule regarding the correspondence of number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). If, then, the suffix *ksnu* were *gid*, the augment *iṭ* would result in the form *bhūṣṇu*; however, this is not a fault.

In the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" as well, the letter *g* is indicated as having undergone the change to *c*; and because this is a Vedic (sautra) formulation, the change to *c* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), so that although the substitution of *u* by "haśi ca" would otherwise apply, it does not occur, and instead the substitution of *visarjanīya* by "kupvoḥ" takes place. Regarding the form *kāmayate*: [it is derived] from the root *kam* with the suffix *ṇiṅ*. Regarding *laigavāyana*: from the word *ligu*, the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule "naḍādibhyaḥ phak. Why is there no prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution by the rule "orguṇaḥ," given that the vowel *o* is indeed an *ik* vowel? This is not the case; [the *guṇa* substitution is not prohibited here].

For here the particle *ca* (and) is employed; thus, the meaning is understood as "that. Consequently, by uttering this word *ekah*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions that would otherwise be prescribed; however, the *guṇa* substitution for *or* [in the case of *mṛj*] is not [included]. Regarding the passage beginning with *mṛjeḥ*: here, the grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) consists of the three sages (*trimuni*), and the established view is that among these sages, authority increases in descending order. Therefore, what was not stated by the author of the Sūtras, the author of the Vārttika states; and he refutes what was stated [by the Sūtrakāra]. Likewise, the author of the Bhāṣya refutes what was stated by the author of the Vārttika.

The status of being a "designator" (*vyākhyātṛtva*) exists for both [the *a* and the *ā*]; thus, although the rule "in a compound, when there is an injunction, the designation applies to that which begins with it" (*yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇam*) would have established the application of the designation to what begins with that [vowel], the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is so that the designation applies to the primary *aj-ādi* (vowels beginning with *a*), and not to those that are merely *aj-ādi* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). [Examples: *tuṇḍaparimṛjaḥ*, *pūyam amṛja*, *tvayā amṛje*. Regarding the phrase "it is called *saṃkrama*" and so forth: it is so called because qualities and augmentations (*guṇavṛddhi*) move toward it or depart from it. Thus, there is a prohibition here even for the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

The meaning here is that in this sūtra there is a prohibition even of the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), and not only of [the rule] "before *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes" (*sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ*). By this, the result of the locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimittasaptamī*) is demonstrated. The word "here" (*atra*) points to the sūtra.

In the case of *acinot*, the substitution of *ti* for the *laṅ* suffix ending in *ṅ* would result in a prohibition of *guṇa* by virtue of the status of being *ṅit* through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. Similarly, in the case of *acinavam*, since the *mip* of the *laṅ* ending in *ṅ* would also possess *ṅittva* through a succession of *sthānivadbhāva*s, a prohibition of *guṇa* would follow; therefore, he says "acinavam," etc. If whatever operation applies to a suffix ending in *ṅ* were to apply to the substitute of that *laṅ* suffix ending in *ṅ* by way of *sthānivadbhāva*, then the explicit mention of *yāsuṭ* as *ṅit* would be purposeless;
for the *ṅit*-operation would already be established in the substitutes of the *liṅ* simply because the *liṅ* itself is *ṅit*.
The [substitution of] Guna and Vrddhi does not take place for the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, nor for a root that has the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the rule *dīdhīvevyoḥ*: this refers to *dīdhīṅ* (meaning "to shine" and "to play") and *vevīṅ* (which is synonymous with *veti*). Now, why is there no inclusion of these other roots: *dīṅ* (decay), *dhīṅ* (disrespect), *veñ* (weaving), and *vī* (motion, etc.)? First, there is no inclusion of *dīṅ*, because by the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅāṃ lyapi ca*, the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel is prescribed specifically for the domain of *ej* (the *iṭ* augment) by means of the word *ca*. Nor is there inclusion of *veñ*, because [for it] there is no possibility of the occurrence of *guṇa*. This is not so; [it is included].

The *ca* (and) [in the rule] would mean that it includes the root *mī* in the sense of "to diminish" (*minoti*); furthermore, the inclusion of *dīṅ* would be for the sake of the *lyap* [substitute]; and in the case of *veñ* as well, in the form *praveyam*, once the substitution of *ī* by the rule *īdyati* has occurred, the *guṇa* [substitution] would apply. If, then, the intention is to include all four [roots], one should have stated "of *vī*, *vedhī*, and *dīṭ*" (*vīvedhīdīṭām*) to avoid ambiguity. Moreover, "the conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of its parts. [The mention of] *iṭ* refers to the augment *iṭ* [prescribed] by the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍvaḷādeḥ*.

Is it not the case that, due to the co-occurrence with a verbal root (*dhātu*), the root *iṭ* (from the rule *iṭa kiṭa gatau*) should be understood? True; however, because of its greater renown, the augment (*āgama*) is understood here, for the augment is indeed more well-known. Furthermore, in this treatise (*śāstra*), because it consists of fewer syllables, the root *iṭ* would not have been placed first [in the compound]; but in the case of *dīdhī* and *vevī*, since they are roots and are the bases (*prakṛti*), they are placed first according to the principle "that which is more venerable (*abhyarhita*) comes first."

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *dīdhī* and *vevī*, since these two are Vedic (*chāndasa*) and in the Veda one follows what is observed? For the guna [substitution] is indeed observed: "hotrāya vṛtaḥ kṛpayann adīdhet" and "adhīdhayuḥ dāśarājñe. Therefore, the prohibition regarding them is useless? Some say: "The fact that the author of the Vṛtti cites 'ādīdhyana' and 'āvevyan' as examples shows that he did not intend these two to be exclusively Vedic; otherwise, he would have cited something from the Veda alone. But this [is the view]:

This contradicts the *Vārttika*, which states: "Because *dīdhī* and *vevī* pertain to the Vedic domain, and because they follow observed usage, and because forms such as *adīdhed* and *adīdhayuḥ* showing [the absence of] *guṇa* are seen in the Veda, there is no prohibition [of *guṇa*]. Thus, in *ādīdhyana*, when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. Regarding *kaṇita*: since *kaṇ* and *raṇ* mean "to sound," when the suffix *luṭ* with *tip* is applied, *ḍā* is substituted, followed by *tās* and the elision of the *ṭi* portion. In the resulting form *kaṇit-ā*, the suffix *tās* has a penultimate light vowel (*laghupadha*), and thus the prohibition applies to the *guṇa* that would otherwise have been required.

But surely, since the term *iṭ* is already being carried over from the rule "naḍvaśi kṛti," the re-mention of *iṭ* in the rule "ārdhadhātukasyeṭ" must be for the purpose of ensuring that only the augment *iṭ* occurs and no other modification takes place. If that were so, then in forms such as *alāvīt* and *pipaṭhīḥ* (derived from *pipaṭhiṣati* by elision of the suffix), the long vowel prescribed by the rules "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" and "rvor upadhāyāḥ" would not occur.

In the section concerning *aṅga* (bases), by the rule of restriction (*niyama*), a modification (*vikāra*) is excluded only when it pertains to the *aṅga*; and here, in the case of *pipaṭhiṣati* with the suffix *apratyaya*, because of the neuter gender, the rule *ajasaḥ śī* applies. Due to the status of the elision (*ato lopaḥ*) as *sthānivadbhūta*, the augment *num* does not occur, and consequently, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *sāntamahataḥ* does not take place; thus, the form *pipaṭhiṃṣi brāhmaṇakulāni* is obtained.
Conjunction is the immediate succession of sounds. 1.1.7.
The word *antara* is used in the senses of interval, space, rule, clothing, disappearance, difference,
purpose, hole, one's own, absence, exterior, opportunity, middle, and the inner self.

The word *antara* has many meanings; here, it is taken in the sense of "gap" (*chidra*), because no other meaning is possible in this context. Those between whom there is no *antara* are *anantarāḥ*—that is, they are without gaps (*niśchidrāḥ*). He demonstrates this very same meaning by means of another explicit term: "unseparated by vowels of a different class, uttered in close contact. For such *haras* (consonant groups) are indeed without gaps, since the mention of "by [vowels] of a different class" implies that separation occurs only in that specific case.

Because of the statement "pronounced in close conjunction" (*śliṣṭoccārita*), this designation does not apply even in the case of an *avagraha* (e.g., *apsu* [in pausa] as *āpsu*), for here there exists an interval of half a *mātrā*. Regarding the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*): if this designation were to apply to each individual consonant (*hal*) when pronounced in close conjunction, then in the word *niryāyāt*, since each [consonant] would individually possess the status of being the designated object (*saṃjñin*), the *yakāra* would be a "conjunction" with respect to the *repha*. Consequently, by the rule "optionally [the penultimate vowel of a root ending] in a consonant cluster beginning with [a semivowel]," the *etva* substitution (of *i* for *e*) would occur.

If the entire cluster were considered the "named" element (*saṃjñin*), then even though there would be doubling of the *y* in accordance with the rule *aco rahābhyām*, there would be an absence of *etva* (the change to *e*) because that [doubling] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). Furthermore, in the case of *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, the augment *iṭ* would apply by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*; in *saṃskriyate*, the *guṇa* substitution would apply by the rule *guṇo'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*; and in *dṛṣatkaroti*, the *lopa* of the *d* by the rule *saṃyogādyoḥ* would occur due to the proximity of the *k*; and in *niryāta*, the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *t* at the end of the suffix (*niṣṭhā*) would occur by the rule *saṃyogāderātaḥ*.

Considering that these faults do not apply when the designatum (*saṃjñin*) is the aggregate (*samudāya*), he says: "The aggregate is the designatum. The purpose of employing this great designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the sake of understanding the etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "In this [aggregate], consonants (*hal*) are joined together with one another. Furthermore, it is logical that the proximity (*nairantarya*) heard in the rule enters into the form of the designatum. In the case of each individual [consonant], however, that [proximity] would merely be an incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the intention is that the aggregate alone is appropriately the designatum.

Fearing that because of the use of the plural form in the expression "haloḥ," the designation might not apply to two [consonants], he says: "and in the case of a genus (jāti). The word "ca" has the sense of "because"; because the plural is used for the genus, it therefore applies to both two and many.

Now, where many *hal* (consonants) are conjoined, does the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) apply without distinction to two or to many? Or does it apply only to many? If it applies only to many, then in this case—where, by the rule "masjinaśorjhali," *num* follows the final vowel after the roots *masj* and *naś*, resulting in *mansj*—there would be a single designation for *nasaj* as a whole, but not for *saj* alone; consequently, the elision of *s* by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ" would not occur. This is not a fault; for *num* should be desired before the final letter of *masj*, so that the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) may take place in forms such as *magna*.

Otherwise, because the two [rules] would depend on different designations (*saṃjñā*), even though the *saṃyoga* and other [conditions] are elided, that [elision] would be unestablished (*asiddha*), and thus the elision of *n* would not occur. If that is so, then in cases such as *nirgleiyāt*, *saṃsvariṣīṣṭa*, *saṃsvaryate*, and *nirglānaḥ*, the substitution of *et*, the *iṭ* augment, *guṇa*, and the *niṣṭhā*-nasality would not take place? Let it be then without distinction. Why? Because there is no difference in the state of being "without holes" (*niśchidratva*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the logic of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it would apply only to the whole [stem].

Just as in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it is impossible to perform the operation simultaneously for both the whole and its parts, such incapacity does not exist here. Furthermore, while it is true that when a whole is reduplicated, its parts are also reduplicated—according to the maxim that "a tree moving moves along with its parts"—yet in this case, the designation (*saṃjñā*) applied to the whole does not effect the grammatical operation (*tatkārya*) for the parts. Therefore, this is not a subject for the principle of reduplication. Consequently, it is established that [the designation applies] without distinction to both two and many.

If that were so, in the case of *indrīyati* (from *indram icchati*) and then *sani* [the desiderative suffix], as in *indidrīyiṣati*, there would be two clusters (*saṃyoga*), namely *na-da* and *da-ra*.
