The meaning is that a long vowel is not possible for either [of the two], nor is a long vowel possible for the *ḷ*-vowel; therefore, only the *ṛ*-vowel occurs for both. Now, one might object: this is not the purpose of the technical designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous). Why? Because regarding the rule "akaḥ savarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), he will state: "In the presence of *ṛ*, there is an option to substitute *ṛ*; in the presence of *ḷ*, there is an option to substitute *ḷ*. And the meaning there is as follows: when a homogeneous *ṛ*-vowel follows an *ak* vowel, *ṛ* optionally takes its place.

This [vowel *ḷ*] consists of two morae (*mātrā*): there are two *ṛ*-sounds in the middle, one mora for which, and another for the vowel-syllable on either side; it is also slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Because of the difference in articulatory effort (*prayatna*), it is not included by the term *ṛ*; because it is not an *aṇ*, the designation "long" (*dīrgha*) does not apply to it, and thus this [rule] is prescribed where it was not otherwise obtained. Regarding the statement "it is optionally like *ḷ* when followed by *ḷ*," this too consists of two morae and is slightly touched; there are two *ḷ*-sounds in the middle, one mora for which, and another for the vowel-syllable on either side. As before, it is prescribed where it was not otherwise obtained.

In that context, regarding the rule *ṛti ṛ vā vacanam*, the word *vān* serves the purpose of including the long vowel (*dīrgha*). Consequently, the long vowel will indeed apply even where it was not previously obtained. Now, if this were stated without first establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), then—due to the connection with the term *ak*—the operation would apply to *aṅ* (vowels) in general before *ḷ*; thus, one would have forms such as *dadhyḷkāraḥ* and *madhvyḷkāraḥ*. However, when the designation is established, since *ṛ* is the homogeneous counterpart only of *ṛ*, the rule remains restricted to that specific case.

Therefore, should the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) be prescribed? It need not be prescribed. Regarding this [rule] "in the presence of *ṛ*" (*ṛti*), it should be stated as "in the presence of *ṛ*" (*ṛta*). Since it is already established that *savarṇa* refers to what is homogeneous, for the vowel *ṛ*, only *ṛ* will be its homogeneous counterpart; thus, the rule will apply only when *ṛ* follows. Then, regarding "in the presence of *lṛ*" (*lṛti*), it should simply be "in the presence of *ṛ*" (*ṛta*). This is for the sake of including non-homogeneous sounds; by this, two forms are established in the case of *lṛ*: *hotṝkāraḥ* and *hotlṛkāraḥ*. Thus, that [separate rule] need not be stated. How so? Even by one who asserts "the statement of *ṛ*" or "the statement of *lṛ*," the status of both as vowels (*actva*) must still be asserted.

Otherwise, there would be merely a prescription for these two [phonemes], but the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not be produced by them. However, since they possess the quality of being vowels (*āctva*), they include even the three-mora (*trimātra*) sounds due to their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*); thus, when the designation "protracted" (*pluta-saṃjñā*) applies, the protracted vowel is established. And so, in the case of *hotṛ ṛkāra*, because the two *ṛ*-sounds are composed of two *r*-phonemes and are open (*vivṛta*), sometimes there will be an *ṛ* composed of two *r*-phonemes, and sometimes there will be an open, pure long vowel.

It is true that even in the case of *lṛ*, sometimes the *ṛ* sound—which is the closest to *ṛ*—is substituted, and sometimes the *lṛ* sound—which is the closest to *lṛ*—is substituted. Regarding this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), it need not be stated [in the rule]; yet if it were so stated, or if this [other formulation] were stated, what indeed would be the difference here? Alternatively, this must necessarily be stated, and by doing so, this also becomes established: "In place of *ak* before *ṛ*, [the substitute is *ṛ*]"—as in *khaṭvalṛkāraḥ* and *mātṛlṛkāraḥ*. Furthermore, regarding the rule "optionally before a verbal suffix (*sup*), according to Āpiśali"—as in *upalṛkārīyati* and *upālkārīyati*. And because of the force of teaching the roots with the marker *ṛt* and those with the marker *lṛt* separately, there is no confusion between their respective grammatical operations (*anubandhakārya*).
Neither *a* nor *jhal* [are considered homogeneous]. Pāṇini 1.1.10.

In this context, the meaning "the vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*) do not become *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with respect to one another" does not hold, because that would leave the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) without any scope. Nor does it mean a prohibition of *savarṇatva* between vowels and the *am*-pratyāhāra, or between consonants and the *hal*-pratyāhāra; for that very reason [the rule] is stated as it is. Otherwise, there would be no long vowel substitution of *ā* for *a* + *ā* by the rule *nādici*, nor would there be the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitution by the rule *nāj-jhalau*. Therefore, what is prohibited here is the mutual *savarṇa* designation between vowels and consonants.

And although it is stated there in general terms that "vowels and *hal*-consonants [are not *it*]" (*nājjhalau*), nevertheless, since the possibility arises for the *a*-sound and *ha*-sound, as well as for the *i*-sound and *śa*-sound, the prohibition applies specifically to those. If this is so, should one not say *nāṇśalau*? There is no difference in brevity in that case. Furthermore, the two previously mentioned alternatives would be possible: *ac ca hal ca*. By this, he shows that there is no mention of *aj* and *hal* here. Even in that case, there is no fault whatsoever; however, it is merely the possibility of another alternative.

In response to the contingency raised by the rule *tulyāsyaprayatna* (P. 1.1.9), he states the reason. He demonstrates the purpose of the prohibition by showing that the substitution of a long vowel for two similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) does not occur. [Objection: But surely the phrase "in the context of the prescription of a long vowel" (*dīrghavidhānavacī*) is understood from the preceding rule, and that must necessarily be understood so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *kumārī śete*; for the prohibition would not be established here by this [present rule]. What is the reason? Because the sentence is not yet complete (*vākyāparisamāpteḥ*).

For here, first there is the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇa*); from that, the designation *it*; from that, the abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) by means of "the first [phoneme] together with the final one"; from that, the establishment of the rule "vowels and *hal*-consonants are not [mutually homogeneous]"; and when that has been established, the technical term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) operates upon its intended domain by excluding the domain of exceptions—but this is not the case at the time of the establishment of this very sūtra.

Consequently, the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca* applies only when its constituent parts—the technical term *upadeśa*, the designation *saṃjñā*, the abbreviation *pratyāhāra*, and the quality of being a *savarṇa*—have been fully established in rules such as *asya cvau*; it does not apply to the *upadeśa* and other elements within the *aṅga*s themselves. Thus, it is established that in the rule *nājjhalau*, there is a reference to vowels (*ac*) that do not include their *savarṇa*s. Furthermore, one must necessarily accept the inclusion of only those vowels that do not include their *savarṇa*s; otherwise, the vowel *i* being grasped by the term *ac* would become a grasper (*grāhaka*) of the letter *ś*.

Moreover, even in this sūtra, this very prohibition does not apply, because it would contradict the principle that an action cannot be directed toward itself (*svātmani kriyāvirodha*). Therefore, the letter *ś* is included by the mention of *aj*, and since it is taught among the *hal* consonants, it is also included by the mention of *hal*. Thus, there would be no mutual designation as *savarṇa* (homogeneous) between the two instances of the letter *ś*.

Furthermore, regarding the expression "more than a hundred tasks" (*paraḥśatāni kāryāṇi*), if one analyzes it as "those beyond a hundred" (*śatāt parāṇi*) or "those exceeding a hundred" (*śatād adhikāni*), then by forming a compound according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* and applying the augment *suṭ* because it belongs to the *pāraskarādi* group, the form becomes *paraśśatāni*. At this stage, when the doubling of the *ś* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca*, the middle *ś* would not be elided by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe*; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of always hearing three *ś*s.

Therefore, since vowels (*ac*) that do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) are being grasped, the homogeneity (*savarṇatva*) between the vowel *ī* and the consonant *ś* would remain unprohibited. Consequently, in the case of "kumārī śete," [the rule] should not apply. To prevent this, the term "in a vowel" (*aci*) must be supplied to the rule prescribing lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*). By the force of that supply, it is understood that lengthening occurs only where there is a vowel (*aj*) that is in no way a consonant (*hal*). Since the consonants *h* and *ś* are grasped by the vowels *a* and *ī* due to their homogeneity, they possess the status of being vowels (*actva*), yet because they also possess the status of being consonants (*haltva*), the absence of lengthening is established. This is true.

The mention of *aj* (vowels) must also be carried over for another purpose; this [mention] is also required to prevent the elision of *y* in cases such as *vaipāśo matsyaḥ* ("a fish from the Vaipāśī river") and *ānaḍuhaṃ carmma* ("the hide of a bull"), so that the elision does not occur. Two examples have been presented to demonstrate that both *daṇḍahastaḥ* ("staff-in-hand") and *dadhiśītam* ("cold curd") are established in either way. Regarding *vaipāśāḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "originating there" (*bhavārtha*). Regarding *ānaḍuham*: the suffix *añ* is used in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) according to the rule *aprāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ*.
A dual ending that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*.

In this regard, four possible positions arise: The first position is that *īdādi* (the group beginning with *ī*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and the dual number (*dvivacana*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Since it is impossible for the dual number itself to possess the property of ending in *ī* and so forth, the meaning is that those items beginning with *ī* which bear the technical name "dual" are *pragṛhya*. The second position is that *īdādi* is the qualifier and the dual number is the qualificand; thus, by the rule of "extension to what ends in [the qualifier]" (*tadantavidhi*), the meaning is that a dual number ending in *ī* and so forth is *pragṛhya*.

When the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) applies by means of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a term (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), then, because the dual ending is subsequently qualified by the vowels *ī*, *ī*, etc., the third interpretation is: "that which ends in a dual [ending] beginning with *ī*, *ī*, etc. In the fourth interpretation, when there is *tadantavidhi* with respect to the dual ending as qualified by *ī*, *ī*, etc., it is: "that which ends in a dual ending beginning with *ī*, *ī*, etc., is *pragṛhya*. Among these, in the first position, [the rule would not apply] in cases such as *agnī*, *vāyū*, or *khaṭve*.

In the first case, because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) would be treated as if it were the beginning of the following element, the rule for dual endings beginning with *ī* or *ā* would apply; however, in forms such as *pacete*, *paceye*, and *pacāvahe*, this would not occur, because the single vowel *e* alone is not a dual ending. In the third case, however, [the rule] would apply even here: *kumāryor agāram* becomes *kumāryagāram*, and *vadhvor agāram* becomes *vadhvagāram*; for in these instances, by the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), what is heard is indeed a form ending in a dual suffix and ending in *ī* or *ā*.

For just as in examples such as *tāvakīnaḥ*, a specific number is manifested by means of a grammatical substitute (*ādeśa*), so too here, when the designation *pragṛhya* is present, duality would be manifested by the retention of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*); thus, there would be a compound even for that which ends in a dual suffix. In the fourth [case], however, there is no such contingency in examples like *kumāryagāram*.

Because the dual ending does not begin with *ī* or end with *ā*, [the rule does not apply]; however, in the case of "aśulke śulke samapadyetām śulkyāstāṃ vastre," this [rule] would also apply here. How so? From the word *śulka*, used in the sense of "clothing" (*vastra*), there is a dual ending *au*; by the rule "from a neuter [stem]," there is the substitution of *śī*; then the *cv-* suffix; then the elision of the *śī* sound by the rule "elision of *sup* after a verbal root"; then, because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix by the rule "in place of this [final vowel] before *cv-," there is *su*; and because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there is elision [of the *su*].

In this case, the word *śī* is a dual ending ending in *ī*, and the entire aggregate ending in that [suffix] would acquire the designation *pragṛhya* by virtue of the rule regarding suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). This same fault applies even in the third alternative. Furthermore, since the prohibition against extending a rule to what ends with a suffix (*tadantavidhi*) applies when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the very proposal of the alternative involving what ends in that suffix is impossible; therefore, relying on the second alternative, he says: "The dual ending ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *e*."

Now, even in this view, since *ī* and *ū* occur only when they are alone, forms such as *agnī* are indeed established; nevertheless, because a dual ending ending in *e* is possible in cases such as *pacete*, [the rule] would apply only there and not in cases such as *khaṭve*. [Objection: It will apply here too by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). [Question: What is the authority for adopting this very view? [Answer: First of all, [the application of the rule] in the third and fourth [cases] is simply impossible.

Because the rule for technical names (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) prohibits the extension of a suffix to that which ends with it (*tadanta-vidhi*) when the suffix itself is mentioned; and because it has been stated that when a technical name depends on a named object (*saṃjñin*), the dual number immediately following is itself the named object, the first [alternative] is also impossible. Here, the fourth position is rejected solely due to its impossibility, not because it possesses defects.

In the case of *śuklyāstām vastraiḥ*, because of the rule "an external elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules," the elision of the case-ending (*supo dhātu*... subverts even the internal substitution of *śī*, resulting in a dual form ending in *-ī*. In forms such as *agnī*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) due to its being a *pragṛhya* by the rule "a protracted vowel (*pluta*) and a *pragṛhya* remain as they are before a vowel. In the counter-examples, however, this does not apply, and thus vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) occurs. If it is argued that the inclusion of the long *ā* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of including those [vowels] of the same duration that differ in quality (*guṇa*), we say no.

Because qualities do not cause differentiation. If it is argued that [the *tapara* marker] is for the purpose of excluding those vowels occurring at different times, we say no; because *ī* and *ū* are not *aṇ*. It might be argued as follows: "Under the view that the phoneme is a genus (*jāti*), although by the force of the long pronunciation and the resulting excess of effort, the short vowels would not be included in cases such as *akurvatrātra*, the long (*pluta*) vowels would certainly be included. Furthermore, since the vowel *e* is an *aṇ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including its *pluta* form as well; therefore, the *tapara* marker is used to exclude the *pluta*. But this is not so, because [the inclusion of the *pluta*] is actually desired."

But for what purpose is the designation *pragṛhya* prescribed for protracted (*pluta*) vowels? [It is so that] the rule "protracted vowels remain in their original form" (*pragṛhyāḥ prakṛtyā*) may apply, such that they retain their original state. [Objection: This need not be so; the rule will simply be "a protracted vowel remains in its original form" (*plataḥ prakṛtyā*). [Response: In that case, where the original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) dependent on a protracted vowel is prohibited by the rule "it is not like a protracted vowel when followed by *upa-sthita*" (*aplutavad upasthite*), there the original state dependent on the *pragṛhya* designation must still apply, as in *agnī3 iti*. Furthermore, in this instance, *agnī3*, the exclusion of nasality (*anunāsika-paryudāsa*) by the rule "of a non-*pragṛhya*" (*apragṛhyasya*) must also apply.

Therefore, since the designation *pragṛhya* is also desired for protracted (*pluta*) vowels, the addition of the marker *t* (in *yvau t*) is not intended merely to exclude them; hence he says: "The addition of *t* is for the sake of removing ambiguity. For if that [marker] were absent, there would be ambiguity when the term *yvau* is used—whether it refers to a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) with the neuter singular short vowel applied, or whether it refers to a distributive copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*). Therefore, the addition of *t* is for the purpose of removing ambiguity.

If the *tapara* designation (the lengthened vowel marker) is employed even for the sake of removing doubt, it would likewise exclude the desired technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the protracted (*pluta*) vowel. [Objection: How then can there be a technical name for the protracted vowel? [Response: Let there be no such name for the protracted vowel itself; however, because that [protracted vowel] is not established as a fact (*asiddhatvāt*), the technical name which applies to its original substitute (*sthānin*) will prevent both vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) and nasality (*anunāsika*). For the protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel-sandhis, as indicated by the rule: "A protracted vowel remains in its original form" (*plutaḥ prakṛtyā*).

Otherwise, since the subject of the operation (*kāryin*) would not exist, for whom would the state of being the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) be prescribed? And for whom would there be the contingency of modification (*vikāra*)? In the section on protracted vowels (*pluta*), the state of being the original form must be prescribed for that which is subject to modification; however, because the protracted vowel is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it cannot undergo modification. Thus, the prescription of the state of being the original form for a non-existent protracted vowel is untenable. Let it be granted that the protracted vowel is established within the section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), yet it is non-existent when a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is being prescribed.

And it is established in the rule for technical designations (*saṃjñāvidhi*). How so? Because the technical designations and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time the operation is to take effect; therefore, since this [rule] is present in the statement "the *pragṛhya* vowels remain in their original form" (*pragṛhyāḥ prakṛtyā*), the designation itself is included within the section on vowel coalescence (*svarasandhi*).

If that is the case, then the point that "the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established among the vowel coalescences" need not be accepted; for by the rule "that which is to become a protracted vowel remains in its original form," the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) will be prescribed for the substituend itself. Even so, the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is not established, because under the view that the rule applies at the time of the operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the protracted vowel is already established even within the technical designation.

If that is the case, then according to the principle "technical names and rules of interpretation follow the order in which they are stated," when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is being applied in this section, the designation would apply to the original element (*sthānin*) because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not yet established as valid. Consequently, that name would obstruct both vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) and the occurrence of nasality (*anunāsika*). Now, although the protracted vowel is not established for the purpose of the technical name, it is indeed established for the purpose of excluding nasality (*anunāsika-paryudāsa*). Therefore, that two-moraic vowel to which the name has been assigned by this rule is not the original element (*sthānin*) with respect to the rule concerning nasality; rather, it is the three-moraic vowel itself.

Nor does that [pluta vowel] possess the status of a *pragṛhya* by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), because it is not a rule concerning a vowel-substitute (*alvidhi*). Furthermore, one must necessarily accept the principle that "the *pluta* is established in vowel-sandhi operations" (*siddhaḥ plutaḥ svarasaṃdhiṣu*), so that in a form such as *daṇḍa-ā3ḍhakam*, the *pluta* may be replaced by a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*). And thus it has been stated by all authors of grammatical treatises in the rule *aṅauṇa*.

Likewise, in the case of *suślokā3* (i.e., *suśloka-iti*), here too, since the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is prohibited by the rule "aplutavad upasthite," the resulting *guṇa* substitution removes only the protracted vowel itself, but not its original locus (*sthānin*); otherwise, the protracted vowel would be heard in the form of the substitute. Therefore, if both technical names (*saṃjñā*) and interpretative rules (*paribhāṣā*) follow the "as-stated" (*yathoddeśa*) view, how is the desired result achieved? And how is the contradiction between earlier and later statements in the treatises avoided? These are questions that must be asked of the learned.

Regarding the phrase "of *maṇīva* and so forth," the word "for the sake of establishment" (*siddhaye*) is to be supplied as the remainder. It does not mean that another prohibition must be prescribed for *maṇīva* and so forth. Nor is this an actual scriptural statement (*vacana*), because it was not recited by either the author of the Bhāṣya or the Vārttika; rather, the meaning is that the justification (*nirvāha*) for *maṇīva* and so forth must be provided. In that regard, in the example "two jewels (*maṇī*) hang from the camel's [neck]," there is the use of the word *vā* in the sense of comparison (*upamāna*). In cases such as "the two worlds (*rodasī*)," the justification is that it is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*).
The [final] *m* of *adas* becomes *ā*.

Regarding the rule "svaritenādhikāraḥ," there are two positions: *arthādhikāra* (governance by meaning) and *śabdādhikāra* (governance by word). Among these, *arthādhikāra* means that whatever meaning is assigned to a particular word in a sūtra where its *svarita* accent is prescribed, that meaning governs what follows. *Śabdādhikāra*, however, holds that the word itself, regardless of its intended meaning, is governed and conveys a meaning appropriate to each respective sūtra.

In that regard, under the heading of *artha* (meaning), since [the rule] ending with *idādi* was previously indicated as extending up to that point, it would follow here by recurrence (*anuvṛtta*) that even in the case of *amuke'tra*, there would be an application [of the rule], because it would be qualified by the word *māt*. However, under the heading of *śabda* (word-form), although only *idādi* recurs here, because there is no element to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply; thus, since there is no fault in qualifying it by *māt*, he relies on that and says: "Those ending in *ī*, *ū*, or *ed* which follow that [i.e., *māt*]"—that is, they receive the designation *pragṛhya*. The term *pragṛhya* is the name (*saṃjñā*) of those [vowels]; they are so described.

Although the term *pragṛhya* was already employed as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) in the preceding sūtra, it does not here denote the designated entities (*saṃjñin*); for it is that term itself, taken in its own form (*svarūpa*), which is continued here. Why is this stated, given that—even though the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*)—the designation is established by the previous rule alone because [the words] end in *e* when in the dual number of feminine or neuter nouns?

In the section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhiprakaraṇa*), since the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), when the modification of the vowel *e* alone would otherwise apply, the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is also established. Furthermore, the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsikaparyudāsa*) is established for the dual number in all three genders under the "time-of-operation" (*kāryakāla*) view. This is because, when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is being applied by the preceding rule—which is present in the rule "aṇo'pragṛhyasya" (*Pāṇini 8.4.57*)—the substitution of *m* is already established. Therefore, this new rule is commenced for the purpose of excluding nasalization in the dual, whereas for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), it serves the purpose of the masculine dual.

But surely, even if this "order of enunciation" (*yathoddeśa*) view is adopted, although the *m*-substitution and *ī*-substitution are established by virtue of being the basis for the formation of the technical name (*saṃjñā*), they would still be considered non-established (*asiddha*) within the section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*). Consequently, there would be the undesirable application of the *ayādi* substitution: *ayādeśa* in *amī āsate*, *āvādeśa* in the masculine *amū āsāte*, and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" in *amī atra*. Nor is the technical name useless, for it serves a purpose by excluding [forms] with an *anunāsika*.

For in that case, since *mutva* and *ītva* are not non-existent (*asiddhatva*) when the [operation] is to be performed, those two [rules] for which this designation (*saṃjñā*) was made apply, but not with respect to that [designation]. However, under the view that the time of application is determined by the operation itself (*kāryakālapakṣa*), even when the designation is to be performed, one need not rely on their being established (*siddhatva*) on account of their basis; because when this [rule] is present in the rule "aṇo 'pragṛhyasya" (P. 8.4.57), *mutva* and *ītva* are already established, and this [designation] has fulfilled its purpose through that much alone. If the purpose had been solely the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika*), he would have simply stated: "The nasalized substitute for *aṇ* does not occur for *adas-* when it is not a *pragṛhya*. In forms such as *amuke* and *amuyaḥ*, there would be no application [of the rule] because they do not contain *aṇ* and because they are not in a pause (*anavasāna*). Therefore, by the force of the introduction of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it is understood that its purpose is also to ensure the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). And since that [preservation] is untenable within the section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) without the established status (*siddhatva*) of the *m*-substitution and the *ī*-substitution, the force of the context overrides the non-established status (*asiddhatva*) in both cases.

"What is the purpose of [the condition] *māt*? [The answer is: In the rule for *adas*, the genitive case [is used]; and in the forms *amī* and *amū*, the original bases (*sthānin*) of the *m*-substitution and the *ī*-substitution—namely, the forms ending in *-ekāra* and *-āba*—are included by the mention of the word *adas*. Consequently, since their substitutes are also included by that same mention, the desired result is indeed achieved. Furthermore, the term *edit* will be removed [from the rule], and since long *ī* and *ū* cannot occur after *m*, there is no risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the question. [The example given is] *ta-amuka-atra*.

The sense is that it is difficult to discern the persistence of a single element among those taught as being in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga*). Nor does the application [of *m*] occur here by virtue of the capacity of the mention of *eṭ* even when *māt* exists; for that would result in the redundancy (*vaiyarthyam*) of *māt*. Nor is there an option (*vikalpa*), because the two possess unequal strength: for *tat* (the previous rule) has already fulfilled its purpose, whereas *māt* has not yet done so. Nor is there the capacity for persistence [of *māt*]; for persistence is possible even in accordance with something else.

Thinking that because the *śe* substitution prescribed by the rule *śeṣe* is without distinction, it would consequently apply even in cases such as *kāśe* and *kuśe*, he asks: "What is this? [The answer is: "It is a substitute for case endings (*sup*). The intention is that in cases such as *kāśe ta*, there is no application because [the word] is derived through a secondary derivative process (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). Regarding *yuṣme*: the genitive plural ending is replaced by *śe* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* etc., and then the remainder is elided by *śeṣe lopaḥ*. Regarding *asme*: the dative plural ending is replaced by *śe*. Regarding *tve* and *me*: the locative singular ending is replaced by *tvam* and *mām* respectively according to the rule *tvamāv ekavacane*.

Having stated that "asame indrābṛhaspatī" is an example from the Vedic (chāndasa) language, and having stated that other instances are worldly (laukika) imitations, it would follow that phrases such as "yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ," "tve rāyaḥ," and "me rāyaḥ" would also have to be considered mere imitations. Therefore, he recites in its actual form that which was intended by the phrase "other than this. He begins with "yuṣme iti" and so forth. Furthermore, by the statement "it is a worldly imitation," he demonstrates the necessity for the commencement of this grammatical rule (*sūtra*).

Expressions such as "asme indrābṛhaspatī" would be established even by virtue of being Vedic (chāndasa); however, this [form] used by the makers of the Pada-texts is merely worldly (laukika) when employed, and therefore its establishment cannot be achieved through its being Vedic.
A particle consisting of a single vowel, except for the particle *aṅ*, [is called pragṛhya].

Because of the indications in the rules *mṛgo vyāharati* and *vyavahṛpaṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*, the term *ekāj* is a *karmadhāraya* compound, not a *bahuvrīhi*; thus he says, "and that [vowel] is single. If this were so, the mention of *eka* would be redundant; one could simply say *nipāto’j*, where the vowel (*aj*) is qualified by the particle (*nipāta*). However, the reverse—that it means "a particle which ends in a vowel"—does not occur; for there is no vowel-ending particle to exclude, and whether or not consonant-ending particles are *pragṛhya*, there is no difference in their status.

[Objection: But surely, because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical operations) for a base ending in a consonant when [the word] "puraḥ" precedes, the substitution of *ru* should not occur. [Reply: This is not so; for the designation *pragṛhya* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *ru*, and furthermore, no other grammatical operation applies to the letter *s*. [Objection: But there is this purpose: what is the point of qualifying the particle (*nipāta*) by a vowel? It is so that it may apply to that which ends in a vowel, and not to every vowel in general. [Reply: If that were the case, the term "an-aṅ" would be meaningless; therefore, the vowel is qualified by the particle, and there is no need for the mention of the single vowel (*eka-grahaṇa*). [Objection: No.

In that case, the mention of "one" (*eka*) is for the purpose of precluding a collective [application]; otherwise, in an expression such as *aiu apehi*, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-sandhi) would apply only to the aggregate as a whole and not to its individual components. Consequently, just as in the rule for the doubling of a single vowel (*ekāj dvirvacanam*), the *prakṛtibhāva* would belong only to that which ends in *a*, while for the preceding two vowels, there would still be a vocalic sandhi (*svarasandhi*).

But surely, because the single term *aj* is a nipāta (an indeclinable) and because singularity is intended to be expressed, [the rule] will not apply to a collection [of vowels]. If this is so, then by making the mention of the word *eka* ("single") for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that it refers to a collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*), he indicates the following: "In the case of references to individual phonemes (*varṇa*), the number of individuals is not intended to be expressed; rather, the genus (*jāti*) alone is what is being referred to. Consequently, it becomes logically established that the mention of the consonant *h* in the rule regarding the root *dambh* (*dambher hal-grahaṇasya*) is valid, as it denotes the genus.

"What is the purpose of [specifying] 'particle' (*nipāta*)?"—this question implies that the status of having a meaning (*arthavattva*) is possible only for a particle consisting of a single vowel (*ekāc*). Regarding "the letter *ca*": in the case of *cakāra*, the suffix *ṇal* replaces *tip* after the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). The intention is that by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), even a suffix possesses a meaning. Here, the vowel *ā* is taken as qualified by the marker *ṅ*; however, in actual usage, the letter *ṅ* is never heard. Therefore, based on the presence or absence of meaning, he establishes the distinction between being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅit*) and not being so marked (*anit*).

Regarding the phrase *īṣadarthe* and so forth: in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), *ā-uṣṇāḥ* becomes *oṣṇaḥ*. It has also been stated that *āṅ* is used in the sense of "slight. In connection with an action (*kriyāyoge*), *ā-itaḥ* becomes *etaḥ*; this is listed among the *prādi* group. Regarding the rule *maryādābhividhau ca*: this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), and because the augment (*āgama*) is not mandatory, there is no application of the nasal augment (*num*). Alternatively, it may mean "limitation accompanied by inclusion" (*maryādāsahito 'bhividhiḥ*). In the sense of limitation (*maryādāyām*): *ā-udakāntāt* becomes *odakāntāt*. In the sense of inclusion (*abhividhau*): *ā-ahicchatrāt* becomes *āhicchatrāt*.

And it is said: "Without that [limit], it is *maryādā* (exclusive limit); with that, it is *abhividhi* (inclusive limit). Furthermore, the prefix *āṅ* is prescribed as having the senses of both *maryādā* and *abhividhi*. The particle *ā* is employed to indicate a change from the previous course of a statement—for instance: "Ā! Do you think thus? Previously you did not think so, but now you think thus. Likewise, the particle *ā* is used as an indicator of memory; then the remembered matter is pointed out: "Ā! That was indeed so."

Now, [one might object that] *aho* and so forth are combinations of particles (*nipāta-samāhāra*): *aha-u* = *aho*; *uta-āho* = *utāho*; *atha-u* = *atho*; *yā-u* = *yo*; *na-u* = *no*; *mā-u* = *mo*; *ca-u* = *co*. Even though no difference in meaning is perceived, nevertheless, since we observe that particles can be devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), their status as combinations is not untenable. Consequently, by virtue of being treated as the first member of a compound (*ādivadbhāva*), the designation *pragṛhya* is established by the preceding rule itself, as in: *eṣo uṣā apūrvyā*.

Having raised the doubt, "Is this [the particle] *eṣā* or *eṣa*?", he shows that these are single indeclinables (*nipāta*) by stating, "an indeclinable ending in *o*. The implication is that they are read as such among the particles beginning with *ca*. Furthermore, in the view of their being a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the rule for *uñaḥ* becoming *ūm̐* would apply in cases such as *āho iti*. Even if they were a collective compound, the sūtra would still have to be formulated in this way for the sake of forms such as *o citsakhāyam* and *o ṣuṃ vartamarutaḥ*.

In the case of *ā-u-o*, because of the treatment as if it were the end of a word (*antavadbhāva*), the prohibition by the rule *anāṅ* would apply. However, this is also established under the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for *āṅ* and *anāṅ* is treated as if it were the beginning (*ādivadbhāva*), it is included by the mention of *anāṅ*. As for the example here, *anado'do'bhavat* ("the ox became not-an-ox"), although it ends in the suffix *cv-* and is thus a particle (*nipāta*), the rule does not apply because the mention of the vowel *au* refers specifically to that which is explicitly stated in the sutra. Even so, in the case of *agaurgauḥ samapadyata gobhavat* ("the non-cow became a cow"), [the substitution] would apply; however, it will not occur because grammatical operations apply to the primary (*mukhya*) meaning rather than the secondary (*gauṇa*) one.

For here, the word "cow" (*go*) applies to the Vāhīka because "cowness" has been superimposed upon him through qualities such as dullness; thus, it possesses a figurative meaning (*gauṇārthatva*). How then do the operations of *vṛddhi* and *ātva* occur in expressions such as "the cow Vāhīka stands" (*gaur vāhīkas tiṣṭhati*) or "bring the cow Vāhīka" (*gām vāhīkam ānaya*)? It is said in reply: when a case ending (*vibhakti*) is produced from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is functioning in its own primary sense, and the grammatical operations have been performed, the figurative nature is perceived here due to the proximity of another word. For the relationship of the factors of action (*kāraka*) is with the verb (*kriyā*), not with one another.

"Bring the cow," "Bring the Vāhīka," "The cow stands," "The Vāhīka stands. However, subsequently, through the presentation of the sentence and due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the figurative sense arises. But here, the distinction is that the designation *pragṛhya* applies at a later time, when the state of having the suffix *-cv-* has arisen following the manifestation of the figurative sense. Therefore, it is established that this rule applies only to operations concerning words (*pada*), not to operations concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
[Rule 1.1.16: In the vocative singular, according to Śākalya, [the final *o*] becomes *it* (i.e., *e*) in non-Vedic usage.

By the word *saṃbuddhau*, the vowel *o* being referred to as the subject is qualified; therefore, he says "on account of the vocative" (*saṃbuddhinimitta*), implying that this is a locative of occasion (*nimittasaptamī*), just like [the rule] *kṅiti*. The point is that if it were a locative of position (*parasaptamī*), the rule would not apply in the neuter, as in *trapo iti*. He explains the meaning of *anāṣa* as "non-Vedic"; for *ṛṣi* means the Veda, as seen in such expressions as *taduktam ṛṣiṇā* ("so it was said by the Seer").

But surely, in the case of *gavityayamāha*, since it possesses meaning through its referent (*anukārya*), it would be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and thus ought to take a case ending; to this he says: "In this case," and so forth. Precisely because there is no case ending, and because it does not stand at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the elision prescribed by *alo'ntyasya* and *lopaḥ śākalyasya* does not occur even in the counter-example provided by Śākalya.

"Because difference is not intended to be expressed. For the relationship between the communicator and the communicated is based on difference; when that difference is not intended to be expressed, it does not exist. Regarding the phrase "if there is no meaningfulness": if it were meaningless, how then could it be employed? It is employed because it possesses a purpose; the purpose is the cognition of the object to be imitated.

Even though there is no function of denotation (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*), nevertheless, the form uttered at that time, by virtue of its similarity, has as its primary purpose the comprehension of the original (*anukārya*); and since the difference [between the two] exists but is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), even if the original is an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*), this [imitation] is not an ungrammatical word. The mention of Śākalya is for the sake of providing an option (*vibhāṣā*). In that regard, the followers of the Ṛgveda study it as a *pragṛhya*, whereas the Taittirīyas study it as not being a *pragṛhya*. AÑ: 1.1.17.

If this were a single rule as read by the author of the Sūtras—namely, *añ ūm̐*—then there would be a connection between *uñaḥ* and the substitute (*ādeśa*) that is explicitly heard in the text, rather than with the designation *pragṛhya*. In that case, however, the designation *pragṛhya* (by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*) would be mandatory, and since the option for the substitute is provided by the continued application of Śākalya’s rule, only two forms would result: *u* and *ūm̐*; but not a third form, *vit*. Therefore, he explains the rule by dividing it.

In this regard, although in the preceding sūtras the term *pragṛhya*—by virtue of being mentioned in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—denotes the dual number and so forth, as it does in those specific rules, nevertheless here, because of the mention in the genitive case, it results in having its own form (*svarūpa*) as its referent. For this very reason, he says: "The *uñaḥ* [the particle *u*] receives the designation *pragṛhya*. The meaning is that the name *pragṛhya* is applied to it. In the previous instance, however, it was stated that "the dual number receives the designation *pragṛhya*"; and by this present rule, since the designation *pragṛhya* itself is made optional, the two forms *u* and *vit* are established.

"According to the opinion of Śākalya, it is also designated as *pragṛhya*. By this, he shows that both [conditions] must be understood as carrying over (*anuvarttyam*) even in this rule (*yoga*). If "of Śākalya" were not required, then the substitute for *uṅ* when it is *pragṛhya* would be obligatory; for the word *pragṛhya*, which carries over, would be transformed into the genitive case. Consequently, there would be only two forms: *ūm̐* and *vit*; *u itī* would not occur. However, because of the mention of Śākalya, since there is an option (*vikalpa*), that form also occurs.

Likewise, if the mention of *pragṛhya* were not carried over [from the previous rule], there would be an option regarding the substitution for both *pragṛhya* and non-*pragṛhya* vowels. In that case, while the desired result would be established even when there is a substitution for a *pragṛhya* vowel, for a non-*pragṛhya* vowel, the *yaṇ*-substitute would be a nasalized *v*. Therefore, the mention of *pragṛhya* must also be carried over. Regarding the phrase "three forms": there are exactly three forms; the meaning is that there are indeed three. Here, in the imitation of what is called *tanūm̐* by the authors of the *Padapāṭha*, this rule—"when a nasal follows, a nasal may optionally take the place of a semivowel (*yar*)"—applies.
And the vowels *ī* and *ū*, when they stand in the sense of the locative case, [are called *pragṛhya*].

Regarding the statement "for Śākalya, these two [words] are elided," this is because [the previous rule] lacks the *svarita* accent. Here, by the word *ca*, the previously mentioned [term] is drawn back (*anukṛṣyate*) by means of its archaic form; since no further designation (*saṃjñā*) follows there, that very [term] is what is drawn back. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *māmakyām* and *tanvām*," this indicates the sense of the locative case. The words *māmakī* and *tanū* have their locative endings elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Thus, *māmakī* and *tanū* are the examples for the grammatical operation (*kārya*).
As for *gaurī adhiśritā*, this is also an example for the grammatical operation even in the *saṃhitā* reading; that very point is demonstrated therein.

"agnā bhava" is an example for the sake of the form (*rūpa*), but the application (*kārya*) occurs at the time of the *pada* formation. [The examples] beginning with "dhītī" show that after the words *dhīti*, *mati*, and *suṣṭuti*, the third-case singular ending becomes the vowel *ī* by way of *pūrvasavarṇa*; this is demonstrated by the forms *dhītyā*, *matyā*, and so forth. [The examples] "vāpyaśvaḥ" and "nadyātis" are locative compounds (*saptamī-samāsa*) formed according to the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*). Now, even if the mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) is made, why does [the substitution] not occur here, since the meaning of the locative case is indeed present here as well? It is said in reply:

In the view that a compound functions by abandoning its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), since the meaning belongs to the compound as a whole, the preceding and following members are devoid of meaning like mere phonemes; thus, there is no referent for the locative case. Even in the view that a compound functions without abandoning its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), the subordinate member does not terminate in its own meaning alone, but rather in the primary meaning as conjoined with it.

In this context, because of the capacity to grasp the meaning, only that much of the meaning expressed by the locative case-ending in the rule—which is in its isolated, uncombined form—is taken; thus, it will not apply to a combined form. If it is argued that the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara* marker) is for the purpose of including those [sounds] of equal duration that differ in their secondary qualities (*guṇa*), we say no; for secondary qualities do not cause differentiation. If it is argued that it is for the purpose of excluding *pluta* vowels of different durations, we say no; for they are not *aṇ* sounds and such a thing is impossible. Indeed, a *pluta* ending cannot possibly occur in the sense of the locative case; therefore, he says: "The inclusion of *t*," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *īdūtāv* and so forth: let it simply be "the [stems] ending in *ī* and *ū* are the seventh case (*saptamī*)," and there would be no need for the mention of "meaning" (*artha*). However, because the mention of "meaning" occurs when [the suffix] is elided (*lupte*), [it serves this purpose]. If the mention of "meaning" were absent, then since a prohibition against "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), the name would apply only to the seventh case itself. Consequently, in the example "Soma is placed upon Gaurī," the name would not apply because [the suffix] has been elided. But when "meaning" is mentioned, this name is caused by the meaning, and not caused by the actual hearing of the suffix.

Therefore, it is argued: "Because the meaning is apprehended even when [the case-ending] is elided. Here, the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) is not elided; rather, the *pūrvasavarṇa* (the single long vowel resulting from the coalescence of the preceding vowel and the case-ending) occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Then, because that [resulting form] is treated as being like the beginning of the word (*tasyādivattvāt*), it is indeed included by the mention of the seventh case-ending under the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101). Thus, one might suspect that the seventh case-ending still exists. The author refutes this: "In the case of the substitution of *āṬ* and *ām*. For if there were a *pūrvasavarṇa* here, then *āṬ* and *ām* would occur, overriding the substitution of the long vowel (*dīrghādeśa*). Therefore, elision (*luk*) alone is appropriate.

Therefore, should the term *artha* (meaning) be included? It need not be included, because since the elision (*luk*) must occur everywhere, the locative case (*saptamī*) does not exist [in the context of the rule]. This is stated: "In that case, by the force of the statement, the inclusion of the final member (*tadantavidhi*) will apply even in the prescription of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhi*). This cannot be obtained from the statement itself; for if it were due to the statement, it would apply only where there is lengthening—as in: 'He did not kill the leather bag lying in the lake while dry.'"

For here, when the *ṅi* suffix following the word *saras-* undergoes the substitution of *ī* according to the rule "the addition of *iy*, *iyāc*, *īkār*, and *ān* [is prescribed]," only the locative case (*saptamī*) would be heard; thus it would apply only there, and not in cases such as *gaurī*. Even in that case, it is established provided that the word *sarasī* exists. How so? If the word *sarasī* exists. This is an expression of doubt regarding what is beyond doubt, just as it is said: "if the scriptures were authoritative."

Furthermore, there is the word *sarasī*; in the Deccan region, large lakes are called *sarasyaḥ*. Therefore, since the word *sarasī* also occurs with the locative case elided, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; this much remains established. If that is so, then [the mention of *sarasī*] would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the status of being a "final element. Regarding the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, four alternative views have been presented; therein, by the phrase "in the case of being a final element," he indicates the third and fourth positions.

In this regard, there must be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, within this section on *pragṛhya* vowels, the rule of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply. If it did apply, then by the previously stated principle—since the inclusion of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) implies the inclusion of what ends with that suffix (*tadantavidhi*)—the technical name would still apply even when the locative case ending is elided, because by the rule of "as if the suffix were present," it would be considered "ending in a locative. What, then, would be the purpose of explicitly mentioning the word "locative"? Therefore, the fault that was raised regarding its being "that which ends in [the suffix]"—namely, that the technical name would undesirably apply by virtue of "as if the suffix were present"—does not occur in the case of a rule prescribing a technical name.

Since there is no rule for "extension to that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, the view that the rule applies to what ends in that suffix does not even arise in that context; thus he says: "or *mā*."
The roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place), when followed by *ghu*, are designated as *adāp*.

Is this an imitation of those forms found in actual usage—meaning that those which are heard in usage as having the form *dā* or *dhā* receive the designation *ghu*? Or is it an imitation of all those forms that can possibly have the shape *dā* or *dhā* as they appear in the root-list (*dhātupāṭha*) during instruction? What follows from this? If it were an imitation of those found in usage, then the designation would not apply to the forms with the suffix *śit*: *do* in *praṇidyati*, *deṅ* in *praṇidayate*, *dāṇ* in *praṇiyacchati*, and *dheṭ* in *praṇidhayati*. Why? Because they do not have the form *dā* or *dhā* [in that specific context].

It would indeed apply in cases such as *praṇidātā* and *praṇidhātā*. Why then is it said that [the rule] does not apply before a *śit* affix? For even in the case of *do*, *deṅ*, and *dheṭ*, once the substitution of *ā* has been made even before a non-*śit* affix, the rule would still not apply because they are *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical operation). This is not a fault; for in the rules concerning the inclusion of *gā*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction [between original and derived forms]. Thus, *do* and *deṅ* are indeed included. And the fact that *daip* is marked with the *pit* designation is the indicator (*liṅga*) for this maxim; otherwise, due to its being *lākṣaṇika*, it would not have been included at all.

And in the rule *do dad ghoḥ*, the mention of *daḥ* serves to exclude the root *dā*; by this, it indicates that [the root *dā*] possesses the technical designation *ghu*. As for the root *dhā*, however, there is no possibility of its being replaced by *dad*, precisely because the substitution of *hi* is prescribed by the rule *dadhāter hiḥ*. If [it were the case that] "in the rules concerning the inclusion of *gam* and *ā*, there is no distinction," then the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a word denotes something meaningful) would also be set aside. What would be the fault in that? [The fault is that] the rule would apply even here in the case of *pranidārayati*.

Let it be so; why does *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) not occur? [The rule] "from a preposition" (*upasargāt*) is understood to carry over, and since this [term "preposition"] is a relative word, we shall understand it thus: when there is a preposition belonging to roots such as *gad*, then, due to the cause situated therein, the *ṇatva* of the *ni-* [prefix] occurs in relation to those very roots, *gad* and the rest. In the case of *praṇidārayati*, that which is the preposition is not in relation to the form *dā*, and that which is the form *dā* is not in relation to the preposition, because the latter is meaningless [in that specific context]. Therefore, the fault lies only in the case of a suffix beginning with a *śit* letter.

However, by following the rule for those [roots] taught with an initial vowel (*upadeśasthānām*), even for the imitations (*anukaraṇa*) of *do*, *deṅ*, and *dheṭ*, the substitution of *ā* occurs due to the presence of the rule "ādeca upadeśe'śiti," and thus it is established for all of them, including *dāṇ*, *dāñ*, and *dhāñ*. This is established because that which has undergone a partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛta*) is not considered different from the original.

Since all [the forms] are being imitated in their own original form (*svarūpa*), the two *paribhāṣās*—"between that which is taught by a technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by its specific wording (*pratipadokta*)" and "that which is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*)"—do not apply; nor is there any over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to the case of *pranidārayati*, for the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) does not belong to the imitation of the root *dīṅ*. Furthermore, an imitation is not contradicted even when some slight similarity exists despite the presence of the *ā*-substitution, just as in the expression *gavityayamāha*, where the word *go* is imitated even though it has undergone the *āva* substitution. Thus, adopting the second position, he says: "The four forms beginning with *dā*," and so forth.

And thus, because the substitute *ā* does not occur for the imitation-form (*anukaraṇa*) of the root *dīṅ*, there is no *ghu*-designation even for that which has the form *dā* when the *ā*-substitution (by the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅām*) applies to forms such as those ending in *tṛc*; consequently, in *praṇidātā*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not take place. In *upādāsta asya svaraḥ śikṣakasya*, the substitution of *i* (by the rule *sthādhvoricca*) does not occur. However, some maintain that the *ghu*-designation does apply; even for them, in the case of *upādāsta*, it does not occur, according to the principle: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration [of sounds] is not the cause of the destruction of that very configuration. In *praṇidadāti* and similar forms, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *nergada*. In *praṇidyati*, the *o* is substituted by the rule *otaḥ śyani*.

The word *dātam* means "barhis that has been cut. Because it lacks the technical designation *ghu*, the rule *do dad ghoḥ* does not apply. Furthermore, in the case of *avadātam*, the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* does not apply. Now, one might object: "Since we are not imitating the roots *dāp* and *daip*, [the rules] will simply not apply. Indeed, imitation is at our disposal, and we shall not perform the imitation of *dāp* and *daip*. To this we reply: no; for if that were absent, the imitation would be understood as referring specifically to the form *dā* (from *dādhā*) as prescribed by the rule itself.

But when that [suffix] is present, the imitation of as many forms as are possible—whether they be derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) or explicitly stated in the rules (*pratipadokta*)—is the imitation of all of them. Furthermore, the mention of the root *meṅ* (in the rule "udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre") after it has undergone the change to *māṅ* indicates that "the status of not ending in an *anunāsika* vowel is not determined by the presence of an *anubandha*."

For the root *mā* (from *māṅ* "to measure") cannot function in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatīhāra*). Therefore, since the letter *p* is actually heard in the case of *daip*, the substitution of *ā* occurs, and thus the prohibition [of *ghu*] applies by the rule *adāp*. Furthermore, the prohibition applies to that form which is *dā* at the time the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is applied; consequently, in the word *praṇidāpayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* takes place by relying on the *ghu* designation which has already been applied prior to the application of the augment *puk*. It should be stated: "The roots *dā* and *dhā* are designated as *ghu* except when followed by *pit*"; that is, they do not receive the *ghu* designation when followed by a suffix marked with *p*.

Alternatively, the letter *ba* may be the *anubandha* for both [roots], and the sūtra should likewise be recited ending in *ba*. However, the contradiction with the Bhāṣya and Vārttika has been explained by us at length in the Mahāpadamañjarī.
In a single [entity], as in the case of the beginning and the end. 1.1.21.

Setting aside the rule "dvandve ghi" (Pāṇini 2.2.32), the rule "ajādyadantam" (Pāṇini 2.2.33) would require that the word ending in *a* be placed first; however, due to this very specific mention [in the sūtra], it does not occur. Nor is there an absolute annulment [of the former rule], because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "antādivacca" (Pāṇini 6.1.85). By the phrase "asahāyasya" and so forth, he states the purpose for the commencement of the sūtra: when something follows, that which has nothing before it is called the "beginning" (*ādi*); and when something precedes, that which has nothing after it is called the "end" (*anta*). Both of these conditions are impossible in the case of what is without a companion (*asahāya*).

Therefore, this undertaking is made so that those operations which were taught and stated for the beginning and the end may apply even to a word that is not accompanied by another. By the term "of one not accompanied" (*asahāyasya*), he demonstrates that the word *eka* here expresses the state of being unaccompanied and does not denote the numerical category of "one. The sense is that if the number "oneness" existed even in what is established among many, then the expression "in one" (*ekasmin*) would be redundant. Since the locative case is heard in the correlate (*upameya*) in the phrase "in one," he states that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) must also be capable of being construed with the locative: "the suffix *vat* is used in the sense of the locative."

The word "from the present" (*vartamānāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. In the rule *tatra tasyeva*, the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of "like" (*iva*). Previously, however, in the expression "of the one without assistance" (*asahāyasya*), the genitive case was employed because it was intended to express the sense of the locative as a residual meaning (*śeṣa*). Since all extensions (*atideśa*) are for the sake of an operation (*kārya*), and since this is primarily an extension of the operation itself, he says: "it occurs in the operation. The designation "as if having an initial and an end" (*ādyantavat-vyapadeśaḥ*) is the cause [for the application of the rule].

The statement "as in the previous case" (*pūrvavat sanaḥ*) is, however, baseless. For while [the rule] effects an extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*), in forms such as *kurute* and *kurve*, even though there is a designation as being "final," the designation of being "final" does not apply to the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "this [suffix] has a final vowel that is the first of the class beginning with *a*" (*ajādi*). Consequently, since the technical name *ṭi* would be absent, the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* (in *kurve*) would not occur. However, in cases such as *kurvāte*, there is no fault if one effects an extension of the observed grammatical operation known as the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi*. Regarding the form *ābhyām*: here two instances of "finality" (*antatva*) are utilized—one for the purpose of the rule "there is lengthening of the final vowel of a stem ending in *ā*" (*āto dhātor lopaḥ* / *ātaḥ* in some recensions), and the other for the rule "there is lengthening of the single substitute for the final vowel of a stem ending in *ā*" (*alo'ntyasya*).

Regarding the term *sabhāsannayana*: if the mention of "the beginning" (*ādi*) were not present, then that which lacks such a designation—namely, that which is neither at the beginning nor accompanied by others in the middle—would be the scope of this extended application (*atideśa*). In the rule "That [word] whose vowels begin with a *vṛddhi* vowel is called *vṛddha*," the very same exclusion would apply to the mention of "beginning. Consequently, there would be an option: sometimes the designation *vṛddha* would apply, and sometimes it would not. Therefore, the meaning of the text is that by relying on the letter *ā*, the designation *vṛddha* does not occur in one alternative case.
The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*.
The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are designated as *gha*.

Although the form *tarap* could theoretically arise from the root *tṛ* through the substitution of *guṇa* by the rule "ṛto ṅi-sarvanāmasthānayoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.110), followed by the presence of a previous *p*, nevertheless, due to its association with *tamap*, only the suffix is understood; thus he says: "The suffixes are *tarap* and *tamap*. Consequently, in the case of *nadītaraḥ* (crossing of the river), the short vowel does not occur [by the rule Pāṇini 6.3.93]. Alternatively, the designation *tarap* is based on the form itself, and the determination of that form occurs either in actual usage (*prayoga*) or in the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*).

In this regard, since the form *tarap* does not occur anywhere in actual usage, it is understood as being based on the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*). Furthermore, there is no form *tarap* here that is derived from such an instruction; or, even if the designation *gha* were applied, there would be no fault, for the rule of shortening is prescribed only when a feminine word in grammatical apposition follows. The assignment of the designation *gha*—which could have been formulated simply as *tādau ghaḥ* or *pitau ghaḥ*—is made by extracting it from its immediate context in order to indicate that there exists another *tarap* as well. Consequently, forms such as *alpāctaram* ("having fewer syllables") and *lopaś ca balavattaraḥ* ("elision is more powerful") are established with the suffix *tarap* used in its own inherent sense (*svārthe*).
Words ending in *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vatu*, and *ḍati* are numerals (saṃkhyā). Pāṇini 1.1.23.

Although the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is mentioned in the rule for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "vat-u-ḍati," nevertheless, since there is no purpose in designating the suffixes alone, the reference is only to those [words] ending in such suffixes. In the case of *bahukṛtvaḥ* and so forth: after a numeral, *kṛtvasuc* is added in the sense of counting the repetition of an action; *dhā* is added in the sense of distribution after a numeral; while the rule "*bahvalpārthāt*" is in force, *śas* is added by the rule "*saṃkhyaikavacanāt*"; and *kan* is added to a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śad*.

Regarding the expression *tāvatkṛtvaḥ*: [the suffix] *vatup* is applied after the words *yat*, *tat*, and so on, in the sense of measure (*parimāṇe*), according to the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup*; and [the substitution of] *ā* occurs for the entire pronoun (*sarvanāman*) by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. Regarding *katikṛtvaḥ*: the suffix *ḍati* (which becomes *ti*) is applied after the word *kim* when denoting a numerical measure, according to the rule *kimaḥ saṃkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca*. As for the statement "of the words *bahu* and *gaṇa*," and so forth: how is it that there is no inclusion [of these two]? This technical term (*saṃjñā*) "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is etymological (*anvartha*); it is called "number" because "by means of this, one is numbered" (*saṃkhyāyate'nayā*). Now, the word *bahu* used in the sense of abundance—as in *bahurodanaḥ* ("much rice")—does not denote a number; nor does the word *gaṇa* used in the sense of a collection—as in *ikṣūṇāṃ gaṇaḥ* ("a group of sugarcane stalks")—denote a number, since by these two [words], one is not actually numbered.

If, then, only those two which denote number are being taken, for what purpose is this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) prescribed for them here? For, in the various rules concerning number (*saṃkhyāpradeśa*), even worldly number is accepted; otherwise, in forms such as *pañcakaḥ* and *saptakaḥ*, the suffix *kan* would not apply by the rule "after a number ending in *ati* or *śat*" (*saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ*), and the prohibition "after [a number] ending in *ati* or *śat*" would be meaningless, because there is no such thing as a technical number (*śāstrīyā saṃkhyā*) ending in *ati* or *śat*. To this, he says: "of *bhūri* and so forth," etc.

By this, he shows that the mention of these two [the words *dvi* and *eka*] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). Since a restriction depends upon its own class (*tulyajātīya*), there is an exclusion only of words such as *bhūri*, which denote an indefinite plurality, and not of the words *dvi* and *eka*, whose domain is non-plurality, nor of words such as *tri* and so on, which denote a definite plurality. Thus he says: "of *bhūri* and so on."

Regarding the rule *aghapūrvapadaśca*: this refers to a compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) is the word *ardha*, and which ends in a ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*). For the word *ardha* can function as a prior member only when it ends in a ordinal suffix, and a prior member is possible only within a compound. An example is *ardhapañcamaśūrpa*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those of whom a half-fifth [is the measure]. Then, by the rule *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), a compound is formed meaning "bought for four *śūrpa*s plus a half," i.e., for four and a half *śūrpa*s.

The suffix *añ*, prescribed by the rule "śūrpādañanyatarasyām," or the suffix *ṭhañ* [prescribed by "śūrpād añ anyatarasyām"], undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule "adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ. But how can there be elision, given that this is neither a compound (*samāsa*) nor does it end in the suffix *kan*? [The answer is: the genitive case in the phrase "for the purpose of prescribing a compound or *kan*" expresses a general relationship; thus, the meaning is: "when a compound is being prescribed, or when something else caused by a compound is being prescribed. [The sūtra] "ṣṇāntāḥ ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 1.1.24).

Why does this not apply here in the cases of *vipruṣaḥ* and *pāmānaḥ*? [The answer is: the term "number" (*saṅkhyā*) is understood [from the previous rule]. But surely that mention of "number" has the technical name (*saṃjñā*) as its primary referent; even though it is carried over here, it would only establish the name for those ending in *ṣ* or *n*, and would not provide a qualifier for the term "ending in *ṣ* or *n*" itself. To this he says: "Because of the indication in the feminine gender. The meaning is that since the feminine form "ending in *ṣ* or *n*" (*ṣṇāntā*) requires a correlative substantive, it will—just as in the specific rules (*pradeśa*)—be connected with the thing named (*saṃjñin*), which is the primary element.

For this very reason, the mention of "ending in" (*anta*) is included here; otherwise, since the rule for "everything ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) would already be established whenever a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, why would it not apply here in the cases of *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*? [Objection: Once the *num* augment is applied, the number becomes "ending in *n*" (*nāntā saṅkhyā*) because that *num* is a part of the preceding element (*pūrvabhakta*). [Response: Let it be so; but why does elision (*luk*) not occur? The *num* is produced by the presence of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix and does not destroy that very presence.

Now, how is there the designation (*saṃjñā*) "eight" (*aṣṭan*) here? And why might it not be so? When the form *aṣṭan-ām* is established, because the rule "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84) applies both by virtue of its position later in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* and its being obligatory, the substitution of *ā* occurs. Consequently, since the word no longer ends in *n*, the designation would not apply, and thus the augment *nuṭ* would not occur. The inclusion of the long vowel in the rule for *aṣṭan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the designation applies even to *aṣṭan* after the substitution of *ā* has taken place. We shall demonstrate this very point in that very context. Alternatively, the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ*) will apply prior to the production of the case-ending, without reference to any specific purpose; and that designation does not cease even when the substitution of *ā* has occurred.
And [the term] *ḍati* [is also included]. (Pāṇini 1.1.25)

"And that which ends in *ḍati* is a number (*saṃkhyā*). By this, he shows the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "number. For if the continued application were absent, then in the case of *pāter ḍatiḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.184], *patayaḥ*, the designation would apply here as well. Now, even if the continued application of the term "number" is present here, why does it not occur in this instance? For is it not the case that the designation "number" is prescribed for *ḍati* in a general sense? It is said in reply: because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with *vatun*, the *ḍati* suffix taken here is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and not the one belonging to the *uṇādi* class.
The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*.

Here, this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on the forms ending in *kta* and *ktavat*, and the apprehension of these forms occurs either in actual usage (*prayoga*) or in the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*). Since a form accompanied by an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*) does not exist in actual usage, that which resides in the instruction must be taken. In this regard, there is an instruction for the suffix *kta* in certain instances, namely "the *kta* suffix is used in the sense of an impersonal action" (*napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*) and "after a root ending in *ñi*" (*ñītaḥ*). If [the designation] were to apply only to that specific [form], it would not apply in other genders, other times, or with other roots.

However, there is no instruction anywhere regarding *kta* and *ktavatu*. Therefore, by what [rule] are these technical names (*saṃjñā*) prescribed for those two that have been enjoined? By this very technical name itself. He will state: "The term *niṣṭhā* [applies to them]. If this is so, a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) would result: the technical name applies to those that have been enjoined, and the injunction applies to those that possess the technical name. This is not a fault, because the technical name is understood as something yet-to-be (prospective), like the case of "the cloth made of thread" (*sūtra-śāṭaka*). For example, someone says to a weaver: "Weave a cloth from this thread."

He observes: "If it is not a cloth, it cannot be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth; to say 'the cloth is to be woven' is a contradiction. Therefore, I think that which is called 'woven' is what subsequently becomes 'cloth'. In the same way here as well, those two [roots] exist in the past time, for which, when prescribed, this designation "niṣṭhā" will apply.
The words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

Since a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa* compound would take the gender of the final member (*uttarapada*), neuter gender would be impossible [for the term *sarvādīni*], and furthermore, a plural number would be untenable, he states "the *bahuvrīhi* [compound] 'those beginning with *sarva*'": "the word *sarva*, etc. [meaning] "that of which *sarva* is the first. If this is so, then because a *bahuvrīhi* has as its primary referent a meaning external to its own members (*anyapadārtha-pradhāna*), the designation would apply only to *viśva* and the others characterized by the word *sarva*, and not to the characterizing word *sarva* itself.

Just as when it is said, "Let Citragu be brought," it is he who is brought—because he possesses those cows—and not the variegated cows themselves, [the author] anticipates this objection and says: "tānīmāni" (these very ones). Here, although "tāni" alone would have sufficed, the use of the word "imāni" (these) with its demonstrative force (*idaṃśabda*) directed toward the perceptible object indicates that the word "all" (*sarva*) is included among those listed in the group; thus, he demonstrates that this is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (retention of the quality) *bahuvrīhi*.

In that [type of compound], the *guṇa*—that is, the meaning of the constituent members—is also understood as the object of the operation (*kāryin*) within that *bahuvrīhi*; hence it is called *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*. For a *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), and the suffix *matup* is prescribed in the case of abundance (*bhūman*) and so forth. Therefore, where a relationship such as owner and owned is the basis for the application of the term, there the subordinate member does not participate in the grammatical operation. For example, in the command "Bring the one possessing cows" (*gomantam ānaya*), a relationship of ownership is indeed possible even with cows situated in the forest.

However, where either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) serves as the basis for the application [of a term], there the subordinate member is connected with the action by its very nature, as in "bring the man with a staff" (*daṇḍinam ānaya*) or "bring the one with horns" (*viṣāṇinam ānaya*). Indeed, a man does not become "one with a staff" merely because a staff is situated in his house. The same applies in the case of *bahuvrīhi* compounds, such as "the owner of brindled cows" (*citraguḥ*) or "the one dressed in white" (*śuklavāsāḥ*).

Here too, the word *ādi* (beginning) denotes a constituent part (*avayava*). A collection (*samudāya*) whose constituent parts are manifest is the meaning of the compound. Since that collection cannot be used simultaneously in the object of grammatical operation (*lakṣya*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to those [parts] included within it; thus, as it does for words like *viśva*, it will also apply to the word *sarva*. And here the evidence is the rule: "The substitute *adaḥ* is for all [cases]" (*adaḥ sarveṣām*), and "The augment *suṭ* is added after a pronoun before the ending *ām*" (*āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*). Regarding *sarve*: this is the substitution of *śī* for *jas*. The presentation of the two preceding forms is intended to show that this [word *sarva*] ends in *jas*. Regarding *sarvasmai* and so on: this is from the rules "After a pronoun, [the case-ending *ṅe* becomes] *smai*" (*sarvanāmnaḥ sme*) and "For *ṅasi* and *ṅi*, the substitutes *smāt* and *smin* [are applied]" (*ṅasiṅyoḥ smātsinau*).

The word *ubha* is employed only within the scope of the dual number; it is never used when the dual is absent. Indeed, one does not say *ubhaputra* for "his two sons" (*ubhau putrau asya*); instead, the word *ubhaya* takes its place here, as in *ubhayaputra*, and so forth. Furthermore, there is no case-ending operation (*sarvanāmakārya*) applicable to the dual; since suffixes such as *smai* and others pertain to the singular and plural, and there is no distinction between the suffixes *ka* and *kāc*, [the author] states the purpose for including this word here: "of the word *ubha*," and so on.

The third and sixth case endings occur after *ubhābhyām* and *ubhayoḥ* respectively; likewise, [the forms] *ubhayeṣām* and *ubhayasmin*. When the word *ubhaya*, being derived as "that which has both parts," denotes a collection in which the distinction between the parts is obscured, it takes the singular: *ubhayo maṇiḥ* ("a gem consisting of both [halves]"). But when it refers to a whole composed of two groups and denotes a collection that follows the distinction of those groups, it takes the plural: *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ* ("both gods and humans").

Regarding the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama*: even when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it refers to that which ends with the suffix, because there is no purpose for the suffix alone.

"By what will be stated" refers to the rule beginning with *prathama-carama* (Pāṇini 1.1.33). "Of that which is a synonym for the word *sarva*" means that the word *sama* is indeed a synonym for the word *sarva*, as seen in such examples as: *nabhantām anyake same* ("May all others perish"), *mā no vṛkāya vṛkye samasmai* ("Not to the wolf, nor to the she-wolf, nor to anyone else"), *uruṣyāṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt* ("Protect us from every one who intends evil"), *uto samasminn āśiśīhi no vaso* ("And bestow upon us everything, O Vasu"), and *mā naḥ samasya dūḍhyaḥ* ("Do not [subject] us to the ill-will of anyone").
