This is understood from the fact that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is given according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*) in the rule *sarveṣāṃ nāmāni*.

For that very word *sama* becomes the name for all [things] which is a synonym for the word *sarva*. If this is a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), why does the substitution of *ṇ* not occur in accordance with the rule "after a preceding word, when it is a proper name" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*)? It is precisely because of this very irregularity (*nipātana*). If [the definition] "those beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns" (*sarvādīni sarvanāmāni*) applies here as well—such as in the case "give to one named Sarva" (*sarvo nāma kaścit tasmai sarvāya dehi*) and "give to Atisarva, who has surpassed everyone" (*iha cātikrāntaḥ sarvasmai atisarvāya dehi*)—then [the rule would indeed apply].

Therefore, it must be stated that there is a prohibition of the designation (*saṃjñā*) for *sarva* and the others when they function as names (*saṃjñā*) or as subordinate members (*upasarjana*). It must also be stated that their recitation does not even exist in the list (*gaṇa*), for if only the designation were prohibited, the grammatical operations (*kārya*) specifically prescribed for pronouns (*sarvanāman*) would not apply to them. However, those operations dependent on their recitation in the list would certainly still apply—such as "the substitution of *a* for *tyad* and the rest" (Pāṇini 7.2.102)—as in: *tannāmakaḥ kaścit* ("someone having that name"), *tatsaḥ*, *tadau*, *tadaḥ*; or *atikrāntastam atitataḥ*, *atitadau*, *atitadaḥ*.

Regarding the rule "from the five beginning with *adaḍḍatara*," as in the example *kataramatikrāntaṃ brāhmaṇakulam atikataram* ("the Brāhmaṇa family that has surpassed which [other] is *atikatara*"), it need not be stated that there is a prohibition against technical names (*saṃjñā*). For: "Those words whose meanings are clearly manifest, which are independent, and well-known in the world—the application of grammatical rules should be made to those words themselves, not to their designations."

In this regard, just as for example, for a certain person named Bāhu, his offspring are called Bāhavaḥ—the suffix *iñ* does not apply because of the rule "bāhvādibhyaśca" [Pāṇini 4.1.96]—or as the offspring of a father-in-law (*śvaśura*) does not take the suffix *yat* [as prescribed by "rājaśvaśurādyat" 4.1.137], or as in the case of "the sister of Dhānyamātṛ," the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] does not occur [by "mātupitṛbhyāṃ svāsā" 8.3.85]; likewise here too, for the words beginning with *sarva* which have become technical names (*saṃjñā*), the designation itself and the grammatical operations based upon that designation, as well as the operations belonging to the internal group (*antargaṇakārya*), will not apply.

Alternatively, in the rule "avyavasthāyām," the term "asaṃjñāyām" (not when it is a technical name) is separated; by this, the list of words (*gaṇapāṭha*) is qualified—namely, that these aforementioned words beginning with *sarva* are to be understood as such only when they do not function as technical names (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore, a prohibition regarding their status as *upasarjana*s need not be made, because the designation of *sarvādi* is prescribed [for the base form]; what possibility is there, then, for that designation to apply to a word ending in *sarvādi* [when it is an *upasarjana*]? As for the word *sarva*, even though it possesses the designation [of *sarvādi*], the suffixes *smāy* and so on would not apply because the *aṅga* (the nominal stem) would not be a pronoun (*asarvanāmatvāt*).

If this were so, then in cases such as *paramasarvasmai*, [the substitution] would also not occur; for that which is a stem (*aṅga*) is not a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and that which is a pronoun is not a stem. [Objection: Let it be that the stem is not a pronoun; however, since the constituent part itself is a pronoun, by the rule "in the context of stems, the operation applies to that [stem] and its following word," the grammatical operation will apply to the entire aggregate. For example, in *paramāsthne* (from *parama-asthi*), the substitute *anaṅ* applies to the stem *asthi*.

And thus, there is no undesirable application [of the rule] even when the word is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as in the case of *atisarvāya* and so forth—unlike the case of *atyasthnē* and so forth—because the relationship is based on the meaning (*arthadvāraka*). That is, a case ending expresses the singularity and other numbers residing in the meaning of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*). Just as in the rules "auś for *aṣṭan*" (*aṣṭābhya auś*) and "elision after *ṣaṣ*" (*ṣaḍbhyo luk*), the substitution occurs in forms such as *paramāṣṭau* and *paramapañca*, but not in forms such as *priyāṣṭānaḥ* and *priyapañcānaḥ*; the same applies here as well. The operations belonging to the internal group (*antargaṇakārya*), such as "the substitution of *a* for *tyad* and so forth" (*tyadādīnām aḥ*), should also be understood in this very same way.

As for the grammatical operation based on *rūpa* (form), namely "yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe," it is not based on the *pāṭha* (the specific wording of the rule), nor is it based on a technical name (*saṃjñā*); therefore, like the substitution of *anaṅ* in *asthi* and so forth, it occurs even when [the stem] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, that which was already applicable prior to the state of being a subordinate member also occurs, as in *atikrānto bhavakantam* → *atibhavakān*. Therefore, there is no purpose in applying the technical name to the whole ending in that [subordinate]. It is replied: [if it were not so], then in the case of *avyayasarvanāmnām akac prāk ṭeḥ*, the suffix *akac* would not apply to *paramabhavakān* because it ends in that [subordinate].

Regarding the forms *paramasarvataḥ* (from the rule *pañcamyāstasil*), *paramasarvatra* (from the rule *saptamyāstral*), *paramatadryaṅ* and *paramayadryaṅ* (from the rules *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* and *viṣvagdevayośca ṭeradryañcatau vapratyaye*), [the substitution] would not occur; therefore, it must be intended that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the whole ending in that [pronoun]. But how can this be obtained even though it is intended? We shall explain that it is obtained through an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Since [the designation *sarvanāman*] would apply to *atisarva* and so on as well—just as it does to *paramasarva* and so on—should the prohibition regarding *upasarjana* (secondary members) also be stated? It need not be stated; for it is established simply by understanding that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*). For in a compound (*vṛtti*), because they are connected with the meaning of the principal member, the secondary members do not denote all objects; and since "denoting all objects" occurs only as far as possible, the designation applies to words like *tad*, *idam*, and so on, even though they express specific distinctions such as being perceptible or imperceptible.

And precisely because they are meaningful [by their very nature], even those that have become technical names (saṃjñā) lack the status of being names. Thus, the application of suffixes such as *smāy* for those items that are subordinate members (*upasarjana*) has been precluded on the basis of their being names. However, the grammatical operations pertaining to the internal group (*gaṇa*) beginning with *tyad* would certainly still apply, since the recitation of that list remains established.

In that case, by resorting to one of the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*, the second word "sarvanāma" is also included; thus, the reading [of the list] is qualified: "those which are the names of all (sarveṣām) are the 'sarvādi' group. Consequently, even the internal operations (*antargaṇakārya*) dependent on the inclusion in the *sarvādi* list will be properly established. Alternatively, since a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) must be meaningful, the inclusion of all things denoting every object (*sarvārtha*) capable of being related to those [terms] must necessarily be accepted.
Therefore, the exclusion of those following other patterns is established simply because there is no authority for their inclusion in the list.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when it is a directional compound (*diksamāsa*), the term *vibhāṣā* [is understood]. Pāṇini 1.1.28.

In this context, it is observed in the *vṛtti* that the designation [of "sarvanāman"] is optionally applied to the members of the compound that begin with *sarva*, as stated in the passage beginning with "taught regarding the directions" (*digupadiṣṭa*). The meaning is that those words which function as members within this compound—namely, "the compound formed between names of directions" (*diṅnāmānyatarāle*)—are subject to this option. Now, there is no practical purpose for this optional application of the designation to the members themselves; for first, the substitution of *smāy* and so forth depends upon the entire stem (*aṅga*), and second, there is no difference between the suffixes *kā* and *ka*, since words denoting directions end in the vowel *a*.

Even with the rule "sarvanāmno vṛttimātre" (P. 1.2.58), which prescribes the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the first member of a compound, there is no purpose [for this specific mention]; for in that rule, the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) is so that the rule may apply even when words previously seen as pronominal (*sarvanāman*) are no longer pronominal at the time of the compound. Thus, it occurs even in the case where *dakṣiṇapūrvā* is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*). It might be argued: "The names belong only to the individual parts, while the grammatical operation applies according to the rule 'aṅgādhikāre tasya ca taduttarapadasya ca' (P. 7.3.10), which states that an operation prescribed in the section on *aṅga* applies to both the *aṅga* itself and its subsequent member."

Even so, [in a compound] such as *dakṣiṇapūrvataḥ* or *dakṣiṇapūrva-tra*, the suffixes *tasil* and others would not occur; therefore, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is optionally applied to a *bahuvrīhi* that ends in a word beginning with *sarva*. However, this passage from the commentary (*vṛtti*), "those beginning with *sarva*," should be explained as intending to convey: "the technical designation, being operative upon that which ends in a word beginning with *sarva*, also encompasses the words beginning with *sarva* themselves. Alternatively, by prescribing the designation for the constituent parts (*avayava*), it is established for the whole ending in those parts as well, because the rule of extension to what ends in [a specified element] (*tadantavidhi*) is accepted.

"What is the purpose of mentioning *samāsa* (compound)? This question arises because a *bahuvrīhi* does not deviate from being a *samāsa*. [The example given is] *dakṣiṇadakṣiṇasyai*. While the rule "one [word] like a *bahuvrīhi*" (*ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat*) is in effect, by the rule "also in the case of intensity" (*ābādhe ca*), the word *dakṣiṇa* is reduplicated. In this case, the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*) does not apply, because that rule also occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *samāsa*. [The next example is] *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.

If the mention of *bahuvrīhi* were not made, just as [the rule] "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" would subvert that prohibition, so too would it subvert the rule "and in a *dvandva*. Now, even when the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is made, why does [the designation *pūrvapada*] not apply in a case such as "give to the one for whom the eastern direction is the northern direction of the bewildered person" (*pūrvottarāya*)? [The answer is: there is the inclusion of that specific compound of directions which is prescribed by its own technical rule: "names of directions [form a compound] in the sense of an intermediate direction" (*diṅnāmāny antarāle*).

If this is so, would it not follow that [the rule] would not apply in a dvandva for that very same reason? True; however, it is thought that the mention of *bahuvrīhi* must necessarily be made for the sake of what follows, and that it will also serve to clarify the meaning here.
Not in a bahuvrīhi compound. 1.1.29.

In this commentary (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the sūtra is observed in two ways: [first] as a locus for prohibition regarding the *bahuvrīhi*—namely, that the designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to the *bahuvrīhi*, or rather, that the designation whose basis is the *bahuvrīhi* does not apply; [second] as a locus for the *sarvādi* group—namely, that those items beginning with *sarva* which occur within a *bahuvrīhi* do not receive the designation of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*). Therein, by means of the phrase "in the case of the pronominal designation," etc., he demonstrates the first alternative, while the second meaning of the sūtra is shown [by the subsequent portion].

How, then, is it known that the rule for the final member (*tadanta-vidhi*) is accepted? Precisely from this very prohibition. He shows the second meaning of the Sūtra with the words "in a *bahuvrīhi*," and so forth. He states an example of the first [meaning]: *priyaviśvāya*. Since the rule "there is an addition for pronouns and numerals" would require the pronoun to be placed first, the word *priya* is placed first by the rule "optionally for *priya*. [An example of the second is: *dvyanyāya*.

Regarding the rule "sarvanāmasaṃkhyayoḥ," when the prior placement of both [the pronoun and the numeral] would otherwise apply, the numeral takes the prior position because it is subsequent [in the rules]. He states an example of the second [case] with the words "and here. Here, the phrase "this prohibition is commenced" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

If this prohibition were not present, and if *akac* were applied instead, the forms would result as *tvakatpitṛkaḥ* and *makatpitṛkaḥ*. However, when *ka* is applied by the rule *prāgivāt kaḥ*, and then the substitutes *tva-* and *ma-* are applied by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, the forms *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ* are established through the addition of the compound-final suffix *kap* by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*. Now, one might object: "This prohibition applies specifically to *bahuvrīhi* compounds, whereas here [the suffix] is applied even before that."

In that case, would the suffix *akac* not apply even while the sentence remains in the state of "tataḥ tvakam pitā asya" or "ahakaṃ pitā asya"? If so, then by the force of the prohibition, the negation will apply precisely to that stage where a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs through the sublation of the sentence. Furthermore, the first meaning of the rule was presented solely to indicate the inclusion of those ending in [the specified words]; however, there is no possibility of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applying to the whole aggregate in cases such as *priyaviśvāya*, because it does not denote "all," just as in cases like *atisarvāya*.

Since the term *bahuvrīhi* is already understood [from the previous rule], for what purpose is the word *bahuvrīhi* mentioned again? He says: "In *bahuvrīhi*, etc., [the forms] *vastrāntara-vasanāntarāḥ*. In the compound *vasanam antaram yeṣām* ("those for whom clothing is an interval"), there is a *dvandva* within the *bahuvrīhi*. Here, if the mention of *bahuvrīhi* were not present, the prohibition would apply based on the current *dvandva*; consequently, the optional form (*vibhāṣā*) would occur only in the *jas* case-ending.

Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the term *bahuvrīhi*, a *dvandva* compound ending in [the word] *antara* was previously a *bahuvrīhi*; thus, the prohibition based on its being a *bahuvrīhi* is indeed constant. This, however, is a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) in accordance with the first position, namely that "there is a prohibition of the designation for that which ends in it. But there is no application (*prasaṅga*) here, because it does not have a universal sense (*asarvārthatvāt*). [In the case of] *vasanam* (an abode), meaning "that in which they dwell" = a house, there is an absence of *ekaśeṣa* by the rule "even for dissimilar [words], if they have the same meaning."
In a compound with a word ending in the third case. (Pāṇini 1.1.30)

Regarding the phrase "in a compound" (*samāse*), it refers to the context beginning with "while [the word] is present," and so forth. The meaning is that since only the primary sense would have been understood [by the previous rule], the term "compound" is mentioned again in order to include the secondary sense as well. Furthermore, he states—"of the preceding, similar," and so forth—to show that there is no unintended application (*prasaṅga*) in a sentence consisting merely of a third-case compound. This is obtained through the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is indicated by a definition versus that which is explicitly stated. [Examples are: *tvayakā* and *mayakā*. In the case of the third-case singular of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, [the rules] "tvamāvekavacane" and "yo'ci" apply; the suffix *akac* is added before the final vowel (*ṭi*) of these two words when they end in a case-ending.
And [the term *para*] is used [in the sense of "the latter"] in a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Pāṇini 1.1.31.

This is a prohibition of the aggregate alone, not of its individual components. Why? First, in the case of *tyad* and the others, there ought to be a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) formation according to the rule "the *tyad*-class [words] with all [others] are always [retained]," and since words ending in *a* precede *tyad* and the others, there would be no difference between the suffixes *ka* and *aka*. Furthermore, the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) of a pronoun in any compound formation is indeed accepted—as in the example *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*—and thus this prohibition makes it known that "in the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), there is an application of the rule to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*)."
In the case of the suffix *jasi*, there is optional substitution [of the final vowel and the following consonant with the corresponding single substitute].

Regarding the statement "the option applies with respect to the operation of *jas*": how is that so? This is an *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option). Alternatively, in the term *jasi*, the locative case is used in relation to the operation—meaning, "when the operation called *śībhāva*, which has *jas* as its locus, is to be performed. Others, however, say: in *jasa ī*, the form *jasī* is a reference to the word-form *jas* itself; the locative case is elided by the rule for the shortening of neuter stems, and it means "when the vowel *ī* is to be applied to *jas*. But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? To that he says: "because of [the rule] *akaci*."

The word *hi* has the sense of "because. If there were an option (*vikalpa*) without distinction, then when *katara* and *katama* are present, if they were to receive their technical designation (*saṃjñā*) at that stage for the purpose of applying the rule for *akac*—desiring to express meanings such as contempt (*kutsā*) and so on—then, by virtue of falling within the scope of those [rules], the substitution of *śī* would apply upon their inclusion; however, when *ke* is applied, it does not occur.
The words *prathama* (first), *carama* (last), *alpa* (few), *ardha* (half), *katipaya* (some), and *nema* (partial) [are indeclinables when used as adverbs]. Pāṇini 1.1.33.

Regarding the phrase "of the word *ubhaya*," and so forth: since it has two parts (*ubhau avayavau asya*), the suffix *tayap* is replaced by *ayac* according to the rule *ubhādudātto nityam*. Due to the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, this [word] is treated as ending in *tayap*; nevertheless, because of its inclusion in the specific list (*gaṇa*), the designation [of the suffix] applies invariably. Now, one might object: the scope for the inclusion in the list is exemplified by forms such as *ubhayasmin* and *ubhayeṣām*, whereas here, in the case of *dvitaye* and *dvitayāḥ*, the inclusion of *tayap* in the rule applies. Thus, when the suffix *jas* follows the word *ubhaya*, this optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) would prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules. This is not a fault; for...
Since an internal designation is permanent because it does not depend on case endings, that very [internal designation] alone operates.

The application of *akac* is according to what is appropriate (*yathāyogam*). This means that the application of *akac* occurs in the word *nema*, while it occurs as *ka-* in other cases; this is the sense of "according to what is appropriate. What fault would there be if *akac* were not applied to the word *nema* with respect to the operation of *jas*? [One might argue: "Let it be so; in the case of *nemake* and *nemakāḥ*, even though *akac* is obligatory, because it is included by the mention of that [word *nema*], these two forms would indeed occur when this option is present. True; the text is intended to mean that in the case of the nominative and other cases, *akac* does not occur as an alternative.

The words *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara* [are optionally termed *sarvanāman*] when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) or as proper names (*asaṃjñā*). Pāṇini 1.1.34.

"In the absence of designation" (*asaṃjñāyām*) means that when there is no designation, if the words "eastern" and so forth do not function as designations. "Establishment" (*vyavasthā*) means restriction (*niyama*); and since this [restriction] here depends on a limit (*avadhi*) by implication, he says "dependent on its own denotation" (*svābhidheyāpekṣa*), and so on. The words "eastern" and so forth depend upon their own denoted object—the entity consisting of direction, place, or time—or that which is depended upon by them is "dependent on its own denotation. "Limit" (*avadhi*) means a boundary (*maryādā*).

The "easternness" of an eastern location exists in relation to a western location, and the "westernness" of a western location likewise exists in relation to an eastern location. This should be understood to apply to space and time as well. Therefore, the object denoted by words such as "eastern" necessarily exists in dependence upon some limit (*avadhi*). In this context, what is intended is that the rule governing this dependence constitutes the "regulation" (*vyavasthā*).

When this regulation is understood, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the very objects denoted by words like "eastern" as they function within that regulation, but not to the mere literal meaning itself.

The meaning is "skilled" (*pravīṇa*). By this, he states the absence of a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). For the word *pravīṇa* does not denote a meaning that is dependent [on another]. With the phrase "only when there is a fixed rule," he shows the etymological appropriateness (*anvarthatā*). In relation to Sumeru as a limit, the word "northern" (*uttara*) applies to the Kuru region; however, it is not stated here that the operation of the suffix *jas* occurs [there], because there is no distinction [in that regard].
The word *sva* (one's own) is used in the sense of "kinsman" and "wealth," except when it is designated as [the name of] a specific person. Pāṇini 1.1.35.

He states the meaning of the rule *ajñātidhanākhyāyām* with the words *na cet* and so on. Where a word denoting "self" (*sva*) expresses its own form independently of any other word, there it functions as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The meaning is "belonging to oneself. Although sons and cows possess the status of being kinsmen and property, the word does not apply to them in that capacity; rather, it applies to them in the capacity of being "one's own. However, if the term *ākhyā* ("name") were not included in the rule, [the designation of "property"] would result here as well, because [the word for "self"] ultimately refers to both kinsmen and property.

"Smoke, as it were," and so forth. Just as firebrands that are unjoined—that is, not in contact—smoke, whereas when joined they blaze up; such is the meaning regarding kinsmen (*jñātayaḥ*) as well. Regarding the phrase "one's own kinsmen" (*svā jñātayaḥ*): the word *jñāti* is employed as a synonym for the word *sva* in order to clarify its multiple meanings; yet the word *sva* itself was not used, for the speech of poets is unrestrained.
The term *antara* [denotes] that which is between the upper garment (*yoga*) and the undergarment (*upasaṃvyāna*). Pāṇini 1.1.36.

"Outside" (*bahiḥ*) refers to an uncovered place. The compound *bahiryoga* is formed by supplying the word *iti* and analyzing it as "the yoga [connection] with what is outside. That [yoga] occurs with an external object that is not covered. *Upasaṃvyānam* means "that which is wrapped around or put on between [the body and the outer garment]"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). The phrase "those outside the city" demonstrates the connection with what is outside. The lower garment (*paridhānīya*) is the inner cloth, while the upper garment (*prāvaraṇīya*) is the outer cloth. The expression "the ascetic in between" [indicates this].

Because the designation (*saṃjñā*) is absent here, *smin* does not replace *ṅi*. Since the term "in the case of *jas*" (*jasi*) is still in force, why is a locative-ending counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) provided? To this he says: "And of the *gaṇa*-sūtra," etc. The *gaṇa*-sūtra is also recited in exactly this same way. Why, then, is a counter-example given for the irrelevant *gaṇa*-sūtra rather than for the [main] sūtra? He will state, "It should be stated that [the rule applies] except for city names" (*apurīti vaktavyam*); this introduction is intended so that this statement may apply specifically to the domain of the *gaṇa*-sūtra. This is the context for it.

In this same manner, the counter-example for the *sūtra* is also understood; therefore, it has not been shown separately. Regarding the term *antarāyām*: the meaning is "situated outside the enclosure wall. Although the word *antara* is listed in the *Gaṇasūtra*, nevertheless, because that very word is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would also be included by the mention of that [word], which would lead to the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying]. Or rather, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply to the form ending in *ṭāp* by means of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā regarding forms qualified by gender), this statement is made. As for the phrase "in the section on the option" (*vibhāṣāprakaraṇe*), etc. [and so forth].
We shall explain how this point is established in the rule "avibhāṣā dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām."
The indeclinables consist of the vowels and so forth, as well as the particles. 1.1.37.

"Beginning with *tasil*": this refers to the section starting from *pañcamyāstasil* up to *edhācca*. *Śastasī*: [the suffix] *śas* after words meaning "many" or "few," and *tasi* in the sense of "in exchange for" (*pratiyoge*) after a word in the ablative case (*pañcamyāstasiḥ*). Regarding numbers: *kṛtvasuc* in the sense of counting the repetition of an action, and *suc* after the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*. Regarding *āsthālau*: *āsi* after the root *iṇ* (as in *ayāḥ*), and *thāl* after *pratna* and *pūrva* (as in *pratnathāḥ*).

Regarding the *cvy-arthas* (the meanings of the suffix *cv-*): "The suffix *cv-* occurs after a word ending in a case-suffix when it expresses the attainment of a state (*sampadyakartari*)," "optionally *sāti* [is used] when expressing totality (*kārtsnye*)," "and *trā* is used [in the same sense] when the object is something to be given (*deye*)," "and *am* [is used] in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)," and "after *kim*, a verbal suffix (*ttiṅ*), and an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in *gha*, the suffix *ām* is added. It will be stated that these are *nipātas*. Now, for what purpose is a separate mention of the *svarādis* made? Could they not simply be read among the *cādis*? No; for the *cādis* which denote non-substances (*asattvavacanānām*) receive the designation of *nipāta*, whereas the *svarādis* receive the designation of *avyaya* whether they denote substances (*sattvavacanānām*) or non-substances—as in the examples *svasti vācayati* ("he causes [someone] to pronounce 'may it be well'" [denoting a substance]) and *svaḥ praśya* ("having looked at heaven" [denoting a non-substance]).

Because multiple powers are observed in connection with verbal action (*kriyā*), [the particle] denotes a substantive (*sattva*). Now, if the formulation of the rule were made as "before *rīśvara*, the *nipātas* beginning with *svar* and those beginning with *ca* are [used] when not denoting a substantive" (*prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ svarādīni cādayo'sattve*), what difference would there be between making the mention of *svarādi* there or here? Furthermore, by the rule "a single-vowel *nipāta* that is not a prefix is a *pragṛhya*" (*nipāta ekājanāṅ*), the designation *pragṛhya* would undesirably apply even to the single-vowel members of the *svarādi* group—such as *kim* in *kimo't*, *dakṣiṇa* in *dakṣiṇādāc*, and the *taddhita* suffixes following a single vowel.

But [words] such as *ken* and others have already become monosyllabic (*ekāc*). Now, if the rule "the first vowel of a word consisting of a single consonant is called *anudātta*" (*cādir ekāj anāṅ*) were formulated, then the qualification that "the particles (*cādi*) denote non-substances" (*asattvavacanatva*) would not be obtained. This is not a fault; [The reason is as follows:]...

In the rule *cādayo’sattve*, the mention of *asattve* (non-substance) is a qualification of the list of *ca*-type particles, just as in the rule *tiṅo gotrādīni*, the mention of *kutsanābhīkṣṇya* (blame and frequency) is a qualification of the *gotra*-type items. Consequently, wherever there is a mention of the *ca*-type particles, it refers exclusively to those specific [listed] names. In this regard, the following point is also established: "Both technical designations (*saṃjñā*)—namely *avyaya* (indeclinable) and *nipāta* (particle)—need not be applied."

How so? Either the rule should have been formulated as "prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ" (those up to [the word] rīśvara are particles) or as "avyayāni" (these are indeclinables). Then, from "svarādīni" up to "avyayībhāvaśca," and then starting from "cādayo'sattve" up to "adhirīśvare" and "vibhāṣā kṛñi";

in that case, wherever there was a mention of "nipāta" (particle), there should have been a mention of "cādi" (the group beginning with ca), and in the sections concerning indeclinables, there should have been a mention of both "avyaya" and "nipāta. However, it was not done in that way.

The term *avyaya* (indeclinable) is a designation based on its etymological meaning. Regarding the phrase "similar," and so forth: this scriptural passage from the Atharva Veda, in the context of the Praṇava-vidyā, states that [the syllable Om] is "similar" across the three genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—because it lacks the capacity to convey any specific gender distinction. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in case-endings," it refers to [its similarity] across the kārakas and the numbers (vacanas).

Regarding numbers such as "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth, even though an *avyayībhāva* compound possesses the capacity for connection with gender and specific number, it is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by explicit rule. The meaning is: "that which does not go away (*na vyeti*), nor becomes manifold (*nānā*), nor takes on different properties (*dharmān*); therefore, it is an *avyaya*. Alternatively, that form of word which does not change (*vyeti*) is an *avyaya*. What, then, is the purpose of creating a designation based on its etymological meaning? It is to prohibit [the application of] the term "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*): as in *atyuccaisau* and *atyuccaisaḥ*.

In this context, because it includes the quality of being a sentient being (*sattvadharma*) for that which has transcended its primary [meaning], the word *uccais* is recited; what occasion would there be for [the rule] to apply to its end? By this, the Teacher indicates: "There is an application of the rule regarding the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) within the technical designation of indeclinables (*avyaya*). Therefore, in cases such as *paramasvaḥ* and *paramoccais*, where the primary status belongs to the words *svaḥ* and *uccais*, the designation applies even to the compound ending in them. The word *ku* should be recited among the *svarādi* group for the purpose of obtaining the designation of an indeclinable.
And a word ending in a taddhita suffix is indeclinable when it does not take all case endings.

In this context, although there is a prohibition against extending a rule (tadantavidhi) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), nevertheless, because there is no purpose for a technical name to apply to a *taddhita* suffix alone, it is understood that the extension applies to that which ends in such a suffix. Thus he says: "the word ending in a *taddhita*. Now, *akac* is prescribed either after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or after a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Furthermore, in the rule "after an indeclinable, there is elision of *āp* and *sup*" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), the elision refers to the *sup* that is prescribed after an indeclinable, not to one that follows it; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *atyuccaisau*.

In the rules "tatpuruṣe tulyārtha," "nāvyayadikśabda," and "khityanavyayasya," there too, the term *avyaya* (indeclinable) refers to the preceding member (*pūrvapada*). That whose related case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not any [specific] one is called *asarvavibhakti*.

But what is this: a qualifier of the *taddhita* suffix itself, or rather, a qualifier of that which ends in a *taddhita*? How is this a qualifier of the *taddhita*, or how is it a qualifier of that which ends in it? If [the compound] refers to the "object" (*kārya*) as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), such that no case-ending whatsoever is related to it—meaning that in its production, no case-ending at all serves as the cause, as in the rule "from the fifth [case-ending], *tasil*" and so on—then it is a qualifier of the *taddhita*; for in that case, the production belongs to the *taddhita* alone.

Regarding the rule *tadantasya*: when there is an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) characterized in such a way, the meaning becomes "that which ends in such a secondary derivative is an indeclinable. However, if the compound meaning (*anyapadārtha*) is taken as the reason—namely, that "it is that from which no case-ending whatsoever arises because no case-ending is connected to it as something to be produced"—then it serves as a qualifier for that which ends in [the suffix]. For there is no possibility of the production of a case-ending from a secondary derivative alone. In that regard, under the former view, [the term] would not apply to *vinā* or *nānā*.
For in the rule *nañbhyām ām*, no specific case-ending (*vibhakti*) is relied upon; thus, *nā* and *ān* occur after both *vi-* and *nañ* when they end in any case-ending.

However, since case-endings such as *su* and so forth—which are prescribed generally—do indeed exist after indeclinables that lack number, even those suffixes like *tasil* and others which are prescribed in the context of words such as *bhavat*—according to the rule "they are also seen after other [words]"—would arise from forms ending in all case-endings, such as *sa bhavān*, *tato bhavān*, *taṃ bhavantam*, and *tato bhavantam*. Consequently, [the desired forms] would not occur in those cases either.

And in examples such as *tasyāpatyam* ("his offspring") and *tatra bhavaḥ* ("occurring there"), only a single case ending, such as the genitive, serves as the cause; it is not the case that all [case endings] do so, for otherwise there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of applying this rule to forms like *aupagavaḥ*. Adopting this second position, he says "yasmāt" and so forth. In forms such as *tataḥ*, because *tasil* and other suffixes are considered case endings by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* ("those before the directions are case endings"), the substitution of *at* for the base of *tyad* and so on takes place.

But how is it that these [suffixes] are not all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*)? For this instruction applies where number is possible; however, under the view that "from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which are devoid of number," and by relying on the *jñāpaka* rule "after an indeclinable, the suffixes *āp* and *sup* are elided" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), they would indeed be all case-endings. Furthermore, if the alternative view is taken—that the meanings of the *svādi* suffixes are number, object, and so forth, and thus this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit with that [general rule regarding number]—then it would follow that those things whose meaning is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*) would simply lack case-endings. It is replied:

In the rule *dvyekayordvivacanaikavacane*, one should remove the word *ekasmin* and make *ekavacanam* a separate sūtra; then [the next rule] would be *dvibahvor-dvivacanabahuvacane*. Consequently, the singular number (*ekavacanam*) will apply even when there is only one [object]. Since the sūtra *ekavacanam* serves to provide what was not previously obtained in the absence of number, object, and so forth, while the dual and plural numbers are sublated by the dual and plural endings when duality and plurality are present, [the singular] follows even from words denoting non-substances (*asattva*).

For all seven case endings, there are likewise seven singular forms. This is the same even for the *avyayībhāva* compound; for even by that much, the rule "of the third and seventh cases" (*tṛtīyāsaptamyoḥ*) would not be applicable to the *avyayībhāva*. Therefore, this is stated: "The singular number shall be applied as the general rule."

This being the case, since not every case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises [from the suffix], the analysis (*vigraha*) is made in the singular; the word "all" (*sarva*) functions here with reference to the entirety of its parts. The meaning is that from which no case-ending—of that triplet for which the technical name *vibhakti* has been prescribed—arises without exception, but rather only a portion of it. Thus he says: "because not every case-ending."

However, if the analysis were made using the plural form *sarvā vibhaktayaḥ*, then—just as in the case of *sarvānnīnaḥ*—the word *sarva* can denote the totality of types (*prakārakārtsnya*). Consequently, even though only the singular number is produced [by the suffix], all case-endings (*sarvā vibhaktayaḥ*) would be produced from nouns denoting non-entities (*asattvavacana*), including the seven singular endings; thus, the sense is that there would be no lack of all case-endings (*asarvavibhaktitva*).

In this context, although both the suffix *aṇ* and the suffix *tas* are prescribed for the same meaning by the rule "tenaikadik-tasi-śca," the *aṇ* has substance as its primary referent, whereas *tas* has the third-case sense (instrumentality) as its primary referent with substance as a subordinate element; thus, *tas* denotes that which is not a substance (*asattvavacana*).

The question "Why [include] *taddhita*? means: let it simply be that "an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is that which does not take all case-endings" (*asarvavibhakti*); let there be no need for this entire section. For those which are *svar-ādi*, those which are *nipāta*s, those which end in *kṛt* suffixes with *m*, those such as *ktvā*, and the *avyayībhāva* compound—all of these do not take all case-endings. Thus, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because from words such as *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, and *bahavaḥ*, only a single number-form is produced even when all seven case-endings are applied. Therefore, the mention of *taddhita* must be made.

The intended meaning is that once that [formation] has been made, the *prakaraṇa* (section) must also be applied. However, words such as *viṃśati* and others, having undergone *ekaśeṣa*, can also appear in the dual and plural; thus, they are not excluded from all case-endings (*asarvavibhakti*). Likewise, the words *dvaya*, *traya*, and *ubhaya* are not formed with the suffix *yaj*. Even so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): for instance, in the case of a village located near two cows (*gavayoḥ*), when the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "and that which is situated nearby" (*adūrabhavaśca*) is elided by the rule "after *varaṇa* and others" (*varaṇādibhyaśca*), the word behaves like the original base (*yuktavadbhāva*). Consequently, since the dual ending would arise in all case-endings, the undesired consequence follows.

This objection might be raised: "If the word *goda* ends in a *taddhita* suffix, then we—who study the rule 'the elision of a suffix occurs when the connection is not perceived' (*lubyogāprakhyānāt*) and 'and when that [connection] is the authority, its absence would be observed' (*yogapramāṇe ca tadabhāve darśanaṃ syāt*)—are certainly not subject to such an objection. Even so, there would still be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): according to the rule 'after a numeral, [the suffix *kan* is added] in the sense of a name, a collection, a sūtra, or study,' the suffix must be added in its own primary sense (*svārtha*) for the sake of forming a name; thus, in the case of "five birds are indeed *pañcaka*s," the suffix would apply here. Furthermore, in forms such as *pacati-kalpam*, only the singular ending would be produced. Thus, the over-extension remains inevitable.

Therefore, the recitation [of the list] itself must be relied upon for the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*); thus he says: "But it is established by the recitation: *tasil* and so forth up to *pāśap*; *śas* and so forth up to the compound-terminating suffixes; the suffix *m* at the end of words expressing frequency; *tasi* and *vat* with the exception of *nānā* and *añ*."
That which ends in a suffix beginning with *m* and having *kṛt* as its marker is called a *pada*.

In this case as well, since it remains established—as in the previous instance—that the technical designation applies to that which ends in such [an element], the mention of "ending in *mej*" (*mejanta*) is a qualifier of that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix: "that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and ends in *mej* is an indeclinable" (*kṛdantaṃ mejantam avyayam*). Alternatively, it may mean "that which is a *kṛt* suffix and ends in *mej*, and that which ends in such [a suffix] is an indeclinable. Regarding the first alternative, consider the forms *pratāmau* and *pratāmaḥ*. From the root *prata* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *ām*, we derive *pratām*. Then, from the causative *ṇic* of the sense "he expresses *pratām*" (*lavam ācaṣṭe*), there is *kvip* suffixation; the *ṇic* is elided, *ūṭh* is substituted [for the penultimate vowel], and by the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, and *ūṭh*" (*etyedhatyūṭhsu*), *vṛddhi* occurs, resulting in *lauḥ*. Here too, the undesirable consequence would arise, because by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), it is indeed a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, and it is heard [in the form *lauḥ*] as ending in *mej*. Having seen this fault, he resorts to the second alternative and says: "that which is a *kṛt* suffix... (*kṛdyo...*).

But surely, even here [in the case of *kārayāñcakāra*], the suffix *ām* would not apply to that which ends in *liṭ*; whereas in the previous case, it was established because *liṭ* is a *kṛt* suffix. Here too, it is established by the inclusion of *ām* among the *svarādi* group. Or, even if its reading there is as a *taddhita* suffix; even so, because it is a *kṛdanta*, the elision of the case-endings (*sup*) produced after it will occur by the rule "of *ām*" (*āmaḥ*), for the word "of *liṭ*" (*leḥ*) does not recur there.

Regarding *svāduṅkāram*: by the rule *svādumi ṇamul*, because the word *svādu* is taken as representing the sense (*arthagrahaṇāt*), we also have *sampannaṅkāram*. [The form] *svāduṅkāram* arises through the irregularity (*nipātana*) whereby the first member of the compound ends in *m*. As for the mention of "end" (*anta*)—since the result would already be established by the rule *yena vidhistadantasya* ("a grammatical operation is prescribed by means of something, it applies to that which ends with it")—the author says: "The mention of the end," etc. Through the understanding that this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound expressing a constant connection (*nityayoga*), there is the comprehension of its being original (*aupadeśika*). Regarding the word *ādhayaḥ*: [it refers to mental anxieties].

From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, [the suffix] *ki* is applied by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*; in the singular dative case, *gher ṅiti* applies to form *ādhaye*. This word is currently [formed with] the suffix *ej* (i.e., it ends in *e*), but not in its original teaching (*upadeśa*). Similarly, in *cikīrṣave*, derived from the root *kṛ* with the desiderative suffix (*san*) by the rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ*, and in the word *kumbhakāraḥ*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, [if the rule were applied here], the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* would apply; and if the designation "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) were applied here, there would be elision (*luk*) by the rule *avyayāt*. This is established even by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the non-disturbance of causes), according to the principle that between a general definition and a specific mention, the specific one prevails. However, the inclusion of the term "final" (*antagrahaṇa*) should be regarded as requiring a further effort [to justify it].
And the *avyayībhāva* [compound] [is also neuter].

Regarding the phrase *luṅ-makha-svaropacārāḥ*: here, the elision (*luk*) and the accentuation (*svara*) serve as the purpose for the application (*upacāra*), because they are what is to be brought about, just as smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes. The elision (*luk*) is due to its being that which is currently being applied. In the case of *upāgni*, there is elision by virtue of the rule *avyayāt*. [The point is that] there is only the original accent of the preceding member; otherwise, by the accent of the compound, there would be udātta on the final syllable. In the case of *upapayaḥkāmaḥ*, [the same applies].

The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the roots *śīl*, *kām*, and *bhikṣā-cari*; alternatively, a *bahuvrīhi* compound may be formed with a word ending in the *ghañ* suffix. In this context, the immediate purpose is simply the removal of the accent on the initial syllable (*mukhasvara-nivṛtti*). As for the elision (*luk*), it is established by the specific prohibition in the rule "not after an *avyayībhāva* ending in *at*" (*nāvyayībhāvādato'm*). Furthermore, in the rule "after *ataḥ* [followed by] *kṛ*, *kami*, *kaṃsa*," the phrase "not standing in a subsequent member" (*anuttarapadasthasya*) is understood to carry over.

But surely other effects of indeclinables are also possible: *upāgnikam* [is formed] by the suffix *akac*; *upakumbhamanyaḥ* [involves] the prohibition of *mum*; *upakumbhībhūtaḥ* [involves] the prohibitory addition (*upasaṅkhyānika*) to the rule *asya cvau*; *upāgnyadhīyānaḥ* [involves] the prohibitory addition to the rule *subāmantrite*. Therefore, from where does this restriction of grammatical operations (*kāryaniyama*) arise? To this, he says: "All this," and so forth.

By the words "iha ca" and so forth, he demonstrates that there is no need to state what he will say under the rule *na lokāvyaya*—namely, that "there is no prohibition [of the accusative] for the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* when there is a prohibition [of the accusative] for indeclinables (*avyaya*)."
The [suffixes] beginning with *ś* are called *sarvanāmasthāna*. (Pāṇini 1.1.42)

Regarding the word *kuṇḍāni*: while the rules *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* and *sarvanāmasthāne* are in force, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*. Although the form *śi* is possible—since the long vowel [of the stem] is replaced by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*, and the form *śī* prescribed by *jasaḥ śīḥ* and *napuṃsakācca* becomes *śi* when its phonetic form (*śabda-rūpa*) undergoes the shortening of the neuter—the former is not taken here because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical operation). In the various instances where *sarvanāmasthāna* is mentioned, the term *śi* refers to the inclusion of the suffix *suṭ*.

It would not [be correct]. Since the rule states *śisuṭoḥ*, it would follow that the *suṭ* of the neuter is also included; therefore, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) must indeed be made. But why is such a long one employed? Some say: "That in which all names (*sarvanāman*) reside is the 'locus of all names' (*sarvanāmasothānam*). Here, *nāman* means a nominal stem (*pratipadika*), and the word *sarva* expresses the totality of parts. Thus, the meaning is: "that in which a name consisting of all its parts resides. By this, it is understood that elsewhere a name may reside with some parts deficient. What is established by this?

In cases such as *upeyuṣaḥ*, once the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed, the elision of the previously applied *iṭ* is established; otherwise, in the absence of a cause for its removal, it would remain. However, in this way, it would not be known which [augment] was deficient in which nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Therefore, this great designation was formulated so as not to reproach the ancient teachers.
The *suṭ* augment is applied before a neuter [ending]. 1.1.43.

"Suṭ refers to the five case-endings. By this, he shows that the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) is formed by the letter *ṭ* following *au*, and not by the word *ṭā*. In the rule *ādirantyena* ("the first [letter] with the last"), a *pratyāhāra* is formed by that which has the designation *it* based on its being the final member. However, in the case of the letter *l*, the intention is that the *pratyāhāra* is formed because of the force of the rule prescribing the *it*-designation for the vowel *a*. "Except after a neuter [noun]"—by this, he indicates that it is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation).

For if there were a general prohibition [of *suṭ*], then in the case of *kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti*, where *jas* is replaced by *śas*, there would arise a suspicion of a prohibition even regarding that which was previously obtained; thus, one would have to resort to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding," and one would have to rely upon an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound). The phrase "there is no rule for the neuter" is because the *suṭ* is introduced in connection with the feminine and masculine genders. The phrase "there is no prohibition" is because a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) has the positive injunction (*vidhi*) as its primary function. Therefore, etc. [refers to the subsequent explanation].

Since its operation is thus by means of the neuter gender, the designation [of the term *jas*] applies to what remains after [the elision of the final *s*] by the preceding rule. Thus, in the case of *sāmanī*, the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule "napuṃsakācca. When there is no elision of the *i* by the rule "vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ," the lengthening does not take place.
The particle *na* [is called *vibhāṣā*] when it signifies an option (*vibhāṣā*). Pāṇini 1.1.44.

This word *nava* is also a single indeclinable (*ekaniṣpāta*) that expresses negation, as in the expression *na vā uktārthatvāt*. If its inclusion were intended, then the prohibition "not in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīhau*)—which occurs while the rule "optionally in a compound beginning with *adi*" (*vibhāṣādiksamāse*) is in force—would be redundant. Furthermore, in the specific rules (*pradeśa*) where the option applies, only the word *na* would need to be employed. For this very reason, the form ending in *n* that denotes a number is also not included. Nor is the word denoting "new" (*pratyagra*) in the feminine gender included, because it is impossible for it to occur in those specific rules.

For indeed, in rules such as *vibhāṣā śveḥ*, it is not possible for the prescribed element (*vidheya*) to possess the quality of being new or old, nor can it have the feminine gender. Therefore, he states that this is a collection of particles by saying "not" (*na*). [He explains] "negation," etc.; by the phrase "of those two, negation and option," he shows that this technical name (*saṃjñā*) refers to the two meanings. Now, one might object that according to the rule *svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* ("the word itself is the referent"), the inclusion of the words *na* and *vā* themselves would be appropriate; to this he replies with "the particle *iti*," and so forth.

The suffix *lyuṭ* [is used here] to form the word *karaṇa*; thus, "the instrument" (*iti-karaṇa*) serves the purpose of providing a designation for the object (*artha*) that is being named. For the particle *iti* effects a reversal of the referent of a word. In common worldly usage, where words primarily denote external objects, the particle *iti* is employed to shift the referent from the external object to the word-form itself, as in: "He said, 'This is a cow' (*gaurityayamāha*). However, in this science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), because of the rule "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*), the word-form itself is the primary referent.

And therefore, because the word "used subsequently" (*prayukta*) follows the two words "new" (*nava*) and "old" (*śabda*), it displaces those two from having their own forms as their referents (*svarūpa-padārtha*) and establishes them as having external objects as their referents (*artha-padārtha*). Consequently, the designation applies only to the two objects.

By the passage beginning with "In certain sections of the *Vibhāṣā*," etc., he shows that negation (*pratiṣedha*) and option (*vikalpa*) are presented together within a single grammatical rule (*yoga*), yet by means of a distinction in their objects (*viṣaya*). The implication is that if this were not the case, the distinction between their objects would be difficult to discern. By the passage beginning with "In that case," etc., he demonstrates that negation operates first and option follows. For if option were to operate first and negation afterwards, the operation of option would be entirely purposeless.

Furthermore, the sequential order heard in the rule-formulating statement (*saṃjñāvidhivākya*) is rightly to be adopted even in the specific application rules (*pradeśavākya*), because they bring about options (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. This is because the assignment of a technical name (*saṃjñākaraṇa*) serves no purpose in either an option for what is already established (*prāptavibhāṣā*) or an option for what is not yet established (*aprāptavibhāṣā*). To illustrate: first, regarding an option for what is already established, in the rule "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne," an option is prescribed when the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has already been established as obligatory by rules such as "svaritañitaḥ."

Furthermore, this word *vibhāṣā* is well known for denoting an option, like [the terms] *vā* or *anyatarasyām*. Therefore, when both existence and non-existence are presented, since the aspect of existence is already established, it is understood that the intent refers to the aspect of non-existence, while the aspect of existence remains as it is.

Even in the case of *aprāptavibhāṣā* (optional rule where [an operation] was not previously established), since the negative portion (*abhāvāṃśa*) is already established by the rule *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*, it is understood that the rule refers to the positive portion (*bhāvāṃśa*). However, in the case of *vibhāṣā śveḥ*, if the scriptural mention of *vibhāṣā* were to operate through the mode of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*), then the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) would be optional only for *pit* suffixes; for *kit* suffixes, however, it would be compulsory due to their inclusion in the *yajādi* group. If, on the other hand, its operation were through the mode of negation (*pratiṣedhamukhena*), then the option would apply only to *kit* suffixes, and not to *pit* suffixes.

Nor can it be said that [the rule] operates by way of affirmation (*vidhi*) with respect to some [roots] and by way of negation (*pratiṣedha*) with respect to others; for since the sentence is a single unit, it would be exhausted merely as an alternative between those two. However, when the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is applied, once the negation has first operated upon the *kit* roots, the entire *liṭ*—whether termed *kit* or *akit*—becomes uniform, because all [of them] are the cause for non-vocalization (*asamprasāraṇa*). Consequently, the alternative (*vikalpa*) everywhere effects vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) in its place by way of affirmation.

And this is the purpose [of the technical designation] in the view that "the grammatical operation applies once to the whole when the word-meaning is the generic form (ākṛti). However, when the operation of the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* applies to each individual instance (*pratilakṣyam*), then it operates in some cases by way of a positive injunction (*vidhimukhena*) and in others by way of a prohibition (*pratiṣedhamukhena*); thus, the desired result is established even without the employment of a technical designation. Consequently, in rules such as *hṛkroranyatarasyām*, whether there is the mention of *anyatarasyām* or the mention of *vā*, the desired result is established in both types of optional rules (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*).

At the beginning of the sūtra, however, *saṃjñā* has the sense of "name" (*saṃjñā*), while *vibhāṣā* has the sense of "optionality" (*vikalpa*). It should be explained that *saṃjñā* [is used] in the sense of "name" and "nine. Regarding *śuśāva*: from the root *śvi* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), with the suffix *tip* replaced by *ṇal*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), followed by the application of vṛddhi and the substitution of *ā*.
The semivowels *i*, *y*, *u*, and *v* undergo *samprasāraṇa*.

"Of *yaṇ*, [there is] the place (*sthāna*). But how is the connection with "place" obtained in a restatement (*anuvāda*)? It is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) in the sūtra "The genitive [case ending denotes] a relationship of substitution (*sthāne-yoga*). Regarding the term "bhūta" (past/perfected): that which is being restated for the sake of another operation is "bhūta," whereas that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is "bhāvī" (future/that which is to come into being). And since the named entity (*saṃjñin*) is "bhāvī," the name (*saṃjñā*) itself must also be "bhāvī. For example: "Weave a cloth for this thread. In the rule "of *vac*, *svap*, *yaj* and so on, before a *kit* suffix," it is understood as: "that becomes [the subject] for which, when it has become [the state of being enjoined], the designation *samprasāraṇa* occurs."

"Iṣṭam" and "uptam": the semivowel substitution (samprasāraṇa) occurs according to the rule beginning with "vacisvapi. "Gṛhītam": [the substitution] occurs according to the rule beginning with "grahijyā," and by the rule "graho 'liṭi dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.12), there is lengthening in the periphrastic perfect (aliṭ).

"Ke-cid-ityādi" and so forth. For those who speak thus, the future designation (*saṃjñā*) need not be resorted to, and the application of the "place" (*sthāna*) is obtained. In the rule "igyaṇaḥ," by supplying the word "bhavati" (it becomes) and because the particle "iti" from the preceding rule is understood to carry over, the meaning of the sentence—"in place of *yaṇ*, *ig* occurs"—is obtained. But how can there be two meanings for a single sūtra? By means of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition). And the evidence for this is the mention of specific case endings.

When [Pāṇini] provides an instruction using a suffix in the sense of a future tense (bhāvyamāna), as in "aṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam" and so forth, he thereby indicates that the meaning of the sentence is the technical name (saṃjñā). For in those cases, the occurrence of a single phoneme is impossible. However, in rules such as "saṃprasāraṇasya," because the instruction uses a suffix in the sense of a past tense (bhūta), it is understood that the phoneme is the named entity (saṃjñin). For in those cases, the meaning of the sentence as a whole is not possible. With the words "tatra" and so forth, he demonstrates the presentation of two meanings through a distinction of their respective domains. [The example is given: *aduhitarām*.

In the case of *duh* in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, in the first person singular of the reflexive construction (*karmakartṛ*), when *iṭ* is added, the suffix *yak* is prohibited by the rule "na duhasnunamām. When the *śap* suffix is elided (*luk*), the form *aduhi* is established. Then, by the rule "tiṅaśca," the suffix *tarap* is added, and by the rule "kimettiṅavyayaghādām," the suffix *ām* is added. Regarding this, an objection might be raised: since *iṅ* is prescribed in place of the *yaṇ* of the *lakāra*, it would acquire the designation of *saṃprasāraṇa*, and consequently, by the rule "halaḥ," lengthening (*dīrghatva*) would apply. He refutes this objection with the phrase "saṅkhyātānudeśāt" (due to the correspondence of numbers). The mention of *tarap* is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*aṅgasaṃjñā*) [of the preceding element].

Since there is a designation of the numbered elements (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) based on equality of number, the vowel *i* in the place of *y* ought to receive this technical name (*saṃjñā*), but this [vowel] is in the place of *l*. In the form *dyubhyām*, after the substitution of *u* by "diva ut" and the subsequent application of the *yaṇ* substitute, the rule "halaḥ" would have required lengthening; however, this does not occur because of the specific mention of the short vowel (*taparakaraṇa*). In forms such as *akṣadyūḥ*, *akṣadyuvau*, and *akṣadyuvaḥ*, once the *ūṭh* has received the technical name "semi-vowel" (*saṃprasāraṇa*), the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca" would require the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*); this is, however, superseded by the *uvaṅ* substitute according to the principle that "an internal operation (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on phonetic elements (*vārṇa*)."
The first and last [sounds] marked by the letters ṭ and k [are termed *saṃjñā*].

In this regard, two alternatives are possible: that [the rule] is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), or that it is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*). Among these, regarding the alternative that it is a technical name, the meaning is as follows: *ṭakitau* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the letters *ṭ* and *k*, which bear the technical designation *it*, are the names for the initial and final elements [of a substitute]. In that context, in the case of [the rule] *iṭ*, by forming a *bahuvrīhi* with the initial letter *ṭ*, the word beginning with *i* is understood as the substitute being prescribed; thus, by the principle of "the most similar" (*antaratama*), it is established that *itavya* occurs in place of *tavya*. Similarly, in the case of [the rule] *ṣuk*, by forming a *bahuvrīhi* with the final letter *k*, the word ending in *ṣ* is understood as the substitute; thus, it is established that *bhīṣ* occurs in place of *bhi*.

Now, one might object: "In this view, a technical name (*saṃjñā*) exists for the purpose of making known the named object (*saṃjñin*); once it has made the named object known, it will cease of its own accord. Therefore, what is the use of including the mention of *it*? Let it simply be stated as *ṭakau*. It is replied: By virtue of having the designation *it*, a specific location is indicated. Consequently, the two letters *ṭ* and *k* become technical names when they reside in that same location which belongs to that which is designated *it*. Thus, in rules such as *ālajāṭacau* and *ṭhasyekaḥ*, the letters *ṭ* and *k* do not function as technical names [because they do not reside in the location of an *it*].

In this view, there is a fault: according to the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*, since the augment *aṭ* is prescribed as a substitute beginning with the vowel *a*, its accentuation alone would apply to the final letter of the preceding element (*alo'ntyasya*), and not to the vowel *a*. This is not a fault; for *aḍudāttaḥ* is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an accented *a* as its initial. The inversion [of the qualifier] is a Vedic usage (*sautra*).

Even so, there is a fault because the term "udātta" (acute) alone would continue to apply from the rule *āḍajādīnām*, making a *bahuvrīhi* compound impossible; therefore, relying on the perspective of a *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim), he says: "The sixth case [denotes] that which is designated (*ādiṣṭi*). The intention is that this follows by association with the subsequent section on *paribhāṣās*. Alternatively, this [term *ādiṣṭi*] is to be understood as continuing from the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*; for this very reason, he says: "of that which is indicated by the genitive."

Therefore, suffixes such as those prescribed by the rules *careṣṭaḥ* and *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ* do not become initial or final [elements]. Even so, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in the cases of *gāpoṣṭak* and *vrīhiśālyor ḍhak*; for in those instances, because of the presence of the markers *ṭ* and *k* (which signify *ṭit* and *kit*), the suffix would, due to its subsequent position, become final. This is not a fault, because of the principle: "Exceptions stated earlier sublate only the immediately following rules, not those that follow further. Thus, this [rule] sublates the connection with a specific *sthāna* (place), but not the status of being a subsequent element (*paratva*) of a suffix. As in *bhīṣayate*: from the root *ñibhī* (in the sense of fear) with the causative suffix *ṇic*. [The rule applies] by *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* and *bhīsmyor hetubhaye*.
The augment *mid* follows after the final [consonant]. 1.1.47.

The genitive case in *acaḥ* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*), and the singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*); thus he says "of vowels" (*acām*) and so forth. Here too, the plural is used for the genus. If, however, this were a fifth-case [ablative] in apposition with "from the last" (*antyāt*), then its application would not occur in the case of final consonants. Consequently, in the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the augment *num* would follow immediately after the final [vowel] in *kuṇḍāni*, whereas in *yaśāṃsi* it would instead apply to the penultimate vowel; the same would apply in rules such as *śe mucādīnām*.

The sense is that, consequently, the designation *mittvam* (the status of being a *mit* vowel) would be rendered meaningless for them. Since selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) occurs only among things of the same class, he states—“after the final vowel”—to show that the final [vowel] is understood to be a vowel (*ac*) alone. Anticipating the objection that, by the rule of "an exception preceding its general rule" (*purastādapavādanyāya*), this should properly be an exception only to the application of the term *sthāneyoga* (substitution), he says: “It is an exception to both *sthāneyoga* and the condition of being followed by an affix (*pratyayaparatva*). Here, there is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) consisting of *sthāneyoga* and *pratyayaparatva*.

The meaning is that because of the grammatical indication (nirdeśa) in the rule *tṛṇahaḥ*, the *m* of the suffix *śnam* is not for the purpose of pronunciation; therefore, by the force of its being designated as *mit*, it is logical that this [designation] also constitutes an exception to the requirement of being followed by a suffix (*pratyayaparatva*). Regarding *masjeḥ* and so forth: if the *num* augment prescribed by the rule *masjinaśorjhali* were to follow the final vowel, then in the form *man-s-ja* (from *masj*), which would stand before the *niṣṭhā* suffix, the elision of *s*—as required by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*—would not take place.

In the view that the designation *saṃyoga* applies to a single group within a collection of many consonants, rather than to each pair of them, even though there is elision of the *va*, because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the letter *ka* would not be a penultimate (*anupadhā*) letter; consequently, by the rule "for those ending in *i* or *t* which are not *it*" (*aniditām*), the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* would not occur. The term *anuṣaṅga* is the technical name used by former teachers for a nasal consonant (*nakāra*) that stands as a penultimate (*upadhā*). Therefore, the meaning is that the augment *num* must be inserted before the letter *ja*.

Regarding the word *magna*: by the rule *oditaśca*, the *niṣṭhā* suffix receives the augment *ṇatva* (nasalization); because that [ṇatva] is considered non-established (*asiddha*), *kutva* (the substitution of *k*) applies. Here, when the term *anta* ("end") is understood from the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau*, the augment *mit* becomes a part at the end of the preceding aggregate. When the term *ādi* ("beginning") is understood, it becomes the beginning of the immediately following element. Alternatively, if both [terms] are withdrawn, it is "not a part" (*abhakta*). Thus there are three positions. Among these, in the case of "not a part": in the form *tātā piṇḍānām*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur.

From that word [tad], by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, [we get] *tāni*; [then] by the rule *śeśchandasi bahulam*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śi* suffix. In *vahaṃlihaḥ* and *arbhralihaḥ*, the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *vahābhre lihaḥ*, and then *mum* is inserted by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya muma*. Because this [suffix] is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*), the anusvāra would not occur. In the case of *trapuṇī*, since *num* is applied first because it is both subsequent and obligatory, the substitution of *śī* for *auṅ* would not occur due to the intervention caused by that [num].

Now, regarding the initial [augment] *parādi*: in the case of *trapuṇe*, the rule "gher ṅiti" would require guṇa; in *atisakhīni*, the rule "sakhyurasambuddhau" causes the status of being *ṇit*-like, which would require vṛddhi by the rule "aco ñṇiti"; in *trapuṇi*, the rule "acca gheḥ" would apply; and in *śucīni*, the rule "nopadhāyāḥ" would not result in lengthening. Furthermore, in *tātā piṇḍānām*, there would be elision of *n* (by "na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ"), and in *vahaṃlihaḥ*, there would be an anusvāra. Therefore, this *mid* augment must be desired as a final element (*pūrvānta*) [of the root].
In place of *ec*, there is the substitution of a short vowel when a light syllable follows.

This technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is intended to restrict the application of the rule; it applies to rules such as "the short vowel [is substituted] in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*). Here, the first portion of the diphthongs *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* consists of a single mora and is guttural, resembling the vowel *a*; the latter portion of *e* and *ai* is palatal, resembling the vowel *i*; and the latter portion of *o* and *au* is labial, resembling the vowel *u*. Thus, since these diphthongs consist of a combination of parts, when a rule for short vowels is prescribed, there is no single short vowel most similar to the whole diphthong. Consequently, the short vowel that occurs as the most similar to the constituent parts might sometimes be *a*, and sometimes *i* or *u*.

This [sūtra] is commenced so that there may never be the form *akāra*; thus he says: "The short vowel is *i* itself. For if this were a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), then the phrase "the short substitute" would be a mere indicator of the domain (*viṣayopalakṣaṇa*), meaning: "In whatever domain there is the contingency of a short substitute for an *ec* vowel, there *i* occurs."

Furthermore, in place of long vowels, only long vowels would occur due to the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*); however, this is not a fault. [The rule] "an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts" is set aside by the statement "the vowel *a*, even when being taught, includes its homogeneous counterparts," as in the case of *diva ut* where the *t* is used to indicate quantity (just as in *amūbhyām*). Likewise, because of the similarity between *eC* and *aiC*, there would also be a correspondence based on numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*), and the mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*) would become redundant.

Therefore, by virtue of the power of the term *ādeśa* (substitute), when there is a short substitute (*hrasvādeśa*), the short vowel must be substituted for the *ik*; the meaning is that while performing the substitution of a short vowel, one should perform the substitution of an *ik*. Alternatively, *ādeśa* means "that which is prescribed" (*ādiśyate*); thus, a short vowel that is a substitute is a "short substitute" (*hrasvādeśa*). The locative case here denotes selection (*nirddhāraṇe*), and the singular number is used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*). Among those short vowels being prescribed, only an *ik* becomes the short vowel; in every respect, this rule functions as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*).

And since a restriction (*niyama*) is preceded by possibility of application (*prāpti*), the restriction applies only to those vowels that are possible as being "nearest" (*antaratama*). Now, since the sounds *ṛ* and *lṛ* are not possible [as nearest], how could there be a correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṅkhya*)? And how could there be the contingency of lengthening? Thus, since the rule would be established by simply saying *iṇ*, the inclusion of *ig* is so that it should not apply to subsequent [sounds]. Examples: *atiri* (one who has surpassed wealth), *atinu* (one who has surpassed a boat); in these *pradi-* compounds, the neuter short vowel is applied because they denote a Brāhmaṇa family that has surpassed wealth or a boat. Example: *upagu*; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound.

The *Bhāṣya* states that the word *rai* occurs only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Because the form *ekāra* is not well-known [in this context], no example is provided. In *atihi brāhmaṇakulam*, the word *he* has been elided. In *atikaṭvaḥ*, there is the shortening of the *upasarjana*. In *devadatteti*, there is the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative (*āmantrita-ādyudātta*). In *devada3tta*, there is the protracted vowel (*pluta*) according to the rule "of a heavy syllable, excepting /ṛ/" (*guroranṛtaḥ*), etc.

"Ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" [Pāṇini 1.1.49] means "for the purpose of restricting the application. Although, under this formulation of the statement—"the genitive case [ṣaṣṭhī] applies only (eva) in the sense of substitution (sthāne)"—the restriction regarding the genitive is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) because the restrictive particle *eva* follows the word [it restricts], nevertheless, the intention is that there is also a restriction regarding the relation, since the meaning is that the relation expressed by the genitive must be one based solely on the occasion of substitution (*sthāna*). Alternatively, "restriction of application" (*yoganiyama*) means a restriction concerning the application itself.

If a restrictive rule (*niyama*) were applied [universally], then such a restriction would apply even in common worldly usage, and the genitive case used for parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth would not be established. Consequently, in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, the substitution of *it* would apply both to the final letter of the root *śās* and to its penultimate (*upadhā*) alone; and in the rule *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, the substitution of *ūt* would apply both to the final letter of the root *guh* and to its penultimate alone. To this, he says: "In this grammar, that genitive which occurs without a restrictive connection... By this, he shows that this is a restrictive rule within the science of grammar—since grammatical maxims (*paribhāṣās*) are auxiliary to the science—and that even therein, there is the contingency of non-restriction (*aniyama*).

Where there is the contingency of non-restriction, a restriction must be made, as in common worldly practice. For example, in the world, someone wishing to go to another village says to another, "Please instruct me on the way. Since there are two paths and doubt arises as to which one to take, he instructs him precisely at that point of uncertainty: "Go by this path at such-and-such a spot. Likewise here, when there is doubt—whether *bhū* is the substitute for *as*, or whether it occurs immediately after *as*—a restriction is established: "It is only in the sense of taking the place [of the original] (*sthāneyoga*)."

He clarifies this very point with the words: "serving as the cause for the application in place" (*sthāneyogasya nimittabhūtaḥ*). [The term] *nimittabhūte* means "having attained the status of a cause. By employing the word *nimitta*, he demonstrates that the locative case in the word *sthāne* is a locative of cause (*nimittasaptamī*).

This word *sthāna* has three meanings: it signifies "inferiority," as in "let the horse be tied in the place of the cow" (*go-sthāne*); it signifies "cessation," as in "bitter medicine [is prescribed] in place of phlegm" (*śleṣmaṇaḥ sthāne kaṭukam auṣadham*); and it signifies "substitution" or "occasion," as in "one should spread [the floor] with *śara* grass in place of *darbha* grass" (*darbhāṇāṃ sthāne śaraiḥ prastaritavyam*). Therefore, he states that here the last meaning is intended: "and the word *sthāna*... The particle *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*) and should be understood as following the word *vācī*, though its position is displaced.

He asks, "How is it that it is expressed only as a *prasaṅga* (contingent application)? and answers with "Just as... (*yathā*). It is not understood as expressing cessation (*nivṛtti*), because of the force of the original instruction (*upadeśa*) of the root *as*. For it is not possible for that which has been made to cease in the *ārdhadhātuka* [domain] to be heard again in the *sārvadhātuka* [domain]; indeed, one who has been killed in Mathurā does not live in Srughna. Nor does it express diminution (*apakarṣa*), for it is impossible to diminish that which is eternally connected with its meaning.

Nor is there an elision (*apakarṣa*) from the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; for when the aggregate of base and suffix is eternal, an elision of the base is not possible.
