Indeed, the non-employment of the root *as-* and the employment of the word *bhū* in the *ārdhadhātuka* context is explained by this very method as being inherent (*svābhāvika*). Therefore, "occasion" (*prasaṅga*) is the locus [of the rule]. "Occasion" means occurrence; the meaning is that upon the occurrence of *as-*, the word *bhū* should be employed.

One who is intent on establishing the meaning of "asti" [as being] should establish it by means of *bhavati* when in the domain of the *ārddhadhātuka* affixes; this is the sense. By the words "of the connection with the contingency" (*prasaṅgasambandhasya*) and so forth, he demonstrates the meaning of the sūtra through an illustration. The mention of *bruvaḥ* is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, since there are many meanings of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), why is this [specific one] being stated? To this he says: "For there are many... There are one hundred and one meanings of the genitive; among these, relations such as that of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) are not possible in the case of a word, whereas proximity (*samīpa*) and the like are indeed possible. Therefore, it is said: "as many as are possible in the case of a word. Even that which is separated is considered "proximate," and thus it is mentioned separately from what is immediately adjacent (*anantara*).

If [the rule] "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā" were not a compound, then the feminine form "yogā" would be incompatible with its grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "ṣaṣṭhī. Even if it were a compound, if it were a *tatpuruṣa*, those two aforementioned faults would persist, and there would be the undesirable consequence of eliding the locative case-ending (*luk*). Furthermore, even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, the elision of the case-ending would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā," and so forth.

Alternatively, there is a word-division as *ayoga* (non-yoga). That which has no *yoga* (connection) is *ayogā*. Since a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) cannot exist without a *yoga*, the meaning is that she has no specific *yoga*. And by taking it this way, it is established everywhere that the presentation [of the mantra] occurs precisely when there is no doubt. Or else—*yogā* means "possessing *yoga*," and since a *yoga* necessarily exists for the genitive case, the suffix *-a* (the *matvarthīya*) is used in the sense of abundance by virtue of the contextual force, meaning "she in whom many *yogas* exist.
Even in this view, it is established that the presentation occurs regarding the object of doubt.

In the Bhāṣya, the Sūtra is rejected. How so? Regarding the rule *asterbhūḥ*, there is a doubt: does "immediate" (*anantara*) mean "in place" (*sthāne*) or "nearby" (*samīpe*)? Following the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*), we shall explain it as "in place. However, this [word *asti*] ends in the genitive case so that it may be joined with "place"; therefore, the genitive is uttered. By this, the principle that "substitutes occur for that which is being specifically indicated" (*nirddiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*) is established.

In that rule (*sūtra*), the word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) is understood; for it is only that which is explicitly indicated by the genitive case that is connected with the *sthāna* (the position of what is to be replaced), not that which is merely implied. Therefore, the meaning of the rule *pādaḥ pat* is this: the word *pat* is the substitute for that word *pād* which is specified by the genitive case in the rule as a constituent part (*avayava*) of a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *pād*; it is not [a substitute] for that which is merely implied as being at the end of such a stem.
In a given place, the most similar [substitute] is used.

If this were an independent rule (*svatantra-vidhi*), it would apply here as well—[to the words] *dadhi* and *madhu*. Let it be so; however, no other substitute is specifically prescribed there, and thus by proximity (*antaryataḥ*), that very same [substitute] would apply to it. No, for that too would have another, leading to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For a rule that operates without a specific purpose operates even repeatedly. Consequently, since everything would be inclined toward cessation, there would be no employment of words for the sake of conveying meaning.

Furthermore, in cases such as *bisaṃ* and *musalam*, when the whole [substitution] applies to the whole, then although there is no possibility of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) because the mere *sakāra* is not a substitute (*anādeśa*), the rule that "a *sakāra* [is replaced] by a *sakāra*" would still result in *ṣatva* for the mere *sakāra*. Therefore, because this belongs to the section on *paribhāṣās* (metarules), this *paribhāṣā* applies wherever there is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, since the prescriptive sentences form a single syntactic unit with this rule, it is stated that at the very time of prescription, the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute is ordained; hence he says: "of those things being obtained in place (*sthāne prāpyamāṇānām*)."

In this case, because the word *eva* (only) is not employed and because of the expression "of those being obtained," this is indeed a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), not a restrictive rule (*niyama*). However, it is shown that by implication there is an exclusion of the closest [substitute]. He states the meaning of "the closest" (*antaratama*) as "the most similar" (*sadṛśatama*). As for the question "from what?"—the question arises because "phoneness" (*śabdatva*) is common [to all phonemes], whereas the specific individuality (*prātisvikaviśeṣa*) is unique [to each]. "She is a young woman who is a Vataṇḍī"—this is the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*); the other is the illustrative example.

In this case, the feminine descendant of Vataṇḍa [is formed as follows]: by the rule *vataṇḍācca* [Pāṇini 4.1.107], the suffix *yañ* is elided by the rule *luk striyām* [Pāṇini 4.1.109]; then, because [the stem] is read in the *śārṅgaravādi* group, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied. When the compound *poṭāyuvati* [is formed], by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* [Pāṇini 6.3.42], the masculine form is substituted for the word *vataṇḍa* which denotes the descendant of Vataṇḍa; thus, the word *vātaṇḍya*, which denotes that same descendant, is derived. Regarding the phrase "of the letter *ca*" and so forth: [properties such as] having a weak breath (*alpaprāṇatva*) have been explained in the section on the technical term *savarṇa*. [The forms] *amuṣmai* and *amūbhyām* [are derived accordingly].

In the singular dative case of *adas*, the substitution of *y* for *t* etc. (*tyadādyatvam*) applies; then, by the rules "for a pronoun, *smai*" (*sarvanāmnaḥ smai*), "in *bhyām*" (*bhyāmi*), and "and in *sup*" (*supi ca*), the lengthening of the vowel occurs.

Regarding the phrase "while [the word] *sthāna* is present": this is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Although in that [preceding] rule it was used in its entirety (as a compound), nevertheless, because it is marked with a *svarita* accent, its recurrence [into the present rule] is not contradictory. As for the mention of *sthāna* again: by the word *sthāna* as it occurs in the original context, the meaning "of those things obtained in place" would have been understood; however, this [second] *sthāna* refers to the physical locations such as the palate (*tālu*), and is connected through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [the sense being]: "that which is most similar in place (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*) becomes [the substitute]."

Where multiple types of similarity exist, the similarity based on place (*sthāna*) is to be resorted to; the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tamap* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this non-differentiation of the sentence. For if only similarity based on place were intended, the inclusion of *-tamap* would be entirely redundant, as all other forms of similarity would be excluded. [Question: Why is the inclusion of *-tamap* stated? [Answer: The intention is that the inclusion of *-tamap* is made because we observe the linguistic usage of the term "very similar" (*sumadṛśya*). Examples include *soṣmaṇaḥ* and *soṣmāṇaḥ*. Here, the word *ūṣman* denotes a mere quality (*guṇa*). The particle *iti* indicates the reason (*hetu*).

The meaning is that because they possess the quality of *ūṣman* (aspiration), the second [consonants] are applicable to the letter *ha*, which possesses the quality of *ūṣman*. The *Śikṣā* states: "The letters beginning with *śa* are *ūṣmans*; by virtue of their place of articulation (*saṃsthāna*), they are the second [class], and by virtue of *ha*, they are the fourth. Here, the word *ūṣman* denotes a quality; the instrumental case in *saṃsthānena* is used in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that just as *ha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* are the *ūṣmans* corresponding to the places of articulation of the second letters of the *khaccha* [guttural] and other classes respectively, so too are the second letters themselves.

There is no sibilant (*ūṣman*) that shares the same place of articulation as the letter *pha*; therefore, its status as a sibilant must be stated specifically. Regarding the phrase "by means of *ha*, [the others] are the fourths," the meaning is that just as *ha* is a sibilant, so too are they. In the same way, the causal sense should also be applied here in the phrase "those possessing resonance (*nādavat*), [the others] possess resonance. In this case, [in the examples] *iṣṭam* and *uptam*, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), a semivowel (*vyañjana*) consisting of half a mora (*ardhamātra*) would undergo semivocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) into [another] semivowel consisting of half a mora.

And here, in the examples *dadhy atra*, *kumārī atra*, and *brahmabandhu artham*, among the vowels (*mātrika*) of one, two, or three morae (*mātrā*), and the semivowels (*yaṇ*) of one, two, or three morae, [the substitution] would apply by virtue of similarity (*āntarya*). However, in neither common usage (*loka*) nor the Veda (*veda*) does there exist a vowel (*iK*) of half a mora (*ardhamātra*), nor does there exist a semivowel (*yaṇ*) of one or two morae; that which exists [as a substitute] will be the one that occurs. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya, the word *antaratama* is also recorded as having a locative ending (*saptamyanta*).

The *saṃhitā* reading "sthāne'ntaratama uraṇ raparaḥ" is not mandatory; in that context, when the words are separated (*padaccheda*), it is also possible for [the word *sthāne*] to end in the locative case. In that case, the meaning is as follows: the term "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood [from the previous rule]. That which is the most similar (*antaratama*) to the substitute (*ādeśa*) is the locus (*sthānin*) for the genitive; thus, it means "of that [locus], there is the substitute. Consequently, in rules such as "akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.101), where a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is prescribed, the desired result is established by restricting the genitive to the most similar locus, namely the *ak* vowels.

Thus, in the rule "vānto yi pratyaye" (Pāṇini 6.1.79), since the genitive case is understood from the previous context, the *vānta* substitute is restricted to the most similar (*antaratama*) vowels *o* and *au*; otherwise, the *vānta* substitute would apply to all *ej* vowels. In this view, there is a fault: according to the rule "iko yaṇ aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the genitive case refers to those *ik* vowels that are most similar to the *yaṇ* substitute; consequently, the substitution would occur only in cases such as *dadhyatra*, but not in cases such as *kumāryatra*.

Likewise, regarding the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī" (P. 1.1.3), if it were interpreted as "the genitive [case] refers to those *ik* vowels which are most similar to the *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*," then it would apply only in cases such as *netā*, *lavitā*, *nāyakaḥ*, and *lāvakaḥ*; however, it would not apply in cases such as *cetā*, *stotā*, *cāyakaḥ*, and *tāvakaḥ*. Thus, because this position is flawed, the interpretation exactly as it has been explained is superior. The author will provide the resolution for this in the rule "vānto yi pratyaye" (P. 6.1.79).
The *u* and *ra* [substitutes] are followed by a *repha*. (Pāṇini 1.1.51)

In this regard, four positions are possible: The first position is that by the rule "in the place of *u*, an *aṇ* followed by *r* occurs," an *aṇ* qualified by the property of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) is prescribed. The second position is that in the place of *u*, only an *aṇ* occurs, and that [an *aṇ*] is followed by *r*; thus, when both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ* are applicable, the *aṇ* is restricted, and for that [restricted *aṇ*], the quality of being followed by *r* is enjoined.

The fourth position is as follows: having referred back to the rule "that which is prescribed in place of *u* is *aṇ*," it is merely the substitution of *ra* that is prescribed for that [substitute] precisely at the stage of its application (*prasaṅgāvasthā*). Regarding this, in the first position—since the *aṇ* is being prescribed when the udātta and other accents have not yet obtained, it would sublate them, because there is no scope [for the *aṇ*] that is not already occupied by them.

For in that case, the formulation of the rule would be as follows: "Since there is no *abhāva* (non-existence) for that which is merely indicated by the genitive case, the closest substitute (*antaratama*) does not occur; rather, for the vowel *ṛ*, [the substitute] is *aṇ* followed by *r*. Consequently, in the word *kṛtiḥ*, this would override the *ṛ*-vowel obtained by the rule "A word beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [udātta]" (*ñnityādir nityam*), and the substitute would be *aṇ* followed by *r*.

Regarding the term *prakṛtam*, there would be the elision of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*) and the circumflex accent (*svarita*); in the case of *nṛm̐ḥ pāhi*, the rule for the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of preceding vowels (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) and its nasalization (*anunāsika*) would be set aside, and the *aṇ* substitute would be followed by *r* (*rapara*). Furthermore, in the cases of *karttā* and *kāraka*, where the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* augmentations are set aside and the *aṇ* substitute occurs, since there is no restrictive rule stating that it must be the letter *a* alone, the letters *i* and *u* could also be followed by *r*. Consequently, in those substitutes for the final element of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) such as "ṝ becomes *it*" (*ṝta iddhātoḥ*), the property of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) would not apply.

In the second [interpretation], however, there would certainly be no fault regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For instance, by the restriction—"when all those designated as *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are applicable, only *aṇ* occurs"—it is established that in forms such as *kartṛ*, since *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are merely the vowels *a* and *ā*, they become followed by *r* (i.e., *ar* and *āl*). Thus, even by this restriction, only that *aṇ* which would have been applicable through another rule occurs; consequently, the vowels *i* and *u* do not occur [in place of *guṇa*].

Now, one might object: "Since it is said that 'restriction [is applied] when there is the possibility of non-restriction,' this would apply only in the case of *vṛddhi*; for in that case, there is indeed the possibility of non-restriction. However, in examples such as *karttā*, only a short *a* (one-mora) would result for a short vowel; and in examples such as *taritaḥ*, only a long vowel (two-mora) would result for a long vowel. This is because, in the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, there is no restriction, and thus in cases like *taritaḥ*, the *guṇa* would instead be *eṅ*."

But in cases such as *kartṛ*, although only the vowel *a* is obtained as the *guṇa* substitute, its status as having *r* as its subsequent element (*raparatva*) is not obtained; for by the restrictive rule that "where there is a possibility of both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ*, it shall be an *aṇ*," *raparatva* is prescribed only for that which is an *aṇ*. Therefore, even in the view that accepts the restriction, the defect regarding the scope of *guṇa* remains exactly as it was? It is said in reply: these two are *paribhāṣās* intended to restrict the substitutes—namely, "in place of [the original], the nearest" (*sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*) and "an *aṇ* is followed by *r*" (*uraṇ raparaḥ*).

In this regard, the scope (*avakāśa*) of the former [rule] is *cajoḥ ku ghiṇnyatoḥ* and so forth; the scope of the latter is where there is no distinction in terms of closest similarity (*antaratama*), such as in *tāraka* and the like, or in cases like *vṛddhīnāṃ karttā tāritaḥ*, where [the rule] applies. When it is stated that "guṇa occurs," since all [possible] guṇas would be applicable, let the restriction be "in place of [the original], the most similar one" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*). Alternatively, because of its posteriority, the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* will prevail, and thus *uraṇ raparaḥ* alone will take effect.

Therefore, it has been well said: "In the view that [the rule] is restrictive (niyama), there is no fault regarding the quality (guṇa). However, the fault regarding the acute accent (udātta) and so forth would remain exactly as it was; for instance, when it is stated that "in *kṛti* and so on, the acute accent occurs," since all vowels designated as udātta would be applicable, by this [rule] the *aṇ*s alone would become acute by virtue of being subsequent, and these would have *r* as their subsequent element (*rapara*). The same should be understood regarding the grave accent (*anudātta*) and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding those rules for substitution such as "ṛta id dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100) and others, since there would be no possibility of non-restriction (aniyama) in their case, the substitution of *ra* would not occur even when a restriction exists; thus he says: "If the statement that *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ* are followed by *ra* (*uraṇ rapara*) is intended to exclude other [substitutes], then there is a fault in the case of the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth."

In the third position, there is no fault regarding the acute (*udātta*) accents and so forth, because the closest possible substitute (*antaratama*) is prescribed by rules such as *ñṇiti*. Nor is there a fault in forms such as *kirati*; however, the aforementioned fault would certainly apply to *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For instance, after the [substitute] has been prescribed, its replacement by *r* (*raparatva*) is subsequently ordained by this rule; yet at the time of the prescription itself, due to proximity (*āntarya*), it would be a monosyllabic (*mātrika*) vowel. While forms like *karttā* are established if the *guṇa* is monosyllabic and followed by *r*, in cases such as *taritā*, the *guṇa* would instead be *eṅ* (i.e., *e*).

Furthermore, at the time of application during the *vṛddhi* substitutions, because there is no internal proximity (*āntarya*) for any one [of the three vowels], all three would apply; and since the vowel *ā* is an *aṇ*, when the rule of substitution by *ra-paratva* applies, although forms such as *kārakaḥ* and *tārakaḥ* are established, undesirable forms such as *vāyakaḥ* and *tāvakaḥ* would still result. Therefore, because these faults exist in these [previous] positions, he states [his view] by resorting to the fourth position:

"In the place of *uḥ*, only when an *aṇ* is being prescribed," and so forth. This is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "two places" (*sthānadvaya*). Therein, one [mention] is for the sake of obtaining the connection with the place even in the restatement (*anuvāda*) that "an *aṇ* is prescribed in the place of *uḥ*. The second, however, is for the purpose of prescribing the time for the *rapara* status, meaning that "that *aṇ* becomes followed by *r* (*rapara*) only at the very moment it is being prescribed (*prasaṅga*)."

For although the word *sthāna* in the rule "In place [of the original], the most similar" (*sthāne'ntaratamaḥ*) refers to the articulatory organs such as the palate, nevertheless, since no purpose is served by that meaning here, it results in being a statement regarding the occasion (*prasaṅga*). And thus, since at the very stage when the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is about to occur, the *aṇ*s have already become subsequent elements (*parapa*), they will—by virtue of the authority of the rule—displace the most similar vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* on the basis of phonetic similarity (*pramāṇataḥ*) and instead become the most similar on the basis of the place of articulation (*sthānataḥ*). Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. Nor does there arise the contingency of the substitute being for the whole (the *sarvādeśa*) because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*); for this is established by the sequential order (*ānupūrvyā*).

When the genitive case in the rule *yadaṅgasya* is understood as referring to the final [element] of the stem (*antyē*), then this [substitute] takes the place of *ay* and *u*; when it takes the place of *ay* and *u*, then it is followed by *r* (*rapara*); and when it is followed by *r*, then it is *anekāl*. It is not possible for it to become a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) by turning back again.

In the word *dvaimāturaḥ*: [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] by the rule *māturutsaṅkhyāsaṃbhadrāpūrvāyāḥ*. In the word *kheyam*: [the suffix *yat* is applied] by the rule *ī ca khanaḥ*. In the word *saudhātakiḥ*: [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] by the rule *sudhāturakaṅ ca*. Here, this substitute *akaṅ* is not followed by *r* because it is not *aṇ*. Now, why is that which is *aṇ* here not followed by *r*? Because it is not a substitute (*anādeśatvāt*); for in this case, the entire complex (*samudāya*) is the substitute.

If this were so, then even in cases such as *khaṭvaśriyaḥ*, the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatva*) would not occur; for here, the substitute would apply to the entire aggregate of the preceding and following sounds, rather than to the constituent *ṛ*-vowel alone. It is replied: because of the dual-number indication in the rule "of the preceding and following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*), the status of being the substituendum (*sthānitva*) belongs only to those two [sounds] individually, not to the aggregate, due to the specific mention (*anudeśāt*). For this very reason, since there would be two substitutes for the two substituenda—just as there is the substitution of *n* in words like *bhinnādi*—the word "one" (*eka*) is employed in that context [to ensure a single substitute]. Consequently, the *ṛ*-vowel indeed retains its status as a substituendum.
This is what is stated: "For that which exists in the place of both receives the designation of either one. Therefore, even in that case, there will be the substitution of *ra* for *r*.
[A substitute] takes the place of the final [element] of that [which is designated by the genitive]. 1.1.52.

If *alaḥ* were in the nominative plural (*jas*), the meaning would be: "the substitutes consisting of *al* [replace] the final [sound]. In that case, the elision of *ra*, *ha*, and *rajas* (as in *nīrajīkaroti*) would have to be a replacement for the entire word (*sarvādeśa*). Furthermore, because the final sound is specifically qualified [by the rule], the substitution of *d* (as in *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ*) would apply to the final sound of the whole word—as in *paramānaḍudbhyām*. To avoid ambiguity, one would have had to state *alo 'ntyasya* [instead of *alontyasya*]. Therefore, it is established that [the term *alaḥ*] is in the genitive case, due to its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *alontyasya*.

If this [sūtra] were to form a single syntactical unit with "The sixth case [is used] in connection with the substituendum" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*), then its meaning would be as follows: "Whatever sixth case occurs in this grammatical treatise, it refers to the final phoneme (*al*) and is connected to the substituendum. Consequently, because the term "final phoneme" (*anta-al*) would be supplied even to the rule "An augment *iṭ* is added to an ārdhadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant" (*ārddhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ*), the *iṭ* would be added only to the very end of the ārdhadhātuka suffix; and since that [augment] occurs before the final element according to the rule "The markers *ṭ* and *k* are placed at the beginning and the end respectively" (*ādyantau ṭakitau*), it would have to be inserted immediately prior to the final phoneme.

For by the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau*, only the status of being connected to a substitute (*sthāneyoga*) is set aside by the genitive case, but not the subsequent application of the term "at the end" (*ante*). Therefore, this constitutes a separate sentence; thus he says: "of that which is designated by a genitive," and so forth. Even though the expression is general, because of the governing rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, it should be understood as "the genitive [denoting] the place of a substitute."

Otherwise, if there were only the governing rule for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhīmātra*), the meaning would be that whatever operation—whether in the form of a substitute (*ādeśa*) or in the form of an augment (*āgama*)—is stated for a specific element designated by the genitive, that very same operation applies to that which ends with it. Consequently, the same fault that arose regarding the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatā*) would persist. Therefore, the entire rule "the genitive denotes the place of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) must be understood as recurring [in all subsequent rules].

And this is the meaning: "Whatever is prescribed for that which is indicated by a locative case ending in 'place' (sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī), that applies to the final phoneme (al) of that [element], not to the whole of it. This application of the grammatical operation to the final phoneme has been demonstrated by the author of the Vṛtti.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the genitive case [in the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*] is the one being carried forward [into subsequent rules], according to the principle: "The genitive [used in a grammatical rule] signifies a substitute for the final phoneme (*al*) of the element [denoted by the base]. In this view, the meaning of the rule *ṅicca* is: "Wherever a substitute marked with the marker *ṅ* is prescribed, the genitive [there] refers to the final phoneme (*al*). This applies everywhere. However, if the operation (*kārya*) were to be carried forward, the genitive would remain exactly as heard in the original statement; in that case, there would be an inconsistency in rules such as *ṅicca*. Therefore, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) has demonstrated the carrying forward of the operation.
That which is permanent [is not elided]. 1.1.53.

Regarding *hotāpotārau*: by the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthāne*, there is *guṇa* substitution; by the rule *aptṛn* etc., there is lengthening (*dīrgha*). Regarding *mātāpitarau*: under the alternative view where *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does not apply, the mother is placed first because she is more venerable, according to the principle: "The mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of respect. Now, why does the substitute *tātaṅ* not occur for the final [letter]? To this he says: *tātaṅi* etc.

The meaning is that this [rule], which has already served its purpose regarding the *ṅit* markers such as *anaṅ* where they have no other function, and which has also served its purpose for the sake of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, is superseded by the subsequent rule "anekāl śit sarvasya" when the *tātaṅ* substitute follows.

Now, an objection may be raised: is it not improper to posit a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), since they are not of equal status? Furthermore, without the substitution being *sarvādeśa* (replacing the whole), the purpose of the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* cannot be realized; thus, must not the utility of the *ṅit*-designation also be reconsidered? We do not say that the *ṅit*-designation is weaker because its purpose—the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—is already certain; rather, even if the substitution were *sarvādeśa*, the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* remains a possible objective for the *tātaṅ* substitute. And by that much, a slight delay in the operation occurs.

Since there is no purpose for the *ṅit*-designation (*ṅittva*) when [the substitute] applies to the whole (sarvādeśatva) in cases such as *anaṅ*, there is not even the possibility of its being intended for the sake of a total replacement; thus, it operates immediately upon those [specific rules]. Consequently, the justification for the triple prohibition (*tripratiṣedha*) is established.

Alternatively—after the rule "eruḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.3), one should state "tuhyostātaṅāśiṣi" (Pāṇini 7.1.35), and [the substitute] would be simply "er". Since this must be stated in this way, it is certain that the application of the *ṅit*-designation is solely for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Thus, the justification for the prohibition is stated: "Because the *ṅit*-designation in the case of *tātaṅ* has its own scope [of application], by virtue of the conflict (vipratiṣedha), [the substitute] is a total replacement."

Alternatively—since the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* as previously demonstrated would not be possible without [the substitution] being a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśatā*), the *tātaṅ* substitute occurs as a replacement for the whole even without [invoking] the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
That which is prescribed [is applied] to the beginning of what follows.

With the intention that this [rule] would be without scope—on the grounds that nowhere in the *Śāstra* is an operation prescribed for a subsequent element by explicitly uttering the word "of another" (*parasya*)—he asks: "And where? and so forth. Regarding the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the meaning is that an operation is prescribed for a subsequent element by the rule "from that, of the subsequent" (*tasmādityuttarasya*). Regarding the word *āsīna*: the root *āsa* (in the sense of "sitting") is *anudātta*. Regarding the word *dvīpam*: since the waters go in two directions there, the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule "of *ṛc*, *pura*, *ap*, *dhur*, *pathin*, [the suffix *a* is added] when not followed by *akṣa*" (*ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe*).
That which consists of more than one letter (anekāl) and that which has ś as its it (śit) replace the whole of the original element.

What is the purpose of including the term *anekāl* (more than one phoneme)? [The purpose is] so that in the rule *asterbhūḥ*, the substitution may apply to the whole [stem], and not just to the final phoneme (*alo'ntyasya*). This is not a valid purpose; for the rule *ṅicca* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "if a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme occurs, it must be one that ends in *ṅ*."

Even so, if there were no mention of "having more than one phoneme" (*anekāl*), then in rules such as *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), where there is a reference to the fifth case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), even a substitute with more than one phoneme would replace only the first element of the following form, according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya*. However, when that [mention of *anekāl*] exists, these two—namely *ādeḥ parasya* and *anekālśitsarvasya*—are both exceptions to the rule *alo'ntyasya*. Among them, the scope for *ādeḥ parasya* is where there is a substitute consisting of a single phoneme or an elision (*lopa*), such as in *ī dāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.101) and *bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), resulting in forms like *āsīnaḥ* and *bhūyān*.

The scope of the rule *anekāl śit sarvasya* is where there is no mention of the ablative case—as in *aster bhūḥ*. Here, however, both rules would apply: *ato bhisa ais* and *anekāl śit sarvasya*. By the principle of "prohibition of an exception" (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), the latter rule alone prevails; thus, the desired result is established.

What is the purpose of including the mention of *śit*? [It is so that] "for *jas*, *śī*" (*jasaḥ śī*) may apply to the whole [stem]. [Objection: It will suffice by the rule "that which has more than one phoneme" (*anekāl*). [Response: Once the letter *ś* is elided, it no longer has more than one phoneme. [Objection: This is established through the sequence [of operations]. When this [substitute *śī*] is a whole-stem substitute (*sarvādeśa*), then it is a suffix (*pratyaya*); when it is a suffix, then it receives the designation *it*; when it has the designation *it*, then there is its elision (*lopa*); and when there is elision, then it has only one phoneme (*ekāl*). Therefore, in this case, the status of having only one phoneme is not possible without the status of being a whole-stem substitute.

In that case, what about the rules *idama iś* and *idaṃ kimor īśkīḥ*? For here, even without [the rule] for universal substitution (*sarvādeśatā*), the designation *it* would apply beforehand. But surely, in these cases as well, the letter *ś* will be elided after having served its purpose of making the substitute multi-alphabetic (*anekāl*), since it has no other function. In that case, what about *ghvasoreddhāv abhyāsalopaś ca*? [The letter *ś* is used] so that the elision (*lopa*) by means of the *śit* designation may apply to the whole. Furthermore, in rules such as *idama iś*, there would be no *it* designation for the letter *ś* due to the absence of any further purpose, and thus there would be the undesirable consequence of its being heard [in pronunciation].
A substitute is treated like the original element, except in the case of an operation concerning an *al* (a phoneme).

Is it not the case that the acquisition of the properties of one thing by another that has taken its place is already established in both common worldly practice and the Veda? In the world, when a single teacher has died, even one who has been appointed to his position acquires the duties of a teacher, such as the right to receive honoraria and so forth; and when a king has gone abroad, even his son or another who is consecrated in his stead acquires those same royal duties. In the Veda as well, barley and other grains that take the place of rice acquire the properties of rice, such as threshing and the like.

In the same way, one might suspect that here too, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would acquire the properties of the original (*sthānin*), such as being a verbal root (*dhātu*) and so forth, and thus there would be no need for this [rule]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the original and the substitute," and so on. The intended meaning is as follows: the properties of a teacher (*upādhyāya*) are occasioned by the status of being a teacher; the properties of a king are occasioned by the status of being consecrated; and the properties of rice (*vrīhi*) are based on its being a means to a transcendental result (*apūrva*). It is logical that these properties belong to those things when they possess that particular form, rather than being based on their mere essential nature (*svarūpa*).

In this context, however, because of the rule *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form"), properties such as being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) and so forth are based on the essential nature of the verb *as-* and others; they are not prompted by the function characterized by the denotation of meanings such as "becoming" (*bhavana*). Since that essential nature does not exist for the substitutes (*ādeśa*), those properties would not belong to them either when they take the place of the original forms. To address this, he says: "Because of their distinctness. This means: "because of the difference in form."

But surely, even for one who possesses this [substitute] nature, the acquisition of its properties is observed when a person standing in the place of another acquires those properties. For instance, when a teacher is invited by a student for the sake of a sacrifice but, due to being occupied with other duties, sends another of his own students, that [student] goes there and receives the properties of the teacher, such as the seat of honor and so forth; here too, because he is a representative of the teacher, those properties are performed with the very same intention as if they were the teacher's.

If this were done, [the rule] would not apply because [the substitute] takes the place of the teacher (*upādhyāya*), nor is such a possibility present here; therefore, the Sūtra must indeed be commenced. [The desired result] is established by the prohibition of substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. When the author says "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when there is no substitute" (*yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*), he indicates that "that which is produced in the original base (*sthānin*) is also produced in the substitute (*ādeśa*). Furthermore, there is no application [of the rule] when the matter depends on the letter *l*, because of the inclusion of the suffix *lyap* in the rule "for *ad*, *jagdhi* [occurs] before *lyap*" (*ado jagdhir lyapi*).

If, in the case of a substitute, the property [of the original] were to depend on the *sthānin* (the original element) even when it is based on an *al* (phoneme), then since the rule would already be established by the mere mention of "before a *kit* suffix," the inclusion of the term *lyap* would be purposeless. This is true; however, the principle "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) must indeed be stated for the sake of subsequent rules. [The author intends: "I shall state that a substitute for an *ac* vowel possesses the properties of the original in specific contexts, and I shall state an exception regarding rules concerning word-final elements and the like. Thus, although it serves another purpose, it is formulated here precisely to avoid relying on such indicative marks (*liṅga*).

There are six types of extended application (*atideśa*): extension of the cause (*nimitta*), extension of the designation (*vyapadeśa*), extension of the rule (*śāstra*), extension of the form (*rūpa*), extension of identity (*tādātmya*), and extension of the operation (*kārya*). Among these, it is impossible to extend the cause, just as in the case of Brāhmaṇahood; for the Brāhmaṇahood that is the cause for a Brāhmaṇa’s right to eat first and so forth cannot be extended to a Kṣatriya even by a hundred utterances.

In the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* as well, a condition residing in the base (*prakṛti*), such as the property of being marked by *ṅ*, is not extended to the form ending in *san*; rather, that very condition residing in the base remains the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) even when there is an intervention by *san*. This much constitutes the justification for the expression "extension of the condition" (*nimittātideśa*).

The extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) does not differ from the position regarding technical names (*saṃjñāpakṣa*); and in that regard, the pointlessness of the suffix *vat* will be stated later. But what is intended by "designation" for your honor? Is it the designation as "the original element" (*sthānin*), such as in the case of the rule "in a single [element], like the beginning and the end," which constitutes the position regarding the extension of designation? Or rather, do those designations belonging to the original element—such as "root" (*dhātu*), "stem" (*aṅga*), and so forth—belong to the substitute (*ādeśa*) as well?

The first position is undesirable even to you, but the second differs greatly from the position regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*). For instance, in the view concerning technical names, an operation would apply only where the form of the substituendum (*sthānin*) is explicitly uttered—as in "āṅo yamahanaḥ" and so forth—and not in cases such as "the *tavya*-suffixes and others [belong] to the verbal root (*dhātu*)," or "the *ina*-suffixes and others [belong] to the base (*aṅga*"); for in these instances, the form of the substituendum, such as "asti" and so on, is not uttered as being employed as a technical name.

That which is uttered as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not itself [the object of] the operation; rather, the operation would apply only to the substitute (*ādeśa*), not to the original element (*sthānin*). For a technical name that is uttered is not itself joined with an operation; however, when the designation of the original element is extended to the substitute—as in "the suffixes *tavya* and others belong to the verbal root (*dhātu*)" or "the suffixes *in* and others belong to the stem (*aṅga*)"—the operation is established for both the original element and the substitute, because the designation exists for both.

However, rules such as "āṅo yamahanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.28) would not apply to the substitute (*ādeśa*) because they are based on the nature of the original element (*sthānin*); for in this case, there is no designation (*vyapadeśa*) belonging to the original that could be extended to the substitute. Even if it is argued that—on account of the rule "one's own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*)—the designation "han" also belongs to the root *han*, and thus when that designation is extended [to the substitute], the grammatical operation is accomplished; even so, the aforementioned distinction still remains, so let this matter rest.

However, because it is not the primary element, there is no designation [of it as such]. For this very reason, there is also no extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). Furthermore, if the form of the original element (*sthānin*) were being extended, the prescription of the substitute (*ādeśa*) would be redundant. Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) based on the authority of two statements, because the option is already established by the rule "optionally before the *liṭ* affix" (*vā liṭi*).

An extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*) is not possible because it is impossible; for an extension of mutual identity occurs only between two things that coexist, as in the case of a nominal stem (*su*) and a vocative (*āmantrita*), whereas here the original element (*sthānin*) has been replaced by the substitute (*ādeśa*), and thus such identity is impossible. Therefore, by process of elimination and due to its predominance, this is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). Thus he says: "the operation dependent on the original element" (*sthānyāśrayakāryam*), and "in the operations dependent on the original element" (*sthānyāśrayeṣu kāryeṣu*). And in its essential meaning, this is described as an extension of the operation.

The substitute letters (*akṣara*) terminate in the sense that they function in the same manner as the original element (*sthānin*); however, when the question arises as to *in what manner* they are equal, [the answer is] "by taking on its function" (*tatkāryāpatti*). Thus he says: "it functions like the original element" (*sthāninā tulyaṃ vartate*). Regarding the term *sthānivad*, [the word] *sthānyāśrayeṣu* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

He explains the meaning of the phrase *analvidhau*: "not in rules depending on vowels" (*analāśrayeṣu*). By this, he demonstrates that *vidhi* means "that which is prescribed," i.e., an operation (*kārya*), and that *alvidhi* is a compound with the loss of the final member, meaning "an operation depending on a vowel" (*alāśrayo vidhir alvidhiḥ*).

But for what purpose is recourse taken to the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*)? It might be argued as follows: when that [elision] exists, there are three types of operations: an operation concerning an *al* (phoneme), an operation concerning an *al* itself, and an operation concerning what follows an *al*. In the case of *yaṣṭaḥ* from the root *yaj*, where the suffix *kta* is applied—resulting in *iṣṭaḥ*—the rule *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.110) would otherwise require the substitution of *u* for the final vowel, as in *ko yaṣṭā* and similar forms; however, because the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element), this substitution of *u* does not occur. Furthermore, in *sa iṣṭaḥ*, the elision of *su* by the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.132) does not take place. An operation concerning an *al*: in *dyukāmaḥ*, the elision of the *u* by the rule *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) does not occur.

But you [the opponent] have already fulfilled your purpose in the case of *ahar vimaladyu*. A rule concerning what follows an *al* (vowel) is as follows: *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*—here, the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *halṅyāb* does not occur. A rule concerning an *al* itself is as follows: *vyūḍhoraskena*. Here, because the substitute for the *visarjanīya* prescribed by the rule *so’padādau* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *aḍvyavāye* does not apply, since the *visarjanīya* was taught as occurring after an *aṭ* (a vowel). Therefore, the resort to the elision of the final member of the compound is for the sake of including the meaning of all case-endings.

Otherwise, if one were to rely solely on a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the rule would have to be understood as applying only to that which has *al* as its locus; however, that is not the case, because the genitive [in this context] expresses a general relationship.

Because the inclusion of the meanings of all case-endings (*vibhakti*) is established even by means of *al-jñāna* (the knowledge of *al*). For in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), since there is no connection with a specific position (*sthāna-yoga*), every rule (*vidhi*) related to *al* will be understood [as applying]. If this is so, then the prohibition should also apply where *al* is resorted to even as a subordinate element (*guṇa-bhāva*), such as in *prapaṭhya*. For here, in the rule *valādeḥ*, the affix (*pratyaya*) is resorted to as the primary element, while *val* is resorted to as a subordinate element; thus, due to its lack of primacy, [the prohibition] would not apply. However, it does apply when there is elision of the subsequent member (*uttara-pada-lopa*), because the injunction for *iṭ* is dependent on *al*.

If the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) did not apply when based on an *al* (vowel), then in the case of *vṛkṣāya*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *supi ca* would not occur, because it would be based on an *al* that belongs to a *sup* suffix beginning with *yañ*. Furthermore, in the case of *aruditām*, when the *tas* ending is replaced by *tām*—which is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix—the augment *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* would not occur, as it is based on a *val* (consonant). Therefore, he says: "those which are based on an *al* belonging to the substituend" (*sthānyalāśrayāṇi*). An *al* belonging to the substituend is *sthānyal*; those for which that is the basis are described in that way.

The intended meaning is as follows: Just as when the rule of extension (*atideśa*)—namely, "one should behave toward the teacher's son as toward the teacher himself, except for eating his leftovers and clasping his feet"—is in operation, when the teacher's son himself becomes the teacher, then one eats his leftovers and clasps his feet. For what reason? Because a prohibition that has attained syntactic unity with the rule of extension prohibits only that specific extension-based application. Similarly here as well, only the extension-based rule regarding *al*-substitution is prohibited.

Furthermore, in the case of *aruditām*, there is no requirement for an extension (*atideśa*) [of the properties of the substitute] to the original element (*sthānin*); this is because it is itself (*svayam*) characterized by having *yañ* as its initial and having *val* as its initial. Consequently, where the original element itself is relied upon as having the letter *l*, that very [original element] is prohibited, as in the case of *prapaṭhya*. For here, the suffix *lyap* is not itself *val*-initial. Now, one might object: "In the case of a teacher’s son, if he himself possesses the status of a teacher, there is not even a trace of requirement for an extension regarding matters such as eating the leftovers; however, in the present case, even though it is itself *yañ*-initial, the long vowel is not established without an extension."

Because it is not *asuptvāt* [the cause of the prohibition]. Even in the case of *aruditām*, although the root itself possesses the *valādi* property, since it is not an *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the optional *iṭ* must be sought through extension (*atideśa*) alone. This is true; however, two operations are involved here: the designation (*saṃjñā*) of *sup* and the lengthening (*dīrghatva*). There is no restrictive rule stating that "only an operation inherent in the actual usage (*prayogasamavāyin*) may be extended"; rather, whatever is scriptural (*śāstrīya*) is what is extended. Nor is the designation *sup* non-inherent (*anāśraya*); once that designation is extended, the lengthening will take place by relying on the status of being a *yañ*-beginning stem, which is inherent to the base itself.

In the case of *aruditām* as well, the augment *iṭ* will occur by relying on the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* (which is extended here by *atideśa*) and its own inherent status of having a *val*-initial suffix (*valāditva*). Now, one might object: in the case of *vṛkṣāya*, since the substitute *ai* takes the place of the original *e* (the *sthānin*), the status of being a *sup* (case-ending) based on that [substitute] would depend solely on the *al*-nature of that [original *e*]. To this it is replied: the status of being an *al-vidhi* depends upon the operation (*kārya*) itself, not upon the specific example (*udāharaṇa*). What is meant is this: when an operation is being prescribed, if some unique form of the *al* itself is relied upon as a cause or other factor—such as in the rules "before *haś*", "before *hal*", "for *v* and *y* before *val*", and "when there is an intervention by *aṭ*"—only that is an *al-vidhi*.

However, in the rule *supi ca*, there is nothing of this nature; rather, regarding the example *vṛkṣāya*, the question is: "What is the example for [the substitution] whose locus (*sthānin*) consists of the letter *al*? The answer is: "The substitutes for verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so forth are the purpose (*prayojana*). In this context, since "purpose" (*prayojana*) means "that by which something is employed," and an example is not itself employed [as a substitute], the response is consistent with the question. Now, one might object: "Since substitutes must occur for the roots *as* and *brū* when followed by an *ārddhadhātuka* affix, what is the point of this extension (*atideśa*)? To this, he says: "In the domain of the *ārddhadhātuka*," and so forth.

*Dādhikam*: prepared in curds; [this is] by the rule *dadhnas ṭhak*. Regarding the term "substitute for an indeclinable" (*avyayādeśa*): since the substitute *lyap* applies to *ktvā* alone, and the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyayasaṃjñā*) applies to that which ends in *ktvā*, how can it be called a "substitute for an indeclinable"? Therefore, this statement is intended to mean that because *lyap* is included within the mention of *ktvā*, the designation applies even to that which ends in it. Even in that case, based on the principle "when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka is also included," it applies to the entire complex.
As for the question "What is the purpose of making the suffix *ṅ*?"—the question is: since its meaning is understood even without it, as in the case of *ṅit-ki-t* and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with *sthāni*: if the suffix *-vat* were not used, then because this is a section concerning technical designations (*saṃjñā*), the designation would be understood to apply to the substitute (*ādeśa*) by virtue of its being the "original" (*sthānin*). To prevent it from being understood in that way, the suffix *-vat* is employed—this is the meaning. But for what reason is it not desired that the designation apply to the original-substitute pair? He says: "even that which depends on its own form" (*svāśrayam api*). For if there were a designation, an operation such as "of *āṅ* and *yama-han*" (*āṅoyamahanaḥ*), which is based on the specific nature of the original, would apply only to the substitute and not to the original; for a designation itself, when uttered, is not directly connected to an operation.

And the phrase "in the case of the ātmanepada endings, optionally" (*ātmanepadeṣv anyatarasyām*) is understood as a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*). The expression "even in its own substratum" (*svāśrayam api*)—what does this mean? It means "even in the original element" (*sthānini api*). Accordingly, in the subsequent text, there is the mention of the locative case in the word "in both cases" (*ubhayatra*).

The question "What is the purpose of mentioning *ādeśa* (substitute)? is asked as follows: Just as when it is said, "He is as stout as his father," one understands from the word expressing a relationship that "his son" is meant, so too here, when it is said "like the original (*sthānivat*)," there arises an expectation as to "what [is like it]? and it is understood that "that which is the substitute (*ādeśa*) is precisely that with respect to which the status of being the original (*sthānitva*) exists. This is the point of the question. Regarding the phrase "of the inferential (*ānumānikasya*)" and so forth: For a substitute is of two kinds—the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), such as "for *as*, *bhū*" (*asterbhūḥ*), and the inferential (*ānumānika*), such as "for *e*, *uḥ*" (*eruḥ*). Here, by means of the vowel *i*, a substitute ending in *i* is inferred, just as a cow is inferred by its horn.

By the mention of *ukāra*, there is a substitution ending in *ukāra*; thus, from *tas* it becomes *tus*. In that context, if the term "substitution" (*ādeśa*) were not mentioned, only an overt (directly perceived) substitute would be understood, and not an inferred one; however, because the repetition [of the word] serves to indicate pervasion (*vyāpti*), every substitute becomes *sthānivat*. Consequently, in the case of *pacatu*, the designation of "word" (*pada*)—according to the rule "that which ends in a *tiṅ* affix is a word"—is established.

But surely, let there be the substitution of *ū* for *i* alone; what is the need for inferring that [the whole word] ends with it? For in this way, the rule *eruḥ* would be explained exactly as it is heard in the text; furthermore, the mention of "substitution" (*ādeśa*) would not have to be made, because the designation of "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) will apply due to the principle that "that which undergoes a partial modification is not different [from the original]. If this is so, then the repetition [of the word in the rule] itself is the indicator that a partial modification is not accepted in the science [of grammar]. Therefore: "All [words] are substitutes for all words, according to Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī;
for if there were a partial modification, permanence (*nityatva*) would not be possible."

Thus it is established that [the term] "dyu-pṛthivī-ty-ādeśāḥ" refers to these: "diva aut," "pathi-mathi-ubhukṣām āt," and "tyadādīnām aḥ. Now, an objection is raised: in the case of a general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*), there is no extension of specific details (*viśeṣānatideśa*). Consequently, just as in the injunction "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one would toward a Brāhmaṇa," only the duties pertaining to a Brāhmaṇa in general apply, and not the specific duties pertaining to particular sub-groups such as the Māṭharas.

Likewise, when it is stated that "a substitute (ādeśa) is not like its original (sthānin)," whatever form the original is heard to have in the rule, the substitute must undergo only those operations conditioned by that specific form. Furthermore, in the rule "the suffix *ktvā* becomes *lyap*," although the property of being followed by a consonant beginning with *v* (*valāditva*) is present according to the actual state of affairs, it is not relied upon as a characteristic of the original form. For instance, the suffix *ktvā* can indeed begin with *i*, as in *iṣṭvā*; it can be the simple suffix itself, as in *datvāya* (where it ends in *ya*); and it can even end in *m*, as in *iṣṭvīnam*.

In that regard, whatever grammatical operation is dependent solely on the suffix *ktvā*—such as being a *kṛt* suffix or having the technical designation *pratyaya*—let that be extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to its substitute. But how can the property of beginning with *val* (i.e., having *v*, *y*, *r*, or *l* as the first letter) be extended? Similarly, in forms such as *ka iṣṭaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ik* for *yaṇ*; in *divaḥ*, the final vowel becomes *ut* or *aut*; in *pathin* and so forth, the final vowel becomes *at*; in *tyad* and so forth, the final vowel becomes *akāra*; and in the case of the *visarjanīya*, there is the substitution of *satva*. Thus, there is a reliance upon the original elements (*sthānin*) through their forms as *yaṇ* and so on.

Consequently, there is an extension (*atideśa*) only of that effect which is occasioned by the specific form [of the substitute], and not of that which is based on specific properties such as *hal*-ness; thus, there is no purpose for the rule *analvidhau*. However, where a specific form itself is resorted to as the *sthānin* (original element), as in the case of the letter *v* in the rule *chvoḥ śūṭh*, let that effect not apply to the substitute—as in *akṣadyūbhyām*, where the elision (*lopa*) of the *val* [consonant] does not take place.

Now, even here, although the original element (*sthānin*) is resorted to in the form "of a stem ending in *v*, [the final] vowel [is replaced] by *uḍ* when followed by *iṭ*," nevertheless this is stated for the purpose of making known the extension of a specific property (*viśeṣātideśa*). Otherwise, just as the property of having *val* as a following letter applies to *lyap*, the property of being *kit* would not be extended [to *ktvā*]; for in forms such as *devitvā*, the suffix *ktvā* can occur even when it is not *kit*. Furthermore, since indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are attached to the original element only for the sake of grammatical operations, the prohibition "not in a rule concerning a phoneme" (*analvidhau*) does not apply to their operations. And there is evidence from the fact that the author says "let *hi* replace *si*, and it is also *apit*"; this indicates that the operations dependent on indicatory letters are indeed extended.

*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (P. 1.1.57). Regarding the statement "the term *ac* is a designation of the *sthānin*": although a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is not obtained here because *ac* functions as a qualifier for the substitute (*ādeśa*) being enjoined, nevertheless, when it is said "the substitute of *ac*," it is understood to be precisely that which occupies its place. The locative in *parasmin* expresses the state of being a cause (*nimitta*), and is not a locative of posteriority (*para-saptamī*); for the sense of posteriority is already expressed by the word *para* itself, and because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*)—as in the rule *kiti ye guṇavṛddhī*—it refers to the substitute occurring after [the cause]. The phrase *pūrvavidhau* indicates the scope (*viṣaya*), since the subject under discussion is the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

"When a preceding rule is to be applied, [the substitute] is like the original (sthānivat). Having thus shown the intended meaning of the *pada*, he states the meaning of the *vākya*: "If [the rule says] 'an ādeśa beginning with a vowel... For what purpose is this stated? In the previous case, the operation belonging to the original (*sthānin*) was extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to the substitute (*ādeśa*); here, however, it is extended that whatever operation belongs to the preceding element when the original is present, that same operation occurs for the preceding element even when the substitute is present.

But surely, even in that case, the cause belonging to the substituend is extended to the other [the substitute], just as in *vṛkṣāya*, where the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *supi ca* applies to the substitute? If this is so, then this [present rule] is for the sake of a rule concerning vowels (*ālvidhi*). For instance, in *vavraśca*, when the udātta accent is applied, the prohibition of the substitution of a semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the letter *va*—by the rule *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam*—occurs on the basis of the original vowel (*sthānyal*) due to this present statement.

And this is the purpose [of the rule] under the view that "the prohibition applies to the subsequent [vowel] when there is a *saṃprasāraṇa*"; however, it serves no purpose under the view that "the prohibition applies only to a *yaṇ* that would otherwise undergo *saṃprasāraṇa*. Here, in the words *acitīkaḥ* and *bahucitīkaḥ*, once the lengthening has been applied to *citi* before the suffix *kap*, the accent based on the original vowel (*sthānyalāśraya*) occurs by the rule "before a short vowel at the end, the accent falls on the penultimate."

Thus, from the root *yā* with the *yaṅ* affix, when *ktic* is added, the *a* is elided; because the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*, and once *y* is elided, the form stands as *yā-yā-ti*. Then, because the elision of the *yaṅ*-augment is subject to the status of being "as if the original," the *ā* is elided by the rule "the *ā* is elided before an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k* and before *iṭ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*). Once again, *y* is elided, resulting in *yāti*. Nor does the elision of *ā* occur again, nor the elision of *y* again, which would result in the undesirable consequence of hearing only the suffix (*ti*), because the elision of *ā* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the maxim of the elision of *ciṇ* in the *luṅ* tense (*ciṇo luṅnyāya*), due to its status as being "as if the original."

And likewise, in the rule for the formation of *yāyāvara*, the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivattva*) is prohibited; [this is done] so that, due to the status of being as if occupying the original position, there might not be the elision of the long *ā* (by *āto lopaḥ*). Similarly, from the root *sthā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, when the suffix *ktic* is added, after the elision of *a* and the elision of *ya* have occurred, leaving *teṣṭhi*, the substitution *iyaṅ* takes place because of the status of being as if occupying the original position of the elided *a*. And thus, in the subsequent sūtra, having raised the objection regarding the possibility of *upaṅ* in the word *kaṇḍūtiḥ*, it is stated: "Let it be; we shall apply *ūṭh* by the rule *chvoḥ śūḍ*. Once *iyaṅ* has been applied and the *ya* has been elided, the form becomes *teṣṭhitiḥ*. Nor does *iyaṅ* apply again, because [the remaining *i*] precedes the vowel that is the original locus of the operation (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*).

Similarly, from the root *pepīy* (intensive of *pā*), after the suffix *ktic*, with the elision of *a* and the elision of *ya*, and then the application of the *yaṇ* substitute by the rule "eranekācaḥ," followed by the elision of *ya*, the form *peptiḥ* arises. From the root *śo* (meaning "to thin"), in its *yaṅ*-intensive form, after the suffix *ktic* and the subsequent elisions of *a*, *ya*, and the final vowel, the rule "śaśāṃ ṣaḥ" applies—because the prohibition against treating the preceding element as a *sthānin* (by the rule "na sthānivat") prevents it from being considered a substitute—the change to *ṣ* occurs, resulting in *śāṣṭiḥ*. This is the general direction for forms such as *cicīyateścektiḥ*.

Likewise, in the case of *titaum ācaṣṭe* (he teaches the sifter), when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, although the *ṭi*-elision would otherwise be subject to the rule of "acting as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the absence of the condition *ñṇiti* means that the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*. Nor is there a prohibition of "acting as the original" regarding the rule for the penultimate syllable (*upadhā*)—namely, *kvilugupadhātv-*, etc.—because that [prohibition] pertains specifically to the domain of suffix-application rules (*pratyayavidhi*). Once the *vṛddhi* has taken place and the *puk* augment is added, the form becomes *titāpayati*. Furthermore, even with the *puk* augment, there is no "acting as the original," because the augment precedes the vowel that is the designated point of reference (*ādiṣṭāt*).

But surely, when an operation on the preceding element is to be performed, it must be as if that element were still present (sthānivadbhāva); and since sthānivadbhāva would apply everywhere here, the attainment of the operation for the preceding element would result—thus there is mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya). It is not the case that sthānivadbhāva applies only after the operation for the preceding element has already been attained; rather, sthānivadbhāva applies whether the operation for the preceding element is desired to be performed before or after [the substitution]. For this very reason, there is a prohibition of sthānivadbhāva in the rule regarding *vārṇa* operations. Therefore, this [sūtra] is for the purpose of [preventing sthānivadbhāva in] operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*).

Furthermore: in the statement "one should behave toward this kṣatriya as one would toward a brāhmaṇa," the duty based on the brāhmaṇa is obtained, but one's own duty, such as fighting and so forth, is not excluded. In the previous sūtra as well, that which is based on the substitute (sthānin) is obtained, but that which is based on the original element (sva) is not excluded; for example, in *vṛkṣāya*, the lengthening is based on the substitute, and in *bhavitā*, *bhavitum*, and *bhavitavyam*, the guṇa substitution occurs. But here, it is desired that [the operation] be based solely on the original *al* (the phoneme to be replaced), and that which is based on the original element itself is not desired.

And likewise, when the *ṭi*-elision is applied in the case of *paṭayati*, the *upadhā*-vṛddhi that would otherwise have occurred does not take place; in *avadhīt*, the [vṛddhi] characterized by a final consonant (*halanta*) does not occur; in *bahukhaṭvaka*, the accent prescribed by the rule "before a short vowel, the penultimate syllable" does not occur; in *vāyvoḥ*, the elision of *y* does not occur; and in *tanvanti*, the substitution of *iṇ* does not occur. Thus, there are many examples of the cessation of operations dependent upon the original form (*svāśraya*). For this very reason, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is prohibited in rules concerning reduplication and the like.

Therefore, this rule must also be formulated for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), so that a substitute for *aj* which has a subsequent element as its cause (*paranimittaka*) shall indeed behave like the original (*sthānivat*) when there is an operation concerning a preceding element, and not itself become a cause [for an operation on the preceding element].

But how can both [the general rule] and the restriction be obtained by a single effort? [The answer is: "By the force of the mention of *vidhi*"; we shall explain this in the discussion of that [sūtra]. Alternatively, the mention of *vidhi* is so that the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) may apply to a mere operation (*vidhi*), whether it be non-grammatical (*aśāstrīya*) or contrary [to the original form]. Therefore, in examples such as *paṭayati*, even a non-grammatical feature—such as the absence of *vṛddhi* seen in the original element (*sthānin*)—is extended [by substitution]. In that regard, the author of the *Vṛtti* has shown examples of non-grammatical cases because they require a specific effort to establish.

The word *vidhi* is derived as a *karmasādhana* (denoting the object); the genitive case in *pūrvasya* is a *śeṣalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī* (a genitive expressing a general relationship). Thus, it means "when an operation (*kārya*) related to that which is previously established must be performed. Here, however, "priority" (*pūrvatva*) is understood in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*), not in relation to the original form (*nimitta*). Furthermore, if "priority" were understood in relation to the original form, the word *vidhi* could not be a *bhāvasādhana* (denoting the action/process). For if it were a *bhāvasādhana*, then because the genitive in *pūrvasya* would be understood as a *karma-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive of the object), the meaning would be: "that which is to be substituted (*vidhātavye*) for the preceding [original] is like the original (*sthānivat*)."

Furthermore, when a vowel (*ac*) remains, something must first be prescribed; however, since it is stated here that "substitutes (*ādeśa*) are like the original (*sthānin*)," the meaning [of the rule] cannot be that the original is replaced by the substitute. In this context, the substitute is conditioned by what follows (*paranimittaka*); therefore, the meaning is that an operation is to be prescribed for something preceding that very vowel which constitutes the original (*sthānibhūta*) of the substitute.

For instance, in the rule "aco ya ādeśaḥ" (P. 1.1.56), the state prior to the substitution is restated; and therefore, by virtue of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), it is logical that the status of being a limit (*avadhitva*) should also belong to the vowel in that very state. For this reason it is said: "The status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies with respect to an operation for that which precedes a vowel that has not undergone substitution. *Ādiṣṭa* means "that which has been substituted"; *anādiṣṭa* means "that for which [substitution] has not been performed. Thus, the meaning is "of that which precedes a vowel for which no substitution has been made," which amounts to saying "in the state prior to the substitution."

Furthermore, it is not possible for the designation "like the original" (*sthānivat*) to apply to an operation prescribed with respect to what precedes this state [of substitution], because at the time of that designation, the vowel has already been replaced by the substitute. Now, even if the term *ādeśa* is derived as a passive noun (denoting the object), the rule "the substitute is like the original" still applies; however, the interpretation "in an operation concerning what precedes an *ac* for which no substitute has yet been made" is not possible here, because at the stage when the status of being "like the original" is established, the vowel (*ac*) has already been removed by the substitute.

The meaning here is not that "the preceding vowel" refers to the immediately preceding one; what then? It means "of that which was perceived as preceding during the state of being a vowel," starting from the stage of being a vowel. Thus, because the quality of being preceding is relied upon in relation to the vowel itself, the word *vidhi* (rule) is derived in the passive sense (*karmasādhana*). But what is the reason for relying on the quality of being preceding solely in relation to the vowel, and not rather in relation to the substitute (*ādeśa*) or the cause (*nimitta*)? It is said:

If "prior-ness" (*pūrvatva*) were relative to that [substitute], then in the case of *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitutions *āy* and *āv* for *ai* and *au* would result. For these two [substitutions] are also operations on what precedes a vowel subsequent to the *yaṇ*-substitution and its cause. Nor should it be argued: "Even though there is the status of being a substitute, since the *āy* and *āv* are to be applied as internal (*antaraṅga*) operations because their cause is included within [the original element], while the *ai* and *au* are external (*bahiraṅga*) due to their dependence on the subsequent taddhita suffix, the *ai* and *au* will not be established [as present]; thus, *āy* and *āv* will not occur."

This is because of the maxim: "An internal operation does not depend on what is external. For example, in the word *akṣadyūḥ*, although the suffix *kvip* is external, the substitution *ūṭh*—which depends on the internal *aj* (the vowel)—is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the *iṇ* (the *ī* in *dyū*). However, regarding the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*) with respect to an *ac* (vowel), there would be no application [of the rule] in cases such as *vi-ākaraṇaḥ* or *su-aśvaḥ*, because at the stage of *vi-aj* and *su-aj*, the *ai* and *au* (the *aic*) do not appear due to the absence of *y* and *v*. Therefore, he says: "The *aic* vowels are established through the understanding that they precede the *ac*."

Furthermore, if priority were dependent upon the cause (*nimitta*), then in the two cases [of *dīyate* and *lūyate*], the *ātva*, *itva*, and *guṇa* substitutions would, by virtue of being "as if the original" (*sthānivat*), apply to their own respective operations—the long vowel and *guṇa* substitutes—preceding their own causes. Consequently, in both of these views, in forms such as *apīpacat*, the "treatment like *san*" (*sanvadbhāva*) prescribed by the rule *sanvallaghuni* would not occur; for, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the short penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasva*), the penultimate would no longer be light (*alaghu*).

But when the state of being prior is disregarded, and the form *pāci-at* is established, although the [requirements for] reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*), and the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇi-lopa*) are all applicable, the elision of *ṇi* occurs first because it is both subsequent (*paratva*) and internal (*antaraṅga*). Then, because the shortening of the vowel occurs due to its being subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*), when reduplication follows, there is no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the original vowel (*sthānin*) of the reduplicated syllable, since that vowel was not previously perceived as being prior.

And thus it is stated in various places: "The status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) applies with respect to an operation concerning that vowel which precedes the non-specified [vowel], and this [vowel] is indeed prior to the specified vowel. Therefore, priority is determined solely in relation to the vowel. If this were the case, then in the form *tanvanti*, when the augment *iṭ* is to be applied, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not be treated as a substitute; for at the stage of *tan u anti*, the stem (*aṅga*) that precedes the vowel does not have the *iṭ*, but rather the substitute itself follows it.

However, when the rule is understood as depending on the *nimitta* (the cause), since the augment *iṭ* is to be prescribed for that very *yaṇ* which precedes the final *kār* (the letter *k*) of the *nimitta*, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is obtained whether the word "prescription" (*vidhi*) is interpreted instrumentally (*karmasādhana*) or abstractly (*bhāvasādhana*). Even when it depends on the substitute (*ādeśa*), it is established in the abstract sense (*bhāvasādhana*) because *iṭ* is to be prescribed by virtue of its position preceding the *yaṇ*; thus, there is no fault. In the rule "ārddhadhātukasyeṅ," the term "upadeśe" (in the original enunciation) is understood from the preceding rule "ekāca upadeśe," so the augment *iṭ* will apply to a root with a single vowel in its original enunciation that begins with a *val* consonant.

In that case as well, because the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], even though both the *iṭ* prescribed by the rule for *valādi* suffixes and the *ciṇvadiṭ* would apply in examples such as *coriṣyate*, the *ciṇvadiṭ* prevails due to its being obligatory (*nitya*). He will state: "And this [ciṇvadiṭ] is obligatory and subverts the cause for the *val*-conditioned [suffix]. That, however, is not tenable; for according to the method already stated, the *iṭ* conditioned by *valādi* suffixes is likewise obligatory. If that is so, then there is an absence of *iṭ* because the *yaṇ* [substitution] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) since it is not internal (*bahiraṅga*).

Alternatively, the compound *pūrvavidhi* (prior rule) may also be understood as a genitive (*pañcamī*) compound, meaning "a rule prior [to the present one]. By this, when the substitution of *yaṇ* is to be applied for what follows after an augment (*iṭ*) that has not been adopted as a cause with respect to the preceding stem, it will behave as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). What, then, are the purposes of the genitive compound? First, there is this purpose: *tanvanti*. Furthermore: *bebhiditā*, *mārthitikaḥ*, *apīpacan*. In the case of *bebhiditā*, derived from the reduplicated root *bebhidi* with the suffix *tṛc*, the substitution of *yaṇ* does not occur because of the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as being like the original element (*sthānivattvāt*). But this is not so.

In the case of *bebhidya*, there arises both the elision of the *tṛ* (the suffix *ktvā*) and the augment *iṭ*. Because it is subsequent, *iṭ* [would apply]. However, the elision of *al* (*allopaḥ*) is permanent (*nitya*), for it applies even when *iṭ* has been added; whereas *iṭ* is non-permanent (*anitya*), for it does not apply once the elision of *al* has taken place, being superseded by that permanent elision of *al*. That whose cause is not obstructed by another rule is permanent; therefore, between these two permanent operations, *iṭ* alone will occur because it is subsequent.

In that case, consider the word *māthitika*, derived from *mathitaṃ paṇyam asya* ("this has *mathita* as its merchandise"). When the substitution of *ṭha* by *ika* is applied and the elision (*lopa*) of *yasya* occurs, the rule "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" would require the substitution of *ka* for the final vowel because the substitute *ika* is treated as the original *ṭha* due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, this does not happen because the elision of *yasya* is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is established either by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of a grammatical occasion) or because the elision is not a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) since it is an *al-vidhi* (an operation concerning a phoneme) and the rule "ṭhasya" refers to a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*).
