In that case, when *apīpacat* is established as *apīpac-a-an*, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) for the final *a* of the root and the *a* of the *caṅ*—by the rule *ato guṇe*—would result in the application of *jus* by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, because that [single substitute] would be treated as the beginning of the following element due to its status as *ādivadbhāva* and would thus be included by the mention of *jhi*. However, this does not occur because of the status of *sthānivadbhāva* belonging either to the elision of the *ṇi* or to the single substitute (*ekādeśa*). Thus, it is established that priority (*pūrvatva*) is relied upon solely with respect to the vowel (*ac*), and that the word *vidhi* is derived as a passive noun (*karmasādhana*), forming a compound with the genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*); therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. This is the settled conclusion.

Regarding *paṭyati*: by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi*. Regarding *avadhīt*: by the rules *hano vadha liṅi* and *luṅi ca*, the substitute *vadh* is applied. Regarding "characterized by having a consonant at the end" (*halantalakṣaṇā*): because the term *halantasya* ("of that which ends in a consonant") is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule *vadavraja*, it is characterized by having a consonant at the end. In the case of *bahukhaṭvaka*, although there is a statement—"In the case of vowel [substitution], lengthening, and the elision of *y*, a substitute for an elided element is not like the original (*na sthānivat*)"—nevertheless, even in a rule concerning vowels (*svaravidhi*), the status of being like the original (*sthānivattva*) indeed occurs here.

Regarding the word *praśna*: the suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule "yajayācayat... (*Pāṇini 3.3.90*), and the substitution of *ś* for *ch* occurs by the rule "chśuvoḥ śūṭh" (*Pāṇini 6.4.19*). [The statement] "it does not behave as a *sthānin* with respect to *tuk*" means that when *tuk* is to be applied, it does not behave as a *sthānin*.

Surely, because it is *antaraṅga*, the *tuk* augment should apply first; and in that case, with a single cause, there would be a simultaneous application (*prasaṅga*) of both the *āṅga* (internal) and the *vārṇa* (phonetic) operation. In such a conflict, the *āṅga* is stronger than the *vārṇa*. For example, when *karoti* is in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense with the suffix *ṇal*, resulting in the form *kṛ-a*, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (P. 7.2.115), which has its scope elsewhere (e.g., in *gaur-ī*), is set aside, and the *vṛddhi* itself prevails over the *yaṇ* substitution that would otherwise apply due to being *antaraṅga*. However, in the word *praśna*, the cause for the *naṅ* substitute is the letter *ś*, whereas the cause for the *tuk* is the letter *ch*; thus, the application of these two occurs at different times.

[Objection: "This [suffix] is not within its scope," one might argue; for when *tuk* is present, by the mention of the letter *ch* together with *tuk* in the rule *cchvoḥ śūṭh*, only that [specific *ch*] is substituted. And even if *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) were to apply here, since the mention of *ch* together with *tuk* in the rule *satukkacchagrahaṇena* would include *ś*, and not merely the mention of *ch*, how could there be any occasion for *tuk*? For this very reason, even the *ṅit*-status of the augment *naṅ* is intended so that the *guṇa* substitution in *viśnaḥ* does not occur. Therefore, this is not a valid counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Consequently, he states another counter-example: *ākrāṣṭām*.

Regarding the rule "the *sic* suffix may optionally be prescribed after the roots *spr̥ś*, *mr̥ś*, *kr̥ṣ*, *t̥p*, and *d̥ṣ*," this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ksa* suffix; thus, in one alternative, *sic* is applied. By the rule "of an unaccented [root ending]," there is the substitution of *am*; then, by *yaṇ*-substitution, the *vṛddhi* is applied according to "vadavraja. Because of the statement "that which was previously established as not valid does not behave like the original [sthānin]," even here [in the case of *atṛpat*], he says "having come" (*āgatya*). [The rule] "optionally before *lyap*" applies.

Regarding the term *yuvajāni*: in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Since the word *yuvati* denotes age (*vayovacana*), it does not express a genus (*jāti*); therefore, the prohibition [of *puṃvadbhāva*] by the rule "not in the case of a genus" (*jāteśca*) does not apply. Regarding the statement "in the case of the elision of *y*, it is not as if it were the original element" (*na sthānivat*): one might object that the substitute (*ādeśa*) here is not the cause of the elision, because that [elision] has as its cause merely the presence of a *val* sound; and that which is the cause, namely the letter *n*, is not a substitute. Thus, the status of being "as if the original element" (*sthānivattva*) should not occur.

Nor does there arise the contingency of the elision of the *ā* (in *jāyā*) on account of the status of *niṅ* as *sthānivadbhūta*, because the word *jāyā* is derived from the root *jan* with the *uṇādi* suffix *yaṅ*, followed by the substitution of *ā* according to the rule *aye vibhāṣā*. For in the *uṇādi* formations, the grammatical operations resulting from the derivation do not necessarily apply [subsequently]. Therefore, another example is presented: *vaiyāghrapadya*. In this case, the form is derived from *vyāghrapāt* (one whose feet are like those of a tiger) using the suffix *yañ* after bases such as *garga*—the elision of *pād* being triggered by the rule *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ*, which depends on a subsequent cause (*aparanimitaka*).

[Objection: But surely, even though there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*), the substitution of *pad* will occur by virtue of the specific rule; if that were so, it would also apply in the case of *pāde*. [Response: However, since this other [rule] exists, namely that the substitution of *pad* has its purpose fulfilled in the case of *vaiyāghrapadya*, there is an absence of the substitution of *pad* in *pāde* because of the status of being a substitute for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). [Question: But how can there be the status of being a substitute for a single-substitute, for this is not a substitute for a vowel (*ac*)? What then? It is said: [it is a substitute] for two vowels (*acoḥ*).

Because the term *jāti* (the class) is understood in the descriptions of phonemes (*varṇa*), and because the singular number in the word *ac* is not intended to be significant, the substitute for even two vowels is treated as the original (*sthānivat*). Alternatively, even if both [vowels] were the substituends, the status of being *sthānivat* would apply based on that which constitutes the single [original] substituend. For this very reason, in the forms *śrāyasau*, *gaumatau*, *cāturau*, and *ānuḍuhau*, the suffixes *num* and *ām* do not occur after the words *śrāyasa-* etc., which end in the suffix *aṇ*, because the single substitute is treated as the beginning of the preceding element.

The word *udakam* flows; by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and in the formation of the name (*saṃjñāyām*), there is the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-*. In the singular locative case, because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as being like the initial element (*ādivattvāt*), it becomes a *bha*-stem; consequently, the rule *vāha ūṭh* does not apply, resulting in *udavāhe*. Regarding the term *ādīdhye*: due to its inclusion in the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. If it were stated that [the substitute] occurs "in the subsequent [element]," then because of the absence of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision would not apply once the substitution of *ṭi* for *e* has been performed. However, since the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* applies both when the elision has been made and when it has not (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitvāt*), it is considered obligatory (*nitya*); therefore, that substitution alone takes place.

But surely, since the other [element] does not exist, even the *ślu* suffix—due to its being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—will not cause the elision (*lopa*) because of that very intervention? No; for by the rule "In the case of *luk*, elision (*lup*), the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*), *aṅ*, *nihnava*, *nihnasa*, and *kutva*, there is a prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* for what has been elided by *luk*."

"He says *gauriti*. [The rule] *goto ṇit* applies. Regarding *bābhravīyāḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: from *babhru*, [meaning] "the offspring of Babhru," the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *madhubabhvrorbrāhmaṇakauśikayoḥ*. Then, by *orguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs, and by *vānto yi pratyaye*, the substitution of *av* takes place. [It is argued that] the substitution of *av* does not behave as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, one might object: even if there were no *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) should not occur here due to the *saṃnipātaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship); this is not so, because this cluster [of sounds] in the word *acaḥ* is brought about by the presence of *y* and other [sounds].

And that [elision] is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the elision; what then? It is merely the letter *v*. If this is so, then the application of the rule of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would also not occur here, because that which is the substitute (*ādeśa*) is not relied upon, and that which is relied upon is not the substitute. [The word] *naiveya* is derived from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ni*: by the rules "the suffix *ki* after a verbal root ending in *ghu* when there is a prefix," "elision of the long *ā*," "after a base of two syllables," and "the suffix *ḍhak* after a base ending in *i* that does not have the augment *ini*. Now, it was stated that there is the status of "behaving like the original" even in a rule concerning what precedes; how then can these be counter-examples? This is not a fault.

In this case as well, because the preceding [element] is adopted without regard for the subsequent, the rule applies to that which follows what precedes an unspecified vowel (*ac*). Even so, in the case of *he gauḥ*, the elision of the *s* would occur even when there is an intervening element, because the term "following" (*para*) functions even with respect to something separated from the *g*; the same would apply to the other two cases. This is not so; the phrase "a prescription concerning the preceding" (*pūrvasya vidhiḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no locative of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); rather, it is a genitive of general relation, meaning "in a prescription concerning that which is related to the preceding."

The relationship [of the preceding element] is of two kinds: either as an effect (*kāryitva*) or as a cause (*nimittatva*). Where it is as an effect, that is a rule (*vidhi*) from what precedes; where it is as a cause, that is [a rule] from what precedes. Consequently, whatever operation is obtained by relying on the cause of that which precedes an unindicated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvaḥ*), that alone is the rule from what precedes, as in *apīpacan*. For here, whether it be the unindicated *ṇic* or the *caṅ*, that which precedes it—namely *apīpac* itself—is the cause for the substitution of *jus* for the following *jhi* of the reduplicated stem.

In the rule *tanvanti*, because the term "of the *aṅga*" (*aṅgasya*) is understood [from a previous rule], that which is relied upon as the cause for the *upapratyaya* (the suffix *u*)—which is not preceded by an enjoined vowel—is taken as the cause; this is precisely the purpose of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "of the *aṅga*" in that context. However, in cases such as *he gauḥ*, the *ga-* sound and so forth, which precede the non-enjoined vowel (*ac*), are not the cause for the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi-lopa*) and the like; and that which is the cause, namely the *o-* sound and so forth, does not precede the non-enjoined vowel. Thus, there is no fault.

In that case, regarding the word *vetasvān*, because the elision of the suffix *ṭi* would be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present) for the sake of a preceding rule, the letter preceding the *s* would not be a penultimate (*anupadhā*) vowel; consequently, the substitution of *v* [for *s*] by the rule *amādupadhāyāḥ* would not occur. Nor can it be argued that, through *sthānivadbhāva*, one obtains the condition "from a stem ending in *a*" by depending on the immediately preceding *a*, since that [elided *ṭi*] lacks the status of being prior to an undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*). If it were dependent on that, then by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva* [the condition would fail]. This is not a fault, because of the principle: "In a rule that is *asiddha* (not yet established) with respect to what precedes it, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*."

What is the purpose of including the term *vidhi* (rule)? Is it not already understood by its recurrence from the preceding sūtra? It is for the sake of including both types of compounds. For if that [term] were absent, when "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is stated, there would be no application in the case of a rule derived from the preceding; and when "from the preceding" (*pūrvasmāt*) is stated, there would be no application in the case of a rule concerning the preceding. This is not a valid objection; because even when "of the preceding" is stated, since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is an absence of the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), and thus every rule connected with the preceding will be understood. If this is so, then the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) should apply to every rule—whether scriptural or otherwise—to ensure the desired result.

Alternatively, the mention of *vidhi* (rule) constitutes a second effort: there, *acaḥ parasmin pūrvasya* is one rule, with *vidhau* alone [as its condition]. By this, in cases such as *vavraśca*, the substitution of an *al* (phoneme) belonging to the original element (*sthānin*) is extended by analogy. Then, in the context of *vidhau acaḥ parasmin pūrvasya*, this is for the purpose of restriction: "A substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*) caused by a subsequent factor is like the original element (*sthānivat*) only in respect to a preceding rule (*pūrvavidhau*), but it is not itself a cause. By this, forms such as *paṭayati* are established.

Now, one might object: even in the absence of a second effort, just as in the case of "there are rice grains in Kashmir like in Cola," or "there is water in this region like in the desert," where there is an extension (*atideśa*) of a property—whether a positive entity or an absence—that is well-known from the example according to how it is observed, so too will it be here? This is an unequal comparison.

That [is] appropriate there, because both existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are well-established; however, here, although existence and non-existence are established through different examples, since it is stated "the substitute is like the original" (*sthānivad ādeśaḥ*), in sentences where the verb is not explicitly heard, the addition of the verb "exists" (*asti*) is well-known; therefore, there would be an extension of existence (*bhāvātideśa*). Enough of this prolixity.

Not [is a preceding sound considered homogeneous] in the rules concerning: the end of a word, reduplication, the *vara-ēya* suffixes, elision (*lopa*), accentuation (*svara*), homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*), the nasal *anusvāra*, lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds. (Pāṇini 1.1.58)

In cases such as *dvirvacana* (reduplication) and *yalopa* (elision of *y*), that very [operation] is to be enjoined, but nothing further to that already established. However, in examples such as *kau staḥ*, since the suffixes *āva* and so on belong to what is already a word-final (*padānta*), there is the possibility of both interpretations: either the operation applies to what is word-final, or the prescription of *āva* and so on applies to what is [already] word-final. The same applies to the prescription regarding *vara*. Nevertheless, for the sake of encompassing all cases, the word *vidhi* (prescription) is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāvasādhana*). "In these" means: in those various prescriptions which are differentiated by the distinctions among the things to be prescribed, such as word-final elements and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the preceding rule" (*pūrvavidhau*), etc.: although in grammar neither individual words nor sentences are directly refined (*saṃskriyante*), nevertheless, when a word such as *kāvi* is being derived within a sentence such as *staḥ*, the mere proximity (*sannidhāna*) of a word like *kāvi* is not contradictory even if it lacks the status of being a formal cause (*nimitta*). Consequently, since the possibility of being prior to an unspecified vowel (*anādiṣṭāt acah*) exists, there arises the contingency of the application of the rule regarding the substitute being treated like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the example *dadhyatra*: by the force of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as the original), the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is invalid with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)" does not apply here either. Even in cases such as *śacyau*, the *yaṇ* substitution is indeed *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon an external element (*aj*); however, due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) expressed by the rule "in *vara*," there is no elision (*aluk*). Regarding *yāyāvara*: the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to the rule "it is obligatory when [the action] denotes crookedness in motion. The statement "the elision of the *at* [of *yaṅ*] has a subsequent cause" refers to the view that the locative case in the rule "before an *ārddhadhātuka*" (*ārddhadhātuke*) functions as a *parasaptamī* (a locative indicating what follows).

And likewise, there is the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*. For if that were not present, it would be understood as "from a root ending in a consonant" (*halantāt*); consequently, the suffix *yuc* would not apply in cases such as *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*. Furthermore, if that [locative case] were a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), then even before the production of the suffix, when the *at* elision has occurred, the suffix *yuc* would be established here as well, because the root would still end in a consonant.

As for what he will say regarding the rule *aco yat*: "What is the purpose of the mention of *ac*, since he will state that *ṇya* follows a consonant-final [root]? It is so that [the suffix] may apply even to those that were previously vowel-final, as in *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*. This should be understood as referring to the view where the locative case (*saptamī*) denotes the scope of the operation (*viṣaya-saptamī*). For under the view where the locative denotes immediate sequence (*parasaptamī*), that [application] would be impossible because the elision of the vowel (*ato lopa*) has not yet occurred prior to the production of the suffix."

The phrase "when *ktin* has been applied after the root *kaṇḍūy*" refers to the rule: "It should be stated that *ktin* is added after [roots] beginning with *nāv*," such is the intention. However, the reading "when *ktic* [is applied]" is more appropriate. In the case of *kaṇḍūtiḥ*, because the elision of *al* (the *y*) would be subject to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution *uvaṅ* would result; let it be so, for the substitution *ūṭ* will occur by the rule "for *ch* and *v*, there is *śūṭh*. Nor does *ūṭ* possess the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, because it precedes the original vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*). For this very reason, *uvaṅ* does not occur again after *ūṭ*.

[The rule states: "In the case of *parasavarṇa*, [the substitute] does not behave as the original (*sthānivat*). Now, one might object: "Once the elision (*lopa*) of the *śn-* and *as-* suffixes has been performed, the *anusvāra* subsequently arises before the vowel that was not yet subject to the original rule (*anādiṣṭāt*); how then can there be any possibility of it behaving as the original when the *parasavarṇa* is to be applied? It might be argued: "Since the original (*sthānin*), the letter *n*, is before the vowel that was not yet subject to the original rule, the substitute *anusvāra* must also—by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*—be before that vowel. But that is not so; for "being before the vowel that was not yet subject to the original rule" is not a technical grammatical property (*śāstrīya*) that could be extended by analogy.

In that case, when an extension (atideśa) is to be applied—based on the requirement of being prior to an unspecified vowel, as in the rule "when a subsequent vowel follows" (acaḥ parasmin)—the rule "a substitute is like the original" (sthānivad ādeśaḥ) operates; therefore, the mention of "homogeneous" (savarṇa) was made.

Regarding the word *śiṣanti*: although *śiṇḍhi* is indeed an example for the rule concerning the *anusvāra*, nevertheless, when that very example is cited, there is a prohibition against the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the rule for *parasavarṇa*. Since this [prohibition] would be untenable without a prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* even for the prescription of the *anusvāra* itself as the original element (*sthānin*), the separate mention of *anusvāra* [in the rule] would otherwise be unnecessary; thus, the example of the solitary *anusvāra* is shown in order to dispel such a doubt.

Regarding *pratidīvan*: from the root *div* preceded by *prati*, the suffix *kanin* is applied according to the rule "kanin is applied after *yu*, *vṛṣi*, *takṣi*, *rāj*, *dhan*, *vidyut*, and *pratidiv*. The mention of the governing heading *bhasya* (of a *bha*-stem) is for the purpose of establishing that [the substitution] is dependent on a subsequent cause. As for what was said—that the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "also when followed by a consonant (*hali*) and when it is a penultimate (*upadhā*)" would not occur—that statement "when it is a penultimate" was written down by scribes through negligence; for he will state under the rule "also when it is a penultimate" (*upadhāyāñca*) that in the word *pratidīvan*, the lengthening occurs by the rule "also when followed by a consonant" (*hali ca*).

The phrase "it occurs from this statement" means that the prohibition "na bhakurchurām" does not apply here, as it concerns a *bha*-stem ending in *r* or *v*. Regarding "the elision of *s* by *jhalo jhalī*"—that is, the rule "there is elision of *s* after *sic*"—is not accepted here; however, if that were accepted, the elision of the phoneme would be due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Regarding the example *bahukhaṭvaka*: here, due to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the vowel preceding the final letter [of the base]—specifically the *a* before the *kh*—does not become udātta according to the rule *hrasvānte’ntyātpūrvam*; rather, only the rule *kapi pūrvam* applies. As for *kiyoḥ* and *giyoḥ*, these have been cited as examples under the view that they are derived [from roots] by the rule *kṛgroricca*.

However, in the rule *upadhāyāñca* (Pāṇini 8.2.78), he will state—relying on the view that they are not derived—that "since *uṇādi* formations are underived (*avyutpanna*) nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there is no lengthening in cases such as *kiyoḥ* and *giyoḥ*."

It should be stated: "In the case of *kvi*, *luk*, *upadhātva*, *aṅ*, *paranirhrāsa*, and *kutva*, a substitute for *ac* (a vowel) is not treated as *sthānivat*. This means that when *kvi*—that is, *kvip*—is prescribed, whatever is to be done there, a substitute for *ac* made anywhere [in its formation] is not treated as *sthānivat*.

In the word *lauḥ*, derived from the root *lū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the *kvip* suffix, there is the elision of the *ya* of the causative (*ṇic*), and there is also the elision of the *ṇi*. Both of these are not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if they were still present) when the substitution of *ū* for the *v*—by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*—is to be applied on account of the *kvip* suffix. Consequently, by the rule *etyedhatyūṭhsu*, the *vṛddhi* (guṇa) replacement occurs. For those, however, who read the rule as *kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*, this [result] would not be achieved.

Similarly, in the case of *pipaṭhiṣateḥ* [derived from the desiderative root] with the suffix *kvip*, when the *a* is elided, there arises the question of whether the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies even when the *num* augment—conditioned by the *jas* ending in the neuter plural—is to be applied, since that elision was caused by *kvip*. However, according to the view that "a rule conditioned by *kvip* does not apply," the prohibition does not hold here; thus, in *pipaṭhīṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, since *num* is absent, the lengthening prescribed by the rule *sāntamahataḥ* does not occur. In the case of *devayateḥ* > *dyūḥ*, the result is established under both views.

When an elision (*luk*) occurs, it is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. For example, the fruit that is a modification of *āmalakī* is formed with the suffix *mayaṭ* according to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after bases ending in long vowels, *śara*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.143). Then, by the rule "there is elision of [the suffix] when there is elision of a *taddhita*" (Pāṇini 1.2.49), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is elided; this elision, being caused by the subsequent *luk*, does not act as a *sthānivadbhūta* in the case of the elision of the *y* in *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Some, however, explain that for this purpose, the vowel *ī* is inserted into the sūtra as *vara-ī-vare*, meaning that it is not *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the application of the suffix *ī*. Furthermore, it is not *sthānivadbhūta* when the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*) is to be established.

When the suffix *ṇika* is applied to the word *parikhā* in the four senses (*cāturarthika*), one obtains *pārikhīya* (meaning "situated near a moat"). In this case, the suffix *cha* would not apply by the rule *vṛddhādakekāntakhopadhāt*, because the elision of the vowel *ā* is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), and thus the letter *kha* is no longer in the penultimate position (*anupadhā*). This [restriction] pertains specifically to the domain of suffix application; that is to say, it applies only where a suffix is intended to be prescribed based on the technical designation *upadhā*. However, in cases such as *ghaṭayati*, this does not occur.

When a short vowel follows *caṅ*, it does not behave like its original substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). For example, in *avīvadat vīṇāṃ parivādakena* ("he caused the lute-player to play the lute"), the *ṇi* that was elided after the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would, by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, prevent the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) in the *caṅ* form; however, the *ṇi* that follows *caṅ* is not part of the stem (*aṅga*), and that which constitutes the penultimate of the stem does not follow *caṅ*. Regarding the substitution of *k* for *s* (known as *kutva*): from *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"), with the suffix *ktic*, we get *pāktiḥ*. The mention of *kutva* is merely illustrative. Other examples include *leḍhiḥ* from *lehayati* ("he causes to lick"), *dogdhiḥ* from *dohayati* ("he causes to milk"), *yāktiḥ* from *yācayati* ("he causes to beg"), and *veṣṭiḥ* from *veśayati* ("he causes to enter"), and so forth.
When a vowel follows, the reduplication [of a verbal root] is treated as a single substitute for both occurrences.

In the rule *acaḥ parasmin*, it is established that "that which precedes a vowel not subject to grammatical instruction [is the substitute]. Since reduplication applies to the entire [stem] including the consonant (*sāckasya*) and not merely to what precedes the vowel, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) would otherwise not apply; therefore, this status is prescribed for the purpose of extending the formal identity (*rūpātideśa*).

In this regard, six alternative views (pakṣas) are possible. The first view is as follows: "aci" is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the substitute (ādeśa), and "dvirvacane" is a specification of the domain (viṣayanirdeśa). Thus, the meaning is: "Whatever substitute for a vowel (aj-ādeśa) occurs in place of a vowel, that behaves as the original (sthānivad) when reduplication (dvirvacana) is to take place. The second view is as follows: the term "aci" is also connected specifically with the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) itself, because "dvirvacane" specifies the domain. Therefore, the meaning is: "When reduplication is to be performed, a substitute for a vowel behaves as the original provided that a vowel follows [the reduplicated element]."

The first [interpretation] is that because it is the cause of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the vowel (*ac*) itself is qualified by the mention of "reduplication," either by means of the suffix *aś* (forming *dvirvacana*) in the sense of "that in which reduplication exists," or by means of an abstract locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*); thus, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is indicated, and the third [view] is: "That substitute of a vowel which occurs when a vowel is the cause of reduplication is like the original (*sthānivat*). The fourth [view] is that the mention of the vowel (*ajgrahaṇa*), thus qualified, serves as a qualification for the status of being *sthānivat*: "A substitute of a vowel becomes like the original when a vowel is subsequent and is the cause of reduplication."

The mention of "doubling" (dvirvacana) recurs; therein, it is qualified by one [term] and the scope is indicated by the other. This being established, that mention of *aj* as thus qualified is a specification for the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*. Thus, the fifth interpretation: when doubling is to be performed, a substitute (*ādeśa*) for an *ac* vowel is treated as the original (*sthānivat*) when an *ac* vowel that causes doubling follows. This being established in exactly the same way, the mention of *aj* is an indicator for the substitute (*ādeśa*). Thus, the sixth interpretation: whatever substitute for an *ac* vowel occurs when an *ac* vowel that causes doubling follows, that substitute is treated as the original when doubling is to be performed.

In this regard, according to the first view, since the vowel (*ac*) is not specifically qualified by the condition of being a cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitute (*ādeśa*) would behave as if it were the original (*sthānivat*) even when the vowel is the cause of reduplication. Consequently, in the case of *acikīrtat*—where there is the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) due to the suffix *ṇic*, followed by reduplication due to the suffix *caṅ*—the result would be *acakīrtat* because of the *sthānivadbhāva*. Similarly, in *dudyūṣati*, the *yaṇ* substitution [of *u* for *v*] following the *ūṭh* augment would also behave as if it were the original.

If one desires the form *bhavanīyati* (derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *san*), then in *bibhavanīyiṣati*—where the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions have been applied—the undesirable form *bubhavanīyiṣati* would result due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. However, in the second case (*dvitīye*), there is no fault in *acikīrtat*, because the *it* (the *i*) is separated from the *t* by the letter *k*; for at the time of prescribing the *sthānivadbhāva* for the substitute, the substitute must be treated as the original (*sthānivattvena*) when an *ac* vowel follows immediately.

For in this way, the status of being a *sthānin* (original substitute) is established only when an *ac* vowel follows. However, in cases such as *dudyūṣati*, it would indeed apply. In the case of *yayau*, once the *vṛddhi* has been effected by the rule "āta au ṇalaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.1.34], there is no longer an *ac* vowel following the substitute; thus, the status of being a *sthānin* would not apply. Furthermore, in cases such as *jagmuḥ*, because the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) governed by "gamahana... [Pāṇini 6.4.98] is separated [by the augment], the status of being a *sthānin* would not apply.

In the third [alternative], however, a restriction of time must be made; otherwise, even after reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the form of the original element (*sthānin*) would persist. In the fourth [alternative], in forms such as *yayau* and *jagmuḥ*, the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not apply according to the previously stated logic, and a restriction of time must also be made. In the fifth [alternative] as well, it would not occur in *yayau*, *jagmuḥ*, and so on; therefore, since such faults are possible in these alternatives, he states—relying on the sixth alternative—the words beginning with "on account of that which causes reduplication" (*dvirvacananimitte 'ci*).

For in this view, because the vowel (*ac*) is qualified by the term "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*), there is no fault in forms such as *acicīrtat*, *dudyūṣati*, and *bibhavanīyiṣati*. Furthermore, since [the term] serves as an indicator for the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is also no fault in forms such as *yayau*. Moreover, by the repeated mention of "reduplication," the determination of time (*kālāvadhāraṇa*) is also obtained.

Now, an objection might be raised: if it were stated that "an *aj*-substitute [is not *sthānivat*] when there is an occasion for reduplication," then in forms such as *nunāvayiṣati*, *cakṣāvayiṣati*, and *pusphārayiṣati*, since the *ṇi*-affix is not the cause of reduplication, the substitute *ā* (for the original *a*) would not be *sthānivat*; consequently, the vowel *u* in the reduplicated syllable would not be heard. This is not a fault, because by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *puyaṇji* (Pāṇini 7.4.80), the status of being *sthānivat* is removed even in the case of a *ṇi*-affix that is the cause of reduplication.

For instance: without the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution) for what was done in the causative (*ṇi*), it is not possible for *oḥ* (the vowels *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*) to be followed by *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *ja* when followed by an *a*-vowel. If it is argued that this possibility exists in cases such as *pipaviṣati* and *yiyaviṣati*, does this much suffice to make the mention of *pu*, the mention of the *pratyāhāra* [yaṇ], and the mention of *ja* meaningful? If this is so, then there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the stated point. [Objection: In the case of *acikīrtat*, because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the short *i* (from *kīrti*), one would get *acakīrtat*; this is not a fault.

Because an indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends upon that which is of the same class, it indicates the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) only in those cases where the first sound of the subsequent portion is a vowel (*avarṇa*) followed by something else. [Objection: Even so, in the rule *oḥ puyaṇ* (P. 7.4.80), since the word *ṇeḥ* is not heard there, the status of being a substitute would be understood in a general sense as the cause for doubling; consequently, this would also apply in *vibhavanīyiṣati*. For here, it is not merely a vowel (*aj*) that is the cause for doubling. Where, then, would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *cakāra* and *cakre*, for in these instances, the suffix consists of a mere vowel (*aj*).

It might be argued as follows: the term *para* (in the sūtra *pareśca*) is qualified by the term *aci* (from the preceding rule); therein, according to the principle that "when a rule applies to something, it applies to that [element] and its initial," the rule applies to the beginning of that element. Thus, since the condition is "when a vowel (*ac*) beginning with *a* (*aj-ādi*) follows," the vowel itself is qualified as the cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Even so, this would apply in the case of *cakratuḥ*, because that which begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) is the cause for reduplication, whereas that is not the cause for the substitution (*ādeśa*); for the *yaṇ* substitution is prescribed only when a vowel (*ac*) follows. Furthermore, that which is the cause for the substitution is not the cause for the reduplication.

In cases such as *papataḥ* and *cakhnatuḥ*, [the rule] would indeed apply. Furthermore, according to the statement "where a prescription [is made]," the rule regarding the beginning of that [element] (*tadādividhi*) applies only where something is being prescribed; however, here, because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*)—"an *ac*-substitute for an *ac"—the application of the rule regarding the beginning of that [element] is impossible, and therefore only the *ac* itself is understood, not the beginning of that [element]. This is said in reply:

In examples such as *cakratuḥ*, although the suffix *atus* is relied upon as the cause for reduplication (*dvirvacana*), reduplication is observed when an *ac* vowel follows; therefore, it is stated that the *ac* alone is the cause of reduplication. This term "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*) is applied even to the entire complex [of the suffix] by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Even so, [one might argue] it would not apply in *papatuḥ*, because the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) has as its cause not merely an *ac* vowel, but [the specific sequence] beginning with an *ac*. This is not a fault; for what is the meaning of the rule "an *ādeśa* which occurs in place of an *ac* when an *ac* follows"? It means: "that which is seen [to occur] when an *ac* follows."

That which is prescribed when *ac* follows, and that which occurs when it begins with *ac*—both are indeed observed only when *ac* follows; thus, it is established in all cases. Alternatively, the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) occurs when [the suffix] begins with *ac*, not when it begins with a consonant (*hal*); therefore, by distinguishing between what is applicable and what is not, the *ac* itself is the cause. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only reduplication (*dvirvacana*) should be performed," he shows this: the mention of "reduplication" qualifies the *ac* and determines its temporal limit.

For the particle *eva* occurs when one thing is connected to both [conditions], as in: "Let Devadatta go to the village; let him alone bring the cow. If, in this case as well, there were an extension (*atideśa*) of the grammatical operation (*kārya*) as in the previous instance, then in forms such as *cakratuḥ*, although reduplication (*dvirvacana*) would not apply because [the original] lacks a vowel (*anackatva*), it would nevertheless occur through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, since it would apply only to that which is joined with the substitutes *yaṇ* and so forth, the form of the original (*sthānin*) would not be heard in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). To address this, he says: "And this is an extension of form (*rūpātideśaḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

How, then, is it understood that this is a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*)? It is because of the mention of *ac*. For in the rule *taddhi jeghrīyate*, the mention of *ac* is made so that the *itva* (the substitution of *ī*) prescribed for roots beginning with a consonant by the rule *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ* shall not be treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. If, however, it were a transfer of the form itself, then even in the absence of the mention of *ac*, there would be reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in the forms *ghrāy-*, *ghrīy-*, *dhmāy-*, and *dhmīy-*; therefore, the mention of *ac* is meaningful for the purpose of preventing that.

For indeed—the substitute (*sthānin*) is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhavati*). Even though it is treated as the original, since reduplication applies only to that which is joined with the vowel *ī*, there would be no purpose in the mention of *ac* [in the rule]. However, in the case of the suffix *kvasu* after the root *bhas*, once the penultimate vowel elision has been performed by the rule "ghasibhasor hali," there is no difference in the resulting form *abhvasan* whether reduplication occurs or not. Furthermore, the suffix *kvasu* is Vedic, and in the Veda one follows what is actually observed; therefore, the mention of *ac* is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In this regard, although the substitute itself assumes the very form of the original, the suffix *vat*—which relies on the distinction between forms that are extended by analogy (*ātideśika*) and those that are not (*anātideśika*)—must nevertheless be applied only to the reduplication (*dvirvacana*). This is precisely what [the author] clarifies. By the phrase "at a fixed time" (*niyatakāla*), he demonstrates that the time is indeed restricted by the statement "when the reduplication has been performed," and so forth.

If, after reduplication has occurred, only the form of the substitute remains—as in *cakratuḥ* and so forth, where after reduplication the *yaṇ*-substitution previously applied is what is heard—then in cases like *ninyatuḥ* as well, since the [root] consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*) prior to reduplication, once the *yaṅ*-substitute is applied, even during reduplication, only *iyaṅ* would occur by virtue of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Because of the rule "asiddhavadatrābhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), which treats this [substitution] as if it were not yet established, the *yaṇ* substitution [prescribed by] "eranekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.82) will take effect, and thus [the original vowel] will not be heard. Alternatively, even though *iyaṅ* had already applied previously, it is withdrawn at the time of reduplication and must therefore apply again; however, in that state, because the stem has more than one vowel (*anekāctva*), it is superseded by *yaṇ*.

If this were so, then in the case of *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa*—derived from the roots *iṣ* and *uṣ* with the *liṭ* suffix *tip* and the *ṇal* augment—the *guṇa* substitution, though applicable at first, would be superseded at the time of reduplication. Once reduplication has occurred, it would apply again; consequently, since the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is seen to precede a vowel that is not the subject of the original rule, when the *uvaṅ* substitution is to be applied to that reduplicated syllable, the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the *guṇa* would trigger the prohibition "not when there is a dissimilar vowel" (*asavarṇe*). [Objection: By the force of the inclusion of the term "dissimilar" (*asavarṇa*), the *sthānivadbhāva* will not take effect.

There is scope for this statement: *iyarti*, *iyṛtaḥ*. For indeed, a single example necessitates the inclusion of the term "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇe*). If this were the only purpose, one would simply say "in *artti*. Why, then, is it said: "upon reduplication, however, only the form of the substitute remains"? For here, because of the word "again" (*punar*) and the expression "remains" (*avatiṣṭhate*), it is understood that what is stated is merely the re-emergence of the very substitute that was previously applied. This is not the meaning.
Rather, this [sūtra] is intended to mean that once reduplication has occurred, the form of the original locus (sthānin) does not persist; instead, whatever is applicable [by other rules] takes place.

The mention of "elision of *a*" (*allope*) and so forth is merely illustrative. In examples such as *taturiḥ* and *papuriḥ*, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if being the original element) also applies to the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ṝta īd dhātoḥ*, the substitution of *ū* by *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*, and the substitution of *y* by *bahulaṃ chandasi*.

Regarding *āṭiṭat*: from the root *aṭ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ*, the reduplication of the syllable *ṭi* occurs according to the rule "the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāderdvitīyasya*), and *āṭ* is prefixed by "āṭ for roots beginning with a vowel" (*āḍajādīnām*). Regarding *nināya* and so forth: when, according to the rule "the final *ṇal* is optionally treated as *ṇit*," the *ṇit*-status is absent, there is *guṇa*; in the case of the *ṇit*-status, there is *vṛddhi*. As for *nenailolā*, this is the reduplication. However, regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, since there is no difference due to their status as *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original), they have not been mentioned.

In *jagle* and *mamla*, the *liṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). The substitution of *ā* (ātvam) is not conditioned by anything else (*anaimittika*), whereas there is a prohibition when a *śit* suffix follows; thus, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply to the substitution of *ā*. Regarding *śravaṇa* and so forth: if the time [of the operation] were not determined, then even at a later stage the form of the original element (*sthānin*) would still persist. Consequently, when the vowel *a* is heard, the *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule "vṛddhir eci" would occur with the following vowel.

Here, in *adhijage*, because the rule "gāṅ liṭi" prescribes the substitute *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ* when a *liṭ* suffix beginning with the letter *l* follows—by the explicit mention of two *l*s—the *liṭ* suffix is not caused by the vowel *a*; therefore, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply.
Disappearance is elision. 1.1.60.

In this context, "seeing" (*darśana*) means knowledge (*jñāna*) or apprehension (*upalabdhi*). And since this discussion concerns the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), that [knowledge] has sound as its object; thus, it is "hearing" (*śravaṇa*). Therefore, he says "non-hearing" (*aśravaṇa*). Now, hearing is the operation of the hearer; if that were negated, the rule *lopo vyor vali* would mean that the *v* and *y* sounds following a *v*-sound (the *val* sounds) are not to be heard. Consequently, the operation of the speaker—articulation—would remain unrestricted.

He says "non-utterance" (*anuccāraṇam*), meaning that if there were no hearing, utterance would be entirely purposeless; thus, by the prohibition of hearing, the utterance which is its cause is itself prohibited. What is the meaning of the rule "there is elision of *v* and *y* before a semivowel" (*lopo vyor vali*)? It means that the sounds *v* and *y*, when followed by a semivowel (*valpara*), are not to be uttered. By this method as well, their very non-existence in this context is explained, for the non-utterance of things that actually exist is not logically possible; hence he says "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

The meaning is that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Regarding "destruction" (*vināśa*): this refers to the observation of the word for the effect (*kārya-śabda*). Regarding "not a different object" (*anarthāntara*): the meaning is that the referent (*artha*) of these words whose objects are sounds does not differ. Because of the rule stating "its own form" (*svarūpam*), in the case of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for the word *adarśana* in the rules concerning elision (*lopa-pradeśa*), the word *adarśana* itself would be the substitute. Therefore, he says: "by these words. And this is obtained through the continuation of the particle *iti* from the rule "the option is expressed by *na vā*" (*naveti vibhāṣā*).

Alternatively, a technical term (*saṃjñā*) is established so that it may be understood according to its meaning—that *lopa* means "elision" (*lopana*). Furthermore, the word "non-appearance" (*adarśana*) is not itself the act of elision. If this were the case, one might ask: "Let the meaning be grasped directly in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), what is the use of a technical term? That is not correct; for if the technical term were not established, then by the rule "one's own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*), the word *lopaś* itself would be substituted in the specific rules. But when the technical term exists, because of the prohibition "not [for] a word" (*na śabdasya*), there is no grasping of the word's own form. Thus, "not for a word."

Although this is established by the very nature of the matter, it is stated again for the sake of clarity. Now, one might object that in the rules prescribing operations (*vidhipradeśa*), there would arise a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): namely, that the designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to a non-appearance (*adarśana*) that already exists, and by means of that designation, the non-appearance is brought into being. This is not so; for it is not the case that a non-appearance which was previously non-existent is brought into being by the statement of the rule of elision (*lopa*), as that would entail the consequence of [the rule] being non-eternal (*anityatva*). What, then, is the case? It is simply that the non-appearance which already exists is designated as being grammatically correct (*sādhutvena anvākhyāyate*).

If this were so, then since everything is not observed by its own nature anywhere other than its own object, it would have the designation *lopa* (elision). Consequently, in the case of *dadhi* and *madhu*, where there is the non-observation of the suffix *ṇic*, the designation *lopa* would apply, and by the rule of "characterized by the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there would be *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* of the base (*aṅga*) and the designation *aṅga* itself are dependent upon the specific grammatical prescription. In that case, when there is the designation *lopa* for the non-observation of the suffix *kvip*, the augment *tuk* would result; to this he replies: "of that which was applicable" (*prasaktasya*). He thinks as follows: the word "in place of" (*sthāne*) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

And "occasion" (*prasaṅga*) refers to the context; therefore, that which is not seen when such an occasion exists is designated as *lopa* (elision). Now, in the case of *dadhī*, there is no occasion for the suffix *kvip* by anything whatsoever. Even so, in the case of *grāmaṇīḥ*, because of the proximity of the agent of the *karmadhāraya* compound, there is an occasion for the suffix *aṇ*; thus, if the non-appearance of that [suffix] were designated as *lopa*, the *vṛddhi* [substitution] would occur. However, whatever occasion there is here for *aṇ*, it is set aside by *kvip*. For a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*), in the presence of a specific one (*viśeṣa*), produces its application only in a domain distinct from that [specific one].
Therefore, in the proximity of the rule "asatsūdviṣa," the cognition that "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the root *nī* when [it has] an object" (Pāṇini 3.2.1) is simply not produced.
The suffixes *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* are substitutes for an affix (*pratyaya*).

Because of the connection with the word "non-appearance" (*adarśanam*), the genitive case in "of the suffix" (*pratyayasya*) is used in the sense of the object (*karma*). If there were a confusion of technical names such as *luk* and others regarding the non-appearance of a suffix, then at the time of its prescription, any non-appearance of a suffix—regardless of which name had been assigned to it—would result in being included even when any arbitrary name is uttered in subsequent rules that refer back to it. Consequently, in the rule "in the case of *ślau*" (*ślau*), the non-appearance of the *śap* suffix—which, although assigned the name *luk* by the rule "it is elided" (*attīti luk*)—would be included, and thus reduplication would occur.

In the case of *juhoti*, there would be the application of vṛddhi by the rule "vṛddhir luki hali"; in the case of *harītakyāḥ phalāni*, there would be the elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule "luk taddhitaluki"; and in the case of *lavaṇāt luk* as in *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ*, there would be the treatment as the base itself (*yuktavadbhāva*). Furthermore, even for that which has been subjected to the designation *lopa*, if it were also subject to the designation *luk*, then in the case of *gomatībhūtā brāhmaṇī*—where the suffix *cvi* is elided—the suffix *luk* would apply by the rule "luk taddhitaluki. Therefore, he says: "Because multiple designations are prescribed," and so forth.

If these designations were to apply even to that which has not been brought about by them, then the formulation of multiple designations would be purposeless; for one could simply have made a single designation and performed all the grammatical operations by means of that alone! Therefore, because multiple designations are prescribed, whichever disappearance occurs by whichever designation, that [designation] belongs to that [specific disappearance] alone; thus, there is no confusion among the designations. If this is so, then in the application of the rules, a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would result; and in this case, a resolution through the doctrine of eternality (*nityatā*) is not possible.

For non-appearance (*adarśana*) is indeed eternal; it is not, however, something produced by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) such as *luk* and so forth. In that regard, if that designation were applied to a non-appearance already produced by that very designation, there would clearly be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To this he replies: "And in the case of the rules for positive injunctions (*vidhipradeśa*). Since the designation *luk* will apply to that which is yet to be (future) after the suffix *śap* following roots such as *ad* and others, there is no fault of mutual dependence because the designation is understood as one that is to come into being (*bhāvinī*).

Since the designation *lop* (elision) is prescribed merely as a perception [of the absence of an element], it certainly occurs even in the domain of designations such as *lug* (deletion), and so forth. Nor is there any sublation by the designations *lug* and the rest; for, apart from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*), designations coexist. Precisely for this reason, there is the prohibition: "When [an affix] marked with *lu* elides, [the substitution of *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* does not take place] for the *aṅga*. In the case of *varaṇāḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *adūrabhavaśca* ("and [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] to denote what is situated near"), and then its *lup* elision is applied by the rule *varaṇādibhyaśca*.

What is the purpose of including the term *pratyaya* (suffix) [in the definition]? It is certainly not for the sake of excluding non-suffixes (*apratyaya*), because in all instances—such as *lug*, *aṇiñoḥ*, *tadrājasya yañañośca*, *śapaḥ*, *yaṅaḥ*, *sicaḥ*, *leḥ*, and *supaḥ*—only a suffix is specifically indicated. Furthermore, in cases of restatement (*anuvāda*), that which has been transformed into a suffix is precisely what is understood. In the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*, the connection is divided: first, "of *go* when it is an *upasarjana*, and of a feminine [stem]"; then, "there is elision (*luk*) when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is elided," where only "of a feminine" remains, and "*go*" is removed.

Otherwise, even if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were included [in the rule], there would still be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ḍa* after the root *gam*; for in the rule "the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are applied to *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, and there is elision," since the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "feminine suffixes ending in *ṅī* or *āp* and nominal stems" (*ṅyāpprātipadika*) is in force, the elision will be understood as applying to the portion following the nominal stem *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, and not to the original base (*prakṛti*) portion.

Even if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were not included [in the rule], there would still be the elision (*luk*) of the phonemes *u* and *s* in cases such as *kaṃsaḥ* from the root *kam-* (where *sa* is a suffix), and *paraśuḥ* from *parā-śṛṇāti* (where *śu* is a suffix). Therefore, the inclusion of *pratyaya* need not be made for the purpose of excluding non-suffixes. But what about where nothing is specifically indicated, such as in the rule "from Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, and Aṅgiras"? In that case, the inclusion of *pratyaya* will be for the purpose of understanding it as a suffix? Not so.

In that case as well, because the term *gotra* (lineage) is understood to carry over from the rule "from *yaska* and others, when [the suffix denotes] lineage" (*yaskādibhyo gotre*), there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix which is prescribed after *atri* and others when denoting lineage; likewise, in the rule "elision (*lup*) in the sense of a country" (*janapade lup*), because the phrase "a suffix after a nominal stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*) carries over, there is elision only of the suffix having fourfold meanings (*cāturarthika*) prescribed in the sense of a country. Furthermore, even in rules such as "elision after *lavaṇa*" (*lavaṇālluk*), since the context is already established, it is not necessary to explicitly state the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) for the sake of understanding.

Furthermore, since the rule "after a nominal stem ending in *lavaṇa*, following *atrya* and others" occurs within the governing context of the fifth case (*pañcamyadhikāra*), it will supply a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the immediately preceding element; and because that connection is not restricted to a specific relation, it will be a locative sixth case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, even for the purpose of understanding this as a locative sixth case, the mention of the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) need not be made.

In that case, the mention of "affix" (pratyaya) is for the purpose of indicating that the replacement applies to the whole [of the original element]; for if that were absent, in rules such as *yañañośca* and *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, where an affix consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the substitution would apply only to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*), whereas in rules such as *lavaṇālluk*, it would instead apply to the initial letter (*ādeḥ*).

But if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is included [in the rule], then by its force, elision (*luk*) and the others become replacements for the whole. This is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*): since, while elision (*lopa*) was already applicable by the rule "there is optionally elision of *ghu* in the *leṭ*," the author teaches elision (*luk*) in the rule "optionally *luk* in *duh*, *diha*, etc.," that indicates: "elision (*luk*) and the others are replacements for the whole. For otherwise, the disappearance of the final letter would already be established by the elision (*lopa*) under discussion in the rule "the disappearance of the final [element]."

The opposite, however, does not occur; for in the rule "ghorlopaḥ" (P. 6.4.100), because there is no conflict at that stage, the rule "alo'ntyasya" (P. 1.1.52) applies first. Subsequently, the mention of *lug* indicates that this [elision] is a substitute for the whole. Furthermore, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) will be established in a general sense: "an absence other than *lopa* is a substitute for the whole. Therefore, the question is: the mention of *pratyaya* (suffix) need not even be made for the sake of making it a substitute for the whole.

The other [author], having understood the intention, offers a rebuttal: "The Āgastyas and Kauṇḍinyas. If the term *pratyayagrahaṇa* ("mention of an affix") were not present, would the mention of *luk* from the rule *lugaṇiñoḥ* be understood to carry over into the rule *āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ*, or not?

In the case of the application [of the rule], there are two substituends and three substitutes including *luk*; thus, due to this inequality, since there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*), all three substitutes would apply to each single substituend in turn. Consequently, the *agastis* would also be the *kuṇḍinas*, and the *kuṇḍinas* would also be the *agastis*. Furthermore, if *luk* were made a total substitute (*sarvādeśa*) based on an inferential indicator (*jñāpaka*), then in both cases there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing only the case-ending.

Now, [the objection] has been refuted: therefore, there is no fault in the forms *agastayaḥ* and *kauṇḍinyaḥ*. However, in the case of *āgastīyāḥ*—meaning "pupils of the Agastis"—even though a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended, the suffix *cha* would not apply because the substitution of *agasti-* for [the base *agastya-*] has not been prescribed as mandatory (*nitya*), and thus the base remains non-vṛddha. But when the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is included [in the rule], by the continued application of the mention of "elision" (*luk*), the portion consisting of the suffix of *agastya* and *kauṇḍinya* does not undergo elision.

The meaning is that, respectively, Agasti and Kuṇḍina [are the original forms] for the two remaining portions. By this, *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ* are established. Furthermore, when a suffix belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *gotre lugaci* is prohibited; consequently, because it is taught as being conditioned by that [elision], the substitute *agastya-* also ceases to apply. Then, since the word *āgastya-* is a *vṛddha* [stem], when the secondary suffix (*cha*) is applied, the *ya* is dropped by the rule *sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām ya upadhāyāḥ*, resulting in the form *āgastīyāḥ*.

Furthermore, there is no distinction [between the two forms] regarding Kauṇḍinya; even when the substitute *kuṇḍinaja-* has been replaced, if the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *kauṇḍinya* by the rule "from Kaṇva and others, in the sense of a lineage" (*kaṇvādibhyo gotre*), and the *y* is elided by the rule "of the secondary derivative" (*āpatyasya*), the form must necessarily be *kauṇḍināḥ*. Therefore, in the rule "of Āgastya and Kauṇḍinya" (*āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ*), the mention of *luk* (elision) must necessarily be carried over. Consequently, in order to avoid the aforementioned fault, the mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*) must also be made. However, we say: "The mention of the suffix, even for the sake of making it a universal substitute, is a general indicator (*jñāpaka*)—the last resort for one who has no other way."
When an affix is elided, the operation conditioned by that affix still takes place. (Pāṇini 1.1.62)

He states the purpose for the commencement of the Sūtra: "for the sake of the appearance of the suffix," and so forth. This word *lakṣaṇa* is used as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) signifying manifestation, and it is also used as an instrumental noun (*karaṇasādhana*) signifying cause. If the first sense were taken, the meaning would be: "when there is the elision of a suffix, the manifestation of that suffix occurs. In that case, if one were to enjoin the re-manifestation of a suffix that has already been elided, the rule for its elision would be rendered useless.

Now, let it be granted that rules such as *aṇer aniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), which prescribe the elision of a suffix itself, may indeed be considered redundant; however, what about the elision prescribed generally by rules such as *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143)? When that elision applies to a suffix—as in *bhikṣayatī* from *bhikṣum ācaṣṭe*—then even though that [suffix] reappears, its [original rule] is not rendered useless, because it has already served its purpose in the formation of the *upapada* suffix (*u*).

If this is so, then one must state that it is the reappearance of a suffix that was previously elided which is intended, rather than saying that there is no elision of the suffix; for the general rule of elision does not apply to the suffix in this case.

Now, if the appearance of another suffix, caused by the elision of a previous suffix, is being prescribed—as in *grāmaṇīḥ*, where, upon the elision of *kvip*, the suffix *su* caused by that [elision] is prescribed—even so, one should simply say: "When a suffix is elided, the suffix [itself] [is considered present]. Thus, by means of the word *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) as a synonym for *nimitta* (cause), a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed, and the resulting effect (*kārya*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, he says: "the effect caused by a suffix."
And due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning is that even when the cause of a particular grammatical operation is elided, that operation still takes place.

"The designation *pada* occurs. But surely the designation *pada* is already established even by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). If that is so, consider this case: *tā tā piṇaḍānām*. Here, after the word *tat*, the suffix *jas* becomes *śi*; then, by the rule "the *śi* [is applied] diversely in the Veda," there is elision (*lopa*); then, by the rule "of a neuter [stem] ending in a consonant or *ac*," the augment *num* is added; and by the rule "in the place of a nominal stem" (*sarvanāmasthāne*), lengthening occurs. In *anaḍvān*, when the nominative suffix *su* is elided, *num* occurs. In *adhok*, the augment *aṭ* and *guṇa* occur. In *nyamārṭ*, by the rule "vṛddhi for *mṛj*" [there is vṛddhi]. In *undat*, in the *laṅ* tense, after the elision of *ti*, the augments *śnam* and *āṭ* occur.

Regarding the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.23): [the form] *auṇat*; and in *agnicit*, when the *kvip* suffix is elided, does *tug* (the augment *t*) occur? These cases are also established solely by means of the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is because they are not operations dependent on an *al* (phoneme). For everywhere, an *al* is simply a suffix (*pratyaya*), and an operation based upon that is called an *al-vidhi*. This is not well stated, for it has been said that the status of being an *al-vidhi* depends on the specific grammatical operation (*kārya*) in question, not on the specific example (*udāharaṇa*).

And in all the rules of the grammatical treatise concerning *num* and so forth—such as [the rules for] a *sarvanāmasthāna*, a *sārvadhātuka*, a *pit* affix, a *kṛt* affix, and that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix—that form which is relied upon is common to both what possesses an *al* (vowel) and what does not; it is merely that in examples such as *tātā piṇḍānām*, by virtue of the meaning, that [form] consists of an *al*.

In this case, then, consider the form *atṛṇeṭ*: from the root *tṛh* in the sense of "injury," with the suffix *laṅ*, the suffix *tip*, and the augment *śnam*; by the rule *itaśca*, there is the elision of the *i* [of *śnam*]; and the substitution of *al* (the *ṇ* of *tṛṇah*) prescribed for a *pit* sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant after the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* [suffix] occurs here from *tṛṇahai*. Likewise, in the form *āśīḥ*, the substitution of *ī* [for the *śā* of *śās*] by the rule *śāsa īdaṅhaloḥ* occurs even though the *kvip* suffix has been elided. But is it not the case that "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the status of being as if a suffix were present) when the operation depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*)"? No, there is no such statement.

The purpose of this second mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is stated as follows: since the result would already be established here by the rule *pratyayalope tallakṣaṇam* ("when a suffix is elided, that which was conditioned by it [still applies]"), the repeated mention of *pratyaya* ensures that the rule applies only where the unique form of the suffix itself is relied upon as the cause—such as in the cases *supi*, *sārvadhātuke*, *kṛti*, and *suptiṅantam*. By this, the substitution of *ava* for *avaṅ* does not occur in the word *gohitam*.

For in the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*, no specific form of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned; rather, what is mentioned is *aci* (in a vowel), which—by implication in the example *gave hitam*—is merely of the nature of a suffix. However, in the case of the augment *it* and the substitution of *ī*, the suffix itself is the primary cause, as they apply when there is a *kṅit* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) or a *pit* *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant; the consonant (*hal*) is merely its qualifier. Therefore, these two [rules] do not depend on the phoneme (*varṇa*). Consequently, this [treatment of *al*] must be undertaken for the sake of rules concerning phonemes (*al-vidhi*).

If this is so, there is a fault regarding the technical term *bha*, as well as the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the suffix *ṣph*. First, with respect to the term *bha*: in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) becoming *rājapuruṣaḥ*, just as the designation *bha* occurs when the suffix is heard, it would likewise occur when it is elided. Consequently, because the designation *pada* would be sublated by that [designation *bha*], the elision of the *l* (in *rājñ-l-ṅas*) would not take place. But surely there are two designations of *pada* here: namely, "a word ending in a *svādi* [suffix]" and "that which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ*. Among these, the designation *pada* defined as "a word ending in a *svādi* suffix" is sublated by the [designation *bha*] which serves as its exception.

As for the technical designation *pada* defined as "that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*"), it should not be annulled—just as, for example, when a suffix is heard, the entire aggregate [such as] *rājñaḥ* [is called a *pada*]? This is not so; for when a suffix is heard, the preceding portion receives the designation *bha*, whereas the aggregate ending in *visarjanīya* receives the designation *pada*. Thus, it is logical that the *pada*-designation is not annulled by the *bha*-designation, as their respective scopes (*avadhi*) are distinct.

When the suffix (*pratyaya*) has been elided, the designation "word" (*pada*) applies to that very limit (*avadhi*) which [was previously defined] by the rule "that which ends in *svādi* is a word," as well as to that same limit which [is defined by] the rule "a word ending in a *sub* [suffix] is a word. In that very same limit, the designation "base" (*bha*) occurs; and just as it subverts the designation "word" characterized by *svādi* because it is subsequent, so too does it subvert the designation "word" characterized by ending in a *sub*, due to its higher status.

In that case, due to the prohibition "na lumatāṅgasya," the designation *bha* will not apply; for the rule *yaci* specifies a locative (*saptamī*) construction. Consequently, although the designation *bha* actually applies to this preceding portion, it is nonetheless merely an operation pertaining to the *aṅga*.

Having understood this, [one sees that] in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*, the elision of *n* is prohibited in the locative singular (*ṅi*). If the designation *bha* were to apply here by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix), then in the example *ardre carmann*, the elision of *n* would not occur simply because of the status of the exception (*apavāda*); so what would be the purpose of that prohibition? In this case, however, consider the word *citrā* derived from the sense "born under Citrā. After the *luk*-elision of the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *citrārevatīrohiṇībhyaḥ striyām upasaṃkhyānam*, and after the *ṭāp* suffix is elided by *luktaddhitaluki*, the form *citrā* remains. Here, by the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, since it ends in *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīp* would have to apply.

[If it is argued that] this [suffix] would apply, there is no such fault; for in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the term *ataḥ* (of *at*) is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*), and therein the vowel *a* of the suffix *aṇ* is qualified—as "the *a* of *aṇ*"—and thus the vowel *a* alone is the cause for the suffix *ṅīp*. Since *aṇ* is merely its qualifier, the suffix *ṅīp* does not occur due to the absence of the condition of being a "suffix-characterized" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) element.

In this case, then, from *vataṇḍa* [the patronymic] *vātaṇḍya*, when the suffix *añ* is elided by the rule "elision of *añ* in the feminine" (*luk striyām*), the suffix *ṅīn*—which would otherwise apply by the rule defining the *śārṅgarava* group—is superseded. Consequently, according to the opinion of the Easterners, because of the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) in the rule "the *ṣpha* suffix is added after [patronymics] of the Easterners in all cases," the *ṣpha* suffix, which applies to bases ending in *yañ*, would result, just as in the case of *āvaṭyā* where *ṣpha* occurs even after overriding the optional *cāp*. Is this not a fault? No, it is not.

Here too, the vowel *a* is qualified as "the *a* of *yañ*"—meaning, "from that which ends in the *a* which is a constituent part of *yañ*. Therefore, even here, the vowel *a* alone is the cause [of the substitution]; however, because it is qualified by *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* does not occur. But then there is this fault regarding the form *parivīḥ*: after the suffix *kvip* has been elided following the root *vī* preceded by *pari*, the semivowel *y* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) and the subsequent position (*pūrvatva*) occurs due to its belonging to the *yajādi* group, whereby the augment *tuk* is required; furthermore, the rule *halaḥ* would require lengthening. In that case, lengthening is desired by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), yet that conflict is not established.

What is the reason? Here, when a suffix is elided (*pratyayalopa*), all operations dependent upon that suffix have already ceased; these are now being reinstated by this [rule]. Thus, the long vowel is produced by this very rule, as is the *tuk* augment—therefore, since they share the same defining characteristic (*ekayogalakṣaṇa*), is it not improper to posit a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between them? This is not a fault; for when a suffix is present, whatever operation is occasioned by it certainly takes place, and it is precisely that which is reinstated by this rule once the suffix has been elided, but not merely whatever was applicable [at the time of its presence].

When an affix such as *parivīya* is heard, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) alone occurs by virtue of its subsequent position, and not the *tuk* augment; therefore, even in this case, if *kvip* alone had been applied, only the long vowel would have occurred. Thus, it is precisely that [augment] which is brought forth by this rule. Consequently, it is established that the sūtra must indeed be commenced, as there is no fault whatsoever.

To this it is replied: As for what was said—that because [the rule] "tṛṇaha im" depends on the term *hal*, it does not depend on *hal*—this is not dependent on *hal*, for the word *halī* will be withdrawn. If it is withdrawn, would [the augment *im*] not also apply here in the case of *tṛṇahāni*? No, because from the rule "nābhyastasyāci," the phrase "not before a vowel" (*nāci*) is carried over; therefore, since it is not a rule concerning an *al*-substitute, the augment *im* is established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original). In the case of *āśīḥ* as well, the presence of *it* is established by the statement: "The addition of *kvip* to the root *ās* [is prescribed] in the sense of the benediction (*āśis*). Even if this [rule *tṛṇaha im*] were indeed commenced, that [exception] must necessarily be stated.

If, first of all, in the rule "śāsa idaṅ-haloḥ" there is the inclusion of *śās* in its entirety, then this [subsequent rule] is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "Let [the substitution of *ī*] occur only after *śās* when followed by *kvip*, so that it does not occur in forms such as *āśāste*. On the other hand, if there is the inclusion of only that *śās* after which *aṅ* is prescribed, then, just as it does not occur in *āśāste* and so on, it would likewise not occur after *kvip*; therefore, in that case, this rule is for the sake of a positive injunction (*vidhyartha*).

In this case, then, consider the many descendants of Bida. From the rule *bidādibhyo 'ñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.104], we have *bidāḥ*. Then, for the young descendant (*yuvan*) of the Bidas, the rule *ata iñ* [4.1.95] applies, yielding *baida-i-*. When the elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañitaḥ* [2.4.58], the elision of the *añ* suffix—which had been produced because of the plurality of the lineage (*gotra*)—is sought to be prohibited by the rule *agotre 'lug aci* [4.1.89]. Would that [prohibition] occur even when the suffix has already been elided by the rule *ajādau* [4.1.4]? This too is not a valid purpose.

The locative case here is one of "domain" (*viṣayasaptamī*); therefore, when *gotra* is intended [as the domain], the elision (*luk*) is prohibited while it is still unproduced, and subsequently the elision of *iñ* occurs—thus the desired result is established. Consequently, since this is accomplished through the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) upon seeing some operation that does not involve an *al* (suffix), there is no purpose for this [rule].

In that case, this [rule] is for the sake of restriction: "When a suffix is elided, let there be only that which is characterized by the suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa), and not that which is characterized by what is not a suffix (pratyayāpratyayalakṣaṇa). What is meant is this: when an operation is prescribed, if it depends upon some unique form of the suffix itself as its cause, that operation indeed takes place even when the suffix is elided; however, that which is prescribed depending on a form common to both suffixes and non-suffixes does not.

In the word *sudṛṣat* (one who has beautiful stones), the rule "the first syllable of the second member is udātta when preceded by *su*, *manas*, or *aloma-uṣas*" does not apply. Otherwise, even though the nominative plural suffix (*jas*) has been elided, there would be the contingency [of applying that rule] because the second member would still be considered as ending in *-as* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle. However, this is not the case under the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle, because of the statement: "The mention of *ani*, *an*, *as*, and *man* causes the application of the rule for what ends in those elements, whether they are meaningful or meaningless," and thus that [suffix] is specifically included in the mention.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, considering that "this [rule] also serves a restrictive purpose and applies everywhere when a suffix is elided," stated that the designation *pada* occurs. Regarding *āghnaya*: [it is derived from] *āṅo yamahanaḥ*.
