Regarding *saṃgmīya*: the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by *samo gamyacchi*; there is the elision of *śap* by *iṭo't* and *bahulaṃ chandasi*; and in both cases, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel by *gamahana*.
A substitute does not take the place of an entire element when it is preceded by *l*. Pāṇini 1.1.63.

Regarding the term *lumatā*: that which contains the word *lu* is *lumān*, such as *lug* and other [technical terms]. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), and the status of being an instrument applies to the elision (*lopa*). Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "when there is elision of an affix" (*pratyayalope*), when there is elision of an affix by means of a word containing *lu*, the operation conditioned by the affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not take place for the stem (*aṅga*). In this context, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning is that the operation caused by that [affix] does not occur for that stem which had acquired the designation of a stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) in relation to the elided affix.

This very point is demonstrated in reality by the statement: "When a suffix is elided by *lu*, that which is the *aṅga* [is defined relative to the original suffix]. Therefore, in the case of *utkrāma*, once the elision (*luk*) has been applied by the rule "*ato heḥ*" (*Pāṇini 6.4.105*), the form ending in the root *kram* is not the *aṅga* with respect to the *parasmaipada* suffix; and that which possesses the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is not the *aṅga* with respect to the *parasmaipada* suffix.

What then? Since there is no prohibition with respect to the *śap* [suffix], the long vowel occurs by the rule "the root-vowel is lengthened before *parasmaipada* endings" (*kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*). Likewise, the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ*—namely, "there is *iṭ* after the roots beginning with *gam* in *parasmaipada* endings" and "not after the four roots beginning with *vṛt*"—apply to forms such as *jigamiṣa* and *vivṛtsa*, even when the *parasmaipada* ending is elided. When the *parasmaipada* is elided by a *lumat* suffix, the prescription and prohibition of *iṭ* do not apply to that base (*aṅga*) which ends in *san*; rather, they apply to the suffix beginning with *s*.

Furthermore, another point is demonstrated in this treatise: by the phrase "not of the *aṅga*," the governing rule regarding the *aṅga* (the stem) is not being referred to in the sense that "when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, it remains an *aṅga*"; rather, when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, everything—both that which is an *aṅga* and that which is not an *aṅga* belonging to that [suffix]—is prohibited.

From that [base], *gargāḥ* and *bidāḥ* are formed by the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*. In *uṣṭragrīvaḥ*, the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of a likeness" (*iva pratikṛtau*), and its elision (*lup*) occurs according to the rule "after *devapatha* and so forth. In *pathipriyaḥ*—meaning "one for whom the path is dear"—the elision of the case-ending (*sup*) occurs according to the rule "before a verbal root or a nominal-stem-suffix" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*). Here, there is a prohibition of the acute accent on the initial syllable, even though it does not belong to the stem (*an-aṅgasya*), by the rules "that which begins with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [acute]" and "for *pathi* and *mathi* before a nominal-stem-suffix" (*sarvanāmasthāne*). For, due to the mention of the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśāt*), this is in fact an operation pertaining to the stem (*aṅgasya*).

Likewise, in the case of *ahardadāti*, the prohibition of *ru*-substitution by the rule "roḥ supi" does not apply. If [the substitution] were prohibited even when it is not part of the *aṅga* (stem), then in the examples *avadhi bhavatā dasyuḥ*, *āgāyi bhavatā grāmaḥ*, and *adhyagāyi bhavatā'nuvākaḥ*, the substitutes for the roots *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅi*—which are prescribed for the *aṅga* when followed by the *luṅ* suffix—would not occur when that *luṅ* is elided by the rule "ciṇo luk". [Objection: The substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅi* are not prescribed specifically for the *luṅ* suffix; rather, they are prescribed for that *ārdhadhātuka* element which occurs within the *luṅ*.

Furthermore, in the case of the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix, that which is the *aṅga* (stem) ending in *ciṇ* does not undergo the substitutions of *han*, *iṇ*, *ṅ*, and so forth; and that for which those substitutions do apply is not the *aṅga* when the *luṅ* suffix is elided (*luk*). Thus, there is no prohibition [of the rule]. In this case, however, in the example "mā hi dātāṃ sarpirāgacchet" (let not the clarified butter come), when the *sij* and the vocative (*āmantrita*) are elided, would the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*)—prescribed by the rule "the first syllable of *sic* optionally, and of a vocative"—not fail to occur? This is not a grammatical operation (*kārya*) belonging to the *aṅga* as ending in *ciṇ*; rather, it belongs to that which ends in it (i.e., the whole word). This is because of the mention of the genitive case [in the rule]. Consequently, in cases such as "payaḥ sām," the designation of a "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) will also be established.

Objection: Even though that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix is udātta on its first syllable and receives the designation of a "word" (*pada*), nevertheless, when the suffix is now elided, since it actually belongs to the stem (*aṅga*), shouldn't there be a prohibition [of the accent]? Response: It is not the case here that what applies to the stem when the suffix is elided is prohibited; rather, even while the suffix remains present, whatever operation would apply to the stem preceding it is what is prohibited.

In examples such as *vṛkṣā mā hi lābiṣṭām*, the designation of a word (*pada-saṃjñā*) and its accent apply to that which ends in the suffix even when that suffix has been elided, provided it is heard [in the form of a suffix] in a rule; thus, in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, although the suffix *ṅasi* is heard, the designation *bha* applies to what precedes it and not to what ends in it. Therefore, even when that suffix is elided, the application [of the *bha*-designation] that would have occurred by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) is prohibited by this [rule].

In that case, consider the word *ātreyaḥ*, derived from *atri* with the suffix *ṭhak* by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*, which undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule *atribhṛgu...*. Once the elision is made, the form becomes *ātrayaḥ*. According to the rule *kitaḥ*, the final syllable of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would be udātta, because it is an operation pertaining to that which ends in the suffix. This is not a fault; for the rule prescribes the udātta accent for the secondary derivative itself, not for that which ends in it.

In that case, for a word like *sarvastomaḥ* (meaning "one whose stoma is all-encompassing"), the rule *sarvasya supi*—which prescribes an udātta accent on the first syllable—would not apply, because the rule is formulated with a locative reference (*supi*). An effort must be made here. And this effort is as follows: the rule *sarvasya supaḥ* should be formulated with a genitive reference; for when there is a genitive reference, the operation applies to that which ends in [the element denoted by] the genitive, and thus it is established, just as in the case of the accent of the suffix *sic*. [Objection: But in both these alternative views, the suffix *jus* would apply to forms such as *abhūvan* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle. [Response: It will not apply, because of the restriction [imposed by the rule] *ātaḥ*.

In this case, then, regarding the form *devadattaṃ yājayāñcakāra*: since the suffix *ām* (of the periphrastic perfect) would block the elision (*luk*) [of the *liṭ*], and once the *tiṅ*-substitutes (*tiptasjhi...*) have been applied and subsequently elided, the entire form would still be considered a *tiṅ*-ending by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule; consequently, the elision of the final *ām* would be obstructed, and the subsequent word would not receive the low-pitch accent (*anighāta*). However, because the term *leḥ* is understood as a governing reference (*anuvṛtti*), the elision will occur precisely while the suffix is still in its *l*-state. Furthermore, in the example *devadatto yuṣmatputraḥ*, the substitutes *vām* and *nau* prescribed for the genitive case do not apply here, because of the specific mention of the term *sthā* in the rule *dvitīyāsthayoḥ*.

The application [of the term *pada*] to that which is actually heard is possible only in the case of the sixth, fourth, and second case endings. However, in this instance—such as in *paramavācā*, *paramagauduhā*, *paramalihā*, *paramadaṇḍinā*, and *paramadivāparamakumāryā*—since the designation *pada* would apply to the final member of the compound by virtue of the case ending belonging to the meaning of the compound, the following rules would consequently apply: "the *k* substitution for *c*" (*coḥ kuḥ*), "the *gh* substitution for a root beginning with *d*" (*dāderdhātorghaḥ*), "the *ḍh* substitution for *h*" (*ho ḍhaḥ*), "the elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ pratipadikāntasya*), "the substitution of *u* for *div*" (*diva ut*), and "according to Śākalya, the short vowel and the *y* substitution for *i* and *u* before a dissimilar vowel" (*iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca*). This is not a fault; [for the following reasons:]... [text continues] ...therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, the *pada* designation does not apply to the entire compound, because it is taught that "the *pada* designation applies to the two words [within a compound]" (*samāsasya dvayoḥ padasaṃjñā bhavati*). Consequently, since the *pada* designation does not apply to the first member, the *k* substitution for *c* does not occur. Nor does the *gh* substitution for *d* occur, because the rule "the *gh* substitution for a root beginning with *d*" is qualified by the condition "when followed by a suffix beginning with *t* or *th*" (*tathoḥ*); and since the *t* and *th* here belong to the compound itself, they are not considered suffixes (*pratyaya*) in relation to the word *parama*. Similarly, the *ḍh* substitution for *h* does not occur, because the rule "the *ḍh* substitution for *h*" is qualified by the condition "when followed by a suffix beginning with *s*" (*saheḥ*); and since the *s* here belongs to the compound itself, it is not considered a suffix in relation to the word *parama*. Likewise, the elision of *n* does not occur, because the rule "the elision of *n* at the end of a nominal stem" is qualified by the condition "when followed by a suffix beginning with *j*" (*jhalām*); and since the *j* here belongs to the compound itself, it is not considered a suffix in relation to the word *parama*. Finally, the substitution of *u* for *div* does not occur, because the rule "the substitution of *u* for *div*" is qualified by the condition "when followed by a suffix beginning with *j*" (*jhalām*); and since the *j* here belongs to the compound itself, it is not considered a suffix in relation to the word *parama*. As for the rule regarding Śākalya, it does not apply because the condition "before a dissimilar vowel" (*asavarṇe*) is absent. Thus, there is no fault. In the domain of the *bha* designation, that very [designation] will indeed supersede the *pada* designation. Now, one might object: "The *pada* designation applies to the whole by the rule *svādiṣu*, and let that be superseded by the *bha* designation which shares the same scope of application (*tulyavidhika*). But how can the *pada* designation that applies to the final member of a compound—by the rule *subantaṃ padam*—be superseded? For their scopes of application (*avadhi*) are different. If this is the case, then the term *subanta* must be carried over (*anuvartanīya*) from the rule *suptiṅantam*. Consequently, the meaning becomes as follows: "When a suffix beginning with *yaj* (i.e., a case-ending) other than a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows, the preceding whole [is designated as *bha*]."

It receives the designation *bha*. And within that aggregate, whatever constituent ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) occurs is also designated as *bha*, provided that a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ja* follows immediately. In this context, the designation *bha* for the aggregate is a primary rule (*pradhāna-śiṣṭa*), whereas for the individual member it is a secondary rule (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*). Wherever one perceives a form ending in a case-suffix, there [the designation applies] to that as well; therefore, in forms such as *rājñaḥ*, the designation applies even in the absence of a case-suffix [in the aggregate]. However, when a case-suffix is actually present, it should be understood that the designation applies both to that [member] and to the aggregate.

Even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], the designation *pada* will not apply because of the prohibition "not when it is a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*asarvanāmasthāne*). Now, one might object: "The prohibition applies only to that application which belongs to the whole [stem and suffix] under the rule *svādiṣu*"; to this he says: no, for even there the term *subanta* (ending in a *sup* suffix) is understood from the previous context, and a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is accepted. By the force of that, the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya vidhir vā bhavati pratiṣedho vā*) is not invoked.

Consequently, the meaning is as follows: "When a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows, the designation *pada*, which would otherwise apply to the preceding aggregate by the rule *svādiṣu*, does not occur. And in that case, for that *subanta* which exists as a constituent part, the designation *pada* does not apply to that *subanta*. If this were so, then in the cases *suvāk* and *surāja*, since there would be an absence of the *pada* designation—whether for the aggregate or for its constituent part—due to the rule *svādiṣu* or the rule *subanta*, the substitution of *kutva* and other such changes would not take place.

In that case, then, in the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, the word *aci* is drawn down from the subsequent sūtra; consequently, in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with a *yajādi* (ya, ja, etc. suffix, whatever designation of *pada* there may be—whether it be [the designation of] *sarvanāmasthāna* itself or any other—is entirely prohibited. However, in the case of the nominative singular (*su*), the designation of *subanta* certainly remains, by virtue of the rules *svādiṣu* and *suptiṅantam padam*.

If this is so, then even while [the second member] is being heard, the designation *pada* would apply to the preceding [member]. What is the fault in that? [The author] will raise an objection regarding the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasya* (P. 8.2.107), stating that the mention of *padānta* ("end of a word") is necessary so that [the substitution of *pluta*] does not occur in cases such as *bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ*. Even if the mention of *padānta* were made there, the modification of *pluta* would still apply. This is not a fault; for it is understood that [the *pluta* applies] to "the final [sound] of a sentence or a word. Thus, it is established that in compounds (*samāsa*), the status of being a *pada* does not belong to the subsequent member.

If this were the case, then in *dadhisecau* and *dadhisecaḥ*, the prohibition of the change to *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would not apply. It is not understood thus—that "the beginning of a word" (*padādi*) means "that which is at the beginning of a word," and that [the rule] does not apply after such a beginning. How then? "The beginning from a word" (*padādādiḥ*) means "that which begins with a word," and [the rule] does not apply after what begins with *da*. How then [do we explain] *agniṣu*, *vākṣu*, and *tvakṣu*? The prohibition regarding *sāt* makes it known that the rule does not apply to what follows a word that begins with *sva*.

And it must necessarily be understood that "the first member [comes] from the word," for otherwise, regarding the rule "there is a prescription for the compounding of prefixes, verbal roots, and secondary words with primary suffixes (kṛt) before the addition of case-endings (sup)," there would be no prohibition in cases where the second member is a word ending in a case-ending.

In that case, however, in examples such as *bahusecau* and *bahusecam*, since the element *bahu* is not a word (*apada*), the prohibition [of *ṣatva*] would not apply. This must indeed be stated: "There is no *ṣatva* for that which is preceded by *bahu*. In that regard, this is the arrangement of the rule (*sūtra-nyāsa*): when *sat* occurs, there is no *ṣatva*; then, "after *bahu*"—there is no *ṣatva* for what follows *bahu*. The mention of "initial" (*ādi*) need not be made, for it is already established by the rule "of the following, the initial" (*ādeḥ parasya*). Thus, this [prohibition] is to be inferred from the inclusion of the term *bahuc*.

"It is caused to be done" (*kāryate*), "it is caused to be taken away" (*hāryate*). Here, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is in the passive sense (*karmani*) from a root ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*; there is the addition of *yak*, and the elision (*lopa*) of *ṇic*. Now, one might object: "In this case, the internal (*antaraṅga*) *vṛddhi* substitution occurs as soon as the *ṇic* is produced, whereas the elision, occurring when *yak* is present, is external (*bahiraṅga*). If that is so, then this is cited as a counter-example under the view that grammatical derivation proceeds by splitting the formation into stages (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*).
In a word, the final vowel together with what follows it is called *ṭi*.

*Antya-bhavaḥ* (occurring at the end): the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *diś* (*dig-ādi*); *antyāt* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Although the word *antya-* is dependent on the term *acām* (of vowels), nevertheless, because it is a relative term that is inherently dependent [on another], this compound is not contradictory. [The genitive case in *acām*] is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). If this is so, then since selection requires more than one basis, the singular number in *acaḥ* is inappropriate; to this he replies: "In the sense of a class" (*jātāv iti*). [The phrase] "the vowel which is final" (*yo 'ntyo 'j*) is used. Because selection concerns members of the same class, the word *ac* (vowel) is understood.

The example for the form [substitution] begins with *icchabda*, and so forth. Regarding the grammatical operation (*kārya*), however, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, the elision of the suffixal *i* occurs by the rule "in place of *iṣṭhan* [the suffixes of the superlative and comparative], as if it were *iṣṭha*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavat*). The examples for the grammatical operation begin with *pacete*, and so forth.
The penultimate letter, preceding the final letter, is called the *upadhā*.

He states that the whole [group] alone is the final element by saying "at the beginning of a root-stem, etc. (*dhātvādau*). If the word *alaḥ* were in the nominative plural (*jas*), then because the final element would not be specifically qualified, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply even to what precedes the entire group; consequently, the vowel *i* would be substituted for the letter *ś* in the word *śiṣṭa*. Furthermore, he would have simply said *ala* (in the singular) to avoid ambiguity. Therefore, he explains that the ablative case in *antyāt* is a genitive of apposition with *ala*, meaning "the *al* that is final" (*antyādalaḥ*).

If this is so, since the preceding [rule] is not specified, the designation would apply to the entire aggregate, and thus the substitution of *it* (short *i*) would result for the aggregate "śā" in the word *śiṣṭa*. However, by the rule "alo'ntyasya," it will apply to the final [element]. [Objection: "The rule regarding the final letter does not apply when [the substitute] is meaningless, except in the case of modifications of a reduplicated syllable. Just as in the example *ābhyām*, where the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "hali lopaḥ" for the form *id* does not affect the final [element], so too here it should not apply. Therefore, he says "aleva" (only the final letter), meaning that the substitute applies to the letter immediately preceding the final one.

The particle *eva* is used for emphasis (*paunarvacanika*), as in the case of the final *al*, so too the preceding *al* is likewise [only that]. But how is this meaning obtained without a second mention of the term *sal*? From common usage (*loka*). For in the world, when it is said, "Bring the one preceding the last of these Brāhmaṇas," only the single person immediately preceding the last is brought, not the entire group. In the rule stating that "the mention of *saṃyoga* and *upadhā* is for the sake of *kṛñ*," the designation of *saṃyoga* and *upadhā* applies to the whole by means of the property of its parts.

*Akāra* and so forth are examples of [vowel] forms (*rūpa*). As for the grammatical effect (*kārya*), in *pācaka* and similar cases, there is *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*. In *bhedaka* and similar cases, there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *punargantalaghūpadhasya ca*. Regarding *śiṣṭa*: it is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *śās*; the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, and the retroflex *ṣ* occurs by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*.
When "in that" (tasmin) is specified, [the operation applies] to the preceding [element]. 1.1.66.

Since the particle *iti* is observed to function as a delimiter by signifying its own form—as in "He said, 'gaur'" (*gaurityayamāha*)—the word *idam* here is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that very [particle] mentioned in the rule *tasminnaṇi ca*. Consequently, its application would occur only in that specific context. Furthermore, there is indeed something to be excluded there: the exclusion of the opposite case, such as "Give us what belongs to you" (*he yauṣmākīṇam asmabhyam dehi*) or "I give to you what belongs to me" (*āsmākīnam yuṣmabhyam dadāmi*). He dispels the confusion regarding this by stating: "The mention of the locative case-meaning in *tasmin*."

By this, he demonstrates that this is a reference to the independent pronoun *sarvanāman*, just as in [the rules] "its offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) or "occurring therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*); and just like those, the expression *tasmin* is a general qualifier for vowels (*ac*), serving as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the conditions] such as *halī*. It is not, however, a mere phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*). This is understood from the use of the particle *iti*; for that particle effects a reversal of the word-meaning (*padārtha-viparyāsa*). In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), its own form (*svarūpa*) is the word-meaning (*padārtha*); the reversal of that is the state of having the meaning of the word as its referent (*arthapadārthakatā*).

The intention is this: if this [rule] were to apply only in the context of *tasminn aṇi ca*, then the mention of the word *pūrva* (preceding) would have been made right there. Why, then, is this [present rule] commenced? It is because of the doubt regarding rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*: is the locative case here a *satsaptamī* (locative of existence), or is it a locative of proximity (*upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*), as in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā"? In that regard, both existence and proximity are possible for what follows as well as for what precedes.

In that regard, for both the preceding and the following [vowels], whether separated by an intervening element or immediately adjacent, the substitution of *yaṇ* would be applicable. However, in cases such as *dadhyudaka*, since it is impossible for one single element to simultaneously function as both the recipient of an operation (*kāryin*) and the cause (*nimitta*), the application of *yaṇ* would result in an alternation (*paryāya*). Yet, it is desired that the substitution occur only for the preceding [vowel] when it is immediate. To this end, the present rule is stated: "When there is a designation in the locative case, [the operation applies] to the preceding [element] and only to that which is immediate. Furthermore, the rule "an *ik* vowel is replaced by *yaṇ* before an *ac* vowel" (*iko yaṇ aci*) applies only once; and since its application has been thus restricted, there is no possibility of any undesirable result.

Therein, he shows the first restriction with the words "of the preceding alone. He shows what is to be excluded with the words "not of the succeeding. Regarding the example *pacaty odanam*: although there is no occasion for an absence of restriction here, nevertheless, since a restriction is established when there would otherwise be an occasion for non-restriction under the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, this too certainly serves as an illustration. He shows the second restriction with the words "the mention of the term *nirdiṣṭa* (specified)."

The root *diś* has the sense of "utterance" (*uccāraṇa*). The prefix *niḥ* signifies "without interval" (*nairantarya*). Thus, *nirdiṣṭa* means "indicated as being without interval"; in this way, its meaning is immediate succession (*ānantarya*). In that context, the syntactical formulation (*vacanavyakti*) is as follows: in rules such as *aci halī* ("before a vowel or a consonant"), the grammatical operation applies to the preceding [element] alone. Therein, "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭe*) means "uttered without interval. Therefore, by implication, the meaning becomes "of the immediately preceding [element]. That is why he says: "Let it not apply to what is separated" (*vyavahitasya mā bhūt*). Otherwise, one would have to say "let it not apply to what is separated" (*vyavahite mā bhūt*);
for since the preceding word exists even when separated [by others], the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow for it.
"Therefore" [refers to] the subsequent [sūtra]. 1.1.67.

The rule "the mention of a specific [term] follows" applies here as well. Therefore, the sense is that even in this case, the operation does not take place when there is an intervention. Here too, someone might have the misconception that it is an *anukaraṇa* (imitative repetition) because of the suffix *-iti*; however, in the rule "tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ," although it is not an *anukaraṇa*—because the lengthening by "ata ādeḥ" is impossible for a preceding *aṅga* and thus serves no purpose—[the same principle applies].

However, in the rules "tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi" and "tasmānnu ḍaci," there is indeed something to be excluded; namely, that which is uttered [as a word] but is not perceived [as such], such as in the case of *gaura-na-aśvaḥ*, so that the rule does not apply to the preceding element. Therefore, this [present sūtra] is an imitation of those two very rules. To dispel this misconception, he states: "The term *tasmāt* is a specification of the ablative sense. By this, it is shown that this is a reference to the independent pronoun *sarvanāman*, just like in the previous sūtra.

In the same way, he shows that the phrase "tasmāt" (from that) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (indicative reference) for specific instances such as "sāmānya," "matiṅaḥ," and so on, rather than a mere phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*). It has been stated that this is understood from the use of the particle "iti. Why, then, is this [rule] commenced? Because in rules such as "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ" (P. 8.1.28), since a case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is impossible, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) must be understood as characterized by direction (*dig-yoga-lakṣaṇā*); thus, a word denoting direction (*dik-śabda*) must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). Since the supply of the words "pūrva" (prior) and "uttara" (subsequent) is possible in that context, this is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) intended to establish a restriction (*niyamārthā*).

Thus he says: "The operation [applies] to the subsequent [element] alone. In this way, the Commentator has shown that both the preceding rule and this present one serve a restrictive (niyamārtha) purpose.

Furthermore, the view that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended as a designation (*praklṛpti*) is also presented in the Bhāṣya. How so? The term "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood [as a governing heading]. When there is a reference to the sense of the locative (*saptamy-artha*), the genitive refers to the immediately preceding [element]; when there is a reference to the sense of the ablative (*pañcamy-artha*), the genitive refers to the immediately following [element]. Therefore, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, where the genitive already exists [in the original formulation], it is stated that the genitive refers to the immediately preceding element and not to the immediately following one.

However, in cases such as *āne muk* and *īdāsaḥ*, where there is no genitive, a genitive is supplied; and because that [genitive] has an unrestricted application, it becomes a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Since the operation applies only to that which possesses a genitive of locus, the restriction of the operation is established everywhere.

But where both [the locus and the element to be replaced] are specified, whichever is without scope (*anavakāśā*) supplies the genitive for the other; for example, in *āne muk*, the locative is without scope, and thus supplies the genitive for the ablative in *ato yeyaḥ*, which had scope in the preceding rule.

Thus, in the rule *īdāsaḥ*, the ablative (*pañcamī*) [is superseded] by the locative (*saptamī*) in the rule *āne muk*; for when both are without scope, the ablative supersedes the locative due to its posteriority, just as in the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ*, where the ablative *sarvanāmnaḥ*—though without scope—is superseded by the locative *āmi*, which is also without scope. Now, even if the locative were for the sake of subsequent rules, nevertheless, because it is in grammatical apposition with the ablative *āt* (which is understood from the previous rule), the ablative *sarvanāmnaḥ*—despite having scope—is made to function as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

In this way, even regarding the position that [the rule] is restrictive (niyamapakṣa), the determination should be understood through the principles of "priority" (paratva) and "lack of occasion" (anavakāśatva). In the rule *dīrghāc che tug bhavati*, because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is explained as being in place of the ablative (*pañcamī*), the augment *tuk* occurs after the long vowel (*dīrgha*) itself, and not after the suffix *cha*; thus, the form *surācchāyā* is justified.
The own form of a word is designated as "word" (śabda), except when it is a technical grammatical term (saṃjñā). 1.1.68.

Since there would otherwise be the possibility of grasping both the primary form (*svarūpa*) and the various derivatives (*paryāya*), this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) serves as a restriction. Because technical rules are auxiliary to the grammar, the restriction applies only within the grammatical system and not in common usage; thus he says: "In the grammar, its own [form] alone," and so forth, ending with "is to be grasped. The word "grāhyam" (to be grasped) is derived from the causative stem (*ṇijanta*) with the suffix *yat*; this is obtained through ellipsis. Regarding the word "śabdasya" (of the word), the genitive case is used according to the rule "the agent of gerundives may optionally take the genitive"; the meaning is that the word causes its own form to be grasped—that is, it makes it known.

On the other hand, if it were a name (*saṃjñā*), then both the occurrence [of the word] and the utterance of the name itself would be untenable. Furthermore, the use of the genitive case in the sūtra would not be particularly appropriate; for in the relationship between a name and the named, coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is generally observed. Moreover, by the word "form" (*rūpa*) here, what is denoted is the universal (*sāmānya*) inherent in distinct individual sound-entities (*śabdavyakti*) as uttered by parrots, starlings, humans, and so forth—namely, the property of being the word "fire" (*agniśabdatva*) and the like.

The meaning is that the universal (*sāmānya*) which is common to all utterances of that individual (*vyakti*) pronounced by the author of the Sūtra—namely, "after *agni*, [the suffix] *ḍhak*"—is what is to be denoted. Since the connection of the universal with grammatical operations occurs through the medium of the individual, the resulting sense is that the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to each respective individual as it is uttered.

He shows what is excluded by the particle *eva*—namely, "not an external object. Regarding the phrase "excluding the designation of the word": the meaning is that in the designations of words, the word's own form (*svarūpa*) is not to be grasped [as the primary object]. Since there would otherwise be the contingency of no restriction, he shows the restriction with the words "by the word," etc. In common usage, when it is said, "Let the cow be perceived," it is understood that the connection with the action pertains to the object itself; for one does not consider the task accomplished merely by perceiving the form of the word.

In grammar, however, operations such as the prescription of suffixes are not possible with respect to the meaning itself, because there can be no sequence (paurvāparya) between the suffix and the meaning. Therefore, when "agner ḍhak" is stated, just as in common worldly usage, the meaning is first understood; yet since [the suffix] cannot coexist with that [meaning], there would be a cognition of all words denoting it—just as when a generic form (*ākṛti*) is intended, individual instances (*vyakti*) are understood. To avoid this fault, this rule is commenced for the purpose of restriction, so that [the suffix] may apply only to what is actually employed [in the rule]. For example: *audaśvitkam*. [This is derived from] "prepared in whey" (*udaśviti saṃskṛtam*); the suffix *ṭhak* is added to a word ending in the locative case, and by the rule "after *is*, *us*, *uk*, and *tānta*, *ka*" [is substituted for *ṭhak*].

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *ghu*-roots," etc.: otherwise, by the rule "after a prefix, *ki* after *ghu*," the suffix *ki* would apply only to that verbal root which has the meaning of sound (*ghoḥ śabdārthāt*), and not to *dā* and *dhā*. However, in the rule "ī halyaghoḥ," because the word *ghu* does not end in the vowel *ā*, the inclusion of only *dā* and *dhā* is established. In the form *kumārīghaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of shortening [the final vowel] by the rule "gharūpa."

But surely, since technical names (*saṃjñā*) are established in the various rules (*pradeśa*) for the purpose of making the named object (*saṃjñin*) understood, it follows by implication that there will be no grasping of the word's own form (*svarūpa*). This is not so; for in this science, both possibilities are admissible. Thus, as in the case of number, object, instrument, and so forth, there would be a grasping of both the own form and the named object in the various rules. [This is] established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In that the rule "those ending in ṣ or n are called ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 1.1.24) prescribes the technical designation *ṣaṭ* for numbers ending in the letter ṣ, this indicates that a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) does not include its own form. Otherwise, since the form *ṣaṭ* itself would also be included in rules such as "elision after the six [cases] and after *ṣaṭ* and *catur*" (Pāṇini 7.1.22), he would not have prescribed the designation *ṣaṭ* for numbers ending in ṣ.

But surely, a technical name (*saṃjñā*) ending in *ṣ* is intended to undergo an operation prescribed for that which ends in *ṣ*, and this name itself indeed ends in *ṣ*; therefore, what is the purpose of the rule "not a technical name of a word" (*na śabda-saṃjñā*)? True; the prohibition is for the sake of avoiding the burden of comprehension. By the word "word" (*śabda*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is meant through a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*); thus, "a name of a word" (*śabda-saṃjñā*) means a name belonging to a word. And in this way, even in the case of technical names of meanings within the science, such as "object" (*karman*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*), there is no grasping of the actual form [of the words themselves].

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term *rūpa*? For in this context, since it is independent of instruction in its cognition, is unique, and possesses an eternal connection, that [word-form] alone is the word’s own meaning; for it is only that which requires the apprehension of a relationship in order to be cognized. Furthermore, because it can be conveyed even by synonyms, it would be common [to other meanings], and its connection would be non-eternal, as it is absent in the state of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). Nor can the meaning be made the apprehender, and if it were the apprehended, the Sūtra would be purposeless. Thus, is there no need for the inclusion of *rūpa*? To this [it is replied]: so it is.

In that case, this indicates: "In the technical treatise (śāstra), a meaning is of equal status with the word-form itself. Therefore, by the mention of "that which has a meaning" (arthavat), it is established that [the rule] applies to what is meaningless (anarthaka). In that context, because of the indicator (jñāpaka), the meaning must also be grasped; and because of the statement "its own form" (svaṃ rūpam), the form is also included. By the force of the expression "and the form," the form of that which possesses a meaning is what is grasped. Consequently, in the example *kāśe kuśe*, the absence of the designation *pragṛhya* for the sound *śe* is established.

He explains the Vārttika *sittadviśeṣāṇām* with the words: "The mention of *sit* (the suffix) must be made; [it should be stated] as *vṛkṣas*. Then he says: "It should be stated after [the rule] *svaṃ rūpam*. To the question "What is the purpose?", he replies: "It should be stated as *vṛkṣādi*"; why then is it said "*vṛkṣādyartham*"? When it is said "its purpose lies in *vṛkṣa* and so on," it follows by implication that "its purpose is for the sake of *vṛkṣa* and so on"—thus there is no fault. We shall explain the logical establishment of this meaning under the rule *vibhāṣā*.

"And of that which is a synonym for *pit*": the word "and" (*ca*) includes its own form and its specific varieties. This is indeed based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). We shall later explain how the rule "of that which is a synonym for *jit*" is established through logical reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*). "And of that which is *jhitt*"—this too is indeed based on explicit scriptural statement. However, they say that for wild animals and birds, the designation *pin* must be applied. Now, regarding "of one"—this is merely a desired conclusion (*iṣṭi*).

An *it* (a letter having an indicatory *i*) and that which is designated as such, when not being a suffix (*apratyaya*), are also [to be understood] as having the same class (*savarṇa*) as their own form.

This is a definitional rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*), not a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*), because its meaning is applied according to what is well-established. "By the subsequent *ṇ*": this has already been explained under the rule *laṇ*. As for the phrase "and of its own form," although it is presented in the nominative case, nevertheless—because the word *ca* ("and") is heard immediately after the genitive form *savarṇasya*, and there is no other genitive form [to which it could apply]—the sense is that it assigns the status of a genitive to that very [term]. "Excluding the affix" (*pratyayaṃ varjayitvā*).

Therefore, in that context, only the form as it is actually uttered is taken; for example, "ād guṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87) and so forth. Just as here [the rule applies] in the case of *devendra*, it likewise applies in cases such as *khaṭvendra*. Regarding the suffix *cvi*: just as here [the rule applies] in the case of *śuklībhavati*, it likewise applies in cases such as *mālībhavati*. Regarding the rule "yasyeti ca" (P. 6.4.148): just as here [the rule applies] in the case of *dākṣi* and *plākṣi*, it likewise applies in cases such as *cauḍi* and *bālāki*. The words *jūḍā* and *balākā* belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

But surely, in cases such as *akaḥ* and *aci*, when there is a reference to a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term), how can there be an inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) by means of the intermediate vowels *i* and so forth? For a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) conveys its referent (*saṃjñin*) only when it is itself uttered; yet there is no utterance of those intermediate vowels. Indeed, they are conveyed as the referents by means of technical names such as *aṇ* and so on. Where, then, would this apply? It applies where there is the actual utterance of the technical name, as in *asya cvau* and *yasyeti*.

In the *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive enumeration), the first letter, because it has been uttered, includes its own class (*savarṇa*). It might be argued: "In the traditional recitation of the alphabet (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), the long *ī*-sounds and others that are uttered are the includers of their respective classes. [Furthermore,] in injunctions such as *agādi*, even the long *ī*-sounds and others are understood precisely by virtue of being designated as short [by the rule], and they are made known by the short *i*-sounds already understood. This is not so, because [the long vowels] belong to a later time [in the sequence].

In this system, first there is the instruction of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Subsequent to that instruction is the designation *it*. Subsequent to the designation *it* is the application of the rule "the beginning [letter] with the last [includes the intervening ones]. Thereafter follows the rule "an [includes] its homogeneous counterparts" (*aṇ savarṇasya*). Thus, when the constituent elements such as the instruction and so forth have been established, the inclusion of homogeneous sounds occurs elsewhere—such as in the rule "of this [root], when *cv-* follows"—but not within those very constituent elements themselves, nor in their own self, because they have not yet been fully established at that stage.

If, however, there were the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) even in this rule, then in rules such as *ādṛgamahanḥ* and *ṝdorap*, the letters *a* and others would also include their homogeneous counterparts. Therefore, in this rule and in the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the traditional alphabet), there is the inclusion of those letters that have not [previously] included their homogeneous vowels. Consequently, the established position remains: that in the *pratyāhāra*s, there should be no inclusion of homogeneous vowels by means of those letters situated in the middle. This is not a fault.

There is no rule that only those sounds being actually uttered must be the conveyors of meaning; rather, it is those [sounds] mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*) that are the conveyors. And there is indeed the mounting upon the intellect of those [sounds] situated in the middle [of a word]. Consequently, even that which is conveyed as a name (*saṃjñin*) will possess the status of a conveyor (*pratyāyaka*). The proof for this is the prohibition [contained in the rule] *dīrghājjasi ca*. For that [prohibition] is intended so that, in examples such as *kumāryau*, the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* does not occur. In that context, the term *akaḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

In cases such as *khaṭve*, however, the prohibition is already established by the rule *nādici*. Furthermore, designations such as *dīdhīvevīṭām* would be justified only if there is a inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) even by those [vowels] situated in the middle. Thus, the acute (*udātta*) vowel mentioned in the Sūtra—such as in *svarānunāsika* and so on—includes even that which differs from other accents; likewise for the grave (*anudātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*). Similarly, a nasalized (*sānunāsika*) vowel includes the non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*), and the latter includes the former.

[The objection is: "It would not become long. However, if [the rule] were simply "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*), then because the term *apratyaya* would include its own homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) by virtue of being a suffix itself, the long vowel might also result. This which is stated—"not a suffix"—is far too little. It should be stated: "Not a suffix, nor a substitute (*ādeśa*), nor that which has the markers *ṭ*, *k*, *n*, or *m*. Regarding the suffix, an example was already given there. Regarding the substitute: in the case of *idam iś* (Pāṇini 5.3.3), as in *itaḥ*; here, because it is specifically prescribed, it would override the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* etc., and a three-moraic substitute would result.

Regarding *ṭit*—[if it were applied], by the rule "the augment *iṭ* is added to an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*)", the long vowel would also occur [in forms like *jighṛkṣati*]. However, the rule "there is a long vowel for the root *grah* in the *liṭ*" would then serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that for *grah*, there is a long vowel [only] in the *liṭ*, and not a short one. Furthermore, the rule "for roots ending in *vṛ*, *u*, or *ṝ*, there is optionally [a long vowel]" would also serve the purpose of preventing a long vowel in the *liṭ* [of *vṛt*, as in] *vavaritha*. Regarding *kit*—by the rule "there is *vuk* after *bhū* in the *luṅ* and *liṭ*", as in *babhūva*, there would also be the nasalization [of the penultimate vowel].

Regarding the statement "miti am sambuddho," O Anaḍvan, it might be [thought that] *ām* would also [be included]. If that is so, then because of the rule *apratyayaḥ*, there is no mention of a technical name (*saṃjñā*) here; what then? It is a mention according to the literal meaning (*anvarthagrahaṇam*). A suffix (*pratyaya*) is so called because it is recognized (*pratīyate*) or prescribed (*vidhīyate*). The meaning is that a [suffix] which is being taught (*bhāvyamānaḥ*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇān*). The vowels *i* and so forth are also being taught. However, for a suffix that is a technical name (*saṃjñā-pratyaya*), a prohibition is not necessary. That by which one recognizes the meaning is a suffix; for there is no denotation of meaning in the case of the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels.

In rules such as *kuhoś cuḥ*, although [the sound *c*] is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), there is no application of the prohibition "it is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) because of the very capacity of its being marked with *u* (*udit*). And thus it is recited: "An *aṇ* that is being taught does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."
That which follows *tapara* denotes its own duration of time. Pāṇini 1.1.70.

He shows that *taparaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that which has *t* as its subsequent [element]. He also shows that *taparaḥ* is a *pañcamī-tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "that which is beyond *t*. Furthermore, this [dual meaning] is to be understood from this very rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*). There is no contradiction in the difference of meaning between the two, since one may resort to either *tantra* (the principle of a single word having multiple meanings) or *āvṛtti* (repetition) regarding the single term *tapara*. In this regard, the evidence for the *bahuvrīhi* is the inclusion of *tapara* in the rule *ato bhisa ais*; the evidence for the *tatpuruṣa* is stated in the commentary on *vṛddhir ādaic*, where it is said that the mention of *aij* is for the sake of that [rule].

"An articulatory feature (*tapara*) is a phoneme (*varṇa*). It is stated that it is a "phoneme" because only a phoneme can possess a homogeneous counterpart (*savarṇa*). The term *tatkālasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "that which has this as its time. This designation is improper. By the word *tat*, the phoneme with the [specified] *tapara* is referred to; and an action of well-known duration is the delimiting factor for another action of well-known duration. For example, regarding time: "He studied for a day. By the word "day," the continuous movement of the sun from sunrise to sunset is expressed.

And since that [duration] is a delimiter of the study, it is time (*kāla*); however, since a phoneme (*varṇa*) is not of the nature of an action, is it not improper for the word denoting a phoneme to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "time"? If this is so, then a compound with elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*) should be understood, as in the case of *uṣṭramukha*. And because the meaning is already implied, there is indeed an elision in usage, just as in the analysis *uṣṭro mukham asya* ("an ox is its face"). And from the capacity of the expression *praṇi praṇyantarasya mukham* ("the face of one phoneme is like another phoneme"), there is the cognition of similarity.

Just as in the expression "one whose face is like that of a camel" (*uṣṭra-mukha*), the similarity of the face is established through the face alone, and not through the entire camel—by implication, the meaning becomes "one whose face is like the face of a camel"—so too here, although color is not duration itself, by implication its activity, being delimited by another [activity] such as a blink (*nimeṣa*), serves to delimit another color; thus, it is said that "color itself is the delimiter."

What is the meaning of the expression "that time belongs to this"? It means that an action connected with that time is the delimiting factor for this [time]. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning with "by itself" (*ātmanā*). Although this word *ātman* is pronounced in proximity to a phoneme followed by *t* (tapara), it refers to the act of pronunciation associated with that [phoneme], because it is impossible for a phoneme to be identical to an action. The meaning is: "the act of pronunciation belonging to this [phoneme] is of the same nature as the act of pronunciation of a phoneme followed by *t*, which is delimited by a blink of an eye (*nimeṣa*) and so forth."

"Of that which is endowed with another quality (*guṇāntarayuktasya*). This means: of that which was previously mentioned as possessing a certain quality, [it refers] to that which is now endowed with a different quality. Furthermore, is this for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), or is it for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartham*)? In that regard, if *aṇ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), it is for the purpose of restriction: "A phoneme followed by *t* (i.e., a *tapara*) denotes only that which has its own duration. If it is not carried over (*nivṛtti*), it is for the purpose of an injunction.

In that regard, regarding the first position—where, under the view that "qualities are differentiators" (*bhedakā guṇāḥ*), there would be no inclusion of a form possessing a different quality than the one specifically mentioned in rules such as *āto dhātoḥ*, *ātāṃ puṅṇau*, *yasyeti ca*, and *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*—he states, adopting the second position: "for the sake of an injunction" (*vidhyartham*). He provides the reason for this here: "the term *aṇ* does not carry over (*nānuvartate*)."

If this [rule] were for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), then, since it would have fulfilled its function with respect to non-*aṇ* sounds (*anaṇsu*), it would apply first to *aṇ* sounds. To this he replies: "and for other *aṇ*s. He clarifies this very point: "therefore, in cases such as *bhisa ais*, etc. [The rule] does not apply at all; the sense is that it is superseded by the subsequent [rule]. For a conflict exists here: by the preceding rule eighteen [sounds] are included, whereas by this [subsequent rule] only six are.

"What is the illustrative example? This question arises because it might be argued that since qualities (*guṇas*) do not differentiate [phonemes], the rule is already established for non-nasal sounds (*anaṇ*). The answer is that this sūtra must indeed be commenced to exclude those nasalized vowels (*aṇ*) that occur at different times; however, that very same rule, by operating through the method of positive prescription (*vidhimukhena*), accomplishes the desired result even for non-nasal sounds. Regarding the rule *viḍ-vanor anunāsikasyāt* (P. 6.4.41), it must be considered what kind of homogeneous sound (*savarṇa*) is intended to be included here. Therefore, this is merely an illustration; its actual purpose lies in rules such as *āto dhātoḥ* (P. 6.4.140) and *yasyeti ca* (P. 6.4.148).

Regarding the question "Why [specify] 'of that time' (*tatkālasya*)?", it is because the rule itself is being challenged by way of its primary constituent parts. As in the example *khaṭvābhiḥ*, in a rule dependent on phonemes (*varṇāśrayavidhi*), the treatment as if being the end or the beginning (*antādivadbhāvaḥ*) does not apply.
The first [phoneme], together with the last, [denotes the entire class]. (Pāṇini 1.1.71)

This is also a technical rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*). Since the beginning and the end depend on what lies between them, it is understood that those situated in the middle are the things named (*saṃjñin*). Because the phrase "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*) is carried over [from the previous rule], he says "of those situated in the middle" to indicate that this refers to the own-form itself. Although the initial and final parts belong to the whole (*avayavin*) which consists of the aggregate, nevertheless, because such a whole is never employed simultaneously in actual usage, he shows by saying "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) that the name applies to the individual members of the aggregate. And [he says] "and its own form."

The [sounds] beginning with the original form (*svarūpa*) alone are grasped, not the final one, because of its lack of predominance. Thus, in the example *dadhyatra*, only the letter *y* operates, not that which is accompanied by *ṇ*. Because of the inclusion of the word "together" (*saha*), the designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the initial and final sounds as a combined whole; therefore, the case-ending arises from the entire aggregate—as in the rule *iko yaṇ*—and not from the initial sound alone. This is so that there might not be a grasping by means of the term *ṭā*. Since this limit is not intended to be significant, this [letter *ṇ*] is not the final one [in the sense of being the last member of a sequence]; rather, it serves as a qualifier for the third-case singular ending in the rules *ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyaḥ* and *dvitīyāṭausvenaḥ*.
A grammatical operation applies to that which ends with the element for which the rule prescribes it.

This undertaking is for the purpose of avoiding [the interpretation of the rule as] an injunction of essential nature (*svarūpavidhi*). This too is a technical definition rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*). In the word *yena*, the third case ending denotes the instrument (*karaṇe*). *Vidhi* means "that which is enjoined" (*vidhīyate*); it is a noun derived from the root with the suffix *kvip*. Thus, "an injunction is enjoined. By the word *vidhi*, a thing capable of being enjoined is denoted; the use of the verb form (*ākhyāta*) serves to indicate its connection with a specific action at the present time, just as in the expressions "he sits on a seat" (*āsane āste*) or "he acts by means of an instrument" (*karaṇena karoti*). The compound *tadantasya* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

By the word *tat*, the term indicated by "by which" (*yena*) is pointed out; thus he says: "of that which ends in *ātman*. Since the word *anta* denotes a constituent part, he states that this is the technical name for the aggregate implied by it: "it becomes the name of the aggregate. Regarding the form *avaśyalāvyam*: it is a compound because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*; the *m* is elided according to the rule: "one should drop the *m* of *avaśyam* before a gerundive suffix."

Now, why does the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) not apply here to that which ends in *ej* (as in the rule "eco 'yavāyāvaḥ")? What would be the consequence? Because they consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the substitutes *ay*, *āv*, and *āy* would replace the whole [of the *ec*]. Consequently, in cases such as *cayana* and *lavana*, the form *ayana* would result. One might argue that the specific meaning would be understood through the force of context, just as in the case of [the word] *akṣa*. This is not a fault; for the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being specifically indicated" will ensure this. Alternatively, just as there is an extension of the rule to include what ends in *ec*, so too shall it apply to *ay* and the others.

Even so, in the rule "ād guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.87), there would be the undesirable consequence of *guṇa* substitution for a group ending in the vowel *ā*, such as in *ādityavarṇaḥ*; and by the rule "aci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77), there would be the consequence of *guṇa* for a group beginning with a vowel, such as in *khaṭvendraḥ*. Furthermore, because no genitive case is specified, the principle "of that which is being pointed out" (*nirdiśyamānasya*) does not apply here either. If this is the case, then this is not its scope at all. It has been stated that the third case in "yena" denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), and an instrument is dependent (*paratantra*), since only that which is presided over by an agent can be an instrument. However, in rules such as "erac" (Pāṇini 3.3.56), the dependence of the vowels *i* and others, and the independence of the verbal roots and so forth, are clearly manifest in their own form.

Or it may be so; therefore, both of these [the status of being a qualifier or a qualificand] for trees and the like are based on the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). That which is intended as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is dependent (*paratantra*) and subordinate (*apradhāna*); that which is intended as a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is independent (*svatantra*) and primary (*pradhāna*). Consequently, it is possible to state that the name [of the compound] applies to the qualificand ending in that [taddhita suffix]. Furthermore, a qualifier exists in proximity to a qualificand, and this proximity occurs in some cases through direct mention, as in the rule "The dual ending *ī*, *ū*, or *e* [is pragṛhya]," where there is proximity to the dual ending.

In some cases [the application occurs] by way of qualification (*adhikāra*), as in "er-ac" (Pāṇini 3.3.56), which [qualifies] the verbal root (*dhātu*). In other cases, it is by way of implication (*ākṣepa*), as in "iko jhal" (Pāṇini 1.2.9), where [the term *dhātu*] is implied by the suffix *san*. In rules such as "eco'yavāyāvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.78), there is no proximity whatsoever to a qualificand (*viśeṣya*); therefore, this [rule regarding qualification] does not apply. If the qualifier were to denote the name of that which ends in it (*tadantasaṃjñā*), then in the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.102), the vowel *ṛ* would be the name of a verbal root ending in it; consequently, the mention of "preceded by a labial" (*oṣṭhyapūrva*) would be a qualifier of the verbal root itself, and not of the letter *ṛ*.

Because a technical name (*saṃjñā*) serves the purpose of making known that which possesses the name (*saṃjñin*), the following would result: [the term *saṃyoga*] would apply here in the case of *saṅkīrṇam*, but it would not apply in cases such as *pūrtam*. Likewise, in the rule "utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt," the phrase *asaṃyogapūrvāt* would qualify the *aṅga* (the stem), and not the *ut* (the letter *u*). This is not a fault; for this technical name depends upon a relationship between the subordinate and the principal. Consequently, in rules such as "utaśca pratyayāt," at the time of connection with the qualifier, the subordinate status is not yet manifest; having experienced that [subordinate status], the name subsequently comes into being through its connection with the qualified element (*viśeṣya*).

Regarding the term *samāse* (in a compound): by this he means the following—words such as *śrita* and so on are subsequently the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and the *sup*-ending [word] is their qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, in rules such as "from *naḍa* and others, the suffix *phak*" (*naḍādibhyaḥ phak*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) beginning with *naḍa* is the qualificand, and [the suffix] is the qualifier. As for the example *kaṣṭaṃ paramaśritaḥ*: since this word ending in *śrita* is not a *subanta* (a word ending in a case-suffix), it must be read as ending in the vocative (*sambuddhi*), for only then does it become a *subanta* by the rule of "treating the final element as having a case-suffix" (*taddhita-pratyaya-lakṣaṇena*), and yet it is heard [in the text] as ending in *śrita*. Regarding the phrase *netyāha* ("he says no"): who is it that says this? It is either the opponent (*uttaravādī*) or the Teacher (*ācārya*).

Regarding *ugidvarṇa*: the meaning is that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by both the *ugit* suffixes and the phoneme (*varṇa*). Since the rule "in which [the operation is prescribed]" (*yasmin vidhiḥ*) is an exception to the rule of "specification of the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) and instead establishes a rule of "specification of the initial element" (*tadādividhi*), the operation applies only through the qualifier itself.
That [stem] whose initial vowel among its vowels is a *vṛddhi* [vowel] is called *vṛddha*.

He says that since only a whole (*samudāya*) can have an initial vowel (*ācām-ādi*), it is that very whole which is expressed by the phrase "of which" (*yasya*): "The word 'yasya' refers to the whole. This is for the purpose of indicating the named entity (*saṃjñin*); otherwise, what would be referred to by that pronoun? If the word *tat* were not employed, the designation *vṛddha* would belong to the *vṛddhi* [vowels] themselves. Regarding the phrase "among the vowels" (*acām madhye*), etc.: here, the word "of which" (*yasya*) is connected with "of the vowels" (*acām*), and the "initial" (*ādi*) is selected as the subject, while *vṛddhi* is the property to be prescribed.

The word *ādi* (beginning) signifies "commencement"—that which is commenced (*upakramyate*) is a commencement (*upakrama*), meaning it is uttered first. The sense is: among the vowels belonging to a given group, that which is uttered first is designated as *vṛddhi*. The plural number in *acām* (of vowels) is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the intention is that this applies even when there are only two [vowels]. It also occurs for a single vowel by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). For example: *śālīyaḥ*.

In this case, although the entire group begins with a consonant (*hal*), the designation "vṛddhi" applies to the first vowel (*ac*) with respect to the vowels. Now, one might object: since selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) pertains to members of the same class, the selected initial must be understood as a vowel alone; the letter *ā* is not a vowel, because it is not taught in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*). If so, how is it that in the expression "the Brāhmaṇa family Somapa," the shortening occurs as a vowel-operation (*ackārya*)? It occurs because of the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*), and not because [the letter *ā*] is itself a vowel. In the present case as well, it is understood [as a vowel] precisely because of the absence of the inclusion of homogeneous sounds.

Let it be so; even while being perceived in that manner, [the term *ac*] will include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), just as when [the term] *aj* is used, the long vowel *ī* and others situated between [the short vowels] are included. Furthermore, since the vowel *a* is uttered as the basis for the selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) in the expression "of the vowels" (*acām*), the vowel *ā* is also perceived. Therefore, even for those being selected, such as *ā*, the status of being a vowel (*actva*) is perceived in exactly that same way. Thus, this objection is trivial.

Regarding the phrase "or of a name" (*nāmadheyasya*): the word *nāmadheya* is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) among technical designations. In the rule "Devadattīyāḥ," the word *devadatta* is listed among the *kāśyādi* group as denoting a place. According to the rule *eṅ prācāṃ deśe*, it receives the designation of "vṛddha" (long vowel) by virtue of its association with the *kāśyādi* group; therefore, for words not denoting a place, only the suffix *cha* applies. However, in the case of the word *devadatta* denoting a village of the Vāhīkas, because it is not a conventional designation (*asaṅketika*) due to its beginningless [usage], and because it does not denote a place of the Easterners (*aprācām*), it lacks the *vṛddha* designation. Consequently, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*—which are conditioned by the *kāśyādi* group—do not apply.

Regarding the phrase "gotrāntāt" and so forth: by the word *gotra*, that which ends in the suffix *gotra* is understood. The meaning is that whatever suffix occurs after a simple [stem] ending in *gotra*—as if it were not compounded—occurs after a [stem] ending in that [suffix] as well.

Regarding *ghṛtarauḍhīyāḥ*: [The derivation is as follows: the descendant of Rūḍha is *Rauḍhi*, formed by the suffix *iñ* according to *ata iñ*. Then, for the sense of "students of," the suffix *aṇ* would apply by *iñaś ca*; however, this is prohibited by the rule *na dvyacaḥ prācyabharateṣu*. Therefore, the suffix *cha* is applied by *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. Similarly, *vṛddhāmbhīyāḥ*: the descendant of Ambhas is *Āmbhi*, formed by *iñ* because [Ambhas] is listed among the *bāhvādi* group, and there is elision of the *s* by the rule *saṃbhūyo'mbhasoḥ salopaś ca*. Regarding *odanapāṇinīyāḥ*: [the derivation is similar].

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the descendant of Paṇin," and due to the rule "gāthividathī" (Pāṇini 6.4.164), there is no elision of the final vowel by the rule "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.143). [Thus we have *pāṇina*. The descendant of Pāṇina who is a youth (*yuvan*) takes the suffix *iñ*. When one intends to express "the pupils of that [youth]," although the suffix *iñ* is elided by the rule "yūni luk" (Pāṇini 2.4.58), the suffix *aṇ* would still be applicable by the rule "iñaśca" (Pāṇini 4.2.112) through the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). However, this does not occur because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning "lineage" (*gotra*).

In the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* ("from Kaṇva and others, when denoting a lineage"), the technical term *gotra* (lineage) is understood; that same term is also carried over into the rule *itaśca* ("and after [a stem] ending in -i"), and therefore the suffix *-yañ* does not apply to denote a youth (*yuvan*). The word *kaśyapa* belongs to the *bidādi* group, and the word *kata* belongs to the *gargādi* group; thus, from *jihvācapala* and *haritabhakṣa*, the suffix *kātya* is formed by means of the *aṇ* suffix. But what is the relevance here of the discussion regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of suffixes, given that this should have been stated under the heading of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*)—specifically, as an exception to the *aṇ* suffix applied to words before *prāgdīvyataḥ*? True; [it is relevant].

Some, however, have prescribed the designation *vṛddha* for the *gotra*-suffix; even so, since the form *vṛddhāmbhīyāḥ* is established [by that rule], the author of the Vārttika—considering that "if the designation *vṛddha* were applied, then for the students of Piṅgalakāṇva, the form *paiṅgalakāṇvāḥ* would require the suffix *cha* by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*, whereas under the extension of the suffix [to the base], the suffix *aṇ* is obtained by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*"—first presented the opinion of others with the preceding statement and then refuted it with this present statement; that very same [refutation] was recited by the author of the Vṛtti.
And the words beginning with *tyad* [are also indeclinables]. 1.1.74.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of what follows": in that [previous] context, it is connected because it serves a purpose and because the relationship "of which the first vowel among the vowels is *eṅ*" is possible. However, here it is not connected. This is because of unsuitability, since selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) pertains to members of the same class (*sajātīya*), and because the pronouns beginning with *tyad* lack the nature of being vowels; for there is no possibility that "the first of the vowels of which are the pronouns beginning with *tyad*. Nor is it appropriate to resort to a strained interpretation—that the word "pronouns beginning with *tyad*" refers to a vowel situated within a pronoun beginning with *tyad*—since the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) is possible even for the sake of what follows.

As it has been said: "It follows for the sake of the subsequent [rule]. This refers to the suffix *tyadādi*. By the rule "udīcāṃ vṛddhādagotrāt," the suffix *phañ* is applied, according to the rule "pratyayottarapadayośca."
In the speech of the easterners, [the vowels] *eṅ* [are substituted for *ai* and *au*]. (Pāṇini 1.1.75)

"Regarding the designation of a region of the easterners (*prācām*). The meaning is: those who dwell in the eastern region are the "easterners" (*prācaḥ*); the designation of the region belonging to them is what is intended. By this, he shows that the mention of "the easterners" (*prācām*) is a qualifier of the [region] as heard in the rule, and not a qualifier of the teachers (*ācāryāḥ*). For if that were the case, the word "in the opinion of" (*matena*) would have to be supplied [as an ellipsis]. Thus, [the examples] such as *eṇīpacanīyaḥ* and so forth are formed by the suffix *chaḥ* after *eṇīpacana* and others. As for *daivadattāḥ*: [this is formed by the suffix *aṇ*].

By the rule "vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca," the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*, which are prescribed [by Pāṇini 4.2.115] after a *vṛddha* base, do not apply. They do not apply even by virtue of the inclusion [of these names] in the *kāśyādi* group, because that group also falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for *vṛddha* bases. Thus, for a village named Kroḍa, the word for one born there is *krauḍa*, formed only with the suffix *aṇ*. However, Kuṇi explained the mention of "the easterners" (*prācām*) as being for the purpose of indicating the specific instruction of the Teacher (Pāṇini); the author of the Bhāṣya likewise relied upon that very view.

From that [base], the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* occur after the two Vāhīka villages, *sepuram* and *skonagaram*, as in: *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca*. Thus we have *saipurikī* and *saupurikā*; *skaunāgarikī* and *skaunagarikā*. Furthermore, because this is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* do not occur after the words *kroḍa* and *devadatta* when they denote places not located in the East. This designation of *vṛddhi* is intended only for the secondary (*śaiṣika*) meanings; therefore, regarding offspring (*apatya*) and modification (*vikāra*), it is established by the fixed option of the Northern Grammarians (*udīcām*) alone.

According to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*, however, all of this must be established through explicit statement. Regarding the term *gomatī*: the river Gomatī in the eastern region is not included under the category of "region" (*deśa*), because in the rule *nadī-deśo 'grāmāḥ* ("rivers and regions, excluding villages"), rivers are mentioned separately from regions. Since the terms "eastern" (*prāc*) and "northern" (*udac*) are heard in rules such as *eḍ prācāṃ deśe* ("in the eastern region") and *udīcāṃ vṛddhād agotrāt* ("among the northerners, from a *vṛddha* [stem] that is not a *gotra*"), he says "the eastern and northern" (*prāgudañcau*) in order to distinguish between those two. The river named Śarāvatī flows toward the north-east; the region situated to the south-east of that river is the eastern region (*prāgdeśa*).

The northern direction is the region of the north (*udagdeśa*); those two [directions] the Śarāvatī river divides. By that boundary, the division between those two is known. Regarding the term *kṣīrodaka*: the singular form is used according to the rule "the genus of non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*). In some places, the reading is *kṣīrodake*; there, because a specific individual instance is intended and there is no intention to refer to the genus, the dual number is used. For what purpose does he divide them? For the sake of establishing the correct usage of words for the learned.

Although such a designation does not apply to the river itself—that words are established and perfected for the learned—nevertheless, by means of her acting as the cause, the established correctness of words is superimposed upon her as a designation. May she, being thus constituted, protect us. In some places the reading is *prāgudīcau*; there, the suffix *ac* is applied through a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from the rule *ac-pratyanvava-pūrvāt*, and the substitution of *ī* for *udak* occurs according to the rule *uda īt*. In the reading *pragudīcam*, it is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule "dvandvāccudaṣahāntātsamāhāre" (Pāṇini 5.4.106). In some places, the reading is "prāgudīcaḥ"; in that case, there is a superimposition of multiplicity upon the aggregate, meaning "from the eastern regions and from the northern regions."
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by Haradattamiśra;
now begins the second quarter of the first chapter.
After the roots beginning with √gāṅ (to go) and √kuṭ (to bend), the affixes that do not have an indicatory letter ñ or ṇ take the augment iṭ when they are marked with an indicatory letter ṅ.

In the bahuvrīhi compound *kuṭādiḥ*, where [the word] begins with *kuṭa*, although it possesses the status of a *pada* due to the case-ending contained within the compound, the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *da*) does not occur; for that would entail the destruction of the form being imitated. Alternatively, it should be understood as an imitation of the root from the Dhātupāṭha, *kuṭa kauṭilye*, together with its indicatory vowel (*anubandha*), namely the letter *a*.

In this regard, four possible positions arise: (1) the establishment of a relationship with the letter *ṅ* bearing the technical designation *it*; (2) a rule (*vidhi*) concerning that which has *ṅ* as its *it*; (3) the assignment of a technical name (*saṃjñākaraṇa*); or (4) an extension of that [designation] by analogy (*atideśa*). Regarding these, in the first position, the suffix following *gāṅ* and the roots beginning with *kuṭ* is *ṅit*—meaning it is joined with the letter *ṅ* bearing the designation *it*, in the sense that "it possesses the *it*-designated *ṅ*.

In this case, for those suffixes such as *yaṅ* and others that already possess the letter *ṅ*, the restatement (*anuvāda*) is redundant; for those such as *tavya* and others that do not possess it, it would be a false effort. Thus, this position is merely a preliminary proposal.

Now, as for the second [interpretation]: by the rule *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used to effect a transformation of the nominative case (*prathamā*) in *añ-ṇit* into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), whereby the substitution of a *ṅit* [suffix] would result. In this case, the nominative is not redundant, as it serves the purpose of brevity (*lāghava*).

In that regard, if *ṅit* is taken as a *karmadhāraya* compound, or even in the absence of a compound, by the rule "of the first of the subsequent," the letter *ṅ* would apply to the beginning of the suffixes *tavya* and so on. But how could that which possesses the designation *it* be a substitute (*ādeśa*) while itself being inclined toward its own disappearance? What is the fault? It will disappear after having caused the original element (*sthānin*) to disappear! This might be argued: "By the force of the mention of *it*, it shall not be a substitute; for if it were a substitute, the designation *it* would already be established by the rule 'laśakvataddhite,' and thus the letter *ṅ* would be prescribed merely as an augment (*āgama*). That is not so.

The inclusion of the word *id* would be for the purpose that the designation *it* should apply only when [the condition] exists by that [rule], and not otherwise. But what is the distinction here between it [the previous rule] being present or this one? This is the distinction: if that [previous rule] were present, there would be elision (*lopa*); however, with this [rule], there is not. Because of the reference to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) by the word *tasya* ("of that"), it means "of this very thing under discussion which has been designated as *it*. And thus, the operations dependent on being *ṅit* (having the marker *ṅ*) take place only while the letter *ṅ* is actually being heard.

In this regard, concerning the rule *'neḍvaśi kṛti'* (Pāṇini 7.2.8), if the term *kṛti* is intended as a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*) of suffixes beginning with *man*, then because there is no prohibition here, forms such as *kuṭiṅā* and *kuṭiṅam* would result. However, if it is instead intended as an illustration of possible examples (*sambhavodāharaṇapradarśana*), then even here, due to the prohibition, forms such as *kuṭṅā* and *kuṭṅam* would result. But in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, those well-known suffixes marked with *ṅ*—namely *ṅa* and so on—which serve as substitutes for *tṛc* and others, would indeed apply.

Nor is the rule established by proximity (*antarya*); for the maxim of proximity (*antaratama-paribhāṣā*) applies only where there is a possibility of both a most proximate and a non-most-proximate substitute. However, in this case, there is no possibility of substitutes such as *tavyat* or *aṅ* being most proximate, because they are not established either in common usage or in the grammatical treatises. Furthermore, the maxim of proximity itself cannot posit those [substitutes], as its function is merely to restrict choice among available options. Even if *tavyat*, *aṅ*, and so on were to exist, since they would be substitutes, they would—by the rule "that which has *ḍ* as an indicatory letter replaces only the final phoneme"—replace only the final letter of the original.

But surely, there is no relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) here that is directly stated by the Vedic revelation (*śrauta*); what then? The word "provided with a *ṅ*-letter" (*ṅit*) means that a suffix (*pratyaya*) following roots beginning with *gāṅ* and *kuṭ* is designated as having the marker *ṅ*. This is merely a restatement of an established fact (*siddhānuvāda*), the function of whose syllables is limited to that.
