However, since such a restatement of an established fact is not possible without a prior injunction, an injunction for the *ṅ*-letter itself, which serves as the marker (*itsaṃjñaka*), is inferred.

What follows from this? If it were so, then since no injunctive statement (*vidhivākya*) has been heard, where could a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) find its application—as in "the genitive denotes the place of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*), or "of that which follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*), or "that which is marked with Ṭ is [substituted for] the whole" (*ḍicca*)? This is not the case, because by means of the assumption of the genitive case, the very relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is established as directly expressed by the text (*śrauta*). Or, let there be an assumed injunction; yet, the *paribhāṣā* becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only to that specific injunction which is being assumed.

Because the *paribhāṣās* are ancillaries (*aṅga*) to the injunctions (*vidhi*). Indeed, since the *paribhāṣās* are constituent parts of the injunctions, they are inferred as injunctional statements themselves through the principle that the literal meaning heard in an explanatory statement (*anuvādavākya*) would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, this position is in every respect flawed.

In the rule *saṃjñākaraṇe 'kṅiti ca*, there would be no inclusion of this [term *kit*] because its technical form (*saṃjñārūpa*) has not been explicitly uttered. The word *ṅit* is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and since the word *ḍit* is what is actually uttered, even though the term *it* is connected to each [of them], the inclusion of this [term *kit*] would only achieve the meaning "that which has *k* as its *it*" (*kid yasya*). Furthermore, because there is no recognition that a technical name is a meaningful compound consisting of two parts, there would be no inclusion of this [term *kit*] at all in the various rules concerning *kṅit*.

Likewise, when the term *ṅit* is uttered in its absolute form (*kevala*), there would be the apprehension of that [term] alone, and not of *yaṅ* and the rest; for between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), the application of an operation is understood to apply to the artificial one. Consequently, the *samprasāraṇa* substitution prescribed for roots such as *grah* and *jyā* would occur in forms like *gṛhṇāti*, but not in forms like *jarīgṛhyate*. Nor is the *ṅit*-marking of *yaṅ* and the others redundant; for in the various rules (*pradeśa*) concerning *kṅit*, where the technical name (*saṃjñā*) itself is not recognized, the *ṅit* serves the purpose of including those suffixes.

But surely, in this case, the prescription of the designation *ṅit* for what follows *gāṅ*, *kuṭ*, and so forth, would result in being purposeless. Why? Because it has already been stated that there is no mention of this [designation] in the rules concerning *ṅit*. Furthermore, the word *hi* occurs only in the rule *grahijyā-*, and there *gāṅ* is not included, nor are all the roots beginning with *kuṭ*; rather, it is only *vyati* [that is mentioned]. What can we do when the matter is established by logic? Let this position be abandoned.

Thus, because these [other] positions are flawed, he states the fourth position, saying: "This is an extended application (*atideśa*). It is understood as the substitute for *iṅ*, which is prescribed by the rules "for *iṅ*, *cāṅ* is substituted in the *liṭ*" and "optionally in the *luṅ* and *luṅ*. This is because the letter *ṅ* has no other purpose. For the *ṅ* that belongs to the substitute for *iṅ* has this sole purpose: that there may be the inclusion of that very [substitute] here. Now, why does it not result in a general inclusion? Because the substitute is not identical [to the original]. The letter *ṅ* serves another purpose; [namely, to indicate the substitution of *cāṅ*].

Since [the desired result] is already established by the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element) for the *ātmanepada*, the [mention of the] verbal root (*dhātu*) serves a purpose. If this is so, then upon the mention of *āP*, only *cāP* would be understood [as the referent], because the letter *P* has no other function; [this is] not so. For if it were thus, the two *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) of *cāP* and the *Ṭ* of *ṭāP* would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, whatever is common and possible—both that which has a realized purpose (*caritārtha*) and that which has not—is relied upon, and not merely that which consists of the form *āP*. [The example is given: *kuṅ śabda* ("to sound").

Immediately thereafter, because we observe the usage "ākūtam" in the formation of the word *vṛt*, the meaning of the suffix *vat* is understood even without the suffix itself, according to the rule "the root *kūṅ* ending in a long vowel becomes like a *ṅit*"; this is just as in the expression "the boy is a lion."

If this is an *atideśa* (extended application), then even in the section beginning with "the *liṭ* [affix] following a root not joined with a consonant is *kit*," an *atideśa* of the *kit*-operation must be admitted. Consequently, in the case of *sisṛkṣati*, even though there is an *atideśa* of *kit*-ness for the *san* suffix by the rule "after a [root] ending in a consonant" (*halantācca*), the augment *am* would still apply by the rule "for the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*" (*sṛjidṛśoḥ*), on the basis of its own inherent (*svāśraya*) non-*kit*-ness; for by means of an *atideśa*, an operation dependent on another is obtained, but one's own inherent [status] is not negated. However, the correct conclusion is established through the principle of absolute prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*): that [the augment] does not occur when there is a *kit* [suffix].

And consequently, because the effect (*kārya*) that would reside in its own locus is absent, there will be a prohibition based on the *ṅit*-ness transferred [from the root]. But in this case, in *uccukuṭiṣati*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would apply by the rule "after a *ṅit* [root]"? The middle voice is prescribed for a root that is *ṅit*; however, here the *ṅit*-ness belongs to the suffix *san* itself through transfer, not to the root. Where a grammatical mark (*liṅga*) has no other scope within a constituent part, it serves as a qualifier for the whole; but here, the purpose of the *ṅit*-ness—such as the prohibition of *guṇa*—applies to the constituent part itself.

In that case, it would not apply even to a root ending in *yaṅ*; therefore, it cannot be understood thus—that [the rule] "of a root ending in *ṅ*" applies—and consequently, one might think that the *ātmanepada* suffix is obtained by relying solely on the single *san* as being *ṅit*. This is not a fault. The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative case: "as if *ṅit*" is *ṅidvat*. But surely, the suffix *vati* is not explicitly mentioned here? True; however, because another word (*para*) is employed in the subsequent rule, the implied *vati* is understood from the commentary to be derived from a locative form.

Even so, would the locative case not still apply to the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) in the rule *añṇiti*? If that is the case, then in the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ*, the word *upadeśe* (in the original enunciation) is understood; thus, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after that which is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* in its original enunciation. As in *adhyagīṣata*: here, the substitution of *gāṅ* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ*, and the change to *ī* occurs by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* within the *ghumāsthā* group.

Regarding *vyaceḥ* and so forth: the root *vyaca* (meaning "to deceive" or "to act fraudulently") is listed among the *tud*-class roots, prior to the *kuṭādi* group. In *udvicitā*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā*.

*Uruvyacas* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. How is it derived? This is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the suffix *asun* by the rule "not in *anas*" (*anasi*); having applied this, the grammatical operation is understood to apply to a *kṛt* suffix similar to that.

"How is it that *likh* is written [in the rule], since it will be written by itself, given that *kuṭ* is recited before *likh*? Someone says: "The term *kuṭādiḥ* means those for which *kuṭ* is the first (*kuṭ ādir yeṣām te kuṭādayaḥ*). When there is a desire to express both a *bahuvrīhi* and a *tatpuruṣa* together—as in 'the *kuṭādi* [group] and the *kuṭādis* [group]'—the rule 'among those whose vowels differ, that after which the subsequent vowel-rule applies is what remains' causes the *bahuvrīhi* to remain. In that case, even *likh*, being included through its occurrence within the *tatpuruṣa* compound, is the cause for the *ṅit* designation."

Having written thus—*likhitvā*, *lekhitvā*; *lilikhiṣati*, *lilekhiṣati*—the [Vārttika] "in the case of birds and scratching" (*śakuniṣvālekha*) would be untenable. Therefore, if it must necessarily be justified: on the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not eternal," there will be no *guṇa* substitution. Furthermore, regarding the root *dhū* in the sense of "shaking," which belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, the *guṇa* substitution does not apply when the suffix *itra* is added according to the rule "after the roots *ṛt*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, *sah*, and *car*, the suffix *itra* is added."

No specific quality (*guṇa*) is intended here; it simply becomes *dhuvitra*. However, the applications found in the *Kalpasūtras* must be justified on the grounds that they follow Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, the formation of a distinct suffix—when one could have simply stated "the suffix *ghurac* is added after the roots *bhañj*, *bhās*, and *mid*, provided they end in *ṅit* (i.e., *cvi*, *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid*)"—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *ṅittva* status [of the root] derived by extension (*ātideśika*) is not invariably obligatory.
The vowel *i* is designated as *it*. 1.2.2.

The root *ovijī* is used in the sense of "fear" and "trembling. As for the *vici* suffix mentioned in the rule "the roots *sṛji*, *vijī*, and *vidi* are without the augment *iṭ* when followed by vowels," that [root] is not intended here, because it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). The other [root], however, is *seṭ* (possessing the *iṭ* augment) by virtue of its being marked with the indicatory letter *ī*. From the rule defining the technical term *vṛddha*, the phrase "of which the first [sound]" is understood; by this, the *iṭ* is qualified as "that *iṭ* which is the first [element]. Consequently, there is no inclusion of the third-person singular ending (*uttamaikavacana*), for that is never the first element of anything.

For this very reason, this rule for the *ṅit*-designation does not apply to the verbal root alone; rather, it applies to the suffix beginning with that [root]. Thus he says: "the suffix beginning with *iṭ*. In the form *udvicitā*, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel due to the *ṅit*-designation.
The substitution of *vi* for the prefix *vi* occurs before the verbal root *ūrṇu*. (Pāṇini 1.2.3)

The root *ūrṇuñ* itself means "to cover"; it has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). Its reading with *ṇ* is due to the rule "after *r* and *ṣ*" (*raṣābhyām*). In *prorṇunāva*, when the *r* is elided, the *n* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is heard. In *prorṇuvīta*, if the root is treated as having the marker *ṅit*, there is *uvaṅ*; otherwise, there is *guṇa*.
A sārvadhātuka affix that is not marked with P (apit) is termed ṅit.

If "api" is taken as a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), then in the case of *cyavante*—where the form is *cyu-a-ante*—the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would necessarily occur because it is both obligatory and internal (*antaraṅga*). Nor can one argue that an operation concerning vowels (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning suffixes (*āṅga*), because their bases (*āśraya*) are different. Once that [single substitute] has been applied, since the subsequent element (*iha*) depends on it, the substitute behaves like the initial (*ādivadbhāva*) with respect to it; thus, the single substitute for *pi* and *api* would be included by the term "api. Consequently, because the *sārvadhātuka* suffix following a root ending in a single substitute would be marked as *ṅit*, the prohibition of *guṇa* would result.

But in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the negation is caused by the *pit* status [of the affix], and thus the preceding element is as if it were "final" (*antavat*) with respect to that [negation]; consequently, there is an absence of *ṅit*-status. Well then, let it be a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*. If that were so, in the form *tudāni*, when the prohibition of *ṅit*-status for the subsequent *pit* [augment] is to be applied to the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) of the *vikaraṇa* and the first person ending (*uttama*), the rule "as if it were the beginning" (*ādivat syāt*) would apply; thus, depending on the first person ending as being *aṅit*, *guṇa* would result. In the rule "as if it were the end or the beginning" (*antādivacca*), the intended referents are the two composite wholes (*samudāya*) consisting of the preceding and following elements, not the individual letters (*aca*).

What is the reason? Because [the vowels] *a* and *c* are constituent parts (*avayava*) at the beginning and end, and because the two substituends (*sthānin*)—*a* and *c*—have been replaced by the single substitute (*ekādeśa*). Therefore, since *a* and *c* are the preceding and following elements of the two composite units (*samudāya*) that possess the ends and beginnings [of the word], the single substitute also comes to have the status of being like the end and the beginning of those very same units; this is the meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*). For this very reason, in the case of *brahmabandhūḥ*, the single substitute also becomes like the end with respect to the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) itself. However, in the case of *dhruvai tu vai*, since the single substitute occurs for the entire pair *pit-apit* in the nominative singular, there would indeed be a fault if only *a* and *c* were treated as having the status of the beginning and end.

In that case, because of the status of the single-substitute (ekādeśa) as being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) with respect to an operation concerning what precedes it, just as the application or non-application of *guṇa* occurs appropriately at the time of the original [vowels] in both alternatives, so too will they occur even when the single-substitute has been applied, by virtue of the cognition of the original.

Thus, even though both [interpretations] are faultless, one must resort to the prohibition of what was previously enjoined (*pratiṣedha*). For in that case—by the very power of resorting to it—there is a prohibition of all the *ṅit*-ness that had been obtained for whatever [suffixes] and to whatever extent from the root *pi*, and thus this also becomes established: *acinot* and *acinavam*. For here, there occurs a prohibition of the *ṅit*-ness which had been obtained for the substitute of the *laṅ* [suffix] by virtue of its being a *sthānivadbhāva* [substitute].

But in the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), because there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the extended application (*atideśa*), that very [element] would be excluded; thus, the *ṅit*-ness produced by the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would certainly remain. Consequently, the explicit statement of *ṅit*-ness for *yāsuṭ* would have to be regarded as an interpretive indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, this meaning—that "what is *ṅit* is not *pit*"—is also desired here.

Therefore, in the example *brūtād bhavān*, because the status of being *pit* (which would apply by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *tātaṅ* substitute) is prohibited, the substitution of *iṇ* for the root *bru-* does not occur on account of its being *pit*. Similarly, in *tṛṇaḍḍhvam bhavān*, the substitution of *iṇ* for the root *tṛṇah-* does not occur. This is the general principle. For this reason as well, a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) must be adopted; for in that case, the negative particle (*nañ*), having been separated [from the verb], can be connected as desired: "the *pit* is not *ṅit*" and "the *ṅit* is not *pit*."

In this regard, it must be distinguished that for that [element] whose *pittva* (the status of being a *pit* suffix) is original (*aupadeśika*), its *ṅittva* (the status of being a *ṅit* suffix)—whether obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) or obtained through the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*—is prohibited; whereas for that [element] whose *ṅittva* is original, its *pittva* obtained through *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited.

"Perform [the action]," [he says]. Because the affix is marked with the *ṅit* indicator, there is an absence of *guṇa* for the *vikaraṇa*, and by the rule "ata utsārvadhātuke," the substitution of *ut* occurs. In this case, the suffix *vat* should be understood as having the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*) as its basis, not as before from that which has the seventh case (*saptamīsamartha*). Consequently, in the form *pacete*, even that operation which belongs to a *ṅit* affix—namely, "āto ṅitaḥ"—also takes place. If this is so, then in *cinutaḥ*, would the rule "tāsyanudāttet" not result in the *anudātta* accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*? This is not a fault; [The reason is: because the *ṅit* marker here serves to prevent *guṇa*, and not to indicate that the *lasārvadhātuka* is *anudātta*. Otherwise, in forms such as *pacete*, the *anudātta* accent would not occur. Therefore, since the *ṅit* marker here indicates the absence of *guṇa*, the *lasārvadhātuka* accent does not apply. Thus, there is no fault.

The term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is connected with both [cases]: "because of instruction with *ṅ*," and "because of instruction with *at*. Alternatively, due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "before *ah* and *iṅ*" (*ahnviṅoḥ*), there is the inclusion of that which is similar to it—namely, that which possesses the *ṅakāra* in its instruction. Thus, everything is faultless.
The *liṭ* suffix is marked with the *k* it-marker when it follows a verbal root that does not end in a conjunct consonant.

He says, "from a root ending in a non-conjunct," because the verbal root (dhātu) implied by the [suffix] liṭ is qualified by the mention of "non-conjunct" (asaṃyoga). Now, one might object: here a *paryudāsa* (exclusion) appears to be intended; and if so, the rule would apply only to those ending in a consonant (*hal*) that resemble a conjunct, such as in *bibhidatuḥ*, *bibhiduḥ*, and so forth.

But would this not fail in cases such as *ninayuḥ*? It is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author prescribes the *guṇa* substitution in *sasmaratuḥ* and so forth by the rule "there is *guṇa* for [a root] ending in *ṛ* that begins with a conjunct consonant" (*ṛtaśca saṃyogāderguṇaḥ*), this indicates that here the maxim of "the negative particle and the word *iva*" (*nañ-iva-yukta-nyāya*) does not apply, and the term refers to the verbal root alone. The purpose of extending the status of being *kit* (even though the status of being *ṅit* is already applicable) is so that there may be vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "for roots beginning with *yaj*, etc., when a *kit* suffix follows," as in *ījanam*, *ījatḥ*, and *ījuḥ*.

They two woke, they woke—so that the *guṇa* substitution may occur by the rule "there is *guṇa* for *jāgṛ* before *viciṇṇalṅit*" (*jāgro 'viciṇṇalṅitsu*). But if, on the other hand, *kittva* were extended even to *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group, this would not be possible; for in that case a fault would arise here: from the roots *ṇu* (in the sense of praise) and *dhū* (in the sense of shaking), with the suffix *tṛc*, we get *nuvitṛ* and *dhuvitṛ*. By the rule "there is a prohibition of *iṭ* after a root ending in *śr*, *ū*, or *ṛ* before a *kit* suffix" (*śryukaḥ kiti*), the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply, as in *lūtvā* and *lūnaḥ*. This is not a fault; for it has been stated that this is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) of the preceding [rule].

In this case, then, having applied the suffix *kuṭ* and *puṭ*, [one might argue] that by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" (Pāṇini 1.2.18), there is a prohibition of *kittva* even for that which is transferred (*ātideśika*), but not for that which is [inherently] transferred. This is true; however, if the mention of *ktvā* were absent, then when it is present, the prohibition of *san* by the rule "na ktvā seṭ" would not be obtained. Thus, it will be stated as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition "na ktvā seṭ" does not apply to that which is transferred. This is true.

If the mention of *ḍha* were not made, then when that [mention of *ḍha*] exists, the prohibition "na ktvā seṭ" would not apply to the suffix *san*; therefore, the mention of *ḍha* there serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Similarly, in the case of the extended application (*atideśa*) of *kit*-status by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit," there would be *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *jāgṛtaḥ* and *jāgrati*; however, if the extended application of *ṅit*-status is intended, there occurs the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "aviciṇṇalṅitsu. Furthermore, regarding the *kit*-status of the *liṭ* suffix after roots with *ṛ* in the penultimate syllable, it is established by a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) over *guṇa*.

The scope for *kittva* (the status of having the *k*-marker) is seen in forms such as *ṛjatuḥ* and *ṛjuḥ*, where there is no possibility of any other rule applying. The scope for *guṇa* (vocalization) is seen in forms such as *varttitvā*, *vardhitvā*, *vavṛte*, and *vavṛdhuḥ*; here, when both [rules] would apply, *kittva* prevails by virtue of the "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). However, in cases such as *bibhidatuḥ* and *bibhiduḥ*, *kittva* is established simply because it is a permanent (*nitya*) rule; for that [status of *kittva*] applies whether the *guṇa* has already occurred or not, whereas *guṇa* does not apply once *kittva* is present.

In the case of *vavṛte*, however, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, the status of being *kit* would not apply because of the presence of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) at the end; thus, since both [rules] are non-permanent (*anitya*), a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is stated. And this must be explicitly stated in the view that the rule effects an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśapakṣa*). For, by this very [rule], there is an extension of the *kit*-operation in forms such as *ījatuḥ*; where another rule does not otherwise apply, the *samprasāraṇa* would have its purpose fulfilled, yet the subsequent *guṇa* would subvert that extension.

Or, in the case of the extension of a rule (*śāstrātideśa*), the rule "before *k* and *ṅi*" (*akṅiti ca*) is extended; and although that [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [general] rule for *guṇa*, nevertheless, because it has already served its purpose elsewhere, the prohibition "before *k* and *ṅi*"—being extended by a weaker extension—is itself weak. Thus, having set aside that [prohibition], the *guṇa* would indeed occur.
And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] after the roots *indh* and *bhū*. (Pāṇini 3.1.6)

In *indh*, the vowel *i* is adventitious (*āgantu*), and not the suffix *ik* prescribed by the rule *ik-śtipau dhātunirdeśe*; therefore, the elision of *n* by the rule *aniditām* does not occur. Regarding *samīdhe*: the root *ñi-indhī* (in the sense of "shining") is anudātta; because the suffix *eś* is *kit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel by *aniditām*, and after reduplication, a long vowel occurs by *savarṇadīrgha*. In *babhūviva* and *babhūvitha*, because the suffixes are *kit*, there is no *vṛddhi* or *guṇa* respectively.
By the phrase "for the sake of the conjunction in *indhe*" etc., he demonstrates that [the previous case] was not established, thereby justifying the formulation of the present *sūtra*.

This grammatical derivation (*yoga*) can be explained; how so? After the root *indh*, the *liṭ* suffix occurs only in the Vedic language (*chandas*). However, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), by the rule *ijādeśca*, the suffix *ām* ought to occur. Furthermore, in the Vedic language, by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the *liṭ* suffix receives the designation of *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule *sārvadhātukamapit*, it is treated as having the *ṅit* marker, which results in the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). If, however, the suffix *śnam* were applied, it would receive the designation of *ārdhadhātuka*; or, due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), the absence of *śnam* may be assumed.

In the case of the root *bhū* as well, the augment *vuk* is prescribed by the rule "vug for *bhū* in the *luṅ* and *liṭ* [tenses]. There, when the forms *bhū-a* and *bhū-itha* have been established, both *vuk* and the operations of Vṛddhi and Guṇa would apply. Since *vuk* applies regardless of whether the other rules have already applied or not, it is obligatory (*nitya*); furthermore, it is not obtained through the acquisition of a different word-form, because that which undergoes modification in one part remains essentially the same. Once *vuk* has been applied, however, because the root no longer ends in a vowel (*anajanta*) and its penultimate vowel is no longer light (*alaghūpadha*), neither Vṛddhi nor Guṇa will occur. One must necessarily understand this point thus: "Vṛddhi and Guṇa are superseded by *vuk*."

For one might think: "Since this [root] has a *kit* suffix, there is a prohibition against *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* by the rule 'not before a *kit*' (*kiti na*), because [the augment] *iṭ* does not have *niṅ* as its defining characteristic. If that is so, then the mention of *indh* is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). It indicates this: "The *ām* [augment] after *indh* is even non-obligatory in the common language (*bhāṣā*)," as evidenced by forms such as *samīdhe* and *samīdhāñcakre*, which occur even in the common language. Furthermore, the *vuk* [augment] after *bhū* is also non-obligatory. What is the reason? Because the word *uḥ* is still in force [from a previous rule], and once *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have been applied, the root *bhū* no longer ends in the vowel *u*.

Does it (the *uru* rule) cease? If it ceases, then in the case of *bobhū*, even when there is *yaṅluk*, the suffix *vuk* would necessarily apply because it is permanent (*nitya*). However, if *uru* continues to apply, then between these two [rules], both of which are non-permanent (*anitya*), the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions take effect first due to their higher priority; once they have occurred, the root no longer ends in a vowel (*anurvarṇāntatvāt*), and thus *vuk* does not apply. Now, why is it that by this very [rule] the *liṭ* suffix is not treated as having the *kit* designation even in the case of *yaṅluk*? Because of the instruction [given] by means of the *śtip* marker.

If, however, the *śtip* designation were made only for the rule prescribing *vuk*, this would not be possible; for in that case, there would be a fault here: *bobhūvat*, *bobhūvuḥ*. But when the *śtip* designation is made for the rule prescribing *kit*-ness and not for the rule prescribing *vuk*, then in the case of *yaṅluk* (elision of *yaṅ*) in the *pit* endings, because the *liṭ* [affixes] lack *kit*-ness, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are applied, and since the context of *uru-* applies, *vuk* does not occur.

In the case of roots ending in *i*, when the *liṭ* suffix is marked with the *k*-sign by the rule "asaṃyogālliṭ kit," there is an absence of *guṇa*; consequently, because the root ends in an *u*-vowel, the *vuk* augment occurs. Now, it was argued: "Even if the *k*-sign is applied, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is not established, because [the *vṛddhi*] is conditioned by *aṅ*. This is not a fault; for the mention of the *ṅ*-sign also continues [from the previous rule], and by its force, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* will apply even to that which is not conditioned by *aṅ*. True; this is indeed a dry logical argument.

But the author of the Vārttika does not accept this, as he says: "Since the root *indh* belongs to the domain of the Veda and since the *vuK* augment after *bhū* is obligatory, the rule prescribing that the *liṭ* suffix is *kit* after these two roots is rendered purposeless."

Regarding *śranthi-granthi* and so forth: [the roots] *śranth* and *granth* mean "to string together" (*saṃdarbhe*); *damb* means "to deceive" (*dambhe*); and *añj*, *piṣ*, and *vañj* mean "to embrace" (*aṅge*). In *śrethatuḥ* and *śrethuḥ*, because the suffix is *kit*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*); here, one must also state that the substitution of *et* (for *a*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-lopa*) apply. In *debhatuḥ*, once the *na*-elision has been performed, the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable occur by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye ’nādeśādeḥ*. Nor is this elision considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), because the unestablished status (*asiddhatva*) of rules pertaining to the *ābhīya* section is non-eternal (*anitya*). In *pariṣasvaja*, [the same applies].

In the case of the root *ṣvañj* (meaning "to embrace"), which is marked with an anudātta accent, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*. However, there is a prohibition of this substitution for the subsequent [root] by the rule *sadisvañjyoḥ parasya liṭi*. Regarding this, some read the word *vā* ("or"); thus forms such as *śaśranthatuḥ* also occur. Now, what happens in the case of *pit* endings? If the statement [of the rule] is solely for the sake of [avoiding] a *saṃyoga*, then it should not apply to *pit* endings. But if it is for the sake of [avoiding] a *saṃyogānta* [consonant cluster] and for the sake of *pit* endings as well, then it should apply even to *pit* endings. Which of these is the true meaning here? May the Lord deign to know it.
The suffix *ktvā* is added after the roots *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas*.

The root *kliś* is listed as ‘*kliśa hiṃsāyām*’ (in the sense of harming), which is *anudātta-it*, belongs to the *divādi* class, and is intransitive (*akarmaka*). The root ‘*kliśū vibādhane*’ (in the sense of afflicting) belongs to the *kryādi* class and is transitive (*sakarmaka*), taking the *parasmaipada* endings. [The sūtra] refers to both of these. But for what purpose is this [sūtra], since by that much alone [the rule] *kṛt* [suffixes] are indeed *kit*? To this he says: “*na ktvā seṭ*,” etc. [This is] an exception (*apakarṣa* = *apavāda*). [Objection: But surely this very [sūtra] will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that “*ktvā* becomes *kit* only after roots beginning with *mṛḍ*, and not after others”; thus there is no need for the [rule] “*na ktvā seṭ*”. [Response: This is not so. For if this were merely a restrictive rule, then [the rule] “*na ktvā seṭ*” would be useless, because even without it, *ktvā* would not be *kit* after roots other than those beginning with *mṛḍ*. However, since it is taught [as a general rule], it follows that *ktvā* is *kit* after all roots, except for those beginning with *mṛḍ*. Therefore, the present [sūtra] is indeed an exception to that. Thus, the meaning of the present [sūtra] is: “*ktvā* is *kit* after roots beginning with *mṛḍ*; but it is not *kit* after roots ending in a *seṭ* vowel. Consequently, the *seṭ* suffix *ktvā* is not *kit* after roots such as *mṛj* and *puṣ*. Thus, the forms *mṛṣṭvā* and *puṣṭvā* are established. Furthermore, the mention of *mṛḍ* is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, *ktvā* is also not *kit* after roots such as *kṛt* and *pṛcch*. Hence, the forms *kṛtvā* and *pṛṣṭvā* are established.
