Regarding the term *aikashrutyam*: it is a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) derived from a *bahuvrīhi* compound; alternatively, by virtue of its inclusion in the *cāturvarṇya*-group, it is a *ṣyañ* suffix added to a *karmadhāraya* compound in its own sense (*svārthe*). Regarding the phrase "recitation" (*saṃpāṭha*): at the time of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), in the mantra "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit," the word *agni* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix [by the rule *agner lopaś ca*]. The word *mūrdhan* is derived from the root *mūrvi* (meaning "to bind"); while the rule *kaniny uvṛṣitakṣi* is in force, the word *mūrdhan* is prescribed in the sūtra *śvann ukṣan pūṣan takṣan* as ending in the suffix *kanin* and being oxytone.

In the root *div* (meaning "to play" and so forth), the suffix *i* [forming *divi*] is acute according to the rule *ūḍidam*. The word *kakud* is acute on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). From the root *pat*, the suffix *ḍati* [forming *pati*]; the word *pati* is acute on the first syllable by the accent of the suffix. From the root *prath*, the suffix *ṣivan* with vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); because of the marker *ṣ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. The acute nature of the genitive singular [of *prathiṣī*] follows the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*. The word *idam* is acute on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem. From the root *āp*, the suffix *kvip* with shortening; [this is governed by] the rule *ūḍidam*.

The case ending is udātta (accented). In the word *retaḥ*, the suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule "ri gatau, sruribhyāṃ tuṭ ca"; by the accentuation of the *nit* suffix, the word *retaḥ* is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding *jinvati*: it is derived from the root *jinva* in the sense of "pleasing" (*prīṇana*); the *tip* suffix is subject to *nighāta* (elision of accent), and by the rule "praṇavaṣṭeḥ," there is the insertion of the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) at the time of recitation.

Regarding "mametyādi": [the word *mama*] has its initial syllable udātta by the rule "yuṣmadasmadorṅasi" (Pāṇini 6.1.211). The word *agneḥ* has its final syllable anudātta due to the *nighāta* rule for vocatives. The word *varcaḥ* ends in the suffix *asun*. In the case of *hvāyaḥ*, derived from the root *hve-* preceded by the prefix *vi-*, the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule "hvaḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca," and it becomes antodātta by the rule "thāthādisūtra. As for the statement "japa is an imitative mantra (*anukaraṇamantra*)," although that very same mantra is being uttered, the designation "imitation" is employed by conceptually positing a distinction based on the manifestation or non-manifestation of the phonemes.

For this very reason, he says: "the practice of whispering" (*upāṃśuprayoga*). It is like the recitation of one submerged in water. In some places, the reading is *akaraṇamantra* (non-instrumental mantra). An *instrumental mantra* (*karaṇamantra*) is that which is enjoined as "one should do this with this"; other than that is the non-instrumental mantra. However, the well-known reading is *antahkaraṇamantra* (internal instrumental mantra). Now, an objection: sound is uttered by the organ of speech; how then can it be designated by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is common to all the senses? True.

In the case of whispered recitation (*upāṃśu-prayoga*), there is no gross activity of the organ of speech, and since that [activity] alone is well-known as its function, it is considered that the mind itself is primary in subtle activity.

Regarding "nyūṅkhā" and so forth: the reading is "ṣoḍaśa" (sixteen) and "okārāḥ" (the *o*-sounds), but these do not end in the letter *m*. Among them, the first, seventh, and thirteenth—these three—are acute (*udātta*) and consist of three morae (*trimātra*); the remaining thirteen are grave (*anudātta*) and consist of half an *o*-sound (*ardhaukāra*). This has been stated by Āśvalāyana in the section beginning with "on the fourth day" (*caturthe'hani*), where it is both defined and illustrated. If the reading were "ṣaḍoṅkārāḥ," another source for the root text would have to be sought. Regarding "e3 viśvam" and so forth: the sound *e* serves to complete the chant; others say it is a particle (*nipāta*).

The word *viśva* ends in the suffix *kvan*, and is thus accented on its first syllable; the connection is "completely burn away the evil that is the counselor"; due to the influence of the chant (*gīti*), the word *viśva* consists of multiple morae (*mātrā*). For chants reside within specific sentences. As it has been stated by the Seer: "The designation *Sāman* applies to chants."
Or rather, the *vaṣaṭ*-call [should be uttered] at a higher pitch. 1.2.35.

And here, by the word *vaṣaṭ*, the word *vauṣaṭ* is indicated; for since they have the same meaning, both of them signify the offering to the deity. The mention of the suffix *kāra* is an indicator that the suffix *kāra* occurs even after a vowel (*a-varṇa*). By this, forms such as *evakāra* are established.

"If it is so," [means: the sense is that in the case of *lakṣaṇā* (indication), there is a heaviness of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*). "For they are diverse" means: in some cases brevity of syllables (*akṣara-lāghava*) is resorted to, while in others brevity of comprehension (*pratipatti-lāghava*) is; such is the diversity. "In a higher pitch" (*uccaistarām*): the word *uccais* occurs in the sense of the production of the acute accent (*udātta*); in that context, the suffix is applied with reference to the action of producing (*bhavana-kriyā*).

The intended meaning is "more acute" (*udāttatara*). This excellence is to be understood in relation to the protracted (*pluta*) accent prescribed by the rule *abrūhipreṣayaśrauṣaḍvauṣaḍvahanāmādeḥ*; for while there are [other] acute accents, this one is more acute. Some say it applies to the final portion (*antyasadeśa*). Others say that because of the force of prescribing a protracted acute, there is no suppression (*nighāta*) of the remaining syllables; or else, because [the protracted accent] is not established [as a fixed rule], the more acute accent occurs for both vowels.

In that case, others maintain that the suffix *tarap* has its own inherent sense of excellence (*prakarpa*) dependent upon the end of the *yājyā* verse; for it is established that the first vowel is merely acute (*udātta*), and thus the rule is prescribed for the second vowel. This word *vaṣaṭkāra* is conventionally used (*nirūḍha*) in the *kalpasūtras* for the word *vauṣaṭ*. It is called *vaṣaṭkāra* because "by this [utterance] the *vaṣaṭ* is performed. In the mantra "mā māṃ pramṛja," as well as in the Brāhmaṇa passage "There are indeed three *vaṣaṭkāras*; he performs the *vaṣaṭ* with *vauṣaṭ*," the *vaṣaṭkāra* is the final [syllable].

Regarding the sūtra, "In every case, [the subsequent mantra] is louder and more powerful than the preceding yājyā," they say that by the term *uccaistarām*, an intensification of the pitch is enjoined.
In the Vedic language, there is an option. (Pāṇini 1.2.36)

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of excluding [the rule] from sacrificial rites": if this rule were restricted to sacrificial rites, then the preceding rule would be without scope. Nor can it be established that the scope of the preceding rule consists of *japa*, *nyūṅkha*, and *sāman* in general, while its scope is distinct from *japa* and the others.

For if this were the case, the mention of *japa* (muttering) and so forth would have to be made right here; what then would be the purpose of mentioning *chandas* (Vedic meters)? From the mention of *chandas*, however, it is understood that this option applies only to those [mantras] consisting of Vedic meters. Consequently, if the phrase "in sacrificial rites" (*yajñakarmaṇi*) were to carry over [from the previous rule], the preceding obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*) would become devoid of scope. Thus he thinks: since *ūha*-mantras (mantras with substitutions) lack the nature of Vedic meters, they fall within the scope of the previous rule; therefore, this very option would apply only to mantras that possess the form of Vedic meters.

If the previous rule (*yoga*) applies with scope to *ūha*-mantras, then—even though [the application of] "in the sacrificial ritual" (*yajñakarmaṇi*) is excluded by the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*)—this very alternative would still apply to unmodified mantras that are of the nature of *chandas* (Vedic), because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. This is not a fault; for the inclusion of the word "ritual" (*karman*) in the phrase "in the sacrificial ritual" is for the purpose that the rule may be obligatory everywhere in the mere performance of a sacrifice.

Even though the mantras being recited (*ūhyamāna*) are not [actual] *mantra*s, nevertheless, when they are employed in a sacrificial rite (*yajñakarman*), they certainly fall within the scope of the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*). As for those who maintain that, by the exclusion of *japa* and so forth, only actual *mantra*s are intended there, for them the exclusion of the phrase "in a sacrificial rite" would have to be understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*); thus, the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) would be redundant. Regarding *iṣa* and so on: *iṣ* is food (*anna*), and *ūrj* is strength (*bala*).

In the fourth case singular, the vowel is acute by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. By the rule *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ*, the substitute *tvā* is grave (*anudātta*). In *agne*, the first syllable is acute because it is the beginning of a vocative. *Āṅ* is a prefix. Regarding *yāhi*: by the rules *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* and *mantre vṛṣeṣapaca...*, the suffix *ktin* is acute; the word *agni* has its final syllable acute. In the case of *ami pūrvatvam*, the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels is acute by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*. Regarding *īle*: from the root *īḍ* (to praise), this is the first person singular present indicative.

The Bahvṛcas prescribe the substitution of *l* for the letter *ḍ* situated between two vowels, as in *purohitam*. Here, by the rule "the indeclinable *puras* [is a *gati*]," it receives the designation of *gati*; then, by the rule "an immediate *gati* [causes the first member to retain its original accent]," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. The word *puras*, ending in the suffix *asi*, is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).

The word *śam* is a particle (*nipāta*). Its substitute *naḥ* is unaccented (*anudātta*). *Devadatta* is listed among the *pacādi* group; because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding the rule "and [the vowel] of that which is unaccented, where there is elision of an acute accent," and in cases such as *abhiṣṭi*—derived from the root *iṣ* preceded by *abhi* with the suffix *ktin*—there is a single-substitute form (*pararūpa*) according to the *śakandhvādi* group. Furthermore, in the dative singular, the word *abhi* is acutely accented on its final syllable by the rule "the original accent of the preceding member [remains] before a suffix beginning with *n* and having *kṛt* or *taddhita* [as its marker]. However, this does not apply in the case of *subrahmaṇyā*, where an acute accent (*udātta*) replaces a circumflex (*svarita*). 1.2.37. *na subrahmaṇyāyāṃ svaritasya tūdāttaḥ*.

"The *nigada* is that which is called *subrahmaṇyā*. The root *gad* occurs in the sense of "unbound prose" (*apādabandha*), as in the word *gadya*; the prefix *ni-* denotes excellence. A mantra-sentence consisting of *yajus* that is recited loudly and in unbound prose is a *nigada*, because it is "uttered intensely" (*nitarāṃ gadyate*). The suffix *ap* is applied here according to the rule *nau gadanada*. And since it is characterized by the word *subrahmaṇyā*, its name is simply *subrahmaṇyā*, retaining the feminine gender.

The syllable *oṃ* is circumflex (*svarita*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix *ti*. [In the word *subrahmaṇī*,] because it is "correct in the *subrahmaṇyā*" (*subrahmaṇi sādhuh*), the suffix *yat* is applied; it is circumflex by the accent of the suffix *ti*. When the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for that [circumflex *ī* and the following vowel]; since this is a combination of a circumflex and an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel, it is circumflex due to their proximity. Then, through the elision (*nipāta*) of the word *oṃ* with the word *nau*, there is a single-substitute for the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex vowels according to the rule "omāṅośca," and thus it remains circumflex. However, the elision (*nighāta*) prescribed in the eighth book—namely, "the vocative (*āmantrita*) is acute on its first syllable"—does not apply here because they do not form a single syntactical sentence (*asamānavākyatva*). [The phrase] "by this of that" refers to that [circumflex].

Nor is that [reason] unestablished (*asiddhatva*), for it has been stated that this section must be transferred to the *Asiddhakāṇḍa*. For this very reason, when this [vowel] is made acute (*udātta*), the subsequent grave accent (*śeṣanighāta*) does not occur either; because under the view that the rule applies according to its enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), when the paribhāṣā regarding the grave accent is to be applied, there is no absence of the [vowels] to be excluded due to their being unestablished. Consequently, two vowels here become acute, while the final one is grave. Nor does the contingency of a circumflex (*svarita*) arise for that [grave vowel] by virtue of the rule "after an acute, [the following] grave" (*udāttādanudāttasya*).

Because it is not established by the extension of the present context, and because of the prohibition "not [a vowel] followed by an acute or circumflex," there are two grave (anudātta) vowels. These are the *va* and the *cha*; the rest is clear. Regarding the rule "the end of 'asau' and 'amuṣya'": in this very *Subrahmaṇyā* litany, the final syllable of both the nominative and the genitive forms becomes acute. For example: *gārgyo yajate* and *dākṣeḥ pitā yajate*. This statement is made because the [general] accentual rule (*titsvara*) would otherwise apply.

"In the case of a word ending in *sya*, both the penultimate and the final syllables are acute. For example: *gārgyasya pitā yajate* ("the father of Gārgya sacrifices") or *nāmedhayasya*; [and] *devadattasya pitā yajate* ("Devadatta’s father sacrifices").
The [vowel] following the words *deva* and *brahman* is unaccented.

"Regarding the statement *svaritasyodātte prāpte* (when the udātta [pitch] would have applied to the svarita): how is it obtained, given that the svarita is *asiddha* (not yet established)? In that case, the Teacher provides this indication (*jñāpaka*): the group of nine rules beginning with *tasyāditaḥ* is to be regarded as following after the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*. The purposes [of this indication] have been stated, and we shall explain them further below. Because the indication applies generally, the entire group of nine rules is displaced, not merely the accentuation of the *subrahmaṇyā* formula alone. [This applies] to both words."

For the second [vocative], the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) does not occur even though it is followed by a word (*padapara*), because the preceding [vocative] is considered non-existent according to the rule "a preceding vocative is as if non-existent. For the first [vocative] either, it does not occur, because they constitute separate sentences (*bhinnavākyatva*).
In continuous recitation (saṃhitā), [the anudātta vowels] following a svarita [vowel take the udātta accent]. 1.2.39.

The plural number in *anudāttānām* refers to the genus (*jāti*); therefore, it applies to one, two, or many. For one: *pacati*; for two: *āgniveśyaḥ*; as for many, it has already been shown in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Regarding the statement "the word *ita-* is oxytone": the stem *idam-* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), while the case-ending is unaccented (*anudātta*); when the substitution of *yat* occurs (yielding *iyat-*), the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* applies, and then by *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the resulting single substitute is oxytone. The phrase "only at the time of the rule's application" (*vidhi-kāla eva*) [is explained as follows].

Although there is no fault whatsoever even if the anudātta [accent] were prescribed here for that which is already enjoined, it was stated nevertheless so that one should deal with it as such [an independent entity]. Therefore, [the rule states] "after a svarita. Nor is that [svarita] non-existent (*asiddha*); because the group of nine sūtras is superior, the effect [of the svarita] occurs just as in the case of *devadatta* and so forth, and thus there is indeed a single audible unit (*ekaśruti*). Regarding the words "of *gaṅgā* etc.": there is no intervention by *yamunā* and so forth; because the genus (*jāti*) is one, and because the individual instances (*vyakti*), though existing, are not relied upon, they are of no consequence.

Regarding the phrase "tataḥ pareṣām" (after those): by the rule "nāmantrite samānādhikaraṇe," the word *māṇavaka* does not become non-existent [for the purposes of the preceding rule]. This is so that [the effect] does not fail to occur when there is an avagraha (word-break). And this very mention of *saṃhitā* (continuous connection) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in the case of a reference in the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), time [or a pause] does not cause an intervention. Therefore, even in the case of an avagraha, the rule "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ" applies—as in *agnim īḷe*. [Now follows: "That which follows an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel becomes more depressed (*sannatara*). (P. 1.2.40)

He states that the word *para* (following) is connected with each [term]: "that from which the following [syllable] is udātta. By the word *sanna*, the meaning "low" (*nīcaiḥ*) is expressed; thus he says "anudāttatara" (more anudātta), as it indicates the quality of being anudātta. The excellence [expressed by the suffix -tara] is in relation to the original anudātta [of the preceding syllable]. Regarding "mātaraḥ" being anudātta: a portion of the compound is extracted and reproduced; when the three vocatives beginning with "devāḥ" are treated as a single unit and become ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable), the remaining syllables are subject to the rule of *śeṣanighāta* (the rest are unaccented).

Regarding the statement, "The plural number is used in the sense of a specific enumeration," when this position is accepted, there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the vocative; the *sakāra* of *jasaḥ* becomes *ru*; for that *ru*, which is subject to elision (*sraṃsana*), the vowel *u* is produced by the rule "ato roraplutāt," and it is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule "ād guṇaḥ," the resulting *guṇa* vowel is also unaccented due to internal correspondence (*āntarya*). For the vowel *ā* of the word *accha*, there is the *śeṣanighāta* (the remaining syllables are unaccented). Between those two unaccented vowels, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) by the rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" is unaccented due to internal correspondence. [This refers to] the vowel *ī* of the word *sarasvatī*.

But has it not been indicated that the ninth sūtra is displaced? And consequently, as in the case of Gaṅgā and others, even for the *sarasvatī* accent, only a single tone (*ekaśruti*) would result from the preceding rule; what then would be the scope for the *sannatara* (lower) accent, which does not follow a *svarita*? [The answer is: "Agni. Nor can the *sannatara* be obtained by means of a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*); for where the preceding is not established, there is no conflict of rules due to the absence of a subsequent [rule].

If that is the case, then in the rule *na mu ne*, the desired result will be established through the separation of the *yoga* (splitting the rule as *na mu* and *ne*). Here, in *devadattasya nyaṅ*, when the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies by the rule *nyadhī ca*, the circumflex (*svarita*) on the vowel *a* of the root *añc*—by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*—is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the preceding lower-pitched (*sannatara*) vowel; this is because of the promotion (*utkarṣa*) of the section [of the rule]. Since the result is already established by the words *udāttasvaritayoḥ* alone, the inclusion of the word *para* (in the full rule *udāttātsvaritaparasya*) is for the purpose of expressing the singular number in a *bahuvrīhi* compound; thus, there is an absence of the *sannatara* accent in forms such as *gaṅge*.
An *apṛkta* suffix consists of a single phoneme. 1.2.41.

Regarding *ghṛtaspṛk*: the substitution of *k* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*. Regarding *arthabhāk*: here, the purpose is the elision [of the *v*] by the rule *ver apṛktasya*. [The author asks: "What is the purpose of including the term *ekāl* [in the sūtra]?"

This question concerns a single phoneme (*ekapada*) by way of the aggregate (*samudāya*); otherwise, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply to the suffix alone, and in the various rules (*pradeśa*), one would have to mention the suffix itself—what would be the use of the designation? If it were to apply to that which ends in a vowel (*al-anta*), then because even a simple [suffix] would possess the status of being "as if ending" (*antavadbhāva*), the mention of *al* would be redundant; therefore, by the force of that [mention], the designation will not apply to an aggregate of vowels (*al-samudāya*). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the word *darvi*: [it is derived from] the root *dṝ* "to tear," with the *vin* suffix added according to the *uṇādi* rules. The intention is that when a specific letter (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the entire class (*jāti*) of letters is understood, and thus groups of consonants (*al-samudāya*) are included. It might be argued: "In the rule *verapṛktasya*, let it be *vorapṛktasya*; and let there be no *ik* vowel in *kvip* and other such suffixes, for there is no other suffix containing the letter *v*. This is not so; for in the case of *rājakṛtvā*—derived from the rule *rājani yudhikṛñaḥ* (P. 3.2.95)—where one says "he causes [someone] to act like a king" (*tam ācaṣṭe*), the *ṇic* suffix is applied, the *ṭi*-portion is elided, *kvip* is applied, and the *ṇic* is elided. Thus, a suffix related to *kvanip* exists which contains the letter *v*.

Furthermore, some *ajakṣara* (non-syllabic element) must necessarily be produced for the purpose of pronunciation in the case of *kvip* and other suffixes; if that were an *a*-vowel, then elision would undesirably follow even in rules such as "after the roots *asṛ* and *śṛ*, [the suffix] *vaḥ*" and others. If it were an *u*-vowel, it would apply in the case of *ṇvul* and similar suffixes. Since there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in other instances, the traditional formulation (*yathānyāsam*) alone is superior. But surely, if the entire collection of vowels (*al-samudāya*) is also understood [by the term *al*], then the mention of *al* itself would be redundant.

Therefore, although in the rule "nipāta ekājanāṅ" (P. 1.1.14) the mention of the word "eka" (single) indicates that when a single phoneme is mentioned, the class (jāti) is intended, nevertheless, because of the force of the mention of "al" here [in P. 1.2.41], this will not apply to a composite group; thus, the mention of "eka" has a purpose that requires further consideration. Likewise, since the requirements for the term *apṛkta* are already fulfilled by the mention of "al" alone in those specific rules, there is no need for the technical designation (*saṃjñā*); much less for such a large one, and least of all for one that was previously specified.

Regarding the word *surā*: [it is derived as follows: from *surāṃ sunoti* ("he presses the *surā*"), with the suffix *kvip*, there is the insertion of *tuk*; then, from *surāsutam ācaṣṭe* ("he describes one who has pressed the *surā*"), with the suffix *ṇic*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion; then with *kvip* again, there is the elision of the *ṇi*. In this case, the elision of the *s* of the verbal root does not occur by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), because it is established by the *pratyayaparibhāṣā* (the rule that when a suffix is mentioned, it includes the whole word ending in that suffix). Furthermore, since the singular number is established through association (*sāhacarya*) with the suffix *tip*, the mention of "suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) is also of doubtful utility.
A Tatpuruṣa compound whose members have a common substratum (samānādhikaraṇa) is called a Karmadhāraya. Pāṇini 2.1.42.

In this context, if both terms "tatpuruṣaḥ" and "samānādhikaraṇaḥ" were taken in their primary senses, then the technical designation would apply only to cases such as *brāhmaṇarājyaṃ śobhanam*, where the *tatpuruṣa* compound stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with an external word, and not to cases such as *paramarājyam*.

Since it is established that because another term is not employed, one of the two must be used in a figurative sense, there is freedom of choice: if the term *tatpuruṣa* were figurative, then the words whose meaning is *tatpuruṣa* would be in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). In that case, because the word "together" (*saha*) would be absent, one might suspect that the designation applies to each [word] individually. Therefore, he says "tatpuruṣa" to show that this term has its primary (literal) meaning. He explains that it refers to a specific type of compound (*samāsaviśeṣa*), and so forth. He states that the other term is used in a figurative sense by saying "words in apposition."

That which possesses words in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by way of its substratum is so described. The sense is that although apposition based on parts is figurative (*aupacārika*), it is nevertheless more intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) than that which depends on other words; therefore, that alone is resorted to. For there indeed occurs the designation of a whole by means of the property of its parts, as in the expression "equal powder" (*samaṃ cūrṇam*). Here, the equality of the powder is mediated through its parts, and not the equality of the entire powder with something else.

Regarding the term *paramarājyam*: in the analysis *akarmadhāraye rājyam*, because of the prohibition by the rule "not in a non-karmadhāraya compound," the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) does not occur; instead, the compound receives the acute accent on its final syllable (*samāsāntodātta*). Regarding *pācakavṛndārikā*: setting aside the prohibition by the rule "not for a word ending in /ka/" (*na kopadhāyāḥ*), the masculine form is applied by the rule "masculine form in a karmadhāraya" (*puṃvat karmadhāraye*).

Regarding the question "What is meant by *tatpuruṣa*?": the inquiry arises because, due to being explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*) or because it is understood from the governing context (*adhikāra*), one might think that only a *tatpuruṣa* compound prescribed under the heading of *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) would be understood here. The example given is *pācikābhārya*. The intention is that this very meaning is difficult to determine with certainty. The example *brāhmaṇarājyam* shows that in this case, there is only the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*).

Now, why was it not stated at the end of this section on "that which precedes in time" (*apūrvakālaika*) that "it is a *karmadhāraya*"? [Namely: "That *tatpuruṣa* which is prescribed under the heading of *samānādhikaraṇa* is a *karmadhāraya*. For if this were so, it would not be necessary to state "a *tatpuruṣa* with a common substratum" (*tatpuruṣaḥ samānādhikaraṇa*). True; [but there is a reason].

However, because there is a governing rule for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation *tatpuruṣa* would be sublated by the designation *karmadhāraya*; therefore, just as in the case of a *dvigu*, the term *karmadhāraya* must be explicitly mentioned in order to re-enjoin the *tatpuruṣa* designation. Furthermore, since there is the possibility of them being optional alternatives (*paryāya*), the particle *ca* ("and") must also be stated so that they may coexist. [Objection: "But surely one could have formulated it thus: 'The *dvigu* and the *karmadhāraya* [are *tatpuruṣas*]'? [Response: But it was not formulated in that way. Precisely for this reason.
In a compound, that which is designated by the first case ending is called the *upasarjana*.

The term "compound" (*samāsa*) here is a locative indication. Since *kaṣṭaśrita* and others are compounds, what among them could possibly be designated as the first member? For when a compound exists, the nominative case is prescribed for that [word] from which [the compound] arises; yet such a thing is not possible. Indeed, once the compound is formed, the nominative is produced from that very [compound] itself, not from its constituent part. Furthermore, by means of the internal case-ending (*antarvartinī vibhakti*), it is the word *śrita* alone that is designated as the first member, not the word *kaṣṭa*.

That [term] also does not arise when a compound (*samāsa*) exists; rather, it arises only at the time of the sentence (*vākya*). Furthermore, the mention of "indicated" (*nirdiṣṭa*) would be redundant, for one should have simply said "that which ends in the nominative case in a compound. Therefore, because the primary sense is impossible, he says "by the nominative," etc., indicating that the compound is taken here in its secondary sense. But how can the word "compound" refer to the grammatical rule (*śāstra*)? He explains: "because it prescribes compounds. The meaning is that it is designated by that name because it serves that purpose, due to its being the prescriber of compounds.

Precisely because of the inclusion of the term "nirdiṣṭa" (specified), a sentence (*vākya*) is not included even though it shares the same status as a compound meaning (*samāsārtha*); for in that case, the nominative case does not serve the purpose of specification (*nirdeśārthā*), since it is employed solely for the sake of the meaning. [The phrase] "the second case" (*dvitīyā*) is what is "specified by the first case" (*prathamānirdiṣṭam*); that is, it is uttered with the nominative case-ending. If this were so, then only that [word "second case"] would receive the technical name (*saṃjñā*), and not words such as *kaṣṭa*, for they are not specified by the nominative in the treatise (*śāstra*). However, the very same specification by the nominative that applies to the word "second case" also applies to *kaṣṭa* and the others, because the former is intended to refer to the latter.

As he will state: "The word 'of that' (tasya) is used as a general term for the purpose of indicating the specific; thus, the priority of those specific [elements] is understood. In compounds such as *kaṣṭaśrita* ("resorted to hardship"), the subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is placed first. The formulation of this technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of understanding it as a descriptive term (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). In common usage, that which is not primary is called subordinate (*upasarjana*); here too, that which is not primary is the subordinate.

The terms "principal" (*pradhāna*) and "non-principal" (*apradhāna*) are relative terms; therefore, that which is non-principal in relation to something else is considered a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) in relation to that very thing. Consequently, in the example *rājñaḥ kumārīśritaḥ* ("the king's girl-resorted-to"), the word *kumārī*, although indicated by the nominative case in the rule *dvitīyā śrita-* (Pāṇini 2.2.34), does not receive the designation [of *upasarjana*]. If it were so designated, there would be no restriction on its position as the first member of the compound, and the shortening of the vowel prescribed for *upasarjana*s would apply.

If, however, the designation is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), then only that which depends on words such as *śrita* (reached) and so forth is an *upasarjana*, and thus there is no over-extension [of the rule]. Likewise, in the case of *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ* ("the king's daughter"), although both are designated as the first member (*prathamānirdeśa*) in the rule *ṣaṣṭhī*, the word *rājan* is an *upasarjana* in relation to *kumārī*, but not she in relation to him. If the technical term is indeed etymological, then this [specific rule] is unnecessary; let the etymological sense be understood directly from the specific applications (*pradeśa*). If that were so, it would also apply to a sentence: *kumārīṃ śritā* ("one who has reached a girl") and *gavāṃ kulam* ("a herd of cows").

Now, why does the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) not apply to the sentence (*vākya*), given that the basis for the nominative indication in the rule "not in a compound" (*asamāse*) is not the designation itself? Likewise, why does shortening (*hrasvatva*)—just like the rule for prior placement—not occur even in compounds such as *gokulam* and *kumārīputraḥ*? Therefore, since the status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatva*) exists only when [the word] is part of a compound, and because the rule for shortening applies to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix whose [prior member] is a subordinate element, and because of the mention of "prior placement" within the governing heading on compounds (*samāsādhikāra*), those two [rules] do not apply to the sentence.

It should not be said that [the rule] does not apply here; rather, the formulation of this technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhāna*) is for the purpose of establishing a fixed order of precedence (*pūrvanipātaniyama*) when both members of a compound are non-primary—as in *unmattagaṅgam* and similar examples—and also so that it may apply even to a primary member where the nominative case ending (*prathamānirdeśa*) serves no other purpose.

In examples such as *yathā-pācakavṛndārakaḥ* (one who is like a distinguished cook), *puruṣavyāghraḥ* (a tiger among men), *ardhapiplī* (half a pipīlikā), and *pūrvakāyaḥ* (the front part of the body), the very purpose of the mention of the nominative case in the rules "vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ pūjyamānam," "upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ," "ardhaṃ napuṃsakam," and "pūrvāparādharottaram" is this: for the formation of a compound where a qualifier is [compounded] with the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) is already established by the rule "ṣaṣṭhī" (Pāṇini 2.2.8).

Is the formulation of this rule for the sake of restriction, so that [the designation] might apply only to objects such as "being honored" (*pūjyamānatā*)? No; for if it were intended merely for the sake of the technical name *upasarjana*, then since a compound such as *ardhapippalī*—where the first member is *ardha* or similar, and which possesses a specific form—could be established by the general rule of compounding, this designation would serve that purpose as well. However, the principle of etymological consistency (*anvarthatva*) serves as a regulator only when possible.
And when there is no prior placement [in the compound], that which has the same case-ending [is placed first]. 1.2.44.

The word *vibhakti* denotes either the case-endings (*sup*) or the expressive power of the grammatical relations (*kāraka-śakti*), on the grounds that "by this, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) is divided. Regarding the phrase "when a compound (*samāsa*) is being prescribed": the meaning is that in that sentence by the suppression of which the compound comes into being; that is to say, when the three words are oriented toward attaining the form of a compound. By this, he shows that here the "sentence" is for the sake of the compound—that is, the compound itself—and not a formal rule (*śāstra*) as in the preceding sūtra.

In the treatise (śāstra), since everything possesses [only] one case-ending (*ekavibhakti*), the term "having one case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*) would be redundant; even in the primary sense of a compound (*samāsa*), its status as having one case-ending must be justified by means of the rule regarding the appearance of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the compound here is actually a sentence (*vākya*). And since in a single usage everything has one case-ending, he says—by the force of employing the qualifier—that what is intended is that which does not possess all case-endings even through a difference in usage, namely: "that which has a fixed case-ending. He clarifies this very point with the words: "in relation to the second correlate," and so forth.

Some say: "That with which one sits together is the second correlate. However, in this case, in the feminine gender option where the compound *pañcakhaṭvī*—meaning the collection of five beds—is formed with the suffix *ṭāp*, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) would not occur. For here, it is the collective whole (*samāhāra*) that is joined with various case-endings, not the word *pañca*; therefore, the second correlate is the word that expresses the subordinate meaning.

In the expression *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, the word *kauśāmbī* ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) precisely because it possesses the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the action of departing; it cannot possibly admit another grammatical function by being related to a different action. The prefix *nis-*, however, primarily signifies "departed" and is not connected with various distinct grammatical functions.

Regarding "Niṣkauśāmbi": the city established by Kuśāmba is Kauśāmbī; the short vowel [in the first member] occurs by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*. Regarding "Nirvārāṇasi": *varāṇā* refers to the water (*vāra*) which is excellent (*vara*); the city situated not far from that river Gaṅgā is Vārāṇasī. In the Purāṇas, however, it is said that there are two rivers, Varaṇā and Asi; it belongs to the *śakandhv-ādi* group, and because it is formed according to the *pṛṣodarādi* class, the vowel *a* of the syllable *ra* becomes long.

By the preceding rule (*ni saḥ*), there is the status of being a subordinate member (*upasarjanatva*); for it has been stated that even a principal member (*pradhāna*) becomes so by virtue of being indicated in the nominative case. Here, however, this [word *ni*] is not indicated in the nominative, whereas the scope of the preceding rule consists of those with multiple case-endings, such as *nīlotpalam* and *arddhapippalī*. In compounds like *kaṣṭaśrita*, words such as *kaṣṭa* have a single case-ending and are indicated in the nominative; thus, when both rules would apply, this [present rule] prevails due to its posteriority. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition "in the absence of prior placement" (*apūrvanipāte*). This is not so.

Because there is no prohibition. This is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)—as in the rule "the negative particle [is placed] first"—but rather, what is it? This is a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation); in the case of a *paryudāsa*, there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition regarding being placed first. Even in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, it is the immediate application that is prohibited. Why is this so? Because either an injunction or a prohibition applies to what follows immediately; the preceding application remains unprohibited, and by that [unprohibited application], the rule will proceed. Furthermore, this [subsequent] application does not sublate the preceding application, because the latter has already been prohibited.
That which possesses meaning, is not a verbal root (dhātu), and is not an affix (pratyaya) is a nominal stem (prātipadika). Pāṇini 1.2.45.

The word *artha* signifies that which is denoted (*abhidheya*). It does not signify purpose (*prayojana*), because [the definition] would then be non-exclusive (*avyabhicāra*). Nor does it signify cessation (*nivṛtti*), for what is the use of a name for that which has ceased of its own accord? Nor does it signify wealth (*dhana*), because a relationship of owner and owned is impossible [in such cases]. Furthermore, that which is denoted is fourfold, distinguished by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and substance (*dravya*): as in *gauḥ* (cow), *śuklaḥ* (white), *pācakaḥ* (cook), and *ḍitthaḥ* (a proper name). If a name applies only to that which possesses a referent (*arthavat*), then names for non-existents such as "the hare's horn" would not be possible, because of the absence of a referent.

Could it not be that [the term *samāsa*] would apply here by virtue of being a compound? No; because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "possessing meaning" (*arthavat*). If this were otherwise, since a rule could apply even to what is meaningless, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa-grahaṇa*) would not serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). It is said in reply: for those who hold that negation (*abhāva*) is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*) cognizable by the intellect, characterized by the absence of a jar or the like in a locus such as the ground, for them there is meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) through that object.

Even for those who maintain that the absence of a counter-positive, such as a jar, is simply the very nature of the locus—such as the ground—or a specific cognition thereof, in their view, the objectivity [of the absence] is established by that very ground; thus, the designation "absence" is indeed proven. Even in the case of the expression "the horn of a hare," one mentally conceives of a horn experienced in cows and the like as residing upon the head of a hare, and employs the word for the purpose of denoting precisely that. For it is the mental apprehension (*buddhyupāroha*) of an object that is the cause for the employment of a word, not its external existence.

If words denoted an object that exists only externally, the usage "the jar does not exist" would be impossible; for in one case it would be a tautology, and in the other a contradiction. However, such usage is appropriate for the purpose of communicating the existence or non-existence of an object as it has ascended into the intellect. Likewise, in cases such as "he cooked," "he will cook," or "weave this cloth for him," the meaning of the roots *pac* (to cook) and so forth is precisely that which has ascended into the intellect; it is not established externally at the time of the word's employment.

Words such as *ḍittha* and the like are examples of those whose etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is not established. In the case where a derivation is established, the form is already proven simply by virtue of being a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Even under the view that "all nouns are born from verbal roots" (*sarvanāma dhātujam*), this sūtra must indeed be commenced for the sake of [defining] indeclinables (*avyaya*) and onomatopoeic words (*anukaraṇa*). Now, in common usage, the determination of the meaningfulness of words occurs only in relation to a sentence, or to a word ending in a case-suffix.

But since it is not [the case that meaning belongs] to the base-component alone, how can there be a determination of its meaningfulness when it is extracted? For those [elements] which are always used together, the meaningfulness belongs to the aggregate alone, as in the case of phonemes. It is replied: the determination of word-meaning is achieved through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). That meaning which is perceived when a particular word is present, and which disappears when that word is absent—that is its meaning.

In cases such as "two trees" (*vṛkṣau*) and "trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*), although there is a deviation from the general suffix, there is no deviation from its specific [suffix]; and in the case of a compound, there is a deviation from the general [meaning], as in "a piece of wood" (*vṛkṣakhaṇḍam*) or "a vegetable from a tree" (*vārksī śākhā*). However, the referent (*artha*) understood by the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) is that which possesses roots, trunk, fruit, foliage, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "not [the word] *anta* because of its being a limit": one might object that these two words are derived from the roots *vana* (in the sense of "to share") and *dhana* (in the sense of "wealth") by means of the suffix *ac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.134), and thus the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*) will apply. If this is so, then this was stated under the view that words are not derivationally formed (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*); for this very reason, these two are presented as examples.

Furthermore, if the term were understood as referring to that which possesses meaning (*arthavat*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the technical name *saṃjñā* applying to every individual phoneme. Nor does the name "verbal root" (*dhātu*) apply to each individual phoneme, nor does the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "that which is not a verbal root and not an affix" imply the inclusion of only those things that possess meaning. For it is possible for both verbal roots and affixes to be devoid of meaning, as in the examples *adhīte* and *yāvaka*. In these cases, the meaningfulness belongs to the root *iṅ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, but not to the root *iṅ* alone, since it is never used in isolation.

In the case of *yāvaka* as well, only the word *yāva* possesses meaning (*arthavattva*), but not the suffix *kan*; for its meaning is understood even without that suffix. Furthermore, it is not known by what property there is similarity [of *yāva* with *yāvaka*]. Nor can there be a selection of the meaningful element based on the paribhāṣā rule "the meaningful is to be understood"? For that rule establishes a restriction when a specific form is being introduced, and here no specific form is being introduced.

[Objection: "But even if the designation *saṃjñā* exists for that which is meaningless, the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) prescribed for number, object, and so forth will not occur. [Response: This is not so; they arise without distinction, and once arisen, there is no restriction regarding their meaning. Consequently, just as with indeclinables (*avyaya*), the case-endings would indeed occur. As for the statement "there would be elision of the *n*" (P. 6.4.24): however, the hearing of the case-ending does not take place, because even though the entire aggregate is designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) separately, the elision (*luk*) occurs due to its inclusion therein.

If this is so, then by the principle of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the [designation] will not apply to the constituent part. It is logical that in the case of *paj*, by the very same vowel (*ac*) through which the whole (*samudāya*) is "single-vowel" (*ekāc*), both the constituent parts—the vowel *a* and the syllable *pa*—are likewise single vowels. However, it is impossible for one thing at one time to be established as a constituent part (*avayava*) with respect to more than one [whole]. Furthermore, when a whole is reduplicated, its constituents are also reduplicated because they constitute its essence. In the present case, however, the status of being a word (*śabdatva*) based on technical designation (*saṃjñānibandhana*) is entirely distinct for the constituents and for the whole.

In that case, the function belongs to the aggregate as a whole, and not to the individual parts. But surely, since meaning is observed in single phonemes—such as *eti*, *ābhyām*, *aupagavaḥ*, and *apehi*—which consist of verbal roots, nominal stems, suffixes, and particles, the phonemes in words like *vṛkṣa* must also possess meaning. Likewise, when the letter *ka* is present in *kūpa*, a certain meaning is understood; when the letter *ya* is added to form *yūpa*, a different meaning arises. Therefore, we consider that whatever meaning is found in *kūpa* belongs to the letter *ka*, and whatever meaning is found in *yūpa* belongs to [the letter *yu*].

Regarding the [word] "of the letter *ya*": likewise, when the word "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) is uttered, the meaning that is understood is not understood even if any one of the letters beginning with *ba* is removed. Furthermore, those whose collection performs a certain function, each individual member of that collection also performs that function; for example, a *khārī* measure of sesame seeds produces oil, and each individual sesame seed does so as well. Conversely, those which are individually incapable of a certain thing, their collection is also incapable of it therein; for example, individual grains of sand do not produce oil, and thus a *khārī* measure of them does not either.

Therefore, since the composite [words] possess meaning, the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves must possess meaning; how then, even when there is the mention of "that which possesses meaning," could there be an exclusion of them? But they are indeed meaningless, because no meaning is perceived for individual phonemes—for when "brā" is uttered, no meaning whatsoever is understood. Thus, the claim that other phonemes also possess meaning on the grounds that single-phoneme elements such as verbal roots (*dhātu*) possess meaning is contradicted by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). In this same way, other reasons [adduced for their meaningfulness] also have their objects sublated.

Furthermore, regarding the words *kūpa* (well) and *yūpa* (sacrificial post), if the letters *ka* and *ya* possess meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then one would have to admit that the four letters in the word *yūpa* are meaningless. Alternatively, if those [letters] were meaningful, then in the word *kūpa* the meaning of *yūpa* would predominate, and the meaning of *kūpa* would predominate in the word *yūpa*; for where there is a positive concomitance of many meaningful elements, there is a predominance of their meanings, while the exclusion (*vyatireka*) belongs to only some. However, in such a case, even among the meanings themselves, there would be a predominance of their application, while the exclusion would belong to only some.

For example: "Devadatta, bring the white cow," and "Devadatta, bring the black cow. Therefore, it is the combinations themselves that possess meaning. Furthermore, the reason "because of the meaningfulness of the combination" (*saṃghātārthavattvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for instance, a lamp exists through the combination of oil, fire, and a wick, but not by each individually; likewise, the act of moving occurs through the combined parts of a chariot, such as the wheels and so forth.

Furthermore, when meaningful [elements] undergo substitution, there is a corresponding substitution of the meaning—as in "āhara pātram" (bring the bowl) and "pātram āhara" (bring the bowl); when they are elided, there is elision of the meaning—as in "gām abhyāja śuklām" (drive the white cow hither) and "gām abhyāja" (drive the cow hither); and when they are added, there is addition of the meaning—as in "gām abhyāja śuklām" (drive the white cow hither). But this is not the case with individual phonemes—for instance, in the words *siṃhaḥ* (lion), *hinasti* (he kills), *hanti* (he kills), and *hataḥ* (killed), or *ghnanti* (they kill). Therefore, only composite units possess meaning.

Regarding the word *ahan*: when the suffix *tiP* is applied to the root *han* in the *laṅ* tense, after the elision [of the *i*] by the rule "itaśca," the elision of the *t* by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt... occurs, and that [elided *t*] is indeed included within the term *han*. In this case, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply even before the production of the *laṅ*, and the status of being a "word" (*pada*) would follow subsequently, the elision of the *n* would take place. Alternatively, the designation as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) might occur at the very same time as the designation as a word; nor would there be a prohibition by the rule "na apratyayaḥ" (not when it is not a suffix), because of the indicative evidence (*liṅga*) in the rule "na ṅisambuddhyoḥ. Otherwise, in cases such as *he rājan*, since it is not a suffix, the prohibition [by "na apratyayaḥ"] would mean it is not a nominal stem, and consequently, the elision of the *n* would undesirably follow.

The term "non-root" (*adhātu*) could be omitted. The mention of "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule *supo dhātu* would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this designation does not apply to roots. This is not a valid indicator, for that [mention of "root"] might be intended to prohibit [the designation] in cases such as *śyenāyate*, where the designation is prohibited by the rule *apratyaya*. However, in forms like *bhid*, *bhūḥ*, and *pūḥ*, which end in the suffix *kvip*, the designation would apply by the subsequent rule because they end in a *kṛt* suffix. Nor is this [present rule] a prohibition of that [subsequent designation], according to the maxim "exceptions [operate] in the middle," or because it is a negative exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Regarding the word *kāṇḍe*: the substitution of *śī* for the nominative dual ending occurs by the rule *napuṃsakācca*; furthermore, by the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there is a prohibition against [the application of the rule] to that which ends in such a suffix. For where a suffix enters into the very form of the technical designation (*saṃjñin*), as in the case of "the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are called *gha*," there is a prohibition of the extension of the rule to the end of a word (*tadantavidhi*) by means of a statement regarding the designation of a word (*pada*).

But here, in the case of *paryudāsa*, the named element (*saṃjñin*) is distinct from the affix (*pratyaya*); and even in the case of *prasajya-pratiṣedha*, there is no mention of the term "affix" in the rule prescribing the name—what then? It is a negation, meaning there is no prohibition [of the application of the name]. [Objection: But surely, in the subsequent sūtra, the mention of *kṛt* and *taddhita* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), such that if the name applies to something ending in an affix, it applies only to that which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* affix. [Reply: It is said in response:

If this prohibition of the designation-rule (*saṃjñāvidhi*) were not present, then because of the prohibition of *tadantavidhi* (the rule that an operation applies to what ends with a specified element), if the designation were to apply to a suffix, it would result in a restriction of the locus (*sthāniyama*), namely that it would apply only to a *kṛt* or *taddhita* [suffix]. However, since this [prohibition] exists, there is first of all a prohibition of that which ends in a suffix; consequently, in the subsequent sūtra as well, there is the inclusion of that which ends in a *taddhita*.

Now, even when [the rule] "apratyaya" (not being a suffix) is applied, why does the shortening of the neuter vowel not occur? In the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is the status of being "final-like" (*antavadbhāva*) for the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) of both the suffix and the non-suffix with respect to what precedes it. Even in the case of *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), because it is an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) applies to the word *kāṇḍa* prior to the arising of the suffix; thus, due to the "final-like" status of the single substitute, the status of being a nominal stem certainly exists.

And thus, in the case of *brahmabandhūḥ*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) ending in *-ū-* is treated as if it were the final element of the preceding stem, the suffixes beginning with *su-* (the nominative) are produced. Nor is the rule *na cāpratyayaḥ* ("it is not [treated as] a suffix") redundant; for it serves a purpose in cases such as *trapuṇī*, where there is no single-substitute. If this is so, then the shortening applies to that which exists in the neuter gender. However, a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*) primarily expresses number and the capacity for grammatical function (*kāraka-śakti*), and neither of these possesses a connection with gender. Furthermore, the meaning cannot be extended by means of the "behaving like another" (*anyavadbhāva*) rule. Therefore, the shortening does not occur.

If this is so, then in cases such as *trapuṇī* and the like, the same would not occur; there would be no need for this [rule], nor is any other suffix (*pratyaya*) possible that could be excluded. For indeed, there are six types of suffixes: those beginning with *san*, *kṛt*, *tiṅ*, *sup*, feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), and *taddhita*. Furthermore, the operations pertaining to the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) include the shortening of vowels as in "the [final vowel] of a neuter nominal stem is short" (*hrasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya*) and "the [final vowel] of a subordinate term ending in *go* or a feminine suffix is short" (*gaustriyorupasarjanasya*), as well as the rule for the formation of suffixes as in "after a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, etc. (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*).

And that [status of being a nominal stem] is desired only for those ending in *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes. Regarding those such as the *san* [desiderative] and others, which possess the status of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the prohibition "not a root" (*adhātu*) applies directly. As for the conjugational suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) such as *śyan*, *śap*, and so on, there is an absence of gender; there is an absence of number, object, and so forth; and there is an impossibility of connection with meanings such as "offspring. The same applies to those ending in *tiṅ* [finite verb endings], as in: "the offspring of one whose form is 'pacati'" (*pacatirūpa*); here, although the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) exists due to the presence of the suffix *-vant*, [the prohibition still applies].

As for those [suffixes] that occur as *svārthika* (denoting the same meaning as the base), they do not apply because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *atiṅaśca*. However, there is simply no connection between feminine suffixes and the neuter gender, which is their opposite. If it is argued that in the case of *kumārīputra*, the shortening prescribed by the rule *go-striyoḥ* would occur, [the answer is: even if the prohibition is applied, why does it not occur in the case of *rājakumārīputra*, since here, due to being a compound (*samāsa*), the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) certainly exists? Therefore, whatever solution applies in that case will apply here as well.

The rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-vidhi*) is indeed accepted. It has already been stated that, under the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the shortening of a vowel does not apply to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Furthermore, there is no possibility of case-suffixes (*sup*) [being applied] because at the time of their prescription, a form ending in them is impossible, and due to the absence of gender, there is an absence of feminine suffixes (*strī-pratyaya*). As for secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), they are indeed intended by the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*. Therefore, this [present rule] is unnecessary, as is the mention of "secondary suffix" (*taddhita*) in the subsequent sūtra; so it is said.

Under the view that rules such as "the plural is used for the plural" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) form distinct syntactical units (*bhinnavākyatā*) from the rule prescribing the *svādi* suffixes, the *svādi* suffixes would apply even after all elements ending in suffixes—just as they do after indeclinables (*avyaya*)—and even after verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*), where derivative suffixes (*taddhita*) expressing the same meaning (*svārthika*) would likewise arise. Therefore, the mention of "not being a suffix" (*apratyaya*) must be made, as well as the mention of "derivative suffix" (*taddhita*). As for the counter-examples *kāṇḍe* and *kuḍye*, we shall establish their status in the context of the rule "the short vowel is used in the neuter" (*hasvo napuṃsake*).

Now, why should the designation (*saṃjñā*) not apply to the suffix alone? For if the designation were applied, then by the logic already stated, suffixes such as *sva* and others would occur in forms like *bahupaṭavaḥ*. It is replied: by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), there will be a prohibition based on the rule that "that which ends in a suffix is not [treated as] a suffix. If this is so, since the application of the rule would be possible even for mere *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes, the subsequent sūtra does not involve a reference to what ends in them (*tadantavidhi*). We shall state the resolution to this point later.
And [the words ending in] kṛt, taddhita, and samāsa [suffixes are called prātipadika]. 1.2.46.

It should be understood that [the term] "kṛta" refers to those [suffixes] beginning with *kṛt*. For here, the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of *kṛt* does not apply; therefore, the compound *mūlakenopadaṃśam* does not receive the designation [of *samāsa*]. According to the maxim of the "intermediate exception" (*madhye'pavādanyāya*), the prohibition by the rule *apratyayaḥ* (P. 1.2.45) is overridden by the mention of *kṛt*, but the restriction on *kṛt* suffixes is not overridden by the mention of *samāsa*. He provides the justification for the fact that even when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), there is an extension to include what ends in that suffix (*tadantavidhi*), by stating: "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*).

This is stated on the basis that the prohibition applies to [a word] ending in an affix, but not to the affix alone. A *vidhi* (rule) is that which provides what has not yet been obtained; and at that time, the designation (*saṃjñā*) does not apply to *kṛt* and *taddhita* affixes alone, but its application is obtained by virtue of their being the end of a word. Therefore, because it serves the purpose of a *vidhi*, only that which ends in such an affix is understood.

However, for those [grammarians] who previously prohibited even the mere suffix (*pratyaya*), since the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) has been removed, the mention of the compound (*samāsa*) would be redundant; for a specific type of meaningful entity ending in that [suffix] would be included by the previous rule alone, as its meaningfulness is established by that very rule. Therefore, he says: "of meaningful aggregates" (*arthavatsamudāyānām*). This is a genitive in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). "Restriction" (*niyama*) means exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Objection: In cases such as *surājā* and *atirājā*, when the internal case-ending has been elided, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to the entire complex. Depending on that [designation], when the suffix *s-* is produced and subsequently elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* etc., the designation [of "suffix"] would apply to that state for the purpose of deleting the *n*. Since this designation would then be barred by the prohibition *apratyaya* ("not a suffix") under the rule *pratyayalakṣaṇam*, this [present rule] would have to serve as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Response: This is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*). The prohibition "not in the case of the locative ending *-ṅi* or the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*)" indicates that there is no prohibition by way of the technical designation of a suffix.

Otherwise, by the logic already stated, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of eliding the *n* in examples such as "he rājan. This [argument] is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). For in cases like "hai surājan," where a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed by the inclusion of the term "compound" (*samāsa*), there would be a prohibition against the elision of *n* whenever its occurrence was otherwise expected. If this is so, then here too the phrase "not being a suffix" (*apratyaya*) is understood to carry over. Consequently, since it is impossible for the mention of "compound" to serve as a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) regarding a compound ending in a suffix, the mention of "compound" serves solely as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

Alternatively, this position is adopted: the designation *kṛt* does not apply without reference to a specific purpose; however, once that designation exists, whatever operation is applicable in a particular state occurs in that state, and the designation need not be repeated for each individual operation. On this view, the designation *samāsa* applies only once immediately after [the application of] the *samāsa* designation, for the sake of generating case-endings (*sub*) and for the sake of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), and not at the stage of the elision of *n*. Thus, since it cannot serve as an injunction (*vidhi*), the mention of *samāsa* serves solely as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

And there is a necessary exclusion of that which is of a similar class (*tulyajātīya*). What, then, is "of a similar class"? It is that for which the prior portion of the meaningful aggregate (*samudāya*) is a word (*pada*); namely, that which is a compound of nouns ending in case-terminations (*subanta*), such as *rājapuruṣa*; and that which is a compound of verbs ending in verbal terminations (*tiṅanta*), according to the rule "a verb may be compounded with another verb to express continuity of action," such as *aśnītapibatā*, *khādatamodatā*; and that which is a compound of both nouns and verbs, according to the rule "a verb is frequently compounded with its object to express repetition," such as *jahijoḍaḥ*, *jahiśakaṭa*; and that which consists of nouns...

And regarding "of nominal stems" (*prātipadikānām*): in the case of [compounds] where a gati, a kāraka, or an upapada is present—such as *vastra-krītī* ("bought for a cloth") and *niṣka-krītī* ("bought for a gold coin")—in all such instances, the preceding portion is indeed a *pada*. Therefore, that which belongs to the same class is necessarily excluded [from being called a *pada* by the rule *naṅ-ky-dhātubhruvām...*, etc.]. Consequently, in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ* ("many cloths"), when the suffix *bahuC* is added before the word ending in *jas*, the preceding portion is not a *pada* within the composite whole; thus, in the absence of the restrictive rule [that the preceding portion is a *pada*], since the suffix *jas* has already been produced, and because the [stem] possesses meaning through the sense of "slight incompleteness," the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies, and [the elision of the case-ending follows] by the rule *supo dhātu...* (Pāṇini 2.4.71).

Thus, when elision (*luk*) has been performed, the *citsvara* (accent on the *cit* suffix) also occurs for the vowel *u* of the word *paṭu*, according to the rule: "The *ati* [suffix] retains its original form for the sake of the meanings of *bahuc* and *kac*. However, if the previously produced *jas* were to remain, the accent would belong to that alone. Regarding the phrase "of a sentence which possesses meaning": since the connection (*saṃsarga*) not apprehended by the individual words is apprehended by the sentence, the sentence possesses meaning; and because a suffix is not prescribed from a collection [of words], the prohibition "not being a suffix" (*apratyaya*) does not apply.

Nor can one resort to the analysis of this as a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which there is no condition is 'without a condition' (apratyaya)," because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of [the term] *bahupaṭu* ("very clever") also being [interpreted as] a negation.
The final vowel of a nominal stem becomes short when it denotes a neuter gender.

He states that in the Sūtra, by the term "neuter" (napuṃsaka), it is the substance possessing that [gender] which is intended, not gender alone: "in the sense of a neuter gender" (napuṃsakaliṅge 'rthe). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose gender is neuter."

Regarding the term *grāmaṇīḥ*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc. [Pāṇini 3.2.61]. The question "What is the purpose of saying 'of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)'? is raised as follows: Neuter gender is a property of the substance (*dravya*) alone, and the capacity to denote a substance belongs only to the nominal stem, not to that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*), because the latter has power (*śakti*) and number as its primary meaning. It does not belong to a verbal root (*dhātu*) or to that which ends in a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), nor to a sentence (*vākya*), because these have action (*kriyā*) as their primary meaning. As for individual phonemes (*varṇa*), they are meaningless; furthermore, feminine suffixes cannot coexist with the contradictory neuter gender. This is the point of the question. The examples given are *kāṇḍe* and *kuṇḍye*.

In this case, because of the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*), it lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*). Now, one might object: since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is, with respect to the preceding element, as if it were the final part (*antavadbhāva*), it is indeed included by the mention of "nominal stem"; therefore, even if the mention of "nominal stem" is made, the shortening (*hrasvatva*) would still occur. To this he replies: "By the force of the mention of 'nominal stem'."

But how is there such capacity [to exclude the neuter], given that in cases where the treatment as ending-in-a-stem (*antavadbhāva*) does not apply—such as in *yāvaḥ*, *vāraḥ*, *trapuṇī*, and so forth—that would be what is excluded? If you argue that because the primary focus there is on the power (*śakti*) and number (*saṅkhyā*), the neuter gender is not applicable, then the same would apply to *kāṇḍe* and so forth; for even though the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) exists through the treatment as ending-in-a-stem, the primacy of power and number is not lost.

He thinks as follows: "If the mention of the *prātipadika* (nominal stem) were not made, then an *ekādeśa* (single substitute) resulting from both that which functions as a neuter and that which does not function as a neuter would be included by the mention of 'functioning as a neuter,' and there would be the undesirable consequence [of applying the rule] even to the word 'napuṃsaka' itself. However, when the *prātipadika* is mentioned, because the purpose is to refer to the primary *prātipadika*, the short vowel—which possesses a transferred status of being a *prātipadika*—is excluded. And the mention of the *prātipadika* is for this very purpose.

In the examples *iha vanāya*, *vanābhyām*, *vanārtham*, and *vanebhyaḥ*, the short vowel does not occur because the long vowels (*dīrghatva*) are considered *asiddha* (non-existent) from the perspective of the external operation (*bahiraṅga*). In the case of *kāṇḍībhūtam*, although it was previously neuter, there is an absence of the short vowel because, at the stage of the suffix *cv-*, it lacks gender due to being an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
The feminine suffix is elided when it is a subordinate member [of a compound]. (Pāṇini 1.2.48)

Regarding the phrase "the mention of the term *strī*," he states the reason here: "because of its being marked with the *svarita* accent. The meaning of the rule "an *adhikāra* [governing rule] is indicated by the *svarita* accent" is that wherever the *svarita* quality is formally asserted, there the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is to be understood. And in this case, the mention of *strī* is marked with the *svarita* accent; therefore, what is included is the mention of the suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others which are prescribed under the governing heading "in the feminine" (*striyām*), and not the meaning, nor the actual form itself. As for suffixes such as *ktin*, they are not included because they do not possess the state of having a short vowel (*hrasva*).

The mention of *upasarjana* is a qualifier for those two [the word *go* and the feminine suffix]. However, because each is connected individually, he states that the dual number does not occur: "of the *upasarjana* *go*, etc. The reading is "of that which ends in a feminine suffix" (*strīpratyayāntasya*). For here, the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) *upasarjana* is what is understood; and it is impossible for a mere feminine suffix to possess the technical status of an *upasarjana*. [He says] "by those two."

If, by the words *upasarjana* (subordinate) and *gośabda* (the word "cow"), as well as by the word ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), the rule of extension to what ends with those (*tadantavidhi*) were not understood, then the meaning would be that there is shortening of the stem (*prātipadika*) which is a subordinate *gośabda* and of the stem which ends in a feminine suffix. Consequently, this [shortening] would apply even in cases such as *gokulam* and *rājakumārīputraḥ*; this is the intended sense. However, in the present case of *kumārīputraḥ*, there is no application [of the rule] precisely because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The reading is: *upasarjana-strīpratyayāntāntasya*.

The meaning is: "that which ends in a feminine suffix and is an *upasarjana*. However, if one were to understand the rule by first qualifying the feminine suffix alone with the worldly term *upasarjana*, and subsequently applying the *tadantavidhi* (the rule of "ending in that") to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—namely, "of a nominal stem that ends in a feminine suffix which is an *upasarjana*"—then it would also apply in the case of *harītakyaḥ phalāni*; for in this instance, the meaning of the feminine suffix is subordinate (*upasarjana*) with respect to the fruit, and the word is a nominal stem because it ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Therefore, it must be understood exactly as follows: "of that nominal stem (prātipadika) which ends in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) that is an *upasarjana* according to the technical rules of grammar. For example, in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*: *kauśāmbī* is an *upasarjana* because it appears with a single case-ending; it ends in a feminine suffix, and the compound nominal stem (*samāsaprātipadika*) ends in that [feminine suffix]. Now, how is there shortening in this case, as in *atirājakumārī*, given that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added after the word *kumāra*, and not after the word *rājakumāra*? True; however, when a feminine suffix is not an *upasarjana*, there is no restriction regarding the initial element of the base.

Now, even though there is the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by means of the word *go* and a feminine suffix, why does it not apply in cases such as *gokulam* and *rājakumārīputra*? For in the rule *ayena vidhistadantasya*, the phrase *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form") is understood to carry over; therefore, when there is an extension to that which ends with something, the actual form of that [element] itself should also be included. If this is so, then, because the nominal stem is qualified by the word *go*, the operation does not apply to the isolated [stem].

Otherwise, [the author] would have prescribed the short vowel for the subordinate element *go* itself; furthermore, in the rule "yena vidhis tadantasya" (P. 1.1.72), the term "svarūpam" (itself) would have to be excluded. Moreover, the status of being "like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) does not apply to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). As for the case of *rājakumārīputra*, however, the resolution is as follows: even that which is technically termed a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is, when possible, etymologically so—namely, that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*). And something becomes non-principal only in relation to a principal (*pradhāna*).

Furthermore, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) for that which ends in a feminine suffix is untenable without a compound (*samāsa*), and a compound consists of constituent parts. In this context, two factors are present: the principal (*pradhāna*) and the subordinate (*apradhāna*). We shall understand it thus: when a compound nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix is involved, the subordinate status of that which ends in the feminine suffix is understood only with respect to what is included within that [compound]. However, in the present case, since the subordinate status is with respect to the son who is not included therein, the short vowel [substitution] does not occur.

"Of *īyas*," and so forth. The meaning is: "of that which ends in a feminine suffix prescribed after a stem ending in *īyasun*. Regarding *bahuśreyasī*: [the rule] *praśasyasya śraḥ* applies; then the suffix *ṅīp*; the compound *bahuvrīhi* is formed as "one who has many *śreyasīs*"; then the suffix *kap* by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*; then the prohibition [of *kap*] by the rule *īyasaśca*; and even in the masculine, there is the elision of the case-ending *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [etc.]. Why "of a *bahuvrīhi*"? [Consider] *atiśreyasiḥ*.
When a *taddhita* suffix is elided by means of *luk*, [the feminine suffix is also elided]. 1.2.49.

The term *strī* (feminine) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], but not the term *go* (cow). Why? Because the technical designation *luk* is prescribed for the non-appearance of an affix, and because the word *go* is an underived (primitive) form; even in the view that it is derived, it lacks the *svarita* accent. Regarding the phrase "and of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)": the word "is carried over" (*anuvartate*) is required [to complete the sense]. Here, the worldly (secular) *upasarjana* is intended, not the technical grammatical one. In some places, the reading "when shortness would have been obtained by the preceding [rule]" is found; in that case, the distinction lies in the word "in some places" (*kvacit*).

For by the preceding sūtra, the technical (śāstrīya) upasarjana is intended; its scope (*avakāśa*) is where there is no elision of the *taddhita* suffix, such as in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. The scope of this [present] rule is where there is a technical upasarjana, such as in *āmalakam*. And as for the elision of the *taddhita* suffix, for example, in *pañcendra*: here, while the sense of the compound involves various case-endings (*nānāvibhaktika*), the form *pañcendrāṇī* has a single case-ending (*ekavibhaktika*), and thus possesses the status of an upasarjana. Therefore, when both [rules] would apply, the meaning is that this very elision (*luk*)—by virtue of its posteriority—sublates the shortening (*hrasva*).
