However, some, based on this very text, maintain that even in the preceding sūtra there is the inclusion of the worldly secondary derivative (*upajana*); according to them, it has been stated that in the case of *harītakyaḥ phalāni*, where elision (*lup*) applies, there would be the undesirable consequence of a short vowel.

It might be argued as follows: by the rule "in the case of *lup*, it is like that which is joined [to it]," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of both the word and its meaning. That is, there is an extension of both the gender of the base-meaning and the suffix that expresses it. In that case, while the original (autonomous) form has shortness, there will be the hearing of the extended (derived) form. If this were so, then in the example "a man is like a young woman" (*yuvatir iva puruṣaḥ*), according to the rule "*lum manuṣye*," the word would be *yuvatiḥ*; thus, two instances of the sound *ti* would be heard.

Therefore, the resolution to this must be stated either by rejecting the elision (*lup*) on the grounds that "the connection [of the parts] is not perceived" (*lubyogāprakhyānāt*), or by accepting the technical (*śāstrīya*) sense of the term *upasarjana*. And the meaning of the text has indeed been explained.

Since elision (*luk*) cannot occur in the sense of non-existence, he states "when *luk* exists" (*luki sati*), indicating that this is a locative absolute (*satsaptamī*). Regarding *pañcendra*: it is a compound formed by the rule *taddhitārtha*; the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by *sāsya devatā*) is elided by *dvigor lug anapatye*; the suffix *ṅīṣ* prescribed by the rule *indravaruṇa-* etc. is elided by this [present rule]; and by the principle that when elements conditioned by a specific grammatical operation (*sanniyoga-viśiṣṭa*) are involved, the absence of one entails the absence of the other, the suffix *ānuk* is also removed. Regarding *pañcaśaṣkula*.

In the case of *tena krītam* ("bought with that"), the suffix *ṭhak* belonging to the *ārhīya* group is elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrva*. Regarding *āmalakam*: by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied, and its elision occurs before the word *phala* by the rule *phale luk*. In the absence of the words *badarī* and *kuvalī*, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *anudāttādeśca*. Words such as *śaṣkulī* and others end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group.

Regarding "Avantī" and so forth: from the words *avanti* and *kunti*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied to form the feminine designating a descendant (*apatya*) according to the rule *vṛddhetkosalājādāñ ñyaṅ*. From *kuru*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*; in the feminine, the *luk* elision applies by the rule *avantī*, while from the word *kuru*, the suffix *ūṅ* is applied by *ūṅ utaḥ*. For the other two [words], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by *ito manuṣyajāteḥ*. Here, the genus (*jāti*) characterized as a descendant is denoted primarily by means of a feminine suffix.
The feminine suffix *goṇī* [is used] in this sense. 1.2.50.

Regarding the term *pañcagoṇi*: the word *goṇi* denotes both a measure (*parimāṇa*) and a container (*āvapana*). From the first sense, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule "before *vati*, *ṭhañ*" (Pāṇini 5.1.18); from the second sense, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for derivatives denoting worthiness (*ārhīya*). In both cases, the suffix is elided by the preceding rule (Pāṇini 5.1.28).

Regarding the phrase "the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by means of *it*": here, the mention of *it* would be purposeless; let there simply be [the rule] "after *goṇī*" and "short vowel" (*hrasva*). Since the elision (*luk*) cannot be carried over due to the lack of capacity in the statement, this very mention of *it* is the indicator (*liṅga*) for the division of the rule. If the division of the rule were made, the substitution of *it* would apply everywhere; to this he says, "And that" (*sa ca*). The sense is that if it were to apply everywhere, the mention of *goṇī* would be useless.

[Objection: But has not the elision (*luk*) also been stated for that *taddhita* suffix, as well as the substitution of *it*? Since there would be an occasion for an option between those two, the mention of *goṇī* must be for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution of *it* occurs invariably. Why then is the scope of the rule distinguished by means of this division (*yogavibhāga*)? [Reply: It is said: First, the Sūtrakāra recited the rule as a single unit. By virtue of that, the process of division also follows [as an implied operation]. And when the rule is undivided, its scope is restricted to a specific domain.

By the force of including the letter *it*, the division (*vibhāga*) being made is understood to have a specific scope; for this very reason it is said: "The desired result is achieved through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Furthermore, that specific scope is to be determined from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). The inclusion of the letter *t* (in *it*) is for the sake of specifying the duration (*tatkāla*), so that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) may not be replaced by a long vowel. Otherwise, the explicit statement [of the rule] would merely serve to block the elision (*luk*) and the short vowel (*hrasva*). If the letter *t* were absent, the long vowel *ī*—which had been previously applicable and then prohibited—would simply be restated (*pratiprasūta*), and a new short vowel *i* would not be enjoined; thus, its status as a "being-enunciated" (*bhāvyamānatva*) would not even exist.
When the elision of the suffix *lup* occurs, the word behaves like that which possesses the suffix, provided there is no change in gender or number. Pāṇini 1.2.51.

Since gender and number would otherwise apply according to the meaning expressed [by the base], this rule is commenced. Because it is impossible to transfer gender and number to *lup*, which is of the nature of non-existence, he says: "In the case of *lup*," meaning "the technical name *lup*," and so forth. In some instances, however, the word *lup* is used in the locative case; even there, it is the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) alone that is intended to be expressed. The use of the locative, however, is because it is so read in the sūtra, just as in the expression *matāv* (in the sense of possession), the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is expressed. Regarding the term *yuktavat* ("like that with which it is joined"), he explains it with "by means of the suffix *niṣṭhā*" and so forth. He states the reason for this with the words "for that... (*sa hi*).

It joins, that is, it connects. Although the meaning of the suffix also connects itself with the meaning of the base, nevertheless it is not taken here [as the referent]; because it would be purposeless, for one cannot enjoin gender and number for that very same thing which is already being enjoined.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha vā" (or else): previously, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) was shown for the form ending in *ktavatu* derived from the root *yuj* in the sense of "joining" (*yoga*). Now, however, it is demonstrated that for that same root ending in *kta*, there is an indication by means of the suffix *vati*, and that this is not a compound. [The phrase] "the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is joined" is explained here by the reason: "it is connected with the meaning of the suffix. Even in this view, as before, there is no inclusion of the meaning of the suffix. [The expression] "the suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative case" is stated.

The meaning is that because of the use of the locative case in the word *lupi* (in the phrase *lupi yuktavad*), the suffix *vat* occurs in the sense of the locative, or in the sense of "like" (*iva*). The word *vyakti* also denotes meanings such as manifestation (*āvirbhāva*). Furthermore, just as Bhīmasena is called Bhīma, one might suppose that even a partial usage of words such as *ekavacana* (singular) and so forth is possible. If that [partial usage] were accepted, then since the genitive case is observed in the sentence "the dwelling place of the Pañcālas," the extension (*atideśa*) would apply to that [genitive] alone.

In the case of the *dvandva* compound "Kuru-Pañcālāḥ," when the prescribed plural suffix is elided (*luk*), there would be no plural ending for the whole aggregate. Therefore, so that this [collective] understanding does not arise, he says: "And [the rule] *vyaktivacane*," etc. He states the reason for relying on the instruction of the earlier teachers with the words: "That very [instruction]," etc. To the question "Why?", he replies: "For thus," etc. For it is not reasonable that one should himself reject what one has oneself composed; the sense is that this follows the maxim: "Even a poison-tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is not fit to be cut down by oneself."

"Pañcālāḥ are Kṣatriyas. [The derivation is as follows: From the word *pañcāla*, meaning "many descendants of Pañcāla," [the suffix] *añ* is applied according to the rule *janapada-śabdāt kṣatriyād añ*; then [the suffix] *tadrāja* is applied by the rule *te tadrājāḥ*; and [finally] the plural marker is applied by the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu*. Their dwelling place is the country (*janapada*). This [term *janapada*] is connected with the upcoming word *pañcālāḥ*. By the rule *tasya nivāsaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *janapade lup*, this suffix is elided. The same applies to "Kurus" and so forth. However, statements such as "Kuravaḥ are Kṣatriyas" have not been explicitly stated because they are understood through the preceding logic.

From the word *kuru*, when denoting offspring, the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule *akurvinādibhyo ṇyaḥ*; when denoting those from Magadha and so forth, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *dvyañmagadha*. The remainder is as before.

"What is the purpose of [mentioning] *lupi*? This question arises because one might think that since *taddhita* (secondary suffix) is carried over by *anuvṛtti*, it will bring forth its meaning through association (*sāhacarya*). [The answer is: "So that [the rule] does not apply when there is *luk*. The intention is that otherwise, due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the condition "when there is *luk* of a *taddhita*," [the rule] would apply only in those cases. [Example: *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* ("salted soup"). [This is derived from] *saṃsṛṣṭe lavaṇāt luk* ("there is *luk* after *lavaṇa* when expressing being mixed with it"). "What is the purpose of [mentioning] *vyaktivacane* (gender and number)? One might think that the suffix *-vat* in *yuktavat* will be understood as having the sense of the past passive participle (*kta*), or that a genitive case reference will be employed. [Examples follow: *śirīṣāṇām adūrabhāvaḥ* ("the state of being not far from Śirīṣa trees"), and so on.

Since the word *śirīṣa* is listed among the *arīhaṇa* group, the *varāha* group, and the *kumuda* group, suffixes such as *vañ* and others are applied to it by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*. Because these [suffixes] are prescribed for specific cases, there should be no elision (*luk*) [of the primary suffix]. This is true; however, he will state that "the general [suffix] is also desired from that," and since the form *varaṇa* and others are observed, there is elision (*lup*) of that [general suffix]. If the mention of "denoting an individual" (*vyaktivacana*) were not made, then the status of being a "large tree" (*vanaspati*) which belongs to the *śirīṣa* trees would also be extended to the village, and consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would result.

In the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*, the specific distinction that "it is a *vanaspati*" (a tree) is not taken into account as being irrelevant. For this very reason, the substitution of *ṇ* indeed occurs when the word refers to a tree, as in the example *śirīṣavanam*. Now, one might object: even when the word *vana* is used in the sense of a village, it expresses the state of being a *vanaspati* as a subordinate quality; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *ṇ*-substitution. Furthermore, in this case, there is no operation dependent upon a primary referent by virtue of which the subordinate quality (*guṇa*) would refrain from initiating its own grammatical effect.

Nor is the inclusion of the term "denoting an individual" (vyaktivacana) redundant; for if it were absent, the genitive case would result due to the extension (atideśa) of even the distinction (vyatireka) residing in the meaning of the base (prakṛti). However, when that term is present, since only the number is extended and the number accompanied by distinction is not extended, this fault does not arise. In that case, just as in the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatvavidhi), the mention of the primary *vanaspati* implies its absence here.

Regarding "the *harītakī* fruits": from the word *harītakī*, which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *añ* prescribed by the rule "anudāttādeśca" is elided by the rule "harītakyādibhyaśca. In this case, only the individual entity (*vyakti*) undergoes the treatment of being like the base (*yuktavat*), while the number remains exactly as that of the thing denoted (*abhidheyavat*). As in the example: "the *khalatika* groves."

The word *khalatikā-* belongs to the *varaṇādi* group. This [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction regarding the elision (*lup*) of the plural ending of the second member in a compound: it is an extension of plurality to the meaning of that which has undergone elision (*lub-artha*), provided that such an extension occurs in the compound, it applies only to the second member. For example: *madhurā-pañcālāḥ*. Here it does not occur: *pañcāla-madhurau*, because of the explicit mention of "plural" (*bahuvacanasya*). However, the extension of duality also applies to the first member: *godau ca grāmaḥ, madhurā ca* = *godamadhurāḥ*.
And [the rule] does not apply to qualifiers that do not denote a genus. 1.2.52.

Previously, the extension (*atideśa*) of gender and number belonging to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*) was established for the meaning of the *luP* suffix, but not for the word ending in *luP*. Therefore, the application of the rule *yuktavadbhāva* (the treatment as if joined with the base) is already established for the qualifiers residing therein. However, the explicit statement [in the rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting it in the case of generic terms (*jāti*). Now, why is this not intended as an injunction for qualifiers in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*), as in "The Pañcālas [belong] to Brahmadatta"? Because of the continued application of the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) from the rule "A *tatpuruṣa* compound whose members have a common substratum... [as in P. 2.4.7]. As in the example: "The two rivers Godāvarī."

The two lakes are Varaṇā and Ādi; the words *grāma* (village) and *janapada* (district) denote a genus (*jāti*). By means of these two, the meaning [of the suffix] is expressed in the form of a genus. Regarding the phrase "and of the meaning of the genus," etc.: the meaning is that it refers to the meaning in the form of a genus, not to the word denoting the genus. He states what is established by this with the words "by this."

By the mention of "the door" (dvāra), he shows this: when a genus (*jāti*) is under discussion, a qualifier that happens to occur qualifies that very genus directly; however, by means of that [genus], the meaning of the elided suffix (*lub-artha*) is understood as qualified. In this regard, there is freedom of choice concerning the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*). Thus, when qualifiers such as *ramaṇīya* ("delightful") occur in relation to a genus, the treatment as if possessing the gender and number of the base (*yuktavad-bhāva*) does not apply; but it does apply when they occur in relation to the meaning of the elided suffix.

If this is so, there is no need for this [sūtra], for this same principle is observed elsewhere in the case of the root *lup*. For example, in the expression "the jujube tree has fine thorns" (*badarī sūkṣmakaṇṭakā*) or "the jujube tree is sweet" (*madhurāvṛkṣa*), when the qualities such as sweetness are subsumed under the jujube tree, they take on its gender and number; and when subsumed under the word "tree," they take on the gender and number of "tree. Furthermore, the word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) itself possesses a fixed gender. In that case, what is stated here and there—that "for words denoting qualities, the gender and number do not follow from their substratum"—is precisely what is being established by this [sūtra].

The meaning is: "of qualifiers that express qualities (*guṇavacana*). "The gender and number are like those of the [substantive] with which [the quality] is joined" means that the gender and number are like those of the substratum (*āśraya*). However, when the qualifier is a genus (*jāti*), this does not apply. And under the view of word-formation (*padasaṃskārapakṣa*), this is a rule based on explicit statement (*vācanika*); for when a word is being formed independently of another word, the universal neuter gender (*liṅgasarvanāma*) and the singular number—which do not depend on any other entity—would result, leading to the form *śuklaṃ paṭāḥ*. Therefore, the gender and number of the future, extrinsic substratum are prescribed.

In the case of a change of gender (*vākya-saṃkāra*), this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); for even the qualifiers, by virtue of being restricted to a specific substratum, do not possess that [new] gender or number. Regarding the rule *manuṣyalupi*: there is a prohibition of qualifiers when the suffix *lup* applies in the sense of "characteristic of a human" (*manuṣya-lakṣaṇa*). However, it does indeed occur when *lup* follows a word ending in *lup*: for example, *cañcābhirūpaḥ*. A *cañcā* is a straw figure of a man; a man resembling that is called *cañcā*. Here, the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *asaṃjñāyām*, and then *lup* is applied by the rule *lummanuṣye*. A *vardhrīkā* is a specific type of leather product.
In that case, it need not be taught, because conventional designations are the standard of authority. (Pāṇini 1.2.53)

"Because of the nature of being a name (*saṃjñā-pramāṇatvāt*). For the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for all means of knowledge consists in their being communicative, characterized by the conveying of their own objects. And this [quality] belongs to all words whatsoever, not only to names. To the objection that "in that case, no distinction would be understood," he says: "For names... and so forth.

Those words which are proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*), even if they possess various genders and numbers, are authoritative (*pramāṇa*)—meaning they convey their own referents—even when their gender and number differ from those inherent in the objects they denote. Let it be that such is the authority of proper names; what follows regarding derivative (*yaugika*) words such as "Pañcāla" and so forth? To this he says: "The Pañcālas, the Varaṇas," and so on. By this, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) has been stated; previously, however, the reason as it exists in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) was explained.

He provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). Even one who undertakes the treatment of words as if they possessed [grammatical] gender (*yuktavadbhāva*) does not exert any effort here; therefore, this must necessarily be accepted as the very nature of the word itself. For some words, by their own nature, denote the number of the aggregate (*samudāya*), while others denote the number of the individual components (*avayava*), as in the cases of "the forest" (*vana*) and "the trees" (*vṛkṣāḥ*). The same should be observed regarding gender (*liṅga*) as well.
Because the connection with the sense organs is not perceived. 1.2.54.

"What is the reason? [The answer is: "In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all [case endings] are generally seen," thus the first or second case ending is used. And so, the subsequent justification is "because of the non-recognition of the connection" (*yogāprakhyānāt*). "Connection" (*yoga*) means the relationship of a region and so forth with [people such as] Kṣatriyas; the meaning is "because of its non-recognition" or non-perception. He says this: "For not... and he explains this very point: "This is not so," [meaning] "these are merely names."

Although even proper names such as *paṅkaja* (lotus) possess a required basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it should nevertheless be understood that in this context they may lack a required basis for their application due to the specific topic at hand. For this very reason, he says: "Therefore, here," and so forth. Now, one might object: "Even when the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is not manifest, a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is still produced—for example, according to the rule 'also from *kambala* when it is a name,' we have *kambalya*, meaning 'one hundred palas of wool. This is true; however, [the rule applies] where there is a distinction in form."

But surely, since it has been established that words such as *pañcāla* are non-etymological (*ayaugika*) on the grounds that "the name is the authority" (*saṃjñāpramāṇatvāt*), the elision (*lub*) is already effectively rejected by implication; what, then, is being done here? It is said in reply: By the phrase "the name is the authority," the reason residing in the example is stated explicitly. However, fearing that this very reason—though understood as applying to *pañcāla* and so forth by implication—is unestablished (*asiddha*), [the author] now supports that very reason by refuting its etymological nature through the argument "because the etymology is not observed" (*yogāprakhyānāt*).
And when there is no [external] object, there would be perception through the means of yoga. (1.2.55)

"Pañcālādayaḥ," and so forth. It has been stated that there is no appearance [of the object] in the prior conjunction; however, he shows that for one who denies this, an undesirable consequence follows, by saying "for, if the conjunction were the means of valid cognition" (*yogapramāṇe hi*). By employing the word "hi" in the sense of a reason, he demonstrates that the word "ca" in the sūtra is also employed as a reason. He explains this very point with "if...": "non-appearance would constitute non-conjunction."

"Vision" (*darśana*) is knowledge (*jñāna*), and that is the fruit of the application (*prayoga*), which is to say, of the pronunciation (*uccāraṇa*). Therefore, he explains that by the absence of the fruit, the absence of the cause is intended. For the manifestation [of the word] is logically dependent upon the connection [with the object], just as in the case of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*); this is the underlying thought. Now, one might object: even something that previously existed can serve as a cause; therefore, even if the connection with the enclosure (*varaṇā*) and so forth is absent at present, that very same previous connection will serve as the cause. This is not so.

For a designation based on a past state would be figurative (*gauṇa*), and this [designation] is not figurative, because it is understood even without the employment of another word. Furthermore, if it were etymological (*yaugika*), why would the designation not also apply based on the connection with other persons? Or why would the opposite not occur? Since the word *pañcāla* applies to kings due to their connection with the region, this word *pañcālādi* must have multiple meanings, just like the word *akṣa* and others.
The statement that the meaning of the suffix denotes the primary sense [of the base] is because the meaning [of the whole] is established by other means of knowledge. 1.2.56.

Regarding the expression "arthavacanam": this is a compound formed with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*). Now, one might object that since both the primary element and the suffix denote the agent (*kartṛ*), the genitive here falls under the rule *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66), and consequently, the prohibition by the rule *karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) would apply. This is not a fault; for in this context, it is intended that the primary element and the suffix function as instruments (*karaṇa*).

Who, then, is the agent (*kartṛ*): the individual (*puruṣa*), or the aggregate (*samudāya*) of the primary and the subordinate, or of the base and the suffix? What is meant is this: by means of the primary and the suffix as instruments, there is a compound (*samāsa*) with the word "expression" (*vacanaśabda*)—whether by the person or by the aggregate—with the word for the object, according to the rules: "The agent and the instrument [are compounded] with a *kṛt*-derivative frequently" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*), and "When a *kṛt*-derivative is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka is also included."

But surely the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also primary in relation to the base (*prakṛti*); why then is it mentioned separately? It is said in reply: when it is established that "the base denotes its own meaning as a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the suffix," then the suffix possesses primacy. That very point is now being defined. For this reason, the former teachers have specified the suffix separately—referring to them as "the primary and the subordinate" (*pradhānopasarjane*) or "the base and the suffix" (*prakṛtipratyayau*). Consequently, in the process of defining their characteristics, [the base is treated first].

The suffix (*pratyaya*) must also be understood as distinct [from the base]. This is because it is impossible [to express them otherwise]; "impossibility" is due to the infinite variety of forms. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is expressed; in a collective (*samāhāra*) such as *plakṣanyagrodham*, there is a co-expression of the two principal members themselves—as in *plakṣanyagrodhau*. Furthermore, in the case of primary derivatives (*svārthika*), both the base and the suffix express the meaning of the base together—as in *śuklatara*; likewise, in verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), it is said that "the verb has action as its primary meaning."

Likewise, in rules such as "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*) and "the third case [is used] for the agent" (*kartari tṛtīyā*), it is stated that "among kṛt suffixes, the substance possessing power (*śaktimat*) is called the primary [meaning]. Thus, when there is a difference in action, another power manifests; in expressions like "look at the cook" (*pācakam paśya*), the predominance of power resides in the case-endings (*vibhakti*). Since such an infinite variety of ways of denoting meaning cannot be exhaustively defined by technical rules (*paribhāṣā*), he asks, "How is this so?"—given that meaning is understood from worldly usage alone—and answers with the words beginning "by whomsoever... (*yairapi...*).
And [the same rule applies] when a word denoting time is compounded as a subordinate member. 1.2.57.

"Because the object [of knowledge] has another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How, then, is this reason obtained here? He says: "The word *tulya* (equal) is for the purpose of drawing forward the reason. How is this so? He says: "And this is a qualification of the non-student. The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. Regarding the phrase "because it is improper": from the night divided into four parts, rising from sleep during the last watch is proper, because it is sanctioned by scripture; and going to bed—that is, sleeping—is proper during the first watch.

In this definition, the two middle watches of the night do not belong to the current day; however, in the second [case], they do. "Midnight on both sides" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning that the entire day is joined with the first half of the coming night and the latter half of the past night. "If it were so" means that because the sense of "if" implies another authority, this very point serves as the reason here as well. "In the previous sūtra alone" implies that, in this way, it would not be necessary to state "it is the same."
When a genus is denoted, the plural may optionally be used for a single individual. Pāṇini 1.2.58.

In the expression *jātyākhyāyām*, the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Similarly, in *ekasmin* as well, these two locatives are in grammatical apposition with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇa*). By the words "the name 'jāti' (*jātināma*)" and so forth, he states the reason for the commencement of the sūtra: "one object" (*eko 'rthaḥ*). Although number as defined by the Vaiśeṣika school does not exist in a *jāti*, because that [number] is a property of substance (*dravyadharma*); nevertheless, number in the form of the counting of distinctions certainly exists. As it has been said:
"A *diṣṭi*, a *prastha*, gold, and so forth, serve to distinguish material objects; time serves to distinguish actions; but number is the distinguisher of everything."

And the Vaiśeṣikas employ [these terms]: "five actions" and "twenty-four qualities. Regarding the phrase "a designation of a genus" (*jāterākhyā*): *ākhyāna* means *ākhyā*, which is the act of making known. Regarding the phrase "in reference to a single object": this plural word used when a genus is designated is etymological (*anvartha*), not technical (*pāribhāṣika*). *Ukti* means speech; *bahuvacana* is the speech of many. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: when there is a speech regarding many [individuals] in reference to a single object, by implication the sense of the suffix *-vat* is understood—that is, it is a speech as if regarding many.

And if it is argued that because a word denoting a genus (jātyartha) behaves like the plural, its expression becomes as if it were many, and thus by implication that very meaning is achieved, he says: "A word denoting a genus behaves like the plural. He asks, "What is established by this? and replies: "By this. However, if the plural number were prescribed for a genus-word [only] when expressing a genus and so forth, then it would not apply to qualifiers such as *saṃpanna* and the like, because they are not words denoting a genus; this is the sense.

Regarding "Devadatta": although, according to the view of those who maintain that a universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, even here the universal as it follows through various states is what is denoted by the word, nevertheless, in this context, the universal inherent in a single, undivided individual (*piṇḍa*) is intended by implication; thus, there is no extension [of the rule]. Regarding "Kāśyapa": from the word *kaśyapa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied [by Pāṇini 4.1.104], and then the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of "resembling" (*iva*) when forming a name [by 5.3.97], with the elision of the suffix [by 5.3.98]. This is a word for a genus (*jātiśabda*), because it denotes a lineage (*gotra*) which is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). However, the genus itself is not directly expressed by this [word].

The intended meaning is "by way of predominance. If the term *asatyākhyā* ("denoting something unreal") were not included, the meaning would be "from a word denoting a genus (*jāti*)," and in that case, just as [the suffix occurs] even after words like *go* when the denotation extends to the individual (*vyakti*), so too would it occur here. But since that term is present, by its force, it occurs when the genus is predominant. As in the example *vrīhiyavau*. Now, one might object: just as in the case of *kāśikosalīyāḥ*, the suffix *vuñ* is prescribed by the rule for designating a country (*janapada*), yet a collective form consisting of a country is not actually initiated by its constituent parts.

Therefore, since that which is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not denote a country, and that which denotes a country is not an independent nominal stem, how could there be any occasion for the suffix *vuñ*? However, this rule applies to the communication of a genus (*jāti*), and since it does not apply to a word that is [merely] a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), the occasion for its application would indeed arise.

Regarding the phrase "in the application of number": the intention is that [this rule] would apply even when the word *eka* (one) is used, provided that a transfer (*atideśa*) of plurality is being made to that very same single entity. Even though this [present rule] is being commenced, it is intended that this injunction applies only to the denotation of the universal (*jāti*) by extracting it [from the individual], as in the cases of "cowness" (*gotva*) or "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*). If, however, the denotation were to extend to the individual (*vyakti*), then since the relationship between the universal and the individual is one of identity (*tādātmya*), the singular number is established when individuals are denoted in the form of the universal. But when the universal is denoted in the form of the individual, the plural number [is required]; therefore, this [rule] serves no purpose.
The substitution of *asmad* occurs for both [the singular and dual] as well. Pāṇini 1.2.59.

He states that the genitive case [in *asmadaḥ*] is used due to its connection with the denoted object (*abhidheya*), saying: "the meaning which belongs to *asmad*" (*asmado yo'rthaḥ*). The intention is that if the ablative were used, the suffix would not apply to the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) occurring therein. Regarding the phrase "in the singular and in the dual": an objection is raised—surely the word *asmad* refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and since that is one, how can there be a connection with duality? Furthermore, even singularity is an inappropriate qualifier for it, because it is never absent (*avyabhicārāt*). It is replied: [The answer follows: ... [text continues] ... [The answer follows: ... When selfhood (*ātmatva*) is superimposed upon another—such as "this is my second self"—or when a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is formed according to the rule "the pronouns beginning with *atyad* [and so on] are always [retained] with all [others]," then a plurality of referents is possible. Now, where the word *asmad* is used in the plural, how is the determination of specific duality or singularity made? It is through context (*prakaraṇa*), just as in the case of the word *dūra* or *antika* [which may be understood as singular or plural]. For example: *aham* [I], [whereby the forms *ṅe* and *prathamā* become *am* by the rule *ṅeprathamayoram*, and *tvāhau sau* applies]; and *vayam* [we].

‘*maparyantasya*, ‘*yūyavayau jasi*, and ‘*śeṣe lopaḥ*. Regarding *āvām*: by the rules ‘*yuvāvau dvivacane*’ and ‘*prathamāyāśca dvivacane*’, the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) occurs. Regarding ‘*saviśeṣaṇasya*’: in the example ‘*tvaṃ rājā vayamapyupāsitaguruprajñābhimānonnatāḥ*’ (*you are the king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom acquired from serving our gurus*), it is precisely the state of being elevated (*unnatatvam*) that is predicated. And since a predicate meaning cannot be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the extension (*atideśa*) [of the dual endings] certainly applies. Regarding ‘*yuṣmadī*’: although not recorded in the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*, it has been included here because it is observed in the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after the words *phalgunī* and *proṣṭhapadā* when they denote a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). 1.2.60.

Regarding the passage beginning with *cakāra* (and so forth), some say: "The status of being a *nakṣatra* (lunar mansion) for luminaries occurs when there is conjunction with the moon; at other times, they possess merely the nature of a *jyotis* (luminary). Since conjunction with the moon requires two [entities] together, the dual number is already established; however, by employing the particle *ca* (*and*) to draw forward the word 'two' (*dvayoḥ*), the Teacher indicates that the mention of *nakṣatra* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any luminary. Since the nature of being a luminary, as thus illustrated, belongs to each individual as well, the word 'two' must be drawn forward in order to exclude the case of a single one."

To this it is replied: although each individual [constellation] possesses the nature of being a light (*jyotis*), the word *phalgunī* does not apply to it [in that sense]. Likewise, the word *proṣṭhapadā* and others denote the aggregate itself in which the distinction of parts has emerged. For this very reason, there is the formulation of the rules: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is the singular number for the two *punarvasū*, and likewise for the two *viśākhā*s. Furthermore, in the *nighaṇṭus*, the word *nakṣatra* is listed as a synonym specifically for *tārakā* (star).

Even in the Veda, in such passages as "The ancestors have adorned the sky with the stars," "Thou art the bright one among the stars," and "Time joined with a star," the author of the *Vṛtti* will say: "But how is time joined with a star, such as Puṣya? That too is untenable; for since this [connection] is occasional, it occurs through Puṣya and others in the form of a star that exists only at specific times. Furthermore, in the case of the expression "of Tiṣya and Punarvasu," the connection with Tiṣya and the others is occasional because they rise [only at certain times].

In the rule "tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ," Tiṣya and Punarvasu are seen as being mentioned in the nominative case (*uditau*). This will likewise be illustrated in the context of conjunction with the moon (*candrayoga*). Furthermore, in the counter-example, he demonstrates that the meaning is indeed the nature of the celestial bodies themselves: "The students are Tiṣya and Punarvasu. Therefore, this is not the view of the author of the Vṛtti—that the term *nakṣatra* refers to a particular state; rather, it denotes the celestial bodies alone.

By means of the word *ca* (and), there is also an attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the term "of the two"—this is for the purpose of demonstrating that a collection (*samudāya*) whose constituent parts are manifest is what is denoted, and not each individual light. Regarding the phrase "of the Proṣṭhapadās," he states that the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative, or that the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive, as in "of the two Phalgunīs" and so forth. The term "of the two constellations" (*nakṣatrayoḥ*) is connected to each [name] individually; however, in the Sūtra, the singular number is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).

In this case as well, because the multiplicity of the meaning is extended [to the compound], it also applies to the qualifier: *pūrve phalgunyau* ("the two former Phalgunīs"). [The derivation is as follows: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "time joined with the two Phalgunīs" or "with the Phalgunīs," according to the rule *lub aviśeṣe*; then, by the rule *lupi yuktavad vyaktivacane*, the gender and number of the original word are maintained. Thus we have *phalgunyau māṇavike* ("two young women born under the Phalgunīs"). Here, the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule *phalgunyaṣāḍhābhyāṃ ṭānau vaktavyau* (meaning that the suffixes *ṭa* and *na* are to be stated after *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā* respectively), and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*.
In the Vedic language, the singular number is used for the two Punarvasu stars.

Regarding the phrase "when two [are meant]," although the term "of two" (*dvayoḥ*) was not carried over from the preceding rule, he shows that this rule applies specifically to two by means of the word *punarvasu*, because it denotes a collection of two luminaries whose internal distinction has become manifest.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *viśākhe*. 1.2.62.

What is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? It is so that I may carry forward the word *chandasi* by means of the particle *ca* in this rule; consequently, the word *chandasi* does not carry forward in the subsequent rules.
1.2.63: In a dual compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-dvandva*), the dual number is obligatory for *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*.

In the expression *tiṣyapunarvasvau*, the locative dual (*saptamī-dvivacana*) is used by virtue of this very rule in consideration of the dual number [of the compound]. Alternatively, in the phrase *nakṣatradvandve*, the locative is used in a locative-absolute sense (*satsaptamī*); that is, when there is a dual compound of lunar mansions (*nakṣatradvandve*), the expression occurs as if denoting two meanings, namely Tiṣya and Punarvasu—thus, the genitive dual (*ṣaṣṭhī-dvivacana*) is used in consideration of the compound. Regarding the phrase *teṣāṃ dvandvaḥ*, the dual number does not occur after the word *tad* (those), because the sentence is under discussion and because [the pronoun] functions with respect to a meaning other than a dual compound.

In this context, if the technical (pāribhāṣika) dual and plural were taken, the dual would be the substitute for the plural. In that case, when *jas* is replaced by the dual of the nominative (*prathamā-dvivacana*), the rule "ajasi ca" would require a *guṇa* [substitution], and furthermore, there would be no [application of] the rule regarding qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇānām*). With this in mind, he says: "in the event of the plural" (*bahuvacanasya prasaṅge*). This means "in the event of expressing many objects. "The dual occurs" means "the expression becomes as if it were two."

Regarding the example *tiṣyapunarvasavo māṇavakāḥ* ("The boys Tiṣya and Punarvasu"): by the words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born under" (*jātārtha*) according to the rule *saṃdhivelādi-sūtra*, and that suffix is elided by the rule *śraviṣṭhā-phalguny-anurādhā*. Here, the *dvandva* compound does not refer to the constellations (*nakṣatra*), but rather to the boys. Furthermore, this usage is not figurative (*gauṇa*), because the application [of the term] occurs through a succession of primary connections (*yoga-paramparā*). Regarding the phrase "also of synonyms": by the force of the repetition of the word *nakṣatra*, this extension (*atideśa*) applies to the meaning itself, regardless of the specific words employed; thus, the inclusion of synonyms is established.

Regarding the question "What is meant by 'dvandva' (copulative compound)?": In the sentence *tiṣyaśca punarvasū ca*, even if it were a compound where the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, plurality would not be possible; furthermore, such a compound is not easily formed. A *bahuvrīhi* is also impossible because the members have different referents (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). Since a *dvigu* is defined as "preceded by a numeral" and this [compound] is neither preceded by a numeral nor an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and an *avyayībhāva* is simply inconceivable here, one might think that it must necessarily be a *dvandva*. [The author replies: "He who is Tiṣya," and so forth.

When a compound is analyzed by its constituent parts (*avayava*), the meaning of the compound is the whole (*samudāya*) in which the distinction between the parts has been manifested. Confused people might think that [the term refers to] only Tiṣya and the others; therefore, he says: "only Tiṣya and the rest. However, in some places it is read as "these, Tiṣya, Punarvasu, and Magadhā. Even there, because the word *unmugdha* expresses a state of transformation, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), meaning "those who are indistinct" (*avivikta*). It is just as one says, "the seasons are confused. This is simply a compound of constellations (*nakṣatra-samāsa*); the intention is that there is no difference between the whole and its constituents. [This applies to] "every *dvandva*," etc.

But surely, in the section on the formation of singular compounds (*ekavadbhāva*), a restriction was adopted such that for parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and the like, the *dvandva* compound must be a collective (*samāhāra*) only, whereas for items such as curds and milk (*dadhipayas*), it must be a copulative (*itaretarayoga*) only. Consequently, since the *dvandva* is established as either collective or copulative by the rule "or when a *dvandva* [is formed] with *ca*" (*cārthe dvandvaḥ*), which is not restricted to that specific section, what is the point of citing an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark)? True; however, the opposite restriction might also have been intended in the Sūtra—that the collective form applies only to parts of living beings and the like.

Therefore, by the inclusion of the plural number, it is indicated that the parts of living beings and so forth are subject to restriction. We shall explain the purpose of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) regarding trees and the like in that very place.
Of words that have the same form, only one remains when they occur with a single case-ending.

Those whose form (*rūpa*) is the same are "homogeneous" (*sarūpa*). By the rule beginning with *jyotirjanapada*, the substitution of *sa* for *sama* occurs. However, it is not the case that they are called *sarūpa* because "they exist together with a form" (*saha rūpeṇa vartante*); for there is no such deviation [from this definition]. Furthermore, the word *rūpa* here refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is related to sound and is perceptible by the ear, and not to white and other colors perceptible by the eye; since this is a treatise on the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), he says: "of homogeneous words. This genitive case is used either for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) or with reference to the whole (*samudāya*).

In this regard, five possible interpretations arise. The first [interpretation] is that the word *eka* means "identical" (*samāna*), as in the rule *tenaikadik*. Since identity (*sāmānya*) is based on difference, when all [words] are distinct yet followed by the same case-ending (*vibhakti*), one [word] remains. This is the first view. The second [interpretation] is that the term *dvandve* (in a copulative compound) is understood [from a previous rule]. In that context, even though the *dvandva* compound finds its scope among dissimilar forms, the *ekaśeṣa* does not exclude it, because the *dvandva* serves as the cause [for the application of the rule]. Thus, once the *dvandva* has been formed for similar forms, the *ekaśeṣa* applies when a single case-ending follows the compound. This is the second view.

In this view, the word *eka* expresses number. From the rule "hrasvo napuṃsake" [Pāṇini 1.2.47], the term "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*) is understood to carry over. The phrase "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*) is an indicator for similarity of form (*sārūpya*). Thus, the third interpretation is that there is an unconditional *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of those nominal stems which are seen to be identical in form when occurring with a single case-ending. The word "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) here denotes the power of the grammatical function (*kāraka-śakti*), since by it the meaning of the nominal stem is differentiated; it means that the expression is produced when a single grammatical function is intended to be conveyed.

The fourth [view] is that there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of distinct words ending in case-terminations. The fifth is that there is a single remainder from a collection of similar forms when a single case-ending follows.

In that regard, concerning the first position: when *vṛkṣaḥ vṛkṣaḥ vṛkṣaḥ* is established, if the two preceding [instances] were to cease, the form would become *s s vṛkṣaḥ*. In this state, while the case-ending (*su*) connected with the middle [instance] would be elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* etc., there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of hearing the other two [case-endings]. The same should be observed regarding the cessation of the first and the last [instances]. Even if the latter two were to cease, the elision of the case-ending connected with the remaining [instance] would simply not be established. Furthermore, in cases such as *godau varaṇāḥ*, if a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) were applied after two separate dual endings, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing those two [endings].

For where there is the cessation of the base (*prakṛti*) caused by a condition (*pratyaya*), there the application of the suffix alone indeed occurs, as in *iyān*. In the second case, however—when *aśva* and *aśva* stand as *aśva-aśva-au*, since the accentuation of the compound-final syllable (*samāsāntodāttatva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the requirement for the case-ending, if the first remainder were applied, the word would be entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*); but if the latter remainder were applied, the word *aśva* would have its final syllable accented. Furthermore, in this case—when *ṛk* and *ṛk* stand as *ṛcau*—since the addition of the compound-final suffix *a* (by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*) is internal, the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would not apply because of the intervention of the vowel *a* of the case-ending.

For a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), being included by the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*), would not itself create an intervention for that [compound], but it certainly does create an intervention for a word of identical form (*sarūpa*). Alternatively, the mention of "single" (*eka*) is redundant; for it is impossible for multiple case-endings to occur simultaneously in a *dvandva* compound. Furthermore, if one were to state that "the *ekaśeṣa* occurs immediately after the formation of a *dvandva*" without including the rule "in a single case-ending" (*ekavibhaktau*), then even so, dual and plural forms would not occur in cases such as *pādau* or *pādāḥ*;
this is because of the restrictive rule that a *dvandva* of limbs of living beings, etc., is treated like a collective (*samāhāra*).

In the third alternative, however, there would be the undesirable consequence of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of only one) everywhere, because even for the word *mātṛ* meaning "mother" and the word *mātṛ* derived from the root *māṅ* ("to measure") with the suffix *tṛc* meaning "measurer of grain," the forms *mātā* and *mātṛbhyām* are identical in some case-endings. Likewise, there would be no such retention for the word *harīṇī*, which results from the word *harita* (a color term) by the addition of the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakāra* according to the rule "from a color term that is unaccented on the first syllable," and the word *hariṇī*, which results from the word *hariṇa* (a generic term) by the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ*;
for although these two are identical when ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, they are not identical in their state as nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
However, in the fourth view, although the word is withdrawn along with its case-ending (*vibhakti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the singular number for that which remains.

Therefore, adopting the fifth position, he says: "of words having the same form (*sarūpāṇām*), when a single case-ending follows. The meaning is: "from a collection of identical forms, when a single case-ending follows."

Now, an objection may be raised: since the rule *aṅyāpprātipadikāt* consists of a dvandva compound of words ending in the singular number, and since singularity is intended there, how can a case-suffix arise from a collection of nominal stems (*prātipadika*)? Let it be that each individual member possesses the status of a nominal stem; however, the collection as a whole is also a nominal stem because it possesses meaning. But what is the meaning of the collection? It is their mutual relationship; by each individual member, a distinct meaning is expressed.

The connection, however, is with the aggregate; and by the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*), there is the exclusion of an arthavat-aggregate that belongs to the same class [as a compound]. What is it that belongs to the same class? It is that wherein the prior portion is a word (*pada*). Since this is not the case here, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) from the aggregate is not contradictory. However, because the distinction between its constituent parts has not emerged, there is either a dual or a plural ending, but not a singular ending.

In examples such as *nāvau* (two boats) and *janāvau* (two people), even after the substitution of *āva* and other suffixes has occurred due to the subsequent presence of the vowel *a*, the single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) takes place because they have the same meaning despite having different forms. This word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) does not apply to the serpent king Ananta, nor to what is subordinate, nor to anything other than that which is relevant; rather, it refers to a state of persistence characterized by cessation. Thus it is said: "one remains, while the others cease."

[Objection: In this view, the mention of "one" (*eka*) is redundant, for it is not possible for multiple case-endings (*vibhakti*) to occur simultaneously within a single aggregate. [Response: It is said in reply: if the mention of "one" were absent, the first alternative—that the case-ending follows after each [word] separately—might also be considered possible. Therefore, that alternative alone in which only a single case-ending occurs for words of identical form (*sarūpa*) is adopted by virtue of the mention of "one."

Alternatively, regarding the fourth position, the text asks: "How then [can it be said] 'when a case-ending follows'? For indeed, there can be no sequence of words based on the functional capacities (*kāraka-śakti*) of the factors of action. It is replied: the word *para* (following) denotes what is intended (*iṣṭa*); that is to say, it is intended within a single case-ending and with respect to a single factor of action.

But was it not said that there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing only the singular ending for what remains? [We reply: Now, the dual and plural endings are not able to arise based on the duality and plurality produced by the entry of a number that is being excluded, because [the remaining form] would not be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) since it would end in a suffix. This is not a fault; for *ekaśeṣa* occurs when there is a desire to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*). What, then, is this "desire to express together"? It has been stated here:
"When a single manifestation arises as if the distinctions were unmanifest, they call that 'desire to express together' in the case of *dvandva* and *ekaśeṣa*. Thus it is said.

This is the meaning: when many objects are presented together in a single cognition—just as, for example, the five fingers of a hand situated before one—and they are applied in that very same way to a single quality or action, such as "they are beautiful" or "they are seen," then there is *sahavivakṣā* (the intention to express them together). For it is thus: the speaker employs a word in order to transmit his own cognition to another.

If the parts were perceived individually—as when [objects] move in succession through a window—then they would have to be designated by distinct words, each ending in the singular number and terminating in its own individual sense. However, there is a single cognition that persists through the differences of the parts and takes on the form of a whole; one who wishes to transfer that [cognition] onto another object must employ a word corresponding to it.

Furthermore, since there is no single word that is unique to such a collection, it must be expressed by means of the words for its parts alone. And expression by means of the words for the parts is indeed appropriate, because of the non-difference between the collection and its constituent members. Moreover, each individual word denoting a part functions with either a dual or plural ending because it expresses a collection in which the distinction between the parts is manifest; thus, there is no consequence of hearing a singular ending.

If this is so, then since such a collective entity can be denoted by a single member-word alone, there would be no consequence of having to employ as many words as there are members. Now, if it is thought that the capacity to denote the meaning of a collective form only manifests when [the members] are in mutual proximity, then how does that capacity belong to a single [member] when the formation of *ekaśeṣa* occurs? For a non-existent capacity cannot be produced for an existing thing by the statement of *ekaśeṣa*. It is replied: in the case of dissimilar items, the capacity to denote the meaning of a collective form manifests when they are in mutual proximity.

In the case of *paṭuguptau* as well, it is precisely the word for "part" (*avayava*) that is employed in the dual number for each instance in order to indicate a collection whose constituent parts are manifest; otherwise, since the dual and plural numbers would be inappropriate, the meaning would be understood only through the successive utterance of words for "parts" that terminate in their own respective referents. And when multiple meanings are perceived successively, the dual and plural numbers do not occur.

And there is also the case of a collective compound (*samuccaya*), such as "eloquent in speech and guarded. Therefore, because we observe this [coexistence] even among dissimilar items, when there is a suspicion that a copulative compound (*dvandva*) might also apply to similar items, it is established by the rule that for similar items, only one [word] possesses the capacity to express multiple meanings.

Others, however, describe even a third position as being established in the text: that *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) occurs among words of identical form (*sarūpa*) when a single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*) follows; the analysis is "when a single case-ending follows, [there is retention] of those which have identical forms," and not merely "retention. The meaning is: when a single kāraka is intended to be expressed, or when a single case-ending follows, those words seen to be of identical form—of these [there is retention]. And in that case, the one that remains expresses the meaning of even that which has been eliminated.

In the case of *agnicit*, when the suffix is elided, the rule *prakṛtivat* (as in the base form) applies, so that the dual and plural endings occur as appropriate. Regarding what was stated—that it would not apply to forms ending in the suffix *ṅī* such as *haritā* and *hariṇī*—that is not correct; for the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not carry over [from the previous rule], and therefore it will apply precisely to those two forms because they possess identical phonetic form (*sārūpya*). Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the possibility of its application to the two words for "mother" (*mātṛ*), it will not occur because their meanings are mutually exclusive (*arthavipratiṣedha*).

For if *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) were applied, the meaning "by them" (*tābhiḥ*) would not be understood in the subsequent usage; if "by them" (*taiḥ*) were said, the feminine sense would not be conveyed. Alternatively, because of the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) here of the particle *eva* which is to be mentioned later, and because of the reliance on the rule "those which have the same form in a single case-ending," and because of the lack of identical form (*asārūpya*) due to the prescription of lengthening in the *sarvanāmasthāna* case for words denoting a male agent according to the rule *aptṛntṛc*, there is no *ekaśeṣa*. In this view, the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) is of questionable utility. Thus, among these five views, three are accepted.

"Tree and tree"—in the view that "the single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) is non-contingent," this analysis (*vigraha*) is presented with an inflected form in order to demonstrate similarity in case-ending. But how can there be an analysis, given that the operation of *ekaśeṣa* is obligatory? This is not a sentence having the same meaning as the formation, for here each individual is intended to be expressed. And therefore it is expressed individually; because here, by means of the word "and" (*ca*), a conjunction based on distinction is illuminated, and even a sentence whose meanings are distinct becomes a [valid] sentence provided there is some slight commonality.

However, when the referents are identical, there is indeed suppression [of one by the other], as in: *vṛkṣau ca vṛkṣau* (two trees and two trees), *vṛkṣāśca vṛkṣāśca* (trees and trees), or simply *vṛkṣāḥ* (trees). Now, if these words—such as *ākāśa* (ether), *dravyatva* (substanceness), and *gotva* (cowness)—are those that adhere to a single referent, then for them there is no *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) even with dual or plural endings. But for those words that adhere to multiple referents—such as *gauḥ* (cow), *śuklaḥ* (white), and *pācakaḥ* (cook)—one must state some single factor residing in the referents that runs through them all, such as the cause *gotva* (cowness) and so forth.

Otherwise, because the apprehension of a relation would be impossible, in this case [of words like] "cow" and so forth, the universal (*jāti*) is not the cause for its being a quality-possessor (*tadguṇatā*), just as it is not in the case of "white" and so forth, which reside solely in qualities. However, in the case of those residing in qualities, the quality becomes unified with the universal inherent within itself. Likewise, in the case of "cook" and so forth, there are universals such as "cowness" and "horseness"; in the phrase "universals are devoid of universals," there is the cause of a non-different cognition regarding things that are different; and in phrases such as "those two," there is the cause of the cognition of mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and immediacy (*pratyakṣatva*).

In this context, regarding the four types of non-existence (*abhāva*), the principle of "being indefinable" (*nirupākhya*) and so forth should be understood to apply everywhere. Furthermore, there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the cause (*nimitta*) and that which possesses the cause (*tadvat*); for every entity is both one and many: it is one in its form as a cow and so forth, and many in its form as individual cows such as Khaṇḍa and others, or in its form as the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This being the case, if the universal (*jāti*) alone were the meaning of a word, then because that universal is one, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of there being no plurality of words [to denote it].

Moreover, even if both [universal and substance] are denoted, the word denotes the substance solely through its universal form (*jātirūpa*) and not by way of its individual specific form (*prātisvikākāra*); thus, there is no contingency of multiple words [being required for a single object]. Even in the view that the substance alone is the referent (*padārtha*), in this case, one must admit that the word possesses the capacity to denote multiple objects—just as in the case of words such as *dvi* (two) and so on—otherwise, even if *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) were applied, that capacity would not exist. Thus, the unity of the word is established. As for the dual and plural endings, they will occur to express the number residing in the substance.

Fearing that this [objection] is not a valid point, he says: "pratyartham" and so forth. Since words are applied to each individual object (*artha*), it follows that the denotation of many things by means of many words is established. This being the case, when the denotation of multiple objects is to be performed, the application of as many words as there are objects would result; yet, a single word-form (*ekaśabdatva*) is desired. Therefore, the *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) is commenced.

This is the intended meaning: in the view that [the word] denotes only the genus (*jāti*), there would be multiple words for such instances as *akṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, and *māṣāḥ*; for indeed, there is no single commonality (*sāmānya*) running through the vibhītaka fruit, the axle of a game-board, and the axle of a cart. For this very reason, a distinct etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) must be sought for each case; the same applies to both [other] views. Even in the view that [the word] denotes only the substance (*dravya*), since we observe multiple words in the sentence "a tree" (*vṛkṣaśca*) and observe compounds (*dvandva*) among dissimilar things, this [treatise] must be commenced.

The question "Why is 'rūpa' (form) mentioned? is asked because [one might think] that identity based on form alone will be understood due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*), not subject to abandonment (*aheya*), and independent of instruction. Furthermore, when it is stated "of similar [words]" (*samānānām*), there is simplicity of comprehension (*pratipatti-lāghava*) because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is understood through the word *samāna* itself as a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*). However, if "rūpa" were mentioned, there would be complexity (*gaurava*), because one would have to first understand the meaning of the constituent members (*varti-pada-artha*) before understanding the meaning of the whole compound. [This applies even] when the meanings are different.

By the inclusion of the word *rūpa* (form) in the rule *svaṃ rūpam*, it is indicated in the grammatical treatise that meaning (*artha*), like form, is also a governing factor (*tantra*). Therefore, the intention is that identity should be understood through both meaning and form.

"Why is the word *eka* (one) mentioned? This is the question: "Is singularity intended to be expressed by the term *śeṣa* (remainder)? [The answer is: "Of two or many. This means: of more than one word, which is the object of duality or plurality. Now, an objection might be raised: since the dual or plural forms would result for "two" or "many," and because that which remains (*śiṣyamāṇa*) is being refined here by way of the rule for the remainder (*śeṣavidhāna*), it is the primary element (*pradhāna*); and in the case of a primary element, number is not intended to be expressed, as in the rule "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). [To this we reply: This is an unequal comparison.

In the procedure for cleansing (*saṃmārjana*), because of the use of the accusative case, the cups (*graha*) are the primary objects, while the cleansing is their consecration (*saṃskāra*). Consecration applies to that which is enjoined as an instrument in another scriptural injunction for a purposeful action, or to that which, once consecrated, is so enjoined; otherwise, a consecration of a mere substance would be purposeless.

If the act of cleansing (*saṃmārga*) enjoined here requires a cup (*graha*) that is already employed elsewhere in another scriptural injunction, then since nine cups are heard of [in that context], the injunction for cleansing, depending upon them, must apply to all nine. As for the singular number in the word "cup" (*graham*), it will serve merely to express the status of being the object of the action. However, in this case, because the remainder [of the sentence] is not determined by any other statement, this very [text] must be intended as the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and thus the number must be significant, just as in the case of "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*). This is true.

This very mention of the singular number (*ekagrahaṇa*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even when the principal element (*pradhāna*) is not understood from another rule, its number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). By this, it is established that in the rule *kartur īpsitatamam* (P. 1.4.49), the number of the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) is not intended to be significant. [Question: Why is the word *śeṣa* (remainder) mentioned? [Answer: The intention is that, since the context is the teaching of what is correct (*sādhvanuśāsana*), it will be understood that among those of identical form (*sarūpa*), one is correct. [Question: [Why is it said,] "lest there be a substitute" (*ādeśo mā bhūt*)? [Answer: For if the word *śeṣa* were absent, then by the statement *ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yoge* (P. 1.1.49), the genitive would be a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); consequently, there would be a substitute (*ādeśa*). [Objection: Let there be a substitute.

"Will it be the closest [substitute] both in terms of sound (*śabda*) and meaning (*artha*)? It cannot be so; for there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). Since the composite of the two *aśva* sounds is the original locus (*sthānin*), and since there are two acute accents (*udātta*) therein, the substitute (*ādeśa*) would consequently have to be doubly acute. By this, the case of being doubly grave (*dvy-anudāttatva*) is also explained.

"What is the purpose of [the condition] 'in a single case-ending' (*ekavibhaktau*)? The intention is that when there are different case-endings, dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is inevitable. For example, in the case of *payaḥ payaḥ*. If this [condition] "in a single case-ending" were not present, there would be no co-occurrence (*saha-prayoga*) of similar forms in all instances. Now, even if this [condition] is applied, why does it not occur here in the view where [the application of the rule] is not dependent on a specific cause (*anaimittika-pakṣe*), since these too are indeed seen to be similar when following a single case-ending? This is not a fault;

It was stated that the inclusion of the word *eka* (‘one’) is redundant in this view; however, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), it will apply only when a single case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the subject. But in this case, if *ekaśeṣa* were to occur, the case-ending would appear in alternation. Alternatively, why resort to this view which must be explained with such difficulty? Let there be only two views: [the view that] *ekaśeṣa* does not occur for numeral words such as ‘one’ and so on because they are not so prescribed (*anabhidhāna*), whereas it certainly does occur for words such as ‘twenty’ (*viṃśati*) and the like.
An elder [is compounded] with a youth, provided that the distinction between them lies solely in those characteristics [of age]. Pāṇini 2.2.65.

In common usage, the word *vṛddha* is well-known as referring to the final stage of life, while the word *yuvan* refers to the second stage; if these were the ones intended here, then [the rule] would apply in cases such as *taruṇaśca vṛddhaśca*, *yuvā ca sthaviraśca*, and so forth. Alternatively, if the technical definitions from the grammatical treatise were intended—namely, "that whose first vowel among its suffixes is *vṛddhi* is *vṛddha*" and "one who lives under a living ancestor is *yuvan*"—then it would also apply in cases such as *aupagavaśca ānantara aupagaviśca yuvaśca*, and so forth.

Therefore, he states "the word *vṛddha*, etc. [to explain that] here, first of all, the artificial word *yuvan* is understood as denoting a descendant who is removed [from the progenitor]; by association with that, the word *vṛddha* is also understood as denoting a removed descendant, as is well-known in other treatises. However, if the term *gotra* were used, since this falls outside the governing rule on *apatya* (descendants), the common worldly sense would apply, and thus there would be a reference to the descendant in general. Furthermore, in some places, an additional passage is recited: "In the expression *yūnā*, this is an instrumental case [denoting] association (*sahayoga*)."

This [example] was interpolated by later [commentators]; by employing the word *saha* (with) in the phrase "with the youth" (*yūnā saha*), he shows that in the Sūtra, the third case is used in connection with *saha*. For this very reason, it is made known that there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) when there is a desire to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*). "Difference" (*viśeṣa*) means "heterogeneity" (*vairūpya*). The sense is that because the words are taken as having the causes for the [suffixes] *vṛddha* and *yuvan*, they are not otherwise. Having shown the meaning of the word, he says "this is the meaning" (*tadayamarthaḥ*), beginning with "only that which has the causes for *vṛddha* and *yuvan*" (*vṛddhayuvanimittakam eva*), etc. "In the same form" (*samānāyām ākṛtau*).

The *ākṛti* (form) is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word, such as being a descendant of Garga and so forth. In some places, however, the reading is *prakṛti*; here *prakṛti* refers to the root form, such as the word "Garga" and so on—as in "Gārgya" and so forth. From the words *garga* and *vatsa*, which end in the suffix *yañ* because they belong to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *phak* is applied according to the rule *yañiñośca* when denoting a younger generation (*yūni*). Thus we have "Gārgyāyaṇau. Here, the fact that they belong to a living lineage is determined by context and other factors, since the word is common to both lineages (*gotra*).

If this is so, then in the case of "Gārgyaśca Gārgyaśca," there is indeed a single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) of the two lineage-names (*gotraśabda*) by means of the former [rule], and the state of being a youth (*yuvatva*) will be understood for one of them through context and the like. For a youth has two aspects: being a descendant of a living person and being a descendant starting from a grandson; among these, when no specific distinction is intended, the general term does not cease to apply—just as, even though in reality the action occurred in the recent past, the *luṅ* suffix occurs in the expression "abhūn nṛpo vibudhasakhaḥ" ("there was a king, a friend of the gods"). Therefore, is there no purpose in this [sūtra]? It is said in reply: [The sūtra is necessary] because... [text continues]

One who wishes to express that two individuals belong to the same lineage by means of a word independent of the specific context would employ a *dvandva* compound, such as "Gārgyāyaṇau. Therefore, this rule is stated for the purpose of precluding the *dvandva*. However, in the counter-examples, a *dvandva* occurs in all cases—such as "Gārgyavātsyāyanau. Now, one might argue: even if other distinctions exist here, since the distinction characterized by that [common lineage] is present, there should be a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one); but this is not a fault.

Thus, the meaning of the statement is expressed as follows: "If that specific feature (*viśeṣa*), by whose existence there was previously non-application [of the rule], possesses that characteristic (*tallakṣaṇa*). And so, since the entire specific feature—which serves as the cause for the commencement of the sūtra—is prescribed as possessing that characteristic through its connection with the predicate (*vidheya*) up to the point of the subject (*uddeśya*), how could there be any scope [for the objection] here? But in this case, it would indeed apply to *bhāgavitti* and *bhāgavittika*, because the entire qualifying feature possesses that characteristic. However, this is excluded by the particle *eva*; for here—
The distinction lies precisely in its characteristic; thus he says: "contempt and the state of being Sauvīra are further distinctions. The meaning is that these are the causes of the distinction.
And a feminine [stem] is treated like the masculine. 1.2.66.

Because of the predominance of femininity (*strītva*) as a cause of deformity, [Pāṇini] will state: "and [the word] is like the masculine" (*puṃvat*). Here, since the word *strī* has a circumflex accent (*svarita*), this refers to the inclusion of suffixes such as *ṭāp* which are prescribed under the heading of feminine (*stryadhikāra*); thus the meaning becomes: "the feminine suffix does not occur, just as there is an extension of non-existence in the rule *puṃvad asya stanau*. Consequently, because femininity has not ceased, in the case of "the Gārgyas who are women and the Gārgyāyaṇas," the elision (*luk*) by the rule *yañañośca* would not take place.

Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*), this fault applies in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). However, in the case of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), since that which remains [the positive term] denotes the meaning of what is being excluded, there exists a meaning similar to the feminine; thus, the desired result is established. But here, in the example *gargān paśya* ("look at the Gargas"), because femininity has not been excluded, this [suffix] *śas* has not arisen in the sense of a masculine plural; therefore, the substitution of *n* for *s* would not occur.

However, if the word were understood as referring to the feminine meaning (*stryartha*), the meaning would be that the form of the feminine word becomes like that of the masculine word upon its apprehension; yet femininity (*strītva*) would still persist. In that case, although there is no fault regarding the nominative plural (*jas*) and other endings when the masculine form—as in *gargāḥ* (the Gargas)—is extended to many [feminine individuals], the specific grammatical operation (*vibhaktikārya*) of the feminine suffix *natva* would not occur. Thus, if the word is taken as referring to the feminine meaning, however, because the masculine meaning is extended [to it], the grammatical operations dependent upon that [masculinity] are established, and therefore there is no fault whatsoever.

When "strī" (woman/feminine) is uttered, only the meaning is understood; because words have meaning as their primary purpose, the apprehension of the word-form itself is not even to be suspected [as an alternative], since the rule *vṛddho yūnā* continues to apply. Therefore, he states that only the meaning is grasped: "The feminine meaning becomes like the masculine meaning. [Examples follow: *gārgī* and so forth. From the words *gārgya* and *vātsya*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca*. [In the case of] *dākṣī*: after the suffix *ṅīṣ* has been removed by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ*, there is lengthening by the rule *prathamayoḥ* when there is reduplication (dvicanam) from a stem ending in *iñ*.
This statement is also for the purpose of excluding the formation of a *dvandva* compound.
A masculine [noun] [is compounded with] a feminine [noun]. 1.2.67.

If the distinction [between the two] consists solely in the characteristics of female and male, then that distinction exists even when the characteristic is conveyed by another word, as in: "This is a bull and this is a cow; these two cows are grazing. In the same way, in cases such as *kanyā* (maiden), *mūṣikā* (female mouse), *kṛkavākū* (hen), *grāmaṇī* (village headman), and *khalapū* (sweeper), it should be understood that the masculine form remains as the remainder.

Why does this not occur here: *haṃsaśca varaṭā ca*, *kacchapaśca ḍuliṣvaruśca*, *rohicca aśvaśca vaḍavā ca*, and *puruṣaśca yoṣicca*?
