Is it not the case that in all these instances the distinction is based solely on gender (*strīpuṃsakṛta*)? [The answer is: the term "of those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇām*) is understood [from the previous rule]; therefore, when there is an identical base (*prakṛti*), the rule applies only where the distinction is based solely on gender.

But here, in the case of *brāhmaṇavatsaśca brāhmaṇīvatsā ca* ("the son of a Brahmin and the daughter of a Brahmin"), [one might object that] the rule for single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would apply; however, this is not a fault. Single-remainder occurs when there is a desire to express a woman and a man together, and that [desire] occurs only when both are primary. Thus, single-remainder applies only where the distinction is made by the primary woman and man; but here, since it is also made by non-primary [factors], there is no single-remainder. Even here, if one intends to express a genus (as in *mṛgakṣīra*, "deer-milk" and so on), forms such as *kukkuṭau* ("a cock and a hen") are established. However, the explicit statement [of the rule] is for the purpose of precluding a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The word *prāk* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

From the root *añc* preceded by *pra*, with the suffix *kvip* and the elision of *asti*, there occurs the elision [of the suffix] according to the rule "the elision of *añc*" (*añcer luk*); its status as an indeclinable follows from the rule "that which is a taddhita suffix and does not represent all case-endings" (*taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*). As for the existence or non-existence [of the object], the formation of a dvandva or a remainder (ekaśeṣa) must be considered.
The words *bhrātṛ* (brother) and *putra* (son) [form a compound] with *svasṛ* (sister) and *duhitṛ* (daughter), respectively. 1.2.68.

This statement is also for the purpose of precluding the formation of a *dvandva* compound. For the word *svasṛ* (sister) has "having the same progenitor" as its cause [for entering into the formation], while the word *duhitṛ* (daughter) has simply "progeny" as its cause. Furthermore, in the case of the words *bhrātṛ* (brother) and *putra* (son), the distinction in both cases lies in their respective genders (masculine and feminine). In that regard, in the expression *bhrātarau putrāv* ("the two brothers and the two sons"), when the gender (masculine and feminine) is not intended to be expressed, the denotation of the sister and the daughter is established. Even if the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) were to be initiated, this very same resolution applies.
When a neuter word is compounded with another neuter word, it may optionally be treated as a singular.

"Śuklā ca śuklaṃ ca" (the feminine and the neuter). Since there is a lack of similarity (*asārūpya*) between the case endings and between those ending in different case endings, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does not apply; for instance, in "śuklaṃ ca śuklaśca," there is a lack of similarity between the two forms ending in case endings. Even if there were similarity in the case endings, the rule would otherwise result in an alternation between masculine and neuter genders; therefore, this statement is made both to ensure the formation of a single form (*ekavadbhāva*) and because the phrase "if the distinction is based solely on that characteristic" continues to apply. This is so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as "śuklaṃ ca kṛṣṇaśca. However, the particle "eva" is used so that it does not apply in cases such as "himahimānyau" or "araṇyāraṇyānyau."

"In this [sūtra], regarding the greatness (*mahattva*) of both snow and forest," he says "greatness" is another specific feature; the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*) is connected with the rule *ekavacca* due to proximity, and not with the rule for *ekaśeṣa*. Thus he says: "as if singular" (*ekavacca*), etc. This mention is so that the phrase *ekavacca* does not carry over into the subsequent [sūtras].

In this case, because there is no distinction in their specific characteristics (lakṣaṇaviśeṣa) among "a white cloth," "a white blanket," and "this white one," the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of identical forms) would not apply. However, when the commonality [of the quality] is intended to be expressed, there will be a single word, singular number, and neuter gender. If that is so, then the same would apply to the expression "this white thing" (*tad idaṃ śuklam*), so what is the purpose of this [rule]? It is stated, however, for the purpose of precluding a *dvandva* compound.

The question "What is the purpose of [the restriction] 'not with a neuter'? is raised because one might think that even when accompanied by a neuter, the rule for a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of similar forms (*sarūpāṇām*) should still apply. The reply is given so that this may occur [in some cases] while it does not occur in others. To the question "What, then, is the distinction here?", he says: "And as a singular" (*ekavacca*).
The word *pitṛ* (father) [is compounded] with *mātṛ* (mother). Pāṇini 1.2.70.

The mother is placed first because she is more venerable, for it is said: "The mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of respect. The use of the dual form *pitarau* (parents) is to be justified by the intention to express merely the state of being progenitors, without intending to specify gender. Even if one were to begin with the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one term), a *dvandva* compound is still desired here; thus, this [explanation] serves no purpose.
The word *śvaśura-* [is used] in the sense of "father-in-law" when accompanied by *śvaśrū-*.

The phrase "the father and the mother-in-law [are formed] from the mother-in-law and the father-in-law" was not stated for the sake of brevity. The word *śvaśrū* is an underived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) with the elision of the *u* and *a* sounds of *śvaśura*. Since it ends in the suffix *ūṅ*, it would not be a nominal stem because it ends in a suffix—just like *brahmabandhū*—and because it lacks its constituent parts. Nevertheless, by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the usage *śvaśrū-śvaśurau*, case endings (*sup*) and secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) occur after this very form. Thus: *śvaśrū-śvaśurau*.

The placement [of *śvaśrū*] first is due precisely to its being more highly esteemed; as it is said, "The mother-in-law and the wife of one's elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to a mother. Here too, even in the case of husband and wife, the intention is merely to express their status as progenitors, and thus the gender need not be intended. Furthermore, even on the view that [the rule] does not apply, if one were to state "mother-in-law and father-in-law" (*śvaśrūśvaśurau*), a copulative compound (*dvandva*) would still be desired; therefore, this point is irrelevant.
The words beginning with *tyad* (the pronominal stems) are always substituted for all [other pronouns].

He states the meaning of the word *sarva* (all): "by *tyad* and so forth, and by others. He clarifies this very point: "the mention of *sarva*," [meaning] "for the sake of that totality which was mentioned as being by *tyad* and so forth, and by others. The sense is that otherwise, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*) or because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "if the distinction is characterized by that," there would be co-utterance only with *tyad* and so forth. And thus: "he and Devadatta."

[Objection: But surely Devadatta can also be referred to by the word *tad* when there is a desire to express the general [form]; thus, the rule would be established simply by the words "of those having the same form" (*sarūpāṇām*). Nor can a distinction be included within the commentary (*vṛtti*) even if the sūtra were composed, because the term *tau* (those two) is common to those of the same form, whereas those of different forms are of various kinds. [Reply: True; this statement is for the purpose of excluding a *dvandva* compound such as *tad-devadattau*. Otherwise, just like other compounds such as *tat-putraḥ* or *tadīyaḥ*, a *dvandva* compound would also occur.

The phrase "whatever is *param*" means that, in the list beginning with *tyad* and so on, one relies on the rule of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict) where the subsequent [rule] prevails; this is the intended meaning. This refers to forms such as *sa ca yaśca yau*. However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated: "Furthermore, an exception to the preceding [rule] is also observed: *sa ca yaśca tau*. And here they say: "I and you two are *āvām*."

*Tyadāditaḥ śeṣe puṃnapuṃsakato liṅgavacanāni*. The suffix *tasi* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *ādyādi* group. The meaning is that when there is a remainder (*śeṣa*) among the words beginning with *tyad*, the gender and number are determined by whichever of those remaining is masculine or neuter, provided it is intended to be expressed together with the others. For example: *sa ca devadattaś ca tau* (He and Devadatta—those two); *sā ca devadattaś ca tau* (She and Devadatta—those two); *tac ca devadattā ca te* (That and Devadatta—they). However, when a masculine and a neuter are intended to be expressed together, the determination is made according to the neuter, because it is the subsequent rule.

And "those two" refers to Devadatta and [Yajñadatta]; here, "that cock and that hen" means "these two, the cock and the hen"; and "those two half-pippalis" refers to that half-pippali and this half-pippali. Thus, by the rule *paravalliṅgam* ("the gender of the latter [member]"), since the gender of the meaning of the compound is extended [to the whole], the pronoun which qualifies it takes that very same gender.
The feminine suffix is applied to denote a herd of domestic animals that are not yet mature.

"Belonging to a village" (*grāmya*) means "produced in a village," according to the rule *grāmādyakhañau*. Regarding the phrase "when the masculine remains": this refers to the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67). Regarding the phrase "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*): the meaning is that since youthfulness and its absence cannot possibly belong to the primary entity—the herd—it follows by implication that these qualities qualify the subordinate entities, namely the animals. As for the example "these two cows": although a herd certainly exists even when there are only two, nevertheless, here the mention of a "herd" (*saṃgha*) implies a collection of many; otherwise, since the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) applies to multiple instances, the rule would not be purposeless.
Regarding the phrase "among those with many hoofs": *śapha* means hooves. As for camels, because they are wild animals (*āraṇya*), there is no application of the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*).
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradattamiśra.
Now begins the third quarter of the first chapter of the *Padamañjarī*:
"The verbal roots (*dhātu*) are those beginning with *bhū* and *vā*. (Pāṇini 1.3.1)

By the phrase "words such as 'bhū' and so forth," he shows that this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on the [traditional] recitation. However, if one were to say that "a root (*dhātu*) is that which expresses an action" without regard for the recitation, then it would also apply to words such as *āṇavedu*.

But how can the instruction of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) be suspected? For from what source could it be known that "āṇaved" and so forth are corrupt forms, given that those which are followed by the treatise are correct (*sādhu*)? Furthermore, a form characterized by [the addition of] *atubandha* and so on must necessarily be shown by its very recitation in the text, for such a form is not possible in actual usage. Therefore, since the purpose is something else, the very recitation in the list of roots (*gaṇapāṭha*) is resorted to; thus, when there is the status of a root (*dhātutva*), the suffix *laṭ* occurs. In the cases of *edhate* and *sparddhate*, they are marked as having an anudātta accent.

If this designation were based solely on the textual reading (*pāṭha*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply even to words such as *yā*, *vā*, and *div*—which denote "option" (*vikalpa*), "heaven" (*svarga*), and so forth—even though they share the same phonetic form. Nor can the meaning, such as "attaining" (*prāpaṇa*) and so on, serve as a restrictive factor, because it is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣatva*), because it was designated by scholars at a later time, and because it is admitted that words have multiple meanings. True; but what is the fault in [accepting] the designation? First of all, there is no possibility of its applying to verbal roots (*dhātu*) or suffixes (*pratyaya*) such as the present tense marker (*laṭ*) and others.

Because of the absence of the agent (*kartṛ*) and other factors, it is desired that [the suffix] *yat* be applied as in *yāḥ paśya*. However, by the rule "āto dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.140), there would be elision [of the final *ā*]. Now, one might object: because of the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*), and because it would not be a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), the case-ending itself would not occur. This is not so; for once the case-ending has been produced, and after the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun [beginning with] *tyad* and the addition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the form becomes *yā*, at which point it possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*). But at the stage when the case-ending is being produced, the form *yad* does not have the status of a verbal root. Furthermore, due to the word *vā* [in the sūtra], the case-ending itself might not even occur; the same applies to the word *div*. Nor does [the rule] "diva aut" (Pāṇini 7.1.84) apply...

This is the indicator (*liṅga*) for the absence of *dhātutva* (the status of being a verbal root), because a form ending in *kvip*, such as *divyati*, is possible when followed by a nominal suffix (*sup*). Even though [the term *dhātu*] possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), only that [specific form] would be grasped; therefore, a prohibition regarding words that are phonetically identical must be stated. To this end, he says: "The word *dhātu*," and so forth. In some versions, however, the phrase "words such as *bhū*" is read immediately after "expressive of action" (*kriyāvācin*); in that case, whatever doubt arises concerning this text should be understood as applying to that [version].

But how is this specific distinction—that it is a word expressing action (kriyāvacana) yet not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra—obtained? To this he says: "The word *dhātu* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) of the ancient teachers. Then he asks: "And what follows from that? and replies: "And those [ancient teachers]. Furthermore, he asks: "And what follows from that? and replies: "Therefore, here too... The sense is that the recourse to the extensive technical terminology of the ancient teachers is solely for the purpose of adopting their specific qualifications (*upādhi*).
Whatever is designated as something to be accomplished (sādhya), whether it be already established or not yet established,
is called "action" (kriyā) because it possesses a nature that depends upon a temporal sequence.

Whether it be established (*siddha*) or unestablished (*asiddha*), that entity which is denoted by a word as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is an action (*kriyā*). And because it is dependent upon a sequential form in its state of being to-be-accomplished, it possesses the nature of having prior and posterior parts and an extended form; this is the form that is denoted. It does not abide in a single moment, as it has been said: "This so-called action is entirely imperceptible and impossible to demonstrate as a solidified whole."

The meaning is that although each individual momentary action (*kriyākṣaṇa*) is perceptible, the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), which consists of a collection [of such moments], is not perceptible. Because these successive moments are brought about with a view toward a single result, they attain a kind of unity and are thus denoted by the verbal root. For example, in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), the actions beginning with placing the pot on the fire and ending with taking it off are delimited by the result of softening (*kledana*). Likewise, in the case of "he cooked" (*apacat*), the action is likewise something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

For in that case, the passing away (*atyaya*) of precisely such a form is perceived as that which is brought about through a sequence of prior and posterior stages. However, in the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), by the word "jar," the jar—even while within the belly of the potter—is said to be of an accomplished form (*siddharūpa*); the meaning is: "by that form which is capable of being seen in a single moment alone. Thus, it is established that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of the acceptance of the rule that "a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes action."

In this context, since the term *bhūvādayaḥ* (beginning with *bhū*) would be grammatically untenable if analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—where the *yaṇ* substitution [of *v* for *u*] has been applied—the author says: "This *va* in *bhūvādīnām* is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). This is a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) of a property belonging to the designator (*abhidhāna*) onto the designated (*abhidheya*). Just as one says "the two-rephed one" (*dvirepha*) for a bee, so too this [term *va*] is employed while residing in the word *bhūvādi*, which denotes that *va* which belongs to the designata (*saṃjñin*) beginning with *bhū*. The meaning is that it is established by an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), as it was not otherwise obtained through the general grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*).

And that [use] is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The acquisition of what was previously unattained is auspicious; furthermore, merit (*dharma*) arises from the employment of correct words (*sādhuśabda*), and the word *bhū* and so forth are correct. Moreover, when the letter *va* is present, the unaltered word *bhū* causes one to recall *vyahṛti* and other such forms, and thus merit also arises.

He states another derivation: "they express the meaning of *bhū*. Alternatively, the meaning is that the designation *bhūv-ādayaḥ* (beginning with *bhū*) refers to those which express the meaning of the verbal root *bhū*. This is merely an explanation of the meaning. As for the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*): *bhū* is the act of becoming (*bhavanam*). Since they express this general action of becoming, this word is derived from the *uṇādi* suffix *iñ* added to the root *vad*, according to the rule "*vasi-vapi-yaji-rāji-vraji-sadi-hani-vāśi-vādi-vāribhya iñ*" in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Thus, the suffix *iñ* is applied to *vad*.

If those who speak of "action" (*kriyā*) as a generality (*sāmānya*) are the ones designated [as *saṃjñin*], then it would apply only to *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati*, and not to *pacati* and others which express specific [actions]. In the case of the specific [view], that [generality] is also accepted by virtue of the power of the recitation in the *gaṇa*-list; otherwise, the recitation of roots such as *bhū* and others—which take the *śap* suffix, are marked with the *iṭ* augment, lack an *anubandha*, and are excluded from the operations of internal *gaṇa*-lists—would be purposeless. As for the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *bhūtvādi* is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

He states the third alternative: "Or, the roots beginning with *bhū* are traditionally known as *bhv-ādi*. Those whose meaning is existence (*bhavana*) are *bhvarthāḥ*; the sense is that such roots beginning with *bhū* are here traditionally known as the designata (*saṃjñinaḥ*). What is this "roots beginning with *vā*"? It refers to those for which *vā* is the first; that is, starting from "vā [is used] in the senses of motion and scenting" up until the end of the *curādi* class. Thus, *bhv-ādayaḥ* (roots beginning with *bhū*) are the same as *vā-ādayaḥ* (roots beginning with *vā*), starting from *bhū* and continuing up to "vā [is used] in the senses of motion and scenting."

In the case of the *bahuvrīhi* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds "vādayaśca vādayaśca" (both the *vādaya*s), when there is a desire to express them together, the rule "among those whose accents differ, that for which the subsequent one prescribes the accent" establishes the remainder (*śeṣa*) as the *bahuvrīhi*. Then, in the sense of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser (*vācyavācakasambandha*), the compound "bhuvo vādayaḥ" is a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) based on the *śeṣa* [category]. In this view, both the specific reading and its meaning are captured by the very syllables of the sūtra.
*Padamañjarī*: "In the *upadeśa*, a non-consonant (*aj*) that has a nasal marker (*anunāsika*) [is called *it*]. (Pāṇini 1.3.2)

"Upadeśa" is so called because "one teaches by means of this"; thus, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the rule "and in the case of a factor other than the agent. Now, one might object: this is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*), and since the rule "in the sense of instrument or locus" applies, the suffix *lyuṭ* would be required; furthermore, under the rule "after a consonant," *lyuṭ* is also restricted to names. To this we reply: *lyuṭ* does not apply here because of the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes occur diversely. In the rule "and in the case of a factor other than the agent," the word "and" (*ca*) is placed out of its logical order; it should be read as "and in the case of a name. Consequently, it occurs in some instances even when it is not a name.

Now, regarding the term *upadeśa* (instruction), what is its meaning in the sense of "that by which something is taught"? It means *vidhāna* (prescription). If this were the case, it would not apply to rules such as *laṇ edha vṛddhau*, for nothing is being prescribed there. Alternatively, if it is defined as the making known of the form of that whose form is not yet known, then it would not apply to the rule *ācāre 'vagalbhaklībahoḍebhyaḥ kvip*, because the vowel *a* in *galbha* and the others would not be part of the *upadeśa*. This is because the suffix *kvip* is prescribed by reference to the fifth case (*pañcamī*), and thus the utterance of *galbha* and so on is not for the purpose of making their forms known.

If this is so, how is it that its form is not yet fully known when it is being taught? In that case, the designation "akāra" will apply to it. Regarding the phrase "scriptural statements": even [the rules] such as *laṇ*, *edha-sparddha*, and so forth, possess the status of "statements" (*vākya*) because they are uttered for the sake of specific purposes. The explanation of this very point is: "the recitation of the sūtras. This includes the recitation of the *khila* (supplementary) texts—the *dhātupāṭha*, the *prātipadikapāṭha*, and the *vākyapāṭha*.

In that regard, the *u*-vowel occurs in the *sūtra*s [in the word] *matup* and so forth; the *a*-vowel occurs in verbal roots [in the word] *edh* and so forth; the *u*-vowel occurs in nominal stems (*prātipadika*) [in the word] *bhavat*; and the *a*-vowel occurs in sentences [in the word] *galbha* and so forth. Now, one might object: "But in all these cases, a pure vowel (*śuddha-ac*) is recited here, not a nasalized one (*anunāsika*). To this he says: "Those whose nasality is based on a formal assertion" (*pratijñānunāsikyāḥ*). Those for whom nasality is understood through a mere formal assertion are so described. However, the well-known reading is *pratijñānunāsikāḥ*.

In this context, the term *pratijñā* (proclamation) should be understood as referring to the nasalization (*anunāsika*), because it is to be understood through such a proclamation. Consequently, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with its members in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, that proclamation does not occur arbitrarily; rather, it occurs only where the Teachers (*ācāryas*) record it. The author of the Sūtras has indeed recorded all the nasalized sounds he intended, just as in the case of the root *ḍulabhaṣ* in the sense of "attaining. However, they were written down in a confused manner by scribes; therefore, the matter must be determined through the tradition of memory (*smṛti-paramparā*). This is the meaning.

Regarding the form *ām̐* in the word *abhra ām̐ apa*: this nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) is not pronounced in its own form in the Sūtras and other such texts; rather, it is prescribed by the rule *“āṅo’nunāsikaśchandasī”* (Pāṇini 6.1.126) as being nasalized. Now, even if the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) were included [in the definition of an *it*], why would it not apply here in the case of *ūm̐* for *uṅ*? Because of the force of the specific prescription itself. For if it were subject to the *it* designation, then by the rule *“tasya lopaḥ”* (Pāṇini 1.3.9), its elision would occur. If that is so, then in this case as well, it will not occur precisely because of the force of the specific prescription. Thus, this has been shown merely as an illustrative direction.

This is the example for that case: *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.57]. From the verbal root *kath* with the suffix *kyac*, followed by *kvip*, there is the elision of *al* (*allope*), then the elision of *v* (*vali lope*), and finally the shortening of the neuter vowel (*napuṃsakahrasvatvaṃ*), resulting in *dadhi*. If the designation *it* were to apply here, then by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.58], the augment *num* would have to be inserted. However, in this case as well, the designation *it* will not occur precisely because of the very force (*sāmarthya*) of the prescription of the nasalization (*anunāsika*).

But surely, where there is no purpose for the *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it"), as in the case of the nominal stems *dadhi* and *madhu*, there is an absence of that *itsaṃjñā*. In such cases, the prescription of the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) would be meaningful. This is not so; for the effect of the elision (*lopa*), which is the function of an "it," is possible everywhere. Therefore, since the *itsaṃjñā* is indeed to be prescribed for the *aṇ* that is not a *pragṛhya*, by the very force of the prescription of the nasalized vowel, elision will not occur here.

In that case, the term "upadeśa" (original enunciation) must necessarily be stated for the sake of subsequent rules; it is thought that it will serve to clarify the present rule as well. Regarding the rule *āto manin* (Pāṇini 3.2.74): here, the letter *m* does not receive the designation *it*. If it were so, then by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.178), which applies to roots ending in consonants, the suffix would follow the final vowel. [The word] *sarvasya* means "even those related to *daridrā* and others."
*Padamañjarī*:
"The final [consonant] in a *hal* [group] is [the marker]. (1.3.3)

In this context, the word *anta* (end) refers to completion (*samāpti*), and not to a part (*avayava*), because [the sense of] a part is impossible here; nor does it mean "nearby" (*samīpa*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). That by which a collection is completed is its "end"; [the suffix] *yat* is applied here because it belongs to the class beginning with *diś*. If [the rule were simply] "at the end of a consonant" (*hal-ante*), there would be the undesirable consequence of applying it to all consonants (*sarva-prasaṅga*), for every consonant is an "end" relative to some preceding limit. The inclusion of the word "end" (*antya*) would then serve only to exclude the "beginning" (*ādi*); therefore, he says: "of the beginning of a verbal root, etc. (*dhātv-ādeḥ*).

By the word "ādi" (beginning), there is the inclusion of *sūtra*, *prātipadika*, *pratyaya*, *nipāta*, *āgama*, and *ādeśa*. The meaning of that which is a collection whose form begins with a verbal root—such as *śīṅ*, *laṇ*, *nadaṭ*, *san*, *āṅ*, *ṣuk* in the case of *trapu* and *jatun*, and *khyāñ* for *cakṣiḍ*—is what constitutes "instruction" (*upadeśa*). The sense is that it does not refer to the meaning of intermediate collections that are necessarily involved; rather, since the final [element] depends upon the collection, the verbal root and so forth are grasped due to their predominance. For example, in the case of *agnicit*, if this were an "instruction," there would be elision [of the *it*].

Nor is the suffix *tuka* redundant, because it has its purpose fulfilled in examples such as *āgatya*. Nor is the *pit*-designation of the suffix *kvip* redundant, because it has its purpose fulfilled in examples such as *āgnicitau*. Although in both these cases the letter *t* is the final element of that specific limit, nevertheless, since it is not the final element of the primary aggregate (*samudāya*), there is no such contingency.

Furthermore, in this case, if the *nakāra* in *daṇḍin* were to receive the designation *it*, then even though its elision would be prevented by the prohibition "not before the *ṅi* [case-ending] or the vocative," there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the initial syllable being udātta because the entire word would be designated as *nit*, just as in the word *śrotriya* under the view that "a word is used for the sake of the sentence-meaning. Now, even if the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], why does [the designation *it*] not apply to the *repha* in *sanutaḥ*? Because of the force of its reading as udātta at the end [of the list] among the *svarādi* group.

In this context, the term *hal*—which is derived from the letter *l* in the rules *śaṣasar* and *hal*—is established only if that *l* has been assigned the technical designation *it*. However, if the pratyāhāra *hal* exists, then because the letter *l* in the rule *laṇ* possesses the property of being a *hal*, it would receive the *it* designation by virtue of being the final member in the sequence *śaṣasarhal*. And if the *it* designation is applied, the pratyāhāra *hal* can be formed. Thus, because they depend upon one another (*itaretarāśrayatva*), the formation of the pratyāhāra is not logically tenable.

Consequently, the designation *it* would not apply to any of the sounds beginning with *ṇ*, and thus the entire system of pratyāhāra usage would be untenable; furthermore, the rule "the first [letter] with the last" (*ādirantyena*) would be rendered useless. This might be argued: in the word *tathal* (Pāṇini 6.4.175), there is an *ḷ* following the *h*; that *ḷ* undergoes a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding *l*, resulting in *lapara* (an *ḷ* followed by *l*). By the rule "in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), a nasalized vowel is designated as *it*," this very sound receives the *it* designation. Thus, in the rule "the final consonant (*halantyam*)" (Pāṇini 1.3.3), it is also indicated by means of that same single substitute ending in *l*.

Even so, this would still result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): namely, that the letter *ḷ* receives the designation *it*, and [only then] from it [the rule *halantyam* applies]. Therefore, a solution must be stated here; he states it with the words "of this, *ḷha*," etc. It would be a common principle (*tantra*), just as a lamp [serves] two people of equal status who are eating together.

And here, this refers to a specific effort (*prayatnaviśeṣa*); just as in the example "The white horse runs" (*śveto dhāvati*), where the result is achieved when two sentences are uttered with a single common effort, so too here, by means of one powerful *tantra*, the second mention of the term *hal* is to be understood as both taken up and grasped. He states the purpose of that second [mention] with the words "of *ha*" (*hasya*). The meaning is that there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) based on the relationship between the proximate and the proximator (*samīpa-samīpisambandha*). He asks, "What follows from that? and replies with the words "by that," and so forth.

This demonstrates that the letter *l* situated near the letter *h* does not receive the designation *it* by virtue of being included in a *pratyāhāra*; rather, it is by means of its direct mention [in the rule]. What is the proof? Precisely the fact that no distinction is perceived. But surely a distinction is perceived: "between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), the artificial is to be understood," and the *pratyāhāra* is indeed artificial. True; however, you yourself have stated that this very [distinction] is untenable in the absence of a systematic framework (*tantra*).
In the *Padamañjarī*:
"The [consonants] *t*, *u*, and *m* are not [elided] when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). (Pāṇini 1.3.4).

In the case of *vṛkṣāt*, if the letter *t* were to receive the designation *it*, then by the rule *titsvaritam*, it would be circumflexly accented (*svarita*). Now, one might object: "Since its status as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) occurs through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) only after the replacement has taken place, the designation *it* ought to apply immediately following the initial instruction (*upadeśa*). This is true; however, by the force of the prohibition [in the following sūtra], the prohibition will apply even when the status of being a case-ending is yet to come into being.

What is the purpose of including the term *varga* (class)? It is so that [the rule] may apply even in the case of *vṛkṣān*. But where else is this *n* final in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*)? For it is not the case that there is ever an enunciation of it as such. One might argue that in the rule *śaso na*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of protecting the *n* from being designated by the technical term *it*. Well then, consider here *jhasya ran* in the form *paceran* and *brāhmaṇāḥ*. This is an example of the form itself. An example of the grammatical operation (*kārya*), however, is *bhavataḥ*. Here, because the condition *siti ca* applies, the word-status (*padatva*) would result, and consequently, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) would occur.

In cases such as *pacataḥ* and *pacathaḥ*, one might argue that [the substitution] will not occur simply because there is no purpose for it; this would also apply to forms such as *apacatām*. The suffixes beginning with *tām* (the ātmanepada endings) should follow the final vowel of those beginning with *tas* (the parasmaipada endings). Since the rule *kimo't* [Pāṇini 5.3.12] states that the suffix *at* is a case-ending (*vibhakti*)—by virtue of the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.1]—and since the suffix *at* in *iṭo't* [Pāṇini 7.1.86] also functions as a case-ending by way of the principle of "acting like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the prohibition [of the substitution of *at* for *at*] would consequently apply to both of them. To address this, he says: *kimo'd* etc. The non-eternality [of this prohibition] is understood from the presence of the indicatory letter *ū* in *thamu* in the rule *idamasthamuḥ* [Pāṇini 5.3.24].

In some commentaries (*vṛtti*), however, it is stated that the non-universality (*anityatva*) [of the rule] is indicated by the mention of the indicatory letter *u* in the rule "idamasthamuḥ," as in the forms *idānīm* and *tadānīm*. For while there is indeed a prohibition regarding the suffix *dānīm*, the non-universality has been made known; it does not, however, imply the non-application of this rule to the *prāgdiśīya* (eastern) suffixes. *Padamañjarī*: 1.3.5. *Ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ*. (The letters *ñ*, *ṭ*, *ḍ*, and *v* are indicatory marks at the beginning of an element.)

The word *ādi* (beginning with) is connected with each [term]; thus, the singular number is justified—this is the intended meaning. Here, the term *ṭu* does not denote the entire *ṭ*-class; this is because the vowel *u* is not marked with an *u*-diacritic (*udit*) due to its being non-nasal (*ananunāsika*), because the *ṭ*-class will be explicitly mentioned later in the rule *cuṭū*, and because of its association with *ñi* and *ḍu*. Regarding *minna*: [it is derived from the root *mī*] by the rules *āditaśca* and *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ*. Regarding *vepathu*: [it is derived from the root *vip*] by the suffix *athuc* after a root ending in *ṭu*. Regarding *uptrimam*: [it is derived from the root *tṛ*] by the suffix *ktri* after a root ending in *ḍu*; the suffix *mam* is added to *ktri* invariably, and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because the root belongs to the *yajādi* group.

Regarding *paṭuyati*: the word *ṭu* is taught among the *pṛthv-ādi* group. Since the designation *it* applies here, the rule that "a characteristic applied to a constituent part qualifies the whole" would result in the undesirable application of the suffix *-athuc* after the entire group. However, the word alone is not an example [of this rule], because there is no operation [triggered] by the letter *i*. Regarding *kaṇḍūyati*: [this is an example of the same principle].

But surely this word is taught in the *kaṇḍvādi* list with a long vowel at the end? If that is so, then one should understand it as follows: from the form ending in *kyac*, namely *kaṇḍūyati* (meaning "he desires itching"), after the elision of the *kyac* suffix (*kvip*), we have *kaṇḍu*; then, [desiring] that [state], one again forms *kaṇḍūyati* by adding *kyac*. In that case, because the designation of *it* is internal (*antaraṅga*), this *ḍu* sound occurs even before the lengthening has taken place; and since the word *kaṇḍū* as read in the list is subject to the rule of "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikṛta*), there would be the undesirable consequence [of applying the *ḍu* designation]. As for *ñikārīyati*, this entire aggregate is not taught anywhere.
*Padamañjarī*: [The rule] "ṣaḥ pratyayasya" (1.3.6).

*Rajakī*: The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṣid-gaurādibhyaś-ca*. But how is there elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) here, given that it is stated [in Pāṇini 6.4.24] that "for roots ending in a consonant other than *n* or *i*, the penultimate vowel is elided before *kṛt* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*"? This indicates that in some cases, even before suffixes not marked with *k* or *ṅ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel of the root *rañj* occurs. *Ṣoḍa*: "One who has six teeth" (*ṣaḍ-dantaḥ*) in terms of age. For the word *danta*, the substitute *datṛ* is applied; for the word *ṣaṣ*, the substitution of *u* occurs; and for the initial sound of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṣ* and *ṭ*) occurs.

The final *ṣ* becomes *ū*, and the initial letter of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes *ḍ*. From the root *ṣaṣ* (meaning "six"), one says "he expresses that which ends in six" (*ṣoḍantam ācaṣṭe*); thus, after the application of *ṇic*, the *ṭilopa* occurs, followed by the addition of *pacādyac* and the elision of *ṇi*. Regarding the form *ṣaḍika*: from the root *ṣaṇu* (meaning "to give"), the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "after a root ending in *ṇam*, [the suffix] *ḍa*" (*ñamantāḍḍaḥ*). Due to the statement "the *uṇādi* suffixes are manifold" (*uṇādayo bahulam*), there is an absence of both the *itsaṃjñā* and the substitution of *ṣatva*. Thus, it is *ṣaḍika*.

*Anukampitaḥ ṣaḍaṅguliḥ*: [The word *ṣaḍaṅguliḥ* is derived as follows: By the rule *bahvaco manuṣyanāmnaṣṭhaj vā*, the suffix *ṭhac* is added; by the rule *ṭhājādāvūrddhaṃ dvitīyādacaḥ*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the word *aṅguli*. Due to the status of that elision as *sthānivat*, there is no designation as *bha* for the base ending in *ṣ* (i.e., *ṣaḍ*), because the intervening case-ending (*vibhakti*) is relied upon, resulting in the designation of a *pada*; consequently, by the rule of *jaśtva*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*. Here, if the designation *it* were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Even though these composite forms are not taught anywhere [as independent bases], the letter *ṣ* exists in its original form of instruction (*upadeśastha*) in the roots *ṣaṣa utvam* and *ṣaṇu dāne*.

Regarding the statement *aviṣaḥ mahiṣa iti* (the word *mahiṣa* is formed with the suffix *ṭiṣac* after the root *maha*): one might object that since there is no purpose for it here, the letter *ṣ* will not receive the designation *it*, because the desired result is already established by the fact that the vowel *ī* is marked with *ṭ*. Nor can the letter *ṣ* be intended for the optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ*, because even when *ṅīṣ* is applied, the vowel would still be udātta by the rule of "acute accent on the syllable following a *cit*" (*citaḥ parasyodāttanivṛttisvara*). True; however, the instruction [of the *ṣ*] might be intended for the sake of hearing one or the other [vowel], and thus one might suspect that the letter *ṭ* [in *ṭiṣac*] is also [intended for such a purpose].
*Padamañjarī*:
*cuṭū* (1.3.7). [The consonants *c* and *ṭ* are termed *itsaṃjñā*.]

"Ādi" means "beginning with"; the sense is that they are present at the start. Regarding "Kauñjāyanya": from a word ending in *cphañ*, the suffix *ñya* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) by the rule "after *vrata* and *cphañ*, when not feminine. Regarding "from *śaṇḍika* etc., *ñya*": the phrase "this is his birthplace" (*so'syābhijanaḥ*) applies there. Regarding "born in a stable" (*manduraja*): the shortening occurs by the rule "the feminine suffix *ṅī* and *ap* are shortened before a proper name or in Vedic meter. Regarding "after *anna*, *ṇa*": the word "having obtained" (*labdhā*) follows from the rule "having obtained wealth or a group."

What is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? One might ask: "Let there be only a single rule, *cuṭūṣāḥ pratyayasya*. To this he replies with the words beginning "separately" (*pṛthak*), etc. [The examples are] *keśacuñcuḥ* and *keśacaṇaḥ*. Here, if the letter *c* were assigned the technical designation *it*, then by the rule *citaḥ*, the word would have an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*). However, the inclusion of the marker *p* would then be for the sake of providing an alternative (*paryāya*). Thus, the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ava* is demonstrated.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The *la*, *śa*, and *ka* [are indicatory letters] when a *taddhita* suffix follows. (1.3.8)

Regarding *priyaṃvada*: [this is an example of] the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*. Regarding *jiṣṇu*: this is an example of the letter *g* in the case where the suffix *snup* is treated as having the marker *g*. Regarding *cūḍāla*: [this is formed] with the suffix *lac* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), according to the rule *prāṇisthādāto lajanyatarasyām*. In this case, one could argue that [the application of the rule] will not occur simply because there is no purpose for it. Regarding *karṇikā*: [this is formed] with the suffix *kan* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārtha*), according to the rule *karṇalalāṭāt kanalaṅkāre*. Here, by the rule *kiti ca*, there would be *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], and the desired form would not be established.

Now, in the case of [roots] such as *tud* and *chid*, by what means would the designation *it* apply to the entire group *ir*? Let it not apply to the group; rather, the designation will apply to the letter *r* by the rule *halantyam*, and to the letter *i* by the rule *upadeśe 'j anunāsika it*. In the rule *irito vā* as well, the analysis is: "the two letters *i* and *r* are *ira*; that which has these two is *irit*"; it does not mean that the group *ir* itself is the *it* of that [root]. Furthermore, the designation *it* must necessarily be applied separately to the letter *i*, so that the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) may occur according to the rule *svaritetah kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*.

If this is so, then by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ*, the augment *num* would apply [to roots ending in /i/]. This does not occur because of the maxim of "one who has grain in a jar" (*kumbhīdhānyanyāya*); for one who has grain either in a jar or elsewhere is not [specifically] called "one who has grain in a jar. However, this maxim cannot be relied upon in the prescription of *num*. For in this case, it would not apply to the root *nadi* in the form *nandathuḥ*. [The objection is answered: It is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author teaches the prohibition of *ksa* in the rule *na haśaḥ*, that indicates that *num* does not occur after roots ending in /e/.

Otherwise, since the root *haś* has an indicatory *it*, the augment *num* would apply; consequently, because it would no longer have a non-guṇa vowel as its penultimate (*anigupadhatvāt*), the suffix *kṣa* would not even be applicable—so what would be the point of its prohibition? Furthermore, another solution regarding this rule for *num* will be stated later.
The elision of that [marker] is prescribed by *padamañjarī* 1.3.9.

What is the purpose of mentioning "that" (*tasya*), given that *lopa* (elision) is the absence [of something], and that absence occurs only of something specific? In this context, by virtue of the topic (*prakaraṇa*), elision would apply only to that which bears the designation *it*. To this, he says: "The mention of 'that,' etc. [referring to] *ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ*. If the mention of "that" were not there, then for those elements such as *ñi* and others that are designated *it* and consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the elision would apply only to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*). However, by the force of mentioning "that," it will apply to the whole. And this has been stated without relying on the rule: "A prescription does not apply to the final letter of a meaningless element" (*nānarthake'lo'ntyasya vidhiḥ*).
*Padamañjarī*: "The designation of equal [elements] is according to their respective order. (1.3.10)

The word "number" (saṅkhyā) here indicates sequence. How so? Because of its non-deviation. Where there is only one thing, being both the subject and the predicate—as in the case of "mudrādaṇ"—there is no occasion for a restrictive rule; therefore, it refers to the number of plurality.

In this context, it is "number" (saṅkhyā) that is being grasped; and that number does not deviate from sequence, because it is impossible to pronounce multiple words simultaneously. However, if taken in its primary sense, this meaning would be: "of those [words] that are equal, i.e., of the same number—such as four and so forth—which are the designata (uddeśinaḥ), the number belonging to them. Since this meaning is already established by the very fact that they are designata, the word "number" must therefore refer specifically to sequence.

The inclusion of the term "in order" (*yathākrama*) was not made so that the equality [of the two groups] might be understood by way of number; otherwise, an equality based on position, effort, and so forth might also be perceived. But even if it were included, since the word "order" refers primarily to sequence, how can the equality of number be understood from it? True; the word culminates in the sense of sequence, yet its primary meaning is also perceived. Once that primary meaning is perceived, it leads to the figurative sense [of number].

Therefore, by virtue of the capacity of the mention of number (*saṃkhyā*), similarity is understood precisely through that [number]. The term *yathāsaṃkhyam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) formed with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), according to the rule *yathā’sādṛśye*. "An *anudeśa* occurs" should be understood as "it becomes related. And so he will state later: "The *anudeśins* (those being designated) become connected. The word *anudeśa* is derived from the root *diś* with the prefix *anu*; although the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for names (*saṃjñā*) when not denoting the agent (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*), here it is used even when not a name, in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The word *anu* has the sense of "after"; since the root *dṛś* (to see) implies an action, he explains that the meaning is "that which is recited subsequently. He demonstrates what was stated—that similarity is understood by way of number—by saying: "of those that are equal," meaning "of those with an equal number. This is further clarified by the phrase: "of those recited equally," namely, "of the subjects (*uddeśin*)."

The mention (*uddeśa*) of some property (*dharma*) for the purpose of enjoining it consists in its presentation in a form capable of being referred to by a well-known term; those possessing such a property are the "mentioned" (*uddiṣṭa*). The subsequent utterance of that same property as something to be enjoined is the "subsequent mention" (*anudeśa*); those possessing it are the "subsequently mentioned" (*anuddeśin*). Although the "mentioned" items are not explicitly heard in the aphorism (*sūtra*), they are nevertheless understood because the word "subsequent mention" is a relative term, and because numerical equality depends upon its correlate.

The two genitive endings in *uddeśinām* and *anudeśinām* are used in relation to the phrase *yathākramam* (respectively). Regarding *yathākramam*: as before, this is an indeclinable (*avyayībhāva*) compound ending in the third case. Thus, the meaning here is as follows: whatever the sequence of the *uddeśins* (the subjects) and the *anudeśins* (the correlates)—that is, their order as first, second, and so on—by that very sequence the *anudeśins* are connected with the *uddeśins*; this is understood by implication to mean "together with" (*saha*). In some places, the reading is *uddeśibhiḥ*; in that case, the third case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). By the statement "the first with the first," and so forth, he applies the meaning of the rule to the examples.

[Objection: In cases such as "they carry," "they rain," and "they roar," since the correspondence [of actions to subjects] is observed in the world according to their respective order, what is the purpose of this [rule]? [Reply: It is said: In the world, correspondence is also observed even by way of inversion—for example, "the maiden and the celibate student" (where the maiden is first, though she is the object), or "those with staffs and balls in hand" (where the staff-bearer is first, though he is the object). [Objection: If it is argued that the correspondence here occurs by virtue of fitness (*yogyatā*), then the correspondence could also occur according to the stated order; for by virtue of that same fitness, rivers are indeed fit for carrying, and clouds for raining.

Therefore, when many properties are prescribed for a single substratum (dharmin), the relation occurs precisely according to fitness—whether following the order of prescription or otherwise—as in the cases: "Anoint him, bathe him, feed him," or "Feed him, bathe him, anoint him. It might be argued that this sequential relation is obtained by its own nature (*svataḥprāpti*). For indeed, when no specific fitness is determined, the relation occurs between those [words] first perceived, provided there is no sublation (*bādhaka*).

For by that much alone, both have fulfilled their purpose; because when the second [element], whether a subject (*dharmin*) or a property (*dharma*), requires its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the first one already heard has fulfilled its purpose, and thus the connection with the second, which has not yet fulfilled its purpose, occurs as the counter-correlate. This applies everywhere; therefore, the sequential relationship established through attainment is proven to be obtained inherently.

If this were so, then even in cases such as *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna* where there is a disparity [in number], the same would apply: that is, the connection of as many [terms] as are equal would occur first in sequence, while the remainder would connect with all [the preceding] or with the immediately following one; therefore, the author begins by stating "of equals" (*samānām*) to prevent this.

"I shall state the distinction [of those marked] with the *svarita* accent. For in some cases, even when there is equality [of status], it is not desired. Now, even if this [rule] were commenced, how could its application occur in rules such as "the *ṇal* etc. for *parasmaipada*s," "the *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* for the first person of the *luṭ*," and "for *ec*, [there are] *ay*, *av*, *āy*, and *āv*"? Since the comprehension of the named elements (*saṃjñin*) by means of the technical names (*saṃjñā*) like *parasmaipada* occurs simultaneously and not sequentially? True;

In the *tibādi-sūtra* and in the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣaramāmnāya*), the suffixes beginning with *ti* appear in a specific sequence; that very sequence shall serve as the regulator. The same applies to *dvandva* compounds. In cases such as *pā-ghrā-*, since the sequence is perceived even when the *dvandva* expresses simultaneous action (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), that sequence itself is the regulator. [Objection: But let there be an instruction given through separate sentences, such as "let *ti* become *ṇal*, *tas* become *atus*, and *pa* become *piba* [and] *jighra*"; for if this were so, the present rule would not need to be stated. [Reply: True.

However, there would be such respect [for the distinction] because its form is not perceived [as identical], and because the case-ending is uttered with a difference therein. Likewise, in the rule *vido laṭo vā*, due to immediate proximity, it would be connected only with *masom*. Therefore he says: "Because of the mention of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) in a compound (*samāsa*), there is the possibility of [the rule] applying to everything; therefore, the subsequent rule (*anudeśa*) is for the purpose of restriction. In this context, the statement of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is for the sake of restriction; the mention of technical terms in a compound is for the purpose of not uttering the individual technical terms and their designata; and within the section (*prakaraṇa*), it is for the purpose of universal comprehension. In forms such as *taudeya*, the suffix is applied in the sense of "this is his ancestral lineage" (*so'syābhijanaḥ*).

"Regarding 'iha' and so forth: [this] is an objection to the view that there is a single *yoga*; however, he will state that in the view where there are distinct *yogas*, the division of the *yoga* is for the purpose of avoiding [the application of] numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Some, however, recite the *yoga* by dividing it, while others recite it as one alone. The phrase beginning with 'svaritena' is the resolution. But how is this distinction obtained? He says: 'By means of the *svarita* [accent], there is an extended application (*adhikāra*)', and so forth. If this were so, then upon seeing a *svarita* accent, doubt would arise: is this for the sake of numerical correspondence, or is it for the sake of an extended application?"

This is merely a doubt; and in all cases of doubt, this principle applies: "The specific understanding [of a rule] is derived from the commentary, for a rule is not rendered non-existent by a doubt. In that regard, the definitive conclusion will be reached through the commentary.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The governing authority [is indicated] by the circumflex accent. (1.3.11)

Considering that if the technical (pāribhāṣika) *svarita* were being referred to here, then in rules such as "raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.1], the fact that a consonant like *na* is a subject of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) would not have been stated, because a technical term is a property of the linguistic element itself, he says: "The *svarita* is a property of the phoneme (*varṇadharma*). This means it is a property belonging to the phoneme alone. And this property, similar to [the distinction between] *sal* and *ādhmāta*, exists only within the sūtras and not in actual usage (*prayoga*). In some places, however, the reading is: "The *svarita* is a defect of intonation (*svaradoṣa*), a property of the phoneme."

In this context, *svaradoṣa* is a defect of pronunciation. The term *adhikāra* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*). It means "application" (*viniyoga*), which is to say, "employment" (*vyāpāraṇa*). Now, he asks: what is the employment of a word that has already been applied? He replies: "Because it has been authorized (*adhikṛta*), it stands over in the subsequent [passages]. This "standing over" (*upasthāna*) is precisely this: its remaining present in the mind (*buddhisthatā*) with respect to those [subsequent passages].

The phrase "in what follows" (uttaratra) is an indicator; sometimes it applies even to what precedes. Because this *svarita* accentation as recited by the author of the Sūtras is so intermingled, the division of its scope is difficult to discern; therefore, he says: "those [terms] whose *svarita* is declared by formal promise (*pratijñā-svarita*). Examples such as *pratyāya* and others follow.

But for what purpose is this stated, since in common usage that which is explicitly mentioned is what governs [the application], just as in the case of "Let a cow and a blanket be given to Devadatta," it is understood that [both] are for Devadatta? Likewise, because [the rules] beginning with *sṛ sthire* (P. 3.3.17) are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), they will be connected only with the *ghañ* and other suffixes that follow by way of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). An explicit mention of something else serves to exclude that [previous rule]; for example, in "Let a cow be given to Devadatta; a blanket to Viṣṇumitra," the blanket excludes the cow. So too here.

If [the suffix] *inuṇ* were prescribed by the rule "in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*) and in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*"), it would supersede *ghañ*; consequently, in cases such as "in the sense of abuse (*ākrośa*), *iṇ* and *ya* are used," only *inuṇ* would apply immediately thereafter. Therefore, this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical metarule).

However, the extent of the governing authority (*adhikāra*) is not known—that is, to what limit does the authority continue? For example, does the authority of "member" (*aṅga*) extend until the modifications [of suffixes] (*vikāra*), or until the substitutes for *l* (*lādeśa*) following the rule "after a root" (*dhātoḥ*), or until the end of the chapter? In that case, this [marking with a circumflex accent] serves both purposes: for the purpose of governing and for the purpose of cessation. How so? By the rule "the governing authority is indicated by a circumflex accent" (*svaritenādhikāraḥ*), the meaning is that when a circumflex accent is seen, the governing authority ceases; therefore, [the suffix] *kha* applies after *viṃśatika*.

In this case, the *svarita* accent should be declared; and because that is observed, the application of the rule "after a word preceded by two or three [prefixes]" (*dvitripūrvāt*) is intended to be excluded. In that regard, a *tāvatitha* suffix should be attached as a marker (*anubandha*), such as the vowel *i* in the rule "after a word preceded by two or three [prefixes], [the suffix] *niṣka*" (*dvitripūrvānniṣkāt*). By means of that, there will be the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the two preceding rules. Likewise, in other instances where no such *tāvatitha* suffix exists, the previous statement must be made; for example, in the rule "before the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of the base" (*aṅgasya prāk ṭeḥ*), that becomes cumbersome.

It might be argued: "The specific measure [of the suffix] will be understood from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). In that case, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) should also be understood from the commentary. When there is doubt between *inuṇ* and *ghañ*, we shall explain it as *ghañ*; for while there is the immediate proximity of *inuṇ*, the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of *ghañ* is also observed—thus, the doubt certainly exists. However, in rules such as "after the roots *grah*, *vṛd*, *niści*, and *gam*" (*grahavṛddhaniścigamaśca*), the governing rule applies only to the immediately preceding [suffix], and not even to *ghañ* by virtue of its observed force of continued application, because [the desired form] is already established either through the governing rule itself or through the commentary.

As for what was also conjectured—that even in a sentence lacking syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), there is a scriptural qualification (*adhikāra*) for the sake of connecting it with the subject at hand, just as in the rule "the second case ending is also used after words meaning 'far' or 'near'," there is the qualification of the fifth case ending—[that too is rejected].

In that case as well, since the commentary itself is the refuge, let that alone suffice for everything; what is the use of this [technical device]? This, then, is the purpose: so that an *adhikāra* (governing heading) seen elsewhere may be indicated by means of the *svarita* accent, as in the case of the mention of "feminine" (*strī*) in the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*; for this is not established by a worldly governing heading, nor is it a secondary purpose of this [device] that there should be the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of a word even when separated by others, provided there is a mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*).
*Padamañjarī*:
"The *ātmanepada* [endings are used] after a root that has an *anudātta* indicatory vowel or an *ṅit* indicatory letter. (Pāṇini 1.3.12)

"Without distinction," and so forth. The meaning is that this section, extending to the end of the chapter, is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because the suffixes *tiP* and others are prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.4.78] as replacements for *L*, and because the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [are prescribed by 3.2.124], *kānac* [by 3.2.106], *Kvasu* [by 3.2.107], and *dvā* [by 3.3.15] for both the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*. If these were prescribed as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatayā*), there would be the undesirable consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

It might be argued: "Just as by the rules 'the plural is used for many,' 'the accusative case is used for the object,' and 'from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī* or *āp*,' there is a specific prescription (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) for the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) through these being part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), so too, in this same manner, let there be a specific prescription for the *tiṅ* suffixes by means of rules such as 'for *la*, [there are] *tiP* and the rest. If this were so, however, the prescription of *tiP* and the other suffixes would depend on the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of 'middle voice' (*ātmanepada*) and 'active voice' (*parasmaipada'), and since those suffixes must first be prescribed before they can be designated by those terms, a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) results."

If the rule were formulated as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) based on the specific form [of the suffix], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the *śatṛ* and other suffixes. It might be argued: "The *ti*, *tas*, *jhi*, *sip*, *thas*, *tha*, *mi*, *vas*, and *mas* replace *la*—that is, *ti* and the others take the place of *la*. Consequently, in the rule *anuparābhyāṃ kṛñaḥ*, the *ti* and others occur after the root *kṛ* preceded by *anu* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. What is the purpose of this? The term 'agent' is mentioned to set aside [the application of] what will be stated in *gandhanāvakṣepaṇasvaritañitaḥ*; it is so that there may not be a sublation (*bādha*) of the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) which is to be prescribed in the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*."

Thus, having proceeded from "abhipratyatibhyaḥ kṣipaḥ" up to "luṭi ca klupaḥ," one will then proceed from "anudāttaṅitastātāṃjhathāsāthāndhvamiḍvahimahiṅ"—whereby *t* and the other affixes replace *l* following a root marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the letter *ṅ*—which is an exception to *ti* and the other [personal endings]—and then from "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ" up to "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne. In that context, this is also the purpose: the mention of the Ātmanepada, the mention of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), and the mention of the Parasmaipada.

It would not need to be performed. Furthermore, in this way, there would be no restriction for the *śastra* hymns and so forth that reside in other contexts; therefore, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) regarding the essential nature [of the act] is not tenable. If, however, one resorts to a technical name (*saṃjñā*), then since it applies everywhere where those two things bearing that name are enjoined, this fault does not arise; yet, a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) results.

If, however, it were understood that this sūtra employs a future designation—just as in the expression "he weaves a cloth"—then there would be no difference regarding the simplicity [of the solution] in terms of mutual dependence; so why the trouble of resorting to a future designation? Thus, the commentator (Vṛttikāra) has adopted the restrictive view by treating the two as distinct sentences.

If this is so, then there would be no application of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) when an affix (*vikaraṇa*) intervenes, because the indicatory letters (*it*) and augments (*anu-bandhas*) of the *liṅ*, *liṭ*, *śnam*, *ślu*, and *luk* suffixes possess meaning. For here, the scope for the *vikaraṇas* consists of the substitutes beginning with *ānaś* (such as *ānaś*, *śnu*, etc.); whereas the scope for the restrictive rule consists of cases where no *vikaraṇas* are present—such as *sparddhiṣīṣṭa*, *pasparddhe*, *āste*, *śete*, *ararti*, *juhoti*, *bhinatti*, *bhūyāt*, and so forth. In instances such as *edhate*, *kurute*, and *niviśate*, where both [the *vikaraṇa* and the restrictive rule] would apply, since the *vikaraṇas* are applied first due to their higher priority (*paratva*), [the restriction does not apply].

Because of that intervention, there would be no restrictive rule (*niyama*). In the absence of a restrictive rule, if first we assume a restriction on the *prakṛti* (the verbal root)—namely, "from roots with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or *ṅit*, only the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs; from the remaining roots, only the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs"—then in this particular case, both [voices] would result. Even if it were a restriction on the suffix (*pratyaya*), since a restriction excludes only those of the same class, if the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada* suffixes were to occur immediately after the *la*-affix following the root, then a restriction would have to be understood in this way: "only after a root with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅit*, or after the remainder, do they occur."

If one were to turn [the suffix] away from the verbal root itself (*dhātu*), then because the restrictive rule would not apply when there is an intervention by an affix (*vikaraṇa*), both [cases] would result. However, this fault does not arise if the prescription is made as a single syntactical unit; for once the substitutes for *l* (tense and mood markers) have been prescribed, they must be accompanied by the affixes which require a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and since the prescription occurs along with this section, there is no possibility of an affix occurring prior to this.

Even though *syat* and the others are prescribed in the *l*-state, they are *bahiraṅga* because they depend on specific *l*-suffixes; therefore, they will only occur after the *antaraṅga* substitutes—which depend merely on *l*—have already been applied. Thus, there is no fault even in that case. This is established by a *jñāpaka*: the fact that [Pāṇini] teaches the option for *sya* in the rule "vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ" indicates that a restriction (*niyama*) is stronger than the *vikaraṇa* affixes. By this, the objection that there would be the undesirable application of the *ātmanepada* endings due to *caṅ* and *aṅ* is also refuted. How so? Because the restriction applies first, and only afterwards do *caṅ* and *aṅ* occur.

He states "anudāttetaḥ" (those [roots] marked with an indicatory *ṅ* that have an anudātta vowel) because the word *iccha* (desire) is connected with each [of these roots] individually. As for the phrase "ye dhātavo ṅitaśca" (those roots which are marked with *ṅ*), if the connection were to the entire group [of rules], it would apply only to *cakṣiṅ*; for that root is recited with an anudātta vowel, and thus [the suffix] *yuc* would apply in the form *vicakṣaṇa*. However, the letter *ñ* is intended to indicate that the ātmanepada (middle voice) conditioned by the anudātta vowel is not mandatory (*anitya*); by this, forms such as "evāyaṃ nāgaḥ sahati kalabhebhyaḥ paribhavam" (this very elephant endures the insults from the young elephants) and "na sahāmi sāhasamasāhasiki" (I do not tolerate violence, O you who are free from violence) are established.

From where is this term *dhātavaḥ* (verbal roots) obtained? Some say: since the term *dhātu-* is understood from the rule "those beginning with *bhū* and so forth are verbal roots" (*bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*), that term *dhātu-* is carried over [into the present rule]; and because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *anudāttaṅitaḥ*, it is transformed into the ablative case. For this very reason, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur after the affixes *caṅ* and *aṅ*.

In that case, [the rule] would not apply even to a root ending in *yaṅ*, as in *bebhid-y-ate*; for here it is the *yaṅ* itself that is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*), and not the verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in it. A grammatical indicator (*liṅga*) that has no function with respect to a part becomes a qualifier of the whole; therefore, the word "root" (*dhātoḥ*) should not be carried over [from the previous rule] here. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the term "roots" was stated because it refers to the majority of cases. As for the exceptions regarding *caṅ* and *aṅ*, the solution has already been stated. If this were a restriction on the base form (*prakṛti-niyama*)—namely, that "only the Ātmanepada occurs after roots marked with anudātta or *ṅ*"—then suffixes such as *-tṛc* and others would not occur. They will occur by virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*).

There is scope for this statement regarding the *parasmaipada* endings; even there, a restriction applies: "From the remainder, only *parasmaipada* [is used]. Therefore, by virtue of that statement, they will occur. Furthermore, by means of this restriction, those of a similar class are excluded. And who is of a similar class? The *parasmaipada* is the counterpart to the *ātmanepada*, and it is that [which is excluded].

Even so, under the view that the rule is one of restriction regarding the verbal roots (*prakṛtiniyamapakṣa*), the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) in the rule *śeṣāt kartari* need not be made. How so? The verbal roots are restricted, while the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the active voice (*parasmaipada*) are unrestricted. Therefore, I shall state [the rule] as *parasmaipadam*; this will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "where both the active voice and something else would otherwise apply, there the active voice alone applies."

However, since the restriction of the conditions cannot be understood without the mention of the *śeṣa* (the "remainder"), the author of the Sūtra, by including the term *śeṣa*, intends exactly this: he states that "the *ātmanepada* occurs after those [roots], and not after others."

If this is a restrictive rule (*pratyayaniyama*)—that is, if in the rule "the *parasmaipada* [suffixes] occur after the *śeṣa* [roots] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed," the restriction were such that "if they occur when the agent is expressed, they occur only after the *śeṣa* [roots]"—then they would not occur after a non-*śeṣa* root when the agent is expressed; however, the *parasmaipada* would still result after a *śeṣa* root even in the cases of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Alternatively, if the restriction were such that "if they occur after the *śeṣa*, they occur only when the agent is expressed"—then they would not occur after a *śeṣa* root in the cases of the action and the object; however, they would still result after a non-*śeṣa* root in all three cases: the action, the object, and the agent.

Furthermore, it is not possible to understand two restrictive rules within a single sūtra—namely, that [the suffix] occurs only after a root ending in a consonant (śeṣa), and that even there, it occurs only when the agent (kartṛ) is expressed. If this is so, we shall establish those two restrictions in that very context by means of a split of the yoga (yogavibhāga). Regarding the forms *āste* and so forth: *āsa* in the sense of "sitting," *vasa* in the sense of "dwelling," *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "birth of living beings," and *śīṅ* in the sense of "sleeping"—these belong to the adādi class. [The rule is: "There is guṇa for *śīṅ* before a sārvadhātuka affix."
*Padamañjarī* [on] *bhāva* (intransitive action) and *karman* (object). 1.3.13.

That which is brought into being (*bhāvyate*) is *bhāva*. [The term is derived] from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the nominalizing suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is said to consist of action (*kriyā*), whereas "object" (*karman*) here is used in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense. However, in the rule prescribing the suffix *ghañ* and others, *bhāva* refers to the state of being (*bhāve*) derived from the simple root *bhū*. *Bhāva* thus means existence (*sattā*); it denotes the state of the verbal root's meaning as something already accomplished (*siddhatā*). To show that this too is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), he states its establishment from another source: "The *l*-suffixes [denote] the object (*karman*) and so forth. (*laḥ karmaṇi ca...*)

But how is this restriction [possible], given that by the previous restriction—"the *ātmanepada* occurs only after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or *ṅ*"—just as the *ātmanepada* is excluded from the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, it would likewise be excluded from the states of being (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*)? Therefore, is it not proper for this [present rule] to serve as an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding those two cases? True; if the application of the previous rule were [already] established, one could indeed state the opposite: "the *ātmanepada* occurs only in the states of being and object. However, once this present restriction is applied, the *ātmanepada* would remain unobtained for roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel or *ṅ* when the agent is expressed. Thus, [this rule is necessary].

The preceding sūtra also has the purpose of prescribing (vidhyartha). Therefore, with respect to the rule *lasya tibādayaḥ*, both [sūtras] serve as restrictive rules (niyamārthatva), yet with respect to each other, they serve as prescriptive rules (vidhyarthatva); this should be understood thus until the end of the chapter. For this very reason, even by one who demonstrates that [the present rule] is established otherwise, the word *eva* was not employed.

In the sūtra for *ti* etc., *ti* and the others are prescribed based on the *lakāra* generally ordained after verbal roots; therein, the former [sūtra] is a restriction meaning "only from these roots," while this [present sūtra] is a restriction meaning "only for these two meanings."

But surely, it is understood from this treatise that there is indeed a restriction regarding the meaning; however, the meaning here is as follows: by the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca," all suffixes beginning with *tiP* will be taught in general for those *l*-suffixes prescribed for the expression of both the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), and not for the *ātmanepada* alone. Therefore, this [new] undertaking is made so that only that [specific form] may occur.

If, however, there were a restriction based on the *pratyaya* (suffix), one would have to state that "the *taṅ* [terminations] will be prescribed generally for the *la* [suffixes] ordained for the *bhāva*, *karman*, and *kartṛ*"; this is true. But the meaning here is as follows: the phrase "in the *bhāva* and *karman*" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication), meaning "in the *bhāva*, *karman*, and *kartṛ*. This was stated in this manner because of the primary mention of *tip* in the rule regarding *ti-bādayaḥ*. The meaning is that the *taṅ* terminations are included within the *ti*-class suffixes; that is to say, they are what is meant by "the *taṅ* and *āna*."

Furthermore, what would happen if this were a restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*)? In that case, [in expressions such as] "What gain has been obtained by you? or "What inheritance has been given by you?", the suffix *ghañ* would not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*). Although there is a defense based on the rule "and when not denoting the agent" (*akartari ca*), which provides scope for [the suffixes] beginning with *apādāna* since the restriction excludes only those of the same class—namely, the *parasmaipada* endings—even so, since the previous rule was a restriction of the suffix (*pratyayaniyama*), the same principle is adopted here as well. [The examples] *glāyate* and *supyate* [are derived from roots] *glai* and *mlai* in the sense of "loss of vigor," and *svap* in the sense of "sleeping."

In the case of *niṣvap* (as in *niṣvap śaye*), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapi-*. When it is said "it is done," whether this be an extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*)—namely, *karmavat karmaṇā*—or an extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*), then, when the rule and the designation are extended, the respective operations occur according to their own original rules. In that context, the scope for the rule "the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs when there is an object" is a pure object; the scope for the rule "the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs when there is a pure agent" is a pure agent; and [the present case] arises when both would apply in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).

Because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the *parasmaipada* ending would apply; therefore, he says: "In the case of the agent," and so forth. This means that the second mention of the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is understood as a carry-over [from the previous rule]. Under the view that this is an extension of the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*), however, only the *ātmanepada* ending applies, according to the rule "when there is a reciprocal action, [the suffixes are used] in the sense of the agent. As for the word "param" (subsequent), this [objection regarding the application of *parasmaipada*] need not be stated as a rebuttal.
