He shows its scope with the words "where," etc.; the meaning is: in a case such as *vṛkṣābhyām* or *vṛkṣeṣu*, where [the two rules] have already achieved their purpose.

But in the view that [the word] denotes the individual (vyaktipakṣa), since the two rules whose objects are those [individuals] cannot have their purpose fulfilled elsewhere, they have another meaning and another purpose; thus, "these two have other purposes. There are two applications (prasaṅgau) where two operations, such as lengthening (dīrghatva) and substitution of *it* (ittva), apply simultaneously. That is "conflict" (vipratiṣedha); the meaning is "the domain of conflict," which refers to a situation where there is an opposition between two rules of equal strength. "The subsequent operation takes place" means that whichever operation is more posterior and is fit to be performed, that one occurs.

He shows the counter-example for the rule "conflict between those of equal strength" with the words beginning "utsargāpavāda," etc. In that context, the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by the rule "śyādvyadha" (Pāṇini 3.1.141) due to the characteristic of having a long vowel (*ākārānta*) is a general rule (*utsarga*). Even though it has scope when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*), it is set aside by the suffix *ka* prescribed by the rule "ātaścopasarge" (Pāṇini 3.1.136), because the latter is an exception (*apavāda*) lacking scope [otherwise]. Thus we have *saglaḥ*, *samlaḥ*.

In the case of *randhayati* (derived from the root *radh* with the causative suffix *ṇic*), the *num* augment is obligatory because it applies whether or not [the subsequent rule] has taken effect, according to the rule *radhijabhor aci*. However, the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by *ata upadhāyāḥ* is non-obligatory, because once *num* has been applied, the vowel *a* is no longer penultimate (*anupadhātva*) and thus the *vṛddhi* does not apply. In that situation, the *num* itself occurs first, resulting in *randhayati*. In forms such as *aśiśriyat* and *adudruvat*, the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions—being internal (*antaranga*) because they depend on the internal *caṅ*—supersede the external (*bahiranga*) *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), even though the latter is subsequent. Furthermore, when there is a conflict between rules such as exceptions (*apavāda*), the internal is stronger than even the obligatory; therefore, the exception prevails. And it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here.]

"Others know that, in the case of the conflict between a subsequent rule and a preceding one, the subsequent prevails; and between a subsequent rule and an obligatory (nitya) rule, the obligatory always prevails. Furthermore, when an internal (antaraṅga) and an external (bahiraṅga) rule conflict, the internal prevails; therefore, a rule concerning the base (prātipadika) is stronger. The term *upapatti* refers to the occurrence of two rules in a single instance—namely, "of the subsequent" and "of the obligatory. Here, since both rules have already fulfilled their purpose elsewhere within the general formation of the word (*samastavyākṛtau*), when a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) arises, there would result a total non-application due to mutual obstruction. This is illustrated as follows: suppose there is a servant belonging to two masters of equal power; he performs his duty for them alternately. However, when a conflict occurs, the subsequent rule takes effect. Thus, it is said: "In the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails. For example: *kṛ-ta* (formed by the suffix *kta*). Here, the suffix *kta* is subject to both the *guṇa* substitution (by Pāṇini 1.1.3) and the *ṛ* → *ir* substitution (by Pāṇini 7.1.100). Since the latter is subsequent, it prevails. Similarly, in the case of an obligatory rule versus a subsequent rule: *pacatu* (let him cook). Here, the substitution of *śap* (the verbal suffix marker) is obligatory (Pāṇini 3.1.68), while the substitution of *ātmanepada* endings is subsequent (Pāṇini 1.4.2). Because the obligatory rule is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Furthermore, regarding the internal versus the external: *puṣyā-mās-* (the month of Puṣya). Here, the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*puṣya-āmāsa* → *puṣyamāsa*) is an internal operation, whereas the substitution of *ṣa* for *s* (by Pāṇini 8.3.59) is external. Because the internal is stronger, the elision takes precedence. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger than a rule concerning the suffix (*pratyaya*). For example: *un-nī-ya*. Here, the *guṇa* substitution (by Pāṇini 6.1.87) is stronger than the *vṛddhi* substitution (by Pāṇini 6.1.90). Thus, the rule concerning the base is stronger. Consequently, the rule "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" is established. As for the statement "between a subsequent rule and an obligatory rule, the obligatory always prevails," this is illustrated by the following: *dīvyatām* (let them play). Here, the substitution of *śap* is obligatory, while the substitution of *ātmanepada* is subsequent. Because the obligatory is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Similarly, in the case of the internal versus the external: *pra-yā-ya*. Here, the substitution of *guṇa* is internal, while the substitution of *vṛddhi* is external. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇa* substitution prevails. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger. Consequently, the rule "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" is established. As for the statement "between a subsequent rule and an obligatory rule, the obligatory always prevails," this is illustrated by the following: *dīvyatām*. Here, the substitution of *śap* is obligatory, while the substitution of *ātmanepada* is subsequent. Because the obligatory is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Similarly, in the case of the internal versus the external: *pra-yā-ya*. Here, the substitution of *guṇa* is internal, while the substitution of *vṛddhi* is external. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇa* substitution prevails. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger. Consequently, the rule "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" is established. As for the statement "between a subsequent rule and an obligatory rule, the obligatory always prevails," this is illustrated by the following: *dīvyatām*. Here, the substitution of *śap* is obligatory, while the substitution of *ātmanepada* is subsequent. Because the obligatory is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Similarly, in the case of the internal versus the external: *pra-yā-ya*. Here, the substitution of *guṇa* is internal, while the substitution of *vṛddhi* is external. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇa* substitution prevails. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger. Consequently, the rule "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" is established. As for the statement "between a subsequent rule and an obligatory rule, the obligatory always prevails," this is illustrated by the following: *dīvyatām*. Here, the substitution of *śap* is obligatory, while the substitution of *ātmanepada* is subsequent. Because the obligatory is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Similarly, in the case of the internal versus the external: *pra-yā-ya*. Here, the substitution of *guṇa* is internal, while the substitution of *vṛddhi* is external. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇa* substitution prevails. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger. Consequently, the rule "in the case of a conflict, the subsequent [rule] prevails" is established. As for the statement "between a subsequent rule and an obligatory rule, the obligatory always prevails," this is illustrated by the following: *dīvyatām*. Here, the substitution of *śap* is obligatory, while the substitution of *ātmanepada* is subsequent. Because the obligatory is stronger, the *ātmanepada* does not apply. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇa* substitution prevails. Therefore, a rule concerning the base is stronger. Because the internal is stronger, the *guṇ

When both [rules] apply simultaneously for two different purposes in different directions, if that [subsequent rule] is for the sake of non-contradiction (*avirodhārtha*), it does not apply to both; in that case, this [subsequent rule] becomes the primary purpose. When that has been performed, if there is also a cause for the former [rule], that too certainly occurs. For example: in the case of *bhindhakī*, when *bhin-d-hi* is established, because the subsequent [rule] applies first, the *hi*-substitution takes place; then, by the principle of "reapplication" (*punah-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the *akac* suffix occurs.

But when the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning, since the science (*śāstra*) operates with reference to all individuals, it follows that its application—which falls upon those [individuals]—would result in optional operation (*paryāyeṇa pravṛtti*) elsewhere as well, having already achieved its purpose. To provide a restriction (*niyama*), this [sūtra] states: "In case of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the latter [rule] alone takes effect, not the former. And from the commencement of this sūtra, it is inferred that the preceding rule does not apply there; thus it is said: "When two rules cannot apply simultaneously in a conflict, that which is sublated is indeed sublated forever."

For example, in the case of *juhutāt* (from *juhudhi*), once the substitution of *tāt* for *hi* has been made due to its being subsequent (*paratva*), the substitution of *dhi* which would have applied by virtue of the status of the original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not take place. The distinction between the scope of these two paribhāṣās is to be understood based on the adherence to the actual linguistic data (*lakṣya*), by resorting to either the individual instance (*vyakti*) or the class-form (*ākṛti*) as the referent of a word.
The words *padamañjarī* and those ending in the feminine suffixes *yū*, when designated as feminine, are called *nadī*. 1.4.3.

In this context, although the designation [of *nadī*] for the long vowels is obtained through the inclusion of their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) when the short *i* and *u* are mentioned, it would also apply to the short ones. Consequently, it would undesirably apply here as well: *he śakaṭe*, *he dheno*; and here, in *śakaṭibandhuḥ*, the rule "the final syllable of the first member is udātta when followed by *nadī* or *bandhu*" would result in an accent on the end of the first member;

and here, in *bahuśakaṭiḥ* and *bahudhenur*, the suffix *kap* would necessarily apply by the rule "after a feminine stem ending in *nadī* or *ṛt*. This is not a fault, for the rule "when a *ṅit* [suffix follows], the short [vowels] are also [called *nadī*]" will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): the short vowels are designated as *nadī* only when a *ṅit* suffix follows, and not otherwise.

A restriction (niyama) occurs because of the purpose [of the rule], on the grounds that there is nothing else to be prescribed; however, here there *is* something to be prescribed. What is it? The designation "river" (nadī-saṃjñā) would apply permanently; therefore, that [designation] must be prescribed as optional (vibhāṣā). Seeing thus the fault that it would consequently apply even to short vowels, he shows that the long vowels are intended by stating: "ī and ū are *yū*. Since the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-vidhi*) falls under the governing heading of *sub* (nominal endings), this is not the analytical expansion (*vigraha-vākya*) of the dvandva compound; rather, it is a demonstration of the meaning.

And here, because the intention is to express the non-difference between the original (anukārya) and the imitation (anukaraṇa), no case ending has been applied. However, in some instances, it is recited with a case ending. Now, one might object that if the long vowels [ī and ū] are being referred to, the designation "yū" would not be appropriate, because of the prohibition of the *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitution] by the rule "dīrghāj jasi ca. To this he says: "This designation is without a case ending (*avibhaktika*). It is called "without a case ending" because the case ending is elided by the rule "dīrghāj jasi ca suluk... or because it is overridden by the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitution according to the rule "vā chandasi"; thus, no case ending is heard in this instance.

Others, however, say that this is not a *dvandva* compound at all, but rather two separate words, as has been stated. Furthermore, the absence of case endings (*avibhaktikatva*) is due to the intention to express non-difference between the original sound and its imitation (*anukārya-anukaraṇayoḥ*). [The term] *stryākhyau* means "those which denote a female."

But surely, [the suffix] *ka* would apply by the rule "for those called feminine" (*stryākhyā*), since [the suffix *aṇ*] is prescribed only when there is no prefix (*anupasarge*). However, as for the *ka* prescribed by the rule "also after [a stem ending in] long *ā*, when a prefix is present" (*ātaścopasarge*), this has its scope when there is no object as a subordinate word (*akarmopapade*); it is superseded by *aṇ* when there is an object. As he will say: "After a stem ending in short *a*, when there is no subordinate word, [the suffix *aṇ* applies]; but when there is an object as a subordinate word, [the suffix *ka* applies] by way of a counter-exception. To this, he replies: "Because it is seen in cases such as *mūlavibhuja* and others. And by accepting this, the following verse also becomes established: "He who, upon the birth of a son, gave ten thousand cows to Brahmins who announced the pleasant news—he now lives by gleaning."

In this context, would this designation be prescribed for *ī* and *ū* alone, or for that which ends in them? In the first alternative, the feminine suffixes (*kṛt*) would not apply in forms such as *ādhyai*, *brāhmaṇyai*, "he lakṣmi," and "he yavāgvi"; for here it is the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) that is designated as feminine, and not merely the *ī* and *ū* sounds. However, [the suffixes] would apply only to the *ṅī* and *ūṅ* suffixes, because they are prescribed for the feminine and because the state of being designated as feminine is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Anticipating the second alternative, he says: "ending in the sound *ī*" and so forth.

In all cases involving the mention of phonemes (*varṇa*), the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained; however, in the rule *suptiṅantam*, because *suP* and *tiṅ* are suffixes (*pratyaya*), the rule of specification by the final element is barred in other instances where suffixes are mentioned. But how is it known that this is a mention of two phonemes alone and not of two suffixes? It is known from the prohibition regarding the substitutes *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. If the technical name (*saṃjñā*) applied to the whole ending in that [suffix], how would he later state: "after a stem ending in *nadī* (feminine suffix) following *śī* or *nadī*"? Since the entire aggregate possesses the status of a *nadī*, the long vowels *ī* and *ū* which constitute its parts are also referred to as such.

Others, however, say: the designation [of *kṛt*] applies only to the two phonemes (*varṇa*), because the feminine gender, which is a property of the aggregate, is superimposed upon its constituent parts. In this case, the grammatical indicator (*liṅga*) is the prohibition of the substitution of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. According to them, there would be no coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *guru* and *nadī*, because they would occupy the same domain.

"What is the purpose of *yu*? [The author] thinks that because of the separate mention of *āp* in the rule "ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ," the suffix will not apply to *āp*. [He asks: "In the case of *mātre* and *duhitre*, would the inclusion of the vowel *ṛ* in the rule 'ṅy-ṛtaśca' be for the sake of feminine forms? [The answer is: In the case of *bahupitṛka*, the fact that bases ending in *ṛ* do not receive this designation (*saṃjñā*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). As for *grāmaṇīḥ* and *khalapūḥ*, these are examples of the actual form (*rūpa*), or they should be understood as being in the vocative case.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *ākhyā* (name/designation), since the fact that [the words] function with reference to the feminine gender is already obtained by the rule *yu striyām* alone? To this he says: "The inclusion of the term *ākhyā*. This means the inclusion of the verbal root *khyā* preceded by the prefix *ā*. However, in some places the question is "What is the purpose of the inclusion of the term *ākhyā*? [The answer is: regarding the femininity of the word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), by the force of including the term *ākhyā*, it is understood that they themselves denote a female without depending on any other word.

In the case of words such as *iṣu* (arrow) and *aśani* (thunderbolt), which possess both genders, since femininity resides in the very meaning of the word, the designation *nadī* (feminine noun) indeed applies by the rule "ṅiti hrasvaśca. Thus, when it is said, "Let the clever one (*paṭu*) be brought," one becomes satisfied even by bringing a woman. Others, however, say that by the force of the mention of the term "name" (*ākhyā*), a restriction is understood: that [the designation applies] only to those that denote a female, and not to those associated with another gender. As for the words *grāmaṇī* (village leader) and *khalapū* (chaff-sweeper), because they are action-words (*kriyāśabda*) and thus possess all three genders, the designation does not apply.

However, in the case of *iṣu*, *aśani*, and so forth, even though they do not have a feminine object, in rules such as *ṅiti hrasvaśca*, only the word *strī* itself is carried over (*anuvṛtti*), and not the mention of *ākhyā*. Thus, for them, in the form *ādhyai brāhmaṇyai*—derived from the root *dhyai* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, with the suffix *kvip* and vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*)—the [application of the rule] would not occur either. Therefore, the former method alone must be adopted.

How, then, is there a counter-example such as *grāmaṇyai striyai* ("to the wife of a village headman") and *khalapvai striyai* ("to the wife of a threshing-floor sweeper")? It is said: although these two words are verbal nouns (*kriyāśabda*), their primary application (*mukhyā vṛtti*) is to the masculine, for it is specifically men who possess the duties known as "leading the village" and likewise "sweeping the threshing-floor. The distinction, however, is that "intense meditation" (*ādhyāna*) is common to both women and men.

"The purpose of [mentioning] the first apprehension of gender is for the sake of the *kvip* suffix, elision (*lup*), and compounds. When a word, having first denoted a substance associated with the feminine gender, subsequently denotes another substance associated with a different gender by some other means, the designation [of "feminine"] is prescribed for it at that time because it has not yet attained the status of being called "feminine" (*astrī-ākhyatva*). *Kvip*: [The derivative] *kumārīyati* (he desires a girl) is formed from *kumārī* with the *kvip* suffix; then, from *kumārīyati*, [another] *kvip* is applied to form *kumārī* (the Brahmin who desires a girl). For that [Brahmin], [one says] *kumāryai brāhmaṇāya* (to the Brahmin who desires a girl).

*Lup*: By the rule "lup manuṣye," there is *lup* [elision of the feminine suffix]; for example, *kharakuṭyai brāhmaṇāya* (to the Brahmin who is a donkey-hut). Although here, due to the application of the neuter-like behavior (*yuktavadbhāva*), femininity also exists, nevertheless, because the inherent masculinity has not ceased, this word does not function solely in the feminine; thus, due to the mention of "gender" (*ākhyā*) [in the rule], the [application of the feminine suffix] does not occur. *Samāsa*: For example, *atitantryai brāhmaṇāya* (to the Brahmin who has surpassed the loom).

It is established because [the term] has as its object a feminine word denoting a part (*avayava*). First, in the case of a compound (*samāsa*), since the word *tantrī*—denoting a part—refers exclusively to a feminine, the designation applies at that very time; consequently, under the view that it is a designation of a phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñā*), the grammatical operation is accomplished because the entire aggregate ends in a *nadī* (feminine) stem. However, under the view that it is a designation of what ends in that [phoneme] (*tadantapakṣa*), by the rule "In the context of the *aṅga*, there is [the designation of the whole] consisting of that [stem] and its subsequent member," the accent prescribed by the rule "A *nadī* [stem] before *bandhu*" is established even in the case of *atitantrībandhuḥ*.

Because the preceding member [of the compound] is qualified by the word *nadī*, and because even after the application of *kvip* and *lup*, it continues to function as feminine, its subsequent application to another meaning does not abandon that prior status. In that case, since the designation (*saṃjñā*) has already taken effect due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal) even before the connection with the other meaning, it will not be revoked—even when a different gender (*liṅga*) is subsequently applied—because that [gender] is *bahiraṅga* (external). If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of prohibiting the *yaṇ*-substitution wherever *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions are prohibited; for the two parts [of the compound] would still possess the status of being bases for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*.

For just as a designation applies to a whole because its parts refer to feminine objects, so too there would be the undesirable consequence of a prohibition applying even to a *yaṇ*-substitute on the grounds that its part (*avayava*) occupies the place of *i* or *u*, as in the cases *dhiyau* and *ādhyau*. However, this is established by the fact that the form of the *aṅga* (stem) is what is referred to; since the prohibition applies to that *aṅga* which possesses *iy* and *uv*, the *aṅga* itself is implied by the very capacity of the rule for prescribing *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Therefore, the designation *nadī* is prohibited for that *aṅga* in which *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are produced.

In the case of *ādhyai*, however, the constituent part (*avayava*) does not possess the status of being a "stem" (*aṅga*); since the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed by the rule *eranekācaḥ*, it lacks the status of being the locus (*sthāna*) for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*. Therefore, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] does not apply here. It is precisely for this purpose that the word *sthāna* is included there [in the rule]: so that the prohibition may take effect when *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are present, but not when they are superseded by an exception (*apavāda*).

Likewise, in the rule "ṅiti hrasvaśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.6), because the term *aṅga* is also implied there, that rule applies to the *aṅga* itself when it denotes the feminine gender, and not to its constituent part—e.g., *śakaṭyai*, *atiśakaṭaye brāhmaṇāya*; *śriyai*, *atiśriye brāhmaṇāya*.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The [stems] *iy* and *uv*, when not in the feminine, are not substitutes for *naḍ* and *uvaṅ*. (Pāṇini 1.4.4)

"*[The term] *iyaṅuvaṅoḥ* means 'the locus of these two (*iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*)'; even though there is a difference in grammatical case (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because the meaning is clearly understood. Others, however, apply the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) and then form a compound with a genitive in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Now, how is it that [one says], "O fair-browed one, whence comes this disrespect in your father's house"? This is simply an error. Others, however, say: "This prohibition is not absolute (*anitya*), because it has been stated once [only]. And thus there is the maxim: "What is stated once is not firm; what is stated twice is well-established. They say the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this is the rule regarding the substitution of *dā* for *tad*.
Or [the suffix] ām is applied after [a word ending in] *pada*. 1.4.5.

Even though the phonetic forms are identical, it is the genitive plural that is understood here, and not the accusative singular, because there is no application of the *nadī* designation [to the latter]; nor is it the locative singular, because the *nadī* designation applies to it only after [the suffix] has been introduced by the rule "ṅer ām nady-ām-nībhyaḥ. Furthermore, the locative case in the word "āmi" cannot be interpreted as a locative of reference (viṣaya-saptamī); this is because of the statement "tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe," which restricts such usage. Thus he says: "The *nadī* designation does not apply when 'ām' follows. For example, in the form *śrīṇām*, if the *nadī* designation were applied, the rule "hrasva-nadī-āpaḥ nuṭ" would require the insertion of the augment *nuṭ*.
*Padamañjarī*: "And [the substitute] is short before an affix marked with Ṅ. (Pāṇini 1.4.6)

If the term *yū* were not carried over here for the purpose of qualifying "short" (*hrasva*), then it would apply here as well in cases such as *mātre* and *duhitre*; therefore, it is carried over here. But even so, the qualification "the two short vowels *yū*" cannot be established: if they are *yū*, they are not short; if they are short, they are not *yū*; thus, "the two *yū* are short" is a contradiction.

Regarding the statement "the short vowels *y* and *v*," we shall understand it thus: "the short vowels [occurring] in place of *y* and *v*. And which are the short vowels in place of *y* and *v* that are homogeneous (*savarṇa*)? To this he says: "and the short vowel related to *y* and *v* which is designated as feminine (*stryākhya*). Here too, the designation "feminine" applies to the short vowels because the property of the whole is superimposed upon its parts; or else, it is an adjective qualifying those [vowels] ending in *y* and *v*. Furthermore, *y* and *v* are those which stand in the place of *iy*, *avaṅ*, and *uṅ*.

[Objection: Surely, the single mention of *yū* continues [from the previous rule], and that has already been exhausted as a qualifier of the short vowels (*hrasva*). How, then, is *yū* obtained once again? [Response: It is said: the letter *ca* is used here, and its purpose is to include the technical term (*saṃjñin*). Since "those which have *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* as their substitutes" is the subject under discussion, and since only those two (*i* and *u*) possess the status of being such substitutes, *yū* is obtained by implication. Furthermore, because it is marked with the *svarita* accent, the continued reference to *yū* serves as a qualifier for the short vowels; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
The *padamañjarī* states:
"The remainder [of the pratyāhāra] consists of *gh*, *ya*, and *sa*, excluding *kha*. (Pāṇini 1.4.7)

Under the governing heading *ā dhṛṣādvā*, the roots *śiṣa* (meaning "not being used for the whole") and *vi-śiṣ* (meaning "excess," preceded by *vi*) are listed. In that context, if the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, the suffix *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.3.56 (*erac*) because it is the object; otherwise, the suffix *ghañ* is applied. The word *hrasva* ("short vowel") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. [The author] asks—"Which one?"—thinking that otherwise, even words like *grāmaṇī* would be included, since they would be "remainder" (*śeṣa*) by virtue of not being feminine (*astrī-ākhyatvena*); furthermore, for anything whose designation as a *nadī* has not been prescribed, if it were merely a "remainder," the rule would apply even in cases such as *mātre*. Thus he asks: "Which one?"

The other [author], however, relying on the non-continuation (*ananuvṛtti*) of the term *yū* for the purpose of qualifying the short vowel, says: "short" (*hrasvam*). This means "ending in a short vowel. As he says: "from that which ends in an *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel" (*ivarṇovarṇāntāt*). In some places, however, the reading is *hrasverṇovarṇāntam*, meaning "that which ends in an *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel consisting of a short vowel. Since the remainder is qualified by the short vowel, there is an application of the rule regarding the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*).

And thus, by the prohibition "not after *sakhi*," the prohibition applies to the word *sakhi* itself and not to the vowel *i* belonging to it; what is established thereby? Here, in the case of *susakhiḥ* (one who has a good friend), derived from *su-sakhaḥ*, the designation *ghisaṃjñā* is established in the form *susakher āgacchati*. For this entire compound is not the word *sakhi*; and since there is a prohibition against [the application of rules] to that which contains a specific mention [of a word], the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) would not apply here either.

If there were no prohibition at the end of that [rule], then regarding the example for the rule *yasyeti ca*—where *ī* replaces the *i*-vowel—namely, when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *sakhi* by the rule *sakhyaśiśrīti bhāṣāyām*, resulting in the form *sakhi ī*, there would be an elision of the *ik* vowel. However, if that elision did not occur, then because the long vowel produced by the rule *savarṇadīrgha* would behave like the final element of the preceding member, in the case of *atisakhiḥ* (one who has surpassed a friend) and *atisakher āgacchati* (he comes from one who has surpassed a friend), the designation *dhi* would be prohibited by the rule *na sakhyuḥ*; thus, that [prohibition] would be untenable.

Even though there is the inclusion [of the whole] by means of the inclusion of the word *sakhi* through the principle of "acting as the final member" (*antavadbhāva*), the aggregate [as a whole] is distinct from the word *sakhi*. Indeed, when the form *atisakhiḥ* occurs even in the masculine gender, what occasion would there be for it to be [governed] by the principle of "acting as the final member"? As for that which will be cited as an example in that context, it should be regarded as a statement made without serious intent (*anāsthāvāda*). The mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) has a purpose that requires consideration; for, precisely because of the governing rule regarding "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), when the designation *nadī* applies to a feminine base ending in a *ṅit* suffix, the designation *ghi* will not apply.
The word *pati* [is the final member] only in a compound, according to Pāṇini 1.4.8.

Regarding the word *siddhāyām*: the meaning is "when it has been reached," and not "when it has been completed," for when it is completed, a cessation [of the rule] cannot necessarily be asserted. It is stated that the word *pati* receives the designation *ghi* only when it is part of a compound. Now, is this designation being prescribed for the word *pati* as a member of the compound, or for the compound ending in it? If it were for the compound, then in the case of *patiśca gṛhaṃ ca* (husband and house), forming the compound *patigṛhe*, the rule "the *ghi* [word] is placed first" in a *dvandva* would not apply.

Now, regarding the word *pati*: [if it were not for this rule], the designation *ghisamjñā* would not apply to *prajāpati* and so forth. Alternatively, what is excluded by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "the word *pati* only in a compound"? It is the non-compounded word *pati*. By what is the designation of *ghisamjñā* excluded for that which ends in *pati*, since the word *pati* itself is being excluded? The intended meaning is that the *ghisamjñā* designation applies based on the vowel *ī* that is related to the word *pati*, provided that it occurs only in a compound.

By that [rule], the substitution occurs even for the word *pati* when it is not at the end of a compound: *patiśca gṛhaśca = patigṛhe*, where the prior placement [of *pati*] is due to the rule "in a *dvandva* compound, a *ghi* [word] is placed first. It also occurs for a compound ending in the word *pati*: *prajāpatinā*. For this very reason, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) has demonstrated the meaning of the sūtra as corresponding to the word *pati*; however, the example shown corresponds to [compounds] ending in that [word]. Now, how is one to interpret the following verse: "When the husband is lost, dead, renounced, impotent, or fallen—under these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women"?

The authors of the *chandovṛtti* [verse-commentaries] act thus. Now, why was it not stated as "asakhipatī" in the previous rule itself? [It was not done] so that in the subsequent rule, the option might apply to *pati* alone. Furthermore, if it were stated as "asakhipatī," then even in a compound, it would not apply to the word *pati*—as in *patigṛhe*. Likewise, because the word *sakhi*, even when being a member of a compound, would lack the designation *ghi*, there would be no fixed rule regarding the prior placement [of the word], as in *sakhigṛhe* or *gṛhasakhāyau*.
*Padamañjarī*:
"In the Vedic language, [the genitive ending] joined with the sixth case [is optionally used for the agent]. (Pāṇini 1.4.9)

"By a word ending in the genitive case": it does not mean "that which is joined with the genitive case-ending. For if that were the case, one would simply say "in the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyām*), and the inclusion of the term *yukta* ("joined") would be purposeless. [Question: Why is the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) necessary? [Response: Here, some think that because a connection (*yoga*) is unavoidable, the specific connection expressed by the word *yukta* will be understood; however, the answer is that without an explicit statement, the specific distinction would be difficult to discern.

In this matter, the following analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) should be made: first, "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), that which is joined with a genitive case [ending], when it is the word *pati*, becomes designated as *ghi*. Then, "Or (*vā*),"—referring specifically to the Vedic language—the meaning is that whatever grammatical operation (*kārya*) is prescribed in the treatise, all of that occurs optionally in the Vedic language; that is to say, all rules are optional in the Vedic language. This is an option applicable in both ways (*ubhayatrabhāṣā*), while expressions such as "frequently in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*) are merely elaborations (*prapañca*) of this very principle.
In the Padamañjarī, a short vowel is light. 1.4.10.

In this context, regarding the form *sarpiṣṭvam*, it is desired that the designation *laghu* (light) coexist with the designation *guru* (heavy) for the sake of applying the rule "hrasvāttādau taddhite" to effect the substitution of *ṣ*. However, in the case of *atatakṣat*, it is desired that the designation *laghu* supersede the designation *guru* in order to prevent the application of the rule for *sanvadbhāva*. Therefore, the two designations must be applied according to their respective domains: so that in rules concerning *hrasva*, a single-mora vowel even when followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) may be included, whereas in rules concerning *laghu*, such a vowel shall not be included.
In a conjunct consonant, [the first vowel] is heavy. 1.4.11.
And [the word] *dīrgha* [is used]. 1.4.12.
*Padamañjarī*:
That from which a suffix is prescribed is the *aṅga* (base) with respect to that suffix; it begins with that [element]. (Pāṇini 1.4.13)

"Kartā" [is formed with] *luṭ*; "kariṣyati" [is formed with] *lṛṭ*; "akariṣyat" [is formed with] *lṛṅ*, where the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "*ṛddhanoḥ sye*". As for the phrase "yasmāt," it is for the purpose of indicating the technical term (*saṃjñin*). Now, one might object: "Is not the technical term indicated by the expression 'tadādi' and not by 'yasmāt'? To this he replies: "Because of its connection with 'tadādi'. For only when the word "yasmāt" exists can the technical term be indicated by "tadādi," and not otherwise.

For when there is something to be referred back (*parāmarśanīya*), there occurs a reference by means of the word *tat*; otherwise, the phrase "beginning with *tat*" (*tadādi*) would be entirely incoherent. Regarding the rule "after the prefix *ni*, [the suffix] *viś*," although *ni* here is a qualifier of the verbal root—meaning "that *viś* which follows *ni*"—and since the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are prescribed for the root, this restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) applies to the root as well as to the prefix; nevertheless, this was stated with the understanding that the prefix also participates in that [application].

What is the purpose of including the word *vidhi* (rule)? The question is raised because when it is stated, "from which [a suffix] follows," there is an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), and one might supply the words "from which it is prescribed. The answer is that the word *para* (subsequent) would also have to be supplied. Regarding the form *strī iyatī*: this is its measure (*parimāṇa*). In the derivation of *iyat*, the suffix *gha* replaces *vat* after *kim* and *idam* (Pāṇini 5.2.40), resulting in the substitute *iy*. Then, by "the substitution of *īś* for *idam* and *kim*" (5.2.40), we get *īś-yat*. By "the elision of *i* when followed by *iti*" (6.4.148), the *ś* is elided, yielding *iyat*. From the feminine stem *strī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by "also after a stem ending in *ugit*" (4.1.6). Finally, from the word *strī*, the case-ending *su* is elided by "the elision of *hal*, *ṅ*, and *y* etc. (6.1.68). Thus, *strī iyatī* is formed.

In this case, when the word *iyat* follows, there would be both the designation *aṅga* and the designation *bha*; consequently, the elision of *y* by the rule *yasyeti ca* would apply. Regarding the elision of *y* resulting from the substitution of *i*, its status as "not yet established" (*abhīya-asiddhatva*) does not hold, because some authorities accept that "the status of being unestablished applies only prior to the application of the *bha*-designation. Furthermore, there is no status of being "as if the original element" (*sthānivadbhāva*), because when the word *iyat* is derived independently of other words, the word *strī* precedes a vowel that has not been subject to grammatical alteration.

[Objection: But surely, if the term *vidhi* (prescription) were not included, the designation [of "base"] would indeed apply here, for there is certainly a prescription of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) after the word *strī*, and this suffix is subsequent. [Response: This is not so; when the term *vidhi* is included, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the meaning becomes that the initial portion of that very element after which a suffix is prescribed is the "base" (*aṅga*).

In this case, [the suffix] prescribed after the word *strī* has been elided, yet the [suffix] that is actually heard was not prescribed from that [word]. Therefore, the mention of "that which begins with it" (*tadādi*) would be purposeless; for by the very fact of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, the meaning "the base (*aṅga*) from which the suffix is prescribed" is already obtained. Hence he says: "The mention of 'that which begins with it'. The *sy*-class elements are the *vikaraṇas*. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of *śap* and so forth.

If the mention of "that" (*tad*) and so forth were not present, then by the principle of supplying the word "that" (*tat*) corresponding to the word "which" (*yat*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply only to that [stem] after which the suffix is prescribed, and not to the entire aggregate beginning from that [stem] up to that suffix. Consequently, in forms such as *kariṣyāvaḥ*, *pacāvaḥ*, *dīvyāvaḥ*, and *tudāvaḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* would not occur; for the entire aggregate ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) would not be considered a "member" (*aṅga*).

Consequently, [the form] would occur only in cases such as *pāpāvaḥ*, where the form is derived from the *yaṅ*-luṅ (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) of the root *pā* meaning "to drink," with the elision of *y* and *v* by the rule "lopo vyor vali. As for *kuṇḍāni*: when the *num* augment is considered to belong to the subsequent element (*parādi*), then the lengthening by the rule "supi ca" is established. However, in cases such as *dadhīni*, this is not established because the stem does not end in *an*; yet, under the view that *num* belongs to the preceding element (*pūrvāntapakṣa*), it is established just as in the case of *sāmāni* and so on. But when the view that *num* is not a part of the suffix (*abhaktapakṣa*) is held, then this is the purpose of including the word "beginning with" (*tadādigrahaṇa*); since the *pūrvāntapakṣa* remains the established position there, this [purpose] is not required.

Now, one might object: "Does not the fact that the author of the *Sūtras* includes the mention of *num* in the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* indicate his intention that *num* is not a part [of the word]? Otherwise, in the case of *māṣavāpāṇi*, since the *ṇatva* substitution would already be established—either because it occurs at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or because the *n* belongs to a case ending—that mention would be purposeless. This is not well stated.

For in that context, the end of a compound nominal stem (*samāsaprātipadika*) is not what is intended; rather, because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "from the preceding member" (*pūrvapadāt*), it is the end of the nominal stem of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as implied by that [term] which is taken. And since the augment *num* is a part of the whole compound, it does not constitute the end of the nominal stem of the subsequent member. Consequently, just as there is no substitution of *ṇ* in the case of *gargabhaginī* (the sister of the Gargas), so too there would be no [substitution of *ṇ*] for *num*.

In that case, would this not apply to the word *gargabhaginī*? It does apply, provided that the analysis of the compound is as follows: "The fortune (*bhaga*) of the Gargas is *gargabhaga*; she possesses that. For in that instance, because it does not stand at the end of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), there is no restriction by the rule "only after a preceding member when it is a name" (*sañjñāyām*). This is just as in the case of *mātṛbhogīṇa*, meaning "beneficial for the mother’s enjoyment. Even so, in the case of *māṣavāpiṇī*, meaning "she whose habit is to sow beans," the suffix *ṅīp* would not be obtained here; for in this case, the final sound of the subsequent member is *ī*, and not the letter *n*.

The letter *n* alone is the final element here; how so? Because it is a rule that words consisting of a verbal root (*gati*), a kāraka, or a secondary word (*upapada*) form a compound with a *kṛt*-affix before the addition of case-endings (*sup*). Therefore, considering that the mention of "beginning with that" (the *kṛt*-affix) made for the sake of the case-endings is intended to apply even to the *num* augment, the mention of *num* was made.

If it is said that [the term] "beginning with that" (*tadādi*) is intended, then [the designation of] "agent" (*kartṛ*) and so forth would not apply in cases such as *kartṛ*, for there is nothing here that begins with "that" (*tat*). What then? It is that very thing itself; it will occur by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), or else through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*): that after which the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya*) is prescribed is its "member" (*aṅga*), and what begins with that is also [the member]. Since this could be established merely by saying "the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth are members with respect to the suffix," the very fact of the heavy formulation is the indicator (*liṅga*) of the split in the sentence.

Now, how does it split [the compound]? In the case of *saṃcaskaratuḥ*, how is the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) applied to the entire complex including the suffix *san*? And how would it not be so? Is there here a reference to that [suffix] itself, or to what begins with it? This is neither that, nor does it begin with that. Yet this too begins with that; how so? It is not understood thus: "that is its beginning, and it is 'beginning-with-that'. How then? It is "its beginning" (*tasyādiḥ*), and then "beginning-with-that" (*tadādiḥ*), and then "this has that as its beginning" (*tadādirasya*). Even so, there is the elision of one word "beginning" (*ādi*), as in the case of *uṣṭramukha*.

When it is understood in this way, in the case of the word *bhinatti*, since the suffix is prescribed after the root *bhid*, its initial letter is *bh*; and being the initial [letter] of that entire complex (the root plus the suffix), the designation is established. Similarly, in the case of *saṃcaskaratuḥ* as well, by the rule "that which falls in the middle of something is included by the mention of that thing," the designation is established in both instances.

Now, why does the technical designation *aṅga* not apply here to the word *bhi*, which precedes the suffix *śnam*? Let it apply; what is the fault? First, as for *guṇa*, it will not occur precisely because of the *ṅit*-characteristic [of the suffix], by the rule "sārvadhātukam apit". Here, in the cases *anakti* and *bhanakti*, the rule "ato dīrgho yañi" would result in lengthening; however, the term *tiṅ* is understood there [in that rule]. Or else, the lengthening would result from the rule "yasmātpratyayavidhiḥ", as the term *tiṅ* is understood there [in that rule as well].

Alternatively, according to the statement "because [the designation of] an *aṅga* occurs when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is prescribed," that alone is the *aṅga* with respect to which something is prescribed by means of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Now, although *rudh* and the others are indicated by the fifth case when *śnam* is being prescribed, they do not stand immediately after (*parataḥ*) it; and although *pra* and the others stand immediately after *śnam*, they are not indicated by the fifth case. Therefore, the designation of *aṅga* does not apply.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of that" (*tadartham*): this is a compound formed by the rule *caturthī tadartha*. For here there is indeed the prescription of the singular dative case; however, if the term *pratyaya* (suffix) were not repeated, then because the word *aṅga* (stem) would lack the status of being a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), the substitution *iyaṅ* would apply to any stem whatsoever in reality. But when the suffix is specified as being indicated in the locative case, the word *aṅga* becomes a relative term; consequently, *iyaṅ* occurs for the stem.

When it is stated "in [the presence of] vowels" (*aci*), since it is understood that the stem is relative to that [vowel], and that [substitution] applies when it begins with a vowel, the substitutions *imaṅ* and *uvaṅ* will not occur when the word *artha* follows.

Furthermore, what is the purpose of the designation "aṅga" (stem)? [It is for] the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the stem. This is not so; for one might think that by saying "of the stem," one intends to say "before an affix. Even so, in forms such as *prākarot* and *praihiṣṭa*, the augmentations *āṭ* and *āṭ* would apply to the verb root along with its prefix. This is not a fault, because when there is a mention of an "affix" (*pratyaya*), the term refers to the beginning of that which the affix is prescribed after.

But where is this technical rule (paribhāṣā) established? Indeed, it is established right here by means of a split in the *yoga* (yogavibhāga). The single rule is simply: "In a rule for the derivation of an affix (*pratyayavidhi*), that which begins with the element from which [the affix is prescribed] is included when the affix is mentioned. The meaning is that when an affix is being referred to, that which begins with the base from which its derivation is prescribed is also included. Consequently, in rules such as "ñ-nity-ādiḥ" (P. 6.1.197), wherever an affix is indicated in the locative case, there the inclusion is of that which begins with it. Thus, in the case of *devadatto gārgyaḥ*, the acute accent on the initial of the entire compound (*saṃghāta*) does not occur.

In the rule *sup-ātmanaḥ kyac*, however, since the analysis of the compound as *sup* qualifying the object (*karman*) establishes the application of the rule to that which ends in a case-ending, there would otherwise be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *mahāntaṃ putram*. This is excluded by the restriction that the rule applies only to that which begins with the word [ending in the case-ending].

If a restriction regarding the initial [vowel] were applied, it would also apply to the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*); consequently, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) prescribed for a preceding member ending in *ṣyaṅ* would not occur in the case of *paramakārīṣagandhīputra*, because that which is the preceding member does not end in *ṣyaṅ*, and that which ends in *ṣyaṅ* is not the preceding member. This is not a fault, because from the rule *neyaṅuvaṅsthānāvastrī*, the term *astrī* (not feminine) is carried over (*anuvartate*). That term, although its primary referent here is the word-form itself (*svarūpa-padārtha*), becomes here a referent to the meaning (*artha-padārtha*).

Thus, the meaning is as follows: when there is the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), that which begins with it is understood; here, even though the subject matter is the word-meaning (*padārtha*), it results in this sense: when there is the mention of a suffix, that which begins with it is understood, provided that "feminine" (*strī*) is not being denoted. The meaning is that there is no restriction regarding that which begins with [the suffix] in the case of a feminine suffix.

If this is so, then [an objection] arises here as well regarding *atikārīṣagandhyā-putraḥ*: even in this case, the prohibition of the restriction beginning with that [suffix] would apply only to a word where the woman is the primary element (*pradhāna*), whereas the restriction beginning with that suffix certainly remains in the case of a non-primary woman. Therefore, only that portion which expresses the woman as the primary element is taken as ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). When that is taken, however, there is also the inclusion of what is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or an agentive factor (*kāraka*); thus, the mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* will be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). A word ending in a nominal suffix (*sup*) is a *pada*. (Pāṇini 1.4.14)

Regarding the statement "the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *suptiṅ*": the term *sub* does not denote the locative plural [ending]; for if it did, since the status of being a *pada* would not apply to the forms ending in *ṅi* (locative singular) and the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*), the elision of the final *n* would not even arise, and thus the prohibition "not in the case of *ṅi* and *saṃbuddhi*" would be rendered purposeless—this is the intended sense. Furthermore, the pratyāhāra for the locative plural is formed with the letter *p*, and not with the *p* of the suffix *kap*.

In that case, since the same would apply to the rule for *svara* (accent) as well, the accent would be established simply by the fact of being in the *su*-case; thus, the designation *pit* would be entirely purposeless. Furthermore, if in the rules concerning *su* one intended the *pratyāhāra* "kap" [which includes *ka*, *pa*, and *ya*] by means of the letter *pa*, one would have simply said "in *su* and in the *asarvanāmasthāna* cases"; the cumbersome reference "in *svādiṣu*" would then be redundant. As in the example *brāhmaṇāḥ*: because of the status of being a *pada*, there is the substitution of *ru* and then the *visarjanīya*.

Now, one might object: since the rule for suffixes (*pratyaya*) is governed by the phrase "that which begins with it" (*tadādi*), the inclusion of that which ends in those [suffixes] is already established by the fact that *suP* and *tiṅ* serve as qualifiers; thus, there is no purpose in mentioning the word "end" (*anta*). To this, he replies: "In the case of the technical name *pada*. If the mention of "end" were not made here, the technical name would apply only to the *suP* and *tiṅ* themselves. Consequently, in forms such as *agniṣu*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "after *s*, and at the beginning of a *pada*" (*sātpadādyoḥ*) would apply. Anticipating this objection, the mention of "end" being made serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned principle. For example: *gaurī-brāhmaṇitare*.

If the designation *gha* were applied to the suffix *tarap*, then when the word *gaurī* stands as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) would be superseded by the rule for shortening (*hrasvatva*) due to its higher priority. However, this would not apply to the word *brāhmaṇī* when *tarap* follows; consequently, one would obtain *gaurībrāhmaṇatarā*, whereas *gaurabrāhmaṇitarā* is what is desired. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, a sentence is cited for the purpose of illustrating the compound formation, but it is not an example of this specific grammatical operation. The form *gaurabrāhmaṇitarā* is the actual form resulting from the compound.
The *Padamañjarī* [is the commentary] on our *kyeḥ* [sūtra], 1.4.15.

The term *ky* refers to the suffixes *kyac*, *kyak*, and *kyaṅ*. However, the mention of *kyap* does not apply to the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ samaja-* (Pāṇini 3.3.99), because there is no purpose for it. First, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) in *manya-* is not a purpose [for including *kyap*], because even though it would be a word (*pada*), it would not be a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*). Alternatively, since the term *subanta* ("ending in a case-suffix") is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), this [mention of *kyap*] does not serve to enjoin [the elision] in the case of *kyap*.

[Objection: Since *kyac* and the others are prescribed after a word ending in a *sup*-suffix, the status of being a *pada* is established by the rule for the treatment of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, this [restriction] is unnecessary. To this he replies: "Since [the status of *pada*] is already established... [He says: "Only that which ends in *n*. However, a reverse restriction—that only *kyac* [and not *kyas*] occurs after a word ending in *n*—does not apply, because of the prohibition in the rule "not before the case-ending *ṅi* or the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*). [Example: *vācyati*. Here, due to the absence of *pada*-status, the changes to *kutva* and *jaśtva* do not occur. As for those who say that *kyac* occurs only after words ending in *n* that have the same number of syllables as *go*, and not after others—for them, the counter-examples for the restriction of both *kyac* and *kyas* must be shown, such as *tapasyati* and so on.
And [the word] *padamañjarī* is neuter. 1.4.16.

In *bhavadīya*, the substitution of *ja* occurs because it is a word (*pada*). In *ūrṇāyuḥ*, because the designation "word" has been set aside, there is no elision of the *ya* (by Pāṇini 6.4.148). Similarly, in *ṛtviya*, the rule "guṇa for *o*" does not apply; the letter *ca* [in the sūtra] serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. Consequently, in the Vedic language, for the suffix *mat* after the roots *bhū* and *dhṛ*, the designation "base" (*bha*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule "tasau matvarthe"—is superseded by the designation "word" (*pada*). Thus, we have *bhuvad-vadbhyaḥ* and *dhārayad-vadbhyaḥ*.
*Padamañjarī*: [The rule] *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.17).

Regarding the phrase "svādiṣu" (in *su* and the following), because of the word *su* and because of the singular number, the inclusion [of the suffixes] does not begin from the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). This is due to the prohibition [contained in the rule] "asarvanāmasthāne. For if the intended prohibition were of the designation "sup-anta" (ending in a case-suffix) as it would apply to *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes in examples such as *rājaśritaḥ*, then the author would have stated "asarvanāmasthāne" right there [in that specific context]. If one argues that in examples such as *rājavān*, the prohibition applies to the internal [case-suffix], we say no.

In *lumatā lupte* (when [an affix] is elided by *lum*), there is an absence of the characteristics of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); furthermore, the designation *bha* is prescribed in order to override the designation *pada* by the rule *tasau matvarthe*. Regarding the phrase *ā kapaḥ*: if, however, twenty-one suffixes up to the locative plural were intended to be included, then one would simply have used the term *sub* or caused it to be supplied from a previous context; for [the desired result] is established through the modification of the locative case [into a genitive] by its connection with the word *asarvanāmasthāne*.

But why are suffixes up to and including *ā* included [in the definition of a word], given that secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes arise from a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) due to the governing rule of semantic competency (*samarthādhikāra*), and even primary suffixes (*svārthika*) likewise arise from a form ending in a case-suffix, as indicated by the rule "in the presence of *gha*, *kāla*, and *tana*" (*ghakālataneṣu*)? Consequently, in cases such as *rājatvam* and *rājatā*, the status of being a word (*pada*) would already be established because it is a form ending in a case-suffix due to the intervening case-suffix. True; however, suffixes up to and including *ā* are included for the purpose of establishing the technical designation of *bha*. This is why examples such as *rājatvam* and so on are presented: although they end in a case-suffix, the designation of *pada* is more appropriately applied here by this [present rule] because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules].

In the case of *rājānau* and *rājānaḥ*, there is an absence of the elision of the *n* because they do not constitute a complete word (*apada*). However, in the case of *rājā* (the singular nominative), the prohibition [of the elision of the *n*] does not apply by virtue of the rule "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*). This [objection] is not tenable as an indicator (*liṅga*), because of the evidence provided by the rule "not before a *ṅi* ending or a vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*). In the neuter form *he varman*, since the case-ending is elided by *lumat* and the status of being a "nominal base" (*sarvanāmasthāna*) is absent, the status of being a word (*padatva*) indeed exists; therefore, the prohibition [against the elision of the *n*] is meaningful in that context.

If that is the case, then this is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)—namely, "not [before] a *sarvanāmasthāna*"—but rather, this is a *paryudāsa* (relative exclusion): "other than a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Thus, regarding a *sarvanāmasthāna*, there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition; if it is applicable by some [rule], it certainly occurs. It is applicable by the preceding rule, or else that application which is immediate is prohibited. Why is this so? Because "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediate."

Alternatively, in the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, the term *yaci* is drawn back (*apakṛṣya*) and connected [to the previous rule]; by this, the designation *pada* is prohibited for suffixes beginning with a vowel (*yajādi*), but not for those beginning with a consonant (*halādi*). Thus, in forms such as *rājā* (where the suffix begins with a consonant), the prohibition does not apply. Furthermore, if this were the case, the expression *asarvanāmasthāne* would not need to be stated at all. However, it is stated for the sake of the subsequent rule so that the designation *bha* may also apply to neuter nouns when the augment *suṭ* is added—as in *sāmnī*—and it should not apply there. As for the designation *bha*, even for that which is not [otherwise] a *bha*, the elision of *an* (*al-lopa*) will occur by the force of the specific statement *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ*.

In this regard, the meaning of the rule beginning with *yasya* is such that it need not be stated that "there is a prohibition [of the elision] before *śi*"; for it is already established by the very fact of its being an *abha*. However, in this case—*supadī brāhmaṇakule*—the substitution of *pad* would not occur because it is an *abha*; and in this case—*sāmāni paśya*—the elision of *al* would occur because it is a *bha*. Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation (*yathānyāsam*).
The suffix *ya* [is applied] after the root *pad*, provided that *bha* follows. 1.4.18.

Regarding "yakārādau" and so forth: the rule "yasmin vidhis tadādāv algrahaṇe" (when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to a specific sound, it applies to that which begins with it, provided no *al* [vowel or consonant] is being mentioned) establishes the application of the rule to the beginning of the word. In examples such as *gārgyaḥ*, because it is a *bha*-stem, there is elision of the suffix *ya* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Regarding the statement "there is an extension of the rule for *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* when the suffix *vat* is used": they say that both of these extensions apply specifically to the domain of Vedic literature (*chandas*). In the example *nabha iva*, since the suffix *vat* is prescribed after a word in the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*), this demonstrates a sense of similarity; the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is "it exists in a manner equal to the sky."

The designation *bha* is prescribed for these [suffixes] solely for the purpose of preventing operations dependent on being a word (*pada*), and not so that operations conditioned by *bha*-ness might occur; for such [operations] are impossible.

For example: *nabhasvat*, *aṅgirasvat*. Here, because they are not words (*apadatva*), there is an absence of *ru*-substitution (as in *manuṣvat*, where if it were a word, *ru*-substitution would occur, but not *ṣa*-substitution, because of the rule stating "not at the end of a word").

In *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ* and *vṛṣaṇāśva*, if they were words, then due to the prohibition "of the end of a word," the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur, and there would also be elision of the nasal (*na*-lopa). Even if they have the status of *bha*, the elision of *a* does not take place, because they are not part of a verbal base (*anaṅgatvāt*).
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffix] *matup* is applied after the pratyāhāra *tasa* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). 1.4.19.

In *nabhasvat* and *aṅgirasvat*, because they are not *pada*s, there is an absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r* for *s*). In *manuṣvat*, however, since it is a *pada*, *rutva* would apply, but not *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), because of the rule stating "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*). In *vṛṣaṇvasuḥ* and *vṛṣaṇaśva*, if they were *pada*s, then by the prohibition "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*), *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) would not occur, and furthermore, there would be the elision of *n* (*nalopa*). Even if they were treated as *bha*s, the elision of *a* (*allopa*) does not take place, because they do not constitute a complete suffixal element (*anaṅgatvāt*).

Regarding the rule *tasau matvarthe*: since the base (*prakṛti*) is implied by the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), it is specified by the letters *t* and *s*; thus, he says "ending in *t* or *s*" (*takārasakārāntam*). Regarding the phrase "in a suffix expressing possession" (*matvarthe pratyaye*): these are two locative cases in apposition (*vyadhikaraṇe saptamyau*), meaning "in that suffix which occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Alternatively, because of its association with the word *matu*, the sense [of the suffix] is indicated as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇe*); the meaning is "in that which has the sense of *matu*."

Regarding *udaśvitvān*: because it is a *bha*-stem, there is no *pada*-status; consequently, *jaś*-substitution does not occur, and by the rule *jhayaḥ*, *va*-substitution takes its place. [The word] *udaśvit* means "it swells (*śvayati*) or increases (*vardhate*) with water (*udakena*). The absence of *samprasāraṇa* is due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) in the rule *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām*; furthermore, the substitution of *ud-* for *udaka-* occurs when it is a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*). Regarding *payasvī*: by the rule *asmāyāmedhāstrajo viniḥ*, the suffix *vin* is applied; because it is a *bha*-stem, the substitution of *ru* (for the final *s*) does not occur.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *artha* (meaning)? Why not simply say *matau* (in the suffix *mat*); [for] *svādiṣu* (in those beginning with *su*) continues to apply, and the two locatives are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), meaning "those *su*-suffixes etc. which occur in *mat*. But how can a word indeed occur in a word, given that it is impossible? It will be understood as occurring in the meaning. If it were possible [to understand it] in this way, then [the mention of *artha*] would be superfluous.

But that is not possible; for when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it is not feasible to understand it as non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Consequently, [the suffix] would apply only to the abstract noun (*mata*), as in *payasvān* and *yaśasvān*, but here it would not apply in forms such as *payasvī* and *yaśasvī*. Therefore, the term "meaning" (*artha*) must be included [in the rule]. If the term "meaning" is included, the suffix *matup* would not be obtained; because it qualifies the meaning [rather than the word-form], this is true; however, while *matup* qualifies the meaning, the form of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is also present therein.

The meaning of the possessive suffix *matup* is "this belongs to him" or "he has this"; and that meaning is no different for *matup* than it is for [words] such as *vini*. For example, when it is said, "Let the Brāhmaṇas sitting in Devadatta’s hall be brought," even though Devadatta is merely a qualifying attribute, he is brought along with the white Brāhmaṇas. Only where the form of the thing to be characterized (*upalakṣya*) is impossible is there an impossibility of the purposeful application of the characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). For instance, in the case of "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," for it is not the case that brindled cows have [other] cows [as their owners].
*Padamañjarī*:
"In the Vedic language, [the suffixes] *mayaṭ* and others are applied after words beginning with *ayas* (iron). (Pāṇini 4.3.143). 1.4.20.

If a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) were being prescribed here, then, due to proximity, the formation would occur solely by way of prescribing the designation *bha*, and the designation *pada* would not apply; furthermore, there would be no coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *bha* and *pada*. Therefore, considering that it is more appropriate to prescribe correctness (*sādhutva*) itself, he says: "By the rule beginning with *ayasmaya*" and so forth. He demonstrates a specific mode regarding correctness: "In the section on the designations *bha* and *pada*" and so forth. "Door" (*dvāra*) means "means" (*upāya*). Regarding *ayasmayam*: it is a derivative of *ayas* (iron/metal), formed with the suffix *mayaṭ* according to the rule *dvyacaśchandasi*.
*Padamañjarī*: "The plural number is used for many. (Pāṇini 1.4.21)

The plural number (*bahuvacana*) has been prescribed. Consequently, since that [number] is already established even though it is indicated by the case-ending of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its status is that of a restatement (*anuvādya*), not that of something to be enjoined; this is the sense. He says, "by this [sūtra], for that... to show that although the plural number is indicated by the case-ending experienced through the rule, it is enjoined because it was not previously established. Furthermore, another point is demonstrated by this passage: for this sentence is distinct from the sentence prescribing the *svādi* suffixes; and even there, it serves the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), not the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

As for the statement that "the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is prescribed," it means it is enjoined as the denotation of the numerical category of plurality (*bahutva*). If, however, there were a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) based on syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), it would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the designation of "plural" (*bahuvacana-saṃjñā*) would apply to *jas* and other suffixes once they are enjoined, and their injunction would depend upon that designation. Furthermore, [if this were the case], suffixes such as *su*, *au*, and *jas* would not occur after indeclinables (*avyaya*). Therefore, it is more logical that they constitute distinct sentences (*bhinnavākyatva*), and even in that case, they serve solely the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*).

In this regard, some maintain that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of five elements: its own referent (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and object (*karman*) and so forth. Others hold that it consists of the first three. Among these, the "own referent" (*svārtha*) is the basis for the application of a word (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), and it is of many kinds: intrinsic form (*svarūpa*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), substance (*dravya*), and relation (*sambandha*). For example: *ḍittha*, *cow*, *white*, *cook*, *staff*, *person*, and *staff-bearer*. Even in the case of words denoting genus and the like, when they are restricted to the genus alone, the intrinsic form itself is the basis for the application of the word.

Due to the superimposition of non-difference between the denoter and the denoted, the object is expressed as being colored by the form of the word. There is a difference in the mode of cognition: "This is the name 'cow'" (*asya gaur iti nāma*) and "This is a cow" (*ayaṃ gaur iti*). The grounds for this are grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and grammatical subordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). In this regard, they consider that even the word's own form—like the universal (*jāti*) and so forth—is apprehended through the word itself and serves as a qualifier of the object. And it has been said: "Just as light possesses two powers—the capacity to be perceived (*grāhyatva*) and the capacity to perceive (*grāhakatva*)—so too these two [powers] exist separately in all words."
Therefore, even the essential nature (svarūpa) is logically the primary meaning (svārtha);
that substance in which the primary meaning finds its rest is accepted as the denotable (vācya).

The meaning is "the stage of final determination. And that [determination] is of many kinds: genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), substance (*dravya*), and essential form (*svarūpa*); for example: "cow" (*gauḥ*), "white" (*suklaḥ*), "cooking" (*pākaḥ*), "Ḍittha," and "he remained silent" (*tūṣṇīm abhūt*). Gender (*liṅga*) refers to femininity and so forth. Number (*saṃkhyā*) refers to singularity and so forth. The specific factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*) and others will be explained later.

Thus, the second view is adopted here by the author of the Vṛtti: the determination of the meaning of a word is indeed established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For that meaning which is perceived when a particular word is present (*anvaya*), and which is excluded when that word is absent (*vyatireka*), is the meaning of that word. In cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree) and *vṛkṣau* (two trees), when those respective case-endings (*vacana*) are present, their respective numbers are perceived; and when those endings are absent, they are excluded, even though the presence of the stem (*prakṛti*) remains constant. Therefore, we consider that number is the meaning of the case-ending.

Likewise, in cases such as *vṛkṣam*, *vṛkṣeṇa*, and *vṛkṣāya*, that respective object (*karman*) and so forth is perceived when there is a connection with the corresponding triad [of case-meanings], and it is excluded when there is an exclusion [of that triad]. Therefore, we consider that the object and so forth constitute the meaning of the triad.

Although in cases such as *payo dadhi madhu* (milk, curd, honey), that respective meaning is understood even without an explicit statement and even without the triplet [of suffixes], its status as the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not thereby lost. For, although the meaning of "offspring" is understood in the word *gargāḥ* even without the suffix *yañ*, it is not correct to say that in the word *gārgyaḥ* the offspring is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) just as it is for the base itself. In examples such as *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, and *pacanti*, since number is associated with the triplet when it is present, and is absent when it is absent, number is indeed the meaning of the triplet, and not [the meaning] of the base.

This is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Although in cases such as *abibhar bhavān* ("you carried"), the agent and number are understood even without a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), it does not follow from this that they must always be the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*). For instance, although the agent is understood in forms like *bhinat* or *chinat* even without a suffix, the agent does not thereby become the meaning of the base in forms such as *bhettṛ*. Thus, the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists precisely of the three factors [gender, number, and the referent].

Since it is held that only action (kriyā) is denoted by a verbal root (dhātu), in the absence of this [rule], because its meaning would be unspecified, the plural suffixes *jas* and so forth would apply only to the "triple" (trika) in its own sense, and not to plurality (*bahutva*). Therefore, it is prescribed as having plurality as its expressed meaning. Even in the sūtra, although there is no abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the reference is primarily to the state (*bhāva*); the meaning is "in plurality. Because plurality, which resides in the substratum, is superimposed upon the quality (*guṇa*), the plural form *bahuṣu* is used.

The purpose of superimposition (āropa) is so that there may be the apprehension of plurality (*bahutva*), which consists of number and has various substrata. Consequently, "extensiveness" (*vaipulya*) residing in a single locus is not the denotation of the plural number—as in the case of *bahurodana* ("much rice").

Some hold the view that number, objecthood (*karman*), and so forth, being mutually unconnected, are expressed by case-endings as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). For instance, in *vṛkṣān paśya*, what is the meaning? It is "many trees are the object," but not "the trees, having become the object, are many," nor "there are many objects."

Likewise, even in the case of the singular number, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the meaning is that "the animal is one" or "the animal is the instrument," but not that "the animal which has become the instrument is one," nor that "one animal is the instrument," because [otherwise] there would be a simultaneous denotation of both instrumentality and oneness. He refutes those [views] with the words "the object and so forth are also others," etc. Regarding the phrase "in its plurality": the meaning is that the plurality expressed by the plural suffix must pertain specifically to the object and so forth, and not merely to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself.

In the view that the substance (*dravya*) is the meaning of the word, it is the plurality residing in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) alone that must be expressed. Since the word "tree" denotes the whole (*avayavin*), and not its parts, there is an absence of the plural number even when there is a plurality of roots, trunks, fruits, leaves, and so forth, because these [parts] are not what is being denoted. Even in the view that the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning, one relies on the plurality residing in its substratum due to proximity, and not on the plurality residing in the parts. It has been stated that the injunction is made through a separate sentence; he states its purpose with the words beginning "And where... (*yatra ca* etc.).

In the Bhāṣya, however, by accepting the view of the fivefold [categories], the restrictive (niyama) view is established. For there, since suffixes whose meaning is not specified apply to their own referent (svārtha), the plural endings such as *jas* are established even when applied to their own referent; because that too is their own referent, and because of the restriction on meaning therein, the rule holds: "the plural is used only for the plural," and "the dual and singular are used only for two and one. Similarly, in rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the restriction on meaning should be understood as: "for the object, only the second case," and so forth.

For in this way, because suffixes are not restricted [by number], the case endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) are established even after indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number and lack grammatical agency (*niṣkāraka*). Alternatively, there is a restriction regarding the suffixes: the plural occurs only when there are many; the dual and singular occur only when there are two and one, respectively. Furthermore, by this restriction, there is an exclusion of what is similar in kind: the plural occurs only for many, not for two or one; the singular occurs only for one, not for another number; and the dual occurs only for two, not for another number.

The same applies to rules such as "the second case-affix [is used] for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*): the second case-affix is used only for the object, not for any other *kāraka*. For in this way, the case-affixes beginning with *su* (the nominative) are established even from indeclinables (*avyaya*).
The dual and singular endings are used for two and one, respectively. (Pāṇini 1.4.22)

By virtue of its association with the word *dvi* ("two"), the word *eka* ("one") here denotes a number. This too is a designation that emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*); for this very reason, the dual form *dvye-kayoḥ* is used. Thus he says: "in the states of duality and unity. Regarding the phrase "this also," etc., he shows by this that this rule also serves as an injunction (*vidhi*).
