How then can it be said "of those prescribed in general" (*sāmānyavihitayoḥ*), given that this [usage] is consistent only if the rule has the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*)? It is replied: the word *sāmānya* is a synonym for *sādhāraṇa* (common/shared); the meaning is "of those prescribed in common to both cases—those with a number and those without a number."

Regarding the term *arthābhidhānam*: "artha" means that which is to be expressed (*vācya*); that by which it is expressed—that is, spoken—is *arthābhidhānam*. In the rule *dvyekayoḥ*, the word *eka* does not undergo prior placement (as required by the rule *saṃkhyāyā alpīyasyaḥ*) precisely because of this specific exception (*nipātana*). Others maintain that among words denoting things to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), "being fewer" (*alpīyastva*) is determined through the meaning (*artha-dvāraka*).
*Padamañjarī*, on the topic of the agent (*kāraka*). 1.4.23.

The governing authority (*adhikāra*) is of many kinds: technical name (*saṃjñā*), qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), locus (*sthānin*), base (*prakṛti*), cause (*nimitta*), and substitute (*ādeśa*). In cases such as *pratyayaḥ*, *śeṣe*, *pūrvaparayoḥ*, *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, *dhātoḥ*, and *ārddhadhātuke mūrddhnyaḥ*, since no element to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is specified and because they are marked with the *svarita* accent, they are established as governing authorities. Regarding this, he states the various types: "the term *kāraka* is a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)... [and] "it is governed (*adhikriyate*). It is not, first of all, a governing authority by way of being a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Because a technical designation (*sañjñā*) is something to be produced [by a rule], the locative case is inappropriate. Now, why was the nominative not used here in accordance with the designation? This would indeed be logical, since it is intended that among the designations of *kārakas* to be mentioned later, only the six beginning with *apādāna* should be understood; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including even "the remainder of the *kārakas*" (as in the example *naṭasya śṛṇoti*). It is replied:

In the case where [the sūtra] is a *sañjñā* (technical designation)—meaning "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) when there is separation (*apāya*) receives the designation *kāraka*, and also the designation *apādāna*"—and so on in other instances as well; then, because the designations *kāraka* and *apādāna* are prescribed simultaneously, there would be no relationship of cause and effect (*nimittanimittibhāva*) between them, and consequently, even that which is not a *kāraka*—being devoid of activity—would incur the designation *apādāna*. However, under the heading of *viśeṣaṇa* (qualification), that which is fixed during separation among the *kārakas* does not incur [the designation].
Therefore, the formulation was made in accordance with the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), and not in accordance with the technical designation (*sañjñā*).

The designation *kāraka*, however, because it is etymologically significant (*anvartha*), does not apply to that which is devoid of activity (*vyāpāra*). Furthermore, there would be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the *kāraka* designation with the designations such as *apādāna* and so forth; consequently, in the case of the word *stamberamaḥ*, when the locative case ending is heard, the accent prescribed by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* would not occur. [In response: the locative case in the term *kārake* is one used for specification (*nirdhāraṇe saptamī*), and the singular number is employed in view of the general category.

This word *kāraka* exists as a derivative formed with the suffix *ṇvul*, meaning "that which acts" (*karoti iti kārakam*); it also exists as an unanalyzed technical term (*sañjñāśabda*) synonymous with "cause" (*nimitta*). In that regard, if the former [derivative] were intended, the term *kāraka* would not apply to the [factors] beginning with the ablative (*apādāna*), just as the term *kartṛ* (agent) does not, because they lack independence (*asvatantra*); or, if they did possess independence, the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-sañjñā*) would undesirably follow in those cases. This, however, is not a fault.

Indeed, every causal factor (*kāraka*), having accomplished its respective intermediate operation, contributes to the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*). And that principal action—which is produced by all the causal factors and consists of the result, such as the softening [of grain]—is the primary action. Alternatively, the principal action is the general action known as "the production of the result," for all causal factors indeed operate toward the production of the result; therefore, whatever constitutes the production of the result is common to all causal factors without distinction.

Indeed, an agent produces a fruit through a specific form; thus, the production of the fruit is uniform across all [factors]. However, when internal distinctions are intended to be expressed, there arises the manifestation of forms such as "instrument" (karaṇa) and so forth.

Furthermore, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas, for us a single action does not inhere in multiple substrates; for action is the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), not merely physical motion (parispanda). And by the verbal root, the operation (vyāpāra) is denoted as unified by being common to all the factors of action (kārakas) and delimited by the fruit, such as cooked rice.

In that single primary action, there is a contribution through various intermediate operations as appropriate; for example: the operation of the *apādāna* (ablative) is its attainment of the state of being a limit (*avadhi*); that of the *sampradāna* (dative), however, is instigation, consent, non-rejection, and so forth; that of the *karaṇa* (instrument), such as wood and the like, is burning and so forth; that of the *adhikaraṇa* (locative), it is the providing of a locus and supporting, and so forth; that of the *karman* (object), it is the production [of the result] and so forth; that of the *kartṛ* (agent) is well known; and that of the *prayojaka* (instigator) is commanding and so forth.

And this being the case, it does not follow that instruments and the other factors would also incur the designation of "agent," because they are dependent. For when there is a direct connection (*samavāya*) with the primary agent, the instrument and the others are dependent; when there is an indirect connection (*vyavāya*), they are independent. This is just as ministers are dependent when in direct connection with the king, but independent when in indirect connection. If this were so, would there not also be an absence of the designation "kāraka" (factor) for the instrument and others in their respective states? No, because of the force of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) stating "the instrument is a kāraka."

The independence conveyed by the term *kāraka* will be understood as pertaining to a different state; for that which is independent in another state is the *karaṇa*, the most effective instrument. However, independence in its primary sense belongs only to the agent (*kartṛ*), and that [independence] is enjoined as being subordinate to the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "agent."

If, then, even in the view that [the term] is derived [from its etymological root], independence (*svātantrya*) exists only when [the agent] has entered into another state, then in the states of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, it would follow that only the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) is admitted. If this is so, what is the point of the trouble taken to refute the objection? Thinking that one should simply accept the synonym *nimitta* (cause), he says: "And the word *kāraka*... [The question is: "Of what is it the cause? The intention is that even a cause whose object is a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*) would result in being a *kāraka*.

Since this word *kāraka* is well-known only in the sense of a cause of action (*kriyāhetu*), he says: "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*). A cause (*hetu*) is a motive (*nimitta*) that does not depend upon an operation (*vyāpāra*), whereas a *kāraka* is one whose operation is dependent [upon an action]. And it has been said: "The cause has substances and so forth as its object; a *kāraka* has a restricted action. And:
"But when the operation is not dependent [on an action], it is accepted as a cause (*hetu*)."

How then was it previously stated that [the general and the particular] are not different in meaning (*anarthāntara*)? For is it not the case that words denoting a general and a particular do not have the same referent? True; however, even for two general terms, it was stated thus with the intention that they function as particulars based on context, purpose, and so forth. As in the example, "The leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*). Here, the tree is intended as a qualifier of the leaf, and not as the cause of the departure (*apāya*); therefore, the technical designation of *apādāna* (ablative) does not apply, nor is it because the departure is not intended to be expressed.

For movement implies a limit (*avadhi*), and cessation [of that movement] occurs only when such a limit exists, not otherwise. Nor is the tree intended here as the limit. To explain: even when a leaf has not yet left the tree, the expression "the leaf of the tree falls" is used when the tree itself has been cut down and is falling. True; for this very reason, being dissatisfied with that [explanation], he says: "the father of the boy."

In this case, the boy (*māṇavaka*) is intended to be related to the father, and not as the cause (*nimitta*) with respect to the act of questioning; therefore, the designation *karman* (object) does not apply. However, if the governing heading *kāraka* were absent, that designation would indeed apply to him as well. As for the genitive case characterized as *śeṣa* (remainder), it finds its scope in examples such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), because it is excluded by the specific enumeration of roots such as *duh* under the rule *akathita*.

If, then, this is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would not be a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for *dhruva* and the others; consequently, in rules such as "only for *kāraka*, *datta*, and *śruta* in the sense of a benediction" (*kārakaddattaśrutayorevāśiṣi*), where the word *kāraka* is employed, one would desire the inclusion of only the six [categories] beginning with the ablative (*apādāna*) that are to be explained hereafter, yet that would not be established. However, there is no fault in the view that it is a technical term; for a technical term, when it recurs, causes its designatum (*saṃjñin*) to be understood.

It might be argued that even in specific rules (*pradeśa*), the term *kāraka* is employed as a synonym for the cause of action (*kriyānimitta*), and that this cause is precisely the *apādāna* and so forth. That is incorrect; for in examples such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor"), [the actor] is a remnant of a *kāraka*. He says: "And in the designations of *kārakas*" (*kārakasaṃśabdaneṣu*). The meaning is that the mention of *kāraka* is indicated by a circumflex accent (*svarita*) in the specific rules; the understanding of a governing heading (*adhikāra*) occurs through what is marked with a circumflex accent.
*Padamañjarī*:
"In the sense of separation (*apāya*), that from which [the separation occurs] is certainly the *apādāna*. (Pāṇini 1.4.24)

Regarding the word *dhruvam*: it is derived from the root *dhru* (meaning "motion" and "stability") belonging to the *kuṭādi* group, with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). For those, however, who read the root as *dhru* (in the sense of "motion" and "stability"), the suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* followed by a short vowel (*igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*, 3.1.135). *Apāya* means separation (*viśleṣa*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*), as well as the specific kind of motion that causes it, which depends upon a limit (*avadhi*). Since disjunction resides in two locations, it is not only the one moving away that is connected with it; rather, that from which the object moves away is also indeed connected with it. Thus he says: "that which is fixed (*dhruvam*) and connected with departure."

But how can we understand that [the action] is connected with separation (*apāya*) even when there is a mention in the locative case (*saptamī*)? To this he says: "When separation is the thing to be accomplished" (*apāye sādhya*). The sense is that because it is the object by virtue of being something to be accomplished, its connection [with the action] is obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).

The term *dhruva* (fixed/steady) is said to denote that which is of a single form—such as "his conduct is fixed" or "his form is fixed. Here, that [single form] is qualified by separation, namely "that which is fixed in separation," and not that which is universal. And that which is called "fixed in separation" is that which is not permeated by separation and is utilized in separation; and since that is, by implication, the limit (*avadhi*), he says: "that which has become a limit."

And thus, in cases such as "fallen from the caravan," "fallen from the chariot," or "fallen while running," although there is motion due to the involvement of another action, there is indeed the status of being fixed (*dhruvatva*) because of indifference toward the resulting separation (*apāya*), since there is no involvement in those specific actions of running and so forth. Therefore, the designation [of *apādāna*] certainly applies. As it has been said: "That which is indifferent toward the separation, whether it be moving or unmoving, is called fixed (*dhruva*) precisely because it lacks involvement in that [action]; it is termed the 'ablative' (*apādāna*)."

Even in the case of "the falling one" (patataḥ) and "the fallen one" (patitaḥ), there is indeed fixity (dhrauvya) with respect to the fall occurring in another. For instance: "The horse from which he falls is certainly fixed for him who is falling; however, when that horse itself falls, the wall or such is said to be fixed."
But here, in the case of "two rams are butting each other," the status of being a limit (avadhitva) is distinct for each ram with respect to the action of the other ram;
likewise, the status of being an agent (kartṛtva) is distinct for each ram with respect to its own action.
But without a limit, there is no going; thus it is said that there is no departure.

Regarding the word *jugupsate*: separation preceded by contact is "separation" (*apāya*), and that is not present here; moreover, that which is mentally constructed is secondary (*gauṇa*), and it is not proper to adopt the secondary sense when the primary one is possible. For this very reason, the author of the *Vākya* [Kātyāyana] intended the formulation of rules such as "of those meaning fear and protection" (*bhītrārthānām*). And in this case, since it is merely a residual factor (*kārakaśeṣa*), the genitive case would apply, as in the example "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*).

The mention of the suffix *tamap* [in Pāṇini 1.4.42]—that "the most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) is the [kāraka]—is an indicator (*liṅga*) that, within the section on *kārakas*, "effectiveness" (*sādhakatva*) applies only as far as possible. Thus, in cases such as *adharmāj jugupsate* ("he feels aversion toward unrighteousness"), once it is established that the verbal activity of *jugupsā* and the like consists in a cessation preceded by *jugupsā* and so forth, this person who acts with foresight perceives: "Unrighteousness is a cause of suffering; I shall not do this. Through his intellect, he reaches [the realization of] that [unrighteousness], and having reached it, he turns away from it.

"He neglects the Dharma, he becomes deluded regarding the Dharma. This refers to that person who is an atheist (*nāstika*); he perceives, "Nothing is gained by this Dharma; I shall not perform it," and thus he reaches that [state] through his intellect. Having reached it, he turns away from it. In that case, it is established that there is indeed a "falling away from" (*dhruvapāya*). Furthermore, this [ablative case] is said to be threefold: that which has a specified object (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), that which has an implied object (*upāttaviṣaya*), and that which requires an action to be supplied (*apekṣitakriya*).

Where the object of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is indicated by means of a noun (*nāman*) characterized as a point of departure (*apāya*), as in "he comes from the village," that is called "having a specified object" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*). Where a verbal root expresses its own meaning as a subordinate part of the meaning of another verbal root, as in "lightning flashes from the cloud," for here the root *vidyuti* functions with flashing as a subordinate part of the act of emerging—meaning "having emerged from the cloud, it flashes."

In the expression *kusūlāt pacati* ("he cooks from the granary"), the root *pac-* (to cook) refers to cooking as a subordinate part of the act of taking; that is, "having taken [the grain] from the granary, he cooks. This is an instance where the object is already included [in the verbal root]. However, an action whose activity is "implied" (*apekṣitakriyam*) is one where the action is not explicitly heard but is understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example, seeing a man approaching by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), someone asks, "Where are you coming from? He too, relying upon that very arrival established by direct perception, replies, "From Pāṭaliputra."

What is the purpose of including the word *dhruva* (fixed)? [It is so that the rule does not apply in cases like: "He comes from the village by means of a cart" (*grāmād āgacchati śakaṭena*), where the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) should not apply to the cart. Now, even if the word *dhruva* is included, why does it not apply here: "He will pierce with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*)? For in this case, the bow is indeed the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) with respect to the departure of the arrows, acting as their point of reference (*avadhi*). True; however, when both [designations] would apply simultaneously, the technical term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) will prevail because it is taught later in the sequence of rules.

Indeed, even if this [rule] were not formulated, it would not apply to the case of "the cart" (*śakaṭasya*), and likewise in all cases involving different designations. However, in the expression "a leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya patraṃ patati*), it will not apply because the departure (*apāya*) is not intended to be expressed and because [the tree] is not a *kāraka*.

However, for the purpose of indicating the technical name (*saṃjñā*), it is not possible to indicate the named entity (*saṃjñin*) by means of the locative form *kārake*; for that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*) must already be established as a named entity. Thus, among the factors of action (*kārakas*) involved in separation (*apāya*), that factor which is not the domain of another technical name is called *apādāna*. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *dhruva* (fixed) is of questionable utility.
*Padamañjarī*:
For verbs meaning "to fear" or "to protect," the cause of fear [is the *apādāna*]. (Pāṇini 1.4.25)

*Bhaya* means fear (*bhī*); *trāṇa* means protection (*trā*). From the root class beginning with *sampad*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Those whose meanings are fear and protection are called "those whose meanings are fear and protection" (*bhītrārthāḥ*). He says "of those whose meaning is 'to fear'" (*bibhetyarthānām*) and so forth, with reference to the use of the genitive case and with reference to the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). Here, the words *bibheti* ("he fears") and *trāyati* ("he protects") refer to their respective meanings; the meaning of which is the meaning of those [words]—this is the sense. Protection (*trāṇa*) is guarding against oppressors, and since oppressors are the causes of fear, for those whose meaning is protection (*trārthānām*), the cause of fear is indeed the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). As in: "from thieves" (*corebhyaḥ*).

From the root *cor* (to steal), with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), we get *coraḥ*. In some places, the reading is *caurebhyaḥ*; in that case, the suffix *aṇ* (of the *prajñādi* class) is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, the word *cura* is listed among the *chattrādi* group; since the suffix *yuc* (by the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*) would otherwise apply as a superseding rule, it is instead derived from that very root by means of a specific irregularity (*nipātana*), resulting in the suffix *a* and the elision of the causative marker *ṇi*. Thus, when the suffix *ṇa* is added in the sense "one whose habit (*śīla*) is stealing (*steya*)," the same meaning is obtained. Regarding *bibheti*: the root *ñibhī* (to fear) belongs to the *juhotyādi* class.

Regarding the word *udvijate*: the root *ovijī* belongs to the seventh (*taudādika*) class, meaning "fear" and "trembling," and is anudātta (unaccented). Regarding the word *araṇye*: here, the fear is from the trees and such things situated therein, not from the forest itself. Now, one might object: "But the term *dhruva* (the fixed point) will be understood by way of anuvṛtti [from the previous rule], and the forest is certainly not intended as the non-agential cause (*apādāna*); furthermore, because it is a subsequent rule, it will simply receive the designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locus). True.

This is an elaboration of the very same [previous point]. How so? In the case of desisting preceded by fear and the like, the roots *bhī* (to fear) and others function; what is the meaning of *bibheti*? It means "he turns away because of fear. What is the meaning of *trāyate*? It means "by means of protection from death at the hands of thieves, he causes him to turn away. How then is there the usage *corabhyaḥ bibheti* ("he fears the thieves") in the case of one standing in the midst of thieves, for there is no actual turning away here? In this case too, the meaning should be understood as "he desires to turn away because of fear."

Thus, since there is an "apāya" (departure) imagined by the intellect, this *apādāna* (ablative case) has its object already grasped. Now that the entire elaboration of usage has been established, what is the use of an inquiry into its constituent parts?
In the *Padamañjarī*, this [sūtra] is not accepted after the root *parā-ji*. (1.4.26)

Here, there is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of only as much as "ji" found in the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*). Therefore, *parājir*—meaning *ji* preceded by *para*—should be understood as a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). [Objection: But since "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam bhavati*), the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-sañjñā*) would be prohibited by the rule "it is not a root" (*adhātuḥ*); consequently, because it would not end in a suffix (*asubanta*), a compound would not be possible. [Response: No.

Because it is not a prohibition; this is not a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) such as "not from a root" (*dhātoḥ na*). What then? This is a *paryudāsa* (relative exclusion)—namely, "that which is other than a root. Thus, there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition regarding the root. Even so, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would still apply; however, because it is subsequent, the *guṇa* substitution [of *e*] will occur by the rule *gher ṅiti*. Or rather, it refers to the whole; the whole is the imitation [of the form]. Of what whole? Of the usage.

If this is so, then [the rule] "he is defeated by study" (*adhyayanāt parājayate*) would apply here; however, the form *parāji* does not exist here. Where, then, would it occur? It occurs where the form *parāji* exists, as in "defeated by study" (*adhyayanāt parājitaḥ*). In the example, the root *parāji* signifies "becoming inferior"—the meaning is that he falters or becomes weary in his study. In this sense, the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have applied, this statement is made. In the counter-example, however, it signifies "overpowering."

In the rule "viparābhyāṃ jeḥ," there is the inclusion of the root *ji* as it occurs in both senses [of victory and defeat]. This detailed explanation also establishes that the term applies to cessation preceded by a state of deficiency. For example, in the case of *adhyayanāt parājayate*, what is the meaning? It means he turns away from study due to exhaustion resulting from a state of deficiency. Therefore, one should not raise the objection that, in the counter-example, the technical designation "object" (*karman*) would apply because of its higher priority [in the sequence of rules].
In the *Padamañjarī*:
"For verbs meaning 'to ward off,' that which is intended [by the agent] is the object. (Pāṇini 1.4.27)

This word *īpsita* (desired) is a synonym for "intended. If it were taken in that sense, then while the barley would be one's own (*ātmīya*), the cows would have to be owned by another (*parakīya*), and not the reverse. Indeed, it is not his intention that his own cows should eat the barley belonging to another; nor is the barley intended to be prevented from being eaten. Rather, it is the cows being prevented who are the ones desiring [the barley]. Furthermore, no such distinction is heard in the rule itself, namely that "that which is desired by the agent" [is the object].

In that case, however, there would not be [the usage]: "He wards off the boy from the fire" or "He wards off the blind man from the well," for neither the fire nor the well is intended by the one warding off or the one being warded off. But if the term *kriyā* (action) is included, it is established because the blind man and others, though being warded off, are connected with the well and so forth through actions such as going; for even though the blind man does not see, he desires to go to what is to be gone to, otherwise he would never engage in activity anywhere. [As in: "He wards off the cows from the barley. The root *vṛñ* in the sense of "covering" belongs to the *curādi* group.

Now, why does the designation *apādāna* (ablative) not apply here to the cows (*gavām*), since that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) is indeed something desired (*īpsita*), just as that which is whitest (*śuklatama*) is also white (*śukla*)? Because of its higher status, the designation *karman* (object) will prevail. The scope for the designation *karman* is in cases other than those involving [words] meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇārtha*); whereas the scope for the designation *apādāna* is that which is desired but lacks excellence. However, when both would apply to that which is most desired, the designation *karman* prevails due to its higher status.

This too is a mere elaboration (*prapañca*), for here also there exists a negative consequence (*apāya*) established by the intellect. How so? He perceives: "If the cows were to go into the field, the crop would certainly be destroyed; with the destruction of the crop, there would be demerit (*adharma*) and fear of the king. Having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he turns them back. Therefore, it should not be objected that in the counter-example the field would have the designation of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the *Padamañjarī*:
"In the sense of disappearance (*antardhi*), [the suffix *ṇamul* is used] when one goes to become invisible. (1.4.28)

Regarding the term *antarddhau* (in disappearance), this is not a locative case governed by the rule *nimittātkarmayoge* ("the locative [is used] after a cause when there is a connection with an action"), as in the example *vetanena dhānyaṃ lunāti* ("he reaps grain for wages"), where there is a connection between the wages and the grain; for here too, there is no connection between the disappearance (*antarddhi*) and the object of the desire (*icchākarma*), namely the non-perception (*adarśana*), in the sense that "one desires non-perception. If it is argued that there is a connection with disappearance because the object of non-perception is the self—namely, "one desires the non-perception of oneself"—and that therefore there is a connection with disappearance, then it would have to be said that the very one for whom there is non-perception is the very one for whom there is disappearance.

Even so, regarding the rule "nimittāt karmayoge" (Pāṇini 1.4.32), what is understood by the term *nimitta*? Is it the cause (*kāraṇa*) or the purpose (*prayojana*)? If it were the cause, then [the suffix] would also apply in the case of "bound by dullness" (*jāḍyena baddhaḥ*), because the dullness exists precisely where one is bound; therefore, it must be the purpose that is taken here. For example, in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti*), the skin is the purpose of killing the leopard. In this case, however, concealment (*antarddhāna*) is the cause of invisibility (*adarśana*), for when someone is concealed, they are indeed not seen.

Therefore, this is either a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*) or a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*). In the word *yena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). But surely, because of its connection with "seeing" (*darśana*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) ought to occur according to the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*. [To this we reply: Because of the restriction that when both [agent and object] are eligible [for the sixth case], it occurs only for the object, the third case will indeed occur. However, in this context, the object of the non-perception is the self (*ātman*). But is it not the case that "of the self" (*ātmane*) is not actually heard? Let it not be heard; for when it is said "by whom one desires non-perception," since there arises an expectation of "whose?", it is understood to be "of the self. [The phrase] "caused by disappearance" (*antarddhi-nimitta*) means...

The meaning is "by means of the cause that is disappearance" (*antarddhinā*). The nominative case is used because of the rule: "In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all [case endings] are generally seen. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where "disappearance" (*adarśana*) is a coreferential qualifier. He says "that causal factor" (*tatkārakam*), for even though the word *tat* is not explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, it is indeed obtained through the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*. "He disappears" (*antardhatte*) means "he becomes hidden. "He hides" (*nilīyate*): the root *līṅ* in the sense of "adhering" belongs to the *devādika* (divādi) class.

"He does not wish to see the thieves"—this is for the purpose that "they may not see him. [Objection: But surely the designation *karman* (object) will apply because it is the most remote (*paratvāt*). [Reply: True; this too is an elaboration (*prapañca*). How so? He sees thus: "If the teacher were to see me, there would certainly be a command or a reproach for me"; having reached this conclusion through his intellect, he desists. If the word "by whom" (*yena*) were not present here, the designation would belong only to the disciple who desires to see, while the word "the fixed point" (*dhruvam*) will continue to apply.

In that case, let there not be a lack of clarity in the Sūtra. For if it were absent, the meaning would have to be: "When disappearance occurs, that which is certainly designated as the *apādāna* (ablative) is so called if one desires its non-perception. But [the Sūtra] does not desire what is certain; and if one desires something, it is not certain. Thus, [without the Sūtra], it would be non-expressive.
*Padamañjarī*:
"When there is instruction, [the ablative case is used] after a verb. (Pāṇini 1.4.29)

"Acquisition of knowledge preceded by a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is because the word *upayoga* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense. For example, regarding the application (*upayoga*) of those mantras, there is a restrictive rule such as "lying on the ground for twelve days," as well as practices like begging for alms. In the expression "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*), is the actor a *kāraka* (participant in an action) or not? If he is a *kāraka*, then the designation "object" (*karman*) would apply to him by the rule "and that which is not otherwise mentioned" (*akathitaṃ ca*). If, on the other hand, he is not a *kāraka*, then the inclusion of the term *upayoga* [in the definition of the dative case] would be purposeless.

Let it be an agent (*kāraka*); for there is indeed no difference whatsoever in the activity of the teacher (*upādhyāya*) compared to that of the actor (*naṭa*), other than this restriction [of the rule]. However, due to the specific enumeration [of verbs] such as *duh* (to milk) and others, the designation "object" (*karman*) does not apply here. In some places, however, the reading is "he hears a song from the actor" (*naṭasya gāthāṃ śṛṇoti*) or "he hears a story from the storyteller" (*granthikasya kathāṃ śṛṇoti*). Even there, the meaning is that he performs the hearing of the song and so forth, caused by the actor and others; the actor and others are not qualifiers of the song and so forth, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of them being non-agents (*akāraka*). A *granthika* is one who causes a story to be recited.

This too is a mere proliferation. How so? In the case of "he perceives the sound issuing from the teacher," the sense of separation (*apāya*) is quite evident here. Then what is the purpose [of this rule]? It is this: "I shall state that it is for the sake of 'attention' (*upayoga*), so that it does not apply to an actor. But surely, even though the actor possesses the status of a limit (*avadhitva*), the genitive will still occur because he is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣa-rūpeṇa*), just as in the expression "one should not eat beans," where the beans are actually the object (*karman*), yet the genitive is used.

True; it is precisely that restriction of intention (*vivakṣā-niyama*) which is demonstrated by the author of the Sūtra: that the status of being a limit is intended when there is attention, whereas elsewhere the status of a residual relation is intended.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The source of the agent of birth [is called the *apādāna*]. (Pāṇini 1.4.30)

The compound *janikartṛ* (the agent of birth) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning "the agent of the root *jan*" (*janeḥ kartā*). Furthermore, this very grammatical indication teaches that the prohibition [of the genitive] stated in the rule *kartari ca* is not absolute (*anitya*). To the question "What, then, is this [exception]?", he says: "of the meaning of the root *jan*. This is what is meant: this word *jani* is derived by forming the suffix *iñ* in the sense of the action (*bhāve*) from the root *jan*, according to the rule *iñādibhyaḥ*.

The prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "janivadhyośca" refers to the word *janya* as a synonym for "born," and not to a form ending in the suffix *ik* according to the rule "ik-stipau dhātunirdeśe"; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule "gamahana-". Nor is the root indicated by means of an adventitious *i*-vowel; for it is impossible for a root, which consists of sound (*śabdātmaka*), to have a connection with an agent. Even if the connection were mediated through the meaning, even so, in the indication of a root, the operation would apply only to that specific form when used, and not to its synonyms—as in the case of "there is arising from limb after limb."

"But here too, [the rule] applies when there is the grasping of an object. This is the explanation of the term *prakṛti*: "the cause" (*kāraṇa*). The meaning is "the material cause" (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Others, however, explain that since the inclusion of *prakṛti* is already established by the recurrence of the mention of *dhruva*, the explicit mention of *prakṛti* is for the purpose of including any cause whatsoever. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "the cause," and not specifically "the material cause. Consequently, the rule also applies in cases such as "joy arises from the son. Now, does that which is born exist (*sat*) or not exist (*asat*)? It cannot be that which exists, because its birth would be purposeless.

If it already exists prior to birth, what is the purpose of birth? Or, if there is birth even in this case, then let the pot be born again and again! Nor is it non-existent; for that which is non-existent cannot possess agency, and it would follow that even things like a hare’s horn could be born. Regarding this, it has been said: "The essence of an object, while not abandoning its prior state and yet touching upon a subsequent property, is designated as 'being born,' as if it were in a state of coagulation."

And we shall establish this point under the rule *ānmahataḥ*. Furthermore, what is the use of this fallacious reasoning for us? There is, at any rate, the usage "an arrow is born from horn," and that alone must be accounted for! This too is a mere elaboration. For in common worldly usage, when something is produced from something else, it is said to have "issued forth" from it; linguistic usage follows worldly convention, whereas the actual nature of things may be one way or another.
The origin of the earth is Padmañjarī. 1.4.31.

*Bhavana* is *bhū*; the suffix *kvip* is applied because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group. Here too, the prefix *pra-* should be understood [as implied]. For the root *bhū*, in its simple form (*kevala*), there is no connection with the sense of "originating" (*prabhavana*); rather, it is [the root] *bhu* when accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*) that is intended. The term "agent" (*kartṛ*) means the agent of the sense of the root *bhū*, or [the agent] of the verbal root *bhu*. But how can a verbal root have an agent? A verbal root is indeed a word; since [an agent] is impossible in the case of a word, it will be understood as referring to the meaning.

In the word *tasu*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), while in *vigatau* (from the root *vi*), the form *vitastā* is derived; its meaning is "that which cannot be dried up. Regarding the phrase "is perceived first," the verb *upalabhate* functions in the sense of the object's activity (*karmavyāpāre*), meaning "it prevails" (*prabhavati*), that is, "it proceeds" (*pravartate*), or "it manifests" (*prakāśate*). By this, he shows that [the definition] is not established by the preceding [definition] because there is an absence of the sense of being produced (*janya*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, it occurs in this sense as well. This too is an elaboration (*prapañca*). How so? The verb *prabhavati* functions in the sense of "emerging" (*niḥsaraṇa*) preceded by "coming into being" (*bhavana*).
*Padamañjarī*:
That which one intends [to benefit] by means of an object is the *saṃpradāna* (recipient). 1.4.32.

"By means of the action functioning as the instrument. But how can one and the same thing simultaneously be both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*)? It is due to the difference in the actions: it is the object with respect to the act of giving, and the instrument with respect to the act [of approaching]. For by means of the cow being given, the student approaches, connects with, or desires to reach the teacher. The root *īh* preceded by *abhi* has the same meaning as *īpsati* (to desire). When "approached" (*abhipreta*) is said, it is understood as "desired" (*īpsita*). And it has been said:
"Because the agent does not reject it, that which is a subordinate part of the act of relinquishing is the desired object;
or, through instigation or consent, it attains the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.32–36)

Renunciation (*tyāga*) is giving (*dāna*). That which is desired to be obtained through an action—such as a cow or other things—which serves as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) or a remnant (*śeṣa*) of that renunciation, attains the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), either because it does not reject [the gift], or by the inference [of the giver's intent] such as "let it be so. For example: "He gives flowers to the gods," "He gives alms to a beggar," or "He gives a cow to his teacher. However, one who rejects [the gift] does not become a recipient; this is the meaning of the verse.

Regarding this, some say: under the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, there is a Vārttika which states, "There is a prescription for the compounding of a particle of motion (*gati*) with a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that possesses an acute accent (*udātta*). Examples include: *yo jāta eva prathamo mahasvān devo kratunā paryabhūṣat*; *yo yaḥ śambaram anvavindat*; *yasmān na ṛte kiṃ cana ījyate*; and *yo vai prayavayatām apy enaṃ pratipadyate*. These and others are the illustrations.

In all these cases, because of the prohibition of the designation *nipāta* by the rule "that which occurs after a compound is always [a *nipāta*]," the verbal form (*tiṅanta*) possesses an acute accent; consequently, even in the case of "tataś cāyam abhipraiti," when a compound is formed, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would result in the production of a case ending.

We say "no," because that [rule] has as its scope the domain of *chandas* (Vedic). If it were the case that whatever one intends through an action is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), then in the example "he leads the goats to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*), the village—which is connected with the goats, which are the objects (*karman*) of the act of leading—would incur the status of a recipient. It does not so incur. Why? Because it was stated that in the rule "by means of the object" (*karmaṇā*), the third case ending denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). And just as the cow is the instrument in the relation between the pupil and the teacher, the goat is not the instrument in the relation between the village and the goats.

But if [the term *īpsita*] has the same meaning as *sampradāna*, then there is even more clearly no application [of the rule]. For instance, when it is said, "whom he intends," the word "whom" (*yam*) indicates that which is the primary object (*śeṣin*), while the cow and so forth, indicated by the word "by means of" (*karmaṇā*), are understood as the subordinate instrument (*śeṣa*). This is just as in the rule "when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent," the agent is the primary object and the fruit of the action is the subordinate element; yet in the present case, such a relationship of subordinate and primary is not perceived.

Furthermore, since the root *nī* ("to lead") is enumerated among the two-object verbs (*dvikarmaka*) in the rule "of *nī*, *vah*, and *hṛ*," for this reason also, the designation will not apply to the village.

Now, he explains why this extensive technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is employed: "Because of the understanding of the designation according to its meaning" (*anvarthasaṃjñāvijñānāt*). Since the term *saṃpradāna* (recipient) is etymologically derived as that "to whom [something] is properly given" (*samyak pradīyate yasmai*), the meaning is that the object toward which one intends through the act of giving is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

Even so, why does [the rule] not apply in cases such as "he gives a cloth to the washerman" (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*) or "he gives his back to the one who strikes him" (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*)? Because it is not a *dāna* (giving). What, then, is *dāna*? *Dāna* is the relinquishing of one's own property with reference to something else, for the purpose that it shall not be taken back; for example: "he gives water to the tree," "flowers to the gods," "alms to the beggar," "a cow to the teacher," or "the teacher Khaṇḍika gives him a slap. [The phrase] "one should not give instruction to a Śūdra" is an example where the word *dāna* is used even though there is no relinquishing of ownership. A "slap" (*capeṭikā*) is a blow with the palm of the hand.

However, because the king is mentioned again, there is an absence of the act of giving; yet, through the force of the comparison, there is the application of the verb "to give. In that case, since he is a residual factor (*kārakaśeṣa*), the genitive case is used, as in the expression "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*).

What is the purpose of the word "karmaṇā" (by means of the object)? For in the sentence *upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti* ("He gives a cow to the teacher"), both the cow and the teacher are intended (*abhipreyamāṇatva*). Since the cow is intended by the act of giving—which serves as the instrument—and the teacher is intended by means of the cow, then, because the cow is mentioned later [in the rule], it would receive the designation of "object" (*karman*), and by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) would belong only to the teacher. This is not so; for even though both are intended, because the "object" is internal (*antaṅga*) to the action, the designation would apply only to the cow and such.

The designation *karmasaṃjñā* (the status of being an object), however, has scope elsewhere than in the case of the act of giving (*dadāti-karman*). Furthermore, in the section dealing with grammatical factors (*kāraka-prakaraṇa*), excellence (*prakarṣa*) is not taken into account, nor even the relationship between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*). If the mention of the word *yaṃ* were not made, the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient) would apply only to the intended person; for once there is a connection with the meaning of the word actually heard, the requirement is satisfied by that alone, making it impossible to supply an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

Even if there were an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), since the word "he" (*saḥ*) alone would be supplied [as the agent], then in the sense of "a cow is given by the student to the teacher," one would have to say "a cow is given to the student by the teacher. For, in the definition of the *karman* (object), the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that which is independent (*svatantra*); thus, even though the student lacks the status of agent, the designation of *karman* for the cow is indeed appropriate. And so, in the expression "he is deprived of his caravan" (*sārthāddhīyate*), the derivation of the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of the *karman*.

What is the purpose of including the prefix *abhi*? For [the root] *yami* means that by means of an action one goes toward, reaches, or connects with—this is the meaning. Is it not the same when one says *abhipraitīti* (he approaches)? If the prefix *abhi* were not employed, there would be an intended restriction to time; consequently, the rule would apply only to that which one is currently reaching (*saṃpratyeti*), but it would not apply to that which one has already reached (*ayām agāt*) or that which one will reach in the future (*yaṃ caiṣyati*). However, when the prefix *abhi* is employed, no such fault occurs.

The prefix *abhi* occurs in the sense of "facing toward" (*abhimukhya*), and the prefix *pra* occurs in the sense of "commencement of an action" (*ādikarma*). Consequently, by the force of employing these two prefixes, an action delimited by another time [the future] is not resorted to. Now, one might object: just as in cases such as "he plays with that" (*tena dīvyati*), there is no intention to express number or time, so too here, the non-intention to express time—just like number—is established. This is true; however, this very meaning, which is established by logic, is demonstrated through the employment of the two prefixes.
But when the meaning of *abhipraiti* is "he desires to obtain" (*īpsati*), then the inclusion of both *abhi* and *pra* must indeed be made.

The *Vārttika* states that "the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) must also be made. He explains this with the words beginning "by action" (*kriyayā*). Now, one might object: in common usage, they even metaphorically refer to an action as an "object," as in "What action will you perform? or "Which action? In such cases, the rule "him whom one intends by means of the object" (*karmaṇā yam abhipraiti*) would already suffice. Even so, it must still be stated [separately]; for between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), the application of a grammatical operation occurs only in the case of the artificial, because [the object] is obtained through seeing, desiring, and resolving.

Action (*kriyā*) is also an artificial activity (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*). For instance: a person who acts with foresight first perceives some object through his intellect, thinking, "This is such-and-such. Having seen it, he desires it, thinking, "O, may this be mine! Then he perceives the action that serves as its means, thinking, "This has that as its result. Thereupon he desires, "How might this be accomplished? and then, having determined the means for its realization, he resolves to perform it.

The status of being a *kāraka* (participant in an action) indeed occurs even with respect to an implied action, as in "Enter, [eat] the cake," where "eat" is understood. And the author of the Sūtras formulates it thus: "And [the dative case is used] for that which has another verb as its object (*upapada*), provided that [the latter] is not present. Even so, the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) must be made [in the rule], because it is the object of the root *dā* (to give). Regarding "he reviles" (*nigarhate*): the meaning is that he censures out of atheism (*nāstikya*). The roots *garha* and *galha* mean "censure" and are *anudātta* (unaccented). "For the sake of battle" (*yuddhāya*).

The meaning is that one forms a resolution regarding the matter of battle preceded by donning armor. The root *nah* is marked with the svarita accent. In the example *patye śete*, the meaning is "she lies down having approached her husband. If, then, the designation applies even to that which is intended through the action, it would follow that it would also apply in cases such as *kaṭaṃ karoti*; for by virtue of the rule, there would be an optionality between the designations of object (*karman*) and recipient (*saṃpradāna*). This is not universal; rather, it is restricted to specific domains according to observed usage.

"Regarding the statement 'the designation of instrument (karaṇa-saṃjñā) for the object of an action' and so forth: this pertains to the domain of Vedic metrics (*chandas*). Since all rules are optional in the Veda (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), usage occurs even according to what is [otherwise] prescribed.

However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase 'the object of the root *dā* (to give)' was not adopted, and there are many usages such as: *aryamṇe caruṃ nirvapet* ("one should offer a sacrificial pap to Aryaman"), *devebhyo brahmodanam apakṣat* ("he cooked the Brahman's rice for the gods"), *devebhyo havyaṃ vahantaḥ* ("carrying the oblation to the gods"), *chandāṃsi vai devebhyo havyam ūrdhāḥ* ("the meters indeed are the upward-moving oblation for the gods"), *yad aṅgam āśuṣe tvam* ("whatever limb you [gave] to the one who desires to eat"), and *śaṃ naḥ karat parvate* ("may he grant us peace on the mountain"), and so forth; according to that view, the mention of "action" (*kriyā-grahaṇa*) need not be made."

How is it that the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is desired in certain cases? In those instances, a distinction between the acts of "showing" (*saṃdarśana*) and so forth and the primary action is intended; consequently, the action itself—which is being reached by those [subordinate acts]—is established as a "pseudo-object" (*kṛtrimaṃ karma*), and thus the status of being a recipient for that which is intended by means of that [action] is established. However, where this is not desired, no distinction is intended; consequently, because the action is unified by being delimited by a single result such as boiled rice (*odana*), that which is reached by that action will simply have the status of an object—as in "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*) or "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).

In the case of verbs meaning "to go," however, both distinctions are intended to be expressed: difference and non-difference. Among these, when difference is intended to be expressed, one uses the construction *grāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the village"); thus, even the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* ("in the case of the object of a verb meaning 'to go'") need not be stated.
*Padamañjarī*:
For roots meaning "to please" (*ruc*), the one being pleased (*prīyamāṇa*) [is the recipient]. (Pāṇini 1.4.33)

"Having the same meaning as *ruc*": this is a statement regarding the actual meaning (*vastu*). As for the analysis (*vigraha*), however, it is "those whose meaning is the same as that of *ruc*. And these [roots] have the same meaning as the root *ruc*. In the case of *prīyamāṇa*: from the root *prīñ* in the sense of "satisfying," belonging to the *kryādika* class and being transitive, the suffix *laḥ* (the present passive participle) is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). The root belonging to the *daivādika* class, however, is marked with *ṅit* and is intransitive; its meaning is "being satisfied. "In the case of another agent": the meaning is that the one who is being pleased (*prīyamāṇa*)—who is the locus of the desire—is such that the agent of the action is other than him.

But how can one thing be the agent of a desire that has a different substratum? For is it not the case that the agent is that whose operation upon the substratum the verbal root expresses as primary? This is not the definition of an agent; rather, it is independence (*svātantrya*). And that [independence] is sometimes real and sometimes merely intended by the speaker (*vaivakṣika*). Thus, in this case, because the sweetmeat (*modaka*) produces a desire for its own object through its excellence of sweetness, having Devadatta as its substratum, it is designated as the "agent" therein.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that the root *laṣ* (to desire) would likewise [be used with an object], as in "Devadatta desires a sweetmeat" (*devadatto modakamabhilaṣyati*). Due to the diversity of expressive power (*abhidhānaśakti*), the desire expressed by *laṣ* has the locus (*āśraya*) as its agent, whereas that expressed by *ruc* has the object (*viṣaya*) as its agent. This restriction regarding the mode of expression is observed elsewhere as well; for example, in "the jar sees" (*ghaṭaḥ paśyati*), the knowledge expressed by the root *dṛś* has the locus as its agent, while in "the jar shines forth" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*), the shining forth expressed by the root *prakāś* has the object as its agent.

For it is the object itself—by virtue of its ease of perception, such as being situated in the midst of clear light—that is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) in the cognition residing in Devadatta; however, no excellence whatsoever is produced in the object by that cognition.

What is this so-called *prakāśa* (manifestation), which the followers of Bhaṭṭa call *prākaṭhya*? Regarding that, this statement is made because the genitive case would otherwise apply, as it is a "remainder" (*kārakaśeṣa*) of the *kāraka* relations. Others, however, maintain that [the rule] provides the designation of object (*karman*) to Devadatta when he is being pleased, as in "the sweetmeat pleases Devadatta," since [otherwise] he would have attained the status of an agent. Still others say: in the example "Devadatta likes the sweetmeat," this statement is made because the cause (*hetu*) relation would otherwise apply; for the sweetmeat is pleasing upon reaching Devadatta, not everyone, since the desires of living beings are diverse. This should be understood in the same way for the subsequent rules as well. And it has been said:

"In the case of being a cause (hetu), being designated as an object (karman), and also in the state of being a residual factor (śeṣa), the kāraka is called 'recipient' (saṃpradāna) by the technical rule [Pāṇini 1.4.33] in the case of verbs meaning 'to please' (rucy-artha) and others.

Thus, regarding the word *pathi*: the intention is that the designation of locus (adhikaraṇa-saṃjñā) would be sublated, just as the designations of cause and object are. Furthermore, precisely because of the inclusion of the term "one who is being pleased" (prīyamāṇa), there is no inclusion of verbs signifying mere shining, such as in the example *ādityo rocate* ("the sun shines").
In the *Padamañjarī*:
"The person being informed [is the object] of the roots *ślāgh* (to praise), *hnuṅ* (to hide/shame), *sthā* (to stand), and *śap* (to curse). (Pāṇini 1.4.34)

Regarding the term *jñīpsyamāna*: the root *jñā* is listed among the *ghaṭādi* group [of roots] in the sense of "killing, pleasing, and perceiving" (*māraṇatoṣaṇaniśāmaneṣu*). Therefore, in the sense of "perceiving" (*niśāmana*), after the causative suffix *ṇic* has been applied, the desiderative suffix *san* is added. Then, by the rule *āpjñapṛdhāmīt*, the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final vowel; by *atra lopo 'bhyāsasya*, the reduplication is elided; and finally, the suffix *laṭ* in the passive voice is replaced by *śānac*. Here, "perceiving" (*niśāmana*) refers to cognition in general, not exclusively visual perception, as he says: "intended to be made aware."

How, then, is it applied? The Teacher makes this known: "A request for instruction reaches fulfillment with masters. Therefore, the reading is *niśāneṣu*. [The root] *śo* (in the sense of "making thin") ends in *lyuṭ*, as in the example *saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ("the animal has been immolated"). The usage *jñīpsyamānaḥ* ("one who is being made to know," i.e., one who is desired to be informed) belongs to the *cur*-class derivative ending in *ṇic*, according to the rule *jñapa micca*.

Others, however, maintain that because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood from the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92) following its recurrence from *vā cittavirāge* (Pāṇini 1.4.35), and because this is understood as a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), there is no shortening in undesirable cases. They explain that the meaning of *ślāghamānas tāṃ devadattaṃ prati* is that he desires to make Devadatta himself aware of that praise. Here, *ślāghā* means "praise"; that is to say, he praises Devadatta directly so that Devadatta may be made aware of it.
Others, however, say the meaning is that he tells Devadatta that he himself is praiseworthy. Thus, it says in the Bhaṭṭikāvya: [text follows].

"The lord of the Rākṣasas went there praising himself before the wives of others"—this means he was speaking of his own praiseworthy qualities to the wives of others. Similarly, in the expression *devadattāya nihnuve* ("he conceals [something] from Devadatta"): since the root *hnuṅ* means "to remove" or "to conceal," the sense is that he wishes to make Devadatta aware of that very concealment directed toward him. Such is the meaning of the word *evam*. Concealment (*nihnuti*) is denial; the meaning is that he denies [the debt] to Devadatta, who is present right there, as if to a creditor or similar person.

Others, however, say that the meaning is "to make known some object of concealment to Devadatta," as in *devadattāya tiṣṭhate*. The meaning is that one makes manifest to Devadatta by means of standing, saying, "I am such-and-such. In *devadattāya śapate*, the meaning is that one makes something known through an oath. In *devadattaḥ ślāghate*, the meaning is that the designation of "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) alone is set aside by the rule concerning that which is intended to be made known (*jñīpsyamāna*), and not the designation of "agent" (*kartṛsaṃjñā*).

Thus, in the expression *ślāghate sabhāyāṃ gārgikayā*, the designations of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) are not set aside [by the designation of the recipient]. However, in some places, the reading is *ślāghate devadattam*. In that case, the intended meaning is as follows: since the one to whom something is related is the "one being informed" (*jñīpsyamāna*), it is logical that the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) applies to the one being related to. But for those who maintain that the "one being informed" is the very person being related to, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs after the one to whom it is related—thus: *devadattāya ślāghate yajñadatto viṣṇumitrasya* ("Yajñadatta praises Devadatta in relation to Viṣṇumitra").
In the *Padamañjarī*, [it is stated that] for the root *dhṛ* (to owe), the creditor is the agent. 1.4.35.

Regarding the phrase *uttamamṛṇaṃ yasya* ("for whom there is a superior debt"): *uttama* means "most excellent. From the root *ucch*, which has the sense of "excellent," the suffix *tamaP* is applied; however, because it denotes an excellence of substance (*dravyaprakarṣa*), the *ām* augment does not occur. The word *ṛṇa* is formed with the suffix *kta* from the root *ṛ*. In the rule *ṛṇam ādhamarṇye*, the mention of *ādhamarṇya* (the state of being a debtor) is intended as an illustration for the exchange of goods to be paid at a later time; thus, the substitution of *na* for *ra* occurs even in the case of *uttamarṇa* (creditor).

In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, regarding the placement of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) at the beginning, the word *daṇḍa* appears at the end because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *sukha* (as per the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ paravacanam*), or else due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*). [The term] "he owes a hundred" (*śataṃ dhārayati*): from the root *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied in the sense that he employs a hundred which, being maintained—that is, remaining in its own form and not deviating from its nature—is owed. Regarding the word "village" (*grāma*): [one might object] that here, by virtue of its higher status, it will indeed receive the designation of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*);
[if so,] then the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) would also receive the designation of "cause" (*hetu*).
In the *Padamañjarī*, [it is stated]:
"The desired object [of the action] in the case of the root *spṛh* (to desire) [is called the *saṃpradāna* kāraka]. (Pāṇini 1.4.36).

It is stated that the root *spṛ* is listed among the roots ending in *-a*. Therefore, in the form *spṛhayati*, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur because the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*). The term *īpsita* (desired) is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188). This technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to anything merely desired. However, when excellence (*prakarṣa*) is intended to be expressed, the designation of *karman* (object) takes precedence, and thus we have *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati* (he desires flowers). But when that which is desired or most desired is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The term *saṃpradāna* applies] to the object toward whom there is anger in the case of verbs meaning "to be angry," "to hate," "to envy," or "to be resentful. (Pāṇini 1.4.37)

Regarding the phrase "in virtues" (*guṇeṣu*): this refers to purity, proper conduct, and so forth. "Manifestation of faults" (*doṣāviṣkaraṇam*) means the attribution (*adhyāsa*) of defects such as hypocrisy (*dambha*). In that context, since the rule *krudhadruhor akarmakayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.37) prescribes the genitive case for the remaining kārakas, the genitive would apply to the actor (*naṭasya*), as in the expression *naṭasya śṛṇoti*. However, because the other two verbs [of the group] are transitive, the accusative case would otherwise apply. This statement [is made] to prevent that.

And although the nature of being a mental defect is common to anger and the rest, these are nevertheless mentioned separately with a view toward their internal subdivisions, in order to exclude other defects of this class such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, and not because they are intended to mean "mental defects" in general. Therefore, in the expression "he hates us," [the suffix does] not [occur], for its meaning is "disapproval. Likewise, it is used even with regard to insentient things—as in "he hates the medicine."

But how can all [the emotions] beginning with anger be qualified by a single instance of anger? To this he says: "First, as for anger... In the expression "he is jealous of his wife," it is merely the wife being seen by others that is intended, not anger directed toward her.
In the *Padamañjarī*:
"The object of the roots *krudh* (to be angry) and *druh* (to bear malice), when preceded by a preposition, is the *karman* (direct object). (Pāṇini 1.4.38)

Regarding the phrase "of those two connected with a prefix" (*upasargeṇa saṃbaddhayoḥ*): since "prefixes" (*upasarga*) are so called because they "approach" (*upa-sṛjanti*) [the verb] when joined with an action—derived from the root *sṛj* with the suffix *ac* (in the sense of the present participle), and the substitution of *k* for *s* by virtue of belonging to the *nyaṅkvādi* group—the meaning of "of those two preceded by a prefix" (*tenopasṛṣṭayoḥ*) becomes "of those two connected with a prefix. Alternatively, it is a term well-known within its own school (*svanikāya*).
The inquiry concerning the lotus-eye of Rādhā [is found] in the Padamañjarī, 1.4.39.

The word *yasya* (of whom) is a genitive used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "that which is asked about in its various forms. The phrase *yatsambandhi* and so forth means "the inquiry concerning the auspicious or inauspicious [fate] related to that person. Regarding the example *devadattāya rādhnoti*: this belongs to the *divādi* class because of the rule *rādho 'karmakādvṛddhāveva* ("after the root *rādh*, when intransitive, the affix *śyan* occurs only in the sense of increase"). Here, the mention of "increase" (*vṛddhau*) is merely illustrative; since the statement specifies "when intransitive," there is no deviation from the intransitive state in the sense of increase. The particle *eva* (only), however, is displaced in order: the affix *śyan* occurs after *rādh* only when it is intransitive, just as in the case of "increase."

Therefore, even though the particle *eva* is present, the occurrence of the term "deliberation" (*paryālocana*) is not contradictory. In that context, because it is subsumed under the meaning of the verbal root, the intransitivity of the verb *rādh* (to succeed) is not contradictory, as in the case of *jīvati* (he lives) and similar forms. The word *nimitta* means "the cause," and the word *nimitta* should be understood as referring to things such as *uñcha* (gleaning) or the seasons such as spring (*vasanta*). The mention of the word *yasya* (of whom/for whom) would be redundant; for if [the rule] were simply "with reference to whom," then what exactly would remain unsatisfied in the syntactical connection "with reference to whom there is an inquiry"? Nothing at all.
Patañjali’s *Padamañjarī*:
"With the prefixes *prati* and *āṅ*, the agent of the preceding action [is the object] of the verb *śru* (to hear). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.40)

He states that because of the dual-number indication, there is a connection with each prefix individually—namely, "of that preceded by *āṅ* and of that preceded by *prati*. To the question, "What then is the prior operation here? he replies with the words "preceded by *prati* and *āṅ*" and so forth, ending with "of that which is employed by another. This means "of that which has been requested," such as "Give this to me. [The phrase] "of the prior action" refers to this.

In the Sūtra, however, the designation "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) is used with the intention of expressing the nature of an action; they say that this statement is made to prevent the usage *devadattena pratiśrāvayati* (he causes Devadatta to hear back), which would otherwise occur when the technical term "cause" (*hetu*) is applicable. And when there is a different intention, the form *devadatto gāṃ pratiśrāvayati* (Devadatta causes the cow to hear back) indeed occurs.
And [the term *anupratigṛṇat*] is also [a substitute for the agent of the action] in the case of *padamañjarī*. (Pāṇini 1.4.41)

Because of its association with what precedes it, he states that here too the prefix is connected to each [verb] individually—namely, *anu-* and *prati-*. To the question, "What then is the preceding action here? he replies: "The Hotṛ first," and so forth. "The other" refers to the Adhvaryu. How, then, is it known that the root *gṛ* (to sing/recite), preceded by *anu-* and *prati-*, functions in the sense of encouraging the reciter? He says: "*Anugaraḥ* (the response), *pratigaraḥ* (the counter-response)," and so forth. That word by which one is encouraged (*anugīryate*) or incited is the *anugara*. Likewise for the *pratigara*; it is a word such as "Othāmo daiva," for by it one is responded to (*pratigīryate*).
*Padamañjarī*:
"The most effective instrument is the *karaṇa*. (Pāṇini 1.4.42)

The word *sādhaka* is derived either from the root *ṣidhū* in the sense of "accomplishment" with the causal suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the substitution of *ā* according to the rule "the root *sidh* takes *ā* when not referring to the next world," or from the root *rādha/sādha* in the sense of "perfect accomplishment" with the causal suffix. Its meaning is essentially action. The agent to be employed is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) for that action, which consists of the object to be accomplished or the state of being accomplished.

[Objection: Surely the accomplishment of an action depends upon the totality [of factors]; indeed, an action is not produced even when any one among the agent and the other factors is absent. Therefore, why should there be a connection with excellence for one among the causal factors (*kāraka*s)? [Reply: It is said: An operation (*vyāpāra*) consists in the penetration into the substance to be cut; in the cooking of wood and such things, it consists in the penetration of the hot touch produced by burning. Immediately after that, the accomplishment of the action occurs. Such penetration into other causal factors, or the production of the action immediately following their operation, does not exist. Therefore: "The complete accomplishment of an action occurs immediately after the operation of which..."
When that which is intended to be expressed therein is the instrument, then it is remembered as such.

By the phrase "is intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣyate*), he shows this: depending on place, time, state, and so forth, when the operation of something—due to its excellence in utility toward an action—is approaching [the speaker's mind] as that which is intended to be expressed, then it attains the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*). For example, although a cooking pot is well known as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), when there is an intention to express its excellence due to having very thin walls, it attains the status of an instrument, as in: "it is cooked by means of the pot" (*sthālyā pacyate*). And it has been said:
"In reality, that [status] cannot be designated, for a thing is not fixed [in one category alone];
since we observe such an intention as 'it is cooked by means of the pot.'"* *The verse is cited from Bhartṛhari’s Vākyapadīya (Kāṇḍa 3, Vṛtti on Kārikā 14.5).*

Nor does it follow that the agent (*kartṛ*) would likewise be intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because they belong to different categories. For the agent is indeed the one who employs all the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); he does not compete with one who possesses only a hundred coins against one who possesses a *niṣka*! How then, in the expression "he travels by horse, by lamp, and by chariot," can there be the status of instrument for many [factors], given that even among those, only that which provides the most immediate assistance is logically the instrument? It is said in reply: the excellence of the instrument is relative to other causal factors (*kāraka*), not within its own class.

Therefore, since it assists by coming together (*saṃnipatyopakārakatva*) in the accomplishment of the action of all [kārakas], its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established. [Question: Why is the mention of the suffix *tamap* (in the word *sādhakatama*) made? [Answer: Since the status of being an instrument (*sādhakatva*) is already established by the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *kārakas*, the repeated mention of "the achiever" (*sādhaka*) must be for the sake of indicating excellence (*prakarṣa*). [Example: "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*). If the mention of *tamap* were not made, then an "abode" (*ādhāra*) would be defined only where the nature of the abode is pervaded by that which is contained within it (*ādheya*). Consequently, it would apply only in cases such as "oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*) or "clarified butter in milk" (*payasi sarpiḥ*), but it would not apply here in the case of "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā."

The inclusion of the suffix *tamap*, however, indicates that in this section, excellence (*prakarṣa*) understood through contextual implication is not required; therefore, it applies here as well. When the property of the location—the state of being a substratum—is figuratively attributed to the stream with respect to the sound, then such is the purpose of including *tamap*. But when the word *gaṅgā* refers to the bank, then there is no need for it, because since pervasion by the contained [the sound] is possible, the status of being a substratum is primary (not figurative).
In the case of the verb *div*, the word *padamañjarī* [is used], and it is also the object. 1.4.43.

One might object: "In the case of *akṣān dīvyati* ('he plays with dice'), the meaning is 'he causes them to fall,' and thus their status as an object (*karman*) is established; whereas in *akṣair dīvyati*, the meaning is 'he plays,' and thus their status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is established. What is the purpose of this [rule]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the preceding [rule], there would have been the designation of instrument (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*)."

In the very same intended sense as "he plays with dice" (*akṣaiḥ krīḍati*), the form "he gambles with dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*) is desired; here, however, only the designation *karaṇa* (instrument) would apply. Furthermore, in the sense of "he causes the dice to fall," the form "he gambles with dice" (*akṣair dīvyati*) is not desired. Therefore, since the designation *karaṇa* would have applied only to that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), this rule is commenced. Now, what is the purpose of the particle *ca*? [The purpose is] so that the designation *karaṇa* may also apply; but this is not a necessary purpose.

"I shall apply the mention of *anyatarasyām* (the option) that is to be stated later right here," he says [in response], "by means of the word *ca* (and), [it is understood] 'and it is also designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*)'. The intention is that both designations should apply simultaneously. However, if the mention of *anyatarasyām* were used, there would be an alternation—when it is the object (*karman*), it is not then the instrument; when it is the instrument, it is not then the object. But by the word *ca*, both designations occur at one and the same time; this is the meaning.

The purpose of [stating] simultaneity is as follows: in the case of *manasā dīvyati* ("he plays with the mind"), because the mind is the object (*karman*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied; yet, because it is also the instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case ending is used. By the rule *manasaḥ saṃjñāyām*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending, resulting in *manasādevaḥ*. In this instance, however, in the sentence *akṣair devayate devadatto yajñadattena*, even though the third case is employed in *akṣaiḥ*, because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the agent *yajñadatta* does not receive the designation "object" (*karman*) in its state without the causative suffix (*aṇ-antāvasthā*) according to the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārtha...*. Furthermore, by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt*, the parasmaipada (active voice) ending is used.

If, then, there is coexistence (*samāveśa*), the third case ending would apply by virtue of its higher status in the rule "he plays with the dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*). However, this fault does not arise in the case of alternation (*paryāya*), because when the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) applies, the designation of instrument (*karaṇasaṃjñā*) is absent. In the case of coexistence, however, there is scope for the designation of instrument—as in *videvanā akṣāḥ* ("the dice are the means of playing"), where the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule "and after [roots ending in] *kṛ*, *han*, and *grah*, when the sense is that of instrument or location. There is also scope for the designation of object—as in *dīvyante bhavatākṣāḥ* ("the dice are being played by you"), where the passive voice (*yag*) and middle endings (*ātmanepada*) are applied according to the rule "when the sense is the state of being (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*)."

In the case of *akṣān*, where there would otherwise be the application of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "fear" (*bhaya*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would occur by virtue of its higher status [in the order of rules]. This is not a fault; for technical designations and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) are operative at the time the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is to take place. Consequently, when this [designation] presents itself in the rule "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), it finds no scope [to apply], and thus the second case ending will indeed occur.

In that case, there would be this fault regarding the coalescence [of functions]: in the expression *dīvyante 'kṣāḥ* ("the dice play"), even though the object (*karman*) is expressed, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not expressed, and thus the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would occur. Or, in the expression *devanā akṣāḥ* ("dice for playing"), even though the instrument is expressed by the suffix *lyuṭ*, the object is not expressed, and thus the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would occur? This is not a fault; for a single functional capacity (*kārakaśakti*) is associated with two designations. Consequently, when one functional capacity is expressed, another functional capacity is also necessarily expressed, because the capacity is one and the same.
In the case of hiring, the recipient (saṃpradāna) is optionally [designated as such] according to Pāṇini 1.4.44.
