In the word *parikrayaṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by relying solely on the *repha* (the letter *r*) residing within the verbal root, according to the rule *raṣābhyām* [Pāṇini 8.4.1], because that [the *repha*] occurs first; this is just as in the case of *krayaṇa* when there is no prefix (*upasarga*). It does not occur by relying on the *repha* situated in the prefix according to the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.29], because that [the prefix] occurs later and is therefore "external" (*bahiraṅga*). Regarding the phrase "by means of wages, etc.": *vetana* means hire; this clarifies that the duration is indeed limited. The expression "it is not an absolute purchase" indicates that the prefix *pari-* signifies proximity.
Purchase indeed means absolute appropriation; however, [the term] "near" (pari) signifies that for a limited time it is merely in its vicinity.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The locus (*ādhāra*) is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). (Pāṇini 1.4.45)

An *ādhāra* (locus) is so called because actions (*kriyā*) are supported (*ādhriyante*) within it; thus, by the rule *adhyāyanyāyodyāva*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Since the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) depends upon action, the word "action" (*kriyā*) is included [in the definition]. If the designation *adhikaraṇa* were to apply to the locus of action alone, it would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), for action resides either in the agent or in the object. What, then, would be the scope for the designation *kartṛ*? It would be for those cases where the action resides in the object, such as: "Devadatta cooks the rice."

But surely, even here, since the agent (*kartṛ*) is the locus of actions such as placing [the pot] on the fire, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would occur? Well then, this is the scope: it was stated that "the sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta" (*devadattāya rocate modakaḥ*); here, the sweetmeat is the agent of the desire residing in Devadatta. Even so, if the designation of agent (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*) has no scope, then there would still be an alternation [of designations]. Now, what is the scope for the designation of object (*karma-saṃjñā*)? It is those cases where the action resides in the agent, such as "he sees the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*).

Therefore, since there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the designation *adhikaraṇa* applying to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) themselves, he says: "Of the agent and the object," and so forth. But how can the secondary (*gauṇa*) locus of action be understood as being intended, when the primary locus of action—which is the substratum of the action itself—is already possible [as the referent], given the intervention of the agent and object which are themselves the substrata of the action? This has been made known by the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tamap-* in the rule for the designation *karaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.4.42), namely that the designation *karaṇa* applies to the locus of action in any way whatsoever. Why, then, should it not apply to the primary locus as well? "He sits" (*āste*) is an example of an action residing in the agent; "he cooks" (*pacati*) is an example of an action residing in the object.

And that substratum (adhikaraṇa) is of three kinds: contactual (aupaśleṣika), objective (vaiṣayika), and pervasive (abhivyāpaka); as in "he sits on a mat," "he dwells with the teacher," and "there is oil in sesame seeds."
The object of the roots √śī (to lie down), √sthā (to stand), and √ās (to sit) is called the locus (adhikaraṇa). 1.4.46.
And [the suffix *kha*] is applied after the root *abhiniviś* to form *padamañjarī*. 1.4.47.

Since the shorter [member] of a compound generally precedes, he states that "abhiniparvasya" is an imitation of the whole compound "abhinip-", saying: "of that which has 'abhi' as its prefix and 'ni' as its prefix. Otherwise, he would have said, "of that which has 'abhi' as its prefix and of that which has 'ni' as its prefix."
*Padamañjarī*:
[The prepositions] *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, and *āṅ* [are compounded with the root] *vas*. (Pāṇini 2.2.19)

Regarding the phrase *aśyarthasya*: the word *artha* here signifies "cessation" (*nivṛtti*). The two genitive cases are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*); the meaning is "of that which expresses the sense of *aś* (to eat). That is to say, it refers to that which denotes the cessation of eating. Alternatively—*śy-artha* means the sense of the root *śī* (to lie down/rest); *na śy-arthaḥ* means "not having the sense of *śī*," i.e., not having the sense of staying. For the root *śī* also functions in the sense of "staying"—as in the example *jalāśayaḥ* ("a reservoir of water"). Therefore, in the sense of "he stays in the village," the expression *grāmam upavasati* ("he observes a fast in the village") occurs.

If it means "not being in a place," then one might ask: must the prohibition [of the locative case] be stated in the rule *grāma upavasati* ("he fasts in the village")? It need not be stated. Why? Because here, the village is not the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the verb *vas-* preceded by the prefix *upa*; rather, it is the locus of the verb without a prefix—meaning, "dwelling in the village, he fasts for three nights. What is meant is this: when Devadatta is already determined to be staying in a specific location, this expression *grāma upavasati* is employed to specify the duration of his abstention from food; in that case, because it is more immediate, the village's status as a locus is understood in relation to the action of dwelling (*vasikriyā*) which is implied.

Since the act of fasting (upavāsana) by its very nature requires time, its internal connection is with time alone; whereas its connection with a village or similar location is external. Thus, even if not explicitly enjoined, the ritual action consisting of three nights and so forth comes to be performed.
That which the agent most desires to reach is the *karman* (object). 1.4.49.

Regarding the phrase "by the action of the agent" (*kartuḥ kriyayā*) and so forth: the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "that which is most desired to be attained by the agent. As for the word "agent" (*kartuḥ*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.67), since there is a requirement for something desired to be attained (*īpsita*). The term "desired" (*īpsita*) is formed with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.188).

The instrumental case in *kriyayā* (by means of an action) denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). For the so-called "agent" (*kartṛ*) is indeed one who performs an action; when it is said that "that which is most desired by the agent," it is understood that he becomes an agent through being permeated by that [action], and thus [the desire] is by means of that which has become the instrument. The meaning is: "that which is sought to be obtained by the agent through his own action. This word *īpsita* is established in common usage (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "intended" (*abhipreta*), as in "the intended is what is desired"; it is also a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*), formed from the root *āplṛ* with the suffix *san* in the sense of "to pervade/obtain" (*āptau*), according to the rule *āpjñapṛdhāmīt*, meaning "that which is desired to be obtained is *īpsitam*. It is shown here that the verbal sense is what is intended—namely, "that which is most desired to be obtained."

Regarding the word *karmaṇaḥ*: [it refers to] the horse (*aśva*). For he desires to obtain the beans through the act of eating. If this is so, then just as—despite the horse being in reality the agent (*kartṛ*) of the act of eating—it is not designated by the technical term "object" (*karman*) for the beans because, at present, it is intended to be the object with respect to the act of binding and thus lacks the status of an agent; likewise, in the case of *sārthād dhīyate* ("he is deserted by the caravan"), although the caravan is in reality the agent of the abandonment (since one who is being deserted is abandoned by the caravan), it is currently intended to be in the form of an "ablative" (*apādāna*) and thus lacks the status of an agent.
Consequently, the passive suffix *yak* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would not occur in the sense of the "object."

On this point, they say: here, the *yaṅ* and *ātmanepada* endings occur in the sense of the agent being also the object (*karmakartṛ*). How so? This root *jahāti* functions in the sense of "departing": "The caravan leaves Devadatta" means it causes him to depart. And this very departure of the caravan consists in performing actions conducive to Devadatta's departure, such as by afflicting him with hunger and the like. But when he departs by himself due to hunger and so forth, then there is the status of the agent being the object; in that case, this is the grammatical usage.

And thus, the phrase "is deprived" means that the essential meaning departs by itself; then, in response to the expectation of "from what is one deprived?", there is a connection with the essential meaning.

Why is the mention of *tamap* (the superlative suffix) used? [The author] considers that the example is established because even that which is "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) can possess the quality of being "desired" (*īpsita*). For instance, in the sentence *payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats rice with milk"), the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa-saṃjñā*) finds its scope in cases such as *dātreṇa lunāti* ("he cuts with a sickle"), for the sickle is not itself the object of the desire to cut. Nor does the rule *tathā yuktam* ("that which is connected in the same way") apply here, because that rule includes things that are detested, indifferent, or merely reached [not desired]. Even though milk is an excellent auxiliary to the act of eating, there is an absence of the intensity of desire (*īpsā-prakarṣa*) regarding it.

In that case, however, where milk itself is the most desired object, [the designation of the accusative] would apply; for example, someone says to another, "Eat what is ready," and he replies, "We have already eaten enough. The other says, "There will be milk," and another, hurrying, says, "One should indeed eat with milk. Here, by distinguishing between what is obtained and what is not yet obtained, it is milk alone that is the most desired object, and not the rice; yet even here, the rice alone is the most desired object, while milk possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) because it serves as a seasoning (*saṃskāraka*).

However, his interest is not in the quality alone; rather, it is in the rice-gruel prepared with that [quality]. For he is not satisfied merely by drinking the milk. If the mention of the suffix *tamap* were made, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as "he eats rice-gruel with milk" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), but it would not apply in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*pacatyodanam*), because [in the latter] it is not the most desired object. In the absence of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), only that which is of the same class as the object becomes the counter-correlative.

And here, no other *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is intended as the desired object (*īpsita*), because milk is already the object being sought (*īpsyamāna*) and thus its status as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitā*) is appropriate. This is not a fault; for even here, excellence is relative to the action. For at the outset, the agent desires the action for the sake of the result; therefore, because it is desired for the sake of the result, the action itself is "desired" (*īpsita*). However, the result, being desired in its own nature, is the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*). Furthermore, the action also possesses the status of an object (*karman*) by competing with other specific [factors] such as perception and so forth.

In that case, it would not apply where there is an absence of a result. And where is there an absence of a result? In the case of something to be modified (*vikārya*), as in "he reduces the wood to ashes"; for the pieces of wood are not themselves the form of the result. Let it be granted that they are not results in their own essential nature; but are they not results in the form of ashes? Then it would not apply to something to be attained (*prāpya*)—as in "he sees the sun" or "he hears the Himalayas"—for in these cases no excellence whatsoever is produced by the action.

In this case as well, an excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced—namely, what is called "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*). For that which someone sees or hears becomes manifest to him; however, it is said that there is no distinction with respect to persons other than the perceiver. Alternatively, by the inclusion of the suffix *-tama*, only that wherein desire is diminished is excluded. Consequently, in cases such as *paśyati* ("he sees"), since the sun and so forth do not exist as counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*), there is an absence of diminution, and thus [the rule] will apply. And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this is: *lalāṭakukkuṭyau paśyati* ("he sees the forehead and the hen").

The phrase "the word *karman* (object) being understood" [is taken] from the rule *adhi-śīṅ-sthāsām*. The phrase "for the purpose of excluding the locus (*ādhāra*)" means that the previous mention of *karman* was connected with the locus; therefore, if it were to recur here, the locus would also recur—this is the intended meaning. He states the fault if the locus were to recur: "For [the designation of object] would apply only to the locus. To the question "Where [would this be the case]? he says: "The house," and so forth. He then states where it would not apply: "He cooks rice," and so forth.

And this most desired object (*īpsitatama*) is threefold: that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*). Likewise, that which is associated with it is also twofold: the hateful (*dveṣya*) and the other. There is another [kind] by the rule "and that which is not mentioned" (*akathitaṃ ca*); and yet another when there is the application of a different technical designation, such as "the object of the root *div*" (*divaḥ karma ca*), and so forth. Thus, the object is of seven types. And it has been said: "It is considered threefold—as that which is produced, that which is modified, and that which is reached; and that most desired object is fourfold, while the others are conceived [as distinct]."
"That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent,
that which is not designated by other names, and that which has another as its antecedent.
Likewise—
That which is non-existent [before] comes into being, or that which already exists is manifested by birth;
such is the "nirvartya" (that which is produced), while the "vikārya" (that which is modified) is established as two-fold.
Some things, such as wood and the like, arise from the destruction of their original nature, like ashes;
others arise through the production of a different quality, like the transformation of gold and the like.
"Where the accomplishment of things characterized by specific actions is not perceived through either perception or inference, that is called 'attainable' (prāpya).

In this context, "to be produced" (*nirvartya*)—as in "he makes a jar"—refers to manifestation, whether intended as an individual instance or as a general class of birth. Now, one might object: "If it is a jar, it need not be made; if it is to be made, it is not yet a jar. Thus, the expression "he makes a jar" would be logically untenable. This is not a fault. The meaning here is: he produces such an entity that, once completed, receives the designation "jar. The same applies to expressions such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).

The *vikārya* (object undergoing transformation) is exemplified by "he turns wood into ash" or "he makes gold into an earring. The *prāpya* (object to be reached) is exemplified by "he sees the sun. For in these cases, no excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the action is perceived either through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), as is the case with the *nirvartya* (object to be produced) and *vikārya* (object undergoing transformation), such as in the examples: "he creates a rope," "he burns wood," or "he angers Devadatta."

The state of being an *kāraka* (participant in an action) for the object to be reached (*prāpya*), however, arises through its approach to manifestation (*ābhāsopagama*) and so forth. For the sun indeed approaches manifestation: because it is seen, because it undergoes revelation, because it is perceived as manifest, and because it endures being seen—that is, because it is possible to see it—this very [process] is "approach to manifestation," "manifestation," and "endurance. These are the specific qualities of the object being reached that are intended when the accomplishment of the action is to be expressed.
And likewise, that which is not desired [by the agent] is also [treated as an object], provided it is connected with the action. (1.4.50)

The word *tathā* is a separate term and is not compounded, because there is no [grammatical] indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) for such a compound. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), since particles have multiple meanings; and he says "by that very [means]" (*tenaiva*) to show that it should be understood as following immediately after *tathā*. Thus, everything other than what is desired is "undesired" (*anīpsita*).

Just as things that are the opposites of the subsequent word-meanings—such as *adharma* (non-dharma) or *anṛta* (untruth)—are expressed by means of their negation, so here, by the word *anīpsita* (not desired), it is not merely that which is hateful (*dveṣya*) that is expressed as the opposite of the "desired" (*īpsita*). What then? It refers to everything other than what is desired, just as in the expression "horse-clod" (*aśva-loṣṭa*); this is the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*). As for the phrase "he eats poison": the sense is that poison is never the most desired thing for anyone.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for a man who is afflicted on all sides by disease and the like, and considers death itself to be better, poison is indeed most desired? Even for one who proceeds toward poison under the delusion that it is molasses or the like, that [poison] is indeed most desired; for it is only the cognition of the desired molasses and so forth that prompts the action there. Therefore, since this is already established by the previous [example], why is another example introduced? [The author replies: "As in the case of 'going to the village'."

In this case, the roots of the trees are not the most desired object because they were not previously intended; for one's approach to them is merely incidental. Nor does the fact that the expression "while going as far as the village" (*yāvad grāmaṃ gacchan*) is not employed here mean that the state of being incidental is not perceived; this is already established by the preceding [argument]. For example, in the sentence "the river erodes its bank" (*nadī kūlaṃ kaṣati*), there is an absence of desire because the bank is insentient; yet, although this is understood through its connection with another word, it does not prevent the designation of "object" (*karman*) due to its being extrinsic (*bahir-aṅga*). Let this be so from the perspective of the cognizer.

Regarding the manner of justification: since one who employs [the term] already knows beforehand the absence of an excellence of desire (*īpsā-prakarṣa*), how could it have been employed? Thus, the [previous] argument remains unestablished. And so, even in the case of "the riverbank" (*nadī-kūlam*), the designation of object (*karman*) occurs by this very [rule]. Likewise, where the intention (*tātparya*) lies in the action itself and not in the result—though the accomplishment of the result is inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*)—there too it occurs by this very [rule].

Now, why has it not been stated that "action" (karman) is that which is connected with the fruit of action? If [the definition] were simply "that which is most desired," then this quality of being connected with the fruit of action would follow everywhere—even in the case of that which is detested or neutral—and thus even the agent (*kartṛ*) would possess the status of an object (*karmatva*), since the fruit of action, namely conjunction (*saṃyoga*), exists there as well. Alternatively, if the definition is "that which is connected with the fruit of an action inherent in another"? Even so, [the definition] would fail to apply in the case of [the injunction] "the Self is to be known" (*ātmā jñātavyaḥ*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is held to be self-luminous, would also incur the status of an object.

In the cognition "I know the jar," indeed only a triad appears: the jar, the cognition, and the self. Among these, cognition is an action; its fruit is practical activity (*vyavahāra*) in the form of the employment of words and so forth. Just as the jar, being connected with that [activity], possesses the status of an object (*karman*), so too would the cognition itself possess it. For cognition is an action that serves as the substratum for the fruit consisting of practical activity; and since it inheres in the Self, which is distinct from the very nature of that cognition, enough has been said on this point.

In the case of "towards thieves" (*corān*) as well, it is already established by the preceding [rule] that one who desires his master, or one who is being deceived by someone in the form of a friend or the like, approaches the thieves.
And [the word] *akathina* [is formed with the suffix *aṇ*], according to *Padamañjarī* 1.4.51.

This word *akathita* is established in the sense of "not being the primary factor" (*apradhāna*), as for example: "I am *akathita* in this village," which is understood to mean "I am not the primary factor. Furthermore, there is a verbal noun (*kriyāśabda*) synonymous with "unmentioned" (*akīrtita*). The root *kath* is listed in the *curādigaṇa* as ending in a long vowel (*adanta*), meaning "to compose a discourse. If the former [meaning] were intended here, then in the sentence "He milks milk into a bronze vessel with his hand" (*pāṇinā kāṃsapātryāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the designation would apply to both the hand and the bronze vessel as well.

However, the scope for terms such as *pacati* (he cooks) belongs to the designations of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*), for there is no application of this [designation] there; because of the specific enumeration in the rule "duhi-yāci" (Pāṇini 1.4.51), the second [interpretation] is taken. Thus he says: "By what is it unspoken?"—namely, by the specific designations such as "apādāna" (ablative) and so forth. What is the authority for this? He says: "By what"—this is a reference to the instrument (*karaṇa*). For in the case of conventional words (*rūḍhi-śabda*), an action is employed merely for the sake of etymological derivation.

In that case, an instrument or other such factor is not connected; for in the expression "a cow (go) because it goes (gacchati)," there is neither a question such as "by what? nor an answer such as "by a chariot" (rathena). Here, because the term *kārake* ("in the presence of a kāraka") is understood from the previous rule, the designation [of *akathita*] must apply only when there is indeed the status of being a *kāraka*; thus, by implication, it is stated [in the commentary] as "by means of specific verbal descriptions."

The enumeration is "dharma and so forth. Its primacy [is established] because all activity is for its sake. "It is connected" (sambadhyate) is an explanation of the meaning of the root *ṣac*; it is *svarita*-accented. However, some read this root along with those that take the *parasmaipada* ending as "ṣaca samavāye," and "rapa lapa vyaktāyāṃ vāci" (to speak clearly).

Regarding this, they say: because the root *sac* (in *ṣacasevane*) is anudātta and possesses multiple meanings, its application here is in the sense of "conjunction" (*samavāya*). Furthermore, since the root *sac* occurs in the sense of the agent's activity (*kartṛvyāpāra*) within the operation of the object (*karmavyāpāre*), the explanation of the meaning of the subject term (*kartṛpada*) by means of the object term (*karmapada*) is not untenable; just as in the case of *rādhyaty odanaḥ*, which means *pacyate*. The word *uktam* is an explanation of *ācaritam*. By the phrase "by the author of the Sūtras," he shows that although the word *kavi* generally denotes any intelligent person, it is used here for the author of the Sūtras due to the context.

"One milks the cow for milk. Now, one might object: here the meaning is that "the cow gives up its milk" (*gauḥ payastyajati*), and "the milker causes the cow to give up its milk" (*dogdhā gavā payastyājayati*). In that case, since the cow is being reached (*āpyamānatva*) through the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), its designation as the *karman* (object) is established. And it should not be argued: "If [the *karman* designation] applies to that which is reached through the operation of an instigator, then by the restriction in the subsequent rule—'only in the case of roots meaning motion (*gatyartha*) and so forth'—it would not apply here, just as in the example: 'he employs Devadatta who is cooking,' expressed as *pācayati devadattena*. This is not correct, because that restriction applies only to causative forms (*ṇyanta*) where the suffix is added after the root has already been modified; however, this [present case] is a primary form (*prakṛtyanta*). This objection does not hold.

Just as in the case of causative (*ṇyanta*) verbal roots, the instigation of an action characterized by another action is perceived—as in "he causes to go" (*gamayati*)—it is not so here, because even non-active entities such as cows and the like are employed in actions such as milking or leading. For instance, a cow that is not itself being milked is said to be "milked," and loads that are not moving are "carried on the head. Therefore, since in the expression "he milks" (*dogdhi*) only a single action is heard, there is no dual status as object (*karman*) for the cow and the milk based on their difference.

But when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is present, there are two distinct meanings—one belonging to the base (*prakṛti*) and one to the suffix (*pratyaya*)—and thus the distinction between the objects is logically established.

[The example] is: *gamayati grāmaṃ devadattam* ("He causes Devadatta to go to the village"). But when the root *duh-* has the meaning of "flowing"—as in *kṣarati goḥ kṣīram* ("The cow's milk flows") and *kṣīraṃ kṣārayati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta causes the milk to flow")—then, although the cow possesses the status of a limit (*avadhi*) in relation to the departure [of the milk], nevertheless, since that [status as a limit] is not intended to be expressed, the example is valid when one considers merely its status as a cause (*nimitta*). And thus, when the status as a limit is intended to be expressed, the technical designation of "ablative" (*apādāna*) indeed applies—as in *geḥ duhyate payaḥ* ("Milk is milked from the cow"). But when the cow is a qualifier of the milk itself, then the genitive case applies—as in *goḥ payo dogdhi* ("He milks the cow's milk").

"He asks the Paurava for a cow. The Paurava is the descendant of Puru. Now, one might object: "The designation of 'ablative' (apādāna) is indeed prescribed here, because he takes the cow from the Paurava; he does not take it merely from the act of asking. He takes it only if, having been asked, the other gives it. Furthermore, even if it has not yet been taken, he intends to take it; yet that too is not the case, because one asks while intending to examine the nature [of the object], even though one does not intend to take it. [And: "He shuts the cow in the pen."

But is it not the case that the meaning here is "he causes the cow to enter the pen," and thus the status of the pen (*vraja*) as the object (*karman*) is established? Or, if the meaning is "he causes the cow to stay in the pen," then the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) has already been stated for it. However, when one intends to express merely the state of being a cause (*nimittatva*) with respect to the action of confinement, rather than its status as either an object or a locus, then this is the example. The meaning is: "he causes [the cow] to stay by means of the pen as the cause."

"One asks the student about the path. [The root] *praccha* is used in the sense of "desire to know" (*jñīpsā*); it belongs to the *tudādi* class, and its vowel is subject to *saṃprasāraṇa* by the rule *grahijyā-vayi-vyadhi-vaṣṭi-vicati-vṛścati-pṛcchati-bhṛjjatīnām*. Now, one might object: has not the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) already been stated here? For he receives instruction from him, and not merely from the question; he receives it only if, having been questioned, he provides instruction. [We reply: Let us grant that it has not been received; yet even if he does not intend to receive it, he still asks for the sake of knowing the nature of things. The root *bhikṣ* (to beg) should be explained in the same way as *yāc* (to ask).

But for what purpose are both *yāci* and *bhikṣi* mentioned? For there is no difference in their meaning; this designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on the object (*artha*), not on the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the verbal roots such as *duh*. Indeed, even when the meaning is the same, [the root] is included—as in the expression "he asks Devadatta for a hundred. It is said: [they are mentioned] in order to include *yāci* when its meaning is not that of begging. Therefore, it also applies in cases such as "he asks the ill-behaved for discipline" (*avinītaṃ vinayaṃ yācate*) and "he asks the angry man for favor" (*kruddhaṃ prasādaṃ yācate*).
Furthermore, since it is impossible for the single root *ur* to have two forms—[one with and one without the prefix *pra*]—*bhikṣi* is also included.

"He gathers fruit from the tree. Although this is a domain for the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) in the sense that "while gathering, he takes the fruit from the trees," nevertheless, when the tree is not intended to be expressed as a limit (*avadhi*) but rather only as a causal factor (*nimitta*), then this is the example.

[The sūtra] says "brūte" (he speaks) and "anuśāsti" (he instructs). [The roots] *brūñ* (to speak clearly) and *śāsu* (to instruct) belong to the second class (*adādi*). Although in these cases the boy is intended as the object of the action of speaking or instructing by means of the dharma, nevertheless, because there is no action of *dadāti* (giving), the designation [of the recipient] does not apply. However, for those who do not rely on the phrase "the action of giving" in that context, they intend merely the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) and not the status of being intended; thus the application of the example is justified.
Now, there are others as well that take two objects:

"The inclusion of the roots *nī* (to lead), *vah* (to carry), and *hṛ* (to take away), as well as those with the meaning of motion, should likewise be understood among the roots that take two objects; this is the settled conclusion."

The phrase "of those meaning motion" (*gatyarthānām*) is an elliptical reference to the subsequent rule. Examples: *nī*—he leads the goat to the village (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*); *vah*—he carries the load to the village (*bhāraṃ vahati grāmam*); *har*—he takes the load to the village (*bhāraṃ harati grāmam*). By the use of the particle *ca*, verbs such as *ji* (to conquer) and others are included: he wins a hundred from Devadatta (*śataṃ jayati devadattam*), he steals a hundred from Devadatta (*śataṃ muṣṇāti devadattam*), he fines Devadatta a hundred (*śataṃ daṇḍayati devadattam*), he pulls the branch toward the village (*grāmaṃ karṣati śākhām*).

This is now considered: when *lādi* suffixes (such as *laṭ*, etc. are produced after roots that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), do they arise with respect to the primary object—that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*)—or rather with respect to that [object] whose status as an object is established by this very rule, namely the secondary object (*guṇakarman*)? Regarding this, it has been said: "When the primary object is to be expressed, grammarians say that *lādi* suffixes follow roots that take two objects; when the non-primary [object] is to be expressed, they follow roots such as *duh* (to milk) and others, as well as causative (*ṇyanta*) roots and roots where the agent is itself the object."*1* *1 Pāṇini 1.4.51–52. This verse summarizes the application of these rules.*

This is the meaning: regarding those verbal roots (*dhātu*) that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), they say that when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*)—that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*)—is to be expressed, the *lādi* suffixes occur; that is, the *lādi* suffixes (the *la*-class, the *kṛtya* suffixes, the *kta*, and the *khalartha* suffixes) are employed. Since it is impossible to express simultaneously two objects of different status—the primary and the secondary—it is logical that only the primary object be expressed, precisely because of its primacy. This is the intended sense. Examples: *√nī* (to lead): *ajā grāmaṃ nīyate* (The goat is led to the village); *neyā* (to be led); *nītā* (led); *sunayā* (easily led). *√vah* (to carry): *bhāro grāmam uhyate* (The load is carried to the village); *voḍhavyaḥ* (to be carried); *ūḍhaḥ* (carried); *suvahaḥ* (easily carried).

√hṛ—*hriyate bhāro grāmam* (the load is being carried to the village), *hartavyaḥ* (to be carried), *hṛtaḥ* (carried), *suharaḥ* (easy to carry). √kṛṣ—*kṛṣyate śākhā grāmam* (the branch is being dragged to the village), *kraṣṭavyā* (to be dragged), *kṛṣṭā* (dragged), *sukarṣā* (easy to drag).

Regarding the rule "duhādīnām apradhāne" (for *duh* and others, when the non-primary [object] is to be expressed): here, words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) and others are also included, not only those recited in the verse beginning with *duhi-yāci*. For these roots beginning with *duh*, they say that the *l*-suffixes and others occur when the non-primary object is to be expressed. This too is established by logic (*nyāya*); since one who desires milk first proceeds toward the cow, the connection of the pure root *duh* is with the cow, whereas the connection of the milk is through the milking of the cow. Thus, because of its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), the *l*-suffixes and others occur precisely there for the "unspoken object" (*akathita-karman*). The same applies everywhere.

*Duhi* (to milk): *gauḥ duhyate payaḥ* (the cow is milked for milk), *dohyā*, *dugdhā*, *sudohā*. *Yāci* (to beg): *pauravaḥ gāṃ yācyate* (the Paurava is being asked for a cow), *yācyaḥ*, *yācitaḥ*, *suyācaḥ*. *Rudhi* (to obstruct): *vrajaḥ avarudhyate gām* (the pen is being enclosed with a cow), *avarodhyaḥ*, *avaruddhaḥ*, *svavarodhaḥ*. *Pracchi* (to ask): *māṇavakaḥ panthānaṃ pṛcchyate* (the boy is being asked the way), *praṣṭavyaḥ*, *pṛṣṭaḥ*, *supracchaḥ*. *Bhikṣi* (to beg): *pauravaḥ gāṃ bhikṣyate* (the Paurava is being begged for a cow), *bhikṣitavyaḥ*, *bhikṣitaḥ*, *subhikṣaḥ*.

*Ciñ*: the tree is being gathered for its fruits (*avacīyate phalāni*), it is to be gathered (*avacetavyaḥ*), it has been gathered (*avacitaḥ*), it is easy to gather (*suvacayaḥ*). *Brūñ*: the boy is being told the Dharma (*ucyate māṇavako dharmam*), he is to be told (*vaktavyaḥ*), he has been told (*uktaḥ*), he is easy to speak to (*suvacaḥ*). *Śāsu*: the boy is being instructed in the Dharma (*anuśiṣyate māṇavako dharmam*), he is to be instructed (*anuśāsitavyaḥ*), he has been instructed (*anuśiṣṭaḥ*), he is easy to instruct (*suanuśāsaḥ*). *Daṇḍi*: the Gargas are fined a hundred [pieces of gold] (*gargāḥ śataṃ daṇḍyante*), they are to be fined (*daṇḍyāḥ*), they have been fined (*daṇḍitāḥ*), they are easy to fine (*sudaṇḍāḥ*). *Ji*: Devadatta is losing a hundred [pieces of gold] (*śataṃ jīyate devadattaḥ*), he is to be defeated (*jetavyaḥ*), he has been defeated (*jitaḥ*), he is easy to defeat (*sujayaḥ*).
*Muṣi*: Devadatta is robbed of a hundred [pieces of gold] (*muṣyate devadattaḥ śatam*), he is to be robbed (*moṣitavyaḥ*), he has been robbed (*muṣitaḥ*), he is easy to rob (*sumoṣaḥ*).

"Of the agent and the object in the causative (ṇyanta) [state]"—the word "denotation" (abhidhāne) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. The meaning is that they state that the *l*-suffixes (*la*) and so forth occur when there is the denotation of that which was the agent in the non-causative (*aṇyanta*) state, but has become the object in the causative (*ṇyanta*) state. This is what is being said: those roots such as "to go" (*gatyartha*) and others which are transitive even in their non-causative state, and which become doubly transitive (*dvikarmaka*) in their causative state by the subsequent rule—in these cases, the *l*-suffixes occur with respect to that object which arises in the causative state by virtue of the subsequent rule.

He causes Devadatta to go to the village (*gamayati grāmaṃ devadattam*), Devadatta goes to the village (*gamyate grāmaṃ devadattaḥ*); [gerundive] *gamayitavyaḥ*, [past participle] *gamitaḥ*; [adjective] *sugamaḥ* (easy to go). [Roots] having the sense of "awakening" (*budhy-artha*): He causes the boy to understand the Dharma (*bodhyate māṇavako dharmam*); [gerundive] *bodhayitavyaḥ*, [past participle] *bodhitaḥ*; [adjective] *subodhaḥ* (easy to understand). [Roots] having the sense of "consumption" (*pratyavasāna-artha*): He causes the boy to eat the rice (*bhojyate māṇavaka odanam*); [gerundive] *bhojayitavyaḥ*, [past participle] *bhojitaḥ*; [adjective] *subhojaḥ* (easy to eat). [Roots] having sound as their object (*śabda-karman*): He causes the boy to recite the Veda (*pāṭhyate māṇavako vedam*); [gerundive] *pāṭhayitavyaḥ*, [past participle] *pāṭhitaḥ*;

[adjective] *supāṭhaḥ* (easy to recite). [Roots] intransitive (*akarmaka*): He causes the boy to sit for a month (*āsyate māṇavako māsam*); [gerundive] *āsayitavyaḥ*, [past participle] *āsitaḥ*; [adjective] *svāsaḥ* (easy to sit).

According to another opinion, in the case of roots whose meanings involve cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), the *l*-affixes and others are applied to the secondary object (*guṇakarman*). Examples include: *māṇavako dharmo bodhyate* ("the boy is made to understand dharma"), *māṇavaka odano bhojyate* ("the boy is fed rice"), and *māṇavako vedo pāṭhyate* ("the boy is taught the Veda").

Thus, the conclusion here is as follows: after the roots *nī*, *vah*, *hṛ*, and *kṛṣ*, the suffixes beginning with *la* (the *l-kartari* suffixes) are used for the principal object (*pradhānakarman*), because its connection [to the action] occurs earlier. After the roots beginning with *duh*, and after *ji*, *daṇḍ*, and *muṣ*, they are used for the non-principal object (*apradhāna*), because its connection is more immediate (*antaraṅga*). After roots whose meaning involves cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), they may be used optionally for either the secondary object (*guṇakarman*) or the principal object, according to one's wish. And after roots meaning motion (*gatyartha*), intransitives (*akarmaka*), and the causatives (*ṇyanta*) of *hṛ* and *kṛ*, they are used for the prompted object (*prayojyakarman*).

Furthermore, because the object of the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is that which is to be reached (*āpyamāna*) by the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), even though that operation is expressed as primary, it possesses primacy. On the other hand, the status of being subordinate belongs to the object of the operation of the prompted agent, which is subordinate; however, the primacy of the operation of the prompted agent is established by the principle of "the purpose of the meaning" (*ārthena nyāyena*), since the operation of the prompter exists for the sake of that [operation of the prompted agent]. And due to that primacy, others maintain that the object of that [prompted agent] also possesses primacy. In any case, it is established that the *l*-affixes and so forth denote the object of the prompted agent.

And for roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), the distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*), and location (*deśa*) are desired to be designated as the object (*karma*). As it has been said: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are indeed designated as the object for intransitive [roots]; furthermore, it should be stated that location is also designated as the object for intransitive [roots]. Regarding the term *adhvagantavya*: it means a path to be traversed (*gantavyo'dhvā*); the word *adhvā* (path) should be understood as belonging to the *kaḍārādi* group [which allows for both prior and posterior compound formation].

The term *gantavya* (that which is to be traversed) is included for the purpose of including things like a *krośa*, which are well-known as objects to be traversed and have a fixed measure; therefore, the expression *adhvānaṃ svapiti* ("he sleeps for the duration of a road") does not occur. Now, one might object: "Is the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) not already established by the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*? What is the use of the technical designation *karman* (object)? To this we reply: First, it must be stated for the sake of [defining] space (*deśa*). Furthermore, even in the case of time and distance, the status of being an *object* (*karmatva*) must be accepted in order to trigger the application of the *L*-suffixes and so forth. Thus, we have examples such as *māsa āsyate* ("a month is sat through"), *āsitaḥ* ("sat for a month"), *āsitavyaḥ* ("to be sat for a month"), and *svāsaḥ* ("easy to sit through"). Similarly, *krośaḥ śayyate* ("a *krośa* is slept across"), and so on. As for the state (*bhāva*): *godoham āste* ("he sits until the milking of the cows").

The meaning is that he remains for as long a time as it takes to milk a cow. Since actions such as milking a cow are not commonly recognized as "time" in the same way that months and the like are, they are mentioned separately as *bhāva* (action/state). Regarding place: examples include *kurūn svapiti* ("he sleeps in the Kurus") and *kuravaḥ supyanti* ("the Kurus sleep"). However, the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* ("in the case of absolute connection with time or distance") is intended for cases of absolute connection with non-actions—such as *māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ* ("jaggery and parched grain [consumed] for a month"), *sarvarātraṃ kalyāṇī* ("she is auspicious throughout the night"), and *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* ("the river is winding for the distance of a *krośa*").

In that case, should it not be said that "because time does not exist, there is no path to be traversed"? It need not be so stated; for here [the verb] does not reside merely in sitting, but rather in the pervasion preceded by that act—*māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"). What is the meaning? He pervades the month by means of sitting. Likewise, one should say *adhīte* ("he studies"); the meaning is that he pervades the month by means of the study of the Veda.

Now, regarding the rule "kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti" (Pāṇini 2.3.65), which prescribes the genitive case for the agent and the object in connection with a *kṛt* suffix, does it apply to the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*) in the case of verbs that take two objects (*dvikarmaka*), or to the secondary object (*guṇa-karman*), or to both? It might be argued that it applies to both, as in the case of the accusative case; however, according to the statement of the Bhāṣyakāra, the genitive is optionally used for the secondary object, while it is obligatory for the primary object—as in the example: *netā aśvasya strughnam*.

"Let there simply be the rule 'here [the object] is called akathita' (Pāṇini 1.4.51); let the two preceding rules not exist, since their objects would also be included under the term 'akathita'. True; however, the enumeration of roots such as *duh* must necessarily be performed so that [the designation of object] does not apply in cases such as "he hears the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*). And when that enumeration is made, [the designation] would not apply in cases such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) or "he approaches the roots of the tree" (*vṛkṣamūlāny upasarpati*); therefore, the two preceding rules are also commenced.
Pāda-mañjarī:

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.52: "In the case of roots meaning motion, cognition, or consumption; those having sound as their object; and those that are intransitive—the agent (kartṛ) of the root in the *aṇ* [causative] sense becomes the object (*karman*) in the *ṇic* [causative] sense."

[One says: "He causes the boy to go to the village. How is it that the village has the status of an object (*karman*) here, given that it is stated that "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), and at present the boy is not the agent, since he possesses the designation of "object"? In this regard, just as in the case of "he ties the horse to the beans," the beans do not receive the designation of "object" despite being what is most desired [by the horse] through its act of eating—for what reason? Because the horse is not currently the agent—so too, in this case, [the designation of object] would not apply.

Let it not be that the boy (*māṇavaka*) is the agent when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) has arisen; rather, he is the agent with respect to the meaning of the root even prior to its arising. And at that very time, there is a connection with the village; he is impelled toward the act of going with the village as its object—[as in the command] "Go to the village. Therefore, in the state in which the village possesses the status of an object (*karman*), the boy does not possess the status of an object; and in the state of the causative suffix (*ṇyantāvasthā*) in which the boy possesses the status of an object, the village does not possess the status of an object, because [the relationship] had already occurred previously.

However, in the case of *māṣeṣvaśvam*, this is not possible [to interpret] as "he causes to go" (*yāpayati*). In the rule *yā prāpaṇe*, movement (*gati*) is indicated by the sense of reaching (*prāpti*); thus, the root *yāti* has the meaning of movement. Regarding the rule *nīvahyoḥ*: one might object that the meaning of these two roots is "causing to reach," which results in movement, but movement itself is not the primary meaning. Furthermore, in the Bhāṣya on the rule *na gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ*, it is stated: "The root *vah* does not have movement as its meaning. This is true; however, the prohibition was stated with the consideration that movement is perceived even as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāvena*).

Regarding the phrase "of that which has no driver" (*vaheraniyantṛkasya*), there is the introductory remark, "I shall explain. In the case of *vāhayati balīvardān yavān* ("he causes the oxen to carry the barley"), in the non-causative form (*aṇi*) the oxen are the agents; however, in the causative form (*ṇyante*), the driver (*sārathi*) is the agent. In that situation, because of the prohibition of the prohibition, the original rule indeed applies. They say that by the mention of "verbs meaning to know" (*budhyartha*), only those expressing knowledge in general are included, and not those expressing specific types of it, such as *smarati* ("to remember") and so on. This is likewise illustrated in the commentary (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the phrase "ādikhādyoḥ": another says that not every action of consuming (pratyavasāna) results in the [karmasaṃjñā] *ad* (eating), nor is it necessarily this very [action] that receives the designation of *karman*; thus, the rule "nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca" does not apply here. This one thing is intended: "kte'dhikaraṇe ca dhrauvyagatipratyavasānārthebhyaḥ"—namely, "this is what has been eaten by them" (*idameṣāṃ jagdham*).

Regarding the word *bhakṣeḥ*: since among roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) and so forth, a causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of instigation (*hetumat*) generally occurs, the rule for the causative suffix applies; and by the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the prohibition is rightly understood to apply to that [causative] alone. Thus, even a root ending in the *curādi* class suffix (*ṇic*) is treated as if it were without such a suffix (*aṇyant*); hence there is the application of the rule to *bhakṣ*. An example is: *bhakṣayati balīvardān sasyam* ("He causes the oxen to eat the grain"). When the barley standing in the field is being eaten, injury (*hiṃsā*) occurs; for at that stage, some maintain that the oxen possess consciousness. Alternatively, the injury belongs to the owner, consisting in the loss of the substance.

In this context, the word *karman* (object) is sometimes taken to mean "action," as in the rule *kartari karmavyatīhāre* ("when there is a reciprocal action, [the suffix *śyan* is used] in the sense of the agent"); and sometimes it means "the object as a grammatical factor" (*sādhanakarman*), as in *veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ* ("after the root *vi*, when sound is the object"). If it is argued that here [in the present rule] it refers to roots whose action consists of sound, [the answer is: "there is a prohibition for *hve* and others"—as in *hvayati putraṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta calls his son") and *hvāpayati putraṃ devadattena* ("he causes Devadatta to call his son"); *krandati putraṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cries out to his son") and *krandayati putraṃ devadattena* ("he causes Devadatta to cry out to his son"); *śabdāyate devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta makes a sound") and *śabdāyayate devadattena* ("he causes Devadatta to make a sound").

Now, if it is argued that this [application of the rule] follows here because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), [we reply: no, because the object characterized by sound (*śabda*) is included within its own meaning, and because another distinct object is impossible. Furthermore, there is the need for a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the root *śru*—because its action does not consist of sound: "Devadatta hears the verse" (*śṛṇoti ślokaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "He causes Devadatta to hear the verse" (*śrāvayati ślokaṃ devadattam*). Nor is the formation of the causative established here on the grounds that it has the sense of cognition (*budhy-artha*), for roots such as *cetati* and others are "cognition-roots" (*budhy-artha*) only insofar as they denote mere cognition.

Let it be, then, that the object of the action is understood as the instrument (*sādhana-karman*). If it is argued that this refers to the "object of speech" (*śabda-karman*), then an addition must be made for verbs such as *jalpati* (he whispers): *devadattaḥ putram jalpati* (Devadatta whispers to his son), *devadattaḥ putram jalpayati* (He causes Devadatta to whisper to his son); *devadattaḥ putram vilapati* (Devadatta laments to his son), *devadattaḥ putram vilāpayati* (He causes Devadatta to lament to his son); *devadattaḥ putram ābhāṣate* (Devadatta addresses his son), *devadattaḥ putram ābhāṣayati* (He causes Devadatta to address his son).

Regarding the root *dṛś* (to see), although there is the inclusion of "action" (*kriyā*), as well as the inclusion of "means" (*sādhana*), or even the inclusion of both—nevertheless, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for *dṛś*. For example: *rūpatarkaṃ kārṣāpaṇaṃ paśyati* (he looks at the coin with the help of a mirror) and *rūpatarkaṃ kārṣāpaṇaṃ darśayati* (he shows the coin with the help of a mirror). This [addition] must be stated when this root *dṛś* refers to a specific kind of cognition whose instrument is the eye; however, if it denotes cognition in general, it is already established by virtue of having the sense of "understanding" (*budh*).
Thus, in both these positions, the Bhāṣya concludes with a dilemma, and neither position is definitively resolved.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, cites those actions which consist of verbal activity and whose objects are words—actions established beyond dispute—as meaning "he makes known by means of speech. The same applies elsewhere as well; in that case, it is established precisely because [the action] has cognition as its purpose.

Even though the cognition (*buddhi*) is one thing and the act of causing to cognize (*bodhanā*) is another, since that cognition still exists as a subordinate element (*upasarjanībhūta*), the state of having "cognition" as its meaning (*buddhy-arthatva*) certainly persists; furthermore, even when an action such as "going" (*gati*) is subordinate, it is still grasped as the meaning. Otherwise, because verbs like *gamayati* would not have "going" as their meaning, they would not apply [to the causative], and thus the inclusion of the term *aṇi* (the causative suffix) would be purposeless. This may hold true for conscious beings; however, how is it in the case of insentient things? When one person makes someone else speak, there is no actual "awakening" (*prabodhana*) involved here at all.

Regarding the term *akarmakāṇām* (of intransitive verbs): here the meaning to be understood is "those devoid of an object other than time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), the distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*), or location (*deśa*). Otherwise, [the rule] would not apply to such cases as *māsam āste devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta sits for a month"), *māsam āsayati devadattam* ("He causes Devadatta to sit for a month"), *godoham āsayati* ("He causes [him] to sit until milking time"), *krośam āsayati* ("He causes [him] to sit for the distance of a *krośa*"), or *kurūn āsayati* ("He causes [him] to sit in the land of the Kurus"); for these would be considered transitive (*sakarmaka*) due to the presence of an object consisting of time and so forth.

In this same way, in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca* ("The suffixes *la* [denote] the object and..."), wherever the term "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is mentioned, it should be understood to apply everywhere. Consequently, in examples such as *māsam āsyate devadattena* ("Devadatta sits for a month"), the suffixes *la* and others are established in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). And it has been said: "But [the formation] is established by the statement that [a verb] becomes intransitive through the time-object. The mention of "time" (*kāla*) is illustrative; because of the use of the particle *vat*, the rule applies even to its own substratum—thus, in *māsa āsyate devadattena*, the suffix *la* occurs in reference to the month as the object.

In that case, should it not be stated that [the suffix] occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) because the verbal roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*)? It need not be so stated. Although it is said "of intransitives," no roots are intransitive by virtue of being associated with time and the like. Roots are intransitive even when associated with time and the like when those factors are not intended to be expressed—as in: "Devadatta lies down; he does not eat. Nor are roots called intransitive merely when their objects are not intended to be expressed; rather, those verbal roots whose objects are absolutely non-existent are intransitive, not their meanings.

That verbal root which is intransitive by virtue of its own essential nature—and not because it has time (*kāla*) or other such factors as its object—is what is intended. Since it is impossible for any root to be intransitive by virtue of its own essential nature when it possesses an object such as time, it is understood by implication that its intransitivity refers to objects other than those.

But why is this stated, given that even for an object (*prayojya*) which is independent in its own operation, when the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is intended to be expressed, it will receive the designation "object" (*karman*) because it is being reached (*āpyamāna*) by that [instigator] which is the primary factor; thus, by virtue of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), it will set aside the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*)—even though the latter would have applied first—and the designation "object" will instead take effect? If this is so, then since the result is already established, the present formulation is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*): if the designation "object" applies to that which is being reached by the operation of an instigator, it applies only to [verbs] such as those meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*), and not to others.

In the sentence "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook rice" (*tena pācayaty odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena*), the instrumental case ending occurs for the agent (*kartari*) because the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ-saṃjñā*), which had already been applied previously, remains in effect. As it has been said: "Having attained the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the act of instigation (*preṣaṇa*) due to its independence in the subordinate action (*guṇakriyā*), [the agent] is expressed by its own grammatical property (*svadharmeṇa*) because of the restriction of the designation 'object' (*niyamāt karmasaṃjñāyāḥ*)."

The third case ending is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) when it is the object of its own action. Now, how is it that [the mountain] "was not able to make the God of Gods accept his daughter without being asked"?

Poets are independent. Alternatively, it should be explained thus: he was not able to make [him] understand or inform him regarding something concerning the marriage of his daughter; in that sense, since the root *budh* (to understand) is involved, the usage is established.
*Padamañjarī*:
"In the case of the roots *hṛ* (to take) and *kṛ* (to do), [the accusative case is used] optionally. (Pāṇini 1.4.53)

Since the meanings of "motion" (*gati*) and so forth have ceased [to apply], this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. When *harati* refers to motion—as in "Devadatta carries the load"—or when it refers to eating—as in "he eats the rice from the boy"—and also when *karoti* is intransitive—as in "the students, full of rice, behave strangely"—then [the rule] is obtained by the preceding [sūtra].

Now, one might argue that according to the rule "a prescription or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes," it would be more appropriate for this restriction itself to be optional. That is to say, the restriction "only in the case of roots meaning 'to go' (gati) and so forth" [as in Pāṇini 1.4.52] is [limited by] the rule "hṛ-kṛ- anyatarasyām" [Pāṇini 1.4.53]. Consequently, since the restriction is absent in one alternative, let there be the status of object (*karmatva*) in the other alternative for meanings other than "to go" and so forth, and let there be the status of agent (*kartṛtva*) in the other alternative; however, when the meaning is "to go" and so forth, the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would necessarily apply.

In that case, this [option] has been read by the author of the Vārttika among the "options for both" (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*). By the force of that, the principle "the rule applies to what immediately precedes" (*anantarasya vidhiḥ*) is not resorted to; rather, the option regarding *hṛ* and *kṛ* proceeds without distinction. Regarding *abhivādi-ddaśoḥ*: for *abhivādayati*, the option applies because it was not previously established [by another rule]; for *ddaś*, it applies either because it has the sense of "understanding" (*budhy-artha*) or because it is already established by the rule "for all [roots]" (*sarvatra*). As for *abhivādayate*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by the rule "and after a causative suffix" (*ṇicaś-ca*). However, in the active voice (*parasmaipada*), as in *abhivādayati guruṃ devadattena*, the agent (*kartṛ*) alone retains its designation as such.

Regarding the form *darśayate*: in the view where there is no designation as an object (*karmasaṃjñā*), because there is no other object, the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *ṇeraṇau*; otherwise, however, it is applied by the rule *ṇicaśca*.
*Padamañjarī*:
The agent is independent. (Pāṇini 1.4.54)

This word *svatantra* has several meanings. It refers to a weaver—*svatantra* being one whose own *tantra* (loom) he possesses; the stretched-out threads are called *svatantra*. It also applies to a person who possesses common property—*tantra* here meaning common property, and *svatantra* being one for whom his own wealth (*tantra*) is common [to others]. Furthermore, it signifies the principal—*svatantra* being one whose own self (*ātman*) is the *tantra*, that is, the principal.

In that case, if the first two [definitions] were accepted, the designation *kartṛ* (agent) would apply to those two even in the domain of the *apādāna* (ablative) and other cases—due to their being subsequent [in the order of rules] and because they are specifically prescribed—as in "he comes from the weaver" (*tantuvāyād āgacchati*). Furthermore, it would not apply here in "Devadatta goes" (*devadatto gacchati*). Having seen this fault in accepting the first two, he states, relying on the third meaning: "the independent one" (*svatantra*). The sense is that the word *svatantra* is more commonly established in that very sense, namely, as that which is the primary factor (*pradhānabhūta*).

Furthermore, since this occurs under the heading of "factors of action" (*kāraka*), independence (*svātantrya*) is understood as pertaining to an action; and a weaver is not employed in the act of weaving merely by virtue of being a weaver, but rather as the primary agent itself. Therefore, it is logical that only the word denoting that [primary agent] should be included. If it is said that the primary agent is intended, then, because the status of being primary depends upon the existence of non-primary factors, this [definition] would apply even in cases where there are subordinate factors such as the locus—e.g., "He cooks rice in a pot with firewood. In this case, the pot would also be considered an agent.

Anticipating the objection that [the agent] is not seen in such cases as *na tvāste* ("you do not sit") or *na tvaṃ śete* ("you do not lie down"), he shows that the state of being a subordinate factor (*aguṇabhāva*) is indicated by its predominance (*prādhānyena*), stating: "that which has become non-subordinate" (*aguṇībhūta*). Therefore, that which lacks the status of a subordinate factor is the agent (*kartṛ*). And even when other factors (*kāraka*) are not intended to be expressed, the state of being non-subordinate certainly exists. But what here is this relationship of subordinate and predominant among the factors? It is when the action is not accomplished even upon the removal of one [factor]. Regarding this, it has been said: "Because [the factor] acquires its capacity from another [source] beforehand, because it is made subservient, because the activity of those already engaged depends upon it, and because it causes those engaged to desist."

"Because no substitute for the agent is observed, because [the instrument] is seen even in its absence, and because it is beneficial even from a distance, independence is attributed to the agent. Wood and other such materials acquire the capacity of instruments and so forth only when set in motion by the agent, whereas the agent exists prior to them. Furthermore, in the presence of the agent, the instruments and others become subordinate, and their activity and cessation are dependent upon him. No substitute for the primary agent is observed, whereas a substitute for instruments and the like is indeed observed—for instance, when rice is unavailable, the sacrifice is performed with wild millet (*nīvāra*). "Separation" (*praviveka*) means non-existence.

Even in the absence of instruments and other factors, as in the cases of "he sits" (*āste*) or "he lies down" (*śete*), the agent alone is observed; however, in the absence of an agent, instruments and the like are never observed.

"Because of being helpful even from afar. This means that although such an agent assists in the accomplishment of the result while remaining external (*taṭastha*), he does not do so by entering into it like an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other factors. And this [status] generally occurs only among sentient beings (*cetana*), not among insentient things—as in expressions such as "the chariot goes"—yet this is not a fault; for two characteristics are observed in the agent defined above: primacy (*prādhānya*) and non-subordination (*aguṇabhāva*). Among these, non-subordination is possible both in the case of insentient things and in the case of sentient beings.

Furthermore, this state of being a non-attribute (*aguṇabhāva*) is not restricted to a specific object; rather, it belongs only to that which one intends to express as such. Thus he says: "it is intended to be expressed independently" (*svātantryeṇa vivakṣyate*). An example of "intended to be expressed" is: *sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks"). Others, however, explain it thus: the agent is that whose operation is denoted as a subordinate factor (*aguṇabhāvena*), while the operation is subordinated—that is, the operation is conveyed by a verbal root that has itself become a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*). And whose operation is conveyed by the verbal root as a non-attribute? It is established everywhere that it belongs to that which one intends to express as such.
*Padamañjarī*:
"And the prompter of that [agent] is also the cause (hetu). (Pāṇini 1.4.55)

By the word "tat" (that), the agent is connected; the meaning is that the one characterized by the technical designation "agent" (kartṛ-saṃjñā) is the independent one (svatantra). But surely, when an instigator (prayojaka) is present, the dependent nature of the one being prompted (prayojya) is like that of instruments (karaṇa) and other factors in the presence of an agent; so how can he be referred to as "independent"? And how much less so as "characterized by the designation 'agent'"? And how much less so in such a construction as *pācayaty odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice")? [The answer is: The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for the one being prompted, while independence belongs to the [actual] agent alone, even prior [to the instigation].

If the agent already exists, for what purpose is there instigation? If it is argued that one instigates so that he might cease [from evil], let it be so in the case of inciting one who is already engaged; but how is it in a case where one is made to act by force? It is said in reply:

Even in the case of instigating one who has not yet acted, as long as the instigator does not perceive his own interest, he is not designated as "one who causes to cook" (*pācayati*) so long as the person to be prompted (*prayojya*) does not act; for even then, the instigation remains present as it is established in memory. Indeed, the persistence of the application is the cause for the prompted person’s engagement until the fruit is accomplished; it is not interrupted in the interim. However, the command (*praiṣa*) expressed by the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) and so forth exists even when the prompted person does not act. And it has been said: "The imperative is prescribed after verbs such as *pṛccha* (ask) when there is a command regarding a mere substance."

"When there is an instigation (*praiṣa*) of one who has already begun [an action], then that is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Thus, the instigation expressed by *ṇic* is understood in the form of an impulsion toward one who has already begun [an action]; therefore, it is not contradictory for the agent—who exists as the subject of the base meaning—to be the "instigator" (*prayojaka*). And it is precisely to demonstrate this meaning that the word *tat* (that) is employed; otherwise, when the expectation arises as to "of what is he the instigator?", since the independent agent would be obtained simply by virtue of being the subject under discussion, its inclusion would be purposeless. [The compound] *tatprayojakaḥ* means "the instigator of that. Now, one might object: "By the rules *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* and *kartari ca*..."

Because [the status of] a *kāraka* is prohibited [by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇayos tṛtīyā*], how can there be a compound here? To this he says: "The compound is established by nipātana (irregular derivation). We shall examine this matter in the very section concerning *vicakṣaṇa*. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of designations (*saṃjñā*). For if that [particle] were absent, then because of the governing rule *ekasaṃjñādhikāra*, the designation *kartṛ* would not apply. The analysis of the phrase *kurvāṇaṃ prayuṅkte* is as follows: the very act of instigation (*prayukti*) that is present in the mind when one is in the state of acting—that alone is what is expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). By the words "because of being the cause" (*hetutvāt*), etc., he demonstrates the purpose of the co-occurrence of designations.
In the *Padamañjarī*, [it is stated]: "The particles (*nipāta*) are those occurring before the word *īśvara*. (Pāṇini 1.4.56)

"Words beginning with *prāk* are particles (*nipāta*). [The word] *prāk* means "in the eastern direction" or "in the past time. Regarding the rule that will be stated as *adhir īśvare* ("*adhi* [is a particle] when meaning 'lord'"), one should understand this as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the portion of the base form *īśvara* together with the final *r* of the preceding word. Because it possesses meaning through its referent (the object being imitated), the case endings are produced; and since it is a particle in the phrase *ca vā*, it receives the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) by the rule *svarādinipātam avyayam*. However, the accent "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*) does not apply here, because those [words] cited in the list are taught as being grave (*anudātta*). For others, however, that accent also applies.

[Objection: But surely, just as an introductory heading (*adhikāra*) such as "suffix" (*pratyaya*) operates upon its intended subject even without the mention of a limit (*avadhi*), so too will this [heading] operate; let there simply be "particles" (*nipātāḥ*), and there is no need for the mention of a limit. To this, he says: "the statement 'before' (*prāgvacana*). By means of the statement "before," the purpose of mentioning the limit has been stated. The meaning is this: if the mention of the limit were absent, then even though the word "particles" would recur with each subsequent rule, because of the governing heading of "one technical name" (*eka-saṃjñā-adhikāra*), there would be an option (*paryāya*) between the names, and not their simultaneous application (*samāveśa*).

But when that [condition] exists, all those sentient beings who existed prior to Īśvara are considered here collectively, and the designation is prescribed once; however, because of the governing force (adhikāra) of each individual sūtra, there is no reversal [of the application], and the purpose of this is their inclusion [within the scope].

Alternatively, what is the purpose of the explicit mention of *prāk* (‘before’), since one could simply supply the word *prāk*—as a directional term—to the word *pañcamī* alone, while no such supply would be necessary for *parāk*, because the rules “*cādayo’satve*” and “*prādayaḥ*” would otherwise result in meaninglessness due to the impossibility of anything being prescribed [by them]? To this he says: “The mention of *prāk*. The intention is this: although [the desired form] could be established by supplying [the word], by the force of the inclusion of *prāk*, two instances of the word *prāk* are uttered simultaneously (*tantra*) [in the rule].

Therefore, this is the meaning: those [words] which are established as being prior to *īśvara* (in the list of particles) receive the designation of *nipāta*; being *nipātas*, they receive the designations of *gati* and so forth. Thus, the designation of *nipāta* is merely the cause for the designations of *gati* and so forth, and consequently, their co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) is established.

Regarding the inclusion of the letter *r* in the expression *rīśvarāt*, he states the purpose: "lest [the rule] apply from *īśvarāt*. That is to say, it is stated as *rīśvarāt* so that this word *īśvara* may serve as a limit (*avadhi*) according to the rule *adhir īśvare*; the meaning is that it is for the sake of preventing the application of the rules *śaki ṇyamulkamulau* and *īśvare tosun-kasunau*. When the sūtras are recited in their joined form (*saṃhitā*), the word *śīśvara* exists; with this in mind, it was stated as *rīśvarāt*.

[Objection: It is established by way of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author teaches that a *kṛt*-derived word ending in *m* or a *kṛt*-derived word ending in *aiC* (e.g., *īśvara*) receives the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the rule "A *kṛt* [suffix] followed by *meC* is [indeclinable]," this indicates that the word *īśvara* is the immediate limit and not separated [by other elements]. Otherwise, since the designation of indeclinable would already be established for *se*, *sen*, and so forth, as well as for *ṇamul* and *kamul* simply by virtue of their being particles (*nipāta*), that [rule] would be purposeless. [Reply: This is not a valid indicator. For even a subsequent [word] ending in *m* derived from a *kṛt* suffix is included; that is, even a *kṛt* word ending in *m* which follows the rule "In the sense of *īśvara*, [the suffixes] *tosun* and *kasun* [are used]" is also covered.

This [rule] would be for the sake of forms ending in *ej*—such as those ending in *ej* used in the sense of the kṛtya suffixes in "tavaikenityādi"—as well as for those ending in *m*, such as the *ṇamul* suffix. However, since it teaches the indeclinability (*avyayatva*) of the *avyayībhāva* compound, that serves to indicate the principle: "the mention of what immediately precedes. Otherwise, because the designation *nipāta* (particle) applies in the second rule, the *avyayībhāva* would already have its indeclinable status established simply by virtue of being a *nipāta*; thus, that [teaching] would be redundant. But this is not the case.

The rule "avyayībhāvaḥ [is taught] among compounds" would be a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) intended to exclude those of the same class, but it does not serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the inclusion of what follows immediately. If that is so, then the inclusion of what follows immediately will occur simply by virtue of common worldly logic (*laukikanyāya*). For in the world, when it is said, "One should follow a loved one as far as the edge of the water," the relatives turn back from that very point which is the immediate edge of the water; would it not be the same here? To this, he says: "And it transcends the worldly [logic]."

Worldly logic itself transcends the world; for, out of excessive affection, people follow even a second boundary of water and then turn back. Therefore, it is said that he is "vīśvara" (the one from whom people turn back), lest there be confusion with "īśvara" (the Lord). Now, one might argue: since the prohibition of the genitive case in the rule "na lokāvyaya... is already established by the fact that words such as *loka* are indeclinables (*avyaya*), their re-inclusion [in this specific context] must serve as an indicator—that is, it indicates that only the immediately preceding rule is to be applied. This is not so.

It would merely indicate the absence of the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable), whereas the designation *nipāta* (particle) would still certainly apply; consequently, in examples such as *cikīrṣvartha*, the designation *pragṛhya* would apply by the rule "a particle consisting of a single vowel, except for *aṅ*, is *pragṛhya*. [The word] *protham* means "sufficiently" (*paryāptam*). [The root] *protha* is used in the sense of "sufficiency"; with the suffix *ac* added according to the *pacādi* group, it takes the neuter gender because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
The words *padamañjarī* and others [are used] when not denoting a substance (asattve). 1.4.57.

"If it does not apply to a sentient being (*sattva*). This means that if it applies to a sentient being, then the designation [of *nipāta*] does not occur; thus he says: "This is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). Now, what is the fault in [interpreting this as] an exclusory negation (*paryudāsa*)? In this case, the word *paśu* is recited [in the list], and it applies to a substance (*dravya*) qualified by a genus (*jāti*); consequently, it would follow that it has the status of a *nipāta*. For a meaning consisting of a collection of both genus and substance is indeed different from the individual [components]. Similarly, regarding the rule for *pra* and so on, [the word] *vipra* is derived from *vi-pra*, with the suffix *ka* added according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*.

In this context, the word *pra* refers to a substance (*dravya*) qualified by an action (*kriyā*). Since the aggregate of that action and substance is distinct from the substance alone, and because it is a particle (*nipāta*), it would—by virtue of being a particle—be designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*); furthermore, since the rule of "extension to what ends with [the particle]" (*tadantavidhi*) is accepted here, the word *vipra* would also receive the designation of an indeclinable. However, under the interpretation of a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the prohibition applies everywhere wherever there is even a trace of a substance.

In what case, then, does the word *paśu* (animal) denote a non-substance (*asattvavacana*)? It is in the sense of "perception" (*darśana*), as in the phrase *paśuṃ manyamānā lodhaṃ nayanti* ("thinking [it] an animal, they lead the lodhra-tree"). Here, the act of thinking is qualified by the sense of perception—the meaning is that this thinking is a perception; that is, "thinking correctly. He dispels the misconception that the word *sattva* is taken here as denoting the universal "existence" (*sattājāti*)—defined as "the state of being existent" (*sato bhāvaḥ sattvam*)—by stating: "And *sattva* refers to a substance (*dravya*). A substance is said to be an entity capable of being referred to by a pronoun such as "this" or "that" (*idaṃ tat*). And it has been said: [The verse follows: "Substance is that which is capable of being designated by the words 'this' or 'that,' which possesses qualities, and which is the substratum of action. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15)
"Wherever a pronoun is employed as a general indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of a thing, that object which is intended to be distinguished is called a 'substance' (dravya).
