The phrase "by its own meaning" (svārthena) is to be supplied [as the condition]. The meaning is: that object which exists in a completed form (siddharūpa) and is intended to be qualified by its own meaning as the substantive (viśeṣya), that is a substance. And it has been said:

"That wherein the primary meaning (svārtha) finds its rest is called the expressed substance (dravya). Having established this, [it is explained as follows]: that in which the genus (jāti) and so forth—which serve as the grounds for the application of a word—settle down or reside by way of being qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), is "substance" (sattva). The suffix *tva* is derived from the root *sad* according to the *uṇādi* rules; by the rule "the *uṇādi* suffixes are used elsewhere than those two," it functions as a locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). The suffix *caṇ* is listed [in the *uṇādi* list]; if it occurs in the sense of "if" (*ced*), the letter *ṇ* serves as a qualifier for the rule "the *caṇ* suffix is joined with *kaccit*, *yatra*, etc. The letter *ñ* in the negative particle *nañ* serves as a qualifier for the rule "there is elision of the *n* of *nañ*."

When it is stated that "there is elision of *n* [in the word] *naḥ*," Vāmanaputra asks: "Does this [elision] also apply here [in *vāmanaputraḥ*]? This is a partial fault. The rule "non-elision (*aluk*) when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*)" continues to apply. In that context, when the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), implied by the term "subsequent member," serves as the qualifier for *naḥ*, then since it is stated that there is elision of the *n* belonging to the preceding member, the elision does not apply here at all. However, if the preceding member is qualified by the word *naḥ* itself, then because the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the elision would indeed occur here as well.

Now, even if the rule "of *nañ*" (*nañaḥ*) were stated in this alternative view, why would [the suffix] not occur in the case of *straiṇaputra*? Because the suffix is not equivalent; the letter *ñ* serves its purpose in respect to the rules for vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and accentuation, whereas the particle (*nipāta*) does not. It is recited as *tathā*; it is an underived form (*avyutpanna*) used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and its initial acute accent is established by the *lit*-accent of the suffix *thāl*. Its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is also established by the rule "and a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that ends in all case-endings."

[Objection: But surely even for one who has not mastered the grammar, the status of these as "pratirūpaka" (counterparts) is already established by the rule *vibhaktipratirūpakāḥ*. [Response: True; the recitation is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). The same applies to forms such as *velāyām* and *mātrāyām*. Regarding the term "svarapratirūpakāḥ" (counterparts of vowels): examples include *ṛti*, *ṛ vā*, *vacanam*, and so forth. Their very existence is established through the provision of the technical name *nipāta* (particle); however, there is no further purpose in their being classified as *nipātas*.
*Padamañjarī*: *prādayaḥ* [1.4.58].

This rule (*yoga*) is separated from both the subsequent and the preceding rules. If, however, it were stated that "the *pra*-class [of words] are *upasargas* when in connection with a verb" (*prādaya upasargāḥ kriyāyoge*), this would not be possible; thus he says: "the making of a separate rule. The meaning is that this separation from the subsequent rule is for the purpose that the qualification "when in connection with a verb" (*kriyāyoge*) may apply only to the designation *upasarga* (and not to the subsequent designation). It should not apply to the designation *nipāta*.

Alternatively—having included the *prādis* (prefixes) within the *cādis* (conjunctions) themselves, for what purpose are they separated from the preceding rule? To this he replies: "The *upasargas* [are used] in connection with action. Regarding the phrase "of *vadis* etc.": here, the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ca* should be understood, thus it becomes "of *vadis* etc. An example is: *parā jayanti senāḥ* ("the armies conquer completely"). Here, *parā* means "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭāḥ*).

Or, because it exists as a substance (*dravyatva*) located there, the word *parā* [does not undergo elision] when situated there. However, where the singular number is read—as in "the army conquers" (*parā jayati senā*)—there it should be regarded as an example of form (*rūpa*); for, due to the elision of the case-ending by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*, and because the word *parā* is udātta on its first syllable.
*Padamañjarī*:
"Preverbs [are so called] when there is a connection with a verbal action. (Pāṇini 1.4.59)

In the term *kriyāyoge*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used; the compound is formed either by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) or by the rule "the agent or instrument [is compounded] with a *kṛt* suffix," due to the word *bahula* (in various cases). Alternatively, since there is a connection between the prefixes (*pra-* etc. and the verbal roots by means of the action (*kriyā*) functioning as the instrument, the compound is formed precisely with the third case in the sense of the instrument. Regarding *praṇayati*: the substitution of *ṇ* occurs according to the rule "after a prefix, even when not in a compound. Regarding *pranāyaka*: one might object that here too there is indeed a connection with the action of going (*gamikriyā*), and this is true; however—

Furthermore, particles such as *pra* and others are of this nature: namely, when a verb is explicitly heard (*śruta*), they qualify that very verb; but when no verb is heard, they imply a verb together with its means. In this context, by the force of the mention of "connection with an action" (*kriyāyoga*), the meaning becomes: "those particles beginning with *pra* which are connected with a particular action receive the designation 'preposition' (*upasarga*) with respect to that [action]. And here, the root *gam* is not employed with the same action that the particle beginning with *pra* is connected with; nor is that action connected with the root *gam* which is actually employed. Thus, there is no possibility of the application of the rule for the substitution of *ṇ*.

Regarding the word *marut*: only the designation *upasarga* (prefix) is intended here, not the designation *nipāta* (particle). For if that [designation as a particle] were present, the rule "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*) would apply, and by the rule "the third case in the sense of the object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*), the preceding member would retain its original accent (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). However, the word *marutta* is intended to be acute on the final syllable. Now, one might object: even if it has the designation *upasarga*, it would still be acute on the first syllable by the rule "prefixes, with the exception of *abhi*, are acute on the first syllable" (*upasargāścābhivarjam*); but this is not so.

By this rule, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is not prescribed as something new; rather, since the status [of *artha*] is already established by the rule "particles (*nipātāḥ*"), this is for the purpose of prohibiting it. Furthermore, if it were designated as a particle (*nipātasaṃjñā*), it would also receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyayasaṃjñā*). Now, why do these two rules—"*kiḥ* after a preverb (*upasarga*) before the root *dhā*" and "*kiḥ* after *ā* when a preverb precedes"—not apply? Because they are not expressed (*anabhidhānāt*).

Regarding the word *marutta*: when the *t* of the word *marut* undergoes doubling by the rule *anaci ca*, there arises a threefold form (*trairūpya*)—either by the elision of the middle *t* according to *jharo jhari*, or by the elision of both middle *t*s according to *jharo jhari*. But how can there be the substitution of *t* here, given that this [word] does not end in a vowel? To this he says: "By the force of the formulation of the technical name (*saṃjñāvidhāna-sāmarthyāt*). It has already been stated that there is no other purpose [for this]. However, in this way, in the case of *marunnayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* would also result even when there is an intervention by *t*; therefore, it is desired [that the substitution of *t* occurs] specifically in the rule for the substitution of *t*.

Regarding the word *śraddhā*: it is desired only for the purpose of forming an *aṅ* stem, for the *kvip* suffix does not apply here; thus he says—by the rule *ātaścopasarge*. It is established either by its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group or by the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in the list beginning with *prajñā-śraddhā-arcā*.
The *padamañjarī* and the *gati*. 1.4.60.

Because of the masculine gender indication in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, it is understood that *gati* is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ktic*; this suffix *ktic* is applied by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām*. Furthermore, due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the prohibition "there is no lengthening in *ktic*" does not apply here. Regarding the word *prakṛtyā*: because it functions as a *gati*, the accent of the verbal prefix (*kṛtsvara*) occurs; the compound itself is established simply because it begins with a prefix (*prādi*). Elsewhere than when preceded by a prefix, the formation of the compound is also a purpose [of using the *gati* designation]. In the word *prakṛtam*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*. As for the phrase *yat prakaroti*: [this illustrates the application of the same principle].

Regarding the accentuation of the finite verb (*tiṅ-lakṣaṇa*), although the rule "with particles [there is no accent]" (*nipātair yadyadi*) prohibits the *nighāta* (absence of accent), the suffix *tip* is unaccented because it is marked with *p*. The suffix (*vikaraṇa*) receives its accent as a *pratyaya-svara*, while the verbal root (*dhātu*) undergoes *śeṣanighāta* (remaining unaccented). Furthermore, by the rule "also when a finite verb is accompanied by an accented word" (*tiṅi codāttavati*), the prefix *pra-* is unaccented. These four purposes should be understood to apply everywhere in the section concerning the designation of *gati*s.

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of designations. The sense is that otherwise, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*) and because two designations would be prescribed for a single thing, there would be an option (*paryāya*). Regarding the word *kārikā*: its meaning is "action," "limit," or "establishment. Others say it means "effort"; [in this case] the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of indicating the root-meaning (*dhātvarthanirdeśa*). As for the word *kārikā* used in the sense of an agent—as in "the *kārikā* is a maidservant"—and that which denotes a verse (*śloka*), those two are not included here.

By the inclusion of *kriyāyoga*, the word *kārikā* is qualified; thus, by the inclusion of the occurrence of action (*kriyāvṛtti*), it refers to that which "performs" (*karoti*) the *kārikā*. Since it is a particle (*nipāta*), it is indeclinable (*avyaya*), and consequently, there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending.

Regarding the term *punarutsyūtam*: because it is a *gati* (a preverb), there is a compound; by the rule "a *gati* [is unaccented] before a *gati*," the *nighāta* (elision of accent) occurs. Although here the *śeṣanighāta* (the remaining parts being unaccented) is already established by the rule "and in the case of *pravṛddha* and others" which makes the final syllable of the second member udātta, nevertheless, the sense is that this very *nighāta* is more appropriate because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. And here in the case of *punarādheyam*: once the compound is formed because it is a *gati*, the word *dheya* becomes udātta on its first syllable by the rule "for words ending in *yat*, except *nau*," which is the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. In *canaḥ hitaḥ*: since the word *canaḥ* is a particle (*nipāta*) and is udātta on its first syllable, the preceding *gati* retains its natural accent according to the rule "a *gati* that is not separated [by another word] [retains its accent]."
*Padamañjarī*:
"The particles beginning with *ūry-* [are indeclinables], as are those formed by the suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc*. (Pāṇini 1.4.61)

"Ending in *cvī* and ending in *ḍāc*. Although it was indicated by the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in") in the definition of the technical term *pada* that "when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical term, there is no extension [of the rule] to what ends with that suffix," nevertheless, the intention is that there is an inclusion of what ends in those suffixes because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase "in connection with a verb" (*kriyāyoge*). For a mere suffix cannot be connected with a verb, since it is itself devoid of meaning due to being a *svārthika* (suffix denoting its own base-meaning), and because *cvī* is not audible [as a distinct element]. "In connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*" means...

Not only that, but the employment of the term *saṃpadya* occurs elsewhere as well; for it is not the case that one says "it becomes *urī*" (*urī saṃpadyate*). Because words beginning with *auṣaṭ* and ending with *svāhā* are listed among the *cādayaḥ*, they possess the status of particles (*nipāta*) even when not joined with a verb. Since the word *āviḥ* is listed among the *sākṣātprabhṛtayaḥ*, there is an option regarding its connection with the root *kṛ*; however, when connected with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, it is obligatory by this very rule.

How then [should one explain] such verses as: "That passion became manifest, as it were," and "The two tongues, flickering, became manifest, licking the streams from both corners of the mouth simultaneously"? Poets are independent [in their usage]. Regarding the form *śuklīkṛtya*: the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *asya cvau*. The word *paṭapaṭā* has been derived under the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ*.
*Padamañjarī*:
An imitation [of a sound] that does not end in *it* [is treated as a word]. 1.4.62.

The word *itiḥ* [is used] because it is that from which [something] follows (*itiḥ paro yasmāt*). A genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*), however, was not adopted due to the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇābhāvāt*). Consequently, [the designation of *gati*] occurs even when *itiḥ* follows [the word], as in the case of *khāṭkṛtya*. [For example: *khāḍiti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat* ("Having made the sound 'khāṭ', he spat"). Here, if the prohibition were absent, there would be a *samāsa* (compound) due to the technical designation *gati*, and since the usage would have to follow immediately after the verbal root (*dhātu*), this very form would not be established. [In *niraṣṭhīvat*: the root is] *ṣṭhivu* "to spit," and the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti*. For what purpose is the mention of the past tense (*bhūtakāla*)? This usage of a certain poet has been cited as an example: *naṣṭvā ca rājye saha putra-dārair bhrājiṣṇunā śārada-candra-lekhā- prabhā-prasādena virājamānam dadarśa dhīmān sa vanecara-stham.* "And having perished in his kingdom along with his sons and wife, the wise man saw him standing in the forest, shining with the radiant splendor of the autumnal crescent moon."* [Note: The commentary explains that if the rule did not apply to the past tense, the *gati*-designation would trigger compounding, resulting in an incorrect form.]
"Intent on kissing her, he spat out his own loosened tooth from his mouth with a 'khāḍ' sound, having touched the root of her tongue. —
*Padamañjarī*
In the case of respect and disrespect, [the suffixes] sat and asat [are applied]. 1.4.63.

"Excitement of joy" (*prītisaṃbhrama*) means a haste preceded by joy, directed toward such acts as rising to meet someone. "Indifference due to contempt" (*paribhavaudāsīnya*) means neglecting what ought to be done, such as rising to meet someone, out of disdain. Why is the inclusion of the term *asat* (unreal/false) necessary? It is so that [the rule] may apply even in the case of *asatkṛtya*. [Objection: Let there not be the designation *gati* for the word *asat*; rather, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) will occur with *satkṛtya*. [Response: This is not possible.

Since the word *sat* exists [as a separate element], it would override the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix and instead result in an acute accent on the first syllable by virtue of the natural accent of the initial member when it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). However, in the case of *asatkṛtam*, once the accent of the word *satkṛta* has applied according to the rule "an immediate preverb [has the acute accent]" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), that same accent remains even after the subsequent negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Furthermore, even when the word *asat* is compounded with the word *kṛta*, because *asat* is a particle (*nipāta*) and thus acutely accented on its first syllable, and because it functions as a preverb (*gati*), it retains its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*); thus, there is no difference in the resulting accent.

Furthermore, in this context, in the expression *yadasatkaroti*, the word *asat* would not undergo the *nighāta* (anudātta accent), nor would it receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*); therefore, the designations of "gati" and "nipāta" must be sought for the word *asat* itself. Moreover, the rule of extension to that which ends with [the stem] (*tadantavidhi*) cannot be applied here by means of the word *sat*, because there is no qualifying element (*viśeṣya*).

But surely, let the designation *sa-* belong to the word *sat* itself; then, in the rules concerning grammatical operations (*kāryapradeśa*), there will be an extension of the designation to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*) because of what is under discussion (*prakṛta*). Indeed, in the case of the designation *avyaya*, there is already such an extension—as in *paramoccais*. Just as in the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, the term *sup* (referring to a nominal ending) applies even though *sup* has ceased [to be mentioned] in its own context, and it qualifies [the preceding element] through its inclusion therein—as in *gatiranantaraḥ*, where *pūrvapada* is the subject under discussion, and in *gatirgatau*, where *pada* is likewise the subject under discussion.

Let it be that the grammatical operation occurs by the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application to that which ends with the specified term); however, from where does the understanding of "disrespect" (*anādara*) come? If the mention of "disrespect" were not present, then because of the negation of respect in the phrase "neither existent nor non-existent" (*na sadasat*), it would not be possible at all; for there would only be the contingency of [mere] respect. Furthermore, in the case of "having shown disrespect to the teacher" (*gurumasatkṛtya*), it would not apply to "having shown disrespect to a Caṇḍāla. Just as the term "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) refers only to a Kṣatriya and so forth, and not to a clod of earth or the like, so too, when the mention of "disrespect" is present, it is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one in whom respect is absent is 'disrespectful' (*anādara*)."

Since a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs in the sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), in the sense of the non-existence of what was expected (*prasaktābhāva*), and in the sense of the non-existence of what was not expected (*aprasaktābhāva*), the designation is established in all cases. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "anādara" (disrespect) is unnecessary. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "asat" (non-existent) could also be omitted. Let it simply be "sat" for both respect and disrespect. In that case, just as in the expression "goṣpadaṃ sevitam" (a cow's footprint frequented), the word "goṣpada" does not apply when it is not frequented—thus the inclusion of "asevita" is for the sake of excluding the case of non-frequencing—so too, since the word "sat" does not apply in the sense of disrespect, the inclusion of "anādara" will serve the purpose of the word "asat."
"Having honored" and "not having honored": the word *sat* signifies either that which is beautiful or that which exists; the word *asat* signifies the opposite of that.
The *Padamañjarī* is sufficient as an ornament for [this] work. 1.4.64.

"Alam" signifies prohibition, and so forth. For example: *alaṃ kṛtvā* (having done enough), *alaṃ bhoktum* (to eat enough), *alaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats enough), and *alaṃ karoti kanyām* (he makes [her] a maiden).
In *Padamañjarī*, [the rule] "antaraparigrahe" (Pāṇini 1.4.65).

"Having struck within" (*antarhatvā*) means "having struck in the middle. Regarding the word *antaḥ* and so forth: this was not stated specifically under the heading of the technical term *upasarga* (preverb), with the thought that "I shall explain this in connection with the word *antaḥ*. And when the designation *upasarga* is indeed applied, then just as in the case of *antarṇayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *antarhaṇyāt* and *antarhaṇanam*—by the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* ("the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for *han* when preceded by *a* other than *pūrva")—is established. Furthermore, in the case of *antarayaṇam*, it is established by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* alone. Therefore, the two rules *antaradeśe* and *ayanaṃ ca* should be understood as intended to prohibit [the application of the aforementioned rules] when the location is inside.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffix *kaṇ* is applied after the words *manas*] when combined with *śraddhā* (faith) and *pratighāta* (hostility). 1.4.66.

The word *kaṇe* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling a locative case ending, used in the sense of an intense longing. Because of its association with it, the word *manaḥ* should also be understood as functioning in the sense of longing. The phrase *kaṇehatya* means "having longed intensely until its cessation, he drinks. This is what [the author] states with the word *tāvat*. The meaning is that "faith is struck down" (or interrupted). This requires the completion of the phrase *iti yāvad asya*. In the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the word *kaṇe* refers to a minute particle of rice (*pūkṣma-taṇḍulāvayava*) acting as a locus; the word *manaḥ* likewise refers to the mind (*cetas*).
The word *padamañjarī* is an indeclinable when used in the sense of "before. (Pāṇini 1.4.67)

The word *puraḥ* ending with the suffix *asi* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). According to the rule *pūrvādharāvārāṇāmasipuradhavaścaiṣām*, the suffix *asi* is applied; the word *pūrva* undergoes the substitution *pur*; it receives the designation of indeclinable by the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhakti*; and the *s* in place of the *visarga* is a conventional usage (*upacāra*). Regarding *puraskṛtya*: the meaning is "having placed in front. [Examples are] *pūḥ*, *purau*, and *puraḥ kṛtvā*. This serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) here.

However, the mention of the other two [cases] is for the purpose of demonstrating that, due to their association with that [word], "puras" ends in the suffix *śas* and is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*). In this context, the substitution of *s* (satva) does not occur by the rule "namaspurasorgatyoḥ," nor does a compound formation take place.
And [the word] *astaṃ* [is used with the accusative]. 1.4.68.

Regarding the word *astaṃ*: it is derived from the root *as* in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*), with the suffix *niṣṭhā*. By the rule *udito vā*, the optionality of the *iṭ* augment is established, and by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies. Now, one might object: since this word is formed according to grammatical rules (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), the [prohibition of *iṭ*] does not apply here even without it; so what is the purpose of the continued mention of the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*)? To this we reply: in that case, it is made known that the word *astaṃ* is an indeclinable. For it is not recited among the *ca*-group (the list of particles) or among the *svarādi* group (the list beginning with *svara*).
*Padamañjarī*:
[The rule] "accha" applies to roots meaning "to go" and those ending in "-vad". (Pāṇini 1.4.69)

In the case of *accheti*, it is an onomatopoeic expression given without a case ending because the case suffix has been elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. It means "facing toward" (*ābhimukhye*). In *acchodyotī*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to its belonging to the *yajādi* group; thus, *udakamacchaṃ gacchati* means "it goes toward clear water," that is, "it goes toward water that is not turbid."
*Padamañjarī*:
"After *ad*, [the substitution of *ṭā* for *ṅi*] does not occur when there is no instruction [to that effect]. (1.4.70)
"Instruction is for the sake of others"—this implies the employment of speech. "Having performed this"—the meaning is: having reflected for oneself that "this is what ought to be done."
*Padamañjarī*:
[The term *tiras* is used] in the sense of disappearance (*antarddhi*). 1.4.71.

Regarding the word *tirobhūya*: its purpose is [to illustrate] the accentuation of compounds (*samāsa*) and primary derivatives (*kṛtsvara*). In the form *tirobhūtam*, since the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Furthermore, in the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the term "object" (*karman*) is understood from the preceding context; therefore, the accentuation of the compound (*samāsa*) and the accentuation of the suffix *thādi* are the purposes here. In the form *tiro bhūtvā*, the meaning is "having become situated at the side" (*pārśvato bhūtvā*).
The *padamañjarī* states that [the suffix *kvip*] is applied after the root *kṛñ* when followed by the word *vibhāṣā*. (Pāṇini 1.4.72)

Regarding the word *tiraskṛtya*: the substitution of *s* [for *t*] occurs by the rule *tiraso 'nyatarasyām*. However, it does not occur in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), because in that case the distinction between the action being imitated (*anukārya*) and the imitation itself (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed; thus, there is an absence of case endings in the sūtra.
*padamañjarī*:
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after [the words] *upāja* and *anvāja*. (Pāṇini 5.2.30)
And [the suffixes] *sākṣāt*, *pramṛti*, and so forth [govern the genitive]. 1.4.74.

Regarding the rule *sākṣāt-prabhṛtiṣu*: this is for the purpose that when something not directly manifest (*asākṣād-bhūta*) is made manifest (*sākṣāt-kriyate*), the suffix should apply; whereas when something already manifest (*sākṣād-bhūta*) is merely produced in another form, it should not. This should also be understood to apply to words beginning with *mithyā*. And this is obtained because of its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*); for instance, when "made manifest" (*sākṣāt-kṛtam*) is said, the production of that very form which was heard [in the source] is understood, and not the production of another form not heard.

[Objection: Even if there is no intention to express the *prakṛti* (base form), that very same form is understood as the instrument (*karaṇa*), yet it does not possess the function of the sense of *cv-*; therefore, the mention of the sense of *cv-* must indeed be made [in the rule]. [Question:

Why then does this option not also apply to words ending in *cv-* such as *sākṣāt* and others? [Reply: Let it be so; since this [option] is set aside, by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānāt*), the rule "after *ūry-ādi* and *ciḍāc*" will apply. [Objection: This cannot be possible, for then even the prescribed substitution of the final *m* for words like *lavaṇa* would occur in those ending in *cv-*.

In this way, substitutes such as *lavaṇa* ending in *-m* will be applied to words like *lavaṇa*. In that case, since a word modified by the substitution of a single part is not considered different from the original, if the substitute *lavaṇam* is optionally applied even to the word *lavaṇī*, there is no fault; for our goal is to establish three forms—*lavaṇaṃ kṛtya*, *lavaṇaṃ kṛtvā*, and *lavaṇīkṛtya*—and this is accomplished in this manner.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, says that "the state of ending in *m* is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). He considers that, among forms ending in *cvi*, the designation [of the word as a particle] is obligatory by virtue of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), whereas the irregularity consisting of the state of ending in *m* is applied optionally. Words such as *agnau* and *vaśe* are particles (*nipāta*) that resemble case-endings; for the words *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ*, the optionality is obtained because they belong to the *ūry-ādi* group.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The rule] *anatyādhāne urasimanasī* (Pāṇini 1.4.75) [is explained as follows].
The words *uras* and *manasi* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). "Having taken to heart" (*urasikṛtya*) means having accepted; "having brought to mind" (*manasikṛtya*) means having ascertained.
In the *Padamañjarī*, [the term] *pada* refers to both a word and a statement. 1.4.76.

"In *madhye* and *pade*, and in *nivacane*. This is an indication [of the forms] without case endings (*avibhaktika*). The words *madhye* and *pade* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). *Nivacana* means the absence of speech. In this regard, due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), they end in the vowel *e*; however, this is not the locative case (*saptamī*). [The sense is] "having restrained one's speech" (*vācaṃ niyamya*). They say that the rule of formation (*nipātana*) applies without distinction based on the explanation, and it is not restricted to the technical term (*saṃjñā*) "silence" (*nivacana*), because it has been cited as such [in the examples].
The word *padamañjarī* [is used] in the sense of "always," "in the hand," "in the palm," and "at marriage. (Pāṇini 1.4.77)

Regarding the term *dārakarma* (the act of taking a wife): others, however, maintain that it refers merely to the act of formal acceptance (*svīkaraṇa*). In the phrase "having taken the great weapons in hand" (*hastekṛtya mahāstrāṇi*), the words *hasta* and *pāṇi* are both indeclinable particles (*nipāta*).
*Padamañjarī*:
[The term] *prādhvam* [is used] in the sense of binding. (Pāṇini 1.4.78)

"It is an indeclinable ending in the letter *m*," because it is listed among the *cādi* group. "It occurs in the sense of favorability (*ānukūlya*). Therefore, the meaning "the word *prādhvam* occurring in the sense of binding" does not hold. If one asks, "In that case, how is there a connection with [the word] 'binding' (*bandhane*)?", he says: "That... [referring to the verse]. Regarding "in binding": the connection with the word *prādhvam* is mediated by the sense of the locative absolute (*satsaptamī*); the point is that when there is favorability in the presence of binding, that favorability is caused by the binding.

Regarding the expression *prādhvaṃ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having made [him] compliant, he departed"): *prādhvaḥ* means "set out on the road. This is a compound formed according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe* ("*ati* and others [form compounds] in the sense of having traversed, etc."). The suffix *ac* prescribed by the rule *upasargādadhvanaḥ* does not apply here precisely because the word is technical (lākṣaṇika). Therefore, they explain that this is the usage of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) itself, and that the "compliance" (*ānukūlya*) is not intended to be caused by a bond (*bandhana*).
The words *padamañjarī*, *jīvikā*, and *upaniṣad* [are used] in the sense of a simile. (Pāṇini 1.4.79)

*Jīvikā* means a means of livelihood; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) according to the rule "in the sense of a technical term" (*saṃjñāyām*). Alternatively, from the causative root *sad*, with the prefix *upa-ni*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "after *sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, etc. (*satsūdviṣa*), and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule "after *sad*, except when preceded by *pra*" (*sadiraprateḥ*). Thus, *upaniṣad* refers to the secret knowledge produced by Vedānta, or the portion of the Veda that is Vedānta. Regarding *aupamyam*: that by which something is compared is *upamā*; the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "after a vowel ending in *ā*, when a prefix follows" (*ātaścopasarge*). The state of being that is *aupamyam*.

This is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*). Due to the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) based on the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, those two [words] which terminate in the object of comparison become the domain of the comparison (*aupamyaviṣaya*). [The examples are] *jīvikākṛtya* and *upaniṣatkṛtya*. The meaning is: "having made it like a livelihood" (*jīvikām iva kṛtvā*) and "having made it like a secret doctrine" (*upaniṣadam iva kṛtvā*). Although a compound with a *gati* is obligatory, nevertheless, when the word *iva* is employed, such a sentence-form indeed occurs because the word retains its own primary sense.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffixes] *te* and so forth [occur] before the verbal root (1.4.80).

This is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Furthermore, would that restriction be a restriction regarding technical names (*saṃjñā-niyama*), or a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga-niyama*)? In that regard, if it were a restriction regarding technical names, then by the word *te* (they), the items beginning with *pra* and ending with *upaniṣad* would be referred to by their own forms, not by a form qualified by the technical names "gati" or "upasarga," because those two technical names have not yet been established. This is because those two [names] are prescribed by the preceding sūtras which have attained syntactic unity with this one.

The meaning is that these particles, beginning with *pra* and ending with *upaniṣad*, when employed before the verbal root, receive the technical designation of "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*). However, in the rule governing their usage, those which have already acquired the designations of "motion" and "preverb" are referred to; the meaning is that those bearing the designations of "motion" and "preverb" must be employed only before the verbal root.

In that case, under the first alternative, there would be a reflection (*parāmarśa*) by way of their own form for particles such as *ca* and so on, just as there is for particles such as *pra* and so on; consequently, there would also be a restriction regarding the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "particle" (*nipāta*). Furthermore, even if it were a restriction specifically concerning the designations "gati" and "upasarga," the statement would still be purposeless; for it is only in actual usage that those [designations] are not desired for what precedes [the verb], but nothing undesirable occurs regarding the designation when they are employed before [the verb].

The two forms of the rule—"in the Vedic language [a suffix is applied] even when followed by another word" and "even when separated"—are redundant; for while the very designation (*saṃjñā*) of those [elements] that are followed by or separated from another is prohibited, their usage (*prayoga*) is not. Nor does that [prohibition] prescribe a designation, as it would serve no purpose.

Furthermore, the mention of "not followed by *iti*" (*anitiparam*) in the rule *anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam* would be purposeless; for in the example *khāḍiti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat*, the designation of "gati" is indeed prohibited for the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) that is separated [from the verb], yet who could prevent its usage? If, however, this were a restriction on usage, the imitation would have to be used only before the verbal root and not when separated by the word *iti*; thus, one would have to say *anitiparam*. Therefore, considering that this is properly a restriction on usage, he says: "those [words] receive the designations of *gati* and *upasarga*."

Now, even in this view, why does the reference by the word *te* not also include particles (*nipāta*)? Because they are separated [from the preceding rule]. How, then, is there a reference to prefixes (*upasarga*)? Prefixes are not referred to by that [same] form; rather, they are referred to by way of their being "motion" (*gati*), since they too possess the nature of motion. It is with this very intention that prefixes are mentioned separately in the Vṛtti. But particles such as *ca* and so on are not referred to in this manner, and thus they are not included.

But surely, where in common usage there is a confusion of forms—such as using *gauḥ* and *gāvī*—there the treatise is purposeful for the sake of discerning the correct word (*sādhu*). However, where usage is entirely unconfused, there is no function for the treatise; nor does anyone ever employ *pra* when they ought to use *pacati*, such as saying *prapacati* instead of *pacati*.

Although no such reversed usage is observed in common worldly speech (*loka*), since such usage separated by another word is seen in the Vedic language (*chandas*), one might suspect that the same usage could occur even in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*). Indeed, even today, the usage of the word *āviḥ* with *gati* status separated by another word in the colloquial language is shown in the rule concerning *ūry-ādi* (Pāṇini 1.4.61).

Furthermore, in the case of *kūlamudvahaḥ* from the rule *udi kūle rujivahoḥ*, since both *udi* and *kūla* are indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*), they would both be considered *upapadas*. Consequently, once the compound is formed, one might expect them to be placed optionally at the beginning according to the rule *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam*. Therefore, this [rule] must be stated to establish the priority and posteriority of elements when there is a conjunction of *upasarjanas*.

If this is so, then regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhūkṛñoḥ*: in examples such as *sukhena kaṭaḥ kriyate* ("the mat is made with ease") and *sukaṭaṃkarāṇi vīraṇāni* ("the vīraṇa grasses make a mat easily"), or *duṣkaṭaṃkarāṇi*, the application of *su* and *dus* before the verbal root (*prāgdhātoḥ*) would result in the form *kaṭaṃ sukarāṇi*. What, then, would be the purpose of the inclusion of the marker *khi* in the suffix *khal*? For it is stated that the augment *muṭ* applies to non-indicative (*anavyaya*) words; however, by the force of the marker *khi*, let it apply even to an indeclinable. Alternatively, according to the principle "when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, it includes a word preceded by a preverb (*gati*) or a kāraka," the change will occur for *kaṭa* when followed by the word *sukara*; yet, an effort must be made here [to justify this].

The mention of the "root" (*dhātu*) would be purposeless. Why? Because when there is an expectation for what comes before, it would be understood as "before that [element] with which the prefixes (*pra* etc. are connected. This cannot be so; for in cases such as *precchati* ("he asks") and *pracikīrṣati* ("he desires to do"), since the prefix *pra* is connected with the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), the prefix *pra* would have to be employed immediately before the suffix itself. However, because of the mention of the "root," the prefix is employed immediately before the root *cikīrṣati* itself.

Regarding the statement "the mention of *te* (them) is for the sake of including the prepositions (*upasarga*"): one might object that if *pra* and the others were only designated as prepositions (*upasarga*) and lacked the designation of "gati," then—in the absence of the mention of *te*—only those [words] immediately preceding would be connected [to the rule], namely the *gatis*, and not the prepositions; therefore, the mention of *te* would have to be made for that purpose. However, they [the prepositions] are also designated as *gatis*. Consequently, even when there is a connection with the immediately preceding *gatis*, the inclusion of *pra* and the others is already established precisely because they possess the status of being *gatis*.

It might be argued: "If the mention of *te* (the suffix *ta*) were not there, then this designation of *gati* would apply only to those [words] that possess exclusively the designation of *gati*, but not to *pra* and the others which possess both designations. This is not so, because there is no such thing as a *gati* that is exclusive [of the other]. But is it not the case that this rule exists: "*anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam*" ("and a mimicry [word], provided it is not followed by *iti*")? No; for that too is a *nipāta*. It is said in reply: if, in the absence of the mention of *te*, there were a requirement for what has been introduced [in the preceding rules], then only a few [words] would be connected [to it], and not all those ending with the *upasargas*.

However, by the logic of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*), when there is a requirement for many [terms], there is no reason for the process to terminate solely with the *pra*-group; thus, the *ca*-group would also be required. But when "them" (*te*) is mentioned, because the designation *gati* follows immediately after it, the reference is made in that form not to only a few [of them], but it pervades even the *pra*-group while simultaneously excluding the *ca*-group. Therefore, the mention of "them" (*te*) is for the purpose of including the prepositions (*upasarga*). The meaning is: so that it may apply to those ending with "them," and so that it may apply to those [prepositions] alone.

Regarding the phrase "the destinies are indeed immediate": the sense is that only those which are immediately following would be grasped, on account of their proximity. However, as for the fault [that would arise] if there were a universal pervasion (*vyāpti*), it has not been explicitly stated because it is easily understood.
In the *Padamañjarī*, it is stated that in Vedic usage, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs even when [the following word] is subsequent (*pare*). 1.4.81.
"And not of others" means that even the case of "motion in motion" is impossible, because [the opponent] considers that only solitary entities belonging to another [category] are ever observed.
*Padamañjarī*:
"And [the rule] 1.4.82 applies even when [words] are separated."

Since the primary application of directional terms (*dik-śabda*) is to that which is not separated [by another word], this statement is intended for the usage of those [terms] when they are separated, both before and after [the noun]. For this very reason, there is no usage of separated [directional terms] in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*).

How then is there the application [of the rule] when a *gati* is separated by an intervention—as in the cases "he rescues" (*abhyuddharati*) and "he cites" (*samudāharati*)? A member of the same class does not constitute an intervention. For example, when asked, "Are these two in an adjacent Brāhmaṇa family?", one replies, "Not adjacent; a Vṛṣala family lies between them," thereby pointing out a member of a different class as the intervening factor. Alternatively, because they share a common basis in their genus (*jāti*), there is no intervention. And thus, the mention of "adjacent" (*anantara*) regarding a *gati*, the statement "a *gati* [is elided] before a *gati*," and the usage "he approaches" (*abhipraiti*) all become logically consistent.
*Padamañjarī*:
The *karmapravacanīya*s [are now discussed]. 1.4.83.

The plural number is used because there are many of the technical terms (*saṃjñins*) to be mentioned hereafter, as in the cases of "particles" (*nipātāḥ*) and "gerundives" (*kṛtyāḥ*). In some instances, however, the singular is used by intending to express the category in general, as in "also a *gati*," "an affix" (*pratyayaḥ*), and "a primary suffix" (*kṛt*). The formation of these "great technical terms" (*mahāsaṃjñās*) is for the purpose of understanding them as descriptive terms (*anvarthasaṃjñā*); that is, those which have expressed an action (*kriyā*) are called *karmapravacanīyas*. In this case, the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule "the gerundive and *lyuṭ* are used diversely."

And who have declared [the existence of] *karmapravacanīyas*? They are those which, when a verbal action (*kriyāpada*) is being employed—as in "the blanket is experienced" (*anubhūyate kambalaḥ*) and so forth—have indicated a specific action, but do not now indicate a specific action; what then? A specific relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*), as for example: "It rained following Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*. For here, the prefix *anu* does not indicate a specific action as it does in "it is experienced" (*anubhūyate*) and so on, because of the absence of a verbal action; nor does it express a mere relation like the genitive case does in the word "*saṃhitām*."

This is because the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) has that [purpose] as its meaning. Nor does it imply a verbal action, as in the case of "he draws a line around the *prādeśa*" (*prādeśaṃ viparilikhati*), where the word *vi-* implies the action of measuring (*vimāna*), such that one measures the *prādeśa* and then draws the line. For if that were the case, there would be the consequence of a case-ending denoting a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), just as in the word *prādeśam*; or else, there would be the consequence of the cognition of a residual relation (*śeṣasambandha*). Thus, the second case-ending expresses a residual relation between the *anu* and the raining together; it establishes that [relation] within a specific context.

Because the relationship is understood through its presence—either by way of the relation between cause and effect or by being produced from a specific action—having perceived the *saṃhitā*, one understands: "It rained. And it has been said:
"This [sandhi] is neither an indicator of an action, nor an expresser of a relationship, nor even an attractor of a verbal form for an action; rather, it is a differentiator of the relationship."

In some cases, however, this technical designation (saṃjñā) is applied by the force of the rule itself even in the absence of an occasion for its application (pravṛttinimitta), as in the rules "suḥ pūjāyām" and "atiratikramaṇe ca."
*Padamañjarī*:
"The [prefix] *anu* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). (Pāṇini 1.4.84)

"Yāvatā": the word *yāvatā* is a particle (*nipāta*) meaning "nanu" (indeed/not so); others say it means "anya" (other). [The rule] is established by the phrase "in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), or in the expression of a state of being (*itthambhūtākhyāna*). In that regard, the mention of *anu* must necessarily be made so that [the suffix *kṛt*] may apply in cases such as the expression of a state of being. Furthermore, the mention of *lakṣaṇa* is for the sake of *prati* and so forth; therefore, since it is common to other meanings and other technical designations (*saṃjñā*), let that [general term] suffice, and this [specific rule] need not be formulated—this is the intended meaning. In the phrase "but for the sake of the causal meaning (*hetvartha*)," the word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position.

*Hetuḥ* means the cause (*karaṇa*); *arthaḥ* means the purpose (*prayojana*), that is to say, the motive for this statement. Now, one might object: "In both that [previous rule] and here, only the term 'characteristic' (*lakṣaṇa*) is employed. Therefore, if the cause is not a characteristic, it would not be included here either; but if it is a characteristic, then there is no need for this [separate mention] even in that [previous rule]. To this he says: "The instrumental case [is used] for the cause" (*hetutṛtīyām iti*). This is true: that by which something is characterized is a characteristic—a mark or an indicator. Furthermore, a cause, being the basis for the certain comprehension of a specific effect, is indeed a characteristic.

It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "A cause (*hetu*) is also pervaded by the definition (*lakṣaṇa*); however, it is not necessarily that which defines [the object] again and again. What then? Even that which serves as a cause even once is a definition. But, according to the principle of *yena nāprāpte*, when used with a *karmapravacanīya*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is an exception specifically to the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*).

Furthermore, the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the particles *anu*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *itthaṃbhūta* finds its scope in cases where [the particle] is not a cause (*hetu*), as in "lightning flashes near the tree" (*vṛkṣamanu vidyotate*). The scope of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) expressing a cause finds its scope in cases such as "the family [is distinguished] by wealth" (*dhanena kulam*). However, when the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself a cause, there arises a conflict between both rules; in that case, the third case would prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules. To ensure that the second case (*dvitīyā*) prevails even over that, the rule for the designation must be restated. Because it is established on a different level of application, the second case indeed sublates the third. And it has been said: "When the connection between cause and effect is delimited by *anu*..."
"From its very inception, the third case [marking] the sense of cause (hetu) is sublated once it has been reached.

By the phrase "the meaning of the third case," however, one must state that—according to the maxim of the prior exception—it is specifically the rule "when joined with *saha*, the non-primary [factor takes the third case]" that is sublated, and not the third case used in the sense of cause.
*Padamañjarī* [on] *Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.2: "In the sense of the third case."

Regarding the expression *nadīmanvavasita*: here, the meaning of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is that of accompaniment (*saha*). The word is derived from the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind") preceded by the prefixes *anu* and *ava*, with the suffix *kta* used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The *Padamañjarī* [is] on the [sūtra] beginning with *hīne*. 1.4.86.

Regarding the statement "the technical term *saṃjñā* [applies] in the case of a relationship between the inferior and the superior": however, the case-ending associated with a *karmapravacanīya* applies only to that which is being distinguished as superior, not to the inferior, due to the inherent incapacity of the expression. Since the relationship residing in both [terms] is expressed by a single second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not apply.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffix *kan* is applied] also after a word meaning "exceeding" (*upo’dhika*). 1.4.87.

In this case as well, since an "additional" (adhika) cannot exist without that which is "more than" it (adhikin), the designation is prescribed for the relationship between the "additional" and the "more than. Furthermore, the case-ending (vibhakti) belongs only to the "more than" (adhikin), not to the "additional" (adhika). For example: *upakhāryo droṇaḥ* ("A droṇa more than a khārī"). The word *khārī* belongs to the *gaurādi* group [and thus takes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*]. The meaning is: there is a *khārī*, and there is also a *droṇa* in addition to it. The locative case (*saptamī*) is used according to the rule *yasmād adhikam*.

The words *apa* and *pari* [are used] in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). This means "by that which is being expressed through the subject matter under discussion. In the example *pari trigarttebhyaḥ*, the ablative case is applied by the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*; furthermore, the doubling [of *pari*] occurs by the rule *parervarjane*. Even though the exclusion is already indicated by the karmapravacanīya [particle] together with the ablative case, the doubling still takes place because both rules have the force of a mandatory injunction.

In *pariṣiñcati*, *pari* signifies "on all sides" (*sarvato bhāve*); since this [term *pari*] lacks the technical designation [of a preposition] in this context, it retains the status of a prefix (*upasarga*), and thus the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*, while the nasal augment *num* is added by the rule *śe mucādīnām*.
*Padamañjarī*: [The rule] *āṅ maryādāvacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.89).

*Maryādaḥ* refers to humans whose nature is subject to death; the suffix *ya* here is of the *auṇādika* class. That which is taken up by them is *maryādā*. The suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, *maryādā* means a limit (*avadhi*). Now, one might object: where a limit is connected with the action itself, that is *abhividhi* (inclusiveness); where it is not, that is *maryādā* (exclusivity). However, a limit (*avadhi*) is common to both. How, then, can a limit be defined as *maryādā*? This is not the meaning here—that whatever is a limit is *maryādā*. Rather, the meaning is: whatever is *maryādā* is a limit. It is called "the grasping of the word" (*vacanagrahaṇāt*).

Although it would have been sufficient to say "here, in the sense of a limit" (*iha maryādāyām*), the word "utterance" (*vacana*) is included for this specific purpose: so that it may be understood thus—"that in which something is spoken" is an utterance; thus, "the utterance of a limit" (*maryādāyā vacanam*) is a compound formed with a genitive case in the objective sense (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). Where the word *maryādā* is used [in Pāṇini’s rule] as in "āṅ in the senses of limit and inclusion" (*āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*), the inclusion of the prefix *āṅ* implies that it also functions in the sense of "inclusion" (*abhividhi*); therefore, here too, there is an inclusion of the sense of inclusion.

Alternatively—the capacity of the term *vacana* (word) implies that the internal subdivisions are not intended to be expressed; rather, the mere limit (*avadhi*) is grasped. In the example *ā mathurāyāḥ*, the phrase *vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it has rained") is required. [The word] *mathurā* is derived from the root *manth* (meaning "to churn") with the *auṇādika* suffix *kurac*. [The mention of *vacana*] is so that [the rule] might not apply in the sense of "slightness" (*īṣadartha*) or in connection with a verbal action (*kriyāyoga*). As for sentences (*vākya*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*), there is no application [of the rule] precisely because they are marked as *aṅit*. In that regard, in the sense of slightness, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) does not occur after *ā* in *ā kaḍāraḥ*; in connection with a verbal action, because it is a compound (*samāhāra*), the elision (*nighāta*) occurs by the rule *gatir gatau*.
*Padamañjarī*:

"In the sense of characterization (*lakṣaṇa*), stating a particular state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), a portion (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vīpsā*), [the prepositions] *prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are karmapravacanīyas]. (Pāṇini 1.4.90)

That by which something is characterized is a *lakṣaṇa*—a mark or indicator. This particular mode (*prakāra*) is "thus" (*ittham*). In this context, however, because there is no proximate object to be referred to by the pronoun *idam* (which would take the suffix *thamu* to form *ittham*), the word *ittham* functions solely to denote a specific mode. The root *bhū* is used in the sense of "attaining" (*prāptau*) and is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); according to the rule "optionally up to *dhṛṣ*" (*ā dhṛṣādvā*), since the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent, the past passive participle (*kta*) is formed in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as the root has the meaning of motion.

Therefore, from the indeclinable word *ittham*, because it assumes the quality of a substantive (*sattvadharmopādāna*) in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule *śritādiṣu gamyādīnām*. One who has attained a certain state is *itthaṃbhūta*; the description of one who has thus become is *itthaṃbhūtākhyānam*. A part that is being accepted is a *bhāga*; however, when the term is used in the sense of a mere portion, as in "a portion of *priyaṅgu*," that is due to its similarity to a share (*bhāgasāddaśyāt*).

"Distributive repetition" (*vīpsā*) is the desire to pervade; this will be explained in the eighth [chapter] under the section on the sixth case. These items, beginning with "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), are not the meanings of *prati* and the others in the same way that "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) and "proximity" (*samīpa*) are the meanings of indeclinables. What then? They are indicated as the domain of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) for *prati* and the others. Thus he says: "and when distributive repetition is the domain. This [phrase] should also be connected with "characteristic" and the others by changing the gender. For example: *vṛkṣaṃ prati*.

In this case, the tree is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) of the lightning flash; however, [the commentators] establish that the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) is produced by the action of reaching (*prāpti*). Thus they state: "having reached the tree, it flashes"; the meaning is "it flashes in the region of the tree. Regarding the example *sādhu* ("good"): here too, the relationship between the object and the subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is indeed produced by the action of reaching—just as when the tree is seen, the flashing is indicated—and thus there is no occurrence of incorrectness (*asādhutva*) here; for this reason, the term *itthambhūtākhyāna* ("description of being in such a state") is included.

Regarding "yadatra mām": the meaning is "let that which is my share be given to me. Here, the relationship between owner and owned is produced by the act of acceptance (*svīkaraṇa*). Regarding "vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam": the repetition (*vīpsā*) is indicated by the doubling of the word. The prefix *pari*, however, is connected only with the verb; furthermore, the accusative case here denotes the object (*karman*). The technical designation *karmapravacanīya* serves to exclude the designation *upasarga*; consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] as prescribed by the rule "upasargāt sunoti" does not occur. [The reason for this is] "due to the association with the word 'aśabda'."

This word *pari* is observed to have irregular usage; it is a *karmapravacanīya* both in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) and non-exclusion (*avarjana*). The word *apa*, however, is used only in the sense of exclusion. Under the governing rule for *karmapravacanīyas*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed; in that context, association (*sāhacarya*) serves as the determining factor.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffix *abhi* is used] in the sense of "for the sake of" (*abhirabhāge*) [Pāṇini 1.4.91].

"What is meant by ‘abhāgi’ (non-participating)? This question is asked in order to understand both the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*). For this very reason, he demonstrates both: a "part" (*bhāga*) is a portion being accepted, as in the thought, "May this accrue to me here. [Objection: But surely, because the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is understood according to its literal meaning (*anvartha*), it will not apply here; for this [term *bhāga*] currently denotes the act of dividing (*vibhajanakriyā*). [Reply: In that case, it would not apply to [words beginning with] *prati* and so on either. [Objection: It will apply there because of an explicit statement (*vacana*).

In that case, [the suffix *ṣatva*] would also apply to *abhi*; therefore, it should be stated as "in the sense of division (*bhāga*). There, because it is a preverb (*upasarga*), the rule "after *upa-* and *prādur-*, when *asti* follows, *ṣatva* occurs" applies. Now, why was it not formulated in this way: "with *abhi* in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), and distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); with *prati* and *pari* also in the sense of division (*bhāga*); by the word 'and' (*ca*), also in the senses of indication and so forth; with *anu* in the senses of indication and the third-case meaning; by the word 'and', also in the senses of division and so forth; then [with *ati*] in the sense of inferiority (*hīna*); and with *upa* in the sense of superiority (*adhika*)"?

In this way, indeed, there would be a double mention of "an" and it would not be necessary to say "abhāge"; for in this manner, the mention of "dvis" is made, resulting in a symmetry between the two words, though the brevity of syllables has not been taken into account.
The word *prati* is used in the sense of "representative" (*pratinidhi*) and "exchange" (*pratidāna*). (Pāṇini 1.4.92)

Regarding the term *mukhasadṛśaḥ*: one who is primary (*mukhya*) is observed to possess the capacity for a certain task, such as the slaying of an enemy; however, that which is substituted (*pratinidhīyate*) or taken up (*upādāyate*) to perform that task in his absence is a substitute (*pratinidhi*). The suffix *kip* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding *dattasya*, it means "by the creditor" (*uttamarṇena*). Regarding *pratiniryātanam*, it means "the act of returning. Regarding *arjunataḥ prati*: the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule "after [words denoting] a substitute or a counter-gift," and the suffix *tasi* is added to the ablative in the sense of a correlative (*pratiyoga*). Regarding *māṣān*: the meaning is that having taken sesame seeds, one gives beans.
*Padamañjarī*:
The prefixes *adhi* and *pari* are sometimes meaningless (*anarthaka*). 1.4.93.

Now, since meaningless words cannot be connected with an action, the designations of *gati* and *upasarga* do not apply to them; therefore, it would seem that the prescription of the designation *karmapravacanīya* for their sake is untenable. Nor is it for the purpose of prescribing the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in connection with the word *pari*, because in the rule prescribing that case, the sense of "excluding" (*varjana*) is specifically required. Furthermore, the fifth case is already established by virtue of its being the *apādāna* (ablative), as in the usage of the word *adhi*: "From where does he come? (*kuto 'dhyāgacchati*). For these very reasons, it is also untenable [to claim] that the rule is for the purpose of prescribing the second case (*dvitīyā*).

Therefore, since the prescription of technical names for two words that lack distinct meanings is purposeless, he says: "expressing no different meaning. For example, in cases such as *tiṣṭhati*, *nitiṣṭhati*, and *paribhavati*, there is an expression of a meaning different from what is conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*); however, this is not the case here. Rather, the very same meaning that is expressed in the usage of *āgacchati* is expressed by those two [prefixes] when used with *adhi* and *pari*. Thus, in this context, the verbal root and the prefixes *adhi* and *pari* possess a joint denotative function (*sahābhidhāyitva*).

Just as the meaning which belongs to the word *gaja* is the very same as that expressed by *mataṅgaja*, so too the meaning which belongs to the word *vṛṣa* is the very same as that expressed by *vṛṣabha*. Thus, because they express no different meaning and are virtually meaningless, they are said to be "meaningless" (*anarthaka*), but not because of their non-existence. And it is shown that for those two [words], the designation *karmapravacanīya* must be prescribed in order to set aside the designation *gati*. [In the example] *kuto 'dhyāgacchati*: from the word *kim*, the suffix *tasi* is applied by the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*; its replacement by *tasil* occurs by the rule *taseśca*; and there is an absence of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *gatir gatau*.
*Padamañjarī*: The [prefix] *su-* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). Pāṇini 1.4.94.

"Is it well-sprinkled?"—here, from the word *bhavat* (your honor), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent. The second case (*dvitīyā*) does not occur because of the rule: "When joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, the case-ending of the *kāraka* is stronger than that of the *upapada*. "Is it well-sprinkled here of yours?"—this is a reproach, not a compliment.
*Padamañjarī*:
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the verb *ati* in the sense of "transgressing. (Pāṇini 1.4.95)
*Padamañjarī*:

The particle *api* is used in the senses of [indicating] a word-meaning (*padārtha*), possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). (Pāṇini 1.4.96)

Regarding the phrase "of another word" (*padāntarasya*) and so forth: first of all, its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) is not grasped because it is non-deviant [from that meaning]; thus, the meaning of another word is what constitutes the word-meaning (*padārtha*). Even in that case, although another word is being employed, the word being used imparts some specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) to that meaning. For example, the word "blue" [is used] with respect to a lotus; however, it does not apply to that very object in a sense that is neither less nor more [than its own primary meaning]. If it were so, it would follow that the words are synonyms (*paryāya*), and consequently, the use [of one when the other is already present] would be improper. Therefore, the point is that it functions toward that meaning only when another word is not being employed.

Regarding the phrase "there might even be [a drop] of ghee": the *liṅ* suffix is used in the sense of a wish (*prārthanā*). The particle *api*, indicating that the object of this wish is difficult to obtain, connects with the word "might" (*syāt*), which results in the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. Furthermore, the difficulty of obtaining pertains to the object itself; if not even a mere drop of it is obtained, then by the force of the particle *api*, the word "drop" (*bindu*) is understood. Thus he says: "The particle *api* occurs here in the sense of 'a measure,' 'a drop,' or 'a little.'"

And when the distinction (*vyatireka*) is produced by that [particle *api*], the genitive case is used in the word *sarpiṣaḥ*. However, the accusative case does not occur, because there is no connection with the particle *api*; for it has been stated that it connects with the word *syāt*. The phrase "by a word expressing an additional meaning" means that it expresses the possibility (*sambhāvanā*) of that [action]. Regarding *api siñcet*: the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of possibility indicates through the particle *api* that the very act falls within the domain of what is difficult to accomplish. "Arbitrary action" (*kāmacāra*) means proceeding according to one's own will. *Api siñcet* means: "Whether you sprinkle or do not sprinkle, whether you praise or do not praise—act as you please."

*Jālma* is a vulgar term (*apaśabda*). "He might even sprinkle" (*api siñcet*)—here the potential suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of censure (*garhā*). [The word *api* is] for the purpose of precluding the designation of [the prefix *ni*] as an *upasarga*. For in the case of *syāt*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in *sic* by the rule "after an *upasarga*, [the *s* of] *sunoti* etc. (Pāṇini 8.3.65).
*Padamañjarī*:
[The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after the word *adhi* when it means "lord" (*īśvara*). (Pāṇini 5.2.97)

Regarding "tadayam": the meaning is that just as in the rule *hīne* there is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the relationship between the inferior and the superior, and in *upo'dhike ca* for the relationship between the additional and the further, so it is here as well. However, he says "in that case, sometimes" because while in those instances the case ending is stated from one of the two [relata], here it is not so. In the rule *yasya ceśvaravacanam*, there are two meanings: first, the word *īśvara* has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary sense; second, another interpretation is that the locative case is applied to that thing which is called the "master" (*īśvara*) of its own.

In that context, when there is a desire to express the distinction (vyatireka) of the owner (svāmin), the seventh case ending is used after that [word denoting the owned]; however, when there is a distinction of the owned itself, it is used after the word "tataḥ" (from that). It does not, however, occur simultaneously from both, because the relationship, though residing in two places, is expressed by a single case ending; thinking this, he said "sometimes. Regarding the example *brahmadatta*: the meaning is that the Pañcālas are the subjects (sva) of Brahmadatta. Regarding *ādhapañcāleṣu*: the meaning is that Brahmadatta is the master (svāmin) of the Pañcālas.
The term *padamañjarī* [is used] in the sense of the *vibhāṣā* [rule] regarding the root *kṛñ*. (Pāṇini 1.4.98)

Since the term *adhi* [in the sense of] "lord" (*īśvara*) is understood from the previous rule, this is an optional provision (*vibhāṣā*). As for the phrase "he will appoint me here," the verb *kṛ* preceded by *adhi* functions in the sense of "assignment" (*viniyoga*), as in: "this person is appointed (*adhikṛta*) here in the village. And because of the rule "an operation is governed by that which is marked with the svarita accent," the meaning is: "He is the lord; thus he will assign me here. This [word *mām*] is in the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) because it is the object (*karman*). If this is so, one asks: what is the purpose of prescribing this technical designation (*saṃjñā*)? To this, he replies: "In the view where there is the designation *karmapravacanīya*..."
Because of the prohibition of the elision of the particle (*nipāta*) by the rule "nipātairyadyadi," the finite verb ending (*tiṅanta*) is accented with the accent of the suffix *syat*.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The *la*-suffixes are *parasmaipada*. (Pāṇini 1.4.99)

The word *la* refers to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Now, what would be the fault if it were in the nominative plural (*prathamā-bahuvacana*)? [The fault is that] by the rule "of *ām*" (*āmaḥ*), the designation *liṭ* would apply to the *liṭ* even while it is still in the state of being *l* (the substitute for *liṭ*). Consequently, in the form *īkṣām*, the suffix *ām* would not occur; for after this [root], a subsequent *liṭ* is impossible, because of the restriction: "the *parasmaipada* suffixes occur only after the remaining [roots]" (*śeṣādeva parasmaipadam*). This is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*): since the author says "like the suffix *ām*" (*āmpratyayavat*), he indicates thereby that *ām* occurs even after roots that take the *ātmanepada*.

In that case, would this fault not arise—that the designation *ātmanepada* would apply only to the letter *l*, and not to its substitutes such as *tiP* and the rest? [Reply: By virtue of the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), it will apply to them as well. [Objection: Then, in the rule *taṅānāvātmanepadam*, the connection between the nominative form *laḥ* and *taṅ* and *āna* would be impossible, for *taṅ* and *āna* are not themselves the letter *l*. [Reply: But surely it can be understood thus: the letter *l* itself, which is to become *taṅ* and *āna*, is what is expressed by the term *taṅānau*.

Even though there is this other alternative interpretation, a defiled (unnecessary) construction is not appropriate; therefore, "laḥ" is a genitive case [indicating] a dependence on a substitute (*ādeśa*). It does not depend on a technical name (*saṃjñā*), as in the case where the name "parasmaipada" applies to the letter *l*. Why? Because technical names are generally prescribed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, whatever fault exists in the case of the suffix *-jas*, that would also apply here; for in both cases, the letter *l* would be the thing named (*saṃjñin*). Therefore, the genitive case indicates a dependence on a substitute.

If this were the case, the designation *puruṣa* (person), having no scope [elsewhere], would subvert the designation *parasmaipada* (active voice), which does have scope in the case of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu*. However, in the case of *jas*, the designation *parasmaipada* applies to the *lakāra* (tense/mood marker), whereas the designation *puruṣa* applies to the *tiṅ* (personal endings); thus, because their domains are distinct, there is no possibility of subversion. Even though, in the view that *jas* is the substitute, the designation *parasmaipada* will apply to the substitutes such as *tip* etc. by the rule "a substitute is like the original" (*sthānivadādeśaḥ*), nevertheless, because that [designation] does not extend beyond the limit of the *ākaḍāra*-section, their coexistence (*samāveśa*) is established.

Even in the view that [the term *taṅ*] is the genitive case, the point is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*). When the author says, "There is *vṛddhi* in the place of *sic* before *parasmaipada*s," he indicates that this designation (*saṃjñā*) applies to *tiṅ* suffixes as well. For the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu* cannot occur in the domain of *sic*. And since this indicator refers to the category in general, it establishes the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designation of person (*puruṣa-saṃjñā*) with the designation of *ātmanepada*. Otherwise, the designations of person—which would have scope in *parasmaipada*s—would be sublated by the designation of *ātmanepada*, which has no scope in *taṅ* suffixes.

Alternatively—the meaning is this: because the mention of the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* designations continues into the rule for the term *puruṣa*, the three triplets of suffixes belonging to the present tense (*laṭ*) which bear the designations *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada*, having come into being, receive the designations "first" (*prathama*) and so forth; thus, their coexistence (*samāveśa*) is established.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes are termed *ātmanepada*. (Pāṇini 1.4.100)

Now, why are these two technical terms (*saṃjñā*) not prescribed immediately after [the rule for] *laṭ*? For in this way, through the technical names of *puruṣa* (person), there would be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of these two with what is already established elsewhere. To this he says: "by the preceding [rule]. The intention is that these two are prescribed in this section so that the technical name *ātmanepada* may supersede (*bādha*) the technical name *parasmaipada*. The use of grand technical names (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is in accordance with the tradition of the ancient teachers.
*Padamañjarī*:
"Of the *tiṅ* [suffixes], there are three triplets: first, middle, and last. (Pāṇini 1.4.101)

The repetition [of the word] "three, three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*) is for the sake of distributive iteration (*vīpsā*). In that case, it is intended that both the aggregate and its individual components function as separate words, so that there may be absolute consistency—just as in *ā pacasi pacasi devadatta* ("O Devadatta, cook, cook")—and so that word-level grammatical operations such as the insertion of an anusvāra may occur even in the preceding member, as in *kuṇḍaṃ kuṇḍaṃ vāg apacannapacann* ("Pot after pot, he was cooking, cooking"). Therefore, at the time of dividing the words (*padaccheda*), "three-three" (*trīṇitrīṇi*) constitutes either one word or two.

In this context, because there is a discrepancy—namely, that there are three groups of three for the *tiṅ* suffixes, whereas there are only three technical names (*saṃjñā*)—the rule of "correspondence according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) does not apply. Although there is no purpose in assigning multiple names to each individual group of three, one cannot thereby obtain the desired scope [of the rule]. To address this, he says: "There are eighteen suffixes of *tiṅ*."

He thinks as follows: "The designations (*saṃjñā*) are also only six; how then can this be a reference using the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) method? In that case, if 'the first and the first' are 'the two firsts,' 'the middle and the middle' are 'the two middles,' and 'the last and the last' are 'the two lasts,' and then a *dvandva* compound were formed from these terms that have undergone *ekaśeṣa*—namely, *prathamamadhyamottamāḥ*—then there would be no correspondence with the intended number."

Therefore, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) after a *dvandva* compound has been formed: "first, middle, and last" (*prathamamadhyamottamāḥ*) and "first, middle, and last" (*prathamamadhyamottamāḥ*), resulting in *prathamamadhyamottamāḥ*. Even so, it is not understood whether three numbers of words are to be taken starting from the beginning; rather, even though the inclusion of triads is desired, does the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyasūtra*) apply here? No; rather, it establishes a sequential connection between the technical terms (*saṃjñās*) and the prescribed [terminations].

In that case, this is established by worldly convention, as for example: "Agni is to be worshipped with two [verses] of the Vihavya. Although it is not explicitly stated that this must be done in sequence, nevertheless, according to the sūtra named Vihavya, Agni is worshipped with two verses at a time starting from the beginning in regular order, and not with just any two verses whatsoever.

In this context, by the statement "there are eighteen suffixes of *tiṅ*," it is shown that the author does not intend for the three groups [of suffixes] to be taken in their sequential order from the beginning; rather, by the mention of *tiṅ*, it is demonstrated that there is a specific arrangement. Furthermore, by the phrase "those termed *parasmaipada*," etc., it is shown that a *dvandva* compound is formed of those items for which the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) reduction has already been applied, but not of those for which *ekaśeṣa* has not yet been performed. Alternatively, the terms *parasmaipada-grahaṇa* and *ātmanepada-grahaṇa* are carried over [from a previous rule], while the mention of *tiṅ* is for the purpose of excluding the suffixes *satṛ* and *kasu*.

And when that [term] recurs, there are two groups (*rāśi*), and this sūtra operates upon them due to the difference in their functions. In that regard, "each one is three triads"—the establishment of the correspondence is according to the order of enumeration. Therein, the two groups are shown by the words beginning with "na ca," while the difference in function is shown by the words beginning with "tatra. Here too, the formation of a technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is as in the previous case.
The Padamañjarī [explains]: "Those [terms]—the singular, dual, and plural—are each [to be understood individually]. (1.4.102)

Regarding the word *ekaśaḥ*: the suffix *śas* is added according to the rule "after a numeral and a word in the singular number, when there is distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)," from a stem ending in the nominative case.
