Since the connection with the word *trīṇi* (three) is already established by the context of the subject matter, the explicit mention of "those" (*tāni*) is for the purpose of ensuring the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations *vacana* (number) and *puruṣa* (person). Otherwise, under the governing heading of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be an option (*paryāya*) based on the authority of the specific statement; consequently, in the alternative where the designation *vacana* applies, the operation prescribed by the rules "the augment *āṬ* is added to the last person (*uttama*) and it is also marked as *pi*" and "it is always [added] after a root marked with *ṅ*" would not take place, because the designation *uttama* would be absent.

But when the word "tāni" (those) is present, because there is a reference to "these three and three" as being distinguished by the designations "first" and so forth, and because the rule for those designations is thereby obtained, their co-occurrence (samāveśa) takes place.

[Objection: "But surely, since the designation *puruṣa* (person) applies to groups of three (*trika*) while the designation *vacana* (number) applies to each individual one, this is not a subject for the governing rule of a single designation due to the difference in their scope. [Response: That is not so. Just as the designation *vṛddhi* applies to each of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* individually, so too the designation *puruṣa*, although it operates upon three [suffixes] because of the statement 'three times three,' operates only on each individual one among *tiP* and the others, and not on the collection as a whole; for that [collection] does not exist in actual usage, since those suffixes arise from the verbal root only individually."

The mention of "three" (tri), however, is for the purpose of establishing a limit, meaning that the designation "first" applies to the first three starting from the beginning; it is not, on the other hand, for the purpose of applying the designation to the aggregate as a whole, such that those [suffixes] become three words each after being called *tiṅ*. In the rule concerning *tiP* and the others (*tibādi-sūtra*), even though it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) consisting of eighteen constituent parts, the word *tiṅ* takes the masculine gender because of its coordination with the word "three by three" (*trīṇi trīṇi*), just as in the rule itself.
*Padamañjarī*:
[The section] on *sup*-affixes. 1.4.103.

The inclusion of *sub* [in the definition of a case-ending] begins with the first singular ending and extends up to the letter *p* of *sup*. However, it does not extend to the *p* of *kap*, because the designation "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) is prescribed for the *prāgdiśīya* suffixes; otherwise, even if they were designated as case-endings, this very mention of *sub* would continue to apply, and since the result would already be established by their being *sub*s, that [mention of *kap*] would be useless. Regarding the phrase "among the triplets of *tiṅ*s":

For what purpose, then, was this stated? Here, someone might think: "Since the word *ca* (and) is not employed in the sūtra, only the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is connected here, and nothing else. To address that, by means of showing an illustration, the meaning is that the recurrence of the two phrases "three" and "three by one" applies to the *sup*s just as the designation of "number" (*vacana-saṃjñā*) was prescribed for the *tiṅ*s. And so, having himself recited the word *ca*, he explains it with the words "of the *sup*s," and so forth.
The word *padamañjarī* and [the term] *vibhakti*. 1.4.104.

The letter *ca* (and) is for the purpose of combining [the two] with the designations "puruṣa" (person) and "vacana" (number). Because they are marked with the *svarita* accent, the term *tiṅ* continues to apply even when separated by other rules. The purpose of treating *tiṅ* endings as case-endings (*vibhakti*) is that the prohibition "not in a case-ending after *tu* or *sm*" applies to forms beginning with *ātām*, whereas for *sup* endings, it also applies to phenomena such as the substitution of *yat* for pronouns beginning with *tyad*.
*Padamañjarī*:
When *yuṣmad* is present as a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) word, the second person [ending] is used, even when [the verb] is in its original position (*sthānin*). 1.4.105.

Regarding the doubt—whether this [sūtra], having attained syntactic unity with the rule "lasya tibādayaḥ," constitutes a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) for *tiP* and the other suffixes, or whether it is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for those *tiP* etc. already enjoined by a separate sentence—the author states that it is a restriction, saying: "having introduced the topic 'of *la*'. For if it were a qualified injunction, there would be a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*): first, the technical names such as "first person" (*prathamā*) would apply to the existing *tiP* etc., and only when those names are established would *tiP* and the others be produced.

Furthermore, that restriction would have to be either a restriction regarding the mode of birth (*upapada-niyama*)—namely, that the second person (*madhyama*) occurs only with *yuṣmad*, the first person (*uttama*) only with *asmad*, and the third person (*prathama*) only with the remainder—or a restriction regarding the person (*puruṣa-niyama*), namely, that the second person occurs only with *yuṣmad*, the first person only with *asmad*, and the third person only with the remainder. In the first case, [such forms as] *kurvaṃs tvam* (you doing) and *kurvāṇas tvam* (you doing), where the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur with *yuṣmad*, would not be possible; nor would suffixes such as *tṛc* be possible, as in *kartā tvam* (you are the agent) or *kārakas tvam* (you are the doer). This is not a fault.

This much is the scope: the entire domain consisting of the secondary words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, as well as the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), is restricted to the [three] persons (*puruṣa*). And since the suffixes such as *tṛc* and others are also mentioned, they will apply by virtue of that statement. Furthermore, the exclusion of similar classes occurs through this restriction: in the case of *yuṣmad*, only the middle person (*madhyama*) applies, not the first or last; in the case of *asmad*, only the last person (*uttama*) applies, not the first or middle; and in the "remainder," the first and last persons apply.

If that is the case, then since they are prescribed in the sūtras beginning with *tib* (Pāṇini 3.4.78), a restriction (*niyama*) regarding them alone is appropriate because of their predominance. Furthermore, due to the mention of the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*), when there is a restriction of the *upapada*, *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are restricted, while the persons (*puruṣa*) remain unrestricted, as is the remainder. In that context, even if only the word "first" (*prathama*) were stated, it would be understood for the purpose of restriction; and since no other restriction is possible therein, the restriction is "only the first. And such a restriction must be applied only where there is the possibility of both the first and non-first [persons] occurring.

Furthermore, since the same contingency would apply to the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) as well, the restriction would occur there [in that case] anyway; so what is the purpose of mentioning *śeṣa*? However, in the case of a restriction regarding the person (*puruṣa-niyama*), the second and third persons (*madhyama* and *uttama*) are restricted to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, while the first person (*prathama*) remains unrestricted. Consequently, there would also be the contingency of using the first person even with *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; thus, a restriction for the first person must be formulated as "the first person occurs only in the case of the remainder. And such a restriction cannot be established without the mention of *śeṣa*. Therefore, the mention of *śeṣa* is indeed necessary. Hence, the mention of *śeṣa*.

The author of the Sūtra also intends this very restriction of persons; therefore, he relies on that alone, stating: "This restriction of persons is made for them. The word "for them" (teṣām) refers to the collection of *ti* and other suffixes whose constituent parts (*avayava*) are distinct; the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in relation to the person (*puruṣa*). The meaning is: "A restriction regarding the accompanying word (*upapada*) is made for that which is the 'middle person' (*madhyama-puruṣa*), which is a constituent part of those *ti*-suffixes and so forth. Although the word *puruṣa* is dependent [on another word], a compound is formed because its meaning is clearly conveyed (*gamaka*).

Alternatively, in the phrase "of them" (*teṣām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). A restriction (*niyama*) by way of the person is called a "restriction of persons" (*puruṣa-niyama*); the meaning is that they are restricted by means of the person. The term *upoccārita* means "that which is uttered near [another word]"; it is a compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapada-lopin*), following the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva*. The prefix *upa-* signifies proximity; therefore, this [explanation] removes the doubt that [the rule] should not apply when there is an intervention [between the words]. Regarding the phrase "and even when there is an intervention": since the status of being "near" would already be established by the mere fact of proximity, the explicit mention of the term *upapada* (in the rule) indicates that even a relative proximity is intended to be included.

The sense is that even that which is separated [from the verb] is considered proximate in relation to what is more remotely separated. However, the inclusion of the term *upapada* is so that [the rule applies] even when *yuṣmad* occurs as a preceding element; otherwise, by the rule "when something is specified as such, it refers to what precedes it," it would apply only when [the pronoun] occurs as a subsequent element. [Objection: But surely, just as by the statement "even in the case of the substituendum (*sthānin*)," the rule applies even when [the pronoun] is not used at all, so too it will apply in the case of a preceding usage because the subsequent element is not used—just as it does for the substituendum. [Response: This is not so; because of the mention of the locative case, in the view that there is actual usage, it would apply only when [the pronoun] occurs as a subsequent element.

Regarding the term *samānābhidheya* ("having the same denotation"): he shows that the word *adhikaraṇa* here signifies "denotation. Furthermore, when there is a common denotation with the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) being restricted by either [the person] or the threefold denotation of the *lakāras*—namely, *bhāva* (state/being), *karman* (object), and *kartṛ* (agent)—since it is impossible for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which denote substances (*dravya*), to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a form ending in a *lakāra* that denotes a state, he specifies that only the agent and the object are intended, stating: *tulyakāraka* ("having the same kāraka").

That which has a single, equivalent agent (*kāraka*) is described as such. Regarding the term *sthānin*: the word *sthāna* here signifies "occasion" (*prasaṅga*). One who possesses such an occasion is a *sthānin*. In that context, there is an occasion for both what is actually employed and what is not employed. This is expressed by saying "this one has an occasion," where, by implication, a restriction is understood: that for which there is only an occasion and not actual employment. Alternatively, this is a technical convention well-known within our own school: that for whose place a substitute (*ādeśa*) is prescribed is the *sthānin*.

In this context, however, [the term] *yuṣmad* is employed by virtue of similarity to that which is not being used; "even when the substituendum (*sthānin*) is present" means even when it is not being used. By the word *api* ("also"), it is meant that it is used even when the substituendum is being used. He states this with the words "even when the substituendum," and so forth. What is the meaning of "even when the substituendum"? It means even when it is being used and even when it is not being used. The word *api* is a restatement of the sense already obtained through the mention of the term *upapada* (governing word). Why specify "in grammatical coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇe*)? [So that it does not apply] in a case such as *tvayā gamyate* ("it is gone by you").

In some recensions of the *Vṛtti*, however, this passage is read as follows: "In cases such as *atitvaṃ pacati* ('he cooks surpassing you') and *atyahaṃ pacati* ('I cook surpassing myself'), because the compound has as its predominant element that which is transcended (*atikrānta*), the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* lack coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it; therefore, only the first person [of the verb] occurs. But here, in cases such as *īṣadasamāptastvaṃ tvatkalpaḥ pacasi* ('you who are slightly incomplete, you who are like you, cook') and *matkalpaḥ pacāmi* ('I who am like me, cook'), the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* themselves—devoid of qualities perceived at other times—are expressed by the words *tvatkalpa* and *matkalpa*; thus, the second and first persons [of the verb] occur."

However, when denoting another object similar to that [object], the first [suffix] applies; likewise, in cases such as *tvattaraḥ pacasi* ("you cook better") and *mattaraḥ pacāmi* ("I cook better"), or *paramatvaṃ pacasi* ("you cook most excellently") and *paramāhaṃ pacāmi* ("I cook most excellently"), it is indeed the referent of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* themselves that is expressed as distinguished by a superior quality perceived at another time. Thus, [the application of the suffixes] is perfectly valid.

And thus, the second person is used for the sense of *yuṣmad* (you) and the first person for the sense of *asmad* (we); by this much it is established that the meaning is: "if the suffixes [of those persons] have arisen for the sake of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, then only the second and first persons [are used]. However, it was not formulated in that way. Here, because "you" (*tvam*) becomes "you" (*ātvam*), the form *tvadbhavati* occurs; for the base itself is the agent when it is transformed into the form of its modification. And this we shall demonstrate under the rule *ānmahataḥ*.

And likewise, in the mantra—"O Agni, may I be you, or may you be me"—and "May I be you, or may you be me," the person (puruṣa) residing in the *prakṛti* (the verbal base) is observed. Here, in the case of "May your honor cook" (*bhavān pacatu*), since the meaning of the word *yuṣmad* ("you") is perceived, the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) would apply even though [the subject] is in its original form (*sthānin*). Or rather, it does not so apply, because the meaning of *yuṣmad* is devoid of gender (*aliṅga*) and has address (*sambodhana*) as its sole scope; whereas the meaning of *bhavat*, however, possesses gender and is not restricted solely to the scope of address.

For just as in the expression "O boy, study," the state of being addressed is understood, so too it is in the case of "You, study. And thus, some say that in all instances of address, the nominative case is used for the word *yuṣmad*, and it bears the acute accent on its first syllable when in the vocative; furthermore, when following another word, it undergoes elision (*nighāta*). And it has been said: "Some maintain that the entire second person [ending] is intended for the purpose of address; likewise, they know that in address, every form of *yuṣmad* takes the nominative case."
"Because the referent of *yuṣmad* is already established [as a pronoun], its initial udātta accent is fixed;
provided that it is the nominative case of *yuṣmad* and does not follow another word. Thus [it is stated].

True; the word *yuṣmad* has as its sole domain the vocative (*sambodhana*), whereas the nominative (*prathamā*) is purely [the expression] of the base-meaning (*śuddha*). Even in the case of being "facing" (*abhimukhībhāva*), this [vocative function] is included within the very meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); however, where it is not so included, the rule "and in the vocative" (*sambodhane ca*) prescribes the nominative for the sake of manifesting that [function], and [it also prescribes] the accent. Otherwise, in such cases as "yuvam hi sthaḥ svarpatī," "yūyam yāta svastibhiḥ," and "haye devā yūyamidāpayastha," there would be final acute-accent (*antodāttatva*) even at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pāda*), and there would be no non-anudātta (*anighāta*) despite being followed by another word (*padātparatve*).

Thus, it is established that because the word *bhavat* is not a subject of address, possesses grammatical gender, and signifies the meaning of "long-lived one" (*āyuṣmat*), the second person [honorific] is not employed.
In *padamañjarī* and in the *prahāsa*, it is stated: "When *manya-* is used as an upapada, the verb *manya-* takes the first person and is treated as singular. (Pāṇini 1.4.106).

Regarding the phrase "when laughter (prahāsa) is implied": where, due to the absence of the actual fact, there is merely deception, laughter is understood when the speaker’s intention is revealed. The word *manyati* is an imitation of a portion of the word *manye*; that which has *manye* as its attendant word (*upapada*) is described as such. Since the suffix *la* is prescribed for verbal roots, and because the second person (*madhyama*) is a substitute for that [suffix], he states that the verbal root is the meaning of the external member of the compound: "when a verbal root has *manye* as its attendant word. This means when it exists as the base form (*prakṛti*). And that [root] is singular.

Furthermore, the singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) of the highest person is based on the sense (*arthadvāraka*); that is to say, it becomes the designator of one [person]. The meaning is that even when there are two or many speakers, the singular number alone is used. For where there are two or many speakers, the singular treatment must be prescribed; elsewhere, however, it is established simply because the speaker is one. Regarding the phrase "and as a singular" (*ekavacca*): the word *ca* (and) implies an inclusive conjunction (*anvācaya*). Therefore, even in the case of singular treatment, both the middle and the highest persons remain prescribed as primary even when there is only one speaker.

To demonstrate the very same *anvācaya* (conjunction), he cites an example that is easily established: *ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyase* ("Come, I think you will eat rice"). This is used toward a brother-in-law or similar person who has come to eat even though rice is already available; thus, it is understood as a jest. As for the examples for two or more [persons], they are: *ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyadhve nahi bhokṣyadhve bhuktaḥ so'tithibhiḥ* ("Come, I think you all will eat rice; no, you will not eat it, for it has been eaten by guests"); and *ehi manye rathena yāsyatha yātastena pitā* ("Come, I think you will go by chariot; your father has already gone by it"). [This occurs] when the second and first persons are applicable.

Since the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are understood [from the context], the mention of the "governing word" (*upapada*) in the present rule is connected with *yuṣmad*, just as in the counter-examples. And that [mention] is to be carried over here exactly as it was; it is stated here so that [the suffixes] do not occur in such cases as: *etu bhavān manyate odanaṃ bhokṣye bhuktaḥ so 'tithibhiḥ* ("Come, sir; you think, 'I shall eat rice'; he has already eaten with the guests"). Since it would be impossible for it to be connected with the verb *man* (in *manyate*), the mention of the governing word is repeated here; otherwise, [the suffixes] would occur only when *man* follows.

Because of the specific mention of *śyan*, there is the inclusion of the root *man* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*), but not of the root *manu* in the sense of "understanding" (*avabodhana*). For instance, in the case of [the statement], "Come, I shall go by chariot," such a thought occurs to him. In the counter-example, there is the speaking of such a matter to a guest.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The first person [is used] for 'we'. (Pāṇini 1.4.107)

Where both *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur as co-occurring words (*upapada*), if the two agentive capacities (*kartṛśakti*) are intended to be expressed as restricted to their respective substrates, then the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is produced separately—as in "you and I cook" (*tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacasi, pacāmi ca*). However, when they are intended to be expressed together (*sahavivakṣā*), a single suffix is produced for both capacities; therein, by the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the middle voice (*madhyama*) applies to *yuṣmad* and the highest voice (*uttama*) to *asmad*—as in "you and I cook" (*tvaṃ cāhaṃ pacāvaḥ*) or "O slayer of Vṛtra, you and I shall unite" (*ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan saṃyujyāvaḥ*).

Even when, according to the rule "yadyatparam" (whichever is subsequent among *tyad* and so forth), the remainder belongs to *asmad*, the middle [person] would still be applicable by the rule "syāt" and "nin" and so forth; however, because of its priority [in the order of persons], only the highest [person] occurs—thus: *āvām pacāvaḥ* (the two of us cook).
In the *Padamañjarī*, this is the first [section] of the *Śeṣa* [chapter], sūtra 1.4.108.

The term *upapada* is no longer [in force]. The term *śeṣa* (remainder) is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), and not a locative of posteriority (*parataḥ*). Thus he says: "In the remainder. This means it is spoken of as other than the scope of the middle and highest [persons]. The meaning is that it is a different scope. Where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there, by this term "remainder," he shows that the "remainder" is the absence of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and not the presence of something else.

What is established [by this]? [The forms] *yūyaṃ ca devadattaśca pacatha* ("you and Devadatta cook"), *ahaṃ ca devadattaśca pacāvaḥ* ("I and Devadatta cook"), and *tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca devadattaśca pacāmaḥ* ("you, I, and Devadatta cook"). Here, although a collection consisting of *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and another is indeed different from *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, nevertheless, since *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are present therein, the first person ending should certainly occur because of their existence. As it is said: "In that case, there is a prohibition of the first person when *yuṣmad* and others are present, because they remain as the remainder (*śeṣatvāt*)."
*Padamañjarī*:
"The closest proximity [of sounds] is *saṃhitā*. (Pāṇini 1.4.109)

The word *para* denotes excellence (*atiśaya*), as in "supreme happiness" (*paraṃ sukham*) or "supreme suffering" (*paraṃ duḥkham*). It does not refer to [the word] existing in the directions and so forth, because proximity (*sannikarṣa*) cannot be joined with direction, place, or time. Otherness (*anyatva*) is relative to another object; proximity is an unerring connection, but it is not physical contact (*saṃśleṣa*), for that is impossible in the case of phonemes. For if that were conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it could not belong to sound, which is a quality (*guṇa*), since conjunction is a property of substances (*dravyadharma*).

If it were inherence (*samavāya*), then one letter would not inhere in another letter, because sound inheres in space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, for those who hold that sound is a substance (*dravya*), sound does not inhere anywhere at all. We do not know what kind of excellence (*atiśaya*) could exist in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). However, due to the difference in the degree of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there can be a connection with superiority or inferiority; therefore, proximity alone is the sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*).

But surely, when phonemes are being articulated in succession, once the activity of the articulatory locations (*sthāna*) and other factors that produce a preceding phoneme has ceased, there begins the activity of those factors that produce the subsequent phoneme. In this case, there must necessarily be some measure of time (*kālakalā*) in between; however, because it is so subtle, it is not perceived—just as the individual distinctions between the hundred petals of a lotus [are not seen when they appear to be joined]. How then can there be "close proximity" (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*)? To this he replies: "with an interval of half a mora (*ardhamātrā-kāla*)."

True; this much of an interval is tolerated because it is unavoidable, but an interval caused by a longer duration of time is excluded by the mention of "another" (para). If this were so, it would apply only to the *druta* (fast) mode of pronunciation, and not to the *madhyama* (medium) or *vilambita* (slow) modes; for in those two, the proximity is not equal to that which exists in the *druta* mode. Rather, the distinction between the modes of pronunciation (*vṛtti*) arises from the difference in the perception of the first phoneme due to the utterance being continuous across all modes.

In the rapid (*drutā*) mode, the duration of perception is very short; in the medium (*madhyamā*), it is longer; and in the slow (*vilambitā*), it is even longer. For sounds are of two kinds: primary (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*). The primary sounds are the producers of the phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the modified ones consist in their repeated perception. However, the intermediate duration is exactly the same in all three modes. Alternatively, in whichever mode a hiatus necessarily occurs for a certain amount of time, a hiatus occurring for more than that is excluded by the inclusion of the subsequent [phoneme].

In common usage, the term *saṃhitā* is well-known to apply precisely to that immediate sequence of one word with another. Accordingly, it is said: "One studies the *saṃhitā*, not the individual words. Consequently, in cases such as *kumāryau*, the grammatical operations pertaining to *saṃhitā* would not apply to the constituent parts of the word; thus, this sūtra is composed.
*Padamañjarī*:
"The pause is the end. (1.4.110)

"Virati means cessation (*virāma*). Here, *virāma* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, *virāma* is the absence of the utterance of a phoneme (*varṇoccāraṇābhāva*). He states another meaning: "Or, *virāma* is that by which one ceases (*viramyate*). According to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, even though this is not a technical grammatical term (*asaṃjñā*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*) by the rule *halaśca*. In the former case, the absence [of utterance] is the thing designated; in the latter, it is the final phoneme, for by that one indeed ceases.

Regarding the first position, [in the rule] *kharavasānayoḥ*, the locative case is one of "subsequent" (*parasaptamī*). But how can there be a sequence with respect to the pause (*avasāna*), since that is the absence of priority and posteriority? Or [if it refers to] the voiceless consonants (*khara*), how so? For when the voiceless consonant exists, the *repha* does not, and when the *repha* exists, the voiceless consonant does not; this is because phonemes arise in succession and perish as soon as they are uttered. If it is argued that in that case there is a sequence constructed by the intellect, then that is equally applicable even in the absence [of actual sequence]. The same applies to the rule *vāvasāne*.

In the second view, however, even though there is only one locative case (*saptamī*) in the rule *khar-avasānayoḥ*, it is divided according to the difference in its scope: "when followed by a *khar* [consonant], the *repha* becomes *visarjanīya*; and when at the end of a word (*avasāna*), with the *repha* as the locus (*sthānin*), the *visarjanīya* occurs. Thus, the status of the locus and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is intended to be expressed. The same applies to the rule *vā-avasāne*. For example: *dadhiṃ*, *madhuṃ*. In the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ*, the phrase *vā-avasāne* is understood to carry over.

But surely the word *avasāna* is well-known in common usage (*loka*) to mean "cessation," even if it were derived from the root *sā-* with the prefix *ava-* in the sense of "understanding" (as in the question, "By what is this understood?"). It is also used in the sense of "defeat," as in "Devadatta has been defeated" (*avasita*). However, the word *avasāna* is specifically established in common usage to mean "pause" or "end. Furthermore, it is not possible for the letter *r* to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) of either understanding or defeat; thus, there would be no purpose in establishing this technical designation (*saṃjñā*). To this, he says: "It is established because [the distinction between] *saṃhitā* and *avasāna* is already known in the world."
The author of the Vārttika considers that the word *saṃhitā* is well-known as referring to mere proximity in general, and not specifically to the proximity of two words alone.
The fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by Haradattamiśra.
The Kāśikāvṛtti – 2 Padamañjarī: Now begins the first quarter of the second chapter.
1. A rule concerning words applies only when they are semantically connected (*samartha*). (Pāṇini 2.1.1)

"This is a general definition (*paribhāṣā*)," [says the opponent]. "It is not a governing rule (*adhikāra*), because of the mention of 'prescription concerning words' (*padavidhi*). Otherwise, since the rules to be stated later—such as the treatment as 'another word' (*parāṅvadbhāva*)—would never deviate from being prescriptions concerning words, that mention would be purposeless. The term *paribhāṣā* is derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, meaning "that by which an operation is explained everywhere (*paritaḥ*): in every instance (*sarvatra*), in a subsequent position (*paratra*), even when separated (*vyavahite*), and even when adjacent (*anantare*). Alternatively, it is used in the sūtra in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), employing a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the means and the action itself.

Even though the word *idam* (this) is employed in the sūtra, it takes the feminine gender because of its coreferentiality with the term *vidheya-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding that which is to be enjoined). [The phrase] "that is *karva*" [is explained as follows]: Now, one might object: since pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the property of that [rule], has already been stated by the general indication "whatever rule concerning words (*pada-vidhi*)", what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning the word *karma* (object)? This is not so; for when it is said, "Let whatever Brāhmaṇa be brought," the exclusion of Kṣatriyas and others is understood, but not pervasion.

Although the word *vidhi* was mentioned first, the author bypasses that capable term and, by virtue of its function as the indicator of the subject (*uddeśya*), explains the word *padavidhi*—which occurs first according to the logical sequence—as a term denoting an injunction (*vidhi*). He shows that the word *vidhi* is derived in the sense of the object (*karman*) by stating: "that which is enjoined (*vidhīyate*) is an injunction (*vidhi*). The meaning is "an operation" (*kārya*). Regarding the phrase "of words" (*padānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*). The meaning is: "the operation that is enjoined for those things which are words."

If, however, the word *vidhi* (rule) were understood as having an active sense—that is, "the act of prescribing" (*vidhānam*)—then, according to the rule for the genitive case denoting the object of a verbal derivative (*kṛd-yoga*), one would have to say "the prescription of words" (*padānām vidhiḥ*). In that case, the operations of compounds (*samāsa*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), case-endings (*sub*), and verbal roots (*dhātu*) would not be included; for in those instances, the formation of compounds and so forth is prescribed for words that already exist, rather than the production of the status of being a word itself.

But surely, even on the view that [the suffixes] are the means of expressing the object (*karman*), the prescription of case-endings would remain unaccounted for; for in that case, it is only words (*pada*) that are prescribed, and not some property of words already existing. It is replied: by rules such as "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), a restriction (*niyama*) is established, but it is not a prescription regarding words (*padavidhi*).

Furthermore, even if the prescription of case endings (*vibhakti*) were by way of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule *svādi* [Pāṇini 4.1.2], even so, in the case of case endings expressing grammatical relations (*kāraka*), there exists a relationship between the action and its factor that is inseparable (*avinābhūta*). However, regarding case endings used as adjuncts (*upapada*)—such as those governed by the rule *antarāntareṇayukte* [Pāṇini 2.3.4]—and case endings used as prefixes (*upasarga*)—such as those governed by *nerviśaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.3.17]—there remains the status of being a "rule dependent on a word" (*padavidhi*) whether they function within a single syntactical unit or as separate units, because the adjuncts and prefixes themselves possess the status of being words (*pada*).

In the phrase "compounds and so forth" (*samāsādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes derivative formations (*taddhitavṛtti*) and the like; these derivatives also arise from words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). As for the purpose of the inclusion of the term "samartha" in the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*, we shall explain it in that very place. Similarly, in rules such as *isusoḥ sāmarthye*, the word *samartha* means "capable"; for the word *samartha* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*) precisely in that context. Indeed, in common worldly usage, one who is capable of accomplishing his own task is called "samartha."

Furthermore, regarding the communication of meaning by words, both worldly and Vedic speakers—who are authorized by the fact that words are taught for the sake of their own specific functions—are capable of communicating any particular [meaning]. When it is said of something, "this is capable," a specific distinction is understood there through that capacity. He states that this specific distinction is of such a nature due to proximity (pratyāsatti): "in the expression of the meaning of the analytical sentence" (*vigrahavākyārthābhidhāne*). An "analytical sentence" (*vigraha*) is so called because by means of it the meaning of the compound is specifically grasped—that is, known.

The compound *tādṛśaṃ ca tadvākyaṃ ca* is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Alternatively, *vigraha* means "analysis" (*viśeṣeṇa grahaṇam*); a sentence for that purpose is a "sentence of analysis" (*vigrahavākyam*), which is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) like *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder") and similar terms.

Alternatively, by means of metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) based on non-difference, the phrase expressing the analytical meaning (*vigrahārtha-vākya*) is called "vigraha"; thus, *rājapuruṣa* is a qualifier compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). For example, this is the compound; its analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). That word *rājapuruṣa* is capable of denoting the meaning of this [sentence], because that [meaning] is understood from it as well—namely, a man qualified by the king. It should be understood as "capable" (*samartha*), with the word "in terms of grammatical correctness" (*sādhutvena*) being the ellipsis.

The meaning of the Sūtra in this view is that whatever rule concerns a compound (*pada-vidhi*) is ungrammatical (*asādhu*) when it is capable of expressing the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*); we do not perceive any other, more excellent meaning. However, that capacity must be inferred from actual usage (*prayoga*). But this is not obtainable from the literal words of the Sūtra—that this particular *vṛtti* (compound) is capable of expressing the meaning of this specific sentence, and no other. Therefore, being dissatisfied with this interpretation, he states another explanation, beginning with "Or rather" (*atha vā*).

In this view, the word *samartha* (capable/competent) is used in a figurative sense; thus he says, "because it depends upon words that are *samartha*. This means [the rule applies] to words that are *samartha*, i.e., to words whose meanings are related (*saṃbaddhārtha*) or whose meanings are integrated (*saṃsṛṣṭārtha*). Whatever operation (*vidhi*) pertains to words should be understood to pertain to words that are *samartha*. What is the meaning of "of those that are *samartha*"? It means "of those whose meanings are related" or "whose meanings are integrated. In that regard, in a sentence (*vākya*), there is the state of having related meanings. For in that case, *sāmarthya* (capacity/competence) consists in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Mutual expectancy means dependence upon one another.

*Vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy) is that mutual relationship which exists when there is *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy), *saṃnidhi* (proximity), and *yogyatva* (compatibility). For in a sentence, the word "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*) expresses a meaning that functions as a qualifier, possessing a relationship manifested through its dependence on a specific related [referent]; it expects a person who is proximate and compatible [with it]. Similarly, by the word "person" (*puruṣaḥ*), the person is expressed as residing in itself, yet it expects the state of being a king (*rājatva*)—which is proximate to it—as a delimiting factor, in the sense of "I am his."

Therefore, by way of the relationship between qualifier and qualified, because the relationship has as its object those related elements that are not fixed [in their order], it connects with whatever is proximate and capable according to expectation—such as "the king's man and horse," or "the man of King Devadatta"—but not with any other meaning. In the *vṛtti* (compound), however, there is the state of having a combined meaning; for in that case, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists precisely in the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

For in a compound (*vṛtti*), the word "king" does not terminate its function merely by denoting the king; it also denotes the man, just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" [denotes] the bank. If, however, it were to terminate its function at that point alone, then just as in a sentence there is a connection with both—as in "the king's man and the horse"—so too would there be such a connection in the case of "the king's man and the horse" within the compound.

There would also be a connection with its own qualifier, as in *ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s prosperous man), which is just like *ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the prosperous man of the king). In that case, the word *puruṣa* denotes a man qualified by the king, not a man in general. If it were so, then just as in a sentence there is a connection with two [qualifiers]—as in *rājñaḥ puruṣo devadattasya ca* (the king’s man and Devadatta’s)—there would likewise be [a connection] in *rājapuruṣo devadattasya ca*. Therefore, that particular state of being (*viśeṣa*) by virtue of whose existence this distinction arises is *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning).

There are other specific points mentioned in the Bhāṣya: "The elision of case-endings (*sup*), separation [of words], connection with either [member] as desired, difference in accent, distinction of number, explicit denotation, qualification of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and conjunction. Likewise, in a sentence, there is no elision of the case-ending—as in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man) or *nīlam utpalam* (the blue lotus)—but in a compound, because the two [words] function toward a single qualified meaning and thus lack separate meanings, the case-ending ceases by its very nature.

And that very inherent cessation (*nivṛtti*) is explained by the treatise through the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.71) by means of the technical designation of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), so that [operations] such as the elision of *n* may take effect. However, when there is no separate meaning, a separate case-ending does not occur. Likewise, among phonemes, intervention is observed only when there is a separate meaning—as in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, where both words are acute-accented on the first syllable due to the *niṭ-svara*. It is observed as non-different, as for example in *puruṣaḥ*, where in the compound (*vṛtti*) a single accent is seen.

Furthermore, a specific number is understood when the referents are distinct—as in *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*, *rājñoḥ puruṣaḥ*, or *rājñāṃ puruṣaḥ*. In a compound (*vṛtti*), however, the expression remains unmanifest, and a doubt arises as to whether it is a vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) or a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), as in the case of *brāhmaṇakambalaḥ*; nor can a decision be reached here by means of accentuation. For in the sentence, there is the suppression of the vocative (*āmantritanighāta*), and since the word *kambala* belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group, it is udātta on the final syllable; this same final udātta occurs in the compound as well. And the qualification of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) has already been explained.

And the word *ca* ("and") occurs when there are separate referents, as in "The king’s cow, horse, and blanket. But in a compound (*vṛtti*), because there is a single referent and an absence of conjunction—which is based on distinction—the word *ca* is excluded, as in "The king’s cow, horse, and blanket. By these specific characteristics, it is understood that the referent in a compound possesses both forms combined, having reached a state of non-distinction like milk and water.

In such cases as "bring the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣam ānaya*) and "bring the royal man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), although only one person is brought because there is no difference in the object of the action, the manner of expression nevertheless differs—just as in the case of "Let a hundred Brāhmaṇas be fed" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ śataṃ bhojyatām*). Thus, it is established that the meaning of the compound (*vṛtti*) and the sentence (*vākya*) differ. And so, in this context, the mention of the option (*vā-vacana*) is of questionable utility, since there is no possibility of the sentence being sublated by a compound whose meaning is different.

Others, however, asserting that the function [of a compound] is one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), claim that the words constituting the compound are entirely devoid of meaning. But we do not find this view acceptable. For, in the case of "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), is the meaning of "king" not understood? If you say "yes," then it would follow that any man whatsoever should be brought. If, on the other hand, it is understood, what is the basis for that comprehension? It cannot be that the power (*śakti*) belongs to the compound itself; for even if that power were based on the word "king," there would be no loss of meaning.

Furthermore, the word *rāja-* (king), which is already established in meaning within the sentence, does not require a new derivation upon entering the compound; rather, the meaning of "king" is understood from that very [sentence]. Therefore, the operation (*vṛtti*) is not one that abandons its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*); rather, it is simply a difference in the manner of expressing the meaning—this alone is correct. In this regard, the fact that the meanings are related and integrated is the cause for the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), and not either of the two [conditions] individually; for, if it were based on mere mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) alone, there would be no restriction against the operation applying even to that which is dependent on another.

If this were the case, that [principle of *ekārthībhāva*] would not apply in the matter of the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) or in the prescription of case-endings (*vibhaktividhāna*), because in those instances *ekārthībhāva* is impossible. Let it not apply; however, regarding the status of being like a subordinate member, the mention of the cause (*nimitta*) will not arise [as a requirement]. Even in the prescription of case-endings, since the mutual expectancy between action and its factor (*kriyākāraka*) is invariably present, there is no fault whatsoever: in some cases there is the mention of "connected" (*yukta*), in some cases the mention of "conjunction" (*yoga*), and in some cases the conjunction is implied by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*).

For this very reason, immediately following [the previous rule], he provides an example of a compound even while bypassing the status of being a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*)—he says, "he will state. [The question] "What is the purpose of the mention of *samartha*? means: what is the purpose of the rule? For nothing at all is accomplished by the mere mention of the term *padavidhi*. [He gives the example] "paśya" and so on. But surely we shall qualify the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) by means of the words beginning with *śrita*—that is, [we will say] "the accusative that occurs in connection with *śrita* and the others."

Even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the compound] being dependent (*sāpekṣa*), as in the case of *mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* ("he has resorted to great hardship"), for here the accusative case ending occurs by virtue of its cause being the action of "resorting" (*śrita*). However, when the term *samartha* ("capable") is included [in the definition of a compound], this does not occur. Although in the state of the sentence (*vākya-avasthā*) there exists the capacity characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣālakṣaṇa-sāmarthya*), we have already stated that in the state of the derivative formation (*vṛtti-avasthā*), the condition of "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is not possible. How then is it that the compound *devadattasya gurukulam* ("Devadatta’s teacher’s family") is a derivative formation (*vṛtta*) despite being dependent? In this case, Devadatta has no direct connection with the "teacher."

What then? [The connection] is by means of the aggregate, and since the connection with the teacher (*guru*) is established through ease, it follows by implication that there is also a connection with the teacher himself. And it has been said:

"Those whose connection is with the aggregate, such as the teacher’s family (*gurukula*) and so forth—even they, having touched the constituent parts, become connected with that which possesses those parts."

Alternatively: when a word whose meaning is already complete enters into a state of syntactic unity (*ekārthībhāva*) with another, and its own meaning is fulfilled through its connection with a correlative (*pratiyogin*), then even that which is dependent [upon it] undergoes composition (*vṛtti*). And it has been said:
"Every word that is a relative term is used in dependence [on another];
this dependence of its own meaning is not lost even when it is in a state of composition."

Regarding the passage beginning with "What will you do?", it can be explained as follows: [The compound] *tatkṛtārthena* is formed by compounding the word *tat*, which refers back to the subject at hand, with a word ending in the third case. That is to say, it means "by the statement of that quality which is produced for its sake. In this context, although a compound might be possible in the case of "with a wedge" (*śaṅkulayā*), where the splitting is not performed for the sake of the wedge itself; and although a compound might be possible in the case of "with a stone," where the splitting is performed for the sake of the stone; nevertheless, since such a compound is not intended here, it will not occur.

Therefore, one should cite as a counter-example a construction that is dependent [on another word], such as "a piece for a large wedge" (*mahatyā śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ*). Or, "Go, you, for the sacrificial post" (*gaccha tvaṃ yūpāya*); here the fourth case ending is used according to the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*. Alternatively, it may be cited according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi*, as in "Go to fetch the sacrificial post" (*yūpam āhartuṃ gaccha*); since this too has that same purpose, the wood (*dāru*) would not be used [as a separate word]—thus, one should cite as a counter-example a dependent construction such as "wood for a large sacrificial post" (*mahate yūpāya dāru*). [In this case] the substitution of *yaṇ* is obligatory, and the *tuk* augment occurs.

Both of these are rules concerning phonemes (*varṇavidhi*); however, the *tuk* [augment] governed by "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) and so forth is indeed permanent, whereas the optional *tuk* governed by "optionally after a word-final [consonant]" (*padāntādvā*) does not apply here because it is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*). Others, however, explaining that the substitution of *yaṇ* is non-permanent and that the *tuk* occurs, describe the elision of the vowel *a* (*akārapraśleṣa*) and explain that the optional *tuk* occurs according to the rule "optionally after a word-final [consonant]."

Is it not the case that this is not a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*)? He replies: Since [the desired result] is established by the mention of "end" (*anta*) there, the purpose of mentioning "end" here is so that the *tug-āgama* may apply as a rule for a long vowel at the end of a word (*padānta*), and not for a word that has a long vowel at its end.
2. In the case of an address, the final vowel of the vocative takes the *parāṅ* accent.

"Like a member of another": the meaning is that the vocative (*āmantrita*) word itself becomes like a member (*aṅgavat*), that is, like a part; it is grasped by the mention of that [whole]. This is an extension (*atideśa*) of identity. Since the word *aṅga* signifies a "member" or "part," its "self" (*tad-ātmā*) is the self of that vocative; the state of being that (*tādātmyam*) means having that very nature. He clarifies this very point with the words "ending in a case-suffix" (*subanta*).

"It enters into"—that is, it is included; the meaning is that when a collection of words ending in case-terminations (*subanta*) has become a single vocative, whatever accent can be applied should be applied. But what is that? It is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*), and since the whole collection follows a word (*padāt paratve*), it undergoes the *nighāta* (suppression of accent). For example: *kuṇḍenāṭan*. Now, if this status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) were to apply here, the acute accent on the first syllable of the collection would be applied, and by the rule of "the rest are unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), the vocative would be suppressed.

If, however, the word *aṭan* occurs at the beginning of this pāda, then there would be no *nighāta* (elision of the accent), and consequently both words would have the acute accent on their first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Furthermore, the word *kuṇḍa* also exists as a masculine noun, as it is said: "He is a *kuṇḍa* while the husband is alive; he is a *golaka* when the husband is dead."

The word *kuṇḍī* is formed by the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra*. Regarding the example *paraśunā vṛścann* ("cutting with an axe"): the word *paraśu* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *kup*, according to the rule *āṅparayoḥ khaniśrṛbhyāṃ ḍicca*. The word *madra* ends in the suffix *rak* according to the rule *madeśca*. The word *kaśmīra* is oxytone because it belongs to the *dhṛtādi* group. [In the case of] the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) for that which has a case-ending (*subanta*), there is the inclusion of its cause; that is, the case-ending itself is included as the cause of that meaning expressed by the vocative (*āmantrita*).

The meaning is "as if it were a part of another. In the examples, the fact that the word ending in the third case functions as a cause (*nimitta*) is indeed established; the same applies to the word ending in the sixth case, for kingship is caused by servants, or a country is caused by its territory. Likewise, this also occurs in the expression *goṣu svāmī* ("the owner among cows").

But when there is an absence of that being the cause [of the preceding word], it does not occur: *maruttvāṃ indra vṛṣabho raṇāya*, *marudbhirindra sakhyaṃ te astu*, *māyābhirindramāyinam*, *etenāgne brahmaṇā vāvṛdhasva*, *kṣettreṇāgne svāyussambharasva*, *mitreṇāgne mitradheye yatasva*. [Question: Why is the word *su* mentioned? [Answer: The question is: since the exclusion of a *tiṅ*-ending word is already established by the very mention of "that being the cause," why include *su*? [Examples of such cases: *pīḍye*, *pūḍyamāne*.

The sense is that the author of the Sūtra does not consider the removal of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to be achieved by the words of the author of the Vārttika. [Grammatical analysis: The root *pīḍ* is used in the sense of "oppressing" (*avagāhana*) with the causative suffix *ṇic* (belonging to the *curādi* class). In both instances, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the passive voice; in one case, the first person singular ending with the augment *iṭ* is applied, and in the other, the suffix *śānac*. With the addition of *yak*, there is the elision of *ṇi*. By the rule "the augment *iṭ* after a root ending in *tās* is unaccented," the *iṭ* is unaccented. The accent of *yak* is the affix-accent (*pratyayasvara*). By the rule "a single substitute for an accented vowel is itself accented," the vowel *e* is accented. In the word *pīḍyamānā*, there is the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) due to its being a vocative (*āmantrita*).

But surely, by the very continuation of the mention of "capacity" (*samartha*), this [prohibition] will not apply here; for there is indeed capacity even in this case. How so? A vocative word is a qualifier of the action itself; and thus, in the example *brajāni devadatta* ("I am going, Devadatta"), the elision of the vocative occurs. And it has been said: "Whatever is a vocative word, that is a qualifier of the action;
such being the case, there is elision of the vocative here in *brajāni devadatta*."

Alternatively, the relationship here is characterized by the nature of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*): "O you who are being tormented, by your suffering I too am tormented. In the example *gehe gārgya*, the word *geha* is oxytone because it belongs to the *uñchādi* group; since both [the house and Gārgya] are factors (*kāraka*) in a single action such as sitting, there is functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) through that medium. [The question is: "Why is the mention of *para* (the following) made? The question implies: "By virtue of proximity, it will apply to the vocative (*āmantrita*) itself. [The answer is: "So that it does not apply to the preceding one."

The sense is that since the status of being a vocative (*āmantrita*) is exhausted by the [word] itself, it would belong to the preceding word as well. And thus, the status of being a vocative for the preceding word is not the governing factor (*atantra*). This occurs even in cases such as *gārgyaḥ kuṇḍenāṭan*, due to proximity (*sannidhāna*). If it is argued that the status of being a non-vocative (*amantritatva*) is also the governing factor; if that were so, only the subsequent [word] would be proximate, and there would be no possibility of the preceding word being subordinate (*aṅga*) to it. In the case of *devadattaḥ kuṇḍenāṭan*, if the preceding word were subordinate, there would be the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the entire compound and the grave accent (*nighāta*) for the remainder.

The accent [of *aṭan*] is the *nighāta* (elision) of an *āmantrita* (vocative). However, when the word *para* (subsequent) is included [in the rule], the word *devadatta* receives the *udātta* (acute) accent on its first syllable as an *āmantrita*. Likewise, there is no *nighāta* for *aṭan* in *kuṇḍenāṭan*, because according to the rule "an *āmantrita* preceding [another] is as if non-existent," the word *devadatta* is treated as non-existent. In the *Chāndasa* (Vedic), however, even a subsequent word is seen to behave like a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the preceding one—as in *ā te pitarmarutāṃ sumnametu*; here, by virtue of the word *putra*, the word *marutām* also undergoes *nighāta*.

"Just as one has become a lump of clay. In this context, since it is impossible for that which possesses a case-ending (the individual) to undergo transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the essence of a lump of clay, this statement is intended to convey a state of oneness. The meaning is: "He has attained unity, just like a lump of clay. Alternatively, there is also the word *piṇḍī*—as in "enter the *piṇḍī*"—and this is its usage here. The word *bhūta* is used in the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*), as in the expression "one who has become a father" (*pitṛbhūta*). Why, then, is an effort made to attain such a state? To this he says: "Of both as well... (*ubhayor api*).

If the designation "member of an *asatya*" were not adopted, there would be the extension (*atideśa*) of one of the rules concerning operations or designations from another [context]. For example, just as the operation of another [word] called an *āmantrita*—namely, its accent or the rule regarding accent—is applied, so too it would apply to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). And in that case, both [the *āmantrita* and the *subanta*] would be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Now, it might be argued: "Since there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for what follows a word, let it be stated that both [the *āmantrita* and the *subanta*] shall not be unaccented. This is true; however, that which was stated applies when the *āmantrita* is not at the beginning of a *pāda*, whereas if it is at the beginning of a *pāda*, that [rule] does not apply. Why is the suffix *-vat* used?

The question is: since the meaning of the suffix *vat* will be obtained simply by the use of another word (*para*) in reference to something else (*paratra*), why is it stated [that the rule applies] "so that it may also apply to its own base" (*svāśrayam api*)? By this, its occasional occurrence (*kvācitkatva*) is not being asserted; for if it were so, the distinction between domains would not be known—where it behaves like a stem (*aṅgavat*) and where it does not. Nor is its temporariness (*kādācitkatva*) intended—meaning that sometimes it behaves like a stem and sometimes it does not—for if that were the case, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) everywhere.

Therefore, for the sake of the *vat* substitute: in the absence of the mention of *vat*, when *ām* [is present] and the form *kuṇḍenāṭan* is established, the rule for *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would apply to *aṭan*; however, because *kuṇḍena* intervenes, the entire phrase *kuṇḍenāṭan* becomes a single *āmantrita* (vocative). Since there is no prohibition on the grounds that it is not "separated by one" (*na ca tadekāntaram*), the *nighāta* would indeed occur. But when the mention of *vat* exists, since *aṭan* is separated by one [syllable], the *nighāta* is prohibited, and thus the initial udātta accent is obtained.

In that state, because of the insertion of *kuṇaḍena* into it, the entire compound becomes udātta on its first syllable. Thus, although the whole compound does not have a single interval [between the verb and the suffix], the very fact that *aṭan* possesses a single interval—attained through the use of the suffix *vat*—is precisely what prevents the *nighāta* (suppression of accent) of the whole and causes it to be udātta on the first syllable. As in the example: *kūpe snāñ*.

In this case, since the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) would apply, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the *s*] becoming part of a single word (*aikapadya*). However, its own inherent status as the beginning of a word (*padāditva*) will remain; for in all cases of extended application (*atideśa*), that which is not contradicted by it remains as its own inherent property. Furthermore, there is no grammatical operation (*śāstrīya-kārya*) concerning the letter *s* here that is derived through extended application; therefore, its own inherent status certainly persists, just as in the example "the staff bends by itself" (*namate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*), where the *śap* suffix occurs despite the prohibition of the *yak* suffix.

In that case, consider this: in the example *carman nāmna*, when the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) applies, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* would occur because the two words reside in the same compound (*samānapadasthatva*). Even though they are in the same compound, it will not occur in non-proper names (*asaṃjñāyām*) due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*): "The substitution occurs after a preceding member [of a compound] when it is a proper name, provided the following word is not *ga*. This is not the scope of that restriction, for the term "preceding member" (*pūrvapada*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to a constituent part of a compound; therefore, the restriction applies only within a compound.

If, however, the term *pūrvapada* were explained as "the word preceding [the subsequent word]"—that is, as a restriction that applies without distinction from the preceding word—then the mention of *svara* (accent) could have been omitted. And if that were not done, the rule "an addition for a word in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇasyopasaṃkhyānam*) could likewise have been omitted.

How, when the status of being a member of a subsequent element (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) has been applied, will the status of being a member of the preceding element also occur through the recurrence of the rule (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*), due to the difference in scope (*viṣyabheda*) according to the principle of *ciṇo luṅ*? However, if there were the mention of accent (*svaragrahaṇa*), then in the example *svahād anyatra paraśunā vṛścann*, the form *vṛścann* would be a nominal stem (*pratipadika*). Nor would there be a prohibition based on the rule *na pratyayalakṣaṇenāpratyayaḥ* ("there is no [application of a rule] by means of a suffix-characteristic if it is not a suffix"), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the prohibition *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*.

In that case, because [the vocative] would enter into the base (prātipadika) by virtue of being like a subsequent member (parāṅgavadbhāva), the elision of the *sup* suffix prescribed by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ" would undesirably apply. But if the term *sva* is included [in the definition of *pada*], then when the elision of *sup* is to be performed, there is an absence of the status of being like a subsequent member. This is not so; in the expression "like a subsequent member," the word *para* refers to the vocative (*āmantrita*) due to its proximity; and since that form consists exclusively of a *sup*-ending element, the status of being like a subsequent member applies only to the operations of a *sup*-ending element, not to the operations of a base (*prātipadika*). As in the example: *uccair adhīyāna*.

The words *uccais* and *nīcais*, being read with an acute (*udātta*) accent on the final syllable, denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) due to the predominance of that locative capacity, and [the word *svarāt*] denotes the cause (*nimitta*) for that [locus].

3. *Prākkaḍārāt samāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.3). There is no reason for skipping the immediately preceding sūtra, *Yathā’sādṛśye*. Now, one might ask: since the term *samāsaḥ* is marked with a svarita accent, let it serve as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), just as *pratyayaḥ* and so on do; what is the purpose of the expression *prāk* [in *prākkaḍārāt*]? To this he replies: *prāgāvacanam* means that *prākkaḍārāt* is a specification of a limit. [He further says: *saṃjñāsamāveśārtham*—otherwise, because there is a single governing heading for technical terms (*saṃjñā*), there would be an optionality (*paryāya*) between them.

However, when there is a specification of a limit (*avadhi*), by the force of that [specification], the term "prior" (*prāk*) is understood to recur. Consequently, the technical designation of *samāsa* applies first; then, being *samāsas*, they receive the designations of *avyayībhāva* and so forth. Thus, the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the designations is established. Alternatively, the word "prior" (*prāk*), which is a directional term, will be supplied as an ellipsis by means of the ablative case itself in the rule *kaḍārāt*. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of having to supply the word "prior" [in every subsequent rule]; for if that were supplied, then rules such as "in a *dik-samāsa* which is a *bahuvrīhi*," "in a *tṛtīyā-samāsa*," and "in a *dvandva*," where the word "compound" (*samāsa*) is used, would become untenable.

Because those [terms] mentioned prior to *kaḍāra* lack the designation of "compound" (*samāsa*), the word "prior" (*prāk*) must be supplied [from the previous rule]; thus, the explicit mention of "prior" (*prāgvacana*) is unnecessary. To this, he replies: "The mention of 'prior'... (*prāgvacanam iti*).
4. *saha* [is compounded] with a word ending in the seventh case. (Pāṇini 2.1.4)

What is the purpose of mentioning "together" (*saha*), since the third case ending alone will imply the sense of "together," as in the example "the old man with the young man"? [The answer is: It is so that the technical designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) may apply to the two things that exist together, and not to each one individually. Otherwise, just as in the expression "the father has come with the son," where the connection with the act of coming belongs to both, so too the designation of a compound would apply to each one separately. But when "together" is mentioned, a single designation applies to the two things existing together.

Furthermore, what would happen if each individual [member] were to receive the designation? In this case, the rule for adding a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) would apply to the expression *ṛkpādaḥ*, and there would be two accents. However, in the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*, it will be explained that the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation applies as "the compound and the compound," whereby the designation is intended as a restrictive rule for a collection of compounds; thus, it will not apply to a single sentence. Otherwise, since every individual compound would end in a suffix, the inclusion of the term *samāsa* [in the rule] would be for the purpose of prescribing [the designation].

In the rule "and from a compound [denoting] that [collection]" (*samāsācca tadviṣayāt*), the term *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") also carries over. Since the status of being a *prātipadika* belongs to the collection (*samūha*) and not to the individual compound, the suffix is established as arising from the collection itself by virtue of the singular number [in *samāsāt*]. Thus, the inclusion of the word "together" (*saha*) is for the purpose that the suffix may apply to the aggregate as a whole and not to each individual member. This, however, is not the purpose; rather, the name "compound" (*samāsa*) is given as a technical designation so that it may be understood as a descriptive (*anvartha*) term.

A *samāsa* (compound) is that in which two words (*pada*) are combined together as a single aggregate. [The word *samāsa*] is derived from the root *as* with the suffix *ghañ* in the locative sense according to the rule *halaśca*. Therefore, the inclusion of the word *saha* (together) is redundant; to this he replies: "The mention of *saha* is for the purpose of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*). *Saha* constitutes one rule: "with *sup*" alone. That is, a *sup*-ending word is compounded with another. With what? Since it is a rule concerning *pada*s, it is with a semantically related word (*samartha*). An example is *anuvyacalat*.

In this case, because the singular number (*ekatva*) is intended to be expressed by *su*, the compound is formed first with *adhi* and subsequently with *anu*; since this is a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), there is no application of the *Śākala* rule (the elision of *a*). However, the general accentuation of the compound does not apply here, because of the suppression (*nighāta*) of the finite verb (*tiṅ*) according to the rule "a finite verb is suppressed after another finite verb" (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*). There is suppression of *anu* according to the rule "a motion [particle] is suppressed after a motion [particle]" (*gatirgatau*). When the *vairyaṇa* substitution occurs, the vowel *a* becomes circumflex (*svarita*) according to the rule "after an acute (*udātta*) and a circumflex (*svarita*...). Others, however, maintain that the general accentuation of the compound applies as a residual rule (*satiśiṣṭa*).

The case-ending (*vibhakti*), however, occurs even though [the word] is a compound (*samāsa*) because it is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); this is because the singular number has already been expressed by the finite verb (*tiṅ*). Alternatively, the mention of "number" (*vacana*) is so that [the suffix] may apply even when the singular number and so forth have already been expressed; thus, the nominative singular suffix is applied, and its elision follows from the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. And in this way, because there is a single word (*ekapada*), in the example *āmanuvyacalad devadattaḥ*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent—by the rule *āma ekāntaram āmantritam anantike*—is established. Furthermore, since the division of the rule (*yaugavibhāga*) is intended for the sake of achieving the desired result, one should not raise the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
5. Avyayībhāva [compounds]. (Pāṇini 2.1.5)

In this context, for the sake of brevity, one might think that a single-syllable technical term (*saṃjñā*) should be employed; why then is such a long one used? To this he says: "And this [term] is descriptive" (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). [The compound *avyayībhāva* is formed as follows: since that which does not undergo modification (*avyaya*) remains unchanged (*avyaya*), it is called *avyayībhāva*; the suffix *ṇa* is added according to the rule "the addition of *ṇa* to the root *bhū*. He asks: what is accomplished by its being descriptive? To this he replies: "By this... The mention of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the indeclinable (*avyaya*).

In cases such as *sūpaprati* and *śākaprati*, [the designation of avyayībhāva] would not apply because the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant. Therefore, it is established that in an avyayībhāva compound, the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is predominant. For in this way, a collection of both indeclinables and non-indeclinables becomes an indeclinable by virtue of possessing the properties of an indeclinable. What is accomplished by this? The over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the avyayībhāva designation to cases such as *samṛddhā madrāḥ* (the prosperous Madras), which would otherwise be called *samadrāḥ* if the meaning of the final member were predominant, is thereby avoided.

In cases such as *pāregaṅgam*, *dvimuni*, and *unmattagaṅgam*, the *avyayībhāva* compound is formed by virtue of an explicit rule (*vacana*). Thus, since the status of being an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is obtained through its etymological meaning—that "what was not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable"—the functional effect of an indeclinable is also secured; therefore, [the objection that] even the rule "and *avyayībhāva*" [is unnecessary] is not valid. To this, we reply: no; for in this very context, let the status of being an indeclinable be understood as pertaining to specific grammatical operations, either by way of enumeration or by virtue of its etymological meaning.

6. An indeclinable (avyaya) [compounds with another word] when it expresses: case-relation (vibhakti), proximity (samīpa), abundance (samṛddhi), prosperity (vyṛddhi), absence (abhāva), passing away (atyaya), "not now" (asamprati), manifestation (śabdaprādurbhāva), sequence (paścāt), accordance (yathā), succession (anupūrvya), simultaneity (yaugapadya), similarity (sādṛśya), attainment (sampatti), entirety (sākalya), or limit (antavacana). Pāṇini 2.1.6.

Since the indeclinable (avyaya) is what is heard [in the rule], the case endings and so forth are qualifiers of that alone, not of the compound; thus he says, "In the case endings and so forth. Regarding the phrase "it is compounded" (*samasyate*): although only the technical name "compound" (*samāsa*) is being enjoined, nevertheless, for the sake of instructing the ignorant, it is said "it is compounded" because in the process of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), a conjunction of two words is performed. The mention of "number" (*vacana*) is connected with each [of the preceding items]; and that [word "number"] is derived as a passive agent (*karmasādhana*) and is in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "case endings" and the rest.

Regarding the statement "the indeclinable which occurs when [cases] beginning with the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are to be expressed": this means that an indeclinable expresses—that is, indicates—the meanings of the case-endings and so forth. By the word "case-ending" (*vibhakti*), the power of the grammatical relation (*kāraka-śakti*) is denoted, on the grounds that by it the meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadika-artha*) is differentiated (*vibhajyate*). The phrase "with reference to women" (*strīṣvadhikṛtya*) is to be construed as "a discourse is set in motion regarding women. The word "with reference to" (*adhikṛtya*) means "having introduced as the subject" (*prastutya*).

And because of their proximity, it is understood that women themselves are the ones who give birth; the meaning is that the discourse has women as its subject matter. Regarding the phrase "it generally proceeds," they say here: the meaning is that the discourse which is undertaken proceeds among women; since there is a single agent for both the introduction and the narration in that context, the suffix *ktvā* is grammatically established.

Others, however, say: *kṛtyasya kathā* means "a discussion regarding what must be done" (*kartavyakathā*). That [discussion] proceeds with respect to women (*strīṣu*) and is applied to women (*strīṣvadhi*), forming a derivative sentence (*prakriyāvākya*); yet this is not fit for actual usage (*prayoga*), because the compound is obligatory (*nitya*). Thus, we have *adhistrī*. Because of the rule "*avyayībhāvaśca*," it is neuter, and by the rule "*hrasvo napuṃsake*" (Pāṇini 1.2.47), the vowel is shortened. The phrase "an indeclinable in the sense of the locative case" shows that it expresses a case-meaning (*vibhaktivacanatā*). For example: *upakumbham*.

The phrase "approaching a jar" (*kumbhasyopaiti*) is a compound with a word ending in the genitive case. Examples include *duḥśakam* and *duryavanam*. The words *śaka* and *yavana* denote human races. But why is the term *vṛddhi* (increase) mentioned again, since the result would be established by the rule for "absence of meaning" (*arthābhāva*) alone? It is not so established; for "absence of meaning" refers to the absence of that very thing with which the compound is formed—here, the absence of the chariot (*ratha*). However, in these cases, there is no absence of the Śakas themselves; rather, there is an absence of their prosperity (*ṛddhi*).

The inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*) in the phrase "non-existence of the object" is intended so that [the rule] applies where there is the non-existence of the very nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), and not in the case of the negation of a mere attribute (*dharma*). For example, someone might negate the Brahminhood of a certain person—having first attributed it to him on the grounds that he was produced by a Brahmin father and a Brahmin mother—by saying, "This man is not a Brahmin, since he urinates while standing. Furthermore, this should not apply to mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), such as "A cow is not a horse"; here too, another entity is being negated, not the nature of the substratum itself.

*Atiśītam* means the absence [of cold] in the past. An absence not delimited by time is understood [there], but here the term *saṃprati* (now) is employed to distinguish it as an absence at the present moment. Regarding *atitaisṛkam*: *Tisṛkā* is the name of a village; according to the rule "the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of 'being there' when it is a proper name," we have *taisṛkam*, meaning a garment produced there. And that is to be used at a particular time. In the words *uṣṇe* (in heat) or *śīte* (in cold), the prefix *ati-* functions in the sense of "not now."

And the action of enjoyment (*upabhoga*) is included within the very function (*vṛtti*) [of the compound], just as rice mixed with curds is called "curd-rice" (*dadhyodana*). Therefore, there is a semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the preceding and following members; the meaning is that the three-fold covering (*taisṛkam ācchādanam*) is not currently fit for enjoyment. Even though the word *taisṛka* depends on the word *ācchādana*, the compound is formed because it is expressive (*gamaka*).

In this case, there is neither the existence of *taisṛka* unconditioned by time, nor its non-existence at present. What then? It is distinguished from the present because of the absence and the passing away of its enjoyment (*upabhoga*). Regarding the word *tat-pāṇi*: the word *tat* is also an indeclinable (*nipāta*). Regarding *pratyartham*: the sentence "with respect to each object" (*artham artham prati*) is also valid here, according to the usage in the *Bhāṣya*. Alternatively, the indeclinable here does not function as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); rather, being a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits a relationship.

Repetition (*vīpsā*), however, is indicated by the doubling [of the word]. The state of being successive is *ānupūrvyam*; the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied here because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class of stems. Because the suffix *ṣyañ* is marked with the letter *ṣ*, it occurs in the feminine as well; its usage is as follows: likewise, *jyeṣṭha*.

Regarding the phrase "in succession" (*ānupūrvyeṇa*): it would be *sacakramita*.
