The word *saha* undergoes elision in a compound; the substitution of *sa-* for *saha* occurs by the rule "in an avyayībhāva compound, except when denoting time. This applies to the subsequent examples as well. Regarding the phrase "even when [the second member] is subordinate" (*guṇabhūte’pi*), etc.: if the word "similarity" (*sādṛśye*) were not stated, then since an avyayībhāva compound has the first member as its predominant meaning, similarity would only be expressed when it is the predominant factor because it qualifies the second member—as in "what is similar to a crow? (*kiṃkṣyaḥ sadṛśaḥ*). It would not be expressed when [similarity] is subordinate, as in "similar to a crow" (*sadṛśaḥ kiṃkṣyaḥ*).

By showing the predominance of that which possesses similarity, he demonstrates that similarity itself is subordinate. [The example] "a *kikhī*"—the short vowel is as before. A jackal (*śṛgāla*) of diminished size is a *kikhī*. This is an obscure example, because it is based on usage from ancient times. Anticipating the objection that the term *sampatti* (attainment) is redundant since it is already established in the sense of "prosperity," he says: "Attainment is a state of being that conforms to [another]. [The example] "the *brahman*-nature of the *Brāhmaṇas*": the meaning is that their state of being *brahman* conforms to [that of the former]. [The example] "together with the grass."

And he says that eating grass here is not literal: "not even anything" (*na kiñcit*). Eating grass is a figurative expression; by that statement, the meaning understood is that one does not abandon any food whatsoever, according to the logic: "how could one who eats grass abandon anything else? This is said with reference to the view of others.

The sense is this: "completion" (samāpti) refers to the limit of the portion of the text that has been grasped—such as "now this much portion is to be studied"—and this occurs even when the study is incomplete. Regarding the phrase "sāgnīti": words such as *agni* refer to the texts whose meaning they denote; at that time, the portion grasped ends with *agni* and so forth, but it does not mean that there is no further study beyond that. Therefore, he says "iyam" (this) to indicate that there is no totality [of the subject matter].
7. [The sixth case ending is used] when there is no similarity (asādṛśye). || 2-1-7 ||

Since a compound expressing similarity would already be established by the preceding rule alone, and since there is no statement such as "in the case of similarity, [the word] *yathā* [is used]," the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle *nañ* is intended here to ensure there is no doubt; thus, the meaning is "in the case of non-similarity. What is the purpose of this sūtra? For example, in the phrase *yathā devadattaḥ*. Here, the word *yathā* indicates that Devadatta is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) with respect to Yajñadatta. In that case, although the standard of comparison depends upon the object of comparison (*upameya*), the intention is that a mutual compounding of the words *yathā* and *devadatta* would result due to their semantic connection.
Now, one might ask: why does this not result in [the meaning] being "similarity with the preceding" or "according to the object"? To this he says: "precisely by the preceding."
8. The particle *yāvat* is used in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇa*). (Pāṇini 2.1.8)

Regarding the expression *yāvanti pātrāṇi*: there exists the indeclinable (*avyaya*) *yāvat*, and there also exists that which ends in a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). Therefore, even though it is not a compound (*asamāsa*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is always with that which ends in a secondary suffix.
*sup-pratinā mātrārthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.9): [The word ending in] a case-ending (*sup*) is compounded with *prati* when the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*) is intended.

In the example *asty atra kiṃcit sūpaḥ*, the word *kiṃcit* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) functioning as a coordinate term (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with *sūpaḥ*, which is masculine. The phrase "while *suP* is present" is derived from the rule *subāmantrite parāṅgavat svare*. The purpose of this [reintroduction of] *suP* is for the sake of excluding indeclinables. Previously, the mention of *suP* was analyzed together with the mention of *avyaya*; however, since words such as *svarādi* (beginning with *svaḥ*) exhibit a predominance of substantive meaning (*sattvapradhānatā*) when they enter into a compound—such as *doṣāmanyam ahaḥ* ("a day considered as night") or *divāmanyā rātriḥ* ("a night considered as day")—the formation of a compound would be possible for an indeclinable alone, provided that the presence of the nominal suffix (*mātrāvat*) is not obstructed. Thus, the compound would otherwise apply even to an indeclinable.
The number of dice or stalks is ten; this is a derivative formation. 2-1-10.

Regarding the phrase "the words *akṣa*, *śalākā*, and numbers": this means the words *akṣa* and *śalākā*, as well as words expressing numbers. In some places, however, the reading is "the word *akṣa*, the word *śalākā*, and number words. "In the practice of gamblers" (*kitavavyavahāre*): gamblers (*kitavāḥ*) are those who play dice; in their practice—namely, the casting of dice and sticks—it is only there that this compound is desired. This is understood from the inherent nature of the rule's formulation. "Crooked or face up" (*karvū uttānā iti*).

Since the *śalākās* (counting-sticks) are also the subject under discussion, the term "all" (*sarve*) is used for both genders—meaning all males and all females—and "upright" (*uttānāḥ*) refers to those who are upright, while "downward" (*avāñcaḥ*) refers to those who are downward-facing; according to the rule "the masculine remains when combined with the feminine," the masculine form is retained. "Of that very one" (*tasyaiva asya*) means "of the thrower. "Defeat" (*vipātaḥ*) means loss. "In the case of a different fall" (*anyathāpāte sati*) means when the fall is other than the one occurring in victory—namely, when some fall upright and some fall downward. "By the thrower" (*akṣeśa*) [is the meaning].

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of the meter. Regarding the word *parameṇa*: it means "beyond this by way of excellence," that is to say, it does not exceed five. The justification for this is provided in the verse: "But when there are five of one form. Here too, the masculine gender remains. The reading *ekarūpāsu* is generally found; in that case, only the counting-sticks (*śalākā*) are understood. [Thus] victory alone will occur.

The meaning of the suffix *lṛṭ* (the future tense marker) must be investigated, since victory occurs only when five [dice] are of one form; therefore, there is a connection with that "supreme" [result] through the fourfold comparison (*catuḥparītyanvaya*). The words beginning with *akṣa* end in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*). The sense is that otherwise this compound is intended in the commentary (*vṛtti*), and in that case, since the dice (*akṣa*) and so forth are the agents (*kartṛ*), the third case alone is appropriate. Regarding the phrase "of what was previously stated": it means "of what occurred previously. Since roots have multiple meanings, the root *vac* here functions in the sense of "occurrence" (*vartane*); that very [meaning] is referred to by the pronoun *tat* in the expression "not as that" (*na taditi tacchabdena parāmṛśyate*).

The meaning is that if, as in the previous victory, the movement of the die (*akṣa*) and so forth was such that it became even (*datta*), but now it is not so, then a compound occurs. The singular number in the phrase "of the previously mentioned" (*pūrvoktasya*) is used with reference to the category in general. That is to say, when the uniform behavior of the die and so forth at the time of victory is contrasted with a contrary behavior, a compound occurs to indicate that transformation. The phrase "as if there were oneness of the die and the counter" (*ekatevākṣaśalākayoḥ*) means that a compound occurs between the words *akṣa* and *śalākā*, both of which are in the singular case-ending.

This too is obtained simply from the inherent nature of the expression; for, as in examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ*, non-dual unity (*abhedaikatva*) would be understood, rather than pure numerical unity (*śuddhaikatva*). However, this is generally recited in the form of a verse: "And in the gambling of a cheat, there is unity of the die and the counter. In that case, another meaning must be sought, and there is the risk of [misapplying] the rules of *saṃhitā*. What is meant by "in the gambling of a cheat"? [For example: "This die did not roll as it did before on the cart."

What is meant by "identity" (*ekatva*)? [The answer is: "This was not played with two dice or with dice"—it is not so formed. What is meant by "dice and so forth" (*akṣādayaḥ*)? [The answer is: "This was not so in the previous victory by chance"; because of the statement "by means of *pariṇā*," it does not occur with a mere word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).
The words *apa*, *pari*, *bahiḥ*, and *añcas* [are compounded] with a word ending in the fifth case-suffix. 2.1.12.

Now, it might be objected: "Since the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is not prescribed by any rule in connection with the word *bahiḥ*, how can there be a compound for that [word] with a form ending in the fifth case? However, in the case of *bahirgato grāmāt* ("gone outside from the village"), this cannot be a compound because of a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). To this, he says: "By the word *bahiḥ*. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the grammatical statement itself, a compound of the word *bahiḥ* with something other than a form ending in the fifth case should be allowed; for the term "fifth case" (*pañcamī*) is explicitly mentioned [in the rule].

In this context, the words *apa* and *pari* are understood to have the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) due to their mutual association; they are both *karmapravacanīya*s, and when used in conjunction with them, only the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed. Furthermore, the root *añc-* is also understood here as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because of its association with *apa* and *pari*; even when used in conjunction with it, only the ablative case—prescribed by the rule for compounds ending in *añc*—occurs. This mention of the ablative case indicates that the ablative is employed in place of the genitive when there is a connection with "outside" (*bahis*). 13. *Āṅ* [is a *karmapravacanīya*] in the senses of limit exclusive (*maryādā*) and limit inclusive (*abhividhi*). (Pāṇini 2.1.13)

The phrase "in the senses of limit (maryādā) and inclusion (abhividhi)" could have been omitted. How so? Because the word "pañcamī" (the fifth case) is understood from the previous rule, and the fifth case is prescribed only in connection with the karmapravacanīya particle *āṅ*. Furthermore, the designation "karmapravacanīya" is assigned to *āṅ* specifically for these two meanings by the rule "āṅ maryādāvacane. In that rule, the inclusion of the word "vacana" (mention/expression) is intended so that [the designation applies] even when there is a mere statement of a limit; thus, it also applies in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Alternatively, in that very rule, one might simply include the mention of "inclusion" (*abhividhi*) itself.
The prefix *abhi-* signifies "towards" (*abhimukhya*) when used with a noun that denotes a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Pāṇini 2.1.14.

*Abhyagni*, *pratyagni*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is *agniṃ prati*. Because *abhi* and *prati* function as *karmapravacanīya*s according to the rules "abhir abhāge" and "lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna-", the second case ending is employed. In this context, fire (*agni*) is the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*), for by it the falling of the arrows is indicated; furthermore, *abhi* and *prati*, having expressed the relationship between the indicator and the indicated (*lakṣyalakṣaṇabhāva*), also express the sense of being directed toward (*abhimukhya*).

In the expression *srughnaṃ pratigataḥ* ("gone toward Srughna"), there arises the understanding that [the person] has gone by way of the same direction as the fire; since the act of going possesses both the fire as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the sense of being directed toward it (*ābhimukhya*), there would be a compound with the words *yena* and *tena*. Regarding *abhyaṅkāḥ* and *pratyaṅkāḥ*: these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "those whose marks (*aṅka*) are new" (*abhinava*) or "those whose marks are renewed" (*pratinava*). Here, the mark (*aṅka*) serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the cows, but there is no sense of being directed toward it (*ābhimukhya*).

But surely, it has been stated that when a non-indeclinable (avyaya) meaning is possible and is predominant, an indeclinable compound (avyayībhāva) occurs; how then is there an occasion for this [present rule]? If this is so, then this [rule] makes known that in this section, even where a bahuvrīhi would otherwise apply, an avyayībhāva may occur. By this, the forms *saṃkhyā vaṃśyena* and *dvimuni vyākaraṇam* are established.
15. The word *anu* [is used] in the sense of "near" (*samayā*). 2.1.15.

The term *yatsamayā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). But how can there be a genitive case when used in conjunction with the word *samayā*, given that by the rule "with *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, and *samayā*, the second case [is used]" (*dvitīyā*), the accusative ought to occur? This is not a fault; for while the primary meaning of the word *samayā* is "proximity" (*sāmīpya*), and the accusative is prescribed in its connection with that sense, here the word *samayā* is used to denote the particle *anu*, which is what the word *samayā* signifies. Thus he says: "*anaryatsamayā*" means "expressing the sense of *anu*."

What is the meaning of *samayā*? It means "expressing proximity" (*samayāvācin*). Here, because it lacks connection with its primary sense, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur; rather, only the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs, and there is a compound with that [genitive]. Nor is there a prohibition by the rule *pūraṇaguṇa-* (P. 2.2.11), because it is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*). For the word *samayā*, when it denotes proximity, is an indeclinable because it expresses non-existence (*asattva-vācitvāt*). But here it functions in the sense of the word *anu* (along/with); in that regard, just as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) does not receive the designation of an indeclinable in cases such as *abhir ābhāge* (P. 1.4.90), so it is with this [word *samayā*] as well.

And thus, the expression *yatsamaya* is a Vedic (sautra) usage without a case-ending. In the commentary (*vṛtti*) as well, the form *yatsamaya* lacks a case-ending by way of imitating the sutra. The word *tena* means "by a word expressing that. Regarding *anuvanam*: it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning "along the vicinity of the forest" (*vanasya anv iti*), expressing a relationship of proximity; its meaning is stated as "along the forest" (*vanaṃ samayeti*).
16. And [the term] "of which" [denotes] the length. (Pāṇini 2.1.16)

The phrase "it continues [from the previous rule] by way of its characteristic" (lakṣaṇena) is understood here. Otherwise, in the sense of "the length of the Gaṅgā," the form would have been *anugaṅgam*. In this case as well, since the word *anu* denotes length because it expresses the same extension (*āyāma*), he says: "the word *anu* which expresses length. The example is *anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī along the Gaṅgā"). This is a compound with the word *gaṅgā* ending in the genitive case; that is, "along the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyā anu*).

The length (*āyāma*) and the state of being a hundred thousand (*lakṣamatva*) are illuminated by the secondary sense (*anunā*), because a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) depends upon that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*); thus, the *lakṣya* is the meaning of the compound. Consequently, the compound occurs in the relation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), resulting in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī: "that of which the length is like that of the Gaṅgā," meaning "Vārāṇasī is as long as the Gaṅgā. Some say the meaning is "extremely long" (*atyantāyatā*). Accordingly, the author of the Bhāgavṛtti employs the expression "this sūtra follows the Gaṅgā" (*anugaṅgametatsūtram*) in the section on the *ekaśeṣa* sūtras. We, however, say this is not so.

When the doubt arises as to whether Vārāṇasī is oriented toward the east or toward the north, this is said: "Vārāṇasī follows the Gaṅgā. The meaning is that just as the Gaṅgā is oriented toward the north, so too is Vārāṇasī oriented toward the north; that is to say, the length of Vārāṇasī is according to the length of the Gaṅgā. It is observed that the length of Mathurā is [determined] by the length of the Yamunā. The Yamunā is not the indicator (lakṣaṇa) by its own essential nature, but rather by its length; likewise, Mathurā is not the indicated (lakṣya) by its own essential nature, but rather by its length.
In this context, through the distinction between what is obtained and what is not obtained, it is stated: "The length of Mathurā is indicated by the length of the Yamunā."
17. And [the compounds] beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* [are neuter]. 2.1.17.

The meaning is that these are taught as ready-made forms (*nipāta*). Their *nipātana* (irregular formation) consists precisely in their being recited thus in the list (*gaṇa*). Consequently, forms such as those ending in *śatṛ* and *śānac* also occur; furthermore, the sense is that the grammatical operations of the *prakriyā* (derivation process), such as "the case endings [are elided] after a verbal root or a nominal stem" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), need not be applied. They possess the designation *avyayībhāva*. It should be understood that the designation *samāsa* (compound) must also be prescribed, as well as the property of having the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*), and so that they may receive the designation *prātipadika* (nominal stem). "Tiṣṭhadgu" refers to a specific time.

The phrase "a specific time" (*kālaviśeṣa*) is connected with the subsequent [terms] as well; for this very reason, he will state at the end: "these are words for time. The meaning is that this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for the expression "such a specific time. They are not connected by means of other case-endings; the meaning is that their usage must be made only when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is not distinct [from the action], and not otherwise. And they function in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*); this connects even with *tiṣṭhadgu*, *vahadgu*, and *āyatīgava*.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be a word denoting time. The particle *ca* is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), since indeclinables have multiple meanings. "Another compound does not occur" means that no other type of derivation (*vṛtti*) occurs. As for the example "ātiṣṭhadgu japansandhyām," there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending by the rule "after an indeclinable," and it is not a compound. In the forms *tiṣṭhadgu* and *vahadgu*, the suffix *śatṛ* replaces the present tense marker (*laṭ*) due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule "of *go* and feminine stems."

In the case of *āyatī-vagam*, however, there is an absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), as well as the substitution of *śatṛ* and the addition of a compound-final suffix (*samāsanta*). In *khaleyavam* and *khalebusam*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. In *lūyamānayava* and similar forms, there is the substitution of the suffix *śānac*. [The examples] *samabhūmi* and *samapadāti* [are explained as follows]: when the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapada*) is predominant—namely, "the levelness of the ground"—it is an *avyayībhāva* compound. In some readings, the forms appear as *samaṃbhūmi* and *samaṃpadāti*; in those cases, the augment *mum* is added to the prior member.

Others, however, read *saṃbhūmisampadā* as "attainment of the earth"; in that case, there is elision of the final vowel of the compound, or the prefix *sam-* is compounded [with the following word]. In the *suṣāmā* group, *samasya* means "excellent," while *vigata* means "gone away," "defective," "departed," or "removed. This is the analysis (*vigraha*). *Āyatosamā* is [formed from] *āyatīsamam*, with the substitution of *śatṛ* and, as before, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). *Samā* means "year. In the same way, one says *pāpasamam* ("equal to sin") and *puṇyasamam* ("equal to merit"). Regarding the four beginning with *prāh* (i.e., *prāh*, *pravaṇa*, *prāk*, *praṅ*), the analysis is "the state of having gone forward (*pragatatva*) of the day" (*ahnaḥ*), and so forth.

The word *samprati* means "presently" or "having come together. Its opposite is *asamprati*. According to the rule *ic karmavyatīhāre*, this suffix *ic* is prescribed even in cases such as *dvidaṇḍi* and others; therefore, these also constitute *avyayībhāva* compounds. In the case of *daṇḍādaṇḍi*: having struck with staffs (*daṇḍaiḥ*) and with staffs (*daṇḍaiḥ*), this battle proceeded. Here, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*. The lengthening of the first member's vowel occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*. Because it is an *avyayībhāva*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); consequently, there is elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*).
The words *pāre* and *madhye* optionally [govern the genitive case] when used with a word in the sixth case. (Pāṇini 2.1.18)

Regarding the phrase "because of the word *vā*": [An objection is raised: "But since the *avyayībhāva* compound is already made optional by the *Mahāvibhāṣā* even when it is an exception (*apavāda*), the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* will also occur as an alternative option; and since that too is optional, the analytical sentence (*vākya*) will also occur. It is replied: When the expression of the meaning through an analytical sentence is applicable, the formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) being commenced would necessarily sublate the sentence. Therefore, by means of the option (*vikalpa*), the sentence itself is permitted as an alternative in one instance.

In that case, since the option (*vikalpa*) regarding the exception (*apavāda*) is what brings about the rule itself, it would be a permanent sublater (*bādhaka*) of the general rule (*utsarga*). However, because of the mention of the word "or" (*vā*), even that [exception] is permitted in one alternative; thus, the three-fold form [of the *lakṣaṇa*] is established. This very mention of "or" is the indicator (*jñapaka*): where both a general rule and an exception are made optional by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), there, when the exception is not applied, the general rule does not apply either.

Therefore, since the *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) applies first in the case of *kāyasya*, a *ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa* (genitive compound) does not occur; and in the case of *dakṣasyāpatyaṃ dākṣiḥ*, since the suffix *iñ* applies, *aṇ* does not occur. The specific prescription (*nipātana*) of the form ending in *-aikāra* is for cases where the locative sense is impossible, such as *pāregaṅgād ānaya* ("bring from across the Gaṅgā"). However, in the case of *pāre* [as a separate word], it is established by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* due to the mention of *bahulam*.
19. A numeral [is compounded] with a word denoting lineage. (Pāṇini 2.1.19)

"Of one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) means a continuum (*santāna*) that has a single nature; because the members of the continuum (*santānin*) possess a single characteristic, the continuum itself possesses a single characteristic. "Two sages" (*dvau munī*) refers to Pāṇini and Kātyāyana. "Three sages" (*trimuni*) refers to those two and the author of the *Bhāṣya*. As for the example of "one characteristic by birth," it is: "twenty-one Bhāradvājas. However, when [the rule] is applied with "together with knowledge" (*vidyayā saha*), this same meaning is established by another method in the rule "*lakṣaṇenābhipratī*."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words meaning "rivers," [to form a Bahuvrīhi compound]. (Pāṇini 2.1.20)

"By words denoting rivers": the intention is that because of the mention of the plural number in "nadbhiḥ," both the word-form itself and the name "nadī" (river) are included. And this [term] is intended for a collective compound (*samāhāra*); otherwise, by the rule of the "prior exception" (*purastādapavāda*), this would be a sublater of the rule "pūrvakāla-eka-".

In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), however, because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], it would be a *dvigu* compound; consequently, in the case of *ekanadī*, if it were an *avyayībhāva*, the suffix *ṭac*—prescribed by the rule "after *nadī*, *paurṇamāsī*, and *āgrahāyaṇī*"—would apply, as would neuter gender. For there is no authority for the restriction that only those words denoting specific [rivers] are intended to be included here. As for the suffix *ac* in the form *godāvaryāśca nadyaśca*, which serves as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), it occurs only in an *avyayībhāva* in cases such as *pañcanadam*, but not in a *tatpuruṣa* in the case of *ekanadī*.

And when there is an intention to express a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), one also has forms such as *ekanadam* (one river), just like *ekāpūpī* (one cake). Likewise, the *avyayībhāva* compound could also occur in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*), as in *dvīrāvatīkaḥ deśaḥ* (a region having two Irāvatīs). Nor can it be argued that here a *bahuvrīhi* applies because it is subsequent [in the rules]; for it is not a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), since this is not a remainder unless the mention of "aggregate" is made. Therefore, it is well said: "And this [compound] is desired in the case of an aggregate"; and this is obtained from the inherent nature of linguistic expression (*abhidhānasvābhāvya*).
21. And [a compound is formed] when another word’s meaning is expressed, provided it is a name (saṃjñā). 2.1.21.
22. Tatpuruṣa [is a compound whose final member is predominant]. 2.1.22.

Regarding the statement "the meaning of the final member is predominant": in cases such as *pūrvākāyaḥ* (the front part of the body) and *ardhapippalī* (half a long pepper), the designation "tatpuruṣa" applies by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*).
23. And [the word] *dvigu* [is a compound]. 2-1-23.

Regarding the term *samāsāntāḥ*: although the suffixes *ṭac* (in *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*) and *ṭac* and *ac* (in *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*) are dependent on the *tatpuruṣa* compound, nevertheless, because there is a distinction between their respective bases, the plural number is used to express that distinction. In the case of *pañcarājam*, there is an absence of femininity because the final member of the compound does not end in the vowel *a*. However, according to the alternative view that "the *samāsāntas* are those [suffixes] at the end of the final member which constitutes the meaning of the compound," it is due to its inclusion in the *pātra*-class.

In some places, there is a reading of *pañcarājī* in the feminine gender; however, that is a corrupt reading because it contradicts the Bhāṣya. Regarding *dvyaha*: the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*, and [the word is masculine] by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*. Regarding *pañcagavam*: the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *gorataddhitaluki*, and as before, there is an absence of femininity.

24. The second case [is used] after words meaning "resorted to" (śrita), "passed beyond" (atīta), "fallen into" (patita), "gone to" (gata), "transgressed" (atyasta), "attained" (prāpta), and "arrived at" (āpanna). Pāṇini 2.1.24.

In words such as *śrita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent because the root has the sense of "going" (*gati*). The word *pati* is also transitive, as in the example: "lest, acting crookedly, we fall into hell. *Atyāsa* means transgression, which is indeed a specific kind of movement. *Prāpti* here is also simply "going," not the resulting fruit. The same applies to *āpatti*. In this context, this compound [with *atyāsa*] should not be prescribed for the words *śrita*, *patita*, and *gata*. Why? Because when someone has resorted to hardship (*kaṣṭa*), it is "hardship resorted to by him"; in that case, the formation is already established by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

There is no difference in meaning, no difference in form, and no difference in accent. Even in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, by the rule "after *ahīna*, *dvitīyā*," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member occurs after words such as *śrita*, *patita*, and *gata*. However, for the sake of establishing the correct accent in the case of [words] like *atīta*, a specific rule must be applied; for otherwise, in those cases, the *tatpuruṣa* would have to take the accent of the *thāthādi* group rather than the *ahīna* accent, because of the prohibition in the rule "in the case of *atīta* and *atyasta* when not denoting a sacrifice (*ahīna*)," whereas for *prāpta* and *āpanna*, there is the specific statement: "after *ahīna*, the second case ending [retains its accent] when it is not a preposition."

In a *bahuvrīhi*, however, the accent should be that of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member; therefore, this compound should not be prescribed by means of [the rule for] *śrita* and so forth. In that case, this [rule] would be purposeless, and even the rule "in an *ahīna*, the second [member takes the accent]" would not need to be stated. As for the contingency of the accent of a genus (*jāti*), when words such as *śrita* follow words denoting a genus, time, or pleasure (*sukha*), then—setting aside the original accent of the first member—the contingency arises of the final syllable being udātta according to the rule "after [words denoting] a genus, time, pleasure, etc., except for clothing."

But surely, even when a *tatpuruṣa* compound begins, since a *bahuvrīhi* is not prohibited when there is a desire to express its meaning, would the accent of the *jāti* class not necessarily occur? Even so, there is a distinction: in the *tatpuruṣa*, by the rule "in an *ahīna* [compound], the second member [takes the accent]," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member; whereas in the *bahuvrīhi*, by the rule "for *jāti*, time, etc.," there is an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*). Thus, two different accents result; however, if [the *tatpuruṣa*] were not begun, there would be only the *jāti* accent.

If that is the case, then instead of saying *jāta* (born), one should say *jāta-śrita-patita-gateṣu* (in the cases of born, resorted to, fallen into, and gone to). Even so, the rule *ahīne dvitīyā* (the second [case-ending] occurs when not meaning "deprived of") would also not need to be stated, and thus there is indeed brevity. However, this much is the distinction: when a *tatpuruṣa* compound begins, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, whereas in a *bahuvrīhi*, there is the accent of the class-name (*jātisvara*); thus, both types of compounds possess a dual accentuation (*dvaitsvarya*).

But if there is no commencement [of the *tatpuruṣa*], would there not be a dual accent (*dvisvarya*) only in the *bahuvrīhi*? To this it is replied: in a *bahuvrīhi* joined with words other than those beginning with "jāti," "kāla," and "sukha," there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of words such as *śrita* according to the rule "niṣṭhā" (Pāṇini 2.2.36), which results in a change of form; likewise, the suffix *kap* would apply everywhere. Now, one might object: that suffix is optional by the rule "śeṣādvibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 5.4.154), and it occurs even when the *tatpuruṣa* is commenced, since the *bahuvrīhi* is also admitted [as an alternative]. Even so, because the dual accent is admitted for the *bahuvrīhi* as well, the suffix *kap* would still result optionally under the view that the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), since the status of being a *bahuvrīhi* is not lost.

However, at the commencement of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, in that very instance, by the rule "in an *ahīna*, [the suffix] *dvani* is applied," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prior member; whereas in a *bahuvrīhi*, the accent of the genus (*jātisvara*) alone applies invariably, so that it is always oxytone. Thus, there is indeed a distinction, as the suffix *ka* does not apply here due to the original accent of the prior member. Likewise, there is also a difference in meaning: by the rule "after roots meaning 'to go' or being intransitive," the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent even when the action denoted by the verbal root is not entirely completed—thus, in "Devadatta has climbed the tree" (*āruḍho vṛkṣaṃ devadattaḥ*), it is stated that Devadatta is merely on the tree.

In the case of an object (*karman*), however, when there is a complete absorption of the whole self, it occurs—as in "Devadatta has climbed the tree. Likewise here, in the expression "he has resorted to hardship" (*kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*), one who is experiencing hardship is so described; or as in "hardship has been resorted to by him," meaning one who has experienced hardship. In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the direct comprehension of the intended meaning of the word "resorted to" (*śrita*) occurs [through the compound itself]; whereas in a *bahuvrīhi*, it occurs by implication. For example, when it is said "the king's friend," it is certainly understood that "the king is also his friend. This is a matter accessible only to those with subtle vision.

Regarding the phrase "of *gamī*, *gāmī*, and so forth": both [terms] are employed for the purpose of including the *uṇādi* derivatives as well as others. In *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"), the suffix *ini* is added by the *uṇādi* rule "from the root *gam*, *ini*" (*gameriniḥ*), and it denotes the future time according to the rule "in the future, *gamyādayaḥ*. In *grāmaṃ gāmī*, the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). Regarding the rule "after a verb meaning 'to go,' when its object is expressed," the mention of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is intended to apply the case even in the scope of an exception; thus, when used with a *kṛt*-suffix, only the accusative occurs. In *oganaṃ bubhukṣuḥ* ("desirous of eating food"), there is the desiderative suffix *san* after the root *bhuji*, and then the suffix *u* by the rule "after *san*, *āśaṃs*, and *bhikṣ*, the suffix *u*. By the rule "not with *loka*, indeclinables, etc.," the prohibition of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies.
25. [The suffix *kta*] is used after a root when it expresses the agent itself (*svayam*). 2-1-25.

The root *dhāv* is listed as meaning "to go" (*gati*) and "to purify" (*śuddhi*). Because it is marked with the *udic* (indicating the optional *iṭ* augment), the *iṭ* is optionally present in the *ktvā* suffix; however, by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the *iṭ* is prohibited. Then, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*, *ūṭh* is substituted for the *v*. Finally, by the rule *etyedatyūṭhsu*, *vṛddhi* is applied. Regarding the form *svayaṃvilīnam*: the root *līṅ* means "to adhere" (*śleṣaṇe*). It belongs to the *svādi-gaṇa* and is marked as *udit*. By the rule *oditaśca*, the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix takes the *natva* (the substitution of *n* for *t*). Since the term "kṛt" [in the rule governing compound formation] includes even those preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, the word *vilīna* ends in the *kta* suffix. "A single word-form (*aikapadyam*) and a single accent (*ekasvarye*) [result] because of its being a compound (*samāsatvāt*). The meaning is: compounding (*samasana*) is *samāsa*; or it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*); therefore, for that reason.
26. [The suffix *khaṭ* is applied] after the verb *kṣip* (to throw) when it means "insulting" (*khaṭvā*). 2-1-26.

"Mounting the couch" (*khaṭvārohaṇa*) and so forth: a "wrong path" (*vimārga*) is a censured way. A celibate student (*brahmacārī*) is one who is worthy of sleeping on the ground; at the time of Vedic study, having studied and performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), he should mount the couch only when permitted by his teachers. However, mounting the couch otherwise than that is setting out upon a wrong path. This serves as an illustration for other similar cases as well; the meaning is that whether he actually mounts the couch or not, one who has set out upon a wrong path is said to be "mounted on the couch. 27. *sāmī* || 2-1-27 ||

"Because that [word] denotes a non-substance (asattva). For the power of action (karma-śakti) has substance as its substratum; therefore, the accusative case occurs only after words denoting substance, not after words not denoting substance—this is the meaning.
28. Temporal expressions [are compounded with the word denoting the object]. 2-1-28.

In this context, one rule should be formulated as *kālā atyantasaṃyoge* ("time-words [are compounded] when there is absolute connection"); since the word *ktena* ("with a word ending in a kṛt-affix") would then have been excluded from that rule, the compound would be established in all cases. To the question, "For what purpose is the compound with a word ending in a kṛt-affix prescribed by splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*)?", he says: "The statement is for the sake of [cases of] non-absolute connection. He demonstrates this very non-absolute connection with the examples: *ṣaṇmuhūrtāḥ* ("six muhūrtas [of duration]") and *carācarāḥ* ("moving and non-moving").

From the root *car* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), there is reduplication and the augment *āg* for the reduplicated syllable, according to the rule: "There is an addition to the list [of roots] *car*, *cal*, *pat*, and *vad*, and the augment *āg* is applied to the reduplicated syllable when the sense is not that of fatigue. Thus, "moving" means being unsettled. "Sometimes the day" refers to the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); "sometimes the night" refers to the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). Consequently, by those six *muhūrta*s, there is no absolute connection with either the day or the night. Regarding "measured by a month" (*māsapramita*): the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*) with the agent as the referent; the meaning is that he has begun to delimit the month.
Regarding the expression "the moon at every new moon": the intended meaning is that there is no absolute conjunction of it with the month.
29. And [the second case ending is used] to express continuous connection (atyantasaṃyoga). Pāṇini 2.1.29.
30. A third [type of compound] is formed with a quality-expressing word whose meaning has been produced by that [prior member]. (Pāṇini 2.1.30)

In the case of the third [case-ending], when there is elision (*luk*) for the sake of Vedic meter, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "guṇavacana" (expressing a quality). The word "arthena" (for the sake of the meaning) is a separate word; for this very reason, it is said: "with both 'guṇavacana' and the word 'artha'. Of what kind of *guṇavacana*? It is "that which is produced by that" (*tatkṛta*). By the pronoun "tat," there is a reference back to the previously mentioned word ending in the third case, and that is a word.

Furthermore, since it is not possible for a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by its own verbal form, it is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*) that [the action] is performed by means of that which is produced by the object denoted by that word. Thus he says: "by that which is produced by the meaning of the word ending in the third case. Regarding the word *yāvat*: the particle *yāvat* indicates a synonym for *tātparya* (intentional focus). And this qualification of the word expressing a quality is mediated by the object; for it is the object itself that is produced by the sense of the third case, not the word expressing the quality.

What is the purpose of including the word *vacana* (speech)? Since a compound cannot occur with the sense of "meaning" (*artha*), it would follow that the term applies only to those words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*). Thus, it should be understood that a "quality-expressing word" is one that has expressed a quality—defined by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*—and not that which has as its cause for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the very quality whose presence causes a word to be applied to a substance; for that [quality] exists everywhere as the meaning of the third case-ending. Examples are *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ* ("broken by a wedge") and *kirikāṇaḥ*.

The words *khāṇḍa* and *kāṇa* are derived from the roots *khaḍi* (meaning "to break") and *kaṇa* (meaning "to close the eyes") respectively, with the suffix *ghañ*. Having first denoted the action (*kriyā*), they come to denote a substance (*dravya*)—either through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Thus, they are termed "expressers of qualities" (*guṇavacana*). Regarding the phrase *dhānyenārthaḥ*: "artha" means that which is sought after (*arthya*), i.e., a purpose (*prayojana*), or the act of seeking (*arthana*), i.e., a request or desire. In all these cases, there is a compound with the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). For example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye").

In this case, [the blindness] is not caused by the eye; what then? It is caused by some other factor such as karma, while the eye is merely characterized as being one-eyed. Therefore, there is an absence of causality by that [eye]. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*) must be made so that [the compound] does not occur in cases such as *dadhnā paṭuḥ* ("clever because of yogurt"). Now, if the intention is to express that the proficiency is produced by yogurt—as in *dadhnā kṛtaḥ paṭuḥ*—"then a compound must indeed occur."

Now, if it is argued that the status of *dadhi* (curd) as an instrument (*karaṇa*) depends on its relation to the act of eating—as in "the clever man eats with curd"—then, due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), [the compound] would not occur. But then it would not occur here either: "The face is red with saffron because of anger. For even here, there is a connection of the instrument with the action of coloring: "made red by saffron. Where, then, would it occur? It would occur only in cases such as "a piece with a mold" (*śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ*), where there is a relationship between the preceding and following words characterized by action and its factor (*kriyākāraka*).

Therefore, even in cases where no action is understood in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the mention of "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*) is included so that the rule may apply when there is a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) mediated by [an action] such as eating, but not otherwise. Why does it say "by a word denoting a quality" (*guṇavacanena*)? Because in the case of words denoting a genus (*jāti*), since a genus is eternal, it is impossible for anything to be produced by it; however, in the case of words denoting an action (*kriyā*), this is indeed desired. Furthermore, according to the rule "the agent and the instrument are compounded diversely with a *kṛt*-derivative," even in the case of words denoting a substance (*dravya*), it is simply impossible for anything to be produced by them.

For the true nature of space (*ākāśa*) is not produced by anything; therefore, the question arises: "Will it [the name] come about through a word expressing a quality? [The example given is] "one who has omentum because of cows" (*gobhir vapāvān*). In this case, his possession of omentum—that is, his fatness—arises precisely from the consumption of curds and other products related to cows; thus, there is indeed a causal connection (*tatkṛtatva*), yet this is not a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).
31. [The sixth case is used] with words meaning "prior," "similar," "equal," "like," "conflict," "skillful," "mixed," and "smooth. (Pāṇini 2.1.31)

Since the compound was established by the word *artha* in the preceding sūtra, the inclusion of the word *artha* here is for the purpose of specifying its meaning. And that [word *artha*] connects only with the immediately following word *una*, not with *pūrva* and the others, because the words *sama* and *sadṛśa* are mentioned separately. "This very [is the case]," and so forth: in other instances, when used with the words *sama* and *sadṛśa*, the third case ending occurs according to the rule *tulyārthaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.72).

In this case, when there is a connection with a word having the same meaning (*tulyārtha*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also optionally prescribed; consequently, in a compound, forms such as *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* ("resembling a mother") are established through that [genitive]. Why, then, is the term *sadṛśa* ("resembling") mentioned here? It is so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member may apply according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārthatṛtīyā*. However, the original accent is already established here by the rule *sadṛśapratirūpayoḥ sādṛśye*.

And in that case, a similar apprehension must necessarily be made so that, when it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), there may not be an udātta accent on the final syllable. Now, one might object: "But surely, due to lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), the genitive compound will not occur? This cannot be maintained; for if it were not a compound, there would indeed be a fault.

Regarding the rule "the sixth case [is used] in the sense of reproach" (*ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*): examples such as *dāsyāḥ sadṛśaḥ* ("like a slave-girl") or *vṛṣalyāḥ sadṛśaḥ* ("like a low-caste woman") show that in those cases it must be applied; however, [one might ask] should this [following example] not be applied? This too must be applied: for the sake of the third case in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), as in *vidyayā hetunā sadṛśaḥ* ("similar by reason of learning," i.e., "similar in learning"). For here the sixth case does not occur by the rule "*tulyārthaiḥ*" (Pāṇini 2.3.72), since that rule prescribes the sixth case only when there is a correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Even so, it need not be stated; for since it is produced by that [the suffix], it is already established by the preceding rule. For that which is similar to a *vidyā* (knowledge/learning) has its similarity produced by that *vidyā*; thus, it is established by the preceding rule alone. [Question: Is the inclusion of the term "mixed" (*miśra*) intended to include even that which is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), as in the example "roasted grains mixed with molasses" (*guḍasaṃmiśrā dhānāḥ*)? [Answer: It is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author makes the mention of "not being accompanied by a prefix" (*anupasarga*) in the rule "And *miśra*, when not accompanied by a prefix, provided there is no euphonic combination" (*miśraṃ cānupasargamasandhau*), this indicates that in the inclusion of the term *miśra*, even that which is accompanied by a prefix is included.
Regarding the phrase "in the east and so forth": the meaning is that the word *avara* (west) should also be recited in the Sūtra.
32. A compound consisting of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix [denoting] the agent and a word denoting the instrument is frequently formed. (Pāṇini 2.1.32)

The form *kartṛkaraṇe* is the nominative dual. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the matter is explained as: "that which is the third case [ending] when there is an agent (*kartṛ*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*). And so he will state later: "An agent and an instrument are compounded with gerundives (*kṛtya*) when expressing an additional sense. The phrase "for the sake of avoiding deviation from the limiting conditions" means for the sake of avoiding under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). The example is *pādahārakaḥ*.

In the word *hāraka*, [the suffix] *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; it is a compound with *pādābhyām*, which ends in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) denoting the source (*apādāna*). Regarding *copaka* in the phrase *gale copaka*: the root *cupa* means "to move slowly"; from this, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added, *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object, and the suffix *yat* is added by the rule *amūrdhamastakāt*. The mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is unnecessary, because there is nothing else [that could apply]. In this context, only the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) occur in relation to the action (*kriyā*), and the action is expressed by a verbal root (*dhātu*). Of verbal roots, there are two types of suffixes: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*.

In this context, because the governing rule is "sup" (a nominal suffix), there is no application [of the term *kāraka*] to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). However, for the purpose of excluding *taddhita* (secondary) suffixes, it is stated: "here, by means of wood, he cooks more" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitarām*), "by means of wood, he cooks in this manner" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatirūpam*), "by means of wood, he cooks to this extent" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatideśyam*), "one who has previously made with the hand" (*hastena kṛtapūrvī*), "one who has previously eaten with curd" (*dadhnā bhuktapūrvī*), and "one who has sacrificed with clarified butter" (*dhṛteneṣṭī*)."
33. The sixth case-affix is used after a word denoting an agent when it is connected with a word expressing an action that must be performed [by that agent]. (Pāṇini 2.1.33)

"Employed for praise or censure" means that which is set in motion by praise or censure; that is to say, it is done for the purpose of praising or censuring. "Speech consisting of superimposed meaning": that which is superimposed (adhyāropita) despite being non-existent is called "superimposed. Regarding the example "by crows" (*kākapeya*): this is praise in the sense that the river has so much water that it can even be drunk by crows standing on its banks; it is censure in the sense that the river has so little water that it can even be drunk by crows. In both cases, the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of possibility (*śakya*). Regarding "lickable by dogs" (*śvalehya*).

"An impure well such that only dogs are fit to lick its water"—this is a censure, using a *kṛtya* suffix in the sense of unfitness (*ahrārthe*). "Grass that is to be cut with steam"—this is a praise, meaning the grass is so tender that it can be cut even by steam; whereas "grass that has been spoken of as such that it can be cut even by steam"—this is a censure. "Rice that is to be gathered with thorns"—this is a praise, meaning the rice is so moist that it can be gathered with thorns.

"Such is the smallness of the rice that it is gathered up by thorns"—this is a censure. This is an elaboration (prapañca) of the very same [rule] mentioned previously. Although the agency and instrumentality are secondary because the purpose is praise or censure, nevertheless, by virtue of the rule allowing for "abundance" (bahula), it is established by the previous rule itself. Thus, in the example *kākapītaṃ nadyā*, a compound is seen even with words denoting action (*ākṛti*) when they express an additional meaning. Therefore, this is merely an elaboration; it is neither a rule for what was not previously established (*aprāptavidhi*), nor is it a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is the meaning.
34. The condiment [is subordinate] to the food. 2-1-34.

Regarding the example "dadhyodana" (curd-rice): [An objection is raised] "But surely no action (*kriyā*) is heard here, and since there can be no mutual connection between substances without an action, this compound cannot occur due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*). Or, even if there were such competency, would the compound occur merely by virtue of a specific rule (*vacana*)? [The opponent continues: "In that case, it would also apply here: 'kiṃ dadhnā, odano bhujyatām' (What with curd? Let rice be eaten! To this, he replies: "Because the action is included within the *vṛtti*. The meaning is that, by its very nature, the action is included within the *vṛtti*; thus, because the connection mediated by that [action] exists, there is semantic competency.
35. Mixing with food. 2-1-35.

Regarding the term *kharaviśadam*: *kharam* means hard (*kaṭhinam*) and having distinct parts (*vibhaktāvayavam*); thus *kharaviśadam* means that which is both hard and distinct, i.e., that which is to be eaten by the movement of the jaw. That which is swallowed is called *bhakṣya*; this is because the word *bhakṣya* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) specifically for that which ends in the suffix *-era-* and the suffix *-eraj-*. However, the verb *bhakṣayati* (to eat) occurs elsewhere as well—as in *abbhakṣaḥ* (one who eats water) and *vāyubhakṣaḥ* (one who eats air). Others maintain that in these cases, the verb *bhakṣayati* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*).
36. The fourth case [is used] for the sake of that, for its purpose, for strength, for what is beneficial, for pleasure, and for protection. (Pāṇini 2.1.36)

The meaning is that "the object (*arthaḥ*) is referred back. Although the word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*)—that is, a word in the dative case—is proximate, nevertheless, because it is impossible for the word itself to possess the status of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*), it is the *meaning* of that [word] which is referred back; this is the sense. [The phrase] "together with these words" means: in that context, the expression "by a word ending in a case-suffix for the sake of that" is a qualifier intended to exclude the literal form, since it is impossible for the mere phonetic form of a word ending in a case-suffix to be "for the sake of that. The second occurrence of the word *artha*, however, is indeed used separately as a noun.

A compound is desired in the case of the relationship between a material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), because of an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). That the author makes the mention of *balirakṣita* serves as an indicator that a word ending in the dative case expressing a modification is compounded with its material cause; otherwise, since the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) is possible even in cases such as *kuberabaliḥ* and *gorakṣitam*, that mention would be purposeless. However, the mention of *hitasukha* is not an indicator, because the dative case can occur even when there is no sense of "being for the sake of," due to the rules "the dative should be stated in connection with *hita*" and "the dative [is used] in a benediction."

If a derivative (vikṛti) is compounded with its source material (prakṛti)—as in *aśvebhyo ghāsaḥ* ("grass for horses"), *aśvebhyaḥ surā* ("liquor for horses") which becomes *aśvasuram* [with neuter gender according to the rule *vibhāṣā senā*], and *hastibhyo vidhā* ("food for elephants") where *vidhā* means a specific kind of food—if [the rule] does not apply here, then *aśvaghāsa* and the others will simply be genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Objection: Is there not a difference in accent when it is a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*), for in that case, by the rule "the dative [is used] for its sake" (*caturthī tadartha*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) should apply; whereas in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), the accent should be on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*)? Reply: This is no difference; even in a dative compound, the original accent of the first member does not necessarily apply.

Because of the [Pāṇinian] indicator (*jñāpaka*): when he states that in the rule "kte ca" (P. 6.2.150), a preceding member ending in the dative case retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), this indicates that this accent does not apply in the absence of a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Otherwise, since the form *gorakṣitam* would also be established by "caturthī tadartha" (P. 2.1.36) alone, that [rule "kte ca"] would be purposeless. This is not a valid indicator; for this [accentuation] is for the sake of expressing benefit (*hitārtha*), as in *go-hitam*, where there is no sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*).

Even so, although one should have stated "and in the case of *hita*," the general statement "and in the case of *kta*" is itself an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is for the purpose of ensuring that in cases such as *kuberabali*, the accent does not occur in every respect; thus, an accent must be desired when there is a relationship of original material and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Now, why does a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) not occur in the example "a pot for cooking" (*randhanāya sthālī*)? Someone says: it certainly does occur, as for instance in *gogrāsa* (cow-grazing), *lālāmbuja* (spittle-lotus), *krīḍāsaras* (play-lake), *vāsabhavana* (residence-house), and *nāṭyaśālā* (theater-hall).

Another says: "Because they are not explicitly mentioned, compounds with the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa) do not occur in cases such as *randhana-sthālī* ('cooking-pot'). To both of these [objections], we reply: let there be only the dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) in those cases where a genitive compound is desired; however, in those cases where it is not desired, let it simply not be desired because of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*). The mention of *balirakṣita* is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). As for the accent (*svara*), even in the case of a dative compound, it will be established precisely through the relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) in the manner previously stated.

Furthermore, this being the case, this very Sūtra would be rendered useless; let there be only the genitive compound even in cases such as *yūpadāru* (sacrificial post-wood), and let the rule *caturthī tadarthe* be replaced by *ṣaṣṭhī tadarthe*. Moreover, the determination of accentuation can be established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*). But [it may be argued that] there is a difference in meaning.

Is it that in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) only a general relation is understood, whereas in a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) a specific relation—namely, "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*)—is understood? This distinction does not exist; even when the dative compound is prescribed, the genitive compound is not thereby prohibited. In that case, the specific meaning is to be determined through context, purpose, and so forth.

If this is so, then even in a simple genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), such a distinction would be understood. Furthermore, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), in cases such as *aśvaghāsa* ("grass for horses"), the understanding that [the grass] is for that purpose (*tādarthya*) occurs everywhere through the force of the context and so forth; why then should this [rule] not serve that purpose? It is replied: first of all, a genitive compound does not occur with the word *hita*; since the dative case is obligatory in its connection, only a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) should be stated. Consequently, the term "dative" (*caturthī*) must also be included in the rule *kte ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.33) for the sake of forms such as *gohitam*.

And thus, in the case of *gorakṣitam*, [the formation] would not occur, because a dative case is impossible there. Furthermore, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36) does not apply here because there is no relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*). Therefore, even according to Rakṣita, a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) must be prescribed. Moreover, since when joined with the word *artha*, a specific relationship of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is invariably understood, a dative case must occur; thus, even by him, a dative compound alone must be accepted.

The inclusion of the term *balisukha* (the pleasure of the offering) must also be made; this is for the purpose that the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is invariably understood within a compound, just as it is from conventional usage (*samaya*). Therefore, the rule (*sūtra*) must indeed be commenced. However, the purpose of the statement that "the compound consists precisely in the state of being the base (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikāra*)" remains to be considered. Regarding the statement "there is a rule for obligatory compounds with *artha*": otherwise, because of the governing authority of the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*), there would also be the syntactical phrase *brāhmaṇāyārthaḥ*. And [it follows] that [the compound] possesses all genders.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the derivative. It demonstrates that the adoption of all genders occurs by virtue of the meaning to be expressed (*abhidheya-vaśena*), and not everywhere. For example: *brāhmaṇārthaṃ payaḥ* ("milk for the sake of a Brahmin"). If [one objects] that there is the designation *sarth* [in the sense of "having the same referent"], then the designation *it* would be absent, and the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would follow. This might be argued: for the sake of that [meaning], in the rule *vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* ("from the modification, in the case of the original material"), the rule *tadarthe sarthavat* should be formulated. The fourth case [ending] is present; when the fourth case ending occurs, the suffix *sarth* is applied when the meaning to be expressed is "for the sake of that" (*tadarthe*). The letter *s* is for the purpose of the designation *pada*. [Examples: *rājārthaḥ*, *gavārthaḥ*; due to the *pit*-designation, there is the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*).

If it is argued that, because the meaning is thus [expressed], the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member need not be prescribed, and because it is a suffix, no analysis (*vigraha*) is made with it, and because it is a *taddhita* suffix, its gender is established as being like that of the referent—this is not so; for it would follow that the letter *s* would lack the designation *it*. Now, if it is argued that the designation *it* would apply by relying on the dual-notation of *s* in the rules "ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ" and "ṣaḥ pratyayasya"—even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *sa* appearing after words such as *tṛṇa* in the case of *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, and other suffixes (e.g., *tārṇasāya*). Furthermore, in the cases of *śryartham* and *bhvartham*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would occur, and in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ātvaka* would be liable to occur.

It might be argued: "Since the milk has the Brāhmaṇa as its purpose, it can be said that the Brāhmaṇa is its *prayojaka* (instigator/purpose). Therefore, one will form a *bahuvrīhi* compound by analyzing [the term] as 'that which has the Brāhmaṇa as its purpose' (*brāhmaṇo 'rtho 'syeti*), using that word ending in the dative case. By this means, the absence of a formal analytical statement (*vigraha*), the preservation of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*), the status of being denotable like the primary meaning, and the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgatā*) are all established. That is not correct; for in the case of the expression *mahadartham*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *tva-kap*. Furthermore, if the word *artha* were substituted for *tadartha*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the final vowel (*udabhāva*).

It might be argued as follows: by means of the rule "the fourth case [is compounded] with that which is for its sake" (*caturthī tadartha*), a compound is prescribed; then, by the portion of that rule stating "for its sake" (*artha*), the word *artha* is ordained as a substitute for the final member (*uttarapada*) when it expresses "that which is for its sake. Furthermore, because the section on "optionality" (*vibhāṣā*) is in force, both forms—*yūpārthaṃ dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post) and *yūpadāru* (sacrificial-post-wood)—will occur. Consequently, even in the cases of *bali* (offering) and *rakṣita* (protected), the word *artha* optionally becomes a substitute, resulting in such forms as *kuberārtho baliḥ* (an offering for Kubera) and *kuberabaliḥ*.

For what purpose is this [sūtra], since it is already established by the preceding one? It is for the sake of providing an indicator (jñāpaka). This indicates that, because there is no relationship of original material and its modification (prakṛti-vikāra), the substitution of meaning (arthādeśa) is permanent elsewhere. By this, forms such as *randhanārthā sthālī* ("a pot for the purpose of cooking") are valid, but not forms such as *randhanasthālī*. However, compounds such as *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder") follow the previous rule.

In this case, once the compound has been formed, there will be no analysis (*vigraha*) with the word *artha* prescribed for the second member; rather, when that [word] remains, its gender will follow from the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) because of the substitution of *artha*. As for the rule regarding the accent of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member as in *artaḥ*, that indeed must be prescribed. But that is not so; for if the word *vīvadha* were substituted by *artha* in the expression "a load for water" (*udakārtho vīvadhaḥ*), then by the principle of the substitute, the substitution of *uda-* (as per the rule *manthaudanādi-sūtra*) would undesirably follow. Therefore, these rules apply only to a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*).

And so, must it be stated that there is an obligatory compound with *ārta* and that it possesses all genders? It need not be stated; since the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the dative case in *brāhmaṇāya*, there will be no analysis using the word *artha*. Furthermore, its possession of all genders is established by the rule: "Gender is non-derivational, because gender depends on common usage.
Let those who have exerted themselves in the Bhāṣya understand this;
others, even if they were a thousand blind men, do not see the sun directly.
37. The fifth [case ending] is used in the sense of fear. (Pāṇini 2.1.37)

Thinking that there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) because the rule takes the specific form (*svarūpa*), he says: "It should be stated as *bhaya-bhī-bhīti-bhībhiḥ*. The meaning is that the formulation of the sūtra should be made in this way. The implication is that if the meaning were taken from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *vṛkebhyastrāsaḥ*. Should the formulation then be made in that manner? No, he says: "By the very previous mention of the word *bahulam* (‘diversely’)."

The meaning is that just as in cases such as *pādahāraka* ("one who takes a foot"), [the suffix] occurs by virtue of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various instances) for the purpose of accounting for all exceptions, so too will it be here. In the expression *adhamajugupsuḥ* ("one who loathes unrighteousness"), the designation *apādāna* (ablative) is applied to *adharma* by the rule *jugupsāvirāmapramādārthānām* ("of those having the sense of loathing, ceasing, and negligence").

38. [The word *apeta* (departed), *apoḍha* (removed), *mukta* (released), *patita* (fallen), and *apatrasta* (frightened) may optionally be compounded with their objects, provided they do not denote a small quantity. 2.1.38.

From the word *alpaśabda*, the suffix *śas* is applied by the rule "from words meaning 'much' or 'little'" (*bahvalpārthāt*). The masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs by the rule "in the case of *śas*, for that which means much or little. Its status as a *kāraka* (participant in an action) arises from being the object (*karman*) of the act of compounding. For this very reason, in the statement "the fifth [case-ending] is compounded," the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the object. Regarding that, he will state later: "In that context, there is a specific mention of words meaning 'much' or 'little' when used in an auspicious sense. Therefore, it is appropriate that *śas* is applied here due to this very derivation. The phrase "a small fifth" (*alpā pañcamī*) means "produced from base forms that signify 'small'. 39. Words signifying "a little" (*stoka*), "near" (*antika*), "far" (*dūra*), and those having the sense of "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) are compounded with a past passive participle (*kta*). 2-1-39. *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* || 2-1-39 ||
40. A word ending in the seventh case-affix is compounded with words meaning ‘skilled in’ (śauṇḍa). Pāṇini 2.1.40.

In this context, due to association (*sāhacarya*), the word *śauṇḍa* is employed among rogues and the like even while not abandoning its own primary meaning, just as in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going. And the proof for this is the use of the plural number; he says "by means of *śauṇḍa* and so forth" because that meaning is understood even without the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). However, by the force of its inclusion in the list (*gaṇapāṭha*), the mention of the plural number is for the purpose of indicating the meaning, or else it serves as the basis for the compound meaning of the plural-ending form; there is no other reason for the locative case here.

Nor can this alone be relied upon as an indicator [of the rule], for it would lead to over-extension (prasaṅga) in cases such as *śauṇḍo devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is a drunkard"). Therefore, he says: "In a compound (*vṛttau*). The word *antar* is listed here; when used in conjunction with it, the locative case is employed to express the sense of the substratum (*ādhāra*) of the whole, as in *vṛkṣe śākhā* ("a branch on the tree") or *vane'ntarvanāntaḥ* ("inside the forest"). Since this [usage] is optional, there is also an avyayībhāva compound, namely *antarvaṇam*, where the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *pra-nir-antaḥ*.

The word *adhi* is recited [in the list of prepositions]. When the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is predominant, it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound: *adhisattri*. However, when the thing located (*ādheya*) is predominant, this forms a *tatpuruṣa* compound: *brāhmaṇādhyayanam*. By the rule "after a word ending in *adhi*, the suffix *kha* [is added]," the suffix *kha* is applied. Thus, the analytical sentence is *brāhmaṇeṣv adhi*.
And [the suffix *khañ* is applied] after the words *sidhma*, *śuṣka*, and *pakva*. (Pāṇini 4.2.80)

"Siddha at Sāṅkāśya" and "Siddha at Kāmpilya": a forest produced from Saṅkāśa is Sāṅkāśya; that produced from Kampila is Kāmpilya. By the rule *cāturthikaḥ saṅkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*, the meaning is one who has become perfected (*siddha*) there through asceticism (*tapas*).
42. [The suffix *ka* is applied after a word ending in *dhvāṅkṣa*] in the sense of "belonging to that. (Pāṇini 2.1.42)

Because of the statement, "one's own [term] is the substitute for the word," it would not apply to synonyms; therefore, he says: "By the word *dhvāṅkṣeṇa*, the meaning is intended. This is understood from the commentary itself: "like a crow at a watering place" (*tīrthe dhvāṅkṣa iva*). The particle *iva* is employed because a sense of reproach is understood only when there is a relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared, and not otherwise. Just as crows do not remain long at a watering place, so one who is unstable in his duties is called a "watering-place crow" (*tīrthadhvāṅkṣa*); thus he says, "the meaning is 'unstable'. In the *Vṛtti*, however, the particle *iva* is not used because its meaning is already included within the compound.
43. [The sixth case ending is used] for *kṛtya* suffixes and for *ṛṇa*. (Pāṇini 2.3.43)

Regarding the statement "it is desired [to apply] only that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix": this is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "in small measure" (*alpaśaḥ*). The plural number in "by *kṛt* suffixes" (*kṛtyaiḥ*), however, is primarily intended to indicate a variety of base forms (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, the mention of "debt" (*ṛṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating "necessity" (*niyoga*). Necessity means inevitability. Because of its association with the inevitability that "a debt must necessarily be repaid," it indicates necessity in general. He states what is established by this: "even here. In the example "to be sung in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇogeya*), the suffix *u* (forming *geya*) is applied according to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, *kṛt* suffixes are used diversely" (*tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*).
Just as a debt must necessarily be repaid, so too there is a rule that this [hymn] must necessarily be recited in the forenoon.
44. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after a word denoting a name (*saṃjñā*). 2.1.44.
45. By means of a word ending in the *kta* suffix, parts of a day and night [are expressed]. (Pāṇini 2.1.45)

Regarding the expression *divā vṛttam*: it does not form a single word (*aikapadya*) nor does it have a single accent (*eka-svarya*). Now, one might argue that since the word *divā* primarily denotes the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti-pradhāna*), when it is expressed [as a case ending], that meaning becomes included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), and thus the nominative case alone should follow from it. Consequently, because the locative case is absent, there would be no occasion for this [rule] to apply here. However, this is not an absolute rule—that it must primarily denote the power of the locus—since we also see such usage as *divā manyā rātriḥ* ("the night is considered as day").

How is it that [the phrase] "intent upon questioning about what occurred during the night"? It is understood according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). In this way, expressions such as "done in another birth" (*anyajanmakṛta*) and so forth also become possible.
In that regard: || 2-1-46 ||

Regarding the statement "tatra" ending in the locative case: since forms such as "tatrabhavan" (your honor) are seen even with other case endings, it is considered that when expressing the sense of "adhrakaṇa" (not being there), the word "tatra" likewise requires the locative case.
47. [The suffix *kha* is applied] after a word denoting censure. (Pāṇini 2.1.47)

The ancient usage "this of yours is like a mongoose staying on heated ground" (avataptenakulasthitam) has its meaning explained as: "the sense is that this is your fickleness. Just as mongooses do not remain for long in a heated place, so too one who, having begun tasks, does not persist due to fickleness is described in this way; such is the meaning. The compound is formed with the word *nakulasthita* according to the rule "when a *kṛt*-derived word is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix or a case-inflected word is also included," and there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending as in the previous example.
And [the compounds] *pātresamita* and so forth [are also *tatpuruṣas* with the first member in the locative case]. 2.1.48.

"Yuktārohyādiparigrahārtham" means that this [rule] is for the purpose of including the *yuktārohī* group and others; the sense is that their inclusion should also occur under the rule "yuktārohyādayaśca. "Pratra eva samitāḥ" means they have gathered at the very time of the meal. "Pātrebahulāḥ" means they assemble only at the time of the meal, not for any other business. "Ubumbaramaśakādiṣu" refers to cases such as the *ubumbara* and the *maśaka*.

The meaning is that the person who is satisfied with that very thing and thinks "there is nothing higher than this" is one who has not seen its full extent; such a person is called a "gnat in a fig tree" (*udumbaramaśaka*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by avoiding what is forbidden": it is forbidden to act as a man toward enemies or toward one's wife, and it is forbidden to act as a man toward one's mother. Regarding the phrase "through lack of effort": a *piṇḍī* is a lump of boiled rice; to be a hero only in that [eating] and nowhere else is "lack of effort. Regarding the phrase "those who meet at the highest vessel": the meaning is that there is no other kind of livelihood of this nature; rather, the statement is simply "the highest among those who meet at the vessel" (*paramāḥ pātresamitāḥ*).
49. The words *pūrva*, *kāla*, *eka*, *sarva*, *jara*, *purāṇa*, *nava*, and *kevala* [form a compound] with a word in grammatical apposition. 2.1.49.

"Of that which has different grounds for application," and so forth. The inclusion of the word *bhinna* (different) is for the purpose of excluding synonyms (*paryāya*). The inclusion of the word *eka* (one) is for the purpose of excluding cases such as "the cow and the horse" (*gauraś ca*). In some places, the reading is *bhinnanimitaprayuktasya*; the meaning is "that which is set in motion by a different ground for application—that is, by a different *pravṛttinimitta*. Since [the rule] *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* already establishes this, the present statement is intended to ensure the prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) of words such as "prior time" (*pūrvakāla*). However, in the case of the word *eka*, it is solely for the purpose of securing its application under the restriction [*niyama*] "directions and numbers [are compounded] when they form a name" (*diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*).

Regarding the phrase "the prior time is the apprehension of the meaning": *pūrvakālaḥ* means that its time is prior; the sense is that it was performed first. And since that [prior status] exists in relation to what is performed later, it is understood by implication that the compound is formed with that very [later element]; thus he says, "with the subsequent time. In the case of *snātānulipta*, the meaning is that one bathed first and was subsequently anointed. Here, because they are verbal nouns, there might be an option for the prior placement [of the first member], as in the case of *pācaka-pāṭhaka* and so on. [The example] is *ekaśāṭi*.

From the word *śāṭī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for *jāti* (gender), and the shortening occurs by the rule *ekata-ddhite ca*. Regarding the example *sarvamanuṣyaḥ*: here, even if it is considered a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no fault in the compound; therefore, a compound consisting of words expressing an action or words expressing a quality must be shown. Similarly, in the case of *jaradādi* (words like *jaraṭ*) as well, [the form] would be *ekasyāḥ śāṭī*. In this case, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) must indeed be formed; therefore, one should provide the counter-example *ekasyāḥ śauklyam*.
