For in this case, the prohibition "not with a quality" (*guṇena na*) applies.
50. The compound of a numeral with *dīkṣā* is formed when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). Pāṇini 2.1.50.

Since the rule "qualifier and qualified" (viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa) already establishes the formation of compounds, this [present rule] is for the purpose of restriction: namely, that it applies only when there is a technical name (saṃjñā), and not otherwise. However, in cases such as *pūrvasūtra*, a compound is formed because the word *pūrva* denotes a direction (*digvācin*).
51. And [the compound is formed] when the meaning of a taddhita suffix, a subsequent member of a compound, or a collective aggregate is expressed. (Pāṇini 2.1.51)

Regarding the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*: since the requirement [of the compound] with a "qualified word" (*viśe�ṣyeṇa*) was already established by the preceding rule, this is a rule for cases where it was not otherwise obtained. Alternatively, because its scope is not restricted, this too can be called a restrictive rule (*niyama*), such that one may say: "This is the restriction; the former is the general rule. He explains that even though there is only one locative case, it is differentiated according to the difference in its scope, using the words "in the sense of a *taddhita* suffix" and so forth. However, if it were understood as "when the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix is to be expressed," then in forms such as *pāñcanīpitiḥ*, the *taddhita* suffix would be difficult to obtain.

The intention is that the meaning of that [term] has already been stated in summary. On this view, the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning) is of questionable utility. One might simply say "in the domain of *taddhita*"; however, if it were understood as "when a *taddhita* suffix follows," a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*) would result: the *taddhita* suffix would have to be prescribed after a compound, yet the compound would depend upon the presence of the *taddhita* suffix.

Furthermore, there is no fault in this position that "when the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix is to be expressed [the suffix is applied]"; the rule prescribing elision (*luk*)—namely, *dvigor lug anapatye*—"elision after a *dvigu* compound, except in the case of the suffix denoting offspring"—serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This indicates that the term *dvigu* refers to *taddhita* suffixes in general; thus, one can understand that in such cases, a *taddhita* suffix must necessarily arise in order to express a specific meaning.

Now, why is it not understood thus: "The *dvigu* compound occurs for the sake of that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix; the *dvigu* is formed so that a *taddhita* may arise"? Just as we exert ourselves for the sake of a wife (*dāra*), thinking "so that there may be a wife," [one might think] the *dvigu* is formed so that a *taddhita* may arise. It is not possible to understand it in this way; for if it were understood thus, the designation of *samāsa* (compound), being prescribed for the production of a *taddhita*, would not apply to other domains.

In this way, the designation *dvigu* would also be prescribed for that very same compound; consequently, in the case of *pañcāratni*, the accent [prescribed by] the rule *igante dvigau* would not occur. However, the scope for a *samāhāra-dvigu* (collective dvigu) is such that, just as the status of being "like the final member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) when an accent is being prescribed does not apply to the rules for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*, so it is here as well. Regarding *paurvaśāla*: when one intends to express a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning, such as "existing in the eastern hall," the compound is formed first, and then the secondary suffix is added. Regarding *pūrvaśālāpriya*: [this is formed] when [the compound] is intended to express a different sense.

In the three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound *pūrvā-śālā-priyā-as-ya*, when the word *priya* stands as the final member (*uttarapada*), if there were an intermediate *tatpuruṣa* [between *pūrvā-śālā* and *priya*], the word *śālā* would receive the accent of the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*). However, if that intermediate *tatpuruṣa* does not exist, then that same *samāsāntodāttatva* applies to the word *śālā*. But if that intermediate *tatpuruṣa* does not exist, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) of the first member, the word *pūrva*, would remain by virtue of the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). Furthermore, a directional term (*dikśabda*) cannot function as a collective (*samāhāra*).

For that [collection], being of the nature of an aggregate, is based on differentiation; and number alone expresses differentiation, whereas a word for direction (*dik-śabda*) is restricted to each individual object. Furthermore, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is elided in a compound. Now, one might object: "Just as in the expression 'a flock of crows' (*kāka-samūhaḥ*), there is an understanding of differentiation even in the absence of a case-ending, so it will be here as well. Therefore, the reason that must be stated here is simply "due to the absence of usage. Regarding *pāñcanāpiti*: in the compound "the offspring of five *nīpitas*," the suffix *iñ* is applied according to the rule *ata iñ*. Regarding *pañcakapāla*: [this refers to an offering prepared] in five vessels.

In the compound *pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.2.16] is elided by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88), resulting in *pañcakapāla-bhakṣāḥ*. Regarding *pañcagavadhanaḥ*: when the three-word *bahuvrīhi* *pañca gāvo dhanam asya* is formed, the word *dhana* being the final member (*uttarapada*), a *tatpuruṣa* is first formed between the preceding two members. Then, by the rule *gor ataddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 5.4.92), the suffix *ṭac* is added. This *tatpuruṣa* within the larger compound would apply optionally due to the governing rule *mahāvibhāṣā*; however, it must be stated that it is obligatory.

Otherwise, one might even have *pañcagodhana*. And it has been stated: "In the case of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, there is a rule for obligatory composition when a final member follows. Thus, in the three-membered *bahuvrīhi* *vāgdṛṣadapriya*—meaning "one to whom speech and stone are dear"—there is a *dvandva* of the first two members, and that is intended to be obligatory so that the compound-ending suffix may necessarily apply. As for *pañcapūli*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "the collection of five bundles" (*pañcānāṃ pūlānāṃ samāhāraḥ*), and not "five bundles collected together" (*pañcapūlāḥ samāhṛtāḥ*).

For the word *samāhāra* (collection) is an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*)—it is the act of collecting (*samāharaṇa*), the piling together in one place of things that are scattered. In cases such as *pañcagrāmaḥ*, *ṣaṇṇagarī*, and *tripurī*, although the locations are distinct, there occurs a mental piling together because they are connected to a single action at one and the same moment.

Now, what is the fault in [interpreting] *pañcakumārī* as a compound where the action (*karman*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? Here, because the meaning of "maiden" (*kumārī*) is predominant, and because it is not designated by a case-ending other than the first (the nominative) in the rule for compounds, and because it lacks the status of having a single case-ending, it does not possess the status of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Consequently, the shortening [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya* would not apply. Granted, the shortening of the neuter form would be established here. However, in the case of *pañca khaṭvāḥ samāhṛtāḥ pañcakhaṭvī*, where the feminine gender is intended and the word ends in the suffix *ṭāp*, the suffix *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule *dvigoḥ* would not apply due to the absence of shortening.

In the case of a formation expressing an abstract state (bhāvasādhana), however, even when the meaning of the compound—a collective aggregate—is joined with various case-endings, the word *kumārī* is invariably connected only with the genitive case; thus, because it possesses only a single case-ending, its status as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is established. Therefore, it is a formation expressing an abstract state.

Regarding the rule "dvigurekavacanam" (a *dvigu* compound takes the singular ending), it is anticipated that [the author] will state "that [compound] is neuter. He asks: how is it that when one says, "bring five bundles (*pañcapūlīṃ ānaya*)," there is the bringing of the bundles? For the bringing of an abstract state (*bhāva*) is not possible without the bringing of a substance (*dravya*). Is it not just as the bringing of fire is not possible without the bringing of fuel? Even so, the mention of "aggregation" (*samāhāra*) would be redundant; for the word *samāhāra* is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*) and is a synonym for "collection" (*samūha*), and since a collection is the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the term "meaning of a secondary derivative" [would suffice].

Thus it is established. If this is so, does it follow that *dadhitotpatti* (the production of curd) would occur? Let *dadhitotpatti* occur; the elision (*luk*) will take place by the rule "of a *dvigu*. [Objection: When elision occurs, rules dependent on it would apply; thus, in *pañcapūlī*, the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "not after *aparimāṇa*, *bista*, or *ācita*" would apply, and in *pañcagavam*, the suffix *ṭac* by the rule "after *go*, when there is no *taddhita* elision" would not apply. [Response: This is not a fault.

Regarding the term *aparimāṇā*, one should set aside the rule *na taddhitaluki* and state instead that it refers to *samāhāra* (aggregation). This is for the purpose of restriction: the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a *dvigu* compound without distinction; however, after a word ending in *aparimāṇa*, as well as those ending in *viṣṭi*, *acita*, and *kambalya*, it occurs only when the sense is *samāhāra*. Thus, the aggregate of five horses is *pañcāśvī*. Where should it not occur? In the case of *pañcāśvā*, meaning "bought for five horses."

In the rule *goratadvitaluk*, one should also exclude *ataddhitaluki* and instead state *dvigoḥ samāhāre*. This is for the purpose of restriction: the suffix *ṭac* applies without distinction to a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in the word *go*, whereas for a *dvigu* compound, it applies only when there is a collective (*samāhāra*). Thus, the collection of five cows is *pañcagavam*. Where should it not apply? As in *pañcaguḥ paṭaḥ* (a cloth bought for five cows). Even so, in the case of *pañcakumārī*, the elision of the feminine suffix would occur by the rule *luk taddhitaluki*.

Therefore, for the purpose of excluding that [possessive suffix], since the term "aggregation" (*samāhāra*) is mentioned, it is explained that the aggregation is to be expressed by the compound itself, not by the derivative suffix (*taddhita*); thus, it is established as desired that the suffix does not arise. Here, in the case of "pañcaguḥ puruṣaḥ" (a man who has five cows), because the meaning of the possessive suffix is already present in the sense of "having," this [compound] would result [as a *tatpuruṣa*], and not a *bahuvrīhi*; for the latter is not exhaustive, its scope being limited to cases such as *citragu*, where direction and number are not involved.

If this compound were to exist, there would be the audible presence of the suffix *matup*. Furthermore, because it does not belong to the *prāgdīvyatīya* class, there would be no elision (*luk*) of the suffix even for a *dvigu* compound. Therefore, a prohibition must be stated regarding the possessive sense (*matvartha*).
52. A compound preceded by a numeral is called *dvigu*. (Pāṇini 2.1.52)

In some cases, the immediately preceding element is expected, as when it is said: "There is either a prescription or a prohibition regarding what follows. In other cases, the entire aggregate is expected, as for example in the rule *na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ*, where it will be stated: "Therefore, neither [of the two] apply. Thus, when there is a doubt as to whether the aggregate is intended here or the immediately preceding element, he says "the one following the taddhita-suffix," etc., to indicate that it is the immediately preceding element.

The intended meaning is as follows: if the rule were understood as referring merely to a compound whose prior member is a numeral and which is in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to the collective whole, then in the case of *dvimuni vyākaraṇasya* (the grammar of the two Munis), this would also be an *avyayībhāva* compound; consequently, the accentuation rule for a *dvigu* ending in *i* (*igante dvigau*) would apply. Even if the rule were understood as referring to a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition, the rule would still apply to *ekaśāṭī* (a single garment). Furthermore, even if the rule were understood as referring to a *tatpuruṣa* specifically prescribed by the inclusion of the word "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*), the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* ("direction and number [form a compound] when it is a name") would also be included; thus, in the case of *saptarṣayaḥ* (the seven sages), there would be the undesired application of the *dvigu* accent.

The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is purposeless; one should instead formulate a single rule: *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyāṃ taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre*. How then is *ekāpūpī* formed? For here, having first formed the compound *ekaś cāsāv apūpaś ca* (‘this is one and it is a cake’) as a *pūrvakāla* compound, and it being a *dvigu*, the suffix *ī* is established by the rule *dvigoḥ*—which states that a *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine—and not otherwise.

And why can a compound not be formed here as in the case of *eka-śāṭī*, by means of the suffixes *ṅīṣ* or *ṅīn*, given that the word *apūpa* alone is masculine? It is said in reply: in this instance, by the immediately preceding rule (*anantarasūtra*), the compound is indeed one of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*). [Objection: But how can a collective aggregation, which concerns multiple objects, be possible for a single thing? [Response: Even when a certain miser gives even a single *apūpa*, he considers it to be many; likewise, due to an excess of faith in giving, or because of the large size of the *apūpa*, he brings together what pertains to many even within a single object.
By this, the recipient who is a pauper has been explained; thus it is established that a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) is that which rests upon a plurality [of items] deposited therein.
53. Words denoting contempt are compounded with words expressing the object of that contempt. (Pāṇini 2.1.53)

Regarding the term *kutsitāni*: the root *kuts* is used in the sense of "reproaching" (*avakṣepaṇe*). In the rule for *matibuddhi* and so forth, because the letter *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccaya*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the present tense. Because of the mention of the plural number, he states that in both cases the meaning is taken rather than the actual form itself—hence, "words expressing reproach. Regarding *vaiyākaraṇakhasūci*: from the root *sūc*, by the rule *icca*, the vowel *i* is substituted. One who, when questioned, in order to cause the question to be forgotten, indicates the sky—that is, looks at the sky saying, "Oh, how clear the sky is!"—he is called a *khasūci*.

In this context, the study of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), though a praiseworthy limb of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), is censured because it is fruitless due to a lack of creative intuition (*pratibhā*). Regarding the term "sacrificial gambler" (*yājñikakitava*): a "gambler" (*kitava*) is one who engages in gambling regardless of caste and other factors, asking only about wealth with the question, "What do you have? Here, however, a "sacrificial gambler" is like a gambler; he is a sacrificer (*yājñika*) who considers only the presence of wealth in the patron (*yājya*) and not his fitness for sacrifice. Thus it is said: "one who officiates for those unfit to sacrifice, being devoted to greed."

Regarding the term *mīmāṃsakadurdurūṭa*: the root *dula* means "to throw up"; with the prefix *dur*, it takes the *auṇādika* suffix *kūṭa*. According to the rule *bahulamanyatrāpi*, there is the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇiluk*), and because the letters *l* and *r* are remembered as being interchangeable in this context, the form *durduruṭa* arises. Regarding the example *vaiyākaraṇacaura*: how can this serve as a counter-example, since the contempt for the grammarian is indeed present due to his being censured for being a thief? To this, he replies: *na hyatra* ("for not here").

Since the application of a word occurs due to proximity, a compound should be formed when there is contempt for the ground of that word's application; and here, it is the grammarian who is being censured as a thief, not his status as a grammarian. In the case of "kutsito brāhmaṇaḥ" (a despised Brahmin), a compound must necessarily occur according to the rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified. If this is not desired, the mention of the term *bahulam* (diversely) is the refuge.
54. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *pāpa* when followed by words expressing contempt. 2-1-54.
55. A word expressing a standard of comparison [is compounded] with a word expressing a common quality. (Pāṇini 2.1.55)

"Upamāna" is derived as that by which something is compared (*upamīyate 'neneti*). This indicates that it is a compound formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*) from the root *māṅ* preceded by the prefix *upa*. However, in the Bhāṣya, the explanation "that which is near to measuring (*mānasya samīpam*)" is merely a statement of the literal meaning. The intention is that if it were an *avyayībhāva* compound, the form *upamānāni* would be grammatically incorrect. Furthermore, the root *māṅ* preceded by *upa* is conventionally used (*rūḍha*) in the sense of discernment based on similarity. That by which another object is discerned through similarity is the *upamāna*; for example: "A gavaya is like a cow."

The cow is the instrument (karaṇa), and the person is the cognizer; for he determines the gavaya by means of its similarity to the cow, thinking, "The gavaya is similar to a cow. Regarding the phrase "by words expressing commonality": the word *samāna* refers to a property (*dharma*), which is the "commonality" (*sāmānya*). Since comparison (*upamāna*) is heard [in the injunction], and since that requires a correlate to be compared with (*upameya*), it is understood that the common property belongs to those two alone; thus he says, "of the object of comparison and the standard of comparison," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by words denoting the object of comparison as qualified by that":

The meaning is that [the word] is qualified by that common property through words denoting the object of comparison (*upameya*), and not merely by words denoting the common property itself. This meaning is obtained from the inclusion of the term "words" (*vacana*): those which, having expressed a generality (*sāmānya*), terminate in the substance (*dravya*) possessing that generality are called "denoters of generality" (*sāmānyavacana*). This is just as one who has expressed a quality (*guṇa*) is called a "denoter of quality" (*guṇavacana*).

And since the word for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is a relative term, it implies its correlate; thus, it is correctly stated that "it is understood as the object of comparison (*upameya*) itself as qualified by that. In the example *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark like a knife"), the knife is the standard of comparison because it is well-known for being characterized by the quality of darkness, while Devadattā is the object of comparison. Their common property is darkness. By denoting that [property], the word *śyāmā* culminates in signifying the [object] as qualified by it; therefore, it is a "word expressing the common property" (*sāmānyavacana*).

"But is it not the case that [the rule] 'with a word in grammatical apposition' (samānādhikaraṇena) applies here? For in this instance, the word *śastrī* refers to a knife, whereas the word *śyāmā* refers to Devadatta—as it has been said: 'Words denoting the object of comparison, being inflected with case endings (*subanta*), [form a compound] with words expressing the object of comparison as qualified by that [object]; likewise, the word *iva* is employed in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*): 'śyāmā is like a knife'? True; however, by the force of the explicit statement, the compound is formed even when there is a lack of grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

If this is so, then in the case of *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle as a deer")—meaning fickle like a female deer—and *haṃsagadgadā* ("stuttering like a female swan"), would the masculine substitution (*puvadbhāva*) not fail to apply, since it is characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*? This is not a fault; for when an instruction is intended to exclude other species, the feminine gender is irrelevant. In that regard, this [application] is established just like the cases of *kukkuṭāṇḍam* ("a hen's egg") and *mṛgakṣīram* ("the milk of a doe"). But surely the fickleness of a woman is one thing, and that of a man is quite another? True; yet...

Even when only the birth (jāti) is denoted, femininity will be understood through the force of context and other factors; and because that [femininity] is extrinsic (bahiraṅga), it cannot be the cause for the feminine suffix. Otherwise, if it were removed by the process of "masculine-like" substitution (puṃvadbhāva), how could you possibly perceive the distinction of the feminine suffix?

Let it be so; however, if the compound is formed with the feminine suffix [in *mṛgī*] as in "fickle like a doe" (*mṛgīva capalā*), then the form *mṛgīcapalā* would result, for that [rule regarding the feminine suffix] has not been barred by the *daṇḍa* (the rule prohibiting such compounds), and the governing rule concerning coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) compounds would be subverted. If this is the case, then this is indeed a coreferential compound: "she who is both a knife (*śastrī*) and dark (*śyāmā*). But how can the word *śastrī* apply to Devadattā? For that word denotes a genus (*jāti*), and its application here is a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) based on similarity, just as one says "the Vāhīka is an ox."

If this is so, then since the word *śastrī* (dagger) has also transferred to the object of comparison (*upameya*), its status as denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) would not be tenable? True; however, its status as the standard of comparison should be understood with reference to its previous state. As for the employment of the word *iva*, it is for the purpose of indicating the standard of comparison and is not a constituent part of the analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*); thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Now, one might argue that because the word *śastrī* is applied to Devadattā through the common property (*sādharmya*) of the quality "dark," the word *śyāma* (dark) is not fit for use [in the same context]; but that is not so.

For there are many qualities in a knife—sharpness, fineness, breadth, and blackness—and among these, the nature of being a "knife" is superimposed [upon Devadatta] by means of the quality of blackness alone. Now, one might object: "Even though the word 'black' does bring Devadatta to mind, it functions for its own literal meaning; thus, the quality of the knife is not actually being indicated. This is not so; for the statement here is not expressed in the form, "That which is black is like a knife."

How then is it that [one says], "Devadatta is dark like a sword"? In this formulation, by the word *iva*, it is first understood as residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*); for a quality residing in the object of comparison necessarily touches upon the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Alternatively, in cases such as "moon-faced" (*candramukhī*), even though a quality such as "loveliness" is not explicitly stated, it is understood—by virtue of common usage—to be the basis for the standard of comparison; so how could that which is heard in relation to the object of comparison not touch upon the standard of comparison? [For example: "Rice grains are like ploughshares," by way of a property such as length.
56. A word denoting that which is compared is compounded with words such as *vyāghra* ("tiger"), provided that the common property [of comparison] is not explicitly expressed. Pāṇini 2.1.56.

Regarding the statement "it is compared" (*upamitam*), he says that the past tense is not intended here: "this is compared, thus it is 'compared'. He explains "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) as follows: since the object of comparison (*upameya*) depends upon a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), by this very implication, when a word expressing a common quality is understood to refer to a specific shared attribute due to the force of context and so forth, then a compound is formed; however, when a word denoting a specific common quality is employed in order to exclude other qualities, then no compound is formed—this is the meaning. For example: "This man is like a tiger."

This is an illustration of the comparison; for here, due to the difference in grammatical case (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the formation of a compound would not otherwise apply. However, when the word *vyāghra* (tiger) is applied to a man by virtue of a common property (*taddharmyatva*), then, because there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the compound is formed. Therefore it has been said: "When [the rule] *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa* applies... as in: "This man is brave like a tiger."

[Objection: But surely, when a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*) is employed, [the compound] will not occur precisely because of its lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*), since it depends upon that [general term]. [Response: If this is so, then this [usage] indicates that a primary element (*pradhāna*) may function even when it is dependent. By this, forms such as *rājapuruṣo 'bhirūpaḥ* ("the king's man is handsome"), *aupagavaḥ śobhanaḥ* ("the son of Upagu is beautiful"), and so forth, are established. This is merely an illustration (*liṅgadarśana*) of a meaning already established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). Precisely because of its primacy, it is possible for it to be assisted by many; thus, expressions such as *puruṣavyāghraḥ* ("tiger-like man") and *abhirūpaḥ* ("handsome") certainly occur.

For in this context, heroism is the common attribute (*samānadharmah*), not the object of comparison (*abhirūpa*). Precisely for this reason, it is stated as "when the commonality is not employed" (*sāmānyāprayoge*), and not as "when the quality is not employed" (*guṇāprayoge*).
57. A qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) is frequently compounded with the qualified (viśeṣya).

Regarding the term *bhedaka* (differentiator): just as in the expression "the sword cuts" (*asiśchinatti*), the suffix *ṇvul* is used here to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the term *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier): from the root *śiṣ* (in the sense of "leaving" or "distinguishing") with the prefix *vi-*, that by which something is distinguished is a *viśeṣaṇa*; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). A word is called a *viśeṣaṇa* or a *bhedaka* when it establishes an object—which is perceived in a general form and possesses many modes—within one specific mode by excluding it from other modes. That which is being established is the *viśeṣya* (the qualified) or the *bhediya* (the differentiated).

But surely, "the qualified" (*viśeṣya*) and [its counterpart] are both relative terms; therefore, when "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) is mentioned, it is already understood that [it relates] "to the qualified," and likewise, when "by the qualified" is mentioned, it is understood that [it refers to] "the qualifier. Why, then, are both mentioned? [The answer is: so that [the rule] may apply only where both the preceding and following words stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified, as in the case of *nīlotpalam* ("blue lotus").

For here, the object "blue" (nīla), being perceived in a form common to bees and other things, is established as a blue lotus by means of the object "lotus" (utpala); and the object "lotus," being perceived in a form common to red lotuses and others, is established as a blue lotus by means of the object "blue. Thus, there is the presence of both [qualifiers] in each case. Where that [mutual exclusion] does not exist, a compound does not occur, as in the counter-example "Takṣaka the serpent"; for Takṣaka does not deviate from the nature of being a serpent.

But is it not the case that there is a deviation [in the application of the term], since the word *takṣaka* is also based on action—namely, "he who hews" (*takṣṇoti*) or "he who cuts" (*takṣati*)? True, it exists; however, this [action-based sense] does not attain equal status with the name [the conventional designation]. For in the case of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), the cognition arises immediately, whereas the word for the action is delayed. In the present case, however, in the compound *śiṃśapāvṛkṣaḥ*, because the word *śiṃśapā* is seen to apply even to the fruit, there is indeed a deviation from the tree [as its sole referent]; thus the compound is valid. Furthermore, in this instance, the cognition of the fruit does not necessarily precede the cognition of the tree such that it would be considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

For just as words such as *pañcāla* and others depend upon a mutual connection between the inhabitants of a region and the region itself in common usage, so it is here as well. As the Blessed One [Patañjali] stated: "The elision of the suffix occurs because the connection is not perceived [as distinct]. How then is it in this case: "Now, for the sake of victory over Meru, the upholder of the earth"? Does Meru ever deviate from being the upholder of the earth (*mahībhṛt*)? Poets are unrestrained.

If, then, a compound occurs where both [members] exist individually and both possess the status of qualifiers, there would be no fixed rule regarding which should be placed first, because both would be designated as *upasarjana*s (subordinate members) due to being indicated by the nominative case—would it not be *nīlotpalam*? Furthermore, in reality, there is a lack of predominance [in both]. Thus, in this case of the encounter between a substance (*dravya*) and a quality (*guṇa*), the substance is predominant and the quality is subordinate. For the substance is directly employed for the accomplishment of the action, whereas the quality is so employed only through the mediation of delimiting the substance.

Therefore, the quality-denoting term alone is placed first, not the substance-denoting term. Now, one might object: "The word *utpala* is also a genus-term (*jātiśabda*), not a substance-term (*dravyaśabda*). If, however, it is considered a substance-term because it ultimately refers to a substance qualified by a genus, then alas, the word *nīla* would likewise be a substance-term, since it also ultimately refers to a substance qualified by a quality. To this it is replied: From its production until its destruction, the genus does not abandon the substance; however, one does not say "the *śābaleya* is a cow" [but rather "the cow is *śābaleya*"].

Therefore, since it is the substance itself that is perceived as being of the nature of a universal (jāti), the word denoting the universal is established as referring to the substance. Qualities (guṇas), however, sometimes appear and sometimes disappear while the substance remains—as in "the whiteness of the cloth. Even though they are distinct from the substance, they are conveyed by their own specific words; thus, the substance does not consist of qualities, and consequently, a word for a quality cannot be established as a word for the substance.

For this very reason, when there is an injunction such as "one should sacrifice a white goat," if a white one is unavailable, a black goat may be sacrificed; however, in the absence of a goat, one does not achieve the goal by sacrificing a ball of flour. This same principle should be understood to apply even when an action and a substance are juxtaposed—as in the case of "a begging Brahmin. But where there is a juxtaposition of two quality-words, two action-words, or a quality-word and an action-word, there no fixed order exists—as in "lame-and-humpbacked" or "humpbacked-and-lame."

"Cook-reader," "reader-cook"; "lame-cook," "cook-lame. In the case of "śiṃśapā-tree," even though there is the mere juxtaposition of two substance-words (*dravyaśabda*), "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) possesses primacy because it is more pervasive (*vyāpaka*), has a wider scope (*mahāviṣaya*), and is perceived first from a distance; whereas "śiṃśapāness" (*śiṃśapātva*) lacks primacy due to the opposite conditions. Thus, even in that case, there is no lack of a fixed rule. [Question: Why is it called a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*)? [Answer: This question arises because the word "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) is a relative term, and therefore the status of being a "qualifier" would already be understood by implication.

"‘Takṣaka the serpent’—but surely the word *takṣaka* is also a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)? It is thought thus: since the word that is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is itself a relative term, the status of the first member as a qualifier is already established; the explicit mention of ‘qualifier’ (*viśeṣaṇa*) again is for the purpose of making it understood that the second member is also a qualifier—that is, a qualifier is compounded with a qualificand, provided that this qualificand is itself a qualifier. And in this case, the second member is not a qualifier, because being a serpent (*sarpa*) is never absent from Takṣaka."

"Red Takṣaka"—here, "Takṣaka" is not the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), because redness is never absent from him. If this were so, then "red" would not be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), since that too requires a qualified object. In that case, one should regard the reading as "Takṣaka is red," for in this reading Takṣaka becomes the qualifier; for redness is never absent from what belongs to Takṣaka.

If this is so, would "redness" (*lohitatva*) also be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)? Indeed, it is the qualificand; however, because the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) lacks the status of being the qualificand, it serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). And having established this, *takṣakaḥ karpaḥ* (the carpenter Takṣaka) is precisely what serves as the counter-example even to this question. Both are mentioned, however, for the sake of clarity.
58. And [the words] pūrva, apara, prathama, carama, jaghanya, sama, madhya, madhyama, and vīra [are also used as ordinal numbers]. 2.1.58.

"This is an elaboration of the very same [rule] previously stated. He considers that this is not for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding the obligatory initial placement of words such as *pūrva* when compounded with words denoting qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*), because that is already established by the mention of the term *bahuvrīhi* itself.
59. Guilds and the like [are designated by their members] through the actions they have performed and so forth. (Pāṇini 2.4.59)

Those who live by a single craft or trade are called *samūhaḥ*—that is, a *śreṇiḥ* (guild). Regarding this, [the author] says: "In the case of *śreṇi* and so forth, there is the mention of the sense of *cvy-artha*" (*śreṇyādiṣu cvyarthavacanam iti*), so that it may apply when those who were previously separate are brought together into a guild, but not when those already situated in a guild are subjected to fines and the like. Thus, *śreṇi* and so forth are enumerated; therefore, in this context, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used in the sense of restriction. Regarding the statement "the *kṛtādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*": a group whose form is to be grasped through observation of usage is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) signifies "type" or "manner."

"Of those ending in *cvyanta*, etc."—the intention is that [this rule] takes precedence due to its posteriority. He recites several examples from the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by form) as illustrations, beginning with "kṛta...mata," and so forth.
60. A word ending in the kṛt-affix *kta*, when not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, forms a compound with a word that is not itself qualified by *nañ*.

This word *viśiṣṭa* (distinguished/superior) is used in the sense of "more" (*adhika*). And this "more-ness" is sometimes restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*), as for example: "Devadatta is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his study of the Vedas. From this, it is understood that he is distinguished by his study of the Vedas alone, while other qualities are equal. Sometimes it is non-restrictive (*niravadhāraṇa*), as for example: "Devadatta is distinguished from Yajñadatta by his study of the Vedas. In this case, it is not determined whether he is distinguished by his study of the Vedas to such an extent that other qualities are equal or even greater.

When a sentence has a single form, the determination of its specific meaning is made through context, purpose, and so forth. In that regard, if one were to adopt the view of non-restriction (niravadhāraṇapakṣa), then the rule would apply even to cases such as *siddhaṃ ca tad abhaktaṃ ca* (it is established and it is not a part [of another word]); furthermore, since there is no difference in number despite the difference in the stems of the two words ending in *kta*, the inclusion of the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) would be redundant, and the rule should simply have been stated as *ktena sa-nañ-nañ*. Therefore, adopting the view of restriction (*sāvadhāraṇapakṣa*), he says: "that which has a qualification by the negative particle (*nañ*) alone."

In the phrase "the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes both suffixes (*pratyaya*) and prefixes (*upasarga*). In that context, "that which is established and not subordinate to another" is the base (*prakṛti*); "that which is to be done and has not been done" is the suffix (*pratyaya*); and "that which has been undertaken and not abandoned" is the prefix (*upasarga*). Thus, he says "not ending in *nañ* and ending in *kta*" because even the preceding member must end in *kta*. The term "not ending in *nañ*" could have been omitted; for when the preceding member does not contain *nañ*, there is no addition of *nañ* to the subsequent member. [The compound] is "that which has been done and not done."

This designation of the whole by means of the property of its parts is not contradictory here; for a single entity is both "done" because one part has been performed and "not done" because another part has not been performed. If, however, the position of absolute restriction (*sāvadhāraṇapakṣa*) were adopted, then a compound would not occur with that which has the augment *nuṭ* or the augment *iṭ* following it; therefore, he says: "in the case of *nuṭ* and *iṭ*."

The mention of *nuṭ* and *iṭ* is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any augment (*āgama*), because the underlying principle (*nyāya*) is the same; by that, even in the case of *channācchannam*, there is the inclusion of the additional *tuṅ*. Regarding *aśitānaśitena*: from the root *aś* "to eat," [the suffix] *kta* is added, and then *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "thereafter, *nuṭ* [is added] before a vowel. Regarding *kliṣṭākliśitena*: by the rule "after *kliś*, [the augment] *iṭ* [is optionally added] before *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*," *iṭ* is applied in one alternative. In that case, *nuṭ* is part of the suffix (*pratyaya*), *iṭ* is part of the suffix, and *tuṅ* is part of the negative particle (*nañ*); thus, all of them are included within the final member (*uttarapada*).

But here, in the case of *chātācchitam*, since the substitution of *i* has been applied by the rule *śācchor anyatarasyām*, a compound would not be possible due to the addition [of that vowel]. Regarding this, some say: the mention of the augment *nuṭ* and the augment *iṭ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any modification whatsoever that does not alter the meaning; therefore, a compound occurs here as well. Others say: the mention of *trātṛ* and *atrāṇa* is an indicator for any modification whatsoever that does not alter the meaning; therefore, a compound occurs here as well.

In the case of *trātātrāṇam*, however, because the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* (the *niṣṭhānatva*) is not established, there is no distinction [between the two parts]; since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is figurative, it would not apply by the previous rule, and thus this rule is commenced. It is also intended to establish a restriction regarding the prior placement of words: so that it may be *kṛtākṛtam* and not *akṛtam*. As for *kṛtāpakṛtam*: because one part is done as desired and another part is done undesiredly, a single entity becomes both "done" and "undone."

"Eaten and [then] discarded" (*bhukta-vibhukta*) means that it was eaten because it was edible, but discarded because it was unwholesome; here the prefix *vi-* indicates unwholesomeness, as in "deformed" (*virūpa*). Likewise for "drunk and [then] discarded" (*pīta-vipīta*). Regarding "going and returning": "going" is *gata*, and "returning" is *pratyāgata*. That going which is accompanied by a return over ground already traversed is "gone-and-returned-to" (*gata-pratyāgata*). And "traversed" (*yāta*) and "followed by traversing" (*anuyāta*)—because of going again at that very moment—is "traversed-and-followed-by-traversing" (*yātānuyāta*). Regarding "buying and selling" (*krayākrayikā*): [it refers to] buying and selling repeatedly.

In the word *alpa*, the suffix *ka* is applied; being so formed, it naturally occurs in the feminine gender. In *krayākrayikā*, the lengthening of the vowel is according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. By the maxim of "the cow and the bull," the word *kraya* (purchase) here refers to a large purchase. Similarly, there are forms such as *puṭāpuṭikā*, *phalāphalikā*, and *mānonmānikā*. Regarding the expression "of *śākapārthiva* and others," the word "for the sake of derivation" (*siddhyai*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

The offspring of Pṛthu is a *pārthava*; some read it as *pārthiva*. A *pārthiva* is one who rules over the earth (*pṛthivī*), formed with the suffix *añ* according to the rule "the lord of that" (*tasyeśvaraḥ*). Among his foods, vegetables (*śāka*) are the primary item because of his fondness for them. In that case, since the designation [of the king] is obtained through association (*sāhacarya*) itself, the elision of the final member of the compound need not be mentioned. However, the compound must indeed be stated, because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is figurative (*gauṇa*).
The words *san*, *mahat*, *parama*, *uttama*, and *utkṛṣṭa* form a compound when joined with those that denote objects of veneration. Pāṇini 2.1.61.

Regarding the statement "because of the word *pūjyamānaiḥ*": the intention is that what is being honored (*pūjyamāna*) necessarily requires an act of honoring (*pūjā*). For this very reason, the mention of *sat* is for the purpose of grasping its own form (the word itself), and not for the participial suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*; for those two do not denote the act of honoring. In the example *utkṛṣṭo gauḥ*, the meaning is "extracted. In cases such as *mahājanaḥ* ("great person") and *mahodadhiḥ* ("great ocean"), even in the absence of an act of honoring, there is a compound according to the rule *viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*. The explicit mention [of *sadādibhiḥ*] in the rule, however, is for the purpose of restricting the prior placement of words like *sat* and others alone, even when they are used as adjectives of quality (*guṇa*) or action (*kriyā*).
62. Being worshipped by hosts of gods, nāgas, and elephants. || 2-1-62 ||

The word *vṛndāraka* denotes a person belonging to a class of deities (*devajāti*), while the other two [words, *nāga* and *kuñjara*] denote classes of elephants (*hastijāti*). In that context, since they function as points of comparison, their status as words denoting honor (*pūjāvacana*) is possible. Since the compound is already established by the fact that *vyāghra* and others belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by their form), this specific rule is stated so that the compound occurs only when honor is intended and not when censure (*nindā*) is intended. Otherwise, one would not have such a case here as: "This boy is an 'elephant' (*nāga*) because he is a fool. Others hold that the rule is also for the sake of allowing the compound even when used with a general term. *Suṣīma* is the name of a particular kind of elephant.

If this is so, then [the compound] will not occur here simply by virtue of the governing rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), for there is no such thing as a "non-serpent Suṣīma. This is true; however, this was shown merely as an indication of the direction for counter-examples. A counter-example is: "This boy is a serpent" (*māṇavako 'yaṃ nāgaḥ*).
63. The [karmadhāraya] compounds *katara* and *katama* [are used] when asking about a birth (*jāti*). 2-1-63.

Regarding the example "katarakaṭha": since "jāti" (generic class) is defined as "the lineage along with the Vedic schools," this serves as a counter-example; the implication is that what was previously presented in the commentaries thus becomes logically consistent.
64. *kiṃ* [is used] in the sense of reproach. (Pāṇini 2.1.64)

65. A generic term [is compounded] with *poṭā*, *yuvati*, *stoka*, *katipaya*, *kṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, *vehat*, *abda*, *ṣaṣ*, *kaṇī*, *pravaktṛ*, *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta*. (Pāṇini 2.1.65)

"Having both sexual organs" (*ubhayavyañjanā*): that by which femininity and so forth are manifested is called a "sexual organ" (*vyañjana*), such as the breasts and so on. She who possesses the sexual organs of both woman and man is thus described; the meaning is a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*), specifically a *poṭā*. However, the word *poṭā* is applied there even when it is associated with femininity, because words possess diverse powers (*citraśakti*), just as the word *ṣaṇḍa* [is used] for a male. The inclusion of the term "rogue" (*dhūrta*) is for the sake of non-contempt; the intention is that if contempt were intended, the form would be established by the rule "words denoting the contemptible [are compounded] with words denoting the cause of contempt" (*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ*).
In that regard, "Kaṭha-Dhūrta" means one who is a Kaṭha and is a rogue; however, the state of being a Kaṭha is not what is being censured.
And [the suffix *kṛt* is used] with words of praise. (Pāṇini 3.2.137)

"Conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*) are understood here as those expressing praise. Although it would have been sufficient to say "by means of praise," the inclusion of the term *vacana* ("expression") indicates that only conventional words which denote praise in its entirety are to be taken here. Consequently, all the following are excluded: (1) derivative words such as *praśasta*, *śobhana*, and *ramaṇīya*; (2) specific descriptive terms such as *śuci* and *mṛdu*; and (3) class-terms (*jātiśabda*) which, when applied to another object, convey praise, such as "the boy is a lion" (*siṃho māṇavakaḥ*). [The examples include] *matallikā* and so forth.

"Matallikā, macarcikā, prakāṇḍa, udgha, and tallaja—these are words expressive of praise," so says Amara. "Because they possess fixed genders (āviṣṭaliṅgatvāt)" means because they have restricted genders. "'Those which take up their own gender' (svaliṅgopādānāḥ)" means those in which there is the assumption of their very own gender. Although a single rule such as "praśaṃsāvacanapoṭāyuvati" could have been formulated, the division of the rules (yogavibhāga) has a purpose that requires consideration.
67. A youth [is not desired] by women who are grey-haired, wrinkled, and aged. || 2.1.67 ||

In cases such as *saṃjñāyūno gahaṇe gārgyāyaṇaḥ khalatiḥ*, [the suffix] would apply only there, yet that [word *yuvan*] lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *jaratī*. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "young Gārgyāyaṇī woman," because the technical designation *yuvan* is prohibited for women (*stri*). Therefore, he states—namely, "the word *yuvan*"—that it is the actual form [of the word] that is being referred to, [as in] "with coreferential terms such as *khalati*."

But how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *yuva* (masculine) and the word *jaratī* (feminine), given that they differ in gender? To this he says: "The mention of the feminine gender. For when this metarule (*paribhāṣā*) exists, since the inclusion of the word *yuva* implies the inclusion of the word *yuvati*, the coreferentiality of the words *yuvati* and *jaratī* is established; but in its absence, it would not be established. Thus, by the principle of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the metarule is understood. [The example is] *yuvakhalatī*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rules "kṛdikārādaktinaḥ" and "sarvato'ktinnarthādityeke. The word *vali* belongs to the *pāmādi* group. Regarding the expression *yuvajarann*, some teachers have taught that there is also a reading *jaradbhiḥ*; the intention is that the compound can thus occur even with a masculine noun. As for *yuvatirjaratī*, one might ask: how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two words with contradictory meanings? It will occur through the superimposition of those forms due to the perception of each other's attributes.

If this is so, then since such grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible even between words of different genders, it must be considered how the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is thereby indicated; the statement is intended to establish the fixed rule for the prior placement of the word *yuvan*, for otherwise, due to its being a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), there would be no fixed order.
68. A word denoting an action is compounded with another word denoting an action, provided they do not denote a genus. (Pāṇini 2.1.68)

"And [the words] *tulya* and *aparyāya*. The intention is that the mention of "name" (*ākhyā*) is for the purpose of excluding the word's own form (*svarūpa*). Since there would otherwise be no fixed rule regarding the order of words in compounds such as *bhojya-uṣṇa*, this statement is intended to establish a rule for the prior placement [of these terms]. Regarding *tulyamahān*: since the rule *sanmahat* (Pāṇini 2.1.61) finds its scope in cases involving non-gerundive (*akṛtya*) terms and names, whereas this present rule applies to gerundive (*kṛtya*) terms and names, the intention is that this very compound is more appropriate due to its superior status. In the case of *bhojya odanaḥ*, because of the force of the prohibition, it is not even considered a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
69. A word denoting color [is compounded] with another word denoting color. 2-1-69.

The rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) applies here; in that case, the status of being a qualifier would arise through the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of both. [For example,] "this is a color, and it is a color. What is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*)? What is concomitant (*anvita*)? Or is there an apprehension of the form of the qualifiers in one instance and [the qualified] in another? [If so,] the expression "this is a white color" (*śuklaścāsau varṇaḥ*) would not be possible, because "color" (*varṇa*) would be the qualifier of "white," since [whiteness] does not deviate from being a color. Therefore, he says "denoting a specific color" (*varṇaviśeṣavācī*) and so forth, meaning that the specific [qualifier] is apprehended in both cases—as in "black-spotted" (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*) and so on.

A *sāraṅga* is a collection of various colors, as is a *sabala*. Since the latter exists even when there is a collection of other colors, its connection with blackness would not be certain; therefore, "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) is used as a qualifier. The same should be understood regarding the word "red" (*lohita*). Now, one might object: the word "black" here refers to a part, not to the whole, because that [whole] is a *sāraṅga*. Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "black," which functions with respect to a part, and the word "sāraṅga," which functions with respect to the whole? To this he says: "by way of the parts," and so forth.

The meaning is that because of its connection with black parts, the whole aggregate itself is called "black. For this very reason, the sūtra is commenced to establish that here there is a metaphorical (gauṇa) grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Now, one might ask: why is the compound not already established by the rule "tṛtīyā tatkṛtena" (Pāṇini 2.1.30)? [The answer is: the word *sāraṅga* is an adjective expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*); since the state of being *sāraṅga* is indeed produced by the black parts, the formation is indeed established.

In this regard, there is also this point: the rule that "the original accent of the first member [is maintained] in a *varṇa* compound" need not be stated, because it is already established by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the original accent remains] after a word ending in the third case when it has the sense of 'equal to'. However, this must be stated as an exception for its specific parts, so that it does not apply here in cases such as *kṛṣṇaitaḥ* and *lohitaitaḥ*.

But is this not something that should not be stated? This too must be stated, so that it may be understood here as well: *śuklababhruḥ* (white-brown), *kṛṣṇaśuklaḥ* (black-white), *haritaśuklaḥ* (green-white), *babhrūkapilaḥ* (brown-tawny). In these cases, when some part of a whole is white and some part is brown, that aggregate is expressed by the two words for its parts; thus, there is no possibility here of [the name] being produced by those [parts].

In this regard, in examples such as *kṛṣṇasāraṅga*, where one word denotes a part and the other denotes the whole, the former is placed first because it is subordinate (*upasarjana*) due to its lack of predominance. However, when both words denote parts, it should be understood that they are used interchangeably.

Here, in a usage where it is intended to convey that a village possesses brave men (*vīra-puruṣavat*), one must first intend to express the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*); thus, the compound *vīrapuruṣakaḥ grāmaḥ* (the village having brave men) must always be formed as a *bahuvrīhi* by means of the construction "brave men exist in this [village]."

Otherwise, if the meaning of the other member had not been previously considered, one might first form a *karmadhāraya* compound such as *vīrāḥ puruṣāḥ* (brave men), and subsequently, when there is a desire to express the meaning of the other member, the addition of a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) would result in the undesirable form *vīrapuruṣavān grāmaḥ* (a village possessing brave men), and so forth. However, a *karmadhāraya* compound of the word *sarva-* with words ending in the vowel *a* is also desired.

Therefore, when the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is intended to be expressed, it must be stated that the suffix *ini* alone occurs, overriding the suffix *ṭhan* prescribed by the rule "ata ini-ṭhanau. Thus, *sarvadhanam* (all wealth) is [the object]; one who has that is *sarvadhanī* (possessor of all wealth), *sarvabījī* (possessor of all seeds), or *karvakeśī* (having curly hair). Where a *karmadhāraya* compound denotes a specific genus (*jāti*), a possessive suffix occurs after that *karmadhāraya*: e.g., *kṛṣṇasarpa-vān valmīkaḥ* (an anthill containing black snakes), *lohitaśāli-mān grāmaḥ* (a village possessing red rice), *gaurakhara-vad araṇyam* (a forest having white asses), or *gauramṛga-vat* (having white deer).
For it is not possible to convey the state of possessing that [genus] through a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The term *kumāra* [is compounded] with words such as *śramaṇa*, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.70).
This statement is for the purpose of establishing the rule regarding the prior placement of the word *kumāra*.
The word *catuṣpād* [is compounded] with a word denoting a pregnant female animal. 2.1.71.

Regarding the term "quadruped genus" (*catuṣpāj-jāti*): some say that the inclusion of "genus" (*jāti*) should be understood as following from the sūtra on *poṭā* and others. Others, however, say that only those words which denote a quadruped genus independently of other words are included here because they are more intrinsic (*antaraṅga*); whereas words like *kālākṣī*, being derivative (*yaugika*), refer to quadrupeds only through the proximity of another word [and thus are not included]. This statement is made for the purpose of placing the word *garbhiṇī* at the end of the list.
72. And *mayūravyaṃsaka* and so forth [are also indeclinable compounds]. Pāṇini 2.1.72.

*Vyaṃsaka* means a rogue; since this *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* (peacock-rogue) involves the word *vyaṃsaka*, which is an adjective (*guṇavacana*), it would normally have been placed first according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.2.37]. This statement [of the Vārttika] is made to prevent that. The same applies to compounds such as *chātra-vyaṃsaka* (student-rogue), up to and including *kamboja-muṇḍa* (Kamboja-shaven-headed).

Others, however, say: "A rogue like a peacock," "a rogue like a student," "shaven like a Kamboja," "shaven like a Yavana"—this is a compound with the word *upamāna* (the object of comparison) as the first member. Since the formation would already be established by the rule "*upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*" (Pāṇini 2.1.55), this further prescription is intended so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member—which is prescribed for a *tatpuruṣa* compound formed with a third-case word having the sense of "equality"—does not apply here. For that [original accent] is prescribed only for a compound formed by the connection of an *upamāna* with a word expressing equality. [The example] "giving again" (*punardāya*) is provided.

Furthermore, the designation *gati* (indeclinable particle) for this [term] "punar" is according to the author of the Vārttika, as stated in the rule "punaścanasau chandasi. This has been recited by the author of the Gaṇapāṭha: *ehīḍam* refers to that action in which one says "come, play"; likewise, *ehīyavam*. *Ehivāṇijā* refers to that activity in which one says "come, merchant. Similarly, *apehivāṇijā* and *pre hivāṇijā*. *Ehisvāgatā* refers to that activity in which one says "come, welcome. *Ihavitarke* is the second person singular present indicative; *prohakaraṭā* refers to that activity in which one says "push aside the crow."

In this manner, [the compounds] beginning with *proha-kardama* and ending with *āhara-vasana* are formed. The root *kṛtī* means "to cut"; that same verbal form is used here, and *num* is added because it belongs to the *muc*-class. *Kṛnta-vicakṣaṇā* refers to an action in which one cuts while looking on; *udhara-utsṛjā* refers to an action in which one draws up while letting go. Although the rule "*ākhyātamākhyātena*" (a verb may be compounded with another verb) already establishes this, the present statement is made for the sake of expressing non-continuity (*asātatyārtha*). Similarly, there are *udghama-vidhamā*, *utpaca-vipacā*, and *utpatanipatā*.

*udakca avākca* becomes *uccāvacam*; *uccaiśca nīcaiśca* becomes *uccanīcam*; *ācitaṃ copacitaṃ ca* becomes *ācopacam*; *niścitaṃ ca pracitaṃ ca* becomes *niścapracam*—all these are irregularly formed (*nipātyate*). *Akicanah* means "one for whom nothing exists. Due to irregular formation (*nipātanāt*), there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound and the absence of the suffix *lyap* after the gerund *snātvā*, as in *snātvākālakādiṣu*. The state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is understood in relation to the implied action: "having bathed, he has become one who is untimely" (*snātvākālakaḥ saṃpannaḥ*). The phrase *jahikarmaṇā* [is explained as follows].

*Jahi* is the second-person singular imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *han*. This [word] is frequently compounded with a verbal noun (*karman*), provided that frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is understood and the agent is expressed by means of the compound. One who says "Kill the fool" repeatedly is called *jahijoḍaḥ*. Where it is constantly stated, "Eat! Drink!", that is *aśnātapibatā*. Similarly, *pacatabhṛjjatā* (from the root *bhrasj*, meaning "to cook"). Where it is stated, "Break the salt," that is *bhindhilavaṇā*. Likewise, *pacalavaṇā*.

"An *tatpuruṣa* compound for which no specific rule has been prescribed": the meaning is that if there is a *tatpuruṣa* for which no formal definition (rule) has been made, yet its usage is established, it should be understood as belonging to this very category because it is included in the *ākṛtigaṇa* known as "peacock-shoulder" (*mayūra-vyaṃsaka*) and others.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Padamañjarī composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
The Kāśikāvṛtti on the second chapter, second quarter; the Padamañjarī:
now begins the second quarter of the second chapter.

1. The words *pūrva* (prior), *apara* (posterior), *adhara* (lower), and *uttara* (upper) [form a compound] with a word denoting a single whole (*ekadeśin*) when they share the same substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*). Pāṇini 2.2.1.

"One who has a part" (*ekadeśin*) means "one who possesses a single part. Since the suffix *ṭhañ* would apply by the rule *ekagopūrvāt*, it must be understood that [the suffix] *ini* is intended here because of this very specific mention. However, the form *ekadaṇḍī* is an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), because its meaning is already established by a *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "one whose staff is one"—and thus the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is difficult to obtain there; how much more so when it is superseded by *ini* or *ṭhañ*? On the other hand, the word *ekadeśa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound denoting a constituent part; therefore, it is not superseded by a *bahuvrīhi* there, as in the example "one who possesses a black snake" (*kṛṣṇasarpa-vān*). By implication, these [words] denote a constituent part.

The capacity [of the definition] is this: a "part-possessor" (*ekadeśin*) exists only in relation to a "part" (*ekadeśa*), and not otherwise. The inclusion of the term "having a common substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇa*) is a qualifier for the part-possessor. The intention is that it functions as a non-co-referential (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) locative absolute (*satsaptamī*); thus he says: "if [the two] are one. This means qualified by the number one. The word *ekādhikaraṇa* does not mean "expressing the same denotation," because co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words "part" and "part-possessor" is impossible, and because the context concerns co-referentiality itself.

It might be argued: "By the maxim that 'words observed to denote aggregates also apply to their parts,' since there is coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the compound *pūrvakāya*—meaning 'that which is both prior and a body'—is established as a qualifier-complex (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*) without need for further effort. Furthermore, by adopting this view, the mention of the term 'tatpuruṣa' in the rule *paravalliṅgam* would not be necessary; why? Because it would be established simply by the fact that the meaning of the final member is predominant. To this, he replies: "This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*)."

The meaning is that while "the front part of the body" (*pūrvakāya*) is established in some way, this rule must nevertheless be formulated specifically to exclude the form *kāyapūrva*. Regarding the phrase *pūrve kāyasya*: although a word is called a "directional term" (*dikśabda*) when it is observed to denote a direction, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) occurs in connection with a word that does not currently denote a direction, as evidenced by the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam*; however, when connected with words denoting parts [of a whole], the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs, as in *pūrve nābheḥ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body from the navel").

In the expression "nābheḥ" (from the navel), the ablative case is used in the sense of spatial relation (*digyoga*). The meaning is: "the part preceding the navel in relation to the body. In that context, since the navel is not a part (*ekadeśin*) itself, no compound is formed with it. However, some say that a compound is indeed formed with that which *is* a part, namely the body—as in "pūrvakāyo nābheḥ" (the front part of the body from the navel)—because the word "pūrva" (prior/preceding) is a relative term and thus necessarily requires a correlative.

Others, however, say that a compound occurs only where the limit (*avadhi*) is understood through the context of the meaning and so forth, and not when it is explicitly expressed by a word—as in *pūrve chātrāṇām* ("the first among the students"). This genitive case here is not used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*); rather, the plural number is used because the collective group of "students" is denoted by this term, just as in the expression "the fifth of the students. Consequently, while the students do indeed possess the status of being a part of a whole, there is no compound because [the group] is qualified by the number "many" (*bahutva*). This is the meaning of the rule beginning with *saṃkhyā-viṣāya-pūrvasya*.

The sense is that otherwise, the state of being "prior" (pūrva) and "subsequent" (apara) in relation to the day would not be logically possible. However, some explain the nature of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) as follows: "A compound with any word denoting a part occurs with a word denoting time, but not exclusively with the word *ahan* (day)"; by this, even the form *madhyarātraḥ* (midnight) is established.
2.2.2. A neuter [word] ending in the half [of a syllable] is called *ardharcādi*.

Regarding the term *āviṣṭaliṅga*: it means having a fixed gender (*niyataliṅga*). This is its inclusion [in the rule] because, in that very sense, its neuter gender is never deviant (*avyabhicāra*). For a word denoting a part possesses all three genders according to the thing expressed (*abhidheya*): "Half of a cake (*apūpārdha*) was eaten by me," "Half of a tooth (*dantārdha*) fell from her mouth," "half of a village (*grāmārdha*)," "half of a city (*nagarārdha*)," and "he anoints with half of the clarified butter (*sarpiṣo 'rdhena*). As it is said: "Having recited half of those [verses], and leaving half remaining, he places the *nivid* in the middle."

In the Bhāṣya, however, the masculine gender used for the word *ardha* as denoting a part (*avayava*) is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). For in some instances, the feminine gender is observed when it denotes an equal division—as in the rule *ekāntṛce rdhā yugmāsu*. This means that having recited half-verses (*ardhāḥ*) among the even-numbered verses, one should place the *nivid*; its validity is maintained by treating it as a Vedic archaism (*ārṣa*). Furthermore, the neuter reference in the form *ardham* could also be understood with respect to the word-form itself, just as in the rules *svamajñātidhanākhyāyām* and *bandhuni bahuvrīhau*; therefore, it is stated to be neuter.

Regarding the term *ardhapippalī*: the word *pippalī* does not receive the designation of *upasarjana* by the rule "ekavibhakti ca" (Pāṇini 1.2.44), because that rule specifies that it must be a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) when it has the same case-ending (*ekavibhakti*). [In this case, it is not so]. [Objection: In that case, the following would not be possible: *ardhāni pippalīnām ardhapippalyaḥ* ("halves of peppers, i.e., half-peppers"). [Response: This is not the case for this particular analysis (*vigraha*); rather, it occurs in reference to a collection of parts: *ardhapippalī ca ardhapippalī ca ardhapippalyaḥ* ("a half-pepper and another half-pepper, i.e., half-peppers"). [Objection: There is no compound with the word *devadatta*. [Response: [This is because] it is not a word ending in the genitive case.

In this case, Devadatta is the owner (*svāmī*), not a part-possessor (*ekadeśin*). However, when there is a part-possessor, such as an animal (*paśu*), a compound is indeed formed: *ardhapuruṣo devadattasya* ("half-animal belonging to Devadatta"), meaning "the half of an animal whose owner is Devadatta. In that instance, because the connection is with the whole (*samudāya*), there is no state of being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*). This rule (*yoga*) could have been omitted. How then [to explain] *ardhapippalī*? It will occur through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): it is both a half and a long pepper (*pippalī*).

But surely, if the half is not the long pepper, and if the long pepper is not the half, then to say "the half is the long pepper" is a contradiction? There is no contradiction; for words observed to apply to a whole also function with respect to its parts. Furthermore, since this same mode of application occurs elsewhere than in the case of an equal division—such as in the case of "half a moon"—let it be the same even in the case of an equal division.

Then what is the purpose [of this rule]? It is so that a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) might not occur in the case of "division" (*pravibhāga*). However, a genitive compound is indeed desired even here; for instance, the venerable Piṅgalanāga employs the expression: *svarārdhaṃ cāryārdham* ("half a vowel and half an āryā"). If that is so, then because the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be figurative (*gauṇa*), a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) would certainly not be possible; thus, this [rule] is commenced.
3. The forms *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* may optionally [be used] in the sense of "second," "third," "fourth," and "fourth" respectively. || 2.2.3 ||

Because of the inclusion of the word *anyatarasyām* (optionally), that [genitive case] also occurs. Now, one might object: these words beginning with *dvitīya* are indeed formed with ordinal suffixes (*pūraṇapratyaya*); therefore, by the prohibition rule "in the case of an ordinal, a quality, *suhita*, etc. (*pūraṇaguṇasuhitādi*), the genitive should not occur. Even when the suffix *an* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*) according to the rule "after an ordinal ending in *tīya*, *an* is added to denote a part" (*pūraṇādbhāge tīyādan*), even then, because the word *artha* is connected individually with each member in the rule "ordinals, qualities, things having the sense of *suhita*" (*pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha*), there is a reference to the meaning of an ordinal, but not a reference to a suffix prescribed under that specific governing heading (*adhikāra*).

A prohibition must necessarily occur; therefore, he asks how that [prohibition] itself comes about, and replies with the words "pūraṇaguṇa... and so forth. The intention is that since the formation of the sentence is already established by the *mahāvibhāṣā* rule, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* is solely for the purpose of allowing the sixth-case compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Previously, however, it was stated—on the basis of the view that the [present] rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth-case compound—that there would otherwise be no application [of the compound]. Alternatively, it was stated thus considering that when this rule exists, both the prohibition of the sixth-case compound and this very rule have the function of indicating the sixth-case compound.

This [alternative] interpretation of the rule is also possible to state; how so? When there is a figurative grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the whole and its parts, forms such as *dvitīyabhikṣā* are established. However, if the word functions in its primary sense and a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed, then forms such as *bhikṣāyā dvitīyam* will result. This is not well said; for by this very mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*), the genitive compound is indeed obtained. How then would it occur in the absence of this rule?
4. And [the words] *prāpta* and *āpanna* [are compounded] with a word in the accusative case. 2.2.4.

Regarding the term *prāptajīvika*: because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) by virtue of the rule "having a single case-ending" (*ekavibhakti*), there is shortening of the vowel. This form is also established even as a *bahuvrīhi* with a past passive participle (*ktānta*) meaning "one by whom livelihood has been obtained," yet this specific statement is made for the sake of ensuring that the compound is oxytone at the end. Furthermore, in cases such as *prāptasukhaḥ* and *prāptaduḥkhaḥ*, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of the words *prāpta* and *āpanna* being placed last in the compound according to the rule "after [words ending in] genus, time, or *sukha*, etc. (*jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ*).

In this context, by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a rule applies also to the feminine form qualified by its gender), this compound also occurs for the word *prāptā*: *prāptajīvikā*, meaning "one who has obtained a livelihood. It should be stated that there is *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) here. However, in the Bhāṣya it is said: "The vowel *ā* is prescribed for the preceding [element]. By means of the particle *ca*, which has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), the elision of the vowel *ā* (*ākārapraśleṣa*) is inferred; and because the expression is *sautra* (belonging to the Sūtra), there is an absence of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form). The meaning is that *prāpta* and *āpanna* are compounded with a word ending in the second case, and for these two—*prāpta* and *āpanna*—there is the substitution of the vowel *a*.
5. Time-words [are compounded] with a word denoting that which possesses a measure (parimāṇin). 2.2.5.

"By implication, they are words denoting measure. This is the implication: that [the suffix] occurs in relation to a measure (*parimāṇa*) when it denotes a measure, and not otherwise. And although time does not function as a measure in every respect like a *prastha* or other such units, it is nevertheless called a "measure" because it is a cause of delimitation (*pariccheda*). Regarding the phrase "of one born for a month": for whom, then, is this month the delimiting factor? It is certainly not for "one who is born," for his measure is days and so forth, and not a month.

Nor is it the act of birth [itself], because that exists for only a single moment and thus lacks a connection with a month. It is said in reply: the limit of the act of birth is not delimited by the month. What is the meaning of "a month-old" (*māsaja*)? It means that a month has passed since his birth; that is to say, his birth occurred in the past month. In this manner, "a month-old" refers to the passage of time, just as in the expression "a debt to be paid in a month," where the limit of the debt's repayment is delimited by the month. Thus, one is called "month-born" (*māsaja*).

Just as in the sentence "he who has cows" (*gomān*), although the possessor (*tadvat*) is indicated by the genitive case, it attains predominance in the compound; for what reason? Because the meaning of the genitive, having been expressed, becomes included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This is as in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "he whose cows are brindled" (*citraguḥ paruṣaḥ*). In the same way, here too, one should understand that although the possessor (*tadvat*) is indicated by the genitive in the sentence, it attains predominance in the compound.

And likewise, in the case of *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"), the connection with the action [of being born] belongs only to that which has been born (*jātasya*), and not to the meaning of the first member of the compound, as is the case with *ardhapippalī* and similar forms. Regarding *dvyahajātaḥ*: it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of two days (*dvayor ahnoḥ*). By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied; however, by the rule *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre*, the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* is prohibited.

How then is the form *dvyahajātaḥ* ("born two days ago") derived? By forming a compound simultaneously of the three words—*dve*, *ahani*, and *asya jātasya*—with the word *jāta* as the final member (*uttarapada*), a *dvigu* compound will result for the two preceding members when followed by that final member. But is it not the case that, according to the rule *sup supā*, since singularity is intended to be expressed, a compound can only be formed between two words at a time, and not among many simultaneously? It is said in reply: this must indeed be stated as a specific rule—that there is an instruction for the compounding of two [words] with a final member (*uttarapada*) that denotes a measure (*parimāṇin*).

For the sake of establishing the *dvigu* compound with a final member that denotes a measure (*parimāṇin*), a rule for compounding must be stated. Now, if it were understood as "of two [things] simultaneously," then by virtue of this statement, this compound would apply even to many [things]. Thus, in the case of "born after two months" (*dvimāsajātaḥ*), when there is a three-word *tatpuruṣa* and the word *jāta* stands as the final member, the preceding two words form a *tatpuruṣa*; consequently, even in a *dvigu* where time is the final member, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member occurs.

The collection of two months is "dvimāsam," belonging to the *pātrādi* group; when the analysis (*vigraha*) "dvimāsaṃ jātasya" (two months [old] of one born) is performed and the compound is formed, it becomes a compound with an udātta accent on the final syllable because it is taught as such by the grammarians (*śiṣṭa*). When the case-ending has ceased in the derivative form (*vṛtti*), there is no evidence for the comprehension of duality or plurality; therefore, even the number of non-differentiated unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) does not apply here, and only pure singularity is understood.

Where a single word-meaning is inherent in two or many things, there alone does the number of non-dual unity exist; however, the word *māsa* denotes an object characterized by a specific measure, and thus, for the cognition of duality or plurality, it depends upon a case-ending (*vibhakti*), whereas unity is its own unique attribute by nature.
6. The negative particle *nañ* [is compounded with a word ending in the genitive case]. 2.2.6.
