The letter *ñ* is pronounced [in the rule] because there is no distinction between the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the letter *ñ*. Since the word *sup* serves as a qualifier, the *n* characterized by the *pām-ādi* group is not included here, precisely because it does not end in a case-ending (*asubanta*). In this context, it is intended that words such as *abrāhmaṇa* denote a Kṣatriya or others; thus, when the word *brāhmaṇa* refers merely to the caste (*jāti*), "one who does not possess Brāhmaṇahood" is a *kṣatriya* or similar person, and the compound is one where the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant.

In that case, because the rule for the *bahuvrīhi* compound would be superseded by the very fact of its being initiated before the *nañ-tatpuruṣa* could even apply, the form *abrāhmaṇakaḥ deśaḥ* ("a region without Brāhmaṇas") would not be established. For there is no restrictive rule stating that this compound applies only to words such as *brāhmaṇa* when they reside solely in their primary denotation (*pravṛttinimitta*), and not when they reside in something possessing that quality (*tadvat*). Furthermore, in the case of *avarṣā hemantaḥ* ("the winter season without rain"), the application of the compound would result in the gender of the whole being determined by the gender of the word *hemanta*, whereas according to the rule *paravalliṅgam* ("the gender of the compound is like that of the final member"), there would be no such fault.

And in this case, because the meaning of the second member (*uttarapadārtha*) in *asau asarvaḥ* is subordinate (*upasarjana*), the grammatical operations pertaining to the *tyad*-class (such as substitution) and the *sarva*-class would not apply. However, when the negative particle *nañ*, which exists in common with non-existence, is qualified by terms such as "Brāhmaṇa"—meaning that one who is not a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of being a Brāhmaṇa, but who exists through other activities, such as a Kṣatriya, is called an *abrāhmaṇa*—then the compound has the meaning of the first member as its primary sense (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*). In that case, because the meaning of *nañ* is predominant, there would be no connection of number with the compound; however, let the rule regarding the gender of the compound being like that of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) be established by specific scriptural injunction (*vācanikī*).

It might be argued: "Due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words (*śabdakti*), the negative particle (*nañ*) does not express an object (*artha*) of a non-substantial nature (*asattva-rūpa*) in a sentence, but in a compound (*samāsa*) it expresses a substantial nature (*sattva-rūpa*); therefore, the connection with number (*saṃkhyā-yoga*) is established. Even so, because this exception (*apavāda*) subverts the *avyayībhāva* compound, forms such as *amakṣikam* would not be established; for its scope of application (*avakāśa*) would be limited to forms such as *nirmakṣikam*, and thus, as before, the suffixes *smāy* and so forth would not be established in forms such as *aso'sarvasmai*.

"Let it be, then, that here the meaning of the final member is predominant. If this is so, does it not follow that any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever would be brought? If the predominance of the final member's meaning is the reason [for your objection], then here too, when it is said 'Bring the king’s man' (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), it follows that any man whatsoever should be brought. There is a distinction here: the king is employed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*).

But here too, the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed as a qualifier. How indeed could the *nañ* be a qualifier? For a qualifier is applied to bring about the cognition of a specific quality for that which possesses indeterminate qualities; it is not applied to destroy that [thing]."

Furthermore, since the meaning of "brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) is negated in its entirety by the negative particle (*nañ*), how could there be any predominance of the non-existent? Therefore, for one who desires the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in this context, the negative particle would be meaningless. However, it must be stated that such a compound—consisting of meaningful and meaningless parts—is grammatically correct (*sādhutva*) due to the force of explanatory tradition (*anvākhyāna*). If that were so, would it not follow that only a mere Brahmin would be brought [into the assembly]? This is not a fault.

In this context, the word *brāhmaṇa*, when employed with its positive referent excluded (*nivṛttapadārthaka*), denotes a primary Brāhmaṇa by virtue of conventional usage (*prasiddhi*); however, through the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is indicated that the status of being a Brāhmaṇa superimposed upon a Kṣatriya or others—on the basis of such factors as similarity—is not real. Thus, since the primary meaning of the word *brāhmaṇa* has ceased and a secondary meaning, such as a Kṣatriya, has arisen, it is established that there is neither the fetching of a Brāhmaṇa alone, nor the non-fetching of anyone at all. And it has been said:
"Prior to the compound, the exclusion of the word-meanings is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*)."
"Of those [castes] who have ceased [to exist] by their very nature, the distinction of form is not perceived.

It might be argued: "A word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning. If the meaning of 'Brāhmaṇa' has ceased to exist, why is the word 'Brāhmaṇa' used in vain? This is not so; for if the word 'Brāhmaṇa' were absent and only "not" (*na*) were said, it would not be known whose meaning is intended to be negated here. But when the word 'Brāhmaṇa' is present, the primary absence of existence of that [Brāhmaṇa] meaning in the Kṣatriya and others is understood. Another view is that all these words refer to a collection of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*), and they are recorded in traditional texts (*smṛti*): [text follows].
"Austerity, sacred learning, and birth—these are the causes of Brahminhood.
He who is devoid of austerity and sacred learning is merely a Brahmin by birth.
Thus says the Śruti:

"O Garuḍa, six afflictions torment a man: those of the body, the heart, the stomach, and the semen; likewise, the heat of summer and the cold of winter. For the sake of remembering him, O Brāhmaṇa... thus [it is said].

Furthermore, there are attributes such as being fair-complexioned, pure in conduct, having reddish-brown hair, and so forth; the word "brāhmaṇa" applies to the collection of these [attributes]. This should be understood to apply to the words "kṣatriya" and others as well. This being the case, according to the principle that "words which function for collections also function for their individual parts," when the word "brāhmaṇa" is applied to something distinct from the [natural] caste (jāti) or distinct from the [specific] qualities (guṇa), the natural exclusion of the caste and the qualities is indicated by the negative particle (nañ). The employment of the word "brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of indicating the existence of the portion [of the qualities] that has not been negated.

If this were so, it would follow that both [the word *brāhmaṇa* and the negative particle] have distinct objects of reference. How so? The word *brāhmaṇa* expresses the existence of a certain part, but the negative particle does not express its non-existence; and the negative particle expresses the non-existence of a certain part, but the word *brāhmaṇa* does not express its existence. This is not a fault.

Both of these [arguments] have been made by relying on the whole (*samudāya*); just as a single object becomes both "made" and "unmade" through the making and non-making of one part, so too here, due to the disintegration of one part, the whole itself is said to have ceased, and because of the existence of one part, that same [whole] is designated as existing—thus, everything is faultless.

In this case, since many people have arrived, the notion of oneness is superimposed upon the two or more, and while the primary [plurality] is negated—just as the status of being a Brāhmaṇa is negated in the case of a Kṣatriya and so forth—the singular number alone remains, yet the number two or more is still understood. Thus, it is established that [the compound] is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*).

And here is the indicative mark (*liṅga*): the inclusion of the term *anañ-samāsa* (a compound not containing the negative particle *nañ*) in the rule *etattadoḥ sulopo'koranañ* [Pāṇini 6.1.132]. Otherwise, since the elision of the *su*-case ending is prescribed for that which is connected to *etad* and *tad* by way of their meaning, how could it apply in cases such as *naiṣo dadāti* ("this one does not give") or *aso dadāti* ("that one does not give")? Furthermore, in the case of *iha na brāhmaṇasya bhāvaḥ*, if the simultaneous connection with both the abstract suffix (*bhāva*) and the negative particle (*nañ*) is intended, then both the suffixes *tva* and *tal* would be applicable, as well as the formation of a compound.

In this regard, if one were to first apply the suffixes *tva* and *tal* because they are of higher priority (*paratva*), and only afterwards form the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) based on the principle that an operation applies again once it has been superseded (*punah-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), then—by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the word] having a meaning similar to *tulya* [takes the original accent of the first member]" (Pāṇini 6.2.2)—the word would have its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) as the original accent of the first member. However, since the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) and the accent of the negative particle (*nañ-svara*) are intended, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* must be applied after the compound has been formed. As it is said: "The negative compound with *tva* and *tal* occurs by prior exception (*pūrva-vipratiṣiddha*) for the sake of establishing the accent of *tva* and *tal*."

In that regard, first of all, an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) does not occur because the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) lacks the required semantic independence due to its being dependent; however, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) does occur because the principal member (*pradhāna*) is dependent.
7. [The suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *īṣat* when it means "slightly" (*akṛta*). 2.2.7.

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] with a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*). The meaning is that the mention of "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) must be made in the sūtra, replacing the term "not yet performed" (*akṛta*). The intention is that if "not yet performed" were stated, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *īṣadrārgyaḥ* ("slightly Gārgya"), and under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *īṣadunnataḥ* ("slightly raised"). Regarding *īṣadrārgyaḥ*: one might object, "Is a person either a Gārgya or not a Gārgya? There is no such thing as a 'slightly Gārgya'. It is replied: [there is].

The application of comparative and similar suffixes to a genus (*jāti*) occurs in relation to those actions and qualities that are inherent in the same substratum as the quality of being a *Gārgya*—namely, *gārgyataraḥ*, *gārgyakalpaḥ*, *īṣadgārgyaḥ*, and *gārgyapāśaḥ*; just as, for example, one says *gotaraḥ*, *gokalpaḥ*, and *gopāśaḥ*.
The sixth [section]. 2.2.8.

"Connected with a *kṛt* suffix," and so forth. That [ṣaṣṭhī case] which is prescribed by the inclusion of the word *kṛt* in the rule "The sixth case is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*) is what is meant by "connected with a *kṛt*. For example: *idhmapravraścanaḥ*. [The root] *vraścū* means "to cut"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). *Palāśaśātanaḥ*: that by which—such as a staff or other tool—the *palāśa* leaves are shaken off (*śātyante*) is the *palāśaśātana*. "Why is this stated? This is a question from one who believes the desired result is already established by the general rule (*sūtra*). "Because it is prescribed as a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhānāt*), and so forth. When there is the commencement of that which is to be stated [as an exception], then this too must be stated.
We shall explain its non-origination in that very place. "Apakarṣa" means an exception (apavāda).
And [the same applies] when [the object] is [conveyed] by means of a ladle and so forth. 2.2.9.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of counter-exception" (*pratiprasavārtham*): a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) is the permission for the re-occurrence of that which had been previously prohibited by another rule. It is stated in a certain commentary (*vṛtti*) that "it should be stated that the genitive case is compounded with qualities residing in that"; the meaning of this is as follows: by the word "that" (*tat*), the qualities alone are referred to due to proximity; thus, the genitive is compounded with those qualities that reside in that self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, it is impossible for anything to abide within itself, for the relationship of container and contained is based on difference; this is especially true in the case of qualities (*guṇa*), since they are dependent upon substance (*dravya*). Therefore, their "residing therein" is stated only with reference to the operation of verbal designation. For qualities such as fragrance are conveyed by their own words as being distinct from the substance—as in "the fragrance of sandalwood"—and never as having attained identity with the substance; indeed, one does not say "sandalwood is fragrance."

However, qualities such as whiteness are sometimes perceived as distinct from the substance—as in "the whiteness of the cloth"—and sometimes they color the substance so that they attain identity with it—as in "a white cloth. In this context, the phrase "by those residing therein" (*tatsthaiḥ*) was stated in order to include those qualities which are perceived by their own specific names precisely as being distinct from the substance.

Regarding the expression "the whiteness of the crane" (*balākāyāḥ śauklyam*), although the word "whiteness" (*śauklya*) denotes that which is indeed distinct from the substance, nevertheless, in the expression "the cloth is that very whiteness" (*tadeva śauklyaṃ paṭaḥ*), that same whiteness is made known as having attained identity with the substance. Since the fact of the object residing therein (*tatsthatva*) is relied upon [in the former case], even though there is a difference in words, the object is the same; however, because whiteness does not reside therein [in the latter sense], there is an absence of the compound.

In the expression *pūpavān paṭaḥ* ("a cloth possessing cakes"), non-difference is determined by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) based precisely on a distinction [between the two]. Thus, since the form resides in that very [cloth], the compound *paṭarūpam* ("the form of the cloth") is indeed valid. This [example] also follows after the prohibition "not with a numeral" (*gaṇana na*). As for *candanagandhaḥ* ("sandalwood fragrance"): in expressions such as *candanagandha*, the word *gandha* is based on the genus (*jāti*), not a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), because it is not observed in cases such as *mālatīkusuma* (jasmine flowers); therefore, the fragrance resides in that very [substance].

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is read as "na tu tadviśeṣaṇaiḥ" (but not with their qualifiers). This means that there is no compound with those qualifiers of the qualities; for example, in "ghṛtasya tīvro gandhaḥ" (the pungent smell of ghee) and "candanasya mṛduḥ sparśaḥ" (the soft touch of sandalwood), there is no compound with the words *tīvra* and *mṛdu*. The authors of the Vṛtti have disregarded this [rule] because it is otherwise accounted for. How so? There is a connection between the ghee and the smell, not with its qualifier, the pungency.

Even when, by virtue of context and other factors, the word *tīvra* refers specifically to the odor, and the genitive case in *ghṛtasya* expresses a distinction produced by that [odor], nevertheless—since we observe the expression *tīvraṃ ghṛtam* (intense ghee)—the formation of a compound would still not apply precisely because of the absence of the quality's residing in the substance itself (*tatsthatvābhāva*).
10. Not so, however, in the case of selection (*nirghāraṇa*). 2.2.10.

"Not in the case of selection (*nirddhāraṇa*). [The phrase] "by means of genus, quality, or action" is an illustration; for selection is also seen in the case of names, as in: "Which of you two, O sirs, is Devadatta? [And in: "The Kṣatriya is the most heroic among men. Here, there would be the contingency of compounding with the word *kṣatriya*; for the genitive in *manuṣyāṇām* depends on that [word *kṣatriya*], not on *śūratama*, and because it is a word expressing a quality (*guṇa-śabda*), there is no contingency of compounding with it. [And in: "The black one among cows."

The meaning here is not that "among cows, that which is black has the most abundant milk," for in this way the word *kṛṣṇā* would be connected with the word *gavām*. Nor would there be the consequence of it forming a compound, because of the prohibition by the rule *nañā kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.2.6). Therefore, the meaning here is: "among cows, that which has the most abundant milk is black. As for the example *dhāvan adhvagānām*, there is no possibility of compounding here with the word *dhāvat*; this is because it possesses the technical designation *sat* (as per Pāṇini 3.2.127).

It must be considered whether the word *śīghratama* is a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*) or not. Regarding the phrase "if it is prescribed by a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhānā ceti*): setting aside that which is characterized as the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), every other genitive is one prescribed by a specific rule. How is it that [we have] "the master of the house" (*gṛhasvāmī*), "heir to learning" (*vidyādāyādaḥ*), and "lord of the earth" (*pṛthivīśvara*), given that the genitive here is prescribed by a specific rule through the rule beginning with "the master and the lord" (*svāmīśvara*)? This [rule] does not prescribe the genitive; what then? It prescribes the locative. However, so that this [locative] might not subvert the genitive, the particle *ca* permits precisely that which is characterized as the "remainder."

For this very reason, the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* was formulated. Even in the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam*, the particle *ca* serves to restore the genitive case characterized as a "remainder" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*); otherwise, that [genitive] would also have been prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipad-vidhāna*), so what would be the purpose of the rule *na nirdhāraṇe*? In the example *sarpiṣo jñānam*, the genitive is applied by the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe*.

Regarding this, they say: In the section on the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-prakaraṇa*), under the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe*, the term *śeṣe* (in the remaining cases) continues to apply. Therefore, as in the example *na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should not eat beans"), the genitive is established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* itself; however, the present section serves a restrictive purpose. The meaning is that while the genitive indeed occurs and is indeed heard, there is no compound formed with it. For if there were a compound, the elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*) would occur by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*.

Therefore, one need not state "and because it is prescribed for each specific word-form" (*pratipadavidhānāt*). Furthermore, having done so, one need not even state "and [the genitive] connected with a *kṛt*-affix" (*kṛdyogā ca*). For it will be stated that in the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-affix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*), the term "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*) has ceased to apply. Consequently, since the genitive case would not have applied at all when there is an intention to express the agent or the object, it is precisely this [genitive] that is being prescribed; how then could there be an exclusion of compound formation?

A word ending in the nominative case is compounded with a word expressing completion (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), the sense of being satisfied (*suhitārtha*), a present participle (*sat*), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), a gerundive (*tavya*), or a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Pāṇini 2.2.11.

"With a word denoting a *pūraṇa* (ordinal), a quality (*guṇa*), the sense of 'satisfied' (*suhita*), a *sat* (past participle), an indeclinable (*avyaya*), or a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "with each [of these]": the meaning is "with the words beginning with *pūraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "a rule for the specific form" (*svarūpavidhi*): the meaning is that it applies to the four [categories] beginning with *pūraṇa*, up to and including those having the sense of a quality. For this very reason, by the word "quality" (*guṇa*), there is no inclusion of the vowels *ā*, *e*, and *o* (*ādeṅ*); rather, what is included is a "quality" as defined by the characteristics such as "that which enters into a substance (*sattva*) and departs from it," and so forth.

Nor is there a restriction of the term *guṇa* (quality) to the negation of a quality where only that which serves as the occasion for the application [of a word]—such as "existence" (*bhāva*) and so forth—is understood, for that would lead to the over-extension [of the term] to universals (*sāmānya*) and the like. Nor is there a restriction to only those qualities well-known in common usage, such as "white" and so forth, since even things like "the sharpness of a thorn" are intended [to be included]. Furthermore, by the term *guṇa*, both words denoting a quality alone and words denoting a substance qualified by a quality are included, by resorting to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In this regard, because a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon that which possesses the quality (*guṇin*), there is a prohibition of compounding with words expressing a quality alone—such as "the sharpness of the thorn" (*kaṇṭakasya taikṣṇyam*). However, with words expressing a quality, there is a prohibition [of compounding] with that which is related to it—such as "the white teeth of the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇasya śuklā dantāḥ*). In this case, the genitive case in *brāhmaṇasya* is not in relation to the teeth; therefore, since there is no connection between the Brahmin and the whiteness, there is no possibility of compounding at all.

When, however, the application of a word such as *śukla* (white) is understood from the sense or the context to refer specifically to "teeth" and so forth, then the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs precisely because of that relationship, and thus there arises the possibility of a compound. This is because of the usage by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), such as in the rules: "after a word ending in *śata* or *sahasra*, [the suffix *kan* is added] when preceded by *niṣka*," "an addition should be made for *krośaśata* and *yojanaśata*," and "he does not give even a hundred *khārīs*. Consequently, in examples such as *goviṃśatiḥ* (twenty cows), a compound with a numeral is not prohibited.

Because we observe such usages as "the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member due to the measure of the notion" (*saṃjñāpramāṇatvād uttarapadārthaprādhānyam*), the negation by means of a quality (*guṇa*) is non-eternal; thus, there is established [the formation of compounds] such as *karaṇapāṭavam*, *buddhimāndyam*, and *yatnagauravam*.

Regarding the phrase *phalānāṃ suhitaḥ*: the genitive case is used here because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). They say that when used in connection with words having the sense of *suhita* ("satisfied"), the intention to express the "remainder" is fixed for the instrument. The prohibition [of the genitive] applies specifically to the genitive characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix when it occurs in connection with a *niṣṭhā* (past participle). As in the example *brāhmaṇasya kurvan*. This genitive is not [used] in relation to a jar or similar object—as in *brāhmaṇasya ghaṭaṃ kurvan*—for in such a case, a compound would simply not arise due to a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*).

What then? One who performs an action is called a *kiṅkara* (servant), for he is indeed one who acts; therefore, it should be understood here that the relationship is direct, just as in the case of "the Brāhmaṇa’s cook," where the connection is with the cook himself and not through the rice. Furthermore, "the enemy of the thief" (*corasya dviṣan*) is an example of an existing entity; in this case, according to the rule "after the root *dviṣ*, the genitive may optionally occur when the suffix *śatṛ* follows," the genitive case is employed. [And] "having done for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasya kṛtvā*).

The meaning is "having done for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa"; the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because [the relationship] is intended to be expressed as a general relation. "Before the rising of the sun" is an example; for here, despite the prohibition regarding indeclinables, the rule "there is no prohibition for *tosun* and *kan*" applies, so the genitive occurs only when [the suffix] denotes the agent. Similarly, "above the tree" (*vṛkṣasyopari*) and other such examples are also illustrations. Regarding "with the suffix *tavyat* which has an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*)," the intention is that "when there is a mention of a suffix without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), there is no mention of one with an indicatory letter. Thus: "that which is to be done by a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇakartavyam*).

This is a compound with a genitive case in the agentive sense (*kartari*); by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived word (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), this [compound] has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable. However, if the compound were formed with the suffix lacking the indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), the final member would instead have the acute accent (*udātta*) on its middle syllable. Thus, this prohibition of the suffix *-tavya* is for the sake of the accent. For example: *śukasya mārāvikasya*.

"He says 'do not cry,'" thus [he is] a *mārāvika*; by the rule "the suffix *ṭhak* is added after words such as *mā-śabda*," the term *mārāvika* denotes one who prohibits an action by means of sound. This is the name of a particular kind of parrot; however, in some places the reading is *mārāvida*, in which case it means "one who gives the word *mārāvi*," and the meaning remains the same. Furthermore, as for the question "what would happen?": there must indeed be a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) here; therefore, let it simply be a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), for what fault would there be? This is the question.

The meaning is that there would be no fixed rule regarding the priority of placement (pūrvanipāta), because both [words] are designated as secondary members (upasarjana) by virtue of being indicated in the nominative case. Now, it might be argued that even in an adjective compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa), where both [words] stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, it has been stated that the word "qualifier" (viśeṣaṇa) is indicated in the nominative; therefore, in that compound as well, the nominative indication of "qualifier" is equal for both.

Now, in that case, "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) means non-primary (*apradhāna*), and non-primacy is established in such a manner among substances, qualities, and so forth; the same rule for establishment will apply even in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Therefore, as for the counter-example given there—"*takṣakaḥ sarpaḥ*"—the fault lies in the fact that a compound would result from those two words ending in the genitive case, and a prohibition must be stated to prevent that.

Thus, in this case, the objection beginning with "what would happen" (*kiṃ ca syāt*) is itself untenable, while the example provided is indeed tenable, provided that the word *mārāvika* is a conventional name (*saṃjñā*). If, however, that word also functions through etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*), then that [objection] too is untenable. The same should be understood regarding the word *pāṭaliputraka*.
And [the instrumental case is used] with a word expressing worship. 2.2.12.

"And [the suffix] *kta* when expressing worship" (*ktena ca pūjāyām*). Regarding the word "of that" (*tasya*): the meaning is that there is a reference to every *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule beginning with *mati-* (Pāṇini 3.2.182), and not only to that which is prescribed specifically for the purpose of expressing worship. If so, how is the mention of "worship" (*pūjā*) to be understood? He says: "The mention of worship. The mention of worship is an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the *kta* suffix intended here, just as a crow indicates a house; it is not for the purpose of prohibiting compound formation. The sense is that, by this, the *kta* suffix prescribed even after the roots *man* and *budh* is also included.

Regarding the phrase "prescribed for worship": the word "from the present tense" (*vartamānāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the word "of kings" (*rājñām*): the genitive case is used according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. How then is [the form] *rājābhimata* [justified], since there is indeed a usage in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "What has he, honored by Rāma, done? (*kānahaṃ sa rāmamahitaḥ kṛtavān*), where the meaning is "honored by Rāma" (*rāmasya mahitaḥ*) from the root *maha* in the sense of "worship"? Someone says: "When the suffix *kta* denotes the present tense, then the prohibition of the genitive compound applies; when the suffix *kta* denotes the past tense, then only the third case (instrumental) occurs in the sense of the agent, as in: 'honored... (*pūjito*).

Regarding the phrase "yaḥ surairapi," there is a compound [formed] with her according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. This would indeed be so if the suffix *kta* were applicable in the sense of the past (*bhūte*); but it is not. For when that [past sense] has not yet been reached, the *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule *bhūtabuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*—which pertains to the present—is an exception (*bādhaka*) to it. And just as, in the case of the word *vaḍavā*, when the sense of "progeny" is intended, the suffix *ṭhak* (which would otherwise apply) is set aside and replaced by *aṇ*, as he will explain: "when progeny is to be expressed, only *aṇ* occurs."

And thus, in the expression "pūjito yaḥ surair api" ("he who is honored even by the gods"), the word *apūjitaḥ* would be an incorrect form (*apaśabda*). [However, this is not so,] for it is certainly known by you and known by me that [the rule applies]; for there is the specific instruction "upajñāta" under the governing heading (adhikāra) of "tena. Another says: In rules such as "ktena ca pūjāyām," there is a prohibition specifically regarding the genitive of the *kāraka* (agentive-genitive). But when that very same *kāraka*, such as the agent, is intended to be expressed in the form of a residual relation (*śeṣa*), then the compound certainly occurs. In that case, however, there is a difference in accent: when the genitive of a *kāraka* is compounded, the accent of the suffix (*kṛtsvara*) prevails; when the genitive of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded, the final syllable of the compound is acute (*samāsāntodāttatvam*).

However, as for what is stated in rules such as "the source [prakṛti] of the agent of birth" and "that which prompts it is the cause [hetu]," where it is said that "the compound is formed by means of an irregular derivation (nipātana)," that is untenable; for the compound is already established through the genitive case of the residual relation (śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī). Furthermore, the novel grammarians who attempt to justify these would fall into the error of rendering their work meaningless. Therefore, the wise maintain that the usage of authoritative masters must be explained in some way or another, but one should not compose verses according to mere whim.

The term *ktena* (with a past passive participle) is no longer [in force]. The mention of *karman* (object) is a qualifier for the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). A genitive that occurs in relation to an object (*karman*) is not compounded. This refers to the genitive [prescribed] by the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*. Examples: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopālakena* — "It is a marvel that the milking of cows was done by one who is not a cowherd. *rocate odanasya bhojanaṃ devadattena* — "The eating of rice is pleasing to Devadatta. *sādhu khalu payasaḥ pānaṃ devadattena* — "Truly excellent is the drinking of milk by Devadatta. *vicitrā sūtrasya kṛtiḥ pāṇininā* — "Wondrous is the composition of the Sūtras by Pāṇini."
And [the genitive case is used] with a word expressing the locus of an action. (Pāṇini 2.2.13)

Regarding the rule *adhikaraṇavācinā ca*: since the term *adhikaraṇa* alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the word *vācin* (denoting) has a purpose that requires consideration. How so? In the rules *kavṛtte lipsāyām* and *yadvṛttānnityam*, this *kta* suffix is not used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*); rather, it is used in the sense of action (*bhāve*). Thus, *kimo vṛttaṃ yasmin* and *yado vṛttaṃ yasmin* are *bahuvrīhi* compounds consisting of non-co-referential terms (*vyadhikaraṇapada*).
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a verbal root ending in a case-ending (*karmaṇi*). 2.2.14.

"And in the case of the object. [The rule] "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] in the case of the object" means that because particles have multiple meanings, this word *ca* has the sense of "and"; therefore, the meaning is that the genitive which is prescribed after the word "object" (*karmaṇi*) is not compounded. For if any genitive in the objective case were to be understood [by the previous rule], the prohibition "and in the case of the agent" (*kartari ca*) would not be necessary; for [the desired result] would already be established by this very [rule]. Example: *sādhu payasaḥ pānam* ("the drinking of milk is good").

Regarding the rule "in the sense of an object (karmaṇi) [the word *sukha* is compounded] with that [which causes pleasure] through contact" (*saṃsparśāt*), he will state that this is an expression for the purpose of forming a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*). In that context, *payaḥ sukham* ("milk is pleasant") will be cited as an example. However, this present case is to be understood when there is no intention to refer to physical bodily pleasure; rather, it refers to when one who is afflicted by disease or the like, being unable [otherwise], drinks [milk] properly.
The sixth case-affix is used after a word ending in a *tṛc* suffix or a *ka* suffix when it denotes the agent.

"By *tṛc* and *aka*, [the genitive is used] when the agent is expressed. The mention of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is a qualifier of the genitive. Now, why is the reverse not accepted—that is, that here the mention of "agent" is a qualifier of *tṛc* and *aka*, while in the subsequent rule it is a qualifier of the genitive? In this way, it would not be necessary to say that "the mention of *tṛc* is for the sake of the subsequent rule. It is replied: [The reason is: ... [text continues] ... [it is said: "In the case of *tṛc*, since the agent is already understood from the verbal root itself, its mention is for the purpose of excluding the passive voice (*bhāva*). If this were not so, then in the case of *pācaka* ("a cooker"), the suffix *aka* would apply even when the action is performed by the object, because the object is also an agent with respect to the action of cooking. Therefore, the mention of "agent" is made in order to exclude such cases. Furthermore, in the case of *tṛc*, since the agent is already understood from the verbal root itself, its mention is for the purpose of excluding the passive voice. In the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*, one might suspect that the mention of the suffix *tṛc* does not recur [from the previous rule], because its connection with the rule *kartari ca* is impossible; for when *tṛc* is employed, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) cannot occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). But will it not be stated later that "in the case of *tṛc* used for play or livelihood, there is no [genitive]; only the suffix *akac* is cited as an example"? If so, then it was simply not relied upon in that way. As in the example *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("the lying down of you"), the suffix *ṇvuc* is used according to the rule *paryāyārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvuc*. Thus, the genitive does not occur with the employment of *tṛc* in the sense of the agent, precisely because the agent has already been expressed by that very suffix.

Regarding "ikṣubhakṣikām": this is a compound with a genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) in the sense of the object (karman). Regarding "me": the dative case (caturthī) is used in the sense of the recipient (saṃpradāna) according to the rule "the creditor [is the recipient] of the verb dhāri."
In the sense of the agent (kartṛ). 2.2.16.

Regarding the agentive [case]: he says "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) because the relationship between qualifier and qualified occurs only when there is both possibility and deviation. Regarding the phrase "of a word denoting a relation": the intention is that the conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts. However, another says: "Because of association with the word *hotṛ*"; but that is not correct, for in that case, a *hotṛ* with many syllables is not intended. That very same word denoting a relation, in cases such as *kṣīrahotṛ*, is understood simply as "one who offers milk."
The suffix *kyaṅ* is used after a word denoting an action that is constant, when it expresses either play or one's livelihood. (Pāṇini 3.1.14)

[The rule applies] always in the sense of play (*krīḍā*) and livelihood (*jīvikā*). [Objection: The word "not" (*na*) has been removed [from the previous rule]. Because of the mention of "always" (*nitya*), and because the prohibition is already established as optional by virtue of the governing heading *mahāvibhāṣā*, a permanent prohibition will occur; what is the purpose of mentioning "always"? [Answer: It is to show that the suffix *tṛc* does not occur in the senses of play and livelihood. However, Vāmana will provide a counter-example for the suffix *tṛc* in the sense of livelihood under the rule *ake jīvikārthe* (P. 3.2.10), stating: "What is the purpose of [the restriction] *aka*? [Consider] *ramaṇīyakartā*."

He [the author] thinks: "Let it be that the suffix *tṛc* does not occur in the sense of 'sport' due to the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); however, why should *tṛc* not occur in the sense of 'livelihood,' just as *ṇvul* does, according to the rule *ṇvultṛcau*? Others, following his lead, explain this as follows: "The meaning is that it does not exist in both senses of 'sport' and 'livelihood,' but rather in only one of them. As for the statement "only *aka* is cited," the meaning is "in both cases," as in examples such as *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*; here, *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.
For there is no understanding of play or livelihood from the sentence, because it conveys only the relationship between an action and its factors.
The words *ku*, *gat*, *prādi*, and so forth [form a compound with a following noun]. 2.2.18.

"Ku and gati-words, etc. [The commentary says: "The word *ku* is understood as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). The intention is that although this is not recited among the *svarādi* group, it ought to be recited there. For this [word *ku*], which belongs to the domain of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), indeclinability applies to the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member; as he will state: "It should be stated that for *nañ*, *ku*, and particles, [the preceding member retains its accent] when followed by an indeclinable. "Not denoting a substance (*adravyavacana*). The meaning is that that which refers to substances such as earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth is not included. "'Duḥ' in the sense of censure (*nindā*).
Censure arises from hatred toward what is praised, whereas evil (*pāpa*) is reprehensible by its very nature; thus, both are mentioned.

Regarding the term *prāyikam*: otherwise, the prescription of the substitution of *kā* for *ku* in the rule *anyatheṣadarthe ca* would be untenable. Regarding *duṣkṛtam*: it is thought that the mention of the scope (*viṣaya*) as "in the sense of censure" (*durnindāyām*) serves as a regulator even for a compound that would otherwise be obtained through its status as a *gati*. However, when [the rule] is a regulator only of that which is obtained through the inclusion of the *prādi* group, then the compound is established here precisely by virtue of its being a *gati*.

In *duratra*, because the word *kṛcchra* (difficulty) is not explicitly denoted, the suffix *khal* does not apply to the root *kṛ*. In examples such as *duṣkara*, there is a compound with an upapada [governed by Pāṇini 2.2.19]. In *āmandrair indra haribhiḥ*, because the prefix *āṅ* does not express a sense of "motion toward" (*agati*) in relation to *mandram*, and because it does not express a sense of "slightness" (*anīṣadartha*), there is no compound; thus, it does not become a single syllable (*ekasvara*). In *suṣṭutam*, the word *su-* expresses excellence (*atiśaya*), not honor (*pūjā*). For this very reason, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs based on its status as a preverb (*upasarga*). In *atistutam*, because *ati* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule "and *ati* in the sense of surpassing" (*atir atikramaṇe ca*), there is no substitution of *ṣ*.

Regarding the rule *prādayo gatādyarthe*: in the context of compound formation (*vṛtti*), prepositions (*prādi*) that possess the sense of "gone" (*gata*) and so forth are compounded by the inclusion of the term *prādi*, even though they lack the technical status of being *gati* particles. In the example *paryadhyayana*, the meaning is "exhausted for the sake of study.

Regarding the phrase *vāsasī iva*: the word *vāsaḥ* ends in the suffix *asun* according to the rule *vaser ṇicca*; the word *vastra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*. Both are invariably udātta-accented on their first syllable.

Regarding the phrase "the undesirable consequence of [forming] a compound with *prāti*": since the mention of *pra* and so forth in the Sūtra is for the purpose of excluding [compounding] when there is no sense of motion (*agati*), a prohibition is stated regarding *karmapravacanīyas*. This prohibition applies specifically to the domain of *prati* and the others. However, a compound does indeed occur with *su* and *ati*, as in *vṛkṣaṃ prati*. Because of the connection with a *karmapravacanīya*, there arises the possibility of forming a compound even with the accusative case, just as in other instances. Regarding the rule that a compound occurs with a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that possesses an acute accent (*udāttavat*) when there is a sense of motion (*gati*), examples include: *yo jāta eva paryabhūṣat* ("He who, as soon as born, overpowered"), *yaḥ śambaram anvavindat* ("He who found Śambara"), *yo'ntarikṣaṃ vimame* ("He who measured out the intermediate space"), *yau vai prajavaṃ yātām* ("The two who indeed went swiftly"), and *apathena pratipadyate* ("He proceeds by a wrong path").
An *upapada* is a term that occurs before a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

“An *upapada* [is compounded] with that which ends in a suffix other than *tiṅ*. For example: *edhānāhārako vrajati* (“he goes bringing fuel”). Here, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*. [The questioner asks: “Why does it say ‘other than *tiṅ*’ (*atiṅ*)? He reveals the intention with which this was asked: “Is it not so? [He replies: “This makes it known. It might be argued: “A prohibition of a primary *tiṅ*-ending word would be purposeless. Therefore, the prohibition is understood to apply to that *subanta* (noun) which has the same meaning as that [verb].

In this regard, although an object denoted by a *tiṅ*-ending—which is characterized by tense, agent, number, and voice, which consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, and whose primary meaning is the form of an action—cannot possibly be the referent of a word ending in a *su*-case suffix, nevertheless, its status as such a referent is accepted on the mere basis of its expressing an action. The meaning is that a word expressing an action (*kriyāvācin*) is not compounded with another word expressing an action. Therefore, in the cases of *kārako gataḥ* ("the agent has gone") and *kārakasya vrajyā* ("the going of the agent"), there is no compounding of the words *gata* and *vrajyā* with the word *kāraka*.

Otherwise, by the rule *kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), which specifies a locative case (*saptamī*), these two [words] would also form a compound because they would function as *upapadas*. That is not the case, however, because they are not *upapadas*. By the locative specification *kriyāyām kriyārthāyām*, it is that which expresses an action (*kriyā*) which functions as the *upapada*; here, it is the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself that expresses the action, and the suffix *ṇvul* is dependent upon that root.

The word *gata*, however, denotes the agent with the action as its subordinate element; likewise, the word *vrajyā*—since suffixes such as *dhañ* occur when there is the state of completion (*siddhatā*) regarding that [action]—functions to express the completion of the verbal root's meaning. Therefore, that which expresses an action and is thus an *upapada* is not a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), and that which ends in a case-suffix neither expresses an action nor is an *upapada*. Consequently, this purpose is not achieved by the inclusion of the term "non-finite verb" (*atiṅ*).

Regarding these two rules: [the questioner asks], "Is it not more logical that the non-connection with a finite verb (*atiṅ*) applies only to this specific rule where the mention of *atiṅ* occurs, and not to the preceding one? [The author] thinks thus: "By means of the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*), the mention of *atiṅ* should be connected even with the preceding sūtra. If that were so, there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word *ku-* and to the group of prefixes (*prādi*), since in those cases too a compound would occur prior to the arising of case-endings (*sup*). If that is the case, then the mention of *gati* in the preceding sūtra should be separated, and the mention of *atiṅ* should be connected with that [separated *gati*] alone.

Regarding the phrase "of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada*," this is its meaning: whatever compound is formed with *kṛt*-suffixes by means of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* according to their respective rules, that [compound] must be formed even before the case-ending (*sup*) arises from the final member (*uttarapada*); however, it is the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), being already ending in a case-ending, that is compounded.

Regarding the *gatis* first: [the word] *vyāghrī* (tigress) is derived from *vyāghrāti*, where the root *ghrā* (to smell) takes the suffix *śa* according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭddaśaḥ śaḥ*. However, because of the prohibition stated in the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied instead by the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, there is a *gati-samāsa* of the prefixes *vi-* and *āṅ* with the word *ghra*. If this [compound] were to occur only after the final member has acquired a case-ending (*sub*), then for the production of that case-ending, the connection with number, object, and so forth would have to be intended; and since the connection with gender occurs even before that, it follows that the word expresses its own primary meaning [prior to the application of gender].

By logical necessity, therefore, if a derivative suffix were to occur based on the indicative mark (liṅga), it would be *āp* because the word *ghra* alone does not denote a genus (*ajātivācitvāt*). Consequently, there would be a compound of *vi-āṅ* with the word *ghra*; and thus, even if the word *vyāghra* were a genus name, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which characterizes genus names—would not apply because it does not end in the letter *a*.

Since the compound occurs prior to the arising of the case-ending (*sup*), it does not even depend upon the connection with gender; thus, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), the compound itself occurs first. Subsequently, when the feminine suffix arises, it is specifically *ṅīṣ*. Furthermore, because the preceding member ends in a case-ending, the operations pertaining to a word (*pada*) take effect: for instance, in *nirgataḥ*, the substitution of *r* occurs (*rutvam*); in *saṃyyanta*, there is the optional substitution of the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇavikalpa*), and so forth.

Regarding the term *abhraliptī* (one smeared with clouds), it is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* ("an agent or an instrument [is compounded] with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, diversely"). If the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) were to end in a case-ending (*subanta*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would apply as before; consequently, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—prescribed by the rules *krītātkaraṇapūrvāt* ("after a word ending in *krīta*, when preceded by an instrument") and *ktādalpākhyāyām* ("after a word ending in *kta*, when denoting a small quantity")—would not occur. Therefore, either because of the governing context of the word *ataḥ* ("from this"), or by the force of the specific statement itself, one must rely on the word *pūrva* as signifying "position" (*vyavasthā*); thus, [the application of *ṅīṣ*] would occur only while the word remains in its sentence state (*vākyāvasthāyām*). Alternatively, the governing context of *ataḥ* would be set aside.

Prior to the arising of the case-endings (*sub*), in a compound, it is accepted as established as before. Here too, because the preceding member ends in a case-ending (*subanta*), operations such as the elision of *n* occur in forms like *carmakrītī*. Regarding secondary members (*upapada*): in the case of "she drinks with her arm" (*kacchena pibati*), the suffix *ka* is applied by means of a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *supi sthaḥ*, resulting in *kacchapī*; this is similar to *vyāghrī*. In the case of "she sows beans" (*māṣān vapati*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*, resulting in *māṣavāpiṇī*. Since the *n* is at the end of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) prior to the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and before the compounding, the change to *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) takes place.

However, in a compound where a *subanta* (an inflected nominal stem) is the prior member, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would not apply because it is the end of the compound and not the letter *n*; yet even here, since the prior member is a *subanta*, word-level operations such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) do indeed occur in cases like *carmakāra*.

Here, the inclusion of the term *upapada* (governing word) is for the purpose of including those governing words that are distinct from both a *gati* and a *kāraka*. For example: *mṛṣāvāpiṇī* ("one who speaks falsely") and *aiṣaddarśeyaḥ* ("the offspring of Aiṣaddarśī"). In the latter case, when there is a compound with the word *darśa*, one might object that—setting aside the suffix *ḍhak* prescribed by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*—the suffix *ḍhak* characterized as a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) would instead apply to the word *darśā*. This is because, even though the restriction regarding the initial element of the compound (*tadādiniyama*) does not apply to feminine suffixes, [the suffix] might occasionally still apply to the word *darśā*. Such is the general direction of the argument.

These are the purposes for which this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has been formulated. But how can this objective be achieved by the inclusion of the term *atiṅ*? For, since the mention of *atiṅ* ending in the nominative case would indicate the exclusion of the nominative-ending *sub* itself, there would be no application of word-level operations (*padakārya*) to the preceding member; furthermore, the desired result regarding the subsequent member would not be established. Thus, this inclusion of *atiṅ*, if performed [in that manner], would achieve exactly the opposite. That too applies only to roots with prefixes and upapadas; however, regarding verbal suffixes (*kāraka*), [the rule] "the agent and the instrument... [is intended].

Is there not, then, no occasion at all for this discussion in rules such as *kṛtā bahulam*? It is said in reply: it has been stated that, by means of a formal separation (*yogavibhāga*), the mention of *atiṅ* (not being a verbal form) is connected with the term *gati* as well. This being the case, we shall qualify the compounds prescribed by the two rules [P. 2.1.4 and P. 2.2.19] by the mention of *atiṅ*: "A *gati* is compounded when it is not a verbal form (*atiṅ*), and thus the compound becomes one where the *gati* is the prior member"; and "An *upapada* is compounded when it is not a verbal form (*atiṅ*), and thus the compound becomes one where the *upapada* is the prior member."

Thus, in cases such as *māṅi luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175) and *mā kārṣīt*, the inclusion of the term *atiṅ*—intended to prevent compounding with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*)—establishes the exclusion of the third-case ending *sup*. Consequently, the desired result for *gati* and *upapada* compounds is achieved. Furthermore, in the *vṛtti*, it is intended that the entire phrase *sup sup* is excluded from connection [with the rule], rather than the mention of the term *sub* alone. Thus, the exclusion of the whole aggregate is what is meant.

A counter-example has also been shown merely by way of illustration; for in that case, there is no compound with a *tiṅ*-ending word. What then? It is a compound of a *tiṅ*-ending word with a *sub*-ending word. Furthermore, in the rule "The agent and the instrument [are compounded] diversely with a *kṛt* [derivative]," the word "*kṛt*" need not be mentioned. Why? Because the agent and the instrument depend upon an action (*kriyā*), they are first compounded with that which expresses the action. And a verbal root (*dhātu*) is what expresses the action. Of the suffixes attached to a root, there are two types: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. Since the governing topic here is *sub*, there is no possibility of compounding with a *tiṅ*-ending word; this is the point.

Some maintain that the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is for the purpose that [the composition] should occur only when [the word] is in the state of being a *kṛdanta*. We, however, say no. The mention of *kṛt* must be made so that there may not be a compound with a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, as in examples such as *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitarām* ("he cooks very well with wood") or *dadhnā bhuktapūrvī* ("one who has previously eaten with curds"). Since the composition of words like *kaṣṭaśrita* ("resorted to hardship") is not established prior to the occurrence of the case-ending (*sup*), forms such as *kaṣṭaśrita* would not be valid. If this is the case, then the maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "of prefixes, kārakas, and subordinate words" was recited by the ancient teachers and was also adopted by the author of the Sūtras through the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not ending in a finite verb).
In this regard, by stating "the cognition [arises] with reference to the general," it makes known the entire meaning of the technical rule (paribhāṣā); thus, what was desired is established.
Let those who have exerted themselves in the Bhāṣya understand this;
others, even if they were a thousand, do not see the sun directly, being as if blind.
The word *am* [is compounded] with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). 2.2.20.

[The rule] "only with an indeclinable" [is stated]. As in *svāduṅkāram*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *svādumi ṇamul*; the final *m* in the first member [of the compound] is due to this very nipātana (irregular formation) [in the word] *svādumi*. Since *svādumi* is taken as a reference to the meaning, it applies here too in cases such as *saṃpannakāram*. Now, when a rule is formulated even though [the result] is already established, it serves as a restriction (*niyama*). What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? It is for the sake of restriction according to what is intended; that is, so that it may be understood as "only with an indeclinable" (*amaivāvyayena*), and not that it should be understood as "only with an indeclinable [that is] an *am* [ending]" (*amāvyayenaiva*).

This restriction will not apply simply because an *anavyaya* (non-indicative particle) is impossible [in this context]. But surely there is such a case as *svaśayaṃ brāhmaṇakulam* ("the Brāhmaṇa family where he sleeps by himself"): here, the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ*, and the substitution of *am* for the nominative case ending *su* occurs by the rule *ato'm*. This restriction would then serve the purpose of preventing a compound with such a non-indicative particle; but that is not so.

For here, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *sā* [suffix] must first undergo composition with the subordinate word (*upapada*) even before it has arisen; subsequently, at the time of the rule prescribing *sup*, since an *ām* that is not an indeclinable is impossible, and since the statement would otherwise be rendered purposeful by another restriction, a contrary restriction will not occur. Therefore, he says: "the use of the particle *eva*. The literal meaning is: "only that subordinate word which ends in *ām* is compounded, and only that is compounded," and not "only what ends in *ām* is compounded."

In that context, regarding the phrase "only an *ām* [suffix] when there is an *upapada*," the ellipsis (*vākyaśeṣa*) is "when it is prescribed by the same rule" (*tulyavidhānam*). Furthermore, "only an *ām* is prescribed by the same rule" means: by whichever rule only the *ām* suffix alone is enjoined, and not together with any other suffix—by that rule, when an *upapada* is enjoined, because of its mention in the locative case, that *ām* is what is prescribed by the same rule.

The particle *eva*, however, which functions as a restrictive adjunct (*niyamāṅga*), is obtained precisely because of its inherent nature as a restriction: namely, that only that which is prescribed by the same rule [is the upapada], and not something that serves as a cause for the production of another suffix. With respect to this, since there is no status of being an "immediately preceding word" (*anupapadatva*), one should not suspect a compound with another indeclinable. For example, in *agre bhojam*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are applied by the rule *vibhāṣāgreprathamapūrveṣu*. What is the purpose of including the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) [in the sūtra]? If the term "indeclinable" were absent, and it were stated merely that "only that which is prescribed by the same rule as *am* is compounded as an upapada," then compounds such as *kumbhakāra* would not be possible.

Now, if it is argued that because the preceding sūtra has no other scope (*anavakāśatva*), and because the word *ama* itself is restricted to the domain of indeclinables (*avyaya*) as its co-occurring term (*upapada*), this restriction should be understood as applying only to that domain—[that is,] "only with *ama* is there a compound for a co-occurring term prescribed in the same manner [as *ama*]"? If that were the case, the restriction would be formulated thus: "A compound with a co-occurring term that is prescribed in the same manner as *ama* occurs only with *ama*. What is the fault in that? It would not apply in the case of *agrebhojam*, but it would certainly apply in cases such as *agre bhuktvā* and *kālo bhoktum*.

However, when the term *avyaya* (indeclinable) is included [in the rule], since it is understood that "a compound with an indeclinable co-occurring term occurs only with *ama* if it is prescribed in the same manner," there is no fault whatsoever.
From the third case onwards, [the feminine suffix] may optionally [be applied]. (Pāṇini 2.2.21)

"From the third case onwards, optionally" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyatarasyām*). Regarding the phrase "from the third case onwards": the sense is that the particle *eva* (only) does not carry over here for the purpose of qualifying the *upapada*, because [the rule] would otherwise not apply when [the word] is used with something other than this [specific *upapada*]. In the example *uccaiḥkāram*: when there is a compound, the accent is that of the original form of the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), and by the rule "the first syllable of a word ending in *ṇamul* is optionally acute" (*ādirṇamulyanyatarasyām*), the initial syllable is acute. However, when there is no compound, *uccaiḥ* has its final syllable acute, because it is read as such among the *svarādi* group; whereas *kāram* has its initial syllable acute.
And [the suffix] *ktvā* [is used after a verbal root]. 2.2.22.

And [the word] *ktvā*: the term *ktvā* ends in the third case (*ktvā*). There is elision of the long vowel *ā* by the rule *ātaḥ*, as in "in a compound not preceded by *nañ*, *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*" and "after *skandi* and *syandi* when *ktvi* follows."
The remainder [of the compounds] are *bahuvrīhi*s. (Pāṇini 2.2.23)

"The *bahuvrīhi* applies to the remainder (*śeṣe*). "The remainder is that which is other than what has been employed. [This is derived from] the root *śiṣ* (meaning "to remain, not being fully employed") with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object. But what is the remainder? Now, it was indeed stated that the remainder is that which is other than what has been employed; this is true. However, since all words are employed in the form of either general or specific [meanings], and since *tatpuruṣa* and *avyayībhāva* compounds are prescribed for all [words] according to their respective application in the senses of the prior member, the subsequent member, or another word, there is no possibility of anything being "other than what has been employed"; thus, the question is asked again.

And it has been said: "If the mention of 'remainder' (śeṣa) were based on the word [itself], it would not exist because [all words] are already included; if it were based on the meaning, it would be indistinguishable [from other categories]. This means that when no other compound, such as an *avyayībhāva*, has been prescribed for certain words in a particular sense, that [sense] is the "remainder."

Now, why is it not understood in this way: that among the three sets of case-endings (*sup*), that set for which composition has not been specifically mentioned by name—such as the nominative (*prathamā*)—is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*)? For composition is desired even for words ending in cases other than the nominative, as in *kaṇṭhekāla* ("one whose throat is black"). Furthermore, the mention of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is necessary under the view that "the operation [of a rule] applies after *kaḍāra*," but it is not necessary under the view that there is only one technical designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*) at a time; this has already been explained in the *ākaḍāra-sūtra* itself.
The word "aneka" [is used] when another word-meaning is intended. 2.2.24.

"Aneka [is used] when another word-meaning [is intended]. This means that several words ending in *sup* (nominal suffixes) are compounded together with one another. By this, he shows that the term *sub* is what is being carried over here, not the term *sup*; for even the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is already established by the very word "several" (*aneka*). [The phrase] "in all case-meanings" (*sarveṣu vibhaktyartheṣu*)...

The meaning is that since the meaning of the suffix is expressed as having the meaning of the base as its subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is predominant; therefore, it is precisely that [predominant meaning] which is grasped by the mention of the "meaning of another word" (*anyapadārtha*). For this very reason, there is the subsequent employment of the word *grāma* in the expression "this village has reached the water" (*prāptodako 'yaṃ grāmaḥ*). Otherwise, if only as much meaning as belongs to the word *grāma* itself were expressed, such usage would not occur because the purpose would already have been served, just as in the case of the word *ca* in a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

But when, in a compound, it is intended that the meaning of the case-ending itself—such as the relation (*sambandha*) and so forth—is expressed, then the case-ending need not be employed. [Objection: Since the substance (*dravya*) has not been expressed, why should there not be the employment of a word denoting that substance? If the meaning of the case-ending is being expressed, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "village" (*grāma*), or how can there be agreement in gender and number, such that a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs—as in "the village to which water has come" (*prāptodakaḥ grāmaḥ*) or "the pot from which rice has been removed" (*uddhṛtaudanā sthālī*)? It is replied: Because the relation and so forth, which constitute the meaning of the case-ending, are dependent [upon a substance].

Because it is a quality (*guṇatva*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through metaphorical attribution of non-difference, and the gender and number will follow those of the substratum (*āśraya*), just as in the case of "white" (*śukla*) and so forth—for example: *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth), *śuklā paṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklaiḥ* (by white things), and *śuklāḥ* (white things). But if this were so, then just as the word "white" sometimes denotes the quality and sometimes the possessor of the quality, the same would apply to the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

There is no such rule that a word denoting a quality (*guṇa-śabda*) must sometimes express the quality alone, for this is not observed in cases such as *paṭu* (clever) and so forth; indeed, one does not say "Devadatta’s cleverness" (*devadattasya paṭuḥ*). Likewise here too, there will always be a state of residing in the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*). Even so, just as the genitive case and others do not occur because the meaning of the case-ending is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, would it not follow that the suffixes expressive of gender and number would also not occur, since those too are expressed [by the compound]? This is not a fault; [The remainder of the argument follows: ...because the gender and number of the possessor of the quality are understood from the gender and number of the quality itself, just as the gender and number of Devadatta are understood from the gender and number of his cleverness. Furthermore, in the case of words like *paṭu*, the gender and number of the possessor of the quality are understood from the gender and number of the quality itself. However, in the case of words like *jñāna* (knowledge), which denote a quality, the gender and number of the possessor of the quality are understood from the gender and number of the possessor of the quality itself. Therefore, in the case of words like *jñāna*, the suffixes expressive of gender and number are indeed employed. Thus, there is no contradiction with the rules governing the application of suffixes. Moreover, since the gender and number of the possessor of the quality are understood from the gender and number of the quality itself, the suffixes expressive of gender and number are not required.
