The suffixes *aṣṭan*, *ādi*, and so forth are *svārthika* (denotative); since they occur after that which expresses the feminine gender, these suffixes will apply even when the feminine nature has already been expressed by that *bahuvrīhi* compound. And by doing so, rules such as "after a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *an*" (*ano bahuvrīheḥ*) become logically justified.

In brief, with respect to external action, since the singular number and so forth are expressed as belonging solely to the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) in the compound—which is devoid of the capacity for [external] objects and the like—the case endings will serve to convey the singularity and other numbers residing in the object and so forth; for example: "Look at the one possessing variegated cows" (*citraguṃ paśya*) and "done by the one possessing variegated cows" (*citraguṇā kṛtam*). Even so, would not the nominative case (*prathamā*) fail to apply because the number has already been denoted by the compound? It will apply because of the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*), just as in the cases of "one," "two," and "many."

Alternatively—only the gender and only the number are expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound, not the specific quality; therefore, one who desires that specific quality must necessarily employ a word expressive of it. And this being the case, even when the meaning of the case-ending is expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* along with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), there is no fault whatsoever.

How can there be the subsequent employment of a specific term when the general term has not been expressed? [Objection: In that case, it would not apply to a general term—for example, in the phrase "Devadatta is someone. [Response: Even a general term is itself a specific [instance]; just as one specific term excludes another specific term, so too is a specific term excluded by a general term. Otherwise, there would be doubt: "Is the general meaning intended here, or the specific?"

"Prāptodako grāmaḥ" (a village reached by water) and so forth are examples in the sense of the accusative case and others, respectively. The analytical explanations (*vigraha*) are: "by whom a chariot was carried," "to whom an animal was offered," "from which boiled rice was drawn out," "whose cows are variegated," and "in which there are heroic men. However, [the suffix] does not occur in the sense of the nominative case because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Similarly, it does not occur in the sense of "immediately following" and so on—as in "whose cows immediately follow [him]"—when used with *citrā gāvaḥ*. Why [is the word] "aneka" (more than one) stated?

The question arises because, by the very governing rule *sup-supā*, even the *bahuvrīhi* compound would not apply to more than one word, just as the *tatpuruṣa* does not. [The purpose of the rule] is so that it may apply to many words as well. Otherwise, since the number [of words] is intended to be specified in the rule *sup-supā*, just as a *tatpuruṣa* is not formed with many words—as in *mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*—so too the *bahuvrīhi* would not occur. [The answer is: its establishment is due to an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Namely, the fact that this [rule] prescribes a *dvigu* when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows a word meaning a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), indicates that a compound may indeed consist of many words.

If this is so, then the same contingency would apply even to a *tatpuruṣa*. Now, why does the designation *upasarjana* not also serve a purpose for the final member (*uttarapada*) in an expression like *citraguḥ*? [The answer is: When the mention of "many" (*aneka*) is present, the term *sup* (the case-ending) is set aside, and by that very [mention of "many"], the final member is also indicated; furthermore, that too is prescribed as the first member in the rule for compound formation (*samāsa-śāstra*), and not otherwise. This is how it is understood: even when the principal meaning—the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—is joined with various case-endings, as in *citragustiṣṭhati* ("The owner of brindled cows stands") or *citraguṃ paśya* ("See the owner of brindled cows").
Since the two words *varti* and *pada* are always in the nominative case, their status as *upasarjana* is already established by the rule *ekavibhakti*.

Regarding the phrase *susūkṣmajaṭakeśena*: it means "one whose matted hair (*jaṭā*) consists of very fine (*su-sūkṣma*) locks (*keśa*). In this four-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound, the shortening of the vowel occurs by virtue of the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasorbahulam* ("the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are diversely elided in names and Vedic meters"). Alternatively, one may analyze it as another *bahuvrīhi*: "those [locks] in which the matted hair is very fine are *susūkṣmajaṭāḥ*; he whose hair (*keśa*) is of such a kind. Similarly, *sugajājinavāsasā* means "by him whose garment (*vāsaḥ*, i.e., covering) is a very excellent elephant-hide (*gajājinam*). This is an example of a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*), because it is so read in the verse: "*susūkṣmajaṭakeśena sugajājinavāsasā*."
"By means of the Samantaśitirandhra [yantra], the two circles do not succeed."

Thus the verse is recited in the Bhāṣya; however, in that context, the mention of the third case (instrumental) is for the purpose of completing the meter. The inclusion of the word *anya* ("other") is for the sake of distinguishing the respective domains of the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa* compounds. If that [word] were absent, the *bahuvrīhi*, having its scope in cases with non-co-referential words (*vyadhikaraṇa*) such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one who has Kāla on his neck"), would supersede the *tatpuruṣa* even in cases of co-referential words (*samānādhikaraṇa*), such as *nīlotpalaṃ saraḥ* ("a lake with blue lotuses"). But when the word *anya* is present, the *bahuvrīhi*—which has its scope in the meaning of its own constituent members (*svapadārtha*)—supersedes the *tatpuruṣa* by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), and thus there is no fault whatsoever.

What is the purpose of mentioning the word *pada* (word)? It is so that [the designation of compound] may apply to the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) and not to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). Someone says to another who wishes to bathe in a river: "There are crocodiles in the river. These words convey the meaning of the sentence, "Therefore, do not bathe there. Consequently, the technical name *bahuvrīhi* would undesirably apply to them.

What is the purpose of including the term *artha* (meaning), given that since a word cannot function with respect to another word, it will necessarily apply to the word-meaning (*padārtha*)? It is so that [the operation] may apply to the entire word-meaning; otherwise, due to its predominance, it would apply only to the meaning of the suffix—the case-role—and not to the substance which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). By this [inclusion of *artha*], that which was stated is refuted: namely, that even though the designation of the substratum (*dharmin*) is established through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), there might still occasionally be a designation of the mere property (*dharma*) alone, as in the case of "white" and so on.

By demonstrating that the *bahuvrīhi* compound is eternally restricted to the substratum (*dharmin*), like words such as "sharp" (*paṭu*) and so on, the rule "the *bahuvrīhi* [is used] for those in grammatical apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇānām*) and others are merely an elaboration of a meaning already established by usage.

As for the example "high-faced" (*uccairmukha*): because the word *uccais* primarily denotes a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the statement is made despite the lack of grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Regarding the rule *saptamyupamāne*: the meaning is that when a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) and a word expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) form the prior member (*pūrvapada*) of a compound with another word, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final member (*uttarapada*) situated therein. In the example *kaṇṭhestha*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*; the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending occurs by the rule *amūrddhamastakāt*. However, if the reading is *kaṇṭhesthita*, the compound is formed through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) based on the mention of the seventh case.

Since the compound is already established by virtue of having a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), this statement is for the purpose of [allowing] the elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*). By this, it is demonstrated that there is also the capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*) here even in the case of a lack of common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Regarding the example *uṣṭrakham iva* ("like a camel's mouth"): because a collective is designated by means of the property of its parts, the word *uṣṭra* (camel) functions as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, the word *uṣṭramukha* has the standard of comparison as its prior member. Here, the statement serves both to indicate the lack of common substratum between the standard and the object of comparison and for the purpose of the elision of the final member. The form *uṣṭramukha* means "one whose face is like a camel."

The compound is a *vigraha* (analytic statement), and since a living being cannot literally enter the mouth of another living being, similarity is understood by implication; furthermore, the similarity between a face and happiness is well-known. Thus, the meaning is "one whose face is like the face of a camel," and therefore it need not be said that there is an elision of the final member of the compound.

Regarding the phrase "of the genitive [expressing] a collection or a modification": the meaning is that when a word ending in a genitive case—whether it denotes a relationship between a whole and its parts (*samudāyāvayava-sambandha*) or a relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛtivikāra-sambandha*)—is followed by another word as its second member (*uttarapada*), the compound formed with that second member is a *bahuvrīhi* when combined with another word. In the example *keśacūḍa* ("a crest of hair"), this is established because the word *keśa* functions here to denote a collection of hairs. Similarly, in *svarṇālaṅkāra* ("an ornament of gold"), this is established because the word *svarṇa* functions to denote a modification of gold.
However, the explicit statement [in the rule] is so that one does not hear the second member pronounced as *keśasamāhāracūḍaḥ* or *svarṇavikārālaṅkāraḥ*.

Regarding the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya*: this indeed need not be stated at all, for particles such as *pra* and others express an action along with its means—just as in the examples *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *nirvārāṇasiḥ*, and *prācāryaḥ*. The same applies to the rule *naño'styarthānām*.

Regarding the section on *sub* (nominal suffixes): [The objection is raised that] the word "asti" is a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix; however, this statement is established because it is a particle (*nipāta*). Particles are those that resemble prepositions (*upasarga*) or case-endings (*vibhakti*), and the word "asti" is recited among the *svarādi* group [of indeclinables]. Here, what about the term "sabrahmacārī"? This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [The question is: "Who are your fellow-students? or "Are you a fellow-student? For in this context, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is desired; thus, the expected response would be, "I am a fellow-student of the Kaṭhas."

As for the statement "I am a Kaṭha," that is not a direct answer; rather, it is an implied one. When it is said, "I am indeed a Kaṭha," it is understood [by implication] that "your [disciples] are also Kaṭhas. For the fellow-students (*sabrahmacārin*) of a Kaṭha are indeed Kaṭhas, and none other. One becomes a fellow-student of Brahmā only by practicing the vow (*vrata*) together in the same Brahman. Thus, when the question "Who are your fellow-students? is asked, the answer is "The Kaṭhas."

In brief, the answer "the Kaṭhas" never occurs in response to a question [about their number], because the meanings of the constituent members [of the compound] are subordinate; for by the compound *sabrahmacāriṇaḥ* (fellow-students), it is the fellow-students themselves that are denoted.

Here, in the case of "two droṇas, half-droṇas, and two-and-a-half droṇas," [the analysis is as follows]: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *ardhatṛtīyā droṇāḥ*, the collective whole in which the distinction of its parts has emerged is the meaning of the compound; hence the plural number. Furthermore, the word *droṇa* applies by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to both the two droṇas and the half-droṇa, and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established.
Numerals, indeclinables, words meaning "near," "not far," "more than," and numerals themselves [are compounded] with a numeral-denoting word (saṃkhyeya) [to form a bahuvrīhi]. 2.2.25.

Numerals, indeclinables, words meaning "near," "not far," "more than," and numerals [are compounded] with a numeral-denoting word (*saṃkhyeya*). In the example *upadaśāḥ*, the suffix *ḍac* is applied by the rule *bahuvrīhau saṃkhyeye ḍaj-abahugaṇāt*, resulting in the elision of the final vowel and its following consonant (*ṭilopa*). Those which exist near ten are thus expressed; they are either nine or eleven. This compound has the meaning of the first member as its predominant sense (*pūrvapadārthapradhāna*). Since this prefix *upa* is synonymous with the word *ārāt*, it denotes both proximity and that which is proximate. In this case, since the proximate object is predominant, it is a *bahuvrīhi*.

When proximity (*sāmīpya*) is predominant, the compound *upadaśam* is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule "an indeclinable [compound] with a word denoting a case-ending or proximity. Regarding *dantoṣṭhāḥ*, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here due to the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the qualities to the substratum. Regarding *upaviṃśāḥ*, there is elision [of the final syllable] by the rule "after *viṃśati*, [the final *i* is elided] before a suffix beginning with *ḍ*. *Āsannadaśāḥ* means those who are near to ten; these may be nine or eleven. *Adhikadaśāḥ* means eleven. *Dvitrāḥ* means two or three; this is a compound in the sense of "option" (*vārthe*).

If the meaning of "or" (*vā*) were a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*), then if there were two [possibilities], the plural number would not occur. Therefore, the meaning of "or" here is doubt (*saṃśaya*), which is a reflection on an indefinite number; since all three [possibilities] are always present therein, the plural is used with reference to them.

Alternatively—there are always only five [factors] here. How so? There is one reflective cognition (*vimarśajñāna*) that rests upon both sides; for example, in the case of "Let two or three men be brought," the plural number occurs both in the word "men" (*puruṣa*) and in the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). For what reason? Because it functions with respect to those two combined. Thus, even a phrase consisting of two or three words functions with respect to the combined [entities]; therefore, this speech has five substrata, and consequently, the plural number alone occurs.

However, for the purpose of bringing [something] and so forth, it occurs according to preference for either two or three; for this is indeed an occurrence (āpad) of the compound just as it is of the sentence. Therefore, when those [numbers] are mixed, the grammatical operation (vṛtti) applies: thus, in the sentence "let two men be brought," from the word *dvi*, only the dual number occurs. Regarding *tricaturaḥ*: [the suffix] *ac* is added by the rule "there is an addition [of the suffix *ac*] after *tri* and *upa* in the section concerning *ac*. Regarding *dvidaśāḥ*: [the suffix *aC* is added].

Here, by the word *dvi*, the number two—which pertains to the repetition of the state of being ten—is expressed, not the number ten itself, because [ten] is singular. Nor are they joined with a number, because [the items] are plural. In that sentence, since the repetition is not understood without the suffix *suc*, the suffix *suc* occurs; consequently, an analysis (*vigraha*) is made using non-co-occurrent words (*asvapada-vigraha*): "twice ten" (*dvirdaśa*), i.e., "two tens" (*dvidaśāḥ*). In the compound (*vṛtti*), however, the word *dvi* itself expresses the number of repetitions even without the suffix *suc* due to its inherent nature; thus, because it denotes a number, it undergoes compounding.

[Objection: But surely this is already established by the preceding rule, since both the sense of *vā* and the sense of *su* [are included] within the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*). [Reply: That is not so; because *su* is an affix expressing its own inherent meaning (*svārthika*), its meaning is also indeed a word-meaning (*padārtha*). The previous rule applies when there is a possessive sense (*matvartha*); this present rule is commenced for the sake of meanings other than the possessive. [Objection: But it has been stated that, excluding cases like *prāptodaka* which express the nominative sense, the suffix occurs according to the expression in all case-sense applications (*sarvavibhaktyartha*). [Reply: If that is so, then this rule is commenced so that it may also apply in the nominative sense.

If, disregarding the statement "except for the first meaning," it is asserted that [the compound] occurs according to the name [of the number], then in that case, the compound of numbers is merely an elaboration of that very [rule]; however, the compound of indeclinables with words denoting the things numbered, such as "fourteen" and so on, must indeed be prescribed.

However, as for those such as *viṃśati* and others which function as numerals, they are already established by the previous rule alone—such as *adhikaviṃśāḥ*, meaning "those for whom there is an excess of twenty," or *āsannaviṃśāḥ*, meaning "those for whom the number twenty is near. In these cases, the rule "of a pronoun and a numeral" (*sarvanāmasaṃkhyayoḥ*) would require the word *viṃśati* to be placed first; therefore, the inclusion of items beginning with indeclinables (*avyaya*) must indeed be made even for the sake of words like *viṃśati*.
The names of the directions [are compounded] when used to denote the intermediate space between them. 2.2.26.

"The names of the directions [are compounded] when referring to the intermediate space. Regarding "south-east": since the intermediate space is the meaning of the external member (anyapadārtha), this rule would already be established by the preceding one; however, this specific statement is made so that the compound may also apply when there is no suffix expressing possession (*atvartha*), when it expresses the primary sense (the direction itself), and even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, in the rule *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* is intended to refer specifically to that *bahuvrīhi* compound which is explicitly taught [by the sūtra], so that in a case such as "Give this to the one who is confused about his directions, for whom the east is the north" (*yasya pūrvā sottarāsyonmugdhasya tasmai uttarapūrvāya dehi*), the suffix might not apply. Therefore, this [new] undertaking is also for that purpose. Moreover, for the sake of avoiding the suffix *kap*, in the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* refers to that *bahuvrīhi* prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*).

In the rule *anekamanyapadārthe* itself, the mention of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) continues to apply; therefore, [the designation of *sarvanāman*] does not occur here. Because of the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) in the rule *sarvanāmno vṛttimātre*, [the designation applies] even when the technical name *sarvanāman* is absent, as in the case of *vibhāṣā diksamāse*.
In that case, when the forms are identical, [the genitive suffix] is used in the sense of "this belongs to that. (Pāṇini 2.3.27)

Regarding the rule *tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*: the word *iti* and so forth [is used] for this purpose. That is to say, if there is a desire to express the worldly meaning (*laukika*) derived from that compound—meaning that the compound exists for this specific purpose and not for any other—the word *iti* is employed to indicate this. He asks, "What is thereby established? and replies, "The worldly meaning. He then asks, "What, moreover, is this worldly meaning? and replies with the words beginning *tataśca*. He explains this very point with the words beginning *yattatra*.

*Grahaṇa* (seizing) is that in which something is seized, such as hair and so forth; *praharaṇa* (striking) is that by which one strikes, such as a staff and so forth; *karmavyatīhāra* (mutual action) is mutual seizing and mutual striking. And this [compound] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), because it is included among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds in the list [of indeclinables]. Now, one might object: since the battle is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) here, the formation is already established by the previous rule [Pāṇini 2.4.14]; [we reply: no, because there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and because it would result in the application of the rule for single-remainder compounds (*ekaśeṣa*).

For instance: since the seizing (*grahaṇa*) and striking (*praharaṇa*) of hair (*keśa*) and so forth are intended to be expressed together (*sahavivakṣitatva*), and because they possess the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktitva*), the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would have applied, but it is set aside by this present rule. How so? When there is no intention to express a collective group (*samūha*), the technical name *bahuvrīhi* does not apply; furthermore, a collective group is not possible in the case of *ekaśeṣa*. Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of this [present rule], the *ekaśeṣa* will simply set aside the *bahuvrīhi* by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratva*)? No, it cannot be set aside; for *ekaśeṣa* is *antaraṅga* (internal), whereas *bahuvrīhi* is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends upon the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*).
"With that together" [is used] in the sense of equal conjunction. 2.2.28.

"With that" (*tena saha*) [is used] in the sense of "equal connection" (*tulyayoga*). Regarding "equal connection": equal connection means a common relation. In *saputra* ("with his son"), the substitution of *sa-* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya*. Now, one might object: "In this case, the father is the primary element and the meaning denoted by the other member of the compound. True; however, this rule is introduced so that [the suffix] may also occur when there is a difference of substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*), even in the sense of the first case (*prathamārthe*), and for the sake of preventing the suffix *ka*. And the absence of *ka* has already been explained in this context. In *daśabhiḥ putrair*, the meaning is "in such a manner" (*itthambhūta*). [The term] "generally" (*prāyika*) [is used].

Because of the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*): namely, that the author prescribes compounds even in the sense of "existing" (*vidyamāna*) in the rules "optionally when there is expectancy" (*vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe*), "even more than one [word] in the Veda when there is expectancy" (*chandasyanekamapi sākāṅkṣam*), "from *pūrva*, the suffix *ini*" (*pūrvādiniḥ*), "and also when preceded by another word" (*sapūrvācca*), "of the first case ending when preceded by another word" (*sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyāḥ*), and "optionally when preceded by another word" (*vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*). This indicates that an adjective is generally [applicable] to all [words].
A copulative compound (*dvandva*) occurs when there is a mutual connection of meaning between the members. (Pāṇini 2.2.29)

The term *dvandva* [is used] in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), and so forth. When word-meanings that are mutually independent are combined with respect to a single correlate, that is conjunction (*samuccaya*). For example: "Day after day leading away a cow, a horse, a man, and an animal, Yama is not satiated, like a drunkard with wine. The meaning is: just as a drunkard is not satiated by wine, so too Yama is not satiated while leading away cows and the other beings.

In this case, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of several items—such as a cow and so forth—in a single action of leading; and because [the meaning] is already understood, the word *ca* ("and") is not employed. In the same way, one should observe that there is a conjunction of two substances in "the king’s cow and horse"; a conjunction of two qualities in "red and white" (referring to a substance); and a conjunction of a quality and two substances in "the red cloth and the earring," and so forth. When, however, because of the predominance of one thing, the other is added in accordance with it, then it is "addition" (*anvācaya*), as in: "Go for alms and bring a cow."

For here, because [the two actions] are not seen [together], one who does not bring the cow still wanders for alms; whereas one who does not wander for alms does not bring the cow, and even while wandering, one does not bring the cow without having searched for it. However, mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) occurs when there is a connection with a single purpose among distinct parts that have attained the status of a collective through mutual dependence, as in: "This task is to be done by Devadatta and Yajñadatta."

Likewise, it occurs even when one [member] is absent; and because there is a manifestation of distinct constituent parts (*avayava-bheda*), the dual and plural numbers are employed. When such [parts] are connected in the form of a collection (*saṃhati*) through the concealment of their individuality, that is their "aggregate" (*samāhāra*), as in the case of *chatropānaham* ("umbrella and sandals"); however, the singular number is used because the collection is the primary focus. Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case," etc.: it might be argued that even in a conjunction (*samuccaya*) where the items are mutually independent, a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists by way of a single action, just as in the case of "curd and rice" (*dadhyodana*); but that is not tenable.

In the case of *dadhyodana* (curd-rice) and the like, there is a single action because of the unity of the act; however, here, due to the difference between the objects (*karman*), the action is divided. Thus, in the rule *samuccaye 'nyatarasyām*, examples such as *bhrāṣṭramaṭa maṭhamaṭa* will be cited based on this division of action resulting from the difference between the objects. But in the case of *anvācaya*, the particle *ca* denotes only the subordinate element and not the principal one; therefore, since there is no occurrence of multiple words in the sense of *ca* [as a single unified meaning], there is an absence of compound formation.

In this case, because there is a collection of multiple attributes in a single substratum—such as "he is both clever and lame"—the designation of *dvandva* would undesirably apply even to two words in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) due to the actual existence of their referents. Consequently, the rule "in a *dvandva*, the *ghi* [word] [stands first]" would become a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Furthermore, if it were treated as a *tatpuruṣa* by the rule beginning with "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇam*), then forms such as *khañjapaṭuḥ* would also be established. Because of the governing rule regarding a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*) and because it is specifically prescribed, there will be only the designation of a Tatpuruṣa compound; otherwise, even in cases such as "that which is blue and that which is a lotus" (*nīlaṃ ca tad utpalaṃ ca*), a Dvandva compound would result. Alternatively, the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, since it has already been employed in the definition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), [the Tatpuruṣa] will not apply here. However, in the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is indeed a Dvandva—as in "the clever and the lame have arrived" (*paṭukhañjāv āgatau*).

Regarding the example *plakṣanyagrodhau*: although the word *ca* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the *dvandva* compound prescribed for its meaning naturally possesses connection with gender and number. But how can there be a dual number here, given that even when the meanings are expressed according to the sequence of the words, there is a sequence of those meanings as well? Consequently, the word *plakṣa* has ceased [its function] along with its sense of "conjunction," and the word *nyagrodha* has appeared; since its referent is one, by virtue of that oneness, only the singular would be expected. And thus, it is said: *ādyantau ṭakitau*.

If it is argued that the application of the term "respectively" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) is based on accepting a sequential cognition, yet a dual number does not occur when two meanings are cognized sequentially—as in the sentence "the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*"—where the very fact that the meaning of the *plakṣa* is not yet cognized at the time the meaning of the *nyagrodha* is being cognized is the cause [of the absence of the dual]; then let it be that the *dvandva* compound occurs when there is a simultaneous expression of the referents (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacane dvandvaḥ*).

What is this "simultaneous expression of multiple substrates" (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacana*)? A substrate (*adhikaraṇa*) is the meaning of the constituent words (*vartipadārtha*). Simultaneous expression regarding the substrate is "simultaneous expression of multiple substrates," and in that case, a *dvandva* compound occurs. But by what means is there a simultaneous expression of two things? By each individual word. This is what is meant: if, for as many words as constitute a *dvandva*, there is a simultaneous denotation of their respective mutual meanings, then a *dvandva* occurs.

For here, the very impossibility of otherwise accounting for the dual and plural endings serves as the proof; this is also seen in the case of the analytical expression (*vigraha*). Indeed, even in the *vigraha*, simultaneous denotation is observed—as in "of the two Pramitras" or "of the two Varuṇas," and "even Heaven and Earth bow down before him. How much more so, then, in the case of a compound (*samāsa*), where distinct powers emerge for each member! But how can the word *plakṣa* denote the *nyagrodha*, or the latter the former? It is through association (*sāhacarya*).

Let whatever the cause be; even if it is observed in worldly usage that the word *plakṣa* alone does not denote a *nyagrodha*, nor does the word *nyagrodha* denote a *plakṣa*, there is no fault here because the members of a *dvandva* compound denote multiple objects while the individual words alone do not. Furthermore, the referents of words are restricted to specific domains, as for instance the word *bhrātṛ* (brother) functions to denote a sister only when used in the form of a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), and the word *putra* (son) [functions to denote a daughter] in the same way.
By this, the following objection is also refuted: "Since that meaning has already been expressed by one [member], the employment of another is not justified.

How is it that this capacity belongs only to the members of the *dvandva* compound through their mutual proximity—just as fluidity exists in ghee only when fire is present, and certainly not when the fire is absent? If, then, both *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* each have two meanings, would there not be a plural number due to the multiplicity [of referents]? No; there are not four meanings here. Rather, the second pair of meanings is precisely the same as those by which the first member has its two meanings.

It might be argued: "If these two are synonyms here, then just as there is a cognition when the dual number is applied—as in *plakṣanyagrodhau plakṣanyagrodhau*—so too would it occur in the case of *plakṣanyagrodhau*. This is not so, because of simultaneous production. Just as when two eyes are opened simultaneously, a single cognition is produced regarding two objects situated in front, so too should it be understood here.

But surely, when the word *plakṣa* is present, the word *nyagrodha* is not, and when the word *nyagrodha* is present, the word *plakṣa* is not; how, then, can there be simultaneous operation here? There is no fault, because their simultaneous operation occurs within memory. For words, as soon as they are heard, cause their respective meanings to be remembered. Subsequently, once expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency have been considered, the meanings residing in memory denote [the sentence meaning]. Since these meanings ascend simultaneously into that very memory, simultaneous operation is indeed possible.

Furthermore, since the recollection of those word-meanings occurs sequentially, the determination of their respective order and so forth is established precisely through that sequence, even when they are denoted simultaneously. Thus, it is settled that a *dvandva* compound occurs when there is a simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*adhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the forms *ekaviṃśati* and *dvāviṃśati*: if this were a *dvandva* compound (meaning "one and twenty"), then in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there would be the undesirable consequence of dual or plural endings; and in the sense of collective totality (*samāhāra*), there would be the consequence of the neuter gender according to the rule *sa napuṃsakam*. Therefore, is it not the case that the compound is formed as *ekaviṃśati*—meaning "twenty plus one"—following the pattern of compounds such as *śākapārthiva*? This cannot be so; for if it were, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) would not occur, because of the rule: "In a *dvandva* of royal titles used in the plural, [the accent is retained] when referring to the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis."

Therefore, this is indeed a *dvandva* compound; it is one of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*) and not of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), because the latter is not expressed [in this context]. As for its neuter gender, it does not follow from the rule "gender is not to be prescribed, since gender depends on worldly usage."
The subordinate member [of a compound] is placed first. 2.2.30.

"The subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first. [The commentary explains: "For there might be the form *ānayamo*. Although such an inverted usage is not seen in common worldly practice, it might be possible—like the case of a sentence—due to the transgression of another person; this is the meaning. Here, in the compound *rājāpuruṣaputraḥ* ("the king's man's son"), although both members are designated as the nominative in the rule for the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the designation of "subordinate member" applies only to that which is non-principal (*apradhāna*), because the term is based on its literal meaning (*anvarthatva*). Since in this instance the "man" (*puruṣa*) is the principal relative to the "king," the restriction regarding the prior placement [of the subordinate] applies.
In the case of *rājadanta* and similar compounds, the last member [is placed first]. 2.2.31.

"In the case of *rājadanta* and so forth, the latter [member] [is placed first]. [The commentary explains: "Not only [the former]," and so on. Regarding the reading *vihitapūrvanipātasya*, the meaning is "of that for which the prior placement has been prescribed. However, the reading *vihitasya* is more common; in that case, the word *apavādaḥ* (exception) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. The meaning is that this is an exception even to the prior placement of other [words], such as those ending in *ghī* (feminine suffixes), which is prescribed according to the grammatical rules (*yathālakṣaṇam*). [The example] *agrevaṇam*: here, the substitution of *ṇa* [for *na*] occurs by the rule *vanaṃ puragā-* and so forth.

In that case, would not that very prescription of *ṇatva* serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the posterior placement [of the word]? No; for that [prescription] is justified as an indicator of this much alone: that the restriction "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first" does not apply. Therefore, how could the posterior placement be established by a restrictive rule? Moreover, since even the absence of elision (*aluk*) occurs here by virtue of a specific technical designation (*nipātana*), the *ṇatva* will likewise not occur; thus, the mention of *agra-* there could have been omitted. [This refers to the rule] *pūrvakālasya*.

The phrase "pūrvakālaika" (the one denoting prior time and so on) means "of that which is a subordinate member," because it is indicated by its nominative case ending. In compounds such as *ulūkhalamusalau* (mortar and pestle), there arises the possibility of the prior placement [of one member] based sometimes on having fewer syllables, sometimes on ending in a long vowel (*ī*), and sometimes on beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in *a*; in some cases, there is no fixed rule. The reading *ddaṣadupalam* is a scribal error; since the posterior placement is already established by that [rule], the inclusion here could have been omitted.
In a copulative compound (dvandva), a *ghi*-stem [is placed first]. 2.2.32.

*Ghi* [ending words] come first in a *dvandva*. Since the rule "in a *dvandva*, there may be many" (*dvandve'nekam*) is indicated by the nominative case, it would follow that all members are *upasarjana*s (subordinate elements), resulting in uncertainty regarding their order. Therefore, this statement is made. Regarding the phrase "when several are applicable": when the word-referent (*padārtha*) is considered as a genus (*ākṛti*), the grammatical operation (*lakṣaṇa*) applies once to the collection as a whole, not by repeating it for each individual instance (*vyakti*). In that case, since the operation has already applied to the genus through the prior placement of one member alone, it does not apply again.

But surely, even in the view that the word denotes the form (*ākṛti*), just as it applies simultaneously to many individuals such as "Paṭugupta" and "Mṛdugupta," so too should it apply here? To this, the following is considered: the simultaneous relationship of limit and limited (*avadhyavadhimadbhāva*) is not possible for a single entity because of contradiction.

Nor can both [terms] be considered prior in relation to the end, because they are separated by one another. In this regard, when a *dvandva* compound is first formed between "sharp" (*paṭu*) and "soft" (*mṛdu*), and subsequently a *dvandva* is formed with the word "white" (*śukla*), then—because it has fewer syllables—it is placed first, resulting in *śuklamṛdupaṭavaḥ* or *śuklapaṭumṛdavaḥ*. As for *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ*: since the word *vispaṣṭa* is an adjective qualifying "sharpness" (*pāṭava*), which is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term "sharp," one analyzes it as *vispaṣṭaṃ paṭuḥ* (sharp in a clear manner) and forms the compound according to the rule *sup-supā*.
A word beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in a short *a* is [the first member of a bahuvrīhi compound]. (Pāṇini 2.2.33)

*Ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33). *Ajādī* is a separate word, or it is a descriptive compound (*viśe�ṣaṇasamāsa*). Examples include *aśvendrau* and *rathāḥ*. When the word *ratha* is placed last in the compound, one also obtains *rathāśvendrāḥ*. Regarding the rule "in a *dvandva*, that which ends in a *ghi* [vowel] comes first," and the rule "that which begins with a vowel other than *a* (*ajādī*) and ends in *a* (*adantam*) [comes first]," there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of "in a *dvandva*, that which is *ghi*" is, for example, *paṭuguptau*; the scope of "that which begins with a vowel other than *a* and ends in *a*" is, for example, *uṣṭrakharam*. In the case of *indrāgnī*, where both rules would apply, the latter—"that which begins with a vowel other than *a* and ends in *a*"—prevails by virtue of the conflict.
That which has fewer syllables [is placed first]. 2.2.34.

[The rule] *alpāctaram* [is stated]. Precisely because it is a *nipāta*, the suffix *tarap* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*), and there is an absence of *kutva*. However, if *tarap* were used in the sense of excellence (*prakarṣe*), then in cases such as *dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ*, where many items are present, this rule would not apply due to the absence of a dual-numbered subordinate term (*upapada*), resulting in a lack of restriction. It would instead apply only to pairs, such as *plakṣanyagrodhau*. As for *śaṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ*, the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur; for in that context, only those who subsist by the craft of musical instruments (*tūryaśilpopajīvinaḥ*) are intended.

When there is an intention to express specific individual substances (*niyatadravyavivakṣā*), since the genus (*jāti*) is absent, the rule "the genus [is used] for non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) does not apply either. Thus, in a *dvandva* compound of *śaṅkha*, *vīṇā*, and *dundubhi*, one may have *dundubhi-śaṅkha-vīṇāḥ*. Similarly, *mṛdaṅgaś ca śaṅkhapaṇavau ca* results in *mṛdaṅga-śaṅkha-paṇavāḥ*; and *dhanapatiś ca rāmakeśavau ca* results in *prāsādo dhanapati-rāma-keśavānām*, and so forth.

Likewise, when many—namely the *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, and *udgātṛ*—are combined simultaneously in a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *ānaṅ* occurs only for the third member immediately preceding [the final one], and not for the others; thus: *hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭṛ-udgātāraḥ*. When they are grouped in pairs within a *dvandva*, *ānaṅ* occurs for all three: *hotā-potā-neṣṭā-udgātāraḥ*. In this way, in other instances of forming *dvandva* compounds as well, the specific difference in form should be understood according to the particular sequence [of the members].

The rule *pūrvābhyām alpāctaram* ("of the two preceding [words], that which has fewer syllables comes first") is not stated in the *vṛtti*, because it is understood by following the previous rule. The scope of *dvandve ghi* ("in a dvandva compound, a word ending in a *ghi* vowel comes first") is, for example, *paṭuguptau*; the scope of *alpāctaram* is, for example, *plakṣanyagrodhau*. In the case of *vāgagnī*, where both rules would apply, the rule *alpāctaram* prevails. The scope of *ajādyadantam* ("a word beginning with a vowel other than *a* or ending in *a* comes first") is, for example, *uṣṭrakharam*; the scope of *alpāctaram* is the same. In the case of *vāgindrāv*, where both rules would apply, the rule *alpāctaram* prevails.

Regarding "of the seasons and the constellations": the sequence of the seasons is determined by their manifestation, and that of the constellations is determined by their rising. Regarding "mother and father": the *Smṛti* states, "The teacher is the best among gurus; some say the mother," and also, "The mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of venerability."

Regarding "śraddhā-medhe": since wisdom (*medhā*) that performs purposeful action exists only when faith (*śraddhā*) is present, faith is more highly esteemed. Regarding "dīkṣā-tapasī": since austerity (*tapas*) is for the sake of initiation (*dīkṣā*), initiation is more highly esteemed. Even though *tapas* has fewer syllables than *dīkṣā*, by virtue of this very rule of precedence (*vipratiṣedha*), it is established that initiation is indeed more highly esteemed.

Regarding the phrase "of homogeneous letters" (*samānākṣarāṇām*), [the author] says "it does not exist. By this, the intention is that the mention of "letters" (*varṇa*) was not made in the rule *ṛtunakṣatrāṇām* alone. Indeed, the sequential order of letters based on their origin is heard in scripture: "He created the Brāhmaṇa from his mouth, the Rājanya from his arms, the Vaiśya from his thighs, and the Śūdra from his feet. Regarding the phrase "of the smaller number," they say it applies both to a *dvandva* compound and to what is not a *dvandva*. In the reading *alpīyasaḥ*, the meaning is "of that which expresses a smaller number. As for "ninety and one hundred," this is a *dvandva*; however, the expression *dvyekayoḥ* is a Vedic (Pāṇinian) usage.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the case ending of] the seventh case is specifically [retained]. (Pāṇini 2.2.35)

"In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the word ending in] the seventh case [is compounded] with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). For example, in *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one whose throat is black"): when it is already known that something exists in the throat, and the word "black" is employed as a qualifier, then the mention of the seventh case serves a purpose; otherwise, however, it is established by its very nature as a qualifier. Regarding "in the sense of deliberation" (*sampradhāraṇāyām*): deliberation is the determination that "let this be," or "this alone [must be]. Regarding "because of being subsequent" (*paratvāt*): the meaning is "due to the conflict-resolution rule (*vipratiṣedha*) favoring the subsequent [term]. And for this very reason, it was not stated as "*saṃkhyāsarvanāmnoḥ*" (of numerals and pronouns). As for "from *gaḍu* etc.": the words beginning with *gaḍu* are to be understood from actual usage.
The completion [of the action]. 2.2.36.

The conclusion: [the word] *avamuktopānatkaḥ* [is formed] because it belongs to the class beginning with *uraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.151), hence the suffix *kap*. Now, as for the phrase "but indeed," etc.: just as in the case of *citraguḥ*, when a quality-word and a substance-word come together, the quality-word functions as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); likewise, even in the case of an action-word and a substance-word, the action itself functions as the qualifier. Therefore, the sense is that [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 2.1.57]. [The phrase] "because it is dependent on the speaker's intention" means that when, after it has been determined that "something has been done by him," the word *kaṭaḥ* is employed, then the mat (*kaṭa*) is considered to be the qualifier.

Or rather, the analysis (vigraha) should be understood as "it was made by means of a mat on a mat. The point is that in such an analysis, there is no possibility at all of suspecting that *kṛta* functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). However, in some places the word *vā* ("or") is not read; in those cases, since [the analysis] is based on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), one should explain it by showing that very intention.

"Regarding the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ paravacanam* (the word following [terms denoting] genus, time, pleasure, etc., is placed last): this is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). By stating *jātikālasukhādibhyo 'nācchādanāt*, he indicates that the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) follows words such as those denoting genus. For example, *śārṅgajagdhī*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom a horn (*śārṅga*) has been eaten (*jagdha*). The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rules *ktādalpākhyāyām* and *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā*. On this point, they say: the term *niṣṭhā* refers to that past passive participle which is prescribed [by the rule *niṣṭhā* P. 3.2.102].
Consequently, in cases such as *susthitam* and *cāruhasitam*, the participle ending in *kta*—which is used in the sense of an abstract action in the neuter (*napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*)—is placed last."
Or [the rule applies] in the case of compounds such as *āhitāgni* and others. 2.2.37.
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the word] *kaḍaśa* [is placed first]. (Pāṇini 2.2.38)
Regarding the rule "kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye," he says "kaḍārādayaḥ" (beginning with *kaḍāra*), because the use of the plural number indicates that the sense of "and others" (*ādi*) is understood.
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
In the Kāśikāvṛtti, now the third quarter of the second chapter:
"When not already expressed" (anabhihite) [2.3.1].

Regarding the term *anabhihite*: this word *anabhihita* has multiple meanings. To explain, this form can belong to both the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *abhi* and the root *hi*; furthermore, the root *dhā* preceded by *abhi* is seen in the sense of "binding"—as in *aśvābhidhānīm ādatte* ("he takes up the horse's halter"); in the sense of "uttering"—as in *abhihitaḥ ślokaḥ* ("the verse has been uttered"); and in the sense of "communicating"—as in *abhihito 'rthaḥ* ("the meaning has been communicated").

The root *hi* also functions in the senses of "going" and "increasing"; however, since the four meanings such as "binding" and so forth are impossible for the [kārakas] like "object" (*karman*) which will be mentioned here, the word *abhihita* is stated in the sense of "expounded. Thus he says: "in what is not abhihita," meaning "not specified" or "not expressed. Here, the root *vac* signifies "expounding."

Regarding the principle that "there is no application [of a case-ending] when the meaning has already been expressed" (*uktārthānām aprayogaḥ*): if it were stated merely in general terms as "when [the meaning] is expressed" (*abhihite*), one might think that in the sentence *kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam udāraṃ darśanīyam*, since the second case ending produced after the word *kaṭa*—which expresses the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—would express the objecthood (*karmatva*) residing in the mat (*kaṭa*) in its entirety, the second case would not occur after *bhīṣma* and the other adjectives. Anticipating this, he asks: "By what is it not expressed? The other, knowing his intention, replies: "By verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)."

When many [factors] are applicable, the exclusion of some while establishing the connection of the operation with others is *parisaṃkhyāna* (exclusive specification). In all counter-examples, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur—as in "He makes a mat beautiful" (*kaṭaṃ karoti bhīṣmam*), and so forth. Regarding this, one of dull intellect might think that just as the suffix *-kta* arising from the root *kṛ* ("to make") denotes the entire object (*karman*) without partiality—such that "the mat is made beautiful, noble, and handsome"—so too should the second case ending denote the whole. For such a person, this enumeration is intended; however, it need not be stated at all for those who possess subtle vision.

For instance, when the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) arises from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it expresses the state of being an object (*karmabhāva*) precisely for that entity as qualified by the form denoted by the nominal stem. Since the word *kaṭha* denotes an entity qualified by the universal (*jāti*) of "Kaṭha-ness" and not by forms such as "Bhīṣma" and so forth, the use of words like *bhīṣma* is employed to convey those specific forms; likewise, the accusative will occur to express the status of being an object for that entity as qualified by its particular form.

The *kta* suffix, however, does not denote the status of being an object (*karman*) for the meaning of the verbal root itself; rather, it is logical that it denotes that which stands in the relation of an object with respect to the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, it expresses all objects without exception.

But surely, since case-roles such as the object (*karman*) and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, it would be redundant to state that they are expressed by *tiṅ*-suffixes and the like, because [the rule] "when [a meaning] is already expressed" (*abhihite*) applies elsewhere as well. Even in cases where the governing heading "when not expressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is not applied, a grammatical operation is not prescribed when the meaning is conveyed by another word. For example: in the case of *bahupaṭuḥ* ("very clever"), because the sense of "incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*) is already expressed by the prefix *bahu*, the suffixes *-kalpa*, *-deśya*, and so on do not occur, even though their application is otherwise possible; likewise, in *dvidaśāḥ* ("twenty"), because the sense of the suffix *su-* (indicating a collection) is already expressed by the compound (*samāsa*).

It is well known that when [a meaning] is expressed by a compound (*dvandva*)—because the sense is conveyed by both members—the word is not employed; likewise, here too, because the case-role is already denoted by the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and so forth, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others will not occur.

But surely, the use of even an expressed meaning is observed—as in "two cakes. True; however, this is the logical principle: that which is prescribed for what has already been expressed would not apply. For a word is not employed out of mere habit, but rather for the purpose of expressing a meaning. If that meaning has already been expressed by another word, why employ yet another word? When a meaning is understood even through a wink of the eye or other such gestures, a word is not used at all; how much less so when it has been expressed by a word itself?

In cases such as "two cakes" (*apūpau dvau*), however, one must somehow justify it by understanding the sentence as beginning with a general reference, such as "bring the two" (*dvāv ānaya*) or "which two are those two? (*kau tau*). Therefore, anticipating the objection that this [discussion] is unnecessary, he says—"by [the rule] 'the plural is used for many' (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and so forth"—demonstrating that number (*saṃkhyā*) is also the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

The meaning is as follows: according to the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consists of the triplet [of number, gender, and case]," numbers such as singularity are the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), just like the object (*karman*) and so forth. In this regard, the Prābhākaras maintain that when the object and other factors are denoted simultaneously by the case-endings, they do not yet stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified; rather, they are denoted as residing solely within the meaning of the nominal stem, such as "tree—one" or "tree—the object," or "cow—one" or "cow—the instrument. Subsequently, however, a mutual connection arises through the force of their co-occurrence in a single action.

The Bhāṭṭas, however, maintain that there is denotation of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhidhāna*), because even though we observe the expression of multiple independent meanings related in a series—such as in "akṣāḥ," "pādāḥ," and "māṣāḥ"—we do not observe such usage without *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one). Furthermore, just as the Prābhākaras accept that in cases like "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists between the effort (*kṛti*) and the action (*kārya*) even though both are simultaneously denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), they consider the denotation of the qualified entity to be exactly like that.

This very position is ours as well. In that regard, action (*karman*) and so forth are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), while oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth are the qualified (*viśeṣya*); thus, when there is oneness in the object, the singular accusative case-ending applies. Or else, it is the reverse: when there is an object qualified by oneness and so forth, the accusative case-ending applies there.

In this regard, although under the view that the object (*karman*) and so forth are primary, there would be no such contingency because the objects—which are the primary factors—are already expressed by the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like; nevertheless, under the view that number is primary, even when the objects and so forth are expressed, the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and others would indeed still occur in order to express the primary factor, which is number. Under the Prābhākara view, however, even though the aspect of the object and so forth is expressed, the second case endings and others would occur in order to express the aspect of number, which remains unexpressed. Thus: "in the case of bases where the object has not been expressed."

The meaning is: "in those [words] which have as their basis (āśraya) the object (*karman*) and so forth that are not already expressed. By this, it is shown that the use of the locative case in the rule *karmaṇi* and so on indicates that singularity (*ekatva*) and the rest are the substrata (*ādhāra*), and not the things to be expressed (*abhidheya*). Thus, "anabhihite" means...

If this were an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), then there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of case-endings even when one of two actions has its *kāraka* expressed by another [word]. For instance, in the expression *prāsāda āste* ("he sits on the palace"), the single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) called "palace" belongs to both the action of sitting (*sadikriyā*) and the action of being (*āsikriyā*). Since that [substratum] is already expressed by the suffix *-ghañ* in the word *prāsāda*—derived from the root *sad-* with the sense "that in which they sit" (*prasīdanty asmin prāsādaḥ*)—if it were said that [the case-ending] does not occur when [the *kāraka*] is already expressed, the seventh case (*saptamī*) would not arise.

In the case of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), however, the locative case is established based on that which is not expressed by the suffix *-āsi*. Now, one might object: "Since the substance called 'palace' (*prāsāda*) is a *kāraka* (participant in action) and is thus already expressed [by the word], there can be no 'otherness' [of the action]? This is not a fault; for the *kāraka* is the capacity (*śakti*). Thus, even though the capacity for the action of sitting (*āsana*) is not expressed when the capacity for the action of being (*sadikriyā*) is expressed, the capacity for the action of sitting remains unexpressed.

[Objection: "In that case, even in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), let there be no case-ending (*vibhakti*) for that power which has been expressed; however, it will exist for that [power] which has not been expressed? [Reply: It is said: In the rule *anabhihite karmaṇi*, the mention of the substratum (*ādhāra*) refers to singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. Furthermore, number (*saṃkhyā*) is a property of the substance (*dravya*). Therefore, by the words *anabhihite karmaṇi* and so on, it is the substance itself that is expressed by way of its power (*śakti*). That is to say: "The case-endings apply to the singularity and so forth of that substance which serves as the substratum for the unexpressed power of objecthood (*karma-śakti*) and the like."

And thus, if it were a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), then because the substance would be expressed by way of its expressed power (*abhihita-śakti*), there would be a negation [of that very substance]; but in the case of *paryudāsa* (relative negation/exclusion), there is a positive injunction by way of an unexpressed power (*anabhihita-śakti*), so the difference in result is indeed clear. How then is it in cases where no difference in power exists, such as "he sits on a seat" (*āsane āste*) or "he lies on a bed" (*śayane śete*)? Even here, by the words "seat," "bed," and so forth, the mere object suitable for the action of sitting or lying down is expressed with its power not yet manifested; therefore, a case-ending will occur to indicate the manifestation of that power.

If, then, this [negation] is conceived as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), then in the case of the expression "having cooked, the rice is eaten" (*pakvā bhujyate odanaḥ*), since the rice is already denoted by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*, one might argue that the accusative case would apply because the rice is not denoted by the *ktvā* suffix—given that the *ktvā* suffix occurs in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). However, if it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), the negation is established by relying on the fact that the rice is denoted by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*. To this, it is replied:

In this case, there is no simultaneous verbal connection (*śābda anvaya*) of the rice with both [the verbs *pacati* and *bhuṅkte*]; rather, it is connected only with *bhuji*, while its connection with *paci* arises from proximity (*sannidhāna*). However, when considering the operation of the word alone, it would not be known whether "having cooked bricks, the rice is eaten," or "only the rice [is eaten]. Therefore, with respect to the operation of the word, since it is indeed expressed (*abhidhāna*), the accusative case will not occur. The rule concerning what is "not already expressed" (*anabhihitavacana*) is redundant, because there is no occasion for the prescription of the nominative case.

The formulation of the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.1] is intended so that the accusative and other case-endings do not occur in instances such as *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is made"). If these [case-endings] were to occur here as well, then where would the nominative case find its scope? [Objection: But surely, because it is without scope (*anavakāśatva*), the nominative occurs only in cases like *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* and not in cases like *kaṭaṃ karoti*; how then can this restriction be maintained? [Reply: It is said: although in *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* and similar examples the status of the mat (*kaṭa*) as the object (*karman*) is understood in proximity to the word *kṛta*, nevertheless, because it constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), it remains non-distinct [from the subject].

The nominative case will occur when the meaning is that of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*). However, in the case of "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), since the object-possessing entity is denoted by the word *kaṭa* itself, the nominative will not occur because the meaning of the nominal stem is not distinct [from the action]. But surely, the nominative has its scope in non-agentive cases, as in "the tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*)? Even here, since the sense of "it exists" is understood, there is the contingency of the instrumental case due to its being the agent (*kartṛ*).

For where no other verb is heard, the verb "is" (asti) is understood there because of its inherent internal connection; for it is only once existence has been established that a connection with other qualifiers can occur.

Furthermore, one might argue that there is indeed scope for [the application of] non-verbs (akāraka) where the intention lies in the exclusion of other qualifiers, rather than in the connection with an action—as in "The lotus is blue, not red," or "This man belongs to the king, not to Devadatta. For in these cases, there is no cognition that "the blue lotus exists" or "there is a man belonging to the king"; therefore, there would be scope for non-verbs. Even so, the nominative case (prathamā) will still apply due to the rule of mutual exclusion (vipratiṣedha). The scope for the accusative and other cases is where there is a distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha)—as in "He makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*).

The scope for the first case (nominative) when there is no grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is, for example, "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*). In the case of "the mat is made" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*), where both [the nominative and the genitive] would apply, the nominative alone will occur because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. [Objection: But surely, even overriding that [nominative], the genitive should occur because it is subsequent; [for] the genitive characterized as "residual" (*śeṣa*) applies to the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) since the rule for the nominative is prescribed [only] when there is no such "remainder. [Response: It will not occur, because there is no "remainder" [in this instance].

In that case, when the word *kṛt* is employed—as in "the mat is to be made" (*kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ*)—the sixth case ending would apply by the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows," thereby subverting the first case ending. To prevent this, the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not [already] expressed") must be applied. Thus, it is established that under the view that number is the meaning of the case ending, the rule must be formulated in this manner.
The second case-affix is used in the sense of the object of an action. 2.3.2.
"The second case [is used] for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*). The phrase "words such as the second case" means that this is a convention established within one's own school (*svanikāya*).

Regarding the rule "of *ubha* and *sarvatas*" (*ubhasarvatasoḥ*), the meaning is: in the usage of the words *ubhaya* and *sarva* when they end in the suffix *tasil*. The word *ubha* is cited as a partial representation of the word *ubhaya*; this is because there is no form of *ubha* ending in *tasil*, since *ubha* is restricted to the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. The mention of *dhik* is a citation without a case-ending. Regarding the phrase "in those ending in *ām* and *ṅit*," the meaning is: in those ending in a *kṛt* suffix or in reduplicated forms. Examples are *ubhayataḥ* and *sarvataḥ*; here, *tasil* is added to the ablative case. *Dhik* has the sense of censure. *Uparyupari* [is an example of repetition].

The doubling [of the word] occurs according to the rule *uparyadhyadhasassāmīpye* ("above, below, and beneath, when expressing proximity"). Since it was stated that this applies "even elsewhere than those," he enumerates those other instances, beginning with *abhitaḥ*. *Abhito grāmam* means "on both sides of the village. *Paritaḥ* means "on all sides. The suffix *tasil* is applied here by the rule *paryabhibhyāṃ ca*. There is also a particle *abhitaḥ* which functions as a synonym for a case ending (*vibhaktipratirūpaka-nipāta*), and that too is included. The words *samayā* and *nikaṣā* are understood here as expressing proximity.

The word *hā* expresses functions such as sorrow, as in "hā kanye" (O girl! and so forth; because it possesses the nature of a case-inflection (*kāraka-vibhakti*), the vocative case ending occurs due to its being *antaraṅga* (more internal). Regarding the statement "it does not occur to one who is hungry" (*bubhukṣitaṃ na pratibhāti*), *prati* here is an *upasarga* because it qualifies the action, and is not classified as a *karmapravacanīya*.
And [the rule] *tṛtīyā ca hośchandasī* (Pāṇini 2.3.3) applies.

"And the third [case-ending] occurs in the Veda, as in *yavāgvāgnihotram*. But where does the word *agnihotra* occur? It occurs in reference to the oblation (*havis*); for we see it used in such passages as "he should place the *agnihotra* on the fire," "the *agnihotra* makes a crackling sound," and "they say that if the *agnihotra* which has been placed on the fire should become impure," and so forth. The root *hu* (to sacrifice) also denotes the act of pouring. Thus, within a single application, there is the third case from the word *yavāgū* and the second case from the word *agnihotra*; the meaning is that one pours the oblation called *yavāgū* into the fire with reference to the deity.

This construction can be explained; how so? The word *agnihotra* occurs in the sense of "flame"—as in "the *agnihotra* is blazing. The root *hu* (to sacrifice) also signifies "pleasing. Thus, when the word *yavāgū* (gruel) takes the instrumental case, the meaning is "one pleases the *agnihotra* with gruel"; but when it takes the accusative case, the meaning is "one casts the substance called gruel, the *agnihotra* oblation, into the fire."

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, say: "The word *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)," and this is seen [in scripture]: "This sacrifice is fivefold: the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," and so forth; and they also say: "Of this very *agnihotra*, there are seven hundred [verses]," and "This *agnihotra* which is offered on the following day is indeed ageless and immortal. Since the instrumental case would be expected because of its being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), the statement of the accusative case is for the sake of an alternative view. And this does not conform to the Sūtra, for the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is indeed the governing rule.
The locative case ending is used after words joined with *antarā* and *antareṇa*. (Pāṇini 2.3.4)

[The rule applies] when joined with *antarā* and *antareṇa*. Regarding the phrase "the words *antarā* and *antareṇa*," etc.: [An objection is raised: "But this is like a boat tied to another boat, which does not serve as a protection for either; for both [words] deviate from being technical particles (*nipāta*). [The author replies: True; however, through association (*sāhacarya*), a commonality (*sājātya*) is indicated. When there is a state of both similar and dissimilar [entities], the cognition of the similar arises. For example, when "Guru and Bhārgava" are mentioned, the understanding is of two planets alone, and not of the teacher [Vasiṣṭha] and Paraśurāma.

Alternatively, because of its association with *antarā* ending in the third case, the word *antareṇa*—even when not ending in the third case—is also understood here, and it is indeed a particle (*nipāta*). Likewise, because of its association with *antareṇa* ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the word *antarā*—even when ending in *ṭāp*—is also understood here, and it too is indeed a particle. "This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth case" means that in the absence of this rule, the sixth case would apply due to the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). But since this rule exists, the sixth case does not apply because [the words] are already accounted for by this specific relation; thus, it is an exception. "The middle is that which is to be placed within."

The meaning is that it is dependent upon that which is to be placed [within it]. That is to say, it functions in the sense of the word "madhya" when ending in the locative case. For example: "The water-pot is between you and me. The meaning is: "The water-pot is in the middle of you and me."

In this case, just as there is a connection between the two pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, which serve as the limits (*avadhi*), with the neutral [person] that depends upon those limits, so too, because the locus (*ādhāra*) is dependent upon the thing located (*ādheya*), there would arise the contingency of a second case ending even from the word *kamaṇḍalu* (the water-pot), due to its connection with the thing located. This is not a fault; for in the word *kamaṇḍaluḥ*, since the verbal roots *tiṣṭhati* or *asti* are supplied, the water-pot is the agent (*kartṛ*), and since that agent is expressed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*), only the nominative case will apply, as it is a case ending belonging to a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

We shall establish this point under the rule "sahayukte 'pradhāne" (Pāṇini 2.3.19). Because of the inclusion of the two particles [antarā and antareṇa], [the rule] does not apply here; what is the use of knowing their distinction! This term [antarā] expresses a specific relation—as in "he dwells in the city of Antarā," where [Antarā] is the rampart of Srughna; here, Srughna is not connected with the meaning of the word antarā, but rather with the rampart.
[The second case ending is used] after words denoting time or distance when there is continuous connection [with an action]. (Pāṇini 2.3.5)

Regarding the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5): "He studied for a month" (*māsam adhīta*). Now, one might ask: is not the accusative case here already established simply by virtue of [the month] being an object (*karman*)? How so? Because of the rule: "Time, state, and the distance to be traversed are designated as objects (*karman*) when [the verb] is otherwise intransitive. It must indeed be accepted that they receive the designation of object—so that forms such as *āsate māsaḥ*, *āsitavyaḥ*, and *āsitaḥ* may occur with the suffixes *la*, the gerundives (*kṛtya*), the past passive participle (*kta*), and the suffixes having the sense of *khal*, respectively. True; however, this must also necessarily be stated: so that the accusative may occur in connection with time and distance even when there is absolute contact (*atyantasaṃyoga*) with a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*).

In that context, although there is absolute connection with the action (*atyantasaṃyoga*), the accusative case is applied by this very rule [Pāṇini 2.3.5] because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. As for "māsasya," the genitive case is applied by the rule "When used with words having the sense of *kṛtvas*, the time is the locus" (Pāṇini 2.3.64).
The third case ending is used in the sense of completion. 2.3.6.

"In the case of completion (*apavarga*), the third [case-ending is used]. "Completion" means the conclusion of an action when the attainment of the result has occurred; the point is that the word *apavarga* is well-known in common usage in this very sense. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the agent's withdrawal": the meaning is that the agent desists due to incapacity or other such reasons. In that case, the action is interrupted midway, which constitutes the cessation of activity (*pravṛttyapāya*), but it is not yet "completed" (*apavṛkta*).
The seventh and fifth case endings are used when [an action] occurs between two factors of action (kāraka).

"The seventh and fifth case endings [are used] when there is an interval between two *kārakas*. Regarding "when there is an interval between two *kārakas*": since an interval depends on two limits (*avadhi*), the compound is formed with a word ending in the dual number; furthermore, this qualifies time and distance. Thus he says: "time and distance which lie between two *kārakas*. As in examples such as "having eaten today... and so forth. Now, one might object: "In this case, Devadatta is the single agent (*kartṛ*); how then can there be time between two *kārakas*? To this he replies: "between two agents (*kartṛ*) and objects (*karman*)."

This would indeed be so if the substance (*dravya*) were the *kāraka*; however, it is the capacity (*śakti*) that is the *kāraka*, and that is what differs here—one is the means for eating today, while the other is the means for eating after two days; thus, the meaning is that "time" lies between these two. Regarding "of the agent and the object": the man who shoots arrows is the agent (*kartṛ*); the object (*karman*) is the target, which is the place of shooting or the place of piercing. Regarding "of the object and the point of departure (*apādāna*)": the object is the same as before by implication; the bow is the point of departure (*apādāna*), from which the arrows go forth.

Regarding the phrase "or [the word] *karman* and *adhikaraṇa*": here, *karman* refers to that very thing which is designated as the *adhikaraṇa*, namely the location (*pradeśa*). In this context, there are two [categories], time (*kāla*) and distance (*adhvan*), and there are also two [case endings], the seventh (*saptamī*) and the fifth (*pañcamī*). Consequently, a correspondence according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would apply—namely, the seventh case after time and the fifth case after distance. Therefore, he says: "correspondence according to numerical order," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because it is not marked with a circumflex accent" (*asvaritatvāt*): it has been explained in that very place that the rule of correspondence according to numerical order applies only when indicated by the mark of a circumflex accent (*svarita*).
The second case ending is used when [a word] is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. (Pāṇini 2.3.8)
The locative case is used for that which is superior to something else, and for that which possesses lordship over something. (Pāṇini 2.3.9)

The locative case is used for that which is "more than" (adhika) and for that which expresses "lordship" (īśvara). Because of the rule stating "that which is more than this" and "this is more than that," both the seventh (locative) and fifth (ablative) cases occur in alternation when joined with the word *adhika*. For example, in the phrase *upakhāryo droṇaḥ* ("A *droṇa* measure is more than a *khāryā*"), the term *upa* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *upo'dhike ca*. Regarding the rule "and that which expresses lordship," and so forth: [the locative is used].

Two things are expressed by this [word *īśvarasya*]: it occurs with both [nouns], and even there, in turn. First, it occurs with both; how so? That by which a lord (*īśvara*) is spoken of is "lordly speech" (*aiśvaravacana*), or else the word *īśvara* has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning: "lordliness" (*īśvaratva*). The meaning is that the genitive case (*saptamī*) occurs after that master whose lordliness is being expressed. Alternatively, by the word "whose" (*yasya*), one's own property (*sva*) is indicated; the meaning is that the genitive occurs after that property of which the lord is being spoken of.

Or it occurs by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*); for in the remaining domains, since the case endings of *karmapravacanīya*s are introduced, the relationship—though residing in two [terms]—is expressed by a single case ending that has arisen from one [of them]. For example: *adhi brahmadatte*. In the alternative where there is compounding according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*, it becomes *brahmadattādhīnāḥ* when functioning as the meaning of the case ending. When functioning as the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*), it is *adhibrahmadattam*.

This application [of the rule] can be stated as follows: the Pañcālas reside in their own lord (svāmin), and Brahmadatta resides in his own substratum (ādhāra). In that case, wherever there is a locus (adhikaraṇa), the locative case will apply. By doing so, the designation *karmapravacanīya* for the word *adhi*—as in the rule *adhir īśvare*—need not be prescribed; for *adhi*, when referring to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), is never connected with an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, it is also not appropriate to argue that [the rule] is intended to set aside its status as a preposition (*upasarga*) or a verb of motion (*gati*).
The fifth case ending is used after the prepositions apa, āṅ, and pari.
And because [the word *prati*] is used in the senses of "substitute" (*pratinidhi*) and "exchange" (*pratidāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.11)

And [the ablative case is used] in the sense of "substitute" (pratinidhi) and "exchange" (pratidāna), because of the very rule beginning with "yasmāt. By this [rule], the fifth case ending is employed. A "substitute" (pratinidhi) is that which is similar to the primary (mukhya). The primary is something established in a particular function; and that which, in its absence, is substituted for it in that same function is its substitute.
