[The word *pratinidhi* is derived as follows: the suffix *ki* is applied after the root *ghu* when preceded by the prefix *pra*, in the sense of the object (*karman*). Similarly, *pratidāna* is also formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object. [The commentary continues with the word] "of what has been given" (*dattasya*).

Now, in this case, the ablative (*pañcamī*) would apply by this very rule, as in the example "from which" (*yasmāt*). If that is so, then the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies when there is an object (*karman*). But surely what was given is not being returned; what then is it? It is another substance. True; however, because the value is equal, there is the cognition that "that very same thing has been returned. *Pratiniryātanam* means returning or giving back; here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, in the phrase "from which [there is] a substitute" (*yasmāt pratinidhiḥ*), the ablative applies just as in the rule itself. The same applies to the expression "from where" (*yataśca*). Examples: *ūrjunataḥ*, *pratīti*.

The suffix *tasi* is applied after a word in the ablative case when it denotes a counterpart (*pratiyoga*). The meaning is that Abhimanyu was like Arjuna, who is well-known for his prowess in battle and other such qualities. Regarding the example "māṣān" and so forth: the *māṣas* (beans) are the counter-gift (*pratidāna*) for those sesame seeds that were previously received. Regarding the phrase "due to the connection with what is connected":

a substitute (*pratinidhi*) exists in relation to a primary object (*mukhya*), and a counter-gift (*pratidāna*) likewise relates to what was previously given. Therefore, the meaning is that when a karmapravacanīya is connected with both a substitute and a counter-gift, it is indirectly connected with those two—the primary object and the previously given thing—by way of them.
In the case of a verb meaning "to go," the second and fourth cases are used for the object when there is physical movement, provided it is not a path. (Pāṇini 2.3.12)

Regarding the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyācaturthyau ceṣṭāyāmanadhvani*: "of actions involving movement" is the actual explanation; however, in the sūtra itself, it says *ceṣṭāyām* (in the locative case). "Of actions consisting of physical motion"—this is the sense, for the word *ceṣṭā* is well-known specifically in the sense of physical motion (*parispandana*). When there is a suspicion that the term refers to its own form (*svarūpa*) because of the statement *svaṃ rūpam*, he says: "the mention of the object (*artha*) is intended, not the form. This is because of the use of the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśāt*). For when the locative case is used, the construction is *anadhvani karmaṇi* ("when the object is not a path").

The meaning of "not [denoting] a path" (*nādhvanaḥ*) is that the word *prakṛti* itself is the object (*karman*), not the word *adhvan*. Therefore, the fourth case (*caturthī*) does not occur after words synonymous with *adhvan*. However, the second case (*dvitīyā*) does occur by the rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*). "Occupied" (*āsthitaḥ*) means "attained," which signifies being presided over by a traveler. Regarding the phrase "but where": the meaning is that when one intends to traverse the very path itself by means of a wrong path (*utpatha*), then the fourth case indeed occurs. Why does it not occur here: "he leads the goat to the village" (*ajāṃ nayati grāmam*)? Because it does not have the sense of motion (*agatyarthatvāt*). For although motion is understood here, it is not the primary meaning of the root *nī*; rather, its meaning is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*).

In that case, does the rule for the fourth case (dative) not apply when one says "he goes to a woman" (*striyaṃ gacchati*)? This is established, however, because of the statement regarding that which has not yet been reached: it should be stated that the fourth case occurs in respect to an object (*karman*) which, though not yet reached, is intended to be reached by the act of going. Since a woman is already reached [as a destination], there is no occurrence of the fourth case. Furthermore, this is not an exception to the rule for the path (*adhvan*). For the path is indeed reached; however, it was stated previously that when the path, being unreached, is intended to be reached, then the fourth case must necessarily occur.

It is not the case that [the dative] alone is used. Because of the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), it connects with the word "optionally" (*vikalpet*). The sense is that when the dative is optionally applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), the accusative will occur by the rule "the accusative is used for the object thus connected. As in *grāmāya gantā* ("one who goes to the village"): first, the accusative supersedes the genitive in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix; and since the dative, which is of equal status to that [accusative], is established by the *dvandva* compound, the dative also occurs in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix—this is the intended meaning.

This application [of the rule] can be explained; how so? Since it is attained through seeing, desiring, and resolving, even the action (*kriyā*) is an artificial object (*karma*). In that context, when the distinction between the nature of going and the natures of seeing and so forth is intended to be expressed, then the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used because the village, which is the goal of the going—characterized by actions such as seeing—is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

However, when non-difference (*abheda*) is intended to be expressed, since there is an absence of "going" as an object, the village itself becomes the object; thus, the use of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is established. This is the position of the Bhāṣyakāra, who holds that this [sūtra] serves no purpose. In that case, when a *kṛt* suffix is employed, only the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs.
[The rule for] the fourth case is: "The fourth case is used for the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.13).

The fourth case [the dative] is used in the sense of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*). Regarding the term *tādarthya*: by the word *tat* (that), the effect is indicated; "this is for that" (*tasmai idam tadartham*)—by this compound, the cause is denoted as having a specific effect as its purpose. *Tādarthya* is the state of being for that purpose; thus, by means of the suffix *ṣyañ*, the relationship between effect and cause is expressed, because of the rule stating that in compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the relationship is denoted by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

In that case, although the relationship resides in both [relata], the fourth case ending occurs from the qualifier alone—just as with the sixth case—as in "wood for the sacrificial post" (*yūpāya dāru*). The third case used for the cause (*hetu*) also does not occur from the qualified [object]. This is because the relation between cause and effect is already conveyed by the fourth case itself, and the third case for the cause occurs only in the domain of the sixth case. Here, however, since there is no deviation from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), only the first case occurs.

If, then, an addition is made [to the rule] for the sake of that purpose (*tādarthya*), there is no need for the dative case in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); for even when a cow is given to a teacher, it is for the sake of the teacher. Nevertheless, the mention of *saṃpradāna* must necessarily be made for the sake of rules such as "the one being pleased in the case of verbs meaning 'to please'" (*rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase *valṛpi saṃpadyamānaḥ*: here, "becoming" (*saṃpatti*) is understood as origination in the form of the manifestation of what was previously non-existent; in that case, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used for the modification (*vikāra*) from which the form arises. For example: *mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel serves for urine"). When there is an intention to express the distinction between the material cause and the modification, the fourth case is used. However, some say that when there is no intention to express such a distinction, the nominative alone occurs, as in *mūtraṃ saṃpadyate yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel becomes urine"). Others, however, maintain that the fourth case is used precisely when there is no intention to express a distinction.

However, when the status of the *apādāna* (ablative) is intended according to the rule "the source of the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*), some say that the fourth case (*caturthī*) does not occur after the word for the modification (*vikāra*), as in: *mūtraṃ saṃpadyate yavāgvāḥ* ("the barley-gruel turns into urine"). Others, however, desire the fourth case even there: *mūtrāya saṃpadyate yavāgvāḥ*. Regarding the term *utpātena*: an *utpāta* is a transformation of the elements that indicates the good or bad fortune of living beings. Regarding *arocakinaḥ*: *arocaka* means "lack of relish"; the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule "when denoting a disease" (*rogākhyāyām*), and due to the statement of "abundance" (*bahulavacanāt*), it does not have the feminine gender.
And [the sixth case-affix is used] for that which stands in the sense of the object of a verb whose upapada (governing word) signifies an action. Pāṇini 2.3.14.

"And [the term *kṛt* applies] to that which has a word expressing an action as its *upapada*, when [the action denoted by the *kṛt*-suffix] stands in the sense of the object (*karman*) of that [action]. [The question is: "What is meant by 'that which has a word expressing an action as its *upapada*'? To this he says: "The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul*," and so forth. Since the technical definition of *upapada* can apply elsewhere, it is precisely this specific scope that is intended here. And in this context, the action itself is the *upapada* expressing an action; thus, such is the meaning obtained—this is the underlying intention.

Relying on the established doctrine of his own school—that "that which is understood as the meaning but is not itself employed is the *sthānin* (the underlying form)"—he says: "of the *sthānin*, which is not being employed. [The example is: *edhebhyo vrajati* ("He goes for fuel"). Now, one might object: "In this case, the dative case is already established by the rule *tādarthye* ('for the sake of that'), so would it not follow here as well in the case of *edhān āhartum vrajati* ('He goes to fetch fuel')? [The answer is: The action of going (*vrajikriyā*) has fetching (*haraṇa*) as its purpose, not fuel (*edhas*) as its purpose; if that were the case, then the same would apply even to the cited example.

However, this is the distinction: the word [denoting the action] is employed in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), but not in the example (*udāharaṇa*). Furthermore, an action that is merely implied (*pratīyamāna*) serves as the basis for the designation of a *kāraka*. In that regard, just as in the counter-example the accusative case occurs because of the requirement of the act of bringing (*āharaṇa*), so too in the example there would have to be the accusative alone due to the requirement of the implied act of bringing; it is for this reason that the present rule is commenced. Here, the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) is the substitute (*sthānin*). This is because [the full sense] is understood as "enter the house and eat the cake" (*piṇḍīm bhakṣaya*). But it is not the case that [this is governed by] the rule *kriyārthopapada* (Pāṇini 3.3.10).

The point is that although entering the house is for the purpose of eating a ball of food (*piṇḍī-bhakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, it does not constitute a technical *upapada* (governing word). Regarding the example "by means of a cart" (*śakaṭena*): one might object that, according to the principle "exceptions [apply] in the middle," the dative case would be superseded by the second case, but not the instrumental case denoting instrument (*karaṇa-tṛtīyā*). If this is so, then this is merely shown as a direction for a counter-example; however, the actual counter-example here should be seen as: "he goes for the sake of fuel for a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasyaidhebhyo vrajati*).

If the mention of the word "object" (*karman*) were absent, this [instrumental case] would also, like the case endings of other *upapadas*, apply only to the domain of the "residual" (*śeṣa*) relation.
And [the suffix *kṛtya*] is used after a verbal noun expressing an action for the sake of another. (Pāṇini 2.3.15)

"Also [the suffixes] expressing an action intended for another (tum-artha-bhāva-vacana). The phrase "having the same meaning as *tumun*" means that the meaning of *tum* is the meaning of *tum-artha*. This is an explanation of the underlying reality (*vastu-vyākhyāna*); however, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which has the meaning of *tum* as its object," whereby the word *tum* indicates the meaning of *tum*. Thus, it refers to a suffix ending in an action-denoting (*bhāva-vacana*) suffix whose meaning is the meaning of *tum*. The mention of "this" refers to that very thing. For that alone is the action-denoting suffix whose meaning is the meaning of *tum*, and nothing else. As in the example: "he goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vrajati*). But surely, in this case, the sense of being for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*) is already established?

Nor does this same undesirable consequence follow from the expression "the cook goes" (*pācako vrajati*), because here the agent (*kartṛ*) is the primary factor, and there is no sense of being for that [agent], but rather for the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). If that is so, then since the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is already indicated by the word expressing the action itself, the dative case would not be established; therefore, the sūtra is commenced. For one who relies on this definition cannot understand that the suffixes *ghañ* and others have the power to manifest the sense of being for that purpose only when they are dependent upon the dative case.

The inclusion of the word *tumun* (the suffix *-tum*) need not be made. How so? In rules such as *pākaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*, and *rāgaḥ*, the phrase "the mention of a word whose object is an action" (*kriyārthopapadagrahaṇam*) will continue to apply. But is it not the case that this [word *bhāve*] is indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), whereas here the sense requires a mention in the ablative case (*pañcamī*)? This change of form will occur by implication (*arthāt*), because of its connection with the rule *bhāvavacanāt*. Indeed, it is not possible for a verbal noun (*bhāvavacana*) to have an action as its subordinate word (*upapada*); what then? It must belong to the root (*dhātu*). Since it is impossible for a verbal noun to belong to a root, it will be understood thus: "that which is prescribed as a verbal noun from a root that has an action as its subordinate word."
And [the word *namaḥ*] is compounded with *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*. (Pāṇini 2.3.16)

"Also [the suffix *kṛt* occurs] after [words] joined with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*. Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the meaning of *paryāpti* (sufficiency) for *alam*": the meaning is that although *alam* is mentioned, it is the sense of sufficiency (*paryāpti*) that is intended there. In that regard, first, the inclusion of the meaning is established by the rule "it is capable of that" (*tasmai prabhavati*). Furthermore, in the example "he makes the girl sufficient" (*alaṃ kurute kanyām*), the accusative case will apply because "the case ending denoting the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is stronger than the case ending of an adjunct (*upapada*)."

Likewise, in the expression *alam odanena*, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), because it is understood that nothing is to be accomplished by means of the rice (*odana*). Therefore, since neither "ornamentation" (*bhūṣaṇa*) nor "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) is applicable here, only "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) is intended. As for the word *punaḥ* (again) and so forth: otherwise, there would be scope for the dative case (*caturthī*) in connection with *svasti*—as in *svasti jālmāya*; this is a statement regarding a past fact, as no benediction (*āśis*) is possible due to his being a rogue (*jālma*).

The scope for the rule "the fourth case is used after words meaning 'welfare' when expressing a benediction" (*kuśalārthair āśiṣi caturthī ca*) is as follows: other meanings of 'welfare'—such as *devadattasya kuśalam* (the welfare of Devadatta) and *devadattāya kuśalam* (welfare unto Devadatta); and *svasti gobhyo bhūyāt* (may there be well-being for the cows). When both [the fourth and the sixth cases] would apply simultaneously, the sixth case would optionally occur due to its higher status in the order of rules.
In the sense of contempt regarding an action, the instrumental case is optionally used for non-living beings. (Pāṇini 2.3.17)

"In the sense of disregard regarding the object of the verb *man*, there is optionally [the use of the fourth case], provided the objects are not living beings. The term "object of *man*" (*manyakarma*) refers to the object of the root *man*. This is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the root *man* belonging to the *divādi* class which takes the suffix *śyan* (i.e., *manyate*), and it does not mean an imitation of that form as it occurs in actual usage with *śyan*. Consequently, the rule applies even in the absence of *śyan*, as in: "Even the joy of the Raghus, considering him as a mere blade of grass (*tṛṇāya matvā*), dispatched the Rākṣasa from the battle with an arrow. However, when *śyan* is present, it excludes only the root *man* of the *tanādi* class meaning "to understand" (*manu avabodhane*).

"Disrespect is contempt. This does not mean merely the absence of respect; how so? Because the negative particle *nañ* expresses the opposite [of the following term], just as in the case of "untruth" (*anṛta*) and so forth—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the Vārttika rule, "In the case of the object of the verb *man* (to think), there is the inclusion of that which is excessively censured": when the dative case is prescribed for the word expressing that [object], the dative occurs only if one intends to convey a degree of excessive contempt, and not when there is a desire to express it in a general sense.

Thinking that the rule for the dative case is established when contempt is associated with a negation, he says: *na tvā tṛṇāya*. Āpiśali used to study [the rule]: "The dative is optionally used for the object of the verb *man* (to think) when expressing disregard, provided it is a comparison involving living beings. In that case, there is no requirement for a negation; thus, the usage by Bhāravi (*Bhaṭṭi*) should be cited as an illustration.

"A stone, a dog," and so forth. This is a statement of the actual facts. Regarding the phrase "whose mother does not see": it refers to that which is capable of being seen. As for the expression "and there is an option based on fixed distribution" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*): one might object, "In those cases where [the suffix] is not desired for living beings, *naḍa* and the others will simply not apply; what is the use of an option based on fixed distribution? The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) himself will state the purpose for this directly.

"Having bowed, [he says] 'it is not a boat' (nāvamiti). Water that is to be crossed by boat is called *nāvya*; as soon as one has crossed it, even though the boat is still present, I do not consider it a "boat," because its purpose has been fulfilled—this is the sense. This should be understood in the same way regarding the phrase "as long as the funeral feast (*śrāddha*) has not been eaten. Regarding "but in the case of living beings, both [apply]," this is according to the distinction of objects. And regarding "this too," we have already stated that this very thing is the direct purpose, since in other cases [the result] is accomplished simply through the state of being a boat and so forth.
The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument. 2.3.18.

"The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument. In the example *prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ* ("naturally handsome"), since no action is explicitly heard and there is consequently no agent or instrument, the sixth case ending would otherwise apply.

Regarding the example *prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ*: the word *prāya* has many meanings; here it means "many," so the sense is "he is a sacrificer by virtue of being among many. Regarding *gārgyo 'smi*: the nominative case would be expected, or perhaps the genitive. Regarding *samena*: here the accusative case would be expected. Regarding *dvidroṇena*: a collection of two *droṇas* is a *dvidroṇa*, which is a measure (*pātra*) and so forth; the meaning is "having made two *droṇas*," and here too the accusative would be expected. Regarding *pañcakena*: a collection of five is a *pañcaka*, which is a measure (*pātra*) and so forth; the meaning is "having made two *droṇas*" (or five measures), and here too the accusative would be expected. Regarding *pañcakena*.

A *pañcaka* is a community (*saṅgha*) whose measure is five; since here one intends to express the non-difference between the community and its members, this [term] stands in apposition with *paśūn* (cattle), and thus the accusative case alone would result here as well. [The example] *sāhasreṇa*: a community whose measure is a thousand is called *sāhasra*. Everything else is as before. This is the intention of one who is proposing this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*).

As for the refutation: here, first of all, even though an action is merely implied by the word *prakṛti* (nature), it serves as the basis for the designation of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth. And here, the action of "making" (*karoti*) is understood; furthermore, the status of the "nature" as an instrument is intended to exclude other instruments. The meaning is: "this person is beautiful by nature," that is, he was made beautiful by his very essence, and not by means of clothing, ornaments, or the like.

The meaning of "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is as follows: "The Brahmins who are in this village mostly studied the sacrifice. In that context, the act of studying—denoted by the word *yājñika*—is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the majority; the sense is that they, having come together, studied the sacrifice. Thus, the majority is the instrument with respect to the study denoted by the word *yājñika*, meaning they studied the sacrifice in unison.

In that case, how does one determine, upon seeing someone in a particular dress, "This person is likely a sacrificer (*yājñika*)"? Here too, the meaning is as follows: first, an abundance of the conduct and so forth of sacrificers is perceived in this person; therefore, by means of this abundance of conduct and so forth, this person is known as a sacrificer by people. In this context, [the abundance of conduct] functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) toward the cognition being produced. Some say that the word *prāyeṇa* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling an inflected form, and that it occurs in the sense of "known."

And it is observed that [the word *guṇa*] generally refers to the arrangement of qualities, as in "generally when the qualities are in harmony," and "generally when the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) departs. Regarding the word *gātreṇa*: by this, in the action of knowing—as in "I am known by my lineage"—or in the action of existing—as in "I am [known] by my lineage"—the lineage (*gotra*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding *samena*: it functions as the instrument in the act of going along a path; the meaning is "by means of a level path. Regarding *dvidroṇena*:

the word *dvidroṇa* and so forth refers to a price consisting of two *droṇas* and so on, and that [price] serves as the cause for the purchase. Furthermore, since two *droṇas* and so forth constitute the price, there is no difference in meaning in the sense that "it is purchased for exactly two *droṇas* and so forth."
When joined with another, the third case ending is used for that which is not the principal factor. (Pāṇini 2.3.19)

Regarding the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne*: when there is a connection between two things through an action (*kriyā*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dravya*), the word *saha* (with) is employed; therefore, examples such as "the father has come with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā*) are presented in sequence as illustrations of the connection with an action and so forth.

Now, in this case, because the nature of the co-occurrent meaning (*sahārtha*) is universal, a relationship such as that between father and son is understood through their coming and so forth; why then is the father considered primary? Some say: when one whose connection to an action and so forth at a specific time is well-known is employed for the purpose of communicating that [action] of another whose connection to an action at a specific time is not well-known—just as, in response to the question "When did this man arrive?", the arrival of the man is expressed by "He arrived with the king"—[the father is primary].

The sentence proceeds in order to establish a specific time [for the principal action], and thus the person (the king) is primary; however, because the king is mentioned merely as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), he is not primary. But if this were the case, the expression "the king has come with his servants" (*bhṛtyaiḥ saha rājāgataḥ*) would not be possible, for the arrival of the servants is not a well-known time by which the time of the king's arrival could be established. Furthermore, it would also not apply in cases where the connection to the action and so forth is unknown for both [the primary and the secondary], such as "the father has come with his son" (*putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā*).

Therefore, its subordinate status must be stated; hence he says: "In this case, [the word] 'of the father' (pituḥ), etc. That which has a connection with an action or the like expressed by a word—whether previously known or unknown—possesses predominance. But that whose [connection] is understood through the necessity of explaining the meaning of the accompanying word (sahārtha) possesses subordination.

By what word is "to whom" expressed, or by what is it perceived? It is that which one intends to speak of. This is what is meant: when there is a connection between two actions, the word *saha* (with/together) is employed. In that case, when the connection of both with the action and so forth is expressed by the word—as in "the father and son have come together"—then, because both are primary, [the rule] does not apply.

But when one intends to convey through the word the connection of action and so forth for one [participant], while for the other it is understood through the impossibility of the meaning of "together" otherwise, then because that [latter] is subordinate, the third case ending is used for its designator. And this being the case, in the rule "He throws the *prastara* grass-bundle together with the branch (*saha śākhayā prastaram praharati*)," although the connection of the *prastara* with the act of throwing is already known from the rule "He throws the *prastara* with the *sūktavāka*," the connection of the branch is not yet known.

Nevertheless, since the instrumental case is established from the word *śākhā* by the aforementioned logic, one should not speak of a "transposition of case endings" (*vibhaktivyatyāsa*). Now, in examples such as *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("he has come with his son"), it is the father alone—the agent—who is expressed by the suffixes such as *kta*; the subordinate son and others are not so expressed. However, the agency of the son is understood through the force of the meaning of the particle *saha*. Thus, the instrumental case is established by the rule *anabhihite kartṛkaraṇayoḥ* ("when [agency] is not already expressed, the third case is used for the agent and the instrument").

In that case, regarding the father’s coming together with his son (*putreṇa sahāgamanaṃ pituḥ*), the genitive case would be required by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*. Furthermore, in the case of "he sows beans together with sesame" (*tilaiḥ saha māṣānvapati*), since the meaning understood is "he sows sesame and beans," the accusative case would be required. Moreover, in cases such as "he is stout together with his son" (*putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ*) or "he possesses cows together with his son" (*putreṇa saha gomān*), the sole intention is to express a relationship between a substance and a quality; thus, because there is not even a trace of an action, there is no trace of an agent either. Therefore, this sūtra must certainly be commenced.

"Because [the rule] is prescribed in connection with the word *artha* (meaning). By the inclusion of the term "connected" (*yukta*), the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is obtained; otherwise, it would have had to be stated simply as "with *saha* when it is the principal [element]. It is sometimes read that [the usage] occurs even without the word *saha*, due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) in the form "the elder [is distinguished] by the youth."

In this context, the mention of "non-principal" (*apradhāna*) is made for the purpose of excluding the "principal" (*pradhāna*), so that the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not occur for the father. [The opponent] asks—"What is meant by 'non-principal'?"—thinking that since the first case ending (*prathamā*) will apply because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal) due to its dependence on the nominal stem alone (*prātipadika-mātra*), there is no need for the mention of "non-principal. [The example given is: "The teacher’s cow along with the pupil" (*upādhyāyasya śiṣyeṇa saha gauḥ*). He thinks that just as the third case occurs here in place of the sixth case when the [pupil] is non-principal, it might likewise occur when he is principal.

On this point, they say: just as in expressions such as *grāmaṃ na gacchati* ("he does not go to the village"), there is first a connection between "the village" and "going," which is subsequently negated by the negative particle (*nañ*), so too here there is first a connection of the teacher with the cow, and subsequently the cow—characterized by that connection—is joined with the word expressing accompaniment (*saha*). Otherwise, whose accompaniment would be expressed? Therefore, since the connection with the cow is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the genitive case will occur after "teacher" (*upādhyāya*); thus, this [rule] serves no purpose.
By which [instrument] there is a modification of a limb. 2.3.20.

"By which there is a modification of a limb (*yenāṅgavikāraḥ*). The word *aṅga* is well known to denote a "limb" or "member. Consequently, the meaning of this sūtra would be: "The third case ending is used for that quality by which a modification occurs in a limb, such as the eye, etc. If this were the case, [the suffix] would only apply in instances such as *akṣikāṇo 'sya* ("he has a blind eye"), and it would only occur after words like *kāṇa* which are themselves adjectives expressing a quality; it would not occur in cases such as *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind with the eye"). Having considered this, he explains it otherwise, beginning with "The word *aṅga* here," etc. The meaning is that the word *aṅga* employed in the sūtra ends in the suffix *ac* added after the root *arśas*, and thus denotes the "body" (*śarīra*).

That which is the basis for the status of being a "principal" (aṅgin) relative to something else is indicated as the cause; by saying "as a cause," just as one says "by another," he shows that the third case ending is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the modified": this is understood through the very force of the context, for an unmodified member cannot be the cause of a modification in the principal. As in the example "blind in the eye": but how can a person be blind, since blindness is a property of the eye, and therefore only the eye becomes blind, not the person? To this he replies: "by means of the property of a part."

Thus, when a modification residing in a member—which is a property of a part—is presented as belonging to the whole through superimposition, then the third case ending occurs after that word denoting the member wherein the modification resides.

But how, then, is the word *akṣi* (eye) employed, given that the word *kāṇa* (one-eyed) expresses a defect located precisely in the eye? When it is said, "Devadatta is one-eyed," no doubt arises as to whether he himself is one-eyed or whether his eye is one-eyed; nor does such a doubt arise as to whether he is one-eyed because of a defect in his eye or in his foot. Therefore, the employment of the word *akṣi* would be purposeless. The same applies to cases such as "lame in the foot" (*pādena khañjaḥ*) or "maimed in the hand" (*pāṇinā kuṇiḥ*). What is the point of mentioning the feet and so forth?

It is said: In a sentence beginning with "the eye" (*akṣi*), when it is stated "of the eye" (*akṣṇaḥ*), it is not known whether it specifies [the person] or whether it means "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*). In that context, the word *kāṇa* is employed to exclude meanings such as "specifies" and so forth, just as when it is said, "Bring two," and one asks "Which two? and the reply is "The two Brāhmaṇas. [The question] "What is the purpose of the mention of 'limb' (*aṅga*)? is a query regarding the inclusion of the term *aṅga*. In some recensions, however, the reading is exactly as follows: "his eye is one-eyed" (*akṣi kāṇam asya*). [Objection: But surely, because of its higher status [in the order of rules], the nominative case (*prathamā*) will apply here; [Response: No.
In the case of grasping what is unreal, this would indeed be primary; however, in the example cited, it is secondary, because the property of a part is superimposed upon the whole.
[The suffix *tṛtīyā* is used] to denote a characteristic mark of a state already attained. (Pāṇini 2.3.21)

Regarding the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe*: from the word *idam*, which denotes what is proximate (*sannihita*), the suffix *thāl* is applied in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*). When the suffix *thamu* is added according to the rule *idamasthamuḥ*, the form *ittham* arises. Since nothing proximate exists here, the word *ittham*—setting aside its literal meaning of "proximity"—expresses a particular manner. The root *bhū* is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*). According to the rule *ā dhṛṣādvā*, in the alternative where the causative suffix *ṇic* is absent, the suffix *kta* is applied in the active sense (*kartari*) because the root has the sense of motion (*gati*). Thus he says: "some" (*kañcit*). The genitive case in *tasya* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*).

That by which something is characterized is a *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic). That by which another is characterized—such as by a white umbrella or the like—as being endowed with a specific mode such as "being a king," is a *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa* (characteristic of such a state). Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means from a present [action]. When a student and a teacher are walking, the water-pot is in the hand of the student; the meaning is that one has recognized, "This is the student, because of his water-pot."

If this is so, would the instrumental case not be established for the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) simply because it is the instrument in such a cognition? If that were the case, then when a knower employs a sentence—such as "This student [is recognized] by means of his water-pot"—in order to communicate a specific quality of his own cognition at the very moment of the act of knowing, the status of being an instrument would be impossible, because the act of cognition is neither manifest nor being communicated at that time. However, the example should be explained in this way: "A cognition of the form 'This is a student by means of his water-pot' has arisen."
What is the meaning? The sense is that here the specific knowledge of the seer (draṣṭṛ) designated by the word "he saw" is being described, not that of the agent of the action.

In this case, when the *bahuvrīhi* compound "kamaṇḍalupāṇiśchātraḥ" (the student with a water-pot in his hand) is formed, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply after the word *kamaṇḍalu*. Nor can the prohibition of the designation *prātipadika*—based on the rule "that which is not a suffix is [a *prātipadika*]"—be invoked by means of the rule "not in the case of a suffix" (*na pratyayalakṣaṇena*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "not before the *ṅi* case-ending or the vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*). Furthermore, the elision (*luk*) of the third case ending that has just arisen cannot be obtained by the rule "of the case-endings in the case of verbal roots and *prātipadikas*" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), because that case ending is not separated from the *prātipadika* of the compound. Therefore, he says: "it does not occur here," because it is included within the compound.

The meaning is that [the word] is subordinate with respect to the sense of the compound (*samāsārtha*). The instrumental case is used for that which is the primary factor in denoting a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of such a state. However, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because the constituent words denote another referent (*anyapadārtha*) with their own meanings as subordinate, there is no primacy [of any single member].
The term *saṃjñā* optionally [takes the genitive case] when it denotes the object [of the action].

The rule *saṃjño 'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 2.3.52] applies. Regarding the form *saṃjānīte*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule *saṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne* [Pāṇini 1.3.46], and the substitution of *jā* for *jñā* and *jan* occurs by the rule *jñājanorjā* [Pāṇini 7.3.79]. However, in the sense of "thinking of" (*ādhyāna*), the genitive case is employed according to the rule *adhīgarthadayeśām* [Pāṇini 2.3.52], as in *mātuḥ saṃjānāti*. But when used with a *kṛt*-suffix, even in the non-"thinking of" sense, the genitive case governed by *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* [Pāṇini 2.3.65] takes precedence, as in *mātuḥ saṃjñātā*.
In the case of a reason (hetu). 2.3.23.

Regarding the term *hetu*: since the rule "the prompter of that [agent] is also called *hetu*" (Pāṇini 1.4.55) prescribes the technical designation of *hetu* for the agent of a scriptural action, and because the instrumental case would already be established by the rule "of the agent and the instrument" (Pāṇini 2.3.18), he states "capable of being a means to an end," etc., to indicate that the worldly *hetu* is intended here. For in common usage, a *hetu*—such as a seed—is the cause for the production of an effect like a sprout when it possesses mere capability and does not depend upon an [intervening] operation; its domain consists of substances, qualities, and actions. As it has been said: "A *hetu* has substances and so forth as its domain, whereas a *kāraka* has a restricted action. And when an operation is not dependent [upon another], it is called a *nimitta-hetu* (efficient cause)."

Since there is an absence of action (*kriyā*) in the examples, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is not to be suspected. In the case of *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), it is the state of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) which is intended to be expressed, and not the causality (*hetutva*), even though it exists; therefore, the nominative case alone occurs after the word *dāru*.
The fifth case-affix is used for the word *ṛṇa* when it does not denote the agent.

The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used for a debt (*ṛṇa*) that is not the agent (*akarta*). Regarding the form *bandhita*: it is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*) of the causative (*ṇyanta*) root *bandh*. "And a hundred is a debt" because it is to be held by the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). And because [the debtor] is the instigator (*prayojaka*), he receives the designation of agent (*kartṛ*); for by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "that which causes one to act is both the cause (*hetu*) and the agent," the designation of agent is prescribed. Now, one might object: in the preceding rule, the worldly (*laukika*) cause was intended, whereas this is a technical (*śāstrīya*) one; yet even a technical cause possesses the nature of being worldly.

Alternatively, for what reason was the technical (śāstrīya) [instrumental] not included in the previous sūtra—[namely], that "the third case-ending is established when denoting the agent"? It is not so; because the fifth case-ending would be unestablished [in that context], the general inclusion here must indeed be for this specific purpose.
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies when a quality (*guṇa*) is expressed, provided it is not feminine.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām*: some maintain that "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to that which is defined by the characteristics "it enters into a substance" (*sattve niviśate*) and "it departs [from it]" (*apaiti*), because the examples and counter-examples accord with that definition. Others, however, desiring the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in instances such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," explain that the term refers to anything that is merely dependent (*paratantra*), just as in the expression "due to the existence of which quality... (*yasya hi guṇasya bhāvāt*).

By means of the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe*, the form "nāstīha paṭo 'nupalabdheḥ" (there is no cloth here because it is not perceived) occurs even in the feminine gender in certain instances. Some, however, maintain that this is the ablative case used for the source (*apādāna*); thus, in the form "nāstīha ghaṭo 'nupalabdhitaḥ" (there is no jar here because of non-perception), the suffix *tasil* is applied according to the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*. For those who advocate the grammatical split, however, the suffix *tasi* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *ādyādi* group.
The sixth case ending is used when a word expressing a cause (hetu) is employed. 2.3.26.

"Sixth case [is used] when there is the employment of the word *hetu* (cause). Regarding the phrase "of the word *hetu*": this is stated because the "employment" (*prayoga*) is a property of words, but it does not thereby exclude the inclusion of the meaning; for even when the meaning is employed, the sixth case is desired by the rule to be stated later, "in the sense of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*. When the word *hetu* is employed, since a specific relation characterized by the state of being cause and effect is invariably understood, this rule ("*hetau*") is an exception to the third case.
And the third case ending is used after a pronoun [when it denotes the agent]. 2.3.27.

Regarding the rule *sarvanāmnas tṛtīyā ca*: the genitive case in *sarvanāmnaḥ* is used in relation to usage (*prayoga*), meaning "when there is the usage of a word denoting a reason (*hetu-śabda*) following a pronominal (*sarvanāman*). If, however, [the genitive were taken] as a fifth case (ablative), this rule would not apply when a word denoting a reason follows [the pronoun]. How then is it that the third case occurs after a pronominal? In this instance as well, the meaning should be understood as "when there is the usage of a pronominal."

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*": although this was read by the author of the Vṛtti (*Vṛttikāra*) in this sūtra, the author of the Bhāṣya (*Bhāṣyakāra*), however, read it under the rule "in the sense of *hetu*" (*hetau*). Consequently, it is understood that this prescription of case endings applies even to non-pronouns (*asarvanāman*). Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyas*) there, the nominative and accusative cases do not occur for non-pronouns; other cases, however, occur according to usage—as in: *annena kāraṇena vasati* (he dwells for the sake of food), *annāya kāraṇāya vasati*, *annāt kāraṇāt*, *annasya kāraṇasya*, and *anne kāraṇe*.

Regarding the phrase "but the inclusion of synonyms": one might object that this is the reverse of what should be done; for when prescribing the actual form (*svarūpa*), synonyms should be included, whereas when referring to the meaning (*artha*), they should not. Furthermore, if the term *artha* were used, there would be the undesirable consequence of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of only one of several identical words), because it is stated that *ekaśeṣa* applies even to dissimilar forms provided they have the same meaning. The [author] thinks as follows: just as in the case of words denoting a class (*ākṛti*), some are recited merely for the purpose of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), so too here, words such as *nimitta* and so forth, though primarily intended to express their own form, serve for the sake of indication. Thus, the expression "of meanings [denoted by] words" is used.
The fifth case ending is used for the ablative (apādāna). 2.3.28.

"The fifth case ending is used for the ablative (apādāna). Regarding the example "prāsādāt" (from the palace): since the meaning is understood even when a form ending in the suffix -lyap is not employed, the second case ending would [otherwise] apply here.

Regarding the word "from the seat" (*āsanāt*): here, the seventh case ending would be expected. However, the [proposed] rejection is as follows: "beholding" (*prekṣaṇa*) is the cognition of objects by means of the eye; the ocular faculty, being composed of light (*taijasa*), goes outwards and grasps the objects. And since the verbal root [√īkṣ] occurs in the sense of beholding—which includes the act of going out as a subordinate factor—the palace becomes the *apādāna* (point of departure) with respect to that subordinate act of going out, which has already been established as its object—thus, "he beholds from the palace. What is the meaning? He grasps the objects after having emitted the ocular light from the location of the palace.

And [the rule applies] in the case of questioning and narration. A specific questioning and narration are understood here—those instances in common usage where the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed. It does not apply here: "Whose wealth is this? or "The king's wealth. In the case of "From where do you come? (*kuto bhavān*), because there is no [explicitly stated] action, it is not an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure). Rather, this is used with reference to an action such as "coming" (*āgamana*) that is established through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is connected with a result. In that context, for both the speaker and the narrator, the action of coming—which is mentally present and expected—is the *apādāna*, namely "from Pāṭaliputra."

The phrase "yataśca" means: from that which is taken as the limit (avadhi) for the demarcation of space and time; that is the meaning. Gavīdhumat is the name of a city, and Sāṃkāśya is a grove of ascetics (tapovana).

The full moon day joined with the *kṛttikā* constellation is called *kārttikī*. The suffix *lup* does not apply here [to form *kārttika*] by the rule "there is *lup* when no distinction is intended" (*lub aviśeṣe*), because of the specific mention in the rule "optionally after *phalgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*" (*vibhāṣā phalgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrībhyaḥ*) within the governing context "that full moon day occurs in this month" (*sā asmin paurṇamāsī*). *Āgrahāyaṇī* means that in which the year begins (*agra-hāyana*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (as a *svārthika*) because the group beginning with *prajña* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). The change of the vowel to *ṇ* [in *āgrahāyaṇī*] is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule "after *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvattha*" (*āgrahāyaṇyaśvatthāt*). [The compound] *tad-yuktāt* means "joined with that."

The meaning is: from words such as *māsa* (month) and so forth, which denote time and are connected by way of their meaning with that which is expressed by a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*). Alternatively, the meaning is: from a word denoting a period of time such as a month that follows that object expressed by the fifth case, such as the full moon of Kārttika (*kārttikī*) and so forth. And since this "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) is based on the actual sense and not on the verbal form, it applies even when there is an intervention; for example, the month situated between the full moon of Kārttika and the full moon of Agrahāyaṇī is subsequent to the full moon of Kārttika.

Regarding the word *adhvan* (path): it is to be understood as being connected with [the word] *tadyukta* (connected therewith). As for the rejection [of this interpretation], it is because here there is the use of only a portion of the sentence. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when four *yojana*s have been traversed after departing from Gavīdhumata, then Sāṃkāśya [is reached]; that is, "when four *yojana*s have been gone over," where the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The meaning is that when the *yojana*s have been traversed by people, then Sāṃkāśya is reached by them.

Alternatively—having superimposed the act of departing (*niḥsaraṇa*) or going (*gamana*) onto those traveling on the road, the use of the suffix *lyap* and the past passive participle (*kta*) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) occurs; its status as an ablative (*apādāna*) is relative to the implied action of departing. Furthermore, in the word *gatān*, because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not differ [from the case-meaning], the nominative is used. The locative in *gateṣu* (in those who have gone) is by the rule "the seventh case is used when one state is characterized by another" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*). Thus, *āgrahāyaṇī nāma* means that when a month has passed subsequent to the full moon of Kārttika, it is the month of Āgrahāyaṇī.
The meaning is "it exists. In that context, the fifth case (ablative) is used by way of connection with direction (*digyoga*), while the seventh case (locative) is as previously explained.

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after words meaning "other than," "different from," "except for," or words denoting directions, when they are followed by a word ending in the sixth case and joined with the words *jāhī* or *yukta*.

[The rule] *anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte* [Pāṇini 2.3.29]. Regarding the statement "the word *anya* is taken here as the meaning," this is because of the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Regarding the phrase "the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of that which is being pointed out": for example, when Devadatta and Yajñadatta have been introduced, one says, "Devadatta is brave, the other is a coward"; in that case, it should be considered whether the meaning of "other" (*anya*) is already included within the word *itara*. As for the example *ṛte yajñadattāt* ("except for Yajñadatta").

How can it be that "whatever [is performed] in the Rājasūya, except for Soma"? This is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). How about "O Rāma, without me, Bālin [cannot do it]"? And how about "Where does an action bear fruit, if not through propitiation of the Person (the Lord)"? Poets are unrestrained.

Regarding the mention of "the apprehension of sound" (*śabdagrahaṇa*): for when that [word] exists, the compound *dikśabdaḥ* ("a word denoting direction") is obtained as a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (compound with the middle term elided), meaning "a word seen in a direction. By means of this, there occurs connection even with something currently existing in a location or time that was previously seen in a direction—such as "the region east of the village" (*grāmāt pūrvo deśaḥ*) or "Phālguna is before Caitra" (*caitrāt pūrvaḥ phālgunaḥ*). However, in connection with words expressing parts, it does not occur—as in "the front part of the body" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya*)—due to the grammatical indication in the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam*.

Regarding the phrase "nanu cāyamapi" (But surely this [word] also...): the meaning is that in examples such as *sadhryaṅ devadattena*, the rule for the inclusion of a word ending in the suffix *añ* does not apply to the sense of a directional term (*dikśabda*), because this too is understood to be a directional term due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with other directional terms. As for "dakṣiṇā": the suffixes *āc* and *āh* are applied by the rules "dakṣiṇādāc," "āhi ca dūre," and "uttarācca."
The sixth case ending is used after a word ending in a suffix expressing the sense of "from this" (atas-artha). 2.3.30.

[The rule] "after a word ending in the sixth case, when followed by a suffix having the sense of *atas*...": here, although the form *atas* could possibly arise from the root √*i* preceded by the negative particle *nañ* with the suffix *kvip*, the suffix alone is understood because it is directly heard in the text and because of the paribhāṣā [P. 1.1.72] regarding suffixes and non-suffixes; thus, the mention of the suffix is not for the sake of the meaning. Regarding "before" (*purastāt*): by the rules "for *pūrva*, *adhara*, and *avara*, there are the substitutes *asu*, *adha*, and *ava* respectively" and "also before the suffix *astāti*," the word *pūrva* undergoes the substitution of *puras*. Regarding "above" (*upari*) and "from above" (*upariṣṭāt*).

The word *upa* is substituted for the word *ūrdhva*, and the suffixes *ril* and *riṣṭāt* are applied; the ablative case is used here because of the usage by the author of the Bhāṣya: "after that, the elephant."
The second case ending is used after [a word] expressing "on account of" (enap). 2.3.31.

The second [view] is as follows: "In that regard, our house is to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth"—because this falls under the domain of feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) necessarily applies; therefore, the grammatical correctness of statements such as "it does not follow after what comes after that" must be considered.
The third case ending is optionally used after words meaning "separately," "without," and "variously."

In the rule *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis tṛtīyānyatarasyām*, because the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* permits what has already been established as the case in its alternative form, when the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is not applied, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply by virtue of [the word] being treated as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Now, one might argue that since particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, the inclusion of *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not for the purpose of optionality (*vikalpa*). Even so, the immediately preceding second case (*dvitīyā*) would be conjoined [with the third].

Even if this [fifth case] is established through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), even so, the sixth case immediately following it would be included, but the fifth case would not be included in any way; yet that [fifth case] is desired. Therefore, he asks "How so? and says: "The mention of the fifth case. Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): in the two preceding rules, there is no continuity of application (*adhikāra*) by way of a frog-leap (*maṇḍūkagati*). If the fifth case is [included] by virtue of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), then for what purpose is the mention of *anyatarasyām*? It is for the purpose of inclusion (*samuccaya*).

In this regard, when the question arises as to what is being combined [by the particle *ca*], it is stated: "The mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti. It should be understood that a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) must be made; even in the absence of a statement from the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali), this interpretation is established solely on the basis of the abundance of usage.

And [the suffix *ktvā*] is used after [words denoting] *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya* when they function as instruments (*karaṇa*), provided that they do not denote a sentient being (*asattvavacana*). Pāṇini 2.3.33.

And [the suffix *am* is used] after the words *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya* when they denote a non-substance (*asattvavacana*) in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). When it is said "when they are mere properties" (*dharmamātra*), those qualities (*guṇa*) by connection with which a substance (*dravya*) receives the designation "small" (*stoka*) and so forth are the "properties" (*dharma*). For these terms are expressive of both; they denote a substance as well as a quality, just like the word "white" (*śukla*). When they are expressive of a quality, then they are expressive of a non-substance—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the case of an object that is an adverbial modifier of an action" (*kriyāviśeṣaṇe karmaṇi*): for by means of a verb, an action in its state of being accomplished (*sādhyamānāvasthā*) is expressed—as in "he moves" (*calati*), which means "he performs moving" (*calanaṃ karoti*).

Therefore, qualifiers such as *stoka* (little) become objects—as in "he performs a little movement" (*stokaṃ calanaṃ karoti*). However, since the word *stoka* here functions as a qualifier of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and denotes a substance (*dravya*), this [rule] does not apply here. Furthermore, where the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is intended to be expressed as an instrument (*karaṇa*) toward another result to be accomplished, there would be no status as a qualifier—as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in a beautiful manner" (*śobhanaṃ jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta*).

For here, just as the instrumental case occurs after the word *jyotiṣṭoma*—which denotes the sacrifice that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the cultivation of the fruit (*phalabhāvanā*)—so too would it occur after the word *śobhana*, which is its qualifier.

However, another says: "Since the action is attained through seeing, desiring, and resolving, the qualifier of that [action] must also possess the status of an object (*karman*). For him as well, the status of being an object would not apply when there is an intention to express the non-difference between the seeing and so forth and the action; for in that case, the action itself does not possess the status of an object.
With words meaning "far" or "near," the sixth case-affix is optionally used [along with the seventh]. 2.3.34.

"With words meaning 'far' or 'near,' [the sixth case-affix] optionally occurs where the sixth case-affix would otherwise apply. This statement is made for the sake of the fifth case-affix; however, the sixth case-affix is already established by virtue of being the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). If this is so, then the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is redundant, because if only the sixth case-affix were prescribed, the fifth case-affix under discussion would be enjoined simply by the fact that the former would otherwise be superfluous. To this, he replies: "The mention of *anyatarasyām*... For if it were understood that the rule under discussion is being enjoined solely by the force of the statement itself, then there would be an injunction for the third case-affix as well.

But surely, the inclusion of the phrase *anyatarasyām* (optionally) must be for the purpose of either allowing an option (*vikalpa*) or for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*). If it were for the purpose of an option, then once the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is set aside, all case-endings (*vibhakti*) would apply by the rule *svādi-sūtra* [Pāṇini 4.1.2]. If it were for the purpose of conjunction, why is the third case (*tṛtīyā*) under discussion not also conjoined? It is said: In the rule *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhiḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.32], it was stated that "by the inclusion of *anyatarasyām*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is conjoined. Therefore, because this present rule belongs to the same section (*praghaṭṭaka*), that very same [fifth case] is conjoined here as well.

Therefore, this objection also should not be raised: "When *anyatarasyām* was already in force, what is the purpose of repeating *anyatarasyām*? For even in that case, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would have occurred.
After words meaning "far" or "near," the second case ending is also used [along with the fifth]. (Pāṇini 2.3.35)

"From words expressing distance and proximity, the second case-affix also [is employed]. The intention is that this rule is an injunction for the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), because no other meaning has been specified. Now, one might object: "Even if no other meaning is specified, this injunction would be appropriate for the scope of the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) and for the scope of the preceding case-affixes; however, in the scope of the first case-affix (*prathamā*), since it is subsequent [to this rule], it alone should prevail. This is not a fault; for this [injunction] also carries over into what follows, and therefore, even in the scope of the subsequent case-affixes, it applies everywhere according to the specific expression intended.

And likewise, in the case of *dūrād āvasathān mūtram* ("urine far from the dwelling"), the suffix occurs even when [the word] denotes a location—the meaning being "far from the dwelling. This rule regarding the application [of the suffix] to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) should be understood as having the examples cited here as its scope. Accordingly, he will state later: "Case endings occur after words denoting substances (*sattva*) according to their respective [grammatical functions]. However, if the application were restricted solely to the meaning of the nominal stem, the phrase "according to their respective [functions]" would be untenable; rather, one would have to say that "only the nominative case occurs."
The seventh case-affix is used in the sense of the locus (adhikaraṇa) as well as [the other senses previously mentioned]. 2.3.36.

"Saptamy adhikaraṇe ca" (Pāṇini 2.3.36) and "Ktasyenviṣayasya" (Pāṇini 2.3.69). The meaning of "inviṣayasya" is: that *kta*-suffix ending whose scope (*viṣaya*), i.e., its domain of occurrence (*vṛttibhūmi*), consists of a word ending in the suffix *in*. For example: *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("one who has studied grammar").

Having analyzed the compound as *adhītam anena* ("this has been studied by him"), and given that the word *anena* follows from the rule *śrāddham anena bhuktam* ("the śrāddha was eaten by him"), when the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *iṣṭādibhyaś ca*, the act of studying (*adhīta*)—which has merged with the agent expressed by the taddhita derivative—cannot be separately connected to grammar or other subjects. Therefore, since grammar and the like are not already expressed by the *kta* suffix, they are related to the act of studying as its object (even though that act is subordinate as the meaning of the base) by means of the action denoted by the base itself, just as in the examples *adhītavān vyākaraṇam* ("he has studied grammar") and *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("he has previously made a mat").

When the second case (*dvitīyā*) is applicable, the seventh case (*saptamī*) is prescribed. In the example "He has studied grammar for a month" (*iha māsam adhītī vyākaraṇe*), there is no seventh case because the time and the object (*kāla-karman*) are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). In the example "Devadatta is skillful toward his brother" (*sādhur devadatto bhrātari*), although skillfulness and lack thereof relate to the mother and father, this statement is made because, due to the absence of an action (*kriyā*), there is no status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). Since the rule would have been established by the words "by *sādhu* and *nipuṇa*" alone, the inclusion of *sādhu* here is for the sake of excluding cases of worship (*anarcā*); therefore, it applies even when stating a fact (*tattvakathana*). The inclusion of *arcā* (worship) therein is for the sake of [restricting] *nipuṇa*.

How, then, will the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) be formulated there—namely, "Is 'bhṛtyo rājñaḥ' (the servant of the king) correct in the sense of 'arcāyām' (in worship)? It is said in reply: there is a verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) between the king and the servant, not with the word "correct" (*sādhu*). [The construction is] "the king's servant; he is correct. In this regard, the phrase "whether toward the king or elsewhere" is not touched upon by that [word "correct"]; rather, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), correctness is understood as pertaining specifically to the king. It is on this basis alone that it should be regarded as a counter-example.

Regarding the phrase "of those worthy of being agents" (*kārakārhāṇām*): the word *kāraka* is derived in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*), meaning "of those worthy of the status of an agent. Regarding the phrase "among the prosperous" (*ṛddheṣu*): the prosperous are "worthy of being agents" (*kārakārhāḥ*) because they are entitled to the act of eating; this statement is made so that [the rule] may apply even when there is no intention to express a relationship between a characteristic and what is characterized (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*). Regarding the phrase "among the poor who are seated": the poor are "not worthy of being agents" (*akārakārhāḥ*) because they are not entitled to eat. Regarding the phrase "and in the case of their reversal": this means when those worthy of being agents are not agents, and those not worthy of being agents are agents.

Regarding the rule *nimittāt karmayoge*: that which is the purpose of an action—that for whose sake an action is undertaken—is here termed *nimitta* (the cause/motive). The seventh case ending occurs after a word expressing such a motive, provided that there exists between that motive and the object (*karman*)—that which is most desired by the agent—a relationship characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) or the like. This is stated because the third case ending for the instrumental cause (*hetu-tṛtīyā*) would otherwise apply. In this context, there is an inherence relationship between the object of the act of killing, such as a *dvīpin* (leopard), and the motive, such as its skin. As in the example *camarīm* ("for the sake of the yak").

From the word *camara*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*). *Puṣkalaka* means a peg; it is "struck" (or driven) into the boundary for the purpose of identifying the boundary. By that peg being struck, there is a conjunction—that is, a connection—with the boundary. Why specify "connection with an object" (*karmasaṃbandha*)? [Because otherwise, one might say: "He reaps grain for wages."
And [the locative case is used] when an action is characterized by the existence of another action. (Pāṇini 2.3.37)

And regarding the rule "by the existence of which there is the indication of another existence": here, the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) is based on repeated observation, as in the case of fire and smoke. Consequently, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as "when the sun has risen, the darkness has vanished" or "when the moon has risen, the ocean has swelled"; however, in a case like "he went while the fires were being offered," where the offering of the fire-sacrifice and the act of going are not repeatedly observed together, that [offering] would not be an indicator of that [going]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "and the action is well-known."

It is the very conventional usage (*prasiddhi*) of an action that is useful for its status as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) with respect to another action, and not its actual perception; what is meant is this: an action whose time is already known, even if employed only once as the cause for delimiting the time of an action whose time is unknown, indeed serves as its defining characteristic.
And the sixth case-affix is used in the sense of disregard. (Pāṇini 2.3.38)

"And the sixth [case-ending] is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). The term "in disregard" is a locative case governed by the preceding rule; furthermore, this is a qualifier of the state that serves as a characteristic mark (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*). He says "excessive in disregard" (*anādarādhika*) to mean that which characterizes a state when disregard is present. The meaning is: "qualified by disregard," i.e., being disregarded. In the example *rudataḥ prāvrājīt* ("He went forth while [his father] was weeping"), the meaning is that he undertook the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*) without regard for the weeping of his father or others.
And [the suffix *ṅasi* or *ṅas*] is substituted for [the sixth case endings] after words meaning "master," "lord," "ruler," "heir," "witness," "surety," and "progenitor. (Pāṇini 2.3.39)

[The suffix *ka* is applied] after [the words] *svāmī*, *īśvara*, *adhipa*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, and *pratibhū*, as well as after [the word *go*] when preceded by *prasūta*. Regarding "an heir to cows" (*gavāṃ dāyādaḥ*): that which is given is a *dāya*—meaning a share. [The term] *dāyāda* is derived with the suffix *ka* according to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), even though the root *dā* is preceded by the prefix *ā* (as in *ādatte*). The phrase "of cows" (*gavām*) is an adjective for the whole [compound], yet it touches upon its constituent part, the share (*dāya*). Thus, the meaning is: one who takes a share consisting of cows. Regarding "born from cows" (*gavāṃ prasūtaḥ*): the meaning is one born to experience cows themselves.
And [the suffix *kṛt*] is used after the roots *ā-yuj* and *kuśala* when expressing habitual practice (*āsevanā*). 2.3.40.

And [the suffix *kha*] occurs after the words *āyukta* and *kuśala* when used in the sense of "practice" (*āsevana*). For example: *āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe* ("a yoked ox for the cart"). Here, the prefix *āṅ* has the sense of "slightness," meaning "only slightly yoked."
And [the sixth case ending is used] when there is a selection from among many. (Pāṇini 2.3.41)

And because selection [is made] "by means of genus, quality, or action"—this is merely an illustration; for selection is also seen to be made by means of a name, as in: "Among these students, Devadatta is clever."
The fifth case ending is used in the sense of separation. (Pāṇini 2.3.42)

"Pañcamī vibhakte" (Pāṇini 2.3.42). "Vibhakta" means that which possesses separation. [The word] "from that which is being singled out" (nirddhāryamāṇāt) is used. What is meant is this: singling out occurs when there is a distinction between that which is being singled out and the basis of the singling out; therefore, since in every case that which is the basis of the singling out possesses separation, an implicit restriction is understood by implication—that in whatever basis of singling out there is only separation, and not identity with it.
The seventh case ending is used after the words *sādhu* and *nipuṇa* when they denote proficiency in an action, provided that the word *apratī* does not follow. (Pāṇini 2.3.43)

Regarding the rule *sādhu-nipuṇābhyām arcāyām saptamy-aprateḥ*: the word *sādhu* is derived from the root *sad* with the suffix *uṇ* according to the rule *kṛ-vā-pā-ji-mi*. From the root *puṇ* (meaning "to purify" or "be auspicious") preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ig-upadhāt kaḥ*, resulting in *nipuṇa*. From the root *arc* belonging to the Bhvādi class (*arca pūjāyām*), the suffix *a* is applied according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*; however, from the Churādi class, the suffix *yuc* would be expected. In the phrase *aprateḥ*, the word *prayoge* ("in usage") must be supplied; thus he says: "provided that *prati* is not employed," as in the example *sādhuḥ mṛtyo rājan*.
This has already been refuted and established previously; however, "the clever son [knows] his mother" is a fitting counter-example for explaining the true nature of the matter.
And the third case-affix is used after words meaning "prasiddha" (well-known) and "utsuka" (eager).

"And the third [case-ending] is used after the words *prasita* and *utsuka*. Regarding the root *ṣiñ* in the sense of "binding," one who is bound intensely is called *prasita*. Thus it is said: "one who is constantly (*nityam*) bound thereto. By the word "constantly," the meaning of the prefix *pra-* is explained. It is "bound as if" (*avabaddha iva*)—the sense being that whoever is attached to something is, as it were, bound to it. By this, it is demonstrated that the form *pramitaḥ* (in the sense of "more white") is not included. In the example *keśeṣu prasitaḥ*, the meaning is "intent upon" (*tatpara*).
[And the third case-ending is used] after a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), when the suffix is elided (*lupi*). (Pāṇini 2.3.45)

Regarding the rule *nakṣatre ca lupi*: the construction of the words of the sūtra is that when a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), [the suffix] occurs after that which expresses the meaning of the affix that is being elided by the technical term *lup*. As for what is said—that in the expression *nakṣatre lupi*, the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative, meaning "after that which ends in *lup* and denotes a lunar mansion"—that would not apply to the example "one should not go north from the two Uttarā-phalgunīs," because that [word *uttarābhyām*] does not end in *lup*.

How then is the *vṛtti* (commentary) to be understood when it says, "from a word ending in *lup* that denotes a constellation"? This was stated by way of general usage (*prāyovṛtti*): that which denotes the meaning of what ends in *lup* is generally [itself] ending in *lup*. The meaning is: "from any word whatsoever that denotes the meaning of a *lup*-ending form. Regarding the term *lubantāt*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which the *lup* is completed" (*asmin*). Furthermore, one should understand that the status of being the final member (*antyāvayavatva*) of the *lup* is established by its position as the original element (*sthānin*). The phrase "the locative case is understood" implies that [the suffix does not apply] even in cases such as *puṣpaṃ pratīkṣate* ("he waits for the flower"), *puṣpāya spṛhayati* ("he longs for the flower"), or *puṣpasya samīpe* ("near the flower").
The first case ending (*prathamā*) is used in the sense of the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender (*liṅga*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and number (*vacana*). (Pāṇini 2.3.46)

"The first case ending (*prathamā*) occurs when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender, measure, or number. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the nominal stem is existence" (*sattā*), this is the definition intended here, and not merely the meaning of the nominal stem in general; for [if it were the latter], it would be impossible in cases such as *gauḥ* (cow), *śuklaḥ* (white), *pācakaḥ* (cook), and *ḍitthaḥ* (a proper name). That meaning which is simply existent, and is not of the nature of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, nor endowed with gender, number, or the capacity for grammatical relations (*kāraka-śakti*), is what is intended here by "the meaning of the nominal stem"; that is to say, it refers to the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

For the meaning of an indeclinable can only be stated as "it exists," but not as "it is such-and-such" or "it is that-and-that. However, in cases such as *gauḥ* (cow) or *śuklaḥ* (white), since the referent is an entity (*sattva*), the [gender] is established simply by the apprehension of gender; this is the intended sense.

Others, however, say: "That meaning which is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that meaning which the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) does not deviate from, and without which the nominal stem is not employed—that is the entire meaning of the nominal stem. The mention of "existence" (*sattā*) is merely illustrative; therefore, examples such as "existence," "cowness," "whiteness," "the white quality," "the cook," "Devadatta," "cow," and "white" are also included. [Objection: But in all these cases, the meaning is already established simply by the mention of gender (*liṅga*); [Response: No.

The inclusion of the term "only" (*mātra*) is made for the purpose of restriction, as in the expression "he observes the vow of milk-only" (*payomātraṃ vratayati*). Consequently, [the suffix] would apply only in cases such as *strī*, *pumān*, and *napuṃsakam*, where gender itself is the meaning; however, it would not apply in cases such as *sattā* (existence), because there exists an additional meaning such as a genus (*jāti*).

Now, one might argue that—just as in the expression "he chooses only a girl" (*kanyāmātraṃ varayati*), where the word *mātra* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*)—the nominative case occurs when there is merely a gender (*liṅgamātre*), because of the interpretation that "the nominative occurs simply because gender exists. Thus, even when an additional meaning is present, the nominative would still occur. To this it is replied: Alas, if that were so, then in expressions such as "look at the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśya*), the nominative would occur simply because gender exists, even though the object (*karman*) and other factors are present! This is because, under the view that the suffixes are restricted (the *pratyayaniyamapakṣa*), objects and the like are not restricted to the second case and so forth. [The rule] states "number, such as singularity," etc.; the intention is that this is based on the established usage of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).

Regarding the word *uccaiḥ*: here, since the nominative case (*prathamā*) is present, in examples such as *grāma uccaistava svam* ("the village is high, it is yours"), the optional application of the suffixes *te*, *me*, and so on occurs by the rule *sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyā vibhāṣā*. Furthermore, the status of being a *pada* (word) is established even for the genitive case; for that meaning for which the accusative and other cases have not been prescribed is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Now, one might ask: since the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is non-numerical (*asaṅkhya*), how could there be a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [to express its relation]? This is because, if the rule were restricted to meanings such as singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth, the genitive would be unrestricted regarding number; and even if the restriction pertained to the suffix itself, such a restriction would depend on things of the same class, and thus singularity and the others would mutually exclude one another. However, in the view that this is an injunctive rule (*vidhi*), the sūtra *svādi-sūtra* forms a separate sentence from rules such as *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*, because its purpose is to enjoin the use of the suffixes when numbers are possible.
