[Objection: But surely, the suffixes beginning with *su* (the nominative) will be prescribed after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *pratyaya*. In that case, when it is stated that "the first case [suffix] occurs in the sense [of the stem]," and there arises the expectation "in whose sense?", it will be understood that "it is in the sense of that from which the suffix beginning with *su* is prescribed. Therefore, the mention of the term *prātipadika* is unnecessary. Furthermore, this has another purpose: the explicit mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) need not be made; cases such as *kumārī* and *sīmā* are established by this very rule. However, if the mention of *prātipadika* were actually made, then even though words like *sīmā* do not deviate from having a meaning associated with the feminine gender...

Since [a word ending in] a suffix would not be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the mention of "gender" (*liṅga*) would have to be made in order to establish the nominative case in its meaning. It is replied: first, it will be stated right here that the mention of "nominal stem" is not connected with the word "meaning. As for the mention of "gender," it is for the sake of words having multiple genders—such as *taṭaḥ*, *taṭam*, *taṭī*; *kumāraḥ*, *kuṇḍam*, *kuṇḍaḥ*, *kuṇḍikā*. Otherwise, the nominative case prescribed merely for that meaning—[namely,] that meaning without which the base (*prakṛti*) is not used, would not apply to words of various genders when they are employed without those specific [gender distinctions].

Now, if one were to accept the statement regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) without mentioning "mere" (*mātra*), would it not follow that even when there is an additional meaning (*adhikārtha*), the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) still undergoes syntactic connection (*anvaya*)? If this were so, then in cases such as *vṛkṣaṃ paśya* ("look at the tree"), where there is an excess of meanings such as the object (*karman*), [the nominative] would occur even under the view that restricts the suffixes. Therefore, in this commentary (*vṛtti*), *kumārī* and *kuṇḍam* are cited as examples; the word *vṛkṣa*, however, is cited by implication. [Objection: Let there be no mention of "mere," let there be no mention of "gender" (*liṅga*), and let the rule *saṃbodhane ca* ("and in the vocative") not be formulated; in all cases, the nominative case will occur simply by the rule *sarvatrārthe*.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence [of using the nominative] for *karman* and so forth, because we adopt a restriction of meaning such that the second case (*dvitīyā*) applies only to the object (*karman*). Even so, in the expression "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the genitive would still apply even to the sense of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), since the genitive is defined as the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). And the "remainder" is that which is other than what has been employed [in the definition of the other cases]. In that case, if the nominative were to apply even when there is an excess over the base-meaning, then the genitive would not occur, because that [base-meaning] too would have been employed in the rule prescribing the nominative.

Now, since the genitive case occurs in relation to the owner-possessed relationship and so forth by virtue of the power of the specific wording, it might also occur with respect to gender as an additional factor. Therefore, the mention of *mātra* (only) must first be made; and when that is done, the mention of *liṅga* (gender) and the rule *saṃbodhane ca* ("and in the vocative") must also be formulated, so that [the genitive] may occur even when there is an addition [of gender].

Why is there a mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*)? One might think that the first case ending is established by [the word's] meaning (*artha*) or its gender (*liṅga*), as in the examples *droṇaḥ* and *khārī*. The underlying intention is this: the first case ending occurs in that meaning without which the base form (*prakṛti*) would not be employed. And words such as *droṇa* do not deviate from their meaning, which is a measure made of metal or wood. However, when they refer to rice and the like measured by a *droṇa*, then because of that deviation, [the rule] would not apply.

Nor is the establishment [of the object] achieved through the apprehension of its mark (*liṅga*) alone—for by that [mark], there would only be the cognition of its mere excess; furthermore, the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "weight" (*unmāna*) and so forth, and thus it also occurs in cases such as "a *pala* of ghee."

Now, regarding the cases such as *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* ("salted soup") and *lavaṇaṃ śākam* ("salted vegetable"), how is it that the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used here? For the word *lavaṇa* does not deviate from denoting a substance belonging to the class "salt," whereas the word *saṃsṛṣṭa* ("mixed") does deviate [from its own specific meaning]. It is replied: this is a common term (*sādhāraṇaśabda*), like the word *akṣa* and others, which applies both to the class "salt" and to that which is mixed. And this is understood from the rule *lavaṇālluk* ("there is elision [of the suffix] after *lavaṇa*"). In that regard, just as the nominative occurs for the words *dadhi* and *dādhika*, so too will it occur here.

In that case, how is it that in the expression "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), the word "white" does not deviate from the quality itself, yet does deviate from that which possesses it, as seen in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth"? To this, [we reply]: even here, by the rule stating "the elision of the suffix *matup* is to be stated after words expressing qualities," the word remains common to both.

In that case, how is it that one says "the Vāhīka is a cow"? For the word "cow" does not deviate from that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, yet it does deviate from the Vāhīka. To this we reply: here too, the word "cow" is applied to the Vāhīka through the superimposition of the form of that which possesses a dewlap and so forth; just as it occurs in reference to that which possesses a dewlap, so too will it occur in reference to the Vāhīka.

If this is so, then the same would apply to cases such as *droṇaḥ* (a drona-measure) and *khārī* (a khari-measure); these would be common nouns like the word *lavaṇa* (salt), or secondary (*gauṇa*) terms like *gaur vāhīkaḥ* (the Vāhīka is an ox), or figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) terms like *gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ* (a hamlet on the Ganges). There is no other possibility; thus, the nominative case is established in every respect. Furthermore, just as the accusative and other cases occur in relation to things that are measurable, so too does the nominative occur.

Now, the inclusion of the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is so that the rule may apply even when there is a distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), as in the case of "rice measured by a *prastha*. If this were so, the instrumental case in *prasthena* would not occur; furthermore, if one intended to express a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the genitive case would not occur; and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *prāstika* would also not occur. Thus, the purpose of including the term "measure" is questionable.

The phrase "even though [the meanings] have been expressed" means that otherwise, because this [rule] forms a single syntactic unit with rules such as "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) under the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"), and because the restrictive enumeration beginning with "by means of verbal suffixes, primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds" (*tiṅkṛttaddhitasamāsaiḥ*) has been rejected, the numbers one and so forth would not be expressed by the words *eka*, *dvi*, or *bahavaḥ*, either because their meaning has already been expressed or because they are considered redundant. Thus: "one, two, many."

Now, one might ask: in cases such as *ekaṃ kṛtam* ("one [thing] was done"), how is it that the accusative case endings (*dvitīyā*) and so forth occur, given that there is no effort [of expression] directed toward them there? It is said in reply: in that instance, two types of meaning are present—namely, the object (*karman*) and so forth, and singularity (*ekatva*) and so forth. Even though singularity and the rest are already expressed, the accusative and other endings will still occur in order to express the object and so forth; however, in the present case (*iha*), they would not occur because there is no other unexpressed meaning [to be conveyed].

But surely, even here, substances qualified by oneness and so forth are denoted by words such as "one" (*eka*) and the like; in that case, the nominative case will serve to denote the quality of oneness and so forth extracted [from the substance], just as from words like "white," which denote a substance where the quality is subordinate, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs to denote the quality serving as the ground for application—e.g., "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śauklyam*). Thus, it would be possible not even to include the mention of "number" (*vacana*) [in the rule].

"What is the purpose of mentioning the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?"—the intention of the questioner here has already been stated. [The answer is: "In the case of a meaningless particle (*nipātasyānarthakasya*)," the sense is that [the designation of *karmapravacanīya*] would not otherwise apply because of the absence of meaning. Regarding the example "he hangs down" (*pralambate*): what, then, is sought by means of the nominative case here? It is the status of being a word (*padatva*).

This is established even by the sixth [case-ending]. For instance: the second case and others are prescribed for the objects (karman) and so forth, while the first case is prescribed for the mere meaning of the base (prakṛti). In that regard, when there is an absence of the base-meaning, yet a relationship such as that between owner and owned exists, the sixth case is established because it is distinct from those [other cases] not joined [to the base]. Nor is there a restriction of that [sixth case] to singularity and so forth; for this has already been answered. Thus, one must necessarily state only this much: "the first case [is used] for the mere gender of the meaning"; even the inclusion of the word "mere" (mātra) need not be made.

Why does [the suffix] not occur when there is a plurality of objects such as *karman* (the object)? Because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*); namely, that he says "and in the case of address" (*saṃbodhane ca*). For if it were to occur even in the case of plurality, that [rule] would be purposeless.

For the sake of the subsequent rule, one should simply have stated "the vocative [is called *samantrita*] when used in address"; what is the point of this formal split (*yogavibhāga*)? Here, because of the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) for the purpose of restriction, or because of the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule "and in address" (*saṃbodhane ca*), the nominative case should not occur when there is an addition [of meaning]. Consequently, in cases such as "the hero is a man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words, the nominative would not apply because the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*)—which is an additional meaning—is perceived. [To this we reply: No; because it is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).

The meaning here is as follows: that which is the surplus [in the sentence] is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Initially, the primary [case-ending] is prescribed for both [words], each being restricted to its own individual meaning; subsequently, however, when a mutual connection arises through the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the resulting comprehension of the specific [sentence-meaning] does not sublate the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) that occurred first, because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

Another says: the definition should be formulated as "the nominative [case-ending occurs] when [the agent, etc. is expressed" (*abhihite prathamā*). The meaning is that the nominative occurs when the agent and so forth are expressed by *tiṅ* suffixes and the like, as in *vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*, *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ*, *śatyaḥ*, and *prāptodako grāmaḥ*. In such cases, even where there is an excess [of qualifiers], as in *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*, the nominative is established because [the agent] is expressed. What is the fault here? [The rule would not apply] where there is no action, such as in *vṛkṣaḥ* or *plakṣaḥ*.

In that case as well, there is an action; how so? In the expression "The tree is a *plakṣa*," it is understood that "it exists. Here, however, in the phrase "He sits in the palace" (*prāsāda āste*), the palace is the single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) for both the action of being (*sadikriyā*) and the action of sitting (*āsikriyā*). That [substratum] is denoted by the suffix *ghañ* in the word *prāsāda*—derived from the root *prasad-* with the sense "that in which one settles"—but it is not denoted by the *tiṅ* suffix in the verb *āste*. In that situation, the nominative case would apply based on what is denoted by the suffix *sad*. Furthermore, where the intention lies in a connection with a qualifier—as in "The lotus is blue, not red"—there too [the nominative] would not occur, because of the absence of an action.

But another says: the rule is that the nominative case occurs when there is coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a finite verb (*tiṅ*). In a case such as "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), where the referent is identical to that of the finite verb, the nominative occurs. However, in "He sits on the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), because of the lack of coreferentiality, that [nominative] does not occur. And in cases such as "The hero is a man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), although there is an excess [of meaning], the nominative occurs because of the suitability for coreferentiality with a finite verb.

What is the fault here? In the derivation "Devadatta pacati" (Devadatta cooks), when the state "Devadatta pac laṭ" has been reached, as long as the *tiṅ* suffixes have not yet arisen, there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a *tiṅ*. Consequently, the restrictive rule that "only the first case ending [is applied]" does not apply. Thus, the case endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) prescribed without distinction for the word "Devadatta" remain in place. Since the condition for the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes—namely, non-coreferentiality with a non-first-case ending—is present, those two alone would occur, and there would be an absence of *tiṅ* suffixes. Yet, the injunction for *tiṅ* suffixes is not purposeless.

Because [the rule for] *tiṅ* and so on has scope [elsewhere], [one might argue] that "only the first case ending" is the intended meaning. However, this would mean that the very same domain would belong to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) as well—this is the fault. And this fault occurs in one of two alternative views. Which view? Regarding the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau*, there are two views: whether it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "not the first," or a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Similarly, in the section beginning with *karmaṇi dvitīyā*, a duality also arises: whether it should be a restriction of the case ending (*vibhaktiniyama*), or a restriction of the meaning (*arthaniyama*).

Thus, when a restrictive rule (*arthaniyama*) and an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) are adopted, this fault arises. How so? Under the restrictive rule "the second case [ending] alone is used for the object" (*armaṇi dvitīyaiva*), since the second case and the others would be non-restricted, they would occur even in the mere sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*); consequently, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, which depend upon those [case endings], would result. However, in the case of a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), since the first case ending also occurs there, the prohibition—which depends upon that [first case]—would apply, and thus there is no fault.

Because there is an absence of the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes when *tiṅ* endings are present, the first case ending alone occurs due to the rule of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), thereby excluding the second and subsequent case endings. However, when there is a restriction for the second and other case endings regarding their respective objects and so forth—namely, that the second case occurs only in the sense of an object (*karman*)—then in the absence of such an object, those [second-case endings] do not occur. Since the first case ending is unrestricted and remains in proximity, there is no possibility of applying the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes either through exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or by way of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

And in the absence of that [agent], since the nominative occurs only there because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the finite verbs (*tiṅ*), the nominative is excluded from the objects and other cases by this restrictive rule; thus, there is no fault. Now, one might object: even if the second case and others are absent there due to the lack of an object and so forth when the case-assignment is restricted, the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would still apply. For instance, if—on account of the restriction that the nominative occurs only in coreferentiality with finite verbs—the genitive were also restricted (like the second case and others) prior to that very rule, then its application there would not arise. But that [genitive] is characterized as being for the "residual" relation.

And where no restriction of another case-ending has been made, that is the *śeṣa* (remainder); consequently, because of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the finite verb (*tiṅ*), since it is still a *śeṣa* prior [to the application of the rule], the genitive would apply, and thus only the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would occur due to coreferentiality with that [genitive]. If it were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there would be no fault, as the nominative would also occur; but if it were a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there would indeed be a fault. True; in both cases, if it were an exclusion, the fault certainly remains.

In the Bhāṣya, however, even if there is an exclusion (paryudāsa) regarding the restriction of case-endings, there is no fault; thus, this statement is one made without firm conviction. The intended meaning is simply that this fault is merely occasional. Furthermore, some slight deviation from the formal text (udgrantha) must be excused, and so we shall conclude.
And [the vocative case is used] in addressing. 2.3.47.

And regarding the vocative: "making [something] present" means that when an object is established in a certain form, making that object present in that very form is the vocative; it does not, however, convey the fact that some meaning is to be performed, as in the case of a rule involving a single hearing (*ekaśrutividhi*), for that would be the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Making [something] present, however, is not the sentence-meaning, because if it were, then the first case ending (*prathamā*) would be established according to the principle that "the sentence-meaning is that which is additional," as in examples such as *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*.

That which is understood only when there is the association with another word is the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). However, in this case, when only "Devadatta" is uttered, the act of addressing (*ābhimukhyakaraṇa*) is understood; therefore, since the meaning of one word is merely an addition to the meaning of another word here, the genitive case would have applied. To address that, he says: "In the case of an addition to that, it is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Furthermore, addressing is not possible through an *ā* that is not established [by grammatical rules]—as in: "O King, be! Fight! Svāhā! O enemy of Indra, prosper!"

In examples such as *he pacan* and *he pacamāna*, although the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed for the vocative case, their capacity to denote the agent and other kārakas exists only when they are devoid of case-endings; this is just as the nominative case occurs by the rule "the [suffix] *loṭ* [is used] independently of reduplication. Alternatively, since that expressed meaning has become included within the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it will be covered by the preceding rule; the division of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
That which is addressed [is called *āmantrita*]. 2.3.48.

"Addressed" (*āmantrita*) means "that word-form which ends with it. The formulation of this great technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of understanding it as a descriptive designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): that which is an act of addressing (*āmantraṇa*) is called "addressed" (*āmantrita*). By a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), it refers to the word that serves as the instrument for that act. The intention is that when a suffix is mentioned in the formulation of a technical name, it includes that which ends in it, provided the mention is made by means of a case-ending.

In the examples, the acute accent on the initial syllable occurs by the rule *āmantritasya ca*. The inclusion of the word *sā* (that) is so that the designation [of vocative] may apply even to that nominative case ending which is prescribed for the expression of address by the rule concerning the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha-sūtra*)—as in *he pacan!* and *he pacamāna!*; for if that word were not present, the designation would apply only to that [nominative] which is prescribed by the immediately preceding rule, according to the principle: "A rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately contiguous."
The singular number [is used] for the vocative case. 2.3.49.

The term *ekavacanam* (singular) refers to the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*). In the example *he paṭo*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "there is *guṇa* for a short vowel" (*hrasvasya guṇaḥ*) in the vocative. Although it could have been stated simply as "the suffix *su* is the vocative," the inclusion of the term *ekavacanam* is for the purpose of designating that specific affix which expresses a single object (*ekaḥ arthaḥ ucyate yena*). Otherwise, to avoid a discrepancy in the grammatical framework, the designation would apply to the entire word ending in that suffix (*tadantasya*).
The sixth case-affix is used in the sense of the remainder (śeṣa). 2.3.50.

"The sixth case-affix [is used] in the sense of the remainder (śeṣa). "Remainder" means that which is other than what has been employed [in the formation of the word]; and since the meanings of the nominal stem (prātipadika-artha) ending with the object (karman) and so forth have already been employed, he says: "other than the object and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "But it is not possible for there to be a distinction from the object and so forth within the meaning of the nominal stem; why? Because a relation is impossible without an action, and because in every instance, those causes of relations—the object and so forth—must necessarily exist. To illustrate: in the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the king is the agent (*kartṛ*).

In the expression "the king gives wealth to the man," the meaning is understood as a transfer of property. In "the branch of the tree," it is well-known in common usage that the tree is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), yet according to the system of logicians (*tārkika*), it is the branch. However, in cases such as "Devadatta's cow," agency (*kartṛtva*) is perceived in relation to acts such as receiving—the cow being understood as Devadatta’s recipient, buyer, barterer, or seizer.

It is said: in the expression "he listens to the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*), the *śeṣa* (residual relation) consists precisely of the connection between action and its factor (*kriyākārakasambandha*). How so? Because of the inclusion of the term "instruction" (*upayoga*) in the rule *ākhyātopayoge*, the actor does not receive the designation of *apādāna* (ablative); and because he is not included in the restricted list of verbs such as *duh* and others, he does not receive the designation of *karman* (object) even though he is not explicitly mentioned [in the rule for *akathita*]. Therefore, this actor is a *kāraka* who is nonetheless a *śeṣa*.

As for what was stated—that because action and its causes exist everywhere, there is no distinction other than that of the meaning of the nominal stem—that is not so; for it is impossible to deny the relationship of ownership and owned, which is produced by acceptance, purchase, and so forth, and is well-known to all the world. Furthermore, if it were argued that even the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) exists everywhere according to the actual state of things, on the grounds that otherwise a relationship would be untenable in the absence of a mutual relation of beneficiary and benefactor, let it be so; there is no fault whatsoever.

For it is not the case that whatever exists according to the actual state of things must be expressed; rather, only that which is intended to be expressed produces its own grammatical suffix (*vibhakti*). In that regard, when there is an intention to express a relationship such as that between owner and owned, even though a relationship between action and factor (*kriyākāraka*) exists, it is not intended to be expressed; thus, in the absence of the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) will occur.

And thus, in cases such as "He remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) or "He should not eat black gram," even though a verbal action is heard—such as in "He imitates the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa"—the intention is merely the relationship, namely that the remembrance is connected to the mother; although the status of being an object (*karmatva*) exists, it is not intended to be expressed, and thus the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs. And it has been said:
"The relation is distinct from the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s); it is preceded by [the relation between] an action and its factor.
It is denoted whether the action is explicitly stated or unstated. |||

If it is argued that "the sixth case [suffix] is used for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*), there is a prohibition regarding the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). A relationship such as that between owner and owned is the meaning of the sixth case, and it resides in both [relata]. In that case, although the sixth case suffix is produced from only one [of the two], the relationship residing in both is understood; therefore, the sixth case does not occur from both. Nevertheless, it might sometimes occur even from the qualificand, and the nominative (*prathamā*) would not occur because of the presence of an additional factor—the relationship—or else, because the relationship constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

In this case, that which constitutes the predominance of the person is the sentence-meaning; because of the proximity of the word "of the king" (rājñaḥ), the connection of the person is understood. However, since the nominal stem *puruṣa* functions solely in its own primary sense, the nominative case will apply there and the genitive case will not.

This is what is meant: when the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) is uttered alone, its status as a relatum is understood as having an unspecified counter-correlate; however, upon the proximity of the word *puruṣa* (man), it is perceived as a qualified relation. Therefore, with respect to an unspecified possessor (*sva*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) first arises as the locus of that relation.

But surely, is there not a distinction created by the utterance or non-utterance of the genitive case-ending, such that you, sir, might as well utter the genitive even after the word *puruṣa* (person)? That distinction will indeed be understood. This is not well said; for the existence or non-existence of a meaning is not produced by the existence or non-existence of a word. Rather, it is the meaning itself—already existing and intended to be communicated—that serves as the cause for the employment of the expressive word.

In that context, because the quality (*guṇa*) is intended to be expressed as something that benefits another, the genitive case occurs at its end; however, because the primary substance (*puruṣa*) is the beneficiary and is intended to be expressed as self-contained, the nominative case occurs for it. Furthermore, the relation, having established itself upon the quality, touches the primary substance as well; and the quality, being engaged for the sake of benefiting the primary substance, assumes another form due to the impossibility of otherwise [accomplishing that benefit]. The primary substance, however, by virtue of being self-contained, does not assume another form. And it has been said: "Although this [relation] resides in both, it is distinguished [and attributed] to the qualities because they exist for the sake of another."
"In that case, being expressed [as a subordinate], it is also employed with respect to the principal.

When, however, the subordination of the person (*puruṣa*) and the predominance of the king (*rājan*) are intended to be expressed, then *puruṣasya rājñaḥ* is indeed possible. And when the connection of the house and so forth with the "king's man" is intended—such as in *rājñaḥ puruṣasya gṛham*—then the relationship of quality and principal belonging to even a single entity toward different objects is not contradictory; thus, the genitive occurs with both [words].

For by the genitive case in *rājñaḥ* (of the king), the relationship is expressed only between the king and the servant, not between the servant and the house. Here, regarding the meaning of the five [cases] within the base-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*), in rules such as "the second case in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the mention of *śeṣa* (remainder) could be omitted under the view that the meanings are restricted. How so? The meanings such as "object" (*karman*) are restricted, while the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is unrestricted. Consequently, when the second case and others, as well as the sixth case for the remainder, would all be applicable by the rule for *svādi* suffixes, the mere statement "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "only the sixth case [is used for the remainder]."

It occurs [in this way]. And where both the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and another suffix would apply, such a restriction applies; thus, by implication, it will occur only in the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Therefore, for the sake of the subsequent rule, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) must certainly be made. However, in the view that [the *kāraka*] consists of three [categories], so that the genitive does not apply to its own meaning (*svārtha*), one must prescribe as the "remainder" to be expressed (*vācyatvena vidhātavya*) something like "object" (*karman*) and so forth, just as with the accusative and other cases.

Likewise, under the view that [the genitive] is restricted to the "condition" (*pratyaya*), since the object (*karman*) and other relations are not restricted, the genitive would also apply to them; therefore, the mention of *śeṣa* ("remainder") must be made for the purpose of restricting the genitive so that it applies only to the *śeṣa* and not to the object and the rest.
The sixth case-affix is used for the instrument of a verb meaning "to know" when it is not derived from the root *vid* (to find). Pāṇini 2.3.51.

Regarding the rule *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.3.46): although one could have simply stated *vidarthasya jñaḥ karaṇe* to avoid ambiguity, the fact that he did not do so indicates that there is a word-break (*padaccheda*) after *avidarthasya*. Furthermore, the root *vid* with the elided suffix (*lugvikaraṇa*) is understood here, because the root *jñā* can only function in the sense of that [root *vid*]. Thus, he says: "of that which has the meaning of non-knowing (*avidartha*), i.e., of that which has the meaning of ignorance. In the example *sarpiṣo jānīte*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rules *apahnave jñaḥ* and *akarmakācca*. "Expressing activity" means occurring in relation to an activity preceded by knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "attached to ghee": attachment (*rāga*) is the cause of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). For instance, Kīcaka, being infatuated with Draupadī, embraced Bhīmasena in secret and said, "Oh, how exquisite the touch of such a noble woman! Or, regarding the phrase "or repelled" (*pratihito vā*): repulsion (*pratighāta*) is the cause of hatred (*dveṣa*), and hatred is the cause of false cognition. For example, someone who is habitually playful might point out an impure substance such as pus and say, "Drink this ghee. That person, being repelled by it, begins to hate ghee from that moment on; and for one who hates it, a cognition arises toward that very thing which is not actually what it is perceived to be.

If everything were indeed graspable, then ghee would be perceived in its own nature; this being the case, the state of being a non-object (avidarthatva) would not be possible. To this he says: "It is merely false cognition (mithyājñāna). The sense is that it does not perform the function of true cognition (jñānakārya). For the delimitation of an unconfused object is the function of cognition, and that is not performed by false cognition. In this view, since the action of water and so forth would lack an object, the ātmanepada suffix would be untenable according to the rule *akarmakācca*; therefore, he considers that the parasmaipada should be cited as the example.
The sixth case ending is used for the object of verbs meaning "to study," of the root √day (in the sense of compassion), and of the root √īś (in the sense of lordship). Pāṇini 2.3.52.

Regarding the rule *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi*: the root *iṅ* (meaning "to remember") includes the letter *k* for the purpose of distinction, so as to indicate that it should be employed only when preceded by the prefix *adhi*. [The phrase] "intended to be expressed as a residual factor" (*śeṣatvena vivakṣita*) means...

[Objection: But surely, when [the word] is intended as a *śeṣa* (remainder), the genitive case is already established by the preceding rule, as in "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*) or "he imitates the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa" (*anukaroti bhagavato nārāyaṇasya*). [Response: True; however, the present context is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that in this specific domain, the genitive case must indeed occur, it is heard [in usage], and it is not elided. What is thereby accomplished? The formation of a compound is precluded—as in "remembrance of the mother" (*mātuḥ smaraṇam*). This should be understood to apply everywhere in both the preceding and subsequent rules within this section.

If a compound were formed, the genitive case ending would be elided by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*; therefore, it is established that a genitive case prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) is not compounded. How, then, can there be a compound in the expression *viśeṣasmṛteḥ saṃśayaḥ*? It is said in reply: the prohibition of compounding applies only to the "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive; here, however, since the intention is to express the object (*karman*), the genitive will form a compound according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.

What, then, is the distinction here—is it a compound with a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), or with a genitive of grammatical function (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*)? This is the distinction: when there is a compound with a genitive of function, the accent of the suffix *kṛt* applies; however, when there is a compound with a genitive of relation, the final syllable of the compound would be udātta. This section [of the rule] is for the purpose of preventing such a final-udātta compound. Furthermore, where a genitive of function is prohibited—as in "remembered of the mother" (*mātuḥ smṛtam*)—there should also be no compound.

Thus, in this section, it should be understood that for both those [cases] not explicitly mentioned and those which serve as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), when used in conjunction with a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), a compound is formed with the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), and not with the genitive of the kāraka relation either. Regarding the word "guṇaiḥ": the meaning is that when the qualities (*guṇa*) are intended to be expressed as the residual relation (*śeṣatva*), because this restriction does not apply, the compound indeed occurs. This alone is the method for understanding the counter-examples in this section.
The affix *kha* is applied after the root *kṛ* when the sense is that of careful preparation.

Regarding *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne*: in the example *edhodakasya*, the singular form (*ekavadbhāvaḥ*) is applied by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*. In *upaskurute*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *gandhanādi-sūtra*, and the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *upāt pratiyatne*.
The sixth case ending is used after words expressing a state that denote pain, provided they do not signify the fever disease.

Regarding the rule *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanāmajvare*: the word *rujaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "breaking," either because it is listed in the *abhidhādi* group or by virtue of this very nipātana (irregular formation), resulting in the suffix *aṅ*. As for the phrase *bhāvavacanānām*: the meaning is not "of those that express a state" (*bhāvavācinām*), because there is no deviation from verbal roots expressing a state. What then? By the word *bhāva*, the "state" (*bhāva*) in its accomplished form, denoted by *ghañ* and other suffixes, is expressed. *Vacana* is a *lyuṭ* suffix used in the sense of the agent.

In this context, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is not intended to be expressed; for in the case of roots whose meaning is "to cause pain" (*rujārtha*), it is not possible for the "state" (*bhāva*) to be the speaker, the communicator, or the utterer. Therefore, only the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), namely the agent (*kartṛ*), is intended—meaning those [roots] for which the state is the agent. Thus he says: "of those whose agent is the state" (*bhāvakartṛkāṇām*). Regarding the example *caurasyāmayati* ("he causes the thief to suffer"): the root *am*, meaning "disease," belongs to the *curādi* group. Because of the statement in the *curādi* list that "others are not marked with *mi* except when preceded by a causal suffix" (*nānye mito'hetau*), the status of being *mit* does not apply here according to the rule *janījṛṣknasurañjo'mantāśca*.

The meaning is that only those roots which have been listed starting from *jñapa micca* up to, but not including, *nānye mito'hetau* become *mit* in the *curādi* group, and no others. In the case of *āmaya*, the *ec* substitute [for the final vowel] of the root *mīnāti* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* is prohibited by the rule *nimimīlīyāṃ khalacoḥ*, which prohibits the substitution of *ā* [prescribed by *mīnātiminoti...*]. In the expression "the riverbank breaks" (*nadīkūlaṃ rujati*), the river is the agent (*kartṛ*), not the state (*bhāva*).

Is it not the case that the word *ruj* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "disease," so that there is no application [of the rule] here? If so, this is merely shown as a direction for providing counter-examples; the actual counter-example is: *śleṣmā puruṣaṃ rujati* ("phlegm afflicts the man"), which means "it causes him to suffer from disease, such as coughing, and so forth. Regarding *jvarayati*: the root *jvara* meaning "disease" belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group. Regarding *santāpayati*: the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied by the rule *hetumati ca*; here, "torment" (*santāpa*) is the abstract state (*bhāva*), and the agent is the one who performs the torment.
The word *nātha* is used in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*). 2.3.55.

Regarding *nātha* in the sense of "blessing" (*āśis*): the form *nāthate* is derived through the addition of the rule "the root *nāth* [takes the ātmanepada suffixes] in the sense of blessing. Since this result would already be established by the fact that the root is marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudāttet*), the rule is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that *nāth* takes the ātmanepada only in the sense of blessing. Consequently, in the counter-example, the parasmaipada suffix is used.
The affix *khaś* is applied after the roots *jas*, *ni-prahan*, *naṭ*, *krāth*, and *piṣ* when used in the sense of injury. (Pāṇini 3.2.56)

Regarding the rule *jāsiniprahaṇanāṭakrāthapiṣāṃ hiṃsāyām*: [the inclusion of] *niprahaṇa* is because of the specific mention of *jāsi* and the statement "in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyām*), which implies that *hana* preceded by *ni* and *pra*—as far as possible—is intended. The substitution of *ṇa* in *niprahaṇa* occurs according to the rule *hanteratpūrvasya*. In *praṇihanti*, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs according to the rule *nergada-nada-pata-pada-ghu-mā-syati-hanti-yāti-vāti-drātipsāti-vapati-vahati-śāmyati-cinoti-dīvyati-muṣati-naṭati-nṛtyati*. *Naṭa* (in *nāṭa*) belongs to the *curādi* group meaning "to cause to flow down"; however, the root *naṭa* meaning "to dance," which is listed in the *ghaṭādi* group, is not included here because of the modified form of the citation. The lengthening of the vowel is due to a *nipātana* (special irregularity).

The inclusion of "ghaṭa" and so forth [in the Dhātupāṭha] is for the purpose that the designation *ṣit* may apply to them by extension according to the rule "ghaṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ," and so that the lengthening of the vowel may optionally occur according to the rule "ciṇṇamulordīrgho'nyatarasyām."
The genitive case is used after the roots *vyavahṛ* and *paṇ* when they have the same meaning [i.e., "to bet"].

[The rule applies] to the roots *vyava-hṛ* and *paṇ* when they have the same meaning. Regarding the phrase "when they have the same meaning" (*samarthayoḥ*): the word *saṃ* in the commentary has the same sense as *sama*; or rather, the view is that the single form [of *sam*] arises through a grammatical substitution (*nipātana*). It is not understood [here] as "having connected meanings," because of the [authoritative] explanation. For a relationship of cause and effect is indeed possible between *vyava-hṛ* and *paṇ*. *Śatasya vyavaharati*: he employs a hundred [coins] in the form of buying and selling, or he plays with it; such is the meaning. *Śalākāṃ vyavaharati*: he counts the tally-sticks; such is the meaning.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *div*, when it has that same meaning [as the preceding noun]). 2.3.58.

Regarding the rule *divastadarthasya*: here, the term *śeṣa* does not carry over [from the previous rule], because of the force of the commencement of the two subsequent rules. Now, one might ask: why was *divaḥ* not also recited in the previous rule itself? For if that were done, it would not be necessary to say *tadarthasya*. To this, he replies: "Because of the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*)."
The term *vibhāṣā* [is used] when a prefix (*upasarga*) follows. 2.3.59.
Regarding the rule *vibhāṣopasarge*: "He plays for a stake" (*śalākāṃ pratidīvyati*). Here, the root *div* functions in the sense of desiring victory and so forth, not in the sense of legal dispute.
The second [vowel] is called *brāhmaṇa* when it occurs before a consonant. 2.3.60.

The second [example] concerns the *brāhmaṇa*. A portion of the Veda distinct from the *mantra* is called a *brāhmaṇa*. [The example is: *gām asya tadahaḥ sabhāyām*. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: *gām asya sabhāyām*. The phrase *tadahaḥ* is the illustration; here, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, and the substitution of *r* by the rule *ahan*. Since the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been obligatory for a verb without a prefix (*anupasarga*), [the author asks]: "Now, since the sixth case would also have been obtained for a verb with a prefix (*sopasarga*) by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 2.3.62], why is this not stated for the sake of making the second case (*dvitīyā*) obligatory? To this he says: 'sopasargasya' etc. [This refers to Pāṇini 1.4.44, which restricts the application of the rule to verbs without prefixes.]
The sixth case affix is used after the words *preṣya* and *bruva* when they denote the deity to whom an oblation is offered.

Regarding the rule *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsaṃpradāne*: [the word] *iṣyate* refers to the root *iṣ* belonging to the *divādi* class. The mention of it by means of the suffix *śyan* (as *iṣyate*) is for the purpose of excluding the roots *iṣ* meaning "to desire" (*icchati*) and *iṣ* meaning "repetition" (*iṣṇāti*). "In that very scope" means ending in the second person singular present indicative (*loṭ*). "When the deity is the recipient" (*devatāsaṃpradāne*) means: the construction is that when the object (*karman*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) in a sense where the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), [the affix ṇamul is used]. "Of the oblation" (*haviṣaḥ*) means of a word denoting a specific kind of oblation. "Preṣya" [is the example].

The protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs in examples such as "brūhi preṣya. [In the injunction] "preṣya agnaye gomayāni," cow-dung (*gomaya*) is nowhere enjoined as a sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Regarding the phrase "of the oblation that has been set forth" (*prasthitasya*): the meaning is "of that which is qualified by the word *prasthita*. And this [phenomenon] occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), because the term "Vedic" (*chandas*) is specified later on.
In the Vedic language, the genitive case is frequently used in the sense of the dative. 2.3.62.

"In the Vedic language, the dative case is frequently used in the sense of the genitive. [As in] "yā kharveṇa" (she who with a small vessel). This explanatory passage (arthavāda) serves to prohibit a menstruating woman from drinking from a small vessel and so forth. Well then, should it be stated that "the dative is used in the sense of the genitive"? It need not be stated; for it is established by means of a formal division of rules (yogavibhāga).

The compound "caturthy-artha" is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound; rather, it should be analyzed as a *yoga* (rule) consisting of "caturthī" and "artha. The term "ṣaṣṭhī" is understood to follow [from the previous rule]: "the genitive occurs in the sense of 'artha,' and also the dative. In that context, since the prescription of both the genitive and the dative in their own respective senses would be redundant, the two case-endings are understood through their mutual proximity to apply to each other's meaning.
And [the suffix *lyuṭ*] occurs after the root *yaja-* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Pāṇini 3.3.117)
When a word expressing time is used in connection with a word having the sense of *kṛtvas* (times), it is placed in the locative case.

"When used in connection with words having the sense of *kṛtvas* (times), [the seventh case ending is used] for time as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The sense of *kṛtvasuc* is indicated here; those suffixes whose meaning is that of *kṛtvas* are called "having the sense of *kṛtvas*" (*kṛtvartha*), as in the example *pañcakṛtvaḥ*. [The rule] "after a numeral, when counting the repetition of an action, the suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added" [is applied]. [The example] *dvis* is formed by "the suffix *suc* is added after *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*. The inclusion of the word *artha* (sense) is for this specific purpose.
The sixth case ending is used for the agent and the object when a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix follows. (Pāṇini 2.3.65)

Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*: here, it is said that there is a means (*sādhana*) for the action (*kriyā*). Through the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), the action is brought into proximity; the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone expresses the action. And for the verbal root, there are two types of suffixes (*pratyaya*): *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. Among these, in the case of the employment of a *tiṅ* suffix, the prohibition [of the sixth case ending] by the rule *na lokāvyaya* must apply.

Furthermore, that [prohibition] must necessarily be stated for the sake of those forms where *l* has been substituted for *la*, such as *odanaṃ pacan*, *odanaṃ pacamānaḥ*, *papiḥ somam*, and *dadir gāḥ*; however, thinking that there is no purpose here for the mention of *kṛt*, he asks: "Why [is it said] 'in the case of *kṛt*'?"; [the example is given: *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*.

But surely, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "a mat was previously made by him" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamanena*), since the suffix *kta* is prescribed after a root with respect to the object, the object is already expressed by that very suffix, and thus the accusative case should not occur; and likewise, its exception—the genitive case—should also not apply.

Here too, because of the governing rule *anabhihite* (Pāṇini 2.3.1), a compound of the word *kṛta*—which requires *kaṭa* as its complement—is difficult to obtain; by this, the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is also explained. Therefore, is this construction simply incorrect? True; when there is a desire to express a specific distinction, neither the compound nor the secondary derivative occurs. However, when the suffix *kta* is produced in the sense of the object in general or in the abstract sense of the action—as in "he has previously made [something]"—then, since there is no longer a state of mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), a compound is possible by the rule *sup-supā*. Thereafter, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rules *pūrvādiniḥ* and *sapūrvācca*.

Nor is there an expression of "mat" (the mat) by means of the *kta* suffix; the *kta* suffix arising after the root *kṛ* denotes only the general object (*karman*), while its expression as a specific object occurs through its connection with that particular object. Furthermore, it is not possible here for that which has become a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhūta*) with the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) to be extracted and connected with "mat"; rather, the connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with the action—which is subordinate—is what occurs, as in: "he made a mat."

Furthermore, this word *kṛtapūrvī* is derived in the sense of "one who has previously done [it]," which is synonymous with "one who previously performed [it]. In that case, the status of the mat (*kaṭa*) as an object (*karman*) depends upon the action of "doing" (*karoti*), and since that [objecthood] is not already expressed [by a verbal suffix], the genitive case would apply according to the rule for *kṛd*-affixes.

Furthermore, the prohibition based on the *niṣṭhā* [past participles] applies only where there is a relationship between the agent and the object expressed by a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, as in "he made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kṛtavān*) or "the mat was made by Devadatta" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭo devadattena*). However, it has already been stated that in this case, there is no relationship between the mat and the act of making. Now, if it were argued that the prohibition applies to those agents and objects which are required by the action denoted by the verbal root within a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix, then this would not be the purpose of including the term *kṛt*; thus, that [objection] is also refuted.

If the mention of the *kṛt* suffix were not present [in the rule], then in the example "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook the rice-cake" (*kaṭaṃ kārayati pācayaty odanaṃ devadatto yajñadattena*), there would result the undesirable application of the genitive case for both the agent and the object (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook), which is the base of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

But if the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] were present, since the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not a *kṛt*, [the prohibition] would not apply; thus, how could it be refuted? Regarding the rule "not with words denoting worldly relations" (*na loka*), it is not understood there as "the agent or object belonging to the verbal root that forms the base of the *la*-affix"; rather, what is meant is that when an action is expressed—either primarily or as a subordinate quality—in a word ending in a *la*-affix, the genitive case is not used for the agent or object thereof. Therefore, this [objection] is also irrelevant.

Now, it might be argued: "In the rule *na lokāvyaya*, the mention of *kṛt* is for the purpose of qualifying the indeclinable (*avyaya*); therefore, in an expression such as *uccaiḥ kaṭānāṃ spraṣṭā* ('one who touches mats loudly'), even though [the word] is not a *kṛt*-derivative, there is no prohibition because it is an indeclinable. That too is not correct; we shall qualify the agent and the object by means of the indeclinable—namely, that the genitive case is not used for those which are the agent and object of an indeclinable—and the status of being an agent or an object is not possible for the indeclinable *uccaiḥ*.

In this case, then, in the word *karoti*, the term *kṛt* refers to the agent (*kartṛ*). Since the genitive case would already be established there by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.65], the restatement is made so that it may apply even when the agent is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*)—as in the example: *bhedikā devadattasya yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("Devadatta’s cutter of Yajñadatta’s wood"). Here, from the root *bhid* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *vuñ* are applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.87 and others; because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*) is predominant, the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) is primary, whereas the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*) is subordinate due to being subordinate to the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛtyartha*).

"In the proximity of both the primary and the non-primary [agent], the [genitive] would arise from the primary alone; however, because of the mention of the *kṛt* suffix, it occurs even from the non-primary. This too is not a purposeful restriction, for it is already established as being like the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*). For example, in such cases as 'the rice was cooked by Devadatta with Yajñadatta,' the instrumental occurs for both the primary and the non-primary agents. Why is that? Because there is no contradiction due to the absence of being expressed by a single word (*eka-śabda-vācyatva*), so the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) will likewise occur."

In this case, then, there is a purpose: so that a *bahuvrīhi* compound may apply according to the rule "when both [kārakas] are applicable, [the suffix is used] for the object" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*). Otherwise, because the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*) would not be explicitly stated, it would be a *tatpuruṣa* compound, and an undesirable consequence will be explained therein. If this is so, the mention of *kṛt* should be made only in the subsequent rule; or else, even when the external member is not explicitly stated, a *bahuvrīhi* will occur by virtue of interpretation, as in the rule "of the first monosyllabic [root], two [are substituted]" (*ekāco dve prathamasya*). Therefore, this mention of *kṛt* has a purpose that is open to question.

Some say that the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] here is for the purpose of excluding those [words ending in] *taddhita* suffixes. Thus, from *prajānāti* (he understands) comes *prajñaḥ*; *prajña* itself is *prājñaḥ*. When the *svārthika* suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *prajñādibhyaśca*, as in *vyākaraṇa-prājñaḥ* (one who is wise in grammar), the genitive case does not occur.

[Objection: But even if the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is made, why does [the sixth case ending] not occur here? For surely there is the employment of a *kṛt* suffix here; for it cannot be said that a connection with grammar by extracting [the base] from a *kṛdanta* word—which has already entered into a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhūta*) with the meaning of the suffix—is impossible, because the suffix is *svārthika* (meaningless in itself) and thus lacks a separate meaning. [Response: This is not a fault. By the force of the mention of *kṛt*, the sixth case ending will be understood to occur only in connection with a *kṛdanta* word. However, in this case, the connection is of one and the same form with both a *kṛt* and a *taddhita* suffix; therefore, it will not occur. Enough of this excessive scrutiny!

The word "remainder" (śeṣa) is excluded; therefore, since the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed where it was not previously obtained, this [genitive] forms a compound. Consequently, it is unnecessary to state that "the sixth case ending used in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded."
When both [the agent and the object] are possible, the sixth case ending is used for the object. (Pāṇini 2.3.66)

"When both [agent and object] are possible, [the sixth case ending is used] for the object. By the word "both," the agent and the object are connected because they are the subjects under discussion. "When both are possible" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, not a *tatpuruṣa*. This means: when the sixth case ending would apply to both the agent and the object. The purpose here will be stated as: "[it occurs] only for the object. However, the reverse restriction does not hold—that it occurs only for the object when both are possible.

For if it were so, the mention of *karman* (object) in the previous sūtra would be purposeless; therefore, one must rely on this very [sūtra] as a specific injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) regarding the abstract state (*bhāva*). Regarding the word *āścaryam*: when a *kṛt* suffix is prescribed after transitive roots in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which would otherwise apply to both the object and the agent is restricted by rule to the agent alone, thereby excluding it from the object.

And because of the mention of "attainment" (*prāpti*), the restriction applies only to that attainment; thus, even when both agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) are employed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for the agent. In the rule *antardhau yenādarśanamicchati*, since "himself" (*ātmanaḥ*) is understood, there is indeed the possibility of both [the agent and the object] being present. And here, by the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding," the application of the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* is restricted; however, the genitive of the remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) certainly remains for the object. The purpose of this restriction is so that the third case may optionally be heard [instead of the sixth].

When the object (*karman*) is also intended to be expressed as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), then the genitive of subordination (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) certainly occurs there as well. And because there is no prohibition for it by the rule "and [the genitive] in the case of the object" (*karmaṇi ca*), it also occurs in a compound. However, the purpose of that prohibition is so that the accent of the suffix *kṛt* (*kṛtsvara*) may not apply. This too has been indicated: that when the genitive would have been obtained by the preceding rule, it is restricted [to this specific case]. "This is a marvel" is one sentence; to the question "What is it?", he says: "of the rice" (*odanasya*).

In this case, because there is a multiplicity of factors—namely, that the rice (*odana*) is the object (*karman*) in the act of cooking (*pāka*), while the Brahmins are the agents (*kartṛ*) in the act of appearing (*prādurbhāva*)—the suffix *kṛt* applies to both, resulting in the form *bhedikā*. In cases such as synonyms, the suffix *ṇvuc* is used, as in *cikīrṣā*. Here, by the rule "after a suffix beginning with a vowel," the third case ending does not occur for the agent in either instance. However, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is established even when there is a desire to express the residual relation (*śeṣa*). A compound also occurs here, as in *dharmajijñāsā devadattasya* ("Devadatta’s desire to know dharma") or *śiṣyasyācāryaśuśrūṣā* ("the pupil’s service to the teacher"), according to the rule "optionally in the residual sense" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*).

In that regard, when the third case (instrumental) is necessarily prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), then—due to the prohibition [contained] in Pāṇini’s rule "karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇ. 2.3.66)—the compounds *pāṇineḥ sūtrakṛtiḥ* ("Pāṇini’s composition of sūtras") and *ācāryasya śabdānuśāsanam* ("the teacher’s instruction in words") would be incorrect; however, the forms *pāṇineḥ sūtrakṛtiḥ* and *ācāryasya śabdānuśāsanam* are indeed correct.
And [the sixth case ending is used] for that which has been mentioned in relation to the present time. 2.3.67.

Regarding "and [the suffix] *kta* [is used] in the sense of the present": in the expression *rājñāṃ mataḥ* ("approved by the kings"), the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the present according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*. Regarding "because of the understanding of the remainder": he rejects the need for a formal addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Even though the status of the student as the agent exists here, it is not intended to be expressed and thus remains hidden; rather, only the mere relationship (*saṃbandhitva*) is intended to be expressed. Consequently, the genitive case is established just as in the example *māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("he should eat beans"). Such being the case: the sense is that this would not be established if one were to rely on a formal addition.
And [the sixth case ending is used] after a word expressing the locus (adhikaraṇa). 2.3.68.

And [the genitive is used] after a word expressing the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). When that [locus] is employed, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs. Wherever it is possible for the agent alone to be expressed, there it is used in the sense of the agent—as in "this is the place where they sat" (*idameṣām āsitam*). However, when the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the locus after transitive verbs, since both the agent and the object are unexpressed (*anabhihita*), the sixth case is applied to both—as in "this is the food eaten by them" (*idameṣām bhuktam odanasya*).

The restriction "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object" applies specifically to the case where there is the possibility of applying the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows. Why is the word *vāci* ("in speech") mentioned? If only "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) were stated, it would be understood as an indicator for the *kta* suffix; consequently, the genitive would occur even in the employment of a *kta* suffix produced from roots such as *dhruva* (to endure) that have shifted to another meaning.

However, when there is the mention of speech (*vācigrahaṇa*), the genitive case occurs only when that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the agent (*kartṛ*); otherwise, when it is another word-meaning, the instrumental occurs for the agent and the accusative for the object—as in "they sat here" (*ihaiir āsitam*) or "he went to the village" (*grāme gataḥ*). Here, regarding the sense of motion (*gatyartha*), there is a fourfold variety: "this has been gone by them" (*idam eṣāṃ gatam*) in the sense of the locus; "these have gone" (*ime ete gatāḥ*) in the sense of the agent; "here has been gone by them" (*iha ebhir gatam*) in the neuter sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*); and when the agent is intended to be expressed, "this has been gone by them" (*idam eṣāṃ gatam*), where the same form is used when the remaining relation (*śeṣa*) is intended.
The sixth case-affix is not used after words ending in *loka*, *avyaya*, *niṣṭhā*, *khalartha* suffixes, or *tṛn*.

[The rule] "not [after a word ending in a vowel] with *loka*, *avyaya*, *niṣṭhā*, or [affixes having the sense of] *khalartha* or *tṛn*" applies here. Because there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of destroying the intended form, there is no *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in the term *tṛnām*. Regarding "u-uketi": by this, he demonstrates the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *u*. In that case, according to the rule "laśca" (Pāṇini 1.3.8), if it were a prior *dvandva* compound, the vowel *u* would have to be placed first; even if it were a posterior *dvandva*, the form would have to be *lavuketi*.

Therefore, having first formed a *dvandva* compound of the two following [elements], the *dvandva* of the word *la* should subsequently be made. Because it is qualified by the letter *u*, the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; and because of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), even the simple [form] is included. Thus, regarding the rule *śatṛśānacau*: the implication is that for the sake of including *śānac*, one need not resort to the *pratyāhāra* *tṛn*. Regarding the rule *kikinau ca*: [an objection is raised]—"But surely, by the mention of *la*, it is proper to include the *lakāras* and their substitutes, as in *kaṭaṃ kārayāñcakāra* and *odanaṃ pācayati*."

The inclusion of *kikin* [in the rule] is improper because they lack the status of being verbal roots (*dhātu*) and because they are substitutes for *al*. This is not a fault; by the rule "the *liṭ* and *kikin* [are treated as such]," an extension of the status of *liṭ* (*liṭtva-atideśa*) is effected, not the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *liṭ*. In that regard, the prohibition observed in cases such as *kārayām* and *pacānaḥ*—which involve *liṭ* and its substitutes—will likewise apply to *kikin*. In all the examples, there is a prohibition of the genitive case of the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*).

The residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), however, certainly occurs—as in *brāhmaṇasya kurvan* ("acting for the Brahmin"), *odanasya pacan* ("cooking the rice"), *apāṃ perur asi* ("you are the drinker of waters"), *narakasya jiṣṇavo guṇaiḥ* ("victorious over Naraka by means of his qualities"), and *tāni dviṣadvīryanirākariṣṇuḥ* ("overcoming the prowess of those enemies"). Regarding the word *āgāmukam*: by the rule *laṣapatapada-* etc., the suffix *ukañ* is applied; the meaning is that the *rakṣas* demons are habitually coming toward Vārāṇasī for the sake of being released from curses and so forth. In the example *dāsyāḥ kāmukaḥ*, the mention [of the genitive] is for the purpose of excluding the accusative; the genitive, however, is established simply through its status as a residual case.

Regarding the phrase *purā sūryasya*: the suffix *tosun* is applied by the rule *bhāvalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 3.4.16). Regarding *visṛpa*: it will be established that in these rules—*sṛpitṛdoḥ kasun*, *pūṅyajoḥ śānan*, *tācchīlyavayovacanaśaktiṣu cānaś*, and *iṅdhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi*—the term *la* does not recur; therefore, thinking that [the application of the suffix] would be unestablished due to the mention of *la*, he says: "The mention of *tṛn* is a reference to a *pratyāhāra*."

"Regarding the statement 'the word [ending] in the suffix *śatṛ* after the root *dviṣ*': the meaning is that when this suffix *śatṛ*—as in the rule *dviṣo'mitre* (Pāṇini 3.2.131)—is employed, a prohibition [of the sixth case] should be stated optionally. However, as for the refutation [of this requirement]: since one may intend to express the remaining relation (*śeṣa*) by means of the sixth case, and in other instances by the second case; and because there is a prohibition of compounding with the present participle (*sat*), there is no need to prescribe a sixth case of the agent (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*) for the sake of the accent of the compound."
The sixth case affix is used after a word denoting a creditor when it signifies a future debt. (Pāṇini 2.3.70)

Regarding the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*: the suffix *in* is applied to the root *ak* when denoting future time, while it is applied to *an* when denoting debt (*ādhamarṇya*). However, Bhartṛhari’s opinion is that the principle of "correspondence of number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) does not apply here, based on the explanation [of the commentators]. Thus we have *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"). One might object: "But surely there is no occasion for the genitive case here; why? Because it was stated under the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi* (P. 2.3.12): 'What is the purpose of mentioning the accusative? Is it not so that the dative alone might be optionally used, so that it would also occur in the domain of exceptions, as in *grāmasya gantā*? This is true."
Since the prohibition is already established by the Śruti itself, he considers that there is no need to rely on the force of the mention of the accusative case.
Or [the genitive case is used] for the agent of actions denoted by *kṛtya* suffixes. (Pāṇini 2.3.71)

"Or [the genitive is used] for the agent of kṛtya-affixes. Why does the question ask "Why 'for the agent'? Since it is stated that "only for those two [agent and object] are the kṛtya, kta, and khal-artha affixes prescribed," and because kṛtyas are prescribed after intransitive verbs in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) and after transitive verbs in the sense of the object (karman), it is possible that the agent alone is not expressed by them. Thus, even though both agent and object are under discussion [in the governing rule], the genitive will occur only for the agent—this is the question. In the example *geya* ("to be sung"), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *bhavyageya*. In the example *sāmnām* ("of the Sāmans"), the genitive necessarily occurs in the sense of the object.

Regarding the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, the *kṛtya* suffix [is used]": the meaning is that when a *kṛtya* suffix occurs where both agent and object are applicable, the genitive case does not apply to either the agent or the object. In the example *kraṣṭavya*, since the root *kṛṣ* is transitive, the *kṛtya* suffix is applied to the primary object and not the secondary one; therefore, the genitive case, which would otherwise be applicable to both the object and the agent, does not occur.

This is obtained through the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). How so? *Kṛtyānām* is one rule; here, the phrase "not [when] both [would otherwise apply]" (*neti ca*) also carries over. The meaning is that when *kṛtya* suffixes are employed where both [the agent and the object] would simultaneously be applicable, the genitive case does not occur for the agent. Following that, *kartari vā* (or [the genitive] for the agent); here, only "genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) continues to apply, while everything else has ceased.
When used with words meaning "equal" (*tulya*), or with the words *atula* and *upamā*, the third case ending is optionally employed. (Pāṇini 2.3.72)

"With words having the same meaning as *atula* and *upamā*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is optionally used. The intention is that the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is governed [by this rule], because it is prescribed in the domain of the remainder. Since the use of the plural number itself establishes that there is no grasping of the word-forms themselves, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of including those words which express similarity independently of other words. By this, particles such as *iva*, which are mere indicators (*dyotaka*), are excluded—examples being *gauriva gavayaḥ* ("the gavaya is like a cow") and *yathā gaus tathā gavayaḥ* ("as is a cow, so is a gavaya"). [An example with *tulā* is: *tulā devadattasya* ("the balance of Devadatta").

The words *tulā* and *upamā* are nouns derived from the action (*karmasādhana*) and have the sense of "equal. In that context, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is prohibited, but the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) certainly occurs. Here, in the phrase "having a clear likeness with Śambhu who is white as snow" (*sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā*), even when joined with the word *upamā*, the third case occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), because that word is derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*), as in the example "that by which something is compared" (*upamīyate 'nena*);

otherwise, the third case would have been carried over [from the previous rule]. Since that [third case] was heard in the immediately preceding sūtra, and since there is no other purpose for the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally), that very [third case] is what is carried over by the particle *ca*.

And the fourth case [is used] with words meaning long life (āyuṣya), prosperity (madra), auspiciousness (bhadra), welfare (kuśala), happiness (sukha), purpose (artha), and benefit (hita). (Pāṇini 2.3.73)

The fourth [type of compound] occurs with words for long life (*āyuṣya*), auspiciousness (*madra*), welfare (*bhadra*), well-being (*kuśala*), happiness (*sukha*), purpose (*artha*), and benefit (*hita*). Having formed a *dvandva* compound of the words beginning with "long life" and ending with "happiness," a *bahuvrīhi* is then prescribed with the word "purpose" (*artha*). Consequently, there is a connection between each of these—beginning with "long life"—and the word "purpose. Regarding this, some say that since the words *madra* and *bhadra* are synonyms, the word *bhadra* need not be mentioned in the sūtra. Others, however, maintain that the word "purpose" (*artha*) is also a distinct cause [for the application of the rule], and based on the commentaries, they explain that the term "purpose" (*artha*) is to be understood in all cases. Even in the Vṛtti, the word "purpose" (*artha*) is sometimes cited as an example.

Regarding the example *hitam devadattasya* ("beneficial for Devadatta"): since the rule "the fourth case is to be prescribed in connection with *hita*" finds its application in cases other than blessings (*āśis*), one considers that in the case of a blessing as well, there must be an option (of using the fourth case) even when connected with *hita*; otherwise, the inclusion of the word *hita* here would be purposeless.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
In the *Kāśikāvṛtti* [or] the *Padamañjarī*:
now, the fourth quarter of the second chapter— “The *dvigu* compound takes the singular number” (2.4.1).

Regarding the rule *dvigurekavacanam* (P. 2.4.1): if "singular" (*ekavacana*) were taken here in its technical sense, then the singular would not occur in the subsequent usage—as in *pañcapūlīyaṃ śobhanā*—because that [compound] is not a *dvigu*. Furthermore, the rule would have been stated with an ablative case as *dvigoḥ*. Therefore, considering that this refers to the term "singular" in its etymological sense, he says: "the expression of one is the singular."

It is called *vacana* because it speaks (*vakti*); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The term *ekavacanam* is a compound formed with a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) meaning "the speaking of a single object" (*ekasyārthasya vacanam*). In this context, the initial statement is made in general terms, namely that it is the designator of a single object; subsequently, when there is an expectation as to what that [single object] is, it is connected with the masculine form *dvigu*, which accounts for the neuter gender of the word *ekavacanam*. He clarifies this very point by saying: "of a single object."

And thus, a *dvigu* compound becomes the designator of a single object (*ekārtha*). If the meaning of the *dvigu* is one, yet it cannot be established as having a single meaning—even by a hundred statements—for that which is in reality multiple meanings, then the extension [of the rule] is understood by implication. To this he says: "In this manner. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*) used to introduce the statement, he asks: what is being said? He replies: "The meaning of the *dvigu* becomes a single unit (*ekavadbhavati*). And this refers specifically to the *samāhāra-dvigu*.

The purpose [of the rule] is so that the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) does not apply to a *dvigu* compound used in the sense of a derivative suffix (*taddhita*), as in the example "cloths purchased for five cows" (*pañcagavaḥ paṭāḥ*). Now, even if the mention of "aggregate" (*samāhāra*) is made, why does it not apply here: "five bundles and five bundles are [collectively] five bundles" (*pañcapūlī ca pañcapūlī ca pañcapūlyaḥ*)? Since the remaining form is a *dvigu*, would the singular form not result for its meaning? No, indeed.

Because it is external (*bahiraṅga*): this meaning of the *dvigu* compound is external because it arises only when the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder formation) has already occurred; since the *ekavadbhāva* (singular treatment) arises later, it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and was already fulfilled by the primary, initial meaning of the *dvigu*. Therefore, the singular treatment will not apply here. If that is so, would the same not also happen in cases such as *pañcagavaḥ paṭāḥ* ("five-cow cloths")? True; [but there is a distinction].

When cloths are made individually by five cows each, or when many cloths are made together by five cows, this is not the domain of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one). If, then, there is a mention of the *samāhāra-dvigu* (collective dvigu), there is no need for this [rule]; why? Because "collection" (*samāhāra*) means a group (*samūha*), and because that is singular, the singular number will apply, as in the cases of "a herd" (*yūtha*) or "a forest" (*vana*).

If, then, the word *samāhāra* is derived as a *karmasādhana* (denoting the object) in the sense that "that which is brought together (*samāhriyate*) is a *samāhāra*," then the meaning of the compound would be five bundles (*pañcapūlāḥ*) whose mutual dependence has been established; in that case, since there is the contingency of using the plural number, the following rule is introduced: "Because a word is produced for each substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) and because of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with number, the singular number is prescribed for a *dvigu* compound. Thus he says: [the singular is used] because a word arises for each substratum and because of coreferentiality with number, the singular number is ordained for a *dvigu*.

The substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substance (*dravya*); the word "five" (*pañca*) and others denote number. When a substance qualified by a particular number is expressed, a verbal form capable of denoting that [substance] arises. By the word *pañcapūlī*, five bundles (*pañcapūlāḥ*) being collected together are expressed; therefore, because there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the meaning of the compound and words such as "five," the singular number is prescribed to prevent the contingency of the dual or plural numbers—this is the meaning.
