By the phrase "due to coreferentiality with a number" (*saṃkhyāsāmānādhikaraṇyāt*), he shows that the word *samāhāra* functions as a *karmasādhana* (a noun denoting the object). However, if it were a *bhāvasādhana* (denoting the action or state), there would be a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between "five" and "baskets. Regarding the statement "or rather, because the aggregate is one" (*na vā samāhāraikatvāt*), the meaning is as follows: the *samāhāra*—which is an aggregate whose internal distinctions are obscured—is the referent of a *dvigu* compound. Since this [aggregate] is singular, the use of the singular number is established just as in the case of a forest (*vana*) and so forth; therefore, there is no need for this rule (*sūtra*).

And one must necessarily resort to a collective compound (*samāhāra*) that functions as a substantive (*bhāvasādhana*); otherwise, in the case of *pañcakhaṭvī* (a collection of five beds), which ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, the shortening of the vowel in the word *khaṭvā* would not occur because it would not be a secondary member (*anupasarjana*). It is a secondary member because it is not specified by the first case ending and because it possesses multiple case endings.

In the sense of an abstract action (bhāvasādhana), however, there is a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of five beds; thus, in the expression *samāhāraṃ samāhāreṇa*, even though the meaning of the compound is connected with various case endings, the word *khaṭvā* always ends in the genitive case. Consequently, by the rule *ekavibhakti ca*, it becomes a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), and its shortening is established. The requirement that it be in the singular number must indeed be applied for the sake of subsequent rules. As in *pañcapūlī*: since it is feminine because of the rule "a *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in *a* is used in the feminine," the suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *dvigoḥ*.
And a copulative compound (dvandva) is formed of words denoting parts of living beings, musical instruments, and divisions of an army. 2.4.2.

"And a *dvandva* [compound] consisting of parts of living beings, musical instruments, and army units [is singular]. Here, if a certain member of a *dvandva* denotes a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), another denotes a part of a musical instrument (*tūryāṅga*), and another denotes a part of an army (*senāṅga*)—as in "hands, drummers, and horse-riders"—then even though its members are intermingled, it would still be a *dvandva* of limbs of living beings and so forth, and thus the rule for singular status (*ekavadbhāva*) would apply. To this, he says: "Of the word *aṅga*, etc."

[Objection: Is it not the case that even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word *aṅga* is complete in each [individual] instance, for a single member (*aṅga*) of living beings, musical instruments, or an army is not possible? [Response: If so, then the word *aṅga*—which already possesses the plural ending as the form of the members themselves—is connected with each [instance], rather than being first completed in each instance and subsequently connected with the plural ending. Thus, three sentences are produced. The intention is that the Sūtra itself is merely a mnemonic statement (*grahaṇaka-vākya*) for those very [sentences].

In this regard, by the first rule, a *dvandva* compound consisting only of parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) is prescribed to be singular; by the second, a *dvandva* of musical instruments (*tūryāṅga*) with musical instruments; and by the third, a *dvandva* of military units (*senāṅga*) with military units—thus there is no possibility of confusion. Likewise, the phrase "of musical instruments" requires that the *dvandva* becomes singular; here the word *aṅga* signifies "auxiliary," whereas in the preceding and following cases it signifies "component part. The phrase "of military units" requires [the same] as before. For example: *pāṇipādam*.

In this case, since the formation would already be established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, the present statement is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of a *vyatikara* (cross-over) compound. Examples include *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* ("the drummers and the pan-plyers"), where the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *śilpam*. In *vīṇāvādaka* ("lute-player"), the compound is formed according to the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*; here, *vipañcī* is a synonym for *parivādinī*, and one who makes a living from that is a *parivādaka*. However, in cases such as *paṇavamṛdaṅgam* ("the small drums and the clay drums"), the formation is already established by the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* alone. An example is *rathikāśvāroham* ("charioteers and horsemen").

How can it be that [the army] is "crowded with chariots, horses, infantry, and female elephants," given that when there is a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*), the neuter short vowel ought to apply? Poets are unrestrained; or rather, it should be explained as: "female elephants together with chariots, horses, and infantry are 'chariot-horse-infantry-elephants' (rathavājipattikariṇyaḥ), and by them it is crowded."

Beginning with *dvandvaśca* and ending with *vibhāṣā samīpe*, he raises the objection that this entire section should not have been commenced, stating *itaretarayoga* etc. His point is that since the singular number is already established [by other rules], the section is therefore unnecessary. He refutes this, saying *idaṃ tu*. To the question "What then is this distinction of scope? he replies: *prāṇyaṅgādīnām*.

But how is it that the statement, "How then does a *dvandva* compound of parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth become singular? has the meaning that for parts of living beings and so forth, there is only a collective (*samāhāra*) [compound]? It is because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). For here the expression is manifested in this way: "That *dvandva* which is singular becomes one of these [categories]," and not by restating that "the *dvandva* which belongs to parts of living beings and so forth" and then prescribing its singularity.

A *dvandva* compound ending in the singular is a collective *dvandva* (*samāhāra-dvandva*). Since that is already established by the rule "a *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*)," the restriction "that alone [applies] to these" is effectively achieved. Furthermore, in cases such as *dadhi-payas* (curd-milk) and so on, for those compounds like *brahma-prajāpati* where the restriction would not otherwise apply by virtue of this specific context, the *dvandva* already obtained by the rule "a *dvandva* in the sense of 'and'" is here prohibited.

By relying on the interpretation that "that which is a singular-number *dvandva* does not belong to these," even for those cases such as *dadhipayasī* (curd and milk) where the restriction "for non-living things, [the *dvandva* is singular] when they are of the same genus" (*jātir aprāṇinām*) would otherwise apply, although a prohibition of that restriction is appropriate according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding," nevertheless—because of the association with terms like *brahman* and *prajāpati*, which require only that the *dvandva* be singular—the prohibition applies solely to the collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva*, and not [to the distributive one].
This is a restrictive rule (*niyama*). We shall explain the purpose of the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) regarding trees and so forth in that very place.

Now, why is it not understood in this way—that in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) is prescribed where it was previously unobtained? It is said in reply: if the singular form were prescribed for a *dvandva* compound formed by mutual conjunction, then the collective suffix *ka* (as in *dvandvāt cudaṣahāntāt*) based on a collective sense (*samāhāra*) would not occur.

However, in the case of *dadhi-paya-ādi* (curd-milk, etc.), the singular number that would otherwise apply to a *dvandva* compound must be prohibited; for even if the singular number of a collective *dvandva* (*samāhāra-dvandva*) is prohibited, the dual and plural numbers would still not occur because of the absence of duality and plurality [in the collective sense]. Therefore, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) must indeed be accepted here, and in this matter, the commentary itself is our only refuge.

Now, even if this is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*), why does it function in this way—that there is a restriction only to the collective compound (*samāhāra*) of parts of living beings and so forth—and not rather that there is a collective compound only of parts of living beings and so forth? It is said in reply: for if it were understood in that way, then in cases such as *dadhi-payas* (curd-milk), where a restriction by this section would not otherwise apply, the prohibition [of the dual] would be redundant; likewise, the mention of the dual number in the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* would be purposeless.

In the case of the *taddhita*, collective (*samāhāra*), and *dvandva* [compounds], there is the possibility of a singular number in the expression *tiṣyapunarvasvidam*. To prevent the occurrence of the dual number in such instances, if the restriction you have stated were valid, then that [rule] would be purposeless; for in this context, since Tiṣya and Punarvasu are not explicitly mentioned, there would be no collective *dvandva* compound. Therefore, the very nature of the restriction as stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* is faultless.
In a derivative formation (*anuvāda*), [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting lineages (*caraṇa*). 2.4.3.

Regarding the mention of *caraṇas* (Vedic schools): the word *caraṇa* is primary when referring to the various Vedic branches such as the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas, and secondary when referring to the persons who study them. Since both of these are designated by the technical term "gotra" according to the rule "gotra and caraṇas [form a compound]," and since the singular form for words denoting Vedic branches is established by the rule "for non-living beings, a class-name is singular," it follows that even the secondary sense—referring to the persons—is what is intended here. Thus he says: "the word *caraṇa* is based on the Vedic branch (*śākhā*)," meaning it is based on the study of a particular branch.

In some places it is read as "gauṇa" (secondary), and in others it is not. Regarding the phrase "of that which is understood through another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntarāvagatasya*): a "means of knowledge other than verbal testimony" (*pramāṇāntara*) refers to perception and so forth. The word "mere" (*mātra*) is used for the purpose of excluding [the notion of] comprehension. [Objection: But the employment [of a word] is for the sake of conveying a meaning; if that meaning has already been understood through another means of knowledge, why is the word employed? [Response: It is for the sake of enjoining another action (*kāryāntaravidhānārtham*).

For when an agreement has been made by us two that we must go there once the *Kaṭha-kalāpa* texts have been recited, and he remains sitting while having forgotten it, then this is said to him: "Has he not risen for the *Kaṇṭha-kalāpa*? Why do you sit? Those who study what was taught by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhas*. [The suffix] *ṇini* is applied because they are pupils of Vaiśampāyana; then, by the rule *kaṭhacarakālluk*, the suffix is elided. From the word *kalāpin*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule beginning with *sabrahmacārī*, the *ṭi*-portion is elided after a stem ending in *n*. In both cases, the suffix *adhyetṛ* (*aṇ*) is elided.

By this, the *Kauthuma* [branch] is explained. As for the statement "when there is instruction by word from the very beginning": the meaning is that it is the primary communication by means of a word of something not previously understood through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding *udaguḥ*: the substitution of *jus* for *jhi* occurs by the rule *ātaḥ*; the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by the rule *usyapadāntāt*. "Adyatanī" is the technical name for the *luṅ* [tense] used by ancient teachers. Regarding *anandiṣuḥ*: the root is *ṭunadi* in the sense of "prosperity"; the substitution of *jus* occurs by the rule *sijabhyasta*. **Pāṇini 2.4.4**: *adhvaryukraturanapuṃsakam* (The compound denoting the ritual of the Adhvaryu priests is neuter).

"The word *adhvaryu-kratu* is not neuter. The word *adhvaryu* is well-known as a specific name for a priest (*ṛtvij*), and it is not appropriate for it to qualify a sacrifice (*kratu*), for there is no sacrifice in which the *adhvaryu* is not involved, nor is there any in which he alone is involved. Since the primary meaning is impossible, he states that it is taken in a figurative sense: "*adhvaryu-veda*. This means the *Yajurveda*; for therein the duties of the *adhvaryu*—both the nature of the ritual acts and their procedure—are prescribed.

And the instruction regarding the result is the prescription [of the rule]: "of words denoting the *adhvaryu* and the *kratu*, provided they are not neuter. How then is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sūtra? He says: "*adhvaryukratur*"—the meaning is that because it possesses such constituent parts, the *dvandva* compound itself is expressed in that way. If, however, by the term "not neuter" (*anapuṃsakam*) the *dvandva* were meant in its primary sense, then this would be understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "it is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*).

Furthermore, when an interpretation without contradiction is possible, a contradictory one is not logical. *Arka* and *Aśvamedha* together form *arkāśvamedham*; *Sāyāhna* and *Atirātra* together form *sāyāhnātirātram*;

and *iṣu* and *vajra* likewise. These are prescribed in the Sāmaveda. The words *Rājasūya* and *Vājapeya* are listed among the *ardharca* group; therefore, they serve as counter-examples, being neuter in gender.
For those whose names are not separated by the study [of the Veda], [the suffix -yaḥ is applied]. 2.4.5.

"By reason of study, [the name] of those whose names are not remote. Here, the word *ākhyā* (name) refers to mere sound—defined as "that by which something is named"—and does not refer exclusively to conventional (rūḍhi) words. To avoid ambiguity, the term is analyzed as *aviprakṛṣṭa-ākhyānām* rather than *viprakṛṣṭa-ākhyānām*, because the latter would imply "those whose names are remote" due to the absence of the prefix *avi-*; thus, the compound is resolved as *aviprakṛṣṭa*. Furthermore, this lack of remoteness does not pertain to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the name itself, but rather through its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), which in this context is "study. This is why he says: "by reason of study."

*Adhītiḥ* means study (*adhyayana*). By means of study, that is, from the perspective of study (*adhyayanataḥ*), the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *ādi*. Because the study, which serves as the cause for their application, is not remote, those whose designations are not remote by way of that [study] are called "those whose designations are not remote from study" (*adhyayanato'viprakṛṣṭākhyāḥ*). He states this very point: "by means of study as the cause," and so forth. Regarding the term *padakakramakam*: one who studies the *padas* (word-texts) is a *padaka*; the suffix *vun* is added after *krama* and others, thus forming *kramaka*.

Commentary: *Saṃhitā*; one who studies that is a *vārttika*, [the suffix] *ṭhak* being applied because it belongs to the *ukthādi* group. Here, he demonstrates the non-separation (*aviprakarṣa*) of the study, which is the cause for the application [of the term]: "recitation" (*saṃpāṭha*). "Recitation" (*saṃpāṭha*) means reciting together (*saṃpaṭhana*), that is to say, study. Regarding "proximate" (*pratyāsanna*): this is because, having studied the words (*pada*), the *krama* must be studied. Similarly, in the case of "the *vārttika* on the *krama*," the proximity should be understood as follows: it is not possible to study the *krama* without having first studied the *saṃhitā*.
The singular is used for non-living beings when referring to their genus. 2.4.6.

"Jāti [is used] for non-living things. This is a figurative designation (*gauṇa-nirdeśa*), because the term "jāti" refers to the members [of a class] that are denoted by the word. Examples include *ārāśastrī* (the goad and the weapon) and *dhānāśaṣkulī* (parched grain and the *śaṣkulī* cake). A *śaṣkulī* is a collection (*kula*) of the six flavors; its form is established by its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group [of feminine nouns]. *Nandakapāñcajanya* (the sword Nandaka and the conch Pāñcajanya): these two are proper names (*sañjñā-śabda*). It is said: "His sword is the Nandaka, and the conch is proclaimed to be the Pāñcajanya."

"And when the genus is predominant" means when the genus is the primary factor. "Not when there is an intention to express specific substances" means that when there is an intention to express specific, fixed substances in a particular place or context, then even though they are words denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*), the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) does not occur. For example, *badarāmalakāni* (the jujubes and the myrobalans); these two words denote the genus of fruits.
A river and a region that do not contain villages are designated by their specific gender.

"A river and a country that do not include villages [are called feminine] when they possess distinct genders. This is an explanation of the term *viśiṣṭaliṅgānām* (of those possessing distinct genders), meaning "of those having different genders. The prefix *vi-* in the root *śiṣ* has the same meaning as *bhid* (to divide). Thus, a distinguishing attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is called the "distinguisher" (*bhedaka*), and the thing to be distinguished (*viśeṣya*) is called the "distinguished" (*bhedya*). Even in the rule *ktena nañviśiṣṭena* ("by a past passive participle qualified by the negative particle *nañ*"), the sense of "excess" (*ādhikya*) is explained precisely through the mechanism of distinction: for that which has *nañ* as its distinguisher becomes "possessing *nañ* as an excess" (*nañādhika*). [This applies to] "those denoting rivers," and so forth.

How then is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the Sūtra through the use of *dvandva* for words such as *viśiṣṭaliṅga*? To this he says: "In the case of a part of a river," and so forth. It should also be understood that *agrāma* means "not a part of a village. Furthermore, the plural form *agrāmāḥ* is used in place of the singular. This is indeed a non-compounded (*asamāsa*) reference; for if it were a compound, the *dvandva* consisting of mixed parts would be treated as a singular.

Regarding the compound *gaṅgākurukṣetre*: the point is that if this were an *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of the dual number; if it were a *samāhāra* (collective) compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of the neuter gender. Regarding *udhyairāvatī*: [the root] *ujjh* means "to abandon," and *udhya* and *airāvata* refer to rivers. Regarding "even a place": the word "is cited" (*udāhriyate*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding "jāmbava-śālūkinyau": *jāmbavam* is a city (*nagara*) and *śālūkinī* is a village (*grāma*). In that case, because they are on both sides of villages, there is indeed a prohibition [of study]. However, a *dvandva* compound whose members are both parts of a village has not been cited as an example; for a *janapada* is a region (*deśa*), meaning a place where people move about. He states "and thus" to show that one must necessarily accept that a *janapada* is a region—[otherwise] one would not study in a village.

In such rules as "village cocks (*grāmakukkuṭāḥ*) are not to be eaten," the mention of "village" (*grāma*) includes the city (*nagara*) as well; likewise here too, the prohibition would apply even to a *dvandva* compound that has a city as one of its members. This is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since [Pāṇini] provides the mention of "city" (*nagara*) in the rule "of villages and cities of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām*) while already mentioning "village" (*grāma*), he thereby indicates that in this grammatical system, when "village" is mentioned, "city" is not [excluded].

Is it being grasped [as a village]? This is not well stated; for he will say there: "Since [the designation] is already established by the very fact of being a *grāma*, the mention of *nagara* (city) is for the purpose of indicating a difference in application; the mention of *grāma* is a qualifier of the first member—as in *pūrva-eṣukāmaśamī*; whereas the mention of *nagara* is a qualifier of the second member—as in *pūrva-pāṭaliputrakaḥ*. Furthermore, in rules such as *vāhīka-grāmebhyaḥ* and *udīcya-grāmāt*, the mention of *nagara* would not be included by the mention of *grāma*; therefore he says: "In the rule *agrāmaḥ*, there is a prohibition of *nagara*. The meaning is that this is a prohibition of the prohibition based on *grāma*.

Regarding the phrase "in both cases": when both [types of places], namely villages and cities, exist, the prohibition must be stated as applying specifically to the village, and not, moreover, as a prohibition based on the city; this is the meaning.
Small creatures. 2.4.8.

Regarding "small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*): this word *kṣudra* indeed exists in the sense of "miserable"—as in "this man is miserable"; it exists in the sense of "deformed in limb" or "lacking virtue"—as in the rule "*kṣudrābhyo vā*"; and it exists in the sense of "diminution of size"—as in "small grains of rice. However, here, because of its association with the word *jantu* ("creature"), the last [meaning] is taken. Thus he says: "A *kṣudra* is one whose size is diminished. The meaning is "one who has a small body."

Since diminution is relative, he introduces a traditional authority (*smṛti*) so that there may be no infinite regress: "There should be a small creature without bones. One for whom bones do not exist is "boneless" (*anasthi*). He cites another traditional authority with the words "or else": "A small creature (*kṣudrajantu*) is one who is to be crushed (*kṣottavya*). The suffix *rak* is applied here in the sense of fitness, according to the rule "after the roots *sphāyī*, *tañc*, etc. Thus, a small creature is one who does not die even when being crushed, such as a leech; whereas one who dies is not fit to be crushed because [death] would be caused by sin.

The meaning is that this [term] is well-known precisely by virtue of its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "the small" (*kṣudra*). He cites another Smṛti: "Or a hundred," etc. This means that for those for whom a hundred [insects] constitute a *prasṛti*—that is, half of an *añjali*—a hundred [insects] fill half an *añjali*. He cites another Smṛti: "Some even up to the mongoose," etc. This means that small creatures include everything down to the mongoose. Regarding the phrase "because of the contradiction with others": the applications shown by the Smṛtis concerning boneless creatures and so forth are not all subsumed by those [other rules]; this is the contradiction here.
And those whose enmity is eternal. 2.4.9.

"And for those whose hostility is perpetual. "Hostility" (*virodha*) means enmity (*vaira*). It does not mean "incompatible coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*) and so forth, because that would lead to over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as "shadow and sunlight. Furthermore, because the term "living beings" (*jantu*), which is carried over from the preceding sūtra, qualifies "hostility," hostility among living beings is indeed enmity. "Perpetual" (*śāśvatika*) means constant. The word *śaśvat* denotes the three periods of time. The suffix *ṭhañ* (forming *-ika*) is applied according to the rule "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) from the word *kāla*; moreover, by exception (*nipātana*), the substitution of *ik* occurs even after a word ending in *ta*, and there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel) for indeclinables when the suffix is merely a *bha*-affix.

*Gopālasyāpatyāni gaupālayaḥ* ("the descendants of Gopāla are Gaupālayas"): here there is an occasional contradiction. The word *ca* (and) [indicates] "again" (*punar*) and so forth. The scope for the rule on the dual number for animals and birds (*paśu-śakuni-dvandva*) is: *mahājorabhram*, *mahājorabhrāḥ*; *haṃsacakravākam*, *haṃsacakravākāḥ*. The scope for the singular collective form (*ekavad-bhāva*) for contradictory things (*virodhin*) is: *śramaṇabrāhmaṇam*, *mārjāramūṣikam*; *aśvamahiṣam*, *kākolūkam*. In these cases, where both rules would apply, the optional rule for animals and birds (*paśu-śakuni-vibhāṣā*) would prevail due to its posteriority; however, because of the word *ca*, this very [singular collective form] occurs.
Of Śūdras who have not been excluded [from the community]. 2.4.10.

"Of Śūdras who have not been excluded. Here, the word *śūdra* denotes any caste other than the three [twice-born] castes (*traivarṇika*), and is not a synonym for *vṛṣala*, because of the prohibition against those who have been "excluded" (*niravasita*). Regarding the term *niravasita*: it is derived from the root *sī* preceded by the prefix *ni-r-ava*, with the suffix *kta* in the passive sense. In this regard, he states the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*): "Exclusion (*niravasāna*) means being cast out (*bahiṣkaraṇa*). The implication is that since roots have multiple meanings, or rather, due to the influence of the prefixes. He explains what is intended here—that it is being cast out from the [sacrificial] vessel—by saying "by whom... [and so on]. "[Even] by means of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*)."...

It is not purified by what has been stated by the authors of the Smṛtis, such as "bell-metal is purified by ashes"; therefore, they do not obtain permission to eat there and are excluded from that place.
And [the compound] beginning with "gavāśva" (cow-and-horse) [is also a dvandva]. 2.4.11.

Regarding the rule *gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca*: because they follow the form of *dvandva* compounds, the neuter gender is established by the word *prabhṛtīni*. These items, beginning with *gavāśva*, are recited as having already undergone *ekavadbhāva* (the formation of a singular collective). By this rule, only their grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*) is prescribed, not the actual occurrence of *ekavadbhāva*; thus he says, "beginning with *gavāśva*. This statement is made because, for the four items beginning with *go-aśva*, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding their being a *paśudvandva* (a *dvandva* of animals). Similarly, one has *uṣṭrakharam* or *uṣṭraśaśam*.

Regarding the compounds beginning with *darbha* and *śara* and ending with *tṛṇa* and *ulapa*, although the option (*vibhāṣā*) for a dual compound would otherwise apply, the absence of the *ekaśeṣa* rule—namely "the masculine remains when joined with the feminine"—in the case of *dāsī*, *dāsa*, and so on, is due to specific technical designation (*nipātana*). The reading of *śāṭīpaṭīkam* and similar forms, which do not denote a genus of living beings, serves the purpose of including multiple bases. For others, such as *kubja* and *vāmana*, the statement is made because [the dual] would not otherwise be obtained. Thus, the operation of the *dvandva* compound occurs exactly as it is uttered.

In a list (gaṇa), the dual compound operation—characterized by the state of being a singular (ekavadbhāva)—occurs only for those forms in which the substitution of *avaṅ* has been applied as they were recited. Regarding the phrase "in other forms": this means when [the substitution] does not occur, because it is optional according to the rule "avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya. By this, it is stated that their specific form as given in the list of gaṇas is intended, and that the purpose does not lie merely in the mention of the preceding and following words.

The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies to compounds preceded by *vṛja*, *mṛga*, *tṛṇa*, *dhānya*, *vyañjana*, *paśu*, *śakuni*, *aśva*, *vaḍaba*, *pūrva*, *apara*, *adhara*, and *uttara*. (Pāṇini 2.4.12)

The *Vibhāṣā* states: "In the case of trees, wild animals, grass, grain, condiments, cattle, birds, horses, goats, and [the pairs] prior-posterior and lower-upper. Here, each of the words beginning with "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) is qualified by being in a *dvandva* compound. Now, it is not the single word "tree" that constitutes the *dvandva*, nor is there the simultaneous employment of two [identical] words, because of the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*). Nor is there the simultaneous employment of synonyms, because of the statement regarding "single remainder" even for dissimilar words that have the same meaning. Nor is there simultaneous employment with a qualifier—as in "the tree and the *dhava* tree"—because the word "tree" alone implies all its specific varieties, making the employment of words such as "*dhava*" redundant.

How then is there the simultaneous usage of the general and the particular in expressions such as "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardau*)? If you argue that this is because, in proximity to the word *balīvarda* (bull), the word *go* (cow) refers only to female cattle, and thus both words denote a particular [sub-class], then here too, in proximity to the word *dhava*, the word *vṛkṣa* (tree) would have a scope distinct from it, and consequently, a *dvandva* compound would result. Furthermore, how is there simultaneous usage even in a sentence—as in: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived; Vasiṣṭha has also arrived"?

If it is argued that the term is employed even when its meaning has already been stated for the purpose of indicating preeminence (*prādānya*), then it would follow that this also applies in the case of a *dvandva* compound. Therefore, one must simply accept non-expression (*anabhidhāna*); for there is no such usage in common speech as "tree-deer" (*vṛkṣadhava*). Consequently, the rule refers to words denoting specific types of trees. The same should be understood regarding "deer" (*mṛga*) and so forth.

"Of these, there is a dvandva compound. Regarding the phrase "of these," although there is only a single genitive case, it is divided according to the difference in its objects: it is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to those beginning with "tree" and ending with "bird," and it is a genitive of selection (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to those beginning with "horse" and "mare. Since those among these that are non-living would necessarily form a collective dvandva (*samāhāra-dvandva*) by the rule "for non-living things, when a genus is involved," this [dvandva formation] is prescribed for both cases.

By relying on the interpretation that "that *dvandva* which has attained the status of a singular number according to the *Vibhāṣā* becomes [singular] for these," the singular status—either obligatory or optional as prescribed—occurs for those very items beginning with *vṛkṣa* when they form a *dvandva* with others: in *vrīhikuśaplakṣam*, the singular is obligatory by the rule "for non-living beings, when expressing a genus" (*jātir aprāṇinām*); whereas in *plakṣaśabdasparśau*, since the words do not denote substances, the rule "for non-living beings, when expressing a genus" does not apply, and thus the singular is obtained in both cases by the general rule "a *dvandva* is used in the sense of 'and'."

The mention of "animals" (paśu) is for the purpose of setting aside the constant rule defining [the term] as a component of an army (*senāṅga*), which would otherwise apply by priority to elephants, horses, and so forth.

What is the purpose of including "deer" (*mṛga*) and "birds" (*śakuni*) [in the rule]? For it is not the case that for these [words], obligatory singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*) is obtained by this specific section (Pāṇini 2.4.6), such that an option would be permitted to set it aside; nor is a restriction—that "for these alone, the *dvandva* compound occurs in both ways"—possible, because since there is no other application [of the term], the *dvandva* would necessarily apply in both cases anyway. Alternatively, if this were a restriction stating that "for these alone the *dvandva* occurs in both ways," then where else would it apply? If you say "somewhere else," then the general definition "a *dvandva* is used in the sense of conjunction" (*cārthe dvandvaḥ*) would become redundant.

In that case, one would have to resort to a specific injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) alone: [that] for *prāṇyaṅga* and so forth there is a collective compound (*samāhāra*), for *dadhi-payaḥ* and so forth there is a reciprocal conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and for *vṛkṣa* and so forth it occurs in both ways? Or rather, by the phrase "for these alone in both ways," the *dvandva* of others is excluded from both ways, while for those [others], it certainly occurs in one way or the other.

Even so, it is not known where else [this option applies], and the rule "every *dvandva* compound may optionally be singular" would be untenable. It is replied: this option applies only to those of the same class; therein alone does the restriction operate—namely, that a *dvandva* of words denoting specific animals occurs with other words denoting specific animals in both cases (i.e., as singular or plural), but with others, it occurs in one way or the other. But even so, it is still not known where "in one way or the other" applies; this might be the case if it were explicitly heard that their *dvandva* occurs in both ways.

In this context, however, it is heard that "the *dvandva* compound takes the singular number optionally" (*vibhāṣaikavacanaḥ*). Consequently, when the formulation of the rule is understood as "that *dvandva* which would otherwise take the singular number optionally [does so] only with words denoting specific animals, and not with others," it becomes clearly known that with other [words], there is a *dvandva* of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).

Now, in this formulation of the statement, what is the purpose of including the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally), given that it is already established that a *dvandva* compound ending in the singular number occurs only optionally? In that case, one might suggest that this much alone should suffice: "That *dvandva* which is singular is [formed] with these [words] and by these [words] alone. It is replied: If the term *vibhāṣā* were not included, another interpretation of the statement would also be possible—namely, that "the *dvandva* is singular only when it is together with these [words]," as is the case with the class beginning with *prāṇyaṅga*. However, since that restriction is impossible, the intended restriction is achieved only when *vibhāṣā* is present.

In this same way, the nature of the rule should be understood regarding "prior and posterior" (*pūrvāparam*) and "lower and upper" (*adharottaram*). Although the form would have been established simply by the rule for "cattle-duals" (*paśudvandva*), the specific mention of "horse and mare" (*aśvavaḍava*) is for the purpose of a *pratipadavidhi* (an explicit, word-for-word prescription). Because it is prescribed by a *pratipadavidhi*, when there is the option of singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) in the case of "horse and mare," the rule "the two, horse and mare, as before" (*pūrvavadaśvaḍavau*) is set aside, and instead only the rule "that [compound] is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*) applies. For, by referring back with the word "that" (*tat*) to that which possesses singular treatment, the neuter gender thus ordained is indeed prescribed by a *pratipadavidhi*, just like the singular treatment itself.

The rule "as in the case of *aśva* and *vaḍabā*" applies to the alternative where there is no formation as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*)—namely, *aśvavaḍavau* and *aśvavaḍavān*. With this very intention, the author of the Vṛtti will state there: "It has been stated that for *aśva* and *vaḍabā*, there is optionally a formation as a singular unit," and so forth. Regarding the term *bahuprakṛti*: that whose basis (*prakṛti*), meaning its cause, consists of many—that is, many base-words (*vartipadārtha*) endowed with the number "many"—is *bahuprakṛti*. Because it denotes that meaning, the *dvandva* compound itself is also called *bahuprakṛti*.

This is not an independent definition; for if it were independent, then in the case of *vanaspati* and so forth, even when there is multiplicity of bases, there would always be the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*), overriding the option prescribed by this sūtra. Conversely, in the case of fruits and the like, even when there is an option, there would be an option regarding multiplicity of bases, overriding the permanent singular collective form obtained through other definitions such as "the genus of non-living things" (*jātir aprāṇinām*). Therefore, this is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to another rule.

In that regard, if—on account of its being recited in the rule "vibhāṣā vṛkṣa"—this [rule] alone were to constitute the remainder (śeṣa), then in the case of *vanaspati* and so forth, even though there is no option regarding their not having multiple bases (*abahuprakṛtitva*), the rule "jātiraprāṇinām" would apply obligatorily; however, there is no fault in the case of fruits and the like, because since this option does not apply there, the restriction is simply due to the application of another rule. Therefore, the remainder of the meaning for the entire section is as follows; thus he says: "Of these, there is only one with multiple bases."

The meaning is that when these items beginning with "fruit" (*phala*) form a *dvandva* compound by this rule or by another definition, they become a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*) only when they have multiple original bases (*bahuprakṛti*). In the example *badarāmalake* ("the jujube and the *āmalaka*"), the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* ("a genus [term] for non-living things") does not apply. In *rathikāśvārohau* ("the charioteer and the horseman"), the rule concerning the parts of an army (*senāṅga*) applies. In *plakṣanyagrodhau* ("the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*"), this option (*vikalpa*) applies; thus, neither *jātir aprāṇinām* nor the mandatory (*nitya*) application occurs.

Regarding *vanaspati* (woody plants), although they consist of many species of trees, this option indeed applies: *āmrapalāśam*, *āmrapalāśau*. Others, however, consider the mention of *vanaspati* to be an illustration for trees in general; thus, in cases such as *rurupṛṣatau* (the ruru deer and the spotted deer) or *haṃsacakravākāv* (the swan and the ruddy goose), there is an absence of this option. In the case of *yūkālikṣe* (lice and nits), there is an absence of the rule governing "small creatures" (*kṣudrajantavaḥ*). But in the cases of *vrīhiyavau* (rice and barley) and *kuśakāśau* (kuśa grass and kāśa grass), both [rules] apply.
And [a compound consisting of] mutually contradictory terms that do not denote a common substratum [is also a dvandva]. 2.4.13.

"Mutually contradictory (*vipratiṣiddha*) and not denoting a substratum (*anadhikaraṇavāci*). This means "mutually opposed. Opposition is characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) and so forth. However, in the sūtra beginning with "of those that are mutually contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddhānām*), it is stated as such in the form of a *dvandva* compound because it denotes the members (*avayava*) that possess that [opposition]. Regarding the phrase "of those not denoting a substance" (*adravyavācinām*): by this, he shows that the word *adhikaraṇa* refers to a substance (*dravya*), not to a locus (*ādhāra*). For it is not possible for the members of a *dvandva* to function as a locus; the intention is that a locus is the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhakti*).

This [sūtra] is also commenced for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha); and the nature of that restriction is as follows: when a dvandva compound in the singular number would otherwise be optional (vibhāṣā), it occurs only if it denotes things that are mutually contradictory and do not denote substances (adravyavācin); however, in the case of things denoting substances (dravyavācin), there is mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga).
Nor curds, milk, and so forth. 2.4.14.

Not [the compounds] *dadhi-paya-ādi* (curds-milk, etc.). Regarding the phrase "as appropriate": because it is an optional rule (*vikalpa*) due to its being a secondary attribute (*vyañjana*), its application would have occurred there—in the first three [cases]—by virtue of the optionality of the preceding sūtra, namely that [the compound is] "white-black" (*śukla-kṛṣṇau*). But here [in the case of *dadhi-paya-ādi*], it does not apply. If this is so, once this optionality is prohibited, would the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) based on the generic characteristic (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) be obligatory? The resolution to this will be stated: "That which was stated regarding the feminine, that is not so. Just as it will be explained in the section on the six [cases], here too only the singular collective form itself is prohibited.

Furthermore, since Brahman, Prajāpati, and others are recited here, by way of prohibiting a collective dvandva (samāhāra-dvandva), an itaretara-yoga dvandva is established; therefore, by association with them, that same [type of dvandva] is appropriate for these four as well.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] when the subject matter is limited to that extent. 2.4.15.

And [the rule applies] when the primary cause is limited to this much. *Vṛtti* means "occurrence"—that is, a compound (*samāsa*). That which possesses it is the member-word (*vartipada*) that constitutes the compound; its meaning is called the "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*). But how is that a locus? He says: "For that... Here, there is a prohibition of the restriction [from Pāṇini 2.4.2]. The restriction—that the co-aggregation (*samāhāra*) of parts of living beings and so forth occurs only in a singular form—does not apply when the limitation of the number of the meanings of the member-words is understood. However, this is not a prohibition of the *samāhāra-dvandva* (co-aggregate copulative) itself, as was the case with the preceding sūtra.

If this is so, even when the restriction has been prohibited, in the case of "ten teeth and lips" (*daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*), where there is a limitation regarding the locus (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*), a *dvandva* compound would still occur in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*) by the rule "a *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*). Furthermore, since the restriction does not apply to those items not mentioned in this context, in the absence of this prohibition, a *dvandva* in the sense of a collective would indeed occur by the rule "a *dvandva* [is formed] in the sense of 'and'"—for example, "ten Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas" (*daśa brāhmaṇakṣattriyāḥ*). Therefore, a singular-numbered *dvandva* does not apply to all cases, both those under discussion and others.

Is it the case that only the collective *dvandva* (samāhāra-dvandva) is to be prohibited by the rule "when the extent of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is [limited]"? It is said in reply: It has been stated that "the substratum is the meaning of the constituent members (*vṛttipada-artha*)," and in a collective *dvandva*, it is impossible to express the limited extent of the meaning of the constituent members. For even when words such as "ten" are employed, it is the specific number of that very collective—the sense of the *dvandva*—that is understood, not the number of the meaning of the constituent members, just as in a *dvigu* compound, such as "ten bundles of five" (*daśapañcapūlyaḥ*).

Therefore, by one who wishes to convey a specific number for the meaning of the constituent members (*varti-padārtha*), a copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*) must necessarily be prescribed; thus, there is no fault in cases such as "ten Brahmins and Kṣatriyas. If this is so, then by this very logic, a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) would not occur even in cases like "ten teeth and lips," and thus the prohibition [of the collective compound] would be unnecessary. Not so; for if this prohibition were absent, because of the restrictive rule that parts of living beings and the like form only a collective compound, the copulative compound would not occur.

Furthermore, even when used in a collective *dvandva* compound with words such as "ten" (*daśa*), it is impossible to convey a specific number for the meaning of the constituent members (*vartipadārtha*). Therefore, since the intended meaning is the limited extent of the substratum (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*), the *dvandva* itself would not occur; thus, this prohibition is commenced. In the example "ten teeth-and-lips" (*daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*), because the word "ten" is connected to each member individually, the quantity of the constituent members is understood. Even if the connection were to the aggregate, the number would still pertain only to the constituent members consisting of teeth and lips.
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies when [the compound] denotes proximity. (Pāṇini 2.4.16)

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā samīpe*: because of the governing context of *adhikaraṇaitāvattve*, it is understood that this refers to "this being in the form of proximity," though in the commentary (*vṛtti*) only the general sense is shown: "in the vicinity of the limitation of the substratum. Here, the word *samīpa* (proximity) is used in a sense where the state [of proximity] is predominant; the meaning is "in the determination of the vicinity of the limitation of the substratum. In this case, the prohibition of the restriction is indeed explicit, for it is not the case that the *samāhāra-dvandva* is to be prohibited by the option (*vibhāṣā*), since the *avyayībhāva* has already been prescribed.

By the rule "avyayaṃ vibhakti... and so forth. Although the word "by a number" (saṅkhyayā) does not appear here, it nevertheless applies even by means of a number. Regarding the term "bahuvrīhi": it is formed by the rule "saṅkhyayāvyayāsanna... and so forth. In that context, when the option for a single unified meaning (ekavadbhāva) is adopted, the avyayībhāva is subsequently applied; thus the sense is "of a single meaning, [with] a single meaning. And its status as having a single meaning arises because proximity is its primary significance. Even though the avyayībhāva is devoid of number due to its being an indeclinable (avyaya), there nonetheless exists a unity of meaning in the form of the absence of differentiation.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is to be established on the basis of the non-difference between that which possesses proximity and the proximate object itself. Furthermore, the limitation of the substratum (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*) is also to be explained precisely by not intending to express the difference between the aggregate (*samāhāra*) and its constituents (*samāhārin*). "In other cases, it is a *bahuvrīhi*": the meaning is that [the term] has a plural sense because it denotes many things. And its having a plural sense is due to its having the proximate objects as its primary referents.

[Objection: But surely, since the meaning of a *dvandva* compound undergoes singularization (*ekavadbhāva*), the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the verb would also be established as being in the singular; what is the use of this laborious interpretation? [Reply: It is said: If the subsequent application were only of an *avyayībhāva*, then because that [compound] is indeclinable (*avyaya*), it would lack plurality, and thus the plural number would not occur. Or, even if that [plural number] were present, once the feminine suffix *āp* (*ām-bhāva*) had been applied, the form would not be *upadaśāḥ*. Furthermore, if the subsequent application were only of a *bahuvrīhi*, there would be a genitive case, as in *upadaśasya pāṇipādasya*; however, the desired form is *upadaśaṃ pāṇipādasya*. Therefore, the previously stated [interpretation] alone is superior.
That [term] is neuter. 2.4.17.

This [rule] concerns the neuter gender. This *yoga* (sūtra) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*). The inclusion of the word "with" (*sa-*) is so that it may apply even to a *dvigu* compound that is separated [from the context]; otherwise, it would apply only to a *dvandva* that is immediately contiguous. But this is not the case; we shall require only the phrase "singular number" (*ekavacanam*), and not the specific term "dvandva. If that were so, would it then also apply to a *samāhāra-dvandva* which is not explicitly mentioned in this section? Otherwise, it would apply only to the *dvandva* and *dvigu* under discussion.

But would not even the context (*prakaraṇa*) be disregarded? If that were so, then in cases such as *ekasaṅkhya*, it would apply to a single meaning; therefore, the context must necessarily be taken into account. And when that context is required, since the *dvandva* compound under discussion consists of things related as parts of living beings and so forth, it would apply to that alone.

However, when this word "sa" (that) is present—even though the context (*prakaraṇa*) is being considered—it results in the neuter gender for every *samāhāra-dvanda* (collective copulative compound), by abandoning the connection with "parts of living beings" (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth, because of the rule "that [dvandva] which is mentioned here [in this section], whether it be a *dvandva* or a *dvigu*, is neuter. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "one" (*eka*) and so on. Thus, it is stated in the rule *yuvoranākau*: "In the case of *yuvoḥ* (of *yu* and *vu*), there would be the contingency of [the whole] being neuter if it were a *samāhāra-dvanda*."
Therefore, it is established that for every *samāhāra-dvandva*—whether relating to the limbs of living beings and so forth, or otherwise—the neuter gender is prescribed.

Regarding the rule "when the final member ends in /a/": here, within the governing context of the word *ataḥ*, the prescription of the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *dvigoḥ* serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*). In the case of *pañcakhaṭvī*, when the feminine gender is adopted, there is shortening of the *upasarjana*. Regarding the rule *ano nalopaśca*: because the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* applies by the rule *uttarapadatve cāpadādividhau*, the status of being a *pada* is absent; hence, the explicit mention of the elision of the /n/ is made.

The dative case in "pātrādibhyaḥ" is used in the sense of purpose (tādarthye); the meaning is that [the suffix] "ṭhak" is applied for the sake of establishing *dvigu* compounds ending in words such as "pātra. The group beginning with "pātra" is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
And the *avyayībhāva* [compound] [is neuter]. 2.4.18.

And [the term] *avyayībhāva* [is used]. Regarding the phrase "of that which has the meaning of the first member as predominant": in cases such as *adhistri*, since the meaning of the first member lacks gender and so forth, it would follow that [the compound] itself would lack gender and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that which has the meaning of another word as predominant": this refers to examples such as *unmattagaṅgam*. As for *puṣyāham*: in a *karmadhāraya*, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules "after *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ṭac*" and "*rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* [are] in the masculine. As for *sudinam*: the word *sudina* signifies "praiseworthy" (*praśasta*). Thus, it is used in such expressions as "this work should be done during the *sudina* months. As for *tripatham*: this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The formation of *dvigu* compounds ending in *pantha* is established because they belong to the *pātrādi* group. *Virūpaḥ panthāḥ* becomes *vipatham*; this is a *prādi-samāsa* (prepositional compound).
Regarding the rule *kriyāviśeṣaṇānāṃ ca*: since adverbs would otherwise acquire feminine gender through their connection with the action (*kriyā*), this statement is made as a restrictive rule.
A Tatpuruṣa compound that is not a negative (anañ) and not a Karmadhāraya [is called a Dvigu]. 2.4.19.

"A Tatpuruṣa compound that is neither a negative (nañ) nor a Karmadhāraya. To avoid ambiguity, the word "Karmadhāraya" is analyzed as follows: the term *nañ-karmadhāraya* refers to a Tatpuruṣa that is both a negative and a Karmadhāraya; a Tatpuruṣa in which those two do not exist is called *anañ-karmadhāraya*. Here, the word "Karmadhāraya" is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Thus, *nañ* and *karmadhāraya* together form *nañ-karmadhārayau*; the Tatpuruṣa in which these two are not found is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: *anañ-karmadhāraya*.

In this case, however, since there is no *tatpuruṣa* consisting of the mere negative particle (*nañ*), a *tatpuruṣa* joined with it would have to be indicated by the word *nañ* through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and furthermore, a change in either the gender or the number would have to be stated. Therefore, the *bahuvrīhi* alone is logical. In the commentary, only the general matter was shown: "excluding the *nañ*-compound and the *karmadhāraya*. [The rule] "optionally, when *senā* [is involved]" applies.

In the subsequent sūtras, this [term] is not of much utility. First, in the rule "sañjñāyāṃ kanthā," an eternal (anādi) technical name (*sañjñā*) is intended; neither a *nañ*-compound nor a *tatpuruṣa* nor a *karmadhāraya* serves as a name for the Uśīnaras. Furthermore, in the rule "upajñopakrama," without a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, the sense of "having that as its beginning" would not be understood. Also, in the rule "chāyā bāhulye," the quality of "abundance" belonging to the meaning of the first member is not conveyed except through a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*.

However, in the case of *sabhārājā*, because of the rule *rājā'manuṣyapūrvaḥ*, there is no possibility of a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) or a *karmadhāraya* ending in *sabhā*. But a *dvandva* would indeed apply—namely, *īśvaraśca sabhā ca* resulting in *īśvarasabhe*; therefore, in that instance as well, the portion [of the definition] stating "it is a *tatpuruṣa*" is certainly applicable.

In the case of the expression *aśālā*, the word *sabhā* denotes a collection (*samūha*); since the dependence of a collection upon its members is most evident, this will necessarily be a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound and not any other type. Thus, [examples would be] *brāhmaṇasabhā* (an assembly of Brahmins), *asabhā* (a non-assembly), and *paramasabhā* (a supreme assembly). Therefore, the intention is that its direct application occurs only in the rule *vibhāṣā senā*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *saṃjñā* when it refers to the region of the Uśīnaras.

Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ kanthośīnareṣu*: because the word *kanthā* functions as a qualifier within a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is stated that there is an extension of the rule to include compounds ending in *kanthā*—namely, "a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *kanthā*. Thus, we have *sauśamikantham*. [In this case,] the *sauśamayāḥ* are the descendants of Suśama.

The word *upajñā* and *upakrama*, when used as the first member of a compound, take the neuter gender when there is a desire to express that [person or thing] as the originator thereof. (Pāṇini 2.4.21)

*Upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.21). *Upajñā* is that which is first known (*upajñāyate*); the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106) in the sense of the object (*karman*). *Upakrama* is that which is begun (*upakramyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the same sense of the object, with the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *nodāttopadeśasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.34). "The first discovery" (*upajñā*) and "the beginning" (*upakrama*) form a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*). This [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in those [two terms].

In the *sūtra*, however, "upajñopakrama" is a *tatpuruṣa* compound used as an adjective in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The phrase "of those two, upajñā and upakrama," and so forth, is its explanation—beginning with "yadi. "Ādiḥ" means "primacy" (*prāthamya*). In the expression "pāṇinyupajñam," there is a compound with a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). Previous grammars were endowed with technical conventions (*paribhāṣā*) pertaining to the present time and so on; however, the grammar initiated by Pāṇini and others was devoid of those [conventions], and thus its status as the "first" (*āditva*) is proclaimed. In the expression "vyāḍyupajñam," [the same applies].

*Aḍa* means the tail of a scorpion (*vṛścika-lāṅgūla*), and by that, sharpness (*taikṣṇya*) is indicated. *Vyaḍa* is one whose *aḍa* has departed; his descendant is the teacher *Vyāḍi*. Because of his inclusion in the list beginning with *svāgata*, the rule "not after *y* or *v*" (*na yvābhyām*) does not apply. *Duṣi* is a conventional term (*saṅketa-śabda*), just as the formation of *vṛt* occurs here. *Nanda* refers to the king. *Mānāni* refers to measures such as the *prastha* and others. The expression *vālmīki-ślokāḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). There is here a desire to express the state of being preceded by him (*tad-āditva*); for it is well known that Vālmīki was the first to perceive the composition of verses (*śloka-prabandha*).
In the expressions "Devadatta is approached by Yajñadatta" and "Yajñadatta is initiated by Devadatta," only the mere connection with an action is intended to be expressed here.
The word *chāyā* [is used in the feminine] when there is multiplicity. 2.4.22.

"In the case of *chāyā* (shadow), when there is multiplicity. Multiplicity is a property of the object denoted by the first member of the compound. How so? The term "in multiplicity" (*bāhulye*) is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). The grammatical connection (*akṣarānvaya*) of the rule is as follows: when there is multiplicity, that which is the word *chāyā* denoting the shadow, a Tatpuruṣa compound ending in that [word] [is neuter]. In this regard, when the question arises as to whose multiplicity it is, since a shadow is caused by an obscuring substance, it is understood to be the multiplicity of that [substance]. Therefore, this rule applies to those many [objects] which, acting together, produce a shadow that is either perceptible or serves as a support.
The word *sabhā* (assembly hall), when preceded by a non-human [word], is neuter. 2.4.23.

The word *sabhā* does not include that which has a non-human being as its primary referent. Here, the word *sabhā* denotes a hall (*śālā*). To the question, "Why does it not apply here [in the case of a specific person]?"—the question implies that by the rule "the word itself is the technical term" (*svaṃ rūpam*), it would be more appropriate for it to apply only here. [The answer is: "Only of a synonym. This means it applies to the synonym alone, and not to the word-form itself, nor to specific individuals such as Candragupta and others. He confirms this very point with the words of an authoritative source: "As it has been said."

How, then, is this obtained? There are two negative particles (*nañ*) here: in *arājapūrvā* and *amanuṣyapūrvā*. In that regard, by the rule of "that which is connected with *nañ* or *iva*," only synonyms of the word *rājan* are understood; however, the word *amanuṣya* is taken in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*). How, then, will *pittaghnaṃ ghṛtam* ("bile-destroying ghee") be cited as an example under the rule *amanuṣyakartṛke ca*? The meaning is that, according to the [traditional] commentary, there the term refers to anyone other than a human being, and not in its conventional sense.
And [the word] *aśālā* [is used]. 2.4.24.

And "aśālā" (not a hall). This word *sabhā* denotes both a "hall" (*śālā*) and an "assembly" (*saṃgha*). Since there is a prohibition regarding the "hall," he states "it denotes an assembly" and so forth, indicating that the other meaning is intended. In that regard, by the preceding rule, [the suffix] will apply even when it denotes a "hall" provided it is preceded by a word for a king or a non-human being; however, by this [present] rule, it applies to that which does not denote a "hall" even in the absence of being preceded by a word for a king or a non-human being.
The feminine suffix ṅīp is optionally applied after the words *senā*, *surā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, and *niśā*.

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyāśālāniśānām*: the term *tatpuruṣaḥ*, which was previously established as being in the genitive plural, is modified here; and *napuṃsakam* becomes a word emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Thus, the literal meaning is that *tatpuruṣa* compounds ending in *senā* and so forth are neuter. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), only the general principle is shown. Alternatively, the genitive is used in place of the nominative. For example, *kuḍyacchāyam*. This option applies when there is no abundance [of objects]; when there is abundance, the form is compulsory, as stated in the rule *chāyā bāhulye*.

Regarding the term *śvaniśam*: that night upon which dogs fast is called *śvaniśam*. That, moreover, is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*), for it is well known that on that day dogs fast.
In a Dvandva and a Tatpuruṣa compound, the gender of the final member prevails. 2.4.26.

"In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa*, the gender of the final member [prevails]. For what purpose is this stated? Here, regarding the *dvandva*, there are three views: first, that the meaning of the *dvandva* consists solely of the meanings of its constituent parts (*avayava*), which require one another, but there is no such thing as a "whole" (*samudāya*) distinct from them; second, that the meaning of the *dvandva* is indeed a whole distinct from the meanings of its constituents, and it possesses the gender of the gender of its constituents; third, that this very whole is itself devoid of gender.

In that regard, concerning the first two types of *dvandva* compounds, since it is impossible for both genders to apply simultaneously when the constituent members have different genders, the rule serves as a restrictive one (*niyama*), meaning that when there is an alternation between the two genders, the gender of the subsequent member alone prevails. However, in the third type, since the meaning of the compound itself lacks a gender, the rule serves as an injunctive one (*vidhi*), meaning that the gender of the subsequent member is assigned to the compound. Furthermore, the *tatpuruṣa* is also of two kinds: that which has the meaning of the prior member as predominant, such as *ardhapippalī*; and that which has the meaning of the subsequent member as predominant, such as *rājakumārī*.

In this context, since the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*) is already established by its very predominance in cases where the meaning of the final member is primary, the rule serves as a prescription (*vidhi*) for cases where the meaning of the prior member is primary. Regarding that, the author of the *Vṛtti* adopts the position of a prescription; thus he says: "that which is the gender of the subsequent member, that [gender] occurs. For in this way, the formulation of the Sūtra remains uniform; otherwise, there would be a discrepancy in the formulation, such that it would be prescriptive in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* and restrictive (*niyama*) in the case of a *dvandva*. This refers to the phrase "of either a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa*."

By this, he shows that this is a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [in the rule *dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*]. If it were a locative case (*saptamī*), however, the meaning would be: "In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa*, that which is subsequent takes the gender. In that case, since no grammatical subject (*kāryin*) is explicitly mentioned, and because of the word "subsequent" (*para*), the rule for gender applies to the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) which is implied by it.

Alternatively, the literal meaning [of the rule] is that in the domain of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, the gender of the subsequent member alone prevails. Even in that case, however, the prescription of gender applies specifically to the first member. In this view, in the example *mayūrīkukkuṭau* ("peahen and cock"), since the gender of the object denoted by the second member is extended (*atideśa*) to the object denoted by the first member, the disappearance of the feminine suffix would follow; conversely, in examples such as *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("cock and peahen"), *rājakumārī* ("the king’s daughter"), and *ardhapippalī* ("half a long pepper"), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a feminine suffix appearing in the first member.

But in this view, is anything desired established, or does it merely result in further faults? He says that something is indeed established: here, in the case of *pūrvakāyaḥ* and *ardhadroṇaḥ*, where the first member is neuter and the second member is masculine, when the gender of the latter is extended to the former, the compound itself takes that very same [gender]. And unlike the previous case, nothing undesirable occurs here.

Even in a *dvandva* compound where the former member belongs to the first two genders (masculine or neuter), such as in *guṇakarmaṇī* ("quality and action") or *dravyaguṇau* ("substance and quality"), where the preceding and following members have different genders, or where the word does not end in the vowel *a* or in a feminine suffix—as in *gatisthāne* ("motion and station"), *yoṣitpūruṣau* ("woman and man"), or *tittiribalāke* ("partridge and crane"—note: this is a *dvandva* of two masculine nouns)—in those cases, although the gender of the latter member is extended (*atideśa*) to the former member and thus both members may function with either gender in turn, everything desired is established, just as before.

Nothing undesirable follows. However, regarding the position that "the meaning of a *dvandva* is distinct [from its constituents] and is itself devoid of gender," in that case, the fact that the meaning of the *dvandva* lacks gender remains exactly as it was; thus, this is merely another fault. The phrase "of the *dvandva* and the *tatpuruṣa*" means "of the meaning of the *dvandva* and the meaning of the *tatpuruṣa*. Therefore, even when there is a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), that same gender applies.

If, then, by resorting to the genitive case, the gender of the subsequent member is extended (*atideśa*) to the meaning of the compound, then in the rule "the dual *aśvavaḍavau* is like the first member," the gender of the first member would also be extended to the meaning of the compound; consequently, since the femininity of the second member remains established, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of hearing the suffix *ṭāp*.

In the seventh alternative (*saptamīpakṣa*), however, even in the rule *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* ("the horse and the mare are as before"), the gender of the meaning of the first member is extended to the meaning of the second member; thus, due to the extension of masculinity to the word *vaḍavā*, its femininity being absent, the removal of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is established. [Objection: This is established by means of an irregularity (*nipātana*). [Question: What is that irregularity? [Response: It is not appropriate to rely on the irregularity of *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau*, because there would be the undesirable consequence of non-extension in other rules, such as in the forms *aśvavaḍavān* and *aśvavaḍavaiḥ*.

If that is so, then in the rule *aśvavaḍavapūrvāparādharottarāṇām*, since the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is not explicitly uttered, the *ṭāp* will be excluded when *aśva* and *vaḍavā* form a *dvandva* compound due to their being indeclinables (*nipāta*).

Another says: "In the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, because of the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of *anekam* (‘more than one’), the [feminine suffix] applies to all the constituent members (*vartipada*) of the meaning. If that were so, would it not then also apply here in the case of *kukkuṭamayūryau*? Let it be; what is the resulting form? It is established by the rule *paravalliṅgam*. What is the meaning of the words *śabda* and *artha* [in this context]? By the word *liṅga*, both the suffix denoting gender and the meaning itself are expressed, either through syntactic coordination (*tantra*) or through the retention of a single term (*ekaśeṣa*).

Thus, the meaning is this: the gender of a *dvandva* compound and of a *tatpuruṣa* compound is like that of the final member, and the suffix denoting it also belongs to the final member alone; [the rule applies] "by means of those two."

Furthermore, in cases such as *ardhadroṇa*, where substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), or quality and action (*karma*), [are combined], and where a suffix denoting gender (*liṅga*) is not possible, only the meaning is extended (*atidiśyate*); however, when both are possible, both are extended—as in *kukkuṭamayūryau*. Consequently, even though the original (*aupadeśika*) form has a short vowel, there will be the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the extended (*ātideśika*) form. And because that [extended form] is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*), and because the whole ending in it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), there is no further shortening of the vowel.

In that case, would not the suffixes *ṣpha* and *ṣyaṅ* apply again after the formation of the compound from *dattāgārgyāyaṇyau* and *dattākārīṣagandhye*, once the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] has been performed? Let them apply; however, by the rule "in the place of *bha*, when a *taddhita* suffix other than *aḍha* follows," there will be the removal (*nivṛtti*) of those two suffixes already produced previously. But where there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) because the word is not *bha*, such as in *dattā ca yuvatiśca* → *dattāyuvatī*, there would follow the hearing of two feminine suffixes. Therefore, the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not occur in a *dvandva* compound.

For the designation *upasarjana* (secondary member) is indeed prescribed for that which is non-primary (*apradhāna*). In a *dvandva* compound, however, because the individual meanings of the constituent parts alone connect with the grammatical operation (*kārya*), there is an absence of non-primacy. Furthermore, in the rule *paravalliṅgam*, it is the meaning itself that is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*). And as for the form *aśvavaḍavau*, it is due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*); this much is the case for now.

Regarding the phrase *dviguprāptāpanna* and so forth: should that prohibition then be stated? It need not be stated; the mention of *tatpuruṣa* will not be made, for it is simply the case that "the gender of a *dvandva* is like that of its final member. How then [to explain] *pūrvakāyaḥ* (the front part of the body) and *ardhapippalī* (half a *pippalī*)? The *ekadeśin* compound will not be commenced; rather, a *karmadhāraya* will occur here—namely, "that which is both prior and a body," and "that which is both half and a *pippalī*."

Words such as *pūrva* ("eastern") refer to a single part (*ekadeśa*), whereas words such as *kāya* ("body") refer to a whole (*samudāya*). How, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between them? [The answer is: because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) to the part. Thus, once the *karmadhāraya* compound is formed, the gender will belong to the meaning of the final member by virtue of its predominance; therefore, there is no need for the mention of the *tatpuruṣa* compound, nor is there any possibility of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) through the rule for compounds denoting a part (*ekadeśisamāsa*). If this is argued, we say: no, because [the latter] is desired and because [the former] is not expressed (*anabhidhāna*).

In this regard, one might argue: "Even though forms such as *pūrvakāya* and so forth are established by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound, nevertheless, since words like *kāya* function in their primary sense, just as there occurs a sentence such as *pūrvaṃ kāyasya*, there would likewise occur a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound such as *kāyapūrva*. Therefore, the *ekadeśisamāsa* was initiated in order to exclude that possibility. But this is not so; for [the desired form] is already accepted, and because [the undesired form] is not actually expressed.

In that regard, first, because the word *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is used in the rule for "second" (*dvitīya*) and "third" (*tṛtīya*), the author of the Sūtras intended a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) there—as in *bhikṣādvitīyam* ("a second portion of alms"). Furthermore, regarding the rule "the neuter [word] *ardha*" (*ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*), the author of the Bhāṣya says: "A genitive compound is also desired here; for example: *apūpārdhaṃ mayā bhakṣitam*" ("half a cake was eaten by me"). Moreover, there is usage in the Paiṅgala-sūtra: *svarārdhaṃ cāryārdham* ("half a *svara* and half an *āryā*"). However, in the case of "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*apara*), a genitive compound will not occur due to the absence of such usage (*anabhidhāna*).
As before, [the words] "horse" (aśva) and "mare" (vaḍabā). 2.4.27.

The horse and mare are as previously stated. Regarding the term *aśvaḍavayoḥ*: although the case of animal compounds (*paśudvandva*) would already be established by the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣa*, the specific mention of *aśvavaḍavau* is for the purpose of a direct prescription (*pratipadavidhāna*). Consequently, because of this direct prescription, when the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) applies—such as in *aśvavaḍavam*—this present rule is set aside, and *sa napuṃsakam* alone takes effect.

For, by referring with that word [“tat”] to that which partakes in the state of being treated as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*), the neuter gender prescribed for it becomes, like the singular treatment itself, prescribed by the specific wording of the rule (*pratipadavihita*). As for the extension (*atideśa*) “as in the previous case,” that serves its purpose in the alternative where the singular treatment does not apply; thus he says: “there, other than in the case of singular treatment. “It is not a technical designation (*nipātana*): for if it were a technical designation, the statement “as in the previous case” would be redundant, meaning it would be unintended. However, if it were a technical designation, that [extension] would be intended, because a technical designation applies only to the form exactly as it is uttered.
In the Vedic language, the forms *hemanta-śiśirau* and *ahorātre* are used as dual neuter compounds.

Regarding the rule *hemantaśiśirāvahorātre ca chandasi*: In the phrase *hemantaśiśirau*, the neuter gender would have been expected here because the word *śiśira* is neuter. However, some authorities consider both [words] to be of both genders, as in the rule *hemantaḥ śiśiro'striyām*; for them, the form *hemantaśiśirau* in this context would be meaningless [as it would not indicate a specific gender]. In the phrase *ahorātre*, the masculine gender would have been expected by the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*. Thus, it is stated that there is a "reversal of gender" (*liṅgavyatyaya*), according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* ("there is extensive substitution").
The words *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine. (Pāṇini 2.4.29)

"Words ending in *rātra*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine"—thus these are stated to be used in the masculine. Some say: "By this rule, the masculinity of *rātra* and the others alone is prescribed; however, as for that which ends in them, the gender is already established by the rule *paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ* (the gender of a dvandva or tatpuruṣa is like that of the final member). But if this were so, then in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (it is neuter) would apply instead, because that [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the final member. Therefore, it is more logical that this prescription of gender applies to the compound itself when it ends in *rātra* and the others. For in this way, even in the case of a collective compound, this very rule prevails due to its superior status (*paratva*).

In the phrase "these are spoken of [as feminine] when applied to a male," the meaning here should be understood as "ending with these. Regarding *trirātra*: this is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), with the compound-final suffix *ac* added by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśe*. Regarding *pūrvāhṇa*: this is a part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*) meaning "the former part of the day. The substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* occurs by the rules *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* and *ahnahna etebhyaḥ*, and the retroflex nasalization (*ṇatva*) is applied by the rule *ahno'dantāt*. Regarding *dvyaha*: there is no substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* because of the prohibition *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre*, and the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva*.

Regarding the rule "anuvākādayaḥ puṃsi": since these are technical names for specific types of sentences, they would normally be neuter by virtue of being formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*); this statement is made to establish their masculine gender.
The word *apatha* is neuter. 2.4.30.

*Apatha* is neuter. This rule is commenced because the previous rule, *pathaḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*, applies at a later stage [of derivation]. Regarding *apatham*: when, by the rule *patho vibhāṣā*, the prohibition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not take effect, then the suffix *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* is applied as the compound-ending. Because of this specific mention of the compound-ending, in the alternative case where it is absent, the masculine gender alone prevails—as in *apanthāḥ*. The term *tatpuruṣaḥ* (masculine) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. For this very reason, it was not placed immediately after the rule *sa napuṃsakam*.
The names of the half-verses (ardharca) are used in the masculine as well. (Pāṇini 2.4.31)

"Ardharcas are [masculine] and [feminine]. By virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), according to the maxim of the "parasol-bearer" (*chattrin-nyāya*), words such as *kārṣāpaṇa* are also included under the term *ardharca*. He states this, for the plural number here is the authority [for this inclusion]. This dual gender is based on the form of the word; the intended meaning here is merely that two genders occur in this specific word-form, and not that two genders occur in every single one of its referents (*artha*). This is the sense.

He asks, "What is established when this is the case? and replies with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*).
