As the venerable Jaimini said: "That which is designated as *Mantra* among the injunctive texts (*codaka*) is the definition of *Mantra*; the term *Brāhmaṇa* applies to the remainder. In the *Hariścandra-Brāhmaṇa* of the Bahvṛcas, this is the statement of Varuṇa to Hariścandra: "His teeth have fallen out."

But how is it that the mention of "mantra" includes the mention of "brāhmaṇa"? To this he says: "The mention of mantra, however... Since a mantra has the nature of *chandas* (Vedic verse), the latter is indicated by the former. However, because they are predominantly seen within the *mantra*, the term "mantra" was used [instead of "veda"].
The word *āma* [is used in the vocative case]. 2.4.81.

[The rule] *āmaḥ* [means]: "There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *liṭ* following *ām*. Although *liṭ* is specified by *sic* [in the previous rule], the sense is that here only *liṭ* continues to apply. In forms such as *vidāmakran* and *vidāṅkurvantu*, elision occurs due to a specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*) regarding the *luṅ* and *loṭ* suffixes. Furthermore, suffixes such as *-tara-* do not arise after a stem ending in *ām*, because that [ending in *ām*] does not express a completed action (*anabhivyakta-padārthatvāt*). And this elision (*luk*), being prescribed when the *tiP* and other suffixes have not yet applied, is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitutes for *l* (i.e., the *tiṅ* suffixes).

Because the *ām* suffix is not a finite verb (*atiṅ*), in the example "the eye [desired]," [the rule] *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* applies; thus, there is no *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent for that [first finite verb], and consequently, the *udātta* (high-pitched) accent for the following one is established. How does the *ām*-ending form possess the status of a word (*padatva*)? Because it ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Since the *l*-suffix possesses the nature of a *kṛt* suffix, it has the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For the prohibition "not a finite verb" (*atiṅ*) applies to a *l*-suffix that is about to become a finite verb (*tiṅbhāvin*), and this [here] is not about to become a finite verb. Why is the case-suffix (*sup*) not heard? Because the *ām* is listed among the indeclinables (*svarādi*) and thus functions as an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Even when accompanied by a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, it is not only that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix that is understood [by the term "nañ"]; rather, because of pervasion (*vyāpti*), even that which does not end in a *taddhita* suffix is included. Consequently, there arises the undesirable contingency of forming a compound with *tu* (the suffix *-tu*) by means of *nañ*, as in *na kārayām* and *na hārayām*. Would this not result in a compound according to the rule "a word ending in *nañ* is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix"? This is not a fault; for the capacity of *nañ* is realized only in connection with a verbal root whose meaning is fully expressed, such as in *yājayāñcakāra*, and not with a mere form ending in *am* whose meaning is not yet fully expressed.

Regarding the prohibition of *ṇal* after forms ending in *ām*: [in the examples] *śaśāma* and *tatāma*, once *vṛddhi* has been applied, since *ṇal* would be included by the principle of "treating as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), its elision (*luk*) would follow because it is included by the mention of the letter *l*. [Response: This is established because of the rule "the mention of that which possesses meaning" (*arthavad-grahaṇāt*). Only a meaningful form ending in *ām* is mentioned, and this [form resulting from the substitution] is not meaningful. [Objection: Even so, in the case of "the root *am* in the sense of 'going' etc.," where *tip* is replaced by *ṇal* to form *āma*, the elision would still apply here because it is meaningful. [Response: No, because of the rule: "Between that which is mentioned by a general definition and that which is mentioned by its specific form, only the latter is to be understood. Therefore, it will not occur in this case.
After an indeclinable (avyaya), the case endings (sup) and the feminine suffixes (āp) are elided.

Regarding the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82): in the example *tatra śālāyām*, because the feminine gender associated with the substance (*dravya*) is expressed through its case-role power (*kāraka-śakti*) in proximity to the word *śālā*, if there were a feminine suffix even here in *tatra*—just as there is in *tasyām*—then the feminine gender would be understood from the word itself. Therefore, to prevent such confusion, the elision (*luk*) of the *ṭāp* suffix must be stated; this is the intention behind the statement that "there is a prohibition [of feminine suffixes] after those bases designated as *ṣat*. However, the author of the Vārttika says: "The statement regarding the elision of *āp* after an indeclinable is unnecessary, because of the absence of gender (*liṅga*)."

Having performed [the action], having taken away—this refers to when the rule for the suffixes *su* and so forth (*svādividhi*) forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule "the plural number is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*), etc.; then, because the elision (*luk*) is prescribed by this very rule for indeclinables (*avyaya*) which lack number and case-role (*niṣkāraka*), the suffixes *su* and so forth arise from them by virtue of that indicative mark (*liṅga*). Even if there were separate syntactic units (*bhinnavākyatā*), under the view of restriction (*niyamapakṣa*), there would be an exclusion of similar classes by way of restriction: the plural suffix occurs only for many, not for two or one; the dual suffix occurs only for two, not for one or many; the singular suffix occurs only for one, not for two or many.

The suffixes beginning with *su* (the case-endings) can arise after indeclinables (*avyaya*) because they occur after many [words]. However, according to the view that [the suffixes] consist of three parts (*trikapakṣa*), the number is prescribed as the expressed meaning only where a number is possible. Since indeclinables are devoid of number, the case-endings (*svādi*) prescribed generally do indeed exist after them; therefore, the production of case-endings from indeclinables must be accepted in every respect—so that the technical designation "word" (*pada*) may apply by virtue of the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the term *tub* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) for the locative plural ending formed by the letter *p*, and not for the suffix *kap*; this is because *āp* is mentioned separately.
The case ending *am* is not substituted for the nominative and accusative dual of an avyayībhāva compound ending in *a*, except for the fifth (ablative) case.

"An *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *at* does not take the suffix *am*, except for the ablative case (*pañcamī*). For what purpose is this prohibition? It is so that the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the preceding rule may not occur. Here, *am* is being enjoined; since it is introduced while the elision (*luk*) has not yet become applicable, it will serve as its sublater (*bādhaka*). But where [the suffix] is prohibited, there the elision (*luk*) would apply to the ablative. However, when the prohibition exists, by virtue of its capacity, two sentences are formed: one is "not after an *avyayībhāva*," and the second is "*am* except for the ablative. And here, the word "ending in *at*" (*ataḥ*) is required [as a reference].

In this context, by the phrase "except for the fifth" (*apañcamyāḥ*), either a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes; thus, the substitution [of *āt*] for the fifth case is prohibited, not the prohibition established by the preceding sentence. The word *tu* (but) clarifies this very point: let there be a prohibition without distinction, namely, "except for the fifth. This is what was stated: "When that [substitution] is prohibited, there is simply the hearing (i.e., retention) of the fifth case. The split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), however, is clear in the Vṛtti itself. [The example is: *upakumbhāt*.

The meaning is "from the jar that has become near. Others hold that it means "from the vicinity of the jar. An indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) such as *unmattagaṅgā* ("the mad Gaṅgā"), which has another word as its predominant referent (*anyapadārthapradhāna*) and denotes a substantive (*sattvavācin*), is a primary example of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) because it possesses the status of an ablative (*apādānatva*) due to the existence of a connection with an action.
The substitution of the genitive case ending for the third and seventh case endings occurs diversely.

The [substitution of *ām* for the case-ending] occurs diversely (*bahulam*) in the third and seventh cases. Regarding *subhadram*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "the prosperity of the Madras"; from that, the seventh case ending is applied, and its final vowel is invariably replaced by *ām*. Regarding *ekaviṃśatibhāradvājam*: this is a compound formed by the rule "a numeral with a word denoting lineage" (*saṅkhyā vaṃśyena*), meaning "twenty-one Bhāradvājas belonging to a lineage. In that case, because the meanings of the constituent words denote another object in which their own referents are subordinate (*svārthopasarjana*), the word *bhāradvāja* has shifted into another object qualified by singularity; thus, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ*.

We say "no," because [if it were so] there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) even in cases such as "the family of the Gargas" (*gargāṇāṃ kulam* = *gargakulam*). Therefore, due to the usage of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), there is no elision (*lugabhāva*) here.
In place of the first person of the *luṅ* (aorist), the suffixes *ḍā*, *ar*, and *iras* are substituted.

[The rule states: "In place of the first person of *luṅ*, there are *ḍā*, *rī*, and *ras*. [An objection follows: If this is so, then since there are three substitutes—*ti*, *tas*, and *anti*, etc.—for the *parasmaipada*, and likewise three—*ta*, *ātām*, and *jha*, etc.—for the *ātmanepada*, there are six bases (sthānin) but only three substitutes (ādeśa). Due to this discrepancy in number (*vaiṣamya*), the principle of correspondence according to number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would not apply.

Let there not be a designation according to numerical order; rather, the determination [of the substitutes] will be based on proximity (*āntarya*). And proximity is determined by meaning: that which has a single meaning replaces that which has a single meaning, that which has two meanings replaces that which has two meanings, and that which has many meanings replaces that which has many meanings. But how can it be determined that the *ḍā* suffixes and so forth have a single meaning, given that that which stands in the place of *tiP* has a single meaning, that which stands in the place of *tas* has two meanings, and that which stands in the place of *jhi* has many meanings? No, he says; for even through observation of usage, it is possible to determine that they have a single meaning and so forth.

Alternatively, only six substitutes are specified; how so? By means of an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical items). It is an *ekaśeṣa* of the compounds *ḍā-rau-ras* and *ḍā-rau-ras*. But if it were a compound of those that have already undergone *ekaśeṣa*—namely, *ḍā* and *ḍā* as *ḍā*; *rau* and *rau* as *rau*; *ras* and *ras* as *ras*; and then *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* as *ḍā-rau-ras*—then an undesirable correspondence of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would result: namely, that *ḍā* would apply to *ti* and *tas*; *rau* to *jhi* and *tha*; and *ras* to *ātām* and *jha*. [This is avoided by the first interpretation. Thus: *kartṛ*.

The substitute *ḍā* for *tip* is a replacement for the whole [stem]. The property of having multiple phonemes (*anekāltva*) is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Let it be, then, that it applies only to the final [phoneme]; the elision of *ṭi* occurs together with the *t* of *tip*. But surely the stem does not end in *t*; [we reply: by the force of the application of the indicatory *ḍ*, it will apply even to what is not a stem, just as in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the rule] applies even to what is not a vowel (*abha*).

Alternatively, it is established by means of sequential order (*ānupūrvya*). How so? Even though this [suffix] occurs in place of the final letter, it would not be a suffix (*apratyaya*); in the absence of the designation "suffix," the letter *ḍ* does not have the designation *it*; in the absence of the designation *it*, it is "more than one sound" (*anekāl*); when it is more than one sound, it is a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*); when it is a replacement for the whole, it is a suffix; when it is a suffix, it has the designation *it*; when it has the designation *it*, there is elision (*lopa*), and thus it becomes "one sound" (*ekāl*). Now, can it not then become a replacement for the final letter (*antādeśa*) through retrogression? This is established by means of sequential order.

*Kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*: by the rule "ri ca," there is the elision of the *tās* and *asti* suffixes. Regarding *adhyetā*: [the root] *iṅ* is used in the sense of studying. Now, why does the substitution of *e* for the final vowel (*ṭi*) not occur here once the replacements *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras* have been applied? Because in this grammatical operation, the [substitution of *e*] has already taken effect upon the original bases (*sthānin*). For here, both the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the word *ta* and the replacement by *ḍā* would apply; since both are subject to the application of a different word-form (*śabdāntara-prāpti*), they are considered non-eternal (*anitya*). Because the substitution of *e* for the final vowel is subsequent (*para*), it is applied first; then, by the principle that a rule may apply again once its conditions are met (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the replacement by *ḍā* occurs. The same should be understood for *rau* and *ras*.

Alternatively—let them first be substituted by *ḍāraurasaḥ*. The statement "thāsaḥ se" (Pāṇini 7.1.41) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the substitution of *et* for the final vowel (*ṭi*) does not apply to those substitutes of *tiṅ*. Otherwise, one would have simply stated "thāsaḥ sa". [In the example] *kartāsī*, there is the elision of *s* by the rule "tāsastyoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.38).
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
*The second chapter is completed.* Homage to that venerable Guru. [End of] the Kāśikāvṛtti.
Now begins the first quarter of the third chapter: *Pratyaya* (Suffixes), according to the *Padamañjarī*.

[This is] the justification [for the rule]. Here, if the technical names were prescribed by explicitly mentioning all the named elements (*saṃjñin*) in their own forms—such as "the suffix *san* is a *pratyaya*, the suffix *kyac* is a *pratyaya*, the suffix *kyaṅ* is a *pratyaya*"—then there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). Alternatively, if the name were prescribed by taking the *sa*-sound from the word *san* and using it as the beginning of a *pratyāhāra* up to the *pa*-sound of *kap*—whether here or in another rule—then, because several instances of the sound *p* are possible, there would be ambiguity.

For if the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) were relied upon, [the *pratyāhāra*] would include the *pakāra* of *sip*; however, if pervasion (*vyāpti*) is accepted, then it includes the *takāra* of *tanap* according to the rule "taptanaptanathanāśca. It might be argued: "Pervasion alone shall be resorted to, yet there will still be no *pratyāhāra* of *tanap* with the *pakāra*."

[Objection: Is this not an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), since the rule "ica ekāco'mpratyayavacca" teaches that *am* is treated like an affix (*pratyayavadbhāva*)? Otherwise, even in the sixth [chapter], because the technical term "affix" (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) applies there as well, *am* would inherently possess the status of an affix, and its treatment as such would not need to be extended by rule. [Reply: That is not so; for in that context, the word *am* occurs twice. Consequently, that extension (*atideśa*) is intended so that specific operations—such as "auto'mśasoḥ"—which are otherwise dependent on what is not an affix, may take place.

But even so, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) would be purposeless; one should simply say "like *am*" (*amvat*). From this mention of "affix," it is understood that even an operation caused by an affix is to be extended by analogy. That will serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the stated meaning. Even so, since *am* is an augment (*āgama*), it would not apply [the rule] like *puK* and others because it lacks the status of an affix; therefore, there must be an extension of its being an affix.

Or, let it be an indicator (*jñāpaka*); even so, why is this pervasion (*vyāpti*) resorted to, rather than proximity (*pratyāsatti*)? Furthermore, as it stands, there would be the very same complexity (*gaurava*) due to the addition of the extra term *sa*. Therefore, to avoid this complexity and over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), this technical name (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed by means of an overarching heading (*adhikāra*). Thus he says: "The word *pratyaya* is introduced as a technical name. The term *kārake* is introduced as its qualifier, just as in the case [of P. 1.4.1]: "In the domain of suffixes beginning with *sva-* and ending with *kap*, this is the base (*prakṛti*)."

When it should have been stated, "The word *pratyaya* is authorized as a technical term (*saṃjñā*)," the expression "as a technical term" (*saṃjñātvena*) is used because there is no difference in meaning. For instance, in the cases "this person here is authorized as a laborer" (*karmakaratvena adhikṛtaḥ*) and "this laborer here is authorized," there is no difference in meaning; however, when one says "the laborer is authorized," it is understood that the laborer is authorized in a particular capacity (or form). But when it is stated again as "as a laborer" (*karmakaratvena*), it is understood that the authorization belongs specifically to that very aspect (or form).

"Is employed"—that is, it is applied by the author of the Sūtra. "Those [channels] etc., which we shall enumerate"—meaning we shall set them forth in sequence. This statement belongs to the author of the Vṛtti, who is acting as if he were the author of the Sūtra.

If, then, the designation [of "suffix"] is made by virtue of this governing rule (*adhikāra*), then because it applies to every individual occurrence, it would follow that the designation applies even to the base (*prakṛti*), the prefix (*upapada*), the condition (*upādhi*), the modification (*vikāra*), and the augment (*āgama*). For example: in the rule *harater ddatināthayoḥ paśau*, *harateḥ* is the base (*prakṛti*); *ddatināthayoḥ* is the prefix (*upapada*); *paśau* is the condition (*upādhi*); *hanasta ca* and so forth is the modification (*vikāra*); and *trapujatunoḥ puk* is the augment (*āgama*). And if the designation were present, there would arise a mutual posteriority (*paratva*) between the base and the suffix, depending on each other in turn.

Is it that the base depends on another word, or that the suffix depends on the base? Since the *upapada* also follows [the base], its priority would prevail over the rule "the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) comes first" in cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, thereby subverting it; and where, due to the absence of a compound, the rule "the subordinate member comes first" does not apply, there the *upapada* would indeed follow. If this were the case, then in the expression *bhoktuṃ vrajati* ("he goes to eat"), this form alone would always be used, and not *vrajati bhoktum*; for the meaning itself is the limiting factor (*upādhi*).

Even though "posteriority" (*paratva*) is impossible [in this context], since there would otherwise be no restriction on the use of terms expressing it, the rule *paraśca* would serve as a restrictive rule. Furthermore, the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) would occur by overriding other accents as appropriate. However, the technical designation of a "base" (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) is contingent upon a specific injunction; and since here the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth are not enjoined by anything, that designation does not apply to what precedes the base and so forth when they are followed by something else. But surely, even if the rule were to apply with each individual operation, the designation for the base and so forth would not occur because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). It is thus.

"Indeed—the first sentence is: 'When *hṛ* [the root *harati*] and *dā* [the roots *dadāti* and *dadhāti*] are the governing words (*upapada*) as objects (*karman*), the suffix *in* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is an animal'; and the second is: 'And those [roots], such as *hṛ* and the rest, are designated by the technical term "suffix" (*pratyaya-saṃjñaka*)'. Is it not the case that when a single sentence is possible, a split of sentences (*vākya-bheda*) is not desired? This is not so; because even for *san* and the others, since they do not yet exist, the designation cannot be established, the designation must be enjoined through a split of sentences. Consequently, one sentence would enjoin *san* and the others, while another would enjoin the designation. Would this same logic then apply to the base (*prakṛti*) and the governing words (*upapada*) as well? To this, he says: "The base, the governing word," and so forth.

The intended meaning is as follows: since *prakṛti* and the other elements are taken as the causes for the production of suffixes such as *san*, they exist for the sake of another (*pārārthya*); therefore, they lack the status of being motivators (*prayojaka*) with respect to their own grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*). For example, in the statement "He who is on the seat is Devadatta," the designation "Devadatta" does not apply to the seat.

Now, it might be argued that in the first rule concerning the derivation of *san* and other suffixes, those [roots] are subservient to another purpose, but not in the second rule, which is intent on establishing the relationship between a technical name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). Furthermore, such a rule as "the suffix *san* follows *gup*, *tij*, and *kid*" is indeed intent on prescribing the technical name; and since even there the roots are indicated by means of a past-participle case-ending (*bhūta-vibhakti*), their status as causes remains established, and thus their subservience to another purpose persists.

Furthermore, due to the absence of a suitable case-ending, there can be no designation (*saṃjñā*) for the base (*prakṛti*) and so forth; for the connection with a designation occurs only for that which ends in the nominative or the genitive, as in the rules "vṛddhir ādaic" and "svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya. Nor can a designation be established in the second sentence by supplying a suitable case-ending, because such an ending has already served its purpose in the case of *san* and other elements specified with their respective case-endings.

However, since the designation of *upapada* is prescribed for that which is indicated by the locative case, it is logical that this occurs through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and the supply of an appropriate case-ending. Furthermore, when both a primary element and another element are in proximity, the application of an operation is understood to pertain to the primary element; and that for which there is an original prescription (*apūrvavidhāna*) is the primary element.

Therefore, it is established as our desired conclusion that in the first sentence, the suffixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth alone possess primacy; and in the second [sentence] as well, the designation (*saṃjñā*), requiring a designated object (*saṃjñin*), requires precisely that which was understood as primary in the preceding sentence, and not that which is secondary due to its dependence on another. Even so, would this not result in [the application of the term *pratyaya*] to modifications (*vikāra*) and augments (*āgama*)? This is not a fault; for a grand designation is being made so that it may be understood as a "significant" designation—namely, that a *pratyaya* is so called because "by means of it, one recognizes (*pratiyantyanena*) the meaning."

Furthermore, people do not comprehend meaning through modification (*vikāra*) or addition (*āgama*). If that were so, there would be no meaning for [suffixes] such as *ka* in *aveḥ kaḥ* and for compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), for no specific meaning is determined for these through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since that meaning is understood from the base (*prakṛti*) alone even in their absence.

As for the claim that "suffixes whose meaning is not specifically stated occur in their own sense," and thus their meaning is indeed their own sense—that too is a mere conceptual construction; for the possession of a meaning is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the designation of a suffix would occur when its own sense is prescribed, and the designation of a suffix would occur when it possesses a meaning because its own sense is prescribed.

If that is the case, then [the augment] will not occur due to the absence of purpose? For, since their status as "prior" (paratva) is impossible—given that they establish both a connection with the sixth case (sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī) and a connection with the whole (avayava-sambandha)—and because the rule ordaining that augments are unaccented (anudātta) makes it impossible for them to have an acute accent on the first syllable (ādyudāttatva); nevertheless, if there were a purpose, even for the augment *śnam*, the designation *it* would indeed apply to its letter *ś*.

Now, why is the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) not applied to the multi-alphabetic substitutes such as *vadha* in the rule *hanaśca vadhaḥ*, *nabha* in *nābhi nabhañca*, and *viraṅga* in *virāga viraṅgañca*, since their status as subsequent (*paratva*) could indeed serve as a purpose? Although, because the original element (*sthānin*) has been replaced by the substitute, there can be no "subsequent-ness" relative to that; nevertheless, "subsequent-ness" would certainly exist in relation to other words.

As was stated previously: "In the case of [suffixes] such as *guP*, they possess meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), they have primacy because they are prescribed (*vidheya*), and they have the appropriate case-ending (*vibhakti*). Therefore, in all cases regarding [the application of suffixes] such as *vadh*, an effort must be made to prevent the designation (*saṃjñā*) [of 'root']. It must be done; it is to be performed. Here, when the designation of a suffix (*pratyaya*) applies, there is the designation of the stem (*aṅga*) for the root, and the *guṇa* substitution for the stem.

Even though [the suffixes] beginning with *tavyat* have been cited as examples despite being separated by intervening elements such as *san* and others, this is because the grammatical operations pertaining to suffixes—such as having an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*)—can still apply to them. However, in the case of *san* and the like, that [suffixal accent] is overridden by the *nit-svara* (the accent of a suffix marked with *n*) and the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*).
And the subsequent [element]. 3.1.2.

"And 'para' (subsequent) as well. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this [term] is an *adhikāra* (governing heading), not only the term "affix" (*pratyaya*). "It stands at each individual rule" (*yoge yoge upatiṣṭhate*): by this, the distinguishing characteristic of an *adhikāra* from a *paribhāṣā* (general maxim) is shown. For a *paribhāṣā* does not stand at every individual rule; rather, while remaining in one place, it operates throughout the entire treatise. "'And it is subsequent,' etc.": by this, it is shown that this very *paribhāṣā*, while situated here [in P. 3.1.1], has its operation everywhere in the prescription of affixes.

This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is characterized by its indicator (*liṅga*), and the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) serves as that indicator. The phrase "or from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ vā*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a base (*prakṛti*) denoting action, including even those ending in *tiṅ* affixes. The phrase "or from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt vā*) is an elliptical expression for a base not denoting action; by this, the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are also included. Thus, [the word] *taittirīyam* [is formed].

"He studies what was proclaimed by Tittiri. [The derivation is as follows: By the rule *tittirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhāc chaṇ*, [the suffix *chaṇ* is added]; by the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi*, [it is understood that this applies to Vedic texts and Brāhmaṇas]; by the rule *tad adhīte tad veda*, [the suffix indicates one who studies or knows that]; and by the rule *proktāl luk*, [the suffix *chaṇ* is elided]. Because the referent is a Brāhmaṇa lineage (*brāhmaṇakula*), there is neuter gender. The particle *ca* (and) serves to include this very same point, because there is nothing else to be included. "By him" (*tena*).

Otherwise, since the use of the word *bahula* (in various senses) implies deviation from all conditions (*sarvopādhivyabhicāra*), one might suspect that even the rule of posteriority (*paratva*) would be optional in the case of the *uṇādi* suffixes. In this context, in rules such as *guptijkidbhyaḥ san*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of spatial direction (*digyogalakṣaṇā*). Since neither "prior" (*pūrva*) nor "posterior" (*para*) is explicitly heard there as a directional term, if they were to be supplied arbitrarily, there would be the undesirable consequence of irregular usage; therefore, this [sūtra] serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) to ensure that the suffix follows immediately after [the root], and not before it.

In cases such as *gāpoṣṭak*, even though there is a mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), since the genitive is understood to denote immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), and since immediate sequence exists even when [the element] is prior, the undesirable consequence (*aniyamaprasaṅga*) remains; therefore, in those instances as well, [the rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) alone.

This purpose is not necessary; the rule "vibhāṣā supo bahuc purastāttu" will serve as a restrictive rule (niyamārtha), meaning that *bahuc* alone occurs before [the stem] and no other suffix does. Consequently, since the position before [the stem] is restricted to *bahuc*, any other suffix will necessarily occur after it. If it is argued that, in the case of rules involving genitive indications (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*), there is the possibility of insertion even in the middle by supplying the word "in the middle" (*madhya*), we say no; because of the restriction "avyayasarvanāmnāmakac prāk ṭeḥ," *akac* alone occurs in the middle of the base (*prakṛti*).

Is it that [the suffix] occurs [only] there and not elsewhere? This is not so. If the restriction were such that "there must be many [suffixes] before and only one in the middle," then there would be no restriction regarding the many and the single. Alternatively, if [the restriction were] that "there must be many before and only one in the middle," then, because the location would be unrestricted, another suffix would certainly occur there; thus, in every case, an undesirable consequence follows. Furthermore, if the restriction were "only *akac* before the final vowel (*ṭi*"), then while another suffix might not occur before the *ṭi*, it would certainly occur in other parts of the middle.

Because the restriction [of the rule] depends on a specific intermediate element (*madhyaviśeṣa*). Nor is priority (*paratva*) established here by the *paribhāṣā* "therefore, of what follows" (*tasmādityuttarasya*), for that is the domain of this maxim where something is prescribed for something that already exists previously—such as: "for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurring after a word and not at the beginning of a metrical foot (*apādādau*), *vāna* and *āvana* are substituted [respectively].

But here, *san* and the others are prescribed as being non-existent before; there is nothing related to them [that exists prior]. If it is argued that their very designation as suffixes (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) is their effect, we say no; even so, their production prior [to the base] would remain unavoidable.

For instance: since the prescription of a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) for non-existent elements such as *san* and others is untenable, one must accept that by the first sentence there is a prescription of *san* and others, and by the second sentence there is the prescription of their technical names. Consequently, in the second sentence, because *san* already exists as an effect, the presence of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) would result in the mere retention of the name for those [elements] previously employed, but their actual production (*utpatti*) would occur at an indefinite location; for the technical rule does not apply in the first sentence.

It might be argued as follows: In rules such as *gup-tij-kid-bhyaḥ san*, there is only one ablative case (*pañcamī*), and it can only supply a single directional term (*dik-śabda*). When a doubt arises as to whether that term should be "prior" (*pūrva*) or "subsequent" (*para*), if the word "prior" were supplied, the natural sense (*svarasa*) of the second sentence would be violated. For the meaning naturally obtained from that [second rule] is: "The suffix *san* becomes known by the technical name 'affix' when it follows *gup* and the others. This natural sense would be destroyed if the word "prior" were supplied in the preceding sentence; therefore, to preserve that sense, the word "subsequent" (*para*) alone shall be supplied.

Let it be that the production [of a word] occurs at an indefinite location; however, the grammatical operation (*śāstrakārya*)—such as the designation of *kṛt* suffixes and *pratyaya*s—which applies to something already existent, does not apply to what is in another location. And that which is in the location where the grammatical operation applies will exclude what is in another location.

Is it because that [suffix] alone is correct due to its being governed by a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*)? Let it be so. But then, how can there be "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) in cases where the designation of a suffix (*pratyayasaṃjñā*) does not even occur—such as in *śameḥ khaḥ* → *śaṅkhaḥ*, *kaṇeṣṭhaḥ* → *kaṇṭhaḥ*, and so on—since there is no operation of the second sentence [of Pāṇini’s definition]? Or how is it for you yourself? For you too define subsequent-ness based on the suffix by stating, "that which is a suffix is subsequent. True.

Under the view that this is a *paribhāṣā* (a general metarule), there would be no status of being "subsequent" (*paratva*); however, under the view that it is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading), the status of being subsequent does not occur preceded by the status of being an affix (*pratyayatva*). Rather, the designation of "affix" applies subsequently to that which has already arisen as qualified by the status of being subsequent. But in this case, due to the statement of "diversity" (*bahulavacana*), the status of being subsequent is not contradicted even in the absence of the status of being an affix. Even so, this [sūtra] serves no purpose; for by the very statement of "diversity," the status of being subsequent will be established here anyway? If that is the case, then this is for the purpose of restricting usage: that the affix must be "subsequent" alone and not merely [the root] by itself.

Otherwise, if one intended to express only the meaning of the suffix, the suffix alone would be employed, as in "what is its pair? (kimasya dvayasam) or "what is its mere measure? (kimasya mātram); or as in the case of expressing excellence, where the comparative and superlative forms appear as *tāratama-bhāvaḥ* and *tāratamyam*.

Is it not the case that [the suffix] is prescribed only after specifying a particular base (*prakṛti*), and thus, by the principle stated previously, only that which is qualified by the suffix is prescribed, so that there is no usage of the base alone? Even so, when there is a desire to express the meaning of the base alone, the base would indeed be used in its isolated form, as in *pac* or *vṛkṣa*. However, where both are intended to be expressed—the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix—there is no possibility of using the base in isolation.

The base alone is not capable of expressing the meaning of the suffix. If it is argued that it is capable through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we reply: no; for even this rule, though being formulated, cannot prevent usage by means of secondary indication. Therefore, the rule is commenced so that when there is a desire to express the meaning of the base alone, the base alone should not be employed. The word *ca* is used for emphasis; the syntactical interpretation is that the suffix "indeed follows" [the base], and it is never the case that it does not follow.

This rule applies until the completion of the word; once the word is formed, it is used exactly as it stands. However, when there is a desire to express another meaning, such as "offspring" (apatya) and so forth, a different suffix is added even after that [already formed] word.
And it has the acute accent on the first syllable. 3.1.3.

And [the term] *ādyaudātta* [is used]. Since it is impossible to pronounce a vowel (*ac*) that lacks a specific accent (*asvaraka*), every rule concerning accents is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). In this regard: only that which is marked with the *cit* sign has its final syllable acute; only that which is marked with the *ṭi* sign has its middle syllable acute; only that which is marked with the *ti* sign is circumflex (*svarita*); only those ending in *sup* or *pit* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*); and only in the case of a vocative from a distance is there monotony (*ekaśrutya*).

Since other vowels are restricted elsewhere, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the suffix will necessarily be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable); it cannot be without an accent (*asvaraka*) nor have any other accent. To this he replies: "there would be the contingency of a suffix with an unrestricted accent. That which has an unrestricted accent is "aniyatasvara"; such a thing being a suffix is "aniyatasvarapratyaya. The meaning is that the purpose [of the rule] is to prevent the contingency of a suffix having an unrestricted accent.

In the reading *aniyata-svara-prasaṅga*, however, the meaning is "the contingency of an indefinite accent. The intention is as follows: even the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) would not be fixed by rules such as *ñ-nityādir nityam* [P. 6.1.197] and so on; there would indeed be no restriction elsewhere where this rule does not apply. Furthermore, under the restriction stated by you, there would be no restriction regarding *cid-ādi* [particles].

Therefore, one must accept that the specific nature of the restriction (niyama) in various instances is such that "only what ends in *ci* is circumflex" (*titsvarita eva*), and so forth; consequently, the suffix itself would remain of unrestricted accent. Furthermore, even under the restriction "only [a suffix] ending in *ri* has its penultimate syllable unaccented" (*rityevopottamanudāttam*), let it be that elsewhere the penultimate is not unaccented; however, the middle part [of the suffix] would certainly still be subject to accentuation, because the restriction depends upon a specific middle portion. Therefore, since there is the contingency of unrestricted accent for those monosyllabic suffixes, this rule is intended for the sake of establishing the acute accent (*udātta*).

Furthermore, regarding those suffixes that consist of more than one syllable, there would result an uncertainty as to the location [of the accent]: sometimes it would apply to the first syllable, sometimes to the middle, and sometimes to the last. Among such suffixes, this rule is stated for the purpose of making [the first syllable] acute; even therein, it is for the purpose of making the first syllable acute.

But for what purpose is this accent prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix), rather than being stated within the very section on accents under the rules "the first syllable of that which is marked with Ñ or Ṅ is always acute" (*ñnityādir nityam*) and "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes and *sup*-affixes ending in *p* or *it* are unaccented" (*pratyayasya ca lasārvadhātukamanudāttaṃ suppitau*)? For in this way, the section would remain undivided. Furthermore, the double mention of "acute on the first syllable" (*ādyudāttagrahaṇa*) would not need to be made twice.

It might be argued as follows: if that [rule] were formulated there, then by the *paribhāṣā* regarding the inclusion of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the accentuation would apply to the end of that [suffix]; however, if it were formulated here, this fault would not occur. For a suffix, once produced, serves as the cause for operations such as the rule of "end-of-that" (*tadantavidhi*) which depend upon it, but while it is being produced, it does not. Indeed, a jar while in the process of being produced cannot be conceived as the cause for actions such as carrying water; therefore, since the rule "and [the first syllable is] acute" (*ādyudāttaśca*) applies at every occurrence, even while it is being produced...

[Objection: "The suffixes beginning with *tavya* are acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), while those beginning with *tiP* are grave (*anudātta*); thus there is no fault, and therefore the accent is prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of 'suffix'. [Response: That is not so; it is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since he states that "a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* is acute," this indicates that in the rule "and of a suffix" (*pratyayasya ca*), the designation of "that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply; consequently, the grave accent will also not apply to that which ends in such a suffix.

This is because of the force of the rule prescribing the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)—namely, that "the final syllable of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is acute"—since the original accent is heard where the suffix is unaccented, as in *yāti* and *vṛkṣābhyām*. However, in cases such as *yātaḥ*, *yānti*, and *vṛkṣatvam*, it is superseded by the acute accent of the beginning of the suffix, which is established later (*satiśiṣṭa*). Furthermore, if the entire word ending in a suffix were unaccented, the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of roots and nominal stems (*prātipadika*) would become devoid of scope.

Then this is the purpose: so that in forms such as *lavitavya*, when the acute accent on the initial syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) has been applied at the very time the suffix is produced, the subsequent augment *iṭ* shall be unaccented (*anudātta*). Otherwise, in the case of *lū-tavya*, the initial acute accent would be non-permanent because it applies to a different word-form; however, *iṭ* would apply to a form already modified by accent. Since both [the initial accent and *iṭ*] are non-permanent, *iṭ* would be applied first due to its posteriority; once it is applied, since it is included by the mention of "suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), the initial acute accent would belong to *iṭ* itself. This too is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely this: [the rule regarding the accent of the root].

He says, "The augment *yāsuṭ* [is applied] after [the suffixes of] the *parasmaipada*, and it is acute (*udātta*) and marked with the *ṅit* designation. This indicates that augments (*āgama*) are unaccented (*anudātta*). Otherwise, in forms such as *cinuyātām*, the acute accent would already be established because *yāsuṭ* is the beginning of a suffix (*pratyaya*); thus, that rule would be redundant. [Objection: But this rule must exist for the sake of the *pit* designation; otherwise, in forms like *cinuyāt*, the *yāsuṭ*—being part of a *pit* element—would be unaccented. [Reply: If its purpose were merely this, he would have simply prohibited the *pit* designation by stating, "The *yāsuṭ* occurs after *parasmaipada* suffixes, and it is also a *liṅ* suffix. Thus, the *pit* status itself would be barred.

This indicator (jñāpaka) must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, even in the rule prescribing initial acute accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) in connection with the technical designation of an affix (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*), in forms such as *laviṣīya*, there would be no accent at the stage of the root *lū* because it lacks a vowel. Consequently, since the *sīyuṭ* augment is specifically prescribed and is subsequent [in application], it would be applied first; then, when the substitute for *lā* is applied later, the initial acute accent of the affix would apply by this sequence, and thus the accent would belong to the *sīyuṭ* itself. However, when the indicator is resorted to, the *sīyuṭ* is unaccented, and the vowel *a* of the *iṭ* augment becomes acute by the rule "iṭo't" (Pāṇini 6.1.167).

How is this so? For when the augment *sīyuṭ* is applied, the initial status (*āditva*) of the vowel *a* is interrupted. This is not a fault; the statement that *yāsuṭ* is acute serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that when the acute accent of the beginning of a suffix is to be applied, augments are treated as non-existent. Otherwise, in forms such as *cinuyātām*, the acuteness would already be established because *yāsuṭ* is the beginning of the suffix, and thus that rule [regarding *yāsuṭ*] would be redundant.

Furthermore, in cases such as *lavitavyam*, although the initial vowel is first acute (*ādyudātta*), why does the subsequent augment *iṭ* become unaccented (*anudātta*) by the rule of "the remainder" (*śeṣanighāta*)? This is not a case for *śeṣanighāta*, because that rule is supplementary to the rules governing accents. The meaning of *śeṣanighāta* is this: in whatever word, at whatever stage, an acute or circumflex accent is prescribed for a particular vowel, the other vowels situated nearby in that same word and at that same stage are suppressed (made unaccented). And this principle is not applicable here.

In this case, then, for the word *straughnī* derived from *strughna*, when the vowel *aṇ* is acute by virtue of the rule for suffixes, the accent of the disappearance of the acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*) for the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is established. Otherwise, if we were in the stage *straughna-ī*, the rule *pratyayasya ca* (P. 6.1.163), which prescribes an acute on the beginning of the suffix, would be set aside by the subsequent rule of elision of the *ya* (P. 6.4.148); since the acute disappearance would not have occurred, the desired accent would not be achieved. Nor can it be argued that [the elision] is exempt from this because it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), for the elision depends upon the production of the suffix *ṅīp*, whereas the accent is independent.

In this case, internal character (*antaraṅgatva*) must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, in the derivation of *kaṃsīyā* (feminine) from *kaṃsena krītā*, where *kaṃsāt ṭiṭhan* applies and *ṭit* triggers *ṅīp*, we would have the form *kaṃsa-ṭha-ī*. At this stage, the rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), which causes the elision of the *ṭha*-suffix, would apply because it is subsequent (*para*), thereby overriding the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed by *ñnityādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.197). Consequently, once the *nit-svara* (the accent of the suffix-initial *ṭha*) has been overridden by that elision, the initial acute accent of the vowel *a*—which was established by the very application of the technical designation *pratyaya* (suffix)—would remain. Upon the elision of that *a*, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the remaining vowel when an acute one is dropped) would then apply to the *ṅīp*.

But surely, because of the *cit* designation of the suffix *ṭhak*, the substitution of the vowel *i* occurs first, and subsequently the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to the beginning of the suffix; thus, there is no loss of an acute accent. In this case, however, consider *utsajātā* (born in a spring), derived from *utsādibhyo 'ñ* with the addition of *ṅīp*. When the form *uts-a-ī* is established, the rule for the accent of the *ñit* suffix would be superseded by the subsequent rule of elision (*yasyeti lopa*), and according to the principle stated previously, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that replaces a lost acute) would apply to the *ṅīp*. This is not a fault.

For the accent of *ñ* and *nit* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of the affix; and a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply where its exception is operative. In that case, the acute accent on the first syllable of the affix occurs here, as it awaits the exception—the accent of *ñ* and *nit*—so how could there be a loss of the acute? In this instance, however, regarding the derivative "Atri's descendant" (*ātreya*), the affix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*. According to the principle "the mention of the original form [of the base] is for the sake of establishing the accent," the substitution of *ey* occurs prior to the accentuation of the affix. When the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in the form *ātreya-ī*, the accent of the *taddhita* affix (by the rule *taddhitasya kitaḥ*) applies.

Since the *yasyeti-lopa* (elision of the *i* or *u* of a suffix) would supersede [the rule for accentuation] due to its being subsequent, the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the acute accent on the vowel replacing a circumflex) would not apply to the vowel *ī*; therefore, one must simply rely on its being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned). In this way, even in the case of *sraughnī*, the desired result is established by virtue of its being *antaraṅga* alone; thus, there is no purpose in the statement that the first syllable is acute by virtue of its being designated as a *pratyaya* (suffix).

In that case, this is the purpose: [the word] *gopāyati* and *dhūpāyati* first receive the acute accent on the initial syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) by virtue of their formation with the suffix *-ya*. Subsequently, when the designation "root" (*dhātu*) is applied by the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, the final syllable becomes acute (*antodāttatva*) by the rule *dhātoḥ*. However, if it were stated that "a root beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* is always [acute], as is a suffix," then the accent of the suffix would override the accent of the root due to its higher status in the order of application. This might be the case.

What, then, is the purpose of making the *anudātta* (unaccented) in this rule? It might be argued as follows: from the word *kārya*, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, because it is *svarita*-marked, once the *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) has been applied, that substitute would—by virtue of being like the final element with respect to the preceding part—be subject to the *svarita* accent (*titsvarita*), and by virtue of being like the initial element with respect to the following part, be subject to the *pit-svara* (the acute accent of the *pit* suffix). Since the latter is subsequent, the *svarita* would prevail. However, if it were stated that "the *lasārvadhātuka* is *anudātta*, as are *sup* and *pit* suffixes," then the *anudātta* would prevail due to its posteriority. That is not so.

For in that case, the circumflex (svarita) occurs even before the suffix *ṭāp* arises; or, even if *ṭāp* is present, since both the circumflex and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) are non-obligatory, the circumflex will be applied first due to its higher priority, and subsequently, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), the single substitute for the circumflex and the unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel will itself be circumflex.

In that case, consider this: in *āmbaṣṭhyā*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, both the accent of a *pit* (a suffix) and the accent of a *cit* (a suffix marked with *c*) would apply; since the latter is subsequent, the *cit*-accent prevails. Would the *pit*-accent not apply elsewhere? Even here, by the very force of the inclusion of the letter *c*, the *cit*-accent will prevail. For if the letter *c* were intended merely to prevent the obstruction of the general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*), one could have prescribed the *ṭāp* suffix for the *yaṅ* formation right within the section on *ṭāp*. If that is so, then that same purpose [for the letter *c*] is simply to ensure that the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply.

As for what was said—that [the rule] is due to the force of the prescription of the *prakṛtisvara*—in that regard, in cases such as *āste* and *śete*, since the *anudātta* nature applies to the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes alone, there remains scope for the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). Furthermore, the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would be necessary for the establishment of the accent in forms such as *agnimān*, *vāyumān*, and *agnīnām*, by means of the rules *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup* and *nāmanyatarasyām*; for here, the term "from an oxytone" (*antodāttāt*) is understood to carry over. Thus, enough with this harsh scrutiny.
The suffixes *sup* and *pit* are unaccented.

"Sup and pit are unaccented. Here, "sup" is a *pratyāhāra* (a technical abbreviation), not the locative plural suffix (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). Since the unaccented nature [of these] is already established by their being marked with *p*, for this very reason the commentary uses the plural form "supaḥ. However, the plural form "pitaḥ" is used here merely to conform to the style of the preceding context. Furthermore, the *pratyāhāra* "sup" is formed by the letter *p*, not by the letter *k*; for if it were formed by *k*, the *ṭāp* suffixes and others would have been marked with *p*. As for the example "pacati": this is an illustration of a word ending in a *śap* suffix; as for the *tip* suffix, however, because it is taught as having an indicatory *u* (*adupadeśāt*), its unaccented nature is already established by the rule "lasārvadhātukam."
The suffix *saN* is applied after the roots *gup*, *tij*, *kit*, and *bhī*.

*Guptijkidbhyaḥ san*. Regarding *gup* in the sense of "to hide": the inclusion here is not of the roots *gup* in the sense of "agitation" (*vyākulatve*) or *gupū* in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇe*), because the *gup* that is read in the list together with *tij* is understood here as well by virtue of its being anudātta (unaccented). Furthermore, the designation *pratyaya* (suffix) is already established [by the governing rule]. What, then, is the concern regarding forgetfulness here? Rather, it is the concern that the designation *pratyaya* is etymological (*anvarthā*); thus, this [sūtra] removes the doubt that the *san* following *gup* and others would not be a suffix if they were devoid of meaning.

The meaning is that by virtue of its governing authority (*adhikāra*), [the suffix] applies even to that which is meaningless. However, being "significant" (*anvarthatā*) is not the reason for selecting the meaningful [roots] when both meaningful and meaningless [roots] are possible. Furthermore, blame (*nindā*) and so forth are the meanings of roots such as *gup*, not of the suffix *san*; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of those roots like *gup* becoming meaningless. Moreover, it is observed in various places that verbal roots possess multiple meanings. Suffixes, however, can also be "self-meaning" (*svārthika*), like those at the end of compounds (*samāsānta*) and so on. Thus: *jugupsate*.

Because this suffix *san* is not designated as a verbal root (*dhātu*) in that manner, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*, since it is not a verbal root. Regarding the term "blame and forbearance" (*nindākṣamā*), this statement of a condition is merely illustrative. Thus, in the passage concerning the word *kṣetriya*—"one who is to be treated in another's field"—the text says: "Alternatively, *kṣetriyāṇi* refers to weeds grown in a field for the sake of grain; they are 'to be treated,' meaning they are to be destroyed. Alternatively, *kṣetriyaḥ* refers to an adulterer; 'another's wife' is like 'another's field,' and therein he is 'to be treated,' meaning he is to be restrained."

Even in cases of doubt, [the suffix *san*] is observed—as in "he hesitated" (*vyacikitsat*), "he who, knowing thus, hesitates," and "the seer, having heard that, hesitated. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": this means from a different verbal root (*dhātu*) that functions with a different meaning. This has been explained more thoroughly under the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ*. As for the statement that the inclusion of the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) in the roots beginning with *gup* is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), this too has been explained in that very same place. The use of the plural in the expression "in the roots beginning with *gup*" (*gupādiṣu*) is intended to include the rules concerning *mān*, *badh*, and so forth.

This [root] is *kit* and *parasmaipadī*, as the subsequent examples have already demonstrated. The letter *n* in *san* is for the sake of the accent; by the power of its being marked with *ni*, the accent of the root does not occur—as in "when you wish to kill your friend, the singer. It also serves a restrictive purpose: [to prevent the application of] *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* and *haneḥ saḥ* [in the formation of] *haṃsa*; and [to prevent the application of] *stauti-ṇyoreva ṣaṇy-abhyāsāt* [in the formation of] *suṣupiṣa indram*.

In the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* as well, although there is no possibility of the suffix *sa* after roots such as *tṛṇ* due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *dhātoḥ* from the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ*, [the mention of *san*] would still apply in cases like *haṃsaḥ* and *vatsaḥ* under the view that Uṇādi derivatives are etymologically derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*). In the case of *pratīṣiṣati*, when the suffix *san* is prescribed after the root *iṇ* preceded by *prati*, this is for the purpose of ensuring that the doubling (*dvirvacana*) applies to the second syllable according to the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya*. It should be stated: "As desired, for denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*)," as in *putrīyiṣiṣati*.

But elsewhere, regarding the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, there is the elision of the vowel *a* (*ato lopaḥ*), whereas for *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, there is a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) with the *śap* augment; thus, there is no difference [in the result].
After the roots *mān*, *badh*, *dān*, and *śān*, [the suffix *san* is added], and there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding the rule *mānbadhadānśānbhyo dīrghaścābhyāsasya*: here, *mān* and *badh* are anudātta (unaccented) roots, while the remaining two (*dān* and *śān*) are svarita (circumflex-accented). The meaning is that the long vowel is substituted for the *i* of the reduplication; that is, after the substitution of *i* by the rule *sanyataḥ*, the long vowel [of the root] occurs in the reduplication.

But surely, since the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is prescribed by a specific rule, it would supersede the short *it* prescribed by a general rule and apply only to the vowel *a*? This is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*): namely, that when [Pāṇini] says "of that which is not followed by *kit*" (*akitaḥ*) in the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ*, he thereby indicates that among modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*), there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). For if such sublation were allowed, [the long vowel] would apply even after the augment *nuṭ* has been added in forms such as *yaṃyamya-te*.

Furthermore, if there were a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between these two modifications [the shortening and the lengthening] occurring through repeated application (*abhyāsa*), then, because the shortening would be specifically prescribed, once it has been applied, the lengthening would not occur simply because the root would no longer end in *an*; what then would be the purpose of the prohibition? For this very reason, in forms such as *ḍīḍhokyate*, the *guṇa* substitution takes place after the shortening has been applied; otherwise, the shortening—which finds its scope in cases like *babādhe*—would be superseded by the lengthening—which finds its scope in cases like *pāpacyate*—due to the latter's higher status.

Another says: Since the very meaning contained in the sūtra has been stated by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), how can there be a word-split (*padaccheda*) such as "of repetition" (*abhyāsasya*)? [The term] *abhyāsa* means a modification (*vikāra*) of repetition; and that is indeed *it-tvam* (the state of having *it*). For instance: first of all, because elision (*lopa*) consists of non-existence, it is impossible to prescribe it as a substitute (*adeśa*). Furthermore, if a short vowel were to become long, the mention of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) would be purposeless; for, by the hearing of the word "long," the rule *acaśca* ("and of a vowel") presents itself, and since a long vowel is prescribed for a base ending in a vowel, there is no distinction between a long vowel and a short vowel becoming long. Therefore, it is precisely *it-tvam* that is conveyed by the secondary suffix.

Alternatively, there is the inclusion of a modification that has been specifically prescribed; this is what he states: "and of the *ik* of the intensive (*abhyāsa*). The phrase "as a supplement to all" means that it applies not only to that [specific case] but also to the two preceding ones. Therefore, it does not occur in certain instances; this means [it does not apply] to other roots (*dhātu*) that have different meanings. This has already been established under the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ*. Forms such as *mānayati* and so on are derived from the *cur*-class with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). In the word *niśāna*, the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*) is applied directly to the causative stem. Regarding the rule *mānerjijñāsāyām*: [the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *mān* when the sense is "desire to know"].

If this is so, is not the suffix *san* established for roots meaning "to know" by the subsequent rule itself? True; however, this statement is for the purpose of prescribing a long vowel and for the purpose of excluding the augment *iṭ*. Regarding "in the case of *badh* in the sense of deformity": deformity (*vairūpya*) is a transformation of the mind caused by the experience of foul odors and the like. Regarding "in *śāni* and *niśāne*": *niśāna* means sharpening; the meaning is that it applies only where this root is read as "śāna tejane" (śāna in the sense of sharpening).
After a verbal root denoting an action having the same agent [as the desire], the affix *saN* is optionally used in the sense of desire (*icchā*).

"From a verbal root denoting an action [which serves as] the object [of another action], having the same agent, when there is a desire, [the suffix san is used optionally]. Since both "being the object" (*karmatva*) and "having the same agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) depend upon an action, and since the desire is already expressed as the meaning of the suffix, these two [properties] are understood as depending on that very [desire]. Thus he says: "The verbal root whose object is the object of the desire, and which has the same agent as the desirer. "By virtue of its meaning" means that the verbal root is designated in such a way because the meaning of the root is the object and because it has the same agent, not by virtue of its own formal nature. What is the reason? Because [otherwise] it would be impossible.

Although in cases such as *karotim icchati* ("he desires to do"), it is possible for the verbal root (*dhātu*) to function as an object even in its own form (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, it is not possible for it to have a "common agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) either in its own form or by way of its meaning. Furthermore, in this instance, because of the mention using the suffix *śtip*, there is a focus on the form itself; however, the base of the desiderative (*san-prakṛti*) has a focus on the meaning alone, in accordance with worldly linguistic usage (*lokavyutpatti*). Therefore, it was rightly said: "The qualification [of the root] is mediated by its meaning."

The meaning is that the suffix *san* occurs after a verbal root whose object is the very same agent as the action of desiring; for example, *cikīrṣati* (he wishes to do) and *jihīrṣati* (he wishes to take).

From the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*, the suffix *san* is applied; *kit*-status is established by the rule *iko jhal*; lengthening occurs by *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*; the substitution of *it* for the root vowel *ṛ* occurs by *ṛta iddhātoḥ*; lengthening again by *hali ca*; the *ṣatva* (retroflex sibilant) of *san* is applied; reduplication (*dvirvacana*) follows; the remainder of the consonants beginning with the first (*halādiśeṣaḥ*) applies; shortening (*hrasvaḥ*) occurs; the change to *cu* sounds (*cutvam*) by *kuhoścuḥ*—the *ka* becomes *ca* and the *ha* becomes *jha*; the change to *jaś* sounds (*jaśtvam*) by *abhyāse carca* results in the *ja* sound; once the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) is established by *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, the *laṭ* and other verbal suffixes are applied.

What is the purpose of including the term *dhātu* (root)? [Objection: It will not apply to a sentence because of the rule "from a verbal root denoting an object having the same agent" (*karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkāt*). For both [conditions] cannot possibly belong to the meaning of a sentence. Furthermore, it will not apply even to a word ending in a case-suffix—as in *putram icchati* ("he desires a son")—because there is no identity of agent. Even in cases where there is identity of agent—as in *gamanam icchati* ("he desires going") or *āsanam icchati* ("he desires sitting")—the suffix *kyac* will serve as an exception [to the application of *saN*].

Although *kyac* finds its scope in cases such as *putram icchati* where the agents are not identical, nevertheless, in cases such as *cikīrṣati*, the suffix *san*—which finds its scope in non-subant forms (*asubanta*)—will supersede [the application of *kyac*] due to its higher status when applied to subant forms with identical agents. Even in cases where *kyac* is prohibited by the rule "there is a prohibition of *mānta* and indeclinables in *kyac*" (Pāṇini 3.1.40), as in *kartum icchati*, it is still superseded by *kāmyac*. Furthermore, even among *ṅyāp*-prātipadikas, there is no identity of agent in examples such as *khaṭvā-putra* or *kumārī-putra*.

In cases such as *āsana* (seating) and *śayana* (lying down), however, there is no status of being an object (*karman*). For a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*) or a long vowel (*āp*) does not denote an object, since objects and other grammatical relations are expressed by case endings (*vibhakti*). If it is argued that, in that case, even for a verbal root (*dhātu*), the status of being an object would not exist; yet, if in that instance the status of being an object exists because the meaning of the root is actually pervaded (*vyāpyamānatva*) by the desire [of the agent], then it should also exist for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If it is argued that it does not exist here for the nominal stem because the form of the object is not expressed, then the same argument applies to the verbal root as well—it would not exist there either. In that case, it will simply not apply here because of the lack of a common agent (*asamānakartṛkatva*).

For in cases such as *śayanāsanādi* (lying down, sitting, etc.), since the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) itself possesses the nature of a single agent and the form of an action, it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*)—which lacks the form of an action—that is excluded. This is because of the traditional rule: "The *ghañ* and other [kṛt] suffixes occur where there is the property called 'accomplishment' (*siddhatā*) belonging to that which has the form of an action. For the very same reason that one does not say *pacatīcchati* for the sense of "he desires to cook" (*pākamicchati*) even after a verb ending in a *tiṅ* suffix, for that same reason the desiderative (*san*) suffix will not occur either. Thus, the question is: since there is no possibility [of the suffix occurring] anywhere apart from the verbal root, how could this objection apply?

[The purpose is] so that the suffix *san* does not arise after a verbal root preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*). Otherwise, since the entire complex (*saṅghāta*) would express a specific action, the suffix *san* would arise from that very complex; and consequently, because that [complex] itself would be a verbal root due to having *san* as its suffix, the augment *aṭ* would result from that very [complex], occurring before the prefix in the *laṅ* tense. Objection: But is it not possible to point out the fault of the doubling of the prefix even in the case of the optative (*liṅ*)? Reply: True; however, the *laṅ* tense was cited in order to demonstrate another fault, namely, the undesired occurrence of the augment *aṭ*.

Is it not the case that the verbal root alone expresses the qualified action, while the prefix is merely an auxiliary by its proximity and does not denote any specific meaning? For example, in the word *bhuṅkte*, the root *bhuj* itself functions in the sense of eating, while the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix denotes the agent; yet, even without the middle voice suffix, the act of eating is not understood [to be restricted to the agent].

In the same way, when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present, the verbal root alone expresses the qualified action; consequently, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the state of having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) are mediated by the meaning, they belong to the root alone and not to the complex (*saṅghāta*). And this must necessarily be understood thus: the verbal root alone denotes the action. Why? For one who thinks that the complex denotes the action, even when the term *kriyamāṇe* (in the sense of "being done") is used, it would follow that the suffix does not arise from the root that is actually present here, because [the complex] lacks the status of being an object and lacks the state of having the same agent.

He thinks as follows: In the proximity of the prefix *pra*, a specific quality known as "intensity" (*prakarpa*) is understood; yet the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself does not denote that intensity either, for otherwise the prefix *pra* would be rendered redundant. This being the case, the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to the entire complex [of root and prefix] together. For the root is not satisfied by the mere sense of "doing," nor by mere intensity alone. Nor does this result in the impossibility of the suffix arising from the root present here, since that too possesses the status of being the object.

And likewise, in the case of "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*) or "fearful, noble, beautiful," even when there is a desire to produce a composite whole (*samudāya*), the accusative case occurs after words such as *bhīṣma*, because those too possess the status of an object (*karman*). Now, one might object: even so, just as a collection of villages is not grasped by the term "village," so too, since a collection of objects is not itself an object, the [accusative] suffix will not arise from the composite whole.

In that case, how is it when the entire complex [of prefix and root] alone constitutes the object (*karman*), as in *pratiṣṭhāsate* (he wishes to set out)? For here, in the word *tiṣṭhati*, the cessation of motion (*gatinivṛtti*) is perceived; however, in the absence of the prefix *pra*, motion is perceived. Just as in *jigamiṣati* (he wishes to go) the object is one and the same, so too should it be here. Consequently, [the suffix *san*] would arise from the complex itself. If this is so, how can the suffix *san* be added to the verbal root (*dhātu*) here, since the root itself is not the object? This [rule], namely *karmaṇaḥ* ("from the object"), is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the verbal root.

Fifth [alternative]: What then? Is it the genitive—meaning "from a root that is a part of an object"? Even in cases such as *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do"), the status of being a part of the object belongs to the root alone by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Even so, the suffix would not apply because there is no common agent, since a mere root does not denote an action. Therefore, it must be explained that the ablative in *samānakartṛkāt* is used in the sense of the genitive. Thus, it is established that the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of excluding a composite [term].

The question "Why [specify] 'the object of the action' (*karma*)? is raised as follows: In usages such as *jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go"), when the desire expressed by the suffix requires an object, that very object which is the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) will be understood through proximity. Although an action also requires an instrument (*karaṇa*), the requirement for an object is more manifest in the case of desire; therefore, that [requirement] will be fulfilled by the meaning of the root itself. Thus, there is no need for the mention of "object" (*karman*) [in the rule], and this is the question. The example *gamanenecchati* ("he desires by means of going") is given so that [the suffix] might not occur in this intended sense.

For if the mention of "action" (*karman*) were absent, then when there is a requirement for an action due to the existence of desire, this statement—"he desires by means of going"—would likewise apply, and thus the suffix *san* would occur even in that case; such is the intention. The question "What is the purpose of [specifying] 'desire'? is asked because one might think: let the term "instrument" (*karaṇe*) from the rule *śabdavairakalaha...* suffice here; and by the very nature of its expressive power, the suffix *san* will occur specifically with respect to the instrument that is "desire," [so that the mention of *icchāyām* is redundant]. The objection "he knows the agent" (*kartuḥ jānāti*) is raised because one who relies solely on grammatical indicators (*lakṣaṇa*) would not understand it in this way.

"Or, because of the word 'vā', the periphrastic construction also occurs. [Objection: But surely the periphrastic construction will occur by the very force of the rule prescribing *tumun* in "samānakartṛkeṣu tumun," for there is scope for it in such cases as *cikīrṣitum icchati*. For in this case, there is no possibility of the suffix *san*, since it will be stated later that "a *san* will not be added after a stem already ending in *san*. With the words "because of the prescription [of the suffix] after a verbal root (*dhātu*)," etc., he demonstrates another purpose for the mention of the term *dhātu*. "Not in the preceding [rule]" means that, consequently, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *jugupsate*.

Regarding the term "in case of apprehension" (*āśaṅkāyām*): apprehension (*āśaṅkā*) means probability (*sambhāvanā*), which is a property of the agent (*prayoktṛdharma*). The suffix is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) because it denotes an action characterized by that [apprehension]. In the example *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati* ("the bank wishes to fall"), since the riverbank is insentient, desire is impossible for it. In the example *śvā mumūrṣati* ("the dog wishes to die"), although the dog is sentient, because life is dear to it, even when overcome by disease and the like, there is no desire to die due to its being an animal. Therefore, the meaning here is: "I apprehend that the bank will fall," and "I apprehend that the dog will die."

As for the refutation: whoever desires something performs its preliminary forms (*pūrvarūpa*), just as Devadatta, wishing to make a mat, girds himself and takes up rope, stakes, straw, and so forth; and the preliminary forms of the riverbank are also observed—clods of earth crumble and fissures arise.

Even dogs that are about to die become solitary in their habits and have swollen eyes; therefore, observing these preliminary symptoms here, "desire" is superimposed—[the inference being] that this [dog] surely desires, since it manifests such preliminary symptoms which are invariably concomitant with desire. Furthermore, the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) is not always adhered to depending on the specific context of what is to be indicated; thus, the cognition has as its basis the superimposed desire. [The question] "What is the qualifier? means: "What is the purpose of including the mention of 'desire'?"

Regarding the term *śaiṣikāt*: because of the possibility of a *san* suffix, another undesirable suffix is excluded. A *śaiṣika* suffix is one prescribed under the heading of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*). A *matubarthīya* suffix is one that occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*. Because the class beginning with *gaha* is understood by its form, the suffix *cha* is applied. The sense of *matup* is *matubartha*; that which possesses this sense is *matubarthika*. [The rule] "from *at*, *ini* and *ṭhan*" applies. From a word ending in a *śaiṣika* suffix, another *śaiṣika* suffix of the same form is not desired. For example: a jar existing in a hall is *śālīya*; water existing therein—another *cha* suffix does not apply again.

However, a different form certainly does occur—for instance, *āhicchatra* means "belonging to Ahicchatra," and *āhicchatrīya* means "located there"; since the suffix *cha* follows a stem ending in *aṇ*, [the rule applies]. Likewise, one who possesses a staff is *daṇḍikaḥ*; although the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are prescribed after a stem ending in *at* (by the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*), the suffix *ṭhan* does not apply again [to the same base]. However, a different form certainly does occur—for instance, *daṇḍimatī senā* ("an army possessing staves"). [The rule] *saniṣyate* (will be formed) does not apply after a stem ending in *san*. It is only when the forms are identical (*sarūpa*) that [the rule holds].

In this context, similarity is indicated by "conformity" (*sārūpya*), and since that is mediated through the object, the meaning remains exactly as stated previously—that [the suffix] follows immediately after the desire. And this is established by logic (*nyāya*).
