For instance: when a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies once to a word-meaning that is a genus (*jāti*), a substance (*padārtha*), or a collection (*samudāya*), then prior to its application, there can be no possibility of that suffix occurring after a base ending in it, because such a base does not yet exist. Thus, there is no contingency for that suffix to apply.

In this context, for one who desires to go to a village, although the village is not desired in its own essential form—as in "let the village be mine"—nevertheless, it is indeed desired in the form of being the object of going. Thus, from the desiderative (*san*) verb expressing desire—such as *jigaṃsyate*, *jigamiṣitaḥ*, *jigamiṣitavyaḥ*, or *sujigamiṣa*—the suffixes *la* and others occur with the village as the object. The status of the village as the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of going is perfectly clear.

Therefore, in expressions such as *grāmaṃ jigamiṣati* (he wishes to go to the village) and *grāmāya jigamiṣati* (he wishes for the village), the second and fourth case endings occur according to the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*.
The suffix *kyac* is added after a verbal root when one expresses an action for oneself. (Pāṇini 3.1.8)

Regarding the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*: since the term "desire" (*icchā*) is understood to carry over here as well, it is understood that the status of being an object (*karman*) for the nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) is in relation to that [desire]. Thus he says: "of the object of the desire. This word *ātman* is taken as a synonym for *sva* (self) in the sense of excluding others; it is not taken in the sense of a conscious substance (*cetana-dravya*). For if that were taken, it would have to be connected either with "desire" or with the nominal stem ending in a case-suffix.

In that case, if the connection were with *icchā* (desire), the genitive would apply to the agent (*kartṛ*); the meaning would then be "in a desire whose agent is the self" or "if the self desires. Consequently, the mention of "self" (*ātman*) would be redundant, because every desire here has the self as its agent, since that [desire] is a property of it. However, if the connection were with the nominal stem (*subanta*), then it would also apply in cases such as "Devadatta desires Yajñadatta's son," for even in the case of another person, what is desired by him becomes desired by the self as well, since he too is a self.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "self" (ātman) would be purposeless, as there would be nothing to exclude. If it is argued that in cases such as "he desires water for the tree" or "he desires a foot for the bed," where something is desired for an insentient object, that [insentient object] is what is to be excluded—this is not so; because even in those instances, the sentient being alone is the ultimate beneficiary. Indeed, everything that is an object of enjoyment exists solely as a subordinate (śeṣa) to sentient beings. Even in the case of "he desires a foot for the bed," it is desired only for the sake of the person for whom that bed and so forth are an object of enjoyment; the bed, however, is merely a means for that person. Therefore, the word "self" (ātman) serves precisely to exclude others.

Even in that case, if the connection were [established] merely by desire (*icchā*), then—as in the previous instance—the mention of "self" (*ātman*) would be redundant when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the agent, because every desire necessarily has a desiring agent as its subject. Therefore, it is connected with the word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*): when a desire is to be expressed regarding an object denoted by a word ending in a case-suffix, the suffix *kyac* occurs; provided that this word ending in a case-suffix is related to "self," that is, to one's own self.

When there is an expectation as to whose [the desire] is, since it is brought into proximity by the desire of the seeker (*eṣitṛ*), it is understood as belonging to that very seeker, the self (*ātman*). Thus he says: "from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) that belongs to the self of the seeker. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in a case such as *ātmanaḥ putraṃ parasya dāsam icchati* ("he desires another's servant as his own son"), because here [in the grammatical rule] it is not intended for any kind of connection with the self whatsoever; rather, the suffix occurs when the very form being desired is sought as being connected to the self—hence *putrīyati*. By the rule *kyaci ca*, the change to *i* (*ittva*) is applied.

If it is asked, "Why [is the word] *sup* mentioned?"—because of the mention of *karmaṇaḥ* (of the object), there is no possibility [of the suffix arising] after a *tiṅ*-ending form, for a *tiṅ*-ending form is not an object. Nor is there any possibility [of it arising] after a root (*dhātu*), because it is superseded by *san*, which is prescribed as a specific rule. Furthermore, even if the suffix were to arise from a *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*, there would be no fault; for by the rule *naḥ kye*, the designation *pada* is prescribed [for such forms]. And that [designation], when the mention of *sup* is made, serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that only a form ending in *n* is a *pada* before *ky*. That very same [mention of *sup*] will serve as an injunctive rule (*vidhyartha*) when the suffix arises from a *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*.

Surely, if the mention of *su* were not present, then since there would be no distinction, the suffixes would have to arise after both *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*s and *sub*-anta words. Consequently, regarding the rule *naḥ kye*, if it were intended as an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a fault in either case. For if it were intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), although there would be no fault in forms like *vācyati*—since the suffix arises after a *prātipadika* or a *sub*-anta—there would be the fault that in the case of words ending in *n*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur if the suffix were to arise after the *prātipadika*.

Now, if [the mention of] *subanta* were for the sake of a mandatory rule (*vidhi*) regarding those [suffixes] arising after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then in cases such as *vācyati*, where the suffix arises after a *subanta*, the word-level operations such as *jaśtva* would apply. Therefore, the mention of *subanta* must indeed be made for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), so that [the suffixes] arise only after a *subanta* and not from a nominal stem. If this is so, then because of the mention of "object" (*karman*), there is no possibility [of the suffix arising] after a nominal stem ending in *ṅyap*; for it is only a *subanta* that denotes the object, since even in the view that [the suffix] expresses the number (*pañcakpakṣa*), a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is required as a signifier (*dyotaka*).
Thus, having considered that there is no possibility [of the suffix arising] anywhere except after a *subanta*, the question is asked.

"From a sentence" (vākyāt) means "from a collection of words" (padasamūhāt). [The example is] *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"). Furthermore, what would happen if this were the case? If there were no mutual connection between the words *mahat* and *putra*, which are subordinate to the meaning of the suffix, there would be no compound; and consequently, the substitution of *āt* based on that [compound] would not occur. Does it then not occur in *mahāputrīyati*? It does occur when the following sentence is present: *mahān putraḥ mahāputraḥ, mahāputram icchati*.

Now, even though the term *sub* is included [in the definition of a word], why does [the suffix -tva] not occur here? Because, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) is not a *subanta*. But is this aggregate the object (*karman*)? Or is the aggregate itself the object? And what follows from this? If it is an aggregate of two objects, it is not grasped by the mention of "object" (*karma*); thus, there would be no application [of the suffix] from the aggregate. If, on the other hand, the aggregate is the object, then the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would not apply to its individual parts because they are not the object. In that case, this is indeed an aggregate of two objects.

The inclusion of the term *sub* (the nominal suffix) here is intended so that [the rule] does not apply from that [base]. Now, even if the inclusion of *sub* were made, why would it not apply from that [base], since it is indeed *sub*-ending (*subanta*)? Because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of capacity? Because that which is dependent [on something else] lacks capacity. However, when the inclusion of *sub* is not made, this is not a "word-rule" (*padavidhi*). For a "word-rule" is one where some unique property of the word itself is relied upon; but the mention of "object" (*karman*) is not a unique property of the word alone, because it is seen even in non-word forms, such as in the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* ("from a verbal root, when there is an object").

But others say: "Since the entire collection (*samudāya*) possesses the status of an object (*karma*), and since the two constituent parts—the son qualified by greatness—are also desired, for them [the rule] would apply to both the collection and the constituent parts; therefore, the mention of *su-* is made so that it does not apply from the collection or from the constituent part. As in: *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son").

[Objection: Surely [the suffix] will not occur here precisely because of lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*). How is there a lack of capacity? Is it because that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) is incapable? [Reply: In that case, let it not occur where the sense of "another's" (*parasya*) is understood even without the employment of a third word, such as in *agham icchati* ("he desires sin") or *vyasanam icchati* ("he desires calamity"), for no one desires sin for themselves. [The opponent says: Regarding the letter *k* and so forth—might this be the case: that the letter *k* should also not be made in the rule *naḥ kye*? [Reply: If that were so, then [the suffix] would also apply here in *sāmasu sādhuḥ* ("skilled in the Sāman chants").

The *cakāra* (the letter *c*) is for the purpose of preventing the elision (*vighāta*) of that [augment]. As for the accent, it is established either by the accent of the suffix or by the accent of the verbal root. Regarding the vowel *a*: in the case of *ddaṣadamicchati*, we derive *ddaṣyadyati*; from *ddaṣyad-yati* we derive *ddaṣadyat* with the suffix *ṇvul*. Then, by the rules "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), "of that which follows a consonant" (*yasya halaḥ*), and "optionally for *kyap*" (*kyasya vibhāṣā*), we obtain *ddaṣadakaḥ*. Here, because of the status of the elided *at* as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), let there not be the *vṛddhi* substitution [of the penultimate vowel] according to the rule "of the penultimate vowel when preceded by *at*" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*).

One desires clay; from the root *mṛd* (in the sense of "to crush"), [the suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule *aco yat*. The elision of the vowel *a* and so forth is as before, resulting in *mṛdyam*. This is done so that the acute accent on the first syllable may apply according to the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*. Furthermore, in forms such as *putrīyati*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the vowel and the following *śap* becomes acute.

Regarding the statement "there is a prohibition for [stems] ending in *m* and for indeclinables": the mention of "ending in *m*" (*mānta*) is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not of the inflected word (*subanta*). Therefore, *kyac* occurs in forms such as *putram icchati*, but it does not occur in forms such as *kām icchati* or *kānic chati*. As for *uccaiḥ* and *nīcaiḥ*: even though these two primarily denote a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), when they function with respect to that which is contained within it (*ādheya*), they possess the status of the object (*karman*). Some maintain that *kyac* occurs after a word ending in *go*, provided it has the same number of syllables and ends in a *n*. That is to say, some hold the view that *kyac* occurs after the word *go*, as well as after words having the same number of syllables and ending in a *n*.

The ten vowels beginning with *a* are the homogeneous vowels (*samānākṣara*). Since there is no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *ḷ* or in the vowel *ṝ*, the seven vowels preceding *e* are understood here. On this view, forms such as *vācyati* would not be established; therefore, they say that this is not the settled position. For this very reason, it is not introduced in the commentary (*vṛtti*). [The phrase] "in the opinion of others" (*parecchāyām*) refers to this.

The compound is formed with the genitive of the "remainder" (śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī), not with the agentive genitive (kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī). Furthermore, the connection with the subsequent element is mediated by the word ending in a case-suffix (subanta), according to the intention of the other; that is to say, it means "in that desire which belongs to the other regarding the meaning of the word ending in a case-suffix. Regarding the form *aghāyavaḥ*: the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *kyācchandasī*, and the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs by the rule *aśvāghasyāt*. This very prescription of the substitution of *ā* when *kyac* follows is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *kyac* also occurs in Vedic usage even when the desire belongs to another; for no one indeed desires evil for themselves.

Nor is it for the sake of [forming] *ācārakya* (the denominative suffix *kyac* in the sense of "behaving like"), because the suffix *kyac* is not observed after the word *agha* in the sense of "behaving" within the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Now, when *lakāra*, *kṛtya*, *kta*, and suffixes having the sense of *khal* occur after this *kyaj*-derived form, where do they apply? They apply, as appropriate, to the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), but not to the object (*karman*). Since the *kyaj*-ending form expresses a desire that is qualified by the meaning of the root and restricted to a specific domain, and since it does not take another entity as its object, the *kyaj*-ending form is intransitive (*akarmaka*), just like the roots *jīvati* and others.

In the case of the denominative suffix *kyac*, although the object of comparison (*upamānakarman*), such as a son, is included [within the meaning of the base], the object of comparison (*upameyakarman*), such as a student, is not so included; therefore, verbal suffixes such as *la* (the *l-affixes*) do indeed occur with that object—as in *putrīyyate chātraḥ* ("the student acts like a son") and *putrāyitavyaḥ* ("he ought to act like a son"), and so forth. This is just as in the case of *śyenāyate kākaḥ* ("the crow acts like a hawk"), where even though the agent of comparison (*upamānakartṛ*) is included [within the base], the suffix *liṭ* occurs for the agent of comparison (*upameyakartṛ*). It is exactly like that.

And here, in cases such as "he shaves the boy" (*māṇavakaṃ muṇḍayati*), "the boy shaves himself" (*muṇḍate māṇavakaḥ*), and "the boy is to be shaved" (*muṇḍayitavyo māṇavakaḥ*), the verbal root ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* is capable of including only the substance qualified by the quality of shavenness (*mauṇḍya*), but not specific particulars such as the "boy. Since those particulars are not included within the verbal root, the *l*-suffixes (tenses and moods) occur there. If this is so, then for this very reason, they would also occur after a root ending in *kyac*.

One desires the boy to be shaven; thus one says *muṇḍīyati māṇavakam* (he causes the boy to shave himself) or *muṇḍīyyate māṇavakaḥ* (the boy is made to shave himself). Should not the suffix *kyac* be applied here? No, because of a lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*). Why is there a lack of capacity? Because that which is dependent [on another] lacks capacity. In that case, would the causative suffix *ṇic* also not be applicable? It might be argued as follows: neither "shaving" nor "the boy" is joined with the action of "making"; for "boy-ness" is not something that is made. Therefore, the suffix *ṇic* is produced in the sense of "he makes him shaven," expressed as *muṇḍayati*.

In the sentence "He makes the boy shaven" (*muṇḍaṃ karoti māṇavakam*), the status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to the shaven state (*muṇḍa*) alone; however, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, the accusative case ending arises after *māṇavaka*. Thus, terms such as *māṇavaka*, when employed for the purpose of indicating a specific substratum (*ādhāra-viśeṣa*) of the shaven state, are not construed with the verb *karoti*.

Furthermore, when both actions are performed simultaneously, the suffix *vṛtti* (the causative *ṇic*) does not occur; for example, "he makes the ox [both] a bull and shaven" (*balīvarddaṃ karoti taṃ ca muṇḍaṃ karoti*), which results in the form *muṇḍayati balīvarddam*. If this is the case, then by this very same reason, the suffix *kyac* would also not apply. Moreover, if the boy (*māṇavaka*) is required even as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is again the fault of being dependent (*sāpekṣatā*).

Furthermore, if it is not correct that "the boy acts" (*māṇavakaḥ karoti*), how does the suffix *lakāra* arise [in the form] "the boy is being shorn" (*muṇḍyate māṇavakaḥ*)? And what is this logic that "the boy is not connected with acting"? For he is not satisfied merely by the state of being shorn; rather, he brings about the act of shaving as it resides in the boy. Thus, although the boy is not acted upon in his own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), he is acted upon in the form of being shorn (*muṇḍarūpeṇa*), and this is indeed accepted.

This being the case, if the *ṇic* suffix occurs, the *kyac* suffix should also occur; and if *kyac* does not occur, then *ṇic* should also not occur—such is the identical argument. If this is so, then [the rule for] *ṇic* applies to words like *muṇḍa*, which are adjectives (*guṇavacana*) and yet require a complement (*sāpekṣa*), and it is stated that *ṇic* shall apply even to such dependent words by virtue of the explicit grammatical rule (*vacana*). However, since *kyac* finds its scope (*sāvakāśa*) with independent words such as *putra* (e.g., *putrīyati*), it will not apply to dependent words in cases such as *māṇavakaṃ muṇḍamicchati* ("he desires the boy to be shaven"). Even though this *ṇic* also applies when there is a desire to express the mere production of a quality (*guṇamātrakaraṇavivakṣāyām*), [it is distinct from *kyac*].

There is scope [for this rule]: "This barber is skilled at performing tonsure. Even though the formation is established by the addition of *ṇic* because he performs that action, this further prescription is for the purpose of ensuring it applies even to words that require a complement (*sāpekṣa*). Alternatively, there are two kinds of items such as *muṇḍa*: verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

In that sūtra, the verbal roots (*dhātu*) are included; from these, which by their very nature denote specific actions, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) will arise. However, in the case of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), there is only analysis (*vigraha*): "he makes the boy bald" (*māṇavakaṃ muṇḍaṃ karoti*). Alternatively, both [the sentence and the suffix] do not occur simultaneously—the sentence and the suffix. Consequently, in the form *muṇḍayati*, only the substance is perceived; therein, one who desires a specific detail must employ the specific term in subsequent usage (*anuprayoga*).

Alternatively—the connection of the bare root *kṛ* (to do) is with *muṇḍa* (bald), while its connection with *māṇavaka* (the boy) is through [the root] as qualified by *mauṇḍya* (the state of being bald). This is just as in the expression *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("he milks the cow for milk"), where the bare root *duh* first connects with *go* (cow), and subsequently the milk connects with the cow-milker. However, the *kyac* suffix does not occur here because it is not prescribed [by grammatical rule]. When one says *māṇavakaṃ muṇḍayati*, a different meaning altogether is understood: "he makes the boy act like one who is bald.
Thus it is established that from a verbal base ending in the desiderative *kyac*, the *l*-suffixes (tenses and moods) occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).
And optionally, [the suffix *ya* is applied]. 3.1.9.

*Kāmyac ca*. For what purpose is this division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) made? Why not simply form a single rule, *supa ātmanaḥ kyackāmyacau*, so that the particle *ca* would not have to be used? To this he replies: "In the case of a division of the rule," and so forth. For if there were a single rule, both [suffixes] would be carried over (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent sūtra. But even with the division of the rule, does it not follow that only *kāmyac* is carried over due to proximity? This is not a fault.

The letter *ca* is used here; it serves to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *kyac*. And the purpose of carrying that forward is so that it may continue into the subsequent rules. However, the suffix *kāmyac* does not continue [into the following rules] because of the force of the formal separation (*yogavibhāga*), and because there is no purpose for it to do so. In examples such as *agnikāmyati*, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution is not the purpose, since *guṇa* simply does not apply because [the suffix] is not an *ārddhadhātuka*.

In the case of *upayaj* [derived from] *upa-yaj* with the suffix *kviṣ* according to the rule *vijupe chandasi*, there is no purpose for samprasāraṇa in the sense "he desires the *upayaj*" (*upayaṭkāmyati*), because the root *yaj* and others serve as qualifiers for the suffix *kit*—meaning "that which is prescribed after roots such as *yaj*. Furthermore, in the case of *vāk-kāmyati*, there is likewise no purpose for samprasāraṇa, because the grammatical operation is understood to apply when a root is mentioned in its own form (*sarūpa*).

Regarding the phrase "or because it begins with the letter *ca*," some explain as follows: The letter *ca* at the end of this [root] is redundant, since its being udātta on the final syllable is already established by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*); therefore, it should have been placed at the beginning. Alternatively, even though it is placed at the end, it serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*), namely that this [root] should be designated as having *cit* [as its marker] and not by any other *anubandha*. Thus, although it is placed at the end, it effectively becomes one that begins with *cit* by producing the result of being treated as such.

Others, however, explain that it begins with the letter *ca* by relying on the mention of two *ca*s in the rules *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* and *kāmyac*; as for the inclusion of the marker *c*, it is so that in the form *putrakāmiṣyati*, the accent of the suffix *syat*, even though it is subsequently applied (*sati-śiṣṭa*), shall indeed be the accent of the *cit* marker.
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after a word used as a standard of comparison, in the sense of behaving like that [standard]. (Pāṇini 3.1.10)

Regarding the rule *upamānād ācāre* ("after a word denoting a standard of comparison, when [the sense of] behaving [is expressed]"): since the locative case is heard in the word *kuḍye* (in the wall) as the object of comparison (*upameya*), the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) must likewise end in the locative. Because this usage would be possible even when the accusative sense is intended, the formulation of the rule was begun. However, the reading *kuṭyām* (in a hut) is more appropriate.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after a word denoting the agent [of an action], and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the *s* [of the verbal root]. (Pāṇini 3.1.11)

"Kyaṅ [is applied] after a word denoting the agent, and there is the elision of *s*. The sense is that since "manner of behavior" (*ācāra*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it is in relation to that [behavior] that the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as the agent is understood. Regarding "and the elision of *s*": if this word *ca* were taken as functioning to express a conjunction (*samuccaya*), then there would be only a single sentence—"Kyaṅ and the elision of *s* occur"—and consequently, *kyaṅ* would only occur where there is the elision of *s*, as in *ojāyate*; however, in this case [of *śyenāyate kākaḥ*], it would not occur.

Therefore, when the particle *ca* is used in the sense of *anvācaya* (secondary addition), a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) must be resorted to: "The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after a verb expressing the agent of comparison without distinction; however, where the possibility of the letter *s* exists, there its elision (*lopa*) occurs. This is what was stated: the elision of *s*, being taught as a secondary addition (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*), applies even when that [possibility of *s*] is absent, so that *kyaṅ* still occurs. In the example *śyenāyate*, the rule "lengthening occurs for [stems ending in] non-*kṛt* and non-*sārvadhātuka* suffixes" applies. Regarding the phrase "even in the rule for the elision of *s*": since the elision of *s* is taught as a secondary addition, when there is a split in the sentence, this [lengthening] also becomes a subordinate feature (*guṇa*).

By the word *api*, he shows this: that [the particle] is connected to the rule for *kyaṅ* first in order to form the sentence, and likewise to the rule for the elision of *sa*. Regarding *ojāyata*: in the context of grammatical function (*vṛtti*), the word *ojas* refers to that which possesses the quality (*tadvat*).

"The [suffix *kyac*] is obligatory after *ojas* and *apsaras*, but optional after *payas*; however, some say it does not occur at all after others such as *yaśas*, while we say it does. The mention of *payas* is for the purpose of indicating any word ending in *s* other than *ojas* and *apsaras*. For this very reason, there is optionally the elision of the *s*. The Vārttika states 'after *ojas* and *apsaras* it is obligatory' as a general rule; by that, forms such as *yaśāyate* also occur. However, the position that the elision of *s* occurs only after *apsaras* is not even established in the Bhāṣya."

In the rule *salopa-vidhau kartuḥ*, the genitive case (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is established. The meaning is that in a rule prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*), whatever ends in the fifth case (*pañcamy-anta*) becomes, by virtue of its connection with the elision (*lopa*), a genitive ending (*ṣaṣṭhy-anta*) through a change of case (*vibhakti-vipariṇāma*). This occurs because the restriction *alo’ntyasya* applies there. Since the agent (*kartṛ*) is qualified by the letter *s*, the rule of "specification by the final" (*tadanta-vidhi*) is understood; and for that very purpose, the word *sa* (meaning "of that [agent]") is treated as a separate word with its genitive case-ending elided.

In some places, the reading is "kvacid alo'ntyaniyame sati"; there, because it is an imitation of a portion of a sūtra, there is no elision of the case-ending even in a compound, as in the example *asyavāmīyam*.

"Ācāra," and so forth. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *kyaṅ*. The roots *galbha* (in the sense of audacity), *klībṛ* (in the sense of lack of audacity), and *hoḍṛ* (in the sense of disrespect) are understood here as ending in the *pacādyac* suffix; furthermore, it is stipulated (*pratijñāyate*) that the vowel *a* of these [roots] is unaccented (*anudātta*) and nasalized (*anunāsika*) within the sentence. Consequently, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after those [roots] formed with *kvip*. Because *kvip* is optionally omitted by explicit statement, *kyaṅ* occurs instead; however, since the nasalization is stipulated in conjunction with *kvip*, the designation *it* does not apply in the case of *kyaṅ*.

But for what purpose is this [rule], since roots such as *galbh* are already listed in the Dhatupatha as having anudātta (unaccented) indicatory letters (*it*), and from them forms such as *galbhate* are established; and from these very roots, by adding the suffix *pacādyac*, forms such as *avagalbhāyate* are established through the addition of *kyan*? Even though roots like *galbh* are listed with meanings such as "boldness," nevertheless, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, they will function in the sense of "acting like one who is not bold" (*avagalbha ivācarati*) as well. True; however, in forms such as *avagalbhāṃcakre*, because it ends in a suffix, the augment *ām* would otherwise apply; it is for this reason that the suffix *kvip* is prescribed.

Now, when the suffix *liṭ* is prescribed after verbal roots (*dhātu*) themselves, how should the forms *avajagalbhe*, *viciklībe*, and *vijuhoḍe* be explained? Others, however, asserting that the suffix *kvip* is prescribed after verbal roots alone, claim that these forms are impossible; but this contradicts the *Bhāṣya*. For the author of the *Bhāṣya* raises the objection regarding their derivation by means of the rule "after all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*) with the words "In that case, not now," and so forth. Indeed, if the mention of "verbal roots" (*dhātugrahaṇa*) were present [in the rule for *kvip*], such an objection regarding their derivation by that [general rule] would not be possible.

The author of the Vārttika as well, by stating "from all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*), intends that the inclusion of the term *dik* (direction) applies even to words such as *galbha* and others. For his meaning is not merely "from *galbha* and so forth," but rather "from all nominal stems indeed. In the expression "from all nominal stems," since the word "all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*) could have sufficed, the specific mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) indicates that the suffix *kvip* is prescribed after the nominal stem itself, and not after a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

Because it lacks the status of being a *pada*, in the case of *aśvatī* (from *aśva*), the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* applies to the *śap* suffix; however, in the case of *vidhavati* and *ravayati*—derived from the roots *vidhu* and *ravi* with the suffix *kvip* followed by *śap* and *guṇa*—the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* does not apply. Furthermore, in *rājatī* and similar forms, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur. In cases such as *vācatī*, the substitutions of *kutva* and *jaśtva* do not take place.

Even for those who maintain that *kvip* is added after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*), they must still include the enumeration of *galbha* and others, so that I may explain the *anubandhas* intended for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
After the words *bhṛśa* and others, when the root *bhū* follows, provided it is not preceded by *ac*, there is elision of the final consonant (*hal*).

Regarding the rule *bhṛśādibhyo vuñ-yaC-cv-er-lopaś-ca-halaḥ*: in this rule prescribing elision (*lopavidhau*), the ablative case *bhṛśādibhyaḥ* is interpreted as a genitive of relation (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, the word *hal* qualifies *bhṛśādayaḥ*. Consequently, when the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the elision being prescribed occurs for those [bases] ending in a consonant (*halanta*). Thus, in forms such as *bhṛśāyate*, the elision does not apply because the base ends in a vowel (*ahalanta*). This is why he says: "If it were understood that [the elision applies] only to those ending in a consonant, then the recitation of [bases] not ending in a consonant would be purposeless. He further states that the term *acveḥ* is connected with each [of the suffixes] individually.

The sense is that, for this reason, the singular number is justified. But for what purpose is this stated? This is a question made with reference to the rule "acveḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.12). "By that" means by the verb *bhavati* which is employed as an auxiliary. Nor can *kyaṅ* occur by setting aside the employment of *bhavati*, because *kyaṅ* has its scope in those roots ending in *ac*. Furthermore, in the absence of *bhavati*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of *cvi* itself, since *cvi* is prescribed only in connection with that [verb].

How then does *kyaṣ* occur after a word ending in *ḍāc*, given that *ḍāc* itself is prescribed in connection with the verb *bhavati*? To this, he will state the solution: the very fact that *ḍāc* occurs even in connection with *kyaṣ*—just as it does in connection with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*—is the *jñāpaka* (indicative proof). [The phrase] "for the sake of understanding its similarity" refers to that.

By the logic of the *nañ-ivayukta* rule (the principle that when a negative particle is joined with *iva*, it implies similarity), how could words ending in *cv-* be understood as being similar to *bhṛśa* and so on? Therefore, the exclusion of those ending in *cv-* is made. Furthermore, this similarity is based on the domain of "becoming what one was not" (*abhūtadbhāva*). Thus he says: "from *bhṛśa* and so on, which have the domain of becoming what one was not," and so forth. Examples include *bhṛśāyate* and others. For those ending in vowels (*ajanta*), there is lengthening by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*; for those ending in consonants (*halanta*), however, there is elision—as in *sumanāyate* from *asumanāḥ sumanā bhavati* ("one who was not well-disposed becomes well-disposed"), and *durmanāyate*, etc.

Regarding the phrase *bhṛśībhavati*: it was just stated that "there is no such contingency here," therefore a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) concerning the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) must be shown—namely, *kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti*. The meaning is: "Where in what place do those stars and so forth, which are intense (*bhṛśa*) at night, become [so] during the day? Here, the word *manas* is listed with its prefixes: *sumanas*, *durmanas*, *abhimanas*, and *unmanas*.

In this regard, there is an inquiry: does the suffix arise from the compound as a whole including the prefix (*upasarga*), or rather from the word *manas* alone when it is divested of the prefix? For that purpose, one must consider: is the prefix a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—as in the case of the word *sumanas*? Or is it a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)—as in *subhavat*, *durbhavat*, *abhibhavat*, or *udbhavat*? But how can it be suspected that a prefix, which is recited together with the word *manas*, is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix? [For] if it were a qualifier of that [suffix],...

Why would *prāgbhavateḥ* be recited [in the rule]? It is not possible to recite it as *prāgbhavateḥ*, for in that case, the suffix would apply to all roots beginning with *bhū* only when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*). However, since it is desired that the suffix apply to the word *manas* itself in this specific sense, the recitation must be together with the word *manas*. In that context, when the words beginning with *su-* form a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *manas*, they become qualifiers of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

But when they are not compounded, then [the compound] is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). In cases such as "he becomes well-minded" (*manasvī suṣṭhu bhavati*), the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs in the sense of the state (*vṛtti*) being applied to that which possesses it (*tadvati*). Alternatively, the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*) is understood here because of the optionality of the causative marker (*ṇic*) prescribed by the rule *ā dhṛṣādvā*. Consequently, the meaning becomes "the mind attains a beautiful state," and so forth. In the first alternative, there is a fault regarding the augment *aṭ*, the suffix *āṭ*, the suffix *lyap*, and reduplication: for instance, *svamanāyata* and *duramanāyata*.

Regarding *āṭ*: [in forms such as] *abhyamanāyata* and *udamanāyata*, since the prefix (*upasarga*) is included within the verbal root when followed by the suffix *kyaṅ*, the augment *aṭ* and *āṭ* would apply before that [root]; however, they are intended to follow it. Regarding *lyap*: in *sumanāyya* and *abhimanāyya*, because the prefix is incorporated into the form ending in *ktvā*, there is no separate word distinct from it; thus, in the absence of a compound, *lyap* would not occur, and the form would have to be *sumanāyitvā*.

Regarding the doubling [of the root]: if the suffix *san* were applied after a form ending in *kyaṅ*, and because the prefix (*upasarga*) would enter into the *san*-ending form, then upon the doubling of that [prefix], one would obtain *susumanāyiṣate* and *abibhimanāyiṣate*; however, *sumimanāyiṣate* and *abhimimanāyiṣate* are what is desired. This is not a fault. In the *curādi* group, the word *saṃgrāma* is listed with the meaning "battle," but it should not be so listed; for from the word *saṃgrāma* itself, which denotes "battle," the causative suffix *ṇic* is already established by the rule "one causes that to be done" (*tat karoti*) or "one describes that" (*tad ācaṣṭe*).

However, its being recited in this manner indicates that when a suffix conditioned by the designation "root" (dhātu) is intended to be applied after a complex form (*saṅghāta*) consisting of a prefix (*upasarga*), the prefixes are separated, and the suffix is applied only to the remainder. For the word *saṃgrāma* is indeed recited in the *curādi* class as a complex form containing a prefix; it is not a different word whose constituent parts merely resemble a prefix. And thus, the optional substitution of a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) prescribed by the rule *vā padāntasya* occurs; otherwise, it would not.

This meaning is recited as follows: so that forms such as *asaṃgrāmayata* (he caused to fight), *saṃgrāmayitvā* (having caused to fight), and *sisaṃgramayiṣata* (he desired to cause to fight) may occur; thus, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned meaning. Or, it is for the sake of a restriction (*niyamārtha*): [the rule] applies only when the suffix that causes the designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) occurs after the word *saṃgrāma* itself, provided it is accompanied by a prefix (*upasarga*).

But surely, since *saṃgrāmayati* is intended here as having an anudātta initial vowel, one would expect the reading to be such that one might think, "I shall add an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) for the sake of the ātmanepada. How then can this [reading] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) or for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)? This might be the case: for if the reading were intended merely to attach an indicatory letter, one should have read simply *grāma yuddhe*; the prefix *sam*, however, is understood from its appearance in usage as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*), just as *adhi* is for the roots *iṅ* and *ik*. But the reading *saṃgrāma* is for the purpose of a restrictive rule.

Even so, just as the prefix *āṅ* does not occur before the root *iṅ* (in *adhyeti*), it would likewise not occur here; therefore, the second alternative is adopted. If that were the case, then just as in *śyenāyate*—where the prefix *āṅ* is not used because the suffix *kyaṅ* has already expressed the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*)—so too it would not occur for *svadīnām*. Since *kyaṅ* is prescribed specifically for that qualified meaning, it is logical that *kyaṅ* arises when the meaning is qualified by a single prefix, such that its expression is accomplished by that [prefix]; however, in this instance, [the meaning] is qualified by more than one.

In this regard, when "manāyate" is uttered, a doubt may arise as to whether it is "subhavati" (he becomes well-disposed) or "durbhavati" (he becomes ill-disposed). To eliminate that doubt, a prefix (*upasarga*) must be employed. However, there is this fault: if the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied to the word *manas*, then for the word "manāyate"—which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)—the rule of *nighāta* (accentual suppression) would apply to what follows it, provided it begins with a vowel and does not itself end in a verbal suffix. In the alternative view, however, forms such as "sumanāyate" result in words ending in a verbal suffix; since there is nothing other than that [verbal suffix] following it, there is no *nighāta*.

If that is the case, then I shall state that in the context of the *bhṛśādi* group, the preposition (*upasarga*) is treated as a subsequent member of the compound (*parāṅgavat*), immediately after the rule *subāmantrite*. But then this would also apply here: *abhibhṛśāyate*, *subhṛśāyate*? If this is not desired, I shall state: *manasyupasarge*; when the word *manas* follows, the preposition is treated like a member of that very following word *manas* when a vowel accent (*svara*) is to be applied.

And thus, in examples such as *devadattaḥ sumanāyate*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of the prefix also occurs by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. As for the one who says that when a suffix is intended to be applied after the word *sumanas*, the prefix is separated [from the base] and the suffix is applied only to the remainder—even by him, the status of being "like a subordinate member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) must necessarily be stated regarding the accent. Therefore, it is established that the suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix, and the suffix is applied only to the word *manas* itself.

If, however, it is intended as a general indicator—that when a suffix is to be prescribed after a compound, prefixes are separated from it—then this does not apply here alone; for instance, as will be stated in the rule *prabhau parivṛḍhaḥ*: "he describes one who is powerful" (*parivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), where, after the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *kṛt* (the suffix *kvip*), the suffix *lyap* occurs in the form *parivṛḍhayya*. Therefore, another indicator must be sought. Furthermore, since nothing remains to be stated beyond what has been mentioned by the learned scholars, we shall desist.
The suffix *k*saṣ is applied after [stems ending in] *lohitā-* and those ending in *ḍha* or *an*.

Regarding the rule *lohitādi-ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ*: [the example] is *paṭapaṭāyati*. When the suffix *ḍāc* is intended after an indistinct imitation of sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*), there is reduplication according to the rule *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve bhavataḥ*. Then the feminine suffix *ḍāp* is added. With the form *paṭat-paṭā* established, the rule *nityam āmreḍite ḍāci* applies; this means that when *ḍāc* follows a reduplicated form, the single substitute for the *t* of the word *paṭat* and the following *p* is the letter *p*. Regarding the statement "the suffix *kyaṣ* is prescribed after *lohita* and words ending in *ḍāc*, while the others [of the *lohita*-group] are included among the *bhṛśādi* group," this is intended as a recitation of the *vārttika* and is not [an original rule].

He says "those which are recited" (*yāni paṭhyante*) to show that by this [mention of] *ādi* (etcetera), others are also excluded. Words such as *nidrā*, *karuṇā*, and *kṛpā* function with respect to their state (*vṛtti*) to denote the possessor of that state (*tadvati*). The suffix occurs in the sense: "one who was sleepless becomes possessed of sleep," "one who was merciless becomes possessed of mercy," and "one who was pitiless becomes possessed of pity. This explains why only the suffix *kyaṣ* occurs after those words listed in the *ūpara* group. Furthermore, he says "this is an *ākṛtigaṇa*" (an open-ended class) to answer the question "Why? He says "and thus... (*tathā ca*) to provide the justification.

But where is the purpose for the inclusion of the letter *k* [in the rule *kyaci ca*]? It is for the sake of [the application of] *kyac* and *kyas*. [The word] *āpatyasya* (of a secondary derivative) is understood [from the previous rule], but this [suffix *kyac*] is not desired in the sense of a secondary derivative (*apatya*). In this case, then, regarding *kyasya vibhāṣā*, [the word] *halaḥ* (after a consonant) is understood, but this [suffix *kyas*] is not desired after a base ending in a consonant. In this case, then, regarding *kyāc chandasi*, this should be stated as *chandasi kyacaḥ*—so that it may apply even to bases ending in *y* derived from the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group, such as *bhuraṇyuḥ* and *turaṇyuḥ*. Alternatively, let the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* simply be *vā yāt*.

And does this not result in an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to forms such as *pāśyā*—derived from *pāśa-* etc. by the rule "yaḥ" [Pāṇini 4.1.137]? This section is for the purpose of restricting the suffixes that are prescribed generally; however, neither Parasmaipada nor Ātmanepada is applicable after a suffix beginning with *pāśa-*. Even if it were possible through a form ending in the denominative suffix *kvip*, one might still argue that the rule should simply be "vā yaṣaḥ. To this, he says: "naḥ kye. By adding the indicatory letter *k* (as in *kye*), the author of the Sūtra intends to indicate that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). He explains this with: "for not... (*na hi*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, the Vārttika is explained solely as being for the purpose of rejecting the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth). The letter *ka* is also rejected. But how can there be the suffix *ḍāc* in the case of *paṭapaṭāyate* when it is joined with *kyaṣ*, given that *ḍāc* is prescribed only in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*? To this he says: "As if with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, etc. The suffix *kyaṣ* is prescribed in the sense of the root *bhū*; it does not occur in actual usage with the verb *bhū* because that meaning has already been expressed by that very [verb]. Therefore, *kyaṣ* must occur only when *bhū* is not employed.

The point is that if there were no connection with *kyaṣ* and no suffix *ḍāc*, then the prescription of *kyaṣ* after a stem ending in *ḍāc* would be untenable. Now, for what purpose is the rule *vā kyaṣ* (*Pāṇini 3.1.12*) begun? Why not simply include the particle *ca* here [in the previous rule], so that it would read: "After *lohitādi* stems, *kyaṣ* occurs, and by the particle *ca*, *kyaṅ* also occurs; thus, in the case of *kyaṅ*, the Ātmanepada is used, and in the case of *kyaṣ*, the Parasmaipada is used"? Ah, how subtle is the vision of the "Beloved of the Gods" (the grammarian), since he has not even seen this: "*kyaṅmāninośca*" (*Pāṇini 6.3.36*).

Thus [it is argued]. In that case, since the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included" applies here, this *kyaṣ* would also occur after the word *lohinī*. This being so, if it were understood that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after a form ending in *kyaṅ* while the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs after a form ending in *kyaṣ*, then under the alternative of the middle voice, when the masculine form is substituted by the rule "after *kyaṅ* and *mānin*" (*kyaṅmāninośca*), one would obtain the undesired form *lohitāyate*—meaning "she who was not red becomes red"—whereas what is desired is *lohinīyate* or *lohinīyati*. Therefore, the difference in result is indeed clear.
The suffix *kha* is applied after a verbal root to form a noun denoting "the act of proceeding toward difficulty. (Pāṇini 3.1.14)

Regarding "for the purpose of stepping toward difficulty" (*kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*): the phrase "from that which is capable [of being joined] with the fourth case" (*caturthīsamarthāt*) has the following meaning. The term *samartha* means "capable"; thus, it is a compound with the third case (instrumental) based on the rule "that which is capable [of being connected] with the fourth case. The meaning is: "from that [word] whose connection with the sense of 'stepping' (*kramaṇa*), which is the meaning of the suffix, is established by means of the fourth case. This is understood precisely from the mention of "for difficulty" (*kaṣṭāya*). Since the word *kramaṇa* is well-known in the sense of "moving the feet," he says "in the sense of stepping, not in the sense of straightforwardness," so that the suffix might not be understood as applying only to that [physical movement].

*Anārjava* means crookedness (*kauṭilya*). However, in this context, the word *anārjava* results in the sense of "striving" (*kramaṇa*) characterized by non-ease; this is implied by the meaning. What, then, is striving? It is enthusiasm (*utsāha*), as it has been explained [in the commentary on Pāṇini 1.4.32]: "He strives (*kramate*) for the study of grammar" means he exerts himself (*utsahate*). [In the example] "he strives for a difficult task" (*kaṣṭāya karmaṇe kramate*), the absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the rule "the root *kaṣ* [takes *iṭ*] in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) and thicket (*gahana*)," where *kṛcchra* means suffering (*duḥkha*).

In this context, however, the cause is sinful action; the meaning is that one strives to perform a difficult sinful deed. The form *vṛttisarge* is used in the ātmanepada. However, the parasmaipada is generally recited there; in that case, the meaning is "one who desires to perform a sinful deed acts crookedly," and the parasmaipada is used because of a lack of resolve (*anutsāhatvāt*).

"This is said to be too little," because it does not include all the bases (*lakṣya*). How, then, should it be stated? He says: "In *sattrakakṣā* etc. In this view, the suffix is applied after words ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), because they function as the object (*karman*) with respect to the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). Regarding the phrase "in the desire to act upon *kaṇva*": this is an indication of the meaning of the entire complex consisting of the base and the suffix. *Kaṇva* means "evil" (*pāpa*). For in the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), words such as *sattra* are synonyms for "evil"; the suffix is applied to them when there is a desire to act, and the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed without using the actual word [for evil], namely: "one who desires to act toward evil" (*pāpaṃ cikīrṣati*).
"The goat traverses the thicket. Here, the root *kram* is used in the sense of "placing the feet"; thus, it means he traverses—that is, he goes to—the thicket, which is a dense place.
The suffix *cha* (forming the word *vartika*) is applied after the words *romantha* and *tapas* when they denote one who subsists by means of those [actions]. (Pāṇini 3.2.15)

[The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *car* when preceded by *romantha* and *tapas*, provided that these are the object of the action. The word "karmaṇaḥ" is in the ablative case, because it is in grammatical apposition with "romanthatapobhyām. It is in the singular number because it is connected to each [of the two words] individually. Regarding "varti": although the suffix *yuc* would be expected after the causative (*ṇyanta*) root *vṛt* by the rule "ṇyāsaśrantho yuc," the feminine suffix *ktin* is used here due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The suffix *yuc* also occurs: *vartanā*. "Car" refers to the act of moving; since it denotes an accomplished state (*saṃpādita*), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). "Hanucalane" means "in the movement of the jaw."

The meaning here is that, accompanied by the movement of the jaw, there is the chewing of what has been chewed by drawing it back into the mouth; thus, "the insect performs *romantha*" (chews its cud). It means that it performs—i.e., makes—*romantha*, a substance called *romantha*, which has been swallowed and emerged from the place of ingestion; that is, it forms balls [of food]. In this case, there is no movement of the jaw. Regarding the rule "for *tapas*, the *parasmaipada* [is used]," it is simply that the word *tapas* should have been included in the rule beginning with "namas-varivas-" and so forth, but it was not done in that way.
In this context, the form "tapasyate" (in the phrase "tapasyate lokaṃ jigīṣuragneḥ") is in the middle voice (ātmanepada) due to its Vedic character.
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after [the roots *ud* and *vas*] when combined with *bāṣpa* and *ūṣman* respectively, provided that they mean "to emit. (Pāṇini 3.1.16)
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after the words *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *megha* when they function as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The suffix *ktvā* is optionally replaced by *lyap* after words such as *sukha*, when the agent of the action expressed by the verbal root is the same as the experiencer of the sensation. (Pāṇini 3.1.18)

[The suffix *ṇini* is applied] after [words such as] *sukha* and others, when the agent experiences the feeling (*vedanā*). Regarding the term "feeling" (*vedanā*): it is derived from the root *vid*, meaning "to perceive," "to inform," or "to dwell," belonging to the *curādi* group; the suffix *yuc* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule "*ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*," or alternatively, it is an augmentative form according to the supplementary rule "*ghaṭṭivandividibhyaśca*. Thus, "feeling" (*vedanā*) means experience (*anubhava*). Experience is direct cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

Although the word "feeling" (*vedanā*) denotes cognition in general, it is nevertheless qualified by the mention of the agent as pleasure and so forth; and considering that for the agent, pleasure and so forth are indeed of the nature of feeling or experience, this was stated in such a manner. Agency is relative to an action, and because of the proximity of "feeling," it is understood as being relative to that alone. Furthermore, pleasure and so forth are qualified by the agent, not by "feeling," because there is no possibility of deviation [between them].

For every sensation indeed belongs to the experiencer alone; thus he says: "If [sensation] belongs to the experiencer, who is the agent, then pleasure and so forth come into being. Furthermore, the relationship is characterized by the nature of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), not by the nature of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*). And thus, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided. Regarding the term *vedayate*: it is listed as an *ātmanepada* verb under the governing rule "from *kusma* onwards, [verbs are] *ātmanepada*. Consequently, the reading of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) in the counter-example is an error born of negligence.
The beautician—the performer of massages and the like—knows the pleasure of the person being treated through inference based on such signs as the changes in the eyes.
The suffix *kyac* is applied after the verbal roots *nam*, *varivas*, and *citraṅ*.

The suffix *kyac* is applied after the words *namas* and *varivas* when preceded by *citra*, provided that a specific instrument such as worship (*pūjā*) and so forth is intended. The sense is this: although the general term "instrument" (*karaṇe*) continues to apply from the previous rule, a specific meaning is understood here due to the inherent nature of the expressive power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) of the word. Thus, in the example *namasyati devān* ("he worships the gods"), the dative case does not occur—as prescribed by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā*—because the word *namas*, being subordinate to the meaning of the suffix, cannot be extracted and connected [to the object] independently. Alternatively, the meaning is: *namasyati* means "he honors with a salutation" (*namaskāreṇa pūjayati*).

In that case, according to the principle that "the case-ending denoting the *kāraka* (grammatical relation) is stronger than the case-ending arising from a secondary word (*upapada*)," the second case (*dvitīyā*) alone occurs. And thus, in examples such as *namaskaroti devān*, the second case likewise occurs. Regarding the term *paricaryāyām*: *paricaryā* means service or attendance. Regarding *citrīyate*: since a characteristic mark belonging to a part serves to distinguish the whole, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root with the *kyac* suffix; furthermore, the substitution of *i* for the vowel [of the root] occurs by the rule *kyaci ca*. For this very reason, the word *citra* was not included in the sūtra beginning with *śabda-vaira-*.

Regarding the word *citrīyate*: some say it means "to be amazed," while others say it means "to cause amazement. Thus, in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, with reference to the illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*), it says: "Then, being thus amazed (*citrīyamāṇaḥ*), he..."
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the words *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*.

[The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the words *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*, when the sense is "throwing up" (*udasanam*) or "throwing around" (*paryasanam*). "Throwing up" (*udasanam*) means lifting up; "throwing around" (*paryasanam*) means tossing about. [Thus one says: *utpucchayate*.

Now, one might object: just as when *kyaṅ* is prescribed after the root *car*, the prefix *āṅ* is not employed—why is that? Because *kyaṅ* expresses the very meaning of "moving" (*carati*) as qualified by *āṅ*. Similarly here, since *ṇiṅ* is prescribed for the sense of "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*), the employment of the prefix *ud* should not occur. To this we reply: there is a distinction here. This [suffix] is also prescribed for the sense of "turning over" (*paryasana*). In that case, the word *ud* must be used to indicate "throwing upwards," and the word *pari* must be used to indicate "turning over. Thus, the two prefixes are required to express their respective meanings.

*Samācayana* means heaping together; *arjana* means the means of acquiring wealth, such as begging and so forth. The inclusion of the letter *ṅ* is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The intention is that, because of this, it would not be possible to list "asking" (*pṛcchā*) and other such terms in the subsequent sūtra.
The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied after the verbal roots √maṇḍ, √miśra, √ślakṣṇa, √lavaṇa, √vrata, √vastra, √hala, √kala, and √kṛta-tūsta.

The suffix *ṇic* is applied after the words *maṇḍa*, *miśra*, *ślakṣṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *vrata*, *vastra*, *hala*, *kala*, and *kṛta-tūsta*. For what purpose is this [rule]? It is not for the sake of establishing the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), since that is already established by the rule "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) [the suffix *ṇic* is added] when the sense of a verbal root is intended. Nor is a restriction on the meaning of the verbal root established there by the rule "he does that" (*tat karoti*), because we also see forms such as *atyararājat* ("he surpassed the king"). [This rule] is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix *ṇic* occurs even after words that require a complement (are *sāpekṣa*), as in *muṇḍaṃ karoti māṇavakam* ("he makes the boy bald"), or it is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

The purpose of the irregular designation (*nipātana*) of *hal* and *kali* as ending in *t* is that otherwise, when *hali* and *kali* are established, the rule "vṛddhi before *ñ* and *ṇ*" would apply, and by the rule "as in the case of *iṣṭhan* before *ṇa*," the *ṭi*-portion would be elided.

In that case, the elision (*lopa*) is non-eternal because another word-form is subsequently obtained, whereas the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is as if it were not even applicable once the *ṭi*-elision has been performed; thus, between these two non-eternal operations, since *vṛddhi* applies by virtue of its higher priority, once *vṛddhi* has taken effect, the elision of the vowel *ai* occurs, and consequently the base (*aṅga*) does not become one where an *ag* is elided. Therefore, the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*)—by the rule "as if *san*" when there is a light syllable—and the lengthening of the light syllable (*dīrgho laghoḥ*) would both apply. However, when the short vowel *a* is specifically prescribed (as a nipātana), although *vṛddhi* still applies by virtue of its higher priority, only the *ag* is elided; thus, the *sanvadbhāva* does not occur. This is what he states: "The prescription of *halika* and *kalika* as ending in short *a*..."

"It is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as *san* (*sanvadbhāva*). This is an elliptical statement; it is also for the purpose of preventing the lengthening of the vowel prescribed by the rule "the long vowel for a short one" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*). In that rule "the long vowel for a short one," the phrase "provided there is no elision of *an*" (*anaglope*) also applies. Thus, from roots such as *bal* and *paṭ*, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), we have *abībalat* and *apīpaṭat*, and not *ababalat* or *apapaṭat*. As for the rule "satyāpapāśa... (*Pāṇini 3.1.25*), words such as *muṇḍa* should have been listed there, but they were not so included.
The suffix *yaṅ* is added after a monosyllabic verbal root beginning with a consonant to express the intensive repetition of an action.

"After a root that has a single vowel and begins with a consonant, the suffix *yaṅ* is added when there is repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). Because of the qualification "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*), the term "having a single vowel" (*ekāca*) is to be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "When it occurs in the sense of repetition of an action" means that it occurs when the action itself is being repeated; by this, he shows that the repetition is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). For the action is indeed what is expressed by the root.

Even when distinguished by repetition (*samabhihāra*), it remains simply an action; therefore, it is logical that it serves as a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛti*). Just as something that is "exceedingly white" is still simply "white," so too the sense of excess belongs to the base meaning itself. Consequently, the *yaṅ* suffix occurs. Where? Since suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed occur in their own [base] meaning, it occurs in that very context.

The meaning is that when "intensive accumulation" (*samabhihāra*) is to be indicated, it serves to indicate that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is being accumulated, just as suffixes such as *-tarap* indicate the excellence of the meaning of the base. Here, the primary sense of "accumulation" (*samabhihāra*) is the gathering together in one place of distinct, material entities existing at the same time, resulting in their becoming a single aggregate (*samudāya*), as in the case of bundles of grass and the like. However, the action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*) is inherently only one.

Although the root *div* is listed as having multiple meanings—namely, "to play, to desire victory, to transact, to shine, to praise, to be beautiful, and to move"—nevertheless, it does not express these multiple meanings simultaneously; rather, it does so through different applications (*prayoga-bheda*). Furthermore, although "cooking" (*pāka*) differs according to the difference in the substratum and the difference in the object—for instance, the cooking performed by Devadatta is one thing, that performed by another agent is another, and the cooking of rice is distinct from the cooking of oil and other substances—[the same applies here].

Nevertheless, that [action] is conveyed as having its distinctions subsumed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). For this very reason, in expressions such as *bhavadbhir āsyate* ("you are sitting"), the plural number does not occur. Indeed, the distinction among agents is not pervaded by a distinction among individual actions; for we observe the use of "they cook" (*pacanti*) even when many people are performing a single action delimited by a single result. Thus, since the principal action expressed by the verbal root is one alone in the form of a collection, there is an absence of cumulative repetition (*samabhihāra*).

However, in the case of subordinate actions such as placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth, even though they are expressed by a single verbal root simultaneously, there is an absence of "conglomeration" (*samabhihāra*). This is because they are produced sequentially, perish as soon as they arise, do not exist simultaneously, and, being immaterial, lack the capacity for such accumulation. Even when expressed by a single verbal root, due to their sequential production, their perishability upon arising, their non-simultaneous existence, and their immateriality, there is no conglomeration.

Thus, since the primary sense of *samabhihāra* (repetition/accumulation) is impossible with respect to the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it is understood in its secondary sense; he demonstrates this by stating: "it is either repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) or intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). The accumulation of substances occurs when they are not separated from other substances; likewise, for actions as well, this same [accumulation] occurs when they are not separated from other actions. In that regard, the *samabhihāra* of principal actions is repetition, for that refers to an object being performed again and again.

Furthermore, it is the principal action (*pradhānakriyā*) itself that is performed repeatedly. However, the "intensity" (*bhṛśārthatā*) of the constituent actions (*avayavakriyā*) constitutes the "intensification" (*samabhihāra*), for that [intensification] has as its object multiple constituent actions that are within the scope of the intellect. In *pāpacyate*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *dīrgho'kitaḥ*. In *dedīpyate*, the *guṇa* substitution applies by the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*. Because the intensification is already indicated by the *yaṅ* suffix itself, there is no reduplication (doubling) either by the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre dve bhavataḥ* or by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*.

The question "Why [specify] 'from a verbal root'? arises because it is impossible for anything other than a verbal root to undergo the repetition (*vṛtti*) of an intensive action. In the example *bhṛśaṃ prāṭati* ("he rains heavily"), since the combination of the verbal root and the prefix denotes a specific action, the suffix *yaṅ* would apply to that whole; consequently, there would be reduplication of the prefix as well.

If the application [of the suffix] in the sense of the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) belonged only to the verbal complex including the prefix (*sopasarga-saṃghāta*), then the suffix *yaṅ* would not apply in cases such as *prapāpacyate*. For that which is the verbal root (*dhātu*) here does not denote the intensification of action, and that which denotes the intensification of action is not the verbal root. Therefore, the verbal root alone expresses the action qualified by intensification, while the prefix is merely an auxiliary by virtue of its proximity. Consequently, since there is no possibility of [the suffix applying to] the complex, there is no purpose in mentioning the "verbal root" (*dhātu*) [in the rule].

In that case, where a specific action is expressed by the verbal complex (*saṃghāta*) itself—as in *pratiṣṭhīyate*—here indeed the simple root *sthā-* denotes the cessation of motion, whereas by the prefix-complex it is the action of motion itself that is expressed, as in *jaṅgamyate*. Even here, because roots have multiple meanings, the root *sthā-* itself functions both for motion and for its cessation; the prefix (*upasarga*), however, is an auxiliary merely by its proximity. Thus, the derivation of the verbal base (*dhātu*) is not contradicted, and therefore [the designation of the complex as] *ārdhadhātuka* is for that purpose alone.

The mention of *dhātu* (root) [is made]; by that, forms such as *bruvo vaciḥ* (P. 2.4.53) and others come about. However, the exclusion of *artha* (meaning) and *ākhya* (denomination) is merely incidental (*ānuṣaṅgikī*).

Now, how is it that the Ātmanepada occurs after a root ending in *yaṅ*? And why should it not occur? It is stated that the Ātmanepada occurs after a root (*dhātu*) marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ*. But that which is the root here [in *yaṅ-luk*] is not marked with *ṅ*; for this [the *yaṅ* suffix] is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) of the entire complex. Furthermore, that which is the *ṅit* affix is not the root.

In a case where a grammatical marker (*liṅga*) applied to a constituent part has not yet fulfilled its purpose, it serves as a qualifier for the whole; however, in examples such as *bebhidya-te*, this *ṅakāra* has already fulfilled its purpose by prohibiting *guṇa*. Someone says: the vowel *a* is elided here in the rule *kriyāsamabhihāre yaṅ*; that [elided *a*] is declared to be both *anudātta* (unaccented) and *anunāsika* (nasalized). In that case, the *anudātta* quality, having no further application within the constituent part, serves as a qualifier for the whole, and thus the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* does not apply.

Regarding the statement that [the *ātmanepada*] is indicated by the mention of *caṅkramya-dandramya* in [Pāṇini 1.3.20], he should be asked: "How then does the *ātmanepada* occur after the root *ṛti-* when followed by the *yaṅ* suffix? For even there, the marker *ṅ* has its purpose fulfilled in the prevention of *guṇa*. If he should reply, "In that case as well, an *anudātta* vowel—either *i* or *ī*—is *praśliṣṭa* (inserted) at the beginning," one should answer him: "If it were *i*, the *num* augment would apply; if it were *ī*, the prohibition of *iṭ* in the rule 'after roots ending in *śvi*, *īdit*, etc., there is no *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* [past participles]' would apply. This is not so.

There is a fault: in the rule for the insertion of *num*, the term "at the end" (*anta*) is understood to carry over from the rule "gauḥ pādānte"; therefore, *num* is applied to those [roots] whose final letter is the augment *it*. Is it not also the case that in the rule "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām," the term "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*) carries over? True.

The Venerable One has provided a solution: this further effort is in vain, for in the rule "anudāttaṅitaḥ" there is no mention of the term "dhātu" (root). What follows from that? From that, this results: the ātmanepada is established by relying solely on the fact that the affix is marked with the indicator *ṅ*. Nor does this lead to an over-extension to forms such as "aśiśriyat" or "avocat" due to the *caṅ* and *aṅ* suffixes; for the section beginning with "anudāttaṅitaḥ" operates prior even to the introduction of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes.

Otherwise, in forms such as *vartate*, the restriction would not apply because of the intervention of the *vikaraṇa* suffix. And just as it has already been established that the restriction operates prior to the *vikaraṇas*, whereas the *vikaraṇa* occurs once the restriction has taken effect, so too has it been explained in that very same place; enough of this.

Regarding the passage beginning with *sūcisūtrī*: it should be stated that the suffix *yaṅ* is added after [roots] such as *sūci*. For what purpose? To ensure that for roots like *sūci*, which have more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the rule applies; for roots like *aś*, which do not begin with a consonant (*ahalādi*); and for the root *ūrṇu*, both to ensure it has more than one vowel and does not begin with a consonant. Thus we have *sosūcyate*. The roots *sūca* (in the sense of "malicious speech"), *sūtra* (in the sense of "untying"), and *mūtra* (in the sense of "urinating") belong to the *curādi* group and take the causative suffix *ṇic*. Here, the elision of the *ṇic* is also required because the *yaṅ* is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. In *aṭāṭyate*, from the roots *aṭa* and *paṭa* (in the sense of "going"), the syllable *ṭya* is reduplicated according to the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* ("of a root beginning with a vowel, the second [syllable]").

Regarding *aśāśyate*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. By the rules "guṇa is substituted for the vowel of a root ending in a consonant cluster" (*guṇo'ttisaṃyogādyoḥ*) and "also in the case of the intensive suffix *yaṅ*" (*yaṅi ca*), the guṇa substitution occurs. Then, by the rule "the first elements of a cluster, such as *n* and *d*, are not doubled," and specifically by the statement "there is a prohibition regarding [the doubling of] a *r* followed by another *r*," the doubling of the *r* takes place. Regarding *aśāśyate*: this is the inclusion of both the roots *aś* ("to reach") and *aś* ("to eat"), which results in the augment. Regarding *prorṇonūyate*: the root *ūrṇuñ* means "to cover. This root has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). The retroflexion (*ṇatva*) is according to the eighth chapter of Pāṇini's grammar; however, because that retroflexion is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) for the purposes of the preceding rule, there is doubling of the syllable *nu*.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that [the rule] 'what is taught in the preceding [sections] is asiddha (non-existent) with respect to reduplication' refers to the reduplication taught in the eighth [chapter], just as in the example *caujaḍhat*, where because the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth is asiddha, the form *dhata* is reduplicated"? That is not so; for if that were the case, it would contradict what will be stated later, namely, that "that which has become *ṣu* is reduplicated. If that is so, then the principle "what is taught in the preceding is asiddha with respect to reduplication" is non-eternal (anitya), as indicated by the evidence of the rule "both [substitutions apply] when there is an abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable)."

Otherwise, if the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* were applied by the rule "aniteḥ" (*Pāṇini 8.4.19*), that substitution would be established; consequently, when the word *ṇi* undergoes reduplication, the form *prāṇiṇiṣati* would be correctly established. Why does this not occur here in the case of *lunīhi lunīhi evāyaṃ lunāti* ("He cuts again and again")? It certainly does occur. However, in the case of *lolūyate*, the imperative (*loṭ*) would not be obtained because it is superseded by the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*); for the *yaṅ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), as it depends merely upon the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), whereas the imperative is external (*bahiraṅga*), since it is prescribed in relation to the agent, object, or state of being (*bhāva*) within a verbal connection (*dhātusambandha*) that relies on a distinction of action.

And there is scope for the imperative (loṭ); what is that scope? It is [the case of] roots with multiple vowels and those beginning with *ha*, such as: "He keeps waking up" (*jāgṛhi jāgṛhi* evāyaṃ jāgarti) and "He keeps looking" (*īkṣasva īkṣasva* evāyam īkṣate). If this is so, then because of the recurrence of the word "or" (*vā*), there will be the suffix *paṅ* optionally; when there is no *yaṅ*, then the imperative (*loṭ*) will occur. The vowel *a* in *yaṅ* is for the purpose of doubling, as in *aṭāṭyate* and so forth.
The [root] kuṭi- is always used in the sense of crookedness and motion. 3.1.23.

The term *nityam* [is used] with respect to crookedness (*kauṭilya*) in the sense of motion (*gati*). The word *dhātoḥ* (from a root) is understood from the previous context; *gatau* (in the sense of motion) is its qualifier, meaning "from a root occurring in the sense of motion. Regarding *kauṭilye* (in the sense of crookedness): by virtue of proximity, crookedness is understood specifically as pertaining to motion. Thus, from the roots *kramu* (in the sense of stepping) and *drama* / *mīmṛ* (in the sense of motion), we have *cakramyate* and *dandramyate*. According to the rule *nugato 'nunāsikāntasya*, one who performs many comings and goings over a short distance is said to produce a crooked motion (*kuṭilāṃ gatiṃ sampādayan*).

The inclusion of the term "nitya" (invariably) is redundant, for the sentence would not arise simply because it is not expressed; indeed, the word *caṅkramyate* in its derivative form (*vṛtti*) cannot convey the meaning of the sentence *kuṭilaṃ kramati*.

For from the sentence, doubt arises: "Is it crookedness of motion, or is it a deceitful behavior based on a crooked heart? In the derivative form (*vṛtti*), however, only the crookedness of motion is invariably understood. And if one were to convey mere crookedness, the sentence could not be excluded and would result in an undesirable consequence; therefore, he says: "The inclusion of 'nitya' is for the purpose of restricting the scope."

The meaning is that "crookedness of motion" (*gatikauṭilya*) is the domain [of this rule], and the suffix *yaṅ* occurs precisely therein; it is for this purpose that he says: "Because it expresses motion, [the suffix *yaṅ*] occurs only when there is crookedness. He shows what is excluded by saying: "but not in the case of the intensification of action" (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

But surely, just as the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the sense of "offspring" is displaced and prescribed instead for the sense of "male descendant of Vaḍavā," or as the suffix *kta* prescribed for the past tense is displaced and prescribed instead for the present tense after roots ending in long *ī*, so too here, although *yaṅ* is prescribed after any verbal root in the sense of "intensive repetition of action" (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), it is [instead] prescribed after verbs denoting motion in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*)? The sublation [of the general rule by the specific one] is established precisely by the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (*takra-kauṇḍinya-nyāya*).

Just as a collection of words does not constitute a sentence when it fails to express the intended meaning, so too, in this case, a suffix will not arise because the sense of immediate succession (*samabhihāra*) is not understood. If, even so, there is still a requirement for a verbal expression (*vacana*), then even when the status of a sentence has ceased, you must still depend upon that expression! Thus, the inclusion of the term "constant" (*nitya*) here is of doubtful utility.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after the roots *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, *daś*, and *gṛbh* when there is censure regarding the action itself.

[The suffix *lyap* is applied after the verbal roots] *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, and *daś*, when there is censure (*bhāvagarhā*) regarding the action. *lup* [is the root] *luplṛ* in the sense of cutting; *sad* is *ṣadlṛ* in the senses of dissolution, going, and sinking. However, the root *sad* from the *curādi* group (which takes the causative marker *ṇic*) ending in *āṅ-sad*—meaning "to fall"—is not included here because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159). *Car* has the meaning of going; *jap* and *jalp* mean "articulate speech"; *jabh* and *jṛbh* mean "bending of the limbs"; *dah* means "reducing to ashes"; and *daṃś* means "biting."

The mention of the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is for the purpose of effecting that elision even in the case of *yaṅ*-elision—as in *daṇḍaśīti*.
