The form *au* occurs for the root *aś* when followed by the suffix *ṇal*; otherwise, after the lengthening of the initial vowel according to the rule *ata ādeḥ*, the forms *atuḥ* and *uḥ* are derived by the elision of the final *ā* before the suffixes *iṭ* and others, as in *cakāsāṃcakāra*. The root *cakāsṛ* means "to shine. As for *daridrāñcakāra*: although the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* prescribes the substitution of *au* for the final *ā* of *daridrā*, the specific prescription of *aukār* (the long *au*) is intended so that even when the *ā* of *daridrāti* is elided due to the elision of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, the long *au* is still heard. Thus, they say that the form *dadaridrāv* also occurs. As for *culumpāñcakāra*: the root *culumpati* is considered correct on the authority of the statement of the author of the Vārttika.

He asks why the *itsaṃjñā* (the designation "it") does not apply to the *m* of *ām* by the rule *halantyam*, and answers: "because of its being *amit*. In usages such as *kārayāṃcakāra*, the word *ām* is *amit*; that which does not have the *m* as an *it* is *amit*, and the state of being such is *amittvam*. Why is this so? He says: "because it ends in *a*" (*adantatvāt*). That which has *a* at the end—that is, in proximity—is *adanta*; the meaning is that at the time of its prescription in the Sūtra, it possesses the letter *a* in proximity.

Therefore, this objection should not be raised: "If it ends in *ām*, how can it be short-voweled (*adanta*); and if it is short-voweled, how can it end in *ām*? For the term *ām* is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the suffix that is being prescribed by the rule. The phrase "the absence of *guṇa* for *vid* is likewise" means that in the form *vidāñcakāra*, the absence of *guṇa* in the *ām* of the root *vid* occurs for the same reason—namely, because [the stem] ends in a short vowel. This point regarding the short-vowel ending was mentioned here incidentally; however, it must be stated in the context of the rule *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām*.

For in that case, the form *vid* ending in the letter *a* is established as a nipātana (irregular formation) in conjunction with the suffix *ām*; there, because the elision of the final *a* is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), guna substitution does not occur. It is not, however, claimed that the letter *a* in the root *vid* "to know" (*vida jñāne*) is intended [to remain]; for if it were, one would have to hear the sound [of *a*] in forms such as *vetti*. Even granting that it ends in *m*, he states that there is an absence of the designation *it*: "because of the prescription of *ām* for the roots *āsa* and *kāsa*."

The phrase "the *ām* [augment] is not a *mit*" is to be supplied [to the previous rule]. For if it were a *mit*, then although the *ām* would occur after the roots *ās* and *kās*, it would follow after the final vowel (*ac*) of the root; and in that case, once the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening) had taken place, it would be of no consequence. Therefore, the meaning is that the *ām* is determined to be a non-*mit* even from the fact that the *ām* is prescribed for *ās* and *kās* by the rules "dayāyāsaśca" and "kāspratyayāt". Others read the text as "and because of the prescription of *ām* for *ās* and *cakās*," but that is incorrect; for there is no prescription of *ām* for the root *cakās* in the sūtra.

Even the inclusion of multiple vowels in *kāsyā* finds its scope in cases such as *culumpa*. Now, one might object that if the view were that [the suffix] ends in *-at*, the rule would have to be stated as *āmāmantraḥ*; to this he replies: "The subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies, as in the case of *katanta*. Just as the subsequent form occurs in the rule "In all cases, after words beginning with *lohita* and ending in *kata*," so too here, by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*), it is stated that the subsequent form is applied.
And after a verb beginning with a vowel that has a heavy syllable (gurumat), except for the root ṛcch, [the suffix ām is added in the perfect tense]. Pāṇini 3.1.36.

Regarding the rule *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ*: "excluding *ṛcch*" means being devoid of that form, that is to say, other than the root *ṛcch*. [The examples] *iyāja* and *uvāpa*: in the case of the third person singular perfect (*ṇal*) of the roots *yaj* and *vap*, because of the absence of the *ṇit* designation by the rule *ṇaluttamo vā*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening, and thus the condition of having a heavy penultimate syllable (*gurūpottama*) is absent. Now, the counter-examples for the *thal* suffix are: *iyajitha* and *iyaṣṭha*; *uvapitha* and *uvaptha*.

But surely, in this case, it will not apply by the *paribhāṣā* regarding the meeting of conditions (*sannipāta-paribhāṣā*) alone; for the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable, which arises from the meeting with the *liṭ* suffix, cannot be the cause for the *ām* ending that destroys that very meeting. For if the *ām* were present, there would have to be *luk* elision of the *liṭ*, and thus it would destroy the meeting with the *liṭ*. In that case, here is a counter-example: *iyeṣa*; for here, the state of beginning with *ij* does not arise from the meeting with the *liṭ*.

Now, even though the mention of "possessing a heavy syllable" (*gurumat*) is made, why does [the suffix *ām*] not occur here? For when a *guṇa* is applied, this very condition of possessing a heavy syllable (*gurumān*) arises. Likewise, in forms such as *īṣatuḥ*, once the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* has been applied, the condition of possessing a heavy syllable likewise arises. True; even when the mention of "possessing a heavy syllable" is present, *ām* does not occur here precisely because of the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), since the state of possessing a heavy syllable is caused by the immediate sequence with the *liṭ* affix. Alternatively, in the expression "possessing a heavy syllable" (*guruṇataḥ*), the suffix *matup* denotes constant connection (*nityayoga*); that is, that which is constantly connected with a heavy syllable.

If this is so, then in the case of *uchī* (meaning ‘to shine’) as in *vyucchāñcakāra*, and *ucha* (meaning ‘to glean’) as in *ucchāñcakāra*, since their roots are heavy (*gurumatā*) due to the augment *āgamana* [of the *liṭ* suffix], the suffix *ām* would not apply. This is established by a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence): the fact that the author says *anṛccha* indicates that *ām* indeed occurs in such cases. In that case, however, for the sake of that *jñāpaka*, the prohibition regarding the root *ṛcch* must be stated.

But surely, this [augment] ought to be prescribed solely for the purpose of preventing *ām*, not for the sake of something other than the prevention of *ām*? This is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): the fact that the rule "of *ṛcchati* and *ṛt*" prescribes *guṇa* when *liṭ* follows indicates that *ām* does not occur after this root. Nor is there, in that context, a reference to the root *ṛcchati* by means of the suffix *tip*; for even the root *ṛ* (as in *ṛcchati*) is included by its very form in the compound "ṛcchati-ṛ-ṛtām. In this inclusion, the plural number is the proof.

We shall explain the purpose for prescribing *guṇa* in the case of the root *ṛcch* under the rule regarding *liṭ* later on. Therefore, the prescription of *guṇa* for the root *ṛcch* is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, the statement that "there is no *ām*" would mean that this very prohibition, "in the case of *anṛccha*," must be made solely for the sake of being an indicator. For in this way, the term "in *liṭ*" functions as a qualifier of what is prescribed—namely, "in that case where *liṭ* is prescribed after a root beginning with *ij* and having a heavy syllable."

Therefore, that which has heaviness (*gurumattā*) caused by a *liṭ* affix will not [be subject to the rule], while that which has heaviness caused by an *ārdhadhātuka* affix will be. As for the prohibition "not after *ṛcch*" (*anṛccha*), let it be applied or let it not be applied. However, regarding the question "why [is it said] 'having heaviness' (*gurumataḥ*)?", the reading *uvoṣa* is given; in that case, the example *uvoṣa* is inappropriate, because the optional rule "after *uṣ*, *vid*, and *jāgṛ*" (*uṣavidajāgṛbhyo vā*) would then have no scope of application.

Regarding the form *prorṇunāva*: the reduplication of the syllable *nu*—by the rules "the second [syllable] of a root beginning with a vowel" and "consonants other than *n* and *r* are not reduplicated when they are the first members of a conjunct"—is for the sake of accomplishing other grammatical operations. It must necessarily be stated that there is the substitution of *ṇu* for the root *ūrṇu*; by that very rule, the prohibition of *ām* is also established. Thus he says: "Or rather, it should be stated. In that context, in the case of *yaṅ*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the state of being [a verbal root]; however, in the case of *ām* and *iṭ*, there is an extension of non-existence (*abhāva*), because those two do not exist [in the base]. The mention of *uṭ* is a prohibition of *iṭ*; the ablative in "optionally before a *guṇa*" (*vibhāṣā guṇe*) is a fifth-case (*pañcamī*).

And here, the status of being a cause (*hetutva*) for the result is as in the example: "He dwells because of his study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). The meaning is that while the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.38) is in force, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11)—for that reason as well—the treatment as *ṇu*-like (*ṇuvadbhāvaḥ*) must be stated. The examples are: *prorṇonūyate*, *prorṇunāva*, *prorṇutaḥ*, and *prorṇutavān*.
And [the suffix *kha* is applied after a word denoting] compassion (*dayā*) and exhaustion (*āyāsa*). 3.1.37.
And regarding *dayāyāsa*: all forms of *dayāyāsa* are anudātta. In the form *palāyāñcakre*, the substitution of *l* for the *y* of the prefix is according to the rule *upasargasyāyatau*.
After the roots √vas (to dwell), √vid (to know), and √jāgṛ (to wake), [the suffix liṭ] optionally [takes the augment ksa].

Regarding the rule *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām*: the root *vid* here means "to know" (*jñāne*). The inclusion of the roots *uṣ* and *jāgṛ* is intended to refer to the two *parasmaipada* forms; there is no inclusion of the *ātmanepada* forms of *vid* meaning "existence" (*sattā*) or "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*), nor of the *ubhayapada* form of *vid* meaning "to obtain" (*lābha*), because of their association with the *parasmaipada* roots *uṣ* and *jāgṛ*, specifically with *jāgarti* from the first class (*ādādika*). In the form *viveda*, the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs, because it is traditionally accepted (*pratijñāna*) that the root *vid* ends in *a* when in conjunction with the *ām* suffix. For this very reason, he says: "Because it is accepted that *vid* ends in *a* when followed by *ām*, there is no *guṇa*."
After the roots √bhī, √hrī, √bhṛ, and √hu, the suffix ślu is applied, and it is as if the suffix luṅ had been applied.

In the rule *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-huvāṃ ślu-vacca*, the genitive case [in *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-huvām*] is used with reference to the grammatical operations [to be performed] as if there were *ślu*; and because of the intended co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*), the suffix *ām* is also understood to follow those very roots. Regarding "doubling and *ittva*": the term *ślau* indicates doubling; *ittva* occurs by the rule *bhṛñāmit*; and the term *ślau* continues to apply there. As for the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, it does not apply here. Why? Because this prohibition applies to the attainment of the rule *pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (the presence of a suffix is recognized even when it is elided), whereas here the suffix *ām* is actually heard [and thus not elided].
The root *kṛ* is employed after [a verbal root] when the suffix *liṭ* follows.

The root *kṛ* is employed after [a verb] when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) follows. Regarding the word "employed after" (*anuprayujyate*), the prefix *anu-* has the sense of "subsequent. Since there arises the expectation of what it is subsequent to, and because the *ām*-affix is the subject under discussion, it is understood that it is subsequent to that very affix; thus he says: "of the *ām*-affix. This *ām*-affix which has been prescribed—this is a *karmadhāraya* compound and not a *bahuvrīhi*: "that from which the *ām*-affix [occurs], this is the *ām*-affix; of that."

For instance, according to the view that "when [the suffix] *sat* is present, it is like [the suffix] *pratyaya*," since the *pratyaya* serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the verbal root (*prakṛti*), the employment of the root *kṛ* would have been stated to occur between the root and the affix *ām*. Thus, it is said: "afterwards, *kṛ* is employed. In the proximity of the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*), this word "anu" is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Regarding the phrase "when *liṭ* follows": the meaning is that the root *kṛ*, which stands when *liṭ* follows, is employed subsequently.

Even in the *sūtra*, "liṭi" (in the case of the *liṭ* suffix) is not an indication of a condition for the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). What then? The explicit statement of the rule is: "When the *liṭ* suffix, prescribed by the rule 'the *liṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of the remote past' (*parokṣe liṭ*), follows [a verbal root], the root *kṛ* is applied after it. This means that a word such as "cakāra" is subsequently applied. Regarding the term "kṛj" as a *pratyāhāra*: it is a contraction starting from the word "kṛ" in the rule "when joined with *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*" (*kṛbhvastiyoge*) up to the *ñ* of "kṛñaḥ" in the rule "the second [augment] of *kṛ*" (*kṛño dvitīya*). And the authority for this is the inclusion of the mention of *kṛ* in the rule concerning the *ām* suffix (*āmpratyaya*).

For if there were the apprehension of the word-form (*svarūpa*) here [in the rule *kṛño dvitīyatṛtīyaśambabījāt kṣetre*], then, because there would be no other application [of the term *kṛñ*], the mention of *kṛñ* there [in Pāṇini 2.4.54] would be purposeless. For this very reason, the reverse is also not the case—that is, that there is the apprehension of the pratyāhāra there and the apprehension of the word-form here; for if only the word-form were being apprehended here, it would not be logical to state an exception (*anuprayoga*) regarding *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* there. "By its force" (*tatsāmarthyāt*) means by the force of the apprehension of the pratyāhāra. Thus, the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not take place.

The intention is that, otherwise, for the sake of removing doubt, one would simply have stated: "In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are employed. Regarding this, there is disagreement concerning the forms when the suffix *iṭ* is present. On both points, some maintain that the substitution of *ha* occurs according to the rule "ha eti" (Pāṇini 8.2.33). Others, however, argue that because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with the suffix *tās*, the substitution of *ha* occurs only before *iṭ*. Still others hold that, precisely due to that association, the substitution of *ha* occurs only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; thus, they conclude that the form in both cases is *īkṣāmāsa*.

In this case, this [verbal root] has its meaning unmanifested; from it, no distinction of state, action, agent, person, or number is understood. It expresses merely an object in the form of an action that consists of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, pertains to non-contemporary time, is remote, and requires specific details such as the means (sādhana) and so forth.

In that case, in order to necessarily eliminate that expectancy, a word expressing a specific [action] must be employed; therefore, the portion stating "it is subsequently employed" (*anuprayujyate*) need not be prescribed as a rule. What, then, is the purpose [of this rule]? It is so that it may apply only to *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, and not to other verbal roots. But for which [roots] would it otherwise apply? It would apply to a general term—such as *kārayām papāca* ("he caused to cook"). Or it would apply to a specific term; in that case too, it would be employed—such as *uṣāmuvoṣa* ("he burned after having burned"), *vidāṃviveda* ("he knew after having known"), or *jāgarāñjajāgāra* ("he woke after having woken").

Or it may have the same meaning as that [root]—as in "he burnt the dawns" (*uṣān dadāha*), and so forth; or it may express a different meaning—as in "he cooked the dawns" (*uṣān apāca*). In the first case, the suffix would not be applied according to the requirement alone, since an additional meaning, namely a specific kind of cooking (*pākādiviśeṣa*), would also be understood. In the second and third cases, however, because the entire meaning is already understood through the application of the suffix itself, the use of the root would be redundant. In the fourth case, only a distinction residing in a different meaning would be understood, but not the meaning [of the root] itself; therefore, [the root is used] to denote a distinction inherent in that [meaning].

[The rule] "tvām-anu-prayoga-vyasanaṃ" [indicates] a predilection for the subsequent employment [of a verb]. For this very reason, there is no subsequent employment of the root *sampadyati*, even though it is included within the *pratyāhāra* (the group of roots beginning with *bhū*); otherwise, there would have to be such employment for it as well. Alternatively, because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "roots" (*dhātu*) from the rule "those ending in *saN* and so forth are roots," there will be no [subsequent employment] for the aggregate of a root and its prefix. Even so, that which is a root here shall be subsequently employed.

For in this way, since a general term culminates in a specific instance that is present, the mention of a specific means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and so forth inherent in that [general term] results in nothing other than the mention of a specific [instance] already contained within it. Likewise, when the roots *bhū* and *as* are employed following an āmantra suffix, they become transitive by virtue of that suffix—as in "his umbrella was borne" (*tasyātapatraṃ vibharāmbabhūve*) and "I indeed expected" (*ahaṃ kila vyapekṣāmāsa*). This is logical, and thus there is the simultaneous employment of both [the general and the specific]. However, if only the general term were employed;

The specific action would not be understood; there would merely be a non-manifestation of the person (puruṣa) belonging to the āmantrita. Therefore, this portion "kṛñ ca" [in the rule] should also not be prescribed. What, then, is the purpose? It is so that it may apply only to that which follows a *liṭ* [perfect tense], and not to that which follows another suffix. To what, then, would it apply by default? To that which follows a *kṛt* suffix. In the case of a *kṛt* suffix, there is no manifestation of the specific person of the verb being subsequently employed (*anuprayujyamāna*). But in the case of *liṭ*, there is indeed a contradiction regarding time (*kāla*), as is also the case with *lṛṭ* and *luṭ*.

In the case of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing other meanings such as injunctions; in the aorist (*luṅ*), only the past in general would be understood rather than the specific qualification of "not belonging to the current day"; and in the present indicative (*laṭ*), non-remoteness (*pārokṣya*) would not be understood.

But surely, just as in the case of the *anuprayoga* (subsequent employment), the general meaning expressed by the verbal root culminates in a specific meaning contained within the *ām* suffix, so too the meaning expressed by the suffix culminates in the specific meanings of the non-recent (*anadyatana*) and the remote past (*parokṣa*) contained within the *ām*; thus, the subsequent employment of *luṅ* is indeed appropriate. Likewise, since in the rule "after *ha* and *śaśvat*, *laṅ* also" (*haśaśvatorlaṅ ca*), *laṅ* is prescribed for the very same meaning as *liṭ*, would it not follow that there should be a subsequent employment of a form ending in *laṅ*? This is not a fault.

The application commenced with one *prakṛti* (archetype) shall belong to the second and the third as well. What is the meaning? The performance must be completed by the very same *prakṛti* with which it was begun—for example, in the case of the option regarding the substance of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), such as "one binds [the animal] to a *khadira* post" or "one binds to a *pālāśa* post," when the performance has been commenced with a *khadira* post, if due to some divine or human error the *khadira* is lost, then even though the primary *pālāśa* is available, one should not abandon it; rather, one should continue with a substitute for the unavailable *khadira*.

The performance is completed by means of the *badara* fruit and so forth; for it is in this way that the performance, once begun, is brought to completion. However, if another substance were taken up, there would be a different performance, because a difference in substance entails a difference in action. A substitute, moreover, is taken up precisely with the cognition that it is the primary substance itself, since a greater number of its constituent parts are present therein.

Likewise here as well, the *liṭ* construction has been commenced with the prefix *ā*, but it remains incomplete and requires a complement. It is logical that this very construction, being completed by filling that requirement through an "after-joined" (*anuprayoga*) element, should be completed only by one following a *liṭ* suffix; therefore, there is no possibility of an after-joined element following any other suffix. Consequently, even this portion [of the rule], namely "in the case of *liṭ*" (*liṭi*), need not be prescribed.

This, then, is the purpose: so that there may be *anuprayoga*, that is, subsequent application—as in *īkṣāṃ cakre*—and not *cakre īkṣām*. It is also for the sake of excluding intervention—as in *īkṣāṃ devadattaś cakre*. How is the exclusion of intervention achieved? Because, in relation to the particle *ām*, the state of being subsequent (*paścādbhāva*) is primary precisely in that case. Thus it is established that the purpose is both the exclusion of what precedes and the exclusion of intervention.

In this case, however, the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa* uses the form "tān ha rājā madayāṃ cakāra," where the separated application of the suffix is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. How then are such forms as "ukṣāṃ pracakre nagarasya mārgān" and "bibhayāṃ pracakārāsau" used in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*? Or how are forms like "taṃ tātayāṃ prathamam āsa" and "prabhraṃśayāṃ yo nahuṣaṃ cakāra" explained? Let the author of the *Vārttika* be questioned, who recites: "It must be stated for the sake of excluding inversion, and for the sake of excluding separation."
The suffix *vidāṃkurvantu* may optionally be used [in place of the imperative]. 3.1.41.

The phrase *vidāṃkurvantu* is optionally [formed] according to the rule. Here and in the subsequent examples, the *lakāra* (tense/mood marker) should be inferred from the following *anuprayoga* (subsequent application of a verb). The suffix *ām* is prescribed for the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *vid*; the word "is prescribed" (*nipātyate*) is to be supplied here, as well as the absence of *guṇa*. This applies likewise to the rule regarding the elision (*luk*) of the imperative, and to the rule stating that the root *kṛ* is subsequently applied after an imperative. All of this is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), since it would otherwise not be obtained. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of illustration; the meaning is that it serves as an indicator for all such imperative forms.

"What is established by this being so? he asks, and replies: "Not only... Because of its frequent usage, the plural number is employed in the Sūtra. However, someone who does not accept that [the plural] is merely illustrative on the grounds that it was not stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika—let him state the purpose of the particle *iti*.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the following forms occur: *abhyutsādayām*, *prajanayām*, *cikayām*, *ramayām*, *akam*, *pāvayām*, *kriyāt*, *vidāma*, and *akrin*. (Pāṇini 3.1.42)

*abhyutsādayām*, *prajanayām*, *cikayām*, *ramayām*, *makaḥ*, *pāvayām*, *kriyāt*, *vidāma*, *akrin*—these [forms] occur in the Veda (*chandas*). Regarding *akar*: from the root *kṛ*, in the *sip* (second person singular imperative), the *cli* suffix is elided by the rule "in a mantra, [the *cli* of] *ghas* etc. (*mantre ghasa*), and the *sip* is elided by the rule "after a consonant, a vowel, or *y*, etc., [the *tiP* ending is elided]" (*halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*). Regarding *kran*: in that same context, the plural suffix *jhi* is used. Regarding *kriyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) of that same root in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). Because of the rule "the optative in a benediction" (*liṅāśiṣi*), it is treated as an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, there is no *vikaraṇa* (conjugational sign). By the rule "riṅ for *śya*" (*riṅśayagliṅkṣu*), *riṅ* is substituted for *śyan*. And regarding "and reduplication": by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, there is no *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *s*).

Regarding the form *abhyudasīṣadat*: from the root *sad* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, there is the substitution of a short vowel for the penultimate vowel due to the *caṅ* suffix; by the rule *caṅi*, reduplication occurs; by *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable is elided; by *samballaghuni*, the reduplicated syllable receives the *it* augment (*i*); and by *dīrgho laghoḥ*, the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable is lengthened. The phrase "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*) is used because the rule *anyatarasyām* (optionally) continues to apply, so that this form also occurs according to usage even in Vedic (*chandas*). However, since this specific form is restricted to the spoken language, it is stated that "*abhyudasīṣadat*" occurs in the spoken language.
The suffix *cli* is applied in the sense of verbal action (*luṅ*). 3.1.43.

In the *Cchluṅ* [sūtra], the vowel *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), because it is impossible to pronounce the conjunct *cchl* as a single unit. However, this is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter), due to the absence of any purpose [for such a designation]. As for the statement "the *ca* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*)," we shall explain this in the subsequent sūtra. [The author] will state that *sij* and the others are substitutes for this [root].

If this is so, for what purpose is this taught? For is an instruction intended for the sake of being heard (*śravaṇārtha*), or for the sake of some grammatical operation (*kāryārtha*)? This *cli* is not heard anywhere [in the Vedic corpus], nor is any grammatical operation seen to occur for it when it is merely assumed—as is the case with *kvip* and other such suffixes. Therefore, why not simply discard *cli* altogether and prescribe its exceptions (*apavāda*) as exceptions to *sic*? This should not be suspected. For if that were the case, many mentions would have to be made in rules such as "ghas in a mantra" (*mantre ghas*); that is, the mention of *aṅ* would have to be made for the sake of including the root *gam*.

Since *dheṭ* is included among those roots ending in long vowels (*ākārānta*), the mention of *caṅ* is for its sake, as it is by the rule "optionally [after] *dheṭ* and *śvi*" that *caṅ* is applied. The mention of *sic* is for the sake of other roots; if the elision (*luk*) of *ciṇ*, which is prescribed after *jan* by the rule "after *dīp*, *jan*, etc.," is observed in the Veda, then that too is included. Thus, there are these three or four mentions. However, in the case of the general rule for *cli*, there is a mention of only that single element which serves as the substitute for all of them.

But surely, even if the general rule (*utsarga*) were not made, those same three instances of *cli* would still occur—namely, in the rules "cli luṅi," "cleḥ sic," and "mantre ghasādayaḥ," where it says "of this *cli*. If that is so, then instead of saying "of *sic*" in the rule "gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ," I shall say "of *cli*"; and that very term "of *cli*" will also carry over into the rule "mantre ghasādayaḥ. In this way, there is economy of expression (*lāghava*).

If it is said that [the suffix] *liṭ* is elided (*luk*), will the elision occur at the very stage of *lyap*, or rather after the substitutes have been applied by virtue of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*)? If the elision occurs at the stage of *lyap* itself, then in forms such as *aguḥ* and *asthuḥ*, the *jus* substitution prescribed by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* would not apply. [Objection: Let it not be by the mention of *sic*; it will instead be by the mention of *āt*. [Response: Even there, the mention of *sic* continues to follow. [Objection: The mention of *sic* will be withdrawn. [Response: If it is withdrawn, then it would undesirably apply even in a case like *abhūvan*.
Why [is this not so]? Because of the rule "after *siC* and after a reduplicated stem" (*sijabhyasta*). No, he says; for it was just stated that the elision (*luk*) occurs only in the state of *lyap*.

Thus, in the rule "of *āt*" (*ātaḥ*), only "after that which has an indicatory *ṅ*" (*ṅitaḥ*) is carried over, not "after *siC*"; otherwise, the same would apply even in the case of *laṅ*. And in the case of the root *dheṭ*, there will be an option due to the restrictions: "optionally for *dheṭ*" (*vibhāṣā dheṭ*) and "only for Śākaṭāyana in *laṅ*" (*laṅa śākaṭāyanasyaiva*). Even so, let them not stand; by the rule "the initial [acute] of *siC* optionally" (*ādiḥ sico'nyatarasyām*), the accent would simply not be obtained.

Now, once the substitutions have been made, the same would apply here in the rule "vibhāṣā ghrādheṭ" as well; and since the *caṅ* affix is also optionally prescribed for the root *dheṭ* by the rule "vibhāṣā dheṭśvyeḥ," then just as there are the presence and absence of *luk* with the *sic* affix, so too are the desired forms—*adhāt*, *adhātām*, *adhuḥ*, *adhāsīt*, *adhasiṣṭām*, and *ādhāsiṣuḥ*—established.

In the case where there is no elision (*luk*) of the *caṅ* suffix, the forms *adadhat*, *adadhatām*, and *adadhan* are established. However, in the case of its elision (*luk*), would not a fourth form, *adadhāt*, also result by means of reduplication (*dvirvacana*) according to the rule for the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)? No, for when the *caṅ* is elided, reduplication does not occur, due to the prohibition: "When [an affix] is marked with *lu*, [the operation] pertaining to the stem (*aṅga*) is not [to take place]."

In that case, when there is *luk* elision of *caṅ* in the plural, an undesired form would result, for a threefold expression is indeed intended: *adhuḥ*, *adhāsiṣuḥ*, and *adadhan*. But surely, even when *caṅ* is elided, *jus* will occur by the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.109), just as it does after *sic*? This is not so; for the mention of *sic* continues [from the previous rule] there.

Will the mention of *sic* be withdrawn? If it is withdrawn, then because the rule "ātaḥ" could serve as an injunction for the elision of *caṅ* after the root *heṭ*, it would not function as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, in the case of *abhūvan*, the *jus* substitution would apply by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix) due to *sic*. For has it not just been stated that the elision occurs once the substitutes have been applied? If this is so, then instead of the rule "ti-j-abhyastāt," I shall state it as "cli-abhyastāt."

What is accomplished [by this]? Even when there is elision (*luṅ-luk*), the substitution of *jus* for *cli* in the case of reduplicated verbs (*abhyasta*) is established. Furthermore, because the term *sic* is understood to carry over into the rule "ātaḥ," the absence of *jus* in forms such as *abhūvan* is established by that restriction. Since the elision occurs after the substitutes have been applied, the accent characterized by *sic* is established. If, however, it were stated as "for *cli* and reduplicated verbs" (*cly-abhyasta*), there would be a fault regarding the *cli* augment in *caṅ*: *adhukṣan*, *avocan*, and *apīpacan*—in these cases too, *jus* would undesirably apply. Therefore, it must be stated simply as "for *sic* and reduplicated verbs" (*sij-abhyasta*).

In the rule *ātaḥ* as well, the mention of *sic* alone must be carried over—so that the restriction may apply, but not the *vidi*. Consequently, that very point remains established: [the rule] *bahuvacane'dhān* would apply. And when the elision (*luk*) of *caṅ* is performed after the root *dheṭ*, then not only in the plural, but in all numbers, because of the absence of the accent characterized by *sic*, there would result a fourfold ambiguity regarding the accent (*svare cātuḥśabdyaprasaṅgaḥ*).
Therefore, in the rule *gātisthāghupā*, one must simply say *sicaḥ*; and thus that very point remains established: those same three mentions [of *sic*].

On the contrary, if the *utsarga* (general rule) were not being set aside, there would be the inclusion of only two [roots] in the sūtra beginning with *mantrighasādi*. How so? Because *caṅ* and *ciṇ* are optional for both *dheṭ* and *jan*, those examples which are cited for *luk* (elision) will actually pertain to *sic* alone. What, then, is the distinction here? This is the distinction: when *sic* is elided, the accentuation must occur according to the rule "the first syllable of *sic* is optionally acute" (*ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām*), whereas this does not apply to *caṅ* and *ciṇ*.

Therefore, since there are three applications [of the rule] in both views, is there no purpose for the general rule (*utsarga*)? To this it is replied: For if the general rule were absent, in the case of *mantre ghasa*, that accent which is prescribed by the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* would apply to those roots from which the elision of *sic* is made. But when this general rule exists, because the elision is prescribed precisely in that state by the rule *ler luk*, the absence of *sic* ensures that the accent is established according to the respective rules.

Likewise, when the *sic* suffix is elided after roots ending in long *ā*, the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.109) and *ātaḥ* (3.4.110) would require the substitution of *jus*; however, in the case of the elision of *liṭ*, that elision itself is internal to the root. Therefore, a general rule (*utsarga*) must be formulated. Similarly, in the rule *śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (3.1.45), the term *aniṭaḥ* should serve as a qualifier for *liṭ*.

Furthermore, in the absence of exclusion (apavāda), that very qualification would apply to the verbal root itself, namely: "that after which [the augment] *iṭ* does not occur. In that case, since the substitutes for *luṅ* and so forth are *sārvadhātuka*, their status as non-*it* (aniṭ) is already established; thus, because it is invariable, it cannot serve as a qualification. Therefore, one must resort to a qualification residing in another suffix—namely, "that after which another suffix [other than the one currently under consideration] has no *iṭ*."

In that case, there would not be the form *aghukṣat*—for after this [root], the augment *iṭ* is optionally prescribed by the rule *svarati-sūtra* (*svarati-sūtrādi*) in forms such as *gūhitā*. Even if it were designated as *aniṭ* (lacking *iṭ*) due to the optional absence of *iṭ*, the suffix *ksa* would necessarily apply; for the term *aniṭ* in the general rule (*utsarga*) serves as a qualifier for that very [suffix]. That [suffix] is sometimes *aniṭ* and sometimes *seṭ*: when it is *aniṭ*, then *ksa* applies; when it is *seṭ*, then *sic* applies. Thus the desired result is established: *aghukṣat* and *aguhīt*. Therefore, the general rule (*utsarga*) must be formulated; the meaning is that it must be prescribed as a substitute (*sthānin*).
The suffix *sic* is substituted for *cli*. (Pāṇini 3.1.44)

The *ikāra* [in *sicaḥ*] is for the sake of pronunciation; it is not an *anubandha*. If this were so, then in the case of *asaṃstet*, since the *aṅga* ending in *sic* would be dependent on an *ātmanepada* suffix marked with *ṅ*, the elision of the *n* [of *saṃsthā*] by the rule *aniditām* would result. This is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author teaches that the *sic* following *han* is *kit* in the rule *hanaḥ sic*, this indicates that there is no elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) in a stem ending in *sic*. How this serves as an indicator has been explained right there [in the commentary on *hanaḥ sic*], so it should be understood from that very place.

"The letter *ca* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*)," meaning it is for the sake of making [the final syllable] udātta. But since the suffix *sic* is devoid of a phoneme (*anackatvāt*), how can the letter *ca* be for the sake of accent? [One might argue: "Once [the augment] *k* is added, it becomes possessed of a phoneme (*sācka*). Even so, [the desired result] would be established by the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*). [The author replies: It is not established; for when another accent has not yet applied, does the low-pitched nature (*anudāttatva*) prescribed for an augment not subvert the accent of the affix? [The opponent says: "In that case, because *cli* is marked with *c*, its accent will occur through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). To this, he says: "For the low-pitched nature of the augment (*āgamānudāttatva*)... [meaning] it would even subvert the accent of the *cit*.

This is due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, one might object: if in *mā hi lāvīt* the augment were unaccented, then the addition of the letter *c* to the suffix *cli* would be purposeless. The [author] thinks as follows: the letter *c* in *cli* serves its purpose in the rule *mantre ghasa...* where it allows for the general inclusion [of the suffix].

Otherwise, because this [term *liṭ*] lacks an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), only this very one would be grasped, and not *liṭ*; consequently, in the rule *āmaḥ*, since a *liṭ* without an indicatory letter is impossible, the term *liṭaḥ* would not be carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. As a result, due to its higher status (*paratva*) and its being more internal (*antaraṅgatva*), the *tiṅ*-suffixes such as *tip* and others would apply first; subsequently, when elision (*luk*) occurs, the form *kārayām* would be considered a *tiṅ*-ending by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of a suffix). Thus, in the case of *devadattaḥ kārayāñcakāra*, there would be the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for that [first member], and consequently, there would be no *nighāta* for the second member. Therefore, in the rule *āmaḥ*, the term *liṭaḥ* must be carried over.

And its recurrence there [in the subsequent rule] is possible only when there has been a prior apprehension of the general form (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). Therefore, since the letter *c* in the suffix *cleḥ* serves its purpose, it would—by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—also subvert the accent of the *cit* element; this is expressed by the potential mood (*liṅ*) in the sense that such subversion is possible. The underlying intention is that since the apprehension of the general form could be established even by another indicatory letter (*anubandha`), one could argue that the accent of the *cit* element alone will prevail in accordance with the letter *c*.

Regarding *aspṛkṣat* and *amṛkṣat*: after the roots *spṛś* (in the sense of touching), *mṛś* (in the sense of touching/grasping), and *kṛṣ* (in the sense of scratching/pulling), the suffix *ksa* would have been expected; however, after *tṛp* (in the sense of satisfying) and *dṛp* (in the sense of exhilaration and release), since they belong to the *puṣādi* group, the suffix *aṅ* would have been expected, yet the *sic* suffix is also permitted as an alternative. Thus, we have *aspṛkṣat*. Following the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* in the *vraścādi* group, and by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, the change to *k* occurs. As for *akāssprākṣīt*: [the derivation follows the same principles].

According to the rule *anudāttasya cardupadhasya ca*, the augment *am* is applied in one alternative; then, by the rule *ṛkārasya yaṇ*, the semivowel *y* replaces the vowel *ṛ*, and by the rule *vadavraja* etc., the vowel *a* undergoes *vṛddhi*. In the alternative where *am* is absent, *vṛddhi* occurs for the vowel *ṛ* itself. The same applies in subsequent cases as well.
The suffix *ksa* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ś*, having a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, provided they do not take the augment *iṭ*.

Regarding the rule *śal-ig-upadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*: one might object that since a root ending in *śal* has *ig* as its penultimate letter, the *guṇa* substitution would necessarily apply at the stage of the *lā* suffix even before the *ksa* affix is added—because the *guṇa* is triggered by the presence of the *liṭ* suffix—and consequently, the qualification "having *ig* as its penultimate letter" (*ig-upadhāt*) would become impossible to formulate. This is not a fault; by the force of the qualification itself, the *ksa* affix will occur precisely prior to the *guṇa* substitution.

But surely, even if the suffix *k* were applied, the suffix *ksa* would still occur by resorting to the status of what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*) or by relying on a qualifier for that which has been prescribed; so what would be the purpose of making *k* kit at this point? It is for the sake of qualifying [the rule] "after *ksa*, when an *ac* follows" (*ksasyāci*). If it were stated simply as "after *sa*, when an *ac* follows" (*sasyāci*), would it not then apply here as well: *vad-i-han-i-kam-i-kaṣibhyaḥ saḥ*—namely, *vat-sau*, *vat-sāḥ*? No, it will not apply, because *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal stems (*avyutpannāni prātipadikāni*) and thus lack [derivative] meaning.

Even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the suffix *sa* would apply after words such as *tṛṇa* within the group beginning with *vuñ-chaṇ*—namely, [the forms] *tṛṇasau* and *tṛṇasā*, meaning "a place where grass exists"? This is not so; for in the section beginning with "The elision of *gho* optionally in the *leṭ*," there is a reference to verbal roots and suffixes. Furthermore, in the rule "The elision (*luk*) of *ksa* optionally after *duh* etc.," the term "of *ksa*" (*ksasya*) is understood from the preceding rule "after *ac*"; and since that [suffix *ksa*] is possible only in the case of roots like *duh*, it will be understood as referring to that very same [suffix] in the previous rule as well.

Thus, it is established that by the power of the insertion of *kit*, no *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding the rule *cler aniṭaḥ*: although the *cli* suffix ought to be replaced by substitutes such as *sij* and others, and since it is not heard in any instance [of its own], it possesses neither the property of being *seṭ* nor *aniṭ*; nevertheless, when the form *duh-la* is present, this is the domain for *ksa*, and therefore *sic* cannot occur.

Even the designation *kṣa* does not apply as long as its status as being without the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*) is not known; since the augment *iṭ* would otherwise apply to the *l*-suffixes there, its prohibition establishes whether it is *seṭ* (with *iṭ*) or *aniṭ* (without *iṭ*), and thus the qualification [of the root] is justified. Examples include *aghukṣat* and so forth. Regarding *alikṣat*: from the root *lih* in the sense of "tasting," *h* becomes *ḍh*. Regarding *abhaitsīt* and *acchaitsīt*: from *bhid* in the sense of "cleaving" and *chid* in the sense of "cutting. Regarding *akukṣat* and *amukṣat*: from *kuṣ* in the sense of "extracting" and *muṣ* in the sense of "stealing. [The rules applied are: *dāderdhātorghaḥ* ("*dh* is substituted for the initial *d* of a root") and *ekāco vaśo bhaṣ* ("*bh* is substituted for *v* or *ś* of a monosyllabic root when followed by a *bhaṣ*-ending suffix").]
The root *śliṣ* is used in the sense of embracing. 3.1.46.

Regarding *śliṣ* in the sense of embracing: the phrase "of the root *śliṣ*" refers to the root *śliṣ* in the sense of embracing (*śliṣa āliṅgane*), and not to the root *śriṣu śliṣu pruṣu pluṣu dāhe* (meaning 'to burn'), because the latter does not function in the sense of embracing, and because [the former] is governed by the heading "it is *aniṭ*" (*aniṭ* iti) and possesses an *anubandha*. In this context, the present rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

But surely this root *śliṣ* belongs to the *puṣādi* class, and thus in the counter-example, the suffix *aṅ* occurs. Consequently, since a rule (*vidhi*) is possible—namely, that the suffix *ksa* should apply in the sense of "embracing" by overriding the *aṅ* obtained from its inclusion in the *puṣādi* list—a restriction (*niyama*) is not tenable. Let it be a rule; even so, is it not established that *ksa* applies in the sense of embracing and *aṅ* elsewhere, which is the desired result? True.

The [suffix] *kta* is established for the *parasmaipada*; however, since there is no *aṅ* in the *ātmanepada*, by the preceding rule, *ksa* would apply both in the case of embracing (*āliṅgana*) and non-embracing. But it is desired that in that case too, *ksa* applies when there is embracing, and *sic* otherwise; and that is possible only if a restriction exists. Yet that restriction is not possible, because there is nothing to be prescribed [by a restrictive rule]. [Objection: It is established through the division of the *yoga*: "After the root *śliṣ*, [there is *ksa*]"—this is one *yoga*. [The next is: "And after *śliṣ*, *ksa* occurs. For what purpose is this? To set aside the *aṅ* of the *puṣādi* group.

In that case, just as it would supersede *aṅ*, it would also supersede *ciṇ*—as in "the girl was embraced by Devadatta" (*samāśleṣi kanyā devadattena*)? According to the principle that "exceptions [apavāda] supersede the immediately preceding rules, not those that follow," the suffix *kso* would apply to the root *śliṣ* both in the sense of embracing and in the sense of non-embracing. What, then, is the purpose of this present rule? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): [the suffix *kso* applies] only in the sense of embracing, and not elsewhere.

By the force of the *yogavibhāga* (division of the rule), every acquisition (*prāpti*) of *kṣa*, as far as it extends, is restricted; however, it does not mean that a rule applies only to what immediately follows. The acquisition [of *kṣa*] by the rule for *śliṣ* is precisely for the purpose of subverting *ṅ*. Even so, the restriction (*niyama*) is not tenable. Why? Because the mention of *śliṣ* is for the purpose of subverting *aṅ*; yet, it is not capable of subverting *aṅ* absolutely.

Because of the force of the recitation of *puṣa* and so forth, a universal option (*vikalpa*) between the two suffixes [the *kta* and the *kṣa*] would result; therefore, the second rule (Yoga) is stated so that the *kṣa* alone may necessarily apply in the sense of "embracing" (*āliṅgana*), lest the *aṅ* [suffix] ever occur. Why, then, is it said that "a restriction (*niyama*) is not tenable"? Is it not true that even Your Honor has stated a restriction by way of another approach? This, however, is the distinction: by me, a restriction on the suffix (*pratyaya-niyama*) was stated—namely, that *kṣa* occurs only in the sense of embracing; whereas by you, a restriction on the meaning (*artha-niyama*) is intended—namely, that [the suffix applies] only in the sense of embracing.

"Or rather, it is *k* alone"—in no way are we released from this restriction. In that case, either because of conformity with the linguistic usage (*lakṣya*), or because of the mention of the case-ending of the predicate (*vidheya*) due to its being the primary element, there will be a restriction on the suffix (*pratyaya*) alone.
The word *ddaś* is not [subject to the rule]. 3.1.47.

It is not seen [as an example]. By the word "pūrveṇa" (by the former), one refers to the rule "śala igupadhāt". "The affixes aṅ and sic occur"—this means that in the parasmaipada, in cases other than this, only sic occurs. *adarśat* is formed by the rule "ṛddhaśo'ṅi guṇaḥ". *adrākṣīt* is formed by the rule "sṛjiddaśorjhalyamakiti". Now, why was not sic alone prescribed immediately after "cleḥ sic" for the purpose of superseding ks, so that aṅ would also occur by virtue of the indicatory letter *it*? True; even in that case, the letter *c* would have to be added in the rule "ddaśaśca", so there is no difference in terms of brevity.
The suffix *caṅ* is applied after the roots *ni*, *śri*, *dru*, and *sru* when expressing the agent (*kartṛ*).

Regarding the rule *ṇi-śri-dru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ*: the letter *c* is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). If, in the rule *caṅi*, it were stated as *aṅi*, then [the suffix] *aṅ* would also apply here in the rules *asyativaktikhyātibhyo'ṅ* and *ṣidbhidādibhyo'ṅ*. However, if this were prescribed as *ṅ*, the letter *c* could be omitted; its purpose must be considered. Examples include *aśiśriyat* and so forth.

In this case, when the suffix *caṅ* is present, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is the base (*aṅga*), whereas when the suffix *tip* is present, the form ending in *caṅ* is the base. Therefore, the prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution—which depends on *caṅ*—occurs only with respect to *caṅ* itself as having the marker *ṅ*. What is the reason? Is it because [the rule] "before *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅiti*) is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*)? This is not a fault; for *viyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are internal (*antaraṅga*) because they depend on the *caṅ* which is included within the base, whereas the *guṇa* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on the *tip* which is outside the base. [The example] *akārayiṣātām*: from the causative (*ṇyanta*) in the passive sense (*karman*), in the *luṅ* tense, second person dual, the suffix *ātām*. 7.2.59) *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.59) *na vṛdbhya

[Objection: But surely the affix *ṇiṅ* is prescribed after the root *kam*, and no other base (*prakṛti*) called *kami* is possible; moreover, [the form] is established by the rule itself from the base ending in *ṇiṅ*. To this he replies: "The rule *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā* [means that] when *ṇiṅ* is absent... [In the case where *ṇiṅ* is present,] there is the treatment as *saṇvat* (like the *sa*-aorist). This is because in the rule for *saṇvat* (*sanyataḥ*), the phrase "a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ*" is relied upon. For in that context, although it could have been stated simply as "*sanvallaghuni caṅi*," the inclusion of the word "following" (*para*) is for the sake of a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therein, *ṇi* is the meaning of the other member of the compound, since nothing else is possible.
The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after the roots *dhā* (to suck) and *śvi* (to swell).

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ*: here, the option [for the suffix] *aṅ* also applies by the rule *jṝstambhu* etc. Thus we have *aśvad*. [In this case], *aḥ* replaces [the root vowel] of *śvi* by the rule *śvayater aḥ*. As for *aśvayīt*, since the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *hmyanta* etc. applies to the *sic* suffix, *guṇa* substitution takes place. In *adhiṣātām*, there is the dual ending *ātām* in the passive (*karmaṇi*). [The *s* of the root becomes *ṣ*] because of the rules *sthāghvoric ca* [which prescribes *it* and *kit* status].
The suffix *ni* is applied after the root *gup* in the Vedic language.

Regarding the rule *gupeśchandasi*: this rule applies where the suffix *āya* does not exist, because the root is cited in its simple form in the sūtra. Therefore, there is no inclusion of the roots *gup* (meaning "to protect") and *gup* (meaning "to be confused"), since one follows what is observed in the Vedic texts (*chandas*). However, if they are actually observed [in such usage], those two are also included. As for *ajūgupatam*: from the root *gup* (meaning "to protect"), with the suffix *thas* changed to *tam* by the rule *tasthasthamipām*, and the lengthening of the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) by the rule *tujādīnāṃ dīrgho'bhyāsasya*. As for *agauptam*: in the alternative case where the augment *iṭ* is absent due to the root being marked with *ūdit*, there is the elision of the suffix *sic* by the rule *jhalo jhali*. As for *agopāyiṣṭam*: this is derived from the root ending in the suffix *āya*.
[The suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the roots *nayati*, *dhvanayati*, *elayati*, and *ardayati*. (3.1.51)

[The suffix *yaṅ* is applied] after the roots *ūnayati*, *dhvanayati*, *elayati*, and *arddayati*. [Regarding *arddayati*: the root *ard* is listed as meaning "to go" and "to beg"; it also includes the root *ard* meaning "to injure," provided that such usage is observed in the Veda. Regarding the phrase "after these": among them, *ūnayati* belongs to the *curādi* (Curyādi) class; *dhvani* is also listed in the *curādi* class under the governing rule "up to this point, roots ending in short *a* [belong to Curyādi]," and it is also listed in the *ghaṭādi* class. *Elayati* belongs to the *curādi* class; *arddayati* is formed by adding the causal *ṇic* suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*). "By the preceding [rule]" refers to the rule beginning with *ṇi-śri-*. [The form] *ūnayī-* [is derived accordingly].

This is the second person singular. As before, since the *vṛddhi* is prohibited, there is *guṇa*. By the rule "na māṅyoge," the augment *āṬ* is prohibited. "Mā tvāyato jarituḥ kāmamūnayīḥ"—this is the speech of the seer Pratisavya. "Tvāyataḥ" means desiring you; "jarituḥ" means of me, the singer; "kāmam" means desire; "mā ūnayīḥ" means do not make it deficient—this is the meaning. Generally, however, it is read with the *tiṅ* ending and with the augment *āṬ*; that should be observed elsewhere. [The form] is "auninaḥ."

In *sipi caṅi*, by the rule *ajāder ddhitīyasya*, there is reduplication of the syllable *na*. Generally, however, this is also read with a verbal suffix (*tibanta*), like the example; thus [we have] *dhvanayīt*. Here, *tip* is the suffix, and by the rule *na māṅyoge*, there is a prohibition of the augment *aṭ*. In *ārdditat*, by the rules *ajāder ddhitīyasya* and *na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*, there is reduplication of the syllable *da*.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied after the roots *as*, *ti*, *vac*, and *khyāti*.

Regarding the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*: "the substitute *brū* may optionally [be used]. The word *vā* (optionally) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The same applies in subsequent cases. [The form] is established by the fact that [the root *as*] belongs to the *puṣādi* group. [The forms] *paryāsthat* and so on [are explained as follows]: in the *ātmanepada*, because of the rule *upasargādasyatyūhyorvāvacanam*, there is the suffix *aṅ*; then [by the rule] *asyatesthuk*, the augment *thuk* is added. [The form] *avocat* [is derived] by the rule *vaca um*. [The form] *ākhyat* [is derived] by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*.
And [the suffix] *lipi* is applied after the verbal root *cih* (to observe). 3.1.53.

*Lipi-sici-hvaś-ca*: *lipi-sici-saha-hvā*—this is a compound formed according to the rule "mayūravyaṃsakādayaḥ. If it were a collective dvandva compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), there would be the shortening of the neuter gender; if it were a copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga*), there would be the plural number. In the genitive singular (*ṅasi*), there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto dhātoḥ. The separation of the sūtra (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows. If there were a single compound, namely "asyati-vakti-khyāti-lipi-sici-hvaḥ," then the inclusion of *as-* and the others would also carry over into the subsequent rules, and consequently, there would be an option for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) even after those [roots].
In the case of the ātmanepada endings, [the substitution of *liṭ* for *laṅ*] may optionally take place. (Pāṇini 3.1.54)

In the case of the *ātmanepada* endings, [the substitution of *iṭ*] is optional. Thus, we have *alipta* and *asikta*. Here, there is elision of the *s* by the rule *jhalo jhali*, and because of the *kit* designation by the rule *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening.
The augment iṭ is applied after roots beginning with *puṣ*, those beginning with *dyut*, and those marked with the indicatory vowel *ḷ* (ḷkārānubandha), when followed by Parasmaipada endings.

"Roots beginning with *puṣ*, *dyut*, and those ending in *ṛ* take the *parasmaipada* endings. Since the goal is achieved by connecting each term with only one word "beginning with" (*ādi*), the inclusion of both [the two groups] has a purpose that requires consideration. Regarding the phrase "within the *divādi* sub-group": this refers to the group starting from "√*puṣ* (to nourish)" and "√*śuṣ* (to dry)" up to the end of the list. As for the occurrence of the marker *vṛt* in the middle for "√*ṣṇih* (to love)," that is intended to mark the conclusion of the *radhādi* sub-group.

And this is understood from the statement of the author of the Vārttika: "The inclusion of this [root *as*] is for the sake of the ātmanepada endings because it belongs to the *puṣādi* group," and not because it belongs to the *bhūvādi* group. [If it were the latter], since [the roots] beginning with *puṣa puṣṭau*, *śriṣu śliṣu pruṣu pluṣu dāhe*, and so forth, would include it, he would not have made a separate mention of the *dyutādi* group, as they are recited immediately after the *puṣādi* group. Or, it may belong to the sub-group (*gaṇa*) beginning with *kryādi*, such as *puṣa puṣṭau*, *muṣa steye*, and so forth.

For in that [Dhātupāṭha], only four [classes] are recited; if those [four] were intended to be grasped there, one should have made them end in *ḷ* (i.e., *lṛdita*), since even the status of having a circumflex accent (*svariteta*) and so forth would be established by that very means. Now, why are the *puṣādi* and *dyutādi* classes not recited as ending in *ḷ*? It is impossible to recite them in that way, because among them there exist roots that are marked with an initial vowel (*āditaḥ*), those not so marked (*auditāḥ*), those marked with *u* (*uditāḥ*), and those not so marked (*ūditāḥ*).

For example: among the *puṣādi* roots, we have *ñiṣvidā* in the sense of "oozing from the body," *madī* in the sense of "joy," *samu* in the sense of "pacification," and *ṣidhū* in the sense of "accomplishment. Among the *dyutādi* roots as well, we have *śvitā* in the sense of "color," *ñimidā* in the sense of "moistening," *ñikṣvidā* in the senses of "moistening" and "releasing," *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *bhraṃsu* in the sense of "falling down," *syandū* in the sense of "flowing," and *kṛpū* in the sense of "capability. [The forms] *adyutat* and *aśvitat* occur because, according to the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi*, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is optionally used in the *luṅ* (aorist). [The form] *aloṭiṣṭa* occurs from the root *luṭa* or *luṭha* in the sense of "striking."
And [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] after the roots *sṛ*, *śās*, and *ṛt*. (Pāṇini 3.1.56)

[The rule applies] after the roots *sarti*, *śāsti*, and *ṛtti*. Because *śās* belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; in the other cases, this is due to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*). [The root] *śāsu* means "to instruct. Due to its association with *sarti* and *ṛtti*, which are *parasmaipada* roots, only this [root *śās*] is understood here, and not the *ātmanepada* root *āṅ-śāsu* meaning "desire," as he demonstrates. Regarding *ṛ*: *ṛ* in the sense of "motion" is the *bhūvādika* (first class) root; *ṛ* in the sense of "motion and breathing" is the *jauhotyādika* (third class) root; and *ṛ-sṛ* in the sense of "motion" is the *jauhotyādika* root.

Some maintain that both [roots] are indicated here; however, we consider that only the two forms *ṛt* (from *ṛ*) and *sṛt* (from *sṛ*), beginning with *jauhoti*, are intended. Regarding *asarat*: by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅi guṇaḥ*, there is guṇa substitution. Regarding *aśiṣat*: by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the root *śās*; furthermore, by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāñca*, the cerebral *ṣ* is substituted [for the final *s*].

The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of the ātmanepada endings. Otherwise, one would have composed a single rule: *puṣādidyutādyuditaḥ sartiśāstyartibhyaḥ*. For in that way, both the separate mention of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the use of the particle *ca* would not be necessary. Regarding *samaranta*: the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *samo gamyṛcchi*; the absence of the augment *āṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi*, because this usage is Vedic—*samanyavo yatsamaranta senāḥ* (when the armies, full of spirit, came together), *saṅkalpā asya samaranta* (his intentions were united).

Likewise, in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, it says: "My desires have been fulfilled now that you have arrived. Someone objects: "This is contrary to the *Mahābhāṣya*; for in the *Mahābhāṣya*, under the rule 'samo gamyṛcchi', the *ātmanepada* forms *māsamṛṣātām* and *māsamṛṣata* are cited as examples with the suffix *sic*. To this they reply: "By association with the root *śās*, the roots *ṛt* and *sṛt* taken here are those belonging to the *juhotyādi* (third) class which lack the augment *śap*;
however, in the rule 'samo gamyṛcchi', the root *ṛt* belonging to the *bhūvādi* (first) class is also included. Thus, the citation of *sic* with the *bhūvādi* root *ṛt* is not contradictory."
Or [the suffix *ir*] is applied after a verbal root ending in *ṛ*. 3.1.57.
Or it is due to the *ir* augment. Regarding "not against a wall": the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because of the *svarita* accent.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the roots *jṝ*, *stambhū*, *mruca*, *mluca*, *gruca*, *gluca*, *gluñcu*, and *śvi*.

[The rule] *jṝ-stambhu-mrucu-mlucu-grucu-glucu-glucu-śvibhyaś-ca* [is stated]. Regarding *astambhat*: by the rule *aniditām*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). Even if only one [of the two roots] were mentioned, all three forms would be established. How so? If, first of all, *gluci* is mentioned, then from that root, with the suffixes *aṅ* and *sic*, the pair *glucat* and *aglucīt* is established; but from *gluñci* with *sic*, the third form *agluñcīt* is established.

Now, if *gluñci* is adopted, its two forms—*aglucat* and *agluñcot*—are established; however, for *gluci*, with the suffix *sic*, a third form, *aglocīt*, is also established. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is both [roots] adopted? he says: "But because of the difference in meaning," etc. "Some say," and so forth. This contradicts the Bhāṣya; for the author of the Bhāṣya, stating that "because roots have multiple meanings, the difference in meaning is not the motive for adopting both," rejected the adoption of either one.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *mṛd*, and *dṛ*, as well as after *ruh*, in the Vedic language.

The suffixes [of the present indicative] are applied after the roots *kṛ*, *mṛd*, and *dṛ* in the Vedic language. [As in the example] *amardat*; the use of the *parasmaipada* ending here is by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The *ciṇ* affix is substituted for *ta* after a verbal root ending in a vowel. (Pāṇini 3.1.60)

"By virtue of the sense (*sāmarthyāt*): because the root is marked for the *ātmanepada*, the form *ta*—which is prescribed by the rule *tasthasthamipām* to replace the third-person plural *parasmaipada* ending—is impossible in this context. Therefore, by virtue of the sense, [the form] *udapādi* [is understood]. [In *udapatsata*], the substitution of *at* is applied by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*. Here, the word *vā* (or) has ceased to apply, because the option (*anyatarasyām*) is mentioned in the subsequent rule."
The suffix *ka* is optionally applied after the verbal roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūr*, *iṣ*, and *pyāy*.

The suffix *ciṇ* is optionally applied after the verbal roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūr*, *āp*, and *pyāy*. [The roots] *janī* (in the sense of manifestation) and *budha* (in the sense of understanding) are intended here; however, the roots *jana* (in the sense of birth) and *budha* (in the sense of awakening), which are *parasmaipadins*, are not included here because they are accompanied by *ātmanepadins* such as *dīp* and the others. Consequently, when there is a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*) with these two *parasmaipadins*, the suffix *ciṇ* does not occur even before the singular *ātmanepada* ending *ta*.

If the inclusion here were only of the *parasmaipada* [roots], it would not apply to the *ātmanepada* ones, because they possess an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Furthermore, this option applies to the agent (*kartṛ*); however, in the case of the passive and impersonal (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), the *ciṇ* suffix necessarily occurs by the rule "ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ," either because that rule is subsequent or because the term "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) is understood to carry over here.
After a verbal root ending in a vowel, when the agent is also the object (karmakartṛ), [the suffix *ya* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.1.62)

*acaḥ karmakarttari* (Pāṇini 3.1.62). Regarding *karmakarttari*: the meaning is "in that case where [the object], having been an object, becomes the agent. This is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*), because by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*, the affix *ciṇ* would necessarily apply. In the example *akāri kaṭo devadattena* ("The mat was made by Devadatta"), when it is a pure object (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), *ciṇ* necessarily occurs by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

[Objection: But surely, the term *kartari* (in the locative) will carry over here [from the previous rule]. [Response: If that were so, it would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, one might argue that by means of a syntactic split (*vākyabheda*), the agent is qualified by the word *karmaṇi*—that is, "when the agent is the object"? This cannot be accepted. When *karmaṇi* is stated, there would be the exclusion of the agent altogether. Even if the particle *ca* ("and") were employed, it would result in a mere conjunction of two locative bases—as in "it occurs when the object is present and it occurs when the agent is present"—but there is no evidence for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *duh*. 3.1.63.

And [the suffix] *duh* [is included]. This is an optional rule (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*), because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* in the rule "there is neither *yak* nor *ciṇ* after *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*" (*na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau*). In that context, the mention of *duh* is for the purpose of prohibiting *yak*, while the mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of *snū* and the others. [The form] *adugdha*: the elision of *ksa* occurs by the rules "after *ksa*, when a vowel follows" (*ksasyāci*) and "the elision of *ksa* is optional after *duh* and *diha*" (*lugvā duhadiha*).
Not after the root *rudh*. 3.1.64.

Not [the root] *rudh*, as in "to obstruct. However, there is no inclusion of the root *rudh* in the sense of "desire" (from *anu-rudh kāme*), because, since its action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), there can be no such thing as a "reflexive object" (*karmakartṛ*).
The suffix *kta* is used after the root *tap* in the sense of repentance. 3.1.65.

Regarding the rule *tapo'nutāpe ca*: "In the case of the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*)," this refers to where the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) has been prescribed by the rule *tapastapaḥ karmakasyaiva*. In that context, [the suffix *liṭ*] occurs also in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Because of the word *api* ("also"), it also occurs where the status of being like the object is extended by the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā*. For example: *atapta tapastāpasaḥ* ("The ascetic performed penance"). The author of the *Vṛtti* himself will explain the meaning of this in the section on *tapastapaḥ karmakasyaiva*. An example is: *anvavātapta pāpena* ("He was tormented by sin").

"By sin" (pāpena) means that he is subsequently tormented or struck by whatever sinful action was previously committed. The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with respect to "sin," while the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). However, when the object is not intended to be expressed, the *lakāra* is used in the sense of the causative (*bhāve*) regarding the root *tap* meaning "to grieve," and the third case is used for the cause (*hetu*) with respect to "sin. When the agent of the act of being struck is intended to be expressed, then, by the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "like the object [is treated] when there is an object" (*karmavat karmaṇā*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed; even then, the third case remains used for the cause.
The suffix *ciṇ* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of the passive (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). 3.1.66.

Regarding the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*: the mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of clarity, because [the term] continues from the rule *ciṇ te padaḥ*, just like the word *te*. As for the mention of the option (*anyatarasyām*) in rules such as *dīpajanabudhipūritāyipyāyibhyo 'nyatarasyām*, that is not the case; for that [option] has already ceased its application in the very rule prescribing the prohibition, namely *na rudhaḥ*. Otherwise, the formulation of the prohibition would be purposeless. Nor is there any suspicion of the continuation of the prohibition itself, for a prohibition must be preceded by a prior possibility of occurrence (*prāpti*). And there is no possibility of the occurrence of *ciṇ* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) by any other rule.
The suffix *yak* is applied after a verbal root when a *sārvadhātuka* affix follows.

In all verbal roots (*dhātu*), the suffix *yak* [is applied] before the *sārvadhātuka* [terminations]. Here, in the case of the benedictive (*liṅ*) and the perfect (*liṭ*), even without a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), and provided that the personal endings (*tiṅ*) alone are present across all roots, all three—namely the state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*)—are understood: *bhaviṣīṣṭa tvayā* (it shall be by you), *kṛṣīṣṭa ghaṭaḥ* (the jar should be made), *bhūyāt* (may it be), *kriyāt* (may it do), *babhūve* (it was), *cakre ghaṭaḥ* (the jar was made), *babhūva* (it was), and *cakāra* (he did). In the case of *ad*, *juhoty-ādi*, and other such roots, the agent is understood. Sometimes, even in the absence of personal endings, these three are understood merely through the proximity of the *ciṇ* suffix, as in "He caused [him] to eat" (*aśāyi*) and "He caused [him] to go" (*akāri*). Thus, even when the *tiṅ* suffixes are absent, all three are indeed perceived.
In expressions such as *adhogavibharati*, the cognition of an agent occurs even when there is only the verbal root;
likewise, in expressions such as *vyatise*, the cognition of an agent occurs even in the absence of a verbal root.

This being the case, the determination of the meaning of a word occurs through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding the various objects [of action]. However, in instances where deviation is observed, it is appropriate to assume that such "power" (mahiman) belongs to that specific word with respect to that specific object; one should not, upon seeing a deviation in one instance, lose confidence in all cases. Furthermore, since such positive and negative concomitances pertain only to the verbal suffixes (tiṅ), it is those suffixes alone whose expressed meanings are the action (bhāva), the object (karman), and the agent (kartṛ).

The author of the Sūtras also says: "The *l*-suffixes [are used] in the sense of the object (*karman*) and, after intransitives (*akarmaka*), in the sense of the state (*bhāva*). Since the substitutes for *l* are the *tiṅ*-suffixes, he—considering that those very suffixes possess those meanings—states: "when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressing the state or the object follows. And in the subsequent sūtra, he states: "when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix expressing the agent (*kartṛ*) follows," as in *śayyate*. [And further: "the substitution of *ayaṅ* occurs before a *kṅit* suffix."

Now, when there are two agents or many, how is it that one says *āsyate bhavadbhyām* (you two sit) or *āsyate bhavadbhiḥ* (you all sit)? Why do the dual and plural endings not occur? Because in the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*), there is no differentiation. For the abstract state is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Even when there is a difference among the agents, the meaning of the verbal root does not necessarily differ, since even when many [agents] produce a single instance of action, it remains one and the same.
"Look, these are cooking"—such is even a difference of action;
observe how, within a single manifestation of action, one says "the rice grains are being cooked."
If there were no identity of the word across a difference in time, [the form] would not have been established nor is it being established;
however, in cases such as *pākau* and *pākāḥ*, there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) due to the identity of the word.
And therefore:
"Every action, regardless of its distinctions, is expressed by the verb;
for it is impossible to conceive a division of distinctions based on what is heard. Thus [it is said].

Thus, since the distinction pertaining to the nature of the action (*bhāva*) is understood through the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), there is an absence of the dual and plural numbers. However, where the distinction pertains to the nature [of the action] itself, the dual and plural do indeed occur, as in: *uṣṭrāsikā āsyante* ("camel-sittings are being performed") and *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("dead-man's-rests are being performed").

For the various ways camels sit are inherently distinct; and when they are killed, they lie down in many different manners—on their backs, face down, with their tails scattered and their garments disheveled. Because of this similarity, even though the verbal root expresses a single action, the plurality [of the verb] arises from the appearance of internal distinctions within the nature of that action. Even without the use of the word "iva" (as if), the sense of comparison is understood; thus the meaning is this: Devadatta and others perform actions of lying down in as many various ways as those exhibited by dead animals.

Some, however, desire the *l*-suffix here in the sense of the object (*karman*), because the state (*bhāva*) characterized by "the sitting of camels" (*uṣṭrāsikā*) or "the lying down of those struck" (*hataśāyikā*) possesses the status of an object according to the rule "time, non-existence, and the distance to be traversed [are objects]. For example: "one sleeps for the duration of milking a cow" (*godohaḥ supyate*).

The letter *ka* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. In the case of *mṛjyate*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*. Regarding the rule for the introduction of *yak*: [an objection is raised]—"But surely *yak* is already established by the extension (*atideśa*) in the rule 'that which has an action equal to that of the object [is treated like the object]' (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*); what is the use of this supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*)? To this he replies: "Because of conflict (*vipratiṣedhāt*). When this rule "like the object" is an extension of the grammatical system (*śāstra*), then by each respective rule within that system, the operations pertaining to the object take place.

In that regard, the scope for the rule *karmaṇi yag bhavati* (the *yaka* affix occurs when there is an object) is, for example, a pure object: *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"); the scope for the rule *kartari śap* (the *śap* affix occurs when there is an agent) is, for example, a pure agent: *bhavati*, *pacati* ("he exists", "he cooks"). When both [rules] would apply simultaneously in the case of a reflexive object (*karmakartṛ*), the meaning is that by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), only *śap* should occur. Should one then provide a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*)? No, it need not be provided. The prohibition of *yaka* in the rule *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* ("there is no *yaka* or *ciṇ* after *duh*, *snu*, or *nam*") makes known that *yaka* does indeed occur in the case of a reflexive object. However, if the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) is intended, then by that very same rule, *yaka* itself becomes the subsequent element.
The affix *śap* occurs after a verbal root when it is used in the active voice (*kartṛ*).

Regarding the rule *kartari śap*: the letter *pa* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it is also for the purpose of prohibiting [the designation] *ṅit*, and for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] by *śap-śyanornityam*. Regarding the statement "the letter *śa* is for the sake of the *sārvadhātuka* [designation]": here the word *sārvadhātuka* refers to the technical name (*sañjñā*) itself, not to that which possesses the name (*sañjñin*); the meaning is that it is for the purpose of establishing the *sārvadhātuka* designation. The mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is utilized in the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā*.

But here, although there are general rules stating that "śap occurs" and "śyan occurs" before a sārvadhātuka affix, since the rule for *yaK* is an exception (*apavāda*) specifically for the meanings of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), the suffixes such as *śap* will occur only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
The affix *śyan* is applied after verbal roots beginning with *div*.

Regarding the rule *divādibhyaḥ śyan*: the root *mṛg* "to search" is listed among the *cur*-class (the tenth class) ending in short *a* as an *ātmanepada* verb; in that case, the form should be *mṛgayate*. However, because it is also listed among the *div*-class (the fourth class), *mṛgyati* is also correct. Alternatively, the word *mṛga* should be understood as belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* group.
Or [the suffix *niṣṭhā*] follows the roots *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, *bhramu*, *kramu*, *klamu*, *tras*, *truṭ*, and *laṣ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.70)

The roots *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, *bhram*, *kram*, *klam*, *tras*, *truṭ*, and *laṣ* [take *śyan* optionally]. This is an optional rule (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*). *Bhram* has the meaning of "unsteadiness" (*anavasthāna*), while *kram* and *tras* belong to the *divādi* class; *truṭ* belongs to the *tudādi* class; the others belong to the *bhūvādi* class.
