In the form *bhrāmyati*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani*. However, this does not apply to the *bhūvādi* root because it is not among the eight beginning with *śam*. For *kram*, the lengthening occurs by the rule *kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*. As for *klam*, the rule *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāṃ śiti* applies. Regarding *tras*, its inclusion in the *divādi* class is questionable as to its purpose; however, its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group is for the sake of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) prescribed for that class.
After the root √yas, when not preceded by a preposition (upasarga), [the suffix kyap is applied]. 3.1.71.

Regarding "from *yas* when not preceded by a prefix": the inclusion of this root in the *divādi* class is for the sake of its occurrence with prefixes. As for the question "why [specify] 'not preceded by a prefix'?", the intention is that the rule "and from *yas*" will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the suffix *kyap* occurs] only after the prefix *sam*, and not after any other. Thus, in forms such as *āyasyati* and *prayasyati*, one might think that the exclusion would apply only to those roots ending in consonants that belong to the same class.
And [the suffix] *saṃyac* [is applied after the root *i*]. 3.1.72.

And regarding *saṃyasaḥ*: here, let it simply be *samaḥ*, and *yasaḥ* will follow by anuvṛtti; however, *saṃyasaḥ* was stated in order to prevent the suspicion that the root *ṣama ṣṭam veklavye* might be intended. If that is so, then let it be *samo yasaḥ* and *anupasargācca*.
The suffix *śnu* is applied after roots beginning with *svap*.
The suffix *śnu* is applied after roots beginning with *svṛ*. Regarding the form *sinoti*: because the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind") is listed in the *kryādi* class, the form *sināti* also occurs.
The word *śruvaḥ* [is replaced by] *śrṛ*. 3.1.74.
The word *akṣa* [is optionally substituted for *akṣi*] in the neuter gender. 3.1.75.
The root *takṣ* is used in the sense of making thin. (Pāṇini 3.1.76)

The root *takṣ* [is used] in the sense of "making thin. This is because roots have multiple meanings; it is precisely for this reason that the multiplicity of meanings is understood from the inclusion of qualifiers. However, the assignment of meanings to roots in the list (*gaṇa*) is merely for the sake of illustration. As in the example *santakṣati vāgbhiḥ*, the meaning is "he reviles" or "he censures."
The suffix *śa* is applied after verbal roots beginning with *tud*.

The suffix *śa* is applied after roots beginning with *tud*. In the case of *tudati*, once the form *tud-ti* is established, the suffix *śa*—being obligatory (*nitya*)—supersedes even the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise apply due to its higher priority.
The suffix *śnam* is applied after roots beginning with *rudh*.

Regarding the rule *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam*: "The suffix *śnam* occurs. Although it has been stated that within the definition of a suffix (*pratyaya-saṃjñā*), one must exclude the base (*prakṛti*), the prefix (*upapada*), the governing condition (*upādhi*), and augments (*āgama*), nevertheless, because *śnam* is being prescribed as the primary element and possesses meaning—just like *śa* and other suffixes—it follows that *śnam* receives the designation of a suffix. Consequently, because the letter *ś* is the initial of a suffix, it receives the designation of an *it*. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*.

Even though both [rules] are possible due to the difference in their scope (*deśabheda*), the present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) because it is introduced before that [general rule] has been reached and because they share the same purpose. For the *vikaraṇas* serve as auxiliaries for the expression of the meaning of both the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes and the verbal root. As for the letter *ś*, it is for the sake of distinguishing [it from *śit*], according to the rule "there is elision of *n* after a *śit*. Why, then, is it not for the purpose of preventing the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "half-verb-affix" (*ārdhadhātuka*)? For if that designation were present, then in *anakti* and *bhanakti*, there would be elision of the final vowel by the rule "*ato lopaḥ*"; and in *ruṇaddhi*, there would be *guṇa* substitution.

In the case of *hinasti* and *tṛṇeḍhi*, the augment *iṭ* would [otherwise] apply; furthermore, the rule "there is no *iṭ* before a *kṛt* suffix ending in *vaś*" would not apply because [the prefix] is not a *kṛt* suffix. All of this is merely laborious effort; [the augment] will not occur because the preceding portion is not part of the *aṅga* (base). How is there *aṅga*-hood? Because of the rule "that after which a suffix is prescribed. What is the meaning? When a suffix is being prescribed, that which is indicated by the fifth case—whether it be a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a nominal stem (*prakṛtipada*)—is the *aṅga* when that suffix follows.

That which was specified [in the rule] as "from the roots beginning with *rudh*" (*rudhādibhyaḥ*) is not the element from which the suffix is prescribed; and that element from which the suffix is prescribed—the preceding portion—is not specified by the ablative case when that suffix is being enjoined. Therefore, the letter *ś* in the word *śnaḥ* serves solely for the purpose of specification.

If it were stated simply as *nānnalopaḥ* ("there is no elision of the *nām* [suffix]"), then even in the case of *yajñānām* and *yatnānām*—derived from the rules *yajayācayatavicchapraccharakṣo naṅ* and *naṅ*—the elision would still apply here. Even if the lengthening by the rule *nāmi* were performed, the designation *nād* would not exist [because the *nām* suffix has been elided], and thus [the elision] would not occur; however, because it is subsequent, the elision itself would indeed prevail. As for the lengthening by the rules *ato dīrgho yañi* and *supi ca*, that does not apply here. Why? Because of the principle: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific configuration (*sannipāta*) is not a cause for the destruction of that very configuration."

In that case, would it not also fail to apply here in *vṛkṣāya*? It will apply because of the specific mention in the rule *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*. But then why does it not apply here in *yatnānām*? Because of the indication that the long vowel occurs when there is a reference to the general category. Even so, since the substitute is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the application of the preceding rule, this remains the word *na*, and thus the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would certainly still occur. Therefore, the letter *ś* must be added for the sake of specification. Now, even if the letter *ś* is added, why does it not occur here in *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*? [The answer is: "Between that which is indicated by a general rule and that which is stated as a specific form, the specific one is to be taken."
The suffix *u* is applied after the verbal roots √tan, etc., and √kṛ.

"From *tan* and the rest, *u* [is the suffix]. This refers to *tan-ī-ti* and so forth—namely, *tanu* (to expand), *ṣaṇu* (to give), and *kṣaṇu* (to injure). "Other operations belonging to the *tan*-class" means that the restriction is with respect to the operations prescribed for the *tan*-class. He shows what is excluded: by the rule *tanādibhyas tathāsor vibhāṣā*, the optional elision (*lug-vibhāṣā*) of *sic* does not occur. Now, one might object: let there be the option of elision; in the absence of that elision, the elision [of the *i*] will occur by the rule *hrasvād aṅgāt*, and there is no sublation by the option, because that which is obligatory is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to an option.

Nor can there be an annulment of the permanent [rule] by means of an option—on the grounds that the reading of the root *tan* and others in the Dhātupāṭha possesses its own force, according to the maxim "the authority of a statement [prevails]," which would otherwise result in the sublation of non-established status—because the reading of *tan* and others has already fulfilled its purpose in the rules prescribing verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*); whereas the option itself finds its scope of application in forms such as *atataḥ* and *atathā*.

On the contrary, if the mention of *kṛñ* were actually made, then because the inclusion of *kṛñ* among the *tan*-class roots would serve no other purpose, the option—by the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*)—would subvert the obligatory rule. Indeed, this mention of *kṛñ* in the rule for the inclusion [of roots] would only be intended so that its recitation among the *tan*-class roots might not be understood as having already achieved its purpose; therefore, we consider the very rejection of the mention of *kṛñ* to be the more logical course.
After the roots *dhinv* and *kṛṇv*, the suffix *a* is also applied [to form the present stem].

Regarding the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*: because of the status of the elision as *sthānivadbhāva*, *guṇa* substitution does not occur. The intention is that for the sake of brevity in the grammatical process (*prakriyālāghava*), only the elision (*lopa*) of the roots *dhinvi* and *kṛṇvi* was not explicitly stated; for if there were an elision [of the penultimate vowel], *guṇa* would have resulted. Nor can one argue that the prohibition "there is no [substitution] when there is elision of a root-vowel before an *ārddhadhātuka*" applies here, because the elision is conditioned by the suffix (*pratyaya-sanniyoga-śiṣṭa*) and thus does not have an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix as its cause.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of [the roots] *dhi* and *kṛ*, which are followed by the augment *num*? It is so that *atva* (the substitution of *a*) may occur when *num* has been applied. If it were stated simply as "of *dhi* and *kṛ*," then once *atva* had been applied, *num* would necessarily follow immediately after that very [root-final consonant]; for *atva* is internal (*antaraṅga*), being prescribed in conjunction with the suffix, whereas the augment *num* is external (*bahiraṅga*), being prescribed for the base (*aṅga*) once the suffix has already arisen. But surely *num* could belong to the base even in the state of the suffix *l* (before the personal endings); for *ti* and the other suffixes are more internal than *num*. In that case, it would occur only before *ti* and the others; but this is not so.

Because it is sublated by the permanent *ātmanepada* [suffix]. But the augment *num* is non-permanent (*anitya*), since it applies to a different word-form. Is the augment *num* then *antaraṅga* (internal)? In its rule, there is the mention of "root" (*dhātu*). For that [mention] is for the purpose that *num* should occur at the very time the technical designation "root" (*dhātusaṃjñā*) is applied; for otherwise, no other [base] beginning with an *udātta* vowel would be possible. How is it impossible? Because it was just stated: "The marking of *tāsi* as having an indicatory *i* (*idit*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the elision of the nasal."

But surely, even in this view, the *num* augment will occur precisely in the original instruction (*upadeśa*), because of the rule stating: "The statement that [the base] is as if it were in its original instruction (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) regarding the prescription of *num* is for the sake of establishing the suffix"? If that is so, then this mention [of the base] is simply for the purpose of indicating the *num* which is already obtained by virtue of being *antaranga* (internal).
The suffix *śnā* is applied after [roots] beginning with *kṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.81)
After the roots *stambh*, *tumbh*, *kambh*, *skumbh*, and *skuñ*, there is also the suffix *śnu*.

[The suffix] *śnu* is also applied after the roots *stambhu*, *tumbhu*, *skambhu*, *skumbhu*, and *skuñ*. Regarding the statement "because it is promised that they are marked with *u*": for it is promised (*pratijñāyate*) that the vowel *u* in these roots is nasalized and bears the technical designation *it*; the purpose of this is that, by the rule "after a root marked with *u*, the augment *iṭ* is optional" (Pāṇini 7.2.56), there is an option regarding the augment *iṭ* when the suffix *ktvā* follows. If these [roots] were restricted solely to the domain of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*), that would not be possible. Therefore, because they are promised as being marked with *u*, it is understood that they serve all purposes; the meaning is that all suffixes are their purpose. Or rather, it means they are supplementary to all suffixes.
After a verbal root ending in a consonant (*hal*), the suffix *śnā* (which becomes *śānac*) is substituted for *śa* when followed by the middle voice marker *jha*.

*Halaḥ śraḥ śānajjhau*: "After a consonant, *śrā* [is substituted] for *hi* when *jha* follows. For example: *puṣāṇ*, *muṣāṇa*. This is the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, second person singular (*sip*); its *hi* is replaced by *śnā* according to the rule *kryādibhyaḥ śnā*, and that *śnā* is replaced by *śānac*. The letter *ca* [in *śānac*] is for the sake of the accent (*svara*). Here, because the *paribhāṣā* regarding immediate contiguity (*sannipāta-paribhāṣā*) is not universally valid, the elision of *hi* by the rule *ato heḥ* does not apply.

But surely, since the *śnā* suffix is the subject under discussion, its substitute will be *śānac* itself; therefore, there is no need for the mention of the original element (*sthānin*) as "śna. To this, he says: "The original element is *śra*, etc. This is for the purpose that there may be the correct understanding—that is, the realization—of what the substitute is. He asks: if that [specification] were absent, what would happen? He replies: "[There would be] another suffix."

"Let there be another condition [for the application of the suffix]; since the word 'from *krī* etc. (*kryādibhyaḥ*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), it will apply only to those [roots] ending in a consonant (*halanta*), so there is no fault. To this he says: "It has all objects as its scope" (*sarvaviṣayam*). The meaning is that it applies even to objects other than *krī* etc. He considers that the governing rule for *krī* etc. is difficult to ascertain. Furthermore, the purpose of making the augment *śit* in *śānac* is to be reflected upon (*cintya*), because the desired result is already established by the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Here, the root *ñimidā* (meaning "moistening") belongs to the *divādi* class; by transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śnā* occurs in the Vedic language, and *śānac* is substituted for it, resulting in *midāna*.

Some maintain that the vowel *guṇa* prescribed for the scope of the prohibition "miderguṇaḥ" does not actually take place, because by the subsequent addition of the marker *ś*, the rule "sārvadhātukamapit" is applied once again. We, however, say no; just as the suffix *śnā* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), so too will the vowel *ik* occur in the scope of *guṇa*.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *śāyac* is also applied [after a verbal root ending in a vowel]. 3.1.84.

In the Veda, the suffix *śāyac* is also applied [after roots ending in long *ā*]. For example, in *gṛbhāya*: there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā-*, and the substitution of *bha* for *ha* by the rule *hṛgrahorbhaśchandasī*. In *badhāna*: from the root *bandh* (to bind), there is the elision of the nasal by the rule *aniditām*.
There is a frequent transposition [of suffixes]. 3.1.85.

"Interchange occurs frequently. Regarding the term *yathāyatham*: the meaning is "in their respective domains. *Vyatyaya* (interchange) is derived from the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *vyati* in the sense of "state" (*bhāve*), with the suffix *ac*. It means "mutual penetration of domains. By the words "in some cases," etc., he demonstrates the manner of this interchange. "It does not die": here, even the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is used interchangeably. "Let him lead": in the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *nī*, there are both *śap* and *sip* suffixes. "May we overcome": [this is the form].

The suffix *liṅ* occurs after the root *tṛ* in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth; thus, the commentary states, "when [the form] *tarema* is expected. Otherwise, one would have to say, "when *tīryāsmahi* is expected. In that case, there would be three affixes—*śap*, *sip*, and *ut*—and the *guṇa* substitution for the root. [In the case of *liṅ*: *taruṣas*; then *yāsuṭ* is added; by the rules "the *s* of *liṅ* is elided when not final," "always [elided] after a *ṅit* [suffix]," and "for *a*, *iy* is substituted," followed by the elision of *y*, and finally by "the *guṇa* of *ādu*," we obtain *taruṣema*.

The inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) is redundant; for if the word *api* (also) were carried over from the preceding rule, then in the Vedic language (*chandas*) there would be "irregularity" (*vyatyaya*), and by virtue of the word *api*, everything that is desired—including what is established by the general rule—would be accomplished. Therefore, he says: "the inclusion of *bahulam*. The meaning is that this is for the purpose of ensuring that there may be a deviation, characterized as irregularity, regarding every rule, whether it be one currently under discussion or one not currently under discussion.

Since the term *bahulam* (variously) is used for this purpose, he demonstrates with a verse what is thereby established: *suptiṅupagraha*, etc. Therein, the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of case-endings (*sup*) is seen in the example *dhuri dakṣiṇāyāḥ*, where one would have expected *dakṣiṇasyām*. Regarding verbal endings (*tiṅ*), it is seen in *caṣālaṃ ye aśvayūpāya takṣati*, where one would have expected *takṣanti*. The primary *upagraha* (voice/mode) is that specific feature of the means of action (*kriyāsādhana*) implied by the substitutes of *l* (the verbal suffixes), such as whether the sense is for one’s own sake or for another’s sake, or whether the voice is active or middle, and so forth. As it has been said: "In some cases, a distinction in the meaning is understood from the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)."

"Others also consider that [the suffix] *l* (the verbal root) is the *upagraha* (the indicator) because of it. This means "because of the *ātmanepada* suffix. Similarly, in the phrase "also because of the *l*-substitute from elsewhere," the word *upagraha* here refers to the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings, as they serve as the indicators for those specific forms. Examples: 1. *sa brahmacāriṇamicchate* ("He desires the student"). This is used when one expects *icchati*. 2. *ūrmiryuvyati* ("The wave struggles"). This is used when one expects *yudhyati*. 3. As for the gender: *madhostṛptā ivāsate* ("They sit as if satiated with honey"). This is used when one expects *madhunaḥ*.

Even in common usage, some employ the word *madhu* in the masculine gender—as in "the trees of the gods bear honey (*madhūn*)"—but that is to be considered doubtful. [In the phrase] "then he should separate with ten heroes" (*adhā sa vīrerddaśabhirviyūyāt*), where *viyūyāt* is used when *viyuyāt* was expected: the root *yu* means "to mix," preceded by *vi-*, in the optative (*liṅ*) for a benediction. [Regarding] "time" (*kāla*) as a suffix denoting time—as in "by one who will establish the fires tomorrow" (*śvo'gnīnādhāsyamānena*)—the *lṛṭ* occurs in the domain of the *luṭ*.

*Hal*—in *triṣṭubhaujaḥ śuṣitamugravīram*, the letter *pha* replaces *bha*; for *śubha* in the sense of "beauty," the *bha* is replaced by *pha*. In the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra* and the *Taittirīya*, however, the letter *bha* itself is read. *Ac*—in *upagāyanti mā patnayo garbhiṇayaḥ*, a long vowel is replaced by a short one. *Svaravyatyaya* (change of accent)—this will be explained under the rule *parādiśchandasi bahulam*. The word *kartṛ* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any grammatical factor (*kāraka*); the meaning is that there is a transposition of words expressing those factors.

"Vibhaktīnāṃ vyatyayaḥ" means "the transposition of case-endings. Regarding "yaṅām"—*yaṅ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) beginning with the letter *ya* of *yaṅ* and ending with the *ṅ* of "liṅyāśiṣyaṅ"; their transposition is demonstrated in the commentary itself by such examples as "āṇḍā śuṣmasya bhedatī. The author of the treatise, the venerable teacher Pāṇini, intends this transposition of *sup* and the other suffixes. That kind of transposition is established through *bāhulaka* (the principle of diversity). *Bāhulaka* is the state of being diverse (*bahula*); the suffix *ruñ* is applied here because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group.

Furthermore, the basis for the application of the word *bahula* is the inclusion of many meanings. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). The meaning is that since an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) of the aforementioned type is established by the very mention of *bahula*, therefore the mention of *bahula* has been made.
The affix *yaṅ* occurs after a verbal root to express a benediction (*āśis*) in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*).

"Liṅyāśiṣyaṅ" is an exception (apavāda) to "śap. [An objection is raised: Since the suffix *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) is treated as *ārdhadhātuka*, how can there be the application of *śap* here? To this he says: "In the Veda, both ways. Furthermore, the mention of *śap* is illustrative; it is an exception to the *śnu* of the root *śak*. He says "sthā-gā-mī" etc., because this *aṅ* is generally seen only after roots beginning with *sthā*. Regarding "upastheyam": [Note: The text provided consists of fragments of grammatical commentary on Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, specifically concerning the substitution of *aṅ* for *liṅ* in the benedictive mood.]

The optative (*liṅ*) suffix is applied after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa* in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). The substitution of *mip* for *mi* occurs; because the *yāsuṭ* augment is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, the rule "the final *s* of the *liṅ* is elided" (*liṅaḥ ssalopo'nantyasya*) applies. Then, with the *aṅ* suffix: by "elision of *ā* before *iṭ*" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*), "the *iy* substitute for *at*" (*ato yeyaḥ*), and "the *guṇa* substitute for *āṭ* and *gu*" (*ādguṇaḥ*), we obtain *upageyam*. Similarly, *gamem* [is derived from] *gam* with the *mas* suffix. *Vocema* [is derived from] *vac*: the *aṅ* suffix, the *um* substitute for *vac*, the *yāsuṭ* augment, the *iy* substitute, and the elision of *v* (*vali lopaḥ*). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *aṅ* is used after *dṛś*": for if *aṅ* were present, there would be *guṇa* substitution according to the rule "there is *guṇa* for *ṛt* and *dṛś* before *aṅ*" (*ṛddaśo'ṅi*).
That which has an action similar to that of the object is treated like the object [in respect to the agent]. (Pāṇini 3.1.87)

"Like an object, [an agent] possesses an action equal to that of an object. By "equal to an object" (*karmaṇā tulyam*), the suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule *tena tulyam* (Pāṇini 5.1.115), and not according to *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116); this is because the correlate (*pratiyogin*) in the term *tulyakriyaḥ* is indicated in the nominative case. Otherwise, one would have to state it as *tulyakriye* or *tulyakriyasya*.

For instance, in a sentence where the suffix *vat* occurs, there are two correlates (*pratiyogin*), with respect to both of which the genitive and locative cases are employed: "the conduct of this man is like that of a Brahmin" (*viprasyeva... śīlam*) and "the rampart at Pāṭaliputra is like that at Mathurā" (*mathurāyāmiva... prākāraḥ*). This is because both possess the status of being related and the status of being a locus. Consequently, even when the suffix *vat* has been produced, those same genitive and locative cases remain applicable to the correlates. However, when used in conjunction with words having the sense of "equal" (*tulyārtha*), the instrumental case occurs only from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), not from the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Because the word *tulya* (equal) resides in the object of comparison (*upameya*), as in "the face is equal to the moon," even when the suffix *-vat* is produced [from it], the nominative case remains for the object of comparison.

By the term "karma" (action), the technical grammatical object (*paribhāṣika-karman*) is intended, not the worldly action (*laukika-kriyā*). For if the worldly action were taken, what would be meant by the phrase "that which has an action equal to an action"? Since [an action] could be equal to just any action whatsoever, this would be incoherent. Therefore, the "karma" refers to the object as a means (*sādhana-karman*). In that case, because there is an absolute difference between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), a primary similarity of the action to the [actual] object is impossible; thus, by the word "karma," the action residing therein is indicated through metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*).

For indeed, by virtue of being located therein, a thing receives the name of that which it contains, as in the expression, "the platforms are shouting. This is what he says: "Action in the object is called 'action' [as a quality].

Thus, the redundancy of the qualifier does not now follow, because the action of the object is not identical to every [other] action. So it is said: "Because of its location, a thing receives the name of that which it contains, just as one says, 'The platforms are shouting. Therefore, he states this: 'Action in the object is called action. In this way, the uselessness of the qualifier does not now result, since the action of the object is not equal to every [other] action."

He says, "having an action equal to the action of the object," because the purpose is to convey that [the agent] has an action equal to the action of the *karman* (object), and not equal to the action of another factor (*sādhana*). Since the word *tulya* (equal) is inherently dependent, a *bahuvrīhi* compound—even one depending on the phrase "having an action residing in the object"—is not untenable, just as in the case of the *sūtra* itself. This word *tulya* exists as a term for "commonality," as in "these two have equal wealth," but its usage as a term for "similarity" is well-established.

In that regard, regarding the first [interpretation], if the term *karmaṇā* (by the object) is used in its primary sense, then it refers to the agent who shares a common action with the object; that is to say, among transitive verbs, it refers to the agent whose action is shared with the object. In that case, the phrase *tulyakriyaḥ* (having an equal action) would be redundant, as it would suffice to say simply *karmaṇā* (by the object). The meaning would be: "the agent who is presented together with the object. Alternatively, if it is used in a secondary sense, then the meaning is this: "one whose action is common [to another] by virtue of the action [itself] as the cause."

"By what action? [The answer is: "By an action residing in the object (*karmasthā kriyā*). Even so, this would undesirably apply even in a case such as "Devadatta cooks rice," because that action consisting of the softening (*viklitti*) which resides in the object is a common action (*sādhāraṇakriyā*). Therefore, in this view, there is the consequence of an unintended result. Furthermore, by employing the word *tulya* as a synonym for *sadṛśa*—which is more widely established—one explains: "The word *tulya* expresses similarity (*sādṛśya*), not commonality (*sādhāraṇya*). "Existing as the agent" (*kartṛbhūta*) means "established as the agent" (*kartari saṃpanna*).

There is an absence [of the application of the rule] here because it is imagined by someone. Alternatively—the word *kartṛ* refers to the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). The form *bhūtaḥ* is derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāptau*), according to the rule *ā dhṛṣādvā*, in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*); thus, the meaning is "one who has attained the state of being an agent. In that regard, in the example *pacatyodanam* ("he cooks rice"), there is an absence of the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) because there is no similarity between the operations of the agent and the object due to their absolute difference.

Even so, one might object that in the case of "the granary, while being split, splits the vessels," this [definition] would also apply there; for the very same action consisting of the dispersal of parts which is observed in the vessels is likewise observed in the granary as the agent. This is not a fault; for when it is said, "an action equal to the action residing in the object belongs to the agent," it is understood that the action which is conducive to agency—that action by the entry of which something becomes an agent—is precisely the action meant here.

But here, while the splitting into two is seen in the vessels, it is also seen by chance in the granary; yet it does not split [the granary] because of its entry into that [action], for even though the granary itself does not split, it certainly splits the vessels as it falls upon them. Likewise, in the cases of "they embrace one another," "they touch one another," and "they seize one another"—does the same [agency] apply here? For is it not the case that whatever action-entrance makes one an agent is seen to exist in the object as well? True, it is so seen.

That [action] is not conducive to the status of being an object (*karman*), for it does not become an object by virtue of being entered into by that [object]; rather, the status of being an object is possible even for one who is not embraced by itself, provided it is embraced by another. This is what is meant: that whose action conducive to the status of agent is similar to the action of an object conducive to its status as an object, that [agent] has an action similar to that of the object.

And thus, it is stated that when the very same action which exists in the state of an object (*karman*) also exists in the state of an agent (*kartṛ*), then that agent is "like the object" (*karmavat*). This too has been stated right here: "in that very action which, though having become the agent... For the meaning here is: "having reached the state of an agent in that very same action. And so, although the action is one, its similarity—based on a distinction—is to be established by relying on the difference between the states of agent and object.

Atideśa (extended application) is of many kinds, distinguished by the extension of form, identity with the cause, designation, scripture, and grammatical operation; however, among these, the first three are impossible here. Furthermore, extension by designation does not differ from the position of mere nomenclature (*saṃjñāpakṣa*), and thus it would be useless to mention it separately. Therefore, there are only two positions: extension of scripture (*śāstrātideśa*) and extension of grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*).

In that regard, regarding the extension of rules (*śāstrātideśa*), when rules such as "in the case of the impersonal (*bhāva*) and the passive (*karman*)" are extended, the respective grammatical operation proceeds by means of each such rule. Consequently, the scope of the rule "in the case of the impersonal and the passive" is the pure passive, as in *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"); and the scope of the rule "after the remaining [roots], the *parasmaipada* [is used] for the agent" is the pure agent, as in *pacati* ("he cooks") or *paṭhati* ("he reads"). If both [rules] were to apply simultaneously in the case of the reflexive-passive (*karmakartṛ*), would not the *parasmaipada* prevail due to its posteriority? This is not a fault.

From the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*, the term *kartṛ* (agent) is understood to carry over; therefore, the *parasmaipada* endings occur only when the agent is indeed the agent, and they will not occur in the case of a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). In this regard, what then is the scope for the rule *karmaṇi yag bhavati*? It applies to a pure object, as in *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is cooked"). What is the scope for the rule *kartari śap*? It applies to a pure agent, as in *pacati* ("he cooks") or *paṭhati* ("he reads"). If both [rules] were to apply simultaneously in the case of a reflexive agent, would not *śap* prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules? This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule *kartari śap*, the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) need not be made. Since the rule *sārvadhātuke śap* is a general provision, it will serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *yaṅ* affix prescribed for the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). This being established, the purpose of including the mention of the agent is this: that the affixes such as *śap* should apply only when the agent is indeed the agent, and they should not apply when [the agent] is designated as the object. True, this has been countered by your venerable self! However, this effort is in vain, because the desired result is already established by resorting to the transfer of operations (*kāryātideśa*).

For in that case, by this very [rule] the ātmanepada is established, and by this very [rule] the yaṅ is established; thus, due to their posteriority, the yaṅ and the ātmanepada are accomplished. Moreover, the primary operation (kārya) is what matters, because other extensions (atideśas) exist for its sake. Therefore, there is an extension of the operation involving the mention of the agent. As for the [rule] under discussion, "kartari śap," since it ends in the locative case, it cannot be connected with "tulyakriyaḥ," which ends in the nominative; regarding this, he says: "from the rule 'kartari śap'."

Regarding the passage beginning with "yagātmanepada... (the *ya*-class suffixes, the *ātmanepada* endings, etc.): the intention is that since it will be stated later that "the agent of a root ending in *l* [i.e., a verbal suffix] is treated like the object," only the *yag* suffixes and so forth are possible here. The three examples beginning with "midyate" (it is split) are, respectively, illustrations for the *ātmanepada* endings and the *yag* suffixes and others. But how can wood possess agency with respect to the act of splitting, given that it is Devadatta who splits it? For one who performs the raising and lowering of the axe and so forth is called the agent of the splitting.

Every causal factor (*kāraka*) possesses its own specific intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*), for it is impossible for that which performs no function to be a causal factor. This has already been established in the section on causal factors (*kārakaprakaraṇa*). In that context, independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to its own operation exists in every case. However, because [the independence] of a causal factor is eclipsed by the operation of the agent (*kartṛ*), its independence becomes subordinate; thus, it does not possess the status of an "agent," but merely receives designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth. This is all there is to it.

However, some transitive roots, even after expressing the operation of the object (*karmavyāpāra*), do not terminate there, but rather express the operation of the agent (*kartṛvyāpāra*) as being subordinate to that [object-operation]. For example, the root *bhid* expresses the act of splitting (*dvidhābhāvana*) as subordinate to the state of being split (*dvidhābhavana*). Indeed, this root does not denote merely the lifting up and the letting down [of the axe]; for if it did, it would apply even to a washerman, since he too lifts up and lets down a garment. And yet, he is not said to "split" [the cloth], because the state of being split does not occur [in his case].

By this, the roots *chid* (to cut) and *lū* (to reap) are explained. Likewise, the root *pac* (to cook) also denotes the act of moistening (*vikledana*), with the softening (*viklitti*) being subordinate. In that context, when the agent’s activity is not intended to be expressed—in order to convey the extreme ease of the object—then the object, having its "impulsion" (*preṣaṇa*) withdrawn, remains situated within its own action; as its status as an object ceases, it abides in its own status as an agent. The verbal root (*dhātu*) also then functions solely in reference to that [agent’s] activity.

But how can a verbal root that denotes both [agent and object] denote merely the operation of the object? What is the contradiction? Verbal roots have multiple meanings, and words that function for wholes also function for parts. Thus, in these cases where the roots denote merely the operation of the object, the fuel and so forth possess only the status of agent (*kartṛtva*), and there is not even a trace of the status of object (*karmatva*); moreover, these roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*) in this particular usage, as in "it softens" (*viklidyati*) or "it becomes two-fold" (*dvidhā bhavati*).

How then is an agent "having an action equal to that of the object" (*karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*) by virtue of the object? We do not say: "in this particular usage, it has an action equal to whatever is the object therein"; rather, we say: "it has an action equal to that which is the object in another usage. [Objection: But if this were so, would it not also apply here: *pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta cooks rice) and *rādhyaty odanaḥ svayam eva* (the rice cooks itself)? [Response: To this, he will state the solution: "because of the governing context of the verbal root" (*dhātvadhikārāt*).

Since the [application of the term] *kartṛ* (agent) and *karman* (object) is already established solely because they cannot possibly apply to anything other than a verbal root (*dhātu*), their recurrence [in the rule] is for the purpose of specifying singularity: "the agent of that very same verbal root which has [something as its] object is one who performs an action similar to it. Therefore, it will not apply when there is a difference in the verbal roots.

He said: "Let this be a superimposition (adhyāropa); what is the point? Is the entire meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) superimposed upon the object (karman)? Why should it be said here that 'Devadatta performs the cooking of the rice'? For in this way, an excellence of facility (saukaryātiśaya) is more effectively demonstrated, just as in the case of the instrument (karaṇa) and the locus (adhikaraṇa), as in: "The sword cuts well" or "The pot cooks well."

In those cases where the entire meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) can occur even with respect to the object—such as "one awakens by oneself," "one is liberated by oneself," "one kills by oneself," or "one strikes by oneself"—the *l*-suffix occurs in the pure passive sense (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), wherein there is agency in one form and objecthood in another form. Likewise, in the case of "the granary is split" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*), even where no conscious agent is perceived, there is either the agency of one among wind, heat, time, or rain, or it is a figurative attribution (*adhyāropa*).

In expressions such as "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) or "the field is reaped by itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*), there is merely a superimposition (*adhyāropa*); the meaning is that "the rice is cooked by its own self, and not by Devadatta," for who indeed could be conducive to the act of cooking [in that sense]? Therefore, since the *L*-suffix arises in the case of a pure (intransitive) object, this [objection] is irrelevant. If this is so, then in the expression "the granary is split by itself" (*bhidyate kusūlena*), the *L*-suffix would not occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), because [the verb] has an object; or else, one might explain it here as having an object, namely: "the self is split by the granary" (*bhidyate kusūlenātmeti*).

Even so, in the case of *kusūlena bhettavyam* ("the granary is to be broken by a lever") or *īṣadbhedaṃ kusūlena* ("the slight breaking by a lever"), would the kṛtya, kta, and khalartha suffixes not occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*)? Nor can it be maintained that they occur there even when the object (*karman*) is present, because the neuter gender is observed [in such forms]. Likewise, in *namate daṇḍaḥ svayameva* ("the staff bends by itself"), *kārayate kaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the mat causes itself to be made"), and *acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the mat caused itself to be made"), even though the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited, the *śap* and *caṅ* suffixes would not occur, because [the agent] is not the agent (*akartṛtvāt*).

Therefore, it is more correct to hold that suffixes such as *la* and others denote the agent and the abstract state (*bhāva*) when they follow verbal roots expressing merely the operation of the object (*karmavyāpāra*). Accordingly, in the case of "the rice is cooked" (*śṛtaṃ pākaḥ*), the word "rice" (*śṛtam*) occurs with respect to both the operation of the object and the operation of the agent, because both are denotable by the word "cooking" (*pāka*).

Thus, the thought that "I shall not compose a treatise," once it has been deliberated upon in this manner, must also be abandoned. For if the *sūtra* were not present, the scope of the prohibition—"there is no application of the *yak* or *ciṇ* affixes after the roots *duh*, *snū*, and *nam*"—would not have been demonstrated. Furthermore, although such usages as "the rice is cooked by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) are justified in the passive sense (*karman*), if the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) were produced in the active sense (*kartṛ*), then usages such as "he cooks the rice" (*pacatyodana*) would also result [as indistinguishable from the passive]. Therefore, the *sūtra* must indeed be commenced.

In these examples, the word *svayam* (self) is employed for the purpose of excluding another agent; however, it is not an integral part of the rule itself. When this [word *svayam*] is employed, since it functions in the sense of *ātmanā* (by oneself), this very action would become transitive (*sakarmaka*)—[the rule is stated] so that it may also apply when the action resides in its own substratum. If the suffix *vat* were absent, the agent would be understood as having the technical designation "object" (*karman*); consequently, because this action would be transitive, the suffix *lo* (the affix *ghañ*) would not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), according to the rule "and after intransitives, [the suffix *ghañ* occurs] in the sense of the abstract state."

But when that [designation] exists, because the designation as "intransitive" (akarmaka)—which is obtained by its own nature—is not set aside, the *la*-suffix is established for intransitive verbs; the meaning is that the *la* which is prescribed for intransitive verbs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) becomes established. How is it established, given that this extended application (*atideśa*) is permanent, and since this is permanent, even the prescription of *la* there would be merely a function of the object (*karmakārya*), and thus the extended application would necessarily occur? By means of the suffix *-vat*, that which belongs to its own base (*svāśraya*) is obtained provided it does not conflict with the extended application, but not if it does conflict.

For this is not the meaning of the alternative—that [the suffix] is sometimes like that of an object and sometimes not. Now, since it will be stated later that "the *l*-suffixes [denote] the agent," the application of the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) must be admitted to occur even prior to the operation of this present sūtra. And that [rule], being operative, applies to the impersonal (*bhāva*) and to the agent (*kartṛ*) because the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*). When it applies to the agent, then this extended application (*atideśa*) takes effect; thus, the prescription of the *l*-suffix for the impersonal is rendered possible.

If this is so, let there be no *vat* affix; rather, let the agent denoted by the *l*-suffixes (*lakāra*) simply receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "object" (*karman*). However, [if that were the case], the application of *yaṅ* and *ātmanepada* endings would be impossible, because the *śab* suffixes and others would apply first, and the *parasmaipada* endings would also follow as a consequence. Furthermore, the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) would not be superseded by the designation "object," since designations coexist elsewhere outside the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for a single designation. True; the solution to this has already been stated: the employment of the *vat* affix here is for the sake of complete similarity. By means of that, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur after words such as "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) in the examples.

Otherwise, [the accusative case] would follow because it is the effect of an action (*karmakārya*); however, it will not occur because [the agent] has already been expressed (*abhihitatvāt*). This might serve as a solution if there were an extension of the *śāstra* (rule), but in the case of an extension of the *kārya* (operation), the operations pertaining to the object are obtained by this very [extension], and since there is no governing rule here concerning what is "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*), the accusative would indeed occur. However, because of the use of the suffix *-vat*, for the sake of total similarity, just as [the accusative] does not occur when the object is expressed, so too it does not occur when the agent is expressed; thus, there is an absence of the accusative.

If, however, because the verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *lakāra* suffix occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāve*), then [the rule for the accusative] would apply; to this he says: "In the case of the benedictive (*āśīḥ*) in the potential (*liṅ*), the suffix *aṅ* [is added]," and so forth. With the intention that the word *la* (referring to the *lakāra*) which has been carried over [from a previous rule] is here transformed into the genitive, he says: "The agent of that which ends in *la*" (*lāntasya kartā*). This means: the agent expressed by the *lakāra*. [He states: "The accusative does not occur after *kusūla*. The point is that in the examples just cited, such as "the granary is split" (*bhidyate kusūlena*), the absence of the accusative is due precisely to the inclusion of the word *vat*, which signifies complete similarity [of the action].

Thus, this is the intended meaning of the author of the *Vṛtti*: that this suffix (*vati*) is for the purpose of expressing complete similarity. Furthermore, it is not necessarily only the second [type of suffix]; in this context, even the *kṛtya*, *akta*, and *khalartha* suffixes are obtained by extension (*atideśa*) when applied to the agent—as in: "the granary breaks itself," "the granary has broken itself," and "the granary is easily broken by itself."

And these [suffixes] are indeed intended to express the state of being (*bhāva*): *kusūlena bhettavyam* (the granary is to be split) or *kusūlasya bhettavyam* (of the granary it is to be split), according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*; likewise, *bhinnaṃ kusūlena* (split by the granary) or *īṣadbhedaṃ kusūlena* (a slight splitting by the granary). In this Vārttika, the mention of the suffix *kta* was recited because it is read together with others elsewhere, just as in the statement: "The letter *ka* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For indeed, since these roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-*.

And likewise, regarding the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied] after the root *si* when the object of the action is the agent," the example *sino grāsaḥ svayam eva* ("the morsel has been eaten by itself") will be cited as an instance of the *kta* suffix used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Therefore, this fault applies only to the *kṛtya* and *khalartha* suffixes; consequently, because the agent of the *lānta* (suffixes ending in *la*) is resorted to there, there is no extension [of the rule].

The question "Why [is it] 'by means of the object' (karmaṇā)? is asked with the following thought: the action expressed by the verbal root resides only in the agent or the object; since similarity must have difference as its locus, an agent who possesses an action equal to an action residing in the agent is impossible. Therefore, thinking that only an action residing in the object will be intended, the question is posed. "By means of the instrument or the locus" (karaṇādhikaraṇābhyām) means "by means of the action residing therein. An example is: "He cuts with an axe" (sādhu asinā chinatti).

Furthermore, in this context, does the verbal root (dhātu) denote merely the operation of the instrument or the locus, or rather is there a superimposition of the entire meaning of the root upon them? It cannot be the first alternative, because the root does not apply to that much alone; even in the case of "he cuts with a sword" (*asinā chinatti*), the operation of the instrument is not denoted by the root at all—there is only the fact that, because it is an instrument, there exists an intermediate operation. As for the second alternative, there is no such application precisely because the actions are distinct.

Therefore, one should understand that the counter-example was provided by accepting that the verbal root (*dhātu*) functions even when there is merely the operation of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). In some cases, however, the status of being like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) is desired for an agent whose action is equal to that of the instrument; as it is said: "An agent whose action is equal to that of the instrument is frequently desired [to be treated as an object]; [examples are] *parivārayati kaṇṭakaiḥ vṛkṣam* (he surrounds the tree with thorns) and *parivārayante kaṇṭakāḥ vṛkṣam* (the thorns surround the tree)—here the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs. The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, considering that the middle voice is justified by the rule *ṇicaśca* ("and after a causative suffix"), did not mention this [specific case].
"Within the same root" (*samāne dhātāv*) is stated because of the governing topic of "roots" (*dhātu*); the meaning is "of one and the same root. This has already been explained previously.

Regarding the phrase "of those [roots] whose state resides in the object" (*karmasthabhāvakānām*), etc.: although the words *kriyā* (action) and *bhāva* (state) have an identical meaning—such that even action is included under the rule "when there is a characterization by means of a state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*), and likewise in the rules "of an action [used as] a characteristic or cause" (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*) and "one whose action is equal to that of the object" (*karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*)—nevertheless, because they are presented as distinct in this treatise, a difference in meaning should be observed: *bhāva* is the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consisting of non-motion (*aparispanda*), whereas *kriyā* consists of motion (*parispanda*).

Where, then, is that [action] located in the object (*karmastha*), and where is it located in the agent (*kartṛstha*)? Some say: "In those cases where the agent's operation is expressed as subordinate to the object's operation, it is located in the object; in those cases where only the agent's operation is expressed, it is located in the agent. We say: no. The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is located in that—whether in the agent or in the object—in which the primary action (*pradhānakriyā*) inheres. That action for the sake of which the operations of the factors of action (*kāraka*) are undertaken is the primary action; for example, the softening (*viklitti*) in the case of *pac* (to cook), and the reaching of another location (*deśāntaraprāpti*) in the case of *gam* (to go).

And having established this, even though the root *ruh* (to ascend) denotes both the state of being subordinate (*nyagbhāva*) and the act of becoming subordinate (*nyagbhavana*), it is one whose action resides in the agent—as in "the elephant-drivers mount the elephant. This is because the reaching of the upper region, which is the intended goal, inheres in the agent. In that case, here [in the discussion of *ruha*], the action of the agent is compared to the action residing in the object (*karmastha*). Since this meaning is impossible in cases where the action resides in the agent, the Vṛttikāra has demonstrated this very point as established by logic. There, he shows by means of a verse merely an example of an action residing in the agent and an action residing in the agent itself: "The state of the root *pac* resides in the object."

In the case of "the jar is cooked" (*pacyate ghaṭaḥ*), this state (*bhāva*) belongs to the jar itself in that location; and it resides in the object (*karmastha*)—in the case of "the rice is being cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*), because the accomplishment of the cooking of that which is to be cooked occurs through the very movement [of the rice], the action of the root *pac* resides in the object. And the action of the root *bhid* resides in the object: in the case of "the granary is split" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*), the action of splitting, which consists of the dispersal of parts, occurs when there is movement; thus, the action of the root *bhid* resides in the object.

"The state of sitting (*āsibhāva*) resides in the agent. In the expression *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), according to the rule "time, state, and distance to be traversed are designated as objects (*karman*) for intransitive verbs," this verbal root *ās* (to sit) has "month" as its object. In that context, the meaning perceived in the root *ās* is "state" (*bhāva*), because it is non-mobile in nature, and that [state] resides in the agent—this is the meaning. And "the action (*kriyā*) of the root *gam* resides in the agent": the meaning of *gam* is action, and that action resides in the agent—this is the meaning.

Therefore, constructions such as *māsaḥ svayam evāsyate* ("the month itself is sat through") or *grāmaḥ svayam eva gamyate* ("the village itself is gone to") do not occur. Now, how is there the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) in this case: *tasmād udumbaraḥ salohitaṃ pacyate phalam* ("therefore, from that, the fruit of the *udumbara* tree ripens blood-red")? On this point they say: in this context, the root *pac* takes two objects, because the ripening of the fruit is impossible without the ripening of the tree. In that situation, according to the rule "in the case of *duh* etc., [the non-primary object is called the object]," the tree is the unexpressed object (*akathitaṃ karma*), and thus the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is applied to it; however, time is the agent (*kartṛ*).

However, this must indeed be stated: "In the case of *sṛji* and *yuj*, however, [the suffix] *śyan* [is applied]"—meaning that for these two roots, *sṛji* in the sense of "emission" and *yuj* in the sense of "joining," when they are transitive, their agent behaves like the object (*karmavadbhāva*). In that regard, for the root *sṛj*, the behavior of the agent like the object occurs when the agent is motivated by faith (*śraddhā*), and in the domain of the *ya*-affix (*yag*), the suffix *śyan* is applied; but in the domain of the *ciṇ*-affix, it is desired that the *ciṇ* itself be applied. Thus: *sṛjyate mālāṃ devadattaḥ*, meaning "Devadatta produces the garland with faith."

When the suffix *śyan* is present, the root (*prakṛti*) retains its original acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*); however, when the suffix *yak* is present, because the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the acute accent would belong to *yak* alone—as in *asaji mālām*, meaning "he fashioned a garland with faith. Regarding *yujir*: the religious student (*brahmacārī*) is joined (*yujyate*) through yoga.
The word *tapas* [is used] only for one who performs the act of austerity. 3.1.88.

The root *tap* [is used] only when its object is the act of heating (*tapaḥ-karma*). He will state later that "this is for the sake of the injunction due to the distinction of the action. Anticipating the objection, "How then is the particle *eva* (only) to be construed?", he explains by means of a split in the sentence: "The agent of *tap* becomes like the object (*karmavat*), and that [agent] only when the object is heating (*tapaḥ-karmaka*). He shows what is excluded by the particle *eva*: "not when the object is something other [than heating]."

This was stated with the thought that the connection of the particle *eva* must be understood as applying specifically to what has been heard (*śruta*), yet there is no further purpose for it. "Because of the difference in action" (*kriyābheda*) means because of absolute difference. Even in the view of restriction (*niyamapakṣa*), a difference among actions is required, since similarity is based upon difference. He demonstrates this very difference in action by saying "fasting and so forth. The meaning is "they cause suffering"; the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the reading in the *curādi* class: "to cause pleasure or pain in an action" (*sukhaduḥkha tatkriyāyām*).

By this, it is shown that when *tāpasa* is the object (*karman*), the meaning of the root *tap* is "to cause suffering. By [the statement] "the meaning is 'to acquire'," it is also shown that when *tāpasa* is the agent (*kartṛ*), the meaning of *tap* is "to acquire. In some places, however, the reading is *ārjayati*; in that case, there is the usage of the prefix *āṅ*. Now, even so, the action characterized by the heating of the body is the same in both states; for is there not any acquisition other than the heating of the body that constitutes the activity (*vyāpāra*) of the ascetic? That is incorrect; [for...]

Even though bodily suffering exists in reality, it is not the meaning of the word [in this context]; otherwise, how could *tapas* (asceticism) have the status of an object (*karman*)? Therefore, *arjana* means "accomplishment" or "the acquisition of what was not previously obtained," whereas *duḥkha* (suffering) is simply bodily torment; thus, the difference between the two actions is quite clear. He concludes that which was stated regarding the purpose of the rule: "The status of being an object, which was not previously established by the preceding rule, is here prescribed. In the example *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*, the suffix *sic* is used because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* by the rule *tapo 'nutāpe ca*; then, by the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is elision [of the *s*].
The affixes *ya* and *ciṇ* do not occur after the roots *duh*, *snih*, and *mā*.

The roots *duh*, *ṣṇu*, *tudu*, *ham*, and *ṇu* are not included [in this rule]. *Duha* means "to fill," *ṣṇu* means "to flow," *tudu* means "to afflict," *ham* means "to laugh," and *ṇu* means "to praise. These are not taken because the actions of *nauti* ("he praises") and *hasati* ("he laughs") do not have their locus of action within the object (*akarmasthakriya*). Furthermore, if their inclusion were intended, the author would have simply said "na dunuhasnamām" to avoid ambiguity; for the conventional meaning of a whole word is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts. [The phrase] "those prescribed as having the status of the object" (*karmavadbhāvāpadiṣṭau*) refers to these.

By this [rule], it is shown that according to the principle "a rule applies to what immediately precedes," this is a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* which would otherwise have applied by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā*; it is not, however, a prohibition of those *yak* and *ciṇ* which apply to the simple object (*śuddhe karmaṇi*) and the abstract state (*bhāve*) by the rules *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* and *sārvadhātuke yak*. In the form *dugdha*: when *yak* is prohibited, the *śap* suffix is applied; because the root belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of that suffix. Then, by the rules *dāder dhātor ghaḥ* and *jhaṣas tathordho 'dhaḥ*, the substitution of *gh* occurs, followed by the change to the voiced unaspirated sound (*jaśtva*).

The root *duh* (to milk) takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*). In this context, according to the rule "for roots such as *duh*, [the agenthood applies] to the non-primary object," there is a desire to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of that object upon which the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is placed; however, the primary object remains simply an object. For example: "The earth, milked by his virtues, yielded treasures for him who was like Vasu. Regarding the form *adugdha*: the suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), followed by the suffix *ksa*; its elision occurs by the rule "the elision of *ksa* is optional after *duh*," etc. (*lugvā duha*).

But has it not just been stated: "By this [rule], *yak* is prohibited for the root *duh*, whereas *ciṇ* was already made optional by the previous rule 'duheśca'? Therefore, this should not be cited here as an example"? [The answer is: In *prasnutaḥ*, since *yak* is prohibited, the *śap* suffix is elided as before; in *prāsnoṣṭa*, since *ciṇ* is prohibited, *sic* is used. In *namate*, the root *nam* here contains an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).

Just as in the case of "Devadatta bends the staff" (*nayamati daṇḍaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the staff bends of its own accord" (*namayate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*), where the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) of the causative form, so too should it be understood here.

Regarding the rule beginning with *ṇi-śranthi-granthi* and so forth: the symbol *ṇi* is a general designation for both the root *ṇiṅ* (to release) and the causative suffix *ṇic*. The roots *śranth* and *granth*, meaning "to string together," belong to the *curādi* class under the sub-class *ādhṛṣīya*; they are included here in their state when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent. Likewise, these two roots are also listed in the *kryādi* class, and they are included there as well. The root *brūñ* means "in distinct speech. Those verbal roots which are specified as being intransitive (*akarmaka*) in the rules prescribing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) become transitive (*sakarmaka*) when they incorporate an implied causative sense; these are what are referred to here as "intransitives [used] in the middle voice."

In the *Vṛtti*, examples of these [grammatical operations] are recited in some places, but not in others. Regarding the causative suffix (*ṇic*): "The mat causes itself to be made" (*kāryate kaṭaḥ svayameva*), "The mat caused itself to be made" (*acīkarata kaṭaḥ svayameva*). When the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes are prohibited, the *śap* and *caṅ* suffixes occur. Regarding the denominative suffix *ṇiṅ*: "He raises his tail" (*pucchamudasyati*) becomes "The cow raises its tail" (*utpucchayate gauḥ*). When that [verb] has the meaning of the causative (*ṇy-artha*) internalized, then it is "He makes the cow raise its tail" (*utpucchayate gām*). Again, when there is a desire to express agency through an excess of facility (*saukaryātiśaya*), it is "The cow causes itself to raise its tail" (*utpucchayate gauḥ svayameva*), and "The cow caused itself to raise its tail" (*udapupucchata gauḥ svayameva*).

Regarding the roots *śranth* and *granth*, which belong to the *ādhṛṣīya* class: *devadattaḥ granthati grantham* (Devadatta ties the book), *mekhalāṃ śranthati* (he ties the girdle); *granthaḥ svayameva granthate* (the book ties itself), *granthaḥ svayamevāgranthiṣṭa* (the book tied itself); *mekhalā svayameva śranthate* (the girdle ties itself), *mekhalā svayamevāśranthiṣṭa* (the girdle tied itself). But regarding the same roots belonging to the *kraiyādika* class: *granthaḥ svayameva grathnīte* (the book ties itself), *mekhalā svayameva śrathnīte* (the girdle ties itself). Regarding the root *brū*: *devadattaḥ bravīti kathām* (Devadatta tells the story), *kathā svayameva brūte* (the story tells itself).

The verbal root *vi* (in *vikurute*) has its action residing in the object (*karmastha*), because its fruit is the manifestation of sound. Regarding the *ātmanepada* forms of intransitive roots—specifically, "after *vi*, when it has sound as its object" (*veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ*) and "also when it is intransitive" (*akarmakācca*)—we have: *vikurvate saindhavāḥ*, meaning "the Sindh horses prance. When another person causes them to prance (*valgayati*), then they possess the status of an object (*karman*). However, when there is a desire to express their agency due to an excellence of facility (*saukaryātiśaya*), as in *vikurvate saindhavāḥ svayameva* ("the Sindh horses prance by themselves") or *vyakṛṣata saindhavāḥ svayameva* ("the Sindh horses pulled themselves up"), the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur.

However, in some commentaries, it is read as: "He strikes the boy" (*āhanti māṇavakam*) and "The boy strikes himself" (*āhate māṇavakaḥ svayameva*). This is incorrect; for in the case of "He strikes the boy," because the root is transitive (*sakarmaka*), there can be no middle voice (*ātmanepada*). Others, however, say: the expression "middle-voice and intransitive" (*ātmanepadākarmaka*) is an elliptical designation for the verbal root itself. Thus, this root *han*—in accordance with the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ*—would be the cause for the middle voice whenever it is intransitive due to the non-intention of expressing an object. Therefore, even though its initial state is transitive, this example is not contradictory.

It should be stated that there is a prohibition of the *yak* and *ciṇ* suffixes for roots meaning "adornment" (*bhūṣā*) and "scattering" (*kirādi*). The word "action" (*karman*) here refers to the activity itself; since the result of adornment, namely beauty (*śobhā*), is perceived as residing in the object of the action, adornment is considered "situated in the object" (*karmastha*). Thus: *alaṃkurute kanyā svayameva*, *alaṃkariṣyate kanyā svayameva*, *alamakṛta kanyā svayameva*; *avakirate hastī svayameva*, *avākīrṣṭa hastī svayameva*, *avakariṣyate hastī svayameva*—in these cases, the *yak*, *ciṇ*, and the substitution of *ciṇvat* do not occur.

"The calf desires to be liberated by itself" (*san-mumukṣate vatsaḥ svayameva*), "the calf desired to be liberated by itself" (*amumukṣiṣṭa vatsaḥ svayameva*); "the mat desires to be made by itself" (*cikīrṣate kaṭaḥ svayameva*), "the mat desired to be made by itself" (*acikīrṣiṣṭa kaṭaḥ svayameva*). Here, the state of having an action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) is relative to the meaning of the root, whereas the desire resides in the agent (*kartṛsthā*). And the primacy belongs to the meaning of the root, because the desire exists for the sake of that [meaning].
According to the Eastern grammarians, the affix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings are applied after the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*.

For the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, when used in the sense of "going," the affix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings are applied. These are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the *yaṅ* affix and the *ātmanepada* endings respectively. Here, *śyan* is an exception to *yak*, and the *parasmaipada* is an exception to the *ātmanepada*. Furthermore, there is a distinction between *śyan* and *yak* regarding the nasal augment (*num*) and the accent: in the case of *kuṣyantī jaṅghā* ("the shank that scrapes"), because the affix is *śyan*, the nasal augment *num* is applied invariably by the rule *śapśyanornityam*; and due to the *nit*-designation of the affix, the word becomes udātta on its first syllable.

However, if there were an optional insertion of *num* by the rule "ācchīnadyornum," and if the *la*-suffixes were unaccented as *sārvadhātuka*, then the accent would belong solely to the *yak*. Thus, in the case of *rajyati*, the elision of the nasal (*na*) occurs by the rule "aniditām. In the alternative view, the *yak* suffix and the *ātmanepada* endings occur in forms such as *kuṣyate* and *rajyate*.

Regarding the rule *liṅ-liṭoḥ*: here the *liṅ* in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) is understood, as it has been stated—namely, that the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is made in the rule prescribing *śyan* for roots ending in *u* and *ṛ* other than *raj*, because if it were not mentioned, there would be a prohibition regarding the *liṅ* and *liṭ*. Regarding "and in the domain of *sy*-suffixes" etc.: by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *sic* and others is intended. Examples: *cukuṣe*, *rarañce*. These are *liṭ* (perfect), middle voice (*ātmanepada*); for these, the substitute *eś* is applied. Regarding *koṣiṣīṣṭa*: [the suffix] *sa* is added to the *liṅ* by the rule *liṅaḥ sīyuṭ*; *suṭ* is added to the *ti* and *tha* by the rule *suṭ tithoḥ*; then the *guṇa* substitution occurs because the penultimate vowel is light. Regarding *raṅkṣīṣṭa*.

There is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ekācaḥ"; there is the substitution of *ku* for *cu* (becoming *g*) by the rule "coḥ kuḥ"; and for that *g*, there is the substitution of *k* by *cartva*. Thus: *akoṣi*, *arañci*. [The affix] *ciṇ*.
[The suffix *ya* is applied] after a verbal root [ending in a vowel]. (Pāṇini 3.1.91)

Regarding the rule *dhātoḥ*: in considering whether this governing authority (*adhikāra*) extends up to the substitution of *l* [for *luṅ*, etc. or until the end of the chapter, the second alternative is adopted—that it extends until the end of the third chapter. This is because of the addition of the marker *ś* to *eś*; for if *dhātoḥ* were the governing authority, then by the rules "after that, the following" (*tasmādityuttarasya*) and "of the first letter of the subsequent element" (*ādeḥ parasya*), the substitution of *e* for the *t* would occur, and then the substitution of *i* for the vowel *a* (by *ṭeḥ*) and the replacement by *ay* (by *ayādeśaḥ*) would result; the marker *ś* is added so that the form *ayeśabda* might not be heard.

Prior to the mention of the *la* designation, however, since the rule "operations [apply] to the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*) is in force within the governing context of verbal roots (*dhātva-dhikāra*), there is no purpose for the letter *e* in the enunciation of the *ekāra*. Therefore, even without the letter *ś*, it will be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) by overriding the application of the *al* (the final letter) through subsequent connection (*anusaṃhāra*). What is the use of the letter *ś*? [This would hold] if this governing context were to extend until the end of the chapter. But if it belongs to the first rule (*yoga*), then they would not occur when there is intervention (*vyavāya*) by *tiṅ* affixes; that is, once those *syat*-class suffixes which are prescribed in the state of *l* (the *la-sthāna*) in the first rule—the *tiptasjhi* sūtra—have been applied, [the desired forms would fail] because of the intervention caused by them.

The *tiP* suffixes and others would not occur [in forms like *kariṣyati*, *hariṣyati*, and *kartā*]; however, there is no fault regarding the *śaP* and other affixes, because they depend on a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and thus have no occasion to apply until the substitution of the *l*-suffixes has taken place; and the *tiP* suffixes and others find their scope (*sāvakāśa*) in those cases. [Objection: The substitution of *et* (for the final vowel) would not occur, since the rule "the *ṭi* of the *ti* suffixes when there is an intervention" (*ṭeṣṭitāṃ vyavāye*) applies—[as in] *pacate*, *yajate*. Where, then, would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *āste*, *śete*, *dhatte*, *rundhe*, *bebhidāte*, and so forth, where there are no *vikaraṇa* affixes.

[Response: Regarding the *śit* status of *eś*: the *eś* in the rule "for *ta* and *jha* of the *liṭ*, *eś*" (*liṭastajhayoreś*) must be marked with the *śit* designation. This has already been explained at the very beginning [of the work].

Furthermore, that which [the rule] prescribes for the *loṭ* suffix would not apply when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa*—such as "the *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*" (*loṭo laṅvat*), "eruḥ" (*eruḥ*), and "for *si*, substitute *hi*, and it is also *apit*" (*serhyapicca*)—in forms such as *pacatu*, *pacatam*, *stautu*, *juhotu*, *bhinattu*, and *āstām*. It would apply only in cases such as these.

Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the *laṅ* and *liṅ* [suffixes], that too would not apply—such as "the *ṅit* [suffixes] are always [marked with K]," "from *it*," "for *tas*, *thas*, *tha*, and *mip*, there are *tām*, *tām*, *ta*, and *am*," "the *sīyuṭ* of the *liṅ*," and "the *yāsuṭ* in the *parasmaipada* is udātta and *ṅit*"—and likewise, in cases such as "thāsaḥ se" [becoming] "pacase" and so on, it would not occur? This is not a fault; for we shall understand this as a qualification of what is prescribed: namely, that [the rule applies to] the *loṭ* prescribed after a verbal root.

If this is so, then even in the rule "vido laṭo vā" (Pāṇini 3.4.83), when it is understood that for the root *vid* and for the *laṭ* affixes such as *tiP* and others which have been replaced [by substitutes], *ṇal* and other suffixes are applied, would *ṇal* and the rest not apply even when there is an intervention by a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) in cases such as *vindati*, *vindataḥ*, and *vindanti*—the latter being the sense of "to find"? No; for the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu*) is never intended as a qualifier of what is immediately prescribed (*vihita*), and thus it must be so in all instances.

Alternatively, we shall qualify here that which is prescribed by means of a verbal root (*dhātu*): [the rule] "after *vid*" refers to immediate succession—meaning "of the *laṭ* prescribed after a root, immediately following *vid*. Likewise, in the rule "after *sic*, after reduplicated forms (*abhyasta*), and after *vid*," that which is prescribed by means of a root is qualified, and with the reduplicated form, there is immediate succession—meaning "of the *jhi* ending beginning with *ṅ*, immediately following a reduplicated form prescribed after a root. Consequently, [the augment *iṭ*] will not occur in such cases as *ajakṣiṣyan* and *ajāgariṣyan*.

Regarding the rule *ātaḥ*: how is this to be understood? If it means "of that which is prescribed after a root-final *ā*," then [the substitution] would apply here as well in *alunan* and *apunan*. If, on the other hand, it means "of that which is prescribed after a root ending in *ā*," then it would apply in *apiban*. Let it be: "of that which is prescribed after a root-final *ā*. In the case of *alunan*, when the form *lunā-jhi* is established, the elision (*lopa*) is effected by the rule *śnābhyastayorātaḥ*; since the *ā* is no longer present, the [substitution] will not occur. But does the elision not apply here at all? It is barred by the substitution of *ī* according to the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*.

Even so, will it not occur because of the *ākāra*? You do not reach this point here: is it sublated by the state of *anti*? Here the state of *anti* does not occur, because it is sublated by the state of *jus*. Thus, in this way: elision (*lopa*) by the state of *ī*, the state of *ī* by the state of *anti*, the state of *anti* by the state of *jus*, the state of *jus* by elision, and elision by the state of *ī*—does this result in a circularity (*cakraka*) and a lack of finality? This is not a fault.

Because of the rule stating that [the substitution] is as if taught [in the original form] (*upadeśivad-vacana*) with respect to roots beginning with *ā* and others, the substitution of *anti* for *jha* occurs at the very time of the original instruction (*upadeśa-kāla*). Once this has been done, the elision (*lopa*) takes place; thus, the grammatical status is established by means of the elision. Furthermore, in the rule *itaś ca*, the mention of *sic* is understood to carry over—meaning "after a root ending in long *ā* from which *sic* has been elided"—and therefore there is no possibility of any undesirable consequence. Thus, it is settled that the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of the verbal root (*dhātu*) extends until the end of the chapter.

He will state [in Pāṇini 3.1.96] that "the suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* [are added]. Furthermore, what would happen if the word *dhātoḥ* ("from a verbal root") were not carried over into the rule for *tavya* and the others? [The concern is that] *tavya* and the other suffixes might then be applied even to *ṅyāp*-prātipadikas (nominal stems ending in feminine suffixes or long vowels). [The answer is: *tavya* and the others are prescribed as being dependent on a *sādhana* (grammatical factor of action), and a *sādhana* belongs to an action (*kriyā*). Since there is no action in a nominal stem, there is an absence of a *sādhana*; and due to the absence of a *sādhana*, *tavya* and the other suffixes will not occur after a *ṅyāp*-prātipadika.

How then do the accusative and other case endings occur when [the noun] is prescribed in relation to objects and so forth? It is not that the accusative and other endings apply to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in its capacity as a factor of action (*sādhana*); rather, they apply when that very same [meaning] assumes the status of an object (*karman*) and so forth in relation to an action expressed by another word.

But since suffixes such as *tavya* and others have their purpose fulfilled by denoting the grammatical agent (*sādhana*) in relation to the action expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), they will not arise from nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in feminine suffixes (*ṅī*) or *āp*. If so, then this is the purpose: so that suffixes such as *tavya* do not occur after corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) like *satyāṇavaya* which denote an action; for these are not verbal roots (*dhātu*), since the technical designation "verbal root" depends upon being listed in the *bhūvādi* group. Furthermore, the governing rule for "verbal root" (*dhātvadhikāra*) is established so that the *laṅ* and other suffixes do not occur after [roots] accompanied by prefixes (*upasarga*).

Otherwise, in cases such as *prākarot*, *prāsthita*, and *adhyaiṣṭa*, since the combination of root and prefix (*dhātūpasargasamudāya*) expresses a specific action, if a suffix were prescribed after that [combination], the designation of "stem" (*aṅga*) would apply to it, resulting in the undesirable occurrence of the augment *aṭ* and so forth. The opponent objects: "The mention of 'root' (*dhātu*) is redundant, because the term 'root' (*dhātu*) is already under discussion (*adhikāra*) in the rule prescribing *yaṅ*. The meaning is this: in the rule *dhātorekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22), which prescribes *yaṅ*, there is a mention of 'root'; because that [mention] is under discussion here [in Pāṇini 6.4.71], [the mention of 'root' in the latter is unnecessary].

He refutes [the objection] with the words: "It is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the *kṛt* and the *upapada*.
