He explains this very point with the words: "In this [sūtra]. The restriction "in this very [sūtra]" is to be understood. He demonstrates that by saying: "Let it not apply in the preceding [rules]. If this governing heading (*adhikāra*) did not exist, the meaning would be merely that "whatever is indicated by the locative case under the governing heading of *dhātu* (root) is an *upapada*"; consequently, it would also apply in the preceding rules—for instance, in the rule *cli luṅi*, where it would mean "when a form ending in *luṅ* is the *upapada*, *cli* [is applied]."

In this way, since the designation *kṛt* would also apply to that which is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) provided it is not a personal ending (*atiṅ*), it would follow in the preceding case as well. Consequently, in the word *kariṣyati*, if the suffix *syapratyaya* were designated as *kṛt*, then by the rule "that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix is a nominal stem" (*kṛdantaṃ prātipadikam*), it would become a nominal stem. Being a nominal stem, even though the number [of one] is already expressed by the personal ending (*tiṅ*), the production of the nominative singular suffix *su* would result due to the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) and because the singular is the default (*utsarga*). Therefore, the verbal root designation (*dhātvadhikāra*) is repeated so that these two [rules] may apply here, but not in the preceding section.

[Objection: "But surely those two technical designations (*saṃjñā*) will be established by way of their governing rule (*adhikāra*), and the designation 'affix' (*pratyaya*) therein will apply to them as well in the preceding [rules]. Anticipating this, he states another purpose: "and for the sake of the designation 'ārddhadhātuka'. [Question: But what is the utility of including the term 'second root' (*dvitīyadhātu*) in the definition of the *ārddhadhātuka* designation? [Answer: He says: "of that which is prescribed by the rule *dhātoḥ* [P. 3.1.91]. [Example: *lūbhiḥ*. Even though this possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it also possesses the status of a root (*dhātu*).

Because the previously established designation of "root" (dhātu-saṃjñā) is not revoked, and since this [suffix] is prescribed after a root alone, the designation "ārdhadhātuka" would indeed apply. However, if in the rule *śam-ādibhyo dhātoḥ* the svarita accent were declared for the second mention of the word "dhātu" for the purpose of establishing the ārdhadhātuka designation, then this governing rule (*adhikāra*) could also be omitted. Furthermore, the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) is already established by that governing rule; therefore, there will be no co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *ksa* and other such suffixes with *sic*.
In that context, a word standing in the locative case is called an *upapada*. (Pāṇini 3.1.92)

In that context, "an upapada standing in the seventh case" [is defined]. He explains the meaning of the phrase "standing in the seventh case" by saying: "indicated by the seventh case. This means uttered with the seventh (locative) case-ending, or expressed by a word ending in the seventh case. In this view, the word "seventh" (*saptamī*) in the sūtra refers to a word ending in the seventh case. The meaning is: the jar (*kumbha*) and so forth, which exist as the object (*karman*) and so on to be expressed within a word ending in the seventh case.

In the first view, however, the indication by means of the locative case found in "karmaṇi" and so forth is the very same as the indication by the locative case in the usage "kumbham" and so forth. Just as in the rule "tasyāpatyam" (the offspring of that), the word "tasya" (of that) is a general term intended to indicate specific instances, and thus the primacy belonging to that [general term] also applies to its specific instances; so it is here as well. In the case of "kumbhakāraḥ," because it contains an *upapada*, it forms a compound (*samāsa*), and it takes the accent of the original form of the final member ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara*).

"Regarding the mention of *sthagrahaṇa* and so forth: the meaning is that it is for the purpose of understanding that only that which is an indication by means of the seventh case (*saptamī*) in the sūtras—whether as its actual utterance or as being expressed by a word ending in the seventh case—is a constituent part of the technical name (*saṃjñā*). Now, one might object: "By virtue of association with the word 'seventh case' (*saptamī*), what is indicated by the seventh case in the sūtras and so on will be understood; there is no need for this specific mention. To this he replies: "For otherwise... Since a secondary sense is not accepted when the primary sense is possible, [if this were not stated], the name would belong to the seventh case itself.

Because the rule for the formation of technical names (*saṃjñā*) prohibits the application of the principle of "extension to that which ends with [the element mentioned]" (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is explicitly mentioned; and since a name cannot be prescribed for a named object that does not exist, the meaning is that this [name] would apply only where the locative case is actually heard. Regarding *stamberama*: the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *stambakarṇayoramijapoḥ*, and the elision of the case-ending is prevented by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*. Regarding *yatra vā*: this means where there is the hearing of the locative case in a sūtra—that is, the actual occurrence of the word "locative" (*saptamī*).

The term "not having a verbal designation" (*aśabdasaṃjñā*) is a concessive statement (*abhyupagamyavāda*) because it serves to prohibit the grasping of the word's own form; the intended meaning here is that what is desired is established in every respect. As for the phrase "but because of the mention of *sthā*": the meaning is that when *sthā* is mentioned, since the designation is prescribed for what is indicated by the locative case in the sūtra, it is established everywhere.

But surely, the purpose of creating a technical term (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of brevity; why then is a cumbersome term being created? To this he says: "The creation of a cumbersome term. A term that follows its own meaning—such as "a word uttered near [another] is an *upapada*"—is an etymological term (*anvarthasaṃjñā*). [It is used] for the sake of the operation of the paribhāṣā concerning semantic competency (*samartha*). Here, when the triad consisting of the word's own meaning, substance, and gender [is present],...

If [the meaning] were that of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then since an object (*karman*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), or other such *upapada* cannot occur without a case-ending (*vibhakti*), a case-ending would necessarily have to be produced; thus, the operation of the Paribhāṣā would be established simply because it is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*). However, even in the view that the word consists of five elements (*pañcaka-pakṣa*), since the nominal stem itself expresses the object and so forth, it would not be a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*), and therefore the operation of the Paribhāṣā would not apply. Why, then, is it forced to apply by virtue of the name being etymological (*anvartha*)? This is not the case.

Even in the *pañcakapakṣa* (the view that a word consists of five elements), it is established that a suffix occurs only when there is "wordhood" (*padatva*) through the production of a case-ending. Now, one might object: "But according to the rule ‘The expression of compounding of prefixes, kārakas, and upapadas with *kṛd*-derived words takes place prior to the production of case-endings,’ how can the *upapada* possess a case-ending? Do you not remember this? For we have already stated that in the rule *upapadam atiṅ*, the term *sup* ending in the third case has ceased to apply, while the term *sub* ending in the first case continues to apply. Otherwise, how could the elision of *n* and other operations occur in forms such as *carmakāra*?

It might be so! Observe: "He makes a jar, he makes a mat. The term *dhātu* (verbal root) is understood [from the previous rule], and words such as *karman* (object) are relative terms; therefore, we shall understand it thus: "the object of whichever verbal root. Even so, would [the designation] apply here in the case of *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a large jar")? It does not so apply; for [the rule states] "the object of whichever verbal root," and in this case, the word *mahāntam* is not the object of the verbal root. Even so, would it apply here in the case of *mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*? It does not so apply.

It is said to be "the great potter" when the sentence is "he makes a great pot" (*mahān kumbho mahākumbhaḥ, mahākumbhaṃ karoti*); however, when the sentence is "he makes a large pot" (*mahāntaṃ kumbhaṃ karoti*), it is not so intended.

Furthermore, what would happen if this were the case? When the word *kumbha* is compounded with the word *kāra*, because its meaning undergoes unification (*ekārthībhāva*), it could not be compounded with the word *mahat*. This is because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on the actual meaning; thus, even though [the word] is specified as being in the locative case, since it qualifies the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), and because the qualifiers of that [base] do not constitute words uttered immediately before [the compound], they do not receive the designation of "subordinate word" (*upapada*).

Now, regarding the mention here—what is the purpose of this inclusion? It is intended to indicate that the governing authority (*adhikāra*) of "roots" (*dhātu*) applies; thus, in this third [section], the governing authority of roots is maintained. This is not a necessary purpose, for even this is established by virtue of the governing authority itself. Then what is the purpose? It is so that that which stands in the locative case (*saptamī-stha*) may serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for the production of an affix (*pratyaya*). How so? The term "affix" (*pratyaya*) is understood to carry over: that which stands in the locative case receives the technical designation "governing word" (*upapada*), and an affix is produced only when such a governing word is present.

Now, if [the locative in] *karmaṇi* and so forth were a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*), then how could there be the contingency of a suffix occurring even in the absence of an upapada? No; the locative in *karmaṇi* and so forth is a Vedic (sautrī) locative dependent on meaning. For if it were so, the object (*karman*) would be the expressed meaning of the suffix *aṇ*—as in the rule "after the root *dhā*, [the suffix] *ṣṭran* occurs in the sense of the object"—and in that case, its status as an upapada would not be perceived. Therefore, just as nasality is postulated for the sake of a technical designation (*saṃjñā*), so too the locative is merely the indicator (*liṅga*) for the designation of an upapada, independent of any specific meaning. Thus it is not [a locative of existence].

The meaning would then be merely that "the root is [the cause] and the object (karman) is the subordinate element (upapada)"; in that case, the fact that the object serves as the condition for the production of the suffix would not be understood. Therefore, for that purpose, the mention of "therein" (*tatra*) is made. Now, is this passage—"in this section concerning verbal roots"—to be rejected? We do not say it is to be rejected; rather, it is supplemented by the following: "In this section concerning verbal roots, that which is indicated by the locative case receives the technical name 'subordinate element' (*upapada*), and when that exists, the suffix is produced."
That which is a *kṛt* suffix, but not a *tiṅ*, [is called a *pratyaya*]. 3.1.93.

*kṛd atiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.93) means "excluding *tiṅ*. That is to say, it is that which has been abandoned by the nature of *tiṅ*, or is devoid of the nature of *tiṅ*; in other words, it is something other than *tiṅ*.

The question "Why [is it said] *atiṅ*? arises with the following thought: even if this prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) were applied here, it would be capable of subverting only the designation *kṛt* belonging to the *tiṅ* itself, but not the *kṛt*-designation that accrues to the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) by virtue of its being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), because of the rule stating, "A prescription or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding. The answer is: the *kṛt*-designation is prohibited specifically for the *lakāra* which is to become a *tiṅ*; or else, by the very force of the prohibition, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) will not occur.

"One should accumulate" (cīyāt), "one should praise" (stūyāt). Now, this is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*): since [the author] teaches a separate prohibition for the *sārvadhātuka* [affixes] in the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ," that indicates that the prohibition [expressed by] "akṛt" does not apply to *tiṅ* [affixes]. If it were otherwise;

In cases such as *cinuyāt* and *sunuyāt*, even though these are *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, the long vowel will not occur simply because of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] that applies to *kṛt* suffixes; so what is the purpose of excluding *sārvadhātuka* suffixes separately? [Objection: But then, in cases like *pacati* and *paṭhati*, the augment *tuK*—by the rule "the augment *tuK* is added after a short vowel before a *pit* *kṛt* suffix"—should not occur. [Response: In the rule prescribing *tuK*, the term "root" (*dhātu*) from the previous rule "after the beginning of a root" (*dhātvādeḥ*) will be carried over (*anuvartate*). [Objection: Even so, it would still apply in cases such as *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*. [Response: It will not occur because of the intervention (*vyavadhāna*) by the *śap* suffix.

Is there no intervention once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been applied? [To this we reply: Because of the rule "A single substitute is treated as the original (sthānivat) for the application of a preceding operation," there is indeed intervention. However, the status of being *sthānivat* does not apply here; it is superseded by the "end-like" (*antavat*) treatment due to its higher priority. Therefore, in forms such as *cikīrṣati*, the prohibition "not after a finite verb" (*atiṅ*) must be formulated so that the suffix *tumun* does not occur.

Furthermore, since a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix would be designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by the rule "that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix is a nominal stem," the following undesirable consequences would follow: in *paceran*, the elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) would apply; in *papāca brāhmaṇī*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would apply; and the derivation of case endings (*svadyutpatti*) would occur in all such instances. Since this [undesirable result] is already established by the very prohibition "except for that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix" (*atiṅ*), the Vṛttikāra considered that there is no need to rely on the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in forms such as *cīyāt*.
Or, when not feminine, the rule of dissimilarity of form applies. (Pāṇini 3.1.94)

*vā'sarūpo'striyām*. The word division is *asarūpaḥ*; otherwise, since there would be no distinction regarding brevity (*lāghava*) and thus no possibility of doubt, he would have said *sarūpo'striyāṃ vā*. This statement is for the purpose that the application of certain *kṛt*-suffixes may occur even in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*). As it has been stated: "The optional rule (*vāvacana*) regarding the dissimilar (*asarūpa*) is for the sake of preventing the operation [of the general rule] in the domain of its sublater."

This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule); within this governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), it pertains as a supplement to those rules that enjoin exceptions (*apavāda*) which are dissimilar in form (*asarūpa*), excluding the governing context of feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*). It is formulated as a general rule because, if the statement were made in each individual instance, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). In that regard, the term "dissimilar" (*asarūpa*) is redundant, for if the option were applied to every *kṛt* suffix without qualification, everything would be dissimilar in relation to some other *kṛt* suffix.

This term *asarūpa* (dissimilar) is relative, because "dissimilarity" (*asarūpatva*) here is understood as having a different form (*bhinnarūpatva*) in relation to a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). For something becomes similar or dissimilar only in relation to something else; thus, when there is an expectation as to "in relation to what is it dissimilar?", that which was applicable to its own domain at the time of its own rule is understood as the counter-correlative present in the intellect. Furthermore, at the time of applying an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*)—which was striving to reach that very same domain—is already present in the intellect. Therefore, [the term *asarūpa*] is used with reference to that.

He states that here, by "dissimilar" (asarūpa), an exception (*apavāda*) of a different form is intended: "the exception-affix is dissimilar. This being the case, if this were an option regarding production—meaning that the exception-affix "may or may not occur"—then an option for it would indeed be obtained within its own domain, but the general rule (*utsarga*) would not apply.

In that case, this [subsequent cognition] does not have that as its object; for when the operations of the cognitions produced by the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exceptional rule (*apavāda*) have already reached their conclusion, only then does this [cognition]—situated in that very same locus—obstruct the application of the exceptional rule to its own domain. Since the cognition produced by the general rule has as its object a domain distinct from the one accepted by the exceptional rule, even if the exceptional rule does not apply, it is not possible for the cognition or the operation of the general rule to occur with respect to that [exceptional] domain, just as in the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

For example: from *dakṣasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of Dakṣa"), when the suffix *iñ* is optionally applied, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur; rather, there is simply the sentence itself. Why is that? Because by the rule "from among those [words] capable [of forming a compound], optionally from the first," the application of the alternative is blocked by a bystander [i.e., the presence of the specific suffix]; it is not, however, that the very attainment [of the general rule] is merely colored by optionality through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). It is the same here as well.

In the case where there is no exception (*apavāda*), the base form itself would be authorized to express the agent and so forth, just as in *agnicit* and similar forms where *kvip* and other suffixes are elided. Thus he says: "In that case, there is either origination or the contingency [of the suffix], just as with a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)."

Having observed this fault in the position that [the suffix] arises through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), he states that it is considered a sublater (*bādhaka*): "or it becomes a sublater. And it has been said: "But it is established that there is an option regarding what sublates that which is dissimilar in form" (*siddhaṃ tvasarūpabādhakasya vāvacanāt*). The meaning is that one must state that "or the sublater is dissimilar in form."

Is it not the case that it is stated here and there—"where no other verb is heard, [the verb] *asti* or *bhavati* is supplied"—and therefore, when it is said "or an asarūpa [suffix]," it is only logical to supply *bhavati*, and not that the suffix *vā* is a sublater? It is replied: the purpose of this option regarding the origin [of the suffix] is the employment of the bare stem (*prakṛti*) alone; however, a bare stem is incapable of expressing its own meaning alone, so how much less will it express the agent and so forth! For [meaningful expression occurs] only in the combination of stem and suffix.

When [words] are employed, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that "this is the meaning of the base" (*prakṛti*) and "this is the meaning of the suffix" (*pratyaya*); however, a base from which a suffix has not arisen does not convey any meaning whatsoever. For its employment is also difficult to find, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) that "a suffix must follow something else. In the case of *taddhita* [suffixes], even under the view that they do not arise [in certain instances], there exists another suffix—the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*)—which functions as a general rule (*utsarga*) and thereby excludes [the application of other suffixes]. But here, it is not so; therefore, by implication, even though it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), it is conceived as having the power to set aside [other rules].

But surely, a rule is sublated by another rule, not an effect by an effect; for it is only by the destruction of the cause that the destruction of the effect can be brought about. Indeed, as long as the lamp is not extinguished, its light is not extinguished either. So why is it called an "exceptional cognition" (*apavāda-pratyaya*)? Should it not rather be called an "exceptional rule" (*apavāda-śāstra*)? It is replied: For every exceptional rule, its own internal dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) is an invariable [criterion] by means of which [the sublation] occurs through the medium of the cognition.

It has been stated that "it must be resorted to" means that it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the [general] suffix-rule. The meaning is that the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) is the prescriber of such a suffix.
Alternatively, because the suffix possesses the capacity for optionality (*vikalpa*) regarding its sublation (*bādhakatva*), the rule itself will also be sublated in one alternative case.

Alternatively, only the general subject matter has been shown in the commentary (*vṛtti*); however, the Sūtra should be explained in such a way that this meaning becomes logically consistent. In this regard, the following is the explanation: it has been stated that this is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule). Just like the *ekaparibhāṣā*, this rule also presents itself as a governing word (*pada*). That is to say, within this governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu*), wherever a dissimilar (*asarūpa*) apavāda suffix is prescribed, the option (*vā*) presents itself; however, it does not present itself within the governing context of feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*).

What is accomplished [by this]? Just as in the case of the rule "There is an option for the roots *dā* and *dhā*" (*dadāti-dadhātyor vibhāṣā*), the valid cognition itself becomes colored by an alternative; consequently, as in that same case, the application of the general rule (*utsarga*) is established. Now, if it were understood that "an irregular (asarūpa) suffix of a general rule may optionally apply even within the domain of an exception (*apavāda*)," what would be the fault? Indeed, there would be no fault at all;

for while an option (*vibhāṣā*) would apply when an exception is already subject to an option, it would be an "option of the unobtained" (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*) regarding the option of the general rule. However, it has been stated that the term "irregular" (*asarūpa*), depending on its correlative, refers specifically to the exception (*apavāda*).

Regarding the rule *astriyām*, three possible interpretations are conceivable: First, it may be a locative of the object (*abhidheyasaptamī*), meaning that when the feminine gender is to be expressed, the "non-identity of form" (*asarūpa*) does not apply. Second, it may be a prohibition of the "non-identity of form" prescribed specifically for the feminine, meaning that those suffixes which are ordained after the word "feminine" (*strī*) has been uttered are not [to be applied]. Third, the mention of "feminine" (*strī*) is intended as a marked accent (*svarita*); since the understanding of a governing context (*adhikāra*) occurs through a marked accent, this indicates that the prohibition applies within the governing context beginning with *striyāṃ kta-niṣṭhāyām*.

In that regard, in the first position, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* would not apply in the sense of "one who scatters," "that which scatters," or "a scatterer" (*vikṣepaka*, *vikṣepikā*, *vikṣeptṛ*). In the second position, however, in the case of *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvakruṣṭi*—formed by the rule "*ṇac* in the feminine when there is reciprocal action"—the suffix *ktin* would not occur, because both [suffixes, *ṇac* and *ktin*] are prescribed specifically for the feminine (*striyām*). Having observed these faults in the first two positions, he adopts the third position and says: "excluding a suffix prescribed under the heading of the feminine (*stryadhikāra*)."

Some say: although it should have been stated as "having excluded the apavāda-pratyaya," the expression "having excluded the pratyaya" is intended to include the pratyaya in general. Therefore, this prohibition applies to both the utsarga and the apavāda when they are introduced within the scope of the feminine gender (stryadhikāra). What is established by this? [The forms] *āsana* and *āsyā*: even though the *yuc* is an apavāda [to the *ṇyat*], its co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the *ṇyat* prescribed after roots ending in *ṛ* and *hal* (Pāṇini 3.1.124) is established. However, there is no such co-occurrence between the *ghañ* and suffixes such as *ktin*, because such usage is not sanctioned (*anabhidhāna*).

Others, however, explain that because "exception" (*apavāda*) is the subject under discussion, it is that very [exception] which is the suffix (*pratyaya*) here; thus, there is no co-occurrence (*asamāveśa*) of the *ghañ* suffix with *ktin* and others. In the case of *āsya*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are general rules (*utsarga*), because they are prescribed for verbal roots in general. The suffix *ka* (as in *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*) is an exception (*apavāda*), because it is prescribed for specific verbal roots.

Furthermore, does this lack of similarity (*asārūpya*) pertain to the application (*prayoga*), or does it pertain to the instruction (*upadeśa*)? What follows from this? If it pertained to the application, there would be a prohibition regarding the substitutes for *l* (the *l*-suffixes)—in the case of "he cooked yesterday" (*hyo'pacat*), the *luṅ* suffix would also apply, because in the application there is a lack of similarity: in the *laṅ* suffix, the suffix is the vowelless *t*, whereas in the *luṅ* suffix, it is the sound *ic* (as in *apākṣīt*).

In the case of *śvaḥ kartā*, would not the *lṛṭ* suffix also apply? This is established by a *jñāpaka*: because [Pāṇini] prescribes the *laṅ* suffix in the domain of the *liṅ* in the rule *haśaśvatorlaṅ ca*, he indicates that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply to substitutes (*lādeśa*) of personal endings. Even so, in cases such as *grāmaṇīḥ* and *grāmanāyaḥ*, where *kvip* and other suffixes are applicable, the *aṇ* and other suffixes would not occur; for *kvip* and the like do not possess a visible form in actual usage, since their elision is prescribed. Therefore, it is the lack of similarity (*asārūpya*) residing in the original instruction (*upadeśa*) that is relevant.

If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) in cases where [roots] differ by means of *anubandhas*. For even in the case of *kāṇ*, the form is different in its technical instruction (*upadeśa*), yet it is the same in actual usage (*prayoga*); regarding this, he says: "not caused by an *anubandha*. Because *anubandhas* are not invariably present [in all stages], the dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) caused by them is not taken into account. Thus, although the letter *ṅ* is heard in the rule "udīyāṃ māṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.4), because that *ṅ* is not invariably present, the status of being "ending in *ej*" remains unimpeded, and consequently, the substitution of *ā* is applied.

The inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* in the rule "dadāti-dadhātyor vibhāṣā" is an indicator (*liṅga*) of this point; otherwise, since there would be dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) caused by the *anubandha*, the substitution of *ṇa* would occur in place of *śa* by default—so what would be the purpose of that [mention of *vibhāṣā*]?

In this context, regarding the suffixes *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and those having the sense of *khala*, the rule of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa*) would apply. For instance, in the examples *hasitaṃ chātrasya śobhanam* ("the student’s laughing was beautiful") and *hasanaṃ chātrasya* ("the student’s laughing"), even though the suffix *ghañ* is not permitted in the domain of *kta* and *lyuṭ*, it would nonetheless apply. Regarding *tumun*: in *icchati bhoktum* ("he wishes to eat"), the suffix *loṭ* would apply by the rule "*liṅloṭau icchārtheṣu*" ("*liṅ* and *loṭ* are used with verbs meaning 'to wish'*"), yet it is intended that *tumun* should supersede it. However, *liṅ* would indeed still occur by virtue of the specific statement "*liṅ ca*" ("and also *liṅ*"). If that is so, then by this very restriction (*niyama*), *loṭ* will also not occur.

Regarding the rule *kālārthād-yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.167), which states that the suffix *yuc* is added after words denoting time, such as *īṣat-pānaḥ* ("drinking slightly"), the suffix would indeed apply here even though it is a feminine form. Now, one might object: "Since there is a prohibition by the rule *na striyām* within the section governing feminine stems (*stryadhikāra*), this suffix will not apply; furthermore, since the section is interrupted thereafter, it will not apply beyond that point either. This would be so if this were a governing heading (*adhikāra*), but it has been stated that this is actually a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Moreover, it is desired that the rule regarding non-identical forms (*vā-sarūpa-vidhi*) should apply even after the section on feminine stems, so that forms such as *āsitvā bhuṅkte* ("having sat, he eats") and *āsyate bhoktum* ("it is sat for the purpose of eating") may also occur.

Otherwise, since a seat (*āsana*) exists for the purpose of eating, its priority would be understood; and because the suffix *ktvā* occurs in the domain of verbal roots ending in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tum-artha*), the *la*-suffixes (tense/aspect markers) apply to that very same [action], so there would be a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhaka-bhāva*) due to their having the same object. Likewise, in the cases "it is time to eat" (*kālo bhoktum*) and "it is time for eating" (*kālo bhojanasya*), the suffix *lyuṭ* would be sublated by the suffix *tumun*.

Therefore, even beyond the scope of the feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), the rule regarding dissimilar affixes (*vāsarūpavidhi*) must be accepted; the mention of *kṛtya* and *tṛc* in the sūtra "arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca" (Pāṇini 3.3.169) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this paribhāṣā is not invariably applicable beyond the scope of the feminine suffixes. Consequently, a prohibition regarding *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and affixes having the sense of *khala* need not be stated at all.
The suffixes forming denominative verbs (kṛtya) occur before the suffix *ṇvul*.

"Derivatives ending in *kṛtya* suffixes [beginning] prior to *ṇvul*. Since he will state [later], "The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc*," this [rule] does not have "the suffix *ṇvul* is used diversely in the naming of diseases" as its limit; for [in the rule] "In the sense of 'deserving,' the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* also," *tṛc* is mentioned separately.

If this is so, then the rule "prior to *ṇvul*" need not be stated; let it simply be "the *kṛtya*s. Due to the very indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the mention of *tṛc*, there will be no subsequent application [of the term *kṛtya*] beyond that point. Furthermore, the indicator—which shows that the governing rule for the technical name *kṛtya* applies prior to the rule "ṇvultṛcau"—depends upon that specific rule. This is true; the author of the Sūtras (Pāṇini) read only "the *kṛtya*s" (*kṛtyāḥ*). However, the author of the Vṛtti (Kātyāyana/Vṛttikāra) inserted into the Sūtra what was read in the Bhāṣya as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Indeed, the composition of the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the commentator (*vṛttikāra*) is most diverse! By using the plural form *kṛtyāḥ*, he intends to include those [suffixes] not explicitly mentioned; therefore, there is no need to provide supplementary rules (*upasaṅkhyāna*) such as "the addition of *kelimar*."
The suffixes *tavya*, *tavyat*, *anīyar*, and *ra* [are used after a verbal root to form gerundives].

The suffixes *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar* [are applied after roots]. Regarding the mention of *vaser*: this refers to the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*vasa nivāse*), and not to the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*vasa ācchādane*) which belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class. Because of the rule "the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal-artha* suffixes apply only to those two [roots, i.e., the transitive and intransitive]," [the suffix] would not apply to the agent; therefore, this statement is made both to ensure its application to the agent and for the purpose of causing the *ṇit*-strengthening (*ṇidvadbhāva*). As for *vāstavya*: alternatively, this may be a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), where *vāstavya* means "that which exists in a dwelling" (*vāstu*), with the suffix *yat* applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group.

In the word *avāstavya*, there is no difference in accent; that which is the final acute (*antodāttatva*) by the rule *kṛtyokeṣṇuc* will likewise apply here by the rule *yayatoścātadarthe*. Regarding *kelima*: the letter *k* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, while the letter *r* is for the purpose of the accent. It is desired that this suffix be used in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*). However, in the Bhāṣya, it is shown in the sense of a pure object (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), as in: "The beans are *pacelima* (easily cooked), i.e., they are to be cooked; the *sarala* trees are *bhidelima* (easily split), i.e., they are to be split."
The suffix *yat* is applied after a word ending in *a*. (Pāṇini 3.1.97)

Regarding the mention of *ac*: "What is the purpose of mentioning *ac*?"—this question implies that the mention of *yat* should have been made in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) itself. [The answer begins with] "As many as... and so forth. For there are two types of verbal roots (*dhātu*): those ending in vowels (*ajanta*) and those ending in consonants (*halanta*). Since he will prescribe the suffix *ṇyat* after a root ending in a consonant, the intention is that by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), *yat* will apply only after a root ending in a vowel. [The phrase] "even from one that was previously vowel-ending" (*ajantabhūtapūrvāt*) is a compound formed according to the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), meaning "that which existed previously as a vowel-ending" (*bhūtapūrva*). Thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "that which is both vowel-ending and previously existing" (*ajantabhūtapūrva*). Examples are *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*.

From the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ*, the suffix *san* is added; there is reduplication; *iṣ* is substituted by the rule "sanimīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadām iṣ ca" (Pāṇini 7.2.49); *t* is substituted for *s* by the rule "saḥ syārddhadhātuke" (Pāṇini 7.4.49); and the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule "atra lopo'bhyāsasya" (Pāṇini 7.4.58), resulting in the forms *ditsa-* and *dhitsa-*. At this stage, even though the *ardhadhātuka* suffix has not yet actually arisen but is merely present in the mind, if the elision of the vowel were performed [only] after the suffix had actually arisen, then because the root would end in a consonant (*hal*), the suffix *ṇyat* would apply instead. However, by virtue of the mention of the vowel (*aj*) in the rule, that which occurs is based on the fact that the root was previously (*bhūtapūrva*) vowel-ending.

Therefore, by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*, [the word] would have an udātta accent; however, with the suffix *ṇyat*, there would be a svarita accent due to the *ti* [of the affix]. But in cases such as *cikīrṣyam*, there is no distinction between *ṇyat* and *ṇya*. For in the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*, the term *dvyacaḥ* (consisting of two syllables) is understood to carry over. However, when the elision occurs before an ārdhadhātuka suffix, then this mention of *ac* (vowel) need not be made at all.

Regarding the passage beginning with *takiśasītyādi*: *taki* means "to laugh," *śasu* means "to injure," *cate* (or *cade*) means "to beg," *yatī* means "to strive," and *janī* means "to be born. According to the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*, the suffix *yat* is prescribed after *janī* for the sake of the accent, resulting in the form *janya*; it is not established by the suffix *ṇyat* either, because the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies by the rule *janivadhyośca*. Some also read *śasi* [in this context]—that is, *nārāśaṃsyaṃ* and *rādvyaṃ*.

Regarding *hana* or *vadha*: either the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *han*, and by its co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*), the substitution *vadha* takes place—as in *vadhyam*. Alternatively, this word may be a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—*vadhya* meaning "one who deserves death" (*vadham arhati*), formed with the suffix *yat* according to the rule "after *daṇḍa* and others. If it were a secondary derivative, a compound would not be possible—as in *asivadhyaḥ* ("slayable by a sword") or *musalavadhyaḥ* ("slayable by a club"). However, when it is a primary derivative (*kṛt*), the compound is established by the rule "a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix is frequently compounded with another word ending in a *kṛt* suffix denoting the agent or the instrument. Regarding *ghātyam*:

the substitution of *t* occurs by the rule "for *han*, [there is *t*] except before *ciṇ* and *nal*" (*hanas to ciṇṇaloḥ*), and the substitution of *gh* occurs by the rule "for *han*, [there is *gh*] before affixes marked with *ṇ* or *ṅ*" (*ho hanter ñṇinneṣu*).
[The suffix *yaṅ* is applied] after a verbal root ending in a consonant preceded by a short vowel. (Pāṇini 3.1.98)

[The suffix] *yat* follows verbal roots ending in a long vowel (*ā*) or a short vowel followed by a single consonant (*upadha*). For example: *pākyaṃ* and *vākyam*. Here, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ka*) for the final consonants *c* and *j* occurs according to the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ. For *kopyam* and *gopyam*, the roots are *kupa* (in the sense of anger) and *gup* (in the sense of agitation). For *āpyam*, the root is *āplṛ* (in the sense of pervasion). In these three cases, the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule "yato 'nāvaḥ"—does not occur; instead, the suffix *ti* (the marker *yat*) retains its own svarita accent.
And [the suffix *ṇini* is applied] after [roots ending in] *śaki* and *saha*. 3.1.99.

"And [the roots] *śaki* and *saha*. Regarding *śaklṛ* in the sense of "ability," this is an illustration; it includes the inclusion of *śaka* in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇe*), which is marked with an optional [parasmaipada] (*vibhāṣita*). Regarding *ṣaha* in the sense of "endurance": now, one might object that only the root *ṣaha* meaning "capability" (*śakyarthe*), which is parasmaipadi and lacks an anubandha, should be understood here. This is not a fault; because the paribhāṣā concerning "that which lacks an anubandha" applies only to the domain of affixation rules (*pratyayavidhi*), both roots are therefore included.
Others, however, maintain that only those two mentioned by the author of the Vṛtti—under the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*—are to be understood.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *gam*, *mad*, *car*, and *yama*, when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them. 3.1.100.

Regarding the rule *gadamadacarayamaścānupasarge*: "from those that are not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargebhyaḥ*). The intention is that in the sūtra, the word *anupasarge* is used in the locative case (*saptamī*) to express the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*), by way of transposition (*vyatyayena*). For this very reason, the meaning does not become "that which is other than a prefix is *anupasarga*; when such an *anupasarga* is present as an *upapada*. If it were so, [the suffix] would not apply to simple roots; furthermore, the mention of *supi* in the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* would be redundant. For the term *anupasarge* continues to be in force there, and by the maxim of "negation joined with 'iva'" (*nañivayuktanyāya*), there will be the inclusion of a *subanta* (a nominal ending) that resembles a prefix.

"Niyamārtham" means: so that [the suffix] may occur only after a root that lacks a prefix (*anupasarga*), and not after one with a prefix (*sopasarga*). How then is it that [the rule] "by that, there should be no *viniyāmya* there"? This is a scribal error; the reading should be *viniyamyam*. By this, the phrase "that which is to be treated with effort" (*iti yatnopacaryam*) is explained. Regarding "after *car-* when preceded by *ā-*, provided it does not mean 'heavy' (*aguru*)," this statement is for the sake of including cases where a prefix is present. In "Ācaya is a region," the meaning is "to be traversed. *Upanetā* refers to the teacher (*guru*).
The term *varya* is used in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "prohibited. (Pāṇini 3.1.101)

Regarding *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "to be excluded": The term *avadya* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*). It is derived from the root *vad* with the negative particle *nañ* as its prefix. Although both the suffixes *yat* and *kap* would be applicable by the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca*, this is an irregular formation for two purposes: first, so that it takes the suffix *yat* specifically; and second, so that it retains the sense of being "blameworthy" (*garhya*) alone. Thus, *avadya* means "sin" (*pāpa*), because it is something unfit to be uttered. The phrase "anything other than *avadya*" refers to such things as the names of one's teachers and the like. For these are not blameworthy (*garhya*), yet they are also not fit to be uttered [in certain contexts].

In this case, the suffix *kyap* is applied; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class; [the *n* of] the negative particle (*nañ*) is elided by the rule *nalopo nañaḥ*; and [the augment] *nuṭ* is added after that by the rule *tasmānnuḍaci*. [The word *paṇya* means] "that which is to be traded. This is because the formation of the irregular form (*nipātana*) serves the purpose of establishing a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), and the word *paṇya* is conventionally established in that very sense. And it has been said: "The formation of irregular forms (*nipātana*) is for the purpose of obtaining [specific] verbal roots (*dhātu*), grammatical operations (*sādhana*), and tenses (*kāla*), as well as for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), and for the purpose of conventional meanings (*rūḍhi*) regarding secondary suffixes (*anubandha*) and modifications (*vikāra*)."

"Pāṇyam" means something else, namely that which is worthy of praise (*stutya*). Regarding "varyā," it is stated that this form is a feminine irregular derivation (*nipātana*). The point is that in the sūtra, words such as *avadya* and so on are separate, indeclinable items (*avibhaktika*), and not a dual-form compound (*dvandva*) ending in the suffix *jas*. In the example "śatena varyā," this is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of the root *vṛṅ* (meaning "to choose" or "to serve"); for in that context alone is the possibility of non-restraint (*anirodha*) possible. In "vṛtyānyā," the suffix *kyap* is applied according to the rule "etistuśāsvṛ... etc., from the root *vṛñ* (meaning "to choose"). In "vāryā ṛtvijaḥ," [the same applies].

In the rule *etistuśāsvṛ*, there is the inclusion of the root *vṛ* (to choose), whereas for the root *vṛñ* (to choose), the suffix *ṇyat* occurs only outside the feminine gender. However, in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, the form *varya* is employed even in the masculine gender—as in: "This one named Sugrīva is worthy of being chosen by you, O you of beautiful prowess."
The word *vahya* is a *karaṇa* [instrument] [when it denotes a means of transport]. 3.1.102.

*vahyam* is the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is an etymological explanation stating that the suffix *yat* is applied irregularly (*nipātyate*) to the root *vahi* when it denotes the instrument. It would have been more appropriate to say: "The form *vahyam* is established as an irregularity (*nipātyate*) when it signifies the instrument."
The word *ārya* [is used] for a master or a Vaiśya. 3.1.103.

The word *arya* [is antodātta] when denoting a master (*svāmin*) or a Vaiśya. It is stated that [the word *arya*] has its final syllable accented acute (*antodāttatva*) when meaning "master. Now, what is the case when it refers to one who is both a Vaiśya and a master? It is said: when the designation "Vaiśya" is intended, it has the initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudāttatva*), but when the designation "master" is intended, it has the final syllable accented acute. Thus, the term "designation" (*ākhyā*) was included in the Phiṭ-sūtra rule: "of *arya*, when the designation 'master' is intended. An *ārya* Brāhmaṇa means one who is to be attained (*prāptavya*).
A cow fit for breeding is called *kālyā* with respect to procreation.

*Upasaryā* means "fit for breeding" (*kālyā prajane*). This is derived from the root *sṛ* preceded by *upa*. Regarding the forms of the root *sṛ*, both the *bhūvādika* and the *jauhotyādika* are included; furthermore, because of the rule "after *sṛ*, *śās*, and *ṛt*, [the suffix *yaṅ* is optionally applied]" (*sartti-śāsti-arttibhyaś-ca*), there is an elision (*luk*) even outside the scope of that specific sūtra. The word *kālyā* means "one whose time has arrived. While the phrase "this has arrived for him" (*tad asya prāptam*) is in effect, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "from *kāla*, etc., *yat*" (*kālād-yat*). *Prajana* means "procreation"; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies here according to the rule "in the case of *jan* and *vadh*" (*janivadhyoś-ca*). Thus, a cow fit for breeding is called *upasaryā*.

The meaning is that she is fit to be approached by a bull for the purpose of conception; that is to say, the time for the bull's approach has arrived. "Upasāryā" means she is to be approached, i.e., she is to be reached.
The word *ajarya* is used in the sense of "companionship. (Pāṇini 3.1.105)

Regarding *ajarya-saṅgatam*: in the rule [Pāṇini 3.4.72] "saṅgamane kartari," he shows that *saṅgatam* is formed with the suffix *kta* in the neuter sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). As for the mention of "the agent" (*kartari*), this is based on the assumption of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) so that the suffixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khala* do not apply to the abstract action (*bhāve*) by the rule "tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.70). Consequently, even when the abstract action has an agent who has come together, only the suffix *ṇyat* occurs—as in *ajārya-saṅgatena*. Regarding *ajarita*: this is the suffix *tṛc*.
After the root *vad*, when followed by a word ending in a case-suffix (*sup*), the suffix *kyap* is also applied.

Regarding the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca*: the term *anupasarge* (without a prefix) carries over [from the previous rule]. As he will state in the sūtra *satsūdviṣa-* etc., the mention of "prefix" (*upasarga*) there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that elsewhere, when the word *sub* (a nominal ending) is mentioned, the mention of "prefix" does not apply. And this must necessarily be accepted in that very way—so that in rules such as *supyajātau* and *spṛśo'nudake kvin*, the mention of "prefix" does not occur. Consequently, there is no purpose here in the recurrence of the mention of *anupasarga*; for [the meaning is] "when a nominal ending (*subanta*) follows as an upapada, provided it is not a prefix."

Although it was previously explained that the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, here, however, because there is no contradiction, the intention is that the locative is used in its own primary sense (*svārtha*) after a *tatpuruṣa*. Regarding the term *brahmodyam*: the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and as before, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). "Brahman" means the Veda; thus, the meaning is "the speaking of that. But how can a *kṛtya* suffix be applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) after a transitive verb, when he will state later that "the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes occur after intransitive verbs in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*)"?

Nor can it be said that [the verb] is intransitive because the object is not intended to be expressed, for the object "Brahman" is explicitly heard in the scripture. Therefore, they say that in this context, the mention of the abstract state (bhāva) must be expected from the subsequent sūtra.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after a verbal root ending in *bhū*, when the action itself (*bhāva*) is expressed.

The word *bhuvo* [is used] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). As for the objection that it does not carry over [from the previous rule], it is because it was drawn over from the preceding sūtra. Now, one might argue: "Since the rule *tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ* prescribes that the *kṛtya* suffixes apply to both the abstract state and the object (*karman*), and since the term *anupasarge* (without a prefix) carries over [from the previous rule], and since the root *bhū* without a prefix is indeed intransitive (*akarmaka*), therefore by implication it will apply only to the abstract state. But is it not the case that the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*) is transitive? True; however, because of the specific mention of the individual form and because of its primacy, only the sense of "existence" (*sattā*) is understood here.

Furthermore, there is no risk of over-extension (prasaṅga) to [the karmans] such as time (*kāla*) and so forth, because they are not denoted [by the verb]. Why, then, is the term "bhāva" (state/abstract action) included? To this he says: "The inclusion of *bhāva* is for the sake of what follows. This is so that, by the rule *hanasta ca*, the suffix may apply in the sense of *bhāva* even after transitive roots like *han*—as in *brāhmahatyā vartate* ("the killing of a Brahmin occurs")—but not in the sense of *karman* (object), as in *tvayā ghātyo vṛṣalaḥ* ("the low-born man is to be killed by you").
And [the substitution of *han*] occurs for [the root] *han*. 3.1.108.

And [the word] *hanas* [is used]. Regarding the expression *brahmahatyā*: this form ending in *kyap* is feminine by its very nature, whereas other *kṛtya* suffixes are neuter when expressing an abstract state (*bhāva*). However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), even a form ending in *kyap* is desired to be neuter—as in: *sanādeva dasyuhatyāya jajñiṣe*. And in the Vedic language, it should also be stated that it occurs in the feminine—as in: *asyai brahmahatyāyai tṛtīyaṃ parigṛhāṇa*. [The commentary states: "The act of striking (*praghāta*) takes place."

What, then, is the reason that the suffix *ghañ* is cited as the counter-example and not the suffix *ṇyat*? To this he says: "But *ṇyat* does not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). The intention is that this applies even when the root is intransitive due to the non-intentionality of the object (*karmāvivakṣā*). However, in the case of a transitive root, there is no possibility at all for *ṇyat* to occur in the sense of the abstract state.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the verbal roots √i, √tu, √śās, √vṛt, and √juṣ.

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *i*, *tu*, *śās*, *vṛt*, and *juṣ*. Why is the root *i* specified here by its personal ending (*tip*) as "eti"? It is so that the reference may apply to the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself and not to something ending in the vowel *i*. In this context, only the root *i* (meaning "to go") is intended, not the roots *iṅ* (meaning "to study") or *ika* (meaning "to desire"), because since those two are always used with the prefix *adhi*, the mention of "eti" would be impossible for them. Thus, it is precisely this [root *i*] that was employed in the *Bhāṣya*: "Grammar should be studied for the protection of the Vedas."

However, some cite *adhītyā mātā* as well, based on the rule stating that "the root *iṇ* should be treated like *adhi*. In *stutya*, there is the insertion of *tuk* after the short vowel. In *śiṣya*, there is the substitution of *it* by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*; the inclusion of the root *āṅ-śāsu* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*) is also intended here because there is no distinction made. Consequently, in *āśāsyam*, the word is oxytone (accented on the middle syllable) by the accent of the verbal root. But if the suffix *ṇyat* were used, the word would instead have a svarita accent on the final syllable according to the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*.

However, some maintain that only the root *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭi*) is intended [in the rule], as in the examples beginning with *orāvaśyake*. Here, the scope of the mention of *stu* is when there is no intention to express necessity (*avaśyakatva*), as in *stutya*; the scope of *orāvaśyake* is, for example, *avaśyalāvyam*. When both would apply in the case of *avaśyastutya*, the suffix *ṇyat* would prevail due to its higher status [in the order of rules]; however, because of the repeated mention of *kyap*, only *kyap* occurs. Regarding the mention of *vṛ*, it is intended that the root *vṛñ* (to choose) is meant, and not *vṛṅ* (to choose as a bride).

This is because of an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence): namely, that the rule "īḍ-vand-vṛ-śaṃs-duhām ṇyataḥ" teaches that the word *vārya* has an udātta accent on its first syllable; and in that context, due to association (*sāhacarya*) with the roots *īḍ* and *vand*, the root *vṛ* taken there is the middle-voiced (*ātmanepadin*) one. [The same applies to] *śaṃs* and *duh*, etc. [The roots are]: *śaṃsu* in the sense of "praise," *duh* in the sense of "milking/filling," and *guh* in the sense of "concealing. Regarding the form *śasyam*: in the alternative view where the suffix *kyap* is applied, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). This supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the phrase "from that preceded by *āṅ*": the root *añjū* means "to manifest, to smear, to shine, or to go. In the word *ājyam*, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; furthermore, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopaḥ*). Now, why was it not stated that the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs specifically with the suffix *ṇyat*? Because [if *ṇyat* were used], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*), and because of the undesirable consequence of the accent (*svaraprasaṅga*) on that suffix. Therefore, this word ends in *kyap*.

If this is so, then a word-break (*avagraha*) would result—would one say *ājyam ity ā* or *ājyam iti*? Let it be broken; what is the harm? For the authors of the *pada-pāṭha* are not to be followed by the rules of grammar; rather, the rules of grammar must be followed by the authors of the *pada-pāṭha*. Indeed, the division of words is a human convention, whereas the *saṃhitā* alone is eternal. Furthermore, they do not break a word when there is no certainty regarding its meaning; for example, in the case of *harivaḥ*, because of the doubt as to whether the word *hari* ends in the vowel *i* or the word *hariḥ* ends in the consonant *t*.
How so? This is a question from one who considers this to be the form of the root *i* (to go). "Eḥ" refers to the root *i* in the sense of "going."
A suffix beginning with *ya* is added after a verbal root that has a short vowel as its penultimate letter, provided that the root is not *kḷp* or *cṛt*.

"Also [the suffix -ya] follows a root with *ṛ* in the penultimate position, except for *klṛp* and *cṛt*. This means excluding *klṛp* and *cṛt*. Since the substitution of *l* for the *r* in *klṛp* (meaning "to be capable") is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and because the rule for the designation of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) applies to the *d* and *ḷ* sounds, it possesses an *ṛ* in the penultimate position. As for *kṝt* (meaning "to sound"), it takes only the causative suffix (*ṇyat*). The intention is that this refers to the alternative where the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent, based on the principle that "the roots of the *curādigaṇa* are not necessarily followed by the causative suffix. This very use of the long vowel *ṝ* (*tapara*) serves as the evidence that the *curādigaṇa* roots are not necessarily followed by the causative suffix. However, when the causative suffix is present, whether the suffix is subsequently elided or not, the form remains the same—as in *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*.

Regarding *pāṇisargya*: it is a *upapada-samāsa* (compound with a subordinate member) meaning "that which is released by the two hands," with the substitution of *k* for *s* as before. The same applies to *samavasargya*.
The augment *ī* is also applied after the root *khana*.

Regarding the rule *ī ca khanaḥ*: for what purpose is the long vowel (*dīrgha*) pronounced? Could it not simply be stated as *i ca khanaḥ*? There is no difference between the long and the short vowel in the application of *ād guṇaḥ*. If it is argued that if a short substitute were used, the *tuk* augment would apply by virtue of the short vowel—on the grounds that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is "not established" (*asiddha*) with respect to the rules concerning *ṣatva* and *tuk*—we say: no.

The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of the end of one word and the beginning of another is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the application of the *tuk* augment; otherwise, in the case of *vṛkṣecchatram*, because the *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *i* + *e*] would be *asiddha* by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*, the *tuk* augment—which is obligatory by the rule *che ca*—would apply based on the short vowel. Therefore, he says: "the mention of the long vowel," etc. By this, he shows that two short vowels are prescribed here, not a long one. However, previously, by relying on the literal reading, it was stated that the substitute is the long *ī*. Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): when there is a *praśleṣa* (conjunction). The phrase "those which are optional" (*ye vibhāṣā*) is for the purpose of setting aside the substitution of *ā*.

Otherwise, there would be no scope for the rule *ye vibhāṣā*; its scope would be [roots] such as *khāyate* and *khanyate*. However, the scope of this [present rule, *kyapi ca*] would be that alternative where the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) does not occur. In the case of the *ātva* alternative, when both [the present rule and *ye vibhāṣā*] would apply simultaneously, *ātva* would prevail because it is both subsequent (*para*) and internal (*antaraṅga*). And this is stated under the view that "in *ye vibhāṣā*, the locative case [indicates] a condition (*viṣaya-saptamī*). For in that case, while the root is still merely present in the mind as beginning with *y*, *ātva* is internal, whereas this substitution of *i* (*itva*) is external because it is prescribed together with the suffix *kyap*. Under the view that the locative [in *ye vibhāṣā*] indicates a cause (*parasaptamī*), however, this very substitution of *i* is internal, since it is prescribed without depending on a subsequent cause.
The affix *kyac* is applied after the root *bhṛ* (to carry/sustain) when it does not denote a name.

Regarding *bhṛño’saṃjñāyām*: "it means 'those who are to be supported'. By this, showing that it is an action-word (*kriyāśabda*), he rejects its status as a technical name (*saṃjñātva*). Regarding "optionally after *sam*-prefixed [to *bhṛ*]": this is an option for the suffix *kyap*, which by the rule would have been obligatory even when not a technical name; thus, the meaning is that it is an option where there was a prior necessity (*prāptavibhāṣā*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the case of *saṃjñā*," the word "of the prohibition" (*pratiṣedhasya*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Since the prohibition expressed by the phrase "not when it is a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) has already fulfilled its purpose by being observed in the masculine form in the example "Bhārya by name is a Kṣatriya," the word *bhāryā* is not established for the female according to the author of the Sūtras. For when a prohibition has been fulfilled in the masculine, the suffix *kyap* must necessarily apply in the feminine.

[Objection: But surely the word *bhāryā* is also a technical name (*saṃjñā*), for even when she is not being supported (*abhriyamāṇā*), she is called "wife" (*bhāryā*). So how can there be any occasion for this [application of] the suffix *kyap*? [Response: We do not say that it must occur by means of this *kyap*; rather, the occasion for its application here is that which is prescribed specifically for names by the rule "in the sense of a name, after the roots *samaja*, etc. (*saṃjñāyāṃ samajani-*). Nor can its exclusion be established by the force of the prohibition [of *kyap*], because that prohibition is already fulfilled in the masculine gender—this is the objection. The answer is stated: "There is an authority [for the suffix] in the feminine."

But will it not be stated under the rule *sañjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada-*—"The term *bhāve* (in the sense of an action/state) is not emphasized; rather, the previous governing topic (*arthādhikāra*) alone [applies]"—so that we have forms such as *samajyā* (an assembly, where they gather together) and *niṣadyā* (a sitting, where they sit down), and so forth? How then can it be said that "the governing topic of *bhāva* applies to the feminine"? This is not a novel objection, for the author of the Vṛtti himself will state there: "How was it said that the governing topic of *bhāva* applies to the feminine?"

In the section on feminine nouns (*strī*), when the suffix *kyap* is prescribed by the rule "in a name, from *samaja*, etc.," there exists an operation characterized by the attainment of the state of being denoted, which is the domain of the abstract action (*bhāva*); this is due to the inherent nature of the word's expressive power. Thus, by that [suffix], *kyap* occurs only for the abstract action (*bhāva*) and not for the object (*karman*); therefore, the intention is that *bhāryā* is established as the object.

According to the rule "when a suffix with one indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is to be applied, [a root] with two indicatory letters is not [taken]," only the root *bhṛñ* "to support" is included in the prescription for the suffix *kyap*, and not the root *ḍubhṛñ* "to hold and nourish. Therefore, another possible resolution here is that the form *bhāryā* is established either from that [root *ḍubhṛñ*] or from the long-voweled root *bhṛñ* "to support."
After the root *mṛj*, [the substitution of *guṇa*] is optional. 3.1.113.
Regarding *mṛjer vibhāṣā*: in the form *parimārgya*, there is vṛddhi by the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*, and the substitution of *k* for *g* (kutva) as before.
The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *ṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya* [are formed with the suffix *kyap*]. (Pāṇini 3.1.114)

The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *avyathya* are irregular formations. Regarding *rājasūya*: "It is to be pressed by the king" (*rājñā sotavyaḥ*). The term *rājā* refers here to an anointed Kṣatriya; the meaning is that it is to be produced by him through the process of pressing. Here, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and the lengthening of the vowel is an irregularity (*nipātana*). Alternatively, "the king is produced here" (*rājā vā iha sūyate*). In this view, the *soma* plant itself is the "king," as seen in such passages as "they buy the king [Soma]" (*rājānaṃ krīṇanti*). In both cases, the root *sū* means "to press."

The addition of the *kyap* suffix in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*) is for the sake of conventional usage (*rūḍhyartha*); therefore, it does not apply to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such sacrifices. Even in the former view, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the *Aśvamedha* and similar rites. Regarding the expression "from *sū* and *sarti*": one might object that since it is stated that "there is *utva* for *sarti*, or a *ruṭ* augment for *sū*," a choice (*vikalpa*) is intended here; however, because there is no semantic distinction [between the two roots], a copulative compound (*dvandva*) would be untenable. Nevertheless, the compound is justified by the usage of the author of the *Bhāṣya*; for it is employed in the *Bhāṣya*: "And from *sū* and *sarti*; there is *utva* for *sarti*, or a *ruṭ* augment for *sū*."

Regarding the term *sartarutvam*: its lengthening is established by the rule *hali ca* itself once *ru* has been substituted for *ra*. Alternatively, [the form] *suvateḥ* with the augment *ruk* is proposed; here *suvateḥ* is in the ablative case, meaning "after the root *sū*" (specifically, after *sū* followed by the suffix *kyap*). In the reading *rugāgamaḥ*, the genitive is used. The vowel *ā* in *sarati* [is explained as follows]: the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" belongs to the *tudādi* class; in the passive sense, it means "that which impels the world," for when that [sun] has risen, people engage in their activities. By using the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*), he shows that this is a conventional derivation (*nipātana*) in the sense of an agent.

The same should be understood for *ruc* and *avyath* as well. And it is said: "In the case of *sūrya*, *ruc*, and *avyath*, [the suffix *kyap*] is used in the sense of the agent. Regarding the word *kupya*: this is desired in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*); it is the name for wealth other than gold and silver. Any over-extension of application everywhere must be avoided by resorting to the fact that these are irregularly formed words (*nipātana*). It is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*). This should be understood as applying to those words which have the udātta accent on the final syllable. For it is said: "In the case of *kṛṣṭapacya*, there is the state of having the udātta accent on the final syllable when [the suffix is applied] in the sense of the object acting as its own agent. But in the simple sense of the object (*karman*), it becomes simply *kṛṣṭapākya*.
The suffixes *udya* and *ddhya* are applied after the verbal root *bhid* to form nouns denoting a river.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *puṣya* and *siddhi* when they denote an asterism (*nakṣatra*). 3.1.116.

*Puṣya* and *siddhi* are [the names of] the two constellations (*nakṣatra*). "In this, objects (*artha*) flourish" (*puṣyanti*); the word "have been undertaken" (*ārabdhāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. "In this, [objects] are accomplished" (*siddhyanti*); here, the word "objects" (*arthāḥ*) is required [as the subject]. The words *puṣpa* and *siddha* are synonyms. However, because they refer to their own forms (*svarūpa*), they form a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the sūtra.
The word *vipūya* is substituted for *vinīya* before the words *jitya*, *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali*. (Pāṇini 3.1.117)

In the words *lipūyavinīyajityā* and *muñjakalkahaliṣu*: *vipūyo muñjaḥ* means that the *muñja* grass is to be purified (*śodhayitavya*) for the purpose of making ropes and the like. *vinīyaḥ kalkaḥ*: This word *kalka* occurs in the sense of a ground medicinal substance—as in the verse: "A paste (*kalka*) consisting of one part each of *pathyā*, ginger, and rock salt should be drunk daily for the destruction of all diseases. It also refers to the dregs remaining when a medicinal substance is thrown into oil or clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Furthermore, it is well-known in the sense of "heat" or "torment"—as in: "Austerity is not torment; study is not torment."

In such cases as these, some maintain that the first [suffix] is to be understood here; however, we hold that it is the specific [suffix], as Māgha employed it: "having disciplined [them] with devotions expanding through agitation. Regarding *jitya*: it means "to be drawn by force. For the purpose of leveling what has been ploughed, a thick piece of wood is cast out by the ploughman (*halin*).
In the Vedic language, the suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *prati* and *api* when combined with the root *grah*.
And [the suffix *khañ* is used] after the words *pada*, *asvairin*, *bāhya*, and *apakṣya*. (Pāṇini 4.2.119)

[The rule applies] to words ending in *pada*, to those that are not independent (*asvairin*), to those derived from *bāhya*, and to those belonging to a *pakṣa*. Regarding *asvairiṇī*: [the root] *īr* means "to impel. The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*) to denote one whose nature it is to impel by herself (*svayam eva īritum śīlam asyāḥ*). The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs according to the rule *svādīreriṇoḥ*. Regarding *bāhyāyām*: that which exists outside is *bāhya*; the suffix *yañ* is applied with the elision of the *ṭi* portion of *bahiṣ*. That which exists in a *pakṣa* is *pakṣya*; the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. [The phrase] "for which the designation *pragṛhya* has been prescribed": now, is it not the case that the designation *pragṛhya* applies to dual endings (*dvivacana*) and so forth which are parts of a word (*padāvayava*), and not to the word (*pada*) itself? True.

This term *pada* is etymological (*yaugika*): that by which a meaning is stepped upon (*padyate*) or reached (*magyate*). Alternatively, in the *Prātiśākhya*, the word *avagṛhya* is well known as being used in the dual number, referring specifically to *padāni*. Here, the root *grah* (to seize) has the sense of "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*). Due to the absence of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), in cases such as *agnī*, the vowels are not in close proximity to one another because they are separated by even a slight interval of time. Thus, it is called *avagṛhya*.

In a compound, the first member is the *pūrvapada*; for at the time of reciting the individual words (*padakāla*), there is a pause (*avagraha*) or separation [between them], as in the sense "these are those who are to be grasped" (*gṛhyakā ime gṛhītikāḥ*). In both cases, the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of compassion. Those such as parrots who have been made dependent through confinement in cages and the like are so called. In the example *grāmagṛhya*, there is a compound with a genitive case characterized as "the remainder" (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*). However, in *vāsudevagṛhya*, the compound is formed with either an agentive genitive or a genitive of the "remainder."
The suffix *a* is optionally applied after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*.
The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*. Thus, *vṛṣyam*; [the root] *vṛṣu* means "to sprinkle."
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the word *yugya* when it means "vehicle. (Pāṇini 5.1.121)

And [the suffix] *yat* is used after the root *pat* to form *pattram*. It is called *pattram* because "one falls by means of this" (*pataty anena*). The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule "after roots ending in *dām*, *ni*, or *śas*, etc. As for the form *yugyam*, it is already established by the *prāgdīvyatīya* suffix *yat* according to the rule "that which carries it: *ratha-yuga-prasaṅgam*. There is also no difference in accent: in the case of *kyap*, there is the accent of the verbal root; in the case of *yat*, there is the initial udātta according to the rule "that which ends in *yat* is udātta, except for *nau*"; and even in the case of *ayugyam*, there is no difference in accent, because in both instances (*yugyam* and *ayugyam*), the final syllable is prescribed to be udātta by the rules "in the case of *yat* and *yat* when not having that meaning" and "the kṛtya suffixes, *uka*, *iṣṇu*, and words beginning with *cāru*."
The suffix *am* is optionally applied after the word *amāvāsya*.

*Amāvasyānyatarasyām*. The word *amā* occurs in the sense of "together with," as seen in examples such as *amātya* ("minister"). In this rule, [the word *amā*] functions as an *upapada*. Its status as an *upapada* is established solely by *nipātana* (irregular derivation), or else the form *amā* is a reference [to the base] with the elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending. Because of the pronunciation of the letter *t*, this is not a *nipātana* of the suffix *kyap* under discussion. However, if it were a *nipātana* of the suffix *yat*—which is not the primary subject here—there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). For if *yat* were applied, in the word *vasyā*, there would be an acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*.

Even if the original accent of the final member of the compound were to remain according to the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*, that same accent would persist; however, when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the final syllable becomes circumflex (*svarita*). Furthermore, since the [suffix] *ṇyat* is not applicable in the sense of a locative (as in *amāvāsyā*), it will instead be formed by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Even so, would the formation of an *upapada* compound not be impossible? It will be possible by virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

Even so, would not the accent prescribed by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* fail to apply? Likewise, in the case of the suffix *ṇyat*, would not the effect of the suffix *yat*—as prescribed by the rule *amāvāsyāyā vā*—fail to apply to the word *amāvasya* ending in *ṇyat*, because they are distinct? Having observed this defect in the alternative involving *yat*, he states that there is indeed a substitution (*nipātana*) of the original *ṇyat* itself: "the suffix *ṇyat* occurs."

What, then, is being stated? That the suffix *ṇyat* occurs; it is not, however, that the suffix *ṇyat* is being irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*). True, that is indeed the meaning: by virtue of this irregular prescription (*nipātana*), the suffix *ṇyat* occurs—this is the sense. "Optionally, the absence of *vṛddhi* is irregularly prescribed. This means that while the suffix *ṇyat* is obligatory, the absence of *vṛddhi* is optional. "They dwell together" means they dwell in close proximity.

Regarding what was stated—that the suffix *ṇyat* is introduced by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*)—he says that this is a case of *guṇa*, namely: "because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. For in the case of *ṇyat*, the form *amāvāsyā* is inherently established; the absence of *vṛddhi*, however, is merely a modification of that very form—this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, when *vṛddhi* has been applied in the case of *ṇyat*, a short vowel is also introduced as an irregularity in certain instances, and that itself is what was described as the "absence of *vṛddhi*. This is likewise the case with the expression *avṛddhitām* in the verse.

In response to the doubt, "What is being elided here?", there is this verse beginning with *amāvasoḥ*. The dual-number designation is based on the distinction between the presence and absence of the augment *vṛddhi*. "I shall elide" (*nipātayāmi*)—the remainder of the sense is "of one [of the two]"; the meaning is that among the two forms of the root *vas* preceded by *amā* and *a*, I shall elide the *vṛddhi* of one. This statement is made regarding that which has attained unity through the author of the Sūtra. To the question, "What is established thereby?", he says: "Thus" (*tathā*).

The meaning is that the single *taddhita* formation succeeds for both of these [words] because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. And "my accent also becomes established": thus, for me who treats them as *nipātas*, the accent is also established. The accent has been explained.

In the Vedic language (chandasi), the following [words] ending in -ya are formed with the suffix *kyap*: niṣṭarkya, devahūya, praṇīya, unnīya, ucchiṣya, arthastarya, ādhvaryava, khanya, khānya, devayajya, āpṛcchya, apratiṣīvya, brahmavādya, bhāvya, stāvya, upacāyya, and pṛḍa. Pāṇini 3.1.123.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), there are the following [irregular formations]: *niṣṭarkya*, *devahūya*, *praṇī*, *unnī*, *ucchiṣya*, *marya*, *starya*, *adhvaryu*, *khanya*, *khānya*, *devayajyā*, *pṛcchya*, *pratiṣīvya*, *brahmavādya*, *bhāvya*, *stāvya*, *upacāyya*, and *pṛḍa*. Regarding the rule "the absence of *nu* and [the suffix] *ghañ*": the sense is that when one performs the act of offering (*juhoti*), that [suffix] occurs. As for the term *upacāyyapṛḍam*: from the roots *mṛḍa* (meaning "to be happy") and *pṛḍa* (meaning "to be pleased"), the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "for roots with *iṅ* as an indicatory letter" (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). Then, the compound *upacāyyapṛḍam* is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "that which is both *upacāyya* and *pṛḍa*. The statement "it should be stated 'and in the case of gold'" means that [this formation applies] when gold is the object denoted. The term "reversal" (*vyatyayam*) means a transposition of the beginning and the end.

"From one [root] the suffix *ṇyat* is applied": the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed after a single verbal root; in the four subsequent forms beginning with *devahūya*, the suffix *kyap* is prescribed after four roots. "The distinction [in form] arises from the difference in prefixes. "Two *kyaps*" means that two *kyaps* are prescribed after two roots. "The rule for *ṇyat* occurs four times": this is a word ending in *su*; the meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed four times, denoting the repetition of an action.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *h*, as well as after the root *al*.

Regarding the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*: [the term] "ending in an *ṛ*-vowel" is intended. However, there is no inclusion of the root *ar* (from *ar-ti*), because of its association with *hal* (consonants), because of the instruction that the operation applies to what follows, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*.
