The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *rava* when preceded by *ora*, provided that necessity (*avaśyakya*) is implied. 3.1.125.

Regarding the word *āvaśyaka*: "that which is inevitable (*avaśyam bhāvaḥ*) is *āvaśyakam*. The suffix *vuñ* is applied because [the word *avaśya*] belongs to the *manojñādi* group; for indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) when followed by any *bha*-suffix. Now, does this suffix apply when an upapada expressing the sense of "inevitability" is present, or rather when the sense of inevitability itself is to be indicated? Regarding these two views, if the first position were held, the suffix would not occur in the absence of an upapada—such as in *lāvyaṃ* and *pāvyam*. Therefore, the second position is adopted; thus he says: "when the sense of inevitability is to be indicated."

Regarding the phrase "the formation of the *svarasamāsa* is untenable": in the view that [the suffix] functions as an *upapada*, the formation of an *upapadasamāsa* is obtained, and by the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*, the final member (*uttarapada*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). However, in the view that it functions as a *dyotaka* (indicator), neither of these two results is established—this is the meaning. In the expression *avaśyalāvyam*, there is the elision of the *m* by the rule *lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye*. Although the meaning is already indicated, the actual use of the word is sometimes observed due to a disregard for brevity (*lāghava*). However, this need not be stated here.

The employment of *avaśyam* [as a separate word] is already indicated by the very rule stating "the indeclinable *avaśyam* is compounded with a gerundive (*kṛtya*)"; for that [rule] finds its application in cases such as "that which must necessarily be done" (*avaśyakartavya*). As for the phrase "because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class," the meaning is that this class is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended group). Regarding the phrase "and in the case of the original accent of the second member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*)," one could also say that the accent will likewise be established simply through the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) of the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class.
The roots *āsu*, *yu*, *pi*, *ra*, *pi*, *lap*, *trap*, and *cam* [take the suffix *uṇ*]. 3.1.126.

Regarding the rule *āsuyuvapirapilapitrapicamaśca*: they say that among the group beginning with *pu*, the term *āsu* is included by forming a *dvandva* compound [with the others]. Thus, he states its connection with the root *su* by saying "from *su* preceded by *ā*. This refers to the root *ṣu* in the sense of "procreation" or "sovereignty," as its inclusion is justified by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The term *yu* refers to the root *yumiśraṇe* ("to mix"); however, the root *yuñ bandhane* ("to bind") is not included because it possesses an *anubandha*. The phrase "an exception to *yata*" [is used] because it is an exception to that.

The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rules "aco yat" and "poradupadhāt. Regarding the form *dābhya*: although the root *dabh* is not listed among the standard verbal roots (*dhātu*), its status as a root should be understood—like *kṣapayati*, *arthayati*, *avadhīrayati*, and so forth—on account of the statement in the *curādi* class that "this [list] is illustrative in many ways" (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*) and because of its usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
The suffix *āṇ* is applied [to form a patronymic] after a word denoting something non-eternal. 3.1.127.

"Ānāyya" [is used] in the sense of "non-eternal. This is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, one should not raise the objection that this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), for its status as a conventional term is established by its being a *nipātana* (an irregular formation). For it has been said: "A *nipātana* is for the sake of conventional meaning. To the question, "But from what does its non-eternality follow?", he says: "And its non-eternality [is due to] constant non-burning. The meaning is "because it does not burn constantly," for its very burning is its waking. He shows that even in the case of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, it is intended only in a specific sense and not everywhere—this is indicated by the words "and which... (*yaśca*).

*Yoni* means the place of origin. By the words "from a Vaiśya family" and so forth, he shows the various types of origins (*yoni-vikalpa*). Regarding the phrase "if [it were] *ānāyya*, it would be non-eternal": the ellipsis is that this would lead to the same consequence for jars and other such things. Regarding the word *bhavet*: the suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility; the meaning is that it is only by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) that it is considered possible. Regarding the phrase "in a single origin": [this refers to] the *āhavanīya* fire. For otherwise, it would be *āneya*. The meaning is that in the case of jars and so forth—which have different origins—and in the case of the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire, which is non-eternal, only the suffix *yat* (as prescribed by the rule *aco yat*) occurs.
The term *praṇāyya* means "not approved" or "disapproved. (Pāṇini 3.1.128)

*Praṇāyyaḥ* means "one who is not approved of. He explains that *asammatāv* (in the dual) is a bahuvrīhi compound, stating: "that in which approval (*saṃmati*) does not exist. Here, *saṃmati* refers to the act of approving—the process of action consisting in the acceptance of something as an object of affection—not the activity of the approver; for if it were the latter, there would be the undesirable consequence of applying this rule to one who is not an approver, and that is not intended. With this intention, he says: "approval is the state of being approved. He further notes that *saṃmati* also denotes desire;
thus, by way of double entendre (*tantra*), the word *saṃmati* also expresses the regard directed toward an object of enjoyment.

The words *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are derived from the roots √pā, √si, √ci, and √dhā respectively] when they signify a measure, an oblation, a dwelling, and a *sāmidhenī* verse. (Pāṇini 3.1.129)

The forms *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are derived from roots] meaning measure, oblation, dwelling, and *sāmidhenī* verses respectively. *Māna* is that by which something is measured (*mīyate 'nena*). *Havis* is that which is offered (*hūyate*). *Nivāsa* is that in which one dwells (*nivasati asmin*). A *sāmidhenī* is a verse for kindling the sacrificial fuel (*samidhām ādhānī ṛk*). Regarding the suffix *ṇyat* after the root *māṅ*: in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), the augment *yuk* is applied according to the rule "āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ. The phrase "anything else is to be measured" means that whatever [suffixes] apply in the senses of state (*bhāva*) and object (*karman*) also apply here. Regarding *sānnāyya*: it is that which is properly led toward the fire for the purpose of offering (*samyak nīyate homārtham agnim prati*); thus, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmani*). It is a specific type of oblation (*haviḥ*).

Regarding the curd and milk prescribed for the new moon day in the injunctions, "Aindra curd on the new moon day" and "Aindra milk on the new moon day," Māgha, however, taking the literal meaning as he heard it, applied it to any sacrificial oblation in general: "The fire has well consumed this offered Sānnāyya. *Dhāyyā*: [Derived from] *dhīyate 'smin dhānyādikam* ("grain and so forth are placed in this"), using the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Regarding *dhāyyā*: [derived from] *dhīyate 'nayā samit* ("the fuel-stick is placed by means of this"), using the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), joined with the prefix *pūrva-vat*. "Of a specific Ṛc verse": such as "pravovājā abhidyavaḥ" and so forth. "What then? Only a certain one": [meaning only a specific verse].

The *pṛthuyāja* verses, beginning with "amartya," which are inserted between the *samidhyamānavatī* and *samiddhavatī* verses in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), are thus established. But how is this specific distinction obtained? He says: "For this is a conventional term (*rūḍhi-śabda*). The sense is that for this very reason, one must rely on grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). He confirms its status as a conventional term with the words "and so too. "He recites the *dhāyyās*" is the injunction found in the *marutvatīya* litany of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
The inclusion of the term *sāmidhenī* is intended to indicate the sphere of practical application; such is the sense.
In the sense of a sacrifice, [the words] *kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya* [are derived with the suffix -yaṅ]. (Pāṇini 3.1.130)

Regarding *kratau kuṇyapāyyasaṃcāyyau*: it was stated that the word *kuṇḍapāyya*, ending in the suffix *yat*, is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed; he states the purpose for this as follows: "because of [the rule] *yato 'nāvaḥ*. The meaning is that the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the final member is established by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*; otherwise, if the suffix were *ṇyat*, there would be a circumflex accent (*svarita*).
The words *paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* denote types of sacrificial fires.

The words *paricāyya*, *upacāyya*, and *samūhya* refer to the fire-altar (*agni*). It does not mean the physical flame; rather, it refers to a specific construction of bricks for that purpose, because the terms are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that sense alone. Here, from the root *ūh* (meaning "to reflect" or "to infer")—which has multiple meanings—the word *samūhya* is derived in the sense of "carrying" (*vahana*), being formed with the suffix *ṇyat* due to its ending in a consonant (*hal*). Thus, it is established as *samūhya*. Accordingly, the Brāhmaṇa explains the word *samūhya* in the sense of "carrying" (*vahyartha*) by means of the root *ūh*: "One desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya* altar; man is indeed cattle; thereby he piles cattle for him. Thus, the word *samūhya* is etymologically defined in the Brāhmaṇa through the root *ūh* in the sense of "carrying."
And [the suffix -ya is used] in the words *citya* and *agnicitya*. 3.1.132.

Regarding *cityāgni* and *agnicityā*: the term *citya* refers to fire (*agni*). Here, the suffix *kyap* is applied as an exception to the rule for the object (*karman*), and by that, the word becomes udātta on its first syllable. [The opponent asks: "Why, then, is not *kyap* itself prescribed here as well? For if it were so, the augment *tug* would not need to be prescribed. To this he replies: "By that [prescription of *kyap*], the word becomes udātta on its final syllable. [The opponent asks: "Is it only with respect to *agni*? That is intended only as a qualifier for the word *citya*, and not for the word *agnicityā*; for the latter is prescribed as being in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). This very point is demonstrated by the statement: "and another thing is to be piled up" (*ceyam anyat*).
The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* [are applied after verbal roots to form agent nouns]. 3.1.133.
The affixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are applied after [verbal roots] ending in *nandi-grāhi*, and after those beginning with *pac*.

[The rule] *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ* [states that] the word "ādi" (beginning with) is connected to each [member of the list]; this is the sense, namely, that they are read [in the Gaṇapāṭha]. The connection is: "those which are read after having been extracted (*apoddhṛtya*) are what are taken. "Having extracted" means having separated them mentally. But for what purpose is the prescription of suffixes made by extracting [the roots], since the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of *nandana* and the others is already established simply by their being read in the Gaṇapāṭha? It is said in reply: if this were not the case, then because [these forms] would find no application anywhere in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, one would conclude that their inclusion in the Gaṇapāṭha is non-Vedic (*anārṣa*).

*Nandivāśī* and so forth: *ṭunadi* means "to prosper," *vāśrṛ* means "to sound," *madī* means "to rejoice," *duṣa* means "to become corrupted," *rādha* and *sādha* mean "to accomplish," *vṛdhu* means "to grow," *śubha* and *śumbha* mean "to beautify," and *ruca* means "to shine. Regarding *dūṣaṇa*: the substitution of *ū* occurs by the rule *doṣo ṇau*. Regarding *sahitapi* and so forth: *ṣaha* means "to endure," *tapa* means "to heat," and *śamu* and *damu* mean "to pacify. Regarding *jalpana* and so forth: *jalpa* and *japa* mean "to speak" (*vaktāyāṃ vāci*).

The root *ram* is used in the sense of playing; *dru* in the sense of joy and release; *krad* in the sense of calling out and weeping; *kṛṣ* in the sense of scratching; and *hṛṣ* in the sense of falsehood. *Arda* is used in the sense of harming; thus, one who "harms people" (*janaṃ mardayati*) is Janārdana. Although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected here by rule, it is not applied. The same should be understood for subsequent cases where a direct object (*karman*) serves as the upapada. *Yu* is used in the sense of mixing; *ṣūd* in the sense of flowing. One who "destroys the demon Madhu" (*madhunāsuram sūdayati*) is Madhusūdana. *Ñibhī* is used in the sense of fear; with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the form *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* applies.

The roots *lūñ* (to cut), *ṇaś* (to disappear), and *damu* (to subdue) take the suffix *ṇic*. Thus, one who destroys the mind is *cittanāśanaḥ*; one who subdues a family is *kuladamanaḥ*. Regarding the words beginning with *grāhī*: the roots *graha* (to seize), *ṣaha* (to endure), *tasu* (to perish), *dasu* (to destroy), and *bhasa* (to threaten or shine) [take the suffix *ṇini*]. For the root *sthā*, the augment *yuk* is added after the vowel *ā*. The root *mantr* (to speak secretly) belongs to the *cur*-class; *ard* means to injure. Regarding the words beginning with *rakṣā*: the roots *rakṣ* (to protect), *śru* (to hear), *ḍuvap* (to sow seeds), and *śo* (to sharpen/thin)—with the word *ni* as a prefix (*upapada*), these take the suffix *ṇini*. Regarding the words beginning with *yācī*: [the same applies].

Regarding the roots *ṭuyācṛ* (in the sense of begging), *hṛñ* (in the sense of taking away), *vraja* (in the sense of going), *vad* (in the sense of indistinct speech), and *vasa* (in the sense of dwelling)—the suffix *ṇini* occurs after these when their meanings are prohibited; that is to say, when their meanings are negated. He shows that this state of having a prohibited meaning occurs when [the roots] are preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. Thus, he gives examples such as *ayācī* and so forth. Although the word *vi-* is also seen to express prohibition in cases such as *vigardabharathi*, the suffix *ṇini* is not observed after *yāc* and the others when preceded by *vi-*. Therefore, it is understood that the suffix *ṇini* applies only when preceded by *nañ*.

"Of roots ending in *a*, etc. [This means: the suffix *ṇini* occurs after verbal roots that end in the vowel *a*, whose agents are non-conscious (*acitta*), and which have prohibited meanings. "Non-conscious" (*acitta*) refers to one who possesses no consciousness; those whose agent is such are described as "non-conscious agents. Examples include *viśayī* (one who lies down) and *viṣayī* (one who binds). [The roots] *śīṅ* (to sleep) and *ṣiñ* (to bind) undergo no *vṛddhi* strengthening due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Examples include *abhibhāvī* (one who has overcome) and *bhūta* (one who has become); "overcome" (*abhibhūta*) means "one who has overcome" (*abhibhāvī*). Examples include *aparādhī* (one who has offended) and *avarodhī* (one who has obstructed). [The roots] *rādha* and *sādha* mean "to accomplish," while *rudhir* means "to obstruct. Examples include *paribhavī* (one who has insulted) and *paribhāvī*; in the alternative form, there is an absence of *vṛddhi*.

"Pac" and so forth: *ḍupacaṣ* means "to cook"; *vaca* means "to speak"; *ḍuvapi* has the meaning already stated [of sowing]; the same applies to *vad*. *Cala* means "to tremble"; *patlṛ* means "to go. Regarding *nadaṅ*: *nada* means "inarticulate sound. The letter *ṭha* is for the sake of the suffix *ṅīp*; the same applies in subsequent cases as well.

*bhaṣ* in the sense of barking; *pluṅ* in the sense of moving; *car* in the sense of motion; *gṝ* in the sense of swallowing; *tṝ* in the senses of leaping and crossing over; *cura* in the sense of stealing; *divu* in the sense of playing and so forth; *sūd* has the meaning already stated; *jṝṣ* in the sense of the loss of vitality; *mṛṅ* in the sense of giving up life; *kṣamūṣ* in the sense of enduring; *ṣivu* in the sense of weaving; *miṣa* in the sense of rivalry; *kupa* in the sense of anger; *midhṛ* in the senses of intelligence and injury; *vraṇa* in the sense of bruising the limbs (belonging to the *curādi* class); *nṛtī* in the sense of tossing the limbs; *ddaśir* in the sense of seeing; *sṛplṛ* in the sense of moving.

The root *ḍubhṛñ* means "to support and nourish. One who supports a paramour (*jāra*) is called a *jārabharā*. Similarly, one who cooks a dog (*śvāna*) is called a *śvapaca*; because the word *śvapāka* is listed among the *nyaṅkvādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* also optionally occurs after the object [of the action]. The *pacādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), because the word *ādi* associated with it expresses a general category (*prakāra*). Thus, in the expression *śiva-śam-ariṣṭasya kare*, the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *kṛ*. And from the root *ghaṭ*, [the form] *karmaṇi ghaṭaḥ* is derived by the rule *aṭhac*.

Likewise, regarding the *yaṅ*-intensive forms, the elision (*luk*) of the *yaṅ* before this vowel (*ac*) has been stated in the rule "yaṅo 'ci ca. And in the Bhāṣya, it is stated: "It should be stated that [the suffix] *ac* is also applicable after all roots. However, the sequential listing [of roots] under the *pacādi* group is for the purpose of attaching the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in cases such as *nadaṅ*; for the purpose of subverting the subverters of those roots which have a root-vowel ending in a consonant (*igupadha*) when preceded by an object as a subordinate word (*karmopapada*); for both purposes in the case of *deveḍ*; and for others, it should be understood as being for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
The suffix *ka* is applied after verbal roots ending in *i* or *u*, as well as after those having *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ* as their penultimate (*upadha*) vowels.

The sūtra *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* [Pāṇini 3.1.135] contains a compound consisting of the items beginning with *igupadha*; since it is a collective (*samāhāra*) dvandva, the neuter gender would require a short vowel, but here it is an associative (*itaretarayoga*) dvandva, and by metarule (*vyatyaya*), the case ending *bhyas* is replaced by the singular ablative *pañcamy-ekavacana*. Among these, because the word *kṛ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root, the imitation follows the form of the original (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), and thus the dual number is applied to the case ending. Regarding *jña*: [the rule] *āto lopa iṭi ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.64] applies. Regarding *priya*: from the root *prīñ* in the sense of "satisfying," the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs. Regarding *kira*: from the root *kṝ* in the sense of "scattering," [the rule] *ṛta iddhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.100] applies.

The meaning is that although the suffix *ap*—like *tṛc* and others—occurs after all verbal roots, these [specific roots] must necessarily be listed among the *pacādi* group for the purpose of setting aside (or overriding) exceptions.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the root *āp-* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it. (Pāṇini 3.1.136)
The suffix *śa* is applied after the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *dhmā*, *dheṭ*, and *dṛś*.

*Pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-daśaḥ śaḥ*: for the roots *pā* (to drink), *ghrā* (to smell), *dhmā* (to blow/sound/fire-contact), *dheṭ* (to suck/drink), and *ddaś* (to see), the suffix *śa* is applied. However, the root *pā* in the sense of "protection" (*pā rakṣaṇe*) is not included here because it belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class. Examples such as *utpiba* and others follow. By the rule *pā-ghrā-ādi-sūtra*, the substitutes *piba* and so on are applied as appropriate. Regarding *vyāghra*: here, only the suffix *ka* applies by the rule *ātaścopasarge*; and in this context, the mention of the group beginning with *vyāghra* serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *limp*, *vind*, *dhārī*, *pārī*, *vedī*, *udij*, *cetī*, *sātī*, and *sāhī*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).

Regarding the rule *anupasargāllimpavindadhāripārivedyudejicetisātisāhibhyaśca*: he explains that the term *anupasargāt* is used in the singular by way of ellipsis (vyatyaya), meaning "after [roots] that do not have prefixes. *Lipa* means "to smear" (*upadehe*). *Vidlṛ* means "to find" (*lābhe*); the inclusion of both forms—with and without the augment *num*—is intended, and by this, other roots of the same form are excluded. *Dhṛñ* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*) and *dhṛñ* means "to stand" (*avasthāne*); both are included here, even though they take the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

The root *pṛ* (in *pāra*) means "completion of an action"; *vid* (in *vinda*) belongs to the *curādi* group, meaning "to perceive," "to tell," and so forth, or it is one of the roots meaning "to know" etc., with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). *Ejṛ* (in *ejaya*) is without the causative suffix; *citī* (in *cetaya*) belongs to the *curādi* group; *sāti* is with the causative suffix (*ṇic*); and *ṣaha* (in *sāhaya*) belongs to the *curādi* group or is with the causative suffix. [Examples: *limpaḥ*, *vindaḥ*. By the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*, the suffix *śa* is applied; by *śe mucādīnām*, the augment *num* is added. In the case of *dhāraya* and others, there is the substitution of *guṇa* and *āyādeśa*. Regarding *limpa* in the sense of "boat," however, we see in the Veda: *chattā ca vidharttā ca vidhāraya*.
Regarding the word *aravinda*: the petals, which are shaped like spokes (*ara*), are denoted by the word *ara*.
The substitution of *a* for the root-vowel of the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place) is optional before an affix beginning with *i*.

The substitution [of *u* for the final vowel] is optional after the roots *dada-* and *dadha-*. Thus, we have *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ*. Here, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap*, reduplication, and the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "the *ā* of *śnā* and the reduplicated stems" (*śnābhyastayorātaḥ*). From the roots *dada* (in the sense of giving) and *dadha* (in the sense of holding), when the suffix *ac* is added, the forms *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* are established. Similarly, when the suffix *ṇa* is added to *dā* and *dhā*, the forms *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ* are obtained. However, this specific rule is for the sake of accentuation—so that in *adadaḥ* and *adadhaḥ*, the rule "the two vowels [at the end of a word] are udātta when the word lacks power [to express a complete meaning]" (*ackāvaśaktau*) does not apply, and instead the accent of the negative particle (*nañ*) alone remains.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after verbal roots ending in *jvaliti*, *kāś*, and *ante*.

Regarding the rule *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ*, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*). The author of the *Nirukta* explains the term *nipāta* by stating that particles (*nipāta*) are so called because they "fall" (*patanti*) upon various meanings; thus, particles have multiple meanings. The form *jvaliti* is a citation without a case ending, meaning "from *jval* and the others. The term *kasantāḥ* refers to those whose end is *kas*. In the opinion of those who read *vṛt* after having studied *kas*, the inclusion of the mention of *kas* is of doubtful utility.

But surely, the root *jval* "to blaze" is recited twice—once among the *ghaṭādi* roots and once later; in the absence of this qualification, there would be doubt as to whether the first *jvali* is the one intended or the latter. Therefore, the qualification "from those beginning with *jval* that are proximate to *kasa*" is meaningful. This is not well said.

If the word *anta* signifies "proximity," then in a *bahuvrīhi* or a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the inclusion of *kas* would not be obtained. Furthermore, if a root such as *jval* were intended in the preceding [sūtra], that very root should have been mentioned immediately thereafter; for the inclusion of *jval* would already be established by the very fact of its being taught later. Moreover, the listing of *ghaṭ* and others serves a purpose in establishing the designation *mit*, whereas the other [the alternative interpretation] would serve no purpose; thus, that alone shall be the initial [element]. The phrase "an exception to [the rule regarding] vowels" (*aco 'pavādaḥ*) implies that this [designation *mit*] also applies to the entire domain of verbal roots.

What is the purpose of including *bhram* in the list of roots beginning with *jval*, given that the form *bhrama* is already established by adding the suffix *ac* (pacādi), and even with the suffix *ṇa* the form remains the same because the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies by the rule "not for a root taught with an udātta vowel"? [The answer is: it is so that in the word *abhrama*, the accent prescribed by the rule "in the case of incapacity, the acute falls on the first syllable" (*ackāvaśaktau*) shall not apply.
The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the verbal roots *syand*, *sru*, *saṃ-svi*, *tṝ*, *nav*, *sā-vah*, *hṛ-liha*, *śliṣ*, and *śvas*. (Pāṇini 3.2.141)

[The rule applies] to *śyai*, *vyadha*, *saṃsvatīṇ*, *avasā*, *vaha*, *lih*, *śliṣ*, and *śvas*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasargāt*). The phrase "provided they are not preceded by a prefix" has ceased [to apply here]. This is because the word "prefix" is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra. The word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) also [has ceased to apply]; it is understood that it has ceased. For the mention of "optionally" was connected with the mention of "not preceded by a prefix"; therefore, when that ceases, this also ceases. Regarding *śyaiṅ*: from the root *śyaiṅ* in the sense of "going," the form *śyād* is derived; thus, there is no inclusion of the root *śīṅ* (which would become *śyā* by the substitution of *yaṇ*) here.

Because of the [authoritative] commentary and because [the meaning] does not immediately present itself to the intellect. By the phrase "from those ending in long ā," he shows that there is no inclusion of roots such as *at* (ending in *ac*), nor of *pati* and others ending in *a*, nor of those ending in short *a*. This too is established solely by the commentary. [The roots mentioned are: *vyadh* in the sense of "striking," *sru* in the sense of "flowing" preceded by *āṅ* and *sam*, *iṇ* in the sense of "going" preceded by *ati*, *ṣo* in the sense of "concluding an action," *hṛñ* in the sense of "taking away" preceded by *ava*, *liha* in the sense of "tasting," *śliṣ* in the sense of "embracing," and *śvas* in the sense of "breathing."

In this context, the suffix occurs only after those roots that have a prefix (*sopasarga*); however, for the remaining roots, it applies without distinction. This is for the purpose of subverting a sublater (*bādhakabādhanārtham*). Specifically, the suffix *ka*, prescribed as a special rule by the sūtra "ātaścopasarge" (Pāṇini 3.1.136), is a sublater of the suffix *ṇa* prescribed as a general rule; this [present rule] is intended to subvert that [sublation]. By this, the inclusion of the root *ava-śyā* is explained. Thus, *avaśyāya* is formed according to the previous reasoning.
The suffix *yu* is applied after the root *du*, provided that no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it.

Regarding the rule *dunyor anupasarge*: the word *dāva* means a forest fire (*vanavahni*). How then is there the form *dava* in that very same context? It is because of the association with *nayati* that the root *du* with its *anubandha* (the causative *dū*) is understood here; the form will instead arise from the root *dav* without an *anubandha*, with the suffix *ac* (forming *dava* as a masculine noun). Alternatively, it is a word derived from the instrument (*karaṇa*), ending in *ap* according to the rule *ṛdor ap*.
The suffix *graha* is used in the sense of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*). 1.3.143.

The term *vibhāṣā* means "optionally. This is an established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), which he clarifies with the examples: "aquatic creature" (*jalacara*) and "existent" (*bhava*). That which exists and never does not exist is called *bhava*, such as a god (*deva*) or *saṃsāra*. *Bhāvāḥ* refers to categories of things (*padārthāḥ*).
The [suffix] *ka* is applied after the word *geha*. (Pāṇini 3.1.144)

Regarding "in the house" (*gehe*): the word *geha* is a qualifier of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, and not an *upapada* (an accompanying word); this is because of the specific instruction "connected with the master of the house" (*gṛhapatinā saṃyuktaḥ*). Thus he says: "in the house, [the word] denotes the agent. As for the phrase "and the wife [is so called] by virtue of being located there" (*tātsthya-dvārāśca*), the word *geham* is to be supplied; by this, he shows that even the secondary sense of "house" is included.

And that [usage] is obtained by resorting to either *tantra* (the method of simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition). In that regard, in the case of the word for "house" (*veśman*), it occurs only in the masculine gender with a plural ending—as in: "He becomes a burner of the houses," "He causes the houses to be looked upon with the [next] verse," "Go to the houses," and "I, having entered the houses with a well-disposed mind. The neuter gender, however, expresses the actual number of objects; the same applies to the word for "wife" (*dāra*).

Others, however, maintain that the word *gṛha* is primary (*mukhya*) only in the sense of a house and secondary (*gauṇa*) when referring to a wife; likewise, they demonstrate its primary application to the house in such passages as, "They say a house is not a house, it is the wife who is called a house. Yet, according to what was stated by the author of the Vṛtti, it appears that the word is indeed primary even when referring to a wife.
The suffix *ṣvun* is added after words denoting artisans. 3.1.145.

Regarding the rule *śilpini ṣvun*: because of its association with the preceding [rule], the term *śilpini* is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), not an *upapada*. Thus he says: "in the sense of an agent who is a craftsman" (*śilpini kartari*). Skill in actions is *śilpa*; one who possesses that is a *śilpa*. [The examples] beginning with *nṛt* and *khan* are illustrative of this very statement; therefore, it does not apply in cases such as *āhvātā* (one who calls) or *āhvāyaka* (one who causes to call). Regarding the rule *rañjeḥ anunāsikalopaśca* ("there is elision of the nasal of the root *rañj*"): this is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Namely, when the author teaches the designation *mit* for the roots *jan*, *jṝṣ*, *knus*, and *rañj* ending in *am*—that indicates that even though *rañj* is not marked with *kit*, there is elision of the nasal.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *gastha*. 3.1.146.

Regarding *gāthaka*: [the rule] says "from the root *gai*. Since there is no distinction regarding the inclusion of roots ending in *m* or *ā* (as per the principle that "in the inclusion of roots ending in *m* or *ā*, there is no difference"), it follows that the root *gāṅ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*) would also be included. However, this does not occur because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). For the suffix *thakan* is capable of denoting only an artisan whose domain is the meaning of the root *gā* (to sing).
And the suffix *ṇyuṭ* [is applied after verbal roots to form nouns denoting the instrument or means]. 3.1.147.

And *ṇyuṭ*. The letter *ṇ* is for the sake of [the suffix] *yug*, and the letter *ṭ* is for the sake of [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that only *ṇyuṭ* may be carried over in the subsequent rules, and not *thakan*.
And [the substitution of *ha* occurs] for [the letter *gh*] in the words *vrīhi* and *kāla*. (Pāṇini 3.1.148)

"And *ha* [is substituted] for [the root] *jahāti* when *vrīhi* and *kāla* are the objects. Regarding "of *jahāti*": the root is *ohāk* (to abandon). Regarding "of *jihāti*": the root is *ohāṅ* (to go). Generally, the reading is "of *jihīti*," but that is incorrect because, since the suffix *tip* is marked with *p*, there would be no substitution of *ī*. Here, the *k* in *jahāteḥ* is for the purpose of general inclusion; otherwise, due to having only one indicatory letter (*anubandha*), the rule would apply only to this [specific form]. If it were stated as *hāṅ*, even then its inclusion would not occur; therefore, both are included. "When *vrīhi* and *kāla* [are the objects]" is a qualifier of the agent (*kartṛ*), not an upapada (object-adjunct).

Thinking that this is because of the rule "tricaturbhyo hāyanasya dāmahāyanāntācca," he says: "In the sense of rice and time, as the agent. Regarding the phrase "they abandon water" (*jahaty udakam*), the word "having done so" (*kṛtvā*) indicates the basis for the application of the term *hāyana* when referring to rice. Some say that certain types of rice produced in the Jāṅgala region are called *hāyana*. Regarding the phrase "it goes toward states of being" (*jihīte bhāvān*), the meaning is that it "goes toward" or "penetrates" those states of being—that is, entities—by means of delimiting them.
The suffix *vun* is added after the verb root *pruṣ* (to sprinkle) when repetition is intended.

In the rule *pru-sṛ-lvaḥ samabhihāre vun*, the form *pru-sṛ-lvaḥ* is the nominative plural (*jas*) in place of the ablative; the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *ossupi*. It is indicated that there is skillful performance (*sādhukāritvam*). Repeated performance is "intensive action" (*samabhihāra*), because such repetition generally accompanies proficiency. Furthermore, for one who repeatedly performs a particular action, skill usually arises; therefore, through general association, skillful performance is indicated. The meaning is that it exists there by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He asks what is established by this and says: "even once" (*sakṛd api*).
And [the suffix *liṅ* is used] in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). 3.1.150.

"And in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). This means when the sense of benediction is understood, not when it is explicitly expressed; for by the rule "the *kṛt*-suffixes denote the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), the agent alone is what is expressed. "A particular kind of request" (*prārthanā-viśeṣaḥ*): a request is the desire to obtain that which is desired but not yet obtained—this is benediction (*āśis*). "If that [request] has action as its object": because of the governing rule "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) and because a verbal root denotes action. "Of this action": such as living and so forth; by this, he shows that benediction is a property of the speaker. "May he live" (*jīvatāt*): by using the imperative (*loṭ*) suffix in the example for benediction, he demonstrates the benediction.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in the *Padamañjarī*, composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
In the *Kāśikāvṛtti*, now the second quarter of the third chapter: *Padamañjarī*. [Sūtra 3.2.1:
"The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after [a verbal root] when an object [is to be expressed]."

Regarding the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*: the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) here is not a reference to the word-form itself, because of the prohibition [stated elsewhere] that "this is not a technical name for a word" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*). Now, one might object: this is a designation for the meaning, not for the word; therefore, the prohibition "not a technical name for a word" should not be understood in this way—as "a technical name for a word is called 'word-designation' (*śabda-saṃjñā*)"; rather, it means "a designation within a word is a 'word-designation'. By the word "word" (*śabda*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), which is the instruction of words, is meant. And when there is no contradiction, it is proper to accept the technical (kṛtrima) sense alone from among both the technical and the non-technical.

Therefore, accepting the technical definition of "action" (*karman*), he states its internal subdivisions: "Action is threefold. He demonstrates those three types as follows: "that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*). That which is non-existent and comes into being, or that which already exists and is manifested through birth, is "produced," such as: "he makes a pot" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) or "she gives birth to a son" (*putraṃ prasūte*).

However, that which undergoes some modification while already existing is the "object of modification" (*vikārya*). This modification is sometimes apprehended through perception, as in "he turns wood into ash" or "he makes gold into an earring"; and sometimes it is apprehended through scripture (*śāstra*), as in "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where it is understood from scripture alone that some excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced in the grains by the sprinkling. On account of this distinction, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there are four types of ritual action, including this "object of refinement" (*saṃskārya*).

But when there is no distinction produced by the action, it is the *prāpya* (attainable) object, as in: "He studies the Veda," or "He completes the *carccā*. Now, is it not the case that the object (*karman*) defined as "that which is most desired by the agent" is threefold, while there is yet another kind defined as "likewise connected [to the action] though not desired," which is twofold—the hateful and the other? Likewise, there is "the unmentioned (*akathita*)," as well as "the object of the root *div*," and "the object of the roots *adhi-śī*, *adhi-sthā*, and *adhi-ās*. Thus, when one intends to express these internal subdivisions, the object is sevenfold. And it has been said:
It is considered to be threefold— namely, that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*)—
whereas the object most desired (*īpsitatama*) is designated as fourfold in other ways.
"That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent, that which is not designated by other names, and that which has another as its antecedent. Thus [it is said].

Why, then, is it said that "action is threefold"? Some say: "In this context, only that which is most desired by the agent is taken [as the object], and nothing else is [an object] except for the case of the root √aṇ. Others, however, say: "To prevent [the application of the term 'object'] in cases such as 'he sees the sun' (ādityaṃ paśyati), it must be stated that [the object] is 'that which is being produced' (nirvartyamāna) or 'that which is being modified' (vikriyamāṇa). Anticipating this objection, the author of the Vārttika stated: "If it is argued that [the definition applies only] to that which is being produced or modified as an object, then an addition (upasaṃkhyāna) must be made for the study of the Vedas," and so forth.

By this, it is demonstrated that all three types of *karma* (object) are included, and not that the "attainable" (*prāpya*) object is excluded; nor is what is stated in other sūtras being set aside. Thus, regarding the rule *divaḥ karma ca*, the purpose of their co-occurrence has been explained: in the case of *manasā devaḥ*, because of its status as an object (*karman*), the suffix *aṇ* applies, and because of its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) applies. And in this way, forms such as *vṛkṣāvāsaḥ* ("dwelling in a tree") and *parvatādhivāsaḥ* ("dwelling upon a mountain") also occur according to usage. [The phrase] "due to non-expression" (*anabhidhānāt*)...

And that non-mention applies only where it has been stated by the authorities; elsewhere, however, it certainly occurs according to the grammatical rules, as he recites: "according to the rules, even when not employed."

Regarding "śīlikāmī" and so forth: *śīl* is in the sense of "to practice" (*samādhi*), *bhakṣ* (meaning "to eat") belongs to the *cur*-class, *kam* (meaning "to desire") takes the suffix *ṇiṅ*, and *car* (meaning "to move") is preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. The addition of the marker *ṇ* after *car* is for the purpose of causing vṛddhi. The rule "the first member retains its original accent" (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) is an exception to the rule that the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative retains its original accent (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). In the example *māṃsaśīlā*, if the suffix *aṇ* were applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would follow; however, even with the suffix *ṇa*, it occurs in some cases as if it were formed with *aṇ*, but this happens only when the suffix *ṇa* has the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*).

The word *māṃsa* ends in a suffix according to the rule *manerdīrghaśca*. The word *kalyāṇa* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) by the rule *laghāvante dvayośca bahvaṣo guruḥ*. Its meaning is as follows: when a light syllable (*laghu*) occurs at the end, or when two light syllables occur at the end, the heavy syllable (*guru*) of a word containing many vowels (*bahvaṣ*) becomes acute (*udātta*). The term *bahvaṣ* means "having many vowels" (*bahvac*). The term *aṣ* is a technical designation for vowels used by ancient teachers.

Regarding the rule *īkṣikṣamibhyāṃ ca*: here too, the intended meaning is simply that the first member retains its original accent (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*); the separation into two distinct rules is for the sake of stylistic variety. In this case, when one says "he who eats meat for a month," the word *bhakṣa* refers to the meat itself; since the root *bhakṣ* ends in the suffix *erac*, the formation is established through a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The same applies elsewhere. However, as for the root *bhakṣ* without the causative marker (*aṇ*), which ends in the suffix *ghañ*, the *bahuvrīhi* formation serves no purpose [in that context].

But is it not the case that in the word *bahubhakṣa*, the rule *baho-rnañ-vat* would result in the final syllable of the second member being udātta? If so, then in this case there will be a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a non-co-referential term ending in the suffix *ac* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*)—namely, "he whose eating is much" (*bahuṣu bhakṣo 'sya bahubhakṣaḥ*). In that instance, because the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*) does not possess plurality (*bahutva*), the accentuation of *bahu* will not apply. True; however, this statement is for the purpose of precluding the suffix *aṇ*. According to the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), [the suffix] *ac* applies after a stem ending in *a*, when there is no accompanying prefix (*anupapada*), as opposed to when there is a direct object (*karman*) as a prefix.

The suffix *ac* is prescribed after roots such as *pac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). The scope for this suffix *akāra* when it is not accompanied by an *upapada* is, for example, *pacati* → *pacaḥ*. The scope for [the suffix] when an *upapada* is present is, for example, *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* or *śaralāvaḥ*. In a case like *odanapāvaḥ*, where both rules would apply simultaneously, this very suffix *aṇ* occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. Consequently, the strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāvṛddhi*) and the obligatory formation of a compound with the *upapada* are secured. However, if the suffix *ac* were used instead, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would be merely optional.

And it should not be argued: "Let there be a conflict when there is a simultaneous intention [to express both]; however, when only the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is intended and the suffix *ac* has been applied, if a connection with *odana* (rice) is subsequently intended, would it not follow that *odanapaca* is also valid?"—because the usage is a single one. For within that very same usage, an object cannot be both intended and unintended. Therefore, *odanapaca* is simply incorrect. However, *gaṅgādharaḥ*, *śrīdharaḥ*, *vajradharaḥ*, *bhūdharaḥ*, and *sragdharaḥ* are technical names (*sañjñāśabda*).

However, when the position is that [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after all verbal roots (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ*), then, precisely because it is an exception (*apavāda*), it sublates that *aṇ*. Similarly, the rule "after a root with an *iṅ* vowel as its penultimate or after *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ*, the suffix *ka* is applied" finds its scope when there is no accompanying object (*anupapada*)—as in *vikṣipaḥ* and *vilikhaḥ*; whereas when an object is present as an accompanying word (*karmopapada*), that same [suffix *ka*] applies. In the case of *kāṣṭhabhedaḥ*, where both [rules] would otherwise apply, this very *aṇ* occurs by virtue of being subsequent in the rules. Likewise, the rule "after roots *limp* and *vind* when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*)" finds its scope when there is no accompanying object—as in *limpaḥ* from *limpati*; whereas when an object is present as an accompanying word, that same [suffix *aṇ*] applies.

In the case of *kuṅmalepa*, when both [suffixes] would apply, this very *aṇ* occurs by virtue of its being subsequent. As for the scope of *ka* [the suffix *kan*] prescribed by the rule *ātaścopasarge* when there is no accompanying word (*anupapada*), it is, for example, *suglaḥ* or *suglaḥ*; and when there is a word as an object (*karmopapada*), that same [suffix *kan*] applies. In the case of *gosandāya*, when both [suffixes] would apply, this very *aṇ* occurs by virtue of its being subsequent.
And [the substitution of] hvāva occurs for [the word] am. 3.2.2.

And [the root] *hvāva* (from *veñ* "to weave" in the sense of continuing a thread). The inclusion of the root *vā* ("to go" or "to smell") does not occur here because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*). For that root has the meaning of "wandering"—as in "the wind blows toward all directions" (*sarvā diśa āvāti*) or "may the wind blow healing medicine" (*vāta āvātu bheṣajam*). Even though the root with a prefix (*sopasarga*) is transitive (*sakarmaka*), it is not included, because the suffix *aṇ* is already established by the preceding rule. Furthermore, the usage *vātā vānti diśo daśa* ("winds blow toward the ten directions") is to be considered problematic.

Even if, in some instances, the root *veñ* is transitive in some way, nevertheless, due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with *hveñ*, only the form of *veñ* that possesses an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*) is understood here. Regarding *māṅ* in the sense of measuring: this is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the form *mā* that has an indicatory *ṅ*; therefore, the root *meṅ* in the sense of "bestowing" is also included. However, the root *mā* in the sense of "measuring," because it is intransitive when meaning "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*), is not included. [The rule] *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3) [applies].

*Ātaḥ-anupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3): The suffix *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Regarding the rule for the application of *ka*: "In all cases where *ka* is prescribed, it should be stated that the suffix *ḍa* is applied after roots containing a *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel. Those which undergo *saṃprasāraṇa* are called *saṃprasāriṇaḥ*. The root *jyā* (meaning "to decay" or "to diminish")—one who conquers the Veda (*brahma*) is a *brahmajyaḥ*. Because of the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) in the rule, it is not necessarily only here [in this specific example] that we have the form *āhvaḥ* or *prahvaḥ* according to *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136). For if there were an occasion for *saṃprasāraṇa* here, then when the form *āhva-a* is established, and once *saṃprasāraṇa* and the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatva*) have been performed, the substitution of *uvaṅ* would result in *āhuvaḥ* or *prahuvaḥ*. Similarly, one would get *brahmajiyaḥ*.

[The objection: "But once *saṃprasāraṇa* has been performed, the elision (*lopa*) of the long *ā* would occur; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would not take place. Furthermore, the elision itself is not established—because it is *antaraṅga*, it would apply first; and when the locus is the same, a rule concerning vowels (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning operations on bases (*āṅga*)? [The response: "In that case, the elision of the long *ā* will occur even before *saṃprasāraṇa*. Because it is subsequent (*para*), *saṃprasāraṇa* is obligatory (*nitya*), since it applies whether [the elision] has occurred or not. However, the elision of the long *ā* is non-obligatory (*anitya*), because once *saṃprasāraṇa* has been performed, [the condition for the elision] is removed by the preceding rule (*pūrvatva*)."

It is being refuted: that which has its cause obstructed by another rule is considered non-eternal (*anitya*). Thus, in this case, first there is the elision of the *ā* (by Pāṇini 6.4.64), then the *saṃprasāraṇa*, and then the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* would follow; however, because the elision of *ā* is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), those two [substitutions] will not take place.

But surely, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies to that which precedes an *ac* which has not been specified (*anādiṣṭa*), whereas this [substitution] precedes an *ac* that has been specified (*ādiṣṭa*)—for it was just stated that the elision of *al* (*allopa*) occurs first, and the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution occurs afterwards? If that is so, then because the elision of the vowel *ā* (*ākāralopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *uvaṅ* will not take place. But then, in cases such as *juhuvatuḥ* and *juhuvuḥ*, because the elision of *āl* is non-existent, the substitution of *uvaṅ* would not apply either? [In response: That non-existence based on the rule of mutual non-validity (*ābhīyam asiddhatvam*) is not universal; thus, it will not apply here.

Alternatively, in the rules *saṃprasāraṇācca* and *eḍaḥ padāntāt*, there is a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the term *eṅ*: "When *eṅ* follows a *saṃprasāraṇa*, a single substitute for both the preceding and the following [sounds] occurs, with the preceding one taking precedence. For what purpose is this? Is it not already established by *saṃprasāraṇācca* alone? It is for the sake of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*): that wherever *eṅ* can follow a *saṃprasāraṇa*, the substitution of *ā* prescribed by *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* does not take place.

If [the substitution] were to exist as something prior, its prescription for removal would be untenable. Therefore, in the case of *juhuvatuḥ*, since it is not occasioned by a specific condition (*anaimittika*), the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *ā* is not applied; rather, because the *eṅ* element is absent, when the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed, the *pūrva* (prior) substitution does not possess the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if the original were present), nor does it have the status of being *asiddha* (unestablished). Thus, the desired result is established. However, in cases such as *āhvaḥ*, *prahvaḥ*, and *brahmajyaḥ*, a suffix characterized by an *ā*-final stem cannot occur if the substitution of *ā* has not yet taken place. Consequently, first the substitution of *ā* occurs, then the suffix, then the elision of *āl* (*allopa*), and then the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization). Because of the status of *asiddha*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* do not occur.
The [substitution of] *su* occurs before the suffixes *sthaḥ*. 3.2.4.

Regarding the term *supi*: this is not a reference to the locative plural (*sup*), but rather to the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated designation). This is because it is that very term which is well-established in such rules as *suptiṅantaṃ padam*, *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*, and *avyayādāpsupaḥ*. As for the example *dvābhyāṃ pibati* ("he drinks from two"): one might object that words like *dvipada* are conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms; therefore, even though the meaning of the constituent parts is absent, the suffix *ka* would be applied by the rule *karmaṇy upapade* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) alone. This is not so.

Since it is possible to derive the meaning through etymology without abandoning the literal sense of the parts—as in the case of *dvābhyāṃ pibati* ("he drinks with two")—this [alternative] assumption is improper where such a derivation is possible. However, that assumption is appropriate only where it is absolutely impossible, as in the case of *tailatapa* ("oil-baking") and the like. By this [rule], it is intended that [the suffix] should apply in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Due to the force of its initial formulation, this [suffix] is withdrawn from the agent (*kartṛ*), and no other meaning is specified.

And suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed apply in their own inherent sense (*svārtha*), and the inherent sense of verbal roots (*dhātu*) is indeed "being" (*bhāva*). [Objection: But is it not the case that the suffix *ka* is established in the sense of "being" by the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*? [Reply: True; however, that statement is for the purpose of making the compound obligatory (*nityasamāsa*), otherwise there would be an optional genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Indeed, the compound with an upapada is always obligatory; thus, in the example *akhūnām utthānam*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with non-compounded words.
In the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*, the mention of the word *sthā* is so that the suffix *ka* may also occur in the sense of other factors of action (*kāraka*), excluding the agent (*kartṛ*).
The suffix *kha* is applied after the roots *tuda* and *śuca*, when they mean "to wipe away" and "to dispel," respectively.

Regarding *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ*: in the case of *tundaparimṛja*, although the rule *mṛjer ajādau saṃkramaḥ* is established by the principle *yasmin vidhis tadādau* ("a grammatical operation prescribed for a certain element applies to that element and what follows it"), the inclusion of the word *ādi* ("beginning with") is intended to capture the primary sense of "beginning with. Consequently, because this [word *parimṛja*] begins with a vowel only by virtue of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (metaphorical treatment as if it were the beginning), the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur here.

"Indolence," and so forth. The meaning is that the suffix occurs when indolence is implied and when the production of pleasure [is also implied]. In this context, by implication, it is stated that the suffix occurs when the agent is indolent and the one who brings about pleasure. "The mere removal of sorrow is another [type]" means that which merely dispels sorrow through the teaching of the impermanence of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and so forth, but does not produce pleasure—that is the "removal of sorrow. "From *mūlavibhuja* and so forth": this dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthya*), meaning "for the sake of establishing the forms *mūlavibhuja* and so forth."

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words), by which forms such as *mahīdhra*, *kudhra*, and *śiroruha* are established. Regarding the term *kākaguhā*: it is intended that the suffix *ka* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in "that which is to be hidden from crows" (*kākebhyo gūhitavyā*); therefore, this should be understood under the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*.
Before [a word ending in] *pra*, [the word *dāja* takes the suffix *kvin*]. 3.2.6.

"From *dājñaḥ*. This refers to the root *dadāti*. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); according to the principle "there is no distinction in the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and *ā*," the inclusion of all forms beginning with *dā* is intended. "And from *jānāti*. This mention is not made by eliding the *a* of the root *jan*; for in rules such as "the suffix *gha* after *khan*" and "the word *vadha* after *han*," the elision of *a* is not performed when citing the verbal root. "Preceded by *pra*" means being connected with the prefix *pra*. The term "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarge*) also carries over [from the previous rule], so the meaning is "preceded by *pra* alone. Consequently, in the case of *gosampradāya*, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.
The word *samī* [is used] in the sense of "near. (Pāṇini 3.2.7)
The suffix *ka* is applied after the verbal roots *gā* (to sing) and *puṣ* (to nourish). 3.2.8.

*gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8). Regarding the word *gāyateḥ*: since it is stated that "in the case of mentions of *gā-* and *mā-*, there is no distinction," it would follow that the root *gāṅ* (of the *luṅ*-class) is also included; however, this does not occur because of its association with *pibati*. In *sāmagī*, the elision of the long *ā* occurs due to the *kittva* of the suffix *ṭak*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because of its *ṭittva*. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *pibati* when *surā* and *śīdhu* are the objects": the mention of *pibateḥ* is merely a restatement of the meaning already obtained through the paribhāṣā concerning roots with and without *luk*-suffixes; the specific enumeration of the accompanying words (*upapada*), however, is indeed based on a direct rule (*vācanika*). In *kṣīrapā*, the feminine gender is cited because there is a specific rule for the feminine alone.
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *hṛ* when it does not mean "to carry."

Regarding "in *ac* when not preceded by *anu*": since it would have been possible to include *ghaṭī* (the feminine form) by means of the inclusion of *ghaṭa* itself through the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the rule that a term including its gender-distinguished forms), the explicit mention of *ghaṭī* is for the purpose of indicating that this *paribhāṣā* is not universally applicable (*anitya*). Regarding "another is one who merely grasps the thread": the meaning is that in the case of one who takes up the thread alone but does not hold it, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.
And [the suffix *ṇini* is used] after a word denoting age. 3.2.10.

And [the rule applies] in the case of age; that is, "or when it is understood. The sense is that even though the actual wearing of armor is absent, when age is implied, the term *kavacahara* (one who wears armor) is still used.
The suffix *āṅ* is used after a verb when expressing habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

Regarding the rule *āṅi tācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.178): by the example "the gathering of flowers" (*puṣpādyāharaṇe*), he demonstrates the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). He explains it as "inherent" (*svābhāvikī*); that which exists in its own nature (*svabhāve*) is "inherent," according to the group beginning with *adhyātma*. The word *sva-* is listed among the *dvāra-* group, and the rule for suffixes beginning with that [group] is intended there; however, due to the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, the grammatical operations of the *dvāra-* group do not apply, as the two words *svārthika* and *svābhāvika* are employed in the Bhāṣya. Its explanation is: "without regard for fruit. But how can one engage in that [action] without regard for fruit? For inherent nature (*svabhāva*) does not admit of questioning.
The suffix *arha* [is applied in the sense of "deserving"]. 3.2.12.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *rami* and *japi* when preceded by the words *stamba* and *karṇa*, respectively.

[The rule applies] to *ram* and *jap* when used with *stamba* and *karṇa*. Regarding the phrase "because *ram* is intransitive": one might object, "But was it not illustrated under the rules *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ* and *upācca* with the example *devadattam uparamati*? [The author] thinks thus: [the word] *anupasarge* ("without a prefix") is understood [to apply here]. Regarding the phrase "and because *jap* has sound as its object": this is because we observe such usage in examples like *mantraṃ japati*, where it clearly takes an object. The meaning is that for the simple roots *ram* and *jap*, no object consisting of a non-linguistic entity is possible. *Sūcakaḥ* means a slanderer (*piśunaḥ*).

Regarding "stamberama": [the compound is formed] with the non-elision [of the middle case-ending] according to the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam. Regarding "karṇe japitā maśakaḥ": the meaning is "one who makes a whispering sound near the ear."
The suffix *śam* is applied after the verbal root *dhā* when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed.

Regarding the rule *śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām*: "from the root alone" (*dhātumātrāt*). By the inclusion of the word "alone" (*mātra*), he shows that the suffix is applied even in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) would otherwise apply. As for the example *śaṅkara*: he is called *śaṅkara* because he brings about happiness pertaining to this world, the next world, and that which is called liberation (*mokṣa*). Demonstrating the purpose of including the word "root" (*dhātu*), he clarifies the very meaning established by the inclusion of the word "alone": *śami saṃjñāyām*. This means: in this sūtra.

If the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) were not made, the scope for the rule *śami-saṃjñāyām* would be cases such as *śambhavaḥ* and *śaṃvadaḥ*; the scope for the rule *kṛño hetu-tācchīlye* would be cases such as *śrāddhakaraḥ*. In the case of *śaṅkaraḥ*, where both rules would apply, the suffix *ṭa* alone would occur due to its higher priority; however, by the force of mentioning the verbal root, only the suffix *ac* occurs. But the teacher Kuṇḍakhāḍava maintains that this form belongs to the root *gṛṇāti* (meaning "to sound"), and that the letter *ka* arises from the letter *ra* due to the inclusion of words like *pṛṣodara* [in the list of irregular forms]; according to his view, the mention of the verbal root is of questionable utility.
The [karmasañjñā] applies to the verb *śī* (to lie) when it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Pāṇini 3.2.15.

[The rule] *adhikaraṇe śeteḥ* [is established]. Regarding the phrase *parśvādiṣu*: this is for the purpose of excluding the sense of "location" (*anadhikaraṇārtham*). He demonstrates this through its analysis (*vigraha*)—namely, *pārśvābhyām*. Regarding *digdhasahaśayaḥ*: [the analysis is] *digdhena saha śete* ("he sleeps with the poisoned arrow"). When the suffix *ac* is applied, a compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. The word *digdhasaha* belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group; thus, it is an upapada-compound (*upapadasamāsa*). Regarding *avamūrddhaśayaḥ*: one whose head (*mūrdhan*) is bent down (*avanata*) is *avamūrddha*; the meaning is that he sleeps face-down (*adhomukhaḥ*). Regarding *girau ḍaśchandasīti*: [this refers to the Vedic rule].

If it is said that [the suffix -śa] occurs only in the Vedic language (*chandas*), how is it that we have such forms as *giriśam upacacāra pratyahaṃ sā sukeśī* ("That fair-haired woman worshipped Giriśa every day") and *āropitaṃ yad giriśena paścāt* ("That which was later placed by Giriśa")? Poets are unrestrained. Others, however, say: here, because [the word] "girīśa" means "he who sleeps on a mountain" (*girau śete*) or "he who has a mountain" (*giris tasyāsti*), the suffix *cha* (which becomes *īśa*) is applied according to its appearance in the list beginning with *loman*. And thus, there is a *vārttika* on this very point: "Or [it may be derived] through a *taddhita* suffix. Furthermore, the mention of the Vedic language (*chandas*) does not apply even to the *loman*-group; therefore, the form *giriśa* occurs even in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
And by taking it in this way, the reading in the Nighaṇṭus also becomes appropriate: "he lies on the mountain" (girau śete), which means "he dwells on the mountain" (girāv āste).
The suffix *iṣṭha* is applied after [a stem] denoting that which is most desired. 3.2.16.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *bhikṣā*, *sena*, and *adāya*. (Pāṇini 4.2.17)

Regarding the examples *bhikṣācarya*, *ādāyacara*, and so on: in the word *bhikṣācara*, the root *car* here functions in the sense of "earning" preceded by that [object]; the meaning is "one who earns alms by wandering. In *senācara*, it refers to one who enters an army. In *ādāyacara*, the meaning is "one who goes after having taken," or "one who eats. How is it that there are forms such as *sahacaraḥ* and *sahacarī*? The suffix *caraṭ* is recited among the *pacādi* group; thus, it is a compound formed according to the rule *sup-supā*.
The suffix *sartin* is applied after the root *sṛ* when preceded by the words *pura*, *agra*, and *agre*.

Regarding the rule *puro'grato'greṣu sarteḥ*: the phrase "in these [words], namely *agre*" shows that the form *agra* is here prescribed as ending in the vowel *e*. This is understood precisely from the fact that *agre* is placed last in the compound; otherwise, according to the rule *ajādyadantam*, *agra* would have been placed first.

But for what purpose is the form ending in *-ā* (ekārāntatva) prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), given that even without the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case, *agresara* is established? Even when the analysis is made as "that which moves to the front" (*agram sarati*) or "that which moves by means of the front" (*agreṇa sarati*), one would still expect only *agresara*. How then is the expression "that herd, proud of its black antelope leading the way" (*yūthaṃ tadagrasaragarvitakṛṣṇasāram*) to be explained? It must be justified by the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely" (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*).
In the preceding [rules], the agent is the referent. 3.2.19.
The suffix *kṛt* is applied after the root *kṛ* in the senses of cause (*hetu*), habitual action (*tācchīlya*), and conformity (*ānulomya*).

Regarding the rule *kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣu*: the meaning is that the root *karoti* is understood here because it is more well-known; thus, this very root [with two anubandhas] is taken, and not the root *kṛñ* in the sense of "injury. Furthermore, the phrase "when *ānulomya* is implied" indicates that *hetu* and the others are not *upapadas*. This is understood from the inclusion of the word *dhātu* in the rule *śami dhātoḥ*, which serves to prohibit the suffix *ṭa* for the root *kṛñ* when *hetu* and so forth are present.

For if it were an *upapada*, since the suffix *ṭa* would not otherwise apply when *śamyā* is the *upapada*, that [suffix] would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, these [words] are neither *upapadas* nor are they the meanings of the suffixes; for if they were, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). And subversion is not appropriate when there is no contradiction. The term "cause" (*hetu*) means an "unconditional cause" (*aikāntika-kāraṇa*). The word "ekānta" should be understood as belonging to the *vinayādi* group [of words ending in -a], meaning "constant" or "invariable. By this, he shows that the term refers to a worldly (empirical) cause.

The sense is that an instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) cannot exist in relation to the root *kṛ* alone. Now, one might object: even by worldly standards, it is improper to qualify the agent by means of a "cause" (*hetu*), because there is no deviation [from this rule]; for there is no such thing as an agent who lacks a cause. True; however, because the word "cause" (*hetu*) is explicitly employed here, an absolute necessity (*aikāntikatva*) is intended, otherwise only a mere "occasioning factor" (*nimitta*) would have been mentioned. "Favorability" (*anukūlatā*) means conforming to the mind of the one to be propitiated. Regarding the phrase "knowledge that brings fame": by the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* etc., the visarga is changed to *s*.

In the case of *divā*, *vibhā*, *niśā*, *prabhā*, *bhāskara*, *anta*, *ananta*, *ādi*, *bahūn*, *nandī*, *kiṃ*, *lipi*, *libi*, *balin*, *bhakti*, *kartṛ*, *citra*, *kṣetra*, *saṃkhyā*, *jaṅghā*, *bāhu*, *ahaḥ*, *yattat*, *dhanus*, and *arus*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.4.87)

Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*): therein, because the word *divā* (by day) functions in the sense of the locative case ending *-i* (as in *ahni*), its status as an object (*karman*) is untenable; therefore, it is connected with the rule *supi*. However, for all the remaining words, the connection is with the rule *karmaṇi*. [The examples are: *divā-vibhā-niśā-prabhā-bhās-karānta-ananta-ādi-bahu-nāndī-kiṃ-lipi-libi-bali-bhakti-kartṛ-citra-tretā-saṃkhyā-jaṅghā-bāhu-ahaḥ-yat-tad-dhanus-arūṣ-ṣu*. In this context: *divā* means "during the day"; since it stands in the sense of a locative (*saptamyanta*), it cannot logically function as the direct object (*karman*). Consequently, it is governed by the rule *supi* (Pāṇini 3.2.4). As for the rest of the terms, they are governed by the rule *karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.1). [The list of examples follows: day (*divā*), distinction (*vibhā*), night (*niśā*), light (*prabhā*), the sun (*bhāskara*), end (*anta*), infinite (*ananta*), beginning (*ādi*), much (*bahu*), joy (*nāndī*), what? (*kim*), writing (*lipi*), manuscript (*libi*), Bali (*bali*), devotion (*bhakti*), agent (*kartṛ*), painting (*citra*), the triad (*tretā*), number (*saṃkhyā*), shanks (*jaṅghā*), arms (*bāhu*), day (*ahaḥ*), that which (*yat*), that (*tad*), bow (*dhanus*), and anger (*aruṣ*). In these cases, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to their respective grammatical roles.

If, however, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) were accepted in the context of the derivative formation (*vṛtti*), as in the cases of *doṣāmanya-ahaḥ* ("a day other than the evening") and *divāmanyā-rātriḥ* ("a night other than the day"), then the word *divā* would also be connected with the rule *karmaṇi*. Regarding the letter *s*: in the word *bhāskara*, the letter *s* is prescribed by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) in connection with the suffix; therefore, in the word *bhāskara*, the *visarjanīya* and *jihvāmūlīya* sounds do not occur. Alternatively: the *visarjanīya* and *jihvāmūlīya* do not occur for the letter *s*; why? Because of the irregularity (*nipātana*).

In the sūtra *bhāskarānta*, the pronunciation of the letter *sa* itself is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding *kārakara*: *kara* itself is *kāra*; the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*) because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group. Regarding *anantakara*: this form is also possible through a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with the word *antakara*; however, there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*), for the accent of the original form of the indeclinable as the prior member (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*)—being the "remaining one" (*satiśiṣṭa*)—would result, whereas what is desired is the oxytone (*anta-udātta*) by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*, which prescribes the accent of the original form of the *kṛt*-derived final member. [The example] *bahukara* is likewise explained.

The word *bahu* signifies "extensive" (*vaipulya*); however, if it were intended to signify "numerical quantity," that would already be established by the inclusion of the term *saṃkhyā*. The words *lipi* and *libi* are synonyms. Regarding *ahaskara*: in the word *ahan*, the substitution of *r* occurs by the rule *roḥ supi*; the change to *s* follows as before. [Examples include] *dhanuṣkaraḥ* and *aruṣkaraḥ*.

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya. However, because the root rule is set aside by the Vārttika "kiṃyattadvahuṣu kṛño 'jvidhānam," the *ṭ* [substitution] does not occur; thus, they say that forms such as *kiṃkarī* are incorrect except in the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) and so forth. In some manuscripts, there is the following text: "Alternatively, it will be included in the list beginning with *vac* (the *vac-ādi* group). The meaning of this is: here, having removed the mention of *kim* and others, one should read "kiṃyattadvahuṣu kṛñaḥ" within the *pac-ādi* group itself.
The [kṛt] affix *kha* is applied after a verbal root denoting an action when it signifies wages (*bhṛti*). (Pāṇini 3.2.22)

Regarding "in the sense of work" (*karmaṇi*) and "in the sense of wages" (*bhṛtau*): the mention of "in the sense of work" (*karmaṇi*) is for the purpose of grasping the word-form itself, because it is qualified by the term "in the sense of work" (*karmaṇi*) which is carried over [from the previous rule]. "The price of work" (*karmanirveśa*) means that "work" (*karman*) refers to action; the meaning is that it is the food and other materials to be given for the sake of compensating that action.
Nor [should one apply it] to words, verses, quarrels, songs, enmity, flattery, urine, mantras, or phrases. 3.2.23.
The affix *iN* is applied after the words *stamba* and *śakṛt* [to form a word denoting the agent].

In the case of *stamba-śakṛt*, the suffix *in* [is applied]. In the form *stambakari*, because of the *niṭ* designation [of the suffix], the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) becomes acutely accented on its first syllable by the rule of the original accent of the subsequent member of a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the roots *hṛ* (to take away) and *dā* (to give), when the object is a domestic animal. 3.2.25.

"In the case of *paśu* [when used] with the roots *hṛ* and *dā*, the agent is [the meaning]. By this, he shows that the animal (*paśu*) is a qualifier of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, and not its sublater. For, since a suffix is prescribed after a verbal root, the suffix ought to express that which is connected to the meaning of that root; and the meaning of the root, being an action, is connected with its instrument (*sādhana*).

The word *paśu* (animal), however, denotes a thing belonging to the class of quadrupeds by way of its own form (*svarūpa*), not by way of its capacity (*śaktimat*), and certainly not by way of its capacity itself. It is therefore rightly stated that "in the case of *paśau* [as] the agent," for it is not logical that the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) should become the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) by way of its own form. Thus, in all cases, the qualifier of the meaning of the suffix should be understood in this manner.
The suffix *ini* is applied after a verbal root to form nouns meaning "one who bears fruit" (*phalegrahi*) and "one who nourishes himself" (*ātmambhari*).

*Phalegrahi* and *ātmambhari*. [The rule] states that the prefix ends in the vowel *e*; however, in Vedic usage, it is also seen ending in the vowel *a*, as in: *yā vanaspatīnām phalagrahiḥ*. This term should be included with the word *kukṣimbhari* by means of the particle *ca* (and).
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *van*, *san*, *rakṣ*, and *math*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix *ini* is applied] after the roots *vana*, *san*, *rakṣ*, and *math*. The meaning is that only the two roots *vana* (meaning "to acquire") and *ṣaṇ* (meaning "to distribute/share"), which belong to the Bhūvādigaṇa and are listed together in the same group, are to be understood here; it does not refer to the two roots *vanu* (meaning "to beg") and *ṣaṇu* (meaning "to give") belonging to the Tanādigaṇa. The reason for this is their association (*sāhacarya*) and their lack of an indicatory letter (*niranubandhakatva*). *Brahmavanim*: with the intention of saying "he acquires Brahman" (*brahma vanati*) or "he acquires Kṣatra" (*kṣatraṃ vanati*), the suffix *ini* is applied, and the second case singular is formed from that stem. *Gosanim*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he acquires cows" (*gāṃ sanati*).
"Pathirakṣī" means "those who protect the path"; this is the analysis of the compound. "Havirmathayaḥ" means those who churn the oblation; [the term refers to] those havirmathas.
The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *ej*. 3.2.28.

Regarding the rule *ejeh khaś*: the mention here of *ej-* is not for the sake of the root *ej-* itself; rather, it is because of the addition of the marker *ś* to *khaś*. For that [marker *ś*] ensures that [the suffix] would be treated as a *sārvadhātuka* so that the suffix *śap* may apply. Now, there is no difference whether the suffix *śap* is present or absent for another root-form (*prakṛtyantara*) such as *ej-*. And since this purpose is possible here, it is not appropriate to assume it serves solely a subsequent purpose. As for the addition of the marker *s* (in *khaś*), it is for the sake of the elision of *m*; this is an indication for the grammatical operations triggered by the marker *kh*.

*Śunindhayaḥ*, *nāḍindhayaḥ*, and *nāsikandhayaḥ*: here, the shortening [of the vowel] is also a purpose [of the rule]. "The letter *śa* is for the sake of the *sārvadhātuka*" means that it is for the sake of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *sārvadhātuka*. Regarding *vātaśunī* and so forth: when *vāta* and the others are the respective governing words (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* occurs after verbal roots beginning with *aj*. In *śarddhajahā*, from the root *ohāk* (meaning "to abandon") belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is reduplication due to the *ślu* affix; then, by the rule "*śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*," there is the elision of the long *ā*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *dhmā* and *dheṭ* when followed by the words *nāsikā* and *stana*.

Regarding *nāsikāstanayordhmādheṭoḥ*: in the form *nāsikandhama*, the substitution of *dham* is applied by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*. By the phrase "And this," etc., he states the reason for the absence of the correspondence between the order of elements (*yathāsaṃkhya*). This refers to the grammatical operation characterized by the absence of such correspondence. By this, it is merely demonstrated that even the author of the Sūtras, as the ultimate authority for commentators, must have had some specific intention regarding this matter.

Therefore, this is not to be urged: why does the connection with each individual [word] not occur as in the subsequent sūtra, or why does the reverse not occur? They say that the suffix *ṅīp* is applied here alone, and not elsewhere. *Stanandhayati*. It is here that *ṅīp* is prescribed, and not anywhere else; so they say.
And [the same applies] to the words *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi*. (Pāṇini 3.2.30)
