And in the case of *nāḍī* and *muṣṭi*: *ghaṭindhamaḥ*, *kharindhamaḥ*. *Ghaṭī* means a jar (*ghaṭaḥ*); *kharī* means a female donkey (*gardabhī*), with the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule for feminine nouns denoting a genus (*jāti*). Others read *khārī*, which is a word signifying a measure (*parimāṇa*). The word *vāta* has not been observed [in this context].
The suffix *u* is applied after the roots *ruj* and *vah*, when followed by the word *kūla*.

In the case of *udi kūle rujivahoḥ*, wherever he intends for each member to be an *upapada*, he pronounces the locative case from the entire compound, as in *nāḍīmuṣṭyoḥ*. Here, however, the reverse has been done; therefore, *udi* is a locative absolute (*satsaptamī*). As for *kūle*, it is the very sign for the designation of *upapada* regardless of its meaning. And in that regard, by the rule *te prāgdhātoḥ*, the word *ut* is placed before the verbal root, and the word *kūla* is placed before that. This is what is shown [by the commentary]: "with *ut* preceding, when *kūla* is the *upapada* in the sense of the object."
The suffix *lih* is applied after the word *vaha* when followed by *abhra*.
The suffix *pac* [is applied] after a word denoting a measure. (Pāṇini 3.2.33)

Regarding the rule *parimāṇe pacaḥ*: the word "measure" (*parimāṇa*) refers to objects such as a *prastha* (a specific grain-measure) made of wood and so forth. It does not have a syntactic connection as an object with the root *pac* (to cook), which denotes the act of softening. Therefore, this is not a reference to the literal form [of the word "measure"]; rather, its specific instances, such as the *prastha* and others, are what are intended. And these [words] refer both to the measure itself and to the things measured, such as rice and the like. In that context, since words denoting the measure itself cannot connect with the root *pac*, the suffix is applied to those words residing in the thing measured. If it is argued that they do not then denote a measure, the answer is no; for the word *prastha* and others are applied to the thing measured through the superimposition of the measure upon it.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after *mitanakhī*. 3.2.34.
And [the term] *mitanakhī* [is derived from] *nakhampaca*; here, the root *pac* signifies "to burn."
The suffix *tud* is applied after the words *vidhu* and *aruṣ*. 3.2.35.

Regarding *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ*: in the word *aruntuda*, the augment *mum* is added after the letter *u* by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum*; then, the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) is elided.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the words *asūrya* and *lalāṭa*, when they are used in the sense of "showing" (*dṛśita*). 3.2.36.

Regarding the forms *asūryalalāṭayoḥ* and *dṛśitapaḥ*: in the case of *asūryampaśyāḥ*, the substitution of *paśya* is according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdrśaḥ śaḥ*. This [usage] has "secrecy" (*gupti*) as its primary sense. As for the statement—"the king's wives are *asūryampaśyāḥ*"—this is principally concerned with secrecy; therefore, the meaning is that even if they do see the sun, such usage is not contradictory. He clarifies that secrecy is indeed the primary sense by saying, "of such a nature."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied after the words] *ugra*, *paśya*, *iramman*, and *pāṇindhama*. (Pāṇini 4.2.37)

*Ugrampaśya*, *irammada*, and *pāṇindhama*. *Ugrampaśya*: "He who sees fiercely. This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). *Irammada*: Regarding the term *irammada*, although the suffix *śyan* would normally apply by rule because the root *mad* (meaning "to rejoice") belongs to the *divādi* class, its absence here is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Irā* means water. *Pāṇindhama*: These are paths. Furthermore, they are so called because travelers on them blow upon their hands—making a sound—to ward off snakes and other dangers.
The suffix *khac* is applied after the root *vad* when preceded by *priya* or *vaśa*.

In the rule *priyavaśe vadaḥ khac*, the letter *k* in *khac* is for the purpose of specification, as in the rule *khaci hrasvaḥ*. If it were stated simply as *khe hrasvaḥ*, would this not also apply to cases such as *ejeḥ khaś*—namely, *aṅgamejayaḥ* and *janamejayaḥ*? It will not apply there because of the principle: "When a term with one *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include a term with two *anubandhas*."

In that case, consider this: in the word *kulīnaḥ* (derived from *kulāt khaḥ*), would there not be the need for a short vowel to prevent the elision of the suffix *ya*, as in the rule *yasyeti ca*? To that, [the answer is]: the mention of a "suffix" (*pratyaya*) here refers to a verbal suffix (*dhātupratyaya*), due to its association with that specific section; thus, the purpose of this *ca* (and) is to be considered. Furthermore, the inclusion of other suffixes is for the sake of subsequent rules. For instance, in the case of *dviṣantapaḥ*, both the shortening of the vowel and the elision of the *ṇi* suffix would apply, but the *śap* augment should not occur. If that is so, what is the purpose of placing the rule here when it ought to have been placed later? It is for the purpose of indicating that [the operation] occurs even after other [suffixes].
Therefore, it need not be stated that "there is an addition [of the suffix *kha*] after the root *gam* when followed by a *sup*-ending word.
As in *mitaṅgama*: this is for the sake of non-technical (*asaṃjñā*) usage; for in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it is already established by the rule to be stated later, "and after *gam*.
Pāṇini 3.2.39: After the root *tap*, [the suffix *kha* is added] when *dviṣat* or *para* precede.

Regarding the form *dviṣantapa* [from the root *tap* with the prefix *dviṣat*]: by the rule *mu-mi saṃyogāntalopaḥ*, there is the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga*. As for the statement that "the citation contains two *t* sounds," therein one *t* sound qualifies the word *dviṣat*—namely, that the word *dviṣat* ends in a *t*. Because this is a Vedic-style (Sautra) citation, the qualifier is placed after the qualified term. Consequently, it does not apply to the feminine. The underlying sense is that otherwise, by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning forms qualified by gender), the undesired application would indeed occur.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *vāc* when it occurs in connection with the term *vrata*.

Regarding *vāci yamo vrate* [Pāṇini 3.2.40]: the term *śāstrita* is derived from the word *śāstra*; the suffix *ṇic* is applied to the verbal root in the sense of its own meaning (*dhātvartha*) when it signifies an injunction (*vidhāna*). From that which ends in *ṇic*, the suffix *kta* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, *śāstrita* means "enjoined by a treatise" (*śāstre vihitaḥ*) or "prescribed by a treatise" (*śāstreṇa*). Regarding *niyama*: it is a specific kind of resolve (*saṅkalpaviśeṣaḥ*). Regarding *vācaṃyama*: the form *vācaṃyama-* and *purandara-* are established by the rule "*vācaṃyamapurandarau ca*" (Pāṇini 6.3.69), which prescribes the addition of the suffix *am* to the first member of the compound. Therefore, the suffix will indeed occur precisely because of that very irregularity (*nipātana*).

In that case, would it not then apply even outside of a vow (*vrata*)? To that very point, the inclusion of the word "vow" (*vrata*) will be made—namely, in the rule *vācaṃyamo vrata-purandarau ca*—but that purpose is questionable. By this, *purandara* is also explained.
Regarding *vāgyama*: when one restrains speech due to incapacity or other such reasons, the suffix *aṇ* occurs there as well.
The word *pūḥ* [is used] with both *dāri* and *sahaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.41)

The term *pūḥ* [is used] after the roots *dṛ* and *sah*. The root *dṛ* taken here is the one meaning "to tear apart" (*vidāraṇe*); it is not the two roots *dṛ* meaning "fear" (*bhaye*) or *dṛṅ* meaning "respect" (*ādare*). The inclusion of *sah* is for the purpose of excluding its technical name (*saṃjñā*), whereas regarding that technical name, he will state [the rule] later. Thus, *sarvasahaḥ* means "a king capable of accomplishing everything."
The suffix *kaṣa* is applied after the words *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *megha*, *ṛti*, or *bhaya*.

Regarding the rule "after the roots *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya*, [the suffix *a* is added] to *kṛ*"—that is, to the root *kṛ* (as in *karoti*). However, the root *kṛṇoti* is not included here, for the same reason as previously stated. Furthermore, the form *śivaṃkara* is also seen in the Vedic language—as in the passage: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the bringer of auspiciousness (*śivaṃkara*)."
The suffix *aṇ* is also applied [after the word *kṣema*] when it means "one who loves" (*priya*) or "one who brings benefit" (*madra*).
The suffix *kviṣ* is applied after the root *bhū* following the word *āśita*, in the senses of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the state (*bhāva*). (Pāṇini 3.2.45)

Regarding the rule *āśite bhuvaḥ karaṇabhāvayoḥ*: here, the word *supi* (after a nominal suffix) is understood to apply, but not the word *karmaṇi* (in the sense of the object), because the root *bhū* is intransitive. The intention is that the suffix *khac* should not occur after the root preceded by a prefix when it has the sense of "attaining," due to the lack of such usage (*anabhidhānāt*). This word *āśita* is derived from the root *aś* (to eat) with the prefix *āṅ*, ending in the *kta* suffix while the object is not intended to be expressed—namely, *āśitaḥ kartā* ("one who has eaten as the agent"), whose initial vowel will be prescribed as udātta.

However, they say that the *kta* suffix prescribed by the rule "after roots meaning staying (*dhrauvya*), going (*gati*), and eating (*pratyavasāna*), [it occurs] in the sense of the action, the object, or the locus" is not included here, because there is no such usage (*anabhidhāna*). Others, however, maintain that the word *āśita* is taken when the *kta* suffix is applied to the causative (*ṇyanta*) of the root *aś* (to eat) in the sense of the object of the caused agent (*prayojya-karman*). Thus, even in the case where the word *āśita-kartṛ* has its initial vowel udātta, it is the caused agent (*prayojya*) who is called the "agent" (*kartṛ*) by way of a former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), because the rule "after roots meaning going, knowing, and eating" prescribes the designation "object" (*karman*) for the agent of the non-causative (*aṇau*) when it becomes the object of the causative (*ṇau*).

And likewise, in the case of *kṛṣann it phāla āśitam kṛṇoti*, no avagraha is observed for the word beginning with an udātta accent. However, the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) there is for the purpose of excluding the "state of being" (*bhāva*). As for *āśitambhava odanaḥ*, that very rice by which a guest or others are fed is so called.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the verbal roots *bhṛ*, *vṛj*, *dhṛ*, *sah*, *tap*, and *dam*, when they are followed by the word *saṃjñā*.

Regarding the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛvṛjidhārisahitapidamaḥ*: "on account of being a name" (*saṃjñāvaśāt*), and so forth. In cases such as *śatruntapaḥ* ("one who torments his enemies"), where the sense of the object (*karman*) is understood, the term *karmaṇi* ("in the sense of the object") is connected [to the rule]. However, in cases where it is not understood, such as *rathantaram*, the term *supi* ("after a nominal suffix") is connected. As for *arindamaḥ* ("subduer of enemies"), the root *dam* (to subdue) takes an object when its causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is implied internally.
And [the word] *gama* [is also used]. 3.2.47.

"And *gama*. [The reason for] this separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that only *gam* may be carried forward in the subsequent rules, and not *bhṛ*, *tṝ*, and the others.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the words *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhvan*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*. (Pāṇini 5.2.48)

[The suffix] *ḍa* [is applied] after [the words] *anta*, *atyanta*, *adhva*, *dūra*, *pāra*, *sarva*, and *ananta*. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the capacity of the marker (*anubandha*)": the letter *ḍ* is not for the purpose of being heard (i.e., it is not *śravaṇārtha*), because the word ending in the suffix *ḍa* is cited in the rule *pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu* after the elision of *ṭi* has been effected. Here, the mention of *atyanta* and *ananta* is redundant; the word *anta* is what is intended here, and since it qualifies the object (*karman*), the rule of "specification by the final member" (*tadantavidhi*) will apply.

However, in the case of a rule prescribing an *upapada* (an accompanying word), the rule of "extension to that which ends with [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply everywhere, because of the restriction: "In a rule prescribing an *upapada*, the mention of 'that which begins with it' (*tadādyādi*) is understood. For example, one who goes as if fallen or dropped is called a *pannaga*. In the rule "after *su* and *dur* when the sense is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), just as in the case of *khala*: thus we have *sugama* ("easy to go") and *durgama* ("difficult to go"). Since it is observed elsewhere as well, the present *sūtra* is for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *han* when used in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*).

Regarding the rule *āśiṣi hanaḥ*: the word *dārau* means the word *dāru*. It is used in the masculine gender because it refers to the word itself. This statement is for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *ṭ*; [otherwise] the suffix *aṇ* would already be established by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. The inclusion of the term *anta-* (final) is for the sake of clarity; [the desired result] is already established by the rule *alo’ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52).
The suffix *ap* is used after words meaning "affliction" (*kleśa*) and "darkness" (*tamas*). 3.2.50.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the words *kumāra* and *śīrṣa*.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after the words *kumāra* and *śiras*. Although this is already established by the rule *supyajātau*, this statement is made for the sake of expressing the sense of "habitual practice" (*tācchīlya*) and to effect the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras*.
The suffix *aṣṭak* is applied after the words *jāyā* and *patī* when they denote a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Pāṇini 3.2.52.

Regarding the rule *lakṣaṇe jāyāpatyoṣṭak*: "possessing a mark" (*lakṣaṇavatī*). By this, he shows that the word *lakṣaṇa* ends in the suffix *ac* (added after the class beginning with *arśas*). This is understood precisely from the formulation of the sūtra itself; for if *lakṣaṇa* were used in its simple form, the suffix would already be established by the subsequent rule. An example is *jāyāghnaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ* ("a Brahmin who kills his wife"). One who has a mole or similar mark on him that is a sign of his wife's death is said to "kill her"—this is a figurative expression (*gauṇaḥ śabdaḥ*). By this, *patighnī* ("one who kills her husband") is explained. There is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopaḥ*) by the rule *gamahana-*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added because of the *ṭi*-marker.
And [the suffix *kṛt* is used] when the agent is a non-human being. 3.2.53.

And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a word denoting a non-human agent. It was stated previously that the term "non-human" (*amanuṣya*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth; however, here it includes everything other than a human. Now, one might object: just as in the previous rule the mention of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) serves as a qualifier of the agent which is the meaning of the suffix, so too here the mention of "non-human" will suffice; thus, there would be no purpose in mentioning the "agent" (*kartṛ*). If it were simply said "in the case of a non-human" (*amanuṣye*), it might also be understood as a subordinate word (*upapada*). Therefore, the mention of "agent" is made. The word *kṛtaghna* should be seen among the *mūlavibhuja*-type compounds.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *śakti*, *hastin*, and *kapāṭa*. (Pāṇini 3.2.54)

[The suffix *ghañ* is used] after the roots *śak* ("to be able") and *han* ("to kill") when followed by the words *hastin* ("elephant") and *kapāṭa* ("door"), respectively. For example: "He kills the elephant with poison. Now, one might object: "In this case too, since agency is impossible for one who lacks capacity, capacity must indeed exist [as a prerequisite]. True; however, by the force of the inclusion of the word "capacity" (*śakti*), what is understood is a pre-eminence [of power], and thus the capacity that exists by its own strength, independent of anything else, is what is grasped. This is shown as follows: "A man capable of killing an elephant is called 'an elephant-killer' (*hastighna*). And so, whether he actually kills the elephant or not, he is called an "elephant-killer" because of his possession of that capability.

"What does it split as one enters?"—thus he derives the word *kapāṭa*. However, the form *kavāṭa* is more commonly known; in that case, the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*) is added to the root *aṭ*, and by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the substitution of *kavaṅ* for *ku* when followed by *uṣṇa*," the substitution of *kavā* for *ku* occurs.
The terms *pāṇigha* and *tāḍagha* denote an artisan. (Pāṇini 3.2.55)

The suffix *khyun* is applied after the root *kṛ*, in the sense of an instrument, when it follows words meaning "wealthy," "fortunate," "stout," "grey-haired," "naked," "blind," or "dear," provided these words end in the suffix *cvī* (or its substitutes) and do not themselves end in *cvī*. (Pāṇini 3.2.56)

In the sense of the suffix *cvy-*, after the words *āḍhya*, *subhaga*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*—provided that *cvy-* does not actually follow—the suffix *khyun* is applied to the root *kṛ* when the agent is the instrument (*karaṇa*). By the phrase "after *āḍhya* and so forth," he shows that these words function as *upapadas*. By the phrase "when the agent is the instrument," he also indicates that the instrument is the meaning of the suffix.

Now, why is it not understood in this way: "when a word from the *āḍhya*-class is a *karaṇa* (instrument) and the agents [of the action] are those [very words]"? It is said in reply: because of the rule "in the sense of *cvy*-derivatives, except when *at* follows" (*cvyartheṣvaccau*), the words *āḍhya* and so on have their own form as the primary meaning; and it is not possible for words themselves to function as agents. But surely, in the case of "the word *āḍhya* produces pleasure by being heard," the status of the word as an agent is indeed possible? If that is so, then such a [literal] interpretation is not accepted due to the nature of the commentary. In the expression "except when *at* follows" (*acvau*), it is either a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*, meaning "that which does not end in *at*" (*acvyanta*).

The singular number is used because the connection applies to each [item] individually. But how is it that they are both *cvi*-derivatives and yet end in the suffix *-ac*? He says: "Because the suffix *cvi* is prescribed optionally. In the form *āḍhyaṅkaraṇam*, the letter *kh* in the suffix *khyun* is for the purpose of eliding the penultimate vowel (*mum*), and by the rule concerning words qualified by gender, it serves to shorten the vowel when feminine bases such as *āḍhyā* and others are the upapadas. The letter *n* is for the sake of accent. The substitution of *an* occurs in place of *y* and *v*.

The meaning is "they are anointing," because verbal roots have multiple meanings. Therefore, in this case, since one who was previously not wealthy (*anāḍhya*) is made wealthy (*āḍhya*), there is an absence of the *abhūtatadbhāva* (the state of becoming what one was not). Or, even if *abhūtatadbhāva* were to apply here, he says that this counter-example is nonetheless appropriate: "when the original state (*prakṛti*) is not intended [to be expressed].

When it is the original state itself that is intended to be expressed as undergoing transformation—as in "the threads become cloth"—then the suffix *cv-* is used; and thus the Vārttika states: "and there is the mention of the non-intention of the original state. Here, "original state" refers to the prior condition of the effect.

"What is the purpose of [the word] *aśvī*?"—this is the intended meaning of what is about to be said, which he reveals with the words "But surely... [he says]. It should be formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* here, according to the rule "and in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Nor is there any difference between *lyuṭ* and *khyun*; for in the case of *lyuṭ*, the form would be *āḍhyīkaraṇa*, and the accent would likewise be the acute on the first syllable of the second member by the accent of the *lit* suffix.

The word *khyun* is also udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the *nitsvara* accent. Furthermore, shortening occurs according to the rules "khityanavyayasya" and "arurdviṣadajantasya mum," and the augment *mum* is prescribed for non-indeclinables (*anavyaya*). Since words ending in *cvī* are indeclinables—because they are included among particles by the rule "ūryādi-cvi-ḍācaśca"—there is no difference in form or accent between the masculine and feminine genders in both cases. The suffix *ṅīp* applies in the feminine in both instances by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... and so forth; therefore, there is no distinction in either form or accent. Moreover, [the mention of the masculine] is for the sake of what follows.

In the subsequent sūtra, since the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are excluded, there must be [the application of] suffixes such as *tṛc*; this is the distinction. Why, then, was it stated previously—"by the force of the prohibition"? The intention is that it refers to the force of the prohibition in this very sūtra. For if it were intended solely for the sake of the subsequent rule, he would have stated "in the case of *ac* and *au*" right there, just as he will state later—"here, in the case of *trapu*. In the Bhāṣya, however, it remains established as being solely for the sake of the subsequent rule.
The suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukan* are added after the root *bhū* when used in the sense of the agent.

The suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khul* are applied after the root *bhū* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. The mention of "agent" (*kartṛ-grahaṇam*) is for the purpose of excluding the instrument (*karaṇa*), and also for the sake of subsequent rules. The letter *kh* is for the purpose of eliding the *m* (in the case of *khul*), the letter *c* is for the sake of the accent (*svara*), and the letter *ñ* is for the purpose of *vṛddhi*. For what purpose is *khiṣṇu* made to begin with the letter *i*, rather than simply saying *khsnu*? To this, the following point is made: [if it were *khsnu*] the letter *c* would not need to be included for the sake of the accent, as it would be established by the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyaya-svara*). [Objection: By what means, then, is its beginning with the letter *i* established? To that he says: "Because of its being acute-accented" (*udāttatvāt*).

The word *bhavati* is udātta; because it is udātta, the augment *iṭ* will occur [after it]. Regarding the phrase "of *nañ*": the term "*nañaḥ*" is in the ablative case, meaning that this is for the sake of establishing the accent of a word ending in *khiṣṇuc* that follows *nañ*. If this [word *aniṣṇu*] were not made to begin with the vowel *i*, then even though *iṭ* were present, there would be no inclusion of it under the rule "the kṛtya suffixes, *uka*, *eṣṇuc*, *cāru*, and so forth," because of the absence of the particle *ca* (in the rule).

If, on the other hand, the particle *ca* were also added here, even so, because the form would be derived through a secondary grammatical operation (*lākṣaṇikatva*) and because the rules for *ṣatva* and *ṇatva* are considered *asiddha*, the form *iṣṇuc* would not exist [to be captured], and thus there would still be no inclusion. Therefore, it is made to begin with the vowel *i*.

But surely, even though it begins with the vowel *i*, by the rules "when there is the mention of that which has such an *anubandha*, [there is no mention of] that which does not have that *anubandha*" and "when there is the mention of that which has one *anubandha*, [there is no mention of] that which has two *anubandhas*," there ought to be a mention only of *iṣṇuc* (in *alaṃkṛñ*), and not of this [suffix *khṣṇuj*]. [To this, the author] thinks: "By the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *i*, there will be a mention of this one as well.

If that is so, let there simply be *khṣṇuj*; since the mention of this one is established even there—by the force of the inclusion of the letter *c* for the sake of the *ṣ*-ness and *ṇ*-ness, and for the sake of the letter *c* itself once the augment *iṭ* has been applied—the fact that it begins with the vowel *i* serves no purpose and is therefore questionable.
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *spr̥ś* when it does not mean "water."

Regarding the phrase *spṛśo 'nudake kvin* and so forth: the objection begins with *nanu ca* ("But surely..."). It was stated under the rule *supi sthaḥ* that "in the case of transitive verbs, [the word] *karmani* (in the sense of the object) is understood, whereas elsewhere, when a *sup*-ending word is present, [it is understood as] *upapade*" (as an upapada). Therefore, the intention is that the statement "the suffix *kvin* occurs when there is an upapada ending in a *sup* [case-ending]" is untenable. The phrase *tatkartṛpracayārtham* means: since the suffix *kvin* is already established in the sense of the agent by the rule *kartari kṛt*, there is no other purpose for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *kartari*; this is the intended meaning. Thus, the accumulation of agents (*kartṛpracaya*) is obtained.

In the case of an object (*upapada*), there is one agent (*kartṛ*), and another [agent] in the case of an instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth; thus, there is an accumulation [of agents]. In the word *ghṛtaspṛk*: by the rule "the *kvin* suffix becomes *ku*," the *ś* is changed to *ṣ* due to internal similarity (*antaratamya*) based on being a voiced aspirate (*soṣman*); then, by the rule "the *jaś* substitutes for *jhal* sounds at the end of a word," the *ṣ* becomes *k*. The *k* of *kvin* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; the *i* is for the purpose of qualifying [the suffix] as "that which has no other [consonant] attached" (*apṛkta*) according to the rule "of *vi* when it is *apṛkta*."

What is the purpose of the letter *n*? For this [suffix] is prescribed after monosyllabic bases (*ekāc*), and in those cases, the desired form is already established by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). If so, what about that which has more than one vowel, such as *dadhr̥k*? To this he will say: "The reduplication and the final acute accent for the root *dhṛṣ*" [Pāṇini 6.1.159]. If that is the case, then when it is stated "of the suffix *kvin*" or "of the suffix *kvip*," there would be a doubt: whether the reference is to *kvi* or to *kvip*. Even if it were the reference to *kvi*, the doubling of the letter *p* would occur according to the rule "also before non-consonants" (*anaci ca*) [Pāṇini 8.4.47].
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the verbal roots *ṛtviñ*, *dhṛk*, *sraj*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, *añcu*, *yuj*, and *kruñc*.

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *ṛt*, *yaj*, *dhṛ*, *sraj*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, *añc*, *yuj*, and *kruñc*. Regarding "he sacrifices at the proper season (*ṛtau yajati*"): this refers to the spring and other seasons. Regarding "he sacrifices the season (*ṛtuṃ yajati*"): this refers to a sacrifice in which the season is the deity, such as—"He offers *kapiñjala* birds to Spring; three tawny ones are for Spring"—wherein he offers the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśūn*); or as in "May summer, winter, and also spring, autumn, and the rainy season [be favorable to us]," and so forth—this is intended in that sense. Or, regarding "impelled by the season (*ṛtuprayuktaḥ*"): this is intended in the sense of the agency [of the sacrificer] in passages such as "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring."

"And [the change to] *ṣ*. Otherwise, there would be the prohibition by the rule "after *sa*, and at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*). "Only when it ends in a case-suffix" (*subantamātre*): otherwise, because it would have an object, the suffix would apply only in the sense of the object (*karman*). "Only from the root alone" (*kevalādeva*): this is also obtained through the force of the prescription of the *kvip* suffix; for there is no difference between *kvip* and *kvip* after the root *yuji* with an upapada, since the change to *k* (*kutva*) is already established by the rule "of *cu*, *ku*" (*coḥ kuḥ*).

However, when there is no upapada, the prescription of *kvip* after the root *yuj-* becomes meaningful for the purpose of changing the *n* to *k* (kutva) once the *num* augment has been applied by the rule *yujerasamāse*. But if it were said that *kvip* occurs after *yuj-*—whether with an upapada or without one—by virtue of its association with the *nipātana* forms, then the mention of *yuj-* in the rule *satsūdviṣa-* could have been omitted. [Question: Why does the elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) not occur? [Answer: These two roots, *kuñc-* and *kruñc-*, meaning "crookedness" and "becoming small," do not have a penultimate *n*.

Similarly, in the case of *nikuciti*, the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *n* is observed; however, due to the substitution of *c* for *j*, the sound *ja* is heard. Because that [substitution] is considered asiddha (not yet established), the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30) does not apply to change the *c* into *k* when followed by the letter *c*. For those who read the root as having *n* as its penultimate letter—as in *kuñcau*, *kuñca*, and so on—the [change to *k*] would indeed occur; in that case, it must be stated that it does not happen because of the rule *saṅijhalī*. Here, *saṅ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term) beginning with the *sa* of *san* and ending with the *ṅ* of *mahiṅ*.

Others, however, say that *kuñci* is a single root, and that the letter *r* following the letter *k* is also introduced by way of an irregularity (*nipātana*) in connection with the suffix *kvip*. Vāmana will explain this very point under the rule *coḥ kuḥ*.
After the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the suffixes *ka* and *kan* are applied to the root *dṛś* when it does not mean "to look at. (Pāṇini 3.2.60)

Regarding the rule *tyadādiṣu ddaśo'nālocane kañ ca*: under the rule *paśyārthaiśca*, he will state that "perception" (*ālocanam*) is cognition (*vijñānam*) whose instrument is the eye; however, here [in the present rule], he considers it to be a prohibition of cognition in general. As for *yāddak* and *tāddak*: while the rule *ddaśavatuṣu* is in force, the substitution of *āt* occurs by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. The letter *ñ* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*).

Since the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is already established even by means of the letter *n*, the purpose of the letter *ñ* as a sub-element is solely for the sake of specification; it is not said that the accent itself is not a purpose. [For example,] in the case of "he sees that" (*taddarśa*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of visual cognition (*cakṣurvijñāna*). But how is it that the root *dṛś*, when being employed [in this context], does not have the meaning of mere observation? To this he says: "Words such as *tāddṛśa* and so on are conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*). He then asks, "What follows from that? and replies: "Not at all in this case."

For conventional words (*rūḍhiśabda*) are derived even by means of a non-existent etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*), such as *tailapāyikā* ("an oil-drinker") and others. It is for this very purpose that the term "non-perception" (*anālocana*) was stated. This rule applies when the object of perception is absent; however, when the object of perception is present, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. In the Bhāṣya, however, the derivation is shown with respect to the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*): "People see him as if he were that [other person]; thus, being seen like that, he sees himself as if he were that. In this regard, it should be understood that either the verbal root *dṛś-* functions solely in the sense of the action of the object (*karman*), or there is a superimposition of the entire meaning of the verbal root to convey an excellence of ease and so forth.
Regarding the rule *samānānyośca*: since the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* is prescribed before the suffixes *dru*, *daśan*, and *vatu*, [the forms] are established.

Regarding the rule *ksaśca*: [it applies] to words beginning with *tyad* and to *samāna* and *anya*. Thus: *tāddakṣaḥ*, *saddakṣaḥ*, *anyāddakṣaḥ*. It should be stated that "before *dakṣa*," whereby there is both the substitution of *sa-* and the substitution of *ā*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *sad*, *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *ji*, *nī*, and *rāj*, even when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present.

Regarding the rule *satsūdviṣadruhaduhayujavidabhidacchidajinīrājām upasarge 'pi kvip*: the phrase "starting from this point" (*ataḥ prabhṛti*) takes the ablative case because it is used in conjunction with the word *prabhṛti*, as seen in the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya. The mention of *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* is intended merely to indicate the general direction of the purpose [of the rule]. For here, the term *anupasarga* (without a prefix) continues to apply; therefore, the purpose [of the rule] should be observed in cases such as *spṛśo 'nudake kvin*. Regarding *suvateḥ*: since the underlying logic is the same, the root belonging to the *divādi* class is not included.

Regarding "śuciṣad": this is a Vedic usage—as in *haṃsaḥ śuciṣad*. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt*. In the reading *śucisad*, it is a common (laukika) usage. The question "How is there the substitution of *ṇ* here? concerns the case of *grāmaṇī*. However, in the word *praṇīḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* certainly exists by the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*. Regarding "by an indicator (jñāpaka)": the meaning is that the indicator provides a general indication that the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* of the root *nī* occurs after a cause situated in the preceding member, even when not part of a technical name (*asañjñāyām*).

Therefore, the [suffix] *aṇ* occurs even in the case of *agraṇī*; however, it does not occur when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*), because the rule of indication (*jñāpana*) applies specifically to instances where there is no visible form [of the action]. Others, however, maintain that based on the statement "it should be stated that [the suffix *aṇ* applies] after *agra* and *grāma* with the root *nī*," the indication also pertains to those specific cases, and in those cases as well, it applies only where there is no visible form. Thus they stand.
The suffix *ṇiv* is applied after the root *bhaj*. (Pāṇini 3.2.62)
In the Vedic language, [the suffix -aC] is applied after the word *sahas*. (Pāṇini 3.2.63)

In Vedic usage, the form *sahaḥ* occurs; however, the employment of forms such as *turāsāham* (having placed at the front), *pṛtanāṣāṭ* (conquering armies), and *pṛtanāṣāṭ* (the much-invoked one who conquers armies) for the purpose of fighting enemies in the common language (*bhāṣā*) are to be considered [as anomalies].
And [the suffix *kha*] is used after a word denoting speed. 3.2.64.
The suffixes *ñ* and *cuṭ* are applied after the words *kavi*, *purīṣa*, and *purīṣya*.
In the word *havya*, the substitute *ananta* takes the place of the final syllable (*pāda*). 3.2.66.
The suffix *viṭ* is applied after the verbal roots √jan, √san, √khan, and √kram. 3.2.67.

The term *viṭ* refers to the suffixes *jan*, *san*, *khan*, and *kram*. And [the word] *uta* is for the purpose of specification. For if it were stated as *vi-vanoḥ*, there would be the inclusion of *kvip* and the others as well. Now, if it is argued that here [in this rule] only this [suffix *van*] is included because it lacks an *anubandha*, then in the rule *verapṛktasya* there too only this [suffix *van*] would be included. Furthermore, if it is argued that here [in *vi-vanoḥ*] there would be the inclusion of *kvip* and the others, then [the same objection applies to the other rule]; thus the reasoning is the same. In *goṣāḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *sanoteranaḥ*. In *agregāḥ*, there is no elision (*aluk*) as in the previous case.
The augment *āṭ* is applied before the aorist marker *an* when it follows a verbal root ending in a vowel. 3.2.68.

Regarding *annāda*: in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), although the suffix *aṇ* would be expected by the rule "after a word ending in *a*, provided there is no upapada," the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādi*) is desired; therefore, in the form *annāda*, the avagraha is made as *anna ada*.
And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after the word *kravya*. (3.2.69)

"And regarding *kravye* [in the rule *kravye ca*]: it is for the purpose of preventing the application of the *vāsarūpa* (optionality of non-identical suffixes) rule. Thus, the Vārttika states: 'The mention of *kravya* after the root *ad-* [when not meaning 'raw meat'] is for the purpose of excluding the *vāsarūpa* rule. [Question: "How then [is the compound formed]? [Answer: The intention is that it would be so if it were for the purpose of preventing the *vāsarūpa* rule. Regarding *kṛttavikṛttapakvamāṃsam*: *kṛtta* means cut; that which is cut (*kṛtta*) is further specifically cut (*vi-kṛtta*). This forms a *pūrvakāla* (prior-time) compound. That [compound] is then again compounded with the word *pakva* (cooked), and subsequently, a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive determinative compound) is formed with the word *māṃsa* (meat).

[The opponent argues: "Because [the word *kravyāt*] belongs to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*, the change to *kravya-* occurs. If this were so, since the form *kravyāda* would be unavoidable, there would be no need for this rule intended to block the formation of dissimilar forms (*asarūpa-bādhanārtha*), and furthermore, one who speaks thus would contradict the Vārttika. Anticipating this objection, he says: "kṛttavikṛtta... and so forth. The intention is that, due to the difference in meaning, neither [of the two forms] exists, as it were.
The [suffixes] *duh* and *kabdh* [are applied after the verbal root *mṛj*]. 3.2.70.
*Duhaḥ* and *kabdhaḥ* [take the suffix *ka*]. *Kāmadudhā*: those which are desired are *kāmāḥ*; that which milks them is *kāmadughā*, namely, the *argha* or *madhuparka*.
The suffix *ṇvin* is applied after the words *mantre*, *śvetavāh*, *ukṣan*, and *puroḍāś*.

"From *mantre*, *śvetavah*, *ukthaśas*, and *puroḍāś* [the suffix] *ṇvin* [is applied]. Regarding the phrase "from these": the meaning is "from verbal roots such as *vah* preceded by [prefixes] such as *śveta*. As for the expression "collections of verbal roots and upapadas": he asks "for what purpose? and replies "because it is not technical (*alākṣaṇika*). In forms such as *śvetavāḥ*, the substitution of *r* occurs due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) stating "in *avayāḥ*, *śvetavāḥ*, and *puroḍāś*. In *ukthaśāḥ*, after the elision of *n*, there is the vṛddhi [substitution] according to the rule "after *at*, [there is vṛddhi] of the penultimate vowel," and then the substitution of *r*.

Regarding the term *ḍaspadasya*: it is connected with each [of the preceding rules]. This is stated on the basis of its future status as a word (*pada*); the meaning is that where the status of being a word will belong to that which ends in *ḍas*, there the suffix *ḍas* should be prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇvi*.

If this is so, then when the *ḍas* suffix is applied here, and after the lengthening by the rule "atvasantasya" and the substitution of *ru*, forms such as *śvetavāḥ* are established; thus, there would be no purpose for the irregularity (*nipātana*) "avayāḥ śvetavāḥ. If that is the case, then the irregularity is for the sake of the vocative: *he śvetavāḥ indra*. For in the rule "atvasantasya," the term "not in the vocative" (*asambuddhau*) is understood to carry over; however, it must also be stated [to apply] to the *ḍas* suffix. It is for the sake of the *utva* (substitution of *u*)—as in *śvetavobhyām* and *ukthaśobhyām*. And likewise, *ukthaśāḥ* should also be an irregularity made for the sake of the vocative, provided it is seen in a mantra.
The suffix *yaja* is applied after the root *ava*. 3.2.72.

*ave yajaḥ*. [The word] *avayājaḥ* [is formed]; the substitution of *ru* (the letter *r*) occurs by virtue of this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). The separation of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows. The meaning is as follows: if there were a single combined rule such as *puroḍāśavayajo ṇvin*, then the suffix *ṇvin* would also apply subsequently to words like *śvetavāh* and others, and the root *yaj* would only follow when preceded by *ava*; however, it is desired that it apply to the root alone. Therefore, the purpose of the separation of the rule is to achieve that result.
The substitution of *viju* for *vi* occurs in the Vedic language. 3.2.73.

"Vijupe chandasi. Now, for what purpose is the mention of "chandas" (Vedic), since [the rule] will not apply to the common language (*bhāṣā*) simply by the continued application of the term "mantra"? To this he says: "The mention of *chandas* is for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas. A portion of the Veda distinct from the *mantras* is the Brāhmaṇa; as it has been stated: "That which prompts [an action] is called *mantra*; the remainder is the word 'Brāhmaṇa'."

But for what purpose is this [sūtra]? The question is: "Why should the mention of *vi-* and the mention of *chandas* not be made in the subsequent sūtra itself? [The answer is: "It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). [Objection: But surely, by the very mention of *dṛśi*, it will not apply to the common language (*bhāṣā*). [Response: True; however, this [present sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very point.
The suffixes *manin*, *kan*, *van*, and *nip* are added after a verbal root ending in *ā*.

The suffixes *manin*, *kan*, and *vanip* are added after verbal roots ending in *ā*. For example: *aśvatthāmā* (Aśvatthāman), who stands like a horse (*aśva iva tiṣṭhati*); here, the letter *s* is replaced by *t* due to the rule for the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Also: *sudhīvā* and *supīvā*; the change to *ī* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali*. The letter *c* in the sūtra is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the suffix *vic*. If this were so, there would be no subsequent application [of *vic*] later on; however, in that case, the letter *c* shall also be carried forward to the subsequent rules.
The suffix *kvi* is also seen after other [roots] as well. 3.2.75.

"Also seen from others. The word *api* (also) is for the purpose of indicating that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from all rules (*vidhi*). "Rule" (*vidhi*) means that by which something is enjoined; it refers to a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Thus, the reading "for the purpose of indicating a deviation from all limiting conditions" is appropriate. The mention of "seen" (*dṛśi*) is for the sake of following actual usage. The sense is that this is based on the interpretation of the statement: "Just as they are seen in usage, so indeed they are."
And the suffix *kvip* [is applied after verbal roots]. 3.2.76.

"Also *kvip*. [This is understood] from the phrase "even when there is no upapada," which is obtained through the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *api* (also/even) for the purpose of excluding all qualifications (*sarvopādhivyabhicāra*), and not through the cessation of the rule regarding *sup* (a nominal stem); for it will be stated in the subsequent sūtra that "the words 'when there is a *sup*' and 'also when there is a prefix (*upasarga*)' continue to apply," and because the word *chandasi* (in the Veda) has already been removed in the preceding sūtra itself by the statement "in both the Veda and the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). [The example is] *ukhāsrat*.

Regarding *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *bhraṃsu* [meaning] "to fall down": by the rule *aniditām*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), and by the rule *vasusraṃsu* etc., there is the substitution of *d* for *s*. Regarding *vāhabhraṭ*: from the root *bhraṃśu* [meaning] "to fall downward," there is the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *vraścādi*, and a long vowel by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*. The analysis of the compounds is as follows: "the leaves fall from the pot" (*ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate parṇāni*), "they fall away" (*dhvaṃsate*), and "it falls from the vehicle" (*vāhād bhraśyati*). The root *dhvaṃsi* has a transitive meaning when the causative sense is inherent within it. In some cases, however, the analytical sentences (*vigrahavākya*) are given directly within the verse itself.
The [substitute] *stha* is applied for both *ka* and *ca*. 3.2.77.

The forms *sthaḥ* and *ka* [are derived from the roots *sthā* and *kai*]. The term *ka* is an indeclinable citation. It depends on the rule "it is seen after others as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*) to establish that the suffix *kvip* is indeed already established. Now, one might object: since the mention of "those characterized by such a habit" (*tacchīlādi*) follows there [in Pāṇini 3.2.178], it must be stated that *kvip* is already established by the rule "and *kvip*" (*kvip ca*). Alternatively, he considers that the mention of "those characterized by such a habit" should not be connected with that [rule].

But even so, would not the suffix *ka*, prescribed as a specific rule by "supi sthaḥ," supersede the suffix *kvip*, which is prescribed as a general rule? [The answer is: By the rule of "option for dissimilar forms" (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*), that [suffix *ka*] will also occur. [However,] in the case of "śami dhātoḥ saṃjñāyām," it supersedes the suffix *ac*. Otherwise, just as [the suffix *ka*] supersedes the suffix *ṭa* after the root *kṛ* when used in the sense of cause and so forth because of the mention of the word "root" (*dhātu-grahaṇa*), it would likewise supersede both *kak* and *kvip* after the root *sthā*. Therefore, the purpose of the repeated statement is so that, having set aside even that suffix *ac*, only *kak* and *kvip* may occur; hence the form *śaṃsthāḥ*.

When the *kvip* suffix is elided, the substitution of *ī* for *u* would apply here by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām aṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) due to the presence of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); however, it does not occur because of the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya. Some, however, read the rule as "the substitution of *ī* occurs when [the suffix] begins with *v* or *y*" (*ītvam avakārādau*); according to them, forms such as *supīvā* and *sudhīvā* would also not be possible.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root ending in *su* (a prefix) when denoting a genus (*ajāti*), provided it expresses habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

Regarding *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78): in the example *brāhmaṇānām āmantrayitā*, the suffix *tṛn* is cited as a counter-example because the sense of habitual tendency (*tācchīlya*) is intended to be expressed; thus, by the rule *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69), there is a prohibition of the genitive case.
Regarding *utpratibhyām*: this new rule is initiated because the previous mention of *su* was for the purpose of excluding verbal prefixes (*upasarga*).

"And in the case of *sādhukārin* (one who does well)": this is for the purpose of excluding the sense of habitual action (*ātācchīlya*). And this is established by the following indicator (*jñāpaka*): since [the author], having stated "one who habitually performs that" (*tacchīla*) in the rule *ākvestacchīle*, nevertheless employs the term *sādhukārin*, he indicates that the suffix *ṇini* occurs even after a word meaning "one who does well," even when there is no habitual action.
"One who speaks of Brahman": *brahmavādī*. This also serves the purpose of excluding habitual action.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after a word denoting the object of comparison when it functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) in a compound.

[The rule applies] when the agent is the object of comparison. Since the object of comparison depends upon the thing compared, and since the suffix is prescribed for the agent, it would be understood that the agent which serves as the subordinate member (*upapada*) is itself the object of comparison; thus he says: "the agent which is the subordinate member. In the example *uṣṭrakrośī* ("one who cries like a camel"), the word *iva* is not used in the compound because its meaning is already conveyed, just as in compounds where the object of comparison is expressed, such as *śastrīśyāmā* ("dark-complexioned like a knife").
In the case of the word *vrata*, [the suffix *ṇini* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.2.80)

This [term *vrata*] is a qualifier of the entire complex [of root and prefix], and not a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). For if it were so, the suffix would apply only when the agent is the vow itself (*vrata*), and not when he possesses that vow—this is the sense. He clarifies precisely that it is a qualifier of the entire complex with the words "root and prefix," etc. *Kāmacāraḥ* means activity according to one's will; when that [activity] is possible, there is a restriction (*niyama*), and that can be of two kinds: either in the form "he sleeps only on the bare ground" or "he eats only what is not from a funeral feast (*aśrāddha*)."

In that regard, concerning the first restriction (niyama), whenever one does not eat at a *śrāddha* due to incapacity or other such reasons, a breach of the vow (*vratalopa*) would necessarily follow. However, there is no such scriptural injunction as "one must sleep on the bare ground" or "one must eat only non-śrāddha food. Rather, there is the injunction: "one must sleep only on the bare ground" and "one must eat only non-śrāddha food. As for the term "vow" (*vrate*), it has been stated that these are scripturally ordained restrictions; therefore, he says "provided there is sleeping," etc., to indicate that a second restriction is understood.
The suffix *bahul* is used in the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). 3.2.81.

The suffix *mān* expresses frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). Frequency means repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). The suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) after two indeclinables (*avyaya*) denoting that which occurs repeatedly; there is elision of the *ṭi* portion of indeclinables when followed by any suffix beginning with *bh*. "Other than [denoting] habitual action (*tācchīlya*)"—by this, he shows that the meaning is not already covered by the rule *supyajātau* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). Habitual action is an activity performed without regard for results. However, people such as the Gāndhāras engage in drinking decoctions and the like due to local custom, for the purpose of balancing the bodily humors (*vāta*, etc.). In the examples, the augment *yuk* is applied by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), and the substitution of *ṇ* is applied by the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.11).
The word *manas* [is used in the sense of "mind" or "intellect"]. 3.2.82.

Regarding "the inclusion of *man*": this refers to the root *man* meaning "to know" belonging to the *divādi* class; it does not refer to *man* meaning "to think" belonging to the *tanādi* class. [If the latter were intended], there would have to be *guṇa* substitution before the suffix *tip*. If that is not desired, one must hold that a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). But what is the reason for making such an effort to exclude the inclusion of *man* (the *tanādi* root), given that here the form remains the same with the suffix *ṇini* for both roots, and there is no difference in meaning? He says: "In the subsequent sūtra... [meaning that the distinction will become clear there].
And the suffix *khaś* is applied after a verbal root when *ātman* is used in the sense of pride (*māna*).

Regarding the rule *ātman-māne khaś ca*: the inclusion of *ca* (and) implies that *ṇini* is also included. Although *ṇini* is already established by the rule of "optionality for dissimilar suffixes" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), it is explicitly mentioned here to ensure its uninterrupted application. Consequently, in the rule *karaṇe yajaḥ*, only *ṇini* is carried forward, not the immediately preceding *khaś*. This word *ātman*, functioning to exclude others, is understood as a synonym for the word *sva* when it denotes the object that serves as its correlative; it does not denote a conscious substance.

*Mananaṃ* (the act of thinking) is *mānaḥ*; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Ātmamānaḥ* is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhyā*), meaning "the conceit of the self. When the question arises as to whose [conceit it is], it is understood that it belongs to the very self who is the thinker (*mantṛ*)—the proximate referent of the suffix; thus he says, "the agent is the referent of the suffix. The phrase "by means of attributes such as being visible" implies that [the self] is qualified [by them]. However, a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari ṣaṣṭhyā*) does not occur here, because there is no deviation from the fact that every instance of cognition has a thinker as its agent.

In this way, even when the word *ātman* denotes a conscious substance (*cetanadravya*), since there is no deviation [in usage] when the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*), the genitive case is not restricted to the object (*karman*). However, there is no contingency of applying the suffix [of the genitive] to an object that is a different conscious entity; therefore, the word *ātman* is indeed a synonym for the reflexive pronoun *sva*. Regarding the expression "one who considers himself beautiful" (*darśanīyammanyaḥ*): transmigrating beings (*saṃsāriṇaḥ*), who perceive non-difference between the body and the embodied self—just as between fire and a heated iron ball—regard qualities such as beauty, which actually belong to the body, as belonging to the self itself. Regarding the expression "one who considers himself learned" (*paṇḍitammanyaḥ*): [the same applies].

It is indeed possible for a single self to possess agency in its own essential nature and to be the object of action in a form qualified by such attributes as being a scholar; as the Teacher has stated: "In that case, the consciousness which arises there, being inseparable from our own cognitive activity and belonging to the agent of knowledge itself, may well have the self as its agent."

The suffix *khaś* consists of the letter *kh*, which serves the purpose of the marker *mum*; it also serves the purpose of [indicating] a short vowel in cases such as "the girl who considers herself beautiful" (*darśanīyammanyā kumārī*). The letter *ś* serves the purpose of providing the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*, whereby the affix *śyan* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *divādi* class. As for the accent, although the accent of the *vikaraṇa* (the *śyan*) is subsequently prescribed, it does not override the accent of the *sārvadhātuka* [affix]; thus, the accent of *khaś* itself prevails, and not the accent of the *nit* [marker]. An example is: "Devadatta, who considers himself beautiful, [compared] to Yajñadatta. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object; and with respect to that [genitive], this word *darśanīya* also forms a compound because it possesses the capacity to convey the meaning (*gamakatva*).
[The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after a word ending in the locative case] when expressing "becoming like that. (Pāṇini 3.2.84)

Regarding the word *bhūte*: that whose existence (*sattā*) is distinct [from others] is denoted by the word *bhūta*; however, it is not known in which *bhūta* [it occurs], or rather, in which meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)? To this, he says: "And because of the governing rule of the verbal root" (*dhātvadhikārāt*). The word *ca* (and) indicates the connection of this with the previously stated meaning. [Thus, it means] "in a *bhūta* which is the meaning of the verbal root."

One might object: "Since the governing topic is the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is correct to say that the suffix denotes 'past' with respect to the root, not that the action expressed by the root has become past. To this it is replied: In actual usage, the state of being past—which is what the suffix indicates—must function as a qualifier of the meaning itself, just like any other qualifier, and not of the word; for the word is occupied solely with conveying its own denotation and is thus unfit to be connected with a qualifier.

Furthermore—since a word is eternal, even if it were non-eternal, the rule for the derivation of a suffix from a "past" (bhūta) form would be untenable; for if "pastness" is defined as having been uttered, then the qualifier is redundant, and consequently, the derivation of a suffix from what has not been uttered becomes possible. Moreover, this word *bhūta* is eternal and denotes that which has passed; thus, the objection that there is no established meaning due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) regarding the formation of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is not to be raised.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *yaj* when it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*).

In the case of the suffix *yaj*, the suffix *ṇini* is understood [from a previous rule], but not *khaś*; the reason for this has been stated here. An example is "agniṣṭomayājī" (one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice). Now, one might object: the word *agniṣṭoma* is the name of a ritual action (*karman*); how then can the Agniṣṭoma be the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the act of sacrificing (*yaji*), for surely that very thing cannot be its own instrument? Is it not rather appropriate to cite these as examples: "one who has sacrificed with Soma is a *somayājī*, one who has sacrificed with the *sānnāyya* offering is a *sānnāyyayājī*"? To this he replies: "The Agniṣṭoma serves as the instrument in the production of the result (*phalabhāvanā*)."

It is true that the Agniṣṭoma is indeed a sacrifice (*yāga*); furthermore, the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the production of the fruit. The meaning is: in that production (*bhāvanā*), which is the bringing into being (*utpādanā*) of the fruit such as heaven (*svarga*). Now, one might object: Is it not the case that the sacrifice known as Jyotiṣṭoma—extending from the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* to the *Udavasānīyā*—is itself the production of heaven, and that there is no activity of the sacrificer (*yajana*) distinct from that, wherein the sacrifice could function as an instrument? To this it is replied: The activity of the sacrificer is twofold: general (*sāmānyarūpa*) and specific (*viśeṣarūpa*).

In this context, the internal [activity] in its general form consists of the departure from indifference (*audāsīnya*) and is denoted by such terms as "action" (*kṛti*) or "effort" (*prayatna*); the external [activity], however, is well known as beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and ending with the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice. Similarly, in cases such as "one should cook rice," the internal quality is effort, while the external is to be seen as the act of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth. For one who desires a result exerts effort for that purpose and does not remain indifferent; since he seeks to know the means, knows it, and having known it, performs the means.

This very volitional activity (*kṛti*), which proceeds with a view toward results such as heaven and the like, is called *bhāvanā*. And that *bhāvanā* requires a triad: the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—in the form: "one should bring this about by means of this, in this manner. As it has been said: "For the *bhāvanā*, being thus required, expects: 'What is the means for my result? What is the assistance to the means? Thus it expects what is not yet manifest."*1* *1 Source: Śābarabhāṣya on PMS 2.1.1.*

This general form of activity does not depend upon the guidance of the scriptures; however, its specific form does depend upon them. For instance, one desiring a result seeks to know its means; seeking to know that means, he hears [the Vedic injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

And in that context, an injunction (vidhi) consisting of the impelling of a person is heard; and since a person does not engage in what is not a human goal (puruṣārtha), the productive operation (bhāvanā), being constrained by the injunction, when it requires an object to be brought about (bhāvya), sets aside even the meaning of the verbal root—which, though expressed by the same word, is of the nature of suffering—and instead takes hold of heaven alone, which, though expressed by another word and subordinate to the person, is of the nature of happiness.

Therefore, when there is a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which is presented within the same word—becomes that instrument; subsequently, the *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, which are mentioned in close proximity, become connected [to it]. This is the established rule (*maryādā*) of the Mīmāṃsakas. However, where the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is not subsumed by an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the verbal root itself becomes the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*); as, for example, in the expressions "he cooks" (*pacati*), which is analyzed as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), or "he goes" (*gacchati*), which is analyzed as "he performs going" (*gamanaṃ karoti*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: how can an external operation (*bāhyavyāpāra*), which is brought about through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in that context? What is the fault here? Indeed, an instrument is everywhere the objective domain of the agent's operation. Even in the case of "he cuts with an axe," it is precisely the axe—being the object to be reached by the agent's operation consisting of raising and lowering—that functions as the instrument therein. But how is it that those two [operations], when delimited by the result in the form of being split into two, possess the nature of "cutting" rather than their own intrinsic nature? It is not by their own intrinsic nature that they are called "washing" in the case of a washerman.

Because it is observed that he too indeed raises up a cloth and lets it fall; now, if it is argued that he does not "cut" because there is no splitting into two parts, then in this way, the nature of raising and letting fall constitutes the basis for the axe being its object, and thus the axe possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) therein. Likewise here as well, in the case of *bhāvanā*, the fact that it has the form of producing heaven is based on its having the sacrifice called Agniṣṭoma as its object; therefore, that [sacrifice] possesses the status of an instrument therein. This is what was stated: "It is the instrument in the production of the fruit."

For this [efficient force] accomplishes both the fruit and the meaning of the verbal root; in that regard, when it takes the form of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward a fruit, the external activity is the instrument (*karaṇa*)—this is the meaning. But even so, does the *agniṣṭoma* not become the instrument with respect to the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice)? Let there be no instrumentality in that case; however, the instrument is indeed related [to the action] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj*. Alternatively, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is expressed by the verbal root itself, not by the suffix.
In that case, one part of the meaning of the verbal root is the instrument for another part, and the word *agniṣṭoma* refers to that other part; thus, there is nothing inconsistent.
The affix *kvip* is applied after the root *han* when it has an object. (Pāṇini 3.2.86)

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ*: the phrase "mention of the contemptible" (*kutsitagrahaṇam*) means that it must be stated that this suffix applies when the agent is censured for acts such as the killing of a paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied after verbal roots when *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, or *vṛtra* are the objects [of the action].

The suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *han* when preceded by the words *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra*. This rule concerns the domain of roots (*dhātu*), upapadas (governing words), time (*kāla*), and suffixes (*pratyaya*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, two types of restrictions regarding upapadas have been demonstrated; it is understood that these serve as illustrations rather than for the purpose of excluding other restrictions. Regarding the restriction on the root—that *han* occurs only with *brahman* and the others—since the word "past" (*bhūta*) is also relied upon in this restriction, the suffix certainly does occur even at another time or with another upapada: e.g., *puruṣahan* ("one who kills a man"), whether he is killing him now, or will kill him.

In rules such as *brahmādiṣu hanter eva*, there is a restriction regarding the governing word (*upapada*); here too, because of the reliance on the term "past" (*bhūte*), the suffix occurs even from other roots at another time—e.g., *vṛtraṃ jayati* or *jeṣyati* results in *vṛtrajit*. There is also a restriction regarding time: that in the past tense, only *kvip* is used, and no other suffix; for example, in the rules *karmaṇi hanaḥ* and *karṇaṇyaṇ*.

However, when there is another accompanying word (*upapada*), even if the action has already occurred (*bhūte*), another suffix indeed occurs—as in *pitṛvyaghātī* ("one who has killed his uncle"). And a suffix with an accompanying word is necessarily excluded [from the rule for past time]. But the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) certainly occurs—as in *vṛtraṃ hatavān* ("he has killed Vṛtra"). Thus, the restriction of the suffix applies only to the case where the action is past; yet here too, because of the reliance on the rule "of the root *han* after *brahmaṇ* etc.," it certainly occurs after other roots and with other accompanying words, even at a different time.

But how is a fourfold restriction obtained within a single *yoga*? To this he says: "This very [rule]," etc. Precisely because no distinction is perceived, a fourfold restriction can be obtained; however, it should be understood that what has been stated therein serves as a supporting reinforcement (*upodbalaka*). [The rule] *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.75) applies here.
The suffix *kṛt* is applied after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the words *sukarma*, *pāpa*, *mantra*, and *puṇya*. (Pāṇini 3.2.89)

Regarding the rule *sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ*: because it was stated immediately after [the rule] *svādiṣu* that one should exclude the word *su*, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the "non-apprehension of the quality" (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) type; it is stated thus by resorting to a general principle, as in the expression "a wealthy village."

"And it is threefold. This is obtained precisely through the continued application of the term "mostly" (*bahulagrahaṇa*). Regarding the domain of time, secondary suffixes, and *upapada* (co-occurring words): therein, due to the restriction of time, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in *karmakāra* ("one who has performed work"), as [the action] was completed in the past. Due to the restriction of the *upapada*, in *mantrādhyāya* ("one who has studied the mantra"), only *aṇ* occurs, and not *kvip*. Due to the restriction of the suffix, when there is the intention to express that one "makes" or "will make" the mantra, only *aṇ* occurs, and not *kvip*, as in *śāstrakṛt* ("author of a treatise"). [The form *mantrakṛt* is derived] by *kvip* according to the rule "and *kvip*."
The word *śūnya* [is used] in the sense of "some. (Pāṇini 5.2.90)

Some [grammarians] hold that [the suffix *kvip*] is restricted by time (*kāla*), root (*dhātu*), immediate constituent (*upapada*), and affix (*pratyaya*). In this regard, because the past tense (*bhūtakāla*) is restricted to the root *su* when followed by the suffix *kvip*, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in the form *somasāv* (one who has pressed the *soma*), as in *somaṃ sutavān*. Likewise, because the root is restricted to the immediate constituent *soma*, the suffix *aṇ* alone occurs in the form *surāsāv* (one who has pressed liquor), as in *surāṃ sutavān*. Similarly, because the root *su* is restricted to the object *soma*, the suffix *kvip* does not occur in the form *somakrī* (one who has purchased *soma*), as in *somaṃ krītavān*; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.

Likewise, because the suffix *kvip* is restricted to the sense of the past (*bhūta*), when there is an intention to express "he presses Soma" or "he will press Soma," *kvip* does not occur; rather, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after [a nominal stem ending in] *agni*, in the sense of "going. (Pāṇini 3.2.91)

Regarding the rule *agnau ca*: "In this case as well," and so forth. Therein, because the suffix *kvip* is restricted to the past tense (*bhūtakāla*), the suffix *aṇ* does not occur [after the root *ci*] when *agni* is the upapada, as in *agnicāya* (one who has piled the fire-altar). Furthermore, because the verbal root (*dhātu*) is restricted to the case where *agni* is the upapada, the form *iṣṭakācit* (one who piles bricks) does not occur. Also, because the root *ci* is restricted to the case of *agni* being the object, the form *agnibhṛt* (fire-maintainer) does not occur. Moreover, because *kvip* is restricted to the past tense alone, there is an absence [of the suffix] in cases such as *agniṃ cinoti* (he piles the fire-altar) or *ceṣyati* (he will pile).
In the case of the word *agni* when it denotes an action, [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.1.92)

Regarding the rule *karmaṇy agny-ākhyāyām*: the term *karman* is carried over from the previous rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ* as the *upapada*; however, this [present] *karman* is for the sake of the meaning of the suffix. Thus he says: "the *kāraka* is indeed [the object] in the sense of the object (*karman*). The particle *eva* (indeed) is for the sake of emphasis. To begin with, the *upapada*, even though it serves as the meaning of the suffix in the sense of the object, is specifically the object itself. The inclusion of the word *ākhyā* (designation) is for the purpose of indicating that this is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

In common worldly usage, the word *agni* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as meaning "flame"; however, in the Veda, its application is frequent even for a structure of bricks in the sense of "fire-altar," as seen in such passages as "he who, knowing thus, piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*) and "one about to pile the fire" (*agniṃ ceṣyamāṇa*). Whether that [meaning] be primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*jaghanya*), if the mention of the verbal designation (*ākhyā*) were not present here, then by force of worldly renown, only the flame would be understood. To prevent this and ensure that the structure of bricks alone is understood, the verbal designation is mentioned—this is the meaning.
One who is free from modification regarding actions. (3.2.93)

"Regarding the word *karmaṇi* [in the rule], it means 'occurring in the object' (*vartamāne*). From the rule *karmaṇi hanaḥ*, the meaning is: when there is an object connected to the action that brings about the censure of the agent, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] in that case. The sale of Soma and other such items is prohibited by the scriptures."
The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the root *dṛś* (to see).

Regarding the rule *ddaśeḥ kvanip*: "In order to exclude other suffixes" means that other suffixes such as *manin* and others, as well as *aṇ* and others, which were mentioned together [with *kvanip*], are excluded. However, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix) certainly occurs when there is an accompanying word (*sopapada*), as in *palokaṃ ddaṣṭavān* ("one who has seen the world").
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛñ* (to do) when *rājan* is the object.

[The rule] "after *rājan* [as an upapada], [the suffix *kvip* is added] after the root *yudh-kṛñ*"—but surely *yudh* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Therefore, the sense [of the objection] is: how can it be said that the word *rājan* is an upapada expressing the object (*karman*)? [The answer is: "with the causative meaning included. Since roots have multiple meanings, or by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), when the root *yudh* itself includes the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*), then it becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*) by virtue of the object being the one who is caused to act (*prayojya*). This is the meaning.
And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after the word *saha*. 3.2.96.

And [the word] *saha* [is also excluded]. Because it does not denote a sentient being (*asattvavacana*), it is not qualified by the object (*karman*) as an attendant word (*upapada*). Therefore, the sense is that the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. However, it is not that there is no connection with the term that is actually carrying over, because it would be of no use in what follows as well.
The suffix *ī* is applied after the word *jana* when it occurs in the seventh case.

In the seventh [case], after the word *janī*, [the suffix *ḍa* is applied]. Regarding the form *manduraja*: "A stable for horses is called *mandurā*"; the short vowel [in *mandura-*] occurs by the rule "after a feminine suffix ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, [the final vowel is optionally shortened] in names and Vedic meters."
The fifth case ending is used for the word *ajāti* (meaning "not a genus" or "non-living being"). 3.2.98.

In the fifth [chapter], regarding "non-origination": cognition and the like are qualities of the self; weariness is passion, because it is observed that from weariness there arises activity toward one's own [objects].
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a preverb when the word is a proper name. (Pāṇini 3.2.99)
And when a prefix is present, [the suffix *aṅ* is applied] to form a name; "prajā" is the name for a class of living beings.
The [kṛt] affix *ana* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). 3.2.100.

In the case of *anu* with the sense of "action" (*karmaṇi*), as in *pumāṃsamanujātaḥ*, the meaning is "born following after a man"; thus, it possesses an object (*sakarmakatva*). In the form *pumanujaḥ*, there is the elision of the final consonant of *puṃsaḥ* due to the rule regarding the elision of a conjunct ending in a consonant (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*).
It is also seen in other cases. (Pāṇini 3.2.101)
It is also seen elsewhere: "He is twice-born. The first birth is from the mother; the second is the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
In that [second birth], the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, and the teacher is said to be his father.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied after a verbal root]. 3.2.102.

It has been stated that *niṣṭhā* refers to the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*. The letter *k* is for the purpose of triggering operations dependent on a *kit* suffix; the letter *u* is for the purpose of triggering operations dependent on a suffix marked with *u* (i.e., having an *ugit* vowel); and it also serves as a qualifier for the rule "of a stem ending in *at* or *as*" (*atvasantasya*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of *niṣṭhā*" and so forth: "non-establishment" means non-formation. Of what? Of either the technical name (*saṃjñā*) or the named element (*saṃjñin*). He asks, "How [is this so]? and replies, "By means of the technical name. If the mention of *kta* and *ktavatu* were made twice—once here and once in the rule prescribing the technical name—then there would be no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*); thus he says, "by means of the technical name. And [he says], "and of those two, which already exist."

The point is that neither in common usage nor in the treatise do these two [suffixes] exist with their full continuity. Even in the treatise, although the suffix *kta* is prescribed in its own form by the rules "ñītaḥ ktaḥ" and "napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ," it does not exist for the past tense; furthermore, the suffix *ktavatu* does not exist anywhere at all. This refers to the fact that the designation is prospective (*bhāvinī saṃjñā*).

Because perception (saṃjñā) is something that comes into being through the process of becoming (bhāvin), perception itself is also something that comes into being, like a cloth from thread. For example, a weaver is told, "Weave a cloth from this thread. He sees that if it is not a cloth, it cannot be woven; yet if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. To say "the cloth is to be woven" is a contradiction. He thinks, "I believe that which, when produced, becomes what is called a 'cloth,' is what is to be woven. This is by way of functional capacity (sāmarthyāt).

By the rule "The suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* are called *niṣṭhā*," there is an absence of the designation *niṣṭhā* for any other suffix that has arisen; this is the [logical] capacity [of the term]. Regarding the phrase "in the case of an initial action" (*ādikarmaṇi*): the word *karman* denotes an action (*kriyā*). An action consists of a collection of moments proceeding toward a single result. Even though the first moment of the action is completed, the statement is made because the action, insofar as it is the meaning of the verbal root, is not yet fully completed. However, it is logical [to apply the designation] due to completion at the beginning. Indeed, this past tense designation is logical, for what reason? Because of completion at the beginning (*ādyapavargāt*).

The first moment of the action is distinguished, and it is in that very constituent part that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), in the form of a whole (*samūha*), is completed. And it has been said:
"That whole, being of such a nature, is completed in each of its constituent parts;
therefore, the distinction of time is possible within those parts."

And thus, the *luṅ* (aorist) is also employed, as in "Devadatta has made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ prākārṣīt*).
