Regarding *mada*, there are two roots: *mada* in the sense of "joy" and *mada* in the sense of "satiety," the latter belonging to the *curādigaṇa*; for that [latter], the form *unmadeti* cannot be derived. *Ruc* means "to shine"; *trapūṣ* means "shame"; *vṛtu* means "to turn"; *vṛdhu* means "to grow"; *ṣaha* means "to endure"; and *cara* has the meaning of "going."

Regarding those [roots] that are mentioned here with their prefixes (*sopapada*), the rule applies from that very form as it is mentioned; therefore, one should not raise this objection: "It should be stated as *udaḥ pacapatamada*—is it by way of its own form (*svarūpataḥ*)? Or is it by reading each [root] preceded by *ud*? For they say that by that [reading], forms such as *samutpatiṣṇuḥ* do not occur. However, for those [roots] that are mentioned without prefixes (*nirupapada*), the rule applies according to what is observed.
In the Vedic language (chandas), [the substitution of *na* for *ni*] is optional. 3.2.137.

In Vedic usage, [the substitution of] *ay* occurs [for the final vowel and following consonant of a verbal root ending in *i* or *ī* before suffixes beginning with *a*, *man*, *tṛ*, *al*, *vāyya*, *et*, *nu*, and *viṣṇu*]. Thus, in the word *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ay* according to the rule "before *ay*, *man*, *tṛ*, *al*, *vāyya*, *et*, *nu*, and *viṣṇu*."
And [the suffix *ṅe*] is substituted for the [genitive case-ending] *bhuvaḥ*. 3.2.138.

It is stated that [the suffix] occurs after *bhuvas* in Vedic usage (*chandasī*). How then can one say, "The Vaiṣṇava [power] is not capable of prevailing over the Lord of the World" (*jagatprabhoraprabhaviṣṇu vaiṣṇavam*) or "to Viṣṇu, the prevailing one" (*viṣṇave prabhaviṣṇave*)? Poets are unrestrained. As for the form *bhrājiṣṇunā*, this has not been adopted in the Bhāṣya.
And [the comparative suffix] *iṣṭhan* is applied after *glājistha* and *gsnu*. (Pāṇini 3.2.139)

"And *glājisthaśca* is *gsnuḥ*. Regarding the phrase "having become a *cartva*": the meaning is that it has attained the state of being a *cartva*, or has been reached by means of becoming a *cartva*. Regarding the phrase "also in the case of *śryukaḥ kitī*" (*Pāṇini 1.4.25*): the ellipsis is that the letter *g* is also indicated as having become a *cartva*.

The vowel *ī* does not occur [after a root] because of the *g*-marker (*git*) in *ksnu*. In the word *sthāsnū*, the vowel *ī* does not occur because of the *g*-marker in *ksnu*; for there is an injunction that the vowel *ī* occurs after *ka* and *ṅit* suffixes. The letter *ka* in *kaṅit* is for the purpose of pronunciation. It is taught that the vowel *ī* occurs after *ka* and *ṅit* [suffixes], but this [suffix *ksnu*] is a *git*. If this is so, would not *guṇa* (vocalic strengthening) apply in *jiṣṇuḥ* and *bhūṣṇuḥ*? — The absence of *guṇa* must be remembered in three cases. The absence of *guṇa* is to be remembered in three cases: *git*, *kit*, and *ṅit*; this is because of the inclusion of the letter *ga* in the rule *kṅiti ca*.

In this case, then, for the word *bhūṣṇuḥ*, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* would not apply?—The absence of *iṭ* after roots ending in *śri* or *uk* applies to both the letter *g* and the letter *k*. That which is the absence of *iṭ* following a root ending in *śri* or *uk* occurs after both the *g* and the *k*, not merely after the *k*; for even there, the *g* is mentioned as having undergone the substitution of *c* (the *cartva* change). If this is so, then because the *cartva* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *u* by the rule *haśi ca* would apply? This is a Vedic-style mention (*sautra-nirdeśa*), or the mention will be made without *saṃhitā* (as separate words) in the Veda, as in the example *daṃkṣṇavaḥ paśavaḥ*. Because the suffix *ksnu* has the marker *g*, there is no elision of the penultimate vowel.
The suffix *knū* is applied after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*.

The suffix *knū* is applied after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*. Regarding the form *trasnu*: there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "there is no *iṭ* before a *kṛt* suffix beginning with a vowel."
The suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied after the eight roots beginning with *śam*.

Regarding the rule *śamityaṣṭābhyo ghinuṇ*, the word *iti* is used in the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*), because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings. In that context, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *śam-ādayo yeṣām* ("those of which 'śam' is the first"), there is elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*). [The roots are: *śamu* (to pacify), *tamu* (to desire), *damu* (to subdue), *śramu* (to exert oneself and to feel fatigue), *bhramu* (to wander/to be unsteady), *kṣamūṣ* (to endure), *klamu* (to be weary), and *madī* (to rejoice). The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).

It is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter). For if it were an *anubandha*, then in the case of *śaminau* and *śaminaḥ*, the *num* augment would undesirably apply by the rule *ugidacām*; likewise, in *śaminitarā* and *śaminitamā*, the optional shortening of the feminine suffix (*nadī*) prescribed by the rule *ugitaśca* would apply optionally. However, the form [with long ī] is required as obligatory by the rule *gharūpakalpacelaḍ*. Therefore, they explain that this is not an *anubandha*, but rather serves only for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In the *Bhāṣya*, however, it is established that "the letter *a* is indeed an *anubandha* for the sake of the operations pertaining to *ugit*."

In that case, shortness (*hrasvatva*) is desired by way of option (*vikalpena*), not as a permanent rule. However, in the rule for the suffix *num*, the term *jhal* will be understood as a governing term (*anuvarttiṣyate*); because the word does not end in a *jhal* sound, the *num* will not apply. Regarding *śamī*: there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "not after a high-pitched vowel" (*nodāttasya*). Regarding *unmādī*: [one might object] that this [prohibition] is already fulfilled in the case of *mādī*; for after the prefix *ut-*, only the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applicable by the rule "after *alaṃkṛñ* etc. (*alaṃkṛñ-prabhṛtibhyaḥ*); yet the suffix *ghinuṇ* will occur by the rule of optional non-homogeneity (*vā'sarūpa-vidhi*). To this it will be stated that the rule of optional non-homogeneity does not apply among suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), though that is merely a general tendency. Regarding *asitā*: from the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing," only the suffix *tṛn* occurs.

The suffix *khaś* is applied after the following verbal roots when preceded by the specified prepositions: *sam-pṛc*, *anu-rudh*, *aṅ-yam*, *aṅ-ya*, *pari-sṛ*, *sam-sṛj*, *pari-dev*, *sam-jvar*, *pari-kṣip*, *pari-raṭ*, *pari-vad*, *pari-dah*, *pari-muh*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *ā-krīḍ*, *vi-vic*, *tyaj*, *raj*, *bhaj*, *ati-car*, and *ām-uṣ*; and also after the root *han* when preceded by *abhi*. (Pāṇini 3.2.142)

The roots *sampṛc*, *anurudh*, *aṅyam*, *āṅyas*, *parisṛ*, *saṃsṛj*, *paridevi*, *saṃjvar*, *parikṣip*, *pariraṭ*, *parivad*, *paridah*, *parimuha*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*, *draha*, *duha*, *yuj*, *ākrīḍ*, *vicati*, *aja*, *raja*, *bhaja*, *aticara*, *acara*, *amuṣ*, and *abhyahana* [are used with the locative]. [Note: Regarding *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact" (*saṃparke*), and *rudhir* in the sense of "obscuring" (*āvaraṇe*); however, the root *anu-rudh* belonging to the *divādi* class is not included here, because of its association with *pṛc*. Others maintain that the *divādi* root is included when it is recited together with *anu*.

The roots are: *yam* (to cease), *yasu* (exertion), *sṛ* (motion), *sṛj* (emission), *div* (play), *jvar* (fever/affliction), *kṣip* (impulsion), *raṭ* (speaking), *vad* (articulate speech), *dah* (reduction to ashes), *muha* (bewilderment), *duṣ* (corruption), *dviṣ* (enmity), *druh* (desire to harm), *duh* (milking/filling), *yuj* (joining), *krīḍ* (sporting), *vicir* (separation), *tyaj* (abandoning), *rañj* (coloring/attachment), *bhaj* (service), *car*.

The roots *gam* (to go), *muṣ* (to steal), and *han* (to kill or to go) have the sense of motion. *Paridevi* belongs to the *bhvādi* class; this is the connection [with the word "is taken"]. However, the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of *krīḍ* (to play) is not included here, because of its association with non-causative forms (*aṇyantaiḥ*) and because it is mentioned by its specific form (*pratipadoktatvāt*). For this very reason, the same does not apply to the root *div* (to lament) in the sense of "moaning," even though it belongs to the *curādi* class. In the word *saṃparkī*, there is the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.

Regarding those [roots] here that are preceded by *sam*, one should form a copulative compound (*dvandva*) of them and state: "the [affix *kha*] comes after these along with *sam*"; likewise for those preceded by *āṅ* and *pari*. Since this is already established, the purpose of reciting it as a specific rule (*pratipadam*) is so that [the affix] may occur only after the form [actually] employed, and not after a form joined with a different prefix.
The suffixes *vā*, *ka*, *ṣa*, *la*, *sa*, *kattha*, and *sra* are added after the root *bhram*. (Pāṇini 3.2.143)
The suffix *laṣ* is applied after the root *ap*.
The suffix *vasu* is applied after the verbal roots *pra*, *lap*, *sṛ*, *drumath*, and *vad*. (Pāṇini 3.2.145)
*Pre lapasṛdrumathavadavasaḥ*. [The roots] *lap* (in the sense of distinct speech), *sṛ* (in the sense of going), *dru* (in the sense of going), and *math* (in the sense of churning).

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the following verbal roots: *nind* (to blame), *hiṃs* (to injure), *kliś* (to afflict), *khād* (to eat), *vināś* (to destroy), *parikṣip* (to surround), *pariraṭ* (to cry out), *parivādi* (to revile), and *vyābhāṣ* (to address); provided that the sense is "envy" (*asūya*).

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the verbal roots *nind*, *hiṃs*, *kliś*, *khād*, *naś*, *kṣip*, *raṭ*, *vad*, *bhāṣ*, and *asūy*. Regarding these roots: *ṇidi* is used in the sense of "censuring" (*kutsāyām*). *Tṛha* and *hiṃsi* are used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*). *Kliśa* is used in the sense of "afflicting" (*vibādhane*). *Khāda* is used in the sense of "eating" (*bhakṣaṇe*). *Ṇaś* (the root *naś*) is used in the sense of "disappearance" (*adarśane*); it is cited here with the causative marker (*ṇic*), though this marker is elided in the actual form, and the vowel *a* is an augment. Some, however, read the form as *vināśī*, which includes the causative marker. *Kṣipi* and *raṭī* have already been explained [in previous rules]. *Vadi* is used with the causative marker (*ṇic*). *Bhāṣa* is used in the sense of "distinct speech" (*vyaktāyāṃ vāci*). *Asūyati* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group and takes the suffix *yak*.

Now, for what purpose is the suffix *vuñ* prescribed after words such as *nindā*? It is not the case that it is already established by the rule *ṇvultṛcau*, since the form would be the same, and as for the accent, it would be the same everywhere except in the case of the root *asūyati*; for in the case of *asūyati* with the suffix *ṇvul*, the acute accent (*udātta*) would fall on the syllable preceding the suffix, whereas with *vuñ*, it falls on the beginning of the word according to the rule *ñnityādiḥ*.

Therefore, the suffix *vuñ* should be prescribed for that one [root] alone; however, for others, it is already established by *ṇvul*. As for this *tṛn* which is prescribed after roots meaning "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, it would result in being an exception (*bādhaka*). [Objection: By the rule of "optional non-identity of form" (*vā'sarūpa*), *ṇvul* will also occur there. To this, he says: "It is established by *ṇvul* alone. This means that suffixes such as *tṛc* and others do not occur. The point is that this is not merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the scope of *ṇvul*, but rather regarding the scope of suffixes in general.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after *deva* and *kruśa* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them. (Pāṇini 3.2.147)

Regarding the rule *devikruśoścopasarge*: the term *devayateḥ* refers to both *dīvya-* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, and to [the root] *divi* meaning "to coo" (*kūjane*) when followed by the *curādi* class suffix *ṇic*.
The suffix *yuc* is applied after a verbal root meaning "motion" that is intransitive.

The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots meaning "motion" (*calana*) that are intransitive (*akarmaka*). For example: *copana* [is derived from] *cupa*, meaning "to move slowly"; and *śabdana* [is derived from] *śabda*, which belongs to the *cur*-class in the sense of "making sound," or alternatively, it is formed by adding *ṇic* to the nominal stem *śabda* according to the rule "that which performs that action."
And [the suffix *ya*] is applied after a verbal root that begins with a consonant and has an anudātta accent. Pāṇini 3.2.149.

[The rule] *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* [is stated]. Regarding the word *jugupsana*: since it has been stated that "the addition of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) in roots such as *gup* is for the sake of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)," and because "a characteristic applied to a part serves to qualify the whole," the whole [root *gup*] possesses the quality of having an anudātta vowel. In that case, if the mention of *ādi* ("beginning with") were absent, there would be an application of the rule to what ends in that [anudātta vowel] (*tadantavidhi*); consequently, this [word *jugupsana*] would not be included. Therefore, the mention of *ādi* is for the purpose of preventing such an application of the rule to what ends in that.
The roots *ju*, *caṅkram*, *daṇḍram*, *sṛ*, *gṛdh*, *jval*, *śuc*, *laṣ*, *pat*, and *pad* [take the suffix *yaṅ*]. (Pāṇini 3.1.24)

*ju-cam-kramya-dam-dramya-sṛ-gṛdh-i-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ*. The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root; some say it denotes "motion," others say it denotes "speed. *Kramu* means "to step"; *drama*, *hamma*, and *mīmṛ* mean "to go"; *sṛ* means "to go"; *gṛdhu* means "to desire"; *jvala* means "to blaze"; *śuca* means "to grieve"; *laṣa* means "to desire"; *śala*, *hula*, and *patlṛ* mean "to go"; and *pada* means "to go."

But surely, since roots such as *caṅkramya* and others have the sense of "moving" (*calana*), and the root *pad* is *anudātta*, the suffix *yuc* is already established for them by the two preceding rules according to their respective applications; why, then, is it mentioned here? To this he says: "of those having the sense of moving," and so forth. The root *pad* preceded by *pra* is transitive (*sakarmaka*). [He says] "for the sake of an indicator" (*jñāpakārtham*); an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is that which makes known (*jñāpanam*), formed with the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) based on the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya. Others explain the mention of the root *pad*; these are the authors of the Bhāṣya and others.

For they think thus: "The suffix *yuc* should not occur after the root *pad*, which takes an object (*sakarmaka*), because it has not been so prescribed. As he said: "The mention of *pad* is useless, since [the suffix] *i* is already established for roots that are *anudātta* and begin with a consonant (*halādi*) by the rule *iran*. [To this, the answer is: "But it is for the purpose of excluding the *vāsarūpa* (optionality regarding dissimilar suffixes) rule. Or rather, it is known from the rule concerning *nindā* and others that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply to *tācchīlika* (suffixes denoting habitual action) when the agent possesses such qualities (*tacchīla*). Thus, in those cases, suffixes like *tṛc* do not occur by virtue of the *vāsarūpa* rule. However, in the present case, it is made known that among *tācchīlika* suffixes themselves, there is no mutual application of the *vāsarūpa* rule.

Regarding the word *alaṃkartā*: the meaning is that the suffix *tṛn* does not occur after the root *alaṃkṛ*. He shows how the mention of the root *pad* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by saying "for instance" (*tathā hi*). [He says] "by the specifically prescribed *ukañ*"—that is, by the rule beginning with *laṣapatapada* (Pāṇini 3.2.154). And this [non-application] is merely general; this will be explained under the rule *sūdadīpadīkṣaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.153). Regarding *gantā*: after the root *gam*, the suffix *tṛn* occurs in the domain of *ukañ*, which is prescribed for *laṣapatapada* and so on. Regarding *vikatthanaḥ*: in the domain of the suffix *ghinuṇ* prescribed by the rule *vau kaṣalaṣa* (Pāṇini 3.2.144), the suffix *yuc*, characterized by its low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*), occurs.
And [the suffix *kha*] is applied after roots meaning "to be angry" (*krudh*) and "to envy" (*maṇḍ*). Pāṇini 3.2.151.
Not [the suffix] *yaḥ*. 3.2.152.

*Nayaḥ*: Since the suffix *yuC* is already established for the root *nī* by the rule "the roots *aya*, *vaya*, *naya*, and *taya* mean 'to go'" because they are *anudātta-it*, this [mention of] *nati* is not its inclusion; rather, thinking that it is a prohibition, he says "from that which ends in *ya*. "By the preceding" refers to the rule beginning with "and from *anudātta-it* roots. *Knūyitā*, *kṣmāyitā*: [from the roots] "knūyī means 'to sound'" and "kṣmāyī means 'to shake.'"
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots] *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*. 3.2.153.

[The suffixes] *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ* [take the suffix *yu*]. [The roots are: *ṣūda* "to flow," *dīpī* "to shine," and *dīkṣa* "to tonsure. Now, it has been established that the rule regarding non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply to suffixes denoting habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Therefore, how can *yu* be obtained here by way of non-identity of form? To this he says: "In the case of suffixes denoting habitual action... This very prohibition is the indicator (*liṅga*) of its being merely occasional (*prāyikatva*). For if the rule of non-identity of form were absent everywhere, *yu* would simply not occur because it would be barred by the suffix *ra* which is specifically prescribed; thus, this prohibition would be purposeless. By the words "And likewise" (*tathā ca*), etc., he demonstrates the purpose of its being merely occasional.

By this prohibition, it is not indicated that there is a simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both [the *kartari* and *bhāve* senses], as appears in the Bhāṣya; rather, what is indicated is merely the commonality (*prāyikatva*) of the rule. Therefore, forms such as "gantā kheṭaṃ vikatthanaḥ" (one who goes about boasting) also occur. And this has already been stated previously.

Alternatively, [the mention of] "in the list beginning with *nandi*" (*nandy-ādiṣu*) is for the sake of variety (*vaicitrya*), while the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) serves the same purpose here.
The suffix *ukañ* is applied after the verbal roots √laṣ, √pat, √pad, √sthā, √bhū, √vṛṣ, √han, √kam, √gam, and √śṝ.

The suffix *ukañ* is applied after the roots *laṣ*, *pat*, *pad*, *sthā*, *bhū*, *vṛṣ*, *han*, *kam*, *gam*, and *śṝ*. Regarding the example *apalāṣukam*, the meaning is "that which is not beautiful. Now, one might object: since this is a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), the suffix *ghinuṇ* should apply here by the rule *ape ca laṣaḥ*; moreover, this [suffix *ukañ*] finds its scope of application only when *laṣ* is used alone or preceded by another prefix. Thus, by the rule of "optionality due to dissimilarity" (*vāsarūpavidhi*), *ukañ* will indeed occur. To this we reply: the principle that "the rule of optionality due to dissimilarity does not apply to suffixes denoting habitual action" (*tācchīlikeṣu vāsarūpavidhir nāsti*) is stated to be merely a general tendency (*prāyika*). For instance, there is the expression *āghātukaṃ pākalikasya sūtram* ("the manual of Pākalika is prone to causing injury").

"Pākala" is a specific disease of elephants; one who has this is called "pākalikaḥ. Although the suffix *ini* would have been expected by the rule "dvandvopatāpagarhyāt," it does not occur here because the word is included in the *vrīhy-ādi* group. The urine of such a "pākalika" elephant, when merely touched or smelled, kills other elephants; this is its inherent nature. Regarding the phrase "they say the Rakshasa is coming to Vārāṇasī": the meaning is that they say he—who has become a Rakshasa through a curse or the like—is habitually returning toward Vārāṇasī for the sake of liberation.
The suffix *ṣākan* is applied after the verbal roots *jalpa*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭ*, and *vṛṅ*.

The suffix *ṣākan* is added after the roots *jalp*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭh*, and *vṛṅ*. [The meanings are as follows: *jalp* and *jap* mean "in distinct speech"; *bhikṣ* means "in begging"; *kuṭṭ* means "in cutting"; *luṇṭh* belongs to the *curādi* (tenth) class and means "in plundering"; and *vṛṅ* means "in sharing."
The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *prajus*. (Pāṇini 3.2.156)
*prajoriniḥ*: the letter *i* in *ini* is for the purpose of ensuring that the *n* does not receive the designation *it*.
The suffix *khañ* is applied after the words *jidda*, *akṣi*, *viśrīṇva*, *māvyathābhyam*, *apari*, *bhū*, and *prasū*.

[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *ji*, *kṣi*, *viśri*, *viśram*, *avyath*, *abhi*, *paribhū*, and *prasū*. *Ji* is used in the sense of "victory" (*jaye*) and *ji* in the sense of "overpowering" (*abhibhave*); both are included. *Draṅ* means "respect" (*ādare*), *śriñ* means "service" (*sevāyām*), *iṇ* means "motion" (*gatau*), *ṭuvam* means "vomiting" (*udvamane*), and *vyatha* means "fear and trembling" (*bhayacalanayoḥ*). The form *avyath* is preceded by the negative particle *nañ*; the mention of the root is made after the elision of the *nañ*, and due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), the *nañ* is compounded with the verbal root, followed by the elision of the *v*, and then the suffix is added. *Ama* means "sickness" (*roge*), and *bhū* means "existence" (*sattāyām*); both are included. Thus it is said: "both are included."

However, because the root *kṣi* in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), it is not included; rather, the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇa*) is what is intended to be included. Furthermore, the two roots *ṣūṅ*—meaning "the release of the embryo from living beings" (*prāṇigarbhavimocana*) and "the birth of living beings" (*prāṇiprasava*)—are also not included because they possess indicatory letters. Should not *pra-ju* also be included here? For if that were so, the particle *ca* would not need to be mentioned. Nevertheless, it was not done in that way.
The suffix *āluc* is added after the verbal roots √spṛh, √gṛh, √pat, √day, √nidrā, √tandrā, and √śraddhā.

The suffix *āluc* is applied after the roots *spṛhi*, *gṛhi*, *pati*, *dayi*, *nidrā*, *tandrā*, and *śraddhā*. Since these are listed in the *curādi* (denominative) class as being without the vowel *a* (*adanta*), the elision of the *a* that occurs when the causative suffix *ṇic* is added is treated as *sthānivat* (as if it were still present). Consequently, in the case of *patayati*, the rule "vṛddhi for the penultimate vowel" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*) does not apply; likewise, in the cases of *spṛhayati* and *gṛhayati*, the guna substitution for a light penultimate vowel does not occur—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the root *dhā* preceded by *śrat*: the root *dheṭ* preceded by *śrat* is simply never used.

Now, for what purpose is *āluc* prescribed, rather than saying it is after *luñ*? What is the resulting form? [The form] *spṛhayāluḥ*—once *śap* has been applied, will there not be lengthening by the rule "lengthening occurs before *yañ*"? For in that rule, the term *sārvadhātuka* is understood from the previous context, but the term *tiṅ* is not; moreover, because the *lakāra* (the marker *l*) lacks the purpose of being designated as an *it*, it will not apply, or else because the suffix begins with *yakāra*.

Is the *yakāra* not heard [in the form *śraddadhātu*]? The *yakāra* has been elided by a specific rule (*luptanirdiṣṭa*). Even so, one who lacks faith does not achieve success; how so? Because of the rule "the *ślau* suffix causes reduplication" and the rule "the long *ā* of *śnā* and the reduplicated stem," the form *śraddadhluḥ* would result. If it is argued that reduplication will not apply because "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not obligatory," even then, the suffix *āluc* is prescribed for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). This indicates that wherever the desired form is established by *āluc* alone, this [suffix] occurs there as well. Consequently, it need not be stated that "there is the mention of *śīṅ* when *āluc* follows."
The suffix *ru* is applied after the verbal roots *dā* (to give), *dhā* (to place), *si* (to sharpen), *sad* (to sit), and *sad* (to perish).

The suffix *ru* is applied after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, *si*, *śad*, and *sad*. Regarding the statement "In the case of the inclusion of *gā*, *mā*, and *dā*, there is no distinction," the forms beginning with *dā* are included according to their specific denotation. *Dheṭ* means "to drink"; *ṣiñ* means "to bind"; *śadlṛ* means "to fall" or "to perish"; and *ṣadlṛ* means "to dissolve," "to go," or "to sink."
The suffix *kmarac* is added after the verbal roots *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *syad*.
The suffix *kmarac* is applied after the roots *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *syad*. There exists another verbal root, *ghasi*.
The substitute *ghurac* is applied in place of *bhañjabhāsa* and *mid*. 3.2.161.
*bhañja* is used in the sense of crushing (*āmardane*), *bhāsṛ* in the sense of shining (*dīptau*), and *ñimidā* in the sense of moistening (*snehane*).
The suffix *kurac* is applied after the roots *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid*.

Regarding the rule *vidibhidi-cchideḥ kurac*: the phrase "not for the root meaning 'to obtain'" (*na lābhārthasya*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) meaning "not for the root meaning 'to know'" (*jñānārthasya*), but not for the root meaning "to obtain. Why? He says: "by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*). Therefore, the principle "between a root with a *luk*-vikaraṇa and one with an *aluk*-vikaraṇa" (*lugvikaraṇālugvikaraṇayoḥ*) does not apply here either. Since the suffix *ghurac*—which is the subject under discussion in the rule *vidibhidi-cchider ṅit*—is already established as having the property of being *ṅit* by means of this extended application (*atideśa*), the creation of a separate suffix is intended to indicate that the *ṅit*-status derived through extended application is non-permanent (*anitya*).

Therefore, regarding the root *dhū* in the sense of "shaking," which belongs to the *kuṭādi* class, when the suffix *itrac* is applied according to the rule *arttilūdhū*, the effect of the marker *ṅ* does not occur. However, some authorities desire only the form *dhuvitram*; this is Vedic—as in the statement "the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the *dhuvitrāṇi*"—and its usage follows that [Vedic] precedent in the *Kalpasūtras*. Regarding the term "in the sense of a reflexive agent" (*karmakartari*): Māgha, however, employs it with a pure (non-reflexive) agent: "The woman, whose nature was to cut through the pride of her elders, did not ask for anything difficult to obtain."
The suffix *kvarap* is added after the roots √iṇ, √naś, √ji, √sṛ, and √tṛ.

The suffix *kvarap* is applied after the roots *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛt*. The letter *p* in *kvarap* serves the purpose of [marking] the accent (*svarārtha*) and the purpose of the *tuk* augment. Thus, from the root *i*, we have *itvarī*; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... and so forth.
And [the word] *gatvara* [is formed with the suffix *kvarap*]. 3.2.164.
The word *jāgarūkaḥ* [is formed by adding the suffix *ūka*]. 3.2.165.
The suffix *yaṅ* is applied after verbal roots ending in *yaj*, *jap*, and *daś*.
The suffix *ra* is applied after the verbal roots √nam, √kamp, √smyi, √jas, and √kaś, when preceded by the prefix *adhi*. (Pāṇini 3.2.167)

The suffix *ra* is applied after the root *aj* [to form *ajasra*] when there is continuity of action (*kriyāsātatye*). The vowel *a* in *ajasra* is an adventitious (*āgantuka*) element. "Continuity of action" means the uninterrupted engagement in actions. How then is it used in the case of fires—as in, "They should kindle the fires that are *ajasra* (uninterrupted) and not being offered into"? And [how about] the statement, "For twelve nights from the consecration (*ādhāna*), they are *ajasra*"? In these cases as well, they are called *ajasra* because they remain awake (*ajasrajāgaraṇāt*) [i.e., they do not go out].
The suffix *u* is applied after the verbal roots *san*, *āśaṃs*, and *bhikṣ*.

The suffix *u* is applied after the roots *san*, *āśaṃs*, and *bhikṣ*. [The rule] "not after the root *san*" means that the roots *ṣaṇu* (in the sense of "giving") and *vana* or *ṣaṇa* (in the sense of "distribution" or "acquisition") are not included here. Why? Because the word *vijigīṣu* is listed among the *gargādi* group. [The rule] "not after *śaṃs* in the sense of praise" is understood from its mention together with the prefix *ā*; for it is taught along with that [prefix] in the sense of "desire," not in the sense of "praise."
The word *vinduri* means *icchā* (desire). 3.2.169.

*vinduricchuḥ* (the word *vindu* means one who desires). Regarding the mention of *vid-*: this refers to the root meaning "to know" (*jñāna*), and not to the other roots [of the same form], because of their specific denotation or due to technical substitution (*nipātana*). As for the word *bindu*, it begins with the labial class (*pavarga*); it is derived from the root *bidi* in the sense of "division" (*avayava*) with the *uṇādi* suffix *u* according to the rule *mṛgayvādayaśca*. In Vedic usage, the substitution of *bha* for *va* is optionally desired, as in the example *vaiśvadevā bhindavaḥ*. Regarding *iṣ-*: this refers to the root *iṣu* in the sense of "desire" (*icchā*); however, the roots *iṣu* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and *iṣa* in the sense of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) are not included here, for the same reasons mentioned previously.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *kāya* in the sense of "desire" (*chanda*) when it occurs in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).

"What is *kyacchasi*?"—the term *kya* is a general designation for *kyac*, *kyaṣ*, and *kyaṅ*. In both the sūtra and the commentary (*vṛtti*), because there is an indication of a suffix possessing the indicatory letter *k* that serves as the cause for the technical name "root" (*dhātu-saṃjñā*), the *yak* suffix of the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class is also included. By this, forms such as *bhuraṇyuḥ*, *turaṇyavaḥ*, *aṅgirasaḥ*, and *nakṣatrasaparyema saparyavaḥ* are established. Furthermore, the word *sumnayu-* in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*) should be understood from its inclusion among the *mṛgayu-* group in the *uṇādi* list. Regarding *mitrayu-*: [it is formed with *kyac*].
The substitution of *i* by the rule "kyaci ca" does not occur, nor does the lengthening by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ," because of the prohibition: "na chandasyaputrasya."
The suffixes *kikin* and *liṭ* are applied after the roots *ād*, *gam*, *han*, and *jan*.

Regarding the rule *āḍgamahanajanakṣiṇibhyaḥ kikinau liṭ ca*: words employed in a sense other than their own primary meaning convey the sense of the suffix *vati* even without the word *vati* being explicitly used—just as in the expression "the Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*). Thus, he says: "And those two are like the *liṭ*. This does not mean that the suffixes *kikin* and *liṭ* actually occur; for if that were the case, he would have simply said "*liṭ* [is applied] after *kikin*. Rather, this is an extension of grammatical operation (*kāryātideśaḥ*).

If this were so, then the designation *parasmaipada* would apply to the suffixes *k* and *kin*, and consequently, they would not occur after roots such as *daiṅ* and *dyaṅ*, which take the *ātmanepada*. [Objection: It is not the letter *l* that receives the designation *parasmaipada*; what then? It is its substitutes (*ādeśas*). [Reply: Even so, since the status of being like the *liṭ* (perfect tense) applies to all three—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the state (*bhāva*)—would it not follow that *k* and *kin* should occur even in the sense of the passive and the impersonal? [Reply: This is not so; what is to be extended by analogy is the operation of the *liṭ* once the suffixes have been produced. And the production of those two occurs only in the sense of the agent.

Because this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit with the rule "kṛt suffixes occur in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), or because of non-utterance (*anabhidhāna*), they will not occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Furthermore, since the governing topic is the present tense (*vartamāna*), the prescription of *kikin* suffixes applies to the present; thus, even the status of the past tense (*bhūtakālatā*) is not extended [to them], as that would involve a contradiction. And since the extension of grammatical operations (*kāryātideśa*) proceeds without subverting the original form (*svarūpa*), there is an absence of the *tiP* and other such suffixes, as well as the *kānac* and *kvasu* suffixes. Regarding the statement "the letter *d* in *ād* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation": the meaning is that this *d* in *ād* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

"But this is not *tapara*. This means that this letter *ta* which follows [the *a*] is not *tapara*; the meaning is that this *takāra* following the vowel *a* has been specified by virtue of being a *jaś* (voiced unaspirated) sound. He asks, "What is the reason? and says, "Lest [this be the case]. However, in the reading "the *takāra* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation" (*mukhasukhārtha*), the meaning is that this *takāra* following the *a* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation, and not for the purpose of effecting the operation of a *tapara*. As in "papiḥ somam": the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule "na lokāvyaya... [Pāṇini 2.3.69] indicates that the *liṭ* suffix is the operative factor; thus, the accusative case is used after the word "soma. As in "taturiḥ."

The substitution of *u* [for *ṛ*] occurs by the rule "bahulam chandasi" (Pāṇini 7.1.10). By the rule "dvirvacane 'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which prescribes the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the element *tṛ* is reduplicated. Thus, we have *jajñiri*. The elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) and the change to *c* (*cutvam*) occur by the rule "gamahana... (Pāṇini 6.4.98). The designation as *kit* is for the purpose of setting aside that [elision]. The meaning is that this is so that there may not be *guṇa* substitution for roots ending in *ṛ*, such as *ṛ* and others, when followed by *kikin*. Regarding the term "utsarga" (general rule): the meaning is that the rule should be formulated as applying to all verbal roots (*dhātu*). He asks "Why? and answers: "Because [the suffix is seen] after ten [roots], beginning with *sad*. Thus, *sedih* and *nemih*; in these, the substitution of *e* (*aitva*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) occur [by Pāṇini 6.1.45 and 6.4.120].

Regarding *sahivahityādi*: here, the phrase "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*) is required [as a governing condition]. As for *pāpatiḥ*, although the augment *nīg* would have been applicable by the rule *nīgvañcu-* etc., it does not occur because of the statement of the Vārttikakāra: "There is the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of *sāsahi*, *vāvahi*, *cācali*, and *pāpati*. This, however, is the sentence as recorded in the *Vṛtti*. The expression "another says" (*apara āha*) is recorded in the *Bhāṣya*; there too, the absence of *nīg* occurs due to the statement of the Bhāṣyakāra. For he has said: "Those very ones are the examples."
The affix *niṅ* is applied after the verbal roots *svap* (to sleep) and *pṛṣ* (to sprinkle).
The suffix *āru* is applied after the roots *śru* and *vand*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *bhī* to form a denominative verb meaning "to fear. (Pāṇini 3.2.174)
The suffix *varac* is applied after the verbal roots *sthā*, *īś*, *bhās*, *pis*, and *kas*.

The suffix *vac* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *īś*, *bhās*, *pisa*, and *kas*. Thus, *īśvara*. There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *neḍvaśi kṛti*. In the feminine, it is *īśvarā*, as in "of the lady (*īśvarāyāḥ*) who has applied auspicious great herbs. However, the form *īśvarīm* (in the phrase *īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānām*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Others say that the suffix *varaṭ* is derived from the Uṇādi list. Others say it is formed by the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām*. Still others say that with the suffix *kvanip* according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are applied by the rule *vano ra ca*.
And [the suffix] yaṅ [is applied] after [a verbal root] ending in yaṅ. 3.2.176.

In the case of *yāyāvara*, as before, when the suffix *iṭ* is prohibited, [the rule] "elision of *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*) applies; then, by "elision of *y* and *v* before a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*), the elision of *ā* (*āllopaḥ*) would be required. However, because the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), this elision of *ā* would be expected; yet, due to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding what is effected by *vṛddhi* (*vare kṛtasya*), it does not take place.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the verbal roots *bhrāj*, *bhās*, *dhur*, *vidyut*, *ūrji*, *pṛ*, *jugrā*, and *stu*. (Pāṇini 3.2.177)

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *bhrāj*, *bhās*, *dhurv*, *dyut*, *urj*, *pṛ*, *ju*, and *stu* preceded by *grāvan*. [The roots are: *bhrājṛ* in the sense of shining; *bhāsṛ* in the sense of shining; *turvī*, *thurvī*, and *dhurvī* in the sense of injuring; *dyuta* in the sense of shining; *urja* in the senses of strength and living; *pṛ* in the senses of protecting and filling; *ju* is a root belonging to the Sūtra (sautra); and *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of praising, preceded by *grāvan*.

"And there is lengthening of *javati*. Some say that in the sūtra, *jū* should be read with a long vowel. Others hold that the mention of *dṛśi* should be drawn from the subsequent sūtra for the purpose of including another rule. Regarding *grāvastut*: even in the absence of an explicit locative indication, the word *grāvan* is desired to be designated as an *upapada*. However, others, based on the wording of the sūtra, form the compound with the verbal root itself and subsequently apply the suffix *kvip*.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is also seen after other [roots]. (Pāṇini 3.1.178)

"It is also seen after other [roots] as well," is said for the purpose of including other rules. When the word *dṛśyate* ("is seen") is used, the meaning becomes that just as roots ending in *kvip* are seen, so too are they to be understood; and they are thus understood provided that doubling (*dvirvacana*) and other operations occur as appropriate. He shows another rule itself with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*). And likewise he says: the author of the Vārttika. *Āyatastūḥ* (one who praises what is long); *kaṭaprūḥ* (one who moves toward a mat); *didyut* (lightning).

In the rule *dyutisvāpyoḥ samprasāraṇam*, there is samprasāraṇa of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). But how can there be the designation "reduplication" (*abhyāsa-saṃjñā*) when, due to proximity, that designation is prescribed only for the doubling [of a root] taught in the sixth chapter (*ṣāṣṭhika*), and not for that which occurs in the eighth chapter? If this is so, then the samprasāraṇa and the designation "reduplication" should be understood as resulting from the very mention of the root *dṛśi*. As for *jagat*: by the rule *gamaḥ kvau*, there is the elision of *m*; here too, the operation is to be understood as before.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *dve ca*, the long vowel is conjoined; through the hearing of the long vowel, the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) is understood to apply, and by resorting to the principle of "specification of that which ends in [the preceding element]," it is understood that this applies only to the root *hu-* when it ends in a vowel, and not to the roots *dyut-* or *gam-*. Thus he says: "and the lengthening of *hu-*" (*juhoter dīrghitvam*). Regarding *juhūḥ*: here, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*).
In the case of *dhīḥ* as well, the instrument alone is intended to be expressed as the agent; for it is the person who meditates (*dhyāyati*), not the intellect (*dhīḥ*).
The word *bhuvaḥ* [is used] in the sense of another name (*saṃjñā*) or in the sense of "another" (*antara*). Pāṇini 3.2.179.

[The rule] "bhuvaḥ saṃjñāntarasoḥ" [is explained as follows]: regarding "between the creditor and the debtor": he to whom a debt is owed is the creditor (*dhanika*), and he who owes it is the debtor (*adhamarṇa*). He who stands between them—that is, in their midst—for the sake of providing assurance is called a guarantor (*pratibhūḥ*). It does not apply when someone stands between two villages. And this is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "seeing" (*darśana*).

If this is so, since this is a technical term (*saṃjñā*), is it not already established by the rule "in the case of a technical term" (*saṃjñāyām*)? To this they reply: as long as things exist, their designations continue; however, the word *pratibhū* ceases to apply once that repayment of the debt has actually occurred.
The suffixes *vip* and *saṃ* take the designation *ṅ* when they do not denote a name.

"From *vipra*, *saṃ*, and [prefixes] ending in *ṅ*, except when there is the designation *saṃjñā*. Regarding "from *mitadrau* and so forth," the meaning is "from verbal roots preceded by *mita* and others. In the word *śambhu*, the root *bhū* here has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) included within it.
The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after a verbal root ending in *dha* when it denotes the object (*karman*).

The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi kārake*), the word "object" (*karman*) here does not function as an *upapada* (an accompanying word). If it were intended as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṣṭran* would have been prescribed in that very same section where *aṇ* is prescribed for roots ending in an object (*karmaṇyaṇ*). One might argue: "But then the suffix *ṣṭran* would have to be mentioned again in the subsequent rule. Let it be so; for mentioning *ṣṭran* is indeed simpler than mentioning "the object" (*karman*). Furthermore, the suffix *ṣṭran* is not applied here in the sense of the present tense; when one says *dhātrī* ("nurse"), only the relationship between the action and its factor is understood. Therefore, "in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*) refers solely to the meaning of the suffix itself, and not to an *upapada*.
The suffix *karaṇe* (in the sense of instrument) is applied after the verbal roots *dam*, *niśas*, *yuj*, *yuj*, *stṛ*, *tud*, *sic*, *mih*, *pat*, *daś*, and *naha*. (Pāṇini 3.2.182)

The roots *dāmnīśasayuyujastutudasisicamihapatadaśanahaḥ* [are used] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding *dāp lavane* (the root *dāp* meaning "cutting"), there is no inclusion of *daip śodhane* (the root *daip* meaning "purifying"), because such a usage is not attested (*anabhidhānāt*). Regarding *yujir yoga* (the root *yuj* meaning "joining"), there is likewise no inclusion of *yuja samādhau* (the root *yuja* meaning "concentration"), for the same reason of non-attestation. Regarding *yujir yoga*, there is no inclusion of *yuja samādhau* as before. As for the phrase "in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) among the kārakas," the word *karaṇa* itself does not function as an *upapada* (governing word), because the word *daṃṣṭrā* is listed among the *ajādi* group [of feminine suffixes].

For this very reason, although there is an elision of the nasal in the sūtra according to the reading, [the suffix] ṣṭran does not occur; rather, it occurs only with lyuṭ. As for that [suffix] which is seṭ (taking the augment iṭ), there is a prohibition of iṭ by the rule "titutra" and so forth.
The suffix *pu* is applied after the words *hala* and *sūkara*. (Pāṇini 3.2.183)

The word *puvaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "the snout" when it refers to the instrument [of the action], provided that it is a part of a plough (*hala*) or a boar (*sūkara*). By this, he excludes the possibility of the words *hala* and *sūkara* being the expressed meanings (*abhidheya*) or being subordinate terms (*upapada*). It is said that "the face (*mukha*) is expressed," meaning no other part such as the ears and so forth. This too is obtained simply by the very nature [of the usage].
The suffix *itra* is applied after [the verbal roots] *art*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, and *saha*. 3.2.184.

The suffix *itra* is taught after the verbal roots *artī*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, and *sah*. The vowel *i* is explicitly taught so that the prohibition of *iṭ*—which applies according to the rules "titutra" and "ekācaḥ"—may not take effect here as appropriate. Furthermore, it serves the purpose of accentuation: for if *iṭ* were present, the augment would be unaccented (*anudātta*), whereas with the suffix *itra*, the first syllable of the suffix itself is acutely accented (*udātta*).
The suffix *puvan* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). 3.2.185.

The suffix *puv* is applied in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). For example, *barhiṣpavitram*. That which is made from *barhis* grass is the *pavitra* (strainer) of the *barhis*; in this case, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), and the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule: "In a compound, [the *s* of *su*] is always replaced by *ṣ* when it does not stand at the beginning of a following word. That by which the clarified butter (*ājya*) is purified is the *pavitra*. Furthermore, it refers to the wrapping around the ring finger during recitations (*japa*) and other such rites.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*, when they function as agent nouns (*kartṛ*).

"In the sense of the agent, [the suffix] is used for the Ṛṣi and the deity. Regarding "in the sense of the instrument for the Ṛṣi": they say that an *ṛṣi* is a Vedic mantra, based on the observation [in scripture] that "it was spoken by the Ṛṣi."
The suffix *kta* is applied after a root ending in *ñī*. (Pāṇini 3.2.187)

The suffix *kta* [is taught] after [roots ending in] *ñī*. Since the *niṣṭhā* suffixes are prescribed for the past tense (*bhūta*), and so forth—therein, by the principle of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāpta*), the domain of the past is set aside for the *kta* suffix because its primary scope is the present; as will be stated regarding the rule "when the male [partner] of a mare (*vaḍavā*) is to be expressed": although [the suffix] would apply to the offspring (*apatya*), it is withdrawn from there and prescribed for the male partner. The same applies to that which is prescribed subsequently. However, the word *jñāta* occurs even in the sense of the past, because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *upajñāta* is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "by that" (*tena*).

For if [the action] were present, the genitive case would have to occur according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*; and thus, the grammatical correctness of such expressions as *pūjito yaḥ surair api* ("he who is honored even by the gods") must be considered.
And [the suffix *ktin* is applied] after verbal roots meaning "to think," "to perceive," and "to honor. (Pāṇini 3.2.188)

And [the suffix *ktin* is applied] after roots meaning "to think" (*mati*), "to perceive" (*buddhi*), and "to worship" (*pūjā*). Regarding *mati*: since *buddhi* is mentioned separately, *buddhi* is not included here. Regarding *mata*: there is the elision of the nasal according to the rule "anudāttopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37).

Regarding the words beginning with *śīlita*: [the roots are] *śīla* (in the sense of concentration), *rakṣa* (in the sense of protection), *kṣamūṣ* (in the sense of endurance), *kruśa* (in the sense of calling out and weeping), *juṣī* (in the sense of pleasure and service), *ruṣa* (in the sense of anger), *hṛñ* (in the sense of taking away); or alternatively, *hṛṣu* (in the sense of falsehood) or *hṛṣ* (in the sense of satisfaction); *tuṣa* (in the sense of satisfaction), *kamu* (in the sense of desire), *yama* (in the sense of cessation), *kaṣa* (in the sense of injury), and *mṛṅ* (in the sense of giving up life). Among these, the first two (*śīla* and *rakṣa*) take the augment *iṭ*; for the others, whether they are marked with *u* or not, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā"; and for those marked with long *ī*, there is a prohibition by the rule "śvīdito niṣṭhāyām".

Regarding *hṛṣṭa*: [the suffix *kta* is applied] by the rule *hṛṣer lomasu*. Regarding *kaṣṭa*: [the suffix *kta* is applied] by the rule *kṛcchragahanayoḥ kaṣaḥ*. Regarding *ruṣṭa*: there is an option by the rule *ruṣyamatvarasaṃdhuṣāsvanām*. Regarding *supta*: although this is already established by the rule *trītaḥ ktaḥ*, the suffix *nañiṅ* is added here so that it may not be superseded by [the suffixes denoting] "one who habitually does that" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; however, in some places, *sṛpta* is read instead.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the third quarter (pāda) of the third chapter:

*uṇādayo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.1]. Regarding the word *vartamāne* ("in the present tense") [in the commentary], the particle *eva* indicates that the mention of "present tense" (*vartamāna*) from the rule *vartamāne laṭ* [3.2.123] continues without interruption. Regarding the phrase *saṃjñāyām ca* ("and when it is a name"), this is from the rule *puvaḥ saṃjñāyām* [3.1.135].

Let the rule "uṇādayaḥ" alone suffice for the purpose of authorizing the correctness of the uṇādi suffixes as recited in other treatises; what is the use of the inclusion of the term *bahula*? To this he replies: "bāhulakam. [The root] *lā* means "to take"; that which takes many meanings is *bahula*; the state of being such is *bāhulakam*, with the suffix *vuñ* added according to the rule for the *manojñādi* group. Furthermore, that taking of many meanings is the ground for the application of the word *bahula*.

Furthermore, there are many meanings—such as "occurrence" in some cases and "non-occurrence" in others—as will be described by their definitions later. Regarding the word *prakṛteḥ*: the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*). In this context, the word *tanu* denotes "merely the quality" (the subtle elements). Having observed that the "thinning out" (*tānava*)—that is, the scarcity—of primary roots (*prakṛti*) occurs, this abundance (*bāhulaka*) has been stated; therefore, the *uṇādi* suffixes occur even from roots not explicitly listed, such as the suffix *ulac* after the root *hṛṣ*, which is prescribed, and it also occurs after the root *śak*—as in the form *śaṅkula*.

Likewise, in the *Pañcapādī*, those *uṇādi* suffixes have been collected for the most part, but not in their entirety; however, due to the rule of "frequent occurrence" (*bahulavacana*), they also apply even where they have not been explicitly prescribed, as in: "from the root *ṛ*, the suffixes *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* occur"—resulting in *ṛphiḍa* and *ṛphiḍḍa*. Furthermore, because the grammatical operations (*kārya*) are prescribed with remainder (*saśeṣa*) rather than exhaustively (*niḥśeṣa*), there are also cases where they occur despite not being explicitly prescribed, owing to the rule of frequent occurrence.

In the case of the root *ṣaṇ* (meaning "to give"), by the rules "*ñamantāḍḍaḥ*" and "*dhātvādeḥ paḥ sa*," the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* does not occur; or, even if the substitution of *s* has already taken place, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs [subsequently]. It might be argued: "Let there be only as many verbal roots (*prakṛti*) as are included in the *Pañcapādī*, as many suffixes (*pratyaya*) as there are, and as many grammatical operations (*kārya*) as have been prescribed; let there be no inclusion of others by means of the term *bahulam* (variously). To this, he replies: "For that which arises from common usage (*naigama*) and conventional etymology (*rūḍhi*) is truly correct."

*Nigama* means *chandas* (Vedic literature); those occurring therein are *naigama*. Since the word *nigama* has its final syllable accented by the rule for *athādi* compounds, the suffix *ṭhañ* would have been expected by the rule *bahvaco'ntodāttāṭṭhañ*; however, because it is listed in the *ṛgayanādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied instead. *Rūḍhi* means established usage; those occurring therein are *rūḍhibhava*, i.e., proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*). Their correctness occurs when, through the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), the base forms (*prakṛti*) and other elements that are not explicitly mentioned are subsumed; otherwise, it would not be so. The word *hi* indicates a reason. The meaning is: since this is the case, therefore the principle of "variousness" (*bāhulaka*) has been stated.

Other teachers as well have provided etymological explanations (*vyutpādana*) of words derived from common usage and conventional meaning (*naigamarūḍhi*) through the division into roots (*prakṛti*) and so forth; therefore, with the intention that we too must do the same, he says: "And the name (*nāma*). For the teacher Yāska, the author of the *Nirukta*, stated in his own treatise that every name is born from a verbal root (*dhātujam*). "Offspring" (*toka*) is a name for progeny. Śākaṭāyana is the offspring (*toka*) of Śakaṭa. Regarding the phrase "that which... (*yan na*).

The meaning of a word (*padārtha*) is that which serves as the purpose for its derivation; thus, "word-meaning" refers to the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth. That which is both a word-meaning and a specific distinction is "the specific word-meaning" (*padārthaviśeṣa*); that which has arisen from this is "arisen from the specific word-meaning. That which is not of such a nature—that is, that which has not been derived by means of employing the specific base forms and so forth—is to be inferred as being born from a verbal root (*dhātu*). How is it to be inferred? From the suffix (*pratyaya*) and from the base form (*prakṛti*).

In a case where a subsequent portion (*parabhāga*) of a word-form is heard as being similar to some well-known suffix (*pratyaya*), one should infer that portion to be a suffix and then deduce (*ūhya*) the remaining portion to be the base (*prakṛti*). For instance, having observed the suffix *ulac* in the rule "from the root *hṛṣ*, [the suffix] *ulac*," the base *śaṅk* is inferred; thus, the status of *śaṅkulā* as being derived from a verbal root (*dhātujatva*) is established.

However, where a preceding portion resembles something already well-known as a verbal root (*dhātu*), one should designate that portion as the base (*prakṛti*) and infer the remaining portion to be the suffix (*pratyaya*). For example: in *ṛphiḍaḥ* and *ṛphiḍḍaḥ*, the elements *phiḍa* and *phiḍḍa* are the suffixes.

And this *ūha* (inference/extension) applies only to those technical terms (*saṃjñā*) for which [the rules] have not been explicitly stated, not everywhere; thus he says, "in technical terms. One should recognize the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters), such as *k*, from the grammatical effect, such as the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution and so forth. By that means, *phiṭ* and *phiḍḍa* are to be inferred as having the *kit* designation. This very same aforementioned science consisting of *ūha* applies to the *uṇādi* suffixes where they have not been explicitly stated.
They are also seen in the case of past things. 3.3.2.

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of the present tense in the preceding [sūtra]": the mention of the present tense (*vartamāna*) has not been withdrawn from that very context. The intention is to demonstrate the distinction that these suffixes generally occur in the present tense, and only occasionally in the past. In the examples, by the rule *tābhyām anyatroṇādayaḥ*, the suffix *manin* is applied to a factor other than the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) or the point of departure (*apādāna*); furthermore, the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti*.
The words *gamyā* and others shall be formed with the suffix *yat*. (Pāṇini 3.3.3)

Just as when it is said "speed (*syada*) means velocity," the word *syada* becomes a synonym for the word *java*, so too here one might suspect that words such as *gamyā* (to be gone) and others would result in being synonyms for the word *bhaviṣyat* (future). Anticipating this, he says: "Of the suffix alone," and so forth. The state of being future, which resides in the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is prescribed as something to be manifested by the suffix alone; it does not, however, belong to the entire complex [of base and suffix] by way of abandoning the meaning of the base. "Not of the base" means "not even of the base."

Among words such as *gamya* and others, some are formed by *uṇādi* suffixes and some belong to the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. For example: *gamī* (one who goes) and *āgāmī* (one who comes). [These are derived] by the rule *gameriniḥ* and *āṅi ṇicca*, which prescribes the suffix *ini*. Similarly, *bhāvī* (one who will be) and *prasthāyī* (one who sets out). In this very section, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rules *bhuvaśca* and *prātsthaḥ*; because the suffix is marked with *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening and the insertion of the augment *yuk*. According to others, the suffix *ini* is added to the roots *rudh*, *budh*, *yudh*, and *yā* preceded by *prati*. Others say this is due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). Still others say it is by the rule *supyajātau*. Thus we have *pratiyogī* (an opponent).

By the rule *saṃpṛcādisūtra*, when the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied, there is the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*) for *ca* and *ja* by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. Others maintain that the substitution of *ku* occurs only when the suffix *ṇini* is applied, either because [the word] is listed in the *nyaṅkvādi* group or due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Regarding the statement "an addition must be made for the non-today time" (*anadyatane upasaṃkhyānam*): what, then, is the reason it is not already established? This indication is made using the suffix *lṛṭ*. *Lṛ...*

Furthermore, since [the suffix] *luṭ* subordinates [the scope of] *anadyatana* (non-today), these [suffixes] would apply only in the domain of *lṛṭ*. Alternatively, because they constitute the meaning of a sentence, words such as "gamya" (to be gone) function by relying on that generality which underlies the particularity. However, the specific quality known as "non-today" is understood through the power of the word "śvas" (tomorrow). When there is an intention to express that specific quality, only *luṅ* occurs—as in "he will go to the village tomorrow" (*śvo grāmaṃ gantā*). And by the rule of "optionality of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), *lṛṭ* also occurs; thus, forms such as *bhaviṣyati* and *gamiṣyati* are justified.
The present tense (*laṭ*) is used after the particles *yāvat* and *purā*. Pāṇini 3.3.4.

The word *purā* is an indeclinable (or a compound in the sense of a *karmadhāraya*). Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the qualifier is placed at the end. These two are irregular forms that indicate certainty. When these are employed, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) does not occur; for the state of being the present time is set aside by the state of being future time.

Regarding "as much as he will give": the suffix *vatup* is applied to the pronouns *yad* and *etad* in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*) by the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup*; the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel occurs by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. Regarding "he will go before [the time]": the root *pṝ* (in the sense of protecting or filling) takes the suffix *kvip* by the rule *bhrājabhās...* etc.; the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya*. The word *asya* is stated in the instrumental case (*karaṇabhūtayā*) in order to indicate its status as the third case ending.

Since the inclusion of the two particles (*nipāta*) would already be established by the fact that they are mentioned explicitly (*pratipadokta*), the explicit mention of "particle" (*nipāta-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating that the *lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding what is formed by a rule versus what is mentioned explicitly) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Consequently, in the rule *ātāṃ puṇau*, the augment *puṅ* occurs even after a verbal root ending in long *ā* that is merely indicated by a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*), as in *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*: *krāpayati* and *jāpayati*.
The particle *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is used after the words *kadā* and *karhi*.

In the rule *anadyatane luṭ* ("the affix *luṭ* is used when [an action] does not refer to the current day"), this same application (*yoga*) must also be understood as carrying over (*anuvartanīya*). Consequently, even in the domain of *luṅ*, *laṭ* optionally occurs. For this very reason, *luṅ* is also cited as an example for the alternative case. This should be understood to apply to the preceding rule as well. [As in the example: *karhi bhokṣyate* ("When will he eat?"). Now, one might object: the word *karhi* refers to a time other than the current day; therefore, in its usage, only *luṅ* ought to occur, not *lṛṭ*. [To this we reply: No, because it serves the purpose of the sentence (*vākya-artha*).

The word *bhokṣyate* functions in the sense of future time in general; however, the understanding of it as referring specifically to the non-immediate future (*anadyatana*) depends on the word *karhi*. Furthermore, the syntactic meaning of a sentence does not serve to effect the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of individual words.
When *lip* (to desire) has taken place [as a prefix], [the suffix *kha* is applied]. 3.3.6.

"What is *kiṃvṛtta*? It is called *vṛtta* because something occurs (*vartate*) therein; thus, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the rule *kto'dhikaraṇe ca*. Precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule *adhikaraṇavācinā ca* does not apply, or else the compound is formed with a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Whatever contains the word *kim* as a constituent part is all *kiṃvṛtta*. Consequently, a specific enumeration is provided to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *kīdṛśaḥ*, *kimīyaḥ*, and *kintarām*. [The phrase] 'by the mention of *vṛtta*'..."

The neuter gender [in the word *tat*] is due to its dependence on the form of the word *śabda*. Regarding the rule *ḍatarad tamau ca*: the meaning is that the forms of the interrogative pronoun *kim* ending in *-ḍatara* and *-ḍatama* [are included]. In the example *kaṃ bhavanto bhojayitāraḥ*, the intention is that this [word *kim*] also carries over (is *anuvṛtti*) into the rule *anadyatane luṭ* ("the suffix *luṭ* is used for the future not of today"). This should be understood to apply to the subsequent rules as well.
And [the augment *iṭ* is applied] when the accomplishment of what is about to be performed is intended. 3.3.7.

The term *lipsyamānasiddhau* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), only the basic fact was shown: "the accomplishment [of heaven, etc. from that which is desired to be obtained. Alternatively, due to this very irregular formation (*nipātana*), it may be a ablative compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*). The meaning is: "in the accomplishment of heaven and so forth, which has as its cause food and other such things that are being desired to be obtained."

But surely, where the accomplishment of what is desired is understood, there desire also exists; therefore, since this is already established by the preceding rule, is there not no purpose for this one? To this he says: "The commencement of this [sūtra] is for the sake of that which is not formed with *kim*. In the previous sūtra, the inclusion of the term *kiṃvṛtta* was intended so that [the suffix] might occur only after that which is formed with *kim* when there is mere desire in the absence of the accomplishment of what is desired, and so that it would not occur when not formed with *kim*.
And [the suffix *liṅ* is used] when the sense of the imperative (*loḍ-artha*) is indicated. Pāṇini 3.3.8.

Regarding the phrase "of the injunction for study" (*adhyayanapraiṣasya*): in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, a locative compound is formed because of the statement that "the instrument [is compounded] with a *kṛt*-suffix," as in the case of *pādahāraka* and similar forms.
And the periphrastic future suffix (liṅ) is used for an action occurring more than an hour later. 3.3.9.

The compound is formed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the second member. Furthermore, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *adhyādi* group. However, in the rule "from a polysyllabic word with an udātta accent on the final syllable," the phrase "of a name that is to be explained" (*vyākhyātavyanāmnaḥ*) is understood to carry over. As for the statement "if the teacher has arrived," one should consider whether the condition of not being "today" (*anadyatana*) can possibly apply to a period exceeding one muhūrta.
The suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* are used after a verbal root when another action is intended as the purpose for that action.

Regarding the example *bhikṣiṣye jaṭāḥ* ("I shall beg for matted locks"), here the matted locks (*jaṭā*) serve the purpose of the act of begging, but they do not possess the nature of an action themselves, because matted locks are substances (*dravya*). Regarding *dhāvataste patiṣyati daṇḍaḥ* ("As you run, the staff will fall"), there is indeed the act of running as a subordinate element (*upapada*), yet one does not run for the sake of causing the staff to fall; rather, the staff falls as a consequence of the one who is running. For "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is distinguished by way of a specific aim (*uddeśa*), and not merely by the state of being a cause (*hetutva*). The objection beginning with *atha* [is as follows].

He refutes [this objection] with the words: “by [the rule] *lṛṭā kriyārthopapadena*. However, an annulment by *tumun* need not be suspected, because their meanings are different: *ṇvul* [denotes] the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *tumun* denotes the action (*bhāva*). How so? Because of the inclusion of the term *tum-artha* (the meaning of *tumun*) in the rule *tumarthe seṣen*. For if *tumun* were to denote the agent on the basis of the statement *kartari kṛt*, then *seṣen* and the others would likewise denote the agent. Therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of *tum-artha*, this [suffix *tumun*] is excluded from denoting the agent.

And no other meaning is specified [for the suffix]; and suffixes whose meaning is not specified apply in their own sense (*svārthe*). What is the "own sense" of a verbal root? It is action (*bhāva*) itself. Although the future suffix *lṛṭ* has its purpose fulfilled in the sense of both action and object (*bhāva-karman*), nevertheless, because it is prescribed for the time of the future when an action is the motive for another action (*kriyārthopapada*), it is a rule of specific application (*viśeṣavidhi*). In the prescription of the suffix *ṇvul*, however, the word "agent" (*kartari*) is not heard; therefore, that [suffix] is superseded by the future suffix *lṛṭ*, which is a rule of specific application.

Alternatively, what is the use of this [argument] that it is "specifically prescribed" (*viśeṣavihita*)? Even though both [rules] have scope, the *lṛṭ* suffix would supersede the *ṇvul* suffix by virtue of its posteriority. He raises an objection again: "By the rule regarding optional forms" (*vāsarūpavidhinā*). He refutes it: "In that case, then... (*evaṃ tarhi*).

Now, an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is employed when there is no other purpose; yet here there is indeed a purpose. What is it? It is so that the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ* may apply when the suffix *akan*—prescribed under the heading of the future tense—is used, as in "one who completes a hundred years" (*varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ*) or "one who sees sons and grandsons" (*putrapautrāṇāṃ darśakaḥ*), and not in other cases. This is the thought: the state of being in the future tense is understood here through the proximity of another word.

For when this [expression] is employed with reference to a child, since at that stage it is impossible for him to complete a hundred years or to see his sons and grandsons, it is understood by implication that he will live for such a length of time; however, in this case, the meaning of the word itself is not "future time."

However, with this rule for the suffix *ṇvul* established, there is no fault even when the future time is the meaning of the word in examples such as "the fulfiller of a hundred years," because of the intention expressed in the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*: this refers to the suffix *aka* prescribed under the heading of the future; therefore, it does not apply in cases such as "the fulfiller of a hundred years" or "the one who shows [his lineage] to sons and grandsons."
And [the suffixes] expressing states of being [are applied after verbal roots]. 3.3.11.

One who speaks is a *vacanaḥ*; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, or else it denotes the instrument—thus, that by which a state (*bhāva*) is expressed is a *bhāvavacana*. Here, persons are the agents; he states that only those [suffixes] prescribed under the heading of "state" (*bhāva*) are *bhāvavacana*s, saying: "by the word 'state' (*bhāva*), [it is meant] 'by the verbal root' (*prakṛtyā*). [The suffixes] would be superseded by the suffix *tumun*. However, the future suffix *lṛṭ* has a different meaning, because it is prescribed for all three: state, object, and agent. Furthermore, the suffixes such as *ghañ* occur when the meaning of the verbal root is established as a completed action (*siddhatā*), whereas the *lakāra* occurs when the meaning of the verbal root is pure (i.e., not yet completed); therefore, they also have different meanings.

In this context, it would have been sufficient to say simply "in the sense of an action" (*bhāve*). For even if that were stated, the meaning—that those suffixes prescribed in the sense of an action occur when there is an upapada (governing word) denoting an action for the sake of another action—is indeed obtained. Thinking that the inclusion of the term *vacana* (denotation) is therefore redundant, he asks: "Now [what is the purpose]?"—namely, so that they may be *vācakas* (denoters). For when the term *vacana* is included, the meaning becomes: "being denoters of an action (*bhāvavacanāḥ*), the suffixes such as *ghañ* and others occur in this domain"; that is to say, they occur while being denoters of an action.

He explains this very point by means of a question: "And how? [He says: "From which bases (*prakṛti*)?"—namely, from those ending in *i* (the vowel *i*), and from those ending in *ṛ* and *u* (the vowels *ṛ* and *u*). Likewise: "By which qualifier?"—by such rules as "after *hasta*, when meaning 'taking,' provided it is not theft" (*hastādāne cerasteye*) and "after *śri*, *ni*, and *bhū*, when no prefix is present" (*śriṇībhuvo'nupasarge*). "Inconsistency" (*asāmañjasyam*) means a confusion, that is to say, an overlapping of their respective domains. In examples such as *pākāya*, the dative case is used according to the rule "and after words expressing an action denoting the sense of the infinitive suffix *tum*" (*tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt*).
And [the suffix *aṇ*] is used after a verbal root when an object is expressed. 3.3.12.

The particle *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*sanniyoga*). Otherwise, there would be an option: sometimes the suffix would apply when the upapada is a verb used for the sake of another action, and sometimes it would apply to a mere object alone. However, the explicit statement [of the rule] would serve to set aside the exceptions (*apavāda*) such as *kā-* and others regarding the future tense. But because of the particle *ca*, which functions as a conjunction, the entire collection [of the root and the upapada] together constitutes the cause for the production of the suffix. The designation of "upapada," however, applies to each one individually, because each is specified in the locative case.

Therefore, a compound is formed even with a solitary verbal noun (*karmaṇ*): *kāṇḍalāvo vrajati* ("going as one who cuts reeds"). Because this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*), it subverts the suffix *ṇvul*. Furthermore, it has been indicated that when *ṇvul* is prescribed, if a verb is present as a subordinate element (*upapada*) denoting an action performed for the sake of another action, suffixes such as *tṛc* do not occur by way of the "non-identity" rule (*vāsarūpa*). However, it is not the case that the "non-identity" rule does not apply within this specific section [of the grammar]. Consequently, this *ṇvul* prescribed by the rule "*tumunṇvulau*" occurs even in a domain where the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise be expected, by virtue of the "non-identity" rule: *edhānāhārako vrajati* ("going as one who brings fuel").

And likewise, by the rule "akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ," the sixth case (genitive) is prohibited for the object when used with the suffix *aka*, which is prescribed under the heading of the future tense; and because [the prohibition] is subsequent, it supersedes the application of the *kā*-suffixes and so forth.

But surely, because it is a restatement (*pratiprasava*) rather than an original injunction (*apūrvavidhāna*), there is simplicity; thus, would not the suffix *aṇ* apply only in the domain of the *aṇ* [of P. 3.2.1], overriding *ṇvul*, and not in the domain of its exception? He thinks as follows: here, the word "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) need not be stated, because by the continued application of the mention of "statement" (*vacana*), the rule "that which is [prescribed] after 'statement' takes *aṇ*" ensures that *aṇ* is established precisely when the object is the attendant word (*upapada*). In that case, the repeated mention of "object" is for the purpose of including the object alone; thus, it applies even in the domain of the exception.

And what is the meaning of "because of being other" (*paratvāt*)? It means because of being superior or because of being more abundant. Others, however, explain it as referring to contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) itself.
The suffix *lṛṭ* is also used for the remaining cases [of future time].

"Remainder" (*śeṣa*) is said to be that which is other than when there is a word denoting purpose (*kriyārthopapada*). The meaning is: "future" refers to a time other than that future time in which there is an action (*kriyā*) that has another action as its purpose (*kriyārthopapada*). Regarding the phrase "by the word *ca*": if it occurs both in the case of a remainder and a non-remainder, then let it simply be "the suffix *lṛṭ* [is used]"; the phrase "when there is an action that has another action as its purpose" will be excluded, and by this, it will apply everywhere in the future. Even so, it would apply only in the case of a remainder; however, in the case of a non-remainder, the suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul* would be obstructors. [Objection: By the rule of "optionality of form" (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffix *lṛṭ* will also occur.

This statement, "and in the case of the remainder," has a purpose that requires consideration. [The example is] "he goes, thinking 'I shall do it. The word *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the mutual connection between the two parts.
The suffix *lṛṭ* may optionally be replaced by *sat*.

The mention of "lṛṭaḥ" is for the purpose of indicating the substituendum (sthānin); otherwise, the two suffixes designated as "sat" would be independent elements rather than substitutes. [This applies] in cases such as when they are not coreferential with a word ending in a case-suffix other than the nominative.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the following are included]: in the scope of the rules "and in address" (*sambodhane ca*) and "in the sense of characteristic or cause of an action" (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*); likewise, under the rule "and in the case of suffixes and subsequent members of a compound" (*pratyayottarapadayośca*): the offspring of one who will act is *kāriṣyataḥ*; *kāriṣyamāṇiḥ*; devotion to one who will act is *kariṣyadbhaktiḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇabhaktiḥ*, *kariṣyantībhaktir asya kariṣyadbhaktiḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇābhaktir asya kariṣyamāṇabhaktiḥ*; *kariṣyattaraḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇataraḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇatamaḥ*, *kariṣyadrūpaḥ*.

*kariṣyamāṇarūpaḥ*, *kariṣyatkalpaḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇakalpaḥ*. How is it that in the expression *śvo’gnīnādhāsyamānena* ("by one who will establish the sacred fires tomorrow"), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur despite the action not taking place on the current day? The solution to this has already been stated: by the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* ("irregularity is frequent"), there is a shift in tense (*kālavyatyaya*), and thus the suffix *lṛṭ* is used. Alternatively, there is a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the term "not of the current day" (*anadyatana*) in the subsequent section; thus, even for that *lṛṭ* which occurs when the action is not of the current day, the suffixes designated as *sat* (namely *śatṛ* and *śānac*) may optionally occur.

But by what [rule] does the *lṛṭ* suffix occur for non-recent time? This very fact indicates that the *lṛṭ* occurs for non-recent time, since this [author] prescribes two suffixes designated as *sat* for the *lṛṭ* in the context of non-recent time.
The suffix *luṭ* is used for the future not belonging to the current day.

Regarding the term *anadyatana*, this is a designation based on a *bahuvrīhi* compound; this has already been explained under the rule *anadyatane laṅ*, and thus it should be understood from that very source. Regarding *paridevane*: *paridevana* means lamentation (*anuśocana*). Regarding *śvastanī*: this is the technical name for the suffix *luṭ* used by ancient teachers. Regarding *bhaviṣyantyartha*: *bhaviṣyantī* is the technical name for *lṛṭ*; the meaning is "in the sense of that [suffix]," i.e., in the general sense of the future. Alternatively, there is a reading *bhaviṣyadartha*, which means "in the sense of the future," i.e., in the sense of a general future form.
