Regarding *yevam*: this refers to a slow or hesitant delivery. Regarding *anabhiyukta*: one who lacks proficiency or familiarity.
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *spṛś* when preceded by *pada* or *ruha*.

"He goes to that" (*padyate'sau*): here, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as the agent (*kartṛ*). As for the word *pada*, it will be established under the rule *khano gha ca*. Regarding *roga*: the substitution of *ku* occurs by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. Regarding *spṛśa upatāpe*: "affliction" (*upatāpa*) means disease (*roga*).
The word *sṛ* [is used] in the sense of "firm. (Pāṇini 3.3.17)

The term *sṛ* is an indeclinable citation. Regarding the phrase "of the root *sṛ*": both *sṛ* in the sense of "to go" (*gatau*) and *ṛ* in the sense of "to go" (*gatau*) are included. Regarding the phrase "when the agent is stable" (*sthire kartari*): by this, he shows that the mention of "stable" (*sthira*) is an attribute of the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix, and not an upapada (a word governing another). This is understood from the inclusion of the word *sāra* in the list beginning with *ardharca*.

[Objection: But surely the word *sthira* is a derivative of the root *sthā*, meaning "cessation of motion," formed with the *uṇādi* suffix *kvin*; whereas *sṛti* denotes "motion. Therefore, how can one who is stationary (*sthira*) be logically the agent of moving (*saraṇa*)? To this he says: "‘Stationary’ means persisting for another time," and so forth. The meaning is that since movement over another period of time is possible, it is therefore logical for [the self] to be the agent of the sense of the verbal root *sṛ* (to move). Furthermore, in the word *tiṣṭhan*, the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used in a causal sense.

*Khadirasāra* means the heartwood of the *khadira* tree; because of its firmness, it is stable. *Atīsāra* is a disease, so called because it excessively causes the substances such as blood situated within the body to flow out (*sārayati*). Here, the root *sar-* carries an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*). The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule: "The vowel of a prefix is often lengthened before a word ending in *ghañ*, except when referring to a human being. *Visāra* refers to a fish, so called because it moves in various ways (*vividhaṃ sarati*). *Sāra* means strength, so called because it causes [the body] to move or exert itself (*sārayati ceṣṭayati*). In this case as well, the causative sense is implied.

The word *sāra* [is used as follows]: for that which is powerful acts; the word *sāra* is masculine when denoting excellence (*utkarṣa*), and it is seen to be neuter when denoting that which does not deviate from justice (*nyāya*).
In the sense of "becoming" (bhāva), [the suffix kyap is applied]. 3.3.18.
In order to prevent the confusion of eternally existing words,
because [the suffix] *ghañ* is prescribed for verbal nouns (*bhāvaśabda*), there is no mutual dependence.

Regarding the word *rāga*: the elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs by the rules "rañjeśca" and "ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ. But how can *pāka* and the like serve as examples, since the definition of the meaning provided by means of the verb *bhavati* (to become) applies only to the domain of *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyati*, and not to the domain of *pacati* and so on? To this he says: "The verb *bhavati* expresses action in general. Even the universal (*sāmānya*) known as existence (*sattā*) is expressed by *bhavati* as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*); thus, *bhavati* becomes a term expressing action in general.

Regarding the phrase "the indication of the meaning (*arthanirdeśa*) being made": the suffix *śānac* is used here in the sense of a causal agent (*hetau*). This is because the indication of the meaning is performed by means of a general term (*sāmānyavācin*), and not by a specific term such as *pac* (to cook) and so forth. Therefore, it becomes applicable to the domain of all verbal roots (*sarvadhātuviṣaya*), since the general property exists within all particular instances—just as "cowness" (*gotva*) exists in individual cows like Śābaleya—and because there is no negation of the substratum of the specific forms.

In this context, "being" (bhāva) is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and that is a process consisting of prior and posterior stages which is not yet fully accomplished. To the question of how that which is expressed by the suffix *ghañ* can be connected with gender and number, he says: "And the meaning of the root... Just as in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and *pācaka* ("cook"), the action is expressed by the base portion (*prakṛti*) while its instrument (*sādhana*) is expressed by the affix portion (*pratyaya*); so too, in words like *pāka* ("cooking"), the base portion expresses the meaning in the form of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the affix portion expresses the very same thing in its accomplished form (*siddha*), presenting it in a manner capable of being connected with the properties of a substance—namely, gender, number, and the capacity for grammatical relations (*kāraka*). And it has been said:

Just as in the case of a verb, the status of being the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is attributed to its two parts according to the treatises, that same sequence applies to words ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes.
"In that context, action, as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is based on the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*);
whereas its state of being an existent entity (*sattvabhāva*) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*."

This matter requires extensive explanation. Here, this reference is made using the masculine gender (*puṃlliṅga*) and the singular number (*ekavacana*). Consequently, in that context, the suffixes would apply only in the masculine gender, only in the singular number, and only in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*); they would not apply in other genders nor in other numbers.

Furthermore, regarding the rule *striyāṃ ktin*, since a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "in the feminine" as "the state" (*bhāva*) is impossible—[otherwise] the suffix *ktin* would apply to the feminine when [the action] is not the agent; whereas in the case of "state," just as in the masculine, under the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*, because the phrase *akartari ca kārake* has ceased to apply, the suffix *kta* would apply to the neuter when [the action] is the agent, and to the masculine when it is the state; and in the case of duality and plurality, such as *pākau* and *pākāḥ*, the suffixes would not occur. Therefore, he says: "The masculine gender and the singular number are non-essential (*atantra*)."
An entity existing as a substance is not expressed without gender and number;
therefore, the employment of these two is a matter of grammatical necessity, not something intended for specific semantic emphasis.
Just as the grasping of straw and the like is considered [merely incidental] by those seeking grain,
so too the purpose of that designation is merely the grammatical refinement of the word.
And [the suffix GHaÑ is used] after a verbal root to denote an agent other than the subject, when it forms a name. 3.3.19.

*Prāsaḥ* means a spear (*kuntaḥ*). *Prasevaḥ* is a specific type of container produced by sewing with a needle. Regarding *madhurāhāraḥ*: this is either a *karmadhāraya* compound or a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound. Regarding *meṣaḥ*: this has been cited as an example without depending on its inclusion in the list of *pacādi* roots; for it is stated under the rule *igupadhajñāprī*—"words such as *deva*, *seva*, and *meṣa* are to be understood as belonging to the *pacādi* group. Indeed, if the word were already present in the list, the statement that it "should be looked for" would not be appropriate. Alternatively, this has been shown merely as a direction for counter-examples; the actual counter-example, however, is: *bharttā* (the bearer), from *bibharti* (he bears).

Regarding the phrase "cakāra" and so forth: this *ca* (the particle "and") is displaced [in the order of the rule], as in the expression "*saṃjñāyāṃ ca*" ("also in the sense of a name"). By this, the suffix *ghañ* occurs even when not denoting a name (*asaṃjñā*). If that is so, let there be no mention of "in the sense of a name," and let the *ca* also be omitted, and let it simply be "in the sense of a factor other than the agent" (*akartari kārake*)? True; however, the mention of "name" (*saṃjñā*) was made to indicate that while it generally occurs in the sense of a name, it occasionally occurs even when not a name. Thus, [we have] *dāya*.

The notion that "everything being given is called *muc* (to release)" does not apply here, nor does it apply to the term "gain" (*lābha*) in this context; in both cases, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "the mention of the *kāraka*," and so forth: for if it were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then according to the maxim of "negation joined with *iva*," the understanding would arise of a *kāraka* other than the agent (*kartṛ*) but similar to it—just as "non-Brahmin" refers to a Kṣatriya and the like. Therefore, the mention of the *kāraka* need not be made if it is an exclusion.

In the case of a non-presumptive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), however, by means of a split in the sentence, the meaning becomes this: "The suffix *ghañ* occurs when [the action] is a name (*saṃjñā*), but it does not occur when [it denotes] the agent. In that regard, because there is no specification of the meaning in the first sentence, the suffix would apply to its own meaning alone, according to the principle: "Suffixes whose meanings are not specified occur in their own meaning. But one might object: "Is it not already prescribed for its own meaning by the preceding rule? He says: "No."

For it has been stated that suffixes such as *ghañ* occur when the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) possesses the property called "accomplished state" (*siddhatā*). But here, [the suffix] would apply to the pure meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) in its form as something to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*). [Objection: But surely, by the force of the prohibition regarding the agent (*kartṛ*), even a *ghañ* whose meaning is not explicitly specified will be understood as referring only to a *kāraka* (participant in the action) connected with the meaning of the verbal root? [Response: This is not so. For if the prohibition did not exist, then because of the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), this [suffix] would not be one whose meaning is not specified. Therefore, the mention of the crow (*kāka*) is for the purpose of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

But it should not be used in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*). If that were so, that very [exclusion] would be resorted to; what then is the purpose of mentioning the "agent" (*kartṛ*)? To this he says: "That is done. But what is the reason that in the case of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the compound is not obtained even with effort? Because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*); for in that case, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the action, as in "he does not become an agent," and not with the word "agent" itself. [This refers to the rule: *ādeca upadeśe 'śitī*.

In this context, if *aśiti* were a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), then the substitution of *ā* would have to occur for [the root-final *u*] in any suffix other than one marked with *ś*, such as those beginning with *tṛc*. Consequently, in forms like *suglaḥ* and *sumlaḥ*, the suffix *ka* prescribed by the rule *ātaścopasarge* would not apply, because prior to the arising of the suffix, the stem would not end in the vowel *ā*. However, if it is a *pratiṣedha* (prohibition), then the substitution of *ā* is unconditional, while the prohibition applies specifically when a suffix marked with *ś* follows; thus, the desired result is established.
After all [roots], when expressing a measure, [the suffix *kan* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.3.20)

Regarding the phrase *parimāṇākhyāyām*: the word *parimāṇa* (measure) is derived in the sense of an action (*bhāvasādhana*). *Ākhyā* means "naming" or "expression"; thus, the meaning is "when there is an expression of measurement. Of what, then, is there measurement? It is of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), which is an abstract state (*bhāva*), and of the factor of action (*kāraka*) excluding the agent. This same meaning applies to the commentary (*vṛtti*) as well: "when the expression of measure is understood. In the example *taṇḍulanicāyaḥ*: it is heaped up or gathered into a pile, hence *nicāya* means a heap; "a heap of rice grains" (*taṇḍulānāṃ nicāyaḥ*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

In this case, delimitation is understood through the singularity of the measure (*rāśi*). Here, since the suffix *in* would otherwise apply, the suffix *ghañ* is used. However, the reading is generally *niścāya*; even there, the meaning is the same. Although the rule "after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *ci*, *niści*, and *gam*, [the suffix *ap* is added]" would also apply, the suffix *ghañ* is used. Regarding *śūrpaniṣpāva*: that rice and so forth which is *niṣpūyate*—that is, purified by the removal of husks and the like—is called *śūrpaniṣpāva*. This is a compound formed according to the rule "the agent and the instrument are frequently compounded with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix," namely, *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. In this instance, delimitation is understood through the number of winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*).

Although the suffix *ghañ* is established here by the rule "nirabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ," nevertheless, because the word *sarva* is employed for the purpose of including all exceptions, it is appropriate that the *ghañ* suffix occurs by this very [rule]; thus it is presented. Regarding the word *kāra*: from the root *kṛ* (in the sense of "scattering"), the *ghañ* suffix is applied in the objective sense (*karman*); *kāraḥ* refers to grain and so forth that has been scattered; here too, there is a delimitation by number.

But surely, since the governing rule "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is general, the suffix *ghañ* will apply even without the mention of "all" (*sarva*), and thus there would be no purpose in mentioning "all"? To this he says: "The mention of 'all'... What, then, is the reason that the sublation of *ap* must be achieved through effort? To this he says: "...the determination [is made] from what precedes. In this case, no limit is perceived by anyone.

But surely, since the word *parimāṇa* (measure) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for [units like] a *prastha* and so forth, it would be appropriate only in cases such as "a *niścāya* of rice measured by a *prastha*," and not in a case such as "two *niṣpāva* measures in a winnowing-basket (*śūrpa*)"? To this he says: "The mention of the word *ākhyā* (name/designation) is for the purpose of excluding conventional usage. If one intended to include the *prastha* and other such units, it would have been sufficient to say simply "in a measure" (*parimāṇe*); what was the point of mentioning the word *ākhyā*? It is because of the mention of *ākhyā* that we understand the elision of the suffix *mātraC*, provided that the name of a mere measure is expressed.

Thus, from that [root], a word denoting measurement (*parimāṇa-śabda*) arises as a word denoting action—namely, *parimitiḥ* (the act of measuring), *parimāṇam* (measurement), and *paricchittiḥ* (delimitation); for delimitation occurs by means of number as well. In the same way, the suffix *ghañ* occurs in *unmāna* and so forth, according to their respective designations. If, then, this *ghañ* suffix supersedes even those [suffixes] following "all" (*sarva-*), it would also supersede feminine suffixes; to this he says: "The enumeration of *ghañ* is for the sake of the scope of *ac* and *ap*. And this is understood from the mention of the ablative case in the rule "from all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*).

For the word *sarva* ending in the fifth case (locative) stands in apposition with the word *dhātu*; therefore, the exception (*apavāda*) is sublated only when it pertains to the base (*prakṛti*), not when it pertains to the meaning (*artha*). Regarding the term *tilocchitti*: the suffix *ktin* is used here either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the state/action (*bhāva*). It refers to a heap that has been turned upright.

Regarding "ṇiluk ca": when there is the elision (*luk*) of the *ṇi*-affix, because of its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were still present), the *vṛddhi* substitution based on the *ghañ* suffix would not occur; therefore, the elision (*luk*) is prescribed. Alternatively, because that [elision] is dependent on a subsequent factor (*paranimittaka*), the prohibition stated in the rule *kvi-luk-upadhā-tva-* prevents its being treated as *sthānivat*, and thus the word *jāra* is established. As for *jarayanti*: the shortening occurs because of the *mit* designation in the rule *janī-jṝṣ-knasurañjo’mantāś-ca*. *Jāraḥ* means a secret husband.
And [the suffix] *iṇ* [is applied after a verbal root ending in a vowel]. 3.3.21.

Regarding the term *upādhyāya*: [it is derived] from the root *adhi-i* with the prefix *upa*, meaning "that which is studied by approaching. The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*), while in the form *adhyāya*, *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the rule "the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for the feminine when [the suffix] *ap* follows," since *ghañ* would not otherwise apply in the feminine, it is here specifically ordained. Thus we have *upādhyāyā* and *upādhyāyī*. This particular form refers to one who teaches by herself; however, in the case of a feminine formed through connection with a masculine (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* necessarily occurs. Furthermore, according to the rule "optionally after *upādhyāya* and *mātula*," the augment *ān* is optionally added—resulting in *upādhyāyī* or *upādhyāyānī*.

Regarding the expression "in *śāra*, *vāyu*, *varṇa*, and *nivṛta*": the form *śṝ* is cited without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). *Śāro vāyuḥ*: [The suffix] *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). *Śāro varṇaḥ*: Here the root meaning is "to cause wonder" (*citrikaraṇam*). That by which a substratum is made wonderful is called *śāra*; here too, *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument. If a color is mixed with other colors, it is *śāra*. *Nivṛtam*: That by which the body is covered or concealed is called a covering (*āvaraṇa*); the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the instrument according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. *Nīśāraḥ*: The long vowel [at the beginning] is as in the previous case.

"Without having made a *nīśāra*" means "without having made a covering (*prāvaraṇa*). The word *śāra* is used even for dice because of the usage by the author of the Vārttika: "of the *śāra*s moving clockwise and counter-clockwise."
The word *samī* is followed by *yudh* and *duvaḥ*. 3.3.23.

*Saṃyāva* is a specific kind of cake (*apūpa*) made from flour; it is so called because it is thoroughly cooked (*sampūyate*) by being mixed with jaggery, cumin, and other ingredients. [Pāṇini 3.3.26: *avo-dorno-nyaḥ*]
Looking downward is *avanāya*; looking upward is *unnāya*; and *unnaya* is indeed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *nī* and *abhi* when they end in the suffix *pūlv*.
Niṣpāva-kośī is a specific type of grain, so called because it is winnowed with a winnowing basket (śūrpa) and other such tools.
The [suffix] *u* is added after the two [roots] *ugra*. (Pāṇini 3.2.29)
Udgāra is an excessively loud sound; nigāra is swallowing.
The root *kṝ* is used in the sense of "winnowing grain. (Pāṇini 3.3.30)

In this context, would "grain" (*dhānya*) be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), or would it be an adjunct (*upādhi*) to the agent, which is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*)? First of all, it cannot be the meaning of the verbal root, because grain is a substance (*dravya*), whereas a verbal root denotes action (*kriyā*). If, however, it were an adjunct to the meaning of the suffix, then since [the agent] has already been expressed by the suffix, the use of the word "grain" in the phrase "the removal of grain" (*dhānyasyotkarṣaḥ*) would not be appropriate. Even so, its use might still occur for the sake of clear comprehension.

Even so, because [the object] is included within the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), the genitive case would not occur in the word *dhanya* (as in *dhanyasya dhānyaṃ*); rather, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone, as in *dṛtihariḥ paśuḥ*. Therefore, this is neither a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the meaning of the suffix, nor is it the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). Rather, he says—“if it is the object of the grain”—that it is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix by way of being its objective domain (*viṣayatvena*). Nor is it not the status of a co-occurring word (*upapadatva*), according to the explanation. “Because of non-expression” (*anabhidhānāt*) means due to the inherent nature of the expressive power of words.
By the two words *utkara* and *nikāra*, only the scattering of grain is denoted, not injury; for one must consider what kind of "injury" there could be to grain.
In the context of a sacrifice, the word *sam* is used when praising. 3.3.31.

"In the place where they gather and praise" indicates that the suffix *ghañ* is used here as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *lyuṭ* when denoting a location (*adhikaraṇe*). *Saṃstava* means familiarity or acquaintance.
In the *pre-stotra* sacrifice. 3.3.32.

Since "in a sacrifice" (*yajñe*) is the subject under discussion, the word division is "not in a sacrifice" (*ayajñe*). Regarding the *prastāra* on conch shells and other such items—it means an expansion or spreading.

As for the term *barhiṣprastara*: *prastara* refers to a specific handful [of grass]; a *prastara* made of *barhis* (sacrificial grass) is a *barhiṣprastara*. The suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *ṛdorap*, and the substitution of *ṣ* is applied according to the rule *idudupadhasya ca*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *prath* in the sense of expansion, provided that it does not denote sound.
Width: the horizontal extent.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a meter. 3.3.34.

*Vṛtta* is a specific arrangement characterized by a fixed number of syllables; "of which *gāyatrī* and so forth" is stated thus because they are well-known. It does not mean the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* [portions of the Veda]. Although their inclusion is well-established in rules such as "it occurs frequently in the *chandas*," nevertheless, they are not included here. Why? He says: "Because of the mention of their names. For example, the term *viṣṭārapaṅkti*.

The term *vistāra* is derived from the root *stṛ* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), meaning "that in which syllables are spread out" (*vistīryante 'sminn akṣarāṇi*). This forms a *karmadhāraya* compound; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *chandonāmni ca*. Although expansion (*prathana*) is understood here, it is not established by the preceding rule because that refers specifically to the domain of sound (*śabda*). However, some do not carry forward the term *vau* [from the previous rule], and thus they maintain that forms such as *prastārapaṅkti*, *āstārapaṅkti*, and *saṃstārapaṅkti* are also valid.

Anticipating the objection—"Just as in rules such as *karmaṇyagnyākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.92), the meaning is that if [a word] ending in a suffix is called 'fire,' so too here, the meaning might be that if [a word] ending in a suffix is the name of a meter (*chandonāman*)?"—he says in response: "The word *viṣṭārapaṅkti* is here the name of a meter. [The phrase] "it exists as a constituent part" [is used]; the ellipsis to be supplied is "the form of the word ending in the suffix *ghañ*. In some places, however, the reading is "it exists therein" (*tadvartate*), where the word *tat* is present and no ellipsis is required.

How, then, is the expression "called *chandas*" to be explained? He says: "The term 'called *chandas*' is in the locative case of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*). The meaning is that the locus of the word ending in the suffix is "that which is called *chandas*"; and since worldly people consider that parts reside within the whole, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
The suffix *ud* is applied [to form a word denoting a vessel] when it refers to a container (*graha*). 3.3.35.

Regarding the term *apavāda* (exception): it is an exception to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca*. The phrase *chandasi nī-* etc. refers to the fact that *srucaḥ* are specific sacrificial vessels characterized by their particular arrangement of parts. However, in this context, only the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles are intended, because of the scriptural injunction: "With *udgrābham ca* he lifts up the *juhū*, and with *nigrābham ca* he holds down the *upabhṛt*. The substitution of *bh* for *h* in *hṛ* and *grah* occurs according to the rule *hṛgrahorbhaśchandasi*.
The word *sami* [takes the suffix *ka*] when it means "in a fist. (Pāṇini 3.3.36)

"If the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) has the fist as its object"—this passage is to be construed in accordance with the rule *kṛ dhānye* ("the root *kṛ* [is used] when the object is grain"), which states that "if the meaning of the verbal root has grain as its object. This word *muṣṭi* exists indeed in the sense of a measure—as in "he pours out four handfuls"—but it also denotes a particular arrangement of the fingers—as in "he strikes with the fist."

In this regard, since the [result] would already be established by the rule "parimāṇākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 4.1.23) upon taking the first [sūtra], he states that the second [sūtra] is taken: "A *muṣṭi* is a particular arrangement of the fingers. The word *aho* expresses wonder. One who is skilled in making a fist is called *muṣṭika*; the suffix *kan* is applied here because it is read in the list beginning with *ākarṣa*.
The suffix *ni* is applied after the roots *pari*, *nyoḥ*, and *nīñ* in the senses of gambling and not missing [the mark]. || 3.3.37 ||

*Dyūta* (gambling) is playing with dice and such. From the root *bhreṣ* "to move," *bhreṣaṇa* is "moving" (*bhreṣa*); *abhreṣa* is "not moving. Regarding the phrase "if it concerns deviation" (*bhreṣaviṣayaścediti*), this passage also should be construed in accordance with what precedes. Regarding "non-transgression" (*anapacāra*): a transgression (*apacāra*) is a contemptible practice; that which is other than this, a commendable practice, is "non-transgression" (*anapacāra*). He clarifies this very point with the words "of that which has been obtained as it ought to be" (*yathāprāptasyeti*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs in whatever manner (*yathā-yena prakāreṇa*)."

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, however, the substitution of *am* would apply. But in some instances, it is taught that "the form should be as it occurs [in the base]. Regarding *pariṇāyena*: the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "*upasargādasamāse 'pi*" (Pāṇini 8.4.14). The word *hanti* means "he obstructs. "By leading around" (*samantānnayanena*) is an explanation of the meaning of *pariṇāyena*. "This is the rule here" (*eṣo'tra nyāyaḥ*) means "this is what occurs here according to the established usage. *Pariṇaya* means marriage; *nyaya* means destruction.
The suffix *kvan* is applied after the root *iṇ* when preceded by *parā*, in the sense of "not passing away."

In this case, the term *pari* is mentioned twice and the term *iṇ* is also mentioned twice; however, it should have been stated only once. One might have said: "The suffixes *ni* and *ya* [are applied] after the root *dyut*, and after the root *iṇ* when there is no deviation (*anupātyaya*), provided there is no error (*nāvabhreṣe*). That is true; yet, it was not formulated in that way.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *śī* (to lie down) following the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-*, when used in the sense of "turning" (*paryāya*).

In the preceding sūtra, the word *paryāya* was derived in the sense of "non-transgression" (*anupātyaya*). Since this would have been established by the governing rule of "non-transgression" alone, the explicit mention of *paryāya* here is for the purpose of re-enacting the rule. Consequently, when there is an intention to express inclusion (*abhividhi*), this suffix *ghañ* itself occurs, overriding even the subsequent suffix *inuṇ*. The meaning is: "the turn (or opportunity) to lie near the king. In the rule "after words denoting time, such as *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*, the suffix *tumun* is used," the term *kāla* includes the word *atyaya*.

The inclusion of synonyms is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*), as in the rule: "All [kāraka] designations are generally seen to apply to *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*. Therefore, the suffix *tumun* occurs even when joined with synonymous words; likewise, forms such as *avasaro bhoktum* ("it is the occasion to eat") and *avakāśo bhoktum* ("there is the opportunity to eat") are also observed. *Viśaya* means doubt (*saṃśaya*); *upaśaya* means lying down nearby (*samīpaśayana*).
The suffix *ca* is used after the root *dā* when it means "taking with the hand," provided that the act is not theft.

"By means of taking with the hand," and so forth. Where something that is to be taken is taken by the hand alone, without depending on any other means, there necessarily exists a proximity (*pratyāsatti*) between the act of taking and the object to be taken; therefore, co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) is the cause for the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*). Regarding "the top of a tree": the meaning is that one gathers the fruits which are at the tip of the tree by means of a staff or similar instrument. Alternatively, even if one takes [the fruit] with the hand after having climbed up, because there is no proximity of the object to be taken [to the hand], the suffix *ghañ* does not occur.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the verbal root *ā-dṛ*, when used with the words *nivāsa* (dwelling), *citi* (hearth), *śarīra* (body), and *upasamādhāna* (placing together). 3.3.41.

Regarding the phrase "in these meanings": here, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary sense, while the others are qualifiers (*upādhi*) of the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) which is the meaning of the suffix. "An assemblage of *cikhallis*" (*cikhallinikāya*): *cikhalli* is a particular region; the meaning is a village or similar locality of residence associated with that [region]. "A heap" (*ākāya*): [derived from] *ā-cī*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*), meaning "that in which bricks are piled. "A body" (*kāya*): [derived from] *ci*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the locative sense, meaning "that in which bones and so forth are piled. "A heap of cow dung" (*gomayanikāya*): the meaning is the piling together in one place of scattered pieces of cow dung.

"Multiplicity is understood here" means that it refers specifically to pieces of wood scattered here and there. While one could have simply said "caḥ kaḥ," the inclusion of the word "ādeḥ" (of the initial) is intended so that [the substitution] may apply to the initial letter even in the case of the *yaṅ*-luṅ form, and so that it does not apply to a non-initial letter or to both [the initial and the reduplicated syllable]. For example: *gomayānāṃ nikecāyaḥ*, which means the repeated piling up of cow-dung.
And [the suffix *cha* is used] after the word *saṅgha*, when there is no superiority or inferiority. 3.3.42.

A "saṅgha" is a collection of living beings (*prāṇin*). Although the word *saṅgha* is prescribed by rule (*nipātita*) as meaning simply a "group" (*gaṇa*)—according to the rule "the roots *sañj* and *udgha* [form *saṅgha*] in the senses of a group and praise"—the intended meaning is that the word *saṅgha* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) specifically for a collection of living beings. Regarding the phrase "by the inclusion of a single property": a single property is that which is common to all. Regarding the phrase "by way of superposition" (*auttarādharyeṇa*): those that are both above and below are "superior-inferior" (*uttarādhara*); the state of being such is "superposition" (*auttarādharya*).

Regarding the term *sūkaranicaya* (a heap of pigs): when they lie down for suckling with one above and another below, this is a counter-example; however, when they stand separately, each like a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), then this indeed becomes the actual example.
The suffix *ṇac* is applied after a verbal root in the sense of mutual exchange of action when the feminine gender is intended.

The term "root" (*dhātu*) is understood [from the previous rule]; its qualification is the mention of "mutual exchange of action" (*karmavyatihāra*), meaning "occurring when there is a mutual exchange of action. Since a root denotes an action (*kriyā*), it is not possible for it to function in the sense of a mutual exchange of the grammatical object (*sādhana-karman*); therefore, he states that the "action-object" (*kriyā-karman*) refers to a worldly action—namely, "mutual exchange of action" means "mutual exchange of activity. This occurs in the feminine gender in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). However, it does not occur when [the mutual exchange] involves a *kāraka* other than the agent (*kartṛ*), because such a usage is not attested (*anabhidhānāt*). This is the intended meaning.

The letter *ca* [in the rule] is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). It does not serve its own purpose, because the accent is already established by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) itself. Furthermore, the vowel *ā* of this [suffix] is never heard [as such], and since the suffix *añ* is invariably prescribed after a stem ending in *ṇac*, there ought to be the accent of the *nit* [element] due to its being "left over" (*satiśiṣṭatva*). If, in the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām*, it were stated as *ṇāt striyām*, then the suffix *ṇa* in *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ* would also be included. Examples include *vyāvakrośī* and so forth.

In the sense of "calling out" (*āhvāne*), from the root *kruś*; in the sense of "arranging letters" (*akṣaravinyāse*), from *likha*; and in the sense of "laughing with laughter" (*hasena*), from *has*—the suffix *añ* is applied after these roots when they end in *ṇic*. And because of the maxim regarding the inclusion of *kṛt*-suffixes, this suffix applies even when the roots are accompanied by prefixes. Since it is a *taddhita* suffix, there is initial *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). However, the rule "not after [roots ending in] *y* or *v*" does not apply here, due to the prohibition "not in the case of reciprocal action" (*na karmavyatihāre*). This was not stated in the section beginning with "the feminine suffix *ktin*" so that the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa*) might apply; thus, the form *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ* also occurs with the suffix *ktin*.

In the case of *vyāvacorī*, the suffix *yuc* would apply by the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ktin*. Likewise, this *ṇac* is also an exception specifically to *ktin* according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte* (that which applies when the other does not). Since an exception (*apavāda*) takes precedence over a conflict, when *yuc* would otherwise apply, this very *ṇac* is desired. Thus we have *vyatīkṣā* and *vyatīhā*. Here, an exception to *ktin*—namely the suffix *akāra* prescribed by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*—is also desired. In the case of *vyātyukṣī* (from the root *ukṣa* in the sense of "sprinkling"), this very [suffix] is desired even in the domain of *akāra*.

"How does this diversity come about?"—the sense is that it does not come about in any way [other than as described]. Regarding the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* ("the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely"): the sense is that the inclusion of the term "diversely" (*bahulam*) alone is what enables such diversity to be produced.
The suffix *inuṇ* occurs after a verbal root to form a noun denoting an action (*bhāva*) when it signifies pervasion (*abhividhi*).

"By means of action (kriyā) and quality (guṇa)": this is a statement defining the scope of the term *abhividhi* (inclusive limit). However, since suffixes are prescribed here after verbal roots (*dhātu*), the *abhividhi* is understood here specifically as referring to action. Regarding the form *sāṃkūṭinam*: the root *kūṭa* is used in the sense of "burning"; the suffix *inuṇ* is applied because it has a long vowel in its penultimate syllable. According to the rule *aṇinuṇaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is added pleonastically (*svārthika*) after a stem ending in *inuṇ*. This suffix, like the previous ones, is applied after a root together with its prefix (*sagatika*) and its kāraka. Due to the rule *inaṇyanapatye*, the original stem-form is maintained, and by the rule *nastaddhite*, there is no elision of the final *ṭi* (the *u* of *inuṇ*).

The meaning is "burning on all sides"; the prefix *saṃ-* indicates pervasion (*abhividhi*). Regarding the word *sāṃrāviṇam*: by the rule *upasarge ruvaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; this [rule] finds its scope of application when there is another prefix and no sense of pervasion. In the word *saṃrāva*, the prefix *saṃ-* denotes honor (*pūjā*). Sometimes the counter-example *sandrāva* is cited, but that is incorrect, because the rule *samiyudruduvaḥ* would then have no scope of application.

But surely, since both [the categories of] *bhāva* (action/state) and *kāraka* (participant in action) are under discussion, by the very nature of the word, it will apply to *kāraka* as before; so what is the purpose of mentioning *bhāva*? To this he replies: "The term *bhāva* is understood [from the previous rule]. Consequently, the suffix *ghañ* does not apply, nor does the suffix *kta* [as prescribed] by the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*. As for the phrase beginning with "by *lyuṭ*, however," the meaning has already been explained. By its very nature, this word ending in *-inuṇ* is neuter in gender.
The suffix *ghan* is applied after the roots *ava* and *ni* when preceded by *ā*. 3.3.45.

This rule is introduced because [the previous rule] *grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca* would otherwise have applied. The phrase *dṛṣṭānuvṛttisāmarthyāt* means that there is an observed capacity for the application [of the preceding rule]. In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the designation is focused on the state [of the capacity], just as in the case of *dvyekayoḥ*; thus the meaning is "because of the observed capacity for application. Alternatively, *anuvṛttisāmarthyam* is the capacity for application; then, a *karmadhāraya* is formed with the word *dṛṣṭa*. "Abuse" (*ākrośa*) means cursing (*śapanam*).

There is no censure, because the word ending in *ghañ* (i.e., *avagraha*) by its very nature has "cursing" (*śapana*) as its object; "cursing" means the wishing of misfortune. "Avagraha" means overcoming. "Nigraha" means suppression. The word "hanta" expresses anger. "Avagraha" also means the cutting off of a word. "Nigraha" means restraint.
The suffix *pre* is used in the sense of desire (*lipsā*). 3.3.46.

*Lipsā* (the desire to obtain) is the wish to acquire. "He wanders with a vessel-grasper" (*pātrapragrāheṇa carati*) means that he wanders having taken up a begging bowl; that is to say, one who has grasped a vessel. However, the mention of the *sruva* (ladle) is an indicative mark for one desiring sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), because the *dākṣiṇa* oblation is accomplished by means of the *sruva*. In the expression "the grasping of Devadatta" (*pragraho devadattasya*), *pragraha* means intoxication or, alternatively, intense attachment.
The word *para* [is used] in the sense of sacrifice. 3.3.47.

Regarding the term *uttaraparigrāha*: the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). The *parigrāha* is the appropriation of the sacrificial altar (*vedi*) with the wooden sword (*sphya*); thus, it forms a *karmadhāraya* compound. In some places, however, it is read as *uttaraḥ parigrāhaḥ* without being compounded.
The suffix *vun* is applied after the word *dhānya* in the sense of "ninefold. (Pāṇini 5.1.20)

"Grains called *nīvāra* are rice. Even though this is a general statement regarding grain, he demonstrates that by its very nature the suffix *ghañ* occurs here in the sense of a specific type of rice (*vrīhi*). In this case, *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and as before, there is lengthening of the prefix vowel. [The example] "a girl who is *nīvārā*" [is explained thus]: according to the rule "after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, *niści*, *gam*, and *ca*," the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of the object itself. But surely, it ought to be in the feminine by means of the suffix *ktin*, because of the statement: "In the feminine, *ap* and *ac* [are superseded] by *strī*, *khal*, and *na*; and *strī* [is superseded] by *khal* and *na* through the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)"? True; [but the present case is not governed by that].

Because of the word "bahulam" (variously) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *ac* occurs even in certain instances where *ktin* and other suffixes would otherwise be expected, as in the examples *pravarā senā* (an excellent army) and *pravarā gauḥ* (an excellent cow). Thus, the rule *ghañajabantāḥ puṃsi* ("words ending in *ghañ* and *ac* are masculine") should be regarded as merely general.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *śri*, *yu*, *pū*, and *dru* when preceded by the prefix *ud*.

Regarding the phrase "to be mentioned later": in this way, an option would result for roots such as *yu* (to join) and others. If that is not desired, it will not occur because of the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* ("the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely").

Others, however, maintain that because this usage is not mentioned in the Bhāṣya, it is indeed incorrect; yet the usage found in the Mahābhārata that was demonstrated can be justified as being archaic (ārṣa).
The suffix *ave* is used after the root *grah* when there is an obstruction to rain.

"From some cause or other" means: "Due to the transgression of beings or their karma, there may be drought for men. The word *sattva* here refers to living beings; *karmāparādha* is a fault regarding action, namely the sin caused by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited—this is the transgression of beings and their karma. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes such [causes] as: "The sun, situated between those two, might even dry up the ocean.
"Drought caused by a deity" means the absence of rain having a deity as its agent.
The suffix *pra* is applied [after a word] denoting merchants. 3.3.52.

Those who bargain and trade are *vaṇijaḥ* (merchants). [The derivation is as follows: from the root *paṇ* in the sense of "to trade" (*paṇa vyavahāre*), the suffix *ij* is applied, and the initial *p* is replaced by *v*, according to the rule *paṇerijyādeśca vaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "by connection with merchants": since a measuring-cord generally belongs to merchants, this association (*sāhacarya*) is the basis for the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As for the alternative "or these two": this is not the purpose of the statement that "the merchants are not the governing factor" (*na tu vaṇijastantram*).
And [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the word *raśmi*.

"Of those joined with chariots and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the cart is included. "Of horses and so forth"—this is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for oxen and the like. "Binding" means restraint. "That [is] the *raśmi* here which is grasped"—the word *raśmi* is masculine, yet it takes the feminine gender here because of the reference to the rope by the pronoun *sā* (she/it). However, the rays belonging to the moon and other celestial bodies are not meant here, as they are not what is intended to be designated. In this context, the root *grah* (to seize/grasp) is employed many times, whereas it could have been performed only once.

How so? I shall state it thus: "The prefix *ud-* [is used] with *grah-*; *sam-* with *muṣ-* for a fist; *ava-* with *ni-* in the sense of reviling; *pra-* with *lip-* in the sense of desire; *pari-* with *yaj-* in the sense of sacrifice; *ava-* with *vr̥-* in the sense of obstructing rain; optionally *pra-* with *vaṇij-*," and so forth. Why not place [the rule] "with *pari-* and *bhrū-* in the sense of contempt" immediately after "with *āṅ-* and *rūp-* and *lup-*"? But it was not done in that way. Thus it stands.
The root *vṛ* is used in the sense of covering. (Pāṇini 3.3.54)

Although it is stated here in general terms as "in the case of clothing" (*ācchādana*), the specific application is understood as before; thus he says: "if [the word] ends in a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*). Regarding "a cloak" (*prāvāra*), the long vowel is applied as before. Regarding "an excellent cow" (*pravarā gauḥ*), the meaning is "praiseworthy."
The suffix *erac* [is applied after a verbal root] to express the meaning of "the act of that. (Pāṇini 3.3.56)

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). For without it, in the rule *thāthādisūtra*, there would be the inclusion of even the term *apratyayāt*. Regarding *varṣam*: from the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, "the bull (*vṛṣabha*) is so called because of raining (*varṣaṇa*)," it follows that *varṣaṇam* also occurs. Regarding *javasavau*: although [the suffix] *ac* was already applicable, it is prescribed here; there is a difference in accent (*svara*). However, there is no such statement as *erajaṇyantānām*; rather, there is only this: "*kalpyādibhyaḥ pratiṣedhavacanam*" (the statement of a prohibition regarding *kalpya* and others).

It is called *kalpa* because it is imagined (*kalpyate*); it is called *artha* because it is sought after (*arthyate*); it is called *mantra* because it is deliberated upon (*mantryate*). When the suffix *ac* is prohibited, the suffix *ghañ* alone occurs.
The suffix *ap* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*.

Regarding the word *lava*: one might ask, "Since it is stated that 'a following *t* makes the preceding [phoneme] also followed by *t*,' and since the *u* here is followed by *t*, should not *ap* occur here? To this he replies: "The *d* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*). This is not a *t*, but rather a *d*. And this is understood from the commencement of rules such as *nirabhyoḥ pūlvoḥ*. By the word "mouth" (*mukha*), the articulatory places such as the palate are meant; "ease" (*sukha*) refers to the lack of effort. For when vowels are pronounced with a consonant intervening, there is lightness of the mouth. Absence of doubt is its incidental purpose (*anuṣaṅgika-prayojana*).
And [the suffix *ka*] is added after the roots *grah*, *vṛdh*, *niści*, and *gam*.

Regarding the statement "there is a prohibition [of *ghañ*] for *ni-√ci*": although *ac* would have applied by the rule *erac*, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed by the rule *hastādāne cerasteye* (Pāṇini 3.3.40). This *ghañ* is desired even after the prefix *ni-*, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), as it has been stated: "If it is argued that this is for the sake of excluding theft, no, because it is not desired. But what is the distinction between *ni-√ci* and *ni-√aj* in the sense of "ascertainment" (*niścaya*), given that their form is identical and their accent is also the same, since both are prescribed as having an udātta accent on the final syllable by the rule *thāthādisūtra*? To this he says: "The mention of *ni-√ci* is for the sake of the accent."

The meaning is that, by virtue of the inclusion of the word *niści*, the *thāthādi* accent does not apply here; rather, by the accent rule for *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), the word becomes specifically middle-accented (*madhyodātta*).

Regarding the rule *vaśiraṇyoḥ*: this statement is made because the suffix *ghañ* would otherwise have applied. *Vaśaḥ* is the act of desiring (*vaśana*). *Raṇaḥ* is battle, in which they "resound" (*raṇanti*) or make noise.

Regarding the term *ghañ-artha*: the meaning of *ghañ* (the nominal suffix) consists of both abstract action (*bhāva*) and a grammatical participant (*kāraka*) other than the agent (*kartṛ*). Thus, *prasthaḥ* (a ridge), *prasnaḥ* (a frying pan), and *prapā* (a water-shed)—in all these cases, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. Regarding *āvidha*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule governing *grah*, *jyā*, and so forth. This word is a synonym for *āyudha* (weapon).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *ad* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it.

Regarding the phrase *aderdhātoḥ*: this is not a reference to verbal roots (*dhātu*) that take the form *ad*; for even by the rule *ghañapośca*, the substitution of *ghas* for *ad* is prescribed when followed by the suffixes *ghañ* or *ap*. [Thus], *vighasaḥ*—meaning food remaining from the *vaiśvadeva* offering—is derived as *vyadyate* (it is eaten). *Ghāsaḥ*, however, means the fodder for four-footed animals. There exists another root *ghasi*; from that alone the suffix *ap* should be prescribed. For in this way, the substitution of *ghas* for *ad* would not need to be stated. However, the mention of *ad* is for the sake of what follows: so that when the suffix *ṇa* is added, it may apply to *ad* as in *adaḥ*, but not to *ghas*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *vyadh* and *jap*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).

In the rule *vyadhajapoh*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe*); *anupasarge* is a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) meaning that [the suffix] does not occur when there is a prefix (*upasarga*). Consequently, it occurs only with the two roots by themselves, and not when there is any other word besides a prefix as an attendant (*upapada*). The commentary (*vṛtti*) text should also be explained in this very sense. *Upajāpa* means the divulging of counsel (*mantrabheda*).
And *kvaṇa* [is used] in the sense of the lute (*vīṇā*). 3.3.65.

The mention of the *vīṇā* (lute) here is for the purpose of including [the term] with its prefix. This should be understood as being for the sake of the prefix distinct from the root itself, because the rule applies generally to both that which is preceded by the prefix *ni-* and that which is without a prefix. The compound *kalyāṇaprakvāṇā* is a *bahuvrīhi*.
The suffix *mad* is applied [after a verbal root] when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it. || 3.3.67 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *vidyāmada*: the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). If the arrangement of the sūtras were made such that immediately after *kvaṇo vīṇāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.65), one placed *nityaṃ madaḥ pramadasaṃmadau harṣe paṇaḥ parimāṇe*, then the mention of "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) here could have been omitted, since [the desired meaning] would be established through mere *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from the previous rule). True; for if such an arrangement were made, one might suspect that the term "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*) would also carry over to the rule *paṇaḥ parimāṇe*.

According to the established grammatical arrangement (*yathānyāsa*), however, because of the statement "also when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*) even later on, it is understood that in the rule *nityaṃ paṇaḥ parimāṇe*, the term *anupasarga* is not connected [to the word *paṇaḥ*]. Consequently, the suffix occurs even when there is a prefix, provided that there is the expression of a measure (*parimāṇa*).

Another says: "The formulation of the rule *mado'nupasarge* is for the purpose of indicating that this rule is non-obligatory (*anitya*); therefore, the form *māda* is established. However, there is no statement of an authoritative teacher (*āpta*) to this effect.
The words *pramada* and *saṃmada* denote joy.

"The purpose of the elision (*nipātana*) is for the sake of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). This means that the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) should apply only to those forms which have acquired a conventional meaning through usage. It is thought that if the rule were stated simply as "after *pra* and *sam*," then [the suffix] would also apply in cases such as *prasaṃmadaḥ*, *saṃpramadaḥ*, and *vipramadaḥ*.
The word *glaha* [is used] in the sense of "stakes" when referring to dice.

Regarding the phrase "the stake (*glaha*) of the die" (*akṣasya*): although it could be interpreted as denoting the state of being (*bhāve*), the meaning is "the taking of the die. Others, however, say: here the word "die" (*akṣa*) indicates by implication the gambling (*devana*) that is accomplished by means of it; that which is to be taken as a wager (*paṇa*) in the activity of the die—that is, in the context of gambling—is expressed by the word "stake" (*glaha*). And so says Māgha: "He played at dice, engaging in a mutual splashing of water as his stake" (*vyātyukṣīm abhiraga-glahām adīvyat*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*) as well, "the stake of the die" means the binding of a wager for the gambling that is accomplished by means of the die.
The suffix *sarter* is applied in the sense of procreation. 3.3.71.

*Prajana* means procreation; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and by the rule "janivadhyośca," the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies. From the causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the suffix *ac* is added. The prefix *pra-* reverses the meaning of the verbal root; just as in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, there is a reversal of the sense of manifestation, namely, the taking of conception. Thus he says: "procreation is first the taking of conception. How [is it that] *avasaraḥ* and *prasaraḥ* [are formed]? [They are formed] with the suffix *gha* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), according to the rule "the suffix *gha* is generally used in the masculine for a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*)."
The substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs for the root *vah*, as well as for *ni*, *abhi*, and *upa* [when followed by *viṣ*]. (Pāṇini 3.3.72)

Forms such as *nihava* and so forth are established from the root *hu* itself, since verbal roots possess multiple meanings; furthermore, even a difference [in root] would be irrelevant here. However, this statement is intended to ensure that the form *nihvāya*—derived from the root *hve* with the suffix *ghañ*—does not occur.
The word *nipāna* is [substituted for] *āhāva*. (Pāṇini 3.3.74)

The form *āhāva* is established as derived from the root *hu* (to sacrifice) itself, because verbal roots possess multiple meanings; moreover, a difference in meaning is irrelevant here. However, this statement is intended to prevent the form *āhvāya* from occurring when the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *hve* (to call). He states that *āhāva* is a nipātana (an irregularly formed word) in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), explaining: "for in that case... (*tatra hi*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after a verbal root that does not have a prefix (*anupasarga*), when the action is expressed as a state (*bhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *bhāva*," etc.: [An objection is raised: "But since both [action and agent] are under consideration, by virtue of observing the intended meaning (*lakṣya*), the rule will apply only to the sense of *bhāva* (action), just as in the case of the rule *karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām*. This is true; this very meaning is expressed by the mention of *bhāva*. Now, just as in the rule *abhividhau bhāve ṇvuṭ*, the mention of *bhāva* is for the purpose of excluding the application of other suffixes of a different form (*vāsarūpa*), why does the same not occur here? [The answer is: because there is no suffix of a different form that needs to be barred."

The *ghañ* suffix is indeed of the same form [as the root], but *kta*, *lyuṭ*, and *ktin* are not its general rules (*utsarga*); for their application does not begin until those [other suffixes] have already become applicable, yet they are desired—as in *hūtaḥ*, *hvānam*, and *hūtiḥ*.
And the substitution of *hana* for *vadha*. (Pāṇini 3.3.76)

"And that [suffix] has its final syllable accented" (antodātta), because it is pronounced exactly so in the sūtra. But for what purpose is there the state of ending in the vowel *a*, and for what purpose is there the state of having the final syllable accented? For this vowel *a* is not heard anywhere [else], and thus its elision (*lopa*) occurs by rule. To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means: when the final syllable is accented. "By the accent of the disappearance of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvareṇa*). According to the rule "And where there is the elision of an acute, [the following unaccented syllable takes its place]," it is called the "accent of the disappearance of the acute" because it is caused by the disappearance of the acute. "After [the suffix] *ghāta*"—this is the example.

In this case, the *ghañ* suffix [is applied] not to a *kāraka* such as the object (*karman*), but rather to the *prakṛti* (the base) by means of the suffix itself. Now, why is it not connected with the *prakṛti*—that is, the verbal root—immediately following which it is heard? [Why not say: "After the root *han*, there is the substitute *vadh*, and after *hvayati* [there is *ghañ*]"? Because of the force of the prescription of *samprasāraṇa* in the preceding rule.
The word *ghana* is used in the sense of a "statue" [when it denotes a specific type of cloud]. 3.3.77.

Regarding the phrase "abhraghana" (dense cloud): the meaning is the solidity (*kāṭhinya*) of the cloud. Regarding the mention of the word "dharma" (property/attribute): the intention is that it is like [the compound] *śulkādi* (white, etc.). If this is so, then because of the prohibition regarding [compounds with] a quality (*guṇa*), a compound would not be obtained; furthermore, the rule "by means of qualities residing in that" (*tatsthaiśca guṇaiḥ*) would also not apply? Indeed, it was just stated that "by the word *dharma*, the substratum (*dharmī*) is expressed"; therefore, a compound must be stated here [in this specific case].
The suffix *antarghana* is applied in the sense of "in a region. (Pāṇini 3.3.78)
That too must certainly be accepted, because it has been set forth by the Teacher for his disciples in both ways.
The words *praghaṇa* and *praghāṇa* denote a portion of a house, namely a porch or vestibule.

"The outer courtyard of the gate is called *bāhya*. Regarding the gate area, there are two courtyards (*prakoṣṭha*), namely the inner and the outer. Among these, the placement [of the term] refers to the outer courtyard, and not merely to a single part of the house. This is understood from the grammatical rule of elision (*nipātana*). It is so called because it is "struck down" (*apahanyate*) intensely by the feet of people entering; thus, the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and in this instance, there is also the substitution of *vṛddhi*.
The word *udghana* means *atyādhāna*. (Pāṇini 3.3.80)

Regarding the term *atyādhāna*: the prefix *ati* denotes "above" or "superiority," while the root *ā-dhā* means "to place. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The same applies to the term *udghana*.
*Apaghana* means a limb. 3.3.81.
Regarding the term *apaghana*: it is formed with the suffix *ap* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
In the sense of an instrument, [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the words *ayas*, *vidruma*, and so forth. || 3.3.82 ||

Regarding the word *drughaṇa*: *dru* is a name for a tree; there is a Vedic citation stating, "The trees (*vanaspati*) are indeed *drus*. According to the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām agaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3), [the *ṇatva* is applied]. Furthermore, this is the name of a specific type of axe.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *stamba*. (Pāṇini 3.2.83)

Regarding the phrase *tatra ca*: even though it was mentioned immediately prior, the substitution of *ghan* does not occur here; for the substitution of *ghan* has already been connected with the preceding [rule]. In the example *stambaghna*, there is a compound with an upapada; the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *gamahana*, and the change to the guttural (*kutva*) occurs by the rule *ho hanteḥ*. The phrase beginning with *striyām* refers to the feminine gender and so forth.

And this [form] *stambakāra* is obtained either because it is prescribed as a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*), because it is an exception to all other rules (*sarvāpavāda*), or by virtue of the statement "the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely" (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). Others, however, maintain that it is *stambaheti*, derived from the root *han* with the suffix *ktin* according to the rule "ūti-yūti-jūti-sāti-heti," since this specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) is an exception to all other rules. Still others say that, by the rule "and in the sense of instrument and locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*), the form should be *stambahananī* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, just as it is stated: "the slayer of Rākṣasas and Yātus. As for *stambaghāta*, it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), followed by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The suffix *gha* is applied after the verbal root *pra-ru*.
Regarding *paligha*: by the rule "the substitution of *l* optionally occurs for the *gh* of *para* before *gha* and *aṅka*," there is an optional substitution of *l*.
The suffix *upaghna* is used in the sense of "resort" (*āśraya*).

Regarding the phrase "the word *āśraya*," and so forth: *āśrayaṇa* (the act of resorting) is *āśraya*. By virtue of proximity, that which is invariably concomitant with it is the cause characterized by this definition. As for the term *parvatopaghna*: it is derived from the sense that one is struck (*upahanyate*) by the mountain—that is, approached in its vicinity—thus it is formed with the suffix *kha* (as in *karmaṇi khaḥ*).
The suffix *udgha* is used after the words *saṃgha* and *gaṇa* when expressing praise. (Pāṇini 5.2.86)

*Saṃhananam* means "the Saṅgha," used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Udghanya* means "it is known as excellent" (*utkṛṣṭe jñāyate*), used here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). Since roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) also mean "to understand" (*buddhyartha*), the root *hanti* is used here in the sense of "knowing. Thus, *udgho manuṣyāṇām* means "he is praised among men"; that is, he is excellent among men.
The word *nigha* is a substitute for *nimitta*. 3.3.87.

Regarding the phrase *samārohapariṇāham*: *āroha* means height, and *pariṇāha* means breadth; that which has these two equal is described as such. Regarding the phrase *nighā vṛkṣāḥ*: they are called *nighāḥ* because they are struck (*hanyante*) or known (*jñāyante*) without distinction; thus it is a *karmakartṛ* (passive-reflexive) formation.
After a verbal root ending in ḍu or vi, the suffix ktri is applied.

The phrase "in the sense of an action (bhāva) and when [the action] is not the agent (akartari) among the kārakas" is understood to carry over. This indicates that the governing rule (adhikāra) is not discontinued. However, this *ktri* suffix occurs only in the sense of an action by its very nature—as in "prepared by cooking" (*paktrimam*), and not as "cooked" (*pakvam*). It is not used alone; therefore, the analysis (*vigraha*) must necessarily be performed with another word. He demonstrates this: "prepared by cooking, thus *paktrimam*. In the case of *uptrimam*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* group.

Now, why not simply say that *kṛtrima* [is used] only in the sense of "artificial"? For if that were so, one would not need to state the rule "*kṛtreḥ mam nityam*" (the suffix *mam* is always applied after *kṛtri*). This cannot be done; because of the governing context of "in the sense of an action" (*bhāve*), it would follow that *kṛtrima* could also apply to an action. Suppose it is argued that even if both [action and agent] are carried over [by the governing rule], by the very nature of linguistic usage (*abhidhāna-svābhāvyāt*), it would occur only in the sense of an object (*karman*) as a participant in an action (*kāraka*). Even so, the past time (*bhūta-kāla*) would not be understood. Let us grant that this too might occur by the very nature of linguistic usage. However, in that case, there would be no distinction in the manner of expressing the meaning. For indeed, people do not consider the words *pakva* and *paktrima* to be synonyms.
The suffix *athuc* is applied after verbal roots ending in *ṭu* or *i*.

This too becomes a noun by virtue of its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*); it is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the application of] the suffix *ghañ* and others. Nevertheless, by the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhāna*), that [suffix *ghañ*] also indeed occurs.
The suffix *naṅ* is applied after the verbal roots √yaj (to sacrifice), √yāc (to beg), √yat (to strive), √vicch (to shine), √pracch (to ask), and √rakṣ (to protect).

The letter *ṅ* in *naṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. Otherwise, because the *tuk* augment would be internal (*antaraṅga*), after the substitution of *cha* with the *tuk*-augmented form according to the rule *cachvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*, there would be *guṇa* due to the lightness of the penultimate vowel. All [roots] ending in *naṅ* are masculine; however, *yāci* is feminine. And the rule regarding dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpavidhi*) applies only as far as they are actually mentioned. Regarding the word *praśna*: why does vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) not occur here by the rule *grahijyā...*? To this he says: *praccheḥ*.
The seventh case-affix is used after a word denoting the object of an action (*karman*) and after a word denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Because the seventh case endings for *karman* (object) and *adhikaraṇa* (locus) are specified separately, both cannot simultaneously function as *upapadas*. In this regard, he states—“when *karman* is the *upapada*”—that based on the explanation, *karman* is the *upapada*, whereas *adhikaraṇa* is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). He further notes that the mention of *adhikaraṇa* is for the purpose of excluding other meanings; by "other meanings" (*arthāntara*) is meant the abstract state (*bhāva*), and by "others" is meant the other *kārakas* such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth.
The suffix *ktin* occurs after a verbal root to form a feminine noun.

Regarding the phrase "the exception (*apavāda*) to *ghañ*, *ac*, and *ap*": by the maxim *yena nāprāpte* (where [a rule] applies where another would otherwise have applied), this is an exception to *ghañ*; however, because they are subsequent rules, *ac* and *ap* are exceptions that override [it]. And it has been stated: "In opposition to [the suffixes] *ac* and *ap*, the suffixes *strī*, *khal*, and *ana* [apply]; and in opposition to the feminine suffix *strī*, the suffixes *khal* and *ana* [apply]. The scope of *ac* and *ap* is, for example, *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*, and *lavaḥ*. The scope of *ktin* is, for example, *kṛtiḥ*, *dṛtiḥ*, *citiḥ*, and *stutiḥ*. Where both would apply, *ktin* occurs by virtue of the opposition [rule], as in *labdhiḥ*.

Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *ṣ*, the suffix *aṅ* also occurs—as in *labhet*. Now, one might object: since the author of the Vārttika stated that "it is established by the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ vā seṭo'kāt*," it is understood that the suffix *ktin* is intended only where the suffix *ap* would otherwise apply by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*; so how can *ktin* be cited as an example in the domain of *aṅ*? True; however, because of the great frequency of usage, he considers that this [suffix *ktin*] also occurs here. And thus, even in the domain of *yuj*, the suffix *ktin* is employed—as in *āstiriḥ*. For this very reason, it was said that "the roots beginning with *ab* are to be followed according to actual usage."

Regarding the rule *śruyajistubhyaḥ karaṇe*: this is a statement made because the suffix *lyuṭ* would otherwise apply; thus, *śrutiḥ* means "the ear," and *iṣṭiḥ* means "a sacrifice" (that by which a deity is worshipped). Regarding the rule *ṛkāralvādibhyaḥ*: after roots ending in *ṛ* and after roots beginning with *l*, the suffix *ktin* undergoes the same grammatical operations as the *niṣṭhā* suffixes—namely, the rules "*radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ*" and "*lvādibhyaḥ*"; the meaning is that the substitution of *n* for the final letter of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is also applied to *ktin*. The phrase *ktinn apīṣyate* ("*ktin* is also desired") is stated because, due to the prohibition "*astriyām*" (which excludes feminine forms), the rule of "non-identical form" (*vāsarūpa*) does not apply here.
The affix *ghañ* is applied after verbal roots ending in *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, and *ca*, when the action is expressed as a state (*bhāva*).

The exception (*apavāda*) of *aṅ* is a sublater (*bādhaka*). It sublates that which would otherwise be obtained by the rules "after *sthā* and others" (*sthādibhyaḥ*) and "also after [a root ending in] *ā* when preceded by a prefix" (*ātaścopasarge*). However, it is an exception to the *aṅ* obtained by the rule due to the *pit*-marker in *pac*. Why does it not also sublate the *ṇvul* and *iñ* suffixes obtained by the rule "optionally in the case of narration and inquiry" (*vibhāṣākhyānaparipraśnayoḥ*), as in the examples *kāṃsthāyikām* and *sthāyimi*? Because of the principle: "Exceptions made earlier sublate only the immediately following rules, not those that follow later."

How so? Not at all; because there is no application of the rule for optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*). Nor does it mean "for an excessive amount"; rather, this is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that invariably functions as a substitute for a word ending in the dative case, just like *cirāya*.
In the words *mantre*, *vṛṣa*, *iṣa*, *pacamana*, *vidabhū*, and *vīra*, [the final vowel] is acute (*udātta*). 3.3.96.

Regarding the phrase "of the base and the suffix" (*prakṛti-pratyayayoḥ*): the dual number is used because there is an intention to express the generality of the bases; otherwise, since bases are many, a plural would have resulted. Regarding the phrase "by means of a change of case": the meaning is that the relationship between the base and the suffix occurs through a transformation of the nominative case—which is present in the *dvandva* compound of *vṛṣ* and so forth—into the ablative case; otherwise, the relationship would be untenable. In the roots *vṛṣu* (to sprinkle) and *iṣu* (to desire), the latter is included because of its association with *vṛṣ*, as it is marked with the indicatory letter *u*.

In the *sūtra*, however, the letter *a* is not intended [as a specific marker]. Both roots *man* (in the sense of "knowing") and *manu* (in the sense of "understanding") are included. The same applies to *vid* and other roots as they appear [in usage]. Regarding the phrase "everywhere": this means both in mantras and in non-mantras (*amantra*). When the suffix *ktin* is to be prescribed after roots such as *vṛṣ*, the explicit statement that it is *udātta* (accented) is for the sake of subsequent rules, so that the suffix *kyap* may be *udātta* in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) after roots like *vraj* and *yaj*. Furthermore, in examples such as *pramati*, it is for the sake of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member by the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau*.
In the case of the root *pā* ("to drink") as well, the suffix *ktin* is seen to be udātta in mantras: "for the drinking of the pressed [juice]," and "for the drinking of the sweet Soma."
And [the words] *ūti*, *yūti*, *jūti*, *sāti*, *heti*, and *kīrti* [are feminine]. 3.3.97.

The word "in a mantra" (*mantre*) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Therefore, this rule applies to the Brāhmaṇas and to the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). Regarding *syateḥ*: this refers to the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*). Regarding "the absence of *it*" (*hatvābhāva*): this is the absence of the *it*-augment that would otherwise be required by the rule *dyatisyati-* etc. Regarding *sanoteḥ vā*: this refers to the root *ṣaṇu* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*). Regarding *hanteḥ hinoteḥ vā*: when it is *han*, the *it*-augment is applied to the *n*; but when it is *hinoti*, there is *guṇa*. Regarding *kīrttayateḥ*: [this is the form derived from the root *kṛt*].

Regarding the root *kṛt* in the sense of "making a sound," which belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and takes the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *ktin* is prescribed by nipātana (as an exception) to the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*, and its high-pitched (*udātta*) accentuation is also prescribed. The absence of the augment *iṭ* is established by the rule *titutra...*. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rules *upadhāyāśca*, *hali ca*, and *upadhāyāṃ ca*. However, the followers of Kālāpa also accept the suffix *yuc*, as in *kīrttanā*.
The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *vraj* and *yaj* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

Regarding the word *ijya*: there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with *vaci-*. Since the term "if it is udātta" (*yadyudātta*) continues to apply [from the previous sūtra], he asks: "What is the purpose of making it marked with *p*? To this he replies: "The addition of *p* is for the sake of the suffix *tuG* in the subsequent rules."
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the verbal roots *sam*, *jan*, *sad*, *ni-pat*, *man*, *vid*, *su*, *śīṅ*, *bhṛ*, and *iṇ*, when they are preceded by *saṃjñā*. (Pāṇini 3.2.99)

"‘Bhāva’ is not marked with a svarita accent. This means that because the mention of *bhāva* in the preceding sūtra is not marked with a svarita accent, it does not carry over (*anuvṛtti*) here. Regarding *samajyā*: due to the statement "there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *kyap* when there is a prohibition of *ghan* and *ap*," the substitution of *vī* does not occur. Others, however, say that because *kyap* is prescribed only when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*), and because the mention of "name" is intended to follow established usage (*rūḍhi*), the substitution of *vī* does not occur; for if the substitution of *vī* were applied, the sense of a "name" would not be understood.

*Samajyā* means an assembly or council; *niṣadyā* means a shop; *nipatyā* means slippery ground; *manyā* refers to the vessels of the neck (the carotid arteries), so called because one "thinks" (*manyante*) by means of them—it is by means of them that a person in anger is recognized. Since [the suffix] *kyap* does not begin with a consonant (*ajhalādi*), the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) prescribed by the rule *anudāttopadeśa* does not occur; and because that elision does not take place, the augment *tug* also does not occur. Others, however, say that because of the statement "in the sense of a technical term" (*saṃjñāyām*), just as the substitution of *vī* for *vi* does not occur in *samajyā*, likewise the elision of the nasal in the root *man* does not occur there, and consequently the *tug* augment is also absent.

There is no authoritative scriptural statement (āptavacana) on this point. "Vidyā" is that by which an object is known or apprehended. "Sutyā" is that in which Soma is pressed or extracted; it refers to the day of the pressing. The neuter gender in the expression "sutyamahar-uttamam" (the final day of the pressing) is according to the usage of the Ṛṣis. "Śayyā" is that upon which one lies, such as a bed; "bhṛtyā" is maintenance or livelihood; and "dīpikā" is that by which one goes or moves, and so forth.

Regarding the statement "In the rule *bhṛño'saṃjñāyām*, it was said: 'There is an extension (*adhikāra*) for the sense of state (*bhāva*) in the feminine; therefore, the word *bhāryā* is established,'" but here it is said, "'The sense of state (*bhāva*) is not extended [to the feminine],' one asks, suspecting a contradiction between the earlier and later statements: "How was that stated? He replies: "It is an extension for the sense of state (*bhāvādhikāra*)."

It is said [in the rule] "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*). Since the suffix *kyap* arises only when there is a state (*bhāva*) of the root *bhṛ*, the term "name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood here; therefore, by virtue of being a name, that very operation which constitutes the state denoted by the word *bhṛtya* is intended as the "state" (*bhāva*) under discussion in this context, and not the technical "state" based on the *svarita* accent. While the term "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is already present [from a previous rule], the repetition of the word "name" (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of referring to the "state" (*bhāva*); for the previous mention of "name" was connected with a "participant" (*kāraka*). However, when it is not a name, only the suffix *ktin* occurs.
And after the root *kṛ*, there is also the suffix *śa*.

Regarding the term *yogavibhāga* (division of the rule): the suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *kṛ*; then *śa* is added, and by virtue of the letter *ca*, that which was already established [by other rules] is also included. Consequently, there are three forms. Otherwise, if the letter *ca* were intended only to include the immediately preceding *kyap* and not *ktin*, then *ktin* would not occur. The letter *ś* serves to designate the affix as *sārvadhātuka*. In that regard, when *śa* occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), then by the rule *sārvadhātuke yak*, the augment *yak* is added, and by *riṅśayagliṅkṣu*, the substitution *riṅ* takes place. In other instances, the substitution *riṅ* occurs only before the letter *ś*, while by the rule *aci śnudhātu* etc., the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs.
The suffix *icchā* [is applied after a verbal root] to express the sense of "desire. (Pāṇini 3.3.101)

Regarding the statement "of the root *iṣ*": from the root *iṣu* in the sense of "desiring," the suffix *śa* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and not in the sense of a non-agentive factor (*akartṛ-kāraka*), due to its inherent nature.

"Paricaryā," etc. This is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of *paricaryā* and others; the meaning is that *paricaryā* and so forth should also be derived as irregular forms ending in the suffix *śa*. In all these cases, the suffix *śa* and [the substitution of] *ya* are irregularly applied. *Paricaryā* means "worship. *Parisaryā* means "wandering about"; here, even the *guṇa* strengthening is irregularly applied.
