The root *mṛg* (in the sense of "searching") belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a long vowel (*adanta*); here, there is no elision of the final *a*, due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). With the suffix *śa*, followed by *ya*, there is the elision of the penultimate *i*: *mṛgayā*.

In the case of the root *aṭ*, when the suffix *śa* is applied with *yaK*, the doubling of the *ṭ* along with the *y*, the elision of the *y* in the preceding portion, and the lengthening—all this is prescribed by rule (*nipātana*). However, the *hal-ādi-śeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) does not apply here, because the designation of "reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*) is prescribed only for reduplication according to the sixth book of Pāṇini. When, however, the suffix *ap* is added to the *yaṄ*-intensive form according to the rule "after roots ending in *aṭ*, *ṛt*, *as*, or *ūṛ*, [the suffix *ap* is used]," and then the *a* is elided and the *y* is elided, the form becomes *āṭāṭā*.

Regarding the statement "or the vowel *a* of *jāgarti*": due to the word "or" (*vā*), in one alternative there is the suffix *śa*; in that case, *yaK* is applied before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, and the *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "there is *guṇa* for *jāgr* except before *viC*, *ciṇ*, and *ṅit* suffixes."
And [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] for a consonant (*hal*) following the root *gur*. (Pāṇini 3.3.103)

Because the root under discussion (*prakṛta-dhātu*) is qualified by *hal* (a consonant), there is an application of the rule *tadanta-vidhi* (the designation applies to that which ends with [the qualifier]); thus he says: "the root which ends in a consonant. Since the word *guru* (heavy), which denotes a specific vowel (*aj*), cannot have its primary application to a root ending in a consonant, he explains that the term is understood as referring to that which possesses such a vowel: "possessing a heavy [vowel]. However, the reverse is not the case—that is, "a root which ends in a heavy [consonant] and possesses a *hal*"—because of the grammatical indications in the rules *ceṣṭāyāmanadhvani* and *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*. [Examples: *kuṇḍā*, *huṇḍā*; from the roots *kuḍi* (to burn) and *huḍi* (to heap together).
The suffix *aṅ* is applied after the roots ending in *ṣit* and those beginning with *bhid*.

Regarding the phrase "in those recited in the *gaṇa*": in the *gaṇa*, indeed, the collective forms ending in the suffix *aṅ*—such as *bhidā*, *chidā*, and so forth—are recited. The meaning is that among these, the verbal roots (*prakṛti*) such as *bhidi*, *chidi*, and others, which end in *aṅ*, are here indicated by the term "the *bhidā*-group" (*bhidādi*). Why is this so? Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots; [the rule applies] "to the verbal roots beginning with *bhidi*."

*bhid* in the sense of splitting; *chid* in the sense of dividing into two; *vid* in the sense of knowing; *kṣip* in the sense of impelling; *guh* in the sense of concealing; *ḍudhāñ* in the senses of holding and nourishing; *midhṛ* and *medhṛ* in the senses of injury and affliction; *ṛ* in the sense of going; *hṛñ* in the sense of taking away; *kṣi* in the sense of destruction, or alternatively *kṣi* in the senses of dwelling and going; *tṝ* in the senses of leaping and crossing over; *dhṛñ* in the sense of holding; *likha* in the sense of arranging letters; *cuda* in the sense of impelling; *pīḍa* in the sense of pressing; *ḍuvap* in the sense of the continuous succession of seeds and threads; *vasa*...
The roots *nivāsa* (in the sense of dwelling), *mṛjūṣ* (in the sense of purification), and *krapa* (in the sense of compassion) are to be understood as such.

*jareti*: "In the case of the suffix *aṅ*, there is *guṇa* for the roots *ṛ* and *dṛś*" (*ṛdṛśo'ṅi guṇaḥ*). Regarding *guhā giryoṣadhyoḥ*: by the word *giri*, a part of that [mountain] is expressed; elsewhere, it is *gūḍhiḥ*, which occurs only with the suffix *ktin*. Regarding *ārā... dhāra*: once *guṇa* has been applied, lengthening is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding *rekhā, lekha*: in the alternative form of the root *likh*, the substitution of *repha* for the letter *lakāra* is prescribed, as is *guṇa*. Regarding *cūḍā*: from the root *cud*, the substitution of *ḍa* and lengthening are prescribed as irregularities. Regarding *mittiranyā*: that which is split is *bhittiḥ*—meaning a wall (*kuḍya*); *chittiḥ* means a hole (*chidra*).

Regarding the word *ārā* in the phrase *ārā śastryām*: *śastrī* refers to the class of weapons (*śastra-jāti*), and a specific instance is understood by virtue of its inherent nature. *Ārā* means a goad (*pratoda*), because horses are driven (*aryante*) or urged forward by it. Regarding *ārtiḥ* as "another": there is a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) according to the rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau*. *Dhārā* is so called because it is held (*dhāryate*) or poured forth (*prapātyate*). Regarding *dhṛtiḥ* as "another": it means joy (*prīti*) and fortitude (*dhairya*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *cintā*, *pūjī*, *kathī*, and *kumbhī*. 3.3.105.

Regarding the statement "when *yuc* is applicable": this is because all [roots] are indeed *ṇi*-derived (*ṇyanta*). For example, *kumbhāgram*; for we see [the usage] "an *udīcīna-kumbā* sacrificial post" (*śamyā*). The *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been mentioned—namely, *tulā* from the root *tulayati*. Now, why was this not placed immediately after the rule "after a heavy vowel and a consonant" (*gurośca halaḥ*)? Why is there this separate prescription of *aṅ*? It should have been done there as well; what, then, is the distinction here? Another says: by the force of the prescription of *aṅ*, the elision of *ṇi* does not optionally occur, so that forms such as *cintiyā* arise. However, there is no statement of an authoritative source (*āptabhāṣita*) regarding this.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the root *āp* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it. Pāṇini 3.3.106.

Regarding the passage beginning with *śraddhāntaror-* and so forth: the meaning is that whatever operation—characterized by the production of suffixes—occurs with respect to a prefix (*upasarga*), that very same operation applies to those two [words] as well. In this context, the word *śraddhā* is established through its inclusion in the *tārakādi* group; furthermore, the fact that [the author] prescribes the *kvip* suffix based on the condition of "disappearance" (*antardhi*) indicates that the word *antar-* functions as a prefix. And having established this, the substitution of *ṇ* in *antarṇayati* occurs by virtue of the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*.
The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots ending in *ṇi* (causative) and after the root *śranth*.

"It will be *ṇyat*. [Objection: But would not *ṇyat* be applied by the rule of "optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*), and is that not prohibited by the rule "not in the feminine" (*na striyām*)? To this he says: "And there is a prohibition of the optionality of dissimilar forms" (*vāsarūpa-pratiṣedhaś ca*). [The compound] "of the general rule and the exception" (*utsargāpavādasya*) is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The meaning is: "of both the general rule and the exception which are situated within the domain of the feminine. [Regarding the rule] "from *ghaṭṭi*, *vand*, and *vid*" (*ghaṭṭivandividibhyaś ca*): the root *vid* is taken in the sense of "obtaining," not in the sense of "knowing."

Since the form *vedanā* is established in the sense of "knowledge" from this very root *vid* belonging to the *curādi* class—as in the rule *vida cetanākhyānanivāseṣu*—the statement [in the commentary] is not intended to exclude the *ktin* suffix from the root *vid* (of the *adādi* class), as we see the form *saṃvittiḥ*. Regarding *anveṣaṇā*: it is derived either from *iṣa* in the sense of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇye*) or from *iṣ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*). The letter *c* in the suffix *yuc* has an inconceivable purpose, for the word *udāttaḥ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]; by its force, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) will result, since the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is already established by the accent of the suffix itself.
The suffix *ṇvul* is frequently applied after a verbal root to form a word denoting a disease.

"Regarding the mention of *ākhyā* (name), etc.: the purpose of mentioning *ākhyā* is so that the suffix occurs only when the name of a disease is formed by means of a suffix, and not otherwise. Therefore, it does not occur when the disease is expressed by another word—for example, *bubhukṣā bhasmakena* ("hunger caused by *bhasmaka*"). *Bhasmaka* is the name of a specific disease in which what is eaten, drunk, and so forth, does not pervade the body, and hunger is constant. The mention of *bahula* (diversely) is for the sake of allowing exceptions."

"Sometimes there is application [of a rule], sometimes non-application, sometimes an option, and sometimes something else entirely"—this is the irregularity (*vyabhicāra*). *Pracchadikā* (a covering). *Vicacikā* (a skin disease). From the root *carca* in the sense of "studying," the perception of a disease arises through the addition of a suffix and a prefix; thus, *vicacikā* refers to *pāmā* (scabies). *Śirottiḥ* means a piercing pain in the head (*śirastodaḥ*). From the root *ard* in the sense of "injury," there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *titutra*. There is the substitution of *r* for the final syllable of the preceding word (*rutvam*). By the rule *atororaplutāt*, there is the substitution of *u*; then *ādguṇaḥ* (the single substitute *o*); and finally *eṅaḥ padāntādati* (the elision of the final *o* before the following *a*). "Specification of the meaning of the verbal root" means the specification of the action.

Regarding the statement "the *śtip* and *śap* [affixes] are for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*)," this means they serve as markers for the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root. Furthermore, due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*), these affixes do not occur in certain instances, such as in the rules "after *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*, there is *san*" and "after *mān*, *vadha*, *dān*, and *śān*. The presence of the *ś* in *śtip* (and *śap*) has the force of making it a *śit* affix; consequently, even when this affix does not denote an agent (*kartṛ*), the *śa*-class affixes (*śab-ādi*) still occur. The same applies when it does not denote a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). In some cases, the *yak* affix also occurs, as in the rule "optionally after *līyate*. Here, the mention of both *lī* and *līṅ* is made by using *yak*; otherwise, if *śyan* were used, the reference would apply only to *līṅ* and not to *līnāti*.

But how can there be the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the marker *śit*, given that in forms such as *pibati* and *jighrati*, the addition of *śit* would be for the purpose of triggering the substitutes *piba-* and so on, and for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *ā* in roots such as *glāyati*? If this is the case, then *śap* and the other affixes will arise by virtue of specific grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*), such as: "after a prefix, [the affix *śnu* is applied] to *sunoti*, *suvati*, and *syati*"; "optionally [to *līyate*]"; "an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of *ṇa* to *bhavati*"; and "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of *dhyāyati*," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from a phoneme" (*varṇāt*): this means "from an imitation of a phoneme that denotes a phoneme," and not "from a phoneme being uttered. What is established by this? In cases such as *kakāraḥ*, the suffix *-kāra* is established even from a composite [sound] containing a consonant; for since the vowel *a* serves the purpose of pronunciation, it is the mere phoneme that is being imitated. The designation *it* (the marker *it*) does not apply to the letter *ka*, because there is no purpose for it. Due to the inclusion of the term "diversely" (*bahulagrahaṇāt*), the suffix *-kāra* does not occur in instances such as *asya cvau* and *yasyeti ca*.

By virtue of the word "bahula" (diversity), [the suffix *kāra*] occurs even from certain clusters of phonemes (*varṇasaṅghāta*) that are onomatopoeic (*anukaraṇa*), such as *ekakāra*. Although the suffix *kāra* is not prescribed after a verbal root (*adhātu*), its designation as a *kṛt* suffix occurs by the force of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *kṛt* suffixes. Consequently, because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, it receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); however, the augment *iṭ* does not occur because it is not part of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix. But why is the suffix *kāra* prescribed at all? For one could simply say "the instrument is *kāraḥ*" and then "the *kāra* of this is *akāraḥ*. This cannot be done; [for the following reasons...]
For if it were understood in this way, there would be no point in the use of the root *kṛ* (in *kakārakaraṇam*), because it would be redundant.

"Rādiph" (ra-ādi-ph): this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *kā*. How then is it that "names beginning with the letter *r*"? By the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffix *kā* will also occur; as before, when the designation *kṛt* applies, there is the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*). Regarding "matvarthāccha": "matvartha" means having the same meaning as the suffix *matup*; from that, the suffix *cha* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). Because of the statement "in various instances" (*bahulavacanāt*), even though it is not a *bha*-stem, the elision of *yasya* (*yasyeti lopaḥ*) takes place, and as before, there is the status of a nominal stem. Due to the statement "in various instances," it does not occur in some cases, such as in the rule "tasau matvarthe."
And precisely because of the word *bahula* (in the rule), the suffix occurs even after a word expressing the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*), according to the rule *śaiṣikān matubarthīyāt*.
Regarding *ājiri*: due to the word *bahula*, there is an absence of the substitution of *vī* for *vi*.
Regarding *ikkṛṣyādibhyaḥ*: this is an exception to the suffix *ṇvul* when the meaning of a verbal root is indicated.
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after [a verbal root] when *saṃjñā* (name) is to be expressed. 3.3.109.

*Uddāla* is the *śleṣmātaka* tree; that [game] in which its flowers are broken off is *uddālapuṣpabhañjikā*. That in which *varaṇa* flowers are gathered is *varaṇapuṣpapracāyikā*. *Abhyūṣa* is a specific kind of fried cake (*pūlikā*); that in which it is eaten is *abhyūṣakhādikā*. That in which palmyra fruits (*tāla*) are broken is *tālabhañjikā*; likewise, *śālabhañjikā*.
The suffix *iñ* is also applied after [a word ending in] *vibhāṣā*, *ākhyāna*, and *paripraśna*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that first there is an inquiry and afterwards an explanation? Then how is it that in the Sūtra, by disregarding the proper sequence, the explanation is presented first and the inquiry afterwards? To this he says: "First the inquiry," and so forth. It is true that first there is the question and afterwards the explanation; however, the meaning is that in the Sūtra, due to the requirements of the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the reverse order has been adopted. But [the author], explaining by way of a rearrangement himself, explains according to the sequence of the actual meaning and provides examples. [The word] *kārikām* [is formed with] the suffix *ṇvul*.

Regarding *kriyām* and *kṛtyām*: from the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca*, the suffix *śa* is applied, and due to the presence of *ca*, the suffix *kyap* is also included. Regarding *kṛtim*: by means of a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), the suffix *ktin* is applied. Regarding *gaṇim*: the root *gaṇa* (meaning "counting") belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in *a*. Regarding *gaṇanām*: the suffix *yuc* is applied. "In this way," and so forth: *kāṃ pācikām*, [meaning] *pacām*. Because it has the marker *ṣit*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied. *Paktiḥ*: the suffix *ktin* is applied according to the rule *sthāgāpāpaca*. *Kāṃ yāji*, *yājikām im*: *kāṃ pāṭhi*, *pāṭhikām*, *paṭhitim*. According to the statement *titutreṣvagrahādīnām*, the augment *iṭ* is not applied.
The suffix *ṇvuc* is applied after verbal roots in the senses of "exchange," "being entitled to," and "arising."

*Paripāṭī*: from the root *paṭ* preceded by *pari*, the suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the rule *iṇajādibhyaḥ*; then, from that [form ending in] *iṇ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. *Tadyorayateti*: by the word *tat*, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is expressed. *Parasmai*: the designation *sampradāna* (recipient) is applied according to the rule *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ*. However, in the reading *parasya*, the meaning is "for the sake of another" (*parasya hita*). *Dhāryate* means "is constrained" or "is bound. *Grāmāmikā*: this is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*). *Udapādi*: [this is the form].

In the rule *ciṇ te padaḥ*, the suffix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). [The phrase] "for the sake of the accent" means that the final syllable should be udātta by virtue of the rule *citaḥ*. However, if the suffix *ṇvul* were used instead, the penultimate syllable would be udātta by virtue of the rule *liti*.
The suffixes *nañ*, *yañ*, and *ni* are applied [to a verbal root] in the sense of reviling.
*Ākreśaḥ* means reviling, not mere abuse; this is because it is its inherent nature. "Akaraṇi" and so forth constitute the sentence of reviling.
The *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely.

Regarding "snānīyam": here the *kṛtya* suffix is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding "dānīya": here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), while in cases such as sprinkling (*avasecana*), it is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

[The examples] *praskandanaḥ* and *prapatanaḥ* [are formed] with the agent (*kartṛ*) as the referent. The mention of "in various ways" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) need not be made; for by the very force of the rule's commencement, *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes will apply elsewhere than where they have been specifically prescribed. Thus, by the mention of "in various ways," the deviation of the primary meaning (*svārthavyabhicāra*) of all *kṛt* suffixes is established. However, the specific indication of meaning in the rules "the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-suffixes [denote] only those two [the action and the object]" and "a *kṛt* suffix [denotes] the agent" is intended to indicate that, due to their abundance, these suffixes occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and so forth, while in some cases they occur elsewhere.

Regarding "pādahāraka": the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is a compound formed by the rule "a *kṛt*-suffix forms a compound with a word ending in the fifth case. Regarding "galecopaka": there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending according to the rule "from *mūrdhan* up to *mastaka*."
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāva*) when it denotes a neuter gender.

But is it not the case that the suffix *kta* is already established for the neuter abstract action (*napuṃsake bhāve*) by the rule "only for those two [roots] are the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes applied"? True, it is established for the past tense (*bhūte*). However, this rule is introduced because it would otherwise not apply to the neuter abstract action when the time is unspecified (*kālasāmānye*). Some say: "Just as suffixes such as *ghañ* occur in the sense of the abstract action even after transitive roots—as in *odanasya pākaḥ* ('the cooking of rice') and *odanasya bhojanam* ('the eating of rice')—so too this *kta* occurs in the sense of the abstract action after transitive roots; for here there is no statement restricting it to 'intransitive roots' (*akarmakebhyaḥ*)."

Now, what case ending occurs for the object (*karman*) at that time? The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix [would apply] to the object; however, that is prohibited when used in conjunction with a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle). [To account for this,] there is the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*): "In the neuter, when expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*), the genitive should be added"—thus [we get forms like] *odanasya bhuktam* ("the eating of rice") and *udakasya pītam* ("the drinking of water"). On this view, this [new rule] is also undertaken for this purpose, for by the rule *tayoreva* ("only those two [roots]"), the *kta* suffix is not established in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) for transitive roots (*sakarmaka*).

Others, however, consider that the phrase "of those two alone" (*tayoreva*) serves to establish the scope even for this *kta* suffix. For while the rule "the *niṣṭhā*" establishes the meaning of the *kta* suffix as being the abstract state (*bhāva*), the phrase "from intransitive roots" (*akarmakebhyaḥ*) establishes its scope; whereas for this [present rule], by restating "the *kta* in the sense of the abstract state," the phrase "from intransitive roots" establishes its scope.
And the suffix *lyuṭ* [is also applied]. 3.3.115.
"The division of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows" means that it is so that only *lyuṭ* may continue to apply in what follows, and not *kta*.
And that [wind] which, through contact with the object of action, produces physical pleasure for the agent. (3.3.116)

The word *kartuḥ* (of the agent) is used in the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). Because of the restrictive rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the genitive is used] for the object," the word *yena* (by which) takes the instrumental case in the sense of the agent. Thus he says: "by which action [the agent] is being touched. In response to the expectation "whose bodily pleasure [is it]?", since the agent is in close proximity, it is understood to belong to that very person; thus he says: "bodily pleasure arises for the agent. What is this so-called "pleasure of the body"? Is it not true that pleasure is a quality of the self, which is distinct from the body? True.

When a pleasure arises such that health is produced even in the body, that is called "bodily pleasure" (*śarīrasukha*). This statement is for the sake of establishing a permanent compound (*nityasamāsa*). How then is it illustrated in the rule *ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi* [Pāṇini 2.3.66] as: "The drinking of milk by Devadatta is indeed good"? It should be understood that this is illustrated in a case where pleasure does not arise due to its being disagreeable; for instance, [the phrase] "the drinking of milk is a pleasure."

In that case, [you might argue] that pleasure arises from drinking and not from touch, and it would be more appropriate to cite this: "The application of sandalwood paste is pleasant. This is not a fault; for where pleasure does not arise without physical contact, the mention of "touch" (saṃsparśa) serves as an illustration of the object [of that pleasure]. In those cases, let pleasure arise from the touch itself, or from drinking and so forth preceded by it; it will be so in all instances.

Regarding the term *tūlikāyāḥ*: a *tūlikā* is a mattress (*kaśipu*) made of cotton (*tūla*); rising after lying upon it is pleasant. Regarding "the worship of the fire-pit" (*agnikuṇḍasyopāsanam*): here, pleasure belongs to one who is not being touched by the fire-pit. Regarding "the bathing of the Guru" (*guroḥ snāpanam*): although in this case the Guru is the agent of the experience of pleasure, nevertheless that [agency] is not what is relied upon here, because it is not invariant. What then? That which is the agency inherent in the base of the suffix *lyuṭ* is what is relied upon. Thus he says: "In the case of the root *snāpaya*, the Guru is not the agent."

"But it is mental joy. When one is being powerfully embraced by a son, there is indeed a physical prickling of the body, yet there is also mental joy. [Objection: But since the suffix *lyuṭ* is employed in all the counter-examples as well, how can they be considered counter-examples? To this he replies: "In all cases, it is the uncompounded form that is cited as a counter-example."
And [the suffix lyuṭ] is used after a verbal root in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) and the locus (adhikaraṇa). Pāṇini 3.3.117.

"Regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) when they are to be expressed. However, when these are used as subordinate words (*upapada*), they do not denote the instrument or the locus, precisely because of the specific instruction [in the rule] "of the instrument and the locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇayoḥ*). For "instrument" is that by which something is done (*kriyate 'nena*), and "locus" is that in which something is situated (*adhikriyate 'smin*); thus, these two are indeed the means (*sādhana*) of the instrument and the locus. If this is so, then there would be a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*): the application of the suffix depends on the instruction, and the instruction depends on the application of the suffix. No; [this is not the case].

Because words are eternal (*nityatva*), the suffix *ta* does not denote the instrument or the locus based on this specific rule. In the case of *idhmapravraścanaḥ*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) with the sense of the object (*karman*); it refers to an axe or similar tool. In *palāśaśātanaḥ*: from the root *śadlṛ* in the sense of "cutting" (*śātane*), there is the causative suffix *ṇic*; by the rule *śaderagatau taḥ*, the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs. That staff by which the leaves of a tree are caused to fall is thus called [a *palāśaśātana*]. *Godohanī*, *saktudhānī*, and *pātrī* are feminine nouns denoting vessels. This application of the rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ghañ*, according to the principle that a rule applies where another would otherwise have applied (*yena nāprāptinyāya*).

The *ajādi* suffixes and feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) sublate [the former] due to their higher status in the order of rules. For it has been stated: "The feminine suffixes, the *khal* and *nañ*, and the *nañ* sublate the *aja* and *ap* suffixes by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)."
The suffix *gha* is generally used after a verbal root to form a masculine noun denoting an agent.

Regarding the term *dantacchada*: the root *chad* in the sense of "covering" belongs to the *curādi* (cur-class) group; the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "the [vowel] of *chād-* is shortened before a suffix beginning with *gh*, when it is preceded by two prefixes. An *ākara* is that in which they conduct their business—that is, a place of origin.
The words *gocara*, *saṃcara*, *vaha*, *vraja*, *vyaja*, *paṇa*, and *nigama* [are used as neuter nouns when they denote a place]. 3.3.119.

"In this, cows move" (*gāvaścaranty asmin*): this is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) synonymous with "object" (*viṣaya*), and its etymological derivation is merely figurative. Thus, we have *gocaraḥ*, *indriyagocaraḥ*, and so forth. "By means of which they move about" (*sañcarante 'nena*): the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *samastṛtīyāyuktāt*. *Sañcaraḥ* means a path; *vahaḥ* means a shoulder-pole; *vrajaḥ* means a cow-pen; *vyajaḥ* means a palm-leaf fan; *āpaṇaḥ* means a marketplace; *nigamaḥ* means a Vedic meter. This [specific] grammatical derivation could not be stated, as it is already established by the preceding rule.

Why does the suffix *ghañ* not apply by the rule "hal-śca"? Because the term "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is understood to carry over there; just as *ghañ* does not apply in the case of *nikaṣaḥ* from the root *kaṣ*, so too it will not apply in the case of *gocara* and the others.
The suffix GHaÑ is applied after the roots *ava* and *tṛ* when followed by the preposition *tri*.

*Avatāra* means a descent, such as [the descent of] form (*rūpa*) and so forth; *avastāra* means a curtain (*javanikā*) and so forth. *Nadyavatāra* means a river-crossing (*tīrtha*). Because the term "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], it occurs even when not used as a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). Now, one might object: since the suffix *ghañ* is that which is to be prescribed (*vidheya*), it is the primary element, and "generally" (*prāya*) is its qualifier (*upādhi*). Consequently, the meaning would be that it does not occur in some cases even when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The author considers this: the word "generally" (*prāya*) is a qualifier of the qualifier itself, namely "in a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*).

It is accepted that a qualifier can qualify a qualifier, or a qualifier can qualify a qualifier of a qualifier; it is not maintained that this is impossible, because it follows the requirements of the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*).
And [the suffix] *hal* [is applied after a verbal root ending in a consonant]. 3.3.121.

*lekhaḥ*—a pen; *lekhanī*. *veṣṭaḥ*—clothing and so forth; from the root *viṣṭa* in the sense of "wrapping. *Vedaḥ*—that by which dharma and adharma are known (*vidyete*) or understood; thus it is called *veda*. *Apāmārgaḥ*—a particular herb; that by which disease and the like are wiped away (*apamṛjyate*). *Vīmārgaḥ*—a broom; [the form is derived] as before, with the substitution of *k* for *g* and the lengthening of the vowel.
The suffixes -ya, -nya, -ya, -a, -saṃhāra, -ādhāra, and -āvāya [are applied after verbal roots] in the sense of the action itself. 3.3.122.

"Āvayanti" means "they come and weave. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; this refers to the Vārttika: "In the rule prescribing the suffix *ghañ*, there should be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the words *avahāra*, *āya*, and [the rest]. However, the author of the Vṛtti (Vṛttikāra), having inserted the words *ādhāra* and *āya* into the sūtra itself, established the word *avahāra* by means of the particle *ca*; for the composition of the Vṛtti by the Vṛttikāra is indeed diverse.
The word *udaṅka* is used in the sense of "without water. (Pāṇini 3.3.123)
Oil is poured out; that in which it is poured out is *tailodaka*, a vessel made of leather.

"Why *gha*?"—the sense is that since *gha* would have been applicable by the rule "in the masculine, when a name [is formed]," etc., the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed; therefore, once *ghañ* has taken its place, *gha* alone ought to follow. [The objection: "But there is no difference"—[one might argue] that if *gha* were used, the accent would be that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), whereas with *ghañ*, the word would be acute on the first syllable due to the *ñit*-accent; so how can there be no difference? To this he replies: "In *ghañ*, [the vowel] is elided," and so forth.
The suffix *mānaya* is applied after the word *jāla*. || 3.3.124 ||

From the root *ghat* in the sense of "to kill" (*jala-ghātye*), when the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule *jvalitikasantebhyo ṇaḥ*, the form *jāla* arises. It is called *ānāya* because fish and other creatures are brought (*ānīyante*) by means of it.
The augment *kh* is substituted for *gha* after the verbal root √khan. (Pāṇini 3.3.125)

What is the purpose of making *ghit* (the marker *gh*)? For there is no part of the root *khan* that undergoes *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *kh*). It is, however, for the sake of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*); it indicates that this [substitution] occurs even after other roots. By this, forms such as *bhaga-* from the root *bhaj*, and *pada-* from the root *pad*—where *gha* is used in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*)—as well as *khala-* from the root *khal* (meaning "to move") where *gha* is used in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), are thus established. Words such as *ākhanādayaḥ* denote digging tools.
The suffix *khal* is used after the words *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *su* when they signify difficulty (*kṛcchra*) or lack of difficulty (*akṛcchra*).

Regarding the term *taddura*: because of the grammatical indication in the rule *suduroḥ adhikaraṇe*, the word *dur* exists as well with a final *r*. Regarding the phrase *sambhavāt*: the occurrence (*sambhava*) of difficulty (*kṛcchra*) is possible only for *dur*, whereas for the other two [prefixes] it occurs only in the absence of difficulty; therefore, even though they are stated in a general sense, the distinction of their respective domains is obtained through this qualification—this is the intended meaning. Regarding *īṣatkāryam*: the word *īṣat* has the sense of "slightly" (*manāk*).

Regarding the rule *kartṛkarmaṇośca bhūkṛñoḥ*: "when the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) is the upapada. However, the agent and the object do not become the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthatva*); for the particle *ca* serves to include the *upapada*. Furthermore, if those two were the meaning of the suffix, the suffix would occur only when *īṣat* and so forth are the *upapadas*; in that case, the inclusion of the *k* (in *khit*) would be purposeless, for it is the addition of *num* that is prescribed for non-indclinables (*anavyaya*). Therefore, it is well said: "when the agent or the object is the *upapada*."

In this context, the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of "conjunction" (*sanniyoga*), meaning that when the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) and words such as *īṣat* etc. are simultaneously present as subordinate elements (*upapada*), then the suffix occurs; however, the compound may occur either simultaneously or successively. But what, then, is the "subordinate element" (*upapada*) here? It is the agent and the object. Why is this so? Because of the insertion of the *khiṭ* augment after the word *khala*. That [insertion] is for the sake of the *mum* augment, and the *mum* augment applies to that which is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*). In that case, if there were immediate proximity between the words *īṣat* etc. and the verbal root, the insertion of *khiṭ* would be purposeless.

Now, let it be granted that there is no immediate sequence with the verbal root (*dhātu*) where this [rule] does not apply—namely, by the rule *te prāg dhātoḥ* (P. 2.2.21). However, where *su-* and *dur-* do exist, their application immediately before the root is indeed appropriate. But the inclusion of the marker *k* would serve the purpose of *mum* (the substitution of *m* for the final vowel and following consonant) in cases such as *īṣadāḍhyambhavantīm*; and since the rule *kṛdgrahaṇe gatikārakapūrvasyāpi grahaṇam* (when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, a term preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included) applies here as well, the *mum* substitution would also apply there, just as in *kūlamudrujaḥ* from the rule *udikūle rujivahoḥ*. This must be addressed here.

The resolution is as follows: [it is governed by] the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). Alternatively, the mention of the term *bahulam* (variously) should be relied upon here. Regarding *īṣadāḍhyambhavam*: the meaning is that "by you, who were not wealthy, one becomes wealthy with ease. Regarding *īṣadāḍhyaṅkara*: the meaning is that "Devadatta, who was not wealthy, is made wealthy with ease. Regarding *svāḍhyena bhūyate*: this is a faulty reading; for here, due to the suffix *khal*, the word *su-* ought to have been placed before the verbal root, therefore the correct reading is *āḍhyena subhūyate*.
It is also seen after other [roots]. (Pāṇini 3.3.130)

"Also from others besides those meaning 'to go' (gatyartha). This means: from those verbal roots (dhātu) which are other than those meaning "to go. Alternatively, there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) here—"also from other roots," meaning "from those not meaning 'to go'.

"In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). This rule is commenced because the governing heading "in the Vedic language (*chandas*)" was previously in effect. [The roots are: *śāsu* in the sense of "instruction," *yudh* in the sense of "combat," *dṛśir* in the sense of "seeing," *ñidhṛṣā* in the sense of "boldness," and *mṛṣa* in the sense of "endurance."
When there is proximity to the present time, the verb may optionally be treated as if it were in the present tense. (Pāṇini 3.3.131)

Regarding this, some explain as follows: "The state of being near is *sāmīpya*; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Vartamānasāmīpya* is a genitive compound meaning 'the proximity of the present. Since the extension of present-tense suffixes is unnecessary for that proximity which the past and future have toward the present—for indeed, those suffixes which apply to the present apply equally when it is near to the past or future—the proximity here refers to that which the past and future have toward the present."

It is said that "proximity to the present" (*vartamānasāmīpyam*) is [the condition for the use of the present tense]. And because the present is connected with proximity by way of its vicinity, the compound is not untenable, just as in the case of "Devadatta’s teacher’s family" (*devadattasya gurukulam*). Nor does the prohibition [of compounding] based on the rule "not with a quality-word" (*guṇena na*) apply; for since the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is a relative term, the prohibition of compounding applies only to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) which is implied by the quality. Furthermore, the present is not the possessor of the quality of proximity, because the past and the future are the possessors of that quality.

This [previous] explanation is flawed, and the mention of the suffix *ṣyañ* would serve only to cause confusion; therefore, he explains it otherwise: "Proximity itself is *sāmīpyam*. He states that even on this view, the suffix *ṣyañ* is not redundant: "It is made known that *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). The meaning is that the mention of *ṣyañ* is made to indicate that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs even when the word retains its own original meaning. [The phrase] "for the sake of establishing *cāturvarṇya*, etc. [is explained as follows].

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such forms as *cāturāśramyam*, *anyasya bhāvaḥ* (the state of being another), and *anyabhāvyam* (the state of becoming another). [For example: "When did you come, Devadatta? This is a question regarding past time. In the illustration, in order to manifest the past time, that form which is inseparable from the act of coming—namely, the appearance characterized by a white turban, a girdle, and so forth—is pointed out with the words "this very one" (*ayam eṣa*). The meaning is: "I have come now."

And thus, an answer is appropriate to the question "When? (*kadā*), and proximity (*sāmīpya*) is thereby indicated. Regarding the form *āgamam*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix; the substitution of *am* for the first person singular ending *mip*; and the addition of the augment *aṅ* because the root begins with *lṛ*. [The example is: "When, O Devadatta, will you go? Here too, since the question in the illustration pertains to the future time, it serves to manifest the future time. [The response is: "I shall go" (*gantāsmi*). This is the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) suffix used for non-todays (*anadyatana*). Here too, proximity should be understood as far as possible.

Now, what is the purpose of the inclusion of the suffix *vat*, since even in its absence this meaning is already obtained—namely, that by virtue of the governing context of "affixes" (*pratyaya-adhikāra*), those affixes prescribed for the present tense also occur in the vicinity of the present? There is no need for the suffix *vat*; therefore, he says: "The inclusion of *vat* is for the sake of complete similarity."

If the suffix *vat* were not used, the phrase "those affixes which [occur] in the present tense" would indicate merely the form of the affixes; consequently, there would be confusion—namely, that an affix prescribed after one root in the present tense might also occur after another root. However, when *vat* is present, because all points of similarity are understood, no confusion arises. He demonstrates this very totality of similarity with the words: "by whatever qualification... and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *upādhi* (limiting condition) and the denotable object (*abhidheya*) is intended. In the examples *pacamānaḥ* ("cooking") and *yajamānaḥ* ("sacrificing"), the suffix *śānan* is prescribed after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj* when [an action] is present; that same suffix occurs after those very roots even when there is proximity [to another time]. In *alaṅkariṣṇuḥ* ("one who is about to adorn"), the suffix *iṣṇuc* is prescribed after the root *kṛñ* preceded by *alam* when the agent is qualified by such habitual tendencies (*tacchīla*) and so forth; that suffix occurs after that very root, preceded by that very prefix, in that very sense, even when there is proximity. *Parut* means "in the previous year."

With the words "For he who thinks," etc., [the author] refutes the specific [notion of] the cognizer with respect to the context. Regarding the phrase "the movement at another time": "another time" refers to a past or future time proximate to the present; its "movement"—that is, its cognition—arises from the sentence "I am going" when it is employed as a response to the question "When, Devadatta, will you go? To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not... [referring to] "the one who understands the meaning of the sentence."

The one who understands that "this is the meaning of the sentence, not the meaning of the word" is the *vākyārthapratipattā* (the cognizer of the sentence-meaning); this is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). The prohibition [of such a compound] by the rule *kartari ca* is non-obligatory, because of the specific mention in the rule *janikartuḥ*; or else, the compound is formed with the genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding the term *prakaraṇam*: from this point onward, a group of eight sūtras is referred to by the word *prakaraṇa*. Thus, for example, [it is said]: "He will do it tomorrow," and so forth.

If time, even though it is understood through the sentence, is utilized in the formation of the word (*pada-saṃskāra*), then such a case as this would not be possible—namely, the assumption that the suffix *luṭ* must necessarily occur for the non-today (*anadyatana*) tense.
In the sense of expectation, [the suffixes] are used as if [the action] were already accomplished. (Pāṇini 3.3.132)

And its object is the future time. "Future time belongs to this" means that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is future time; that [future time] is the object of the wish (āśaṃsā), while the wish itself pertains to the present time. Thus, by implication, it is understood that this extended application (atideśa) has the future as its object; so he says: "in the future time. "When a wish is being understood" means: from a verbal root expressing an action that is being wished for.

The phrase beginning with "upādhyāyaśced" (if the teacher) is an example of a sentence expressing hope (*āśaṃsā*). In that case, both the arrival of the teacher and the study of grammar are things hoped for; therefore, the suffix occurs in both instances. Regarding the form *adhyagīṣmahi*: by the rule "vibhāṣā luṅ-lṛṭoḥ," there is the substitution of *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ*; by the rule "gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ," the *sic* affix is marked as having the *ṅit* property; and by the rule "ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām," there is the substitution of *ī* for the vowel.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of a general extension" (*sāmānyātideśe*): in this sūtra, by the word *bhūta*, mere past time (*bhūtamātra*) is expressed, and not its specific sub-variety, the non-recent past (*anadyatana*). Furthermore, when there is a general extension, the specific detail is not extended; for instance, when it is said, "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa," the action resulting from the mere category of "Brāhmaṇa" is understood, but not that which is specifically enjoined for a particular individual such as Māṭhara. Therefore, the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes, which are prescribed for the non-recent past, do not occur here.

In this case, when something is not yet accomplished, the word "accomplished" (niṣpanna) must be explained to the student as follows: if it is said, "The rice is accomplished because the rain has fallen," this is merely a statement of the nature of things (vastusvarūpa); there is no intention (āśaṃsā) here. Therefore, does this [intention] not apply to that sūtra? This is not a fault; for the very conjunction of water and the rice seed is the accomplishment of the rice, since the occurrence of accomplishment takes place right there. For this very reason, common worldly usage does not tolerate the employment of a word denoting a future state [for what is already present].

When it is said, "If the god rains, the rice will be produced," people say, "Do not speak thus; say rather that the rice has been produced. This is established because the time [of the cause] is observed as the basis for the effect. That very time which belongs to the cause—such as rain—is observed as the time of the effect; that same time is determined to be the time of the effect itself in order to demonstrate the absence of dependence on any other cause.

Furthermore, since the cause itself is intended to be expressed in the form of the effect, and because of the determination of non-difference (*abheda-adhyavasāya*), the fact that the cause has come into being establishes that the effect has also come into being—this is the meaning. In this context, however, someone wishing to travel along a path might see [a sign] and think, "In that space, a well will exist" (*kūpo bhaviṣyati*); having reached it, he thinks, "A well exists" (*kūpo 'sti*); having passed beyond it, he thinks, "A well was there" (*kūpo 'bhūt*); and having passed beyond it and stayed there, and then forgetting, he thinks, "A well came into being" (*kūpo babhūva*). Because of having stayed there after passing beyond, he thinks, "A well existed" (*kūpa āsīt*). Thus, through the determination of non-difference, the past tense is established even for the effect. This is the sense. In the same way, here too, the effect is understood as past by means of the determination of non-difference with the cause. Therefore, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Alternatively, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is" (*asti*) or "exists" (*vidyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar exists" (*ghaṭo vidyate*), it is understood that the jar is present. Similarly, when one says, "The effect exists" (*kāryaṃ vidyate*), it is understood that the effect is present. Or again, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "manifests" (*prādurbhavati*). For example, when one says, "The jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ prādurbhavati*), it is understood that the jar is manifesting. Similarly, when one says, "The effect manifests" (*kāryaṃ prādurbhavati*), it is understood that the effect is manifesting. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "becomes" (*saṃpadyate*). For example, when one says, "The milk becomes curd" (*kṣīraṃ dadhi saṃpadyate*), it is understood that the milk is becoming curd. Similarly, when one says, "The effect becomes" (*kāryaṃ saṃpadyate*), it is understood that the effect is becoming. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is produced" (*jāyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is produced" (*ghaṭo jāyate*), it is understood that the jar is being produced. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is produced" (*kāryaṃ jāyate*), it is understood that the effect is being produced. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is perceived" (*upalabhyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is perceived" (*ghaṭa upalabhyate*), it is understood that the jar is being perceived. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is perceived" (*kāryam upalabhyate*), it is understood that the effect is being perceived. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is designated" (*vyapadiśyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is designated" (*ghaṭo vyapadiśyate*), it is understood that the jar is being designated. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is designated" (*kāryaṃ vyapadiśyate*), it is understood that the effect is being designated. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is named" (*nirdiśyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is named" (*ghaṭo nirdiśyate*), it is understood that the jar is being named. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is named" (*kāryaṃ nirdiśyate*), it is understood that the effect is being named. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is described" (*varṇyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is described" (*ghaṭo varṇyate*), it is understood that the jar is being described. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is described" (*kāryaṃ varṇyate*), it is understood that the effect is being described. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is explained" (*vyākhyāyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is explained" (*ghaṭo vyākhyāyate*), it is understood that the jar is being explained. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is explained" (*kāryaṃ vyākhyāyate*), it is understood that the effect is being explained. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is established" (*sādhyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is established" (*ghaṭaḥ sādhyate*), it is understood that the jar is being established. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is established" (*kāryaṃ sādhyate*), it is understood that the effect is being established. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is proven" (*siddhyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is proven" (*ghaṭaḥ siddhyate*), it is understood that the jar is being proven. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is proven" (*kāryaṃ siddhyate*), it is understood that the effect is being proven. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is accomplished" (*niṣpādyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is accomplished" (*ghaṭo niṣpādyate*), it is understood that the jar is being accomplished. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is accomplished" (*kāryaṃ niṣpādyate*), it is understood that the effect is being accomplished. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is completed" (*parisamāpyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is completed" (*ghaṭaḥ parisamāpyate*), it is understood that the jar is being completed. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is completed" (*kāryaṃ parisamāpyate*), it is understood that the effect is being completed. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Moreover, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is finished" (*samāpyate*). For example, when one says, "The jar is finished" (*ghaṭaḥ samāpyate*), it is understood that the jar is being finished. Similarly, when one says, "The effect is finished" (*kāryaṃ samāpyate*), it is understood that the effect is being finished. Thus, the statement "the effect comes into being" (*kāryaṃ bhavati*) is not contradictory. Furthermore, the word *bhavati* may be used in the sense of "is concluded" (*upasaṃhriyate

In this regard, since the existence of the well (*kūpa-sattā*) is present here everywhere—taking on both past and future forms—the *laṭ* (present tense) suffix alone would be applicable everywhere; yet, the *luṅ* (aorist) and other suffixes must also be stated. Thus he says: "For verbs meaning 'to exist,' all case-endings (*vibhakti*) occur in the sense of 'being' (*bhavanti*), because their agent (*kartṛ*) has the sense of being present. The word *bhavantī* is the technical term for the *laṭ* used by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).

If the *luṅ* (aorist) and other suffixes were prescribed to denote only the present time by means of verbal expression, then when one ought to say "the well existed" (*kūpo 'bhūt*), one might instead say "the well will exist" (*kūpo bhaviṣyati*). Therefore, these case-endings are employed according to their respective times. How so? Because the operation of the sense organ, as a temporal factor, is adopted as the differentiator with respect to the existence of the well, that [existence] also possesses that same time. Consequently, it is established as desired: when the operation of the sense organ is future, the future tense ending is used; when it is present, the present tense ending; and when it is past, the past tense ending. And it has been said:
Existence itself is qualified by its connection with a particular faculty;
for linguistic usage based on distinction is indeed dependent upon another entity.
"The existence of the mere thing is grasped by the intellect;
however, that distinction which arises from its specific acquisition is not intended to be expressed therein."
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used in the sense of speed.

The inclusion of the word *vacana* (utterance) is for the sake of including synonyms (*paryāya*). If that were not present, then by the rule "the word’s own form [is the technical term]," the suffix would apply only when the word *kṣipra* itself is the attendant word (*upapada*); however, because the synonym is included, it applies even to synonyms. Now, one might object: this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132), and since that rule concerns the future tense, one should simply say "it does not apply there. Once that is prohibited, the suffix *lṛṭ* is established by the rule *lṛṭ śeṣe ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.13) alone; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *lṛṭ* here? To this he replies: "When one ought to say 'not,' etc. [This means that if the exception were not stated, the prohibition of *bhūtavacca* would apply to all cases, and thus the mention of *lṛṭ* serves to restrict the scope of the exception.]

If it were not stated thus, then when the suffix *lṛṭ* would occur by the rule "lṛṭ śeṣe ca," it would not apply to the non-immediate future (*anadyatana*), because it would be superseded by *luṭ*. Therefore, the mention of *lṛṭ* is made so that it may also apply to the domain of *luṭ*; this is the meaning.
The suffix *liṅ* is used in expressions of hope (*āśaṃsā*). 3.3.134.

Regarding the form *adhīyīya*: from the root *iṅ* (to study), with the suffix *liṅ*, [the substitution] *icaḥ* applies; then *sīyuṭ* is added; there is elision of the *s* of the *liṅ*; the *iyaṅ* substitution occurs for the root vowel; and with the prefix (*upa-sarga*), there is the lengthening by *savarṇa-dīrgha*. In the case of expressing "speed," the suffix *lṛṭ* is used, whereas in the case of expressing "hope" (*āśaṃsā*), the suffix *liṅ* is used, according to the rule of "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule "in the case of expressing speed, *lṛṭ*" is seen in: *kṣipram adhyeṣyāmahe* ("we shall study quickly"); the scope of the rule "in the case of expressing hope, *liṅ*" is seen in: *āśaṃse yukto 'dhīyīya* ("I hope that I, being diligent, might study").

In this case, two [suffixes] are obtained: one expresses "I hope that I may study quickly," and the *liṅ* suffix occurs by way of conflict [between rules]. He demonstrates this very point in the example: "I hope that I may study quickly."
The [use of the present tense] does not apply when there is a continuity of action or proximity to the current day, even if it is not as if it were occurring on that very day. Pāṇini 3.3.135.

Regarding "proximity of times" (*kālānāṃ sāmīpyam*): since this section primarily concerns time—beginning with the rule *vartamānasāmīpye* (P. 3.3.131)—the intention is that even though proximity is mentioned generally, only proximity related to time is intended here. Regarding "by one of the same kind" (*sajātīyena*): the intention is that in common worldly usage, the term "proximity" is applied only in such cases. Regarding *adāt*: the suffix *sic* is elided by the rule *gātisthā* (P. 2.4.77). Regarding *adhyāpipat*: the root *iṅ* takes the causative suffix *ṇic*;

the vowel substitution *ā* occurs by the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* (P. 6.1.48); the augment *puk* is added by the rule *arttihrī* (P. 7.3.36); and in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix, the syllable *pi* undergoes reduplication according to the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (P. 6.1.2), followed by the elision of the *ṇic*.

Regarding the phrase "this full moon day that has passed": this is said with reference to that full moon day which is immediately followed by another full moon day. Although that [full moon] is indeed separated from the new moon day and other lunar days, nevertheless, because it is not separated by anything of its own kind—that is, by what is called a full moon day—it does not transcend proximity. Regarding the form *ādhitā*: from the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the substitution of *i* occurs according to the rule *sthāghvoricca*; the elision of the suffix *sic* occurs according to the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*. Regarding the form *ayaṣṭa*: [it is derived from the root *yaj*].

By the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is the elision of the suffix *sic*; by the rule for the *vraśca*-group, there is the substitution of *ṣ*. Regarding *adita*: the form of the root *dā* is as before. Regarding *yakṣyate*: after the substitution of *ṣ* by the *vraśca*-rule, there is the substitution of *k* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*; in all these cases, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *svaritañitaḥ*.

In this context, the suffixes *luṅ* and *lṛṭ*—which denote the present tense (*adyatana*)—are intended for the cases of continuous action (*kriyāprabandha*) and proximity (*sāmīpya*), and not the suffixes *laṅ* and *lṛṭ*, which denote non-present time. Even though those two suffixes, *luṅ* and *lṛṭ*, would indeed be established by the rule stating "in the cases of continuous action and proximity, [the suffixes] are treated as if they were present," why are two prohibitions stated? To this he says: "two prohibitions. Regarding the phrase "of that which is obtained as it is": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs in whatever manner (*yathā*) or by whatever means (*yena*)."

In the case of an *avyayībhāva* compound, however, there would be the substitution of *am*. Since this rule is understood as being prescribed here in reference to the present tense (*laṭ*), when the application of the present tense arises under the previous rule, because there is no suffix prescribed by the term "present" (*adyatana*) itself, there would be an extension (*atideśa*) of whatever was seen in the present tense. And since the present tense (*laṭ*) is also seen in the present, its application would consequently follow for the past and future as well; furthermore, the prescription of *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* would occur out of their proper time—*lṛṭ* in the domain of *luṅ*, and *luṅ* in the domain of *lṛṭ*.

But surely, because the suffix *vat* has the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), there will be no confusion? This is not so; for here, the *luṅ* and *lṛṭ* suffixes are seen to apply to the past and the future, as well as to the recent past (*adyatana*). In that case, if it were stated simply "like the recent past" (*adyatanavat*), the extension (*atideśa*) of those two [suffixes] to that very same recent past would be redundant; therefore, some portion must be excluded. When the extension is understood by excluding the portion referring to the recent past, it is established that *luṅ* applies to the non-recent past and *lṛṭ* applies to the non-recent future.

But when the extension [of grammatical rules] occurs by abandoning the distinction between past and future, then there would certainly be a confusion: that which was seen in the past present would be prescribed for the future present, and that which was seen in the future non-present would be prescribed for the past present; and the *laṭ* suffix would consequently apply in both cases. However, the use of the term *vat* (in the rule *tadhvamau... vat*) is for the purpose that whatever suffix is prescribed after a particular verbal root under a particular condition, it should occur after that very root under that very same condition.

Therefore, in rules such as "pūṅyajoḥ śānan," only a displacement of time occurs, not a displacement of the verbal root or other elements. If, however, this [author] were to remain silent after applying two prohibitions, then by their own prescriptive rules, the *laṭ* and other suffixes—the general rules—would apply in their respective times when freed from exceptions; thus, there would be no risk of confusion. Consequently, since this permits what has already been established by default, this is not a *vati* suffix.

What then? [The suffix] *matup*—[the formation] "that which has what is not of today" (*anadyatanavat*)—is neuter because of the intention to express a general quality. The meaning is that there is no rule for the application of suffixes as if they were "not of today" (*anadyatana*). Furthermore, the phrase "the rule for that suffix which is both 'not of today' and a suffix" means that everything prescribed for the "not of today" period does not occur. In the *Vārttika*, the statement "there is a prohibition of *laṅ* and *luṭ* which are prescribed [for that time]" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The suffix *lyap* shall be used after a verb when it expresses a limit in time that is posterior. (Pāṇini 3.4.136)

The statement is made for the purpose of excluding the continuity of action (*akriyāprabandha*) and for the purpose of excluding proximity (*asāmīpya*). The phrase "in the case of continuity of action and proximity" (*kriyāprabandhasāmīpyayoḥ*) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. For if it were to carry over, this [present rule] would be for the sake of a restriction—meaning that [the suffixes *luṭ* and *lṛṭ*] would apply only in the future tense, or only when expressing a limit (*maryādā*), or only in the latter case. And since both a general injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the intention is that the injunction alone is superior. "When there is the expression of a limit" (*maryādāvacane sati*) means: when there is the mention of a limit.

The inclusion of the term *vacana* (mention) is for the sake of denoting "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). For when the term *vacana* is included, the meaning of the expression *maryādāvacana* becomes "that which expresses a limit. Indeed, that very same limit, when connected with an action (*kārya*), is called "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent division": the meaning is that if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) pertains to the posterior portion, [the rule applies]. Because of the mention of "in the subsequent" (*aparasmin*), it is understood that one must conceive of two parts of that which has the limit. Regarding the word "to be gone to" (*gantavya*): [this refers to the destination].

By showing that the journey will take place in the future, he shows that the eating and other activities to be performed therein will also be in the future. Regarding the phrase "that which is subsequent to it": by this, the division of the path is indicated; and by the word "twice," the absence of a continuous flow of action is shown—meaning "twice" indeed, not "without interruption. The phrase "this person who has gone on the journey" indicates the past tense. In the form *adhyaimahi*: it is the root *iṅ* (to study) in the *laṅ* (imperfect), with the elision of *śap*, [the addition of] *āṭ* by the rule *āḍajādīnām*, and [the substitution of] *ai* for *āṭ* by the rule *āṭaśca*. In *abhuñjmahi*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule *bhujo'navane*; there is the elision of *al* (the *a* of *śna*) by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, and the change to *j* by the rule *cutvam*.
In that regard, he will state the distinction in the subsequent sūtra by means of the phrase "of those [days] which are not days and nights."
And [the suffixes] expressing divisions of time, with the exception of *ahorātra*. 3.3.137.

Regarding the phrase "when there is a division of time and limit" (*kālamaryādāvibhāge sati*): "limit and division" (*maryādāvibhāgam*) is a collective *dvandva* compound; with that [compound], the word "time" (*kāla*) forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). [The phrase] "if it is not a division related to a day-and-night" (*na cedahorātrasambandhī vibhāgaḥ*) shows by this that the genitive in "of non-day-and-nights" (*anahorātrāṇām*) expresses a general relation (*sambandhasāmānye*), and is not [the genitive] prescribed by the rule "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*). This being so, he demonstrates what is intended to be established by the words "by them" (*taiḥ*).

By those [days and nights], there is a division of another time, or by another [unit] of those [days and nights], or by those very [units] themselves; in every way, there is a prohibition. Now, one might object: "In the previous sūtra itself, it should have been stated as 'of non-days-and-nights' (*an-ahorātrāṇām*); for even so, by implication, the prohibition would be understood to apply only to the division of time, since there is no connection between the division of space and days-and-nights. So what is the purpose of this separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? To this he replies: "The separation of the rule is for the sake of the subsequent [sūtra]. This is so that in the following sūtra, the option (*vibhāṣā*) may apply only to the division of time, and not to the division of space. *Āgrahāyaṇī* means *Mārgaśīrṣī*.

"An example is threefold": the first [refers] to the disjunction of those [two]; the second, to the disjunction of them [the parts]; and the third, to their contact with day and night—that is, the scent of day and night—and this is obtained by resorting to a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). And the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* has been shown [in the text] as "if the disjunction is not connected with day and night"; otherwise, he would have said, "the disjunction is in that which is not connected with day and night."
The conditional (lṛṅ) is used when there is a cause indicated by a sign (liṅ-nimitta), provided that the action is not realized (kriyātipatti).

"Due to some deficiency" means that the deficiency consists either in the arising of an obstacle or in the incompleteness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). "The cart would not have overturned by way of the southern path" is because that path was straight and free from obstacles such as stumps; "overturning" (*paryābhavana*) means breaking. "Kamalaka" refers to a certain man who, by employing supports such as a pestle, was a driver of carts and other vehicles even on uneven ground. "You would not have been deprived of the ghee."

Even when the action of eating has been completed, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs upon the non-occurrence of the ghee alone; for, due to the difference in causes, the action of eating itself is distinct. Therefore, when the ghee fails to occur, the action of eating ghee is likewise considered non-occurrent. This statement refers to a future time. How, then, is there an understanding of a future matter at present? To this he says: "the non-occurrence of the future. In that context, "having a cause" means being the cause. By this, he demonstrates the relationship of cause and effect as the occasion for the conditional suffix (*liṅ*). [He concludes: "having understood by means of the conditional."

Having observed that on numerous previous occasions the overturning of the cart occurred when Kamalaka was summoned, and having perceived through a logical mark (*liṅga*) that even a future summons of Kamalaka will be the cause of the cart’s overturning—where the mark is, again, the fact of being a summons of Kamalaka—the meaning is: "One understands thus: 'A future summons of Kamalaka is also a cause of the cart’s overturning, because it is a summons of Kamalaka, just like previous summonses of Kamalaka.'"

Regarding the phrase "the non-occurrence of that" (*tad-atipattim*): due to the context, this is a compound ending in a dual number, meaning "the non-occurrence of those two," namely, the summoning and the overturning. Among these, the non-occurrence of the summoning of Kamalaka is understood from his departure for another country and so forth; and by that very non-occurrence, the non-occurrence of the overturning [of the cart] is also understood, due to the loading of a heavier burden upon the cart and so on. From this sentence, the non-occurrence of these two in the future time is understood, because one realizes: "Kamalaka cannot be summoned now, and that cart will surely be overturned as well."
And [the suffix *ṇini* is used] after a word denoting a living being (*bhūta*). 3.3.140.

"One who wanders seeking food" means one who, desiring to eat, walks in a crooked manner due to hunger. "And another twice-born man seeking a Brahmin"—the phrase "was seen wandering" is to be supplied here. "Seeking a Brahmin" means searching for someone to eat with him; he too walks in a crooked manner out of agitation. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "If," and so forth.

If it is read somewhere as *yadi dṛṣṭo 'bhaviṣyat*, that is because the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs when *yad* is the cause for the conditional mood according to the rule *yadāyadyor upasaṃkhyānam*; however, this is optional by the subsequent rule. Therefore, the reading *dṛṣṭaḥ* alone is appropriate, and not *bhuktavān*. This demonstrates the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*). The reason for this is stated: "He went by another path."
The suffix *ya* is applied after [a verbal root] ending in *vā* or *tāp*.

The phrase "vā ā utāpyoḥ" indicates the elision (praśleṣa) of the particle *ā*. In that context, because it is connected with the rule "utāpyoḥ," or because it is *antaraṅga* (internal) due to its dependence on fewer factors, the *guṇa* substitution occurs first with the following vowel. Then, by virtue of the preceding element being treated as if it were the final element of the preceding word (*antavadbhāva*), the *pararūpa* (single substitute of the form of the subsequent element) applies according to the rule "omāṅośca. For example: *ā-ūḍhā* becomes *oḍhā*; *adya oḍhā* becomes *adyoḍhā*; and *kadoḍhā*.

In this context, regarding the rule *atontāpyoḥ samarthayoḥ*, that which ends in the locative case is taken as the limit (*avadhi*). Since "an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is treated like its original (*prakṛti-vat*)," the imitation itself lacks the status of a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*) due to the prohibition [of suffixes] by the rule *anukaraṇam apratyayaḥ*. Consequently, even when joined with *āṅ*, there is no occurrence of the ablative case. The phrase *maryādāyām āṅ* is understood from the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): *vibhāṣā garhāprakṛtau prāgutāpibhyām*. Here, *garhāprakṛtau* means when the meaning of the root (*prakṛtyartha*) is qualified by censure (*garhā*).

The mention of *garhā* (censure) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other causes of the optative (*liṅ*), such as *anavaklṛpti* (impossibility) and so forth. Because there is an absence of the causes for the optative in the case of *katham*, the subsequent sūtra (*vibhāṣā kathaṃ liṅ ca*) is bypassed.
The suffix *laṭ* (the present tense marker) is also employed after the particles *api* and *jātu* when expressing censure (*garhā*).

"It does not apply to the general tense (*kālasāmānya*). By the word "is prescribed" (*vidhīyate*), [the author] indicates the exclusion of specific times such as the future (*bhaviṣyati*) and so forth, thereby showing that the prescription applies to time in general. As for the phrase "and those prescribed for specific times," etc., this is the conclusion in the *Bhāṣya*: "The prescription of the *laṭ* [present tense] in the sense of censure is purposeless, because the completion of the action is not intended to be expressed."

In this context, the reproach arises from the indication of habitual practice; consequently, whatever he performs is all for the purpose of officiating at sacrifices for a *vṛṣala*, and thus he is always engaged in officiating for a *vṛṣala*. Therefore, since the completion of the action is not intended to be expressed, the rule "the suffix *laṭ* is used in the sense of the present" (*vartamāne laṭ*) is established as sufficient.

"If this were so, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would also apply; yet we see both *śatṛ* and *śānac* used in such expressions as 'see me sacrificing' (*māṃ yājayantam paśya*) and 'see me performing the sacrifice' (*māṃ yājamānam paśya*). On the contrary, since the suffix *luṭ* is prescribed for the present time, those two [suffixes] would not apply when the rule is formulated; thus, the formulation of this rule is defective."
The *vibhāṣā* rule states: "And [the suffix] *liṅ* is used in the sense of 'how' (*katham*). (Pāṇini 3.3.143)

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *vibhāṣā*," etc.: the meaning is that this is for the purpose of ensuring that there is no sublation of those *laṅ* and other suffixes which are prescribed for their respective times. If this is so, since the *laṭ* will also occur by virtue of the very mention of *vibhāṣā*, what is the purpose of the particle *ca*? True; it is established for the present time, but it is not established for other times. Therefore, the particle *ca* serves to include the *laṭ* for that purpose. Here, the condition for the *liṅ* exists; how so? Because this [particle] also expresses censure (*garhā*).
The suffixes *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* are used after a word ending in the interrogative particle *kim* when it expresses a condition (*vṛtte*).

In the rule *kiṃvṛtte lipsāyām*, the term *kiṃvṛtta* has been explained. Here, one might object: "It should be stated that when a word ending in *kim* is present, the *lṛṭ* [future tense] occurs; by the force of the word *ca* (and), the previously mentioned *liṅ* will also apply. Thus, there is no need for the explicit mention of *liṅ*. To this, he replies: 'The mention of *liṅ*... The intention is as follows: by the word *ca*, there would be a conjunction of the *laṭ* as well, just as there was of the *liṅ*, because the *laṭ* is also part of the preceding context. Therefore, the mention of *liṅ* is for the purpose of excluding the *laṭ*."
The particle *na* is used with the sense of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) and "impatience" (*amarṣa*), even when it is not preceded by *kiṃ*. Pāṇini 3.3.145.

The inclusion of the term *api* could indeed be omitted. How so? Just as in the rule "after *upaka* and others, the suffix *anya-ra* is optionally used when not in a *dvandva*," the mention of "not in a *dvandva*" (*advandve*) is for the purpose of terminating the governing context of *dvandva*, so too here, the mention of "not being a *kiṃvṛtta*" (*akiṃvṛttagrahaṇam*) is for the purpose of terminating the governing context of *kiṃvṛtta*. When this [term *api*] is not present, two suffixes will occur both when there is a *kiṃvṛtta* and when there is not; it is included here for the sake of clarity.

Likewise, the inclusion of the term *akiṃvṛtta* ("not containing an interrogative pronoun") is also for the sake of clarity; since [the word] *kiṃvṛtte* is not svarita-accented, it does not carry over [into this rule], and thus both suffixes will apply without distinction. And it has been said: "Because there is no governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *kiṃvṛtta*, the mention of *akiṃvṛtta* in the subsequent rule is redundant. Now, by the mention of *akiṃvṛtta*, a word other than *kiṃvṛtta* is understood through the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); therefore, the mention of *akiṃvṛtta* would be for the purpose of stating that such a word shall receive the designation of *upapada*.

But what, then, is the purpose of the technical designation *upapada*? [Is it] for the sake of compound formation (*samāsa*)? No; because of the prohibition by the rule *atiṅ*. If that is so, then when the suffixes designated as *sat* are applied to *lṛṭ*, there should be compound formation. [Answer: These *sat*-designated suffixes do not apply to this *lṛṭ*. In the rule *laṭaḥ sad vā*, the *lṛṭ* is understood as that which is prescribed specifically under the heading "future" (*bhaviṣyat*).

Although this [present *lṛṭ*] occurs because it is prescribed for time in general, nevertheless, since it is not prescribed under the heading "future," the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes do not apply to it.
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after the particle *kiṃkila* when expressing matters that are possible or existent.

"The compound is the *upapada*. This is because the word *kim* alone cannot function [as a verb] in the senses of "impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) or "intolerance" (*amarṣa*). "An exception to *liṅ*" means it applies where *liṅ* would otherwise not have been obtained by the preceding rule. Regarding the phrase "there exists," etc.: the meaning is that there exists a sacrifice performed by you, O Vṛṣala. For it has been stated: "Verbs such as *pac* (to cook) become the agents of the action of *bhū* (to be)."
The optative suffix (liṅ) is used after the particle *jātu* when expressing possibility (*yadā*).

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *lṛṭ*" means that since both *liṅ* and *lṛṭ* would be applicable by the rule beginning with "anavaklṛpti" (*Pāṇini 3.3.145*), the purpose [of this rule] is so that only *liṅ* occurs and *lṛṭ* does not.
"The addition of *yadā* and *yadi*" means that, like the [original] sūtra, it is an exception to *lṛṭ*.
The suffix *yat* is applied after [the words] *yad* and *tad*. (Pāṇini 5.2.39)

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) specifically to *lṛṭ*. [This refers to] that which was previously applicable. The particle *eva* is for the sake of emphasis (*paunarvacanika*).
