"The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent [sūtra], there should be the recurrence of only *yac* and *yat*, so that it does not apply to *jātu* and *yad*. Here, there are two [meanings]: non-acceptance (*anavaklṛpti*) and impatience (*amarṣa*); and since there are exactly two words, *yac* and *yat*, as the governing terms (*upapada*), would there not then follow a correspondence by number (*yathāsaṅkhyam*)? To this he says: "Correspondence by number is not intended here," because of the deviation from the previous definition and because the word with more syllables is placed first.
And [the suffix *kha* is used] in the sense of reproach. (Pāṇini 3.3.149)

If he were poor, even performing sacrifices for *vṛṣala*s (outcasts) would be appropriate; therefore, it is said "prosperous" (*ṛddha*). Even for a prosperous man, [offering sacrifices] might be suspected due to an abundance of enjoyments; therefore, it is said "aged" (*vṛddha*). Even for an aged man who is a *brāhmaṇa* by birth alone, [such acts] might be appropriate; therefore, it is said "an excellent *brāhmaṇa*" (*sadbrāhmaṇa*). This means that one born of a noble lineage and possessing virtuous conduct is, by implication, unworthy of censure.
In the remaining cases, [the suffixes] *lṛ*, *ya*, and others [are applied]. 3.3.151.

Regarding the rule *yaccayatrābhyām*: the remainder (*śeṣa*) [of the sense] does not depend on wonder (*citrīkaraṇa*), because that [remainder] is here under the governing influence (*adhikāra*) by virtue of being marked with the *svarita* accent. For example: "It would be a marvel if he were to eat. Here, two things are understood: improbability (*anavaklṛpti*) and wonder (*āścarya*). In this case, since the *lṛṭ* (future) is prohibited when wonder is the cause, and since the *liṅ* (optative) is prescribed after *yad* and *yadi* when [improbability is meant], the *liṅ* occurs in the sense of improbability according to the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*): "The addition of *yad* and *yadi* [is made] for the sake of improbability."

In the *Bhāṣya*, however, it is stated: "The word *yadi* is employed in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*); therefore, the intended meaning here is possibility, not wonder (*citrikaraṇa*). Consequently, the phrase *ayadāu* need not be mentioned, for the optative (*liṅ*) is already covered by the rule *sambhāvane 'lam-iti-yoge ca*. As he says: "If [the word *yadi*] were used in the sense of wonder, the prohibition would be redundant because the meaning would be different."
The suffix *liṅ* is used after the particles *uta* and *api* when they express capability.

Regarding the phrase "of two [words] that are semantically compatible" (*samarthayoḥ*): in the sūtra, the word *sama* is either treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) resulting in the elision of the vowel *a* (as per the rule *ato lopaḥ*), or it takes the form of the subsequent vowel through the *śakandhvādi*-group. Alternatively, the word *saṃ* itself has the same meaning as *sama* in the commentary (*vṛtti*). This is the intended sense, as in the examples: "with *pra* and *upa* when they are semantically compatible" (*propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*), and "of one who is face-to-face" (*mukhasammukhasya*).

It is understood that [the particle *api*] signifies both a question (*praśna*) and concealment (*pracchādana*). In the first case, a question is understood; in the second, concealment. Now, one might object: the particle *api* is also seen in the sense of a question—as in "Even the foremost of the seers who composed the mantras" (*apyagraṇīrmantrakṛtṛmṛṣīṇām*) and "Is your mind also pleased with the deer? (*api prasannaṃ hariṇeṣu te manaḥ*). Therefore, since these two [uses] have the same meaning even in the case of a question, would it not be impossible to provide a counter-example such as "Will the staff fall? (*uta daṇḍaḥ patiṣyatīti*)? The [author] thinks as follows: in examples such as "even the foremost," the particle *api* depends upon another matter that is to be questioned.

The particle *api* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) alone, whereas the sense of a question is understood from the context and so forth; therefore, these two do not have the same meaning in the case of a question.
The particle *akaccit* is used in the sense of making a request regarding a desire.
"The disclosure of one's own intention is the expression of desire. He establishes this very point by elucidating the meaning of its constituent parts: "desire" means "wish."

"I ask you, O Mārāvida. One who utters the sound "mārāvi" is called *mārāvida*; that is to say, he should not make the sound "mārāvi. This is the name of a particular type of parrot, which someone holds in their hand and fondles. Pārvatī also has a certain beloved parrot. However, the reading is generally "I ask my mother and father," and the sentence beginning with that is: "I ask my mother and father. What is asked here? "Is your mother living?"
When expressing capability with respect to a possibility, the suffix *kṛt* is used after a verb even if the word *alam* is not employed. (Pāṇini 3.3.154)

"Ascertainment of fitness" (*yogyatādhyavasāna*) means the determination of fitness. He clarifies this very point with the words "belief in capacity" (*śaktiśraddhāna*). "Capacity" (*śakti*) means efficacy; that by which it is believed—that is, made an object of cognition—is what is thus described. By the phrase "by way of sufficiency for possibility," he indicates that the word *alaṃ* here has the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*), not in the sense of "ornamentation" (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth; hence he says: "If it is thus, [it is] possibility."

If one asks how the word *alam* can be construed with that which ends in the seventh case (the locative), and considering the objection that this particular qualification would thus be untenable, the author explains by means of a grammatical transformation (*vipariṇāma*): "And if that [expectation]... Here, both *sambhāvanam* and *alam* are repeated: "The *liṅ* suffix occurs when there is an expectation (*sambhāvana*), provided that such an expectation consists of the nature of *alam*. Thus, the connection is established through this final resolution; therefore, the word *iti* should not be connected here. Consequently, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "When *alam* is used in its established sense [of 'sufficiency']."

In this context, the word *cet* ("if") should not be connected [to the preceding]; for it is impossible to connect it with that which ends in a locative case. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, only the matter itself is shown—namely, "if it is established, enough with its non-employment"—but there is no syntactic connection of the word *cet* here. Regarding the term *paryāptam*: it means capable of accomplishing its own function. Its own function, moreover, is the determination of the object without error; he shows this by the word *avitatham* ("not false").

The falsity (*vaitathya*) of a cognition consists in its having as its object an entity that does not exist in that manner—as, for example, the cognition of silver with respect to mother-of-pearl. That which is the opposite of this is non-false (*avitatha*), meaning it has as its object an entity existing in that very manner. Regarding the phrase "conditioned by such a possibility" (*tadīdṛśasambhāvanopādhika*): the word *tat* is used to introduce the sentence; the three-word *bahuvrīhi* compound means "that whose limiting condition (*upādhi*) is a possibility characterized by such a specific object. However, in some places the reading is *īdṛśe sambhāvanopādhaka*, which is an uncompounded form; in that case, the term *īdṛśe* (locative singular) would not be consistent [with the rest of the construction].

Indeed, no form of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) has been previously demonstrated such that it could be described as being "of this kind. [The phrase] "an exception to all verbal suffixes" (*sarvalakārāṇām apavādaḥ*) means that since the act of imagining (*sambhāvana*) has the future as its object, it is an exception to all verbal suffixes whose objects are the future. For example: "He might even split a mountain with his head."

In this context, the capacity regarding the splitting of mountains which is imagined for a man exists indeed in someone such as Bhīmasena; since that imagination is not false, it serves as an illustration concerning that [capacity]. "One might even eat the cooking of Droṇa" (*api droṇapākaṃ bhuñjīta*): eating what has already been cooked is precisely "eating the cooking"; or else, the word *pāka* is derived in the sense of the object (*karman*). "A resident abroad" means one who has gone to another country. "He will likely go."

Having conjectured the arrival [of someone] from a fallacious sign such as the frequent twitching of one's own right eye, one then employs this [expression]; it may turn out to be true, or it may be the opposite. "Enough, Devadatta!"—the meaning is that he will be sufficiently struck. Because the conjecture concerns a future object, the *lṛṭ* suffix is cited as the counter-example in all cases.

Another explanation: *sambhāvanā* (possibility) is the imaginative projection (*utprekṣaṇa*) of a future thing; it is the cognition that "this must happen," provided there is no occurrence of a contrary cognition, as in the counter-example—"he will probably come. Its qualification is "if [it is] sufficient" (*alam iti cet*). The connection is made by changing the word order: "if it is sufficient, then that is possibility" (*alam iti cet tat sambhāvanam*).

In this regard, just as when it is said, "the cognition 'this is a jar'" or "the cognition 'this is a cloth'," the indication of the object of the cognition is understood, so too here, if it is argued that this is the indication of the object of the cognition called "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*), namely, "it is sufficient" (*alam*); the meaning is that if that possibility has the object-entity (*artha*) as its domain, then "sufficient" (*alam*) refers to adequacy (*paryāpti*) and not to ornamentation or the like. Furthermore, since the suffix is prescribed after a verbal root, the capacity (*sāmarthya*) is understood precisely as having that [root-meaning] as its sphere.

The meaning is that "possibility" (*sambhāvanā*) consists in the form: "this person is capable of performing this particular verbal root-meaning. In the case of the usage with a verb in the past tense (*siddhāprayoga*), the word *alam* occurs due to proximity [to that action]. Thus far is the interpretation of the words of the Sūtra. As for the Vṛtti, however—the determination of fitness regarding actions—that is the definition of "possibility" (*sambhāvana*) intended here in the Sūtra, and not mere possibility (*sambhavana*) in general.

Otherwise, the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) would be untenable, for in that case, the apprehension of capacity (*śakti*) is not understood. But how is such a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) grasped here? To this, he says: "Now, that... This means that indeed, at the time of composing this sūtra, there was such a possibility regarding this sūtra. If it is asked whether the word *alam* is qualified by its object (*viṣaya*), [the answer is: if *alam* signifies possibility, it means sufficiency (*paryāpti*). Sufficiency is the meaning of *alam*, not ornamentation (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth.

He demonstrates the logical sequence through transformation: "If that [be] a possibility (*sambhāvanā*). It is called "adequate" (*paryāpta*) because it is the object of adequacy; it is called "non-false" (*avitatha*) because its object is not untrue. The meaning is: if there is a possibility characterized by the thought, "He is capable of performing this verbal root-meaning; this undertaking, though potentially false, is directed toward this verbal root-meaning. For example: "He might even split a mountain with his head. This means, "He is indeed so powerful," whether he actually splits the mountain or not.
The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies when expressing possibility (*sambhāvana*) within the context of a verbal root (*dhātu*), provided that the particle *yad* is not present.
"I imagine that you will eat" means "I conjecture that you are capable of eating."
The conditional (liṅ) suffix is used to express the cause and that which arises from the cause. Pāṇini 3.3.156.

"And there will be a time"—the word "is intended" (*iṣyate*) is to be understood [as the ellipsis]. But how is this pair [of meanings] obtained even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra? To this he says: "In that case," meaning "while *liṅ* [is] present. This refers to the rule beginning with "utāpyoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.152). "He strikes, therefore he flees": here, striking is the cause (*hetu*), and fleeing is the effect (*hetumat*). "It rains, therefore it flows": here, raining is the cause, and flowing is the effect. In the word "fleeing" (*palāyate*), the substitution of *l* for *y* occurs by the rule "upasargasyāyatau" (Pāṇini 8.2.19).

In this case, the substitution of the suffix *śatṛ* (as in *kurvan*) by rule Pāṇini 3.2.126 (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*) does not occur either, because the provision for the suffix *sat* (i.e., *śatṛ*) when used with the root *han* is listed among the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionals).
The suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used in the sense of desire.

"It should be stated as 'in the expression of a wish' (kāmapravedane). [Objection: Then what is the purpose of this rule, "in the expression of a wish, after the word *kaccit*," since [the desired result] is already established by this very rule even in cases such as "I wish that you would eat" (*kāmo me bhuñjīta bhavān*) or "I desire that you would eat" (*abhilāṣo me bhuñjīta bhavān*)? [Response: It is so that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) may also occur in cases where there is no accompanying word expressing the sense of "wish," but where the expression of a wish is understood through the context of the meaning or other factors.

What, then, is the purpose of this? It is for the sake of *loṭ*; however, the mention of *liṅ* is so that there may be no sublation by *loṭ*. Even so, since one could simply say "and *leṭ*," what is the point of mentioning *liṅ*? The previously mentioned mention of *liṅ* is connected with the option (*vibhāṣā*); therefore, if it were drawn forward [into the present rule], it would be possible that the mention of *vibhāṣā* would also be drawn forward.
The suffix *tumun* is used when the agents of the two actions are the same. (Pāṇini 3.3.158)

Regarding the phrase *tumunprakṛtyapekṣam*: if the agent who is the basis of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) of the suffix *tumun* is also the agent in the case of roots meaning "desire," this is understood from the immediate proximity [of the rule]. For example, in *icchati bhoktum* ("he wishes to eat"), the meaning is "he desires eating for himself. Since the very same person who is the agent of the root *iṣ* ("to desire") is also the agent of the root *bhuj* ("to eat"), there is here a commonality of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). However, because the purposefulness (*tādarthya*) of the act of eating toward the desire is not perceived, the suffix *tumun* is not established by the rule *tumunṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10); therefore, this [present rule] is commenced.

Even if, for some reason, there were a need for that [suffix], this present undertaking is intended with the thought: "I shall state [the rule] as *samānakartṛkeṣu* (when the agents are the same). Therefore, in the case of *devadattena bhoktumicchati yajñadattaḥ* ("Devadatta desires to eat by means of Devadatta"), it does not occur. Regarding *icchan karoti* ("desiring, he acts"), the meaning is that in this sense, *icchan kartum* does not occur. In examples such as *icchan kartuṃ gacchati* ("desiring to act, he goes"), the suffix *tumun* is applied by the rule *tumunṇvulau*.

But surely the suffix *tumun* is prescribed when an action (*bhāva*) is to be expressed; so how can there be the possibility [of its application] to the agent (*kartṛ*) in the case of "he does desiring" (*icchankaroti*)? Even so, because of the possibility [of its application] in the case of "it is done by one who desires" (*icchatā kriyate*), one must simply resort to the principle of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
And [the suffix] liṅ [is used]. 3.3.159.

For what purpose is this stated? So that the *liṅ* [optative] may occur. Is not the *liṅ* already established here by the rule "the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [imperative] occur after verbs meaning 'desire'" (*icchārtheṣu liṅloṭau*)? That [rule] would be superseded by the rule for the *tumun* suffix when the agents are the same (*samānakartṛkeṣu*). Furthermore, the rule for alternative forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) is prohibited in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and *khal* suffixes; therefore, just as the *loṭ* would not occur there, the *liṅ* likewise would not occur. Even if the rule for alternative forms were to apply, this [present rule] must still be commenced so that only the *liṅ* occurs and the *loṭ* does not.
After verbal roots expressing desire, the suffixes of the present tense are optionally used.

Regarding the word *aśyāt*: the root *vaś* (meaning "to desire") belongs to the second class (*adādi*); the semivowel is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule governing roots beginning with *grah*.
The potential suffix (liṅ) is used in the senses of injunction, invitation, permission, request, inquiry, and entreaty. Pāṇini 3.3.161.

*Vidhi* (injunction) means impelling. It signifies the commanding of a subordinate person, such as a servant, to engage in a certain action. *Nimantraṇa* (invitation) is that performance or undertaking which occurs by necessity (*niyogataḥ*), meaning with certainty; this is the object of an invitation. That is to say, it is the impelling of a grandson (*dauhitr*) or similar relative toward a necessary duty, such as eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony; for a grandson invited to a *śrāddha* incurs sin if he does not eat. *Kāmacāra-karaṇa* (acting according to one's own will) means...

*Āmantraṇa* (invitation) is the performance or execution of an action through *kāmacāra*, which is activity according to one's own desire; the meaning is that it is an invitation regarding such a matter. That is to say, it is an instigation to act in cases where there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) even if the action is not performed. For instance, one who is invited to a festive meal (*kalyāṇa*) and does not eat does not incur sin. Regarding *adhīṣṭa* (authorization): the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) from the root *iṣ* preceded by the prefix *adhi*. A masculine reading is incorrect. It refers to an activity preceded by respect (*satkāra*).

The meaning is "by the instigation of one worthy of honor, such as a guru," [the suffix] *ac* being added to the causative form (*ṇyanta*). "Deliberation" (*sampradhāraṇa*) is the investigation consisting of thoughts such as, "This should be done, or that should be done. Just as it is well known that "this is deliberated upon here" constitutes a request (*yācñā*).

Furthermore, for the purpose of explaining the system (*nyāya*), and also for the sake of elaboration, the four [categories] beginning with injunction (*vidhi*) have been presented in their proper order.
There exists a form of instigation permeating all four [means of knowledge];
it is precisely there that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) should be employed—what is the use of intending to express a distinction?

There are four positions regarding this: whether the injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth constitute the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), a qualifier of the meaning of the base, or a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. Among these, according to the first position, the meaning would be "from a verbal root occurring in the sense of an injunction and so forth. Consequently, it would apply only where the base itself expresses the injunction and so forth—namely, in cases such as *vidadhyāt* (he should command), *nimantrayeta* (he should invite), *āmantrayeta* (he should address), *adhīcchet* (he should desire), *saṃpracchet* (he should inquire), and *prārthayet* (he should request).

In that case as well, it would be understood only that the meanings of the verbal root consist of the abstract action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*); nothing else, such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, would be understood apart from the meaning of the verbal root. This is just as, for example, after roots expressing desire, when the optative (*liṅ*) occurs according to the rule "optionally in the present tense" (*vibhāṣā vartamāne*), forms such as *icchet* (optative) and *icchati* (present indicative) and so forth do not occur; because they are sublated by this optative suffix.

In the second alternative, if the meanings such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth were indicated while the factors of state (*bhāva*), object (*karman*), and agent (*kartṛ*) have not yet been attained, they would act as sublaters (*bādhaka*) of those [latter factors]; consequently, there would be no denotation of the agent and so forth by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and the occurrence of dual and plural endings would be untenable because injunctions and the like are singular in nature. In the third alternative, however, where the verbal root itself expresses the injunction and so forth, it would not occur—such as in "one should enjoin" (*vidadhyāt*) or "one should invite" (*nimantrayet*); for in these cases, there are no injunctions and the like distinct from the meaning of the root that could serve as qualifiers of it.

In the fourth [case], however, the distinction between the injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, as well as the agents (*kartṛ*) and so forth, is indeed manifest; thus, there being no fault, he relies on that very point, stating: "And these are the injunctions and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in those qualified by injunctions and so forth" (*vidhyādiviśiṣṭeṣu*): injunctions and so forth are specific types of instigation (*pravartanā*); the meaning is "in those instigated, being qualified by those [instigations]. As for the cases of inquiry (*sampraśna*) and request (*prārthanā*), they apply to the agent who is being questioned or who is being requested.

But surely, according to the principle that "that which has already been expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) need not be expressed again," the suffix (*pratyaya*) should apply only where the meaning is not already denoted by the root, and not where it is already denoted by the root. Consequently, even in this view, the same undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) would persist in cases such as *vidadhyāt* ("one should perform")? If this is so, then indeed there exist here distinct [meanings] such as injunction (*vidhi*) and the rest, due to the difference in their objects (*viṣayabheda*). To illustrate: in the sentence *śrāddhe māṃ nimantrayeta bhavān* ("May you invite me to the funeral feast"), the meaning is that "an invitation having me as its object must be performed by you."

In this regard, the invitation expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) concerns the act of eating, whereas that expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) concerns the invitation itself; thus, the distinction between the two types of invitation is quite clear. Just as in the expression *eṣitum icchati* ("he wishes to wish to go"), there is a grammatical connection based on the distinction between the two instances of "wishing" due to differences in time and the means of accomplishment, so it is here. The same should be understood for injunctions (*vidhi*) and other such cases. And having established this, even in the view where the meaning of the root is qualified [by the suffix], there is no great fault. For example, in the case of an invitation: *iha bhavān bhuñjīta* ("May you, sir, eat here"), the meaning is "if he wishes."

"Adhyeṣyāmahe" is a corrupt reading; for this form is not possible from the root √iṣ (to desire), as √iṣ also takes the *parasmaipada* ending, and the *guṇa* substitution is difficult to obtain in the *śyan* affix. Furthermore, the meaning of √iṅ (to study) is not applicable here, and √iṅ is not employed in the sūtra where "adhi-iṣṭa" occurs. Therefore, the correct reading is "adhīcchāmaḥ. Regarding "upanayet," the *ātmanepada* ending is used in the sense of "acting as a teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇa*).
And the imperative (loṭ) [is used in these senses]. 3.3.162.

"The division of the *yoga* is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent rule, only the *loṭ* suffix should continue to apply, so that the *liṅ* suffix does not. Regarding *adhyayai*: there is the augment *iṭ*; this is the first person singular; the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* ending; by "eta ai," *ai* replaces *e*; by "āhuttamasya picca," the augment *āṭ* is added; by "āṭaśca," there is *vṛddhi*; and then the *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* substitutions apply to the base.
The *kṛtya* suffixes are also used in the senses of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*).
Regarding the word *kṛtya*: the suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ*. The ellipsis of the sentence, such as "for you have been sent," should be supplied in all the examples.

"Not in a general sense" means that the mention of "bhāva" (state/being) and "karman" (object) is merely illustrative; for [the suffixes] *bhavya*, *geya*, and so forth, occur even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended. If this were so, one might think it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). However, this is not for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) such as "kṛtya suffixes occur only in the sense of commands (*praiṣa*) and the like, and not elsewhere," because such a restriction is undesired. Kṛtya suffixes are indeed seen elsewhere—for instance, in *tṛṇena śoṣyam* ("it is to be dried by grass") and *budhena bodhyam* ("it is to be awakened by a wise man"), or *agnistokaṃ tṛṇena dīpanīyaḥ* ("the fire is to be kindled slightly with grass"). These are merely statements of the nature of things (*vastusvarūpakathana*), and there is no perception of a command or similar sense in these cases.

"Beyond the governing rule (*adhikāra*). In connection with the suffix *enap*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) must be sought. "Not necessarily" means that it occurs in some instances, but not in others.

"What is the distinction?"—since it was explained previously that *vidhi* (injunction) is *preraṇā* (impulsion), the question is raised that there is no difference at all. If there is no difference, one might ask, "How then is there a dual designation (*dvandva-nirdeśa*)? [The answer is: because the form of the word itself is the denotable object (*abhidheya*). The meaning of "What is the distinction? is: what is the specific denotable object of these two words? By the phrase "some say" (*kecit*), it should be understood that a distinction also exists between *āmantraṇa* (addressing) and *atisarga* (permission). By the use of the word "some," it is implied that others do not accept a distinction between these two.

For them as well, the inclusion of *praiṣa* (command) and *atisarga* (permission) must indeed be made, so that the *kṛtya* suffixes may apply in those very cases. For if it were stated simply as "and in the sense of the time being appropriate (*prāptakāle*)," the *kṛtya* suffixes would also apply to *nimantraṇa* (invitation) and so forth. By means of the particle *ca*, the *loṭ* suffix should also be drawn in—so that [the suffixes] may apply in the sense of the time being appropriate.
The suffix *liṅ* is used [after a root] when the action is to occur after a period exceeding one muhūrta. Pāṇini 3.3.164.
The word "and" (ca) implies "as it occurs," namely, the imperative (loṭ) and the gerundive suffixes (kṛtya).
The suffix *loṭ* [is used] in the sense of *sme*. (Pāṇini 3.3.165)

"An exception to the *liṅ* [optative] suffixes": this refers to those [suffixes] obtained by the immediately preceding rule. Regarding "karotu sma": the word *sma* indicates a governing context (*adhikāra*), meaning "you are the one authorized here."
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a verb meaning "to authorize. (Pāṇini 3.3.166)

"O King, indeed!"—the word *aṅga* is used here as a term of conciliation. The meaning is that teaching Brahmins alone is one's livelihood; therefore, "O King" is used to show him respect (*abhyarhita*).
The suffix *tumun* is used after verbal roots when expressing time, occasion, or specific junctures.

The phrase "the inclusion of *praiṣa* and so forth" is connected [to the previous discussion]. The sense is that *praiṣa* (commands) and the like are not understood here. [The question] "Why here? refers to the time for eating. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is "May you eat," and thus the question arises: "Is a command (*praiṣa*) understood here? [The response is] "By the rule of *vāsarūpa*. But surely, since the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed for commands and the like, and it has been indicated that the *vāsarūpa* rule does not apply after the section on feminine formations? To this he says: "It has been stated."

The meaning is that only impermanence (*anityatva*) is indicated therein, not total non-existence (*sarvathābhāva*). The inclusion of a synonym (*paryāya*) is for the purpose of excluding other synonyms. Others, however, say: "The suffix *tumun* is also seen in expressions such as *avasaro bhoktum* (it is time to eat); in the rule *vyupayoḥ śeteḥ*, the commentator (*vṛttikāra*) employed the expression *rājānam upaśayituṃ paryāyaḥ* (it is the turn to lie near the king). Therefore, the inclusion of the synonym is for the sake of capturing the general sense (*arthagrahaṇa*), just as in the rule *nimittakāraṇahetuṣu*."
The suffix *liṅ* [is used] when [the word] *yadi* [occurs]. 3.3.168.

"An exception to *tumun*": although the suffix *liṅ* has its own scope of application regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), it is an exception to *tumun* used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), because it is both more specific (by being a *pratipadavidhi*) and subsequent [in the order of rules]. This is the meaning.
The kṛtya suffixes and the tṛc suffix are also used after a verbal root when it denotes one who is worthy (arha).

"Arhati" means "one who deserves" (*arha*). [The suffix] *ac* is added according to the rule *pacādyac*. "One who is worthy of that"—by the word "that" (*tat*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is referred to. Regarding the phrase "when the agent is understood as one who deserves": it is stated as "understood" (*gamyamāna*) in order to accommodate both cases—where [the sense of deserving] is expressed (*vācya*) and where it is merely implied (*gamyamāna*). There is also a reading "whether expressed or implied," in which case the connection is "according to what is possible. In that regard, the suffix *tṛc* occurs in words such as *ajarya* and *akupya*, while the *kṛtya* suffixes occur when [the sense of deserving] is expressed.

The suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of "fit to be" (*bhavya*), "to be sung" (*geya*), and so forth; and the *kṛtya* suffixes occur in both senses. Now, why is the plural used in the rule *kṛtyatṛcau* with the intention of expressing a distinction between types of *kṛtyas*, while here the dual is used with the intention of expressing the general category? In some instances, however, even in the commentary (*vṛtti*), the plural alone is read. This is so that there might be no sublation [of the general rule]. And it was stated immediately after that the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not necessarily apply in every case.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root to form a word expressing necessity (*āvaśyaka*) or debt (*adhamarṇya*).

"Avāśyakam" means "that which must necessarily happen. The suffix *vuñ* is applied because [the word *avaśya*] belongs to the *manojñādi* group; for indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* portion when any case-ending (*bh*) follows. The term "condition" (*upādhi*) means a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. It is not an "immediate constituent" (*upapada*), because of the specific grammatical indications in the rules: "after *śīta* and *uṣṇa*, [the suffix *ṇini* is used] in the sense of one who performs," and "also after words ending in *senā*, and after *lakṣaṇa* and *kārin*. For if it were an immediate constituent (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇini* alone would not occur; by association with that [rule], even the state of being a debtor (*ādhamarṇya*) is merely a condition and not an immediate constituent. Thus, in the example "one who gives a hundred" (*śataṃ dāyī*), the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "the genitive is not used after a word ending in *aka* or *in* when expressing future time or debt," so only the accusative case occurs.
And [the suffix] Kṛtya [is applied after verbal roots]. 3.3.171.

"Bhavya-geya-ādayaḥ kartṛ-vācakāḥ kṛtyāḥ" means that among the *bhavya-geya* group and others, the *kṛtya* suffixes stand as constituent parts (*avayavatvena*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is not only the inclusion of those specifically mentioned in the *bhavya-geya* sūtra; rather, there is also the inclusion of *ajarya*, *rucya*, *kupya*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, *avyathya*, *avyadhya*, and so forth. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of subsequent purposes.
The suffixes *śaki* and *liṅ* [are used] also [to express capability]. 3.3.172.

"It is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)," [it is said]. It is not an *upapada*, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "the forms *kṣayya* and *jayya* are used in the sense of 'capable'. For if they were *upapadas*, the forms *kṣayya* and *jayya* alone would not be possible in the sense of "capable. The ellipsis of the sentence "you are indeed capable" is to be supplied in all cases, so that there may be no sublation by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). There is a suspicion of sublation by the optative because the rule regarding non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) after a feminine suffix is not universal. In the rule "the root *ji* [takes *kṛt* suffixes] after *para-* and *asah-*," the meaning of *asah-* is "that which cannot be endured"—i.e., that which is not capable of being endured.

The suffix *kta* is explained here in the sense of possibility (*śakya*); it may be justified either by the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* ("the kṛtya suffixes and *lyuṭ* are used diversely") or by the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*).
The suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*).

The term *āśīrviśiṣṭa* means "that which is being wished for. The mention of *āśis* (benediction) was not made in the very first sūtra [Pāṇini 3.3.161], *vidhyādi*, so that this rule might also apply in cases such as *sme loṭ* [3.3.165], since that [latter] rule is subsequent. Furthermore, the mention of *āśis* must necessarily be included here for the sake of what follows.
And [the suffix *kyaṅ*] is applied after verbal roots ending in *ktic* or *kta*, when a name is being formed.

Regarding *tanti*: by the rule "anudāttopadeśa... (*Pāṇini 6.4.37*), the elision of the nasal would apply, and by "anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti" (*Pāṇini 6.4.15*), lengthening would also apply; yet neither of these two occurs, because of the prohibition "na ktici dīrghaśca" (*Pāṇini 6.4.39*). Regarding *sāti*: when *san* takes *ktic*, there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule "lopaścāsyānyatarasyām" (*Pāṇini 6.4.45*). The *c* in *ktic* has a purpose that must be considered; for in the rule "na ktici dīrghaśca," the exclusion of *ktin* is already established by the *ekānubandhaka-paribhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning monosematic suffixes).
And *laṅ* [is used] after *smi* when it expresses censure. (Pāṇini 3.3.175)

In this context, the word *uttara* signifies "subsequent" (*ādikya*) and not "direction" (*dig*); therefore, it applies even when the particle *sma* occurs earlier. This has been demonstrated by the phrase "accompanied by the word *sma*."
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the third chapter: *Padasañjari*—“Affixes [occur] when there is a connection with a verbal root. (3.4.1)

Since two verbal roots (*dhātu*) occupied with expressing their own respective meanings cannot have a mutual relationship during their application (*prayoga*), the word *dātu* here functions only figuratively (*upacaritavṛtti*). Thus he says: "The word *dhātu* [is used] in the sense of the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*). The connection between the meanings of the roots is "root-connection" (*dhātusambandha*). The intention is that because a connection has multiple loci, even when it occurs as a single unit (*vṛtti*), a specific number is understood. Furthermore, the plural form is used in view of all possible instances.

However, when each [suffix] is intended to be expressed individually, it should be understood that the relationship pertains to the meanings of the two verbal roots. If, on the other hand, one were to maintain that the relationship between the two roots—mediated through their meanings—is a qualifier of the suffixes (just as "objecthood" and "having the same agent" are qualifiers of the suffix), then this would not apply in cases such as *gomān āsīt* ("he was rich in cows") or *gomān bhavitā* ("he will be rich in cows"). For a relationship exists only when two [verbal roots] are actually employed together, and in these instances, the root *as* ("to be") is not employed in the present tense.

But what kind of relationship between the *dhātu* (verbal root) and [the suffix] is this? He says: "The relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*). In that regard, the meaning expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is the qualified, because the sentence has that as its primary focus; whereas the meaning expressed by a nominal suffix (*subanta*) is the qualifier, because a case-role (*kāraka*) is subordinate with respect to the action (*kriyā*). "Even when uttered at an incorrect time" means: even when employed at a time other than that for which they were prescribed.

By this, he demonstrates that here there is a sublation (*bādha*) of time alone, but not of the meanings of the upapada, the adhi, the prakṛti, or the pratyaya. And this is understood from the fact that, beginning with the rule "vartamānasāmīpye" (Pāṇini 3.3.131), there is generally an exposition of the difference in time. "Agniṣṭomayājī" refers to past time; it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose time is past. By this, the case of future time is also explained. "Therein" means between those two.

The word "agniṣṭomayājī" (one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice), being in the past tense, becomes grammatically correct when connected with the future tense word "janitā" (will be born). The meaning is that this [past tense] word also becomes correct while remaining in the future tense. Alternatively, it means that even by itself, when connected with the future tense, it abandons its own time and becomes future.

For this is the meaning here: "He is his son, and he shall sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma. In that case, if the suffix -ṇini were restricted solely to the past tense, then the understanding of the sacrifice as being in the future would not be possible; thus, this [present] undertaking is begun. This should be understood in the same way for the other two examples as well.

Now, why does the reverse not occur—that is, why is it not the case that the future time, being connected with the past time, abandons its own time and becomes valid in the past, so that the meaning of the sentence would be: "A son has been born to one who performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice"? To this he replies: "The qualifier [is subordinate] because of its quality-status.

A quality follows the principal; the principal does not follow the quality. Since a connection between two things each fixed in its own time is untenable, the meaning is that the quality abandons its time in accordance with the principal.

Regarding the phrase "the section on suffixes" (*pratyayādhikāra*): although the word *pratyaya* (suffix) currently under discussion has its own form as its referent (*svarūpapadārthaka*), nevertheless, because it is mentioned here by way of its technical name (*saṃjñā*), the intention is that it should be understood as referring to the thing named (*saṃjñipadārthaka*). The phrase "even those prescribed outside the section on verbal roots" (*adhātvadhikāravihitā api*) is used because otherwise there would be a reference only to the verbal roots and suffixes currently under discussion. However, since the mention of "suffix" (*pratyayagrahaṇa*) is intended to include all [suffixes], even *taddhita* suffixes remain grammatically correct even at other times [not immediately following the base]. For example: *gomān āsīt* ("he was rich in cows") and *gomān bhavitā* ("he will be rich in cows").

The possessive suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of "this belongs to him" or "it is in this," denoting an object qualified by the meaning of the base noun as characterized by present existence. However, when there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātusambandha*), it remains grammatically correct even if the meaning of the base noun pertains to the past or the future. Consequently, the meaning here is as follows: "He had cows, thus he was 'possessed of cows' (*gomān āsīt*)," and "He will have cows, thus he will be 'possessed of cows' (*gomān bhavitā*)."

Since the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is already established by the governing context of "roots," the repeated mention of "root" is for the purpose of specifying a particular type of root. Therefore, some maintain that when *as*, *bhū*, and *jan* are involved, only their specific qualifiers attain correctness through a change in tense. However, this position has not been established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the *Bhāṣya*; therefore, others hold that it occurs without such distinction.

Furthermore, this [distinction] based on the difference in time is observed elsewhere as well: in the verse, "Those roaring incessantly upon the earth with pride, who shall inundate everything on all sides," the word *nadantaḥ* (roaring) refers to the present time, while its connection with *plāvayiṣyanti* (shall inundate), which refers to a non-present time, results in it being understood as the future time.

As for the rejection of this rule (*sūtra-pratyākhyāna*): in the case of *agniṣṭomayājī*, the suffix *ṇini* denotes one who has already performed the sacrifice (*bhūta*); however, due to its connection with the word *janita* ("about to be born"), there is merely a cognition of the future state of the designation, just as in the expression "weave a cloth for him" (*asya sūtrasya śāṭakaṃ vaya*). Consequently, because of the cognition of a future designation, the difference in time of the qualifier will be understood on the strength of the sentence-meaning, even in the absence of the formulation of this rule.

Furthermore, the application of temporal suffixes must necessarily be accepted as occurring only at their own respective times; otherwise, in the case of the expression *bhāvikṛtyam āsīt* ("the future task was [in the past]"), since the word *bhāvi* (future) would possess a past tense, the words *bhāvi* and *āsīt* would become synonyms, and their simultaneous usage would be impossible. Therefore, its meaning there is simply "it existed now. In the case of *gomān āsīt* ("he possessed cows"), although Devadatta exists in the present, the past suffix is used because the state of possessing cows (*gomat-rūpa*) has passed.

There, by implication, the pastness of the cows themselves is understood; however, the word *gomān* by its own power expresses the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) as qualified precisely by present existence.
The *loṭ* suffix is used to express the repetition of an action; after this *loṭ*, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* may optionally take the place of *ta* and *dhvam*.

"The connection with the verbal root (*dhātu-sambandha*) is understood [from the previous rule]. This means there is a connection with the verb used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). However, this passage is not read in some versions. Furthermore, the statement "this is a qualifier of the meaning of the base form (*prakṛtyartha-viśeṣaṇa*)" serves to dispel the suspicion that it might be a subordinate word (*upapada*). Moreover, the absence of its status as a subordinate word follows from the explanation itself. The phrase "because it denotes an action qualified by repetition" (*samabhihāra-viśiṣṭa-kriyāvacanāt*) is stated because a verbal root cannot function with respect to mere repetition, which is a property of the action.

In this context, if by the rule "for *loṭ*, *hi* and *sva*" (*loṭo hisvau*), only those [suffixes] belonging to *loṭ* itself were to become *hi* and *sva*, then there would be an annulment of the *tiṅ* suffixes prescribed in general by *hi* and *sva*, just as there is an annulment by *śatṛ* and *śānac*. Consequently, since *tad* and *dhvam*—which are substitutes for *loṭ*—would not exist, their mention as substitutes in the rule "and optionally for *tad* and *dhvam*" (*vā ca tadhvamoḥ*) would be untenable. Therefore, it is understood that the word *loṭ* here includes its substitutes.

Let it be so; what is the fault? For here, because the *hi* substituted in place of *tips*, *sip*, and *mip* would—by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like its original)—be considered *pit* (having a *p* as an indicatory letter), it would lack *ṅittva* (the property of having a *ṅ* as an indicatory letter). Consequently, in *lunīhi*, the substitution for *ītvam* would not occur; in *brūhi*, the rule *bruva īṭ* would apply; in *tṛṇḍhi*, the rule *tṛṇaha im* would apply; and the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatvam*) of *hi* would also result. This is not a fault.

In the case of the rule *serhyapicca*, a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) will be made. By virtue of that, the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes" is not relied upon; thus, *hi* is substituted for *si*, and *apit* is also applied, meaning that whatever is called a substitute for *hi* is included. If that is so, then for the two substitutes *hi* and *sva* used in the first person, the augment *taṅ* would apply—such as in *lunīhi lunīhi evāhaṃ lunāmi* ("I cut, indeed, while you two cut") or *adhīṣva adhīdhvam evāham adhīye* ("I study, indeed, while you two study")? This is not a fault.

Once *āṭ* has been applied, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* will occur, because a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) fulfills its purpose through a single application. However, *āṭ* will not occur again after *hi* and *sva* have been substituted. For in this case, when there is a conflict between the two options—"let *āṭ* be applied" or "let *hi* and *sva* be substituted"—since both are non-obligatory (*anitya*), the rule "a rule that applies to a different word-form is non-obligatory" dictates that *āṭ* occurs first due to its higher priority; thus, once *āṭ* has been applied, the desired result—that *hi* and *sva* are substituted for the form including *āṭ*—is established.

Even so, by means of this *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), although there is an absence of *pit*-ness [for the suffixes], because the substitutes *hi* and *sva* themselves possess *pit*-ness, the elision of the vowel *a* prescribed by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* would not apply in cases such as *bhuṅkṣva bhuṅkṣva evāhaṃ bhuñje*, nor would the augment *īṭ* prescribed by *bruva īṭ* apply in *brūṣva brūṣva evāhaṃ bruve*. Furthermore, both *hi* and *sva* would apply alternately to all *tiṅ* suffixes, as there is no restrictive rule stating that "only *hi* applies to *parasmaipada* suffixes and *sva* to the others."

Therefore, considering that this position is indeed faulty, he demonstrates that the substitutes *hi* and *sva* must be understood as belonging to the *l*-suffix itself; hence the phrase "of that [suffix], namely the *loṭ*. Now, it was argued that in this view the rule "and optionally for *ta* and *dhvam*" (*vā ca tadhvamoḥ*) would be untenable; to this he replies: "But it optionally occurs for that which is about to become *ta* and *dhvam*. The meaning is that, since the primary sense is impossible, the *loṭ* suffix itself—which is about to become *ta* and *dhvam*—is spoken of in that way.

If, then, the substitutes *hi* and *sva* belong only to the imperative (*loṭ*) itself and not to its substitutes, then by the rule "the *la*-suffixes are the *parasmaipada*," both would receive the designation *parasmaipada*. Consequently, both would occur only after roots that are inherently *parasmaipada*. Furthermore, because they would not be situated within *tiṅ* suffixes, a form ending in them would not be considered a *tiṅanta* (a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix); consequently, the rule "a *tiṅ* is unaccented after another *tiṅ*" would not apply, and the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) would not be obtained.

Since these two *hi* and *sva* are treated as having the status of suffixes (*pratyaya*), and since only that which ends in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) or a future participle suffix (*śānac*) possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the addition of case endings (*svādi*) would necessarily follow. In that case, because these two—*hi* and *sva*—resemble case endings (*vibhakti*), they would receive the designation of "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) by the rules "those that resemble case endings are particles (*nipāta*)" and "a particle is an indeclinable. Consequently, although the case endings themselves are not heard [as distinct sounds], the rule "a verb ending in *tiṅ* is unaccented after an item that is not *tiṅ*" (*tiṅ-ṅatiṅ*) would necessitate the application of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent to what follows them. Furthermore, both would apply only to the agent (*kartṛ*), and not otherwise.

But [if it were so], the substitution would apply to the *bhāva*, the *karman*, and the *kartṛ*. Therefore, this position is also indeed faulty; regarding that, he says: "only *loṭ*. By this, he shows the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *loṭ* ending in the nominative case in connection with the second [word]. And there, by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), *hi* and *sva* are qualified by this term "*loṭ*," not by a transformation into the genitive; nor do *hi* and *sva* become *loṭ* endings.

And this is stated [in Pāṇini’s sūtra]: "For *hi* and *sva* are substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*). From this, an extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) is understood; thus he says: "The meaning is that those two possess the properties of the imperative. Here, by the word *loṭ*, the *hi* and *sva* substitutes related to the imperative are meant, because it is impossible for the actual properties of the primary imperative to be extended. Therefore, the meaning is: "those two which are the well-known *hi* and *sva* related to the imperative—prescribed by the rules *serhyapicca* and *savābhyāṃ vāmau*—possess those properties."

What is established? He shows that with the words "by that" (*tena*). For the status of *parasmaipada* (active voice) and *ātmanepada* (middle voice) is established as distinct between those two: *hi* has the status of *parasmaipada*, while *sva* has the status of *ātmanepada*. Therefore, by the extension of those properties (*dharmātideśa*), here too both of them are established as distinct; the meaning is that they will exist as distinct. And the status of *tiṅ* (verbal suffix) also occurs. And thus: for *hi*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is to be expressed; but for the word *sva*, however, the agent, the object (*karman*), and the state (*bhāva*) are to be expressed.

However, because of the force of the specific injunction, the singular number and the masculine gender do not apply [to the *loṭ* suffix]. For if those two were also to apply, the prescription of *hi* and *sva* by this rule would be untenable, since such forms are already established by another rule. Examples include *lunīhi lunīhi*, etc. The meaning is "he performs the act of cutting repeatedly," and so forth. In that case, the word ending in *loṭ* expresses the repeated cutting, while the verb used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)—by expressing the action directed toward that [cutting]—makes it manifest, though its specific means (*sādhana*) and so on remain somewhat indistinct.

And thus, because there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified between the general and the particular, the connection with the verbal root (*dhātu*) is established; this is the purpose of the two words *eva*. The two words ending in the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) serve the purpose of expressing the connection. However, the words *ayam*, *tvam*, and *aham* are the causes for manifesting the specific person. Now, as for the word *atha vā*: he demonstrates the result of the rule "vā ca tadhvamoḥ."

Regarding *alāvīt*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] before *sic*, the augment *iṭ* for *sic*, and for *tip* there is *iṭ* by the rule "for *asti* and *sic* before an *apṛkta* suffix. Then, by the rule "the elision of *sic* occurs before *īṭ*," there is the elision of *sic*. Regarding the elision of *sic*, it should be stated that it is established as having taken effect when a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is to be applied; thus, the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality) occurs. In this same manner, examples for the middle and first persons may be cited: *lunīhi lunīhi*—thus you have mown (*alāvīḥ*), or *alāviṣṭam*, *alāviṣṭa*; or alternatively, *lunīta lunīta*—thus you all have mown (*alāviṣṭa*). *Lunīhi lunīhi*—thus I have mown (*alāviṣam*), or *alāviṣva*, *alāviṣma*.

The same applies to the middle and the highest [persons]. "Cut! Cut!"—thus you will cut, you two will cut, you all will cut; or rather, "Cut! Cut!"—thus you [plural] will cut. "Cut! Cut!"—thus I will cut, we two will cut, we all will cut. In this manner, examples should be provided for all the *lakāra*s (tense/mood markers). "Cut! Cut!"—thus he cut, let him cut, may he cut, let him be cut, he cut, he will cut, he would cut.

"Study! Study!"—thus he studied; [the forms] *adhītām*, *adhīyīta*, *adhyeṣīṣṭa*, *adhijage*, *adhyagīṣṭa*, *adhyaiṣṭa*, *adhyetā*, *adhyaiṣyata*, and *adhyeṣyate* [are derived]. In the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), [it is used as]: "This field is being reaped," [just as one says] "Reap! Reap! and so forth. However, regarding the abstract state (*bhāve*), it should be considered whether the word *sva* is seen as established [in usage] or not.

Now, regarding the examples, how can there be reduplication? For reduplication is prescribed to indicate the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), and that [intensification] is already indicated here by the *loṭ* suffix itself, which is prescribed for that very purpose. Even if that [intensification] has been indicated, one might argue that by the force of the rule stating "there are two [forms] when there is intensification of action," reduplication would apply here even in the case of the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix; or rather, must some distinction be stated? To this, he says: "In the manifestation of the intensification of action... (*kriyāsamabhihārābhivyaktau*).

Because of the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca," its [the *yaṅ* affix’s] denotable meanings (*vācya*) are the action, the object, and the agent; however, the intensification (*samabhihāra*) is expressed solely by reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Since there is nothing else to be denoted or expressed by the *yaṅ* itself, and because the intensification of the action is already expressed by that very [affix], there is an absence of reduplication.

But surely, let the state of being an object (*bhāva*), an action (*karman*), and an agent (*kartṛ*) be the denotable meanings (*vācya*) of this [imperative suffix]; furthermore, "intensive repetition" (*samabhihāra*) is also heard as a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*). Let that too be manifested by the *loṭ* suffix, just as "present time" and so forth are manifested by the *laṭ* and other suffixes? If this is the case, then since the form of the pure *loṭ* suffix and that of this [repeated *loṭ*] would be identical in the absence of reduplication, reduplication is necessarily required for the manifestation of the intensive repetition.

And the cause here is the wonderful diversity of the expressive power of words (*śabdaśaktivaicitrya*); for instance, femininity is sometimes indicated by a single suffix, sometimes by two, and sometimes by the nominal stem alone, as in *dṛṣat*. Enough with this elaboration.
In the case of a conjunction, [the particle *ca*] may optionally [be placed after the first word]. 3.4.3.

Although the term "conjunction" (*samuccaye*) is stated in general terms, it is observed that it refers specifically to the conjunction of actions (*kriyā-samuccaya*), because suffixes are prescribed after verbal roots (*dhātu*). Thus he says: "Conjunction is the bringing together of multiple actions. The meaning is: the accumulation (*nicīyamānatā*) of several actions upon a single related entity. By this, the distinction between conjunction and "repetition" (*samabhihāra*), which has a single action as its object, is demonstrated.

Since a verbal root denotes action, its application does not occur in the mere sense of a collective property of action; with this intention, he says: "from roots denoting the actions being collected. The meaning is: suffixes [are applied] after those roots which denote the actions that are collected within a single instrument (*sādhana*).

*bhrāṣṭramaṭa* and so forth. The meaning is that one performs such acts as wandering about a frying pan (*bhrāṣṭra*). In this context, the root being subsequently employed (*anuprayujyamāna-dhātu*) expresses the activity of "doing" (*kṛti-vyāpāra*) which persists through various wanderings differentiated by their respective instruments (*sādhana-bheda*); thus, it illuminates the instruments and other factors inherent therein—this is the mutual connection [between the two roots]. *Bhrāṣṭram* means a hearth (*cullī*); *khadūram* means a distant place from a well, namely a room (*apavarakam*); *sthālyapidhānam* is that place where, having washed the cooking pots (*sthālī*), they are set down and covered.

Regarding the word *atha vā*: by the first *atha vā*, he shows the operation of the rule *vā ca tadhvamoḥ*; by the second, that of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*. This should be understood in the same way for the second example as well.
In the former case, there is the subsequent application according to the rule.

Regarding the term *yathāvidhi*: when there is no deviation from the meaning of the word (*padārtha*), the compound is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule "an indeclinable used in its own sense" (*yathārthe yad avyayam*). In the expression *anuprayoga*, the prefix *anu* restates the meaning of the verbal root; it does not signify "subsequent occurrence" or "immediacy. Consequently, even a usage separated by preceding elements is permitted. The mention of "in the preceding [rule]" (*pūrvasmin*) is for the sake of clarity. For he will state that the employment of a general term occurs in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*); therefore, this rule applies elsewhere than that, and its scope is distinct from the previous injunction regarding the imperative (*loṭ*).

"Because suffixes are prescribed when there is a connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*). Now, one might object: "But this form ending in *hi* or *sva* has its word-meaning unmanifested, because number, tense, and person are not manifested; therefore, the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of a verb is established for the sake of manifesting that meaning. Let it be so; even so, does this not still serve as the reason stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*? Or rather, it was said thus considering that the subsequent employment is established when there is a desire to express exactly as much meaning as the form ending in *hi* or *sva* is capable of manifesting.

"According to the rule, there is the employment of the word. Now, one might object: since he will state [later] that "in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*), there is the employment of a general term," a restriction (*niyama*) will be understood therein—that is, the employment of another root occurs only in the case of conjunction; consequently, in the case of the intensification of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the employment will occur according to the specific rule [of that section]. The [author] thinks as follows: because of the restriction that "in the case of conjunction, there is the employment of only a general term," it would follow that in other cases there could be the employment of even a different root. Thus, [if this were so], the form *chinatti* would not be employed [as an auxiliary].

However, there is no possibility of such [an auxiliary] for verbs like *pacati* which have a different meaning, because they cannot be syntactically connected with a form ending in the imperative suffix (*loṭ*). But for a verb that has the same meaning, such a connection is possible, as in the case of that very [verb]. Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an auxiliary being used after general verbs like *karoti*, for even these can indeed be connected, since they too terminate in a specific sense denoted by the proximate form ending in the imperative suffix.

But surely, once the usage of one *ākṛti* (morphological class) has been employed, it does not apply to a second or a third; this was explained under the rule "the root *kṛ* is subsequently employed," where it was shown that just as one cannot say "the master of cows and of horses," so too here, the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix should be concluded with the very same verbal root with which its employment began? No; for this principle also has exceptions both in the Veda and in common usage.

First, in the Veda: in the section on the fourth case-usage, we see "sūkaraḥ" (boar) in the sense of "for King Indra"; "varttikā te dhātuḥ" (the quail is your portion), where the genitive is used; and "mayuḥ prājāpatyaḥ" (the wild beast belongs to Prajāpati), where a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is seen in connection with a deity. In common usage as well: in the instances "sasnuḥ" (they bathed) and "payaḥ papuḥ" (they drank milk), the imperfect (*laṅ*) "anenijuḥ" (they washed) is employed alongside the perfect (*liṭ*). Therefore, this [treatise] must indeed be commenced.
In a copulative compound, the word expressing the general class [is placed first]. 3.4.5.

But surely, since the forms ending in *hi* and *sva* have their word-meanings unmanifested (*anabhivyakta-padārthaka*), and since suffixes are prescribed in connection with verbal roots (*dhātu-sambandha*), the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) is already established; thus, is there no purpose for this [rule]? To that he says: "sarvaviśeṣa... (in all particulars). In its absence, that root from which the imperative (*loṭ*) was prescribed would be employed subsequently. Even so, the manifestation of the meaning of the forms ending in *hi* and *sva* occurs, and the connection with the verbal root is likewise justified.

Now, one might object: even when there is the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of a word denoting the totality (*sāmanya*) that pervades all the particulars (*viśeṣa*), that generality—having its fulfillment in the particulars present before it—manifests the meaning for all of them, and there is also a connection with the verbal root (*dhātu*). In this regard, when deliberating whether the subsequent application should be of a single word expressing the generality or of many words expressing the particulars, it will be of the former alone, because of its brevity (*lāghava*); to this he says: "And [the reason is] brevity."

The point is that otherwise, only words such as *taru* and *druma* would be employed, and not words such as *vanaspati*. [Objection: But in examples such as *bhrāṣṭram aṭa*, since there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of that very same word, how can it be considered a term expressing a general meaning? To this he says: *bhrāṣṭram aṭa*, etc. [This applies] when there is a difference in action due to a difference in the grammatical factor (*kāraka*). In this way, even a conjunction (*samuccaya*) based on such differences is to be explained here.
In the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses] [are used]. 3.4.6.

In the examples, the connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*) must be sought. Regarding *akarad*: by the rule *kṛmṛdṛruhibhyaśchandasi*, there is the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli*; and by the rule *ṛdṛśo'ṅi guṇaḥ*, there is *guṇa* [substitution] before *aṅ*.
The suffix *leṭ* occurs in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*).

Regarding *joṣiṣat*: the root *juṣ* (meaning "to please" or "to serve") is anudātta; the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). By the rule *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, there is elision of the *i*; by *leṭo'ḍāṭau*, the augment *aṭ* is added to the suffix *tip*; by *sibbahulaṃ leṭi*, the suffix *sip* is added, followed by the augment *iṭ*. Regarding *tāriṣat*: it is stated that in the application of *sip*, there is frequently the status of being *ṇit*, from which follows the *vṛddhi* vowel lengthening. Regarding *patātu*: the root *patlṛ* means "to go"; the augment *āṭ* is added to *tip*.
And [the same applies] in cases of agreement and suspicion. 3.4.8.

With the words "If you [should grant] to me," etc., he shows the nature of the agreement (*upasaṃvāda*). With the words "By reason of [the cause]," etc., he explains that the "following" (*anusaraṇa*) of doubt means its pursuit. Regarding "I alone," etc.: these are the words of the Lord when he was entreated by the gods for the conquest of Tripura. In the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), the suffix *iṭ* is applied to the root *īś*; the substitution of *etva* (for *īt*) occurs; and by the rule "*vaitonyatra*" (Pāṇini 6.1.79), the vowel *ai* is substituted. "Beasts" (*paśavaḥ*) refers to both bipeds and quadrupeds.

The gods said to Vāyu, "Let us slay King Soma. He replied, "I choose a boon: let the cups (grahas) be drawn for you with me at their head. Those whose cups have me at their head—that is, first—are thus described. The form *madagrahaḥ* is derived from the root *grah* (to seize) in the sense of the object, taking the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix *yak*; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule beginning with *grahi-jyā*; the augment *aṭ* is added after the suffix *jha*; and the elision of the final vowel follows the previous rule.

The gods killed the Soma; it became putrid and reached a state of unfitness for consumption. They said to Vāyu, "Make this palatable for us. He replied, "I shall choose a boon: let the vessels be declared to have me as their deity. Those [vessels] whose deity is he are thus described. Regarding the form *ucyāntai*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with *vacisvapi* etc.; the rest is as before. Regarding the phrase *nejjihyāyanta*: the particle *na* indicates a doubt or apprehension.

The meaning is: "May there not be a fall into hell through crooked conduct (*jihmacaraṇa*). *Jihma* means crooked or evil; [the suffix] *kyac* is applied according to the rule *chandasi parecchāyām*, and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the split rule (*yogavibhāga*) *aśvāghasyāt*. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, only the bare fact is shown: "*jihmācaraṇena*" (by crooked conduct). Furthermore, the suffix *kyac* does not occur after the root *car* except when preceded by an object of comparison. The present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used here in the sense of a causal reason (*hetu*). This is precisely the sense of the optative (*liṅ*).

Regarding the relationship between cause (*hetu*) and effect (*hetumat*), how is it so? First, in the case of an agreement (*upasaṃvāda*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the cause, and the giving (*dāna*) is the effect. Otherwise, the potential mood (*liṅ*) would not occur in the sense of "if Your Honor were to do this for me," though there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the *liṅ*. Furthermore, the future tense (*lṛṭ*) occurs in the sense of "I too shall give this to you. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the *liṅ* is also employed after the verb *dadāti*. Even in the case of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*), there is a pursuit of the effect from the cause; therein, the cause is the *hetu* and the effect is the *hetumat*.

Furthermore, if the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the limit (*avadhi*) and the giving (*dāna*) is that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*), then in the case of a formal agreement (*upasaṃvāda*), it is the relationship between the limit and that which possesses the limit (*avadhyavadhimadbhāva*) that is understood, not the relationship between cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*). Even if one were to say that there is no certain causal relationship even in the case of a mere suspicion, nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), a causal relationship must necessarily be stated here; therefore, the meaning is that this [usage] is precisely the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅartha*). As for the statement "but the statement is for the sake of [indicating] what is constant" (*nityārthaṃ tu vacanam*), [it means as follows].

One might think that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is seen here as obligatory in the Vedic language; nevertheless, if it is argued that this is established by means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), then that very point is what is being made known by the statement.
For you (tumarthe), [the suffixes] śe, sena, se, asen, kse, enadhyai, adhyain, kadhyai, kadhyain, śadhyai, śadhyain, tavaite, taveṅ, and tavenaḥ [are used]. 3.4.9.

"How is this known?"—this question arises because, according to the rule *kartari kṛt* ("kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent"), it is not logical for the suffix *tumun* to express the abstract state (*bhāva*). "Removal" (*apakarṣa*) means taking away; and since the abstract state (*bhāva*) of verbal roots is their own inherent meaning, it takes the form of something yet to be accomplished (*sādhyamāna-rūpa*). For that alone is the abstract state expressed by the verbal root. However, the abstract state expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ* is distinct from the meaning of the root and takes the form of something already established (*siddhatā-rūpa*). Regarding *pibadhyai*: there is elision (*luk*) of the *yak* suffix according to the rule *yako bahulaṃ chandasi*, and the substitution of *piba* occurs. Regarding *mādayardhyai*: where *yak* would otherwise apply, the *śap* suffix is used by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *dṛś* and *vikhyā*.
The analysis of the grammatical rule (yogavibhāga) has an intended purpose that must be considered.
The suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* are used after a verbal root when *īśvara* (the agent) is the object.
Regarding "vitṛda": the root *tṛd* (with prefix *vi-*) means "to injure" and "to disregard."
The suffixes *tavya*, *anīya*, *ya*, *enya*, and *tva* are used in the sense of what ought to be done (*kṛtyārthe*).

"The meaning of *kṛtya* [suffixes] is the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Although in the case of words such as *bhavya* and *geya*, the agent (*kartṛ*) is also the meaning, and in cases such as *vahyam* (the vehicle) and *snānīyam cūrṇam* (bathing powder), the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth are the meanings; nevertheless, it is not by virtue of being a *kṛtya* that they are prescribed for the agent and others. What then? They are prescribed in their own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*). Therefore, the point is that prescription by way of being a *kṛtya* applies only to the abstract state and the object. Regarding *didṛkṣeṇya*: the suffix *kenya* is applied to the root *dṛś* followed by the desiderative suffix *san*. Regarding *śuśrūṣeṇya*: [it is derived] from the root *śru*. "Also in the rule beginning with *sayādi*" refers to this.

The meaning is that [the suffix *śeṣ*] is used in those instances where suffixes such as *sa* and *ya* are prescribed, namely in the rule "for the sense of the infinitive (*tum-artha*), [the suffixes] *śeṣ*, *enap*, and *se*. The phrase "other than for the sense of the infinitive" means elsewhere than that. Otherwise, since the sense of the infinitive would already be established by this very [rule] even in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*), that [subsequent rule] would be redundant.
And [the suffix] *avacakṣe* [is applied]. 3.4.15.

Regarding the term *eś-pratyaya*: the addition of the marker *ś* is for the sake of [the suffix] being treated as *sārvadhātuka*; by virtue of that, the substitution of *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ* does not occur.
The suffix *tosun* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *kṛ*, *vad*, *car*, *hṛ*, *mi*, and *jan* when expressing a characteristic of an action (*bhāva-lakṣaṇe*).

Configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and the others function as defining characteristics by virtue of being the limits [of the process]. "Until completion" (*ā samāpteḥ*): for the verb *tiṣṭhati* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is conventionally established in the sense of "completion," as seen in such examples as "the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is completed" (*santiṣṭhate*). "Until exhaustion" (*ā tāmiteḥ*): [this refers to] the root *tam-* in the sense of "weariness" (*glāni*).
In the dialect of the easterners, the suffix *ktvā* is used after the prohibitive particles *alam* and *khalu*. (Pāṇini 3.4.18)

"Only [in the sense] of 'for you' (tumarthe)"—as in *alaṃkṛtvā*. Due to the restrictive rule "only with an indeclinable" (*amaivāvyayena*), there is no compound with an upapada. The meaning is that [the suffix] should not be applied. Regarding the phrase "if [it is argued] by the rule *vāsarūpa*": previously, in the section on commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth, it was indicated by the statement concerning the kṛtya suffixes that "after the section on feminine endings (*stryadhikāra*), the *vāsarūpa* rule does not necessarily apply. With the intention that this [rule] is absent here, it was stated that the mention of *prāk* (before) is for the purpose of providing an option.
According to the Eastern grammarians, the suffix *ām* is used after the root *māṅ* when expressing reciprocity.

Regarding *apamitya*: the root *miṅ* means "to borrow" (*prāṇidāna*). After the suffix *ktvā*, when replaced by *lyap*, the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *gayateridanyatarasyām*, followed by the insertion of *tuk* after the short vowel. The phrase "because there is no prior time" (*apūrvakālatvāt*) is used because one first borrows (*yācate*) and only afterwards returns (*apamayate*). When the suffix *ktvā* is applied to the root *mī* (from which *miṅ* is derived) based on this statement, it applies to the act of borrowing according to the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ* etc., since the present case supersedes that general rule—just as the second doubling of a consonant supersedes the first doubling. Alternatively, it is due to non-usage (*anabhidhānāt*). This is explained by the passage beginning with *meṅaḥ*.

The meaning is that this reference is made to the root *meṅ* after its *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) has been applied, and not to *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring," because the latter cannot function in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatihāra*). If this is so, one should simply say "*meṅ*" [in the rule]; in that case, even the mention of "reciprocal action" (*vyatīhāra*) would not need to be included. To this he replies: "For the sake of providing an indication" (*jñāpanārtham*). He asks: "What is being indicated? and says: "That which is caused by an *anubandha* [does not affect the form]. He states the purpose: "By means of that... [and so on].

If this meaning were not made known, then when the root *daip* is heard, its substitution of *āt* would not occur because it would not end in a vowel (*ajantatvāt*). Consequently, in the prohibition [of the augment *it*] by the rule *adābit*, there would be no inclusion of that [root *daip*], and the rule would apply only to *dāp* in the sense of "cutting."
And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after a word ending in the locative case when it denotes a connection with what is superior (*para*) or inferior (*avara*). 3.4.20.

Since the words *para* (higher/further) and *avara* (lower/nearer) are relative terms, their status as "higher" or "lower" depends on a point of reference. It is understood that the connection between these two—*para* and *avara*—occurs only with respect to what precedes and follows them; thus he says: "of the preceding by the following. Here, by the word "preceding," the "nearer" (*avara*) is intended. Regarding the phrase "without reaching the river": the meaning is "the region prior to the river. Consequently, the river becomes the "further" (*para*) limit. Thus, the mountain is qualified by its connection to the further river. Regarding the phrase "having crossed the mountain": the meaning is "on the far side of the mountain."

And thereafter, there is the Avara mountain; by that connection with the Avara mountain, the river is qualified. This commencement also serves to indicate a time not previously mentioned; it must be considered what kind of transgression occurs here.
When two actions have the same agent, [the suffix -ktvā is used] for the action occurring at the earlier time. 3.4.21.

Since the status of being an agent depends upon the action, even though the context concerns verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is understood that the "identity of agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*) applies only to the meanings of those roots, not to the roots themselves; thus he says: "those two meanings of roots which have the same agent. This word *samāna* signifies "one"; by using the locative case in the phrase *tatra*, he indicates a sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*). There would be no fault even if the genitive were used, but the locative has been adopted. [The compound means] "from that which exists in the meaning of the root pertaining to a prior time."

The Prābhākaras, however, explain [the rule] as "because of that which is employed first," and they do not respect the priority of sequence in actual performance; this must be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. For it is stated: "An addition should be made [to the rule], 'having opened his mouth he sleeps' and 'having closed his eyes he laughs,' because of the non-priority of time. Now, if it is argued: "Capacity (*śakti*) is the causal factor (*kāraka*), and since that capacity differs with each action, how can there be a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*)?"—to this he says: "Of the capacity and the possessor of the capacity."

In this context, the dual number is employed in the expression *samānakartṛkayoḥ* ("of two having the same agent").
