Consequently, [the rule] would apply only when there are exactly two actions occurring in prior time (*paurvakālya*), and not when there are many; to this he replies: "The dual number is non-essential (*atantra*). The meaning is as follows: a reference must necessarily be made by some number or other. Since the properties of having the same agent and of occurring in prior time are based on distinct entities, and since the dual and plural numbers—which are grounded in such distinctions—occur first [in the grammatical system], the dual was employed; however, it is not essential to the rule.

Even so, this is not established by common worldly understanding; for example, in the world, when it is said, "Let the first among these Brahmins be brought," the very first one is brought. Likewise here too, it would follow that [the suffix -ktvā] applies to the very first action. Therefore, it should be stated thus: in all these cases, priority belongs to the act of going—namely, "having bathed, he goes," "having eaten, he goes," and "having drunk, he goes."

For the action expressed by the verb is the primary element because it is that which is to be qualified; therefore, since all [other elements] are qualifiers with respect to it, they have no mutual connection with one another. As it has been said: "And because subordinate elements (guṇas) exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection between them due to their equality. And this being the case, the order of usage is also unrestricted: one may say *snātvā bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* ("having bathed, eaten, and drunk, he goes") or *pītvā snātvā bhuktvā vrajati* ("having drunk, bathed, and eaten, he goes").

Regarding the example *bhuktavati brāhmaṇe*: Now, since this falls under the governing rule for the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*), the suffix *ktvā* should denote an abstract action (*bhāve*), whereas *ktavatu* denotes the agent (*kartari*). If that is so, then one must state that in this particular context, [the suffix] does not denote an abstract action; thus, it serves as a counter-example. Consequently, usages such as *śrīśailaśikharaṃ dṛṣṭvā sarvapāpaiḥ pramucyate* ("Having seen the peak of Śrīśaila, one is liberated from all sins"), which involve different agents, would indeed be ungrammatical. Regarding *vrajati jalpati ca*: here, because there is simultaneity, there is no "priority of time" (*pūrvakālatā*). This is because there is no priority of time.

For in that case, he first sleeps and afterwards opens [his eyes]; at the very moment he laughs, he closes [his eyes]. This is not because sleep occurs at a different time, for in this instance, having opened [his eyes], he sleeps even for a moment, and having closed them, he laughs; therefore, the priority [of one action over another] is relative to the laughter and so forth occurring at a subsequent time, and the cognition is based upon that. Why does this not occur here—namely, "he eats first, then he goes"? Because it has already been expressed by its own word.

Even by the rule *vibhāṣāgre*, [the suffix *ktvā*] does not apply here. What is the reason? In that rule, words such as *agrya* are understood as referring to the priority of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana-paurvākālya*); for example, "having eaten before other eaters, he then departs. But here, the suffix *ktvā* is enjoined with respect to the priority of the eating relative to the departure (*vrajyāpekṣaṃ bhojanasya yat paurvakālyam*), which is what is expressed by the word *pūrva*. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even when [priority] has already been stated by the force of the specific wording.

Regarding the priority of the means (*sādhana*), since [the temporal relation] has already fulfilled its purpose when applied to words such as *agrya* (foremost) and so on, and because the conventional usage of time pertains to action, the priority of the means should be understood as being mediated by that [action]. For it has been said:
"Time serves to differentiate actions, while number is the differentiator of everything."

In the expression "it is sat here in order to eat" (*ihāsyate bhoktum*), the present tense suffix *laṭ* occurs by virtue of the rule *vāsarupeṇa*. When the suffix *ktvā* is applied to the root *ās-* (to sit), then only *laṭ* and other such suffixes are applied to the root *bhuj-* (to eat)—as in "having sat, he eats" (*āsitvā bhuṅkte*)—but not the infinitive suffix *tumun*; this is because such usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*). When one says "having sat, in order to eat" (*āsitvā bhoktum*), a connection with words such as "he begins" (*prakramate*) is understood.
The suffix *ṇamul* is also used [after a verb] when frequency is indicated. 3.4.22.

"Accompanied by reduplication. But by what means does reduplication occur here? He says: "Reduplication occurs because of the supplementary rule (upasaṅkhyāna) stating that 'two [words] are used in the sense of repetition (ābhīkṣṇya). However, regarding the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, Vāmana will state: "'Perpetuity (*nityatā*) applies to finite verbs (*tiṅ*) and to indeclinable suffixes (*avyayakṛt*). According to his view, reduplication occurs here precisely because of the mention of *nitya*. [The example is] *pāyaṃpāyam*, [formed] by the rule *āto yuk*."
Not so, if there is no desire for it. (Pāṇini 3.4.23)

Regarding the term *anākāṅkṣa*: it is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with a word ending in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* class), as has been shown; that is, "it does not desire anything else. As for the suffix *ktvā*, although it is prescribed by the preceding rule—as stated in the rule "*ṇamul ca*"—the status of being "preceding" is relative to that. By the force of the word "also" (*api*), the prohibition applies even to that which is prescribed by the immediately following rule. The meaning is that there is a prohibition of the suffix *ktvā* alone when used in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*). And this is understood from the fact that the prohibition is recognized in relation to the context, namely: "that which would otherwise apply to the prior action does not take place."
The word *vibhāṣā* is optionally [used] before the words *agra*, *prathama*, and *pūrva*.

The word *agra* also signifies a specific place—as in "he eats in front of the master"—but here, due to its association with the word *prathama*, it is understood as denoting a specific time. Furthermore, because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there is no elision of the case-ending in *agre*, just as in the expression *asyavāmīyam*. The phrase "in the sense of repetition" (*āmīkṣṇye*) does not carry over [to this rule]. This is the reasoning for why this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the application] was not previously established.

For if that [term *ābhīkṣṇye*] were to follow from the previous rule, there would be an option (*vibhāṣā*) where [the suffixes] are already required by that preceding rule; and by speaking thus, it is implied that *agrya* and so forth apply to the domain of the priority of the means of action (*sādhana*). Since the priority of the action is already expressed by *agrya* and the others, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* would not apply even in the case of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*); thus, even if *ābhīkṣṇye* were to follow, it would result in an option for what is otherwise unestablished (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*).

Furthermore, since it is impossible to indicate frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) without a reduplication, the prescription of the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* for the purpose of indicating that [frequency] is also not tenable. Now, even if the mention of "frequency" (*ābhīk�ṣṇya*) were not carried over [from the previous rule], there would still be scope for the preceding sūtra in cases where [roots] such as *agrya* do not exist; whereas the scope of this [present] rule would be those cases where frequency does not exist.

Since both [rules] would apply when *ābhīkṣṇya* (frequency) and words such as *agrya* (foremost) are present, this option (*vibhāṣā*) would prevail due to its later position; thus, why is it appropriate that this be an option for both? He thinks as follows: by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the rule is indeed obligatory in the case of frequency—e.g., *agre bhojam bhojam vrajati* (he goes eating first, eating first), or *agre bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati* (he goes having eaten first, having eaten first). The same should be understood for *pūrva* and *prathama* as well.

One might object: "In this case, since the suffix *ktvā* would apply by default [under P. 3.4.21], and the suffix *ṇamul* would also apply by the rule 'when there are two actions having the same agent' (P. 3.4.21), this new rule must be an initiation [of a specific option]; therefore, it is more appropriate that this be considered an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applicable in both cases. This is not so. This is stated as an "optional rule for what was not previously established" (*aprāpta-vibhāṣā*) with reference to those instances of *ktvā* and *ṇamul* prescribed by the immediately preceding sūtra, where it is intended to indicate the absence of the rule regarding non-identity of form (*vā-asarūpa-vidhi*). It is not, however, with respect to *ktvā* and *ṇamul* in general.

"The suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* occur. But for what purpose is *ktvā* prescribed again, since it is already established even in cases where there is no repetition (*nābhīkṣṇye*) by the rule "when two actions have the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*)? True; he will state that by the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*), the absence of the *vāsarūpa* rule is indicated. And it is not intended that this absence be indicated only in the prescription of *ṇamul*; rather, it is intended in the prescription of *ṇamul* together with *ktvā*.

Therefore, so that the rule for *ṇamul* may apply together with *ktvā*, the term *ktvā* is also restated by virtue of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "and *ṇamul*" (*ṇamul ca*). For in this way, the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) when both [suffixes] are introduced together to be prescribed simultaneously indicates that the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in such a case; thus, the desired result is established. The example *agrebhojaṃ vrajati* means: "having eaten before other eaters, he goes. Regarding the statement "the *laṭ* and other suffixes do not occur in the sense of frequency (*āmīkṣṇya*)," the meaning is that it does not take the form *agre bhuṅkte bhuṅkte tato vrajati* (he eats repeatedly first and then goes).

Why does this not become an *upapada* compound? In this case of an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*), words such as *agrya* serve as the cause for the non-occurrence of the suffix in one alternative, but not for its occurrence; for both [the occurrence and non-occurrence] are prescribed without distinction by the rule "In the sense of repetition, the suffix *ṇamul* and [the suffix *ktvā*]" (Pāṇini 3.4.22). Thus, there is no *upapada*. However, in the case of a non-applicable optional rule (*aprāptavibhāṣā*), since words such as *agrya* are the cause for the production of the suffix, and because the technical term *upapada* is prescribed for that which is the cause, an *upapada* compound would result—this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase "that which is prescribed by the same rule as *ama*," this has been explained in that very place.
The suffix *khamuñ* is added after the root *kṛ* when it means "to revile" and is used with an object.

In these examples, the root *kṛ* (to do/make) functions in the sense of utterance (*uccāraṇa*), and its object is necessarily of the nature of sound (*śabda*). In this context, words such as *cora* (thief) have sound as their primary element. [The expression] *coraṅkāram*: what is the meaning? It means "having uttered the word *cora*. Thus he says: "You are a thief," and so forth. *Corakaraṇam* (the making of a thief): this refers to the utterance of the word *cora*. [It is said to be] "for the purpose of effecting an insult" (*ākrośasampādanārtham*), because it is impossible to effect that [insult] without the utterance of a censurable word. But it is not the case [that the person becomes a thief], for one does not become a thief merely by the statement "you are a thief."
The suffix *ṇamul* is used after a verb when it is construed with the word *svādu* (sweet). 3.4.26.

"‘The inclusion of the word *artha* [is for the sake of] ‘sweet things’ (*svādu*). This is understood from the commentary. Regarding "in the sense of sweet things": the suffix *-mat* also occurs after all [of these words], because it is possible in the sense of "object. Furthermore, the words *lavaṇa* and *sampanna* are synonyms for the word *svādu*.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of prescribing the indeclinable *svādumī* with a final *m*, given that *khamuñ* is the current topic and it will continue to apply; thus, its status as ending in *m* would be established by the rule *arudviṣadajantasya mum*? To this he replies: "The prescription of the indeclinable ending in *m* is for the sake of preventing the vowel *ī*. The meaning is that when the form is prescribed as ending in *m* in the context of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not occur according to the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*, because it ends in *m* and lacks an ending in *u*. [This refers to] that which ends in the suffix *cvī*.

The suffix *mum* is not established everywhere even for *khamuñ*; the intention is that this is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of an indeclinable" (*avyayasya*). If that is so, then let only the final *m* be prescribed as a nipātana (irregular form), while the suffix *khamuñ* itself—being the one under discussion—should be enjoined? This is not correct; for if the addition of the final *m* were merely for the sake of making it an indeclinable, then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would necessarily follow. However, in the case of *ṇamul*, the addition of the final *m* is prescribed as something new, and it is understood to serve three purposes: to prevent the long vowel *ī* [from appearing], to apply to forms ending in *cvī*, and to provide the final *m*.

Furthermore, since the suffix *ṇamul* must necessarily be prescribed later on, this [suffix] has been applied here for the sake of brevity, as there would otherwise be no economy of expression. The example "having made it sweet" (*asvādvīṃ svādvīṃ kṛtvā*) involves the simultaneous mention of two sentences. "Having made the gruel sweet, he eats it" (*svādvīṃ kṛtvā yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte*) is an example of the absence of the long vowel *ī*; "he eats what was not sweet, [making it] sweet" (*asvāduṃ svāduṃ bhuṅkte*) is an example of the indeclinable form.

Here, if suffixes such as *ktvā* were to denote the agent—on the basis of the rule "the *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent"—then in the sentence "rice is eaten by Devadatta after having been cooked," the instrumental case would not apply to Devadatta, because the agent has already been expressed by the *ktvā* suffix.

Now, even though the agent is expressed by the *ktvā* suffix, since the agent is not expressed by the *bhuj* suffix, does the case-ending based on what is "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) occur as the third case? If that were so, the second case would result for *odana*; what is the reason? Because, although it is expressed by the *bhuj* suffix, it is not expressed by the *ktvā* suffix as the object (*karman*). Likewise, if [the endings] were applied to the object, one would have *paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte devadattena*, but in fact it is only *paktvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*.

Likewise, in this case, because the suffix *ṇamul* is used with the sense of "eating so as to make it sweet" (*svāduṅkāram*)—as in "Devadatta eats barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) so as to make it sweet"—the accusative case is not employed for the *yavāgū*. However, in the sentence "Devadatta eats the barley-gruel so as to make it sweet" (*svāduṅkāraṃ yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*), the accusative case does indeed occur for the object (*karman*), and the instrumental case does not occur for the agent (*kartṛ*). The same principle should be understood to apply to the suffix *tumun*.

Likewise, regarding the rules "tamunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām" and "samānakartṛkeṣu tumun," even in cases involving the suffix *tumun*, such as "bhoktum odanaḥ pacyate devadattena" (rice is cooked by Devadatta for the purpose of eating), "iṣyate grāmo gantuṃ devadattena" (Devadatta desires to go to the village), "bhoktum odanaṃ pacati devadattaḥ" (Devadatta cooks rice in order to eat), and "grāmaṃ gantum icchati devadattaḥ" (Devadatta wishes to go to the village)—in all these instances, because of the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), the case endings for the agent and the object occur in accordance with that very subsequent verb where the *l*-suffixes (*lādayaḥ*) are present.

Therefore, it must be stated that "an indeclinable *kṛt* [suffix] forms a coordinate construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)"; with what is there this coordination? With the verb subsequently employed (*anuprayoga*). This is what is meant: the *l*-class suffixes and others are prescribed for whatever grammatical participant (*kāraka*) [the action] occurs in relation to the root to which they are added; the indeclinable *kṛt* suffixes likewise occur in relation to that very same participant. For in this way, since both [the indeclinable and the subsequent verb] express the agent or the object, the case-endings are established according to their respective roles.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, states the following in order to establish this point differently: "And because of the governing rule for the sense of *tumun*. In that regard, by the inclusion of the term *tum-artha* (the sense of *tumun*) in the sūtra beginning with *seṭ*, it is indicated that *tamun* occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). And that very inclusion of *tum-artha* continues to apply up until the sūtra *śakadhṛṣajñā*. Therefore, all these suffixes beginning with *ktvā* occur in the sense of the abstract action. To this, he raises an objection: "If this is so," [he asks], "why does the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) not occur?"

This is also an illustration; one should also consider why the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur in the sentence *svāduṅkāraṃ yavāgūrbhujyate devadattena* ("A sweet gruel is being eaten by Devadatta"), where the object (*karman*) is expressed. This objection applies if "anabhihite" (when not [already] expressed) is interpreted as a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation); for in that case, whether the expression exists or not, the case ending would apply based on whatever constitutes the non-expression. He provides the solution: "by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*" (*bhujipratyayena*). The intention is that "anabhihite" is understood as a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (prohibitory negation).

For in that case, the negation would have as its basis that [capacity] from which the expression originates. But surely, capacity (*śakti*) is the factor (*kāraka*), and the capacity regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) is one thing, while the capacity regarding the act of eating (*bhujiviṣaya*) is another; if there were both expression and non-expression of a single capacity, this resolution—that the negation has as its basis that from which the expression originates—might be valid. However, since there is a difference in capacities, is this not improper? To this, he says: "And not in this... and so forth.

What is the reason that the distinction [between the two powers] is not intended? He says: "For the state of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) would be contradicted. Now, one might object: "Granted that the distinction between the two powers is not intended in this particular context, why is it not intended in the rule *anabhihite*? This is irrelevant; for how could there be both intention and non-intention regarding the very same usage at the very same time?

Something—[it is argued]: the mention of "in what is not expressed" (*anabhihite*) as the locus for singularity and so forth means that when action (*karman*) and so on are not expressed, [the question arises] where that singularity and so forth resides; and since the substance (*dravya*) alone is the locus of singularity and so forth, not the power (*śakti*), therefore even in that case, it is said that "the substance itself is not expressed. And since, given the presence or absence of expression through the medium of the power, the prohibition applies based on that which *is* expressed, this is indeed logical.

Even having accepted the intention to express a distinction between powers (*śakti*), he states the resolution: "And when the power of the principal [action] is denoted. The action expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) is the principal because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); that which serves as its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), however, is non-principal. By means of that [qualifier], there is also a relationship of subordinate and principal between the two powers that have it as their object. In this regard, since subordinate elements follow the principal, they look toward it; and because they do not initiate their own effects in contradiction to it, the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are established according to their respective roles. And it has been said: "Where there are two distinct actions of a substance, one principal and the other subordinate..."
Power resides in the qualities; therein, the primary matter (pradhāna) is conformed to.
"The power whose primary object [is the principal] is denoted by the suffix;
when [it is directed] toward a subordinate element, then, in that same manner, it is understood even though not explicitly stated.

We, however, say: because there can be no simultaneous syntactic connection with both [the principal and the subordinate] for a single heard word, the verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) is with the principal alone, while with the other [the subordinate], it is through implication (*ārtha*) due to proximity.
The suffix *siddha* is used after the words *anyathā*, *evam*, *katham*, and *ittham*, provided that they are not employed in a compound. 3.4.27.

But how is this [term] *siddha-aprayoga* established? In examples such as *siddha odanaḥ* ("the rice is cooked"), the word *siddha* means "accomplished" or "completed. Therefore, the question is: if it is *siddha* (established), why is it called *aprayoga* (not used)? And if it is not being used (*aprayujyamāna*), how can there be a rule (*vidhi*) for the suffix *ṇamul* after it? The answer is that the word *siddha* here signifies "that which is already obtained," just as in the maxim: "When something is already established, the formulation of a rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). [The phrase] "because of its meaninglessness" (*nirarthakatvāt*) means "because of its lack of purpose. [The phrase] "in this very way" (*evameva*) means "being indeed meaningless."

This very point is elucidated by the phrase "otherwise he eats" (*anyathā bhuṅkte*). Regarding the expression "whatever the meaning may be": in the examples provided as subsequent applications (*anuprayoga*), the words *anyathā* and so forth denote the manner of that action. For instance: "Having done otherwise with his head, he eats. However, in this case, without the verb *karoti*, the "doing otherwise" of the head is not perceived; rather, it is understood only as a manner pertaining to the act of eating. Therefore, the verb *karoti* must necessarily be employed.
The substitution of *yathātatha* occurs in response to a statement made with malice. 3.4.28.

"If he asks while being envious, he replies" means that when he asks, he replies while being envious. The root *asu* (in the sense of "mental affliction") belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. Regarding the word *tatra*: the meaning is that in such a situation, whatever reply is given is a "reply characterized by envy. Regarding *yathākāram*: this is the response if one who is unworthy to ask nevertheless asks; for example, "I shall eat according to how [it was done]. This is a statement of the actual facts.

But how is it that the suffix *ktvā* occurs here, given that by the rule "when the action is established [and not expressed]," the verb *karoti* (to do) is redundant? Consequently, since there is an absence of priority in time—which is based on a distinction—and an absence of a common agent, the suffix would not apply here; whereas the suffix *ṇamul* occurs even in the absence of both, by virtue of the power of the specific grammatical rule? It is said in reply:

The root *kṛ* expresses action in general, while its specific modes are expressed by the words *yathā* and *tathā*. Since a general term finds its culmination in a specific instance that is present, the mode in question is said to have that very [action] as its object. Consequently, just as much meaning as is contained in "he will eat" (*bhokṣyate*) is already established by this [expression] "even though there is the act of doing" (*karoti sati*); thus, it is stated that the usage is redundant (*siddhaprayogatva*), yet not because of an absolute absence of denotation. Therefore, the suffix *ktvā*, which is based on a distinction between actions, is indeed logically justified.

And by adopting this view, the suffix *ktvā* occurs even in the preceding sūtra by virtue of the rule *vāsarūpa*. It is also employed in various places in the Bhāṣya—for instance: "Having formulated the objection in one way, the resolution has been stated in another way," and "In what manner does it act as a sublater? and so forth.
The affix *kha* is used after the roots *dṛś* and *vid* when they have an object and denote completeness.

"With *karman* as the upapada, [the suffix is used] when distinguished by totality (*sākalya*). This means that when *karman* is the upapada, it must be qualified by totality. In the example "he chooses [all] maidens to be seen" (*kanyā-darśaṃ varayati*), there is totality because all maidens who have become objects of sight are connected with the meaning of the sentence. In the case of "he chooses all maidens" (*sarvāḥ kanyā varayati*) as well, the meaning is that they are those who have become objects of sight. Furthermore, this is intended to express an excellence (or intensity), for even if some are excluded, the usage still occurs.
The sense is that [the root *vid*] is not included because, in its meaning of "existence," it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), even though it may mean "he knows," "he obtains," or "he investigates."
The [augment] *iṭ* is applied before the roots *vid* and *jīv*. (Pāṇini 3.1.30)

*Vindeti* is an imitation of the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining," for in forms such as *vindati*, there is the augment *num* by the rule *śe mucādīnām*. The meaning is: "as much as he obtains, so much he eats. By this, he shows the lack of totality (*asākalya*); for if there were totality (*sākalya*), it would already be established by the preceding rule.
The suffix *pūra* is applied after the words *carman* and *udara*. || 3.4.31 ||

Since the term *karmani* (in the sense of an object) is understood from the previous rule, this refers to the causative form of the root *pṛ*, because the simple root is intransitive; thus he says "of *pūrayati*. In the example *udarapūraṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats until his belly is full"), the meaning is "he eats filling his belly. In such cases as these, there is generally no prior temporal sequence [between the two actions]; therefore, they say that the phrase "prior in time" (*pūrvakāle*) should not be connected here.
The elision of the *u* of the word *varṣa* is optionally applied when it follows [the word *ūna*] as a measure of time. 3.4.32.

Regarding "goṣpadapūra" (filling a cow's footprint): the meaning is that it rained so as to fill a cow's footprint. Since the root *vṛṣ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). On this point as well, they say that the rule "pūrvakāle" (when a prior action is indicated) should not be applied. Regarding "sītāpūra": *sītā* refers to the track of a plow.

"What is the purpose of mentioning *asya*? This question implies that the elision of *ū* would be understood from the proximity (*sannidhāna*) alone. [The answer is: "So that it does not apply to the *upapada*. If *asya* were not stated, the elision of *ū*—just like the measure of rain (*varṣapramāṇa*)—would be understood as referring to the entire complex; that is, the elision of the vowel *ū* which is present in the complex consisting of the verbal root and the *upapada*. Consequently, the intention is that the elision would then apply to the *upapada* as well.

The rule *ūlopaścāsyānyatarasyām* could have been omitted. How is *goṣpadapram* formed? From the root *prā* (in the sense of filling), by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*, we derive *pra*. Because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), it takes the neuter gender and the accusative case. There is no difference in form, no difference in meaning, and no difference in accent. When the suffix *ka* is added, the word is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule *thāthādisūtra*.

When the suffix *ṇamul* is used with the elision of *ū*, since there is no preceding vowel possessing an accent (*svarabhāj*), the rule *liti* does not apply; thus, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) remains, which, by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*, stays as oxytone. Therefore, the result is indeed oxytone.

But surely, when *ṇamul* is present, because [the suffix] is an indeclinable by the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*, there would be no hearing of case-endings; and in the case of *tarap*, we have *goṣpadapratarapam*; and in the case of *kalpa* and so on, we have *goṣpadaprakalpa*; and in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, because it is an indeclinable, the suffix *akac* occurs. But if *ka* were present, all of this would not be established? It is replied: the hearing of case-endings is indeed desired in one instance, as in *goṣpadapreṇa*; however, the forms cited for *tarap* and the others are simply not desired. And this is understood from the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the elision (*ūlopa*) in the Bhāṣya.

But is it not the case that even forms such as *goṣpadapūra* are established by the suffix *ghañ* alone? It is not so established. For if one were to apply *ghañ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and then form a compound with a genitive case-ending in the sense of the object (*karman*) using that derivative, then by the accent rule for *sthādi* suffixes, the word would be oxytone (have the acute accent on the final syllable). Alternatively, if *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a non-co-referential term (*vyadhikaraṇa-pada*) is formed—namely, "that in which there is the filling of a cow’s footprint"—then there would be the undesirable consequence of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applying.

Furthermore, expressions such as *goṣpadapūrantarām* (having an interval filling a cow's footprint) and *goṣpadapūraṅkalpam* (resembling what fills a cow's footprint) would not be established; therefore, it should be stated as "*varṣapramāṇe*" (in the measure of a year).
[The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the verbal roots] *cel* and *knop*. (Pāṇini 3.4.33)

Regarding the phrase "from this root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*)," the fact that it is a causative form is determined precisely by the mention of the *puk* augment; furthermore, based on the commentary, he states "in the sense of *cela*" (clothing) to indicate that the meaning is being taken [rather than the specific word]. The example given is *celaknīpaṃ vṛṣṭaḥ*. The meaning is: "it rained while making the clothing *knopayan*," that is, making it produce sound. In other words, it means it rained in such a way that the clothes made a noise as they were being soaked.
The affix *khaś* is applied after the root *kaṣ* when it is preceded by the words *nimūla* and *samūla*.

In this context, there is indeed a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Regarding the term *nimūlakāṣam*: the root *kaṣ* has the meaning of "to harm. When there is a distinction between two aspects of the same verbal meaning—one general and one particular—there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). That from which the root has departed is *nimūlam*. One performs a *kaṣaṇa* (uprooting) together with the root; the meaning is that one uproots it along with its root. This should be understood throughout the entire treatise.
The roots *han*, *kṛ*, and *grah* take the affix *kvip* when used with the words *samūla*, *akṛta*, and *jīva*.

Regarding the term *jīvagrāham*: that which lives is a *jīva*; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. The meaning is "one who seizes [it] while it is still living."
The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *han* when it denotes an instrument.

"And for the sake of making the compound obligatory": by the rule "of words meaning injury" (*hiṃsārthānām*), when *ṇamul* is added, a compound would be optional according to the rule "the [words] beginning with the third case, optionally" (*tṛtīyāprabhṛtīny anyatarasyām*). Therefore, the meaning is that even in the sense of injury, the compound must be desired by this very [present rule] when *ṇamul* is added.

But how can [the desired result] be obtained even when it is intended, given that this rule (*vidhi*) finds its scope (*avakāśa*) in the verb *han* when used in the sense of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), whereas for the rule "of those meaning violence" (*hiṃsārthānām*), the scope is the sense of violence other than *han*; and since both rules would apply when *han* is used in the sense of violence, the latter rule alone would prevail by virtue of being subsequent? To this, he says: "by means of a prior exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*).

How then will the example "daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kālayati" (he drives the cows, striking them with a stick) or "daṇḍenopaghātam" be illustrated under the rule *hiṃsārthānām*? On this point, they say: its scope is that case where a single verbal root-meaning, being differentiated through the relation of general and particular, undergoes the status of qualifier and qualified; for there is the rule: "In the case of *kaṣ* and others, the subsequent use [of the root] is according to the original form. However, when there is a connection between two entirely distinct root-meanings, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs by that very [rule].

And thus, the meaning of "always forming a compound" (*nityasamāsa*) is the same as the meaning of "the subsequent application according to the rule" (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*); what is the meaning? The meaning is that being for the purpose of the subsequent application according to the rule is the meaning of always forming a compound.

In this case, both the inclusion of *dvārāṅga* (the door-frame) and the inclusion of *samūla* (with the root) are being performed; however, these could have been accomplished all at once. How so? I would have stated it thus: "After the roots *graha* and *kṛñ* when used with *jīva* and *akṛta* [respectively]; after *piṣ* when used with *śuṣka*, *cūrṇa*, and *rukṣa*; after *kaṣ* when used with *nimūla*; and after *han* when used with *samūla*—and by the word *ca* ('and'), *kaṣ* is also included; then, for the instrumental case, simply 'after *han*'. Furthermore, that which was stated as "in the case of *kaṣ* and the others, there is the subsequent application of the verb according to its original form" (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*) should have been stated as "in the case of *grah* and the others. But it was not done in that way. Thus it stands.
The root √piṣ takes the suffix *kha* when used in the sense of "smearing. (Pāṇini 3.4.38)

He states that by the word "vyākhyāna" (explanation), the meaning "snehana" (moistening) is understood, saying: "expressive of moistening. Regarding "udapeṣam": the substitution of *uda* for *udaka* occurs by the rule "peṣaṃ-vāsa-vāhana-dhiṣu ca. In the case of "śuṣka-cūrṇa," the mention of "snehana" was not made; there, the suffix is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), whereas here it is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *vṛt* when preceded by *hasta*, provided that the sense is "taking hold. (Pāṇini 3.4.39)

It was not stated [in the rule] "jīve grahaḥ, haste ca, vartteśca" that there is an object (karma) as a secondary word; however, in this case, it is the instrument (karaṇa). The root *vṛt* is here taken with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*). The very mention [of the word *hastavarttam*] is the proof for this. The phrase "he causes the hand-cylinder to revolve" means he revolves with his hand, that is, he makes a ball.
The [augment] *puṭ* is applied after the word *sva*. 3.4.40.
Regarding "svapoṣam": [the rule] applies even when the word is used in its own form, provided it is a synonym for *pitṛ* (father).
In the case of *saṃjñā* (a name), [the suffix *cha* is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.4.42)

This undertaking is for the purpose of excluding the sense of "location" (*anadhikaraṇārtha*), whereas the preceding rule was for the purpose of excluding "technical names" (*asaṃjñārtha*). How then is it that we have the form *grāme bandhaḥ*? It will be formed by the application of the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) which permits the suffix *ghañ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after verbal roots ending in *a* when they denote the agent, provided that the agent is neither the individual soul (*jīva*) nor Śiva. 3.4.43.

"Perished by the living soul (jīva)" means that he has met with calamity through the instrumentality of the living soul. "Carried away by a person (puruṣa)" means that Devadatta or another has been brought to another place through the instrumentality of that person.
After the word *śuṣi*, [the suffix *pu*] is applied when it means "full. (Pāṇini 3.4.44)

"Ārdhvaśoṣaṃ śuṣyati" means that it withers while standing upright; the meaning is that trees and the like wither while remaining in an upward position. "Ūrdhvaḥ pūryate" means that it is filled while facing upwards; the meaning is that jars and the like become full of rainwater and so forth while being oriented with their openings upward.
The word *upadaṃśa* [is compounded] with a word in the third case-ending. (Pāṇini 2.1.30)

From this point onward, there is also the case of prior time [expressed by the instrumental]. For example: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* ("He eats with a radish as a side-dish"). Now, one might object: "In this case, there is no connection between the word ending in the third case and the word *upadaṃśin*; for it is not something else that is 'sided' (*upadaśyate*) by the radish; what then? That very same thing [the food] is 'sided. However, a connection with the verb *bhuj* (to eat) is indeed possible."

Since that [root] functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), however, because there is no semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*) with the *upapada*, the suffix would not be applicable, and the designation of *upapada* would not occur; due to the absence of that, even the *upapada-samāsa* compound would not be applicable. But would there not be scope for the rule in cases such as "he eats after showing with his teeth" (*daśanair upadaśya bhuṅkte*)? To this, he says: "and *mūlaka*, etc. (*mūlakādi*).

It is true that there is no verbal (śābda) connection between the act of eating (*bhuj*) and the radish (*mūlaka*) and so forth; however, when there is a requirement for an object (*karman*) for the act of eating, a factual relationship certainly exists due to proximity and semantic compatibility. Otherwise, its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the act of eating would not be logically established. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: "He eats with a radish. Having done what? Having used it as a side-dish (*upadaṃśya*). Using what as a side-dish? That very same radish.

If, however, this suffix were intended only where there is a verbal connection (śābda-anvaya) with that which ends in the third case, he would have simply said "in the instrument" (*karaṇe*), as in the rule *hanaḥ karaṇe*. Therefore, when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) through a logical (ārtha) relationship, everything—including the suffix—will take place.
And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after verbs having the sense of *artha*, provided they have the same object (*samānakarmaka*). 3.4.48.

Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe*), it is understood that there must be identity of object with the root used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*); thus he says: "of those [roots] which have the same object as the root used in subsequent application. *Kālayati*. The root *kala* meaning "to throw" (*vikṣepe*) belongs to the *cur*-class (*curādi*). *Daṇḍatāḍam*. The root *taḍa* meaning "to strike" (*āghāte*) likewise belongs to the *cur*-class. In *upahatya*, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) by the rule "optionally when *lyap* follows" (*vā lyapi*), and the augment *tuk* after the short vowel.
In the locative case, [the suffix *kha*] is applied after [roots ending in] *upapīḍa*, *rudha*, and *karṣa*.

The word *upa* applies to each [of the following]. Having formed a collective *dvandva* compound of "pīḍā" and the others, there is a compound with the prefix *upa-* where the final member is elided, as in the rule "pīḍa-rudha-karṣa. The masculine gender used in the Sūtra is for metrical reasons. Regarding the case endings for the prefixes, two types appear depending on whether one intends to express them as instruments (*karaṇa*) or loci (*adhikaraṇa*). The term "of *karṣati*" refers to the root belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, and not to the root *kṛṣ* of the *tudādigaṇa*; this is known because the reference is made by means of the suffix *śap*, which indicates that the guṇa substitution has already been applied. The use of the suffix *śap* is understood from the fact that the form is uttered with the guṇa already prescribed.

In the Sūtra, however, the nominative case is used in the sense of the ablative. Furthermore, what would be the consequence if there were a reference to the root belonging to the Tudādi class? For since both roots have the meaning "to scratch" (*vilekhana*), there is neither a difference in meaning nor a difference in form. Even though both are recited with the meaning of scratching, nevertheless, the root of the Tudādi class functions in the context of scratching a field—as in "he plows with five ploughs" (*pañcabhir halaiḥ kṛṣati*). Therefore, when one has plowed in the field and then plowed with a plough, only the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the Tudādi root, not the suffix *ṇamul*.
In the case of proximity. 3.4.50.

"In the seventh [case], the third [case] is understood to carry over. Even in the previous rule, the third case carries over precisely because it is marked with a *svarita* accent; however, the particle *ca* is employed so that its cessation might not be understood in the seventh case. Therefore, one should not raise the objection that "what is drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) does not carry over to what follows. [The phrase is] "due to the intensity of battle" (*yuddhasaṃrambhāt*).

*Saṃrambha* is a transformation of speech and body preceded by mental agitation caused by anger and the like. *Yuddhasaṃrambha* is a *ṣaṣṭhī*-compound (genitive compound) meaning "strife for the sake of battle," similar to the term *aśvaghāsa* ("grass for horses"). The meaning is that they fight while being extremely close together. Whether this mention of "seizing by the hair" is intended to illustrate such close proximity or not, it is immaterial.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a word denoting a measure. 3.4.51.

"Only [the words] *tṛtīyā* and *saptamī* [are understood]"—this is a demonstration of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the sense, for no such word has been introduced in the context. "An elevation of two finger-breadths" (*dvyaṅgulotkarṣam*): the combination of two fingers is *dvyaṅgulam*; by the rule "*tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.4.86), the compound suffix *ac* is applied. The meaning is: having elevated and measured by two finger-breadths. "Short pieces" (*hrasvāḥ khaṇḍāḥ*) means small fragments (*khaṇḍikāḥ*).
[The sūtra] "In the ablative case when there is a desire for speed" (Pāṇini 3.4.52).

Regarding *parīpsā* (desire for haste): the root *tvar* is included in the *ghaṭādi* group according to the rule *ñitvarā saṃbhrame*; since it is marked with the *ṣi*-sign by the rule *ghaṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ*, it takes the suffix *aṅ*. Regarding *śayyotthāyam*: by the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ*, the *s* of the root *sthā* is replaced by *t*, as explained previously. Regarding "even that which must necessarily be done": this refers to such acts as washing one's eyes and so forth. [The rule applies] only when there is a second sense of haste (*parīpsā*).

In the rule "anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam" (P. 6.1.158), there is indeed a sense of urgency (*parīpsā*). How so? This is a *paribhāṣā* (a metarule), and the mention of the word "pada" is for the purpose of the *paribhāṣā*. Therefore, wherever an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent is prescribed, at that very moment, with the exception of one vowel, the remainder must be made unaccented (*anudātta*); one must not delay.
[The suffix *kan* is applied after a word denoting] one's own limb (*svāṅga*), provided that it is not permanent (*adhruva*).

The definition of its own limb (*svāṅga*) will be stated in the fourth [chapter]: "that which is not liquid, possesses form," and so forth. Regarding the term *akṣinikāṇam*: the root *kaṇ* (meaning "to close") belongs to the *curādigaṇa* when preceded by the prefix *ni*. Regarding the phrase "having raised his head, he speaks": one might object that *dhruva* means "eternal," as in "the sky is eternal, the earth is eternal"; whereas *adhruva* means "non-eternal" or "impermanent," and the head is indeed impermanent because living beings themselves are impermanent. To this, he replies: "in which limb... [and so on].

The meaning is as follows: by the force of the qualification, excellence (*prakarpa*) is intended; that which is non-permanent even when excellent. And this excellence refers to the fact that [the thing] may at some time cease to exist while the living being is still alive.
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a word ending in the locative case when it means "being afflicted. (Pāṇini 3.4.55)

Regarding the term *parikliśyamāna*: this is the form of the root *kliś* meaning "to afflict" (*kliśū vibādhane*), and not of the root *kliś* meaning "to suffer pain" (*kliśa upatāpe*). He explains that the prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides," thus stating: "affliction (*parikleśa*) is oppression from every direction."
The roots *viśi*, *pati*, *pad*, and *skand* are used in the sense of pervading (*vyāpyamāna*) and frequenting (*āsevyamāna*). 3.4.56.

"Without parts" (*anavayavena*) means "in its entirety. "Of the objects" (*padārthānām*) refers to houses and so forth. "Intent" (*tātparyam*) means repetition or frequency (*ābhīkṣṇyam*). By the phrase "pervasion in the case of a substance" (*dravye vyāptiḥ*), etc., he shows the distinction between the domains of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and practice (*āsevā*). Regarding "entering the house," one might object: "Since repetition is understood in the case of pervasion and constancy in the case of practice, the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* would require reduplication; why does it not occur here? To this he replies: "By means of the compound" (*samāsena*).

Although a compound is not prescribed for these two meanings, nevertheless, by their very nature, they are expressed by it, as in *saptaparvā* ("seven-jointed"). This refers to the repetition (*vīpsā*) inherent in the joints—as in "there are seven leaves on every joint" (*parvaṇi parvaṇi sapta parṇāny asya*). And so he will state [later]: the author of the Bhāṣya will state this under the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*. The term "permanence" (*nityatā*) is an illustration; it should also be understood to include "indeclinable formations" (*avyayakṛt*).

"If it is argued that [the rule] is for the purpose of excluding *ktvā*": the meaning is this—if it is argued that since both *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed by the rule "In the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*), *ṇamul* also," then *ṇamul* alone should occur after roots such as *viś* and others, and for the sake of ensuring that the suffix *ktvā* does not occur, *ṇamul* is stated again. He refutes this: "Because it is desired. For it is indeed desired that *ktvā* occurs after roots such as *viś* in the sense of repeated action (habitual action)—as in: "He remains having entered the house again and again" (*geham anupraviśya anupraviśya āste*). "Then it is for the sake of the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) as the accompanying word (*upapada*)."

For here, by virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "and in the case of the second [case-ending]," that which ends in the second case obtains the designation *upapada*. Why, then, is the status of being an *upapada* desired? To this he says: "the compound with an *upapada*" (*upapadasamāsa*). It is stated that [this occurs] optionally because of the rule "the third case and those following are optional. For by that [rule], when there is an absence of an *upapada*, [the compound does not apply]; since there is no word whatsoever situated in the seventh case [that could serve as an *upapada*].
The seventh case ending is used for words expressing time when they denote an interval between two actions, provided that the roots *as* (to throw) and *tṛṣ* (to thirst) are not involved.

The root *asu* is used in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*), and *tṛṣ* in the sense of "thirst" (*pipāsāyām*). [The term] *kriyāntara* means that which "interrupts an action. From the word *antara*, which signifies "interposition," the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "one who performs that" (*tat karoti*), followed by the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. Thus, from the root *pā* (to drink), with the addition of *ṇic*, the form *pāyayati* is derived; the augment *yuk* is applied according to the rule *śācchāsāhvā* etc. Regarding the phrase "by excessive drinking" (*atyasanena*) and so forth: because it occurs between the drinking that takes place today and the drinking that will take place after two days have passed, it is situated in the interval between those two acts of drinking and thirsting. Clarifying this very point, he states the meaning of the example: "having made him drink today," and so forth.

Regarding *dvyahamupoṣya*: the suffix *lyap* is applied to the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *upa*, with *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) occurring because it belongs to the *yajādi* class; the change to *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*. Here, eating is interrupted by fasting. Regarding *ahar* (day): the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*. The meaning is that he has passed the entire day, having cast [the meal] away. Regarding *yojanamatyasya*: the meaning is that having made [the child] drink [milk] somewhere, such as Sṛghna, he then makes him drink after having gone beyond a *yojana*.
The suffix *śas* is applied after words beginning with *nāman* and *ādiśigraha*.
Regarding the phrase "ādiśer graheś ca": by this, he demonstrates that the prefix *āṅ* is connected only with the root *diś*, and not with *grah*.
After the root *kṛ*, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are used when an indeclinable (*avyaya*) expresses something that was not intended.

In the phrase "ayathābhipretākhyāne," the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) is understood from its subsequent placement; otherwise, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, it would have been placed first. Furthermore, the word *ayathābhipreta* is an adverbial modifier of the action of telling (*ākhyāna*); the meaning is "telling in a manner that is not as intended. For example, having approached a Brahmin who was praying for the birth of a son, someone told him in a low voice as if it were a secret: "O Brahmin, a son has been born to you. Unable to bear this, the Brahmin asked: "What then? (i.e., what do you mean?)

Although the announcement of the birth of a son is pleasant, it serves as an example because the manner of the announcement is unintended; thus it is said to be an "announcement not intended," and not an "unpleasant announcement. Regarding the form *ācakṣe*: this is the present tense (*laṭ*), with the suffix *thās* changed to *se*, the elision of the *śap* augment, the elision of the letter *ka* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, and the change of *ṣa* and *ḍha* to *ka* before *si*. In the example, he demonstrates the announcement that was not intended: "uccairnāma... (by name Uccaiḥśravas).

The word *nāma* [is used] in the sense of "well-known"; furthermore, this was stated in the rule "upadaṃśas-tṛtīyāyām" [Pāṇini 3.4.47] as "the statement is for the sake of forming a compound. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*).

In the rule *ktvā ca*, the phrase *tṛtīyāprabhṛtīnyanyatarasyām* ("the words beginning with the third case [are optionally compounded]") is understood to carry over. Therefore, by this [rule], compounding is obtained only in the alternative (*pakṣe*) for that *ktvā* which is prescribed [by *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle ktvā*], but not for that [form] prescribed by the rule concerning "common [agent]" (*samāna-*) and so forth; for the meaning is that *ktvā* is not prescribed by that [latter rule] when words beginning with the third case are present as attendant words (*upapada*). The mention of *ṇamul* is redundant, because it is already under discussion there; should it not rather have been stated as *ktvā ca*? To this he replies: "The section on *ṇamul*" and so forth. "Equal status" (*tulyakakṣatva*) means equal strength (*tulyabalatva*).

"Teneti," and so forth. If, however, *ṇamul* were attracted by the word "ca" (and), it would not carry over to the subsequent rule, because there would be no effort [to do so]. But when *ṇamul* is mentioned again, the carrying over of both elements specified in the *dvandva* compound to the subsequent rule is established.
The suffix *ap* is applied after a word denoting an animal (*tiryak*) to express exclusion (*apavarga*).

Regarding the term *tiryakṛtya*: [it is derived] from *tiro'ñcati* (he goes across). By the rule *ṛtvig-ādi*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule *tirasastiryalope*, the substitute *tiryak* is applied. This is merely an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*); however, there is no meaning for the individual components here, for this whole word (*samudāya*) refers to completion (*apavarga*), as has been shown. The meaning is "having finished" or "having gone. Thus, *tiryakṛtya* means "having made crooked," that is, having cast to the side what was standing in front.

The formulation "tiryaci" is incorrect; for if the designation *bha* were applied, the vowel *a* would be elided by the rule "acaḥ," and the form should have been *tiraścī*. To this he replies: "This [form] 'tiryacī' is an imitation of the word. The term "ac" refers to the meaningful sound *aj*; and that meaning is understood as it is well-known in common usage, according to the maxim: "Those whose meanings are clearly manifest, which are independent, and renowned in the world [are accepted]. Therefore, there is an elision of the *a* of the root *añc* when it occurs in its own sense.

This, however, is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form of the word as it exists there; therefore, it possesses meaning by virtue of that imitated form, but not by virtue of its worldly meaning. The implication is that for this reason, there is no elision (*lopa*). Now, even so, since it is said that "an imitation is like the original (*prakṛti*)," elision would indeed still apply; to this he says: "And an imitation need not necessarily be like the original. Why? He says: "Because it would result in the destruction of the form being imitated."

The meaning is that the form one intends to imitate would not be perceived as such; rather, only the worldly (secular) meaning would be perceived. To show where an imitation occurs just like the original (*prakṛti*), he says: "In *etado’ś*," etc. If the imitation were to occur just like the original even when the form being imitated is destroyed, then in both cases—*etadaḥ* and *adasaḥ*—once the original’s grammatical operations such as the substitution of *yatva* for pronouns have taken effect, the forms would become *etasya* and *amuṣya*.

Is it not the case that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) follows the purpose? If so, does this [substitution] not result in the elision [of the final vowel]? How so? In the case of *yattadetebhyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad*; in *asyavāmīyam*, there is the elision of the suffix *yasya*; in *gavityayamāha*, there is the substitution of *ava*; and in *paṭiti karoti*, although the form being imitated is destroyed, there occurs the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) by the rule "for an unmanifest imitation, when *ataḥ* followed by *itau*."

Therefore, since both types of instruction are observed, it must be stated that in some cases an imitation follows the original form (*prakṛti*), while in others it does not. And thus, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this very sūtra, it says: "This is a technical (sautra) expression."
When a reflexive limb is the object, the suffix *kha* is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*, provided that the suffix *ta* follows.

He states that "tas-pratyaye" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, explaining: "that [limb] from which a suffix beginning with *ta* occurs is thus designated. Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that a limb would be considered a *svāṅga* even when it is not currently ending in such a suffix, merely because it was previously seen to end in one—as happens with the rule "the *ku* [substitution] for the suffix *kvip*"—because of the force of the explicit mention of the suffix beginning with *ta* (*tas-pratyaya-grahaṇa*). Alternatively, this may be a *karmadhāraya*: "when a limb is present as an upapada before a suffix beginning with *ta*. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, only the bare fact is shown.

"In this case, a correspondence according to numerical order (yathāsaṃkhya) is not intended," because of the [author's] explanation. Regarding the word *mukhataḥ*: the suffix *tasi* occurs in the sense of the locative case because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādyādi*.

Thus, [the derivation is] from the root *tasu* meaning "to perish" (*upakṣaye*), with the word *mukha* as an attendant word (*upapada*), and the suffix *kvip* by the rule "it is seen after other [roots] as well. Hence, *mukhataḥ*. The lengthening of the vowel [as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.14, *atvasantasya ca*] does not occur here, because of the prohibition [by 6.4.14, *adhātoḥ*].

Since the non-application [of the lengthening] is already established by the paribhāṣā "the technical name *pratyaya* applies only to what is actually a suffix," there is no purpose in the explicit mention of the word *pratyaya* [in that sūtra].
The suffix *kyaṅ* is not applied after a word ending in *na*, when the sense of "becoming" (*cvyartha*) is intended.

"Not having an object" (*nārtha*) means that neither the substratum (*ādhāra*) nor the object (*artha*) associated with the substratum is expressed by the two words [beginning with] *na*. That which has no object is "objectless" (*nārtha*); this is the meaning. By this, "having an object" (*sārtha*) is explained. [The compound] "that from which there is a suffix" (*pratyaya-yasmāt*).

If the analysis (vigraha) were made using the ablative case (pañcamī), then the mention of the "base" (prakṛti) would not serve as an indicator for the inclusion of the suffix *nañ*; thus, even though the suffix does not end in that [ablative], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its application to the base alone. It is not such a consequence; for if it were so, one would have to state "vinañ-saṅkhyāsu," and the analysis should rather be made using the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī): "that composite whose part is a suffix having the sense of 'not' (*nañ*)."

Alternatively, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *lyablope* should be explained as referring to that aggregate with respect to which a suffix having the sense of separation (*nādhārtha*) is prescribed. [Examples include: *vinākṛtya*, *nānākṛtya*—here the suffixes *nānāñ* and *añ* are applied by the rule *vinañbhyāṃ nānāñau na saha*. [The example] *dvidhākṛtya* is formed by the rule *saṅkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*. [The example] *dvaidhaṃkṛtya* is formed by the rule *dvitryośca dhamuñ*. The words *hirak* and *pṛthak* signify "without" (*vinārthe*).

"Having made the pieces of wood separate, he has gone. This means that the pieces of wood were already separate, and having placed them elsewhere, he has gone. Regarding the statement "the mention of *artha* is for the sake of the meaning": there are indeed many suffixes (*pratyaya*) whose meaning is to be conveyed (*dhārtha*). In the absence of the mention of *artha*, only the suffix itself would be understood, and not the others; however, by mentioning *artha*, those [meanings] are also included.

The inclusion of the word *artha* is for the sake of that which is an *ādeśa* (substitute) having the meaning of *dha*, according to the rule: "The suffix *ḍa* is seen after a stem ending in *dhamuñ* in its own sense"—as in *dvaidhakṛtya*, *dvaidhakāram*, *dvaidhabhūya*, and *dvaidhabhāvam*. As for the suffixes *dhamuñ* and the rest, [the required form] is established simply through the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (treated like the original), because in the formulation of those rules, one resorts to the view of substitution (*ādeśapakṣa*) by means of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "when *dha* follows. Now, why is the inclusion of the word *artha* not also for the sake of the *artha* (meaning) itself? To this he says: "But *na* is indeed only one."

But surely there are two types of suffixes that are not *pratyaya*s: those without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*) and those with an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*). In that case, if the term "meaning" (*artha*) were not mentioned, would not only the suffix without an indicatory letter be understood, and not the other? It is thought thus: by resorting to one of the methods—*tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*—the [suffix with an indicatory letter] will also be included.
The suffix *anvac* is used in the sense of conformity (*anulomya*).

Regarding the term *anvagbhūya*: the meaning is that one remains having become favorable—either from the front, the side, or the back. Regarding *anvagbhūya*: the meaning is having come behind. One is not touched by the expression "favorable" or "unfavorable."
The suffix *tumun* is used after the roots *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, *jñā*, *glā*, *ghaṭ*, *rabh*, *labh*, *kram*, *sah*, and *arh*, when they have the sense of "being able" (*asti-artha*).

In this context, the word *artha* is connected specifically with the word *asti*, because *ghaṭa* and so forth are mentioned separately from *śak*, *dhṛṣ*, and *jñā*. Thus he says: "when *śak* and others are the governing words (*upapada*), or when they have the sense of *asti*. [The suffix] *tumun* occurs; that is, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). The purpose of this rule is for cases where the governing word does not denote an action, since [the suffix would otherwise be] established by the rule "when a word denoting an action is the governing word, *tumun* and *ṇvul* [occur]" (Pāṇini 3.3.10). In that regard, in the examples *śaknoti bhoktum*, *dharṣṇoti*, and *jānāti*, proficiency in eating is understood.

"He is weary of eating" (*glāyati bhoktum*)—here there is incapacity (*aśakti*). "He is fit for it" (*ghaṭate arhati*)—this is capability (*yogyatā*). "He begins," "he undertakes"—these are the initial stages of the act of eating itself. "He obtains [the opportunity] to eat" (*labhate bhoktum*)—the meaning is that he obtains food that has not been refused. "He exerts himself to eat" (*utsahate bhoktum*)—the meaning is that he applies himself to the act of eating. "There is [an occasion] to eat" (*asti bhoktum*)—the meaning is that food exists.
In expressions such as "skilled at eating," "proficient at eating," or "dexterous at eating," when sufficiency (*paryāpti*) is intended, the suffix *tumun* occurs by the subsequent rule.
In words expressing sufficiency, when they have the sense of "being able" (alam). Pāṇini 3.4.66.

*Paryāptiḥ* means non-deficiency, that is to say, completeness. Non-deficiency occurs in two ways: either through the abundance of food, or through the capacity of the eater. Therefore, he qualifies it with the word *alam*, which signifies capacity. [The rule] states: "in the sense of *alam*, when words expressing sufficiency (*paryāpti*) are used. For example: *prayāpto bhoktum* ("sufficient to eat"). This means one is capable of eating and does not fall short in the act of eating. *Paryāptam* means "abundant."
"It can be done thus" means that this is easy to perform; or rather, what is intended here is mere possibility—that the performance of such a thing is indeed possible.
A *kṛt* suffix [is applied] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Pāṇini 3.4.67.

For what purpose is this stated? Because it is understood that the suffixes denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) express their own meaning (*svārtha*) when they are taught in a specific rule. Where a meaning is indicated by a specific rule, there the suffix occurs in the sense of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) itself due to proximity; for example: "The suffix *saN* [is added] after roots ending in *gup*, *tij*, and *kit*" and "The suffix *kaN* [is added] after *yāva* and so forth. Thus, these [suffixes] would apply in their own meaning; [this statement is made] so that they do not apply in their own meaning, but rather in the sense of the agent.

But is it not the case that when one desires [the suffix] for the sake of the action itself (*bhāva*), he says: "The *ghañ* occurs in the sense of the action"? That will be for the purpose of restriction—namely, that *ghañ* alone occurs in the sense of the action, and no other *kṛt* suffix. For if this sūtra did not exist, only the sūtra "ghañ" would have to be formulated—meaning "ghañ occurs after a verbal root"—and in that case, since no specific meaning is specified, *ghañ* would occur only in the sense of the action (*bhāva*).

Then, the second rule, "padarujaviśa," should be formulated, and the rule "bhāve" need not be formulated. However, if it were formulated, it would serve as a restrictive rule (niyama), meaning that the suffix ghañ occurs only in the sense of an abstract action (bhāva) and no other kṛt suffix does so. Consequently, other kṛt suffixes will occur when the agent is implied by the meaning of the verbal root. An objection might be raised: since the object and other grammatical relations are also implied by the meaning of the verbal root, would kṛt suffixes not also occur in those senses? No; [they do not].

In the rules "the suffix *ṣṭran* [is used] after a root signifying action in the sense of the object" (*dhaḥ karmaṇi ṣṭran*), "the suffix *lyuṭ* [is used] in the sense of the instrument or the locus" (*karaṇādhikaraṇayor lyuṭ*), "the suffixes *dāśat* and *ghāt* [are used] in the sense of the recipient" (*dāśagāghnau sampradāne*), and "the suffixes *bhīma*, etc., [are used] in the sense of the point of departure" (*bhīmādayo 'pādāne*), a restriction will be understood such that "*ṣṭran* alone [is used] in the sense of the object, and no other [suffix is used in that sense]," and so forth. If it were the case that the grammatical relation (e.g., the object) is fixed while the suffixes are not, then suffixes like *ṣṭran* might occur even when another kāraka is intended. This is not a fault; for...

This is a single statement: "The suffix *ṣṭran* occurs after [roots] ending in *dh* in the sense of the object (*karman*). How then could that which is prescribed for the object occur in another *kāraka*? Alternatively, a second restriction will be understood: "*ṣṭran* occurs only in the sense of the object. This applies everywhere. As for any other suffix remaining from this point onward, it will occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) even without an explicit statement.

In both rules—"kṛtari bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau" and "kartari ca ṛṣi-devatayoḥ"—the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) is solely for the purpose of the injunction, intended to exclude the instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, there will be no restriction regarding the agent in the case of suffixes such as *khiṣṇuc*. Is that then the very purpose—namely, that these suffixes should not occur in their own primary sense (*svārtha*)? But was it not already stated that "the restriction will be understood as applying to the abstract state (*bhāve*)"? That "state" other than the primary sense is what is called the "accomplishment" (*siddhatā*) of the root-meaning.

[The opponent argues: "They [the *l*-suffixes] would be used in their own sense (*svārtha*) by the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.69). In that case, this restriction (*niyama*) will apply: 'only *l*-suffixes [are used] in the impersonal sense (*bhāva*)'? [Reply: This restriction cannot be understood, because since the *l*-suffixes have already been assigned their meanings through the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), they would not occur in their own sense; therefore, this [rule] must be for the purpose of stating 'after intransitive verbs' (*akarmakebhyaḥ*). Thus it has been well said: 'The statement that *kṛt*-suffixes [denote] the agent is for the sake of understanding their own sense when there is no specific designation [of agent or object]."

And here there is a dilemma: would the meaning be assigned by this [sūtra] subsequently to those words formed by their own prescriptive rules independent of this statement—namely, those derived from the *kṛt* suffixes such as "the *ṇvul* and *tṛc* suffixes are used in the sense of the agent," or "the *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* suffixes are used in the sense of the agent" after roots like *nandi*, *grahi*, and *pac*? Or would this [sūtra] be a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the original rules for the production of *kṛt* suffixes? Regarding the first position, just as the meaning is assigned by this [sūtra] to the *tṛc* suffixes and others, it would likewise have to be assigned to the *khyun* suffixes and others as well, because no distinction is made.

Consequently, these suffixes would also apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) by this rule, because in their respective prescriptive rules (*vidhivākya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors are also mentioned, and thus they would apply to the instrument and so forth as well. Now, one might object: "In the case of suffixes such as *khyun* and others, since the meaning of the instrument and so forth is specifically prescribed (*viśeṣavihitatvāt*), it will set aside the agent. This is not so, because the rules constitute distinct sentences (*nānāvākyatvāt*). In this world, when it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," because the time is the same, it is a single sentence that conveys a qualified act of giving; thus, the buttermilk sets aside the curd.

But when, in the context of feeding Brahmins during the forenoon, it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins," and in the afternoon, "Let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya," there is no relationship of sublation (bādhyabādhakabhāva) at that time. Likewise, even in this view, because two sentences are uttered at different times, a relationship of sublation is not obtained. Therefore, since this position is indeed faulty, he states—relying on the second position—the following: "This [general rule] shall be a supplement (śeṣa) to the originative injunctions of the kṛt-affixes."

Is the previously mentioned fault not still in force? To this he replies: "In those [sentences]... and so forth. Why is this so? He says: "Because they require a meaning. Those sentences in which a meaning is not explicitly stated are those that require a meaning (*arthākāṅkṣāṇi*).

For instance: when it is stated, "The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur," an expectancy regarding their meaning arises: "In what [meaning] do these two occur? And there is an expectancy for the rule "A *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*): "Which *kṛt* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent? Therefore, when rules such as those prescribing *tṛc* and others are not present, they come to that very place from there for the sake of satisfying the mutual expectancy between both the subsidiary (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*). This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "in the sentences concerning *khyun* and so on": the word "they come" (*upatiṣṭhante*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).

He states the reason: "Because when there is a direct indication of the meaning, they [the suffixes] are devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). Nor is it appropriate for the rule to apply by raising an expectancy according to the analogy of the "red cloth" (*raktapaṭa*), since the remainder [of the word] already fulfills its purpose through its own inherent expectancy (*svata eva sākāṅkṣe*) without the application of the rule for the *tṛc*-suffix and others. In the case of "The red cloth exists" (*raktaḥ paṭo bhavati*), although the phrase "the cloth exists" is itself devoid of expectancy, there is a syntactic connection by raising an expectancy because the referent of the word "red" (*rakta*) possesses expectancy.

Nor should it be asked how there can be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) for those [rules] situated in different parts of the treatise; for in this science (*śāstra*), even for subordinate sentences located in different places, syntactic unity is observed by virtue of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). For example: elision (*luk*) is taught in the second chapter, while its exceptions (*apavāda*) regarding non-elision (*aluk*) in the fourth and sixth chapters are stated as "non-elision before a *gotra* name ending in *ac*" (*gotre 'luc aci*) and "non-elision when the following member is a word" (*aluk uttarapade*).
Or [the suffix -ya] is applied after the words *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, *upasthānīya*, *janya*, *āplāvya*, and *āpātya*. || 3.4.68 ||

Regarding *bhavya*: by the rule *aco yat*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs, and by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye*, the *vānta* substitute (*au*) is applied. In the example *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("the boy is to be sung [to] with the Sāmans"), this shows that this is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) of the root *kai* or *gai* in the sense of "sound," and not of *gāṅ* in the sense of "motion. This is obtained through the *nipātana*. By the rule *īdyati*, the change to *ī* occurs. Regarding *janya*: here, by the statement "there is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for *taki*, *śasi*, *cati*, *yati*, and *janī*" under the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied. Regarding *āplāvya*: by the rule *orāvaśyake*. Regarding *āpātya*: by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
The suffix *la* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) and also in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) after intransitive verbs (*akarmaka*).

He dispels the doubt that the term *laḥ* might generally denote both the *laṅ* and *laṭ* suffixes (which have the marker *a*) as well as the singular number—by stating that "the single general form *la*, with its markers discarded, is what is grasped," and that this is the nominative plural. [Objection: Even though the general category is one, according to the rule "the plural is used for a single thing when expressing a genus" (*jātyākhyāyāmekasmin bahuvacanam*), why is it not accepted as the genitive singular in relation to the substitutes (*ādeśa*), such that *laḥ* would mean "that which is the substitute for *laḥ*," just as in the rule "*laḥ parasmaipadam*" [Pāṇini 1.4.99]? [Reply: It is said:

If it were understood in this way, the meaning of the *lādeśas* (substitutes for *l*) would be indicated by this [sūtra], and consequently, the meaning of the *lakāra* occurring in a context other than *ām* would not be specified; moreover, *luk* (elision) is an *ādeśa* (substitute). And it is not appropriate to assign a meaning to that which has the form of an elision (*luṅ*); therefore, it [the *lakāra*] would apply only to the agent according to the rule "kṛt suffixes occur in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*). [Objection: But surely, once its [the *ām*] elision has occurred by the rule "of *ām*" (*āmaḥ*), the manifestation of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and so forth will take place through those very *lādeśas* used in the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)? [Reply: This is not so.

Since it is established that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) has no other scope than the agent (*kartṛ*) alone, then—due to this contradiction—an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) expressing the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) would not at all be applicable. Furthermore, since the connection is possible with the suffix as it is heard (*śruta*), it is not proper to supply (*adhyāhāra*) the term "substitute" (*ādeśa*). Therefore, it is correct that [the word] ends in the nominative plural. In that regard, the *lakāra* is of two kinds: that which results in a finite verb (*tiṅbhāvī*) and that which does not result in a finite verb (*atiṅbhāvī*).

In that regard, for those [kṛt suffixes] that do not occur after a finite verb (atiṅbhāvin), because the designation *kṛt* is prohibited, the rule "kṛt [suffixes] occur when the agent is expressed" (*kartari kṛt*) does not apply; consequently, they would result in being prescribed in their own sense as abstract action (*bhāva*). However, for those [kṛt suffixes] that do occur after a finite verb (tiṅbhāvin), by virtue of the statement "kṛt [suffixes] occur when the agent is expressed," they would be correct only in the sense of the agent, and not in the senses of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), as in examples such as *āsyamānam* and *śayyamānam*. It is for this reason that the present rule is commenced.

Now, an objection might be raised: "The *ātmanepada* endings are prescribed for the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), while the *parasmaipada* endings are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) from the remaining [roots]. Therefore, the meanings of the action, the object, and the agent will be inferred from the *l*-suffixes themselves. Alternatively, since these meanings do not co-occur with the use of the *l*-suffixes, they must belong to the substitutes (*ādeśas*) alone; so what is the purpose of this [rule]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "They do not occur in the sense of the action after transitive roots."
