Just as when this [term *bhāva*] is not being employed [in its technical sense], suffixes such as *ghañ* prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*) occur even after transitive roots—as in *odanasya pākaḥ* ("the cooking of rice") and *sūtrasya kṛtiḥ* ("the making of a thread")—so too, by the rule "for the abstract state and the object" (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would occur in the abstract state even after transitive roots. Consequently, the usage *pacyate yavāgūṃ devadattena* ("the gruel is being cooked by Devadatta") would result; therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced with the intention of stating: "and in the abstract state, after intransitive roots."

Now, if it were stated right there [in Pāṇini’s sūtra] that "the [kṛtya, kta, and khalartha suffixes] occur after an intransitive verb when expressing the state (bhāva) or the object (karman)," then the mention of "intransitive" (akarmaka) would have to be repeated there as well. But is it not already included here? It must certainly be included here: "Only after those two [verbs] do the kṛtya, kta, and khalartha suffixes occur in the sense of the state, and after intransitives [they occur] in the sense of the state. Therefore, it is established that this [present rule] is begun for the purpose of preventing these suffixes from occurring in the sense of the state after transitive verbs. Furthermore, this must also be stated for the sake of teaching the meaning of the l-suffixes whose scope has not yet been defined; otherwise, the aforementioned fault would follow. Enough of this.
The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khalartha* suffixes have those two meanings alone.

Regarding the phrase "of those two, the state (bhāva) and the object (karman)": the meaning is that in the preceding sūtra, the terms "state" and "object"—which were explicitly mentioned—are referred to by the pronoun *tat*, and not the agent (*kartṛ*) brought to mind by the particle *ca*. For this very reason, the subsequent sūtra states again, "and in the case of the agent. If, indeed, there were a reference here to both the agent and the state brought to mind by the particle *ca* in the immediately preceding sentence, then the mention of the "agent" would be redundant; for the agent would already be established by this [preceding] rule alone.

Regarding the phrase "the word *eva*," and so forth: since the suffixes known as *kṛtya* are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of being *kṛt* suffixes, they would normally apply to the agent; however, by the use of the word *eva*, the agent is drawn away—that is, excluded. Now, one might object: "Surely the exclusion of the agent will occur according to the logic of the case of Takra and Kauṇḍinya. For instance, as will be stated in the rule *vaḍavāyā vṛṣe vācye*—where [the suffix] is applicable to offspring, it is drawn away from that and prescribed for the bull (*vṛṣa*), while for offspring only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. True; this very meaning, which is already established by logical principle, is merely restated here by means of the word *eva*.

Regarding the form *śayitam*: because the rule "niṣṭhā-śīṅ-ṣvidi-midi-kṣvidi-dhṛṣaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.2.19] prescribes that the suffix *niṣṭhā* does not take the marker *k*, *guṇa* substitution occurs. Furthermore, the phrase "and in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) from intransitive verbs" is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. However, we say this: it has already been stated that the particle *eva* (in the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi ca...*) is not intended to exclude the agent; rather, its utility here is as follows: the *kṛtya* suffixes and others occur only for those two—neither more nor less—namely, the *bhāva* and *karman* for which the *l*-suffixes were previously mentioned. For if they were to apply to the abstract state (*bhāva*) even after transitive verbs, then the *kṛt* suffixes would not be restricted to those same two categories.
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), and it may also denote the agent (*kartṛ*).

The term *karmadhāraya* is used here, and since the word *karman* denotes "action," he explains: "the initial moment of action is *ādikarman*. However, the "object as the means of accomplishment" (*sādhanakarman*) is not intended here, because of the qualification by the word "initial" (*ādi*). When many things are gathered together, there exists the distinction of beginning, middle, and end; since the object as the means of accomplishment is always present, what would be the purpose of the word "initial" in that context? Therefore, it refers to that which is intended to be expressed as having become [accomplished] in the state of *ādikarman*.

By this [explanation], he shows that the suffix *kta* is established by the rule "niṣṭhā" itself for the beginning of an action (*ādikarma*), and not that one must specifically state that *niṣṭhā* occurs in the beginning of an action. For when the first moment of the action has occurred, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) itself becomes "past"—either through the superimposition of the form of a whole upon its parts, or according to the maxim that "the whole exists in its parts. Thus, the suffix *kta* is indeed appropriate in such cases as *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*, which means "Devadatta has begun the mat. In *prakṛtaṃ devadattena*, since the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and therefore the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*) itself. The same applies to *prabhuktaṃ devadattena*.
And [the *kta* suffix is used] after roots meaning "to go," after intransitive roots, and after the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.72)

Regarding "anūṣita": [the rule] "vasati-kṣudhor iṭ" applies. "Anujāta" means born after having approached. Likewise, "anujīrṇa. In these cases, when the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*) with respect to transitive roots (*sakarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
The [kṛt] suffixes *dāś* and *goghn* occur in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Pāṇini 3.4.73.

Regarding the term *goghna* ("cow-killer"): here, the root *han* functions in the sense of killing preceded by the act of giving (*dānapūrvaka*). Regarding *arghārha* ("worthy of the guest-offering"): *argha* refers to the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture); the killing of a cow is prescribed as an integral part (*aṅga*) of that rite. These are the occasions for the ritual slaughter (*ālambhana*) of a cow: a guest (*atithi*), the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*), and marriage (*vivāha*). If the form *goghna* were derived through the application of the rule for the recipient (*sampradāna*), then it would follow that even a *caṇḍāla* or similar person could be designated by that term; for friends and others are indeed worthy of giving a cow to such a person when he has arrived. Therefore, he says: "By the force of the technical derivation (*nipātanasāmarthyāt*)."
"And even when [the action] is absent" means that just as one who is not currently cooking is still called a "cook" by virtue of his fitness [for the task], so it is here as well.
The words *bhīma* and others [are used] in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*).

"These [words] end in *uṇādi* suffixes"—this was stated because they are the majority; for even *praskandana* and *prapatana* are derived from the *uṇādi* group. Thus, the prohibition (*paryudāsa*) "the *uṇādi* suffixes occur elsewhere than those two" would apply. Even if this rule did not exist, since the *ablative* (*apādāna*) is the subject under discussion, the reference "than those two" would not be appropriate; nevertheless, that meaning must indeed be stated there: namely, "the *uṇādi* suffixes occur elsewhere than that ablative," and consequently, the prohibition would certainly take effect—this is the sense.
The *uṇādi* suffixes occur after those two [roots] and others. 3.4.75.

But surely, even if it were stated that "elsewhere [the suffixes] uṇādi [are applied]," it would be understood from the context alone that they apply elsewhere than to those two? To this he says: "for the sake of the recipient" (*sampradāna*). By the example "kṛṣitaḥ" and so forth, he shows the occurrence [of the suffix] in the sense of the object (*karman*). Here, the introduction of the augment *iṭ* is to be considered; the same applies to "tanitaḥ."

Some say: "The prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* is not permanent (*anitya*), because of the addition of the marker *it* to the roots *kṛt* and *nṛt*. For that [marker] is added for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*; since the *iṭ* is already optional (*vibhāṣita*) there by the rule *se'sici kṛti*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by *yasya vibhāṣā* will occur anyway—so what is the use of adding the marker *it*?
Another says: "In the *curādi* group, the roots *kṛp* and *tan* should be read as ending in a short vowel (*adanta*)."

The [karmapravacanīya] *kta* [is used] in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after verbs whose meanings involve staying still (*dhrauvya*), motion (*gati*), or consumption (*pratyavasāna*). Pāṇini 3.4.76.

"Established in their own school" (*svanikāyaprasiddhiḥ*): Just as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *caṣāla* (the wooden ring on the top of the post), and so forth, are well-known only to ritualists (*yājñika*), so too is this [usage] established within the school of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). However, the inclusion of the word *pratyavasāna* in the *Nighaṇṭus* as a synonym for "eating" (*abhyavahāra*) is rooted in the usage established among grammarians. Regarding the phrase "this is their sitting" (*idameṣām āsitam*): the genitive case is used according to the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaś ca* ("and [it is used] after words denoting the locus").

As for the question beginning with "How? (*katham*): this is a question from one who considers the *niṣṭhā* suffix to denote the agent (*kartṛ*). "The vowel *a* has the sense of possession" (*matvarthīya*): the meaning is that the suffix *ac* is applied because the group beginning with *arśas* (*arśādigaṇa*) is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

In this [rule], the mention of roots meaning "motion" (*gati*) that are "intransitive" (*akarmaka*), as well as the mention of the suffix *kta*, are made twice; however, it could have been done only once. How so? I shall state it thus: "From roots meaning 'stability' (*dhrauvya*), 'motion' (*gati*), and 'eating' (*pratyavasāna*), [the suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Then, from roots meaning 'motion' that are 'intransitive', [it is used] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as well; because of the word 'and' (*ca*), also in the sense of the locus. Because the word 'and' is carried over (*anuvṛtta*), it is also used according to what is otherwise prescribed. Then, from the roots *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*, [it is used] in the sense of the agent; indeed, 'in the sense of the agent' applies here too. And from these [roots], the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent."

The word *ca* (and) implies that [the suffix *kta*] occurs both as it is already established [by previous rules] and [in this specific sense]; however, the mention of *adhikaraṇe* (locus) does not recur here because of the force of making a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). Therefore, in the sense of the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of the word *ca*, as well as as it is already established; hence [the forms] *dāśa* and *goghna* and so forth? But it was not done in that way.
[The suffix] *lasya* [is applied after a verbal root]. 3.4.77.

The letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and is not an *anubandha* (indicatory letter); otherwise, there would be the apprehension of only *laṅ* and *laṭ*. Consequently, the rules prescribing operations such as "for the parasmaipada endings, *ṇal* and so forth," "the *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*," and "for *e*, *uḥ*" would be untenable, because the *ti* and other suffixes of *liṅ* and *loṭ* would be absent. Thus, the mere *lakāra* is designated as the substitute. [Objection: But in that case, wouldn't elision (*lopa*) apply due to the designation of *it*? [Response: By the force of the explicit statement, even though the designation of *it* occurs, there will be no elision.

Even so, would not the *lit-svara* (the acute accent on the *li*-marker) apply? The insertion of the *li*-marker [in Pāṇini’s rules] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *lit-svara* does not apply to substitutes for *la*. Furthermore, what is this? This question is asked by one who thinks that there might be a reference to the letter *la* alone. With the intention of stating what will be explained later—that "the governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*) continues"—he says: "there are ten *lakāras*. The meaning is that they are designated by means of indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) such as *a*, which follow the same sequence as the vowels *a* and so forth in the traditional phonetic list (*akṣara-samāmnāya*), and not according to the order of their formal prescription.

Why does the inclusion of the letter *l* alone not apply? The intention is that it certainly does apply, because no specific distinction is made. Furthermore, the paribhāṣā "in the case of the mention of phonemes, [only] meaningful [elements] are included" does not operate; thus, the elision of *y* (yasyeti lopaḥ) occurs even for what is meaningless—as in *daivadattiriḥ*—and the substitution of *yaṇ* (yaṇādeśaḥ) occurs as in *akurvyatratra*. "The governing rule for verbal roots (*dhātu*) continues" means that the mention of "verbal root" (*dhātu*) continues.

Even so, [the rule] would apply here as well: *agnicit lunāti*. Is it not the case that the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is intended as a qualifier for what has been prescribed? Even so, [the rule] would still apply here: *śālā*, *mālā*, *mallaḥ*—these being derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes according to the rule *śāmāmalibhyo laḥ*. [Answer: The *uṇādi* formations are underived nominal stems (*avyutpannāni prātipadikāni*). Nevertheless, he states another solution: "the agent and so forth" (*kartrādayaḥ*).

In the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, the meanings specified—namely the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the abstract state (*bhāva*)—are carried over here; and by these, the *l*-suffixes are qualified, meaning "of the *l* prescribed for the agent and so forth. Consequently, only that *l* whose scope is thus qualified is understood, not every *l* without distinction.
ti, tas, jhi; si, thas, tha; am, vas, mas; ta, ātām, jha; thās, āthām, dhvam; iṭ, vahi, mahiṅ. || 3.4.78 ||

*tib-ādīnām* is a collective *dvandva* compound. The statement "the letter *pa* is for the sake of the vowel" is merely illustrative; other purposes such as [the rule] *sārvadhātukam apit* are also intended. Regarding the letter *ṭ* in *iṭaṣṭakāra*, etc.: one might object that in the rule *iṭo't*, the word *liṅ* is understood from the previous context, so even if the substitution of *at* for the vowel *i* is prescribed, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even so, the substitution would apply to a part of *ti* and the other suffixes, just as in the case of *eruḥ*, where even though *loṭaḥ* is understood, the substitution occurs for a part of *ti* and the other suffixes.

For there is no evidence that the genitive case in *avayava* (in *liṅo 'vayavasya*) denotes a part, whereas the genitive in *liṅaḥ* denotes a position (*sthāna*). Now, one might ask: why does the letter *ṭ* in [the rule] *ādyantau ṭakitau* not serve the purpose of a positional injunction (*deśavidhi*)? To this he says: "by *tiP* etc. and so forth. "Similarity" means likeness; and that [similarity] exists because they are taught in a single grammatical operation (*ekayoganirdiṣṭatva*), namely, the single genitive *lasya*. In that context, the seventeen substitutes beginning with *tiP* require a connection with a position (*sthāne yogaṃ prayojayanti*); the meaning is that a single [element, such as *ṭ*], is not able to set those aside. As for the *ṅ* in *mahiṅaḥ*, etc. [the same principle applies].

The term *tiṅ* is an illustration; *taṅ* is also a pratyāhāra. However, in forms such as *cinumahe*, it does not serve to prohibit *guṇa*, because this is already established by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*. Why then does it not serve to provide the *ṅit*-character where there is an *ārdhadhātuka*, as in *eṣiṣimahi*? Because there is no evidence that a marker (*anubandha*) attached to a whole (*samudāya*)—which has already fulfilled its purpose within that pratyāhāra—can function as a marker for its individual parts (*avayava*).

How [can there be] three? For the *ṇakāra* in that [suffix *ṣṇam*] has already served its purpose in the pratyāhāra "na-lokāvyaya" (Pāṇini 2.3.69), and regarding "auṅa āpaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.18), it will be stated: "The *ṅakāra* is for the sake of including the general category; otherwise, only the first dual ending (*au*), which is without an anubandha, would be included, and not the *auṭ* ending, which possesses an anubandha. But that [statement] would be contradicted, because the *ṭakāra* in that [suffix *ṣṇam*] also serves its purpose in the pratyāhāra "suṭ," and thus the *au* vowel [of *auṭ*] remains without an anubandha.

Therefore, the letter *ṅ* in *mahiṅ* is for the purpose of forming a pratyāhāra, and not an indicatory suffix (*anubandha*) belonging to a constituent part; in this matter, the tradition of the teachers' oral transmission is the sole refuge.
In place of the *ṭi* (the last vowel and following consonant) of the *ātmanepada* endings, *ṭer* is substituted.

"Of the *ṭit* [element] in place of *sthā*"—by this, he shows that the two genitive cases in *ṭitaḥ* and *ātmanepadānām* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The point is that if one were to assume a singular number based on a connection with each [term] individually and adopt the reading "*ṭitām ātmanepadānām*," then the rule would undesirably apply even to forms such as *akurvīta*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *prakṛtaiḥ*: among those *tiṅ* suffixes and others that have been introduced as the subject matter (*prakṛta*), those for which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has been prescribed are thus specified as being the middle voice. Since the suffix *śānac* is not included among the *tiṅ* suffixes, there is no possibility of its application; this is the meaning. In this way, one should simply say *taṅām*. However, some explain the mention of *āne muk* [in Pāṇini 7.2.82] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this substitution of *muk* applies only to *tiṅ* suffixes and not to others; otherwise, one would have had to say *ānayi*.
"No," [they say], "this is a reference to that *āna* which is the substitute for *al*, namely the *śānan* suffix prescribed after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj*—as in *pavamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*."
The substitution of *thās* for *se* [occurs]. 3.4.80.

Regarding *peciṣe*: this is the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix. By the rule "ata ekahalamadhye" and so forth, there is the substitution of *et* (the *i* for the root vowel) and the elision of the reduplication. The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*. Here, it should be stated that "th becomes s. When the letter *th* is changed to *s*, and the *e* of the following portion (*se*) is substituted, the desired form is established. Does this [substitution of *s* for *th*] also apply here in *pacathaḥ* and *pacatha*? The phrase "of the ātmanepada endings" is understood [from the previous context]. Even so, would it not apply to the *th* of *āthām*? The word "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is understood—meaning, the *th* that immediately follows the verbal root.

In that case, it would not apply here either—to *pacase* and *cinuṣe*—because of the intervention by the *vikaraṇa*. Where, then, would it apply? To those [verbal bases] which have the *luk*-vikaraṇa, the *ślu*-vikaraṇa, or the *śnam*-vikaraṇa. Therefore, it should be stated: "For *thās*, [the substitute is] *se*. Even so, should not the substitute *sa* alone be prescribed, since it is already established by the substitution of *et* for *ṭe*? It is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This indicates that the substitution of *et* for *ṭe* does not occur for those substitutes of the middle-voice endings (*ātmanepada*). Consequently, in forms such as *paktā*, *paktārau*, and *paktāraḥ*, the substitution of *et* for *ḍā*, *auras*, and [others] does not take place.
In place of the *ta* and *jha* suffixes of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], *eś* and *irec* are substituted respectively.

It was made known in the previous sūtra that the substitution of *et* for the final *ṭi* does not occur for substitutes of the ātmanepada; therefore, the two substitutes *iś* and *rac* were not prescribed. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of making the substitute apply to the whole [stem]. Otherwise, because of the governing rule *dhātoḥ*, the rule *ādeḥ parasya* would result in the substitution applying only to the initial letter, namely the *t*. Now, why was it not simply stated as *śe*? For if it were stated as *śairej*, there would be a saving of one mātrā. This cannot be so; for if it were *śe*, it would receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *pragṛhya*.

Furthermore, in this case, in the word *pape* (from the root *pā*), the substitution of *piba* would apply; and in forms such as *jagle* and *mamle*, the substitution of *ā* would not occur. However, if *eś* is used, there is no fault, according to the maxim: "Whatever [substitution] is prescribed for a phoneme, that applies to the beginning of that [phoneme]."
For the *parasmaipada* [terminations], there are substituted in their place: *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *atha*, *us*, *a*, *ṇal*, *vam*, and *ma*.

Regarding the phrase "of *tib* and so forth": this is understood from the context; therefore, the *ṇal* and other suffixes do not occur after *kvasu*. Alternatively, the absence of *ṇal* and the rest after *kvasu* is due to the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of its rule of formation. As for the statement "the *lakāra* [suffix] has its own meaning (*svārtha*)": otherwise, even though the suffix would be unaccented (*anudātta*) because it is marked with *p*, once the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) is applied, the principle that "reduplication (*dvirvacana*) consists in a double usage" would result in both [the root and the suffix] being acute-accented (*udātta*). The rule "a word (*pada*) is unaccented except for one [syllable]" would not apply, as simultaneous occurrence is impossible; rather, it would result in an alternation (*paryāya*).

Regarding the statement "the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of [indicating] *ṇit*-status": this is established otherwise. In the rule *ṇaluttamo vā*, there is a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*): first, *al ṇid bhavati* ("the suffix *al* becomes *ṇit*"); then, *tata uttamo vā* ("thereafter, the last [suffix] optionally [becomes *ṇit*]")—meaning it optionally becomes *ṇit*. Thus, we have *papāca*.

How is this a replacement for the whole [stem], given that "the fact of having multiple *al* sounds is not caused by a suffix" (*nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam*), and consequently, due to the governing rule "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) and the rule "for the first of what follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*), it would apply to the letter *v*? Is it established because it is not an *it*? No; for at the time of the prescription of *ṇal*, this is not yet a suffix, and thus, because it is not an *it*, the *ṇakāra* is a replacement for the whole because it has multiple *al* sounds; thereafter, the designation of *u* (as an augment) for the *ṇakāra* is established through this sequence.

But was it not said that the letter *ṇ* should not be applied? If that is so, then the letter *l* is placed at the beginning; since that too is not an *it*, the result is established. It must be stated that "the last [suffix] optionally [becomes *l*]. Similarly, [in the rule] *āta au ṇalaḥ*, and in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*, the mention of *hal* is an indicator (*liṅga*) that *ṇal* is a substitute for the whole [stem]. For that [mention of *hal*] is intended so that it does not occur in cases such as *papāca*; and that is possible only if it is a substitute for the whole. [Thus we have] *papaktha*.

The augment *iṭ*, which would have been required by the rule *krādiniyamāt*, does not occur here due to the prohibition in the rule *upadeśe'tvataḥ*. In some places, the reading is *pecitha*; in this case, *iṭ* is applied by the restriction *ṛto bhāradvājasya*, and the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) occur by the rule *thali ca seṭi*. As for *peca*: because of the governing context of the word *dhātoḥ*, the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* combined with *ādeḥ parasya* changes the *th* of *thali* to *a*; then, by the rule *ato guṇe*, the *guṇa* substitution of the two *a*s results in the single substitute *pararūpa*.
The suffix *laṭ* is optionally used [after a root] when preceded by *vid*.

Regarding the statement "vida jñāne": since the roots meaning "existence" (*sattā*) and "investigation" (*vicāra*) are ātmanepada, the occurrence of *tiP* and other suffixes is impossible; furthermore, because even the root meaning "acquisition" (*lābha*) is separated by a verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*), the immediate [suffixes] are impossible—this is the intended sense.
Of the five beginning with *āha*, the substitute *āho* is used for *bruvaḥ*.

"Five, beginning with *ṇal*": there are exactly five substitutes as well; among them, the first five begin with *ṇal*, and it does not mean that there are five according to one's whim. But how is this distinction regarding the substitutes obtained without a second mention of "five" and the mention of "beginning with" (*ādi*)? For surely, it would be logical for all five, beginning with *ṇal*, to take the place of the five [originals]? It is said in reply:

In the preceding sūtra, [the rule] operates according to the respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*); consequently, the connection of *ṇal* and the others with their specific substituends (*sthānin*) is established therein. Since those very [elements] are carried over (*anuvartante*) here as well, it will function in the same way here too. Therefore, the phrase "due to the connection with the substituend" means that in the preceding sūtra, the connection with the specific substituend has already been determined. Regarding *āttha*: [it is derived from] *āha* + *tha*. Regarding "of others": [it refers to] *tha* and the following [suffixes].

But surely, since this term *bruvaḥ* ending in the fifth case (ablative) will—by the principle of "change of case" (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*) based on the sense of the context—be understood as ending in the sixth case (genitive) when connected with the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is no need for the word *bruvaḥ* to be stated again? To this he replies: "*bruva iti* [is] a repetition," and so forth. "For it would apply only to the *parasmaipada*s. The meaning is that a change of case occurs when no related word is explicitly heard; however, here, because the word "of the *parasmaipada*s" (*parasmaipadānām*) is explicitly heard, the rule would apply only to them.
The imperative (loṭ) is treated like the imperfect (laṅ).

"The operation of *laṅ* occurs for *loṭ*. Here, the word *loṭ* refers to the substitutes of *loṭ*, and the word *laṅ* refers to the substitutes of *laṅ*; the meaning is that the operations belonging to the substitutes of *laṅ* apply to the substitutes of *loṭ*. Thus he says: "The suffixes *tām* and so forth, as well as the elision of *s*. Although these [suffixes] are not explicitly prescribed for *laṅ*, they are extended [to *loṭ*] because they are observed in *laṅ*. As for the question, "Why do *aṭ* and *āṭ* not occur?": the objection is that since *aṭ* and *āṭ* are explicitly prescribed only for *laṅ*, it would be more appropriate to extend those two [suffixes] instead.

Likewise, regarding the substitution of *jus* for *jhi*: why does it not occur? This is to be supplied by changing the case of the word [from the previous rule]. The substitution of *jus*, as in the rule "of the *laṅ* according to Śākaṭāyana," is prescribed specifically for the *laṅ* [tense] alone. However, here in cases such as *jāgratu* and *vidantu*, the substitution of *jus* seen in the *laṅ* tense would apply [undesirably] by the rule "after the *sic*, after reduplicated stems (*abhyasta*), and after *vid*. [The answer is: the term "optionally" (*vā*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

Because the genitive case is used for the *upameya* (the object of comparison) in the word "loṭ," it is understood that the *upamāna* (the standard of comparison) must also end in the genitive; thus, "whatever operation applies to *laṅ* applies to *loṭ*. This is an alternative way of avoiding [the application of] *aṭ* and *āṭ*. However, regarding the replacement of *jhi* with *jus*, he himself will state an alternative solution in the rule "laṅaḥ śākaṭāyanasya."
eruḥ || 3.4.86 || [The substitution of] *eru* [occurs for the root *i*].

Regarding the phrase "of the *i* belonging to the substitutes of the imperative (*loṭ*)," if the intended meaning were "of that *i* which is a substitute for the imperative," one would have simply said "of the augment *iṭ*. Furthermore, the grammatical rule *tuhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.35), which prescribes the form *vidāṅkurvantu*, would be untenable. Now, why does the substitution of *i* not also apply to the augment *iṭ* by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)? [The answer is: Because of the recognition that the rule applies again (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānāt*), the substitution of *i* will occur for the *ṭe* (the final syllable of the root). Nor can it be argued that it is due to the power of the specific pronunciation [in the rule].

If there were *utva* (the substitution of *u*) for *hin* and *ni*, one would have simply said *sernuḥ* and *mernuḥ*; for in this way, there would be brevity in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*). The indication [in the sūtras] that *āni* occurs in the imperative (*loṭ*) and that *dhi* replaces *hi* after *hujhal* (consonants other than semivowels and nasals) serves as evidence for the absence of *utva* for *hin* and *ni*.
The substitution of *śar* for *ha*, *ya*, and *va* occurs before a following *ca*. 3.4.87.

Regarding the word *lunīhi*: because it lacks the property of being *pit*, when the *ṅit* designation applies, the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*. In the case of *rāghnuhi*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Here, it should be stated that the suffix *si* (the imperative ending) is *ṅit*.

But surely, if this is the case, let the operation of being *ṅit* occur because of the *ṅit*-designation; however, since by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) there is also the status of being *pit*, would not the property of being *anudātta* (unaccented) also result? It will not occur, because of the explicit statement: "Even if it is *ṅit*, it is not *pit*. For example, in *api stuyādrājānam*, the *vṛddhi* prescribed for a *pit* suffix by the rule "vṛddhi occurs before a *pit* suffix beginning with a consonant when *luk* [of *ya*] follows" does not take place. In *brūtādbhavān*, the substitution of *iṇ* for *bruvaḥ* does not occur. Furthermore, since the *ṅit*-designation is initiated when the *pit*-status has not yet taken effect, it will supersede that [status].
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ai* for *e* and *au* for *o* is optional]. || 3.4.88 ||

"It is considered to have the *pit* designation" because it follows immediately [after the rule defining *pit*]. "It is not a substitute" because it is separated [by other elements]. Regarding *yuyodhi*: due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is reduplication of the root after the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*. Here, because it has the *pit* designation, the *ṅit* designation is absent; consequently, by the rule *aṅitaśca*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs.
The suffix *merni* [is applied after a word ending in *mā*] to express the sense of "measuring. (Pāṇini 3.4.89)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rules] *eruḥ* and *loṭo laṅvat*. That is to say, it applies respectively to those [operations] obtained by *eruḥ* and *loṭo laṅvat*, as well as to the elision of the vowel *i* obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), since such elision is seen in the case of the *laṅ* [tense] by the rule *itaśca*. However, we maintain that this is an exception to the substitution of *ām* which is obtained by the rule *loṭo laṅvat*.
The suffix *āman* is applied [after a word ending in *a*] to express "this" (*āmetas*). 3.4.90.

"Belonging to *loṭ*" means belonging to the substitutes (*ādeśa*) of *loṭ*. By this, he shows that the single phoneme *e* (ekāra) is qualified [by *loṭ*]. However, if *loṭ* were qualified by the single phoneme *e*, then, by the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), the suffix *ām* prescribed for *loṭ* ending in *e* would be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) because it consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*). In that case, one would have to state the following solution: "Substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out (*nirdiśyamāna*). This is the intended meaning.
In the case of the root √ad, when it is followed by the suffix -tama, the substitution of *pi* for the final vowel and the following consonant occurs.

And that *uttamapuruṣa* (first person) is *pit*. Why is it not understood that the *āṭ* itself has the property of being *pit*? For a relationship between two items with identical case-endings is indeed appropriate—as in "the *āṭ* is *pit*. [Reply: Because it would be meaningless. First of all, its being *anudātta* (unaccented) is already established simply by virtue of being an *āgama* (augment). Furthermore, in forms such as *karavāṇi* and *mārjāni*, it is the suffix (*pratyaya*) alone that is the cause for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitution, not the *āgama*.
These are for you. 3.4.93.

Regarding the question "Why here?": the sense is that there is the possibility [of the substitution] because the *guṇa* is included by the mention of the *loṭ* suffix due to its being treated as having an end (*antavadbhāva*). As for the phrase "because it is characterized as external" (*bahiraṅgalakṣaṇatvāt*): the *guṇa* is external because it depends on two words, whereas the *aikāra* (the single vowel *ai*) is internal because it depends on a single word; for this very reason, the rule "āmetaḥ" also does not apply.
In the *leṭ* [mood], the suffixes *aṭ* and *āṭ* are applied.

"By way of alternation," that is, not simultaneously; because of the functional force of the rule prescribing *aṭ*, otherwise, if the long vowel by *savarṇadīrgha* were to apply, the prescription of *aṭ* would be rendered useless.
[Pāṇini 6.1.95: *āta e*]

Regarding *karavaite*: because of the rule "in Vedic [usage], both ways," it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; thus, due to its being *ārddhadhātuka*, there is an absence of the *ṅit*-marker, which results in the guna-vowel of the suffix and the absence of the substitution of *ū* for the vowel of the root *kṛ*. Similarly: *pavaite*, *aśnavaithe*, *pravaite*, *vigranthaithe*.
The suffix *vati* occurs in other cases as well. 3.4.96.

"Having this as its object" (*etadviṣayam*): this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). However, the reading "having such an object" (*evaṃviṣayam*) is more appropriate. The examples have been explained under the rule *upasaṃvādāśaṅkayośca*.
Regarding *dadhasa*: [the suffix] *thās* becomes *se*; the substitution of *śnu* for *śap*; the augment *aṭ*; and the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *ghorlopo leṭi vā*.
And henceforth, there is elision [of the augment *iṭ*] before the *parasmaipada* endings. (Pāṇini 3.4.97)

Regarding the mention of *parasmaipada* (the active voice), and so forth: otherwise, the scope for the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* would be all other *lakāra*s, while the scope for the elision of *it* would be *leṭ* as well, but only where there is an *ikāra* other than [the one in question]. Since both rules would apply in the case of *iṭ* and the others, the elision of *it* would occur by virtue of its being the subsequent rule.
That [suffix] occurs after the word *uttama*. 3.4.98.

"Let us cause to do," "let us cause to do"—as before, there is the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and by the rule "āṭ for the *leṭ* [augment]," the augment *āṭ* is applied. Regarding the mention of "the subsequent [element]" and so forth: here, only the mention of *vas* and *mas* should be made. In that case, this further purpose follows—it is unnecessary to state "that [which is subsequent to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix]," because it is already established by the rule "of the final [phoneme] (*alo’ntyasya*)."

And when *vas* occurs in place of another person-ending (*puruṣa*), and another person-ending ending in *s* occurs in place of these two, then too—by the continued application of the mention of the option (*vā*) alone—the elision and non-elision will be established according to what is observed. Even if the mention of "the last" (*uttama*) were not made, the mention of the option (*vā*) would still follow; however, in the subsequent rule, there would be a mention of "always" (*nityam*), as in "always [elision] after an affix marked with *ṅ*" (*nityaṃ ṅitaḥ*).
The augment *sīyuṭ* is added after the optative suffix *liṅ*.

He states "of the substitutes of *liṅ*" because the word *liṅ* is used here by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute) for the various forms of *liṅ*. Regarding the augment *sīyuṭ*: its *s* is heard when it follows an *ardhadhātuka* *liṅ*, whereas in the case of a *sārvadhātuka* *liṅ*, there is elision of the final *s* according to the rule "there is elision of the final *s* of *liṅ*. As for the *y*, it is heard when followed by vowels (*ajādi*), while in other cases it is elided.
The affix *yāsuṭ* is acute-accented and marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* when applied to *parasmaipada* endings.

"Of that which has the *parasmaipada* as its scope": because it is impossible for *parasmaipada* suffixes to follow a *liṅ* [optative] verb ending. "An exception (*apavāda*) to *sīyuṭ*" is said because the rule is formulated when *sīyuṭ* would otherwise have applied; therefore, one should not object that once *yāsuṭ* has been applied, since it is a portion of a *tiṅ* suffix, *sīyuṭ* would consequently apply to that which begins with it. For even when there is a possibility of coexistence, a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) overrides a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*).

How, then, is it that *sīyuṭ* occurs in forms such as *kṛṣīṣṭa*, where *suṭ* has already been applied? Is it not the case that even there, *sīyuṭ* ought to be superseded by *suṭ*? Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti* himself will state the solution in the rule for *suṭ*: "Because it is an augment (*āgama*), it would [otherwise] be unaccented. For this very reason, it is understood from the explicit statement that *yāsuṭ* is accented that augments are unaccented; otherwise, since *yāsuṭ* is a part of the suffix (*pratyayabhakta*), its accentuation would have been established by the accent of the suffix itself.

This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Those rules concerning *piṭ* would exist for that purpose. If this were the only objective, one should have simply said "api. Therefore, this mention of the acute accent (*udātta*) is indeed an indicator: namely, that augments (*āgama*) are unaccented (*anudātta*). This is because the application of those [accentual] operations is possible therein. Even in the rule regarding *grahi*, *jyā*, and so forth, when the root's own form (*svarūpa*) is being grasped, since the operation is understood to apply to its suffixes, it is the suffix itself that is grasped—as in the example *kuryāt*.

The *guṇa* substitution for the verbal root (*dhātu*) occurs by virtue of the absence of an affix (*vikaraṇa*). Then, the substitution of *u* [for the vowel] occurs by the rule "ata utsārvadhātuke," and the elision of the letter *u* occurs by the rule "ye ca. Thus, we have *kuryuḥ*. Here, *jus* is substituted for *jhi*, and the elision of the *s* of the *liṅ* occurs by the rules "liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya" and "usyapadāntāt."

Regarding the phrase "simply by virtue of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva)": it was not stated that this is due to the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, because the designation of *ṅit* is for the sake of the *pit* [suffixes]. As for the statement "the *ṅit* designation of *yāsuṭ*": the meaning is that there is a *ṅit* designation for the *liṅ* [optative] beginning with *yāsuṭ*. For it was just now stated: "The *ṅit*-ness, however, is prescribed for the *liṅ* itself. And this is an indication (*jñāpaka*) stated without relying on the principle that "a *pit* suffix is not *ṅit*. If, however, that [principle] were not accepted, then the *ṅit*-ness obtained through *sthānivadbhāva* would be sublated by the original (*aupadeśika*) *pit*-ness; thus, the *ṅit* designation would serve merely as a means of obtaining [the *ṅit*-ness].
The suffix *liṅ* (the precative) is used in the sense of benediction. 3.4.104.

"For that [liṅ], *yāsuṭ*... becomes as if it were *kit*. This means that *yāsuṭ* is applied to that [liṅ], and it (i.e., *yāsuṭ*) becomes as if it were *kit*. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the immediately following text: "This *kit*-ness belongs to the affix (*pratyaya*). [The opponent asks: "Because there is no purpose [for this rule]. [The author replies: Even in the case of the rule *vacisvapi...* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), by the principle "when the form of a root is mentioned," this would have to be understood as referring only to the affix; otherwise, it would also apply in cases such as *vācyati*, *vācikam*, *kathayati*, and *vāg jahāti*.

"The prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is the same. To the question, "For what purpose, then, is the designation *kit* prescribed?", he says: "for the sake of *saṃprasāraṇa*. [The example is] *jagaryāt*. Here, the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule "there is *guṇa* for *jāgr-* before affixes other than *vi*, *ciṇ*, and *ṅit*s."
The substitution of *ra* occurs in place of *jha*. (Pāṇini 3.4.105)

Because of the pronunciation of the vowel *a* in the term *jhasya*, there is the apprehension of the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*) and not of a single phoneme (*varṇa*); otherwise, as in the rule for the substitution of an end-element (*antādeśa*), he would have simply said "of *jha*. Thinking thus, [the author] says: "of *jha*, which is a substitute for *liṅ*. "An exception to the end-substitution of *jha*" means that it is an exception to the end-substitution of the phoneme *jha*; or, it means it is an exception to the rule "an *anta* [is substituted] for *jha*."

But surely, since *jha* is an *antādeśa* (a substitute for the final letter) and *ran* is for the entire group (*samudāya*), how can there be a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between two things that occupy different domains? This is because they are in conflict and because of the maxim *yena nāprāpte*. Furthermore, the statement that *jha* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the final letter is merely an illustration; in forms such as *kṛṣīran* and *tṛṣīran*, it is also an exception to [the rule] *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.5). Objection: But due to the prohibition of an exception (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), shouldn't the absence of *ṭ* (*adbhāva*) alone apply? No; because a rule prescribed by a specific mention (*pratipadavidhi*) is stronger, and the substitution of *ran* is indeed prescribed by a specific mention.

Alternatively, let the substitution of *at* for *it* apply even in the cases of *kṛṣīran* and *tṛṣīran*; nevertheless, even when that [substitution] has occurred, by the principle of "reapplication" (*prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the suffix *ran* will be applied to the entire cluster.
The suffix *at* is applied after [a verbal root] ending in *iṭ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.106)

"This [augment] is not a part of the substitute. This means that there is no purpose for designating it with the technical name *it*, because it ceases to exist by itself. On the contrary, if it were designated as such, it would possess the property of being *svarita*. Regarding this, it was stated in the context of the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* by way of a hypothetical argument: "In this case, the prohibition [of the *it*-designation] does not apply to the augment *iṭ*, because this [rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*). Regarding the phrase "in the case of the mention of a meaningful element" (*arthavad-grahaṇe*), etc.: even due to the qualification "that *iṭ* which occurs in place of *la*," there is no inclusion of the augment *iṭ*.
The suffix *suṭ* is applied after the word *tithi*. (Pāṇini 3.4.107)

Is the word *tithoḥ* in the locative case (*saptamī*) or the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)? In the first alternative, according to the rule "in a mention of 'that which begins with [a letter],' the operation applies to that which begins with it," the augment *suṭ* would have to apply to the substitutes for *liṅ* (optative) beginning with *t* and *th*. Consequently, it would occur only in forms such as *kṛṣīṣṭa* and *kṛṣīṣṭhāḥ*, but not in *kṛṣīyāstām* and *kṛṣīyāsthām*. Furthermore, *suṭ* would supplant *sīyuṭ*, because both are part of the *liṅ* substitute. Therefore, adopting the second alternative, he says: "of the *t* and *th* belonging to the *liṅ*."

He clarifies this very point with the words "the letters *t* and *th*. Regarding the phrase "the *liṅ* [suffix] and its qualifier": by the word *liṅ*, its substitutes (*ādeśas*) are meant. Similarly, in the expression "of those connected to the *liṅ*," the form *kṛṣīṣṭa* is cited as an example. Since the *liṅ* used for injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, the suffix *suṭ* would not be heard because of the elision prescribed by the rule "there is elision of *s* after *liṅ*" (*liṅaḥ salopaḥ*); therefore, only the *liṅ* used for benediction (*āśis*) has been cited.
jher jus || 3.4.108 || The suffix *jus* is substituted for *jhi* [the first-person plural ending] when it follows a verbal root ending in a vowel.

Regarding the phrase *jho'ntāpavāda* ("an exception to [the substitution of] *jhi*"): it is to be explained as before. Furthermore, in cases such as *jāgṛyuḥ*, there is likewise an annulment of the rule *adabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4), just as previously. In *paceyuḥ*, there is the substitution of *iy* by the rule *ato yeyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.80), and with the *śap* suffix, the *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) rule applies.
And [the suffix *ktvā*] is substituted for the gerundive suffixes (*kṛtya*) after roots ending in *s*, after reduplicated (abhyasta) roots, and after the root *vid*.

Since the roots *vid* in the senses of "existence" (*sattā*) and "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) are ātmanepada, the suffix *jhi* is simply impossible [after them]. Even for the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābha*), because it is separated by a verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*), the immediately following *jhi* is impossible. Therefore, he says "of *vid* [ending in] *luK*" (*vetteśca*), meaning that only the root *vid* with the *luK*-affix is intended. [An objection: "If so, the mention of the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) *vid* would be for the sake of [the rule regarding] *asi*. [The author replies: "And there is no such undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in the case of the imperative (*loṭ*) and other moods," as he says: "and the term *ṅit* is understood [from the previous rule]."
From this point [onward]. 3.4.110.

[The rule] "after *sic* and after that which ends in long *ā*, [there is *jus*] for the following *jhi*"—the meaning is "immediately following both. [The question is: "How so? The question implies that because of the intervention of *sic* after [a root ending in] *ā*, immediate succession (*ānantarya*) from both cannot occur. What is being stated is that *jus* occurs for *jhi* after a form where *sic* has been elided. As in *abhūvan*: by the rule "there is *vuk* for *bhū* in the *luṅ* and *liṭ*," *vuk* is applied. And [it is said] "because it depends on a similar class": since immediate succession from both is not explicitly heard [in the rule], it is stated that the form ending in the elision of *sic* is what is intended.

By this—because of the reliance on the restrictive rule (niyama) that [the augment *iṭ*] occurs only after a root ending in long *ā* when followed by *sic* with the *luṅ* affix—the meaning is that it indeed occurs even after roots not ending in *ā*, such as in *akārṣuḥ* and so forth, when *sic* is actually heard.
According to Śākaṭāyana, the suffix *laṅ* [is used] only [in the sense of past time].
*āyuḥ*, *āvuḥ*: [from *āyus* and *āvas*] there is elision of the *śap* suffix, and by the rule "usi apadāntāt," there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).

"Only in *laṅ*"—the sense is that while there must be [the substitution of] *jus* for both *luṅ* and *liṅ*, in the case of *lṛṅ*, there is an intervention by the suffix *syap* after *jh*. [The examples] "yāntu," "vāntu": this meaning is established here even by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from the rule "the *loṭ* is like the *laṅ*. Now, one might object: "Surely, by the mention of *laṅ*, let this *jus* substitution not occur for the *loṭ*; however, would this [substitution] prescribed by 'for *sic*, reduplicated stems,' etc., not still take place? To this he replies: "For *sic*, reduplicated stems," etc. He asks: "How so? and answers: "For the mere *jus* substitution..."

But how, while "ātaḥ" is being carried over, can the mere state of being *jus* be qualified by the primary term *laṅ*? It is thought that a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) should be made as "laṅaḥ. Now, it was stated that "ātaḥ" serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*) through the continued application of the mention of *sic*; therefore, since [the substitution] does not apply to anything else in cases such as *āyuḥ*, this [rule] must be for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartham*). Why then is the particle *eva* used? To this he replies: "The particle *eva* is for the sake of what follows. He will demonstrate its utility in the rules "liṭ ca" and "liṅāśiṣi."
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after a word meaning "enemy. (Pāṇini 3.4.112)
The root *dviṣ* belongs to the *adādi* (second) class.
The *tiṅ* and *śit* [suffixes] are called *sārvadhātuka*. (Pāṇini 3.4.113)

In *tarati* and *nayati*, because the *tiṅ* affix is *sārvadhātuka*, there is the *śap* augment; and because the *śap* is *sārvadhātuka*, the root undergoes *guṇa*. In *roditi*, due to the elision (*luk*) of *śap*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "after roots such as *rud*, etc., before a *sārvadhātuka* affix. In *pavamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*, the *śap* and *guṇa* are as in the previous case.
The remainder is termed *ārdhadhātuka*. (Pāṇini 3.4.114)

"By the mention of 'dhātu' (root)" means by uttering the word *dhātu*. For here, in the rule prescribing the *yaṅ* suffix, both the mention of "the root" (*dhātu*)—as in "of the root *śam*"—and the mention of "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*) are carried over (*anuvartate*). Among these, one excludes non-root affixes (*adhātupratyaya*), while the other qualifies the root-affixes (*dhātupratyaya*) as being "prescribed after a root. Thus, the meaning is as follows: [the forms] *lūbhyām*, *lubhiḥ*, and *jugupsate*.

Although here [the suffix] is prescribed after the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, it is nevertheless not prescribed by explicitly uttering the word "verbal root" (*dhātu*); thus, this serves as a counter-example. The inclusion of the term *śeṣa* (remainder) is intended to prevent this from applying to *tiṅ* and *śit* affixes; otherwise, in the absence of the governing rule for a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), there would be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of designations, just as occurs with the designations of suffixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth.
The particle *eva* (only) continues to apply here, and it would have been possible to omit the mention of *śeṣa*.
And the suffix liṭ [is used for the expression of the past]. 3.4.115.

"pecitha," "śekitha"—here, by the rule "ṛto bhāradvājasya," the augment *iṭ* is applied; then, by the rule "thali ca seṭi," the substitution of *e* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication occur. In "jagle" and "mamle," because they are *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the elision of the long *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca. As for what was stated—that this [the designation *liṭ*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the designation *sārvadhātuka*—he refutes that with the words "nanu ca" (but surely...). He establishes its status as an exception with the words beginning "satyam" (it is true).
In the Veda, [the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*] occurs in both ways. Pāṇini 3.4.117.

"The entire section" refers to the group of four sūtras beginning with *tiṅśitsārvadhātukam*. [The statement] "the substitution of *bhū* does not take place" is because at that time, due to its being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* does not apply.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the *Padamañjarī*, composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra—the *Kāśikāvṛtti* commentary. 4.
*Padamañjarī*.
[The suffixes taught from here on] are applied after a nominal stem ending in a vowel or a consonant.

"This is an *adhikāra* (governing heading)," because neither that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) nor a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) has been specified, and because the suffixes beginning with *su* (the case endings) to be mentioned hereafter depend upon a base (*prakṛti*), as well as because it is marked with the *svarita* accent. "Up to the end of the fifth chapter" indicates the limit of the governing heading. There are several types of governing headings—namely, a heading of technical names (*saṃjñādhikāra*), a heading of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇādhikāra*), and a heading of bases (*prakṛtyadhikāra*). To the question, "What kind of governing heading is this? he says: "From *su* up to the end of *ka*, the base is governed."

Regarding the phrase "of *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp*": the term "general reference" (*sāmānyagrahaṇam*) is to be supplied. "A collective designation" (*samāhāranirdeśaḥ*) means that this is a designation of those [suffixes] beginning with *ṅī* by means of a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). Consequently, because the collection is a single unit, the singular number alone is appropriate, not the plural; such is the intended meaning.

For what purpose is this stated? [It is so that] "the case endings (*svādayaḥ*) may follow after *ṅī*, *āp*, and nominal stems (*prātipadika*)," lest there be the employment of them alone. Would it not be the case that they would not be employed alone because of the rule stating "and [they are] subsequent" (*paraśca*)? This, then, is the purpose: [to ensure] that they follow *only* after *ṅī*, *āp*, and nominal stems, and not after other bases (*prakṛti*).

In the absence of this governing rule (*adhikāra*), there would be four types of bases (*prakṛti*)—namely, verbal roots (*dhātu*), verbal endings (*tiṅanta*), sentences (*vākya*), and nominal stems (*subanta*) distinct from those ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—as well as four types of suffixes (*pratyaya*) to be mentioned hereafter: those beginning with *su* (case endings), those beginning with *ṭāp* (feminine suffixes), those beginning with *aṇ* (primary suffixes), and those that are self-referential (*svārthika*). Therefore, this governing rule must indeed be established so that the four types of suffixes do not apply to all four types of bases indiscriminately.

It need not be stated. [Objection: But if this were not stated, then because of the governing context of "root" (*dhātu*), these suffixes would apply only to roots; furthermore, the technical designations of *kṛt* and *upapada* would apply, and the rule regarding optional forms of different types (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) would also apply. [Response: No; because the mention of "root" has ceased [to govern]. Even if they were to apply to the root as well, that too is not possible; because the object (*karman*) and other factors are absent. For the *svādi* suffixes are prescribed when there are grammatical relations (*kāraka*) such as the object and so forth, and when there is a number such as singularity and so on; and it is not possible for the meaning of the root to be connected with the object and other such factors.

How, then, do suffixes such as *tavya* occur when there is an object (*karman*)? It is not the case that *tavya* and the like occur simply because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the object; rather, they occur when that which is the object with respect to the meaning of the verbal root is to be expressed—as in "the mat must be made" (*kartavyaḥ kaṭaḥ*). However, suffixes such as *sva* (possessive) have their purpose fulfilled when the object belongs to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), and they cannot occur when something else is the object. Furthermore, because they are superseded by *tavya* and the like, these [possessive] suffixes do not occur after a verbal root.

But is it not observed that the objecthood (*karmatva*) belongs precisely to the meaning of the verbal root—as in *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do") and so forth, which are based on the *san*-affix? Even so, the absence of number (*saṃkhyā*) is indeed established; however, suffixes beginning with *su* (the nominative case endings) occur after indeclinables (*avyaya*) by virtue of the metarule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. As for what was stated under the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam*—"where number is possible"—that is not accepted in this particular state [of the verb].

[Objection: In that case, let the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth not apply to the verbal root (*dhātu*). [Response: The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are prescribed for the feminine gender, and there is no connection between the meaning of the verbal root and the feminine gender. [Question: How then are the suffixes *ktin* and so forth prescribed for the feminine? [Response: Here, the suffixes *ktin* and so forth are not taught to denote the femininity of the meaning of the verbal root; rather, they denote its property called "accomplishedness" (*siddhatva*). Furthermore, because the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are superseded by *ktin* and the others, they do not occur.

[Objection: "In that case, let there not be *aṇ* and other suffixes for the verbal root (*dhātu*)? [Response: *Aṇ* and other suffixes are prescribed in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth; however, there is no connection between the meaning of a verbal root and offspring and the like. Furthermore, because of the absence of a compatible case-ending (*samartha-vibhakti*), *aṇ* and other suffixes do not arise. For instance, suffixes such as *aṇ* are prescribed after words ending in case-endings like the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), as in the rules "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), "colored by that" (*tena raktam*), and "occurring therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*). But a case-ending is not possible for a verbal root. Even primary suffixes (*svārthika*) will not apply to the verbal root, precisely because they are superseded by suffixes such as *tumun* which express the same meaning (*svārthaka*).

[Objection: In that case, let there be no *svādi* suffixes after a verb ending in a *tiṅ* (conjugational) affix? [Response: In verbal forms (*tiṅanta*), the action (*kriyā*) is the predominant factor and the agent (*sādhana*) is subordinate. Since the object and other factors do not exist for that predominant action, the *svādi* suffixes will not occur. If it is argued that agency is observed in such cases as "he is cooking" (*pacati bhavati*) or "the teachers indeed prompt even what is being done" (*bhavati vai kiñcid ācāryāḥ kriyamāṇam api codayanti*), even so, the absence of number (*saṃkhyā*) remains established. As for the agent who is expressed as subordinate;

In that case, the absence of a case-ending is established precisely because [the agent] has already been expressed. Furthermore, it is not possible for an agent who has become subordinate (guṇabhūta) to enter into another action; for if that were so, case-endings such as the accusative would occur, as in examples like "see the cook" (*pācakam paśya*).

[Objection: But would this not be like the case of *putrīya*? Just as from the word *putrīya*, which expresses an action whose object is internally contained, the *L*-suffix arises in the sense of the agent—as in *putrīyati*—so too here, from the word *pacati*, which expresses an action qualified by an agent, the accusative and other case-endings should indeed occur in relation to the sequence [of cooking] and so forth. [Response: This is not a fault; for it has already been stated: "The *svādi* suffixes, having fulfilled their purpose when the objecthood belongs to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), cannot apply when the objecthood belongs to anything else."

Furthermore, it is not possible for two distinct means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that depend on a single action to be expressed simultaneously within a single word. However, since the word *putrīya* denotes a qualified action—just like verbal roots such as *jīvati*—the derivation of the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) is not contradictory. Moreover, this must necessarily be understood in this way: that case endings beginning with the accusative (*dvitīyā*) do not arise after a word ending in a *tiṅ* (finite verb) precisely because of the absence of an object (*artha*). For one might think that they do not arise simply because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a *pratyaya*"; [but this is not the case].

From forms ending in *rūpa* and so forth, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and subsequent cases would indeed occur, as in examples such as *pacatirūpaṃ paśya* ("see the form of the cooking") and *pacatirūpeṇa kṛtam* ("done by means of the form of the cooking"), for this is indeed a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). How then does even the singular nominative (*prathamā-ekavacana*) occur from forms ending in *rūpa* and so forth? Because the number [of the agent] has already been expressed; for the singular number does not apply to the number of that agent. If it were otherwise, then from *pacatirūpa*, there would be dual and plural forms, such as *pacantirūpam*.

However, in the rule *prātipadikārtha*, because of the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the nominative case occurs as being connected solely to the nominal stem. Even there, only the singular number applies, according to the statement: "The singular shall be established as the general rule. Nor does this result in an over-extension to verbal endings (*tiṅanta*), because those are not nominal stems.

If that is so, then let the suffixes *ṭāp* and the others not apply after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*)? The suffixes *ṭāp* and the others are prescribed for the feminine gender, and there is no connection of the primary meaning with femininity in a verbal ending. Even if it were the case that *ṭāp* and the others would apply when the instrument (*sādhana*) is feminine—such as "the Brāhmaṇa cooks" (*pacet brāhmaṇaḥ*) or "the Brāhmaṇī cooks" (*paceyuḥ brāhmaṇyaḥ*)? That too is not possible; for by their very nature, verbal endings take on only the number residing in the instrument, not the gender. And it has been said:
"Even though unity resides in the action expressed by the verb, [it is expressed] by the number residing in the instrument."
"The distinction called gender is not split; rather, the distinction residing therein [is split].

In examples such as *śobhanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks well"), the adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) alone is connected with gender, not the action itself, and even there, it is by means of the neuter. In cases such as *pacati rūpam* ("the form [of] he cooks"), the action expressed by the verbal suffix (such as *-ti*) is naturally connected with gender, and even there, it is by means of the neuter. For the powers of words are manifold and must be accepted according to observed usage; they cannot be established by inference based on general observation.

And this must necessarily be understood in this way: that because of the absence of femininity (*strītva*), the suffixes *ṭāp* and others do not occur after verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*; otherwise, in cases such as *pacatirūpā brāhmaṇī*, the suffix *ṭāp* would indeed occur after [the nominal stem] ending in *rūpa*.

Why is it that *aṇ* and the other suffixes do not occur after verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*? The suffixes *aṇ* and so forth are prescribed for meanings such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and the like; however, there is no connection between the primary meaning of a word ending in *tiṅ* and offspring or similar categories. Furthermore, because a non-primary element is simply non-primary, it lacks a connection with offspring and the like; thus, the absence of *aṇ* and the other suffixes is established by the absence of a compatible case-ending (*samartha-vibhakti*). This must necessarily be understood in this way, for otherwise, if one were to say "the offspring of that which has the form *pacati*," the suffixes *aṇ* and the rest would indeed apply even to words ending in *rūpa* and so forth.

Even the *svārthika* suffixes will not occur after verbal roots (*tiṅanta*) because of an indicative rule (*jñāpaka*), namely that [Pāṇini] employs the mention of *tiṅ* in certain rules for the formation of *taddhita* suffixes—such as "the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*) and "also after *tiṅ*" (*tiṅaśca*). Furthermore, case endings (*svādayaḥ*) cannot possibly arise from a sentence (*vākya*), because there is an absence of objects (*karman*) and so forth. Indeed, it is impossible for the meaning of a sentence—which consists of an action, a relation, or a distinction—to be connected with objects and so on, or with feminine gender, offspring, and the like.

If it is argued that [number] is observed in cases such as "the deer runs" (*paśya mṛgo dhāvati*), even so, the absence of connection with number remains established. Furthermore, since there is no denotation of their own meaning, even primary suffixes (*svārthika*) will not arise from a sentence. To explain: from the sentence "Devadatta’s horse-mounting" (*devadattārohāśvam*), when the *ke* suffix is applied in the sense of the *prāgivīya* group and the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending occurs, because the meaning of the sentence has become a non-substantial entity (*asattvabhūta*), there is an absence of connection with gender, number, and [case-]power; consequently, since the case-endings (*svādi*) cannot arise, the form would have to be *devadattārohāśvakā*. And yet, by such a form, the contempt and other qualities residing in the meaning of the sentence are not conveyed.

The case endings beginning with *su* (the nominal suffixes) cannot possibly arise even from that which ends in a *sup*. For when the *svādi* suffixes are being prescribed, it is not possible for a base (*prakṛti*) ending in them to exist, as it has been stated: "A desiderative suffix will not be applied after that which already ends in a desiderative suffix. Furthermore, even that which ends in a *sup* is primarily concerned with number or primarily concerned with the power of the grammatical relation (*kāraka-śakti*), and its connection with other factors such as the object (*karman*) and so forth is not possible.

The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth will also not occur because of the absence of femininity. Furthermore, there is no distinction regarding the suffixes *aṇ* and others, whether their production occurs from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) or from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). We shall demonstrate how this is so under the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*. In any case, since an undesired suffix would result even from a nominal stem ending in *rūpa* and so on—just as it would from a root and so forth—there is no purpose in this [rule]. Thus the objector first raises the doubt with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
The base is obtained by virtue of its dependence on the suffix; the meaning is that, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this very base is what is obtained.

He addresses this by saying "even so" (*tathāpi*). The meaning is that the mention of *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* is for the purpose of ensuring that, in a rule prescribing a suffix where old age (*vṛddhi*) and so forth are the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or cause (*nimitta*), the *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* is understood as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The phrase "otherwise" (*itarathā hi*) means if the mention of *ṅy-āp-prātipadika* were not made. In that case, this [mention] would become a qualifier of "that which is capable" (*samartha*), because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of those that are capable, optionally from the first. Furthermore, what is "capable"? That which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*).

If there is a qualification of "capacity" (*samartha*), what is the fault? [The rule] "after a *vṛddha* [stem] that is not a *gotra*, the suffix *phin* occurs for the Northern grammarians" would apply here: *jñānāṃ brāhmaṇānām apatyam* ("the offspring of Jñāna-brāhmaṇas"), for this is a compound consisting of a *vṛddha* [stem]. And it would not apply here: *jñānāṃ brāhmaṇānām apatyam* ("the offspring of Jñāna-brāhmaṇas"), for this is not a compound consisting of a *vṛddha* [stem].

For where the manifestation of a specific number occurs by virtue of an injunction (*ādeśa*) and so forth, there the application of dual and plural endings does not take place—as in *tāvakaḥ* and *māmakaḥ*. Just as here the suffix *phiñ*, being produced, would imply plurality because its occurrence is impossible without plurality due to the requirement of *vṛddhi*, so too the suffix *phin* might imply duality; thus, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would indeed arise.

Regarding *avarṇa*: [if the rule] "ata iñ" were applied here alone, it would apply to "the offspring of Dakṣa," but it would not apply in cases such as "of two Dakṣas" (*dakṣayoḥ*) or "of many Dakṣas" (*dakṣāṇām*). Regarding *svara*: [if the rule] "anudāttāder añ" were applied here, it would undesirably apply to "a modification of speech" (*vāco vikāraḥ*) and "a modification of skin" (*tvaco vikāraḥ*), for these are capable of being *anudāttādi* (beginning with an unaccented vowel), since the case ending is acute by the rule "sāvekācaḥ."

But surely, since they maintain that *mayaṭ* must always be used after a monosyllabic stem (*ekāca*), should *mayaṭ* not be applied here? Consider this case: in *pañcānāṃ vikāraḥ*, when the case-ending is acute according to the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*, the resulting form begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttādi*) and is thus capable [of taking *mayaṭ*]. However, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *nraḥ saṅkhyāyāḥ*. And in this case, it would not apply: in *sarveṣāṃ vikāraḥ*, the word is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *sarvasya supi*, whereas the nominal stem is prescribed as having the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

[Otherwise,] the rule "from a two-syllable [word]" (*dvyacaḥ*) would apply here as well—such as in *vācā tarati* ("he crosses by means of speech") and *tvacā tarati* ("he crosses by means of skin")—for these are indeed capable of being two-syllable words. However, the mention of the word *nau* ("boat") would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*), meaning that if a word ending in the vowel *au* is used, it must be the word *nau* itself. Consequently, in cases such as *ghaṭena tarati* ("he crosses by means of a jar"), the suffix would not apply. On the other hand, in cases such as *sāmnā tarati* ("he crosses by means of a Sāman chant"), the result is established in both ways.

However, when there is the mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika*, by virtue of that very [mention], *vṛddha* and so forth become qualifiers of that [stem] alone; and because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding "capacity" (*samartha*), the suffix is applied from that which is "capable. In this regard, the connection is as follows: "From that *ṅī*-ending, *āp*-ending, or *prātipadika* stem which is *vṛddha* and so forth, and which is 'capable,' the suffix is applied."

Regarding the statement "because it is a rule concerning suffixes" (*yasmāt-pratyaya-vidhiḥ*), the purpose [of this rule]—namely, that the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *aṅga*, *bha*, and *pada* which are prescribed when a suffix is enjoined by means of the ablative case should apply to the *ṅyāp-prātipadika* (stems ending in feminine suffixes or nominal stems)—is not [the primary motive]. Why? Because these designations belong to that [stem] from which the suffix is enjoined by the omniscient Lord (*daiva*); let them be indicated by the ablative case, or let them not be indicated at all.

Furthermore, the purpose [of this governing rule] cannot be that the *luk* elision of the suffixes *cha* and *ya*—as in the rule "In the case of *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, there is *yañ* and *añ*, and *luk* [of the suffix]"—should apply to these two suffixes when they follow a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but should not apply to the suffixes *u* and *ka* belonging to the *uṇādi* group; for why? Because "the *uṇādi* suffixes are underived nominal stems" (*uṇādayo 'vyutpannāni prātipadikāni*), which means that in the *uṇādi* lists, the grammatical operations based on derivation do not necessarily take effect. This is understood from the fact that in the rule "After *ataḥ*, before *kṛ*, *kami*, *kaṃsa*, etc. (*ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa*), although the result would have been established by the mention of *kami* alone, the mention of *kaṃsa* again is made. Therefore, the governing rule has as its sole purpose the restriction to those [suffixes] beginning with *vṛddhi*.

The mention of *ṅyāp* is made because [the base] would not otherwise be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to its ending in an affix. However, in the case of *yuvati-* from *yūnaḥ tiḥ*, there is the status of being a nominal stem because it ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Regarding *ūṅutaḥ*, the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed after bases ending in *u*; therein, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) behaves like the final element, there is the status of being a nominal stem. As for *śvaśrū-* from the rule "there is also the elision of the *u* and *a* of *śvaśura*," the formation of the case-endings and so forth is established through the specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) "both *śvaśuraḥ* and *śvaśrūḥ*. This being the case, the objection is raised: "Now then" (*atha*).

"Not when there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). The meaning is that this is already established because the negative particle *nañ* is used with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), or because particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings; thus, the word *na* here should be understood in the sense of the word *nanu*. "Of that which is qualified by gender" means: of that which is augmented by a suffix conditioned by gender.

The purpose of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is [to apply] the designations of pronoun (*sarvanāman*), accent (*svara*), compound (*samāsa*), metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), and the treatment as if ending in *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*). Regarding the pronoun: the designation of pronoun prescribed for the word *bhavat* applies to the word *bhavatī* as well; thus, by the rule "the third case [is used] after a pronoun," we have: *bhavatā hetunā*, *bhavato hetoḥ*, *bhavatyā hetunā*, and *bhavatyā hetoḥ*. Regarding accent: in the rule "in the sense of a hole, the words *kuśūla*, *kūpa*, *vumba*, and *śāla* [are compounded with *bila*]," we have *kuśūlabilam* and *kuśūlībilam*.

Compound (*samāsa*): *pūrvasadṛśa*, *mātṛsadṛśaḥ*, *mātṛsadṛśī*; by the rule "of *sadṛśa* and *pratirūpa*," the accent (*svara*) also occurs here. Likewise, *kumāraḥ śramaṇādibhiḥ*: *kumārīśramaṇā*, *kumāraśramaṇā*; similarly, *yuvatirvalinā*, *yuvavalinā*. Metaphorical application (*upacāra*): *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsakumbha*, *ayaskumbhaḥ*, *ayaskumbhī*. The treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*): *ṇāviṣṭhavatprātipadikasya*, he describes a young girl (*kumārīmācaṣṭe*), [expressed as] *kumārayati*.

But here, regarding the rule *acittahastidhenoṣṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.47), which states that the suffix *ṭhak* is added after words denoting non-sentient beings, *hastin*, and *dhenu*, the form *hāstikam*—meaning "a collection of female elephants"—is established as follows: by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), which prescribes masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel other than *āṬ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is removed; thus, this is simply the word *hasti*, and the application of *ṭhak* is achieved. For the term *taddhite* in that rule is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Furthermore, masculine substitution must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, if *ṭhak* were added directly to the word *hastinī*, the elision of *y* (by *yasyeti ca*) would be subject to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, and consequently, the elision of the final *ī* (by *nastaddhite*) would not occur.

And here, in the case of *innanta-siddha-badhnātiṣu ca sthaṇḍilaśāyini*, because of the rule stating that "the statement regarding the compounding of preverbs, objects, and secondary words with *kṛt*-suffixes occurs prior to the arising of case-endings," the compound is formed while the feminine suffix *ṅīp* has not yet arisen; thus, since the final member of the compound ends in *-in*, the prohibition of elision (*aluk*) is established. Similarly, in *grāmevāsinī* according to the rule *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt*, there is no elision.

Likewise, by the rules *māninaśca* and *svāṅgāccetomānini*, forms such as *darśanīyamāninī* and *dīrghamukhamāninī* are established; since the word *mānin* itself is the final member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is achieved. Furthermore, here, because of the understanding that "the sixth case [genitive] which occurs in connection with the affixes *tṛc* and *aka*, when they denote the agent, does not undergo composition with whatever [word it might otherwise combine with]"—as per the rules *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* and *kartari ca*—the prohibition of composition is established even in the case of *apāṃ sraṣṭrī*.

If "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): the rule "for *tāpa* preceded by *dviṣat*" would apply even in the case of *dviṣatītapa*.
