Regarding this, it has been stated: "In the mention 'preceded by *dviṣat*,' this is a reference containing two *t*s; the word *dviṣat* ends in a *t*. Furthermore, in the cases "the descendant of Gārgī" and "the descendant of Dākṣī," the suffix *phak* (by the rule *yañiñośca*) would supersede the suffix *ḍhak* (by the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*) due to its higher status [in the order of rules].

And here, in the case of *dākṣiḥ* and *glucukāyaniḥ* according to the rule *ñnityādinityam*, once the acute accent on the first syllable has been applied in this state, and subsequently the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ*, only the accent of the suffix remains as the "later taught" (*śiṣṭa*) accent—thus *dākṣī* and *glucukāyanī*. At this stage, the acute accent on the first syllable does not apply again, because it has already taken effect previously.

Similarly, in the case of *bahugomatī*—meaning "she who has many cows"—the suffix *ṅīp* is applied only after the formation of *bahusvarā* (having many vowels) has already occurred; because the suffix is marked with *p*, it becomes *anudātta*. Furthermore, the rule *bahoḥ nañvat* does not apply again here, as it has already been applied previously. Moreover, since the *ṅīp* suffix is produced from the compound itself, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is not qualified by gender.

In that case, then, in the example *madrāṇāṃ rājñī* ("the queen of the Madras"), the suffix *ṭac* would apply by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*. Consequently, by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply, whereby the long vowel *ī* would be removed and the *ṭi*-portion elided; then, because the suffix is marked with *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be added, resulting in *madrarājī*, whereas the desired form is *madrarājñī*. Similarly, in the case of *mahatīpriyaḥ* ("one whose beloved is great"), which is a subject for the prohibition of masculine form, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ānmahataḥ* would occur.

Likewise, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *tathā''ryayor brāhmaṇakumārayoḥ* and *rājā ca rājabrāhmaṇī*. Furthermore, there is a fault regarding any operation dependent on a case-ending (*vibhakti*), whether that operation occurs when a case-ending follows or when it precedes; for example, in *śunā* and *śunaḥ*, the acute accent of the case-ending—which would have been required by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*—does not take place because of the rule *na gośvan-sāv-avarṇa*.

Likewise, from *gaurī* ending in *ṅīṣ*, in forms such as *śunyā* and *śunyai*, there would also be a prohibition of the rule "udāttayaṇo halapūrvāt" [Pāṇini 6.1.174]. In *gomatī* and similar forms, the *num* augment prescribed by "ugidacām" [Pāṇini 7.1.70] would also apply. In *anaḍvāhī*, the *ām* prescribed for *catur* and *anaḍuh* [Pāṇini 7.1.98] would follow after the vowel *ī*. In *supathī*—derived from the analysis "she in whom there is a beautiful path" (*śobhanaḥ panthā asyām*), where the compound-final suffix is prohibited by "na pūjanāt" [Pāṇini 5.4.69], and then *ṅīp* is applied by "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp" [Pāṇini 4.1.5] with the elision of the final syllable of the *bha*-stem—the [augment *num*] would also apply here.

Since, under the heading of *aṅga*, there is the inclusion of that which ends in such a [suffix], as in the case of *supanthāḥ*, the rule *puṃso 'suṅ* would also apply here in *supaṃsī*. [One might object: "In the list of words beginning with *uraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.151), because *pumān* is read as a word ending in a case-suffix, the suffix *kap* occurs invariably only after the singular form; however, for the plural form, since the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā* applies, *kap* is indeed optional. In the alternative where *kap* is absent, there is the substitution of a short vowel for *puṃs*, and the suffix *masu*; the letter *ā* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In that case, because the suffix is marked with the indicatory letter *u* (*ugit*), [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added].

By the rule *ugitaśca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. By the rules *sakhyurasambuddhau* and *anaṅ sau*, the forms *sakhau* and *sakhyau* would also occur [by the addition of *anaṅ*] because of its *ṇit*-status. However, the prescription of *ṅīṣ* in the rule *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* would be for the sake of forms such as *sakhībhyām*.

In the rule *vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām*, the word *ava* is specified as occurring in the vocative case (*sambuddhau*). Consequently, because of the principle *yena nāvyavadhānam* ("that by which there is no intervention"), the substitution of *o* (otva) does not take effect here when there is an intervention by even a single phoneme—as in *he bhagavati* and *he aghavati*. Due to the absence of that [substitution], the substitution of *r* (rutva), which is taught in conjunction with it, also does not occur. Furthermore, in the rule *śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite*, because the term *anaḥ* is carried over from the preceding rule *allopo'naḥ*, there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) in the form *yuvatīḥ paśya*.

Thus, there are indeed purposes for this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding gender-distinction, and there are also defects. For the sake of those purposes, this rule must be formulated; however, one must provide remedies for the defects. And the remedy is as follows: since the form *ghaṭī* would already be included by the mention of *ghaṭa* in the example *śaktilāṅgala*, the specific mention of *ghaṭī* is intended to indicate that this technical rule is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

Therefore, this remains established: the mention of the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* is redundant when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, because the mention of the stem includes the form qualified by gender as well.

He refutes this, saying: "This is not so. Regarding the phrase "it has as its object an injunction concerning the word-form" (*svarūpavidhiviṣaya*): an injunction that takes the word-form itself as its basis is an "injunction concerning the word-form" (*svarūpavidhi*); the meaning is "in that which is both such an injunction and an object. He asks, "What is being stated? and replies: "When there is the apprehension of the word-form of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Why is this so? To this he says: "And thus," etc. Just as the statement regarding the compounding of the word *yuvañ* with the word *jaratī* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this point, so too is it demonstrated in that very same place. "Of that very kind," etc.

The meaning is that this is entirely consistent with what was stated: "When there is the mention of the actual form of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is also the mention of that which is qualified by gender. If this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) concerning the domain of rules prescribing the actual form [of a word], how is the treatment as an *iṣṭhan* suffix established—as in *kumārayati* from *kumārīm ācaṣṭe* ("he describes a young girl")? He considers its establishment to be due to *bāhulaka* (irregularity/variety). For this is recited in the *curādi* group: "From a nominal stem, in the sense of verbal action, [the suffix *nic* is added] diversely, and it is treated like *iṣṭhan*."

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned in any way whatsoever, that which is qualified by gender is also included. Accordingly, according to the view "from all nominal stems, some say," the suffix *kvip* occurs even after a word ending in a feminine suffix—as in *yāminayantyahāni* ("the days that cause the nights to pass").

With the words "kiñca" and so forth, he adds another purpose [for the rule]. Regarding "kālitara": from the word *kāla*, by applying the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra* and then the comparative suffix *tarap*, the shortening occurs by the rule *gharūpakalpa* etc. He asks: what is the reason that the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) from that ending is not established? He says: "Because of conflict" (*vipratiṣedhāt*). The scope for the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is when excellence is not intended to be expressed, as in *kālī*; the scope for the suffix expressing excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*) is when femininity is not intended to be expressed, as in *kālatara*.

If there were an intention to express both [the feminine suffixes and the *taddhita* suffix], and both were applicable simultaneously, the *taddhita* suffix would occur by virtue of its higher status [in the order of rules]. However, when the mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *g* is present, then by the force of the governing context of the three bases (*prakṛti*) in the rule for *tarap*, *ṅī* and *āp* occur first, and subsequently *tarap*; thus the desired result is established.

Now, one might object: since femininity (*strītva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), the suffix caused by it is also internal; whereas excellence (*prakarṣa*), because it depends on an external correlative, is external (*bahiraṅga*), and therefore the suffix caused by it must also be external. Furthermore, even the suffix *ka* prescribed after words beginning with *prāg* (Pāṇini 5.3.70) in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth is indeed external, because it depends on the meaning of "unknown" and the like; for the connection with meanings such as "unknown" occurs only after the word has already ended in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*), and case-endings themselves depend on [factors] such as number and grammatical object (*karman*).

Even before the connection with number, object, and so forth, the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is connected with gender (*liṅga*). And it has been said: "Having denoted its own meaning (*svārtha*), a word denotes the substance (*dravya*) inherent [in it] independently; but in the expression of that which is inherent, having denoted gender, number, and case-ending, and disregarding those particularities, it then reaches its full self in relation to affection, contempt, and the like; thus, the cognition of the qualified object arises from that [stem]. Therefore, first the own-meaning, which serves as the qualifier, must be denoted, and afterwards the substance qualified by it."

Because that [the base] is the primary element as the substratum (*dharmin*), the gender (*liṅga*) follows next because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Number (*saṃkhyā*), however, is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on differentiation; yet even that is more internal than the case-roles (*kāraka*) which depend on factors of a different class such as action (*karman*) and so forth. Therefore, number is denoted first, followed by the case-roles. Thus, once the meaning is complete, there is subsequently a connection with contempt and the like. For the causes of contempt and so forth are the meanings of the suffixes themselves (*svārtha*), since this is how it is understood in cases such as *paṇḍitaka* ("a pseudo-scholar") and the like, where the contempt applies to the substance itself.

Thus, in this way, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is *antaraṅga* (internal), while the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are *bahiraṅga* (external); and a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the internal and the external is improper. In that case, consider the rule "in the sense of a color when it is not permanent" (*varṇe cānitye*), along with "when it means 'dyed'" (*rakte*) and "and after *kāla*" (*kālācca*). Its scope is exemplified by *kālaka*, where there is no intention to express femininity. The scope of the feminine suffix is exemplified by *kālī*. In the instance *kālikā*, where both would apply, the suffix *kan* would occur by virtue of its being subsequent [in the rules]. Furthermore, because that [suffix *kan*] is strictly *svārthika* (expressing its own meaning), the feminine suffix does not possess *antaraṅga*-status in relation to it.

There is no distinction here; for even if [the suffix] arises from the word *kāla*, the form *kālikā* would be established by [Pāṇini 7.3.44] *pratyayasthāt* [which prescribes *it*]. However, when [the suffix] arises from the word *harita*, since the suffix *kan* would apply by virtue of being subsequent (paratva), overriding both the feminine marker *ṅīp* and the *nakāra* by the rule *na sāmivacane*, the form *hariṇikā* would not be possible.

The word *hariṇa* has the same meaning as the word *harita*; therefore, [the suffix] will apply when it functions as the object (*karma*). But why would it not also apply after the word *harita*, resulting in *haritikā*? In that case, consider the following: the suffix *kan* added in the sense of "extreme" by the rule *lohitān maṇau* would, due to its higher status, supersede the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the shortening of the vowel (*nakāra*) prescribed by the rule *varṇādanudāttāt*. Consequently, one would only get *lohitikā* and not *lohinikā*; yet both forms are desired. For that purpose, the mention of *ṅīp* and *āp* is made.

But is this not already established by the rule "there is also the sublation of gender after *lohita*"? In that case, it need not be stated. How so? In the rule "after a non-udātta vowel [ending in] a color-name," the word "optionally" (*vā*) is understood to carry over. Thus, when the suffix *kan* is applied to the words *lohinī* and *lohitā*, which end in the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*, the desired forms *lohinikā* and *lohitikā* are established once shortening (*hrasvatva*) and the substitution of *itva* have been applied as appropriate.

This being the case, it need not be stated—either as "or there is the sublation of gender [by the suffix] after *lohita*"—for the purpose that, when *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, there should be optional sublation by a suffix caused by gender, rather than obligatory sublation. Nor should it be stated for the purpose that, although the suffix *kan* (which is prescribed by a specific rule) would otherwise cause the obligatory sublation of the suffix caused by gender, there should instead be optional sublation; for the mention of *ṅī* and *āp* serves no other purpose.

If the suffix *kan* were intended here as an absolute superlative (*atyantasvārthika*) derived from the words *eta-* and *śveta-*, then, since the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* would have served its purpose there, a constant (*nitya*) sublation of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would result for the word *lohita-* by means of the *kan* prescribed by the specific rule (*pratipadavihita*). In that case, must this [exception] be stated? Or rather, need it not be stated, because even the rule "after *lohita-* when denoting a gem" has its application in the masculine and neuter genders? Thus, although *kan* is an absolute superlative, the mention of *ṅī* must indeed be made so that the suffix may occur after a word ending in *ṅī*.

The inclusion of *āp* (the feminine suffix) is for the sake of clarity. In that regard, there is a fault concerning the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*): when a *bahuvrīhi* is formed in the sense "in this city there are many *gomat* [possessors of cows]," since the feminine form is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), both the suffix *ṅīp* and the suffix *kap* would be applicable. If *ṅīp* were applied due to the mention of *ṅy-āp*, then *kap* would follow; consequently, the form would become *bahugomatīkā*, whereas the desired form is *bahugomatka*. This is not a fault, because the compound-final suffixes are added to the final member of the compound even before the compound itself is fully formed; subsequently, the compound is formed with that which ends in the suffix. Thus...

For the status of being a final constituent (*pratyantāvayavatva*) with respect to a compound is appropriate for compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*); and so he will state in the rule *na kapi*. Regarding this, some hold that the compound-final suffixes are placed before the case-ending (*vibhakti*) belonging to the meaning of the compound within the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Others hold that when the compound-final suffixes follow, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided (*luka*), and because the word then ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the case-ending (*sup*) is added again, whereby the compound of the inflected word (*subanta*) is formed.

In every respect, the form *bahucarmikā* would result [from the rule *prātipadikāt*], because of the prohibition [contained in] *asupaḥ*, as in the case of *bahuparivrājakā madhurā*. An effort must be made here [to resolve this]. However, regarding [the rules] such as *nañastatpuruṣāt*, we shall resolve the contradictions with the text in their respective places. Thus, it stands established: the mention of *ṅy-āp* is for the purpose of prescribing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) after a stem ending in those [suffixes]; for, by the principle of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the secondary derivative suffix is more powerful.

If this is so, then the suffixes *ti* and *ūṅ* should also be included in the rule "yūnastiḥ" and "ūṅutaḥ" for the purpose of prescribing secondary (*taddhita*) affixes after words ending in them—e.g., *yuvatitarā*. Due to the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur by the rule "tasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ. Alternatively, because the shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "khid-dhādiṣu puṃvadbhāvāt," it prevails over the masculine substitution through the operation of a grammatical maxim (*parjanyavat lakṣaṇapravṛtti*), as the latter is sublated by the former.

In the case of *brahmabandhūtarā nadī*, when the short vowel is not applied under the rule *śeṣādanyatarasyām*, there is a prohibition of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule *jāteśca*. However, in the previous instance, this prohibition is not obtained because youth (*yauvana*) is not a genus (*jāti*); for a genus is that which persists as long as the substance exists, and thus *yuvajāniḥ* is cited as an example.

But surely, *ty* and *ūṅ* will occur here precisely because they are internal (*antaraṅga*). As for the suffix *kan* in the sense of an absolute self-meaning (*atyantasvārthika*), there is no difference between the form *brahmabandhukā*—where the shortening prescribed by *ke’ṇaḥ* occurs—and the case where the suffix arises from a stem ending in *ūṅ*, or from one ending in *u*. Even in the case of the word *yuvati*, when *kan* is added, there is no difference at all, since the masculine form (*bhvāya*) results through the application of *puṃvadbhāva*. Furthermore, there is no evidence that *kan* is intended to be applied after this [word]. Therefore, there is no purpose in including *ty* and *ūṅ* [in the rule].

The suffixes *su*, *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*, *śas*, *ṭā*, *bhyām*, *bhis*, *ṅe*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*, *ṅasi*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*, *ṅas*, *os*, *ām*, *ṅi*, *os*, and *sup* [are called *vibhakti*]. Pāṇini 4.1.2.

"The *u* and other [sounds] are *anubandhas*," and so forth. In that regard, the *u* of the nominative singular is for the sake of pronunciation, because in the rules "there is elision of *su* after *etad* and *tad*" (*etattadoḥ sulopaḥ*) and "after a long vowel, before *su*, *ti*, and *si*" (*dīrghātsutisi*), a consonant alone cannot be uttered. However, in this particular rule, because of its proximity to the diphthong *au*, it is possible to utter the letter *s* alone. Furthermore, it does not serve as a qualifier in the rule "anaṅ before *su*" (*anaṅ sau*), because there is nothing to be excluded [by such a qualification].

Nor does the objection apply that if *anaṅ si* were stated, there would be the undesirable consequence [of *anaṅ*] applying even to the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*), because when a specific phoneme is indicated, a rule may apply to what begins with it; for the term *sarvanāmasthāne* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*). Furthermore, the letter *j* in *jasaḥ* is for the sake of unambiguous pronunciation in this very sūtra; otherwise, there would be doubt regarding the substitution of *āv* for *au*—namely, whether the pronunciation is of the diphthong *au* or of the sequence *a-u*. However, it is not intended as a qualifier in rules such as *jasaḥ śī*.

Even if one were to say "asaḥ śī," there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because *śas* and the other suffixes possess indicatory letters (*sānubandhaka*). The letter *ś* in *śas* and the letter *ṭ* in *auṭ* are for the purpose of unambiguous pronunciation; otherwise, there would be doubt as to whether [the suffixes] were *ḍakāra* or *ṭakāra*. However, in rules such as "tasmācchasaḥ," they do not serve to qualify [the suffix], because *jas* and the others also possess indicatory letters. In the case of "ṭā," the letter *ṭ* serves to qualify [the suffix] in the rule "ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ."

Otherwise, there would also be the inclusion of the vowel *ā* prescribed by rules such as *supāṃ suluk...* [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. Thus, among these four [suffixes], the initial vowels (*u*, etc. serve the purpose of specifying their pronunciation. Their designation as *it* is so that they might not be heard in actual usage; however, there is no grammatical operation (*it-kārya*) to be performed by them. The letter *ṭ* in *auṭ* is for the purpose of including it in the pratyāhāra *suṭ*. The letter *ṅ* in *ṅe* and the subsequent suffixes is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] *gher ṅiti* [Pāṇini 7.3.111].

The letter *ṅ* in *ṅasi* is for the purpose of ensuring that [the term] is not included in the rule *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso 'ś*. The letter *p* is for the purpose of including [the letters] in a pratyāhāra. Since the meaning of the statement "the indicatory letters (*anubandha*) beginning with *u* serve as qualifiers for pronunciation as appropriate" has already been established, this was stated here. And thus, there ought to be a subsequent passage stating: "The letter *ṭ* in *auṭ* is for the purpose of including [the letters] in the pratyāhāra *suṭ*."

But where do these [grammatical categories] such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and object (*karman*) occur? He says: "Number, object, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by another rule" (*śāstrāntareṇa*): this refers to rules such as "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*) and "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*). "It forms a single syntactic unit with that" means that it constitutes a single sentence together with those other rules. Previously, however, the expression "by another rule" was stated with reference to the distinction between intermediate subordinate sentences. Indeed, by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), even those [words] read in different sections form a single syntactic unit.

However, due to the difference in context, the recitation [of the rule] is intended so that there may be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) even with the rules for *tiṅ* and other suffixes. In the case of the rule "the plural is used for many" (*bahuṣu bahuvacanam*), it is stated by assuming a separate sentence: "From *ṅyāp*-prātipadikas, *svādi* suffixes [are applied]; from *la*, *tibādi* suffixes. Thus, the plural number is prescribed here as the denotable meaning (*vācyatvena*) of that [suffix] which was previously enjoined. Furthermore, in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*), since they lack number, the *svādi* suffixes are indeed present as those prescribed by general rules.

However, if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), then because the suffixes *svādi* (case endings) would be prescribed for number (*ekatvādi*) and so forth—which are already associated with a specific meaning such as the object (*karman*)—it would not be possible for them to be "prescribed generally" (*sāmānyavihitatva*). Therefore, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) provided by the rule "after an indeclinable, *sup* [is elided]" (*avyayād āpsupaḥ*), which prescribes the elision of the *sup* suffix produced after an indeclinable, the production of *svādi* suffixes from indeclinables follows in this view. Examples will be made manifest in their respective sentences as appropriate.
In the feminine gender. 4.1.3.

"Because of the application of this very rule [Pāṇini 6.4.69] regarding *ṅī* and *āp*. This is the reason why, in this particular section, only the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is connected [to the suffix]. And this is stated with reference to the context; however, at the time of the operation of other rules, a base (*prakṛti*) ending in a suffix prescribed by another rule is certainly possible. [Objection: But in this entire section, whenever possible, the word "from *at*" (*ataḥ*) is connected [to the rule], and a feminine form ending in *ṅī* or *āp* does not end in *at*. Furthermore, since its meaning has already been expressed, there is no possibility of applying *ṅī* or *āp* after such forms? [Response: True; however, the underlying logic (*nyāya*) is being examined here.

He objects: "It is said, 'in the feminine' (striyām). The meaning is that by means of this locative indication (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), the term is restated for the purpose of prescribing another grammatical operation. He then asks: "What is this so-called 'feminine'? The meaning is that since "feminine" is not defined within this treatise (*śāstra*), and since adopting the worldly sense of "feminine" would result in the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) to words such as *khaṭvā* (bedstead), which are feminine in common usage, this restatement based on what is already well-known is untenable.

Since the nature (*svarūpa*) itself is what is sought to be known, the question is formulated with a nominative case, as in "in which woman? (kasyāṃ striyām); for if it were stated as "of which woman" (kasyāḥ striyāḥ), the question would concern a specific instance. Furthermore, the mention of "woman" (*strī*) is intended to indicate by implication the masculine and neuter genders as well. For this very reason, in the answer, the general and particular characteristics—femininity and so forth—are presented, thereby demonstrating the nature of all three genders. Thus, it would have been appropriate to define the nature of gender at the very first occurrence in the rule "the short vowel is [used] in the neuter" (*hrasvo napuṃsake*); however, that was not done. In this regard, the definition according to common worldly usage is as follows:
"A woman is one who possesses breasts and hair; a man is traditionally said to be one who is hairy (*lomaśa*).
That which is the difference between the two, in the absence of which there is a neuter (*napuṃsaka*).

In this context, the suffix *matup* is used for "earth" and so forth, and likewise the suffix *śa* is used in the word *lomaśa*. The possession of breasts and hair is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the female gender, as it is well-known to be a cause for recognizing a woman even when she is a young girl (*kumārī*) or otherwise. Similarly, the state of being hairy is an indicative mark for the male gender, as it is a cause for recognizing a man even when he is a boy (*kumāra*) or otherwise. The meaning is that the "difference between the two"—that is, the similarity consisting of both sets of characteristics such as breasts and hair—is what constitutes a neuter.

Therefore, even though the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) or a verb (*ākhyāta*) lacks both femininity and masculinity, it does not follow that it possesses neuter gender. Otherwise, if only "in the absence of those" (*tadabhāve*) were stated, such an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would arise. By specifying "in the absence of those" (*tadabhāva*), it is shown that the neuter gender does not apply to the meaning of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) such as *kukkuṭamayūrī* (cock-and-peahen), which consists of a collection of both female and male entities. For a collection is similar to its constituent members; thus, the aforementioned undesirable consequence would otherwise occur.

This objection does not apply, because by the rule "the gender of the latter" (*paravalliṅgam*), the gender of the subsequent member is extended to the whole compound. True; however, this [present discussion] should be understood as being concerned with the determination of the actual nature of things. By this, it is stated that femininity and so forth are either the connection with breasts, hair, and the like; or the breasts themselves in their specific configuration; or the classes (*jāti*) characterized by those [features].

In this view, the suffix *ṭāp* would undesirably apply to the word *bhrukuṃsa* (an actor wearing female attire), for a connection with breasts and hair is perceived in him; furthermore, since barber shops (*kharakuṭī*) and the like possess hair, when they are masculine, the rule for changing *t* to *n* would apply in the phrase "look at the barber shops" (*kharakuṭīḥ paśya*). A barber shop is called *kharakuṭī*. Now, one might object: "In this context, the intended connection is with breasts and so forth that possess natural development, not just any [connection whatsoever]."

Since "breasts" and so forth were stated as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other well-known [female] things as well, how can this objection (*prasaṅga*) arise? If that is the case, then "beds" (*khaṭvā*) and "trees" (*vṛkṣa*) would not be established [as feminine], because beds, trees, and the like lack breasts, body hair, and so on. One might argue: "Just as objects covered by a cloth are not perceived, likewise the existing gender-mark (*liṅga*) of beds and trees is simply not perceived. That is not correct.

Objects covered by a cloth are perceived when the cloth is removed; yet, in the case of a bedstead and a tree, no sign [of their existence] is perceived even at that very moment [when they are covered]. Just as the motion of the sun, though it exists, is not perceived through direct perception but is inferred from its arrival at another location, so too the sign of the bedstead and the tree, though existing, is not perceived due to its subtlety.

For even existent entities may fail to be perceived for six reasons: due to extreme proximity, as with collyrium and the like applied to one's own eye; due to excessive distance, as with a bird that has flown away; due to being concealed by another physical object, as with gold or similar items hidden behind a wall or the like; due to being enveloped in darkness, as with a jar or similar objects shrouded in gloom; and due to the weakness of the sense organs, such as when the eyes are impaired by cataracts or other defects.

"From excessive negligence"—negligence (*pramāda*) is a lack of attentiveness; for one whose mind is distracted by other objects does not perceive even a nearby object. As for subtlety (*saukṣmya*), it is included within the weakness of the senses, since one possessing divine sight and hearing perceives even a subtle object. Likewise, "confusion with similar things" (*samānābhihāra*) is also included therein; for example, a bean thrown into a heap of beans is not perceived separately.

The same applies to suppression (*abhibhava*); for example, the stars, overwhelmed by the rays of the sun, are not perceived during the day. But how is it determined that the mark of the bedpost and the tree is never perceived? Because we observe the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and others, which are produced by those [words] and have no other function.

If this were so, a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*) would result: namely, that the application of words such as *ṭāp* and others arises from the comprehension of gender, and the comprehension of gender arises from their application. It may be argued that the weakness of the sense organs is sometimes the cause for perceiving something at one time and not perceiving it at another; however, since gender is never perceived in objects such as a bedstead (*khaṭvā*), and since perception—which grasps the object of the bedstead as distinct from gender—ascertains the absence of gender therein, an inference contrary to that perception cannot arise.

For it cannot be argued that "the monk’s house is like an elephant-stable because it is a location, like an elephant-stable; however, the elephant is not perceived because of the weakness of the sense organs [in that case]. Therefore, even a non-existent sign (*liṅga*) is perceived in words such as *khaṭvā* (bed) through the power of linguistic usage. Granted that this may be the cognition of the listener, by what means does the speaker—who is the one employing the word—perceive that sign so as to employ a word corresponding to it? Furthermore, in the case of *kumāry-arthaḥ* (the object of a girl) and *kumārī-vastu* (the thing that is a girl), there would be an inconsistency regarding the masculine and neuter genders of the words *artha* and *vastu* when applied to feminine entities such as a girl. However, in the Bhāṣya...
Manifestation, disappearance, and persistence—
these imperishable attributes are observed as the defining characteristics (liṅga) in all embodied forms.

Manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) is increase (*upacaya*), which is masculinity; concealment (*tirobhāva*) is decrease (*apacaya*), which is femininity; and the intermediate state (*antarālāvasthā*) is stability (*sthiti*), meaning neuter-ness. Of what, then, are manifestation and the others the gender-marks? They are the marks of the qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—and of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are their transformations and consist of them.

Furthermore, all material forms consisting of aggregates such as sound and so forth, as well as the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest, are by nature subject to transformation at every moment; they do not remain in their own self even for a moment. This applies equally to sound and the like, to space and the like, and to jars and the like.
And it has been said:
"In every group of the qualities such as sound, which constitute the essence of all material forms..."

"The three factors, such as existence (sattva) and the rest, are omnipresent. And: "Their unstable mode of operation, like boiling water, is described incessantly in the Bhāṣya regarding all entities."
Likewise:
"Of form and of its constituent elements, such as white and so forth, some part perishes every moment while some other part somehow increases."

"For all those possessed of activity are constantly not separated from the three types of activity, and it is within this [realm] that speech arises. This means that it is the word itself, ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp*, that brings these states within its range. Although the Puruṣa is indeed unchanging (*apariṇāmī*), nevertheless—
In insentient things, consciousness appears as if it has been transferred;
that which occurs through the principle of reflection is the basis for verbal expression.
And therefore:
That which has the nature of non-activity and whose purpose is consciousness is grasped as the very form of consciousness;
it follows, as it were, the various activities of others that have diverse supports.

Even a universal such as "cowness" possesses the property of being active because it is non-different from the individual; however, in cases such as the "horn of a hare," this is so only by way of that [individual].
Therefore, because the aforementioned categories are possible, they possess the capacity for logical marks (*liṅga*);
for there are indeed these three types of activity (*pravṛtti*).

Masculinity, femininity, and neuterhood—by these there would be the state of having other genders. Thus, because they pervade all objects, these three genders exist in the states of growth, decline, and the intermediate stage. And so, even for a single object, the connection with various genders is established—as in *nakṣatra*, *tārakā*, and *tiṣya* (for a star), or *kumārī*, *artha*, and *vastu* (for a young woman). This is because the triad of manifestation and the rest is always possible within that very same object due to the differentiation of qualities (*guṇa*). Nor does it follow from this that every word denoting such [an object] would necessarily possess all three genders.

For there is no such rule: that every aspect (ākāra) present in a particular meaning must be denoted by the word that culminates in that meaning; rather, it is only this much: that whatever aspect is denoted must exist [in reality]. For example—*takṣā* (carpenter), *yuvā* (young man), *kṛṣṇaḥ* (dark), *kāmukaḥ* (lover)—although these words such as "carpenter" and the rest culminate in a single referent, the aspect expressed is strictly determined. The same should be observed regarding gender (*liṅga*) as well. And it has been said: "When word-meanings are in proximity, only a certain one among them is the motivator."
"Just as there is a restriction regarding gender for words such as *takṣan* (carpenter), so it is here.

Even in the case of "the girl grows" (*upacīyate kumārī*), the word *kumārī* by its own power expresses only the diminution of some property; however, through the employment of another word, the growth of another property is understood. Likewise, in "the tree decays" (*kṣīyate vṛkṣaḥ*), there is diminution. Thus, this entire view is free from confusion. But the author of the *Vṛtti*, because ordinary people do not understand it in this way, presents a position that conforms to their understanding—namely, "they are generalities and particulars. This means that some are generalities (*sāmānya*).

Alternatively—the term "general-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is conventionally established for universals that are distinct from pure existence (*sattā*). The meaning is that there are three intermediate classes. And it has been said:
"These three classes alone exist in some [entities], being non-contradictory with contradictory classes such as those of cows, buffaloes, and so forth."
"The cognition of 'femaleness' persists in both an elephant and a mare;
therefore, they maintain that this universal (jāti) inheres in substances and other categories."

Now, one might object: "The existence of these three—universal, particular, and individual—must be admitted in all objects, not merely in a few objects such as 'cowness' and the like. Otherwise, how could words with different genders, such as *artha*, *vyakti*, and *vastu*, be applied to a single referent? Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the appearance of all three genders would occur everywhere. To this, he says: "Individuals (*vyakti*) of many kinds. They are called *vyaktis* because the universals and particulars are manifested (*vyajyante*) by them; they are the substrata (*āśraya*).

This is what is meant: because substrates—that is, manifestors—are diverse, a particular substrate is the manifestor of a particular universal-particular, but not every [substrate] is the manifestor of every [universal]. In that regard, among sentient beings, an individual possessing breasts and so forth is the manifestor of femininity; one possessing hairiness and so forth is the manifestor of masculinity; and one possessing both sets of characteristics is the manifestor of neuter-ness.

How is it [determined] in the case of insentient things (*acetana*), since no gender-indicative mark (*liṅga*) whatsoever is manifested there? If that were so, then even in the case of sentient beings, there would be the impossibility of words such as *artha*, *vyakti*, and *vastu* having different genders; and furthermore, why would the masculine word *dāra* not apply to a wife? To this he says: "In some cases, due to the absence of a specific substratum (*āśrayaviśeṣa*). A specific substratum is that which is capable of manifesting that [gender]. In the case of insentient things, manifestation occurs everywhere solely through instruction (*upadeśa*). Instruction, moreover, is found in works such as the *Liṅgānuśāsana*.

Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: "just as [the qualities] such as Brāhmaṇahood. Because there is an extreme similarity between individual instances of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, the manifestation of Brāhmaṇahood and the like occurs only through instruction. Indeed, when a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya are standing before one, the cognition "this is a Brāhmaṇa" or "this is a Kṣatriya" does not arise prior to receiving instruction.

Just as in the absence of individual cows or horses, even in cases such as a hare’s horn, there is a connection with a universal (*sāmānya*) mediated by the meaning of the latter member of the compound—the universal being the *jāti*—so too, even within a universal, there exists another universal, such as the universal of existence (*sattā-sāmānya*) in respect to cowness (*gotva*) and the like. For according to us, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas, universals are not themselves devoid of universals.

This word *strī* (woman/feminine) functions both with respect to the quality alone and with respect to the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), just like words such as *śukla* (white). In that regard, when the word *strī* refers to the quality alone, then the rule "when the meaning to be expressed is femininity, the suffixes *ṭāp* and so on occur after a nominal stem denoting a substance" applies; thus, one position is that femininity is the meaning of the suffix. However, when a substance endowed with femininity is expressed by the word *strī*, then two further positions are possible: that femininity is either a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

In that regard, regarding the first [view], the position is that *ṭāp* and other suffixes are added to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denoting a substance characterized by femininity, [the condition being] "this [suffix is added] when [the stem] is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a feminine [word]. Regarding the second [view], however, the position is that [the suffix is added] to a nominal stem that denotes a substance endowed with femininity and which has accepted that femininity; thus, in this case, femininity is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).

If it is argued that [the term "woman"] must be in grammatical apposition with a feminine noun, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "element" (*bhūta*), etc.—for instance, "this Brāhmaṇī woman is an element," "this Brāhmaṇī woman is primordial matter" (*pradhāna*), or "this small jar is a receptacle" (*āvapana*). However, this fault does not apply to either of the two positions [under consideration]. How so? Because terms such as "element" function by virtue of the possibility of the predominance of consciousness, and they do not function by way of assuming femininity. Thus, since a fault is seen in this position, he states—beginning with "And femininity"—that one of the other two [positions] must be adopted.

"It is appropriate in both ways. [Objection: But if the meaning of the suffix is the primary referent (*pratyayārtha*), then the use of dual and plural endings, as well as multiple suffixes, would be untenable. How so? This single referent called "femininity" (*strītva*) is denoted by the suffix as subordinate to the meaning of the base; since it is singular, only the singular ending should apply. Furthermore, multiple suffixes would be impossible—as in *gārgyāyaṇī*, *kārīṣagandhyā*, and *kālitara*. Why? Because this single referent called "femininity" has already been expressed by one [suffix].

Does this not result in the non-application of the second suffix, according to the rule that "those whose meaning has already been expressed are not employed"? Furthermore, the vowel *ī* would not occur in the word *strī*, because the state of being female (*strītva*), which is contraction (*saṃstyāna*), is already expressed by the word *strī* ending in the suffix *ḍraṭ* (according to the rule *styāyater ḍraṭ*). Moreover, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not exist in the case of "the girl Devadatta," because two instances of femininity—each delimited by its own respective base-meaning—would be denoted as primary entities; consequently, a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) based on distinction (*vyatireka*) would arise. Why? Because... [text ends].

First, it cannot arise from one [word] with respect to another, because there is no relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇaguṇibhāva*) between them; nor can it arise from the base of a feminine suffix, because it is sublated by suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others. In that case, where a feminine suffix is prohibited in relation to a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the genitive case would apply—as in "five Brahmin women" (*pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ*) or "a beautiful sister" (*svasābhirūpā*). However, according to the other view, since both [words] reside in the substance (*dravya*), there is no distinction [between them], and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs; furthermore, because the substance may be manifold, the dual and plural numbers also occur.

This is correct. Just as the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth occur even when femininity has already been expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), so too it is not illogical for multiple suffixes to occur; for in that case, the various suffixes serve to indicate that [femininity], and it is observed that even multiple things, such as lamps and the like, can function as indicators. Furthermore, there is no fault even under the view that the meaning of the suffix is [the feminine gender] itself.

Although the suffix is applied when only femininity is to be expressed, nevertheless—due to the intention to express non-difference between femininity and its substratum, or because of the inherent nature of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal being observed in both cases—there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as well as a difference in number. Furthermore, in forms such as *gārgyāyaṇī*, femininity can be expressed by both [the primary and secondary suffixes] alone, and not by one alone, due to their inherent nature.

Alternatively, by the force of the inclusion of the *ṣ* in *ṣpha*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is established; and by the force of the rule "yaṅaścāp," the suffix *cāp* will also occur after *ṣyaṅ*. For instance, two markers (*anubandha*) were attached to *ṣyaṅ* here in order to include both *yaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ* generally and to prevent their obstruction. In a form such as *kālitara*, one [instance] is joined with excellence (*prakarṣa*) and the other is not joined with excellence. Since the single meaning is differentiated there due to the difference in state, the feminine gender of that which is joined with excellence remains unexpressed; therefore, for the sake of expressing that, [the suffix *cāp* is applied].

The suffix *ṭāp* will also occur. Even in the case of the word *strī*, the long vowel *ī* is established by this very rule (*striyām*) as a formal exception (*nipātana*); thus it is well said that "it is appropriate in both ways."
The suffix *ṭāp* is applied after a feminine stem beginning with a vowel other than *a*, or after a stem ending in short *a*, provided it does not begin with a prefix such as *aja*.

"Also after what ends in *at*": this means "after that which ends in the vowel *a*. It does not, however, refer to the phonetic form itself; for [the suffix *ṅīp*] follows feminine bases such as *nīta*, *parīta*, and *kaliṅgaga*, because of the rule "when there is a desire to express that as the beginning" (*tadādyācikhyāsāyām*) and other such indications. The letter *p* is for the purpose of general inclusion, as in the rule "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *prātipadika*" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*). The adherence to the letter *p* serves the purpose of including the suffixes *ṭāp* and *ṅīp*. The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of general inclusion.

Otherwise, because this [suffix] alone would have a single subsequent element (*ekānubandhaka*), only its own [substitution] would occur, and not that of *ḍāp* or *cāp*. As in *khaṭvā*. But how, one might ask, is it determined here that the base ends in *ā*, given that this [word] always occurs in the feminine with the suffix *-āp*? From both scripture (*śāstra*) and usage (*prayoga*). For in the view of Śākaṭāyana, all [words] are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*). In examples such as *pañcakhaṭvaḥ*—"bought for five *khaṭvās*"—where the feminine suffix has been elided, the fact that the base ends in *ā* is seen in actual usage.

"Śubhaṃyāḥ" and "kīlālapāḥ"—these are formed by adding *ṭāp* according to the rule "it is seen [to be applied] after other [roots] as well. He asks: what fault is there here when *ṭāp* is present? He replies: "by the rule *halḍyābbhyaḥ*, there would be elision (*sulopa*) of the nominative suffix *su*.
Regarding the phrase "in some cases, by the characteristic of a genus (*jāti*)," he will demonstrate the distinction during the occasion of reciting the *gaṇa* lists.

Regarding the phrase "but for those ending in consonants," etc., the word "ajādi" (beginning with 'a') is included because it is impossible for the current subject, which ends in the nominative case, to be construed [with that term]; the remainder of the sense is that the mention of "ajādi" is for the sake of that [consonantal ending].

Regarding the term *amahatpūrvā*: because the word *mahat* is used here as a mere imitation (anukaraṇa) and thus lacks the expression of a worldly meaning (*laukikārtha*), the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel] as prescribed by the rule *ānmahataḥ* does not occur. As for the case of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), however, only the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies. He states the purpose of including the mention of "jāti" (genus): [one might object,] "But since in the case of connection with a male, the word for another [person] is applied to another through the relation 'this is that,' it will not apply simply because it is figurative (*gauṇa*); therefore, the mention of *jāti* is for the sake of easy understanding. He explains the meaning of the phrase *amahatpūrvā*: "if preceded by *mahat*."

Here too, the term "jāti" (caste/class) is connected [to the rule]; let there be no prohibition here in the case of *mahatī śūdrā* = *mahāśūdrā*, for in this instance the compound preceded by *mahat* does not denote a caste. Where, then, is the prohibition applied? It applies where the compound refers to a caste. This has been demonstrated: for the word *mahāśūdra* denotes the *ābhīra* caste.

If this is so, then since the word denotes the genus (*jāti*) in reference to the whole, there is no meaning for the individual parts—as in the case of *gaurakhara* and similar compounds—and thus it is merely a derivative formation (*vyutpatti*). In that case, because the feminine gender of the individual parts is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), when a masculine compound is formed, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *ṭāp*. To this, the prohibition [in Pāṇini 5.1.128] "not when preceded by *amahat*" (*amahatpūrva*) becomes meaningful. What follows from this? In the rule "not when preceded by *amahat*," the term "genus" (*jāti*) should not be connected.

How is it that the term *mahāśūdrā* is formed as "great Śūdra woman"? Here, because the suffix *ṭāp* is applied first due to its being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, the case-ending (*sup*) is subsequently added; since the compound is formed from that which ends in a case-ending, the prohibition regarding the suffix *ṭāp* does not apply, as it has already been realized. True; however, for the sake of clarity, the word "jāti" (genus) is indeed connected here as well. But the word *śūdra* is listed [in the Gaṇapāṭha]; what possibility is there for this [prohibition] to apply to the word *mahāśūdra*? To this he says: "there is no rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) [to the prohibition]. Thus, we have *atidhīvarī* and *atipīvarī*.

When the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the roots *dadhāti* and *pibati* by the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*, the substitution of *i* occurs for the final vowel by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām hali*. Thus, we have *atikrāntā dhīvānam* (one who has surpassed the wise) and *atikrāntā pīvānam* (one who has surpassed the fat), which are *prādi*-compounds (*avyayībhāva*). In these cases, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* are applied by the rule *vano ra ca*. However, if this [specific] instruction were not given, the term *vana* would be taken as referring to the suffix *van* itself. Furthermore, even if it were taken as referring to the entire *kṛt*-derived word, in any case, the suffixes would not apply in a compound where the surpassing element is the predominant factor, such as *atibhavatī* and *atimahatī*.

In the rule *ugitaśca*, it is accepted that the term *ugit* refers specifically to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in an *ugit* [vowel]; based on this, the present purpose has been demonstrated. However, regarding that point, he will state later: "The term *ugit* includes both nominal stems and non-nominal stems; therefore, because there is no prohibition against a nominal stem that possesses a suffix, the rule of extension by suffixation (*tadantavidhi*) applies. And as he says: "From whatever [stem] an *ugit* occurs in some way or another, from that nominal stem ending in such [an *ugit*]."

In the word *atimahatī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule for words ending in *ugit* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), because of its treatment as if it were a present participle (*śatṛvat*). Some explain that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because the word is listed in the *gaurādi* group; however, that is incorrect, because of the governing rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14). Furthermore, we do not see any purpose for including it in the *gaurādi* list. Now, one might object that the word *mahatī* is intended to have an udātta accent on the final syllable; this is true, but that is already established by the rule *bṛhanmahatorupasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.173) under the heading *śaturanumaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.172), which prescribes the udātta accent for feminine stems ending in *nadi* or *aj* when they follow a word ending in *śatṛ*.

If it is argued that [the mention of *udātta*] is for the sake of making the accent high-pitched (*udātta*), then that very [mention] will serve the purpose of making the *ṅīp* suffix high-pitched as well. Furthermore, since the absence of *ṅīṣ* has already been stated in cases such as *atimahatī*, an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be desired even for the sake of making the *ṅīp* high-pitched, provided that the rule of "reference to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is being indicated. [Objection: In the case of *pañcājī*—meaning the aggregate of five goats—the suffix *ṭāp* would also apply to the *dvigu* compound. To this they reply: In the rule *ajādyataḥ* (A 4.1.4), the genitive case indicates that when femininity (*strītva*) is inherent (*samaveta*) in the meaning expressed by a word denoting a female—whether that word begins with *aj* or ends in *at*—then [the respective suffixes apply].

Thinking that, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only those bases which indicate the specific quality of femininity are understood to be the *prakṛti*, the author of the Vṛtti stated: "From nominal stems beginning with *aj* and from those ending in *ā*. Furthermore, in the case of *pañcājī*, the femininity inherent in the meaning of the *ajā* [goat] does not belong there; rather, it belongs to the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).

In this way, the prohibition "not after *amahat*" could have been omitted, for in the term *mahāśūdrī*, the feminine suffix does not denote the gender of the word *śūdra*. However, the rule regarding suffixes ending in [a specific element] will be explained under the rule *anupasarjanāt*. Regarding *satprākkāṇḍā*: in the Vārttika on *pākakarṇa* it says, "There is a prohibition [of the suffix] after *puṣpa* when preceded by *sat*, *adat*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, or *eka*"; and in the Bhāṣya on that very point it says, "*prākpuṣpā* and *pratyakpuṣpā*.
Therefore, even here, the word *prāk* should not be read; one should read only *sadackāṇḍa*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after stems ending in short *ṛ*.

"The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of including [the suffix] in general," as in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* and others. However, the statement "the letter *p* is for the purpose of preventing the inclusion of [suffixes] in general" was not mentioned here because it is already understood by following the previous [explanation]; furthermore, even here, the adherence to the letter *p* is for the sake of its being unaccented (*anudātta*).
And [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a stem ending in an *ugit* vowel.

"In whatever way" (*yathākathañcit*): whether it is a *varṇa* (phoneme) that can be designated as having the *ugit* [marker], or a suffix (*pratyaya*), or even a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—the meaning of "in whatever way" is that wherever any one of these modes is possible. This very point is clarified by the phrase "that word-form which has the *ugit* [marker]": the referent of the compound is the word-form itself, whether it be a suffix or not a suffix, a nominal stem or not a nominal stem; the meaning is that it is neither exclusively a nominal stem nor exclusively a suffix.

In this regard, he states that because the *prātipadika* is qualified by the term "ending in an *ugit*," the rule applies to that which ends in such a form: "from that which ends in [an *ugit*]. For example, in *pacantī*, the suffix *śatṛ* is an *ugit*, and the *prātipadika* ending in it is likewise so. This also applies in cases such as *atibhavatī* and *atimahatī*. However, the prohibition regarding "a *prātipadika* accompanied by a [specific] designation" applies only where the unique form of the *prātipadika* is explicitly mentioned in the rule; nevertheless, in the present case, it still occurs by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

However, this prohibition—"the treatment as if possessing a designation does not apply when [a word] is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo'prātipadikena*)—occurs even in the case of *atigomatī* when there is the grasping of the unique form of the nominal stem itself. The paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), on the other hand, occurs only when there is the grasping of the unique form of the affix itself.

"But there is a prohibition for the root *ghu* because it is marked with *u*. The word "it must be stated" (*vaktavya*) is the ellipsis. Should it then be stated? No, it need not be stated. Since [the formation] is already established by the fact that [the root *añc*] is marked as having an *uk* vowel in the rule *ugidacām*, the mention of *añcati* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). In this grammar, whatever operation is prescribed for that which is marked with *uk* applies only to the root *añc*—thus the operation itself is restricted, not merely the addition of the augment *num*. Furthermore, it will be explained in that very place that the mention of "non-root" (*adhātu*) is for the sake of adding *num* even to that which is preceded by a non-root element.

Another says: "The word *ca* in the rule *ugitaśca* serves to include the root *añc-* with its nasal elided; the case-ending is dropped by the rule *supāṃ suluk*; and the mention is made by taking into account the future elision of the vowel *a*. Consequently, the inclusion of *añc-* is for the sake of restriction: since the elisions of the vowel *a* and the nasal *n* are not the governing factors, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs even in cases where the prohibition of elision applies according to the rule *nāñceḥ pūjāyām*, as in *prāñcī* and *pratyañcī brāhmaṇī*. [Examples such as] *ukhāsrat* and *parṇadhvat* are derived under the rule *kvip ca*."
And [the suffix] *ra* is substituted for the final phoneme of a word ending in *van*. 4.1.7.

The term *vanaḥ* is a general inclusion of the suffixes *kvanip*, *vanip*, and *ṅvanip*; it does not refer to the two roots *vana* (in the sense of "to share") and *vanu* (in the sense of "to beg") with the suffix *vic*. Why? Because of the rule: "When there is a choice between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix alone is to be understood. For this very reason, [the suffix is not applied] in cases such as *niḥśunī* ("one who has gone out from a dog") or *atiyūnī* ("one who has surpassed a youth"), because [there the suffix would be] meaningless; or alternatively, because [the forms are derived] from the root *śvan* and *yuvan* with the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Regarding *śarvarī*: from the root *śṝ* (in the sense of "to injure"), the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. Regarding *paralokadṛśvarī*: from the root *dṛś*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied.

Regarding the phrase *vano na haśaḥ*: the mention of *haś* is a qualification of what has been prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*). The meaning is that the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* do not occur after a nominal stem ending in *van* which is prescribed after a verbal root ending in a *haś* letter (i.e., a consonant other than *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v*). Consequently, there is no prohibition in the case of *śarvarī*. Likewise, in the case of *avāvā*—derived from the root *oṇṛ* ("to remove") with the suffix *vanip*, where the vowel substitution (*ātva*) by the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt* applies and the *ava* substitution occurs—the prohibition certainly applies because it is prescribed after a root ending in a *haś* letter, even though the *haś* letter itself is no longer present (*paratvābhāve’pi*). Thus, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) remains as stated.
In the Vedic language, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* should generally be stated [as applicable]: *yajvarīriṣaḥ*. Furthermore, after the root *īr*, there is the augment *tuṭ*: *pretvarī*.
The word *pāda* [is optionally treated as a neuter] in the other case. 4.1.8.

The word *pāda* is indicated here as having the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) applied; this is because it is only that [form] which is possible when the referent is a *ṛc* verse in the subsequent sūtra. Therefore, there is no inclusion of the form derived from the root *pād* with the *kvip* suffix. Regarding *dvipadī*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one who has two feet," the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*, and the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs by the rule *pādaḥ pat*.
The suffix *ṭāp* is applied after [a stem ending in] *ṛc*. (Pāṇini 4.1.9)

The term "ṛk" is an indication of the object [of the rule]; this is because of pervasiveness (*vyāpti*). For if it were an indication of the subject matter (*viṣayanirdeśa*), the application would occur only in the case of the *Ṛgveda*, and not elsewhere.
Not [is the suffix *cha* applied] after the six beginning with *svasu* (sister). 4.1.10.

He dispels the doubt that the prohibition here applies to the *ṅīp* suffix immediately following [the *ṭāp* suffix]—since the *ṭāp* prescribed by the rule "ṭābṛci" (Pāṇini 4.1.9) is not applicable here—by stating: "whichever [suffix] from whichever [base]. In that case, the *ṅīp* would apply after all [bases], whereas the *ṭāp* applies only after the six [specific bases] once the final *n* has been elided and the state of ending in *ā* has arisen. However, the reading "whichever [suffix] is applicable" (*yo yaḥ prāptaḥ*) is more appropriate; otherwise, one would have to say "that [suffix] does not occur after that [base]," and the full scope of the rule would not be understood. As for the example "pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ": *pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ* (five Brahmin women). Here, the *ṅīp* is applied after the word *brāhmaṇa*, which ends in *a*. Since the number five is a bahuvrīhi compound, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.12 (*taddhitāḥ*), and the resulting form is *pañcabrāhmaṇī*. When the plural marker *jas* is added, the *ī* is replaced by *ya* by Pāṇini 7.1.2 (*jasi ca*), yielding *pañcabrāhmaṇyaḥ*. The prohibition of *ṅīp* does not apply here because the base does not end in *a* at the time the suffix is introduced. Regarding the phrase "from whichever [base]": this indicates that the prohibition applies to any suffix that would otherwise be applicable, regardless of its specific nature. If the reading were simply "whichever," it might be interpreted as referring only to the immediate successor of the *ṭāp*, thus failing to encompass all potential applications. By using the form "whichever is applicable," the author ensures that the prohibition covers every instance where a suffix might arise, thereby avoiding the need for a separate statement such as "that [suffix] does not occur after that [base]" and ensuring the rule's universal application is clearly understood. The example *pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ* serves to demonstrate that even when a base like *brāhmaṇa* is modified by a numeral, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* remains applicable under the general rules of formation.

But surely, in this case, femininity is understood due to the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *brāhmaṇī*, whereas the numeral, by its own power, expresses the counting of distinct entities. For instance, when "five" is uttered, only the multiplicity of the substance is understood, not any specific gender; and thus, in the grammatical treatises on gender, it is stated that "a number ending in *ṣ* or *n* is without gender."

If this is so, would there not also be no [feminine] suffix in cases such as *ekā*, *dve*, or *bahvyaḥ*? For, by virtue of being number-words (*saṃkhyāśabda*), the meaning of the word consists merely in the enumeration of distinct entities. If, on the other hand, femininity is also the meaning of the word in those cases, then it would apply to *pañca* and so forth as well. Or rather, a distinction must be stated: even when that [suffix] is prohibited, since the manifestation of femininity and so forth in words like *pañca* cannot occur without the employment of a subsequent word (*anuprayoga*), they are declared to be "without gender" (*aliṅga*) in the grammatical treatises on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*).

If there were no prohibition, however, one would not be able to understand—relying solely on the authority of the grammatical treatise—that the feminine suffix does not occur after *pañca* and so forth, but does occur after *eka* and so forth. Now, since the substitution of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* occurs when a case-ending follows by the rule "tricaturor striyām," the absence of the suffix *ṅīp* is already established there by the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the destruction of a cause); why, then, is the inclusion of the words *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* in the *svasṛ*-class? It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). It indicates this: that the *saṃnipāta-paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory; therefore, once the substitution of *yatva* for *tyad* and so forth has taken place, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs—as in *yā*, *sā*, *ime*, and *dve*.

Relying on the view that this prohibition applies specifically to the immediately preceding case of the *ṅīp* suffix, he raises an objection: "Of those termed *ṣaṭ*. Why would it not apply? Because [the rule] "from this" (*ataḥ*) would indeed apply; however, the elision of *n* (*nalopaḥ*) is not established (*asiddha*). Since it is unestablished, this [word] does not end in short *a*. The elision of *n* is unestablished only with respect to the operations enumerated [in the rule], because the rule "the elision of *n* before *sup* and in accentuation" (*nalopaḥ supsvarasaṃjñātugvidhiṣu*) is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

Is this not included there? This too is included there; how so? The term *sub* is not a pratyāhāra (abbreviation) formed by the locative plural suffix; rather, it is formed by the *pakāra* of *yaṅśca āp* [Pāṇini 7.1.37]. Consequently, since the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is also included within that pratyāhāra, its rule is likewise a *sub*-rule. Thus he says: "and because of the pratyāhāra *cāp*. The word "it would not be" (*na syāt*) is to be supplied. The question is: why would it not be? The answer is: because of the pratyāhāra *cāp*. And this is the statement of one who is a follower of the Teacher's school.

To demonstrate the teacher’s established position (*ācāryasiddhānta*), he refutes this [view] with the words: "The fault is established, however, in the case of *ittva*. It is true that this is established in the *pratyāhāra* *cāp*; however, a fault arises in the case of *ittva*. "The fault is established, however, in the case of *ittva*. Indeed, it is established in the *pratyāhāra* *cāp*, but a fault occurs regarding *ittva*: namely, in the case of *bahucarmikā* (meaning "she who has many skins"). How so? In that context, the rule for *sub*-suffixes (*subvidhi*) is relied upon as a compound whose members end in all case-endings—namely, "the rule for *sub*" (*supo vidhiḥ*) and "the rule [governing] *sub*" (*supi vidhiḥ*).

And thus, just as in the case of *rājabhyām*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *supi ca* does not occur, so too the *it*-augment (*i*) prescribed for the *ṭāp* suffix when it follows a *su*-ending is also a *sub*-operation; therefore, since the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that operation, the vowel preceding the *k* would not be the one [prescribed], and consequently the *it*-augment would not apply—this is the meaning. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Therefore, neither both... The meaning is that what was said there regarding the mere sense of "in the feminine" does not hold; thus, both the *ṅīp* and the *ṭāp* suffixes are to be prohibited.

But surely, a prohibition operates only once; and at the time of its own operation, it prohibits only that which is applicable. Consequently, since the *ṅīp* has already been prohibited and the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) has already occurred, how can there be a prohibition of the *ṭāp* that would otherwise apply subsequently? For this would result in self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*)—the operation depending upon its own operation.
Therefore, by resorting to one of the principles of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*, this rule operates twice; therein, by the second operation, the *ṭāp* is prohibited.
The mind. 4.1.11.

Regarding the rule *an-in-as-man-grahaṇāni*: in the inclusion of these—*an*, *in*, *as*, and *man*—the paribhāṣā "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat-paribhāṣā*) does not operate; therefore, there is the inclusion of even those that are meaningless. The meaning is that through both these meaningful and meaningless elements, the rule of "having that as its final member" (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies. The word *sīman* is an un-derived nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*). In *atimahimā* (one who has transcended greatness), here too only the element *-iman-* possesses meaning, but not the suffix *-man*.
[The suffix *ka*] is applied after a Bahuvrīhi compound [ending in *a*, provided that the final member is not a word denoting a part of the body]. Pāṇini 4.1.12.

"A *bahuvrīhi* compound that does not elide its penultimate vowel (*anupadhālopī*) is the example here. From what [source] is this known? He says: "For regarding those that do elide [the penultimate vowel] (*upadhālopinaḥ*), etc.," because he will state an option (*vibhāṣā*) by means of the rule: *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām*. Examples include *suparvā* and so forth. [In these cases,] it is a *bahuvrīhi*: "she whose joints (*parvan*) are beautiful" or "she whose hide (*carman*) is beautiful. And this [compound] is one that does not elide its penultimate vowel because the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is prohibited by the rule *na saṃyogādvamantāt*.
[The author asks: "Why say *bahuvrīheḥ*? The intention is that it should have been stated as *samāsāt* ("from a compound").

Regarding the term *atirājñī*: the suffix *ṭac* [prescribed by] "rājāhaḥ sakhibhyaḥ" does not occur here, because the rule for adding a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is not universally obligatory. [The suffix] *ḍāp* is optionally applied after both [of these]. (Pāṇini 4.1.13)

Why is the mention of *antar* included? This should not be done for the purpose of ensuring that the prohibition applies when *ḍāp* is excluded. How so? *Ḍāp* is also prescribed; both [the suffix *ḍāp* and] the prohibition will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. For if there were no hearing of the form ending in *n*, then, because *ṅīp* would be superseded by the exception *ḍāp*, the prohibition would be rendered useless.

Now, is the mention of *anyatarasyām* intended so that *ṅīp* may also occur when [the suffix] is exempt from the prohibitions of *ḍāp* and *ṅīṣ*? That too is not the case; for in examples such as *bahurājñī*, *ṅīp* is already established by the rule *ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām*. If it is argued that this [rule *anyatarasyām*] would then be necessary for cases where it is not established by that [previous rule], such as *atiśarmā* and the like—then if that were so, since [the formation of *atiśarmā*] would be established by this very [present] rule even for those with a penultimate vowel elision (*upadhālopin*), the rule *ana upadhālopinaḥ* would be rendered useless.

If that is the case, then [you might argue] that this mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally") is made so that we need not have mentioned one or the other; how so? Since by this very mention of *anyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṅīp* would already be applicable both to those whose penultimate vowel is elided (*upadhālopin*) and to those whose penultimate vowel is not elided (*anupadhālopin*), the rule "for a Bahuvrīhi ending in *an*, provided its penultimate vowel is elided" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*)—even if formulated in this abbreviated form alone—would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): namely, that the prescription of *ṅīp* for a Bahuvrīhi ending in *an* applies only to those whose penultimate vowel is elided. Consequently, the mention of *anyatarasyām* would not need to be made at all?

That [the mention of *anyatarasyām*] must necessarily be made; for if it were absent, then—since by this mention of *anyatarasyām* the suffix *ḍāp* and the prohibition of *ṅīp* would apply to all three types of *bahuvrīhi* compounds alike—the rule for the compulsory *ṅīp* of those compounds ending in a penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*) would override both the *ḍāp* and the prohibition of *ṅīp*, and thus the *ṅīp* alone would invariably occur. Therefore, that [mention of *anyatarasyām*] must certainly be made; the question is: why then should this [mention of *anyatarasyām*] not be made?

He refutes [the objection] with the words "in a bahuvrīhi. This is the intention: this mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is first intended so that the suffix *ṅīp* may also occur when both the suffix *ḍāp* and its prohibition have been set aside. Nor is the rule "of a word ending in *an*, provided there is elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*) redundant; for it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the optional prescription of *ṅīp* after a bahuvrīhi ending in *an* applies only to those cases where there is elision of the penultimate vowel.

Therefore, by this option (*anyatarasyām*) [in Pāṇini 4.1.32], the suffix *ṅīp* is not applied in cases such as *suparvā* and *suśarmā*, whereas it does apply in cases such as *bahurājñī*. Now, one might object: "In that case, let this mention of 'option' (*anyatarasyām*) be omitted; let the rule 'ana upadhālopinaḥ' (Pāṇini 4.1.28) itself serve as the injunction. What is the difference? [The answer is: By this mention of 'option,' the suffix *ṅīp* would be introduced after every *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, the present rule serves to restrict it. Otherwise, in the absence of this [restriction], [the suffix] would apply only in the presence of the *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*].

When [the suffixes] *ḍāp* and *niṣ* have been obtained, the *ṅīp*—which was not previously applicable—is prescribed as an alternative option. This is the distinction: when this term *anyatarasyām* is present, once [the word] is released from both *ḍāp* and the prohibition (*niṣedha*), the *ṅīp* that occurs by its own respective rule does so in the case of words ending in *van* precisely by the rule "vano ra ca" (Pāṇini 4.1.7), whereby the *repha* (the letter *r*) also appears in forms such as *bahudhīvarī*.

Thus, when by this [rule] the suffixes *ṅīp* and *repha* (ṛ) are caused to apply to a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in a word whose penultimate vowel is elided (*upadhālopin*), such as *bahudhīvan* and *suparvan*, and when elsewhere—in cases like *bahurājan* and *suśarman*—only the suffix *ṅīp* is caused to apply, the rule "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.28) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). By that restriction, the suffix *ṅīp* is excluded in cases such as *suśarman*. When *ṅīp* is excluded in cases such as *suparvan*, the *repha* (ṛ) is also not applied, because it is prescribed in obligatory association (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) with that [suffix].

In cases such as *bahurājñī*, however, the suffix *ṅīp* remains as it is obtained by default; and in cases such as *bahudhīvarī*, both *ṅīp* and *repha* (the *r*-sound) remain as they are obtained by the rule "vano ra ca. Thus, everything desired is established. If this [rule] were not present, and if that [other rule] were intended as a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*), then a previously non-existent *ṅīp* would be enjoined by it alone. Consequently, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *van*, the rule "vano ra ca" would not apply because it is restricted by the rule "ṛnnebhyo ṅīp. As a result, with only *ṅīp* applied, the form would be *bahudhīvnī*.

Therefore, the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* here is for the purpose of making the rule "ana upadhālopinaḥ" restrictive—so that it may function as a restriction and not as an independent injunction. This the author of the Vṛtti will clarify under the rule "ana upadhālopinaḥ. If, by this inclusion of *anyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṅīp* were also obtained optionally in cases such as *dāmā* and so on, would it not follow [undesirably] even after words ending in the suffix *man*? This is not a fault; [because...]

A division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made: the suffix *ḍāp* occurs after both [suffixes]; then follows "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*). The rule "of the *an* [ending] in a *bahuvrīhi*" continues to apply, while "after *manas*" (*manaḥ*) is withdrawn.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after a word that is not a subordinate member [of a compound]. (Pāṇini 4.1.14)

He states that this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), because [the rule] effects a prohibition of the secondary member (*upasarjana*) in the subsequent sūtras. What is the fault in [interpreting it as] a *paryudāsa* (relative negation/exclusion)? [One might argue: in the case of *kukkuṭīpāda*, [the suffix] would not apply because the first member is a secondary member. [Reply: No; because of its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied first, and only then does the compound occur for that which ends in it.
