Thus, even if there were a prohibition of *ṅīṣ* due to being a secondary member, it is of no consequence, because [the suffix] has already been produced. Furthermore, this same fault applies equally even in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha*.

In that case, [the rule] would not apply to *kukkuṭī*; for what reason? Because "subordinate" (*upasarjana*) is etymologically defined as "that which is non-principal. Let it be so; however, "non-subordinate" (*anupasarjana*) means everything other than the subordinate, and not only the principal. Therefore, even in the absence of something to be related to it, the rule will still apply because it is simply different from the subordinate. But when the word *anupasarjana* expresses opposition—just as in the case of *adharmā*, *anṛta*, and so on—then the rule would not apply; therefore, it must be a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).

"‘Only from what is not a subordinate member (anupasarjana)’—this is what that [sūtra] means. The meaning is that it does not occur after a subordinate member. He will say: ‘[The suffix] ṅīp [is applied] after [stems ending in] ṭi, ḍha, aṇ, and añ. How is there a connection here of the word ending in the nominative case with the phrase ‘he will say’? On this point they say: the text is only as far as ‘he will say: ṭiḍḍhāṇañ’; the meaning is ‘he will say [the rule] beginning with ṭiḍḍhāṇañ. But which suffix is intended here? To this he says: ‘ṅīp.’"

Likewise, in the case of *jāti*, there is also a break in the text at the point where *ṅīṣ* [is prescribed]; and in that previous instance, the word "he will state" (*vakṣyati*) is to be supplied as a continuation. Regarding *kurucarī*: [it is formed] by the rule *careṣṭaḥ*. Regarding *bahukurucareti*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound in which all members are subordinate (*sarvopasarjana*).

"But how [is this]? and so forth. In the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), that which is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not denote a female (*striyām*); and when it does denote a female, the suffix certainly occurs—as in *bahukurucarīkā* ("she in whom there are many Kuru-women") and *bahukukkuṭīkā madurā* ("the city of Madurā having many hens"). Since the *bahuvrīhi* compound that denotes a female is not marked with the *ṭi*-sign and does not denote a genus (*ajāti*), there would be no application [of the rule]. For instance, a *prātipadika* marked with the *ṭi*-sign is taken [as the basis for the rule], and some such forms are directly marked with *ṭi*, such as *nadaṭ* and *coraḍ*.

[The *ṭi*-designation] occurs by way of being contained within a constituent part (*avayava*) [of a word]. For where the status of being contained in a constituent part is irrelevant, it is understood there as serving the purpose of the whole (*samudāya*). That constituent part is, in some cases, a verbal root—as in *stanandhayī*; in some cases, a suffix such as *kṛt*, *lyuṭ*, and so on; and in some cases, a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) such as *ṭyu* or *ṭyul*. In this regard, the *ṭi*-status of a constituent part belongs to that which does not deviate from its role within a particular whole. Thus, only the word *kurucara* possesses the *ṭi*-status; therefore, how could there be the possibility [of the feminine suffix] arising from the word *bahukurucara*? This is the question.

He refutes [the objection] by saying, "by the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to what ends with that). [Objection: But is it not the case that the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* is prohibited when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is used in its specific form (*grahaṇavatā*)? Furthermore, "being used in its specific form" (*grahaṇa*) means merely being mentioned [as such], and not necessarily being uttered in its own phonetic form; so how can there be a *tadanta-vidhi* here? [Response: This might be so—where the form being grasped is unique to the nominal stem itself, there the prohibition of *tadanta-vidhi* applies. However, in this case, *coraḍ* and so on are nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that are *ṭit*, the suffixes such as *lyuṭ* are also *ṭit*, and the verbal root *dheḍ* is also *ṭit*. Therefore...

Just as in the rule *ugitaśca*, where—whether it be a phoneme (*varṇa*), a suffix (*pratyaya*) marked with *u* or *i* (ugit), or a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—the rule of "extension to that which ends in [the aforementioned]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, so too might such an extension apply here? This objection would hold if the nominal stem were qualified by the *ṭit* [suffix]; however, when the *ṭit* suffix is itself qualified by the nominal stem, there can be no "extension to that which ends in" based on this qualifier, because it is impossible for the *ṭit* suffix to be a nominal stem. Therefore, the objection does not apply to the word *bahukurucara*. To this, he says: "And this has been indicated."

This has been made known by the rule "śūdrā cāmahatpūrvā. And he says "tathā ca" (and so too), because this which has necessarily been made known must also be maintained in subsequent cases. For if the indicator (*jñāpaka*) were not relied upon, the *ṅīp* suffix prescribed after a word ending in *aṇ* would apply only to the word *kāra* itself—by virtue of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix—and not to the word *kumbhakāra*, which ends in *aṇ*. However, by means of the indicator, it occurs even from that [word *kumbhakāra*]; such is the meaning.

But is it not the case that by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes, the word *kumbhakāra* ends in the suffix *aṇ*? No, he says: "and not [ending] in *aṇ*. Regarding the phrase "mention of *kṛt*," he asks: "What is the reason? and answers: "Because there is also an *aṇ* which is a *taddhita* [suffix]. This technical rule applies where the form being mentioned is unique to *kṛt* suffixes alone; however, in this case, since the form *aupagavī* is also a *taddhita*, it is not within the scope of this rule. This is the meaning.

Now, what fault would there be if [the suffix] were produced from the word *kāra*? [The form] *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* would not be established. Because of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied after feminine bases according to [Pāṇini 4.1.120], the rules for Vṛddhi and accentuation would apply only to that very word *kārī*. [Objection: It will be like the case of the substitution of Samprasāraṇa for *ṣyaṅ*. Just as the Samprasāraṇa prescribed for a stem ending in *ṣyaṅ* occurs even in a compound such as *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, because there is no restriction to the initial element (*tadādiniyama*) when a feminine suffix is involved; so too here.

Likewise, even if it were derived from the word *kāra*, since the word *kumbhakārī* ends in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), it will [be formed] accordingly; nevertheless, it might also sometimes arise from the word *kārī*.

Now, you might argue: "The word *kumbha* will be compounded with the word *kārī*; and in the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*, by the force of the three governing rules (*adhikāra*)—namely *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*—the suffix will be prescribed after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a feminine suffix; since the status of being a nominal stem for that which ends in a feminine suffix is untenable without a compound, the suffix *ḍhak* will arise from the word *kumbhakārī* itself; and by the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, this will also apply in the case of *sauparṇeya*."

Even so, because of the continued application of the rule *apiṅ*, the suffix *ṅīp* could occur even after the word *kārī*, as in the case of *sauparṇeya*. Furthermore, due to the rule "of [words ending in] a gati, a kāraka, or an upapada," a compound is difficult to obtain when the suffix *caṅ* has been applied; therefore, so that the suffix *ṅīp* may occur from the word *kumbhakāra* itself, one must also accept the principle of "reference to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) in the subsequent rule as well.

Furthermore, even if [the suffix] were produced after the word *kumbhakāra*, there would be no restriction regarding its initial element, and consequently, the suffix *ḍhak* would undesirably apply after the word *kārī*. Why? Because of the rule "not when a feminine suffix is not a subordinate member" (*strīpratyaye cānupasarjane na*), which—when a suffix is mentioned—permits the inclusion of that [word] and what follows its beginning, but not of anything preceding it.

But surely, even if the rule of "extension to that which ends in [the stem]" (tadantavidhi) applies hereafter, let it apply to the whole in the case of *kumbhakārī*; nevertheless, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying to the word *kāra* alone as well, just as in cases such as *aupagavī*. Consequently, the form *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* would be defective in one alternative. If this is so, then even when the suffix arises from the word *kāra*, since that much [of the base] has already entered into a state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*) with *kumbha*, it cannot be extracted and joined with the descendant; furthermore, because there is no restriction to "that which begins with" (tadādi-niyama), the suffix *ḍhak* will arise from the whole [base] itself.

Alternatively—since the *kā* suffix, which has already entered into a single semantic unity (*ekārthībhūta*) with *kumbha*, cannot be connected with femininity, no feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) will arise at all; and since there is no subsequent rule for "specification by its final element" (*tadantavidhi*), a feminine suffix would not apply here even in its absence. Why? Because that which ends in *aṇ* is not extracted and connected with femininity, and that which is connected with femininity does not end in *aṇ*. Therefore, even in the subsequent case, one must necessarily accept a "specification by its final element" based on the principal member (*pradhāna*); and in that regard, it occurs just as it does through the principal member.

Likewise, since this rule would apply even when [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), this prohibition is now commenced. Thus, in the previous case, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to a form ending in that which is specified) does indeed occur even with a subordinate member; for example, in "priyapañcā draupadī" (Draupadī who loves five) according to "na ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ," and in "atikrāntā bhavantam atibhavatī" (one who has surpassed you).

It might be argued as follows: "In the previous [sūtra], that which ends in *ṭi* (or *ṭid*, etc. is qualified by the word *striyām* ('in the feminine'); whereas in rules such as *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, only *ṭi* and so forth are mentioned. Therefore, even if the rule of 'extension to that which ends in X' (*tadantavidhi*) were made known [by this sūtra], [the suffix] would not apply in cases like *bahukurucarā* because *ṭi* and so forth do not denote the feminine there. However, in *kumbhakārī*, since the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the feminine, the [suffix] will apply even from that which ends in it. Thus, there is no need for this [sūtra]. That is not correct; for the distinction between the scopes (*viṣayavibhāga*) you have described is difficult to discern. Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced in order to make known that distinction between the scopes.

But surely, even if this [work] has begun, this distinction of subject matter cannot be maintained; for in the case of *pañcājī*, since the word *ajā* is feminine, its derivative ending in *-ī* would function as feminine, resulting in the undesirable application of the suffix *ṭāp* by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*.

Therefore, since there is freedom of choice regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), why is it not the case that in rules such as *ajādyataṣṭāp* and *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the term [the base] mentioned there is qualified by "femininity" (*strītva*), while in rules such as *vano ra ca*, it qualifies both the base mentioned there and that which ends with it? If this is so, then this rule is commenced for the purpose of making known the application of the suffix to what ends with the base (*tadantavidhi*). Furthermore, the phrase *amahatpūrva* ("not preceded by *mahat*") could have been omitted; for in the word *mahāśūdrī*, where the whole expresses a caste (*jāti*), the word *śūdra* does not denote a feminine.

Another says: Here, there is the inclusion of that which is worldly, non-primary, and subordinate. [The word *Āpiśilā* is derived as follows: it is "proclaimed by Āpiśali"; from this, by the rule *iñaśca*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, for one who studies that [text], by the rule *tadadhīte*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied again; and for that [second *aṇ*], by the rule *proktālluk*, there is elision (*luk*). Thus we have *Āpiśilā brāhmaṇī*. In this case, because the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *iñaśca*—which is the suffix expressing "proclaimed by"—is subordinate, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after a word ending in that [subordinate *aṇ*].

Now, one might object: "Since the suffix *aṇ* has been elided when the notion of the student (*adhyetṛ*) is present, the base form itself expresses that meaning; therefore, because the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a feminine base, the *ṅīp* suffix ought to appear. This would indeed be so, if it were stated that [the rule applies] "after a non-feminine subordinate element ending in *aṇ*" (*anupasarjanāt*). We, however, shall qualify the suffix *aṇ* itself by its status as a non-subordinate element—namely, "the *aṇ* which is not subordinate"—and the predominance or non-predominance of the *aṇ* is determined through its meaning.

This is what is meant: when the meaning in which the suffix *aṇ* was produced is expressed as the primary element, then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs after that which ends in it; but when it is expressed as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāva*), then it does not. And here, because the meaning of the first *aṇ* has been transferred to the female student (*adhyetrī*), its meaning is subordinate; therefore, the *ṅīp* does not occur based on that. Nor does it occur based on the one produced for the female student, because that [suffix] has been elided. It does not occur even by virtue of the "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because the suffix *aṇ* is used as a qualifier for the vowel *ā*.

In the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the word *ataḥ* (from "a") is understood. In that context, if it were understood as "from that which ends in the suffix *aṇ*," then the suffixal characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) would apply; however, when *aṇ* is used to qualify the vowel *a*, how could the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is caused by a phoneme (*varṇanimitta*)—be applicable by virtue of the suffixal characteristic? [Objection: But we shall qualify *aṇ* by the continued application of the word *striyām* ("in the feminine"), so that it means "that *aṇ* which is prescribed in the feminine"? [Reply: Even so, in the case of "the Mīmāṃsā taught by Kāśakṛtsna is *Kāśakṛtsnī*; she who studies it is a *Kāśakṛtsnā* Brāhmaṇī woman," there is a second *aṇ* [suffix].

Even though [the suffix] is elided by the rule "proktālluk," the first *aṇ* was produced only after a feminine stem; consequently, there would be the undesirable application of the *ṅīp* suffix after that [stem] when it denotes a Brāhmaṇī woman. Therefore, the purpose of this sūtra is to ensure that [the suffix occurs] after the principal [element], and not after the non-principal.

The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied after nominal stems ending in the affixes *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇa*, *añ*, *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, *mātraC*, *tayaP*, *ṭhak*, *ṭhaÑ*, *kaÑ*, *kvarap*, and *khyun*. (Pāṇini 4.1.15)

Regarding the question "Why here?"—the point of the inquiry is that the substitute for *laṭ* possesses the property of being *ṭit* by virtue of its status as a *sthānin*. [The examples given are] *pavamānā* and *yajamānā*. Now, one might object: since the rule "of *laṭ*" has been removed from the section on *śānan* and so forth, the position that there is no substitute has been established; therefore, *śānac* should have been cited in examples such as *pavamāna*. [The answer is: because *laṭ* has two indicatory letters (*anubandha*). The intention is that even the vowels *a* and others are indicatory letters in the case of *laṭ* and the rest. By this, *liṅ* and *luṭ* are also explained—as in *anūcānā* and *yakṣyamāṇā*.

Regarding the question "How [is it] in the case of *laṭ* and so forth?": the question implies that since those [suffixes] also possess two indicatory letters (*anubandha*), they ought not to be included [in the rule]. [The answer is: "By virtue of the force of the addition of the *ṭ*-indicatory letter. He says "In the other case" to show that the force of adding the *ṭ*-indicatory letter does not apply to *laṭ* and so forth as well. "Knowledge has been recited"—the word "how" is to be supplied here. The question is: "Would the *ṭ*-indicatory nature of *iṭ* serve both purposes? [The answer is: "The *ṭ*-indicatory nature of an augment is not a cause [for the application of *ṅīp*]. This means that the *ṭ*-indicatory nature of augments does not function as the cause for the suffix *ṅīp*.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the indicative mark [in the rule] *ṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca*. The sense is that if the *ṭi*-status of the augment (*āgama*) were the cause for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, then in forms such as *sāyantanī*, the *ṅīp* would already be established by the *ṭi*-status of the augment *tuṭ*; thus, the assignment of *ṭi*-status to *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* would be purposeless. Now, one might object: "By the reference in the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu*, when *tuṭ* does not occur, the *ṭi*-status of those two [suffixes] must exist for the sake of the *ṅīp* suffix? That is not so.

Since the word *purāṇa* is listed among the *bahu*-group [of words], the suffix *ṅīṣ* ought to apply; for the form *purāṇī* is indeed acutely accented on the final syllable—as in the example *purāṇī*, meaning "she who is born again and again. Even so, this is not a conclusive indicator (*jñāpaka*), because in the rule *bahvādibhyaś ca*, the particle *vā* (or) is understood to carry over; thus, since *ṅīṣ* is optional, the *ṭi*-marker [assigned] to the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* would be intended to ensure that *ṅīp* occurs when *ṅīṣ* is excluded—this point remains to be considered.

Regarding the term *sauparṇeyī*: from the word *suparṇa*, by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *pākakarṇādi-ṅīṣ*, and then applying the suffix *ḍhak* according to the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*, [the form *sauparṇeya* is derived]. Now, one might object that because this [suffix *ḍhak*] possesses an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), it ought not to be included in the application; to this he replies: "without an indicatory letter" (*niranubandhaka*). Although there exists a suffix *ḍha* without an indicatory letter in the rule *śilāyāḍhaḥ*, it is stated that because it is neuter by its very nature, it does not apply here in the feminine gender.

Even the suffix *ḍha* [which forms the word *sabhya*] in the rules "sabhāyā yaḥ" and "ḍhaś chandasi"—that too does not apply to the feminine. How so? Because in that context, the term "tatra sādhuḥ" (good/skilful therein) is understood. And how could a woman possibly be "good" (*sādhu*) in an assembly? For in a sacrificial assembly (*yajñasabhā*), only learned men have the right to participate! [Objection: Granted, she may not be "good" in a sacrificial assembly; however, she will be "good" in a hall (*śālā*) or in a women’s assembly (*strīsabhā*). [Reply: In that case, there would be the same over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even for the expression "an assembly of Brahmins good in a sacrificial assembly" (*yajñasabhāyāṃ sādhu brāhmaṇapariṣat*). It is thus.
In such a case, the reason for the absence of the word *sabheyī* in Vedic usage is precisely this.

[The question is: "Does the operation of *aṇ* also take place in some instances for a suffix that is not *aṇ*? [The answer is: "In the case of the suffix *ṇa* prescribed by the rule ‘*chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ*’ (Pāṇini 4.4.62), the operation of *aṇ* takes place. How so? "By means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Namely, when this [author] provides a specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*) in the rule ‘*kārmastācchīlye*’ (Pāṇini 6.3.10) for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* portion. For if the operation of *aṇ* did not apply to a suffix *ṇa* used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), the specific substitution would be useless; because once the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the word *karman* according to the rule for *chattra* and others, the elision of the *ṭi* portion would already be established by the rule ‘*nastaddhite*’ (Pāṇini 6.4.144).

Nor does the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical changes) apply here by the rule "na ca," for that *prakṛtibhāva* applies specifically when the suffix *aṇ* follows. Thus we have *caurī* and *tāpasī*. The words *cura* and *tapas* should be included among the *chattrādi* group [of words]. He shows what is excluded by the phrase "in some cases" (*kvacit*)—namely, *dāṇḍā* and *mauṣṭā*. From the words *daṇḍa* and *muṣṭi*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "that which is the weapon in her hand."

*Autsi*, *audapānī*. [These are formed] from the words *utsa* and *udapāna* by adding the suffix *añ* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārthe*) according to the rule *utsādibhyo 'ñ*. Now, what is the purpose of the re-mention of the suffix *añ* in the *sārṅgaravādi* list, since the forms are already established by this very rule, and there is neither a difference in form nor a difference in accent? To this, he says: "In the case of the *śārṅgaravādi-añ*, etc. *Baidī* is the female descendant of *Bida*, formed by *añ* according to the rule *anuṣyānantarye bidādibhyo 'ñ*. Since "lineage" (*gotra*) is considered a "class" (*jāti*) along with "Vedic schools" (*caraṇa*), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which applies to classes—is applicable here. In cases such as *autsī*, that *ṅīṣ* would prevail, overriding the *ṅīp* suffix which was intended for those specific instances. Thus, the re-mention of *añ* is necessary to prevent the application of *ṅīṣ* in such cases.

If, then, there is a basis for that [application], let that itself be the inclusion of *añ*; what is the use here of including *añ*? Or rather, it is not so, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "of a genus" (*jāteḥ*). For the word "of a genus" (*jāteḥ*) is operative there; for if it were not a governing context, the suffix *ṅīp* would undesirably apply in the case of a name derived from connection with a male—such as *baidī*, meaning "the wife of a Baida. In cases such as *urudvayasī*, the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *dhaN*, and *mātraC* are applied according to the rule "the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *dhaN*, and *mātraC* are used when denoting a measure" (*pramāṇe dvayasaCdhaNmātraCaḥ*).

Regarding the term *pañcatayī*: the suffix *tayap* is applied [by Pāṇini 5.2.42] in the sense of "a part of a number. In the case of suffixes such as *dvayasaC* and others, the mention of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is intended to ensure that the base words themselves are not included—lest one ask, "What is its *dvayasa*? or "What is its *mātra*? The word *taya* can also be derived from the root *taya* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac).

The phrase "for the purpose of excluding *ṭhan* and so forth" means that it should not apply in cases such as *daṇḍikā* (derived from *daṇḍa* by the rule *ata iniṭhanau*, Pāṇini 5.2.115) or *kāśikā* (derived from *kāśi* by the rule *kāśyādibhyaṣṭhaññiṭhau*, Pāṇini 4.2.116), and so on.

Regarding "tādṛśī": [it is formed] by the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca* and *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*. The pronunciation of the letter *ñ* in *kañ* is for the purpose of preventing [the application of] *āto'nupasarge kaḥ* in cases such as *godā*. Regarding *itvarī*: [it is formed] by the rule *iṇ-naś-jisarti-bhyaḥ kvarap*. Regarding *āḍhyaṅkāraṇī*: [it is formed] by the suffix *khyun* according to the rule *āḍhya-subhaga-* etc.

Regarding the rule *nañ-snañ-īk-ak-taruṇa-talunānām*: in the Bhāṣya, however, there is only the sūtra *kañ-kvarapaḥ*; the reading of *khyun* is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*), and thus its addition was made as a mere supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Examples are *straiṇī* and *pauṃsnī*, derived from the rule *strī-puṃsābhyāṃ nañ-snañau bhavanāt*. Examples are *śaktīkī* and *yāṣṭīkī*, derived under the heading concerning weapons (*praharaṇa*) by the rule *śakti-yaṣṭyor-īkak*. Examples are *taruṇī* and *talunī*.

The purpose of including these two [words] is as follows: regarding *taruṇī*, [the form] is established by the rule "in the first age" (*vayasi prathame*). But regarding *vayas*, it is not established; because of its inclusion in the *gaura*-group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply. Therefore, there is an option between *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ* for both *vayas* and *avayas*. As for the statement that it is established in some cases due to its inclusion in the *gaura*-group, that should be understood as intended merely to establish the specific form; however, an addition must indeed be made for the sake of the accent.
And [the suffix *yañ* is applied after a word ending in *a*] when it denotes a sacrifice (*yaña*).

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of *apatya*": the meaning is that the rule should be formulated as *apatyād yañ*, where *āpatyaḥ* means "that which pertains to offspring" (*apatye bhavaḥ*). As for *dvaipya*: here too, *yañ* is applied in the sense of "pertaining to" (*bhavādi*) and so forth. The division of the yoga-sūtra is for the sake of what follows; it is so that only *yañ* may be carried over into the subsequent rules, and not *ṭi*-stems and the others.
The suffix *ṣpha*, which is a *taddhita* suffix, occurs after [stems ending in] vowels in the eastern dialects.

"The letter *ṣ* [indicates] that *ṅīṣ* [is applied]. But surely, since the feminine gender has already been indicated by the suffix *ṣpha* itself, *ṅīṣ* should not occur? To this he replies: "By means of two suffixes. The mention of the term *taddhita* is for the purpose of establishing the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, the designation of a nominal stem is for the sake of *ṅīṣ*. But is it not the case that *ṅīṣ* is already established here by the force of the marker *p* [in *ṣpha*]? As for the roots *trap* and so on, their status as having the marker *ṣ* (*ṣittva*) is useful for the application of the augment *aṅ*, and thus there is an absence of *ṅīṣ* in forms such as *trapā* and *kṣamā*. Let this point, along with its proposed solution, rest for now.

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the word *sarvatra*," and so forth: first of all, the inclusion of the word *sarvatra* need not be made in the subsequent rule (*sūtra*), because once the word *prācām* (of the Easterners) has been withdrawn by the force of the very commencement [of this new rule], the desired result is established everywhere. Therefore, that [word *prācām*] is drawn back here [to this rule]. Thus, the meaning becomes this: even in cases where there is a sublater (*bādhaka*), according to the opinion of the Easterners, the suffix *ṣpha* occurs after a stem ending in *yañ*. In this way, the sense of the locative case [in the original rule] also becomes consistent. [The author] will state [later] that the suffix *cāp* occurs after the word *āvaṭya*.

Furthermore, if there were no *apakarṣa* (downward displacement) and the view of those from the North were not accepted, the suffix *ṣpha* would, by virtue of its subsequent position, supersede [the suffix *āvaṭya*] when there is scope for it; however, because of the inclusion of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), only *ṣpha* occurs. And thus, by the rule "after *yañ*, [there is] *ṣpha* and *ca*" (*ṣācca yañaḥ*), even in cases where *cāp* would otherwise apply, only *ṣpha* occurs according to the Easterners—as in *śārkarākṣyāyaṇī*, *pautimāṣyāyaṇī*, and *gokakṣyāyaṇī*.
In all cases, [the suffix *kan* is applied] after words beginning with *lohita* and ending with *tanta*.

*Lohitādī* is a separate word with its case-ending elided (*luptavibhaktika*). In the previous rule, according to the opinion of the Easterners (*prācām*), the suffix *ṣpha* was prescribed; here, however, it is according to all opinions. What is the meaning? It means "in the opinion of all. Thus he says: "in the opinion of all teachers (*sarveṣām ācāryāṇām mataḥ*). Regarding the reading *matena* ending in the instrumental case, the suffix *tral* is applied to the word ending in the genitive in the sūtra. "Independent" (*svatantram*) means that which is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of anything else is an independent nominal stem (*prātipadika*). To the question "What, then, is this? he says: "that which follows the word *kapi*."

The group beginning with *Lauhityāyani* is included within the *Garga*-class; the word *babhru* is also recited in that very same class, whereas [the formation of its feminine] occurs by the rule: "In the case of *madhu* and *babhru*, [the suffix *yañ* is applied] when they refer to a Brāhmaṇa and a Kauśika respectively."

Regarding the passage beginning with *kaṇvāt tu*: the word *śakala* is intended to follow after the word *kata* and precede the word *kaṇva*; the meaning is that their arrangement should be performed as *kata-śakalaka-kaṇva*. What happens when this is so? He says: "the former and the latter. Those two groups, the former and the latter, are described as such because the word *śakala* is respectively at the end and at the beginning of them. The meaning is that the former group, beginning with *lohita*, has the word *śakala* at its end, and the latter group has the word *śakala* at its beginning.

"This is indeed true; however, what is the purpose [of this]? To this he says: "In the *sphāṇau*. He explains the verse: "The reading in the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is otherwise. The arrangement in the *Gargādi* group is as follows: *kapikata*, *kurukata*, *anaḍuh*, *kaṇva*, *śakala*. This very [arrangement] must be established. "Thus" means according to the sequence mentioned in the verse. That is to say, the words *anaḍuh* and *kurukata* should be removed from this position and read elsewhere, while the word *śakala* should be recited between *kataka* and *kaṇva*.

But in that case, the word *śakala*, having fallen away from both groups, would not obtain either of the two suffixes, *ṣ* or *phan*. To this he replies: "from those ending in *kata*" (*katantebhyaḥ*). This means there is a single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) of both the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*. By the *tatpuruṣa* analysis—"that which is near the end (*anta*) of *kata* is *katanta*"—the word *śakala* is expressed; the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs either by virtue of its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group or by irregular derivation (*nipātana*).

Likewise, *katantāni* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which *kata* is the final member. In that context, when both the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa* are intended to be expressed together, the *bahuvrīhi* alone remains, according to the rule: "Among words differing in accent, that one whose subsequent phonological operation is prescribed remains. The phrase "likewise" and so forth means that in the case of the rule "from *kaṇva* and others" (*kaṇvādibhyaḥ*) as well, there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) between the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*.

The word *śakala* is "one beginning with Kaṇva" (*kaṇvādi*), meaning it is situated near the beginning of the *Kaṇva* group; those whose first is *Kaṇva* are the "Kaṇva-beginners" (*kaṇvādīni*). From that, as before, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Among the two compounds—the *bahuvrīhi* and the *tatpuruṣa*—it is by means of the *tatpuruṣa* compound. "Situated in the middle" refers to the two groups. "Both suffixes as well" means both *ṣpha* and *aṇ*. [The form] *śākalāḥ* results from the elision of *ya* according to the rule "āpatyasya ca."

Another says: the remainder is that the preceding and succeeding [groups] are to be understood as ending with and beginning with those [terms], respectively. The preceding group is to be understood as ending with them—namely, "after all [the terms] from lohita to śakala"; the succeeding group is to be understood as beginning with them—namely, "after [the terms] from śakala onwards, the suffix gotra is applied. Thus, the purpose for the two groups (ṣpha and aṇ) is established.
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after the words *kauravya* and *māṇḍūka*. (Pāṇini 4.1.19)

Regarding the passage beginning with "kauravyamāṇḍūkayoḥ" and so forth: in this sūtra, the inclusion of Āsuri must also be made. The meaning is that it should be stated: "and after [the names] Āsuri, Kauravya, and Māṇḍūka."

Regarding *āsurāyaṇī*: because the suffix *ṣpha* is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is the elision of the *iñ* suffix according to the rule "and that which begins with *ya*" (*yasyeti ca*). This very mention of the *taddhita* suffix serves as the indicative mark that *ṣpha* is also applied after *āsuri*. As for the forms ending in *yañ* and so forth that end in the vowel *a*, the form is established even by means of the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). And this applies to the secondary meanings (*śaiṣika*) as well. This has been stated here in connection with *āsurī*; otherwise, the mention of *āsuri* would have to be made twice. Regarding *āsurīya*: *āsuri* is the offspring of *asura*; that which was taught by him is the *āsurīya* ritual manual (*kalpa*).
In the first stage of life. 4.1.20.

"By hearing alone" (*śrutyā*) means by mere hearing, without depending on context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. "A maiden" (*kumārī*): this word denotes the first stage of life; it is not caused by the absence of union with a male, because it is applied even to males—as in the case of "an old bachelor" (*vṛddhakumārī*), which should be understood as being due to the common property of lacking union with a male. "In the non-final stage of life" (*vayasyacarama*): *carama* means final, and *acarama* means non-final. Here, some maintain that there are four stages of life: childhood (*kaumāra*), youth (*yauvana*), middle age (*madhyatva*), and old age (*vṛddhatva*). As they say:
"What was not studied in the first stage of life, nor wealth acquired in the second, nor austerity practiced in the third—what will one do in the fourth?

Others, however, [mention] three: The final answer to the problem is: Final Answer: The final answer is "What was not studied in the first stage of life, nor wealth acquired in the second, nor austerity practiced in the third—what will one do in the fourth? I hope it is correct.
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence.
Others, however, [divide life] into three stages: childhood, middle age, and old age.
"Until sixteen one is a child, subsisting on milk and rice; until seventy one is middle-aged, and beyond that one is called old.

In all these systems of thought, youth constitutes the second stage of life, and the words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī* denote youth; therefore, [the application of the suffix] would not be obtained [in those cases]. To this he says: "These two [words] denote the second stage of life. However, when there are only two stages of life characterized by growth and decline, then this need not be stated; for even youth would then be of the nature of the first stage of life.

He shows what is to be excluded by that which was stated—"it exists by means of direct audition" (śrutyā)—with the words: "The 'one lying on her back,' the 'red-footed'—these are not [mere] words (vayaḥ). The meaning is: "by means of direct audition"—that is, by mere hearing—these do not establish [the object as] a word (vayaḥ). Here, first of all, in the case of "lying on her back," only the relationship between action and agent is perceived, and that alone is the ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta).

In the case of "those who lie on their backs" (*uttānādiṣu kartṛṣu*), the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *śī* (to lie down). While everyone lies down on their back at some time or another, it is nevertheless said, "one who lies on his back" (*uttānaśaya*); in that context, a restriction is understood—that because he is unable to sleep otherwise, he lies only on his back.

Even so, there remains doubt: [is she] a child or an old woman? Therefore, when the restrictive rule "she lies on her back" is established, and the absence of old age is determined through context and other means, childhood is understood. In the case of "red-footed" (*lāhitapādikā*) as well, only the referent of the compound is cognized through direct audition (*śruti*). When, through context and other means, the cognition arises that her feet are naturally red and not [colored] by lac or similar substances, then "childhood" is understood. The word *iti* indicates a manner; the meaning is that the scriptural mentions of age are not of this kind.

For this very reason, the plural number is used; consequently, it does not occur in cases such as *dvivarṣā* (two-year-old). Here too, the age is understood through context and so forth, whereas the mere measure is the literal meaning of the word, since it is employed even in reference to things like houses (*śālā*). In the case of *dve varṣe bhūtaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied, which is then elided by the rules *varṣālluk ca* and *cittavati nityam*.
The feminine suffix ṅīp is not applied after the words *aparimāṇa*, *viṣṭi*, *cita*, and *kambalya* when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has been elided.

The genitive case in *para* (in *parasaptamī*) is not appropriate, because a sequence of priority (*paurvāparya*) is impossible with a *luk* elision that takes the form of non-existence. "Measurement from all sides" (*sarvato mānam*) means the inclusion of the rule "but measurement is from all sides" (*parimāṇaṃ tu sarvataḥ*), and not merely anything that delimits.

"Bought for five *ai* coins" (*pañcabhiḥ śvabhiḥ krītā*): here, a *dvigu* compound occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of being worth (*ārhīya*).

Time and number are not *parimāṇa* (dimension). For it is not by means of these two that an object is measured from all sides, both in height and in circumference. Thus, since "time" and "number" are mentioned for the sake of illustration, "measure" (*pramāṇa*) also does not constitute *parimāṇa*. Accordingly, the author will state in a subsequent sūtra: "because the word *kāṇḍa* does not denote a [specific] dimension," and also: "*kāṇḍa* is a particular kind of measure."

Because of that [rule], when the suffix *mātrac* is applied in the sense of "its measure is this," as in *dviśama* or *triśama*—where the *lopa* (elision) occurs by the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam*—the forms *dviśama* and *triśama* arise. If this is so, would not *unmāna* (height/measure) also fail to be included under *parimāṇa*? Someone says: "This is indeed accepted; even *unmāna* is not included here by the mention of *parimāṇa*—for example, in the case of *dviniṣkā* or *triniṣkā*, meaning 'purchased for two *niṣkas*' or 'three *niṣkas*,' where the suffix *ṭhan* is elided by the rule *dvitripūrvānniṣkāt* following the same principle as before."

Another says: the mention of *bista* and *kambalya* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that here, even "measurement" (*unmāna*) is included under the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*), because those two are specific types of measurement; for instance, in the rules *suvarṇabistau hemno’kṣe* and *kambalācca saṃjñāyām*, [it is stated] that a *kambalya* is one hundred palas of wool. However, the author of the *Nyāsa*, analyzing the compound as "that which has two *bistas* as its measure," considers *bista* itself to be a measure. Regarding *dvivarṣā*: this has already been explained. Regarding *dviśatā* and *triśatā*: [the suffix *kan* is applied].

Regarding the form *dvābhyāṃ śatābhyāṃ krītā* ("purchased for two hundred"), although the suffix *yat* would normally apply according to the rule *paṇapādamāṣaśatādyat*, the rule *śāṇādvā* allows for an alternative; furthermore, by the statement *śatācceti vaktavyam* ("it should be stated that [the suffix *kan* applies] after *śata*"), the suffix *kan* is optionally applied by the rule *saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*. This *kan* is then elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrvāt*.

Regarding *dvibisti*: when it denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*), there is elision of the suffix *ṭhañ*; when it denotes a weight (*unmāna*), there is elision of *ṭhak*. Regarding *dvyācita*: ten *bhāras* would constitute an *ācita*. In the expression "he cooks two *ācitās*," according to the rules "after *āḍhaka*, *ācita*, and *pātra*, the suffix *kha* optionally" and "after a *dvigu* compound, also *ṭhaṅ*," the suffixes *ṭhan* and *kha* may apply; when these are not applied, the suffix *ṭhañ* from the *prāgvatīya* group applies, and its elision occurs as before. Regarding *dvikambalya*: there is elision of *ṭhañ* in the sense of "purchased. The forms *dvyāḍhakī* and *dvyācitā* are similar to this.

Regarding the term *pañcāśvī*: this is a *dvigu* compound formed by a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). These two prohibitions are stated here; however, one of them could have been omitted. How so? I would have formulated it thus: "After a word ending in a measure-word (*parimāṇa*), when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. This would serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning: "The feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs only after a word ending in a measure-word when there is elision of a *taddhita* suffix. Consequently, it would apply in cases such as *dvyāḍhakī*, but not in cases such as *pañcāśvī*; and then why would it not apply in cases such as *bistācikambalyebhyaḥ*? It cannot be done in this way.

A reversed rule might also be possible—such as *dvikuḍavī* or *pañcāḍhakī*. However, in cases such as *pañcāśvā*, the suffix *ṅīp* would certainly apply due to the absence of any [other] distinguishing factor. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it is in the established system.
The suffix *cha* (forming the word *kha*) is applied after a word ending in *kāṇḍa* when it denotes a field.

The Section on the Measure of Honor (Mānadaṇḍa): The Section on Stalks (Kāṇḍa). Since the rule for compounds ending in [a specific term] is already established by the governing heading "dvigoḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.21), just as in the preceding rule, for what purpose is the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in")? If the word *anta* were not included, the term *kṣetre* would be understood as a qualifier of *kāṇḍa* alone—meaning "from a *dvigu* compound that ends in the word *kāṇḍa* when it occurs in the sense of 'field'"—because that is what is explicitly heard in the text, rather than qualifying the entire compound. This would be similar to the subsequent rule, where [the word *pramāṇe* qualifies] the word *puruṣa*, meaning "from a compound ending in the word *puruṣa* when it signifies a measure. Consequently, the following undesired application (*prasajyeta*) would occur: [the formation of a feminine suffix] from *dvābhyāṃ kāṇḍābhyām*.

"A mare bought for two fields measured by *kāṇḍas* is called *dvikāṇḍī*"; however, in this case [of the following example], it would not apply: "a field-division whose measure is two *kāṇḍas* is *dvikāṇḍā*. But when the mention of the suffix *-anta* (ending in) is made, the field alone is qualified by that ending, not the *kāṇḍa*, because in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the *kāṇḍa* is a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*).
The suffix *mātraC* is optionally applied after the word *puruṣa* when it denotes a measure.

Regarding the phrase "the word *puruṣa* [is used] in the sense of a measure": those learned in the *Śulba-sūtras* state that "a *puruṣa* is five *aratnis*. In that case, in the sentence "two *puruṣas* are the measure," the word *puruṣa*, although denoting a genus (*jāti*), functions in the sense of a measure due to its connection with the word "measure" (*pramāṇa*). However, in the case of a derivative form (*vṛtti*), its application to a measure should be understood as arising from its very nature.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*.

Regarding the rule *ūdhaso'naṅ*: since the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied [after the first member], the compound-ending suffix—which occurs after the final member of the compound—occurs first, and only then does the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) follow. The statement *ano bahuvrīheḥ* is merely illustrative; its meaning is that both *ano bahuvrīheḥ* and *ḍābubhābhyāmanyatarasyām* apply. In the example *kuṇḍodhnī*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she whose udder is like a jar" (*kuṇḍamiva ūdho'syāḥ*). When the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *allopo'naḥ*.
In *prāptodhāḥ*, the compound is a *tatpuruṣa* by the rule *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyayā*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *atvasantasya*.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has *upadhā*-elision" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*), and so forth: if this [word] were not being carried over (anuvṛtti), then by the maxim of "the intermediate exception" (*madhye'pavādanyāya*), this *ṅīṣ* would be a sublater only of the *ḍāp* and the prohibition [of *ṅīp*], but not of the *ṅīp* prescribed by the rule "of that which has *upadhā*-elision" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*).

[Objection: But surely, in the rule "ḍābubhābhyām," the *ṅīp* is also obtained through the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) therein; and since the rule "of that which has *upadhā*-elision" is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), how can this undesirable consequence arise? [Response: True; however, this was stated on the assumption that the rule "of that which has *upadhā*-elision" is indeed an original injunction (*vidhi*).

In this context, it should be stated that for a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *ūdhas*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied and the final letter is replaced by *n*. Thus, for a *bahuvrīhi* ending in the word *ūdhas*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine, and by its concomitant application (*sanniyoga*), the final letter becomes *n*. However, in the section on compound-final elements (*samāsānta-prakaraṇa*), it need not be stated that "for *ūdhas*, there is *anaṅ*"; rather, one should simply read "for *dhanus*, there is *anaṅ*. What advantage is gained by doing so? It is that the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of this rule need not be relied upon in the rule "for [a stem] ending in *an*, provided it undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel" (*ana upadhālopinaḥ*).

Furthermore, [the forms] *mahodhāḥ* (having great udders) and *vuṇḍodho dhainukam* (a cow with a small udder) are established [by this rule]. Otherwise, in the rule *ūdhaso'naṅ*, one would have to specify "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Therefore, he says: "And the compound-ending suffix occurs only in the feminine. The word "is desired" (*iṣyate*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]; the meaning is that the restriction "only in the feminine" must be stated in that very rule. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of the suffix *kap*. The scope of *kap* is other *bahuvrīhi*s, such as *ayavakaḥ* (one who has no barley) and *avrīhikaḥ* (one who has no rice); whereas the scope of *ṅīṣ* is when *kap* is optional (*vibhāṣā kap*), specifically when *kap* does not apply—that is its scope. When there is the contingency for *kap*, both [suffixes] would apply, and by the principle of priority (*paratva*), *kap* would occur.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a numeral or an indeclinable [ending in a consonant] to form feminine nouns.

Since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been applicable by the preceding rule, *ṅīp* is here specifically prescribed. This applies to a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the accent of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) prevails. However, in a *bahuvrīhi* that is oxytone (ending in an acute accent), there is no difference between *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*; for example, in *sūdhnī*, the oxytonic quality is established by the rule "after *nañ* and *su*" (*nañsubhyām*). In that case, when the *al*-lopa occurs, even with *ṅīp*, the vowel becomes acute by the rule concerning the restoration of the accent (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*). Examples include *dvyūdhnī* and so forth. The analytical explanations (*vigraha*) are: "she who has two udders" (*dve ūdhasī yasyāḥ*), "she whose udder is surpassed" (*atigatam ūdho'syāḥ*), and "she from whom the udder has departed" (*nirgatam ūdho'syāḥ*).

What is the purpose of including the word *ādi* ("and so forth")? The question arises because, if it were understood that "the [term] *ūdhas* which follows a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [forming a bahuvrīhi compound ending in that word, takes the feminine suffix *ṅīp*]," then forms such as *dvayūdhnī* would already be established. Regarding *dvividhodhnī*: the point is that if the inclusion of *ādi* were absent, then by the rule "from a numeral or an indeclinable" (*saṃkhyāvyayābhyām*), which specifies an ablative case (*pañcamī*), the suffix would apply only when the word *ūdhas* immediately follows those two; however, it would not apply when there is an intervention by another word.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a word ending in *dāman* or *hāyana*.

Regarding the rule "svīritenādhikāraḥ" (an indicatory circumflex accent serves as a heading), there are two positions: that it is a heading for words (*śabdādhikāra*) or a heading for meanings (*arthādhikāra*). In the first position, only that word which is established as having the circumflex accent continues to apply; in the second, however, because the meaning of a *dvandva* compound is singular, its continuation might or might not occur. Therefore, adopting the first position here, he says: "The mention of 'number' (*saṅkhyā*) continues, but the mention of 'indivisible' (*avyaya*) does not."

"‘*Hāyana* is prescribed [as the substitute] when age is indicated’—the word *prakṛtiḥ* (base form) is to be supplied as the remainder. The meaning is that the teachers have recorded that a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in *hāyana* is the base form (*prakṛti*) for the feminine suffix *ṅīp* when age is understood. For example: *trihāyanā śālā* (a three-year-old shed). Since age is a property of living beings, it cannot apply to a shed. Now, one might ask: why does the nasalization (*ṇatva*) introduced by the supplementary rule ‘*tricaturbhyāṃ hāyanasya*’ not occur here, as it does in the primary examples? To this he says: ‘And the nasalization (*ṇatva*), etc.

Because the rule for compounds ending in [a specific element] is established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *bahuvrīhi* itself, the inclusion of the word *anta-* (ending in) is for the sake of clarity."
In this context, for a word ending in a *u* that undergoes elision of its penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is optionally applied.
Thus, that [suffix] for which elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is possible when followed by another element is called *upadhālopī*.
As for the objection beginning with "But they are already established," etc., this has already been explained in the very rule *ḍāb ubhābhyām*.

The statement "this rule is for the purpose of prohibiting the *ṅīp* suffix after [a word] whose penultimate vowel is not elided" means that the optional prescription of *ṅīp* after a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *an* is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) applicable only to those compounds where the penultimate vowel is elided. Since the result of this restriction is the exclusion of *ṅīp* after compounds where the penultimate vowel is not elided, it is figuratively described as a prohibition. In the example *bahurājñī*, the substitution of *śī* occurs by the rule *auṅa āpaḥ*. The mention of the dual number is for the sake of manifesting the *ḍāp* suffix; for if the singular were used, the form would be identical whether *ḍāp* or the prohibition of *ṅīp* applied.

Regarding *bahumatsya*: because the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is prescribed by the rule "sūryatiṣyāgastya," this *bahuvrīhi* compound is one in which the penultimate vowel is elided. Regarding *suparvā*: because of the prohibition "not after a conjunct consonant ending in *m* or *v*," this is not a case where the penultimate vowel is elided.
The suffix *nitya* is used in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "desire" (*chanda*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the Vedic language (*chandas*) one follows only what is actually observed, and does not invent something unprecedented? And in those cases, if only the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is observed, and there exists a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for it, who then is capable of effecting its absence? Furthermore, even technical terms (*saṃjñāśabda*) employed by ancient authorities have a fixed sequence [of phonemes]; in those cases too, only *ṅīp* is observed, and its absence cannot be established. For what purpose, then, is this sūtra? [Answer: The phrase "in technical terms and in the Veda" (*saṃjñā-chandasoh*) must be stated for the sake of subsequent rules. The mention of "always" (*nitya*) is for the purpose of precluding optionality in what follows.
And solely from the auspicious medicine prepared by noble persons who are not inferior, yet equal to me in their own misfortune and ill-fortune. || 4.1.30 ||

"In the sense of 'mere'" means in the sense of "not being a technical name" (*asaṃjñā*). Regarding *māmakī*: [the derivation is as follows: from the thought "this belongs to me" (*mameyam*), the suffix *khañ* is applied by the rule *yuṣmadasmador anyatarasyāṃ khañ ca*; then, by the rule *tavakamamakāvekavacane*, the substitution *mamaka-* occurs. Since the form ends in *aṇ*, it would have been established by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* [which prescribes the feminine suffix *ṅīp*]; however, the explicit mention of *māmaka-* is for the sake of restriction—namely, that *ṅīp* occurs only after these two [words] when they are names or in Vedic meter, and not otherwise. Thus, we have *māmikā*. In the case of *bhāgadheyī*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, and the substitution of *ī* is effected by the rule *māmakanarakayor upasaṃkhyānam*. Regarding *bhāgadheyī*: [the derivation is as follows: from *bhāgadheya* (meaning "one's share"), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *samarthānām prathamād vā* [in the context of the *taddhita* suffixes]. Here, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *prāg dīvyato 'ṇ*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is derived from *bhāga* with the suffix *dheya* by the rule *bhāgarūpanāmabhyo dheyaḥ*. The meaning is "that which is to be given as a portion. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *dheya*. According to the rule *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu*, it becomes *puṃvat* (masculine-stem-like) because it is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. By the rule *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu*, it becomes *puṃvat* because it is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. Therefore, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. By the rule *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu*, it becomes *puṃvat* because it is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. Hence, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. By the rule *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu*, it becomes *puṃvat* because it is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. Therefore, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. By the rule *puṃvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu*, it becomes *puṃvat* because it is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*. Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. The word *bhāgadheya* is a *tatpuruṣa* ending in *dheya*.
