Regarding the word *dityauhī*: the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rules "in the Veda, after *sah*" and "after *vah*"; there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; with the addition of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, the substitution *ūṭh* is applied to *vāh*; because the term "vocalization" (*samprasāraṇa*) is understood from the previous rule, the substitution of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied by the rule "after a vocalized element"; and finally, vṛddhi is applied by the rule "before *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*."
In common usage, [the word] *sakhī* is used for a woman who has not borne a child. (Pāṇini 4.1.62)

It is stated that [the rule applies] "in the spoken language" (*bhāṣāyām*); however, in that case, this [form] is not established: *sakhī saptapadī bhava*, *ā dhenavo dhunayantāmaśiśvī*. This is not a fault; for here the particle *iti* is employed, and it should be understood as having its position shifted, occurring immediately after the word *bhāṣāyām*. Furthermore, that particle (*iti*) functions in the sense of "manner" (*prakāre*); therefore, it will also occur in the Vedic language (*chandas*) in certain instances. The mention of "spoken language," however, is for the sake of making the rule obligatory (*nityārtham*).
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a feminine genus-denoting word (*jāti*) that does not have a corresponding masculine form and whose penultimate vowel is not *a*. (Pāṇini 4.1.63)

Regarding the phrase "not having women as its object" (*astrīviṣaya*), he explains that the word "object" (*viṣaya*) here refers to the state of being non-different (*ananya-bhāva*), saying: "nor [is it] feminine" (*na ca straiṇam*). That which functions invariably only with respect to a woman is "having women as its object" (*strīviṣaya*); anything other than that is "not having women as its object" (*astrīviṣaya*).

In this context, since there is a dispute among theorists regarding whether universal classes such as "Brāhmaṇahood" (*brāhmaṇatva*) and so forth, as well as lineages (*gotra*) such as "Nāḍāyana," constitute universals, and since words denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*) such as "Kaṭha" and others—being based on their connection to the act of study—are action-words (*kriyāśabda*) like "cook" (*pācaka*) and thus would not be included, he defines the intended universal (*jāti*) as follows: "A universal is that which is apprehended through form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇā jātiḥ*).

The word *grahaṇa* is refined [grammatically] as a general instrumental term, based on the etymology "that by which something is grasped" (*gṛhyate 'nena*). Subsequently, when it occurs in conjunction with a word denoting a generic form (*ākṛti*), the femininity that is perceived does not serve as the cause for the suffix, because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). The meaning is that, in the expression "that whose generic form is the object of grasping" (*grahaṇam ākṛtir yasyāḥ*), the state of being a generic form is prescribed with reference to the state of being the object of grasping; it is not the case that the state of being the object of grasping is prescribed with reference to the state of being a generic form.

*Ākṛti* means configuration (*saṃsthāna*). That which has this as its basis of apprehension is *ākṛtigrahaṇā*; the meaning is that it is manifested by a specific arrangement of parts. By this, the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is indicated. However, the universal such as "Brahmin-ness" (*brāhmaṇatva*) is not included, because the physical configuration of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others is similar. To include that, he says: "and of genders" (*liṅgānāṃ ca*). The intended meaning is that [the universal] does not partake of all genders.

In this context, although the word *sarva* depends on gender (*liṅga*), the suffix *ṇvi* is applied to the root *bhaj* because it conveys the meaning, and a compound is also formed. In the expression "of genders" (*liṅgānām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). This statement is intended to provide what has not been previously established; it is not a restriction of the rule "by virtue of grasping the form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇāt*). Therefore, even though words such as *taṭa-* possess all genders, they still qualify as "classes" (*jāti*) because they do grasp a common form. Why does this [designation of *jāti*] not apply here in the case of "Devadatta, Devadatta"? This definition depends upon instruction (*upadeśa*).

What is the meaning? The meaning is that [the universal] occurs only in those things which, despite not possessing all genders, the Teacher teaches to be denotative of a genus (*jāti*). He states the characteristics of the genus—which is apprehended through its form—namely, its unity, eternity, and its complete presence in each individual, with the words "once" (*sakṛt*), etc. Even when taught only once in a single individual, such as "this is a cow," it is capable of being grasped—that is, it can be determined—in another individual. And if it were not one, it could never be so grasped.

Likewise, even though it lacks permanence, because it perishes along with one particular body (*piṇḍa*), it would not be perceived in another body. Furthermore, if it were not fully present in its entirety within each individual [body], then it would not be perceived in its entirety even in that specific body where it is said to reside; how much less so in another body! But how can a single entity exist simultaneously in many places in its entirety? For Devadatta cannot be in Srughna and Madhurā at the very same time. If it is observed, however, what is the fault? Indeed, there is none.

What is unestablished in what is observed? It is called "lineage" (*gotra*). The meaning is "offspring. By the word "branch" (*caraṇa*), those who study a particular recensional school (*śākhā*) are understood. Because lineage is not apprehended through physical form and because it possesses all genders, it is mentioned separately, as seen in the rule: "The word *nāḍāyana* is neuter. Furthermore, the word *caraṇa*, because it functions through its connection with the act of studying, is strictly a term for an action (*kriyāśabda*), not a term for a genus (*jātiśabda*).

*Kukkuṭī* (hen) and *sūkarī* (sow) are examples of a genus (*jāti*) apprehended through its form. *Brāhmaṇī* (Brahmin woman) and *vṛṣalī* (outcaste woman) are examples of a genus that does not possess all genders; among these, *brāhmaṇī* is an example of the word-form itself. Because this [genus] is included in the *śārṅgarava* group, *vṛṣalī* is specifically an example for the suffix *ṅīp*. *Nāḍāyanī* and *cārāyaṇī* are examples of a genus characterized as a lineage (*gotra*), derived by the rule "from *naḍa* etc., the suffix *phak*. Since it refers to offspring in general, it applies even to immediate offspring—*avantī* and *kuntī*, where the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs by the rule "after a word denoting human genus ending in *it*."

In this case, however, because the word *kulīnā* means "the offspring of a family," the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply to the word *brāhmaṇī*; they say this is because [the formation] is seen among the *ajādi* group. Regarding *kaṭhī*: [it is derived from] that which was taught by Kaṭha. Since he is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana, the suffix *ṇini* is applied; this is elided by the rule *kaṭhacarakāt*. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that," and this is elided by the rule *proktālluk*. Regarding *bahvṛcī*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "she whose *ṛc*s are many. The suffix *akāra* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *bahvṛścaraṇākhyāyām*.

But how, then, can a woman be said to "study"? Let it not be that she actually studies; rather, the designation will apply to her because she belongs to that lineage, just as one might say of a boy who is not currently studying.
Regarding this, another definition of a genus (*jāti*) is stated in the Bhāṣya: "By the appearance and disappearance of a being, simultaneously with its qualities..."

"Poets know that *jāti* (universal) to be non-universal in its gender (*asarvaliṅgā*) and manifold in its objects (*bahvarthā*). This means that it undergoes manifestation and disappearance through the appearance and destruction of the substance (*sattva*), and thus it exists as long as the substance does. Furthermore, it is simultaneously connected with the qualities (*guṇa*) and with the substance; the meaning is that just as there can be no substance devoid of qualities, so too there can be no [substance] devoid of *jāti*. Regarding "manifold in its objects": the word *artha* here denotes an object (*viṣaya*); thus, it means having many objects, or pervading many individuals (*vyakti*). "Non-universal in its gender" is another defining characteristic from the previous [text].

In that regard, just as according to the previous definition [it would follow that] "the wife is a maiden" (*kumārībhāryā*), how so? Because even though it does not persist as long as the substance (*ayāvad-dravyabhāvin*), it is still a genus (*jāti*) because it is grasped through its form (*ākṛtigrahaṇatvāt*); and consequently, by the rule "and of a genus" (*jāteśca*), there would be a prohibition against the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*). Furthermore, in cases such as *vṛddhā* and *sthavirā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by virtue of the definition of a genus. However, according to the subsequent [view], *kaumāra* and the like are not a genus; this is because they do not persist as long as the substance.

In this regard, the former definition is intended by the author of the Bhāṣya, not the latter; for it says, "another says. Likewise, in the rule on feminine suffixes (*ṅyāp-sūtra*), regarding the form *yuvatitarā*, the prohibition of the masculine-like transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule "in the case of *tasil* and so forth"—is relied upon by the rule "and [the prohibition applies] to a genus" (*jāteśca*). For this very reason, some say that the Vṛttikāra also presented this same definition.

Even so, in the case of *yuvajāni*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not apply; therefore, we consider the second definition alone to be more correct. For this very reason, in the words *vṛddhā* and *sthavirā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is prescribed for feminine nouns denoting a genus (*jāti*)—does not occur. However, in the case of *yuvatitarā*, the absence of the masculine substitution is due to the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya.

Regarding *muṇḍā*: this is a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*). Regarding *makṣikā*: this is restricted to the feminine gender alone. Why does [the suffix] not occur here in the case of *mālā* and *balākā*? The word *mālā*—derived from the root *mal* with the suffix *ghañ*, meaning "wearing" (*malanam*)—is masculine when referring to a particular field, neuter, and feminine when referring to a garland. The word *balākā*, however, is etymologically derived as "one who makes strength" (*balām kāyati*) and thus possesses all genders; yet, when it denotes the species of crane (*baka*), it is feminine.

In this context, it is not intended that the term *astrīliṅga* (non-feminine gender) refers to anything whatsoever; rather, what is meant is this: when a word occurs in another gender while retaining the very same ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as that which caused it to be feminine, then it is "not having the feminine as its object" (*astrīviṣaya*). We shall explain how this meaning of the word is established in the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*. Therefore, due to this difference in the ground for application, this rule does not apply to words that possess multiple genders.

If this is so, why does [the rule] not apply here in *droṇī*, *kuṭī*, and *pātrī*? The word *droṇa* is masculine when denoting a specific measure, but feminine when denoting a cow or similar animal; the word *kuṭa* is masculine when denoting a jar, but feminine when denoting a house; [the forms are] established by their inclusion in the *gaura*-group. Regarding *haya-gavaya* and so forth: it is understood from the statement of the author of the Vārttika that words such as *haya* were added to the *gaura*-group by modern [grammarians].
And [the suffix -matup is applied] after words ending in *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, *bāla*, or those where these are the final members of the compound. Pāṇini 4.1.64.

"Because these [words] have women as their referents. The sense is that since, in the previous case, it was accepted that [the word] refers to something other than a woman when the form is identical, these words of various genders do not succeed due to the difference in the causal basis (nimitta). Words such as *odanapāka* ("rice-cooking") and others, being technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), may be etymologically derived in whatever way possible.
From this [word] *manuṣya-jāti* [the suffix *cha* is applied]. 4.1.65.

*Avantī*, *Kuntī*. From the words *Avanti* and *Kunti*, in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*), the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied by the rule *vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ*; its elision (*luk*) occurs in the feminine by the rule *striyāmavantikuntikurubhyaśca*. *Dākṣī*, *Plākṣī*. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*. *Viṭ*, *Darad*. From the word *viṭ*, which is a name of a region (*janapada-śabda*) and denotes a Kṣatriya, the suffix *añ* is applied; from the word *darad*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *dvyañmagadha-* etc. The elision (*luk*) of both occurs by the rule *ataśca*. The recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ataḥ* cannot be relied upon merely for the sake of establishing these examples; thus, this same contingency applies here as well.

"Audameyī": *udameya* means "he whose measure (*meya*) is water (*udaka*)," with the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* by the rule "udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām. From that [name], the suffix *iñ* is applied in the sense of "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*), according to the rule "ata iñ.
Regarding *sautaṅgamī* and *maunicittī*: the suffix *iñ* is applied after the words *sutaṅgama* and *municitta* in the sense of "produced by him" (*tena nirvṛttam*).
The suffix *ūṅ* [is applied] after [a word ending in] *uta*. (Pāṇini 4.1.66)

Regarding "Kuru": by the rule *kuru-nādibhyo ṇyaḥ*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs in the feminine by the rule *striyām avanti-*, etc. Regarding *brahmabandhuḥ* and *jīvabandhuḥ*: these two function as *bahuvrīhi* compounds referring to the Brāhmaṇa caste that is devoid of proper conduct and Vedic study.

Regarding the passage beginning with *ṅakāra*: if it were stated as *nodhātvoḥ*, then in forms such as *yavāgvā* and *yavāgvai*, there would be a prohibition of the accentuation of the case-ending (*vibhaktyudātta*) which would otherwise apply by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*. This is because the paribhāṣā "the mention of a meaningful item [includes its substitutes]" (*arthavadgrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) does not apply when a mere phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned. Now, what is the purpose of pronouncing the long vowel *ū*? Could one not simply say *uṅutaḥ*, since the form would be established through the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*)? It is not so established.

Even though the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) applies, the shortening prescribed by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya* would follow. It does not apply; for what reason? Because "when relying on both [ends], the resulting form is neither like the end nor like the beginning. For instance, the designation of a nominal stem (*pratipadika-saṃjñā*) must be established for the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) by treating it as if it were the end [of the preceding element], since there is a prohibition against it being a suffix (*apratyaya*). Furthermore, its status as a feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*) must be established by treating it as if it were the beginning [of the following element].

If that were so, then in the case of *brahmabandhūcchatram*, because the rules for *ṣatva* and *tuk* are not established (*asiddha*), the *tuk* characterized by a short vowel would necessarily apply; however, due to the pronunciation of the long vowel (*dīrghoccāraṇāt*), even though the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not established, this [vowel] remains long, and thus the optional rule "after a long vowel or at the end of a word" (*dīrghātpadāntādvā*) is successfully achieved. This too is not a valid purpose; for the single-substitute between the end of a word and the beginning of a word is not established, and this is not a single-substitute between the end of a word and the beginning of a word.

Raising the objection that, therefore, the long pronunciation [of the *u*] is useless, he says: "The long pronunciation is for the purpose of subverting the *kap* suffix. The scope of the *kap* suffix [prescribed by the rule] *śeṣādvibhāṣā* is, for example, *ayavakaḥ* and *avrīhikaḥ*; the scope of the *ūṅ* suffix [prescribed by the rule] *ūṅutaḥ* is, for example, *kurūḥ*. In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *brahmabandhū*, where both [suffixes] would apply, the *kap* suffix would prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules; however, because of the long pronunciation, it does not occur. How so? Two *u*s are indicated by the long vowel; therein, the second *u* is for the purpose of subverting the *kap* suffix.

Regarding the term *adhvaryu*: because it is seen among the *uṇādi* suffixes in the rule "and *mṛgayū* etc.," the suffix *ku* is applied to the word *adhvara*, with the elision of its final syllable. This is a caste (*jāti*) defined by Vedic school (*caraṇa*); the meaning is that he belongs to a lineage that studies the *Adhvaryu* branch [of the Yajurveda].

Regarding the rule *aprāṇijāteśca*: here, the requirement of the suffix *utaḥ* (from a stem ending in *u*) is not required; therefore, it applies even to the long-final stems *alābu-* and *karkandhū-*. While the rule *kṛṣicamitanidhanisajikharjibhya ūḥ* is in force, there is also the addition of the marker *ṇit* from the rule *ṇitkaśipadyarteḥ*. Furthermore, regarding the rule *nañi lambernalopaśca*: the root *labi* means "to hang down"; from this root preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *ū* occurs and there is elision of the nasal (*n*), and because the suffix is marked *ṇit*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening. Thus, by the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) "andūdṛmbhūkarkandhūḥ," the word ends in the vowel *ū*.

The word *karkandhū*. Likewise, the words *alābū* and *karkandhū* end in long vowels. The prescription of the suffix *ūṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the acute accent on the case-ending according to the rule *noṅdhātvoḥ* in forms such as *alābvā* and *karkandhvā*. [The word] *kṛkavāku*: by the rule *kṛke vacaḥ kaśca*, when the word *kṛka* is an upapada, the suffix *uṇ* is added to the root *vac*, and there is the substitution of *ka* for the final portion [of the prefix]. [The word] *rajju*.

Regarding *sṛj* with the suffix *asu*: the elision of the initial vowel (*ādi-lopa*) is the rule under discussion; the suffix *u* is added to the root *sṛj*, there is elision of the initial vowel (*ā*), and the augment *asuk* is inserted. Then, by the rule *ṛto yaṇādeśaḥ*, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *yaṇ*; finally, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) and the retroflex (*cartva*) apply to the letter *s*. Thus, "that rope is produced" is *sṛjyate’sau rajjuḥ*. Regarding *hanu*: by the rule *yusnihi* etc., the suffix *u* is added to the root *han*.
And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the word *paṅgu*. (Pāṇini 4.1.68)

Regarding the word *śvaśura*: the suffix *ūṅ* is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṅīṣ* which is conditioned by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). [The rule] "after the root *aś*, when meaning 'attainment,' the suffix *uran* occurs after the word *śu*" applies. What is this *śu*? It is the substitution of an initial elision (*ādilopa*) for the word *āśu*. One who is to be attained quickly is a *śvaśura*; his wife is *śvaśrūḥ*. Due to the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) beginning with "the father-in-law is *śvaśura*," the operations pertaining to nominal stems (*prātipadika*), such as case endings and so forth, take place.
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied after a word ending in *ūrū* when it is the second member of a compound used in a sense of comparison (*aupamye*).

That by which something is compared is *upamā* (the simile); the state of being that is *aupamya* (similarity). How is it that [one says] "and he scattered [them] with the trunks and thighs of the female elephants"? Poets are unrestrained; the reading is "with the trunk and the beautiful thighs"—meaning he scattered them with the trunk and with the beautiful thighs.
The augment *ṭi* is added after a word ending in *saṃhita*, *śapha*, *laṅkṣa*, or a word beginning with *vāma*.
The word *saṃhita* is a synonym for *sahita*; the word *lakṣaṇa* ends with the suffix *ac* according to the rule beginning with *arśas*; and the word *vāma* is a synonym for *śobhana*.

Regarding the phrase "and with *sahita* and *saha*": when the *m* is elided by the rule "optionally after *sama* in the sense of *hita* and *tati*," the form *sahita* is already established by the very mention of *saṃhita*, because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. However, they say that this is the inclusion of the word *sahita* derived from the analysis "that which exists together with (*saha*) what is beneficial (*hita*). Regarding *sahorū*: the meaning is "she whose thighs (*ūrū*) are *sahau*," that is, those which bear together (*sahete*). Alternatively, the word *saha* is employed even though it is already present [in the compound] for the purpose of expressing an excellence of the thighs.
In the Vedic language, [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the feminine gender of *guggulu* and other such words is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The word *patayālu* ends in the suffix *-āluc* according to the rule beginning with "spṛhigṛhi" (Pāṇini 3.2.158).
The suffix *ṅīn* is applied after [stems ending in] *śārṅgarava* and those that take the suffix *aṇ*.

"These end in *aṇ*": from *śṛṅgara*, *kapaṭu*, *guggulu*, and *brahman*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *prāgdīvyato'ṇ*; from the word *gotama*, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied (as this word is also listed among the *gaura*-group). "These end in *ḍhak*": this is stated because they are the majority. From the word *kaṇva*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied according to the rule *catuṣpādbhyo ḍhañ*; from the others, however, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule *śubhrādibhyaśca*. "These two end in *phak*": from the word *vātsya*, which ends in *yañ* (from the *garga*-group), the suffix *phak* is applied in the sense of a descendant (*yūni*) according to the rule *yañiñośca*.

But surely the designation *yuvan* does not apply to a female, because of the rule "the *yuvan* [suffix] is used for the descendant of a *gotra*, except in the feminine," and because regarding the *gotra*, there is the restriction "only one [suffix is used] in the *gotra*"? If this is so, then by virtue of the word *vātsyāyana* being read in this list (*gaṇa*), the designation *yuvan* will apply to the female; or else, both suffixes may apply to the *gotra* itself. The word *muñja* belongs to the *naḍādi* group. Regarding "a genus" (*jāti*): it is defined as a *gotra*. Regarding "ending in *ḍhak*": the word *kīkasā* belongs to the *śubhrādi* group. Regarding "ending in *ñyaṅ*": [these are the two types].

By the rule *vṛddhet-kosalājādāñ-ñyaṅ*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after the words *kavi* and *śibi*; consequently, the suffix *cāp* would apply here by the rule *yaṅaś-cāp*. [Examples are] *ehi* and *paryehi*. In the case of *īha* (meaning "effort"), the suffix *in* is applied after the root preceded by the prefixes *āṅ* and *pari* according to the rule *sarvadhātubhya in*. The word *aśmaratha* belongs to the *garga*-class, while the word *udapāna* belongs to both the *śuṇḍika*-class and the *utsa*-class; regarding this, he says: "The word ending in *aṇ* from the *śuṇḍika*-class is employed. However, at the end, there is no difference whether the feminine suffix is *ṅīp* or *ṅīn*. [The term] "jāti" [is used].

The status of *arāla* and *caṇḍāla* as *jāti*s (castes/kinds) is due to their not being of universal gender (*asarvaliṅgatva*). Because the word *vataṇḍa* is a *gotra* (clan name), [the following applies]: the feminine descendant of *vataṇḍa* takes the suffix *yañ* by the rule *vataṇḍācca*; then, by the rule *luk striyām*, there is elision of that suffix. Regarding the phrase *bhogavad-gorimator*: since it ends in the suffix *matup*, the suffix *ṅīp* would have been required by the rule *ugitaśca*; therefore, this specific statement is made.

[Objection: But surely the word *bhoga* ends in the suffix *ghañ*, and the word *gaurī* ends in the suffix *iñ* by the rule *ata iñ*; both of these are acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) due to the accent of the *ñit*-suffixes. To them is added the suffix *matup*, which is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it is marked with *p*. Consequently, there would be no difference here between the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ṅīṣ*. To this, he replies: "In the case of *gha*-class [suffixes], it is obligatory. If the suffix *ṅīp* were applied by the rule for *ugit* stems, then shortening would occur optionally by the rules *nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām* and *ugitaśca*. However, when *ṅīn* is applied, the shortening occurs obligatorily by the rule *gharūpakalpa*. Thus, there is a distinction.

How is this so? For a *vikalpa* (optionality) has been prescribed for a river-name that follows an *ugit* [stem], and the suffix *ṅīp* also follows an *ugit*; since [the stems] *bhogavat* and *gaurimat* possess the quality of being *ugit*, would this not be a fault? This is not a fault. The particle *ca* in the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6) has the sense of "and" (*ityarthe*). A river-name that is prescribed by the specific designation of *ugit*—namely, by the word *ugit* itself—is what is intended here; it is not the case that a river-name is prescribed merely by this [general rule for *ṅīp*]. Just as in the commentary on the rule *yuvoranākau*, so too it remains established that [the option applies only to] a river-name that follows an *ugit*.
In the case of *saṃjñā*, it is only *hī* that occurs, and the short vowel is also optionally prescribed.

Regarding *nṛ* and *nara*, there is the rule for *vṛddhi*. Since the suffix *ṅīp* would apply after the word *nṛ* by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*, and the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply after the word *nara* by the characteristic of being a genus (*jāti*), this statement is made. As for the mention of *vṛddhi* and "I shall state [it]," even if only one of these were mentioned, the desired form *nārī* would be established; however, both are employed in order to exclude the undesired forms.

In that case, when the *vṛddhi* [substitution] applies to the final letter of the word *nara*, the elision of the *ya* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) results in its becoming meaningless; thus, the elision of *ya* indeed takes place first. Once that has been done, the *vṛddhi* would apply to the *repha* (the *r*). Which [vowel]? Indistinctly, by way of alternation, would it be every vowel? This is not a fault; for in the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*, an alternative interpretation has been explained wherein the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) refers to the most similar substitute. Consequently, this genitive in the expression *nṛ-narayoḥ* is construed with the original base (*sthānin*)—which is a constituent part of *nṛ* and *nara*—that is most similar to the *vṛddhi*.

And where there is a genitive case, the substitution occurs only for the letter *a*, according to the rule "where there is a genitive, there is a substitute. Here, some read the word *putra*; however, since that word alone does not denote the feminine, the term refers to a compound ending in it. Even so, in cases such as *bahuputrā* and *atiputrā*, the substitution does not occur because of the governing rule regarding non-qualifiers (*anupasarjana*). Where, then, does it occur? It occurs when the son (*putra*) is the predominant element. But is it not the case that in a compound where the son is predominant, that very same masculine gender applies? True; [the substitution occurs when the feminine suffix is added after such a compound].

Regarding the statement by the author of the *Vārttika*, "after *sūta*, *ugra*, *rājan*, *bhoja*, and *meru*, there is the substitution of *putraḍ* for the daughter," these are the examples: *sūtaputrī* and *rājaputrī*. Here, the intention of those who recite [the text] is that, by its very nature, the word *putra* has the same meaning as the word *duhitṛ*, and thus it is not a case of the substitution *putraḍ*.

Others, however, maintain that *pradyotaputrī* and *śailaputrī* are examples of the suffix *ṅīn* entirely distinct from the scope of the *Vārttika*; they hold that the substitution *putraḍ* is intended merely for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*) when the suffix *ṅīp* follows. In this matter, there is nothing spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*).
And [the suffix] yaṅcāp. 4.1.74.

The letter *pakāra* (the *p* in *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*) is for the purpose of including the general category [of suffixes], whereas as for the accent, because it is subsequent, the *citsvara* alone occurs. Thus, there is a general inclusion of both *ñaṅ* and *ṣyaṅ*. Although *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed only for the feminine, nevertheless, the intention is that it is also included here by virtue of the force of its being marked with the *ḍi*-indicator. Examples such as *Āmbaṣṭyā* and so on: from *ambaṣṭha* and others, the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied to denote offspring when the stem begins with a *vṛddhi* vowel, according to the rule *vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ*. *Kārīṣagandhyā* has been explained in the *svādi* section of the sūtras.

From the word *varāha*, [the suffix] *iñ* is applied by the rule *ata iñ*. The words *śarkarākṣa*, *pūtimāṣa*, and *gokakṣa* belong to the *garga-ādi* group. Now, one might object: "But the word *gaukākṣya* is listed among the *krauḍyādi* group; therefore, when the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied, the feminine suffix *cāp* is already established by the rule *yaṅaḥ*. So why list it there? Do not say so; even without that listing, the form *gaukākṣī* is established by the rule *ṣācca yañaḥ*, just like *śarkarākṣī* and others. If this is the case, then in the form *gaukākṣīputraḥ*, would the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *ṣyaṅ* not apply? Vocalization is not desired here; the form remains simply *gaukākṣyāputraḥ*.
For thus the Saunāgas recite: "There is a prohibition of the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *gaukakṣyā* after [the suffix] *ṣyaṅ*."
The secondary suffixes (taddhita). 4.1.76.

Regarding the word *yuvati*: when the designation *taddhita* applies, the designation *prātipadika* occurs by the rule "kṛt, taddhita, and compounds [are also *prātipadikas*]. As for the plural number and so forth: although the singular should have been used—as in the case of the term *pratyaya*—the use of the plural indicates the multiplicity of the things designated (*saṃjñin*); thus, it is understood that even though not explicitly mentioned, the *taddhita* suffix is included.

If the section on feminine suffixes were placed at the beginning of the section on *taddhita* suffixes, then the mention of "taddhita" in the rule *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ* would not be necessary; the mention of the particle *ca* in the rule *yasyeti ca* would also not be necessary; however, in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*, the mention of *ṅyāp* would indeed have to be made in order to prescribe *taddhita* suffixes after those [stems] ending in them. True; [if that were so], the marker *ṅ* in *ṅīp* and other such suffixes would not receive the designation *it*, because of the prohibition in the rule *ataddhite*. Or, even if that were granted, the rule *orguṇaḥ* would apply in cases such as *paṭvī*. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was originally formulated.
The suffix *ti* is applied after the word *yuvan*.

Regarding the word *yuvati*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply after a stem ending in *t* denoting a human species, because femininity is already expressed by the suffix *ti* itself, or because youth (*yauvana*) is not a genus (*jāti*).
The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem ending in *aṇ* or *iṇ*, provided that the penultimate syllable is long and the stem is not a Vedic (*ārṣa*) formation.

The relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) occurs only when there is both co-occurrence (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, in the rules "in *gotra*" and "of non-Vedic [names]," the terms "the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*" qualify the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ* alone, whereas "having a heavy penultimate syllable" qualifies that which ends in them. Thus he says: "of those ending in *aṇ* and *iñ* which are prescribed for *gotra* and are non-Vedic. Although elsewhere—outside the scope of the definition of offspring (*apatya*)—the term *gotra* refers to the worldly sense of lineage, here it refers to the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense.

Since the inclusion of the term *laukika* (worldly/common) is already established by relying on the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not [the names of] sages" (*anārṣayoḥ*), one might ask here: is this suffix *ṣyaṅ* a secondary suffix (*pratyaya*) or a substitute (*ādeśa*)? For even in the case of a rule for suffixes, such as "gāpoṣṭak" (Pāṇini 3.2.8), the genitive case is observed; yet, because of the use of the ablative case in the subsequent rule "krauḍyādibhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.80), the view that it is a suffix is indeed possible.

In that regard, according to the first position, the feminine descendant of Udamegha is formed as *audameghe* by the rule *ata iñ*; when the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is subsequently applied to that form, one would have *audameghyāyāś chāttrāḥ* (the students of Audameghī) or *audameghāś chāttrāḥ*, and *audameghyānāṃ saṅghaḥ* (the assembly of Audameghīs). In these cases, the suffix *aṇ*—which is prescribed after stems ending in *iñ* by the rules *iñaś ca* and *saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇe*—would not apply.

Furthermore, even if—by virtue of the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a rule stated with reference to a specific gender applies also to the word qualified by that gender)—the suffix *aṇ*, which is prescribed after a stem ending in *iñ*, were to apply even after a stem ending in *ṣyaṅ*, there would still be no elision of *y* according to the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite'nāti*. This is because *ṣyaṅ* does not denote a descendant (*apatya*)? This is not a fault; for, by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, the *ṣyaṅ* is replaced by the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) prior to the arising of the *aṇ* suffix. Once that [masculine form] has taken effect, the *aṇ* will apply by the rule *iñaḥ*, and there will be no audible *y*.

"In that case, for the feminine form *audameghyā*, [the derivative] *audamegheyaḥ*—formed by the suffix *ḍhak* according to the rule *strībhyaḥ ḍhak*—would not undergo the elision of *yalopa*, nor would there be *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution), because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *aḍhe*. Having observed this fault in the first position, he states the second position: 'The substitute *ṣyaṅ* occurs.'"

Now, one might object: in this view, regarding "the female descendant of Uḍuloma," since the word *loman* is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group, and because there is no connection with the suffix *iñ* for the simple stem alone, it follows by implication that the form ending in that [suffix] is what is intended. Consequently, when *iñ* is replaced by *ṣyaṅ*, the rule "there is no substitution of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) when *ya* follows, except in the case of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) or actions (*karman*)" would prevent the elision of the final *ṭi* by the rule "the final *ṭi* is dropped before a *taddhita* suffix. Thus, the form would have to be *auḍulomanyā*, whereas *auḍulomyā* is desired. In the view where the suffix itself is the basis, however, there is no *prakṛtibhāva* due to the intervention of *iñ*; and even after the elision of the *ya* by the rule "of that which ends in *y*" (*yasyeti ca*), [the elision of *ṭi* still occurs].

Is there not an intervention [of the suffix] because of its status as a substitute (*sthānin*)? This is not a fault; for here, *ṣyaṅ* does not apply before the elision of the *ṭi*-portion has taken place. What is the reason? Because the word would not have a heavy syllable in the penultimate position (*agurūpottama*). Therefore, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs only after the *iñ* suffix has been applied; then there is the condition of having a heavy syllable in the penultimate position, and then *ṣyaṅ* follows—thus it is established by this sequence. But then this is the fault: by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), there is the inclusion of those ending in *aṇ* and *iñ*. Since *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed for these two, it would result in a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) because it consists of more than one letter (*anekāl*). [To this we reply: By the rule "ṅit" (*ṅicca*), it will apply to the final letter; however, by the logic of *tātaṅ*, a total replacement would still result.

For where another purpose for the marker *ṅ* is possible, there the rule "an element marked with *ṅ* [replaces only its own place]"—which finds scope in cases like *anaṅ* where the *ṅ* serves no other purpose—is set aside by the rule "that which has more than one letter or is marked with *ś* or *ṭ* replaces the whole," as is the case with *tātaṅ*. However, in this instance (*yaṅ*), even though it would replace the whole, the purpose of the qualification "after *yaṅ*" (in the rule *yaṅaścāp*) is still possible; therefore, it follows that it should replace the whole. To this, he says: "Of that which is being specifically indicated," and so forth.

If this word *uttama* were derived [by adding the suffix *tamaP*], then after the word *ud*, when *tamaP* is applied, would the suffix *ām* not be required by the rule "after *kim*, *tiṅ*, and indeclinables ending in a consonant (*ghat*), [the suffix *ām* is added] before *tamaP*"? No, because it is not the excellence of a substance (*dravya*). For the word *ud* denotes an action accompanied by its instrument and refers to that which has risen; its excellence is mediated through the action—namely, "risen to the highest degree. Consequently, since the excellence resides in the substance, the prohibition "when there is no excellence of a substance" will apply.

Even so, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word *uttama* being acute-accented on its first syllable due to the suffix *tamap*? No; because it is listed among the *uñchādi* group. For in the *uñchādi* list, both *uttama* and *śaśvattama* are read as "everywhere" (*sarvatra*). Even if that were the case, that reading [of the *uñchādi*] must be established [as a specific rule]; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *ām* suffix in *uttamām* when expressing the excellence of an action in general. Therefore, one must accept that the suffix *tamap* does not arise after the word *ut* due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

Furthermore, the word *uttama* (superlative) applies to four or more [entities]. How so? It is "risen above" (*udgata*), and that [state] depends upon what was uttered first. Thus, among three, two are "risen above," and between those two, the second is "risen above" to a greater degree. Since the suffix *-tarap* is used for comparison between two, it would follow that it could only occur where there are exactly three "risen above" entities—as in *kārīṣagandhyā* and similar forms; however, it would not occur in cases such as *vārāhī*.

Thus, seeing the fault in the view that [the suffixes] are derived through etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*), he states—relying on the view that they are not so derived (*avyutpatti*)—"the word *uttama*. "By its own nature" means: not by virtue of etymological derivation. By the mention of "three and more," [the suffix] does not apply in cases such as *dākṣī* or *plākṣī*; rather, only the suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*. This was stated with the intention of referring merely to what would otherwise be applicable; for here, because it is a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīn* ought to apply by the rule *śārṅgaravādyañaḥ*. As for *vāsiṣṭhī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca*.

Regarding *āhicchatrī*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "born from" (*jāta*) and so forth. In this way, the position that [the word] is a substitute (*ādeśa*) has been established. If this is so, then consider the case of *hastiśiras* (having an elephant's head): the suffix *iñ* is applied because it belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group; by the rule *aci śīrṣaḥ*, there is the substitution of *śīrṣa*; then, by the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* for *iñ*, the word *śīrṣa* would—by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—be included under the term *śiras*, and thus the substitution of *śīrṣan* would apply by the rule *ye ca taddhite*. Let it be so; the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) will occur by the rule *nastaddhite*.

Regarding the rule "ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ," the status of the *prakṛti-bhāva* (non-substitution) would apply; consequently, the form would have to be *hāstiśīrṣaṇyā*. However, in the view that [the suffix] is a *pratyaya*, because it is not separated by the *iṅ* augment, there is no substitution of *śīrṣan*. Even when the *yasya* elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is still a separation due to the status of the *sthānivat* (as if it were the original element); thus, the form *hāstiśīrṣā* is established. Therefore, the view that it is a *pratyaya* should be adopted.

Regarding this, Vāmana will say under the rule *ye ca taddhite*: "If [the suffix] is a *pratyaya*, how is the form *audameghya* derived? The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed after a patronymic (*āpatya*), and that too is indeed a patronymic; therefore, the form is established by the elision of *y*."

Jayāditya, however, held the view: "Since the substitution of *śīrṣan* occurs by virtue of the conjunction [of conditions], that [substitution] will not cause the obstruction of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*. If this is so, how could the substitution of *śīrṣan*, which is dependent upon a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*), obstruct that very vowel-initial suffix? What follows from this? Even the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* would not apply, because the Paribhāṣā regarding the obstruction of a conjunction of causes (*sannipātaparibhāṣā*) is not eternal; therefore, *ṣyaṅ* occurs, and the substitution of *śīrṣan* will not take place.

In that case, there is this objection regarding the view that [the suffix] is a substitute (*ādeśa*): two *anubandhas* must be added to the suffix *yaṅ* by the rule *yaṅaścāp* for the sake of its general inclusion and to prevent its disruption; otherwise, if *ṣyaṅ* were a substitute for *aṇ*, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* etc., whereas if it were a substitute for *iñ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *ṅīṣ* by the rule *iña upasaṅkhyānam*. This is not a fault; for in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the word *ataḥ* (containing the vowel *a*) is understood, and therein the vowel *a* is qualified by *aṇ*—meaning "the vowel *a* other than that which follows *aṇ*. Thus, there is no application of *ṅīp* or *ṅīṣ*.

In that case, when the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs, the suffix *ṅīp* will not apply because of the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "analvidhau" (Pāṇini 1.1.56). For if [the rule] were understood as "after a stem ending in *aṇ* and ending in *a*," then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṅīp* applying, since the status of ending in *a* would be inherent to the word itself (*svāśraya*), while the status of ending in *aṇ* would be due to *sthānivadbhāva*. Furthermore, in the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "of *iñ*," the term "ending in *it*" (*itaḥ*) from the rule "of the human class ending in *it*" (*ito manuṣyajāteḥ*) is required—meaning "after that which ends in the *ikāra* of *iñ*."

Alternatively, if it is understood that [the suffix] is applied after a word ending in *iñ* or one ending in long *ī*, then when the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs, the absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* in forms such as *vārāhyā* is established because there is no modification [of the stem]. Even so, the accent must still be considered; otherwise, since the substitute *ṣyaṅ* for *iñ* would be treated as having the marker *ñ* by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, and since *ṭāp* is also anudātta due to its being marked with *p*, the word would become udātta on the first syllable by the accent of the *ñ*-marker.

It might be argued: "Since the designation *it* for the *ñ* of *iñ* is prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) even before the substitution of *ṣyaṅ*, and since there is no accent caused by an *it* (as the *ñ* has been removed), the accent will instead be that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*); thus, the accent is established even when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. [The response is: In that case, just as the accent caused by an *it* does not occur, so too would the *vṛddhi* increase not occur. Therefore, one must accept that the substitution takes place once the *it*-designation of the *ñ* has already occurred; consequently, because of the resulting fault regarding the accent, two markers (*anubandhas*) must indeed be applied for this purpose.

But when the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is present as a secondary element (*pratyaya*), once the accent of the suffix has been applied, the desired form is established even after adding *āp* to that which ends in it; there is neither a difference in form nor a difference in accent. Now, one might object: "Since femininity is already expressed by *ṣyaṅ* itself, *āp* should not occur? This is not a fault; just as in forms such as *gārgyāyaṇī*, where femininity is expressed by two [suffixes], so too here the capacity belongs to both, and thus *ṭāp* will also occur.

"In that case, you too must apply two indicatory letters (*anubandha*) for the sake of specification in the rule *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, so that [the suffix] does not occur here: *pāśyā* (a collection of nooses), formed by *pāśādibhyo yaḥ*, and then *pāśyāpatiḥ*. If that is so, then only one indicatory letter will be used. Which one? [If it were *ka*,] there would be the undesirable application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* in the word *ṣakīra*."

If the rule "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel in *yaṅ*" were stated, would it not also apply in the case of *lolūyāputra*? No, because after the application of the suffix *apratyaya*, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), and since the [semivowel] is then separated from the *yaṅ* by that *a*-vowel, the rule will not apply. But then, in the case of *vārāhīputra*, there is separation by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*? There is no separation, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding member.

Now, in the rule *iṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, the term *dhātuḥ* (root) is understood to carry over from the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ*. This is for the purpose that the substitution of *āt* [for the final vowel] by the rule *ādeca upadeśe 'śiti* should apply only to a root—as in *gobhyām* and so forth—and not otherwise.

In that context, when it is stated that "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in *yaṅ* when followed immediately by the words *putra* or *patni*," a root such as *lolūya* is not immediate [to the suffix], and that which is immediate, such as *vārāhī*, is not a root. In such cases, since either the status of being a root or the state of being immediate must be relinquished, the vocalization occurs—as in *vārāhīputra* and so on—by relying solely on the state of being immediate even in the absence of the status of being a root; likewise, in *lolūyāputra*, it would occur by relying on the status of being a root even in the absence of immediacy.

Now, you might say: "There is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two suffixes *yaṅ* and *dhātu*; rather, there is a conjunction—namely, 'of the son (*puttra*) and the husband (*pati*) immediately following [the word], and of *yaṅ* and the verbal root (*dhātu*)'? In that case, it would apply in instances such as *vārāhīputtra*, but not in instances such as *lolūyāpati*, because of the intervention of the verbal root. Consequently, by implication, the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*) results in its continuation only for the sake of what follows.

If this is so, then in the case of *vākpati*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *vac*. In that case, the term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) will be removed [from the rule], and the substitution of *ā* will not apply to nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *go*, because they lack an original instruction (*upadeśa*). An "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is a mention whose primary purpose is to make known the specific form [of a word]. However, in cases such as *godvyacaḥ* and *naudvyacaḥ*, the pronunciation is for the sake of another grammatical operation (*kāryāntara*), not for the sake of making known the specific form. Therefore, in this way, only one marker (*anubandha*) need be employed in the view that [the suffix] is a secondary element (*pratyaya*). On this point, there are these summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*):

In the case of a non-jāti [term], there is *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment), and even when the *yalu* (elision of *ya*) occurs, when a subsequent *ṣyaṅ* follows—as in *Audameghi*, where *ṣyaṅ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*)—then, by the rule of *tadyaluk*, the form *Auḍulomi* would arise here in sequence.
However, the acquisition of the *ṣyaṅ* suffix depends upon the head [of the compound]; for the destruction of that [head], the *hāsti* (elephant) is not capable in the *śīrṣya* (head-position).
Even though it is a universal substitute (sarvādeśa), like *tāt-aṅ*, it does not [apply] because of the stated reason regarding the substituends *yaṅ* and *aṇiñ*.
Even when [the suffix] *strī* is mentioned, since [the vowel] *ā* is easily obtained in the subsequent [rule], *ṣ* and *ṅī* should not be prescribed here.

If it is argued that [the rule] "for *iñ*, *aṇ*" is intended to prevent the application of *ṅī* when there is the substitution of *aṇ*, then there is no fault, as there are two things to be qualified.

However, because of the *ñit*-designation, the acute accent would apply to the first syllable; furthermore, if the substitution were simultaneous (*sahajādeśana*), the *vṛddhi* [vowel] would not occur.

In the case of *pāśyāputtra*, for the sake of cessation [of the application of rules], let there be *yaṇ* and *ika*; here, because of the *ṣit* designation, let there be only one [application]; but let there be *ṅīṣ* and *yaṅ*.

In the case of *lolūyā-putra*, even though there is no immediate intervention [by another element], the suffix should be treated as having a long vowel at its end (*dīrghāntavat*) when it occurs in connection with the immediate sequence of a verbal root (*dhātu*). This rule applies just as it does when immediately following a verbal root (*dhi*); for in this context, those two [the suffix and the root] do not require each other, O Lord of Speech.
For it is taught that "the cow" is the subject here; thus, for me, that alone is one.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [a word denoting] a part of a lineage (*gotra*). 4.1.79.

This word *gotra* has several meanings: it is a technical term [in grammar] defined as "the lineage beginning with the grandson" (*apatyaṃ pauttraprabhṛti gotram*); it is a common worldly term denoting offspring in general; and it has an etymological derivation: that by which those born from one's own lineage are praised or designated—that is, the primary progenitor—is called *gotra*, because he provides the name for the lineage of offspring originating from him, such as Bharata, Raghu, or Yadu.

The word *avayava* (part) has several meanings: first, it refers to a single portion, by connection with which a whole (*avayavin*) is designated as such; second, it means separation, as seen in usages such as *avayutya-anuvāda* (reiteration after separating), where the root *yu* preceded by the prefix *ava-* is observed to signify separation; and third, it signifies that which is subordinate—as in the expression "this person is a part (*avayavabhūta*) of this village."

In that case, this statement would be redundant regarding the technical sense of *gotra*, as well as regarding its partial sense (*ekadeśa*) and its constituent sense (*avayava*). How so? The collection of offspring beginning with the grandson is *gotra*, and its constituent parts—the fourth descendant and so on—are also *gotra*. Since the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is already established by the preceding rule for a word ending in *aṇ* or *iñ* denoting such [a *gotra*], [this rule would be unnecessary]. Alternatively, if it refers to the intermediate *gotras* within some major *gotra*—such as *cyavana* and others within the *bhārgava* *gotra*—then these are indeed constituents of a *gotra*, and this new rule is commenced for the sake of those cases where the penultimate syllable is not heavy (*agurūpottama*).

If this were so, then since eight great *gotras* of the Seven Sages with Agastya as the eighth are recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix *ṣyaṅ* applying to all others distinct from them; yet this is not desired, for it is intended that *ṣyaṅ* applies only to those such as the Puṇikas even when they do not have a heavy penultimate syllable (*agurūpottama*). However, if the word "separate" (*pṛthak*) is stated [in the rule], then when *ṣyaṅ* is prescribed after a word denoting a part of a *gotra*—that is, a word other than a *gotra* ending in *aṇ* or *iñ*—the mention of "gotra" in the preceding rule would be purposeless.

Now, if the word *avayava* (member/part) refers to what is not primary (*apradhāna*), then *gotra* would be purely technical (*pāribhāṣika*) because it is read in the *Pravarādhyāya*, and its non-primacy [would follow from that]. In that case, the meaning would be this: *ṣyaṅ* is applied after those [patronymics] ending in *aṇ* or *iñ* which denote a *gotra*-descendant but are not listed in the *Pravarādhyāya*. Among these, for those [names] derived from non-sages (*anṛṣi*) where the penultimate syllable is heavy (*gurūpottama*), the formation is already established by the preceding rule; however, for those that do not have a heavy penultimate syllable, the application is desired only for those that function as proper names (*saṃjñākārin*). And since the status of being a proper name is not obtained as a specific feature within the technical definition of *gotra*, [the rule remains necessary].

In this case as well, the following undesirable consequence would follow: suppose there is someone named Tuṣajaka; his lineage (*gotra*) is a woman, *Tauṣajakī* (formed with the suffix *iñ* according to the rule *ata iñ*). Now, regarding the term for the offspring (*apatya*) itself as a lineage (*gotra*), if it is taken as a part (*avayava*)—that is, if the offspring beginning from the grandson (*pautra*) onwards is considered a constituent part of the aggregate of offspring—then the formation is already established by the previous rule (*aṇ* or *iñ*) for that which denotes such a [lineage]. However, if it is taken as something distinct, then there would be the undesired application of the suffix only to words like *Āhicchatra*, which denote something other than the offspring.

However, when [the suffix] is not primary, it is not desired in all cases for a word ending in *aṇ* or *iñ* that denotes a non-primary descendant and has a heavy penultimate syllable; rather, it is desired only after those [words] that function as proper names (*saṃjñākārin*), and even there, only in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). In the case of a derived lineage name, the word "part" (*avayava*) cannot refer to a single constituent part [of the body], for it is impossible for the *aṇ* or *iñ* suffixes to apply to a lineage based on a limb such as a hand or foot from which a person is named because they belong to his own progeny.

Now, if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the lineage (*gotra*) and its constituent part (*avayava*"), then there would be the undesirable consequence [of the suffix applying] to those such as Cyavana, who provide intermediate designations within lineages such as that of Bhṛgu. Furthermore, if they were separate [words], it would apply only to those such as Tuṣajaka, who are distinct from those who provide the primary designation. Therefore, since faults arise in these alternative views, the word *gotra* is derived [in this specific sense], the word *avayava* denotes something subordinate, and the compound is a *karmadhāraya*.

The placement of the qualifier at the end [of the compound] is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and its lack of primacy is because it is not recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*. This is what he states: "those that are parts of a lineage (*gotra*) are considered as the lineage. That is to say, they are considered to be the lineage; they are well-known in the world as designating the lineage, but the meaning is that they are not those recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*. To the question "Which ones, then, are they?", he replies: "those called by family names (*kulākhyā*)."

"Kulākhyāḥ" (clan-names) are so called because the family is designated by them; for a family is indeed designated by names such as Puṇika and others—as in "We belong to the Puṇika lineage," and so forth. "From those" means from those clan-names characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers. The purpose of the commencement [of this rule] is to exclude the condition that the penultimate syllable be heavy (*agurūpottama*); the sense is that while the phrase "when the penultimate syllables are heavy" (*gurūpottamayoḥ*) is no longer operative, everything else continues to apply. Examples include *Pauṇikī* and so on. From the words *puṇika*, *bhuṇika*, and *mukhara*, the suffix *iñ* is added, which is then replaced by *ṣyaṅ*. The meaning is that these [names] should be understood as belonging to the *krauḍyādi* group, since they have not been excluded from it.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after [words ending in] *krauḍi* and others. 4.1.80.

The suffix *ṣyaṅ* occurs. This is stated thus because of the ablative indication in the rule "from *krauḍi* and so forth" (*krauḍyādibhyaḥ*), and because there is no fault even in the view that [the suffix] is added directly to these bases. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of those whose penultimate syllable is not heavy" (*agurūpottamārtha*) and so on: therein, the words beginning with *krauḍi* up to, but not including, *caupayata*, end in *iñ*; the words beginning with *caupayata* up to, but not including, *saudhātaki*, end in *aṇ*; and the word *saudhātaki* ends in *iñ* according to the rule "after *sudhātṛ*, [the suffix] *akaṅ* also [is applied]" (*sudhāturakaṅ ca*). [The term] "young woman" (*yuvati*) refers to a female charioteer (*sūtā*).

The word *sūta* produces the suffix *ṣyaṅ* when the meaning to be expressed is a young woman who has attained puberty—*sūtyā*; otherwise, from this verbal noun, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs—*sūtā*; but when it denotes a caste (*jāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs—*sūtī*. Regarding *bhoja* as a Kṣatriya: this is an exception to the *ṅīṣ* prescribed for castes—the form is *bhojyā*; however, from the verbal noun "one who causes to enjoy," only *ṭāp* occurs—*bhojā*, because she causes [others] to enjoy. Those that follow end in *iñ*. The word *gaukakṣya* ends in *yañ* from the *garga*-class.
The patronymic suffixes *cha* and *aṇ* are optionally applied after the names Daivayajñi, Śaucivṛkṣi, Sātyamugri, and Kāṇṭheviddhi.

The gods are to be worshipped by him through sacrifice; this is his *devayajña* (sacrifice to the gods). A tree that is pure is his *śucivṛkṣa* (pure tree). Truth is fierce for him; thus he is *satyamugra*. Due to irregular grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), the qualifier is placed first and the suffix *mum* is added. "Pierced in the throat" means either "pierced in his throat" or "his throat is pierced"; according to the rule *amūrddhamastakāt*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. Others read *kāṇḍeviddhibhyaḥ*; "pierced by a shaft" (*kāṇḍena viddhaḥ*) forms a compound by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, and due to irregular derivation, the word *kāṇḍa* takes the vowel *e*. All [these names] end in the suffix *iñ*.
When [the suffixes] capable [of expressing the sense of the agent] follow, the first case ending may optionally be used.

It is declared here that each individual word possesses the *svarita* accent, and not that the entire group as a whole has one; thus he says, "all three. Furthermore, the purpose here is so that when one [word] is excluded, another might not also be excluded. He clarifies this very point by saying, "and [the rule] 'of those that are semantically connected' (*samarthānām*)," and that this [rule] extends up to the limit of *svārthika* suffixes.

Svārthika suffixes are those applied for the sake of the base itself (*svasyāḥ prakṛteḥ arthe bhavāḥ*). This includes *adhyātma* and so forth; however, due to the usage of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), there is an absence of the application of suffixes such as *dvārādi*. Yet, because the word *sva* is included among the *dvārādi* group, there is an occasion [for its inclusion]. For in that context, the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) applies; since the *dvārādi* words serve as qualifiers for the initial vowel (*ādyaj*), as in: "this belongs to the gatekeeper (*dvārapāla*)," hence *dauvārapāla*. This continues up to the rule "before the case-endings, [the suffix *ṭāp* etc. after words beginning with *prāc*. (*prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ*).

From that point onward, indeed, suffixes with the same meaning as the base (*svārthika*) are prescribed. But what is the reason that this [rule] does not apply to those *svārthika* suffixes? To this he says: "In the case of *svārthika* suffixes," and so forth. In that context, "of those that are capable" (*samarthānām*) means "of those whose meanings are connected" (*sambaddhārthānām*). In that regard, there is a connection of meaning in the sentence; for in that case, "capacity" (*sāmarthyam*) is "mutual expectancy" (*vyapekṣā*). Expectancy is "desire" (*ākāṅkṣā*), and mutual expectancy is "reciprocal dependence. When these—expectancy, proximity, and compatibility—are present, the relationship [between words] is characterized by this [mutual expectancy].

In a *vṛtti* (compound), there is the quality of having a unified meaning (*saṃsṛṣṭārthatā*). For in that case, semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) is indeed the capacity (*sāmarthya*). Indeed, in a *vṛtti*, subordinate words (*upasarjana*) subordinated their own meanings and become directed toward the primary meaning; for example, in "the cowherd on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ gopaḥ*), the word "Gaṅgā" denotes the bank by subordinating itself. Likewise, in "Aupagava" (*aupagavaḥ*), the word "Upagu" denotes the offspring by subordinating its own meaning. For this very reason, in the expression "the wealthy Aupagava" (*ṛddhasyaupagavaḥ*), the quality of being wealthy does not function as an adjective qualifying Upagu.

For the connection with a qualifier occurs precisely where a word finds its final semantic rest. If, as in a sentence, a compound (vṛtti) were to find its final rest in its own primary meaning alone, then it would likewise be connected with qualifiers; indeed, even principal words express their own meanings only as qualified by their subordinate elements.

If, however, as in the case of a sentence, even in a compound (*vṛtti*) the principal words were to express only their own individual meanings, then—just as in the expression "Upagu’s offspring is Devadatta, who is auspicious" (*aupagor apatyaṃ devadattaḥ kalyāṇaśca*), where the meaning of "offspring" is connected with both [Devadatta and auspiciousness]—one would likewise expect the statement "the descendant of Upagu is auspicious" (*aupagavaḥ kalyāṇaśca*). But this is not the case. Therefore, that particular kind of relationship which, by its presence, results in this distinction is *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning).

Furthermore, in the case of secondary suffixes (*svārthika*), no distinct meaning other than that of the base word (*prakṛti*) is possible, for which a different word would need to be employed to convey it, such that there could be a capacity (*sāmarthya*) [for composition] with it. By this, the point regarding "priority" (*prāthamya*) is explained. Therefore, since both capacity and priority are absent in secondary suffixes due to the lack of dependence on a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), it is established that these [rules] have no application therein. As for the "option" (*vikalpa*) mentioned there, it is not fixed; it occurs in some cases. This will be stated in the rule concerning *aṣaḍakṣa* and so forth.

In this context, the qualifier "from the first" (*prathamāt*) is taken as referring to the sentence within the technical rule (*śāstravākya*), and not to the analytical explanatory sentence (*vigrahavākya*); for the latter is unrestricted. Since usage in a sentence is unrestricted, it is possible for everything to be "first. Consequently, sometimes the suffix might occur after a word denoting the offspring itself, and sometimes after a word denoting that which possesses the offspring. This alternative would be obtainable even without the phrase "from the first," and thus that [phrase] would be redundant.

[Objection: But surely, the purpose [of the qualification] would be that in a given sentence, [the operation] should occur from that which is uttered first therein, and not from that which is uttered last? [Reply: That is not so; for there is no simultaneous employment of both the *vṛtti* (commentary) and the *vākya* (sentence). Consequently, since primacy within the sentence serves as the regulator, the employment of the *vṛtti* is not fixed; thus, the qualification "from the first" (*prathamāt*) would be entirely redundant. Therefore, he states—beginning with "the definitional sentences" (*lakṣaṇavākyāni*)—that it is precisely the primacy found within the scriptural sentences that serves as the regulator.

The genitive case in *samarthānām* is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Consequently, since selection pertains to members of the same class, the suffix occurs after the first [word] among those that are *samartha*. While it would have been sufficient to say "after the first *samartha* word" (*samarthāt prathamāt*), the expression "after the first among those that are *samartha*" (*samarthānām prathamāt*) is intended to demonstrate that even the principal member (*pradhānapada*) enters into a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) with the subordinate member (*upasarjanapada*). Otherwise, as in the case of a sentence, one might suspect that even within a compound (*vṛtti*), the principal member could be connected with something else.

If, then, the suffix occurs after that which is uttered first in the defining rule (*lakṣaṇavākya*), this being the case, in examples such as *tasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of him"), the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) would be what is designated first; therefore, the suffix should arise from that [pronoun] alone, and not from *upagu* and so forth, for the latter is not designated first in the defining rule. To this he says: *tasyeti*. The phrase "the general," etc., is a definition by way of specification; the meaning is that it is a specification of a particular instance.

For in expressions such as "tasmātpatyam" (the offspring of him), it is precisely the specific individuals that are intended to be designated; however, if all of them were to be mentioned individually, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). If only one were mentioned, [the rule] would not apply to other unspecified individuals, as in the case of "purified by water" (*adbhiḥ saṃskṛtam*) and so forth. Therefore, the phrase "of him" (*tasya*) and so on is employed as a comprehensive indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all of them—meaning "of him," such as Upagu and the others.

But it is not [the case] that [the suffix] functions as the agent itself; for, since the general statement "of him" (*tasya*)—lacking a specific context or other indicators—is not restricted to a particular [referent], it is impossible for it to provide the assistance known as the exclusion of other related entities by specifying a particular related entity with respect to the offspring.

The general sense of "relative" (*sambandhi*) for the word *apatya* (descendant) is already understood precisely because it is a relative term; therefore, the suffix is not applied to that which is directly mentioned first in the rule (*sūtra*) as denoting a general category. And that from which the suffix is applied is not directly mentioned first in the rule. Thus, out of necessity, the priority belonging to the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is understood to apply to the things indicated (*upalakṣya*). As it has been said: "The priority pertaining to that [indicator] is understood to belong to the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*)."

"Kambalopagoh," and so forth. The point is that just as the word *apatya* (offspring) may be connected with either the preceding or the following term as desired, so too might the suffix *aṇ* be considered [to function in such a way]. Furthermore, when this suffix is present, the entire compound—even if it is semantically empty—would receive the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Consequently, even in the absence of number (such as singularity), case endings (*svādayaḥ*) would arise from it, just as they do from indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Is it not the case that there is no such contingency here, since the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is understood when there is an expectation for a related term (*sambandhin*) as heard in the rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*)? This is not so; for there is no utterance of a case-ending in the definitional statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), because a general relation intended to convey a connection cannot itself be a [further] relation. What then? It is for the purpose of prescribing a suffix after a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*).

Even so, might there not be a connection by way of indicating a specific distinction? Even in that case, [the suffix] would indeed arise even from a dependent form, as in "the offspring of Upagu the wealthy" (*ṛddhasyopagorapatyam*). In that case, will the determination be made by the technical rule regarding semantic capacity (*samartha-paribhāṣā*)? It would indeed be so, provided that it were established prior to this very sūtra that "secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) follow that which ends in a *sup* [case-ending]. However, here, because the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a primary nominal base" (*ṅyāpprātipadika*) applies, the secondary suffixes would arise only from that [nominal stem], since it functions in the sense of the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and other case-endings.

However, since the comprehension of this relationship depends upon the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) arise from the nominal stem (*subanta*) alone; and this being the case, there is no undesirable consequence of [the stem] being treated as a word (*pada*). For instance, in examples such as *rājanye* or *vārtraghne*, the designation of "word" (*padasaṃjñā*)—which would otherwise apply based on the elided case-ending—is superseded by the designation of "nominal base" (*bhasaṃjñā*) that has arisen [by rule], because of the governing principle of "one designation takes precedence" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*). On the other hand, in cases such as *rājatvam* or *rājatā*, even when the suffix arises from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the designation of "word" does indeed occur by the rule *svādiṣu*.

But surely there is a fault when the *taddhita* suffix is elided (*luk*) before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [case ending], as in the case of "those who study what was taught by Kāśyapa"—where, according to the rules "after the sages Kāśyapa and Kauśika, the suffix *ṇini* is applied" and "the *chandas* and *brāhmaṇa* texts," that suffix would be subject to elision.

Regarding the rule "one who studies that or knows that" (*tadadhīte tadveda*), when the suffix *aṇ* derived from the word *kāśyapin*—which ends in the second case—is elided by the rule for elision after what is taught (*prokta-luk*), although there is no fault in forms such as *kāśyapinaḥ* because the designation *pada* (word) subverts the designation *bha* even though the latter is caused by the elided case-ending; nevertheless, in forms such as *kāśyapanau* and *kāśyapinaḥ* where a *sarvanāmasthāna* (nominal ending) follows, since the designation *bha* does not apply, the designation *pada* would occur by relying on the internally situated (*antarvatini*) elided case-ending.

And there is no prohibition [of the term *pada*] by the rule "not in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. What is the reason? The prohibition applies only to that application which arises by the rule "in the case of *svādi* suffixes" (*svādiṣu*). If that is so, then the word "not in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*" (*asarvanāmasthāne*) is split [into two separate rules], and a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is adopted. By the force of that, the principle "a rule applies only to what immediately precedes" (*anantarasya vidhir vā*) is not relied upon. Consequently, when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows, whatever designation of *pada* belongs to the preceding portion—whether it be that derived from "in the case of *svādi* suffixes" or that derived from "ending in a *sup* suffix" (*subanta*)—all of that will be prohibited.

If this were so, then even in cases such as *rājā daṇḍī* (the king with a staff), the designation *sā* would not occur; for from the rule *yacchibham*, the term *aci* is required in the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, and by that, the designation *pada* would be prohibited only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). However, there is no fault, because [the designation *pada*] will apply either by the rule *sau halādau* or by the rule *svādiṣu* as "ending in a *sup*. Thus, it is established that when this statement exists, there is no defect whatsoever regarding the formation of *taddhita* suffixes from a word ending in a *sup*.

For this very reason, in examples such as *pūrvāhṇetarām* and *pūrvāhṇetamām*, the non-elision (*aluk*) will be prescribed by the rule *ghakālataneṣu*. Now, one might object: even if this [non-elision] exists, since it does not operate within *svārthika* suffixes, how can the suffix *tarap* follow a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*)? To this we reply: such is indeed the sequence of meanings here, namely that first there is a connection with the case-suffix, and afterwards with the *tarap*. For it has been stated: "In the case of words expressing affection, contempt, and so forth, that [suffix] proceeds after the word has already ended in a case-suffix. And by adopting this view, the prescription of non-elision also becomes logically consistent.

If, however, that very rule prescribing the *aluk* (non-elision) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*), then in examples such as *tasyāpatyam*, the intention does not lie merely in the sense of the case-ending; rather, it is intended to indicate only those forms ending in case-endings such as the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Since the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "feminine suffixes (*ṅī*), *āp*-ending stems, and nominal stems (*prātipadika*)" is utilized precisely as a qualifier for "vṛddha" and so forth, that being the case, the determination is established by the maxim of semantic competency (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) itself, because it is a rule dependent on words (*padavidhi*). Furthermore, due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*), there will be no application where there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*); thus, there is no need for an explicit statement regarding semantic competency.

Then this is the purpose: so that [the rule] may apply to that which is capable of expressing the intended meaning. What, then, is that? It is the word whose sequence of phonemes has been established—such as *sautthitiḥ* and *vaikṣamāṇiḥ*. Here, once the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrghatva*) has taken place, the suffix occurs; it does not occur at the stage when it is *su-utthita* and *vi-īkṣamāṇa*. If it were to occur then, the forms would have to be *sāvutthitiḥ* and *vāyīkṣamāṇiḥ*, because of the application of the rule "an operation concerning a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a suffix (*āṅga*)," which would result in the occurrence of *vṛddhi*.

But surely, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the suffix will apply after the phonemic operations have been performed? If that is so, then by making this statement regarding "samartha" (semantic compatibility), he indicates this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "The followers of Pāṇini do not [allow the application of] *vyūha* (grammatical operations) once they have been performed," meaning that even an operation already established by the rules is set aside.

"Vyūha" refers to the operation of a grammatical rule (*śāstrakārya*). Those who, even though such an operation has been reached because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), do not perform it—thinking that a subsequent destruction of its cause (*nimittavighāta*) will occur—are called "those who do not form the array" (*akṛtavyūha*); this is the meaning of being "Pāṇinian" in this sense. In the phrase "even when performed" (*kṛtam api*), the word "or" (*vā*) is to be supplied; the meaning is that they even set aside a grammatical operation that has already been performed when the absence of its cause is about to arise. By this, forms such as *papuṣaḥ* are established.

In this case, although the augment *iṭ* was previously applied, it is nullified by virtue of this paribhāṣā because it is internal (*antaraṅga*); or rather, it is not applied at all beforehand. Consequently, when the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) has taken place before the suffix *śas*, there is an absence of *iṭ* because the suffix begins with a consonant (*valādi*). "From that which ends in the nominative" means: from a word such as *Devadatta*, which is indicated in the nominative case and denotes a specific descendant.
