Otherwise, just as in the rule "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*), where a suffix occurs in the sense of the genitive after a word ending in the nominative—as in *aindraḥ sthālīpākaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake for Indra")—so too would it happen here: *daivadattir upaguḥ* ("Upagu is the descendant of Devadatta").

The question "What is the purpose of including the word *vā*? is raised because one might argue that the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between a derivative formation (*vṛtti*) and a sentence (*vākya*) will not occur simply due to a difference in meaning—namely, the distinction between mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) and the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). [The answer is: "So that the sentence-form may also occur. For example, the word *gāvī* is set aside by the word *go*, even though the feminine gender is understood in both; likewise here, when it is said "bring the son of Upagu" (*aupagavam ānaya*), the very same person who is brought when it is said "bring the offspring of Upagu" (*upagor apatyam ānaya*) is the one intended. Thus, the idea is that the sentence would be sublated by the derivative formation due to a difference in the primary meaning. If this were so, then the compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*) would be sublated by the secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*).

The principle is: "Where there is both a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*), as well as an option (*vibhāṣā*), the general rule does not apply once the matter has been resolved by the exception. Thus, in cases such as *rājānantaraḥ* ("one immediately following a king"), the formation of a compound (*samāsavṛtti*), which would otherwise have scope, is superseded by the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhitavṛtti*). The underlying idea is that, for example, the suffix *aṇ* in *dākṣiḥ* is superseded by the suffix *iñ*. The phrase "this too" means that the grammatical operation known as the formation of a compound is likewise superseded.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form derivatives] from words beginning with *prāgdīvya*.

He will say, "one plays with that. If this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of that [term], it ought to be stated as *prāgdīvyateḥ*; why then is it indicated as *prāgdīvyataḥ*? To this he replies: "it is a part of that. For it is possible to imitate a part separately, even when that part has become subordinate to a whole—as in the case of the expression *asyavāmīyam*. This is the intended meaning.

If there were only the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "aṇ," as in the case of [the rule for] *pratyaya*, then the *aṇ* suffix—which has been interrupted by the section on exceptions (*apavāda*) such as "ata iñ"—would not apply to meanings such as those expressed in "tena raktaṃ rāgāt" (colored by that). Therefore, the phrase "prāgdīvyataḥ" (before the word *dīvyat*) is stated in order to indicate the extent of the governing rule. Regarding the phrase "in all three views," and so forth:

But surely, even under the view that [the suffix] is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading), since it applies to every individual rule (*pratiyogam*), the suffix *iñ* would apply, and thus *aṇ*—as in the case of *aṇvā*—would also follow. Even under the view that it is a *paribhāṣā* (a general metarule), since *aṇ* is prescribed after all those bases that fall under the category of *prāgdīvyatīya*, why would it not occur in the domain of an exception (*apavāda*)? Likewise, under the view that it is a *vidhi* (an original injunction), there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) everywhere? The answer is this: by the fact that he begins the rule "pīlāyā vā" ("after *pīlā*, optionally"), he indicates (*jñāpayati*) that *aṇ* does not occur in the domain of an exception.

Otherwise, the suffix *ḍhak* would be established by the rule "dvaya-caḥ," and thus the prescription of *aṇ* by this [rule] would be purposeless. Furthermore, the statement of an option in the rule "udaśvito 'nyatarasyām" is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this same meaning.

We, however, say this: the term *prāgdīvyataḥ* is not an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the word *dīvyat*, which is a portion of the word *dīvyati*; rather, its meaning is being indicated—namely, "prior to the meaning of *dīvyat*. In that context, when the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is applied to the root *div*, the suffix *śatṛ* is substituted for *laṭ* because it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *arthāt*, even though *arthāt* is not actually employed in the text and is not in the nominative case, since its meaning is already understood by that term.

In this context, because the limit (*avadhi*) itself constitutes the meaning, those things which possess the limit (*avadhimant*) are also understood as being the very meanings [of the suffix]; for the relationship between a limit and that which possesses the limit is more commonly established when they share the same class of objects. Consequently, in all three of these views, the operation of this [suffix] applies only to those meanings which occur prior to the word *dīvya*. In that regard, since a specific base (*prakṛti*) gives rise to an exception (*apavāda*) when the meaning is the same, it is established that the desired result is achieved by the exception setting aside the general rule (*aṇ*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *aśvapati* and others. 4.1.84.

Regarding the phrase *prāgdīvyatīyeṣu*: from the avyayībhāva compound *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā*, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārthe*) by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*. The elision of the *ṭi*-portion (the final vowel and following consonant) does not occur because of the restriction in the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre* ("for indeclinables, [elision occurs] only before a *bha*-suffix"), as this is included in the list of exceptions under *luṅmukhasvaropacārāḥ*. For this very reason, the suffix *tayaP* also does not apply after an indeclinable, due to the restriction in the rule *amehakvatasitrebhyaḥ*. Since the word *gaṇapati* is not included in the list [of words taking the suffix *cha*], the form *gāṇapatyaḥ mantraḥ* is an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). By this, the case of *kṣaitrapatya* is also explained.
The injunction "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Kṣetrapati," however, is Vedic; "they consume the *kṣaitrapatya*," for the seers act according to the Vedas.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [a word ending in] *ditya*, *āditya*, or a word having *āditya* as its final member.

He states "after a word ending in *pati* and having *uttarapada* as its subsequent member" (*patyuttarapadāt*) because, when a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the word *uttarapada*, a *dvandva* follows subsequently; it is not that a *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *uttarapada* as part of a *dvandva*. This [interpretation] is obtained either through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) or from the commentary. However, the mention of *aditi* would be for the purpose of including that which has it as its subsequent member; for a word ending in *aditi* does not become a word ending in *diti*. It is not stated as "after a word ending in *pati*" (*patyantāt*), so that [the rule] may not apply to a word preceded by *bahu*.

Regarding the phrase *vāḍamatipitṛmatām*: the inclusion of the words *mati* and *pitṛmat* in [the list beginning with] *kurū* is so that the suffix *ṇya* may apply even in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*) when the sense is "offspring" (*apatya*). By this rule, however, the application of *ṇya* occurs in Vedic (*chandas*) after all [stems] ending in *prāgdīvyatīya* suffixes. Some read the word *vāk* in that very same [list], whereby the usage "these calves are to be spoken of (*vācyāḥ*)" is justified. Regarding *yamācca*: the meaning is that the word *yama* should also be recited in the Sūtra. Regarding *pṛthivyā ñāñau*: since there is a distinction for feminine forms in the case of the suffixes *ña* and *añ*, he says: *pāthivā*, *pārthivī*.

Regarding the word *sthāman*: this is a term denoting strength (*bala*). Although that [word] alone has no connection with a descendant (*apatya*), its connection with [patronymic suffixes such as] *jātādi* is certainly possible. Furthermore, this rule applies to all [suffixes] beginning with *prāgdīvyatīya*. Therefore, based on the example given in the Bhāṣya, "aśvatthāma," there is here an application of the rule for a compound ending in that [word] (*tadantavidhi*). As for "aśvatthāma": in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose strength (*sthāma*) is like that of a horse (*aśva*)," the vowel *a* undergoes *ṭilopa* (elision of the final phoneme), and by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is changed to *t*.

Regarding the rule *lomno'patye bahuṣu*: since this [word *loman*] is listed among the *bāhv-ādi* group, the suffix *iñ* would otherwise apply; however, the vowel *a* is substituted when the descendant is plural. Because the word *loman* alone cannot be connected with the sense of "descendant," the rule of "reference to that which ends in [the stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies by virtue of the requirement of meaning. Thus, we have *uḍulomāḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: "one whose body hairs (*lomāni*) are like stars (*uḍūni*)" or "one whose body hairs are like arrows (*śarāḥ*)."

But surely, even when the suffix *iñ* is applied according to the rule for *bāhu-* and so on, that suffix is elided by the rule "when [a stem] has more than two syllables" (*bahvacaḥ*). Since the *iñ* is produced from a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the technical designation "word" (*pada*) applies by the rule of "characterized by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), namely "that which ends in a case-suffix is a word. Thus, the elision of the *n* is established? Granted, this may be established; however, in cases such as *uḍulomebhyaḥ*, because the elision of the *n* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) for the application of case-suffix rules, the replacement with *ais* and so forth would not occur. Furthermore, the elision of the *iñ* is not established except in the case of the lineages of the Easterners (*prācya*) and the Bharatas. Moreover, there is no designation of "word" (*pada*) here, due to the prohibition "not before a case-ending other than a sarvanāmasthāna."

And just as that prohibition applies even to the technical designation of "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*)—namely, the term *subanta*—which is otherwise obtained by the characteristic of being a condition (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), so it has been stated previously.

"Everywhere" means not only in the sense of *apatya* (descendant), but also in the sense of *prāgdīvyatīya* (relating to what precedes the suffix *dīvya*) and elsewhere; thus, from *gavā carati*, we also get *gavya*. Regarding *gorūpyam*: by the rules "after words denoting cause or a human being, *rūpya* is optionally used" and "also *mayaṭ*," the suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* are applied. Regarding "the *ṇya*-class [suffixes]": according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, the *ṇya*-class suffixes are exceptions (*apavāda*) specifically to *aṇ*; however, since they would be superseded by *ḍhak* and other suffixes—which are exceptions to *am*—due to their higher status in the order of application, the Vārttika is commenced to establish them.

That which has a specific object—characterized by offspring and the like—as its cause is "that which has a specific object as its characteristic" (*arthaviśeṣalakṣaṇa*). However, that [suffix] characterized by a general object—which is the exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of "this belongs to him"—occurs because it is subsequent [in the rules]. For example, from *uṣṭrapati* (name of a leaf), the form *auṣṭrapata* is derived; by the rule "*tatra adhvar-yupariṣadaś ca*" [Pāṇini 4.3.120], the suffix *añ* occurs, but not the suffix *ṇya*. In the case of *diter apatyam* ("the offspring of Diti"), the suffix *ḍhak* does not occur by the rule "*itaścāniñaḥ*" [Pāṇini 4.1.122]; rather, it occurs only in cases such as *ḍauleya*. In the case of *vānaspatyam*, the suffix *ṭhak* characterized by the rule for non-sentient objects (*acittāt*) does not occur; it occurs only in cases such as *āpūpika*.

"How is *daiteya* [formed]?"—to this he says, "In that case, here... Since it is already understood [from the context], it is not explicitly stated. The meaning is: if the suffixes beginning with *ṇya* (i.e., *ṇya*, *ṇyaṅ*, etc. occur by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) to the exception to *aṇ* based on specific meanings, then how is *daiteya* established? [The answer begins: "From the word *diti*," and so forth. But surely, according to the rule "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included," the suffix *ṇya* itself would apply even after a form ending in *ṅīṣ* (i.e., *diti* + *ṅīṣ* = *ditī*)? To this he says: "And the paribhāṣā regarding that which is qualified by gender is non-eternal. Others, however, maintain that *daiteya* is incorrect because it is not mentioned in either the Bhāṣya or the Vārttika.
The suffix *añ* is applied after [words ending in] *utsa* and others.

"And of their exceptions" (*tadapavādānām*): this refers to [the suffixes] *iñ* and so forth. Regarding the example *baṣkayāsaḥ*: the word *baṣkaya* produces the suffix *añ*, provided that it is not in composition (*ase*), meaning "not in a compound. This is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) of the ancient teachers; thus, [the derivative form is] *bāṣkayaḥ*. Why does it say "not in composition" (*asa*)? Consider *gobaṣkayiḥ*. [Objection: Since there is a prohibition against the application of a rule to a base ending in a specific element when that base is itself a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) accompanied by a suffix, this [suffix] will not apply here anyway. [Response: It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). By this, it indicates that in this case, the rule of extension to what ends in such an element (*tadantavidhi*) does indeed apply.

What is established [by this]? The word *dhenu* is listed here; from that which ends in it, there is also [the formation]: "a collection of non-cows" (*adhenūnām samūhaḥ*) is *ādhenavam*. Regarding "a region named Udasthāna": when a region is to be expressed, the word *udasthāna* produces the suffix *añ*: a region is *audasthānaḥ*. When it is something other than a region, if someone is called Udasthāna by chance, his offspring is *audasthāniḥ*. Regarding "Pṛṣadaṃśa": when a portion (*aṃśa*) is to be expressed, the word *pṛṣat* produces the suffix *añ*: a portion is *pārṣataḥ*. When it is something other than a portion, it occurs with the suffix *aṇ*.

Regarding the statement "graiṣmī triṣṭubh": if one intends to express the full meaning that "Grīṣma is its deity," the general suffix *aṇ* applies by default; however, if one intends to express a specific derivative meaning such as "existing in the summer" (*grīṣme bhava*), then the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* is established. For there is no possibility of this suffix *añ* subverting the suffix *aṇ* used in the sense of a derivative (*śaiṣika*), because suffixes characterized by specific meanings are the ones subverted by suffixes such as *ṇya*. On the other hand, *ṛtvaṇ* is prescribed for the general remainder (*śeṣamātra*) and is not characterized by a specific meaning; furthermore, it is obtained through a different stage of application.

How so? [The suffix] *añ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *aṇ* [prescribed by Pāṇini 4.3.16], and *tsa* is likewise an exception to *ṛtvaṇ*. Here, "Vedic" (*chandas*) is understood as meter (*vṛtta*), that is, that which has specific varieties such as *triṣṭubh* and so forth. It does not mean the Veda itself. Therefore, even in the domain of the Veda, when a meter is to be expressed, because *añ* is prohibited, only *aṇ* occurs—thus, for example, *graiṣmī triṣṭubh*.

[The rule: *strī-puṃsābhyāṃ nañ-snañau bhavanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.87). [This means that the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are applied after the words *strī* and *puṃs* respectively, in the sense of "being" (*bhavana*).]

Regarding the phrase "from the word *strī*, from the word *pūm*, and from the word *puṃs*": there is no inclusion of the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth prescribed under the heading of *strī* (feminine), nor of the suffixes prescribed under the heading of "the suffix *gha* [is used] when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed in the masculine" (*puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ*), because the words *strī* and *puṃs* themselves are not marked with the *svarita* accent. Nor is there an inclusion of the meanings "female" and "male," because of the rule stating "the form itself [is the meaning] of a word" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*). Thus, the form is *pauṃsnam*.

By the rule "there is elision of a final conjunct," the *s* of the word *puṃs* is elided; for when that [elision] is to be performed, because the *anusvāra* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *s* constitutes a final conjunct. For this very reason, due to the contingency of the elision of a final conjunct, *nañ* alone is not prescribed by both [the preceding and following rules]. If one were to argue: "Let there be no *nañ*, and let there be no *snañ*; let only *añ* be the subject at hand, and let it be stated simply as 'let *nuk* be added after *strī* and *puṃs*'; in that case, the long vowel *ī* in the forms *straiṇī* and *pausnī*—derived from *añ*—would also be established. This suspicion is not to be entertained.

Regarding *straiṇāḥ* and *pauṃsnāḥ*, the rule "yañañośca" would require the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes when there is plurality. Furthermore, in the case of *straiṇānāṃ saṅghaḥ*, the rule "saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣvañyañiñām" would require the suffix *aṇ*. This is not a fault; for in both cases, the word "gotra" (lineage) is understood from the context. Moreover, what is grasped here is the worldly sense of "gotra," and in common usage, "gotra" refers to the progeny of sages (*ṛṣiprajana*). Now, even a female sage does not possess a generic property that can be denoted by a masculine term.

If so, does the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) not apply by the rule "nastaddhite"? [Response: The status of the base (*prakṛtibhāva*) will apply by the rule "prakṛtyaikāc," as the phrase "in the case of iṣṭhan, īyasun, and īyas" is understood to carry over there. If that is the case, then by the force of the prescription of *nuk*, the elision of the *ṭi* will not occur? [Objection: That rule for which the teaching [of a particular form] would otherwise be purposeless is sublated; however, that which is merely the cause for another rule is not sublated. In this regard, the prescription of *nuk* would indeed be for the sake of the elision of the *ṭi*.

The word *strī* is also the cause for the elision of *nu*; otherwise, because it is subsequent to the elision of *ya* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*), there would be a *vṛddhi* [vowel] substitution—as in *śrāyam haviḥ*, where *śrī* is the deity (*śrīr devatā asya*). Therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original formulation. Regarding the phrase "and with reference to the rule": this means that the rule *strī-puṃsābhyām* does not apply in the sense of the suffix *vat*, and this is the nature of the indication; it does not mean, however, that the suffix *snañ* does not apply in the sense of *vat*. How then are the forms *strītvam*, *strītā*, *puṃstvam*, and *puṃstā* derived? The resolution for this will be found under the rule *ā ca tvāt*.
In a *dvigu* compound, there is elision of the suffix when it does not denote a descendant.

The phrase "of the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [is used] because if the ablative (*pañcamī*) were understood as characterized by immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then the suffix *aṇ*—by the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that")—would also apply in the case of *pāñcakapāla*, as in *pañcakapālasya puroḍāśasyedam*. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, if the genitive were also used in connection with immediate succession, the same fault would occur as in the case of the ablative; therefore, considering that recourse to the genitive would be purposeless, he says: "that which is related to the *dvigu* compound by way of being its cause."

That *taddhita* suffix for whose meaning a *dvigu* compound is prescribed by the rule "in the sense of a *taddhita* [suffix] or when it is the final member of a compound" is the relevant cause (*nimitta*). For example, in *pañcakapāla*: when the sense expressed by the rule "food items prepared [by baking]" is intended, a *dvigu* is formed; then the feminine suffix *ām* is applied, and its elision (*luk*) occurs. In *dviveda*: when the sense expressed by the rule "one who studies that or knows that" is intended, a *dvigu* is formed.

*Dvaidevadattiḥ* means "the offspring of two Devadattas. According to the rule *ata iñ*, "offspring" (*apatyam*) refers to one who does not fall away [from the lineage]. Thus, this term is used for someone whose father or ancestors have two individuals named Devadatta; or, he may be the adopted son of one and the biological son of another. The phrase "because of the recognition of the cause of the *dvigu*" means because of the application of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix that is caused by a *dvigu* compound. In the case of *pañcakapālasyedam* ("this belongs to the five-pot-sherd"), the suffix that first arose in the sense of "prepared therein" (*saṃskṛta*) is itself the cause of the *dvigu*; it is not the second suffix. Therefore, there is no elision of that [first suffix]. Alternatively, etc. [the rest follows].

Previously, it was explained by relying on a grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the suffix brought forward by the rule "elision" (*lug*) and the term "of a *dvigu*" (*dvigoḥ*); now, however, there is the distinction that they are co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But how is it that elision is obtained for the *dvigu* alone? To this he says: "The term 'of a *dvigu*' (*dvigoḥ*) is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*)."

Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu ca" (But surely...): the technical terms *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* have been prescribed for the non-appearance of suffixes (*pratyayādarśana*). Consequently, the expression "dvigor luk" (the elision of the suffix after a *dvigu* compound) is not at all consistent; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the passage beginning with "upacāreṇa tu" (But by metaphorical transfer...): "metaphorical transfer" (*upacāra*) is the attribution of a form to what does not possess it; "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is the employment of a word for something other than its primary referent. Thus, the meaning is: "by that indication which is based on the cause of metaphorical transfer. Others, however, state that the phrase "by metaphorical transfer" (*upacāreṇa*) is itself an explanation of the term "by indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*).

When a *taddhita* derivative ending in *-dvigu* is intended by the intellect to be expressed as having the form of a *dvigu* compound, that is *lakṣaṇā*, which is indeed a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*). The basis for this metaphorical transfer is its being caused by a *dvigu*. For there is indeed a metaphorical transfer of the effect onto the cause—as in the expression "clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*). [The opponent asks: "In that case, even that which is caused by a *dvigu*... and so forth.

Even with respect to an effect, usage [of a term] as if it were its cause is observed, as for example: "ancient karma is being experienced. Consequently, in the case of a *dvigu* compound, that which is the cause of a suffix is intended by the word "quality" (*guṇa*) through the metaphorical attribution of a quality—that is, the property which serves as the basis for the metaphorical usage. The "attribution of a quality" (*guṇakalpanā*) is the conceptualization based on that [property], and not the cognition consisting of the metaphorical usage itself. Why, then, is it not called a *dvigu* by means of that [cognition]? The meaning is: it certainly deserves such a designation. He provides the rebuttal: "not of that... (*na tasya*).

For in that case, although the state of being a *dvigu* is present, it is not utilized for the production of the suffix; for this [suffix] is not prescribed by the rule "after a *dvigu*" (*dvigoḥ*), but rather by the rule "after a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*). "The other," however, refers to the suffix whose elision (*luk*) has been shown. "The cause of the state of being a *dvigu* itself": for the compound is prescribed for the sake of that [meaning], and the designation *dvigu* belongs to that very [compound]; therefore, it is the cause of the state of being a *dvigu* itself.

"If this is so," and so forth. This objection applies to both positions. For here, the *taddhita* suffix is neither connected as the cause (*nimitta*) of the *dvigu* compound, nor is it fit to be designated as such through metaphorical usage because it is the cause of the *dvigu*. The meaning of the objection is that once the *dvigu* has been formed in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), the *taddhita* suffix is subsequently produced; yet that [suffix] does not serve as the cause for the *dvigu*. He refutes this: "In this case, the *taddhita* suffix is not produced at all. The underlying intention is that this is because there is no such linguistic expression (*anabhidhāna*).

If [the suffix] does not arise, how is the formation of the form *pañcakapāla* established in this sense? Therefore, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) must indeed arise here, and its elision (*luk*) must be prescribed. To this he says: "For there is a threefold designation" (*traiśabdyaṃ hi*). A "threefold designation" (*traiśabdya*) consists of exactly three words, such as *cāturvarṇya* and others. For in this case, we must establish a threefold designation; and since that is accomplished even without the arising of a secondary derivative from the word *pañcakapālī*, the secondary derivative does not arise from it.

He shows those same three words: "in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu*). Regarding the two words: the *dvigu* compound formed in the sense of a collective aggregate and that formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—both of these have the same meaning. Of these two, the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed with the former. A restriction should be understood here: the analysis occurs only [with the first], not the production of the secondary derivative; because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*). From the other, namely *pañcakapāla*, the derivative is produced.

This is called the "sheep-ewe" maxim (*avyavikanyāya*). For example, in the case of *aver māṃsam* ("the meat of a sheep"), the analysis (*vigraha*) is indeed by means of the word *avi*, yet the suffix is produced from the word *avika*, and the analysis is *avikasya māṃsam* ("the meat of an *avika*"). And that [rule regarding the suffix] is one where the option is fixed (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). By adopting this principle, the elision (*luk*) does not occur in cases such as *traividyaḥ*, *pāñcanadam*, and *ṣāṭkulam*. Alternatively—*trividyā* is a science consisting of three parts (following the *śākapārthiva* class of compounds); one who studies that is a *traividyaḥ*. Since the status of being a "science" (*vidyātva*) is intended for the whole aggregate consisting of the three sciences, there is no difference in meaning.

The collection of five rivers is *pañcanadam*; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *nadībhiśca*. By the rule *godāvaryāśca nadyāśca*, the suffix *ac* is added at the end of the compound, resulting in *pañcanada*. That which exists in the *pañcanada* [region] is *pāñcanada*. Alternatively, when there is an actual denotation, a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is indeed applied even to a collective *dvigu* compound. Thus, for example, one born among the families of the six primal sages is *ṣāṭkulaḥ*. Furthermore, by the logic of the words *ava* and *avi*, the analysis is simply: "he studies three sciences," or "that which exists in five rivers," or "that which exists in six families"; here there is neither a *dvigu* nor a secondary derivative suffix.
There is no elision [of the final vowel] of a *gotra* [patronymic] before a vowel-initial suffix.

Because elision (*luk*) is prescribed both previously and subsequently, the negative particle (*nañ*) is understood here [in the rule *yaskādibhyo gotre*] by implication. However, the displacement of this section [to the end of the *gotra* rules] is for the sake of depending upon the rule *prāgdīvyataḥ*; furthermore, this is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Regarding the term *aci*: if this were a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*), a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would result in the application of the suffix *cha*: in forms such as *gārgīyāḥ* and *vātsīyāḥ*, the suffix *cha* would have to occur after the elision (*aluk*) of the *yañ* ending, and the suffix *cha* would have to occur because of the status of being "vṛddha" only when that elision has taken place.

But surely, *aluk* is prescribed only when [the suffix] *cha* follows; what then? It applies to any [suffix] beginning with *aj* (vowels) in general. In that case, *aluk* will occur only where such a [suffix] beginning with *aj* is possible. For example: *gargāṇāṃ chāttrāḥ* ("the students of the Gargas"). Here, by the rule *prāgdīvyato 'ṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Then, by the rule *yañañośca*, which prescribes *luk* (elision) when these suffixes follow, *luk* would have been obtained; however, by the prohibition of that *luk*, the form *gargāḥ* is established. Even if *luk* were present or absent here, there would be no difference, because the elision of *y* is prescribed by the rule *āpatyasya ca taddhite*.

In this case, however, the descendants of Atri are many; when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule "itaścāniñaḥ" and then elided by the rule "atribhṛgu...", the form "āttrīṇām" results. When the suffix *aṇ* is subsequently applied in the sense of "students of the Āttris," if the prohibition [of the elision] were not in force, the form would be "āttrā"; but because the prohibition exists, the form becomes "āttreyāḥ. This would indeed be so if the reappearance of an elided suffix were being prescribed; however, in this instance, by the statement "aluk," a prohibition of the elision (*luk*) is what is to be enjoined, and a prohibition applies to that which has already been obtained but has not yet come into effect.

Cessation can be effected; therefore, if [a suffix] beginning with *a* or *ā* were intended here, the application of *luk* must be admitted to have occurred even before [the application of the suffix]. Otherwise, because of the status of being "vṛddha," there would be only *cha*, and if *luk* has already applied, what would the prohibition accomplish? For if one were to say to someone who has already eaten, "Do not eat," what would that person achieve by it? Thus, in this case, once [the suffix] beginning with *a* or *ā* has applied, there must be *aluk*; and once *aluk* has applied, there must be [the suffix] beginning with *a* or *ā*.

Clearly, this is a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). It is established by contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*): the scope of *luk* (elision) is where the sense of "descendant" (*prāgdīvyatīya*) is not intended to be expressed—as in *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*; the scope of *cha* is—as in *śālīyaḥ*. In the case of *gargāya*, where both would apply, *cha* will occur because it is subsequent. In that situation, there is a prohibition of *luk* with respect to what follows. Furthermore, *luk* is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends merely on the plurality of the descendant, whereas *cha* is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on the sense of "descendant" as defined by the *prāgdīvyatīya* rules. And a contradiction between the internal and the external is improper.

If it is argued that this [rule] states that elision (*luk*) occurs after [a suffix] beginning with *aja* when followed by another [suffix], and that if the cause were present merely by that much, the elision would apply regardless of the mere plurality [of the referent], then the formulation of the prohibition would be purposeless. Therefore, it must be understood that as long as a suffix beginning with *aja* belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group has not been produced, the elision does not take effect. Consequently, when the suffix *cha* is applied because of the status of being a *vṛddha* [gotra], and the elision is prohibited, the desired form *gargīyaḥ* is established.

In the case of the locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), however, nothing requires effort to achieve [the desired result]. When there is a desire to express the meaning "the students of the Gargas" (*gargāṇāṃ chāttrāḥ*) and a suffix beginning with *aj* (such as *cha*) is intended, even though the elision (*luk*) has not yet occurred, it is prohibited by being situated in the intellect; because the [base] is considered "vṛddha," the suffix *cha* then applies. Therefore, relying on the locative of scope, he says: "when a suffix belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is in the state of being the scope. Regarding the form *khārapāyaṇīyāḥ*: these are the many descendants of Kharapa. The elision (*luk*) which would otherwise apply by the rules "*naḍādibhyaḥ phak*" and "*yaskādibhyo gotre*" is here prohibited.

*Kaubalam*, *bādaram*. The words *kubalī* and *badarī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (by the *gorādi* class) and are oxytone; from these, by the rule *anudāttādeśca*, the suffix *añ* is applied to denote a product (*vikāra*). Regarding the elision (*luk*) of that suffix which would otherwise apply by the rule *phale luk*, there is no prohibition when one intends to express the meaning "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*). Consequently, because the stems are not *vṛddha*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. [Thus we have] *gargarūpyam*. If there were no elision (*aluk*) here, it would be *sārgyarūpyam*. [And] *gārgīyam*: the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *tasmai hitam* (for its benefit), as it precedes the *krīta* group.

He demonstrates the result precisely by means of the locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*) with the words "of the *gotra*" and so forth. "Of the *gotra*" means "of the *gotra*-suffix. "In the case of many [words] that undergo elision" means "in the case of an elision prescribed for many meanings. "Upon the occurrence of a word ending in the plural" means "upon the occurrence—that is, the transition to another meaning—of that which exists as ending in the plural. "In the case of two or one" [is added].

The meaning is: "wherein there is a transfer (*saṃkrānti*) to another referent (*arthāntara*), while duality and singularity [of the original] still exist. And that transfer to another referent occurs when a suffix (*pratyaya*) denoting that [new referent] arises and its elision (*luk*) is performed; for when the secondary suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) is elided, the base (*prakṛti*) itself expresses that meaning, and thus the transfer takes place. As in the example: *bidānām*.

The descendants of Bida are many; by the rule *anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo’ñ*, the suffix *añ* is applied, resulting in *bidāḥ*. When there is the intention to express "the young descendant (*yuvan*) of those Bidas," or "the two young descendants," and the suffix *iñ* is intended by the rule *ataḥ*, this [present sūtra] prohibits the elision (*luk*) of the *gotra*-suffix *añ* which would otherwise have been required. Since the suffix *iñ* is then subject to elision by the rule *ṇyakṣattriyārṣa-*, the forms *baidaḥ* and *baidau* result. However, according to the view that the locative case in the previous rule is a governing locative (*parasaptamī*), elision would not apply here; for the condition of being "beginning with *aj*" (a vowel) is absent.

This must be considered here: "Let there be the elision (*luk*) of *iñ*, or let this non-elision (*aluk*) take place? Because it is subsequent, the non-elision occurs. The elision of *iñ* is obligatory; it applies whether this non-elision has occurred or not. This non-elision, however, is non-obligatory (*anitya*), for it does not apply once the elision of *iñ* has taken place; [one might argue] because of the absence of that which begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*)? It will occur by virtue of the "characteristic of the affix" (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*). [One might object: "There is no 'characteristic of the affix' when the basis is a phoneme (*varṇa*)"? Here, the phoneme is not the cause; rather, it is the affix itself, and "vowel" (*ac*) is merely its qualifier.

In that regard, just as the rule *tṛṇaha im* prescribed for a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *pi* applies even in the case of *atṛṇeḍ*, by virtue of the suffix being a formal cause (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), so too will it apply here. True; however, under the view that the locative case indicates the domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), such a difficulty need not be experienced. But surely, even under both views, the rule would not apply here: in the case of "the offspring of the Bidas are many young men, [namely] the Bidas"? This is not a fault.

In this case, there are two types of plurality: plurality of the *yuvan* (descendant) and plurality of the *gotra* (clan). Let there be a prohibition of the elision (*luk*) based on the plurality of the *gotra*; however, the elision will still occur based on the plurality of the *yuvan*. For in the rule prescribing elision, it is the worldly *gotra* that is intended; and even a *yuvan* is metaphorically designated as a "gotra" in common usage—as in: "I am a Gārgyāyaṇa by *gotra*."

Now, why is there not a further prohibition of *luk* (elision) even for that which is based on plurality among *yuvan* [descendants]? Regarding the locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), in whatever state *luk* is applicable, if at that state some [word] beginning with *aj* constitutes the scope, then there must be *aluk* (non-elision). In this case, however, although a word beginning with *aj* was produced and subsequently elided, when it later shifted to refer to a plurality of *yuvan*s, *luk* became applicable; yet, in this state, no word beginning with *aj* constitutes the scope, and thus there is no further *luk*.

It will be so. Even in the case of the *para-saptamī* (locative of reference), there is elision (*luk*) for that which resides in a *gotra* [patronymic] when followed by an *aj-ādi* (vowel-initial) suffix. In what kind of *aj-ādi*? When it is stated, "in those meanings which occur before *prāgdīvyataḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83) that begin with an *aj-ādi*," it is understood to mean: "in that *aj-ādi* belonging to a meaning prior to *prāgdīvyataḥ* other than that for which elision was obtained when residing in a *gotra*. And here, since the *aj-ādi* is indeed such [belonging to a meaning prior to *prāgdīvyataḥ*], and the elision occurs in the *gotra* precisely for that purpose, the prohibition will not apply.

Alternatively—the word "from the first" (*prathamāt*) is carried over from the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamāt*; that [word] is transformed into the genitive case, and because it functions in the sense of "first," its status as being first is relied upon. Thus, the meaning becomes this: there is no elision (*luk*) of the first *gotra* suffix; that elision which would otherwise apply to a suffix occurring in the very same sense in which it was originally produced does not take place.

In this case, however, since the elision (*luk*) would apply when transitioning to the second meaning, it is not prohibited. This must necessarily be understood in this way—that the elision of the first [suffix] is prohibited—otherwise, consider the following: the descendant of Atri is formed with *ḍhak* by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*; his many young descendants are formed with *iñ* (yielding *ātreya*), which undergoes elision by *ṇyakṣattriyārṣa-*, and the *ḍhak* undergoes elision by *atribhṛgu-* (resulting in *attrayaḥ*). If the prohibition did not apply to the first, the *luk* of the *ḍhak* would have already occurred. Thus, the elision of the first is indeed prohibited.

From the word *bharadvāja*, the suffix *yañ* is applied by the rule *vidādibhyo 'ñ*. When there is a plural of the *yuvan* generation derived from that, the suffix *iñ* is elided (*luk*). Then, by the rule *yañañoś ca*, the suffix *añ* is also elided. Thus, *attrayaḥ* (descendants of Atri) and *bharadvājāḥ* (descendants of Bharadvāja) form the compound *attribharadvājāḥ*. From this copulative compound (*dvandva*) expressing a matrimonial alliance, the suffix *vun* is added, resulting in *attribharadvājikāḥ*; in this case, the elision (*aluk*) [of the first member's case-ending] would apply. Similarly, from *kutsa*, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied, which is elided by the rule *atribhṛgu*. From *kuśika*, which ends in the suffix *añ*, the suffix *iñ* is elided, resulting in *kuśikāḥ*. Thus we have *kutsakuśikikāḥ*, *vasiṣṭhakaśyapikāḥ*, and *bhṛgvaṅgirasikāḥ*.

Or rather—[the word] *gargabhārgavikā* is recited in the *Gopavana* and other lists; this will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for the purpose of prohibiting the elision (*luk*) that would otherwise apply to the word *bhārgava* when denoting a plurality of *yuvan* descendants. That is to say, the non-elision (*aluk*) occurs only when [the suffix] has transitioned to this second meaning. Or again, in this case, non-elision does not even apply to that which denotes a plurality of *yuvan* descendants. What is the reason? Because it is stated "in the sense of *gotra*. Although, outside the context of the section on offspring (*apatya*), the worldly (*laukika*) *gotra* is understood, here there is the adoption of the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) definition, due to its association with the word *yuvan*.

Otherwise, regarding the fault that will be stated concerning the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designations *gotra* and *yuvan*—namely, that for the descendant of Śālaṅki, by the rule *yañiñośca*, the suffix *phak* is applied; then, by *pailādibhyaśca*, there is elision (*luk*); and when one intends to express "the pupils of the young descendant of Śālaṅki," the non-elision (*aluk*) would apply by *gotre'lugaci*. Consequently, since the elision of *yuvan* by *yūni luk* is optional by *phakphiñoranyatarasyām*, there would result the undesirable hearing (*śravaṇa*) of *phak* in one alternative, and thus that fault would remain exactly as it was. This remains true even if there is no co-occurrence of *yuvan*.

Since it would follow that the suffix *aluk* would apply [to the word *laukika*] precisely because it belongs to the *laukika*-group (*gotra*), it is established that one need not state such things as "of the *gotra* ending in many vowels" (*bahuṣu lopinaḥ*) and so forth.

"Of that which ends in the singular or dual number," and so forth. This means: when a *gotra*-suffix ending in the singular or dual undergoes a transition—that is, when it is applied—to refer to many individuals who bear the designation of *yuvan* (descendants). "Lopa" means elision (*luk*). For if there were merely elision (*lopa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of *vṛddhi* and accentuation by virtue of the rule regarding the presence of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Now, one might object: since the elision here is already established by the rule "of *yañ* and *añ* [there is elision] in the plural" (*yañañośca*), why state this? To this he replies: "For in this case, *añ* has not been produced in the plural."

The meaning is that if it were understood as "that which ends in *añ* when there are many [descendants]" and "that which ends in *yañ* when there are many," then elision (*luk*) would not be established. However, when it is understood as "that which ends in *añ* [denoting] those who are many" and "that which ends in *yañ* [denoting] those who are many," then elision is indeed established; for in that case, both the worldly *gotra* (lineage) that occurs among many *yuvan* (junior descendants) ending in *añ*, and the mere descendant (*apatya*) ending in *yañ*, are included therein.

And likewise: *gārgyaśca vātsyaśca vājyaśca* becomes *gargavatsavājāḥ*, and *baidaśca aurvaśca bhāradvājāśca* becomes *bidaurvabhāradvājāḥ*. Although there is no plurality at the time of the derivation of the suffixes *yañ* and *añ*, in a *dvandva* compound, because the suffixes denote multiple substrates simultaneously, the elision (*luk*) occurs due to the emergence of plurality for that which ends in *yañ* and that which ends in *añ*.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there are many representations of a single Kāśyapa such that they would be called "Kāśyapas," for if the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule *ive pratikṛtau* were elided by the rule *jīvikārthe cāpaṇye*, then—despite the statement that "in the case of *harītakyādi* words, the individual [is expressed]" which implies the absence of the treatment as a plural—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision (*luk*) for the form ending in *añ* when used in the plural, since elision is specifically ordained only when there is a plurality of lineages (*gotra*).
There is elision [of the suffix] when a young person [is denoted]. 4.1.90.

In this case as well, if *aci* were a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffixes applying in any order whatsoever. When the *yuvan*-suffix is being heard [in the derivation], that which is applicable must first be applied; once that has been done, when the *yuvan*-suffix undergoes elision (*luk*), its hearing [in the final form] would result. However, if it is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*), then even when the *yuvan*-suffix—which serves as the domain—is elided before an *ac*-beginning [suffix], whatever is applicable from whichever source occurs, that very thing becomes established as desired.

This will be clarified in the examples; thus he says: "when a suffix beginning with *a* or *j* is intended," and so forth. [The rule] "after *iñ*, there is *aṇ*" applies. However, if the locative case (*parasasaptamī*) were used, only *cha* would apply after a *vṛddha* stem. Regarding the rule "after *phe*, there is *cha*": the enumeration by the author of the Bhāṣya—namely, "Yamunda, Suyāman, and Vārṣyāyaṇi are recorded as having the suffix *phiñ"—is not accepted. Consequently, *cha* also occurs after *taikāyani*, resulting in *taikāyanīyāḥ*.

In this case, there is no fault even if [the locative] is taken as a *parasaptamī* (a locative of reference). However, regarding the rule *ṇyakṣattriyārṣañitaḥ*, the author of the *Vṛtti* has cited the elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix—namely, "Taikāyani is the father; Taikāyani is the son"—which should be understood as being based on a specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*). Consequently, in that context, "taikāyanīyāḥ" would not serve as an example. As for "kāpiñjalādāḥ": here too, if [the locative] were a *parasaptamī*, the suffix *cha* would apply after a word marked with the marker *vṛddhi*. The same should be observed in the case of "glaucukāyanāḥ". But in the present instance, when the students of the young descendant of Upagu (*aupagava*) have the *iñ* suffix elided, the suffix *cha* applies after a *vṛddha* base; whereas if [the locative] were a *parasaptamī*, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule *iñaśca*.

This is not an illustration of this rule (*yoga*). Why? Because in the rule *iñaśca*, the term "in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*) is understood from a previous context; therefore, we shall qualify the suffix *iñ* by that: "that *iñ* which is prescribed in the sense of a lineage. Furthermore, what is taken here is the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense of "lineage. How so? In the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the "lineage" mentioned in the rule *gotre kuñjādibhyaḥ*: "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in that suffix which was prescribed in the sense of a lineage after the *kaṇva*-group. And in that context, it is precisely that technical sense which is taken.

And that very [rule] is also carried over (anuvartate) into the rule "iñaśca"; therefore, how could there be any possibility of the suffix aṇ after a word ending in a secondary suffix (yuvapratyaya)? This must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, even when the suffix iñ has been elided, the suffix aṇ would still occur by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa).

Here, then, are the examples for this [rule]: those ending in *khac* and *śānta*. For instance: *rāja-śvaśurād-yat*. From *śvaśura*, "the offspring of a father-in-law," comes *śvaśuryaḥ*; from that, "the offspring of *śvaśurya*" is *śvāśuriḥ*. Regarding his students (*chāttrāḥ*), when the suffix *iñ* is elided (*luki*), the suffix *aṇ* applies by the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*, resulting in *śvāśuraḥ*; otherwise, the suffix *cha* would apply by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*. From *kula*, by the rule *kulātkhaḥ*, we have *kulīnaḥ*. From that, "the offspring of *kulīna*" is *kaulīniḥ*. Regarding his students, when *iñ* is elided, we have *kaulīnaḥ*.

Regarding the forms *svasuśchaḥ*, *svasrīyaḥ*, its offspring *svāsrīyiḥ*, and its pupils (*tasya chāttrāḥ*) with the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ* resulting in *svasrīyāḥ*: these are not the correct examples. According to the rule “there is an addition [to the rule] for the elision of the youth-suffix (*yuvan-pratyaya*) after a non-Brāhmaṇa [stem] when it denotes merely a lineage (*gotra-mātra*),” once the elision of *iñ* has been applied, the forms should be *śvaśuryaḥ* (the father) and *śvaśuryaḥ* (the son), *kulīnaḥ* (the father) and *kulīnaḥ* (the son), and *svasrīyaḥ* (the father) and *svasrīyaḥ* (the son).

Furthermore, no suffix that does not cause *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) can occur after a *brāhmaṇa* *gotra*, such that when the suffix *iñ* is applied, the suffix *cha* would subsequently apply. However, there is no distinction in the case of a *gotra* suffix that does cause *vṛddhi*, because even when *iñ* is actually heard, it must be replaced by *cha*; and even when that [suffix] has been elided, since the word ending in the *gotra* suffix is still "old" (*vṛddha*), it must take *cha*, as for example in *aupagavīyāḥ*. Thus, it is established that an example for *iñ* is not possible here.

If, however, the term *gotra* in the preceding sūtra refers to the worldly (laukika) lineage, then this [example] would indeed serve as an illustration. For instance, in the case of the suffix *iñ* derived from *śvaśurya* and similar words, even though its elision (*luk*) occurs by means of an augmentative rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*), if there is a desire to express a descendant in the *prādīvyatīya* sense, the suffix *cha*—prescribed by "the suffix *cha* after a *vṛddha* stem"—would arise based on that *iñ*, because of the prohibition "there is no elision (*aluk*) of a *gotra* suffix before a vowel" (*gotre 'lug aci*). This would happen if the elision of that [suffix] were not performed by the rule "elision of the *yuvan* suffix" (*yūni luk*).

Therefore, it is concluded that even the prohibition of *iñ* as an example [from this rule] indicates that the Bhāṣyakāra intended "gotra" in its technical sense (*pāribhāṣika*) in the previous sūtra.

But for what purpose is this stated, since even in the case of a youth (*yuvan*), if he is intended to be expressed in the form of a "gotra," he will be denoted by a gotra-suffix; the specific status of being a youth will be established through the meaning, context, and so forth, and the distinction must necessarily be understood through meaning, context, and so on, because the word remains common [to both] even when this sūtra has been commenced?

For it is not known whether the students of Bhāgavitti are called *Bhāgavittāḥ* because they belong to Bhāgavitti himself, or because they belong to one who is a descendant of Bhāgavitti. Therefore, this [rule] is intended so that when a specific distinction is intended to be expressed, the form shall be *Bhāgavittāḥ* alone, and never *Bhāgavittikīyāḥ*.
The suffix *phak* or *chañ* is optionally applied [after a word denoting a place of origin]. 4.1.91.

For what purpose is this [sūtra], since the word is common to both when one intends to express the form of a youth (*yuvan*)—as in *gārgyāyaṇīya*—and when one intends to express the form of a lineage (*gotra*)—as in *gārgīya*? To this he says: "by the previous sūtra. It was stated that the rule "elision in the case of a youth" (*yūni luk*) must be commenced; and if this [present sūtra] were not stated while that [previous rule] is being commenced, there would be a permanent elision even of the suffixes *phak* and *phiñ*, and consequently the form *gārgyāyaṇīya* would not occur. Therefore, the meaning is that this [sūtra] must also be commenced.
The descendant of that [person]. (Pāṇini 4.1.92)

"This is a specification of the meaning" means that by this [sūtra], the meaning of the suffix—namely, the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) qualified by the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), which takes the form of "offspring" (*apatya*)—is specified. By this, the indication of the genitive case as the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*) is also clearly shown. Regarding the phrase "by preceding and by succeeding [suffixes]": first, it is connected with the preceding [suffixes] such as *aṇ* and others.

Because [the sūtra] is formulated as unconnected [to the preceding], otherwise he would have composed a single rule simply as "tasyāpatyam ata iñ" (from that, the suffix *iñ* is used for offspring). But since he formulates it as unconnected, it is understood that it connects with what precedes. It also connects with what follows, because those [subsequent rules] possess the *svarita* accent and are expectant [of a prior reference]. The phrase "tasya" means "from that which is governed by the genitive case. Here, "tasya" is a general term intended to indicate specific genitive-ending forms, and in the expression "samarthānām," the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇa*).

In this context, because there is a selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) from among things of the same class (*tulyajātīya*), the following meaning is established: "from a [stem] ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) that is semantically capable (*samartha*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of 'offspring' (*apatyam*)," since it is impossible for the word *apatya*, which ends in the nominative, to be construed otherwise, this ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is understood. As for the expression "as prescribed" (*yathāvihitam*): the term *yathā* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) used in the sense of "according to," and thus forms an *avyayībhāva* compound with the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). The meaning is: "that suffix which has been prescribed by rules such as *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83) and so forth, [is applied] from that [base]."

Here, this designation "tasya" (of him/it) is made using either the masculine or neuter gender and in the singular number; therefore, it would not apply from a different gender or a different number—such as *somātraḥ* (the offspring of Sumātṛ), *kṣāttriḥ* (the offspring of Kṣattra), or *aupagavaḥ* (the offspring of Upagu).

The designation "apatyam" (offspring) is made using the singular number and the neuter gender. One might therefore suspect that it would apply to only one offspring, not to two, nor to many; and that it would apply only to the neuter, not to females or males. Anticipating this objection, he says: "prakṛtyartha... and so forth. The "meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyartha*) refers to specific individuals such as Upagu and others; for the word "tasya" (of him) is intended to indicate those specific [progenitors]. The phrase "and mere offspring" (*apatyamātram*) uses the word "mere" (*mātra*) to exclude [restriction to] gender and number. The phrase "gender, number, and so forth" refers to these very factors.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), time (*kāla*) is included; for here there is the perception of a reference to the present time, as it has been said: "Where no other verbal action is present, the verb 'to be' (*asti*) in the third person is understood to exist even if it is not explicitly employed. Consequently, if that [present] time were intended to be expressed, it would not occur at another time. [Objection: "Everything is unintended. [Response: Because its inclusion is inseparable, a reference must necessarily be made by some gender or other.

Regarding the statement "tasyedam apatye 'pi" (the rule "this belongs to him" applies even in the sense of offspring): the ellipsis is that the prescription of suffixes such as *aṇ* and others is established. For the specific instances of "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*) include offspring, collections, modifications, and so forth; since all particular cases are included within the general category of relationship, the prescription of *aṇ* and other suffixes for offspring is already established by the rule "this belongs to him" alone. Therefore, the purpose of the objection is: why are *aṇ* and other suffixes prescribed for offspring through a separate rule (*yogavibhāga*), rather than having the meaning of offspring indicated solely in connection with exceptions (*apavāda*) such as "from this [stem], *iñ* is added in the sense of offspring" (*tasyāpatyam ata iñ*)?

He refutes [the objection]: "It would be for the purpose of sublation. The meaning is that the prescription of *aṇ* and other suffixes in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) would be for the purpose of sublating that *cha* which is prescribed by the rule "tasyedam" (Pāṇini 4.3.120) as a sublater of them. Now, one might object: "The *cha* suffix is a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*). A 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is any meaning other than those starting from 'offspring' up to the fourth category; so how could there be any occasion for the application of *cha* in the sense of 'offspring,' such that this [prescription of *aṇ*] would be for the purpose of sublating it? To this he says: "The general rule (*utsarga*) applies only to the remainder."

If, without performing a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), one were to state simply "the suffix *iñ* is applied after [a word ending in] *ataḥ* to express its offspring" (*tasyāpatyam ata iñ*), then the meaning of "offspring" would be applicable only when connected with that specific base; consequently, any other sense of "offspring" would be considered a *śeṣa* (remainder), and thus the suffix *cha* would indeed apply after a *vṛddha* base to denote offspring. However, when there is a *yogavibhāga*, because the meaning of "offspring" is already utilized in the prescription of suffixes such as *aṇ* and others, it lacks the status of being a *śeṣa*; therefore, *cha* does not apply at all. This very non-application is what is called "sublation" (*bādha*) in this context.

The term *utsarga* refers to the general meaning connected with the common nature [of the suffix], which is stated as having the sense of "offspring. He gives an example for the purpose of setting aside [the general rule]: "vṛddhānyasya prayojanam" (wealth is his purpose). Regarding "śyāmagavaḥ": one whose cows are dark is "śyāmaguḥ."
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied after a word denoting a *gotra* (lineage) to form a patronymic. || 4.1.93 ||

This word *eka* denotes [the senses of] "other," "principal," "without companion," "number," "first," and "common. First, regarding its sense of "other": in the rules *ekānyābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*, *prajāmekā rakṣatyūrjamekā*, *ekān bandhuraparānnirāsuḥ*, *ityeke manyante*, and *yajuṣyekeṣām*; however, some say that in these two usages, the word *eka* is a synonym for the word *kecit* ("some"). In the sense of "principal," as in *ekaḥ pārtho dhanuṣmatām*.

In the rules "as if one thing had a beginning and an end," "in that which begins with a single consonant," and "between two single consonants," the word *eka* is used in the sense of "unaccompanied" (*asahāya*). In the expression "one, two, many," it is used in the sense of "number" (*saṅkhyā*). In the expression "some have little breath," it is used in the sense of "first" (*prathama*). In the rule "in the same direction as that" (*tenaikadik*), it is used in the sense of "common" (*samāna*). In the expression "Devadatta and Yajñadatta possess the same wealth" (*ekadhanau*), it is used in the sense of "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*). Among these, the meaning of "number," "shared," or "first" is accepted [for the present context], because the other meanings are impossible. The term *gotra* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*).

Because, between the artificial (*kṛtrima*) and the natural (*akṛtrima*), the understanding of the grammatical operation applies to the artificial, and because of the mention of *gotra* in the section on offspring (*apatya*).

Why is this stated? So that when an offspring beginning with a grandson (*pauttra*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix may occur from the original base itself, such as *uparava*, and not from a form already ending in a suffix, such as *aupagava*.

This objection has no force. This will be like the case of the suffix *san*. Just as when *san* is prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), it does not occur after [a form] already ending in *san*; for what reason? Because a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies only once to a generic form (*ākṛti*), which is the meaning of the word and constitutes a single unit. And when *san* is being prescribed, a verbal root ending in *san* is not possible. Similarly here too, when a patronymic suffix is being prescribed, a base (*prakṛti*) ending in a patronymic suffix is not possible; therefore, the suffix will not occur. [Reply: This is an unequal comparison.

Since there is a single condition (*pratyaya*) and only one defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that is applicable therein, it is not possible for a base (*prakṛti*) ending in that [suffix] to exist while it is being prescribed.

Furthermore, in this case, there are many rules such as *tasyāpatyam*, *ata iñ*, and *yañiñośca*, and there are many suffixes (*pratyaya*). When one suffix is being prescribed, it is indeed possible for a base (*prakṛti*) ending in another suffix to occur; and thus, for instance, a *san* suffix may follow a *san* suffix of roots like *gup*, as in *jugupsiṣate*. What would happen, however, if this were not undertaken? It is said: here some maintain that the word *apatya* is a synonym for the word *putra*.

This is because it is so recited in the *nighaṇṭus* and is observed in common usage. For example, seeing a child sitting on his grandfather’s lap, someone asks, "Whose son is this? Whose offspring is this? He identifies the progenitor, saying, "He is Devadatta’s" or "Yajñadatta’s," and not himself; therefore, just as he is not the son in relation to the grandfather, so too he is not the offspring (*apatya*). Only the progenitor is connected with the offspring, and not even the grandfather and others.

Others, however, maintain that the word *apatya* is based on action; it is not derived from the etymological rule "that by which one does not fall (*na patanti anena*) is *apatyam*" with the *yat* suffix added according to the *uṇādi* rules, but rather that for whom there is non-falling by means of another, that is his *apatya*.

Even one born through an intervening generation, such as a grandson, becomes a cause for the non-falling [from heaven] of the grandfather and others; for it is heard in scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: to the sages by means of studentship, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny; he alone is free from debt who has a son. By this, since it is established that one becomes free from debt to the ancestors after producing a son, the benefit to the ancestors is seen to be effected through the progeny produced by the son. And it is recorded in Smṛti: "Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality."
"Then, through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.

And in the *Itihāsas*, such as those concerning Jāratkāru and others, there is a great tradition—that even one born of a remote ancestor can be a benefactor. Furthermore, the author of the *Sūtras*, the preeminent among those who know the science of words (*śabdavid*), formulates the rule: "Offspring beginning with the grandson is called a *gotra*. From this, it is understood that the word "offspring" (*apatya*) is applied even based on the causal action [of benefit]. Otherwise, just as it would be untenable for the grandson and subsequent descendants to be called "sons," so too would that [usage] be.

This being the case, whether directly or through a lineage, whoever is produced by someone is that person's *apatya* (offspring); thus, even all ancestors such as the grandfather and others would be connected with the offspring, and not only the progenitor. Regarding this, in the first position, if this [rule] were not commenced, then in each respective case of offspring, that particular suffix would apply based on the word for each respective father—for example: from Upagu comes Aupagava; from him, Aupagavi; from him, Aupagavāyana.

In this way, for the hundredth descendant, there would be ninety-nine conditions for being a descendant—which leads to an undesirable result—and the desired form "aupagava" would not be established, because from the third generation onward, [the descendants] would no longer be considered descendants in relation to Upagu. However, in the second alternative, the fifth descendant of Upagu is the offspring of the four preceding ones; therefore, when the suffix is applied to Upagu, the desired form "aupagava" is indeed established.

Furthermore, one arrives at undesired forms; and that undesired form is not fixed for Aupagavi—namely, from him [comes] Aupagavāyana, and from him [comes] Aupagavāyani. In the fifth generation there are three undesired forms, in the sixth four, and so on, until as many descendants as are intended to be named, that many minus two undesired forms are reached—for example, in the hundredth generation, there are ninety-eight. This being the case, the following is undertaken.

Even when this [treatise] is commenced, if the first position is adopted, would this then be for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*) or for the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*)? And how would it serve as an injunction, or how as a restriction? If, by the word *gotra*, the entire collection of descendants beginning with the grandson is denoted by each individual descendant, then it would be for the purpose of an injunction; in that case, however, it is possible for it to be for the purpose of a restriction, because there is no possibility of multiple suffixes occurring for a single descendant.

First of all, there is no contingency of multiple suffixes arising from a single base within a single application (*prayoga*), because its meaning is expressed by one [suffix] alone. Nor is there a contingency of multiple suffixes arising from multiple bases through a difference in applications, for that would always result [only] from the mention of one's own father. Thus, in the third instance and beyond, the suffix is not obtained after the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*) in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*); likewise, it is not obtained after *aupagava* in the fourth instance and beyond. Therefore, why is it not prescribed? Because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). For in this case, the expression is manifested as follows: "In the lineage (*gotra*), one [is designated]."

The meaning is that the suffix occurs only from that [stem] from which a single suffix can be applied; this sense is obtained by the force of the mention of "one" (*eka*). Now, one might object: even when the suffix is prescribed, would not the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix remain unrelated? There is no fault here, for by the force of the statement, the suffix will apply through the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the descendant's descendant as being a descendant itself.

Since the suffix would not have its purpose fulfilled in the case of the primary offspring, it must indeed be prescribed [for that case as well]. On this view, although the desired form *aupagava* is established for all [descendants], the contingency of a series of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*) remains exactly as it was; for by this rule, the suffix obtained from the respective paternal words is not prohibited. Thus, when a suffix is applied to the word *upagu* for the fifth offspring, the sixth descendant—meaning "his offspring"—would be *aupagavi*.

However, when the term *apatya* (offspring) in the rule *apatyaṃ pautraprabhṛtigotram* is used to indicate the entire collection of offspring beginning with the grandson (*pautra*) by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and the designation *gotra* is prescribed for that very collection—whereby the word *gotra* is applied to each individual offspring according to the maxim that "words functioning for a whole may also apply to its parts"—or when the collection of offspring beginning with the grandson is denoted by the word *gotra* here through the transfer of the property of the parts to the whole, then [the rule] serves as a restriction: namely, that only one suffix occurs for the collection of *gotras*.

Although it follows that a single suffix applies to each individual descendant, nevertheless, since one suffix applies to the grandson and another to his offspring, it is established by a comprehensive analysis that many suffixes would be applied to the entire collection; thus, the restrictive rule is justified. However, there is a defect in this position: a suffix would apply to the third generation from a word already ending in a suffix for an immediate descendant. For the restriction is established by the inclusion of the term *gotra*—namely, that there shall be only one suffix for a *gotra*—and therefore, let there not be multiple suffixes for a *gotra*.

Why should there not be more than one [suffix], such that one follows immediately and another follows in the third [generation] and so on? Even so, only one would be applied to the *gotra* (lineage). Alternatively, what is accomplished by the phrase "only one" (*eka eva*) with respect to the collection of lineages? It serves to prohibit [the application of a suffix] to the third generation and beyond when it would otherwise have been applicable in the fourth generation and so forth. If it were to apply to the third generation and beyond, then multiple suffixes would be applied to the collection. However, that which is applicable immediately in the third generation is permitted; the purpose of the restrictive rules (*niyama*) is the exclusion of others, as expressed by "only one."

And therefore, since when a suffix is applied [to a compound], multiple suffixes would have been applied to the aggregate, it follows that the meaning of the rule is simply "it does not occur. In this way, the designation of the fourth descendant by means of a patronymic suffix would not be obtained; for a suffix produced from the second [member] denotes only the third, and does not arise from the third itself, but rather there would only be the sentence: "the offspring of Aupagavi."

Furthermore, in the case of the fifth [descendant] and beyond, even verbal expression would not be possible; for there exists no derivative word ending in a patronymic suffix that could be analyzed as signifying those respective ancestors. Moreover, in the case of the *paramaprakṛti* (the ultimate source) in the third [descendant] and onwards, a suffix would never apply anywhere due to the lack of connection (*ayogāt*). Thus, under this view, one must state the production of the *paramaprakṛti*, and one must also state a prohibition of what would otherwise apply from the immediate [source] in the third [descendant].

It might be argued as follows: the production of the supreme material cause need not be stated, since it is established through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference. And this metaphorical attribution of non-difference occurs, for example, between Upagu and the descendant of Upagu, or between the lineage of Upagu and his offspring.

Thus, even in the case of a hundredth descendant, the designation "Aupagava" is established through a succession of metaphorical applications of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). Yet, if the desired result were achieved solely by such metaphorical application of non-difference, would the Sūtra not be rendered useless? No; for its purpose is to prevent the occurrence of a string of secondary suffixes (*pratyayamālā*) when there is an intention to express distinction (*bhedavivakṣā*). Even so, if there is an intention to express distinction regarding the immediate [descendant] and the third [descendant], the third would have to be called *Aupagavi*. Likewise, this would apply wherever a suffix differs, as in the case of the Gargas and others, whether in the immediate [descendant] or in the third and beyond.

In that case as well, an undesirable consequence follows. If, first of all, there is a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) of the name Garga to Gārgya, then his offspring would also be Gārgya; yet it is intended that he be Gārgi. Alternatively, if there is a metaphorical transfer of non-difference between Garga and his offspring, even so, [the offspring] would be Gārgya. Thus, in such instances as these, a metaphorical transfer of non-difference is inherently faulty. Therefore, since faults would follow in both the injunction and the restriction under the first alternative, the second alternative is adopted; and in that case as well, it is a restriction.

Although in each individual application only one suffix would be applicable to a single base, nevertheless, in the case of *upagu* in the fifth [derivative], where there is the contingency of various suffixes arising from the four preceding bases due to the difference in applications, a restriction is made—namely, that it must be this very [suffix]. This is what was stated: "When there is the contingency of various suffixes due to a difference in application, a restriction is made."

But is it not the case that it is not known which one becomes [the suffix]: is it that which follows the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*), or that which follows a further derivative suffix (*pratyayānta*)? Is it not said that there is only one? And if the suffix were obtained from a further derivative suffix, then more than one would have been applied. Where [is this]? Not in the fifth [chapter], for the previous suffixes would apply here in this usage because they have as their domain other types of offspring (*apatya*).

Now, within the aggregate of *gotra* (lineage), by what could this [restriction] be prevented? It cannot be by this very [rule], for the aggregate of *gotra* is not grasped by the mention of *gotra*. Even if it were so grasped, it would still remain unknown whether [the suffix applies] to one who is further removed from the original source (*paramaprakṛti*) or to one immediately following it. Furthermore, if the mention of *gotra* were not made, or if, being made, it were understood as referring merely to "offspring" (*apatya*), this fault would not arise; for there is a restrictive rule that within the aggregate of offspring, [the suffix] occurs only once.

Does this fault arise because of the mention of *gotra* (lineage) under the heading of *apatya* (descendant)? This is not a fault; for the term *apatya* continues to apply, and the explicit formulation of the rule is: "In the case of a descendant that is a *gotra*, only one single affix denoting a descendant occurs. Furthermore, if an affix were added after [a stem already ending in] another affix, then multiple affixes denoting descendants would have been applied to the *gotra*. Alternatively, by implication, the affix is qualified: "only one among those capable of expressing a *gotra* [is used]."

Furthermore, if a suffix were added after another suffix, many suffixes capable of denoting lineage (*gotra*) would have been created, since the first one is already capable of doing so. Even though in this particular application it refers to a different descendant, there is still the capacity for a fifth [suffix] as well. Alternatively, by means of such rules as "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*), only a single suffix should be applied; where? To the *gotra*, meaning: in that suffix where the lineage is intended to be expressed.
Furthermore, when a suffix follows another suffix within that very same application, there would have to be many instances of the restoration of the original form of the base.

Alternatively, if the word *eka* (one) refers to the first [suffix], what is the "first"? It is that without which it is impossible to apply another suffix. Or, it may mean "common" (*sādhāraṇa*); and because of the governing context of "descendants" (*apatya*), that which is common to all descendants is alone [the one] that occurs in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). Thus, from the word *garga*, only *yañ* occurs. The meaning is that only that *yañ* which is applicable from the word *garga* occurs, and not the suffixes applicable from other bases; thus he says: "the suffix is restricted."
The meaning is that another condition is excluded; by this, the statement that "the material cause is restricted" is also explained.

Now, regarding the phrase "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth: in this alternative view, it is shown that the word *śabda* (sound/word) is used in the nominative case. The term *prakṛti* (base) is in the nominative. However, in the grammatical rule (*sūtra*), the masculine gender is employed with reference to the word *śabda*. Thus, it is shown that "the word is one and the same. Alternatively, in this view, the word *eka* (one) has a general sense; the "ultimate base" (*paramaprakṛti*) is common to all suffixes, or the word *eka* denotes number. Since there is no reason to skip over the first [possibility], the ultimate base is understood by the word *eka*.
Of these two views, the first is the primary one; it should be understood as an explanation of the word "one" (eka) by way of its meaning.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [stems ending in] *gotra*, etc., when the feminine gender is not intended.

In this case as well, if this rule (*yoga*) were not commenced, then when a descendant is connected with a progenitor, the designation *gotra* would be superseded by the designation *yuvan*; consequently, in the absence of the operation of the preceding rule, the suffix would not be obtained after a third [progenitor] for a fourth [descendant], nor after a fourth for a fifth, nor after a fifth for a sixth, and so on, in the case of a *yuvan*. This is because, with respect to that [further descendant], there would be no status as a direct offspring (*apatya*). Thus, the desired result would not be established. However, if all [progenitors] are connected with the status of being an offspring, then for a fifth *yuvan*, the suffix would be obtained from the four preceding ones.
