In that regard, when [the suffix] is applied from the third [generation], the desired form *gārgyāyaṇa* is indeed established; however, an undesired result also follows, because there would be the contingency of the suffix being applied even after other bases. Therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced. Here too, if the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is adopted, then does this [sūtra] serve as an injunction (*vidhi*), or as a restriction (*niyama*)? If by the word *yuva* (youth) one single descendant is meant, then—since there is no possibility of application from the *gotra* or the non-*gotra* in the case of a single youth—the rule serves as an injunction for the *gotra* in the case of a youth separated by the fourth generation, such as the fifth and so on.

Now, if the group beginning with the fourth descendant is denoted by the term *yuvan*, then, since there would be the contingency of applying the suffix both from the *gotra* (to the fourth) and from the non-*gotra* (to the fifth), the rule "from the *gotra* alone" (*gotrād eva*) serves as a restriction. In that case, regarding the injunction, the desired form *gārgyāyaṇa* is established; however, the fault of the contingency of a series of suffixes (*pratyayamālā*) would indeed remain, because the suffix obtained from the word denoting the father is not prohibited.

In the case of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), this results in a prohibition of the suffix that would otherwise apply from the fourth generation onwards—on the grounds that if it were to apply from the fourth generation onwards, a suffix might have been applied even from the *gotra* [stem] when forming a collective group of *yuvan* [descendants]. Consequently, there would be no undesirable consequence [in that case]; however, for the fifth generation and beyond, the production of a suffix from the *gotra* [stem] for a *yuvan* descendant would not be applicable, because [the *gotra* stem] is not considered a direct offspring (*anapatyatvāt*) in relation to him. Thus, the fifth-generation descendant would have to be expressed by a full sentence: "the offspring of Gārgyāyaṇa" (*gārgyāyaṇasyāpatyam*).

But even by means of a sentence, the sixth [case] is not established, for there exists no word denoting a father that ends in a suffix expressing "offspring" (*apatya*) by which it could be analyzed. Therefore, in this case as well, the second alternative is adopted, and there is a restriction (*niyama*); thus he says: "This too is a restriction," namely, "only from a *gotra* [ancestor]. It is not the case that the restriction is the reverse, i.e., "only in the case of a youth" (*yuvan*), because since there is already the restriction "one [suffix] in the *gotra*," there is no possibility of a *gotra* suffix occurring elsewhere than in the *yuvan*. [The restriction is] "not from the immediate original base (*paramaprakṛti*) or from a youth. Otherwise, due to differences in usage, [the suffixes] might apply to those as well.

"But what is it that is being prohibited here? This question arises because faults are seen even when everything is prohibited. He reveals that very fault [with the words]: "If it is a restriction" (*niyama*). The sense is that the prohibition is syntactically connected with that [restriction]. [The consequence would be] that there would be no restriction regarding the feminine gender; the meaning is that the suffixes characterized by *parama*, *prakṛti*, *anantara*, and *yuva* would occur alternately according to different usages. [Objection: "Then the *yuvan*-suffix is what is prohibited."

The intention is that, by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) and by relying on a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), [the application of the suffix] is restricted to non-feminine forms. Thus, designation by means of a *gotra* suffix would not be obtained. For example, in the case of "Garga and others take *yañ*" (*gargādibhyo yañ*), one would have *gārgī* or *gārgyāyaṇī*; however, the suffix would instead be one conditioned by the general definition of *apatya* (descendant). To the question, "For what reason does non-designation result?", he says: "Because the technical name *gotra* is sublated by the technical name *yuvan*. And how this sublation occurs will be explained in that very same place.

It might be argued as follows: the elision (*luk*) of the *yuvan* suffix will be applied in the feminine. How so? Immediately after the rule "elision in the sense of *yuvan*" (*yūni luk*), I shall state "and in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*). Thus, "elision in the sense of *yuvan*" remains in force, while the phrase "prior to *dīvya-t*" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*) is no longer applicable.

Or rather, I shall state [the rule] as: "Also after *vataṇḍa*; there is elision (*luk*) in the feminine, and in the sense of a youth. [The first part] would simply be "elision in the feminine. Consequently, when the *phaK* suffix produced from the word *gārgya* is elided, the base itself expresses even the meaning of that which has been elided; thus, since it ends in *yaÑ* and denotes a feminine, the suffixes *ṅīṣ* and *ṣpha* will occur. Even so, when the *iÑ* suffix is elided from the word *aupagava*, the long *ī* [of *aupagavī*] would not be obtained, because of the governing rule regarding non-derivatives (*anupasarjana*), which states that the suffix *aṆ* applies to what is not a derivative (*anupasarjana*).

Because the *aṇ* suffix is not primary, as it has been transferred to the youth (*yuvan*). [Objection: Let it not be that the *aṇ* is not a secondary element (*anupasarjana*); rather, the rule will apply as "from a word ending in *aṇ* which is not a secondary element. [Reply: This cannot be so.

For here there would be a fault: the grammar was taught by Āpiśali; by the rule *iñaśca*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form *Āpiśala*]. Then, in the case of *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brāhmaṇī who studies the Āpiśala grammar"), when the suffix *aṇ*—which follows the word ending in *aṇ* derived from the sense of "one who studies that"—is elided after a word formed with the suffix *prokta* (meaning "taught by"), the suffix *ṅīp* would be required because the suffix *aṇ* has transferred its status to the primary feminine referent (*adhyetry*). Therefore, one must necessarily rely on the formulation *aṇyo 'nupasarjanam* ("the *aṇ* which is not a secondary member") or "the *aṇ* prescribed for the feminine. Otherwise, the long vowel *ī* in *satyaupagavī* would not be obtained.

Even if, in this case, the vowel *i* were to occur by virtue of the rule "the addition of *iñ* [is prescribed] as a characteristic of a suffix," here—in the case of *glucukāyani*, where the general suffix *aṇ* has been elided—the suffix *ṅīp* would not apply; however, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will indeed occur by the rule "after a word denoting a human class ending in *it*."

In that case, consider *yāskaḥ*, the descendant of *Yaska* (formed with the suffix *aṇ* after *śiva* etc.). His female descendant would require the suffix *phiñ* by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*. Since there is elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix, the long vowel *ī* would not be obtained. For here, the suffix that has been elided is not the cause for the *ī*; and that which is actually heard [as the suffix] is neither prescribed in the feminine nor is it an *upasarjana*. What, then, is the solution? To this he says: "Therefore..."—namely, that only the designation *yuvan* (younger generation) is prohibited.

Now, it was stated that "what is prescribed for the *yuvan* [descendant] does not apply to the feminine," yet the technical designation *yuvan* (*yuvasaṃjñā*) was not explicitly taught as applying to the *yuvan*; for indeed, prior to the application of the *yuvan*-designation, there is no such thing as a *yuvan*-designation. There is no fault here, because the word *yuvan* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for a descendant belonging to the fourth generation and beyond who is still living within the lineage. Another says: the word *yuvan* refers to its own form (*svarūpapara*), and this is a metarule (*paribhāṣā*): wherever the word *yuvan* is heard, the phrase "provided it is not feminine" (*astriyām*) is understood to apply. Or rather, it should have been clearly stated as: "But when the ancestor is living, the *yuvan* [is used], provided it is not feminine."
Therefore, the suffix *iñ* [is applied]. 4.1.95.

Regarding the phrase "from a nominal stem ending in *a*": this does not include the root *at* (as in *ata sātatyagamane*) nor words like *kurvat* that end in the suffix *ac*. If it did, then the reading of words such as *śiva*, *proṣṭha*, and *prauṣṭhika* in the *Śivādi* list—which is intended to block the application of the suffix *iñ*—would be redundant. Furthermore, by the principle of "treating a thing as if it possessed its own designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix *iñ* also applies here: [the form] *asyāpatyam* becomes *iri*; when the *ya* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, only the suffix remains audible.

But here—[in the case of] "the grandson of Erā" (erapatyam asya), being a youth (yuvan)—after the suffix *phak* has been applied by the rule "yañiñoś ca," and having overridden the elision of the *y* (yasyeti lopa) because it is subsequent, once the initial *vṛddhi* has been performed, the form becomes *āyāyana*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *bāhu* and the others. 4.1.96.

Regarding the phrase "in some cases": in the case of [names] beginning with Ajīgarta and ending with Udaṅka, since they end in a vowel (a), the suffix *iñ* would be applicable by the preceding rule; however, that is superseded by the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "ṛṣy-andhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaś-ca. All other [names] end in consonants (*anakārānta*); among them, for those beginning with Bāhu and ending in *u*, as well as for those beginning with Puṣkarasat and ending in consonants (*halanta*), the suffix *aṇ* is applicable. From the word *cūḍā*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applicable by the rule "dvyacaḥ"; from words such as *vṛkala*, the suffix *tannāmika-aṇ* is applicable. The forms *śiras* and *loman* are included here because they are used as final members of compounds.

Although it would have been sufficient to state simply, "There is elision of *s* when [the suffix] follows *sambhū*, *ombha*, and *mitaujas*," the separate mention of "elision of *s*" (*salopaśca*) is for the sake of stylistic variety. The form *udañcu* is recited; in this case, the suffix does not follow a stem ending in *u*, but rather follows a stem ending in the *kvip* suffix, while the non-elision of the nasal (*n*) is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, the offspring of one who faces north (*udīc*) is *audañciḥ*. All of this is understood from the inclusion of the word *audañci* among the *pailādi* group.

Regarding the phrase "in *bāhu* and so forth": by the inclusion of the word "so forth" (*prabhṛti*), those [names] to be mentioned later, such as *kuñja*, are included. "Worldly" (*laukika*) clan-status means being known in common usage; the meaning is that it consists in being a name-giver and being a primordial person (*ādipuruṣa*). And this is established by logical principle (*nyāya*). How? By the rule "when there is the mention of something meaningful, that which is meaningless is not included," there is the mention of meaningful items such as *bāhu* and so on; and that meaning is well-known, because it is immediately perceived.

Since the *Smṛti* treatise is, by its very meaning, beginningless, it is logical that only those [names] which denote beginningless referents should be included. For instance, there was a certain person named Bāhu; likewise, one named Kuñca or Naḍa—therefore, the suffix *iñ* alone applies, resulting in Kauñji and Nāḍi. However, in cases where a grammatical operation (*kārya*) is not prescribed by the inclusion of the specific form itself, but rather by another means, it applies even to names denoting contemporary referents, such as in "from *ata* comes *iñ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.95), resulting in Daivadatti.

Regarding the phrase "and of relative terms," the genitive case is used in relation to the grammatical operation (*kārya*); that is, when an operation prescribed for relative terms such as *śvaśura* ("father-in-law") is mentioned, its prohibition applies to something similar to them. This refers to the rule *saṃjñā-śvasurasya*. A person is called *śvasura* by virtue of being a name (*saṃjñā*), not because of a [blood] relationship. Thus, in the form *śvāsuris*, since the word *śvasura* derived in the *uṇādi* suffixes does not necessarily undergo the grammatical operations based on its etymological derivation, the rule *na yvābhyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.3) does not apply to this etymologically derived word *śvasura* [which ends in /r/].

Likewise, in the rule *mātṛpitṛbhyāṃ svasā*, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) does not occur when the word refers to a female relative by marriage (*dhānyamātṛ*). This too is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*); for while the technical term *śvaśura* has a beginning [in time], the relative term [itself] is beginningless. Even in the case of *mātṛpitṛbhyām*, the word denoting one's biological mother is understood because it is more commonly known. And it has been said:

"Those words whose referents are clearly manifest, which are independent, and renowned in the world—the purpose of the treatise should be applied to those words, and not to their mere verbal expressions."

The letter *ca* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; it indicates that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). The intention is that the inclusion refers to words not explicitly listed.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after *sudhātṛ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.97)

Regarding the passage beginning with *vyāsarudra* and so forth: one who arranges (*vyasyati*) the Veda is a *devavyāsa*; [the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*. This is an instance of using a part [of a word] for the whole—just as *Bhīmasena* is called *Bhīma*. *Varuḍas* and others are specific castes (*jāti*). Should that [suffix] then be stated? It need not be stated; these are simply other verbal roots ending in the *kan* suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*), according to the maxim of *avya* and *avika*, for the *kan* suffix is applied here and they do not form a sentence. Furthermore, even from the word *vyāsa* when denoting a seer (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *iñ* occurs because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *bāhu* (the *ākṛtigaṇa*).
The suffix *cphañ* is applied after words denoting a place of origin (*gotra*) such as *kuñja* and others.

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). If the letter *ca* were not used here, then one would have to state [the rule] as "after *vrāta* and *phañ*, when not feminine" (*vrātaphañor astriyām*); consequently, there would be no inclusion of the suffix *phañ* in the rule "after *aśva* and others, *phañ*" (*aśvādibhyaḥ phaṅ*). Regarding *kauñjāyanya*: the suffix *ñya* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*); however, in the plural, because it is a *tadrāja* suffix according to the rule "those beginning with *ñya* are *tadrāja*," there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "of a *tadrāja* suffix in the plural," and so forth.

Furthermore, in this case, does the accent belong to the *ñit* [suffix] or the *cit* [suffix]? To this, he says: "In the singular and dual numbers. For there, the *ñya* suffix is heard, and since it occurs later, the *ñit*-accent based upon it is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied). But in the plural number, once the *ñya* has ceased to apply, there is a deliberation: whether the accent belongs to the *ñit* or the *cit*. In that situation, the *ñit*-accent would prevail due to its posteriority; however, by virtue of the functional power (*sāmarthya*) of the marker *c*, the *cit*-accent will occur.

By virtue of the addition of the marker *ñit*, the accent of a *ñit* [element] would apply. But there is another purpose for adding the marker *ñit*: what is it? The letter *ñ* is for the sake of [triggering] *vṛddhi*. [Objection: Even in the case of adding the marker *cit*, there is another purpose; what is it? It is for the sake of [providing] a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). One could have attached another marker here for the purpose of providing a qualifier. In that case, the accent of a *cit* [element] will occur by following the presence of the letter *c*. [Reply: Then one could also attach another marker for the sake of *vṛddhi*. In that case, the accent of a *cit* [element] will occur by following the presence of the letter *c*.

In that case, another suffix (*anubandha*) could have been attached for the sake of *vṛddhi*; there, due to the presence of the marker *ñ*, the accent of a *ñit* suffix would have applied. This being the situation, the following is stated: even setting aside the subsequent accent of a *ñit* suffix, only the accent of a *cit* suffix is desired. The thought is as follows: a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding accent must be made: first, "of a *cit*" (*citaḥ*)—meaning the final syllable of a *cit* [suffix] becomes acute; then, "of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)"—meaning "of a *cit* [suffix] belonging to a *taddhita*," so that the final syllable of a *cit* suffix belonging to a *taddhita* becomes acute.

For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of subverting the *ñit*-accent which would otherwise apply by virtue of its higher status. Consequently, the rule "after *kit*, the end of a *taddhita* suffix is acute" applies. However, if the suffix *cphañ* were used, the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) "of a *taddhita*" could be dispensed with. Why, then, is it not formulated thus: "In the sense of a lineage (*gotra*), *cphañ* after *kuñja* and so on; *phak* in the sense of many; and [the same] after *naḍa* and so on"? It cannot be done in this way.

For in this case, there would be a fault: a young brahmin who is the descendant of the Kauñjāyanas is called *kauñjāyanyaḥ* (singular) and *kauñjāyanyau* (dual). In these forms, the suffix *ya* is heard [after the base]. Indeed, the suffix *cphañ* is prescribed for the formation of patronymics from bases ending in *iñ* when there is one or two descendants (*dvyekayoḥ*). However, when *ñya* is prescribed after a base ending in *cphañ*, then—since the *iñ* produced for a junior descendant (*yuvan*) undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule "the suffixes *ṇya*, *kṣatriya*, and *ārṣa* are elided" (*ṇyakṣattriyārṣañitaḥ*)—and since the elision of *ñya* itself would follow from the rule "there is elision of the *tadrāja* suffix" (*tadrājasya*), the hearing of the suffix *ya* occurs because of the prohibition in the rule "there is no elision (*aluk*) of the *gotra* suffix before a vowel" (*gotre 'lug aci*). Thus, the form *kauñjāyanya-* is established.

Just as there are many descendants of Kauñjāyana, when the suffix *iñ* is elided, because the term denoting a royal lineage (*tadrāja*) itself applies to the plural, the suffix *ñya* is also elided, resulting in the form *kauñjāyanāḥ*.
The suffix *phak* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *naḍa*.

"Śalaṅku" and "śalaṅkam": both end in the nominative case. The neuter gender is used with reference to the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*). The meaning is that this word-form "śalaṅku" becomes "śalaṅkam"; it transforms into that form. [The rule] "as in other cases, *iñ*" is stated because the group beginning with *bāhu* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. Even assuming that the suffix *phak* is prescribed only for the sake of denoting a lineage (*gotra*), he states the rebuttal: "Or rather... This refers to the state of being *iñ*. This is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the attainment of the state of being "śalaṅka. In the previous rebuttal, that very reading should be understood as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [attainment].

Regarding the rule *agniśarmanvṛṣagaṇa*: the word *agniśarman* takes the suffix *phak* when it belongs to the *vṛṣagaṇa* lineage; thus, if he is a descendant of Vṛṣagaṇa, he is called *āgniśarmāyaṇa*, whereas if he is otherwise, he is simply *āgniśarma*. Since the form *amuṣya* is recited [in the rule], although the base word *adas* alone should have been recited, because the form ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*) is recited, the elision (*luk*) does not occur even when *phak* is produced. Consequently, there is no need to include this term in the rule for non-elision (*alugvidhi*) regarding the forms *āmuṣyāyaṇa* and *āmuṣyaputrika*.

Regarding *kṛṣṇaraṇau* [as derived] from *brāhmaṇa* and *vāsiṣṭha*: if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he is *kārṣṇāyana*; otherwise, he is *kārṣṇirnya*. If he is a Vāsiṣṭha, he is *rāṇāyana*; otherwise, he is *rāṇiranya*. Regarding *kroṣṭu*, [the forms] *krauṣṭāyana* and *krauṣṭi* [are used]. *Krauṣṭāyanaḥ*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after words such as *harita* and others [to form patronymics].

In the rule *haritādibhyaḥ* and *añaḥ*, the two ablative endings are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which ends in the suffix *añ* that follows after [a word] beginning with *harita*. The author of the Vṛtti also explains this very point in reality by saying: "from those beginning with *harita* which end in *añ*. However, the meaning "the suffix *añ* occurs after *harita* and others in the sense of a lineage-descendant (*gotrāpatya*)" does not hold, because they are already included in the *bidādi* group.

"By implication (*sāmarthyāt*). This means that another *gotra*-suffix does not occur after a word already ending in a *gotra*-suffix; this is the implication. Therefore, even though the governing topic is *gotra*, it is understood that the suffix applies to the *yuvan* (descendant). And so, he says "the governing topic of *gotra*" to show that the governing topic of *gotra* is not interrupted in this way; the meaning is that the mention of *gotra* continues for the sake of what follows.
And [the suffix] *yañ* is applied after [a stem ending in] *īn*. (Pāṇini 4.1.101)

"By the mention of *gotra*, [the suffixes] *yañ* and *iñ* are specified," meaning those *yañ* and *iñ* which are prescribed in the sense of *gotra*. Since the descendant (*apatya*)—which is the meaning of the suffix—is not further specified in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix applying to any descendant whatsoever; therefore, he says: "This suffix applies only to the *yuvan* (descendant of a *yuvan*) following that [base ending in *yañ* or *iñ*]. The word "only" (*eva*) is for emphasis: not only does the previous suffix apply to the *yuvan*, but this one also applies only to the *yuvan*. Why? He says: "Because of the statement 'from *gotra* to *yuvan*.'"
The substitution of *śaradvata* for *śaradvat*, *śunaka* for *śunaka*, and *darbha* for *darbha* occurs before the patronymic suffixes *-bhṛgu*, *-vatsa*, and *-āgrāyaṇa*.

For those such as Śaradvat and others, who originate from lineages like that of Bhṛgu, there are both adopted sons and sons born of their own lineage; in that context, a specific qualification regarding offspring is made. In this regard, Bhṛgu is not the offspring of Śaradvat, because he existed prior to him.

Likewise, regarding *śunakasya vatsaḥ*: from that [name] come both *bhārgava* and *vātsya*, and *āgrāyaṇa*. In the case of a *dvandva* compound, because it expresses multiple referents simultaneously through a single substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*), the suffixes denoting lineage (*gotra*) are elided by the rule *atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca* and *yañañośca*. Thus he says: "if one is a Bhārgava and another a Vātsya. Regarding *dārbhiḥ*: the word *darbha* does not denote a seer (*ṛṣi*); rather, it should be read among the *bāhvādi* group.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is optionally applied after the words *droṇaparvata* and *jīvantā*.

It was stated previously: "And the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after *gotra*, starting from *śiva*," and so forth; here too it is stated: "only after *gotra*. To this, the objection arises: "How so? The meaning of the word *eva* (only) is that the [suffix] whose inclusion you have accepted as causing a fault in the case of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not included at all here. For example: *droṇa* in the *Mahābhārata* is *mahābhāratadroṇa*. Regarding the term "beginningless" (*anādi*): for it was just now stated: "in the list beginning with *bāhu*, etc. and so on.

"Is it not the case, then, that such an application is utterly untenable? To this he says: "But now... The meaning is "modern," and it does not mean that Droṇa of the *Mahābhārata* was contemporary with the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*); for the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) uses the term "Droṇa" equally for the beginningless [Vedic] figure and for the modern one. Among those, the descendants of the beginningless Droṇa who were contemporaneous with Aśvatthāman are called the *Droṇāyanas*.

In this regard, that which is observed as "gotra-ness" (the state of being a lineage) is superimposed by cognizers whose intellects have faltered upon Aśvatthāman as well, because he is the offspring of one denoted by the word Droṇa. Through that superimposition, the designation "Drauṇāyana" occurs for Aśvatthāman by means of the suffix indicating *gotra*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the group beginning with *bida* to form patronymics from names that do not belong to the *ṛṣi* class and which do not involve immediate succession.

"Only as a *gotra*. By this, he shows that those words denoting seers (*ṛṣi*) such as *Bida*, *Urvaya*, and so forth, [function] here only as a *gotra*; otherwise, they would not do so. Thus, he indicates that the term "*gotra*" must be understood as carrying over (*anuvartanīya*) here, by saying "but those which... and so on.

But how is this meaning obtained when the section on *gotra* (lineage) is under discussion? To this he says: "The meaning of *anṛṣyānantarya* is as follows. The term *anṛṣi* is an indication made with the elision (*luk*) of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*), and *ānantarye* contains the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, in cases such as *pautrāḥ* ("grandsons"), there is the designation of only the immediate descendant (*anantara*), and not of the *gotra*, nor of the general category of offspring (*apatya*). This is the meaning [of the rule].

For in this matter, since [the rule] applies to non-sages for the sake of prescribing [the suffix] for descendants who are not immediate, there would be no prohibition in a case where there is an uninterrupted succession of sage-descendants—that is, where there is an uninterrupted succession of those who are both sages and descendants (ṛṣyapatyāni), such that the descendants in the form of sages are continuous. What fault would there be in that? To this he says: "In that case, this... and so forth.

The sage Kaśyapa’s offspring is also a sage; thus, there are seven sages in uninterrupted succession, the seventh of whom is named Indrahū, [who belongs] to the Kāśyapas. In this case, the grammatical application [of the suffix *añ*] would not be appropriate; for if the suffix *añ* were present, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its elision (*luk*) by the rule "yañañośca. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the phrase "anṛṣyānantarye" (in the absence of non-sage succession) must be explained as: "when there is no interval—that is, when there is immediate succession—among sages, the suffix does not occur. He first establishes the correct usage: "in the form of an immediate offspring."

The meaning is "in the form of a general offspring" (*apatyasāmānyarūpeṇa*). It is not, however, prescribed that the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* applies to a descendant who is not immediately following [the founder]. In this regard, just as in examples such as "there was a king" (*abhūn nṛpaḥ*), where—despite the fact that there is actually a specific instance of what has come to be—the elision (*luk*) occurs because of the intention to express the general, so too here, although there is actually a lineage (*gotra*), the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* occurs by disregarding that specific form and intending to express the general form of offspring. But what is the reason for resorting to this laborious interpretation? To this he says: "And this must necessarily be understood in this way."

That prohibition whose scope is the uninterrupted lineage of the sages' offspring is described as such. [The text says] that Kauśika, namely Viśvāmitra, becomes defiled. What is the reason? Viśvāmitra performed austerities with the thought, "May I not be one who is not a sage, but rather may I indeed become a sage"; thereupon, your honor became a sage. He performed austerities again with the thought, "May I not have a son who is not a sage"; thereupon, Gādhi also became a sage.

He performed penance again, thinking, "May I not be the grandson of a non-seer (an-ṛṣi)"; thus, the venerable Kuśika also became a seer. Therefore, this continuity of seers (ṛṣyānantarya) is possible.

"Parastrī and paraśu. The word "occurs" (āpadyate) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. This means that the word *parastrī* gives rise to a suffix and undergoes the substitution (*ādeśa*) of *paraśu*. Thus, the offspring of another's wife (*parastriyā apatyam*) is a *pāraśava*, born from a Brāhmaṇa father and an unmarried Śūdra mother; and she, by birth, is a woman of excellent status (*varastrī*). However, one born from the wife of another is a *pārastraiṇeya*, which belongs to the *kalyāṇy-ādi* and *anuśatikā-di* groups.
In the case of *pāraśava*, because of the confusion between the preceding and following members of the compound, the grammatical operation prescribed for the *anuśatikā-di* group does not apply.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [patronymic bases] beginning with *garga*.

This will apply to the general category of offspring. Others, however, maintain that "Manu-tantu" is a single compound word and not two separate words recited; thus, there is the usage in the Brāhmaṇa: "He spoke to Mānutantavya," and it appears as such in the *pravara* formula: "Of the Kālavas, Manutantus, and Kuśikas."

"How is *mānavī* [formed]?"—the sense is that because [the word *manu*] is listed in the *lohita*-group, it ought to take the suffix *ṣpha* (which becomes *īna*) as a rule. "But when the immediate descendant is intended" means that one should understand this to apply even to the *gotra* [descendants]; thus, there is the usage in the *pravara* lists: *jāmadagnāḥ*, *vātsāḥ*. Regarding *vājāse*: the word *vāja* causes the suffix *yañ* to arise, provided it is not in a compound (*ase* = *asamāse*). However, in a compound, we have *sauvājiḥ*; the prohibition "not in a compound" (*ase*) is for the purpose of making known that the rule "by a nominal stem accompanied by a suffix that has a marker" (*grahaṇavatā prātipadikena*) is non-universal.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *madhu* and *babhru* when they are names of Brāhmaṇas belonging to the Kauśika lineage.
One should simply say "the Gaṇa Babhru-Kauśika," for in that case the mention of "two Babhru-s" would not have to be made; however, it was not done in that way.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *kapibodha* when followed by *āṅgirasa*.
*Kāpeya*: the suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule "itaścāniñaḥ. *Baudhi*: since he is not a *ṛṣi*, the suffix *iñ* is applied, or alternatively, [the name] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *vataṇḍa*. (Pāṇini 4.1.108)

"What is the purpose?"—this is the question: why was it not simply stated as *vataṇḍālluk striyām* (P. 4.1.103), and what is the purpose of this split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? He provides the answer: "Even in the *śiva* group, etc. The sage named Vataṇḍa is already established by the suffix *aṇ* due to his being a seer (*ṛṣi*); therefore, his inclusion in the *śiva* group is for the sake of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the *yañ* suffix from the *garga* group. The meaning is that the split of the rule is intended to prevent that [co-occurrence] even in the case of one belonging to the *āṅgirasa* lineage, just as it occurs when one does not belong to the *āṅgirasa* lineage.
The suffix *luk* is applied in the feminine. (Pāṇini 4.1.109)

Regarding "Vātaṇḍyāyanī": the suffix *ṣpha* applies by virtue of the characteristic [rule] beginning with "lohita. Regarding "Vātaṇḍī": because she is a seer (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *ṣyañ* will not apply.
The suffix *phañ* is applied after [words ending in] *aśva* and others.

As for those which are listed here as having the suffix *pratyaya* [denoting lineage]—namely *bailya*, *ānaḍuhya*, and *āttreya*: among them, the word *bailya* ends in *ñyaṅ* according to the rule "after a *vṛddha* [stem], after *kosala*, and after *ajāda*, [the suffix] *ñyaṅ* [is applied]" (*vṛddhetkosalājādāññyaṅ*); it refers to a royal sage named Vili. The word *ānaḍuhya* ends in *yañ* according to the *gargādi* group; and *āttreya* ends in *ḍhak* according to the rule "after a [stem ending in] *it*, except when it is *aniñ*" (*itaścāniñaḥ*).

Regarding "Śaya Ātreyi": the suffix *phañ* occurs after the word *śaya* if it refers to an *Ātreya*; thus, *śāyāyana*. If it is other than an *Ātreya*, it is *śāyi*: because he is not a seer (*ṛṣi*), the suffix *iñ* applies, or [the word belongs to] the *bāhv-ādi* group. Others, however, cite *aṇ* as the counter-example. Regarding "born of a male" (*puṃsi jāta*): *puṃsi* is a qualifier of the base noun; the offspring of one born [as a male] is *jātāyana*. But in the feminine, the offspring of one born [as a female] is *jāteya*, where only the suffix *ḍhak* occurs; otherwise, by the rule concerning gender-distinction (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), *phañ* alone would apply. Regarding "Ātreya Bharadvāja": [the suffix *iñ* applies].

If [the patronymic] Bhāradvāja is derived from Ātreyāyana, then—provided it is not from this [specific case] where *iñ* is elided by the rule "ṇyakṣattriya"—[the suffix] is applied as *bhāradvājāt* before *ātreye*. That is to say, when one born of the *Attri* lineage is adopted as a son by one born of the *Bhāradvāja* lineage, then the suffix [is applied]. For he is both an *Ātreya* and possesses the lineage (*gotra*) of *Bhāradvāja*. If *Bhāradvājāyana* is an *Ātreya*, then for another who is a *Bhāradvāja*, there is only the suffix *añ* from the *Bidādi* group.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words beginning with] *śiva* and others.

"Yathāyatham," etc. Among these, [the inclusion of *munika*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *iñ*. In the case of *muni*, *sandhi*, *bhūmi*, and so forth, the suffix *ḍhak* applies by the rule "after [a word] ending in *it* that does not have *iñ*. In the case of words ending in feminine suffixes, the suffix *ḍhak* is obtained by the rules "from feminine [names], *ḍhak*" and "from a word with two vowels. As for the words *gaṅgā* and *vipāṭ*, the [suffix] that would apply has already been stated by the author of the Vṛtti itself. However, the purpose for including the word *jārakāru* in the list must be considered. Some say: it should be read among the *śubhra* group so that the form *jāratkāreya* may occur; its inclusion there, however, is for the sake of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffix *ḍhak*.
However, the sublation of the *ṇya*-suffix is not desired; the reason for this will be stated in the rule "udīcām-iñ" (Pāṇini 4.1.135).

Regarding the rule *śubhrādibhyaś ca*: he will state under the rule *śubhrādibhyaś ca*—"The particle *ca* serves to include those not explicitly mentioned; it indicates that this [word] belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* (class of words defined by its form), whereby forms such as *gāṅgeyaḥ* and *pāṇḍaveyaḥ* are established. It is with this intention that the following was said. The words *rāvaṇa* and *viśravaṇa* are listed; these two are substitutes (*ādeśau*) for the word *viśravas*, or they occur as distinct bases (*prakṛtyantare*) having the same meaning in the context of derivative formation (*vṛtti*). Thus, the offspring of *viśravas* is *vaiśravaṇaḥ*, [also known as] *rāvaṇaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *dvyaco nadyāḥ*: for those two-syllable (*dvyaca*) words denoting rivers, such as *kulyā* and others, when the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply as an exception to the suffix *tannāmikāṇ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is prescribed by the rule *dvyacaḥ*; however, in this case, *aṇ* occurs instead. Thus we have *triveṇī* and *traivaṇam*. [The form] *traivaṇaḥ* means "the descendant of Triveṇī"; although the suffix *aṇ* is already established by the aforementioned rule, this specific statement is made for the purpose of providing the phonetic substitution (*ādeśa*).

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? Could it not simply be stated as "that which is prescribed by *yat*" (*yathāvihitam*)? If this were said, only suffixes such as *iñ* and others would apply, since they are prescribed; yet, by the force of the rule's restatement, that which is prescribed but does not otherwise obtain would become *aṇ*. In that case, the following is the purpose: the word *ṛṣṭiṣeṇa* is listed here. If it were stated merely as "that which is prescribed by *yat*," then *iñ* (by *ata iñ*) would be applicable; however, the suffix *ṇya*—characterized by the condition of ending in *senā*—would be applicable as its superseder. In that situation, by the force of the rule's restatement, *iñ* would still result. But because of the repeated mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs.
[The suffix ṅīṣ is applied] after names of rivers that are not feminine in the elder [sense], provided they are named after those [rivers]. 4.1.113.

In other treatises, the term *vṛddha* is defined as "an offspring that has disappeared" or "grown old," and its inclusion [in this context] is also observed; furthermore, the honorific use of *vṛddha* is seen in the rule *vṛddho yūnā*. However, here, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is stated that only the *vṛddha* established by this very treatise is intended—namely, "that which has *vṛddhi*" (*vṛddhir yasya*). The phrase "except for those beginning with *avṛt*, *u*, and *ṛ*" (*avṛdbhyaḥ*) is a property of the word (*śabdadharmah*). This is because, when there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *vṛddha*, by the maxim of "negation joined with *iva*," there is the cognition of a word similar to that [excluded one].

The feminine gender designation, however, is due to its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "from [names of] rivers and female humans" (*nadīmānuṣībhyaḥ*). But how can there be coordination between that which refers to a meaning and that which refers to a word-form? It is through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Because they are denotable by the term "non-vṛddha," only those female humans who are rivers are called "non-vṛddhas. Thus, the phrase "from [names of] rivers and female humans" refers to the property of the meaning. It is not a reference to the actual phonetic form (*svarūpa*), because of the use of the plural number and because of the exclusion of *vṛddha* [names]; furthermore, even a name that is a river is not included.

Because of the association with the word *mānuṣī* (human female), which functions in its worldly sense, the pronoun *tad-* in the expression *tannāmikābhyaḥ* refers back to the base of the suffix. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those rivers and human females for whom those non-*vṛddha* bases are their names. Thus, although the meaning itself is indicated by all three words, since it is impossible to prescribe a suffix directly upon that meaning, the suffix is produced from the bases that express that meaning.

This has been stated: "Therefore, because of non-difference, the *prakṛtis* (bases) are indicated. This means: because of the non-difference of the meaning. What is meant is this: the suffix *aṇ* occurs after those feminine names of rivers and human beings which are not designated by *vṛddhi* [vowels]. What is the sense? That the suffix occurs after those words that denote them. This is what he says: "Those which are not *vṛddha*, etc. And having done it in this way—namely, that it should have been stated as "after non-*vṛddha* names of rivers and human beings"—it was not stated in that manner; such is the point. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ḍhak*.
The intention is that because of the specification of the feminine gender, this rule does not apply to words such as *bhaidya*, *uddhya*, *śoṇa*, and so forth.
And [the suffix *yañ* is applied] after the names of seers (*ṛṣi*) and [the tribes of] Andhaka, Vṛṣṇi, and Kuru. Pāṇini 4.1.114.

The *ṛṣis* are well-known [sages] such as Vasiṣṭha and others. *Ṛṣis* are those who have seen the mantras; they are the well-known ones beginning with Vasiṣṭha, just like the deities beginning with Indra, who are to be designated by their respective names—this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "known as lineages" (*vaṃśākhyā*): the meaning is that these are the designations for certain lineages; that is to say, certain lineages are thus named. With the intention that "exceptions in the middle set aside preceding rules, but not subsequent ones," he says: "this is an exception to the suffix *iñ*. [This refers to the rule] "from *atṛ* and so forth."

In this regard, the scope (*avakāśa*) for the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*—as in *vāsiṣṭha*, by the rule "also after [a word] other than one ending in *-iN*"—is as follows; the scope for the suffix *ḍhak*—as in *ḍuler apatyam* (the descendant of *ḍuli*), namely *ḍauleya*—is as follows; in the case where both would apply, such as in *ātreyi*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs because it is subsequent in the order of rules. The scope for the suffix *ṇya* characterized by the word *senānta*—as in *hāriṣeṇya*—is as follows; for here, because the substitution of *ṣ* (by the rule "there is *ṣ* in a name when preceded by *a*") is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this [word] ends in *senā*; whereas the scope for *ṛṣyaṇ* is that same [case].

There is a sage named Jātasena; when both [suffixes] are applicable, because it is subsequent, the suffix *ṇya* occurs—*jātasenyaḥ*. Similarly, with the *iñ* of the Northerners—*jātaseniḥ*; this is the scope for the *aṇ* of the Andhakas—*śvāphalkaḥ*; for the *ṇya*, it is the same; from Ugrasena, who is an Andhaka, when both are applicable, because it is subsequent, the *ṇya* occurs—*augrasenyaḥ*. This is the scope for the *vṛṣṇyaṇ*—*vāsudevaḥ*; for the *ṇya*, it is the same; from Viṣvaksena, who is a Vṛṣṇi, the *vṛṣṇyaṇ* occurs—*vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*. This is the scope for the *kurvaṇ*—*nākulaḥ*; for the *ṇya*, it is the same; from Bhīmasena, who is a Kuru, the *kurvaṇ* occurs—*bhaimasenyaḥ*.

"By way of the 'crow-and-palm-fruit' maxim" means by chance. "Without confusion" means not mixed with other words. "Collected" means gathered together. "Very many" means all those that are intended to be etymologically explained. It is observed that even an eternal [entity] is explained through recourse to something non-eternal, as for example, time is explained through its locus in the Śakas. Or else, etc.: according to the principle stated in the rule "one should name [a child] after three ancestors," the lineages of the Andhakas and others are also indeed eternal. "The words which exist among them" refers to this.
The meaning is: from those very words such as *andhaka* and others that are used even today;
[the suffix *ṇyaṅ* is applied] after the word *mātṛ*, when preceded by a numeral, *ut*, *saṃ*, or *subhadra*. (Pāṇini 4.1.115)

Regarding *dvaimātura*: this is a *dvigu* compound for the sake of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), followed by the secondary derivative suffix. He has one biological son from one mother and an adopted son from another; thus he possesses two mothers (*dvaimātura*). Regarding *sāmmātura*: this is a secondary derivative following a *prādi* compound. Regarding *bhādramātura*: this is the suffix *aṇ* following a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

With the words "tena" and so forth, he demonstrates the purpose of the feminine gender designation with respect to the meaning. Regarding the term *dhānyamātuḥ*: one who measures grain (*dhānya*) is a *dhānyamātṛ*; this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) according to the rule for words beginning with *yājaka*. The meaning is that the word *mātṛ* occurring in *dhānyamātṛ* is not included [in the application of the rule]; therefore, in the form *sāmmātraḥ* (derived from *san-mimīte*, "he measures well"), the substitution of *u* does not occur. Furthermore, this feminine gender designation is a statement of the established principle (*nyāya-anuvāda*).
For since a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*) is more commonly known, it is logical that only that [the relative term] should be taken.

Regarding the question, "Why [is it said] 'preceded by a numeral or *saṃbhadrā*'?": First of all, there is no possibility of an application from the word alone, for the qualification "the offspring of a mother" (*mātuḥ apatyam*) is not possible; this is because the relationship with the mother is never absent in the case of offspring. Therefore, since the rule applies to that which ends in [the word *mātṛ*], the form preceded by a numeral and so forth is already established; this is the meaning of the question. The answer is: "It would also apply to that preceded by something else. [The example is given: *saumātraḥ*.

In some places, the following passage appears immediately after: "Because of the recitation of *śubhra* and others [in the list of *mātṛ*], he is a *vaimātreya*. The intention is that, for this reason, the word *mātṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* should not be cited as a counter-example. We, however, say: since the term *strī* in the rule *strībhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120) is understood as referring to a suffix (*strīpratyaya*), the suffix *ḍhak* does not apply here even if the meaning (*artha*) were not explicitly mentioned. This passage actually belongs immediately after the rule *aiḍaviḍo dāradaḥ* (4.1.120), but it has been written here by scribes through error.
The word *kanyā* may optionally take the suffix *kanīna*. (Pāṇini 4.1.116)

The term *ḍhaka* is an exception (*apavāda*) to what would otherwise be obtained by the rule "from a word ending in two syllables. Thus, the offspring of a *kanyā* is called *kānīna*. The basis for the application of the word *kanyā* is the absence of sexual intercourse with a man preceded by the sacramental rite of marriage as prescribed in the scriptures; it is not merely the state of having an intact hymen (*akṣatayonitva*). For a woman who has sexual intercourse with a man without the sacramental rite of marriage does not lose her status as a *kanyā*.

Therefore, this objection should not be raised: "If she is not an offspring (*apatya*), then she is not a maiden (*kanyā*); if she is an offspring, then she is not a maiden; for it is a contradiction to say she is both a maiden and an offspring. Another says: "Due to the greatness of a sage or a deity, she does not lose her status as a maiden even upon union with a man—just as Kuntī, just as Satyavatī; this is the example here. Thus he says: "Karṇa is *kānīna* (born of a maiden), Vyāsa is *kānīna*."
The suffix *cha* is applied after *vikarṇa*, *śuṅga*, and *chagala* when followed by *vatsa* and *bharadvāja*, provided that three generations have passed.

In this context, since Vatsa and the other *mūlaprakṛtis* cannot be offspring (*apatya*) in relation to Vaikarṇa and the others, the words *Vātsya* and so forth—which end in an *apatya*-suffix—function as a *dvandva* compound denoting multiple substrates; consequently, the plurality inherent in each member is already accounted for by the elision (*lopa*), and thus the *apatya*-suffix is indicated by its elision (*luk*). This is what he states: "If [the person] is a Vātsya, he is a Vaikarṇa," and so forth.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after words denoting females [to form patronymics].

Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *strī*," and so forth: it does not mean the inclusion of the word-form (*svarūpa*) itself, because of the use of the plural number (*bahuvacana*). Nor does it mean the inclusion of the referent (*artha*) of the word *strī*, because the referent of the word *vimātṛ* is listed among the *subhrādi* group [of words]. Its status as referring to a female (*stryarthatva*) is to be understood from its association with the word *vidhavā*. Furthermore, the *svarita* accentuation of the word *strī* is prescribed, and through the *svarita* accent, the governing scope (*adhikāra*) is understood; therefore, it is proper that only those words ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others are included.

However, suffixes such as *ktin* and others are not included because they involve an intervention [of other elements]. For example, in *aiḍaviḍaḥ* and *dāradaḥ*: from the word *iḍaviṭ*, by the rule *janapada-śabdāt kṣatriyād-añ*, and from the word *darada*, by the rule *dvyañ-magadha-* etc., the suffix *aṇ* is applied. In the feminine form of these two, by the rule *ataś-ca*, there is elision (*luk*); thereafter, for the descendant (*apatya*) of those, only *aṇ* occurs. Regarding the phrase "when *vṛṣan* is to be expressed": *vṛṣan* means a stallion. Because that specific meaning is prescribed by a particular rule, it subverts the suffix *ḍhak* in the sense of a descendant; therefore, only *aṇ* occurs for the descendant. In the case of *vāḍavaḥ*, even the suffix *ḍhañ*—which is prescribed for quadrupeds—does not apply, because it does not denote a quadruped.

"Aṇ" [is applied] after "kruñca. The word "vṛṣa" is not required; this rule applies specifically to the offspring. It is an exception to the suffix "ḍhak. In the compound "kruñcā-kokilā," which is a collective dvandva, there is the shortening of the feminine vowel.
A word consisting of two syllables [is called a *gati* when it precedes a verb]. || 4.1.121 ||
The suffix *kāṇ* with that name is an exception (*apavāda*), because it is established elsewhere by the preceding rule alone.
And [the suffix *cha* (i.e., *īya*) is applied] after [words beginning with] *śubhra*. (Pāṇini 4.1.123)

"According to the application," and so forth. In that regard, [the suffix] *iñ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to those ending in *ad*; for words such as *śalākā*, there is the suffix *aṇ* derived from their own names (*tannāmika*); from the word *vidhavā*, however, there is the suffix *ḍhrak* characterized by the rule for small animals (*kṣudra*); for words denoting four-footed animals, there is the suffix *ḍhañ* characterized by the rule for four-footed animals; from the word *godhā*, there is *ḍhrak* according to the rule "of *godhā*" (*godhāyā ḍhrakaḥ*); because of an explicit statement (*vacana*), that [suffix] also occurs. In some cases, there is the general suffix *aṇ*. As in *pāṇḍaveya*: the elision [of the final vowel] does not occur by the rule "*ḍhelopo'kadravā*" (Pāṇini 6.4.144), because by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *kadrū*, a feminine form is understood; or rather, the suffix is applied directly from the word *pāṇḍava*.

Regarding "lākṣaṇeya" and "śyāmeya" as [patronymics] of Vasiṣṭha: if he is a descendant of Vasiṣṭha, he is *lākṣaṇeya*, whereas another [descendant] is *lākṣaṇi*; if he is a descendant of Vasiṣṭha, he is *śyāmeya*, whereas another [descendant] is *śyāmāyana*, due to the suffix *phañ* [applied after the word *śyāma*] because it belongs to the *aśva*-class.
Or [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *kulaṭā*. (Pāṇini 4.1.127)

The term *kulaṭā* is derived from the sense "one who wanders among families" (*kulāny aṭati*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words such as *mūlavibhuja* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). The suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādy-ac*) is not applicable here, because if it were, the suffix *aṇ* would have to apply by the rule of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*)—namely, that when there is no upapada, an *akārānta* stem takes *aṇ*, whereas a stem with a *karmopapada* takes *ac*. However, the intended meaning is: "she who, while wandering among families, breaks her character. That is to say, a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) who, having entered one family, wanders to another family is of bad character; she is a *kulaṭā*. Regarding the phrase "because of the priority of the rule *kṣudrābhyo vā*" (Pāṇini 4.1.132): *kṣudrāḥ* refers to those who are physically deformed or deficient in character. But this [present] rule includes the case of one who, though of good character, wanders among families out of a desire to obtain alms.
The suffix *airak* is applied after the word *caṭakā*. (Pāṇini 4.1.128)

He says that because the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) is specified, the suffix does not apply after the masculine form; thus he states, "it should be stated [the rule applies] even after *caṭaka*. In this way, the masculine form alone should have been mentioned, for by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim that a word denotes also its gender-specific forms), it would also apply after the feminine form. However, it was not done in that manner. Regarding the statement, "in the case of a feminine [stem], the elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix should be stated," as in "the offspring of *caṭakā*" (*caṭakāyā apatyam*), it should be understood that this also applies to the masculine *caṭaka*. Thus, in the form *caṭakā*, once the feminine suffix *ṭāp* has been elided by the rule *luktaddhitaluki*, the *ṭāp* characterized by beginning with a vowel (*ajādilakṣaṇa*) must be applied again.
The suffix *āru* is applied after the word *āra* in the sense of "northerly."

[The objection is raised: "Because [the suffix] *rak* is already established. [The reply is: There is no distinction even in the case of the *avagraha*, according to the principle that "word forms are not to be followed by means of a grammatical rule" (*lakṣaṇa*). However, the phrase "for the sake of an indicator" (*jñāpakārtham*)—the word *jñāpaka* here has the state of being [an indicator] as its primary meaning—or rather, it should be read as "for the sake of making known" (*jñāpanārtham*). [Examples are] *jāḍāraḥ* and *pāṇḍāraḥ*. Since this suffix [is taught] after bases ending in a short vowel, there would be no establishment [of the form] with the suffix *rak*.
Or [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting small things. 4.1.131.
"Those with deficient limbs" refers to those who are one-eyed and so forth. "Those deficient in virtue" refers to female slaves who have no fixed master and others of that sort.
There is elision of the suffix *ḍhak*. (Pāṇini 4.1.133)

"But how," and so forth. The question arises because, in the rule for the suffix *ḍhak*, there is a mention of words ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others, yet this word is not included among the *śubhra* group. "This very [point]," and so forth: for that which does not exist cannot function as a cause (*nimitta*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *mātṛṣvasṛ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.134)

The phrase "of the father's sister" (*pitṛṣvasuḥ*) is understood here; that is to say, it is drawn forward by the particle *ca*. He demonstrates the meaning that results from its recurrence: "that which was stated regarding the father's sister. What, then, is that? He says: "the suffix *chaṇ* [is applied], and there is elision (*lopa*) when *ḍhak* follows. The sense is that, according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding," only the elision (*lopa*) of *ḍhak* would apply, and not *chaṇ*; thus, one should not raise an objection.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after words ending in *catuṣpād*.
The word *kamaṇḍalu* has four meanings; for it is seen [in usage]—such as "one should place the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*)". *Jambu* means a jackal.
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the words beginning with *gṛṣṭi*. (Pāṇini 4.1.136)

Regarding the term *aṇādīnām*: by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the suffix *ḍhak* is included. The plural number is used because those two [suffixes] are numerous due to the diversity of their bases. Among them, for the words *aja*, *basti*, and *mitrayu*, this [suffix *yañ*] is an exception to *aṇ*; for the remaining [bases], *ḍhak* applies according to the rule "*itaścāniñaḥ*. As for the word *gṛṣṭi*, it means that every female who has given birth once is a *gṛṣṭi*, not only four-footed animals such as cows; this is the intended meaning. Another [author] says: the word *gṛṣṭi* is applied figuratively even to non-quadrupeds on the basis of the common property of having given birth once.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *rājan*, *śvaśura*, and others.

"If it is the *kṣatriya* caste" means that the *kṣatriya* caste would be understood through the combination of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). Regarding "rājanya": there is the preservation of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule "and [there is no elision] when [the suffix] denotes non-existence or an action. Regarding "rājano 'nya" (one other than a king): this refers to one born of a Vaiśya or Śūdra woman; there is the preservation of the base form by the rule "aṅ."
The suffix *ha* is applied after the word *kṣatra*.

The suffix *gha* occurs. It is the word *gha* itself, and not the suffixes *tarap* or *tamap*; otherwise, since *gha* would be understood as referring to *tarap* and *tamap* in every rule prescribing a suffix, the statement regarding the substitution of *iy* for the initial *gh* of the suffix would be untenable. Nor can it be argued that *ghan* (in *tugrāddhan*) and *ghac* (in *ghacchau ca*) provide scope [for the term *gha*], because even there, a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) accompanied by an *anubandha* is employed. This is possible because the *anubandha* serves to distinguish the specific technical term, just as in the case of the rule *ṅamuṇnityam*.

Even in the rule "kim-id-abhyāṃ vo ghaḥ," it is understood that only the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are subject to replacement by *gha*. This [suffix *gha*] is also a word denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*). The meaning is that when denoting the *rājanya* genus, the suffix *gha* occurs; however, when produced from a *vaiśya* or a *śūdra*, only the suffix *iñ* occurs.
The suffix *kha* is applied after a word denoting a family (*kula*).

Regarding the phrase "in the subsequent sūtra" (*uttarasūtra*) and so forth: the purpose of this negation of the preceding word (*pūrvapadapratiṣedha*) is to prevent [the application of the suffix] to words such as *āḍhyakula*. Since the rule prohibiting the extension of an operation to that which ends with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a suffix (*grahaṇavatā*) already ensures that it will not apply to *āḍhyakula* and the like, the Teacher perceives that this prohibition does not actually apply to the word *kula*. Consequently, in this context, there is indeed the inclusion of that which ends in [the word], because of the continued application of the principle "that by which an operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it" (*yena vidhistadantasya*), whereas in other cases, there is the inclusion of the simple form itself (*svarūpa*).

And the indicator depends on the general rule (*sāmānyāpekṣa*): "The *paribhāṣā* which contains the hearing of the term *prātipadika* does not apply to the word *kuśala*; therefore, the [rule] *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* also does not apply. In the case of *kulīna*, because the word *anyatarasyām* is included in the subsequent sūtra, the suffix *kha* occurs even from the simple base [by this rule]. A "family" (*kula*) is an excellent lineage; its offspring means the offspring of one who originates from that [lineage].
After a word that does not have *apūrva* as its first member, the suffixes *yaṅ*, *ḍhak*, and *kañ* are optionally employed [to form a feminine derivative].

But surely, the term *pūrvapada* (first member) is conventionally restricted to a constituent part of a compound; thus, its application to the word *kula* (family/clan) would not be appropriate? To this he says: "belonging to a compound," and so forth. A first member belonging to a compound is also somehow related to the word *kula*, since both are constituents of the same single compound. Furthermore, no doubt regarding [the term's] being used in a restrictive sense (*vyavasthāvacana*) should be raised here; for the term *pūrvapada* is conventionally established as denoting a constituent of a compound.
Therefore, one should not entertain any suspicion of a prohibition in a sentence such as "Devadatta is well-born" (*devadattaḥ kulīnaḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "even from that which has *bahuc* as its prior member": if it were stated simply as "from that which does not have [another] prior member" (*apūrvāt*), then in the case of the word *bahukula*, since it consists of *bahuc* followed by a prior member, the suffix would not apply there. Furthermore, a prohibition would also apply in cases such as "Devadatta is well-born" (*kulīna*). Therefore, the mention of the word (*pada*) must be made in order to include those that are conventional (*rūḍhi*).
The suffix *vyansac* is applied in the sense of "enemy" (*patna*).

But surely, since the word *sapatnī* itself is derived as feminine in the rule "nityaṃ sapatnyādiṣu," how can there be a masculine usage? To this he says: "the word *sapatna*," and so forth. "In the sense of *iva*" means in the sense of similarity; that is, the similarity that just as a wife (*patnī*) is a cause of suffering, so too is an enemy (*śatru*). "If [it is] by the whole [compound]" means...

By this, he demonstrates that the meaning here is the collective whole (*samudāyārtha*), namely "rival" (*sapatna*), and not the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), nor even a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix; thus, both the base and the suffix are indeed devoid of independent meaning in this context. Now, why is it that *sapatna* does not serve as a qualifier of the descendant (*apatya*) which is being carried over [from a previous rule]? To this he says: "In this case, the sense of 'descendant' simply does not exist. He clarifies this very point by means of an example: "by the evil rival (*pāpmanā bhrātṛvyeṇa*)."

For an evil person (pāpmā) is not the offspring of a brother; therefore, since the word *bhrātṛvya* is seen to apply to any mere rival (*sapatna*), it does not here have the sense of "offspring. Furthermore, even that rival who might be the offspring of a brother is understood from the word *bhrātṛvya*—which has an acute accent on the first syllable—as being merely a rival (*sapatna*) and not as an offspring. Thus, the co-occurrence of the forms *bhrātṛvyaḥ* and *bhrātṛvyaḥ* occurs for two words ending in different suffixes (*vyat* and *yat*); hence it is rightly said: "There is no sense of 'offspring' at all."
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [words beginning with] *revatī*. (Pāṇini 4.1.146)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *ḍhak* and others. In that context: the word *revatī* ends in *ṅīṣ*; from the root *pālayati* with the words *aśva*, *maṇi*, and *dvāra* as upapadas, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), followed by *ṅīp*. In these cases, the suffix *ḍhak* would otherwise have been applicable. From the root *vañcu* in the sense of "deceiving," with *vṛka* as an upapada, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "when the agent is a standard of comparison" (*kartaryupamāne*); here, the suffix *aṇ* would have been applicable. From the root *grah* with *vṛkakarṇa* and *daṇḍa* as upapadas, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*). [The compound] *kukkuṭākṣaḥ* means "one whose eyes are like those of a cock"; in these cases, the suffix *iñ* would have been applicable.
The suffix *ṇa* is also applied after the word *gotra* when used in the sense of contempt for a woman.

He states that the term *gotra* is taken here in its technical sense: "the offspring [is called] *pautra*. It does not, however, refer to the worldly sense of offspring in general; for if that were the case, he would have simply said *tatstriyāḥ*, since the meaning would already be obtained by referring back to the relevant offspring (*apatya*) through the word *tat*. As in the example: *gārgaḥ*.

The word *gārgī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *yañaśca*. By the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite*, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) other than one beginning with *āḍha*; thus, from the word *gārgya*—which denotes a female descendant in the lineage (*gotra*)—the suffix is applied. Then, by the rules *yasyeti ca* and *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'nāti*, the elision of the *i* and the elision of the *ya* occur. Thus, [we derive] *glaucukāyana*.

The descendant of Glucuka is formed by the suffix *phin* according to the rule "for Easterners, *phin* is frequently applied after a non-vṛddha [stem]," and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule "after a word denoting a human species ending in *i*. The [feminine marker] is then removed through the application of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). From that [base], the suffix is applied; the *ṇ* in the suffix is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi*, because in cases such as *gārgya*, the base itself is already *vṛddha*.

In this case, however, the feminine descendant (apatya) in the lineage (gotra) of Vataṇḍa is *vataṇḍī*, according to the rule *vataṇḍācca luk striyām*. Her descendant is *vātaṇḍaḥ*—meaning "a wretch"—where, by virtue of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), the suffix *ṅīp* is removed. Because the prohibition *gotre 'lug aci* applies to the rule *luk striyām*, the suffix is added directly from the word *vātaṇḍya* itself.

And here, in the case of *gārgābhārya*—meaning "one whose wife is a Gārgī," a female descendant of Garga—the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is established by the rule *jāteśca* alone; for in the rule *gotraṃ ca caraṇaiḥ saha*, "lineage" (*gotra*) is taken to mean "any offspring" (*apatya*) in general. Therefore, the prohibition of the masculine form based on the rule *vṛddhinimittasya ca* is not required as a purpose [in this instance].

Furthermore—there is no suffix in the sense of "the female descendant of Garga" (gārgyā apatyaṃ strī), because the prohibition "not when [denoting] a female" (astriyām) precludes the designation *yuvan*, leaving only the designation *gotra* to remain; and since there is the rule "only one [suffix] in the *gotra* lineage" (*eko gotre*), another *gotra*-suffix cannot possibly follow a word already ending in a *gotra*-suffix. Consequently, there is no such form as *gārgā*, and certainly none for *gārgābhāryaḥ*.

Another says: There exists [the form] *gārgī*; how so? A female descendant of Gārgya is neither a *yuvati* (a young woman) nor a *gotra* (lineage); for she is not the direct offspring (*apatya*) of Garga, since the designation *gotra* is prescribed only for a descendant from the grandson onwards. Due to the absence of that [direct descent], the restriction "in the case of a *gotra*" does not apply, and consequently, because the suffix *ṇa* is present, *gārgī* exists.

However, those who say "there is no [such rule]," Gārgi, think as follows: both lineages—the maternal and the paternal—contribute to this offspring; for it is the cause of its descent (*apāta*). Consequently, where there is an offspring of Gārgī who is female, she is indeed the offspring of Garga. Furthermore, the mention of "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for even more remote offspring. Thus, because she belongs to the *gotra* of Garga, by the restrictive rule "only one [suffix] is used in the *gotra*," there is an absence of any other suffix.

In the *Vṛtti*, however, it is sometimes read: "The suffix occurs in reference to a youth (*yuvan*) after [a word denoting] a lineage (*gotra*) and so forth. That too is consistent with this very position; thus he says: "The male offspring of Gārgī who is a youth is a *gārgeya* boy. This usage is intended as an illustration for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others, and thus there is no censure.
In the Sauvīra country, the suffix *aṭhac* is frequently applied after a word ending in *vṛddhi*.

Here, "vṛddha" is understood in the sense of "that [stem] whose initial vowel among its vowels is *vṛddhi*," as defined by this very treatise; it is not the "vṛddha" defined in other grammatical systems as "a descendant whose lineage is remote. For the author will state in the subsequent sūtra: "The mention of *phin* is not for *phin*, because of the governing context of *vṛddha*. The phrase "among the Sauvīras" is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*). This means that since the term "gotra" is carried over from the rule "of a female of the gotra" (*gotrastriyāḥ*), it serves as a qualifier for that base which ends in a gotra suffix. Thus, the meaning is "from a *vṛddha* gotra belonging to the Sauvīras."

This also applies only when "vṛddha" is understood in its technical (pāribhāṣika) sense; otherwise, it should have been stated as "from that which is *vṛddha* among the Sauvīras. Regarding *bhāgavittāyana*: the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *yañiñośca*. Regarding *tārṇabindavaḥ*: since Tṛṇabindu's descendant is formed with the general (*autsargika*) suffix *aṇ*, [the form] is *tārṇabinda*, from which *ṭhak* is then applied. The previous mention of *ṭhak* was connected with *ṇa*; therefore, if that were to recur here, *ṭhak* would also recur. Hence, it is mentioned again here.

"Bhāga" as the first member [of a compound] results in "vitti. This means that it ends in *vitti*; that is to say, the word *bhāgavitti*. Regarding the rule "the suffix *ṭhak* is frequently applied after a *gotra* [term]," since the mention of *gotra* is carried over from the rule "after a female *gotra*," the suffix *yaṣṭhak* is stated to be applied frequently after a nominal stem denoting a *gotra*. The meaning of this verse of enumeration is that this [suffix] occurs only after those three, namely *bhāgavitti* and the others, and not after any others.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the mention of *gotra* (lineage) continues [from the previous rule], and since a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) belonging to the Sauvīra lineage and its usage is necessarily "vṛddha" (possessing a vṛddha vowel in the first syllable), for what purpose is the mention of *vṛddha* made? [Response: To this he says: "The mention of *vṛddha* is for the purpose of excluding the feminine. For that mention of *gotra* is a qualifier of the feminine; therefore, if it were to continue, the mention of the feminine would also continue. However, by the force of the mention of *vṛddha*, they explain that only the mention of *gotra* continues, and not the mention of the feminine.

Regarding the statement "the offspring is hidden when it is old," if one were to take this as referring to an actual aged person, this passage would be inconsistent. For example, [the form] *aupagaviḥ*.

But surely, [one might argue], this [undesired application] will not occur here simply because of the enumeration? That is not so; for the author of the Sūtras does not intend to prevent over-extension by relying on a recent enumeration. He states the purpose of the inclusion of the term *bahula*—namely, "the inclusion of *bahula*, etc."—in order to demonstrate the very variety [of application], beginning with the rule "of a woman belonging to the *gotra*," and so forth. Among those, the last [case] refers specifically to a *gotra* of the Sauvīras; this is precisely the point that must be established through effort.
And [the suffix] *pheś* is applied after the word *cha*. 4.1.149.

Regarding "Yāmundaśca" and so forth: here, the neuter gender in the word *vārṣyāyaṇī* is used in view of the form of the word [as a generic term]. Regarding "phiñ": the meaning is "those ending in the suffix *phiñ*. Regarding "smṛtāḥ": the meaning is that these three bases ending in *phiñ* are traditionally recognized [as such]. Regarding "and in the case of the Sauvīras, when expressing contempt": the word *ca* ("and") was not repeated out of fear of breaking the meter. This point, which is established by the inclusion of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of "in various cases"), was previously shown by the author of the Vṛtti; however, since it is now presented by the author of the Ślokavārttika, there is no redundancy.

The word *suyāma* also belongs to the *tikādi* group. *Vārṣyāyaṇi* is the offspring of *vṛṣa*. This too belongs to the *tikādi* group; for according to the rule, "In the case of *dagu*, *kosala*, *karmāra*, *chāga*, and *vṛṣa*, there is the augment *yuṭ* when *āyana* is prescribed," the augment *yuṭ* is added once the substitution of *āyana* has been made.
The suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* are applied after [the patronymic bases] Phāṇṭāhṛti and Mimat respectively.

Therefore, in this case, there is no application according to the respective order of enumeration (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). By adopting this view, the designation of *ṇ* as having the marker *ṇit* becomes purposeful; for that [designation] serves the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* in the word *mimataḥ*. However, if the rule were applied according to the respective order of enumeration, then because *phāṇṭāhṛti* would already be a *vṛddha* (possessing a *vṛddhi* vowel in the first syllable), the designation of *ṇ* as *ṇit* would be redundant. In this context, however, one should observe that in a form such as *phāṇṭāhṛtābhāryaḥ*, rules such as the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) apply, just as in the case of *gārgābhāryaḥ*.

However, according to the Vārttika, the correspondence [of the rules] is accepted here as follows; as it says: "The addition of the marker *ṇ* to the root *phaṇṭāhṛti* is unnecessary because [the word] is already considered *vṛddha*; furthermore, it is for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); or else, it has already been stated."
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *kṛvṛ*.

But surely, since the suffix *ṇya* is already established for the word *kuru* by the rule *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*, for what purpose is it listed here? To this he says: "There is yet another [suffix] after the word *kuru*. It is true that there will be another suffix *ṇya*; however, by the phrase *tattriyāt*, he indicates a difference in meaning. By the phrase *tadrājasaṃjñakaḥ*, he indicates a difference in form. "Because of its inclusion among the *tikādi* group"—both the words *kuru* and *kauravya* are listed there. But as for the *kārin* [suffix], it is from the word *rathakāra*. *Kārin* means an artisan (*śilpin*). He considers that the *rathakāra* caste, however, does not have the occupation of an artisan.

The rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) does not apply to this [word]. This is because [the rule] prescribed by "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" would, if it were to apply, result in the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule "nastaddhite. Why does it not apply? He says: "By virtue of the mention of the feminine suffix. Even though the masculine form is also recited, the suffix is established from the word *keśinī* as well by the *paribhāṣā* "a word qualified by gender [includes its feminine form]. However, the sense is that it will not occur from the masculine form due to a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).

He explains the statement regarding the *gaṇa* (list) that "for *vāmaratha*, as for *kaṇva* and others, [the suffix is elided] except for *svara* (accent)" with the words beginning "the word *vāmaratha*," etc. "Of that" (*tasya*)—by virtue of the context, this should be understood as "of that which ends in the suffix *ṇya*. "Like *kaṇva* and others" (*kaṇvādivat*): since no specific grammatical operation is prescribed for those [names] alone, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of whatever operation applies to *kaṇva* and others when they end in *yañ*. "Elision and so forth" (*lugādikam*).

In the case of [the suffixes] ending in *yañ* such as those beginning with *kaṇva*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of only that grammatical operation which is observed [in the base], but not of the status of being a member of the *kaṇva*-class and so forth; for this very reason, he says "with the exception of accent" (*svaravarjam*). By this, elision (*luk*) and other operations are also extended, but not the rule for the introduction of the suffix itself, namely, "after [names] beginning with *kaṇva*, in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*). Regarding *vāmarathāḥ*: by the rule "and after [stems ending in] *yañ* and *añ*" (*yañañośca*), there is elision (*luk*) when the plural is expressed. Furthermore, from the suffix *yañ*, the secondary suffix *ṣpha* is applied according to "the *ṣpha* of the Easterners is a secondary suffix" (*prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*); and in the sense of a descendant (*yūni*), the suffix *phak* is applied according to "after [stems ending in] *yañ* and *iñ*" (*yañiñośca*).

When secondary (śaiṣika) meanings are intended, although *cha* would otherwise apply, *aṇ* occurs by virtue of the rules "from Kaṇva and others, in the sense of lineage" (*gotra*) and "in the sense of a corporation, a limb, or a characteristic" (*saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣu*). Thus, from *samrāj*, [the form] *sāmrājyaḥ* is derived provided he is a Kṣatriya; otherwise, he is not a *sāmrāja*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *senānta* and after words denoting characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). 4.1.152.

He states that "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the grasping of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), by saying "from the word *lakṣaṇa*. He states that "agent" (*kārin*) refers to the grasping of the meaning (*artha*), by saying "and from words denoting an agent" (*kārivacanebhyaśca*). Those who perform [their work] well are "agents" (*kāriṇaḥ*), namely, artisans (*śilpinaḥ*). Regarding "nāpitya": according to the opinion of the Easterners (*prācām*), the suffix *ṇya* is cited as the example. However, according to the opinion of the Northerners (*udīcām*), because it is of higher priority, only the suffix *phiñ* applies by the rule "udīcāṃ vṛddhāt," resulting in *nāpitāyaniḥ*.
The suffix *min* is applied after a word denoting a direction in the north (*udīc*) [to form a feminine noun]. 4.1.153.

Regarding *tākṣṇa*: by the rule *ṣapūrvahandhaṛtarājñāmaṇi*, there is elision (*allopa*) of the penultimate vowel. Regarding *tākṣaṇya*: by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Here, it should be stated that [the suffix] is optional after words ending in *senā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kārin*; there is no need for this specific mention of *iñ*, nor for the inclusion of the word *takṣan* in the *śivādi* list. For if the suffix *ṇya* were made optional, then whichever suffix would apply from a given base would indeed apply—namely, *aṇ* by *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* after *tākṣṇa*, and *iñ* by *ata iñ* after others? This cannot be so; for if it were thus, then after names such as *jātasena*, the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed for *ṛṣi* names) would undesirably apply.
The suffix *phiñ* is applied after words beginning with *tika*.

Regarding the phrase "denoting a Kṣatriya": this refers to [the word] derived by the rule *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*.
