Regarding the word *auraśa*: one who lies on the chest (*urasā śete*) is an *uraśa* Kṣatriya; the form is according to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. His descendant is formed with the suffix *añ* by the rule *janapadaśabdātkṣatriyāt*.

Why, then, is the inclusion of the term denoting a Kṣatriya explained with such effort? To this he says: "And thus," etc. "It has been illustrated" means that it has been so stated even by previous commentators (*vṛttikāra*).

From the root *tiki* with the suffix *ka*, because its penultimate vowel is *ṛ*, we have *tika*. One who acts as if asking "What do you have? is a *kitava*; this is derived from the *pṛṣodarādi* group. From the root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*; in the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is added, resulting in *saṃjñā*. One whose crest (*śikhā*) is bound by children is *bālaśikha*. Others say there are two words: from the causative of the root *bal* comes *bāla*, and from that, *bālāyani*. By the word *śikhā*, one possessing it is indicated; thus, *śaikhāyani*. The word *uraśa* has been etymologically explained.

From *śaṭha* with the suffix *kutsā*, the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*) is applied; then, by virtue of belonging to the *gargādi* group, the suffix *yañ* is added—yielding *śāṭya*. From this, the suffix *phiñ* is applied for the junior descendant (*yūni*). From the word *sindhu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *dvyañmagadha*; thus *saindhava*. Here too, *phiñ* is applied for the junior descendant. That which drinks Yama is *yamunda*; this belongs to the *śakandhvādi* group. That which possesses an excellent form (*praśastaṃ rūpam asya asti*) takes the suffix *ya* by the rule *rūpād āhata-praśaṃsayoḥ*; thus *rūpya*. That which exists in a village (*grāme bhavaḥ*) is *grāmya*. For the root *nīla* meaning "color," the suffix *ka* is applied because it has a semivowel (*ig*) in its penultimate position; thus *nīla*. For the root *am* meaning "disease," the suffix *itra* is applied according to the *auṇādika* rules; thus *amitra*.

*Gaukākṣya* is derived from *garga* with the suffix *yañ*. *Kuru*: by the rule *kṛgroruḥ*, [the form] *kuruḥ* is obtained. *Devaratha*: one whose chariot is like that of a god. *Titila*: [from *tila*] *tila-tilaḥ*; this belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group; from that, the possessive suffix *in* is added (*titil-in*), and the regular *aṇ* is applied for the descendant (*apatyam*); by the rule *nastaddhite*, there is elision of the final *i*, resulting in *taitilaḥ*. The word *auraśa* has been etymologically explained. *Kauravya*: by the rule *kurunādibhyo ṇyaḥ*.

*Bhūrika* means one who possesses much, such as rice and other grains; in its place, by the rule for *kapila* and others, there is the substitution of *la*, resulting in *bhūlika*. From these two, with the suffix *iñ* after the suffix *a*, we have *bhauriki* and *bhauliki*. From the root *cupa* (to move slowly), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is substituted for the present tense marker (*laṭ*); his descendant is *caupayataḥ*. Similarly, *caitayataḥ*. From the root *ciṭa* (to serve another), with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is substituted for the present tense marker (*laṭ*); his descendant is *caiṭayataḥ*. From the root *śīkṛ* (to sprinkle), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and so forth are applied as before; [his descendant is] *śaikayataḥ*.

*Kṣitayan* means he tells of the earth (*kṣiti*); his descendant is *Kṣaitayataḥ*. *Dhvajavān* means one who has a banner (*dhvaja*); his descendant is *Dhvājavataḥ*. Others say there are two words: from the root *dhvaja* "to go," with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the suffix *ac*, we get *dhvāja*; and from the root *van*, with the suffix *taṣ* [and *vat*], we get *vataḥ*. From the root *cad* "to delight," *candra* is formed; its descendant is *Cāndramasāyaniḥ*, namely Budha. *Śubhaḥ* means he shines; the suffix *ka* is applied because it is a root with a semivowel as a penultimate letter (*igupadha*). From the root *gam*, *gaṅgā* is formed. From the root *vṛ*, the suffix *eṇya* is applied, resulting in *vareṇyaḥ*.

From *sarvadhātu* comes *manin*. *Yāna* [is derived from] *yām*. That which has a beautiful *yāma* (time/measure) is *suyāma*. *Ārada* is the name of a country; from that, by the rule "from the word for a country" (*janapada-śabdāt*), the suffix *añ* is applied to form *ārada*, denoting a descendant. *Vahyam* means a vehicle; *vahyam* itself becomes *vahyakā*, where the absence of the shortening of the vowel (*itvābhāva*) is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Khalyā* means beneficial for a threshing floor (*khala*); the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "for *khala* and *yava*" (*khalayava iti yat*). From the root *vṛṣu* (to sprinkle), with the suffix *ka* after a root having *i* as its penultimate letter (*igupadhāt kaḥ*), we get *vṛṣa*. *Lomakā* is that which desires hair (*loman*).

One who desires water for oneself is *udanya-*; according to the rule "for food, water, and wealth" (*aśanāyodanyadhanāya*), there is the substitution of *udana-* for *udaka-*, followed by the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* group). One who is engaged in sacrifice is *yajña-*. These are examples beginning with *tikan*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *kausalya* and *kārmārya*. (Pāṇini 4.1.155)

He dispels the doubt that the forms *kosala* and *karmāra* might be intended here—by means of the suffixes *ñyaṅ* (applied after *vṛddha* stems ending in *kosala* and *āja*) and *ṇya* (characterized by the agent)—by stating: "only from the ultimate base (*paramaprakṛti*). [The objection: "How then is a modified form heard as having the nature of a base? To this he replies: "But by connection with the suffix... Nor is this merely his own invention; he says: "And thus... [Regarding] "yuḍādiṣṭasya": if it were treated as a prior element (*pūrvānta*), there would be no *guṇa* substitution for the *o* in *dāṃgavyāyani*; therefore, it is treated as a subsequent element (*parādi*).

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been assigned" (ādiṣṭe): this means "of that for which the substitution of *āyana* has already been performed. If this were not stated, then once the suffix *yuṭ* had been applied, the substitution of *āyana* would not take place because it would no longer be initial (*anāditvāt*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in two vowels that expresses a measure.

Regarding the example *kārtrāyaṇi*: [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the descendant of a *kartṛ*," resulting in *kārtṛ*. From that, the suffix *phiñ* is applied in the sense of a youth (*yuvan*), and because the rule states "not from a non-Brahmin *gotra*," the elision (*luk*) does not occur, due to the force of the specific formulation. Another says: *kārtṛ* means "the student of a *kartṛ*"; in such cases as "his descendant" (*tasyāpatyam*), the statement is made for the sake of the *caritra* [suffix] even when it is not a *gotra*. Still another says: the term "descendant" (*apatya*) is repeated; there, by one instance it qualifies the suffix *aṇ*, and by the other the meaning of the affix is indicated. Thus, since only the *aṇ* used in the sense of "descendant" is being grasped, the force of the specific formulation indeed exists.
According to the Easterners, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a word denoting a *vṛddha* (a person of the third generation or further) that is not a *gotra* (patronymic).

"Also from the word *kārin*. This refers to the scope of the suffix *iñ*, which characterizes the agent (*kārin*) according to the rule for the Northeners (*udīcām*): *tāntuvāyiḥ*; and the scope of the suffix *phiñ*: *āmraguptāyaniḥ*. When both would apply to the word *nāpita*, *phiñ* occurs: *yājñadattiḥ*. [This is because] "it should be stated that a personal name (*nāmadheya*) may optionally be designated as 'vṛddha'"; thus, in the alternative case, *yājñadattāyaniḥ* indeed occurs.
And for *vākinā* and others, there is the substitution of *kuk*. (Pāṇini 4.1.158)

Regarding "the lineage of Vṛddhagotra" mentioned here: these three are Vākina, Gāredha, and Kāka. *Vāk* means speech; one who possesses that is *vākina*, which is to be explained in the same way as *barhiṇa*. *Gāredha* is derived from *edh* with the prefix *agāra-*; the initial [syllable] is elided because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, and the substitution of the following form occurs because it belongs to the *śakandhvādi* group. *Kāka* is derived from the root *kai*; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *anyeṣām api*. *Kārkaṭya* is the descendant of *karkaṭa*, belonging to the *gargādi* or *kurvādi* groups. *Laṅkā* is derived from the root *lagh*; by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the substitution of *ka* for *gha* occurs. The words *varman* and *carman* belong to the *vrīhyādi* group.

Regarding the phrase "an exception to *iñ*": the suffix *aṇ* would apply to *varmin* and *carmin*; the suffix *ḍhak* would apply from the word *laṅkā* by the rule *dvyacaḥ*; the suffix *phak* would apply to those ending in *yañ* by the rule *yañiñośca*; and the suffix *iñ* would apply to the remaining cases. When the augment *kuk* is added by the rule *varmicarmiṇornalopaśca*, the base word (*prātipadika*) no longer ends in the letter *a*, so the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not otherwise apply; therefore, it is prescribed [here]. Furthermore, if this *kuk* were made a subsequent element (*parādi*), the substitution of *āyan* would not occur, because *phak* would not be the initial element.

When, by the paribhāṣā "a word qualified by its gender," a suffix does not occur after the words *varmiṇī* and *carmiṇī*, then the rule "in the case of a *bha*-stem, when a *taddhita* suffix other than one beginning with *aḍha* follows" would not apply, and thus the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not take place.
The case ending of the word *putra* may optionally be elided when it occurs at the end of a compound.

Since the suffix is already established by the preceding rule alone, it is here specifically prescribed [for this particular case]. If one asks, "How then is there an indication by means of the ablative case? he says: "from that which ends in *putra*, etc."
The suffix *phin* is frequently applied after Eastern [place names] that do not end in a *vṛddhi* vowel.

"Vikalpārthāḥ" means "having optionality as their purpose. In this context, the inclusion of the term *ācārya* (the Teacher) indicates the absence of the suffix in other opinions (*matāntara*). However, the mention of the term *bahula* (various/abundant) refers to its occurrence in certain instances and so forth. The word *anyatarasyām*, on the other hand, signifies optionality itself. Since [the desired result] is established by any one of these, it is understood from the context that they serve the purpose of providing an option. If so, for what purpose are all of them mentioned? To this he replies: "In that regard... The mention of *bahula* is for the sake of variety (*vaicitryārtha*).

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is stated that the mention of "another" is for the sake of providing an alternative; he demonstrates this very variety with the words "in some cases."
After the word *manas*, when followed by the suffixes *añ* and *yat*, the augment *ṣuk* is added.

And likewise: if it were intended in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), then by the rule *yañañośca*, there would result the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes in the plural, because in that context the term "lineage" (*gotra*) is understood in its worldly sense.

[The phrase] "a contemptible offspring" (*apatye kutsitaḥ*): this is for the purpose of prescribing the substitution of *ṇ* (in *māṇava*), since the substitution of *aṇ* is already established. Nor can the substitution of *ṇ* be established by the rule *na daṇḍamāṇavāntevāsiṣu*, because the specific meaning [of the word *māṇava*] is not determined therein. His stupidity arises from not having studied the Vedas. His contemptibility arises from the non-performance of prescribed duties and the practice of prohibited ones.
Offspring beginning with the grandson is called *gotra*. (Pāṇini 4.1.162)

Regarding the statement "it becomes known as that *gotra*": if it is argued that this is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) rather than a formal designation (*saṃjñā*), because in common usage the term *gotra* applies to offspring in general, whereas its restriction to a specific type of offspring is a rule (*niyama*), we say no. A technical definition is characterized by a specific indicative mark (*liṅga*), such as "guṇa and vṛddhi [substitute] for *ik*," or it serves as a supplement to another rule, such as "in case of conflict, the subsequent operation prevails. This [present rule], however, is not like those.

Furthermore, even [words] such as *vṛddhi* and the like, though capable of conveying all meanings, are restricted by the delimitation of their power to specific named objects (*saṃjñin*). And just as those are names (*saṃjñā*), so too will this one be. As it has been said:
"The restriction of names to a named object occurs in certain cases for the sake of linguistic usage;
however, the relationship is indeed eternal, as in the case of *ḍittha* and the like, or like 'cow' and so forth."

"And in this treatise, the relationship of *vṛddhi* and the others is indeed non-artificial (*akṛtrima*), characterized by the delimitation of capacity (*śaktyavaccheda*), just like that between a qualifier and a qualificand.

[Objection: If the designation *gotra* is applied to offspring starting from the grandson onwards, then it would apply to Garga as well, since he too is certainly a grandson in relation to someone; what is the fault in that? [Fault: There would be the undesirable consequence of applying a suffix for the younger generation (*yuvan*) according to the rule "after a *gotra*, the suffix is used for the *yuvan* except in the feminine" (*gotrādyūnyastriyām*). Yet, it is intended that the suffix be applied to Gārgya and others specifically for the *yuvan*. [Response: This is not a fault.

In this context, the mention of "offspring" (*apatya*) need not have been made; since the grandson is already offspring, it is established that the term refers to offspring starting from him onwards. It is nevertheless included for the purpose of ensuring that the rule applies to one who appears as offspring, even if he is not actually offspring in reality. Consequently, it will not apply to Garga, who appears as offspring [by name] but is not such in fact.

[Objection: But surely, even if the mention of "offspring" (*apatya*) were omitted, since the designation would be understood for that which appears in the form of a grandson (*pautra*) and so forth, it would not apply to a *marga* (a distant descendant) who does not appear in that form; so what is the use of mentioning "offspring"? [Response: If that were the case, then it would not apply to an *aupagava* either, for he too appears in the form of offspring, but not in the form of a grandson and so forth. Furthermore, because the suffix is prescribed for offspring in general, it would apply only to cases such as *gārgya*, where the suffix occurs specifically in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*).

And from what source is this meaning obtained—that [the self] appears in the form of a grandson and so forth? If it is argued that it is obtained by the force of the mention of "him" (tat), then since everything, in relation to some object or other, invariably possesses the status of being a grandson and so forth, the mention of "grandson and so forth" would be unnecessary. Is it then said that this meaning is obtained by the force of that mention? That is not so; for its purpose is to specify the bearer of the designation (*saṃjñin*) and to exclude non-conscious things.

For if only "lineage" (*gotra*) were stated, of what would the designation be? Moreover, chariots and the like do not possess the status of being a "grandson" (*pautra*) and so forth even in reality. Therefore, the term "offspring" (*apatya*) must be included so that the designation may apply to one such as Garga—who is in reality a grandson and so forth—but who appears in the form of an offspring.

Furthermore, because they are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*), the designation *gotra* is understood to apply only with respect to that person toward whom there is the status of being a descendant starting from a grandson (*pautraprabhṛti*) and the status of being an offspring (*apatyatva*). Therefore, it does not apply to one who is a grandson of Aṅgiras but an immediate descendant of Garga; thus, the suffix *yañ* [prescribed] by the rule "from *garga* etc., *yañ*" (*gargādibhyo yañ*) does not occur. All of this has been stated.

"Because it is a relative term," and so forth. The meaning is that [the word] appears as "the offspring of someone. This is the sense of the intended meaning of the *sūtra*: in reality, a referent such as a grandson (*pautra*) and so on, which appears in the form of offspring, is designated by the technical term *gotra* with respect to that person toward whom it appears as offspring, and with respect to whom it is in reality a grandson and so on. "For the purpose of the designation 'offspring'"—the word "of the named entity" (*saṃjñinaḥ*) is to be supplied. The meaning is: for the sake of ensuring that there may be a designation of the named entity—which appears in the form of offspring—as "offspring."

Why does this not occur here: *gargāpatyasya tṛtīyāder apatyam* ("the offspring of a third-generation descendant of Garga")? For in this case, since the technical designation *gotra* applies to the actual grandson and those beyond him—who appear as offspring in relation to Garga by virtue of the word *gargāpatya*—then for the fourth living descendant of Garga, a suffix would be required after the word *gargāpatya* by the rule *gotrād yūni*. This is not a fault.

While this very section on technical names (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*) ought to have been composed at the outset when the secondary suffixes for offspring (*apatya-pratyaya*) were being prescribed, the placement of the section on technical names in the middle is for the purpose of delimiting the "offspring" expressed by those suffixes. Specifically, the offspring that was indicated as the meaning of the suffix starting from the rule *tasyāpatyam* (P. 4.1.92) is designated by the term *gotra*; therefore, the technical name will not apply to an offspring that merely appears through the word "offspring" (*apatya*) itself.

But surely, in the rule *te tadrājāḥ*, the inclusion of only those beginning with *añ* (i.e., *añ*, *yañ*, and *ṭhak*) by means of the word *tat* would have been intended so that [the designation] does not apply to the preceding ones; thus, the assignment of this technical name (*saṃjñā*) in the middle [of the section] would be for that purpose. If this were the only purpose, one could simply have said *añādayas tadrājāḥ*. Therefore, the direct purpose of assigning this technical name within this specific context is exactly as stated. Even though this purpose has already been established, it remains valid; for this very reason, he will say there: "The designations *gotra* and *yuvan* are separated by the section [on *tadrāja*]."
But if a descendant of the lineage is living, the younger [takes the title]. Pāṇini 4.1.163.

"Lineage (*vaṃśa*) is a continuous succession (*prabandha*) of ancestors. Ancestors (*abhijana*) are those such as fathers and so forth, so called because sons and others are born from them. A "succession" (*prabandha*) is a lineage (*santāna*). One who belongs to that is "of the lineage" (*vaṃśya*); the suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *diś*. The term "descendant starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛtyapatya*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). If, as in the previous case, one were to qualify "descendant" (*apatya*) by the term "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then even a third-generation ancestor who is still living would receive the designation of "younger relative" (*yuvan*).

What is the fault here? Because the designation *yuvan* (younger descendant) would sublate the designation *gotra* (lineage), the suffix *yañ* would apply after [names] such as *Garga*, and no affix denoting a descendant (*apatya*) would occur. Why? Because of the restrictive rule that [the *yuvan*-suffix] applies only after a *gotra* [name], and not after an immediate descendant nor after the original base-form (*mūlaprakṛti*). Consequently, the expression would have to be conveyed through a periphrasis alone—such as "the descendant of Garga" or "the descendant of Gārgi. By this, the case of Upagu’s third descendant, whose lineage members are still living, is explained. Therefore, he states that the qualification is expressed through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) by saying "starting from the grandson" (*pautraprabhṛti*).
Regarding the phrase "the sixth case having been changed," here the commentary itself is the only refuge.

As for the word *tu*, it serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Since particles have multiple meanings, he states that its position should be seen after the word *yuvan*, despite its different order [in the sūtra]: "He remains a *yuvan* only, not a *gotra*. If this restriction were not present, because of the governing rule on "single technical designation" (*eka-saṃjñā-adhikāra*), and because elsewhere the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of designations is admitted—as in the case of the designations for *kṛt* and *pratyaya* suffixes—there would be a co-occurrence of the designations *gotra* and *yuvan*.

Let it be so; what is the fault? The patronymic *gotra* derived from *Yaska* is formed with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *śivādibhyo 'ṇ*. From that form ending in *aṇ*, when deriving the *yuvan* (descendant) form, the suffix *phiñ* is applied by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*. After the vowel-vṛddhi and the elision of the *y* in *yasya* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*), the form becomes *Yāskāyani*. However, in the plural, the elision (*luk*) of *phiñ* would undesirably apply by the rule *yaskādibhyo gotre*, because a form modified in one part is not considered different from the original. Now, the elision of *phiñ* is prescribed for a *gotra*-suffix that follows immediately after [a name] in the *yaskādi* group, but here the *phiñ* does not follow immediately.

In the case of *śivādyaṇ*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Regarding that [elided element], even when a grammatical operation is prescribed based on what precedes it, one should understand—by means of the status of being "as if in its original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—that the operation applies to what is immediately following a word beginning with *ya* (i.e., the *ya* of *yaskādi*). And here, for example: the descendant of Kaṇva is *Kāṇvyaḥ*; his youthful descendant (*yuvan*) is *Kāṇvyāyanaḥ*; and his students are *Kāṇvāyanīyāḥ*. In this instance, the suffix *aṇ* is not applied by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* ("*aṇ* after *kaṇva* etc. in the sense of a lineage"). This is because the rule is understood to apply to a word ending in that which follows *kaṇva* etc., whether it is immediately subsequent to them or prescribed in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*) after them.

And here, in the case of "aupagavir" as the offspring of "aupagava," the restriction "only one [suffix] is used for the *gotra*" will be set aside by the specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) "for the *yuvan* [descendant], after a *gotra*. If it is set aside, then since the fourth *yuvan* descendant of "aupagavi" would possess the status of a *gotra*, the suffix *phak* would apply to the fifth *yuvan* descendant? This is not a fault; when the fifth *yuvan* descendant is intended, the suffix *iñ* that was produced [after the original stem] undergoes elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision of *iñ* in the *yuvan* [descendant]," and once this elision has been performed, the suffix *iñ* itself will be applied again from the word "aupagava," which now ends in the suffix *aṇ*.

In that case, when one intends to express the meaning "the offspring of Dākṣāyaṇa"—that is, the offspring of the offspring of Dakṣa—the suffix *iñ* would apply after the form ending in *phak*, provided that *phak* has not been elided by the rule *phakphiñor anyatarasyām*. Furthermore, in the case of "the offspring of Aupagavi," even though *iñ* has been elided, the suffix *phak* would apply again by virtue of the technical designation *pratyayalakṣaṇa*. If this is so, then in the rule *gotrād yūni*, the word *eka* ("single") will be understood as carrying over; consequently, there will not be multiple successive suffixes applied.

If that is the case, then the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *gotre 'lug aci* would apply in instances such as *strīṇāṃ yūnāṃ chātraḥ* ("the student of young women"), since even a youth (*yuvan*) is considered a lineage-descendant (*gotra*). Let it apply; however, it will be superseded by the subsequent rule for the elision of the suffix in the sense of "youth" (*yūni luk*), which takes precedence. This cannot be maintained, for there would be a fault regarding the suffixes *phak* and *phiñ*. Consider the following: from *Śālaṅkiḥ*, the offspring of Śālaṅka—wherein the suffix *iñ* is applied because *Śālaṅka* is listed among the *Paila* group, and the substitution of *Śalaṅka* occurs—then the offspring of that Śālaṅki who is a youth is derived with *phak* by the rule *yañiñoś ca*, and subsequently, the elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *pailādibhyaś ca*. From that...

In the case of *śālaṅker yūnaś chātrāḥ* ("the students of the young Śālaṅki"), when there is a desire to express a meaning belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] prescribed for the *paila* class by the rule *gotre 'lug aci* would be prohibited. Consequently, since the elision of the *yuvan* suffix is mandatory by the rule *yūni luk*, there would arise the undesirable consequence of hearing the suffix *phak* in some instances due to the rule *phakphiñor anyatarasyām*. However, if the *yuvan* does not receive the designation *gotra*, the rule *gotre 'lug aci* does not apply, and thus the elision [of the *yuvan* suffix] occurs within the *paila* class as expected.

However, this option (*vikalpa*) provided by the rule *phakphiñoranyatarasyām* applies immediately after the rule *yūni luk*, and not to the *luk* elision of *paila* and others which is more remote and internal (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, by the rule *iñaśca*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, resulting in *śālaṅkāḥ*. Similarly, the offspring of *Pīlā* is *Pailaḥ* (by the rule *pīlāyā vā*), and his youthful descendant is formed with *phiñ* by the rule *aṇo dvyacaḥ*; this *phiñ* is then elided by the rule *pailādibhyaśca*. Thus, the students of the youth *Paila* are called *pailīyāḥ*.
And [the suffix ṭhak is applied] after the word *bhrātṛ* when it denotes an elder brother. 4.1.164.

Regarding the terms "younger brother" (*kanīyān bhrātā*) and "elder brother" (*bhrātṛjyāyaḥ*): this meaning is obtained because these are relative terms (*sambandhiśabda*). Regarding the phrase "due to not being the cause": in common usage, one who is the cause—whether directly or indirectly—is called a "lineage-descendant" (*vaṃśya*). Regarding the expression "while a Gārgya is living": the meaning is "while an elder brother is living. The same should be understood for [the cases of] Vātsyāyana and so forth.
Or while another sapinda who is older remains alive. || 4.1.165 ||

"Ending with the seventh person" means those for whom the limit is the seventh person when counting from oneself among ancestors such as the father, or among descendants such as the son. Generally, however, the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is not recited; rather, it is read simply as "ending with seven persons" (*saptapuruṣāvadhayaḥ*), and we do not see a correct meaning in that case. "Sapiṇḍas" are those who have the same *piṇḍa* (funeral cake); the change to *sa-* [from *samāna-*, meaning "same"] occurs by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). "They are recorded in the Smṛtis" means...
For example: "But sapinda-relationship ceases with the seventh person. The meaning is that it ceases when the seventh [ancestor] has passed. "In both cases" means in birth and in death.

"In such actions as these": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), actions such as "giving, receiving, offering oblations, and Vedic study are suspended" are included. "While [the father] is living" (*jīvati*): this is an explanation of the actual meaning. In the *sūtra*, however, the verbal form is "he lives" (*jīvati*); if that offspring is living, then either the locative case is to be explained as having the sense of the nominative (i.e., "while he lives"), or it is derived from the present participle ending in *-śatṛ*. "The mention of the comparative suffix (*tarap*)" and so forth.

In its absence, from the word *sthavira* alone, only the excellence of age would be understood; however, by means of the suffix *-tarap*, the excellence of position (*sthāna*) is indicated. Consequently, by virtue of the power of employing that [suffix], just as in cases such as *gotaraḥ* (a better ox) or *aśvataraḥ* (a better horse), where the excellence of the suffix *-tarap* applies even to qualities like the capacity for carrying or milking—which are not the primary grounds for the application of the base words but are related to the meaning of the base—so too is it here. "Position" (*sthāna*) refers to rank, such as being a father and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "inferior in station and age": the meaning is "inferior by way of station and by way of age. Now, one might object: since the word *jyāyasī* is understood from the previous context, excellence in both [station and age] is already obtained, because the rule "for *praśasya*, *śra*" (Pāṇini 5.3.60), along with "and *jya*" (5.3.61) and "and for *vṛddha*" (5.3.62), prescribes the substitution of *jya* for both. This is not so; for a single word employed once is not capable of denoting multiple meanings. Even so, one might argue that the suffix *-tarap* should not have been used, since excellence in station is obtained simply through the recurrence of *jyāyasī*. This too is not the case; for...

When the qualification "the elder" (*sthavira*) is employed as an additional attribute, it is difficult to discern whether the term "the senior" (*jyāyasī*) is being carried over [from the previous rule]. As for the question "What does 'living' mean?", the inquiry refers to both what has been heard and what is under discussion. For this very reason, he demonstrates the purpose of both by saying, "if he is dead, or if he is dead. In that context, "he is dead" refers to one's own father; "or if he is dead" refers to the descendant beginning with the grandson who has become an offspring.
And [the suffix *kan* is used] after the word *vṛddha* when honor is intended. 4.1.166.

"Offspring has disappeared," and so forth. This is understood because the term "offspring" (*apatya*) serves as a qualifier for the "elder" (*vṛddha*), and because that which is defined here by the technical rule [of grammar] cannot possibly be offspring in the literal sense of the word. "When respect is implied": what, then, is respect in this context? It is simply youthfulness.

Although the word *yuva* (young) is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) whose basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not required [for its primary meaning], nevertheless, since it is generally possible for one of little age to belong to a living lineage, when that [belonging] is superimposed, the age associated with it is also conveyed; thus, honor is achieved. This is "by the power of the technical name."

The designation "yuvan" (descendant) is prescribed for one who already possesses the designation "gotra" (lineage). If the designation "gotra" has already been applied, the restriction "only one [suffix] in the lineage" would apply; consequently, because the meaning would have already been expressed by a suffix produced from the primary base itself, the suffix would not otherwise be applicable. However, by this rule, the suffix does occur even though it was not required. This is the meaning.

Since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) was established in the preceding rule through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it would have been appropriate to establish the designation in that same manner for the sake of consistency in the method of exposition. To the question, "What is this use of the genitive case in *vṛddhasya*? he says: "*vṛddhasyeti*. Regarding the phrase "the use of the genitive case": the particle *iti* indicates the reason; furthermore, this is a *vārttika*-rule inserted by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) into the sūtras. By this, the subsequent rule is also explained.
And [the suffix *kan*] is used after *yuvan* in the sense of contempt. 4.1.167.

The alternative [interpretation] holds that cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the primary sense, and not activity (*pravṛtti*), because [the activity] has already occurred previously. As it says: "and for a youth" (*yūnaśca*). For this designation would not be appropriate if that [activity] had not already taken place. But one might object: even cessation, if it has not yet occurred, cannot be brought about; for what would be achieved by one who says to someone who has already eaten, "Do not eat"? Therefore, the designation "and for a youth" (*yūnaśca*) is intended as a technical rule (*lakṣaṇārtha*) regarding the domain of the term "youth" (*yuvasaṃjñā*).

It should be stated that [the term] refers to one who is a fourth descendant or further from the living progenitor (*jīvadvaṃśya*), and not to one designated by the technical name *yuvan* (youth). And in this way, an option regarding its application is also justified; thinking that such an application is obtained even in the absence of the rule, it was said that [the rule] is primarily intended for its exclusion (*nivṛtti*). "When the designation *yuvan* has been prohibited" means: in the case of its non-existence. "A wretched Gārgya" (*gārgyo jālmaḥ*).

What, then, is the censure here? It applies only to those who superimpose the status of a *gotra* [upon others], for those designated as *gotra* are indeed descendants of the deceased; since they are generally in their final stage of life, there is censure when that status is superimposed upon them.
The suffix *añ* is applied after a word denoting a country (*janapada*) when it refers to a *kṣatriya*.

Regarding the statement that "the word *janapada* denotes a Kṣatriya": one might object—these words such as *Pañcāla* and so forth are indeed words for Kṣatriyas; however, through their connection [to those Kṣatriyas], when the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is applied according to the rule *tasya nivāsaḥ* ("his residence"), and then that suffix is elided by the rule *janapade lup*, they come to denote the country (*janapada*). Therefore, how can their status as permanent Kṣatriya-denoting words be indicated by their later status as words for a country? Furthermore, who says that they denote the country only because of their connection to Kṣatriyas? The author of the Sūtras, at any rate, [states otherwise].

By stating "because the connection [of the name] with the country is not perceived" (*lubyogāprakhyānāt*), he asserts that the word *Pañcāla* and others apply naturally to the country as well as to the Kṣatriyas—this is expressed by the word "Pāñcāla. Furthermore, although words such as *Pañcāla* end in the plural when referring to a country, but in the singular when referring to a Kṣatriya, nevertheless, it is the status of being a country (*janapadatva*) that qualifies the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not the inflected form (*subanta*); thus, the suffix is indeed applied even from a singular ending. As for *Aikṣvāka*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the word *Ikṣvāku* is prescribed by the rule *dāṇḍināyanādi-sūtra*.

Regarding "Drauhyava": this is a designation for a *kṣatriya* alone and is not a word denoting a country (*janapada*). As for the phrase "of a Brāhmaṇa who is a Pañcāla," since it has been stated that [the rule] applies to those whose names appear in the list beginning with *bāhu*, one must consider how this case could possibly fall under that rule.

"From a word denoting a country that has the same sound as the word 'kṣatriya'": *samāna-śabda* means "having the same sound"; from that country-name which has the same sound as the word *kṣatriya*, when the sense to be expressed is a king (*rājanya*), there occurs a suffix denoting a descendant (*apatya*), provided it is in grammatical apposition with a word ending in the sixth case. This is an exception to the suffix *vuñ* which would otherwise apply by the rule "even after a non-*vṛddha* [word]". In some versions of the commentary (*vṛtti*), this very text is read as follows: "Māgadha"—[here the suffix] *aṇ* applies by the rule *dvy-añ-magadha*.
The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied after the words *vṛddha*, *it*, *kosala*, and *āja*.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed": the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the final vowel (*ṭilopa*), and the letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) that would otherwise be triggered by the cause of *vṛddhi*. The phrase "from another" means from words denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) and from words such as "Yudhiṣṭhira’s father. In some places, it is read as "the suffix *aṇ* should be prescribed after *purū-* [to form] *paurava*"; since the word *purū-* is not a name of a country (*janapada*), the suffix *aṇ* is already established by the rule for derivatives meaning "belonging to that" (*prāgdīvyatīya*), so this specific statement is intended to assign it the technical designation of *tadrāja*. If it were a word denoting a country, it would be established by the rule "*dvyañmagadha*" itself.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [words ending in] *kuru-nādi*.

The word *ādi* (beginning with) is connected only with the letter *n*, not with the word *kuru*; for there is no country that begins with that [letter]. Thus he says: "from the word *kuru* and from those beginning with *n*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to *am*. It is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "from *dvyañc* and *magadha*" when applied to the word *kuru*, and an exception to the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by the rule] "from those beginning with *n*" (*na-ādi*). Regarding *naiṣadhya*: how is it that one says, "If a Naiṣadha should deserve sin"? The sages are speakers who act according to their own will. How is it that one says, "He [was born] in the daughter of the lord of wealth, the Naiṣadha"? Poets are unrestrained. Alternatively, if one intends to express the remainder (*śeṣa*), the suffix *aṇ* must be justified in both cases.
The suffix *iñ* is applied after [the names of] Sālva, Avayava, Pratyagratha, Kalakūṭa, Aśmaka, and others, to denote a descendant.

The reading is *sālvā kṣatriyā* because of the statement "it is named after that"; for this was stated for the purpose of obtaining [the suffix] *aṇ* for those names. Nor is there an application of that [suffix] from the word *sālva* itself, because it is *vṛddha* (containing a long vowel in the first syllable), and thus the suffix *vap* applies. It is desired that even *aṇ* occurs; this is because of the mention of *sālvāt* in the rule regarding a descendant of a part of the Sālvas (*sālvāvayave apadātau*). Nor is the prescribed *aṇ* an exception to *ḍhak*, because of the mention in the rule: "*sālveyagāndhāribhyāṃ ca*" (and from Sālveya and Gāndhāri). "From those who follow the profession of Kṣatriyas"—this is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "from a country-name denoting a Kṣatriya" (*janapadaśabdātkṣattriyāt*).

The verse beginning with "udumbarāstilakhalāḥ" is intended for illustrative purposes. By this, [the suffix] also occurs after *busa*, *ajamīḍha*, and *ajakanda*; thus it is exemplified in the Bhāṣya as *bausī*, *ājamīḍhiḥ*, and *ajakandiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "designated as parts of the Sālva," the meaning is that they are designated by the term "parts of the Sālva."
Those [words] ending in -tad are called rājā [when they denote a king]. 4.1.174.

And thus it has been illustrated. In that context, under the rule "tadrājasya bahuṣu tenaivāstriyām," an illustration based on the grammatical operation (*kāryāśraya*) was given; however, in this present section, the illustration is based on the form (*rūpāśraya*).
The suffix *luk* is applied [to the patronymic suffix] after the word *kamboja*. 4.1.175.
In *cola* and *śaka*, [the suffix] *aṇ* applies by the rule "from *dvyañ* and *magadha*. In *kerala*, [the suffix] *añ* applies.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the words *avanti*, *kunti*, and *kuru* when they denote a feminine.

*Avantī* and *Kuntī*: when the suffix is elided, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "after a word denoting a human class ending in *it*. *Kurūḥ*: [the feminine suffix] *ūṅ* is applied by the rule "*ūṅutaḥ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.66).
And for this reason also: 4.1.177.

The letter *t* is for the sake of clarity. For if it were not there, the reference would be "asya" (of this), and from that a doubt would arise: is this a reference to the phoneme (*varṇa*)? Or is it a reference to "this" (*idam*)? And if there were a reference to "this," the elision (*luk*) of the immediately preceding *iṅ* would result; however, when the letter *t* is present, this fault does not occur, because the designation "with a following *t*" (*tapara*) is predominantly established with respect to phonemes, and because the technical term "that which has a following *t*" (*tapara*) is prescribed [by Pāṇini] as "denoting its own duration" (*taparastatkālasya*).

How is it that [the text says] "the two sons of Mādrī are abundant in flowers and fruits"? The sages speak according to their own will; or rather, it should be read as "madrīsutau" (the two sons of Madrī).

Regarding the statement "because of the rule for elision (*luk*) after *Avanti* and so forth": if there were here an application of the rule regarding the final member of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*), then the rule prescribing elision after *Avanti* and so forth would be purposeless, since the result would already be established by this very [present rule]. However, when the rule regarding the final member does not apply, the elision is established by the inclusion of the mere vowel *a*; thus, the rule for elision after *Avanti* and so forth becomes meaningful.
The suffix *cha* is not applied after [words denoting] the eastern [tribes], such as Bharga, nor after [words denoting] the Yaudheya and others.

Regarding "Pāñcālī" and so forth: Pañcāla and the others are the eastern regions [janapadas] situated along the Śaravatī river. The inclusion of Bharga and the others is for the purpose of excluding Prāg-deśa (the eastern lands). From the root *bhṛ* (to carry), the suffix *ga* is added, yielding *bharga*. From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *u* is added, yielding *karu*; because it consumes (*oṣati*) or hates (*dveṣṭi*) darkness, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for *mūlavibhujādi* words, resulting in *karūṣāḥ*. From the root *ci* (to gather), *kaya* is substituted and *ka* is added to the initial; by virtue of the general rule (*bahulavacana*), the elision of the *it*-marker does not occur, resulting in *kekaya*. From the root *kaś*, the suffix *mira* is added, yielding *kaśmīra*. The word *sālva* has been etymologically explained [elsewhere]. One who possesses beautiful highlands (*sthalāni*) is *susthala*. One who lies down with his chest (*urasā śete*) is *uraśaḥ*.

From *kuru* and others, the suffix *ṇya* is applied: *kauravyaḥ*. As for *yaudheyī* and so forth: [it denotes] the offspring of *yudhā*, the offspring of *śubhrā*; by the rule "from a word of two syllables," the suffix *ḍhak* is applied. From the word *śubhrā*, by the rule "and from *śubhra* etc.," [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]; then, in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), by the rule "from *parśu* etc. and *yaudheya* etc., the suffix *añ* is applied. If there were elision (*luk*) of *añ*, then when the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is characterized by the presence of *ḍhak*—is applied, the accent would be the udātta on the final syllable (due to the rule regarding the cessation of the accent). However, since that elision is prohibited, when the suffix *ṅīn* is applied by the rule "after *śārṅgarava* etc. and *añ*," the word becomes udātta on the first syllable.

Regarding the question "Of whom, then?", the intention of what is about to be said is revealed by the phrase "How, then?". He provides the answer: "This very thing, namely 'Parśu'. *Parśu* is a Kṣatriya whose name is identical to that of a country; his descendant is a clan (*saṅgha*), specifically in the feminine gender. By the rule *dvyañ-magadha*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; its elision occurs by the rule *ataśca*. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is added again in the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*) according to the rule for *parśu* and so on, and this too is elided. It is the same with "Rakṣā."

*Rākṣasī* is the feminine descendant of a *kṣatriya* Rākṣasa, a community characterized by femininity; the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before, with elision (*luk*) of both [the patronymic and the feminine marker], and the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *atvasantasya ca*. Regarding *āsūrī*: when the suffix *añ* (characterized by being derived from a country name) is elided, there is elision of the suffix *aṇ* (characterized by being derived from the *parśu* group), and the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added because it denotes a genus (*jāti*). He confirms that this is indeed an indicator (*jñāpaka*) by stating: "And so it has been said. This was stated by the author of the Vārttika; three [examples] have been explained among those beginning with *yaudheya*.

That which has a bowstring (*jyā*) and an arrow (*bāṇa*) is *jyābāṇā*; its offspring is *jyābāṇeya*. Others read *jyāvāneya*, in which case that which has a bowstring (*jyā*) and a bow (*vāna*) is *jyāvānā*. From the roots *ghṛ* (to flow) and *dhṛ* (to hold), with the suffix *ktic*, and then by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, resulting in *ghārtteya* and *dhārtteya*. Those who have three *gartas* (hollows/fortresses) are the *trigarttas*. From the root *bhṛ* with the suffix *atac*, we get *bharata*.

From the root *vaś* with the suffix *ki* in the sense of the object, we get *uśi*; one whose men are desirous (*uśaya*) is *uśīnara*, with the lengthening of the vowel according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the second quarter of the fourth chapter. — 4 *Padamañjarī*
That which is colored by that [color] is so called because of its attachment to it. 4.2.1.

The root *rañj* exists in the sense of attachment—as in "attached to food"; it exists in the sense of a specific color—as in "a red cow," meaning "ruddy"; and it exists in the sense of transforming a white object into another color—as in "a red cloth. Considering that if the first two meanings were taken, [the term] would also apply in cases such as "attached to a beautiful woman because of her form" or "a face flushed with anger," he relies on the third meaning and says "of a white [object]," and so forth. This is obtained from the inherent nature of the word itself: *rāga* is that by which one is colored (*rajyate*).

The elision of the *n* occurs by the rule "ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ. However, the word *rāga* here is not used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), for the act of coloring itself cannot be the instrument (*karaṇa*) of that very same act of coloring. [The term refers to] "that which expresses a specific kind of color"; it does not, however, refer to the word-form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*) itself, because later on, the word *rāga* is used as a qualifier for lac (*lākṣā*) and other such substances.

The question "Why [is it] from attachment (*rāgāt*)? is asked as follows: [the opponent argues that] because it is not explicitly stated, the suffix will not apply to a word denoting an agent, for when one says "Daivadatta’s garment," there is understood only the relationship of owner and owned. To this it is replied: "One who relies solely on grammatical definition cannot understand this. The question "How so? is asked because [the opponent thinks] no other phoneme has been added here. [The answer is: "From comparison (*upamānāt*)," meaning from the cause of similarity of form.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *lākṣā* when it occurs before *rocanā* and *naṭṭha*. (Pāṇini 4.2.2)
The inclusion [of the terms] *śakala* and *kardama* in the sūtra is because they are seen in the vārttika.

Regarding the word *nīlyā*: *nīli* is a specific medicinal herb; this statement is for the purpose of precluding [the application of other rules]. As for the word *nīla*, since it is a quality-word (*guṇaśabda*), it is already established that it applies to cloth dyed with *nīlī*. Regarding *pītāt*: the word *pīta* denotes a specific dye. This statement also serves solely to preclude [other rules]. However, the word *pītaka*, which ends in the suffix *kan* used in its own sense (*svārthika*), is obtained as a quality-word when applied to cloth.
Time conjoined with a lunar mansion [is expressed by a compound]. 4.2.3.

In this regard, the followers of the Great Sage (the Pāramarṣas) maintain that time is of the nature of action (*kriyā*), as it has been said: "Others, who know time, understand time— which is distinct according to the various obstructions— to be the movement of the sun, the planets, and the lunar mansions."

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, regard time as a substance similar to space; and it has been said: "Some describe time as a single, eternal, all-pervading substance that possesses magnitude and is the locus of all actions."

In both views, the conjunction of the asterism with time is not possible. Why? Because conjunction (*yoga*) is an attainment preceded by non-attainment; for in common usage, words such as "Pauṣa" and so forth are employed for the purpose of determining a specific period of time, and it is only such a conjunction that serves as the cause for determining a specific period of time. In the case of the view that [the asterism] is a substance (*dravya*), since both the asterism and time are eternal and time is all-pervasive, there is never a lack of conjunction.

Even regarding the category of action (*kriyā*), the conjunction characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) with an action residing in a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)—which is designated as "time"—is not a qualifier because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). However, [the conjunction] with an action residing in the sun and so forth is not a qualifier because it is impossible [to apply it to all time]. If, however, conjunction were understood in some way or another, then there would be no absence of deviation; for there is no day-and-night (*ahorātra*) that is not conjoined with a lunar mansion. Therefore, the designation "time conjoined with a lunar mansion" is untenable.

How, then, should the rule be formulated? The suffixes are prescribed after words such as *nakṣatra* ending in *yukta*, when the time joined [with that asterism] is intended, and there is the elision of the word *yukta*. For example, "the moon is joined with Puṣya" is *puṣyayuktaḥ*; then, from the word *puṣyayukta*—which refers to the moon—the suffix is applied, and the word *yukta* is elided. Thus we have *pauṣī rātriḥ* ("the night of Puṣya") and *pauṣamahaḥ* ("the day of Puṣya"). This applies everywhere in the same way.

In that regard, there is a fault in the application of the *yuktavadbhāva* (the treatment of the compound as having the gender and number of its first member). If a suffix were added to the word *maghāyukta* and then elided (*lup*), the feminine gender and plural number of the form *maghāḥ* would not be established; rather, the gender and number of the moon (*candramas*) alone—which is what is joined—would result. Therefore, considering that the application of the suffixes is possible only when [the word] denotes the asterism itself, he asks: "But how [is it]? It is not by being joined with the moon alone that *puṣya* and the others acquire the status of an asterism (*nakṣatra*); for the word *nakṣatra* denotes light in general.

However, for those who maintain that the status of being a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) for Puṣya and the others occurs only through conjunction with the moon, this question is inappropriate. The point is that when the primary meaning is impossible, one resorts to a secondary (metaphorical) sense—as in the expression "one situated near Puṣya" (*puṣyādisamīpastha*). In that case, words such as *maghā* and so on apply to the moon without abandoning their own gender and number, just as in the examples "the platforms [are] women" (*mañcāḥ striyaḥ*) or "look at the platforms" (*mañcān paśya*). Consequently, there is no fault even regarding the application of the rule *yuktavadbhāva*.

The meaning is that [the month] is conjoined with the moon when it is situated near Puṣya. Although the conjunction of the moon with time is constant because the moon is eternal, its conjunction with the vicinity of Puṣya is occasional, because being near Puṣya occurs only at certain times. In the form *pauṣī*, there is the elision of the *y* according to the rule "sūryatiṣya" and so forth.
[The suffix *viś* is applied] after [a word ending in] *lub*, when a specific [quality] is to be expressed. 4.2.4.

If the suffix *lub* occurs when there is no specific distinction (*aviśeṣa*), then it would also apply here in the cases "the night of Pauṣa" (*pauṣī rātriḥ*) and "the day of Pauṣa" (*pauṣamahar*), because even here, no specific distinction such as "today" or "yesterday" is perceived. Now, if [it is argued that] the suffix does not apply because the specific distinctions "night" and "day" are understood, and thus the prohibition based on those [distinctions] applies, then in this case too it would not occur: namely, in "today is Puṣya, yesterday was Kṛttikā," because the specific distinctions such as "today-ness" (*adyatva*) and so forth are indeed understood.

"But this would apply only in cases such as 'one should eat milk-rice under the Puṣya asterism,' where there is not even the slightest determination of a specific [time]. To this he says: "If not," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "night and so forth," moments (*muhūrta*) and other units are included. "A specific [time] is denoted" means by means of a word ending in a suffix. He clarifies this very point with the words: "As much as... [He asks: "And for how long a time is one conjoined with an asterism? To which he replies: "A day and night (*ahorātra*)."

The meaning is that it consists of sixty *nāḍikās*; for during that much time the moon remains in proximity to a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Thus, when a certain duration of time is joined with a lunar mansion, the designation of that entire duration by means of a suffix is the general rule (*aviśeṣa*), whereas the designation of a specific portion of it is the particular case (*viśeṣa*). And this [particular case] is obtained because of the entry into the end of the suffix and because of its being more internal (*antaraṅga*).

This is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). Therefore, in the case of "the *pauṣa* day-and-night," even though it is perceived as a whole, it is perceived as consisting of two parts; thus, the negation applies based on that [whole]. [Objection: In cases such as "the full moon day joined with *puṣya* is *pauṣī*" or "the full moon day joined with *maghā* is *māghī*," would there not result the elision (*lup*) [of the suffix] by rule P. 4.2.4? [Response: This is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). By the fact that he states, "Optionally [there is elision] after *phalgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*," he indicates that there is no elision in the case of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*).

From the word *śravaṇā*, however, [the form] *śravaṇākārttikī* arises precisely from the specific grammatical rule (*nirdeśa*). How then is it that we have *śrāvaṇyāṃ paurṇamāsyām*? For there are also exceptions (*nipātana*) which do not constitute contradictions.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *śravaṇa* and *śvattha* when they denote a name (*saṃjñā*).

This undertaking is for the sake of a specific meaning; it is not, however, for the purpose of a restrictive rule regarding technical names (*saṃjñā*), because a restriction is inappropriate when a direct injunction is possible, and because we observe the elision (*lup*) even in cases that are not technical names, such as *śravaṇākārttikī*. [Question: Why does the treatment of the compound as if it were its constituent member (*yuktavadbhāva*) not apply here when there is an elision? [Answer: As in the case of *śravaṇā rātriḥ*. [Explanation: It is due to a formal exception (*nipātana*). Here, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), based on the understanding that "the vowel *a* which follows the suffix *aṇ* [is the one affected]."
The suffix *cha* is applied after a copulative compound (*dvandva*).

The term *nakṣatra-grahaṇa* (the mention of "asterisms") is carried over [from the previous rule] and is modified to end in the genitive case; it serves as a qualifier for the *dvandva* compound, as he states: "from a *dvandva* of asterisms. For example: *rādhānurādhīyā rātriḥ* ("the night belonging to Rādhā and Anurādhā"). Through its parts, the night and so forth are connected with the two asterisms. For example: *adya rādhānurādhīyam* ("today belongs to Rādhā and Anurādhā"). Although the word *adya* (today) is genderless, its qualifier takes the neuter gender because gender is dependent on common usage (*lokāśrayatvāt*). Furthermore, the elision (*lup*) [of the suffix] prevails over this by virtue of being subsequent in the rules. [He asks: "Why? (cha).

[Objection: "But a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) occurs when two rules apply simultaneously; however, there is no simultaneous application of two *lup*s, for the technical term *lup* refers to the non-appearance of a suffix. How, then, could there be a simultaneous application of that [non-appearance] with a suffix? Therefore, this is the meaning here: 'Exceptions (*apavāda*) sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones. Thus, this *lup* applies only to the suffix *aṇ*, not to this *cha*. Consequently, this *cha* is heard in the domain where *lup* would otherwise apply; it is precisely this *cha* that sublates *lup* due to its posteriority—this is what constitutes its status as a sublater."
"Because it is subsequent": since this [rule] is subsequent, *lu* does not apply to it; therefore, even in that domain, it is heard [in its original form].
The *sāman* has been seen. 4.2.7.
When the application of a particular Sāman to a specific ritual purpose is known by someone, it is said that the [purpose] has been "seen" by him.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the word *kali*. (Pāṇini 4.2.8)

"Everywhere" means that the suffix *ḍhak* is not applied only in the sense of "this is its deity" (*sāsya devatā*), nor is the suffix *ḍhak* applied to *kali* only in the sense of "the *Sāman* seen by him" (*dṛṣṭaṃ sāmā*); rather, the meaning is that [these suffixes] apply to all *prāgdīvyatīya* (patronymic/derivative) meanings.

In the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*), the reading is: "In the sense of 'born there' (*jāti*), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed twice, or it is optionally marked with the *ḍi*-sign. This means that the suffix *aṇ* which is prescribed in the sense of "born there" may optionally be treated as having the *ḍi*-sign.
"Not from *vidyā*" means that the suffix *īkak* does not occur after a word denoting "knowledge" (*vidyā*).

"Like a mark from its source" (*gotrādaṅkavat*): whatever suffix is observed in the case of a "mark" (*aṅka*) is entirely extended [to other cases], for it is not the "mark" itself that is specifically prescribed. Therefore, there is an extension of the suffix *aṇ* from the rule "in the case of *saṃgha*, *aṅka*, and *lakṣaṇa*" (*saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣu*), and of the suffix *vuñ* from the rule "from *gotra* and *caraṇa*, *vuñ*" (*gotracaraṇād vuñ*).
After *vāmadeva*, the suffixes *ḍya* and *ḍyaṅ* [are applied].

"Why is the *ḍi*-marker applied? This question arises from the thought that the desired result is already established by the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix itself. [The answer is: "So that there might not be the inclusion of these two. Now, even if the *ḍi*-marker is applied, why would there still not be the inclusion of these two? To this he says: "In the case of the inclusion of that which lacks an *anubandha*... According to the rule "when there is the inclusion of that which lacks an *anubandha*, there is no inclusion of that which possesses an *anubandha*," when *ya* is included, there is no inclusion of *ḍya* and *ḍyat*. However, by the paribhāṣā regarding "that which has only one *anubandha*," when *yat* is included, there is an absence of the inclusion of *ḍyat*.
Regarding *avāmadevyam*: by the rule for the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of an indeclinable as the first member of a compound, it retains its initial udātta accent.

In the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*), the phrase "not in that sense" (*atadarthe*) indicates the sūtra "yayatoścātadarthe. Regarding "the accent of the negative particle" (*nañsvara*): the accent dependent on the negative particle *nañ* is the "nañ-svara"; the meaning is that when the final udātta accent of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is being prescribed, this applies.
The word *ratha* (chariot) [takes the suffix *ka*] when preceded by *pari*.

Regarding *cārmaṇa*: the term *an* indicates the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Regarding "a chariot surrounded by [something]": this requires the inclusion of the condition "exclusive" (*ekānta*); it must be stated that the chariot is surrounded by that which constitutes its exclusive covering. Therefore, it occurs only in the case of leather, cloth, and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying even to students (*chāttra*) and the like. Thus he says: "completely encircled," etc. The root *vṛ* means "to encircle," and the prefix *pari-* denotes the sense of "on all sides. "Of which no part [is exposed]" means...

This [statement] intends abundance; for the wheel-rims and so forth are not covered by leather, nor are the internal parts. But is this not one who acts accordingly, when he says "surrounded by students"? And is this not one who acts contrary to that, when he says "encircled on all sides" and so forth? This is not one who acts accordingly; this usage is figurative: he is "surrounded" as it were, though not actually surrounded.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *pāṇḍukambala*, etc.,] to denote that which is made thereof. 4.2.11.

"It is established by the suffix itself expressing possession (*matvarthīya*). For when something is surrounded by another, it possesses that [surrounding thing]. "In order to exclude *aṇ*" means: if this were not commenced, then when one intends to say "a chariot surrounded [by cloth]," the suffix *aṇ* would undesirably apply by the preceding rule.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *dvaipa* and *vaiyāghra*.

Regarding the phrase "of the leopard and the tiger": by the rule "even for dissimilar [words] that have the same meaning," a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would apply; however, this must be resolved by noting that because there is a difference in meaning due to the distinction between their intermediate species (*avāntarajāti*), the rule will not apply. It is stated "two hides" (*carmaṇī*) because the covering of a chariot is possible only with the hide itself, and not merely with its modification. From the words *dvīpin* and *vyāghra*, the suffix *añ* is applied according to the rule "from animals, silver, etc., the suffix *añ*"; in the case of *dvīpin*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
In the case of the word *kaumāra* when it does not denote a previously married woman. Pāṇini 4.2.13.

Regarding the term *apūrvavacana*: the word *apūrva* has the state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning. The expression of the state of being unprecedented is *apūrvavacana*; [the rule applies] in that case of *apūrvavacana*. To the question, "Of what, then, is the state of being unprecedented spoken? he says: "of the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). And this is obtained through the force of the irregular formation (*nipātana*). [The word *ubhayataḥ* is used] because the suffix *tasi* occurs after words beginning with *ādya*. This irregular formation is intended for both the female and the male; and the meaning is that in both cases, the state of being unprecedented belongs to the woman alone, not to the man.

In this context, because the term *kaumāra* is indicated as a mere nominal stem (*prātipadika*) common to both female and male, it is understood that the irregular formation (*nipātana*) applies to both genders. However, the fact that it refers specifically to a woman is obtained by the force of the irregular formation itself. Regarding the term *apūrvapati*: she whose hand has not been previously taken by anyone is an *apūrvapati*, in the sense that "a previous husband does not exist" for her; one who has approached such a woman—meaning he has attained her or accepted her as his wife. This may have occurred through a prior marriage ceremony, or it may not.

Regarding the term *apūrvapati*: this too is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and here also the person (*puruṣa*) is as previously described. Regarding the rule beginning with *kaumāra* and so forth: the form *kaumāra* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when [the husband] has not been married before. What is irregularly formed here? The suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after the word *kumārī*. When? When she is one who has not been married before. The meaning is: when the girl (*kumārī*) is unmarried, but not the man. Or, "it occurs because of the girl" (*kumāryā bhavati*). By this, the application of the rule is rejected; for he belongs to her who has obtained the girl, since the performance of religious duties and so forth depends upon her. Consequently, the suffix *aṇ* is established by the rule "that which occurs therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*).

Although the term *vāṇī* and others may also apply to a young girl (*kumārī*), nevertheless, when there is a true designation [of her as such], the suffix *bhava* (denoting "being therein") certainly applies. For even at the commencement of the rule (*sūtra*), this is not prohibited by force; thus, first of all, the form *kaumāra* is established. It is also established for the feminine: how so? The feminine of *kaumāra* is *kaumārī*. And by virtue of proximity, it is precisely that woman who, having attained the designation *kaumāra*, is denoted [by the word], and not any other woman; and this must be accepted even at the commencement of the rule.
In that case, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words meaning "vessels" when they have been removed from them. 4.2.14.

In this context, the root *ud-dhr* (to take out) refers to placing [something] after having first taken it out; therefore, the use of the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) [in the compound] is not justified. Regarding the term *bhuktocchiṣṭam*: "remnant" (*ucchiṣṭa*) means that which is left over after eating (*śiṣṭa*), just as in the expression "he cuts off a portion, he does not offer the whole"; thus, the meaning is "that which remains after being eaten. In the phrase *yasyoddharaṇam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the past passive participle (*bhūte karmaṇi*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The phrase *śarāveṣūdḍhṛtaḥ* means "taken out and placed upon the plates."
The suffix *ini* is applied after the word *sthaṇḍila* when it denotes one who observes a vow of sleeping on the bare ground. 4.2.15.

Regarding the term *śāstrita*: it means "one in whom the scripture has arisen. Alternatively, from a base ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāsamartha*), in the sense of "being enjoined," the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *prātipadikāddhatvarthe*; then the suffix *kta* is applied in the passive sense (*karmani*), meaning "enjoined by the scripture. Regarding the phrase "one whose vow is to lie on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)," the suffix *tumun* should have been used here, because a "vow" (*vrata*) is not of the nature of an action (*akriyārūpa*).
The word *saṃskṛtam* [is used] in the sense of "prepared as food. (Pāṇini 4.2.16)

The term *saṃskṛta* is derived in the sense of "prepared" in general; therefore, it takes the neuter gender and the singular number. The term *bhakṣāḥ*, however, is derived in the sense of specific types of edible food such as cakes (*apūpa*) and the like; therefore, it takes the masculine gender and the plural number.

In this context, since the meaning understood from the sentence as a whole is not applicable to the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the individual words, it follows that [the word *bhakṣāḥ*] is already refined (*saṃskṛta*). For this very reason, he demonstrates the connection by pausing: "that which is refined—if they are the *bhakṣas*. This is like the rule *aṇau yatkarma ṇau cet sa kartā* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), where the pronoun *tat* takes on the gender of the referent being pointed out. "Hard and distinct" (*kharaviśadam*): *khara* means hard; *viśada* means distinct. It is expressed by the word *bhakṣa*.

The sense is that although the verb *bhakṣ* is used in other contexts—as in "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣa*) or "one who subsists on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*)—the word *bhakṣa* itself is well-known specifically in that [sense of eating].
The suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *śūla* and *ukhā*.

Regarding the term *śūlokhāt*: this is a collective dvandva compound; *ukhā* refers to a specific type of vessel. However, the word *ukhā* when it denotes a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is not included here, because there is no object to be prepared within a bodily part. As for the expression *ukhya agniḥ* (the fire belonging to the *ukhā*), this [fire] is certainly not something to be consumed; rather, it should be understood as expressing the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*), according to the rule beginning with *dig-ādi*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *dadhi*. (Pāṇini 4.2.18)

In this case, however, the curd is merely the substratum (*ādhāra*). Just as a spit (*śūla*) is for meat being prepared on it; although here the curd is also a seasoning agent (*saṃskāraka*), nevertheless that is not what is intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). Rather, the sense is that only that seasoning which the substratum undergoes by means of another substance is intended to be expressed.
The word *udaśvit* may optionally [be compounded with a word ending in the genitive case]. 4.2.19.
Regarding the term *audaśvitka*: [it is formed] by [the rule] *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*.
The suffix *aḍḍhañ* is applied after the word *kṣīra*.

In this context, the term "prepared" (saṃskṛta) alone is connected, not the word "foods" (bhakṣāḥ); therefore, it applies even to barley-gruel (yavāgū). [The form] *kṣaireyī* is derived by applying the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...* and so forth.
The suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied after [a word ending in] *paurṇamāsī* when the resulting form is a name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 4.2.21)

"If there is a desire to speak from that": the meaning is that if the world's desire to speak arises from that which ends in a suffix, then such a suffix occurs, and not otherwise. "In the case of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is a condition for the whole [word]. He clarifies this very point with: "if by that which ends in a suffix. Regarding *pauṣī paurṇamāsī*: it was already stated previously that the elision (*lup*) does not occur for the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) by the rule "when there is no distinction" (*lubaviśeṣe*). And regarding "in the month of Bhṛtaka."

"Those who are supported" means laborers; the "month" belonging to them is that which consists of thirty nights starting from the commencement of their work. When that month possesses the full moon of Pauṣa, it does not, in reality, bear the designation of Māgha and so forth—this is the meaning.

"The result is indeed equal. What, then, is that? He says: "according to the application" (*prayogānusāraṇam*). The suffix *lyap* is used because of the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*). "Equal with the word that is a technical name" (*saṃjñāśabdena tulyatām*)—the meaning is "equal in terms of the result" (*tulyaphalatām*). "In order to make known this to Kaṇa"—what, then, is this which is to be established by the *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark)? To that he says: "For this [is not]... He shows the purpose of the *jñāpana*: "But if it were for the sake of a technical name" (*saṃjñārthatve tu*). The meaning is: "if there were equality of result with a word that is a technical name."

And this meaning is made known through a distinction in the application [of the rule]. In the case of *saṃjñāyām*, there is the application of the accusative case; here in the grammar (*śāstre*), the word *iti* is to be understood as having the sense of "in the meaning of" (*ityarthe*). Thus, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is established. Regarding *pūrṇamāsādaṇ*: in the compound *pūrṇo māso 'syām tithau* (the full moon day on which the month is complete), the suffix *aṇ* is applied because *prajñādi* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), or else due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). It is said that *mā* refers to the moon (*candramas*); this is a usage of a single part of the word *candramas*, just as in the cases of *satyabhāmā* for *satyabhāmā* and *bhāmā* for *bhāmā*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvattha*.

The full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) occurring at the beginning of the year is called *āgrahāyaṇī*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied because [the word] *agrahāyaṇa* belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *prajñā*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule "after a preceding member [ending in a vowel], when it is a name. The full moon day joined with the *aśvattha* [nakṣatra] is called *aśvattha*; here, the elision (*lup*) of the suffix occurs even for the term *paurṇamāsī* due to a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
That is its deity. 4.2.24.

"The deity is the recipient (*sampradāna*) of the sacrifice. Although the word *deva* (god) denotes a genus—just as [the words] *manuṣya* (human) and so forth do—and the suffix *-tā* is a reflexive (*svārthika*) one, nevertheless, by virtue of its collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), the word *devatā* applies to everything that is enjoined as the recipient in a sacrifice, such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); the meaning is that it does not denote a specific genus. [The deity is] "the owner of what is to be given," such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

He demonstrates the etymological derivation of the word *devatā* from the sense of "diverse sovereign action" (*divera-aiśvarya-karman*). And by adopting this view, the grammatical rules "the suffix *yat* after *vāyu*, *ṛtu*, *pitṛ*, and *uṣas*" and "after words for time, like *bhava*" become logically consistent; for there is no genus (*jāti*) in the seasons, the ancestors, or the dawn. Likewise, the usage of terms such as *pitṛ-devatyam* ("having the ancestors as its deity") and *deva-devatyam* ("having the gods as its deity") is also justified in this very way.

"How so? This is the question: since there is an absence of an offering such as the *puroḍāśa* cake, Indra cannot possess the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*). Regarding the phrase "even in the praise of the mantra," etc.: by this, the usage is not said to be figurative; rather, it is a primary usage. It is universally recognized that the term is used for the recipient of a sacrifice; the only distinction here is that this particular usage belongs to the etymologists (*nairuktas*). When they say "they employ [the term] figuratively" (*upacaranti*), the meaning is "they apply [it]."

"How so? and so forth. The question is: "The two modes previously mentioned do not exist here. Regarding the phrase "because of being metaphorical" (*upamānāt*): the meaning is that this usage is figurative (*gauṇa*), like the expression "the two ears of a donkey are reddish-brown" (*kāṣāyau gardabhasya karṇau*). Regarding the phrase "that [refers to] what is under discussion" (*prakṛte*): for the term *sā* (she/it) is connected with the technical name (*saṃjñā*) in the context under discussion; therefore, when that [term *sā*] recurs, the technical name would also recur.
[The suffix] *ka* [is applied after a word ending in the genitive case] to express "belonging to whom. (Pāṇini 4.2.25)

He dispels the doubt—namely, that after applying the substitution of *ka* for the case-ending *kim*, one might wonder what is being referred to by "of *ka*"—by stating "the word *ka*. And having done so, the injunction is "recite for *kāya*. As for "for whom (*kasmai*) recite," the change to *smai* is Vedic, as in "to no god shall we worship with oblation" (*na kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema*), or like "O Indra and Agni, in the lowest [place]" (*yad indrāgnī avamasyām*). Regarding *kāyam*: once the substitution of *it* (the *yaṇ*-sandhi) has been applied, the elision of the *i* (as in *yasya*) would have been required, but it is superseded by the initial *vṛddhi* because it is subsequent; this is like the form *śrāya* in "whose deity is Śrī" (*śrīr devatāsya śrāyaḥ*).

In the rule "somāṭ-ṭyaṇ," even if the mention of *k* were made, although the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) would occur because it is subsequent to the elision of *y* (*yasyeti lopaḥ*), the elision of *y* would still certainly take place even after the *vṛddhi* has been applied.
The suffix *gha* is applied after the words *aponatṛ* and *pānnatṛ*.

"Aponapāt" and "Apāṃnapāt" are names of deities; their grammatical correctness is established by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Regarding these two, however, [the specific forms] occur in connection with particular suffixes. Thus, the ritual injunctions (*sampraiṣa*) are: "Recite for Aponapāt," "Recite for Apāṃnapāt," "Sacrifice to Aponapāt," and "Sacrifice to Apāṃnapāt. In the Veda, however, the form "Aponaptre svāhā" is a Vedic usage.
And [the suffix] cha [is applied after a word denoting a part of the body]. 4.2.28.
