Regarding the phrase "yogavibhāga" (division of the rule), and so forth: if the suffix *cha* were included in the previous sūtra itself, there would be two suffixes, *gha* and *cha*, and two bases; thus, there would be a correspondence based on number (*saṅkhyātānudeśa*). As for the word *śatarudrīyam*: the word *śata* signifies "infinite"; since its deity is "a hundred Rudras," the suffixes *gha* and *cha* are applied. By virtue of the power of that specific rule, the elision prescribed by "dvigor lug anapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88) does not take place.
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after *mahendra* and *ghana*. 4.2.29.
Regarding "saumī": because it ends in a *ṭi* vowel, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; then, by the rule *halastaddhitasya*, there is the elision of the *y*.
The word *yat* is compounded with *vāyu*, *ṛtu*, *pitṛ*, and *uṣas*. (Pāṇini 4.2.31)

Regarding "vāyavyam": by the rule "orguṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 6.1.87], the guṇa substitution occurs; and by "vānto yi pratyaye" [Pāṇini 6.1.79], the final *au* is replaced by *av*. Regarding "pitryam": by the rule "rīṅṛtaḥ" [Pāṇini 7.4.27], *rīṅ* is substituted for the ṛ of the suffix *taddhita*, and then the elision of the *ya* suffix occurs by "yasyeti ca" [Pāṇini 6.4.148].
The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*. (Pāṇini 4.2.32)

The suffix *aṇ* and *ṇya* are exceptions [to other rules]. From the word *vāstoṣpati*, it is an exception to *ṇya* when *pati* is the final member; from the remaining words, it is an exception to *aṇ*. Regarding *dyāvāpṛthivyau*: the substitution of *dyāvā* occurs by the rule "for *div* there is *dyāvā*" and "also for *divas* before *pṛthivī*. Regarding *śunāsīrau*: the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs by the rule "also in a dual compound of deities. *Śunaḥ* is Vāyu and *sīraḥ* is Āditya. Others, however, considered *śunasīra* to be a single entity, a quality (*guṇa*) of Indra, as Āśvalāyana says: "Indra indeed is Śunāsīra."

And there is also an indicative mark (liṅga) in the mantra: "We invoke Indra Śunāsīra at this sacrifice. Indra is "possessed of the Maruts" (marutvān), for he has the Maruts as his attendants. Regarding the term *agnīṣomīya*: [the rule] "īd is substituted for the final vowel of *agni* before *soma* and *varuṇa*" applies. *Vāstoṣpati* is [derived from] *vāstoḥ patiḥ*; it is correct precisely because of this specific grammatical instruction. The Bahvṛcas consider the word *gṛhamedha* to end in the vowel *a*. Āśvalāyana states: "The [offering] to the Gṛhamedhas, who are the Maruts, follows next. And there is the indicative mark in the mantra: "O Gṛhamedhas, come hither!"

"An evening rice-mess cooked in the milk of all [the cows] is for the Maruts who are householders," so says the Taittirīyaka; regarding this, there is a disagreement as to whether [the word *gṛhamedhibhyaḥ*] ends in the vowel *e* or the consonant *n*.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the word *agni*.
He recalls the very meaning stated in the rule *kaler ḍhak* by saying: "in the case of [suffixes] belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group."
[The suffix *vat* is applied] after words denoting time, in the same manner as [the suffix *vat* is applied] after words denoting existence. 4.2.34.

"From those expressing specific times": this refers to the actual forms [of the words], for if it were not so, the plural number would have been used. Regarding the mention of "vat" (as if): if the term *vat* were not employed, and it were stated simply that "the suffixes [occur] after words for time in the sense of 'born therefrom' (*kālebhyo bhavaḥ*)," then if the connection were made such that "those suffixes which are prescribed after words for time in the sense of being born therefrom occur in the sense of 'this is its deity' (*sāsya devatā*)," the base [meaning] "deity" would remain unspecified; consequently, the suffix *ṭhañ* [prescribed by the rule] *kālaṭṭhañ* would apply even to [words like] *indra* and others.

Alternatively, the connection might be as follows: "Are those conditions that will be prescribed for *bhava* [to be understood as] 'from words denoting time and deities'? Even so, the conditions for *bhava* would not be specified; consequently, the suffix *yat*, which is prescribed by the rule "the suffix *yat* after *diś* and others," would also apply to words denoting time in this sense.

Furthermore, if the connection were as follows—that those suffixes which occur after words for time (*kāla*) are used [in the sense of "arising from"], and that they are used after words for time specifically in the sense of a deity—then it would first of all be difficult for that word *kāla*, being heard only once, to be connected with both meanings in such a way. Even if it were possible, even so, any suffix whatsoever occurring after a word for time would apply to any deity whatsoever; thus, the suffix *aṇ* would result after words like *ṛtu* (season) and even *muhūrta* (hour), and so forth.

But when there is a specification by means of a suffix (*vati-nirdeśa*), there is an inclusion based on similarity; therefore, whatever suffixes are prescribed for the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) from certain bases (*prakṛti*) with a certain qualification, here too those same suffixes occur from those same bases with that same qualification—thus, nothing undesirable occurs.
The suffix *aṭṭhañ* is applied after [the word] *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada*.

Mahārāja Vaiśravaṇa; [the mention of] the asterisms prior to the word *proṣṭhapada* is for the sake of specific instruction; *navayajña* refers to the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice. Regarding the suffix *-aṇ* after *pūrṇamāsa*, it means "that which occurs in this. Thus, *paurṇamāsī*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that lunar day (*tithi*) in which a full month (*pūrṇa-māsa*) occurs. And this very etymology is also shown in the rule *sāsmin paurṇamāsī*.
Paternal uncle, maternal uncle, maternal grandfather, and paternal grandfather. || 4.2.36 ||

Regarding the rule *pitṛmātṛbhyām*: because the two words denote their own forms (*svarūpa*) as the referents, there is no distinction in terms of being more venerable (*abhyarhita*); therefore, the word with the fewer syllables is placed first. Furthermore, because it denotes a non-uterine relationship, the suffix *anaṅ* does not occur. Regarding the rule *ḍāmahaj*: how then is there a pause (*avagraha*) in the form *mātāmahaḥ*, *pitāmahaḥ*? Some say that the suffix *tasa* is added after *pitṛ* and *mātṛ*, and the suffix *maha* is applied to these two, with the substitution of *anaṅ*.

The author of the Vṛtti, however, considers that since the *saṃhitā* reading alone is obligatory, one should not apply the *avagraha* (separation) according to the maxim: "The makers of the *pada-pāṭha* must follow the characteristics of the [original] words. Regarding *mātari ṣicchet*: the meaning is that the status of being marked with *ṣ* (*ṣitva*) must be added as an exception; it does not mean that the letter *ṣ* itself should be made an *anubandha*, because such a case does not exist—[for instance], *mātāmahāḥ* is also seen in the mantra.

Regarding *averdugdham*: *dugdham* means milk. In cases such as *soḍha*, the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* does not occur, due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *s*.
Regarding the phrase "the sesame is fruitless": it is said to be devoid of fruit while in the state of a crop; others say it means useless while in the state of grain.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [the word] "tad" to form a collective group. (Pāṇini 4.2.37)

Because every object [of grammar] is already encompassed by exceptions (*apavāda*), he asks: "What is the example here? The words *kāka*, *śuka*, and *vaka* are acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "for living beings beginning with *k*" (*prāṇināṃ kupūrvāṇām*). Its meaning is as follows: there are two genitive cases in grammatical apposition; furthermore, from the rule "the initial [syllable], before *śakaṭi*" (*ādiḥ prāk śakaṭeḥ*), the word *ādiḥ* is carried over and is transformed into the nominative plural. Thus, for those words denoting living beings whose initial vowels precede the guttural class (*kavarga*), the acute accent occurs. In that regard, *śaukam* is not an example [of this rule]; because it is listed among the *khaṇḍika*-type words. However, the word *vaka* is to be cited as an example.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words ending in] *bhikṣā* and so forth. (Pāṇini 4.2.38)

"The mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting a sublater. This word *bhikṣā* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *a* [by the rule] *gurośca halaḥ*; from that, the suffix *añ* [prescribed by] *anudāttādeḥ* would apply as a sublater of *aṇ*. The mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting that. But surely, if *añ* were applied here, the repetition [of the rule] would be useless? It is not useless.

Because it is subsequent, the suffix *ṭhak* prescribed by its respective rule would apply; to prevent that, there would have to be a restatement here, and thus *añ* would indeed occur. However, because of the repeated mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs. In the case of *gārbhiṇam*: by the rule "in the case of a *bha*-stem before a non-*ādhaka* secondary suffix" (*bhasyā'ḍhe taddhite*), there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), which results in the removal of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. Then, when *aṇ* follows, because of the rule "there is no change to the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) before *iman* and *añ* when not denoting descent" (*imaṇyanapatye*), the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*ṭilopa*) by the rule "the final vowel and following consonant are elided before a secondary suffix" (*nastaddhite*) does not take place. It is precisely due to the force of the inclusion of this [suffix *aṇ*] that the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur.

If [the form] were to exist, then by the rule "because it is already established, [the substitution] occurs when the suffix is being prescribed," the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) would have to apply even before the *taddhita* suffix has been produced. Furthermore, since the word *yuva-* ends in the *kanin* suffix according to the rule "kanin after *yuvan*, *vṛṣan*, etc.," it is *ādyudātta*; thus, the regular *aṇ* suffix is already established, and its inclusion here [in the list of *bhikṣādi* words] would be purposeless. Regarding the form *yauvatam*: according to the Vārttika, however, *puṃvadbhāva* is desired. For it says: "The mention of *yuvati-* among the *bhikṣādi* words is useless, because *puṃvadbhāva* is already established by the rule 'when the suffix is being prescribed.'"
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [the words] *gotra*, *ukṣan*, *uṣṭra*, *urabhra*, *rājan*, *rājanya*, *rājaputra*, *vatsa*, *manuṣya*, and *aja*.

"Because the context concerns *apatya* (offspring), [the rule applies] elsewhere. If this is so, then the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* is redundant, as it is already established by the rule for the *gotra*. These two are certainly not formed with *apatya*-suffixes; for the meaning of the suffix is "birth" (*jāti*). For it has been stated: "In the case of a king's offspring, there is the inclusion of *jāti*; for *manu*, the suffixes *añ* and *yat* are used in the sense of *jāti*, with the augment *ṣuk*. What then is meant by saying, "By *prakṛti* (the base form), *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan* [retain their forms]," implying that the elision of *y* does not occur? [The objection is: since they are not *apatya*-suffixes, the elision will not occur anyway. True.

This is stated while assuming that [the suffix] has the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). If it were assumed that it has the sense of "offspring," would the mention of *rājanya* and *manuṣya* be purposeless? It is not purposeless; it is for the sake of making known [a specific rule]. It makes this known: that for these two, [the suffix] does not occur by virtue of being offspring. Consequently, the elision of *y* does not take place. Thus, in no case need it be stated that "in the case of *rājanya*, *manuṣya*, and *yuvan*, [the suffix] is by its own form (*prakṛtyā*) when followed by *aka*. As for *aupagavakam*, just as here the suffix *añ*—even though it follows—is not applied because it begins with an unaccented vowel (*anudāttādi*), so too will be explained under the rule "and after *khaṇḍika* and others" (*khaṇḍikādibhyaśca*).
The suffix *yañ* is applied after the words *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, *vāḍaba*, and so forth. 4.2.42.

The letter *ṇ* [in *brāhmaṇa*] is for its own sake, so that the acute accent on the first syllable may occur by the rule "that which begins with *ñ*, *ṇ*, etc., is always acute. But for what purpose is *yañ* prescribed after words such as *brāhmaṇa*, rather than simply prescribing the already-mentioned *yañ*? For there is no difference between *yañ* and *yañ* when applied to bases ending in *vṛddhi*—the form remains the same and the accent is the same. Why then is *ṭhañ* not carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], given that it is not marked with a svarita? It is for the sake of an informative indication (*jñāpana*). This indicates that this suffix applies even to other words. What is thereby established? He will raise the objection regarding the need for an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for the word *pṛṣṭha*; that need no longer be stated.

"A collection of *pṛṣṭhas*": the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes a specific type of hymn of praise (*stuti*). [In the expression] "the six-day period consisting of *pṛṣṭhas* (*pṛṣṭhyaḥ ṣaḍahaḥ*"), there is a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) of the term to that which possesses it.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṇa* should be prescribed": the letter *s* is for the purpose of designating the word as a *pada*; by means of this, in the case of *pārśvam*, because it lacks the status of a *bha*-stem, the *guṇa* substitution of *o* does not occur.
The suffix *añ* is applied [to form a patronymic] after a word whose first syllable is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Since there is no suffix *ac* following [the root], the suffix *ṭhak* ought to apply. However, those words containing the suffix *ac* have been cited. The words *kapota* and *mayūra* are oxytone because of the rule "when a light vowel is at the end" (*laghāvante*). The word *tittiri*, ending in the suffix *ki*, is derived from the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ka* added after an *ig-upadha* root, and by the rule "the reduplication of *tṛ* is like that of *san*" (*sanvattuk cābhyāsasya*), it is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvareṇa*). It does not become ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) through the application of the *san*-like behavior (*sanvadbhāva*), because of the use of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule "the *uṇādi* suffixes are variously applied" (*uṇādayo bahulam*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after [words beginning with] *khaṇḍiraka*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.45).

"And *kṣudrakāḥ*": [the form] *kṣaudrakāḥ* means "the offspring of the *kṣudrakas*. There is elision (*luk*) of the *tadrāja* suffix prescribed by the rule "from words denoting a country" (*janapada-śabdāt*), whereas from *mālava*, there is the suffix *ñyaṅ* characterized by the [condition of being] "vṛddha. As for the statement "it is established by the preceding [rule] with the suffix *añ*": this is because, when the final member of the compound is accented (*samāsāntodāttatva*), it begins with an unaccented vowel due to the "subsequent suppression" (*śeṣanighāta*).

"But [you argue] because of its being 'other' (paratvāt). This was stated having provisionally accepted that it is a *gotra*; however, he says that this very thing does not exist: "Nor is a collection of *gotras* a *gotra*. In that regard, just as a collection of districts (*janapada*) is not included under the designation "district," so that in the case of *kāśikosalāyaḥ*, only the suffix *cha* applies and not the suffix *vuñ* characterized by a district, so too here the suffix *vuñ* characterized by a *gotra* would not apply; such is the sense.

It might be argued: "Let the aggregate not be the *gotra*; however, the word *mālava* itself is the *gotra*, and consequently, by the rule governing suffixes at the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*), the suffix *vuñ* would apply even to the aggregate. To this he replies: "Not so" (*na ca*). For in the rule *yena vidhistadantasya* ("that by which a rule is prescribed applies to what ends with that"), it has been stated: "There is a prohibition regarding the prescription of compounds and suffixes. [The opponent says: "If that is so," and so forth.

How can both be made known by a single effort? He says it is possible: it becomes a signifier through *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise), for the prescription of the suffix *añ* would not be possible without both [conditions]. What is impossible here? In that regard, the purpose of making known the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) is [seen in the forms] *aupagavakaḥ* and *kāpaṭavakaḥ*.

The scope (*avakāśa*) of *vuñ* is when [the word] has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), such as *glucukāyaniḥ* (the descendant of Glucuka), where [the suffix] *phin* applies by the rule *prācām avṛddhāt phin*; the collective thereof is *glaucukāyanakam*. On the other hand, the scope of *añ* is [words] that are not *gotra* names, such as *kāpotam*. When both [suffixes] would apply after a *gotra* name beginning with an anudātta vowel, *añ* would prevail due to its being the subsequent rule; however, by this *jñāpaka*, only *vuñ* occurs. The purpose of making known the application of the rule regarding the final member of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) is as follows: the collection of forest-elephants is *vānahastikam*; [the collection of] cows from the Gaudha region is *gaudhenum*. In these cases, there is an optional lengthening of the final vowel of the second member by the rule *jaṅgaladhenuvalajānatasya*.

Furthermore, intending to describe the restrictive nature (*niyamārthatva*) of this very rule, one might ask: "How can both—namely, the indication (*jñāpana*) and the restriction (*niyama*)—be obtained by a single effort? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By as much as [the mention of] *kṣaudrakamālava*. The meaning is that two efforts are resorted to through a split in the yoga (*yogavibhāga*). [The examples are: *kṣaudrakamālavī* and *kṣaudrakamālavakam*. In both cases, when the suffix *ñyaṅ* derived from *mālava* is prohibited from being elided by the rule "there is no elision (*aluk*) in the case of a gotra [suffix] before a vowel-initial [suffix]" (*gotre 'luc aci*), the elision of *y* occurs by the rule "of the descendant" (*āpatyasya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "añ-siddhi" and ending with "anudāttādeḥ": the phrase "anudāttādeḥ" (beginning with an unaccented vowel) is a qualifying attribute containing a *hetugarbha* (an implied reason). Since this word *kṣudrakamālava* begins with an unaccented vowel, the suffix *añ* is established for it precisely by the rule "anudāttādeḥ. What is the purpose? The ellipsis is "by its inclusion in the *gaṇa*-list"; the meaning is that there is no purpose [for its inclusion]. If it is argued that the suffix *vuñ*, which characterizes a *gotra* (clan), would otherwise apply, and therefore its inclusion in the list is intended to block that, the author replies: "from a *gotra*, *vuñ*."

The suffix *vuñ* is prescribed after a word denoting a *gotra* (lineage), and the meaning is that the forms of the words *kṣudraka* and *mālava* do not constitute such a *gotra*. Regarding the phrase "after that which ends in [it]": since the word *mālava* is a *gotra*, the rule applies by means of the extension of the rule to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding the phrase "it does not apply everywhere": the suffix *tasi* occurs after a locative ending because it belongs to the *ādyādi* group; the meaning is that this *tadantavidhi* does not apply in all cases. Regarding the phrase "if it ends in that": the meaning is in the sense that the *tadantavidhi* exists. And so forth.

"The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *dhenu* when not preceded by a negative particle (*nañ*)," such is the rule of Āpiśali. In this context, a marker (*anubandha*) for the purpose of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) must be sought; furthermore, it should be understood that the substitution of *ka* occurs only after an *ik* vowel (i, u, ṛ, ḷ) followed by the letters *is*, *us*, or *uk*. Alternatively, only the general meaning was indicated by Bhāṣkāra. The term *ikak* means *ṭhak*. Thus, "a collection of cows" is *dhainukam*. Why specify "not preceded by a negative particle"? [Consider: "a collection of non-cows" is *ādhenavam*, where the suffix *añ* is applied because of its inclusion in the *utsādi* group.

Although the word *dhenu* is recited in the sūtra, nevertheless, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form *baṣkayaṇī*, the suffix also occurs after the word *adhenu*. In that case, if the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) did not apply to collective formations, the prohibition "not after a negative particle" (*anañ*) would be purposeless.

He states another purpose as well: "In the case of an army" (*senāyām*). Regarding "just as" (*yathā*): the meaning is that its inclusion in the list [of *uṇādi* suffixes] is for the sake of ensuring that the suffix *vuñ* should supersede the suffix *añ* by means of the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). The word *ulūka* is read here; according to the rule "when a light syllable is at the end" (*laghāvante*), it has the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). However, in Vedic usage, as in "what the owl speaks is in vain" (*yadulūko vadati moghametat*) and "thus the owl has flown down" (*itthā ulūka āpaptat*), there is an acute accent on the first syllable; that is a Vedic peculiarity (*chāndasa*).

In common usage (*bhāṣā*), however, [the word *aulūkya*] has the middle syllable as the udātta accent; in that case, the desired form is already established by the previous rule (*añ*). Therefore, it must be stated as follows: the word *aulūkya* ends in the suffix *yañ* from the *garga*-class, because the form is produced when the elision (*luk*) of both *yañ* and *añ* occurs in the plural according to the rule "yañañośca"; that [form] is what is listed here [in the *gaṇa-pāṭha*]. For if it were not listed there, then when one intends to express the meaning "a collection of *ulūkas*," the suffix *vuñ*—which depends on the *gotra* [status]—would apply after the word *aulūkya*, because of the prohibition of elision (*luk*) by the rule "gotre 'lug aci."

The word *śuka* is recited here [in the rule for forming collective nouns]; however, regarding the rule "the collection thereof" (*tasya samūhaḥ*), it is cited as an example under the statement "and that for which no other specific rule of formation exists"—namely, *kākam* and *śaukam*. Therefore, in that context, instead of reading *śaukam*, one should read *bākam*. The word *baka* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule "of living beings beginning with *ku-*, etc. (*prāṇināṃ kupūrvāṇām*).

The form *yugavaratrā* is recited; regarding this, they maintain that it expresses both a collective (*saṅghāta*) and a distributive (*vigṛhīta*) sense—namely, *yaugavaratram*, *yaugam*, and *vāratram*. In that case, if one follows the collective view, then according to the rule "a compound of non-living things denotes a genus" (*jātiraprāṇinām*), the dual-membered compound would undergo singularization (*ekavadbhāva*), and upon the shortening of the feminine vowel (*napuṃsakahrasvatva*), the long-vowel reading *yugavaratrā* would be untenable. Therefore, the compound must be analyzed as *yugasahitā varatrā* (a leather thong together with a yoke); or else, because there is no intention to denote a genus (*jātiparatvābhāva*), there is no singularization.
The suffix *matup* is applied after words meaning "feet" (*caraṇa*) when expressing a connection with the Dharma. 4.2.46.

"Starting from the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ*, suffixes will be explained. Now, one might object: "In that [rule], there is no mention of *dharma*; how then is the extension (*atideśa*) 'like *dharma*' appropriate? To this he says: "In that regard, this... This very statement, "like *dharma*," serves as the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the rule *caraṇād dharmāmnāyayoḥ*. The suffix *-vat* is intended to signify complete similarity.

In the absence of that [word *caraṇa*], if it were stated simply "Dharma from the *caraṇas*," and if the connection were such that "those suffixes which will be prescribed after the *caraṇas* for Dharma occur," then the base of the collective (*samūha*) would remain unspecified; consequently, suffixes such as *vuñ* would undesirably apply even to words like *kāka*.

Alternatively, the connection might be as follows: "Those suffixes that will be prescribed for *dharma* occur after [the names of] the *caraṇas* when they denote a collection"? Even so, the suffixes applied to *dharma* would not be specified; consequently, even the suffixes such as *aṇ* which are to be prescribed by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*) would result in being applied after [names like] Kaṭha and others.

Furthermore, suppose the connection were as follows: "Those suffixes (*pratyaya*) which [apply] to *dharma* after [the word] *caraṇa*—they [apply] to a collection (*samūha*) after *caraṇa* itself"? In that case, it is first of all difficult for the word *caraṇa*, being heard only once, to have such a dual connection. Even if it were possible, whatever suffix might apply to *dharma* after any *caraṇa*-word whatsoever would result; thus, the suffix *aṇ* would apply after *kaupiñjala* and *hāstipada*, and it would also apply after *Kaṭha* and others. However, when there is an indication by means of the suffix *-vat*, there is the inclusion of all points of similarity.

It occurs as follows: by whatever bases, with whatever qualification, and by which suffixes suffixes are prescribed for a *dharma* [in the Vedic literature], here too, from those same bases, with that very same qualification, those same [suffixes] occur; thus, nothing undesirable arises. For example: *kāṭhakam*, *kālāpakam*—[these are formed] by the suffix *vuñ* after [words denoting] a lineage (*gotra*) or a school (*caraṇa*). *Chāndogyam*—[this is formed] by the suffix *ñya* according to the rule *chandogaukthika*. *Ātharvaṇam*—[this is formed] by the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *ātharvaṇikasyekalopaśca*, and there is also the elision of the suffix *ik*.
The suffix *iṣṭhakā* is added after the words *acitta*, *hastin*, and *dhenu*. || 4.2.47 ||

The phrase "an exception to *aṇ*" means that among words not signifying a sentient being (*acittārtha*), this [suffix] is an exception to *aṇ* according to the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*). However, in the case of *kapota* and other such words denoting sentient beings, since the suffix *añ* has already found its scope of application, it is an exception to *añ* because it occurs later [in the order of rules]. As for the words *hasti* and *dhenu*, since they are both oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of the accent of their respective suffixes—*hasti* ending in the suffix *ini* by the rule "after *hasta*, [the suffix] *ini* [is added] when denoting a genus" (*hastājjātau*), and *dhenu* ending in the suffix *nup* by the rule "from the root *ghaiṭ*, [the suffix] *nup*" (*gheranuśca*)—this [suffix *aṇ*] is an exception to *añ*, which would otherwise be characterized by an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudāttādi*). Regarding the form *ādhenavam*: the suffix *añ* is applied because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *atsa*; furthermore, there is an absence of *vṛddhi* substitution in accordance with the rule "of that which ends in *jaṅgala*, *dhenu*, or *valaja*" (*jaṅgaladhenuvalajāntasya*).
The suffix *ya* is applied after [words ending in] *pāśa* and so forth. || 4.2.49 ||

That which ends in the suffix *ya* is feminine by its very nature. The word *vāta* is listed here [in the sense of "wind"]: "a collection (*samūha*) of winds is *vātyā*. [Objection: Since individual winds are not perceived, a "collection" is inappropriate here; therefore, it should be stated that the suffix denotes "swiftness" (*śīghratva*). [Response: This is not a fault. Even for a single composite wind, a distinction based on different directions is superimposed, and the "collection" is based upon that.

Alternatively, it is the parts of the wind itself that are divided according to each direction, and thus there is such a perception: "the east wind," "the north wind," or "winds blow from all directions. And it has been said: "The mingling of winds with winds is the mark of their diversity.
[Pāṇini 4.2.50: *khalagorathāt*].

Now, why are *khala* and the others not also listed among *pāśa* and the rest, so that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) need not be explicitly uttered? To this, he says: "Because they are not included among *pāśa* and the others."
And [the suffixes] ini, tra, ka, ṭyaP, and caC [are applied after a verbal root]. 4.2.51.

The separation of the *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of establishing a correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyārtha*). There would be a discrepancy, as there are four suffixes—namely, *anyat*, *hanit*, *kaṭyac*, and *astrac* due to the word "and" (*ca*)—whereas the bases (*prakṛti*) are only three.
Regarding the phrase "from *khalādi*" etc., the members of the *khalādi* group are to be understood from usage. These suffixes also, by their very nature, apply only to the feminine.
The word *viṣaya* [is used] in the sense of "region. (Pāṇini 4.2.52)

Now, one might object that since the term "object" (*viṣaya*) is never found apart from a location (*deśa*), the qualification "location" is redundant. To this he says: "This word 'object'... It is "extremely familiar" (*atyantaśīlita*), meaning it is extremely well-practiced [in common usage]. In that context, the inclusion of the word "location" is for the purpose of conveying a collection of villages. If this is so, one might ask: let there be only the word "location" and let the word "object" not be used? This cannot be done; for the word "location" (*deśa*) also has multiple meanings, as it can be a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*) meaning "the act of pointing out" (*deśana*).

The region that is the domain of the Śibis is called *śaiba*. How is it that the Śibis [are said to] be the country? When there is the intention to express their residence, the suffix *lup* will apply according to the rule "the suffix denoting 'his residence' is elided when referring to a country" (*tasya nivāsaḥ*, *janapade lup*). But surely there is a difference in meaning: in the expression "the country is the residence of the Śibis," the relationship of owner and owned is not perceived, because residence is possible even in a country belonging to others.

In the expression *śibīnāṃ viṣayaḥ* ("the territory of the Śibis"), however, the relationship of owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) is understood, rather than the sense of residence; for even those who do not dwell there may possess ownership. True; that very suffix *lup* is prescribed by tradition (*smṛta*) when their residence is in the very same country that constitutes the territory of those [people], and not merely upon residence in general. And here, the inherent nature of the designation (*abhidhānasvābhāvya*) is the reason. Thus, in the sense of "the territory of the Śibis," the form *śaiba* occurs, and the word *viṣaya* is also used [in this context].

In this way, the territory of the Vasātis is *vāsātaḥ*, while their very dwelling place is the *vasātayaḥ*. Likewise, the territory of the Gāndhārīs is *gāndhāraḥ*, while their dwelling place is the *gāndhārayaḥ*. In the cases of the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Srughnas, and Puṇḍras, it is only the nature of the dwelling place that is intended to be expressed, not the nature of the territory.

Even in the rule *eṣāṃ rājanyādibhyo vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.53), when there is a desire to express the sense of "territory" (*viṣaya*), we have *rājanyakam*, meaning "the territory inhabited by the Rājanyas. In that same context, regarding words such as *bailvata* and others, it is only the sense of "territory" that is intended; therefore, forms such as *bailvatakam* and *āmbarīṣaputrakam* alone occur. In all cases, the sole cause is the expressive power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) itself. Thus he says: "When expressing the territory, there is elision (*lup*) [of the suffix] after [names of] countries; or optionally after *gāndhārī* and others, or necessarily after [words] beginning with *rājanya*, provided they denote a plural number of inhabitants; or not at all, because the thing denoted is the territory itself."
When there is a desire to express the dwelling place, there is elision (*lup*); but when there is a desire to express the object of perception, there is the suffix.
The word "so" (he/that) [is used] as the initial [member of a compound] in the case of *pragāthas* belonging to the Vedic meters. 4.2.55.

The term *chandas* does not denote its own form, nor does it refer to the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* texts; what then? There is a word *chandas* which expresses a specific measure of syllables, and it is that whose particular varieties are the *jagatī* and so forth that is being referred to; since this [word] is possible at the beginning of the *prāgāthas*, the suffix is applied after words such as *paṅkti* and the like.

In cases where two *ṛc*s are made into three—such as by repeating the fourth and sixth quarters of a *bārhata* *pragātha* and then pausing before the following two verses—in this manner and others like it; for example: *yajñāyajñā vaḥ priyaṃ mitraṃ na śaṃsiṣoṃ priyaṃ mitraṃ na śaṃsiṣam ūrje nipātam*. The specific mode of utterance therein is "weaving" (*grathana*). Thus, it is called "from weaving" (*pragrathanāt*).

He shows the cause for the application of the term *pragātha*: it is called a *pragātha* because it is "chanted forth" (*pragrathyate*). The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "also when [the action] is not the agent" (*akartari ca kārake*). The letters *r* and *n* are elided due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *gā* with the prefix *pra*. According to the rule "the *ṇatva* [substitution of *ṇ*] occurs after a *kṛt*-suffix ending in a vowel," there is the substitution of *ṇ*. From the root *gai* (meaning "to sound") with the prefix *pra*, we have *pragīyate*; thus it is a *pragātha*, formed by adding the suffix *than* to the roots *uṣi*, *kuṣi*, and *garti*. Regarding the word *traiṣṭubham*:
just as in the word *kuṭīra* there is a change of gender despite the suffix being applied in its own sense (*svārthika*), so too here one should understand the neuter gender.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *saṃgrāma*, when it denotes the purpose for which warriors fight. 4.2.56.

Anticipating the objection that—on account of the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*—the suffix would apply to words denoting the battle (*saṃgrāma*) rather than to the final members mentioned, namely the purpose and the combatants—he says: "The case-ending of the *samartha* [word] is 'that belongs to this' (*so'sya*)," and so forth. The word "first" (*prathamā*) is a qualifier of the *samartha* [word]. Thus, by way of the qualified [word], it is the purpose and the combatants themselves that are indicated as being first. The word "battle" (*saṃgrāma*) is a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix. Thus, by way of that [suffix-meaning], the battle is indicated as being the final member.
The suffix *ñ* (forming *-ī*) is applied after a word ending in the *ghañ* suffix to denote "that in which this action occurs. (Pāṇini 4.2.58)

"In this [suffix]" refers to the meaning of the suffix; by this, he shows that gender is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*). "From a word ending in *ghañ* which denotes an action" means: from that which ends in the *ghañ* suffix used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Regarding *śyainampāta*: falling is *pāta*; "the flight of hawks" (*śyenānāṃ pātaḥ*) is a compound with a genitive in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), followed by the suffix *ñ*, and the augment *mum* according to the rule "after *śyena* and *tila*, *ñ* is applied in the sense of falling. Regarding *prākāra*: [it is derived from *pra-kṛ* with the suffix *ghañ*].

This word is denotative of a substance (*dravyavacana*), ending in the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). The lengthening of the vowel in the prefix *pra-* occurs according to the rule "the [vowel] of a prefix is diversely lengthened before *ghañ* when not referring to a human being. And since this rule is a general injunction, he confirms it by means of an example: "falling of a staff" (*daṇḍapāta*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote one who studies or knows that [work]. Pāṇini 4.2.59.

In this world, it is established by the mention of either one that whoever studies a text knows its form, and whoever knows it necessarily studies it; for what purpose, then, are these two meanings taught? Their coexistence is not necessary, for "study" is the recitation of the words, while "knowledge" is the comprehension of the meaning; and it happens that someone recites the text without knowing the meaning, and someone else knows the meaning without reciting the text.

Regarding the phrase "the double mention of 'tat'" and so forth: if it were stated simply as "one who studies that or knows that" (*tad adhīte veda*), a conjunction (*samuccaya*) would be understood; consequently, the [suffix] would apply only to one who both studies and knows it, but not to one who merely studies it or merely knows it. However, with the double mention of "tat," a distinction between the two suffixes for the student and the knower is established through a division of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

But surely, in the rule *tad asya tadasmin syāt*, since there is an indication of multiple meanings, the case endings expressing the respective capacities must be connected to each one; thus, by the double mention of *tat*, the underlying principle will be established. For this very reason, in the rule *tena dīvyati*, the suffix occurs for each individual meaning? We do not say that the double mention of *tat* here is for the sake of prescribing separate rules for those who study and those who know. What then? It is for the sake of [avoiding repetition] in subsequent rules such as *kratūkthādisūtrāntāṭ ṭhak* and *vasantādibhyaṣ ṭhak*.

In this case as well, what would be the reason [for the restriction]? The word *kratu* is a name for a ritual action (*karman*), and terms such as *vasanta* (spring) and so forth are its referents; however, their study is not possible, because that [study] has sound (*śabda*) as its object. Study is indeed possible with respect to the text associated with those [referents], but it is not accepted there because it would be secondary (*gauṇa*). Rather, since knowledge is possible only in the primary sense, [the qualification] would apply only to those who know [the rituals], not to the student. However, because of the repeated mention of "that" (*tat*), and because the secondary sense is also grasped through effort, it applies there as well.
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after words ending in *kratu*, *uktha*, and so forth, as well as after words ending in *sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "from those denoting specific sacrifices": there is no inclusion of the word-form itself [the root *yaj*]. If that were the case, it would have been recited only among *uktha* and so forth. Nor does it apply to synonyms for general sacrifices such as *soma-yāga* and others, because the word *yajña* is already recited among *uktha* and the rest. Therefore, the suffix is applied to those specific terms when they function in their primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) to denote a knower [of the sacrifice], and when they function in a text intended to explain them, it denotes a student. Thus, one is called a *vārttikasūtrika*.

The term *vārttika* means "that which is good for the commentary (*vṛtti*)," derived from the rule *kathādibhyaṣṭak*. The suffix is applied here based on a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "it is both a *vārttika* and a *sūtra*. Similarly, one says *sāṃgrahasūtrikaḥ*. The term *kalpasūtra* is either a *karmadhāraya* or a *samāhāra-dvandva* compound.

Regarding the expression *yajñāyajñīyātpareṇa*: the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in connection with the suffix *enaP* is questionable; for even *enaP* is only optional after the word *para*, since in its rule of formation, the phrase *uttarādharadakṣiṇādātiḥ* does not apply, but rather only *dikśabdebhyaḥ*. Furthermore, a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*) is not desired when [the word] refers to one who studies those [texts]. Thus, neither of the two suffixes—*ṭhak* nor *aṇ*—is desired; consequently, the expression *ukthānyadhīte* remains merely a sentence (and not a nominal derivative).

And in this matter, the very designation itself is the refuge; [it is found] in the *Prātiśākhya*, which is characterized by the *Sāman*. Regarding the term *aukthikya*: it is the traditional corpus (*āmnāya*) of the *Aukthikas*; the suffix *ñya* is applied according to the rule "after *chandoga* and *aukthika*" in the sense of "belonging to" (*idamarthe*). It means that no further suffix is added after the word *aukthikya*; rather, the suffix *aṇ* is applied—this was mentioned incidentally. Regarding the phrase "after a word ending in *sūtra*": he says that what has been stated is too little, adding that one should say "after words ending in *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *kalpasūtra*."

The statement beginning with "vidyā ca" (and *vidyā*) serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to what was previously over-extended. The meaning is that the word *vidyā*, when preceded by [the term] *aṅga* and so forth, does not produce a suffix. Regarding the form *traividya*: *trividyā* is a knowledge consisting of three parts; one who studies that is a *traividya*. However, if the analysis were "one who has studied three sciences" (*tisro vidyā adhīta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of elision (*luk*) according to the rule "dvigor lug anapatye" (Pāṇini 4.1.88).

Regarding the term *yāvakrītika*: a narrative composed concerning Yavakrīta is referred to by the word *yavakrīta*; likewise, a work composed concerning Priyaṅgu is called *praiyaṅgava* by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Regarding *vāsavadattika*: a tale (*ākhyāyikā*) composed concerning Vāsavadattā; in the sense of "a book composed concerning [someone]," the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*, which is then elided by the rule *lubākhyāyikābhyo bahulam*, after which this suffix *ṭhak* is added. The same applies to *saumanottarika* and *aitihāsika*.

"Itihāsa" is that which is said as "it was thus"; it is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Regarding the phrase "of all [beginning with] *sarva*": the meaning is that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix produced after a word beginning with *sarva*, as well as after a *dvigu* compound; since the term *sa-* is understood as having a specific meaning, the word *sarva-* is mentioned separately. By the rule "and after a *dvigu*," this very elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule "elision after a *dvigu* when not denoting a descendant" is recalled. In the example *sarvaveda*, there is elision of the *aṇ* suffix [from the sense] "he studies all the Vedas. In *savārttika*, [the same applies].

In the expression *varttikāntam adhīte* ("he studies up to the end of the Vārttikas"), there is an *avyayībhāva* compound with the word *saha* used in the sense of "limit" (*anta*). By the rule *avyayībhāve cākāle*, the substitution of *sa-* for *saha* occurs, followed by the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding *anusū-*: the word *anusū* produces the suffix *ṭhak*, as do words meaning "the characterized" (*lakṣya*) and "the characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). In the form *ānusukaḥ*: [one who] has studied the *anusū* takes the suffix *ṭhak*; its replacement by *ka* occurs by the rule *isusuktantāt kaḥ*, and the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*. Regarding *padottarapada-*: that of which the word *pada* is the final member (*uttarapada*) is so described. One who has studied the *pūrvapada* is called *pūrvapadikaḥ*. Likewise, one who has studied the *uttarapada* is called *uttarapadikaḥ*.

Regarding the term *śataṣaṣṭeḥ*: the suffix *ṣikan* is applied to a word ending in the word *pathin* which follows either the word *śata* or the word *ṣaṣṭi*. The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*.
The suffix *ini* is applied after [words such as] *anubrāhmaṇa* and others. 4.2.62.

Regarding the expression *brāhmaṇāsadṛśa*: the compound *asadṛśa* is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule "the indeclinable [is compounded] with its correlative meaning" (*yathārthe yadavyayam*), here signifying similarity. [The opponent] objects: "It would have the sense of possession (*matvartha*). [The author] replies: "In that case, [the suffix would be derived] from this [base]. [The opponent] refutes this: "Because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*). [The author] states the direct solution: "But the statement [of the rule] is for the purpose of excluding the suffix *aṇ*. However, in some recensions, the passage beginning with "it would have the sense of possession" (*matvartha*) is not read.
The suffix *ṭhak* is added after [words denoting] spring (*vasanta*) and so forth.

Regarding the term *vasantasahacarita*: it refers to that which describes springtime, or that which is to be studied during springtime. It receives its designation through association with spring (*vasanta-sāhacarya*). Should these [names] be recited in the *uktha* group, or those [groups] in the *vasanta* group? They were simply not arranged in that way. The word *atharvan* is recited here; it refers by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*) to the treatise composed by Atharvan. One who studies the *Atharvaṇa* is an *Ātharvaṇika*; the absence of *ṭi*-elision (of the final syllable) is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule "dāṇḍināyana-hāstināyana," which supersedes the general rule "na-staddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144).
The elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending] is prescribed after what has been mentioned [in the preceding rules]. 4.2.64.

Regarding the phrase *proktasahacarita* ("associated with what is taught"): since the word "taught" (*prokta*) refers to the meaning (*artha*), and because it is impossible for a suffix to have a temporal sequence (priority or posteriority) with respect to a meaning, the primary sense is untenable; therefore, the secondary (metaphorical) sense is accepted—this is the meaning. Another says: here the word *prokta* is accented (*svarita*); by that, the suffix prescribed under that governing rule (*adhikāra*) is understood. Or rather, *prokta* means "that which exists in what is taught," and this is a Vedic (Pāṇinian) elliptical expression (*ataddhitānirdeśa*). [The example is] *pāṇinīyam*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that one who possesses a *paṇa* (bet) is called *paṇī*; his descendant is *pāṇinaḥ*; the youthful descendant of *pāṇina* is *paṇina-yuvan* = *pāṇiniḥ*. Then, when there is the intention to express the meaning "taught by him," the suffix *iñ* is elided by the rule "elision of *yuvan*" (*yūni luk*), and subsequently, by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule "*iñaśca*" [Pāṇini 4.1.95]? [Response: This is not a fault. In the rule "*iñaśca*," the word "*gotre*" (in the sense of a lineage) is understood as a carry-over from the rule "*kaṇvādibhyo gotre*" [Pāṇini 4.2.111]. Therefore, we shall qualify the suffix *iñ*: "after that which ends in an *iñ* prescribed in the sense of a lineage. Thus, since the *iñ* here was not prescribed in the sense of a lineage, the application of *aṇ* does not occur.

And in that context, the technical term *gotra* is understood; therefore, the suffixes *yu* and *un* will not apply, and instead, the suffix *cha* will follow by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*. From the word *āpiśali*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *iñaśca*; in both cases, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting the student. Now, one might object: "Whether this elision occurs or not, the form remains the same, so there is no difference? To this, he replies: "There is a difference regarding the feminine gender and the accent. If the elision did not occur, in the feminine gender the suffix *ṅīp* would be applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*, and the word would have an udātta accent on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix *aṇ*.

When there is elision (*luk*), however, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs, and by the accentual rule for *cha*, the word becomes middle-accented (*madhyodātta*). In the system of Āpiśali, there is no difference regarding the accent; however, just as *ṅīp* does not occur here even when there is elision—as was explained under the rule "from that which is not a subordinate member" (*anupasarjanāt*)—so it is in this case as well.
And from a sūtra, when accompanied by the word *sopadha*. (Pāṇini 4.2.65)

Regarding the term *aṣṭakaṃ sūtram*: its measure consists of eight chapters (*adhyāya*). According to the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṅghasūtrādhyayaneṣu*, and specifically by the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*, the suffix *kan* is applied.

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] to a suffix whose base is a numeral. This means it should be stated that [the suffix *ka* is applied] after a word ending in a numeral which is the base of a suffix, provided that the word has a *k* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*). For example: *kālāpakaḥ*, meaning "one who studies the *Kālāpa*. The *Kālāpa* [Veda] is so called because it was taught by Kalāpin; thus, from *kalāpin* we derive *kālāpāḥ* by the rule *kalāpino’ṇ*. Then, by the supplementary rule *nāntasya ṭilope sabrahmacārī*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonants). From that, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule *tadadhīte*, and the suffix *prokta* is elided by the rule *luk*.

The traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) of the Kālāpas is called *Kālāpaka* by the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ*. From that, the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of "one who studies that" (*tadadhīte*). The elision (*luk*) of this suffix does not occur; for if it were to occur, the word would be acute-accented on the first syllable due to the accent of the *ñit*-suffix, whereas in the absence of elision, the accent of the suffix *aṇ* itself prevails. Furthermore, in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding the word *catuṣṭaya*: since it has four parts (*avayava*), the suffix *tayap* is added according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*. The cerebral [ṣ] occurs by the rule *hrasvāttādau taddhite*.
And the *chandobrāhmaṇa* texts have that [Veda] as their subject matter. 4.2.66.

The phrase "the mention of *prokta*" (proktagrahaṇa) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Indeed, although it carries over, it does not connect with the preceding sūtra because of the force of its initial formulation. "Vedic meters (*chandāṃsi*) and Brāhmaṇas" means those word-forms which denote them. It is not a reference to their own phonetic forms (*svarūpa*), because of the use of the plural number and because they do not end in the suffixes that form words meaning "proclaimed by" (*aproktapratyayānta*). [The term refers to] those ending in the suffixes that form words meaning "proclaimed by" (*proktapratyayānta*).

The word "proktāt" (from what is taught), which ends in the ablative case, is modified into the nominative plural to agree with "chandobrāhmaṇāni" (the Vedic hymns and Brāhmaṇas); this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "objects of the cognition of those who study or know them," he demonstrates the following: by the word "tat" (that), the cognition of the student or knower is referred to, because it is the primary element as that which is to be enjoined; it does not refer to the students or knowers themselves, because they are subordinate elements in the injunction regarding the suffix.

What is established? It follows that the sentence is also excluded from having the student as its referent (*viṣaya*). This is because "having no other state" (*ananyabhāva*) is the meaning of the term *viṣaya*. Furthermore, the word *viṣaya* is not taken here in the sense of a collection such as a village, because that is impossible in this context. In this regard, if the phrase "one who studies the Veda" (*vedam adhīte*) were to carry over [from the previous rule], then its status as a *viṣaya* would be prescribed only when there is the intention to speak of the student or the knower; consequently, it would exclude only that specific sentence, but not sentences concerning other actions, nor independence, nor connection with other qualifiers (*upādhi*).

As it has been said: "In that context, there is an application to that subject matter according to the specific qualification (*yathādhikāra*). Therefore, only the mention of *prokta* (that which is taught) continues [from the previous rule], and not the phrase "one who studies the Veda. By the word *tat* (that), the suffix (*pratyaya*) is referred to, and the word *viṣaya* (subject matter) is intended in the sense of "nothing else" (*ananyabhāva*). By this, all these [other conditions] such as independence (*svātantrya*) and so forth are excluded. And it has been stated: "But it is established [that the suffix applies] under the heading of *prokta*, because of the statement regarding its subject matter. The meaning is that only the mention of *prokta* is governed [by the rule], and not the two meanings [of the root *iṅ*] "one who studies" or "the Veda."

In this context, the suffixes prescribed [by the rule] are seen to have many varieties: independence (*svātantrya*), connection with another attribute (*upādhyantarayoga*), a sentence (*vākya*), and the suffix applied to the student or the knower (*adhyetṛ-veditṛ-pratyaya*). Independence, for instance: "proclaimed by Pāṇini" (*pāṇininā proktam*) results in *pāṇinīyam*; here the derivative (*vṛtti*) has the same meaning as the original sense of "proclaimed. Connection with another attribute: "the great *pāṇinīya*" (*mahatpāṇinīyam*). A sentence: "he studies the *pāṇinīya*" (*pāṇinīyam adhīte*). The suffix applied to the student: "students of the *pāṇinīya*" (*pāṇinīyāś chātrāḥ*).

However, for words denoting *chandasaḥ* (Vedic texts) and *brāhmaṇāni* (Brāhmaṇas) that end in the suffixes prescribed [by Pāṇini 4.2.66], it is desired that they always denote those who study or know them, and not independence (*svātantrya*) and so forth; for this purpose, the present rule is commenced. Thus he says: "by that" (*tena*). And by doing so, he shows that the analysis (*vigraha*) of both meanings should be performed by means of a single common expression (*tantra*).

Those who study what was proclaimed by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhas*. [The suffix] *ṇini* is applied because he is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana; for that [suffix], there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "elision after *kaṭha* and *caraka*. Then, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that," and subsequently, that too is elided by the rule "elision after [a suffix] denoting 'proclaimed' (*prokta*). From the words *muda* and *pippalāda*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied as the general rule (*autsargika*). The remainder is to be understood as before, according to the appropriate application. *Ṛcābha* is a pupil of Vaiśampāyana. Similarly, *Tāṇḍya*. The word *Vājasaneya* belongs to the *Śaunakādi* group. [Thus] *Tāṇḍins*.

In the word *apatyasya*, there is the elision of *y*. The word *bhāllavi* ends in the suffix *iñ*. From the word *śāṭya*, which ends in *yañ* (from the *garga*-class), the suffix *phak* is applied by the rule *yañiñośca*. The word *aitareya* ends in *ḍhak* (from the *śubhra*-class); from these [words], the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu*, and in all cases, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting the student.

"For the purpose of indicating a specific [type of] Brāhmaṇa": the specific quality of the Brāhmaṇa is that he is "proclaimed in the Purāṇas. Regarding "Yājñavalkyāni": the word *yājñavalkya* belongs to the *kaṇva*-class; by the general rule (*utsargika*) for names beginning with *sulabha*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and here there is independence [of formation]. He will state under the rule "purāṇaprokteṣu" (Pāṇini 4.3.105): "For Yājñavalkya and others have appeared in recent times; thus, they are mentioned in the narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*). Regarding "Kāśyapinaḥ" and "Kauśikinaḥ": [the suffix] *ṇini* is applied after the two sages Kāśyapa and Kauśika.

Regarding "Pārāśariṇaḥ": from the word *pārāśarya*, which ends in the *yañ* suffix belonging to the *garga*-class, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "from *pārāśarya* and *śilālin*," and as before, there is the elision of *y*. Regarding "Karmandinaḥ": [the suffix] *ini* is applied by the rule "from *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva*, *ini*. Regarding [the word derived from] *piṅga*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "in the case of those proclaimed in the Purāṇas."
The suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied [to a word denoting a thing] in the sense that "it exists in this," when the place has that name. 4.2.67.

Regarding the phrase "if there is the intention [to refer] by means of the particle *iti*": now, one might ask, "Will there not be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) simply by mentioning the name itself? That is not so; for a name is of two kinds: that which is sometimes designated by someone at some time, and that which is eternal and follows worldly usage. The particle *iti* is employed here for the purpose of including the second type, as well as for the purpose of including specific categories such as the *bhūman*.

The phrase "in that name" (*tannāmni*), however, serves to override even stronger cognitions that contradict its status as a proper name; otherwise, since the suffix *matup* would apply when [the name] has not yet been reached, this [suffix *ini*] would be its sublater. But if one were to weigh it against the exceptions to that—namely *ini*, *ṭhan*, and so on—then by the rule of "prohibition of an exception" (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), the suffixes *ini*, *ṭhan*, and the rest alone would prevail.
That which has been produced by that [is expressed by the suffix -maya]. (Pāṇini 4.3.135)
The word "nirvṛttam" is derived from the root *vṛt* with the sense of the causative (*ṇy-artha*) inherent within it, and the suffix *kta* is applied in the passive sense (*karman*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a place of residence. 4.2.69.
"Of you two who are straight" means: those whose boat is straight.
And [a word] meaning "situated not far from" [is compounded with its object]. 4.2.70.

"Adūrabhavaḥ" means that which exists not far from (*adūra*) or near (*antika*) a place; it is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) by virtue of a formal rule (*nipātana*). Regarding the word "vidiśāyāḥ": the genitive case is used according to the rule "with words meaning 'far' or 'near,' the sixth [case] is optionally employed. As for the particle *ca* and so forth: if it were not present, this very meaning would be connected with what follows immediately thereafter due to proximity.
And after *aura*. 4.2.71.

*Āraḍu* is a specific Kṣatriya name. Regarding the rule "after a river name, [the suffix] *matup* [is applied]," this is the scope for *arañ*, as in *āraḍava* and so forth; whereas the scope for the rule "after a river name, *matup*" is exemplified by *audumbarāvatī* and so forth.
And [the suffix -matup] is applied after a word ending in *mātra* when it means "having many legs. (Pāṇini 5.2.37)

Regarding the term *caturarthika*: a collection of four meanings is a *caturarthī*; that which exists therein [is called] *caturarthika*, by virtue of the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the rule beginning with *adhyātmādi*. However, when a *dvigu* compound is used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there would be elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*.

The question "Why is there the mention of *aṅga*? is asked because one might argue: "Let it simply be 'matośca bahvacaḥ'; since the two ablative cases are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), when it is understood that [the suffix] is prescribed after a *matup* that follows a base consisting of many syllables, the intended meaning is indeed established. The intention is to prevent the word *bahvac* from being a qualifier of the *matub*-ending itself. Otherwise, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, it would be improper to assume a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); thus, the concern is that it would become a qualifier of that very [suffix].
Is there now any instance where a word ending in many vowels occurs, for which the inclusion of the term "bahvac" (having many vowels) would be necessary? He says that there is: *svavān*, *śvavān*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied after the word] *udaka* when it means "free from" (*vipāśa*). 4.2.74.
"A great and subtle scrutiny"—this is a praise of the Teacher, implying that the Teacher has indeed applied such careful attention even to the vowels.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [place names] beginning with Suvāstu.

Regarding the word *aṇ*: this refers to the intention of the sūtra as it stands without the mention of *aṇ*. He himself will state its purpose: "The mention of *aṇ* is for the sake of superseding *matup*. Therefore, in reality, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to *matup* as well. Now, what is the purpose of mentioning *aṇ*? One might ask: why not simply say "as prescribed from *suvāstu* and so on"? Because of the repetition [of the rule], that which was prescribed once and does not otherwise apply will indeed come to be; and since that is *aṇ*, would it not suffice? To this he replies: "The mention of *aṇ*... [etc.]

If the mention of *aṇ* were not present, then by the rule of "an intermediate exception sublates [the preceding]," that which is prescribed by *yat* would sublate only *añ*, whereas *matup*—being subsequent—would sublate it; however, because of the repeated mention of *aṇ*, it occurs even in the domain of *matup*. Furthermore, it has been stated that for the rule *orañ*, *matup* is a sublater due to its posteriority; in that case, if the mention of *aṇ* were absent and it were said that "that which is prescribed by *yat* [sublates]," then in the case of a river (*nadī*), only *orañ* would apply, and the explicit statement [of *añ*] would merely serve to sublate *matup*.
Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* must be made for this purpose as well.
The suffix *roṇī* [is applied after the word *kārṣāpaṇa*]. 4.2.78.

[The rule applies] both to the simple [stem] and to that which ends in it. Otherwise, because of the prohibition against *tadantavidhi* (the application of a rule to that which ends in a given element) when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is accompanied by a suffix, the operation would apply only to the simple [stem], not to that which ends in it. However, regarding the word *roṇī*, since the mention is made independently of any technical rule (*śāstra*), the independence from a rule is indicated here; thus, by the Paribhāṣā [which states that] "when there is no expectation [of another rule], [the operation applies] even to that which ends in it," the operation occurs even for that which ends in it. Now, one might object: this *roṇī* is not a nominal stem, because it ends in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).

And in the rule *grahaṇavatā prātipadikena*, there is no inclusion of that which is qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*), such that the extension of a suffix (*tadantavidhi*) would be prohibited even for that which ends in a feminine suffix; for this is a paribhāṣā concerning rules involving the actual form (*svarūpa*) of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), since it has been stated that when the actual form of a *prātipadika* is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included. This was stated on the basis of the position of the author of the Bhāṣya, who holds that whenever a *prātipadika* is mentioned in any way whatsoever, that which is qualified by gender is included.

Thus, this is precisely the position of the author of the Vṛtti as well; it is understood that the opposing view is presented in the rule regarding *ṅī* and *āp*. What is established by this? In the case of *kumārayati* (he describes a young girl), the elision of the suffix *ṭi* is established by the rule "as in the case of *iṣṭhan*" (*ṇāviṣṭhavad*).

[The suffixes] vuñ, chaṇ, kaṭhac, ila, sa, ini, ra, ḍhañ, ṇya, ya, phak, phiñ, iñ, ñya, kak, ṭhak, and orīhaṇak, [are applied] after the groups beginning with *kṛśāśva*, *arīhaṇa*, *kumuda*, *kāśatṛṇa*, *prekṣā*, *aśman*, *sakhi*, *saṅkāśa*, *bala*, *pakṣa*, *karṇa*, *sutaṅgama*, *pragadin*, *varāha*, and *kumuda*. In the sūtra, the word *kumuda* is mentioned twice; there, because two *dvandva* compounds—namely, *arīhaṇakṛśāśvarśyakumudāḥ* and *kāśatṛṇādayaḥ*—are formed, there is no application of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) rule. Thus it is said: "after the *kumuda*-group, etc."

He confirms with the usage of an authoritative source (āpta) that which was stated previously—that even the general rule (*autsargika*) is accepted there in the case of *ṛśya* and so forth—by saying, "And thus it has been said. This was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the rule *lupi yuktavat*. Now, why not say that based on this usage, the elision (*lub*) occurs optionally only for those [suffixes] prescribed by specific rules? Let it be so; in any case, it is precisely this fourfold form (*cātūrūpya*) that we desire here.
Or [the suffix *kan* is added] after the word *śarkarā*. 4.2.83.

Regarding "in *kumuda* and so forth": this refers to those [words] immediately following *ṛśya*. "By the force of its recitation" means that if the *lup* were obligatory, the recitation of this [term] in the two lists would be purposeless. Regarding *śākara*: there is *lup* of the *aṇ* suffix; thus *śārkaram*, where that very [suffix] is heard. Regarding *śarkarikam*: because it belongs to the *kumuda* group, there is the suffix *ṭhañ*. Regarding *śārkarakam*: because it belongs to the *varāha* group, there is the suffix *kak*, and by the rule "shortening before *ka*" (*ke'ṇaḥ*), the vowel is shortened. Regarding *śārkarikam* and *śarkarīyam*: these are formed by the suffixes *ṭhak* and *cha* according to the subsequent sūtra.
The suffix *matup* is applied after the word *nadī*. (Pāṇini 4.2.84)

Since the suffix *matup* is established by the rule "tad asyāsti asmin" (Pāṇini 5.2.94), this specific statement is intended to set aside the suffix *aṇ* which would otherwise apply by the rule "tad asminn asti" (Pāṇini 4.2.67), and for the sake of including meanings such as "ceased" (*nivṛtta*) and so forth. This is indicated by the term *cāturarthika*. The word *nadī* (river) serves as a qualifier of *deśa* (region). Although it was stated under the rule *viśiṣṭaliṅga* that "the mention of *nadī* [is made] because it is not a region, for a *janapada* (province) is indeed a region," here, however, it is said that the river itself is the region.

By virtue of its inherent connection, a non-human region (*ajanapada*) is included by the term "region" (*deśa*); thus, the fourfold secondary suffix (*cāturarthika*) applies even to mountains. Others, however, say: "A river is indeed a region, as is well-known in common usage. But in the rule *viśiṣṭaliṅga*, the mention of "river" (*nadī*) is for the purpose of including that *dvandva* compound whose every constituent member denotes a river, so that it does not apply where one constituent member denotes a river and another denotes a different kind of region.
In *udumbarāvatī* and similar forms, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *matau bahvaco'najirādīnām*. In *bhāgīrathī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tena nirvṛttam*.
The suffix *ḍmatup* is applied after the words *kumuda*, *naḍa*, and *vetasa*.

In examples such as *kumudvān*, the substitution of *v* for *m* occurs by the rule *mādupadhāyāśca*. Now, why was not [the suffix] prescribed with an initial *v* from the start? It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*); it indicates that this suffix also occurs after other bases. By this, the form *mahiṣmān* is established, and it becomes unnecessary to state the rule *mahiṣācca*. By this, the following view is also refuted: that the form is established simply by extending the *ḍit*-status to the suffix *matup* itself; for if the *ḍit*-status were extended, the aforementioned indication would not be supported.
The suffix *valac* is applied after the words *naḍa* and *śāda*.
The word *śāda* has the letter *d* as its penultimate; as it is said: "Mud (*paṅka*) is not feminine [and is called] *śāda* and *kardama*."
The suffix *valac* is applied after the word *śikhā*.

Regarding the statement "it will burn the crest," this is by the rule *danta-śikhā-t saṃjñāyām*. That [previous rule] is for the purpose of excluding the location; however, this present rule is for the sake of excluding *nivṛtta* and so forth, and for the purpose of subverting the suffix *aṇ* when the name refers to a location.
In the case of *naḍa* and others, the suffix *kuk* [is added]. (Pāṇini 4.2.91)

Regarding the rule *takṣan-lopaśca*: if, however, this *kuk* were made to follow the end of the word (*parādi*), then the elision of *n* would be established because the final syllable would possess the status of a word (*padatva*); however, there would be the impossibility of applying the substitute for the beginning of the suffix after *kuṭ*, because *cha* would not be the beginning of a suffix, and thus the substitution of *īya* would not apply.
In the remaining cases. 4.2.92.

"Remainder (*śeṣa*) means other than those already employed. This is a statement regarding the meaning of the word. He states its specific qualification as it arises from the context: "from [the suffixes] *apatya* and so forth. For these are what have been employed here. Regarding the expression "ending with the four meanings": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which the four meanings—beginning with 'that exists in this' (*tadasminn asti*) and so on—are the limit (*paryanta*). In the reading *cāturarthyaparyantebhyaḥ*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in its own sense (as a synonym) to the *samāhāra-dvigu* compound *cāturarthya*, according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇyādi*.

However, those who read "from [roots] ending with *cāturarthya*" desire the suffix *aṇ* because *prajñā* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups). But for what purpose is the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*)? It is so that the suffixes *gha* and others may apply to the "remainder," and not to [meanings such as] "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth. Are "offspring" and the rest already excluded? Then let them not apply to the four meanings either.

Otherwise, just as the suffixes beginning with *orañ* and ending with *naḍādīnāṃ kuk ca* occur in the sense of the four [suffixes], so too would the suffixes beginning with *gha* and ending with *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām* occur in that same sense. For a section is not interrupted without cause. [Objection: Then will the four senses be discontinued? [Reply: No, because they are not marked with an *svarita* accent and because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely that the author reads certain words from the *utkarādi* group as *vṛddha*—such as *ārdraka* and *śālā*.

Otherwise, [the suffix] *cha* would already be established by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ. Well then, let the suffixes *gha* and so on not apply in their own sense (*svārtha*). For, since no specific meaning is prescribed for them, they would indeed apply in their own sense; however, these suffixes [beginning with *cha*] are not prescribed without a specified meaning. Will the suffixes *gha* and so on then recur in the senses of genus (*jāti*) and the rest? If they do recur, then for whichever subsequent base there is, the preceding suffix would have to apply again and again. There can be no mutual connection between two elements that are both preoccupied with specifying their respective meanings.

And from an indicative mark (*liṅga*): the fact that [Pāṇini] in some instances combines the previously mentioned [element] with the word *ca*, as in "In the case of *raṅku*, when not denoting a human, there is also *aṇ*," indicates that each preceding suffix does not apply to each subsequent base. Alternatively, the worldly governing rule (*adhikāra*) is characterized by mutual expectancy; however, the suffixes beginning with *gha* have no expectancy for other bases, nor do bases such as *grāma* have expectancy for other suffixes. Therefore, the purpose [of this argument] is that these [suffixes] should not occur in their own primary sense (*svārtha*).

Then that very purpose [of the rule] remains: namely, that [the suffixes] should not apply to offspring and so forth. But was it not already stated that "offspring and the like have long since ceased [to be relevant], and the fourfold meaning (*cāturarthī*) is not required"? We do not say that there is a direct connection between these [suffixes] and offspring and so forth; rather, what do we mean? By the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"), they would also apply to offspring and the like. How so? He says: "For offspring, groups, and so forth are indeed specific instances of 'this belonging to that' (*tasyedam*)."

Just as by the rule "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*), suffixes such as *cha* occur in specific instances like "students" (*chāttra*) and so forth, so too should suffixes such as *gha* occur in specific instances such as "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, because the general category exists within the particulars.

But surely, when a general term is employed in proximity to a specific term, it culminates in that specific [meaning]—as in "The Kauṇḍinya is a Brāhmaṇa," or in another specific case, "Curd for the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk for the Kauṇḍinya. In that context, the general term *tasyedam* ("belonging to him") is employed in proximity to specific instances such as offspring; if it were to culminate only in those specific instances [of offspring], the employment of the general term would be redundant. Therefore, it will culminate in another specific [meaning].

Furthermore, if *gh* and other suffixes were to apply even to [the meanings of] "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, they would have been prescribed right there in the rule *prāgdīvyato ’ṇ* along with *aṇ* and the others. Moreover, on account of an indicatory mark (*liṅga*), *gh* and the others will not apply to "offspring" and so forth. What is the indicatory mark? In the rule *pheś cha ca*, one need only say *phervā* for the purpose of prescribing *ṭhak*; once *ṭhak* is excluded, the suffix *cha* is already established by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. That very prescription of *cha* serves as an indicator—that indeed, *gh* and the others will not apply to "offspring" and so forth.

Likewise, since the suffix *vuñ* is already established by the rule "from *gotra* and *caraṇa*, *vuñ*" when the sense of "belonging to" (*idam-artha*) is included within the sense of "collection" (*samūha*), the fact that it is prescribed again by the rule "*gotra-ukṣoṣṭra-*" is also an indicator (*liṅga*) for this meaning. Similarly, in the rule "*rājanyādibhyo vuñ*", the word *daivayāta* is listed among the *rājanyādi* group; and *daivayātavāḥ*—meaning "the descendants of the Daivayātus"—ends in a *gotra* suffix.

Likewise, in the *Arihaṇādi* group, the word *bhāstrāyaṇa* is listed as ending in a *gotra* suffix; there too, [the form] is established by the rule "vuñ after a *gotra* or a *caraṇa*. Therefore, by these indicative marks (*liṅga*), suffixes such as *gha* will not occur in the sense of offspring and so forth. Thus, since this purpose [of the rule] is not tenable, he states another purpose with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*).

If the term *śeṣa* (remainder) were not included, it would be understood that the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth have fulfilled their purpose through connection with the first meaning alone. Consequently, regarding the second and subsequent meanings—those specifically delimited by the boundary "prior to *dīvya*"—only *aṇ* and the other suffixes prescribed therein would apply. However, since the word *śeṣa* is capable of denoting meanings such as "born" (*jāta*) and others by excluding those already employed, the suffixes *gha* and so forth are established in all cases. Therefore, the specific mention [of *śeṣa*] must be made for the sake of completeness.

[The sūtra] consists of "the definition" (lakṣaṇa) and "and the subsequent mention" (adhikāra). In that regard, [derivatives such as] *cākṣuṣa* and so forth are established simply by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*); however, [derivatives such as] *pārṣada* and so forth are established by the rule "prepared foods" (*saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*). Therefore, the status of being a "definition" is not of much use here.
The suffixes *dhak* and *kha* are applied after the word *rāṣṭra*, when it is preceded by *avārapāra*.

"It is also accepted [that the rule applies] even from a compound" means that in the Sūtra, however, only the aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is mentioned; otherwise, due to the inequality [of the number of elements], there would be no correspondence of number (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). "And because it is the reverse" means that this too is merely an accepted view (*iṣṭi*).
The suffixes *aṇ* and *khañ* are applied [after a word ending in the first case] to form a derivative meaning "belonging to" or "originating from" a village (*grāma*) and so forth.
The word *grāma* is listed among the *katryādi* group; therefore, the suffix *ḍhakañ* also occurs [after it].
The suffix *ḍhakañ* is applied after [words ending in] *kattrya*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.95).

Regarding *kāttreyaka*: either it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those who have three (*trayaḥ*) that are contemptible (*kutsitāḥ*)," which is *kat-trayaḥ*; by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the substitution of *kad-* for *ku-* occurs, so that one need not state the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the addition of *trau*" after the form with *kad-*. [The rule] "and there is elision of *y* after *kulyā*" is stated; however, some read the third letter as *l*, while others read it as *ḍ*.

Regarding the forms *kauleyaka* (a dog), *kukṣeyaka* (the mouth), and *grīveyaka* (an ornament): this grammatical derivation can be explained. How so? When the word *kula* refers to the "lineage of dogs," then its offspring is also simply a *śvan* (dog); in that case, the form is established by the suffix *ḍhakañ* according to the rule *apūrvapadād anyatarasyām*.
