From the words *kukṣi* and *grīvā*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied by the rule *dṛtikukṣikalaśivastyastyaherḍhañ*; then, for the meanings "mouth" (*āsya*) and "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), the suffix *kan* will be added as a pleonastic (*svārthika*) suffix.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after words such as *nadī* (river) and others [to denote "born there" or "originating there"].

In the *gaṇa* [list], "nadī" is taken as its own form (*svarūpa*), not as a technical name (*saṃjñā*), because "nadī," "mahī," and so forth are mentioned separately. In examples such as "paureya," the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which exists in the city," "that which exists in the forest," or "that which exists on the mountain. Both views are authoritative, since the Teacher has taught his disciples in both ways.
The suffix *tyak* is applied after [the words] *dakṣiṇa*, *paścāt*, and *puras*. (Pāṇini 4.2.98)

The word *dakṣiṇā* is understood here as an indeclinable ending in the suffix *āc*, according to the rule *dakṣiṇādāc*; this is because of its association with *paścāt* and *puras*. Therefore, there is no inclusion of the feminine form ending in *ṭāp* which signifies "proficiency."
The suffix *ṣphak* is applied after the word *kāpiśī*.

Regarding the term *bahv-ṛdiparda*: this statement is made because the suffix *vuñ* would otherwise apply by the rule "even after a word that does not contain a *vṛddhi* vowel [in its first syllable]."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *raṅkoḥ* when it refers to a human being.

There is a country named Raṅkava. From that [name], the suffix *aṇ* is first applicable by the rule "prāgdīvyato ’ṇ. This is superseded by *vuñ* according to the rule "avṛddhād api. Then, since it is a name of a region (*ordeśa*), *ṭhañ* applies; from that, *aṇ* applies by the rule "kopadhādaṇ. Then, *aṇ* is again applicable by the rule "kacchādibhyaś ca. Subsequently, the suffixes *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* are prescribed. Since *aṇ* would already be established simply because the word has a *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), the inclusion of the word *raṅku* in the list of *kacchādi* words is for the purpose of prescribing *vuñ* when it denotes either a human being or something residing therein. It is said that [the application of *vuñ*] takes precedence over [the others] because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].

The meaning is "because it is superior" or "because it is an exception. [An objection: But surely, since the suffix *aṇ* is already established for non-humans due to the inclusion [of the word] in the *kaccha*-group, that inclusion in the list must be for the purpose of prescribing the suffix *vuñ* for humans and things belonging to them; consequently, in a domain other than those, where *aṇ* is prescribed, there would only be the suffix *ṣpha*. [Response: This is not so; for there is no obstacle to the inclusion in the *kaccha*-group serving both purposes. By the maxim of the "negation-like" (*nañ-iva-yukta*), the understanding is produced as referring to a living being similar to a human.

As for the word *manuṣya* which is conventionally used (*rūḍha*) for *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth, it is not that alone which is being referred to here; [the author] considers this because such a meaning is not expressed [by the rule]. Now, why is it not understood in this way: since the suffix *vuñ* would already be established by the subsequent rule, the prohibition of *manuṣya* indicates that these two suffixes, *ṣpha* and *gaṇa*, also supersede the rule "of *manuṣya* and what pertains thereto" (*manuṣyatatsthayoḥ*). Consequently, in the case of "what pertains thereto," only *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* would apply, and not *vuñ*? That is not so, because it is not desired [that this should be the case].

For in that case, the suffix *ṣpha* would not be prescribed; rather, it would be *vuñ* alone. [The objection is: "In the expression *rāṅkavaḥ kambalaḥ*, the suffix *ṣpha* does not occur. However, according to the Vārttika and the Bhāṣya, *ṣpha* is indeed prescribed here, and the prohibition regarding humans has been rejected.

As it has been said: "The mention of *raṅku* and the exclusion of *manuṣya* [in the rule for the suffix *vuñ*] would be redundant, because *vuñ* is prescribed for [words denoting] humans and for things located therein (*tatstha*). If it is argued that this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the existence of the suffixes *ṣpha* and *gaṇa* when something is located therein, we say no, because such a result is not desired; furthermore, the mention of *aṇ* would be redundant, since *aṇ* is already prescribed after words beginning with *kaccha*. And by the suffix *ṣphak*, which is prescribed as a specific exception. Otherwise, since the reading of the *kacchādi* group would already have its purpose fulfilled in the sense of a living being (*prāṇin*), the suffix *ṣphak* alone would apply to a living being.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *dyu*, *prāc*, *apāc*, *udac*, and *pratīc*. (Pāṇini 4.2.101)

The term *dyu* is used here as a designation for *diva* by means of its substitution with *ut*. However, it does not include the word *dyu* itself, according to the explanation. Regarding the phrase "not to be expressed" (*avācyam*): *avācī* refers to the southern direction.

Regarding the rule "after an indeclinable expressing time": just as the suffix *ṭhañ* (as in *kālāṭṭhañ*) does not apply after an indeclinable expressing time, the same principle applies here due to the equality of the underlying logic.
The affixes *vuñ* and *vuk* are applied after [a word ending in] *varṇa*.

The region near that [river] is called Varṇu. In the sense of "situated not far from," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *suvāstvādibhyo 'ṇ*; this *aṇ* is then elided by the rule *janapade lup*. "Expressing an object whose domain is that" means: expressing an object for which that region of Varṇu is the domain (*viṣaya*). By the use of the term *viṣaya*, he indicates that in the expression *varṇau*, the locative case is used in the sense of a domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).
The suffix *tyap* is applied after an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Regarding *amehati*: the meaning is that the suffix *tyap* prescribed after an indeclinable is traditionally taught as occurring only after [indeclinables] beginning with *amā*. The word *amā* is a synonym for "near" (*samīpa*) and belongs to the *svarādi* group; thus, one who exists near (*amā*) is an *amātya* (minister). Regarding *aupariṣṭa*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the sense "existing above" (*upariṣṭāt*), the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs by the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of indeclinables when any suffix beginning with *bha* follows. The word *parataḥ* ends in *atasuc* according to the rule "optionally [after the words] *para* and *avara*"; [the suffix *aṇ* is added] in the sense of "existing there. Regarding *ārātīya*: because the rule "of *bahiṣ*, there is elision of the *ṭi*" is known to be non-universal (*anitya*), there is no elision of the *ṭi* here.

Regarding *tyap* in the sense of "fixed" (*dhruva*): when the word *dhruva* is to be expressed, the suffix *tyap* occurs after the prefix *ni*. Thus, that which exists invariably at all times is *nitya*. Regarding *nis* in the sense of "gone": when the word "gone" (*gata*) is to be expressed, the suffix *tyap* occurs after the prefix *nis*. Thus, *niṣṭya*. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "after a short vowel, before a suffix beginning with *t*, in a *taddhita*," and the *t* is changed to *ṣṭ* by the rule for *ṣṭu*-substitution. Similarly, that which has become manifest is *āviṣṭya*. Regarding *araṇyāṇṇa*: since the suffix *ṅīp* would have occurred if *aṇ* were applied, *ṇa* is prescribed instead.

Regarding the word *dūretya*: the suffix *etya* is used in the sense of "come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*). Regarding *auttarāha*: this statement is for the purpose of ensuring the initial udātta accent. In the form *auttarāham*, the suffix *āh* is applied by the rule *uttarācca*; since the suffix *tyap* does not apply here due to its exclusion from the specific enumeration (*parigaṇana*), the form is established through the suffix *aṇ*.
The words *aiṣamas*, *hyas*, and *śvas* may optionally [be compounded with a word ending in the seventh case]. 4.2.105.

The suffix *ṭhañ* is also the third [suffix]. Its status as the third is relative to the prescriptive rule (*vidhivākya*), but in relation to the suffixes [of that section], *ṭhañ* is the fourth; however, because the option (*vikalpa*) is in force in the rule "śvasastuṭ ca," the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* also occur.
The suffixes *añ* and *ña* are applied after a compound whose final member is *tīra* or *rūpya*.

There is a specific rule regarding feminine forms of words ending in *añc*: namely, *kākatīrī* and *cāṇārarūpyā*. This is so that [the suffix] might not apply after a word preceded by *bahuc*; otherwise, it would apply even after the word *bahutīra*. However, because the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is restricted to the context of compound formation, there is no possibility of its application after a word preceded by *bahuc*.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after a word beginning with a cardinal direction, provided it does not form a proper name.

Regarding the phrase *asaṃjñāyām*: this is not an indication by means of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), such as *asaṃjñāyāḥ*, because that meaning can also be obtained through the locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Thus he says: "from the scope of a name" (*saṃjñāviṣayāt*). Regarding *paurvaśāla*: this is a compound formed for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning "situated in the eastern hall" (*pūrvasyāṃ śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*); from that, the suffix is applied. Regarding the mention of the word *pada* and so forth: if it were stated simply as *dikpūrvāt*, it would refer to the actual form [of the word], and consequently, only forms such as *diggaja* (the elephant of the direction) would be possible.

However, when the word *pada* (foot/word) is included [in the definition], there is the inclusion of those words that denote specific directions. How so? It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a non-co-referential term (*vyadhikaraṇapada*): "that in which the first member (*pūrvapada*) is a direction. The genitive case in *diśaḥ* is used in relation to the denotative word; thus, the meaning is "that in which the first member is a denotative of a direction."
The suffix *añ* is applied after [words denoting] mothers. (Pāṇini 4.2.108)

The word *madra* denotes a country (*janapada*); the use of the plural number is for the purpose of including all that which signifies a country. Therefore, a synonym for *madra* is not included [in the list]. As for the term *paurvamadra*: since the word *madra* applies to a specific part of the Madra country, when it is placed in grammatical apposition with a directional word (*dikśabda*), the compound is formed according to the rule "the meaning of a secondary suffix" (*taddhitārtha*).
And [the suffix ṭhak is applied] after a name of a village in the north that has more than two syllables and ends with an udātta accent.

Regarding the term *śaivapuram*: the suffix *vuñ* does not apply here according to the rule "after [words ending in] *prastha*, *pura*, or *vaha*," because the word "after a [word with] *vṛddhi*" is understood in that context.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [compounds] having *prastha* as their final member, and after [words] such as *paladyādi* that have *ka* as their penultimate element (*kopadha*).

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *añ*, which is prescribed for names of villages in the northern regions. Therefore, elsewhere—in cases such as *vrīhiprastha*, *giriprastha*, and *karikā*—the general suffix *aṇ* applies. In the case of names denoting places with a long vowel (*vṛddha*), such as *kailāsaprastha*, *kāka*, and *śāka*, the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ. However, for place-names like *mālāprastha*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule "prasthapuravahāntācca. In the case of *ikṣvāku* and similar names, the suffix *aṇ* will be taught by the rule "kopadhādaṇ" as an exception to the *janapada-vuñ*. And in the case of *arīhaṇaka* and others, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule "vṛddhādakekānta."

Therefore, it is well said that [the suffix] *añ* is an exception (*apavāda*). Due to the mention of the term "final member" (*uttarapada*), it does not apply here: *uttaromāhakiprasthaḥ* (a village situated on the northern slope of Mount Māhakī) and *uttaramāhakiprasthaḥ*, because [the suffix] *bha* applies there. However, if it were stated as "after a word ending in *prastha*," it would apply even in this case.

The inclusion of the term *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting that which subverts [the rule]. If the inclusion of *aṇ* were not made, then, since *aṇ* would be applicable here by the rule "after a word denoting a Vāhīka village, *aṇ* is applied in the sense of 'descendant' or 'belonging to' (*prāgdīvyataḥ aṇ*)", the suffix *cha* would also be applicable by the rule "after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel, *cha* is applied. That *cha* would then be subverted by the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhiṭha* according to the rule "and after Vāhīka villages," yet because of its re-enactment [in this specific context], *cha* alone would result. Therefore, by including *aṇ*, even that *cha*—which is a subverter—is itself subverted, and only *aṇ* occurs.

The word *yakṛlloman* is recited [in the Gaṇapāṭha]; from *yakṛlloman*, the suffix *bha* is applied to form *yākṛllomaḥ*. They say that the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form) by the rule *an* does not apply here, because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is specifically prescribed for this entry in the Gaṇa.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after [names] such as Kaṇva and others to form patronymics (*gotra*).

In this context, "lineage" (*gotra*) does not mean a derivative suffix (*pratyaya*), because that would entail the sublation of the governing rule for the remaining [suffixes]. Nor does it qualify the base (*prakṛti*), because it is impossible for the word *kaṇva* and others—which already end in a lineage-suffix—to function as a lineage again. When it says "the suffix prescribed after *kaṇva* and others in the sense of lineage," only the suffix *yañ* prescribed by the specific rule (*pratipadavihita*) is understood.

By doing so, "lineage" is taken here in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense; otherwise, since the governing rule for "descendants" (*apatya*) applies elsewhere, the worldly sense of lineage would be taken, resulting in the inclusion of mere descendants—as in "Kaṇva is his deity."

Now, one might object: "If it is stated 'from Kaṇva and others' (*kaṇvādibhyaḥ*), how could there be the possibility [of the suffix] *aṇ* from a stem ending in *aṇ*, or how could it apply to stems ending in *yañ*, such that what is desired is accomplished? [The author] thinks as follows: the general suffix *aṇ* is indeed established for the simple stems beginning with Kaṇva; however, because this rule is an exception (*apavāda*), the word "Kaṇva and others" will function [metaphorically] to refer to those items ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that have Kaṇva as their constituent part.
And [the substitution of *iṇ*] for *iña*. 4.2.112.

"Regarding the phrase *gotra eva* (only a *gotra*): it was stated previously that the technical term (*pāribhāṣika*) *gotra* is what is intended; here too, that same [term] is carried over. Therefore, since only the technical *gotra* is intended here as well, the following do not occur: *pāṇiner yūnaś chātrāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ* ("the students of the young Pāṇini") and *sautaṅgamer idam* ("this belongs to Sutaṅgami"). From the word *sutaṅgama*, the suffix *iñ* is applied in the sense of the fourth case (descendant) by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*. Since in this case there is no status of being a descendant at all—and even less the status of being a *gotra*—it serves as a counter-example."
A patronymic derived from a stem consisting of two syllables is not formed with the suffix *aṇ* when it refers to people of the East or to the Bharatas.

But surely the Bharatas are indeed Easterners (*prācya*); for what purpose, then, are they mentioned by their own specific name? To this he replies: "By virtue of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) elsewhere. Regarding the rule *bahvaca iñaḥ prācyabharateṣu*, this is the meaning indicated: "In other instances where 'Easterners' (*prācya*) are mentioned, the Bharatas are not included. Another says: the construction is "by virtue of an indicator elsewhere," meaning that because this matter has been made known elsewhere.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied after a word ending in *vṛddhi* [in the first syllable] to denote a descendant.

Regarding the passage beginning with *avyayatīretyādi*: the scope for the rule "after an indeclinable, *tyap* occurs" (*avyayād dhyap*) is, for example, *amātyaḥ*; the scope for *cha* is, for example, *śālīyaḥ* and *mālīyaḥ*; and after the word *ārāt*, *cha* occurs, as in *ārātīyaḥ*. This conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is established without regard for the restriction (*parigaṇana*) found in the rule "after *ama*, *iha*, *kutaḥ*, *tas*, and *itra*" (*amehakvatasitrebhyaḥ*). The scope for the subsequent rule regarding *tīra* is, for example, *kāśyatīraḥ*; the scope for *cha* is the same; and after *vāyasatīra*, *cha* occurs, as in *vāyasatīriyaḥ*. The scope for the subsequent rule regarding *rūpya* is, for example, *cārarūpyaḥ*; the scope for *cha* is the same.

The suffix *cha* is obtained [by P. 4.2.139] after *māṇirūpya*, but this is superseded by the suffix *vuñ*, which is characterized by having *y* as its penultimate letter—thus we have *māṇirūpyakaḥ*. However, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between *cha* and the suffix *ñya* (characterized by having *rūpya* as its final member) was stated on the basis of their mere potential application. The scope for the rule characterized by "northern villages" (*udīcyagrāma*) is, for example, *śivapura* → *śaivapuraḥ*; whereas after *vāḍavakarṣa*, the suffix *cha* occurs—thus *vāḍavakarṣīyaḥ*.

The rule concerning the suffix *kopadha*—namely, "the suffix *aṇ* after words ending in *prastha*, those having *paladyādi* as a subsequent member, and those having a penultimate *k* (*kopadha*)"—is intended here. Its scope (*avakāśa*) lies beyond that [other rule], as follows: *nilīnaka* → *nailīnakam*; [and] *aulūka*, meaning "there are owls (*ulūka*) in this place," with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is applied when something exists in a place" (*tadasminn asti*), [referring to] a village named Aulūka; from that [village name], the suffix *cha* occurs, resulting in *aulūkīya*.

As for the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "aṇ after a word ending in *ka*," that is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* used for country names; furthermore, the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule "after a word with a *vṛddhi* vowel, after *akekānta*, etc."—wherein the mention of "ending in *ka*" is for the sake of [excluding] *sosuka* and so on—becomes a sublater (*bādhaka*) of even that *aṇ*.
The suffixes *tasi*, *thañ*, and *cha* are applied after the word *bhavat*.

Regarding the statement "these two are *ṭhak* and *cha*": it is understood from the inclusion of the letter *s* that this is a reference to the suffix *chas*, not *śas*; for in the case of *śas*, the status of being a word (*pada*) is already established by its inclusion in the *svādi* group. The letter *s* is for the purpose of the technical designation "word" (*padasaṃjñā*). By means of this, in the form *bhavadīya*, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) occurs. In the case of *bhāvatka*, although the suffix *kak* could have been prescribed [by the rule] *isusuktāntāt kaḥ* for the sake of brevity in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), the prescription of *ṭhak* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*: thus, *bhāvatkī*. As for the phrase "but from one that is not *vṛddha*," this refers to a word ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. In some places, however, the reading is simply *bhavataḥ śatuḥ*.
The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* are applied after [words ending in] *kāśi* and others.
Regarding the phrase "only from *vṛddha* [words]": if that is so, how is it that suffixes occur after non-*vṛddha* words such as *yuvarāja* and others? To this he says: "But those which...

If the two suffixes occur after non-*vṛddha* words by virtue of the authority of the explicit statement (*vacana*), for what purpose then is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *vṛddha* words? To this he says: "The word *devadatta*, etc. As for the question "How is it illustrated in the *Bhāṣya*?": although he himself indeed illustrates the *cha*-suffix there, he has stated "in the *Bhāṣya*" because that is based on the authority of the author of the *Bhāṣya* and not independently.

Regarding the rule "from *āpad* and so forth as the prior member": *āpadādi* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Regarding the rule "from *kāla*": the meaning is "from that which ends with the word *kāla*."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the names of villages belonging to the Vāhīkas. 4.2.117.

"Regarding the two exceptions to *cha*": thus, those cases which are sublated by *cha* itself—namely, the domains of *avyaya*, *tīra*, *rūpya*, a word as the final member (*uttarapada*), and a village name of the North (*udīcya*) having *ka* as its penultimate (*kopadha*)—in those very domains these two suffixes (*kan* and *kāp*) also occur, provided there is no sublation by another rule. For example: *ārān* is the name of a Vāhīka village; [the derivatives are] *ārātkī* and *ārātkā*, according to the rule "after a word ending in *i* or *uk*, *ka* is added. Likewise, *kāstīra* is the name of a Vāhīka village; [the derivatives are] *kāstīrikī* and *kāstīrikā*.

But here, there is a Vāhīka village named Dāśarūpya; by the rule "from words ending in *dhanvan* or having *ya* as a penultimate letter," the suffix *vuñ* supersedes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhiṭh*: [the derivative is] *dāśarūpyakaḥ*. Likewise, there is a northern village named Śākala, meaning "that in which there are pieces (*śakalāni*")—it is also a Vāhīka village—and from that, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhiṭh* occur: *śākalikī*, *śākalikā*.

In this case, however, the suffix *cha*—which supersedes the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *prasthottarapadādi-sūtra* (Pāṇini 4.2.110) due to its being subsequent (*paratva*), and which itself supersedes that [suffix *aṇ*] because it is an exception (*apavāda*)—supersedes the suffix *cha* characterized by having *ka* as an upadhā, according to the statement: "In the rule *vṛddhādakekānta* (Pāṇini 4.2.143), the mention of *kopadha* is for the sake of forms such as *sausuka*. Thus, we have *sausukīyaḥ*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a word denoting a region (*ordeśa*). 4.2.119.

*Naiṣādakarṣukaḥ* and *śābarajambukaḥ*: from the words *niṣādakarṣū* and *śabarajambū*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; then, by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is added, and by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ*, the vowel is shortened.
According to the Eastern grammarians, [the suffix *cha*] is applied after [a word ending in] *vṛddhi*. (Pāṇini 4.2.120)

Regarding the rule *vṛddhādeva prācām*: the restriction is not the reverse—namely, that it applies only to the easterners (*prācām*) from a *vṛddha* [name]—because there is no *vṛddha* name ending in *u* or *ū* that does not denote a place in the eastern region, which would otherwise result in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the preceding rule. In the example *āḍhakajambuka*, the substitution of *kā* and the shortening of the vowel are as explained previously.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a word ending in *dhanvan* when it has a *y* as its penultimate letter.

Regarding the phrase "denoting a desert" (*dhanvavācinaḥ*): the meaning is that it refers to specific deserts such as Airāvata and the like. There is no inclusion of the actual word-forms themselves nor their synonyms, because of the governing rule concerning *vṛddha* [words]. In the example *pāredhanvakaḥ*: the compound is an *avyayībhāva* formed by the rule "pāre-madhya- with the genitive [is optionally compounded]"; the suffix *ṭac* is added as a compound-final element by the rule "acaśca"; and when the suffix *vuñ* is applied, there is the elision of the final vowel and what follows it (*yasyeti lopaḥ*).

If, however, the word *dhanva* is neuter, then, in the alternative where the suffix *ṭac* is absent according to the rule *napuṃsakād anyatarasyām*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied; in that case, there is elision of the final vowel by the rule *naḥ taddhite*. The words *sāṅkāśya* and *kāmpilya* end in the suffix *ṇya* by virtue of the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādayaḥ*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *prastha*, *pura*, and *vaha*. (Pāṇini 4.2.122)

The word "from a *vṛddha*" is understood [to carry over]. If this is so, then the mention of the suffix *-anta* is redundant, since the rule for that which ends in such a suffix will apply to *prastha* and the others simply because they are not *vṛddha*. This is not the case; for by the rule "optionally in the case of a proper name" (*vā nāmadheyasya*), it is possible for the words *prastha* and the others themselves to be *vṛddha*.

Furthermore, even if there is no such place by that name, nevertheless, just as in the previous sūtra there was a mention of a specific desert region (*dhanvan*), so too here one might suppose [the same]: there is a village named Nādīpura among the Vāhīkas; in that case, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*, which characterize Vāhīka villages, would be exceptions (*apavāda*) to *cha*, and this *vuñ* would also be an exception to *cha*. But here, due to the prohibition of an exception (*apavādavipratiṣedha*), *vuñ* occurs. And thus, in cases such as *pātanaprasthakaḥ* and *kauñjīvahakaḥ*, *vuñ* alone occurs.
In the speech of the easterners, the augment *it* is added after a verbal root beginning with the letter *r*.

Regarding the phrase "and [after] that which ends in *ī*": the short vowel (*hrasva*) is not included [in the definition], because it is impossible for that which ends in a short vowel to denote a region of the East. For example, in *ekacakra*: there is a city named Ekacakra in the Eastern region; according to the rule *eṅ prācāṃ deśe*, it receives the designation *vṛddha*. The city established by Kakanda is *Kākaṃdī*; for feminine forms, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *sauvīrasālvaprākṣa*. The inclusion of the marker *t* (in *it*) is for the sake of clarity; it is not, however, for the purpose of excluding the short (*hrasva*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels.

Because it is impossible for that which ends in *t* to denote a region in the east, and because the vowel *ī* is not an *aṇ*, those two [the suffixes *ta* and *tha*] would not be included. However, if the letter *t* were absent and it were merely said "of those ending in *r* and *u*," it would not be clearly known what is intended to be grasped here. When the letter *t* is present, however, the reference to the specific phoneme (*varṇanirdeśa*) is determined, since it is well-known in that very context. If the instruction were given as "of those ending in *ī* and *r* or *u*," there would be the consequence of unnecessary prolixity (*gaurava*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words *janapada* and *tadavadhi*. (Pāṇini 4.2.124)

The meaning is that even that limit (*avadhi*) is understood as the country (*janapada*) itself; thus, the term *tadavadhi* is taken as a *karmadhāraya* compound (meaning "that which is the limit"), and not as a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) meaning "the limit of that. For if it were so, then in the case of *mauñjīya*—derived from *mauñjī*, the name of a village that serves as the limit—the form would also apply there [to the inhabitants]. If one asks, "Of what, then, is this the limit? it is understood to be of the country alone, due to its proximity.

Regarding the phrase "having set aside the suffix *cha* after a compound whose final member is *garta*": otherwise, there would be scope for the rule that the suffix *cha* occurs after a compound ending in *garta*, as in *vṛkagartīyaḥ*; and there would be scope for the suffix *vuñ* after the word *janapada*, as in *āṅgakaḥ*. When both [suffixes] would apply to the word *trigarta*, the suffix *cha* would prevail due to its subsequent position in the rules. Consequently, one would have to state a "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) such as: "after a word ending in *garta*, the suffix *cha* is applied, and the suffix *vuñ* after a *janapada* is [set aside] by this prior counter-exception. Thus, [the form] *traigartakaḥ* is derived with the suffix *vuñ* by the subsequent rule. By this, he demonstrates the utility of including the mention of that limit (*tadavadhi*) in the later rule.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] even after a word that does not end in the plural number, provided it denotes a plurality. 4.2.125.

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* and *cha*. This means it is an exception to *aṇ* after a non-*vṛddha* [stem] and to *cha* after a *vṛddha* [stem]. Here, [the desired form] is already established even from a non-*vṛddha* [stem] by the rule "after a plural [stem]" (*bahuvacanāt*). The word *bahuvacana* is etymological (*yaugika*): "that which expresses many meanings" (*bahūnām arthānām vacanaḥ*). Or, if [it is taken as] "from a plural [stem]," meaning "from that which ends in a plural suffix," then what is the purpose of including the mention of the "domain" (*viṣaya*)? To this he replies: "In the case of plurality resulting from the collective remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of country names. The meaning is: "in that case where there is plurality by virtue of the collective remainder of country names. [The example is] "the Vartanīs."

The *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is based on the distinction between the individual members [of the group]. This [term] does not have a mandatory plural ending, because it is seen even in the dual and singular. Regarding the phrase "by the principle of the curd and Kauṇḍinya": for in the preceding sūtra, the suffix *vuñ* was prescribed after a word denoting a general country (*janapada*), just as the giving of curd is prescribed for Brahmins in general.

But here, in the context of the plural number, there is a specific rule: *vuñ* after a non-*vṛddha* [base], as in "the giving of buttermilk to the Kauṇḍinyas. Consequently, since *vuñ* would also apply after a *vṛddha* base due to the plural number, the *vuñ* prescribed after a non-*vṛddha* base—which is being introduced here—would sublate the *vuñ* that follows a *vṛddha* base; thus, it is combined with the word *api* (even) in the sense that it applies even in those cases. Here, the point is established by the mere phrase "from the context of the plural number" that this introduction is for the sake of the non-*vṛddha* meaning. However, the statement "even from a non-*vṛddha*" is made in order to interrupt the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of the *vṛddha* [rule].
The suffix *cha* is applied after a compound whose final member is *kāca*, *agni*, *vaktra*, or *garta*.

The mention of the word "uttarapada" (subsequent member) is for the sake of the meaning of the term *kaccha*. For that [term *kaccha*] occurs even by itself to denote a region known as a bank (*kūla*); however, since it is impossible for the others [the items in the list] to occur by themselves to denote a region, the rule of application to what ends with those terms (*tadantavidhi*) is already established. If it were stated simply as "after *kaccha* and so forth," it would apply even after a form preceded by the prefix *bahuc*; therefore, the mention of "uttarapada" is made.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words such as *dhūma*. (Pāṇini 4.2.127)

"An exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffix] *aṇ* and others": it is an exception to *aṇ* after words beginning with *dhūma* that are not *vṛddha*; to *cha* after *vṛddha* words; to *tvañ* after villages of the North; and to *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha* after villages of the Vāhīkas. Regarding "after *kūla* when referring to the Sauvīras": it is *kaulaka* when referring to the Sauvīras, but *kaula* elsewhere.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *nagara* in the senses of "censuring" and "skill. (Pāṇini 4.2.128)

The question is, "By whom was this stolen? The answer is, "By a man in this city. The statement beginning with "This is possible," and so forth, is the speech of the questioner. Regarding the expression "the city of Saṃjñā is recited": due to its association with the word *Māhiṣmatī*, the meaning is that the word *nagara* (city) has become a proper name (*saṃjñā*) here.
The suffix *manuṣya* is added after *araṇya* [to form a bahuvrīhi compound].
Regarding the term *aupasaṃkhyānikasya*: this refers to that which is obtained through the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating, "The suffix *ṇa* should be prescribed after *araṇya*.

[The objection] "The mention of *manuṣye* is insufficient" is addressed by saying: "after *pathin*, *adhyāya*, etc. An *āraṇyaka-adhyāya* is so called because it is a portion of the Upaniṣads that is studied in the forest (*araṇya*). *Vihāra* means play or sport.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *kuru* and *yugandhara*.

Since the word *kuru* is listed among the *kaccha*-group [of bases], how then is the application of the suffix *vuñ* from the word *kuru* stated [in the rule], given that *vuñ* is already obtained by the rule "from those two, even if they are non-vṛddha" (*tābhyām avṛddhād api*)? That statement was made with the intention of referring to the initial application [of *vuñ*], and not with the intention of referring to that which is subsequently sublated by this optional rule. As for those who read "it is established in *vuñ*," the meaning is "it is obtained."

Just as when something is already established, a new undertaking is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so too, intending to demonstrate that the mention of *vibhāṣā* is unnecessary for the meaning of the word *kuru*, he says: "The word *kuru* is recited among the *kacchādi* group. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). To the question "For what purpose, then, is the mention of *vibhāṣā*? he says: "This very [mention]... (*saiṣā*).

[Objection: But surely, since the suffix *vuñ* would be established even from the word *yugandhara* by the rule "even after a non-*vṛddha* [word]" (*avṛddhād api*), an option would be understood through this repeated statement even without the mention of *vibhāṣā*? [Response: This cannot be so; for the opposite might also occur. That is, the *vuñ* after the word *yugandhara* could be compulsory, while by the rule "even after a non-*vṛddha*" it could be optional; thus, the restatement would indeed be justifiable in that way as well. [The rule] "of a human and one situated therein" (*manuṣya-tatsthayoḥ*)... [follows].

And this [restriction] is obtained through the force of its recitation in the *kacchādi* group; otherwise, since *vuñ* and *aṇ* would already be established by this very option (*vibhāṣā*), its recitation there would be purposeless.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *madra* and *vṛjya*.

The word *madra* ends in the suffix *rak* according to the rule *sphāyitañci*. The word *vṛji* ends in the suffix *kip* according to the rule *vṛjī varjane igupadhātkiḥ*. It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *vuñ* used for designating a country (*janapada*). [This applies] even from bases that do not have a *vṛddhi* vowel, according to the rule *avṛddhādapi*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in *kopadha*.

But why is this [suffix] not desired for words that do not denote a place, since the term "place" (*deśa*) is carried over from the previous rule? To this he says: "elsewhere. By the preceding rule, namely the *prasthottarapada* sūtra and others, the recurrence of the word "place" is for the sake of the subsequent rule; it is not for the purpose of excluding non-places. Now, one might object: the suffix *aṇ* is already established by the *prāgdīvyatīya* rule even for words denoting non-places, while the *prasthottarapada* sūtra is intended merely to set aside the suffix *añ* prescribed for northern villages; so why say, "elsewhere, by the preceding rule alone"? True.

If this is indeed the intended meaning, then since the rule is prescribed specifically for its commencement, it is logical that the suffix *aṇ* alone should apply everywhere; so, what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *aṇ*? One might ask: why not simply say "as prescribed for [stems] ending in *ka* and so forth"? For, by the force of the rule's commencement, that very suffix which is prescribed but does not otherwise apply will come into effect. To this, he says: "The mention of *aṇ*..."

From the word *ikṣvāku*, the suffix *ṭhañ* would be applicable by the rule "ṭhañ after a name of a region. Since that [suffix] is superseded by *vuñ* in the sense of a country (*janapada*), if the mention of *aṇ* were not made, then due to the repetition [of the suffix], *vuñ* alone would apply. However, when *aṇ* is mentioned, *aṇ* itself occurs—as in *aikṣvākaḥ*. Here, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is effected by the rule for the *dāṇḍināyana*-class. Thus, it is precisely because of the mention of *aṇ* that this [suffix] supersedes *ṭhañ* in the sense of a region, and not because it is subsequent [to it].
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *kaccha* and other such words. 4.2.133.

"An exception to *vuñ*": this is an exception to *vuñ* for those [names] denoting a country (*janapada*) that take the plural number; it is an exception to *ṭhañ* after the words *sindhu* and *varṇu* when referring to a region. The word *sālva* is listed [in the *gaṇa*] so that *vuñ*, which would otherwise apply by the definition of a country, might not occur. The rules "after *sālva*, except when meaning 'pedestrian'" (*apadātau sālvāt*) and "and after *go* and *yavāgu*" (*goyavāgvośca*) will serve as restrictive rules—meaning "only after *go* and *yavāgu* when meaning 'pedestrian'"—since [otherwise], due to the presence of the *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffix *cha* would be applicable.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *sālva* when it refers to a non-foot-soldier (*apadāti*).

In the word *padāti*, the substitution of *pada-* for *pāda-* occurs according to the rule "pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu" (Pāṇini 6.3.52), because [the person] goes on foot (*pādābhyām atati*). Thus, *apadāti* means one who is not a foot-soldier. An *apadāti* is someone mounted on a horse and so forth. The phrase "only when referring to a human being standing upon that [vehicle]" is stated because the term is presented as a *dvandva* compound; however, there is no possibility of a foot-soldier standing upon such a vehicle. Furthermore, the restrictive rule "only after *sālva-* etc., when referring to an *apadāti*" does not apply here, because of the introduction of the rule "goyavāgvośca" (Pāṇini 6.2.40).
The suffix *cha* is applied after a compound whose final member is *garta*.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of a Vāhīka village": although the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* are prescribed by the rule *vāhīkagrāmebhyaś-ca*, nevertheless, because there is no difference in their phonetic form (*ṭha*) once their anubandhas have been dropped, they are referred to in the singular as "the characteristics of a Vāhīka village. Regarding *śvāvidgartīyam*: [the word] *śvāvidh* is derived from the root *vyadh* with the suffix *kvip* (meaning "one who pierces a dog"), followed by vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and lengthening according to the rule *nahivṛti-*. Thus, *śvāvidgartah* means "the hole of a porcupine."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the words beginning with *gaha*. (Pāṇini 4.2.138)

Regarding the phrase "an exception to *aṇ*": therein, from the word *māhakiprastha*, there is an exception to *vuñ* [by the rule] *prasthapuravasantācca*; from words such as *vālmīki* ending in *iñ*, there is an exception to *aṇ* [by the rule] *iñaśca*; and for the remaining [words], there is an exception to the default *aṇ*. The phrase "with respect to possibility" means that this qualification applies only to those [words] such as *gaha* whose occurrence is possible both in their own region (*deśa*) and in another region (*cādeśa*), but not to those such as [words] with an internal *sthā* as a prior member. The phrase "of the middle of the earth" (*pṛthivīmadhyasya*)... [is used].

The meaning is that the word *madhya* should be understood as denoting the "middle of the earth" (*pṛthivīmadhya*), and not as denoting some other kind of middle. By virtue of its connection with a *caraṇa* (Vedic school), the suffix *aṇ* signifies "residence. That *aṇ* which is prescribed by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after a *caraṇa*" should be regarded here as signifying residence. The meaning is that this [suffix] occurs in the sense of "this is their residence"; therefore, when the sense is "the middle of the earth is the residence of these *caraṇas*, such as the Kaṭhas and others," the form *madhyamāḥ* arises.

Regarding the rule *mukhapārśvatasorlopaḥ*: there is elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *-tas* and *-tasa* when attached to the words *mukha* and *pārśva*, by virtue of their connection with that suffix; and since [the rule] *alo’ntyasya* applies, this elision occurs of the final letter. Once that has been performed, the elision of the *y* (by *yasyeti ca*) follows. The explicit mention of "elision" (*lopavacana*) is for the purpose of making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ*; by means of this, the form *ārātīya* is established.
The suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *vṛddhi*, after *adaka*, and after a monosyllabic word having *kh* as its penultimate letter.

*Ārīhaṇakīyam*, *drauhaṇakīyam*. In the sense of "completed by that," the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*; this example has been shown as an illustration of the ending in *-aka*. For here, the suffix *cha* is indeed established by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*; for *ārihaṇaka* and *drauhaṇaka* do not denote a *janapada* (country), which would otherwise have given rise to the application of *aṇ* after a word ending in *ka*.

In this regard, the following example should be observed: there is a country named Brāhmaṇaka, where the Brāhmaṇas live by the profession of arms; [the form] *Brāhmaṇaka* is correct due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) "in the sense of a name, [the suffix -ka is added after] *brāhmaṇa* and *uṣṇika*" (Pāṇini 4.2.103). One born there is called *Brāhmaṇakīya*. Regarding the mention of "having *ka* as an upadhā" (*kopadha*), it means that the mention of "not having *eka* as an upadhā" (*akekānta*) in the sūtra should be removed and it should be stated simply as "from that which has *ka* as an upadhā" (*kopadhāt*), because this is more comprehensive (*vyāpaka*) and more concise (*laghu*).
[The suffix *cha* (i.e., *īya*) is applied] after a compound whose final member is *anyāpala*, *nagara*, *grāma*, or *hrada*. (Pāṇini 4.2.142)

This is established by the mention of *antagrahaṇa* alone; there is no purpose in mentioning the subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Nor is there the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] when preceded by *bahuc*, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the region of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ deśe*).
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is optionally applied when [the action] is performed by one who is not a human being.

If there were no elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*) here for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, one would simply say "optionally in the case of *manuṣya*," since there is no difference in brevity. Thinking this, he says: "when *amanuṣya* is the referent. He shows by way of an example that the word *amanuṣya* is taken here in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), and not in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*) as referring to *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, and so forth, [as in the phrase] "fruits from the mountains" (*parvatīyāni phalāni*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *kṛkaṇaparṇa* when it belongs to the Bhāradvāja lineage. 4.2.145.
"It is not the word 'lineage' (gotra). Why? He says: "And this is a qualifier of the primordial nature (prakṛti). For the word "and" (ca) has the sense of the word "because" (hi).
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the third quarter of the fourth chapter—
the *Padamañjarī*.
After the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the suffix *khañ* is optionally applied [in addition to the previously mentioned suffixes].

The mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*) is for the sake of what follows: namely, that these three suffixes (*pratyaya*) occur. Now, one might object: by the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), the non-occurrence of *khañ* and *cha* in certain instances is indicated; since they do not occur, there is no exception (*apavāda*), and thus by the rule of our own grammar, "before *dīvya-taḥ*" (*prāgdīvyataḥ*), the suffix *aṇ* alone occurs. Therefore, how can this [rule] be the injunction of three suffixes? Even *cha* is certainly not enjoined by this [rule], for its *ca*-suffix is merely permissive (*abhyanujñāpaka*)—if something else were also applicable.

That [suffix] also occurs; therefore, by its own rule, "vṛddhācchaḥ," the suffix *cha* also occurs, but only the previously non-existent *khañ* is prescribed [here]. Now, since everything for which this [rule] has application is intended to be prescribed by this [sūtra], the prescription of *cha* by this [sūtra] follows.

If this is so, then by this very [rule], the suffix *aṇ* is also prescribed; the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) does not intend merely the non-occurrence of *khañ* and *cha*, since that is already established by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*). What then? It intends its occurrence even alongside *aṇ*. Therefore, it has been stated that from the perspective of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), these three suffixes come into being, and that three suffixes are prescribed for each [base]. In that context, by the statement "the suffix *khañ* occurs," it is shown that *khañ* itself is prescribed as something previously unestablished.

By the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), the suffix *aṇ* is permitted by the rule "and as [already] established" (*yathāprāptam*). Since *yuṣmad* and *asmad* belong to the class beginning with *tyad*, the suffix *cha* is obtained by the rule "after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Thus, by this [latter rule], the suffix *cha* is also permitted. However, in the Bhāṣya, the absence of a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyābhāva*) is demonstrated through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): "After *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" is the first rule, where *cha* is carried over from the rule "the suffix *cha* after a word ending in *garta*"; then follows the second rule, "and the suffix *khañ*."
And in that [context of the suffix] aṇ, the forms yuṣmāka and asmāka [are substituted for yuṣmad and asmad].

"Directly" (*sākṣāt*) means prescribed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that is, prescribed by the explicit mention of its own form (*svarūpa*). This qualification contains a logical reason (*hetugarbha*): because it is prescribed directly, therefore it is designated by the suffix *khañ* itself. When that [suffix] is enjoined, the cognition arises immediately regarding that very [suffix], and not regarding the suffix *cha* which is merely drawn in (*anukṛṣṭa*). For the particle "and" (*ca*) ceases after merely indicating the assistance of the neighboring *khañ*.

In that case, because no companion [word] is specified, there is a search for the relevant [rule]; and while searching as far as the rule "the suffix *cha* after a compound whose final member is *garta*," the cognition of *cha* occurs only after a long time, and therefore it is not fit to be referred back. However, when there is a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) in the preceding sūtra in order to avoid a correspondence between terms (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), then there is no attraction of *cha* by the particle *ca*, and thus there is no suspicion of its being referred back.

"Regarding the two causes," and so forth. There are indeed two causes—*khañ* and *aṇ*—and there are likewise two things caused by them—the two substitutes (*ādeśau*). Therefore, considering that there must be a correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) due to this equality, the question is raised. "A separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made": although one could have simply stated "for *khañ* and *aṇ*, [the forms] *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-*," the statement "in that [case of *aṇ*] and in *aṇ*" indicates a split in the sentence by means of the word *ca*. The meaning is that the two substitutes are not connected individually with the two causes.
The forms *tava* and *mama* are substituted [for the sixth case endings] in the singular. || 4.3.3 ||

"Between the artificial and the natural, the artificial [term] is to be understood as the singular number. Since that [singular number] applies both when the suffix has been added and when it has not, once the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) has occurred by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," the status of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* as being followed by a singular suffix is no longer possible; therefore, it must be established by means of the principle of "the characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Anticipating the refutation of even that application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*, he says: "But surely... [and so on]. "[Because of] the statement... [is the reason].

If, however, *aṇ* and *khañ* were qualified by their status as following a singular number (*ekavacanaparatvena*), what would be the fault? In that case, [the suffixes] would apply here: *yuṣmākaṃ chāttraḥ* → *yauṣmākīṇaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*; yet they would not apply here: *tava chāttrāḥ* → *tāvakīnāḥ*, *māmakīnāḥ*. Therefore, in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtre*), *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are qualified by their status as following *khañ* and *aṇ*; and here too, those very same [words] are qualified by their status as following a singular number. Consequently, by virtue of this statement, in *āsmākīnaḥ*, the condition for the suffix is met through the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇam*)—this is the only logical conclusion.

"Anvarthagrahaṇam" (the term is taken according to its literal meaning): that by which a single object is expressed is "singular number" (*ekavacana*). And in this view, the word "ekavacane" ends in the nominative dual, not in the locative. [The rule] *ardhādyat* || 4.3.4 ||.
The substance for the sake of the bali offering is "bāleya"; half of that is one part; that which exists therein is "bāleyārddhika."
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [a word ending in the locative case] preceded by *para*, *avara*, *adhama*, or *uttama*. 4.3.5.

This is a rule [vacana] intended for when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applicable by means of the supplementary statement (*aupasaṅkhyānika*) "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be stated after a compound whose prior member [ends in *ka*]."

The word "from [the word] *ardha*" (ardhāt) is understood to carry over. Consequently, because of the force of the qualification "the word *ardha* which follows *para*, *avara*, *adhama*, or *uttama*," it will be understood that the word *ardha* must be preceded by *para*, *avara*, and so on; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "preceded" (*pūrva*)? Thus, he provides this support for the objection just mentioned: "the words *para* and *avara*. However, due to this mention of "preceded" (*pūrva*), only the suffix *yat* occurs. The intention is that this is indicated by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Pāṇini 4.3.6: *dvikpūrvapadāṭ ṭhañ ca* (And the suffix *ṭhañ* [is applied] after a word ending in *dvi* as its prior member).

"An exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*": this was stated with reference to the application [of the suffix] prescribed by the Sūtra, because it has been stated that "the suffix *ṭhañ* should be mentioned when preceded by a prior member.

Regarding the mention of the word *pada*, etc.: if it were merely stated as "preceded by a direction-word" (*dikpūrvāt*), it would result in a rule concerning the specific form [of the word itself]; consequently, it would apply only in cases such as "born in the eastern half" (*digardhe jātaḥ*). However, when the word *pada* is included—where *pada* means "that by which one goes"—the compound is formed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) as "that from which the direction-word *pūrva* is prior."
The suffixes *añ* and *ṭhañ* are applied [to a word denoting] a part of a village or a district.

Regarding the term *paurvārddhāḥ*: it is a compound (*samāsa*) formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), meaning "those who exist in the eastern half of the village"; from that, the suffix [is applied]. Although the word *ardha* (half) requires a relation to the village, nevertheless, because it is invariably dependent (*nityasāpekṣa*) and is the primary member (*pradhāna*), both types of formation—the compound formation (*samāsavṛtti*) and the secondary derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*)—are not contradictory. For what purpose is the mention of *ṭhañ*? Why not simply say "and *añ*" (*añ ca*)? Nor does this imply that *yat* would also be included by way of conjunction; for in the preceding rule, *yat* has already been carried over (*anukṛṣṭa*). Therefore, the mention of *ṭhañ* is for the sake of clarity.
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after [a word ending in *ṣaṣṭhī*] when the sense is "suitable for that" (*sāmpratika*). || 4.3.9 ||

It is stated that *sāmpratika* means "proper," "justified," "righteous," "fitting," or "equal. The employment of multiple words is because a particular term is well-known for a specific meaning; although the word *samprati* is well-known in the sense of "now" (*idānīm*), it also functions in the sense of "justified. For instance, we see: "The four-night sacrifice is deficient, or the six-night sacrifice is excessive; this five-night sacrifice is *samprati* (proper). It is neither deficient nor excessive; the meaning is "equal" (*sama*). And since it is listed among the words beginning with *prajñā*, the forms *sāmpratam* and *sampratī* are synonyms.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *dvīpa* when followed by *anusamudram*.

Regarding the term *anusamudram*: it is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *anuryatsamayā*. This word ends in the locative case and serves as an adjective for the island; thus he says: "the island which is near the ocean."
[The suffix -ta] is used in the sense of time [past]. 4.3.11.

Regarding the phrase "denoting specific times": there is no inclusion of the word-form itself nor its synonyms; for by the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra*, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after words such as *saṃdhivelā* and *trayodaśī* when they are not *vṛddha*. That [prescription] is indeed for the purpose of superseding the suffix *ṭhañ*; and if the term were taken as denoting the meaning, then *ṭhañ* would apply after those [words].

Here, one might raise the objection: "According to the maxim that 'between the primary and the secondary senses, the understanding applies to the primary,' this cognition [of time] should arise only from those things that denote time through their primary function—such as 'month' or 'fortnight'—and not from things that denote time through a secondary (metaphorical) function, such as 'the *kadamba* is time because of its association with the *kadamba* flower,' or 'the *vrīhi*-straw is time because of its association with *vrīhi* straw. Anticipating this, he says: "in whatever way" (*yathākathañcit*). This means by any manner whatsoever. He clarifies this very point by saying: "even by a secondary function" (*guṇavṛttyāpi*).

A *guṇa* (quality) is that which serves as the basis for the application of a word denoting something else (*paraśabda*) to another object; the application [of a word] based on that is *guṇavṛtti* (metaphorical application). This is understood from the fact that in the rule *sandhivelādi-sūtra*, by the inclusion of the term "time" (*kāla*), the [names of the] lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are qualified by it. For there is no primary meaning of the word "time" that could possibly apply to the lunar mansions. Rather, the words such as *puṣya* and others function with respect to time through *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on indication), because of their conjunction with the moon when it is situated near the *puṣya* mansion and so forth.

And that very [time] is also explained by the rule "lub-aviśeṣe" (Pāṇini 4.2.4), which prescribes the elision of the suffix in order to exclude terms such as *pauṣa* and others; however, this does not mean that time is their primary meaning.
The suffix *śarat* is used in the sense of "autumn" when referring to a *śrāddha* rite. || 4.3.12 ||

The word *śrāddha* refers to the ritual action (*karman*). The suffix *aṇ* in the sense of possession—according to the rule *prajñā-śraddhā-arcābhyo ṇaḥ*—is applied because "faith" (*śraddhā*) exists in this [action]; thus, the meaning is that the ancestral rite (*pitrya karman*) which is to be accomplished through faith is denoted by the word *śrāddha*. It does not refer to a person who possesses faith. When that same suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of the genitive case, then the word *śrāddha* functions as a term for a person. But how is this specific distinction obtained when the word-form is common to both? To this he says: "Because of non-denotation" (*anabhidhānāt*).

Regarding the term *śāradikaṃ śrāddham*: the suffix *ṭhañ* (forming *-ika*) is applied in the sense of "occurring therein" (*bhave*), meaning that whatever is prescribed for this [autumnal] occasion occurs at that time.
And after *śvas*, there is the augment *tuṭ*.

"And of that" means: of the suffix *ṭhañ*, not of the word *śvas*. Why is this so? Because *ṭhañ* is primary as that which is to be prescribed (*vidheya*). And it should be understood that the augment *tuṭ* occurs after the substitution of *ik* has been made.

But surely, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the augment *tuṭ* should apply before the substitution of *ik*, whereas the substitution of *ik*—being prescribed within the governing rule for bases (*aṅgādhikāra*)—occurs after the designation of the base has been established and is therefore external (*bahiraṅga*). Furthermore, once *tuṭ* has been applied, since the substitution of *ik* is prescribed for the initial sound of the suffix, as in *karmaṭha*, it would not take effect here either; however, if this *tuk* were made a prior-final element (*pūrvānta*), [the fault would be avoided].

This cannot be so; for by the rule "is-us-uk-tāntāt kaḥ," there would have to be the substitution of *ka*. Therefore, let it be that [the augment] occurs at the very beginning of the suffix (*parādi*). How then is the substitution of *ik* established? It is established through an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence): namely, that the author makes the marker *ṭh* in the *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi* group serve as an indicator (*cit-karaṇa*), which indicates that the substitution of *ik* indeed occurs even prior to internal operations (*antaraṅga*). If it were not so, then once the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*)—which is prescribed in conjunction with the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of the suffix—had been applied, the substitution of *ik* would occur afterwards, and thus the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) would be established.

The suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* also occur [after this word]. Since the word *śvas* is an indeclinable denoting time by virtue of the rule "sāyaṃ-ciram... and so forth, [the suffix *ṭyu* applies]. Thus we have *śauvastikam*. Because it belongs to the *dvārādi* group, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi*, and the substitution *aij* (for *o*) occurs.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after words denoting *saṃdhivelā*, etc., as well as names of seasons and lunar mansions [to form derivatives indicating time].

The inclusion of *aṇ* is for the purpose of superseding the suffix *cha* after a *vṛddha* [base]. If *aṇ* were not included, and it were stated that "after *sandhivelā* and so forth, the suffix is applied as prescribed," then—even though by the force of the rule's commencement the suffix *ṭhañ* would not apply after a word denoting time (*kālāt*)—the suffix *cha* would still apply to the word *paurṇamāsī*, which is listed among *sandhivelā* and so forth, as well as to words like *svāti* because they are *vṛddha*. However, the explicit statement [of *aṇ*] would serve only to supersede *ṭhañ* after a word denoting time. Therefore, the inclusion of *aṇ* must be made for the purpose of superseding the suffix *cha* after a *vṛddha* base. Thus we have *sauvātam*.

From the root *sāti* in the sense of "continuous movement," the suffix *iṇ* is applied by the rule *ajyatibhyāṃ ca*. [The word *svāti* is formed from *su* + *at* with this suffix. Then, by the rule *svātyā yuktaḥ kālaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to denote the time connected with *svāti*; this *aṇ* is elided by the rule *lubaviśeṣe*. Subsequently, the suffix *aṇ* is applied again in the sense of "occurring therein" (*bhava*), etc.; the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *na yvābhyām* applies, and the augment *aij* is introduced. However, in the sense of "born under" (*jāta*), because of the elision by the rule *śraviṣṭhāphalgunī*, the form becomes simply *svāti*. As for *taiṣam*: [it is derived similarly].

Here too, as in the previous case, there should be elision (*luk*) when the sense is that of "born under" (*jāta*); thus the suffix is applied in the sense of "bhava" and so forth. By the rule "in *tiṣya* and *puṣya*, the elision of *ya* occurs when referring to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)," there is elision of the *ya*. Regarding the rule "from *saṃvatsara*, [the suffix *aṇ* is added] in the sense of fruit (*phala*) or festival (*parvan*)," [we have] *sāṃvatsaraṃ phalam* or *parvam*; anything else is *sāṃvatsarikam*.
The suffix *eṇya* is applied after the word *prāvṛṣ*.

It rains, thus it is *prāvṛṭ* (the rainy season); the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule beginning with *nahivṛti* when the suffix *kvip* is applied. Regarding *prāvṛṣeṇya*: this is an affix used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*). However, he will explain the suffix *ṭhañ* for the sense of "born in" (*jāta*) under the rule for *prāvṛṣ*. Although the form would have been established by the rule *raṣābhyām* alone, the explicit pronunciation of the letter *ṇ* in the affix is for the sake of the change to *ṇ* in *prāvṛṣeṇya* when one says *prāvṛṣeṇyayati*—that is, after the application of *kvip*, the elision of the causative marker *ṇic*, and the elision of *y* by the rule *lopo vyor vali*. Otherwise, the prohibition [of the change to *ṇ*] by the rule *padāntasya* would apply.
The suffix *aṣṭhak* is added after *varṣā* [in the sense of "born in that"]. 4.3.18.
Regarding "the rainy-season residence" (*vārṣiko vāsaḥ*): the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "proper" (*sādhu*) according to the rule *kālāt sādhu-puṣpyat-pacyamāneṣu*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied [to form patronymics] in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). 4.3.19.

"Nabhaḥ" and "nabhasyaḥ" constitute the rainy season (*vārṣika-ṛtu*). In this sense, the suffix [is applied] in the meaning "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*); and the word *ṛtu* refers here to two months which are parts of the season. The meaning is that these two months are components of the rainy season.
And in all cases [of the word *sarva*], there is the elision of the *t*. 4.3.22.

Regarding the word *haimanam*: when there is the elision (*lopa*) of the entire word *tat*, then because of the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form) by the rule *an-*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) by the rule *na-staddhite* does not occur. However, when the elision of the letter *t* occurs by this [present] rule and the elision of the letter *a* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*, then, because that [elision of *t*] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *asiddhavad atrābhāt* and because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original element), there is no elision of the *ṭi*.

But will [the word] *chandasi* not follow [from the previous rule]? No, because it is not marked with a svarita accent. "That very [rule]," and so forth: that which was a non-svarita following is designated by the word *sarvatra* (everywhere). For what purpose? He says: "by means of an additional effort. But then, for that same reason—because of the non-svarita accent—the word *chandasi* would not follow even in the preceding sūtra; therefore, the inclusion of the term *sarvatra* is indeed for the sake of clarity. [The commentators] remember that the suffix *ṭhan* applies even in the *bhāṣā* (secular language).

However, this is not accepted in the Bhāṣya; for it is as follows: this sūtra has been rejected. How so? There exists the word *heman* as a synonym for *hemanta*, based on the observation: "O *heman*, they reach toward the ears; therefore these two do not wither in *heman*; thus *heman* perishes, and it becomes *hemanta*. In that regard, in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), from the words *heman* and *hemanta*, the two forms *haimana* and *haimanta* are established by the suffix *ṛtvaṇ*. But in the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the form] is *haimana* from *heman*, and from *hemanta*, [the form is *haimantika*] by the rule "and from *hemanta*" (*hemantācca*).

Thus, with the suffix *ṭhañ*, we have *haimantikam*; and because "all rules are optional in the Vedic language" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), from the word *hemanta* itself with the suffix *aṇ*, we obtain *haimantam*. Consequently, these three forms are established. However, the author of the Sūtras has prescribed the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) for the word *hemant*—which denotes a season—in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), because that word is not used elsewhere than in the scope of this specific derivative. Furthermore, the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* applies as it occurs by default; and as for the immediately preceding suffix *ṭhañ*, its application is established everywhere through its connection with the term *sarvatra* (in all cases) in the preceding rule, so it is not explicitly added here.

"But what is the distinction between these two?"—the sense is that there is none at all. There are three forms: one with the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the previous rule; a second with the suffix *aṇ* and the elision of the final syllable (*antalopa*) according to this [present] rule; and a third with the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* and the elision of the *y* (in *ya*) according to the rule *yasyeti ca*. Thus, there are three forms.
After the indeclinables *sāyam*, *ciram*, *prāhṇe*, and *prage*, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are applied, and the augment *tuṭ* is added [to the beginning of these suffixes].

In this case, since the substitution *an* for *yu* and *vu* is prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*), it is *bahiraṅga*; however, the augment *tuṭ* is *antaraṅga* because it is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix. Therefore, the *tuṭ* must indeed occur first. Once that has been applied, the substitution *an* does not apply. Why? Because the substitution *an* applies to the *yu* or *vu* that serves as the cause (*nimitta*) for the stem; but when *tuṭ* is present here, the cause of the stem is the word *tyu*, not merely the word *yu*. Consequently, just as the substitution *an* does not occur in *mṛtyu*, so too it does not occur here.

It might be so. But if this *tuk* were made a part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), it would not be possible; for in the word *prātastanam*, the *visarjanīya* would not occur because [the *n*] would not be at the end of a word (*apadāntatvāt*). Therefore, this must be made a part of the following element (*parādi*). In that case, however, the substitution (*ādeśa*) would not apply? To this he says: "But when those two have been substituted, the augment *tuṭ* occurs. The phrase "when those two have been substituted" means "when they have undergone substitution."

And this meaning is obtained from the word *ādiṣṭa* by virtue of its ending in the suffix *yat* (from the root *diś* with the prefix *ā-*): that which is pointed out (*ādiśyate*) is "pointed out" (*ādiṣṭa*); those two [words] for which that exists are "the two pointed-out ones" (*ādiṣṭau*), and [the rule applies] "of those two pointed-out ones. This is understood from the technical indication (*nirdeśa*) in the rule *ghakālataneṣu*; for if the augment *tuṭ* were prescribed for words that are not "pointed out," the form *nata* would not be possible. It was not stated that in the case of *prātastanam*, the suffix *cha* (prescribed after a *vṛddha* stem) supersedes [the suffix *tanaC*] due to its higher status; rather, it is because [the suffix *tanaC*] is applied to a word that has already been "pointed out."

Even though *cha* is an obstructor [of other suffixes], there is no possibility of a comparative evaluation (*sampradhāraṇā*) between it—which is weak—and the two suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul*, which possess superior strength, even while they are themselves obstructing *ṭhañ*. The statement "a word ending in *m* is an indeclinable" is because it is listed among the *svarādi* group. Regarding the phrase "of the action of ending": this means "of that which has the action of ending," namely, of the root *ṣo* in the sense of "ending" (*antakarmaṇi*). Although this [root] denotes merely the conclusion [of an action], the word *sāyam*, derived with the suffix *ghañ*, denotes the end of the day; therefore, there is no suspicion of subverting the governing rule for time (*kālādhikāra*). The phrase "in connection with the suffix" means: *chasya bādhakam api ṭhañaṃ bādhamānayos ṭyuṭyulor utkṛṣṭabalayor durbalena chena saha sampradhāraṇābhāvāt |* *makārāntaṃ padam avyayam iti |* *svarādiṣu paṭhitam |* *antakarmaṇa iti |* *antakriyasya, 'ṣo'ntakarmaṇi' ity asyety arthaḥ |* *yady apy asāv avasānamātravācī, ghañantas tu sāyaśabdo divasāntavacana iti na kālādhikārasya bādhaśaṅkā |* *pratyayasanniyogeneti |*

In other cases, however, it ends in *a*, as in *sāyāhnaḥ* and *sāyataraḥ*. And it has been said: "Of *ahna* preceded by a numeral or *vi* or *sāya*" [Pāṇini 5.4.91]. Regarding the form ending in *e*: the word *nipātyate* (it is an irregularity) is to be supplied. This irregularity (*nipātana*) is for the sake of cases where the sense of the locative case is absent—as in *prāhṇaḥ soḍho 'syā* ("this person has endured the forenoon") and so forth. But when the meaning is "born there" (*jāta*) and so on, the form is established by the non-elision (*aluk*) rule in *ghakālataneṣu* [Pāṇini 6.3.17].

Regarding the rule *ciraparutparāribhyaḥ*: because the word *cira* is included in this sūtra, the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are applied; there is no sublation of the sūtra as there would be in the case of the rule *kiyattadvahuṣu kṛño’jvidhānāt*. *Parut* means "in the previous year"; *parāri* means "in the year before that. The word *pratna* signifies "ancient" (*purāṇa*).

Regarding *agrāpaścāḍḍimac*: some read the word *ādi* here as well, [reading] *agrādipaścāt*; they do not read [the rule] *madhyānmaḥ*, [thinking] that the addition of *ādeḥ* must be stated there. The inclusion of the marker *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) in *paścāt*. This is merely an elaboration of the rule: "In the case of indeclinables, there is elision of the *ṭi* whenever a *bha*-suffix follows."
The suffix *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is applied after the words *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*. (Pāṇini 4.3.24)

The rule that there is no *aluk* elision in the case of the seventh case-ending was determined under the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*; namely, that secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are produced from a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), which should be examined in that very place. If a secondary suffix is produced from a word ending in a case-suffix, how does it occur in the case of *pūrvāhṇatana*? To this he says: "But when... (*yadā tu*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a place of birth [to form a patronymic]. (Pāṇini 4.3.25)

From this point forward, their meanings and the case endings that express their semantic competency (*samarthavibhakti*) are being specified. However, both of these are not to be explicitly stated. Why? It has been said: "The term *śeṣa* (remainder) serves both as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and as a governing heading (*adhikāra*). In that regard, by virtue of being a defining characteristic, suffixes such as *aṇ* are established even for meanings such as "born from" (*jāta*), just as in the case of "visible form" (*rūpa*) in the expression *cākṣuṣaṃ rūpam*. And by virtue of being a governing heading, [suffixes] such as *gha* are established. Thus, the meanings need not be explicitly stated; furthermore, because it is the very nature of a suffix to denote its own meaning, the case endings expressing semantic competency are also obtained.

Since the case endings that express capacity are also obtained through the sense of the suffix and by virtue of the inherent nature of the expression, their specification too should not be made at all. If it is argued that this is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), we say no, because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭatvāt*). In this regard, one might think: "The secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) should apply only to meanings such as 'born in' (*jāta*) and so forth, and should not apply in cases such as 'he stays there' (*tatrāste*) or 'he sleeps there' (*tatra śete*); therefore, the meanings beginning with 'born in' are enumerated. But that is not so, because it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

For *taddhita* suffixes are accepted elsewhere as well—such as in *cākṣuṣaṃ rūpam* (visible form), *śrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ* (audible sound), *cāturdaśaṃ rakṣaḥ* (a demon appearing on the fourteenth day), and *dārṣadāḥ saktavaḥ* (flour ground on a stone)—but where they are not accepted, as in the case of *āste* (he sits) and so forth, they will not occur there due to the absence of such usage (*anabhidhāna*), just as in cases like *aṅgulyā khanati* (he digs with a finger). Therefore, there is no purpose in enumerating the universals (*jāti*) and so forth.

However, for the purpose of stating exceptions (*apavāda*), I shall explain those exceptions—beginning with *prāvṛṣaṣṭha* and others—in their respective places without confusion; thus, these meanings must necessarily be presented in sequence. Although they serve other purposes, they are also indicated as the meanings of *aṇ* and other suffixes through a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Furthermore, for the sake of clarity, those instances where no exception exists because the meaning is not observed—such as in the case of "those who are skilled in what is made, obtained, bought, or practiced" (*kṛta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ*)—can be left unstated.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [a word ending in] *śarat* when it occurs in a compound with *saṃjñā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.27)

"If it is by means of a collection" means that if the collection of base and suffix constitutes the technical name (*saṃjñā*). "Up to 'skilled in what is made, obtained, or bought'"—the word *yāvat* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) used to indicate a limit.
Or on the new moon day. 4.3.30.

"Because that which has undergone a modification in one part is not something else. Regarding the rule *amāvāsyad anyatarasyām*, it is stated: "In the case of the suffix *ṇyat* after the root *vas* preceded by *amā*, the absence of *vṛddhi* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in one alternative. Since *vṛddhi* is generally prescribed for the penultimate vowel by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* when the suffix *ṇyat* follows, the form *amāvāsyā* is the regular one; thus, the meaning is that the substitution of a short vowel for the long penultimate vowel constitutes a modification of only one part of that very word. However, for those who read this sūtra and the list beginning with *sandhivela* as having a short penultimate vowel (*hrasvopadha*), the form with a long penultimate vowel (*dīrghopadha*) would not be valid, because it would not be a modification of that [short-vowel base].
And [the suffix] *a* [is applied after a word ending in *ca*]. 4.3.31.

What is the purpose of this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)? One might ask: "Why not simply state *‘vāmāvāsyāyā vā’* (or ‘after *amāvāsyā*, or’), so that by the force of the word *ca* (‘and’), the suffix *vuñ* would apply, and by the mention of the option (*vā*), the suffix *aṇ* would also apply when both [suffixes] are absent? This is true; however, in the subsequent rule, one might suspect that the option (*vikalpa*) continues to apply. But when there is a separation of rules, because the suffix *aṇ* is permitted for *saṃdhivelā* and so forth, the option is established for this case as well by the force of the mention of *vā* in the preceding rule. Consequently, the word *vā* need not be carried over (*anuvarttya*) here. Thus, due to the intervention [of the intervening rule], the cessation of the option in the subsequent rule is established.
And [the suffixes] aṇ and añ [are applied after the word *māṇava*]. 4.3.33.
The separation of the yoga (yogavibhāga) is for the purpose of establishing a correspondence (yathāsaṃkhya).
The suffix *luk* is elided after the names of the lunar mansions *śraviṣṭhā*, *phalgunī*, *anurādhā*, *svāti*, *tiṣya*, *punarvasu*, *hasta*, *viśākhā*, *āṣāḍhā*, and *bahulā*.

In this context, the word *bahulā*—which is a synonym for *kṛttikā*—is indicated in the neuter gender with a short vowel due to its treatment as a singular compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*), and not because it is the word *bahulā* meaning "many" (which would require a long vowel); this is because of its association with *śraviṣṭhā* and the others. Regarding the term *citrā*: once the elision (*luk*) has been applied by the rule "the feminine suffix is elided when a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is elided," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added again.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *ṅīṣ* [is applied] because of their inclusion in the *gaura*-group": it is recited there that "Revatī is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), Rohiṇī is a lunar mansion," yet these two are not denoters of lunar mansions, because they function in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the meaning is that the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies here due to their being included in the *gaura*-group by the rule "and *pippalī* etc. are also [included] among the *gaura* etc.," since they have not been excluded from that group.

Regarding the statement "the suffixes *ṭāp* and *ṅīṣ* should be stated": the word "in the feminine" (*striyām*) is required [as a governing condition].
