The letter *ṭ* in *ṭāp* is for the purpose of [triggering] the suffix *ṅīp*; the letter *n* in *ṅīṣ* is for the sake of the accent (*svara*); and by virtue of the power of their specific prescription, elision (*luk*) does not occur for these two. Regarding the statement "the suffix *chaṇ* should also be stated": in this case, "in the feminine" is not required.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *sthāna*, as well as after *gośālā* and *kharaśālā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.35)

Regarding *gośālā*: by the rule *vibhāṣā senā*, there is shortening when the word is neuter. Due to its association with that [term], *kharaśāla* is also understood as neuter; however, the shortening does not occur here through the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) of a *dvandva*. Because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding member, the elision (*luk*) occurs even after feminine forms, by virtue of the maxim *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*. Although the elision after neuter forms would also be established—even if they were read with the feminine suffix *ṭā*—since the modified part is not different from the original, the reading of the short vowel is for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*).
Or [the word *nakṣatra*] may optionally [be used as a neuter noun] when it refers to Vatsaśālā, Abhijit, Aśvayu, or Śatabhiṣaj. 4.3.36.

Regarding "Vatsaśālā": this refers to the inclusion of both forms ending in a short vowel and those ending in a long vowel. This is an elaboration specifically of the term *bahulagrahaṇa* (the mention of "in many cases"). This was stated with reference to the words *aśvayuj* and *śatabhiṣaj*, because the other two [words] do not denote lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Regarding *abhijit*: although there is indeed a lunar mansion named *abhijit*—as it is said, "The lunar mansion named *abhijit* is situated above the *aṣāḍhās*"—there is also a *muhūrta* (a specific time-unit) so named.
The suffix *cha* is frequently applied after words denoting lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

Since the elision (*luk*) is established through the continued application of the word "or" (*vā*) and by understanding the rule as having a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the mention of "variously" (*bahulam*) is for the purpose of indicating that in some cases something else occurs; by this, the requirement that the suffixes *ṭā* and *naū* be stated [as exceptions] and so forth becomes established. Regarding the form *rohiṇa*: the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyānam*) "an addition regarding *citrā*, *revatī*, and *rohiṇī* in the feminine" is intended to ensure the mandatory elision in the feminine, and not merely to restrict the elision to the feminine alone. Pāṇini 4.3.38: *kṛta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ*. (The suffix *aṇ* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case to denote one who has performed, obtained, purchased, or is skilled in that thing.)

Whatever is produced here, even if it has arisen, it belongs to that [place] where it was made. Although not everything that is produced is necessarily "made"—since there are things that arise spontaneously—everything that is "made" is indeed produced; for nothing can be made that lacks the nature of being born, just as, for example, space cannot be made. And whatever is purchased, even if it is obtained, it belongs to that [person] from whom it was bought. Here too, not everything that is obtained is necessarily "purchased," since acquisition may occur through gifts and other means; however, what is "purchased" is indeed a form of acquisition.

The meaning is that purchase (*kraya*) is also a cause for acquisition (*lābha*). If so, why is it mentioned separately? This is the question: "Is it not already included within 'born' (*jāta*) and 'obtained' (*labdha*)? [The answer is: "Because the meanings of the words are distinct. A form produced by the operation of another is called "made" (*kṛta*); that which is devoid of such [operation] is "born" (*jāta*). Likewise, a form produced by the operation of the recipient consisting in the payment of a price is called "bought" (*krītā*); that which is devoid of such [operation] is "obtained" (*labdha*).

In this regard, just as there is no difference in meaning between the words "soaked rice" (*viklinna odana*) and "cooked rice" (*pakva odana*), so it is here as well—this is the sense. He clarifies this very point with the words "by the mere thing" (*vastumātreṇa*). This means "in reality. What is intended is this: in reality, that which is purchased is simply "obtained," whereas by means of the word, a different form is expressed. Likewise, even that which is "done" (*kṛta*) is in reality "produced" (*jāta*), but by means of the word, a different form is expressed; thus it should be understood.

He concludes: "The meaning of the word, however, is indeed distinct. In that regard, if the terms *kṛta* (made) and *krīta* (bought) were not employed, then just as when asked, "Where was this jar made, or bought? the answer "It was produced or obtained in Srughna" would not be used, so too the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) would not occur. Therefore, the terms *kṛta* and *krīta* are mentioned separately in order to express their meaning through the secondary derivative.
The suffix *cha* (forming *prāya*) is applied after a word denoting a place (*adhikaraṇa*) to express that which mostly exists there. 4.3.39.

"Prāyeṇa bhavaḥ": this is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). The meaning is that since it is produced by means of "existence" (*bhava*), the very thing that was to be established by the term *yatprāyabhavaḥ* has already been established by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53). For indeed, one who exists mostly in a kingdom exists in that very place; thus, it is already established by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. [The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that 'mostly existing' (*prāyabhava*) means 'impermanent existence' (*anityabhava*)."

The meaning is: if it were argued that what exists there only at certain times and not at others is not a *prāyabhava* (an occurrence by way of pervasion), whereas that for which the relationship of locus and located is constant is designated as "*tatra bhavaḥ*" (occurring therein)—this distinction being necessitated by the force of their separate mention—[the author] refutes this by stating: "it is the same as [the case of] one whose doubt has been removed."

As for that which Your Honor, free from doubt, considers to be a logical example—namely, "Devadatta is a native of Śrughna"—it is exactly the same [as the case in question], for he too sometimes emerges from that region of water. If it is appropriate in that case according to Your Honor, let it be seen as appropriate here as well. Now, if this too is an example of "being for the most part" (*prāyabhava*)—as in "Devadatta is a native of Śrughna"—then what is the example for "being there permanently" (*tatra nityabhava*)? It is: "The rampart is a native of Śrughna" (*sraughnaḥ prākāraḥ*).

If this were so, then the rule prescribing the suffix *cha* for the words *jihvāmūla* and *aṅguli* under the heading "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) would not apply when an exception is observed; yet such an exception is indeed seen:
"O illustrious lady, I am a monkey, a messenger of Rāma in accordance with righteousness;
O Queen, look at this ring engraved with the name of Rāma."

Therefore, since the specific "mostly" (*prāya*) existence is included within the general "existence" (*bhava*) there, is the inclusion of the term "mostly" redundant? This, then, is its purpose: so that [the suffix] may apply in the sense of "mostly existing"—as in *upajānu-bhavaṃ gaḍu* ("a goitre occurring mostly on the knee")—but not in the sense of "always existing."

Now, why does the suffix *yat*—prescribed by the rule "śarīrāvayavād yat" (Pāṇini 4.3.55) under the heading "tatra bhavaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.53)—not apply here to the word *upajānu*, which denotes a body part located near the knee? Because it is not so prescribed [by tradition]. But then, for the same reason of not being prescribed, the suffix *ṭhak* will also not apply? Thus it stands: this mention of "mostly" (*prāya*) is useless, because the matter is already settled by the rule "tatra bhavaḥ."
The suffix *thak* is applied after the words *upajānu*, *upakarṇa*, and *upanīvi*.
Compounds such as *upāñju* are *avyayībhāva*s when expressing proximity; the masculine gender used for the *samāhāra-dvandva* is based on a Vedic (sūtra) usage.
In the word *sambhūta*, [the suffix *kha* is applied]. 4.3.41.

"Avaklṛpti" means possibility, and "pramāṇānatireka" means the non-excess of the measure of the contained over the measure of the container. The sense is that even for a single application [of a word], multiple meanings are not contradictory, because of the recourse to principles such as *tantra* (simultaneous application). In this context, *avaklṛpti* is possibility—the cognition that "this may be thus"; *pramāṇānatireka* is the state where the measure of the contained does not exceed the measure of the container, such that the entire contained object fits within the container. Regarding the example *sraughna*: the meaning is that Devadatta is now possible to be found in Srughna; or, the meaning is that the army and so forth do not exceed the dimensions of Srughna.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the word *kośa*.

"Kauśeya" means "silk cloth. Now, one might object: cloth cannot exist within a cocoon (*kośa*), because when the cloth is produced, its cause—the cocoon—has already been transformed; nor can cloth exist within another cocoon, for that is not accepted there. Therefore, since the suffix *ḍhañ* would arise from *kośa* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) and yet the meaning would be untenable, the *Vārttika* itself is the refuge. The meaning is that within the section beginning with "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*), immediately after the rule "from *eṇī*, the suffix *ḍhañ*" (*eṇyā ḍhañ*), one should state: "and also from *kośa*. (*kośācceti vaktavyam*).

Regarding the phrase "the meaning is untenable": the worldly meaning of the word *kauśeya*, which is characterized by a cloth made of silk thread, would be untenable; that is, the worldly meaning would not be followed by the treatise (*śāstra*). Rather, the intended referent (*abhidheya*) would have to be the silkworm itself, for it is that which exists within the cocoon (*kośa*). Furthermore, because the term is stated without qualification, it would follow that the word could also evoke the notion of a sword-sheath (*khaḍgakośa*); therefore, he says: "This is a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)."

It is held that in conventional (rūḍhi) words, the meaning of the individual components need not necessarily be sought, as in the case of words such as *tailapāyikā* ("crane" or "oil-drinker"). However, the author of the Sūtras has prescribed the suffix *sambhūta* on the basis of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). For since the effect exists even in the state of its cause, it is possible for it to be [said to be] there; yet this is untenable [in the present context], because the relationship between cause and effect is one of identity (*tādātmya*), not a relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
The suffix *kha* is applied after a word denoting time when it signifies that something is being sown, flowering, or ripening [at that time]. 4.3.43.
The phrase "from those expressing specific times" does not refer to the literal form [of the words themselves]; for later on, the words *aśvayujī* and so forth are qualified by this term "time."
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after [a word ending in a vowel] when it means "sown. (Pāṇini 4.3.44)

The Sūtra shows that the past tense is not intended to be expressed [in the examples]. The phrase "they are sown in winter" (*hemante upyante*) is used. The division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows; it is so that the suffix prescribed by the preceding rule may apply to the two subsequent rules, but it should not apply to words such as *sādhu* and others.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied [to denote the day of a lunar month] after the word *āśvayujī*. (Pāṇini 4.2.45)

The letter *ñ* is for the sake of the vowel [in *aśvayuj*], and for the sake of the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] in subsequent forms. The reading is *aśvayugbhyāṃ yuktā* (joined by the two Aśvayuj [stars]), because the dual form *aśvayujau* is observed in the expression "Salutation to the two Aśvins, the two Aśvayujs" (*namo 'śvibhyām aśvayugbhyām*). It is also read as a synonym for *aśvinī*; Amarasimha states, "The stars Aśvayuj and Aśvinī. The well-known reading is *aśvanī*, where the suffix *in* is added to *aśva-pūrva-an* according to the *uṇādi* rules, and the initial vowel is shortened due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
[The suffix *vuñ* is applied after the words] *kalāpa*, *aśvattha*, and *vyavaba*. Pāṇini 4.3.48.

Since words such as *kalāpin* (peacock-feathered) and others, which are well-known to denote peacocks and so forth, cannot possibly apply to time, how can it be said that [the suffixes apply] "after words denoting specific times"? To this he says: "The words *kalāpin* and so forth. Because there is no deviation in the relationship between the *aśvattha* tree and time, it is not a qualifier; thus, the word *aśvattha* ends in a *luk* elision according to the rule "phale luk. He explains this by saying: "in which the *aśvattha*s bear fruit. *Yavabusam* refers either to a distinct species of grain inferior to barley, like *yava* itself, or to the chaff of barley grains themselves.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after [the word] *grīṣma* when preceded by *avara*. 4.3.49.

"Avarasamam" is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Furthermore, the word "avara" does not denote direction; if it did, the compound would not be valid due to the restriction "only when denoting a name [is a compound formed] with a word for direction or a numeral. Regarding "āvarasamakam," the meaning is that it is to be paid in the first year of those years yet to come. Another says: "That which was due to be paid in the past year but has not yet been given even today is called *āvarasamakam*."
After the words *saṃvatsara* and *āgrahāyaṇī*, the suffix *ṭhañ* also [is applied].

Regarding the phrase "it should be stated": since the suffix *vuñ* is optional, it is thought that in the alternative case, the suffix *ṭhañ* will apply by its own default rule. As for the mention of *ṭhañ* and so forth: if the mention of *ṭhañ* were absent, then because of the entry in the *sandhivelādi* group—"from *saṃvatsara*, [the suffixes are used] for *phala* and *parvan*"—when *phala* is intended to be expressed as a debt (*ṛṇa*), the suffix *vuñ* would be excluded and *aṇ* would occur instead; however, due to the mention of *ṭhañ*, only *ṭhañ* occurs.
The word *mṛga* takes the suffix *aṇ* when meaning "to speak. (Pāṇini 4.3.51)
He speaks—he utters sound.
That has been endured by him. (Pāṇini 4.3.52)

Regarding the word *asya*: this genitive case is not the "agentive genitive" (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to *soḍha* (endured), because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini] in the rule *na lokāvyaya*. What then? It is the genitive characterized as "residual" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*) intended merely to express the relationship of the agent. By saying "study associated with the night," he shows that in this rule, what is meant by time is the activity associated with it, since time in its own nature cannot be "endured."
The suffix *bhava* [is applied] in that sense. 4.3.53.

The phrase "it ceases from [the rule concerning] time" means as follows: since the term *tatra* (therein) under discussion in the rule *tatra jātaḥ* ("born therein") is connected with the governing heading on time (*kāla-adhikāra*), its recurrence would imply the recurrence of that [time-rule] as well. Therefore, the term *tatra* is repeated here so that only the sense of the locative case (*saptamy-artha*) may be grasped, and not the sense of the locative as qualified by its connection to time; this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Is not the term *tatra* under discussion separated from the word *tat* in the preceding rule by the first-case ending used as a case-ending expressing grammatical competency (*samartha-vibhakti*)? He says: No; for it is possible to read it elsewhere as well.
The suffix *yat* is applied after words such as *diś* (direction) and others.

Regarding the term "senāmukhya": it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) consisting of the word *senā* followed by that which ends in *-mukhya*, rather than a suffix being applied directly to the word *senāmukhya*; for there is no rule for [suffix application] to that which ends in such a compound.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after a word denoting a limb of the body. 4.3.55.

"Body" (*śarīra*) refers to the collection of living beings (*prāṇikāya*). However, usages such as "the body of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya śarīram*) are figurative (*gauṇa*). Regarding the phrase "it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ*": it supersedes *cha* derived from a *vṛddha* [stem] because of its higher priority [in the rule order]. For example, that which exists in the foot (*pāde bhavam*) is *padya*; here, the substitution of *pad* occurs according to the rule *padyatyatadarthe*. That which exists in the nose (*nāsikāyām bhavam*) is *nasya*; here, the substitution of *nas* occurs according to the rule *nasa nāsikāyā yattatkṣudreṣu*.

How can it be said that "the speed resides in the shanks and thighs"? And why should it not be so? For a collection of body parts is not grasped by the mention of a single body part. Nor is there a rule of extension to the end of a compound (*tadantavidhi*) here? Poets are unrestrained.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the words *dṛti*, *kukṣi*, *kalaśi*, *vasti*, and *asthi*.

*Dṛti* refers both to a leather product and to a part of the body. *Kukṣi* refers to smoke and so forth, while *vasti* is a part of the body located below the navel. *Āheya* refers to poison and the like. The word *asti* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*); it is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles a case ending and has the same meaning as a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), as in "the cow has milk" (*astikṣīrā gauḥ*); it also expresses possession of wealth, as in "one who possesses [it]" (*astimān*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the word] *grīvā*.

Regarding the term *dhamanīvacana*: this means a word denoting a collection of vessels (*dhamanī*). When that [word] refers to a collection in which the distinction between its constituent parts is manifest, it takes the plural; however, when it refers to a collection in which the distinction between its constituent parts is concealed, it is used in the singular.
The suffix *añ* is applied after [stems ending in] *gambhīra*. 4.3.58.

It should be stated that [the suffixes] apply after *badhira*, *deva*, and *pañcajana*. This was stated under the rule *prāgdīvyataḥ*: "After *deva*, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* are applied, and there is elision of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhi*) of *bahiṣ*. That must necessarily be stated so that [the suffixes] may apply even in other meanings. However, this mention of *bahiḥ* and *deva* here is for the purpose of further elaboration (*prapañca*).
And [the suffix *ṭac* is added] after an *avyayībhāva* compound. (Pāṇini 4.3.59)

"What is the purpose of [mentioning] *parimukha* and so forth? Furthermore, he asks how this specific restriction can be obtained when there is a general statement, and answers: "And of *parimukha* and so forth. The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Immediately after *digādi*, the group beginning with *parimukha* is recited; no other purpose for its inclusion is possible, since it can only be construed as a qualifier for the mention of *avyayībhāva*. Therefore, the rule will apply only to *parimukha* and so forth, and not to every *avyayībhāva*.

If this is so, one should have simply said "from *parimukha* and so forth"; therefore, he says "of those very [compounds]. If it were stated as "*parimukhādeḥ*," the suffix *ñya* would apply even after Bahuvrīhi and Tatpuruṣa compounds; however, because of the inclusion of the term "avyayībhāva," only the suffix *aṇ* occurs after them. Furthermore, the mention of "avyayībhāva" must necessarily be made for the sake of the subsequent rule; therein, regarding those compounds preceded by *pari*, if exclusion (*varjana*) is understood, then an Avyayībhāva compound is formed according to the rule "apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā."

Now, if it means "on all sides," then it is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). In the case of those preceded by *upa*, it denotes proximity; in those preceded by *anu*, the compounds are formed according to the specific rules: *anuryatsamayā*, *yasya cāyāmaḥ*, and *paścādarthe yadavyayam*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after [the word] *pūrvada* when it occurs within a compound. (Pāṇini 4.3.60)

Regarding the term *ādhyātmika*: the suffix *ṭac* is applied by the rule *anaśca* as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Similarly, *ādhyātmika* and *ādhibhautika* are formed; here, both members of the compound undergo *vṛddhi* (strengthening) because they belong to the *anuśatikādi* group. Thus, the *adhyātmādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). Furthermore, the passage beginning with "from the word *samāna*" is an elaboration of this very point. The word *ūrdhva* has the same meaning as the word *ūrdhva*; moreover, that [form] occurs only within the scope of this specific grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*). Another teacher says: "By the force of the application of the suffix *ṭhañ*, the word *dama* is substituted for the following word *ūrdhva*, and its final syllable is prescribed to have the vowel *m*. In the case of *ūrdhvadeha*, however, there is no substitution of the final syllable with *m*.
Regarding the term *aihaukika*: as before, there is vṛddhi of both members [of the compound].

In the cases of *mukhatīyam* and *pārśvatīyam*, the suffix *tasi* is applied to the words *mukha* and *pārśva* ending in the locative case by virtue of their inclusion in the *ādyādi* group; from that, the suffix *īya* is added, and because these are indeclinables (*avyaya*), there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*). This is merely an elaboration of the reading in the *gahādi* group. By this, the other [term] is explained.

Regarding the term *maṇmīya*: in the list beginning with *gaha*, it is stated that where *madhyamadhyamaṃ cāṇ caraṇe* is recited, the word *madhya* is understood there as signifying the "middle of the earth. However, for the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārtha*), the rule prescribing the suffix *mīya* is stated so that the form *madhyamīya* may occur even outside of that specific context. In the categories such as *jātādi*, the form *madhyamīya* occurs only when *madhya* signifies the "middle of the earth," and not when it signifies other types of middles.

Likewise, by virtue of its inclusion in the *gahādi* group, the form *mādhyama* is established in the sense that "their dwelling is in the middle of the earth" (*pṛthivīmadhya*). The suffix *maṇ* is prescribed so that it may also apply in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*) for words denoting a middle position, as expressed by the rule:
"The word *madhya* becomes *madhyama*, and from this [word], the suffix *dinaṇ* occurs. This means that the word *madhya* undergoes the change to *madhyama*, and the suffix *dinaṇ* is added after it.

Regarding *sthāmnaḥ*: this means "from a word ending in *sthāman*. Regarding *aśvatthāma*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose strength (*sthāma*) is like that of a horse (*aśva*). Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*. Then, for the sense of "belonging to that" (*bhava*), the suffix *a* is added according to the rule "*sthāmno 'kāraḥ*," and from that [suffix], there is elision (*luk*).
Regarding *vṛkājina*: this is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *aṇ*.

Regarding the rule *samānasya tadādeśca*: the genitive case here is characterized by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*). Regarding the phrase *adhyātmādiṣu*: this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Regarding *ūrdhvandāmācca dehācca*: the meaning is "from the word *ūrdhva* and from words ending in *dāma*. Furthermore, it is accepted that [the suffix] applies only after words preceded by *ūrdhva* and ending in *deha*. For it was stated previously: "*ūrdhvadehācca*, [forming] *aurdhvadehikam*. Regarding *sthāmno lugajināttathā*: in both readings, the rule for [compounds] ending in those [words] (*tadanta-vidhi*) applies.
In the word *aśabda*, [the suffix] *yat* or *kha* may optionally be applied.

Regarding the term *vāsudevavargīya*: since the suffix *cha* (as prescribed by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*) is subsequent [to the rules for *yat* and *kha*, which would otherwise apply], those two (*yat* and *kha*) act as exceptions; therefore, even after a *vṛddha* stem, the suffix *cha* must be desired here by this very rule.
And [the suffix *cha*] is added after the name of that which is to be explained, in the sense of "its commentary. (Pāṇini 4.3.66)

Regarding the phrase "from that which is in the genitive case" (*tasyeti ṣaṣṭhīsamarthāt*): one might object, "But you will state that this [genitive] is for the purpose of providing a governing context (*adhikāra*), since both the *bhavya* and the *ākhyāna* are governed simultaneously for the sake of prescribing exceptions (*apavāda-vidhāna*), as those two have already been specified. Why, then, is it explained here as being for the purpose of prescribing according to what has been previously ordained? It is said in reply: although the governing context is intended primarily for the prescription of exceptions, what fault is there in its secondary (*anuṣaṅgika*) function of prescribing suffixes such as *aṇ* and so forth? For when one intends to express a specific distinction, one resorts to a general rule as a last resort (*agatikagati*).

For this very reason, expressions such as *kṛta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ* ("skilled in what is made, obtained, or bought") are teachings of meaning that are without exception. Regarding the phrase *tatra bhavet*: this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it is prescribed by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53) within this very same specific context. Now, one might object: the particle *ca*, when heard in proximity to the meaning of an affix (*pratyayārtha*) that is being explained, effects a conjunction only of an affix-meaning of the same class, not of a case-ending (*samarthavibhakti*).

Just as in the rule "kedārād yañ ca," by its proximity to the suffix (*pratyaya*), it is the suffix itself that is conjoined [with the particle *ca*], and not the base (*prakṛti*); and in the rule "ṭhañ kavacinah ca," it is the base alone [that is conjoined] and not the suffix; therefore, here too, because of the employment of the word "tasya" (of that), it is logical that the suffix occurs after a word ending in the genitive case even when the sense is "belonging to it" (*bhava*). To this, he says: "in proximity to the meaning of the sentence. Here, the particle *iti* is employed with the intention: "I am referring back to the contextual meaning of the sentence."

And the purpose of this retrospective reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) is precisely this: that there may be a conjunction only with that which is of the same class (*tulyajātīya*). It is with the intention of establishing this very principle that the restatement (*anuvāda*) "in that case, and in the sense of 'becoming'" (*tatra bhave ca*) was made previously.

Regarding the question "Why [is it said] 'that which is to be explained' (*vyākhyātavya*)?", the inquiry arises from the thought that since the word *vyākhyāna* (explanation) is a relative term, it is understood that for every explanation there is something belonging to it, as indicated by the phrase "that very thing belongs to this. [The author] asks this question with this in mind. In the expression "Pāṭaliputra is explained by Sukauśalā," this instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is not used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); rather, what is it? It is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). The meaning is: "It is explained by persons using Sukauśalā as the instrument. To the question "How so?", he says: "Having such an arrangement" (*evaṃsanniveśam*).

For the arrangement of the walls and other structures in Pāṭaliputra is exactly like that in Sukauśalā; therefore, it is explained by means of that [analogy]. If this is so, then since the word "Pāṭaliputra" is also the name of that which is to be explained, how can it serve as a counter-example? To this he says: "But not... The meaning is that although this is intended here as something to be explained, the word [Pāṭaliputra] does not function as its name [in this context].

What, then, is intended here? It is that which is well-known in the world as having the nature of a text (*grantha*) and which is to be explained. For it is for this very purpose that the name of "that which is to be explained" is mentioned; for the word "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*), being a correlative term, implies "that which is to be explained" (*vyākhyātavya*) by its very nature. But surely this [suffix] might have the sense of "being" (*bhāva*); for in that case, "that which is to be explained" would not be obtained through implication. If that is so, then the mention of the name will serve to include what is well-known [in common usage].

Regarding the phrase "of *bhava* and *vyākhyāna*": the meaning here is not that this simultaneous governing authority (*adhikāra*) over *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is for the purpose of prescribing exceptions (*apavāda*); for the status of being a governing authority has not yet been explained previously. Therefore, the meaning is that this simultaneous governing authority over *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is not an indication of the meanings of *aṇ* and the other suffixes. To the question "For what purpose is this governing authority?", he says: "for the purpose of prescribing exceptions."

Why is this explanation of meaning not applied to the suffixes *aṇ* and others? To that he says: "For those two have already been explained. For those two meanings have already been explained in this way: one by the rule "tatra bhavaḥ" (P. 4.3.53), and the other by "tasyedam" (P. 4.3.120). Therefore, this [present rule] does not serve that purpose. However, it was previously explained that while this must necessarily be performed for the sake of governing (*adhikāra*), this [present statement] is incidental (*anuṣaṅgika*) and serves to explain the meaning.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after a polysyllabic word that has its accent on the final syllable.

"The exception (*apavāda*) [is] 'amo'. However, the suffix *cha* (forming the word *sāmastika*) supersedes it due to its higher position in the order of rules. *Sāmasta* is the name of a treatise; its commentary is *sāmastika*. The treatise that prescribes rules such as *ṣatva* is referred to by the term *ṣatvādi*. *Nataḥ* means "having an unraised accent" (*anudātta*); *anataḥ* means "having a raised accent" (*udātta*). "The bases (*prakṛti*) have the acute accent on the final syllable. Although only two examples were cited, the plural number is used with reference to other bases of this kind, and these include those subject to changes such as *kutva* and *rutva*.

Regarding the phrase "by the accent of the preceding member" (*gatisvareṇa*), this refers to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*. The term *udātta* here is a mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*); by this, the rule of "specification of that which ends in X" (*tadantavidhi*) is established, as in the case of the rule *varādanudattāt*. Therefore, the explicit inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity.
And [the suffix -aṇ] is applied after words denoting *kratu* sacrifices. 4.3.68.

The words *agniṣṭoma* and so forth, as they occur in the *mantras*, *brāhmaṇas*, and *kalpas* concerning the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites, serve as the examples here. The commencement [of this rule] is for the sake of [establishing] a final acute accent (*an-antodātta*). In that regard, the words *rājasūya* and *vājapeya* have the acute accent on the middle syllable by virtue of the original accentuation of the subsequent member in a *kṛt*-derivative compound (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*). In *rājasūya*, [it is derived as]: "the King is consecrated" (*rājā sūyate*) or "he is consecrated by the King" (*rājñā iha sūyate*), with the suffix *kyap*; the compound is formed either through a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) or as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). In *vājapeya*, [it means]: "that in which one drinks," with the suffix *yat* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe yat*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

*Vāja* is a specific kind of gruel (*yavāgū*); *peya* means "to be drunk"; thus, *vājapeya* [is a compound meaning] "that which is to be drunk as a *vāja*. *Stuti* is *stoma*; [the term] *agnistoma* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is a *stoma* of Agni. According to the rule "the first member and the last member [of a compound may be accented]," it is oxytone (accented on the final syllable). *Navayajña* is the sacrifice with new rice; it is the *āgrayaṇa*. The compound is formed according to the rule "frequently, [a word ending in] a *kṛt* suffix [is compounded] with a word denoting an agent or an instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*). By the rule "by the preservation of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛdanta* compound, the accent of the suffix *naṅ* itself remains," it is oxytone.

The word *pāka* has a limited range of application; thus, that which is both a *pāka* and a *yajña* is a *pākayajña*. By the accentuation rule for compounds (*samāsasvara*), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). Since this [sūtra] is commenced for the sake of another purpose, even though it follows a word denoting a sacrifice that is oxytone, the suffix *ṭhañ* is more appropriately applied by this very rule; therefore, there is the presentation of these oxytone words.

"It is established by the word *kratubhyaḥ* alone" means that the intention is that *kratu* and *yajña* are synonyms. "Even from non-Soma sacrifices" means that otherwise, since the word *kratu* is conventionally restricted (*rūḍha*) to Soma sacrifices, it would not apply elsewhere; however, because of the inclusion of the word *yajña*, it applies to those [non-Soma sacrifices] as well. Thus, even when only *yajña* is mentioned, the same defect occurs as when only *kratu* is mentioned; therefore, both are employed for the purpose of including both the primary and the secondary senses.
The suffix *ṛṣi* is applied [to denote a person] only in the case of chapters (*adhyāya*). 4.3.69.

The word *ṛṣi* refers to the names of the *pravara* lineages. They are called *pravara*s because they are invoked (*pravriyante*) by the *hotṛ* and the *adhvaryu* priest; these are [the sages] such as Bhṛgu and others. For example: "Bhārgava-Cyāvana-Āpravāna-Aurva-Jāmadagna" is the invocation by the *hotṛ*, and "Jamadagni-vat, Urva-vat, Āpravāna-vat, Cyavana-vat, Bhṛgu-vat" is the invocation by the *adhvaryu*. By this, although the word *ṛṣi* is well-known in the sense of those who have seen the mantras, he shows that here it refers to those recited in the *pravara* section and so forth. Regarding the explanation of Vasiṣṭha: the mantra seen by Vasiṣṭha is figuratively called "Vasiṣṭha."
The suffix *aṇ* in *vāsiṣṭhī* is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhavārthe*); the particle *eva* is for the purpose of indicating that all statements are restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇatva*).
The suffix ṣṭhan is applied after the word *pauroḍāśa* to form a derivative meaning "made from that. (Pāṇini 4.3.70)

"Puroḍāśas are balls of flour. [The word *puroḍāśa* is derived as follows: from the root *dāśṛ* in the sense of "giving," with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive/objective sense; thus, *puroḍāśāḥ* means "those which are given (*dāśyante*) or offered (*dīyante*) before (*puras*). The compound is formed according to the rule for *pṛṣodarādi* words, and the letter *da* is changed to *ḍa*. By this, he states that the word *puroḍāśa* denotes a physical form (*ākṛti*), and is not based on an unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭanimitta*) like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) or the Āhavanīya fire. "The mantra is the purifier (*saṃskāraka*) of them" refers to such mantras as "Thou art the head of Makha. The mantra associated with the *puroḍāśa* is called "the *puroḍāśa* [mantra]. For it is the mantra alone that must be explained, not the *puroḍāśa* itself.
In Vedic (chandasa), when the suffixes ya and aṇ follow, [the substitution of vṛddhi for the first vowel of the stem does not take place].

In this context, although there are two meanings for *bhava* and two suffixes (*yad* and *aṇ*), they do not correspond respectively [to those meanings]. This is because the suffixes *yad* and *aṇ* apply both to the sense "in the explanation of that" (*tasya vyākhyāne*) and to the sense "occurring therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), as they are taken together in a collective sense. Regarding the phrase "when *ṭhak* is applicable after a word ending in two syllables": the meaning is that *ṭhak* would be applicable by the subsequent rule due to the mention of "two syllables" (*dvyac*).
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [words ending in] *dvyañ*, *aja*, *brāhmaṇa*, *arka*, *prathama*, *adhvara*, *puraścaraṇa*, *nāman*, and *ākhyāta*. (Pāṇini 4.3.72)

Regarding the phrase "an exception to *aṇ*": by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is intended. In that regard, in the case of words ending in *ṛk* and those with two syllables, it is an exception to *aṇ*. Furthermore, the word *puraścaraṇa*, being formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*, has its middle vowel acute (udātta) due to the accentuation of the original form of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*). Since the suffix *as* is produced from a word ending in the locative case, the word *puras* functions as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*); alternatively, by the rule "indeclinables such as *puras* are *gatis*," it is a *gati*. Therefore, in this case too, it is specifically an exception to *aṇ*. Among the *brāhmaṇa*-class words which have the acute accent on the final syllable, it is an exception to *ṭhañ*; among those ending in the vowel *ṛ*, it is also an exception to *aṇ*.

However, among those [words] that have many syllables and are oxytone (antodātta), this [suffix] *ṭhañ* supersedes [the previous rule] due to its posteriority. The mention of both "noun" (*nāman*) and "verb" (*ākhyāta*) is for the purpose of including both compounds and their separated forms; the mention of "separated form" (*vigṛhīta*) is for the sake of the verb, whereas for words ending in "noun" (*nāman*), the desired result is already established simply by virtue of having two syllables.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after words such as *ṛgayanā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.73)

Regarding the phrase "of *ṭhañ* and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *ṭhak* and *cha* is intended. Among these, from the words *vidyā*, *nyāya*, and *śikṣā*, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṭhak*, which is characterized by having two syllables; from the word *vyākaraṇa*, it is an exception to *cha*, because it is a *vṛddha* [stem]; the remaining [stems] have many vowels (*bahvac*) and are oxytone (*antodātta*), and for them, the suffix is *añ*.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? Could it not simply be stated that [the suffix] is applied to words such as *ṛgayaṇa* according to the rule already prescribed? By the authority of the statement itself, that which is prescribed but would not otherwise apply—because it is barred by another suffix—will indeed be this *aṇ*. To this he replies: "The mention of *aṇ*. If the mention of *aṇ* were absent, then in the case of a polysyllabic word with a *vṛddhi* vowel in the penultimate syllable and an acute accent on the final syllable, such as *vāstuvidyā*, the suffix *cha* (which would replace *ṭhañ*) would be barred; however, due to the repeated statement, *cha* alone would apply. But because of the mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs.

Regarding the term *ṛgayanam*: the substitution of *ṇ* (as in *ṛg-ayana*) does not occur because of the prohibition "not after [a word ending in] *ag*" in the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyāmagaḥ*. Furthermore, the word *ayana* is derived in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), and by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), it refers to the treatise; it is oxytone (*antodātta*) according to the rule *ano bhāvakarmavacane*. The word *padavyākhyāna* is oxytone according to the rule *manktinvyākhyāna*. The word *chandomāna* has been explained by the term *ṛgayanam*; it is oxytone by the accentual rule for *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*) applied to the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

The word *chandoviciti* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of the suffix *ktin*. The word *punarukta* [is accented] by the rule for *athādi* compounds. The word *nirukta* [is accented] by the rule "in a technical name (*saṃjñā*), except for *anācita* and others. The word *nigama* is a root-stem ending in *gha*, prescribed as *antodātta* by the rule beginning with *gocara*. The words *vāstuvidyā*, *kṣattravidyā*, and *aṅgavidyā* [are accented] by the accent of compounds. The words *utpāta* and *utpāda* [are accented] by the rule for *athādi* compounds. The word *saṃvatsara* has its final syllable accented by the rules "the suffix *saran* after the root *aś*" and "the suffix *cid* after the root *vas* preceded by *sam*."

The words *muhūrta* and *nimitta* [have their accent] by the rule for the accent of nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*). From the root *sad* preceded by the prefixes *upa* and *ni*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus the word *upaniṣad* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by the rule for the accent of primary derivatives (*kṛt-svara*).
The suffix *tasi* is applied in the sense of "come from that. (Pāṇini 4.3.74)

The word "tataḥ" (from that) refers here to that which is intended as the primary *apādāna* (ablative point of departure), precisely because it is the primary one. However, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna* applies even to that which is secondary (*gauṇa*), for in the section dealing with grammatical factors (*kāraka*), no distinction between the primary and the secondary is observed.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words ending in] *ṭhak*, *āyasthāna*, and [the rest of the group]. (Pāṇini 4.3.75)
"Āya" means the portion to be taken by the owner; it is so called because the owner comes toward it, or because it comes toward the owners.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words] such as *śuṇḍika*.

The rule "āyasthānaṭhaka" is an exception (*apavāda*). This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it is also an exception to the suffix *cha* [prescribed] by the rule "kṛkaṇaparṇādbhāradvāje. It is also an exception to the suffix *vuñ* [prescribed] by the rule "dhūmādibhyaśchaḥ" for the word *tīrtha*. It is also an exception to the suffix *yañ* [prescribed] by the rule "utsādibhyo 'ñ" for the word *udapāna*.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of *aṇ*? Why not simply say that [the suffix] after *śiṇḍika* and so on is "as prescribed"? For by the force of the statement itself, that which is prescribed but does not otherwise apply—because it has been superseded by another [suffix]—will indeed be *aṇ*. To this he replies: "The mention of *aṇ*. The word *udapāna* is read here, and it belongs to the *utsādi* group. If the mention of *aṇ* were absent, then, having superseded the *ṭhak* of *āyasthāna*, the suffix would be only *añ* by the rule "*utsādibhyo 'ñ*". But because of the mention of *aṇ*, it becomes *aṇ* alone.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words denoting a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or a relationship through the womb (*yoni*).
Regarding the term *vidyāyonikṛta*: since its meaning is already conveyed by the bahuvrīhi compound, the word *kṛta* is not employed.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the word *ṛtaṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.78)

In these examples, [the rule] "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" applies. Thus, for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), this suffix should have been prescribed as *kañ*; however, it was not done in that way.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *pitṛ*. (Pāṇini 4.3.79)
Regarding *pitrya*: [the substitution of] *rīṅ* for *ṛt* [is applied], and [the elision of] *y* [follows] by the rule "and that which ends in *i*" (*yasyeti ca*).
[The suffix *yañ* is applied] after a *gotra* [name], as if it were a numerical marker (*aṅka*). 4.3.80.

By the mention of "in the *aṅka*," the general sense of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*) is indicated. How can a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) be resorted to when the primary sense is possible? In this matter, the commentary is the refuge. Another says: what is seen in the *aṅka* is extended [by analogy], but it is not prescribed directly for the *aṅka*. Since the suffix *vuñ* in the rule "from *gotra* and *caraṇa*, *vuñ*" is also seen in the *aṅka*—even though it is prescribed in the general sense of "this belongs to that" for cases other than those beginning with *añ*—there is an extension of that as well. Thus, we have *aupagavakam*.

The examples for *vuñ* are: *vaidam*, *gārgyam*, and *dākṣam*. But for *aṇ*, they are: *vaidam*, *gārgyam*, and *dākṣam*. The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of complete similarity, as in the rules "after words denoting time, [the suffix] is like *bhava*" and "after words denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), [the suffix] is like *dharma*."
After the word *hetu* and words denoting humans, the suffix *rūpya* is optionally applied [to form a noun of agency].

Regarding the term *samādāgatam*: the meaning is "come for the sake of [that] cause. In that case, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be required by the rule for the "cause" (*hetau*). This is established by way of an indicator (*jñāpaka*); namely, the fact that [Pāṇini] prescribes an affix after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) as the cause indicates that the fifth case occurs when there is a cause. This is not a valid indicator. For where there is the fifth case in the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe*, this [usage of *samādāgatam*] might be intended for that purpose—as in *jāḍyād āgataḥ* ("come because of dullness"). Therefore, in the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe*, by means of a separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) through the word *vibhāṣā*, the fifth case occurs even after words that do not denote a quality (*aguṇavacana*).
And the suffix *mayaṭ* [is used in the sense of "made of" or "consisting of"]. 4.3.82.

The purpose of the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is to prevent [the application of] *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence in order). By using the term *anyatarasyām* in the sense of an option (*vikalpa*), the non-occurrence of the suffixes *-rūpya* and *-mayaṭ* is established as an alternative; in the absence of those, the suffix is obtained by the rule of one's own grammatical system itself. Therefore, since this [rule] prescribes only *-rūpya* and *-mayaṭ*, the intention is that *yathāsaṃkhya* would indeed apply if there were no *yogavibhāga*.
The suffix *prabhavati* [is applied]. 4.3.83.

Regarding the word "prākāśate" (it shines forth): the root *prabhavati* (to originate) is not taken here in the sense of "origination," because that meaning is already covered by the expression "born therein" (*tatra jātaḥ*).
The suffix *añ* is applied after [the word] *vidūra*.

He says, "This explanation is incorrect," beginning with "But surely... [regarding] *vālavāya* and *vidūra*. The word *vālavāya* gives rise to the suffix (*pratyaya*), while *vidūra* undergoes substitution (*ādeśa*). However, in the Sūtra only the substitute (*ādeśa*) is mentioned; therefore, the corresponding base (*sthānin*), the word *vālavāya*, is implied, just as in the case of *śiva* and others, where by the two substitutes *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* being taught, the word *viśravas* is understood. Or rather, it means that *vidūra* itself is the base: the word *vidūra* denotes both a city and a mountain, and that very word is the base here.

"If one should say, 'It is not so there,'" the word *cet* (if) here expresses dissatisfaction. If one should say that the word *vidūra*, which denotes a mountain, is not well-known [in that sense], he would employ it through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), as in the case of *jitvarī*. Just as merchants alone use the term *jitvarī* for Vārāṇasī for the sake of auspiciousness, so too do grammarians alone employ *bālavāya* as a metaphor for *vidūra*. The meaning is that even a conventional usage (*prasiddhi*) occurs with reference to specific persons. [The rule] "In the sense of 'going to that,' [the suffix *cha* is applied after words denoting] a path or a messenger" (Pāṇini 4.3.85).

The root *gam* (to go) occurs in the sense of movement toward an attainment (*prāpti*), and since there is no movement in a path, he says "in those situated therein" (*tatstheṣu*) to indicate that the movement residing in the person is metaphorically attributed to the path. Alternatively (*athavā*), the root *gam* also occurs in the sense of attainment, as in the expression "gone to godhood" (*devabhūyaṃ gataḥ*).
The word *abhiniṣkrāmati* [governs the accusative case] when it means "to go out through a gate. || 4.3.86 ||

Regarding the phrase "the door in the act of going out": by this he means that when those [senses] situated therein go out, because the door serves as their instrument (*karaṇa*), it is said that "the door itself goes out" through the superimposition [of the action] upon it. It was not stated that "the going out is the door"; for since there is the governing rule of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) in the word *tad* (in the expression *tad dvāram*), otherwise the genitive case characterized by its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛd-yoga-lakṣaṇā*) would result.
[The suffix -aṇ] is applied to a word when it denotes a treatise composed concerning that [subject]. 4.3.87.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of narratives" (*ākhyāyikābhyaḥ*): this is the dative case used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). A narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) is a specific type of prose composition; the meaning is that the suffix which has been produced to denote it is frequently elided (*lup*). Nor need this be explicitly stated, because through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the word for the object itself is obtained, and since the suffix is characterized by denotation, it is produced in some cases and not in others.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *śiśukranda*, *yamasabha*, *dvandva*, *indrajana*, *nāndī*, and others.

The group beginning with *indrajana* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). By this, the expression "we shall explain the chapter on forbidden foods" (*viruddhabhojanīyam adhyāyaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*) is established.
That [suffix] denotes his residence. 4.3.89.

In this context, for one whose residence is Srughna, he is "one who exists in Srughna" (*srughne bhavati*); thus, [the designation] is already established by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ*. However, it is mentioned separately because of the difference in the meaning of the words.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *abhijana*. 4.3.90.

"Lineage (*abhijana*) means former relatives (*pūrvabāndhava*). This is because one is born from them; "former relatives" refers to ancestors such as fathers and so forth. The word *bandhu* belongs to the *prajñādi* group [of suffixes]. Thus, by virtue of that connection, there is also a substitution of the term for the place. Just as the word "staff" (*yaṣṭi*) is applied to a person due to his connection with a staff, so too is the word "lineage" (*abhijana*) applied to a region. "What, then, is this region? To this he says: "In which... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "that here" (*tadiha*), the word "that" (*tat*) is used to introduce the statement.

But how can there be a derivative suffix from a secondary sense when the primary sense of "noble lineage" (*abhijana*) is possible? To this he says: "due to the proximity of the word 'residence' (*nivāsa*). This means that because the word for residence—which is proximate, that is, immediately adjacent—qualifies the noble lineage. For here, when the noble lineage is qualified by the residence as "that noble lineage which is [located] in the residence," the suffix is applied only to that which denotes a place.

"What is the distinction between *nivāsa* (residence) and *abhijana* (ancestral home)? The meaning is that there is no distinction at all, since *abhijana* is also understood as being a place of residence. Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): that where one resides oneself is one's *nivāsa*; whereas that where one's ancestors, such as one's father and so forth, have dwelt is one's *abhijana*.
[Pāṇini 4.3.91: *āyudhajīvibhyaścha parvate*]

The phrase "āyudhajīvibhyaḥ" (from those who live by weapons) is in the dative case to express purpose (*tādarthye*), and so forth. However, if "āyudhajīvibhyaḥ" were in the ablative case, it would have to be explained as an ablative used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (as in "from a mountain"). In that case, the meaning would be: "When 'those who live by weapons' are the source and 'the mountain' is the intended object, the suffix *cha* occurs when the mountain is to be expressed. In that scenario, the governing rule "so'bhijanaḥ" (that [place] is his native land) would be contradicted.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after [words beginning with] *śaṇḍika* and others.

"An exception (*apavāda*) to [the suffixes] *aṇ* and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *cha* and others are included. In that regard, if words such as *śaṇḍika* denote mountains (*parvata*), then by the preceding rule, *cha* would be applicable. If, however, they denote regions (*janapada*), then by the rule "also after a non-*vṛddha* [stem] when the sense is plural," *vuñ* would be applicable. From the word *śaṇḍika*, since it has a *ka* as its penultimate letter (*kopadha*), *aṇ* would be applicable.
The suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied after [place names] such as Sindhu and Takṣaśilā.

Regarding the phrase "Sindhuvarṇu and the others": by the word "and the others" (prabhṛti), Madhumat, Kamboja, Śālva, Kaśmīra, and Gandhāra are included. In the case of the four beginning with Kiṣkindha, since the suffix *vuñ* would have applied by the rule "even after a non-vṛddha [stem]," this specific statement is made. Furthermore, although the suffix *cha* would have applied to Vṛddha stems such as Takṣaśilā, and the suffix *aṇ* would have applied to the remaining stems by the rule "before *prāgdīvyat*, the suffix *aṇ*," [these specific suffixes are prescribed].
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [words denoting] non-minds (*acitta*), as well as those not restricted by place or time (*adeśakāla*).

Regarding the term *acittavācin* (denoting that which is not the mind): it does not denote its own form (*svarūpa*), because of the prohibition of [specifying] place and time. Due to its association with those [two], there is also no denotation of the own form of place and time.
The suffix *vun* is applied after the words *vāsudeva* and *arjuna*.

Regarding the objection concerning *chāṇoḥ*: he will state that "the word *vāsudeva* is a proper name" (*saṃjñā*); therefore, in that case, the suffix *vuñ* does not apply to the subsequent [element]. As for the word *arjuna*, whether it denotes a specific type of tree or a specific type of warrior (*varṇa*), the suffix *vuñ* does not apply there either. The point is that even when it denotes a *kṣatriya*, because of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *vuñ* simply does not apply.

Regarding the passage beginning with "nanu ca" (But surely...): [the word *Vāsudeva*] is the offspring of Vasudeva, formed by the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca. And as for the phrase "na cātra" (And not here): there is no distinction regarding the *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], since it was already present previously. As for the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) based on the rule "vṛddhinimittasya," that too does not apply here because of the rule "na kopadhāyāḥ" (not when *ka* is the penultimate letter). This is a name of a specific deity; it is a designation for the Supreme Self (paramātman) based on the etymology "in whom everything dwells. It is not a name of a Kṣatriya. This is merely an illustration; one should also understand that it is not a name of a lineage (*gotra*).

He demonstrates another incidental purpose for the inclusion of Vāsudeva: namely, the rules "that which begins with *aja* and ends in *at*" and "that which has fewer syllables. The particle *iti* is connected to each [rule]. Although this is what is being made known, nevertheless, because of the specific mention in the rule "of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when not followed by a *taddhita* suffix," there are instances where it occurs otherwise as well.
The suffix *vuñ* is frequently applied after words denoting a *gotra* (clan) or a *kṣatriya* (warrior lineage).

Regarding the phrase *gotrakṣatriyākhyebhyaḥ*: the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *khyā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, because it belongs to the *mūlavibhujādi* class. Regarding the mention of *ākhyā* (designation): the meaning is that the root *khyā* preceded by *ā* is what is being referred to. Regarding the expression *yathākathaṃcit* (in whatever way): the meaning is that this [suffix] should not apply to those words which, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *kṣatriya*, have their application in the sense of a *kṣatriya*, such as in "a brave man is a *kṣatriya*" (*śūraḥ kṣattriyaḥ*). Thus, the suffix should not occur in such cases.

In the plural number, for words denoting inhabitants of a country that have the same form as the word denoting the country itself, the rules for the country-name apply to all [the inhabitants]. 4.3.100.

Regarding "janapadinām," which means words denoting a country; "janapadavat" means like words denoting a country; "janapadena" means by a word denoting a country; "samānaśabdānām" means having identical forms; and "bahuvacane" means when expressing a plurality of objects. This same meaning applies to the term *vṛtti* as well—namely, the suffix (*pratyaya*) and the base (*prakṛti*). By this, the meaning of the entire word is shown. "Janapadinaḥ" means the lords of the country; thus, he demonstrates the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) in the sense of a relationship between owner and owned.

With the passage beginning "The Aṅgas are a country" (*aṅgā janapadā*), he explains the manner of application in the example; with "in the same way" (*tadvat*), however, he provides the formal illustration (*udāharaṇa*). In all cases where there are many referents, when the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule "dvyañmagadha... has been elided by the rule "tadrājasya bahuṣu," and when the suffix *vuñ* is intended for the plural because the base is a homogeneous word that is not *vṛddha*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied after the word *āṅga* by virtue of the statement "gotre 'lug aci. Thus, we have "Pañcāla brahmins" (*pañcālā brāhmaṇāḥ*). Because of the metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) based on non-difference, the word *pañcāla* applies to the brahmins; since there is no extension [of the suffix] in that case, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs.

"Regarding the phrase 'the mention of "all" (sarva),' etc.: if the mention of 'all' were not made, then because of its predominance, only the suffix (*pratyaya*) would be extended (*atideśa*), and not the base (*prakṛti*). However, the mention of the word *vat* is for the purpose that, when certain people belong to certain regions (*janapada*), the suffix belonging to those very regions should apply to them, and not a suffix belonging to another region. But by this [mention of *vat* alone], the extension of the base is not obtained; therefore, the mention of 'all' is made for that purpose. And the reading is: 'and it applies to two or one.'"

And that extension by nature (*prakṛtyatideśa*) necessitates the inclusion of the term *sarva* for the dual and singular, but not for the plural; for in that case, the form is not different. As it has been said: "In the plural, [the rule applies] to words that are identical. However, in the dual and singular, the form denoting a country (*janapada*) is *vṛddha*, whereas the form denoting a country is *avṛddha*; thus, the purpose of including *sarva* is precisely in those cases. Whether the reading is *atideśaḥ prayojayati* or *atideśaṃ prayojayati*, we do not perceive a correct meaning [in either].

Regarding the phrase "in cases where there is an occasion for Vṛddhi," and so forth: for in those instances, even though the original form (*prakṛti*) is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), it must again undergo Vṛddhi; thus, there is no distinction [between the two]. As for the question, "What is the difference between *madravṛjyoḥ*?"—it is because Vṛddhi is impossible in that case. Regarding the expression "when the reduction of the original form has been made": "reduction" (*nirhrāsa*) means decrease, that is, diminution. Examples are *mādrakaḥ* and *vārjikaḥ*. However, if there were no extension of the original form, the forms would have been *mādrakakaḥ* and *vārjyakaḥ*.

"Regarding the mention of the plural number (*bahuvacanagrahaṇa*), etc.: it is for the purpose of demonstrating—that is, indicating—the definition of the scope of what constitutes 'identity of word-form' (*samānaśabdatā*). For otherwise: if the mention of the plural were not made, then [the rule would apply] only where; that is, only where the *tadrāja* suffix has been elided (*luk*) in the plural, would there be identity of word-form. It would not apply in the singular or dual, because in those cases, due to the absence of elision (*lugabhāva*), there is an absence of identity of word-form."

Now, one might object: "Is not the inclusion of the word *sarva* (all) intended for the purpose of extending the original rule (*prakṛty-atideśa*), and since it has been stated that this applies even to the dual and singular, why would it not apply to the dual and singular? Therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of *sarva*, the extension of identical words is established here in all instances. To ensure the clear understanding of this very point, the term *bahuvacane* (in the plural) has been employed as an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
That which has been stated by him [is expressed] with the suffix *tena*. (Pāṇini 4.3.101)

"Proclaimed with excellence" (*prakarṣeṇoktam*) means that it was not previously revealed through teaching or by the explanation of its meaning. By the inclusion of the word "excellence" (*prakarṣeṇa*), even though the *Kāṭhaka* and other texts may be recited by Devadatta and others in every village, no suffix is applied [to those names]. However, this is not the case for the word *kṛta*. The intention is that the root *vac*, preceded by the prefix *pra*, also functions in the sense of "making" (*karaṇa*).

*Mādhuraḥ* means "one who exists in Madhurā. From that [word], although the suffix *cha* would have been expected by the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.114], the suffix *aṇ* is applied because the mention of *aṇ* in the rule *kalāpino 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.108) is intended to provide an additional prescription. Regarding *pāṇinīyam*: that which was composed by Pāṇini himself or by another [on his behalf] is so called.
The suffix *chaṇ* is applied after the words *tittiri*, *varata*, *tantu*, *khaṇḍika*, and *ukha*.

"In the Veda (chandas), this [suffix] is also desired. This means that it occurs when the Veda is the expressed object. It does not occur in the case of "a verse (śloka) proclaimed by Tittiri. They say that it is not only the suffix *chaṇ* that is absent, but the suffix *aṇ* as well, due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). But how can it be obtained in the Veda even though it is merely desired? To this he says: "From Śaunaka and others.
By the rule "from the sages Kāśyapa and Kauśika, the suffix *ṇini*," [the suffix *ṇini* is applied].

The letter *ṇ* [in the suffix] is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* in subsequent cases; however, in this instance, since *vṛddhi* is already established by the preceding rule, it serves no purpose here. Furthermore, as for the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) based on the rule "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause," that too is not a requirement, because a derivative ending in *ṇin* refers to one who studies or knows, and thus does not apply to the feminine. Even if it were to apply, the desired form is established by the rule "and of a genus" (*jāteśca*), since [the term] is a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being a *caraṇa* (Vedic school). [This applies] to that as well.

How is it that the *kalpa* comes under the scope [of the term *chandas*] when it is stated [in Pāṇini 4.2.66] "for the *chandasaḥ* and the *brāhmaṇāni*"? To this he says: "after Śaunaka and others. But even if that [term *chandasaḥ*] is carried over there, this *yoga* does not make the *kalpa* a *chandas*, nor a *brāhmaṇa*. Therefore he says: "and of those prescribed under the heading of *chandas*."

In the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni*, the term *chandas* (Vedic meters) is marked with the *svarita* accent; since an *adhikāra* (governing heading) is understood through the *svarita*, this [suffix] *ṇini* also falls within the scope of that [heading] because it occurs in the middle of the section on *chandas*. As for the explanation that the particle *ca* in *chandobrāhmaṇāni* has the sense of an inclusive "and so forth" (*ādi*)—thereby establishing that [the suffix applies to] the *kalpa*s and other such texts—that should be regarded as a different method. [The phrase] "by the contemporary Gotrakāśyapa" is used because he is not a seer (*ṛṣi*), as he is not a seer of mantras.
And [the suffix ṇini is applied] after the words *kalāpin* and *vaiśampāyana*, when they denote pupils. 4.3.104.

"Of the Kalāpy-antevāsins," and so forth. In the Sūtra, however, the designation is based on the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of them as non-different [from their teacher]. "The Kalāpy-antevāsins are four," and so forth. Now, one might object: since the conventional usage of the term "student" (*śiṣya*) is observed in the world even for the disciples of disciples, how can there be such a restriction that they are only this many? To this he replies: "those who perform [the action] directly" (*pratyakṣakāriṇaḥ*). The root *kṛ* expresses action in general, but here, by virtue of the context and so forth, it refers specifically to study. [He states] "because of the mention of Kalāpin and Khāṇḍāyana. He explains this very point with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

Kālāpin was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana; if pupils of pupils were also to be included, then the mention of Kālāpin would be redundant, as it would already be established by the rule "from the pupils of Vaiśampāyana," since the pupils of Kālāpin are also pupils of Vaiśampāyana.

Likewise, there is Kaṭha, the pupil of Vaiśampāyana, and Khāṇḍāyana, the pupil of Kaṭha. In that case, even if those separated by an intermediate link were included, since [the status of] being a pupil of Vaiśampāyana would already be established for Śaunaka and others by this very rule, the inclusion of the word "Khāṇḍāyana" among them would be redundant. In the examples, the scope is determined by the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni* (A 4.2.66), and the suffix denoting the student is elided by the rule *proktālluk* (A 4.2.64).

Regarding the phrase "with the fourth, *ulapa*": the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). This [term] *kālāpaka* belongs to the *kalāpin*; it is formed with the suffix *vuñ* according to the rule "from *gotra* and *caraṇa*. In that context, the word "in the sense of *dharma* and *āmnāya*" is recited; therefore, here the usage is for a group of disciples (*śiṣyasamūha*) based on a comparison. Regarding "the *ālambi* and the *caraka* of the Easterners" (*prācām*): there was a disciple of *Caraka* born in the eastern region named *Ālambi*. Likewise, both *Phāliṅgika* and *Kalmāṣa* belong only to the Easterners; thus these three are called Easterners. Regarding "of the *Kaṭha* and the *Kalāpin*": [this refers to their respective schools].
The elision (*luk*) is prescribed [for the suffix] after *Kaṭha* by the rule "kaṭhacarakālluk"; likewise, the *aṇ* suffix is prescribed after the word *Kalāpin* by the rule "kalāpino'ṇ."
In the case of Brāhmaṇas and Kalpas proclaimed in the Purāṇas. (Pāṇini 4.3.105)
"Bhāllavinaḥ," and so forth: the suffix *ṇini* is applied after these—namely, *bhallu*, *śāṭyāyana*, *aitareya*, *piṅga*, *aruṇa*, and *parāji*.

The words *yajñavalkya* and *aśmaratha* belong to the *kaṇvādi* group; even though they end in the suffix *yañ*, there is elision of the *ya* by the rule "āpatyasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.151). Now, one might object: "But aren't the works of Yājñavalkya and others also indeed proclaimed by ancient sages (*purāṇaproktāni*), since they are contemporary with other Brāhmaṇas such as the Śāṭyāyanaka? To this he says: "For Yājñavalkya and others... [The word] *ākhyānāni* refers to the *Mahābhārata* and similar texts. The meaning is that whether the usage [of the name] is based on those [texts] or otherwise is irrelevant. Why, then, would these not be the objects [of the rule]?

The question concerns the scope of Yājñavalkya and others; the sense is that [the designation *chandas*] would apply there because, in the rule "chandobrāhmaṇāni ca," no specific qualification such as "proclaimed by ancient seers" (*purāṇaproktatva*) is relied upon. Regarding the term "pratipada": this is obtained through the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by its own form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*). And it is precisely for this purpose that the word "brāhmaṇa" is included there, since [the status of being *chandas*] would already be established by the very fact of being *chandas*.

If that is so, why does [the suffix] not occur in *kalpa* as it does in *kāśyapinaḥ* and *kauśikinaḥ*? To this he says: "Or rather, this [is not the case]. The meaning is that while it is appropriate there—because that rule (*yoga*) continues to apply under the heading of *chandas*—this [word *kalpa*] is not like that, and thus its scope does not extend to *kalpa* either. Nor is there an absolute prohibition.

Although the form [is] already established by the very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in "siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandhaiś-ca," the indicators "śuṣaḥ kaḥ" and "paco vaḥ" show that "even irregular derivations (*nipātanas*) are subverters [of other rules]. However, as it stands in the *Bhāṣya* on the *sarvādi* sūtra, it is established that "even irregular derivations that have other purposes are indeed subverters."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *kalāpin*.

"It should be stated exactly as prescribed. The intention here is that, by the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), that very suffix *aṇ* which is prescribed but does not otherwise apply will indeed occur. Regarding the phrase "these and others" (*evamādīni*): by the word "others" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Maudas, Paippalādas, and Śākalas is intended. In this case, after the words *muda*, *pippalāda*, and *śākalya*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇini* [prescribed] by the rule "in the case of those proclaimed in ancient times" (*purāṇaprokteṣu*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *pārāśarya* and *śilālin* to form the names of a mendicant and a dramatic manual, respectively. (Pāṇini 4.3.110)

"For that purpose, the mention of *chandas* (Vedic meter) must be understood as continuing [from the previous rule]. Now, one might ask: "Even if that continues, how can the *bhikṣusūtra* and the *naṭasūtra* possess the status of *chandas*? To this he says: "And by the attribution of qualities (*guṇakalpanayā*). A quality (*guṇa*) is the property that serves as the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), such as obedience to teachers (*guruśuśrūṣaṇa*) and so forth; the attribution based on that is "the attribution of qualities. Regarding the term *pārāśariṇaḥ*: the elision of *y* is as before. Regarding *śailālinaḥ*: [one who] "adorns with stones" (*śilām ālute*) is a *śilālī*. From the root *ala-* in the sense of "adornment," "sufficiency," or "prohibition" (*alaṃ bhūṣaṇaparyāptivāraṇeṣu*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*supyajātau ṇiniḥ*). Then, in this *ṇini*-suffix, there is the elision of the *ṭi* vowel.

Regarding *pārāśara*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.114 (*kaṇvādibhyo gotre*). Regarding *śailāla*: when the general suffix *aṇ* is applied, the elision of the final syllable occurs by the rule "the elision of the *ṭi* of *sabrahmacārin*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.174).
The suffix *tena* [is used] in the sense of "in one direction" (*ekadik*). Pāṇini 4.3.112.
Regarding "saudāmanī": the term "an" indicates the absence of sandhi (prakṛtibhāva). Sudāman and others are specific names of mountains.
And [the suffix] *tasi* [is applied after a word ending in the locative case]. 4.3.113.

Because it is listed among the *svarādi* group, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). It should be understood that even though this word is prescribed for that very same meaning, its lack of gender and number is inherent to its nature.
In the case of "upajñāta" (invented/discovered), [the sixth case ending is used]. 4.3.115.

"Upajñāta" means known without instruction; the sense is that the root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *upa-* is well-established in that sense. "Akālakam" means devoid of technical rules regarding time, such as those beginning with "from improper rising. "Gurulāghavam" is a treatise on meaning (*artha-śāstra*) wherein the heaviness or lightness of methods is considered. That in which a conventional term (*saṅketa-śabda*) is employed—such as "vṛt" in Pāṇini's system—is called *duṣkaraṇa-vyākaraṇa*; others call it the *kāma-śāstra*.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word denoting a work when it signifies "composed by. (Pāṇini 4.3.116)

The sūtras beginning with "tittirivaratantu" are not recited in this section. For Tittiri and the others are the expounders of the Vedas (chandas), not their authors; for the Vedas are eternal and are not created by anyone.
[The suffix *khañ* is applied] after [a word ending in the sixth case] when it signifies a name (*saṃjñā*). (Pāṇini 4.3.117)
This has no meaning as a literal composition.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *kṣudrā*, *bhramara*, and *vaṭara*. (Pāṇini 4.3.119)

Regarding the phrase "an exception to *aṇ*": this was stated because of its predominance, for the suffix *cha* would otherwise apply after the word *pādapa*. Others, however, read the word *padapa* in place of *pādapa*.
This belongs to him. (Pāṇini 4.3.120)

He recalls the very meaning already stated in the rule *tasyāpatyam* with the words "of the base and the affix," and so forth. In the base (*prakṛti*), only the sense of the genitive case is intended; in the meaning of the affix (*pratyayārtha*) as well, only that which is related to it [is intended], because the genitive occurs in connection with it. When that is to be expressed, the affix is employed. He shows what is excluded by the word *mātra* (only) with the words "whatever else. The word *idam* (this) expresses what is perceptible, while the word *tat* (that) expresses what is remote from perception. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the quality of denoting a universal (*sāmānyābhidhāyitva*) is included.
"All that is not intended to be expressed. The reason for this has already been stated in the rule *tasyāpatyam* ("his offspring").

Regarding *vahes-tuḥ*: there is a general inclusion of both the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*. Regarding *sāvahitram*: because the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth are considered *asiddha*, when *iṭ* is first applied here, those substitutions do not take place due to the absence of their cause.

"Agnīdh": [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *indh* (to kindle) with the prefix *agni*, resulting in *agnīdh*. He is a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). In the phrase "you are addressed as *agnīdh*," the shortening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). "Śaraṇam" means a house or a place; that place where the *āgnīdhrīya* altar (*dhiṣṇya*) is located is called the *āgnīdhra*. However, the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* apply this term to the priest himself by virtue of his being situated there—just as one says "the platforms are shouting"—as seen in the passage: "The *āgnīdhra* should respond to the call for the *potṛ* and the *brahmā* at the *āgnīdhra*."

And then they take refuge [in it] with the suffix *cha*, because of the statement regarding the refuge: "having gone around the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth to the north of the *āgnīdhrīya* fire. Regarding the term *samidhām-ādhāne*: that by which the fire is kindled is a *samit*; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule beginning with *sampadādi*. That *ṛc* verse by which the *samit* is placed upon the fire is a *sāmidhenī*; the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added because of the presence of the suffix *ṣit*, and there is the elision of *ya* according to the rule *halas-taddhitasya*.
[The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ratha*] and others. 4.3.121.

It is intended that the term *rathāṅga* (chariot-part) itself [denotes the chariot]. As for the usage of *rathya* as "one who carries a chariot" (*voḍhṛ*), that should be understood as falling under the rule *tadvahati rathayugaprāsaṅgam*. One might argue: "Let this very term *rathya* be intended even for the carrier; do not include the mention of 'chariot' (*ratha*) in the rule *tadvahati*. This cannot be so; for in the case of *dvirathya*, meaning "one who carries two chariots," the elision (*luk*) of the secondary suffix (*prāgdīvyatīya*) would apply by the rule *dvigorluganapatye*.
However, when it refers to a part belonging to two chariots, the form remains simply *dviratha*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after [a word ending in] *pattra* when it occurs as the first member [of a compound].

That by which one flies is a *pattra*; [the suffix] *ṣṭran* is applied according to the rule "after *dāman*, *ni*, and *śas*, etc. A chariot yoked with horses is an *aśvaratha*; in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the meaning of "yoked" is understood through the inherent nature of the formation. Its limb is the *āśvaratha*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the words *pattra*, *adhvaryu*, and *pariṣad*.
In this context, "pada" signifies the meaning, while the other two [terms] signify their own forms; and here, the commentary is the authority.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied after a copulative compound (*dvandva*) to denote enmity or sexual union. Pāṇini 4.3.125.
