*Vaira* means hostility; it is so called because it belongs to heroes (*vīra*). *Maithunikā* refers to the act of pairing; the suffix *-vuñ* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *manojña*. *Mithuna* means a husband and wife, and *karma* means the performance of an action. In the term *bābhravaśālaṅkāyanikā*, the word ending in *-vuñ* naturally functions as a feminine noun.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied [to form patronymics] after words denoting a lineage (*gotra*) and a branch of learning (*caraṇa*). Pāṇini 4.3.126.

The prescription of *vuñ* for *vun* in the case of non-*vṛddha* [words] is for the sake of *vṛddhi*. In the case of *vṛddha* [words], there is no difference between *vun* and *vuñ*: the form is the same and the accent is the same; furthermore, the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* [substitution] by the rule "not after a word ending in *ka*" applies to both.
The suffix *maṇ* is applied after [stems ending in] *añ*, *yañ*, and *iñ* when they denote characteristics of the Saṅgha.

"It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding *yuñ* [sūtra]. The intention is that because the term "clan" (*gotra*) is understood to carry over, the suffixes denoting clans that begin with vowels (*ajādīnām*) are what are included here.

Regarding the statement "the mention of *ghoṣa* must be made here": *ghoṣa* means a cowherd settlement (*ābhīrasthāna*); the purpose is so that the suffix may also apply there. He states another incidental purpose for the mention of *ghoṣa*: "on account of that disparity."

Now, what is the distinction between *aṅka* and *lakṣaṇa*? The meaning is that there is no distinction at all, because they are listed as synonyms in the *Nighaṇṭus*. [The opponent asks: "Should a distinction be accepted here on the strength of their being mentioned separately? To this he replies: "*Lakṣaṇaṃ lakṣyasyaiva*" (the mark belongs only to that which is marked). The word *svam* means "one's own" or "related. *Baidīvidyaḥ* means one who possesses the knowledge (*vidyā*) that is unique to the Baidas.
Or [the suffix ṭhak is applied] after the word śākala. 4.3.128.
Regarding the objection that this is a *vuñ* suffix: since the word *śākala* is a name of a Vedic school (*caraṇa*), he demonstrates this by stating, "proclaimed by Śākala."
The suffix *ñya* is applied after the words *chandoga*, *aukthika*, *yājñika*, *bahvṛca*, and *naṭa*.
"An exception to *vuñ*": this is an exception to *vuñ* after words denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), and not to the general *aṇ* prescribed for [words beginning with] *naṭa*.
Nor [is the suffix *ka* applied] to the words *daṇḍa*, *māṇava*, and *antevāsin*. (Pāṇini 4.3.130)

"The young brahmins are characterized by punishment" (daṇḍaprādhānā māṇavāḥ). This is an explanation of the meaning; as for the compound, it is a *karmadhāraya*. Because they always carry a staff (*daṇḍa*), the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is applied to the young brahmins.
The suffix *cha* is applied after [patronymic stems] such as *raivatika*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.131).

Regarding the word "pūrveṇa" (by the preceding rule): by the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ*, we have *raivatikīya*. [Derivation: The offspring of Revatī is *raivatika* (formed by *ṭhak* according to *revatyādibhyaṣṭhak*), and from that, the suffix *cha* is applied. Other [names] end in *iñ*; in those cases, the prohibition from the immediately preceding rule will carry over. When the prohibition of *vuñ* after *raivatika* and others is understood, where there is no exception—such as in *raivatīkīya*—it is established simply by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*. From the words *kṣema* and *vṛddhi* as well, the suffix *cha* applies because they belong to the *gaha*-class. For the others, the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule *iñaśca*; therefore, the mention of *cha* [in the rule] is necessary.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the words] *kaupīñjala* and *hāstipada*.

Regarding the statement "it is an exception to the rule for *gotra*": why? He says—"because of the governing context of *gotra*. *Kaupiñjala*: the descendant of Kupiñjala; by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and from that form ending in *aṇ*, another *aṇ* is added. *Hāstipada*: one whose feet are like those of an elephant is *hastipāda*; here the elision of the word *pāda* does not occur, because of the rule stating "not after *hasti* and so forth. The descendant of Hastipāda is [formed] by the rule "the descendant of that" (*tasyāpatyam*), by virtue of this very irregular derivation, with the substitution of *pad* for *pāda*. Then, for "this belongs to Hāstipada," another *aṇ* is added.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *aṇ*? If the mention of *aṇ* were absent, the suffix *cha* would apply immediately [to the preceding rule]. Is it not already established here by the rule "cha after a *vṛddha* [patronymic stem]" (*vṛddhācchaḥ*)? It is not so established; for the suffix *vuñ* would apply instead, according to the rule "vuñ after a *gotra* or a *caraṇa* [stem]. If that were the case, and if *cha* were intended after these two [stems], one should have read them exactly as they are in the *Raivatikādi* group; for in that way, there would be brevity due to the non-utterance of the case-ending. Therefore, since they are treated separately, *cha* will not occur.

But that which is prescribed [by another rule] and does not otherwise apply will indeed take place, and that is the *aṇ* suffix. If this were so, then in a case where the application of *vuñ* is prohibited—such as in the rule "not after *daṇḍa*, *māṇava*, and *antevāsin*"—this [mention of *aṇ*] would serve to prescribe *vuñ*. Therefore, the mention of *aṇ* must be made. The addition of the marker *ṇ* is for the sake of forming the feminine with *ṅīp* and for the sake of prohibiting the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*)—as in *kaupiñjalīkriyaḥ* (one whose action is like that of a *kaupiñjalī*).
For the word *ātharvaṇika*, there is also the elision of one [of the two final syllables].

Regarding the statement "the suffix *caraṇa* is an exception": the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan is called *Atharvan* through the metaphorical treatment of identity (*abhedopacāra*). One who studies that [Veda] is an *Ātharvaṇika*; here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied because [the word *Atharvan*] belongs to the *vasantādi* group. Alternatively, the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan is [denoted by] *Atharvaṇa*, formed with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *tena proktam*. Then, by the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni*, since the word *Atharvaṇa* also falls within the scope of that [rule], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied to the student because it is read in the *vasantādi* list; due to the force of that specific prescription, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *proktālluk* does not occur—thus, *Ātharvaṇikaḥ*.
This preceding sūtra and this one were inserted among the sūtras because they are seen in the Vārttika.
Its modification. 4.3.134.

"Of the *prakṛti* (the base)" means of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). "Another state" means a change [of form]. The question—"What is an example here?"—is asked because an object that is not overridden by an exception (*apavāda*) is difficult to find. "Not denoting a living being" (*aprāṇi*): he will teach the suffix *añ* after words denoting living beings. "Acute on the first syllable" (*ādyudātta*): he will teach the suffix *añ* even after words with an anudātta initial vowel. "Not having *vṛddhi*" (*avṛddha*): he will teach the suffix *mayaṭ* after words with *vṛddhi* vowels. "And that which has no other [suffix]" (*yasya ca nānyat*): as in the rule "the suffix *yat* after *go* and *payas*. "By the accent of the *nit* [suffix]" (*nitsvareṇa*): the words *aśman* and *bhasman* end in the suffix *manin*. "The suffix *takan* after *mṛd*" (*mṛdastikan*): *mṛttikā*.

Regarding the phrase "in its context": this refers to the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that"). The repetition [of the word *tasya*] is for the purpose of excluding the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes. For the previously mentioned mention of *tasya* was connected with the secondary suffixes beginning with *gha*; therefore, if that were to recur, those suffixes would also recur. However, this new mention of *tasya*, being made, serves to exclude the mention of *tasya* as connected with *gha* and the others, and thus excludes *gha* and the other suffixes as well.

But surely, since roots such as *ghu* are primary because they are what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), they ought not to cease even when their [the suffixes'] inclusion ceases, for the primary does not follow the subordinate; rather, it is the subordinate that follows the primary. True; however, by virtue of the power of including those [suffixes], there is the cessation even of the primary roots like *ghu*, whereas the *aṇ* and other suffixes do not cease, because they have been introduced with a specific delimitation of scope, namely "prior to *dīvya-t*" and "prior to *bhavān*."

Regarding the phrase "of the modification and the part": the point is that the exclusion of the suffixes *gha* and so forth is already established by the subsequent governing rules (*adhikāra*), namely "prior to *vahati*" and "prior to *hit*. One might object: "Let it be that *gha* and the others do not apply here because they have been set aside by the mention of *tat*; however, they would still apply by virtue of the rule 'this belongs to that' (*tasyedam*), since the categories of 'modification' and 'part' are specific instances of 'belonging to that'. This is not so.

Since the suffixes *aṇ* and others are already established for derivatives denoting modifications (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*) by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), the restatement of those [suffixes] is solely for the purpose of setting aside the secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*). Why, then, is it said: "The repetition of the word 'of that' (*tasya*) is for the purpose of excluding the secondary suffixes"? For is it not the case that the very application of the rule itself serves to exclude the secondary suffixes? True; however, if the mention of "of that" were absent, the application of the rule might still encompass the secondary suffixes. Therefore, this is the specific burden of the mention of "of that": namely, that the secondary suffixes are excluded.

Regarding *hālaḥ sairaḥ*: the word *hala-* is acute on the first syllable by the rule “*navviṣayasyānisantasya*” (Pāṇini 6.1.213). The word *sīra-* is acute on the first syllable due to the accent of the *nit* suffix because it ends in the suffix *-kan*. Since there is no occasion here for any of the exceptions that will be mentioned later, the suffix *aṇ* applies.

And this demonstrates the purpose of prescribing the suffix *aṇ* and others through the method of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For if [the sūtra] were stated solely for the sake of prescribing exceptions, such as "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*) and "from *bilva* etc., the suffix *aṇ*" (*bilvādibhyo 'ṇ*), then in the case of "the modification of a plow" (*halasya vikāraḥ*), the suffix would have to be prescribed by the rule "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*). Consequently, setting aside *aṇ*, the suffix *ṭhak* would apply by the rule "from *hala* and *sīra*, the suffix *ṭhak*" (*halasīrāṭ ṭhak*), and likewise in other specific instances of "belonging to that."

However, because the suffix *aṇ* and others are prescribed through a formal separation (*yogavibhāga*), only *aṇ* occurs; the purpose of including that [term] is the exclusion of *gha* and the other suffixes. Thus, the modification of the *vṛji*s is "vārja," where *aṇ* applies because the word *vṛji* is optionally prescribed as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) in the *Phiṭ-sūtras*, resulting in an initial accent (*ādyudātta*) in the alternative case. If, however, the suffix *aṇ* were applied here by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), or if *gha* and the others were prescribed by this very rule, then the suffix *kan* would apply by the rule "after *madra* and *vṛji*, *kan*."

Similarly, in the case of *traigarta*—meaning "the modification of the Trigartas"—the word *trigarta* is acutely accented on the first syllable by virtue of the original accent of the first member of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Here, four suffixes would otherwise apply: first, the *aṇ* prescribed by "prāgdīvyato 'ṇ" (Pāṇini 4.1.83); second, the *vuñ* characterized by the rule for [suffixes after] country names (*janapada*); third, the *cha* characterized by the rule for words ending in *garta*; and fourth, the *vuñ* prescribed by the inclusion of that limit [in Pāṇini 4.2.125]. By this [present rule], however, only *aṇ* occurs.

Just as the derivative of *raṅku* is *rāṅkava*: here, first, there is the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*; second, one of two suffixes of equal status—either *vuñ* by *avṛddhād api* or *ṭhañ* by *ordeśe ṭhañ*—which are exceptions to that; third, the suffix *aṇ* by *kopadhādaṇ* or by its inclusion in the *kacchādi* group; and fourth, the suffix *vuñ* by *manuṣyatatsthayor vuñ*. By this [latter rule], the *aṇ* that would have been obtained is superseded by *orañ*, but it is then restored by the rule *kopadhācca*.

If, then, suffixes such as *gha* and others do not apply to derivatives formed from modifications (*vikāra*) or parts (*avayava*), one might object: "In the case of 'the palaces of Pāṭaliputra'—where *pāṭaliputrakaḥ* means 'parts of Pāṭaliputra'—the suffix *vuñ* [prescribed] by the rule *tasyedam*, *ropadhetoḥ prācām* would not be applicable. This is not a fault; for the exclusion of *gha* and other suffixes applies specifically to parts derived from living beings, herbs, and trees. What possibility is there that their exclusion would apply to parts derived from things that are not living beings, herbs, or trees?
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after words denoting parts of living beings, herbs, and trees. (Pāṇini 4.3.135)

Regarding the word *maurva*: the word *mūrvā* is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule "and for grasses and grains that have two vowels [the first is acute]. Regarding the word *khadira*: the word *khadira* is derived from the root *khād* with the suffix *kirac*, which is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātita*); consequently, the suffix *vuñ*—which applies when the initial syllable is unaccented—would be required. However, if the suffix *aṇ* is desired, it should be included among the words listed in the *bilvādi* group.

"For those two have already been explained" means by the rule "tasyedam" (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Although it was stated that the purpose of the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) was to exclude secondary suffixes (*śaiṣika*), nevertheless, disregarding that, this was said with the intention that, for instance, in the cases of *bhāsmana* and *mārtika*, the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth are established.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *bilva*.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to both *mayaṭ* and *añ*. In this regard, by means of the words *kāṇḍa* and *pāṭalī*, there is an exception to *mayaṭ* characterized by [the rule for] *vṛddha* stems; whereas for the remaining [words], there is an exception to *añ* characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*). For the word *bilva*, the final syllable is either circumflex (*svarita*) or acute (*udātta*), according to the rule: "In *bilva* and *tiṣya*, the final [syllable] is circumflex. The words *vrīhi* and *mudga* have their final syllables acute because they belong to the *ghṛtādi* group. The words *masūra*, *godhūma*, and *gavīdhuka* have their middle syllables acute, according to the rule: "When a light syllable is at the end, or when there are two [light syllables]."

From the root *iṣ* comes *ikṣu*, which is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The word *veṇu* is optionally oxytone by the rule "vibhāṣā veṇvindhānayoḥ. The word *karpāsī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* by virtue of its being a genus name (*jāti*). The word *karkandhū* is middle-accented due to the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule "alābūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ. The word *kuṭīra* is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix in the rule "kuṭīśamīśuṇḍābhyo raḥ. [The mention of these examples is] for the purpose of precluding the suffix *mayaṭ*.

The mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting the subverter [of *aṇ*]. For if it were stated simply that "from *bilva* and so on, as prescribed," then in the case of the word *pāṭalī*, which ends in *ṅīṣ*, since the suffix *añ*—which is conditioned by the rule regarding words with an initial anudātta vowel—would be subverted by *mayaṭ*, the repetition of the rule would result in *añ* alone being applied; however, because of the mention of *aṇ*, only *aṇ* occurs. And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word having *ka* as its penultimate letter (4.3.137).

Regarding the phrase "an exception to the year": this refers to what would otherwise be obtained by the rules *orañ* and *anudāttādeśca*. Words such as *tittiḍīka* and others have the acute accent on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante* and so forth.
The suffix *ṣuk* is applied after the words *trapu* and *jatun*.
"Because it is not among living beings and so forth" means that it lacks the quality of being any one of the categories of living beings, plants, or trees.
The suffix *orā* is applied [after a verbal root] to form a feminine noun denoting the action. || 4.3.139 ||

The words *devadāru* and *bhadradāru* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their first syllable by the rule beginning with "of those whose meaning is yellow liquid" (*pītadravārthānām*). *Pītadruḥ* refers to the *sarala* tree, also known as *navaspati*; the meaning of the rule is that for those words whose meaning is "yellow tree" (*pītadru*), the first syllable becomes acute.
And [the suffix] after a root that begins with an anudātta vowel.

*Dādhittha* means "belonging to the *kapittha* tree. [The derivation is as follows: from the sense "that which stands in curd" (*dadhi tiṣṭhati*), the suffix *sthā* is applied by *Pāṇini* 3.2.4 (*supi sthaḥ*). This forms an *upapada-samāsa*; by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the letter *s* is replaced by *t*. The final syllable is udātta by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛdanta* compound.
Alternatively, it is derived from *palāśa* and other such words by *Pāṇini* 4.3.141.

"This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. He asks, "How so? and replies with the words beginning "palāśa-khadira," etc. The word *palāśa* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. The word *khadira* is a conventional form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *kirac*, according to the rule beginning with "ajira-śiśara. The word *śiṃśapā* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) by the rule "of those ending in *p* and those beginning with a heavy syllable," while the phrase "the second [syllable] before the *īṣā*" is in effect.

The suffix *yuc* is applied by the rules *spadi kiñciccalane* and *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*, resulting in *kirateḥ īran*: *karīra*. From the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*, the suffix *īṣan* is added; from *śṛ* and *pṛ*, the suffix *īṣan* is added with the *kit* designation, resulting in *śirīṣa*. By the rule regarding the accent of the *niṭ* suffix, both of these (*karīra* and *śirīṣa*) have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). The words *vikaṅkata-mūla-āsa-yavāsa* have the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule *grāmādīnāṃ ca*.
The suffix *lañ* is applied [after a word denoting a measure] when the object measured is eight *śamyās*. 4.3.142.

Regarding the phrase "an exception to the [general] rule": the word *śamī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the *gaurādi* group. Thus we have *śāmīlī sruc* ("a ladle made of *śamī* wood"). This is based on the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) stating that at the Varuṇapraghāsa rites within the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, "the ladles are made of *śamī* wood."
The suffix *mayaṭ* is optionally used in the common language after these two [words], provided they do not refer to food or clothing. Pāṇini 4.3.143.

"Maudgaḥ sūpaḥ" (lentil soup) and "kārpāsam ācchādanam" (a cotton garment): in both cases, the suffix *aṇ* derived from the class beginning with *bilva* does not apply, respectively, because they are neither a derivative (*vikāra*) nor a part (*avayava*), and because they are non-edible and a covering (*ācchādana*). This is because the mention of "derivative" and "part" as separate terms indicates that each is connected [to both categories].

It is so that [the suffix *mayaṭ*] may also apply to those objects. If it were not stated "of these two," then in a conflict with the subsequent specific suffixes such as *añ* and others, those very suffixes would apply because they are subsequent (*paratvāt*). Since the preceding specific suffixes have scope when the option of *mayaṭ* is absent, and since *mayaṭ* alone is obtained by virtue of being subsequent in the case where *mayaṭ* applies, it was stated [in Pāṇini 4.3.154]: "After words denoting living beings and *rajata* etc., [the suffixes] *añ* and others [apply]. However, the mention of "of these two" results in a re-enactment (*punarvidhāna*), whereby *mayaṭ* occurs even in the domain of the subsequent suffixes.
The suffix *nitya* is applied after words such as *vṛddha*, *śara*, and others.

The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs invariably. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules governing the *prāgdīvyatīya* suffixes. As for the suffix *aṇ*, which is characterized by having a *k* as its penultimate letter, it is superseded by *mayaṭ* because the latter is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Examples are *śākamayaṃ* and *āmramayaṃ*. The word *āmra* ends in the suffix *ran*, according to the rule "the suffix *ran* is added to *am* and *tam*, and there is lengthening [of the vowel]. The phrase "this is made by that" (*tadanena kriyate*) is the basis for this. The word "invariably" (*nityam*), being redundant [if taken literally], serves as a reminder of a sūtra recited by the ancient teachers. And thus, the inclusion of the word *mṛd* among the items beginning with *śara* should be understood as intended for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition (*prapañca*) of this very point.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *go* when it means "cow-dung."

Regarding the example *gavyaṃ payaḥ* ("cow's milk"): how can there be an application [of the rule] here, given that the rule continues with the words "of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*"), whereas milk is neither a modification nor a part? To this he replies: "The dung is not a modification," and so forth. If the mention of *purīṣa* ("dung") were not made, then for the sake of establishing the desired result, one would have to formulate the rule *gormayaṭ* under the heading *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120); consequently, the undesired application would arise even in this case—this is the meaning.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *piṣṭa*. (Pāṇini 4.3.146)

Regarding the phrase "piṣṭamayaṃ bhasma" (ashes made of flour): when there is a desire to express the general sense that "this belongs to that," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "tasyedam" (Pāṇini 4.3.120), as in the example, "Let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha."
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied after the words *asaṃjñā*, *tila*, and *yava* [to form derivatives meaning "made of" or "belonging to"]. 4.3.149.

Regarding the word *yāvaka*: from the word *yava*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*); then, from that form ending in *aṇ*, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*) according to the rule "from *yāva* and so forth."
The suffix *matup* is applied after words ending in *vat*, *vardha*, and *bilva*. 4.3.151.

Regarding *mauñja*: from the word *muñja*, the suffix *aṇ* applies by the general rule (*autsargika*), because [the word] has the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule "of grasses and grains, those with two vowels" (*tṛṇadhānyānāṃ ca dvyaṣām*). Regarding *gārmuta*: the word *garmut* has the acute accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *uti* according to the rules "from *mṛgrī*, *uti*" and "*gormuṭ ca*"; thus, the suffix *añ* applies by the rule "and that which begins with an anudātta" (*anudāttādeśca*). How then is there a final acute accent in the phrase "for him he should offer this *gārmuta* oblation" (*tasmā etaṃ gārmutaṃ caruṃ nirvapet*)? Because all rules are optional in the Veda (*chandasi*), the suffix *aṇ* will apply here. Regarding *vādhrī*.

The word *vardhra* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) by the rule "laghāvante" [Pāṇini 6.1.197]; from it, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, and then the suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ" [Pāṇini 4.1.15]. Regarding the mention of the suffix *matup*, etc.: if that were not present, the mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) would cause the rule of "specification of what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) to apply everywhere; thus, there would be a *tadantavidhi*. For example, in the case of *vaiṇavī*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *bilva* and others [by Pāṇini 4.3.136].
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words ending in] *tāla* and others.

The phrase "an exception to *mayaṭ* and others" includes *añ* by the word "and others" (*ādi*); the plural number is used because those two [suffixes] themselves become numerous due to their various bases. In that regard, from *tāla* and *śyāmāka*, *mayaṭ* is obtained because they are "heavy" (*vṛddha*) [by Pāṇini 4.3.143]. From *barhiṇa*, the derivative *bārhiṇam* is formed; since it is an animal name, *añ* is obtained by [Pāṇini 4.3.154]: "After [words denoting] animals, *rajata*, etc., [the suffix] *añ*. From that [base ending in *añ*], *añ* is again obtained by [Pāṇini 4.3.152]: "And after a base ending in *ñ*, when that same suffix [is applied]. For the remaining [bases], the suffix characterized as having an initial anudātta vowel [i.e., *añ*] is obtained.

The word *indra* is derived from the roots *liś* and *dṛśi* with the word *indra* as an upapada; by the rule *mūlavibhujāditvāt kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is added, and by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs. The word *cāpa* is formed from the root *cap* (meaning "to soothe") with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). The word *pīyūkṣā* has its acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*) according to the rule *laghāv ante*; for in that case, the accentuation of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* takes effect even before the application of the rule *phiṣ*. The compound *indrāyudha* has its acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) by the rule governing the accent of compounds (*samāsasvara*).

Regarding the rule "from *tāla*, [the suffix] *dhanus*": elsewhere, it simply becomes "*tālamaya*. The inclusion of the term *aṇ* is for the purpose of subverting a sublater; otherwise, if it were stated as "according to what is prescribed," the suffix *mayaṭ* characterized by *vṛddhi* would arise from the word *bārhaṇa*. However, this specific statement serves to subvert the suffix *añ* [prescribed] by the rule "also after a word ending in *ñi* and a *tat*-suffix."
The suffix *kan* is added after words meaning "gold" (*jātarūpa*) when expressing a specific measure.

"An exception to *mayaṭ* and others": by the word "others" (*ādi*), the suffix *añ* is included; the plural number is as before. Among these, it is an exception to *mayaṭ* after [words] such as *hāṭaka* that are marked with *vṛddhi*, and an exception to *añ* after [words] such as *tapanīya* that are marked with an *anudātta*.
The suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting living beings and after *rajata* ("silver") and so forth [to form patronymics].

Regarding the term *aṇādīnām*: by the word *ādi* (and so forth), the suffix *mayaṭ* is included; the plural number is as before. In that context, it is an exception (*apavāda*) to *aṇ* after words denoting living beings with an udātta accent on the first syllable, and an exception to *mayaṭ* after words with a *vṛddhi* vowel on the first syllable. Even among words such as *rajata*, it is an exception to *aṇ* when the word has an udātta on the first syllable, whereas *mayaṭ* applies to those with an anudātta on the first syllable. For example: *kāpotam*, *māyūram*, *taitiram*. The word *tittiri* ends in the suffix *kvi* derived from the root *tṛ* according to the rule *sanvaccābhyāsasya*, and thus has the udātta accent on the final syllable. The other two [words, *kapota* and *mayūra*], however, have the udātta accent on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante*.

It has been stated that there is an additional example here; therefore, the parrot (*śuka*), the crane (*baka*), the vulture (*gṛdhra*), and others should be cited as examples in this context. The words *śuka* and *baka* have their initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "of living beings whose penultimate vowel is short" (*prāṇināṃ kupūrvāṇām*). The word *gṛdhra*, ending in the suffix *ran*, has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).

How then is it that examples such as *kāpotam* have been cited? [The opponent] thinks: "Even when the meaning of 'living being' (*prāṇin*) is present, since this rule applies even after a living being whose first syllable is unaccented (*anudāttādi*), the suffix *-añ* ought to occur by this very rule alone. And he says: "By the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) of the *añ* [rule] for those beginning with an unaccented vowel against the *añ* [rule] for living beings. But what is the distinction here between that [previous rule] and this one? That rule is subject to exceptions and is superseded by the subsequent suffix *mayaṭ*; this one, however, is without exception, for by this very rule, due to its posteriority, *mayaṭ* is superseded.

What is established? The form *śauvāvidha*, meaning "a modification of a porcupine," is established. How is it established? [The word] *śvāvidh* is derived from the root *vyadh* (to pierce) with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "one who pierces a dog" (*śvānam vidhyati*). There is lengthening by the rule *nahivṛti* etc., and vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā* etc. Because it is oxytone due to the accent of the original base of the second member of a *kṛt*-derivative compound, it begins with an unaccented vowel. In that case, this suffix *añ*—being subsequent—supersedes the suffix *mayaṭ*, which would otherwise apply by the rule concerning unaccented vowels. Furthermore, because it belongs to the *dvārādi* group, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the addition of the augment *aij*.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after [a word ending in] *ñi*, by virtue of that [same] condition. 4.3.155.

The relation which exists between those two as denotators is the "relation of that" (*tat-pratyaya*); this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Regarding the phrase "only in the case of a modification or a part": if a suffix ending in *ñit* can denote a living being, a herb, or a tree, then it applies to the part as well, because both [modification and part] have been introduced as the subject matter. This was stated thus without regard for specific illustrative examples (*lakṣya*).

But surely, in cases such as "the eastern Pañcālas" or "the cloth is burnt," we see that a word denoting a whole is applied to a part, and a word denoting a material cause is applied to its modification—as in "he eats rice with mung beans," which means "with modifications of mung beans [mixed] with modifications of rice. Consequently, since words like *devadāru* function to denote both parts and modifications of themselves, the suffixes *añ* and so forth will apply to those modifications and parts by their respective rules; thus, there is no need for this [present rule]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "It is an exception (*apavāda*) to *mayaṭ*."

It is true that the desired result is achieved in some way or another; nevertheless, the suffix *mayaṭ* must be prescribed for this very purpose so that it does not apply to [materials] characterized by the elders (such as *śamī*). Otherwise, by the same reason for which this statement—"the modification of *devadāru*," "the modification of *śamī*"—is made, *mayaṭ* would also apply; for by that same reason, *mayaṭ* would also be obtained from a material subject to modification (*vikārya*). [Objection: It will not occur because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). [Response: Then that very non-usage is established by means of the formal rule.

If this is so, then in the case of "its modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*), and [the rule] "from *uṣṭra*, the suffix *vuñ*" (*uṣṭrād vuñ*), as in *auṣṭrakam carma* ("an ox-hide") and its modification *auṣṭrikī upānah* ("a sandal made from it"), the suffix *ṅīp* would be required by the rule "*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*" (*ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*), yet this is not desired. For thus the followers of Śākalya (the Saunāgas) recite: "There is the contingency of *ī* for *añ* following *vuñ*. Therefore, the word for the whole is used for the part, and the word for the modification is used for the original material; thus, by those respective grammatical rules, the suffixes *añ* and others will apply.

However, since there is no linguistic usage [to support it], the suffix *mayaṭ* will not occur after a word ending in a suffix denoting a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*); this alone is correct. Regarding the example *bailvamayam*, the author of the *Vṛtti* holds the view that "by making an effort to exclude *mayaṭ* from words ending in *ñi*, the author of the Sūtra desires *mayaṭ* elsewhere. The authors of the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, however, state: "And that non-usage must be accepted; for if there were such usage, there would be the undesirable consequence of *mayaṭ* even elsewhere—as in 'the modification of *bilva*' (*bailvasya vikāraḥ*)."
[The suffix *kan* is applied] after a word denoting a measure of what has been purchased. 4.3.156.

This is equivalent to [the rule] "from *caraṇa*, as in the case of *dharma*. And number (*saṅkhyā*) is included by the mention of "measure" (*parimāṇa*). Because of the word "and" (*ca*), "weight" (*unmāna*) is also included; the meaning is that the word *parimāṇa* is etymological (*yaugika*), derived from "that by which something is measured" (*parimīyate 'nena*). Thus he says: "it is not only the conventional measure (*rūḍhi-parimāṇa*). Regarding *naiṣkika*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "after *niṣka* and so forth, when not in a compound. Regarding *śatyaḥ* and *śatikaḥ*: [the suffixes] *ṭhan* and *yat* are applied by the rule "after *śata*, [the suffixes] *ṭhan* and *yat* occur, except for the sense of 'one hundred'. Regarding *sāhasram*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "after *śatamāna*, *viṃśatika*, *sahasra*, and *vasana*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs."

The suffix *vati* has the sense of "complete similarity. What is established by this being so? He states that: "When preceded by *adhyardha*, etc. By the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of the rule regarding the base and the suffix (*prakṛti-pratyayayoḥ*), the rule "before *vati*," the inclusion of compounds where the first member is a numeral (*saṅkhyā-pūrva-padānām*), the inclusion of the rule for taking what ends in that (*tad-anta-grahaṇam*), and the inclusion of the rule for the inclusion of what ends in that (*tad-anta-vidhiḥ*). There is no elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending].

This is what is meant: from whatever bases (*prakṛti*) and by whatever qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) certain suffixes (*pratyaya*) are prescribed, those same suffixes occur after those same bases with that very same qualification when expressing a modification (*vikāra*). In the case of *dvisāhasram* ("worth two thousand"), there is optionally elision (*luk*) [of the suffix], and by the rule "after a numeral and a word denoting a number of years," there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member (*uttarapada*). In the case of *dvinaiṣkikam* ("worth two *niṣkas*"), as before, there is optional elision of the suffix *ṭhañ* by the rule "after *niṣka* preceded by *dvi*, *tri*, etc.," and there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member by the rule "of that which ends in a measure-word."
Or [the suffix *khañ* is applied] after words ending in *um* or *ūrṇā*. (Pāṇini 4.3.158)

The word *umā* has an udātta accent on its first syllable according to the rule "tṛṇadhānyānāṃ vā," while the word *ūrṇā* has an udātta accent on its final syllable by the general accentuation of nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*). Since the suffix *vuñ* does not apply after these two, the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied respectively.
The suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after the word *eṇī*.
He states the purpose of the feminine gender designation: "But for the male, she becomes [the female]."
The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *go* and *payas*.
Regarding the phrase "but in the domain of mayaṭ": it refers to the domain of the suffix *mayaṭ* prescribed by the rule "mayaḍ vaitayoḥ."
And [the suffix *ṇa* is applied] after the root *dru*. (Pāṇini 4.3.161)

Regarding the phrase "an exception to the year": this refers to the rule *orañ*, and it is intended to show that the application of the sūtra [in question] is not established. Since they desire the suffix *mayaṭ* invariably after a monosyllabic word, *mayaṭ* would actually apply here instead. As for the term *dravya*: it is called *guṇasaṃdrāva* because it is gathered together with, or reached by, qualities (*guṇaiḥ saṃdrūyate prāpyate*).
The suffix *vayas* is applied after the word *māna*. || 4.3.162 ||
That by which something is measured is a measure (*māna*), such as a *prastha* and so forth.
There is elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] in the sense of "fruit" (*phala*). 4.3.163.

Regarding the phrase "tadviśeṣe" (in its specific variety): this refers to a specific modification or constituent part. In the examples provided, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mayaṭ* after the word *āmalakī* because it is a *vṛddha* stem; for the other two [words], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because they belong to the *gaurādi* group; and from those two, the suffix *añ*, characterized by an initial anudātta vowel, is applied. In all cases, the feminine suffix is elided by the rule "luktaddhitaluki" (Pāṇini 1.2.49).

But is it not the case that the fruit is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the tree? For a modification is of two kinds: either that which destroys its material cause (*prakṛti*), such as "khadira-wood ashes," or that which produces a different designation for the material cause, such as "a ladle made of khadira-wood. But the fruit is not of this nature; therefore, even while remaining on the tree, it is not a modification of it—just like a crow perched upon it—nor is it a constituent part (*avayava*), because it does not originate [the tree].

For when a tree has arisen, the fruit subsequently comes into being; so how can the elision of the suffix be prescribed for that which has arisen in the state of a modification (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*)? To this he says: "of that which has borne fruit" (*phalitasya*). The word *phala* belongs to the *tārakādi* group [of words taking the suffix *itac*]. It has been stated that "a modification is a different state of the original substance" (*prakṛti*); and indeed, the state of having borne fruit is simply a different state from the state of not having borne fruit.

In that case, "tree-ness" (vṛkṣatva) persists in both [the tree and its parts], and in all instances, a subsequent state is a modification (*vikāra*). Furthermore, no part exists prior to its own production and thus cannot be its producer; for example, although horns, teeth, and so forth are parts of a cow or similar animal, they do not exist before the animal's birth. This same principle applies to the fruit as well. The word *pallava* belongs to the class beginning with *ardharca*. The rule prescribing the elision (*luk*) of the suffix when referring to the fruit is redundant, because it constitutes a different base form (*prakṛti*).

The word *āmalaka* and others denote the fruit; it is not etymologically derived [from the tree]—as in "the fruit of the *āmalakī*"—in the same way that the word *āmalaka* does not apply to the tree because of its connection with the *āmalaka* fruit, nor as in "this [tree] belongs to the *āmalaka* fruit. It is like the word *aṅga*, which applies to both a Kṣatriya and a country. However, for the sake of excluding the [secondary] suffix (*pratyaya*), just as this sentence occurs—"a derivative of the *āmalakī*, a derivative of the *kuvalī"—so too would the suffix [otherwise] occur.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [words] such as *plakṣa*.

Regarding the phrase "an exception (apavāda)": by means of the words *śigru* and *kākṣatu*, there is an exception to that which is characterized by a final *u*-vowel; whereas from the remaining [words], there is an exception to that which is characterized by a low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*). In this regard, the word *plakṣa* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule "phiṣaḥ" (*phiṣ* being the technical name for a nominal stem). The word *nyagrodha* is middle-acute (*madhyodātta*) by the rule "laghāvante. The word *aśvattha* is oxytone because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. The words *iḍgudī* and *bṛhatī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* of the *gaurādi* group. [The phrase] "by the force of the specific injunction" [is used].

If there were elision (*luk*) of this [suffix], the rule prescribing it would be purposeless; for once the elision of either *aṇ* or *añ* has been performed, no distinction whatsoever remains. As in the case of *naiyagrodha*: by the rule "and [the word] *nyagrodha* when standing alone," the augment *aij* is applied.
Or [the suffix -mayaṭ] is used after the word *jambū*. (Pāṇini 4.3.165)

But *añ* indeed occurs; for there is no capacity in the rule for *añ* [to produce this form], since it is heard elsewhere than as a result [of a specific suffix]. Regarding *jambūni*: because the fruit is the meaning expressed (*abhidheya*), the neuter short vowel applies; then, by the rule *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*; then *num* is added; and finally, by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*, the long vowel is applied.
The suffix *lup* [is applied] in the sense of disappearance. 4.3.166.

Regarding the phrase "there is a distinction in the case of *yuktavadbhāva*": for when there is *lup*, by the rule "when *lup* occurs, the gender and number are like those of the joined [base]," the gender and number belonging to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) are maintained; however, in the case of *luk*, the gender and number would instead be those of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*).

Regarding the term *phalāpākaśuṣām*: those that wither through the ripening of their fruit are called *phalāpākaśuṣaḥ*. Examples are *vrīhayaḥ* (rice) and *mudgāḥ* (mung beans). In the case of *bilva* and others, the suffix *aṇ* is elided (*luk*). The words *yava*, *māṣa*, and *tila* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable according to the rule "and for grasses and grains consisting of two syllables," etc.; from these, the default suffix *aṇ* is elided. The word *mallikā* has the acute accent on the middle syllable according to the rule "for [words] beginning with *ma*. The meaning of this is as follows: here, the phrase "the second [syllable] before *īṣ*" applies, and the expression "of those consisting of three syllables" (*tryaṣām*) is understood; thus, for words beginning with *ma* that consist of three syllables, the second syllable becomes acute.

The word *navamālikā* is a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) with the middle syllable accented, according to the rule "laghāv ante. The words *vidārī* and *bṛhatī* end in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* (belonging to the *gaurādi* group). The word *aṃśu* is oxytone by virtue of its nominal stem accent; from it, the suffix *matup* is added, which is initial-accented according to the rule "hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup"; the *ṅīp* suffix is unaccented. Thus, in the word *aṃśumatī*, the vowel *m* of the *matup* suffix is accented. Regarding *pāṭalāni*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied because they belong to the *bilvādi* group; the word *sālva* is oxytone by virtue of its nominal stem accent. "In some cases, something else also occurs."

There is another matter as well: there are certain instances where both *lu* and *lup* do not occur. In examples such as *kadamba*, the suffix *aṇ*—which is characterized by having an initial low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*)—is elided by *luk*. Words such as *kadamba* have their middle syllable accented because they end in the suffix *laghu*. In the case of *bailvāni*, there is the absence of both [suffixes]; here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after *bilva*.
And [the suffix -mayaṭ] is applied after *harītakī* and others. (Pāṇini 4.3.167)

In the case of *harītakyādi* (the group beginning with *harītakī*), there is elision (*lup*) of the suffix *mayaṭ* after words such as *drākṣā*; there is elision of the suffix *aṇ* after words beginning with an acute accent (*udātta*); and there is elision of the suffix *añ* after words beginning with a non-acute accent (*anudātta*).
After the words *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*, the suffixes *yañ* and *añ* respectively are applied, and there is also elision (*luk*) [of the final phoneme].

"Prior to *krīta*, [the suffix] *cha* [is applied], as in *kaṃsīya*. This means that within the governing rule "prior to *krīta*, [the suffix] *cha*," the word *kaṃsīya* is derived by means of the suffix *cha* according to the rule "beneficial for that" (*tasmai hitam*). By this, the word *paraśavya*—derived from the *ugavādi* group with the suffix *yat*—is also explained. Furthermore, by virtue of its association with that [suffix], there is elision (*luk*) of both *kaṃsīya* and *paraśavya*. Since the technical term *luk* is prescribed for the non-appearance of a suffix, the meaning is that there is elision of the two suffixes that constitute parts of those words.

Now, in the case of the word *kaṃsa*, the suffix *sa* is applied by the rule "after the roots *vṛt*, *han*, *kaṣ*, and *kam*, the suffix *sa* [is added]. Furthermore, regarding the word *paraśu* (axe), derived from the sense "that which cuts another," the suffix *ku* is applied by the rule "after the roots *khan* and *śṛ* with the prefixes *āṅ* and *pari*, the suffix *ku* is added and is marked with *ṇit*. Why, then, does the elision (*luk*) of those two suffixes not occur? To this he replies: "Because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of 'nominal stem' (*prātipadika*). For it is within the governing heading of "nominal stem" that [the elision applies].

The elision (*luk*) occurs for the two suffixes *cha* and *ya*, but not for the root or the primary suffix (*pratyaya*). As it is said: "The mention of *ṅī*, *āp*, and *prātipadika* is for the sake of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of 'stem' (*aṅga*) and 'word' (*pada*), and for the sake of the elision of *cha* and *ya*. Now, one might object: "In the rule *ataḥ kṛkami*, the inclusion of the word *kaṃ* is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the grammatical operations of derivation (*vyutpatti-kārya*) do not apply to the *uṇādi* derivatives; therefore, the elision of the vowel *u* and the consonant *s* will not take place [in such cases]. True.

In the rule for the application of suffixes characterized by *vṛddhi*, *avṛddhi*, vowel (*svara*), and double-consonant (*dvyañjaka*) features, the incidental purpose of the necessarily required mention of "the nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or a *prātipadika*" has been demonstrated in order to ensure that [these] are understood. For this very reason, this was not shown by the author of the Vṛtti in the rule "from a *prātipadika* ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or [a consonant]."
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter—
the *Padamañjarī*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [a word ending in] *prāgvahat*.

Regarding this, he says: "He will state that 'this rule for the suffix is prescribed after a sentence,' yet a second case-ending cannot occur after a sentence because it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*). Therefore, the word *tat* indicates the mere object (*karman*) itself, and not a case-ending capable of being construed with a second case."

"Māśabda ityāha" means "he says 'let there be no sound'. This analysis (*vigraha*) is offered with the thought that when the sentence-meaning, which consists of a relation (*saṃsarga*), is referred to by the particle *iti*, it can function as the object (*karman*) of the act of speaking; otherwise, this would not be possible. The rule for deriving this suffix from a sentence is obtained from the fact that words such as *prabhūta* are mentioned again [in the sūtra]; otherwise, let *prabhūta* and so on simply be included among *māśabda* and the like—what would be the point of a separate mention?

Regarding the example *āha*: in the word *āha*, the imitation of the demonstrative pronoun *idam* occurs through the addition of the incoming vowel *i* to the base portion [of the word]. Since a grammatical operation cannot apply to the sound itself, there is a rule for conveying the meaning based on the qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇāt*). The meaning is that [the suffix applies] to that which denotes the end of that [base].

"Let them ask"—this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. Likewise, "let them go. However, in the case of the meaning of a *tiṅ*-ending verb, a suffix [is added] to form a noun. "He asks whether [you have] well-bathed": the meaning is that he asks, "Have you well-bathed? or "Are you well-bathed? Regarding "one who asks after a happy night" (*saukharātrika*): he asks about a happy night. One who asks in this manner is so called. By this, the term *saukhaśāyanika* ("one who asks after a comfortable sleep") is explained. There is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group. Regarding "one who violates his teacher’s bed" (*gaurutalpika*): by the word *talpa*, the wife is indicated.
He plays with it, he digs with it, he conquers with it, or it has been conquered by it. Pāṇini 4.4.2.

The meaning of the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) is that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) applies in every instance where there is an instrument (*karaṇa*). Since [in examples] such as *dīvyati* ("he plays"), the agent (*kartṛ*) is already expressed by the verbal suffix, the third case for the agent is not applicable; therefore, by association with those cases, even when joined with the word *jitam* ("won"), the third case occurs only for the instrument—this is the meaning of "everywhere. Consequently, in the sentence *na devadattena jitam* ("not won by Devadatta"), it does not occur. Furthermore, the third case expressing cause (*hetu*) is not suspected here; because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*), for there is no expression of the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) by the suffix *ṭhak* which arises [after a word] ending in the third case expressing cause.

Regarding the phrase *pratyayārthe* ("in the meaning of the suffix"): this locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇa*), and the singular number (*ekavacana*) is used with reference to the category as a whole. In examples such as *iha dīvyati*, there are many meanings for the suffix *tip*: the number one (*ekatvasaṅkhyā*), the present time, and the exclusion of the second and first persons (*yuṣmadasmadvyatireka*). The meaning is "among these. That very point has been demonstrated by the statement: "there is no intention to express (*avivakṣā*) the number or the time," because they are necessarily implied (*nāntarīyakatvāt*).

For it is necessary that there be a designation by some number and at some time; thus, those two [number and time] are mentioned, but they are not intended to be emphasized. Consequently, forms such as *ākṣikaḥ* (singular) and *ākṣikāḥ* (plural) occur even when referring to two or many, and *ākṣikaḥ* occurs at another time in expressions such as "one who plays with dice" (*akṣair adīvyat*). Since this principle is the same, the person is also not intended to be emphasized; therefore, it also occurs in cases such as "you are a gambler" (*akṣikas tvam*) and "I am a gambler" (*ākṣiko 'ham*).

If that is the case, then just as there is no intention to express number, time, and person, it would follow that the agent is also not intended to be expressed, since all are denoted by a single suffix. This is not a fault; for if the agent were not intended to be expressed, the employment of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) would be useless. However, the reverse does not occur—that is, the non-intention of the agent while the intention of time and so forth persists—because the agent is the primary factor.

Indeed, the agent qualified by number and so forth is the primary meaning of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*); therefore, that [agent] is intended to be expressed, while the others are not intended because they are invariably concomitant with it. Furthermore, if even the means (*sādhana*) were not intended to be expressed, the employment of the word *jita* would be purposeless.

Here, in verbal suffixes, the action (*kriyā*) is the primary element and the agent is subordinate; for this very reason, when asked "What does Devadatta do?"—which is a question regarding the action—the answer given is "He cooks" (*pacati*) by means of a verbal suffix, and not "A cook" (*pācaka*) by means of a *kṛt* suffix, because the latter has substance (*sattva*) as its primary element.

Furthermore, if the agent were the primary element in verbal forms (ākhyāta) just as it is in primary derivatives (kṛdanta), then—just as there occurs a connection with [words like] "offspring" in the case of "the offspring of a cook" (pācakasyāpatyam)—there would likewise be such a connection for that which is expressed by the verb, such as "this one cooks" (pacatyayam), and there would be an entry of the action [into the agent], as in "the cook stands" (pācakastiṣṭhati). Therefore, the verb has the action as its primary element.

Furthermore, if the suffix (*pratyaya*) prescribed after that [noun] were also primarily expressive of action (*kriyāpradhāna*), then there would be no connection between the word ending in that suffix and terms such as "offspring" (*apatya*), nor would there be the infusion of action [into the compound], as in the case of *ākṣikasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of an Akṣika") or *ākṣikaṃ paśya* ("look at the Akṣika"). To this, he says: "Even though the verb (*ākhyāta*) is primarily expressive of action... A verb (*ākhyāta*) is so called because by it action is expressed as the primary element; it is a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. This is a convention well-known within its own school (*svanikāyaprasiddhi*). [He concludes with: "...by its very nature."

Just as in the case of the suffixes *aṇ* and *taṣi*, which are prescribed in the sense of "being in the same direction as that" (*tenaikadik*) and "and [the suffix] *taṣi*" (*tasiśca*), they denote things that have become substantial entities (*sattvabhūta*), whereas the opposite is true for *saudāmanī* and *vidyut*—as in *saudāmanī vidyut* and *sudāmataḥ vidyut*—so it is here as well; for an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) does not admit of questioning.
Sanskrit. 4.4.3.
"The division of the rule (yogavibhāga) is for the sake of what follows," meaning that the subsequent exception (apavāda) should apply only to words that are *saṃskṛta* (grammatically formed).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the word] *kulattha* when it is compounded with *kopa*.
The word *kulattha* means "one who remains in the family"; by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the letter *s* is changed to *t*. Others, however, read it with the letter *s* itself.
They did not look around twice. 4.4.7.

In this context, within the section on the suffix *ṭhak*, the *ṅīṣ* suffix is required for certain rules where the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) of the suffix is *ṣ*. Regarding the doubt as to whether that [ṣ] is merely phonetic (*sāṃhitika*) or indeed an *anubandha*, the author of the *Ślokavārttika*, intending to provide a systematic enumeration of the cases, enumerates all those ending in *ṣ*: "from *ākarṣa*, etc. For if he were to mention only those cases where there is doubt and state, "so many [suffixes] in the *ṭhak*-section are marked with *ṣ*, then one might suspect that the suffixes in the *ākarṣa*-group are not marked with *ṣ* because they are not Vedic (*anārṣa*). [The phrase] "from the rule concerning *kusīda*" [is added].
The term *kusīdasūtra* refers to a sūtra beginning with the word *kusīda*, as well as the words *kusīda* itself and *daśaikādaśa*.

[Objection: But are there not seven here, since two *ṣits* are prescribed by the *kusīdasūtra*? To this he says: "And the state of being six is relative to the prescriptive statement. By resorting to the figurative designation of "sixness" for the seven suffixes in relation to the prescriptive statement, it was said: "these six are *ṣits*."
The suffix *ṣṭhal* is applied after [a verbal root] in the sense of "attracting. (Pāṇini 4.4.9)

Regarding "ākarṣa": the suffix *gha* is used here in the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa), according to the rule "the suffix *gha* is generally used after a root ending in a consonant when forming a masculine name."
The suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *parpa*.

In the *parpādi* group, the rule "pādaḥ pat" is recited; thus, one who moves on two feet is called *padikaḥ*. Regarding the rule "padyatyatadarthe," he will state: "The substitution of *pad-* for *pāda-* in the sense of 'moving' (*carati*) must be added as an exception (*upasaṅkhyāna*) when the suffix *ika-* follows. This [recitation in the *parpādi* group] is for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition (*prapañca*) of that very point.
And [the suffix] -aṭṭhañ follows the word *śvagaṇa*.

Regarding the term *śvāgaṇika*: [an objection is raised]—"But surely the word *śvan* is listed among the group beginning with *dvāra*, and the rule for suffixation after such words (*tadādividhi*) is intended there; so how is it that we have *śvāgaṇika*? To this, he replies: "In this case, by the rule *śvādibhyaḥ iñ*" (Pāṇini 4.2.107).
He lives on wages and so forth. 4.4.12.

The mention of "taking up the bow-staff" (*dhanurdaṇḍagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of expressing both the collective and the individual; this is because one may resort to any one of the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words denoting price, purchase, or sale.

The value of goods is the price. The mention of "purchase and sale" is intended to include both the compound and the distributive senses; the reason for this has already been stated. In the term "krayavikrayeṇa," it is a collective dvandva compound.
And [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the word *āyudha*.
That by which one fights is "āyudha" (a weapon); the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the suffix *ghañ*."
The suffix *ha* is applied after [roots] such as *utsaṅga* to form the sense of "taking away from. (Pāṇini 4.4.15)
It carries away—meaning it leads, or it takes up.
The suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied after [the words] *bhastrā* and others. 4.4.16.

*Bhastra*—a leather product, by which iron and the like are blown, or by which grain and the like are carried; the suffix *tran* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule *hūyāmāśrubhasibhyastran*. *Śīrṣabhāra*: it is read as *śīrṣebhāra*, where the form *śīrṣa* arises through irregular derivation (*nipātana*) and there is a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*). The non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending occurs according to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *vibhāṣā*, *vivadha*, and *vīvadha*.

And regarding the term *paryāhāre*: that by which rice and other goods are carried around is called *paryāhāra*—specifically, a particular kind of wooden pole with two slings tied to its ends for carrying on the shoulders. The word *vīvadha* has been inserted into the sūtra because it is seen in the Vārttika.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after the word] *aṅkuṭilikā*. 4.4.18.
The cessation of crooked hunters: *kuṭilikā*, with the suffix *kan* added in the sense of a name.
The suffix *nityam* is added after the word *tri*. 4.4.20.

The word *tri* in the rule *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ* is understood here as the numeral; however, it is not taken in its sense of "three" because such a meaning would not yield a valid expression (*anabhidhānāt*). Regarding the form *uttrimam*: the semivowel is vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacyādi*. The inclusion of the word *nitya* is for the purpose of precluding independence (*svātantrya-nivṛttyartha*). Independence refers to the usage of a stem ending in *tri* without the suffix *ktri*. Since independence is precluded, he demonstrates the resulting benefit: a stem ending in *tri* must always end in the suffix *map*. He shows what is excluded by the particle *eva* (only): it should not be used in any other context.

[Objection: But surely, since the *vibhāṣā* (optionality) would apply to the sentence, the inclusion of the word "nityam" (always) ought to exclude that very sentence which falls under the scope of the suffix *taddhita* *nirvṛtta*, such as "prepared by a cook" (*paktriṇā nirvṛttam*), just as in the cases of "ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām" and "nityaṃ saṃjñācchandasoh. Consequently, the verbal form ending in the suffix *tryanta* would indeed have its independence established in other contexts by the rule for artificial *arhat*. [Response: It is thought thus: a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) must be made here: "The suffix *man* occurs after the suffix *tri*..."

The word *nirvṛtte* constitutes one rule (*yoga*), followed by *nityam*. In this case, only *tremab* is required, not *nirvṛtta*; this is due to the force of the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). Consequently, the universal application of independence [of the suffix] is set aside by the mention of *nityam*. [Objection: Even so, since *nirvṛttam* is not required in the rule for *nityam*, would it not follow that the qualifier *nityam* applies to other instances of independence? [Response: True; however, such a thing is not accepted because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhāna*).

It should be stated that [the suffix] *ima* occurs after words ending in abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the sense of "produced by that" (*tena nirvṛttam*). For example: "produced by cooking" (*pākena nirvṛttam*) is *pākimam*. In this way, even after a word ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*), when *ima* is added and the *ya* is elided by the rule *yasya*, forms such as *kṛtrimam* are established; furthermore, there is no difference regarding accent, for the udātta quality is maintained precisely by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent of the elision of an udātta vowel). However, the formulation of the rule [with the word *nitya*] should be understood as intended to exclude independence (*svātantrya*) by means of the inclusion of the term *nitya*.
The suffixes *kak* and *kan* are applied after the words *apamitya* and *ayācita*, respectively.

Regarding the word *apamitya*: when the suffix *ktvā* is applied according to the rule *udīcāṃ māṅo vyatihāre*, there is a compound with the word *apa*; *lyap* replaces *ktvā*, the vowel *i* is substituted by the rule *mayateridanyatarasyām*, and the word receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the rule *ktvātosunkasunaḥ*. Therefore, the suffix here is not derived from a word standing in the third case.
In the case of a mixture. || 4.4.22 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever is mixed with something becomes refined by it? And therefore, even in the case of "mixed," the suffix *saṃskṛta* would be established simply as "refined"? [Reply: It is not so established. Refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists in the imparting of excellence to what already exists, whereas mixing (*saṃsarga*) is a state of becoming one. Now, excellence is not necessarily present wherever there is that [mixing]; for indeed, in the case of contact with impure substances, there is rather a degradation. Therefore, it must be said to be "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).

If there is a basis for this [suffix], let it be just that; need there be the term *saṃskṛta*? This must certainly be stated so that it may apply here as well—as in "one refined by knowledge is a *vaidyaka*," for in this case there is no contact [of the sense organs with the object], since that is a property of material things (*mūrtidharma*). Furthermore, it must be stated that the suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after [the word] *kulatthaka* when it has *upa* as its prefix, so that it may apply only when [the person] is "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) and not when they are merely "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*); for this purpose, the term *saṃskṛta* is employed.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *cūrṇa*, etc.,] in the sense of "made from that. 4.4.23.

Is it not established by the possessive suffix *ini* itself that those which are mixed with powder possess powder? True; it is established when one intends to express that specific form [of the substance]. However, when the intention is to express the mixture (*saṃsarga*), the suffix *ṭhak* would apply. But the fact that [the formation] does not occur is difficult to ascertain.
The suffix *luk* is applied after [the word] *lavaṇa*. 4.4.24.

Regarding the phrase "denoting the substance salt," and so forth: this word *lavaṇa* exists as a quality-denoter—meaning it denotes one of the six tastes—and it also exists as a substance-denoter, as in the case of *saindhava* (rock salt) and other such things. Among these, that which is a quality-denoter does not necessitate the elision [of the suffix], because its application to a substance is established through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), just like words such as *madhura* ("sweet"). However, the substance-denoting word applies to the substance by virtue of the connection "this is that" (*so 'yam*).

Although in expressions such as *praṣṭhī*, *pracarī*, and *yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya* (bring in the female leaders, the attendants, and the staff-bearers), we observe that even a word denoting a substance (*dravya-śabda*) is sometimes used through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), nevertheless, when distinction (*bheda*) is intended, it is seen even in its original form—as in *praṣṭhasyaiyaṃ prāṣṭhī* (this belongs to the leader) or *yaṣṭimataḥ puruṣān* (the men who possess staves). Therefore, the word *lavaṇa* denotes only a substance and thus triggers the elision (*luk*); and that [elision] indeed triggers [the application of the rule].
[The suffix *khañ* is applied] after [a word ending in the seventh case] when it means "sprinkled with seasonings. (Pāṇini 4.4.26)

That by which the flavor (*rasa*) in rice porridge (*odana*) and other such foods is manifested is called a *vyañjana* (condiment). The use of the plural number is intended to exclude the injunction regarding the specific nature [of the condiment itself]. "Saturated" (*upasikta*) means made soft by the act of pouring. In this context, whatever is saturated by something becomes mixed with it; since the term "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) would already suffice in that case, this statement is for the sake of a restriction (*niyama*): so that the rule applies only when there is saturation from condiments, and not merely to anything that is mixed, as in the expression "a pot mixed with curds."
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *īṣat-loma-kūla* in the sense of "slightly resembling that. (Pāṇini 5.3.28)

"An adverb," and so forth. For a verb expresses the necessity of performing the meaning of the verbal root—*vartate* means "he performs the act of existing" (*vartanam karoti*); *supyate* means "the act of sleeping is performed" (*svāpaḥ kriyate*); *śobhanam odanaṃ pacyate* means "a beautiful cooking having rice as its object is performed" (*odana-karmakaḥ pākaḥ śobhanaḥ kriyate*). Thus, the meaning of the root *pac* (to cook), when it is itself that which is to be performed, becomes the object; and whatever qualifier is in grammatical apposition with it, that too becomes an object.

*Prātīpikaḥ* and *ānvīpikaḥ*. [The former is derived as follows: "In this, waters have gone toward (*pratigatā āpaḥ*)"; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*, the suffix *ikāra* is added at the end of the compound, and by the rule *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt*, the substitution of *īt* for *ap* occurs. This is merely an etymological derivation; these two words, however, are synonyms for "contrary" (*pratikūla*) and "favorable" (*anukūla*). The substitution of *ūt* does not occur here by the rule *ūdanordeśe*, because this is not a location (*adeśatvāt*), and if it were a location, it would be impossible for it to be a qualifier of an action (*kriyāviśeṣatvāsambhavāt*). This is because the word *īp* is specifically mentioned in the sūtra. [Similarly,] *prātilomikaḥ* and *ānulomikaḥ*.

The bahuvrīhi compound is as before; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *ac pratyanvavapūrvāt*. Here too, this is merely for the sake of etymological derivation; the meaning, however, remains exactly as stated previously. Regarding *prātikūlika*: the bahuvrīhi is as before. Here also, there is no sense of "bank" (*kūla*); rather, the meaning of these two [words] is "opposition" (*pratisaraṇa*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *parimukham*. 4.4.29.

Regarding the term *pārimukhika*: here the word *pari* is used; it receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "apaparī varjane" (Pāṇini 1.4.88), takes the ablative case by the rule "pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.3.10), and forms an *avyayībhāva* compound by the rule "apaparibahirañcavaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.12). From this [base], the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. A servant who attends upon his master while avoiding his face is called *pārimukhika*. Alternatively, the word *pari* signifies "on all sides"; thus *parito mukham* is a *prādi*-compound, meaning he attends from whichever direction the master’s face is turned. Similarly, one is called *pāripārśvika* [one who stands at the side].
[The suffix *cha*] is applied [after a word denoting a person] when it conveys something blameworthy. 4.4.30.

"Twofold for the sake of twofold" means: one who deals in doubling [the principal] is called a *dvaiguṇika*, i.e., a creditor; yet he does not give back twice as much, but rather, having given back the single-fold [principal], he takes back double. Therefore, it is censurable. Consequently, the word "twofold" (*dviguṇa*) should be understood here as meaning "for the sake of twofold" (*dviguṇārtha*).

Regarding the term *vārdhuṣika*: the word *vṛddhi* refers to interest on money lent for the purpose of profit. [The suffix *ṭhan*] is indeed a separate primary element (*prakṛtyantara*). This [rule] applies specifically to the formation of the word *vārdhuṣika*. For words have restricted domains of application; since there is no conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*) for the word *vṛddhi* [in this specific sense], the undesirable consequence of the form *vārdhika* does not arise. Therefore, how is it that [the Vedic verse says]: "The son of the usurer (*vārdhudāsa*) trembled at the usury (*vārddhuṣeṇa*) of another"? The sages are free in their speech.
The suffixes *ṣṭhan* and *ṣṭhac* are added after the word *kusīda* ending in the first case, provided it does not end in the eleventh (i.e., the locative) case.

The wealth for that purpose is "kusīda" (lending at interest). Here too, it is intended that the term *kusīdika* refers to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*); yet, it is not the creditor who provides the *kusīda*, but rather the debtor (*adhamarṇa*). Furthermore, the giving of interest by the latter is not censurable. Therefore, the sense is that the name [of the object] is applied to the person because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*).

Since ten things are expressed by the word *ekādaśa* (eleven) for the sake of [conveying] eleven, the word *ekādaśa* also functions with reference to those very ten things. Thus, when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) is formed. According to the rule "the smaller number [is placed first]," the word *daśa* is placed first. Because of the specific mention of *daśaikādaśāt*, the suffix *a* is added at the end of the compound. In this way, the sentence also ends in *a*: *daśaikādaśān prayacchati* ("he gives eleven").
It protects. || 4.4.33 ||
Regarding the term *sāmājika*: *samāja* means a collection (*samūha*), based on the derivation "that in which people gather" (*samajati asmin*); such is its arrangement.
He makes a croaking sound like that of a frog. 4.4.34.

Regarding the expression *śabdaṃ karoti* ("he makes a sound"): here the root *kṛ* functions in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*), meaning "he knows [the sound] through its analysis into base, prefix, and so forth. This is obtained from the inherent nature of the verbal designation; thus, it does not apply here: *śabdaṃ karoti kharaḥ* ("the donkey makes a sound"). The word *dardura* denotes a particular type of vessel, according to some; others say it is an imitative sound (*anukaraṇaśabda*).
He kills birds, fish, and wild animals. 4.4.35.

It is intended that there be the inclusion of the own form (*svarūpa*), its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), and its synonyms (*paryāya*). The reason for this has already been stated under the rule *svaṃ rūpam*. Regarding the example *mātsyika*: the elision [of the suffix] by the rule *sūryatiṣya* does not occur, because [the word] *matsya* is included in the list [of exceptions] for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅī*. Similarly, *hāriṇikaḥ* and *saukarikaḥ*.

Why has an example for the synonym *mṛga* not been shown here, as was done for the two previous cases? For both of those are indeed specific instances of this term: wild quadrupeds are called *mṛgas*, and the word *mṛga* is also a synonym for *hariṇa*; with reference to that, *hāriṇika* is given as an example of a synonym.
And he stands as an obstacle. || 4.4.36 ||

The word *tad* [is used] in the sense of the second case (*dvitīyā*). The term *paripantha* is either an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*)—like *parimukha*—or a determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*). In that regard, even in the case of the indeclinable compound, although the root *sthā* (to stand) is intransitive, *paripantha* functions as the object because it is an adverbial modifier of the action. However, in the case of the determinative compound, *paripantha* means "the path all around" (*paritaḥ panthāḥ*), and according to the rule "time, state, and distance to be traversed are objects," it is the object; others say this is due to the force of the governing context of the word *tad*. Thus, a *pāripanthika* is a thief.

He who stands having avoided the path, or he who stands pervading the path, is described in this way. [The phrase] "for the purpose of illustrating a common worldly expression" means that the second utterance is for the purpose of illustrating the worldly expression *paripanthaṃ tiṣṭhati* ("he stands blocking the path"). Now, what is established by this second utterance in this sense? He says: "It is a synonym for *paripatha*" and so forth. What is the purpose of making this known? He says: "It [is used] even in other domains."

If, however, there were no indication [of this rule], it would be understood that the substitution of the word *paripantha* occurs only in conjunction with the suffix; consequently, its usage elsewhere than in that context would not be possible.
The word *mātha* follows after a word that has *uttara* as its final member, as well as after the word *pada*. 4.4.37.
The word *mātha* is a synonym for "path," because it is traversed or frequented by travelers; a staff-shaped path is a *daṇḍamātha*.
And [the suffix] ṭhañ is applied after the word *ākranda*. (Pāṇini 4.4.38)

Regarding the phrase "the region of crying" (*ākranda*): it is called the "resort of the distressed" (*ārttāyana*), meaning the place where those who suffer go for refuge; that is, it is resorted to or reached by the afflicted. It is called "crying" (*ākranda*) because it is the protector of the afflicted; that is, it is cried out to or invoked by those in distress.
He takes up the subsequent word. 4.4.39.

When the term *pada* is mentioned, its own form (*svarūpa*) is understood, not that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), because there is no deviation from the status of being a *pada* for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For this very reason, he says: "that of which the word *pada* is the subsequent member."
And [the suffix -matup] is applied after a word ending in *kaṇṭha* when it signifies something that is a "beauty" (*lalāma*) for that which it qualifies. 4.4.40.

*Pratikaṇṭham* means "toward each throat" (*kaṇṭhaṃ kaṇṭhaṃ prati*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*), according to the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] when it has its own meaning. Alternatively, it may express "facing toward," according to the rule "*abhi* and *prati* [are compounded] with a word denoting a mark when expressing 'facing toward'. However, the *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound) consisting of *prati-gataḥ kaṇṭham*—meaning "gone toward the throat"—is not included here, because such a usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (*anabhidhānāt*).
He practices the Dharma. || 4.4.41 ||

It should be stated that [the suffix] also applies after *adharma*. This statement is necessary because the rule prohibiting the extension of grammatical operations to what ends with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a suffix would otherwise apply here. Thus, we have *ādharmikaḥ*. In this context, the negative particle *nañ* expresses opposition; the meaning is "one of evil conduct."
The augment *ṭhaṃ* is also applied after the root *i* when it means "to go along a path. (Pāṇini 4.4.42)
Regarding "pratipatham": as before, this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), with the suffix *akāra* added according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ".
It inheres in the inherent relations. 4.4.43.

"Samavāya is said to be a collection (*samūha*)," because [the root *i*] "they come together in it" (*samavayanti tasmin*). It is not "deliberation" (*sampradhāraṇā*), for he considers that the root *i* preceded by the prefix *sam-* is also used in the sense of deliberation. The meaning is: "having come together, it becomes a part of that. In that case, the use of the accusative in "samavāyam" is with respect to the act of coming together as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).
