Furthermore, by saying *prāgvateṣṭhañ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* that is proximate would be understood, rather than the remote ones such as *lokasarvalokāṭ ṭhañ*. To this, he says: "The meaning [is taken] as the limit."

"Grasped" (*gṛhīta*) means intended to be grasped. This is the intention: an object must necessarily be taken here as the limit (*avadhi*). Otherwise, if it were merely stated "prior to *ṭhañ*," since there would be no possessor of the limit (*avadhimat*) of the same class [as the limit], it would follow that either the objects or the bases (*prakṛti*) would be grasped as the possessors of the limit—namely, "the objects prior to *ṭhañ*" or "the bases prior to *ṭhañ*."

In that regard, if the *prakṛti* (base) were the governing factor (*adhikāra*), then because [the base] would present itself before every individual *prakṛti* in the manner of a river's current, and because of the proximity of both *ya* and *cha* in the rule "from *u*, *go*, and so forth, *ya* and *cha*" (*ugavādibhyo yacchaśca*), there would be no distinction between general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*); rather, there would simply be an option (*vikalpa*), as in the case of *tavyat*, *tavya*, and *anīyar*. However, when the meaning (*artha*) is taken as the limit (*avadhi*), its application occurs only for those meanings prior to "bought" (*krīta*).

For that which possesses a limit (*avadhimān*) must be of the same genus as the limit (*avadhisajātīya*). For example: in "after a month" (*māsātparaḥ*), time is understood; in "east of the village" (*grāmātpūrvaḥ*), space; and in "before the final letter" (*alo'ntyātpūrvaḥ*), it is the letter itself. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). How so? When a suffix such as *yad* arises after a specific base (*prakṛti*) in a sense identical [to other rules], it subverts the suffix *cha*, which finds its scope elsewhere. For instance, in the case of *takram kauṇḍinyāya dadhi*, curd is [the gift] for Kauṇḍinya instead of buttermilk; thus, the object is taken as the limit.

But surely, even if it were stated "prior to *ṭhañ*," let it be granted that this refers to those bases which occur prior to *ṭhañ*; nevertheless, the suffix *cha* would still not apply in cases such as *yadādi*, because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author teaches the optionality in the rule "optionally after *havir* and *apūpa*-type words" (*vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ*), that indicates that *cha* does not occur in other domains. And having done so, let the governing rule (*adhikāra*) simply be "after [a word ending in] *cha*"; there is no need for the specification of a limit (*avadhi*), and by virtue of the indicator, even though [the rule] applies to each individual sūtra, it will not occur in other domains.

In the section beginning with *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), however, this [term *taddhita*] does not hold as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), because that section is already occupied by another governing heading. This is true; nevertheless, the mention of a limit (*avadhi*) is for the purpose of avoiding excessive complexity in understanding. Furthermore, that limit should be specified as a meaning (*artha*), not as an affix (*pratyaya*); otherwise, one would fall into the situation described by the proverb: "The garlic was eaten, yet the disease did not depart."
The suffix *yat* is applied after nominal stems ending in *u*, as well as after the group beginning with *go*. (Pāṇini 5.1.2)

The meaning is not that [the suffix] *yat* occurs after words beginning with *u* such as *go* or *vastra*, because [the word *go*] is listed in the *gavādi* group. Regarding *sanaṅgu* and so forth: the scope for the suffix *añ*, which is characterized by being applied to derivatives of *carman*, is seen in examples such as *vārdhra carma* (leather from a goat) and *vāratraṃ carma* (leather from a ram); the scope for *yat*, which is characterized by being applied to words ending in *u*, is seen in examples such as *śaṅkavyam* (suitable for a peg) and *picavyam* (made of cotton). When both [suffixes] would apply to *sanaṅgu*, the suffix *añ* prevails due to its higher status in the order of rules. *Caru* refers to an oblation (*havis*).

The word *caru*, which primarily denotes a cooking vessel (*sthālī*), functions here through metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to refer to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) contained therein. In the rule *vibhāṣā havirapūpādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.4), the term *havis* refers to words denoting specific types of sacrificial offerings, not to the generic form itself; for that [generic form] is already included in the list beginning with *go*. However, the reverse does not occur—that is, that the specific types are taken there [in the rule] while the generic form is taken here [in the application]; for since no contradiction has yet arisen regarding the items in the *go*-list, there is no obstacle to taking the generic form there.

Therefore, since it is established that the specific mention [of the word] occurs only in the rule "vibhāṣā haviḥ-apūpādibhyaḥ," its scope is as follows: *āmikṣyam* and *āmikṣīyam*; *puroḍāśyāḥ* and *puroḍāśīyāḥ*.

It is stated that [the suffix] *yat* is also prescribed after words ending in *anna*. The scope for this is as follows: *surāḥ*, *suryāḥ*, *surīyāḥ*, *odanyāḥ*, *odanīyāḥ*; since the suffix *yat* applies to those ending in the vowel *u*, it would otherwise result in the optional (*vibhāṣā*) application of *yat* due to its subsequent position in relation to both *caru* and *saktu*. In that case, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the suffix *yat* alone is desired in all instances. This is the meaning: that the suffix *yat* is indeed obligatory.

Regarding the statement "it attains the designation *nabha*": this does not mean that it does not possess the technical name *bh* (the *bha*-saṃjñā), for such is not the intended meaning according to the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Indeed, it is precisely for that purpose that the *gaṇasūtra* has been explained; for generally the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) does not explain the *gaṇasūtras*. In the expression *nabhya-akṣaḥ*: the *nābhi* is a specific part of a chariot characterized by a hole; the *akṣa* is a specific wooden shaft inserted into that hole. Because it is suitable for that [hole], it is said to be "beneficial for it" (*tasmai hitam*).

Collyrium and oil-massage are [also excluded], for because they are lubricating, they are not beneficial for the navel. As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya—"In the case of the word *nabhya*, there is no impossibility of the suffix because of the absence of the base"—that is intended with reference to the usage *nabhyaṃ cakraṃ* ("the nave of the wheel"). For the nave is not a modification (*vikṛti*) of the wheel, but rather a constituent part (*avayava*). Nor is there the sense of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*); for a whole does not exist for the sake of its parts.

Therefore, in the sense expressed by "tadartha-vikṛteḥ prakṛtau" [Pāṇini 5.1.12], the form *nābhyaṃ cakra* ("a wheel for the nave") is not at all established. However, since the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitārtha*) is indeed suspected there, the intended meaning is that the suffix is not altogether impossible in that context. Regarding the statement "after the word *śarīrāvayava*, when *yat* is applied," the intention is that it applies because of its higher status in the order of rules. Thus, one would expect the form *nābhyaṃ taila* ("oil for the nave"). Now, why does the substitution of *na* for *nabhas* not occur here as well? To this he says: "by the rule *gav-ādi-yat*" (Pāṇini 5.1.2). As in the case of *śunaḥ* and so forth.

In the case of *śvan*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), as well as the suffix *yat*, and optionally a long vowel (*dīrgha*) by virtue of that [suffix]. When the long vowel occurs, it forms *śunyam* or *śūnyam* (meaning "beneficial for a dog"), because the rule *nastaddhite* ("the final *n* is dropped before a *taddhita* suffix") applies there. Furthermore, once the vocalization has taken place, this word no longer ends in *-an*. While it might be argued that in the case of the long vowel, the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) should not occur due to the specific power of that rule's formulation, it would nonetheless apply in the alternative case. The vocalization is intended to prevent the sublation of what is to be sublated; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of sublating the original base form (*prakṛti*).

In that case, two *ca*s are recited here. Of these, one should be understood as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with *samprasāraṇa*; since there is no other thing to be conjoined there, *samprasāraṇa* itself is prescribed once again. This re-prescription will serve to ensure the preservation of that very form [of the stem]. [The rule] is: "And *anaṅ* for *ūdhas*. It is not stated as "*naśca*" (and *na*); for there is no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*). The substitute *anaṅ* occurs for the word *ūdhas*, and by its co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*), [the suffix] *-ya* is added—as in *ūdhanyaḥ*. By the rule "and when *-ya* follows, there is the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) except in the sense of an abstract quality (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*)," there is the preservation of the original form.
And after *kama*, when a name is formed. 5.1.3.

This *yoga* (rule) can be stated as follows: how is *kambalya* formed? This is established simply by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*), according to the rule: "The suffix is not elided after words denoting measure, *vistra*, *cita*, and *kambalya*, when there is no elision of the *taddhita* suffix. If it is argued that the purpose [of this rule] is so that one may say "I shall state [the condition] 'when it is a name' (*saṃjñāyām*)", even this is not a purpose; for since the exclusion [of the suffix] would already apply by the exclusion of "measure" (*parimāṇa*), the mention of *kambalya* therein is intended to show that the word *kambalya* is a name for a measure.

In that case, the statement is for the sake of the accent; for by means of the *nipātana* (irregular derivation), it is understood only that the word *kambalya* is correct when denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*), but not that it ends in the suffix *yat*. Consequently, the circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable would not occur. If, however, the circumflex on the final syllable were recited within the *nipātana* rule itself, then the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) would have to be relied upon [to justify it], and from the commentary, the rule would become unnecessarily cumbersome.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* (optionally) [is applied] after words such as *havis* and *apūpa*. Pāṇini 5.1.4.

Regarding the phrase "from words denoting specific types of sacrificial offerings" (*havirviśeṣavācibhya*): there is no inclusion of the word-form itself [as a source for the suffix], because that [word-form] is already included among the words beginning with *go*. Nor is the reverse the case—that is, that the specific types are included there while the word-form itself is included here—because it is more logical that the inclusion of the word-form occurs precisely there, since it has not yet encountered any contradiction. Regarding the phrase "and from modifications of food" (*annavikārebhyaśca*): "modifications of food" means varieties of food, that is to say, specific kinds of edible things. From these also, the suffix *yat* optionally (*vibhāṣā*) occurs: *odanyāḥ*, *odanīyāḥ*.

If this is so, then the enumeration of items beginning with *apūpa* (cake) and ending with *kiṇva* (ferment) is purposeless, since they are already established as such simply by being modifications of food (*anna-vikāra*). Is *kiṇva* the raw material for *surā* (liquor)? No, it is not purposeless, because it serves to provide detailed elaboration (*prapañca*).
Another says: when [the words] are used metaphorically (*upacāra*) for things other than cakes and so forth due to similarity and the like, it is for that purpose that these are enumerated.
That which is beneficial for him. 5.1.5.

Regarding the word *tasmai*: the dative case is used according to the rule, "The dative should be stated when used in connection with *hita*. Another says: this very grammatical indication (*nirdeśa*) is the indicator that the dative occurs in connection with *hita*; however, this is to be considered; for the dative is possible in connection with *hita* within the specific scope of a benediction (*āśis*), by the rule: "The dative is used [with words] expressing long life, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita*, in the sense of a benediction."
The suffix *yat* is applied after words denoting parts of the body and so forth.

"Body (*śarīra*) means the collection of living beings (*prāṇikāya*). By this he shows the following: although the word "body" (*śarīra*) is derived by adding the suffix *-īran* to the root *śṛ* (meaning "to decay"), such that it is etymologically explained as "that which decays" (*śīryate*), nevertheless, because it is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*), it refers only to the collection of living beings and not to objects such as jars.
The word *brahmaṇya* is formed from *khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaḥ* [with the suffix *yat*]. [The term] *brahmaṇya* means "one who is friendly toward Brahmins. (Pāṇini 5.1.7)

There is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) as in previous cases. This word *vṛṣan* is taken as ending in *a*, and not as ending in *n*; otherwise, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity, it would have been cited without eliding the *n*, as in the rules for *ātman* and *viśvajana*. Furthermore, there exists a form ending in *n* for which [a specific rule] must be stated, and from that too, [a particular result] occurs; otherwise, in that case, after the application of *cha* and the elision of the *ṭi*, the form *vṛṣīya* would result, and for that, a substitute for the word *vṛṣan* would have to be prescribed, otherwise [the form] would be *vṛṣaṇya*.

The word *brahman* is taken as ending in *-n*, whereas the word *brāhmaṇa* ends in *-a*. In that regard, it must be stated that [the suffix] occurs even from the word *brāhmaṇa*; otherwise, the suffix *cha* would apply after it, and its substitute would have to be the word *brahman*. Otherwise, the form *brāhmaṇyam* would result? To this objection, he says: "beneficial to the bull (*vṛṣṇo hitam*)," and so forth.

The suffix *cha* also does not occur. The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that the suffix *yat* first does not occur simply because it is not mentioned in the rule, and not only that, but the suffix *cha* as well does not occur. He asks why, and says: "Because of non-usage" (*anabhidhānāt*). By this, the logic of the *avyavika* [and *avya*] is also demonstrated. For our goal is to establish three forms: *vṛṣāya hitam*, *vṛṣṇe hitam*; likewise, *brahmaṇe hitam*, *brāhmaṇyam*, and *brāhmaṇāya hitam*.

In that regard, between two words of identical meaning, in one case there shall be only the analytical statement (*vigraha*), while in the other there shall be both the analytical statement and the compound formation (*vṛtti*). For example: *avikasya māṃsam* (the meat of a sheep) and *āvikam* (sheep-meat); likewise, *aver māṃsam* (the meat of a goat) and *āvikaṃ māṃsam* (goat-meat). The inclusion [of the word *aratha*] among the *go-ādi* group was not accepted for the purpose that the suffix *yat* should apply only when the sense is "beneficial" (*hita*)—so that it might not occur in other senses. Some desire the application of the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) here, according to the rule: "After *ratha*, *sītā*, and *hala*, when *yat* is prescribed. Others, however, hold that because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with *hala* and *sītā*, the extension to what ends with those words applies only to the fourfold set of meanings (*cāturarthika*), and not to this particular instance.
The suffix *thyan* is applied after the words *aja* and *avi*.

The word *aja* used here is taken in the masculine gender; for this very reason, in the compound *ajāvi*, the rule *ajādyadantam* (Pāṇini 2.2.33) causes the word *aja* to be placed first, thereby overriding the rule *dvandve ghi* (Pāṇini 2.2.32) which would otherwise have required the word *avi* to stand first. Furthermore, according to the principle that "when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, it includes its feminine form as well," the suffix *thyan* occurs even from the feminine stem: *ajathyam*, meaning "beneficial for a she-goat. The masculine form is applied here because the word is included in the list of exceptions under the rule *tasilādiṣu thyantālau* (Pāṇini 7.1.47).
The suffix *kha* is applied after the words *ātman*, *viśvajana*, and those ending with the word *bhoga*.

In this context, does the inclusion of the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) connect with all [words] according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or only with the word "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) according to the principle of proximity (*pratyāsatti*)? Regarding these, he refutes the first position by stating: "in *ātman*," [showing that] the elision of the nasal (*n*) has not been applied.

The meaning is as follows: the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) was not performed so that I might indicate the intended base (*prakṛti*) in its entirety; furthermore, if there were a connection with each [word] individually, this much would not constitute the base by virtue of the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). Therefore, by the non-performance of *nalopa*, the individual connection being precluded, it is connected with the word *bhoga* alone. Regarding the phrase "the *karmadhāraya* is desired": here, the detailed explanation (*vyākhyāna*) is the refuge. Regarding "from the genitive compound" (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsāt*): *viśvajana* means "the people of the universe," such as one who is common to all, and so forth. Regarding "and from the *bahuvrīhi*": *viśvajana* means "one for whom the people are universal," where that very same person and so forth constitutes the external referent (*anyapadārtha*).

Regarding the term *pañcajanāt*: the four castes with the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) as the fifth are the "five people" (*pañcajana*). This is a compound formed according to the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. The phrase *pañcajanīyam anyat* means that the suffix *cha* occurs only after a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). Furthermore, when, by virtue of context and other factors, it is determined that numerals function to denote specific things to be numbered, then the compound is not contradictory because there is no lack of independence (*sāpekṣatva*), since the connection is direct through [the word] *jana* itself.

Otherwise, however, the exclusion (*vyatireka*) would belong only to the *saṃkhyeya* (the thing numbered) in relation to people, and by means of that, it would belong to the quality of number (*saṃkhyāguṇa*). Since there would be no direct connection [between the quality and the people], a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would be difficult to justify.

Regarding the term *sarvajanāt*: it is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the rule "pūrvakāla-eka-sarva" [Pāṇini 2.1.49]. Regarding the phrase *mahājanān nityam*: the inclusion of the word *nityam* is so that the suffix *kha* (i.e., *īya*), which was prescribed after *sarvajana*, should not apply here.

Regarding the phrase "only from a *tatpuruṣa*": here it is not stated "only from a *karmadhāraya*," because the exclusion of the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is already established by the very mention of the suffix *tvan*.

In this context, it is intended that words such as *pitṛbhogīṇa* (beneficial for the ancestors) denote an object that is beneficial to the ancestors and so forth; however, [if taken literally], they would instead denote something beneficial for the enjoyment of the ancestors and so forth. Furthermore, this word *bhoga* indeed exists with the meaning of a substance (*dravya*), as for example: "This region is called *bhogavat*, in which cows and crops flourish"; for it is that which is enjoyed (*bhujyate*) that is called *bhoga*. And it also exists with the meaning of an action (*kriyā*), as for example: "This Brahmin is called *bhogavat*, who experiences actions such as ritual bathing correctly."

And there is also a sense in which it denotes the body, as seen in the expression, "He encircles the arm with coils like a snake. Here, the word *bhoga*, which applies to the whole [of the serpent], is used for its parts, namely the hoods; yet the "coil" (*bhoga*) is not merely the body of the snake, but rather the entire body. This is because, since the scope of usage is infinite, it is impossible to establish a definitive restriction. However, in the *Nighaṇṭus*, due to the frequency of usage, it is employed to denote the body of a snake. Furthermore, in all cases, the intended meaning would not be achieved [if the term were restricted].

Therefore, this suffix *kha* should not be prescribed after the word *bhoga* as the final member; rather, the suffix *bhogīna* should be prescribed after words such as *pitṛ* and others—as in *pitṛbhogīṇa*, meaning "beneficial for the father. If that is the case, the mention of the option (*vā*) must be made, so that forms such as *mātrīya* and *pitrīya* may also occur; otherwise, because [the suffix] *kha* would be superseded by *bhogīna*, the suffix *cha* would not apply.

In this case, for *grāmaṇibhogīnaḥ* and *senānibhogīnaḥ*, the shortening of the vowel based on the final member of the compound—according to the rule *iko hrasvo’ṅyo gālavasya*—would not occur; and in the case of *abbhogīnaḥ*, the substitution of *t* prescribed by the rule *apo bhi* would apply when a suffix beginning with *b* follows. However, if the suffix *kha* is prescribed after a word ending in *bhoga*, these faults do not arise. Yet, there is a contradiction regarding the meaning; he resolves that by stating: "the word *bhoga* here signifies the body."

In this regard, because there is no difference between the body and the embodied one, the very same meaning that "it is beneficial for the mother" also occurs when analyzed as "it is beneficial for the enjoyment of the mother"; this is the intended sense. Thus, having avoided a contradiction in meaning even when the suffix *kha* is prescribed after a compound ending in *bhoga*, he states an additional advantage in that very context: "the suffix *cha* alone occurs after *mātṛ* and the others when they stand alone. The word "alone" (*eva*) should be understood as following the word "occurs" (*bhavati*). The meaning of the word "alone" is that the suffix *chan* would certainly not occur if the suffix *īnan* were prescribed instead.

Regarding the phrase "from *rājan* and *ācārya*": the meaning is that if a suffix is introduced for the sake of expressing what is beneficial (*hitārtha*) from *rājan* and *ācārya*, it occurs invariably, and moreover, that suffix is specifically *kha*. It is not [introduced] from the bare stems alone. In this context, only the requirement "a suffix is desired" is expected, and not "the suffix *kha* is desired," because there would otherwise be no possibility [of its application]. For this very reason, some read the text separately as "the suffix *kha* is desired."

"And the substitution of *aṇ* for [the suffix] after *ācārya*," it is understood from the phrase "when *bhoga* follows as the second member," for it was just stated: "it is always [so] after *rājan* and *ācārya* when they have *bhoga* as their subsequent member."
The suffixes *ṇa* and *ḍhañ* are applied after the words *sarva* and *puruṣa*. [The word] *sarva* is included [in the rule]. (Pāṇini 5.1.10)

Because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the grammatical operations associated with pronouns (*sarvanāma*) do not apply; for, based on the understanding that the technical designation "pronouns" (*sarvanāmāni*) is etymological (*anvartha*), even the rule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*) does not result in its being a pronoun, since it is an imitation of the mere form of the word without regard for its meaning.

Regarding the phrase *puruṣādvadhe*: by the force of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as the governing case is obtained; however, when [the suffix] *tena* is employed, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is already included. Furthermore, based on the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya, the word *tena* may be inserted even in the middle of a compound (*dvandva*). In that context: in the sense of "killing" (*vadha*), it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*); in the sense of a "modification" (*vikāra*), it is an exception to the suffix *añ* prescribed by "from living beings, *rajata*, etc., the suffix *añ*" (*prāṇirajatādibhyo'ñ*); and in the sense of a "collection" (*samūha*), it is likewise an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by "a collection of that" (*tasya samūhaḥ*). Even when the sense is "made by him" (*tena kṛta*) and the object is a literary work (*grantha*), it is an exception to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by "in a work made [by someone]" (*kṛte granthe*). However, in the case of *pauruṣeyaḥ prāsādaḥ* ("a palace built by a man"), there is no exception to any rule.
The suffix *khañ* is applied after [the words] *māṇava* and *caraka*.

*Manor apatyam* (the offspring of Manu) is *māṇavaḥ*, where the substitution of *ṇ* occurs according to the rule *apatye kutsite mūḍhe*. *Carati* (he moves) forms *caraḥ* by adding the suffix *ac* (as in *pacādyac*). Because the doubling [of the consonant] prescribed by the rule *caricalipativadīnām* is optional, it does not occur here. From that, with the suffix *kan* used for a name (*saṃjñāyām*), we have *carakaḥ*. The addition of the marker *ñ* to the suffix *khañ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi* and for the sake of the accent. It serves to cause *vṛddhi* in *caraka*; and in the case of *māṇava*, it serves to prohibit the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *vṛddhinimittasya ca*, as in the example *māṇavībhāryaḥ* (one whose wife is a young girl).
For that purpose, [the rule applies] to the modification in relation to the archetype; for the archetype is the material cause. || 5.1.12 ||

That from which an effect is derived is the *apādāna*; that which is both the material (*upādāna*) and the cause (*kāraṇa*) is the "material cause" (*upādānakāraṇa*). For an effect has three types of causes: the material cause, the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Among these, that which does not exist in a location separate from the effect, and whose cognition persists through the effects—such as "this is clay, this is a jar," "these are threads, this is a cloth," or "this is gold, this is an earring"—is the material cause.

The non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is that which is proximate to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), such as the conjunction of threads for a cloth. An external cause, however, is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), such as the weaver and the loom. Among these three, that which is the material cause is *prakṛti*; and a subsequent state of that very material cause is the modification (*vikṛti*). By this, he states the non-difference between the effect and its material cause.

For just as a "sling" (*śikya*) is not a different reality from the "rope" (*rajju*), yet the cognition of "sling" does not occur with respect to the rope alone; so too here, clay is indeed the jar, threads are indeed the cloth, and gold is indeed the earring, yet the cognition of the jar and so forth does not occur with respect to the clay and so forth alone. Although the cognition of the seed and so forth does not occur in relation to the tree and its subsequent stages, the cognition of it certainly occurs in relation to that state which immediately follows the seed. In this same way, the cognition of each preceding stage should be understood to persist through the subsequent stages.

Thus, it is entirely clear that for a tree, the seed is the ultimate material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "denoting the modified form" (*vikṛtivācinaḥ*): one might object that because of the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamāt* ("from the first [word] among those capable [of forming a compound]") and because the meaning of that [first word] is indicated here as the first, and since the primary derivative (*prakṛti*) has that meaning, the suffix would logically apply only to what denotes that [primary derivative]. To this he says: "By the pronoun *tad*, the modified form (*vikṛti*) is referred back. The sense is that the modified form itself is indicated as the first in every respect.
Thus, the suffix occurs when the primary derivative has the meaning of the modified form.

By this [statement], he shows that the nominative case is used in place of the locative case *tadarthe*, and the neuter gender is used in place of the feminine gender. Regarding the phrase "by the inclusion of the term *tadartha*" and so forth: here, in sentences concerning material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra*), sometimes only mere suitability is intended, as in "barley-gruel serves for urine" (*mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ*); sometimes there is the exclusion of other possible causes, as in "roasted barley grains from barley," or "flour from roasted grains."

In some cases, the material cause (*prakṛti*) has no other purpose [than that of its modification], as in: "these pieces of wood are for the limbs. In this context, the mention of "for that purpose" (*tadartha*) is made to demonstrate that it is this final meaning which is intended to be expressed. What is established by this? He says: "not [the relation of] material cause and modification," and so forth. For a suffix is prescribed when the material cause is intended for the sake of a modification; its being "for that purpose" can be made known only by the dative case—this is the functional capacity [of the rule]. However, according to some, the dative is obtained from the very statement [of the rule itself].

Regarding the example "yavānāṃ dhānā" (barley-grains for barley): this is a counter-example for those [grammarians] for whom the dative case is obtained through semantic implication (*sāmarthya*). However, for those who carry forward the word "tasmai" (to that), it should be understood as "yavāgūḥ kalpate mūtrāya" (rice-gruel is suitable for urine).

"Whatever [it may be]" means even that which has not become a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). To this, one might object: "The well is not at all the material cause of the water"; to this he says: "If that were so... Why? He says: "In that case... For just as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are the material cause of the Saurya and other sacrifices because they are the locus of the origin of their constituent properties (*dharma*), such as the *prayāja* offerings, so too the well is the material cause of the water because it is the locus of the origin of the water's properties, such as salinity; this is the meaning.

If this is so, is water also a modification (*vikṛti*) of that [earth], like the *saurya* oblation and others? To this he says: "But not... Why? He says: "Because of absolute difference. Regarding the statement that "a subsequent state of that very thing is a modification," there is no absolute difference between cause and effect, because of the cognition "this is clay, this is a jar. Nor is there absolute identity, because the cognition of a jar does not occur when there is merely clay. Therefore, there is difference in some respect and non-difference in another respect. By this, the difference and non-difference of the genus and the individual, as well as of the quality and the possessor of the quality, are explained.

But the sheath is not its material cause (*prakṛti*), because it is not the cause of that [fire] and because it is not the substratum of its production. A "sheath" (*kośī*) is a container made of wood or similar materials, covered with leather, intended for the depositing of fire and other such things.

But surely, "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) and "evolute" (*vikṛti*) are relative terms, and relative terms invariably bring to mind their correlative; for example, when it is said, "one should behave properly toward one's mother," it is not explicitly stated that she is "one's own mother," yet it is understood as "the mother who belongs to someone. Thus, even if only one of the two is mentioned here, the cognition of the other is established? To this, he says: "of both."

He thinks as follows: this verb *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of "displeasure" or "injury," as in "Fate works havoc upon my misfortune"; it is used in the sense of "diversity of action," as in "the students act differently"; it is used in the sense of "impropriety," as in "this independence of women is indeed a deformity"; and it is used in the sense of "transformation of a product," as in "the cloth is a modification of the threads."

Likewise, the root *kṛ* preceded by *pra* also has multiple meanings. It is used in the sense of "cause," as in "the threads are the *prakṛti* (material cause) of the cloth. The Sāṃkhyas, however, call the state of equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇa*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—the *prakṛti*. It is used in the sense of "freedom from defects," as in "the mind is established in its *prakṛti*. It is used in the sense of "inherent nature," as in "he is handsome by *prakṛti*. And it is used in the sense of the "substratum for the arising of properties," as stated previously. Thus, because it has these various meanings, these two terms [prakṛti and vikṛti] do not possess an absolute status as relative terms; therefore, by the employment of either one...

The intended relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is thus obtained. However, in the rule *tasya vikāraḥ*, the effect is understood solely by the very nature of the denotation, and not [the meaning of] "benefit" (*upakāra*) and so forth.
The suffix ḍhañ is applied after the words *chadi*, *rūpa*, *ādhi*, and *bala*.

That by which something is covered is *chadis*. [The suffix] *isi* is applied according to the rule *arciśucihusṛpiccadibhya isiḥ*, and the shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *ismantrankviṣu ca*. Thus we have "grass for a covering" (*chādiṣeyāṇi tṛṇāni*). However, when *chadis* refers to a product of leather, then because of its higher status in the order of rules, the suffix *añ* would apply according to *carmaṇo'ñ*; in that case, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), only the suffix *ḍhañ* is desired—hence "leather for a covering" (*chādiṣeyaṃ carma*)—and it has been said: "The suffixes *yañ*, *ñya*, and *añ* are superseded by *ḍhañ* through a prior counter-exception."

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, says that this [objection] was not raised because the rule for each specific word (*pratipadavidhi*) is stronger. This is not correct; for even the suffix *ḍhañ* finds its application in such cases as *chādiṣeyāṇi tṛṇāni* ("grass for a covering") and *bāleyāstaṇḍulāḥ* ("rice for an elephant"). But how can there be a relationship of material cause and product (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) here, when those very same rice grains exist even in the state of being an elephant's food? It is not necessarily the case that only that which comes into being through the destruction of the material cause is a "product" (*vikāra*); rather, that which possesses different qualities (*guṇāntarayukta*) is also a product.

Furthermore, in the state of being raw (balyavasthā), there is an acquisition of a different quality (*guṇāntarayoga*) for rice grains through contact with turmeric; ultimately, by washing, whiteness, moisture, softness, or a particular configuration (*sānniveśaviśeṣa*) arises. [The term *upadhi*] is formed by adding a suffix in its own sense (*svārthe*) to the word *upadhi*. This is the accepted view (*iṣṭi*). But what is the reason that it is not accepted as being included within the governing context (*adhikāra*)? To this he says: "It is called *upadhi* because it is placed upon (*upadhīyate*)," and so forth.

For that very *rathāṅga* (wheel), because it is being placed down (*upadhīyamāna*), is expressed by the word *upadhi* ending in the *kvip* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*). Although its *prakṛti* (base form) exists, nevertheless the suffix *ḍhañ* does not apply there; what then? It applies to that very *rathāṅga*. And here, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is the reason, for that [suffix] does not become the *prakṛti* of that [word]; therefore, a suffix must be sought in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).

Now, is this [term] *upadhāna* [the same as] *upadhi*? The word *upadhi* denotes an action (*kriyā*), yet its application to the purpose [of that action] is also possible, because the substance exists for the sake of the act of placing (*upadhāna*). Even so, it is not a modification of the action; rather, the action itself is a modification. This is seen from such instances as, "This man, who undergoes many modifications, laughs, dances, and sings. True.

However, in the rule "tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau," only a specific relationship between material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is intended—namely, that wherein there is either the destruction of the material cause or its transformation into another form. For this very reason, it is stated therein that the relationship of material cause and modification is what is intended to be expressed.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after the words *ṛṣabha* and *upānaha*. For example: *ārṣabhya* (a calf from a bull). 5.1.14.

The term *mahāprāṇaḥ* refers to one who possesses great vital strength, is well-knit, and has well-formed limbs—a calf that is nourished for the purpose of attaining the state of a bull. Regarding the rule *carmaṇyapī* (Pāṇini 5.1.15): the scope of the suffix *ñya* is, for example, *aupānahyo muñjaḥ* ("mūñja grass used for making sandals"); the scope of *añ* here is "outer skin" (*vāhyaṃ carma*). When the word *upānat* is intended to signify the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the skin, *añ* would apply by virtue of its higher status; however, by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), *ñya* alone occurs. As for those who maintain that being specifically prescribed (*pratipadavidhāna*) is the reason for superiority even when both rules have scope, for them this prior counter-exception would be untenable.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the word *carman*.

The word "carmaṇaḥ" is in the genitive case. However, if it were in the ablative case, the suffix would apply when the base word *carman* denotes the material cause (*prakṛti*) for the sake of the object—such as in examples like *carmaṇe dvīpī* ("a leopard for the sake of its skin")—but such an expression does not exist.
"Then that [quality] would belong to this, or it would be in this"—this is the meaning of Pāṇini 5.1.16.

Regarding the rule "the potential suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility" (*sambhāvane liṅ*), [the author] demonstrates the meaning of the sūtra through examples by means of the passage beginning with "in the sense of possibility" (*sambhāvane*) and "enough" (*alam*). By the passage beginning with "due to the multiplicity of bricks" (*iṣṭakānāṃ bahutvena*), he shows the application of the sūtra's meaning in the examples. By the passage beginning with "the relationship of original material and modification" (*prakṛtivikārabhāva*) and "for the sake of that, of the modification" (*tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ*), he establishes the justification for the formulation of the sūtra while demonstrating what is already established. Regarding the phrase "mere fitness" (*yogyatāmātram*): likewise, even in the case of bricks intended for another purpose, speakers say, "these are bricks for the wall" (*prākārīyā iṣṭakāḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the double mention of that" (*dvistadgrahaṇam*), etc.

[Objection: Is this not the reverse? For if the connection were with each [word] individually, then the mention of "both" (*dvi*) here would be purposeless; therefore, because of the mention of "both" here, it is logical that elsewhere the connection is with the aggregate. [Response: True; however, since this mode is also possible, he shows the connection with each [word] individually—which follows from the rule—by way of an illustration while remaining within this sūtra. This is what was meant by the phrase "for the sake of demonstrating the rule. "Demonstration" (*pradarśana*) means a directional example (*dig-udāharaṇa*).

If, however, this principle were not demonstrated here, then in the rule *tadasyāstyasminniti matup* ("the suffix *matup* occurs when 'this belongs to him' or 'this exists in this'"), the connection with the case-ending expressing grammatical competency (*samartha-vibhakti*) would be understood as applying to the entire complex [of base and suffix]. Consequently, this would apply only in cases where the case-ending expressing competency can be connected with both meanings of the suffix, such as *śākavān vṛkṣaḥ* ("a tree possessing shoots"); but it would not apply in cases where the connection is with only one of the two meanings, such as *gomān devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta possesses cows") or *vṛkṣavān parvataḥ* ("a mountain possessing trees").

Regarding the phrase "here [it is not so]": when one perceives and esteems a palace built for the sake of a Brahmin and Devadatta who possesses virtuous qualities, then there is the possibility of such a connection.
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied after words ending in *vat* [in the sense of "excelling" or "abounding in"]. 5.1.18.

He will state [later] "pārāyaṇa-turāyaṇa" etc. However, in this particular instance, its formulation is for the sake of ensuring that the suffix *ṭhañ* applies to those cases which are excluded by the subsequent sūtra—such as *gaupucchikaḥ* and *sāmpratikaḥ*.

Since the rule for *ṭhañ* is already established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*), the statement "before *vat*" (*prāgvateḥ*) serves this purpose: even when there is an interruption caused by an intermediate governing rule that is an exception—such as "from *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*, [the suffixes] *aṇ* and *añ*" or "after *śīrṣaccheda*, [the suffix] *yat*"—it ensures that *ṭhañ* alone applies in cases such as *pārāyaṇa* and *turāyaṇa*. Although here the suffix is taken as the limit (*avadhi*), it nevertheless applies only to the meanings (*arthas*) and not to the bases (*prakṛtis*); therefore, it does not apply in the domain of those exceptions.
And thus, the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) in the rule *śūrpādañ anyatarasyām* becomes meaningful.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words meaning "worth" (*arha*), and after words denoting the number of cows' tails (*agopuccha*) or a measure (*parimāṇa*).

The intention is that he will state "it deserves that," and thus the word *arha* (deserving), which is a part of that [compound], is being pointed out. He says this: "up to this designation *arha*. However, the word *ārhāt* is not a limit (*avadhi*); for if it were a limit, the mention of *ārhāt* would be redundant, as [the desired result] would already be established by the rule *prāgvateḥ*. Now, one might object: "Is the statement *ārhāt* intended so that the suffix *ṭhak* may also be prescribed in the sense of the suffix *vat*? Even so, the indication should have been made simply with *āṅ*; the vowel *ā* in *vateḥ* is used precisely to denote inclusion (*abhividhi*).

Even so, in the rule "upasargācchandasi dhātvarthe," the suffix *ṭhak* would also apply in the sense of *vat*. Therefore, the only recourse here is the [traditional] commentary: "excluding *gopuccha* and others. This does not mean that [the suffix applies] after words denoting numbers or words denoting measure when they follow a word other than *gopuccha*. If that were the case, the inclusion of the word *droṇa*—which denotes a measure—and the word *ṣaṣṭhi*—which denotes a number—among the *niṣka*-group would be purposeless, as [the desired forms] would be established by this very rule. It is not purposeless, because [the specific mention is required for other reasons].

Could this be a restatement for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that [the suffix] might occur only when there is no compound? This is not so; for when both a primary injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction is superior. Or rather, this letter *ā* signifies "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*). If it were to signify "limitation" (*maryādā*), its mention would be useless, since the desired result would already be established by the continued application of the term "before" (*prāk*). What, then, is established by this? He says: even in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*), the suffix *ṭhak* certainly occurs.

What is the distinction between number (*saṅkhyā*) and dimension (*parimāṇa*)? The question is: that by which something is measured or delimited is "dimension," yet number also delimits. [The answer is: Number is the counting of distinctions (*bhedagaṇana*). A "distinction" (*bheda*) is that which is distinguished; it refers to mutually distinct objects. That by which these are counted is the "counting of distinctions. It is not the case that number is simply the counting of distinctions because it begins with the universal of oneness (*ekatva-sāmānya*) and so forth; rather, by the term "counting of distinctions," he indicates that it is established upon separateness (*pṛthaktva*).

As it has been stated: "Because they are established as distinct, there would be a division of actions according to number. Even the number one, when applied by the intellect to many things, expresses a distinction as a single [unit]. Regarding the terms *gurutvamānam* (measurement by weight) and *unmānam* (measurement by capacity): having placed [an object] upon a scale or similar device, that by which the weight of gold or other substances is measured—by means of another substance such as a stone, designated by terms like *pala*, whose weight is already determined—that is *unmānam*. *Āyāmāmānam* (measurement of length) is *pramāṇam* (measurement).

Length (*āyāma*) is extension; that by which it is measured is the measure of length (*āyāmamāna*). This occurs in some cases for an object facing horizontally, such as the hand and so forth of a garment; in other cases, it pertains to an object situated in the vertical direction, such as "elephant-sized water" or "water reaching to the thighs. Measurement of height and circumference (*ārohapariṇāhamāna*) is called dimension (*parimāṇa*). Height (*āroha*) is elevation; circumference (*pariṇāha*) is breadth.

That by which grain and the like are measured—by means of a measure made of wood or other materials, according to those two dimensions of height and circumference inherent in it—is *parimāṇa* (measure). The prefix *pari-* signifies "on all sides. When asked for the distinction between number (*saṃkhyā*) and measure (*parimāṇa*), this demonstration of the lack of distinction from *unmāna* (weight) is provided incidentally in order to remove the ignorance regarding that specific distinction as well.

"Height-measurement" (*ūrdhvamāna*) means that the measurement of weight by raising [an object] upward is "unmeasured" (*unmāna*); this is precisely the meaning stated previously. The word *kila* indicates well-known tradition. Regarding "measurement, however, on all sides": although the term *māna* was already compounded as "height-measurement," it is required here [as a separate term]. For this reason, some read it separately as "height" (*ūrdhvam*) and "measurement" (*mānam*). "Length" (*āyāma*): the word "measurement" (*māna*) is required [to complete the sense], with the genitive case used in the objective sense (*karman*). However, the well-known reading is "length, however" (*āyāmas tu*).

In this context, the term "length" (*āyāma*) is used figuratively to denote that which is to be delimited by length. As for the phrase "but number is external on all sides": it is external to all [the measures] previously mentioned, such as measurement (*unmāna*), because it is not included therein. Furthermore, its etymological derivation—*saṃkhyā* being that by which one counts (*saṃkhyāyate'nayā*)—should be understood as having the characteristic of enumerating distinctions (*bhedagaṇanalakṣaṇatva*). This is how it should be investigated.
The suffix *ka* is applied after words such as *niṣka* when they do not form a compound. || 5.1.20 ||

"An exception to *ṭhañ*": according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, since *ṭhak* would apply by exclusion (*paryudāsa*) to words denoting measure from *niṣka* up to *droṇa*, as well as to the word *ṣaṣṭhi*, it is precisely *ṭhañ* that would otherwise apply; therefore, this [rule] is an exception to that very [suffix].

"Regarding the non-prohibition of that which ends in it": this means there is no prohibition in the case of a rule involving "that which ends in it" (*tadanta-vidhi*). If, then, the suffix is understood as following that which ends in it, in that case, would [the application of] the principle "the designation of a thing is extended to what resembles it, except in the case of a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*) not fail to apply to simple [stems]? This is not a fault; for by the inclusion of the word *asmāt* ("from this"), the cessation of the technical rule "that which possesses a marker" (*grahaṇavat-paribhāṣā*) is indicated. When that is ceased, the status of being "that which ends in it" is established by the rule "a rule [is applied] to that which ends in that by which the operation is prescribed. Since its own form is also the subject under discussion here, the suffix occurs even from a simple [stem].

As for the one who thinks that [the result] might arise even from the mere capacity of the material cause (*upādāna*) mentioned previously—for him, the recitation of the [causes] alone would have been for the sake of brevity; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

"And so on, from here onwards. But how can the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to that which ends with the specified element) be obtained when it is desired, given that it is prohibited by the principle: "There is no *tadanta-vidhi* with a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that functions like a word-form (*grahaṇavat*)"? Furthermore, the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this paribhāṣā is understood from the prohibition of compound formation (*samāsa-pratiṣedha*) in the case of the *garga*-class [of surnames] by the rule *vājāse*. For if [the paribhāṣā] were universal, there would be no possibility at all for a suffix produced after the word *vāja* to occur in a compound; thus, one would not have made a prohibition regarding compounds.

Regarding *dviśūrpa*: having formed a *dvigu* compound for the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning "purchased with two winnowing baskets" (*dvābhyāṃ śūrpābhyāṃ krītam*), this base is not yet one ending in *luK*. Therefore, by the rule "after a word preceded by a numeral, *añ* is optionally applied after *śūrpa*," the suffix *añ* itself is applied; subsequently, its *luK* elision occurs by the rule "there is *luK* elision of the suffix after *adhyardha* and a *dvigu* compound, except when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is involved. Thus we have *dviśūrpikam*. In this form, the vowel of the final member is lengthened by the rule "there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of a word ending in a measure-word, except in the case of a technical name or the word *śāṇa*."

Regarding what was stated—"From here onwards, the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element) is desired for those compounds whose prior member is a numeral"—and what was further stated—"However, it is not desired for a base ending in a *luk*-elision"—he says "And so it has been said," etc., in order to stabilize both of these points by means of authoritative tradition (*āptāgama*).
After the word *śata*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *yat* are applied [to form ordinals], except when the meaning is "one less than a hundred" (*avaśate*).

Regarding the question "What is the exception (*apavāda*) for *kan*?"—it refers to that which would otherwise be obtained by the subsequent rule. In the case of *śatakam*: while the phrase "that is its measure" (*tad-asya parimāṇam*) is in force, when the sense of a "collection" (*saṃgha*) is intended as the meaning of the suffix according to the rule "after a numeral, [the suffix *ka* is added] in the sense of a name, a collection, a sūtra, or a lesson" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā-saṃgha-sūtrādhyayaneṣu*), it is precisely *kan* that occurs by the subsequent rule. Here, the "collection" (*saṃgha*) is the meaning of the suffix. That is to say, the meaning of the suffix here is a work called the *Nidāna* whose measure is one hundred chapters; and since that consists of a group of chapters delimited by the number one hundred, the "collection" (*saṃgha*) becomes the meaning of the suffix.

"Exactly one hundred in reality. Because it is non-different from the hundred, it does not differ from the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); for that very same hundred which is denoted by the base is also denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, there is no difference here between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix. By this, it is explained that where the meaning of the base is non-distinct from the meaning of the suffix, the prohibition applies, but not where it is distinct.

But surely, in the rules "saṃghe cānauttarādharye" and "saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃjñāsaṃghasūtrādhyayaneṣu," the word *saṃgha* is understood to refer to a collection of living beings; how then can it be taken here as referring to a literary work? There is no fault, for this is by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Alternatively, in the rule "saṃjñāsaṃghasūtra," a specific kind of collection is understood due to its association with the word *saṃjñā*; whereas in "saṃghe cānauttarādharye," because the term *chandas* is understood to carry over from the preceding rule "chandonāmni," it refers to a living being.

But here, since there is no other effort [required], the inclusion of the word "book" (*grantha*) is not a fault. Now, one might object: "When 'hundred' (*śata*) is the meaning to be expressed, it should not occur; yet when one says *śatyam śāṭaka-śatam* ('a hundred of cloth worth a hundred') or *śatikam śāṭaka-śatam* ('a hundred of cloth consisting of a hundred'), a 'hundred' is indeed understood. Why, then, does the prohibition not apply? To this he replies: "By means of a sentence," and so forth. The words *śatya* and *śatika* are general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*), and general terms do not function with reference to a specific instance without the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors.

As long as the other word "a hundred garments" (*śāṭakaśatam*) is not employed, the quality of being a hundred (*śatatvam*) regarding the meaning of the suffix is not determined. Therefore, because it is understood only through the proximity of another word, this becomes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and not [the meaning] of the direct expression (*śruti*). The connection is that "it is understood."

Where the hundredfold nature of the meaning of the suffix is expressed by a word ending in a suffix independently of other words, there it is understood through direct audition (*śruti*) by the mere hearing of that suffix-ending word; as, for example, in the counter-example, when it is said "this has a hundred as its measure" (*śatakam*), it is understood that the meaning of the single suffix is indeed a hundred. But here, the hundredfold nature is understood from the sentence (*vākya*). Furthermore, at the time of the formation of the individual word (*pada-saṃskāra*), the sentence-meaning does not have the status of a subordinate factor (*aṅga-bhāva*), because at that time the sentence-meaning is not yet present.

The prohibition applies when the meaning of the suffix is not distinct from the meaning of the base; for it does not apply when [the meaning] is distinct, as that is understood through the sentence itself. To reinforce this with the words of an authoritative person (āpta), he says: "And so it has been said," and so forth. When a prohibition of "hundred" (śata) is to be applied, there is no prohibition if the meaning of the suffix is something other than the meaning of the base and yet constitutes a "hundred. This is what is meant: where the meaning of the base is one hundred and the meaning of the suffix is another hundred, in that case there is only a positive injunction (vidhi), not a prohibition.

But by what [rule] would a compound be obtained here, such that the particle *ca* is employed for the purpose of prohibiting it and for the purpose of carrying forward the term *asamāsa* (non-compound)? To this he says: "Prior to *vati*, etc."
The suffix *kan* is added after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śad*.

"Pañcakaḥ paṭaḥ" (a cloth worth five) is an example of a worldly number (*laukikī saṃkhyā*). "Bahukaḥ" (many) is an example of a technical number (*pāribhāṣikī*). "Cātvāriṃśatkaḥ" (worth forty) [is formed] by the rule "is-us-uk-tāntāt kaḥ. [The objection is raised: "Because of the mention of the word *ti* as being meaningful (*arthavat*)," that is, by the maxim of mentioning meaningful elements (*arthavad-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*). [The reply is: "[The suffix] *ḍati*"—this means the element *ti* which is a constituent part [of the suffix *ḍati*]. [Thus,] it is not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), for that [element *ti*] is not meaningful. "Katikaḥ" (how many)—[this is formed] by the suffix *iti* according to the rule "kimaḥ saṃkhyā-parimāṇe ca. [The meaning is: "those whose number or measure is what? (*kā saṃkhyā parimāṇaṃ yeṣām*)."

In the case of the word *saptati*, however, since it denotes seventeen objects, the suffix *ti* occurs after the word *sapta*—which has "measure" as its limiting adjunct—in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), meaning that the word *ti* is meaningful. The same applies to the word *navati*. As for the word *aśīti*, although the usage of the stem *aśī* is not seen elsewhere than in the number eight, this is the established rule in the grammatical treatise: "The substitution of *aśī* for the eight [objects] and the suffix *ti*."

In the word *viṃśati*, however, there is the elision (*lup*) of two instances of *daśat* and the suffix *śat* is added; thus, the syllable *-ti* is indeed meaningless. Consequently, the suffix *kan* is indeed applied after it, as in *viṃśatikaḥ*. This being the case, the grammatical rule "after *viṃśatika*, [the suffix] *kha* [is applied] to form *śatamāna-viṃśatika*" becomes logically consistent. However, because the suffix *ḍvun* is prescribed by the rule "after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*, [the suffix] *ḍvun* [is applied] when not a name," the suffix *kan* occurs only when it is a name.

In the rule *atiśadantāyāḥ*, the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the suffix] even in cases such as *ekasaptatyā krītam* ("bought for seventy-one"); otherwise, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the rule would not apply.
The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after a root ending in *v*.

Regarding the phrase "but for that [suffix], by this [rule]": a different suffix, such as *iṇ*, does not occur here—as in the case of the rule "after *car*, *ṭa*"—because of the force of the marker *ṭ*. Is there another purpose for the marker *ṭ*? [One might think: so that *ṅīp* may apply by the rule "for that which has *ṭ* as a marker" (*ṭitaḥ*). [The answer is: under the governing heading "from *at*" (*ataḥ*), *ṅīp* applies; however, this [suffix *i*] does not end in *a*. Nevertheless, by the force of the marker *ṭ*, *ṅīp* shall apply even after what does not end in *a*, just as in the word *saraja*, where by the force of the application of the marker, *ṭilopa* (elision of *ṭ*) occurs even though [the base] is not *bha*.

In that case, would the augment not occur by virtue of the capacity of the suffix *kan* being drawn forward through the formal agreement (*pratijñāna*) regarding its circumflex accent (*svaritatva*)? There is another purpose for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*): lest there be an annulment by the augment *iṭ*, so that the rule for *kan* may also apply. Or rather, will *kan* occur simply because of the mention of the option (*vāvacana*)? Then this might be the purpose: that both *iṭ* and *kan* occur, while in the alternative case, the suffix *ṭhañ* prescribed by the general rule applies. Therefore, a mere explanatory interpretation (*vyākhyāna*) alone is the refuge.

But surely, there is no mention here of the suffix *kan*; even that which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is indicated by the nominative case, whereas here the meaning requires something indicated by the genitive case. [One might argue: "The word *vatoḥ* is in the ablative case, and it will effect a change of the nominative *kan* into a genitive—according to the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67). [To this we reply: *tāvatkaḥ*. This means "that much is its measure. [The suffix] *vatup* is applied after the pronouns *yat*, *tat*, and *etad* when expressing measure; then [the final *u* is replaced by *a*] according to the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.114).
The suffix *ḍvun* is applied after the words *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*, provided that they do not form a technical name (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the form *viṃśaka*: by the rule *ti-viṃśater-ḍiti*, there is the elision of the word *ti*; by the rule *ato guṇe*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. However, the elision of the stem-final vowel (*yasyeti lopaḥ*) does not occur, because the elision of *ti* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*. Now, one might object: since secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are produced from words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*), the designation "pada" (word) occurs by relying on the intervening case-suffix; how then can the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) apply?

But as for the designation *bha* which depends upon the designation *ḍvu*, does it subvert only that designation of *pada* which is [derived] by the rule "in the case of *su* and so on" (*svādiṣu*) according to the maxim "that which is not otherwise obtained" (*yena nāprāptinyāya*), and not also the [designation of *pada*] defined by the rule "a word ending in a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix is a *pada*" (*suptiṅantaṃ padam*)? It subverts this one as well. Why? Because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules]. For this very reason, there is no elision of the *n* in forms such as *sāmanaḥ*.

But how is it here? It concerns the [suffix] *kan* added to *triṃśat* (thirty), as in the question and answer. However, the derivation of *kan* from the word *viṃśati* (twenty) has already been explained previously. But when the view is that the suffix *ti* occurs after the elision (*lopa*) of the *valiśa* (the *śat* portion) of two *daśatas* (tens), then it applies even with reference to *viṃśatika*.
The suffix *ṭṭhiṭhan* is applied after the word *kaṃsa*.

He shows that this word *kaṃsa* denotes a vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), and is understood here as a term for a specific measure, because of its association with the preceding and following words which denote measures; it does not signify a particular type of metal, nor does it refer to the son of Ugrasena. Regarding the phrase "an exception to *ṭhan*": the vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation. One might ask: "In that case, for the sake of brevity in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*), should one not simply say *ṭikan*? It is simply that [the author] did not do so. Regarding the word "additional" (*adhika*): since the word *ardha* is conventionally established (*nirūḍha*) as referring to half of a *kārṣāpaṇa*, one should not suspect a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*) regarding the "half" in relation to a part.
Another says: when the specific deity is determined by the force of the context and other factors, there is no lack of capacity [in the word].
The suffix *ṭhak* (ika) may optionally be applied after the word *śūrpa*.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṭhan*. This is because the word *śūrpa* denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*). Although a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is a specific type of winnowing implement, it nevertheless possesses a particular shape that serves as a measure for grain and the like; or rather, grain and so forth measured by a winnowing basket is expressed by the word *śūrpa*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *śatamāna*, *viṃśatika*, and *sahasra* when they denote a garment. 5.1.27.

It is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffixes *ṭhak* and *thañ*. *Śatamānam* is a measure (*parimāṇa*); *sahasram* is a number (*saṃkhyā*); [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is an exception to those two. *Viṃśatikam* (bought for twenty): this is a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*). If it were not a technical term, the suffix *ḍvun* would have applied by the rule "after *viṃśati* and *triṃśat*, *ḍvun* occurs when not a technical term. If that [word *viṃśati*] is a technical term for a measure, then *ṭhañ* is an exception even to that. But if it refers to something else [than a measure], then *ṭhak* applies. However, after the word *vasana*, only *ṭhak* applies.
In the case of a *dvigu* compound preceded by *adhyardha*, there is the elision [of the suffix] when it does not denote a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*).

"Adhyardha" means that which has one and a half [units] added to it; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule *prādibhyo dhātujasya*. "Adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ" is a collective *dvandva* compound; the masculine gender used here is based on the Vedic (sautra) usage. Therefore, the meaning is "after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) preceded by *adhyardha*, and after a *dvigu* [compound]. By this, it is indicated that the ablative case in "adhyardhapūrvadvigoḥ" is relied upon.

If this is so, then regarding the elision (*luk*) of a *dvigu* compound, one must state: "The elision occurs of that secondary derivative (*taddhita*) which is the cause of the *dvigu*. This is so that in cases such as *dviśūrpam* ("bought for two *śūrpa*-measures") and *dviśaurpikam* ("bought with two *śūrpa*-measures"), the elision does not occur for the second [derivative]. Likewise, when there is no perception of a specific difference in meaning, even where [the form] is caused by that [specific condition], if the meaning is not distinct from the *dvigu* whose purpose is the secondary derivative, then it applies even where it is not caused by that [condition].

It must be stated that the elision (*luk*) occurs even after a *dvigu* compound for which that *taddhita* suffix is not the cause—for example, when one analyzes "purchased with two *śūrpa*s" as *dviśūrpyā krītam*, the form should likewise be *dviśūrpam*. Therefore, in the rule "after a *dvigu*" (*tasmād dvigoḥ*), this is not an ablative (*pañcamī*); what then? It is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*): "the *taddhita* suffix belonging to the *dvigu*. And which *taddhita* suffix belongs to the *dvigu*? That which is its cause, in the presence of which the *dvigu* comes into being.

Regarding the expression *dviśūrpyā krītam* ("purchased for two winnowing baskets"), however, the suffix will not occur due to the absence of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). For us, three forms must be established: *dviśūrpam*, *dviśūrpyā krītam*, and [the other]. In that regard, of the two words having the same meaning, the analysis (*vigraha*) alone is expressed by one—namely *dviśūrpyā krītam*—but there is no derivative formation (*vṛtti*), because of the absence of conventional usage. By the other word, both the analysis and the formation are expressed: *dvābhyāṃ śūrpābhyāṃ krītaṃ dviśūrpam*, according to the logic of the *avyavika* rule.

The principle regarding *avyavi* has been explained. This is the true nature of the matter; and in the rule *dvigor lug anapatye*, the author of the *Vṛtti* has also explained it in exactly this way. However, here [in the present context], because it is understood by following that [previous rule], it was not explained with such detailed analysis. It was stated as "of that which follows a *dvigu*" simply on the grounds that the *taddhita* suffix for which elision (*luk*) is desired must also follow a *dvigu*. Examples are *pāñcalohitikam* and *pāñcakalāpikam*.

The analysis is as follows: "five red ones (lohinyaḥ) are its measure" and "five bundles (kalāpāḥ) are its measure. Having thus analyzed the compound for the purpose of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule "that which is its measure" (*tadasya parimāṇam*). Due to the masculine transformation (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "in the case of a secondary suffix beginning with a vowel other than *a*, in a neuter base," the short *i* and the *n* of the word *lohini* are dropped. These two are names for specific measures.

The mention of "not being a name" (*asaṃjñā*) is a qualification of the suffix ending [in *taddhita*], but not of the *dvigu* compound even though it is proximate; this is because the locative case is used in the expression "when it is not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*). However, the author of the Vārttika considers that "the mention of 'not being a name' is a qualification of the *dvigu*; for the words *pañcalohita* and *pañcakalāpa* are indeed *dvigu* compounds in which the *taddhita* suffix has been elided, and they are names. Therefore, there is no purpose in the prohibition 'when it is not a name'. Thus he says: "And the prohibition of the name is useless, because the elision is caused by that [name]. The meaning is that the very fact of being a name is the cause for that elision.

"The word *adhyardha* is a number itself" means that it denotes a number, because even *adhyardha*, like "one" (*eka*) and so forth, serves as a means of delimitation. For this very reason, in the expression *adhyardhakena krītam adhyarddhakam* ("purchased for one and a half [units]"), the suffix *kan* occurs according to the rule for numbers; and in expressions such as *adhyarddhakaṃsa*, there is also a *dvigu* compound for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). "In some cases" means elsewhere than after the suffix *kan*, a compound, or a final member subject to *vṛddhi*. [The rule] "of a number, in counting the repetition of an action" [is also applicable].

When, having once completed that action which has a single result, one desists while performing it halfway, then, due to the absence of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, the expression "one performs it with a half added" (*adhyardham karoti*) occurs.
The word *vibhāṣā* [is used] after the two words *kārṣāpaṇa* and *sahasra*. (Pāṇini 5.1.29)

Regarding the term *adhyardhasahasram*: according to the rule *śatamānaviṃśatikāt*, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed; in the case where there is no elision (*aluk*), there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca*. For it has just been stated that "the word *adhyardha* is indeed a number."

Regarding the form *adhyardhasuvarṇam*: there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhañ*, but not of *ṭhak*. This is because in the rule *ārhāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.19), the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is understood as referring to that which is based on an action [of weighing]. However, according to those who hold that the term there refers to conventional measures (*rūḍhiparimāṇa*), there is elision of *ṭhak*. Thus, the form is *adhyarddhasauvarṇikam*. Here, by the rule *parimāṇāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.17), there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member; for in that context, even weights (*unmāna*) are included, since there is a specific prohibition regarding the *śāṇa*. In this case, the application of the rule *adhyardhe kārṣāpaṇasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.16) and *dvigau sahasrasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.15) is not desired to follow the respective order of the rules.
The suffix *niṣka* is added after the words *dvi* and *tri* when they precede it.

The mention of *adhyardha-pūrva* (preceded by *adhyardha*) from the previous rule is carried over for the sake of subsequent rules, but here it is not connected [to the current rule]. However, the mention of *dvigu* (a compound denoting a multiple) is indeed connected, so that [the suffix] might not apply to a genitive compound such as *dvayorniṣkam* or *trayāṇāṃ niṣkam*. In this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge; otherwise, one would understand the rule as a conjunction: "from *niṣka* preceded by *adhyardha*, and also preceded by *dvi* or *tri*. Thus we have *dvinaiṣkikam*. [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is added according to *prāgvateṣṭhañ*; there is vṛddhi of the final syllable of the second member according to *parimāṇāntasya*.

Since the formation would be established simply by the rule "from *niṣka* preceded by *dvi* or *tri*," the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (preceded by) has a purpose that requires further consideration.
And because of the detailed exposition. 5.1.31.

The word "and" (ca) is drawn along [from the previous rule]. The sense is that what is drawn along by it does not recur in what follows; thus, there is no recurrence in the subsequent [rules]. The word *bista* denotes a measure of quantity.
After *viṃśati*, the suffix *kha* [is applied] to form ordinal numbers. 5.1.32.
When the suffix *aṇ* would otherwise apply [to form] *śatamānaviśatika*, its elision (*luk*) occurs, and the suffix *kha* is prescribed here instead.
[The suffix] *īkan* is applied after *khārī*. (Pāṇini 5.1.33)
When the suffix *ṭhañ* would [otherwise] apply in the sense of "measuring a *khārī*," its elision (*luk*) occurs and the suffix *īkan* is prescribed instead.

Regarding the phrase "and of the simple [word]": because of the governing rule "after *adhyardha*-preceded and *dvi-gu* [compounds]," the suffix would not apply to the simple word; hence this statement. Now, if it were not connected with "preceded by *adhyardha*," then since the suffix *īkan* would have found its scope in the simple word, the elision (*luk*) would apply to the *adhyardha*-preceded *dvi-gu*. Why is the long vowel (*dīrgha*) pronounced? Why not simply say *īkan*, since the desired form would be established through the application of the *savarṇa-dīrgha* rule? [Objection: The elision of the final syllable (*yasyeti-lopa*) would apply. [Response: It will not occur due to the force of the explicit pronunciation of the letter *i*; otherwise, he would have prescribed merely the suffix *kan*.

When the shortening [of the vowel] is effected by the rule "ke'maḥ," the form is established. Does it not follow that there must be an *avagraha* (word division)? No; the authors of the *pada-pāṭha* are not to be followed by the rules of grammar, for rather, the rules of grammar are to be followed by the authors of the *pada-pāṭha*.
[The suffix -ka is applied] after words such as *paṇa*, *pāda*, *māṣa*, and *śata* [to denote a price or value]. 5.1.34.

In this case, the substitution of *pad* does not occur, according to the rule *padyatyatadarthe*. He asks, "What is the reason? and replies: "Because it refers to a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). In the rule *pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu*, the word *pāda* is understood as referring to a limb of a living being, because only such a *pāda* has a connection with words like *ājya* that denote movement; therefore, its application continues in examples such as *padyati* and so forth. But here, "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is what is taken—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. The intention is that [the word *pāda* here] is understood through its association with the two words *paṇa* and *mā*.
Or [the suffix -maya] is applied after the word śāṇa. (Pāṇini 5.1.35)

"An exception to *ṭhañ*": although the word *śāṇa* denotes a measure (*unmāna*), nevertheless, because the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is understood in the rule *ārhāt* [Pāṇini 5.1.19], this too is excluded; thus, the sense is that *ṭhañ* alone would otherwise apply.

"It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *śata*" means that since the suffix *yat* would have applied invariably by the preceding rule, this statement is made. In the alternative where *yat* does not occur, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *kan*, which is conditioned by its being a number (*saṅkhyā*).
The suffix *aṇ* also [is applied] after a word preceded by two or three [other words].

Because it is observed in the *Vārttika*, this has been interpolated into the sūtras: that there are three forms. The first is when [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied; the second is when *yat* is applied; and the third is when there is elision (*luk*) of *ṭhañ*.
[The suffix -ka is applied] after [the word *krīta*] when it means "bought by him. || 5.1.37 ||

Regarding the word *teṣām* ("of them"): its connection is only with the phrase *asya samarthavibhaktayaḥ* ("the case-endings of this [word] are [the ones] whose meaning is compatible"), not with the phrase *pratyayārthaḥ* ("the meaning of the suffix"). For the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) would not be logical if it were "the meanings of those suffixes are being pointed out. Alternatively, a connection might somehow be possible, as in the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*).

"From that" means "from the price. The meaning is that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) for denoting that which constitutes the price is the "case of semantic competency" (*samarthavibhakti*). "Price" (*mūlya*) is said to be that which is not bent down by the root (*mūla*), namely, profit (*lābha*). "Elsewhere" means: in cases where [the word] is not the price, or where it is not the instrument, whatever instrumental case occurs—there [the rule applies]. The word "only" (*eva*) is for the sake of emphasis (*paunarvacanika*).

Furthermore, words such as *prastha* (a measure of capacity) denote objects of fixed dimensions; they do not apply when there is even a slight degree of deficiency or excess. For instance, just as the word "water" applies to both a *prastha* and a *kuḍava*, or as the word "fire" applies to both the fire in a frying pan and a forest fire; or just as in expressions such as "one grain of rice has ripened," a unity of all individual instances is perceived through the nature of the genus (*jāti*), so it is not the case with measures like the *prastha*.

Therefore, in the absence of case endings (*vibhakti*) for those [words], only as much as is expressed by the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) itself is understood. In a sentence, however, from forms such as *prasthābhyām* (by two measures) or *prasthaiḥ* (by many measures), through the force of the dual and plural endings, there arises the comprehension of that many distinct entities—such as "a pair" or "a triad.
