The suffix *ka* is applied after a word denoting time when it signifies that which occurs immediately or at the very end [of that time]. Pāṇini 5.1.114.

Regarding the statement "the word *ākālika* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*)," having stated that it refers to the whole [compound], he now demonstrates the specific derivation by analyzing it—starting with "of the word *samānakāla*" and so forth. The connection for all these sentences is with the phrase "it is an irregular formation," which will be mentioned later. Furthermore, this is a qualifier of the first and the last; the meaning is that this state of being simultaneous (*samānakālatva*) is irregularly formed as a qualifier of the first and the last, because it is heard [as such] in the rule *ādyantavacane*. And the suffix is *ikaṭ*.

In what sense [is this used]? Because of the governing rule *asya* ("of this"), it is used in the sense of the genitive case. Thus he says: "its beginning and end are simultaneous. "Simultaneous" means occurring at one and the same time. "Beginning" is birth; "end" is destruction. Since it is impossible for birth and destruction to exist at the very same moment, "simultaneity" here refers to their being immediately contiguous in time. For when time is continuous, because the distinction between moments is not perceived, there arises the cognition that "it is the same time. Thus he says: "the meaning is that it perishes immediately after having arisen."

Regarding the rule *ākālāṭ ṭhañ ca*: the author of the Vārttika maintains that the word *ākāla* is not a substitute for the word *samānakāla*, nor is the suffix *ikaṭ* prescribed. What then? The sūtra should be formulated as *ākālāṭ ṭhañ ca*. The particle *ca* serves to include the suffix *ṭhañ*, which is already under discussion. What is this *ākālāt*? That whose time is obstructed (*āvṛta*) is *ākāla*. Since an obstruction of time is impossible, the meaning is this: that whose time of destruction is simultaneous with and immediately following its time of origination.

For in this way, at the very time of its arising, there occurs the cognition that "its destruction has returned. Consequently, the suffix *ṭhan* should be prescribed in its own sense (*svārthe*) when the meaning is "beginning and end. In that case, under the rule for *ṭhañ*, there would be the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the initial udātta accent; however, if another suffix were substituted, the initial udātta accent would not be established. Thus he says: "The mention of 'time' (*kāla*) [in the rule] is redundant because of the context of *ṭhañ*."

The author of the Vṛtti, however, considering that the mention of the suffix *ṭhak* indicates the derivation of a different suffix altogether, does not accept the accentuation caused by the *ñit* marker. In his view, the word *ca* has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the rule of derivation, and the derivation must be performed; furthermore, the suffix *ṭhan* should also be prescribed after the word *ākāla*. The meaning of the word *ākāla* has already been stated, and the suffix *ṭhan* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*). Moreover, the state of being "not yet elapsed" (*avṛttakālatā*) pertains to the beginning and the end.

Another says: *āvṛttaḥ kālaḥ* (the time has returned) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; therefore, by virtue of the governing rule [Pāṇini 4.3.51], the suffix is applied in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*). In every respect, the meaning of the suffix *-tip* and of *-ṭhan* is one and the same: that its beginning and end are simultaneous. Others explain it thus: those things, such as rain and so forth, whose production occurs at the very same time—such as midday—and whose destruction occurs at that same time belonging to the second day, are called *ākālika*; this is because they persist from that time [of production] until [the end]. For indeed, for them, there is only one single time, namely midday and so forth, which constitutes both the beginning and the end.
The suffix *vati* is used when the comparison is with that [word] and the word denotes an action (*kriyā*). Pāṇini 5.1.115.

"That which is that [is the same] if it is an action"—by this, he shows that because of its identical case-ending and its predominance, the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). However, if one were to follow the order of presentation, then since the root-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), which is mentioned first, would be the qualifier, there would be a discrepancy in case-endings; consequently, something would have to be supplied in the remainder of the sentence: "That which is that third-case-competent [element], if it is an action, then it becomes [so]."

The word *tulyam* (equal) here ends in the nominative case and is not used as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), as stated in the commentary: "in the sense of this [word] *tulyam*. The term *kriyā* (action) is its qualifier. Because it begins with a general term, the neuter gender is used for *tulyam*, just as in the expression *hitam bhakṣāḥ* ("wholesome foods"). Thus, the phrase is *brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ vartate* ("he behaves equally to a Brāhmaṇa"). Now, one might object: the word *brāhmaṇa* denotes either a genus (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*), and an action cannot be equal to those two because of their absolute difference.

However, where there is some commonality and some distinction, that alone is the domain of similarity. It might be argued: the word "Brāhmaṇa" functions with reference to an action such as studying and so forth that is concomitant with being a Brāhmaṇa—[in the expression] "he acts like a Brāhmaṇa. What is the meaning? The meaning is: he acts in the same manner as a Brāhmaṇa acts. "Acting" refers to the performance of actions such as studying; since [the other person] is indeed endowed with that, there is similarity.

Even so, when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to adopt a secondary one. What, then, is the primary [meaning]? That which expresses an action (*kriyā*). Now, in the case of verbs such as *pacati* ("he cooks") and the like, because they express an action, they do not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and because they denote that which has not yet attained substantial existence (*asattvabhūta-artha*), it is impossible for them to be construed with the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā-samarthatva*). As for indeclinable gerunds (*avyaya-kṛt*)—such as *kṛtvā*, *hṛtvā*, *kartum*, *hartum*, and so forth—although they do express an action (just as in the expression *pañcakṛtvaḥ kṛtvā*, where the suffix denoting frequency [of action] arises), [they are treated differently].

Nevertheless, because it denotes an object that has become a substance (*sattvabhūta*), it lacks the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). Furthermore, since *ghañ* and other such suffixes occur when the meaning of the root is established as a completed state, they denote objects that have become substances and do not express an action. For this very reason, there is an absence of suffixes expressing frequency (*kṛtvas*) in those cases. Indeed, one does not say "five times cooking" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ pākaḥ*), but rather "five cookings" (*pañcapākāḥ*). Just as one says "five jars" (*pañcaghaṭāḥ*), one does not say "five times a jar" (*pañcakṛtvo ghaṭaḥ*).

In expressions such as "to cook in order to eat" (*bhoktum pākaḥ*), the *tumun* suffix disregards the action denoted by the verbal root. Furthermore, cases such as "the cooking of oil is equal to the cooking of ghee" (*ghṛtapākena tulyas tailapākaḥ*) do not constitute [valid] instances [of this rule].

Now, one might object: since the suffix *kṛtvasuc* in "five times" (*pañcakṛtvaḥ*) implies that Devadatta must sleep five times, and since words such as "must sleep" (*śayitavya*) denote actions, what follows? There would be scope for such comparisons as "Devadatta’s sleeping is equal to the King’s sleeping," and so forth; likewise, "walking is equal to sleeping because of its slowness," or "walking is equal to dancing because of its many variations. Furthermore, just as in cases like "cooking in order to eat" (*bhoktum pākaḥ*), the suffix *tumun* occurs in dependence upon the action expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), so too [would it apply] in the case of "with the cooking of ghee" (*dhṛtapākena*).

In cases such as *tulyastailapākaḥ* ("equal to the cooking of oil"), the suffix *-vat* may also occur; thus, that too is a possible scope. Therefore, even when the meaning of the suffix is qualified by "action" (*kriyā*), because of the inherent force (*sāmarthyāt*) of the mention of "action," the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) must also be an action itself. For an action cannot be equal to what is not an action; consequently, the suffix *-vat* must necessarily follow bases that denote actions. This being so, how can the suffix apply to words like *brāhmaṇa*, which—through much effort—are made to signify an action? It is replied:

That by which something is compared, that which is compared, and the common property shared by the two—depending upon these three, the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) proceeds. In that context, when an action (*kriyā*) is intended to serve as the standard of comparison, it necessarily depends upon a substratum for its common property; consequently, it abandons its form as an action and attains the status of a substance (*sattva*). Thus, by implication, one must resort to the notion of "having previously been" (*bhūtapūrvagati*)—that is, a thing which formerly possessed the form of an action but now, having transcended that form of action [functions as a standard].

Even when it has attained the state of a sentient being (*sattva*), that which is denoted by a word ending in the third case is accepted [as the basis for the suffix]. Thus, since a primary action is currently impossible [in the case of nouns like *brāhmaṇa*], even words such as *śayitavya* (one who ought to lie down), which denote a meaning consisting of a past action, are only secondary (*gauṇa*) [in expressing action]. And since this secondary expression of action is possible even for [words] such as *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix occurs after them as well. However, the distinction is simply this: in no circumstance whatsoever do those [words like *brāhmaṇa*] possess the quality of expressing a primary action.

If, then, the suffix [expressing comparison] were to denote the equality of two actions, in the case of "he studies like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇavad adhīte*), another common property would have to be expected, such as "he performs a study equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, it is more logical that the suffix denotes the equality of two substances (*dravya*) themselves, while the action is the common property. This is not correct; for in a case such as "the Kṣatriya is equal to the Brāhmaṇa with respect to studying," since a substance is capable of being connected with gender and number, [the suffix would have to denote the substance].

[Objection: It will be so because of its inclusion in the list [beginning with] *svar* (Pāṇini 1.1.37). [Response: In that case, it would also apply here: "upasargocchandasi dhātvarthe" (Pāṇini 1.4.59), as in "ya udvato nivato yāsi. Furthermore, even if the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) were established by virtue of being listed, who can prevent its connection with gender, number, and the power of the grammatical relation (*kāraka*), as in "svaḥ paśya"? Moreover, in common usage, a similarity is perceived only between two actions, not between two indeclinables (*avyaya*) that possess such qualities. As for what was said—that a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) must be required—this is not a fault.

Just as in expressions such as "her face is like the moon," qualities such as loveliness are understood even though they are not explicitly expressed by words, so too here, qualities such as excellence will be understood. Therefore, it was rightly said: "If that which is equal to it is an action, then [the suffix *vat* is used]. Regarding the term "equal in quality" (*guṇatulya*), it means "equal by means of qualities" (*guṇaiḥ tulyaḥ*). This is a compound with the third case ending according to the rule for "prior similar" (*pūrvasadṛśa*) compounds. For example: "He is as stout as his son. The meaning is that whatever degree of stoutness belongs to the son, the father possesses that same degree.
In that case, [the suffix *ṣyañ*] is applied after [a word ending in *taddhita*] *tasi*, provided it has the same referent as the base. 5.1.116.

For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the preceding rule? It is not so established; for in that [preceding] case, the suffix occurs after a word in the third case (instrumental), whereas here it occurs after a word in the seventh or sixth case (locative or genitive). If that is the case, then by the rule *tulyārthaiḥ* ("with words having the sense of 'equal'"), all case-meanings are encompassed by that very third case when used in conjunction with the word *iva*. For example: *brāhmaṇa iva adhīte* ("he studies like a Brāhmaṇa") is equivalent to *brāhmaṇena tulyam adhīte* ("he studies equally to a Brāhmaṇa"); *brāhmaṇam iva paśyati* ("he sees like a Brāhmaṇa") is equivalent to *brāhmaṇena tulyam paśyati* ("he sees equally to a Brāhmaṇa").

"He has studied like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇenevādhītam*), "he has studied equal to a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyam adhītam*); "he gives to one like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāyeva dadāti*), "he gives equally to a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ dadāti*); "he studies from one like a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇādivādhīte*), "he studies equally from a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyam adhīte*); "the property of a Kṣatriya is like that of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasyeva kṣattriyasya svam*), "the property of a Kṣatriya is equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ kṣattriyasya svam*); "he behaves toward a Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇa iva kṣattriye vartate*), "he behaves toward a Kṣatriya equally as toward a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ kṣattriye vartate*)—therefore, by the preceding rule, the suffix shall indeed be applied to that which ends in the third case.

And likewise, the suffix *vat* is seen after a word ending in the ablative case in the rule "pūrvavatsanaḥ. Even so, this [explanation] is not established. Why? Because in the previous rule, the suffix is applied when there is equality of action (*kriyā*), and that requires the explicit mention of "action" (*kriyā*)—for the purpose of preventing [the application of the suffix] in cases such as "the *gavaya* is equal to the cow" (*gavā tulyo gavayaḥ*). Consequently, since the suffix *vat* would not apply when there is equality between a substance (*dravya*) and a quality (*guṇa*), this [suffix] is prescribed by this rule for the sense of "like" (*iva*) after words ending in the genitive or locative case.
The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting a person worthy of that [action]. (Pāṇini 5.1.117)

The word *tat* [in the rule] is in the second case (accusative). The word *arha*, ending in the suffix *ac* by the rule *pacādyac*, would require the sixth case (genitive) for its object when used in conjunction with it; however, the second case is used here due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). Another says: this refers to the intention of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*); when it is analyzed with a finite verb as "he deserves the king" (*rājānam arhati*), then the second case is the "competent" one. In the sūtra, however, the suffix *ac* is applied to the word *arha* with the object (*karman*) as a subordinate element (*upapada*).

In this context, the mention of "action" (kriyā) continues—meaning that when something is worthy of that [action], it becomes [the suffix -vat] provided that it is an action: *rājānam arhati vṛttam* ("conduct worthy of a king") results in *rājavat vartate* ("he behaves like a king"). Here it does not occur: *rājānam arhati chattram* ("an umbrella is worthy of a king") or *brāhmaṇam arhati dadhi* ("curd is worthy of a Brahmin").

If this is so, is it not already established by the previous rule alone through the analysis (*vigraha*) "he behaves similarly to the king"? In that case, here in the example "the king behaves like a king," since there is no distinction [between the two], there is an absence of similarity (*sādṛśya*) based upon it; therefore, the suffix *vati*—which would otherwise not apply—is prescribed by this [rule]. Here too, those such as Bharata and others who are well-known for their kingship serve as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*) for people of the present day; thus, the application of *vati* is established.

When, however, the word *rājan* (king) is used as a general term, or refers to a well-known specific individual—as in "Bharata behaves like a king"—then there is no application [of the suffix] due to the absence of similarity (*sādṛśya*). In the examples "he waited upon him like one who is disciplined" (*vinītavad upasthitam*) and "he cut [it] like one with a trained hand" (*kṛtahastavad*), it is understood that "this kind of waiting upon is appropriate for those who are disciplined" and "this kind of cutting is appropriate for those with a trained hand," but not that there is a similarity. And it has been said:
"It is taught that *tadarham* is used to illustrate the meaning 'suitable' or 'appropriate for a king';
however, when the intention is to express a comparison (*upamāna*), the form *tadvat* is prescribed."

However, when a single object itself is intended to function as both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), by means of a distinction imagined through its different states, then this [sūtra] is not required. Indeed, the use of the particle *iva* is observed in such cases: "This king fights like a king," "The grammarian speaks like a grammarian," and "The battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. As it has been said: "The rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117) was not commenced in another grammatical system, because even in the case of a comparison, a distinction can be conceptually constructed."
In the Vedic language, [the suffix -ka] is applied after a preposition when it denotes the meaning of a verbal root.

Regarding the phrase "in the meaning of the root together with its instrument" (*sasādhane dhātvarthe*): if the meaning of a root is merely action (*kriyāmātra*), how can it be understood as being "together with its instrument"? It is replied: here, the mention of the word "meaning" (*artha*) need not be made; it is established simply by saying "in the root" (*dhātau*). But how could a noun or a prefix apply to a root, since it is impossible for a word to apply to another word? Its application will be understood as being to the *meaning*.

Likewise, in the rule *dhātusambandhe*, that [suffix] is applied so that the *bahuvrīhi* compound may be understood as follows: "from that which occurs when there is a means (*sādhana*) whose purpose (*artha*)—that is, its motive—is the verbal root (*dhātu*), meaning the action (*kriyā*) which is the sense of the root. The meaning of the expression *sasādhane dhātvarthe* is also exactly this: "in a means qualified by the sense of the root," and not "in a sense of the root qualified by a means."

Furthermore, prefixes (*upasarga*) are of such a nature that they qualify the very action (*kriyā*) that is expressed; for example, as in *āgacchati* ("he comes"). However, where no action is heard, they express a means (*sādhana*) qualified by an action—as in *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī"). In those cases where no action is heard, the term "meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*) is stated for the purpose of ensuring that [the prefix] occurs [there]. [Examples include] *udgatāni* ("gone up") and *nigatāni* ("gone out"). Because "forests" (*vanānām*) is the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), it takes the neuter gender.

He considers that the masculine gender in *udvataḥ* and *nivataḥ* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. Furthermore, what we have stated—that "the action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), the means (*sādhana*) is primary (*pradhānabhūta*), and therein lies the function of the prefix (*upasarga*)"—is also demonstrated by this [example]. By the word *sādhana*, a substance possessing power (*śaktimat dravya*) is meant, not power alone; therefore, because it is connected with gender and number, the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable), which is based on its literal meaning (*anvartha*), does not apply.

The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used in the sense of "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*). This word *bhāva* exists indeed with the sense of intention (*abhiprāya*), ending in the suffix *ṇa* according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix *ṇa*] follows the root *bhū*"; for example: "this is the state of affairs" (*athaiṣa bhāvaḥ*). It also exists as a term denoting any category of object (*padārtha-mātra*); for example: "for the powers of being (*bhāva-śakti*) are manifold. And it exists in the context of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others, as in "the stable emotion" (*sthāyī-bhāva*) and "the transitory emotion" (*sañcārī-bhāva*). But when ending in the suffix *ghañ*, it denotes the act of becoming (*bhavaty-artha*) and functions as a kāraka other than the agent.

The term *bhāva* has multiple meanings: for instance, in "that which exists therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), it has the sense of existence (*sattā*); in "the place where grains grow" (*dhānyānāṃ bhavane*), it has the sense of production (*utpatti*); in "having become thus" (*itthambhūte*), it has the sense of attainment (*prāpti*); in "one who is prosperous, desiring prosperity" (*bhūṣṇur bhūtikāmaḥ*), it has the sense of success (*samṛddhi*); and in rules such as "when there is a characterization by means of an action" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*), it denotes the mere meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvarthamātra*). Furthermore, another meaning is shown by the author of the Vṛtti; consequently, would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "his state of mind" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*) when it refers to intention (*abhiprāya*) and so forth? To this, he says: "from which [something] comes into being," and so on.

Since the designation "cow" and so forth proceeds with respect to cows and the like on account of the cause that is cowness (*gotva*) and so forth, and since there arises a cognition of an undifferentiated form such as "cow, cow," that object is here called by the term "existent" (*bhāva*), serving as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of words such as "cow."

In this context, the phrase "from this being" (*bhavataḥ asmāt*) is intended to demonstrate the meaning; however, no one has prescribed the suffix *ghañ* here in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Therefore, it should be understood that the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the rule "after the roots *śri*, *ni*, and *bhū*, when there is no prefix. Furthermore, because [qualities such as] intention (*abhiprāya*) and so forth are not denoted [by the word], they are not included. And it has been said: "When a word is applied to a substance on account of the presence of a certain quality (*guṇa*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote that [quality]. By the term "quality" (*guṇa*), whatever distinguishing factor dependent on another—such as a universal (*jāti*) and so forth—is meant; all such things are included here.

If only "from whose existence" (*yasya bhāvāt*) were stated, then because the word "father" (*pitṛśabda*) is applied due to the existence of the son, there would arise the notion that "fatherhood" (*pitṛtva*) resides in the son and "sonship" (*putratva*) resides in the father; thus, the mention of "existence" (*bhāva*) is for the sake of grasping the quality. "Existence" (*bhāva*) means being present (*vidyamānatvāt*). "Substance" (*dravya*) refers to that which has become the substratum (*viśeṣyabhūta*), having attained the state of being an entity (*sattvabhāvāpanna*); "application of the word" (*śabdaniveśa*)—meaning the operation (*pravṛtti*) of the word—refers to that [substance] as the denotable object (*abhidheya*) of the suffixes *sat* and *tal*. This is the meaning.

In this regard, those words such as *rūpa* (color/form) which denote the quality alone, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to them refers to the specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) inherent in that quality—thus, *rūpatva*. However, those words such as *śukla* (white), which apply to both the quality and the qualified substance either through the metaphorical identification of the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇaguṇinorabhedopacārāt*) or through the elision of the possessive suffix (*matublopāt*), take the abstract suffix to refer to the universal inherent in the quality when they apply to the quality, but to the quality itself when they apply to the substance.

Terms such as *aṇu* (small), *mahat* (large), and *dīrgha* (long) always reside in that which possesses dimension (*parimāṇin*). From these, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) denotes the quality of dimension. Likewise, in the case of [expressions] such as *ṣatvam* (the state of being *ṣ*) and *ṇatvam* (the state of being *ṇ*), the cognition refers to a specific universal inherent in distinct individual phonemes. When words like *go* (cow) denote the genus alone, then the cognition from them refers to the form of the word itself; for in this way, the form of the word is superposed upon the genus as its meaning—the thought being: "That which is the word 'cow' is the meaning of the word. Thus, in that context, the form of the word alone is the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and nothing else.

However, from words such as *go* (cow) which denote a substance, the suffix occurs in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). As for compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), although they do not denote the relation alone, they nevertheless reside in the relatum and thus require the relation as the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*); therefore, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurs after them to express that relation.

Thus, in *rājapuruṣatvam*, the relation of owner and owned is understood; in *pācakatvam*, the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*); and in *aupagavatvam* and the like, the relation between offspring and progenitor.

Some maintain that in the case of *aupagavatva*, the suffix denoting offspring (*apatyapratyaya*) expresses a genus (*jāti*). According to their view, an example of [the suffix] occurring with a different meaning (*arthāntaravṛtti*) is to be cited as follows: "In compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), there is the expression of a relation (*sambandha*), except in the cases of conventional terms (*rūḍhi*), words whose form is not distinct [from the base], and relations that are invariable. Since conventional terms such as *gaurakhara*, *saptaparṇa*, *lohitaśāli*, and so on, denote substances delimited by specific genera, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to them only in the sense of the genus itself.

In this way, "the state of being a potter" (*kumbhakāratva*) and "the state of being an elephant" (*hastitva*) are of an undifferentiated form. Even though words such as *śukla* ("white") and others are understood to end in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) when the possessive suffix *matup* is elided (*luk*), nevertheless, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to them denotes the quality (*guṇa*) itself. It does not denote a relation between the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), because—as in the case of a genus and its instances—the relation of difference has been suppressed by the worldly convention of identity expressed as "this is that" (*so 'yam*).

By means of the rule prescribing elision (*luk*)—namely, "there is elision after words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacanebhyo luk*)—it is explained that the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) is denoted by the word itself without [the addition of] a suffix, and not through the production of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) based on a relation. Because the connection is invariable, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in *sattā* (existence) refers to the genus (*jāti*) alone; for an existent entity does not deviate from its connection with existence, and thus, since there is no dependence on a connection with existence, the suffix does not denote the relation.

Since the relationship between "king" and "man" is occasional (*kādacitka*), the word *rājapuruṣa* denotes its own referent in dependence upon that [relationship]; therefore, it is logical that the suffix conveys the relationship. Consequently, among existing things (*padārtha*), it is existence (*satta*) itself—which is eternally inherent (*nityasamavāyin*)—that is the cause for the application of words and is denoted by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), and not the relationship called inherence (*samavāya*) between "existent" and "existence."

In the case of *dhavakhadiratvam*, there is a cognition of a collection of universals (*jātisamudāya*) arising from a dvandva compound of universals; in cases such as *kutvam*, there is a cognition of the name-form superimposed upon the named objects. Others, however, say that it is the "relation between the name and the named. And it has been said: "From a universal or a quality [a suffix occurs] with respect to a universal or a quality; from a compound, a primary derivative (*kṛt*), or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [it occurs] with respect to a relation; and in the case of *ḍittha* and so on, [it occurs] with respect to its own form; and from *dhava-khadira*, [it occurs] with respect to a collection of universals."

In this context, however, regarding such instances as "diversity" (*nānātva*), "simultaneity" (*sahatva*), and "simultaneous occurrence" (*yaugapadya*), the word *nānā* functions with respect to its referent in the sense of being non-coexistent; the word *saha* refers to that which is coexistent; and the word *yugapat* also refers to that which occurs simultaneously. Consequently, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied to [the states of] non-coexistence and so forth. This should be understood similarly in other cases as well, according to what is applicable.

In this case, when it is intended to express the non-existence of the state of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*) through its simultaneous connection with both the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, first there is a *nañ*-compound; subsequently, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied. Thus, in the forms *abrāhmaṇatvam* and *abrāhmaṇatā*, because the *tva* suffix is "remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*), the *nañ*-compound is established first, followed by *tva* and *tal*; consequently, the state of being a non-Brahmin (*abrāhmaṇatva*) results. It does not have an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the prior member of the compound.

[Objection: But would not the suffixes *tva* and *tal* apply [to form *abrāhmaṇatva* and *abrāhmaṇatā*]? [Reply: No, because it is dependent (*sāpekṣatvāt*). Wherever the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) depends on the meaning of another word—such as in the case of a *nañ*-compound—it does not apply. [Objection: In that case, even the *nañ*-compound would not be possible, since the word "Brāhmaṇa" depends on the state of being (*bhāva*)? [Reply: Not so; for here the word "Brāhmaṇa" is the primary element (*pradhāna*), and a *nañ*-compound has the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as its primary element. Furthermore, a compound is indeed possible even when the primary element is dependent, as in the example: "the king's man is handsome" (*rājapuruṣo 'bhirūpaḥ*).

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), in certain instances, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are applied first, followed by the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*)—as in *ayonitvāya* (for the sake of not being born) and *aśithilatvāya* (for the sake of not being loose). In these cases, the accent of the negative particle (*nañ-svara*) alone prevails; however, in some instances, the reverse occurs. Regarding suffixes expressing abstract state (*bhāva-pratyaya*) other than *tva* and *tal*, it is desired that the same [suffix] be applied first, followed by the negative compound; thus, in examples such as *aprathimā*, because the suffix is established first, the accent of the negative particle alone prevails.

Furthermore, in cases such as *aśauklyam* ("non-whiteness"), since the negative particle (*nañ*) is not included within the base word (*prakṛti*), the suffix *vṛddhi* would not apply to the word *śukla* and so on prior to the *nañ*-compound; moreover, because of the prohibition "not after a word preceded by *nañ*" (*na nañpūrvāt*), the suffix *ṣyañ* would also not occur. Or, even if *ṣyañ* were applied, the *vṛddhi* of the negative particle would still occur. [This objection is answered: It is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For this reason—that he teaches the prohibition of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) when a *nañ*-compound is the object of application in the list of *yuvādi* words, specifically in *puruṣātve* and *hṛdayātve*—it indicates that a suffix which is an exception to *tva* and *tal* occurs after a word related to the meaning of *nañ*, overriding the *nañ*-compound due to its higher priority.
And [the suffix] *āc* [is applied] before *tvat*. 5.1.120.

Regarding *prathima*: there is elision of the *ṭi* suffix by the rules "*turiṣṭhemeyassu*" and "*ṭeḥ*"; the substitution of *r* for the vowel *ṛ* occurs by the rule "*raṛto halāderlaghoḥ*". Regarding *pārthava*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "*igantācca laghupūrvāt*".

"By exceptions," and so forth. [The author] will state the exceptions (*apavāda*) to *imanij* and the others, as well as to *tva* and *tal*; this [present rule] is for the purpose that there may be co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with those. [Objection: But surely, by the very fact of being marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*), *tva* and *tal* will be carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], and thus they will apply even in the domain of the exceptions? [Reply: That is not so. Because the subsequent sentences lack expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) due to the specific mention of suffixes, and because *tva* and *tal* were already prescribed in the preceding sūtra, there is no expectancy [for them]. Therefore, it cannot be understood that *tva* and *tal* are being carried over.

"And for the sake of prescribing [suffixes] in the sense of the object (*karmani*). From those very bases to which the suffix *ṣyañ* and others are prescribed in the sense of the object, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* also occur in that same sense of the object, and not from every nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī*, *āp*, or *p*. The particle *ca* (and) is intended to include them even after *nañ* and *snañ*; otherwise, if the rule "from *strī* and *puṃs*" were treated as a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*), then since *nañ* and *snañ* would be prescribed in that very same section with reference to the meanings prior to the word *bhavana*, they would lack proximity (*sannidhāna*) within this particular context, and thus their inclusion (*samāveśa*) would not be established, just as in the case of *imanij* and other such suffixes.

Even though [the rules for] *nañ* and *snañ* are technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*), under the view that the rules are taught according to their enunciation (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), the proximity of *nañ* and *snañ* occurs only within this very section, namely "from *strī* and *puṃs*" (*strīpuṃsābhyām*). They do not, however, appear in the midst of suffixes such as *imanij* and others. Even under the view that the rules apply at the time of operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), since the meanings [of the base] exist prior to the suffix *-bhavana*, *nañ* and *snañ* must present themselves there.

In this regard, if the presence of the suffixes *nañ* and *snan* occurs at the very point of understanding the meaning "the state of being" (*bhāve*)—as in the rules "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* [denote] its state" (*tasya bhāvastvatalau*) and "The suffixes *nañ* and *snan* [denote] the state of feminine and masculine" (*strīpuṃsābhyāṃ bhāve nañsnañau*)—then, even though they are in proximity, they occur before the rule "And up to *tvāt*" (*ā ca tvāt*). However, if the presence of *nañ* and *snan* occurs after the understanding of the application of the general rule and the specific prescription, then *nañ* and *snan* occur after the rule "The suffix *tva* [denotes] Brahman" (*brahmaṇastva*).

In every respect, [the suffixes] *nañ* and *snan* do not apply within the scope of the rule "up to and including *ā ca tvāt*. In the rule "guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca," one should not suspect the presence of *nañ* and *snan* in the sense of "karma" (object); for since the meaning of "karma" is introduced here as being connected to specific bases (*prakṛti*), it cannot be connected with other bases. However, according to the view that the governing heading (*adhikāra*) applies, because *nañ* and *snan* recur with every sūtra and are included within the group beginning with *imanij*, their inclusion is established by the very fact of the heading "up to and including *ā ca tvāt*."

Furthermore, since even there the meaning itself serves as the limit, the application occurs only to meanings; therefore, even under the view that [the suffix] has governing authority (*adhikāra*), it does not possess internal status. Consequently, in every respect, the co-occurrence with *nañ* and *snañ* must be stated by means of the particle *ca* alone.

The suffix *taddhita* *ṭhaÑ* (i.e., *ika*) is not applied after a *tatpuruṣa* compound beginning with the negative particle *nañ*, except in the case of the words *catura*, *saṅgata*, *lavaṇa*, *vaṭa*, *ac*, *budha*, *katara*, *sala*, and *seba*. Pāṇini 5.1.121.

The statement "a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately follows" serves to dispel the misconception that this prohibition applies to the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. The phrase "those suffixes which follow from here onwards" is understood through its connection with the rule "up to and including *tvat*. The expression "beginning with *catur*" means tatpuruṣa compounds ending in *catur* and so forth, provided they are preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. Now, one might object: the suffix *vati* is prescribed after bases derived by rules such as "the suffix *imanij* optionally [is added] after *pṛthu* and others."

Furthermore, no base (prakṛti) preceded by the negative particle *nañ* is taken there [in those rules], and the rule regarding suffixes added after a specific element (*tadantavidhi*) is prohibited when the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is used as a marker of its own form. However, where there is no such mention of the specific form—as in "the suffix *yañ* occurs after a word ending in *pati*," "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in *hāyana*," "also after a word ending in an *ik* vowel that has a light penultimate syllable," and "the suffix *vuñ* occurs after a word with *y* as its penultimate letter that has a heavy penultimate syllable"—there is indeed the possibility of application from a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by *nañ*. He demonstrates this: he will state that "the suffix *yañ* occurs after words ending in *pati* and after *purohita*, etc. Thus, we have *apatitva* and *apatitā*.

It has been stated that this [rule] is under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "up to *tvatal*" (Pāṇini 5.1.119). Consequently, by the rule "after a word ending in *pat*" (Pāṇini 5.1.128), the suffixes *tva* and *tal*—which are themselves governed by that heading—are also prescribed. What follows from this? Just as in the case of the suffix *yak*, a prohibition would apply to *tva* and *tal* as well. Let it be so that there is a prohibition of the governed *tva* and *tal*; however, *tva* and *tal* will still occur by virtue of the rule "the state of that" (Pāṇini 5.1.119), since there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) of that.

If its application were restricted only to those [bases] ending in *pati* and so forth, then this [rule] should have been stated immediately after the rule for "ending in *pati*" (*patyantāt*), and that same [rule] would have continued to apply in subsequent instances as well. If that is the case, then because the governing heading of the prohibition (*pratiṣedhādhikāra*) is introduced at this point, it is understood that the prohibition applies to suffixes such as *-imanij* and others as well. But was it not said: "There is no possibility [of the rule applying] because there is no rule regarding 'that which ends in that' (*tadantavidhi*)"? If so, then this [introduction of the prohibition here] indicates that there *is* a *tadantavidhi* in subsequent rules.

What is the purpose of making this known? It is so that suffixes such as *iman* and others may be established after a *bahuvrīhi* compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, and after a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by another word ending in *pṛthu* and so on—for instance, "that which has no broad [parts] is *apṛthuḥ*," and "the state of being that is *paramapṛthu-bhāvaḥ*. However, the suffix *iman* and others are not desired here; for this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* also demonstrated the exclusion of such cases by showing examples like "he does not have clever [parts], thus he is *apaṭuḥ*. Therefore, the purpose of including this [rule] here must be considered. In examples such as *ācāturya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because the word belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* group.
The suffix *iman* is optionally applied after the group of words beginning with *pṛthu*.

"The mention of the word *vā* (or) is for the purpose of allowing the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of suffixes. Here, in the case of words such as *pṛthu* and *mṛdu*, which end in *ik* and have a light vowel (*laghu*) preceding the final consonant, there is the co-occurrence of the suffix *aṇ*. In the case of quality-expressive words (*guṇavacana*) such as *caṇḍa* and *khaṇḍa*, there is the co-occurrence of *ṣyañ*; and in the case of words expressing age (*vayovacana*) such as *bāla* and *vatsa*, there is the co-occurrence of *añ* characterized by that category. But as for the co-occurrence of *tva* and *tal*, is it not already established by the rule "and up to *tva*" (*ā ca tvāt*)? To this he replies: "But *tva* and *tal* indeed occur everywhere."
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied after [words ending in] *varṇa*, *dṛḍha*, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "from those expressing specific castes (*varṇa-viśeṣa*)," there is no inclusion of the word-form itself (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*). If that were the case, one would have listed the word *varṇa* itself among the *dṛḍha*-group. Furthermore, the word *varṇa* denotes physical appearance (*rūpa*), not [castes] such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth; this is because of its association with quality-words (*guṇa-vacana*) like *dṛḍha*. For this very reason, due to that association, the inclusion of synonyms does not occur through the mention of the word *varṇa*.

How so? For words such as *dṛḍha* (firm) and *āyasa* (iron) denote substances (*dravya*) where qualities (*guṇa*) are subordinate; therefore, by association with them, the word *varṇa* (color/quality) is also understood in that same sense. Thus, since words like *varṇa* and *dṛḍha* are already established as quality-words (*guṇavacana*), their explicit mention [in the rule] is for the sake of the suffix *-aniC*. [Examples: *aucitī* (propriety), *yāthākāmī* (acting according to one's will). Because the group beginning with *brāhmaṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *-ṣyaÑ* is applied, followed by *ṅīṣ*; then, by the rule "the *y* of a *taddhita* suffix following a consonant," there is the elision of *y*.

Regarding the phrase "of *viyāta*, *vilābha*, *vimati*, and *vimanaska*": the meaning is that the suffix *ṣyañ* occurs immediately after compounds ending in those [words] beginning with *vi-* and so forth. Thus: *viyātatvam*, *viyātatā*, *viyātimā*, *vaiyātyam*; *vilābhatvam*, *vilābhavatā*, *vilābhimā*, *vailābhyam*; *vimatitvam*, *vimatitā*, *vimatimā*, *vaimatyam*—since it ends in a short vowel (*iganta*), the suffix *aṇ* also occurs, as in *vaimatam*; *vimanastvam*, *vimanastā*, *vimanimā*, *vaimanasyam*.

*viśāradatva*, *viśāradatā*, *viśāradimā*, and *vaiśāradya*; [the suffix] *ṣyañ* occurs after *sama* when it is followed by *mati* or *manas* in a compound: *saṃmati* and *saṃmanas*. From these two compounds, the suffix *ṣyañ* follows immediately: *saṃmatitva*, *saṃmatitā*, *saṃmatimā*, and *sāmmatya*; as before, there is also *saṃmata* with the suffix *aṇ*. [Likewise: *saṃmanastva*, *saṃmanastā*, *saṃmanimā*, and *sāṃmanasya*.

The suffix *ya* is applied after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*) and after the class of words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, in the sense of the object (*karman*), and also [in the sense of the agent].

The word *karman* denotes action (*kriyā*), not the object as a grammatical factor (*sādhana-karman*); for it is action that can possess a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Furthermore, words such as *sattva*, *guṇa*, *brāhmaṇa*, and so forth denote [entities], and therefore they have no connection with the object as a grammatical factor. Rather, action is produced by them for the sake of its own manifestation.

How, then, is poetry (*kāvyam*) the "object" (*karman*) of the poet (*kavi*)? For in that case, no action (*kriyā*) is denoted; rather, what is it? It is the work (*grantha*) produced by him. To this they reply: the suffix is prescribed precisely for the object of an action, but its application to that which is produced by it is figurative (*aupacārika*). Another says: both the word *karman* in the rule (*sūtra*) and the word *kriyā* in the commentary (*vṛtti*) are derived from the root *kṛ* (to do/make) as their basis of derivation; thus, the meaning is "the effect of an action. Therefore, the suffix occurs only with respect to the "instrumental object" (*sādhana-karman*), which is that which is pervaded by the activity (*kṛti*).

The group beginning with "brāhmaṇa" is an *akṛtigaṇa* because it has not been formally closed by a specific rule (*avṛtkṛtatvāt*). He demonstrates this very point by stating: "the word 'ādi' (beginning) expresses a type (*prakāra*)."

For what purpose, then, is there the mention of "words expressing qualities" (*guṇavacana*) and the enumeration of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth? [The answer is: for some, it is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*); for some, it is for the sake of prescribing suffixes in their own sense (*svārthe*); and for some, it is for the sake of subverting what would otherwise subvert [the rule]. In that regard, from the word *brāhmaṇa*, since the suffix *añ*—characterized by denoting a genus of living beings (*prāṇabhṛjjāti*)—would [otherwise] apply, [the mention is made] to prevent that. From *māṇava* and *vāḍava*, since the suffix *vuñ*—characterized by denoting a lineage (*gotra*)—would apply, [they are mentioned]. The reading [of *arhat*] is for the sake of the augment *num*; [specifically], the suffix *śatṛ* applies according to the rule "the root *arh* is used in the sense of praise," resulting in *ārhantya*.

Since *cora* and *dhūrta* belong to the *manojñādi* group, the suffix *vuñ* would apply; however, that indeed occurs here as well. Regarding the four terms beginning with *ārādhya*, since they denote a *janapada* (region), the suffix *añ* is applied. When the elision (*luk*) of that suffix is prescribed by the rule "there is elision after *kamboja* and others," the *gotra-vuñ* would then apply; the recitation [of these terms] is for the purpose of establishing the suffix in its own sense (*svārtha*) for all terms from *ekabhāva* up to *anyabhāva*. Accordingly, there is a usage in the Vārttika: "But the state of being otherwise (*ānyabhāvya*) [is established], because of the intervention of time-words."

Regarding the words *akṣetrajña* and *anīśvara*, the prohibition [of the suffix *aṇ*] by the rule "not after a word preceded by the negative particle *na*" would have applied; regarding *kuśala* and others, the suffix *aṇ* (called *am*) would have applied because they belong to the *yuvan*-class; regarding the word *bāliśa*, the suffix *añ* characterized by the *vyañ* group would have applied; regarding the word *rājan*, the suffix *yak* would have applied because it belongs to the *purohita*-class; and regarding *gaṇapati* and *adhipati*, the suffix *yak* characterized by the ending *-pati* would have applied. The inclusion of the remaining words such as *alasa* and others is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

Regarding the rule *sarvavedādibhyaḥ svārthe* (Pāṇini 5.1.124): *sarvavedāḥ* means "all the Vedas"; this is a *pūrvakāla-* compound (meaning "those [Vedas] which are all"). From *sarvaveda*, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule *tad adhīte tad veda* (Pāṇini 4.2.59). Then, by the rule *sarvasāder ddhigoś ca laḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix. Thus, *sarvaveda* itself becomes *sārvavedya*. Regarding *cāturvaidya*: from the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a *dvigu* compound is formed for one who studies four Vedas; the suffix *aṇ* is elided, and thus *caturveda* itself becomes *cāturvaidya*. Note that in the case of *cāturvaidya*, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound.

In some places, however, the reading is *cāturvaidyasya*; in that case, the word *siddhayaḥ* (accomplishments) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "after *vidyā*, *lakṣaṇa*, *kalpa*, and *sūtra*, when preceded by *catur-*," etc., as before; there is elision (*luk*) as before, and thus *cāturvaidyaḥ* means one who has studied the four *vidyās*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after the words *stena*, etc., and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel and the following consonant (*an*).

Regarding the word *stena*: from the root *stai* meaning "to steal," the suffix *ap* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied, resulting in *stenaḥ*. The phrase "of the word *na*" indicates that this refers to the entire compound (*saṅghāta*). However, if it were taken as referring to the individual phoneme (*varṇa*), then once the *n* is elided, the *a* would be subject to elision by the rule *yasyeti ca*; and because of the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* regarding a preceding operation, the substitution of *ay* would result. [Objection: Even if it refers to the entire compound, does not the rule *allo 'ntyasya* apply to the final letter? [Response: The elision of the final letter is already established by the rule *yasyeti ca*.

In that case, by virtue of the capacity of the initial undertaking (*ārambhasāmarthya*), it will apply to everything; furthermore, they recite the metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "The rule concerning the final letter does not apply to what is meaningless, except in the case of modifications of reduplication. They also perform a split of the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) as *stenāt*. Although this was not stated in the Bhāṣya, it has been mentioned here because of the great frequency of the usage of the word *stainya*.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *kapi* and *jñāti*.

In this case, since there are two [items] belonging to the *kapin* class and exactly two meanings—namely, the state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)—the rule of "correspondence by number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) would apply. Anticipating such an objection regarding rules like "after words ending in *pati*, and after *purohita* etc., [the suffix] *yak*" and "after words ending in *hāyana*, and after *yuvan* etc., [the suffix] *aṇ*", he says: "Correspondence by number is not intended in this section. The meaning is that the quality of being *svarita* (which triggers such correspondence) has not been declared for these items.
The suffix *ya* is applied after words ending in *patyanta*, *purohita*, and so forth.

The word *rājan* takes the suffix *yaK* when it is not in a compound (*ase*). That is to say, the word *rājan* produces the suffix *yaK* in an uncompounded state: the state or action of a king is *rājyam*. Why "not in a compound" (*ase*)? [Consider] *ādhirājyam*, which takes the suffix *yaÑ* because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Even though the word *rājan* is listed there [in the *brāhmaṇa*-class], this very prohibition (*ase*) indicates that "there is an application of the rule by extension (*tadantavidhi*) to this word *rājan*. And thus, since the listing in the *brāhmaṇa*-class finds its purpose in compounds, in an uncompounded state only the specifically prescribed suffix *yaK* occurs.

Another says: "Since [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is already established after words ending in *brāhmaṇa* and so forth because they belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇas*, the inclusion of the word *rājan* there is for the purpose of its co-occurrence with *yak*; and thus it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya under the section on the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice: 'The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the action belonging to that [word]. "

The suffix *añ* is applied after words denoting living beings (*prāṇin*), genus (*jāti*), age (*vayas*), speech (*vacana*), and the group beginning with *udgātṛ*. Regarding "living beings" (*prāṇabhṛt*): these are sentient creatures (*prāṇin*). The term "living being" was not used [instead of "sentient creature"] for the sake of variety. Because of the mention of "living beings," the suffix does not apply in cases such as *tṛṇatvam* or *tṛṇatā*; because of the mention of "genus," it does not apply in cases such as *devadattatvam*. However, when a word ending in *iṅ* has a light vowel preceding it, the suffix *aṇ* applies by virtue of its higher priority, as in *taittira*. Among the words in the *udgātrādi* group, those that denote officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would otherwise require the suffix *cha* by the rule *hotrābhyaśchaḥ*; therefore, *añ* is specifically prescribed here.

When the suffix *guṇavacana-lakṣaṇa* *ṣyañ* applies to *su* and *duṣṭhu*, and the suffix *aṇ*—characterized by having *vadhū* as its initial—is applicable, and when *tva* and *tal* are applicable to the remaining [bases], the following occurs: Regarding the rule *subhagaṃ mantre*: the word-form *subhaga* produces the suffix *añ* when used in the context of a mantra—as in *mahate saubhagāya*. Because all grammatical rules are optional (*vikalpita*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the rule *hṛdbhagasindhvanta* (which prescribes vṛddhi of the first vowel of the second member) does not apply here.
For this very reason, the suffix *añ* is sometimes absent in a mantra—as in *saubhāgyam asyai dattvāya*.

*Hāyanāntayuvādibhyo’ṇ*: This prescribes *aṇ* after words ending in *hāyana*, as well as after the group beginning with *yuvan*, where *tva* and *tal* would otherwise have applied. Thus, from *yuvan* we get *yauvanam*. Here, by the rule *an*, the original stem (*prakṛti*) is retained; furthermore, because it belongs to the *manojñādi* class, the suffix *vuñ* may also occur. The word *sthavira* is listed [in the *yuvanādi* group] because the suffix *añ* would otherwise apply to it by virtue of its denoting an age (*vayaḥ*). As for the word *hotṛ*, since it belongs to the *udgātrādi* class, it likewise takes *añ* only. [The form] *pauruṣeyāsaḥ* [is derived similarly].

The word *puruṣa* produces the suffix *aṇ* when not in a compound, as in *pauruṣam*. Since it denotes a genus of living beings (*prāṇabhṛjjāti*), the suffix *añ* would otherwise be expected; however, this word refers to the human species and is not a synonym for the word *pumān* (male), though it expresses the masculine gender. This is seen even in the feminine, as in the example: "In this and that [place], one should give two female oxen (*puruṣī*) and two female cows (*dhenukā*). Why is the word *asa* mentioned? [To exclude cases where it forms a compound, such as] *rājapuruṣatvam*. As for the word *kamaṇḍalu*, since it ends in the vowel *i*, the suffix *aṇ* is already established by rule; its inclusion here is for the purpose of excluding the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. [The examples are] *hṛdayāsa* and so forth.

The word *hṛdaya* produces the suffix *aṇ* when not in a compound: *hṛdayasya bhāvaḥ* (the state of the heart) becomes *hārdam*. By the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu*, there is the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya*. Why [is it said] "not in *alaṃs*" (*ase*)? [Consider: *ahṛdayatvam*. Since the prohibition of the application of rules to a base ending in a specific word is already established by the fact that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) possesses a specific form, the prohibition regarding compounds (*samāsa*) is of doubtful utility. For words beginning with *kuśala* and ending with *kṣetrajña*, the suffix *ṣyañ* also occurs because they belong to the *brāhmaṇa*-class.

Regarding the rule *śrotriyasya ghalopaśca*: when the view is that in the expression *śrotriyam̐śchandodhīte* ("one who studies the Veda is a *śrotriya*"), there is a substitution of *śrotṛ* for *chandas* and the suffix *gha*, then there is the elision of *gh*. However, when the view is that "the word-form expresses the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthe padavacanam*), then by the word *gha*, the form *ya* is indicated. In some places, however, the reading is *yalopaśca* ("elision of *ya*").

In that case, if there were elision of the *y* (the *yaṇ*), the term "group" (*saṅghāta*) would have to be mentioned; however, if only the letter (*varṇa*) were elided, then when the *y* of *yakārasya* is dropped, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the *yaṇ*-substitution to the vowel *i*. But if the group as a whole is elided, then the *y* of *yakārasya* is indeed dropped, resulting in the form *śrautra*—meaning "the state of being a *śrotriya*."
And [the suffix *aṇ*] is applied after a stem ending in *i* or *u*, provided that the preceding syllable is light.

By the inclusion of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as a whole is qualified. If this is so, the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) must mean either a "part" (*avayava*) or a "position" (*vyavasthā*). In the first case, the suffix would apply only to words like *iṣu* where the very first letter is light; in the second case, however, it would apply even to words like *pāṇḍu*.

One might raise the objection: "When it is said that 'the preceding [element] is light,' the word *pūrva* (preceding) refers specifically to a constituent part; yet even that functions only with reference to a limit (*avadhi*). In that case, if nothing specific is mentioned, one would understand 'the very first of all'; however, here, due to proximity, it must refer only to the immediately preceding element. To demonstrate this, he says: "that which has a light preceding [element]," and so forth. By the phrase "by that," he means by a stem ending in *iK* that has a light vowel preceding it. In this interpretation, the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is redundant, because the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is already established by the fact that the stem ending in *iK* is qualified by the condition of having a light vowel preceding it.
"How is it 'kāvyam'?"—the question is whether it ought to be "kāvam."

"From a word having *y* as its penultimate (*yopadha*) and having a heavy syllable (*gurūpottama*) as the penultimate-to-the-penultimate, the suffix *vuñ* [is applied]. Regarding "of three or more," and so forth, this has been explained under the rule *aṇiñoranārṣayoḥ*. "It should be stated that [the suffix is applied] optionally after *sahāya*"; since the suffix would have applied obligatorily by the preceding rule, this provides an option.
And [the suffix *ka*] is added after a copulative compound (*dvandva*) and after words such as *manojña*. (Pāṇini 5.1.132)

From *patyantadvandva*, the suffix *yak* is obtained; from that ending in *hāyana*, the suffix *aṇ* is obtained; from others, however, *al* is obtained. Even among the *manojñādi* group, *ṣyañ* is obtained because they are qualities (*guṇavacana*). From *cora* and *dhūrta* as well, *ṣyañ* alone is obtained because they belong to the *brāhmaṇādi* class. From the word *yuva*, *aṇ* is obtained because it belongs to the *yuvādi* class. From the remaining words, *tva* and *tal* are obtained. In the case of *amuṣyaputra*, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case occurs by way of a formal exception (*nipātana*).

The suffix *cha* is applied after [a word denoting] a lineage (*gotra*) or a practice (*caraṇa*) to form derivatives expressing praise (*ślāghā*), disregard (*atyākāra*), or the acquisition of that [quality]. (Pāṇini 5.1.133)

Regarding the phrase "denoting a lineage" (*gotravācina*): since this occurs outside the section governing *apatya* (descendants), the term *gotra* is understood here in its worldly sense; that is to say, it refers to that which denotes a descendant. In other words, it means "ending in an affix that signifies a descendant."

Another says: "The *gotras* mentioned in the chapter on *grāmaṇī* are what is intended here. Regarding the rule *caraṇavācinaśca*: the word *caraṇa* is conventionally used for persons who study a particular Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Since both [the *gotra* and the *caraṇa*] are classes (*jāti*)—as in the expression "together with the *gotras* and the *caraṇas*"—the suffix *añ* would have been required by the rule *prāṇabhṛjjāti*. Regarding the phrase "respectively for the two meanings of state and action": it was already stated previously that "in this entire section, a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) is not desired. Regarding the phrase "when *ślāghā* and so forth are the objects": [this refers to the construction where these verbs take the dative].

The meaning of the suffixes [denoting] *ślāghā* (praise) and so forth does not apply here, because the meanings of the suffixes—namely *bhāva* (action/state) and *karman* (object)—are what are currently under discussion (*adhikṛta*). Nor can they be qualifiers of the meaning of the suffixes—i.e., that those two, *bhāva* and *karman*, are specifically *ślāghā* and so forth; for such a thing is impossible. For *bhāva* is indeed the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word, and praise and so forth are not the ground for the application of words denoting *gotra* (lineage) and *caraṇa* (Vedic school); nor is there any established renown for words denoting *gotra* and *caraṇa* as being the objects of praise and so forth.

Therefore, in the case of [words] such as *ślāghā* (boasting), the meaning is simply that the agent (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) have become the objects of the action as things to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*). "One who has understood that" (*tadavetaḥ*) means "one who has attained that," because the root *iṇ* has the sense of "attaining. Or, "one who knows that" (*tajjñaḥ*), because the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ava* is well-known in the sense of "knowing. By the word *tat* (that) here, the agent and the object belonging to the lineage (*gotra*) and the school (*caraṇa*) are referred to. In the example *gārgikayā*, there is the elision of *ya* according to the rule *āpatyasya ca*.

The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *hotrā*. The word *hotrā* denotes the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). It is derived from the root *hu* with the suffix *tran*, and by its very nature, it is feminine even when referring to the priests. Examples include *ācchāvākīyam* and *brāhmaṇācchaṃsīyam*. Even the feminine gender is observed in the Veda, as in: "He should perform his *ācchāvākīyā*."
The suffix *tva* is applied after the word *brahman*.

Regarding *brahmaṇastvaḥ*: although one should have said *na* (negation), since the suffix *cha* is prohibited, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are established by the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau*. The intention is that there is economy (*lāghava*) because the case-ending need not be uttered. As for the statement "that which is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*)," he shows its purpose through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *hotrābhyaḥ*.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra;
now begins the second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
The suffix *khañ* is applied after the word *dhānya* when it occurs in the sense of a place where grain is grown, i.e., a field.

From the root *dhinoti*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the final letter and the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *i*. Thus, that which nourishes (*dhinoti*) is *dhānya*. Indeed, it is seen [in the Vedic text]: "Thou art grain (*dhānya*); nourish the gods. In the expression *dhānyānām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent with respect to the act of becoming (*bhavana*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) to form *bhavana*. From the root *kṣi*, the suffix *ṭran* is applied to form *kṣetra*. It is called *bhavana* because things exist (*bhavati*) or are born (*jāyate*) therein.

By this, he demonstrates that the root *bhū* is understood here in the sense of "origination" (*utpatti*), and not in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*). And this is obtained from the inclusion of the word "field" (*kṣetra*). For the word "field" denotes the substratum for the origination of grasses and grains. Indeed, the earth does not receive the designation "field" with respect to the mere existence of grains; rather, the "receptacle" (*kusūla*) is the place where beans exist. The point is that if the word "field" were not included, there would be the possibility of including the root *bhū* even in its sense of "existence."

Furthermore, one might argue that since the word *bhavana* is conventionally restricted (*ruḍha*) to mean "house," the rule would apply only to cases such as *mudgānāṃ gṛham* ("the house of mung beans"). If, then, the inclusion of the word *kṣetra* ("field") is necessary here, let that alone suffice; what is the purpose of including *bhavana*? [In the example *dhānyānāṃ kṣetram*] the genitive case in *dhānyānām* is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), while the field (*kṣetra*) serves as the meaning for the suffix. Nor does this lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because even though the word *kṣetra* has multiple meanings—such as "body" or "wife"—it refers here specifically to the place of origin due to its connection with grain. Thus, the inclusion of the word *bhavana* has a questionable purpose.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied after the words *vrīhi* and *śāli*.

Here too, the genitive case is the governing case (samarthavibhakti) precisely because of the specific mention [in the rule]; however, the author of the Vṛtti did not state it because it is already understood by following the previous [rule].
[The suffix -mayaṭ is applied] after *yava*, *yavaka*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and so forth. 5.2.3.
In this case, the genitive case as the governing inflection is obtained through the force of the meaning of the suffix.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *tala*, *māṣa*, *umā*, *bhaṅgā*, and *aṇu*.

Regarding the statement that "the suffix *kañ* occurs optionally after [words for] grains," it is logical that *kañ* occurs optionally after words such as *aṇu*, *tila*, and *māṣa*, because they are grains (*dhānya*); however, since *umā* (hemp) and *bhaṅgā* (dried hemp) are not grains, this would seem incorrect. For indeed, only grains are recited in the *camaka-anuvākas* beginning with "These rice-grains of mine" (*vrīhayo me*), and these alone are grains; yet *umā* and *bhaṅgā* are not recited therein. To this he replies: "The status of being a grain is certainly attributed even to *umā* and *bhaṅgā*."

The *camaka-anuvāka* is not intended for the purpose of enumerating grains, because stones and other non-grains are recited therein, and even among grains, some such as *kodrava* are not included. Therefore, the determination of what constitutes a grain must come from another source; in this regard, there is the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "There are seventeen kinds of grains," and in that list, both *umā* (flax) and *bhaṅga* (hemp) are recited. Consequently, it is entirely correct that the suffix *khañ* occurs in the alternative case by means of those two as well.
The suffixes *śa* and *khañ* are applied after the word *sarvacarman*.

Regarding the phrase "from that which is in the third case": since the word *kṛta* has the sense of "made," and because the hide (*carman*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the third case is obtained through semantic necessity (*sāmarthya*); this is the governing case (*samartha-vibhakti*). This reference is made after forming a compound of the word *sarva* with the word *carman*. Someone might mistakenly think that because the compound *sarvacarmaṇaḥ* occurs only when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*), the word *sarva* must therefore be connected specifically with the word *carman*; to preclude this, he says: "And here the word *sarva*... [is connected with *kṛta*]. If so, how then is the compound formed? To this he replies: "In this case, this... [is the construction].

The meaning is that this is due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*). But what is the reason that the word *sarva* is connected with *kṛta* and not with *carman*? To this he says: "All [the leather] by means of the hide," and so forth. The intended sense of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is the sentence-meaning "made entirely from leather. If it were connected with *carman*, then if there were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) such as *sarvacarma*, the meaning would be "made from leather belonging to all [of something]."

Now, if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound, it would mean "made by the entire hide," but in neither case is the entirety of what has been made obtained. Therefore, the sense is that it is logical for [the word *sarva*] to be connected only with "what has been made" (*kṛta*).
The suffix *kha* is applied after [the word] *yathāmukha* when it means "facing toward. (Pāṇini 5.2.6)

"It is seen in this seeing" (*dṛśyate 'smin darśane*); [the suffix] *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). What, then, is this? He says: "a mirror and so forth" (*ādarśādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), water and the like are included. "The substratum of the reflection" (*pratibimbāśraya*): for in that which is the substratum of the reflection of a face and so on, the face and so on are seen. Regarding the compound *yathāmukham*, which means a reflection similar to the face—how is the compound formed here given the prohibition against using *yathā* with words denoting similarity? To this he says: "by way of irregular derivation" (*nipātanāt*).

In the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*, however, the word *yathā* is employed in the sense of "not exceeding the object" (*padārthānativṛtti*). Thus, regarding the illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*), there is a verse: "Becoming manifold, he leaped about, appearing as if facing Sītā" (*yathāmukhīnaḥ sītāyāḥ pupluve bahulo bhavan*). Here, the indeclinable compound *yathāmukham*, meaning "in accordance with the face," is used; since the word *yathāmukha*—like *unmattagaṅgā* and others—is a substantive, when it is joined with the power of the object (*karmaśakti*) and further connected with the word *darśana* (seeing), the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied by the rule governing connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. Subsequently, the elision of the final vowel (*am-bhāva*) occurs according to the rule *nāvyayībhāvāt*.

For this very reason, it was stated previously: "from the words *yathāmukha* and *saṃmukha*, when [used] with a word in the genitive case. In the expression *samam mukham saṃmukham*, the word *sama* is a synonym for the word *sarva*. The elision of the final syllable occurs by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). The genitive case in *saṃmukhasya* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Because the elision of the final syllable is an irregularity prescribed in connection with the formation of the suffix, this [form *saṃmukhasya*] is not fit for actual usage; rather, it is a sentence for the purpose of grammatical derivation (*prakriyāvākya*). Furthermore, the prefix *sam-* is not seen to have the meaning of the word *sama*. [The form is] *sammukhīnaḥ*.

That in which the entire face is seen, such as in a mirror and so forth, is described in this way. How then [to explain] the expression, "Who could withstand him as he rose up, facing the battle"? This will be due to the similarity [of the meaning] arising from the state of being face-to-face (*abhimukha*).
The word *sarva* governs [the following] from *aṅga*, *karman*, *patra*, and *pātra*. (Pāṇini 5.2.7)

The remainder [of the rule] is a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti-viśeṣaṇa*). Since simple words such as *pathin* cannot possibly belong to the *sarvādi* class, the rule applies by extension (*tadanta-vidhi*) to nominal stems ending in those words; furthermore, he states that the first case ending (*prathamā*) may optionally take the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamyarthe*), saying: "ending in *pati*, *aṅga*, *karman*, *pattra*, or *pātra*. In the word *sarvapathīna*: there is a compound according to the rule "pūrvakāla" (P. 2.1.49); the suffix *a* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ" (P. 5.4.74). Because the mention of the compound ending in *pathin* includes this specific form, the nominal stem is indeed one ending in *pathin*, and thus the suffix *kha* is applied.
He reaches as far as the toes of his feet. 5.2.8.

"Āprapadam" refers to the tip of the foot; this is understood by taking "the beginning of the foot. This forms an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.6]. Regarding the phrase "from that which has the second case as its correlate": since it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case is used for the object (*karman*). The meaning is: "it reaches the entire body in such a way as to reach up to the tips of the feet. Although the cloth is not actually connected to the body, its measurement is thus described because of its suitability; for it is indeed capable of reaching the body up to the tips of the feet.

Regarding the statement "it pervades" (*vyāpnoti*) in the present context, the expression "it reaches" (*prāpnoti*) is used because of a difference in meaning: "reaching" (*prāpti*) denotes mere relation, whereas "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) denotes a relation characterized by totality. However, in the term *āprapadam*, pervasion is understood in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*), not in the sense of exclusive limit (*maryādā*).

He does not follow the path of all the scriptures, whether they concern what is permitted or what is forbidden, nor does he adhere to the rules regarding what is edible or inedible, or what is to be done or not done.

Regarding the term *anurāyāmam*: the meaning is that it is an *avyayībhāva* compound, either by the rule "and [that which has] length" (*yasya cāyāmaḥ*), or by the rule "whatever indeclinable [is used] in the sense of 'according to'" (*yathārthe yadavyayam*). The phrase "in the sense of the measure of a word" (*padapramāṇa*) means this very same thing when referring to length; even in the case of similarity (*sādṛśya*), since similarity consists in having an equal dimension, the meaning remains the same. Regarding the expression "a mendicant who eats all food" (*sarvānnīno bhikṣuḥ*): here the word *sarva* signifies the totality of types (*prakārakārtsnye*). The meaning is that he eats all those foods that are obtained—whether they be hot, cold, savory, or tasteless.

He dispels the doubt that the word *ayanamaya* refers merely to "going" (*gamanamātra*) and that its negation is expressed by the word *anaya*, by stating: "*Ayaḥ* means 'clockwise' (*pradakṣiṇam*). That is to say, it means movement to the right. Similarly, *anaya* means "counter-clockwise" (*prasavyam*), which is movement in the direction of the left. This is understood through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

For this term *ayānaya* is conventionally established as referring to the clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*) and counter-clockwise (*prasavya*) movements of the *śāra*s—those specific implements of gambling known as *śvāna*s (dice), so called because "messengers (*dūta*) hear [the results] from one another by means of them"; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. In that context, when two gamblers playing face-to-face move clockwise toward one, that very same movement is counter-clockwise toward the other; thus, it is both *aya* and *anaya*, forming the compound *ayānaya*.

Alternatively—there is only one way of bringing about the conditions (*pratyayānayana*). How so? By means of a division of paths (*vīthī*). There are four paths; therein, on the first path, one's own pieces (*śāra*) situated on the opposite side will move clockwise around themselves, on the second they will move counter-clockwise, and likewise on the two following ones. In that context, when there is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), the masculine gender is used because it depends upon common worldly usage (*lokāśrayatva*).

Another says: the designation "bringing" (*ānaya*) is applied to the entire collection of movements by way of a single part; this is simply a compound in apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-samāsa*), like the expression "done-and-undone" (*kṛtākṛta*). It is not intended to refer merely to movement clockwise or counter-clockwise, but rather to a specific [type of] movement. Thus he says: "of those moving clockwise or counter-clockwise," and so on. This refers to that specific mode of movement in which [the state of being] "those who move" and so forth occurs. The plural number is used for the purpose of indicating the cause for both bringing and taking away.

If the pieces move both clockwise and counter-clockwise, then there is "mine" and "theirs," but not otherwise. In that case, these pieces move clockwise, while those belonging to the opponent move counter-clockwise.

For those pieces moving in such a manner, when there occurs a specific mode of movement consisting of both clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*) and counter-clockwise (*prasavya*) motion, wherein there is no encounter—meaning no pressure, no crowding, and no being stepped upon—by opposing pieces that have become active, this is called *ayānaya*. It is not merely the clockwise and counter-clockwise movement itself that constitutes it. This kind of *ayānaya* is to be understood as occurring when the squares (*pada*) are traversed by pieces accompanied by their allies.
