For indeed, the positions of pieces (*śāra*) that have companions cannot be occupied by others; however, for those without companions, it is possible through mere devotion (*bhakti*). "Situated on the head of the board" (*phalakaśirasi sthita*): where on the board they play with dice, the position at its head—which is well known among gamblers—is where a piece situated there is called "the invincible" (*ayānayīna*), because the word *ayānayīna* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense.

Others, however, say: "That which is to be carried (*neya*) is not [already] carried (*nīta*); therefore, since the meaning 'standing on the head' is untenable there, the text must mean 'it is placed on the head of the board' (*phalakaśirasi sthāpyate*). Or rather, that which has been carried (*nīta*) is what is to be carried (*neya*), because the former serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the latter; it is stated with reference to a future state. Even though all [the words] are connected to both "carrying" and "not carrying," it has already been stated that the suffix arises from the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) alone.

Even though the context is already governed by the second case (*dvitīyā*), the repetition of the word "second" is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix occurs after a word ending in the second case that is actually perceived as such. Consequently, the suffix arises from words like *neyavacana* when they are qualified by a second-case ending—as in *ānaya*—and not from the mere term *neyavacana* alone. That very qualification is what is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "the method (*naya*) which proceeds clockwise and counter-clockwise," and so forth.

Regarding the word *ayānaya*: what is this term? For if it were a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), then because of its neuter gender, it ought to be *ayānayam*. Or if it were in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), then because it would have two referents, it ought to be *ayānayau*. This is not a *dvandva*; rather, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*, meaning "an *anaya* (misfortune) accompanied by *aya* (fortune)," i.e., *ayānaya*.

Now, regarding the expression *baddābhakṣayatineyeṣu*, how can there be a *dvandva* compound of a verbal form (*tiṅanta*)? Who, moreover, says that this is a *dvandva*? If it is not a *dvandva*, how is the plural ending in *neyeṣu* justified? It is because the formulation is *sautra* (belonging to the Sūtras). Or rather, by means of the substitution of case endings (*subvyatyaya*), the plural is appropriate in place of the singular in Vedic usage. But surely the substitution of case endings is prescribed for Vedic usage; is this not Vedic? It is indeed a *naya* (a leading principle), and thus that which is to be led (*neya*) is so called.

In the rule "baddhābhakṣayatineyeṣu," a dvandva compound consisting of verbal forms (tiṅanta) is established by means of nipātana; however, in the alternative where it is not a compound, it would result in an inconsistency, as "baddhā" would then be a nominative singular and "neyeṣu" a locative plural.
One experiences [the results] for oneself, for others, in succession, and for one's sons and grandsons. || 5.2.10 ||

"Parasyautvam" means that the substitution of *o* for the initial [sound] of the word-form "para" is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). In that case, the rule "ādguṇaḥ" (P. 6.1.87) applies. Alternatively, the substitution of *o* for the final phoneme (*al*) of the word "para" is prescribed; then, by the rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" (P. 6.1.109), there is a single substitute of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa-ekādeśa*). Thus, one would expect "parasyautvam," but the mention is made using the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) because of the rule "śakandhvādiṣu pararūpaṃ vaktavyam. In the expression "paraparatarāṇāṃ ca," the particle *ca* has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*), referring back to the requirement of placing the shorter term first (*pūrvanipāta*).

The plural number [in *pārovaryāṇām*] arises from superimposing multiplicity upon the word for that which has gone beyond (*atigata*). It should be regarded as a distinct word altogether; it is an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) expression denoting a lineage. For this very reason, it lacks feminine gender and takes the singular number. As for the form *pāramparya*, it likewise derives from that same base with the suffix *ṣyañ* added in its own sense (*svārthe*). How then can there be the form *pārovaryavat*? This is simply incorrect; for by the rule of *nipātana*, the form *pārovara* is established in conjunction with the suffix *kh*.
The suffix *gāmin* is applied after *avāra*, *pāra*, and *atyanta* when followed by *anukāmam*.

Regarding "gāmī": by the rule *gameriniḥ* and *āṅi ṇicca*, because of the word *bahula* (diversity/optionality), the suffix *ṇini* will occur even from the root alone. Regarding "gamyādayaḥ": although the root *gam* preceded by *āṅ* is listed among the *gamyādi* group, nevertheless, due to the *bahula* rule itself, the suffix *ṇini* will occur even for the future tense; this is the intended meaning. As for the statement "there is a prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *akernorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*," [it refers to the following].

Regarding what was stated under the rule *gatyarthakarmaṇi*: "The mention of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is for the purpose of providing an exception (*apavāda*); therefore, when a *kṛt* suffix is employed, the genitive case does not occur—as in *grāmaṃ gantā* (one who will go to the village). This [objection] is not accepted, because in the case of a prohibition, there is simply no possibility for the genitive to arise. In the word *avārapārīṇa*, the suffix is applied after a *dvandva* compound. Since the pair *avāra-pāre* ("this shore and that shore") is included in the list beginning with *āhitāgni*, both forms are valid: *avārapāre* and *pārāvāre*. The word *antam* [is explained as follows].

This is an adverbial modifier; "evamanukāmam" means "according to desire. Desire (*kāma*) is longing; that which corresponds to it is "anukāmam," meaning conforming to desire. The compound is formed according to the rule: "An indeclinable used in the sense of 'as' [forms a compound]."
She gives birth every year. 5.2.12.

Regarding the phrase *samāṃsamām abhi*: the word *praṣṭavyā* (to be asked) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In this instruction, *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) is to be seen; therefore, the meaning is that there is a dual number. Alternatively, the term *vīpsā* refers to a collective expression denoting repetition—that is, it means "that which expresses repetition. This is because the entire verbal form (*subanta*) is the base (*prakṛti*), even though the governing rule concerns nominal stems (*prātipadika*), due to the force of the specific statement here. As for the meaning "she conceives a fetus": the root *jan* is indeed observed in the sense of "conceiving," as in the passage: *sa vijāyamāno garbheṇātāmyat* ("He, being born, was distressed by the fetus").

"It should be stated that there is no *luk*-elision of the case-ending (*sup*) in the prior member. Otherwise, when a secondary suffix (*taddhita*) arises, just as elision occurs in the subsequent member by the rule "the case-ending is elided after a verbal root or a nominal stem" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*), it would likewise occur in the prior member.

Regarding the words "some, however," and so forth: one might object that the accusative case should occur here because of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). To this he replies: "but in the case of releasing the fetus. In that context, the meaning of the word "only" (*mātra*) is that by the act of releasing, only the suffix *-ya-* is elided, not the entire case-ending. Regarding the phrase "of the remainder": it should be stated that there is no *luk*-elision of the suffix *-ām*.

[Objection: Since the suffix *su* is a case-ending (*sub*), its elision is already established by the elision of the case-ending itself; in that case, the mention of the elision of *y* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), meaning that only the *y* is elided and not the entire suffix. So why is it said that "non-elision (*aluk*) must be stated"? [Response: It is thought thus: just as by virtue of the irregularity (*nipātana*) the elision of the remaining portion of the first member does not occur, so too it might not occur in the second member. Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-origination": even in a sentence, the elision of *y* for both the preceding and following members must be stated optionally; thereby, the two forms are established.
The word *adyaśvīna* is used when referring to something seized on the same day or the next day.

The explanation for *avaṣṭabdha* and *vijana*, respectively, is "near birth. But how can the word *avaṣṭabdha* have the meaning "near"? To this he says: "For [it is used] in the sense of proximity (*āvidūrya*). Although the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed even in the sense of support (*ālambana*), nevertheless, because the sense of support is impossible for *vijana*, its meaning is only proximity. What, then, is elided here? It is a compound in the sense of "option" (*vā*)—either *adya* or *viśvaḥ*—with the suffix *kh*; the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is established simply by its being an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

Regarding the example *adyaśvīnā vaḍavā* ("a mare that will bring forth [a foal] today or tomorrow"): the feminine gender is cited here for the sake of compatibility with the verb *vijāyate* ("she gives birth"), but there is no specific mention of the feminine gender in the sūtra itself. This is because the desired form is also required in cases such as *adyaśvīno gosamūhaḥ* ("a herd of cows that will give birth today or tomorrow") and *adyaśvīnaṃ gomaṇḍalam* ("a group of cows that will give birth today or tomorrow"). The citation of the base ending in a short vowel (*hrasvāntasya*) is without case endings (*avibhaktika*).

Regarding the phrase "some, however" (*kecittu*): for them, a verbal action must be supplied according to the expression. The term *avaṣṭabdhamātre* means "even in the sense of 'it exists' (*bhavati*) and so forth. The example *adyaśvīnaṃ maraṇam* ("death today or tomorrow") indicates that the suffix is applied in the sense that it will occur either today or tomorrow.
The suffix *āgavīna* [is applied after a word ending in the locative case to denote "one who returns by that time"]. 5.2.14.

Regarding the phrase *gorāṅpūrvāt*: the meaning is "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *go* (cow) and preceded by *ā*. The expression *ā tasya goḥ pratidānāt* means "until the return of that cow"; *pratidāna* signifies "restoration" or "returning. By this, he shows that in the context of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the word *go* refers to the "return of the cow. Regarding *kariṇī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). Regarding *āgavīna*: after forming an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*, and after applying the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*), the suffix *kha* is added; then, by the rule *orguṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the word *anugu*, when it denotes that which goes along with [the river].

Regarding *alaṅgagāmī*: the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau*. Regarding *anusvit*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "behind" (*paścāt*), with the first member shortened as it is an *upasarjana*. Regarding *paryāptam*: this is indeed an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Regarding *anugv*: the suffix is therefore applied after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*). However, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection to a verbal derivative (*kṛt*) does not apply to an adverbial modifier; for example, one says *śobhanaṃ pācakaḥ* ("a good cooker"), not *śobhanasya pācakaḥ*.
The suffixes *yat* and *kha* are applied after the word *adhvan*.

Regarding the phrase "from that which is not capable of governing the second case" (*dvitīyāsamarthāt*): when the analysis (*vigraha*) is with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), as in "he goes to the road" (*adhvānaṃ gacchati*), then there is the state of being incapable of governing the second case. Even when the analysis is with the form *gāmī* as included in the rule itself, even then only the second case is used, and the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix does not occur, because of the prohibition [stated in the rule] "*akenoḥ*". In this context, the suffix *yat* is established by the rule "*adhvano yacca*"; and by the word "and" (*ca*) in that rule, the suffix *kha* is also included. If it were stated in this way, then in the subsequent rule, only the immediately preceding *yat* would be drawn forward (*anukṛṣyate*) by the word "and," and the *kha* would not be drawn forward.
Therefore, the expression "*yat-khau*" is used so that both *yat* and *kha* may be understood as recurring.
And [the suffix *cha*] is added after *abhyamitra*.

Regarding "abyacāmitram": it is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye" (Pāṇini 2.1.14). Because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the second case ending is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied after the word *goṣṭha* when expressing that which formerly existed there.

"Goṣṭha" means "that in which cows stand. The suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the suffix *chañ*; by the rule "sthāsnāpāvyadhihrīānayudhyaḥ," the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), and by the rule "ambāmbagobhūmi... the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. "Bhūtapūrva" means "one who existed previously"; this is a compound formed according to the rule "sup-supā. The word "goṣṭha" functions as an adjective by way of its meaning, not by its own form; for a suffix cannot be prescribed after the word "goṣṭha" when it is already in the state of having existed previously (*bhūtapūrva*). "The cow-pen exists" indicates the current location of the cows.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *asva* when it means "arriving in one day. 5.2.19.

"Ekāhagama" means that which is traversed in one day (*ekāhena gamyate*). Here, the suffix *ap* prescribed by the rule "grahavṛdṛniścigamaśca" is set aside by the rule "parimāṇākhyāyāṃ sarvebhyaḥ. Is there indeed a designation of measure (*parimāṇākhyā*) here? Yes, because from the expression "it is traversed in one day," a delimitation (*pariccheda*) is understood. It should be seen as derived from this very irregular formation (*nipātana*). The compound is formed according to the rule "kṛt-karaṇe bahulam. The word "aśvasya" (of the horse) takes the genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). "Having fallen [to the ground] a hundred *aśvīna*s" means having gone a hundred times the distance that can be covered by a horse in one day.
The words *śālīna* and *kaupīna* are used in the senses of "timid" and "an improper act," respectively. || 5.2.20 ||

"In whatever manner" (*yathākathañcit*) means that one should not be overly insistent on the literal meaning of the individual components (*avayava-artha*). For if one were so insistent, how could there be a designation for one who is timid in the house because he is dominated by his wife, yet is bold elsewhere; or for one who performs improper acts such as urinating in a well? How, then, is the intended meaning conveyed? To this he says: "He deserves entry into the house. The meaning is that because that improper act must be concealed, he deserves to descend into a well. And [the rule] "with the elision of the final member" (*uttarapadālopaśca*) applies.

In the domain of verbal activity (*vṛtti*), the words *śālā* (house) and *kūpa* (well) refer to the action whose object they are; since this [action] is understood [by implication], its non-employment constitutes elision (*lopa*). As for the expression "the private part (*kaupīna*) is sin": the word *kaupīna* refers to the male organ because it is the instrument (*sādhana*) of sin, or because of a similarity (*sādharmya*); the similarity consists in its being something to be concealed (*gopyatva*). And by association with that [organ], it also refers to the piece of cloth used to cover it. Another says: in the word *kārya*, the root *kṛ* denotes action in general; therefore, the male organ is called *kaupīna* because it is not to be seen due to being a cause of shame, and the covering is so called because it is not to be touched.
He lives by a troop. 5.2.21.

In common usage, the word *vrāta* denotes a mere multitude; however, to show that it does not mean that here, he cites the passage from the Bhāṣya: "not of the same kind. By this, groups of Kṣatriyas and others who are of a single caste are excluded. Regarding "those of unsettled livelihood," there is a prohibition against groups whose livelihood is fixed as living by arms. He explains the term "living by their physical bulk" (*utsedhajīvinaḥ*) as follows: "the body is the *utsedha* (bulk)," because of its height (*ucchrāyatvāt*). [He further explains] "that which results from exertion" (*tad-āyāsya*): from the root *āyas* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *lyap* is applied; thus, it possesses an object.

In the reading where the root is not marked with *ṇ* (i.e., *vrāta*), its transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) should be understood as resulting from the inclusion of a causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyarthatva*). The meaning is that they live by means of physical exertion, such as carrying loads, and not through intellectual activity. Regarding the word *vrātāḥ*: this term, which denotes a "group," is used here to refer to the members of the group; thus, the meaning is "the group of those who are such. Even so, [one might object] that the rule would apply to those who live by such a group, yet this is not intended. To this, he says: "Their work is *vrāta*."

When the suffix *cha* would otherwise apply in the sense of "this object," the suffix *aṇ* is used here precisely because of this specific grammatical rule (nipātana). As for the phrase "but that which is other," and so forth, the reason here is non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).
Friendship is formed by walking seven steps together. || 5.2.22 ||

"The term *sāptapadīna* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*). What, then, is irregularly formed here? The case-ending of the governing word is the third case. "Is obtained" is the meaning of the suffix; "obtained by seven steps" is a *dvigu* compound used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and the suffix *khañ* is added to the word *saptapada*. "How so? [The questioner asks: "Friendship (*sakhyam*) is the state or action of a friend (*sakhi*); why is there not a question using the word 'friend' for that which is derived from it? [The answer is: "By way of metaphor (*upacāra*)," as in the phrase "the primary quality."

A quality (*guṇa*) is an existence (*bhāva*), and an action (*karman*) is also an existence; it is called a "quality" because it serves as the basis for the application [of a word]. For it is said that "by the presence of which quality... and that actions are called a "quality" because they are denotable by the word *sakhi* (friend).
The word *haiyaṅgavīna* [is formed] in the sense of "at twilight. (Pāṇini 5.2.23)

"Hyogodohasya vikāraḥ" means: *doha* (milking) is that which is milked, i.e., milk; *godoha* is a genitive compound meaning "the milking of a cow. Then, by the rule *sup supā*, there is a compound with the word *hyaḥ*. From that, the suffix *khañ* is applied as an exception to the suffix *añ* characterized by an anudātta vowel, to denote a modification (*vikāra*). This is the technical name for a specific kind of ghee. It does not refer to all ghee, but rather to that very [ghee] whose smell and appearance remain unchanged.
Because the word *hyaḥ* expresses proximity in time, *navanītam* (fresh butter) is designated as *haiyaṅgavīnam*; the word *ghṛta* is also used in reference to that same thing.
The suffixes *kuṇap* and *jāhac* are applied after the words *pīlu* and others, as well as *karṇa* and others, when they follow [the word] *tasya-pāka-mūla*. (Pāṇini 5.2.24)

*Pāka* means transformation; *mūla* means the primary source or undertaking. This rule is introduced because [suffixes] such as *aṇ* (which would apply by the rule "this belongs to that") would otherwise be applicable; since the letter *j* serves no purpose here, it lacks the designation *it*.
The suffix *ti* is applied after the word *pakṣa*. (Pāṇini 5.2.25)

Even in the case of words remaining from a single *yoga*, according to the view that the word itself is the governing factor (*śabdādhikāra-pakṣa*), only that word for which the status of being *svarita* is declared continues to apply. Thus, in the rule "dāmahāyanāntācca," the mention of "number" (*saṅkhyā*) continues, but not the mention of "indivisible" (*avyaya*). However, under the view that the meaning is the governing factor (*arthādhikāra-pakṣa*), because a *dvandva* compound is prescribed for words that simultaneously express mutually distinct meanings, there can be no continuation of a single part once the meaning of the *dvandva* has been severed. The root of a wing is called *pakṣati*; it refers to the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), and it is also used for the base of a bird's wing.
The suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* are added after the word *vitta*.

Regarding the form *vitta* meaning "renowned" (*pratīta*): because of the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) stating "the word *vitta* [is formed] in the senses of 'wealth' and 'cognition'," just as the letter *c* in the suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* does not receive the technical designation *it*, so too has it been stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the very rule *cuṭū*.
After the words *vi* and *na*, the suffixes *nānāñ* and *añ* are applied respectively, provided that they do not co-occur with the word *saha*.

The phrase "nasaheti" is an adjective qualifying the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*). If it were the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), then two negations would convey the very same sense as the base word; thus, the meaning "together with" (*saha*) alone would be understood, and not "not together," but rather "indeed together. Therefore, it pertains specifically to the meaning of the base word. This is obtained from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

If this is so, let the meaning of the suffix be simply "together" (*saha*), since *nañ* and *vi-* have the sense of negation; for even in examples such as *vigardabhārathaka*, the word *vi-* is clearly seen to function in the sense of negation? True; however, one would understand the suffix to mean "together" from the word *vi-*, which denotes action—as in "gone together" (*vigata*) or "altered together" (*vikṛta*). Furthermore, the letter *ñ* in *nañ* is for the purpose of [triggering] vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and for the sake of accentuation (*svara*).
The suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* are added after the word *vi*.

But where do these [words] such as *śālaja* and so forth occur? To this he says: "Because they express an action along with its instrument (*sasādhanakriyāvacanāt*). This means: because they express an instrument qualified by an action. And this was established in the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*. Regarding the word *upasargāt*: since the technical designation *upasarga* is seen elsewhere, the term *pra* and so on are applied even in other contexts. Regarding *svārthe*: because no specific meaning has been specified. Regarding *vigata*: he shows that the root *vi-* functions with respect to the agent of the action of departing. Regarding *tadyogāt*: because of the connection with large constituent parts; the sense is that, according to the view of etymological derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*), there is no other way [to explain the formation].

He states the extensive application [of the term]: "But in the ultimate sense... "Vastness" (viśālatva) is the quality (guṇa) known as extensiveness (vistīrṇatva); therefore, these are words denoting a quality (guṇavacana). The plural number is used in view of the suffixes that will be explained later. Consequently, the intended meaning is that since the application [of the word] to a horn is due to its connection with that quality, the application to a cow is established by virtue of that very same connection with the quality. And thus, one also sees such usage as "a vast region" (viśālo deśaḥ).
The suffix *kaṭac* is applied after the prefix *sam* and the root *proda*.

The suffix *kaṭac* occurs [after these words] in their own sense (*svārthe*), as previously [stated] for words expressing an action along with its instrument: *saṅkaṭaḥ* means "well-known," that is, "manifest"; *utkaṭaḥ* means "eminent"; *vikaṭaḥ* means "deformed."

Regarding the passage beginning with *alābūtila* and so forth: the reading is *bhaṅgābhyaḥ*, where the word *bhaṅga* ends in the suffix *ṭāp*. Just as the suffix *kaṭac* occurs after words such as *alābū* when "dust" (*rajas*) is to be expressed—as an exception to the suffixes denoting a modification because dust is a modification—so too, after the word *alābū*, it is an exception to both the suffix *orañ* and the suffix *mayaṭ* [prescribed by the rule] *mayaḍ vaitayoḥ*. After the words *tila* and *umā*, which are oxytone (ending in the acute accent) due to belonging to the *ghṛtādi* group, the suffix *añ* [is applied] according to [the rule] *anudāttādeśca*, as well as the suffix *mayaṭ*.

In the case of *umā*, there is the suffix *vuñ* according to the rule "or after *umā*" (*ūrgomayorvā*), and the suffix *mayaṭ* according to the rule "after *tila* and *yava* when not forming a technical name" (*asaṃjñāyāṃ tilayavābhyām*). In the case of *bhaṅgā*, because of the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule "and for grasses and grains that have two vowels," there is the suffix *aṇ* and also *mayaṭ*.

Regarding the term *goṣṭhādayaḥ*: that which consists of the suffixes occurring in actual usage (*prayoga*) has been indicated. The particle *ca*, however, is to be understood as an *anubandha* for the sake of the accent. For instance, this [suffix] was rejected in the Bhāṣya on the basis of the compound (*samāsa*), since in a compound the final syllable bears the acute accent (*antodātta*). Everywhere the word "etc. (*ādi*) indicates a class. In the sense of "the place of cows," when the suffix *yat* would otherwise apply by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to that"), the suffix *goṣṭhaC* is applied according to the rule: "In all cases where *yat* would apply after *go* followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel, [it is replaced by *goṣṭhaC*]."

A collection (*saṅghāta*) is an aggregate whose constituent parts are not spread out; an expansion (*vistāra*), however, is one whose constituent parts are spread out. Both of these are exceptions to the general rule for collections. Regarding the term "in the sense of duality" (*dvitve*): the meaning is that the duality of the base-meaning is to be indicated. In the example *uṣṭragoyugam* ("a pair of camel and cow"), the singular number is used because it denotes a collection consisting of two members, just as in expressions such as *dvayaṃ yugam*. The same should be understood in cases such as *hastihastinī-gavam* ("a pair of male and female elephants").

Regarding the word *sneha*: *sneha* is that by which things become oily (*snihyanti*); it is a liquid substance, a derivative of *iṅguda* and similar plants. In this regard, the word *iṅguda* is acute-accented on the first syllable according to the rule "the acute accent falls on the first syllable when followed by a light vowel" (*laghāvante*). From that, the suffix *aṇ* would be expected by the rule "its derivative" (*tasya vikāraḥ*). From the word *tila*, however, the suffix *añ* would be expected by the rule "and [words] beginning with an anudātta vowel. Yet even that is desired—namely, "oil (*taila*) is a derivative of sesame seeds (*tila*). Is it then necessary to say all this? No, he says; it is established through comparison (*upamāna*).

How so? A "goṣṭha" is that in which cows stand; by analogy with that, even the place where camels and other animals stand is called a "goṣṭha. In order to convey a specific distinction therein, it is qualified by [the names of] those animals—such as "uṣṭragoṣṭha" (a camel-pen) or "mahiṣagoṣṭha" (a buffalo-pen); and in order to convey the primary meaning, it is also called "gogoṣṭha" (a cow-pen) by means of the word "gobhiḥ" (by cows).

Just as when the word *gopati* is used in the sense of a mere master, it is qualified by "cows" in such expressions as "O Indra, you alone are the sole master (*gopati*) of cows" and "having abandoned the brave master of cattle," so too, since a mat (*kaṭa*) is a collection of various materials such as grass and *vīraṇa*, by analogy any other collection is also called a "mat," and that will be qualified by terms such as "goat"; thus, a collection of goats that is as extensive as a cloth is called a "goat-cloth" (*avipaṭa*).

Likewise, by the word *yuga*, a pair is expressed—as in *gavoryugam* (a pair of cows) or *goyugam* (a cow-pair). Because of the commonality of being a pair (*dvayātmatva-sāmānya*), any other couple is also called a *goyuga*. This is then qualified by terms such as "camel" (*uṣṭra*) and so on, and even by the word "cow" (*go*) itself, for the sake of understanding the primary sense of a cow-pair. Similarly, six cows brought together are a *ṣaḍgavam*; here the suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule *gorataddhitaluki*, and it is neuter because it belongs to the *pātra*-class. The phrase "due to its similarity to that" (*tatsādharmyāt*) and so forth is to be understood as before.

Likewise, "oil" (*taila*) primarily refers to the modification (*vikāra*) of sesame; by similarity to that, any liquid modification is simply called "oil. Consequently, there is a qualification by *iṅguda* and so forth, as well as by sesame. And this being the case, it also follows that "oil is the modification of sesame"; for if it were not so, it would be sublated at the beginning of the sentence by [the term] "oil."

The opponent says: "Just as the term 'pravīṇa' (skilled) in relation to the lute (*vīṇā*) is formed merely through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), yet skill alone is its actual cause—so that one can say 'skilled in the lute' (*vīṇāyāṃ pravīṇaḥ*)—and just as the term 'oil' (*tailam*) is a mere etymological derivative meaning 'a product of sesame seeds,' yet its actual referent is a liquid product; and thus [the use of] specific qualifiers like *iṅguda* is established; we do not accept that view. For when 'oil' is said, people do not understand it as merely a liquid product. As for the terms *śākaṭa* and *śākina*, they must indeed be explained [separately]."
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *avāt* and after *kuṭāra*. 5.2.30.
*Avakuṭāram*, *avakaṭam*: meaning downward-facing, that is to say, unestablished.
After the word *nata* and after a word denoting the nose, the suffixes *ṭīṭan*, *ṇāṭac*, and *bhraṭac* are added [to form a bahuvrīhi compound]. 5.2.31.

"Namana" means "natam" (bowed). The suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning "the state of being low. [The phrase] "connected with the nose" (*nāsikāyāḥ sambandhinī*)—the connection here is by way of the nose being the agent of the act of bowing. However, in the Sūtra, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyānam*): "The neuter abstract sense [of the suffix *kta*] is to be added [to the rule for the agent]. Alternatively, it is established through the understanding of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*); thus, it is simply characterized as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). In words such as *avaṭīṭa*, the suffix is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) after an upasarga that denotes an act of bowing performed by means of the nose.

How, then, is it said that the nose and the person are likewise [designated]? He says: "Because of connection with that" (*tadyogāt*). The fact that the letter *ṭ* in the suffix *ṭīṭañ* is subject to the designation *it* has already been explained in the rule *cuṭū*.
The suffixes *ini* and *ka* are applied after [a word ending in] *ina*, *cipiṭa*, and *ca*. 5.2.33.

"The letter *ka* is the suffix (*pratyaya*). Here, the word *kāra*—as in *akāra*, *cakāra*, *evakāra*, and so forth—is intended to mean "the letter *a*" or "the letter *ca*"; thus, *kapratyaya* means "the suffix *ka*. And so it has been said: in the Sūtra, two substitutes (*ādeśa*) and two suffixes (*pratyaya*) are prescribed for the word *ni*; therefore, this was stated by the author of the Vārttika for the purpose of prescribing these substitutes and suffixes. [This refers to the rule] regarding the meaning "his eyes."

Although the two eyes are qualifiers of the meaning of the base (prakṛti), and the suffix denotes the sense of the genitive case in "of this" (asya), nevertheless, it was stated in this way with the understanding that the fact of being moist belongs to the eyes and is manifested by the suffix itself.

Regarding the phrase "of this" (*asya*) and "by this" (*anena*), he rejects [the interpretation that these refer to] a portion of the sentence. Why? Because there is no purpose [for such an interpretation], he says: "It is the designation of the two eyes themselves. This means that the suffix is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) to the word *klinna* (moist) when it refers to the two eyes. If so, how is there a designation of the person (*puruṣa*)? He says: "Through connection with that," and so forth. In the list beginning with *arśas*, the rule "*svāṅgāddhīnāt*" (after a word for a limb of one's body that denotes deficiency) is recited; by that, the suffix *-aka-* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*).
The suffix *tyakan* is used after words denoting a limiting attribute (*upādhi*) to express that which has not yet arrived or has already ascended [to that state]. (Pāṇini 5.2.34)

"Having a fixed object" means having a mountain as its object. The point is that [the suffix -ka] does not occur in such cases as *āsena vṛkṣasya* ("near the tree") or *ārūḍhaḥ plakṣasya* ("climbed the fig tree"). Now, why is the substitution of *i* (by the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasya*) not applied in the words *upatyakā* ("valley") and *adhityakā* ("plateau")? To this he says: "By the rule *pratyayasthāt kāt*... If the substitution of *i* were to occur here, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) would not be established; for the technical names are not of the form *nopatyikā* or *adhityikā*. Therefore, because this falls under the heading of technical names (*saṃjñā-adhikāra*), the substitution of *i* does not take place.
The suffix *aṭhac* is applied after a word ending in the accusative case when it denotes an action.

By the word "karmaṇi," he shows that the term *karma* is being used in its own specific form (*svarūpa*). Why, then, is the technical definition (*paribhāṣika*) of "object" (*karman*) not taken here? Because it is impossible. It is impossible because the root *ghaṭ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). The pronunciation of the vowel *a* in the suffix *aṭhac* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *ekādeśa* (the single substitute for *ṭha* and *a*).
The suffix *itac* is applied after this [word] when it means "born from" (sañjāta), provided it begins with *tāraka* and so forth. (Pāṇini 5.2.36)

The words *bubhukṣā* and *pipāsā* are recited among the *tārakādi* group [of roots]. For what purpose is their inclusion there, since the forms *bubhukṣitaḥ*, *pipāsitaḥ*, and *pipāsitaḥ* are already established by adding the suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta) along with the augment *iṭ* to the desiderative (*sannanta*) roots? It is true that they are established in the sense of the object (*karman*)—as in "the rice is hungry" (*bubhukṣita odanaḥ*) or "the water is thirsty" (*pipāsitam udakam*)—but they do not apply in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), as in "Devadatta is hungry" (*bubhukṣito devadattaḥ*) or "Devadatta is thirsty" (*pipāsito devadattaḥ*). By this [inclusion in the *tārakādi* list], however, the suffix arises for one in whom hunger and thirst have actually arisen.

In that case, for what purpose is the listing of roots such as *puṣpa*, *mūtra*, and *vraṇa*—namely, ‘*puṣpa* in the sense of blossoming,’ ‘*mūtra* in the sense of urinating,’ and ‘*vraṇa* in the sense of wounding’? Is it not established that by these [roots], being intransitive (*akarmaka*), the forms *puṣpitaḥ* and *mūtritaḥ* are derived with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*)? True, they are established in the sense of the past (*bhūte*). However, they are not established in the sense of the present (*vartamāne*); therefore, their inclusion [in this list] is for the sake of the present tense.

But how, then, does this [suffix] occur in the present tense? Since here too the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of the past as "sañjāta" (born/produced), [the answer is: in that case, by virtue of the inclusion of words such as *puṣpa* in the list (*gaṇa*), the past time is not intended to be expressed in the word *sañjātam*. Regarding the rule *garbhād aprāṇini*: the suffix *itac* occurs after the word *garbha* when a non-living being is denoted—e.g., *garbhitāḥ śālayaḥ* (rice plants bearing grain); but when a living being is denoted, [the suffix is *ini*, as in] *garbhiṇī gauḥ* (a pregnant cow).
The suffixes *saC*, *daghnaC*, and *mātraC* are added after a word denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*).

"That which is the first [referent] is valid cognition (pramāṇa) if it exists"—by this, he shows that validity is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (prakṛtyartha). However, if it were a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (pratyayārtha), it would be: "that which is indicated as 'this belongs to it' is valid cognition if it exists."

In that case, since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is dependent upon its object of cognition (*prameya*), the object of cognition would be the meaning of the base form (*prakṛti*). Just as when it serves as a qualifier of the base meaning, the object of cognition becomes the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), so too here [the following] would result: "water is the object of cognition of this mountain. But this is incorrect; for since the means of valid cognition have various objects of cognition, it is improper to use one as a qualifier [of another], whereas words such as *ūru* (thigh) and so forth are employed to indicate that the object of cognition has a fixed relation to its specific means of valid cognition.

"First and second. That by which something standing upright is measured is "upward measurement" (*ūrdhvamāna*), such as *urvā* and so forth. Regarding this, some say: "In the rule, only that which is a measure of length (*āyāmamāna*) is understood as *pramāṇa*; and only a transverse measurement is a measure of length. Therefore, since upward measurement is not included [by that definition], the suffixes *dvayasaC* and *jaghnaC* are prescribed here by being drawn away from the general category of *pramāṇa*. Others say: "Even that by which a length is delimited when standing upright is included in the rule as *pramāṇa*, because it too is a measure of length."

"The statement is for the purpose of restriction, so that [the measurements] may apply only to vertical measurement and not to horizontal measurement. Another, however, says: "In this context, 'measurement' (pramāṇa) is understood as merely that which delimits [an object]. In that case as well, this is for the purpose of restriction. "Merely" (mātra) refers to the measurement; therefore, this is a restatement of what is established by logic. By the word "also" (api) in the phrase "even a measure of a *prastha*," it is implied that "even a measure of a thigh" (*ūrumātra*) is also possible.

Regarding "pramāṇe la": *luk* is a technical term (saṃjñā) used by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). "Those which are well-known as measures" means those words which are established as denoting measurement—namely, *diṣṭi*, *vitasti*, and so forth. In this case, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *mātrac*; for the other two [suffixes, *dvayasaC* and *daghnaC*], it is impossible, because words such as *śama* do not measure vertically.

Regarding the rule *dvigornityam*: since a *dvigu* compound is not a measure (*apramāṇa*) and because the rule for elision (*luk*) by extension to the final member does not apply, this elision is prescribed where it was not previously obtained by the preceding rule. The question "What is the purpose of the mention of *nityam* (‘always’)? arises because no option (*vikalpa*) is currently under discussion. [The answer is: He will state the word *saṃśaye* (‘in case of doubt’) later on.

*Śravaṇa* means hearing (*śrāva*). By the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied. That which possesses this [hearing] is called *śrāvī*. Regarding the suffix *mātrac* which will be mentioned in the rule *pramāṇaparimāṇābhyāṃ saṅkhyāyāścāpi saṃśaye*, the elision (*luk*) does not occur by the rule *pramāṇe laḥ*, because the latter [rule] takes precedence. Therefore, it is called *śrāvī*. The meaning is that although hearing would have occurred even in the case of a *dvigu* compound, the elision is now prescribed. For example: *dviśamaḥ*, meaning "that of which two *śamas* are the measure."

But how, then, does the suffix *mātrac* arise here in the sense of "doubt"? It is by means of the rule for extension to that which ends in [the base] (*tadantavidhi*). This very mention of elision (*lugvacana*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is indeed such an extension to that which ends in [the base]. Whether this [suffix] has as its domain certainty or doubt is to be determined from the context and other such factors in usage.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *ḍaṭ* should be prescribed for *stoma*": since a physical measurement is impossible here, when *stoma* is to be expressed as the meaning, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied to a number that serves as a limiting adjunct (*paricchedopādhika*). The addition of the marker *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the word-final *ti* in forms such as *ekaviṃśa*, and for the elision of the *ṭi*-portion in forms such as *trayastriṃśa*. In cases like *pañcadaśa*, the form is already established by the rule *nastaddhite*; thus: "that which has fifteen mantras as its measure" is a *pañcadaśa* *stoma*, and "that which has seventeen [mantras] is a *saptadaśī* night."

Due to its association with *stoma*, the word [derived from *śat*] functions in the feminine gender when referring to things such as nights; because of the marker *ṭi*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. However, in the rules "that is its measure" (*tadasya parimāṇam*) and "of a number, a name" (*saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā*), the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed for *śata*; in that case, the suffix *ṭāp* occurs if there is usage, but if there is none, then this very [rule regarding *ḍa*] is its detailed exposition (*prapañca*). As for the statement "the suffix *ḍin* is to be prescribed for *śan* and *śata*": since *ḍin* is thus ordained for both Vedic and common language (*bhāṣā*), the specific mention in the rule "of a number, a name or a collection" (*saṅkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā-saṅgha*)—namely, "for *śan* and *śata*, *ḍin* in the Veda" (*śan-śator-ḍiniś-chandasi*)—is solely for the purpose of detailed exposition.

Regarding "the Viśis and the Aṅgirasas": twenty divisions are stated according to the distinction of *pravara* lineages. In this context, from the word *viṃśati*, which denotes the number itself, the suffix *ḍini* is applied to the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) as the thing to be measured; by the rule "*ti-viṃśater-ḍiti*," there is elision [of the final syllable], and by the rule "*yasyeti ca*," there is further elision [of the *i*].

Regarding the phrase *pramāṇaparimāṇābhyām*: these two are conventional (*rūḍhi*) terms, as they are mentioned separately. Regarding *śamamātram*: the suffix *mātrac* is used in the sense of "may this have *śama* (measure/extent) or not. Regarding *pañcamātrāḥ*: the suffix is applied in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*) to a word expressing an object about which there is doubt—namely, whether there are five or not. Thus, *pañcamātrāḥ* means those whose measure (*pramāṇa*) may be the number five or not. Regarding *tāvadeva*: that is its measure (*parimāṇa*), such as grain and so forth; hence, the suffix is added in the same sense (*svārthe*). However, in the subsequent sūtra, the meaning will be stated differently: "The state [of being] is established for words ending in *ḍa* and *vat*."
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *puruṣa* and *hiṣṭi*.

Regarding *hāstinaṃ*: there is the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *inaṇyanapatye*. As for the statement "the suffix is always elided after a *dvigu*": this is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule *pramāṇe lo dvigornityam*, because *puruṣa* and *hastin* are not commonly recognized as measures (*pramāṇa*) in the same way that *śama* and other such terms are. For this very reason, in forms such as *puruṣadvayasaṃ*, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *pramāṇe laḥ* does not occur; otherwise, even if the elision were absent due to the specific power of the prescription of the *aṇ* suffix, the elision would certainly apply to *dvayasañ* and the others. Therefore, in this context, the elision is being newly prescribed (*vidhīyate*).

And that [suffix] *ṅīp* does not apply after words such as *dvayasañ* and *ajādi*, because there is a prohibition of the rule regarding suffixes applied to what ends in a word (tadantavidhi) when the base is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that already possesses a suffix; furthermore, since a *dvigu* compound cannot take the suffix *aṇ*, the application of *ṅīp* would otherwise be impossible. Thus, in the case of *dvipuruṣī*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "after *puruṣa*, *ṅīp* optionally occurs when denoting a measure."
The suffix *vatup* is added after the words *yad*, *tad*, and *etad* when expressing measure.

Regarding the word *yāvān*: the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ*; the augment *num* is added by *ugidacām*; the lengthening occurs by *atvasantasya*; and the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the following vowel (*aṅya*) as well as the final member of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) apply. If someone were to object—thinking that "measure" (*pramāṇa*) and "dimension" (*parimāṇa*) are identical—that the mention of "dimension" (*parimāṇa*) is redundant because the context of "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is already established, the author replies to him: "While [the word] 'measure' (*pramāṇa*) is being carried over," and so forth.

Furthermore, this distinction between the two has already been explained previously: "Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is on all sides, whereas length (*āyāma*) is the measure (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the term *ḍāvatī*: here we have prescribed the suffix *vatup*, and then applied the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of a pronoun according to the rule "ā sarvanāmnaḥ. However, the ancient teachers (Pāṇini and others) prescribed the suffix *ḍāvu*; this reference is made with respect to their system.

That which is distinguished is a *viśeṣa*; the state of being that is *vaiśeṣya*. Due to the distinction in meaning—that is, due to a difference in meaning—there is a separate mention of *parimāṇa* from *pramāṇa*; this is what is stated or expressed. It might be argued: "Even though the meanings of the words *pramāṇa* and *parimāṇa* differ, nevertheless, by following the term *pramāṇa* alone, the suffix *-vat* should be applied only to those [words] qualified by it."

In this regard, the following point is also established: this too is proven—namely, "as much distance as there is," "as long a rope as there is," for here the measurement of length (*āyāma*) is understood. As for those usages regarding quantity (*parimāṇa*), such as "as large a heap of grain as there is" and so forth, these will also arise from analogy (*upamāna*). Just as in the established doctrine [of the grammarians], there are expressions such as "as much distance as there is," "as long a rope as there is," and "as many times as he eats. To this, he replies: "so that there may be no obstruction to [the suffixes] *mātra* and the others."

If it were done as previously stated, then because [the suffixes] *ḍāc* and *turi* are prescribed for specific cases, they would sublate (*bādheta*) the general suffixes *mātrac* and so on. However, when the term "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is included, there is no relationship of sublation and sublated because their bases (*upādhi*) are different; thus, forms such as *tanmātram* and *yanmātram* are established as denoting measure. Regarding the phrase "and the state (*bhāva*) is established": the meaning is that the length of this grain is such that it is also of that same measure. Thus, since the domains are distinct, suffixes such as *mātra* are established after words ending in *vat*.

If, however, there were identity of object (*ekaviṣayatva*), then since the qualified object of knowledge would already have been expressed by the suffix *vatup* itself, suffixes such as *mātra* and others could not follow it. For in that case, the word *tāvat* alone would have to be employed even there, as in the expression "the measure of that which has such a measure" (*yasyā hi tāvat pramāṇaṃ tasya tat pramāṇam*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an endless series of suffixes such as *mātra* and the rest.
[Pāṇini 5.2.40: *kim-idam-bhyāṃ vo ghaḥ*.

"How much? This much. [The form] *iyān* is derived from *kim* with the suffix *īyas*, and the elision of *ya* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*. "This very same [suffix]"—the suffix is inferred because the prescription of the substitute would otherwise be inexplicable. Or, "by means of a split of the yoga (yogavibhāga)"—when explained in this way, there is brevity (*lāghava*). Since the result is already established by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the mention of *vaḥ* is for the purpose of indicating that it is a substitute (*ādeśa*); for otherwise, *gha* would be understood as a distinct suffix (*pratyaya*).
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *kim* when expressing a numerical measure. 5.2.41.

Regarding the phrase "the measure of number" (*saṅkhyāyāḥ parimāṇam*): the genitive case in *saṅkhyāyāḥ* is used for the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, because there is an intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the agent. "Measure" (*parimāṇam*) means "delimitation" (*parimitiḥ*). Thus, the meaning is: "in that delimitation which number effects. Furthermore, the substitution of the letter *gha* for that letter *va* occurs because of the continued application of the rule "of *va*, *gha*" (*vo ghaḥ*).

Now, in the phrase "What is the number and the dimension of these?", does the word *kiṃ* (what) refer to the number that performs the delimitation (*paricchedikā saṅkhyā*), and not to the act of delimitation itself? To this he replies: "Because it is being asked" (*pṛcchyamānatvāt*). It is the number, as qualified by its status as a delimiter, that is being asked—"What is the number that delimits these?"—and since the act of delimitation is included within the form of what is being asked, the meaning is that [the word refers to the number] because it functions to delimit the number.

Another says: "In the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). It is said that [the word] which occurs in a question concerning the determination of number (*saṃkhyāpariccheda*) occurs in the determination of number. The meaning is: 'from that which occurs in a question when a number is intended to be determined. Thus, *kati*. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the plural alone is used for the word *bahu*. And it has been stated: 'The plural should be employed when the referent is not specifically determined (*anirjñāte*)."*

How then [should one understand] "how many" (*kiyān*) or "how many" (*kiyantau*)? Here, the word *kim* does not refer to a question regarding number; rather, it refers to a question regarding measure (*parimāṇa*) alone. However, when there is a question regarding number, even in that case the plural is used—such as "how many Brāhmaṇas? When the specific number belonging to something is asked, then suffixes [are applied]; therefore, in that case, the suffix must be formed with a numeral—such as "how many cows are in this herd? (*kati gāvo 'smin varge*).

However, when there is an intention to express the non-difference between the group and those who constitute the group—as in "How many cows are in this herd?"—it does not refer to a herd associated with a fixed number; rather, in the case of a question regarding the number of groups, one asks, "How many herds are there?"

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "athavā" (or else): in this view, *saṃkhyāparimāṇa* is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the inversion of the order of the qualifier is due to irregularity (*nipātana*), and the word *parimāṇa* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). The explanation of the term *evamātmikā* (of such a nature) is "having the nature of delimitation" (*paricchedasvabhāvā*). Regarding the phrase "where it is intended [to be expressed] as non-delimiting": the meaning is that it is not intended to be expressed as a delimiting factor. Or rather, the reading is exactly as it stands. But where is it not so intended? To this he says: "for in the case of censure" (*kṣepe hi*). "What is this of theirs? means: what is this number ten belonging to such things?
"Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on mere birth—even if they assemble by the thousands—there exists no status as an assembly (pariṣad).

Thus, there is a rejection of number by means of the door of enumeration. The term "measure" (parimāṇa) under discussion is not fit to be connected with number because it is a conventional term; therefore, it is taken up here again as denoting mere delimitation.
The suffix *tayap* is added to a numeral to denote a part [of a whole].

In this context, by virtue of the governing rule "of this" (*asya*), a suffix does not first occur in its own sense (*svārthe*) for a numeral that denotes a part (*avayave vartamānāyāḥ*); rather, it would apply to the owner of the parts (*avayavasvāmini*). For example, [one might think the suffix applies] in the case of "Devadatta has five parts. To this, he says: "[It refers to] the related [owner] of the part and the whole (*avayavāvayavinaḥ sambandhinaḥ*). Since the word "part" (*avayava*) is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*), the meaning is that the suffix occurs only with respect to that whole (*avayavin*) for whom there is the status of being a part.

Just as in words such as *dvayasaja* and others, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is the meaning of the suffix while the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is the object of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), so it is here. When the letter *r* is replaced by *visarjanīya*, and that [visarjanīya] becomes *s*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule "after a short vowel, before a suffix beginning with *t*, in a *taddhita*," and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "after a word ending in *ṭi*, *ḍha*, *āṇ*, or *añ*."
After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *taya* is replaced by *ayaj*.

[Objection: Surely *taya* is the subject under discussion and will carry over [into the subsequent rule]; since "from two or three" (*dvitribhyām*) is in the ablative case, the rule "after that, of what follows" (*tasmādityuttarasya*) will effect its change into a genitive form. So what is the purpose of the mention of *tayasya*? To this he replies: "The mention of *taya*, etc. The point is that in the absence of a specific requirement for it, the carry-over [of the previous term] and the original base of the genitive case would be difficult to determine.

Now, what is the fault in [accepting] another suffix? [The fault is that] the rule *trayī gatiḥ* would not apply, and consequently the vowel *ī* based on that suffix would not occur; furthermore, this rule *prathama-carama-taya-ka-ala-* would not apply, as in the forms *dvaye* and *dvayāḥ*. In some places, the passage beginning with "what is the fault there? and so forth is read in the Vṛtti itself. As for the mention of the particle *ca*, it is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). By means of that, through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the unaccented nature (*anudāttatva*) does not occur.
That which has both [the first and the last syllables] acute is always [called *ubhayatodāttá*]. 5.2.44.

"By the force of the statement [that the word is] accented" means that since its final syllable being accented is already established by the *cit*-accent, it cannot be entirely accented, because of the rule "A word is unaccented except for one [syllable]. Nor does the statement of the accent serve to subvert the unaccented status of the vocative *ubhaya* (in *he ubhaye*) or the initial accent of the vocative *ubhaya*; rather, by the principle of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāya*), it subverts only the *cit*-accent itself.

If the word *ubha* signifies a number (*saṃkhyā*), then when *ubhau* is uttered, there is the cognition "two. If, on the other hand, it does not signify a number, this is because no grammatical operations pertaining to numbers—such as those involving the suffix *kṛtvasuc*—are observed; furthermore, in common worldly usage, one does not see such counting as "one," "both," or "three. Regarding the rule "for that [word *ubha*, the substitute] *ayac* is always [applied]," why is it not assumed that *ayac* is simply another suffix? In that case, the purpose would be this: it would not be necessary to state "acute-accented" (*udātta*), since it would be established by the accent of the suffix itself.

Furthermore, regarding what was stated in the section on the technical name *sarvanāman*—namely, that for the word *ubhaya*, when followed by the suffix *jas*, the designation [of *sarvanāman*] is obligatory because it is listed among the *sarva-ādi* group, and not optional under the rule *prathamacaramatayālpārdhakati-paya-nemāśca*—that too becomes unnecessary effort. How so? Because this [suffix] is not a substitute for *tayap*. True; however, in the case of *ubhayī*, the long vowel *ī* would not occur based on *tayap*.

But if, in the prescription of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, the term *mātraj* includes *ayac* by means of the letter *c* (as a *pratyāhāra*), then the long vowel *ī* is established even though *ayac* is a distinct suffix.

The mention of *udātta* (acute accent) and the mention of *nitya* (invariable) could have been omitted, as could the mention of *tayap* in the rule prescribing the suffix *ṅīp*. Alternatively, even the mention of *daghnac* and *mātrac* there could have been omitted; let there be a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference) for *ayac* alone by means of the letter *c* in the word *dvayasa*. However, it was not adopted in that way. In the example *ubhayo maṇiḥ* ("a jewel with two [parts]"), the designation of the whole (*avayavin*) is based on its parts (*avayava*), meaning "that which has both yellow and red parts. In the example *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ* ("both gods and men"), this is a designation of the members of the groups whose distinctions are not obscured, with reference to two classes.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the word *daśan* in the sense of "more than this," [forming the word *adhika*]. (Pāṇini 5.2.45)

In this [sūtra], because of the mention of both "in which there is more" (*asminn adhikam*) and "more than which" (*yasmād adhikam*), the locative and ablative cases occur when joined with the word *adhika*. Thus, in the example *adhikā khārī droṇena* ("a khārī is more than a droṇa"), the instrumental case also occurs when the agent is expressed. [The examples are: *ekādaśa adhikā asmin śate* ("eleven more in this hundred"). Furthermore, the rule regarding "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*) is prohibited by the base noun (*prātipadikena*). And so on, including [the prohibition] regarding the meaning of the suffix. The meaning is that the suffix occurs when the meanings of the base and the suffix belong to the same category. And this meaning is established by logic.

For instance: in a sentence, first of all, the eleven cows—which are expressed as a qualification of the hundred by the phrase "there are eleven more in this herd of cows"—touch upon the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as well due to their proximity. Even in a compound (*vṛtti*), when it is said "one hundred and eleven cows," the cows are perceived as being present precisely as the meaning of the base. However, where a word denoting a different kind of thing to be numbered is employed, that [other] thing, which is proximate through the word itself, sets aside the other [proximate] meaning.

Furthermore, in a compound (vṛtti), the meaning of the base cannot be qualified by such a word, because it has already attained a unified meaning with the meaning of the suffix, as in the case of "the son of Upagu who is old" (vṛddhasyopagavaḥ).
"And it will be desired for [the numbers] one hundred and one thousand"—this is precisely the *iṣṭi* (intention).

The particle *iti* has the sense of "intended meaning" (*vivakṣārtha*). From that, all of this is obtained. Although the preceding matter is obtained through logic alone, nevertheless, the point that "it will be desired for one hundred and one thousand" is obtained from the particle *iti* itself; thus, for the sake of brevity, a common reason is taught.

"How so? and so forth. When "hundred" or "thousand" is the intended meaning, the suffix does not apply here; for in this case, there is another number, namely "hundred-thousand," and it is not simply "hundred" or "thousand"—this is the sense. He says "of hundreds" or "of thousands" to show that even here, it is one of the two—either hundred or thousand—that constitutes the meaning of the suffix, and not some other number.

In this case as well, because of the traditional rule "of the smaller number" (*saṃkhyāyā alpīyasyāḥ*)—which applies both in a *dvandva* compound and in a non-*dvandva* compound—the word "hundred" (*śata*) alone is placed first. In the former analysis (*vigraha*), since hundreds are being numbered, they themselves constitute the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*): "in which eleven hundred thousand are exceeded by eleven hundreds. In the latter, however, since thousands are the objects to be numbered, they themselves constitute the meaning of the base: "in which eleven hundred thousand are exceeded by eleven thousands. And by the force of context and so forth, it is determined whether the hundreds are the objects to be numbered.

He demonstrates the very same point by means of a verse: "When [the suffix] occurs in the sense of a superior [number] within the same genus (*samānajātīya*). The meaning is that the suffix occurs when the genus of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is identical to the genus associated with the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), provided that the suffix denotes a greater number. Alternatively, "within the same genus" (*samānajātau*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. However, the suffix *cha* does not indicate the end of a genus (*jātyanta-lakṣaṇa*); this is because of its usage in the *Bhāṣya*. The meaning is: "from that which occurs in an object belonging to the same genus as the meaning of the suffix. "Desired" (*iṣṭam*) refers to the grammatical operation (*kārya*) known as the suffix.

Regarding the statement "eleven hundred thousand," he says [the following] for the sake of providing an explanation: "of which the number... It has been stated that "hundreds and thousands are counted," and also that "when there is an addition of the same kind. Therefore, "of which the number" means that whatever kind of number is being counted; the singular number is used with reference to the general category. In the case of an addition to that, it is my view that the [plural] should be applied. This has already been made clear in the very example provided; nothing new has been said here.

Regarding the rule *śadantaviṃśateśca*: the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is redundant, because there exists no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) consisting of the word "hundred" (*śata*) alone; by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of an affix, the rule will apply to that which ends in it. Furthermore, since words such as "thirty" (*triṃśat*) are prescribed in the sūtra on *paṅkti* etc. as ending in the affix *śat*, [the author] says here: "In the mention of 'śat', the mention of 'end' [is intended]."

By means of the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of the referent (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), when the rule for "that which ends with [the element mentioned]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, there would be a restriction to that which begins with it (*tadādiniyama*). However, because the word "end" (*anta*) is included here, the inclusion applies to as much of a whole aggregate as has the word *śat* at its end. And regarding the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyāgrahaṇam*): the meaning is that the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*) must be carried over from the rule "the suffix *tayap* occurs after a number to denote a part" (*saṃkhyāyā avayave tayap*). By this, the meaning is that the suffix occurs after a word denoting a number that ends in *śat*.

The words *ekatriṃśat* and so forth denote a specific number, but not a collection; therefore, they are included [in the rule]. However, words such as *gotriṃśat* do not denote a number, and thus they are not included. Regarding the phrase *viṃśateśca*: the meaning is that the word *anta* (ending) should be read immediately after the word *viṃśati*; otherwise, due to the prohibition by the rule *grahaṇavatā*, there would be no application for those ending in *viṃśati*.

Regarding the rule *saṃkhyāyā guṇasya nimāne mayaṭ* and the rule *tadasya sañjātam ityataḥ*: first, it is declared that the entire compound *tadasya* possesses the svarita accent, and this is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) through many subsequent rules. However, in the rule *tadasminn adhikam*, because the word *tat* is mentioned again, it does not connect [with the previous *tadasya*]; that is all.

But here, because there is no obstacle to its application, that very same collective [term] continues to follow; this is the meaning. Therefore, it is logical that the word *tat* (in the compound *tadasmin*) alone follows by immediate proximity. It should not be objected that the continuation of *asya* is improper because it is interrupted by the word *asmin*. "The measure is the price" (*nimānam mūlyam*): from the root *mīṅ* in the sense of "giving" (*praṇidāne*), with the prefix *ni*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the instrumental sense (*karaṇe*); the meaning is "that by which something is measured," i.e., purchased. In the phrase "of the quality" (*guṇasya*), the genitive case is used in the objective sense (*karmaṇi*). And "that too, by virtue of the context" (*so 'pi sāmarthyāt*).

Even a word denoting a quality expresses a form that is dependent [on something else]; for instance, when it is said "twofold" or "threefold," it is understood that this is in relation to something. In that case, the state of being a quality (guṇatva) of the object to be measured is established in dependence on the measure (nimāna) present there—this is the force of the context. As in the expression, "two parts of barley."

Although in both cases the relinquishing of one's own and the taking of what belongs to another are equal, nevertheless, in some instances, a certain course of action is more prevalent. For example, when the act of relinquishing is the same, one says "he sells grain," but no one says "he sells a kārṣāpaṇa coin. Therefore, the status of being the object of exchange (nimāna) belongs only to the portions of barley, not to the portion of whey (udaśvit). Alternatively, the relationship between the means of exchange and the object of exchange depends upon place and time.

Since a measure (*nimāna*) depends upon that which is to be measured (*nimeya*), the purpose [of the measure] is to convey the object to be measured; the meaning is that two measures of barley are the price for one measure of buttermilk. For example: "for one *prastha* of buttermilk, there are two *prasthas* of barley," or "barley is twice the measure of buttermilk. The employment of the word "barley" (*yava*) and so forth as a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is for the sake of conveying a specific portion.

Furthermore, since the word *dvi-* (two) in its derivative usage (*vṛtti*) refers only to the two parts that are the objects of counting, it is a relative term (*sambandhiśabda*) and thus necessarily dependent [on another]. Therefore, its occurrence as a compound with *taddhita* is not contradictory. But how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *udaśvit* when the suffix is prescribed for the "part" (*bhāga*) consisting of curdled milk, and not for "curdled milk" (*udaśvit*) itself? To this he says: "But even when prescribed for a part... In this case, the reason is the inherent nature of linguistic expression (*abhidhānasvābhāvya*).

Another says: where a portion of buttermilk (*udaśvit*) is purchased for twice as much barley, there, by implication, the whole aggregate is also purchased for twice as much barley—whether by many [barley grains] or by one; it is with reference to that [aggregate] that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, the singular number in the word *guṇasya* is intended to be significant; for this very reason, the lighter expression *guṇanimāne* was not employed. [The example is: "two parts of barley and three of buttermilk."

This was not cited with the thought that "the word *bhūyasaḥ* has already been stated [as the indicator]," for in this case, the word *dvi-* is not the indicator of *bhūyas*. Alternatively, this is merely shown as an illustrative direction; one should rather show "three of barley, two of buttermilk," or inquire into the relationship between the standard of measure (*nimāna*) and the thing measured (*nimeya*). Regarding the phrase "of the greater" (*bhūyasaḥ*): the meaning is that the suffix denotes that number which indicates the greater sense of the base (*prakṛti*) relative to the sense of the suffix itself. It does not occur here [in the following example].

The meaning is that [the rule] does not apply to the case of the equality between the standard of comparison (*nimāna*) and the object compared (*nimeya*); otherwise, even if one intended to express the singular number for the word *guṇa*, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would indeed still arise. Why, then, does it not apply? Because it is not so stated.

Since the word *bhūyas* is derived according to the rule *bahorlopo bhū ca bahoḥ*, the suffix must occur when there is a greater degree of the base-meaning; consequently, one might suspect that it would not apply after the word *dvi*. Anticipating this, he says: "And [the word] *bhūyasaḥ*," and so forth. The term "quality-word" (*guṇa-śabda*) and so on: for this does not denote a mere portion (*bhāga-mātra*), but rather it expresses the equality of that portion as well.

"And it is also seen in the case of *nimeya*. How is this obtained? By resorting to one of the [grammatical devices] known as *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*. Here there are two words; therein, one is *vyākhyā* (explanation), and the second is *nimāna* (measure). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are applied diversely" (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*).

Regarding the word *guṇasya*: when there is an intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the agent (*kartṛ*), the genitive case is used for the agent. Since that which is measured (*nimeya*) depends upon the means of measurement (*nimāna*), the suffix has the means of measurement as its meaning; everything else remains as explained previously. Why is it said "of a number" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*)? [Consider the example: *yavabhāgau nimānam udaśvidbhāgasya*. A suffix does not occur after the word *yavabhāga* ending in a dual suffix (*dvivacanānta*). In the case of *vrīhiyavau*, here the means of measurement is two portions of curd (*udaśvit*) itself, not a portion of those [grains]; therefore, the form *dvimayam udaśvid vrīhiyavau* does not occur.
"Oil is cooked with double the milk" means that there are two measures of milk in relation to this oil; therefore, it is said that the oil is cooked together with that very milk.
The suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied after [a word ending in] *taddhita* *pūraṇa* to denote that which completes it.

In the word *tasya*, the singular number is not intended to be significant, because it is impossible for a single entity to be completed [by a fraction]. Therefore, the suffix is applied after words such as *dvi* and others ending in the dual and plural numbers. The term *pūraṇa* means "that by which something is completed"; here the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). As for the form *pūryate*, it is derived from the causative stem (*ṇyanta*) in the passive voice (*yak*), and not from another verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*) in the active voice (*kartari śyan*).

If a suffix is prescribed after a word expressing a number to denote a "completer" (*pūraṇa*), then it would follow here as well: "the jar which completes five camel-loads that have already acquired the number five"? To this, he says: "by which" (*yena*). This is an explanation of the term "number" (*saṃkhyā*): "counting" (*saṃkhyāna*). Here, a suffix is ordained after a word expressing a number; therefore, by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood that the suffix denotes the completer of that counting—such as "fiveness" (*pañcatva*)—which is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of that specific word expressing the number.

The meaning is that [the term] does not apply to something remote (*viprakṛṣṭa*), such as that which is not included within the denotation of words like *pañca* (five) and so on—as in the case of the rules "the suffixes *tamaP* and *iṣṭhan* are used in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*) or "in the sense of being contemptible" (*kutsita*). Regarding the phrase "the completer of eleven" (*ekādaśānāṃ pūraṇaḥ*): likewise, in the expression "a wretched grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ*), even though there is a contempt for the ground of application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is "a contemptible grammarian" (*yāpyo vaiyākaraṇaḥ*), and not "a contemptible state of being a grammarian" (*yāpyaṃ vaiyākaraṇatvam*). Similarly here too, when the completion of a number is intended, an analysis using a word expressing the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*) is not contradictory. Thus, [it is said] "eleven."

When counting is performed again, it should be understood that he is the one by whom the number eleven is completed as it resides in the intellect upon reaching the feet (*caraṇa*). And thus, when the eight chapters are counted in reverse order, when the chapter beginning with "A grammatical rule concerning words depends on their mutual connection" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*) is counted last, then even for the second [chapter] from the end, the designation of being "eighth" certainly occurs according to the sequence of counting.

But surely, there ought to be a meaning for the suffix distinct from the meaning of the base; for here, since "eleven" is included within the group of eleven, when it is said, "Let the eleven be brought," even the eleventh is brought. True; however, because of the distinction between the whole and its part, the whole is the meaning of the base and the part is the meaning of the suffix, just as in the case of "a branch of a tree" (*vārkṣī śākhā*), where the branch is a part of the tree.
The suffix *maṭ* is not applied after a word ending in *anta*, nor after a word beginning with *asaṃkhya*.

"An augment *maṭ* occurs after [a stem ending in] *ḍaṭ*. But how can this augment be understood, since no augment has been specified here, and even that which is under discussion (the context) ends in the nominative case? Furthermore, what is the purpose here of [specifying] the genitive case? To this he says: "After one ending in *n*" (*nāntāt*). The mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) continues [from the previous rule], and its recurrence is not for the sake of prescribing it anew, because it has already been prescribed previously.

Nor is the recurrence of the suffix *ḍaṭ* intended for the purpose of its prescription when there is the possibility of it being superseded by the specifically prescribed suffix *maṭ*; for if that were the case, the particle *ca* would have been used in the present context to signify a conjunction with the preceding, as is done elsewhere—namely, [the rule would have read] "and *maṭ*" (*maṭ ca*). Therefore, by the force of its recurrence, it is understood that [the suffix] is indeed an augment (*āgama*) once the sixth case has been established. But what is the difference between *maṭ* being a suffix (*pratyaya*) or an augment (*āgama*), since its form is the same and its accent is the same? True.

There is no difference between the suffixes *ḍaṭ* and *maṭ*; however, if this *tamaṭ* were a suffix (pratyaya), as in the rule "from *viṃśati* etc., *tamaṭ* optionally," it would be udātta on its first syllable. Since it is an augment (*āgama*), it follows the rule that augments are anudātta; thus, it does not take the accent of a suffix, and consequently, *viṃśatitamaḥ* has its final syllable udātta.

Regarding the term *ekādaśa* ("eleven"): this is not a collective aggregate of numbers; rather, it is a distinct number itself. For this very reason, the suffix *ḍaḍ* occurs here; otherwise, even that would not apply. Indeed, a collective aggregate of numbers is not grasped by the term "number," just as a collective aggregate of countries is not grasped by the term "country"—as in the case of "the inhabitants of Kāśi and Kośala. Even if this were a collective aggregate of numbers, it must nevertheless be stated as "not beginning with a number" (*asaṃkhyādeḥ*) for the purpose of indicating that such an aggregate is indeed included under the term "number"; thus, all grammatical operations pertaining to numbers apply to *ekādaśa* and the like as well.
The suffix *thuk* is applied after the words *ṣaṭ*, *kati*, *katipaya*, and *catur*. (Pāṇini 5.2.51)

Therefore, in this case, the locative case (*saptamī*) is substituted [for the genitive].
