If, as before, a substitution for the genitive were intended, it would have been indicated by the ablative case (*pañcamī*); however, because it is indicated by the genitive, it is understood that only *ṣaṣ* and the others possess the status of being augmental (*āgamin*). Consequently, the meaning is that the suffix *ḍaṭ*, which has been carried over [from a previous rule], is effectively transformed into the locative by implication. And by doing so, the formulation "from *ṣaṣ* and *aṣṭama*, [the forms] *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, and *caturtha*" becomes logically consistent. Furthermore, the word *katipaya* is not a numeral.

Although this term denotes a plurality devoid of excessive accumulation, nevertheless, it is not recognized as a number (*saṃkhyā*) in common usage, as in the expressions *dvitrāḥ* (two or three) and *pañcaṣāḥ* (five or six). Furthermore, its designation as a number has not been prescribed even in the technical treatises (*śāstra*). [The opponent asks: "In that case, how is the suffix *ḍaṭ* applied? To this he replies: "Of that" (*tasya*). But why is the augment *thuk* prescribed? Why should the suffix *thaṭ*, which is already present in the context, not be prescribed by means of a reference to the fifth case (*pañcamī*)? This cannot be so.

In this case, [if *thaṭ* were applied first], the sixth [suffix] would undergo the substitution of *jaś*, and the fourth [suffix] would undergo the substitution of *visarjanīya* for the *repha*, followed by the substitution of *satva*; this is because, due to the initial position of *thaṭ*, the preceding element would be treated as a word (*pada*). If, however, *thuk* alone were prescribed in the previous rule, it would not be possible; for instance, in *pañcathaḥ* and *saptathaḥ*, there would be no elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

Here, by the maxim regarding the inclusion of gender-distinct forms (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), *thuk* occurs even after words ending in long *ā* derived from *katipaya*; in that context, since the masculine form is applied only when the suffix *ḍaṭ* is the domain of application according to the rule "in a *bha*-stem before a non-*ḍha* secondary suffix" (*bhasyāḍhe taddhite*), the form becomes *katipayathī*—meaning "the female ordinal of those who are few."

Regarding the phrase "caturaśchyatāviti": the suffix *ḍaṭ* is not superseded by the two [suffixes] beginning with *chay*; this is because the rule for *thuk* is prescribed when *iṭ* follows. Regarding the phrase "and the elision of the first syllable" (*ādyakṣaralopaśca*): a consonant accompanied by a vowel is denoted by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*), meaning the first consonant together with its accompanying vowel. If the word "syllable" were used to denote a vowel accompanied by a consonant, then by the principle of doubling (*dvirvacananyāyena*), there would also have to be an elision of the letter *t*.
The suffix *tithuk* is applied after [the word] *bahupūgaga* when it is followed by *saṃgha*.

Here too, because of the mention in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśāt*), only *bahvī* and the others possess the status of being a feminine suffix (*āgamitva*). The rule beginning with "pūga-saṅghayoḥ" constitutes a single textual unit. In this context, the term "the ordinal of many females" (*bahvīnāṃ pūraṇī*) follows the previous [rule], whereby the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied and there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*).
The suffix *athuc* is applied after the verbal root *vā* (to blow). || 5.2.53 ||

Here too, as before, only that which ends in *vat* is the augment. In this case, the suffix is applied by the rule regarding the inclusion of forms qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), resulting in the form *tāvatithī* (the ordinal number for so many), and there is also the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). But how can the rule regarding forms qualified by gender apply here, given that it has been stated that it applies when the specific form of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is being grasped? Even where a qualifier of the nominal stem is taken in its own form, that rule still applies; for example, in the rule "after [stems ending in] *tṛc* or *aka*, [the genitive suffix is used] when denoting the agent," as in the example *apāṃ sraṣṭrī* ("the creator of waters").

Here too, the qualifier *vatuḥ* is taken in its own form; therefore, the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*) indeed occurs. And it has been stated: "The suffixes *bahu* and *katipaya* are produced from [bases] qualified by gender; for when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is also included."
The second [case-affix] is used in the sense of the accusative. 5.2.54.

[The objection is: "The suffix *tīya* occurs [after a word ending in *dvitīya*]; thus, it is not a substitute for the suffix *ḍaṭ* nor for the word *dvi*, because of the specific mention [in the rule] as *dvitīya*. If this is so, then is its correctness (*sādhutva*) not established by that very mention? [Response: Let its correctness be established; however, how is the meaning of 'ordinal' (*pūraṇa*) obtained? Furthermore, if one were to rely on that [mention], there would be no distinction between base and suffix, and consequently, by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it would have an udātta accent on the final syllable. Moreover, according to the view that 'even those [forms] which are not exceptions are treated as irregularities (*nipātana*),' there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *ḍaṭ* applying [instead of *tīya*]."
There is also vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the vowel *tṛ*.

The term *aṇ* is understood to carry over there [from the previous rule], from the rule "When *ḍh* or *l* is elided, the preceding vowel becomes long, provided it is an *aṇ*. Even so, if the pratyāhāra were formed with the subsequent *ṇ*, the lengthening would still occur; however, that is not the case. Thus he says: "by the preceding [ṇ]. This has already been explained under the rule "laṇ. The form *trestr̥ ca* was not stated [in the rule] so that it might not be understood as a suffix (*pratyaya*).

[The rule] *viṃśatyādibhyastamaḍanyatarasyām* [means] "after *viṃśati* and the others. But how is it that, although the suffix *ḍaṭ* is interrupted by the suffix *tīya* in the rule *dvestīyaḥ*, the sense of "ordinal" (*pūraṇa*) is not interrupted? That [sense] continues; therefore, it is understood that the augment *tamap* applies to that which was prescribed for the purpose of ordinality. And there is no other suffix prescribed after *viṃśati* and the others for the purpose of ordinality than *ḍaṭ*.

But what is the fault in accepting [the interpretation] as indicated by the sūtras beginning with *paṅkti*? To this he says: "For in that case... It might be argued: "By the rule of extension to the end of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*), it will apply even from numbers such as twenty-one (*ekaviṃśati*) and so on. To this he says: "Like that which is explicitly mentioned (*grahaṇavat*). Now, when he says "from *ṣaṣṭi* etc., provided they are not preceded by another number," that indicates that the rule of extension to the end of a compound applies within the section concerning ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*). Therefore, it will apply even from twenty-one and so forth.

This has been stated; however, it would not apply to simple [stems] alone because they do not end in that [suffix]. It will occur by virtue of the principle "treatment as having a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), according to the rule "the treatment as having a designation applies except in the case of a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*)". And so forth.

If this refers to worldly numbers such as twenty and so forth, then in the rule "ṣaṣṭyādeśca" (Pāṇini 5.2.58) as well, only worldly numbers like sixty and so forth are understood. Consequently, since the suffix *tamaṭ* would necessarily apply to numbers beginning with sixty-one, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule "asaṃkhyādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.48) is indeed appropriate; it is not in any way inappropriate, as there is not even a trace of an undesirable consequence. However, if the reference were to the numbers specifically included within the Sūtra itself, then the exclusion would be appropriate for the purpose of indicating that the rule applies to those ending in such numbers (*tadantavidhi*).

The meaning of the *vṛtti* is that [the rule] applies only [to those ending in *kāraka*], but it does not apply to *kevala* (the word "only" itself) because there is no possibility of its occurrence as such. However, according to the *bhāṣya*, the inclusion is of those words situated within the *sūtra*; and it is established that the extension to forms ending in [a specific element] (*tadantavidhi*) occurs by virtue of an implied indication (*jñāpana*). The body of this indication is that there is no non-occurrence for *kevala* alone, but rather that it also occurs for those ending in [that element]; it does not mean that it occurs only for those ending in [that element].

Alternatively, this is a general indication that where there is the explicit mention (śruti) of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—as in the rules "by a nominal stem possessing [the suffix] *grahaṇa*" and "the treatment as having a designation applies to what is not a nominal stem"—neither of those two [restrictions] operates. By doing so, the following is also established: "the filler of nineteen" (*ekānnaviṃśatitama*). For this word contains the number ending in "twenty" (*viṃśati*) situated within the sūtra, and it is a denoter of number. However, if the worldly (laukika) numbers were being taken, this would not be established;
because this number occurs prior to twenty.
The suffix *nityam* is used after [words denoting] a hundred and so forth, as well as after *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*. (Pāṇini 5.2.57)
The section beginning with "māsādayaḥ" and ending with "vijñāyate" constitutes a single block of text.

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "śata" (hundred) and so forth, since this would already be established by the upcoming rule "ṣaṣṭyādeśca"? To this, he replies: "by that very [rule] 'ṣaṣṭyādeḥ'. If it were established by that, it would not apply to words such as "ekaśata" (one hundred and one), because of the prohibition "asaṃkhyādeḥ" (not from a word beginning with a numeral).
And [the suffix *kan* is added] after words beginning with *ṣaṣṭi*, provided they do not begin with a numeral (*asaṃkhyādi*).

"But in the case of number and so forth, there is only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this is not a negation even of conceptual construction; rather, this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of number and so forth, neither a positive injunction nor a negation. If something were to be obtained by some means, it would indeed exist; and since it is obtained by what precedes, [the rule] excludes that which follows immediately, not that which is separated. Even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), that which is immediately proximate is prohibited, not that which is remote.
The word *matu* [is substituted] for the suffixes *sūkta* and *sāman*. 5.2.59.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of possession" (*matāv*), this refers to the meaning of the possessive suffix *matup*. Due to association, the primary [meaning] is not what is being grasped here. For how could the possessive suffix itself be the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) of a word? [The text continues: "By the inclusion of the sense of possession," and so forth. The case-ending expressing grammatical competency (*samarthavibhakti*) is the nominative. The qualifier—namely existence (*astitva*)—is connected to the base word (*prakṛti*) through its meaning. The meaning of the suffix consists of both "this belongs to him" and "in this. In that regard, although the expressed meaning of the suffix is indeed the denotation of the possessive suffix (*matup*), the other [aspects] are not its denotation.

Nevertheless, since concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is indistinguishable, all of this is implied—meaning it is brought near (*sannidhāpyate*), that is, it is presented (*upasthāpyate*). Alternatively, because subordinate elements (*guṇa*) are dependent upon the principal element (*pradhāna*), once the principal meaning—the sense of the suffix—is presented, the subordinate factors such as the case-ending expressing capacity (*samarthavibhakti*) are likewise necessarily presented, just like the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and so forth. For example, when it is said, "Let the Brahmins be fed," even though they are not explicitly mentioned, subordinate acts such as rinsing the mouth are implied.

Since both the genitive and nominative cases are observed here in the expression *ihāsyavām* ("it exists here in this"), this is a collection of multiple words; consequently, because the rule regarding compounds (*samāsa*) is intended as a restrictive one for collections that possess meaning, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) does not apply. Thus, a suffix would not be obtained from such forms. Therefore, he says: "and [this applies to] words that are imitations (*anukaraṇa*). "In which the mere form itself is predominant" means that at that time, the actual form of the imitation as it was uttered is not intended to be expressed; rather, what is intended is the form of the original object being imitated (*anukārya*).

The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding external objects; this is what is meant: just as words such as "cow" (*go*) convey an object characterized by the form of possessing a dewlap and so forth, and thereby give rise to the possessive suffix *matup* with respect to that object—as in *gomān* ("possessing cows") or *vṛkṣavān* ("possessing trees")—so too do imitation-words (*anukaraṇaśabda*), when they are in the nominative case, give rise to the suffix *cha* with respect to their own original (*anukārya*) which possesses that [imitation-word]. By the phrase "imitation-words," he excludes the status of being a collection of words (*padasamudāyatva*).

For a collection of words (*padasamudāya*) is that which is to be imitated (*anukārya*), but not the imitation itself (*anukaraṇa*). What, then, is the difference between the object of imitation and the imitation? Is it not the case that no difference in form (*rūpabheda*) is perceived? Even so, there is a distinction due to the difference in meaning: the object of imitation has an external referent (*bāhyārtha*), whereas for the imitation, that very [external object] is what is being imitated. For this very reason, in cases such as *asyāvāmīyam*, because the meaning of the case-ending is not conveyed, the status of being a nominal stem (*subantatva*) is absent; consequently, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffixes in words like *sya*.

Furthermore, those rules regarding the words of the Vedic tradition—such as "one should not study in a cremation ground," "one should not study on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight]," and "if one hears the Veda from a Śūdra, one's ears are to be filled with lac and molten lead"—these do not apply to imitations. For the hymn known as the *Asyavāmīya* is employed everywhere, at all times, and in the presence of everyone. Therefore, other words are imitative sounds (*anukaraṇaśabda*), whereas the words being imitated (*anukāryaśabda*) possess meaningfulness by virtue of presenting the mere form of the original.

"Even from multiple words" (*anekapadād api*) means: even from that collection (*samudāya*) in which there are multiple words. This is stated according to the opponent's own established view; the meaning is: "even from that which you consider to be a collection of multiple words. However, in reality, there is no state of being multiple words here—for instance, in the case of *asyavāmīyam*, the two words *asya* and *vāmasya* as they are recited in the Veda, the word *asyavāma* is the base form (*prakṛti*) for the suffix *cha* belonging to the single constituent part *asyavāma*.

The term *pratipādaka* (designator) signifies meaningfulness; and because it lacks the status of being a collection of words (*padasamudāya*), while possessing the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), a suffix is applied. But what is the proof here that the base of the *cha*-suffix is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*)? It is the *cha*-suffix itself. For this [suffix] is not possible without the status of being an imitation. Therefore, just like the word *iti*, the *cha*-suffix is also proof for the status of being an imitation.
The suffix *luk* (elision) is applied to the [secondary] nominal suffixes denoting chapters (*adhyāya*) and sections (*anuvāka*).

"But by what [is it established]?"—this is the question, since the suffix *cha* is prescribed only for *sūkta* and *sāman*. "This very [suffix]"—for if it were non-existent, the prescription of its elision (*luk*) would not be logical. "And optionally"—how is it that, when this very sūtra ought to have been formulated within the section on the possessive suffix *matup*, the elision of *cha* is instead prescribed here? Therefore, an optional elision is inferred. On this point, some say: because of its association with the *anuvāka*, the Vedic chapter (*adhyāya*) is understood [to be meant].

Others, however, maintain that the term *adhyāya* should also include specific human-authored texts; and this is indeed seen in medical treatises, such as in the passage: "We shall explain the chapter on Longevity (*Dīrghajīvitīya-adhyāya*)."
In that case, [the suffix -ya] is applied after the word *kuśala* when it means "path. (Pāṇini 5.2.63)

Regarding the expression *pathi kuśalaḥ*: the locative case is used here by the rule *āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām*. Since proficiency (*kauśala*) has an action as its object, the word *pathin* indicates the action of going and so forth that takes that path as its object. Furthermore, this grammatical construction is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *ākarṣa*.

*Ākaṣa*: that in which gold and so forth are drawn (*ākaṣati*) is called *ākaṣa*. The suffix *gha* is applied by the rule "in the masculine, when it is a technical name" (*puṃsi saṃjñāyām*). The suffix *ghañ* does not apply here because the word "mostly" (*prāyas*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], as in the case of *nikaṣa*. However, for those who read the root as *ākarṣ* with a *repha* (i.e., *ākarṣ*), the form is derived from *ghañ* in the sense of "that in which something is drawn. *Tsaruka*: [The root] *tsakara* means "to move stealthily. The suffix *u* is added according to the rule beginning with "the group starting with *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śṛ*" (*bhṛmṛśrṛ...*). *Tsaru* is the part of a sword where the hilt is grasped.

This introduction of another suffix (*pratyaya*) ending in *i* is for the sake of words ending in *i*; however, in the case of words ending in *a*, such as *ākārṣa* and others, the formation is already established by the suffix *vuñ* under discussion.
The suffix *kāmaC* is applied after *dhana* and *hiraṇya* in the sense of "desire for."
"Desire" (kāma) is intended [by the suffix]; however, the desirer is not grasped [as the agent], because it is not expressed [by the suffix].
The suffix *kha* is applied after a word denoting one's own limbs when it signifies something spread out from those limbs. || 5.2.66 ||

"Prasitaḥ" means "attached" (*prasakta*). [The suffix] *kta* is applied to the root *ṣiñ* (meaning "to bind") in the sense of the object (*karman*); thus, one who is attached to something is as if firmly bound (*prakarṣeṇa baddha*) to it—this term is used based on such a comparison. In the example "prasitaḥ keśeṣu," the locative case is employed according to the rule "the third case is also used with *prasita* and *utsuka*. By saying "in the arrangement of hair, etc.," he shows that the word "hair" (*keśa*) and so forth functions to denote the arrangement situated upon the hair. And this is understood from the attachment [of the person] to the activity, since that activity has the hair as its object.

Regarding the phrase "the plural number," etc.: the plural number is not intended for the purpose of prescribing the word's own form (*svarūpa*), because since "limb" (*svāṅga*) has been defined by the rule beginning with "not liquid" (*adrava*), it is impossible for the word's own form to be grasped [as the meaning].
The suffix *ane* is applied after [a word ending in] *udara*, *aṣṭhīva*, and so forth. || 5.2.67 ||

*Ādyuna* means one who desires victory; this is because the rule for the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past participle suffix) in that context prescribes the substitution of *na* for *t*. *Udaraka* refers to one who is intent on such things as massaging the belly.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied after the word *sasya* when it means "grown from. (Pāṇini 5.2.68)

The two words *sasya* and *śasya* denote a quality (*guṇa*) and do not denote grain (*dhānya*), because [grain] is not so designated. However, some read the word *śasya* as ending in the suffix *kyap*, according to the rule "after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*, [the suffix *kyap* is optionally applied]. In the expression *sasyena*, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The term *parijāta* means "completely grown" (*parigato jātaḥ*); it is a compound formed by the rule "prepositions [such as *pari*] are compounded with a word in the first case when they mean 'gone' (*gata*) and so forth. It means "completely connected" (*samantāt saṃbaddhaḥ parigataḥ*). In this context, the crop (*sasya*) functions as the agent; thus he says: "that which has become connected with qualities."
The word *hīrī* [is substituted for *hrī*] before the suffix *aṃś*. 5.2.69.

In that context, [the objection] is "because of the prohibition of the sixth case (genitive) by the rule *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*. Now, one might ask: does that [rule] refer to the suffix *aka* prescribed under the heading of the future tense (*bhaviṣyat*)? True; however, the suffix *in* is also included without distinction, precisely because of this mention of the accusative case.
The suffix *ṭyaP* is applied after the word *tantra* when it means "recently removed. (Pāṇini 5.2.70)

*Tantra* means that in which threads (*tantavaḥ*) are stretched (*tanyante*); it refers to a weaver’s shuttle. Alternatively, from the root *tan*, with the suffix *erac*, there is the elision of the causative marker (*ṇi*). Regarding the phrase *acirāpahṛta* ("recently removed"): since "a short time (*aciraḥ kālaḥ*)" has elapsed for what was removed, this is a compound formed according to the rule *kālāḥ parimāṇinā*. Regarding the phrase *pañcamīsamarthāt* ("from that which is in the fifth case"): when used in connection with *apahṛta*, the fifth case is employed by the rule *apādāne pañcamī*.
The word *brāhmaṇaka* is substituted for *brāhmaṇa* before the suffix *uṣṇika* when it denotes a name.

[The two words] ending in the suffix *kan* are treated as irregular forms (*nipātyete*). What, then, is irregular here? From the word *brāhmaṇa*, when qualified by the condition of being "one who lives by weapons" (*āyudhajīvī*), the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the locative case (the seventh case-ending); from the word *anna*, when qualified by the condition of "smallness," the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the locative case itself; and for the word *anna*, there is the substitution of *uṣṇa* for *uṣṇa*. Thus he says: "where [there are] those who live by weapons," and so forth.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* when they denote the agent of an action. || 5.2.72 ||

That which makes cold is "cold-making" (*śītaka*), and that which makes hot is "hot-making" (*uṣṇaka*). What follows from this? [The rule] would apply to frost and the sun; for the primary meanings of the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* are specific types of touch, and those two certainly produce them. Seeing the fault in accepting the primary meanings, he says—"from an adverb"—showing that there is an adoption of figurative meanings. In that context, the function of the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* arises through comparison: "cold as it were cold," meaning "slight action."

For "cold" (*śīta*) is associated with slowness, because when it is cold, there is a lack of proficiency in performing an action. Likewise, "hot" (*uṣṇa*) means that which acts with skill or acts quickly; such is the meaning. Thus, the suffix is applied by means of these two adverbs. Regarding the phrase "from that which is in grammatical relation with the second case" (*dvitīyāsamarthāt*): it has already been stated previously that "the genitive case, characterized by its connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛt*), does not occur at the end of an adverb. However, the suffix is not applied to words used in their primary sense (*mukhyārtha*), because they are not so designated.
The suffix *adhika* [is applied in the sense of "exceeding"]. 5.2.73.

Regarding the word *adhyāruḍha*: if, however, the suffix *kan* were applied after the word *adhi*—which denotes an action accompanied by its instrument—then it would follow that only one of the two, either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), could be expressed. Since the word *adhyāruḍha* expresses both meanings, it is appropriate that this irregular formation (*nipātana*) should be accepted for that very word, wherein the distinction of the instruments is already admitted. Thus: "A *droṇa* is more than a *khārī*," or "A *khārī* is exceeded by a *droṇa*."

He demonstrates how these two applications are justified by stating: "the word *adhyārūḍha* [is used] in both the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). By the rule beginning with *gatyarthākarmaka*, the suffix *kta* is prescribed after the root *ruh* in both the sense of the agent and the object. And by the force of the irregular formation (*nipātana*), even though it is mentioned only once, it includes both distinct grammatical relations (*sādhana*). In that regard, when it denotes the agent, the nominative alone occurs because [the agent] is not otherwise prescribed there, and not the instrumental.

But when [the word *adhika*] is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), since the agent (*kartṛ*) is not expressed, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) applies; however, because the object is expressed, the first case (*prathamā*) applies. And when [the word *adhika*] is used in the sense of the agent, since the object is not expressed, just as the second case occurs in connection with the verb *adhyārūḍha*—as in "a *droṇa* measure has been loaded onto a *khārī*" (just like "he has gone to the village")—so too, although the second case would be expected in connection with the word *adhika*, the fifth (*pañcamī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) cases occur by virtue of the rules "that from which there is more" (*yasmād adhikam*) and "that in which there is more" (*tadasminn adhikam*).
The suffix *kā* is applied after the words *anu*, *abhi*, and *abhī* when they mean "a lover" (*kamitṛ*). || 5.2.74 ||

In the Sūtra, there is a change of gender in the collective dvandva compound; he states that the suffix *kan* is applied in its own sense after the words *anu* and *abhi*, which denote an action together with its instrument—as in "he desires following [it], thus *anuka*. The word "he desires intensely" (*abhikāmayate*) is not explicitly stated because it is already implied.
He seeks by means of the side. 5.2.75.

"An oblique means is 'pārśva' (the side). Because it is situated askance, the side is not straight; likewise, another [type of] means that is not straight is also called *pārśva*. One who seeks objects that ought to be sought by a straightforward means (*ṛju-upāya*) by means of a non-straight one is a *pārśvaka*. A "bad path" is a "crooked way" (*kusṛti*); a "net" is a "snare" (*ānāya*). One who operates by means of these two is a *kausṛtika* (one who uses crooked ways) or a *jālika* (one who uses nets).
The suffixes *ka* and *ṭhak* are applied after the words *śūla* and *daṇḍājina*, respectively, when the sense is "wearing" (*kaṭhaka*). (Pāṇini 5.2.76)

Regarding the phrase "from those [words] having the third case as their governing factor" (*tṛtīyāsamarthābhyām*): this is the third case, not the fifth, precisely because of the specific mention [in the rule], and because of its association with the preceding [word]. The example *tīkṣṇa upāyo 'yaḥśūlam* ("an iron spike is a sharp means") means that just as an iron spike is sharp, so too another sharp means is metaphorically called an "iron spike. Regarding *dambhodaṇḍājinaṃ* ("the staff and deerskin of hypocrisy"): this is because they are the instruments of hypocrisy. For those possessed of hypocrisy generally carry a staff and a deerskin. As for the word *tena*: the meaning is "whether one carries them out of hypocrisy or not"; in all cases, the reason for the non-application of the term is simply the failure to grasp the primary sense.

Regarding the rule *tāvatitham grahaṇam iti lug vā* (5.2.77): just as in the expression *tasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of that"), the term *tasya* is a general reference to words ending in the genitive case, so too here *tāvatitham* is a general reference to words ending in ordinal suffixes (*pūraṇapratyaya*). And regarding the phrase *pūraṇapratyayasya ca*: this refers to the elision of the ordinal suffix itself, not to the elision of the suffix *kan*; for if it were the latter, the inclusion of the word *vā* ("optionally") would be rendered meaningless, since the optional production of *kan* is already established by the governing principle of *mahāvibhāṣā*. Thus, both forms—*pañcamaṃ grahaṇam* and *pañcamakaṃ grahaṇam*—are duly established.

And thus the Vārttika states: "The mention of elision (*lug*) in the rule 'the *tāvatitha* [ordinal] is elided' is purposeless, because of the context of the optional (*vibhāṣā*) section. Therefore, for the author of the Sūtra who employs the expression "optionally elided" (*lugvā*), the view is indicated that the elision of the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*) is prescribed; this is seen from the second form: "he grasps the text with the second [form]. In this grasping, this sentence is intended to demonstrate the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the second [form]. In reality, however, the analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as "Devadatta’s second grasping."

"Two-fold apprehension": it will be stated that there is also a cognition of the apprehender; therefore, since the apprehension—which serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the base—is not necessarily perceived, the word "apprehension" is employed [in the compound]. However, the example "the two-fold form of Devadatta" was not cited because the application of words proceeds according to one's own preference. Regarding "four-fold": by the *sanniyogaśiṣṭa* paribhāṣā (the rule that when two things are taught together, they are removed together), when the suffix *ḍaṭ* is removed, the *thuk* augment is also removed; the *repha* becomes a *visarjanīya*, and by the rule *idudupadhasya ca*, the *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) occurs.

Regarding the phrase "by that manyfold" (*tāvatithena*): since a suffix prescribed in its own sense would not apply to the recipient (*grahītṛ*), this statement is made. And I shall state that there is always elision (*luk*). As for the word *ṣaṭka*: although the word *rūpa* is employed in the sentence, it is not used in the compound (*vṛtti*) because it is already understood; furthermore, due to its status as a nominal stem (*padatva*), the changes to *jaś* and *cart* [are applied].

In this context, when one uses the sixth form [the genitive] to express "he grasps with six forms," what is the point of the numeral? One should simply say "he grasps with that"; for if it were so, the rule "or there is elision" (*lug vā*) would not need to be stated. But it cannot be said thus; for if it were stated in that way, it would apply here as well—to the case of "he grasps with one form. However, the ordinal suffix does not occur after the word *eka*, and therefore it is understood that the application of the suffix is restricted only to the subject matter of the treatise (grammar). Consequently, it does not occur here: *dvitīyo hasto grahaṇo daṇḍasya* ("the second hand is the grasper of the staff").
He is their leader (grāmaṇī). 5.2.78.

In expressions such as *tvatko matko vā vijayaḥ* ("victory is yours" or "victory is mine"), the suffix *kan* is used by this rule. Thus, *tvatkaḥ* means "you are the leader of this," and *matkaḥ* means "I am the leader of this. However, this suffix is generally employed in the sense of the thing itself (*arthamātre*).
The word *śṛṅkhalam* is used in the sense of a fetter for a young camel.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a camel is not bound by the chain alone? What then? By the rope and the peg. Therefore, it is not proper to say that "the chain is its bond. Rather, one should say: "The binding of the camel is considered to be by means of the chain, which is the instrument (karaṇa) [of the action]. To this, he replies with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*). Let there be the status of being an instrument for the rope and so forth as well; let there certainly be the status of being an instrument for the chain too; for the meaning is that without it, the binding would not be accomplished.
*utka* means *unmanāḥ* (one whose mind is distracted). || 5.2.80 ||

"From the word *ud* [meaning] 'expressing an action together with its instrument' (*sādhanakriyā*). The instrument is the mind (*manaḥ*), and the action is the act of going (*gamana*). Thus, the meaning is "from that which exists when the mind has risen. Regarding "that which possesses it": the meaning is "in one whose mind has risen. *Utsukaḥ* means "eager" (*utkaṇṭhitaḥ*).
In the case of a disease, [the suffix *ṇa* is applied] after [a word denoting] time and purpose. 5.2.81.

Regarding the term *arthalabhyā*: it is that which is obtained through the force (*sāmarthya*) of the meaning. In that case, the locative case is the governing case (*samarthavibhakti*), for "being" (*bhava*) is the meaning of the suffix there. In the sense of purpose (*prayojana*), the instrumental case is used, for "produced" (*janita*) is the meaning of the suffix there. But when the fruit (*phala*) is the purpose, the nominative case is used. A purpose is both a cause and the fruit of a disease; it is called a "purpose" because it brings about both.

If, then, the cause is also called a "purpose" (*prayojana*), the mention of "time" (*kāla*) is redundant. How so? That fever which occurs on the second day has that very second day as its cause, since it does not arise on any other day. True; even though it possesses the status of being a cause, when that status is not intended to be expressed and one intends only to say "occurring therein," the mention of "time" is for the sake of ensuring that [the suffix] still applies—such as in the case of "occurring on the second day."

Even though the word *dvitīya* is a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*), it is designated as a "word for time" (*kālaśabda*) because it applies to time within its scope of usage (*vṛttiviṣaya*) through the force of context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors. But what is the reason that the suffix does not occur after words like *māsa*, which directly denote time, whereas it does occur after [words like] *dvitīya* and so on? Furthermore, why is it that even in those cases, the suffix occurs only in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*) when derived from bases in the seventh case, in the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇa*) when derived from bases in the third case, and in the sense of "result" (*phala*) when derived from bases in the first case—yet none of this is explicitly stated in the words of the Sūtra?

Regarding this, he says: "The mention of *saṃjñā* (name) from the subsequent sūtra is drawn back (*anukṛṣyate*) here. This is according to the maxim of the "lion's backward glance" (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), just as lions, while running, look back over their shoulders. Another [teacher] says: there is a division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) in the subsequent sūtra: first, "when food is mostly in this," and then "in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*). The meaning is that whatever has been introduced [by the previous rule] should be understood to apply when it is a name. Thus, the mention of *saṃjñā* is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both; and this alone is intended as the "drawing back" (*anukarṣaṇa*). *tadasminnannaṃ prāye saṃjñāyām* || 5.2.82 || "When food is mostly in this, [the suffix *ṭhan* is added] in the sense of a name."

"Food that is not to be consumed" (*annam-avyavahāryam*), because it is something that is eaten. *Guḍāpūpa* refers to cakes mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*). *Kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame seeds; others say it is crushed sesame. *Traibila* is a three-layered cake. Regarding the suffix *-in-* [in *vaṭakin-*], since the suffix *-ka-* would otherwise be expected, this rule is stated as an exception. Now, one might argue: "Since this is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *-ka-* will not apply; and in its absence, the possessive suffix *-in-* will apply. This is not established, because of the rule: "And [the suffix *-in-*] does not apply after a word ending in the seventh case, nor when it is a technical name."
The suffix *añ* is applied after *kulmāṣa* [to form a word denoting a place where that food is regularly eaten]. 5.2.83.
Kulmāṣas are mung beans.
The word *śrotriya* denotes one who studies the Vedic meters (*chandas*). Pāṇini 5.2.84.

Regarding the term *vākyārtha* (sentence-meaning): by the mention of "sentence-meaning," the person who studies the Veda (*chandodhyāyī*), which is the substratum of that meaning, is figuratively designated. Why? Because the primary sentence-meaning consists of an action or a relation, and that is not a substantive entity (*asattvabhūta*). However, the word *śrotriya* denotes a substantive entity; the meaning is that the word *śrotriya* is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) in the sense of that sentence-meaning, wherein the division between stem and suffix does not exist.

Now, how is the attainment of the accent (*svara*) established in this alternative view, given that an accent is prescribed when the letter *n* (the *nit*) follows [a word], whereas here such a distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) does not exist? Let there be no such separation; nevertheless, by the force of the designation *nit*, it will occur even in its absence. Alternatively, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound: *nit* means that which is both *n* and *it*; [the rule applies] when that follows.

"How so? and so forth. The question is: if the suffix *ghan* is applied to the word *chandas* to form the state of being a *śrotra*, resulting in *chāndasa*, this is not established; for the suffix *ghan* would subvert the suffix *aṇ*, and the word *chandas* itself would be replaced by the state of being a *śrotra*. [The answer is: "The mention of the option (*vā*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Another says: the term *śrotriya* applies to one who studies the Veda (*chandas*) and practices its meaning, whereas the term *chāndasa* applies to a mere student; thus, because there is a difference in meaning, there is no relationship of subverter and subverted. According to the Dharmaśāstra, "Having studied one branch [of the Veda], one becomes a *śrotriya*."
The suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* are added [to a word] to form a derivative meaning "one who has eaten this at a Śrāddha. (Pāṇini 5.2.85)

The word *śrāddha* is the name of a rite (*karmanāmadheya*). The term *śrāddha* is the designation for the ancestral rite (*piṇḍya-karman*) which is accomplished through faith (*śraddhā*); the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule "after *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, *arcā*, and *vṛtti*, [the suffix] *ṇa*" in the sense that "faith exists in this. It refers to the substance used as a means for that rite, because it is impossible for one who possesses primary faith to eat. This is the inclusion of the simultaneous time.

The purpose of using the suffix *ka* (as in *adyabhukta*) is so that the word may be employed at the same time as the act of eating (*bhujinā*), even though the action of eating is accomplished in only a few moments. Nevertheless, the "same time" refers to the duration during which the signs of satiety from that meal persist for the eater; and since this generally occurs on the very same day, the suffix is used only in that case. However, when someone who is weak has eaten on the second day and the food is still undigested, then there is no such usage. This is what [the author] says: "So that the usage of the suffix *ka*—as in *adyabhukte śvaḥ śrāddhikaḥ* ('one who ate today and will perform a Śrāddha tomorrow')—does not occur."
The suffix *niḥ* is applied after [stems ending in] *pūrva* and so forth. (Pāṇini 5.2.86)
"Previously gone by him," and so forth: the suffix is applied after a word ending in the accusative case that functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.
And [the suffix *kta*] has the sense of "having previously done" (*sapūrva*). 5.2.87.

The term *sapūrva* means "that which has something preceding it" (*pūrva* being present in this). Because the rule "with that, in the sense of equal connection" (*tena saheti tulyayoge*)—which prescribes an attributive compound—is generally applicable, a compound is formed even with the word *vidyamāna*. The word *pūrva* here denotes a constituent part (*avayava*). No other word can logically function as a constituent part of the word *pūrva*; however, the letter *pa* is constant (in its occurrence), and therefore this serves as a qualifier for the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself: namely, "that nominal stem which has *pa* as its preceding element."

And thus, the word *pūrva* (preceded by) is also a qualifier of that very [base]; and since there is the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) when there is a qualifier, he says: "there is extension to what ends with that by means of the word *pūrva*. Regarding the phrase "from that which is preceded by" (*sapūrvāt*), etc.: although a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the word *pūrva* is necessarily already "preceded by" something, nevertheless, if the expression "preceded by" (*sapūrva*) were not used, the extension to what ends with that would not be obtained; therefore, it is stated as "from that which is preceded by" (*sapūrvāt*). This usage has been explained under the rule *kṛtakarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of two rules" (*yogadvayena*): if this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—namely, "the treatment as if possessing a designation [does not apply] when followed by a non-prātipadika" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*)—did not exist, then one would have composed only a single rule, *pūrvādiniḥ sapūrvāt*. Since the treatment as if possessing a designation would allow [the suffix] to occur even from a simple [word], what would be the purpose of composing two rules? In that case, the particle *ca* (and) would not need to be employed here.

Furthermore, if this paribhāṣā—"a nominal stem [is understood] as being accompanied by that which is expressed by the suffix"—did not exist, one would simply say "pūrvādiniḥ" (P. 5.2.86). Since the rule for extension to what ends in that (tadantavidhi) would ensure that the suffix occurs even after a word preceded by another, what would be the purpose of the second rule? Therefore, in this case, two paribhāṣās are indicated by the two rules.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffixes *paripanthin* and *pariparin* are used in the sense of one who stands as an obstacle or an adversary.

In this context, the suffix *ini* is added to the word *paryavasthātṛ* in its own sense (*svārthe*), and the substitutions of *panthi* for *avasthātṛ* and *pari-* for *pari-* are prescribed by way of technical derivation (*nipātana*). However, the usage of the word *paripanthin* in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is ungrammatical (*asādhu*).
The suffix *an* is applied after the root *pad* when it means "to search for. (Pāṇini 5.2.90)

"Anupada" is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "after" (*paścāt*). The suffix *ini* is applied irregularly (*nipātyate*) to the word "seeker" (*anveṣṭṛ*). Thus, we have *anupadī gauḥ* ("a cow that follows its tracks"). The genitive case is used in relation to "track" (*pada*); the search for the cow's tracks is specifically for cows, and it does not occur when gold or other things are to be sought, because in those cases there is no "track. However, if the suffix *ini* were applied to the word "seeker" (*anveṣṭṛ*) itself in its own sense, then the word "track" (*pada*) would be prescribed as an irregular substitute (*ādeśa*) for the word "seeker" (*eṣṭṛ*).

Alternatively, if it were treated as an irregular form (*nipātana*) like *śrotriya*—meaning one who seeks out the root and suffix that do not exist [as separate entities]—then the genitive case in "of cows" (*gavām*) would not be obtained; instead, a second case would be required, as in "one who has previously made a mat" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*), or "one who seeks a wife" (*anukā bhāryām*) or "one who seeks a slave-girl" (*abhikā dāsīm*). Furthermore, when gold and so forth are the objects sought, it would result in "one who seeks gold" (*anupadī hiraṇyam*). Therefore, the explanation exactly as stated is indeed superior.
The suffix *saṃjñā* is applied [to a word] when it denotes one who sees directly. Pāṇini 5.2.91.

The word *sākṣāt* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Therefore, according to the rule "an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is like its original (*prakṛtivat*)," there is no elision of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamyā aluk*) in the sūtra; and in the example, there is the elision of the suffix *ṭi* by the rule "for indeclinables, [elision occurs] when a nominal ending (*bha*) follows. Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of the technical term (*saṃjñāgrahaṇāt*)," etc.: something is seen directly (*sākṣāt*) by three parties—by the one who gives, by the one to whom it is given, and by the one standing nearby who witnesses it. In all those cases, the suffix would apply. The meaning is that because of the mention of the technical term, it does not apply to the creditor and the debtor.
A hereditary disease is to be treated in another's field (i.e., in a different person). 5.2.92.

From the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go," the word *kṣetra* is derived by adding the suffix *ṣṭran* according to the appropriate grammatical rule (Pāṇini 3.1.141), signifying a locus or place. Thus, *parakṣetra* refers to the body of another birth (*janmāntaraśarīra*). It is called a *kṣetra* because it is the dwelling place of the Self (*ātman*); the term *parakṣetra* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both other and a field. In this context, it is "to be treated"—meaning it is to be remedied or managed—but it does not mean that one should act as a physician toward it. As it has been said: "Not [for] the immortal one... (Gītā 2.21).

The phrase "or rather" (*atha vā*) indicates that conjunction (*samuccaya*) alone is intended here, not an alternative (*vikalpa*). He will state later: "All of this is authoritative. The suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of possibility (*śakyārthe*) in the former case, but in the sense of mere object (*karmamātre*) in the first [instance], and in the sense of fitness (*arhārthe*) in the latter two. Regarding the term "for the sake of grain" (*sasyārtha*): by this he expresses that the field belongs to another—just as one speaks of "another's wife" (*paradārāḥ*) or "another's field" (*parakṣetram*). The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied in the sense of the object; thus, "fields" (*kṣetra*) refers to those who are to be approached (*gantavyāḥ*), that is, wives fit for sexual union. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means in that context. "Should be restrained" (*nigṛhītavyaḥ*): by means of punishment and so forth.
Or [the word *indriya*] means "a mark of Indra," "seen by Indra," "created by Indra," "beloved by Indra," or "given by Indra. (Pāṇini 5.2.93)

Regarding the term *antodātta*: this is due to its association with the word *kṣetriya*. Regarding the claim that it is a conventional (*rūḍhi*) term: what is the proof for this? He says, "And thus," for there is no lack of restriction regarding the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of derivative (*yaugika*) words. "Indra is the Self" because he is the Lord (*īśvara*) over the aggregate of cause and effect. And it is known from scripture: "They call him 'Indra' by an indirect name, though he is indeed Indra. "By means of an instrument": this is a qualifying attribute containing a reason. He demonstrates how this is a reason as follows: "it is not without an agent."

The particle *iti* indicates the reason: for an instrument such as an axe does not function unless presided over by an agent. "Seen by Indra" means known; and thus, with reference to the aggregate of cause and effect, there occurs the statement: "He saw this very person as the Brahman-tattva," and "I saw this," and so forth. But how could the eye and other organs be created by the Self? To this he says: "By what is done by that [Self]."

Wholesome action is prescribed, and unwholesome action is prohibited; these two combined are the cause of production, because desirable and undesirable forms and so forth are perceived by the eyes and other sense organs. "In accordance with each" means: whatever is the object of a particular [sense organ]—such as form for the eye, odor for the nose, and so forth—it is for the sake of grasping that [object].

"It must also be performed otherwise" refers to, for example, [the statement] "it is difficult to conquer by Indra. "Being connected to each one" is a qualifying attribute containing a reason; the meaning is: because it is connected to each one individually, therefore [it is so].
The suffix *matup* occurs after a word [ending in the first case] in the sense of "this belongs to him" or "this is in this. (Pāṇini 5.2.94)

Regarding the statement "the meanings of the suffixes are 'of this' and 'in this'": [An objection is raised: "But surely, if something belongs to someone, it also exists in that which possesses it; and if something exists in something, it also belongs to that thing. For example: 'the branch of the tree' and 'the branch in the tree. In such cases, the meaning is established by the mention of either one alone; for what purpose are both meanings mentioned? [The answer is: "The simultaneous occurrence of these two is not necessarily required."

For instance: when there is a mere indication of the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), if the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to be expressed in that very form, and not a residual relation (*śeṣasambandha*) produced by it, then no suffix would occur there—for example, in the case of "trees are on this mountain. For here, a residual relation preceded by an action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) is not observed; since the mountain is not composed of the trees, there is no relation of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*). However, a relation such as immediate proximity (*ānantarya*) and so forth is possible; yet, in that case, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) does not occur.

Because it is not so designated. Likewise, if only the meaning of the locative case were indicated, a relationship preceded by another *kāraka* would not be grasped; consequently, forms such as *putravān* ("having a son") and *gomān* ("having cows") would not be possible. For in these cases, the relationship is produced by the agency [of the father] with respect to actions such as procreation or acceptance, and is not preceded by the [mere] locus; this is because the designation "possessing that" (*tadvān*) applies even when the son or cow has gone to another country. Furthermore, a locative sense based on proximity (*sāmīpika-adhikaraṇa*) is also impossible.

It might be argued: "Since a son is dependent on his father and cows are dependent on their owner, [the term *adhika*] will function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), just as in the expression 'dwelling with the teacher' (*gurau vasati*). For when the designation of instrument (*karaṇa*) applies, because excellence is not intended in the section on grammatical relations (*kāraka-prakaraṇa*) by the inclusion of the suffix *-tamap*, the designation of locus applies even to a secondary (*gauṇa*) substratum. Let this be so regarding the designation of locus; however, the possessive suffix (*matup*) would apply only to a primary locus—as in "a mountain possessing trees" (*vṛkṣavān parvataḥ*) or "a country possessing cattle" (*gomāñ janapadaḥ*).

It does not apply in a figurative sense—as in "Devadatta has a son" (*putravān*) or "Devadatta possesses cows" (*gomān*)—for in these cases there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the inclusion of the figurative. Therefore, the mention of both [the primary and the figurative] must be made. Regarding the phrase "of the qualifiers of the base (*prakṛti*) such as 'exists' (*asti*)," it should be understood that this is by way of the meaning (*artha*).

Now, it might be argued that the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) occurs only when there is both possibility and deviation, as in the case of "blue lotus"; however, no object ever deviates from existence (*sattā*), for it is impossible even to utter a word without it. For as long as an object has not been made an object of cognition (*buddhi*), there is no employment of the word; thus, the word takes as its domain an object already permeated by the existence of cognition. It is precisely for the sake of communicating the external presence or absence of that very [object] that one employs such expressions as "the tree exists" or "the tree does not exist."

If an object were denotable as being conjoined with an external existence (*sattā*), then this usage [of words] would not occur due to contradiction and redundancy. In the same way, even for objects that are absolutely non-existent externally, such as a hare’s horn, there is the employment of words signifying them after they have been made objects of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, existence as it is metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) and mounted upon the intellect is the cause for the employment of words; thus, the word-meaning (*padārtha*) does not deviate from that [existence]. As it has been said: "The word-meaning does not deviate from existence. Does this mean that the meaning of any given word does not deviate from such a kind of existence?

This, then, is the purpose: [the term *gomān*] should apply to that external existence which is primary, characterized by the present, and currently real; it should not apply to that existence which is conceptualized through metaphorical form by a cognition reflecting upon past or future entities. Therefore, there is no usage of the word *gomān* in such senses as "he had cows" (*gāvo 'syāsan*) or "he will have cows" (*gāvo 'sya bhavitāraḥ*).

If this is so, when Devadatta exists [in the present], the expressions "he was rich in cattle" (*gomān āsīt*) and "he will be rich in cattle" (*gomān bhaviṣyati*) are employed to indicate the pastness and futurity of those cattle; in that case, since the existence of the referent of the base (*prakṛti*)—namely, the cattle—is absent at the present time, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the suffix not occurring? This is not a fault; for here the existence of the cattle themselves is not directly stated. What, then, is stated? It is the existence of the possessor of the cattle (*gomat*) that is stated. If, on the other hand, the existence of the cattle themselves were being stated;

Just as here the use of the verb *as* does not occur—as in "he possesses cows" (*gomān*), because the adjunct of the base meaning is already understood through the suffix itself—so too it would not occur here [in the past and future] either, as in "he was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) or "he will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhaviṣyati*). Or, even if such usage were to occur, just as the plural number is used here—as in "he was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) or "he will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhaviṣyati*)—and just as the plural is used when one says "his cows were" (*gāvaḥ asya āsan*) or "his cows will be" (*gāvaḥ asya bhavitāraḥ*); so too it would occur here as well, namely, "he was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) and "he will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhaviṣyati*).

Therefore, this is not stated as the existence of cows; what then? This is stated as the existence of one who possesses cows (*gomat*). In that regard, although the one who possesses cows exists, the form of "possessing-cow-ness" (*gomattva*) belonging to him may be past or future; thus there is usage in the past and future tenses. For example: "This man was wealthy," or "This man will become poor."

In that case, by implication, the pastness or futurity of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is also understood; however, since this arises by virtue of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it is considered external (*bahiraṅga*) and does not preclude the internal (*antaraṅga*) grammatical refinement (*śabda-saṃskāra*). For example, in the expression "he does not go to the village" (*grāmaṃ na gacchati*). Thus, it is established that the word "is" (*asti*) is employed so that [the action] may exist in the present, and so that it may not exist in the past or future—as in the case of "he does not go to the village."

But surely, where another verb is not heard, the verb *asti* (is) or *bhavati* (becomes), in the third person and unexpressed, is understood; thus, when it is said "his cows" or "in this [place] his cows," in response to the expectation of "what?", it is understood that "they exist. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the term *asti*? This is not universally the case; for when there is the intention to express "his cows and not another's" or "in this [place] and not in another," then existence (*astitva*) is not perceived. Therefore, it must be stated: "*asti*" (is).

Now, even if the term *asti* (is) were included [in the definition], why does [the suffix] not occur here: *gāvo 'syānantarāḥ* ("he has cows immediately following him")? Because of its dependence [on another word], it lacks syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). Why does it not occur here: *citraguḥ*, *śabalaguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows," "one who has spotted cows")? Because the meaning is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself. However, in the case of the analytical sentence (*vākya*), namely *citrā gāvo 'sya santi*, it does not occur because each individual word lacks syntactic capacity; nor does it occur from the whole [sentence] because a sentence is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*).

But here, in the case of *pañcaguḥ* ("one who has five cows") and *daśaguḥ* ("one who has ten cows"), both the *dvigu* compound and the *bahuvrīhi* compound would apply by virtue of the rule "in the sense of a secondary derivative" (*taddhitārtha*). Now, in cases such as *citraguḥ*, the *bahuvrīhi* has its scope; however, in the presence of words expressing a number, the *dvigu* would exclude it. Consequently, when the meaning of a secondary derivative is the intended object, the *dvigu*—which is prescribed for that specific context—is applied because the meaning of the secondary derivative has not yet been expressed. Thus, just as a secondary suffix occurs here in forms like *dvaimāturaḥ* ("son of two mothers") and *pāñcanāpitih* ("descendant of five barbers"), so too does the elision (*luk*) apply by the rule "there is elision of the *dvigu* [suffix] except in the case of *apatya*" (*dvigor lug anapatye*), provided the suffix belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group.

Because [the suffix] is prescribed [in that way], the *luk* elision of the *matup* suffix is obtained. Therefore, regarding what was stated in the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 5.2.36)—namely, "there is a prohibition in all cases where a possessive sense (*matvartha*) is intended"—that alone is the refuge here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhūma": the meaning is that those suffixes such as *matup* which are prescribed when the sense of existence (*asti*) is intended to be expressed, occur when the domains of "abundance" (*bhūman*) and so forth are present.

*Bhūman* is the state of being many (*bahūnām bhāvaḥ*); [the suffix *matup* occurs] in that sense of plurality. For example: *gomān* (possessing cows), *yavamān* (possessing barley). Furthermore, this plurality must be understood as specifically determined by the force of the expression itself, as it has been said: "Indeed, existence [denoted by the suffix] is predicated only of as many cows as suffice for the purposes of carrying, milking, or breeding; for someone, these may suffice with even four, while for another, they may not suffice even with a hundred. And thus, although plurality exists in three or more [cows], the form *yavamān* does not occur [if fewer than the required number are present].

In this context, when it is said, "one sprinkles the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with as much water as is required," only the connection with the genus (*jāti*) is intended; thus, even in the absence of abundance (*bhūman*), the suffix occurs. However, the mention of "abundance" and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating the inherent nature of the denotation (*abhidhāna*). In the sense of censure: *kakudāvartinī kanyā* ("a girl with a hump"); in the sense of praise: *rūpavān* ("handsome"); in the sense of constant association (*nityayoga*): *kṣīriṇo vṛkṣāḥ* ("trees that always bear fruit"); in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*): *udarī kanyā* ("a girl with a large belly"). In the sense of contact (*saṃsarga*); *saṃsarga* means conjunction (*saṃyoga*): *daṇḍī* refers to one who has a staff attached [to him]. But one who merely has a staff while staying at home is not called *daṇḍī*.

In some recensions of the commentary, there is the statement: "When there is the intention to express 'exists,' [the suffix] *matup* occurs. In that context, the compound should be explained as a conjunction: "when there is abundance (*bhūman*) and so forth, and when there is the intention to express 'exists,' the suffixes *matup* and others occur. The word *asti* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*) identical in form to a case ending; it denotes existence qualified by an agent, and is not the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *as*. Another derivative suffix is also observed: *astitva*, *astiteti*. Because [existence] is never absent [from the substrate], there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *asti*; therefore, the suffix is prescribed when there is the intention to express "exists."

And this is obtained from the Sūtra by resorting to the elliptical indication of the base form with the fifth case ending elided, [expressed] as *asti* "exists" by way of *tantra*. Furthermore, in the context of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), the word *asti* "exists" refers to wealth as a specific agent; for it is not possible for the meaning of the suffix to be qualified by the agent in a general sense, since everyone always possesses something or other.

Regarding the rule *guṇavacanebhyaḥ*: here, only words such as *śukla* (white) and the like are understood, which possess an identical form whether they denote a quality (*guṇa*) or that which possesses the quality (*tadvat*). However, terms such as *rūpa* (form) and the like, which always denote only the quality itself, are not included. In this regard, although the expression "the white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*) and so forth is established through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*), nevertheless, because we also observe the desire to express distinction—as in "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śuklaḥ*)—there would otherwise follow the hearing of the suffix *matup* in such cases; therefore, its elision (*luk*) must be stated.
And [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after *rasa* and the following words. 5.2.95.

"Not by the former alone. Because of the use of the particle *na* with a change in intonation (*kāku*), the meaning is that [the suffix] is indeed established. Or rather, the word *na* should be understood in the sense of "but" (*nanu*). "Others" refers to [suffixes] such as *ini* and *ṭhan* in the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*, and so forth.

How so? The sense is that if the word were stated again for the purpose of excluding others (*anyanivṛtti*), then [the designation] "possessing form" (*rūpin*) and so forth would not be established. Regarding the term "mostly" (*prāyika*): the meaning is that its purpose of excluding others depends on whether its usage is frequent or infrequent. What follows from this? He says: "In some cases. How, then, is it "mostly"? He says: "By the particle *iti*. Therefore, the meaning is this: wherever the common usage intends to express [the quality] precisely through the suffix *-mat*, only in those instances is the exclusion of others effected by this [particle], and not everywhere.
And this was stated as "from the guṇa" and "from the gaṇa," without regard for the *gaṇapāṭha*; however, having in mind the necessity of that [reference], he says:

Now, regarding the word "atha vā" (or else): here, in this list, the term "guṇāt" (from a quality) is recited, and that serves as a qualifier for each of the items beginning with *rasa* (taste), rather than being independent, nor is it in apposition with the term "ekācaḥ" (having a single vowel). Therefore, those qualities which are perceptible by the sense organ of taste and so forth—the word "ādi" (and so forth) including the eyes and other senses—it is these very things that are listed here. By this [term], the exclusion of others from them is effected. [The examples are] *rūpiṇī* (possessing form) and *rūpikaḥ* (possessing beauty); for beauty is indeed a state of excellence. True.

Regarding the phrase "due to a quality" (*guṇāt*), by the force of this qualification, there is a mention of those qualities that are most well-known as being perceivable by the sense organs, such as the tongue and so forth. Regarding the phrase "connection with a state" (*bhāvayoga*): "states" (*bhāvāḥ*) refers to the dramatic elements (*nāṭyadharmāḥ*) such as love, laughter, and so on.

However, in the *Bhāṣya*, because it is observed that—as in the statement "Urvaśī is indeed the embodied one among the Apsarases; Vāyu is the tactile one"—there can also be another cognition according to the specific designation [of the object], this rule (*sūtra*) is rejected on the grounds that its restriction is undesirable.
Regarding the term "having a single vowel" (*ekāca*): here, the requirement "due to a quality" (*guṇāt*) is not required—[as in the examples] *svavān* and *khavān*.

*Prāṇisthād āto laj anyatarasyām* (A 5.2.96). Regarding *cūḍāla*: *cūḍā* means a tuft of hair (*śikhā*), not the ornament called an *āpīḍa*. Similarly, *karṇikā* here does not mean an ear-ornament; what then? It refers to a specific part of a living being that resembles such an ornament. For the suffix *lac* is desired only after words denoting parts of a living being. The example *śikhāvān dīpaḥ* (a lamp with a flame) is shown as a counter-example; it is presented merely as a direction, since the suffix *lac* would not apply here because the word *śikhā* is not included in the *vrīhy-ādi* list. A proper counter-example to provide would be *cūḍāvān vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree with a crest).

"It should be stated that [the suffix *matup*] follows a member of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*). This is obtained through the continued application of the particle *iti*. In the example *cūḍālo 'si*: the word *asi* undergoes *nighāta* (enclitic accentlessness) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*; from the word *cūḍāla*, the suffix *su* is added; then *ru*-tva (substitution of *r* for *s*); then, by the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute*, the substitution of *u* occurs. Since that *u* possesses the quality of falling away (*sraṃsana*) among the consonants (*hal*), it is *anudātta* (unaccented). Then, by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, there is the *guṇa* substitution; by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the single substitute is *udātta*. Then, by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati*, there is the single substitute of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*). Regarding that, by the rule *svarito vānudātte 'padādau*, [the resulting vowel is optionally *svarita*].

A *svarita* accent would result [from the suffix], but it does not occur due to the power of the marker *c*. If this is so, then in the case of *cūḍālaḥ*—where there is the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative (*āmantrita-ādyudātta*), the subsequent syllables would not be unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*); nor would there be the unaccented status of the vocative in "he *cūḍāla*" (*he cūḍāla*); and in cases such as *cūḍālatvam*, there would be no unaccented status for the remaining syllables when the accent belongs to the suffix (*pratyayasvara*)? If this is desired, a solution must be stated here; if it is not desired, then this very [result] will serve as the purpose for the accentuation by the marker *c*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the group of words beginning with *sidhma*.

By the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām*, the suffix *bha-tuP* is conjoined [with the suffix *laṅ*]. Since particles have multiple meanings, the meaning here is that the inclusion of *anyatarasyām* functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, the Vārttika states: "The inclusion of *anyatarasyām* in the rule for *laṅ* is a conjunction. It does not mean that the suffix is made optional; the point is that, unlike other instances where the inclusion of *anyatarasyām* signifies an option (*vikalpa*), it is not so here. What is established by this being the case? To that, he says: "Therefore... (referring to the subsequent statement).

If the mention of *anyatarasyām* were for the sake of option (*vikalpa*), then when the suffix *lac* is excluded, it would follow the general rule; consequently, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* would apply after bases ending in long *ā*. However, if the meaning is conjunction (*samuccaya*), then only the suffix *matup*, which is under discussion, is conjoined, and thus there is no fault. How, then, is it known that the meaning here is conjunction and not option? From an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*): namely, that [Pāṇini] lists the *piccha*-group and the *tunda*-group separately.

How does this function as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? Here, regarding the rule *tundādibhya ilacca*, four suffixes are intended: *ilac*, *ini*, *ṭhan*, and *matup*. In that context, if the mention of *anyatarasyām* were for the purpose of optional application (*vikalpa*), then the set of four suffixes would apply even to words such as *piccha* and others. How so? Because *ilac* is optional, *ini* and *ṭhan* would follow; and since those two are also optional, *matup* would follow as well. Consequently, either *piccha* and others should have been listed among the *tunda* group, or *tunda* and others should have been listed among the *piccha* group.

It is understood from the separate recitation [of these rules] that: "By the inclusion of *anya-tas*, the suffix *matup* is added in conjunction, rather than merely permitting what was already established. For in this way, two suffixes—*ilac* and *matup*—are applied after words such as *piccha*, and four suffixes are applied after words such as *tuṇḍa*; thus, the separate recitation becomes meaningful. Now, one might object: "But isn't it the case that *ini* and *thañ* are prescribed even after words like *tuṇḍa* which do not end in *n*, whereas [the suffixes] after words like *piccha* are prescribed only for those ending in *a*?"

In that case, if words such as *piccha* were listed in the *tunda*-group, then the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* would apply even after *piccha* and other words ending in *-ā*. Alternatively, if words such as *tunda* were listed in the *piccha*-group, then *ini* and *ṭhan* would not apply even after *tunda* and other words ending in *-ā*. Therefore, by listing some words ending in *-ā* in the *piccha*-group and others in the *tunda*-group, it will serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned meaning. Likewise, the rule "optionally *va* after *keśa*" need not be stated.

Since the suffixes *in*, *than*, and *matup* are already established by the recurrence of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) from the preceding rule, the fact that the present rule is formulated for the purpose of applying *ka* after *tad* and *ini* indicates that the preceding "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is intended as a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*).

[The suffix] *lac* is applied after *pārṣṇi* and *dhamani*, as in *pārṣṇilaḥ* and *dhamanīlaḥ*. [The suffix] *ūṅ* is also applied after *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*. Thus, *lac* occurs after *vāta* and the others, and for that *lac*, the augment *ūṅ* is added: *vātūlaḥ*, *dantūlaḥ*, *balūlaḥ*, *lalāṭūlaḥ*. [The suffix] *lac* is applied after *jaṭā*, *ghaṭā*, and *kalā* when contempt (*kṣepa*) is implied. These words produce the suffix *lac* when contempt is understood—as in *jaṭālaḥ*, etc. Why "when contempt is implied"? [Answer: "A mendicant possessing matted hair" (*jaṭāvāṃs tāpasaḥ*). [The suffix] *lac* is also applied after [words denoting] small creatures and suffering (*upatāpa*).

"Small creatures" refers to those from the mongoose downwards. "Affliction" means disease. Regarding the phrase "in the case of *vipādikā*": *vipādikā* is "cracking of the feet. The reading of the words *sidhma* and *gaḍu* is for the purpose of excluding [their inclusion as] afflictions.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa* when the sense is "desire" (*kāma*) or "strength" (*bala*).

"Kāmavatī" and "balavatī. By this instruction ending in the suffix *mat*, he shows that the words "kāma" and "bala" end in the suffix *aṇ* (the *ac* suffix) according to the rule beginning with *arśas*.

But surely, the words *vatsa* and *aṃsa* are conventional (*rūḍha*) for specific stages of life and specific parts of a living being respectively, and not for desire and strength. Therefore, how can one who possesses desire or strength be expressed by those two words ending in the suffix *la*? To this he says: "In the domain of *vṛtti*. How is this known? He says: "For not here," meaning that the well-known meaning of these two in a sentence does not exist in the *vṛtti*. To show what meaning does exist, he says: "*Vatsala* means one who possesses affection (*sneha*). Here, *sneha* is passion (*rāga*), which is desire (*kāma*).

He dispels the doubt that "since the suffix *matup* is included everywhere in this context, it must also be present here" by stating "and not. For this very reason, even the sentence itself does not exist.

In this [compound], there are two words, *vatsa* and *aṃsa*, and there are likewise two meanings for the suffixes, namely "in this" (*asyām*) and "in this" (*asmin*). Nevertheless, the rule of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not apply here. Why? Because, although by the rule "that which begins with a vowel, ends in a short vowel, or has fewer syllables is placed first" (*ajādyadantam...*), the words *aṃsa* and *bala* would have been expected to be placed first, they are instead placed last; this serves as an indicator of the deviation from the general rule regarding word order. This should be understood to apply everywhere in this section.
The suffixes *śa*, *na*, *ila*, and *ca* are applied after words beginning with *loman*, *pāman*, and *piccha*.

Regarding *aṅgakalyāṇa*: the word *aṅga*, when occurring in a sense qualified by "beautiful" (*kalyāṇa*), causes the suffix *na* to arise—thus, *aṅganā* ("a woman"), which is a designation specifically for a female whose limbs (*aṅgāni*) are beautiful. Why say "beautiful"? [Because otherwise it would be] *aṅgavatī*. And regarding *śākī-palālī-dadravāṃ hrasvatvaṃ ca*: the suffix *na* occurs after *śākī* and the others, and there is shortening of the vowel. Thus, *śākinam* and *palālinam*. A large *śāka* (vegetable) is *śākī*; or it is a collection of various kinds [of vegetables].

*Palālī* means "chaff" (*palālakṣoda*) or "broken grains of *śāli*, *kodrava*, and so forth. According to the rule *daridrāteryālopaśca*, the suffix *ū* is added to the root *daridrāti*, with the elision of the letters *ri* and *a*. *Dadrū* is a specific skin disease; one who has this is called *dadruṇaḥ*. Regarding *viṣvak*: the suffix *na* is added to the word *viṣvañc*, with the elision of the subsequent member (*uttarapadalopa*). This [elision] applies to the form as it stands, before the application of sandhi rules—that is, before the substitution of *yaṇ*.

*Viṣvañci* means "going in various directions" (*viṣu nānā añcanti*); that which possesses these is *viṣuṇaḥ*—the time known as the *viṣuvant*. For in that time, the days have various courses, since the variation in the length of other days depends upon it. Likewise, death, wind, and humans and others of unstable nature are *viṣuṇaḥ*. In this context, because the action of moving is included within the function [of the word], they maintain that the designation of the beginning of the sentence is "one who moves in various directions" (*viṣvaggamanam asyāstīti*).

If, however, the elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*) were to occur after the substitution of *yaṇ*, then when the elision of *val* takes place, the form would result in *viṣṇu*. [Likewise,] regarding *lakṣmyā acca*: the suffix *nañ* is applied to the word *lakṣmī*, and the letter *a* is substituted for its final; thus, one who possesses *lakṣmī* is *lakṣmaṇaḥ*. Regarding *jaṭā-ghaṭā-kalāḥ kṣepe*: the words *jaṭā* and others take the suffix *ilac* when contempt (*kṣepa*) is implied—thus, *jaṭilaḥ*, *ghaṭilaḥ*, *kalilaḥ*. Other than in cases of contempt, it means "one who has matted hair" (*jaṭāvān*).
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the words *prajñā*, *śraddhā*, *arcā*, and *vṛtti*.
The word *vṛtti* has been interpolated in the Sūtra because it is seen in the Vārttika: "vṛtti, because of the counteracting of interruption.

For what purpose is the inclusion of *prajñā*? It is so that this form *prājña* may be obtained. This is established by the addition of the suffix *aṇ* [by the rule] *prajñādibhyaśca*; for one who possesses wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed wise (*prājña*), since he knows. True; however, when *aṇ* is applied to a feminine noun, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs—thus *prājñī*—but here, with the suffix *ṇa*, only *ṭāp* occurs—thus *prājñā*.

But here, when there is a connection with grammar and so forth through an action that has become subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), there is grammatical analysis (*vyākaraṇa*) for both the suffix *ṇa* and the suffix *an*: thus [the form] *prājña* arises. This is just as in the case of *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*; for it has been stated that when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is employed, the genitive case does not occur.
The suffix *vin* is applied after the words *tapaḥ* and *sahasra*.

The vowel *i* in *vinīnī* [is used] so that the letter *n* might not receive the designation *it*.
