However, some read it as *vinīnau*, with the vowels *ī* and *ā*; for if it were read with a final *n*, the *it* designation would apply. As for the phrase "of the two meanings of the suffixes," etc., it has already been stated previously how the correspondence of order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) does not occur even when it is not intended. As for the phrase "because of being non-existent" (*asantatvāt*), etc.

Since the suffix *vin* is established for the word *tapas* by the rule "asmāyāmedhās... [Pāṇini 5.2.121], and since the suffix *ini* is established for the word *sahasra* by the rule "ata iniṭhanau" [Pāṇini 5.2.115], this further prescription is made so that there may be no sublation (*bādhā*) by the suffix *aṇ* which is about to be mentioned. The term "by *aṇ*" (*aṇā*) uses the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of cause (*hetau*).

But in the case of the agent (*kartṛ*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix would not apply; for, according to the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the genitive] applies only to the object," the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) would result. [One might argue: "Let there be no sublation of the suffixes *vin* and *ini*, since the object is also implied, as in the example: 'by which he desires non-perception' (*yenādarśanamicchati*)"? This is not so, because the restriction is prohibited when the suffixes *aka* and *āka* are employed. Therefore, the instrumental occurs only in the sense of cause (*hetu*). Alternatively, the word *bādha* should be read as ending in *ghañ*. Even the suffix *aṭṭhan* is sublated after the word *sahasra*; however, the suffix *ṭhan* is not [sublated] because of the specific (prātipadika) prescription of *inaṇ*.
And [the suffix] *aṇ*. 5.2.103.

Regarding the phrase "in the section on *aṇ*," and so forth: "section" (*prakaraṇa*) means a topic (*prastāva*) or a chapter (*kāṇḍa*). This refers to the words listed in the sūtra beginning with *jyotsnā-tamisrā*. The example is *jyautsnaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("the moonlit fortnight"). Furthermore, this is the first fortnight (*pūrva-pakṣa*), for in that period, moonlight (*jyotsnā*) exists during all fifteen lunar days (*tithi*); thus, the entire fortnight is pervaded by moonlight. By this, *tāmisra* is explained: *tāmisra* is a mass of darkness (*tamaḥ-samūha*), with the suffix *ra* used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

For in that [dark fortnight], darkness exists as its constituent part; thus, that other fortnight is *tāmisra* because "it contains this" (*tad asmin asti*). Alternatively, it is *tāmisra* because "the night of darkness" (*tamisrā rātriḥ*) exists therein. This is the name for a specific hell. One who is worthy of earrings is *kauṇkaḍala*. In that case, the possessive suffix must be applied in some way or another. However, one who has earrings attached to him becomes *kuṇḍalī*. And this restriction is obtained through the continuation of the particle *iti*.
And [the suffix -mayaṭ is applied] after the words *sikatā* and *śarkarā*. (Pāṇini 5.2.104)
"Śārkaraṃ madhu" (sugar-based honey). Here, "śarkarā" refers to sweetness, not molasses, because that [molasses] is absent in honey.
This is cited as an example of a non-place (*adeśa*), since a specific rule regarding place will be stated later.
And *lub* and *ilac* [are substituted] for [the suffixes] *deśe*. 5.2.105.

"And [the suffix] *matup*": because of the inclusion of *matup* everywhere through the mention of "either one" (*anyatarasyām*), [the suffix *matup* is added]. "A region of sand" (*sikatā deśaḥ*): here, when there is elision (*lup*), there is the treatment as if the suffix were present (*yuktavadbhāvaḥ*).

Why does [the author] ask "Why [is the word] 'region' (*deśe*) mentioned?"? By this, even the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is effectively questioned; the meaning is: why was it not simply formulated as "after *sikatā* and *śarkarā*, there is elision (*lup*) and also [the suffixes] *ilac* and *ca*"?
The [suffix] *unnata* is applied after the word *danta* when it refers to the chest (*uraḥ*). 5.2.106.

Regarding the word *dantura*, it is derived from the term *danta* (tooth) with the qualifier *unnata* (protruding). In the grammatical rule (*sūtra*), however, the nominative case is used in the sense of the ablative, or alternatively, the locative: "one whose teeth are protruding is *dantura*. Expressions such as *himaśilāśarkarādanturāṇi* ("studded with snow-stones and pebbles") are examples of metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*).
The suffix *ra* is applied after the words *ūṣa*, *suṣi*, *muṣka*, and *madhu*.

In this *samāhāra-dvandva* compound, the masculine gender is used according to the Vedic (Sautra) usage. While the suffix *matup* would have been applicable after both *suṣi* and *madhu*, the rule prescribes *ra* for the other two (*ūṣan* and *muṣkan*) as well as for *ini* and *thañ*. *Ūṣāḥ* refers to yellowish dust; *suṣi* means a hole or cavity; *muṣkau* refers to the testicles. *Madhu* denotes a specific kind of taste called sweetness, and not honey (*mākṣika*) or grape wine (*mādhvīka*), because those meanings are not expressed by the word here. Consequently, the usage "this is sweet like honey" (*madhvidam madhuram*) is justified even when referring to [sweet] honey itself. However, in the following case, the suffix does not occur: "there is honey in this jar" (*madhv asmin ghaṭo vidyate*).

Regarding the term *raprakaraṇa*: *prakaraṇa* means context or occasion. The phrase "the throat-cavity is large" shows the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *gardabha*. However, the word *khara* is not derived from sharpness (*taikṣṇya*). *Mukhara* means talkative; for such a person has a "mouth" (*mukha*)—that is, the organ of speech—for everything that ought to be said, due to the lack of discrimination between what should and should not be spoken. *Mukha* here refers to the vocal organ. It is stated that the elephant's jaw is called by the word *kuñja*; this is said with the intention of asking why the literal meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), which is possible here, is abandoned. But the word *kuñjara*, like the word *hasti*, is a class-name (*jātiśabda*).

Regarding the word *nagaram*: "nagas" refers to trees and mountains. This too is a generic term (*jātiśabda*); thus, in the case of *nagarī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs by virtue of its being a generic term. Since the word *naga* is listed among the words beginning with *aśman* [in the *gaṇapāṭha*], it is established by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādi-sūtra*; therefore, the suffix *ra* need not be mentioned. Regarding *pāṇḍuram*: *pāṇḍu* is the white color; that which possesses this is *pāṇḍura*. However, the word *pāṇḍara* is unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) and applies to both the quality (*guṇa*) alone and the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*).
The suffix *ma* is applied after verbal roots ending in *dyu* or *drū*.

The word *dyu* is also a derived nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the vowel *u*. Furthermore, the possessive suffix *matup* is not optionally applied to conventional (*rūḍhi*) words, because it is impossible to express its meaning by means of *matup*.
The suffix *vaḥ* is optionally applied after the word *keśa*.

It was stated that "that" [the suffix *matup*] is for the purpose of including a collection; this has already been explained under the rule *sidhmādibhyaśca*. Regarding the phrase "in the section on *v*":

*prakaraṇa* means context or occasion. *Maṇivaḥ* is a particular kind of serpent. *Hiraṇyavaḥ* is a particular kind of treasure, though others say it is a particular kind of elephant. *Bimbāvaḥ* and *kurarāvaḥ*: the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*. *Rājīvaḥ*: the suffix is added to a word ending in *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*.

Regarding *arṇava*: *arṇa* means water; [the suffix] *-asun* with the augment *nuṭ* [is applied] according to the rule *arteḥ-asun-nuṭ ca*. Furthermore, by the rule *chandasi-iva-nipau ca*, because of the word *ca* ("and"), the suffix *-vala* is also included, and due to the continued application of the option (*anyatarasyām*), the suffix *-matup* is also available. Thus he says: "and *-vala* and *-matup*. Regarding *rathī*: the meaning is "one who possesses a chariot" (*ratha*). Regarding *sumaṅgalī*: "excellent auspiciousness"; it is a *prādi*-compound according to the rule *suḥ-pūjāyām*. From that, the vowel *ī* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) by this [rule]. The principle that a *bahuvrīhi* compound should be used for the sake of brevity is set aside here because of the Vedic character of the passage.

Regarding "maghavānam": the suffix *vanip* is applied because he possesses *magha*, which means wealth; however, the word *maghavan* is formed with the suffix *matup*. Why, then, is it said that "the suffix *vanip* is used diversely (*bahulam*) for *maghavan*"? We shall explain that very point later. Regarding "or *udvatī*": from the word *ut*, expressing the sense of "gone up," the suffix *vapratyaya* is added, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding *udvatī*: the substitution of *va* for *m* occurs by the rule "after a consonant ending in *jhay*" (*jhayaḥ*), and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Regarding "from *medha* and *ratha*": this also pertains to the Vedic domain (*chandoviṣaya*).

Regarding the rule *gāṇḍyajāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.110): "The bow is called *gāṇḍīva*"—this refers to Arjuna’s. "The bow is called *ajagava*"—this is the *pināka*. The Sūtra has been formulated in two ways by resorting to the principle of the *tantra* (the system of simultaneous application). Usage occurs in both ways as well: "With his two arms, [Arjuna] grasped the *gāṇḍīvī*, which resembled a slab of gold," and "He ascends the great arrow upon the *gāṇḍiva*. This is merely an elaboration of the mention of the word *saṃjñā* (name/designation).
The suffix *valac* is applied after the words *rajaḥ*, *kṛṣi*, *āsutī*, and *pariṣad*.

Regarding *āsutīvala*: the root *ṣuñ* means "to press"; with the suffix *ktin*, we have *āsutiḥ*, meaning "pressing. Regarding *pariṣadūla*: those who sit around (*paritaḥ sīdanti*) are the *pariṣat*. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa* etc., and the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *sadiraprateḥ*. Others read the word as *parṣat*; [the suffix] *adi* is added to the roots *śad* and *bhas* by the rule *śadibhaso'diḥ*, and by virtue of the irregularity (*bāhulaka*), it also occurs after the root *pṛṣ*. For it is seen in usage: "this assembly (*parṣad*) consists of at least ten members," and in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "this is the composition of the assembly (*pārṣadakṛti*) of your honors," and "for this treatise is attended by all the Vedas (*sarvavedapārṣadam*)."

And in the Bhaṭṭikāvya it is said: "The assembly (parṣad) arrived from the Kaṭha hermitage along with Mahābrahmans. The word *pariṣad*, however, is well-known—as in Manu: "Among those gathered by the thousands, the status of an assembly (*pariṣat*) does not exist [without certain qualities]. And in this present sūtra, both meanings apply, because the sūtra has been composed in both ways.

Regarding *bhrātṛvala*: in the word *valaḥ*, there is no lengthening of the vowel because of the continued application of the rule for the suffix *aṇ*. However, in *putravalaḥ* and *utsāhavalaḥ*, there is no lengthening because these are not proper names (*asaṃjñā*). But when they are proper names (*saṃjñā*), there is lengthening; for in the rule for *valaḥ*, the term "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is understood from the preceding rule, "in the case of *vana* and *giri* when it is a name."
In the sense of a name, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *dantaśikha*. Pāṇini 5.2.113.

*Dantāvalaḥ* means an elephant; as Amarasimha states: "The words *dantī* and *dantāvalaḥ* denote an elephant. Regarding the city name *śikhāvalam*: one might object that this is already established for a place-name by the suffix *valac*, which belongs to the fourfold group (*cāturarthika*), and that this [suffix] must necessarily be applied for the sake of meanings such as "produced there" (*nirvṛtta*) and so on. True; however, the inclusion of the word *śikhā* here is also necessary for the sake of non-place-names, so that it may apply here as well—namely, in the case of *śikhāvalā stūpā* ("a spire with a crest"). If such a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) exists, then since the suffix *la* is prescribed for a place-name in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), and because this [suffix *valac*] is subsequent [in the order of rules], one considers that it is formed by this very suffix and thus cites *śikhāvalaṃ nagaram* as an example.
The suffixes *tamap*, *tarap*, and *iṣṭhan* are applied after words ending in *jyotsnā*, *tamisrā*, *aśrṛṅgin*, *ūrjasvin*, *ūrjasvala*, *gomin*, *malina*, and *malīmasa*. (Pāṇini 5.2.114)

In the case of *jyotsnā* (moonlight), it is called "the radiance of the moon" (*candraprabhā*). Since there exists a constituent light (*jyotis*) therein, the formation of the word is justified by the sense of possession (*matvartha*). By this, the word *tamisra* (darkness) is explained as a collection of darkness (*tamaḥ-samūha*). However, in the *Nighaṇṭus*, the word *tamisra* is listed as a synonym for *tamaḥ* (darkness); in that case, there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the collection and that which is contained within it. As for the statement that "femininity is not essential," the commentary is the authority here. [The suffix] *-naC* is applied after the root *śṛṅg* and others.

Although the particle *ca* is not explicitly uttered in the Sūtra, it is nevertheless inferred from the fact that [the word] is pronounced with an udātta accent at the end. [The rule states: "the augment *asu* is added after *ūrj*. Thus we have *ūrjasvatīḥ* and *payasvatīḥ*. While the suffix *matup* is seen following words ending in the suffix *asun*, such as *ūrjasvat* and *payasvat*, the primary reason for not adopting that here is [the presence of the particle *ca*]. In the Sūtra, in the expression *ūrjasvingominn*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) was not performed in order to make manifest its ending in *n*.
The suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* [are applied after a verbal root] in these senses. (Pāṇini 5.2.115)

Regarding the phrase "from that which ends in the vowel *a*": this refers to the phoneme itself and not to the word-form [as a whole], because [the rule] would otherwise apply to forms such as *kurvat* and *pacat*, which end in the word *ac*. This is because of the subsequent mention of "from *rasa* and so forth," which is stated for the purpose of overriding the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* that would otherwise be obtained by this [general rule].

Regarding the purpose of adding the *tapara* (the long vowel marker): the question is raised that the inclusion of words such as *vrīhi* and others ending in long vowels like *mālā* in the list will serve a restrictive (*niyama*) function. The intention behind the answer—that the addition of the *tapara* must necessarily be made—is that a doubt arises as to whether this restriction concerns words ending in long *ā*, or those ending in feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*), or perhaps those ending in long *ā* (āp). [The rule] "from a single syllable" (*ekākṣarāt*).

It has been stated that the repetition [of the word] after *rasa* and so forth is for the purpose of excluding others; and in that context, the term *ekācaḥ* (having a single vowel) is recited, by which this is established: *kāryī*. This is a suffix [added] to the word *kārya*, which ends in a *kṛt* suffix. *Tandulī*: [this is formed] from a genus (*jāti*).
And [the suffix -maya] is applied after vrīhi and the other words listed in that group. (Pāṇini 5.2.116)

Regarding "from *śikhā* and so forth": the words beginning with *śikhā* will be mentioned right here. Regarding "in *ika*, *kan*, *ya*, *kha*, *da*, etc.": this is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). These suffixes as well will be enumerated right here. "*Ikan*" means the suffix *ṭhan*. This mention of "*ikan*" is in accordance with the system of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) and is for the purpose of completing the verse. "From the remaining [words], both [suffixes]"—all of this is obtained through the continued application of the particle *iti*.

If that is so, then there is no reversal—namely, that in that case there is the grasping of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas here there is the grasping of the object (*artha*); for it is precisely the grasping of the essential nature that is logical, since its opposition has not yet arisen.

Regarding the rule *śīrṣān nañaḥ*: after the word *śīrṣa* that follows the negative particle *nañ*, the suffixes *ini* and *iṭhan* occur—thus, *aśīrṣī* and *aśīrṣikaḥ*. One who has no head is described in this way. By the rule *aci śīrṣe*, the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras* takes place; even in the explanatory sentence (*vākya*), it is that very form which undergoes the substitution that is mentioned.
After the words *tuṇḍa* and others, the suffix *ilac* is also applied [to form a feminine noun].

Regarding the phrase "from a body part that has increased" (*svāṅgādvivṛddhāt*): suffixes such as *ilac* and others occur after words denoting a body part when that part is qualified by increase. For example, one who has large ears is called *karṇilaḥ*, *karṇī*, *kaṇikaḥ*, or *karṇavān*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* is always applied after [a word ending in] *go-pūrva*. 5.2.118.

"It has one hundred and one" means "that which is both one and a hundred. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound formed according to the rule beginning with "pūrvakāla" (Pāṇini 2.1.49). It does not arise from a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*, a *bahuvrīhi*, or a *dvandva* compound, because such forms are not conventionally expressed (*anabhidhāna*) and because the particle *iti* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

"How so?"—this is a question because even the word *eka-go* does not end in the letter *a*. [The answer is: "Because the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has been applied," namely, the suffix *ṭac* by the rule *gorataddhitaluki*. "How so?"—this is a question from one who thinks that the word *śaka-kaṭi* exists only as ending in the vowel *i*. [The answer is: It will not apply after words such as *ekaviṃśati* simply because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*); what is the use of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ata*? To this he says: "And necessarily (*avaśam*)," etc. "For the sake of such cases" means for the sake of such a sūtra as this.
As for the other suffixes (*yogāḥ*) such as *vātātīsārābhyām* and so forth, there is no application of the word "hence" (*ataḥ*) in those cases.

Regarding the mention of "the inclusion of the term *nitya*" (*nityagrahaṇam*), etc.: otherwise, because of the inclusion of the option (*anyatarasyām*) throughout this entire section concerning *ann*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its application here as well, due to the addition of the suffix *matup*. Regarding the phrase "or by one [suffix]": the sense is that if it must necessarily be justified. In that case, the compound is formed according to the rule *supsupā*. How then is the form *ekadaṇkaḍī* derived? The specific grammatical instruction (*nirdeśaḥ*)—namely, *ekadeśinaikādhikaraṇe*—indicates that the suffix *ini* also occurs in certain instances.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *niṣka* when it ends in *śatasahasra*.

The word *niṣka* is connected even with the hundred and thousand which function as subordinate members (*guṇabhūta*), and not only with that which ends in *-taddhita*; thus he says: "If those two... [referring to] *suvarṇāniṣkaśatam*, etc. The meaning is that this applies where the word *niṣka* does not stand as the prior member (*pūrvapada*).
Why is the mention of "end" (*anta*) made? For if it were stated simply as "*niṣkācchatasahasrābhyām*," there would be doubt: "Is it the prior member?"—thus.
The suffix *yat* is applied after [the word] *rūpa* when it means "unassailable" (*āhata*) or "praiseworthy" (*praśaṃsā*).

"A silver *dīnāra*": the *dīnāra* and the *kārṣāpaṇa* are specific measures of gold marked with the forms of a man or other figures, devised for the sake of conventional usage. "By means of hammering with a *nighātikā*," etc.: a *nighātikā* is an iron rod with a sharp point by which goldsmiths bring out the form of a man or other figures upon gold and other materials. According to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *ṇvul* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*); thus, it is that by which something is struck—a *nighātikā*. By "hammering with that," and so forth; by the word "etc.," the stamping of seals and similar processes are included.

In some cases, the form of a person or similar object is produced by striking with a hammer; in other cases, such as with coins like *dīnāras*, it is impressed by means of a seal (*mudrā*). Because it is produced through striking (*āhanana*), it is called "struck" (*āhata*). Generally, the word *kedāra* is recited [in this context], though its usage in such a sense must be sought.

"The snowy mountains" (*himyāḥ parvatāḥ*): *Himavat* and those situated on its borders; the suffix *yap* is used in the plural. "The virtuous ones" (*gupyāḥ*): those possessing qualities (*guṇavantaḥ*). The suffix *ini* is also seen—as in: "He did not distinguish between the virtuous and the non-virtuous."
The suffixes *vin*, *ni*, and *ṅīṣ* are applied after the words *āsmāya*, *āmada*, and *āsraj*.

The suffix *matup* is indeed included everywhere. The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is this: by the previous mention of the term "nitya" (invariable), the mention of "anyatarasyām" (optional) was not connected there; however, it is certainly connected here. And so, in the rule *tasau matvarthe*, the examples *payasvān* and *yaśasvān* were cited in the Bhāṣya. As for *payasvī*: because of the designation *bha* by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, there is an absence of *jaśtva* (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop).
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *u* for *ū*] occurs frequently.

Regarding *aṣṭrāvīti*: *aṣṭrā* is [derived from] the root *aś* with the suffix *traṇ*. This word, which is a synonym for *daṃṣṭrā* (tusk/fang), is employed in the mantras—as in "Pūṣan shook his loose *aṣṭrā*" and "The matted-haired one moved about with a good *aṣṭrā*"—and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied here precisely because of this very reading. Regarding "from both *dvaya* and *ubhaya*, *hr̥daya*": since other words are already long by nature, the suffix *āluc* is added after *hr̥daya* according to the rule "after *hr̥daya*, *āluc* optionally. By the mention of "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*), the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* are also obtained; the letter *c* in *cakāra* receives the technical name *it* according to the rule "the letters *c* and *ṭ* [are *it*]. The same applies in subsequent cases. However, at the end, the letter *c* does not exist at all. Regarding "after *himā*, *celu*": the suffix begins with the vowel *e*.
Regarding *balādūla-jiti*: an alternative derivation for *balūla* and *vālūla*—which belong to the *sidhma*-class and denote the sense of possession (*matvartha*)—has been shown.

The word *marutta* is derived from *parvan* and *marut*. The letter *n* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable udātta (accented). Marutta was a king about whom this is heard: "The Maruts were the attendants in the house of Marutta. However, regarding the technical designation of an *upasarga* (prefix), because the word *marut* is specifically included [in the rule], the substitution of *t* for *s* occurs according to the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ*, even though the word does not end in a vowel (*anajanta*). The etymological derivation is shown as "May the Maruts grant him [the kingdom]—thus he is *marutta*. In that case, by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would apply.

The word *marut* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *uti*, according to the rule "mṛgorutiḥ"; however, in that case, one should observe that its initial syllable is udātta according to the rule "upasargāścabhivarjam."
The suffix *yus* is applied after the word *ūrṇā*.
Regarding the term *ūrṇāyuḥ*: because it consists of more than one word (*bahupadatvāt*), the elision of the suffix *ya* (as prescribed by *yasyeti ca*) does not take place.
The suffix *gmini* is applied after the word *vāc*.

Regarding the term *vāggmī*: through the application of *kutva* and *jaśtva* to the letter *ca*, there is the hearing of two *ga* sounds. Now, why not simply say *min*? For even in that case, *vāggmī* would indeed be established through *kutva* and *jaśtva*. But [one might object]: in this way, there would be only one *ga* sound, and there would be no doubling according to the rule *anaci ca*, because the prohibition of the suffix *kap* applies by the rule *dīrghādācāryāṇām*.

Furthermore, if it were argued that there is no difference whether both [the *yaṇ* and the *anunāsika*] are heard or only one of them, even so, by the rule "before a nasal [consonant]" (*yaro'nunāsike*) and the rule "it is obligatory in the secular language" (*pratyaye bhāṣāyāṃ nityavacanam*), a nasalized form would necessarily result; thus, one would have to say *vāṅbhayam* and *tvaṅbhayam*.

The suffixes *ālaj* and *āṭac* are applied [to the root *bhāṣ*] when it means "one who speaks much. This refers to one who indeed speaks correctly; the sense is that he speaks even though there is much to say.
The [taddhita] suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *svāmin* when the sense is "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*).

Regarding the phrase "from the word *sva* denoting sovereignty": although elsewhere the word *sva* also denotes self (*ātman*), one's own (*ātmīya*), kinsmen (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*), in the scope of this particular grammatical formation (*vṛtti*), its denotation of sovereignty occurs by its very nature. Therefore, one who possesses wealth or is even destitute is called a "ruler" (*īśitṛ*) or a "master" (*svāmin*); however, this [word *sva*] does not denote wealth itself. Consequently, the expression "the master of wealth" (*dhanasya svāmī*) also occurs; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the suffix *matup* being superseded by *āminac*.

Even if the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* (optionally) were intended to aggregate the suffix *matup*, it would follow that one could say "svavān" (possessing self) of wealth, just as one says "śvavān" (possessing a dog); therefore, it is established that the word *sva* denotes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), not wealth and the like. Nor is it the case that sovereignty arises from the possession of wealth, for this is observed even in the case of speech and so forth—as in "Vācaspati" (Lord of Speech) or "the master of speech"—and yet there is no common recognition of speech as being "wealth."
The suffix *ac* is applied after [the group of words] beginning with *arśas*.

Regarding the rule *svāṅgāddhīnāt*: "deficient" (*hīna*) means "impaired" (*vikala*). The suffix *añ* occurs after a word denoting a deficient limb. For example: one who has a lame foot is called *khañja*; one who has a blind eye is called *kāṇa*. How is it that one who has a withered hand is called *kuṇi*? It is through the metaphorical treatment of identity (*abhedopacāra*). If that is so, will the same apply to words like *khañja* and others? Then this is the purpose: so that the possessive suffix *matup* does not occur when the distinction [between the person and the limb] is intended to be expressed. Now, why does *matup* not occur after the word *kuṇi*? Because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

[Objection: In that case, the suffix *matup* will not occur after words such as *śaṅkha* simply because it is not prescribed [by rule]. [Response: But it is for the sake of the final acute accent (*antodātta*). For those words denoting inferior body parts which have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), the final acute accent should occur, provided it is possible. Regarding the word *varṇāt*: the suffix *ac* occurs after the word *śukla* when it denotes a color—e.g., "a cloth that has whiteness" is a *śukla* cloth. Is this not already established by the rule: "The elision (*luk*) of *matup* should be stated after words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*)"? [Response: But it is for the sake of the final acute accent.

This is so that, among those words denoting color which have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), there may be the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) when they denote the possessor of that quality (*tadvat*). Another says: this suffix is prescribed after words denoting qualities (*guṇivacana*) to express the possessor of that quality; therefore, from the expression "the palaces in this city are white," one obtains the form *śuklaṃ nagaram* ("the city is white").
The suffix *ini* is applied after a word ending in *pra*, *niṣṭhā*, or *ādi*, when it denotes something censurable due to being afflicted by a pair of opposites (*dvandva*).

Regarding the phrase *tadviṣayebhyaḥ*: by the word *tat*, "affliction" (*upatāpa*) and "blameable" (*garhya*) are referred back, not the *dvandva* compound; for it is impossible for that [compound] itself to have those as its objects. Regarding *prāṇisthārthavācibhyaḥ*: this, however, includes all [of the aforementioned categories]. In the example *citralalāṭikāvatī*, because there is a desire to express a specific substance, the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* does not apply, and thus the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) is absent, resulting in the audible suffix *ṭāp*. Regarding the statement "the suffix being already established": this refers to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*. The phrase "for the purpose of excluding *ṭhan* and others": by the word "others" (*ādi*), the suffix *matup* is included.
The suffix *kuk* is applied after [the word *vāta*] when combined with *atisāra*.

"Because of the affliction caused by wind and diarrhea. The intention is that, due to the association with diarrhea (*atisāra*), only the disease (*vyādhi*) called "wind" is understood here, and not the element of air (*vāyu*). Regarding the phrase "the suffix is established," the meaning is that it occurs only with the suffix *-in*. It is sometimes read as "and this [suffix] is desired in the sense of a disease," where the reason has already been stated.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after a word denoting age, in the sense of "fulfilling. (Pāṇini 5.2.130)

The meaning is that, by virtue of the context and other factors, the word *pañcama* (fifth) functions to denote time—such as a month or a year—and therefore the qualification "when age is to be expressed" is appropriate in that instance.
And [the suffix -matup is applied] after the words *sukha* and so forth. 5.2.131.

"The suffix *ini* is restricted. In the previous rule, the nature of the restriction was shown as "only *ini* occurs"; here too, the restriction is exactly the same. Now, one might object: since the restrictive particle *eva* is attached to "from which [the suffix arises]," the restriction applies to everything other than that; thus, only *sukha* and the others would be restricted. Why, then, is it said that "the suffix is restricted"? There is no fault here, for a restriction (*niyama*) is defined as an establishment characterized by the exclusion of others.

The statement is for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *matup*, but not for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ṭhan*; the intention is that *ṭhan* has already been excluded by the rule "the suffix *ini* is to be prescribed after words such as *śikha*."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, and *varṇa*. (Pāṇini 5.2.132)
Regarding the term *brāhmaṇavarṇī*: the "color" (*varṇa*) of the Brāhmaṇas is their caste (*jāti*); one who possesses that is a *brāhmaṇavarṇī*, which is simply a Brāhmaṇa.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *hasta* when it means "born from the hand. (Pāṇini 5.2.133)

It is stated that the suffix *ini* is being restricted. In this context, the expression of a restriction (*niyamavācoyukti*) is based merely on the possibility of the possessive sense (*matvartha*). In reality, however, this is a positive injunction (*vidhi*). How so? This word is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), like the word "elephant" (*gaja*); here there is not even a trace of a possessive sense. Thus, even when an elephant lacks its trunk, it is still called an "elephant" (*hastī*) because the genus (*jāti*) is present. And when there is an intention to express the connection with a trunk, the suffix *matup* occurs even in the case of a female elephant (*hastinī*)—as in "possessing a trunk" (*hastavān*, *hastī*)—just as one says "a man possessing a hand" (*hastavān puruṣaḥ*).

The same should be understood regarding the subsequent yogas as well. Furthermore, the mention of "taking by the hand" (hastagrahaṇa) is considered to be illustrative; by this, forms such as *dantī* (having tusks), *viṣāṇī* (having horns), and *kesarī* (having a mane) are established.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *varṇa* when it denotes a *brahmacārin*.

Regarding the phrase "brahmacārī," it is intended to mean a member of the three [upper] castes (*traivarṇika*). Although the word *brahmacārī* is well-known in its primary sense as referring to one in the first stage of life (*āśrama*) who dwells in the teacher's house, nevertheless, here—due to the requirements of the subject matter—it is intended to mean simply a member of the three castes, and not the stage of life itself; this indicates that the latter possesses the practice of celibacy only occasionally. He explains this with the words "for he... (*sa hi*). One is a *brahmacārī* because he practices (*carati*) the *brahman*; here, *brahman* means the Veda. However, what is intended here is a specific rule (*niyama*) for the purpose of studying it; thus he says: "the rule" (*niyamam*).

In this context, the term *brahmacārī* is formed by the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of "one who observes a vow" (*vrate*). He states the reason for the word *brahmacārī* abandoning its primary meaning and referring instead solely to the three social classes (*traivarṇika*)—namely, the Brāhmaṇas and the other two castes—by saying: "the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas."
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied after] *puṣkara* and other [words] when [the derivative denotes] a region (*deśa*). 5.2.135.

"Arthī" means one for whom an object (*artha*) is not present (*asannihita*). This non-presence is in terms of time, not in terms of space. In that regard, because of the contradiction, the word "exists" (*asti*) cannot be connected [to the suffix]; therefore, the suffix *ini* is prescribed for one who has not yet obtained [the object]. And by the logic of the curd and Kauṇḍinya, there is an absence of the suffix *ini* when it is conditioned by existence (*sattā*). "Arthavān" refers to one for whom an object is present. Regarding the rule "tadantācca": this rule is commenced because the prohibition against treating a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a suffix as having that suffix as its final member applies to stems that possess a suffix (like *grahaṇavat*). An example is "dhānyārthī."

The meaning is that there exists an object in the form of grain (*dhānya*) which is not present; [the suffix] *ini* is applied after a *karmadhāraya* compound. Now, one might argue: "This is established by the suffix *ṇini* from the root *arthayati*—one who seeks grain is a *dhānyārthī*. Even so, by the rule for *ṇini*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member would result. If that is the case, then it should be explained as follows: *artha* means seeking (*prārthanā*); one who possesses that is an *arthī*. A *dhānyārtha* is a seeking of grain—that is, a desire for grain; one who possesses that is a *dhānyārthī*. By explaining it thus, the forms *arthikaḥ* and *pratyarthikaḥ* are also established.

If, however, it were stated as "and from *artha* when not preceded [by another word]," then because the suffix *ini* alone would be prescribed, the suffix *ṭhan* would not occur. The prohibition "after a monosyllabic word, after a *kṛt*-derivative, and after a genus-name" is non-universal (*anitya*); therefore, just as in the case of *kāryī* and *kāryika*, the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* will occur. But the possessive suffix *matup* will not occur due to lack of usage (*anabhidhānāt*). Nor is there any possibility of *ini* and *ṭhan* occurring even when the word *artha* denoting wealth is proximate, because of lack of usage. Thus it is established that one need not state: "and from *artha* when not preceded [by another word] and when ending in that [i.e., *artha*]."
The suffix *matup* may optionally [be applied] after words beginning with *bala*.

Regarding the phrase "by the mention of *anyatarasyām*," and so forth: [one might argue] that since it occurs in a collective sense (*samuccaye*) as before, why was the particle *ca* not used? What can we do about it? However, if by this [particle *anyatarasyām*] meaning "optionally" (*vikalpārtha*) the suffix were made optional, then when the *matup* suffix is excluded, both *ini* and *ṭhan* would occur according to what is otherwise prescribed. But if this were the case, the formulation of the rule (*sūtra-ārambha*) would be purposeless, because even without it, all three suffixes would be established; therefore, only *ini* would occur. From what, indeed, would it follow that only *ini* occurs and not *ṭhan*? Therefore, it is a collective sense (*samuccaya*).
[The suffix *matup* is applied] after [a word ending in] *saṃjñā*, when the words *manas* and *mat* [are present]. 5.2.137.

In *prathamini* and *dāminī*, the rule for suffixes ending in a specific element applies according to the principle that "the mention of *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* includes both meaningful and meaningless [suffixes]"; thus, there is an application of the rule for suffixes ending in those elements (*tadantavidhi*), and the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by the rule *nastaddhite*.
The suffixes *ba*, *bha*, *yu*, *tu*, *ti*, *ta*, *ya*, and *sa* are added after the words *kaṃs* and *śam*.

Regarding the statement "the two ending in *m* are *kam* and *śam*": although the word *ka* ending in *a* is well-known as denoting happiness, water, wind, Brahman, and the head, the phrase "ending in *m*" is stated to demonstrate that there is also a word *ka* ending in *m*. As for "denoting water and happiness," this is not according to the respective order; rather, it is according to what is possible. Thus, *kam* denotes both water and happiness, while *śam* denotes happiness alone.

Regarding the rule "alpāctaram" (the word with fewer syllables is placed first), the precedence of *sukha* was applicable but was not applied by the author of the Sūtras themselves, because it is subject to exceptions. In the examples, there are the anusvāra and the parasavarṇa; therein, for the letters *y* and *v*, there are nasalized (*sānunāsika*) *y* and *v* sounds.
The suffix *yu* is applied after the words *aham* and *śubham*.

"It is simply another word [for 'I']. [Objection: But here no word has been introduced as a subject matter such that there could be "another word" in relation to it? [Response: True; however, by virtue of common usage, the word *aham*—which is a substitute for *asmat* according to the rule *tvāhau sau*—is present in the mind and is practically already indicated. It is in relation to that [word] that it is called "another word. Regarding the statement "it occurs in the sense of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*)," this expresses a difference in meaning: "Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) is pride (*garva*) or self-conceit (*abhimāna*). [Examples: *ahaṃyuḥ*, *śubhaṃyuḥ*. As before, there is the anusvāra and the subsequent assimilation (*parasavarṇa*).
Regarding the rule *ūrṇāyā yus*, for those who do not carry forward the term *chandasi* [from the preceding sūtra], the mention of *ūrṇā* must be made right here.
Thus ends the second quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by Kṣīrasvāmin Miśra;
now begins the third quarter of the fifth chapter of the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
The case endings [are called *vibhakti*] after the words beginning with *prāk-diś* (Pāṇini 5.3.27).

"They should be understood as having the technical designation 'vibhakti'. This means that those for whom the word *vibhakti* is the designation are so described. Now, an objection may be raised: the word *vibhakti* has already been employed as the designation for *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes. Furthermore, in the various rules (*pradeśa*), it is the designation that conveys the designated object (*saṃjñin*), not its own form. Therefore, it is more appropriate that the *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes themselves possess the status of the designation, rather than the word *vibhakti*. True; however, if the *su*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes were to serve as the designation, they would have to do so either individually or collectively.

First, they do not function individually, because there would be no purpose in assigning multiple designations [to a single item]. Nor do they function collectively, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and because the designation does not recur. For designations are indeed recurrent, but a collective aggregate (*samudāya*) does not recur. Another says: "Just as in the rule *kinau liṭ ca* the status of being like *liṭ* (*liḍvadbhāva*) is prescribed, so too here the status of being like an inflectional suffix (*vibhaktivadbhāva*) is prescribed. However, one should not suspect that the actual prescription of *su*-suffixes and *tiṅ*-suffixes occurs here, since they have already been prescribed previously. Thus, these are the rules concerning *tyad* and so forth.

The "rules for *tyad* and so forth" (*tyadādividhi*) are those operations which are conditioned by being *tyad* and so forth, whether they pertain to their specific forms or to their status as *tyad* and so forth. This is merely an illustration; another purpose is the prohibition of the technical designation *it* for the *m* of *dānīm* by the rule "not [the *m*] of *tu*, *sa*, or *ma* in a case-ending" (*na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*). From this follow examples such as *tataḥ* and *yataḥ*, where the substitution of *a* occurs by the rule "for *tyad* and so forth, *a*" (*tyadādīnām aḥ*). Here, because the *s* is not final, it lacks the designation *it*. In *kṛtaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ku* by the rule "for *ha*, *ku*" (*kṛti hoḥ*). In *kadā*, there is the substitution of *ka* for *kim*.

In the examples *kva* and *iha*, the forms *kva* and *iha* arise through the substitution of *kva* for *ati* and *ha* for *idam* respectively—specifically by the rules *idamo haḥ* and *idama iś*. Here, the acute accent (*udātta*) is already established by the accent of the suffix itself. Therefore, *itaḥ* alone is the illustrative example for the accentuation of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*); otherwise, by the rule *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix would be acute.

But surely, according to the maxim *madhye’pavādāḥ* ("intermediate rules are exceptions"), the accent of the case endings (*vibhaktisvara*) is an exception only to the rule *anudāttau suppitau*, and not to the accent of the *lit* suffix; thus, the *lit*-accent would subvert the case-ending accent because it is subsequent? This is not a fault; for here, the case-ending accent does not apply while the *lit*-accent has yet to be applied. Why? Because the term *antodāttāt* ("from that which has an acute on the final syllable") is understood [in the rule]; thus, the *lit*-accent itself is the very cause for the application of the case-ending accent.

Although in the rule *ūḍidam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171), the mention of "the third case and those following" (*tṛtīyādigrahaṇam*) is understood as a carry-over from the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (6.1.168), nevertheless, since every suffix bearing the technical name "case-ending" (*vibhakti-saṃjñaka*) up until the completion of the fifth chapter is considered to begin with the third case, even the suffixes beginning with *tasil* are indeed included by that mention of "the third case and those following."

"From here onwards," and so forth. This has already been explained under the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*. However, the word *vā* (or) indeed continues to apply [to the subsequent rules], because it is separately marked with the svarita accent. Now, could one not simply say *prāgdiśaśca* right after *supaḥ* and *vibhaktiśca*? It cannot be done in this way; for if it were stated thus, it would not be known from where the *prāgdiśīya* suffixes begin.

Furthermore, there are many words denoting direction—such as those derived from *diś* and others by the rule *digādibhyo yat*, as well as *ka* and so forth—and consequently, the limit (*avadhi*) would not be determined. Moreover, for the sake of restricting the scope of operations such as *kiṃsarvanāmabahubhyaḥ*, the term *prāgdiśaḥ* would have to be stated here once again.

If, on the other hand, it were stated right here that "the suffixes *sup* and *tiṅ* [are also prātipadika]," even so, in the rule *tiṅastrīṇitrīṇi*, the mention of *tiṅ* and *sup* would still have to be made there for the purpose of designating them as *puruṣa* (person) and *vacana* (number); thus, there is no difference [between the two approaches].

"From [words ending in] *kiṃ*, *sarvanāman*, and *bahu*, except for *dvi* and so forth. This indicates whether it is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) or a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). It should be understood as a suffix (*pratyaya*). Thus, in the cases of *dvābhyām* and *dvayoḥ*, the suffixes *tasil* and *tral* do not occur.

"Enumeration of the base" (*prakṛtiparisaṃkhyāna*) means "counting of the base. Regarding the phrase "the snare of the grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇapāśa*): since suffixes such as *astāti* and others are prescribed after bases that possess [specific] markers (*grahaṇavat*), an enumeration of the base is impossible in that context; therefore, even though it is separated [by other rules], *pāśa* is cited as a counter-example. Regarding the phrase "due to the exclusion of *dvi* and so forth": if, however, this [suffix *kan*] were recited before *dvi* and the others, it would not be possible in this way;

for there would be a fault in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Among pronouns beginning with *tyad*, whichever is subsequent remains; thus, *tvaṃ ca kaśca* would result in *kau*, and *bhavāṃśca kaśca* would result in *kau*.

Regarding the statement "in the mention of *bahu*, there is the mention of number": how are the named items (*saṃjñin*) indicated here by means of the technical name (*saṃjñā*) "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*)? By association (*sāhacarya*) with those [other named items], the word *bahu* is also understood as a named item—that is, it is understood as that for which the technical name "number" (*saṃkhyā*) has been prescribed by the rule "the words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vat*, and *uṭati* are numbers"—and not as the word signifying abundance (*vaipulya*). Therefore, even in this context, there is no inclusion of the latter.
The substitute *idam* is applied [in place of the pronoun *adas*] before the case-ending *iś*. 5.3.3.

The substitute *śakāra* (the letter *ś*) is for the purpose of applying the rule to the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). Otherwise, because it is specifically prescribed, it would set aside the substitution of *at* for the *tyad*-class stems; consequently, by the rule "of the final [alophon]," the substitution of *it* would apply to the *m*, and upon the elision of the *hal* (consonant), the undesirable forms *etaḥ* and *eha* would result.
These two [suffixes] are used after the word *ratha*. (Pāṇini 5.3.4)

"An exception to *iś*": the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāve*). The meaning is that the sublation of *iś* is effected by these two. However, the singular number is used with reference to the rule (*yoga*), meaning "this rule is an exception to *iś*. Alternatively, the singular number is used because each [suffix] is connected individually with the substitutes, as in the rule "after *bhū*, *śas*, etc., there is *bhuva* except after *acvi*. Or rather, one should read "two exceptions to *iś*. The vowel *a* in the letter *r* is for the sake of pronunciation, because there is no *prāgdiśīya* substitute ending in *r* that possesses the vowel *a*.
The suffix *oṣ* is applied after this [word] to form the sense of "speed. (Pāṇini 5.3.5)

Śakāra is for the purpose of making [the substitute] apply to the whole (sarvādeśa). Otherwise, by the rule *alo'ntyasya*, it would apply only to the final letter. But surely the substitution of *at* is already established for the final letter by the rule for the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so on; once that has been done, the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *a* would follow. Since there is no purpose in pronouncing *ā* for an *a*, will it not therefore become a substitute for the whole? There is indeed another purpose for pronouncing *ā* even for an *a*: what is it? It is so that any other rule that might otherwise apply shall not take effect. Which one is that? It is the accent (*svara*) prescribed by the rule *liti*.
For example, in the rule *mo rāji samaḥ kvau*, the explicit mention of the letter *m* (as in *makārasya*) is for the purpose of overriding the *anusvāra*.

Regarding the "separation of the rule" (*yogavibhāga*), it is for the purpose of overriding [the application of] *aś*. As for the phrase "the suffix *thamu* again," otherwise, that very *thakārādi* which is prescribed without distinction by the rule *prakāravacane thāl* would apply only there. Should it then be added as a supplement? No, he says; we shall qualify the *thakārādi* by means of this [word *idam*]: "that which begins with *th* belonging to *idam*"—and that is precisely *thamu*. Consequently, by this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), *thamu* will occur, and by it, *thāl* is overridden.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that the substitute is *an*, ending in *n*, according to the rule *etado 'n*. Since this substitute consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole of the original. Consequently, because it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) through the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle, the final *n* is elided—thus [we have] *atra*.
The suffix *di* optionally follows *sarva* in the sense of "one of many."

The word "di" is the locative case of the letter *d* (*dakāra*), and according to the rule "yasmin vidhiḥ," this is understood to include the beginning of that [word]. Thus he says: "when a suffix beginning with the letter *d* follows."

Regarding "sarvadā brāhmaṇī": for what purpose is the feminine gender introduced? For one who thinks—"In *dāti*, this is the seventh [case-ending] from the word *dā*, and not from the letter *da*; therefore, there is the substitution of *lyap* for *ktvā*, as in the rules *halaḥ* and *śnaḥ*, and thus there is the elision of the long *ā* [by the rule *ato lopaḥ*]"—against such a person, the word *dā* is cited as a counter-example. Even so, might it be argued that because the word *dā* here is derived through a secondary formation (*lākṣaṇika*), the rule will not apply? In that case, this should be viewed as a word ending in a primary suffix (*vijanta*); and by doing so, it indeed serves as an example even in the masculine gender.
The suffix *tasil* is added after the fifth case ending.

The suffix *tasil* occurs [after the seventh case-ending]. However, if *tasil* and the other substitutes were understood as replacements for the fifth and other case-endings by relying on the genitive (as in "of the fifth," "of the seventh"), there would be prohibitions regarding the elision of case-endings (*subluk*), accent (*svara*), the formation of *guṇa*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), the substitution of *aitva* and *autva*, and the addition of *smāyādi*. Regarding the elision of case-endings (*subluk*): after the rule "the suffix *tyap* follows an indeclinable" (*avyayāttyap*), we have *tatastyaḥ* and *tatratyaḥ*. In these cases, the rule "the case-endings are elided after verbal roots and nominal stems" (*supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*) would result in the elision of *tasil* and *tral*. Regarding accent (*svara*): in *tadā* and *yadā*, the rule "the case-endings *sup* and the suffix *pit* are unaccented" (*anudāttau suppitau*) would result in their being unaccented.

[Objection: There would be *guṇa*—why? Because [the rule] "gheṅiti" prescribes *guṇa*. [Reply: Then there would be lengthening (*dīrghatva*)—because [the rules] "ato dīrgho yañi" and "supi ca" prescribe lengthening. [Objection: Then there would be *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *at*)—because [the rules] "ato dīrgho yañi" and "supi ca" prescribe lengthening. [Reply: In the case of those [forms], such as *teṣu* and *tatra*, [the rule] "bahuvacane jhalyet" would apply. [Objection: There would be *autva* (the substitution of *au* for *at*)—in forms like *kasmin* and *kutra*, because [the rule] "acca gheḥ" prescribes *autva*.

From that [word] ending in *smāy* and so forth, in that [case], there, the forms *smāt* and *smin* would apply according to the rule "for the *ṅasi* and *ṅi* [cases], *smāt* and *smin* [are substituted]. Therefore, it is correct to say "of the fifth" (*pañcamyāḥ*) and "of the seventh" (*saptamyāḥ*), as well as "the suffixes beginning with *tasil*" (*tasilādayaḥ*). For this very reason, there is the mention of the fifth case in the rule "from the others" (*itarābhyaḥ*); otherwise, one would have to say "of the others" (*itarāsām*). If, then, *tasil* and the others are suffixes (*pratyaya*) and not substitutes (*ādeśa*), then there is also a fault regarding the verbal root *tasi* in the rule "and of *tasi*" (*taseśca*).

Is it not the case that, because [the suffix] *tasil* is a substitute for the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) in the rules "after a word in the sense of pratiyoga, *tasi* is used" and "also after [a word denoting] the apādāna, except for *ahīya* and *ruha*," this *tasi* is a substitute for the fifth case-ending, and thus the rule for *tasil* would apply? There is no fault even in the view that it is a suffix (*pratyaya*); since the vowel *i* in *taseḥ* is intended to be significant, [the suffix] will not apply to a verbal root (*dhātu*).
And [the suffix *ṭāc* is applied] after words ending in *tasi*. 5.3.8.

Regarding the phrase "of that *tasi*": because it is subsequent [in the order of the rules], *tasil* has its scope in cases such as *kuto 'vahīyate* ("from where does he fall away? and *kuto 'varohati* ("from where does he descend?"); whereas *tasi* has its scope in cases such as *grāmata āgacchati* ("he comes from the village"). When both would apply in instances such as *kuta āgacchati* ("he comes from where?"), *tas* occurs by virtue of being subsequent, and its replacement by *tasil* is effected by this rule. The statement that the mention of *tasil* for *tasi* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtham*) refers to the purpose already stated for the inclusion of the *liṭ* marker. And the phrase "for the sake of the case-ending designation" (*vibhaktyartham*) means for the purpose of assigning the technical name "case-ending" (*vibhakti-saṃjñā*).

Otherwise, because that [suffix] would be subsequent, once it is applied, it would not belong to the *prāg-diśīya* class; consequently, due to the absence of the designation "case-ending" (*vibhakti*), the substitution of *tadādi-ātva* (the replacement of the initial of *tad* etc. would not occur, and thus the desired form itself would not be established.
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the prepositions *pary-* and *abhi-*.

Regarding the phrase "from those [words] existing in the sense of 'all around' (sarvatas) and 'both ways' (ubhayatas)": here, the inherent nature of the expression (*abhidhānasvābhāvya*) is the reason. Therefore, it does not occur here in cases such as *pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles around") or *abhiyāti* ("he goes towards"); for in these instances, *pari* has the sense of "above" and *abhi* has the sense of "facing. However, in the case of *odanaṃ pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles rice all around"), although the sense is "all around" (*sarvatobhāva*), because the option (*vāvacana*) applies, there is optionally an absence of *tasil*, resulting in *sarvataḥ* and *ubhayataḥ*. The suffix *tasi* is applied to words ending in the locative case by virtue of their inclusion in the *ādyādi* group.
The suffix *at* is applied after the interrogative pronoun *kim*.

The prohibition of the *it*-designation for the letter *t* in the rule "na vibhaktau tusmāḥ" does not apply here, because that [prohibition] is non-eternal (*anityatva*). Its non-eternality, however, is known from the fact that in the rule "idamasthamuḥ," the letter *u* in *thamu* is intended to prevent the *it*-designation of the letter *m*. In the case of *dānīm*, the prohibition of the *it*-designation for the letter *m* indeed applies. For what is being indicated is its non-eternality, and not its total absence in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).

Regarding the phrase "from the subsequent sūtra": the sūtra *kimo'dvā* should be recited. Their view is that by the inclusion of *tra* and *tara* through the particle *ca* in the rule *ha ca chandasi*, the desired result is achieved. However, the author of the Bhāgavṛtti does not accept this for the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).
They are also seen after other [suffixes]. 5.3.14.

"Otherness (*itaratva*) is in relation to the fifth and seventh [cases]," because those two have been mentioned immediately prior. "For the sake of a general rule (*prāyika*)," means for the purpose that this rule should be generally applicable. What is established by this? He says: "By this," as in *sa bhavān*, *tato bhavān*, and so forth. Examples of *ha* include *ayaṃ bhavān*, *iha bhavān*, and so forth; examples of *ataḥ* include *ko bhavān*, *kva bhavān*, and so forth. Regarding "in the case of *dīrghāyus* and so on," the substitution of *s* (as in *nityaṃ samāse*) does not occur.

Because it occurs as part of a compound ending in the final member (*uttarapadastha*), the optional application [of the suffix *dā*] prescribed by the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* does not take place either; for that rule relies upon the relation of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) between words.
[The suffix *dā* is applied after the words] *sarva*, *eka*, *anya*, *kiṃ*, *yad*, and *tad* when expressing time: *sarvadā*, *ekadā*, *anyadā*, *kadā*, *yadā*, *tadā*.

The term "of the seventh" (saptamyāḥ) is understood [as the governing rule] because it is marked with the svarita accent; however, "not from the others" (na tvitarābhyaḥ) is not so understood, because of the opposite [lack of svarita].
The suffix *rhil* is applied after the pronoun *idam*.

The *lakāra* (the letter *l*) is for the sake of accent (*svara*). For instance, in the case of *hita*, an accent occurs by the rule "ūḍidam" and so forth, but such an accent does not occur here [in *itarāt*]; because the status of being marked with *l* (*litva*) has already served its purpose elsewhere. However, the status of being marked with *l* in *tasil* has already served its purpose in other instances of *idam*.

In this case, *idam* becomes *iś*, and *dhunā* is the suffix. Therein, by the rule *ūḍidam* etc., the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) applies; and that [accent] occurs by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* etc. However, in the Bhāṣya, the suffix *adhunā* is adopted; there, the *iś* of *idam* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and its middle-acute (*madhyodātta*) nature results from irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
Then, moreover: || 5.3.19 ||
Regarding the term *dāvacana*: another says, "This is the suffix *adā*, not the suffix *dā*"; in that case, the acute accent on the first syllable occurs optionally.
The suffixes *dārhi* and *lau* are applied after these two [roots] in the Vedic language.
The term *tayoḥ* is a citation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*); by transposition, the genitive case is used in place of the ablative.

The suffixes -sadyas, -parut, -parāri, -aiṣamas, -paredyavi, -adya, -pūrvedyus, -anyedyus, -anyataredyus, -itaredyus, -aparedyus, -adharedyus, -ubhayedyus, and -uttaredyus [are added to the word "day" (ahan) to denote various temporal relations]. 5.3.21.

"Denoting 'day' (ahani)" means the meaning of the word *ahar* ending in the locative case. He demonstrates this by saying "on the same day, *sadyaḥ*. In the same way, this should also be understood for expressions such as "denoting 'year' (*saṃvatsare*)," and so forth.

The reading is *ubhayedyuḥ* (on both days). However, it is generally read as *ubhayasminnahani* (on both days); in that case, it is stated that *ubhayamahaḥ* refers to the two-day period which has both days as its constituent parts (*avayava*).
The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a manner or kind.

A particular (*viśeṣa*) is that which differentiates a general category (*sāmānya*); it is a "manner" (*prakāra*). For example, Māṭhara and others are particulars of the general category "Brāhmaṇa. By this, he shows the following: although similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also a manner—as he will state under the rule *prakāre guṇavacanasya*: "Manner is both difference and similarity; therefore, here 'manner' is understood as similarity"—nevertheless, similarity is not taken here [in this specific context], because it is not so expressed (*anabhidhānāt*). Thus, by that manner, it is "so" (*tathā*).
But it does not occur after a word ending in the nominative—such as *sa prakārastathā* ("that manner is so")—precisely because it is not so expressed; this is the intended meaning.

Fearing that the suffix *thāl*, which is prescribed specifically for words beginning with *kiṃ* and *sarva* (and others), might exclude the suffix *jātīyar*, which is prescribed generally, he says: "Even *jātīyar*... It is true that even *jātīyar* has this very same definition, namely, "in the sense of expressing a manner (*prakāra*). How then is there no exclusion? To this he says: "But that... The meaning is that the difference [between them] arises from a difference in their respective meanings.

And having established this, they employ *thāl* in the sense of mere manner, and then apply *jātīyar* after a word ending in *thāl* to express that which possesses such a manner—as in *tathājātīyaḥ* ("of such a kind") and *yathājātīyaḥ* ("of such a kind").
And [the suffix *kim*] also [is used in this sense]. 5.3.25.
The separation of the *yoga* rule is so that the suffix *kim* may continue to apply in subsequent rules, while *idam* shall not.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting directions. 5.3.27.

The suffix *astāti* is applied after words in the seventh, fifth, and first cases when they denote direction (*dik*), place (*deśa*), or time (*kāla*). "Words for directions" (*dikśabda*) refers to a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*); that is, those words which are expressive of directions. The meaning is that those which are observed to function as expressions for directions are intended here by the term "words for directions," and not only those that directly denote the cardinal points themselves. "After those" (*tebhyaḥ*) [refers to those words].

Although words such as *pūrva* and others, when denoting direction (*diś*), are feminine in gender and end in the suffix *ṭāp*, whereas when denoting place (*deśa*) or time (*kāla*), they are base forms (*prakṛti*)—and thus there is a difference in form—nevertheless, because the suffix *ṭāp* is pleonastic (*svārthika*), there is no difference in their expressive form; therefore, there is no contradiction in the linguistic usage that those very same directional words denote place and time. As for those who maintain that there is a difference in meaning, for them the designation [of the words] as such is based on similarity. But how do directional words denote place and time? By their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).

For words such as *pūrva* (eastern) and so forth are denotative of space and time by their very nature, just as they are of direction. How is it, then, that these words, while applying to all three [space, time, and direction], are designated by means of a single direction—as in the expression "words for directions" (*diśśabdebhyaḥ*)? What is the fault in this? For this designation is made on the basis of common occurrence (*anvaya*), and not through the restrictive definition that they are "only those words which denote directions."

Now, why are [the suffixes] not designated by either "space" (deśa) or "time" (kāla)? This is an objection regarding the term *śiṃśapā*. Furthermore, there is brevity in the mention of "direction" (*diś*). Since the word "direction" is used as an illustration, the term "direction" is mentioned again; otherwise, [the rule] would apply only to those residing in space and time, and not to those residing in direction. Here, because the meanings of the case-endings beginning with the seventh (locative) and the meanings such as "direction" are similar, there might be an assignment according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). To this, he says: "In this case, assignment according to numerical order is not intended," because [the rule] lacks the svarita accent.

Regarding "purastāt" and "adhastāt": by the rule *astāti*, the words *pūrva* and *adhara* undergo the substitutions *pura-* and *adha-* respectively. [In the example] "he dwells in the eastern direction" (*aindryāṃ diśi vasati*), this word *aindrī* denotes merely a feminine entity related to Indra; however, because of its proximity to the word *diś* ("direction"), it refers to a direction and thus is not itself a directional term (*dik-śabda*). Furthermore, if the phrase "from directional terms" (*dik-śabdebhyaḥ*) were absent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the suffix would apply even to place-denoting terms like *pañcālāḥ* and time-denoting terms like *māsaḥ*.

But since this [rule] exists, the suffix occurs only from those words denoting direction (*dik*) that apply to space (*deśa*) and time (*kāla*). Why does [the author] ask, "In the case of *dik*, *deśa*, and *kāla*"? He asks this thinking: "By the inclusion of the word 'word' (*śabda*) in the rule *dikśabdebhyaḥ*, the suffix is established even for those applying to space and time—on the basis of the etymological derivation that a 'direction-word' (*dikśabda*) is a word seen to denote a direction—and thus it would be like the fifth case [in the rule] *dikśabdāñcūttarapada*. Regarding the example *pūrvasmin gurau*: here the word *pūrva* applies to the teacher (*guru*) due to his connection with the [cardinal] direction, and not to the direction itself.
The suffix *atasuc* is added after the words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*.

For what purpose is *ataḥ* stated here? Why not simply say *ataḥ* alone? To this, the following is the meaning: the letter *ca* need not be included for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), as it is already established by the accent of the suffix itself. What then is the accomplishment of the form? These two words, *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*, end in the vowel *a*. When they denote a direction and end in the suffix *dāp*, the letter *a* is [stated] so that the elision of *ṭāp* may occur by the rule *yasyeti ca*; thus, the elision of *ṭāp* is established here. How? By the rule *tasilādiṣvākṛtvasucaḥ*, which prescribes the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) due to the presence of the suffix *ka*.

But surely, when the form (*ākṛti*) is the same, there is the substitution of the masculine for that which has been spoken of as masculine; yet these two [words] belong to different forms—how so? Words such as *pūrva* and the like, when denoting direction (*diś*), are independent of other causes [of gender], whereas when denoting place (*deśa*) or time (*kāla*), they depend upon a specific arrangement (*vyavasthā*).

How then does the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) apply to words denoting directions, given that it is stated [in the rule] "when there is a restriction" (*vyavasthāyām*)? On this point, they say: although for words denoting directions, restriction is not the ground for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), yet in reality such a restriction exists; therefore, the designation indeed applies. For in the phrase "when there is a restriction," the scope (*viṣaya*) is specified, but not the ground for application.

And likewise, in the case of the word *uttarāḥ kuravaḥ*, because linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is firmly established there, even though the actual restriction (*vastuto vyavasthā*) is not taken into account by the speakers, the prohibition "provided it is not a technical name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) was formulated to prevent the application of the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-saṃjñā*). Thus, due to the difference in form (*ākṛti-bheda*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is not established in the case of suffixes such as *tasil*.

If that were the case, then by the rule "in all derivative formations (*vṛtti*) involving pronouns, there is masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*)," masculine substitution would occur—as in the example *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*—and therefore, there would be no need for the inclusion of the letter *a*. To this, he says: "The letter *a* is for the sake of specification. If it were stated simply as "*ṣaṣṭhī tasarthapratyayena*" (the genitive occurs before suffixes having the sense of *tasi*), then even when joined with *tasi* in the phrase *tato grāmād āgataḥ*, the genitive would still apply. [To prevent this, the rule specifies the locative: "The case ending of the subordinate word (*apapada*) is superseded by the case ending of the factor of action (*kāraka*)."

In that case, when there is a connection with words such as *anya* (other), as in "another than that village" (*tato grāmād anyaḥ*), would not the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occur instead of the ablative (*pañcamī*)? [Response: It will not occur in connection with *tasil* and the like, because of the principle: "When a term without an *anubandha* is mentioned, it does not include one with an *anubandha*. However, what about those suffixes without an *anubandha*, such as in "the suffix *tasi* occurs after the fifth case in connection with *prati*" (*pratiyoge pañcamyās tasiḥ*), and "with that in the same direction" (*tenaikadik*), and "also *tasi*" (*tasiśca*)? In those cases, let it not be so: for example, *arjunataḥ pratyabhimanyuḥ* ("Abhimanyu is opposite Arjuna") or *sudāmato vidyut* ("lightning is opposite Sudāman").
The elision of the suffix *añc* [occurs]. 5.3.30.

Regarding the phrase "from those ending in añc": this applies both to the simple forms and to those qualified by gender-markers. Consequently, the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is also elided. Thus, there is neither the elision of the vowel *ā* nor the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *cau*. Therefore, in *prāk*, there is the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*), and in *pratyak*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*.
Afterwards. 5.3.32.

Regarding the phrase "of *apara* there is the substitution of *paśca*": this applies to the word *apara* alone, as well as when it is qualified by a nominal stem (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*). Regarding the phrase "also when preceded by a word denoting direction" (*dikpūrvapadasya ca*): that which has a word expressing a direction as its prior member is so described. For example, *dakṣiṇapaścāt*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule "names of directions [used] in the sense of an intermediate direction" (*diṅnāmānyantarāle*), meaning "that which is between the southern and western directions. From this, the suffix *āti* is applied in the sense of "dwelling there," and *apara* undergoes the substitution of *paśca*. Regarding the phrase "also when the second member is *ardha*": this also refers to *apara*. The phrase "even without a preceding directional word" connects with "of *apara*" and "when the second member is *ardha*."
The suffix *āti* is applied after [the words] *uttara*, *adhara*, and *dakṣiṇa*. || 5.3.34 ||

The suffix *āti* occurs [after these words]. The suffix *atasuc* also occurs after *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*, and the suffix *astāti* also occurs after the word *adhara*; this is indicated by the rule "and when *astāti* follows," which prescribes the substitution of *adha-* for the word *adhara*. Here, although there is a parity between *uttara* and the others on one hand and the locative case (*saptamī*) and the others on the other, as before, there is no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Furthermore, the suffixes beginning with *astāti* are not possible after *uttara* and the others, because the word *dakṣiṇa* cannot function in the sense of time.
The suffix *enap* is optionally used after a word denoting proximity (excluding that which ends in the fifth case). 5.3.35.

Regarding the passage beginning with "not far" (*adūre ca*) and so forth: although neither a limit (*avadhi*) nor that which possesses a limit (*avadhimat*) is explicitly mentioned in the sūtra, nevertheless, words denoting direction (*dik-śabda*) function by depending upon a limit. And since a limit requires that which possesses a limit, the specific distinction is obtained through the very force of the context (*sāmarthya*). In this regard, there is no dispute concerning the dependence on a limit for space (*deśa*) and time (*kāla*), but regarding direction (*diś*), people do disagree.

Regarding the phrase *prāgaseḥ*: [this refers to] from the rule *asi-puruṣa-udharvaścaiṣām*. Regarding the phrase *divaśabdamātrāt*: by this, forms such as *pūrveṇa vasati* (he dwells to the east) and so forth also occur. However, it does not occur after a word ending in *añc*; for this is understood to be a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Or, let it occur even after a word ending in that [suffix], since *luk* will apply due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *añcerluk*. The letter *p* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*); it is not for the sake of a qualifier in the rule *enapā dvitīyā*. Let there be [the form] *enena*, because of the continued application of the rule *atasarthapratyayena*, the application of the rule *dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ* will not occur here.
The suffix *āc* is applied after the word *dakṣiṇā*.

The letter *ca* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*). Otherwise, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) would also occur in connection with that *ā*-vowel which is not an *anubandha*, as found in the forms *vākya* and *smaraṇa*. Even if it were argued that the *ā*-vowel denoting "direction" (*atasa*) is intended here due to its association (*sāhacarya*) with words ending in *añc* and with *ahi*, nevertheless, since the word *paścāt* is also prescribed (*nipātita*) as ending in *ā*, the fifth case would still occur in connection with it.

The word *paścāt* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), for in the Veda there is conformity with what is observed. [Objection: Then it is for the sake of removing doubt; for if it were stated simply as *añcūttarapadāddhiyukte*, one would have to explain the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*. [Response: The rule will be formulated as *añcūttarapadāddhyāyukte*; therefore, the purpose of the letter *ca* must be stated so that the rule *svarito vānudātte 'padādau* does not apply in the case of *tasmākṣaiṇāsī*.
And [the substitution of *ā* for *a* occurs] when followed by *āh* and *dūre*. || 5.3.37 ||
The word "and" (ca) implies "up to and including" (ācca). Otherwise, if "far" were intended to be expressed, only the specifically prescribed suffix *āhi* would apply.
And from the north as well. 5.3.38.

"Let there be the addition of *ā* and *pra*. Although *ā* is immediate [to the preceding rule], the intention is that by means of the word "and" (*ca*), there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) even with *āc*, which is separated [by other rules].

Of the words *pūrva*, *adhara*, and *avara*, the substitute *apara* is applied [in place of *avara*] when followed by the word *pur*. And for these [three], the substitute *para* is also applied [in place of *pūrva*].

The genitive case is used here because of immediate proximity (*ānantarya-yoga*). The term *asi* is a citation (*nirdeśa*) without a case-ending. The expression "of these" (*eṣām*) is for the sake of clarity; for, by virtue of their proximity, it would have been possible to understand that only the preceding [elements] and so forth are the substituends (*sthānin*).
And [the suffix] *asti* [is applied] after *astāti*. 5.3.40.
The word *astāt* ends in the seventh case; [the suffix] *asi* refers to the suffix *āti*, which is also applied after the word *adhara*.
The term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) applies to what follows. 5.3.41.

This substitution *avit* occurs. But how, when many substitutions are applicable, is it determined that this one alone should occur? Because of its specific recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). Alternatively, it should be understood that what was stated regarding the suffix *avaḥ* applies optionally (*vibhāṣā*) when *asat* follows.
The suffix *dhā* is added after a numeral in the sense of "dividing" (*vidhā*).

The word *vidhā* means "kind" (*prakāra*), and this is connected with the upcoming term "is understood" (*gṛhyate*). Although even a ball of rice (*odanapiṇḍaka*) can be denoted by the word *vidhā*, the meaning here is that only "kind" is intended. By this, [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *ekā govidhā*. This is understood from the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning). For, although one could have simply said *vidhāyām*, the fact that the word *artha* was included has this purpose: so that the word *vidhā* may be understood in its most well-known sense.

Just as the word *vidhā* is well-known in the sense of "manner" (or "kind") in expressions such as *trividha* ("threefold") and *bahuvigha* ("manifold"), it is not so in the case of *odanapiṇḍa* ("a lump of boiled rice"). Furthermore, in the Sūtra, the meaning of the word *vidhā* is "the object of distribution," which forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The same applies in the Vṛtti. And that [distribution] has action as its domain; this is obtained from the very nature of the expression. Therefore, he states the meaning as follows: "in the manner of action."

How then is it that we have expressions such as "substance is ninefold," "qualities are manifold," "the Ṛgveda has twenty-one branches," or "the Atharvaveda is ninefold"? For in all these cases, an action is understood—either "it is taught" (*upadiśyate*) or "it exists" (*bhavati*). In phrases like "he goes in two ways," one understands a distinction between sub-types of a single action of going. However, in "he eats in one way," the action is excluded by the demonstration of the unity of its mode.

In expressions such as *ekaḥ pākaḥ* ("one cooking"), however, what is intended to be expressed is the oneness of the individual instance (*vyakti*) of the cooking, and not a state of having a single mode due to the absence of internal distinctions between modes; hence there is no suffix *dhā*.
