But when that [latter] sense is intended, the suffix certainly occurs—as in *ekadhā pākaḥ* ("cooking in one way"). In expressions such as *pañca pākāḥ* ("five cookings"), distinct instances of cooking are indeed intended, and not the possession of multiple modes by a single entity. But when that [latter] sense is intended, the suffix must likewise occur there—namely, *pañcadhā pākāḥ* ("cookings in five ways").
And also in the case of a change of the subject matter. 5.3.43.

"Substance (*dravya*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," and so forth; this is because universals (*jāti*) and the like possess the quality of being loci. "Shifting" (*vicāla*) means changing—namely, making otherwise—from the root *cal* with the causative suffix (*ṇij*), followed by the suffix *ac*. Since number is present here, he says that this shifting consists in the production of another number: "its shifting is the production of another number. For example, "make one heap fivefold," which means "make it into five heaps. This rule is commenced because no distinction of manner is understood here, much less a distinction regarding the object of the action.

In that regard, even a substance (dravya) is expressed in the form of non-existence by means of a suffix ending in *dhā*, and thus possesses the nature of an indeclinable (*avyaya*); for example, "lightning from Sudāman," where the word ends in the suffix *tasa*.
After the word *eka*, the suffix *dhyamun* is optionally applied [to form ordinals].

In the case of *ekadā*, because the word is predominant [as a noun], there is an absence of the grammatical operations associated with pronouns (*sarvanāma*). An example for the sense of "changing the location" (*adhikaraṇavicāla*) is: *ekadhā rāśiṃ kuru* ("make the heap into one"). For the sense of "manner" (*vidhārtha*), it is obtained from the very context. In what context is it obtained? When the suffix *dhā* functions as a substitute (*sthānin*). For here, the mention of *dhā* is carried over from the preceding rule; and since that has already been prescribed, its status as a substitute is understood precisely because a further prescription is impossible.

[The rule] is stated so that it may apply even to that which is prescribed for the sake of exclusion (*vidhārtha*). This very purpose is why the absence of both the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) has been resorted to, since there is no such defect even when another suffix follows. But what is the reason that it would not apply to that which is prescribed for the sake of exclusion? To this he says: "For [a rule applies] only to what is immediately preceding. The sense is: "A prescription or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately contiguous."
And after the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *dhamuñ* [is applied to form ordinals].

Regarding the term *bhatidvaidhāni*: the plural number is used by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical forms). In some places, the reading is *pathi dvaidhāni*. Although a word ending in *dhamuñ* lacks gender and number, this suffix—being prescribed in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) after such a word—is nevertheless joined with gender and number due to its inherent nature; therefore, it does not possess the status of an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
And [the suffix] *edhāc* [is applied]. 5.3.46.
The separation of the yoga-rule is for the purpose of avoiding [the application of] numerical correspondence (yathāsaṃkhya).
The suffix *pāśap* is applied after a word denoting something that is merely tolerable (*yāpya*).

The word *yāpya* has two possible derivations: it is derived from the ablative case (*apādāna*) as "that from which qualities have been removed," meaning contemptible; or it is derived from the accusative case (*karman*) as "that which is to be sent away" (*yāpayitavya*), meaning one who is to be conveyed to another place, or that which is to be removed from the body, such as a disease that cannot be cured and must be palliated (*yāpya*). In this context, because of the inherent power of its denotation, the first sense is intended; thus he says: "the word *yāpya* denotes something contemptible."

In that regard, why does it not occur? The sense is that even for one who is proficient in grammar, because he is censurable due to his bad character (*duḥśīlatva*), the suffix must necessarily occur. Regarding the phrase "of which quality" (*yasya guṇasya*): a "quality" (*guṇa*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and a "substance" (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). The suffix occurs when there is censure of that [quality]. And this is obtained because of its being internal (*antaraṅgatva*). For the ground of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is proximate, since it is directly expressed by the word (*śabdavācyatvāt*). Other properties (*dharmāntara*), however, although they exist there in reality, are not touched upon by the word.

However, where the basis for the application of the suffix is not a contemptible [quality]—as in examples such as *asako devadattakaḥ* ("this Devadatta is a non-giver")—there the suffix indeed occurs based on the contempt for a quality or action associated with the primary referent. And thus, forms such as *devadattapāśaḥ* also occur when there is actual denotation.
This [suffix] was not prescribed specifically under the rule "when contempt is expressed" (*kutsite*), because that would lead to its undesired application even after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*).
The suffix *an* is applied after a word ending in the ordinal suffix *tīya*, when it denotes a part of a whole.

He says that because it is prescribed for the purpose of denoting an ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), the suffix *tīya* itself is expressed by the word "ordinal" (*pūraṇa*): "the suffix *tīya* which is an ordinal. The statement is for the sake of the accent (*svara*). This is so that, when [the suffix] denotes a part (*bhāga*), there may be an acute accent on the first syllable due to the *nit*-accent; however, there is no difference in the form itself. He says "the mention of 'ordinal' is for the sake of what follows," meaning it is not for the sake of this [present rule]. Why? To this he says: "for not... [is it not the case that] this exists—namely, "there is elision of *mukha* and *pārśva* before *tas*, as in *mukhatīyaḥ*"? To that he says: "the *tīya* in *mukhatīya* and so forth is meaningless. The meaning is that the word *tīya* in *mukhatīya* and similar forms is devoid of meaning.
Before eleven [in the sense of "more than"], the suffix *kan* is applied in non-Vedic usage. 5.3.49.

"Prior to the eleven numerals" means those numeral words which precede the word "eleven" (ekādaśa); or alternatively, it means those numeral words which apply to the objects to be numbered (saṃkhyeya) that come before the number eleven.
After the sixth and eighth case endings, the suffix *ñya* is also applied.
There is no application of correspondence by number here, because [the desired result] is already established by the preceding rule alone from either one of the two.
After the words *māna* and *paśvaṅga*, the suffixes *kan* and *luk* [are applied respectively].

"Māna" refers to gold measured by a *vrīhi* (grain of rice). "The eighth part"—of what, then, is there elision (*luk*) here? He says: "There is elision of *ña*, or of *an*. This is because the suffixes *ta* and *ya* are prescribed after the word *aṣṭan* in those two cases [the ordinal and the distributive]. Why is the mention of elision (*lugvacana*) necessary, since the optional absence of *ña* and *an* is already established by the Great Option (*mahāvibhāṣā*)? It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpanārtham*). For this indicates that in the preceding rule, *ña* and *an* are obligatory (*nitya*).
The suffix *cha* is applied after [a word ending in] *ekā* when it is accompanied by *dākṣī*. (Pāṇini 5.3.52)

Regarding the rule *ākinicaḥ kano vā*: since these two suffixes alone are prescribed by this very sūtra, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix prescribed by another sūtra in cases such as *ekadhā* and so forth; for [that other suffix] is not present here.

"Regarding the phrase 'for the purpose of excluding the word for number' (*saṃkhyāśabdanirāsārtham*): otherwise, because it is well-known [in that sense] and because of the context of numbers, only that [well-known meaning] would be understood. Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says: 'For in the case of taking that [meaning]' (*tadupādāne hi*). 'In the case of two or many' (*dvibahvoḥ*) means in the case of duality and plurality. For the number one does not exist in two or in many. However, 'being without a companion' (*asahāyatvam*) occurs even for many things by virtue of the absence of any companion distinct from themselves."

In this case, it should be stated that [the rule] *akinic-eva* applies; for when the long vowel by position (*savarṇadīrghatva*) is established, the desired result is achieved. Furthermore, the elision of *yasya* (*yasyeti lopaḥ*) will not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*. Nor is the letter *a* intended for the purpose of preventing the *avagraha*; for grammarians (who formulate rules) are not to be followed by those who compose the word-texts (*padakāras*), rather, it is the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) that must be followed by the composers of the word-texts.
The suffix *caraṭ* is applied after a word denoting time when it signifies "in the past."

Regarding the phrase "the word *bhūtapūrva*," and so forth: the word *bhūta* alone is used in the sense of "kinship," as in "this Brāhmaṇī woman is a *bhūtā*"; it is also used in the sense of "truth," as in "one who speaks the truth (*bhūtavādī*). Others maintain that here the word *bhūta* signifies "that which exists. Furthermore, the word *pūrva* is used for both "direction" and "place. Therefore, if only one of the two were employed, the intended meaning would not be understood; hence, both are included. Regarding the term *āḍhyacara*: just as the letter *c* does not receive the designation *it* in this case, so too has it been explained under the rule *cuṭū*.

It was not stated in the very rule *goṣṭhāt khañ* that [the suffix] *khañ* is used, lest there be an annulment (*bādhā*) of *caraṭ* by *khañ*, which is specifically prescribed; for the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) occurs when they are in close proximity, not when there is a difference in time.
And [the suffix] *rūpya* is used after a word ending in the sixth case. (Pāṇini 5.3.54)

Because it is prescribed for the remaining scope (*śeṣaviṣaya*) and functions to exclude what follows it, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is subordinate (*apradhāna*). On the other hand, that which is merely a related entity (*sambandhimātra*) implied by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) because it is what is to be excluded; thus, it is primary (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, since the understanding of an operation pertains to the primary element when another [element] is in proximity, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is first understood as applying to that very [primary element]. Consequently, even the mention of "having existed previously" (*bhūtapūrva*) is a qualifier of that same [primary element]; thus he says: "the prescription of the suffix is from that which ends in the genitive."

This designation contains a reason (*hetugarbha*): "because the suffix is prescribed after [a word] ending in the sixth case. "Now" (*samprati*) means that although it was previously connected only with the *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*, it is now connected in this manner. Regarding the word *vidhāne*, which ends in the locative case, and the word *samprati*, some commentators—fearing redundancy—explain the word *vidhāna* as being derived in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), referring to the rule (*sūtra*).
The suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used to express excellence (*atiśāyana*).

*Atiśayanam*, *atiśāyanam*: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Although he will state immediately below that "the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*)," nevertheless, since "irregular derivations do not necessarily override [general rules]," the form without the lengthened vowel is also justified for the sake of the meaning. Others, however, read it as *atiśayaḥ*, *atiśāyanam*; and others still hold that *atiśāyanam* means "excellence" (*prakarṣaḥ*). Regarding "excellence": although the root *śī* alone functions in the sense of sleeping, it functions in the sense of excellence when preceded by *ati*.
Through the influence of prefixes, a verbal root brings about a play of different meanings,
as in the cases of *vihāra* (wandering), *āhāra* (eating), *saṃhāra* (withdrawal), *prahāra* (striking), and *parihāra* (avoidance).
And here, excellence does not mean "superiority" (in quantity), but rather it is intended as "distinction"; for this [verb] is transitive, as in the expression "he surpasses the white."

"By way of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). This very long vowel pronunciation in this sūtra constitutes that irregular derivation. The resolution "it is a Vedic-style (*sautra*) usage" is not proposed here, because its application is accepted even outside of the sūtras. And for this very reason, the word *prakarṣa*, though concise, was not employed [in the sūtra]. Furthermore, this [word *atiśāyana*] is a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*). It is not the case that [the suffix applies] from that which occurs in the sense of "exceeding" (*atiśāyane*); for if that were so, [the suffix] would apply only to words such as *atiśaya* and *prakarṣa*.

Nor is it the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), for if that were the case, one would have to say *āḍhyasyātiśayanam* (the surpassing of the rich) rather than *āḍhyatamam*. In the expression *āḍhyasya*, the genitive case is used either in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the agent (*kartṛ*); in either case, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the form *āḍhyatamo devadattaḥ*. Nor is it a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix itself, because no other meaning of the suffix has been specified. Nor is it a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*) alone, [as the rule states] "from a nominal stem ending in a feminine suffix or a consonant (*ṅy-āp-prātipadika*) which is qualified by the sense of surpassing."

It is logical that the excellence manifested by the suffix should qualify the very meaning denoted by the base (prakṛti), which is the primary element; it does not, however, qualify the word itself, which is subordinate with respect to the expression of the meaning. But when the word is not subordinate, then there indeed occurs a connection with excellence—as in "a higher sound" (uccataraḥ śabdaḥ) or "a lower sound" (nīcataraḥ śabdaḥ).

[Objection: But surely this could be like "white" and so forth; for example, in the expression "a whiter cloth," the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of whiteness—which is itself a quality (*guṇa*)—is the cause of the excellence of the substance (*dravya*). Why should it not be the same in the case of sound? [Response: This is an unequal comparison; the excellence of whiteness is the cause of the excellence of the substance, but such is not the case with sound.

For qualities such as whiteness are inherent in substances; it is logical that they, being themselves intensified, cause [the substance] to be intensified. But sound is not like that—how then could a substance be intensified by the intensification of that [sound]? [The rule states] "from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*). This is an elliptical expression for the base (*prakṛti*); however, the suffix is added after that which ends in a case-ending (*subanta*). For it has been said: "In cases of affection, censure, and so forth, that [suffix] proceeds from that which ends in a case-ending. Furthermore, the prescription of the non-elision (*aluk*) in the rule "in the presence of *gha*, *kāla*, and *tana*, [the elision of the case-ending] of a word denoting time" is likewise justified in this way. [The term] "its own meaning" (*svārtha*) refers to...

If this is so, then since "kumāritamā" denotes an age that is not distinct from childhood, would the suffix *ṅīp* not apply by the rule "vayasi prathame"? [Response: Since the feminine gender of the meaning qualified by age is already expressed by the *ṅīp* produced from the word *kumāra*, the suffix *ṅīp* will not occur; however, from the form ending in *tara*, the suffix *ṭāp* will occur to manifest the feminine gender alone. For if *kumāritama* were uttered, another gender would be understood, just as in the case of *kuṭīraḥ* or *śamīraḥ*.

Alternatively, here the term *prājña* is not intended to have an entirely literal (*atyantasvārthika*) sense—such as in the case of *prajña* itself being *prājña*, or *yāva* being *yāvaka*—but rather, because the quality [of whiteness] exists to some degree in what is slightly white and to a greater degree in what is whiter, the word *śukla* (white) is rightly applied there; however, this is not the case in instances such as *aupagava*. It is by this much alone that the expression "having a literal sense" (*svārthikatva*) is employed.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, in this application, the ground for the application of the word *śukla* is the excellence itself, whereas for the form ending in *tamap*, it is the excellence residing in that [excellence]. Thus, how could there even be the possibility of the suffix *ṅīp* here? This is what was stated: "For suffixes added in their own meaning (*svārthika*), that which qualifies the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) becomes the indicated (*dyotya*)."

In this case as well, although many qualities (*guṇa*) exist in that substance (*dravya*), nevertheless, the application of a word to a substance occurs because of a particular quality; the cognition [of excellence] is based on the preeminence of that [quality] due to its proximity. For example: from words such as *śukla* ("white"), there is a cognition of the preeminence of a quality; from words such as *pācaka* ("cook"), there is a cognition of the preeminence of an action (*kriyā*); and from properties such as "carrying" or "milking," there is a cognition of their preeminence.

For example: "This is a cow, which draws a cart"; "This is a bull, which draws both a cart and a plow"; "This is a cow that gives birth every year"; "This is a bull that gives birth every year to a female calf"; "This is a horse that travels four yojanas"; "This is a mule that travels eight [yojanas]. By this, the terms for number (*saṃkhyā*), measure (*parimāṇa*), weight (*pramāṇa*), and capacity (*unmāna*) are explained.

For excellence does not belong to a substance inherently, as in the cases of "more than two," "more than a *prastha*," "more than a *vitasti*," or "having more beautiful wings. In every respect, the excellence of a substance is mediated by its qualities (*dharma*), not inherent; just as a cloth is designated as "white" due to its connection with the quality of whiteness, so too is the designation of excellence [derived from that]. The meaning is that it arises precisely from the excellence of those [qualities].
And it has been said:
"The quality which is attributed to a substance that is itself indefinable..."
"The differentiator is for the sake of designation; its excellence is what is expressed.

Regarding the term "indesignable" (*avyapadeśyasya*), the meaning is that it is impossible to designate by way of its own nature in the absence of a connection with attributes (*dharma*). Thus, it is established that the word *atiśāyana* functions as an action-noun (*bhāvasādhana*), serves as a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), and the suffix is *svārthika* (having its own meaning). For this very reason, the gender and number follow those of the base.

If, however, it were a *kartṛ-sādhana* (denoting the agent), then, if it were the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it would apply only to things such as "exceeding" (*atiśāyana*), "that which exceeds" (*atiśāyaka*), or "the one who exceeds" (*atiśayitr*); even in that case, it would not apply to the excellence of the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) within its own sense. If, on the other hand, it were the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), then the case-ending required by the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) would be obtained. And if that [suffix] were analyzed with a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*), then the second case would be used—as in "it exceeds the white," i.e., *śuklataraḥ*.

Now, if [the word] *atiśāyana* is taken as having a *kṛt*-suffix ending (*kṛdanta*), then the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply—[resulting in] *śuklasyātiśāyanaḥ* (the excelling of white) or *śuklataraḥ*. Likewise, it would follow that *kālaḥ* (black) "excels" *kālīm* (a black woman), resulting in *kālītaraḥ*, and that *kālī* "excels" *kālam* (a black man), resulting in *kālātaraḥ*. Furthermore, in this case, *gārgyaḥ* (a descendant of Garga) "excels" the *gargān* (Gargas), resulting in *gargātaraḥ*, and likewise, the *gargāḥ* (Gargas) "excel" *gārgyam* (a descendant of Garga), resulting in *gārgyātaraḥ*.

Now, suppose it is derived as an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*). Even in that case, if it refers to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*), the suffix would apply only to words like *śauklya* (whiteness) which denote the quality by which one exceeds another; for it is by means of whiteness (*śauklyena*) that a white thing exceeds another white thing. However, if it refers to the meaning of the suffix, then from a word such as *śukla* (white), the suffix would apply to the quality in the sense of "excelling," and there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substratum of the quality—such as in the expression *śuklataraḥ paṭaḥ* ("a whiter cloth"). Furthermore, if it were formed with the suffix *vyat* followed by the agentive suffix *lyuṭ*—meaning "that which causes to excel" (*atiśāyayatīti atiśāyan*)—even so, the same fault remains as in the case of the instrument.

For qualities indeed impel the possessor of qualities [with the thought]: "By us, being preeminent, you shall surpass those of your own kind. Consequently, whatever fault arises when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) after a verbal root, that very same fault occurs here as well. Alternatively, if the root *śī* is taken in the sense of "lying down" (as in *pakvāśaya*, "receptacle of digested food," or *jalāśaya*, "reservoir of water"), then the meaning would be: "The qualities lie down—that is, they abide—in the possessor of qualities; he causes the qualities to excel, that is, he causes them to abide with excellence within himself. And in that case, the very same fault occurs as when *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*) after a different verbal root.
Furthermore, the word *atiśāyana* would not be established as having a nominal suffix (*prakṛtyanta*). Therefore, the meaning demonstrated by the author of the Vṛtti alone is logical.

Regarding *paṭiṣṭha*: by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu*, there is the elision (*ṭilopa*) of the suffix *ṭi*. Regarding *gariṣṭha*: by the rule *priyasthira* etc., the word *guru* undergoes the substitution *gara*.

To one who thinks that "another suffix of excellence (*prakarṣa*) cannot follow a suffix of excellence, because excellence has already been expressed by the first," [the author] says in response: "And when... (*yadā ca*). Regarding *ātiśāyikāntāt*: that which arises in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*) is *ātiśāyika*; the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *adhyātmādi*, and both members of the compound undergo *vṛddhi* according to the rule *anuśatikādi*. Thus, *śreṣṭhatama-ārya*.

Regarding the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ*: the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed here for that excellence which exists in relation to a counterpart lacking excellence; whereas the suffix *tamap* applies to that excellence which is manifested by the suffix *iṣṭhan* in relation to a counterpart possessing excellence. Thus, there is no tautology. Furthermore, because two distinct suffixes are being prescribed, these constitute two separate rules: in the first, *iṣṭhan* is applied, and in the other, *tamap* is applied after a stem ending in *iṣṭhan*.

Therefore, this should not be objected to: just as a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) cannot follow another present participle suffix because the original verbal root is absent at the time of that subsequent formation, so too there ought not to be another suffix of excellence following a suffix of excellence.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is established that no further suffix of excellence can follow another suffix of excellence. How so? First, there is no possibility of a further suffix following one ending in *tarap*—for the possibility is indeed suspected only in a case where, among three things, one is white, the second is somewhat more excellent, and the third is most excellent; in such a case, the excellence of the second, though present, is rendered ineffective in the presence of the third, just as the status of a minister is nullified in the presence of a king.

First of all, [the suffix] *tarap* does not occur after a second [item]. Nor does it occur after a third, because in that very same usage, since all three are being considered, there is an absence of a dual-numbered subordinate term (*upapada*). By this, the suffix *īyasun* is also explained. Furthermore, there is no possibility of another [suffix] occurring after a word ending in *tamap*. For the possibility of such an occurrence is indeed suspected only in a case where, among four items, two are white, the third is slightly superior, and the fourth is extremely so.

In that regard, although the third [suffix] possesses excellence (*utkṛṣṭatva*), it is, as before, ineffective in the presence of the fourth; rather, it becomes subordinate (*tama*) to the fourth. By this, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is explained.

How then is the expression "for the most excellent action" (*śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe*) to be understood? Because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), the suffix *tamap* should be seen as having its own meaning (*svārthika*). As for the statement "Yudhiṣṭhira is the most excellent of the Kurus," however, he considers that to be merely figurative (*aupacārika*).
And [the suffixes] tiṅ. 5.3.56.
Regarding the form *pacatitamām*: the suffix *ām* is applied by the rule *kimettiṅavyayaghād ām* and so forth.

This is because its application is restricted to words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*). For this very reason, it was stated even at the time of explaining the meaning of the sūtra that the suffix *tamap* occurs [in such cases]. Nor can the restriction be set aside by the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*), since the continued application remains valid even when the suffix *tamap* is prescribed.
The suffixes *tarap* and *īyasun* are added [to a word] when it is accompanied by a dual case form or by the word *vibhakti*.

"The term *dvivacana* means 'the expression of two meanings' (*dvayor arthayoḥ vacanam*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), and there is a compound with the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). The meaning is: that word by which two meanings are expressed is *dvivacana*. By this, he shows that what is being taken here is the etymological (*anvartha*) *dvivacana*, not the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) one. For if the technical one were taken, [the rule] would not apply in a case such as "Between us and Devadatta, Devadatta is more handsome."

However, this occurs when the term is taken according to its literal meaning (*anvarthagrahaṇa*); for instance, by the word *asmākam*, one meaning is expressed, because by the rule *asmado dvayośca*, the plural number is prescribed for the singular meaning [of "we"]; and by the phrase *devadattasya ca*, a second meaning is expressed. Thus, how could this be non-literal? [The answer is: the dual is the *upapada*. It is that which is to be divided—that is, to be separated—and it is that which is being surpassed. For it is that [dual] which has the status of *upapada*, not the surpasser, because the suffix is prescribed after the latter.

Another says: the suffix is prescribed because of the qualifier *atiśayitr* (that which surpasses) following words such as *ādya*, but not because of the surpasser itself, such as *mādhura*. Thus, its status as an *upapada* (governing word) is not contradictory. Furthermore, its separate mention is no different [from others]. The form *yad* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*); it is an exception to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*. Consequently, the form *vibhāgyam* does not occur at all. As for the word *vibhājya*, which is employed in the legal codes (*smṛtis*), its grammatical correctness is to be considered [as derived from a different source]. And [the rule applies] when the two-syllable word *vibhajya* is the *upapada*.

In the Sūtra, however, *dvivacana* (dual) and *vibhajya* (separable) form the compound *dvivacanavibhajyam*; since this is both that [term] and a subordinate word (*upapada*), the locative case is used based on a *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, *upapada* is etymologically defined as "a word uttered near [another]" (*upa-uccāritaṃ padam upapadam*). And that [subordinate word] is employed only in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*); in the formal derivative (*vṛtti*), it is not necessarily used because its meaning is already conveyed. Thus, the mention of *upapada* is for the sake of clarity.

In this context, there are two subordinate words (*upapada*) and two bases (*prakṛti*)—namely, *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* and *tiṅśca*—and there are likewise only two suffixes; consequently, would there not be the undesirable consequence of a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*)? To this he says: "according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). This is merely a desired rule (*iṣṭi*). "Of these two" (*anayor*): here the word *anayoḥ* has a dual sense as the subordinate word (*upapada*). "Paṭīyān": as before, there is the elision of *ṭi*; since it does not end in *it*, there is the insertion of *num*; by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*, there is lengthening; and finally, the elisions of the final consonant (*hal*) and the *ṅy-ādi* suffixes due to their being a *saṃyoga*.

"Madhurā," and so forth. What, then, is being distinguished here? He says: "The people of Pāṭaliputra. And thus, in that case, the ablative case occurs by the rule "the fifth [case-ending] when there is distinction" (*pañcamī vibhakte*). Although here too there is a twofold meaning with respect to the two groups—the group of the Madhurans being one and the group of the Pāṭaliputrakas being another—nevertheless, this is not what is expressed by the word; rather, it is the very difference between the parts. For this reason, the plural number is used.

And here, in the statement "The people of Mādhurā are more handsome than those of Pāṭaliputra and Sāṃkāśyaka," there is no dual meaning even with respect to the two groups. Therefore, the mention of the *upapada* (the word in composition) was made separately. In this case—"The teeth of Dantoṣṭha are smoother, and the hands of Pāṇipāda are softer"—the suffix *tarap* would not apply. What is the reason? Because the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is a single entity.

Furthermore, the suffix does not have as its basis the individual items that constitute the subordinate members (*guṇabhūta-varttipadārtha*), because they are many—such as "thirty-two teeth" or "two lips. Regarding this, they say: the constituent words (*varttipada*) assume the number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) within the composite (*vṛtti*); and thus, through the abandonment of distinction and the assumption of the number of non-dual unity, the suffix has as its basis the two meanings characterized by such teeth and lips. However, in a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*), because there exists a distinction between the meanings of the individual members, there is no duality [of meaning in the sense of a single integrated whole], and therefore the suffix *-tarap* does not occur.

In the case of "plakṣanyagrodhānāṃ plakṣā dīrghatamāḥ" (among *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees, the *plakṣas* are the tallest), it does not even depend on a subordinate term (*upapada*) for its analysis. Why? Because excellence (*prakarpa*) depends upon a correlative (*pratiyogin*). Since the distinction is obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), the mention of a subordinate term in the analysis is for the sake of restriction—meaning that only where the distinction is explicitly conveyed by the word [is this rule applied]. Here, however, the mention of the basis of selection (*nirdhāraṇāśraya*) is common to both the basis and the thing being selected; thus, it is not merely a distinction alone, but also includes non-distinction.

By this, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) as prescribed by the rule "the fifth [case-ending] in the sense of distinction" (*pañcamī vibhakte*) is explained. Here, in the example "He was clever last year, but he is even more clever this year," although there is only one substratum (*dharmin*), a distinction is superimposed due to the difference in qualities; thus, there is a degree of excellence (*prakarpa*) relative to a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and the suffix is based upon that. And it is said: "You have become quite another person," and "Are you truly that same Dhanañjaya?"
The suffixes *aC* and others [beginning with vowels] are applied only after words expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? It is so that a restriction (*niyama*) may be understood. Otherwise, since the suffixes *añ* and *ādi* are prescribed for excellence (*prakarpa*), they would apply even in the absence of excellence. [Objection: The term "in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane*) will carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, its repetition here must be for the sake of restriction. What need is there for the particle *eva*? To this he replies: "The particle *eva* is used for the purpose of restricting [the application] according to one's intention. For if this were absent, a contrary restriction might also be possible: namely, that the suffixes *añ* and *ādi* are applied only after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*).

What is the fault here? The suffixes *vyañ* and *añ* would not apply after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*); for those two [suffixes] are restricted to words beginning with *aj* and so forth. Since the restriction applies to that which follows the particle *eva*, while the restriction does not apply to words beginning with *aj* and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of those two suffixes applying even after a word denoting a quality.

This is being made far too complex—stating that "aj-ādi [suffixes] follow only from words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanāt*). Rather, it should be stated thus: the suffix *tamap* is used for expressing excellence (*atiśāyane*); *iṣṭhan* follows from words denoting qualities; *iyasun* is used when there is a dual number or a distributive sense as an accompanying word (*dvivacanavibhajyopapade*); and *tarap* also follows from words denoting qualities. Thus, the requirement "from words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanāt*) would be removed [from the rule for *aj-ādi*]. This is not so; however, the term "aj-ādi" was stated for the sake of rules such as "the substitute *śra-* is used for *praśasya*" (*praśasyasya śraḥ*).

If that is so, then let it simply be "praśasyasya śra ajādyaḥ"; for even in this way, the particle *eva* need not be stated. Even in your position, the particle *ca* is added in the rule "tarap ca," and thus the situation remains the same.
The suffix *tu* is used in the Vedic language [after a verbal root ending in a vowel].

"By the preceding [rule]," and so forth. The meaning is that by setting aside the restriction (*niyama*), there is merely the permission (*anujñāna*) for another base (*prakṛti*), and not an entirely new injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*); therefore, there is no confusion of grammatical conditions (*upādhi-saṅkara*). In *kariṣṭha*: the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied after the word *kartṛ*, which ends in the suffix *tṛn*. For this very reason, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*). Alternatively, let it be derived from the word ending in *tṛc*; however, the second case ending should be understood as in the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"). In *dohīyasī*: the suffix is applied to the word *dogdhrī* by means of the rule regarding words qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*).

In the case of a taddhita suffix following a word ending in *bhas*, there is the removal of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by virtue of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). Alternatively, according to the rule "and [the base form] is established when a suffix is prescribed," once *ṅīp* has been removed, the suffix is added directly to the word *dogdhṛ*. Thereafter, when the *tṛc* suffix is removed by the rule "the *tṛ* is elided before the superlative suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun*," there is also the removal of the *ghatva* and *jaśtva* substitutions due to the absence of their cause.
The suffix *śra* is applied after a word denoting that which is praiseworthy.

"Following the two affixes beginning with *ac* (*ajādī*). Now, one might object: "But *ajādī* is introduced as a nominative form; it is not in the locative case. Therefore, how is this meaning obtained? To this he says: "Of the introduced [term] *ajādī*, etc. The case-ending of the introduced term, which is nominative, is transformed into the form of the locative; that is to say, it is inferred.

"If that is so," and so forth. Now, why does this substitution not occur only after those two suffixes which are possible—namely *tarap* and *tamap*? It cannot be thus, because of the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "beginning with a vowel" (*ajādī*). Now, why is it not understood that the rule for the vowels applies right here—that after the word *praśasya*, the suffixes beginning with a vowel occur, and *śra* is its substitute? In that case, this further advantage would follow: there would be no need to change the case of the words. This, however, is not possible.

For [if it were not so], the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* would indeed occur, and the specifically prescribed suffixes beginning with *a* (such as *aC*) would sublate them; furthermore, there would be a confusion of conditions (*upādhi*), such that *īyasun* would apply in the domain of *iṣṭhan*, and *iṣṭhan* in the domain of that [suffix]. Regarding the phrase "in its domain" (*tadviṣaye*): that which has the word *praśasya* as its domain is "its domain. In the reading where the locative case ending is used, however, the meaning is that "that very [word] is the domain therein. As for the statement "the restrictive rule does not operate": the meaning is that the status of being a suffix beginning with *a* is indicated by way of making known the non-operation of the restriction, but not directly.

Otherwise, however, there would be both the sublation of the rules regarding *ajādi* (words beginning with vowels) and a confusion of grammatical conditions (*upādhi*). Since the rules for *ajādi* are taught by the very system of our own grammar in the manner already stated, neither of these two defects occurs. But how can one resort to a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) when the connection [of the case-ending] is possible as it stands in the text? Listen: if the injunction for *ajādi* were intended, it would have been indicated by the ablative case. Furthermore, the particle *ca* (and) would also have been employed for the purpose of conjoining them in this way.

Regarding the expression "ṭilopa-yasyetilopau": the term "yasyetilopaḥ" is a compound formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, meaning "the elision [of the suffix] by means of the word 'yasya'. Since this is a formal imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the case-ending is not elided, as in the case of *asyavāmīyam* and similar forms. Furthermore, the rule *ādguṇaḥ* (which prescribes guṇa substitution for *a* followed by *ā*) is not prohibited here because the preceding element is not part of the same grammatical unit (*anaṅgatvāt*).
And [the suffix] *jya* [is applied after the same stems]. 5.3.61.

The separation of the *yogavibhāga* is so that, in what follows, only the substitution of *jya* may occur, and not the [other] substitute. In the expression "the best of these two" (*ayamanayoḥ*), it is expected through the transformation [of the compound] as "the most praiseworthy," and not because it forms a single textual unit with what follows. This is the case everywhere.
And [the suffix *kan* is added] after the word *vṛddha*. (Pāṇini 5.3.62)

He states that there is the apprehension of the word's own form (*svarūpa*), and not of the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) term defined as "that [word] whose first vowel among its *ac* vowels is *vṛddhi*," by saying "of the word *vṛddha*. In this matter, the commentary itself is the sole refuge. Regarding the phrase "of those two" and so forth: that which was previously stated—"the same should be understood for the subsequent rules as well"—is precisely what is being recalled here.

By virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), that [suffix] also occurs in the sense of "excellent" (*pakṣe*). Now, one might object: would not *imanij* then find its scope of application in the word *varṣā* (rainy season)? No; because the suffix *imanij* does not occur after the word *vṛddha*. If this is the case, then the substitution of *varṣin* for *vṛddha* should have been stated right here—as in "for *vṛddha*, there is *varṣin*"—so that the mention of *vṛddha* need not be repeated twice. True; however, it was simply not done in that way. Another says: the existence of *imanij* is also postulated after the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*; therefore, *varṣiman* also occurs.

In his view—since the substitution of *varṣa* has already fulfilled its purpose through the suffix *imanij*, the substitution of *jya* would necessarily apply to both *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* by this very rule. Therefore, the word "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) from the rule "the substitution of *kan* optionally occurs for *yuvan* and *alpa*" is understood here; thus, when the substitution of *jya* is not applied, the substitution of *varṣa* takes place in that alternative case.
The substitutes *nedas* and *ādha* are used for *antika* and *bāḍha*, respectively.

It is considered here that a correspondence between the two signs (*nimitta*) according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended. This is because, since the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* are understood from the context of the rule "ajādyoḥ," and since these two are taught in a specific sequence, they are perceived as retaining that very order; thus, one might think that a correspondence according to sequence would necessarily follow. Why, then, does this desired correspondence not occur? Because it is possible for them to occur in the reverse order as well.

For instance—when there is an expectation as to "of which two [suffixes], ajādi and so forth?", first, by virtue of proximity (*ānantarya*), the suffix *īyasun* is understood; however, because of the requirement of the dual number, the sequence "even though *iṣṭhan*" is also possible. Thus, since neither of these two sequences can be definitively determined, it is proper not to rely upon either of them at all.
The substitute *kan* may optionally be used for the words *yuvan* and *alpa*.

The term *yuvan* here does not refer to the specific designation of "youth," but rather to the word-form itself; this is because of its association with the word *alpa* (small) and because of the [authoritative] commentary. The inclusion of the option (*anyatarasyām*) is for the sake of the meaning of the word *alpa*. As for the word *yuvan*, however, the option is already established by the rule *sthūladūrayuvahrasvakṣiprakṣudrāṇāṃ yaṇādiparam* (Pāṇini 6.4.156). Regarding *yaviṣṭha*: by the aforementioned rule *sthūladūra-*, the *yaṇ*-class vowels and subsequent sounds are elided, and the preceding vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution. Regarding *kanīyān*: depending on the context and other factors, one determines whether it refers to "youth" or "smallness.

Due to the status of being a *prakṛtibhāva* (original form retention) according to the rule *prakṛtyaikāc*, there is no elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*), nor does the elision of *an* (*allopo'naḥ*) occur.
The *luk* elision of the suffixes *matup* and *vin* [occurs after a word ending in] *m*.

The genitive dual *vin-mat-oh* is a compound of the two suffixes *vin* and *matup*, which have been designated as having "dropped indicatory marks" (*utsṛṣṭānubandha*). Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of *vin*? For even without it, since *matup* also occurs after those same bases after which *vin* occurs, its elision (*luk*) would result in forms such as *srajiṣṭha* being established; nor is there any possibility of hearing the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* [in place of *vin*], because those two do not occur after a base ending in *vin*. Indeed, it is precisely from this statement regarding elision that it is indicated that those two suffixes do occur after a base ending in *vin*.

When, however, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to a word ending in *vin*, according to the rule "one who does that [which is denoted by the base] takes *ṇic*," then the statement that there is elision (*luk*) of *vin* is for the purpose that the suffix *vin* itself should not be heard; for example, one says *srajayati* when meaning "he describes one who possesses a garland" (*sragviṇam ācaṣṭe*).
The suffix *rūpaP* is used in the sense of praise. (Pāṇini 5.3.66)

And this [term *praśasta*] is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). If it were the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), then for the word *vaiyākaraṇa*, the form *vaiyākaraṇarūpa* would result as a praise; consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "Devadatta is of the form of a grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇarūpo devadattaḥ*). Therefore, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the base—[meaning] "from those qualified by praise. Furthermore, that which is praised is [the object], not the praiser; for [otherwise] there would be no linguistic usage (*anabhidhāna*). [The term] "its own meaning" (*svārtha*) refers to this.

If this is so, then in the case of *kumārīrūpā*, since the age is not distinct [from that of a maiden], would the suffix *ṅīp* not apply? This is not a fault. Because the femininity residing in the meaning qualified by age has already been indicated by the *ṅīp* produced from the word *kumārī*, the suffix *ṭāp* alone is employed for the form ending in *rūpa* to manifest mere femininity. Nor is it the case that this [femininity] has already been manifested by *ṅīp* alone, such that there would be no occasion for *ṭāp*. For if one were to say *kumārīrūpaḥ*, another gender would be understood, as in the case of *kuṭīra* and similar forms.

Alternatively, there is no occasion for the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* because of the difference in the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the two terms: the word *kumāra* has "age" as its ground, whereas for *rūpavat*, it is the praise pertaining to that [age]. Thus he says, "and those which have their own meaning," and so forth. Here too, this suffix occurs when there is praise of the ground for the application; therefore, in the case of one who is unskilled in grammar but praised for his lineage, character, and so on, the form *vaiyākaraṇarūpa* does not occur.
However, in some cases, it also occurs when there is praise of a quality associated with the object—for example, "this is a 'cow-form' (gorūpa) person, since he draws [the cart] well."

Now, how is it that a suffix [denoting excellence] arises from words such as *vṛṣala* (outcaste), since at that time they are expressions of censure, because their referents—like crows and the like—are of an inferior nature? To this he says: "of the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthasya*). "Distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) means fullness; when that exists, praise occurs. Thus, even words such as *vṛṣala*, when their own referent is complete, function toward a referent qualified by praise. The sense is that the suffix is therefore established even from those words.

Regarding the phrase "in the form of a *vṛṣala*": although this word denotes a caste (*jāti*), and a caste neither becomes deficient nor complete, nevertheless, deficiency and completeness should be understood here as referring to the smallness or largeness of the qualities associated with it, in relation to one another. Alternatively, since the word functions with respect to a collection of qualities, both of these [deficiency and completeness] belong to the referent of the word itself. In the expression "he who [eats] with an onion," the third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*).

A certain *vṛṣala* eats *palāṇḍu*; another drinks *surā*; but he who does both possesses the full status of a *vṛṣala*. Likewise, the meaning of the word "thief" (*cora*) reaches its fulfillment through the theft of a well-guarded object. [The phrase] "he should remove the collyrium from the eyes" uses the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of possibility; the meaning is that such a form of theft is possible for him.

"Whether collyrium is applied to the eyes or not, let it be; even so, when [the term] 'vṛṣalarūpa' (having the form of a low-born man) and the like are employed to express censure, it still does not succeed. For in that case, there is indeed censure because of the specific quality (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*). Therefore, instead of including the mention of 'praise' (*praśaṃsā*), one should simply include the mention of 'specific quality. As it has been said: 'But it is established by the statement of the specific quality of the meaning of the base word.'"

The author of the Vṛtti, however, maintains that in expressions such as "this man is like a thief," praise alone is the literal meaning of the word, while the perception of censure is based on the sentence. Furthermore, it is observed that even those [words] intended for praise can have the sense of censure; for example, in the case of the term "Rākṣasa" (demon), when used in a statement praising an excellence of prowess, praise is understood, but when used to demonstrate cruelty, censure is understood.

[One might ask: "Why is there no occurrence of the dual or plural [endings] in *pacatorūpam* or *pacantirūpam*, given that suffixes added in the sense of the base (*svārthika*) follow the gender and number of the base? To this he replies: "The verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning. Although a verb possesses multiple meanings—consisting of the action, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), person (*puruṣa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), time (*kāla*), and voice (*upagraha*)—nevertheless, among these, action alone is its predominant meaning.

How is this known? When asked about an action, one answers with a verbal form (tiṅanta): "What does Devadatta do?"—"He cooks. But surely, when asked about a substance as well, one also answers with a verbal form, as in: "Who among these is Devadatta?"—"The one who cooks. This is correct here because, by means of the other word *yaḥ* ("who"), the action is brought to a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) for the purpose of indicating the substance. For this very reason, there is no answer consisting of a finite verb alone; for it is not the case that one could say, "Who is Devadatta?"—"He cooks."

Therefore, a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning; and the primacy of action is said to be in relation to the meanings expressed by the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). However, in cases such as "he threshes the rice" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), threshing and the like have subordination in relation to the rice, precisely because they serve the purpose of preparing the substance. Another says: even here, threshing and the like possess formal primacy (*śābdam prādhānyam*) because they are that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); but the rice and so forth do not, because they are the means (*sādhana*). Their primacy, however, is functional (*ārtham*).

And there is only one action: "In all verbal expressions, action is understood as that from which distinctions have ceased. How then do the dual and plural numbers occur—as in *pacataḥ* (they two cook) and *pacanti* (they cook)? These dual and plural endings are not dependent on a distinction in the action; rather, what then? They are dependent on a distinction in the means (*sādhana*). For this very reason, in cases such as *bhavadbhir āsyate* ("you are being sat by"), where only the action is expressed, there is an absence of the dual and plural numbers. Nor is a distinction in the agent pervaded by a distinction in the action.

Since we observe expressions such as "you all are cooking" (*bhavantaḥ pacanti*) and "it is being cooked by you all" (*bhavadbhiḥ pacyate*), even when many people are performing a single specific act of cooking directed toward a single result, it is established that the action denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is one and the same. Consequently, dual and plural endings do not occur after a word ending in the *rūpam* suffix.

Now, just as dual and plural endings occur after finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) based on the distinction of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), why do they not occur after words ending in nominal suffixes (*rūpabant*) as well? This has already been answered: "The verb (*ākhyāta*) is primarily concerned with action (*kriyā*). For when a suffix is added in a sense identical to the base (*svārthika*), the gender and number are obtained from the base itself; and in that case, the action is the predominant factor, and it is singular. Therefore, in accordance with the meaning of the base which is the predominant factor, the resulting number is necessarily the singular.

In expressions such as *pacatirūpam* ("the form of cooking"), the number of the agent is expressed [by the suffix]; however, by means of the nominal suffix (*sup*), the singularity of the action is expressed. Alternatively, because it has already been stated by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the dual and plural will not occur after a word ending in the suffix *rūpa*; but the singular will occur, because it is the default rule—as it is said: "The singular shall be made the general rule. And this has been explained in various places.

If, then, the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action (*kriyā*) as its primary meaning, there would also be no neuter gender for the word *rūpavat*, because action, being non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), lacks gender. To this he says: "But the neuter gender... Now, what is the distinction between the scope of the superlative suffixes (*tamap* etc. and the word *rūpa*, since even excellence (*atiśāyana*) can be the object of praise or censure—as in *paṭutamaḥ* ("most clever") and *pāpīyān* ("more wicked")?

Is the cognition of form (*rūpapratyaya*) also directed toward both [the object and its quality], such as "a sharp form" or "a thief-form"? It is said: excellence (*atiśāyana*) depends upon a correlate possessing a similar quality, whereas distinctness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is independent of that; thus, the difference in their objects is indeed clear.
The suffixes *kalpa*, *adeśya*, and *deśīya* are used after a word when there is slight incompleteness [of the quality expressed by that word]. Pāṇini 5.3.67.

"Completeness" (*sampūrṇatā*) means the fullness of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). By the word "referent of the base" (*padārtha*), the ultimate point of resolution (*paryavasānabhūmi*) is intended. And this [completeness] is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), not of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). If it were so [i.e., a qualifier of the suffix], then in the case of "a grape that is slightly incomplete as compared to molasses" (*guḍasya īṣadasamāptiḥ drākṣāyāḥ guḍakalpā drākṣāyāḥ*), there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substance [grape] in the form "a grape that is like molasses" (*guḍakalpā drākṣā*); furthermore, there would have to be only the singular number, whereas it is desired that the gender and number should be like those of the expressed object.

Therefore, it is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Regarding the term "its own meaning" (*svārthe*): even in the case of *kumārikalpā*, there is no contingency for the suffix *ṅīp* because "age" (*vayas*) is not something additional [to the base]; for "being nearly [an age]" (*kalpa*) is not the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word [to the age], but rather it is the slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*) residing in that [age]. For example: one who is slightly incomplete in skill is *paṭukalpaḥ*, or *mṛdukalpaḥ*.

But surely, when an object is fully known as being of such-and-such a magnitude, it must either be complete or incomplete; however, the quality of proficiency (pāṭava) is not definitively known to have such a fixed magnitude, for proficiency can indeed exist in varying degrees. So how can there be even a slight incompleteness in this case? By this, words denoting universals (jātiśabda) are explained; for they do not express an object of a determined measure. However, these are appropriate examples to cite: *kṛtakalpa* ("almost done") and *bhuktakalpa* ("almost eaten").

For the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is a collection of operations delimited by a result, and its extent has already been stated. Now, one might object: "In this case as well, the suffix *kta* denotes the past; and when the result is accomplished, the meaning of the root becomes past. How, then, can there be 'incomplete' (*īṣadasamāpta*) status for that which is past? To this we reply: When the suffix *kta* in the past tense refers to the completion of a single part of the action, then [the following] is the example: "a garment almost finished" (*kṛtakalpaṃ vastram*). And thus, usages such as *kṛta-* and others are observed to refer to the performance of only a portion [of the whole action].

When the suffix *kta* occurs in the future tense because an action that is slightly incomplete in the future is being wished for—according to the rule "in the sense of wishing (*āśaṃsā*), it is treated as past"—then this too serves as an example. Likewise, according to the rules "from roots ending in long *ī*, *ktā*" and "also from roots meaning 'intellection,' 'cognition,' or 'reverence,'" the suffix is appropriately applied even when the *kta* refers to the present time—as in *pūjitakalpam* ("almost revered") and *jātakalpam* ("almost born").

Likewise, there is also an example involving a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) that pertains to the three times: *pacatikalpam* (he cooks somewhat), *pakṣyatikalpam* (he will cook somewhat), and *apākṣītkalpam* (he cooked somewhat). However, [the objection that] it is improper for it to be called "expressive of a quality" (*guṇavacana*) is not correct. That too is appropriate; for has it not been stated that even the extent (*yāvat-tāvat*) constitutes proficiency, and thus there is no "incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpti*) in this case? This is not so; for the very measure of a quality is already known from common worldly usage (*loka*). In the world, indeed, one is said to be "clever" (*paṭu*) when he accomplishes his goals by means of a swift method.

That which does not accomplish [its purpose] in that manner, but is slightly deficient, is "almost capable" (*paṭukalpa*). By the reverse of that, "weak" (*mṛdu*) and "almost weak" (*mṛdukalpa*) are explained. How is it that when expressing a genus (*jāti*), one says "grapes are almost molasses" (*guḍakalpā drākṣā*) or "clear liquor is almost oil" (*tailakalpā prasannā*)? It is said: because the quality of molasses inherent in the molasses is superimposed upon the grape by relying on its sweetness, yet due to the absence of the actual genus of molasses, the molasseness of the grape is only slightly incomplete. Likewise, the expression "molasses that is almost molasses" (*guḍakalpo guḍaḥ*) also occurs.

But how, then, can that very same thing be "slightly incomplete"? Due to the loss of its qualities: as much sweetness as is well-known in molasses does not remain when it is afflicted by defects such as aging; therefore, it is called "slightly incomplete molasses."
The *vibhāṣā* rule [applies] to a case-ending (*sup*); however, when the suffix *bahuc* follows, it is placed before [the stem].

"From that which denotes a meaning qualified by being slightly incomplete"—this fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs due to the elision of *lyap*. The meaning is: "having relied upon such a nominal stem (*subanta*) as the base. However, in the sūtra, because of the rule "of a sup [ending]" (*supaḥ*) and the rule "with a suffix having the sense of 'atas'," the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. And that [suffix] occurs only before [the word]. By this, he shows that since particles have multiple meanings, the word *tu* functions in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).

The intention is that if the word *tu* were not present, then because the status of being prior to the suffix would also be something to be enjoined, it would be primary; consequently, it might be connected with the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*).

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, considers this: "In rules such as *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām*, why is the status of being posterior (*paratva*) not made optional? Because it is the suffix itself that is prescribed as qualified by posteriority; therein, due to the subordinate nature (*guṇatva*) of the qualifier, there is no connection with the option, according to the maxim: 'Qualifiers exist for the sake of another. Likewise here too, by the mention of *vibhāṣā*, it will be connected only with *bahu* (the suffix *bahu*), and not with the word *purastāt*."

However, the purpose of the word *tu* (but), which has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), is something else entirely: namely, that everything occurs precisely as it was previously. By this, the gender and number are also exactly those which were observed in the state of the base (*prakṛti*) prior to the production of the suffix; and the usage occurs prior to the formation [of the compound]. Thus, in examples such as *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes with much molasses") and *laghur bahutṛṇo naraḥ* ("a man who is light despite having much grass"), the gender is like that of the base, not like that of the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*). And in this way, the reading of the feminine form *bahuguḍā* should be regarded as resulting from an error.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: "Since these suffixes are merely self-referential (*svārthika*), their gender and number will follow those of the base word (*prakṛti*). If this is so, then this [rule] teaches the following: in the case of self-referential suffixes used to denote slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*), the gender and number are exactly like those of the thing expressed (*abhidheya*). By this, forms such as *guḍakalpā drākṣā* ("grapes that are somewhat like molasses") and *tailakalpā prasannā* ("clarified butter that is somewhat like oil") are established.

The suffix *cit* is prescribed for the purpose of making the final syllable of a word have the acute accent (*udātta*). And that final acute accent belongs to the entire complex consisting of the base together with the suffix, not to the *bahu*-suffix alone; for there is a rule stating that the *cit* suffix serves to make the final syllable of the base plus the suffix acute. If this is so, then in the case of *bahupaṭavaḥ*, since the suffix would arise before the nominal ending (*sub*), the acute accent would apply to the *jas* ending? This would indeed be the case, were it not for the fact that the *jas* which arose previously remains [as part of the complex].

In this case, however, when the suffix *bahuc* has been produced, because the whole (*samudāya*) possesses meaningfulness characterized by the slight incompleteness [of the original sense], it becomes a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending; then another suffix *jas* is produced again. And because that [suffix] is not a constituent part of the base (*prakṛti*), it does not receive the udātta accent.

[Objection: But surely, because the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) would not apply to the aggregate of base and suffix? [Response: This is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author teaches the prohibition "not when it is a suffix" (*apratyaya*), that indicates: the designation of "nominal stem" does indeed apply to the aggregate of base and suffix, and there is no exclusion of it by the mention of "compound. [Regarding the phrase] "because of the statement of the option" (*vibhāṣāvacanāt*), etc.: otherwise, the suffixes *kalpa* and so on—which have their scope in verbal forms ending in *tiṅ*—would be superseded by *bahuc*, which is specifically prescribed for words ending in *sup* (nouns) and has the same meaning even when there is a difference in location.

Regarding the mention of *sub* (the nominal suffix), and so forth: otherwise, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "also after *tiṅ*," the suffix *bahuc*—just like *kalpab* and others—would also precede a *tiṅ*-ending form. However, the mention of *sub* is not for the purpose of excluding the base noun (*prātipadika*), because there would be no distinction [otherwise].

But surely there is this distinction: when the suffix is produced after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the prohibition of *ṣatva* by the rule "sātpadādyoḥ" is established; however, if it were produced after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of *ṣatva*. This is not a fault. Even if the suffix is produced after a word ending in a case-suffix, an effort must necessarily be made here to prohibit *kutva*; that very same effort will serve to prohibit *ṣatva* when the suffix is produced after a nominal stem.

And that has already been demonstrated under the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. Here, the scope (*avakāśa*) of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* is the expression of excellence (*prakarpa*) without the expression of slight incompleteness (*īṣadasamāpti*)—as in *paṭutaraḥ* (more clever) and *paṭutamaḥ* (cleverest); while the scope of the suffixes *kalpap* and so on is the expression of slight incompleteness without the expression of excellence—as in *paṭukalpaḥ* (somewhat clever) and *mṛdukalpaḥ* (somewhat soft). When both [suffixes] would apply because both meanings are expressed, the suffixes *kalpap* and so on are applied first due to their higher priority (*paratva*). Then, by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punah-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are applied again to the word ending in those [suffixes] in order to indicate excellence—resulting in *paṭukalpataraḥ* and *mṛdukalpataraḥ*.

If the two suffixes [kalpa and deśya] apply to that which ends in *yat* when it is the predominant element, and they occur in the sense of its excellence (*prakarpa*), then what is the predominant element of that which ends in *yat*? Is it the predominance of "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*)? And is this desired in the sense of the excellence of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)? This is not a fault; for the excellence of "slight incompleteness" is not possible, because neither in the excellence of the sense of "slight" nor in the excellence of "incompleteness" does "slight incompleteness" itself come to be.
The suffix *jātīyar* is used in the sense of expressing a kind or variety. (Pāṇini 5.3.69)

Regarding the phrase "of that word" (*tasya vacane*): *vacanam* means "illumination" (*dyota*). Regarding "after a word ending in a case-suffix" (*subantāt*): here too, he shows that the term *supaḥ* ("after a case-suffix") is understood from the previous rule in order to exclude verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). Regarding "and this [suffix] occurs in the sense of 'belonging to a class'": the point is that because the domains of application differ, there is no sublation of the suffix *jātīyar* by *thāl*, even though *thāl* is prescribed for a specific instance; thus, *jātīyar* is established after a word ending in *thāl*. And in this context, the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of the suffix is the reason.
The suffix *ka* is applied after words ending in *prāgīva*.

The intention is that this suffix is not desired after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) and so forth; therefore, in this case, one must connect [the rule] only with "of *sup*" (*supaḥ*). The intention is that for the sake of [the suffix] *akac*, in that case as well, one must connect [the rule] only with "of *sup*" (*supaḥ*).

But how can that which is being carried over (anuvartamāna) be prevented from continuing? To this he says: "The word *tiṅ* is understood to carry over. And in this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge. Here, one should have said "prior to *kuṭī*," for there is no utility for this [rule] starting from "after *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*, the suffix *ra* [is applied]," because [the forms] are already occupied by other suffixes. However, this much limit is taken for the sake of what follows; for in the rule "optionally after many," the mention of the option (*vā*) is for the purpose of [the suffix] *akac*.

Even so, it should be stated that "the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of 'formerly'" (*prākkana*), for this [rule] "the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of 'throwing down'" (*avakṣepaṇe kan*) is the limit. Why indeed is this so? This very [rule] regarding *kan* is the limit, and not the rule regarding the "short" (*hrasve*); otherwise, one of these two—either "the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyāṃ kan*) or "the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of contempt when it is a name" (*kutsite saṃjñāyāṃ kan*)—would have to be the limit.

"Before the suffix *ṭi*, the affix *akac* is added to indeclinables and pronouns. [The question is: "Is this an exception (*apavāda*) to *ka*? Now, an exception-and-sublated relationship (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) occurs only when there is a conflict; however, since *ka* and *akac* occupy different positions, there is no conflict between them. So how can it be an exception to that? It is not necessary that conflict be based solely on position; rather, it may also be based on purpose. Furthermore, *ka* and *akac* have one common purpose: namely, to indicate meanings such as "unknown. Once *akac* has been applied for that purpose, *ka* will not occur because its purpose is no longer served. Thus, [the form] is *sarvake*.

Because that which falls in the middle of [the elements] *aka* and *ac* is included by the mention of those two, the substitution of *śī* for *jas* occurs; however, if *ke* were present, it would not occur. Both [rules] are understood here as being in force. If this is so, would there not be the undesirable consequence of suffixes occurring everywhere before the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of both nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and inflected words (*subanta*)? To this he says: "In that regard... [He specifies: "In some cases, of the nominal stem"—that is, when the case-ending begins with *o*, *s*, or *bh*. "In some cases, of the inflected word"—that is, in case-endings other than those mentioned. In the form *tvayaki*, the second vowel *a* of *akac* is for the sake of pronunciation. The inclusion of the marker *c* (in *akac*), however, is for the purpose of making the entire complex [of the suffix] have an udātta accent on its final syllable.

This is because of the rule: "The suffix *kā* is added after *cit* together with its *prakṛti* for the sake of expressing multiplicity. This very addition of *kā* is the indicator (*liṅga*) that the acute accent (*udātta*) applies to *cit* along with its *prakṛti*, and not to *cit* alone.

Regarding the rule *tūṣṇīmaḥ kā*: it is applied in the senses of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, as far as possible. The letter *m* is for the purpose of a specific grammatical operation (*vidhi*). The suffix *kā* occurs after the final vowel. When there is no intention to express the senses of "unknown" and so forth, the form remains simply *tūṣṇīm*.

Regarding the rule *śīle ka*: "habit" (*śīla*) means natural disposition (*svabhāva*) and also restraint (*niyama*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the senses of "unknown" and so forth. One who is habitually silent by nature or disposition is called *tūṣṇīka*; it does not refer merely to the state of being silent at that moment.
And [the suffix] *da* is used after the word *kasya*. (Pāṇini 5.3.72)

The phrase "not including all nouns" should be understood as also excluding the mention of *iṅ*; for the reason is the same. In forms such as *adhok* and *avak*, the substitution of *ku* (the guttural) is not established. In cases like *aśāśak* from the root *śak* and others when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), followed by the present tense marker (*laṭ*) and the third-person singular ending (*tip*), with the elision of the vowel by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...*—here the elision of *yaṅ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and in the Veda, one follows what is actually observed. The word *dhik* shows that this indeclinable ends in the letter *k*.
[The suffix *kha* is applied] after [the word *ajñāta*]. (Pāṇini 5.2.73)

"Unknown" is stated in a general sense; however, the employment of a word is not possible with respect to something that is entirely unknown. Indeed, one who does not know "this is a horse" is not capable of employing the word "horse. Therefore, he says that there must be the apprehension of a specific [quality]: "the specific is known. He demonstrates that very specific [quality] by saying "in its own form. This is an elaboration of the phrase "in its specific form": "To whom does this horse belong? and so forth.

In this case, when there is a desire to express two meanings—being "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and being "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*), as in the sense of "very clever" (*paṭuḥ*)—the suffix *ka* is applied later, resulting in *paṭutamaka*. And here, when there is a desire to express that something is "bad," as in "half a long pepper" (*ardhapippalyāḥ*), the compound is formed first, and then *ka* is applied, resulting in *ardhapippalīka*. By this, the suffixes *kalpa*, *bā*, and so on, are explained. And it has been said: "The suffixes *ka* and others, as well as the superlative suffixes (*tamap*) and so on, [are applied] by the rule of prior precedence (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*); and the compound is one where the subordinate member is predominant (*ekadeśipradhānaḥ*)."

But here, in the case of *chinnakatara*, the suffix *tarap* occurs because, by the rule "after a word ending in *kta* when not expressing absolute completion," the suffix *kan* is applied later; thus *tarap* follows. Sometimes there is a *dvandva* compound: either *plakṣanyagrodhakau* or *plakṣakanyagrodhakau*.
In the sense of contempt. || 5.3.74 ||

"And this is a qualifier of the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*). This means that this is a qualifier of the meaning of the base, not a mere incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). For if it were an incidental indicator, then when it is understood as "from that which denotes something contemptible," the suffix would apply even to the word *idam* in expressions such as *idaṃ ghṛtakam* ("this ghee") and *idaṃ tailakam* ("this oil"). However, if it is accepted as a qualifier, the suffix occurs from that which possesses contempt as its admitted attribute—that is, from that which is in grammatical apposition with the contemptible—and not from that which merely has contempt as an accidental characteristic; [the suffix occurs] from that which is in apposition with the contemptible.

If, however, [the suffix] were to express the meaning of the suffix itself, then according to the principle that "the base and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix, and among those two, the meaning of the suffix is primary," it would follow that the meaning of the base is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the contemptible thing is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Yet, in common worldly usage, the opposite is perceived. Therefore, it is well said that [the suffix] is a qualifier of the meaning of the base. Regarding the example *aśvaka*: one who, being indeed a horse, does not properly perform the action to be accomplished by it, is called thus.

For it has been stated that in the case of suffixes used in their own sense (*svārthika*), where it is impossible for the qualifier of the basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) to exist, the suffix comes to depend on another property co-occurring with the expressed meaning. And thus, forms such as *devadattakaḥ* and *ḍitthakaḥ* also occur for one who does not properly perform the purpose to be accomplished by them. However, when [the qualification] is possible, even here the censure (*kutsā*) depends solely on the property conveyed by the word itself; for example, in *paṭukaḥ* (clever) and *paṇḍitakaḥ* (learned), the censure is directed at the thing itself.

"Having encountered the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, know the Kauravas to be women"—this is "contempt for gender," meaning: "Are these Kauravas actually men in the presence of Arjuna? In some cases, there is "contempt for number," as in: "This is but a single *śata* (hundred)," where the contempt for the state of being a hundred lies in the fact that the suffering involved in supporting a hundred is the same as that of supporting a single one. In every case, the suffix arises from the acceptance of such contempt.

Now, what is the justification here for the suffix [ka] in the word *kutsitaka*? And why should it not be so? Because the contempt (*kutsā*) is already expressed by its own word. [Answer: It will occur in another sense, such as compassion (*anukampā*). Or rather—the suffix occurs there when there is a contempt for that which is already contemptible; the meaning is: when the state of being contemptible itself is contemned, as in "this is not properly contemptible. Just as the suffix *tamap* occurs in the sense of excellence upon excellence, as in *prakṛṣṭatama*, so it is here as well.
By this, the suffix after the word *anukampita* in the sense of compassion has been explained.
In the sense of compassion, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]. 5.3.76.

"By compassion" (*kāruṇyena*): compassion itself is *kāruṇya*. "Acceptance" (*abhyupapatti*): this means favoring, that is to say, assistance. "Of another" (*parasya*): here the genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
