True; this question should be understood as being asked by one who wonders why the meaning of the sūtra cannot be "after a word ending in *akṣi* that does not denote seeing. [The author replies: "It is a synonym for the eye" (*cakṣuḥ-paryāya*). The intention is that this is because [the word *akṣi*] is more well-known [in that sense].

The following compounds are *avyayībhāva* by virtue of their specific forms: *acatura*, *avicatura*, *sucatura*, *strīpumsa*, *dhenvanaḍuh*, *ṛksāma*, *vāṅmanasa*, *akṣibhru*, *avadāra*, *gavāśva*, *goṣṭhaśva*; as well as *goṣṭhaśvāḥ*; and the following: *uṣṭravāmi*, *padaṣṭhīva*, *aṣṭhīvac*, *naktaṃdiva*, *rātriṃdiva*, *ahardiva*, *ahardiva*, *saraja*, *saniśreyasa*, *puruṣāyuṣa*, *dvyāyuṣa*, *tryāyuṣa*, *ṛgyajuṣa*, *jātokṣa*, *mahokṣa*, *vṛddhokṣa*, *upaśuna*. (Pāṇini 2.4.77)

"Regarding the establishment of compound types (*samāsavyavasthā*): This refers to a rule or restriction (*niyama*) such as that in some cases there is only a *bahuvrīhi*, while in others there is only a *dvandva*, and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that other matters, such as the elision of the suffix *ṭi*, also occur solely by virtue of this specific nipātana (irregular formation). "A man [is brave] toward a woman": the meaning is that a man is brave in relation to a woman.

Regarding *akṣibhruvam*: because it is a part of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), it takes the singular form (*ekavadbhāva*). Regarding *dāragavam*: "Every *dvandva* optionally becomes singular. The compound of two indeclinables (*avyaya*) used in the sense of the locative case also occurs only by virtue of a specific rule (*nipātana*). Because there is no connection with the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*), [the rule] does not apply here, for one does not say, "here and thus" (*iha ca, evaṃ ca*). Regarding *ahardivam*: the *repha* (r) is substituted [for the visarga] by the rule "ro'supi. How can there be a *dvandva* of these two? Not at all, because the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is initiated even for words that are dissimilar in form provided they have the same meaning. Regarding "in the sense of repetition" (*vīpsāyām*), etc.

When [the term] is prescribed for the sense of *cā-artha* (conjunction), it would not apply in the sense of *vīpsā* (distribution/repetition), because of the introduction of the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). Therefore, a *dvandva* compound is irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of *vīpsā*; and because of the indication of *vīpsā*, one should not suspect that the meaning is already conveyed by a single word, as in the case of reduplication—e.g., "every village is beautiful" (*grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ*). Regarding *sarajasam*: the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule "in an *avyayībhāva* compound, when not denoting time. Regarding *niḥśreyasam*: this is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix). Regarding *niḥśreyaska*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is certain. The suffix *kap* is added according to the rule for "remainder" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and the change to *s* occurs by the rule "after *sa-*, when not at the beginning of a word" (*so 'padādau*).

Regarding the term *ṛgyajurunmugdha*: one who considers the *ṛc*s and the *yajus* to be "three or four" (*tricaturaḥ*). In the vicinity of the number four, the form is *upacaturaḥ*. This prescribes the substitution of *ad-* as an exception to the suffix *kaḍac*, which would otherwise apply according to the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* containing a numeral."
The suffix *matup* is applied after the words *brahman* and *hastin* when the sense is "possessing splendor" (*varcas*).
*Varcas* means luster. In the examples provided, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The suffix *tama* is applied after words meaning "blind" (*ava-sa*) and "darkness" (*andha*).

*Tamo'vatamasam* means "penetrating darkness"; *santataṃ tamaḥ* is *santamasam*. These are compounds with the prefix *pra-* (as *prādi-samāsa*). One makes blind (*andaṃ karoti*) is *andhayati*; from the root *andhayati*, the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*) yields *andham*. That which is both *andha* (blind) and *tamas* (darkness) is *andhatamasam*.
The suffix *śvas* is applied after [words denoting] "better" (*vasīyas*) and "more excellent" (*śreyas*).

From the word *vasu*, which denotes "praiseworthy," the suffix *īyasun* is added to form *vasīyaḥ*; then, by the rule "the substitute *śraḥ* is used for *praśasya*," it becomes *śreyaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "by its very nature" (*svabhāvāt*) and so forth: although the word *śvas* here refers to a specific point of time (tomorrow), nevertheless, in this compound, it expresses a blessing directed toward the excellence of the object denoted by the second member of the compound. Why? By its very nature. The phrase "of this very [word]" means "of the word *śvaḥśreyasa*."
The suffix *raha* is substituted for the final vowel and following consonant of the word *anvavatapta* [before a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel]. 5.4.81.

The word *rahas* occurs here in the sense of "that which is not manifest. [In the term *anurahasam*,] it is either a *prādi* compound meaning "that which has followed into secrecy," or a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that in which secrecy has entered. Similarly, *avahīnam rahas* is *avarahasam*, meaning "that in which secrecy has been cast down" (i.e., hidden). And *taptam ca tadrahaśca* is *taptarahasa*, meaning "secrecy that has been heated"; the sense is "extreme secrecy."
The suffix *prati* is compounded with a word ending in the seventh case that denotes "from the chest" (*uras*).
"It exists in the sense of the locative case" means that the word *anyad-uraḥ* itself does not possess the status of being "situated in the locative," such is the intended meaning.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied after [a word ending in] *anugava* in the sense of "extent" (*āyāma*).

Regarding the statement "the meaning to be expressed is length": length (*āyāma*) is the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*), while the final referent is that which possesses it. Alternatively, the word *āyāma* may end in the possessive suffix *-ka* (i.e., *āyāmika*), meaning "that which possesses length. Otherwise, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "a carriage following the ox" (*anugavaṃ yānam*). As for the analysis of the compound as "the length of which [is the ox]," one might object: "But does not the rule 'by means of a characteristic' (*lakṣaṇena*) apply there? True; even here, the oxes indeed function as a characteristic with respect to the external carriage.

Since the suffix must be expressed by the word *anu-gu*, the recourse to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*) is for the purpose of including well-known usage; therefore, it occurs only in that which is external to cows.
The sacrificial altar (vedi) is twice or thrice as large [as the fire-altar]. || 5.4.84 ||

"And the compound is formed by way of an irregular derivation (nipātana), because [otherwise] there would be a lack of smoothness (*ślakṣṇa*). By the words 'to whatever extent is the archetypal state' (*yāvatī prakṛtatā*) and so forth, he shows the scope of the irregular derivation: that in which the ritual properties (*dharma*) are taught is the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; that by which they are utilized is the ectype (*vikṛti*). 'In a certain ectype' means in the Aśvamedha and others. 'Twice that much' (*dvistāvat*)."

By the word *tāvatī*, the measure (*vṛtti*) related to it is indicated; that very measure is what is counted by the word *dvis*, and thus the suffix *suc* is applied, as well as the mutual semantic connection (*parasparasāmarthya*). The form *dvistāvatī* is not a compound. In the Sūtra, gender is not intended to be significant; for one also sees the expression *dvistāvo 'gniḥ*. Now, is it not the case that neither the fire-altar (*agni*) nor the altar-ground (*vedi*) is being denoted here? [The answer is: The fire-altar is indeed the altar-ground itself, because it is a modification of the *uttaravedi*, according to the scriptural statement: "The fire is established upon the *uttaravedi*."
[The suffix *ṭac* is applied after a word denoting a road] following a prefix [to form a bahuvrīhi compound]. Pāṇini 5.4.85.

Since the word *adhvan* does not denote an action, it lacks the designation of "preverb" (*upasarga*) with respect to that [root]; therefore, the mention of "preverb" (*upasargagrahaṇa*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the group beginning with *pra*.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *aṅguli* following a numeral or an indeclinable [takes the suffix *ṭac*]. (Pāṇini 5.4.86)
Regarding the phrase "of that which ends with the word *aṅguli*," and so forth: in all instances where there is a connection with a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), the genitive case is used.
[The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the words *ahar*, *sarva*, a portion [of a whole], a numeral, *puṇya*, and also after the word *rātri*. Pāṇini 5.4.87.

The inclusion of the term *ahaḥ* (day) is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound, and not for the sake of a *tatpuruṣa* compound; for a *tatpuruṣa* is impossible when two words function in their primary senses, since it is not possible for there to be both "night" (*rātriḥ*) and "day-and-night" (*ahorātriḥ*). However, if by the word "night" one means the day characterized by the qualities of night, and by the word "day" one means the night characterized by the qualities of day, then a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) might indeed be possible; yet in that case, the meaning would be figurative (*gauṇa*).

Furthermore, when the primary meaning is possible, it is not appropriate to adopt a secondary (metaphorical) one; therefore, the mention of *ahaḥ* (day) is for the sake of forming a *dvandva* compound. Accordingly, in the rule “*hemanta-śiśirāv-ahorātre ca chandasi*” (*Pāṇini 2.4.28*), the suffix for a *dvandva* compound is prescribed [as *ṭac*]. Thus, *ahorātraḥ* is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound). By the rule “*rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi*,” [the neuter gender is overridden by] the masculine gender; then, after the substitution of *ru* for the final *n* of *ahan*, the rule “*rūparātrirathantareṣu*” prescribes *ru* for the *n*; and by the rule “*haśi ca*,” this *ru* is changed to *u*. *Dvirātraḥ*: This is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective. *Nīrātraḥ*:
This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes), where by the rule “*ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho’ṇaḥ*,” the preceding vowel is lengthened.
The word *ahna* is substituted for *ahan* before these [suffixes]. (Pāṇini 5.4.88)

Regarding the phrase *tasmin parabhūte* ("when that has occurred as subsequent"): because this is within the section on compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), it is understood that this substitution occurs when that [suffix] follows; it is not an exception (*apavāda*) to it, and since that [suffix] is prescribed only as *ṭac*, this meaning is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Furthermore, the substitution of *ahan* is established through formal explanation (*vyākhyāna*), for it is not itself recognized as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*), unlike [the suffix] *anaṅ* in the rule *ūdhaso'naṅ* and others. Regarding the phrase "and by implication" (*sāmarthyācca*) and so forth: it is not recognized as a compound-final suffix, unlike *anaṅ* in *ūdhaso'naṅ* and others. He demonstrates this very implication with the words "for not" (*na hi*).

First of all, a *dvandva* compound is impossible because of the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one member). Because of that very rule, there is no connection between them, so it cannot be a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound), nor can it be a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (attributive compound), for a thing cannot be its own qualifier. By this, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is also explained [as impossible]. In the case of *dvy-ahnaḥ*: it is a compound in the sense of a *taddhita* derivative; the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "that which occurs therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*), and that suffix is elided by the rule "elision of the *aṇ* of a *dvigu* when not denoting a descendant" (*dvigor lug-anapatye*). In the case of *sarvāhnaḥ*: the substitution of *ṇ* is applied by the rule "of *ahan* after a word ending in *a*" (*ahno 'dantāt*).

The mention of *ahan* [in the rule for the suffix *ṭac*] is redundant because of the restrictive rule regarding *ṭa* and *kha*. The sūtra should have been formulated simply as "after these [words], [the suffix] *ac* is applied to *ahan*" (*ahna etebhyaḥ*). The term *ac* is understood from the previous context; thus, when *ac* follows the word *ahan* after these [specific words], it serves as an exception to *ṭac*. When *ac* is applied there, by the restriction "only after *ahan* with the suffixes *ṭa* and *kha* [does elision occur]," the elision of *ṭi* is prevented. Consequently, upon the elision of the final *a*, forms such as *dvay-ahnaḥ* are established. Since the statement "the words *rātri*, *ahna*, and *aha* are masculine" precludes their application in the feminine, there is no distinction between *ṭac* and *ac*.

The expression "from these" is for the purpose of indicating number and the meaning of an indeclinable; otherwise, because they would not have been drawn forward [by the previous rule], they would not be connected.
The suffix *taddhita* does not occur after a numeral or the like when forming a collective compound (*samāhāra*). Pāṇini 5.4.89.
The phrase "of number and so forth" need not be stated, because it is impossible for anything else to function as a collective aggregate (samāhāra).
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *uttama* and *eka*. (Pāṇini 5.4.90)

"Some [say]... and so forth. Just as in the rule *prathamayoḥ*, there is the inclusion of both the first and second [cases] due to the mention of the dual number, so too here, by the force of the mention of the "last" (*uttama*), there is the inclusion of both the penultimate and the last; such is their intention. In this view, since there would be three—two that are last and one other—the dual mention in the sūtra is used despite the contingency of the plural. The non-initial placement of the word *eka* is for the purpose of indicating that the rule *alpāctaram* is not universally obligatory."
The suffix *ṭac* is applied after [the words] *rājan*, *aśva*, and *sakhi*.

Why is this so? Furthermore, what would happen if the suffix *ṭac* were applied here? By the rule "in the case of a *bha*-stem before a non-*ādh* secondary suffix" (*bhasyāḍhe taddhite*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be removed through masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*). Once *ṭac* is applied and the *ṭi*-portion elided, the suffix *ṅīp* would be added again because of the *ṭit*-designation, resulting in the form *madrarājī*; however, *bhadrarājñī* is what is desired. Therefore, the point is that the non-occurrence of *ṭac* must be stated here. The addition of the *c*-marker to *ṭac* is for the purpose of making it oxytone (*antodātta*); otherwise, since a suffix is part of the composite whole, the accent of the suffix (as in *vidhuraḥ*, *pradhuraḥ*, etc. would be overridden by the accent of the first member of the compound (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).
[The elision of the feminine suffix] *ī* occurs after a word ending in *go-rat*, when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel follows, provided that the suffix does not have the marker *luk*.

Regarding the term *pañcagavām*: it is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*). In the case of *pañcaguri*, it is used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). As for *pañcagavarūpyam* and *pañcagavamayam*, just as in this instance the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *rūpya* and *mayaṭ* does not occur according to the rule "elision of the *dvigu* [suffix] except in the sense of a descendant" (*dvigor lug anapatye*), so too has it been stated in that very same place.
The term *agra* is substituted for *uras* [in a Bahuvrīhi compound] when the latter member is one denoting a limb of the body. || 5.4.93 ||

The locative case in "agrākhyāyām" is used in the sense of the ablative, because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word "uraḥ," which ends in the ablative. This apposition is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "sa ceduraḥśabdaḥ."
The suffix *śun* is applied after the root *at*.
The meaning is "impulsion" (*javana*), and so forth. This determination of the meaning of the word "dog" is based on specific objects and other such factors.
The suffix *kan* is applied after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) when it refers to non-living beings (*apraṇin*).
Regarding the example *aśvā loṣṭaḥ*: here, there ought to be a prohibition by the rule *nañastatpuruṣāt*; therefore, *niḥśvā loṣṭaḥ* should be cited as the counter-example.
According to the Eastern grammarians, [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the word *khārī*.

Regarding "dvikhārī": in the alternative view where the suffix *ṭac* is absent, the neuter short vowel applies. Could this rule (*yoga*) be omitted, as in the case of "trikhāram"? There exists a word *khāra* that has the same meaning as the word *khārī*, just as there is a Vārttika under the rules "tadasya parimāṇam" and "saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃjñā" stating: "it is seen after other words as well, for the sake of forms such as *khāraśata*."
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *dvayaṅgula* and *tryaṅgula* when they denote a measure of capacity (*añjali*).

The term *dvyañjali* means "purchased for two *añjalis*. Here, an *añjali* refers to a measure of rice or other grain equal to the capacity of two cupped hands (*añjali*), not merely the two palms themselves, because it is impossible for those [palms] to have a price. Consequently, since it denotes a measure, the suffix *ṭhak* (which would otherwise apply by the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ*) is elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrva*. Thus we have *dvyañjalipriyaḥ*. They say that, because the optionality is restricted (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the suffix does not occur after a *dvigu* compound consisting of an *uttarapada*.
The suffix *śas* is applied after a word ending in *an*, as well as after words that do not end in a neuter gender.

Regarding *sutrāmāṇam*: [the derivation is] "one who protects well" (*suṣṭhu trāyate*), formed with the suffix *manin* after a root ending in *ā* (Pāṇini 3.2.74), followed by a compound with an *upapada*. Regarding *anehasam*: [the derivation is] from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *ā*, with the suffix *isi* according to the rule *nañyāhana eha ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.120); there is the substitution of *i* for the root and the prefix; then a compound with the negative particle *nañ* as an *upapada*, in the second case singular.
The inclusion of the word *anta-* is for the sake of clarity.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *brahman* when it denotes a person belonging to a particular region (*jānapada*).

Even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the word *jānapada* has the abstract sense as its primary meaning, just like the expression "of two or one" (*dvyekayoḥ*). Thus he says: "And by means of the compound, the state of being a *jānapada* of Brahman is expressed. Although there is only a single mention of "Brahman," and by that [mention] the compound is qualified, nevertheless, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood that the qualification "state of being a *jānapada*" belongs to Brahman alone; therefore, this is the formulation of the rule for the suffix. For only from that [qualification] can the state of being a *jānapada* of Brahman be expressed when the suffix is prescribed.
As in the example *devabrahma*: it is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*).
A neuter compound ending in *dvandva*, *ac*, *ud*, or *ṣas* denotes a collective aggregate.

"Lest it [apply] from a *tatpuruṣa*": the meaning is "lest it apply from a *tatpuruṣa* compound alone. For if the word "from a *dvandva*" were not stated, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *tatpuruṣa* would not be suspended.
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after words beginning with *śarad*.

Regarding *jarāyā jaras ca*: the suffix *ac* is applied after the word *jarā*, and in an *avyayībhāva* compound, the substitution of *jaras* occurs—as in *upajarasam*. Regarding *pratiparasamanubhyo'kṣṇaḥ*: when the word *akṣi* follows the words *prati*, *para*, *sama*, or *anu*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied; since the word *para* cannot form an *avyayībhāva* compound, the rule here refers to a *tatpuruṣa* compound—as in *pratyakṣam*.

In the expression *yathārthe yadavyayam*, the term *avyayībhāva* refers to the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). In *parokṣam* (from *parakṣmaṇaḥ*), it is an ablative compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) because of the rule "the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is used for what is out of sight" (*parokṣe liṭ*); furthermore, the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is placed last, and the vowel *u* is substituted for the *kṣya* of *akṣya*. In *samakṣam* (meaning "suitable for the eyes"), the *avyayībhāva* occurs in the sense of suitability (*yogyatā*) according to the rule *yathārthe*. In *anvakṣam*, the *avyayībhāva* occurs in the sense of "afterwards."
After a neuter [stem], [the suffix *śas*] is optionally [used]. (Pāṇini 5.4.109)

The mention of the neuter gender is a qualifier of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), not a qualifier of the *avyayībhāva* compound; for [the neuter gender] does not deviate [from being a qualifier of the subsequent member].
[The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after [words ending in] *nadī*, *paurṇamāsī*, and *āgrahāyaṇī*. (Pāṇini 5.4.110)
The term "river" (nadī) refers to the essential form itself, not to the technical name [of specific rivers], because the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī) and the Āgrahāyaṇī day are mentioned separately.
The suffix *jhac* [is applied after a word ending in *kṣipra*, etc., to form adverbs]. 5.4.111.

The term *jhaya* is understood as a collective inclusion (*pratyāhāra*). However, there is no inclusion of the letters *jha* and *ya*; for it is impossible for an avyayībhāva compound to end in those sounds. The purpose of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is to be considered further.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied after the word] *gireḥ* when [the sense is that of] *senaka*. 5.4.112.

Regarding the term *antargiram*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed with a case-ending (*vibhaktyarthe*). The option (*vikalpa*) indeed continues to apply; otherwise, the inclusion of certain words ending in *jh* among the *śarat-prabhṛti* group would be purposeless, as the desired result would already be established by the rule *jhayaḥ*. By this, one should not raise the objection that—since "between two optional rules, the rules are mandatory"—this mention of Senaka must be for the sake of making the preceding rule mandatory.
The suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a limb of one's own body, provided that *brahma-vrīhi* follows.

The term *svāṅga* (limb of one's own body) is understood here according to its technical definition as "not liquid" and so forth. Regarding the phrase *duḥśliṣṭavibhaktīni*: the prefix *dur-* signifies censure (*nindā*). Thus, those are so described in which the case-endings (*vibhakti*) are joined or connected in a censurable manner. For instance, from the word *bahuvrīhi*, there ought to be either a fifth case (*pañcamī*) or a sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) when connected with a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), as in the rule: *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ*; however, in this instance, the locative singular (*saptamyekavacana*) is heard.

The form *sakthyakṣṇoḥ* is either a genitive dual or a locative dual. A bahuvrīhi compound cannot be qualified by such a word, because their case-endings and numbers differ. Furthermore, the form *svāṅgāt* is a nominative singular, and it cannot logically function as a coreferential qualifier for *sakthyakṣṇoḥ*, yet that is what is intended. Therefore, it was stated that "the case-endings are poorly joined," meaning that one must resort to a transposition of the case-endings to establish the connection between them.

Regarding the example *sthūlākṣirikṣu*: by the rule *akṣṇo’darśanāt*, the suffix *ṣac* ought to apply here. However, if its application is not desired, one must state that the rule for suffixes at the end of a compound (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*); for that very reason, the suffix *ṣac* will also not occur. Therefore, they say that in cases such as *sthūlākṣā* or *sūkṣmākṣā veṇuyaṣṭiḥ*, one should provide counter-examples using the feminine suffix *ṭāp* itself. Regarding *dīrghasakthī*: "she whose thighs are long" is *dīrghasakthī*; here, if *ṣac* were present, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would be udātta (accented), but if *ṭac* were present, the suffix *ṅīp* would be anudātta (unaccented).

[Objection: But surely the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ṭac* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta; and consequently, by the rule regarding the "anudātta-nivṛtti-svara," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* will also be udātta? To this, he says: "And it is possible from what is preceded by *ākānta*" and so forth. Regarding "optionally": because of the continuation [of the option] from the rule "vibhāṣotpuccha," the addition of the *cit* marker to the suffix *ṣac* is for the sake of accentuation (*akṣya*). When *sakthi* follows what is preceded by *ākānta*, it is invariably udātta at the end—e.g., *cakrasakthaḥ*, *vakrasakthaḥ*. However, in cases such as *gaurasaktha*, there is no purpose served by the addition of the *cit* marker.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *aṅguli* when it occurs before the word *dāru*.
"Having limbs resembling fingers," and so forth. The sense is that, in the case of the compound meaning "wood," a primary connection with actual fingers is not possible.

But is it not possible [to apply the suffix] in the case of *dve aṅgulī pramāṇam asya dāruṇaḥ* ("a piece of wood whose measure is two fingers")? To this he replies with the words beginning "yasya tu" (but for whom...). Here, this suffix is prescribed after a *bahuvrīhi* compound; however, in the example cited by you, a *tatpuruṣa* compound must be formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In that case, the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ* would have to apply. Therefore, the meaning is that when a piece of wood is to be expressed within a *bahuvrīhi*, the word "finger" (*aṅguli*) is used only in a figurative sense; thus it was well said.
After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *ṣa* is added to the word *mūrdhan*.

Now, for what purpose is a separate suffix *ṣa* employed here, instead of simply carrying forward the previously mentioned *ṣa*? It is so that in forms such as *dvimūrdhaḥ* and *trimūrdhaḥ*, the optional final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhasu* may occur. If the suffix *ṣac* were used, however, the accent would necessarily be final due to its being marked with the indicatory letter *c*.

However, because the rule "dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhaśu bahuvrīhau" (Pāṇini 5.4.117) prescribing the compound-ending suffix is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), there are cases where that suffix is absent, such as *dvimūrddhā* and "trimūrddhānaṃ saptaraśmiṃ gṛṇīṣe. That would be its scope. But when the suffix *ṣ* is present, even if the compound-ending suffix is applied, two accents are established: in one case, the final syllable is udātta; in the other case, by the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), the initial syllable is udātta. And the non-obligatory nature of this rule is understood precisely from the prescription of the suffix *ṣ*.

For if [the suffix] were permanent (*nitya*), then even when the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣ*) is prescribed, the accent of *dvitribhyām* would supersede the *cit*-accent—which is of the nature of an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*)—because there would be no other scope for it. However, if it is non-permanent (*anitya*), then in the alternative where the compound is not formed, the accent of *dvitribhyām* finds its scope and thus supersedes the *cit*-accent; therefore, the creation of a separate suffix becomes meaningful. And by doing so, the mention of the form ending in *n*, namely *mūrdhasu*, becomes justified.

Otherwise, he would have pointed out the form ending in *a*, as in the rule "sakyaṃ cākrāntāt. If [the word] were pointed out as ending in *n*, how could [the accent] apply when a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) has been added? This is not a fault; for he will state there: "Even when the compound-final suffix is applied, because the *bahuvrīhi* is the subject of the operation and because the compound-final suffix is a part of that [compound], the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) certainly occurs.
[The rule: "The feminine suffix *ap* [is not acute] when it denotes a ordinal number (*pūraṇī*) or a measure (*pramāṇī*). (Pāṇini 5.4.116)

"Ending in a suffix denoting completion" means those words ending in suffixes prescribed for the sense of completion, such as *ḍaṭ* in the rule "tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ" and others. "Feminine gender" is because they are indicated by the form *pūraṇī*, which includes the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. They are understood through the mention of *pūraṇī* due to their association with the meaning of completion.

"Also, there is the inclusion of the principal ordinal (*pradhānapūraṇīgrahaṇam*). The meaning is that it must be stated: "Even when [the rule] is being prescribed, that which is the principal ordinal is to be understood. But where, then, does the ordinal have primacy? To this he says: "Where... It is not only in the case of the meaning of the *vṛtti*-word itself. A *vṛtti*-word is a word that constitutes a member of a compound; its meaning is the "meaning of the *vṛtti*-word. This [term *varttipadārthe*] ends in the nominative case, not the locative. The word "ordinal" (*pūraṇī*) is supplied [from the previous rule], but it does not enter into [the compound].

In that example, because the aggregate whose constituent parts are manifested is denoted by the word *rātri* through the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the fifth [night] is included within the nights. Thus, we have the expression *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("a fortnight having an auspicious fifth [night]"). Here, the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *nadyṛtaśca*. In this case, the ordinal (*pūraṇī*) refers only to the meaning of the member of the compound (*vartipadārtha*), and not to the meaning of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*); for the "fortnight" (*pakṣa*), as the external referent, is an entity whose internal distinctions between parts are obscured. Just as the word *vṛkṣa* denotes the whole (*avayavin*) and not its parts such as the branches—since what is merely inferred is not the direct meaning of the word—the ordinal is thus subordinate.

Regarding "neturnakṣatre": the meaning is that [the suffix ṭac] is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *netṛ*. Regarding "chandasi ca" (and in the Vedic language): this is for the purpose of excluding cases where the sense is not "constellation. Regarding "pañcakamāsikaḥ": a month whose wages are five [coins] is a "five-month" (*pañcaka*); from the word *pañca*, the suffix *kan* is added according to the rule "saṃkhyāyāḥ kan" (Pāṇini 5.1.22). When the *bahuvrīhi* "pañcako māso 'syāsti" (he has a five-month [period]) is formed, the suffix *ṭac* is added. This is intended to override the rule "apaḥ pit kṛtvasu ca" (Pāṇini 6.2.173), which prescribes that a *bahuvrīhi* beginning with *apa-* is oxytone; thus, in *apañcamāḥ* and *supañcamāḥ*, the oxytonic accent prescribed by "nañsubhyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.172) does not occur.
In place of the word *añjana*, [the substitute] *na* is used before a nominal stem ending in the locative case, provided that it does not denote something gross (*asthūla*).

*na-samiti*: The second mention [of *nas*] is for the sake of variety. Regarding *draṇasa*: his nose is like a tree (*dru*); the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām gaḥ*. Regarding *vādhrīṇasa*: that which exists in a *vadhrī* (a type of animal) is *vādhrī*; her nose is his, thus he is *vādhrīṇasaḥ*. The prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies here by the rule *vṛddhinimittasya ca taddhitasya*. Regarding *gonasa*: his nose is like a cow (*go*). Regarding the statement "the suffix *nas* should be stated after *khura* and *khara*": the mention of the mere substitute is for the purpose of excluding the [separate] suffix. Thus: *khuraṇāḥ*, *kharaṇāḥ*. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *atvasantasya ca*.

*Śitināḥ*: his nose is black; *śitiḥ* means black. *Ahināḥ*: his nose is like that of a serpent (*ahi*). *Arcanāḥ*: his nose is like that of an image (*arcā*); the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule "ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.63).
And [the suffix *ka*] is added after a preverb [to form a feminine noun]. 5.4.119.

The mention of "upasarga" (preverb) is an illustration intended to include words such as *prādi* (the group of prefixes beginning with *pra*); for there is no connection with an action (*kriyā*) in relation to the nose (*nāsikā*). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that *gra* replaces *vi*": the substitution of the word *gra* occurs for the word *vi* when it follows [another word], but the suffix remains unchanged.
The words *suprāta*, *suśva*, *sudiva*, *śārikukṣa*, *caturaśra*, *eṇīpada*, *ajapada*, and *proṣṭhapada* [are neuter]. || 5.4.120 ||

Regarding the phrase "the elision of *ṭi*, etc.": in examples such as *suprātaḥ* and *sukhaḥ*, there is an elision of *ṭi*. However, the rule "there is elision of *ṭi* for indeclinables (*avyaya*) when a *bha*-stem follows" has not been adopted here. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the substitution of *pad* for the words *ṇaṇīpa* and *ajapa* is intended. They say that because the word *prātaḥ* primarily denotes a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with the following noun]; therefore, by means of *prātaḥ*, the action belonging to the morning (*prātastanaṃ karma*) is indicated, while Devadatta and others constitute the meaning of the external member (*anyapadārtha*).

And how is it that [the compound] "varadaḥ karotu suprātamahnāmayaṃ nāyakaḥ" is explained? For this is certainly not a *bahuvrīhi* compound, since its meaning would then be "may this leader of days perform a beautiful morning [ritual]. It is replied: its interpretation is achieved with difficulty by taking it to mean "may he perform that [ritual] which has a beautiful morning activity, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth."
After the negative particle *nañ*, and after the words *duḥ* and *suṣ*, the long vowel is optionally substituted for the final vowel of the words *hali* and *sakthi*.

Is the inclusion of *halin* (the possessor of a plough) purposeless? [One might ask: how could there be *ahalaḥ* (without a plough) or *suhala* (with a good plough)? Is there not a word *hala* ending in the vowel *a*? [The opponent replies: But surely there is a difference in meaning—*halin* refers to one who possesses a large plough, whereas *hala* refers to the mere plough itself. [The author replies: This difference in meaning is of no consequence; even if the inclusion of *halin* were made, a compound with the word *hala* would not be prohibited by *daṇḍādi* [the list beginning with *daṇḍa*]. Consequently, the specific distinction must be understood through the force of context and other such factors.

And if this were the case, would not the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable be understood even in a compound ending in *a*, by means of context and so forth? In that case, here—in the compound *durhala*—even though it ends in *a*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) would result; however, when the compound suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied, the *cit-svara* (the acute accent on the suffix) occurs. In *ahalaḥ* and *suhalaḥ*, there is no difference because the rule "after *nañ* and *su*" prescribes an acute accent on the final syllable. Furthermore, by the rule "optionally after the remainder" (*śeṣād vibhāṣā*), the suffix *kap* would undesirably apply after the word *hali*; therefore, the term *hali* is mentioned [in the rule]. Some, however, read it as *hali-śaktyoḥ*. The word *śakti* is a synonym for *asthi* (bone).

*nityamasic prajāmedhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.122). This suffix *asic* is not prescribed for the sake of non-service (*asevā*), so that the designation *sakāśit* might not apply. "In that case, etc."—this [objection] is not accepted in the Bhāṣya. The addition of the marker *c* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta in forms such as *duṣprajāḥ* and *durmedhāḥ*. In other cases, it is already established by the rule *nañsubhyām*.
The suffix *aṇic* is applied after the word *dharma* when it stands alone.

The term *paramasvadharma* means "one’s own supreme duty. Regarding this, the word *sva* does not undergo prior placement [in the compound] because of the rule "there is an addition [of the prohibition] for pronouns and numerals"; however, it should be explained that the established [rule of prior placement] is not barred here, or alternatively, because [the compound] belongs to the class of *āhitāgni* and others (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the words *jambha*, *suharit*, *tṛṇa*, and *soma*.
Or it means "one whose speech is controlled," as seen in the expression: "Drink this water."
The word *dakṣiṇermā* is formed with the suffix *kan* when used in connection with a hunter (*lubdha*).

"Lubdha" means a hunter; however, poets employ it in the sense of mere injury—as in the example: "The one adorned with a garland of golden lotuses, a treasury of virtues, was made *dakṣiṇermā* (wounded on the right side) by an arrow. Regarding the word *vraṇitam*: it is formed from the noun *vraṇa* with the suffix *itac*; or alternatively, it is derived from the root *vraṇ* (meaning "to wound the limbs") with the causative (*ṇic*) suffix and the past passive participle (*kta*) suffix.
The suffix *ic* is applied after a verbal root when there is a reciprocal exchange of actions. 5.4.127.

This refers to the *bahuvrīhi* compound, because it occurs in the sense of mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*). In the examples provided, the lengthening of the initial vowel of the first member (*pūrvapada*) occurs according to the rule "it is seen [to happen] in other cases as well" (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*). Since this [term] is listed among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds, it receives the designation of *avyayībhāva*; consequently, being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the elision of case-endings (*subluk*) takes place—this is the intended meaning.

If this is so, since the designation *avyayībhāva* would sublate the designation *bahuvrīhi*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) would be established by the accent of the compound itself; thus, there would be no purpose in making the letter *c* (in *tiṣṭhadgu*) a marker (*cit*). However, it is for the sake of specification. For if that [marker] were not present, only the vowel *i* would be listed in the *tiṣṭhadgu*-class, and consequently, the rule "after a vowel, *i*" (*aca iḥ*) would also be included.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *dvidaṇḍi* and the others. 5.4.128.

If the intended meaning is that "words such as *dvidaṇḍi* are grammatically correct," how is the wording of the rule (*sūtra*) "from *dvidaṇḍi* and so forth" (*dvidaṇḍyādibhyaḥ*) to be explained? To this he says: "From *dvidaṇḍi* and so forth. This dative case (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*tādarthye*), and so on. Regarding the phrase "by way of the citation of the whole form" (*samudāyanipātanāt*): the meaning is that the citation of the whole form is for the sake of restricting their inclusion—i.e., establishing them—to only those cases where they are well-known as such wholes. For example: "He strikes with two sticks" (*dvidaṇḍi praharati*).

The analysis of the compound is: "two staffs in this striking instrument. Regarding the statement "it does not occur here": what does not occur? The meaning is that the word-form *dvidaṇḍī* is not grammatically correct.

Regarding the phrase "even though [the topic is] the *bahuvrīhi*": here too, the reason is precisely this: "and because of the technical designation (*nipātana*) of the whole compound. Now, one might object: "The correctness of forms such as *dvidaṇḍi* is already established simply by their being listed among the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in the suffix *ic*; so what is the point of this [rule]? That is not so; for correctness cannot be understood through mere listing alone. Consequently, the designation of *avyayībhāva* would not apply. Furthermore, the listing would be suspected of being non-Vedic (*anārṣa*), since it serves no purpose anywhere else.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *jñā*, following the prepositions *pra*, *sam*, and *abhi*, when the knees (*jānu*) are the object.

The term *jñu* is this substitute (*ādeśa*); however, it is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), because it is indicated by a genitive dual ending. For here, although the word *jānu* is singular, the indication *jānvoḥ* is made for the purpose of ensuring that it is understood without doubt as a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), by relying either on a duality residing in the meaning or on a duality based on the accompanying word (*upapada*).
In Vedic usage, however, the word *jñu* is seen even independently: e.g., *upajñubādho nabhasā* and *sadema vatsajñuṃ paśukāmasya*.
The substitute *anaṅ* is applied in place of the final portion of the word *ūdhas*.

By virtue of the inclusion of the marker *ṅit*, it is determined that this is a substitute for the final letter and that it begins with the vowel *a*; having ascertained this, he says, "the substitute *anaṅ* occurs. As in *kuṇḍodhnī*: [this is formed] by the rule *bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ* and *allopo'naḥ*.
The prescription of *anaṅ* is for the sake of subsequent rules, but here the form is established even by the substitution of *n*.
The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *gandha* when it follows *ut*, *pūti*, or *su-surabhi*.

The substitution of the phoneme *i* occurs; this determination of its status as a substitute (*ādeśa*) follows from its mention in the genitive case. Furthermore, its status as a substitute is established in order to distinguish it from the context [of the suffix], yet there is no fault whatsoever even in regard to this suffix itself.

This word *gandha* (fragrance) has both a denotation of substance (*dravyavacana*)—as in "this [river] carries water" or "this [grinder] grinds fragrances"—and a denotation of quality (*guṇavacana*)—as in "the fragrance of sandalwood. Among these, in order to include the sense of the quality, it says: "the substitution of *it* for *gandha*. Substance is a collection of form (*rūpa*) and other qualities; fragrance is its quality (*guṇa*) that constitutes a single part (*ekānta*) or a portion (*ekadeśa*). However, according to the view that substance is a composite whole (*avayavin*) distinct from form and the rest, the term "single part" (*ekānta*) is used figuratively (*iva*), because [the fragrance] is perceived as residing therein.

"Sugandha-āpaṇika" means one appointed to a shop (*āpaṇa*); *āpaṇika* is derived by adding the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule for words beginning with *prāgvahati*. Alternatively, the suffix *ṭhak* is added in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*) because the word belongs to the *adhyātma* group. Now, how can there be such expressions as "sugandhir vāyuḥ" (fragrant air) or "durgandhir vāyuḥ" (foul-smelling air), given that this odor is not a quality (*guṇa*) of the air? Let it not be its quality; nevertheless, the air is characterized (*lakṣyate*) by the odor because it has attained inseparability (*avibhāgāpanna*) from it. It is precisely this state of inseparability that is intended to be expressed, not the fact that it is a quality of that [air].

And having established this, even when an ointment such as saffron becomes non-distinct from Devadatta and so forth, the designation "Devadatta is fragrant" indeed occurs; in every respect, there is no cessation of the expression denoting the substance.
In the case of a word denoting something small. (Pāṇini 5.4.136)

"‘Supo’lpo’sminsūpagandhī’—this is an illustration of the meaning; however, the formal analysis (*vigraha*) is ‘in this there is a scent, that is, a trace, of soup. Otherwise, because the word *gandha* is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would have to be placed first [according to Pāṇini 2.1.57]. Or rather, the placement of the word *gandha* at the end occurs precisely due to this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*).”
The suffix *pāt* is elided after [words] other than *hastin* and so forth.

[The suffix] *lopa* (elision) occurs as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*). For if this were not a compound-final element, then by the rule "of the subsequent [element], [the operation applies] to the initial [sound]" (*ādeḥ parasya*), it would apply to the beginning [of the subsequent word], and furthermore, the suffix *kap* would also be liable to occur by the rule "optionally after what remains" (*śeṣādvibhāṣā*), because that rule relies upon a "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in relation to a compound-final element. But how can an elision, which is of the nature of a non-existence, be a final member (*antāvayava*)? To this he says: "by means of its substituendum" (*sthānidvāreṇa*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *kumbhapadī*. 5.4.139.

He says "starting with *kumbhapadī* and so forth" because the meaning of "beginning with" (*prabhṛti*) is understood from the use of the plural number. [The question is: "How then is there a mention in the sūtra using the locative case, which denotes 'having become' (*bhūta-vibhakti*), since it is the entire group that is being treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*)? To this he says "therein" (*tatra*). By the inclusion of the word "object" (*viṣaya*), he shows that in the sūtra there is a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), indicating how forms such as *kumbhapadī* and others are established. Because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the meaning to be understood is that "in the preceding case, elision occurs in that manner."

But for what purpose are the entire compounds taught as such, rather than simply listing *kumbha* and the others in the gaṇa and prescribing the elision of the word *pāda* that follows them? To this he replies: "And of the reading of the entire compound... He demonstrates the restriction of the scope itself: "...only in the feminine. And here, even in the feminine, only the suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]. The meaning is: only when [the suffix] *pādo'ntarasyām* is the domain for *ṅīp*.

Regarding the phrase "yac ca" and so forth: examples where the first member is a word of comparison include *kumbhapadī* (having feet like jars) and *jālapadī* (having webbed feet), and so on; examples where the first member is a numeral include *ekapadī* (one-footed) and *śatapadī* (hundred-footed). As for the form *aṣṭāpadī*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by way of an irregular grammatical rule (*nipātana*), or else the long *ā* is substituted according to the rule "aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām."
The suffix *datṛ* is applied after the word *vayas* in the sense of "having teeth. (Pāṇini 5.4.141)
Regarding *dvitanni*: because the vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering an *ugit*-operation, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *ugidacām*.
In the sense of "three nights," [the suffix *cha* is applied]. (Pāṇini 5.4.143)

This is for the sake of the absence of desire (*acchanda*). Regarding *ayogadantī*: she whose teeth are like iron is *ayodatī*; because of the *ugit* designation, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Regarding *samadantī*: by the rule beginning with "nāsikodaroṣṭha," the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* (optionally) [is applied] after the words *śyāva* and *lāroka*.
"Without light" means "without radiance. [The root] *ruc* means "to shine"; thus, *roka* is "shining," and it is so called because that [light] does not exist in him.
And [the suffix *matup* is applied] after words ending in *agra*, *anta*, *śuddha*, *śubhra*, *vṛṣan*, and *varāha*. (Pāṇini 5.2.145)
The particle *ca* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned;
[this applies to] "ahidat" and so forth. This has not been relied upon in the Bhāṣya.
There is elision of the [final vowel] of *kakuda* in the state of being a hump.
Regarding the phrase "produced by time and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the transformation of food and other such factors are included.
*trikakud* occurs [as a Bahuvrīhi compound]. 5.4.147.

Since the primary meaning of "hump" (*kakuda*) is impossible in the case of "mountain," which is the other word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*), he says: "a horn having the shape of a hump," and so forth. As for the phrase beginning with "na ca" (nor is it...), the word "ucyate" (it is said) is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). The statement beginning with "this is a technical designation" (*saṃjñaiṣā*) and so forth is obtained through irregular derivation (*nipātana*). And thus, the inclusion of the word "mountain" (*parvata*) is for the sake of clarity.
The suffix *kap* is applied after [stems ending in] *ara* and so forth.

"vyūḍhoraskaḥ" (broad-chested) and "priyasarpiṣkaḥ" (fond of ghee). [In these cases: by the rules "so'padādau" (Pāṇini 8.3.30) and "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.39), [the sibilant becomes ṣ]. From the root *nah* preceded by the prefix *upa*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the object because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group; thus, *upanaddhā* means "a shoe" (*upānat*). By the rule "nahivṛti" (Pāṇini 6.3.116), there is lengthening [of the vowel]; thus, one by whom the shoes have been taken off is *avamuktopānatkaḥ*. [In *dadhnaḥ* and *madhunaḥ*: by the rule "naho dhaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.34), [the *h* becomes *dh*], followed by the application of *jaś*-ness and *cartva*-ness.

"It becomes only a *vikalpa* (an optional rule). From the word *lakṣmī*, the suffix *kap* prescribed by the rule "nadī-ṛtaś-ca" does not occur as a mandatory (*nitya*) one; for the reading with the singular ending serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*). Regarding the phrase "after *artha* following *nañ*": the suffix *kap* necessarily occurs after a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the word *artha* which follows *nañ*. For example: *anarthakaḥ* ("one who has no purpose").
The [suffix] *ina* occurs in the feminine. (Pāṇini 5.4.152)
"The inclusion of the terms *ani*, *na*, *as*, and *m* causes the rule for what ends with them (*tadanta-vidhi*) to apply, whether [the preceding element] is meaningful or meaningless."
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *nadyṛt*. (Pāṇini 5.4.153)

Regarding the phrase "from a *bahuvrīhi* ending in a river-name (*nadī*)," the word "end" (*anta*) here refers to the final member of the compound; thus, the meaning is "from a *bahuvrīhi* that has a river-name as its final member. Alternatively, the term "*bahuvrīhi*" refers to the final member for the sake of the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself; thus, the meaning is "from [a *bahuvrīhi*] ending in a river-name. What is established by this? In cases such as *bahugrāmaṇīrnagarī* ("a city with many chiefs") and *bahukhalapūrnagarī* ("a city with many winnowers"), the suffix *kap* is prevented from occurring.
Optionally [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the remaining [stems]. (Pāṇini 5.4.154)

Regarding the phrase "from the bahuvrīhi": this ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "having resorted to"), thus signifying "having resorted to the bahuvrīhi. Consequently, even where a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) functions as a substitute—as in *vyāghrapāt*, *sugandhiḥ*, and *kuṇḍodhnī*—this [substitute] is also not considered a remainder (*śeṣa*). Alternatively, because the compound-final suffix is essentially a suffix (*pratyaya*), it is stated as "from that which [is the base]."

In this context, three possible interpretations of the term *śeṣa* (remainder) arise: it may refer to [the remainder] in relation to *kap*, or it may refer to the immediately preceding governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the *bahuvrīhi* compound, or it may refer to the requirement for a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). Regarding the first interpretation: in cases such as *vyāghrapāt*, *sugandhiḥ*, *dvidaśāḥ*, *anṛcaḥ*, and *vidhuraḥ*, the suffix *kap* would apply everywhere except where it is prescribed as mandatory (*nitya*). Furthermore, the mention of *śeṣa* would be redundant, because there is no possibility of an optional application (*vikalpa*) in a domain where *kap* is mandatory; otherwise, the mandatory rule itself would become purposeless.

Thinking that the undesirable consequence would still arise even in the second view regarding examples such as *dvādaśa*, he resorts to the third position: "the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) has not been prescribed. In cases like *bahukhaṭvaka*, there is the shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule *āpo'nyatarasyām*; in cases like *bahukhaṭva*, there is the shortening by the rule *go-striyor upasarjanasya*. The question "How so? and so forth refers to the inquiry: if "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is understood in relation to the compound-final suffix, [how can it apply here]? The answer is: "It is desired in specific instances. The implication is that in other domains—namely, in the case of the *sūkta* and the *sāman*—the status of being a "remainder" for a *bahuvrīhi* does indeed exist in relation to the compound-final suffix.

But for what purpose is the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) made? For, as long as compound endings (*samāsānta*) are prescribed, they alone will be the sublaters (*bādhaka*), since rules that have no other scope (*anavakāśa*) are sublaters, and those [compound endings] do have scope. What is their scope? It is the optional *kap* suffix; when *kap* does not apply, that is its scope—namely, other bases than those for which *kap* is specifically prescribed. When there is a conflict between both possibilities regarding specific bases, *kap* would apply because it is subsequent. Therefore, the mention of "the remainder" is necessary.
And [the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a word ending in the superlative suffix *īyas*.

"All *prāpti* (occurrence) is prohibited. However, the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is that the prohibition applies only to the suffix *kap*, which is characterized as being "residual" (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), according to the principle: "A rule or a prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding. This is understood because the term "from the remainder" (*śeṣāt*) has ceased to apply, while only the suffix *kap* continues to apply. In the case of *bahuśreyasī*, the prohibition applies here due to the inclusion of the feminine form (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇāt*). Just as the elision of the nominative singular suffix *su* occurs here by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* and so forth, we shall explain that very point in its proper place. Furthermore, even the shortening of the vowel (*hrasvatva*) does not take place.

The rule "gostriyor upasarjanasya" would have applied here. Why? To this he says: "īyaso bahuvrīhau," etc. By the statement regarding the treatment as masculine (puṃvad-bhāva), the intention here is not the removal of the feminine suffix; rather, its absence follows from the context of the section on short vowels (hrasva). Thus, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule "gostriyoḥ," it is stated: "A prohibition must be stated for [the application of] īyas in a bahuvrīhi compound."
The suffix *kha* is applied after [the word] *vandita* when it denotes the brother. || 5.4.157 ||

"Vanditaḥ stutaḥ" (praised as "worshipped"). Although the root *vadi* is listed in the sense of both "salutation" and "praise"—as in the rule "vadi abhivādana-stutyoḥ"—nevertheless, he shows through his commentary that only the sense of "praise" is to be understood here. Consequently, in the example *vanditabhrātṛkaḥ*, the suffix *kap* indeed occurs.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the words *nāḍī* and *tantrī* when they denote one’s own limb.

The word *nāḍī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, which marks it as belonging to a genus (*jāti*). The word *tantrī* ends in the vowel *ī* according to the rule "from the roots *avi*, *tṛ*, *stṛ*, and *tantrī*, [the suffix] *ī*. In the case of *bahurnāḍiḥ*, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel because it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). However, in the case of *bahutantrīḥ*, [shortening] does not occur due to the specific statement: "There is a prohibition for that which has already formed a feminine derivative (*kṛtstrīyaḥ*)."
And [the word] *niṣpravāṇi*. (Pāṇini 5.4.160)

"Pravāṇī" means "that in which weaving occurs. [The suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) to the root *veñ*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is according to the rule "kṛtyacaḥ."
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fifth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra;
now begins the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
A monosyllabic root has two occurrences of its first part.

In this context, although it is illogical for something to serve another's purpose when its own purpose is possible—and since its own purpose is indeed possible here due to the mention of both the rule to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and the agent of the action (*kārin*)—nevertheless, because of the consequence of futility in cases such as *liṭi dhātoḥ* where no thing to be enjoined is mentioned, this is not a mere injunction (*vidhi*) like *aṇ kuṭilikāyāḥ*, nor is it both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*) like *śeṣe*.

For if that were the case, since the reduplication of the first monosyllabic root (*ekāc*) would be established for all roots by this very rule, the rule "in the *liṭ* [perfect], after a verbal root" (*liṭi dhātoḥ*) and so forth would be redundant. If it is argued that there is no redundancy because of the restrictive rules (*niyama*)—"only after a verbal root in the *liṭ*" and "only in the *liṭ* after a verbal root"—we say no; for when both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restriction (*niyama*) are possible, the injunction is always superior. And if it is argued that [the injunction] has the purpose of being subservient to another [rule], we say no; for when both an injunction and a restriction are possible, the injunction is always superior.

For when this [rule] exists for the sake of another, its description is appropriate only insofar as those [other rules] possess the status of injunctions (*vidhi*); therefore, this is indeed for the sake of another. Even in that case, it is not a *paribhāṣā* stating that "the doubling being enjoined should be understood as belonging to the first single-vowel (*ekāc*)"; for if that were so, since its operation would occur only in the rule *sarvasya dve*, one would have had to state "of the first single-vowel" right there in that rule. Furthermore, rules such as *liṭi dhātoḥ* would become useless, because there would be no mention of anything to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Therefore, having determined that this is indeed a governing rule (*adhikāra*) by means of the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and because of its *svarita* accent, he says: "of a monosyllable (*ekāc*) and if it ends in /i/ (*it*)". While it could have been stated simply as "this is a governing rule," it was stated in this way in order to demonstrate its distinct *svarita* accent. Regarding these three [rules]: their purpose is that wherever something is required, there it is connected; for example, in the rule "of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), the phrase "of a monosyllable" (*ekāco dve*) is connected; in "the reduplicated [verb] is called *abhyasta*" (*abhe abhyastam*), the word "two" (*dve*) is connected; and in "in the *liṭ* [perfect], of the root" (*liṭi dhātoḥ*), all [three] are connected.

"From here onwards," and so forth, is an elaboration of what was just stated. [The phrase] "prior to the rule concerning *samprasāraṇa*" means that from that point onward, this [rule] has no connection; for either because another thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*) is indicated, or because of the interpretation that once the circumflex accent (*svarita*) has been applied, there is no governing heading (*adhikāra*).

He demonstrates that what was stated in general is established through an illustration—namely, "he will say. Here, if there were a connection based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*), it would apply only to roots such as *pac* and the like, and not to [roots] such as *jāgarti*. Furthermore, the mention of "the first" (*prathama*) would be purposeless, for among roots consisting of a single vowel, there is no second or subsequent single vowel. Nor can there be a connection with the phrase "of the first root" (*prathamasya dhātoḥ*).

For if that were the case, [the rule would apply] only to the root *bhū*, which is listed first in the Dhātupāṭha; consequently, one would have to mention *bhū* alone. Alternatively, could there be a connection [of the word *prathamasya*] with "of the first syllable of a monosyllabic root"? That is incorrect; for it is improper to abandon the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two items mentioned together, which is obtained by its very nature. Therefore, he states—[referring to the phrase] "of a part of the root"—that the connection is through grammatical apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). And [the phrase] "and of the second [syllable]"...

Although the mention of the second [suffix] is not present here, nevertheless, it is indeed governed by the rule "liṭi dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.8), and its meaning is being demonstrated; thus, there is nothing inconsistent. The examples beginning with *jajāgāra* are given in order according to their primary and secondary applications.

If this [term] *ekāc* were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, would there then be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [the word] *dhātoḥ*? In that case, [the rule for reduplication] would apply only to forms such as *iyāya* and *āre*; however, if there were lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then even though reduplication would occur in forms such as *papāca*, it would belong to the single consonant (*ajmātra*) alone. Consequently, [rules] such as *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*, and *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayesām* would become untenable.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "eka" (one) would be redundant; for, by the qualification "of the first vowel," and because a single root cannot have more than one initial vowel, the singularity of the vowel would already be intended by the term "vowel" (*ac*) itself. What, then, is the purpose of including "eka"? Therefore, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Thus he says: "The mention of 'ekāc' is a *bahuvrīhi* indication. The "indication of a *bahuvrīhi*" refers either to the expression of the intended meaning by means of a *bahuvrīhi*, or to the actual utterance of the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself. The presentation of the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is for the sake of clear understanding.

If this were a reference to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then—since a *bahuvrīhi* is primarily concerned with an external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—just as when it is said, "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought," it is the person who owns those brindled cows who is brought, and not the brindled cows themselves; so too here, only the two consonants situated on both sides of the vowel which they characterize would be doubled, and not the vowel (*aj*) that serves as the characteristic. To this, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).

Indeed, even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there are instances where the constituent member (*vartipada*) itself is connected with a grammatical operation (*kāryayoga*). For example: "Bring the one with white clothes" (*śuklavāsasam ānaya*), where the *bahuvrīhi* is used in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). In that case, just as in the words *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") and *viṣāṇī* ("horned"), when a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is produced to denote a relation (*saṃsarga*), that suffix, being inherent in both [the possessor and the possessed], results in the grammatical operation affecting the quality (*guṇa*) as well; likewise, in a *bahuvrīhi*, wherever the relation is the expressed meaning, the connection of the grammatical operation with the quality is not contradictory. The term "internal" (*abhyantara*) means "included within" (*antarbhūta*).

Regarding the reading *ābhyantaram*, it means "internal" (*abhyantara*), that is, the middle; what exists therein is "internal" (*ābhyantaram*). The meaning is that reduplication occurs only for a consonant (*sācaḥ*); just as another constituent part situated near it is reduplicated, so too is the vowel *a* which serves as a marker. And here the evidence is the rule "a long vowel is substituted for [the reduplicated syllable] when it is not followed by *kit*" (*dīrgho'kitaḥ*), and so forth. An objection is raised: "And thus in *pacityatra*..."—by that very [rule], the sound *ta* and the sound *pa* would be [reduplicated] as constituents of that [syllable].

And because of the principle of "designation as if possessing the property" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the letter *a* [in *acakāra*] is treated as a single vowel (*ekāj*), just as Devadatta is called "finger-possessing" (*aṅgulimān*) when pointing with a finger, even though his hand also possesses fingers; it is the same here. Consequently, the implication is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubling for all of them.

[Objection: "But surely, by the principle that 'when a meaningful element is mentioned, an meaningless one is not,' this will apply only to the whole (the root *jāgṛ*) and not to its parts. However, in that case, it would not apply to [roots] such as *jāgṛ* and *pac*. Furthermore, this paribhāṣā applies only where a specific verbal form (*śabdasvarūpa*) is mentioned, as in the rule for *śe*; here, however, since *jāg*, *pac*, and so on, are grasped through an external indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)—namely, 'a monosyllabic part of a root' (*dhātor avayavasyaikācaḥ*)—and not by their own form (*svarūpeṇa*), this paribhāṣā does not operate here. [The author] answers: "In that case... (*tatra*).

Among those [cases], such as the collection (*samudāya*) and so forth, when there are single-syllable [words], the first single-syllable members are not reduplicated. Why? He says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*), etc. The intention is this: Is it enjoined that all [members] be used simultaneously in a single application (*prayoga*), or alternatively (*paryāyeṇa*), or rather, by means of different applications, such that some [member] occurs in some [place]? The first alternative is not tenable, because both [the requirements of] cognition (*pramiti*) and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) would be impossible.

For instance: reduplication must be understood as being predicated of that which is characterized as having a single vowel (*ekāc*). However, it is not possible to simultaneously characterize a single constituent part (*avayava*) as having multiple constituent parts. Therefore, how could it be cognized simultaneously? Or, even if it were cognized, how could it be performed? For when one single-vowel element is being reduplicated, another single-vowel element cannot be reduplicated at that very same time, because speech occurs sequentially. Nor is the second alternative [the case]; for there is the prohibition "of that which is not repeated" (*anabhyāsasya*), and because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, since the undesirable consequence [of over-extension] applies to all cases due to the difference in grammatical application (*prayoga*), this very position is the only one that is possible. In that regard, when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the syllable *ni* for the root *ṇijir* (meaning "purification and nourishment") according to the rule for *ślau*, then in forms such as *nenekti* and *nenikta*, there is no fault whatsoever. However, in forms such as *nenijati*, *anejijuḥ*, and *nenijat*, the substitution of *at* by the rule *adabhyastāt*, the augment *jus* by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, and the prohibition of the suffixal marker *num* by the rule *nābhyastācchatuḥ* would not occur.

Is the fault not simply that, due to the intervention of the letter *ja*, the doubling of the letter *i* and the word *iccha* would fail to produce the correct form? The refutation of that is: "Because it would entail the abandonment of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). For when a constituent part is doubled, the treatise concerning other constituent parts and concerning the whole collection is abandoned.

[Objection: But surely, if that which is indeed established by the treatise (*śāstra*) were not put into practice, there would be a failure of the treatise. Here, however, it has been stated that [the doubling] is perceived in turn; and since that very thing has been performed, how can there be a failure of the treatise? [Reply: My friend, please explain this: when the word *paśu* is pronounced twice, why is the letter *c* not pronounced twice? If you say, "Because its doubling is not perceived at that time," then why is it not perceived? If you say, "Because it has not been determined to be a single vowel (*ekāc*) together with that [consonant]," then why is it not so determined? Silence is the answer here.

Therefore, in whatever application, whatever [element] and however much can be determined as having a single initial syllable, the reduplication of all that must be recognized and performed. Otherwise, if it were done differently, it would bring about a violation of the scripture in respect to both the theoretical understanding and the practical performance. Thus, there is reduplication of the whole. And even in this view, there is no violation of the scripture regarding the individual parts.

Since a composite whole consists of its parts, it is certainly not possible to utter the whole twice without uttering the parts twice; for example, when a tree moves, it moves together with its parts.

Now, how can there be reduplication in *papāca*, given that this is a root itself and not a part of a root, nor is it "first"? For when there are second [sounds] and so on, that which has nothing before it is called "first. Furthermore, how could this apply in cases such as *iyāya*, where there is no external referent for the rule "of a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*)? To this he says: "In *papāca* here... [and] "also the state of being a single-vowel (*ekāctva*)"; by the word "also," the state of being "first" is included; in both cases, it is a part relative to the root. [The principle of] "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) applies.

The meaning is that for those things which possess both primary designation (*mukhya-vyapadeśa*) and part-designation (*avayava-vyapadeśa*), such as "waking" and so forth in the states of waking and the rest—just as it happens for them, so it happens for these [states] as well. Nor is this a mere statement; rather, this is a worldly principle (*laukika-nyāya*). For in the world, even when there is no external difference in substance, a distinction in designation based on a difference in state is observed, as in the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*).
That which is seen as a "stone statue" is designated as "this is its body" by way of a perceived difference in state, such as being in a condition of being bought or sold.

In the case of *papāca* as well, it can be designated as a "part" (*avayava*) because the form ending in the *liṭ* suffix currently being employed is a part of the root *pac*, whose domain of application is infinite. Furthermore, just as in common usage the word "first" (*prathama*)—even when applied to a single entity such as in "she was killed first" (*hatā prathamam*)—is used by mentally postulating non-existent second instances and so forth due to its similarity to a primary "first," so too is it here.

Even in the case of *iyāya*, the referent for the single vowel *i*—as found in the various usages such as *itaḥ*, *yanti*, *āyan*, *āgāt*, and *jigamiṣati*—is likewise postulated as the meaning of the other word (*anya-padārtha*). Furthermore, the distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*) is determined by what is well-known (*prasiddhi*) and what is not. Since such usage is well-established even in the case of the primary sense, there is no fault of being secondary. And having established this, [the grammatical rules] such as *vyatho liṭi*, *bhavateraḥ*, *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, and *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* become logically consistent.

In this context, since the word "two" (*dve*) requires a correlate to be numbered, and because the subject under discussion is the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the correlate is the form of the word. By the rule "the genitive denotes the element to be replaced" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*), when there is a genitive of the locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) in the rule "for a monosyllable, the first [is doubled]" (*ekācaḥ prathamasya*), the meaning becomes: "two forms of the word take the place of one. This is as in the case of "asterbhūḥ" and similar rules; thus, the position that "doubling occurs in place of [the original]" (*sthāne dvirvacanam*) is established.

When the word *uccāraṇe* (in the act of utterance) is connected with the number [denoted by *dvir*], then—since a connection between the action-form (*kriyārūpa*) and the word (*śabda*) as the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is impossible—the genitive case *ekācaḥ* is understood as a genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to the supplied action of utterance; thus, the meaning is "two utterances of that which has a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ dve uccāraṇe bhavataḥ*), or "one should utter that which has a single vowel twice. In that case, the view is that "reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is the double employment (*dviḥprayoga*)."

In that regard, in the first position, although no fault arises—since by the rule "the most similar [substitute] occurs in place" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*), two [substitutes] most similar in terms of sound are prescribed, and thus whatever [substitutes] might apply would be valid—nevertheless, in the case of *cicīṣati*, because the genitive case in the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* will be established as denoting the "place" (*sthāna*), when *cis* is replaced by the different word *ciscis* as a substitute, there is no authority for the *s* residing therein to be considered *san* (the suffix *san*). Consequently, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *ajjhanagamāṃ sani* would not occur.

The status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is stated for the substitute itself, not for a part of the substitute; therefore, by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, the property of being a *san* [suffix] does not belong to that part. However, its scope (*avakāśa*) is where the entire *san* undergoes reduplication and acquires the status of a *san* through *sthānivadbhāva*, as in the case of *iṇaḥ san*: *īṣiṣati*.

But surely, since reduplication applies when another form is obtained and lengthening applies when it is not obtained, both rules being of equal force, lengthening would take effect first, and then reduplication would occur? In that case, consider the root *hvayati* with the suffix *san*, resulting in *hnās*; here, there is reduplication of the whole [stem] as a substitute for the whole. In that situation, the distinction "this is the base" and "this is the suffix" does not exist; consequently, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by the rule *hvo'bhyastasya* would not occur, whereas it would occur only in forms such as *juhāva* and *juhuvatuḥ*, where—

Is there not the fault that *hvām* would undergo reduplication by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)? This is not a fault; for in the rule *hvo 'bhyastasya*, both genitives are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). First, there is the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) and the substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*) of the root *hvayati* before it becomes reduplicated. Then, lengthening occurs either by the rule *halaḥ* or by *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani*. Finally, the reduplication applies to the form *hvās*.

And here, in cases such as *pipakṣati* and *udvivakṣati*, [the rule] "what is previously established is not valid for reduplication" applies. However, in forms like *āṭiṭat* and *āśiśat*, even though the *ṇi*-suffix has been elided, because of the rule "in place of a reduplicated syllable before a vowel," there is a status as if it were the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*). Since no other word-form takes its place, and because this is obligatory, reduplication occurs first. Consequently, the entire complex becomes a substitute for the entire complex; therein, because the original state is lost, the nature of base and suffix is destroyed. Thus, that *ṇi* no longer exists, and the elision of *ṇi* should not occur. Its scope, however, is in cases such as *kārayati*.

Furthermore, in this case, when the entire complex *jighāṃsati* is substituted for the complex [desiring to kill], the root *han* would no longer exist; consequently, the substitution of *k* (kutva) in the form *abhyāsācca* [Pāṇini 7.3.55] would not apply to *han*. However, forms such as *jaghanitha*, *jaghantha*, *ahaṃ kila jaghana*, and *jaghanvān* provide the scope [for that rule], because in these instances, the simple root *han* itself undergoes reduplication, thereby allowing for the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus, since the first position is flawed, he states—relying on the second position—that "reduplication occurs through double employment" (*dviḥprayoge dvirvacanam*). The word *ca* is used here for emphasis.

But how, given the paribhāṣā "the genitive [case ending] is used in the sense of 'in place of'," can the view of double utterance (dviḥprayoga) be maintained? To this he replies: "For the number belongs to the repetition. If the number were prescribed for the repetition itself, then a triple utterance (trirvacana) would result. For the initial utterance is not a repetition; thus, that one [initial utterance] plus the two repetitions would lead to the undesirable consequence of a triple utterance. Therefore, the number is produced by the repetition.

Of what is the number of repetitions [the attribute]? Of the utterance; the meaning is that the repeated utterance is prescribed. And it has already been stated that in that case, the relationship of substituend and substitute (sthānyādeśabhāva) is not possible.
