In this view, he demonstrates how no fault occurs in examples such as *aṭiṭat* and so forth, by means of the words beginning with "by that" (*tena*).

But surely, even in this view, in forms such as *nematuḥ* and *sehe*, once the substitution of *n* for *ṇ* and the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* have been applied, the status of the root as "beginning with a substitute" (*ādeśāditva*) does not cease even when there is reduplication; thus, the substitution of *e* for *ai* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) would not occur. However, in the alternative view, there is no designation [of the reduplicated form] as "beginning with a substitute. There is no fault here because, due to its dependence on the letter *a* (*alāśrayatva*), the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) does not apply, and because the entire form is a single substitute (*samudāyādeśatva*), it lacks the status of "beginning with a substitute. Furthermore, by the qualification "in the context of *liṭ*," the substitutions of *n* and *s* are not dependent on external conditions (*anaimittikatva*).

In that case, regarding the form *vebhiditā*: from the word *vebhidya*, when the suffix *tṛc* is added and the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) and the elision of *y* (*yal-lopa*) have been performed, since this [root] is the very same one that was a single vowel (*ekāc*) and unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), there would be a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. However, in the other view, because the designation as "having a single vowel" (*ekāj-vyapadeśa*) does not depend on the presence of the elided *a*, and because *vebhidy-* consists of two syllables (*dvy-actva*), there would be no prohibition. Even with the doubling [of the root], there is no fault; for even in an operation based on what precedes, the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) retains its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were still present).

In that case, one might object: "In *jarīgṛhīta*, there would be lengthening of the vowel of the root *grah* when followed by the *liṭ* affix, for here the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply, as it is prohibited in rules prescribing lengthening. This is not a fault; for the term "single-vowel" (*ekāc*) from the rule "ekāca upadeśe" will be carried over [into this rule]. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Lengthening occurs for that *iṭ* which is prescribed after an *ārddhadhātuka* affix following the root *grah*"; thus, it will not apply to the *iṭ* prescribed after the word *jarīgṛhya*. And likewise in *siṣecati*, even though the *liṅ* affix is prescribed after the root *sic*.

Nevertheless, when reduplication has been performed, the designation *pada* applies to the whole complex and not to its individual parts. Since the rule for including the beginning of a word (*tadādigrahaṇa*) does not cease even when the word *sec* is designated as a *pada*, it is impossible to exclude the reduplicated syllable; thus, there is no prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*. In this case, however, in forms such as *vibhidvān*, the status of being a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is not attained even if the root is uttered a hundred times, let alone twice; consequently, there would be the undesirable application of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *vasvekājāddhasām*. This is not so.

Because when a contradictory number arises due to a difference in pronunciation, the designation established by the previous number is set aside. For this very reason, the mention of "ādi" (beginning with) was made [in the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*] for the sake of the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *papivān*. [Objection: In that case, here in *viśuṣvāpa*, since it is merely the doubling of that very meaningful root, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would possess meaning. Consequently, in the rule *supeḥ ṣatvam* ("the substitution of *ṣ* after *su*"), the example *viṣuṣupuḥ* which is about to be cited would be contradicted, because [there the reduplicated syllable] is meaningless. [Reply: This is not a fault.

The determination of all meanings of a word occurs through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, in this case [of repetition], no new meaning arises when the repetition is produced, nor does it disappear when it ceases. [Objection: But if that very same thing is uttered twice, there must also be a recurrence of the cognition of the meaning, just as in "Snake! Snake! Wake up! Wake up! [Response: What can we be reproached for here? It is not the cognitions of the meaning that recur! Let it be seen thus: just as in cases such as "dream," "slept," or "did not dream," [the form] is sometimes unaltered and sometimes altered.
In some cases, it conveys its meaning by depending on the augment *aṭ*; likewise, in examples such as *suṣvāpa*, it conveys the meaning only when it is repeated.
Of that which begins with a non-initial consonant, the second [syllable] is reduplicated.

This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the first doubling (*dvirvacana*). Now, an opposition between two rules (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) occurs when there is a contradiction and they yield the same result, as in the case: "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the Vājapeya should be made eight-cornered" and "it should be four-cornered"—here, the eight-corneredness and four-corneredness are in opposition. Similarly, in the rule "The rice-porridge (*caru*) is of wild grains (*naivāra*), [prepared from] those [grains] winnowed by the nails," the threshing (*avaghāta*), which has the result of removing the husk, is superseded by the winnowing with the nails, which also results in the removal of the husk; thus, the mortar and pestle are set aside by the nails.

But where this pair [of rules] does not both apply, there is no sublation (*bādha*), as in the case of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for *kṛt* and *kṛtya* suffixes, or as in the case of the technical designations for *taddhita* and *tadrāja* suffixes. However, in the present instance, there is no equality of result (*samānaphalatva*).

Because there is no such thing as a "third" fruit, how could it be possible for both to exist? One might argue: "When two people are seated and a third person sits down between them, he becomes the second; likewise, when the first is repeated, the second becomes the third. Thus, the possibility of a 'third' certainly exists. This might be so, provided that the repetition of the first necessarily occurs beforehand. Furthermore, what is being stated here is not the repetition of an inherently second entity; rather, what is it?
[The rule applies] to the second member alone; what follows from that? It will apply to that which is the second [member] when the first has been doubled.

But surely, in this way, it would be equivalent to the objection regarding the non-commencement (*anārambhasama*). How so? [Consider] *aṭ* with the suffix *san*: after the first [consonant] has been doubled, we have *aṭ-aṭ*. At this stage, both the rule for the "retention of the initial" (*halādiśeṣa*) and the doubling of the second [consonant] apply. Because it is subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*), the "retention of the initial" applies first; then the doubling follows. When we have *a-aṭ-aṭ*, and the "retention of the initial" has applied, there are three *a*s. By the rule "guṇa for *at*" (*ato guṇe*) resulting in the single substitute form (*pararūpatva*), the form would be *aṭiṣati*. However, even if the doubling had not occurred, the form would be exactly the same; for in both cases, there is merely the single substitute form resulting from two *a*s.

It is equal in its various operations; how so? First, there is reduplication, then the rule that only the initial consonant remains (*halādiḥśeṣaḥ*). When the form *a-aṭ* has been established, both the substitution of *i* by the rule *sanyataḥ* and reduplication apply. Between these two obligatory rules, the substitution of *i* takes precedence because it is subsequent in the order of the rules.

[Objection: But since *itvam* (the substitution of *i*) depends on both the presence of the suffix *san* and repetition (*abhyāsa*), it is *bahiraṅga*; what follows from that? [Answer: The *antaraṅga* substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇaḥ* would apply; and when the locus (*āśraya*) is the same, that which pertains to the phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to the morphological element (*āṅga*). [Reply: If that is so, then even after the *pararūpa* has been applied, *itvam* would still apply because of the treatment as being "as if the final" (*antavadbhāva*); and since it would also apply before the *pararūpa* is applied, it possesses two grounds for its superiority: its *nityatva* (invariable necessity) and its *paratva* (subsequent application). The *pararūpa*, however, has only one ground for its superiority, namely its *antaraṅgatva*. Therefore, *itvam* indeed takes effect first.

But when that [doubling] exists, both *iyaṅ* (by the rule "abhyāsasyāsavarṇe") and doubling apply. In that case, if doubling occurs after *iyaṅ* has been applied, the suffix *yaṅ* applies; but if it has not been applied, *aṅ* applies. Because it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*), it is non-eternal (*anitya*). Therefore, because it is subsequent and eternal, once *iyaṅ* has been applied, there is doubling of the word *yaṅ*, followed by *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* (retention of the first consonant), and then *itvam* (the substitution of *i*); thus we get *iyiṭiṣati*. From the root *oṇ*, we get *uvuvoṇiṣati*. If the second doubling did not exist, we would get *iyaṭiṣati* and *uvoṇiṣati*; thus, there is no parity between the two cases regarding the effort required.

If that is the case, then because of the prohibition "of what is not repeated," it would be impossible for one thing to be uttered twice when another cannot be uttered twice; thus, this very [rule] would be unestablished. Alternatively—when a rule is prescribed for a specific instance, it sublates a rule prescribed for a general instance even if both are possible, just as in the case: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇkaḍinya.

If you argue that here there is a sublation of the curd because the result called "sprinkling the rice" is the same, then here too there is a single result called "denoting the meaning," for the double utterance is for the sake of denoting the meaning, and that is accomplished by the first [utterance] alone.

Now, is the fruit called "a specific excellence of form" distinct? For the form of the first [element] in the case of reduplication is one thing, and that of the second is another? In the other case as well, the fruit called "a specific excellence of satisfaction" differs; for the satisfaction derived from curd is one thing, and that from buttermilk is another. Therefore, it is not impossibility, but rather the fact of being commenced when [the general rule] has not yet applied, that is the basis for sublation. For general terms, in the proximity of specific terms, are restricted either to those specific instances or elsewhere—just as in the cases:
"Vasiṣṭha is a Brāhmaṇa," and "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived, Vasiṣṭha has also arrived."

[Objection: But since Kauṇḍinya is also a Brāhmaṇa, would the curd not also apply to him? Furthermore, since the doubling (dvirvacana) being prescribed here for the first [element] does not apply to the second, how can it be said that "there is no non-application" (yena nāprāpti)? [Response: It is not that the sequence applies to the second; rather, the doubling of the first, which is prescribed generally for verbal roots, applies to a root beginning with a vowel. In that case, the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) differs—namely, the curd and the buttermilk—but here it is the grammatical operation (*kārya*) that differs, while the thing to be enjoined, the doubling, is one and the same: this much is the distinction.

Alternatively, even there, it is giving alone that is to be enjoined; its distinction arises from the difference in the objects to be given, while here the distinction arises from the difference in those who seek a favor. Thus it has been said: "This second dual number is an exception to the first dual number. In every respect, the first dual number is superseded by the second dual number.

If this were the case, then just as the first reduplication would apply to a monosyllabic root (*ekāc*) in its original state, so too the second reduplication would be its sublater; since this [second reduplication] applies to the root together with its consonant, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the consonants also do not repeat. This would indeed be the case if something were either prescribed or prohibited for the first monosyllable in the context of roots beginning with vowels (*aj-ādi*); however, here, because of the presence of a specific [rule], the general term [for "first"] applies elsewhere than that, specifically in the case of roots beginning with vowels.

Since the form of the first doubling is not perceived, its non-occurrence is inferred, which constitutes the sublation (*bādha*). Furthermore, when a consonant serves as the *kāryin* (the subject undergoing an operation), it is then considered a member (*aṅga*) of that [consonant]; thus, because it is included within the single instance of the second [doubling], by what could its doubling along with that [consonant] be prevented? In this regard, the evidence is the prohibition "not *n*, *d*, or *r*" (*na ndrāḥ*).

Now, in cases such as *athaiyāya* and *āreyāya*, by what rule does the doubling [of the vowel] occur? It cannot be by this [present rule], because it is not applicable to a second [vowel]; nor can it be by the preceding [rule], because that rule does not apply to vowels beginning with *a* (*ajādi*). Is it not the case that where this [present rule] does not apply—namely, where it does not operate due to the absence of a second [vowel]—there its application is not precluded? Even there, its application is indeed precluded, because of the general designation "beginning with *a*" (*ajādi*).

For if there were a general designation, it would subvert [the rule] everywhere, even in a particular individual that possesses a second [consonant], just as it will be stated regarding *halādiśeṣa*: "The *halādiśeṣa* rule, though applying in some instances, effects an exclusion everywhere. This is not a fault;
for here the individual is grasped primarily as characterized by its genus (*jāti*). Therefore, this [rule] operates only upon that individual which possesses a second [consonant].
"And where this [process] proceeds, there it first ceases;
however, in the case of the *halādiśeṣa* rule, the *jāti* (the universal) is primarily relied upon. Thus [it is said].

"And with respect to a quality (*guṇa*)," [it is said]. Because of its permanence (*nityatva*) and its superiority (*paratva*), the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply. Consequently, after the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of *isa*, and after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* and the lengthening (*dīrghatva*), there would be the undesirable contingency (*prasaṅga*) of the form *arīṣati*. Nor is the augment *iṭ* here the cause for the reduplication; the point is that only that after which the reduplication is prescribed is its cause. What then is the subject of the operation (*kāryin*)? It is the root, because of the recourse to the genitive case in the rule *sanyaṅoḥ*. What follows from this? He says: "And not... and so forth.

The meaning is that even though the state [of the cause] exists when the effect exists, its status as a *nimitta* (cause/condition) is not established in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) because there is no mention of it in the locative case (*saptamī*). He says "for instance" (*tathā hi*) to show that this must necessarily be understood in this way. Regarding "of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*": since *vṛddhi* is also prohibited by the rule "before *k* and *ṅ* suffixes" (*kṅiti ca*), the expression "of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*" is used. In the example *śayitā*, the prohibition of *guṇa* does not apply. However, some read *śāyaka* instead; that is incorrect, because here the *vṛddhi* is not part of the base form (*aprakṛtitvāt*). Furthermore, in the subsequent text, only the mention of *guṇa* is made.

The phrase "of those, the second" is for the sake of clarity; [it means] that the word "tasmāt" (from that) will refer only to the immediately following second [element], and not to the third and so on. However, when there is a genitive case from a *bahuvrīhi* compound—such as "that root whose beginning is a vowel"—then, since the rule would apply even in a sense other than the nominative by virtue of the syntactic connection (*sāmarthya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying to the third and subsequent elements as well.
The letters *n*, *r*, and *l* are not [subject to doubling] when they are the first members of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Pāṇini 6.1.3.

The roots *undī* (in the sense of moistening), *adḍa* (in the sense of assault)—which has *d* as its penultimate letter—and which undergoes the change to *ṣṭu*; *arca* (in the sense of worship); *īkṣa* (in the senses of seeing and marking); *ana* (in the sense of breathing); *drā* (in the sense of contemptuous motion); and whatever needs to be said regarding the root *ubj*—all that has already been stated in the very rule *hayavaraṭ*.
Regarding the phrase "preceded by *ya*" (*yakārapara*): the meaning is that of which the letter *y* is subsequent to the letter *r*.

"Of the *vyañjana*": this means of a monosyllabic root (*ekāc*) accompanied by a third consonant. In that case, there is no doubling of the letter *ṣ*. "But others," however: in this alternative view, the explanation should be "when *san* has been applied to the root *īrṣyati*, because a third monosyllable related to that [root] is impossible. "Nominal roots" (*nāmadhātavaḥ*): these are verbal roots derived from nouns (*subdhātavaḥ*).
"The preceding is the reduplicated syllable" (*pūrvo 'bhyāsaḥ*). 6.1.4.

"By implication (*arthāt*). By force of the context, this word *pūrva* denotes a member (*avayava*); and a member belongs to a whole (*avayavin*). Since no such [whole] has been specified here, the word "two" (*dve*) must necessarily be supplied here. Nor is it the case that even when supplied, the word ending in the nominative case alone is sufficient to fulfill the requirement for a whole; this is what is meant by "by implication. "In this section" means that this technical name (*saṃjñā*) does not apply within the section beginning with "doubling of everything" (*sarvasya dve*); therefore, in that context, there is an absence of [rules such as] the substitution of a single substitute for homogeneous consonants (*halādiśeṣa*).

If this is so, would [the rule] "there are two [substitutions] for *dyuti*, *gami*, *juhoti*, and so forth" not fail to apply here? An effort must be made in this regard. [The phrase] "the former part of those two" implies that the ablative case is not used in connection with directional words (*dikśabda*) that denote parts; this is indicated by the evidence of the rule "its repetition is *prāmreḍita*. In forms such as *papāca*, the various operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) apply as appropriate: "the first consonant remains" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), "for *a* in *saN*" (*sanyataḥ*), "long vowel for non-*kit* roots" (*dīrgho'kitaḥ*), "for *ku* and *hu*, *cu*" (*kuhoścuḥ*), "for *ca* and *ja* in the reduplication" (*abhyāse carca*), "like *saN*" when the penultimate is light (*sanvallaghuni*), and "long vowel for a light [penultimate]" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).
Both [the preceding and following vowels] become *abhyasta* [when they form part of a reduplicated stem]. 6.1.5.

The phrase "two" (*dve*) is understood from the context of "the present tense," and so forth. The mention of "both" (*ubhe*) is for the purpose that the single designation *abhyasta* (repeated) should apply to the entire repeated group, so that two separate designations do not apply to each of the two parts; it is not, however, for the purpose of specifying the technical term (*saṃjñin*). This is because the specification of the term is already established by the recurrence of the word "two" (*dve*) itself. In forms such as *dadati*, there is the substitution of *at* by the rule *ad abhyastāt*, and the elision of the long *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "in *nenijati*," and so forth: if both [the terms] were not included [in the rule], then because one observes that each individual word completes the sentence in rules such as *vṛddhir ādaic*, here too [the rule] would apply to each [word] individually. Consequently, in *nenijati*, there would be a separate initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) for each. Nor could there be the single [word] being unaccented according to the rule *anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*; for the reason for identifying the specific word to be excluded—such as its being *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining when others have been elided) and so on—is impossible. Even if this were the case, there would still be an alternation (*paryāya*).

But surely, by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *bhī-hrī-bhṛ-hu-mada*, [the augment] will not apply to the subsequent [vowel]? Then it would not apply to the preceding one either, because of the intervention by the subsequent [vowel]. And since the accent (*svara*) is prescribed, that very same contingency of alternation (*paryāya-prasaṅga*) would follow.

If, however, the use of a "great designation" (mahāsaṃjñā) is for the purpose of conveying that the name is descriptive (anvartha)—just as in the case of designations such as *saṃyoga* or *samāsa*—and it is therefore stated that the designation applies only to the whole (*samudāya*) upon the understanding of its descriptiveness, then the mention of "both" (*ubhe*) could be omitted. [Objection: But surely the mention of "both" must be made so that the rule applies where both [the vowel and the consonant] are heard, and not where one or the other is absent?

Otherwise, in the case of the root *ṛdh* and the root *āp* in the form *sanīvantaḥ*, when the suffix *iṭ* is absent, the substitution of *ī* by the rule "āpjñapyṛdhāmīt" would apply because it is subsequent and specifically prescribed (*pratipadavihita*). Then, after applying the doubling of the second monosyllable (excluding the *r*) due to the prohibition "na ndrāḥ," the designation "abhyasta" (repeated) would occur before the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*atra lopo'bhyāsasya*) because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). Now, would that designation apply to each [monosyllable] individually or to the whole aggregate? In the first case (individual application), even if the reduplicated syllable were elided, the subsequent [portion] would not be removed.

Even in the view that [the term] refers to the aggregate (*samudāya*), the designation (*saṃjñā*) previously applied to the aggregate would persist in what remains even after one part has been removed—just as the designation "taddhita" persists in *bhūyān* even when the *ī* of *īyasun* has been elided. And if that designation were present, then in forms such as *īpsanti*, *aipsan*, *īrtsanti*, and *airtsan*, there would result the occurrence of *adbhāva*, *jus*, *bhāva*, and *num*. Therefore, must the mention of "both" (*ubhe*) be made for the sake of understanding what is actually heard? No; because it is established just as in the case of *pratīṣiṣati* and so forth.

For instance, in the case of *ajāderdvitīyasya* ("of the second [syllable] beginning with a vowel"), when the suffix *san* is reduplicated, even though the designation *abhyasta* applies to both audible [syllables], the substitution of *at* and so forth does not occur. And just as in examples such as *putrīyiṣati*, where the suffix *san* is reduplicated according to the rule *yatheṣṭaṃ nāmadhātūnām* ("one may choose any [part] of nominal stems"), it will likewise not occur here.

For here, when *īpsa-jhi* and *īrtsa-jhi* have been established, the substitution of *ad* occurs first because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Indeed, the substitution of *ad* would not apply once the suffix *śap* has been added, as it would be intervened by that [suffix]; thus, it is non-obligatory (*anitya*). Consequently, the substitution of *anta* (as prescribed by *jño 'ntaḥ*) would apply, along with the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding vowel; however, due to its priority, the *anta*-substitution takes effect. The single-substitute is obligatory: it applies whether the *anta*-substitution has occurred or not. The *anta*-substitution, however, is non-obligatory; for once the single-substitute has occurred, the [root] is treated as if it were the end of a word (*antavadbhāva*), and being thus included by the term "reduplicated" (*abhyasta*), it is superseded by the substitution of *ad*.

And that for which the cause is destroyed by another rule is *anitya*. Now, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *antaraṅga* because it depends on the phonemes (*varṇa*), whereas the final-substitute (*antādeśa*) is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on the stem (*aṅga*). Furthermore, when both depend on the same basis, "that which depends on the phoneme is stronger than that which depends on the stem. However, the final-substitute is also *antaraṅga*, for he will state: "In the case of *āyan*, *ādin*, etc., there is the instruction to treat them as if they were original (*upadeśivat*).

Thus, since both are *antaraṅga* and both are *nitya*, the final-substitute prevails due to its posteriority. Consequently, because the letter *jha* is absent, the substitute *āt* does not occur, as it would lack a basis in a vowel (*al*) and thus the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original) does not apply.

Or, let there be the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) first; even so, in the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*, because the term *anataḥ* is connected with the preceding rule *adabhyastāt*, the substitution of *at* will not occur due to the status of the single substitute as the original locus (*sthānivadbhāva*), even when the operation is based on the preceding rule. Similarly, in the case of *īpsan*—where, after *īpsa-jhi* has been established, both the *śap* augment and the *jus* substitution would apply—the *śap* is applied first because it is obligatory; once *śap* has been applied, the *jus* substitution does not occur because of the intervention by that [augment].

Furthermore, even when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding element has been applied, there is no recurrence of the *jus* replacement because that [single substitute] is treated as the final element (*antadbhāva*). This is because, according to the rule "in the application of a grammatical operation following a preceding element, the substitute is treated as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), it retains its status. In the case of *īpsan*, the present tense suffix *laṭ* is replaced by *śatṛ*. When the form *īpsa-śatṛ* is established, since the addition of *śap* depends only on the *sārvadhātuka* suffix and is thus an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation, it is applied first. Then, after the *guṇa* substitution of the following form (*pararūpa*)—where the *a* of *san* combines with the root vowel—the locative case ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*) arises. At that stage, although the insertion of *num* would otherwise be applicable, [it does not occur].

Because there is no separation (*vyapavarga*) between the two [sounds] following the root, and because the status of being "end-like" (*antavat*) or "beginning-like" (*ādivat*) is absent due to their dependence on both phonemes, there is no application of the prohibition. This is likewise the case in forms such as *pratīṣiṣanti*. However, in cases such as *cikīrṣanti*, where the vowel *a* of the suffix *san* is not reduplicated, there is an absence of the substitution of *at* (for *it*) and so forth, because of the intervention by that very [vowel].
The six [roots] beginning with *jakṣ* [are termed *ad*]. 6.1.6.

In this context, when the *śtip* affix is applied to the root *jakṣ*, and the augment *iṭ* is added by the rule "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke," the form becomes *jakṣiti*. If it were understood that "those which have *jakṣiti* as their first" constitute the group *jakṣityādayaḥ*, then the seventh root, *vevyati*, would not be included. For the sake of brevity and to avoid ambiguity, one should have simply designated them as *jakṣyādayaḥ*. Therefore, this is not the aforementioned analysis; rather, he says: "The word *jakṣa* is a separate word," meaning that these six roots beginning with *jakṣa* [are the ones intended].

By the word *iti*, the immediately preceding *jakṣi* is indicated. The word *ādi* signifies proximity; it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities of the members do not apply to the whole (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). "This very [form]" means that which has been described in the manner stated. "This accent" [is used] because otherwise, due to the *ṅit*-designation, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would be unaccented, leaving the accent of the verbal root; then, upon the substitution of *yaṇ*, the rule "of an acute and a circumflex" would result in a circumflex accent [for the *yaṇ*]. It is established by the transposition [of voice] in the case of the *śatṛ* suffix; since a *parasmaipada* ending is impossible due to the *ṅit*-designation, there is a transposition [to the *ātmanepada*].

The mention of "six" (ṣaḍ) is redundant; let *jakṣ* and the others be included up to the end of the *āgaṇa*. Why does [the rule] not apply to those which are recited after *vevīṅ*? Here the reading of the *gaṇa* is as follows: immediately after *vevīṅ*, "ṣasa svapne, vaśa kāntau, carkarītaṃ ca, hnuṅ apanayane"; some read "āṅaḥ śasu" immediately after *vevīṅ*, and "ṣasti svapne". Among these, *āśās* is not a distinct [root].

The majority of reduplicated (abhyasta) verbal forms belong to the *parasmaipada* (active voice), whereas this [root] is *ātmanepada*. Furthermore, there is no distinction regarding the accent of the reduplicated form (*abhyastasvara*). How so? Even when it is not reduplicated, following a root that has an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta*, as is the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). The *carkarīta* formation is indeed non-reduplicated; *ṣasa* and *ṣasti* are Vedic, as is *vaśi*; moreover, its usage in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is not considered correct, provided the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* are authoritative. As for *hnuṅ*, because it bears the marker *ṅit*, the occurrence of *parasmaipada* endings is impossible.

In that case, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) would be obtained. However, by the force of the prohibitive statement "of *aṅ* and *niṅ*" (*aṅnviṅoḥ*), it will not occur. If it were to occur, then in forms such as *apahnavate*, since the accent of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyastasvara*) is present, the subsequent *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would necessarily be subject to the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*); thus, the prohibition would be purposeless. Therefore, so that the accent of the suffix may indeed apply and the lack of accent for the *lasārvadhātuka* (*lasārvadhātukānudāttatva*) does not occur, the prohibition "of *aṅ* and *niṅ*" becomes meaningful. Consequently, by the force of this prohibition, the accent of the suffix itself will occur, and not the accent of the reduplicated syllable.

Now, it might be argued that the accent of the affix (*abhyasta-svara*) is prescribed when [the root] begins with a vowel; what follows from this? Even though that [affix-accent] would apply when [the root] begins with a vowel, if the prohibition "in the case of *ah* and *iṅ*" were not made for forms such as *ṣehu*, *hnu*, and *hnuve*—even after the elision (*hruta*) has occurred—then the word would become acute on the first syllable by virtue of the verbal root accent (*dhātu-svara*). To ensure that it is instead acute on the final syllable, the prohibition is made. This being the case, since there is a purpose [for the rule], the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) is established by the force of the prohibition, overriding the accent of the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta-svara*).

In that case, even in the rule "the first [of] those that are repeated" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*), the phrase *ahniṅoḥ* will continue to apply; therefore, there is no purpose in the mention of the word *ṣaṭ*. As it has been said: "Or rather, there is no inclusion [in the list], because it is at the end of the group."
In the case of roots beginning with *tuj* and others, the long vowel is substituted for the reduplicated syllable. 6.1.7.

This grammatical formation (*yoga*) can be explained. How so? This lengthening is Vedic (*chāndasa*); and in the Vedas, such lengthenings cannot be exhaustively enumerated, as they are seen even in other words, such as *pūruṣaḥ* and *nārakaḥ*. Furthermore, because it involves multiple vowels (*anekāj*), it is not observed in the actual usage of those very forms for which it is prescribed—namely, *māmahānaḥ* or *mamahānaḥ*.
In the case of the *liṭ* suffix, reduplication occurs for a verbal root that is not already reduplicated (*anabhyāsa*).

The question "Why [specify] 'of a root'? arises because nothing else can follow *liṭ*; for that [doubling] is prescribed only for a root. [The example given is] *viśrṛṇvire*. Because [the suffix] is treated as both [sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka] by the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the suffix *śnu* is applied and the root changes to *śrṛ* by the rule "for *śru*, *śrṛ*. Here, since the entire complex ending in the *vikaraṇa* suffix is not a root when followed by *liṭ*, there is no doubling of the first *ekāc* (single-vowel) element belonging to it. However, in cases such as *īkṣāñcakre*, the complex ending in *ām* does not have *liṭ* following it.

The term *āmaḥ* [is used] because [the suffix] is elided (*luk*), hence there is an absence of reduplication; thus [the form] is established. [Question: Why is it stated "of that which is not a reduplicated base" (*anabhyāsasya*)? [Answer: First of all, there is no possibility of a further reduplication in forms such as *nunāva* or *papāca* when the *liṭ* [suffix] occurs there, because the grammatical rule has already fulfilled its purpose through a single application, and because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, that which possesses reduplication in other suffixes such as the desiderative (*san*) cannot possibly occur with the *liṭ* suffix; for in that case, the augment *ām* must occur by the rule *kāspratyayād ām am ca*. This is the point of the question. [The example] is *nonāva*.

Because of the prohibition "not in mantras," there is no *ām* here. Regarding *sammimikṣuḥ*: from the root *mih* preceded by *sam*, with the suffix *san*, [the changes] *ho ḍhaḥ* and *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* apply; then the suffix *liṭ*, *jher us*, and the elision of the vowel *a*. Regarding the phrase "in the section on reduplication": because of the mention of "section" (*prakaraṇa*), it is not only every case of reduplication that is optionally applied in the Veda. And thus, both [rules], "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) and "of the non-reduplicated" (*anabhyāsasya*), are for the sake of subsequent rules. Precisely because of this optionality, [reduplication] will not occur for those ending in verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) or for reduplicated stems (*sābhyāsa*).
[The substitution of *sa* for *śas* occurs] before the locative plural ending *su*.

This [word *sani*] ends in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). In that case, by the technical rule regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), reduplication applies to that which ends in it, and not to *san* and *yaṅ* alone; as he says: "and of that which ends in *san*. In the alternative where it is taken as locative (*saptamīpakṣe*), however, the meaning would be that reduplication occurs of the preceding verbal root when *san* and *yaṅ* follow; and consequently, there would be no reduplication of the augment *iṭ* which is a part of *san*, in forms such as *aṭiṭiṣati* and *aśiśiṣati*; likewise, in forms such as *pratīṣiṣati*, the *san* affix itself would not occur.

In such cases as *arāryate*, the suffix *yaṅ* [is applied]; likewise, when the seventh case (*saptamī*) is desired, one should form a single compound with either the preceding or the following [element]. For example: *jugupsiṣate*. Here, from the root *gup*, the suffix *san* is applied by the rule *guptijkidbhyaḥ san*; there, reduplication occurs for the *san* suffix, and then the *san* suffix of desire (*icchā-san*) is added again. Since the condition has not yet been fulfilled, there is the contingency of reduplication occurring once more. For example: *lolūyiṣate*. Here too, reduplication occurs for the *yaṅ* suffix, but not for the *san* suffix; thus, there is no contingency of reduplication [occurring twice] due to the *san*.

The author of the Bhāgavṛtti states: "In the previous sūtra, the commentator (the Bhāṣyakāra), having rejected both [the terms] 'of a root' and 'non-repeated,' said: 'Let the mention of the root for the sake of the general rule stand aside. The intention is that it is for the sake of the subsequent rule. However, no purpose was stated for the mention of 'non-repeated'; from this, the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra is perceived to be that even for the sake of the subsequent rule, that [mention] does not apply. Therefore, reduplication must necessarily occur here."
When *ślu* [is applied], [the substitution of guṇa for the final vowel and the following semivowel of the verbal root] does not take place. 6.1.10.

Regarding the phrase "when *ślau* follows": since even phonemes lack simultaneous existence, their sequence is conceptually constructed by the intellect; and that [sequence], being of the nature of an absence, is compatible with *ślau* as well—this is the intended meaning. As for the term "of what is not a reduplication" (*anabhyāsasya*): this is stated merely as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), for when *ślau* occurs, it does not become accompanied by a reduplication. This should be understood in the same way regarding the rule "and of the second" (*dvitīyasya ca*).
[The substitution of *guṇa* for *ik* occurs] before the suffix *caṅ*. (Pāṇini 6.1.11)

This is the sequence of operation for these grammatical operations. This has been established under the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57), and one should understand it from that very source. He says "for instance" (*yathā hi*) to show that this sequence is not adopted merely because it is logical, but because there is also a purpose that cannot be established otherwise: "because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the short vowel, it is not prohibited. The meaning is: "that which was stated—'it is prohibited because of the status of being a substitute for the short vowel'—does not occur here, because there is an absence of the status of being a substitute."

But how is it that, this sequence of operations being in place, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original)? To this he says: "And because it is not prescribed (*anādiṣṭāt*). [In the sense of the instrument or cause. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been set forth regarding the rule *acaḥ parasmin*: that for that which precedes an unprescribed vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*), there occurs the status of being like the original with respect to the grammatical operation (*vidhi*). Now, in this sequence, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not precede an unprescribed vowel; rather, it precedes one that is indeed prescribed, because the reduplication arises only after the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been applied.

Therefore, when that [shortening] is to be performed, the status of being "as if in the place of" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply to the short vowel; thus, because lightness (*laghutva*) is not removed, the treatment as *san* (*sanvadbhāva*) is not obstructed. However, if the shortening were applied after reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has already taken place, then the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) would precede a vowel that has not been previously enjoined (*anādiṣṭa*). Consequently, the status of being "as if in the place of" would indeed apply to it during the operation, and because of its long vowel, there would be an absence of the designation "light"; thus, the treatment as *san* would not occur. Where, then, would it occur? It would occur in cases such as *aśīśamat*.

For here, the shortening of *ṇits* [roots] is indeed prescribed only before the affix *ṇa*. If this sequence of operations were followed, then in forms such as *āṭiṭat*, the reduplication of the second monosyllabic element *ṭiśabda* would not be obtained. To this, he says: "In *āṭiṭat*, etc.
Although the rule could have been formulated as a single compound, *ślucaṅoḥ*, the separation into two distinct rules (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of variety.
The words *dāśvān*, *sāhvān*, and *mīḍhvān* [are formed with the suffix *kvasu*].

Thinking that this sūtra is Vedic because forms such as *dāśvān* are seen to be used predominantly in the Veda (*chandasi*), he says in response: "without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*). The sense is that no specific qualification is provided. Regarding the term "parasmaipada" (active voice): since the root *mī* belonging to the *bhū* class is ātmanepada, others hold that in the case of the *cur* class, when there is an absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) by the rule "optionally up to *dhṛṣ*" (*ā dhṛṣādvā*), the lengthening of the vowel and the absence of the augment *iṭ* are treated as irregularities (*nipātana*). In the example *mīḍhvastokāya*, the substitution of *ru* for the *num* augment occurs according to the rule "matuvasoḥ".

What, then, is the underlying force [of this rule]? He says: "For, in the case of *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant), etc. Regarding *carācara*: due to the force of the long vowel pronunciation, the short vowel does not occur. Regarding *ṇiluk ca*: since the elision of *ṇi* is already established by the rule *ṇoraniṭi*, the repetition is so that, by virtue of the technical designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there may be no further occurrence of *vṛddhi*. Regarding *pāṭūpaṭa*: as before, there is an absence of *halādiśeṣa* and an absence of shortening. Precisely because of the long vowel pronunciation, or by virtue of the statement *abhyāsasyānaci*, there is an absence of *halādiśeṣa* in both cases. The meaning is that what is prescribed for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) does not apply when an *ac* (vowel) follows.
In a Tatpuruṣa compound, there is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the final vowel of the word *ṣyaṅ* when followed by the words *putra* or *pati*.

Regarding the statement "The *ig* [vowels] are the substitutes for the *yaṇ* [semivowels]," it was said therein: "The meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) as well as the individual phoneme (*varṇa*) is the technical name (*saṃjñin*). Since the meaning of the sentence presents itself in the rule (*vidhi*), he says—relying on that—the meaning is: "The *ig* vowel occurs in the place of the *yaṇ*."

Regarding the rule *tadantāt ṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78): since the alternative view of substitution (*ādeśapakṣa*) has been established for the prescription of the suffix *ṣyaṅ*, this ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used with the elision of the word *al* (i.e., *tasmāt*), meaning "having recourse to that which ends in [the suffix] *aṇ*. Here, the compound is a *bahuvrīhi* of the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type; the meaning is that *ṣyaṅ* follows that which has the suffix *aṇ* as its final or proximate element, such as *kārīṣagandhi*. Indeed, the master Vāmana favors the view that this refers to the suffix itself. Thus, he will state under the rule *ye ca taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.1.61): "The suffix *ṣyaṅ* is to be desired after words ending in *aṇ* or *iñ*."

In the case of *ibhyā* (derived from *ibham arhati*), according to the rule *daṇḍādibhyo yaḥ*, there arises the contingency of applying the suffix *ya* to that which ends in *ṣyaṅ*. Here, in the compound *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ*—meaning "the son of one who has surpassed Kārīṣagandhyā"—even though the entire complex (*samudāya*) does not end in *ṣyaṅ*, the suffix *ya* would still apply to that part of it which does end in *ṣyaṅ*, due to the technical paribhāṣā concerning the inclusion of the constituent element (*pratyagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*).

Similarly, in the case of *putrasya kulam* (the family of the son), which becomes *putrakulam*, and *kārīṣagandhyā-putrakulam*, because the rule for "taking the initial" (*tadādividhi*) is understood to apply when a vowel is being taken, and since that [vowel] is absent here, even though the rule for taking the initial does not apply, the elision of the *saṃprasāraṇa* would still occur based on the immediate sequence of the son (*putra*) and the wife (*patnī*). Consequently, the form *kārīṣagandhīputrakulam* would not be obtained at this point.

And there occurs this statement: "The son of Kārīṣagandhā is Kārīṣagandhīputra; his family is the Kārīṣagandhīputrakula. The meaning of the objection is that [this formation] is not established. Likewise, in cases such as *atikārīṣagandhyāputrakula* and so forth, there would everywhere be the undesirable consequence of vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) by relying on the immediate sequence of the suffix *ṣyaṅ* with both "son" (*putra*) and "wife" (*patnī*).

It might be argued: "Just as in the case of 'the branch of the tree,' the tree is understood to be the whole (*avayavin*) of which the branch is a part, so too here—given the rule 'a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *ṣyaṅ* [i.e., feminine suffixes] with the words 'son' (*putra*) or 'husband' (*pati*) [is neuter]—by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood that only that *tatpuruṣa* whose constituent part ends in *ṣyaṅ* takes this form, and not in this other case. Even so, since a part of a part is indeed a part of the whole, does the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) not still apply? This is not a fault.

From the mention of "putrapatyoḥ" in the locative case (saptamī), it is understood that there is a sequential order (*paurvāparya*) between the element ending in *ṣyaṅ* and the words "putra" and "pati," as well as their status as constituents of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, according to the principle stated previously. Furthermore, a *tatpuruṣa* consists of two constituents situated in a sequential order. Thus, when it is said here that "this [suffix] occurs when there is a sequential arrangement of the two constituents of a *tatpuruṣa*," it is understood that those two constitute the *tatpuruṣa*. The meaning is: when the word ending in *ṣyaṅ* is the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and "putra" or "pati" are the subsequent members (*uttarapada*).

In a compound, that which has nothing before it is the *pūrvapada* (first member), and that which has nothing after it is the *uttarapada* (second member). That which ends in *ṣyaṅ* is not a *pūrvapada*, and that which is an *uttarapada* does not consist of "son" (*putra*) or "offspring" (*patya*), and that which consists of "son" or "offspring" is not an *uttarapada*; thus, there is no such contingency. But then, would this [rule] not fail to apply here as well: *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*? To this he replies: "The mention of *ṣyaṅ* is a reference to a feminine suffix."

Because it is prescribed with "in the feminine" (*striyām*) as its governing context, it possesses the status of a feminine suffix either by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (acting like the original element) or because it is itself a suffix; thus, it is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). To the question, "If there is the mention of 'feminine suffix,' then what [is the consequence]? he says: "By that" (*tena*).

"Non-principal" means subordinate (*upasarjana*). This is what is meant: when a feminine suffix is prescribed for a certain meaning, the entire aggregate up to that point—in which that meaning is expressed as the principal—should be understood as ending in that [suffix]. However, in the case of a non-principal element, the rule does not apply to that which begins with the element after which the suffix was prescribed, nor to that which ends in it. The intention is this: when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) implied by the *tatpuruṣa* compound is qualified by "son" (*putra*) or "husband" (*pati*), then there would be the possibility of application to that which ends in them; but here, the son and the husband are qualified by the subsequent member.

Regarding the phrase *nirdiśyamānasya* ("of that which is being specified"): this has been explained under the rule *ṣaṣṭhīsthāne yogā*. However, the paribhāṣā *anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya* ("when there is no modification of the final element, [the substitute applies] to that which stands in the place of the final") is not adopted here because it serves no purpose. The mention of *samprasāraṇa* is for the sake of what follows; however, in this case, it is established even by the rule *īśāpi*, and the letter *ś* is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśa*). In that regard, this is also the meaning: by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule), the prescription of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) need not be enjoined; he demonstrates that very fact of being for the sake of what follows with the words *samprasāraṇam iti ca*, etc.

Wherever a word ending in *ṣyaṅ* occurs first, followed by a subsequent word consisting of *putra* or *pati*, one should recognize that *ṣyaṅ*-tatpuruṣa compound here as a case where an *ig* vowel is to be substituted in place of the *yaṇ*.
In whatever sense *ṣyaṅ* is applied, even when it exists [in such a context], this *guṇa* substitution is not desired at its end.
Where the sense of "yatra" (in which) is not predominant, that [word] from which the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is derived remains as it is at the beginning of the compound.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the word] *bandhu* [is optionally acute on the final syllable]. || 6.1.14 ||

Regarding the phrase "with respect to the word-form": the neuter designation is made with respect to the word-form *bandhu* itself, as in the expression "this word-form *bandhu*. Why is it explained in this way? To this he says: "But this has a masculine referent. This means that the word *bandhu* which is employed in this sūtra [is masculine]. Why is this so? Because its neuter gender also exists; for instance, in the sense "that in which a genus is bound," there is the neuter substance *bandhu*, according to the rule *jātyantāccha bandhuni*.

If this is so, does it not follow that only that [specific form] should be included? This is not a fault; because of its association with *paripūta*, it will be understood as referring specifically to the genus (*jāti*).
[The rule] *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

This word *ādi* (beginning) is connected only with *yaj*, not with each of *vac* and the others individually; this is because of the separate mention of *svap*. Otherwise, since the inclusion of *svap* and the others would already be established by the inclusion of *vac* and the rest—given that they are listed in the grammatical list (*gaṇa*) as "vaca in the sense of speaking," "vid in the sense of knowing," "as in the sense of being," "mṛjūṣ in the sense of cleansing," "rudir in the sense of weeping," and "ñiṣvap in the sense of sleeping"—the author would not have made a separate mention of *svap* and the others. Regarding the phrase *āgaṇāntāḥ*: the end of the list is the *gaṇānta*; those which have reached the end of the list are *āgaṇāntāḥ*.

Regarding "ukta": [the *k* is substituted for *c*] by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*. Regarding "iṣṭa": [the *ṣ* is substituted for *ch*] because it belongs to the *vraścādi* group. Regarding "ūḍha": [the *h* is replaced by *ḍh*] by *ho ḍhaḥ*; [the *dh* is replaced by *ḍh*] by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*; [the *ṣ* is substituted for *t*] by *ṣṭutvam*; [the first *ḍh* is elided] by *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*; and [the preceding vowel is lengthened] by *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ*. Regarding "uṣita": [the augment *iṭ* is added] by *vasatikṣudhoriṭ*; [the *ṣ* is substituted for *s*] by *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*. In *saṃvīta* and similar forms, there is lengthening by the rule *halaḥ*. Regarding "śūna": [the *ṇ* is substituted for *n*] by *oditaśca*.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of the root by its own form" (*dhātoḥ ka-svarūpa-grahaṇa*): where a root is taken in its own form and not by means of the word *dhātu*, there the grammatical operation is understood to apply only to that suffix which is prescribed after a root by the rule *dhātoḥ*. This will be made known by the specific technical designation (*nipātana*) in the word *bhrauṇahatya*. In the cases *vācyati* and *vācikam*, although words ending in *kvip* do not lose their status as roots, nevertheless, because no suffix is prescribed after them by the rule *dhātoḥ*, there is an absence of *samprasāraṇa*.

In the case of the roots grah, jyā, vayi, vyadhi, vaṣṭi, vicati, vṛścati, pṛcchati, and bhṛjjati, [the substitution of samprasāraṇa occurs] before an affix marked with Ñ or Ṅ, and also before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than a nasal.

It has been accepted; although the sequence was explained first as "vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) when a *ṅit* suffix follows, and [also] when a *kit* suffix follows" (due to the word *ca*), nevertheless, out of disregard for that order, the example for the *kit* case was given first. Regarding the statement "the substitute *vij* is taken": by virtue of association with what precedes and what follows, it is logical to take that root *vape-* for which the possibility of a parasmaipada ending exists; however, the root *vayi-* in the sense of "going" (*aya vaca gatau*) is *anudātta* and takes the ātmanepada. If this is so—meaning, if the substitute *veñ* is what is being taken.

The meaning is that since *veñ* is recited among the roots beginning with *yaj*, the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is established by the preceding rule alone. "It cannot be understood thus" is the sense; the word "to understand" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that it is not possible to understand the inclusion of *vay* as redundant on this basis. In this way, the prohibition would also apply.

In this context, the word "also" (*api*) does not express a conjunction (*samuccaya*); rather, it indicates that just as a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) is obtained through the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), so too is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) obtained, because the status of being like the original is equal in both cases. For this reason, equality is indicated by the word "also," meaning that only the prohibition would apply. Regarding *uṣṭa*: it ends in the suffix *tasa*. *Vyadh* belongs to the *divādi* class; *vyaci* and others belong to the *tudādi* class. Regarding *vṛkṇa*:

there is the elision of *s* according to the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for the *th* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix as before. In forms such as *varīvṛścyate*, there is the substitution of *rīk* according to the rule *rīgṛtvataḥ*.
In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, when there is no reduplication, both [the initial and the reduplicated syllable] undergo the substitution [of *guṇa*].

Regarding the form *vivyathe*: according to the rule "it should be stated that *vyac* belongs to the *kuṭādi* group when followed by *manas*" (*vyaceḥ kuṭāditvamanasīti vaktavyam*), the term *kṛt* here refers to suffixes similar to *ap* through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*). Consequently, because there is no *ṅit* suffix here, there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root.

Regarding the Vārttika stating, "There is no distinction between the roots *vṛścati*, *pṛcchati*, and *bhṛjjati*," that was refuted by the Bhāṣyakāra with respect to the case of *vṛścati*, beginning with the words: "As for what was said, 'there is no distinction for *vṛścati*,'" and so forth. In this regard, he states the intention of the Vārttikakāra: "of *vṛścati*. The meaning is that the Vārttikakāra said this with the intention that whatever form exists when the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.46] is absent, that very same form remains when it is present. He then states the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra: "when the formulation of the yoga (rule) is present."

The meaning is that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has stated this by superimposing the view of the Vārttikakāra, who said that there is no difference whether the semivowel *ṛ* undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) or not. [The objection is: "This [rule] applies when a *kit* suffix does not follow. To the question "How then [does it apply] when a *kit* suffix follows?", he says: "For when a *kit* [suffix follows]... [He continues: "Simply because of the governing context (*adhikāra*). Is this a technical grammatical governing context (*sāstrīya-adhikāra*)? No; rather, it is characterized by mutual requirement (*apekṣā-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, one should not suspect a connection with roots such as *vac* and others from the preceding rule. Alternatively, due to the force of the word-splitting (*yogavibhāga*), they are not connected to the preceding rule.

"Even setting aside the *halādiḥśeṣa* rule"—otherwise, because it is subsequent, the *halādiḥśeṣa* would apply. The intention is that the re-enunciation [of the rule] occurs by virtue of the mention of "both" (*ubhayeṣām*), for the purpose of subverting that which subverts [the present rule], so that the *samprasāraṇa* alone may take place.
The substitution of *śvāp* occurs for the root *śvas* before the affix *caṅ*.

The term *svāpeḥ* refers to the root preceded by *su*, ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and not to the root preceded by *su* without the suffix; for the reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*) is impossible in that case. Nor does it apply to the root ending in the causative suffix itself, because of the governing rule "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*). In *svāpyate*, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the passive sense, with the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopaḥ*). In *svāpitaḥ*, the elision of the causative suffix occurs according to the rule "before a *seṭ* niṣṭhā suffix."

But surely, from the rule *grahijyā* etc., the term *ṅiti* will be carried over [by anuvṛtti], and there is no other *ṅit* suffix for *svāpi*—for the *yaṅ* affix does not exist because the root has more than two syllables (*anekāctva*), while the *apit* sārvadhātuka suffix is separated by the *vikaraṇa* affixes, and the *aṅ* and other affixes have not even been prescribed [for this root]? To this he says: "The term *ṅiti* alone," and so forth. Now, one might object: since the term *kiti* was carried over from the preceding rule, it will not be carried over here; why then is the difficult-to-understand mention of *ṅit* made? [Response: In that case, the mention of *ṅit* also does not carry over from the preceding rule; because a *ṅit* [affix] after *liṭ* is impossible, its carrying over here is difficult to ascertain.
The substitution of *ī* for the vowel of the roots *svap*, *śvas*, and *vyen* occurs when the suffix *yaṅ* follows.
Regarding "svapna": [the suffix] *nañiṅ* is applied after the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*.
The suffix *ka* is applied after [the word] *cāya*. 6.1.21.

Is the long pronunciation [of the vowel] useless, since even when a short substitute is applied, the lengthening is established by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*? To this he replies: "The long pronunciation," and so forth. But how can a substitute being prescribed for the *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅ*) apply when the *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*)? By means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the presence of the suffix as a formal condition). [Objection: Is it not the case that *na lumatāṅgasya* (P. 1.1.63) prohibits such application? [Reply: If that is so, then by the force of the long pronunciation itself, it will apply even when there is elision; however, the *prasāraṇa* (vocalization) enjoined by the preceding rule certainly does not occur when the *yaṅ* is elided.

Nor does the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occur prior to elision (*luk*) on the basis of the maxim "an operation dependent on *samprasāraṇa* is stronger [than elision]"; for this maxim is not universally accepted (*pratyākhyātatvāt*). Consequently, since both types of roots were included in the previous rule, that inclusion would have been redundant if—by this very maxim—the *samprasāraṇa* had occurred before the *halādiśeṣa* (elision of all but one consonant). Thus: *sāsvapīti*, *sāsvapti*; *sāsvaptaḥ*, *sāśvapītaḥ*; *vāvyeti*, *vāvyāti*.
The [substitution of] *stya* occurs for [the root] preceded by *pra*.

"In both of these cases" means that it would apply to both, because the form [of the suffix] is characterized by its specific technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*). "When the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been performed" means that because that [substitution] is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), the vocalization occurs first.

"It is already established by [the rule] *prastyah* alone," as in the case of *prastyo 'nyatarasyām*. Nor does this being stated lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the rule would apply to the *repha* (the letter *r*) of the prefix *pra-* as well; for there is the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the word "dhātu" (root). In *prasaṃstītaḥ*, the substitution of *m* (matva) by the rule *prastyo 'nyatarasyām* certainly does not occur here. "How so?"—this question asks how this meaning is expressed by the word. "[It is expressed] by a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the genitive."

Because the word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), as in the expression "the front part of the body" (*pūrvaṃ kāyasya*). [The phrase] "with two genitives in different grammatical relations" means that the genitive in *prapūrvasya* is a partitive genitive in relation to the word *styā*, while the genitive in *stya* is also a partitive genitive in relation to its constituent *yaṇ*. He demonstrates how this meaning is relevant to the present context with the words "In that case" (*tatra*).
The suffix *sya* occurs after the words *drava*, *mūrti*, and *sparśa*.

Regarding "liquidity and solidity": solidity is a specific subsequent state of the state of liquidity. Regarding "and touch": touch is a quality that coexists with color and the other [sensory qualities]. As for "cold air": how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *śīta* (cold), which denotes merely a quality (*sparśa*), and the word *vāyu* (air), which denotes the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality? To this he replies: "merely a quality," and so forth. The intended meaning is that it is like words such as *śukla* (white) and others.
The substitution of *vi* for *ava* is optional when preceded by *abhi*.

"This [rule] is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases": it is applicable by the preceding rule regarding the domain of fluidity and form, and it is not applicable elsewhere. Now, what is the purpose of including the word "preceding" (*pūrva*); why not simply say "optionally after *ava* and *vi*" (*vibhāṣāvyavābhyām*)? To this he replies with the words beginning "of the inclusion of 'preceding'" (*pūrvagrahaṇasya*). Even when the inclusion of "preceding" is made, why does it not apply here? He says: "it is said, indeed, not so" (*na kila*). He shows his lack of approval, which is indicated by the word "indeed" (*kila*), with the words "he who [thinks] here" (*yo'tra*).

Let it be that there is no large composite whole (*mahāsamudāya*) preceded by *abhi* or *ava*; however, a subordinate composite (*avāntarasamudāya*) does exist that is so preceded, and thus a grammatical option (*vikalpa*) would apply based upon that. Therefore, another effort must be undertaken; the meaning is that the mention of the term *vibhāṣā* must be understood as referring to a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Furthermore, another purpose for the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (in the rule) must be stated. Moreover, in cases such as *abhisaṃśīnam*, *abhisaṃśyānam*, *avasaṃśīnam*, and *avasaṃśyānam*, it is precisely the application of this option that occurs.
And how that [result] is obtained when the term *pūrva* is included has been explained in the commentary on the rule *astyo prapūrvasya*.
The word *śr̥ta* [is used] in the sense of "cooked. (Pāṇini 6.1.27)

Regarding the root *śrā* in the sense of "cooking": the root *śrā* in the sense of "cooking" is listed in the *adādi* (second) class; *śrau* in the sense of "cooking" is listed in the *curādi* (tenth) class; and *śrā* in the sense of "cooking" is also listed among the *ghaṭādi* roots for the purpose of making them *mit*. Here, all of these are included. This form also occurs from the causative *śrāyati* after the vowel has been changed to *ā*; furthermore, by the force of this specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*), the maxim regarding "that which is taught by a general rule versus that which is taught by a specific rule" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*) is not applied here. Thus, it applies both to the causative and the non-causative forms. Accordingly, it has been stated: "The substitution of *śrṛ* for *śrā* and *śrap* is prescribed as a specific rule (*nipātana*)."
For this very reason, the original *samprasāraṇa* itself is not sublated, so that even from the root *śrī*, the form *śr̥tam* may indeed occur.

If the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) were to apply here [to all cases], then an option would result for *kṣīra* and *havis* everywhere else as well; therefore, he says: "And this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). As for the passage beginning with *yadā tu*, etc.: the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), characterized by commanding and so forth, is expressed by the word *prayojaka*; and its externality (*bāhyatva*) is due to its being pervaded by the external *ṇic* suffix. Even then, it is not desired. And thus it has been said: "The form *śrṛtam* occurs after the root *śrap* in other instances than when there is a cause [of action]. For example: *śrapitaṃ kṣīraṃ devadattena* ("the milk was cooked by Devadatta").

Even though the prompted agent (*prayojya*) is that which is reached (*āpyamāna*) through the operation of the prompter (*prayojaka*), it does not receive the designation of "object" (*karman*), because of the restrictive rule: "In the case of [verbs denoting] motion, cognition, and eating... (Pāṇini 1.4.52). But how can the formation of the causative (*ṇyanta*) be obtained here? For when one says *pāka* ("cooking"), the causative suffix denotes "causing to cook" (*pācanā*), not "cooking" (*pāka*). If, however, even in the sense of "causing to cook," "cooking" is understood as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*), and the irregularity (*nipātana*) were based on that, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying it even to a second causative suffix. For in that case as well, "cooking" is not perceived as a subordinate element.

If it were argued that, because it is merely a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) there, the *nipātana* (irregular formation) will not apply since its purpose is fulfilled by the primary factor (*pradhānabhūta*) which is the cooking (*pāka*), [we reply: even in the first case [of the patient], it would not apply; or else, a distinction must be stated. He states that [distinction] with the words "this root *śrāti*" and so forth. This is the intended meaning: cooking (*pāka*) is of two kinds—characterized by softening (*viklitti*) and characterized by moistening (*vikledana*). For the verb *pac* is seen to be used in both senses, as in "the rice cooks by itself" (*pacyate odanaḥ svayameva*) and "Devadatta cooks the rice" (*pacatyodanaṃ devadattaḥ*).

Although this root *śrāti* is listed without qualification as "in the sense of cooking" (*pāke*), it nevertheless functions in the sense of the root *pac* when it has a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). Even when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it expresses the natural state—that is, the meaning of the base root *pac* devoid of the causative marker—and thus denotes the act of cooking itself, not the meaning of the causative *pācayati*. For example: *siddhyaty odanaḥ* ("the rice is being cooked") and *sādhayaty odanam* ("he cooks the rice").

In that regard, when the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *śrāti*, because it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the form occurs in the sense of the agent—as in *śṛtaṃ kṣīram* ("the milk has been boiled")—whereas for the root *śrap*, it occurs in the sense of the object—as in *śrṛtaṃ kṣīraṃ devadattena* ("the milk was boiled by Devadatta"). However, in the second case, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added, the operation of the causer characterized as "causing to cook" (*pācanā*) is primarily denoted, and not the act of cooking itself; thus, there is no irregularity (*nipātana*) [in the form].

In the Vārttika "The substitution of *śrṛ* for *śrap* occurs elsewhere than when there is a cause [for it]," it was previously stated that "the substitution of *śrṛ* for *śrā* and *śrap* is prescribed as a nipātana. Therefore, by the force of accepting the primary original characteristic—the operation of the instigator—it should be understood that the operation of the instigator characterized as the cooker (*pācayitṛ*) is prohibited.

This process of cooking (*pāka*) consists of two aspects here: that which is cooked (*pākya*) and the act of cooking (*pakti*). It is of the nature of softening (*viklitti*) and the agent of softening (*vikledana*).

The verbal root *śrā* expresses one [aspect], while *śrapayati* expresses both, because both are stated in both cases. Alternatively, when the sense of cooking is present, the form *śrapeḥ* applies to its respective denotation; it does not apply to a second [denotation].
The state of being boiled (*śṛbhāva*) occurs eternally in milk and in the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), but not in cooked foods or other substances.
The substitute *pī* is applied in place of *pyāya*. 6.1.28.
Andhu means a well.
And [the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* for *ik*] occurs in the *liṭ* and *yaṅ* suffixes as well.

"‘Vibhāṣā’ (optionally) is understood [to apply here] because the term ‘vibhāṣā’ is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra. The [term] *pyāyaḥ pī* is drawn along by means of the particle *ca*. If the particle *ca* were not present, there would be a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) from the governing context alone, as occurs later on. As for the statement ‘when the change to *pī* has been effected due to its being subsequent (*paratvāt*)’: one might object that priority (*paratva*) applies between two rules that both have scope (*sāvakāśa*), whereas the change to *pī* is without scope (*anavakāśa*). To this, the sense is: it is because it is subsequent, superior, and without scope. [The rule applies] because of the principle of ‘recognition of recurrence’ (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānāt*).”

In this case as well, that which was stated under the rule *vipratiṣedhe param* is not intended [as a general principle]; rather, the meaning is that there is a recurrence (*punah-prasaṅga*) of reduplication (*dvirvacana*). If, then, the substitution of *pī* is without scope (*anavakāśa*), would it not follow that reduplication is sublated by that [substitution], since it is introduced when reduplication has not yet taken effect? This is not a fault; for the relationship of the sublated and the sublater (*bādhyabādhaka-bhāva*) occurs only in close proximity (*paraspara-sannidhi*). Here, however, the section on reduplication is interrupted by the section on *samprasāraṇa*. For this very reason, it will be stated later: "The sublation of reduplication by the substitute *di* is accepted."
The substitution of *śvi* is optional [before the suffix *kvasu*]. 6.1.30.

Regarding *śuśāva*: here, although the rules for *vṛddhi* and *āy-ādeśa* apply later, the *samprasāraṇa* takes precedence because it is *nitya* (obligatory) and *antaraṅga* (internal); furthermore, by the rule of *pūrva-tva* (priority), it occurs first. Regarding *śuśuvatuḥ*: here too, although *iyaṅ* applies later, the *samprasāraṇa* takes precedence because it is *nitya*. Once that has been performed, although the *yaṇ* substitution prescribed by "eranekācaḥ" applies later, the *pūrva-tva* (priority) takes effect because it is *antaraṅga*, followed by the substitution of *uvaṅ*. "Elsewhere" means in the *pit* (strong) case-endings. In all those instances, there is an option; first, the option is applied in the *pit* endings.

Because there is no prohibitor [to prevent it]. Even in the case of *kit* suffixes, this option prevails because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. The scope of the rule characterized by *yaj*-class roots is, for example, *śūnaḥ* and *śūnavān*; the scope of this present rule consists of forms with *pid* affixes. When both would apply in the case of a *kit* suffix in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, this option prevails due to its subsequent position. [Question: Why does it not also apply to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)? [Answer: It is not that it is sublated by this option due to its subsequent position; rather, this option pertains to the verbal root (*dhātu*), not to the reduplicated syllable. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "both" (*ubhayeṣām*), it is so that this very same rule may apply to both cases.

Therefore, in this matter, the scriptural statement alone is the refuge, as it says: "There is a prohibition of the characteristic [application] of the reduplication when the *liṭ* [affix] follows a root ending in *s*."
And [the substitution of *guṇa* for *vṛddhi*] does not take place before the affix *ṇau*, nor before the *saṅ* (i.e., *san*) and *caṅ* (reduplication).

The term "in *ṇau*" (*ṇau*) is a locative case (*parasaptamī*) in relation to *śvi*, while "of *san* and *caṅ*" (*saṃścaṅoḥ*) is in relation to *ṇi*. Thus he says: "when *ṇi* follows, provided that *san* or *caṅ* follows. [He adds] "even though it is *antaraṅga* (internal). Its status as *antaraṅga* is due to its depending on *ṇi* alone. [He refers to] "the *vṛddhi* substitution and so forth."

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the substitution of *ā* is included. However, when the paribhāṣā—"substitution by semivowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and an operation dependent on that semivowel are stronger"—is rejected due to a lack of purpose, then [the rule] applies as "when *ṇi* and *saṅ* are the objects [of the rule]. This is seen in rules such as *oḥ puyaṇjī*. How this serves as an indicator has been explained in the commentary on the rule *dvirvacane'ci*. In this context, the word "api" (also) should be read before the words "sthānivadbhāvāt" (due to the status of being a substitute); or rather, the word "tena" (by that) should be read [there].
A vowel that results from *samprasāraṇa* [is called *saṃdhyakṣara*]. 6.1.32.

"Because the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is stronger"—and its strength is as explained previously. "Established by the very same rule" means that since no cause for [the application of] the subsequent rule is mentioned in relation to the reduplicated base (*abhyasta*), the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the root *hve* is already established even when followed by *ṇi*, *saṃ*, or *caṅ*. "With a suffix that is not a cause of the reduplicated base" means: with that which does not serve as a cause for the reduplicated base. "In the case of intervention" means: if the subsequent rule were to apply, then the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless; thus, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
And [the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs] for that which has been repeated (*abhyasta*). 6.1.33.

In this context, if the term *hvah*, which is being carried forward (*anuvarttamāna*), were to stand in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase *yadi abhyastasya* ("if [the root] is reduplicated"), then the process of vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) would have to occur once the reduplication has been performed and the designation "reduplicated" (*abhyasta-saṃjñā*) has arisen. Consequently, there would be no vocalization of the reduplicated syllable, because of the prohibition: "There is no vocalization [of a semivowel] when another vocalized semivowel follows" (*na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam*). If it is argued that there is no prohibition because [the semivowel] is separated from the preceding vowel by the letter *ā* and the letter *h*, we say no; for the prohibition applies to vocalization within the same morphological unit (*samānāṅga*).

One might object that the term *samānāṅga* (having the same member) should be included there [in the rule]; but this is not so, because of the prohibition of *samprasāraṇa* when the members are identical. One will raise the objection regarding the inclusion of *samānāṅga* there, and this will be explained clearly at that very point. Anticipating this fault regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says later: "By the phrase *tadabhyastasya*, [the compound] is in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*). He clarifies this very point: "The *hvayati* which belongs to the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) [root]. What is established by this? He says: "By that... [and so on].
The forms *apaspṛdhethām*, *ānṛcuḥ*, *ānṛhuḥ*, *cicyuṣe*, *tityāja*, *śrātāḥ*, *śritam*, *āśīr* and *āśīrttāḥ* [are formed with the substitution of ṣ for s]. 6.1.36.

Another teacher says: In one Vedic recension (*śākhā*), the form *apaspṛdhethām* is read with an acute accent on the first syllable; in another, however, it is read as two words. Both readings are subsumed by this rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*). In the case where it is a single word, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would require the enclitic accent (*nighāta*) on the verb, but this is prohibited by the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*. Consequently, the word becomes acute-accented on the first syllable due to the accent of the augment *aṭ*.

But when there are two words, then, because the prohibition of *nighāta* applies, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes become unaccented by the rule *tāsyanudāttet*; thus, by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), the word *spṛdhethām* is udātta on its first syllable, and by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati*, the word *apaśabdaḥ* receives *nighāta*. This is because the plural number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Furthermore, this is because they do not rely on the restrictive rule that the substitution of *śrā* occurs only when *soma* itself is plural; otherwise, even if plurality were not intended to be significant, the absence of *śrā* would not occur in cases other than *soma* for those who maintain a distinction between the scope of application.
When a *samprasāraṇa* vowel has occurred, a subsequent *samprasāraṇa* substitution does not take place.

This prohibition is stated because, for those [roots] for which *samprasāraṇa* is prescribed, all their *yaṇ*s would otherwise be subject to *samprasāraṇa*.
