One might object: "But surely, by the *paribhāṣā* 'the substitute takes the place of the final letter' (*alontyaparibhāṣā*), it will apply only to the final [yaṇ]. This *paribhāṣā* cannot be invoked here, because there is no *yaṇ* at the end of roots such as *vaci* and others. If it is argued that by the *paribhāṣā* "when a change does not affect the final letter, it affects what stands in the vicinity of the final" (*anantyavikāre 'ntyasadeśasya*), then it will apply only to that which stands in the vicinity of the final, and not to any other; [we reply: this *paribhāṣā* does not exist.

Because there is no purpose [for it]. This has been established by us in the work titled *Paribhāṣāprakaraṇa*. If that is so, then it is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*): namely, that this [rule] teaches the substitution of *pī* for *pyā*, which indicates that not every *yaṇ* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*. For if it were otherwise, [the rule] would have simply prescribed *saṃprasāraṇa* for *pyā*. If both *y* sounds were to undergo *saṃprasāraṇa*, and the preceding [vowel] were applied, and the lengthening by the rule *halaḥ* were applied, then the form *pīnaṃ mukham* would be established. But surely, in *pyā*, the final *yaṇ* is [the one affected]?

Would it belong only to that which follows [the *yaṇ*]? It would indeed be so if the genitive case were understood as a locative-genitive (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), meaning "that which takes the place of"; however, this will be understood as a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*)—meaning "of that *yaṇ* which is a vowel.

Even so, by this [rule] only this much is indicated: it is not indicated that the *samprasāraṇa* occurs for every *yaṇ*. In that case, how is it known that it occurs only for the subsequent [vowel] and not for the preceding one? Nor can it be concluded from the mention of "pierces" (*vidhyati*) and so forth that it belongs only to the subsequent one, because that [usage] is also possible through alternative application (*paryāyeṇa*). Therefore, this very rule must indeed be commenced.

Now, is it not the case that the *samprasāraṇa* characterized by a single conjunction applies to both the preceding and the following semivowels (*yaṇ*)? If it has been accomplished for the following one, it must necessarily have been accomplished for the preceding one as well; and it cannot be understood that what has already been accomplished can be set aside by a prohibition—just as if one were to say to someone who has already eaten, "Do not eat," what could that person possibly do? On the other hand, if it has not been accomplished for the preceding one, then it has likewise not been accomplished for the following one; in that case, its reliance [on the following] as a cause (*nimitta*) would be untenable? To this [it is replied]: [The text continues: ...therefore...

He says: "Even the definition of a single *yoga* [is applicable]. Another interpretation: Let it be that both [the *samprasāraṇa* and the *pūrva-vaṅtva*] have already been produced; how then is it negated? It is not the *samprasāraṇa* itself that is negated, but rather its status as being prior (*pūrva-vaṅtva*). That very status is here figuratively referred to by the word *samprasāraṇa*; when that is negated, the desired result is established by means of the *yaṇ*-substitution. Or, let it be that neither of the two has yet been produced.

How, then, is it a cause (*nimitta*)? It is not that there is a cause for *samprasāraṇa* here; what then? That *yaṇ* which is to become that [vowel] is itself designated by the word *samprasāraṇa* with a locative ending. [The author says: "There is a repetition of the mention of *samprasāraṇa*. If that were not present, then according to the principle "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding," the prohibition would apply only to the *samprasāraṇa* prescribed in the preceding section, and not to one located elsewhere. A different location is called "elsewhere" (*videśa*).

"Simply because of the inclusion of *saṃprasāraṇa* [in the rule]. Here, however, in the case of *vivyathe* from the root *vyath* with the suffix *liṭ*, *saṃprasāraṇa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *halādiḥśeṣaḥ*. Since an exception occurs in the same location as its general rule (*utsarga*) due to the context, the desired result is established by the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the subsequent [vowel] alone. For this very reason, it must be accepted that there is a prohibition even when the *saṃprasāraṇa* is situated in a different location (*videśastha*), because otherwise one would have to say "there" (*tatra*). It is this much separation (*vyavadhāna*) that is being relied upon.

In forms such as *upeyuṣaḥ*, derived from the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *upa*—where the suffix *kvasu* is applied to the root *vas* according to the rule *bhāṣāyāṃ sadavasaśruvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.108), and where the semivowel *v* of *vas* undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) before the case-ending—the prohibition of vocalization that would otherwise apply to the root due to its being a *yajādi* root (by Pāṇini 6.1.15) does not take effect. The point is that this is because there is an intervention by the directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) *ṣakāra*. However, if the prohibition were to apply merely upon any kind of intervention, then it would be necessary to include the condition "belonging to the same stem" (*samānāṅga*).

It should be stated that a prohibition applies where both the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) reside in one and the same member (*aṅga*). In the case of *upeyuṣī*, the verbal root is the member (*aṅga*) with respect to the suffix *kvasu*, while the entire form ending in *kvasu* is the member with respect to the case-ending; thus, there is no prohibition. Alternatively, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root occurs here even earlier.

Regarding the rule "in the Ṛgveda, for *tri*": the authors of the Kalpasūtras, however, employ the vocalization of the word *dvi* as well—as in "the *pratipad* and *anucara* verses are *tṛca*s" and "the *pragātha*s are *dvaca*s."
In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, *vaya* is substituted for *yaḥ*.
The mention of *liṭ* is for the sake of what follows; it serves no purpose here, because elsewhere the substitution of *vay* is impossible.
And the substitution of *v* for [the final consonant] of this [root] optionally occurs before an affix beginning with *k*.

By the mention of *asya*, the element *ya* is indicated; otherwise, since there would be no evidence for the vowel *a* being merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), this [substitute] might be suspected of replacing the entire word (*sarvādeśa*). However, when *asya* is mentioned, even if the substitute contains the vowel *a*, the desired result is nonetheless established by the elision (*lopa*) of that *a*.

Furthermore, the mention of *va* (the root *veñ*) could have been omitted. How so? The rule should have been formulated as: "Optionally, when a *kit* affix follows, for *veñ*"; this would mean that when a *liṭ* affix follows, the *samprasāraṇa* of *veñ* does not occur optionally—resulting in *vavatuḥ*, *vavuḥ*. When the *samprasāraṇa* alternative applies, there is the substitution of *upadhā* (vocalization), followed by reduplication and the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), resulting in *ūcatuḥ*, *ūcuḥ*; and according to the rule "for *veñ*, [substitute] *vayi*", one obtains *ūyatuḥ*, *ūyuḥ*.

As for *vavau* and *vavitha*, the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule "also when *lyap*" (*lyapi ca*) brings forward the *liṭ* from the previous context; that will serve to establish a permanent prohibition when a *pit* affix follows.
And also after *lyap*. 6.1.40.

Furthermore, if its inclusion were made earlier, the rule should have been formulated as a single compound: *lyapi vyo jyaśca*; for in this way, even the repetition of the particle *ca* would not be necessary.
In the original instruction (upadeśa), *ai*, *au*, and *añ* are substituted for [the final elements of verbal roots], except when followed by the suffix *as*. (Pāṇini 6.1.45)

Regarding the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti*: if the term *dhātoḥ* (of the root) were not carried over [from the previous sūtra], then, due to the absence of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*), there would be no "specification by its end" (*tadantavidhi*). Consequently, the meaning would become "the *ai* and *au* sounds that exist in the original instruction (*upadeśa*) are replaced by *āt*"; and as a result, this substitution would undesirably apply even in forms such as *ḍhaukitā* and *traukitā*. Now, one might object: "But it is stated 'when followed by something other than *śit*' (*aśiti*); we do not see anything other than *śit* here [in *ḍhauk* and *trauk*]."

Nor is it only the letter *ka* that is *aśit*. What is the reason? Because, according to the maxim regarding connection with *nañ* (negation) and *iva* (likeness), there is the grasping of a suffix (*pratyaya*) similar to *śit*. This would indeed be the case if *aśiti* were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), but it will be stated that this is rather a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Therefore, he says "the word *dhātoḥ* (from a root) continues," meaning "the word *dhātoḥ* is understood. And because it qualifies *ec*, there is the inclusion of what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*); thus he says, "a root which ends in *ec*. Regarding "in its original enunciation" (*upadeśe*):
the first pronunciation of something whose true nature is not yet known, for the purpose of making its nature known, is "original enunciation" (*upadeśa*).

[If it were so,] the rule for *guṇa* substitution in the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes would serve only for the purpose of [the suffix] *ātvam*; this is according to the maxim: "An instruction is for the sake of that specific operation toward which it is directed. Furthermore, the prescription of *guṇa* is already fulfilled in cases such as *karttā*, *harttā*, and *hatyā*. Even so, one might argue that it will not apply here precisely because it is based on a secondary derivative (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). Moreover, there is an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*): the fact that [Pāṇini] teaches the substitution of *ātvam* for the roots *krī*, *jī*, and *nī* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi* indicates that the substitution of *ātvam* does not occur for a vowel (*aic*) whose cause lies in a subsequent element.

This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*); rather, this [mention of *upadeśe*] would be for the sake of restriction—namely, that the substitution applies only after the roots *krī*, *jī*, and *mī* when followed by the affix *ṇa*. Well then, does the substitution of *ā* (as in *mīnāti*, *minoti*, *dīṅ* + *lyap*) exist here? In that case, the mention of *upadeśe* must certainly be made for the sake of subsequent rules; therefore, it is placed right here for the benefit of those of dull intellect.

"How so? [The question is: "In this case, *aśit* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; when a prohibition regarding *śit* is being applied, it would apply to every *śit* [affix] without exception, and consequently, one would have to say *jaglāye*. This is the question. The answer relies on the fact that it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound and that the *lakāra* (the letter *l*) denotes the action (*bhāva*). But what is the advantage of it being a *tatpuruṣa*? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). For in a *tatpuruṣa*, this refers to the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), and when there is a mention of a phoneme, the grammatical operation applies to that which begins with it.

Regarding the word *stanandhaya*, however, when the suffix *khaś* is applied by the rule *nāsikāstanayoḥ*, a prohibition [of the substitution of *na* for *ṇa*] occurs based on the fact that the suffix *śap* is attached to a root ending in *m*. If it is argued that *śap* should not be considered here simply because there is no purpose [for its presence], [we reply]: But this very thing—namely, the prevention of the substitution of *at*—is precisely the purpose. [This is indicated by the condition] "when followed by a vowel other than *a*" (*aśiti*).

If this were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—meaning that "non-śit" (*aśit*) is that which is other than *śit*, and [the rule applies] "in that non-śit"—then in forms such as *glāyanti* and *malāyanti*, once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of the letter *ś* and the final vowel *ā* has been made, because that substitute behaves like the initial (*ādivadbhāva*) with respect to what follows, the condition "being other than *śit*" would apply, and consequently, the substitution of *ā* for *i* (by Pāṇini 6.4.66) would result here. However, in the case of a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there is no fault; because the single-substitute behaves like the final (*antavadbhāva*) with respect to what precedes it, it is included by the mention of *siddh* [in the rule], and thus the prohibition indeed applies to *śit*.

But what is the reason that the application of *āttva* (the substitution of *ā*) is raised as an issue only in the case of a single portion [of the root], and not also in cases such as *glāyati*, where *āttva* would apply to the letter *l* when followed by an affix beginning with *a* other than *śit*? It is not possible to raise such an objection; for if it were so, the prohibition "not when followed by *śit*" (*aśiti*) would be rendered purposeless. Furthermore, in the rule *pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-dṛśaḥ*, the *śap* affix following *dheṭ* is not a case where the root is preceded by nothing else [to which the *āttva* could apply]. Indeed, a single example does not necessitate the prohibition of *śit*. If this were all [that were required].

If there were a purpose [for the rule], one should simply say "aśe. Or rather, would it not be urged that [the substitution] should occur first because it is internal (antaraṅga) and obligatory (nitya)? This is not a fault; for by virtue of the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva) in a rule concerning what precedes, there is no occurrence of another suffix beginning with 'ā'. In this case, however—[in forms such as] *suglaḥ*, *suglā*, and *suglānam*—would not the suffixes *kāṅ* and *yaṅ* conditioned by a stem ending in long *ā* fail to apply? This too is not a fault; for all suffixes conditioned by a stem ending in long *ā* are understood to follow a monosyllabic root (*ejanta*) that undergoes *āttva*. Furthermore, by the rule *hrasvādaṇaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* applies again.

In that case, for *glai* and *pai*, when the suffix *-anīya* is applied, both the substitution of *ā* (āttva) and the *āy*-substitutions (*āyādayaḥ*) would apply. Since the *āy*-substitutions are subsequent (*paratvāt*), would they not take effect first? True; however, once those [āy-substitutions] have been applied, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel (*alontyasya*) and the lengthening by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) result in forms such as *glānīyam*, which are thus established.

Now, one might object: "Once the *āy*-substitutions have been made, this [stem] no longer ends in *ej* (a vowel other than *a*); and since the rule depends on the letter *a* (*al-āśrayatvāt*), there can be no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if it were the original). This would indeed be so if it were said that the substitution of *ā* applies to whatever ends in *ej* at the time [of the operation]. But here, the quality of ending in *ej* belongs to the original instruction (*upadeśagatamejantatvam*), not to the current state; therefore, there is no need to rely on the *sthānivadbhāva*.

But even so, in cases such as *jaglātuḥ*, once the substitution of *ya* for *i* has been applied, we have the form *jaglā-ā-atus*. At this stage, would not the elision of the *ā* (by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*) apply, overriding even the internal *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) of the two *ā*s? Furthermore, one cannot obtain the elision of the preceding *ā* again, because the elision of the *yakāra* and the *ākāra* would be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) with respect to the preceding operation, and because of the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt* (which treats such operations as non-existent for subsequent rules within the same *abhāt*). This is not a fault.

Regarding the rule *samānāśraye vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (an internal operation [āṅga] is stronger than a phonetic operation [vārṇa] when they share the same locus), here, however, because they have different loci (*vyāśrayatva*), the substitution of *ekādeśa* occurs first as an internal operation, and subsequently the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) follows; thus the desired result is established. Even so, by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (when a vowel follows, there is reduplication), since the substitutes for *āy* and other suffixes would be treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the reduplication of the root *glai* would result in the abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) ending in an *i*-vowel. But in the alternative view, since the substitution of *āt* is not dependent on any external cause (*anaimittikatva*), and because it is not prescribed with reference to the vowel that causes reduplication, there is no fault. Furthermore, there is no fault even in the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) interpretation, as in the case of the rule *liṭi vayo yaḥ*.

This instruction contains two *lakāra*s; and since there is no purpose for such an instruction in that [other context], it is connected here by means of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) as it recurs: "the substitution of *āt* occurs only before *aśit* (non-*liṭ* suffixes)," whereas in the case of *liṭ*, it occurs only while the root is still in the state of *l* at the beginning of the *liṭ* suffix. Consequently, because the substitution of *āt* lacks the status of being caused by a non-duplication cause (*advirvacana-nimitta*), there is no application of the rule of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) to it. As for the substitutes *āy* and so forth, they simply do not apply at all before *liṭ*.

Thus, since the position of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) involves many points that must be refuted, he states that this is a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), saying: "In [the word] *aśiti*, this is a *prasajyapratiṣedha*. What is established by this? He says: "By this, etc. This and so forth are established. By the word "etc.," the inclusion of *aṅ* in the rule *ātaścopasarge* is intended for the case of *sugla*. Many other purposes have already been demonstrated by us.

Why does this not occur here in *gobhyām* and *naubhyām*? It is because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). When [the author] teaches the substitution of *ā* in the rule *rāyo hali*, that indicates that the substitution of *ā* does not apply to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). This is not a valid indicator; for this [rule] might be intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the substitution of *ā* for *rāya-* occurs only before a consonant (*hal*).

But as for the rule *aut-as-asoḥ*, in the case of *gāṃ paśya* ("look at the cow"), because of the *ṇit*-designation in *goto ṇit*, a vṛddhi [vowel] would be required; whereas in the case of *gāḥ paśya* ("look at the cows"), because of the prohibition *na-aśiti*, that [vṛddhi] would be prohibited. Thus, [the fact that the rule works] would be established [without needing this new definition], so is it not a non-indicator (*ajñāpaka*)? In that case, it is said that "instruction" (*upadeśa*) is intended. However, there is no instruction for the word-forms *go* and *nau*; the pronunciation found in rules such as *gopayasoryat* and *nauvayodharma* is not "instruction," but rather "reference" (*uddeśa*), since they are presented as already established.

Let it be that there is no formal instruction (*upadeśa*) for the words *go* and *naus*; however, there is an instruction for the *ec*-vowels, namely: "from the root *gam*, the suffix *ḍo*" and "from *glā* and *nud*, the suffix *ḍau*. And the prescription of the suffixes *ḍo* and *ḍau* is not purposeless, as they find their application in forms such as *gām* (accusative singular). If this is so, then [the objection does not hold], because it has been stated that the term "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) continues to apply [and thus the rule does not apply to nouns].
The substitution of *vī* for *vyo* does not occur before the *liṭ* suffix.

Whether kittva (the status of having an indicatory *k*) is present or absent, since there is no difference [in the result], the commentator has shown this as an example for the [rule concerning] *thali*: "The augment *iṭ* [is applied] after roots ending in *ṛ*, *at*, and *vyay*" (*iḍatyartivyayatīnām*).
The substitution of *krī*, *ñī*, and *nā* occurs before the causative suffix *ṇi*.

Although the form of the root *īṅ* "to go" is possible through the substitution of *yaṇ* when followed by a *ṅit* suffix, nevertheless, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of *ec*" (*ecaḥ*), the inclusion of *kṛ* is not possible; likewise, the inclusion of *īṅ* is also not possible, due to its association with the subsequent *jayati*, which ends in a short vowel.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used after the root *sidh* when it does not refer to the other world (*apāralaukika*).

The term *pāralaukika* means "having the other world as its purpose. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "the purpose of this," and there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both parts of the compound because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group. It "subsists in a particular kind of knowledge" (*jñānaviśeṣe vartate*). This "particular kind of knowledge" is the realization of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted (*heyopādeyatattvāvabodhaḥ*). "The ascetic (*tāpasaḥ*) succeeds" means that one who desires to know the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted proceeds [to practice]. Thus it is said: "he attains a particular kind of knowledge. "He applies austerity" (*tapaḥ prayuṅkte*) means he makes himself possessed of a particular kind of knowledge.

The explanation of "the other world" (paraloka) is "another birth" (janmāntara). Whether it be in this world or in heaven and so forth, the term "pāralaukika" (pertaining to the other world) is used for the purpose of indicating another body. "Concluding" (upasaṃharan): here, the suffix -śatṛ is used in the sense of a causal agent (hetau).

Regarding the question "Why is this so?": the question is why the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), when performed with the intention "I shall give to the Brahmins," results in a purpose pertaining to the next world. By the words "the meaning of the root is 'accomplishment' (*siddhi*)," etc., he shows that the meaning of the root pertains to this world. "Its purpose" means because one engages in the action for the sake of that [purpose]. Again, "accomplishment itself" should be connected by changing the gender to "pertaining to the next world. Thus, "accomplishment" means "accomplishment itself."

The term *pāralaukikī* (pertaining to the next world) is to be connected [with the word *siddhi*] by changing its gender. *Siddhiḥ* means accomplishment (*niṣpatti*). Since that accomplishment in which the verbal root (*dhātu*) resides is not *pāralaukikī*, the substitution of *āt* is therefore not excluded. Regarding the word *sākṣāt*: if the exclusion were intended to apply only to the direct, immediate meaning of *siddhyati* that pertains to the next world, then there would be no purpose served by resorting to an indirect (*pāramparya*) sense. However, this [exclusion] finds its application in a specific kind of knowledge regarding the next world in a direct sense; therefore, it does not operate in such a case [as the one under discussion]. This is the meaning.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots *mī*, *atimī*, and *dī* occurs before the suffix *lyap*.

Because the substitution of *āt* is prescribed only in the context of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), and because the suffix *lyap* cannot follow [the root] at that stage, he states "in the domain of *lyap*" (*lyapi viṣaye*) to indicate that this is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Regarding "from a monosyllabic root" (*ekācca*): although this was previously a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), nevertheless, here—due to the governing heading of "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) and because roots such as *mīnāti* cannot end in *ej* (*e*, *o*, *ai*, *au*) in their original instruction—it is understood by implication that this too is a qualifier of the scope; thus he says, "and from *ej* in the domain. The meaning is: in that suffix where *ej* is about to occur, that suffix is present in the mind.
The phrase "only in the original instruction" is explained as "prior to the production of the suffix."

He demonstrates the purpose achieved by the prescription of *āt* (long *ā*) specifically in the case of *upadeśa* (the original formative stage), stating: "Because of the prescription of *āt* specifically in the case of *upadeśa*. The suffix *erac* is characterized by having a final *i*-vowel, whereas *ghañ* is characterized by having a final *ā*-vowel. Although it is not explicitly stated that *ghañ* follows a stem ending in *ā*, nevertheless, when *āt* is present [in the original form], *ghañ* occurs; when it is absent, it does not. It is by this much that *ghañ* is said to be characterized by a final *ā*. Thus: *upadāyaḥ vartate* ("he exists as one who takes up"). Here, the augment *yuk* is applied according to the rule: *ghañi āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*.

The term *īṣadupadānam* is formed with the suffix *yuc* in the sense of the *khal* suffixes [by Pāṇini 3.3.126, *āto yuc*]. However, for the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti*, only the two *khal* suffixes (*kha* and *lu*) occur; this is because it will be stated later that "there is a prohibition of [the suffixes] *khal* and *cu* after the roots *mī*, *mīl*, and *li*" (Pāṇini 3.1.141). Therefore, *dīvyodānam* has been cited as an example.
The suffix *ap* is optionally applied after the root *lī* [to form the word *vilaya*].

The meaning is that this designation is made for both of them; however, if only the *divādi* [class] were designated by means of *śyan*, one would simply say "of *līṅ*. Furthermore, by the power of the *śit* marker in *śitap*, the *yag* suffix occurs even when there is no expression of agent or object, just as *śap* and others occur despite not expressing an agent—as in "the root *bhū* becomes *a*" (*bhavateraḥ*), and so forth. Regarding "of *khal* and *ac*": there is a general inclusion of both the *ac* suffix from the *pacādi* group and the *erac* suffix. And regarding "in this way": the meaning is precisely because of the understanding of the rule as having a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
Regarding the word *ullāpayate*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule "after the root *lī*, [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of honoring and making someone humble."
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *i* for *e*] occurs before the word *khi*. 6.1.52.

He causes to eat (*cakhādeti*). The *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), because the substitution of *ā* (in *khād*) is not dependent on any external condition (*anaimittika*); thus, due to the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule "when a vowel follows in reduplication" (*dvirvacane'ci*), the reduplicated syllable does not end in an *i*-vowel. This grammatical rule could have been omitted. How so? From the root *khād*, we have *cakhāda*; from the root *khid*, we have *cikheda*. Since roots possess multiple meanings, even a difference in meaning is of no consequence here.
The substitution of *apagura* occurs before the suffix *ṇamul*.

If the root *gṛ* (to swallow) is used in the sense of *gur* (to speak), then this grammatical rule can be stated. How so? *gireḥ* means "swallowing again and again" (*apagāram-apagāram*), while *guroḥ* means "speaking again and again" (*apagoram-apagoram*).
The suffix *vi* is applied after the root *jan* in the sense of procreation.

If it also occurs in the sense of "procreation" (*prajana*), then this grammatical derivation (*yoga*) can be established. How so? From the root *vāti*—it causes to propagate (*pravāpayati*)—and from *vīyati*—it causes to propagate (*pravāyayati*). This reading as *vīyati* is also recorded in the tradition (*smṛta*), because since *veti* belongs to the first class (*adādika*), the suffix *śyan* is impossible [there]. Indeed, the purpose of the reading with *yak* must be considered. Regarding the phrase "the commencement of birth" (*janmana upakrama*): the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *jan* in the sense of "becoming," and the prefix *pra-* indicates the beginning of an action. Regarding "the taking of the embryo" (*garbhagrahaṇa*): for an embryo is born only after it has been taken [into the womb]; therefore, the taking of the embryo is the commencement of birth.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *bhī* when the cause of fear (*hetu-bhaya*) is expressed. || 6.1.55 ||

Regarding the term *hetubhayam*: this is a compound formed according to the rule *pañcamī bhayena* ("the fifth [case-ending] with the word *bhaya*"). Thus he says: "the fear caused by a cause" (*hetor bhayam*). What, then, is that? He says: "that fear of which... And since that [substitution] does not occur in the case of the *āttva* (the substitution of *ā*) [in the root *bhi*], one might ask: since a form modified in one part is not considered different from the original, why does it not apply here? He answers: "Because of the explicit mention of the long vowel *ī* through the elision of the short *i* in the forms *lī* and *bhi*."

Regarding the rule "līlor nuglukau," the augment *nuk* is prescribed for the root *lī*, and the suffix *ṣuk* is prescribed for the root *bhī*; however, neither of these two operations applies to roots ending in long *ā*. Why? Because they are prescribed as ending in short *i*, through the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ī*—that is, as *lī-ī* and *bhī-ī*. Alternatively, according to the Vārttika which states "due to the mention of *lī* and *bhī* together by way of elision," the inclusion here is specifically of the root *lī*.
The suffix *ya* is applied after the root *smi* (to smile) when it denotes a habitual action.

Regarding the phrase "due to the commonality of the root-meanings" (*dhātvarthasāmānyāt*): *sāmānya* means similarity. The commonality of the two root-meanings is "dhātvarthasāmānyam. Since the meanings of both roots consist in a modification of the mind (*cittavikārasvabhāva*), the meaning of the root *smi* is expressed by the word *bhaya*. Thus, although *smi* was not explicitly mentioned in the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau*, [the author] intends to state the condition *hetubhaye* ("when there is fear caused by a cause").
The augment *am* is added after the roots *sṛj* ("to emit") and *dṛś* ("to see") before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, provided that the affix does not have *kit* as its marker.

Since a grammatical operation is understood to apply to a suffix when the root's own form is mentioned, the suffix is brought to mind here; thus, being qualified by *jhal*, the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) is understood, which is why he says "when preceded by *jhal*. Regarding the phrase "when a suffix beginning with *ak* follows": the meaning is that it does not occur when a suffix beginning with *kit* follows. For this is intended as a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), and this has been correctly established in the rule concerning *gāṅ* and the *kuṭādi* group. This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).

The *vṛddhi* substitution does indeed occur as "akiti," and it is not superseded because there is no absence of its application. That [vṛddhi] also occurs once *am* has been applied. This is its very explanation: "But first it is superseded" [by the *am* augment]; for that [augment] is obligatory (*nitya*). Examples are *rajjusṛḍbhyām* and *devadṛgbhyām*. Some hold that in both cases, after the application of *ṣatva* by the rule *vraśca-ādi-sūtra*, there is *jaśtva*. Others, however, desire *kutva* by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*. Now, are these two not ending in *kvip*, but rather ending in *kvip*? This is not a fault.

Because *kvip* is prescribed after a certain verbal root (*dhātu*), the substitution of *k* for *s* occurs when another suffix follows; this will be explained by the statement that although it could have been said simply "of *kvip*, [there is] *ku*," the inclusion of the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is for a specific purpose. Due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*), this substitution does not occur in forms such as *sraṣṭā* and *draṣṭā*; we shall provide the definitive explanation regarding this in the very section prescribing the *kutva* substitution.
And for a root with an unaccented vowel as its penultimate letter, provided it has a short vowel as its penultimate letter, [the substitution of *ya* for *iṭ*] may optionally take place.

The term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) is understood [from the previous rule]. This is for the purpose of qualifying that which is unaccented (*anudātta*); therefore, although in the case of *drapta-*—where the suffix *tṛn* is prescribed—the root becomes accented by the *nit*-accent, nevertheless, because it is unaccented in its original enunciation, the suffix *ām* does not apply. In the case of *vardha-*, where the suffix *tṛc* is applied, although the root becomes unaccented by the principle of "the remainder is unaccented" (*śeṣanighāta*), nevertheless, because it is not unaccented in its original enunciation, the suffix *ām* does not apply.

But for what purpose is it stated "of that which has an anudātta [vowel]"? Why not simply say "of that which does not have *iṭ*"? For if that were the case, the rule would be more concise. To this he replies: "The root *tṛp* in the sense of 'pleasing,' etc. By the rule *radhādibhyaśca*, the addition of *iṭ* is optional. Consequently, because those two [roots] would possess *iṭ* in one alternative, the [suffixes] would not apply; yet if they were to apply even when *iṭ* is absent in the other alternative, then it would also apply in cases such as *varḍhā* and *varḍhum*. This is the intended meaning.

If, then, the option for *iṅ* is prescribed for those two by the rule "radhādibhyaśca," for what purpose is their designation as having an anudātta vowel in the upadeśa? He says: "The designation as having an anudātta vowel in the upadeśa, moreover, is for the sake of [the formation of] *am*. [The word] *śīrṣan* [is used] in the Veda. (Pāṇini 6.1.60)

However, this substitution does not apply to the word *śiras*. Even though the form *śirasaḥ* is not explicitly mentioned as the original element (*sthānin*) in the rule, it is nevertheless implied by the substitute because they share the same meaning; this is just as there might be a suspicion that the word *viśravas* is a substitute for the words *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa* in the case of [the names] Śiva and others, since that too is employed in the Veda. The point is that, according to the view that it is a substitute, the word *śiras* would not be used, as it has been superseded by that substitute.

But surely, because of the recurrence of the term "anyatarasyām" (optionally), its usage will also occur; this is true, yet since one might suspect that the option would recur even in what follows, the alternative view of a different root has been adopted.
And [the final vowel of] those [stems] which take a *taddhita* suffix [is elided]. 6.1.61.

"It is established by the preceding rule alone in Vedic usage. This [sūtra] is for the purpose of the spoken language (bhāṣā), provided that here too, as in the previous rule, *śīrṣan* is understood to be a separate base (*prakṛti*). Thinking that if a taddhita suffix beginning with *ya* were produced from the word *śiras*, then its [original form] would necessarily be heard, he says: "This is intended to be a substitute (*ādeśa*). "How so?"—the question is: how is that substitute obtained? It is not obtained at all, because the original element (*sthānin*) has not been mentioned, as was the case in the previous rule.

On account of that [suffix], it implies a corresponding base (*prakṛti*)—both in terms of sound and meaning—that is the closest (*antaratama*), namely the word *śiras* itself. Thus, one says *śirasyāni*. By the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, when the suffix *kyac* is applied, the option is provided by the rule *vā keśeṣu*. Since the word *śirasya* here refers exclusively to hair, the word *keśa* should not be employed when it is already used; however, because the word *śīrṣaṇya* is a general term, the word *keśa* must be employed when it is used in order to convey the specific meaning.
The word *aci* is the head [of the following rule]. 6.1.62.
The meaning is that, because *śīrṣan* would otherwise undergo its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) due to the presence of the suffix *ani*, another substitute ending in *a* has been prescribed.

"An effort must be made here" means that this is the effort: the substitution of *ṣyaṅ*, which is produced by the occurrence of the substitute *śīrṣan*, does not become the cause for the destruction of that very [substitute]. Alternatively, the phrase "or after a word ending in *aṇ* or *iñ*" implies that one should either abandon the view of it being a substitute (based on the rule *aṇiñoranārṣayoḥ*) and instead adopt the view that it is a suffix, or else, while remaining within the view that it is indeed a substitute, an effort must be made. This is the sense of the word "or" (*vā*).

The forms *padan*, *nomān*, *śṛṅgiṇan*, *niśan*, *sanyūṣan*, *doṣan*, *yakān*, *śakan*, *udan*, and *āsan* [are substituted for their respective bases] before the suffixes beginning with *śas*. (Pāṇini 6.1.63)

Here too, because the cause [of the substitution] is specified as "in the case of *śas* and so forth," the corresponding bases are implied, and *pada* and the others are understood as the substitutes; thus he says, "pāda, danta," and so on. The word *āsana* is recited at the end, but the word *āsya* should have been recited; for in such instances as "the whelp of the wolf in the mouth (*āsni*)," "even though bound by the neck, [it is] in the mouth (*āsani*)," and "that you two released the head of the wolf from the mouth (*āsnaḥ*"), the meaning of "mouth" is understood. The form *āsanī* is the form when there is no elision (*allopābhāva*) according to the rule "optionally in the locative singular (*ṅi*) and the nominative-accusative dual (*śi*)."
Others, however, maintain that there is no distinction [between the two cases]; but in the Bhāṣya, it is established that this is merely a Vedic usage.

The word *prabhṛti* is used in the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*). However, if it were used in the sense of "limitation" (*vyavasthā*), then [the suffixes] before the case-endings beginning with *śas* would not apply. Regarding *doṣṇī*: this is the nominative dual; the substitute *doṣan* is applied to the word *doḥ*, and *auṅ* is replaced by *śī*. Regarding *māṃsapacāyā ukhāyāḥ*: the elision of the final syllable will be stated [by the rule] *māṃsasya paci yuṭghañoḥ*; this is another derivation for that word. Regarding *nasyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting a part of the body in the sense of "beneficial for" (*hitārtha*) or "belonging to" (*bhavārtha*). Regarding *nastaḥ*: the suffix *tasi* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) after the root *sah* (in the form *sāhi*) and *ruh*.

Regarding the word *naḥkṣudraḥ*: some say it is a compound formed by the rule *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena* ("the third case [ending] is compounded with a word meaning 'done by that'"). Others say it is due to a split in the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*) beginning with *saptamī*. Still others say that in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *kṣudra*, being a qualifier, is placed at the end because of its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group.

"One should state [the rule] as *yati-varṇa-nagarayoḥ*. Should it then be stated? It need not be stated. Here, first, in the case of *nāsikya-varṇaḥ*, the suffix *ñya* is applied because of its inclusion in the *parimukha* group; in the case of *nāsikyaṃ nagaram*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied because of its inclusion in the *saṅkāśa* group. Since the specific accentuation is prescribed by the rule "The initial vowel of *rājanya*, *sāṅkāśyaka*, *kāmyilya*, *nāsikya*, and *dārvāghāṭa* is optionally acute," there is no difference in accent either. On the contrary, if the suffix *yat* were used, then in the case of *anāsikyam*, the rule "*yayatoścātadarthe*" [would apply].
Thus, the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound would result; however, the accentuation of the *kṛt* suffix, with the indeclinable as the first member, is desired.
The sibilant *ṣ* at the beginning of a verbal root is replaced by *s*.

Regarding *siñcati*: the augment *num* is applied by the rule *se mucādīnām*. Regarding *ṣoḍan*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one who has six teeth" (*ṣaḍ dantā yasya*), the word *danta* becomes *datṛ* by the rule *vayasi dantasya datṛ*; then, by the rule *ṣa, uttvaṃ datṛdaśadhāsu*, the *ṣaṣ* changes its vowel to *u* (becoming *ṣoḍ*) and the initial letter of the following member becomes *ṭ* (becoming *ḍatṛ*). The augment *num* is added by the rule *ugidacām*, and the elision of the final consonant occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. In some places, however, it is read as *ṣoḍa*; that form arises when the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he expresses one who has six teeth" (*ṣoḍantam ācaṣṭe*), followed by the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*) and the addition of the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class). The word *ṣaṣ* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) formed through irregular derivation (*avyutpanna*).

*Ṣaḍaṅguli* (six-fingered) becomes *ṣaḍika*; by the rule "the suffix *ṭhañ* is added after a human name consisting of more than two syllables," and by the rule "in a suffix beginning with *ṭha* or *ja*, [the preceding part] is elided," there is the elision of the word *aṅguli*. Regarding the form *laṣati*: the inclusion of the letter *ṣ* in its original instruction (*upadeśa*) would serve to prohibit the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in forms such as *pranilaṣati* by the rule "optionally [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] in the remaining cases when the prefix *ni* is followed by a root beginning with a non-*k* sound and ending in *ṣ* in its original instruction. Furthermore, it serves to provide the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in forms such as *leṣatuḥ* and *leṣuḥ* by the rule "the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for *s* when it follows a *repha* or a consonant other than *y*, provided that the *s* belongs to a substitute or an affix. In some places, however, *kaṣati* is also read; that is incorrect.

By the very force of the instruction [of the root] with the letter *ṣ*, it will not occur here; even in the case of *praṇikaṣati*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* is established by the rule "after *ka-kha* etc. (*kakhādau*), and there is neither the substitution of *ādi* nor the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*)—thus: *cakaṣatuḥ*, *cakaṣuḥ*.

But for what purpose are the *ṣādi* roots taught? Why should not only those beginning with *sa-* be taught, so that this rule (*sūtra*) need not be composed? To this he replies: "In the case of substitutes and suffixes," and so forth. This is a restriction of the application: certain roots beginning with *ṣ* are taught so that the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) may occur only for those beginning with *sa-* when followed by a substitute or a suffix, and not for roots such as *sṛp*, *sṛj*, and others. Thus, the *ṣādi* roots have been taught for the sake of establishing this specific rule.

Otherwise, a further effort would have to be made for the sake of establishing the status of *sa* and the others as being six; and that [effort] would be cumbersome—this is the sense. But who are they? This is a question arising from the possibility of an error in the recitation. "Those which are recited in such a manner" means that they should be recited with care. Alternatively, "the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is being formulated" means for the purpose of favoring those of dull intellect. Regarding the phrase "those beginning with *s*, followed by vowels (*aj*) and dentals (*dantya*"): those for whom vowels and dentals are subsequent are "followed by vowels and dentals" (*ajdantyaparāḥ*); the word *para* here denotes a constituent part.

And since that status of being "other than a non-palatal and non-dental" (an-aj-dantyayoḥ) is understood as being relative to another constituent part, it is understood—due to proximity—to be relative to the letter *s*. [The roots] *smiṅ*, *svid*, etc.: *ṣmiṅ* "to smile slightly," *ñiṣvidā* "to perspire," *ṣvanja* "to embrace," and *viṣvap* "to sleep"—these are recited in their own phonetic forms (*svarūpeṇa*). Because the letters *v* and *m* are neither non-palatals nor non-dentals, the letter *v* also does not have exclusively a dental place of articulation (*kevaladantasthāna*). [The root] *svada* "to taste": some also recite *svadi*. [The rule begins with] *sṛpisṛjī* etc.

Excluding *sṛpṛ* (in the sense of "going"), *sṛj* (in the sense of "emission"), *stṝñ* (in the sense of "covering"), *satyai* and *ṣṭyai* (in the senses of "sound" and "collection"), *sekatir* (which has the meaning of "going"), and *sṛ* (in the sense of "going")—those other roots that have a non-jhal consonant followed by a dental (*dantyapara*) are termed *ṣopadeśa*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *subdhātu*: a *subdhātu* is one ending in *kyac* and so forth. For the roots *ṣṭivu* (in the sense of spitting) and *ṣvaṣkati* (in the sense of moving), which are *anudātta*, a prohibition of the substitution of *s* must be stated. Among these, it need not be stated for *subdhātus*, because the word "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) is understood [from the previous rule], and *subdhātus* are never enunciated [as such]. Having established this, the mention of the word *dhātu* could have been omitted. Furthermore, because of the very absence of an enunciation, the substitution will not occur for *ṣoḍa* and others; nevertheless, it is included in order to indicate the cessation of the application of the term *dhātu*.

Therefore, by the rule "lopo vyor vali," the elision occurs without distinction; thus, *ṣṭhīvati* and *ṣvaṣkati* both have two sibilants (*ṣ*). In that case, let there be *satva* (the substitution of *s*) for the preceding [sibilant], and *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) will occur for the following one due to its proximity (*sannipāta*). If this is so, then in *liṭ ṣvaṣkate*, since *ṣatva* is considered asiddha (not yet established), would the augment *dhuṭ* not be improperly applied by the rule "ḍaḥ si dhuṭ"? If that is the case, then *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣvaṣkati* begin with *y*; however, the *y* is elided by "lopo vyor vali. As for *ṣṭhīvati*, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti."

Now, if its second consonant is *ṭha*, then *teṣṭhīyate* is not established; if it is *tha*, then *ṭeṣṭhīyate* is not established. Since both forms are desired, he says: "of this [root] *ṣṭhīv*" and so forth. The sense is that the Teacher has taught his pupils in both ways.
The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs [before a following *ṇa*]. 6.1.65.

It is called *aṇati*. However, if it were taught with an initial *ṇ* (as *ṇopadeśa*), then in forms such as *niraṇati*, the rule "after a prefix, even in non-compounds, there is *ṇatva* for a root taught with an initial *ṇ*" would apply to ensure the change to *ṇ*. This [root] is also not desired after a nominal stem (*subdhātu*). Thus, in usage, all [roots] beginning with *n* are treated as before. Examples include *nṛtī*, *nandī*, and so forth: *nṛtī* in the sense of "shaking the limbs"; *ṭunadi* in the sense of "prosperity"; *nard* and *gardd* in the sense of "sound"; *nakka* in the sense of "destruction"; *naṭa* in the sense of "flowing" (belonging to the *curādi* class); and *nāthṛ* and *nādhṛ* in the senses of "begging," "affliction," and "sovereignty."
There is elision of *v* and *y* before a semivowel (*val*).

"Of the root," as is the subject under discussion, and so forth. This has been explained in the commentary on the rule *ṣaḥ saḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.64], which states "the *ṣ* at the beginning of a root becomes *s*. Regarding *didivān*: this is the form of the root *div* with the suffix *kvasu*. By the restrictive rule *vasvekājādghasām* [Pāṇini 7.2.67], there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*. There is something to be said regarding this, and we shall explain it in the commentary on the rule *vasvekājādghasām*. For *ūyī* (meaning "to weave") and *knūyī* (meaning "to sound"): regarding *āsremāṇam*, the root is *srivu* (meaning "motion" and "drying"); the suffix *manin* is added according to the Uṇādi rules, and it forms a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with the prefix *a-*.

But surely, since that which possesses an effect must exist prior to the effect, it would be more logical to state the possessor of the effect first and the effect afterwards—as in "there is elision of *y* and *v* before a semivowel" (*vyor vali lopaḥ*)—and thus there would be brevity by half a *mātrā*. Why, then, was the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) placed first? To this he says: "The mention of 'elision' first," and so forth.

Previously, by the mention of *lopa* (elision), this meaning was indicated: that this elision occurs even before other rules apply. Thus, from the root *kaṇḍūyati*, both the elision of *yak* and the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix *vi* would be applicable; however, because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal), the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix must occur first. [This refers to the formation] *kaṇḍūḥ* from *kaṇḍūyati* with the suffix *kvip*. Regarding the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*, the Bhāṣya states: "The suffix *kvip* is not seen after these. Therefore, one should understand that *kvip* is applied here to a form ending in *kyac*, namely *kaṇḍūmicchati*. For the *kaṇḍvādi* group is of two kinds: roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

In that context, since the suffix *ya* is prescribed after verbal roots (*dhātu*), suffixes such as *kyac* certainly occur after nominal stems (*prātipadika*). When *kvi* follows a stem ending in *kyac*, both the elision of the final vowel (*ataḥ lopaḥ*) and the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix *vi* (*ver apṛktasya lopaḥ*) would apply; however, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the elision of the *apṛkta* suffix must occur first.

Furthermore, if one assumes that the term *ārdhadhātuka* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), then the elision of the *at* [of *kṛ*] would occur first, and subsequently the *kvip* suffix would be applied. Even so, both the elision of the *k* (by *kvilopa*) and the elision of the *apṛkta* vowel *i* (by *verapṛktalopa*) would be applicable. In that case, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*), the elision of the *apṛkta* [vowel] would occur first. Once that has taken place, since the cause for the other elision is absent—and because there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule when the operation depends on a letter (*alāśraya*)—and because the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply here, the elision of the *val* [consonant] would not occur. However, it does occur precisely because of the inclusion of the word "previous" (*pūrva*) in the rule.

Now, one might ask: why does not *uvaṅ* substitution occur here due to the status of the elision (*al-lopa*) as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*)? It is said in reply: it has been stated that [the suffix] *kvip* follows a stem ending in *kyac*; what follows from that? Even by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, since the element *kaṇkaḍū* alone lacks the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*), *uvaṅ* does not occur. If it is argued that the *yaṇ* substitution would then apply, let there be *yaṇ*; for that, *uṭ* will be applied. Furthermore, even when *uṭ* is to be applied, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the elision, because the letter *v* precedes the original *ac* (vowel) that has been substituted. For this very reason, in forms such as *kaṇkaḍuvau*, when *ūṅ* or *uvaṅ* substitutions are to be applied, there is no *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision *al*.

Now, regarding *vraścakaḥ*, *vraścanaṃ*, and so forth: why does the elision of the letter *v* not occur before the letter *r* when it follows [the *v*]? To this he says: "In the case of *vraśc-* etc. [Objection: But surely the purpose of this instruction would be so that the sound of the *v* is heard in forms such as *vṛścati* and *vavraśca*, where, after the application of *samprasāraṇa* and *halādiśeṣa*, the elision does not take effect because the condition of being followed by a *val* (semivowel or nasal) is absent. To this he says: "Even in *vṛścati*, *vavraśca*, etc. [The reason is] "because it is *bahiraṅga* (external)."

The substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) is external because it depends upon a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *ḍ*, whereas the replacement of the first consonant by the second (*halādiśeṣa*) depends upon the reduplication; consequently, although the elision of the semivowel (*valopa*) would have applied even while those two operations were still unperformed, it does not take place precisely due to the force of the original instruction (*upadeśa*).

In this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the elision of the *val* (the consonants v, y, r, l) is rejected. In the forms *āsremāṇam* and *jīradānuḥ*, there is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) elision of phonemes; likewise, the suffix *kvasu* is also purely Vedic. For roots such as *div* and others when followed by the *yaṅ*-lopa (*yaṅluganta*), the augment *ūṭh* must occur before suffixes beginning with *ta* and so on; it must also occur before *tip* and *sip* in those alternative cases where the augment *īṭ* is absent. As for those who do not carry forward the condition "before a *kṅit*" (*kṅiti*) from that rule: [they derive] *dediviti* and *dedyoti*, *dedivīṣi* and *dedyoṣi*; however, in the case of *mip*, it occurs precisely because of the nasalization (*anunāsikatva*), resulting in *dedivīmi* and *dedyomi*. But for those who do carry forward that condition, even for them, the *yaṅ*-lopa is considered Vedic.
[The substitution of *o* for *au* occurs] when [the word *go*] is joined with a word beginning with a vowel. 6.1.67.

The *kvip* and other such suffixes are understood [here], because there is no other *vi* that is not a *apṛkta*. In the example *ghṛtaspṛk*, the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ* applies; since the term *apṛkta* is mentioned, this refers specifically to the letter *v*, and the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation.

After a verbal root ending in a consonant (hal), or in a long vowel (dīrgha) followed by a *y* or *v* (*yaṅ* or *yaṅluk*), the suffix *s* (the third person singular present indicative marker) is elided, provided it is not joined with an augment (*ayapṛkta*) and is followed by a consonant (*hal*).

The inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) serves as a qualifier for *ṅ* and *āp* alone, based on the principles of possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The inclusion of *ṅy* and *āp* is likewise a qualifier for that [long vowel]. And the inclusion of "conjoined with a consonant" (*halapṛkta*) applies to both [the long vowels and the short ones]. The terms *su*, *ti*, and *si* constitute three words. The meaning of the phrase "In this case... and so forth is that there can be no syntactic connection between the word *lopa*, which is under discussion and functions as a technical term denoting an action (*bhāvasādhana*), and the nominative forms *su*, *ti*, and *si*.

Another says: by the rule *il-ly-ābbhyaḥ*, when the genitive case is substituted for the nominative case beginning with *su*, *ti*, and *si*, there is no fault even in the technical term *lopa*. Thus, in *abhino'tra*: from the root *bhid* in the *laṅ* tense, there is the elision of *s*; by the rule *daśca*, the letter *d* becomes *r*; by the rule *ato ror aplutād aplute*, that *r* becomes *u*; by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, [the *u* and the following *a*] form *o* through *guṇa* with the *a* of *śnam*; and by the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati*, the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied.

The form *niṣkauśāmbi* is established. But surely, by the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇa*), this [suffix] will not apply here simply because of the inclusion of that which begins with it; in that case, it would also not apply here in *paramakumārī* and *paramakhaṭveki*. [Answer: It will apply, because the restriction of "beginning with that" (*tadādiniyama*) does not operate when a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*).

In examples such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, does the restriction that the compound begins with that [first member] indeed apply because of its status as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)? If so, this teaches the following: even though there is the status of a subordinate element in cases like *ardhapippalī* by virtue of the rule *ekavibhakti ca*, the elision [of the feminine suffix] still occurs. Here, *pippalī* is not a subordinate element, because of the statement: "In the case of having a single case-ending, [the word] which is not ending in the genitive [is the subordinate element]. For this very reason, the shortening [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule *gostrīyoḥ upasarjanasya* does not take place.

Let it be that [the word] is not a technical *upasarjana* (secondary member); nevertheless, it certainly remains non-primary—as in the case of *bahuśreyasī*, meaning "one who has many excellent things. Yet, its status as a technical *upasarjana* also exists: there is the prohibition of the suffix *kap* by the rule *īyasaśca*; and because of the statement "a prohibition must be stated for *īyas* in a *bahuvrīhi*," there is the absence of the shortening [of the final vowel].

Another says: "In examples such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, although the entire compound (*samudāya*) ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*), the elision of the case-ending *su* that would otherwise apply to what follows the feminine suffix *ṅyāp*—namely, the word *kauśāmbi* and the like—is precluded by the inclusion of the term 'long vowel' (*dīrgha-grahaṇa*). But surely, one might argue, this should be understood as a qualifier of the rule's application (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*): "of [the case-ending] prescribed after a word ending in a feminine suffix (*ṅyāp*)"? This cannot be so; for in cases such as *yā*, *sā*, and *kā*, the rule would not apply, because in these instances the case-ending (*sub*) is not prescribed after a word ending in *ṭā*. Let it not be thus; rather, it will be understood as: "prescribed after a word ending in a consonant (*hal*)."

If this were so, then [the elision] would apply in cases such as *yaḥ*, *saḥ*, and *kaḥ*, but it would not apply in cases such as *kartā* and *hartā*, because here the suffix *t* is not prescribed after a consonant (*hal*). Therefore, it must be accepted that the elision applies to any suffix prescribed after [a consonant], provided it does not end in a *hal*, a *ṅ*, or a long vowel (*āb*). And in this way, the elision which would otherwise result in forms like *niṣkauśāmbi* must be excluded by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule. Regarding the phrase "of that which is accompanied by *tip*": the meaning is that due to association with the word *tip*—that is, through co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) with the term *ti*—only a *tiṅ* suffix is understood.

Now, as for the phrase "for what purpose" and so forth: the meaning of the objection is that one should simply state, "su [is substituted] after a long vowel ending in *ṅī* or *āP*. [The opponent asks: "But surely, because of the rule 'not before *ṅi* or the vocative,' which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) will already be established when the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is to be applied? [The author replies: No; for otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *pacan*.

When a negation (*na*) is understood as occurring immediately after a *saṃbuddhi* (vocative singular ending), it indicates that the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is established only when there is immediate proximity between two *na*-sounds of the same class. One might object: "In cases such as *pacan*, because the sound is separated by the letter *t*, there is no elision due to the absence of such an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Anticipating this doubt, he states another fault: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*. [The word] *datvam* (the substitution of *d* for *t*) is to be supplied with the phrase "it would not occur."

When *ukhāsras* stands [as the form], the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29) applies because it is an exception (*apavāda*) that overrides the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Once the original *s* has been elided by this rule, the *s* that remains audible does not belong to the stem *vasu* and so forth; therefore, the substitution of *d* [for *s*] by the rule *vasusraṃsu* (Pāṇini 8.2.72) would not occur. Nor can the substitution of *d* for the original *s* be obtained prior to the elision of the initial member of the conjunct, because [the preceding element] is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Indeed, while the suffix *sau* is audible, the preceding element does not receive the designation "word" (*pada*), due to the prohibition contained in the rule *asarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.17).

Even so, might there be the status of being a word (*padatva*) by resorting to the position that "this [suffix *su*] also possesses the status of being a word"? Even in this case, because the substitution of *d* for *t* (*datva*) is not yet established, there would first be the elision of the initial member of the cluster (*saṃyogādilopa*). But will it not be stated there that the substitution of *d* for *t* in words such as *vasu* is established when the long vowel occurs after the nominative singular suffix (*sau*), and that in that context the mention of "the long vowel in *sau*" will not be made, but rather simply "the substitution of *d* for *t* in *vasu* and so on"? And thus, the substitution of *d* would occur even earlier? Even so, in cases such as *rājā* and *takṣā*, since the status of being a word applies even to the suffix *su*, and because the elision of the final member of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not yet established, [the elision of *s*] would occur first.

If there were elision of *n*, then because the word would not end in a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyogāntatvāt*), the elision of the nominative suffix *su* would not occur. Therefore, it was rightly stated that "the substitution of *d* would not take place. Regarding "the substitution of *u*": the phrase "it would not [occur]" is to be supplied as a continuation. The reason for this is the same: "because the elision of a final conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is [regarded as] non-existent (*asiddha*). Regarding "the substitution of *u*": the phrase "it would not [occur]" is to be supplied as a continuation. The reason for this is the same: "because the elision of a final conjunct consonant is non-existent. And this was stated without relying on the rule: "The elision of a final conjunct consonant after *ru* is to be declared as established (*siddha*) before the substitution of *u*."

But if one relies on that [interpretation], it is established—just as in the case of *harivo medinīm* and so forth—that by the rule *rātsasya*, there would be no elision at all. Now, one might object: "Since the rule *rātsasya* employs a dual notation of the letter *t* (*tta*), the letter *t* is also included through *praśleṣa* (conjunction), and thus the elision will be prescribed for the *t* following the *r* as well? If this were so, then from the root *kīrt* with the suffix *kvip*, the form would be *kīḥ*; however, according to the other arrangement, it becomes *kīrt*. Therefore, it is settled that the mention of *sic* need not be made once, while everything else must be performed.

"Regarding *saṃyogāntasya lope hi* and so forth: this is a summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*). The word *hi* indicates the reason; by the phrase 'elision of *n* and so forth' (*nalopādī*), the elisions of *d* and *ū* are included. For those who advocate for the elision of a consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), however, there would be no elision at all of the *t* following *r* in forms such as *abibhar bhavān*; therefore, the elision of the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si* after a consonant (*hal*) is prescribed."
After a vocative ending in *eṅ* or a short vowel, [the *s* of the nominative-accusative dual is elided]. Pāṇini 6.1.69.

In this context, if the mention of *hal* (consonant) were not carried over [from the previous rule], then only *sambuddhi* (vocative case ending) would be qualified by *eṅ* and *hrasva*—meaning that the *sambuddhi* following what ends in *eṅ* or what ends in a short vowel (*hrasva*) is elided—and consequently, the elision would not occur in the example "he kuṇḍa."

How so? When *kuṇḍa-su* is present, both elision (*lopa*) and the substitution of *am* (*ambhāva*) are applicable. In that case, elision is non-permanent because it is superseded by the attainment of another form; for if *am* were substituted, the rule "of what follows" (*ādeḥ parasya*) would cause the elision to apply to the letter *a* of *am*, whereas if it were not substituted, it would apply to the letter *s*. On the other hand, the substitution of *am* is non-permanent because it is absolutely precluded once elision has occurred. Since both are non-permanent, the substitution of *am* takes precedence due to its posteriority in the rules; once *am* is applied, both the substitution of the preceding vowel (*ami pūrvasya*) and elision become applicable.

In that case, since *ami-pūrvatva* (the substitution of *am* for *au*) has been applied, there would be no *vyapavarga* (separation of vowels), and because both [rules] would depend on the same substratum, the status of being "like the end" (*antavad-bhāva*) or "like the beginning" (*ādivad-bhāva*) would not apply; thus, elision (*lopa*) would not occur. Furthermore, once elision were applied, *am* would no longer exist, so *ami-pūrvatva* would not apply. Since both rules are equally non-obligatory (*anitya*), *ami-pūrvatva* would take precedence due to its higher position in the order of rules, and consequently, elision would not occur. Therefore, the mention of *hal* must be carried over [from the previous rule]. Thus he says: "and *hal*" (*haliti ca*). This is understood to mean "it continues. It is not governed by the term *apṛkta*; for if it were governed by it, [the rule] would not apply in a form such as *he kuṇkaḍe*.

Because the designation *apṛkta* does not exist [in this context]. But how is it known that this [rule] is not operative? To that, he says: "And so" (*tathā ca*). Even though the mention of *hal* (consonant) continues [from the previous rule], if the vocative (*sambuddhi*) were qualified by *eṅ* and the short vowels (*hrasva*), then the consonant would be qualified by that [vocative]—namely, "the consonant at the end of a vocative following what ends in *eṅ* or a short vowel is elided. In that case, [the elision] would not occur in *he kuṇḍa*, for the very reason stated previously.

Therefore, considering that the *eṅ* vowels and the short (*hrasva*) vowel must be qualified by the vocative (*sambuddhi*) and the consonant (*hal*) respectively, he says: "from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *eṅ*, etc. Since the nominal stem implied by the vocative is qualified by the *eṅ* and the short vowel, the rule of "ending-in" (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained. In this view, in the case of *kuṇḍa*, because the substitution of *ām* for the preceding [vowel] behaves as if it were the end of the word relative to what precedes it, a consonant follows a short vowel; and thus, the elision of the vocative suffix is established by the rule *sambuddheḥ*.

Regarding the term *ac-chabda*: this will be explained in that very place. As for the phrase "due to the absence of a short vowel" (*hrasvābhāvāt*): [an objection is raised]—is it not the case that the vowel *ā* in *adaḍ* itself is short, and since a consonant follows it and it is connected with the vocative (*sambuddhi*), the elision (*lopa*) would certainly occur? Furthermore, if the vocative were being qualified, then upon the elision of the stem-vowel *ā*, the vocative would no longer follow a short vowel, and thus the elision would not apply. It is replied:

It has been stated that "the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) implied by the vocative case-ending (*sambuddhi*) is qualified by the terms 'long' (*eṅ*) and 'short' (*hrasva*). By this rule, [the elision] will not occur in *kuṇkaḍe*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the final element of the preceding part, and thus it is included by the mention of the "base form" (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, it will not occur in *he katarat*, because once the *ṭi*-elision has been applied, the base form ends in a short vowel. [The reason given is] "because the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative is stronger. Otherwise, when *agni-su* is situated there, both the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative and the elision [by the rule] "after a short vowel" would apply simultaneously.

In that case, because the word is eternal (*nitya*) and because it is subsequent, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied by the rule for the vocative singular (*sambuddhi*), the [elision] would not occur because the word no longer ends in a short vowel (*ahrasvānta*). Now, might it not be understood that the term "short vowel" (*hrasva*) qualifies the condition under which the vocative is prescribed—that is, "the vocative that is prescribed after a word ending in a short vowel"? Even so, it would not apply in the case of *he khaṭve*. One might argue: "Let it not occur by this [rule]; it will occur by the preceding one, since the word ends in *-ā*. But even so, it would still not occur in the case of *he khaṭve*.

"Let it not be [the case that the rule does not apply] because of this [suffix]; since it ends in *ā*, it will be covered by the preceding rule. Even so, in forms such as *he nadi*, *he yavāgu*, and *he kumārī*, [the elision] would not occur; nor can elision be obtained here on the basis of its ending in a *ṅ* (feminine suffix), because of the explicit mention of the "long" (*dīrgha*) vowel. "In that case, both [interpretations] shall be understood: as a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*) and as a qualifier of the subsequent element (*para-viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, it will apply everywhere in cases such as *agne* and *kumārī*. In that regard, it is first of all difficult for the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva-grahaṇa*), which is heard only once, to serve as a qualifier for both.

Even so, it might be obtained. For instance, in the case of *katarat*, although the elision of the *ṭi* suffix occurs, there is no subsequent short vowel (*hrasva*) following the vocative ending; nevertheless, since the vocative ending is prescribed after what ends in a short vowel, the elision would indeed take place. Therefore, the mention of *eṅ* (the vowels *e* and *o*) must be made.

We, however, say that the inclusion of *eṅ* (the vowels *e* and *o*) must be made even for the sake of those words that end in *eṅ* by their very nature. For example: a Brāhmaṇa who has surpassed the word *ahi* is called *atihi*; his vocative is *he atihe*. One by whom the word *pacate* is imitated is called *anukṛtapacate*; his vocative is *he anukṛtapacate*. Pāṇini, by whom the suffix *īra* was prescribed, is called *vihitereḥ*; his vocative is *he vihitere*, and so forth. Regarding this, there is a summary verse: "If the vocative were not distinct from the base form, then it would neither be like the beginning nor like the end."
This fault remains even when there is *lup* after the elision of *hal*, because the substitution of *am* by *pūrvarūpa* takes precedence due to its being a subsequent rule.

The prescription of *lup* applies after a stem ending in a short vowel, whereas *hal* [refers to] the elision of *ṭi* after a stem ending in a consonant—as in *kataraḍ*—and thus it cannot apply here. Furthermore, because of the explicit mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*), a rule prescribed subsequently does not supersede one that is otherwise established; therefore, even in the case of *atihe*, the *aṅ* substitute does not occur.
*Lopana* is *lup*; the meaning is "elision."
In the Vedic language, the elision of *ś* occurs diversely.

Regarding the word *kṣetrī*: when the suffix *śi* is elided, the augment *num* is applied by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, and lengthening occurs by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*; then the *n* is elided. This grammatical operation (*yoga*) could have been omitted; how so? Because it is already established by the substitution of *ḍā*. But how about the form *agnetrī*? When *tri-ī* remains, it is established simply by the long vowel of the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the first two cases. It is not established, because it is separated by *num*. [Answer: In Vedic usage, the neuter should be treated as masculine; for the sake of forms such as *madhorgṛhṇāti*, the elision of *num* occurs precisely through the masculine treatment.

Even so, the rule "jasi ca" would entail *guṇa*; however, he will state this: "In the Vedic language, there is an option regarding the suffixes beginning with *us*, prior to the rule concerning the penultimate vowel before the causative *ṇi* and *caṅ*. Furthermore, in the case of *yā kṣetrā tā tā piṇḍānām*, when *tā-i* remains, the *ikāra* is changed to *akāra* by the rule "supāṃ suluk," and the form is established through lengthening by the rule "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ."
The augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel before a *kṛt* suffix that begins with a *pi*t (a vowel other than *a*).

A verbal root (*dhātu*) is attracted [by the rule], and it is further qualified by the term "short" (*hrasva*); therefore, the rule of application to that which ends in such [a root] occurs. Thus he says: "of a verbal root ending in a short vowel. Examples are *agnicit* and *somasut*. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rules "after the root *ci* when *agni* precedes" and "after the root *su* when *soma* precedes. As for *grāmaṇikulam*, if the words are analyzed separately (*vyasta*), there is the shortening of the neuter; however, in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the *kvip* suffix is applied by the rules "the *ik* vowel is shortened before a feminine suffix according to Gālava" and "after the root *su* when *soma* precedes."

If, however, this *tuṭ* augment were placed at the beginning [of the suffix], it could not be done in this way; for here, in the case of *agnicit-soma-sut*, the elision of *v* by the rule "verapṛktasya" would not apply. And here, in the case of *paritanoti* with the *kvip* suffix, there would be the elision of the nasal by the rule "kvau ca gamādīnām," followed by the lengthening by the rule "nahivṛti" etc.—resulting in *parītat*. Since the *tuṭ* would then be part of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *iṭ*. Furthermore, in the case of *avacchya*, the substitution of *et* by the rule "vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ" would be wrongly applied.

Now, if it were not an *abhakta* (an integral part of the preceding word), then in the case of *madhucchādayati*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would not apply, because of the intervention of the letter *t*. Nor is the letter *t* itself an *atiṅ*; for it does not constitute a word (*apadatvāt*). Therefore, it must indeed be treated as a *pūrvānta* (the final element of the preceding word). If this were so, however, the following would not be established: the shortening of the neuter (*napuṃsakahrasvatvam*), the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjanahrasvatvam*), and the accent of the *dvigu* compound (*dvigusvaraḥ*). Regarding the shortening of the neuter: *ārāśaṣkulicchatram*, *dhānāśaṣkulicchatram*. Regarding the shortening of the subordinate member: *niṣkauśāmbicchatram*.

Regarding the accent of a *dvigu* compound—as in *pañcāratnicchatram*—once the augment *tuk* has been applied, these rules do not apply because [the final vowel] is no longer final? No, for they are *antaraṅga*. The *tuk* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on the conjunction with the letter *ch*; these rules (*antaraṅga*) will therefore take effect even before that [conjunction] occurs.
In the *saṃhitā* [text], [the rules of this chapter apply]. 6.1.72.

The locative case in "saṃhitāyām" is a locative of domain (viṣaya-saptamī). The meaning is that the grammatical operation to be described takes place when *saṃhitā*—the conjunction of the phonemes—is the domain, serving as both the locus of the operation and its cause. He will state: "A semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) replaces an *ik* vowel before an *ac* vowel. However, the underlying intention for bypassing the rule of proximity (*antaraṅga*) must be sought. [Example: *dadhi atra*.

But surely, in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, this locative case is one of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), and since no such location other than immediate proximity (*upaśleṣika*) is possible among phonemes, a substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* prescribed when [the vowel] is proximate to a vowel will not occur when there is an intervention by another phoneme or an intervention by time; thus, what is the purpose of the governing heading on *saṃhitā*? It is, however, for the sake of providing a technical indication (*jñāpaka*); it indicates this: "In the application of the maxim regarding the specified [element], an intervention by time is not taken into account."

Therefore, even when there is an intervention by time, an operation such as *aluk* (non-elision) prescribed for the initial sound of the subsequent member still indeed takes place—for example, *ākhareṣṭhaḥ* [from *ākhare sthaḥ*] and *agnāviṣṇū* [from *agnā viṣṇū*], and so forth.
And [the suffix *cha*] after [a stem ending in] *ca*. 6.1.73.

The letter *cha* and the letter *kā* are for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), as seen in such rules as "vidi-bhidic-chideḥ" and "śācchor anyatarasyām. Regarding the governing context (*adhikāra*), there are two positions: that it governs meaning (*arthādhikāra*) and that it governs the word-form (*śabdādhikāra*). In the first position, since the verbal root (*dhātu*)—which was implied by the previously mentioned rule—is qualified by the term "short" (*hrasva*), the word "short" indicates that which ends in a short vowel; thus, in this [present] rule as well, only that which ends in a short vowel would be understood.

In this context of the rule concerning sounds (*śabdādhikāra*), however, only the word *hrasva* (short vowel) is carried forward here, not the previously mentioned meaning; nor is there any thing to be qualified here.
