Thus, due to the absence of a rule governing the inclusion of what ends with that [word], only the short vowel becomes the augment. Regarding this, he says—“only the short vowel is the augment here”—because the second alternative has been adopted. What is established by this being so? To that he says—"by that. For if *tuk* were to belong to that which ends in a short vowel, then because *tuk* would be included by the mention of "reduplication" (*abhyāsa*), its disappearance would occur through the rule of "remaining after consonants" (*halādiśeṣa*).

However, when a short vowel is the augment (*āgama*), this [hal] is not a part of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*); therefore, this undesirable consequence does not arise. But how is it that a short vowel, when it is an augment, is not included by the mention of "guṇa" and "reduplication"? To this he says: "not a part of a part. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

If a part of a part were not to be a part of the whole, then in the case of *śerate*, the augment *ruṭ*—being a part of the substitute *ad* which is itself a part of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix—would likewise not be a part of the *sārvadhātuka* as a whole. What would be the fault in that? The rule "there is guṇa for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka*" would not apply, because of the intervention by *ruṭ*. For while *ruṭ*, being attached to the [substitute] part, would not intervene with respect to that [substitute] itself, it certainly does intervene with respect to the *sārvadhātuka*.

And from what reasoning does this principle derive—that "the part of a part is not a part of the whole"? In common worldly usage, the finger, which is a part of Devadatta’s hand (which is itself a part of Devadatta), is indeed a part of Devadatta as well, as expressed by the phrase "Devadatta with his fingers. Therefore, the intended meaning here is that the single rule *cha āhbhāṅośca* should have been formulated; [and] by virtue of the word *ca*, it would apply both to the immediately preceding [element] and to that which was previously mentioned.

Since this is already established, the reason he employs a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) and the letter *ca* is this: by abandoning the application of that which ends in *tat* (the previous rule), he intends to carry forward only the short vowel (*hrasva*) alone. For if the augment *tuk* were a constituent part of the entire complex (*samudāya*), this effort would be purposeless.
And [the substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] after the augment *āṭ* and after *māṅ*.

They state the purpose for including the prefix *āṅ* and the specific mention of the *ṅit* markers: "of *āṅ* when it is *ṅit*" (*āṅo ṅitaḥ*). The meaning is that the inclusion of the two forms distinguished by the *ṅit* marker is for the sake of accomplishing a specific meaning. In the case of *ācchāyāyāḥ*, the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* applies because of the rule "āṅ in the sense of a limit" (*āṅ maryādāvacane*), and the ablative case is used according to the rule "the fifth [case] with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" (*pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ*). In the case of *ācchāyam*, it is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "āṅ in the senses of limit and inclusion" (*āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*). In the case of *mācchidad*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule "optionally after a root ending in *i* or *ī*" (*irito vā*).

*Āchāyā*, *ācchāyā*: here the vowel *ā* is used in the sense of recollection, according to the rule "in the case of a sentence or recollection, [the suffix] is *aṅ*. Regarding *pramā*: from the root *mā* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "after *ā* when there is a prefix. Although the verbal root here has the marker *ṅ*, the word ending in *ṭāp* (*pramā*) is not *ṅit*. Consequently, the principle "there is no distinction in the inclusion of *gām*, *ā*, and *āṅ*" would lead to the undesirable consequence of including even this derivative form [which is not a primary root]. In both these cases, however, the option "optionally after a word-final [ṅ]" applies.
[The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] after a long vowel. 6.1.75.

"In the case of an instruction involving an ablative (*abhayanirdeśa*), an ablative instruction is more powerful. Furthermore, the ablative [in *dīrghāt*] has not yet fulfilled its purpose; therefore, by means of this ablative, the genitive of the locative *chaḥ* is substituted, and [the author] dispels the misconception that the augment *tuk* must belong to the letter *ch* itself—by stating "that which follows a long vowel," and so forth. By this, the connection with the ablative is shown; however, for the sake of consistency in the grammatical sequence, he shows that the letter *ch* is the cause (*nimitta*) and the long vowel is the object of the operation (*kāryin*).

"In that [context], of the preceding of that very same long vowel. And here the evidence is the mention of *śācchā*, *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyā*, and so forth; for since both the relationship of limit and limited (*avadhyavadhimadbhāva*) and the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇabhāva*) are intended, the locative case is employed in the rule *tasmin pūrvasya*. *Hrīcchati*: from the root *hrīccha* in the sense of "shame. *Mlecchati*: from the root *mleccha* in the sense of "indistinct sound. *Apacācchāyate*: from the root *cho* in the sense of "cutting," with the intensive suffix *yaṅ*, and by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*.
Or [the substitution of *anusvāra* for a non-nasal homorganic consonant] may optionally occur after a word-final [consonant]. 6.1.76.

Since the rule for "that which ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantavidhi*) is already established by the fact that the long vowel is a qualifier of the word (*pada*) under discussion, the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) is intended to ensure that this is a rule regarding the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*), so that the augment *tuK* may apply there; it is not a rule regarding a word (*padavidhi*). Consequently, because the maxim concerning semantic compatibility (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) does not apply here, the optional application of the augment occurs even in such cases as *tiṣṭhatu kumārī chatraṃ hara devadattasya*.
A semi-vowel (yaṇ) is substituted for an *ik* vowel before a following vowel (*ac*).

The substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik* occurs. Because of the similarity between the *iks* and the *yaṇ*s, the correspondence is established by numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*), or it is determined by internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*). Why is "for *ik*" stated? So that it does not apply to a consonant—e.g., in *vāk* here. Since the rules for *kutva* and *jaśtva* are considered non-established (*asiddha*), the substitution of *yakāra* for the letter *ś* would [otherwise] result. And where there is no possibility of *kutva* and so forth at the end of a word, as in *pacati*, would there still be the application [of this rule]? This is not a fault.

The term "from a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*) is understood [from the previous rule], and since that was established as the *sthānin* (the element to be replaced) in that very context of the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), it is carried over here in the same way. If the *yaṇ* substitute occurs for a long vowel, how is it that we have forms such as *dadhy atra* and *madhv atra*? [The answer is: the term "for a short vowel" (*hrasvasya*) is also carried over; thus, because the *yaṇ* is prescribed for both short and long vowels, there is no possibility [of its application] to a consonant. Furthermore, in cases such as *cayanam* and *cāyakaḥ*, the *pluta* vowel must undergo *prakṛtibhāva* (the state of remaining in its original form), because *ecām ay-ādayaḥ* (P. 6.1.78) and other such rules serve as exceptions (*apavāda*). This applies where [the general rule] has not yet taken effect.

Is it because of its commencement at that point? O Lord of the Gods, in cases such as *khaṭvaudana*, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions will serve as exceptions [to the rule], just as even when the term "vowel" (*ac*) is not mentioned, the long vowel substitution for homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-dīrghatva*) occurs in *dadhi-indra* and so forth; therefore, there is no need for the mention of "vowel" (*ac*). If so, then this is the purpose: that the *yaṇ* replacement of *ik* should occur only before a vowel (*aci*), and whatever else might otherwise apply, that should not happen. What else might apply? The *śākala* doubling. And there is no absolute exclusion of that either, due to the force of the rule's very commencement.

This being the case, that which is traditionally recorded by the ancient teachers—that there is a prohibition of the Śākala rule regarding the *sinnitya* compounds—is accomplished by this very mention of *in*.

Regarding the phrase *ikaḥ plutapūrvasya*: that which has a *pluta* vowel as its predecessor is so described; the meaning is "after a *pluta* vowel. In the sequence *bho 3 i indra*, since the word *bhoḥ* is *pluta* due to its being sung (*gīti*), and the vowel *i* is a particle (*nipāta*) because it is listed among the vowels and so forth, it would receive the designation *pragṛhya*. When the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would have applied to it, the *yaṇ* substitution is prescribed. This was stated with the intention that [the rule] prevents the application of the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening) and other such rules. Thus, [it refers to] "that which has a *pluta* vowel as its predecessor."

The inclusion of the term "protracted" (*pluta*) is for the purpose of including vowels other than those of one or two morae (*mātrā*); by this, it also applies to [vowels] of four morae and so forth. Thus do the Chāndogas sing; furthermore, this [term] is intended only for the *Sāmavedic* chanters, as even the expression "he sings 'bhoy indram'" is an imitation of a *Sāmaga*. Such is the position established in the Bhāṣya, and it should be understood in the same way in the Vṛtti as well.
The substitution of *vā* occurs before the suffix *yi*.

For whom, then, is this the prescription of *vānta* (the "ejected" sounds)? It follows from the rule for *ec*. If that is so, would it not also apply to *e* and *ai*—as in *ceyam*, *jeyam*, and *raiya-ti*? In that case, the mention of *vānta* will not be made; let there simply be the rule: *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*. But even so, the substitution would still apply here: *ceyam*, *jeyam*. [To this we reply: the rules *kṣayyajayyau śakyārthe* and *kryyastadarthe* will serve as restrictive (*niyama*) rules: [they will mean] that if an *ec* occurs, it happens only in the case of the roots *kṣi* and *ji*.

Even so, would the substitution of *ā* not apply in the case of *raiyatī*? The word *rai* is Vedic, according to the rule: "In the Veda, one follows what is observed. However, the use of the word *rai* in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is incorrect because it contradicts the Bhāṣya. Alternatively, this restriction may be adopted: "If [the suffix] occurs after a word other than one ending in *u*, it occurs only after *kṣi* and *ji*"; then the second rule, "in the sense of possibility," would mean that even after *kṣi* and *ji*, it occurs only in the sense of possibility. This is established; but what is the interpretation of the Sūtra itself? It is said:

This word *vānta* refers to that which is proximate (*sannihita*), not to whatever [sound] occurs anywhere; and what is proximate here is that which stands in place of *au* or *ai*, due to its connection with the rule of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*). In that case, just as no arbitrary substitute for *vānta* occurs, so too none will occur in place of anything else, because only a specific [substitute] is brought into proximity. This is what was stated: "this [substitute] which occurs in place of *ec*. Regarding *bābhravya*: [the suffix] *yañ* is applied by the rule "after *madhu* and *babhru*, [the patronymic suffixes are added] when [the descendants are] Brāhmaṇas and Kauśikas. The word *maṇkaḍu* belongs to the *garga*-class.

By means of the words *śaṅku* and *picu*, in the sense of "for that purpose, from a derivative back to its original material" (*tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau*), the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *ugavādibhyo yat*. *Nāvyam* means "to be crossed by boat"; here, *yat* is applied according to the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūlasītātulābhyastāryatulyaprāpyavadhyānāmyasamasamitasammiteṣu*. The phrase *adhvaparimāṇe ca* is for the sake of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). *Gavyūtiḥ* means a pair of *krośas*.
[The rule applies] only to that [root] which is the cause of that [suffix]. Why is it stated "to a root"? For there is no possibility of a restriction applying without qualification—

"If [the substitution] occurs before the suffix *yi*, it must be of that very cause"; for in this way, a specific rule (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)—namely, "when *yi* follows, the *vānta* [substitution] applies to that which is the cause of it"—would have to be resorted to, and thus the entire [system of] rule-separation (*yogavibhāga*), the particle *eva*, and the restriction (*niyama*) would become useless. Therefore, the question is: even in the absence of the mention of "root" (*dhātu*), will there be a restriction regarding a specific domain? The answer is: that specific domain might also include nominal stems (*prātipadika*). [Consequently, the substitution] would apply only in cases such as *vābhravya*.

Because this is the cause for that; [the objection] "it would not occur here" is due to the opposite case. Regarding *upoyate*: it is the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive (*karmaṇi*), with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) suffix, the *yak* augment, *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) because it belongs to the *yajñādi* group, lengthening by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*, and *guṇa* by *ādguṇaḥ*. Because that [resultant form] is treated like the initial element with respect to the following [suffix], it is included by the mention of "root" (*dhātu*). Regarding *oyate*: likewise, the aorist (*laṅ*) in the passive. Regarding *lāuyamāni*: the suffix *iñ* after a root ending in *a*, with vṛddhi of the first vowel.

[Objection: But surely, in this case, the *guṇa* [substitution] is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two words (*padadvayāpekṣatvāt*), and the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is likewise *bahiraṅga* because it depends on an external *taddhita* suffix? [Reply: True; however, both of these do not apply in the case of *auyatā*; therefore, the rule must necessarily be commenced for that purpose. Since the result is established by the commencement of the rule itself, forms such as *upoyate* are cited as counter-examples (*pratyudāhṛta*). [Question: What is the purpose of employing the particle *eva* (in the rule)? [Answer: The objection is that when a rule is already established, its commencement serves the purpose of restriction (*niyamārthatva*), and not even the employment of the particle *eva*. [Reply: The answer is that it is for the sake of restriction according to what is desired (*iṣṭato’vadhāraṇārtha*).
The suffixes *kṣayya* and *jayya* occur in the sense of "capable of" (*śakya*).
In the example, the kṛtya suffixes are used in the sense of possibility; in the counter-example, however, they are used in the sense of necessity.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is used after a word denoting the price of something, in the sense of "that for which it is the price."

In the word *krayya*, the meaning of the suffix is the object (*karman*), since the kṛtya suffixes are prescribed in the sense of the object; and the meaning of the base is the exchange of goods. In that case, the meaning of the suffix is primary (*pradhāna*) and the meaning of the base is subordinate (*upasarjana*). Therefore, if the meaning of the suffix were intended by the pronoun *tat* due to its primacy, then since the word *krayya* functions in that very sense, there would be no purpose in including the phrase "having that as its meaning" (*tadartha-grahaṇa*).

Now, does the phrase "in that which has that as its object" (tadarthe) mean "in that word whose referent is that [object]"? That too is incorrect, because a word cannot have such a function. Therefore, he shows that even though it is subordinate, it is indicated as being precisely within the meaning of the base (prakṛti)—namely, "in that which has that as its object," meaning "in that which is for the purpose of buying. "That which is spread out for the purpose of buying" means that which has been placed in the shop with the intention that "buyers might purchase it. "To be bought" (kreya) means that which is to be acquired by means of a price.

"And there is nothing here for sale" means that there is no grain spread out in the marketplace for the purpose of selling. Some, however, say that in the word *krayya*, the root *krī* (to buy) functions in the sense of selling; thus, an item spread out in the marketplace for the purpose of selling is called "krayya."
The forms *bhayya* and *pravayya* are [valid] in the non-Vedic (secular) language.
Regarding the word *vītya*: it is derived either from the root *vī* in the sense of "motion" and so forth, or according to the rule *ajervyaghañapoḥ*.
Regarding *hradayyāḥ*: there is the substitution of *ay* for the vowel *ā*.

"One [element] takes the place of both the preceding and the following. In the section to be explained, two elements situated in a sequence of priority and posteriority are indicated—such as "before *āt*" (*ādaci*) and "after *āt*" (*ādecī*), etc. The meaning of the sūtra is that the substitution (*ekādeśa*) to be explained, such as *guṇa* and so forth, occurs in the place of those two, the preceding and the following.

Now, what is the purpose of [the mention of] "the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*)? It is for the purpose of indicating the substituend (*sthānin*). For if that were not present, in rules such as *ādguṇaḥ*, there would be no indication of the substituend, and consequently, what would the substitute—such as a *guṇa*—replace? This is not a valid purpose, because a fifth case (ablative) such as *āt* will effect a sixth case (genitive) for a seventh case (locative) such as *aci*; and by that [sixth case], the *guṇa* will occur in place of those very two, namely the preceding and the following. Therefore, this [mention] is unnecessary. To this he says: "The mention of 'preceding and following'," and so forth.

"For the sake of understanding the simultaneous application of two rules" means for the sake of understanding the simultaneous application of two substitutions. But if that [simultaneity] were not present, which [rule] would apply? Therefore, it is said: "Neither the locative nor the ablative case endings are both [simultaneously] applicable. The meaning is that neither are they both applicable at once. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*). In that regard, in the rule *ādguṇaḥ*, this locative case ending in *aci* has its purpose fulfilled by the prescription of *yaṇ* and other such operations.

In the rule *ādityeṣā tu pañcamī*, however, this fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) has nowhere else fulfilled its purpose; consequently, it would itself project a sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the seventh case (*saptamī*), and thus the *guṇa* substitution would occur only in place of the vowel *a*. But in the rule *vṛddhireci*, since the prescription of *guṇa* has already fulfilled the purpose of the fifth case, that [fifth case] would project a sixth case for the seventh case *eci* (which otherwise has no purpose), and thus the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply only to the vowel *a*.

In rules such as "upasargād ṛti dhātau" (Pāṇini 6.1.91), even though both [the upasarga and the dhātu] have not yet fulfilled their purpose, there would be an alternating assignment of the genitive case to each other, rather than simultaneous status as the recipient of the operation (*kāryitva*) and the cause (*nimittatva*); for these two are mutually contradictory at once, and consequently, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) would also occur alternately. Therefore, should one not state "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*)? It need not be stated; for by the force of the mention of the word "one" (*eka*), and by the rule "as if it were the end and the beginning" (*antādivacca*), the substitution will occur for both the preceding and the following together, and not for either one alone. This is true.

However, it was stated that [the mention of] "the preceding and the following" is for the sake of ease of comprehension (*sukhapratipatti*); otherwise, if the intended meaning were conveyed simultaneously by means of assuming two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhī*), there would be complexity in comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*).

Now, for what purpose is the word "one" (*eka*) used? Having bypassed what was mentioned first, the purpose of the latter-mentioned term "of the preceding and the following" was stated previously; this is because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). How so? An existing subject (*kāryin*) must exist prior to its effect (*kārya*), and the mention of "one" is an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that effect, such as the *guṇa*.

But surely, in rules such as *ādguṇaḥ*, only a single substitute is mentioned; since the number [of the substituends] is intended to be significant and there is no reason to abandon the number thus expressed, there will therefore be only one substitute, such as *guṇa*.

It might be argued: "Since the injunction (*ādeśa*) is primary by virtue of being that which is to be performed (*vidheya*), and since in cases such as 'one cleanses the cup' (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*) the number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) when it concerns the primary element, there would follow the contingency of cleansing multiple cups. This is incorrect, because the cleansing is enjoined with reference to the cup as the object to be benefited (*śeṣin*); furthermore, that which is enjoined in another scriptural passage becomes the object to be benefited here, and those cups known from other scriptural passages are associated with different numbers. Therefore, if one were to intend the singular number here, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result. Thus [the singular is not intended].

It is said that in the case of the "single cup" (*grahaikatva*), singularity is not intended to be significant. It is not so in the case of the injunction regarding the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the cups, where singularity is indeed intended. Under the heading of the nine cups prescribed in another scriptural passage—"There are nine cups for Prajāpati"—the purificatory rite of cleansing is enjoined. In that context, although singularity is mentioned in the text, it cannot be included within the scope of the subject matter (*uddeśya*), because the cups have already been enjoined as being associated with a different number (nine). Consequently, if that singularity were intended to be significant, it too would become an object of the injunction, which would result in the fallacy of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

In cases such as "He cleanses that which he grasps," the distinction arises from a difference in the mode of expression (vacanavyakti), namely, that he grasps it and he cleanses it, and that it is singular. However, in the present case, although the quality and so forth are primary by virtue of being the object of an injunction, there is no risk of syntactical split (vākyabheda) because a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) is possible; furthermore, since there is no reason for non-intentionality, singularity is intended, just as in common worldly usage. For example, when one says in the world, "Make a jar from these two lumps of clay," even though it is not explicitly stated that it should be "one," the person makes only one.

Nor can it be argued that, due to the context or other factors, only one [substitute] is applied there; for we observe [multiple applications] even in the absence of such [contextual factors]. Therefore, the singular mention [of "one"] does not serve the purpose [of restricting the application]. To this, he says: "The mention of 'one' is for the sake of precluding separate injunctions. He demonstrates how the contingency of separate injunctions arises: "Because of the difference in the substituenda (*sthānin*). From the expression "of the preceding and the following," a difference in the substituenda is understood; consequently, by virtue of that, even though unity is heard in the rule regarding the substitute (*ādeśa*), it would be unintended, resulting in the contingency of multiple substitutes. This is the meaning.

He demonstrates by means of an example that this must necessarily be accepted: "as in the case of *natva* and so forth. The meaning is that just as, according to the rule "after *r* and *d*, the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *n*, and the preceding *d* also [becomes *n*]," the substitution of *n* occurs (*pratisthāni*) without any intention to express numerical unity, so it is here as well.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the mention of the singular number (*eka*) is rejected. To begin with, it is not logical to assume a distinction in the substitute (*ādeśa*), which is the primary element, on account of the original (*sthānin*), which is subordinate; for a subordinate element conforms to the primary, but the primary does not conform to the subordinate. As for what was said—"In the case of *bhinn* and so forth, there is indeed *natva* [the substitution of *n*]"—it is certainly not the case that because the singularity is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*) in the rule prescribing *natva*, two *n*s come into being. What then? From the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and of the preceding" (*pūrvasya ca*), a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) is understood.

In that context, by the former [rule], the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the final *n*, and by the latter, for the *d* of the root; and here, regarding the form *prāṇiṇiṣati*, since the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* immediately following the prefix is already established by the rule *aniteḥ*, the inclusion of the word *ubhau* (both) in the rule *ubhau sābhyāsasya* would not be necessary—since the substitution of *ṇ* for both *n*s would be established by the mere statement "of that which has the reduplication" (*sābhyāsasya*) alone. Thus, the mention of *ubhau* is intended to specify the substituends: namely, that both *n*s undergo the substitution of *ṇ*.

Therefore, the mention of "both" (ubhau) is understood for the sake of a specific instruction: that when there are two *ṇakāras* in place of the *ani* root along with its reduplication (*abhyāsa*), both of them become *ṇakāras*. Consequently, even in this case, because singularity is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*), two [ṇakāras] occur for the two [roots]; however, since it is due to the mention of "both," there is no fault whatsoever.

In this world, certain actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti are performed only once, such as initiation (upanayana), the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), and sipping water for purification (ācamana); for one who has been initiated is not initiated again, nor does one who has established the fires establish them again, nor does one who has sipped water sip it again—provided there is no specific occasion [for repetition]. Other actions are performed repeatedly when there is no specific occasion, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. For example, according to the rule "An elderly Brāhmaṇa should be greeted by rising," whenever any elderly person arrives, one must rise to greet him.

The prohibition "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" and "Liquor must not be drunk" is carried out with respect to every individual instance; one does not, however, refrain from killing a single Brāhmaṇa or drinking a single instance of liquor and then act as one pleases elsewhere. And grammar is a Smṛti (traditional law); thus, when the injunction "A Guṇa [substitution] must be performed" is issued by this Smṛti rule "ādguṇaḥ," if—thinking that the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled by performing the Guṇa substitution once in a single instance such as *khaṭvendra*—one were not to perform it in cases such as *mālendra*, then [the rule would be invalid]. Therefore, like the act of rising to greet [a guest], it must be repeated for each instance.

What, then, is the basis for this distinction—that some acts are performed once, while others are repeated? Initiation (*upanayana*), for instance, is a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) for the boy; once he has been consecrated by it, he becomes fit for study and other such duties. The establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is likewise for the purpose of consecrating the fires; once the fires have been successfully established, they are not performed again because there is no further need for them. Even sipping water (*ācamana*) is for the sake of purification; in the absence of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), it is not performed again.

As for the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites, if they are obligatory (*nitya*), they are performed in the spring to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*); if, however, they are optional (*kāmya*)—as in the case where it is said, "In that world, the Apsarases become his wives and lie with him"—then they are performed again and again by those desiring to repeatedly obtain that exaltation (*abhyudaya*). Regarding the former stage of life, a fault is shown for failing to rise in greeting a Brahmin, while exaltation is shown for doing so: "For the vital breaths of a youth depart when an elder approaches; through rising to greet and saluting, one recovers them once more. (Manusmṛti 2.120)

And that return [to the ritual] is not distinguished [by specific conditions]; therefore, they are performed again and again for the sake of removing faults. Or rather, because they are occasional (*naimittika*), there is a repetition for every occasion. Likewise, regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa and the drinking of *surā* liquor, a fault has been declared; since that fault applies to any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever and to any *surā* whatsoever, one performs [the expiation] everywhere [in all such cases] so that we may not be possessed of fault.

In this context, the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) through the knowledge and correct application of words has been shown: "A single word, correctly understood and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) that fulfills all desires in the heavenly world. Furthermore, the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from the use of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) in sacrificial rites has been shown: "Those Asuras were *helayaḥ*" and "An *āhitāgni* priest, having employed a corrupt word... For this very reason, even those [rituals] involving qualities and so forth are performed again and again.

Thus, in this way, the status of being obligatory (*nityatva*), occasional (*naimittikatva*), or optional (*kāmyatva*) is based on repeated performance. Although this applies universally to all scriptures, it was stated by the author of the *Vārttika* and demonstrated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*; we too have established it here for that very reason.
And as in the case of the end and the beginning. 6.1.85.

Since the words *anta* (end) and *ādi* (beginning) denote specific parts, they require a whole (*avayavin*) as their referent; because the terms *pūrva* (prior) and *para* (subsequent) are understood by way of ellipsis (*anuvṛtti*), and since that [whole] serves as a qualifier for the specific substitutes such as *guṇa* which are about to be mentioned, the term *ekādeśa* (single substitute) is obtained. This is what was stated: "the rule 'one [substitute] in place of the prior and the subsequent' continues," and so forth.

What, then, is the meaning of this extension (*atideśa*) here? Does it mean that the two [sounds], the preceding and the following, which are the substituends (*sthānin*) of the single substitution (*ekādeśa*), become respectively the end and the beginning [of their respective constituents]? Or rather—does it mean that when the single substitution has not yet been performed, the two composite units consisting of the preceding and the following, with respect to that very single substitution, become respectively the end and the beginning? Or else—do the end and the beginning of the two composite units consisting of the preceding and the following phonemes, which are the substituends of the single substitution, become respectively the end and the beginning of that [single] substitution as well? Among these, the first position is not possible, because of the single substitution.

Because the preceding and following elements have been replaced by their respective substitutes, how could that which is non-existent [in its original form] possess the status of being like the end of the former or the beginning of the latter? In the second alternative, in the case of *vṛkṣau*—where *vṛkṣa-au* is situated—the single substitute for both the *sub* and the *sup* would not be treated as if it were the beginning of the following element, because there is no subsequent element relative to the *sub*.

Therefore, the third position is adopted. But surely even this position is not possible. For instance: in the case of *brahmabandhūḥ*, when we have *brahmabandhu-ū*, the letter preceding [the *ū*]—namely the *u* which is the final (*anta*) of the word *brahmabandhu*—no longer exists at all in the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), because the original *u* has been replaced. And as for that which does exist—the form ending in *dh*—the substitute *u* is not its final (*anta*), because it was not the originator (*anārambhakatvāt*) of that [final element]. If this is so, then the meaning is as follows: the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of that which possesses the designation of the two original elements (the prior and the posterior) also possesses the designation of the final (*anta*) and the initial (*ādi*) of those very same elements. Thus, although the *u* is no longer the final of *brahmabandhu*, the single-substitute *ū* is treated as if it were the final of that word. Similarly, although the *ū* is not the initial of the following element, the single-substitute is treated as if it were the initial of that following element. This is the sense.

What is meant is this: prior to the single-substitute (ekādeśa) operation, when the preceding and following elements stand separately, there is observed a designation (*vyapadeśa*) concerning the aggregate of the preceding and following [elements]—such as "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) or "inflected word" (*subanta*). That same designation persists even after the single-substitute has been applied. This is what was stated: "Just as its end or its beginning is included within it," and so forth.

By the word *tasya* ("of that"), the preceding and following composite units situated prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) are indicated; and since the terms "end" (*anta*) and "beginning" (*ādi*) do not exist [independently], the preceding and following elements are the substituends (*sthānin*) of the single-substitute. By the statement "it is grasped by the mention of that," what was stated by us immediately after beginning with "this is what is meant" has been demonstrated. Furthermore, by the statement "it is grasped by the mention of that," what was stated by us immediately after beginning with "this is what is meant" has been shown.

"This is the meaning of the extension (atideśa). It is called "extension" (atideśa) because it is extended (atidiśyate). This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "the meaning which is the extension," meaning that this particular meaning is extended here.

Regarding the phrase *varṇāśrayavidau* and so forth: the meaning is that what is prescribed based on the very nature (*svarūpa*) of a phoneme (*varṇa*) is not extended by way of the treatment as being "the end" or "the beginning. How so? Here, an operation (*kārya*) conditioned by identity with that [phoneme] is not extended; rather, this single substitution (*ekādeśa*) becomes like that which was previously situated as the final or initial element before the substitution—namely, like the preceding and the following [elements]. Thus, it obtains the operation induced by them. And in this case, one should simply say *tadvat* ("like that"), for by the word *tat*, the preceding and following elements are referred to.

For if this were established, then by the rule *antādivat* ("as if it were the end or the beginning"), let the operation conditioned by being an "end" or a "beginning" apply to the single substitute (*ekādeśa*). But by what would the operation conditioned by the specific nature of the preceding and following elements (*pūrva-parasvarūpa*) be effected? Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) here in the statement that the *tuk* augment is "not established" (*asiddha*); otherwise, in forms such as *adhītya*, the *tuk* would already be established simply because the single substitute has the status of being the "beginning," and thus that rule would be rendered purposeless. [The example] *khaṭvābhiḥ* [is given]. However, the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of cases where there is no single substitute—such as *śubhaṃyābhiḥ*. [The example] *juhāva* [is given].

Regarding the rule "and [the substitute] for *abhyasta*": when the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) is applied to the root *hve*, the resulting single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) of the vowel *ā*—namely *juhu-ā*—does not behave like the initial element. That is to say, it does not possess the same status as the initial *ā*; therefore, the rule "for *ā* before *ṇal*, there is *au*" does not apply. In the example *asyai aśvaḥ*: the single-substitute *vṛddhi* (long *ai*) resulting from the combination of the case-ending suffix *syāṭ* (which contains the phoneme *e*) and the phoneme *a* of the word *aśva*—by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* for *eC* before *eC*"—does not behave like the initial element of the following word. Therefore, the rule "for *eṅ* at the end of a word, there is *ai* before *at*" does not apply.

Furthermore, where both [the end and the beginning] are simultaneously relied upon—such as the end and the beginning—the treatment of one as being like the other does not occur; for example, in the rule "eteliṅi," the shortening of the vowel *i* prescribed after a prefix (*upasarga*) does not apply in cases such as *abhīyāt* or *parīyāt*.

For if this single unit (ekādeśa) were perceived by the intellect as being like the end with respect to the preceding element, how could it at that very same time be like the beginning with respect to the following element? Likewise, if it were like the beginning with respect to the following element at that very same time, its status as being like the end with respect to the preceding element would also be untenable; because it is contradictory for a single entity to be simultaneously dependent on both [elements] in such a manner.

Regarding the phrase "pūrvāpara" (the preceding and the following): that by which something is replaced is the *sthānin* (original element) of that [which replaces it], as for example, the root *as-* is the *sthānin* of the root *bhū-*. And here, it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) that is being replaced; consequently, if there were any grammatical operation (*kārya*) conditioned by that [aggregate], it would occur by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), but not [an operation] conditioned by the preceding and following parts individually. It might be argued: "Since the two constituent parts are also being replaced, should they not also possess the status of being *sthānin*s? To this, he says: "tatra" (in that case). Both instances of the particle "iti" are used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

In that context, regarding the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) belonging to two parts within a whole (*samudāya*), that status is inferential; for it is impossible to cause the whole to cease without the cessation of its parts, and thus there is a cessation of the two parts. However, this is not because they are explicitly prescribed as such. Consequently, an operation (*kārya*) based upon them does not apply by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original), because in that case one relies solely upon the *sthānin* as directly heard in the rule. And yet, such an operation is desired; therefore, the rules for "behaving like the end" (*antavadbhāva*) and "behaving like the beginning" (*ādivadbhāva*) are prescribed for that purpose.

Is this not, however, the reverse—that the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) belongs inferentially to the two individual parts? Because of the mention of the *dvirvacana* (doubling) in the rule "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*), the status of being a *sthānin* is heard to belong to those two alone; there is no word for the composite whole. Rather, when the two [parts] are being replaced, the composite whole is excluded by implication—this is all that occurs. And thus it was stated in the previous rule: "Due to the difference in the *sthānin*, as in the case of *natva* in words beginning with *bhinna* and others."

And this has been stated elsewhere as well: "For that which exists in both positions receives the designation of one or the other. Therefore, in the case of *khaṭvarśyaḥ*, the subsequent status (*paratvam*) applies, and there is also the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvaḥ*) for the vowel *ṛ*. How so? In the rule *sthānivadādeśaḥ* ("a substitute is like the original"), although the inclusion of the substitute is already established because the word *sthānin* ("original") is a relative term, the explicit mention of the word *ādeśa* ("substitute") is for the purpose of extending the status of being a substitute even to an inferred substitute. Consequently, an inferred original (*sthānin*) is also accepted, just as in the rule *eruḥ*.

Regarding the example *pacatu*: here, by means of the vowel *i*, a substitute ending in *i* is inferred as the original (*sthānin*), and by means of the vowel *u*, a substitute ending in *u* is inferred; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, it receives the designation *pada* according to the rule "that which ends in a *tiṅ* is a *pada*.

Even so, is the *sthānivadbhāva* established here since the status of the two parts as *sthānins* is merely inferential? If that is the case, then since *sthānivadbhāva* has been stated to apply except in the case of an operation concerning an *al* (a phoneme), this [present rule] is for the sake of operations concerning an *al*; for example, in *kṣīrapeṇa* and *surāpeṇa*, because of the status of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the two case-endings of the second member as being like the final element (*antavadbhāva*), the substitution of *ṇ* according to the rule "when the second member consists of a single vowel, *ṇ* is substituted" occurs even though it is an operation concerning an *al*.

But is it not the case that the prohibition "not in the case of an operation concerning *al*" (*analvidhau*) applies only to operations that depend upon the *al* of the substituendum (*sthānin*), whereas in this instance, what must be sought through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* is precisely that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) possesses the status of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*) of the subsequent word (*uttarapada*)?

The status of being a vowel (*actva*), however, is established by its very nature; therefore, just as in the case of *aruditām*, where the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* applies the augment *iṭ* by relying on both the fact that the suffix begins with a consonant (*valāditva*)—which is established through the substitute (*sthānivat*)—and the fact that it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix—which is inherent to the suffix itself—so too here, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by relying on both the fact that the subsequent word lacks the suffix *val* (established through the substitute) and the status of being a vowel (*actva*), which is inherent to the vowel itself. That [status of being a vowel] is indeed dependent upon the form of the original element (*sthānin*), and in such cases it is precisely what is intended, as in *khaṭvābhiḥ* and so forth, where the replacement of *ais* for *bhis* and other operations apply.
Therefore, the purpose of the term *ac-bhasya* is to be considered.
The substitution for *ṣatva* and *tuk* is not established [as having taken effect] when another rule is subsequently applied.

"In the case of *ṣatva* and *tuk*": this means in the rule (*śāstra*) concerning *ṣatva* and in the rule concerning *tuk*. "A single-substitute (*ekādeśa*)": this means the rule for single substitution, such as *ādguṇaḥ*, and so forth. "It becomes as if unestablished (*asiddha*)": that which is *siddha*—meaning accomplished—is the opposite of that, namely *asiddha*. In that context, since the nature of the rule itself is indeed accomplished, its meaning is understood through the use of the word "other" (*para*) with respect to what follows, and there is a similarity because it performs those same functions. Thus he says: the meaning is that it does not perform the functions of established [rules].

In the presence of the rules concerning *ṣatva* and *tuk*, the rule regarding *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) does not perform its own operation—that is, it does not apply or bring about the operation known as *ekādeśa*. This is the meaning. He states the purpose of the Sūtra: "the statement that [the substitute] is *asiddha*. When an operation is to be applied based on a cause that arises once a substitution has been made, that is termed "characterized by the substitute" (*ādeśalakṣaṇa*), considering that the substitute is the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) or cause (*nimitta*) for it. The statement that [the substitute] is *asiddha* is for the purpose of prohibiting such an operation.

The term *utsarga* means "the place of departure" (*sthānī*). Because it is generally set aside (*sāmānyotsṛṣṭatvāt*), that which has this as its characteristic is called *utsargalakṣaṇa*; the statement regarding what is not established (*asiddha*) is for the purpose that its operation (*pravṛtti*) may take place accordingly. As for the form *ko'sicat*: by the rule *lipisicihvaśca*, the suffix *cl* is replaced by *aṅ*. From the word *ka*, there is the substitution of *u* for *s* (by *soḥ*); then, by the rule *ato roraplutādalute*, there is the substitution of *u* for *r*, followed by *guṇa*. [The rule] *eṅaḥ padāntādati* applies because, with respect to the following element, the preceding [element] behaves as if it were the beginning of a word (*parampratyādivadbhāvāt*).

For if the treatment as being "like the original" (*ādivadbhāva*) were applied, the word would end with *osicad*, and since the *s* following it would not be the beginning of a word (*padādi*), the prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* would not apply. Consequently, one might expect the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) by relying on the single-substitute *o* (*ekādeśa*). However, because that [single-substitute] is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) relative to the rule for *ṣatva*, the substitution does not occur. Indeed, due to its unestablished status, the rule for *ṣatva* does not perceive the rule for the single substitute; thus, the form of the word remains as *ko asicat*. In that state, because of the intervention of the vowel *a*, there is no occurrence of *ṣatva*. This is the case in *ko'sya*.

This is the genitive singular of *idam*. [The substitution of] *yat* for *tyadādi* occurs; then, by the rule "ṭāṅasiṅsāminātsyāḥ," there is the replacement with *syā*; then, by "hali lopaḥ," there is elision [of the *y*]; the rest is as before. Thus, examples have been shown for the prohibition regarding the characteristics of the substitute.

He now shows the other case—namely, *adhītya* and *pretya*. [He says: "Because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*)," and so forth. For if it were non-existent, then in the presence of the rule for *tuk*, the form of the word would remain exactly as *adhi-i-iy-eti*; consequently, *tuk* would apply based on the short vowel (*hrasva*).

If, however, it is stated that only the primary single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) itself is *asiddha*, then there is no fault regarding the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*); how so? The vowel *o* does not perform its own function of *ṣatva*, nor does *ṣatva* apply based on the *k* and *y* sounds preceding it, because they are separated by that very *o* vowel. Regarding the insertion of *tuk*, the desired result is not achieved; why? Because the short vowel is replaced by the single substitute, and yet the single substitute does not fail to perform its own function.

By this, the restoration of the original element (sthānin) is possible; therefore, since [the substitution] is possible, one must simply resort to the fact that the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddhatva*). And it has been said: "The statement regarding 'behaving like the original' (*sthānivadbhāva*) is redundant because of the non-existence of the rule."

Regarding the rule *samprasāraṇaṅīṭsu*: it must be stated that the prohibition of the "asiddha" status applies to that single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) which occurs in place of a *samprasāraṇa*, the suffix *ṅī*, and the augment *iṭ*. In the example *śakahūṣu*: from the root *hvayati* ("to call") preceded by *śaka*, there is *samprasāraṇa* (the substitution of *u* for *ha*) because the root belongs to the *yajñādi* group; then follows the suffix *kvip*, and the lengthening of the vowel by the rule *halaḥ*. In the example *parivīṣu*: from the root *vyeñ* ("to weave") preceded by *pari*, the suffix *kvip* and so forth are applied as before. Because [the preceding rule] would be *asiddha*, the substitution of *ṣ* (by P. 8.3.59) would not apply. For if the *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute resulting from the *samprasāraṇa*) were *asiddha*, the form of the word would remain as *śakahu-ā*.

In the examples *vṛkṣecchatram* ("an umbrella for the tree") and *apacecchatram* ("an umbrella for one who cooked"), [the latter] is the first person singular of the imperfect (*laṅ*) of the root *pac*, with the augment *iṭ* and the suffix *śap*. [The objection is raised: "Because the *guṇa* substitution [of *a* and *i* to *e*] is not yet established. For if that were unestablished, the word-form would remain as *vṛkṣa i chatram* and *apaca i chatram*. In this regard, a prohibition concerning *samprasāraṇa* need not be stated; for it is said that "a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is unestablished," and we do not perceive a single-substitute here, because it has been replaced by the long vowel [*e*].

Furthermore, because it is not long, there is no inclusion [of the substitute] by the mention of "single-substitute" (ekādeśa) due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, since it is not a rule concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). However, a prohibition must indeed be stated for the case endings *ṅi* and *ṅas*.

Alternatively—for the sake of brevity—it should have been stated as *padasya*. Furthermore, the mention of "end" (*anta*) and "beginning" (*ādi*) must be carried over from the preceding rule; thus, the meaning becomes: "An *ekādeśa* (single-substitute) that occurs at the end of a word or at the beginning of a word is considered *asiddha*. If this were the case, then in the example *supippalā oṣadhīḥ kṛdhi*, there is the second-person plural ending after the word *oṣadhi*; by the rule *oṣadheśca vibhaktau aprathamāyām*, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*); then, by the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*, there is the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound; and finally, the substitution of *ru* and *visarjanīya*.

In this case, one might argue that the substitution of *s* for the *visarjanīya*—as prescribed by the rule *kaḥ karat karati kṛti*—is not obtained because of the statement *padāntapadādyoḥ*. Furthermore, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *visarjanīya* follows an *iṇ*-vowel, and thus the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] as prescribed by *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* would apply. [Objection: Is it not the case that, if non-existence were applied without distinction, then in forms such as *oṣadhī-as kṛdhi*, the *visarjanīya* would not follow an *iṇ*-vowel due to its position, and thus the application of *ṣatva* would not arise, thereby establishing *satva*? [Response: This is established through an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).

The fact that he recites the word *bhrātuṣputra* in the list of *kaskādi* compounds indicates that the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for a *visarjanīya* following a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). If it were otherwise, then from the word *bhrātṛ* in the *ṅasi* case—after the substitution of *u* by "ṛta ud" and the subsequent substitution of the single substitute with a following *r* (i.e., *rapara*), and after the elision of the *s* by "rātsasya"—there would be a sixth-case compound. In that case, due to the non-elision (*aluk*) by "ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ," the *visarjanīya* would replace the *repha*, and because the single substitute *u* (from "ṛta ud") is established as already accomplished, [the rule] "idudupadhasya ca" [would apply].

Since the substitution of *ṣ* would thus be established by this rule alone, one need not have included [the word *kaska-*] among the *kaskādi* group; yet the author does include it. From this, it is understood that the substitution of *ṣ* does not apply to what follows a single substitute (*ekādeśa*). [Objection: In that case, it would not apply even in the example *śakahūṣu*. [Reply: This is not a fault; for this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding items of the same class. And what is of the same class? That which immediately precedes *k* or *p*.

And here, in the case of *caṭu* from the root *veñ* with the suffix *kvip*, after the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) and the subsequent single-substitute replacement (*pūrvatva*), the rule "a short vowel before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *pit*" would require the insertion of the augment *tuk*. However, since the single-substitute replacement (*pūrvatva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule [P. 6.4.22], one might think the *tuk* does not apply. But because of the specific statement "at the end of a word and at the beginning of a word" [P. 6.1.85], the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) does not apply here, and thus the *ud* augment indeed occurs. For the long vowel *ā* is not the final element of a word in the state prior to the single-substitute replacement of *u* and *ā*; nor is the short vowel *a* the initial element of a word, because there is no case-ending (*vibhakti*) present. Nor can it be argued that the case-ending arises even before the single-substitute replacement, on the grounds that the form ends in a *kṛt*-suffix; for the single-substitute replacement is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).

Furthermore, even if the case-ending were produced first—so that *u-āsu* remains, where the letter *u* is at the beginning of a word (*padādi*) and the letter *s* is at the end of a word (*padānta*), for a "word" (*pada*) is indeed that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*) and not what precedes it—even so, there is no fault. For in the case of *bhyām* and the following forms, when *u-ābhyām* remains, the designation "word" (*padasaṃjñā*) applies by the rule *svādiṣu*, and thus the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs between the end of one word and the beginning of another. Nevertheless, there is no defect; for the phrase "of the preceding and the following" (*pūrvaparayoḥ*) continues to apply, as does the mention of "end and beginning" (*antādī*).

In this context, due to the connection according to the respective order of enumeration, the meaning that results is that the single-substitute (ekādeśa) for the final letter of the preceding word and the initial letter of the following word is considered asiddha (non-existent). Furthermore, since the vowel *ā* here is not the beginning of a word, nor is the vowel *u* the end of a word, the *tug* augment indeed occurs because of its being asiddha.

But for what purpose is it stated that the substitution of *ṣatva* and *tuk* is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not yet established? For, since the single-substitute depends on two words (*dvipadāśraya*) and is thus "external" (*bahiraṅga*), while the *ṣatva* and *tuk* substitutions depend on a single word (*ekapadāśraya*) and are thus "internal" (*antaraṅga*), their status as non-existent is already established by the rule: "The external is non-existent with respect to the internal" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam antaraṅge*). It is, however, for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpanārtham*). This indicates the following: "Wherever the proximity of vowels (*ac-ānantaryam*) is relied upon as the cause for either an external or an internal operation, there the paribhāṣā regarding the external [being non-existent] does not apply."

Therefore, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, because the substitution of *ūṭh*—though it is extrinsic (*bahiranga*)—is not treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *yaṇ* becomes established. This very point is recited as a metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "When there is immediate succession of vowels (*ajānantarya*), the status of being extrinsic is not applied."
The *guṇa* substitute [is applied] in place of [the vowels] *ā*, *e*, and *o*. (Pāṇini 6.1.87)

What is the purpose of mentioning the "quality" (*guṇa*)? For since the term *ac* is understood [from the previous rule], as well as the phrase "one [substitute] in place of the preceding and the following," then by virtue of proximity (*antarya*), in place of the *a*-vowel and *i*-vowel—which belong to the throat (*kaṇṭhya*) and the palate (*tālavya*) respectively—there will be a corresponding *e*-vowel; and in place of the *a*-vowel and *u*-vowel—which belong to the throat (*kaṇṭhya*) and the lips (*oṣṭhya*) respectively—there will be a corresponding *o*-vowel.

Would there not then be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the *ai* and *au* vowels [would also be called *vṛddhi*]? No, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "vṛddhir eci. This [rule] is now for the purpose of restriction, since the status of *ai* and *au* as *vṛddhi* is already established by this very [definition]; it means that *vṛddhi* occurs only before an *ec* vowel. And the restriction will be explained in both ways: either "vṛddhi [occurs] only before an *ec* vowel," or "only *vṛddhi* [occurs] before an *ec* vowel. In that case, in forms such as *khaṭvārśyaḥ* and *mālārśyaḥ*, would not the retroflex *ṛ*—being the closest in measure (*pramāṇataḥ*)—be obtained? No, because of the rule "the substitute is followed by *r*" (*raparaḥ*), which is based on the place of articulation (*sthāna*); thus, [the substitute] is the closest in both respects.

In that case, would not the substitution of *ākāra* (long *ā*) apply? [One might argue: "The rule *upasargād ṛti dhātau* will serve to restrict its scope—meaning that *ākāra* occurs only when the following verbal root begins with *ṛ*, and not elsewhere. Then would not the protracted vowel (*pluta*) apply—as in *khaṭvendraḥ*? For it is traditionally taught that "the protracted vowel [occurs] in its proper domain," and once the rule for protraction is established, shouldn't this very [substitution of *ākāra*] also take effect in the very domain where protraction is prescribed? Since the protraction belonging to the eighth book (*Aṣṭādhyāyī*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when this [substitution] is to be performed, the protracted vowel does not occur in that alternative case, as it would result in the fault of being a redundant restatement (*anuvādadoṣa*).

In that case, here [in the examples] *śaṭveṣā* (from *śaṭvā + īṣā*) and *khaṭveṣā* (from *khaṭvā + īṣā*), as well as *śaṭveḍhā* (from *śaṭvā + ūḍhā*) and *khaṭveḍhā* (from *khaṭvā + ūḍhā*), a substitute of four morae (*caturmātra*) would result by virtue of phonetic proximity (*āntarya*). However, when the term "guṇa" is included [in the definition], since the designation "guṇa" is made for the sake of all purposes by adding the suffix *-para*, those consisting of three or four morae are not considered "guṇas," and thus there is no such contingency. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "guṇa" is necessary. There are two verses on this point: "If the substitute were a 'guṇa,' by what [criterion] would it be the most similar in place? For *ai* and *au* are not taught as substitutes for *e* and *o*; nor is *ṛ* the most similar to both."
The vowel *ā* is prescribed as long (*pluta*) in the *nartti* musical mode when it occurs in its proper domain;
due to proximity (*āntarya*), it may also consist of three or four morae (*mātrā*), and the *guṇa* vowel followed by *t* (as in *at*) is likewise considered long.

In this case, from the word *vṛkṣa* with the suffix *ṅi*, when *vṛkṣa-i-indram* is established, both the *guṇa* substitution for the *a* and *i* sounds and the long-vowel (*dīrgha*) substitution for the two *ī* sounds (by the rule of homogeneous vowels) would apply. Therein, due to the "subsequent rule" (*paravipratiṣedha*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the long vowel; however, this is not a fault, because the *guṇa* will occur within a single word (*ekapada*) as an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), being prior even to the proximity of another word. Furthermore, the *it* designation for the *ḷ*-sound is by virtue of its place of articulation (*sthāna*); how this is obtained has been explained in the commentary on the rule *laṇ*.
The substitution of *e* for *ā* occurs before the suffixes *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*.

"But not in the case of *edh*, because of its non-deviation"—this was stated with the intention of referring to the majority of cases. For indeed, there is also deviation in this case; they say that in the form *mā predidhat* (with the *caṅ* suffix), where the penultimate vowel is shortened, this [rule] does not apply. Regarding *praṣṭhauha*: it means "one who carries the leader" (*praṣṭham vahati*). By the rules *chandasi sahaḥ* and *vahaśca*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied. Then, by the rule *vāha ūṭh*, *ūṭh* is substituted, followed by *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), the replacement of the preceding [vowel], and subsequently *vṛddhi*. This [substitution of *vṛddhi*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the single-substitute rule (*pararūpa*) that applies to *eti* and *edhati* before *ehi*; the phrase "vṛddhi is prescribed" is to be supplied as the remainder of the statement.

If that is so, then just as [the rule] *eṅi pararūpam* is sublated, so too would *āṅi pararūpam* be sublated; for this increase (*vṛddhi*) is introduced when the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) has not yet taken effect. To this he says: "And this [rule] applies to *om* and *āṅ*. Why? He says: "By which... That [subsequent rule] becomes the sublater of that [preceding rule]. This means it becomes the sublater of that very [rule], because the sublation of that [preceding rule] is inevitable, and because the sublater fulfills its purpose by that much alone.

Furthermore, this *vṛddhi* substitution is not commenced when the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule for *eṅ* has not yet applied; rather, it applies where *pararūpa* for *āṅ* has already applied, as in *ā itaḥ* → *etaḥ*, *pretaḥ*, and *paretaḥ*. However, in cases such as *upaiti* and *praiti*, where *pararūpa* has not applied, [the *vṛddhi* rule does not operate]; therefore, it does not sublate [the subsequent rule]. He states another solution: "In the preceding [rule]. The sense is that once the immediately preceding [rule] is known to be sublated, the present statement achieves its purpose through that sublation; thus, in competition with the subsequent [rule], the latter alone prevails due to its higher status (*paratvāt*). Regarding *akṣauhiṇī*: [it is derived from] *akṣaiḥ ūhate avaśyam* ("one necessarily moves by means of dice"), where *ṇini* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*), and the compound *sādhanaṃ kṛtā* is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.33.

Regarding the word *svairam*: the root *īr* means "to go. *Īraṇa* (the act of going) is *īraḥ*, formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Svairam* is the act of going (*īraṇam*) according to one's own intention (*svena abhiprāyeṇa*). It is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. Its neuter gender is due to its being an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatva*), or because gender is dependent on common usage (*lokāśrayatva*). One who goes according to his own intention is a *svairī*; here the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau*. [Objection: The inclusion of the root *īr* is redundant; for one who goes according to his own intention is a *svairī*, and the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supyajātau*.

The inclusion of the term *īrin* is redundant; it is established by the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule "padāsvairibāhya. It is also established by the suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) applied to the word *padāsvaira* and others. However, the suffix *ṇini* will not occur here due to lack of expressive power (*anabhidhāna*).

The words *prāditya* and so forth; the subsequent members [of the compounds] are *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, and *eṣya*. When the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the roots *iṣ* (to send), *iṣ* (to desire), or *iṣ* (to go), then it becomes *praiṣya*; when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, then it becomes *praiṣa*. In the case of the word *īṣya*, however, it becomes *preṣya*. Likewise, in *ā-ūḍhā*, *oḍhā*, and *proḍhā*, the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) occurs according to the rule "omāṅośca. That other debt which is contracted for the purpose of clearing a previously incurred debt is called *ṛṇārṇa*. The word *daśārṇa* is a proper name for a particular river and also for a particular country.
And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *āṭ*. 6.1.90.

The examples for these roots—*īkṣa* (in the sense of seeing), *ubha* and *umbha* (in the sense of filling), *ubja* (in the sense of straightening), and *ṛdhu* (in the sense of increasing)—are provided. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of prescribing an additional rule; this is explained by the statement: "and before *us*, *om*, and *āṅ*. It is for the purpose of subverting the application of the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) rule. The meaning is that it serves to subvert whatever single-substitute would otherwise apply before *usi*, *omi*, and *āṅ*; otherwise, because it is a subsequent rule, that very single-substitute would take effect. The example *ausrīyat* arises here because the single-substitute is prescribed even when *usi* is meaningless.
When a vowel beginning with *ṛ* follows a prefix (*upasarga*), [the final *a* of the prefix is replaced by *o*] before a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Regarding the word *upārcchati*: the root *ṛcch* is used in the senses of "going," "loss of the senses," and "assuming a form. In the example *prarcchako deśaḥ*, since the rule "prefixes (*pra-* etc. are [verbal prefixes] when connected with an action" applies specifically toward the verb *gam* (to go), the prefix *pra-* is not a prefix toward the verb *ṛcch*. Thus, this serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). For otherwise, by the rule *vā supy āpiśaleḥ*, there would have been an option. Therefore, the intention is that the mention of the suffix *ta* (in *tāntāt*) is for the sake of the subsequent rule.

The mention of "root" (*dhātu*) would be redundant, because where the status of being a prefix (*upasarga*) is not possible, there the mention of "prefix" implies *prādayaḥ* as well—just as in the rule for changing *nāsikā* to *nas* [in the word *nasa-karṇa*]. But here, the primary status of being a prefix is indeed possible; so why the mention of "root"? To this he says: "Precisely because of the mention of 'prefix'... This is the *śākala* [rule] of Śākalya; the mention of "root" is repeated again in order to exclude that.

However, when the mention of the "giver" (*dātṛ*) is present, the rule for *vṛddhi* is enjoined again through a split in the yoga-rule (*yogavibhāga*), and thus the *śākala* [variant] is set aside. In its absence, however, by the opinion of Śākalya, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would indeed occur because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].
Or, according to Apiśali, [the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the first member occurs] even when the word ends in *su*.

Since it is impossible for a verbal root (*dhātu*) to end in a nominal suffix (*sub*), the term "ending in a *sub*" (*subanta*) is a qualifier of the root by way of its constituent part; thus he says: "in a root that is a constituent of something ending in a *sub*. Although both honor (*pūjā*) and optionality (*vikalpa*) are established by the mention of the Teacher (*ācārya*) alone, the repetition of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is made to indicate that the mention of the Teacher is primarily for the purpose of honoring him.
[The substitution of *am* for the case-ending *su* occurs] before the affixes *ām* and *su*. (Pāṇini 6.1.93)

"Look at the cow" (*gāṃ paśya*). Now, one might object: since the suffix here is marked with *ṇ* by the rule *goto ṇit*, once *vṛddhi* has been applied [to *go* + *ṅas*], the vowel *o* would no longer exist; therefore, the substitution of *ā* (by *auto 'mśasoḥ*) should not occur. Furthermore, the prescription of *ā* would then be for the sake of the word *dyo*. Indeed, there is no *ṇ*-marking in that case, because of the specific statement *gotaḥ*. To this, he says: "The word *dyo* also," and so forth. It is true that [the substitution of *ā*] would not occur if there were no *ṇ*-marking; however, there *is* *ṇ*-marking even there, because the term *gotaḥ* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words ending in *au*, as it is well known that in the specification of phonemes, a following *t* indicates the inclusion of the homogeneous class. What follows from this? He says: "By that," and so forth.

"By virtue of association with *śas*": for here, the possibility of *śas* arises only after a *sup* [case-ending], not after anything else, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after a vowel" (*aci*).

Regarding the forms *acicītavam* and *asunavam*: these are the *laṅ* [aorist] of the roots *ci* (to gather) and *su* (to press); when the suffix *am* is applied by the rule "*tasthasthamipām*", the *guṇa* strengthening and the substitution of *ā* occur for the *vikaraṇa* [suffix].
When *eṅ* (e or o) is followed by a vowel, the single substitute for both is the form of the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*).
The root *il* is listed in the *curādi* group with the meaning "to impel" (*preraṇe*), while *okhṛ* and *śākhṛ* are recited in the *bhūvādi* group.

Some maintain that the rule *vā supyāpiśaleḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.92) continues to apply here. If this were so, then because of its syntactic unity with that [rule], this [suffix] would not apply to roots beginning with vowels; therefore, he says: "And that... In this matter, the commentary itself is the only refuge.

Regarding the rule *śakandhvādiṣu*: the words beginning with *śakandhu* are to be followed according to actual usage; in these cases, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) must be stated. The indications such as "or for *kulaṭā*" and "after those ending in *kat*" serve as evidence for this meaning. *Andhu* means a well; she who wanders among many families and does not remain in a single family is called *kulaṭā*. This word should be listed among the *pacādi* group [of suffixes], otherwise the suffix *aṇ* would apply by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*.

Regarding the phrase *eve cāniyoge*: "niyoga" means necessity (*avaśyambhāva*), while "niyama" means restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore, in a sense other than that [restriction], the external form (*pararūpa*) is possible. In the examples, the word *eva* is used in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), as in: *kveva bhokṣyase* ("Where indeed will you eat?"). However, when used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs—as in *amaivāvyayena*, *dhātostannimittasyaiva*, *ihaiva santatvāya*, and *mamaiva havyāny agne*, etc.

*otuḥ* means "cat. Regarding the rule *tunvor vi nipāta upasaṃkhyānam*: because of the mention of *vi* in the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśāt*), the rule applies to that which begins with it; when a particle (*nipāta*) beginning with *va* follows, the single substitute (*pararūpa*) occurs for both *tu* and *nu*. Thus: *tu vai*, *tvai*; and *anubhūtatamaṃ ca ekam* (and also the most commonly experienced one): *nu vai*, *nvai*. This is indeed a single particle because there is no difference in meaning, as he said: "Or rather not, because of the oneness of the particle. For this very reason, this was not included by the author of the *Vṛtti*.

In the *sūtra*, the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) is for the sake of subsequent rules; however, here [in the present rule], it is established by the mere mention of *eṅ*—namely, that when *eṅ* follows, a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs. The inclusion of the term "form" is therefore of questionable utility, and accordingly, the term "form" was not employed in the rule "before *am*, the preceding vowel is substituted" (*ami pūrvaḥ*).
[And also] in the case of *om* and *āṅ*: 6.1.95.

Regarding "adyoḍha": since the single substitute for *āṅ* and *anāṅ* is included by the mention of *āṅ*, this serves as an example. Here, according to the principle that "an operation concerning a root and a prefix is internal (*antaraṅga*"), the *guṇa* substitution [of *o*] occurs first due to the rule *ād guṇaḥ*. Subsequently, when the connection with the word *adya* takes place, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply; thus, the form of *āṅ* remains unaltered. In cases such as *adya gaāgataḥ*, the desired form is established through the long vowel of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*).

"It is argued that the substitution of a long vowel for two homogeneous vowels (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghatvam*) is what is being sublated. But surely, according to the maxim of 'an intermediate exception,' it would be more logical for the *vṛddhi* rule alone to be sublated, not the substitution of a long vowel? This is not a fault; the particle *ca* is added here, and it will serve the purpose of re-enjoining [the long vowel]."
[The substitution of *u* for *v* does not occur] after a word-final [consonant] followed by *u*. (Pāṇini 6.1.96)

*bhindyuḥ*: This is the *liṅ* (optative) of the root *bhid*. The suffix *yāsuṭ* is added, followed by *jher jus* (the substitution of *jus* for the *jhi* ending). By the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, there is elision of the *a* of *śn*. Then, by the rule *liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya*, there is elision of the *s* of *yāsuṭ*. Thus we have *bhindya-us*; by this [present rule], the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied. *aduḥ*: This is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *dāñ*. By the rule *gātisthā* etc., there is elision of *sic*. By the rule *ātaḥ*, *jher jus* is substituted. Thus we have *adā-us*; by this [present rule], the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is applied.

[Regarding] *koṣitā*: Now, one might object that because it is meaningless (*anarthaka*), this *us* will not be included [by the rule]. If that is so, then this [mention] serves to indicate that even a meaningless *us* is included; therefore, in forms such as *bhidyus*, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) occurs for *us*. For here, the entire complex beginning with *yāsuṭ* is meaningful, but the *us* which is its constituent part is not. [Thus we have] *koṣitā*.

In *uṣitaḥ*, the suffix *kta* is added to the root *vas*; by the rule *vasatikṣudhor iṭ*, the augment *iṭ* is inserted; by the rule *yajāditvāt saṃprasāraṇam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); and by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Because that [substitution] is treated as not established (*asiddha*), the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) does not take place before the suffix *usi*. Furthermore, its exclusion is established simply because it is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical rule). Regarding *abibhayuḥ*: this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *bhī*; there is *ślu* (elision) of the *śap* (present marker); by the rule *sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*, *jus* replaces *jhi*; and by the rule *jusi ca*, *guṇa* (vocalization) occurs.
Therefore, [the suffix *taddhita*] is applied after a quality (*guṇa*). (Pāṇini 5.1.123)

"‘Akaḥ savarṇe’ is an exception (apavāda) to the rule for long vowels. [Objection: But according to the maxim that "an intermediate rule is an exception to what precedes it," this should properly be an exception only to the *vṛddhi* rule, not to the rule for long vowels. [Response: Because of the mention of *guṇa*, it will also be a sublater of the long vowel; otherwise, one would have simply said: "After *at*, not at the end of a word" (*ato 'padāntāt*), and "before *eṅ*" (*eṅi*), and then "also before *jus*" (*jusi ca*), and "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntāt*). This being established, since this rule applies to *guṇa* in general because of the mention of *guṇa*, it will also sublate the long vowel. [Question: Why is "after *at*" (*ataḥ*) stated? [The answer is implicit: It is understood from the context that "after *at*" (*aditi*) indeed continues to apply. [Question: What is the purpose of the *tapara* (the *ḥ*) marker? [Answer: That is the intended meaning.
In the case of an imitation of an indistinct sound, the suffix *at* is applied before the word *iti*.

"Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) means having indistinct phonemes (*aparisphuṭavarṇa*). That in which the phonemes, beginning with *a*, are indistinct—that is, unmanifest—is so described. If this is the case, then its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) must also be of that same nature; for an imitation is indeed similar [to the original]. Consequently, just as in the original, even there [in the imitation] the word-sound (*śabda*) cannot be determined, and if it is not determined, it is impossible to apply the "other form" (*pararūpa*) rule. To this he replies: "That imitation occurs because of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore he says: "By some degree of similarity."

Furthermore, that similarity [of the sound] is due to its being equal to the *dhvani* (the manifesting sound); for by means of it, the person (*puruṣa*) imitates the unmanifest object of imitation (*anukārya*). Here, the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is the agent (*kartṛ*) which imitates the unmanifest object (*karman*). Since there is no intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the agent, the agentive suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) is used; however, the word "imitation" (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) is derived solely from the sense of the instrument. Thus, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) takes the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*).
