This applies even to the entire word "ac," and not merely to its final letter; this is because of the rule "there is no application of the final-letter rule to that which is meaningless" (*nānarthake'lontyavidhiḥ*), and because of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*).

When [the author] employs the mention of the "final" (*antyagrahaṇa*) in the rule *āmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā*, he indicates that "the paribhāṣā concerning the final vowel (*alontyaparibhāṣā*) does not operate here. Furthermore, it has been stated that the entire preceding-and-following aggregate (*pūrvāparasamudāya*) is the locus (*sthānin*) of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*); therefore, one must consider what kind of application of this paribhāṣā could possibly occur with respect to its constituent part, namely the preceding element. The form *paṭaditi* is a sentence of the analytical derivation (*prakriyāvākya*), not fit for actual usage (*prayoga*); for the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is compulsory (*nitya*).

Regarding the term *pāṭiti*: how, moreover, does it become a communicator of that which is being imitated (*anukārya*) once the substitution of another form (*pararūpa*) has been applied, and from what source does its status as an imitation (*anukaraṇatva*) arise? This is not a fault. Just as in the expression *gavityayamāha* ("he says 'cow'"), even though the substitution [of *v* for *o*] has been applied, it remains an imitation of the word *go* due to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), so too will it be here. This is an imitation of a form ending in *d*; however, if it were an imitation of a form ending in *t*, this very form would not occur, because, lacking the status of a word (*apadatva*), the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *d* for *t*) would be absent—as in the case of *paṭiti karoti*.
But for the final syllable of a reduplicated word, [the substitution of *pluta*] is optional.

Regarding the rule *avyaktānukaraṇasyāmreḍitasya*: the two genitive cases are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*); the meaning is "of that which is the reduplicated portion (*āmreḍita*) belonging to an imitation of an indistinct sound. Regarding the statement "the doubling [occurs] by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*": the connection with distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) should be understood in some way or another. Another says: this [mention of] *nityavīpsayoḥ* is merely illustrative; because of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *ḍāci bahulaṃ dve bhavataḥ*, there is doubling even for other cases.
As for the phrase "if, however": there occurs a difference in meaning for the imitation of a whole compound that has been doubled.
The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after a word denoting repetition when it signifies "constantly."

This is indeed a *vārttika* [of Kātyāyana], which was read by the author of the *Vṛtti* (*Patañjali*) as if it were a *sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "when *ḍāc* is intended to be expressed": the suffix *kta* refers to the future tense according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*, meaning "that which is intended to be prescribed" (*vidhitsita*). Otherwise, the suffix *ḍāc* would not occur at all, because the condition of having "at least two syllables in the latter half" (*dvyajavarārdhatva*) would be absent. Thus, it is stated in the rule prescribing *ḍāc*: "The suffix is applied after that which, when reduplicated, has at least two syllables in its latter half. Furthermore, he will state in the eighth book that the locative case in the word *ḍāci* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).

He states another purpose for the fact that the reduplication is performed precisely when the suffix *ḍāc* is intended to be applied—namely, "And that" (*tacca*). The particle *ca* here has the sense of *hi* (for/indeed). For that reduplication is desired to occur prior to the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel). And thus it is established first, provided that the reduplication occurs only when *ḍāc* is intended; not otherwise. For if the reduplication were to occur after [the suffix has been added], then, because the elision of the *ṭi* is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it would take effect first; subsequently, if the word ending in *ṭ* were reduplicated, the form *paṭapaṭā* would not be established.

Alternatively, the meaning is "when the suffix *ḍāc* has been prescribed and produced. Now, was it not said that the suffix *ḍāc* itself would not even occur? This is not a fault; the expression "from a base consisting of at least two syllables" (*dvyajavarārddhāt*) is a prospective designation (*bhāvivyapadeśa*). The meaning is: "from that which will possess the status of having at least two syllables once reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has been performed. If it was argued that since reduplication is prescribed for *ḍāc*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) due to its higher priority, he says in response: "And that," etc. Because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*bahulam*) in the rule "*ḍāci bahulam*," the elision of the final vowel occurs after reduplication has been performed.
When *akaḥ* (the short vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*) is followed by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is substituted [in place of both].

In the case of *agnaye*, once the *guṇa* substitution [of *i* for *e*] has been applied by the rule *gher ṅiti*, there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening (*dīrghatva*). In the case of *dadhy atra*, if the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) were not present, one would not know how to distinguish between the scope of the *yaṇ* substitution and that of lengthening; consequently, they would apply alternatively (*paryāya*).

"The girl lies down. Now, one might object: "Even though the place of articulation and the effort are identical, there is no *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) here, because of the prohibition in the rule *nājjhalau*? To this he says: "In the case of *nājjhalau*... The statement *āṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* is the "informative sentence" (*grahaṇaka-vākya*); and that has not yet come into existence at the time the rule *nājjhalau* operates, for it is dependent upon the technical designation *savarṇa*. Therefore, as long as that [designation] has not been applied, it has not yet come into existence.

The designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) also does not apply as long as its own exception, namely the rule *nājjhalau*, has not yet taken effect; therefore, first the rule *nājjhalau* applies, then the designation *savarṇa*, and finally the *grahaṇaka-vākya* (the defining statement). This is the sequence. Consequently, in the rule *nājjhalau*, there is the inclusion of vowels (*ac*) that have not yet been grasped by the *savarṇa* designation; thus, the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *i* and the consonant *ś* is not prohibited. Therefore, the term *ac* must be carried over [from the previous rule]. Regarding the statement "when *ṛ* follows, *ṛ* [is substituted]," there are two *repha*-portions (*bhakti*) in the middle, and half a *mātrā* of the *aj*-portion at the beginning, and likewise at the end.

In the same way, here too in the case of *lṛ*, there are two portions of the letter *l* in the middle, with [the other parts] on both sides as before. Thus, because these two [sounds] have a duration of two morae (*mātrā*), they are only slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*); consequently, due to their lack of similarity (*asāvarṇya*) with the open (*vivṛtta*) vowels *ṛ* and *lṛ*, they are not included [in the *savarṇa* group], and thus, in the absence of the designation "long" (*dīrgha*), this statement [is made]. Others hold that it is because they have a duration of two and a half morae, and therefore lack the requisite duration [of two morae for a long vowel]. This has been explained in detail under the section on the designation of similar sounds (*savarṇa*). As for the phrase "but in the view that they are long":

The combination of the sounds *ṛ* and *lṛ* is the substituendum (*sthānin*), and since no corresponding long vowel (*dīrgha*) exists for that combination, only that which is most similar (*antaratama*) to its constituent parts occurs. Furthermore, because a long vowel is impossible for the sound *lṛ*, only that which is most similar to the sound *ṛ* occurs; and even there, because a long vowel is impossible for the sound *lṛ*, only the sound *ṛ*—which is the most similar to the sound *ṛ*—occurs.
In the case of the first two [vibhaktis], there is the substitution of the homogeneous vowel of the preceding [syllable]. (Pāṇini 6.1.102)

The word *prathamā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to a specific case-ending (*vibhakti*), because in rules such as "of the first case preceded by something" (*sapūrvāyāḥ prathamāyāḥ*) and "from the seventh, fifth, and first cases" (*saptamī-pañcamī-prathamābhyaḥ*), it is precisely that [case-ending] which is understood. Now, one might object: the word *prathamā* is conventionally established there as feminine, yet there is no evidence for its being feminine; on the contrary, since the word *prathama* is employed in this very grammar as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the two triplets of verbal endings (*tiṅ*), it is more appropriate to understand it as referring to that alone.

Consequently, in forms such as *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*; *pacate*, *pacete*, *pacante*; and *cakāra*, *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*; *cakre*, *cakrāte*, *cakrire*, this rule is appropriate because it sublates other rules that would otherwise apply. Furthermore, if this were the case, the dual number in the expression "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*) would be justified even for the primary sense of "first," since the "first" is divided by the distinction between the Ātmanepada and Parasmaipada? It is replied: if that were so, the use of the dual number would be purposeless.

This is because [the rule] is established by analogy with "luṭaḥ prathamasya" and so forth. Alternatively, the term *sup* will be carried over from the rule "vā supyāpiśaleḥ"; therefore, only the first two [cases] of the *sup*-suffixes are understood. And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this. What is the indicative mark? It is the rules "dīrghājjasi ca" and "tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi. For this very reason, by virtue of that indicative mark, the first two of the *sup*-suffixes are also understood; furthermore, because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "aci," for [the suffixes] beginning with *su* and *jas* are not [included].

[Objection: Does the rule not apply here in cases such as *surāpi kuṇḍam tiṣṭhati*? [Response: This rule does not apply here. Why? Because it is sublated by the preceding [rule]. Therefore, it is established that there is the mention of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*). By association with that, the second [word] is also said to be "the first" (*prathamā*). And the dual number here is the proof.

Now, is it not the case that a word heard only once must function either in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) or in its secondary sense (*jaghanyavṛtti*), but not in both simultaneously? In this instance, within the aggregate of the first and second [cases], this word functions only in its secondary sense; and since that aggregate has its constituent parts manifested as distinct, the use of the dual number is justified, just as in the expression "the umbrella-bearers are going."

"Vṛkṣāḥ," "plakṣāḥ"—here too, one might argue that by the rule *ato guṇe*, the single substitute of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) ought to occur, because that rule was formulated precisely for cases where no other rule would otherwise apply. One might further object: "Just as the rule *prathamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), which prescribes lengthening, sets aside other rules even when they have not yet found scope—as in the case of *agnī* and so on—so too shall it set aside the *pararūpa*. To this we reply: In the context of vowel sandhis (*svarasandhi*), *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are general rules (*utsarga*), whereas *vṛddhi*, *savarṇadīrgha*, and the substitution of a homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇādeśa*) are their exceptions (*apavāda*). Thus, [the rule for] lengthening does not override the *pararūpa* here.

Those [cases] falling under the second rule would be superseded by the subsequent form, which falls under the third rule; thus, that very [subsequent form] would be obtained. If this is so, then a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) will be made: first, "of the two initial vowels" (*prathamayoḥ*), and then "of a vowel homogeneous with itself" (*akaḥ savarṇe*). By this, in examples such as *vṛkṣāḥ*, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) will be set aside, and the lengthening of a homogeneous vowel for the two initial *ak* sounds will take place.

If, then, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) subverts the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), then in cases such as *vṛkṣam*, it would likewise subvert the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) under the rule "before *am* there is the preceding form" (*ami pūrvaḥ*). What, then, would be the scope for that [rule], such as in *agnim* and so forth? This is not a fault; for in the rule "before *am* there is the preceding form," by means of a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) within the word *ami*, the meaning is that even the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) that would otherwise be obtained does not take place.

Even so, in the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi*, the word *tat* refers back to the immediately preceding long vowel (*dīrgha*), so that in an example such as *etān gāś carato balīvardān paśya*, the substitution [of *na*] does not occur due to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule *auto 'mśasoḥ*. What follows from this? If a split of the *yoga* (rule-segmentation) were made, the substitution of *na* would apply only in cases like *agnīn* and *vāyūn*, but not in cases like *vṛkṣān*, where a long vowel is prescribed by the split of the *yoga* in the rule *prathamayoḥ*. This too is not a fault.

By the word *tasmāt* (from that), the long vowel (*dīrgha*) whose place of occurrence is *ak* is referred to, not the immediately preceding one, nor merely any long vowel; this is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ak*. Or rather, let there be no splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [into two parts, the first being] *prathamayoḥ*. But was it not said that in forms such as *vṛkṣāḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the single-substitute form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*)? This is not a fault; the activity of the Teacher (*ācāryapravṛtti*) makes it known that the single-substitute form of the subsequent element does not occur for *jas* and *śas*, since he employs the mention of *i* in the rule *nādici*.

Otherwise, since there would be no possibility at all of a long vowel for that which does not end in a vowel, what would be the purpose of including the letter *i* [in the rule]? For if it were intended solely for the sake of the subsequent rule, it should have been placed right there. Or rather, one might simply say "after a long vowel, before *śas*" (*dīrghācchasi*); why then is this [present rule] stated? It is for the sake of the word *nīyam*—to ensure that [the substitution occurs] only after a long vowel before *śas*. Consequently, it will not apply to *jas* and *śas*. However, the author of the Vṛtti, fearing that the aforementioned solution would lead to a burden on the intellect (*pratipatti-gaurava*), offers a logical solution: "Since *ato guṇaḥ* [prescribes] the single-substitute form [of the preceding and following vowels] when an *a* follows, and so forth. He demonstrates the logic with the words "because it precedes" (*purastād iti*). The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason.

Regarding the example *agnī iti*: if the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) were absent, then because there would be no long vowel among the substitutes that is most similar to the entire preceding composite (*samudāya*) which is the original element (*sthānin*), the substitute that is most similar to a part [of it] would apply. Since there would be no restrictive cause stating that it must belong to the preceding [element alone], the *parasavarṇa* (the same sound as the following) might also occur. Therefore, the mention of "the preceding" is for the purpose of excluding that. Furthermore, the mention of "the preceding" is for the purpose of removing the conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*); otherwise, in the case of *agnī iti*, a conflict of rules would arise.

How so? The word "long" (*dīrgha*) is understood [from the previous rule]. [The meaning is: if the preceding [element] is not long, or if it is long but not the preceding [element]. But surely, by the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "long," the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) will be understood as referring to the preceding form (*pūrvākṛti*)? How, then, is there such force, given that the continued application of "long" would be for the purpose that the rule applies only where the preceding individual instance (*vyakti*) has become long—as in *kumārīḥ paśya* ("look at the girls") or *bhastrāḥ paśya* ("look at the bellows")—and does not apply in cases like *agnī* ("two fires")? If this were the only purpose, [the rule would be restricted accordingly].

One might say that [the rule] should have been stated as "let there be the preceding vowel before the nominative plural suffix *śas* and before *am*" (Pāṇini 6.1.102). However, since the rule begins with "in the case of the first two cases" (Pāṇini 6.1.102), it is understood that by the rule "in the case of the first two cases," a long vowel is not intended to be prescribed only for instances such as "look at the girls" (*kumārīḥ paśya*), but rather also for cases such as "two fires" (*agnī*). And this is justified when there is an intention to express the generic form (*ākṛti*). True; that very point is made even clearer by the inclusion of the term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*)—namely, to prevent the substitution of a three-mora vowel for a three-mora base.

Because of its internal nature, only that which possesses three moras (trimātra) would be applicable. Only where there is the possibility of both a protracted (pluta) and a non-protracted vowel is that the domain of the rule "and a protracted [vowel] is prescribed in its specific scope" (*plutaśca viṣaye smṛtaḥ*). However, since here there is the possibility of only a protracted vowel, this is not its domain.
Therefore, [the substitution of] *naḥ* occurs for *śas* in the masculine. (Pāṇini 6.1.103)

By the word "tasmāt" (from that), the internal long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is indicated; thus he says: "from that long vowel of the same class as the preceding. [The phrase] "of the following *śas*" means: the word "following" (*uttarasya*) is an adjective qualifying the member of *śas*; thus, it refers to that which is the following member of *śas*, and not to *śas* itself, because that is impossible. For a *śas* never occurs immediately after a long vowel of the same class as the preceding. Nor does the rule of "treating the end as the beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) apply here, because it would involve relying on both sides simultaneously.

For this very reason, even though not explicitly mentioned, the phrase "of a part" (*avayavasya*) is understood. In the rule *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* ("the plural [suffix] is used for many"), it was stated that "the triplet is the meaning of the nominal stem" (*trikaṃ prātipadikārthaḥ*). Consequently, the word *pumsi* ("in the masculine") serves as a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*), meaning "of the suffix *śas* which is a part [of the word] following a masculine noun. If this is so, then forms such as *vṛkṣān* (accusative plural) are valid examples ending in the letter *n*.

Although the words *ṣaṇḍha* and *ṣaṇḍhaka* here refer to the neuter according to worldly convention, they nevertheless convey a meaning that is accompanied by masculinity, just as the word *artha* when applied to things such as girls conveys [a meaning] associated with femininity; for femininity and so forth are indeed specific universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), and not merely the physical marks such as breasts and so on. This has been established in the rule concerning women (*strīsūtra*).

The two examples beginning with *sthūrakān* are inappropriate. How so? [One might argue: "The offspring of *sthūrakā* and the offspring of *ararakā*"—from *gargādibhyaḥ* [we derive] *yañ*; in the plural, there is elision (*luk*); and by the rule *luk taddhitaluki*, there is also elision of the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*). Thus, *sthūraka* and *araraka* are here feminine words, and the suffix *śas* follows them; it does not follow masculine words. To this, he says: "All these... [meaning they are all masculine].

The meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is that it refers not only to trees and the like, but to these two as well; for even when the suffix is elided, the base itself functions in that sense, and here the meaning of the suffix is this distinct form: "qualified by masculinity. The point is that although these two are well-known as denoting females, in this particular usage they are words denoting males.

If this is so, one might object: in the case of *cañcāḥ pumāṃsaḥ* ("men who are like dolls"), when the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule *ive pratikṛtau* is elided by the rule *lummanuṣye*, the base word *cañcā* itself expresses the referent qualified by masculinity in this usage; thus, why would the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) not arise? To this, he says: "But here," and so forth. The meaning is that even here, the meaning of the suffix is not qualified by masculinity; rather, due to the extended application (*atideśa*), it is qualified by femininity.

Regarding the question "What does 'from that' (tasmāt) mean?", the inquiry is whether the rule is established by the transformation of the genitive case of the previously mentioned mention of "long" (dīrgha) into an ablative. In the example *etān gāḥ paśya*, there is the substitution of *ā* (*ātva*) by the rule *auto'mśasoḥ*, which is governed by the general heading *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*; consequently, one might think that the change to *n* (*natva*) would apply only within the scope of that [substitution]. [Objection: But if this were so, then the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* should have been stated right there—namely, under *śaśo naḥ puṃsi*. Why then is it applied here immediately following the [general] section? [Response: That very point is made clear by the inclusion of the word *tasmāt*.
The substitution of *nādici* [occurs] before a vowel other than *i*.
Regarding *khaṭve*: by the rule *auṅa āpaḥ*, the substitution of *śī* occurs for *auṅ*. Regarding *kuṇkaḍe*: here too, it is by the rule *napuṃsakācca*.
And [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of a stem ending in a long vowel occurs] before the suffix *jas*. (Pāṇini 6.1.105)

The word *āt* does not follow [from the previous rule], because the force of the particle *ca* (and) serves to draw in *ic*; otherwise, since the prohibition would already be established by the preceding rule even for a long vowel followed by *ic*, what would be the purpose of the particle *ca* for the sake of that continuation? What is the purpose of including the term "long" (*dīrgha*), given that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the substitution of *guṇa* is prescribed for the vowel *ṛ* by the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ*? Similarly, for *i* and *u* as well, the substitution of *guṇa* is prescribed by the rule *jati ca*. In these cases, however—such as *vṛkṣāḥ*, *agnī*, *vāyū*—[the rule applies].

In this case, would there not also be a prohibition [of *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*] even after a short vowel? This is not a fault. The rule *nādici* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), and since no specific distinction is being grasped, the restriction applies in both ways: namely, "only after *ā* and *ī*, when followed by *ic*" and "only after *ā*, when followed by *ī*. Among these, by the first restriction, forms such as *vṛkṣāḥ* are established; by the second, forms such as *agnī* and *vāyū* are established. If that is so, just as the prohibition does not apply in cases like *agnī* and *vāyū*, it would likewise not apply in cases such as *kumāryau* and *vadhvau*; therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "after a long vowel" (*dīrghāt*).

The mention of *jas* is for the purpose of excluding *śas*; otherwise, in examples such as *kumārīḥ paśya* (look at the girls) and *vadhūḥ paśya* (look at the wives), there would also be a prohibition regarding *śas*. [Objection: It will not apply because of an indicator (*jñāpaka*); namely, that this author makes the mention of "masculine" (*puṃs*) in the rule *tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi* ("after that [stem], *na* replaces *śas* in the masculine"). That indicates: the prohibition does not apply to *śas*.

For that [prohibition] was indeed made for the sake of excluding the feminine, since a long vowel by *savarṇa-dīrgha* is impossible in the neuter. And if this prohibition were to apply even to the feminine—as in examples such as *kumārīḥ paśya*—then, precisely because of the absence of the *pūrvasavarṇa-dīrgha*, the [substitution of *ru*] would not occur; so what is the use of the mention of the masculine (*puṃgrahaṇa*)? This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [prohibition] must rather be for the sake of those feminine stems ending in a short vowel—such as *kṛtīḥ paśya* and *dhenūḥ paśya*. Therefore, the rule *jāsi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109) must certainly be stated as well. *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106). [In the Vedic language, the substitution of *ru* for the final *s* of a word ending in *as* or *an* before a case-ending beginning with *jhal* is optional.]

Regarding *mārutī*: since the Maruts are their deities (*maruto devatā āsām*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sāsya devatā*; then the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and in the nominative plural (*jasi*), the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatvam*) occurs. Regarding *vārāhī*: since it is a modification (*vikāra*) of a boar (*varāha*), the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *avayave ca prāṇyoṣadhivṛkṣebhyaḥ* (and when denoting a part, after words for living beings, plants, and trees), specifically *prāṇirajatādibhyo'ñ*; then *ṅīp* is added, and in the dual, the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding occurs. The word *upānahau* is the object of qualification (*viśeṣye*).
The word *ami* [is substituted] for the nominative plural ending when it follows a stem ending in a vowel. 6.1.107.
The word "dīrghāt" (from a long vowel) is not repeated [in the subsequent rule], because of the force of its initial introduction.

Regarding the mention of "pūrva" (the preceding), etc.: it is so that it may be precisely that which was previously heard; for what else could possibly apply? To this he says: "lest there be a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding. In some places, however, a compound is recited; that should be understood as a *karmadhāraya*.

This is what is meant: if the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) were not present here, the mention of "the preceding" from the current context would have to be carried over (anuvartate). And while that is being carried over, its correlative, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*), would also have to be carried over. Consequently, only that which is homogeneous with the preceding sound would be subject to the rule as the most similar (*antaratama*). What would be the fault in that? It might be argued that in cases such as *vṛkṣam*, where a long vowel is the substitute for two [short] vowels, there would be no occurrence of a long vowel because the substitute would be two-moraic; for by the force of the specific statement, "the homogeneous of the two preceding vowels" (*prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*), the long vowel is already established. To this, he says: "in the case of *kumārīm*."

"Or [it applies] only in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). This is connected by means of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); otherwise, it would not apply in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Regarding "and *śamyam*": because of the force of the rule enjoining an option (*vikalpa*), even the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) does not occur in the absence of the preceding [condition], since there is no distinction between those two here; thus, only the *yaṇ*-substitution takes place.
And [the substitution of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* does not take place] after a *samprasāraṇa*. (Pāṇini 6.1.108)

"By virtue of the power of the rule prescribing *samprasāraṇa*. But how can there be such power, given that the *yaṇ* substitution is prescribed for *saṃhitā*, whereas *samprasāraṇa* finds its scope in non-*saṃhitā* (i.e., when words are separated)? This is not so; because of the statement: "In a single word, *saṃhitā* is obligatory. [The phrase] "or as in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*) is connected as before by means of a split in the sentence. Regarding the example "yajyamāna": but was it not just stated that the hearing of the separated form would result? How then is there the *yaṇ* substitute here? To this he says: "For, in the prescription of the preceding state..."

True; if priority (*pūrvatva*) were not established, one would encounter the hearing of the separated [vowels], so that the prescription of *samprasāraṇa* might not be rendered useless. For when the prescription of priority exists, the *samprasāraṇa* is meaningful within the scope of its realization. Thus, in the alternative where priority is absent, the substitution of *yaṇ* indeed occurs. [The rule] "In the case of *samprasāraṇa*-priority, there is the mention of 'the same member'" (*samprasāraṇapūrvatve samānāṅgagrahaṇam*) is intended so that it may apply only with that vowel which is included within the very member in which the *samprasāraṇa* resides; let it not apply here: *śakahvau*.

Regarding the term *śakahvartham*: from the root *hve* (to call) with the suffix *kvip*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajñādi* group. That final vowel *ā* of the root is included within that very stem (*aṅga*), and thus it possesses the status of being "prior" (*pūrvatva*). However, the vowel *u* belonging to the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the vowel *a* of the word *artha* are not included within that stem; therefore, they do not possess the status of being "prior."

The solution to this is as follows: that *ik* which occurs in place of a *yaṇ* is called *saṃprasāraṇa*; however, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is not in the place of a *yaṇ*. Furthermore, because it depends on the individual phonemes (*varṇāśrayatva*), the treatment of it as being like the final or initial element (*antādivadbhāva*) does not apply. Thus, the preceding [vowel] itself is not a *saṃprasāraṇa*, let alone the long *ū* that takes its place; therefore, there is no absence of the single-substitute in the case of the preceding vowel. As for the lengthening of the *saṃprasāraṇa*, by the force of the specific rule (*vacanasāmarthya*), the single-substitute is treated as if it were the final element with respect to the preceding one, and thus receives the designation of *saṃprasāraṇa*. The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, having accepted the status of *saṃprasāraṇa*, offers another solution: "And when [the operation] is internal" (*antaraṅge ca*).
Here, spatial remoteness is described as being external;
temporal remoteness, however, consists in occurring later.
Its externality is established by its not being included within the [eighteen] elements (dhātu), while its subsequent occurrence is indeed evident.
And [the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of a stem occurs] before the endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas*.

The phrase *eṅa uttarayoḥ* means: when the letter *y* follows those two [suffixes] *ṅasi* and *ṅas* which follow *eṅ*. For example: *agner āgacchati* (he comes from Agni), *agneḥ svam* (his own [belonging] to Agni). Although there are two *eṅ*s and likewise two *ṅasi-ṅas*s, there is nevertheless no "correspondence by number" (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), because here no operation is prescribed for *ṅasi* and *ṅas* themselves; rather, it is for the *ya* connected to them, and that *ya* is only one. Even if its distinction were based on the distinction of its correlates, there would still be no fault, as evidenced by such rules as *īd agneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* ("the substitution of *ī* for *agni* occurs before *soma* and *varuṇa*") and *dhātoḥ* ("of a root").
The augment *ut* is added after the word *ṛta*.

"Of the two [roots] specified by the genitive case," and so forth—this is a demonstration of what is obtained through logical necessity (*nyāya*), and not because anything undesirable would follow if *aparatva* (the quality of being short) were not applied. The use of the *tapara* marker (*ṛtaḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding the long vowel; thus, [the substitution] does not occur in cases such as "the inclusion of *un* and *nyoḥ*" or "in *preṣṭhaḥ*, except in a sacrifice. Likewise, the use of the *tapara* marker in "uc" is also solely for the purpose of excluding the long vowel, for by virtue of internal similarity (*āntarya*), a long vowel of two morae (*dvimātra*) would otherwise result from a [substitute] of two morae.

Is it not the case that "a vowel being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous counterparts"? If so, then this teaches that "even an *u*-vowel being taught includes its homogeneous counterparts"; therefore, in the form *amūbhyām*, by the rule *adasoserdādu do maḥ*, the long *ū* replaces the long *ū*. Here, after the suffixes *ṅasi* and *ṅas* have been applied to roots such as *gamlṛ*, and after the substitution of *ṛ* and *lṛ* for *ṛ* and *lṛ* respectively, and after the designation of these as homogeneous (*savarṇa*), and after the substitution of *utva* and the subsequent application of *laparatva*, the final consonant is elided (*saṃyogāntalopa*), resulting in the form *gamul*.

[The substitution of *u* for the final vowel of a verbal root occurs] before a suffix beginning with a consonant that is marked with *k* or *ṅ*, provided that the suffix is not one of those called *kṛt*.

Regarding the expression "kh-śabda-śī-śabdayoḥ" and so forth: once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, both [forms] are included because they have become identical in form. It is precisely for this purpose that the *yaṇ* substitution is made with an adventitious vowel (*ākāra*) and the term is presented in its modified form; otherwise, if there were a reference to the two short vowels as in "kh-tyoḥ," it would not apply to the long vowels, and if there were a reference to the long vowels, it would not apply to the short ones. However, when presented in its modified form, it applies to both. Furthermore, there is no inclusion of those ending in /a/ which primarily denote "offspring" (*apatya*) and so on, because of specific grammatical rules such as "sakhyuryaḥ," "patyurno," and "āpatyasya ca."

The word *sakhī* is derived from the verbal root *sakhīyati* with the suffix *kvip*. Now, one might object: "Since the elision of the *ā* (in *sakh-ī*) must be treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), then once the *ya*-elision (*yalopa*) has occurred, the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited [by P. 1.1.58]. Furthermore, because the remaining portion begins with a vowel (*ādiṣṭadacaḥ pūrvatvāt*), there is again no *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, when the *ya* is elided by the rule 'lopo vyor vali', forms such as *saśyuh* would not be established. This is not so; for the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies here by the rule: "That which is elided before *kvip* is not subject to *sthānivadbhāva*."

He states another purpose for the mention of the modified form (*vikṛta*), saying: "Because of the mention of the modified form. Regarding *atisakheḥ*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one by whom a friend has been surpassed" (*atikrāntaḥ sakhā yena*). Alternatively, *atisakhā* means "an excellent friend" (*śobhanaḥ sakhā*); the prohibition of the suffix [for the final member] is applied by the rule *na pūjanāt*. Now, one might ask: why does the *yaṇ* substitution not occur here [in *atisakher*], since it is blocked by the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule *gher ṅiti*? No; because the designation *ghi* is prohibited by the rule *śeṣo ghyasakhi*. Therefore he says: "For it is only the word *sakhi* itself... This has already been explained in that very place.
Therefore, [the substitution of *u* for *o* occurs] after a *ru* that is not protracted (*apluta*), when followed by a vowel that is not protracted (*apluta*).

Regarding the phrase "of that which has *u* as its *anubandha*": if the entire word-group *ru* were the substituendum (*sthānin*), then [the rule] would undesirably apply even in cases such as *agurvartham* and *tarvartham*. Furthermore, in the rule *sasajuṣo ruḥ*, the employment of the *anubandha* *u*—by virtue of the formal agreement (*pratijñā*) that it is nasal—would be purposeless, for it is introduced precisely for the sake of qualification in this very sūtra. As for the phrase "even the state of being *ru*": the word *api* has the sense of *punaḥ* (furthermore). If, moreover, the state of being *ru* were unestablished (*asiddha*), then its recourse as the substituendum would be untenable; for there would be no instance of *ru* whatsoever that possesses *u* as its *anubandha*.

"Of that too" means "of that which has become the cause. In the phrase *susrotā3 atra nvasi*, the prolated vowel (*pluta*) occurs according to the rule "and in calling from a distance"; the word *nu* expresses a question. In *aśvin ātra*, the suffix *ini* is added to the word *aśva* in the sense of possession; this is a vocative form, and the prolation occurs according to the rule "of a heavy syllable not containing ṛ. The meaning is: "O Aśvin, let the water remain right here in this place. However, it is generally read with a final *t* (i.e., *aśvint*), in which case the etymology of the word *aśvin* must be sought.

[Objection: But surely, by the very inclusion of *ta* (in the rule *taparaḥ*), [the substitution] will not occur after a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, nor when a protracted vowel follows, just as it does not occur after a long vowel? To this he replies: "Because the protracted [vowel] is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Objection: But the protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*), since [the grammarian] teaches the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the rule "protracted vowels and *pragṛhya* vowels remain as they are before a vowel" (*plutapragṛhyā aci*). For the preservation of the original form must be prescribed for that which would otherwise undergo a modification; and if the protracted vowel were unestablished, there would be no occurrence of a modification for an existing protracted vowel, so that [the teaching of *prakṛtibhāva*] would be purposeless. [Reply: Let it be so.
In the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*), a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established as valid; however, the substitution of *u* for *ru* (*rorutvam*) does not constitute a vowel-sandhi.

If, however, one relies on the interpretive indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the rule applies only to those things prescribed within the governing heading of "euphonic combination" (*saṃhitā*), then the rule "aplutādaplute" could have been omitted.
And [the suffix] *iṣ* [is applied] after a word ending in *ṛ*. 6.1.124.

"Apluta" means "protracted"—as in "susrotā3 dehi. The particle *ca* serves to draw forward the word "atīta" (protracted); by this, its recurrence occurs in what follows, and not that of "haśī," for there is no other purpose for drawing it forward.
By nature, [the *yama* doubling] does not occur within a *pāda* when followed by a non-*vyañjana* (consonant) other than *v*.

"Only after [the preceding vowel]," not "before *haś*. The reason for this has already been stated: namely, that the word *eṅaḥ* ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyantam*), and so forth. First of all, the word *eṅaḥ* continues to apply even though it is separated [by other rules], but not the word *ror* which is immediately adjacent; in this matter, the commentary alone is the refuge. Therefore, the meaning does not become "when *haś* follows, provided there is no *ava* or *para*, the *ru* remains in its original form (*prakṛtyā*). This is because a connection with the word *prakṛtyā* is not possible for that which ends in the fifth case. Regarding the phrase "the original form," and so forth: [The commentary continues: "The word *prakṛti* means 'one's own nature' (*svabhāva*). That which exists by its own nature is called *prakṛtyā*. It is said that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when followed by *haś*. The meaning is that the *ru* remains as it was before. Why? Because it is not modified. What is meant by "not modified"? It is that the *ru* does not undergo any change such as elision (*lopa*) or substitution (*ādeśa*). Thus, the sense is that the *ru* remains in its original state. Alternatively, the word *prakṛti* means "cause" (*kāraṇa*). That which arises from its own cause is called *prakṛtyā*. It is said that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when followed by *haś*. The meaning is that the *ru* remains as it was before. Why? Because it is not modified. What is meant by "not modified"? It is that the *ru* does not undergo any change such as elision or substitution. Thus, the sense is that the *ru* remains in its original state. Or again, the word *prakṛti* means "non-modification" (*avikāra*). That which consists of non-modification is called *prakṛtyā*. It is said that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when followed by *haś*. The meaning is that the *ru* remains as it was before. Why? Because it is not modified. What is meant by "not modified"? It is that the *ru* does not undergo any change such as elision or substitution. Thus, the sense is that the *ru* remains in its original state. Or yet again, the word *prakṛti* means "that which is produced" (*kriyate*). That which is produced from its own cause is called *prakṛtyā*. It is said that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when followed by *haś*. The meaning is that the *ru* remains as it was before. Why? Because it is not modified. What is meant by "not modified"? It is that the *ru* does not undergo any change such as elision or substitution. Thus, the sense is that the *ru* remains in its original state. Or finally, the word *prakṛti* means "the state of being" (*bhāva*). That which exists in its own state is called *prakṛtyā*. It is said that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when followed by *haś*. The meaning is that the *ru* remains as it was before. Why? Because it is not modified. What is meant by "not modified"? It is that the *ru* does not undergo any change such as elision or substitution. Thus, the sense is that the *ru* remains in its original state. Therefore, the word *prakṛtyā* is used here in the sense of "remaining as it was before" (*pūrvavat-sthiti*). It is not used in the sense of "being the cause" (*kāraṇatva*). This is because the word ending in the fifth case cannot logically be connected with the word *prakṛtyā*. Furthermore, since the word *eṅaḥ* is present in the fifth case, it is understood that the *ru* becomes *prakṛtyā* when preceded by *eṅ*, not when followed by *haś*. Thus, the intended meaning is established. [End of section] "Because of that purpose" (*tadarthāt*): For a connection with the word *prakṛtyā* is not possible for that which ends in the fifth case. Regarding the phrase "the original form," and so forth: [The commentary continues as above].

The word *prakṛti* is seen in both senses—as in "nature is difficult to abandon" (*dustyajā prakṛtiḥ*) and "milk is the *prakṛti* of curds" (*dadhnaḥ kṣīraṃ prakṛtiḥ*). [Regarding the term] *antar*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and so forth. By means of that word *antaḥ*, which denotes the middle, a distinction (*vyatireka*) is produced; consequently, the genitive case is applied after the word *pāda*, and an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed with that [genitive form]. It is intended that only the quarter-verse of a *ṛk* (Vedic verse) is to be understood here; this is indeed a specific rule (*iṣṭi*).

Others, however, by means of the "frog-leap" (maṇḍūkapluti) from the rule *vā chandasi*, carry forward the word *chandasi*. Having thus shown the meaning of the individual components, he shows the meaning of the whole through the phrase beginning with *avakārayakāraparaḥ*. "It remains in its own nature" (*svabhāvenāvatiṣṭhate*): when the word *prakṛti* refers to one's own nature, then this is the meaning—the sense being that it does not undergo the effects of *saṃhitā* by abandoning its own nature.

But when it occurs in the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇa*), then this is the meaning: "it exists by way of the nature of the cause. The cause of the effect *ai* is the quality of having *para* (the subsequent vowel) as its predecessor; its "self" (*ātman*) is its own form (*svarūpa*). It exists by that very [form]. The meaning is that it remains in that very form which was its nature prior to the application of the *saṃhitā*-rule for *ai*. He clarifies these two meanings just mentioned with the word "thus" (*iti*). For it exists by its own nature (*svabhāva*) only if it does not have a characteristic other than its own nature.

It attains [that state]; likewise, it exists as that which has such a cause, meaning provided it does not undergo modification—that is, provided it does not transform into the form of an effect. Regarding the phrase "if those two": the cause is the vowel *a*, and the effect is the *eṅ* diphthongs. In the examples, there is an absence of the preceding quality (*pūrvatva*) and the substitution of *ay* and *āv* as appropriate, according to the rule "after an *eṅ* at the end of a word, before *ati*. In the case of *ete 'rcayanti*, this word ends in a word-final position, and the vowel *a* of *arcayanti* occurs at the beginning of the subsequent quarter-verse (*pāda*).

Regarding the phrase "some": if they read "not within a foot" (*nāntaḥ pādam*), then in that case, a prohibition would apply only to what immediately precedes, and not to *ay* and *avaḥ* when separated [by other sounds]. To this he says: "in *saṃhitā*. If only the condition "in *saṃhitā*" is required here, and not the state of being a single substitute (*pūrvarūpatva*), then the meaning is that whatever was stated under the heading of *saṃhitā* regarding *eṅ* does not apply here.

Therefore, this objection also is not to be raised: "If this prohibition were not undertaken, there would be no application of those two [rules], because they would have been sublated by the preceding one; however, when the preceding rule is sublated by this prohibition, those two would arise, and at that stage, this [prohibition] has no function, as it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya)."

How is this objection resolved? If this were a prohibition of "prior-ness" (*pūrvatva*) itself, then it would prohibit it with reference to that very [prior-ness]. However, since it prohibits it generally with reference to the rule "in *saṃhitā*," its purpose is this: so that there may also be a prohibition of the two vowels *a* and *i* which arise after the operation of the [rule] itself has taken effect.

And here, the phrase "after a word-final [consonant]" (padāntāt) must be understood as carrying over; otherwise, in cases such as *agnerahaṃ suhuvasya praṇītau* and *vāyoriva sūnṛtānāmudarkkaḥ*, the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) prescribed by the rule *ṅasiṅsośca* would also incur the prohibition of *prakṛtibhāva*.

The root *av* (to protect) takes the augment *iṭ* in the forms *avyāt*, *avadyāt*, *avakramuḥ*, and *avavrata*; it also takes *iṭ* in the Aorist (*luṅ*) when used with words meaning "desirous" (*avaśyu*).

Because *avyāt* and the others are imitations (of Vedic forms), they form a compound and take case endings. *Avyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a blessing from the root *av*. *Avadyāt*: this ends in the singular of the ablative case. *Avakramuḥ*: this is the form of the perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us* from the root *kram* preceded by *ava*, where there is no reduplication according to the rule "In the section on reduplication, it may optionally be stated for the Veda. Some, however, read *avacakramuḥ* in the sūtra as already reduplicated; for them, an example must be sought elsewhere, as the Rigvedins indeed recite *avakramuḥ*. *Avratā*: [this refers to those who do not observe vows].

In the case of *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli* by the rule "in a mantra, [the suffixes] *ghas* etc. and the substitution of *ad* for *at* by the rule "in the ātmanepada, [for roots ending] in *a*. Regarding the word *ayam*: from the stem *idam*, the nominative singular suffix *su* is added, and by the rule "in the masculine, *id-* becomes *ay-*," it becomes *ayam*. Regarding *avantu*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *ava*; from that same root ending in the *asu*-suffix, the desiderative suffix *kyac* is added, and by the rule "in the Veda, after *kyac*," the suffix *u* is added—thus forming *avasyuḥ*. Therefore, the Ṛgvedins recite the text as "may the fathers protect us in our invocations" (*tenovantu pitaro haveṣu*), preserving the original form (*pūrvarūpa*). [The Yajurvedins], however, read "may they speak over us; may they protect us" (*adhibruvantu te 'vantvasmān*).
The word *āpaḥ* [is substituted for *apaḥ*] when followed by *juṣāṇaḥ*, *vṛṣṇaḥ*, *varṣiṣṭhe*, *ambe*, *ambāle*, *ambike*, or *pūrve*. (Pāṇini 6.1.118)

*Āpaḥ* and the following words are separate items that function as phonetic imitations (*anukaraṇa*). However, because the distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, no case-ending (*vibhakti*) occurs. Alternatively, the elision of the case-ending occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. The word *ambikepūrva* is likewise an imitation. Among these, the first ends in the nominative plural suffix *-jas*, the second ends in the locative singular suffix *-su*, the third ends in the accusative plural suffix *-śas*, the fourth ends in the feminine nominative singular suffix *-ṅī*, and the others end in the vocative singular. The expression "preceded by the word *ambike*" is a compound with a fifth-case member (*pañcamī-samāsa*), made possible by this very irregularity (*nipātana*).

"From this very irregular derivation (nipātana)" refers to the case of *ambe*. However, for the other two [vocatives], since it will be stated later that "the word *ambā* consists of two syllables," there is no possibility of shortening at all.
And [the substitution of *aṅ*] occurs in place of [the final vowel of] *aṅga*, etc., [before a case ending beginning with a consonant]. 6.1.119.

Regarding the word *aṅga*, "that which begins with *eṅ*"—this is connected with what will be stated later: "that remains in its original form" (*sa prakṛtyā bhavati*). Regarding "that which precedes the *ā* which begins with that," the term "*eṅ*" is expected [as a reference], and the connection is as before. By the word *tat* (that), which refers back to what has passed, the meaning of the word *iti* is expressed; "that which begins with that" (*tadādi*) means that which begins with the word *aṅga*.

What is the purpose of the particle *ca*? If *ca* were not present, the meaning would be that the *eṅ* of the word *aṅga* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) only when followed by *ati* at the beginning of a subsequent word; consequently, this would apply only in cases such as *aṅge aṅge*. However, when *ca* is present, the meaning becomes: the *eṅ* of the word *aṅga* remains in its original form wherever *ati* follows, and furthermore, any *eṅ* whatsoever remains in its original form when followed by *ati* at the beginning of a word. By this, [the rule] applies in both instances: *aṅge adīdhyat* and *prāṇo aṅge*.
And [the substitution of *t* for *d* occurs] before an unaccented vowel when followed by *k* or *dh*.

Regarding the phrase "when followed by a guttural consonant (*kavarga*) or the letter *dh*": that after which a guttural consonant or the letter *dh* follows is so described. In the word *dh*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The word *agni* ends in the suffix *nip* according to the rule "aṅgenirnalośca," and is thus oxytone (*antodātta*). The word *adhvara* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*) because it ends in the suffix *yaṅ*. It is prescribed as being initially acute (*ādyudātta*). In the list of *uṇādi* suffixes beginning with "ṛnnendrāgra," the word *agra* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem.
In all cases, there is an option regarding the word *go*.

"In both Vedic (chandas) and colloquial (bhāṣā) usage. Although "in Vedic" was not the subject under discussion, nevertheless, because of the statement "within a quarter-verse in the Yajus," and because of the imitation of Vedic forms such as *avakramuḥ* and *avrato 'vasyuḥ*, the sense is that the preceding sūtras belong to the Vedic domain. The inclusion of the term *sarvatra* ("everywhere"), however, makes it applicable to the Yajus as well as elsewhere. Only after a word-final [consonant]—as in *go-r-āgatam* ("come from a cow") or *goḥ svam* ("the property of a cow").
The substitution of *avaṅ* for *ava* occurs according to the opinion of Sphoṭāyana.

*Sphoṭāyana* refers to one for whom *sphoṭa* is the goal (*ayana*) and the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇa*); that is, a teacher of grammar (*vaiyākaraṇācārya*) devoted to the exposition of *sphoṭa*. As for those who read [the name] with the vowel *au*, they consider it to be included in the *naḍādi* or *aśvādi* groups [of the *gargādi* list]. The word "at" (in the rule) is understood as meaning "ceased" (*nivṛtta*). Otherwise, [the suffix] would not apply in cases such as *gavaudana*. One might ask: "If this is so, does it not lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? To this he says: "But as for the word 'aci'... In all such instances here, the explanation itself is the only refuge.

If the term *aci* (before a vowel) continues to apply [from the previous rule], how is it that it was stated under the rule *iko yaṇ aci*: "The governing force (*adhikāra*) of *aci* extends as far as the rule *samprasāraṇācca*"? There is no fault here, for that statement was intended to refer to uninterrupted continuity. Examples: *gavāgram*, *gavājinam*. These are either *bahuvrīhi* compounds or *tatpuruṣa* compounds. *Gavoṣṭram* is a *dvandva* compound. Regarding the mention of *gorag*—it should be stated as *gorag*; even there, it is indeed established by the substitution of *ava*. Nor does there arise the contingency of the preceding [vowel] being substituted by *eṅaḥ padāntāt*.

Because that [the final *au*] is included by the inclusion of that [the rule for *o*], the vowel *o* is not considered "not at the end of a word" (*apadānta*). What is the purpose? First, there is brevity; furthermore, there is no fault regarding the accent (*svara*).

How is it that the augment (*āgama*) is unaccented (*anudātta*)? In this regard, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *gavāgra*, the unaccented nature of the augment is possible by virtue of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prior member. However, in the case of the substitution (*ādeśa*) of *avaṅ*, since [the substitute] must be identical in its internal properties (*āntarya*), the *avaṅ* substitute would necessarily be oxytone (*antodātta*), as the original is oxytone. Now, one might argue: "Since this [word *go*] is a single-syllable (*ekāc*) word, its oxytonic status must be accepted through the principle of 'behaving like that which possesses a designation' (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). From that very same [principle], its initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) status will also follow. Therefore, what prevents an initial-accented substitute from replacing an initial-accented [original]? This is indeed true.

However, there is no such rule as "the first syllable of a nominal stem (prātipadika) becomes udātta"; rather, this rule exists: "the final syllable of a nominal stem becomes udātta. Consequently, regarding that which is [already] antodātta by virtue of a grammatical rule, an antodātta substitute would result by way of proximity (āntarya). [Objection: But is not the suffix Ḍa prescribed after the root gam? [Reply: What of it? Once the accentuation of the initial syllable of the affix has been applied, an ādyudātta substitute will occur by way of proximity.

But how is this [stem] acutely accented on the first syllable, given that it consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) by virtue of the principle of designation as if it were multiple (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*)? If that is so, then for that very reason it would also be acutely accented on the final syllable; in that case, by the rule of closest proximity (*antaryataḥ*), an *avaṅ* substitute acutely accented on the final syllable would result. True; however, there is indeed this rule: "The suffix is acutely accented on the final syllable," whereas this other rule states: "The beginning of the suffix is acutely accented. Therefore, in the case of that which is acutely accented on the first syllable by virtue of the rule, an acute-accented substitute will occur by way of closest proximity.

This might be the case if there were an extension of the rule from the scripture stating "as in the case of the beginning and the end in a single [element]. However, when by this [rule] only the effect—namely, the acute accent (*udātta*)—is extended to the state of being the "end" while the state of being the "beginning" is absent, then since the designation "beginning" does not apply to the vowel *au* itself, how could its substitute possess an initial acute accent? Consequently, in the alternative view that the initial acute accent would occur at an indefinite position by rotation, the aforementioned defect would follow. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras, disregarding brevity, has instead provided the substitute *avaṅ*.

In this regard, he demonstrates how no fault occurs with respect to the accent: "The substitute *avaṅ* is prescribed as having the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) on its first syllable. When the Sūtra is recited in a single tone (*ekaśruti*), the fact that it is here pronounced with effort as acute-accented is understood to be for the purpose of setting aside its status as having the acute accent on the final syllable; otherwise, it would be overridden by the general rule of the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound.

And this [result] is obtained through the statement in the Bhāṣya, "The treatment as if it were taught [in the original form] must be stated"; otherwise, because [the rule for] the accent of the final member of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*) applies earlier due to its higher status, once *avaṅ* has been applied, the accent of *avaṅ* alone would remain as the *satiśiṣṭa* (the remaining one). But when there is the treatment as if it were taught, *avaṅ* is applied first and the compound later; thus, because it is *satiśiṣṭa*, the accent of the compound itself occurs. Only after [the word] ends in a word-final [consonant]—as in *gavo*, *gavoḥ*, *gavām*, *gavi*.
And [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after the word *indra*. (Pāṇini 6.1.124)

In this context, if *aci* is the qualifier and the word *indra* is the qualificand, then the meaning would be "the word *indra* when preceded by a vowel-initial [word]. Consequently, forms such as *gavendrayajña* would not be possible, because [in such cases] the word *indra* is not the final member of a compound (*anuttarapadatvāt*). Although there is no explicit mention of the term "final member of a compound" here, this rule nonetheless applies to compounds by implication; for the word *indra* cannot occur immediately after the word *go* in any other context.

And since a rule of application within a compound would, by implication, apply only to the final member—just as in the case of the *ṣyaṅ* substitution involving *samprasāraṇa*—the vowel (*ac*) is the qualified element and the word "Indra" is the qualifier; thus, it means "in whichever Indra there exists [a vowel] when followed by a vowel. This is what was stated: "in the vowel situated in the word 'Indra'."
Pluta vowels and pragṛhya vowels are always [unchanged] before a vowel.

[Objection: Is it not the case that *prakṛtibhāva* (the state of remaining as the original form) must be prescribed for that which has undergone a modification (*vikāra*), and yet no modification has been prescribed for the protracted vowel (*pluta*), because it is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*)? [Response: To this, it is said that "the protracted vowel is established (*siddha*) by virtue of its basis. The meaning is this: since this protracted vowel is relied upon as the cause (*kāritvena*) for the *prakṛtibhāva*, one infers from this very indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "the protracted vowel is established in the context of vowel-sandhis."

The purpose is to include the vowel that serves as the cause for the substitution. This means it is for the sake of ensuring that the very vowel for which a substitution is prescribed is also included as the cause for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). In the example *jānu u asya*, the particle *u* undergoes a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding vowel; since the cause of this [substitution] is not something following a *pragṛhya* vowel, and that which follows it is not the cause of the single-substitute, the preservation of the original form does not occur, and thus the single-substitute indeed takes place.

If, however, the mention of *ac* were not repeated, then when it is stated that "a *pragṛhya* remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by an *ac*," the original form would apply even to that change which was previously obtained in conjunction with the preceding vowel. But when *ac* is mentioned again, this does not happen; for once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been made there, because of the rule regarding the treatment of the substitute as the initial element (*ādivadbhāva*), it is included by the mention of *pragṛhya*, and thus the *yaṇ*-substitution prescribed by "the *iK* vowels become *yaṇ* before an *ac*" does not occur due to the application of the original form. Furthermore, by the rule "after *m* [ending a word], *uÑ* optionally becomes *v*," the letter *v* may optionally appear in place of *uÑ*.

"The term *nitya* (invariable) is understood [from the previous rule]. The inclusion of the word *nitya* was indeed made for this very purpose in the preceding sūtra; however, there, the rule was established as invariable solely by virtue of its formulation. The meaning is: "so that the *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) may occur invariably," that is, so that this very *prakṛtibhāva* may be invariable and not accompanied by any other grammatical operation (*kāryāntara*) through another rule.
In the Vedic language, the nasalized vowel [āṅ] is substituted for the particle *ā* before a word beginning with a vowel.

Therefore, in this case, [the augment] does not occur. It occurs only for the meaningless *ā*; for instance, in examples such as *abhra ām̐ apaḥ*, the meaning of that [prefix] is already expressed by the locative case itself, so the prefix *ā* functioning with that meaning is meaningless (*anarthaka*). On the other hand, in *ātarat*, it is meaningful because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action.
But how can there be the status of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittva*) for something that is meaningless, given the rule:
"That which is used in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadartha*), in connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), or in the senses of 'limit' (*maryādā*) and 'inclusiveness' (*abhividhi*)..."?
Is it not stated that "one should know this *āṅ* as having the marker *ṅ*; [however], when used in the sense of speech or recollection, it is without the marker *ṅ*"?

True; the intended meaning lies precisely in the statement "when used in the sense of speech or recollection, it is without the marker *ṅ*," whereas elsewhere in all other instances, *āṅ* should be understood as having the marker *ṅ*. Such is the position established in the Bhāṣya.
According to Śākalya, an *ik* vowel followed by a non-homogeneous vowel may optionally be replaced by its short form.

For what purpose is the particle *ca* used here? Is it for the purpose of drawing back (*anukarṣaṇa*) the word *prakṛtyā* [from the previous rule]? But surely, by the very force of the prescription of short vowels (*hrasva*), there will be no vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)? It might be argued that while there would be no vowel-sandhi for long vowels due to the force of the prescription of short vowels, it would nonetheless occur for short vowels. However, a short vowel does not become a short vowel, because there is no purpose [in doing so].

Is there a purpose [for this rule]? [One might ask: "Is it so that sandhi by its own inherent nature (*svarasandhi*) should not occur? In that case, the purpose is this: so that the state of being the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) may occur in some instances. By means of this, the mere preservation of the original form in words such as *akṣa* and others within the Vedic language (*chandas*) is established.

The mention of Śākalya is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*). [An objection is raised: "Why then does it not serve the purpose of providing an option (*vikalpārtha*)? To this he replies: "Precisely because of the force of the initial undertaking. Since the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*) applies when a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) follows, the scope of the *yaṇ* substitute is restricted to non-homogeneous vowels (*asavarṇa*). This present rule also has that same scope; therefore, since the option is already established by the identity of their scope, the mention of the Teacher (Śākalya) is not for that purpose.

Regarding the rule *sinnityasamāsayoḥ*: a *nityasamāsa* (an obligatory compound) is a compound prescribed under the heading of "obligatory" (*nitya*) which does not admit analysis into its constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). Although there is only one locative case (*saptamī*), it is divided according to the difference in scope: [it applies] when *sit* follows, and when there is an obligatory compound. Thus, *śākalaḥ* means "the rule pertaining to Śākalya," where the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre*. Regarding *ṛtviya*: [it means] "one for whom the season has arrived," formed with the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *ṛtoraṇ*, or *ghas* in Vedic usage. Regarding *vyākaraṇam*: this is a compound by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*; in that context, the word *nityam* ("obligatorily") is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*).

Regarding "kumāryartham": this is for the sake of a maiden (*kumāryai idam kumāryartham*); it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) whose analysis is not into its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*).
The substitution of *ṛ* for *ṛti* occurs before a suffix marked with the technical term *ak*.

"The statement [is made] for the sake of the homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*) and for the sake of preventing elision (*anigara*)," as in *hotṛ ṛśyaḥ*, *khaṭva ṛśyaḥ*, and so forth; because in these cases, [the result] is already established by the preceding rule.
The suffix *kvasu* is applied in the sense of "having bathed" when the action is imminent.

The *ṛṣi* is the Veda; that which originates therein is *ārṣa* (Vedic), while anything other than that is *anārṣa* (non-Vedic). Having been extracted from the collection—that is, separated from the sentence—it is established in its own form by whom? By the *padakāras* (arrangers of the word-text). For the purpose of determining the extent of a word, it behaves as if it were not protracted (*aplutavat*). He shows by what common property it possesses this quality of being "as if not protracted"—namely, that it undergoes the grammatical operation of a non-protracted vowel. Furthermore, he shows that by the term "protracted" (*pluta*), there is a prohibition of the operation prescribed for a protracted vowel—namely, that it effects the state of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

Otherwise, there would be a prohibition even of vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), because that too has *pluta* as its effect. In the examples, since the effects of *pluta* are prohibited, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs by supplanting the *pluta* itself; this is because *pluta* is established within the section on vowel-sandhi. In that case, what is the fault? Since the *pluta* is being set aside by the single-substitute, it should not be heard; therefore, let the *pluta* itself simply be prohibited. Why resort to this extension (*atideśa*)? [The answer is: "In *agnī3 iti*," where both the absence of sandhi (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on *pluta* and that based on a *pragṛhya* vowel would apply.

In that case, even though there is a prohibition regarding the basis of prolation (*pluta*), since there is no prohibition regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) based on the *pragṛhya* status, the hearing of the prolated vowel is established; however, if a prohibition of the prolation itself were made, then its hearing would not occur here either.
The [patronymic] *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of the word *cākravarmaṇa*. (Pāṇini 6.1.130)

In the Sūtra, the mention of *ī* (in *ī ceti*) indicates that [the vowel] has three moras (*trimātrika*). The phrase "when followed by a vowel" (*aci parataḥ*) implies that the requirement of being "present" (*upasthita*) is removed because it is not marked with a svarita accent. Consider the example: *astu hī3 ity abrūtām*. Here, the protracted (*pluta*) vowel occurs according to the rule *vibhāṣā pṛṣṭaprativacane heḥ*; the form *astu* is derived from the root *as-* in the imperative (*loṭ*), with the ending *tip*, which becomes *uḥ* by the rule *eruḥ*. The purpose of the word *anupasthite* ("when not present") is as follows: in the case of what is "present," the status of not being treated like a protracted vowel (*aplutavadbhāva*) is already established permanently by the preceding rule; therefore, *anupasthite* is used to establish the application of this rule where [the vowel] is not "present," since in that case it would otherwise not apply by any means. Furthermore, the word *anyatrāpi* ("even elsewhere than after *ī*") is intended to show that the rule applies beyond just the vowel *ī*. Thus, the Bhāṣya states: "There is no need for the mention of the vowel *ī*," and so forth.
The substitution of *ut* occurs for the word *divā* [before a case ending beginning with a vowel]. 6.1.131.

The term *pada* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Even though it is combined with the term *anta*, only the term *pada* itself carries over; consequently, by implication, it becomes a word ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*). Because it is qualified by the word *div*, the rule applies to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). However, the principle "by a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a suffix" pertains specifically to the domain of suffix-vidhis (rules for adding suffixes). By virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the rule must apply even to the solitary [word] *div*. Furthermore, the statement "the principle of behaving like that which has a designation does not apply to a nominal stem" also pertains exclusively to the domain of suffix-vidhis.

"Because of having an *anubandha* (indicatory letter)": the letter *u* is the *anubandha* of the verbal root *div*, but there is no *anubandha* whatsoever for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). "Of the word *div*" means: of a word ending in that [root]. "Desirous of heaven" (*dyukāma*): from the sense "he desires heaven," the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule *śīlikāmibhikṣācaribhyo ṇaḥ*. "Pure heaven" (*vimaladyu*): this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one in whom the sky is pure. "From *akṣa* and *div*" (*akṣadyubhyām*): when the word *akṣa* is an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *div*; therein, by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanāsite ca*, the substitution *ūṭh* occurs.

Now, what is the purpose of the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara* marker) in the rule *ṛta ut*, even though it has been indicated by that very *tapara* marker that "even when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the vowel *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts"? Nevertheless, on account of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*), would not a consonant having a duration of half a *mātrā* become [substituted] for a vowel of exactly one *mātrā*? To this he says: "The inclusion of *t*... Even though a long vowel would not be obtained by this [rule], it is indeed obtained; however, he says that it is obtained by another rule, namely: *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*.

The scope for *utva* is where a suffix beginning with *ay* or *aj* follows—as in *vimaladyu*; the scope for *ūṭh* is—as in *dyūtvā* and *dyūtam*. However, where both would apply simultaneously, *ūṭh* would prevail due to its posteriority in the rules; yet, because of the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*taparakaraṇa*), *utva* alone occurs.

If it is argued that the inclusion of *t* (in *tapara*) is for the purpose of excluding the *ūṭh* that has already been obtained, then how can this be reconciled with what will be said later in response to the objection regarding the forms *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* under the rule *cachvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*: "Once *ūṭh* has been applied, because of the *tapara* [specification] in the rule *diva uṭ*, there will be a duration of one *mātrā*"? For would not the meaning of that [statement] be that once *ūṭh* has been applied, that very *ūṭh* itself will have a duration of one *mātrā*? This is not a fault.

The connection of the phrase "when *ūṭh* has been applied" is with the preceding section of the objection: "How [can there be] *dyubhyām*, *dyubhiḥ*, when *ūṭh* has been applied? The extent of the response is: "Because of the use of the *tapara* marker (*u*) in the rule *diva ut*, it will have the duration of one mātrā. However, the sole purpose of the *tapara* marker is the exclusion of *ū*. Therefore, the substitution of *utva* alone should be performed here, and not *ūṭh*; such is the meaning.
The elision of the *su* (nominal suffix) of *etad* and *tad* occurs before a consonant, provided they do not contain the vowel *a* and are not part of a negative (*nañ*) compound.

By this [statement], he explains that in the rule *etattadoḥ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by relation is used in dependence upon the word *su*. If this is so, since the word *su* is dependent [on another], would it not follow that a compound with the word *lopa* is impossible? This is not a compound at all; rather, *su* is a separate word whose genitive case ending has been elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. And which is the word *su* among those two?

If that *su* which is prescribed by those two [the *parama-* and *utkṛṣṭa-*] were to become related to them, then forms such as *paramas dadāti* and *paramaiṣa dadāti* would not occur; thinking thus, he asks. The other, having understood his intention, replies: "That which is connected with the meaning of those two. And this connection is mediated by the meaning; the sense is that it expresses the singularity residing in the meaning of those two.

In examples such as *paramasa dadāti*, since the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, the word expresses the singular number inherent in that very object; thus, the elision is established. Here, the term *su* refers to the nominative singular ending, not the locative plural. For its occurrence is possible only in this specific case, as seen in the rules *syaś chandasi* and *so 'ci lope cet pādapūraṇam*.

In that case, why does there not occur a general inclusion of both [forms]? If so, then by the rule "when there is a mention of a form without an *anubandha*, [it does] not [include] one with an *anubandha*," there is the inclusion of only the nominative singular; for in that case, the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), not an *anubandha*. As for *eṣaḥ*: [the process involves] the substitution of *sa-* by the rule "for *ta-* and *do-*, *sa-* occurs before the nominative ending," then the substitution of *ya-* for the *tyad*-class stems, and finally the substitution of *ṣa-* for *sa-*. As for *eṣakaḥ*: the suffix *akac* is added by the rule "after indeclinables and *sarvanāman*s, *akac* is added before the final vowel."

[Objection: But surely, because of the difference in form, these two [words] themselves do not exist when there is a *sakakāra* (the sound *k* with a following vowel); so what is the purpose of the prohibition "of *ak*" (*akoḥ*)? To this he says: "because it falls in the middle of that" (*tanmadhyapatita*). And the very existence of this prohibition is the indicator (*liṅga*) for the existence of this *paribhāṣā*. [The reason given is] "because the meaning of the final member is predominant. This has already been explained in the *nañ*-sūtra itself. Why is this not placed immediately after the rule "after *hal*, *ī*, *ū*, and *āb*" (*halṅyābbhyaḥ*)—so that it would apply in *saṃhitā* but not in non-*saṃhitā*? [Note: The *paribhāṣā* "that which falls in the middle of something belongs to that" (*tanmadhyapatitaṃ tadgrahaṇena gṛhyate*) is invoked here to justify the application of the prohibition *akoḥ* even when the *k* is part of a compound.]
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *sya* for *saḥ* occurs diversely.

The word *sya* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the nominative form *yat*, with the genitive case ending elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Since the distinction between the original (*anukārya*) and the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed, the genitive case ending does not arise at all. In the example, the substitution of *satva* and so forth is as previously described.
That [elided *a*] is treated as present (*aci*), provided that its elision serves to complete the metrical foot.
The term "it" (saḥ) is a reference as before.
Regarding the phrase "some": he himself, however, considers that because of the governing context of *chandas* (Vedic meter), only the quarter-verse (*ṛkpāda*) is intended to be understood.
The augment *suṭ* is placed before the suffix *kāt*.

Regarding the form *saṃskaroti*: according to the rule "for *sam*, *puṃs*, and *kān*, *s* should be stated," or because the mention [in the sūtra] as *samaḥ suṭi* contains two *s*s, the *s* of the *makāra* of *sam* is [retained], and by the rule "here the nasal [is substituted], but optionally for the preceding," the nasal is substituted for the preceding [vowel].
