In cases such as *samparyupebhyaḥ karotau bhūṣaṇe* ("after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, *suṭ* is added to *kṛ* when meaning adornment") and *kiratau lavane* ("to *kṛ* preceded by *vi* when meaning cutting"), since the augment begins with *k*, *suṭ* is obtained before that *k* precisely because of its *ṭit* status.

In rules such as *hrasvāccandrottarapade*, since the condition of being preceded by *k* (*kātpūrvatva*) is possible, the mention of *kātpūrva* would be useless and therefore meaningless. One might argue: "In forms like *saṃcaskāra*, once reduplication has occurred, the entire form including the reduplicated syllable is considered the root *kṛ*; thus, *suṭ* would be placed before *c*. To prevent it from being placed before *c* and ensure it is placed immediately after *k*, the mention of *kātpūrva* is necessary. This is not correct; for in this case, both reduplication and *suṭ* apply simultaneously to the root *kṛ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

In this regard, before the *suṭ* augment has been applied, reduplication would apply to the root *kṛ*; but once it has been applied, it applies to the form *skṛ*. Furthermore, even after reduplication has been applied, the *suṭ* augment would apply to *cakṛ*, whereas before it has been applied, it applies to *kṛ*. Since both rules are non-obligatory (*anitya*), the *suṭ* is applied first because it is subsequent. Once *suṭ* is applied, it is included by the term "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule for reduplication; thus, when the remaining consonants (*khayaḥ śeṣe*) are applied according to the rule "the *khayaḥ* preceded by *sa*" (*sarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*), the form *saṃcaskāra* is established. Nor does there arise a further possibility of applying *suṭ* to the form with the reduplication (*sābhyāsa*)—as in *akṛta-sukaḍ*—because the grammatical rule has already operated upon this very formation.

Now, an objection might be raised: according to the view that "the verbal root is first joined with its means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*), when the *lakāra* expressing the *sādhana* and the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) based upon it have first been applied—both being *antaranga* because they depend on a single word—the suffix *suṭ* would subsequently be applied as *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two words; furthermore, in forms such as *samaskarot*, since *aṭ* is applied first due to its *antaranga* status and its higher priority, *suṭ* could not occur at all because it would be separated by that *aṭ*. For the augment *aṭ*, being part of the stem ending in a *vikaraṇa*, would not separate that very stem, but it would indeed separate the root *kṛ*.

It certainly creates an intervention. Furthermore, in cases such as *samaskṛta* and *saṃskṛtha*, where the augment *aṭ* itself is the element [intervening], the augment *suṭ* would apply immediately before that *aṭ* because *aṭ* is included within the term *kṛ* (in the rule *kātpūrvaḥ*). Therefore, should the mention of "before *ka*" (*kātpūrva*) be made so that *suṭ* occurs even when both *aṭ* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) have been applied, preceding the *ka*? It need not be made. This is established by the very statement: "*even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and the reduplication*. Nor was the mention of "before *ka*" intended for the purpose of saying "I shall do it" (*kariṣyāmi*) in that context, because even if this were done, [the result] would still be unestablished due to the rule of "asiddha" (non-application).

For instance, this [rule] might be intended to determine the time [of the suffix], meaning: "the *suṭ* augment occurs for that *kṛ* in that state in which, when it occurs, it precedes the *ka*"; or it might be intended to determine the action [of the root], meaning: "the *suṭ* augment occurs for that *kṛ* in which, when it occurs, it precedes the *ka*."

In that regard, according to the first view, although the augment *suṭ* occurs first—by virtue of the force of the mention of "before *ka*" (*kātpūrva*)—thereby overriding even the internal operations of the augment *aṭ* and reduplication, the desired result is established once those two have subsequently taken effect. However, according to the second view, on the contrary, the mention of "before *ka*" (*kātpūrva*) would serve solely for the sake of bringing about the state of having the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsavat*); for if it were applied to that which possesses [the reduplication], it could not be considered as occurring "before *ka*."

It might be argued as follows: "The mention of 'before *kā* (*kātpūrva*)' is not for the purpose of restriction; rather, it is an extraction (*apakarṣa*) of the rule. The augment *suṭ* applies everywhere after the root *kṛ*; however, having obtained its place elsewhere, it must be placed before the *kā*. Even so, while forms such as *samaskṛta* and *samaskṛthāḥ* would be established—since the *suṭ* which was to occur before the augment *aṭ* is instead drawn forward to precede the *kā*—there is indeed no establishment of forms such as *samāskaroṭ*. Why? Because an extraction of a rule occurs when it has already obtained its place elsewhere, and that is not the case here.

Since *suṭ* is obtained immediately before the suffix *ac*, how could the rule be applied by extraction (*apakarṣa*)? And how [could it apply] in cases such as *saṃcaskāra*, where, because there is a difference in utterance due to reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in the application of *ddhi*, there is a difference between words—such that "he performs two [actions]" (*dvau karoti*)—wherein that which is immediately preceded by *sam* does not have the letter *k*, and that which has the letter *k* is not immediately preceded by *sam*? Thus, since it would not otherwise be applicable, why would it not be prescribed before the *k*? Furthermore, if there is reduplication in place (*sthāne dvirvacana*), then by the principle of "as if being the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is only one *karoti*, and since that is not separated [by anything], it would indeed be before the *k*.

Since the [augment] *aṭ* is obtained before the *k*, it is considered "prior to the *k*" (*kātpūrva*), and thus there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, in this way, the verbal root (*dhātu*) is first joined with its grammatical means (*sādhana*); consequently, even if the rule for "being prior to the *k*" (*kātpūrvagrahaṇa*) were applied, the desired result would not be established. Thus, one must simply state: "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplication" (*aḍbhyāsavyavāye’pi*). The author of the *Vārttika* maintains the position that the mention of "prior to the *k*" (*kātpūrvagrahaṇa*) can indeed be omitted.

If, however, by the mention of the instrumental case in the rule *samparyupeḥ karoto*, the augment *suṭ* is prescribed for the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *pari*, or *upa*, then this objective can also be achieved by the inclusion of the term *kātpūrva* (that which precedes the *ka*), even in the case of a separated prefix. How so? In examples such as *samaskarot*, the augment *aṭ* will not occur even without the inclusion of *kātpūrva*; for that [augment] does not belong to a part of the root *kṛ*. However, it will occur for the root *kṛ* itself, because even a separated prefix is considered a *upasarga* (prefix).

In cases such as *samaskṛta*, it is desired that [the substitution] occur before the *k* of the suffix *aṭ*; and in cases such as *saṃcaskāra*, where there is reduplication in place [of the root], it is desired that it occur before the *k*. In *saṃcaskāra* and similar forms, although [the substitution] would apply before the *k* of both instances of the root *kṛ* due to the reduplication, it will be applied before the *k* of the first instance alone; for it is established that what was done before the *k* of that [first instance] remains as it was done before the *k*. Thus, the desired result is achieved.

But the author of the Bhāṣya held that neither [of these two views] should be adopted. First, the root is joined with the prefix; then, while the suffix has not yet arisen and the form *saṃskṛ* stands, when *suṭ* is applied, the *lakāra* follows; thereafter, the augment *aṭ* and the reduplication will occur for the very form that includes *suṭ*.

But surely, an action that has acquired its own form requires a qualifier, and since the acquisition of that form occurs through another factor (the means), the verbal root must first be joined with the means. As for the phrase "having acquired its own form," what is the meaning? Does it mean that its form has been cognized (*pratipanna*), or that its form has been brought into existence (*niṣpanna*)? While the completion (*niṣpatti*) of the form is indeed useful for the connection with the qualifier, the cognition (*pratipatti*) of the form is possible even prior to the action's connection with the qualifier.

Furthermore, a qualified action is connected with its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For instance: in "he stands" (*tiṣṭhati*), the connection with a means is understood as the cessation of motion; in "he sets out" (*pratiṣṭhate*), it is [the cessation] of going; in "he goes" (*gacchati*), of moving; in "he comes" (*āgacchati*), of coming; in "he does" (*karoti*), of mere activity; and in "he embellishes" (*saṃskaroti*), of decoration. Since a qualified action is perceived only when there is a connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), the prior connection with a prefix must be required, whether [the verb root] functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*) or as an expresser (*vācaka*).

And this must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, since the root *bhū* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), when a *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is produced in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), and it subsequently connects with the prefix *anu*—as in the example "the blanket is experienced by Devadatta" (*anubhūyate kambalo devadattena*)—how could there be a *lakāra* in the sense of the object (*karmani*)? Therefore, the view that "first the verbal root is joined with the prefix" is the one accepted. And thus, since the desired result is established by the previously mentioned formulation (*nyāsa*), there is no purpose in the inclusion of the rule for "that which precedes *ka*" (*kātpūrva*), nor in the rule "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* or reduplication" (*aḍabhyāsavyavāye’pi*).

If the verbal root (*dhātu*) were to be joined with the prefix (*upasarga*) first—such that in examples like *adhyetā*, *pratyetā*, or *pratyāyaka*, the root and prefix undergo a single substitution (*ekādeśa*) first, and because that [substituted form] would then be treated as the initial element of the root, the suffix would be generated from that very point, resulting in an undesirable outcome—is this not a fault? No, this is not a fault. This has been made known by the rule *nendrasya parasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.128): first the grammatical operation applies to the two members, the preceding and the following, and only afterwards does the euphonic combination of vowels (*svarasandhi*) take place. Alternatively, the very mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) is the indicator of this principle.

But the author of the Vṛtti, considering that both [the suffix and its augment] must be stated, first states the purpose of the mention of "preceding *k*" (kātpūrva), beginning with the words "The mention of 'preceding *k*'... What, then, is the purpose of it not being part of the suffix? To this he says: "For instance... [and gives the example] "saṃskṛṣīṣṭa."

In the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the suffix *liṅ* is used in the *ātmanepada*. By the rule *uśca*, there is *kittva*; then *suṭ* is added. Since *suṭ* precedes the *ka*-portion of the root, and because it is a part of the root *kṛ*, it would be included by the mention of *kṛ*; thus, since *kṛ* begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* would cause the augment *iṭ* to apply. [The form] *saṃskriyate* is derived from the root in the passive (*karmani*) with the present suffix (*laṭ*), according to the rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu*.

In this case as well, if *suṭ* were a suffix (*bhakta*), then because it begins with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*), the rule "guṇo 'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ" would cause *guṇa* substitution [of the vowel in *kṛñ*]. To prevent this from occurring in forms such as *atakṣīt*, it must be intended that *suṭ* is not a suffix (*abhakta*). [Objection: In that case, would not even the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) fail to apply? [Response: No, because the word *samaḥ* is separated from the suffix *suṭ*, and *suṭ* itself is not a word (*apada*).

How is this a quality (*guṇa*)? Because the augment *suṭ* is not a part of the base (*abhakta*), the base lacks the property of beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāditva*); thus, there is no objection. Regarding the rule "that which falls in the middle of it is included by the mention of that," it has been stated that in both the view of doubling the substitute (*sthāne-dvivacana*) and the view of double utterance (*dviḥ-prayoga*), the designation of the base (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) applies only to the entire aggregate. Consequently, what falls in the middle of that base is included by the mention of that base.

"Even so, does the state of being 'not joined with a consonant' (asaṃyogāditva) remain as it was? To this he says: "And the mention of the augment *suṭ* as being conditioned by conjunction (*saṃyogopadhagrahaṇaṃ ca*). Since the technical term *upadhā* is prescribed for the sound preceding the final vowel, it follows that "whatever falls between [the first consonant and] that [final vowel] is included by the mention of that [consonant]," provided that *suṭ* is not [already] joined [with the initial consonant]. If it is not so joined, for what purpose is the marker *ṭ* applied? To this he says: "The application of the marker *ṭ* is for the sake of *ām*."

If it were stated as "su-tu-stu-svañjām," then there would be the inclusion of the word *su* in forms such as *sura*, as well as the inclusion of any prefix (*upasarga*). Consequently, [the rule] would also apply in cases such as *surāṃ paricaṣṭe* and *parisurayati*.
[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs even when there is an intervention by a vowel (*aṭ*) or a semivowel (*yaṇ*). 6.1.136.

*Vyavāya* means intervention (*vyavadhāna*); by the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is implied that even in the absence of intervention, [the rule applies], whereas in its absence, there would be intervention alone. As in *saṃcaskaritha*: because of the statement that even the rule "*ṛto bhāradvājasya*" is intended to apply only when *suṭ* is not present, the augment *iṭ* is added. Regarding "first, the root," etc.: although under the view that "the root is first joined with its grammatical factor" (*sādhana*) this [rule] would certainly be unnecessary to commence, nevertheless, this very view is presented because it belongs to his own system and is logically consistent.

Another says: "The passage beginning with 'Why, then, is this said? should be read immediately after [that], and the section consisting of the objection ending with 'therefore, subsequently, there would be the repetition of the suffix aṅ' follows from that. He refutes this with the words "and because it is not a part" (*abhaktatvāt*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*). Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): it means "in the case of being a non-part. As for the phrase "this being so," etc. (*etasmistu sati*), and so forth.

But surely, on the basis of this very statement, even when the two [augment] *abhyāsas* have been applied, let the *suṭ* augment be placed before the *k* even if there is an intervention by that [vowel]; as for the *suṭ* which would apply at this stage (*saṃskṛ*), by what could it be prevented? It is said in reply: because this [rule] is commenced while that [other rule] has not yet taken effect, the latter is superseded by the former. Others, however, out of fear of this objection, consider the view of the Bhāṣyakāra himself to be superior. As for what was further stated—that there would be the contingency of *guṇa* substitution [by *ādguṇaḥ*]—this is not a fault; [End of excerpt]

In the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*, the term *upadeśe* (in the original enunciation) continues to apply. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt*. What follows from that? [The interpretation is: "In the case of a root beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādi*) that is not [originally] marked as such in its original enunciation (*apadeśe*), [the augment *suṭ* does not apply]. Thus, once *suṭ* has been applied, the rule will not operate. In the rule *guṇo'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*, the term *nityam* (always) also continues to apply. Where was it previously mentioned? In the rule *nityaṃ chandasi*. What follows from that? [The interpretation is: "There is always guna for that which begins with a conjunct consonant. Thus, once *suṭ* has been applied, the rule will not operate.
The prefix *sam* and the prefixes beginning with *upa* [i.e., *pari* and *upa*] are compounded with the root *kṛ* when it signifies adornment. || 6.1.137 ||
It is accepted that the prefix *sam-* [is used] in some cases even when it does not signify adornment; this is understood from the rule "saṃskṛtamaśnāti bhakṣāḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.15).
And [the suffix *ṭhak* is used] after the word *samavāya*. (Pāṇini 5.1.138)
In the examples, the *niṣṭhā* suffix denotes the state (*bhāva*); the same applies here in the case of the word *samuditam*.
The particle *upa* [is used] in the senses of effort, alteration, and ellipsis of a sentence. 6.1.139.

Regarding the passage beginning with *sataḥ*: when qualities are previously imparted to an object that has already acquired its existence (*labdhasattāka*), for what purpose is that further imparting of other qualities? He says: "for the sake of increase" (*ādhikyāya*). "Increase" means growth (*vṛddhi*). Or, "for the sake of maintaining the state of that which has grown. The meaning is: for the sake of avoiding the loss of that state endowed with growth. "Effort" (*samīhā*) means exertion (*ceṣṭā*). "Of a meaning not being understood" means by means of context, subject matter, and so forth. "Of the sentence" means of a portion of the sentence. The example is "fuel for water" (*edho dakasya*).

This is a copulative compound (*jātidvandva*). The genitive case is used by the rule *kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* ("after the root *kṛ*, [the genitive is used] in the sense of improvement"), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule *pratiyatnaprakathanopayogeṣu kṛñaḥ* ("after *kṛ* in the senses of improvement, detailed description, and employment"). In the phrase *upaskṛtaṃ bhuṅkte*, "upaskṛtam" is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*); the meaning is that he eats it prepared (*vikṛtam*). In the phrase *upaskṛtaṃ jalpati*, the meaning is that he prattles in such a way as to require a supplement (*sādhyāhāram*). Now, why was it not formulated thus: "*sampratibhyāṃ karotau bhūṣaṇasamavāyayoḥ, upātpratiyatnavaikṛtavākyādhyāhāreṣu ca*" (Pāṇini 1.3.42–43)? Ask the author of the Sūtras!
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *kṛtī* and *lū* to form agent nouns.

Regarding the phrase "kirati in the domain of cutting" (lavana-viṣaya): the status of *kṛ* as having cutting as its domain is mediated by its meaning; that is to say, it refers to that instance of *kṛ* which occurs in the sense of scattering when it pertains to the domain of cutting. Thus he says: "the meaning is that they cut after having scattered. However, if [scattering] were the direct object, the very act of cutting would be the meaning of *kṛ*.
As for the statement "the suffix *ṇamul* should be prescribed here": this is because the conditions for *ṇamul*, such as frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) and so forth, are absent.

"In the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) and with *prati*. This means when the sense of injury is the subject matter; it does not mean when it is the expressed meaning (*abhidheyā*). Rather, it is "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) that is the expressed meaning. He demonstrates this very point with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). In the example, the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter gender in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and the word *haṃ* expresses anger. The change to *ṣ* for the augment *suṭ* occurs only after *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*, but not after *prati*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after words denoting animals that do not move on feet (such as snakes), quadrupeds, birds, and tools for scratching.

"In that object" means not in the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*). Rather, *vikṣepa* (distraction) itself is the denoted meaning; thus he says: "the meaning is 'having drawn [it], he distracts [himself]'".
Regarding "joy, livelihood," and so forth: *harṣa* is delight; *jīvikā* is the means of preserving one's life; *kulāya* is a refuge.
Why, then, does the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occur only in the primary example (*udāharaṇa*) and not in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*)? To this he replies: "joy, livelihood," and so forth.
The word *kustumburu* is a synonym for *jāti*. 6.1.143.

Raising the objection—“Since the rule in the Sūtra is stated using the neuter gender and the plural number, should the augment *suṭ* apply only to the genus of fruits (*phalajāti*) and not to the genus of medicinal herbs (*auṣadhijāti*)?”—he says: “The indication in the Sūtra. The mention of the neuter gender is also an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the plural number.
The word *aparaspara* is used in the sense of continuous action.

Regarding the term *aparasparāḥ*: it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "others and others" (*apare ca pare ca*). Due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the word with fewer syllables is placed last. "Traveling as caravans" means traveling in the form of a caravan. "Constantly and without interruption" means that the movement upon this great path is never interrupted at any time. And this meaning is illuminated by the presence of the augment *suṭ*. As for the question "What is this?": [it refers to the following].

The question is raised: if it is stated that "the elision of *m* occurs by virtue of this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*)," then the form *satatam* would not be established, because the word *tata-* is mentioned in the sūtra with the suffix *-añ*. How so? Because no specific rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for the elision of *m* is observed. Alternatively, one might suppose that the irregular derivation itself, namely *sātatye*, serves as a general indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *m* of the prefix *sam-* is elided when followed by the word *tata-*. However, the questioner considers that in such a case, *santatam* would not be established, on the grounds that irregular derivations (*nipātana*) act as exceptions (*bādhaka*) to general rules. Thus arises the inquiry.

"By means of the entire [rule] with the option"—this is the intended meaning: by one who utters the word *sātatya*, which is established by the definition of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*), the definition of the ancient masters has been relied upon; therefore, by that [definition], the elision of the letter *m* is prescribed as being equal [to the preceding vowel]. And having done so, the elision of the letter *m* in words such as *avaśyam* when followed by kṛtya-suffixes and the like is also established. They recite that very definition of the ancient masters as "one should drop [the *m*]," etc.; the word "final" (*antya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the rule].

When a word ending in a *kṛtya* suffix follows the word *avaśyam*, one should drop its final letter; that is, one should effect its elision (*lopa*). By the rule *śe mucādīnām*, the augment *num* is added. "That which must necessarily be done" (*avaśyakāryam*) is the example. The genitive case is not used for the word *tum* out of fear of breaking the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*). One should drop the final letter of a word ending in the *tum* suffix when the words *kāma* or *manas* follow—such as *kartukāmaḥ* (desirous of doing) and *kartumanāḥ* (minded to do). They say that the *tum* suffix is also included here because it does not have a verbal root as its upapada.

One should elide the final letter of the word *sam* optionally (*vā*) when followed by the words *hita* and *taya*: *sahitam*, *saṃhitam*, *satatam*, *saṃtatam*. This is a *nañ*-compound (negative compound). One should also elide the final letter of the word *māṃsa*, where? In the verbal root *pac* (*pacati*). Under what conditions? When followed by the suffixes *yuṭ* or *ghañ*; that is to say, when *pac* occurs before *yuṭ* or *ghañ*. Examples: *māspacanam*, *māspākaḥ*. This is a compound with a genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*). They say that this elision of the *m* occurs in both *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) and in compounds. Now, as for whether the suffix *pyañ* occurs after the word *saṃtata* or not—namely, in the form *sāntatyam*—they say "it does."

*Goṣpada* [is used] in the sense of "measured by whether it has been traversed or not traversed. It is derived as that "in which cows (*gāvaḥ*) tread (*padyante*). By the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyām*, the suffix *gha* is applied in the locative sense; then, a compound is formed with the genitive case of the agent. [Examples include: *agoṣpadāny araṇyāni* ("forests where no hoofprints of cattle exist"). Now, since the word *goṣpada* is already included in the sūtra, why is this [additional statement] made? To this he says: "not traversed," and so forth. This mention of "not traversed" is made for a specific purpose, yet the word *goṣpada* cannot logically apply there [in the literal sense]; therefore, it is understood that *goṣpada* is an irregularly prescribed form (*nipātana*) for the meaning "not traversed."

"It is not for this purpose" refers to the mention of "not being practiced. How can there be accomplishment without that? To this he says: "Because of the negation of a cow's footprint. "It is true": he considers what was said regarding the negation of a cow's footprint to be true, but not that "it is not for this purpose. If that is true, then for what purpose is the mention of "not being practiced"? To this he says: "But where..."

For a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is a *tatpuruṣa* by its very nature, and it denotes a meaning similar to that of the subsequent member—as in *abrāhmaṇa*. Consequently, when the negative compound *agoṣpadam* (not a cow’s footprint) is formed from *na goṣpadam*, it would apply only where there is a possibility of the footprint being present, for only such a place is similar to a cow’s footprint; however, it would not apply where the presence of a footprint is absolutely impossible.

However, by virtue of the capacity of the term *asevita* (unfrequented) to function as a qualifier, it is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound; and such a compound can apply even in the case of absolute non-existence. Therefore, those forests where the existence of cows is absolutely impossible are designated by the word *asevita*. Consequently, the expression *agoṣpada* (cowless) applies there as well. He clarifies this absolute impossibility by saying, "those which are great forests. Regarding this, some say: the word *agoṣpada* should be employed only where cows are absolutely impossible, and not merely where they are impossible [in a relative sense].

Others, however, maintain that this applies without distinction. Nor is the inclusion of the term *asevita* (not previously used) redundant; for if it were absent, the rule would not apply in cases where [the usage] is absolutely impossible. Regarding the example *goṣpadapūram*: the suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule *varṣapramāṇa ūlopaścāsyānyatarasyām*. Now, one might object: "But *goṣpada* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*); its meaning is 'the footprint belonging to a cow,' and not a measure. To this he replies: "In this context, *goṣpada* is not employed for the sake of conveying its own primary meaning."

And likewise, one says, "It rained enough to fill a cow's footprint," even though there was no filling of a cow's footprint; similarly, one says, "It rained enough to soak a cloth," even though there was no soaking of a cloth.
The word *āspada* is used in the sense of a foundation or support. (Pāṇini 6.1.146)

Regarding the term *ātmayāpanāya*: sustaining the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is "sustaining the self" (*ātmayāpana*); the place for that purpose is "the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*). Regarding the term *āspada*: from the root *pad* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of a locus as before; its neuter gender is due to its being a refuge for the world, or else it is due to this specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), and *āpada* is an avyayībhāva compound.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *āścarya* when it is used in the sense of "impermanent. (Pāṇini 5.1.123)

If the term *āścarya* (wonder) were applied to that which is impermanent (*anitya*), would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to things such as a jar? To this he says: "By way of impermanence," and so forth. In the world, whatever is perceived as improper or unprecedented is pervaded by impermanence, specifically its occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*); therefore, impermanence becomes the objective domain [of wonder]. Thus, by means of that which has become the objective domain, the state of being wonderful—namely, the quality of being a cause for astonishment—is indicated. In the example, the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of impossibility (*anavaklṛpti*), according to the rule: "In the sense of impossibility and impatience (*amarṣa*), even when *kiṃ* is not present. This refers here to the impossibility of occurrence.

For one who is ill or slow of ear, eating and study at times and in places that are not distinct [from those prescribed] are seen to occur, which were never seen before; thus they become marvelous. Regarding the word *āścarya*: it is derived from the root *car* with the prefix *āṅ* according to the rule "after *car*, when *āṅ* follows, provided it does not mean 'to go'"; the meaning is "that which is to be performed as a wonder."
The word *avaskaraḥ* is used in the sense of excrement.

*Varcaska* means contemptible excrement (*varcas*). The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *kutsite*; the substitution of *s* for *r* occurs by the rule *so'padādau*. The mention of the suffix *kan* is so that [the term] might not be understood as "splendor" (*dīpti*), for the word *varcas* also functions in the sense of splendor. "Food-impurity" (*annamala*) refers to that which adheres to vessels and, having been scraped off with wood or other tools, is scattered for crows and the like; this is what is meant by "it is scattered" (*avakīryate*), meaning it is cast upon the ground. "The place also [is so called] because of its connection with that" refers to the place where the vessels are wiped clean.

And likewise Yājñavalkya says: "By one who has cleansed the refuse-heap and whose hand is not loose in expenditure. Another says: *purīṣa* is excrement and its place; *avakara* refers to the emission of semen by a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) into a woman, from which he becomes an *avakīrṇin*.
The word *apaskara* means a part of a chariot.
In this sutra, it is the third prefix; in the preceding one, it was the sixth.
The word *viṣkira* optionally becomes *vikira* when it refers to a bird.

Regarding the passage beginning with *viṣkirau vā*: the meaning is that by merely stating that the word *viṣkira* is irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when denoting a bird, the optional application of the suffix *suṅ* is established. Regarding the phrase beginning with *vikiragrahaṇam*: if that [second] mention of *vikira* were absent, this rule would serve only to provide an option for the word *vikira* ending in the suffix *kap* when it denotes a bird; thus, the usage of the word *vikira* elsewhere would not have been precluded. However, since the mention of *vikira* occurs again, it functions as intended.
According to the Bhāṣya, however, the sūtra is simply: *viṣkiraḥ śakunau vā*.
In a mantra, when the word *candra* follows, [the final vowel of] a short [word] is [lengthened].

The augment *suṭ* is applied. Previously, it was stated that *suṭ* is not a part of the word (*abhakta*) because of the mention of "prior to *ka*" (*kātpūrva*); however, in this case, being prior to *ka* is impossible, and since the characteristic of an augment (*āgamaliṅga*), namely *ṭit*-ness, is present, the intention is that *suṭ* is indeed stated to be an augment. When it occurs, according to the principle "in the case of a dual mention, the mention in the ablative case is stronger," it applies only to the word *candra*, as in "the sun and moon" (*sūryācandramasau*). This is a *dvandva* compound, with the form *ānaṅ* substituted by the rule "and in a *dvandva* of deities.
The phrase "the subsequent member," etc., refers to what is well-known within one's own school (*svanikāya*).
And *pratiṣkaśa* [is formed] from the root *kaś*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra yadyapi" and so forth: the sense is that there is no other purpose for the inclusion of the verbal root (*dhātu*) than [the one already stated].
Praskaṇva and Hariścandra are [names of] ṛṣis. 6.1.153.

Hariścandra is a royal sage (*rājarṣi*). Prakaṇva is a region. *Kaṇva* means evil; that from which evil has departed is thus called *prakaṇva*. *Haricandra* refers to one whose moon (*candra*) is golden (*hari*).
[The suffix *ini* is applied after the words] *maskara* and *maskarin* when referring respectively to a bamboo staff and a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). (Pāṇini 6.1.154)

Regarding the word *parivrājaka*, however, the suffix *ini* is also applied. Since the suffix *ini* would not otherwise apply due to the absence of the sense of possession (*matvartha*), it is therefore also introduced here as a nipātana (irregular formation). For a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) does not possess a *maskara* [in the sense of a "maker"], but rather possesses a *maskara* in the sense of a bamboo staff (*veṇu*); this is because he carries a staff. What follows from this? It is established that the form is derived from the word *maskara* with the suffix *ini*.

Even so, because the suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*) is prescribed in the sense of conjunction, one would have to say "a *maskarī* is one who possesses a staff" (*maskara-saṃyukta*). To prevent this from being a term that refers merely to any wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the word is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*). Alternatively, since no etymological derivation is evident here, it is not clearly an irregular formation; he shows this by saying "some [say]... [as follows]: "one whose nature is to carry" (*mākaraṇa-śīlaḥ*). This means "one whose nature is to prohibit. Regarding the phrase "because of censuring action" (*karma-apavāditvāt*): here, by the word "action" (*karman*), optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) are intended, not obligatory or occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*), for those must be performed even by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). As they say: [The passage continues with a citation: "By abandoning all actions, one becomes free from desire; by abandoning desire, one becomes free from suffering; by abandoning suffering, one attains immortality. (Mahābhārata 12.178.13) Thus, the prohibition of optional rites is what is meant here. Furthermore, the word "staff" (*maskara*) is used in the sense of "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*), based on the similarity of sound (*śabda-sārūpya*). For example, the word "lotus" (*ambuja*) is used in the sense of "water" (*ambu*) because of the similarity of sound. Or else, the word "staff" (*maskara*) is used in the sense of "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) because of the similarity of form (*rūpa-sārūpya*). For example, the word "elephant" (*gaja*) is used in the sense of "earth" (*gaja*) because of the similarity of form. Therefore, a "staff-bearer" (*maskarī*) is one whose nature is to prohibit—that is, one who censures action. Thus, the word "staff-bearer" (*maskarī*) is a designation for a mendicant who has renounced all action. It is not a designation for one who carries a physical staff. This is the view of some. Others, however, hold that the word "staff-bearer" (*maskarī*) is a designation for a mendicant who carries a physical staff. They say: "The word 'staff' (*maskara*) is derived from the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *nis*, meaning 'to make' or 'to create. Because he makes [the world] through his teaching, he is called a 'staff-bearer' (*maskarī*). But this is incorrect, because the suffix *ini* is not prescribed after the root *kṛ* preceded by *nis*. Therefore, the former view is correct. Thus, the word "staff-bearer" (*maskarī*) is a designation for a mendicant who has renounced all action. It is not a designation for one who carries a physical staff. This is the view of some. "One seeking liberation should not engage in optional (kāmya) or prohibited (niṣiddha) acts; one should perform the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites for the sake of averting transgression. One whose nature is to disparage or prohibit those actions is a "disparager of action" (karmāpavādī). However, the Paramahaṃsas disparage action in its entirety, saying, "Do not do it"; the meaning is that they should not be performed. [The suffix] *luṅ* is used here in the sense of an imperative (*karmani*).
In the city of Rājastunda, [the word] kāstīra [is used]. || 6.1.155 ||

Some maintain that *nagare* is in the nominative dual; however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is explained as being in the locative. Regarding *kātīram*, there is the elision of *kā* by the rule "and in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣadartha*)."
The word *kāraskara* denotes a tree. || 6.1.156 ||
"Only in the *Pāraskara-prabhṛtis* [is this recited]. This means that this particular sūtra is not studied [in other texts].
And the words beginning with *pāraskara* [form a compound] when they denote a proper name (saṃjñā). Pāṇini 6.1.157.

These are conventional (ruḍhi) words that must be derived in some way or another. One who performs the *pāraskara* [sacrifice] is called *pāraskara*; here, the suffix *ṭa* is applied by the rule "after *kṛ*, when denoting cause," and so forth. One who goes by chariot (*ratha*) is a *rathaṣyā*; here, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in *ā*, when no upasarga is present. The change to *ṣ* is also introduced here as an irregularity (*nipātana*); others, however, read the letter *sa* instead. From the root *kṛ* ("to do") in the sense of "what does he do?", the suffix *ḍu* is applied; there is elision of the final letter of *kim*, the augment *suṭ* is added, and thus *kiṣku* is formed. That which holds even a little (*kim api dhatte*) is *kiṣkindhā*.

As in the previous case, there is reduplication of *kim*, elision of the *m* of the former, and the addition of *suṭ*; furthermore, in both instances here, the substitution of *ṣ* is also prescribed by technical rule (*nipātana*). Thus, "he does that" (*tat karoti*) becomes *taskaraḥ*. For here, by the word *tat*, one refers to the well-known, censurable act of stealing.

Regarding *prātumpatau*: after this root *tupa* and *tumpa*, which mean "to injure," the augment *suṭ* is added when preceded by the word *pra*, provided that the meaning of the root has "cattle" (*go*) as its agent. Thus, in *prastumpati* (he injures cattle), the *suṭ* is present in the *tiṅ*-ending form expressing effort. Because the root is mentioned by its own name (*svaśabdena*), the augment also occurs when the root begins with that [suffix], as in *prastumpato gāvau* (the two cows are injuring) and *prastumpanti gāvaḥ* (the cows are injuring).

Regarding *citti-cittayoḥ*: from the root *citī* (meaning "to perceive"), there is the suffix *ktin*; alternatively, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) in the neuter gender. It is said: "Austerity (*tapas*) is called *prāya*, while resolve (*niścaya*) is called *citta*."
Austerity joined with firm resolve is known as expiation according to the Smṛtis.
A word has one unaccented syllable, with the exception of one [which may be accented]. 6.1.158.

Regarding the phrase *ekavarjam*: the meaning is "having excluded one. The suffix *ṇamul* is used here according to the rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca*. For in that context, the condition *parīpsāyām* (in cases of haste) is merely common. Here, if the word *padam* were used in the singular to denote a class (*jātāvekavacanam*), then by proximity, the word *eka* in the compound *ekavarjanam* would also refer specifically to a *pada*. Consequently, the meaning would be: "In a sentence, the words are unaccented, having excluded one word."

If the word *anudātta* (unaccented) is now understood in its worldly sense, then in common usage, when vowels possess qualities such as being unaccented, the consonants (*hal*) associated with them are also perceived as having those same properties because they are colored by them. Thus, one designates the entire word—consisting of the collection of vowels and *jhal*-consonants—as "unaccented" through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In this view, since there is no restrictive cause to determine which single [element] should be excluded, all words would be excluded in turn, and consequently, there would be no fixed rule for accents. Therefore, the term "word" (*pada*) refers to an individual instance (*vyakti*), and singularity is intended to be expressed.

Furthermore, since the word *anudātta* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*), referring to a specific vowel as defined by the rule "that which is low-pitched is *anudātta*," it is logical that only that [vowel] should be understood [by the term]. By the word *eka* ("single") as well, only a vowel is meant due to its proximity [to the preceding context]. How then can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between a word consisting of a collection of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*) and the word *anudātta*, which denotes only a vowel? It is because of the metaphorical treatment of the part and the whole as non-different (*abhedopacāra*), or because the word itself is *anudātta* since it ends in the suffix *ac* (as in *an-udāt-ta*). Thus, the word whose single vowel is *anudātta* is itself called *anudātta*.

If this is so, then even by the word *anudātta*, it is the *pada* itself that is primarily denoted by virtue of the absence of the quality (*guṇa*) of vowels; thus, when the single word [“one”] again requires something to be numbered, would not the *pada*—being the primary element—be what is obtained as the object to be numbered? It is replied: it has already been stated that singularity is intended with respect to the *pada*. In that context, the meaning “one *pada* becomes *anudātta* in one vowel, having excluded one *pada*” is not possible; therefore, by implication (*sāmarthya*), it is the vowel (*ac*) itself—which is subordinate—that is denoted by the word “one.”

Alternatively, the word *pada* may also be used by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to those vowels residing within it; in that case, since the status of being part of a *pada* is never absent from vowels, the mention of the word *pada* is solely for the purpose of intending singularity (*ekatva*). In any event, this is the intended meaning: "the vowels existing in a single *pada* become unaccented (*anudātta*), with the exception of one vowel. This being the case, if this were an independent rule (*lakṣaṇa*), it would have to be either a restriction (*niyama*)—meaning "with the exception of one vowel, the remainder becomes exclusively unaccented"—or a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

In that regard, concerning the first position: for those vowels (*ac*) for which an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent is prescribed by another rule, this [present rule] applies only to cases other than those, because there is no possibility of an absence of restriction (indeterminacy) in their case. Indeed, there is a possibility of such indeterminacy there, since it is impossible to pronounce a vowel that lacks an accent. Regarding the phrase "with the exception of one" (*ekavarjam*): the meaning is that whichever vowel has an acute or circumflex accent prescribed for it, that very one is to be excluded.

Furthermore, in cases such as *tataścatur*, there would be the undesirable consequence of four separate accents for the [suffix] *āgam* and so forth; in *āmalakīja*, there would be a simultaneous occurrence of four udātta accents: the udātta of the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the udātta of the word *ja* by the rule "a *kṛt*-suffix following a preverb, an agentive noun, or a subordinate word is udātta," the udātta of the first member of the compound by the rule "in a *je* suffix, the first syllable of *dīrgha*, *kāśa*, *tuṣa*, *bhrāṣṭra*, and *vaṭa* is udātta," and the udātta of the vowel preceding the final syllable in a polysyllabic word by the rule "the syllable preceding the final one in a polysyllabic word is udātta. Thus, there would be the simultaneous occurrence of a quartet of udātta accents.

Now, one might object: since the *kṛt-svara* (the accentuation of a *kṛt*-suffix) has not yet applied when this rule is being introduced, it will simply not occur because it is set aside by the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) in forms such as *dīrghakāśa*. Likewise, the initial acute in cases like *kuṭīja* has its own scope, while in cases like *upasaraja*, it will be superseded by the subsequent rule "the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word" (*antyātpūrvaṃ bahvacaḥ*). The relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) exists when there is a contradiction between two rules that yield the same result; "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*) is indeed nothing other than such a contradiction. Since neither of these two conditions exists in the case of accents, there would follow the undesirable consequence of their simultaneous application (*samāveśa*), just as occurs with the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *kṛt* and *kṛtya* suffixes. Even if a conflict were present, once the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the *ṅīṣ* suffix has been applied, even if the rule "the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic word [is acute]" subsequently applies, the previously established acute accent of the *ṅīṣ* would not be removed, resulting in an undesired outcome.

Furthermore, if the meaning were that whatever has the prescription of an acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita) accent is excluded and everything remaining is simply unaccented (anudātta), then both [rules]—"the word" (padam) and "with the exception of one" (ekavarjam)—would be redundant. One could simply state, "vowels are generally unaccented"; in cases where the initial vowel of a suffix is acute and so forth, the lack of anudātta would not occur precisely because those [other rules] would have sublated it. Therefore, because of the statement "the word with the exception of one," this is not an independent restriction.

Now, what is the purpose of this rule? If it were a mere injunction (*vidhi*), then in the case of those vowels for which an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent has not been prescribed by another rule, an injunction would be inappropriate because the grave (*anudātta*) accent would already be obtained as an alternative option (*pakṣe*). Therefore, the meaning must be that those vowels for which an acute or circumflex has been prescribed by another rule become grave when they occur in a single word, with the exception of one vowel.

It would not be known which one [of two rules] is to be excluded! Furthermore, even if the application were determined by the principles of "the later" (*para*) or "the permanent" (*nitya*), even so, there would be no determination by the "more specifically prescribed" (*atiśiṣṭa*). In the case of *aupagavatvam*, why would there be two cases of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the affix? Among those, if the non-acute (*anudātta*) status were being enjoined for one, for which [of the two] would it apply? Moreover, there would result the undesirable consequence that for vowels other than the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*), there would be no fixed rule. Thus, under this independent rule—whether as an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restriction (*niyama*)—what is desired is not established.

Now, if this were a governing rule (*adhikāra*), then upon its application in the rule "the final vowel of a word ending in *ghañ* preceded by *kṛ*, *ṛṣ*, or *ā* is acute," the following meaning would result: "In a word containing the letter *ā*, the final syllable of the word *karṣa* becomes acute; excluding that one [acute] syllable, the remaining vowels (*ac*) occurring in that word become grave (*anudātta*). Likewise elsewhere—in every instance where there is an application [of a governing rule], it serves to indicate the accent being prescribed therein.

Therefore, in cases such as *tavaicāntaśca yugapat* and *ubhe vanaspatyādiṣu yugapat*, there is the exclusion of both [rules]. In the case of *indrābṛhaspatī*, because the word *bṛhaspati* belongs to the *vanaspatyādi* group, it is doubly udātta; when it forms a *dvandva* with *indra* according to the rule *devatādvandve ca*, both [words] retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*). Thus, there is the exclusion of all three [accents], and consequently, there is no defect whatsoever regarding the accentuation prescribed in the sixth [chapter].

If [the rule] "anudāttaṃ padam" were the governing principle (adhikāra), then in rules located in other sections—such as "ādyudāttaśca," "samānodare śayita o codāttaḥ," and "asthidadhisakthyakṣṇāmanaṅudāttaḥ"—which prescribe specific accents, this [governing principle] would not apply; consequently, the remaining syllables in those cases would not be unaccented (anudātta). Furthermore, the phrase "ekavarjam" (with the exception of one) would be redundant. [Objection: Why not let "anudāttaṃ padam" alone be the governing principle? [Reply: Even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even the accents prescribed by those specific sūtras would become unaccented. [Reply continued: This is not so, because of the inherent force (sāmarthya) of those specific prescriptions.

Having thus determined that this is a *paribhāṣā* because other alternative views are possible, he says: "This is a *paribhāṣā*. And since this [rule] possesses a characteristic mark (*liṅga*), and the rule for accentuation (*svaravidhi*) is that characteristic mark, he says: "It concerns the domain of the rules for accentuation (*svaravidhiviṣaya*)."

Regarding the phrase *yatrānyaḥ*: "otherness" (*anyatvam*) is in relation to the *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel. The statement "*udāttaḥ svarito vā*" (whether acute or circumflex) implies that the exclusion of the *anudātta* from the *anudātta* category would be redundant; therefore, due to that contradiction, it must be understood as a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*) concerning the *udātta* or *svarita*. The sense is that this [rule] applies only when those two are being prescribed. By the word *upariṣṭāt*, it is shown that this [rule] forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rules prescribing accents. The question *kaḥ punaḥ* (but which? arises because no specific thing to be excluded is mentioned in the sūtra. The answer is *yasya svaro vidhīyate* (that for which an accent is prescribed).

Wherever this [rule] applies, the accent that is prescribed there is stated as "this one" (*asau*). For if even this were not excluded, the instruction regarding its accent would be purposeless. [The rule] "the accent of *śna* (the *śnā-pratyaya*) sublates the accent of the root," because the establishment [of precedence] by means of being "later-prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*) will be explained later. [The phrase] "the accent of *śna* [sublates] the accent of *ta*"—the word "sublates" (*bādhate*) is to be supplied here as well. The reason for this will also be stated in the passage: "But the accent of the *vikaraṇa*, though later-prescribed... where [it says] "the accent of *ta* [sublates] the accent of the root. As before, the word "sublates" is to be supplied; the state of being "later-prescribed" is the reason.

"Of the traditional scripture," and so forth. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). For it is stated that the purpose of this [rule] is the prevention of the simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of many acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) vowels produced by their respective specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Nor is this the only purpose; for even in those cases where no acute or circumflex is prescribed by anything—such as the vowels other than the first and last in multi-syllabic suffixes or verbal roots—the restriction to the grave (*anudātta*) accent depends upon this very rule.

Regarding the word *catvāraḥ*: by the rule *cateruran*, the word *catur* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Regarding *anaḍvāh*: by the rule *anasi vaheḥ kvib ab uścānasaḥ*, there is the suffix *kvip*; because [the root] belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). The word *anas-* ends in the suffix *asun* and is acutely accented on the first syllable; however, by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*, the final syllable of the verbal root is acutely accented due to the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member of the compound. Regarding *asthanī*: [the same applies].

The word *asthi* has its initial vowel udātta by the rule *asisañjibhyāṃ kyin*; the word *dadhi* has its initial vowel udātta by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya*. Here, *naṭ* is a designation for the neuter gender. It has been stated that when a specific accent is prescribed for a word, that [neuter] word is excluded. Since the accent is prescribed for all elements, including augments (*āgama*) and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of excluding them all without distinction; therefore, he says: "by the rules [regarding] the subsequent, the permanent, the internal, and the exceptional."

In that yoga-rule, for all of them who desire to apply an accent other than their own specific svarita—namely, the anudātta—a mutual contradiction arises; therefore, a systematic determination (*vyavasthā*) is established based on factors such as posteriority (*paratva*) and so forth, and by the principle of "that which is taught later" (*satiśiṣṭa*). The word "determination" (*vyavasthā*) is required [to complete the sense]. He explains this very point with the words "for he who... (*yo hi*). He brings the general statement down to the level of concrete examples with "for instance" (*tathā hi*). And this capacity of that which is taught later to sublate [the preceding] is established through logical reasoning (*nyāyataḥ*).

It has been stated that the suppression of the remaining [accents] (*śeṣanighāta*) is effected by this [rule], which forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rules for the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents; what follows from that? This [rule] applies at the final occurrence of either a general rule (*utsarga*) or an exception (*apavāda*). Thus, when this [rule] applies to the very last occurrence of a particular grammatical characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the preceding occurrence is sublated; for example, as in *aupagavatvam*.

For here, when the rule *ādyadāttaśca* is applied repeatedly to each suffix, this [present rule] effects the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) when it applies to the suffix *tvap*. If a later-accented (*satiśiṣṭa*) accent were the sublater, then the accent of the *vikaraṇa* would also necessarily become the sublater of the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*. To this he says: "The accent of the *vikaraṇa* [does not sublate], because of *ti*. He thinks as follows: the fact that [Pāṇini] teaches the unaccented nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned principle.

Otherwise, even though *tās* is prescribed in the state [of the verbal root] ending in *l*, nevertheless, because it depends upon the presence of the *l*-suffixes (*lakāra*), and since the internal substitutes for *l* (*lādeśa*) are applied first, *tās* would follow later; thus, its accent being *satiśiṣṭa* (later-arisen), it would be established by the *śeṣanighāta* (the non-accentuation of the remainder) alone, making that [specific rule] redundant. "From the accent of the case-ending" (*vibhaktisvarāt*): this is a statement [providing an exception] when the accent of the case-ending would otherwise apply due to its being *satiśiṣṭa*. "By the accent of the negative particle" (*nañsvareṇa*): by that which is prescribed as the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the rule "In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, [the first member retains its accent] when meaning 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*)," etc.

"From the accent caused by the case-ending" means: from that accent which belongs to that whose cause is the case-ending. Regarding the phrase "For in the sentence," etc.: the word *devadatta* is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule for the name-accents (*āmantrita-svara*). *Gām* is acute on the first syllable; this is the accent of the suffix *ḍo* after the root *gam*. The substitution of *ā* [for *o*] in *gām* by the rule "oto'mśasoḥ" is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), and by the rule "the single substitute is acute when the other is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*), it becomes acute. As for *abhi*, since it is excluded from the rules "particles are acute on the first syllable" (*nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*) and "prepositions, with the exception of *abhi*" (*upasargāścābhivarjam*), it takes the final acute by the rule "phiṣ" (*phiṣityanenāntodāttatvam*).

*Phiṣ* is the technical term for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) according to the ancient teachers. The prefix *āṅ* is acute on its first syllable by virtue of the accentuation rule for prepositions (*upasarga*). The suffix *loṭ* [applied] to the root *aj* results in [the form] *aja*; it is followed by the elision [of the preceding *tiṅ*] because of the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. The word *śukla* is acute on its final syllable by virtue of the accentuation rule for nominal stems. By the *ṭāp* suffix and the case-ending, the single substitute [for the two vowels] is acute by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*. Thus, because of the mention of the "word" (*pada*), the accent remains distinct within the sentence.

But surely, if the *śeṣanighāta* (the low-pitched accent for the remainder) were to apply even within a sentence, then—since the determinants such as the *satiśiṣṭasvara* (the accent remaining when others have been elided) would be impossible there—it could not be known which single [syllable] should be excluded? True; because no specific distinction is perceived, the exclusion will occur by way of alternation (*paryāyeṇa*).

If, then, the mention of the word *pada* is made, this being the case, as long as the designation *pada* has not yet occurred, there should be no occurrence of the *śeṣanighāta* (the low-pitched accent for the remainder); and consequently, in the example *kauvalam*, meaning "a modification of *kuvalī*," the suffix *añ* [prescribed by] *anudāttādeśca* would not apply. For this word *kuvala* is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) due to its inclusion in the *grāmādi* group; and even when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group, it does not lose its status as *ādyudātta* because the designation *pada* has not yet been established? To this, he says: "And for the sake of defining the limit."

What is intended here is a secondary (gauṇa) designation of "word" (pada), which will receive the technical name *pada* rather than a primary one; for otherwise, since the word *pada* is already under discussion (*padādhikāra*), there would be no reason to mention *pada* again. Furthermore, it has been stated that the elision of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*) occurs by combining with the rules governing the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents; at that stage, the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) is already established in instances such as *yuṣmad-asmadoḥ ṅasi* and *ṅayi ca*, and not during the subsequent application of rules like *dhātoḥ* after the initial teaching (*upadeśa*) of verbal roots and so forth.

And for this reason, since the word *pada* has become one with those [phonemes], its function will apply even to a single part thereof. If this is so, then wherever there is the presence of this [word *pada*], that is a *pada*; and elsewhere, being deficient, it is not present as a functional unit (*kāryitva*), and thus the remaining [phonemes] therein will be unaccented (*anudātta*). Is there, then, no purpose in the mention of *pada* for the sake of excluding the sentence (*vākya*)? It is said: [there is].

If the term *pada* were not used, and it were stated that "the final syllable of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is acute and the remainder is grave," it would be understood that only that which remains of the verbal root itself is grave. This would also apply in cases such as "and [the first syllable] is acute" (*ādyudāttaśca*). Consequently, the accentuation of the root and the suffix would remain distinct. Therefore, the mention of the word *pada* is for the purpose of ensuring that all syllables belonging to a single word (*ekapada*) are grave.

It effects the cessation of the governing influence (*adhikāra*) of the word *pada*. This mention of the word *pada* serves a secondary purpose (*gauṇārtha*), as it causes the cessation of the governing influence of the primary word *pada*. What is established by this? To that he says: "By that" (*tena*). He also shows an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this meaning: "and the word *garbhiṇī*. In the word *garbhiṇī*, the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) because "she has a fetus" (*garbho 'syā asti*), followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. The word *garbha* belongs to the class beginning with *grāma*.

In this regard, if the state of being *anudātta* (unaccented) occurs for the suffix *ini* at the very same time as the rule for its *udātta* accent is applied, then—since the word *garbhiṇī* would begin with an *anudātta* vowel—the suffix *āñ* would be applicable by the rule "after a word beginning with *anudātta*" (*anudāttādeḥ*). Consequently, its inclusion in the *bhikṣādi* group is justified for the purpose of overriding that [application of *āñ*]. On the other hand, if the state of being *anudātta* were to apply to the remaining portion of the word only after the designation of the word (*pada-saṃjñā*) has occurred, then the word *garbhiṇī* would be *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). In that case, it would not need to be listed among the *bhikṣādi* words for the purpose of overriding the suffix *āñ*.

The words *kuvala* and *garbha* have their initial syllables accented (*ādyudātta*). In that regard, the very same method has already been stated; therefore, it must be accepted for the sake of establishing the suffix *añ* after the word *kuvala*. Furthermore, the word *garbhiṇī* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this rule]. This is the intended meaning. Here, the following objection is raised: "Even if this [rule] is unified with the rules for acute and circumflex accents, if it is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), it would apply only to those cases where no accent has been prescribed; if it is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*), it would apply only to those cases where an accent has been prescribed. Thus, the previously mentioned defect remains exactly as it was? It is replied:

It has been stated that by the mention of the word "pada," all [suffixes] included within a single *pada* are *anudātta*. Therefore, this rule will proceed in such a way as to be appropriate—either as a positive injunction (*vidhi*), as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), or as both. Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.159: *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ*. (The final syllable of a *ghan* suffix following a root ending in *karṣ* or a letter of the *āt* group is *udātta*.)

Because it possesses *āt*, it is called *ātvān*; by the rule "tasau matvarthe," it receives the designation *bha*. The compound *karṣaścātvāṃśca* is a collective dvandva. Regarding the phrase "an irregular indication": the intention is that this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), and not an indication of a form ending in the suffix *ghañ*. Now, what is the purpose of indicating the possessive suffix *matup*, given that since there is no *ghañ* following an *ā* anywhere, the reference will necessarily be to that which possesses it by virtue of the context? It is said in reply:

By the rule "the root ending in ā is [replaced]," the element *ghañ*-attracted would be qualified. In that case, when the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) is understood, because immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is impossible, the prescription would be qualified as "that which is prescribed after a base ending in long ā. Consequently, it would apply only in cases such as *dāya*, but not in cases such as *pāka*; however, because of the mention of *matup* (in the commentary), it occurs everywhere. It is desired that even a derivative form (*lākṣaṇika*) ending in ā be included, because words such as *kāmapā* and *apāmārga* are read among the *vṛṣādi* group.
Although the result is established by the rule "of the final letter" (*alo'ntyasya*), the inclusion of the word "final" (*anta*) is for the sake of subsequent rules.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *uñcha* and others. 6.1.160.

*Uchi-ucche*, *mleccha* in the sense of an indistinct sound; *jaji* in the sense of battle—here the absence of *kutva* (the substitution of *ja* for *ji*) is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*); *jalpa* in the sense of distinct speech; *vyadha* in the sense of striking. From *vyadh* and *jap* with the suffix *ap* when there is no prefix, we have *vadha*. In the rule "and from *han*, *vadha*" (*hanaśca vadhaḥ*), the suffix *ap* is applied. "A particular time" refers to the *Kṛta*, *Tretā*, and so forth. From *ghṛ* and *gṝ* in the sense of swallowing, with the suffix *ap* according to the rule "*ṛdorap*". By the word "poison" (*viṣa*), he demonstrates the specific usage of the term "corruptible" (*dūṣya*).

The roots are: *vida* in the sense of "knowing," *ovijī* in the sense of "fear" and "trembling," *veṣṭa* in the sense of "encircling," *bandha* in the sense of "binding," *ṣṭuñ* in the sense of "praising," *yu* in the sense of "mixing," and *dru* in the sense of "going.

This [list] is for the purpose of including [roots] preceded by prefixes (*upasarga*), because for simple roots ending in *kvip*, the accent is already established by the accent of the root itself. Regarding *pariṣṭud*: since it belongs to the *sampadādi* group, *kvip* is applied; thus, there is a prepositional compound (*prādisamāsa*). The cerebralization (*ṣatva*) occurs by the rule "after a preceding word" (*pūrvapadāt*). When the original accent of the indeclinable as the prior member would apply, the final syllable is instead acute (*antodātta*). However, when *kvip* is added after a root accompanied by an object (an *upapada*), the accent is correctly established by the accent of the primary suffix (*kṛtsvara*).

"Except in the case of *madhyodātta* (where the middle syllable is acute). For that [word] is derived from the root *vṛt* "to turn" with the suffix *ini*. [The root] *dṝ* means "tearing. Regarding *sāmbatāpa*: *sāmba* [is used] when there is censure of the action; *sāmba bhikṣate* ("Samba begs")—begging together with one's mother is censurable. This is an exception to the rule concerning the original accent of the first member in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. *Tāpa* refers to the affliction of robbers (*dasyu*). When robbers inflict affliction upon righteous people, that is censurable. Although the rule *karṣātvataḥ* would have already established this, the statement is made to ensure that the initial syllable is acute in cases other than the censure of the action.

Regarding *uttama* and *śaśvattama*: these two are formed with the suffix *-tamap*. When there is a desire to express excellence (*prakarpa*) of a substance (*dravya*), the suffix *-ām* is absent; since [the suffix] would otherwise be unaccented due to its being marked with *p*, this specific reading is provided. Regarding *sarvatra*: it applies both in the sense of censuring an action (*bhāvagarhā*) and elsewhere. Others say it applies in both Vedic (*chandas*) and common (*bhāṣā*) usage. *Bhakṣa* (in eating) belongs to the *curādi* group; *mantha* (in stirring); *bhuja* (in crookedness); and *diha* (in accumulation). Regarding the rule "for roots ending in *i* that do not have *ṇic*": for those who claim this statement is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*), the purpose for including the word *bhakṣa* in the list must be sought.
And [the substitution of *y* occurs] for an unaccented vowel where there is the elision of an acute accent.

The word *kumāra* has its acute accent on the final syllable by the rule *phiṣ*. One should understand that elsewhere as well, the final acute accent of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established by this very same principle. The word *pathin* has its acute accent on the final syllable because it ends in the suffix *-in* according to the rule *patestha ca*. The words *kumuda* and others have their acute accents on the final syllable: the word *kumuda* ends in the suffix *ka* because it belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*; the word *naḍa* is an unanalyzed (irregular) formation; [the word *naḍa*] is derived from the root *vi* in the sense of "motion" and so forth, with the suffix *asac* and the augment *tuṭ*; and *vetasa* has its acute accent on the final syllable by virtue of the *cit* accent.

Regarding the word *prāsaṅgya*: it is called *prāsaṅga* because it is attached (*prāsajyate*), formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object; then, by the rule "that which carries it" (*tadvahati*) and "the suffix *yat* after *pra* and before *hit*" (*prāgghitādyat*), the suffix *yat* is applied. The statement "this is not so" refers to the fact that the acute accent (*udātta*) is elided. This is a prohibition of that [elision]. How is it that this is not so? He says: "For in the case of a circumflex (*svarita*)," etc. It was stated previously that "even before the designation of a word (*padasaṃjñā*), the suppression of the remaining accents (*śeṣanighāta*) will occur at the very same time as the prescription of the accent. Therefore, from what could there be an elision of the acute accent? The meaning is: from nothing whatsoever.

Regarding the passage beginning with *tadetad* and so on: since there is no possibility of anything else to be excluded by the mention of *anudātta* (unaccented) in this manner, therefore this mention of *anudātta* is for the sake of [specifying] that the first syllable is unaccented. Now, if the mention of *anudātta* were not present, to what would [the accentuation] belong? To this he says: *anta* (the end). For example, in *mā hi dhukṣātām*: from the root *duh* with the prohibitive particle *māṅ*, there is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the Ātmanepada; *ātām* and *āthām* are the suffixes; and for the *cli* (aorist marker), there is *ksa*. By the rule *adupadeśāt*, the *lasārvadhātuka* (suffixes of the verbal base) are unaccented; the suffix *ksa* is accented on its final syllable by the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*); and by the rule *ksasyāci*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*.

The employment of *māṅ* is for the purpose of preventing the arrival of the augment *aṭ*; for if *aṭ* were present, the word would become acute-accented on its first syllable. The employment of the word *hi* is for the purpose of prohibiting the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule "hi ca. Here, if the mention of *anudātta* (unaccented) were not made, the acute accent would fall on the second vowel of *ātām* and *āthām*, because of the governing context of "the end" (*anta*); but since this [mention of *anudātta*] exists, it occurs on the first vowel. This must be addressed: when it is stated "where there is the elision of an acute accent" (*yatrodāttalopaḥ*), how could there be a possibility of it applying to the final [vowel], since that is not the cause of the elision of the acute accent? It is said in reply:

In that case, it would not apply even to the first [vowel], because it is not the cause for the elision of the unaccented vowel (*anudātta*), since the rule "after *kṣa*, before a vowel-initial suffix" (*ksasyāci*) prescribes it only before a suffix beginning with a vowel. Therefore, if the meaning of the sūtra were "where there is an elision of an accented vowel, the unaccented vowel connected to that [elided vowel] becomes accented," then—due to the governing context of "final" (*anta*)—there would be the undesirable consequence of it applying to the final [vowel]. However, if the meaning of the sūtra is taken as "regardless of whether it is a cause [for the elision], wherever there is an elision of an accented vowel when followed by an unaccented one, that [unaccented vowel] becomes accented," then there is no such consequence for the final [vowel].

Regarding *bhṛgavaḥ*: by the rule *atribhṛgukutsa-* etc., there is elision (*luk*) when [the patronymic suffix] refers to many. In that context, "many" is taken as the meaning, not as the plural number itself. Regarding *vaidī*: from a word ending in *yañ* derived from *vid*, [the feminine suffix] *ṅīn* is applied by the rule *śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*.
The suffix *cita* [is applied after a word denoting a measure when it signifies a heap]. 6.1.163.

Regarding *bhaṅgura*: the substitution of *k* (kutva) occurs by the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ. Regarding *kuṇḍinaḥ*: from the word *kuṇkaḍa*, the possessive suffix *ini* is added; in the feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in the word *kuṇḍinī*, which is udātta on the middle syllable. The descendants of many *kuṇḍinīs* [are expressed as follows]: the suffix *yañ* from the *garga*-class is elided (*luk*) when denoting many, and the remaining portion undergoes the substitution of *kuṇḍina*.

Regarding the phrase "in a *cita* suffix": one might object that here there is no mention of the term "*cita*" as a suffix, since [the rule] would apply even to [suffixes] beginning with *kuṅ*, *kaḍi*, and *na*. Therefore, the meaning here is this: where a *cita* suffix occurs, the operation is intended for the entire complex. But how is this obtained? This genitive case in "of a *cita*" (*citaḥ*) refers to a constituent part, not to the recipient of the grammatical operation; thus, the complex which is related to the *cita* constituent is the recipient of the operation.

Alternatively: "citaḥ" means "that which has *cit*," where the suffix *ac* is applied because the group beginning with *arśas-* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*; the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. Thus, the meaning is "of the aggregate possessing *cit*. And here the evidence is the addition of the marker *CIT* after *ak-*; otherwise, since it would consist of only one vowel (*ekāc*), that marker would be purposeless. The status of possessing *cit* for *kuṇḍinaja-* and others is established through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
[The elision of the final vowel and consonant of] a taddhita suffix [is optional]. 6.1.164.

*Kauñjāyanāḥ*: these are the many descendants of Kuñja. [The suffix] *cphañ* is applied by the rule *gotre kuñjādibhyaś cphañ*; then, by the rule *vrātacphañor astriyām*, the suffix *ñya* is substituted; [the resulting forms] *kauñjāyanya-* and so on are *tadrāja* (royal/tribal) suffixes according to the rule *ñyādayas tadrājāḥ*; and in the plural, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule *tadrājasya bahuṣu*. [Question: "For what purpose [is this rule stated]? [Answer: This is a question implying that the result is already established by the preceding rule. [Explanation: The letter *ca* in the rule *vrātacphañor astriyām* has its purpose fulfilled as a qualifier for that specific context. The letter *ñ* is also for the sake of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening). If that [letter *ñ*] were not present, then because of its higher status (*paratvāt*), the accentuation would be determined by the *ñit-svara* (the acute accent on the first syllable of a stem ending in *ñ*).
The suffix *jas* is substituted for the case endings of the three [feminine] numerals.

The plural number, which belongs to the meaning, is superimposed upon the word, and thus there is an indication by means of the plural form. Regarding the word *tisraḥ*: in place of the word *tri*, which is oxytone (acute-accented on the final syllable), the substitute *tisṛ* is applied; because it possesses the status of the original base (*sthānivadbhāva*), it is also oxytone. By the rule "sup and pit [suffixes] are anudātta," the suffix *jas* is anudātta. There, when followed by a vowel (*aci*), the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" applies. Why is "*jasaḥ*" mentioned? Consider the word *tisṛkā*; here the suffix *ka* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*), and the substitute *tisṛ* is applied by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name. [Objection: In this case, the accent of the *nit* suffix will be the sublater. [Response: True. However, since that [substitution] is not taught in the context of the *jasa* suffix, the present rule is necessary for the sake of establishing the accent. Furthermore, if the word *tisṛkā* were formed with the suffix *kan* in the sense of "one who possesses three" (*bahuvrīhi*), then the accent would be governed by the rule "the first syllable of a *bahuvrīhi* is udātta," and the accent of the *nit* suffix would not apply. Therefore, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Alternatively, one might argue that even if the accent of the *nit* suffix were to apply, it would still be anudātta because of the rule "sup and pit [suffixes] are anudātta. Thus, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" would be useless. To this we reply: the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in cases other than *jas*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛkā*, where the suffix *kan* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or rather, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛbhiḥ*, where the suffix *ṅīp* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or again, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *śas*.
