For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛḥ*, where the suffix *śas* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or yet again, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *ām*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṝṇām*, where the suffix *ām* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or finally, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *ṅasi*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛbhyaḥ*, where the suffix *ṅasi* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Thus, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is established as being purposeful. Now, regarding the word *tisṛkā*: if it is derived from *tisṛ* with the suffix *ka* in the sense of "one who possesses three" (*bahuvrīhi*), then the accent would be governed by the rule "the first syllable of a *bahuvrīhi* is udātta," and the accent of the *nit* suffix would not apply. Therefore, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Alternatively, one might argue that even if the accent of the *nit* suffix were to apply, it would still be anudātta because of the rule "sup and pit [suffixes] are anudātta. Thus, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" would be useless. To this we reply: the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in cases other than *jas*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛkā*, where the suffix *kan* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or rather, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛbhiḥ*, where the suffix *ṅīp* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or again, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *śas*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṛḥ*, where the suffix *śas* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or yet again, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *ām*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in the case of *tisṝṇām*, where the suffix *ām* follows. But since the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" is superseded by the rule "the substitution of *tisṛ* occurs before the suffix *kan* when it is a name," the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is indeed meaningful. Or finally, the mention of "*jasaḥ*" is for the purpose of excluding the application of the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" in the case of the suffix *ṅasi*. For if it were not so, the rule "for *ṛt*, *ra*" would apply even in

The accent of *tisṛ* is not commenced when another [subsequent] vowel has not yet been reached; for just as it subverts the rule "the endings *suP* and *pit* are unaccented," so too would it subvert the accent of the *nit* [marker]. This is not a fault. The subversion will apply to that [rule] by the principle "when [a new rule] is commenced, it subverts that which was not already applicable. However, the accent of *tisṛ* is not commenced while the rule "the endings *suP* and *pit* are unaccented" is still not applicable; for even in the case of *tisṛkā*, since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the suffix *ṭāp* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the accent of the *pit* [suffix] would [otherwise] apply.

Alternatively, according to the principle that "exceptions in the middle set aside preceding rules," the accent on *tisṛ* will set aside only the rule "anudāttau suppitau" and not the *nit*-accent; for since [the former] applies to the domain of the plural number, it does not apply to the dual or singular. However, in the case of the *śas* ending, the accent must indeed occur by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt."

All other case endings beginning with *hal*, such as the accusative and so forth, would have to be subject to the accentuation prescribed by the rules "ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ" and "jhalyupottamam"; therefore, even without the explicit mention of *jas*, the accent would apply only to *jas*. To this he replies: "The mention of *jas* is for the sake of [the form] compounded with another. Thus, even in a compound, the *jas* following the word *tisṛ* will be subject to that accent.

Regarding *atisrāvi*: here, by the rule "the final syllable is udātta when *ati* is followed by a non-ṛt suffix," the resulting udāttatva of the suffix would set aside the udāttatva of the case-ending that would otherwise apply by the statement "it should be stated that [this applies] when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) after *ati*. However, because of the inclusion of *jas*, the *svarita* occurs by the rule "after a *yaṇ* that follows an udātta or a *svarita*. But in the case of *atisras* (nominative plural), the udāttatva of *jas* indeed occurs by this very rule.
The [substitute] *śas* is applied after the word *catur*.

Because it functions as a mere imitation (*anukaraṇa*), it lacks referential meaning (*arthaparatva*); therefore, the singular number is used. Here, in the case of *catasraḥ paśya*, once the substitution of *catasr-* has been applied, this accent would apply by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). To this, he says: "the substitution of *catasr-*. Since the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is already established through the status of the original element, the explicit mention (*nipātana*) of the initial acute accent is for the purpose of overriding this [other] accent. This is the intention.

In that case, just as the accent of the irregular formation (*nipātana-svara*) subverts the accent of the suffix *śas*, so too would it subvert this accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*) prescribed by the rule "after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the suffix] beginning with a consonant" (P. 6.1.173)—as in the word *catasṛṇām*? This is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*). By the fact that he employs the term "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi*) in the rule "after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the suffix] beginning with a consonant," he indicates: "the accent of the irregular formation does not subvert the accent of the case-ending."

For that [suffix] should not be applied there; how so? Because all [stems] fall under the scope of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), the dual (*dvivacana*) and singular (*ekavacana*) endings are not possible. Nor is their occurrence possible when [the stem] is compounded, because one must rely on the specific qualification as prescribed. In that case, first of all, for the six [stems], there must be elision (*luk*) of *jaś* and *śas*. All other case-endings (*vibhakti*) beginning with *hal* [consonants] apply. Furthermore, even for the word *strī*, it should not occur in the *jas* [plural nominative].

Because of the governing rule *asarvanāmasthānam*, [the accentuation] must apply to the *śas* [ending] by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*; the others are those beginning with consonants (*hal*). In the word *tisṛ* as well, [the accentuation] must apply to the *jas* ending by the rule *tisṛbhyo jasaḥ*, and also to the *śas* ending by the rule *udāttayaṇo halapūrvāt*; the others are those beginning with consonants. In the word *catur* as well, there is a prohibition regarding the *jas* ending because it is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*; for the *śas* ending, only this [rule] *caturaḥ śasi* applies; the others, however, are those beginning with consonants.

This inclusion of the term "beginning with *hal*" was made precisely so that [the rule] would not apply in the case of *catasraḥ paśya*; for if the accent of the case-ending were to be superseded by the accent of the irregular formation (*nipātana-svara*), the mention of "beginning with *hal*" would be purposeless.

In the case of *catasraḥ paśya*, since the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) is already precluded by the accent of the enclitic particle (*nipātanasvara*), there would be no occasion for its application; so what is the purpose of including the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*)? Its inclusion serves to indicate that the accent of the case-ending is stronger [than the accent of the enclitic], and thus the accent of the case-ending is established in the form *catasṛṇām*. Regarding the phrase "and of the *yaṇ* substitute": this refers to the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* according to the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ*, which is applied after this accent because it is subsequent [in the order of rules].

This is what is meant: when the substitution (*ādeśa*) is made due to its being "para" (subsequent), it does not apply to the vowel *ṛ*, nor does it apply to the vowel *a* of the word *tas*; this is because of the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor is there a prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule in the case of vowel operations (*svaravidhi*), because of the statement: "In the case of vowel changes, long vowels, and the elision of *y*, only an elided substitute (*lopajādeśa*) is not treated as the original."
A case ending beginning with the third [case] that has a single udātta accent is unaccented (anudātta).

The mention of *su* refers to the seventh case plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*), not the nominative singular (*prathama-ekavacana*), as is clear from the commentary. The purpose [of this distinction] will be explained later. Regarding *pāta*: the suffix *śatṛ* is substituted for the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *pā*. Regarding *rājñā*: if the word *sau* were not present, the meaning would be that "the third case and subsequent case endings following a monosyllabic (*ekāc*) [stem] become acute"; and indeed, once the elision of *a* (*allopa*) has been performed, this [stem *rājñ-*] is monosyllabic. But one might object: should we understand the rule as qualifying the prescribed [suffix], such that it means "the third case and subsequent [suffixes] which are prescribed after a monosyllabic [stem]"? No.

Because there is no evidence [for such an interpretation]; for it is the locative plural that is being taken. However, in the case of the nominative singular, once the substitution of *tvā* has been applied by the rule "tvāhau sau," the word *yuṣmad* becomes monosyllabic (*ekāc*). Then, when the remaining portion is elided, because it ends in the vowel *a*, the prohibition "sāvavarṇa" will apply. Therefore, one must consider what the reason is for not including the nominative singular here.
In an optional compound that is not necessarily permanent, the acute accent may optionally be placed on the final syllable of the second member provided that it is oxytone.

"The word *nitya* is marked with the *svarita* accent" means that its *svarita* quality is applied. In this context, the *svarita* is specified as a functional property (*guṇa*). To the question "What happens when there is the *svarita*? he says: "by that" (*tena*). This meaning has also been explained under the rule *svaritenādhikāraḥ*: "That which is the governing scope (*adhikāra*) here is to be understood by the mark of the *svarita*. Consequently, the compound prescribed under the governing scope of *nitya* is prohibited here. [The example] *avāca* is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). This is a *tatpuruṣa*.

It is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Therefore, by the rule *nañ-subhyām*, the final syllable does not become udātta; rather, the meaning is that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable preceding member prevails. However, the reading is generally *suvācā* and *sutvacā*. In that case, it should be explained that this is merely shown as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), for there is no actual occasion (*prasaṅga*) here; because a *prādi*-compound is necessarily a *nityasamāsa*.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *uttarapada* (subsequent member), given that one could understand the locative case in *anityasamāse* as a locative of location—meaning "the third-case ending and those following it which follow a monosyllabic word that is acutely accented on the final syllable when situated within an optional compound"? And if [the rule] applies only to the subsequent member, he says: "The inclusion of *uttarapada*... The intention is this: it might be understood as a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*), and consequently, because the compound would be the locus, its own status as a monosyllable and its acute accent on the final syllable would become the qualifying conditions.
[Examples: *agnicitā*, *somasutā*. [These are formed with] *kvip* by the rules *agnau ceḥ* and *some suñaḥ*.
Regarding what was stated, "the word *nitya* is intended in its own sense," he states its purpose: "But he who... and so forth.
In the Vedic language, the case endings other than those called *asarvanāmasthāna* do not cause the substitution of the long vowel in the word *añc*.

Regarding *dadhīca*: [the derivation is as follows: from the root *dadhyañc*, the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvig... etc.; there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*); the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "acaḥ"; and lengthening occurs by the rule "cau". The phrase "also for the sake of including *śas*" means that the mention of *śas* and so forth was not made [in the rule] so that [the augment *suṭ*] would not apply to the neuter form in the *śas* case-ending, but would apply when *suṭ* is present.
The acute accent (*udātta*) is placed on the vowel following the final *ū*, *ṛ*, or *ī* of a word that begins with *am*, *pād*, *ādi*, *ap*, *pum*, *raih*, or *dyu*.

Regarding *praṣṭhauhaḥ*: the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rules "in the Veda, after *sah*" and "after *vah*. When *ūṭh* is substituted for *vāh*, the rule "vṛddhi is substituted for [the final vowel] before *eti*, *edhati*, and *ūṭh*" applies, resulting in vṛddhi.

As for the phrase "the mention of *upadhā* with respect to *ūṭh*": the meaning is that the *ūṭh* which constitutes the *upadhā* (penultimate) is taken, not the final one. Since the rule would otherwise have prescribed the substitution of the final letter due to the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), this statement is made as an exception.

Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from that which has the udātta accent on the final syllable" (*antodāttāt*), [the substitution] does not occur in the case of an *anvādeśa*. For this very reason, it also does not occur by the rule "sāvekācaḥ. If it were to occur, the governing rule concerning the final udātta would be rendered useless here. Now, one might object: if [the substitution] were to apply in "yadi ime nānuśaso abhyavarṣat," then its purpose would be to prevent it from occurring in the *anvādeśa* of "śas"; however, this is already established by the governing rule "ekācaḥ" alone. Furthermore, forms such as *tadasmai*, *tathya*, *tadasya priyam*, *preṇā*, and *tadeṣām* are recited with all syllables unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).

The items beginning with *pada* and ending with *niḥ* are understood [to be included]. They are specified in the rule *padannomās*; however, because the term *ekācaḥ* (monosyllabic) is understood to carry over there, those [forms] following *niḥ* are not included. But when they become monosyllabic after the elision (*lopa*) has taken place, then the acute accent of the case-ending is established by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent resulting from the removal of an acute accent). Furthermore, those substitutes (*ādeśas*) which are prescribed in place of words that are originally acute on the first syllable are themselves specifically prescribed (*nipātyante*) as being acute on the final syllable in those instances. This very point should be seen as stated in the *Vṛtti* as well. Regarding *āsanī*: this is the substitute *āsana* for the word *āsya*. In those cases where they are monosyllabic, their inclusion is for the sake of the suffix *śas*.
[The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] after an *aṣṭan-* that ends in a long vowel. 6.1.172.

The meaning is that because *ghṛta* and others are listed [in the *ghṛtādigaṇa*], they are *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable); thus, there is no contradiction here even for the term *antodāttāt*, which continues to apply for the sake of subsequent rules. [The word] "in eight" (*aṣṭasu*) [is used].

But is not the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) here redundant? For, by the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*, [the substitution of *ā*] ought to occur, since there is no optionality in that rule. To this he says: "This very [mention]. For if the substitution of *ā* were obligatory, the mention of the long vowel here would be redundant because there would be nothing to exclude. And [the phrase] "of that which has undergone the substitution of *ā*, the designation *ṣaṭ*"—the connection is that this very mention of the long vowel makes known [the fact regarding] *aṣṭan*. How so? To this he says: "Otherwise, indeed..."

The inclusion of the term "long" (dīrgha) is indeed for the purpose that this accent should not apply in the alternative case where the substitution of *ā* does not occur. For if the designation *ṣaṭ* were not applied to *aṣṭan* even after the substitution of *ā*, then—while this accent of *aṣṭan* would have its scope in the case of the substitution of *ā*—it would be superseded by the accent prescribed by the rule "the penultimate syllable in words ending in *jhal*" (*jhalyupottamam*) when the designation *ṣaṭ* applies in the case where *ā* is not substituted, because the latter rule is subsequent. Thus, the inclusion of the term "long" would be redundant.

When, however, the designation *ṣat* applies to *aṣṭan* after it has undergone the substitution of *āt*, then the accentuation of *aṣṭan* being commenced would apply even in the alternative where *āt* is not substituted, since the *ṣaṭ-svara* (the accent prescribed for words designated as *ṣat*) would otherwise have already applied. Therefore, the rule is meaningful as it is formulated to prevent that [undesired application]. But how can both things be indicated by a single effort? What is the fault? For when a meaning cannot be accounted for otherwise, multiple meanings may be indicated; thus, since this [single rule] cannot be justified without both [meanings], it indicates both. [The rule continues: "After a word ending in the suffix *śatṛ* or in *num*, the feminine suffixes *nadi* and those beginning with vowels [take the acute accent on the final syllable]. (Pāṇini 6.1.173)

It means "piercing" or "pushing. Because it belongs to the *tudādi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied; the augment *num* is optional by the rule *ācchīnadyornum*. In that regard, the example provided is for the alternative where *num* is absent, while the counter-example is for the alternative where *num* is present.

Regarding the word *tudanti*: there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*. Here, the form ending in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix. With the words "In that case," etc., he removes the deficiency of the counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) in having two parts—namely, that the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* is not desired here. And in this matter, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is precisely this prohibition [of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*] by the term *anumaḥ*; for indeed, there is no present participle ending in *śatṛ* followed by *nuṭ* that is oxytone except through the accent of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

Regarding the statement "there should be an addition [of the feminine suffix] for *bṛhat* and *mahat*": since this is already established by the application of the *śatṛ*-like behavior (*śatṛvad-bhāva*), this rule is for the sake of restriction—meaning it should not apply to words such as *pṛṣṭha* and so on. It has already been stated in the section on feminine nouns that "the inclusion of *bṛhat* and *mahat* among the *gaura*-group is purposeless."

*Udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*: This is a rule [introduced] because the [previous rule], *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito 'nudāttasya*, would otherwise apply. For example: *vahutitavā brāhmaṇyā*. The mention of the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*) is for the purpose of excluding the form *nābhi*. [The derivation is as follows: from the root *tan*, by the rule *tanoter ḍauḥ sanvac ca*, we have *titauḥ*; and according to *cālanī titauḥ pumān*, *titauḥ* is masculine. Then, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed: *bahutitauḥ*. By the rule *bahor nañvad uttarapadabhūmni*, the final syllable of the *uttarapada* is udātta. In that case, by the rule *udāttasvaritayoḥ*, the case-ending becomes svarita.

And it must be stated that the inclusion of the letter *n* [in the rule] is necessary; the meaning is that one must declare that the vowel of the feminine suffix *nadi* following even a *nakāra* (*n*) in place of an acute-accented vowel is itself acute. For that purpose, some consider that the rule should be recited as "udāttahalo halpūrvāt" (P. 6.1.176). In the example *vākpatnī*, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Since the rule "patyāvaiśvarye" (P. 6.2.18) would normally cause the first member to retain its original accent, the prohibition "na bhūvākciddidhiṣu" (P. 6.2.19) applies; consequently, the compound receives the acute accent on the final syllable by the rule "samāsāntodāttatva". Then, the *nakāra* is substituted by the rule "vibhāṣā sapūrvasya" (P. 4.1.35).
[The substitution of *u* occurs] for the vowel *o* and the semivowel *v*, [when followed by a vowel]. 6.1.175.

Regarding the rule "ūṅ, and that which has a *udātta* *yaṇ* preceded by a consonant": this indicates that the present [prohibition] is a negation of the application of the previous [rule]. Therefore, the case ending beginning with the third [case] follows after that. Although in the previous sūtra the term "nady-ajādī" (feminine stems in *ī*, *ū*, and those beginning with vowels) is understood to carry over and not "tṛtīyādiḥ" (beginning with the third case), nevertheless, because here it is mostly possible for only the third case and so on to occur, this was stated. For instance: first, a feminine stem in *nadī* cannot follow after *ūṅ* or a *yaṇ* derived from a verbal root; nor can the nominative plural suffix *śas* follow after *ūṅ* or a *yaṇ*; however, it is possible for it to follow after a *yaṇ* derived from a verbal root.
The suffix *matup* is applied after a short vowel or after a word ending in the particle *nuṭ*.

Regarding *akṣaṇvatā*: the suffix *anaṅ* is applied by the rule "it is also seen in the Veda" (*chandasy api dṛśyate*), and the augment *nuṭ* is added by the rule "after *an*, there is *nuṭ*" (*ano nuṭ*), with the elision of the preceding *n*. Regarding *śīrṣatvata*: the word *śīrṣan* is established as such by the rule "in the Veda, [the word *śiras* becomes] *śīrṣan*" (*śīrṣañ chandasi*). Regarding the fact that the word *vasu* has its first syllable accented: the suffix *u* is added to the root *vas* under the governing rule "the suffix *niṭ* is applied after [roots] meaning 'to dwell' when [the word refers to] grain" (*dhānye niṭ*). Now, why does this not occur here: *marutvān*, meaning "one who possesses Maruts"? For the word *marut* ends in the suffix *uti* according to the rule "after the roots *mṛ* and *gur*, there is *uti*," and thus, by the accent of the suffix, it is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable).

And there is no intervention by the letter *t*, because in a rule concerning vowels (*svaravidhi*), a consonant is as if non-existent? To this he says: "here. But how is it known that [the *nuṭ* augment] is not elided? From the mention of *nuṭ*. For that [mention] is for the purpose that it should occur in cases such as *akṣaṇvatā*; otherwise, since a consonant is treated as non-existent even when it has been elided, there would be no occurrence [of the *nuṭ*] due to the intervention of the letter *n*, as it would be as good as non-existent in the application of the vowel rule.

If, in this case, the consonant (*vyañjana*) were as if non-existent, then because that [consonant] would be non-existent even for the purpose of what is "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the vowel would be established by virtue of its very non-existence; thus, the mention of *nuṭ* would be redundant. This is not correctly stated; for if the consonant *n* were as if non-existent even when the elision of *n* is unestablished, then the rule stating that the elision of *n* is as if unestablished for the sake of vowel-application (*svaravidhi*) would be meaningless.

Therefore, since the treatment as non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*) does not apply in the domain of elision of *n* (*nalopa*), the mention of *nuṭ* must indeed be made. If this is so, then this is merely a desired conclusion (*iṣṭi*): "In this matter of accentuation, the paribhāṣā regarding treatment as non-existent does not operate. The reading is "reśabdācca" (and from the word *re*). [The example is] *ārevān*. Since he possesses wealth (*rayi*), the suffix *matup* is applied; by the rule "the substitution of semivowels occurs abundantly for *rayi* in the sense of *matup*," there is a vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatvam*), and the addition of *āṬ* as the augment. Then, because there is no short vowel [preceding], this specific statement is necessary. [The example is] *trivatīḥ*. By the rule "in the Veda, *ira* becomes *ir*" (*chandasīraḥ*), there is the substitution of *vat*; then, by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*), there is the lengthening of the homogeneous preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*).
The substitution of *na* for the final vowel of a word ending in *n*, when followed by a case-ending beginning with *m*, is optional.

Regarding the phrase *matupi ca*: by virtue of the word "ca" (and), it results in a locative sense [meaning "in the presence of the suffix *matup*"]. Otherwise, it would apply only to the case of immediate presence (*sāmpratika*). For when there is an absence of immediate presence, one resorts to the notion of what existed previously (*bhūtapūrva*), but not when it is actually present. Consequently, in forms such as *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*, because the prohibition of lengthening by the rule *na tisṛcatasṛ* applies, the short vowel exists only in the sense of immediate presence; thus, the [substitution] would occur only there. However, in cases such as *agnīnām* and *vāyūnām*, since lengthening occurs by virtue of its higher status and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), the short vowel would be absent and therefore the substitution would not take place. Therefore, the short vowel is qualified by the suffix *matup*.

If this is so, would not the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rules "matau bahvaco'najirādīnām" and "śarādīnāṃ ca"—which state that lengthening occurs in the sense of *matup*—fail to apply to those [words]? This is not a fault; for the word "in a technical name (*saṃjñāyām*)" is understood [from the previous rule], and consequently, the lengthening in *matup* applies only in the sense of the fourfold suffixes (Pāṇini 5.2.127), and not in the sense of "that belongs to him, is in him, or exists in him" (Pāṇini 5.2.94). In that latter case, since the word ends in a short vowel, the desired form will be achieved.

Even so, would this not fail to apply in the cases of *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*, since the forms *tisṛ-* and *catasṛ-* themselves do not exist there? This is indeed intended to be included. For here, by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī-atricaturbhyo halādiḥ*, the acute accent of the case-ending is desired as being invariably [present]. In *dhenvām* and *śakaṭyām*: the word *dhenu* ends in the suffix *nup* according to the rule *dheṭa icca*, and is thus oxytone; the word *śakaṭī* is also optionally oxytone according to the rule *śakaṭi-śakaṭyor akṣaram akṣaraṃ paryāyeṇa*.
The words *trapu* and *vasu* are ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable).
After [the stems] ending in six, three, or four, when followed by a consonant, [the suffix *tamaP* is applied].

"The phrase 'from that which has the udātta accent on the final syllable' (antodāttāt) is discontinued. If this were to continue to apply, then [the rule] would not apply in the cases of *pañcānām*, *navānām*, and *caturṇām*, because these have the udātta accent on the first syllable by the rule "nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ" (P. 6.1.173). Where, then, would it apply? In *saptānām* and *aṣṭānām*; for the words *sapta* and *aṣṭa* have the udātta accent on the final syllable due to belonging to the *ghṛtādi* group. The term "nraḥ" means "of a word ending in the letter *r* or *n*.

As for the example *catasraḥ paśya*, we have already explained here how this is an instance excluded by the inclusion of the term "beginning with a consonant" (*hal-ādi*), just as we stated in the rule "caturaḥ śasi" (P. 6.1.167).
Before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, the penultimate vowel is acute.

When a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows, because there is an absence of three or more syllables in the words "ṣaṭ," "tri," and "catur," there is the inclusion of a word (*pada*) ending in such a *jhal*-initial case-ending; as it has been said: "In a word ending in a case-ending, the penultimate syllable becomes acute (*udātta*)."

Regarding the rule *na gośvan-sāv-avarṇa-rāḍ-aṅkuṭ-kṛdbhyaḥ*: if the word *sau* were taken as the locative plural (*supsu*), then the rule would not apply in examples such as *tebhyaḥ* and *kebhyaḥ*. This is because when the substitution of *yat* for the pronouns *tat* and *kim* occurs before the locative plural, the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* prescribes the change to *e*; thus, the rule would apply only in cases like *tābhiḥ* and *yābhiḥ*, but not in *tāsu* and *yāsu*, since those end in an *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*). Therefore, he states that *sau* refers to the nominative singular: *sau prathamaikavacane*.

Since the immediate [preceding] element to be negated is impossible, it is understood that the negation applies to every sixth-case (ṣāṣṭhika) accent. Thus he says: "That which was stated after these [rules] does not take place. And in this way, in examples such as *vṛkṣavān*, there is also a negation of the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*; however, a negation of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent resulting from the removal of an acute) is not desired. In *sugunā*, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is shortening by the rule *gostriyor upasarjanasya*, and final acute accent by the rule *nañsubhyām*.

[The opponent says: "But [in the case of] *śunā*, once the *n*-elision (*nalopa*) has been performed, does this not end in *s* or *avaṇ*? [Vājapyāyana replies: No; because in a rule prescribing accent (*svaravidhi*), the *n*-elision is considered as if it had not taken place (*asiddha*). [The opponent asks: But is this not a rule for accent, but rather a prohibition of accent? [Vājapyāyana replies: In that case, by making this prohibition regarding *śvan*, he indicates that in this prohibition, the *n*-elision is treated as *asiddha*.

Therefore, from the word *nṛ* in the seventh case singular (*nar-i*), the vowel of the case-ending becomes acute according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*; and in forms such as *pitṛmān*, the suffix *matup* becomes acute according to the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*. Otherwise, the prohibition [of accentuation] by the rule *sāvavarṇa* would apply. Regarding *prācā*: as before, there is elision of *n* and lengthening of the vowel. Regarding *kruñcā*: the root is *kuñca* or *kruñca* in the sense of "crookedness" and "becoming small"; the suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-*, etc., and in that very rule, because *kruñcā* is an irregular form (*nipātana*), there is no elision of *n*. Regarding *kṛtiḥ* or *vā*: the root is *kṛtī* in the sense of "cutting."
After the word *div*, [the suffix] *jhal* [is applied].

Regarding the phrase "beginning with *jhal*": how, moreover, can there be a rule concerning what follows (tadādividhi) when there is no mention of the locative case (*saptamī*), since there exists no case-ending (*vibhakti*) consisting solely of *jhal*? Well then, let it be a rule concerning what precedes (tadantavidhi). But which case-ending ends in *jhal*? It is the one beginning with *śas* and ending in *s*. In that case, the term "beginning" (*ādi*) is understood from the previous rule, "after *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, and *catur*, [the case-ending] beginning with a consonant (*hal*)," so that a case-ending following *div* does not become udātta; of what kind? One whose beginning is *jhal*.

This formulation of the rule (*yoga*) is capable of being stated. How so? I shall state it thus: "After *aṣṭan* when long, after *div* when followed by a *jhal*-initial [suffix], and after *śatṛ* and *anum* when they are *nadī*s. Furthermore, I will not include the mention of *div* in rules such as "*ūḍidam*" and so forth. Even so, in the subsequent rule "*nṛ cānyatarasyām*," the mention of *jhal* would have to be made there, and the particle *ca* would have to be added in the form "*nadi ca*"; thus, there is no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*).
The *svarita* accent [is applied] to the final syllable of a word ending in *iti*. 6.1.185.

If it is asked: "Why does [the rule] *ṛta id dhātoḥ* not apply here in the cases of *āstīrṇam* and *vistīrṇam*, since its purpose is fulfilled by the inclusion of that specific time (the short vowel)? Answer: No; for the markers (*anubandhas*) are seen to have multiple purposes. For example, in the case of *ākṣikaḥ* and similar forms, when the suffix *ṭhak* is present, both the accent and the vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*) occur. If this is so, then this *ikāra* (the letter *i*) is not followed by a *takāra* (*tapara*), but rather is followed by a *dakāra* (*dapara*). If that is the case, would not a long vowel be obtained in place of the *ṛkāra* by virtue of internal similarity (*āntarya*)? [The answer is: "An *aṇ* which is being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)."

If this is so, then in the case of *adas* [in the forms] *imūbhyām*, by the rule *adaso'serdādu do maḥ*, would there not be no long vowel in place of the long vowel? This is not a fault; for it has been indicated by the use of the *tapara* marker in the rules *diva ut* and *ṛta ut* that even an *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). But then, does it not follow that those two *u*s must be *svarita*? They too are not *tapara*; what then? They are *dapara*.

How, then, is it an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? In the rule *taparastatkālasya* ("a [phoneme] followed by *t* denotes its own duration"), the letter *d* is also indicated as being subject to the substitution of *c*. This is because of the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayastaparaḥ* ("an *aṇ*, or one marked with *u* or *it*, denotes its homogeneous phonemes, provided it is not a suffix and is followed by *t*"). If the letter *d* were also indicated there, then in the rule *ṛdorap*, because of the inclusion of *d*, the suffix *ap* would apply only in cases like *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ*; it would not apply in cases like *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*, since *ap* follows a *ta*-marked (*tapara*) vowel even after a *ta*-marked consonant (*tāt*).

In that case, in the rule *ṛdorap*, the letter *d* is indicated for the purpose of pronunciation as having become a *jaś* sound; since *jaś*-hood is considered *asiddha* (not yet established) there, this *ṛ* is not followed by a *da*. For those, however, who recite the paribhāṣā—"Of both suffixes and non-suffixes, only the suffix is to be understood"—there would still arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of this accent [the udātta] in rules such as *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, even though the suffix is marked with *t*. Furthermore, in the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, the letter *d* should not be included by *praśleṣa*;
for that paribhāṣā is absent from both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.
Because it has not been seen before, this great effort has been undertaken by us.

*tāsyanudāttenṅidadupadeśāllasārvadhātukamanudāttamaṅgviṅoḥ*. This is a collective *dvandva* compound consisting of *tāsi*, etc. Regarding *adupadeśāt*: "upadeśa" means that which is taught (*upadiśyate*). Because it is qualified by the vowel *a*, the rule applies to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). Thus, *adupadeśaḥ* means "that which ends in the vowel *a* at the stage of being taught. The meaning is: "after that [root] which ends in the vowel *a* at the time it is being taught. Regarding *akāropadeśāt*: the meaning is "from a root taught as ending in the vowel *a*. Examples include *kartā*, etc.

In the Ātmanepada, for the first person, there are the substitutes *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*; [and] *tās* [is added]. In the singular, there is elision of the *ṭi* [portion]; elsewhere, there is elision of *s* by the rule "ri ca. In forms such as *āste*, there is elision of *śap* due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class.

The forms *tudataḥ* and so forth end in the suffix *tas*. But how can there be a vowel *a* at the end when this [root] is taught with a final *p*, since it is taught as ending in *p* there? To this he says: "Because an *anubandha* is not invariably present, it is indeed taught as ending in *a*. From the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *udīcām āṅaḥ*—which refers to the form [of the root] after the substitution of *ā*—it is inferred that even when *anubandhas* are heard in grammatical operations, they do not act as obstructions. Thus we have *pacamānaḥ* and *yajamānaḥ*; here, the suffix is *śānac* from *laṭ*. Now, is there not an intervention by the augment *muk* here? To this he says: "In whatever case... and so on.

"Syāt" (it may be) indicates possibility (*sambhāvanā*), expressed here by the potential mood (*liṅ*). This alternative is possible because one relies on the rule that *muk* is substituted for the *akāra* of the stem (*aṅga*). In that case, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies according to the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* following a verbal root taught with a low vowel (*adupadeśa*)". However, the substitution of *iy* by the rule "āto ṅitaḥ" does not take place; why? Because of the inclusion of the long *ā* (*taparakaraṇa*) in the word *kaata* [in the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*]. The ablative case in "following" (*anantara*) should be understood as expressing immediate sequence, or the word "param" (after) should be supplied. Alternatively, the phrase "of a stem ending in *akāra*" is used because the stem is qualified by the vowel *a*. [This refers to] "the *lasārvadhātuka*".

The word *siddham* (established) is connected with what is to be stated hereafter, and the term *nighātaḥ* (elision) is supplied by way of *anuṣaṅga* (elliptical extension); thus, the meaning is that the elision of the *lasārvadhātuka* [suffix] is established. Regarding the phrase *asiddhaḥ* (unestablished): because of the context, it is understood to mean "the augment *muk*. Regarding the phrase *bahiraṅgatvāt* (because of being external): the status of being external (*bahiraṅgatva*) for *muk* arises from its dependence on many factors. For *muk* depends upon a stem (*aṅga*) qualified by the vowel *a*, as well as a specific suffix (*pratyaya*) such as *āna*. This accent (*svara*), however, depends only upon the fact of being taught with an initial *a* (*adupadeśa*) and the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix in general; therefore, it is internal (*antaraṅga*).

"Even the *citsvara*," and so forth. The scope of the *citsvara* is [in cases such as] *calanaḥ* (from the rule) "The suffix *yu* occurs after roots meaning movement that are intransitive. Its scope is [in cases such as] *āste*, *śete*. In examples such as *pavamānaḥ*, this *nighāta* (non-accentuation) prevails over the *citsvara* due to its higher status. Now, one might object: "A conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) arises when a single element is subject to two operations, but here a single element is not joined with two operations. How so? The *anudātta* (low-pitched accent) applies to the initial [syllable], while the *citsvara* applies to the final [syllable]; here, it is not the initial syllable that undergoes the *anudātta*, but rather the entire complex (*saṅghāta*) is the subject of the operation."

We shall state the evidence for this later on. Consequently, since the root *ci* would have to be entirely unaccented (sarvānudātta), rather than having an acute accent on its first syllable, there is indeed a contradiction; thus it is quite logical that this [rule] sets aside [the previous one] by virtue of its being subsequent (*paratva*).

Examples: *cinutaḥ*, *cinvanti*. But surely, according to the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, the suffix *śnu* is also treated as having the marker *ṅ*; so how can this serve as a counter-example? To this he says: "This *śnu* is treated as having the marker *ṅ* with respect to the operation of what precedes it. For in that context, whatever operation applies to a suffix marked with *ṅ* is extended [to *śnu*]; as it has been said: "But it is established by the extension of the operation of what precedes."

This is not an established conclusion; for he will state under the rule *āto ṅitaḥ* that in the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, it is accepted that [the suffix] behaves like one marked with *ṅ* (*ṅit-vat*), even though it is not itself marked with *ṅ*, and so forth. However, in this view, the solution is as follows: the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) is connected with both [phrases]: "because of being originally enunciated with *ṅ*" and "because of being originally enunciated with *a*. Thus, we have *pacāvaḥ* and *pacāmaḥ*. If the term *upadeśa* were not present, then after the long vowel had been substituted by virtue of its higher status and its obligatory nature, the substitution would not take place because of the specific mention of the short vowel *a* (*tapara-karaṇa*).

But surely, the inclusion of *t* (in *at*) need not be made? If it were not made, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *yātaḥ* and *vātaḥ*, as well as *hataḥ* and *hathaḥ*. Here, once the nasalization (*anunāsika-lopa*) has been effected by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa... (*Pāṇini 6.4.37*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix follows the letter *a*; nevertheless, because of the mention of "original enunciation" (*upadeśa-grahaṇa*), [the rule] does not apply. For the root *han* is not taught (*upadiśyate*) as ending in *a*.

Now, why does the *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent not apply here to the short *ha* sound (*haśabda*), which is the basis for that [accent]? Because it has not been taught as such; for the teaching of the root *han* refers to the whole [root], as in the example: *katīha pacamānāḥ* ("How many are cooking here?"). Here, the suffix *śānan* is applied by the rule *pūṅyajoḥ śānan*, and since the word *laṭaḥ* has ceased to apply there, this is not a substitute for *lādeśa*. In the form *śiśye*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*, and this is an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix by the rule *liṭ ca*. In the phrase *yad adhīte*, the use of the word *yat* is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment of the particle (*nipāta*) by the rule *nipātairyadyadi*.
**Ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām** (Pāṇini 6.1.187). [The initial syllable of the augment *sic* may optionally be acute.]

"Let them not do it"—regarding the use of *hi* and *māṅ*, the purpose has already been stated. [The opponent asks: "But here the suffix is not one beginning with *v*; rather, there is the augment *iṭ*, and augments are unaccented (*anudātta*). Therefore, even in this case, the word should have its final syllable accented (*antodātta*)? To this he replies: "Because of the *cit* designation of the suffix *sic*."

Regarding the rule *aniṭaḥ pita*: when a *pit* suffix follows a *sic* that does not take the augment *iṭ*, it is optionally acute (*udātta*), while in the other case it is grave (*anudātta*). Consequently, in the form *mā hi kārṣam*, the finite verb ending is optionally acute on the first syllable and optionally acute on the last syllable. Otherwise, by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), it would always be acute on the first syllable. By the phrase "only acute on the middle," he indicates that it is acute due to the accent of the *sic* suffix, and by the word "only" (*eva*), he shows that it is not acute on the final syllable.

The substitution of *sva* for *su* occurs before a non-*iṭ* augment beginning with a consonant, when it follows a verbal root ending in *pā*, provided that the root does not involve injury to oneself.

"Up to the root *svap* and including the cause [of the designation]," meaning up to the end of the *gaṇa*. In that context, following the roots *ñiṣvap śaye* ("to sleep"), *śvasa prāṇane* ("to breathe"), and *ana ca* ("to breathe"), the roots beginning with *jakṣ* are designated as *abhyasta* (repeated). Among these, because of their posteriority, the accent "the first syllable of *abhyasta*s" applies. However, those following them—namely *ṣas svapne* ("to sleep"), *vaśa kāntau* ("to desire"), *hnuṅ apanayane* ("to remove"), and the *carkarīta* [reduplication]—in that regard, the *carkarīta* is also *abhyasta*.

Others, however, maintain that *ṣaṣ* and *vasi* are Vedic (*chāndasa*), and in the Veda, one follows whatever is observed [there]. This accent does not occur for the root *hnuṅ* either, because of the continued application of the rule *ahan-viṅoḥ*. By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), this accent applies only to the first three [roots] mentioned. Regarding *hiṃsanti*: the root *hisi* meaning "to injure" belongs to the *rudhādi* class; there is the elision of *n* by the rule *śnānnalopaḥ*, and the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*. [The rule] *abhyastānām ādiḥ* [6.1.189] [applies].

The word "initial" (*ādi*) is understood from the present context, [referring] to the rule *ādiḥ sico'nyatarasyām* (6.1.187). The repetition of the word "initial" is for the sake of making the application obligatory; otherwise, the mention of *anyatarasyām* ("optionally"), which is connected with the mention of "initial," would continue to apply. And [the augment *it* is added] after [a root ending in] a non-acute vowel: 6.1.190.

This [rule] is for the sake of excluding meanings such as "beginning with *an*. In the forms *jihīte* and *mimīte*, by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*, the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes become unaccented (*anudātta*) because the suffix is marked with the *ṅit* indicatory letter. By stating "that in which no *udātta* exists," it is indicated that this term *anudātta* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. He states the purpose of this there: "that in which no *udātta* exists" means it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound and so forth; that is, an *anudātta* is that in which no *udātta* is found. As in the example *mā hi sm dadhāt*.

If the term *anudātta* (unaccented) were understood in its technical (*śāstrīya*) sense, then because the elision of the vowel *i* would be either obligatory (*nitya*) or internal (*antaraṅga*), there would be no unaccented vowel following it; consequently, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) would not occur. However, this [initial accent] does occur when the word is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Furthermore, in the case of "it places here" (*dadhātyatra*), the accent is established even by virtue of the fact that the *yaṇ*-substitution is non-existent (*asiddha*) due to being external (*bahiraṅga*).
The word *sarva* takes the augment *suP* before all case endings (*sup*).

The word *sarva* is prescribed as having an udātta accent on the final syllable in the *uṇādi* list so that the suffix *añ*, characterized by an anudātta initial vowel, may apply in the sense of "a modification of *sarva*" (as in *sārva*).

[The phrase] "even by means of the characteristic of the suffix" and so forth has been explained under the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. [The statement] "the accent of *sarva* applies when *kak* is not present" [is made].

In the case of the roots *bhī*, *hrī*, *bhṛ*, *hu*, *mad*, *jan*, *dhan*, *daridrā*, and *jāgar*, the augment *iṭ* is placed before the suffix beginning with *pi*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*). The mention of *jāgarām* is a Vedic (sautra) usage. Here, *mad* belongs to the *divādi* class; *daridrā* and *jāgr* belong to the *adādi* class; the others belong to the *juhotyādi* class. Regarding "the fifth *lakāra*": in the sequence of *l* shown here, the fifth *lakāra* is *leṭ*. The term *leṭ* is considered vulgar (*jugupsita*) in the regions of the Vṛttikāra, just as the word *nīvī* is in the Draviḍa country. The form *dadhanat* [is explained as follows].

Furthermore, there is the elision [of the *ā*] by the rule "there is elision before the *parasmaipada* endings," and the augment *aṭ* by the rule "in the *leṭ* there are *aṭ* and *āṭ*. Thus we have *daridratī*. Here, if the elision of the long *ā* were applied first because it is a subsequent rule (*paratvāt*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the vowel *i* becoming udātta. Now, what is the purpose of including the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) [in the rule], since only a *pit* affix can possibly follow roots such as *bhi*? Is this not the case: "the final syllable of the first person plural is *pit* and *āṭ*"? In *bibhayāti*, it is indeed the *loṭ* first person plural that is prescribed as *pit*, and not the *āṭ*; yet the *loṭ* first person plural together with *āṭ* becomes *pit*, and that [form] is indeed an affix.

Therefore, one should not say that the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is for the purpose of excluding [the augment] *āṭ* from occurring before the *pit* [marker], since *āṭ* occurs before the substitute *loṅ* but not before the affix itself, because the [augment] *āṭ* along with [the substitute] is not an affix. Why? Because just as the status of being an affix belongs to [the substitute] together with *āṭ*, so too does the status of being *pit* belong to that very same [unit].

In this case, then, the purpose is that the acute accent (*udātta*) should apply to the vowel preceding the suffix, and not to the entire cluster; this itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in rules governing accent, the entire cluster is the subject of the operation. Consequently, what was stated—that the *nighāta* (elision of accent) prescribed by the rule "tāsyanudāttet" overrides the *cit-svara* (accent of a suffix marked with *c*) in forms such as *pacamānaḥ* because it is subsequent—is thereby justified.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word "prior" (*pūrva*) [in the rule]? One might say that it should simply be stated as "when a *pit* suffix follows. In that case, by the principle "when something is specified by the locative case, the operation applies to what precedes it," the result would apply to the preceding element alone. However, this is the purpose: so that when a *pit* suffix follows, the preceding element should undergo the grammatical operation, and not the suffix ending in *pit*. But how can there be an application to the ending in *pit* when there is a locative specification? This very fact makes it known: in rules concerning accent (*svara-vidhi*), locative specifications refer to the ending in that [suffix]. What is thereby established? That the penultimate syllable [receives the accent].

Regarding the rule *riti*: when a suffix ending in *rit* follows, the penultimate syllable becomes udātta, but it does not apply to what precedes *rit*. As for the rule *caṅyanyatarasyām*, it applies to that which ends in *caṅ*. If this were so, then by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, the accent would apply to that which ends in the suffix *śas*; however, it will not apply because of the force of the specific mention of *śas* [in the rule].

For if the acute accent of the suffix *śas* were intended by the rule "caturaḥ śasi," then [the author] would have stated "caturaśca" immediately after "ūḍidam"; for in that case, due to the continued application of the term "asarvanāmasthāna" and because the rule "ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ" prescribes an acute accent for the initial vowel of a suffix beginning with a consonant, the accent would belong to *śas* alone.
The suffix *liṭ* [is applied after a verbal root to express the sense of the past]. 6.1.193.
The phrase "before the suffix" (pratyayāt pūrvam) continues to apply; therefore, one should not raise the objection regarding the occurrence of a vowel at the end of a *liṭ* [perfect] formation.
The augment *ṇamul* may optionally be applied after a verbal root beginning with a vowel.

"Lolūyaṃ-lolūyam": since there is no difference between the accent of the *liṭ* suffix in single-syllable roots and this [case], it is cited with multiple syllables. It is stated that the *āmreḍita* (the repeated portion) is unaccented by the rule "anudāttaṃ ca" (Pāṇini 8.1.3).
When the causative suffix *ṇic* is replaced by *yak* with the sense of the agent, [the substitution of *ī* for the penultimate vowel] does not occur after a vowel. (Pāṇini 6.1.195)

The *yak* prescribed when a *sārvadhātuka* affix denoting the agent follows is called *kartṛyak*. Regarding the statement "the term *upadeśa* is understood [from the previous rule]," the mention of *upadeśa* in the rule *adupadeśāt* (P. 7.2.62) is connected here as well, even though it was compounded there, because its status as a *svarita* vowel has been formally promised; and considering that this term effectively becomes a locative ending (*saptamyanta*) by virtue of its meaning, it has been stated thus. However, a locative mention of *upadeśa* is not actually present in the current context. If the mention of *upadeśa* were not carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], then in forms such as *kāryate*, the substitution of *ra* for *ya* would not occur once the *raparatva* (substitution of *ra* in place of *ya*) has taken effect; therefore, the term *upadeśa* must be understood as being carried over.

If this were so, [the rule] *jāyate svayameva* and others would not apply; for when the substitution of *ā* (by the rule *ye vibhāṣā*) has occurred, *jana* and the others would subsequently end in *ā*, but they do not [end in *ā*] at the stage of their original instruction (*upadeśa*)? To this, he says: "of *jana* and the others. In the rule *ye vibhāṣā*, the term *upadeśe* (at the time of instruction) is understood from the preceding rule *anudāttopadeśe*; and since that is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), the substitution of *ā* for *jana* and the others occurs precisely at the stage of their original instruction. Thus: *jāyate svayameva*. Here, the root *jan* has its causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized and refers to a case where the agent is also the object (*karmakartṛ*).
Furthermore, the usage of a verb with the causative sense (antarbhāvita-ṇyartha) is observed, as for example: "The One was born twelvefold."
And *thāl* and *seṭ* endings [are optionally treated as having an indicatory *k*]. 6.1.196.

While the term *anyatarasyām* is already in force, the inclusion of the word *vā* is for the purpose of allowing an option regarding the operation (*kārya*). By the mention of *anyatarasyām*, the operation is made optional; by the mention of *vā*, the operands (*kāryin*) are made optional. Consequently, [grammatical operations] such as *iṭ* and so forth obtain their application alternately. Now, one might object: "In rules such as *antaśca tavai yugapat*, the alternation is established elsewhere simply by the mention of *yugapat* (simultaneously). Is this not so? True; however, even when the rule *ader api* applies, the mention of *vā* is included.

Otherwise, if only the two forms ending in *hi* and *danta* were heard, one would have to choose between them as the objects of the operation; however, when the particle *vā* is present, whether the meaning is an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*), it applies to all [forms] beginning with *ādi*.

"What is the purpose of [specifying] *seṭ*?"—this question implies that the *thal* suffix will be understood as *seṭ* (having an augment *iṭ*) simply by virtue of the mention of *iṭ*. "As in *yayātha*"—the intention here is this: when the augment *iṭ* is applied by the mention of *iṭ*, it would be for the sake of its being acute (*udātta*). Consequently, just as in forms like *lulavitha*, where the acute accent is optionally prescribed for any one of the four [suffixes], so too in forms like *yayitha*, even though the fourth [suffix] is absent, the acute accent would occur by way of option; thus, it would also occur even in the absence of *iṭ*.
That which begins with a vowel is always pluta. 6.1.197.

The statement "it is an exception to the accent of the suffix" is made because of its general prevalence. In the case of *śrotriyaṃś chando 'dhīte*, there is no occasion for the accent of the suffix under the view that "the word-form is stated [here] for the sake of the sentence-meaning."

"It is not desired that there be an operation based on the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) here. But surely, because of the prohibition "not when [an affix] marked with *lu* elides" (*na lumatāṅgasya*), an operation based on an affix will simply not take place; why then is it said, "it is not desired that there be an operation based on an affix here"? This has been made known from another source: "In rules prescribing accent (*svaravidhi*), locatives [denoting case endings] refer to those ending in that [case ending]. Consequently, just as in the preceding rule the element ending in *thaN* is the subject of the operation, so too here the element ending in *ñNi* is the subject, and not the stem (*aṅga*) preceding it;
thus, since it is not an operation upon the stem, the prohibition does not apply. [The rule] "in *yaÑ* and *kan*"—the word "and" (*ca*) implies "also in *yaÑ* following *bid* and others."
And [the substitution of *e* for *o* occurs] when a vocative is addressed. 6.1.198.

In this context, the application of the rule "after a *kāraka* [word], only for *datta* and *śruta* in the sense of a blessing" (*kārakād dattaśrutyor evāśiṣi*) is prohibited; the meaning is that it is set aside by the prohibition of the *śeṣa* (the remaining case). It is accepted here that there is a formal characteristic based on the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), because the operation resulting from that suffix is made clear by the mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding *sarpiḥ*: from the root *sṛp*, with the suffix *isi*, the word *sarpiḥ* is oxytone (acute-accented on the final syllable); the suffix *su* is elided by the rule "after a neuter [stem], *su* and *am* are elided" (*svamornapuṃsakāt*). The word *sapta* is oxytone because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group; the suffix *jas* is elided by the rule "elision after the six [numerals]" (*ṣaḍbhyo luk*).
The [final] *ṛ* of *pathin* and *mathin* is replaced by *ar* before a nominal stem suffix (*sarvanāmasthāna*).

Regarding the words *pathin* and *mathin*, and so forth: the suffix *ini* is applied by the rules "from the root *gam*, *ini*" (*gameriniḥ*), "from *puṣ*, *kit*" (*puṣaḥ kit*), "the word *mantha*," and "from *pat*, with *tha*" (*patestha ca*). Due to the *kit* designation, there is elision of the penultimate vowel in *mantha*, resulting in *panthāḥ* and *manthāḥ*. Then, operations such as those prescribed by "for *pathi*, *mathi*, and *ṛbhukṣan*, [substitute] *āt*" (*pathimathyṛbhukṣāmāt*) are applied. In the example *pathaḥ paśya* ("look at the paths"), there is elision of the final *ṭi* (the *i*) of the *bha*-stem. Here too, the principle of "characterized by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) is not desired. As for the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is to be understood as before.
And [the suffix] *antaś* occurs after the word *tava* when used simultaneously. 6.1.200.

Regarding the word *karttave*: the suffix *tavai* is applied according to the rule *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ*. But what is the reason for making an effort to exclude synonyms? To this he says: "For [it is said] 'excluding one [of the synonyms]' (*ekavarjam*)," and so forth.
The word *kṣaya* [is substituted for *ni*] before the word *nivāsa*.

From the root *kṣi*, meaning "to destroy" or "to go," the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), resulting in *kṣayaḥ*. In the expression "the destruction of the Dasyus," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *vṛṣan* and the others. 6.1.203.

The roots *vṛṣu* (to sprinkle), *janī* (to appear), *jvara* (to be feverish), *hi* (to go), and *kai*, *gai*, *rai* (to sound) all end in the suffix *ac*. This is because they belong to the *pacādi* group; this is stated on account of their great number. In the case of *vṛṣaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule for roots having a penultimate *i*. The roots *ṇīñ* (to lead) and *tāyṛ* (to extend and protect)—some read *taya* instead—and *aya*, *paya*, *taya* (all meaning "to go"). In some places the word *caya* is read; it should be understood as derived from the root *ci* (to gather).

The root *iṇ* means "to go"; *aṃs* means "to support"; *vida* means "to know"; *ṣūda* means "to cast away"; *du* means "to burn"; *vada* means "to speak clearly"; and *ata* means "to move continuously. Some do not include these two [roots]. *Guhū* means "to conceal"; *śama* means "to become calm"; and *aṇa* and *raṇa* mean "sound."

Regarding the rule *sammatau bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*: the terms *śama* and *raṇa* are understood [to follow]. When the sense is "consent" (*sammati*), the verbal roots *śam* and *raṇ*, in the senses of "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) respectively, have their first syllable udātta. *Śāntiḥ*: from the root *śam* with the suffix *ktic*. *Kāntiḥ*: from *kam* in the sense of "desire" (*kānti*). *Rāntiḥ*: from *yam* in the sense of "restraint" (*uparama*); some do not recite the word *yam*. *Ārtiḥ*: from *ṛ* in the sense of "sound" and "motion. *Ghṛtiḥ*: from *ghṛñ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*). *Kīrtiḥ*: from *kṝ* in the sense of "scattering" (*vikṣepa*); the vowel lengthening occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the *bhidādi* group. *Vāhiḥ*: from *vah* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇa*). *Kṛpā*: from *kṛpū* in the sense of "capacity" (*sāmarthya*). *Pattiḥ*: from *pad* in the sense of "going" (*gati*).
In the case of a name, there is the use of comparison. (Pāṇini 6.1.204)

"If this is so" means: if, in this context, there is the elision (*lup*) of the suffix *kan*. "This very [point]" and so forth: in the absence of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), even when there is a mention of the locative case (*saptamī-nirdeśa*), the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) would not occur; for, by the indicator that "in rules concerning accent (*svaravidhi*), locatives refer to the end of the word," the entire form ending in that suffix becomes the subject of the operation. "In some cases": due to an explicit statement (*vacana*), it indeed occurs in some instances, as in the rule "of the whole (*sarvasya*) before a case-ending (*supi*)."
And the final [vowel] is substituted for [the penultimate vowel] when followed by two consonants. 6.1.205.

Here, because the single-substitute (ekādeśa) *adyātta* is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga*, there is no application of the prohibition *anāt*. The word *bhīṣma* ends in the suffix *man* according to the rule *bhiyaḥ ṣuk ca*.
Regarding *cintita*: the root *cit* in the sense of "recollection" belongs to the *cur*-class (*curādi*).
The agent [of the action] when preceded by the prefix *ā-śas* [takes the genitive case]. 6.1.207.

Regarding the word *āśeḥ*: it is derived from the root *aś* in the sense of "eating" (*bhojane*), preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, with the object not being intended to be expressed. For it has been said: "An action is intransitive due to its well-known usage or because the object is not intended to be expressed. Regarding the suffix *kta*: it is applied according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning motion or intransitives," and so forth. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that "the suffix *kta* is introduced [here] as an irregularity (*nipātana*) in the sense of the agent. If, then, the form *āśitaḥ* belongs to the root *aś* preceded by *āṅ*, the *avagraha* (separation) would follow; therefore, the author of the Vārttika states: "The lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrghatva*) is also introduced as an irregularity."

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, maintains that "the *saṃhitā* reading alone is eternal, whereas the *pada* reading is a human composition; therefore, the authors of the *pada* text are not to be followed by the rules [of grammar], nor indeed are the rules to be followed by the authors of the *pada* text. Another says: the form *āśitaḥ* arises from the root *aś* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*ṇi*), with the agent who causes the action (*prayojyakartṛ*) designated as the object (*karman*) according to the rule "roots meaning motion, cognition, or eating," and in this context, that very person is intended to be the agent by way of having previously been so.
When [the word] *rikta* is used, there is an option.

Regarding the word *rikta*: the root *ric* is used in the sense of "purging" (*virecana*). [The rule] beginning with *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.10) applies. The scope of the rule *niṣṭhā ca dvyajanāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.49)—which prescribes the substitution of *t* for *th* after a double-consonant—is exemplified by *dattaḥ*, *guptaḥ*. The scope of the present rule (*saṃjñāyām*) when not forming a name is exemplified by *rikto ghaṭaḥ* ("an empty jar"). When both rules would apply in the case of a name, the former is superseded by the subsequent rule (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
The words *juṣṭa* and *arpita* [are used] in the Vedic language (*chandas*). 6.1.209.

Regarding *juṣṭa*: the root is *juṣ* in the sense of "pleasure" and "service. By the rule *śvīdite niṣṭhāyām*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Regarding *apita*: the root is *ṛ* with the suffix *ṇic*; by the rule *artyādibhyaḥ puk*, the augment *puk* is added.
The suffix *nityam* is applied before a mantra. 6.1.210.
Since [the meaning] is already established by the very force of the initial statement, the inclusion of the word "nitya" (constant/permanent) is for the sake of what follows.
The genitive singular ending ṅasi is substituted for the endings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.

Regarding the rule *yuṣyasibhyāṃ madik*: *yuṣ* is a root belonging to the *sautra* (Vedic/technical) class. [The forms] *tava* and *mama* [are derived from it]. Regarding the rules *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso's* and *tavamamau ṅasi*: the substitutes *tva-* and *ma-* replace [the portions of] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* up to the final *m*; then there is elision (*lopa*) of the remainder; then, by the rule *ato guṇe*, the substitution of the single substitute form (*pararūpatva*) occurs; and although the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending would follow from the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, this [present rule] is stated [to override that].
And [the substitution of *ṅa* occurs] before *i*. 6.1.212.

"tubhyam," "mahyam": [the forms are derived] by [Pāṇini 7.1.28] *ṅe prathamayoram* and [7.1.29] *tubhyamahyau ṅayi*. Now, for what purpose is this split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*)? Why not simply say *yuṣmadasmadorṅeṅasoḥ*, so that the particle *ca* would not have to be used? To this he says: "The making of a separate rule... He shows that it can be argued that because of the mention of the word *āśaṅkā* (in the previous rule), there will be no correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṃkhya*) precisely because [the present rule] is not marked with an indicatory vowel *u* (*asvarita*). Here too, as before, the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) was applicable.
The suffix *an* is applied after [a stem ending in] *nau*. 6.1.213.

In this context, the prohibition "anāvaḥ" indicates that, in a rule concerning accents, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent; otherwise, since the initial *n* is not suitable for an accent and the *a* suitable for an accent is not the initial, the prohibition would be purposeless.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the roots √īḍ, √vand, √vṛś, √saṃs, and √duh.

In the sense of "praise" (*stuti*), there are the roots *vadi* (in the sense of salutation and praise), *vṛṅ* (in the sense of choosing/bestowing), *śaṃsu* (in the sense of praise), and *duha* (in the sense of filling). How is it that the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in the word *vārya*, given that the suffix *kyap*—which is prescribed as a specific rule by the sūtra beginning with *eti-stu-śāsu*—should have applied instead? To this, he says: "In the case of *vārya*, etc. Now, why does *kyap* not also apply to the root *vṛṅ*? To this, he says: "For in the rule prescribing *kyap*, etc. This has already been explained in that very place.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the verbal roots *veṇi* and *nāth*.

"Ending in the suffix *ṇu*": here, "after the root *sthā*, the suffix *ṇu*" is understood to carry over. "By the accent of the removal of the acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*)" means because of the elision of the acute vowel *a* of the suffix *śnas* according to the rule "the elision of *a* in *śna* and *as*. Regarding "veṇuḥ" and so forth: the scope of the rule "in a name, that which is the object of comparison [retains its original accent]" is exemplified by *cañcā vardhrikā*; the scope of the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is exemplified by a bamboo (*veṇuḥ*) that is not being compared, such as one that is dry in a grove. In the case of "veṇuḥ" where it is a name and an object of comparison, there is a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). [The rule] "of *tyāga*, *rāga*, *hāsa*, *kuha*, *śvaṭha*, and *kratha*" (Pāṇini 6.1.216).

The roots *kuha* (in the sense of "wondering") and *śvaṭha* and *kratha* (in the sense of "speaking") belong to the curādigaṇa and end in the letter *a*. Is it not appropriate that this [rule] should be an exception (*apavāda*) specifically to the rule for the loss of accent (*nighāta*)? This is not so; for if this were an exception to the rule for the loss of accent, he would have stated it right there: "A word has one vowel unaccented, except for its own [meaning]. [This is not the case here.]
The substitution of *caṅ* optionally [takes place] in the case of either [of the two roots].
In the example, the reason for the departure from the singular number must be sought. In *mā hi daghat*, the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśyoḥ*.
[The following is the sūtra: *matoḥ pūrvam āt saṃjñāyāṃ striyām* (P. 6.1.219).

"Before *mat* [there is] *ākāra*"—this is the explanation of the meaning. In the sūtra, however, the neuter gender is used in reference to the form of the word (*śabdarūpa*). Some, however, read the word *pūrva* in the sūtra as masculine. In the example, *cāturarthikaḥ*, there is lengthening according to the rules "after *nadī* there is *matup*" and "in the presence of *mata*, there is lengthening for polysyllabic stems and for *anacirādi*. Why say "*mataḥ*" (after *mat*)? [Consider] *gavādinī*.

If this [condition] "after *matur*" were not present, the mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) would not even be made; consequently, there would be the undesirable application of the rule to the mere vowel *ā* that is connected with the technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*). The mention of "preceding" is so that [the substitution] may apply to what immediately precedes *matur*, and not in cases such as *sānumatī*.
The suffix *matup* is applied after a word ending in *avati*, provided it does not denote a country.
In this case, for the sake of removing doubt, the elision of the letter *a* (in *avaty-anta*) is established because the expression "ending in *vatī*" (*vatyā antaḥ*) was not stated [by Pāṇini].

He asks about the purpose therein: "What is meant by 'ending in *vatī*'? Now, even if "ending in *vatī*" were stated, why does [the rule] not apply in the case of *rājavatī*, since this too ends in the word *avatī* once the *n*-elision has been performed? To this he replies: "In a rule concerning vowel [accentuation]," and so forth. But surely, even in the example [given], because the substitution of *vat* for *mat* is not established, there is no ending in the word *avatī*? To this he says: "The substitution of *vat*, moreover... The word "moreover" (*punaḥ*) highlights the distinction from the [mere] elision of *n*.
[The suffix *īyasun* is applied] after words ending in *īvat*. 6.1.221.
In *ahīvatī* and similar forms, the long vowel occurs first, and the suffix *vat* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. The purpose of the word-split (*yogavibhāga*) is to be considered.
The substitution of *cau* [for *ku*] occurs before the suffix *au*. (Pāṇini 6.1.222)

This is an exception to the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. By the rule of the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*), the vowel *a* of the root *añc-* is acute; its elision by the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138) is caused by the case-ending.

It must be stated that "it does not apply when a taddhita suffix follows. The meaning is that the accent which belongs to the *cu*-portion [of a compound] does not occur when a taddhita suffix follows. Otherwise, just as in cases such as *dadhīcaḥ paśya* ("look at Dadhīca"), where an unaccented suffix [would cause the accent of the preceding member to disappear], this [proposed rule] would override the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent resulting from the removal of an acute), so too in cases like *dādhīcaḥ*, the accent of the suffix—being the later-enunciated (*satiśiṣṭa*)—would override [the accent of the compound]. Therefore, it must be stated "not when a taddhita follows"; and this being so, [the present rule] becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*.
[The substitution of *ṅīp* occurs] for a compound [ending in a short vowel]. 6.1.223.

Regarding the term *rājadṛṣad*: one might object, "Is it not the case that the letter *d*, which is the final element of this compound, does not participate in the accentuation, and that the vowel *a* preceding it is not the final element of the compound? To this, he says: "In the rule for accentuation (*svaravidhau*). It is not only the prescription of an accent itself that is meant here; rather, even a rule such as "*añ* after a word beginning with an unaccented vowel" (*anudāttāder añ*) is also a "rule for accentuation," because it depends upon an accent. Therefore, that rule also applies when [the following element] begins or ends with a consonant. And the proof for this is the prohibition of the word *pṛthivī* after stating, "not when the second member of the compound begins with an unaccented vowel."

Regarding the objection that there would be various accents (*nānāsvara*): although there is the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]," nevertheless, because a specific exception is required for the exclusion (*varjana*), there arises the contingency of various accents occurring alternately. In this regard, the word *rāja-* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *kanin* according to the rule "kaniny-uvṛṣi-takṣi... etc.; *puruṣaḥ* is derived from *puras* with the suffix *kuṣan*; *brāhmaṇāḥ* is the offspring of *brahman*, ending in the suffix *aṇ*; *kambalaḥ* is formed by the rule "and *kalatṛpa*" (ending in *aṇ*), "from *vṛṣa* and others *cit*" (with the *cittva* accent), and "after *kam*, *buk* [is added]" (with the *buk* augment).

In the rule "The [final vowel] of *kanyā*, *rājanya*, *śiṣya*, and [certain] human names [is unaccented]," the word *kanyā* has its final vowel unaccented (*an-udātta*). By the rule "After *svan* and *han*, [the suffix] *ap* [is optionally used]," the suffix *ap* is applied, and the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*) remains. In the case of *paṭaha*, derived from the sense "it is struck while making the sound *paṭat-paṭat*," it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group and is oxytone (*antodātta*). By the rule "After *svan* and *han*, [the suffix] *ap* [is optionally used]," the suffix *ap* is applied, and the accent of the verbal root remains. In the case of *paṭaha*, derived from the sense "it is struck while making the sound *paṭat-paṭat*," it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group and is oxytone. Regarding *nadī*: by the rule "From *śā* and *śap*, [the suffixes] *dan* and *au* [are added]," the suffix *nadaṅ* is listed among the *pacādi* group; because of the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in *nadī*. Here, the accent is that of the "cessation of the acute" (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*).

The word *poṣa* ends in the suffix *ghañ*; *dṛṣat* is derived from the root *dṛ*, with the suffix *adi* and the substitution of *ṣu* for the root vowel and its shortening—its accent is that of the suffix; *samit* is that by which one is kindled, formed with the suffix *kvip* because it belongs to the *sampad-ādi* group—its accent is that of the original form of the final member of the compound. These are various [instances of] accents, and this [rule] is an exception to them.
Thus ends the first quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent.

In this context, that which has undergone a modification must have its original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) prescribed. Now, it is not the case that a modification characterized by the *śeṣanighāta* (the low-pitched accent for all remaining syllables) applies to the entire preceding member (*pūrvapada*); rather, it applies only to the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents residing therein. Therefore, the term "preceding member" (*pūrvapada*) refers specifically to those two [accents]. This is what he expresses with the words "the mention of the preceding member," and so forth. By the phrase "for when there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound," etc., he demonstrates the occurrence of the modification.
