This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, because it is commenced before that [general rule] has already taken effect.

But surely, an exception (*apavāda*) occurs where a specific rule operates independently of the operation of a general rule, as in the case of *karmaṇyaṇ* and *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*. However, here, since the state of being the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is to be enjoined when a modification (*vikāra*) would otherwise have occurred—and since that occurrence of modification applies to the compound—how can this [rule] be an exception to it, given that it depends on its operation? Therefore, it is more logical that this is an exception specifically to the elision (*lopa*) that would have been obtained once the rule *samāsasya* had operated. This is not so.

If this were an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for elision (*nighāta*), he would have stated it right there: "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the preceding member is unaccented, with the exception of one [word]. Now, if this were not stated, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the natural unaccentedness of the preceding member in cases such as *samapādaḥ* would be prohibited; for what reason? Because a rule or a prohibition applies only to what immediately precedes. Therefore, since this is begun immediately after the rule "of the compound" (*samāsasya*), it is an exception specifically to that.

But has it not been said: "How can there be an exception (*apavāda*) to that which depends upon its very application? It is replied: the destruction of the primary cause (*nidāna*) makes possible the destruction of that which possesses the cause (*nidānin*). And the fact that the final member of a compound is accented (*antodātta*) is the cause for the modification of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-vikāra*), which is characterized by the placement of the remainder (*śeṣa-nighāta*). Therefore, by the absence of that [cause], the non-application of the compound-final-accent itself—which serves as the cause—is declared in this case.

But surely, if various word-accents were thus obtained, then because the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound (*samāsāntodātta*) is introduced, its non-application would result in both the preceding and following members of the compound retaining their original accents (*prakṛtisvara*). For if that were the case, the rule "not [for] a *bahuvrīhi*" (*na bahuvrīheḥ*) would preclude the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. Alternatively, let there be the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound; or let there be the preclusion of the remaining rules (*śeṣavidhāta*). However, subsequently, by means of the phrase "retaining their original accent" (*prakṛtyā*), that specific accent is prescribed for the preceding member, prior to the application of the rule for the remaining cases (*śeṣavidhātāt prāk*).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Alternatively, by the word "by its original nature" (*prakṛtyā*), when a specific accent is indicated, this meaning follows: in a *bahuvrīhi*, whatever is the natural accent of the preceding member—such as being acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) and so forth—that remains. Thus, just as when it is stated that "the beginning of the preceding member becomes acute," there is no dependence on the application of the rule "of the compound" (*samāsasya*); in the same way, this [rule] is appropriately understood as an exception (*apavāda*) to that. For example: *kṛṣṇo mṛgaḥ* ("a black deer"); that whose skin is a black antelope skin is called *kṛṣṇājina*.

The word *brahmacārin* has its final syllable accented (antodātta) by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent of the second member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). Thus it is recited: "The student (*brahmacārī*) wanders among those who hate the objects of the senses. In such cases as "Whose student are you? (*kasya brahmacāry asi*), the suffix is *ṇini*; however, the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member does not occur, for that [suffix] is intended to belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* because it is listed among the *pravṛddha* group. In the *Vṛtti*, however, the phrase "by virtue of the original accent of the second member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix" is merely illustrative. Another says: according to the rule "in the Veda, the beginning and the end [may be accented]," it has the final syllable accented.

The meaning here, however, is as follows: in the expression *brahmacārī* ("one who moves as Brahmā"), the first member of the compound is a comparison (*upamāna*). Consequently, by the rule that "the comparison [is treated as such] only when it constitutes the base form of the word's meaning," the accent remains that of the base form of the final member of the *kṛt*-derivative. As for the word *snātaka*, it ends in the suffix *-kan*; it is listed among the *yāva*-type words in the sense of "one who has bathed upon completing the Veda."

From the root *man*, with the suffix *uṇ* and the augment *ṣuk*, we have *manuṣya*. Now, if this rule for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) were to subvert the accentuation of the final syllable of a compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*), it would also subvert it even when the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*), for its application there too cannot be prevented by anything. Furthermore, a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), when it operates, subverts a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) even when both are possible, just as the giving of buttermilk (*takradāna*) supersedes the giving of curd (*dadhidāna*). Therefore, he says: "The mention of 'acute' (*udāttagrahaṇa*)," and so forth.

This point is also established by logic: for whom a modification (*vikāra*) has occurred, for him the original state (*prakṛtibhāva*) must be prescribed; and the occurrence of a modification applies only to the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents. For this very reason, it was stated previously that [the vowel] exists as either acute or circumflex.

Regarding the term *samabhāga*: the word *sama* is derived from the root *su* with the suffix *ḍamap*, and is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*). Now, one might object: even if the accentuation of the final syllable of a compound does not apply here, the word *bhāga*—by virtue of the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ*—is oxytone; therefore, the compound *samabhāga* will necessarily be oxytone as well. Consequently, this is merely shown as an illustrative direction; one should rather cite *samapāda*, for the word *pāda* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.

But for what purpose is this stated? [It is said] so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member may occur, and not the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*). [One might argue: "The rule *nañ-subhyām* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that if an oxytone accent occurs in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, it happens only after *nañ* and *su*. [Response: This is not so. Even if the restriction excludes the rule prescribing the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound when there is a possibility of various word-accents (*nānāpadasvara*) arising, there remains the contingency that both the preceding and following members would alternately (*paryāyeṇa*) undergo their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

Because the rule *śitinirantābahvac* is for the purpose of restriction—meaning that if, in a *bahuvrīhi*, the final member (*uttarapada*) remains in its original form (*prakṛti-svara*), it must follow specifically after *śiti*—the restriction expressed by *nañsubhyām* would not be applicable. This is because in cases such as *anudaraḥ* and *sūdaraḥ*, a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is possible, since it serves to override the default rule whereby the penultimate syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is acute (*udātta*) when used in a derogatory sense (*kṣepa*).

This rule—"śiti-nitya-bahvac"—would also be restricted by the rule "śiti-nitya-bahvaj-eva," thereby removing the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*) only in cases such as *śītilalāṭa* and the like, but not in cases such as *citragu* and so forth; therefore, this [present] rule must indeed be commenced.

However, the mention of *bahuvrīhi* could have been omitted; why does [the rule] not apply to a *tatpuruṣa*? It will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for the *tatpuruṣa*: namely, that [the suffix] occurs in a *tatpuruṣa* only after words such as those meaning "equal" (*tulyārtha*), etc.—that is, only in a *tatpuruṣa* where the first member means "equal" and so forth; or only in the case of "merchants" (*vāṇija*) when the object is "to be traveled to" (*gantavya*); or only in the case of *dvigu* compounds when the subsequent members are those beginning with "gone" (*gata*), etc. Why does it not apply to a *dvandva*? This will serve as a restrictive rule: namely, that [the suffix] occurs in a *dvandva* only in the case of a *dvandva* consisting of a plural of *rājanya*.

Why does [the rule] not apply in the case of *avyayībhāva* compounds? It will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—namely, that *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *apa* [occur] only in *avyayībhāva* compounds. However, the reverse restriction would not apply everywhere; for the operation of a grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is never for the sake of something unintended.

Even so, if the mention of the *bahuvrīhi* were not made, then because the accentuation of the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*) and the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) would have the same scope and would be in conflict, an alternation (*paryāya*) would result in cases such as *tulyaśvataḥ* and *pañcāratni*. For a restriction has been established for *tatpuruṣa* compounds and the like, stating that "only those first members whose meaning is 'equal' (*tulyārtha*) and so on receive their original accent, and no others"; it does not state that "in *tatpuruṣa* compounds and the like with first members whose meaning is 'equal' and so on, the first member must exclusively retain its original accent."

Now, because no specific distinction is perceived, there would be a restriction for both [types of compounds]: that in *tatpuruṣa* compounds and others, only those beginning with "tulyārtha" (having the same meaning) and so forth are included, and in them, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member alone applies. And thus, while the rule *bahu anyatarasyām* is in effect, the option *diṣṭivitastyośca* is prescribed; this is so that in cases such as *pañcadiṣṭiḥ* and *pañcavitastiḥ*, the rule *igante dvigau*—which mandates the constant application of the original accent of the first member—should not apply. Even so, in the case of *bahuvrīhi* compounds like *citraguḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the accent] applying alternatively. This is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

When [the rule] "yadayam dvitribhyāṃ pādadanmūrddhasu" teaches an optional final acute accent (*antodāttavikalpa*) for [compounds] such as *dvipād*, it indicates that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final acute accent does not occur optionally. Even so, this indicator would apply only to the domain of the acute accent (*udātta*), [implying]: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final acute accent occurs optionally. Furthermore, what would follow? There would be the undesirable consequence of optionality when the acute and circumflex (*svarita*) accents reside in the preceding and following members [of the compound].

Furthermore, it is not appropriate for that which is based on the acute (udātta) [vowel] within a circumflex (svarita) to serve as the indicator (jñāpaka), for the designation "acute" applies to vowels (ac), and a single part of a phoneme (varṇaikadeśa) is not grasped [as a vowel]. If, however, setting aside the distinction caused by being a phoneme or not being a phoneme, one were to state the indicator as referring to what follows the perception of an acute [vowel], then the mention of the *bahuvrīhi* compound could have been omitted.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the first member retains its original accent when it has the sense of "equal to" (*tulyārtha*), or when it is a word ending in the third case, the seventh case, or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), or when it is a word ending in the second case, or a gerundive (*kṛtya*). Pāṇini 6.2.2.
The phrase "the word *sadṛś* also," and so forth, refers back to [the rule regarding] the original accent of the final member in a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).

The phrase "the word *kumuda* also," and so forth, is explained as follows: when it ends in the suffix *kap*, it is oxytone by the rule *thāthādisvara*; thus, in the rule *anudāttasya ca yatro dātalopaḥ*, the form *kumudvān* is cited as an example, and it has been stated that "words such as *kumuda* are oxytone. However, when it is treated as an underived (non-etymological) form, it is stated that it is ādyudātta by the rule *nabviṣayasya nisantasya*.

Another says: the word *kumuda* when referring to a water-born lotus is neuter, whereas the word *kumuda* used for a particular kind of monkey is masculine; here, the example cited refers to the water-born [lotus], while in the rule *anudāttasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.159), it refers to the monkey.

Regarding the words *dūrvākāṇḍa* and *śarakāṇḍa*, etc., this is shown as an instance where the first syllable would otherwise be obtained [as udātta]; however, by the rule *ṣaṭ ca kaṇḍādīni* (Pāṇini 6.2.135), the initial syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) should be udātta there.

Regarding the phrase "of *nañ* and particles": although [the accentuation] is already established by the fact that they are particles (*nipāta*), the explicit mention of *nañ* is for the purpose of overriding even the subsequent accent of a *kṛt*-suffix in cases such as *akaraṇi*. Thus, in *avyathī*, where *nañ* is mentioned together with a *kṛt*-suffix, the accent belongs to *nañ* alone; likewise, the accent of *nañ* is stronger than the accent of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). As for the mention of *ku*, it is because it is not included among the *cādi* group; however, it ought to be included there, otherwise it would not receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), since it is also not listed among the *svarādi* group.

Regarding the term *snātvākālaka*: this belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. If that is so, it will be recited in that very list as having its final vowel udātta. Even so, an explicit enumeration must be made [of such cases] so that in examples like *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done") or *svayandhautam* ("self-washed"), the original base (*prakṛti*) does not become subordinate. Why does [the rule] not apply here: *paramaṃ kārakaṃ paramakārakam*, *parameṇa kārakeṇa paramakārakeṇa*, *parame kārake paramakārake*? For there is no restriction stating that a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consists only of words ending in the nominative case.

Therefore, the objection is that the preceding word (*pūrvapada*) ends in the second case (*dvitīyā*) and so forth. The resolution, however, is by means of the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*: this accent applies to those compounds where the third case and so on are employed *pratipadam* (i.e., specifically prescribed for each individual rule). This [present compound], however, is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) formed without specifying a particular case ending.
In the case of *varṇa*, [the elision of the final vowel occurs] before all vowels. 6-2-3.

Because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 6.2.175] *anete taiti* and because of the mention of the plural number, there is no taking of the actual form (*svarūpa-grahaṇa*) in the case of the subsequent member; by association with that, the same applies to the preceding member as well. The word *kṛṣṇa*, ending in the suffix *naṅ*, is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable). However, according to the *Phiṭ-sūtras* (specifically Phiṭ-sūtra 2.28), *kṛṣṇasyāmṛgākhyā cet*, it is oxytone in the Vedic language when it is not a name of a meter; otherwise, its being ādyudātta (having the acute accent on the first syllable) is established.
The sixth case ending is used after the words *gandha* and *lavaṇa* when they denote quantity. 6.2.4.

Regarding the term *samyag-ādham*: the root *gādh* means "to stand firm" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*). That which is stood upon is a *gādha*; it belongs to the class beginning with *ardharca*. "Limitation of extent" (*iyattā-pariccheda*) refers to the delimitation of quantity. Here, the word for action is taken as the word for measure (*pramāṇa*), rather than in its conventional sense of spatial dimension. This is the meaning.
The word *dāyādya* takes the substitution [of *yat*] when it occurs in the sense of "an heir. (Pāṇini 6.2.5)

*Dātavyaḥ* means that which is to be given—a portion, a share; such is the meaning. One who takes the inheritance (*dāya*) is an *dāyāda*; the suffix *ka* is applied here because the word belongs to the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*. The state of being an heir is *dāyādya*. But what is this? It is either the taking of the inheritance or a relationship connected to it. However, in this context, the word *dāyādya* is used specifically to denote that which is being received as an inheritance.

"Now," and so forth. This refers to the intention that is about to be stated. He reveals that very point with the words "if it is thus. Regarding the phrase "only as characterized by the *śeṣa* (remainder)": the meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is that here the genitive case is used solely in the sense of the general relation (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and not according to each specific rule (*pratipada*). If the genitive here is indeed only in the sense of the *śeṣa*, he asks, "For what purpose, then, is it prescribed there again? and answers with "But of that [genitive]... First, the locative must be prescribed, because it has not been previously established.

In that case, if that very [genitive] were to be prescribed, then, because it would be specifically prescribed, it would be understood as an annulment of the genitive characterized by "remainder" (śeṣa); lest this be understood, that same genitive characterized by "remainder" is again permitted, but the meaning is that it is not being prescribed as something previously unestablished.
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the roots *prati-bandh* and *cirā-kṛ*, provided that the action is performed with difficulty. || 6.2.6 ||

It is called *pratibandhin* because it obstructs the accomplishment of the task; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). It is a descriptive compound (*viśe�ṣaṇasamāsa*). Now, one might object that such a compound occurs only when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), yet that is not present here, since the word *gamana* denotes "going" and the word *cira* denotes "time. This is not a fault, for in this context the word *cira* refers to a going that takes a long time to occur. Furthermore, this is a *mayūravyaṃsakādi* type of compound.

The meaning is that "going" (*gamana*) alone is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), whereas "long time" (*cira*) and "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) are its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, in order for the substantive to be placed first [in the compound], it must be accepted as belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. He establishes that the first member of the compound expresses the sense of an obstacle by saying, "For going," and so forth. Indeed, because of a deficiency in the means, the going occurs after a long time and is associated with difficulty; "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) means suffering, and that which is associated with it arises as an obstacle to the accomplishment of the task.
In the case of *pada* and *apadeśa*. (Pāṇini 6.2.7)
*Accāraḥ*—the act of purification.
In *nivāta*, meaning "protected from wind. (Pāṇini 6.2.8)

Others maintain that [the word *kavi*] ends in the suffix *ḍyak* and is oxytone; they study the rule as *kavater ḍyak*. The letter *ḍ* does not receive the designation *it*, because the letter *k* is an *anubandha* intended to prohibit *guṇa*.
The word *śārada* is used when it does not refer to the season. 6-2-9.

In the example *rajjudhṛta*, the word *rajju* [is used]; in *dṛṣatpiṣṭeṣu*, the word *dṛṣat*. Thus, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound whose analysis (*vigraha*) does not contain its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). In the rule *sṛjer asum ca*, the phrase "and the elision of *sa*" (*salopaḥ*) from the preceding rule *skandeḥ salopaśca* is understood to carry over; therefore, this suffix *asum* follows the final vowel of the root *sṛj*. When the elision of *sa* occurs and the semivowel substitution (*yaṇādeśa*) takes place, and the *jaś*-substitution of the *s* of *asum* is applied, the form *rajju* is produced.
The suffix *jāti* is applied after the words *adhvaryu* and *kaṣāya*. 6-2-10.
"Of restricted objects" means they are determined by specific coverings (varaṇa).
The [taddhita suffix] *ya* is applied after the words *sadṛśa* and *pratirūpa* when expressing similarity. 6-2-11.

The mention of *sadṛśa* (resembling) is redundant because of the rule for the third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). A compound with the word *sadṛśa* is called a third-case compound by the rule "the words *pūrva*, *sadṛśa*, *sama*, and those having the sense of *artha* [form a compound with a word ending in the third case]. In that case, it is already established by the rule "in a third-case compound, the preceding word retains its original accent" (*tṛtīyā-pūrva-pada-prakṛti-svara*) that the desired result is achieved; therefore, he says: "and for the sake of the sixth-case compound. Since the sixth case is also prescribed when used in connection with words having the sense of "equal," the mention of *sadṛśa* is for the purpose that [the rule] should apply even when a compound is formed with that sixth case.

But surely, because it is not prescribed [by Pāṇini], the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) will not occur; for our goal is to achieve threefold expression—namely, *mātuḥ sadṛśaḥ*, *mātrā sadṛśaḥ*, and *mātṛsadṛśaḥ*—and this is indeed accomplished even without the genitive compound. To this he replies with the words "here," etc.: since a specific form exists when there is no elision (*aluk*), the genitive compound must necessarily be formed; and for that purpose, the inclusion of the term *sadṛśa* (resembling) is necessary here.

If this is so, then the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* (similar) applies to the third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*), as in: *vidyā-sadṛśaḥ* ("one similar to knowledge"). For in this case, there is no genitive sense (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*), but rather a third-case sense; the meaning is "similar by means of knowledge" (*vidyayā hetunā sadṛśaḥ*), where another person such as Devadatta serves as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Another says: even in the absence of elision (*aluk*), the third-case compound is employed—as in *manasā-sadṛśaḥ* ("similar to the mind") when forming a name (*saṃjñāyām*). Regarding the phrase "in this case," etc. [the commentary continues].

From the root *daśi*, meaning "to bite" or "to touch," the suffix *ṭap* is applied according to the rule *daṃśeṣṭo na ā ca*; the *na* is replaced by *ā*. Because of the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added; the *u* of *yasya* is elided, and the vowel becomes udātta according to the rule *anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ*. From the word *vṛṣala*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied as a characteristic of a genus (*jāti*).
In a Dvigu compound, when it denotes a measure, [the final vowel is acute]. 6.2.12.

In the rule *kardamādīnām ca*, the term "beginning with" (*ādi*) from the preceding sūtra—*makara-kukkuṭa-kuṭa-pārevata* and so forth—is understood to carry over. Now, regarding the second [sūtra], *prāg īpāt*: here, the mention of "second" (*dvitīya*) is for the sake of excluding the first. [The example] *paramasaptasamam* [is explained as follows]: it is a *dvigu* compound in a collective sense (*samāhāre dviguḥ*), and it is neuter because it belongs to the *pātrādi* group; however, in the original example [of the previous sūtra], it is a *dvigu* where the subsequent member expresses a derivative meaning (*taddhitārthe dvigur uttarapadam*).
Or merchandise intended for transport [is exempt] for a merchant. 6.2.13.

*Vaṇija* means "trader"; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *prajñādi*. These [compounds] are locative (*saptamī*) compounds, formed by the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "after a word ending in the seventh case. However, *govāṇija* and others are genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds.
The word *mātrā* is used in the neuter gender when it signifies a measure, an offering, or shade. 6-2-14.

By the first method, the word *samudra* indicates the entire group of four sūtras beginning with *śāntanavīyam*. In that context, the word *samudra* has an udātta accent on the final syllable because it belongs to the *gāgara* class.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *sukha* and *priya* when they denote something beneficial (*hita*).

"These are compounds of apposition (samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa). He considers that because "going" and so forth function as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), they should be placed first [in the compound]. However, if "pleasure" (sukha) and "dear" (priya) are the qualifiers, then one must accept that the compound belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. "In the future" (āyatyām) means in the end, in the coming time—that is to say, in the time yet to come.
And [the suffix *kta* is used] in the sense of pleasure (*prīti*). 6.2.16.

In this case, however, one should formulate the sūtra as "in *sukha* and *priya*" and then state "and in *hita*. Since in the first sūtra (*sukhapriyayoḥ*) the word *prīti* (joy) will be understood precisely because it is never absent from *sukha* and *priya*, he says: "Regarding *sukhapriyayoḥ*," and so forth. The word *brāhmaṇa* ends in the suffix *aṇ*. The word *chāttra* ends in the suffix *ṇa*, according to the rule *chattrādibhyo ṇaḥ*. The word *kanyā* ends in a circumflex accent (*svarita*), because it is listed in the *phiṣ* [section] with the statement: "The finals of *tilya*, *śikya*, *martya*, *kāśmarya*, *dhānya*, *kanyā*, *rājanya*, and *manuṣya* [are circumflex]."
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the word *pati* when it signifies sovereignty over [a group]. (Pāṇini 4.1.87)

Regarding *dhānyamantaḥ svaritam*, this is according to the *phiṭ-sūtra* recited immediately following [the previous rule]. As for *gav-ādi* and so forth, however, the statement of their accentuation has already been made previously.
The suffix *didhiṣu* does not occur after the words *bhū*, *vāk*, or *cit*. 6-2-19.

In the compound *bhūvādīnām*, which is a collective dvandva, the neuter short vowel [is applied]; here, because there is a prohibition of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, the Vṛttikāra has explained the accentuation of the preceding members. Among those, the first three end in the suffix *kvip*. The word *didhiṣūḥ* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word ending in the suffix *kū*, as stated in the rule: "andū, dṛbh, bhū, jambū, kaphelū, karkandhū, and didhiṣū."
Or [the suffix *ṇya* is applied] after the word *bhuvana*. (Pāṇini 6.2.20)
The word *bhuvana* is grammatically correct in the vernacular due to its frequent usage.
In cases where there is a proximity of apprehension and affliction, the neutral state (*samā*) is applied. (6-2-21)

The root *śaki* means "to doubt" and *bādhṛ* means "to agitate"; from these two, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). *Nedīyaḥ* means "very near," being the superlative form of *antika*; [this is according to] the rule *antikabāḍhayornedasādhau*. "The determination of existence" (*astitvādhyavasāyaḥ*) is "the certainty of existence" (*astitvaniścayaḥ*). "Fears of going" (*gamanāśaṅkādayaḥ*) and so forth are either *viśeṣaṇasamāsa*s (descriptive compounds) or belong to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* (irregular compounds).
The word *pūrve* [is used] in the sense of "formerly occurred" (*bhūtapūrva*). 6-2-22.

"Rich in former times" (*āḍhyo bhūtapūrvaḥ*) refers to one who was previously rich; this is how he is described. Regarding "here," etc.: "supreme and formerly" (*paramaś cāsau pūrvaś ca*). This sentence-meaning, characterized by being honored, is what is intended here by the compound in this example. "But not" (*na tu*): [in the case of] "supremely formerly" (*paramo bhūtapūrvaḥ*). This sentence-meaning, which takes the form "he was formerly supreme," does not constitute a compound there. For what reason? He says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*), in the sense of *hi* (for/indeed).
The [taddhita] suffix *cha* (i.e., *īya*) is applied after the words *savidha*, *sanīḍa*, *samaryāda*, *sasīmā*, and *savedika* when expressing proximity (*sāmīpya*). (Pāṇini 5.2.23)
In the examples, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*); the accentuation of *madrā-* and the others has already been stated previously.
The words *vispaṣṭa* and others [are used as adjectives] when expressing qualities. 6.2.24.

Regarding the word *vispaṣṭa*: from the root *spaś* in the sense of "afflicting" or "touching," the form *spaṣṭha* is derived in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule beginning with *vā dānta-*. It forms a *gati-samāsa* with the prefix *vi*. The root *cit* belongs to the *curādi* class in the sense of "making variegated. From this, with the suffix *erac*, we derive *citra*; with the prefix *vi*, it becomes *vicitra* (a *prādi-samāsa*). The root *citī* means "to perceive. One whose perception (*cita*) has departed is *vicitta*. The root *añjū* is used in the sense of "manifestation" and so forth; when preceded by *vi*, its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) takes the accent of the *gati* [prefix]. In that case, the *yaṇ* substitute for the vowel *i* becomes an *udāttayaṇ*.

Regarding the word *sampanna*, [the udātta accent] is by the initial vowel of the following word (*athādi*). It does not, however, take the accent of a *gati* (preverb). What is the reason? Because the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is understood to carry over there [from the previous rule], whereas this [suffix] *-kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). As for the words *paṭu* and *paṇḍita*, [the udātta accent] is by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). They are expected to be oxytone (*antodātta*). Having changed the number of that which was introduced in the singular, the connection must be made as "they are both oxytone."

From the root *pāṭ* (to split), the suffix *u* is applied according to the rule "pharipāṭinamijanīnāṃ gukpaṭinākidhaśca," resulting in the substitution of *paṭi* for the root; the letter *i* is for the sake of pronunciation, hence *paṭuḥ*. From the root *paḍi* (to go), with the suffix *niṣṭhā*, we have *paṇḍitaḥ*. From *kuśān lāti* (he takes up the kusha grass), *kuśalaḥ*; from the root *lā* (to take). As for the word *capala*, it is [derived] by the accent rule *citsvara*; it is expected to be oxytone (*antodātta*). The phrase "after *cit*" continues [from the previous rule], as seen in the rule "vṛṣādibhyaścit. Regarding the word *nipuṇa*, etc., the connection is as before. From the root *puṇ* (in the sense of action) with the prefix *śubhe*.

In a *karmadhāraya* compound, when the final member denotes a state (*bhāva*) and begins with *śraji-*, *avama-*, *kanyā-*, or *apava-*, [the first member retains its original accent]. (Pāṇini 6.2.25)

In the examples, the qualifier is placed first because it belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group. [The suffixes] *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* [are applied after a word denoting excellence]; for *praśasya*, [the substitute] *śra* is used, and for *yuvan* and *alpa*, *kan* is optionally substituted. [Thus we have] *pāpiṣṭha*; here, the *vin* and *mat* suffixes are elided. And [the word] *kumāra* [is also placed first]. 6.2.26.

Regarding the term *kumāraśramaṇa*: by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning the qualification of gender, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the word *kumārī* when in a compound. From the root *kumāra* in the sense of "playing" (*krīḍā*), the suffix *ac* is added according to the *pacādi* group, resulting in *kumāraḥ*. However, some [commentators] say that because the particle *ca* is present here, it serves to include this very same type of formation as a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The initial [vowel] of [the word] *pratyenas* [is elided]. 6-2-27.

Regarding the term *pratigata enasā*: it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule that words such as *ava*, *prati*, etc., are compounded with a word in the third case when they have the sense of "deficient" (*kuṣṭa*) and so forth; however, in the second analysis, it is a *bahuvrīhi*. But how is the acute accent (*udāttasvara*) obtained without explicitly mentioning the word "acute"? To this he says: "The word 'acute' (in the rule)... He demonstrates the very necessity [of this] by saying: "In the preceding word... For the word *prakṛtyā* is understood [from a previous rule]; the connection there is as follows: the accent which was established by the state of being a base-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the preceding word *kumāra* becomes the initial [accent] here.
In a *dvigu* compound, the feminine suffix is applied when the final member is *iṅguda*, *kālakapāla*, *magāla*, or *śarāva*.

"Those in which the suffix *aṇ* has been elided" (*kṛtāṇapratyayalopāḥ*): those in which the suffix *aṇ* has undergone elision are so described. Why [is the condition] "in a *dvigu* compound" (*dvigau*) stated? [Consider] *paramaśarāvaḥ*; this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). However, in a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member would necessarily apply. Regarding the rule for the original accent of a stem ending in an *ik* vowel (*iganta-prakṛtisvaratve*), there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the cases of *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitution—such as *pañcāratnayaḥ* and *daśāratnayaḥ*. Since this accent "in a *dvigu* ending in an *ik*" would not apply once *yaṇ* and *guṇa* have been performed, he says "of *yaṇ* and *guṇa*" and so forth. [This applies] prior to the production of case-endings (*prāk subutpatteḥ*).

The vowel substitution (*svara*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions are external (*bahiraṅga*) because they depend upon a case-ending (*sup*). Or rather, it is due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor is there an absence of the status of being a substitute here in the rule for vowels, because this is not a substitute for a letter (*alopa-ādeśa*). As for the example *pañcāratnyaḥ*, this is a Vedic usage; in that context, the *guṇa* [substitution] does not occur by the rule *jasi ca*, because of the statement: "In the Veda, the application [of the rule] is optional in the case of *jas* and other endings."
The plural may optionally be used for the word *bahu*.

The word *bahu* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). This is because it is derived from the root *bṛh* with the suffix *ku*, according to the rule "landhibṛhyorna lopaśca" while the rule "kurbhuśca" is in effect.
The seventh case ending is used after a word denoting time when it follows words meaning "accomplished," "dried," "cooked," or "bound. (Pāṇini 2.2.32)

Regarding the suffixes ending in *ṇya*: in the list beginning with *vuñ* and *chaṇ*, the suffix *ṇya* is applied after words such as *saṅkāśa*. The suffix *kak* is applied to the root *av*; by the rule *jvaratvara-*, etc., the augment *ūṭh* is added, resulting in *ūkaḥ*. From the words *kumbha* and *kalaśa*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for generic names (*jāti*). The word *bhrāṣṭra* is derived from the root *bhrasj* with the suffix *ṣṭran* and the application of *vṛddhi*. The word *cakra* is derived from the root *kuñc* with the suffix *rak* and the doubling of the consonant.

Regarding the passage beginning with *saptamīsvara*: in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound formed with words having the sense of "equal" (*tulyārtha*), etc., the *prakṛtibhāva* (original accentual status) of the word ending in the locative case is superseded by the *thāthādi-svara* (the accentuation rule for suffixes such as *tha*, *atha*, etc. because it is of higher priority. However, where the reading is *kṛtsvareṇa bādhita tha-iti*, the meaning is that it is superseded by the accentuation of the *kṛdanta* (words ending in *kṛt* suffixes) characterized by the rule for *thāthādi*.
The suffixes *pari*, *prati*, *upa*, and *apa* [are karmapravacanīyas] when they signify exclusion (*varjyamāna*) with respect to parts of days and nights. 6-2-33.

"Paritrigarttam": the meaning is "excluding the Trigarttas. *Apa* and *pari* receive the designation of *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of exclusion (*varjane*). The ablative case is used according to the rule *pañcamyagāṅparibhiḥ*. The compound is an *avyayībhāva* according to the rule *apaparibahirañcavaḥ pañcamyā*. *Sauvīra* and others are also specific names of regions. "Pratipūrvāhṇam": this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*. "Upapūrvāhṇam": this is formed in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpye*) according to the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti...*. What, then, [is the difference]?

The example for the exclusion [of the rule] has been cited only for *apa* and *pari*, not for the other two; regarding this, he says: "In that case. Now, why are the parts of day and night (*ahorātrāvayavāḥ*) not cited as examples for the other two, *apa* and *pari*? To this he says: "The parts of day and night also. Regarding the phrase "in *parivanam*": this is the scope (*avakāśa*) of the rule *pari-praty-upa-apa-* (Pāṇini 2.1.12), namely *paritrigartam*; whereas the scope of the rule *vanaṃ samāse* (Pāṇini 6.2.178) is *pravaṇam*. In the case of *parivanam*, the rule *vanaṃ samāse* prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedhena*).

And here, the reason is its status as an exception (*apavāda*), not its contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*). Since the formation of a compound would already be established by the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*) alone, the purpose of the repeated mention of "forest" (*vana*) is this: for the sake of setting aside those other exceptions to it. Just as it sets aside both the accent of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and the accent of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, so too will this [mention of *vana*] set aside [the present rule].
In a dvandva compound consisting of multiple words denoting Kṣatriyas, the name of the first member retains its original accent when the members belong to the Andhaka or Vṛṣṇi clans.

The reading *śvāphalkacaitrakarodhakāḥ* is an erroneous recitation. For in a three-word *dvandva* compound, the accentuation required for the preceding member applies only to that specific word; consequently, the assignment of the acute accent (*svaravacana*) to the word *caitraka* would be untenable. Therefore, the correct reading is *śvāphalkacaitrakāścaitrakarīdhakāḥ*. However, one instance of the word *caitraka* was omitted by scribes due to the fear of redundancy. As for the word *śini*, it is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), because the suffix *nin* is applied to the root *śi* with a short vowel by virtue of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*).

Regarding the phrase "in their offspring": although the word *śini* is the subject under discussion, since it is impossible for that word itself to have offspring, the meaning is "in those who are the offspring of Śini, who is a Kṣatriya. "By way of non-difference" means by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). Now, one might object: because of the rule stating that the term for a king's offspring denotes the caste (*jāti*), the word *rājanya* expresses the Kṣatriya caste; therefore, [the terms] *dvaipya*, *bhaimāyana*, and so forth...

Thus stated, the counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) is not tenable, because they too are Kṣatriyas; therefore, he says: "The mention of *rājanya*, etc. The sense is that since the status of being a Kṣatriya is never absent in the case of the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis, the mention of *rājanya* is for the purpose of including the specific category already mentioned.
Number [is compounded with another number]. 6-2-35.

Regarding "ekādaśa": the word *eka* is placed first because it is the smaller number [according to Pāṇini 2.2.35]. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 6.3.76]: "In the Veda, [the final vowel of] words ending in *eka* is long before the numbers beginning with *daśan*. Regarding "dvādaśa": the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel of *dvi*] occurs according to [Pāṇini 6.3.47]: "The substitution of *ā* takes place for *dvi* and *aṣṭan* when followed by a number."
And a pupil is [designated] by means of the name of his teacher. (Pāṇini 6.2.36)

That whose subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is "teacher" (*ācārya*) is *ācāryopasarjana*. One who dwells at the end [of his teacher's life] is an *antevāsī*; the absence of elision (*aluk*) occurs here by the rule *śayavāsavāsiṣvakālāt*. Furthermore, this designation is figurative (*gauṇa*). Those constituent words of the *dvandva* compound are so called because they denote a subordinate teacher and because they denote a resident pupil. The *dvandva* consisting of those parts is also so called by virtue of the property of its constituents. It has already been stated previously that the suffix *iñ* does not apply after the word *pāṇini*.
Nor does it apply after the word *rauḍhi*, due to the prohibition: "not after a two-syllable [word], nor after [names of] Easterners or the Bhāratas."

The inclusion of the term *ācāryopasarjana* is a qualifier of the *dvandva* compound; it is not a non-qualifier as in the previous case. The nominative case, however, should be understood in the sense of the locative. Why, then, is it understood as a qualifier of the *dvandva*? He says: "so that the entire *dvandva* [is affected]," lest it apply here—whereas if it were a qualifier of the prior member (*pūrvapada*), it would apply even in this instance.
And [the suffixes] *kārttakīja* and so forth [are applied after the word *pāda*]. 6.2.37.

Regarding the phrase *prakṛtisvarapūrvapadāḥ*: the word *prakṛti* here signifies "natural" (*svābhāvika*). Those whose accent is natural are *prakṛtisvarāṇi*; thus, the term *prakṛtisvarapūrvapadāḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those [compounds] which have such [naturally accented] words as their prior members. Examples are *kṛtasyāpatyam* ("the descendant of Kṛta") and *kuñjasyāpatyam* ("the descendant of Kuñja"). These two end in the suffix *aṇ*, since the suffix *aṇ* is applied after these two because they denote seers (*ṛṣi*). The etymological derivation of the latter member is incidental; however, the derivation of the prior member itself must be shown for the sake of establishing its accent. The word *māṇḍūka* ends in the suffix *ḍhak*, according to the rule *ḍhak ca maṇḍūkāt*.

Regarding *avantyaśmakāḥ*: the word *avanti* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). From it, by the rule *vṛddhet-kosalājādāñ*, the suffix *añ* is applied; since it denotes a king (*tadrāja*), there is elision (*luk*) when referring to many [inhabitants]. The country inhabited by the Avantis is the meaning of the base; for the suffix *aṇ* used in the sense of "born there," there is elision when referring to a country. From the word *aśmaka*, the suffix *iñ* is applied by the rule *sālvāvayava-* etc.; the elision and so forth are as before. Regarding *śyāparṇī*: from the group beginning with *śārṅgarava*, the suffix *yañ* is applied, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīn*. Regarding *kapir antodāttaḥ*: this is by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). The root *kam* (in the sense of "desire") takes the suffix *ktic*; by the rule *pṛṣodarādi*, the vowel *a* is changed to *u*.

The word *kunti* has its accent on the final syllable; the *Kuntis* are like the *Avantis*. One whose kingdom is excellent is *Surāṣṭra*; his many descendants [are called] *Saurāṣṭras*, following the rule for the suffix *añ* after a word denoting a tribal territory (*janapada*) belonging to the Kṣatriya class, with elision (*luk*) and so forth as previously explained. From the root *cit* (in the sense of "to remember"), with the suffix *ktic*, we have *cinti*; those who think like Kunti are *Cintis*. From the root *taḍ* (in the sense of "to strike"), we have *Taṇḍa*; from that very same root, because it begins with the letter *v*, we have *Vataṇḍa*, where the vowel *a* is elided according to the rule: "Bhāguri effects the elision of the *a* of the prefixes *ava* and *api*. From the root *mad* (in the sense of "joy"), with the suffix *kta* preceded by the prefix *vi*, there is no substitution of *n* according to the rule "not in the case of *dhyai*, *khyai*, etc."; thus, one who is not intoxicated is *Avimatta*.

*Śalaṅku* and *śalaṅkaṃ*: this is recited among the *ṇaḍādi* group. The offspring of *Babhru* is *Bābhravaḥ*; [the suffix] *aṇ*. One who has fallen from giving is *Dānacyutaḥ*; his offspring is likewise *Dānacyuta* [with the suffix *aṇ*]. The word *kaṭa* ends in the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* class); one whose eyes are in the world (*loke*) is *Lokakṣaḥ*;
his offspring is *Laukākṣiḥ*; his pupils are *Laukākṣāḥ*. *Strīkumāram*: this is a collective *dvandva* compound.

*Mud* means joy; by the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied, resulting in *mudaḥ*. *Pippalādaḥ* is derived from *pippalam atti* (he eats the pippala fruit), using the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇyaṇ*). From the root *vad*, the suffix *sa* is added, yielding *vatsaḥ*. From the root *jṛ*, the suffix *atṛn* is added, yielding *jaran*. These two form a collective dvandva compound.
By the rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo’ṅ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied, resulting in *jarā*. From the roots *bhuj* and *mṛ*, the suffixes *tyu* and *tyuk* are respectively applied, resulting in *mṛtyuḥ*.

The suffix *cha* (forming the feminine *ī*) is applied after the words *mahat*, *vrīhi*, *apara*, *ahna*, *gṛṣṭi*, *iṣvāsa*, *jābāla*, *bhāra*, *bhārata*, *helihila*, *raurava*, and *pravṛddha*. 6-2-38.

The word *mahat* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*), because of such a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) in the rule *pṛṣadbṛhanmahat* [Pāṇini 6.2.101]. Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*) and so forth: this is obtained through the technical paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a definition versus that which is taught by its own form. If this is so, the mention of *pravṛddha* would be redundant, since the desired result would already be established by the rule to be stated later, *aniṣṭhā karmadhāraye* [Pāṇini 6.2.46], and because the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix includes even those preceded by a non-agentive factor, as the word *pravṛddha* ends in a *kta* suffix. To this he says: "This [rule] *aniṣṭhā karmadhāraye* also..."

In that case as well, by the technical rule regarding terms mentioned by their specific definitions (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), the meaning is that there is a reference to that *karmadhāraya* compound which is mentioned by its specific definition through a word ending in the suffix *-kta*.
And the *kṣullaka* [sāman] is used in the *vaiśvadeva* [stotra]. 6-2-39.

One who takes hunger is *kṣulla*. [The suffix] *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in long *ā* when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it; then, by the rule *tor li*, the letter *t* is replaced by its homogeneous substitute (*parasavarṇa*).
The word *uṣṭra* [takes the suffix *aṇ*] when compounded with *sādi* or *vāmya*. 6.2.40.

The word *uṣṭra* ends with the suffix *ṣṭran*. This is because, while the suffix *ṣṭran* is in force [after the root] *uṣ* "to burn," it is derived according to the rule *uṣikhanibhyāṃ kit* ("after the roots *uṣi* and *khan*, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied as *kit*").
The word *go* [is substituted for *gavi*] before the suffixes *sāt*, *ādi*, and *sārathi*. (Pāṇini 6.2.41)

Regarding *gosāda*: [the word] *sāda* is derived from the root *sad* with the suffix *ghañ*; then, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is formed. Alternatively, it is said that [it means] "one who causes the cow to sit" (*gāṃ sādayati*): here, the suffix *ṇic* is added to the root *sad*, followed by the suffix *aṇ* for the object; and from that very [root with *ṇic*], the suffix *ṇini* is applied, resulting in *gosādī*. In this case, there is an exception to the accentual rule (*kṛtsvara*) for both *sāda* and *sādin*, whereas in the case of *sārathi*, it is an exception to the accentual rule of the compound (*samāsasvara*).
The words *kurugāri*, *hapata*, *riktaguru*, *asūta*, *jaratī*, *aślīla*, *dṛḍharūpa*, *pārevaḍava*, *taitilaka*, *drū*, *paṇyakambala*, and those ending in *dāsībhāra* [form neuter nouns]. 6.2.42.

In this context, there are seven compounds beginning with *kurugārhapatya* and ending with *paṇyakambala*. Among them, the first two lack case endings (*vibhakti*), while the others end in the nominative singular. That nominative case should be understood as standing in place of the genitive by way of a transposition of case endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). Regarding the expression *dāsībhārāṇām*, the plural indication is explained as having the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi-artha*).

From the roots *kṛ* and *bhṛ*, and from *kṛ* and *gṛ* with the suffix *ru*, we have *kuru*. From the root *vṛj* (in the sense of "avoiding"), under the governing rule that *ni* is applied to roots ending in an *it*, the suffix *ki* is added, resulting in *vṛji*. However, according to the rule *phiṣi tu igantānāñca dvyacām*, when the suffix *phiṣ* is applied, the final syllable of two-syllable words ending in an *ik* vowel is udātta. Its meaning is as follows: the term *janapada* (country) is understood from the context, as is the option between the penultimate or the final syllable being udātta. Thus, for two-syllable names of countries (*janapada*) ending in an *ik* vowel, the first syllable is udātta or the last syllable is udātta—such as *kāśayaḥ* and *cedayaḥ*. By this, the word *kuru* is explained.

*rikta-pūrva-ādayaḥ* are *karmadhāraya* compounds. The word *śrī*, in the sense that "she possesses *śrī*," denotes beauty (*lāvaṇya*). Because [the word] belongs to the *kapilaka*-class, there is the substitution of *la* for *ra*; this will be explained under the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ*. Thus, one who possesses *śrī* is expressed by the word *śrīla*. He establishes this very point: "for she is not lacking in beauty, nor is her form unfirm. She is beautiful merely by way of her physical configuration (*saṃsthāna*), because of the absence of deformities such as hunchbackedness and because of the firmness of that configuration. He shows what is excluded by the word "merely" (*mātra*)—namely, that she is not "devoid of *śrī*"—and he clarifies this very meaning by stating: "she is devoid of *lāvaṇya*."

Regarding the form *taitilina*: the suffix *ini* is added to the word *tila* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). Due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the syllable *ti* is reduplicated. In that context, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*) occurs by the rule *na-staddhite*. However, when it is applied in the sense of a student (*chātra*), the elision of the final vowel occurs by means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) beginning with *nāntasya ṭilope*. Those who read the word *taitili* in that [list of *pṛṣodarādi*] words analyze the formation here as well as *taitilinaḥ apatyam*, and the derivation of the form is established through the *pṛṣodarādi* category itself. The word *paṇya* ends in the suffix *yat* (as in *avadya-paṇya-ya*), and by the rule *yataḥ anāvaḥ*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.

"Paṇyakambalaḥ" [is used] as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). This is the designation for a woolen blanket (*kambala*) of fixed dimensions and unrestricted price. [One might ask: "But since the word *paṇya* ends in a *kṛtya* suffix, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a word meaning 'equal' (*tulyārtha*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member should apply according to Pāṇini 6.2.2; why then is it said that the final syllable of the compound is acute? To this he replies: "For regarding what is explicitly stated... That accent applies only in the case of a *kṛtya* compound that is explicitly prescribed by the rule "A *kṛtya* compound with a word denoting a non-genus (*ajāti*) is called *tulyākhyā*" (Pāṇini 2.1.68). In that specific instance, that accent occurs.

But this [term] is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), as prescribed by the general rule (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because the word *kambala* is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*). For the rule *kṛtyatulyākhyā ajātyā* is intended to ensure that a word ending in a *kṛtya* suffix takes the first position when there is an unrestricted possibility of prior placement for words expressing qualities or actions; it is not for the purpose of prohibiting genus-words. The statement "provided it is not a genus-word" (*ajātyā*) is merely a restatement of a meaning established by logic; such is the settled conclusion. Furthermore, in the case of *mithuna*, the suffix *asi* is applied after the root *māṅ* with *candra* as the object, according to the rule *candre māṅo ḍicca*, and it is treated like the preceding [suffix].

The suffix *asi* is understood from the preceding context as applying to all [cases]. When the word *candra* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *asi* is applied to the root *māṅ* (to measure), and it becomes *ḍit*. Because it is *ḍit*, there is elision of the vowel (*ṭilopa*). That which is measured like the moon is *candramāḥ*. The word *candra* refers to silver and nectar. Alternatively, that which is measured as "the moon" is *candramāḥ*. As for the word *candra* itself, it ends in the suffix *rak* according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*.
By the rule beginning with *yasya tatpuruṣasya*, he shows that the group beginning with *dāsībhāra* belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class.
The fourth case ending is used for that which is for the sake of that [denoted by the word in the first case]. 6.2.43.

"tasmai idam" means "for that purpose"; by the word "tat," the meaning of the dative case-ending is expressed, as he says: "that which is for the sake of the object denoted by that. The meaning is: "for the sake of that which is denoted by that [word] ending in the dative case. It is called a *ratha* (chariot) because those situated upon it rejoice (*ramante*); [the suffix] *kyan* is applied after the roots *hani*, *kṛṣi*, *nī*, *rami*, and *kaśi*; there is the elision of the nasal according to the rule "anudāttopadeśa..."; and the word *vallī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* belonging to the *gaurādi* group.

What is the purpose of the phrase "for that purpose" (*tadartha*)? [The answer is: as in *kuberabali* ("an offering for Kubera"). Since the state of being "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) exists here, they consider *gosukha* ("cow-comfort") to be a counter-example. It is intended that this accentuation applies only when there is a relationship between a material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). This has been properly established in the section on compounds (*samāsa-prakaraṇa*), and he will provide an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for it here as well.
In the sense of "in the matter of" (arthe). 6-2-44.

The meaning is that only the specific instances (viśeṣa), such as wood, gold, and so forth, become "for that purpose" (tadartha). That is to say, wood, gold, and the like, being specific instances themselves, serve that purpose. For "being for that purpose" (tādarthya) consists in being a subordinate element (śeṣabhāva) to it, and that [subordination] belongs only to specific instances, not to the universal (sāmānya); this is what he considers.

"But some," and so forth. They think as follows: "This is not a royal decree—that only specific [words] have that [particular] meaning; therefore, even when the word *artha* expresses a general sense, the formation is established by the previous rule alone. Regarding *aśvaghāsa*: one might object, "It has been stated that a compound occurs when there is a relationship of material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) by means of the word *tadartha*; thus, *aśvaghāsa* and others are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). To this they reply: "When it is established here that the relationship of material cause and modification applies to the word *sva*, then there is a fault even in the case of a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) such as *aśvaghāsa*. Regarding *śvaśruśvaśuram*: neuter gender is applied by the rule beginning with *vibhāṣā senā*.
And [the substitution of *k* occurs] before *kte*. (Pāṇini 6.2.45)

"It is given for the sake of the cows, protected"—thus, the fourth case (dative) is used in the sense of the recipient (*sampradāna*). Now, what fault is there in using the fourth case in the sense of "for the purpose of" (*tādarthya*)? [One might argue: because the accent is already established by the rule *caturthī tadarthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.36). This is not a valid example; for how could the accent apply here when it was stated that it occurs in the relation of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*)? And yet, there is no such relation of material cause and modification here. True; however, this was shown as the purpose of including the word *rakṣita* in the rule prescribing compounds (*samāsa-vidhi*).
In a karmadhāraya compound, [the feminine suffix] aniṣṭā [is not applied]. 6-2-46.

The word *śreṇi* is derived from the root *śri* (meaning "to serve") with the *auṇādika* suffix *nin*. The words *pūga* and *gaga* are derived from the roots *mud* and *gras* respectively; because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *gak* is also applied to the root *pū*, resulting in *pūga*. Regarding the term *kṛtākṛtam*: this is a compound formed by the rule "a negative (*nañ*)-qualified [word] with a *kta*-ending word that is not itself negative. If the condition "not being explicitly taught" (*anihṣṭa*) were not stated here, this very compound would fall under the rule, for it is directly taught (*pratipadokta*) as a specific formation following the *śreṇyādi* group, since it is prescribed by the technical designation *kta*.
The accusative case ending is used for what is not excluded [from the action]. 6.2.47.

*Hīna* means "abandoned. [The rule] *ahīnayācini samāse* (P. 6.2.153) refers to a compound; by way of the first member (*pūrvapada*), that compound possesses the sense of "not abandoned" (*ahīna*). Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the word] *anupasarga* (a non-prefix) [is required]," the meaning is that one should remove the mention of *ahīna* and instead employ the mention of *anupasarga*, because it is more comprehensive (*vyāpaka*). "Ihāpi mā bhūt" means "let it not occur even here. If the mention of *anupasarga* were made here, the word *khaṭvārūḍha* would not need to be included among the *pravṛddhādi* group, because the word *ārūḍha* is a prefix-possessing (*sopasarga*) form. This is because, in the absence of this specific accent, the final acute (*antodātta*) would already be established by the accent rule for *thā-thādi* compounds (P. 6.2.144).
The third case ending is used for the object of the action. 6.2.48.

This is also an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule concerning the accent of *thā-thā* and so forth. Regarding the statement "the word *ahi* is udātta at the end": the suffix *ḍi* is applied to the root *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, and the vowel of *āṅ* is shortened. Thus, *ahiḥ* means "it strikes others" (*āhanti parān*) or "it is struck by others" (*āhanyate paraiḥ*). Regarding the phrase "some [teachers]": they carry forward the mention of the term *udātta* from that context; accordingly, they recite it as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), as in the examples: *ahan ahim* ("he slew the serpent") and *ahir iva bhogaiḥ* ("like a serpent with its coils").
The word *gati* is immediately preceding [the verb]. (Pāṇini 6.2.49)

Because of the masculine designation in the word *anantaraḥ*, the word *gati* is derived from the root with the suffix *ktic*; furthermore, the nasal is elided by means of a formal irregularity (*nipātana*), as in the words *prakṛtaḥ* and *prahṛtaḥ*. Here, although the following would have applied—the accentuation of the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*), the preservation of the original accent of the first member when preceded by an indeclinable (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*), the accent of the suffix *kṛt* (*kṛtsvara*), and the accent beginning with *thā-tha* (*thāthādisvara*)—the rule prescribing the preservation of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtibhāva*) is enjoined.

"This [suffix] does not apply when there is an intervention in the application. But surely, the mention of "nirdiṣṭa" (specified) is for the sake of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), and by the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the word *hṛta* ends in a *kta* suffix; so how could that which is prescribed after a *kta*-ending form apply to something separated [from it], given the maxim regarding the mention of a *kṛt* suffix?

If it is argued that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word *ud* [being included] because of its entry into the category ending in a *kta*-suffix, then even if the mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) were made, this would still occur; for the word *uddhṛta*, being a *kta*-suffix form, has *gati* immediately following it. This is not a fault, because by the force of the mention of "immediate," the *gati* immediately following a verbal root (*dhātu*) will be understood as the intended referent.

[Objection: Even so, since the rule *gatir gatau* (P. 8.1.70) is subsequent [in the order of the Aṣṭādhyāyī], the *nighāta* (elision of accent) will occur here; and when that occurs, because of the governing scope of the rules for the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member cannot apply anyway. Therefore, the mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) need not be made for the purpose of excluding those cases separated by an interval; rather, it is for the purpose of ensuring the application to immediate cases. And in that regard, where there is only one *gati* [particle], this [mention of "immediate"] serves no purpose.

However, where there is more than one *gati* [prefix], that [rule] does not apply; by the rule *tānantaraḥ*, when there is a concurrence of multiple *gatis*, the immediately preceding [word] would be subject to the application [of the accent]; and by the rule *tadanantaraḥ*, when there is a concurrence of multiple *gatis*, the immediately following [word] is obtained [as the subject]. Otherwise, in the case of *abhyuddhṛtam*, since the word *uddhṛta* ends in the suffix *kta* according to the *paribhāṣā* regarding the inclusion of *kṛt*-suffixes, the final member of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*) would apply; then, in its exception (*tadapavāda*), the accent of the *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛtsvara*) would apply; and as an exception to that, the accent beginning with *āthādi* (*ādyudātta*) would result.

Now, one might object: "Just as in the first compound the accent of *thā-thādi* (P. 6.2.144), which was superseded by the *gati*-accent (P. 6.2.49), is again applicable in the second compound, so too the *gati*-accent, which is an exception to that, will likewise apply here again. This is not so, because [in this case] there is no prior word (*apūrvapadatvāt*).

In the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, for the application of word-level operations (*padakārya*) to "niṣkrānta" and the others, the term *sup* (the nominal suffix) must be understood as carrying over; since singularity is intended there, and because a collection of items ending in *sup* is not itself *subanta*, simultaneous compounding of the two is not obtained, and thus this [compounding] must be prescribed sequentially. By the rule *gatikārakopapadānām*, [the status of] the final member [is also determined].

The compound is stated to occur prior to the production of the suffix *su*; it does not apply to the first member (*pūrvapada*) alone, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word-formation operation (*padakārya*) failing in cases such as *niṣkrānta-carmakārāt*. Therefore, the compound of the word *ud* occurs first; subsequently, the compound of the word *abhi* occurs with the word *uddhṛta*. Consequently, the word *abhi* alone is the first member (*pūrvapada*), and not the word *ud*.

Since the rule "the first member [of a compound] does not have the word *ud*" prohibits the *prakṛtisvara* (original accentuation) of the first member when it is prescribed for a *gati*, this would not apply to a case where there is no first member. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) is for the purpose that the *prakṛtibhāva* (retention of the original accent) may occur even for what is not the first member—or for that which is immediately following—by means of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), thereby overriding even the *thāthādi-svara* (accentuation rules such as P. 6.2.144) that resides in another section. Thus he says: "But it is desired in the case of what is immediate."

If this were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the sequence of verbal roots (*kāraka-pūrva*). In the example *dūrād āgataḥ prāpto devadattena* ("Devadatta has arrived from afar"), when the compound *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena* is formed with the word *āgata*, one would expect the accent of the *thā-thādi* group in that state; however, even setting that aside, the accent of the initial syllable (*apūrvapada*) itself would result instead. This is not a fault, because the inclusion of the term "motion" (*gati*) in the rule *thā-thādi-sūtra* will be restricted; consequently, in cases such as *prakṛtam ityādi*, since the accent of the suffix *kta* itself is what applies, that alone [remains].

This is an exception to the accentuation of the *gati* [prefix], but it does not entail the application of the accentuation rules for *thā-thādi* [compounds]; in those cases, that very rule will apply. Furthermore, in instances such as *abhyuddhṛtam*, where even at another level (*kakṣā*) the accentuation of the *kṛt*-suffix alone is applicable, that very rule will likewise apply. Consequently, there is no need to formulate a separate rule for the subsequent member of the compound.

How so? When the accent of the *gati* [particle] has already taken effect upon the word *uddhṛta*, and subsequently the compound with the word *abhi* is formed, the rule *gatir gatau* (P. 8.1.70) applies the *nighāta* (elision of accent) to the preceding *gati*. Because this occurs within the governing scope (*adhikāra*) of the rules for acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents, the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of original form) of the preceding member *gati* does not apply. Consequently, the *kṛtsvara* (accent of a *kṛt*-derived word), which is an exception to the general accent of a compound, takes effect; and by the technical rule regarding the mention of *kṛt*, since the word *uddhṛta* ends in a *kṛt* suffix, its accent will simply be the acute accent of the syllable *uc* (the first part of *uddhṛta*). This would be the case even if the mention of *gati* were excluded from the rule *thāthaghana...* (P. 6.2.144).

Regarding the term *prabheda*: by the accent rule for *kṛt* suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), because the suffix *ghañ* has the marker *ñ*, the verbal root would become udātta; however, an udātta on the final syllable is desired. If that is so, then the mention of *gati* (preverb) continues [from the previous rule], but it is not connected with *kta*. Therefore, how is it that the mention of *kta* must be separated from the rule *thāthadikkitktyānām* and removed from there, and in that place the mention of *gati* will be withdrawn? Even so, in cases such as *viśuṣka*, where the word ending in *kta* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) denoting the agent—as in the rule *śuṣkadhṛṣṭau* and so forth—the initial part [of the compound] is treated accordingly.

However, in the case of a word preceded by a *kāraka*, because it is taught later [in the rules], only the accent of the *thā-thādi* group occurs, as in *dūradāgataḥ*. [If the rule were applied otherwise,] the first syllable would be udātta due to the *dinā* [rule]; in that case, while the *kṛtsvara* (the accent of a *kṛt*-suffix) would apply, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would become udātta on its first syllable, whereas it is desired to be udātta on the final syllable. Therefore, even by the mention of *kṛt*, the mention of a "motion" (*gati*) must necessarily be connected; and consequently, the aforementioned defect would follow. To this, he says: "But in the case of one preceded by a *kāraka*... and so forth.

The intended meaning is as follows: this word *anantara* functions in dependence upon what is immediately preceding it; and when it is stated that "the immediately preceding [member] is *gati*," by virtue of proximity, even that which is not immediately preceding is understood to be a *gati*. Consequently, the inclusion of the term *anantara*—even though its referent has not been previously mentioned—effects the *prakṛtisvara* (original accentuation) of the immediately preceding member only when two *gatis* are in conjunction. Thus, there is no fault in examples such as *dūrādāgataḥ* ("come from afar").

Alternatively—in the rule *kārakāddattaśrutayorevāśiṣi*—"from a *kāraka*" (*kārakāt*) is to be separated [and applied elsewhere]. There, the mention of the suffix *kta* (*ktaprahaṇa*) is understood to follow from the previous rule, as are the terms "ending in an acute accent" (*antodāttaḥ*) and "a *gati* word" (*gatiḥ*). The meaning is that a subsequent member ending in *kta* following a *kāraka* becomes acutely accented on its final syllable. In that regard, since in examples such as *dūrād gataḥ*, the acute accent on the final syllable is already established by the rule *thāthādisūtra*, this rule *kārakāt* is understood to be an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of a *gati* word prescribed by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*—which applies specifically to an immediately preceding *gati*—by means of the inclusion of the term "immediately preceding" (*anantara*), which serves to exclude the meaning of a non-immediate prior member, as seen in cases like *dūrād āgataḥ*.

If this is the case, the mention of "immediately preceding" (*anantara*) need not be made. For how could, in the absence of that mention, the rule *kārakāt* (P. 6.2.148) serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—applying when a second compound has been formed in all instances such as *abhyuddhṛta-taila* and so on, where only the accent of the suffix *thāthadi* (P. 6.2.144), being the "remaining" (*atiśiṣṭa*), would otherwise be obtained? Furthermore, in that context, the term "motion-word" (*gati*) must be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, the meaning here is: "Only when following a kāraka, a final member ending in a *kta*-suffix that is accompanied by a motion-word is acutely accented on the final syllable.
Thus, in cases such as *abhyuddhṛta*, once the accent of the *thāthadi* class is excluded by this restrictive rule...

By virtue of the rule regarding *kṛt*-suffixes (*kṛtsvara*), because the word beginning with *uddhṛta* is a *kṛdanta* (ending in a *kṛt* suffix), its accent—namely, the initial acute (*ādyudātta*)—will indeed occur. Now, one might suspect that the restriction could be reversed: namely, that "only that which is accompanied by a prefix (*sagatika*) follows a case-factor (*kāraka*). If that were so, in the example *pūrvāhṇa-śuṣka*, the accent of *śuṣka* and *dhṛṣṭa* (as prescribed by the rule *thāthādisvara*) would result in an initial acute due to the *kṛtsvara*. This is not a fault; for the Teacher’s practice indicates that the restriction is not reversed, as he [states] this: [The text continues: "If this..."

He says that the rule applies only when *datta* and *kṣuta* follow [the word] in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). For if the restriction were otherwise, there would be no possibility of the final syllable of any other *kta*-ending word being udātta when *datta* or *kṣuta* follow a *kāraka* (agentive noun); therefore, there is no purpose in including the mention of "immediately following" (*anantaram*) for the sake of the meaning of the preceding word.

If that is so, then the inclusion of the word "immediate" (*anantara*) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] when there is an intervention. But has it not already been stated that, because the rule *gatir gatau* (P. 8.1.70) is subsequent, once the suppression (*nighāta*) has been effected, the occurrence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of original accent) does not even arise due to the governing scope of the rules concerning acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) accents? In that case, the occurrence [of the *prakṛtibhāva*] would apply where the suppression by the rule *gatir gatau* does not take place. And where does that [suppression] not occur?

Regarding "at the beginning of a pāda": for he will state that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "not at the beginning of a pāda" extends until the end of the chapter on pādas. Thus, in the example *caupapretakuśitāścetadhvam*, the word *upa* at the beginning of a pāda is recited as acute even though it signifies motion (*gati*). Similarly, in the case of *abhyuddhṛtam*, when the word *abhi* occurs at the beginning of a pāda, there would be no elision of the accent (*nighāta*), and by this [rule], the original accentuation (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the *gati* would apply even when it is separated [from the verb]. This is not so; because, according to the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*), the word *hṛta* is understood as ending in the *kta* suffix, whereas *uddhṛta* is not.

In that case, this [rule] makes it known that when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, the inclusion of a preceding *gati* or *kāraka* also takes place. Now, it might be objected: "It has been made known that when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, there is the inclusion of what precedes a *gati*, but how can it be said that there is the inclusion of what precedes a *kāraka*? To this we reply: first, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) was indeed established by the ancient teachers; here too, by means of the mention of the immediately preceding [element], the entire sense of the technical rule is made known through a partial indication.

If, when there is the mention of a *kṛt* suffix, there is also the inclusion of that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, how can *samuddhṛtaḥ* be given as a counter-example? For the word *uddhṛta* ends in a *kta* suffix, and *sam* is immediately before it. To this he says: "Because of the lack of purpose in mentioning 'immediate' (*anantara*). The sense is that here, because the mention of "immediate" has the result of excluding what is separated [by other words], this rule serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the *paribhāṣā*; thus, the result is obtained even at the end [of the compound]. In the example *prakṛtaḥ kaṭam*, the suffix is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca*.
And [the substitution of *n* for *t*] occurs before suffixes beginning with *t*, *n*, *i*, *kṛt*, *tya*, and *tu*. (Pāṇini 6.2.50)

Regarding the term *prajalpāka*: [the suffix] *ṣākan* occurs after the root *jalpa*. Here, the accent (*svara*) is prescribed for a *gati* (preverb). Furthermore, the designation *gati* applies when there is a connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), and a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an action. Of roots, two types of suffixes occur: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. Among these, since a preceding member is impossible in the case of a *tiṅ*-ending word, [the accent] will apply only to a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix; thus, there is no purpose in explicitly mentioning *kṛt*. However, this is the purpose: so that the mention of *ta* (in the rule *ta-ādy-anta-t*) may be understood as a qualifier of *kṛt*, meaning "in a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *ta* which has an indicatory *n*" (*nitī kṛtī*). Otherwise, by the rule *nitī* alone...

By the paribhāṣā regarding the inclusion of that which ends in a suffix, there would be the presentation of that very [suffix], and thus the qualification "beginning with the letter *t*" would apply only to that final member (*uttarapada*). Consequently, this [rule] would apply only here: *prataritā* and *prataritam*; it would not apply here: *prakartum*.

This purpose is not necessary; for even if the mention of *kṛt* were made, an undesirable result could still be understood [from the rule] "when a *nit* suffix follows a *kṛt* suffix," as in the case where the subsequent word begins with *ta*. And even if it were not made, the desired result would follow from the understanding that "the subsequent word ends in a *nit* suffix beginning with *ta*. Consequently, just as in the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*, the vowel *u* is qualified by the mention of "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) and not the suffix itself, so too here, the mention of "beginning with *ta*" (*tādi*) will serve as a qualifier for the *nit* suffix alone. To this, he replies: "The mention of *kṛt* is for the sake of [specifying] those [suffixes] beginning with *ta* in their original instruction (*upadeśa*)."

This is the intended meaning: by the inclusion of the term *kṛt*, it is understood that "that which begins with *t*" refers to the form at the time when the designation *kṛt* applies. He asks: what is accomplished by this? To this he replies: "In this case also. If the inclusion of *kṛt* were not there, then by the inclusion of "beginning with *t*," it would be understood as "that which begins with *t* at the time of the application of the accent"; consequently, in forms such as *pralapitā*, once the augment *iṭ* has been added, the rule would not apply because it no longer begins with *t*. However, due to the inclusion of *kṛt*, it does apply.

The inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning), however, could have been omitted, according to the principle: "In a rule where a designation is made with reference to a beginning, that which is designated is understood as starting from that point. [One might ask: "How is it that the meaning 'the final syllable becomes udātta' is obtained even without the explicit mention of the word *udātta*?
