[The answer is: It is thought that the term *prakṛtyā* (by its original accent) is understood here; thus the connection is made as follows: "Whatever accent belonging to the base (*prakṛti*) was applicable to the element ending in the suffix *tavaī*, that [accent] now belongs to the final syllable," and that [accent] is specifically the *udātta*.
The word *yugapat* (simultaneously) is for the purpose of excluding successive occurrence (*paryāya*).
The augment *an* is applied before the suffix *vap*, provided that the root ends in *añc*.

Regarding the term *vapratyaya*: that which has the phoneme *va* as its suffix (*pratyaya*) is so described. Regarding *prāṅ*: by the rule *ṛtvig-*, etc., the suffix *kvin* is applied; and this [suffix] consists of the phoneme *v* alone, because the phonemes *k* and so forth are merely indicatory markers (*anubandha*). By the rule *ugidacām*, the augment *num* is added; then the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) applies after the *hal-ḍyādi* rule. By the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*, there is the substitution of guttural (*kutva*)—the phoneme *ṅ* for the phoneme *c*. Regarding *parāṅ*: the word *pāra* is acutely accented (*ādyudātta*); therefore, the rule *svarito vānudātte 'padādau* does not apply here. Regarding *pratyaṅ*.

But surely, since the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply here by virtue of its being an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) ought to occur because the stem no longer ends in *i*; for the rule "not ending in *i*" (*anigantaḥ*) finds its scope in examples such as *pratīcaḥ*, where, due to the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*, there is an absence of the *yaṇ* substitution. Nor can there be the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original) for the *yaṇ* substitution, because it is not a rule concerning something previously established (*apūrvavidhi*). Furthermore, since the rule ordains that the accent of the preceding member remains its original (*prakṛtisvara*), [the author] therefore teaches the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for the prefix *adhi-* in the case of *nyadhīca*.

This indicates that this vowel does not belong to the domain of *yaṇ*. If it were so, then in the case of *adhy-aṅ*, it would already be established by this very rule. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*), for this [rule] might be intended for cases such as *adhīca*, where there is no *yaṇ* substitution. Furthermore, since the word *ni-* consists of a single syllable (*ekāc*), there is no distinction between the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) and the subsequent accent in forms such as *nīca*. Therefore, the fact that [the rule] prescribes the original accent for *ni-* serves as the indicator.

Even this is not a proving indicator (*jñāpaka*). By the force of the statement itself, this [prohibition] would apply to the word *ni-* for the sake of its accent (*svara*) even before the internal (*antaraṅga*) *yaṇ* substitution has taken place; for once the *yaṇ* substitution has occurred, there is no longer any element that possesses the accent. However, in cases such as *pratyaṅ*, the *yaṇ* substitution itself prevails because it is the internal operation. Therefore, a prohibition regarding the scope of *yaṇ* must be stated. It need not be stated, for it is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). But was it not said that "the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member does not belong to what precedes the *yaṇ*"? This is not so. For it has been stated that the word "preceding member" (*pūrvapada*) refers to that which occurs when the preceding member is accented acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*).

Regarding *coriti*: the fact that the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is prescribed to be udātta is indicated here by the word *cu*. Thus, the meaning is "due to the accent of *cu*" (*cusvarāt*). The sense is that this accent prevails by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope (*avakāśa*) of the *cu*-accent is seen in forms such as *dadhīcaḥ* and *dadhīcā*, where there is no possibility for the accent of the non-*aniganta* [non-terminating in *-añc*] rule to apply. The scope of the non-*aniganta* accent is seen in forms such as *parāṅ*, *parāñcau*, *parāñcaḥ*, and *pāraca*, and so on. When both would apply simultaneously, the accent of the non-*aniganta* rule alone prevails because it is subsequent in the order of rules (*paratvāt*).

This contradiction is not tenable; for how can it be said that the *cu*-accent is "remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*) when it is stated as *cau*? It occurs where this form exists, namely when a suffix conditioned by the designation *bha* follows and the elision (*alopa*) has been performed. If this is so, then this contradiction was not put forward; rather, this is a desired rule (*iṣṭi*), for it is desired that this accent apply according to the rule: "In *cau*, after a root ending in a consonant and not having *u* as its penultimate letter, when no suffix follows."
And [the suffix *ṇi* is applied] after the word *nayati*. 6.2.53.
Regarding "adhīca": here too, he shows that this very [term] is intended to have the kṛtsvara accent.
The suffix *ka* may optionally be applied after a word meaning "slight" (*īṣat*) when it is used with another word [in apposition]. 6.2.54.

In cases such as *īṣadbheda*, however, the accent of the entire compound indeed occurs, because of its higher status [in the order of rules]. Another, moreover, says: since the rule *īṣadakṛtā* refers to a compound that is explicitly mentioned (*pratipadokta*), the application of the rule for upapada compounds does not take place here.
The word *hiraṇya* takes the neuter gender when it denotes a measure of gold.

The phrase "denoting a measure of gold" means that it denotes gold as qualified by its specific measure. In this context, the word *suvarṇa* refers to the measure itself, and when used with a qualifying prefix (*upapada*), it refers to the gold delimited by that measure—just as the word *prastha* and others refer both to the measure fashioned from wood and to the rice or other grains measured by it. Five *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one *māṣa*; sixteen of those [māṣas] constitute one *suvarṇa*; four *suvarṇas* constitute one *pala*; and two *suvarṇas* combined form a *dvisuvarṇa*, such as a vessel or similar object.

Regarding the phrase "the measure of two *suvarṇas*": here, the word *suvarṇa* refers to a weight-measure (*upala*). As for the expression "gold-wealth" (*kāñcanadhana*): if one were to say simply "gold" (*hiraṇya*) without mentioning the measure, it would apply here as well, because the word *kāñcana* denotes gold; however, this [word *suvarṇa*] does not denote gold, but rather a specific measure.
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, [the word] *katara* and *katama* [are placed first]. (Pāṇini 2.2.57)

Regarding the passage beginning with *iha tu*: the rule *katarakatamau jātiparipraśne* (Pāṇini 2.1.63) prescribes a *pratipada-samāsa*; it is that [compound] which is intended here, and it is indeed a *karmadhāraya*. Therefore, the intention is that the mention of *karmadhāraya* in the rule is not for the sake of the augment *iṭ*. [This concludes the discussion on] *rājā ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.59).

Regarding the example *rājābrāhmaṇaḥ*: because the word *rājan* is applied to a Brāhmaṇa due to his similarity [to a king], it forms a *karmadhāraya* compound through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Since the word *rājan* ends in the suffix *kanin*, it is acute-accented on its first syllable. The reason for making a separate rule is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that this prescription may apply only to the word *rājan* and not to the word *ārya*. Furthermore, the absence of a sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyā*) is also a purpose for making a separate rule, though that much has not been explicitly stated here.
The sixth case ending is used [in apposition] with a word meaning "enemy" (pratyenasi).
The term *pratyenāḥ* belongs to the king; the suffix *ul* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in the genitive case, when expressing reproach."
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of what is constant (*nitya*). (Pāṇini 3.2.186)

The word *nitya* occurs in the senses of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) and "immovability" (*kauṭasthya*); here, however, it refers to repetition. Why is this so? Because it is stated that [the suffix] *kta* is used, and it is stated that *kta* follows a verbal root; furthermore, *kta* is prescribed after a verbal root, and a verbal root denotes an action. Since action is momentary, immovability is not possible. Therefore, the word *nitya* here signifies repetition. This is a compound with the second case ending (*dvitīyā-samāsa*).

The second [interpretation], however, concerns continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Alternatively, according to the rule "time, state, distance, and the path to be traversed are designated as the object (*karman*) when [the verb] is otherwise intransitive," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), and so forth. But when the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), then by the rule "an immediately preceding *gati* [is unaccented]," it becomes acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the original accent of the first member of the compound. The accent of the compound (the *samāsasvara*) sublates the accent of the first member being original (*dvitīyā-pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*); that [sublation] is further sublated by the accent of the *thā-tha*-class; and this [latter] is the exception (*apavāda*) to that.
The word *grāma* [is used] in the sense of an artisan. In this rule, *grāma* is taken as its own form (*svarūpa*).
And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is used after a word ending in the genitive case] when expressing praise of a king. 6-2-63.

Regarding the phrase "and in a genitive compound": the word *praśaṃsā* (praise) is to be supplied [from the previous rule]. By the phrase "because of his suitability for a king," it is meant that he, being skilled in action, becomes fit for a king. Furthermore, when the expression *rājārhaḥ* ("fit for a king") is used, praise is understood.
The first syllable is acute-accented. 6.2.64.

In the case of the word *pūrvapadaka*, there is here a transformation of the sixth case [ending] due to the sense of the context; or rather, throughout this section, in the domain of the *pūrvapada*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the sixth case.
The seventh case is used for the agent in the sense of "taking away" when the object is something that can be maintained [in one's possession]. 6.2.64.

The suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of "necessity" (*avaśyaka*) after the root *hṛ*. In the term *gharmya*, there is an inclusion of the meaning; because of the prohibition of taking away (*haraṇa-pratiṣedha*), by association with that, the meaning "that which must be maintained" (*dhārī*) is included. Regarding the phrase "fixed by custom" (*ācāraniyata*): it is fixed by custom (*ācāreṇa niyatam*), meaning it is necessarily to be performed due to the force of custom. But how is it "pertaining to that" (*tāddharmyam*)? To this he says: "For custom (*dharma*) is established practice (*anuvṛtta ācāra*). This means it has been handed down through tradition (*paramparāyāta*) within a country, a village, a school (*caraṇa*), or among the Kurus.

Therefore, [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule "that which does not deviate from that is *dharmya*" (Pāṇini 4.4.92), or by the rule "in the sense of *dharma*, *pathin*, *artha*, etc. Alternatively, [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule "after *nau*, *vayas*, *dharma*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.3.120). In cases such as *yājñikāśva*, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

By the rule beginning with "and *cit*" (Pāṇini 5.1.121), he shows the fixedness of the practice regarding the giving of items such as *śāṇa*. [The phrase] "of the sacrificers (*yājñika*) and others, [the items] such as horses (*aśva*)" implies that these are "to be given" (*dātavya*).

In some cases, this practice is established as follows: that which is called *varddhitaka* is a lump of boiled rice, thick at the base and thin at the tip; it is given to a laborer so that he might perform his work, for otherwise he would not do so. However, this is not the Dharma. *Bījāvāpa* means the sowing of seed, that is, conception (*garbhādhāna*). Regarding "the taking of the *vāḍava*": in some cases, this practice is established such that after the sowing of the seed, suitable food and other sustenance must be given to the *vāḍava* for the sake of nourishing the body.

The word *haraṇa* is derived as a noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*). Here, when this accent has ceased and the general *kṛt*-accent would otherwise apply, the rule *ano bhāvakarmavacanaḥ* causes the final syllable of the second member to be udātta. Now, one might object: "Since this accent is subsequent [to the previous rules], it will simply prevail; so what is the purpose of the prohibition regarding *haraṇa*? To this he replies: "Even though it is subsequent," and so forth. In this context, the accent of the preceding members has not been mentioned because it serves no purpose.
And [the suffix *ktvā* is used] when there is a connection [between two actions]. (Pāṇini 3.4.21)

Words such as *vallava* and others denote the guardians of cows (*gavādi*) and so forth. *Maṇinda* means "one who gives curds" (*mathaṇiṃ dadāti*); it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations]. *Gosaṃkhya* means "one who counts the cows"; it is formed with the suffix *ka* by the rule *sami khyaḥ*, resulting in an *upapada* compound. Now, one might object: "In this case, because it is subsequent, the accent of the *thāthādi* group would apply, whereas the scope for *goballavādi* is elsewhere. This is true; however, a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior exception) must be stated here: the accent of *dhāri* takes precedence over the *cit* accent—as in *pitṛgavaḥ* and *mātṛgavaḥ*—and the accent of *kṛt* takes precedence over the *vāḍavahārya* accent.

"And *yuktasvara* [occurs] in place of *kṛtsvara*" means that the accentuation of *yukta* takes place in place of the accentuation produced by the rule *atha ādiḥ sūtreṇa* (Pāṇini 6.2.140), by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). "Yuktaḥ samāhitaḥ" means that this form [is derived] from the root *yuj* in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhau*), according to the Dhatupatha.
The suffix *adhyakṣa* is added after a word denoting a Vibhāṣā (option) to form a Tatpuruṣa compound.

Since the word *adhyakṣa* also denotes that which is joined [with another] when used in a compound, an option is provided by this rule where a compulsory application would otherwise have occurred by the preceding rule.
And the word *pāpa* [is compounded] with a word denoting a craftsperson. 6-2-67.
"Sin" (pāpa) is a reference to its essential nature (svarūpa), while "the artisan woman" (śilpinī) is a reference to its function (artha), according to the commentary.
The sixth case ending is used after words denoting lineage (*gotra*), disciples (*antevāsin*), young brahmins (*māṇava*), and brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*) when expressing censure.

In the case of *gotra* and *antevāsī*, there is the inclusion of the meaning (*artha*); in the case of the other two, there is the inclusion of the essential form (*svarūpa*). By the statement "except in the context of offspring, the worldly [term] is *gotra*," it is understood that in ordinary usage, *gotra* refers simply to offspring. [For example: "I give a gift of a leg" (*jaṅghādānaṃ dadāni*) means "I shall perform the act of giving a leg" (*jaṅghādānaṃ karavāṇi*), just as in the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*). In this context, when the Śāṇḍilyas and Vātsyas perform the washing of feet, one who is not a Vātsya says, "I am a Vātsya," for the sake of obtaining that [benefit].

"Jaṅghāvātsya" is an example of a disparaging term. The word *vatsa* here refers to Sauśruta. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being dominated by his wife," he shows that this is a compound with elision of the second member (*uttarapadalopa*), following the rule for compounds such as *śākapārthiva*. In the expression "vaśābrāhmakṛteya," *vaśā* means a barren wife; it is a compound similar to that of Sauśruta. *Dākṣa* is that which was taught by Dakṣa; one who studies that is a *dākṣa*, or a student of Dakṣa is also called a *dākṣa*. The word *cāra* belongs to the *naḍādi* group; one who studies what was taught by Cārāyaṇa, or his disciple, is a *cārāyaṇīya*.

"Likewise, *pāṇinīyaḥ*. Regarding "those desiring the acquisition of girls and so forth": even when there is no faith in the treatise taught by him (*tatprokte granthe*), those who engage in it out of a desire for the acquisition of girls and so forth are thus censured. The compound is as before. *Māṇava* and *brāhmaṇa* are mentioned separately because they are not commonly known to denote offspring (*apatya*). Another [scholar] says: the two are included as ending in the suffix *aṇ* [meaning] "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*); and by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the *ṇatva* occurs in *māṇava*.

"A fearful Brāhmaṇa" (*bhaya-brāhmaṇa*) refers to one who, being a Brāhmaṇa by birth, performs the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa out of fear of royal punishment and the like, and not out of faith; he is thus [described].

It is set aside [as an exception]. According to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32), because of the mention of the word *bahulam* ("variously"), a compound is formed even when not joined with a *kṛt*-suffix. Thus, *dāsīśrotriyaḥ* is like *dāsībrāhmaṇaḥ*.
The word *aṅga* [is used] in reference to *maireya*. (Pāṇini 6.2.70)

"Aṅgam" means a constituent part; the plural number is used to exclude the possibility of it being a rule regarding the essential nature [of the substance]. "Madya other than *surā*" refers to *daireya*. The phrase "expressing its constituent part" refers to the word *daireya*, which is the subject under discussion; however, here the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers back to that very meaning. Regarding "flower-liquor" (*pauṣpāsava*): *āsava* is a specific type of liquor; when it is prepared from flowers, honey, or another substance, the flower constitutes its constituent part (*aṅga*). However, the reading "puṣpāsavaḥ kaḥ" would be more appropriate.
The words called *bhakta* [are used] in the sense of those things. (Pāṇini 6.2.71)

Since the rejection of a rule prescribing the original form (*svarūpavidhi*) is already established by the very use of the plural number, the inclusion of the term *ākhyā* (name) is for the purpose of including words such as *bhakṣa* which denote specific types of food; otherwise, only synonyms such as *anna* and the like would have been included. For some, *bhikṣākaṇḍayaḥ* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), while for others, there is the view that they are dative compounds (*caturthīsamāsa*) when there exists a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛtivikārabhāva*). For others still, they are indeed dative compounds.

In the case of *go*, *viḍāla*, *siṃha*, and *saindhava* when they are used as points of comparison [with the word following them], [the final vowel of the first member is optionally long]. (Pāṇini 6.2.72)

In the examples "like a cow," "like a cat," "like a lion," and "like a Sindhu horse," the singular number is used because the word expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is connected individually with each [subject], such as the cow and so forth. The phrase "the meaning of the standard of comparison" means that whichever word functions as the standard of comparison in a given example must be applied there accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "as it is well-known in the world," whichever example has a certain established usage in common parlance, it should be applied in that manner. He shows a mere indication of this by saying "in the form of a cow," and so on.
"Form" (ākṛti) means configuration; "arranged" (saṃniveśita) means established. In this same way, whatever similarity [is applicable] elsewhere should also be applied.
The suffix *ka* is applied after a word denoting a livelihood when it occurs in the sense of "for the sake of. (Pāṇini 6.2.73)

"Living by means of [the act]" (*jīvikāvājinī*): this is a statement regarding the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term; the meaning is that its ground for application consists in the form of "livelihood. However, the ultimate referent (*paryavasānabhūmi*) is those who possess that [act]; thus he says: "those whose [livelihood] is by means of scraping teeth and so forth. Regarding "delightfulness" (*ramaṇīyakatā*): here too, the compound is formed according to the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*; for the sense is that a word ending in the suffix *-tṛc* is possible only in the sense of "play," and not in the sense of "livelihood."
In the sense of "play," [the suffix *khañ*] is applied after [a word ending in] the locative case, according to the Eastern grammarians. (Pāṇini 6.2.74)

Considering that it is not appropriate to supply the word "according to the opinion" (*matena*) because the connection is possible between the two words heard in the phrase "of the Easterners in play," he says: "the play of those from the eastern region."
The augment *aṇ* is applied after [the suffix] *niyukta*. || 6 - 2 - 75 ||

Regarding the word "niyukta," he states that this is a form of the root *yuj* in the sense of "joining" (*yoga*), explaining: "niyukta means 'appointed' (*adhikṛta*). Furthermore, such a person does not become intent upon some particular duty, because an appointment can apply to other tasks as well.
The affix *ṇvul* is applied after a verbal root denoting an artisan, provided it does not end in the root *kṛ*.

Since the rule would have been established by the mere statement "and in a *yukta* [compound]," the explicit mention of *kṛñaḥ* is for the purpose of prohibiting [the *yuk* suffix] in certain cases. In *tantuvāya*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *hvāvāmaśca*; hence the *yuk*. In *ayaskāra*, the change of the visarga to *s* occurs by the rule *ataḥ kṛ-kami-kaṃsa-kumbha-pātra-* etc.
*gauta* and *tiya* are suffixes after the root *pāl* (to protect). After the root *tan* (in the sense of extension), with the suffix *ktic*, we have *tanti*: a rope for tethering calves.
The comparison [suffix] occurs only when the word-meaning is the base form itself. 6-2-80.

In examples such as *uṣṭrakrośī* ("one who cries out like a camel"), the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *kartary upamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.79). This is because of the phrase "the censure of the object of comparison" (*upamānagarhaṇam*), and so forth. Otherwise, by means of the force of the division of the sūtra and the reliance on a restrictive rule (*niyama*), one would only understand that the restriction applies to a specific domain; however, the intention is that the desired distinction between domains would not be established.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the verbal root (prakṛti) of the word-meaning (śabdārtha)": what is the purpose of formulating this sūtra? It means: for what reason is the rule begun? [The example] *vṛkavañcī* shows that only the kṛt-suffix accent occurs. "Only the root," and so forth. If the mention of "the root" were absent, one would understand the rule to mean: "when the word-meaning is followed by a suffix ending in *ṇini*, provided that suffix stands before a subsequent member. Consequently, even in a case where *ṇini* follows the composite of a verbal root and a prefix—which constitutes the word-meaning—the rule would still apply; for, since the mention of a kṛt-suffix includes that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or an object (*kāraka*), the subsequent member would be understood as ending in *ṇini*. However, when "the root" is mentioned, it does not apply.

That which is the verbal root (*dhātu*) here is not the meaning of the word; and that which is the meaning of the word—the composite of root and prefix—is not prescribed with the suffix *ṇini*. Since a rule is commenced even when the matter is already established, it serves as a restriction (*niyama*) by means of the particle *eva*, even in the absence of another [restriction]. There is no purpose for the particle *eva* there, so he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*," and so forth. For if that were absent, the restriction would be the opposite: namely, that if [the suffix] occurs in the sense of a word-meaning (*śabdārtha*), it occurs only when it is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). In this way, the base (*prakṛti*) would be restricted, but not the object of comparison (*upamāna*).

Therefore, the particle *eva* is employed for the purpose of restricting the scope to the comparison (*upamāna*). But what is the reason for resorting to this restriction to the comparison? To this he says: "in the case of the original form of the word-meaning" (*śabdārthaprakṛtau*). The word *tu* indicates the reason: for if there were a restriction to the comparison, since the original form of the word-meaning would not be restricted, then even in that case, the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) would result without distinction for everything; it would not be otherwise. Furthermore, if there were a restriction to the original form (*prakṛti*), because this [comparison] would not be restricted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the acute accent on the first syllable in cases such as *vṛkavañcī*.
And [the compounds] beginning with *yuktārohī* [are also bahuvrīhis]. 6.2.81.

The phrase "for the purpose of restricting the preceding and following members" means that it should apply only in cases where words such as *yukta* and so forth are exclusively the preceding members (*pūrvapada*), and words such as *kaāroha* and so forth are exclusively the following members (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, in compounds such as *āgatamatsya*, the construction may be either a *bahuvrīhi* or a *karmadhāraya*.

Regarding the term *ekaśitipād*: by the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* of the word *pāda*; the meaning of that rule is that the final *ā* of the word *pāda* is elided when it occurs at the end of a compound preceded by a numeral or the word *su*. Now, one might object: since the word *eka* here ends in the suffix *kan*—according to the rule *iṇbhakāpāśalyatimarñcibhyaḥ kan*—it is acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Consequently, the acute accent on the first syllable would already be established in this *bahuvrīhi* compound by the rule *prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*. To this he replies: "In this case, *ekaḥ śitiḥ pādo'sya* is a three-word *bahuvrīhi*."

He asks "What follows from that? and says: "In that case" (*tatra*). If the word *ekaśiti* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound when followed by a subsequent member, he asks "What follows from that too? and says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Of that word *ekaśiti*, which bears the designation *tatpuruṣa*, the rule for the acute accent on the final syllable of a compound would apply. [Objection: But surely the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* is an exception to the accent of the compound; to this he replies: "Because the accent of the cause is stronger. The words "of the compound accent" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

The meaning is that the accent of the compound is stronger because the latter member (*uttarapada*) is the cause [of the accent], while the *dvigu* is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*. Its strength, moreover, arises from its being *satiśiṣṭa* (left over after others have been applied). It is *satiśiṣṭa* because it occurs subsequently once the *tatpuruṣa* has already taken place within the *bahuvrīhi*.

"Even so," and so forth; the meaning is clear. "Also [the rule] regarding the greater strength of the accent of the cause (*nimittisvara*)," and so forth. And thus, there is a *vārttika* on the *samartha-sūtra*: "The mention of the accent for 'one-footed white' (*ekaśitipāt*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the greater strength of the accent of the cause. Since the mention of 'one-footed white' would otherwise be untenable even without both [conditions], it indicates both.
The [final] *t* of the words *dīrgha*, *kāśa*, *tuṣa*, *bhrāṣṭra*, and *vaṭa* is changed to *j* before the suffix *je*.
Regarding "kuṭīja": the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *jan* when preceded by a word in the locative case.
In a compound consisting of many words, the case-affix of the word preceding the last member is elided.

Regarding the term *āmalakīja*: even when the long vowel occurs at the end, this same accentuation applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], despite the presence of multiple syllables.
Not residing in a village. 6-2-84.

The suffix *jhac* is added to the root *vas* preceded by *ni* according to the *Uṇādi* rules in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, "those who dwell here" (*nivasantaḥ*) means those in whom one dwells. Regarding the term *devagrāma*: this word "village" (*grāma*) refers to a region enclosed by boundaries in the east. If that is so, and it denotes those who dwell there, he says: "having the gods as its owners. Therefore, the point is that this village does not exist in relation to the gods as its inhabitants; rather, it belongs to them. As for the phrase "in which the Dākṣis and others dwell," etc.: the meaning is that even if others dwell there, or perhaps do not, they are designated as "belonging to them" simply on the grounds that they have resided there.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words such as *ghoṣa*. (Pāṇini 6.2.85)

"Those which are here" refers to Ghoṣakuṭa and so forth. "Others, however" means that for them, [the designation] applies even to words such as Ghoṣakuṭa, but not to those which are names of inhabited places.
The words *chattra* and so forth [denote] a hall (*śālā*). 6.2.86.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yadā śālānta* and so forth: by the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurā* and so on, the optional neuter gender of a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *śālā* has been stated. In that context, the scope (*avakāśa*) of this [present rule] is when the compound does not have a neuter gender—for example, *chāttriśālā* (the hut of the students) and *gośaritiḥ* (the cow-path). The scope of the rule *tatpuruṣe śālāyām* is when the first member is not *chāttri* and so on—for example, *vārāhmaṇaśālam* (the hut of the Brahmins) and *kṣattriyaśālam* (the hut of the Kṣatriyas). [The scope of the present rule applies] to that which has *chāttri* and so on as its prior member and is also neuter in gender.

In that case, because a form that has undergone a partial modification is not considered different [from the original], this [rule] would also apply; however, regarding the rule *tatpuruṣe śālāyām*, by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), this very [latter rule] prevails.
In the word *prastha*, the vowel is not lengthened when it follows *a* or *ka* (the first letter of the *karkyādi* group), except for the word *amā*. 6-2-87.

Because of the statement "and in the case of *mālī* etc.," the word division is *avṛddham*. However, the prohibition of [the names] *karki* and so forth would serve the purpose of defining the technical name—that is, it must be stated that the designation *vṛddha* applies to the technical name ending in *-vuñ*.
A monosyllabic word ending in a vowel, as well as a dissyllabic or trisyllabic word beginning with a vowel, is called *arma* when it denotes a color. 6.2.90.

Regarding *vṛhadarmam*: in this rule concerning vowel changes (*svaravidhi*), the principle that "a consonant is as if non-existent" is not applied here, because that principle is not universal (*anityatva*). Regarding *nāharmam*: once the substitution of *ā* has been made, there is the possibility [of the rule applying] because the word ends in the vowel *a*. Regarding *navāmam*: the word *nava* signifies "fresh" and ends in the vowel *a*.
Nor [should one use] *bhūtādhika*, *sañjīva*, *mṛd*, *aśmaka*, or *kajjala*. (6.2.91)

The inclusion of the term *madrāśman* is for the purpose of excluding both the compounded and the uncompounded forms; that is to say, it serves to prohibit the application [of the suffix] to the word *madra* alone as well as to the compound *madrāśman*.

Regarding the example *madrāśmārmam*: when the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applies by the rule *ano’śmāyaḥsarasāṃ jātisaṃjñayoḥ*, this form arises because it ends in the vowel *a*. Thus, *madrārmam* and *madrāśmārmam* are indeed examples provided by the Teacher himself. However, a third example, *aśmārmam*, is generally recited; that is incorrect, because the word *aśman* ends in the letter *n*. Nor does it become vowel-ending (*avarṇānta*) once the *n* has been elided, because in rules governing vowels (*svaravidhi*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*).
And so he will state later: regarding *pañcārma* and *daśārma*, [the rule] "in *arma*, there is no elision of the vowel, and the accent does not occur for a word of two or three syllables" applies.

Another says that because the mention of *madrāśma* is not seen in the Bhāṣya as being for the sake of both the compound and the separated forms, the reading in the Vṛtti is unauthoritative (*anārṣa*).
Regarding *divodāsa*: the sixth-case elision is not applied by the rule *divaśca dāse*.
The [final] vowel [of the preceding word is elided]. 6.2.92.
In this context as well, the nominative case, due to the qualification of the preceding word, should be understood as having the sense of the genitive.
In the case of the totality of all qualities, [the suffix *ka* is applied]. 6-2-93.

Where there is an absence of any other quality, there the entirety of the quality exists, as in the case of "all-white. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the rule beginning with "pūrvakāla-eka-" (Pāṇini 2.1.49). Here, it is understood that all parts are pervaded by the quality of whiteness.

"Supremacy [is established] by pervasion of the substratum. Although supremacy can also occur through brilliance and so forth, the meaning here is that such a form of supremacy is intended. "Entirely golden": here, "entirety" (*kārtsnya*) refers to the scope of the modification. As for the question "Why 'entirely' (*kārtsnye*)?": the question is raised because, when the subsequent member is a word denoting a quality, the word *sarva* does not deviate from the sense of entirety. For example: "the whitest of all" is *sarvaśveta*.

The word *sarva* [is used] when there is the totality of qualities (*guṇa*), not when there is the totality of the substratum itself. In the expression *sarveṣām*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a relationship with the quality, as in "the whiteness of the cloth" (*paṭasya śauklyam*). Furthermore, the suffix is applied to that which expresses the quality; the meaning is: "a quality of whiteness that is superior in comparison to that white quality of all cloths which resides in other substances. Regarding the phrase *guṇāt tara-ena*: the suffix *taraP* is added after a word expressing a quality, and the compound is formed with that which ends in such a suffix. This is indeed a specific statement [of the rule]; therefore, it sets aside the prohibition found in Pāṇini 2.2.11 (*pūraṇaguṇa...*) and allows for both the compound and the elision of the suffix *taraP*.
In the sense of a name, [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the words *giri* and *nikāya*. (Pāṇini 6.2.94)
Regarding "Añjanāgiri": there is lengthening of the vowel by the rule *vanagiryoḥ saṃjñāyām*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after a word denoting age when it refers to a maiden. || 6.2.95 ||

Regarding the term *vṛddhakumārī*: this is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). Regarding *jaratkumārī*: by the rule *pūrvakāla-eka-* [Pāṇini 2.1.49], and by the rule *puṃvat-karmadhāraya-* [Pāṇini 6.3.42] et cetera, there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) in both cases. Now, one might object: the word *kumārī* refers to the first stage of life; thus, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed here by the rule *vayasi prathame* [Pāṇini 4.1.20]. How, then, can it be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words *vṛddhā* and *jaratī*, which denote the final stage of life? To this, he says: "The word *kumārī*... and so forth.

For in the case of a maiden (*kumārī*), two things are observed: first, youth, and second, non-union with a male. In this context, for one who abandons the first object and adopts only the second object—namely, mere non-union—co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible; such is the meaning. And "that" refers to the fact that it is denotable by other words such as "old woman" (*vṛddhā*) and so forth. "Only maidenhood" means that the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *kumārī* is not taken here as [mere] age.

And this [meaning] is obtained through the force of the inclusion of the term *vayograhaṇa* (the mention of age); otherwise, since the use of the word *kumārī* necessarily implies the first stage of life, its [explicit] mention would be redundant.
In the case of *paramakumārī*, only the state of being a *kumārī* is perceived, not another stage of life; thus, this serves as a counter-example.
In the case of *udaka*, when it does not denote "entirely" (*akevale*). || 6-2-96 ||

To eliminate any doubt, since the word "only" (*kevala*) is not used in the phrase "in water," the compound is analyzed as *a-kevale* (not in [pure] water). *Maśram* means conjoined with another substance.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *dvigu* when it denotes a sacrifice (*kratu*).

*Gargatrirātra* and similar compounds are genitive *ṣaṣṭhī*-compounds. *Trirātra* is the collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) of three nights; the suffix for the compound-final member is applied according to the rule *ahaḥ sarva-* etc. Regarding *atirātra*: it is a *prādi*-compound meaning "that which has transcended the night" (*rātrim atikrāntaḥ*).
In the word *sabhā*, the neuter gender is optionally used. || 6.2.98 ||
In cases such as *gopālasabha* and *aśālā*, the neuter gender is due to the word *sabhā* [occurring at the end of a compound].
In the case of *ramaṇīyasabham*, the neuter gender is due to the influence of the meaning (*abhidheya*), and not because it is explicitly prescribed by the rule for specific compounds.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa*, preceded by [the word *pūrva*]. 6.2.100.

What is the purpose of including the word *pūrva*? The question is: should it not simply be stated as "of *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa*"? [The answer is: so that the rule may apply here as well. For when *pūrva* is included, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is obtained—namely, a compound in which *ariṣṭaga* and *gauḍa* are the prior members. Consequently, in cases such as *ariṣṭāśritapura* and *gauḍabhṛtyapura*, the first member (*pūrvapada*) retains its final acute accent (*āntodātta*). However, if *pūrva* were not included, because the words *ariṣṭa* and *gauḍa* would be separated by the words *śrita* and *bhṛtya*, they would not qualify as "prior members" (*apūrvapadatvāt*), and thus the desired result would not occur for them; furthermore, the two composite forms as a whole are not mentioned in the rule.
The suffixes *ha*, *aṇ*, *ini*, *phaka*, *ka*, and *mārdeya* do not apply [to words ending in *gotra* suffixes]. 6-2-101.
Regarding "mārdeya": by the rule "ḍhelopo'kadr̥vāḥ," there is the elision of the letter *u*.

"Words denoting directions [are compounded] with names of villages, districts, and Cānarāṭa. (Pāṇini 6.2.103). In the case of *cānarāṭe*, there is a reference to the word-form itself; in the other cases, there is a reference to the meaning. For example: *pūrveṣukāmaśamī*. This is a compound by the rule "Direction and number [are compounded] when forming a name" (Pāṇini 2.1.50). Regarding *pūrvapañcālāḥ*: since words that apply to a whole may also apply to its parts, the word *pañcāla* here refers to a specific part of Pañcāla. Consequently, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed according to the rule "The first, the last, the foremost, etc. (Pāṇini 2.1.58). As for the mention of the "word-form," and so forth...

The term *dikśabda* (direction-word) is a compound formed by the elision of the final member of the phrase *diśi dṛṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ* (a word seen in the direction); because of this, it also includes words denoting time, so that [the rule] applies even in cases such as *pūrvāyatam*.
And [the name] of the pupil [is compounded with the name of] the teacher as a subordinate member. 6.2.104.

The inclusion of the term *ācāryopasarjana* (having the teacher as a subordinate member) is an adjective qualifying *antevāsinaḥ* (pupils); the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative. Thus, it means "expressing pupils who have the teacher as a subordinate member. In the compound *ācāryopasarjanāntevāsī*, that which has the teacher (*ācārya*) as its subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is *ācāryopasarjana*; this, together with *antevāsī* (pupil), forms *ācāryopasarjanāntevāsī*, and [the suffix -cha is applied] to that which expresses such a thing. Regarding the example *pūrvapāṇinīyāḥ*: the compound is formed in the same manner as before; those who are students (*chāttra*) of Pāṇini are *pāṇinīyāḥ*. Here, the pupil is the primary element (*pradhāna*), while the teacher is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*).

From the word *kāśakṛtsni*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by rule 4.3.79 (*ataśca*). "The *pāṇinīya* treatise is prior" means that the *pāṇinīya* treatise is earlier, i.e., ancient. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.2.105: "In the case of the strengthening of the second member, [the first member becomes] *sarva*."

Since the inclusion of the subsequent word would be established by the mere mention of "vṛddhau" alone, the explicit mention of "uttarapada" (subsequent word) indicates that this is the governing heading for that section.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the word *viśva* [is treated according to Pāṇini 6.2.106]. When derived from the root *viś* with the suffix *kvun*, the word *viśva* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*). Examples include *viśvāmitra* and so forth. The scope (*avakāśa*) of this rule is: *viśvadeva*, *viśvayaśas*. The scope of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *mitra* or *ajina*, when used as a proper name" (Pāṇini 6.2.175) is: *kulamitra*, *kulājina*, *viśvāmitra*, *viśvājina*. Where both rules would apply simultaneously—as in *viśvāmitra* and *viśvājina*—the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* ending in *mitra* or *ajina*, when used as a proper name" prevails by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
The suffix *ka* is applied after the words *udara*, *aśva*, and *iṣu*. || 6.2.107 ||

This also is an exception to the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. The word *vṛka* is acutely accented on the first syllable according to the rule *praṇināṃ ca kupūrvāṇām*. Thus, one whose belly is like that of a wolf is *vṛkīudaraḥ*. One who has a rope (*dāman*) in his belly is *dāmodaraḥ*; the word *dāman* ends in the suffix *manin*. [The word *hari*] is derived from the root *hṛ* with the suffix *in* (according to the rule *sarvadhātubhya in*), as in *haryaśvaḥ*, one whose horses are bay. The word *yauvana* is an unanalyzed nominal stem (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*); it is acutely accented on the first syllable according to the rule *laghāvante dvayośca bahvaṣo guruḥ*.

In the case of *yauvanam* (youth), derived from *yuvan* with the suffix *-aṇ*, because the accent of the suffix would result in an oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule of "accent of the suffix" (*pratyayasvara*), it is established as having its original accent on the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*). Regarding *suvarṇapuṅkheṣuḥ*: those whose color (*varṇa*) is beautiful (*śobhana*) are *suvarṇāḥ*; by the rule *nañsubhyām*, this results in an oxytone. Those whose feathers (*puṅkha*) are *suvarṇa* are *suvarṇapuṅkhāḥ*; by the original accent of the first member, there is an acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *iṣu*. Regarding *maheṣuḥ*: [it is formed similarly].

It has been stated in the rule *mahān vrīhi-aparāhṇa* that the word *mahat* is oxytone (*antodātta*). Therefore, since the desired accentuation would already be established by the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) of that compound, this new rule is commenced for another purpose; its presentation is based on the principle that, due to its status as an exception (*apavāda*), the oxytonic quality is properly achieved by this very rule alone.
In the sense of reproach (kṣepa). (Pāṇini 6.2.108)

The word *kuṇḍa* is acutely accented on the first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya*. The word *ghaṭa* ends in the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*). Its mention here is for the sake of comparison with *maheṣu*. From the word *kaṭu*, the suffix *kan* is applied when it is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*). The word *spandita* ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. [The compound] *nighāta* is derived from *nihanyate 'nena*; anything other than that is *anighāta*. Therefore, there is the original accent of the indeclinable as the prior member (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). Regarding the words *cali*, *cali*, *pati*, and *vadi*, there is optionally reduplication (*dvitva*) and the substitution of *acyāc* for the reduplicated syllable: *calācalaḥ*.

Regarding "anudara" and so forth: its scope of application includes examples such as *kuṇḍodara*. The scope of application for the rule *nañsubhyām* includes examples such as *ayaśas* and *suyaśas*. Such being the case, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
The word *nadī* [is used] in the sense of "kinswoman. (Pāṇini 6.2.109)

The neuter designation in the word *bandhu* is made with reference to the form of the word itself; from the words *garga* and *vatsa*, by means of the suffix *yañ* belonging to the *gargādi* group, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *yañaś ca*, resulting in the forms *gārgī* and *vātsī*; these two words are udātta on the first syllable due to the accent of the *ñit* suffix. The word *brahman* is derived from the root *bṛh* with the suffix *manin* as a conventional formation (*nipātita*).
When preceded by *niṣṭhā* or an upasarga, [the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*] is optional. 6.2.110.

Regarding the term *prakṣālitapāda*: the root *kṣal* (meaning "to cleanse") belongs to the *curādi* class; *dhāv* (meaning "to move" or "to purify") [is used here]. By the rule *cchvoḥ śūṭh*, *ū* is substituted for *ū*; by the rule *etyedhatyutṣu*, there is *vṛddhi*. Thus, the words *prakṣālita* and *pradhauta* have their initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the prefix (*gatisvara*).

The statement "mukhaṃ svāṅgam" (the word *mukha* [is] a *svāṅga*) means that it becomes so. An optional rule (*vikalpita*) applies for the final acute accent (*antodātta*) of the subsequent member; thus, when the word *mukha* denotes a *svāṅga*, three accents occur: by this [rule], there is the final acute of the prior member (as in *mukhaṃ svāṅgam*); and when both [of those conditions] are absent, there is the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (P. 6.2.49), due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the prior member. Regarding the phrase *na cet*: it is connected with the term *svāṅgavācī*; the meaning is "if the word *mukha* does not denote a *svāṅga*."

The word *prasecaka* is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the original accent of the second member of the compound; the word *śuṣka* is initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule *śuṣkadhuṣṭau*.
The initial vowel of the second member [is acute]. 6.2.111.

The term *uttarapada* (subsequent member) refers to a non-compounded word ending in the suffix *thak*, with the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) elided. Here too, when the subsequent member is specified within this context, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used in the sense of the genitive.
The word *karṇa* [is optionally substituted for the final vowel of the first member] when followed by *vartana*, provided that it denotes a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). 6-2-112.

Regarding the examples *dātrākarṇaḥ* and *śaṅkukarṇaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "one whose ear is a sickle" (*dātraṃ karṇe yasya*) and "one whose ear is a peg" (*śaṅkuḥ karṇe yasya*). As for the inversion [of the order], the rule *gaḍvādibhyaḥ paravacanam* prescribes that the word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) is placed first. The lengthening of the vowel is by the rule *aviṣṭādiṣu ca*. That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); consequently, one might ask why the form *sthūlakarṇaḥ* ("thick-eared") would not also result here, since even thickness can serve as a characteristic. To this he replies: "For the purpose of indicating the classification of animals," and so forth.

And this [rule] is obtained even from the general statement because of the mention of *varṇa* (color); otherwise, since it would be indicated by *varṇa* as well, that [mention] would be purposeless. [The word] *śvitra* is derived from the root *śvit* in the sense of "color," with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*). [The word] *kūṭa* is from the root *kūṭ* in the sense of "burning," with the suffix *ka* (by the rule *igupadhala-kṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). [The word] *śobhana* is from the roots *śubh* and *śumbh* in the sense of "beauty"; [it takes] the suffix *yuc* (by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*). In all counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*), there is only the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. Due to the formation of a neuter compound in the sense of a collective aggregate (*samāhāradvandva*) of *aṇ*, *ṭhak*, *araṇ*, etc., there is the shortening of the vowel.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied after a word ending in *kaṇṭha*, *pṛṣṭha*, *grīvā*, or *jaṅghā*] to denote the whole. 6.2.114.

Regarding *sugrīva*: here, by virtue of its priority, the rule *nañsubhyām* would require the final syllable to be udātta; however, this [rule] finds its scope in cases such as *daśagrīva*. If, however, this is not desired, then the particle *ca* itself must be explained as having the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for the purpose of the injunction. Regarding *nāḍījaṅgha*: he whose shanks (*jaṅghe*) are shaped like reeds (*nāḍī*) is *nāḍījaṅgha*.
The negative particle *naÑ* [is compounded] with *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta*. (Pāṇini 6.2.116)

*Jaraṇam* (the act of growing old) is *jaraḥ*; [this is formed] by the rule *ṛdorap*. *Maraṇam* (death) is *maraḥ*; here, *ap* is applied by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). From the root *ṛmid* (in the sense of "to moisten"), the suffix *ktra* is added, resulting in *mitram*.
The words *sormanasi* and *alomoṣasī* [are formed with the suffix *kvin*]. 6.2.117.

And *manasī* [is derived from] *mam̐śca*. Regarding *suprathimā*: it is the state (*bhāva*) of *pṛthu*; by the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanic*, the suffix *iman* is added; by the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ*, there is the substitution of *r* for *ṛ*. *Pacaḥ* [is derived from] *pibati*; by the rule *pibater iñ ca*, the suffix *asun* is added. Regarding *yaśaḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *aś* in the sense of playing (*devana*); by the rule *aśer devane yuṭ ca*, the suffix *asun* is added along with the augment *yuṭ*. Regarding *srotaḥ*: [it is derived from] the roots *sru* and *stru*; by the rule [adding] *tuṭ*, we have *srotaḥ*. Regarding *susrat* and *sudhvad*: [they are derived from] the roots *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* with the suffix *kvip*. By the rule *vasusraṃsu...*, there is the substitution of *d* for *s*; because that [substitution] is treated as not having taken effect (*asiddha*), the word here ends in *as*.

The words *rāja* and *takṣa* end in the suffix *kanip* according to the rule *kanin yuvṛṣitakṣi...* etc. From the root *lū*, the suffix *manin* forms *loman*; from *uṣ* (meaning "to burn"), the suffix *as* is applied while the rule *mithune'siḥ* is in effect, and the suffix is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*).

Regarding the expression *an-in-as-man-grahaṇāni*: those sūtras in which the terms *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* are included are so designated; by the statement that they cause the application of the rule regarding "that which ends with [the aforementioned suffixes]," it is implied that even meaningless forms such as *an* and the others are included. Thus, the intention is that examples such as *suprathimā*, *susrat*, and *sudhvad* are also appropriately established.

Regarding the rule "after a *kapi* [suffix]" (*kapi paratvāt*): the scope of the rule *sormanasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.117) is, for example, *sukamā*, *suśarmā*; the scope of the rule *kapi pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.2.173) is, for example, *ayavakaḥ*, *suyavakaḥ*. In a single instance where both would apply, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
In the Vedic language, a two-syllable word beginning with a single consonant has its first syllable accented acute.

While the rule "kurbhraśca" is in effect, [the following roots] also take the suffix *ku*: *arji*, *daśi*, *kami*, *yami*, *paśi*, *bādhā*, *mṛji*, *pasi*, *tugi*, *dugi*, as well as those ending in long vowels and the letter *h*. That by which one overcomes others is called *bāhu*.
And [the words] *vīra* and *vīrya* [are used in the same sense]. 6.2.120.

The root *vīra* is used in the sense of "valour" (*vikrāntau*) and belongs to the *curādi* group; from it, by adding the suffix *ac* (via *pacādyac*), we derive *vīraḥ*. By the rule *aco yat*, we derive *vīryam*; or, by the rules *tatra sādhuḥ* and *tasmai hitam*, we derive *vīryam* as that which is beneficial for heroes (*vīreṣu*). Regarding the phrase "therein," etc., he asks: "How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He replies: "For in that case... [the rule] *phiṣi ca bilvabhakṣyavīryāṇi chandasi* establishes that in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) the final syllable of these words is circumflex (*svarita*), whereas in the common language (*bhāṣāyām*) they have the acute (*udātta*) accent on the first syllable.
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, the words *kūla*, *tīra*, *tūla*, *mūla*, *śāla*, and *akṣa* take the neuter gender. || 6.2.121 ||

In examples such as *suṣamam*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *suvinirdurbhyaḥ supisūtisamāḥ*. Because that [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this remains simply the word *sama*. These [words] are listed among the *tiṣṭhadgu*-type compounds; therefore, they receive the designation of *avyayībhāva*. Regarding the rule beginning with *paryādibhyaḥ*: the scope of the rule *paripratyupāpāḥ* is where words such as *kūla* do not exist—for example, *paritrigartam*; whereas the scope of the rule for *kūla* and the others, which have the acute accent on the first syllable, is where *pari* and the other prefixes do not occur—for example, *avakūlam* and *tatkūlam*. Thus, when *kūla* and the others follow *pari* and the other prefixes, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
In a *dvigu* compound, the words *kaṃsa*, *mantha*, *śūrpa*, *pāyya*, and *kāṇḍa* [retain their original accent]. 6.2.122.

*Dvikaṃsa*: "Purchased for two *kaṃsas*"; this is a compound formed in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the rule *kaṃsāṭ ṭiṭhan*, the suffix *ṭiṭhan* is applied; its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *adhyardhapūrva*. *Dvimantha*: By the rule *ārhād agopucchasaṃkhyāparimāṇāṭ ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied; the remainder is as before. *Dviśūrpa*: By the rule *śūrpād añ anyatarasyām*, the suffix *añ* is applied. *Dvipāyya*: This is an irregular form (*nipātita*) in the sense of a measure (*parimāṇa*), according to the rule *pāyyasānnāyya...*. The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *prāgvateṣ ṭhañ*. *Dvikāṇḍa*: [This is formed similarly].

In the section on *deva*, by the rule "in the sense of measure, [the suffixes] *dvayasaC* and so forth" (*pramāṇe dvayasac* etc.), the suffixes *mātraJ* and others are introduced; for these, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "after a *dvigu* compound, the suffix *loP* is obligatory."
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound denoting a building, the final vowel is shortened when the word is neuter. || 6.2.123 ||

Regarding *dṛḍhaśālam*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In that case, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member alone occurs, and the first member is oxytone because it ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. Now, one might object: "Will this not be established by the *paribhāṣā* concerning 'that which is taught by a specific rule' (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*)? True; however, the mention of the *tatpuruṣa* must necessarily be made for the sake of subsequent rules. It is placed here precisely so that the *paribhāṣā* need not be relied upon.
And [the word] *kanthā*. 6-2-124.

The offspring of one whose tranquility (*śama*) is beautiful (*śobhana*) is *Sauśami*. From the root *hvā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ātaś copasarge*; from the root *cap* meaning "to move" or "to go," the suffix *pa* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules, and due to the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*), there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*—thus, *cappaḥ*.
The initial [vowel] of words such as *cihaṇa* and others [is elided]. (Pāṇini 6.2.125)

From the root *cin* with the suffix *kvip*, we have *cit*. From the root *han* with the suffix *pacādyac*, we have *hanaḥ*. *Cihaṇam*—here, by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the suffix *tal* and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. The roots *mal* and *mall* mean "to hold. From these two, the suffix *rap* is added; by irregular derivation, the *l* is changed to *ḍ*, resulting in *maḍaraḥ* and *madduraḥ*. That which is without comparison (*tula*) is *vaitula*. It cries out "paṭat"—thus it is *paṭatkaḥ*. [The suffix] *ka* is applied after roots ending in long *ā* when no prefix is present, according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*. It eats all things (*biḍam ādatte*)—thus it is *biḍālaḥ*. The roots *kai*, *gai*, and *rai* mean "to sound. [The suffix *ka* is applied here as well.]

The word *baiḍālika* is derived from the root √lā (to take), with the suffix *ka* added even after a prefix due to this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). His offspring is *baiḍāli*; one whose ears are like those of a *baiḍāli* is *baiḍālikarṇa*. However, some read it as ending in the vowel *i*: *baiḍālikaṇi*. One who cries out "kukku" is a *kukkuṭa* (cock); here, by exception (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the sound *ra*, and from the root √ci (to gather) with the suffix *kvip*, we get *cit*; from √kaṇ (to sound) with the suffix *ac*, we get *kaṇa*; that which has a sound (*kaṇa*) like that of a *cit* is *cikkaṇa*. By exception, the letter *ta* is replaced by *ka*. Others, however, read it with the letter *ta*. These words, beginning with *cihaṇa*, are recorded in tradition as names of lineages (*gotra-nāmadheya*).

Regarding the phrase "the word 'ādi' [is] understood": for previously, the mention of *ādi* was connected with the subsequent member of the compound; here, however, it is intended that the first syllable of the preceding members—such as *cihna* and others—is acute-accented. Therefore, the mention of *ādi* is repeated for that purpose.
The words *cela*, *kheṭaka*, *kaṭuka*, and *kāṇḍa* are used in the sense of reproach. 6-2-126.

"Putracela" means as empty as a cloth; "kheṭa" is a name for grass, and like that, it is weak, hence "upānatkheṭa. "Kaṭuka" means tasteless; likewise, even curd is called "kaṭuka" because its sweetness has departed. "Kāṇḍa" is a name for an arrow; just as that causes pain to living beings, so too is this [state] of being.
The word *cīra* is an example [of a compound where the final vowel of the first member is lengthened]. 6-2-127.
Regarding "vastracīra": it is a *vyāghrādi* compound, meaning "cloth like bark," as explained previously.
The words *kūlasūda* and *sthalakarṣa* [form a tatpuruṣa compound] when they denote a proper name (saṃjñā). || 6.2.129 ||
Regarding the word *bhājīsūdam*: the term *bhājī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra*.
The word *rājya* [is used in the neuter gender] except when it forms a *karmadhāraya* compound. 6-2-130.

"From the accent of *cela*, *rājya*, etc."—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the accents of *vargī* and so forth. The scope for the accent of *cela*, *rajā*, etc., is [in examples such as] *bhāryācela* ("the wife's garment") and *brāhmaṇarājyam* ("the kingdom of a Brahmin"). The scope for the accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* and so forth is [in examples such as] *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("one who has departed from Kauśāmbī"), *kucelam* ("a bad garment"), and *kurājyam* ("a bad kingdom"). When both [rules] would apply simultaneously, the former prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) takes effect.
The suffix *putra* is applied after masculine [bases] to form a feminine derivative. || 6.2.132 ||
The offspring of Kunaṭa is Kaunaṭi. The words *dāmakam* and *māhiṣaka* end in the suffix *kan*, according to the rule "the suffix *kan* [is applied] in the sense of a proper name."
Not [to be given] to those designated as teachers (ācārya), kings (rājan), officiating priests (ṛtvij), or kinsmen (jñāti). 6.2.133.

"Connected ones" refers to those related through marriage, such as brothers-in-law and so forth; this is a *yogarūḍhi* (a term whose meaning is both etymological and conventional) for them, just like the word *sambandhin* ("relative"). "Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) refers to those who are relatives by virtue of connection to one's mother and father; however, in common usage, the word *jñāti* is well-known specifically for those related on the father’s side. The mention of the term "name" (*ākhyā*) is connected individually with each [category], beginning with "teacher" (*ācārya*). In the case of *bhrātuṣputra* ("brother's son"), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because it is included in the *kaska-* group.
The word *cūrṇa* and others [are used] with a word denoting something other than a living being in the sixth case-ending. 6-2-134.

From the root *cūri* (to burn), the suffix *kta* is applied to form *cūrṇam*. From the roots *vā* (to move/to smell) and *pā* (to protect)—with the word *kari* as an upapada—the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*, resulting in *karivaṃ* and *karipaṃ*. From the root *mahi* (to increase), the suffix *inaṇ* is added; because of the rule regarding "variety" (*bahulavacanāt*), this also applies to the root *śaki* (to be able), resulting in *śākinam*. From *śaka* and other roots, the suffix *aṭac* is applied to form *śakaṭam*. That which carries it is called *śākaṭam*, formed from *śakaṭa* with the suffix *aṇ*. *Drākṣā* is that which flows quickly (*drāk kṣarati*); it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. From the root *tusa* (to sound), the suffix *kta* is applied by virtue of the rule regarding "variety," and there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatvam*).

It distresses (*du*); or, it distresses in a contemptible way (*kutsitaṃ dunoti*)—thus, with the suffix *kvip*, and by this very irregularity (*nipātana*), there is the absence of *tuk*; furthermore, the prefix *mum* is added to the first member, resulting in *kundu*. It measures (*mimīte*) the *kundu*, thus *kunduma*. From the root *dala* with the suffix *kap*, *dalapa*. From *camasac*, *camasa*; from that, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* as a marker of a genus (*jāti*), *camasī*. From the root *kanī* (in the senses of shining, beauty, and motion), with the suffix *pacādyac*; by this very irregularity, there is reduplication, resulting in *cakkana*. Others read *ckana*; even in that case, the form is established solely through irregularity. The offspring of *cola*—with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule "for a word of two syllables"—is *caula*. These are the words beginning with *cūrṇa*.
"By the practice of the former teachers" means that "practice" (upacāra) refers to application (prayoga).
The word *kuṇḍa* [is used] in the sense of a forest. 6-2-136.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this case, from the word *kuṇḍa*," etc.: the meaning is that since the word *kuṇḍa* denotes a specific person (a sacrificial pit-attendant), its application elsewhere—in a forest—is not possible without some similarity [to that person]. Others, however, maintain that even in the case of a forest, the word *kuṇḍa* is used in its primary sense.

In this context, by the qualifying term "forest" (*vana*), the specific vessel is excluded; furthermore, the word "forest" here denotes a collection (*samudāya*) and not water. For it has been said: "When [the first syllable of] *kuṇḍa* and so forth is acute, there is the inclusion of that collection. By the word "that" (*tat*), the meaning of the preceding rule is referred to. Another says: "It should be stated as 'in a collection of forests' (*vanasamudāye*), and not as 'in a forest' (*vane*); therefore, a collection of reed-forests is expressed by the term *śarakuṇḍa*."
The word *bhagāla* [is used] by nature [to denote a skull]. 6-2-137.

He states that *bhagālam* is a word for "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) by saying "it denotes *bhagāla*. In this matter, the commentary itself is the authority. For it is stated: "Words such as *bhagāla* have an udātta accent on the penultimate syllable," according to the rule: "In a word with many vowels (*bahaṣ*), if the penultimate is light, the heavy vowel [is acute]; and likewise when there are two [light syllables before the end]."
In a bahuvrīhi compound, the word *śiti* is not elided when it occurs after *bahu-ja-ba*, except when it is followed by *asat*.

Regarding the words *aṃsa* and *oṣṭha*, and so forth: from the root *am* (to be sick), with the suffix *san*, we have *asa*; from *uṣ* (to burn), by [the rule] "after *uṣi*, *kuṣi*, and *gāti*, the suffix *than* is added," we have *oṣṭha*. The word *darśanīya* ends in the suffix *anīyar* and has the acute accent (*udātta*) on the middle syllable. The word *śiti* has the acute accent on the first syllable, according to the rule "for colors ending in *taṇ*, *ni*, or *ti*, etc."
A *kṛt* suffix is applied after a word denoting a destination (*gati*), an agent (*kāraka*), or a subordinate word (*upapada*).

In *prakāraka* and similar forms, there is a compound according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*. In *idhmapravraścana* and similar terms, there is a compound with a genitive case [ending] denoting the object; the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes the instrument. That by which fuel (*idhma*) is cut is here called *idhmapravaścanaḥ*. [The root] *śadḷ* means "to cut down"; with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and because of the rule *śaderagatau taḥ*, the suffix *ta* is applied. That staff by which leafy branches (*palāśāni*) are cut down is a *parāśaśatanaḥ*. That by which a beard (*śmaśru*) is trimmed is a razor or similar tool, called *śmaśrukalpanaḥ*. [The root] *kṛpū* meaning "capability" takes the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), or remains unmodified. Thus, we have *īṣatkaraḥ*.

This is the direct illustration for the inclusion of the term *upapada*. However, in the case of *su* and *dur*, the [desired form] is established even by virtue of their being *gatis*; and in cases such as *stamberama*, it is established by virtue of their being *kārakas*. Expressions such as *uccaiḥ kṛtya* and *uccaiḥ kāram* are also illustrations specifically of the inclusion of the term *upapada*. As for the phrase "of Devadatta" (*devadattasya*), this is a genitive case characterized as a *śeṣa* (remainder); it is not a genitive case characterized as an *object* (*karman*). For if it were so, Devadatta would be a *kāraka*, and there would consequently follow the prohibition of compounding based on the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari ca*.
Now, for what purpose is the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes]? [It is] so that [the rule] does not apply in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"). This is not a valid purpose.

Those [words] such as *pāra* receive the designations of "gati" (indeclinable prefix) and "upasarga" (preverb) only when they are connected with an action (*kriyā*), and there is no connection with an action toward the word *Kaiśambī*. Furthermore, a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is possible only in relation to an action. An *upapada* is also defined as a cause for a suffix, specified in the locative case within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*). Thus, by all three—*gati*, *upasarga*, and *upapada*—an *uttarapada* (subsequent member) denoting an action is implied. And a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes an action. Regarding a verbal root, there are two types of suffixes: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. Among these, in the case of a *tiṅ*-ending [word]:

Since a compound is impossible here, only a *kṛt*-derived form can occur; however, in the case of *anuvyacalat*, there is no compound based on its being a *gati* (preverb). Rather, it is based on the rule *sub* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) through a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules). This is for the purpose of including the entire collection of root and suffix; otherwise, because the status of being a *gati* would apply only toward the root according to the statement "that which is connected with an action [is a *gati*] toward that," the accent would occur only when the root is the final member of the compound—as in *praṇīḥ* and *unnīḥ*—but it would not occur here in *praṇayakaḥ* and *unnāyakaḥ*.

This purpose also does not hold, for it is not understood thus: "that which is connected with the action of whom"—meaning, [the designation applies] toward that person whose action it is. If it were understood in this way, then by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the action would be expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone; consequently, the technical designations of motion (*gati*) and prefix (*upasarga*) would apply only toward that [root]. How, then, is it to be understood?

Whatever action (*kriyā*) there is, and whatever belongs to that action—that object characterized by action—having approached it, the two [words] receive the designation *upasarga*. Furthermore, since there is no subsequent word (*uttarapada*) that expresses action alone, [the designation applies] everywhere—in cases such as *praṇīḥ* and *prakāraka*, which denote a means (*sādhana*) qualified by action; in cases such as *prabhavanam*, which expresses the state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*); and so forth. Therefore, this mention of a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛdgrahaṇa*) is unnecessary; thus he says: "The mention of *kṛt* is for the sake of clarity.
The meaning is that it is made for the sake of clarity for one who is unable to understand it in this way.

If, then, the mention of the *kṛt* suffix is made even for the sake of clarity, it would not apply in the case of forms ending in *ām*, such as *prapacatitarām* and *prapacatitamām*; consequently, instead of the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*), the accent of the indeclinable (*avyayasvara*) alone would occur. To this he says: *prapacatitarām*, etc. For here, the word *pra* is compounded with that which ends in *tarap*, not with that which ends in *ām*.

How is it that, due to its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*) first? At this stage, because the case-ending (*sub*) is absent, no compound (*samāsa*) has been formed; then comes the finite suffix (*tiṅ*). Even at that stage, the case-ending is absent. Then comes the comparative suffix *tarap*; since it ends in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the case-ending *sup* is added, and by means of that, the compound is formed. Then comes the suffix *ām*, and finally, the suffix *ām* is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining when others have been applied).

But how, then, can there be a compound with [the suffix] *tarap*, and why would it not be so? Because of the rule stating, "There is a prescription for the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-suffixes," it is not restricted here that the compound must be with *kṛt*-suffixes alone; rather, if the compounding of *gati*s and the others occurs by means of their respective grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*), then [it follows] that the *prakṛti* [stem] undergoes case-suffix addition (*sup*) after the *kṛt*-suffixes. [Objection: Even so, a compound with [the suffix] *tarap* is still not obtained. What is the reason? Because it is not a word ending in a case-suffix (*asubanta*). For, since the governing context is "starting from a nominal stem" (*pratipadika-adhikāra*), it follows from that very point [that only nominal stems may be compounded].

The suffix *ām* occurs by the rule *kimettiṅavyayaghādām*, and not from that which ends in a case-suffix (*subanta*); nor does the principle "the [preceding] *gati*, *kāraka*, or *upapada* [are compounded with the following word]" apply here, because [the element *am*] is not a *kṛt* suffix. Regarding this, they say: on the basis of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ghakālataneṣu*, all secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) arise only from that which ends in a case-suffix; however, the mention of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ṅī* or *āp* is prescribed specifically for the sake of [the formation of] *vṛddhi* and so forth. Consequently, for the production of *am*, there is a compound with that which ends in the case-suffix used for its derivation.

Another says: because of the anticipation (pratikarṣa) of the term "not a verbal root" (atiṅ), which will be stated in the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, only that which ends in a non-suffix (*asubanta*) is compounded with the following word; therefore, a compound with a form ending in the suffix *-tarap* is obtained.
Thus [ends] the view of some. Regarding this, they explain that the mention of *kṛt* [in the rule] is for the sake of clarity, and that no fault arises even when [the suffix] *-am* follows.

Regarding the phrase "but for the sake of [the forms] *prapacatideśya* and so forth," the word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position. By the word *ādi* (and so forth), there is the inclusion of *prapacatikalpam*, *prapacatideśīyam*, and *prapacatirūpam*. That which has its purpose (*artha*)—meaning its objective (*prayojana*)—in *prapacatideśya* and the others is described as such.

This is what is meant: the mention of the *kṛt* suffix *ghañ* is not for the sake of clarity; rather, it is seen as having a specific purpose, namely that in formations such as *prapañcita*, where no other *satiśiṣṭa* accent exists, this [specific] accent should not occur, so that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) preceding member may prevail.

However, this must be addressed: in forms such as *prapacatitarām*, when a compound is formed with the suffix *-tara* (in *pacititara*), and the suffix *ām* is subsequently added, then by the paribhāṣā "the mention of a suffix [refers to that which ends in that suffix]," the word *pacititara* alone would be considered ending in a verbal root (*dhānta*). What is the fault in that? Because the entire complex including the prefix (*sopasarga*) would not be treated as a single word (*ekapada*), the rule "an vocative [ending in] *ām* is separated by one word [from the preceding verb] when not distant" (*āma ekāntaram āmantritam anantike*) would not apply in examples such as *āmaprapacatitarāṃ devadatta*. Furthermore, the rule for the low-pitched accent of the remaining words (*śeṣanighāta*) would not apply to the prefix *pra* because it would belong to a separate word. Therefore, the formation of a compound between the prefix *pra* and the form ending in *ām* must be accepted.

It should be formulated [with the suffix *kṛtya*], not with *tarap*. In that case, because it is a compound (*samāsa*), the entire aggregate becomes a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus there is a single word-form (*ekapadya*) when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows. However, since a fault would arise regarding the accent (*svara*), it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes must also be abandoned; yet we do not know what the status would be for forms such as *prapacatideśīya*.
The suffix *um* is applied to words such as *vanaspati* when they denote simultaneous action. 6.2.140.

The word *vana-* is udātta on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya*. The word *pati-* is derived from the root *pāti-* with the suffix *ḍati*. The word *tanu-* has its udātta on the final syllable; however, some maintain that it is also udātta on the first syllable here, and thus they recite [the mantra] *tanūnapād ucyate garbha āsuraḥ* with the udātta on the first syllable. [The compound] *narā asmin* and so forth [is explained as follows]: the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *śaṃs-* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) by the rule *akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*; it ends in *-an* because of the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, specifically the suffix *ap* after roots ending in *ṛ* or *u*.

Regarding *śunaḥśepa*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending occurs by the rule *śunaḥ puccha-śepa-lāṅgūleṣu*. "Both [words] have the acute accent on the first syllable": the word *śvan* [is acute on the first] by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), and the word *śepa* [is acute on the first] by the rule *svāṅga-śiṭām adantānām ca*. Here, *śiṭ* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for the words beginning with *sarva*; the meaning is that for words denoting body parts (*svāṅga*) and for those ending in *śiṭ* (the sibilants) which do not end in *a*, the initial syllable is acute. [The word *śaṇḍa*: from the root *śaḍi* in the sense of "injury," with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), we have *śaṇḍa*; it has the acute accent on the first syllable because it belongs to the *pramādi* group.

From the root *mṛc* (in the sense of "to mark"), the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *imbhī-kā-pā-ślyati-mṛcibhyaḥ kan*. By the rule *titutra-tathasisusarakaseṣu ca*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. There is also *kutva* (the change of *c* to *k*). Thus, the word *marka* is udātta on its first syllable. Regarding the word *tuṣṇīm*: from the root *tṛṣ* (in the sense of "thirsting"), the absence of *iṭ* occurs due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the formation of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*). Furthermore, by the rule *niṣṭhā ca dvyajāt*, it is udātta on its first syllable. The root *labi* (in the sense of "slipping down") takes the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*). Due to this very irregular derivation, the letter *l* is changed to *b*. [Thus we have *labaka*]. The term *viśvavayāḥ* means "one whose offspring (*vayas*) are all-encompassing. Regarding *marit*: from the root *mṛḍ* (in the sense of "to be gracious"), the suffix *vic* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*. From the roots *bhuj* and *mṛj*, the suffixes *tyuk* and *tyuk* are respectively applied, resulting in *mṛtyuḥ*.
And in the case of a dual compound of deities, [the first member retains its original accent]. 6.2.141.
