In the examples, by the rule *devatādvandve ca*, the substitution *anaṅ* occurs for the first member; here there are three acute accents (*udātta*), meaning the initial syllables of the three members [are acute].

The first vowel of the first member of a compound retains its original accent when followed by a second member that begins with an unaccented (anudātta) vowel, provided that the second member is not *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, or *manthin*.

The word *agni* ends in the suffix *ni*, according to the rule *agner ṇit nalopaś ca*. [The word *vāyu* is derived from] the roots *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, *ci*, *mi*, *svad*, *sādh*, and *aś* with the suffix *uṇ* and the augment *yuk*; thus, *vāyuḥ*. The mention of the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is for the following reason: otherwise, in this section, since the locative case is used to indicate a *dvandva* compound, the phrase "beginning with an anudātta vowel" would qualify the locative-ending *dvandva* itself. Consequently, there would be a prohibition in cases such as *candrasūryau*. However, when the term "subsequent member" is included, the qualification "beginning with an anudātta vowel" applies specifically to that very [subsequent member] which is heard in the text.

"Beginning with *anudāttādau*," and so forth. Otherwise, because the injunction (*vidhi*) and the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) would have the same scope, an option (*vikalpa*) would result. [The suffix] *ṣivan* is added to the root *prath*, along with vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). This word *śukra* is established as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by the rule beginning with *ṛjrendrāgra*.
The word *antaḥ* [is used as an indeclinable when expressing location]. 6-2-143.

Regarding the phrase "there, of the compound or of the final member": the meaning is that in some cases the acute accent (udātta) occurs at the end of the compound, while in others it occurs at the end of the final member. He will demonstrate the distinction between these domains further on.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of a verbal root occurs before the affixes *tha*, *thas*, *dha*, *kta*, *ktavatu*, *ja*, *ni*, *tra*, and *kā*.

The meaning is that the final member of the compound would have its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) if this [rule] were not stated. Regarding the example *dūrādāgataḥ* ("come from afar"): here, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Since a village or similar location is the thing to be expressed, the rule *kṛtā āṅo gatisamāse gatiranantaraḥ* applies, resulting in the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtibhāva*) for *āgata*, which thus has its first syllable accented. Consequently, the compound is formed by the rule *stokāntikadūrārthakṛcchrāṇi ktena*; the ablative case ending is not elided by the rule *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*. In that case, because the word follows a kāraka (the source), the phrase *paramāgatam* would—by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*—have its first syllable accented.

Regarding the word *viśuṣka*: since the root *śuṣ* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). By the rule *śuṣkadhṛṣṭau*, it has an initial udātta accent; thereafter, a *gati-samāsa* (compound with a prefix) is formed. Regarding *ātapaśuṣka*: this is not a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) with *siddha-śuṣka*, because by the rule *saptamī siddha-śuṣka-pakva-bandheṣvakālāt*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the initial member retaining its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*). Therefore, it is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

*prakṣayaḥ*, *prajayaḥ*. [The suffix] *ac* [is applied]. Now, one might object: since the final acute accent (*antodātta*) is already established here by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), he says: "In the sense of 'dwelling' (*nivāsa*), etc. [This refers to the rule *kṣayo nivāse*]. *pralavaḥ*, *prasavaḥ*, etc. [The suffix] *ap* [is applied] after roots ending in long *ṝ* or short *u* (*ṝdorap*). *pralavitram*: [the suffix] *itra* [is applied] after the roots *ṛ*, *tu*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, *sah*, and *car*.

Regarding *govṛṣa*: the root *vṛṣu* (in *vṛṣu mṛṣu*) means "to serve. Regarding *sustutam*: *suḥ* is used in the sense of praise (*pūjāyām*), and *ati* is used in the sense of exceeding (*atikramaṇe*); thus, by the rule "those beginning with *su* and *ati* are called *karmapravacanīya*," they receive that designation. Then, by the rule "*sva* and *ati* [form a compound] when meaning praise," this is a *prādi-samāsa*.
The suffix *kta* is applied after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*sūpamāna*).

Regarding "vṛkāvaluptam" and so forth: the roots *lūñ* (to cut), *cyuṅ*, *pruṅ*, *pluṅ* (to move), and *nard*, *gard* (to sound) are used here. In all these cases, the compound is formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is "cut by a wolf" (*vṛkeṇa avaluptam*). Regarding the phrase "even from a standard of comparison" (*upamānād api*) and so forth: here, the word *prāptaḥ* ("attained") is to be supplied immediately after the word *iti*.
In a compound denoting a name, the elision of the case-ending does not occur after words such as *anācita* and others. 6-2-146.

Words such as *sambhūta* and others are proper names (*saṃjñā*) for works like the *Rāmāyaṇa*; the word *rāmāyaṇa* is neuter, though it is generally recited as masculine. Regarding *upahūta*: after the root *hve* (to call), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group when followed by the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Regarding *parijagdha*: after the root *ad*, *jagdhi* is the substitute. Regarding "from the root *bhū* in the sense of 'attaining'": under the heading *ādhṛṣādvā* in the *curādi* class, it is stated that *bhū* takes the *ātmanepada* endings when meaning "to attain."

But what is the reason that the suffix *kta* is applied with effort to the root *gam*? To this he says: "For [it is stated] in the rule *gātiranantaraḥ*... This [statement] is for the purpose of setting aside that [rule]. This refers to the example under discussion, not to the intention of the *sūtra* itself. In the form *ghanuṣkhātā*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya*.

The roots *ci* (in the sense of piling), *sthā* (in the sense of cessation of motion)—both with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*) and in its simple form (*kevala*), *grah* (in the sense of taking), *vac* (in the sense of speaking), *pad* (in the sense of going), *śliṣ* (in the sense of embracing), and *dhā* (in the sense of supporting and nourishing)—all take the suffix *kta* when preceded by the word *karṇam*. These are the roots beginning with *ā-ci*.
The rule *saṃhitā’gavīti* is a metarule (*gāṇasūtra*). He explains it as follows: "If [the word] other than *go* [is present]."
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after [words ending in] *pravṛddha* and so forth. 6.2.147.

The roots *vṛdh* (to grow), *yu* (to mix), *ḍudhāñ* (to hold), *ruha* (to sprout from a seed), and *śasu* (to injure) [are mentioned]. Regarding the term *khaṭvāruḍha*: this is a compound formed with the rule *khaṭvā kṣepe* ("with *khaṭvā*, in the sense of reproach"). We have already stated in the section on "the second case in the sense of *ahīna*" (*ahīne dvitīyā ta*) that this [usage] need not be recited here. [The form] *kavibhiḥ śastaḥ* is an exception to the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi ta*. [The phrase] "for the purpose of showing the predominant usage" means: for the purpose of showing that usage which occurs predominantly—that is, most frequently—in meanings such as "vehicle" (*yāna*) and so forth.

Regarding the word *punarutsyūtam*: from the root *sīv* (to sew), the substitution *ūṭh* occurs by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike*; then, by the rule *panaścanasośchandasi*, it receives the designation of a *gati* particle, and thus forms a compound.
In the sense of a benediction, [the suffix *ktin*] is used after a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*) only when it is not preceded by *adatta*. (Pāṇini 6.2.148)

In the rule *saṃjñāyām anācitādīnām*, the fact that the final syllable has the udātta accent (antodāttatva) for words ending in *-ta* is restricted by this [sūtra]. Devadatta is so called because he was "given" (*datta*) by the gods who were thus entreated: "May the gods give him. Since the context of the rule *āśiṣi liṅ-loṭau* is still in force, the suffix *-kta* is applied by the rule *ktic-ktau ca saṃjñāyām*. [In the root *dā*,] *da* becomes *dha* before *ghu* affixes. Thus, *saṃsūtaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "Rāmāyaṇa. If it were stated simply as *kārakāt*, then—since there is a governing authority over three categories beginning with *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada*—just as the restriction would apply to the *kāraka*, it would likewise apply to the *gati* as well.

What is the purpose of employing the particle *eva*? The question is this: since a rule is being initiated when its application is already established, it will serve the purpose of restriction even without the particle *eva*. [The answer begins with] "the restriction of the *kāraka*," and so forth. For if the particle *eva* were absent, there would be a contrary restriction—namely, that [the udātta accent occurs] only after a *kāraka* in the case of the words *datta* and *śruta*. In that case, the accent would not occur after a non-*kāraka* in those two words, yet such is desired. Furthermore, because the *kāraka* would be unrestricted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an udātta at the end of a word in cases such as *devapālita*.

Therefore, the purpose of the rule is so that there may be a determination of the *kāraka* (participant in an action), and not a determination of the [specific] word-form as it was heard (*datta-śruta-avadhāraṇa*). This restriction (*niyama*) is also intended. And this is obtained from the fact that the two sūtras are pronounced by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) even though they are in a single sūtra; for the particle *eva* has a distinct scope (*bhinnakarmatva*), namely that [the designation] applies only in the case of a benediction (*āśis*).
And [the suffix *ṇamul* is used] after a word meaning "done by one who is thus. (Pāṇini 6.2.149)

"Seven types of pralāpita," and so forth. But how can these be examples, given that it is said "done" (*kṛta*), whereas *pralāpita* and the others are not "done"? For the root *kṛ* (to do) functions only with respect to the manifestation of what has not previously existed; therefore, one should have cited examples such as "well-done," "well-spoken," or "well-produced. To this he replies: the root *kṛ* functions in the sense of action in general.

And therefore, just as in the rule "the verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes action, [when another action] for the sake of that action [is present]" and so forth, there is the inclusion of specific instances as well, so it is here too. *Abhūtaprādurbhāvaḥ* means "bringing into existence" (*niṣpādanam*).
The word *bhāvaka* denotes the object of the action (*karma*). (Pāṇini 6.2.150)

In *payaḥ-pāna* and similar examples, there is a compound without a subordinate member (*amupapada-samāsa*). In *rāja-bhojana* and similar cases, there is a compound with a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Regarding all such counter-examples and so forth, this demonstrates that the present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *gati-kāraka-upapadāt*.
[The suffix *ka*] is applied after [the words] *man*, *kṛt*, *vyākhyāna*, *śayana*, *āsana*, *sthāna*, *yājaka*, and so forth, when they denote that which has been purchased. (6.2.151)

Regarding *rathavartma*: the suffix *manin* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the action; the compound is formed with a genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Regarding *pāṇinikṛti*: the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*); the compound is as before. The word *vyākhyāna* is derived by means of the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas the words *śayana*, *āsana*, and *sthāna* are derived by means of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding *prakṛti* and *prahṛti*: by the rule *tādau ca niti kṛtyatau*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member remains here.
The merit [accrues] from the seventh [day]. 6-2-152.

Regarding the phrase "but in the case of the *uṇādi* [suffixes]": since the form would have been established by the mention of the root *kami* alone in the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa-*, the fact that *kaṃsa-* is specifically mentioned indicates that the grammatical operations based on etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) are optional (*pākṣika*) in the *uṇādi* suffixes;

this is the intended meaning. From the root *pū*, the suffix *yat* is applied, along with the augment *ṇuk* and the shortening of the vowel, resulting in *puṇya*. Because of the prescription of the short vowel, there is no *guṇa* substitution. By the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the word is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).
The word *ūna* (deficient) forms a compound with a word denoting an object [of deficiency] when used in the sense of a quarrel; this applies after the third case-ending.
In the examples, *pūrvasadṛśa* is a third-case compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "here some [say]" and so forth: [an objection is raised] "But in this way, the inclusion of the word-form (*svarūpa*) of the word *ūna* would also follow; consequently, other words having that same meaning would not be included. To this he replies: "But by the word *ūna* itself... That it serves the purpose of indicating the meaning, however, is to be understood from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
And a mixed [vowel] that is not preceded by a prefix remains unchanged when there is no sandhi. 6.2.154.

But how can the word *miśra*, when being prescribed, apply to the word *sammiśra*; or how can that which is expressed by the word *miśra* be obtained when it is accompanied by a prefix? To this he says: "In this case," and so forth. He demonstrates the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the counter-example: *bāhmakaṇaiḥ*. He clarifies this very point by saying: "attaining a single meaning. But how is this the meaning of the word *saṃdhi*? To this he says: "*Saṃdhi*" means a "stipulation" (*paṇabandha*), that is, a "negotiation" (*paribhāṣaṇa*) of the form: "If you do this for me, I too will do this for you."

Regarding the phrase "some, however": that proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in which a perceived distinction—that is, a differentiation—is present is described as such. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In that case. Although the king also has proximity with the Brahmins, nevertheless, even while that [proximity] exists, a difference in nature consisting of the mutual distinction of their forms is perceived; thus, the counter-example is established—this is the meaning. He states that it is not so in the actual examples: "In the examples..."

When a negation (*nañ*) expresses the negation of a quality, the taddhita suffixes having the senses of "to be accomplished" (*sampādya*), "worthy" (*arha*), "beneficial" (*hita*), and "sufficient for" (*alam*) are elided.

*Sampādi* means "excellent. *Kārṇaveṣṭakikam*: here, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ*. *Chaidika*: here, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rules *chaidādibhyo nityam* and *ārhādagopucchādibhyaḥ*. *Vatsīya*: here, the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *prāk krītāc chaḥ*. *Sāntāpika*: here, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule *tasmai prabhavati santāpādibhyaḥ*, as it belongs to the *prāgvatīya* group.

"Why is there no *nañ*?"—this question arises because, generally, the negative particle *nañ* is seen to function only in negation. "It is *vigārdabharathika*"—here, only the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) preceding member occurs; [the compound means] "one other than a charioteer of donkeys," and so forth. To demonstrate the distinction of this [rule] from the example, he explains the portion of the sūtra beginning with "guṇapratiṣedhe": "guṇa" refers to the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), such as "having accomplished" (*sampādya*), and its "occasion for application" (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the state of having accomplished (*sampāditva*), and so on.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), qualities such as "being worthy of that" (*tadarhatva*) are included; this is what is called a "quality" (*guṇa*). For it has been said: "Whatever is perceived as having an operation that distinguishes a connection, its status as a quality is declared in the treatise because of its dependence on another.

How then is the negation of that quality stated? He says: "Not [fit] with ear-rings" (*karṇaveṣṭakābhyām na saṃpādī*). Regarding *vaveḍhā*: the suffix *tṛc* is used in the sense of being worthy (*arha*), and after the application of *ḍhatva*, *dhātva*, *ṣṭutva*, and the elision of *dha*, there is the substitution of *o* for the vowel of the roots *sah* and *vah* according to the rule *sahivahorodavarṇasya*. Thus, the form *vaveḍhā* is derived.
The suffix *cha* (forming the word *yāyāvara*) is applied after the names *yayāti* and *yati* when the sense of "one who habitually performs that" is not intended. 6.2.156.

By the words *pāśa* and *tṛṇa*, the suffix *ya* is applied [after these] in the sense of a collection (*samūha*) according to *pāśādibhyo yaḥ*. By the words *danta* and *karṇa*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhavārtha*) according to *digādibhyo yat*, and also by the rule *śarīrāvayavācca*.

Regarding *pādyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied after *pāda* and *argha* according to *pādārghābhyāṃ ca*. Regarding *adeyam*: in the sense of "worthy of" (*arhārtha*), the suffix *yat* is applied after a vowel (*aco yat*), and the substitution of *ī* for *ā* occurs according to *īdyati*, followed by *guṇa*. The two rules concerning "those without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*)" and "those with one indicatory letter (*ekānubandhaka*)" are both indicated in the rule *vāmadevād ḍyaḍḍyau*.
The suffix *ka* is applied after a word denoting inability, when it is used in the sense of "not capable of. (Pāṇini 6.2.157)

Regarding the term *avikṣipa*: because it occurs in association with the suffixes *kṛt*, *u*, *ke*, and *ṣṇuc* which are to be mentioned later, this refers to the formation of nouns ending in those suffixes; thus, by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes, the word *vikṣipa* is understood to end in the suffix *kā*.

Just as the initiated student (*dīkṣita*) and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) do not cook due to scriptural prohibitions and not because of incapacity, so too in that case, a religious vow (*vrata*) is understood, not mere incapacity.
And also after the verb *ā-kruś* (to revile). 6-2-158.
"This fellow is uncooked"—here, greed is intended, not incapacity.
In the case of *saṃjñā* (a name), [the elision of the final vowel and consonant of the first member does not take place]. 6.2.159.
"Non-Devadatta": one who, being Devadatta, does not perform his duty, is thus reviled.
The words *kṛtya*, *okeya*, *uṣṇika*, *cāru*, and so forth [are used as adjectives]. 6.2.160.

"Even that which has two suffixes (*anubandha*) is included. This is to be connected with what follows, namely "it occurs. The reason for this is stated as: "by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing [the suffix] after the vowel *i*. Since the root *bhū* is udātta, it is already established that the *iṭ* augment following it (in the case of the suffix *khiṣṇuc*) begins with *i*; therefore, the prescription here of [the suffix] beginning with *i* is solely for the purpose of including it generally. Regarding the example *acāruḥ*, and so forth.

From *car* with the suffix *ṇvuṇ*, *cāruḥ*; from *sādh* with *uṇ*, *sādhuḥ*. From *yudh* with the suffix *ṭhak*, *yaudhikaḥ*. From *ej* with the suffix *khaś*, *aṅgamejayaḥ*; other than that, *anaṅgamejayaḥ*. From *vad* with the suffix *ānyaḥ*, *vādānyaḥ*. [The term] *akasmāt* is not [derived] from *kasmat*. The roots *vṛtu* (to turn), *vṛdhu* (to grow), *ñitvarā* (in confusion), *ruca* (to shine), and *dhṛṅ* (to stand)—these are understood as ending in the suffix *śānac*. With the suffix *kan* when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), [we have] *gṛhapatikaḥ*. Others read *gṛhapatiḥ*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *ṣaṣṭhī* (ṣaṣ) is applied after the words *idam*, *etad*, and *tad*, when they denote either the first [ordinal] or a count of actions.

The term *prathama-* [in the rule] indicates the mention of the word-form itself. Because the word *pūraṇa-* (ordinal) is marked with the svarita accent, it includes those suffixes prescribed under that governing heading. In the case of *prathama* [as a Bahuvrīhi], only the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the third case-ending in the prior member occurs. In the case of *yatprathama-*—which is a Bahuvrīhi meaning "he who is the first among these"—here too, only the original accent of the prior member occurs.
The meaning is "having this as its primary referent.

By this, he shows that the word *prathama* denotes the primary element (*pradhāna*) and not the number one, thereby stating the absence of counting—namely, "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*), and so forth. Here, "of the compound" (*samāsasya*) is the subject under discussion; from the rule beginning with "the initial [element] of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadādiḥ*) up to "of the subsequent member" (*uttarapadasya*), the subsequent member is taken as the basis for the operation. Therefore, when the suffix *kap* arises, that which precedes *kap*—namely *prathama*—becomes udātta at its end, but the form ending in *kap* does not.

For the suffix *kap* belongs to the end of the compound as a whole, not to the final member alone. And even when one holds the view that the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied before the compound has been formed—specifically from the final member which conveys the meaning of the compound—the accent still applies only to those two [words] that have been explicitly mentioned, because of the specific mention of the forms "prathama" and "pūraṇa," and because *kap* is included therein.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the word ending in *kap* which serves as the *uttarapada* here has not been explicitly mentioned (*anupātta*), while that which is explicitly mentioned is not the *uttarapada*, because it forms a single unit with the *kap*? Thus, there is no occasion for the accentuation of *kap* here, nor should there be an accentuation of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) by virtue of it being a *seṣa*. Therefore, in this view, the mention of "the *uttarapada*" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (indication) of what is actually employed. For that [word] is generally the *uttarapada*, since the *kārti* (the suffix *ka*) is intended to apply to the *uttarapada*. What is the meaning? It means that the *kārti* is intended to apply to the first and the ordinal numbers when they have become, in general, the *uttarapada*.
In the Vedic language, there is optional substitution [of the genitive case-ending]. 6.2.164.
*dvistanā*—this is oxytone; *catustanā*—this is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
In the case of *saṃjñā*, [the suffix *cha*] is applied after the words *mittra* and *ajina*. (Pāṇini 6.2.165)

Regarding *viśvāmittra*: by the rule *mittre carṣau*, a long vowel [is substituted], and because this [rule] applies later, it would result in the final syllable being udātta; however, that is prohibited, and consequently, by the rule *bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*, the final syllable of the first member becomes udātta.
The *vyavāyin* (the intervening element) is the *antara* (that which comes between). 6-2-166.

In the example, from the word *antarā* meaning "separation," the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *tat karoti*, followed by the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). In the counter-example, however, the word *antara* signifies "other."
The word *mukha* [is used] in the sense of one’s own limb (*svāṅga*). (Pāṇini 6.2.167)

"In *dīrghamukhā śālā* (a long-faced hall)," it is said. Here, by the word "face" (*mukha*), the entrance region of the hall is meant. [Objection: But surely it is one's own limb (*svāṅga*), and therefore the [shortening] ought to occur here as well; to this he replies: "A 'limb of one's own' (*svāṅga*) is understood according to the definition beginning with 'not liquid' (*adrava*)."
The suffix *kan* is not applied after indeclinables, words denoting direction, *go*, *mahat*, *sthūla*, *muṣṭi*, *pṛthu*, and *vatsa*. (Pāṇini 5.2.167)

The words *uccais* and *nīcais* are udātta on the final syllable due to their inclusion in the list beginning with *svarādi*. The word *prāk* is udātta on the first syllable because it is formed with the suffix *añcu* preceded by a non-iṇ-ending prefix. In *pratyaṅ*, the accent follows the rule for the original form of the second member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). The accent for *go* and *maha* has already been stated. The word *sthūla* is listed among the *ṛjrendra* group and others, and is thus udātta on the final syllable. From the root *muṣ* with the suffix *ktic*, we get *muṣṭiḥ*. From the root *prath* with the suffix *ku* (which replaces *ka*), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowel and the elision of the suffixal *s*, resulting in *pṛthuḥ*. From the root *vad* with the suffix *sa*, we get *vatsaḥ*. [The rule] beginning with "preceded by *go*, *muṣṭi*, or *vatsa*" [applies].

The scope for this prohibition is where there is no comparison with "cow" (*go*) and so forth—such as *gaurmukham iva yasya* ("one whose face is like a cow"), *muṣṭirmukham iva yasya* ("one whose face is like a fist"), or *vatso mukham iva yasya* ("one whose face is like a calf")—in all these cases, "cow" and the rest are the objects of comparison (*upameya*), not the standards of comparison (*upamāna*). The scope for the subsequent optional rule (*vikalpa*) is where "cow" and so forth do not occur as the prior member (*pūrvapada*)—such as *siṃhamukhaḥ* ("lion-faced") or *vyāghramukhaḥ* ("tiger-faced"). When both [the prohibition and the optional rule] would apply in the case of "cow" and so forth being the standard of comparison, this very prohibition takes effect by means of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
The suffix *niṣṭhā* may optionally be used after a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). 6.2.169.

From the root *hiṃs* (to injure), the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *pacādyac*; due to its inclusion in the *paṛṣodarādi* group, there is a transposition of the initial and final sounds, resulting in *siṃha*. From the root *vyāghrā* (to smell about), *vyāghra* is formed; the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*. The suffix *śa* does not apply here according to the rule *pādhrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ*, because of the specific statement that there is a prohibition of *śa* after the root *jighrati* when forming a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

The suffix *kta* is used after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, when they do not denote clothing (*anācchādana*), provided that the action has not been completed (*akṛti*), nor is it measured (*mita*), nor is it comparable (*pratima*). (Pāṇini 6.2.170)

One might object: "In the examples and counter-examples, since the rule *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 2.2.36] applies, the word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix should be placed first. To this he says: "In these," etc., beginning with "in the counter-examples. Among those, the word *putra* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). From the root *vas* with the suffix *iṣṭran*, we have *vastra*; from the same root with *lyuṭ*, we have *vasana*. The word *kuṇḍa* has its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* [Pāṇini 6.2.172].
Or when [the word] *jāta* follows. (Pāṇini 6.2.171)

The words *danta* and *stana* have their initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by the rule "of [words ending in] *svāṅga*, *śiṭ*, or those ending in short *a*. The word *māsa* has its initial syllable accented acute by the rule "and of *prāma* etc. The word *saṃvatsara* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*) by the rule "of *baṃhiṣṭha*, *vatsara*, *tiśat*, and those ending in *tha*. The meaning of this is: for words ending in *baṃhiṣṭha*, *vatsara*, *tiśat*, and *tha*, the final syllable is acutely accented—namely, *baṃhiṣṭhaḥ*, *saṃvatsaraḥ*, *saptatiḥ*, *aśītiḥ*, *triṃśat*, *catvāriṃśat*, *gūtham*, and *pūtham*.

The words *sukha* and *duḥkha* have their final syllable accented (*antodātta*) because they belong to the class beginning with *aśama* and ending in *kha*. The meaning of this rule is: for a word ending in *kha*, the final syllable is accented provided it does not begin with the letter *a* or *śa*; for example, *nakhaḥ* and *taukhā*. Why "not beginning with *a* or *śa*"? [Consider] *śikhā* and *mukham*. The suffix *rak* is applied to the root *tṛp* by the rule *sphāyitañci* etc.; thus, *tṛp* + *rak* = *tṛpra*. By the rule *kṛteśchra ca*, we have *kṛcchram*. From the root *as*, the suffix *rak* is applied due to the frequentative nature of the rule, resulting in *asram*. Furthermore, by the rule *ambikādayaśca*, the word *ambaka* is established as a conventional form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *ikan*.

The waters have returned here against the current (*pratīpam*). [The suffix] *uṇ* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, and *ji*: *kāruḥ* (artisan). [The suffix] *kyun* is applied after the root *kṛp*: *kṛpaṇaḥ* (miserable). [The suffix] *kta* is applied after the root *sah*: *soḍhaḥ* (endured). These ten are the *sukhādi* group.
The suffix *ka* is applied after a word ending in the negative particle *nañ* or the prefix *su*, provided that the word is not a *prātipadika* ending in *a*.

Regarding the phrase "of the compound" (*samāsasya*) and so forth: although both "the compound" (*samāsa*) and "the final member" (*uttarapada*) are under discussion, nevertheless, here it is intended that the compound alone is the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryitva*). This is understood from the rule stating "before *kap*" (*kapi pūrvam*). For if, by this [rule], the final member were to become oxytone (*antodātta*), then in examples such as *akṛtārīka*, since the desired result would already be accomplished by this very rule, the statement "before *kap*" (*kapi pūrvam*) would not need to be stated. Furthermore, the suffixes added at the end of a compound (*samāsānta*) constitute parts of the compound itself.

The inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in the rule *samāsāntāḥ* is for this purpose: that the *samāsānta* suffixes should be understood as included by the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) itself. Consequently, in forms such as *anṛcaḥ*, once the *samāsānta* suffix has been applied, it is precisely that *samāsānta* suffix which receives the acute accent. The example *bahvṛcaḥ* is cited here because of the extended application (*atideśa*) from the rule *bahoḥ nañvat*. And this is stated on the assumption that *samāsānta* suffixes are members of the compound itself, not of the final member (*uttarapada*). However, regarding the rule *na kapi*, he will later state that the *samāsānta* suffixes are applied first, and subsequently the compound is formed with that [form] ending in the suffix.
The word *kapi* [is used] before [the suffixes mentioned in the preceding rule]. (Pāṇini 6.2.173)

Since the suffix *kap* would have been required by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.4.153] due to the presence of the vowel *ā*, the acute accent (*udātta*) is then assigned to the syllable preceding it; however, because of the rule "before a short vowel, the penultimate [syllable is acute]" (Pāṇini 6.2.174), only examples with long vowels are cited here. The suffix *kap* is applied by the rule "after *nadī* and after a word ending in ṛ" (Pāṇini 5.4.153).
When a short vowel follows, [the augment] is placed before the final consonant. (Pāṇini 6.2.174)

Regarding the term *hrasvānte*, he explains that the referent of this bahuvrīhi compound is either the final member (*uttarapada*) or the entire compound itself—stating: "that of which the end is short," and so forth.

In this context, because of the separate mention of "when *kap* follows," both the final member devoid of *kap* and the compound are understood; otherwise, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* would be redundant, since the phrase "before *kap*" (*kapi pūrvam*) is already supplied by way of anuvṛtti. To address this, he says: "while the word *pūrva* is being carried over," and so forth.

When there is a second mention of "pūrva" (preceding), a distinction in application (*pravṛtti-bheda*) occurs. Therein, by one application, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is prescribed for the syllable preceding the final short vowel; by the other, however, it is restricted: "only that which precedes the final short vowel becomes acute, but not that which precedes the suffix *kap*. He states what is established by this: "By that [restriction]... [The examples are: *ajñakaḥ* ("one who does not possess knowledge") and *sujñakaḥ* ("one who possesses good knowledge").

In this regard, if this restriction were not in place, then since there would be no preceding element that is to become acute (udātta) relative to the final one, the accentuation "the preceding [element] in a *kap*-suffix" would apply here as well. However, because this restriction exists, it does not occur; rather, by the rule *nañ-subhyām*, it applies only to that which ends in *kap*. How it applies to that which ends in *kap* has been explained in that very same context. Furthermore, this mention of "preceding" (*pūrva*) was made with reference to the view that words denote individuals (*vyakti*).

However, when recourse is taken to the genus (*jāti*), just as in the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, a consonant (*hal*) belonging to the genus—even if occurring anywhere—effects the removal of all non-initial consonants everywhere; likewise, here too in the rule *hrasvānte 'ntyātpūrvam*, because recourse is taken to the genus "short vowel" (*hrasva-jāti*), the application of the rule *kapi pūrvam* is precluded everywhere where a short vowel ends [the word], by way of the maxim of the curd-milkman (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*).
In the sense of "abundance," the suffix *matup* is applied after a word ending in the negative particle *nañ*, provided that the subsequent member of the compound denotes "ground" (*bhūmi*).

*Nañvat* means "like *nañ*. From this very [sūtra], the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) due to the inclusion of the particle (*nipāta*). Alternatively, the sixth case (genitive) is used for the general sense of relationship; since all case-meanings are subsumed under it, the suffix *vati*—as in *tatra tasyeva*—is applied even in the sense of the fifth case, and thus it follows a word ending in the sixth case. *Bhūmā* is the state of being many (*bahūnāṃ bhāvaḥ*). According to the rule *baho-lopo bhū ca bahoḥ*, the final syllable of *bahu* is elided and *bhū* is substituted for it. By the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), its meaning is understood, because the subsequent member itself cannot possess plurality. Thus he says: "in the plurality of the meaning of the subsequent member."

But for what purpose is this extended application (*atideśa*) resorted to? Why not simply say: "after [compounds] with *nañ* or *su*, [the suffix *ka* is added] when there is abundance in the final member"? Even if it were stated thus, because of the possibility of occurrence and the exclusion of others, the phrase "when there is abundance in the final member" would serve as a qualifier for *bahu* alone. Furthermore, regarding the prohibition "not when *guṇa* and so forth are constituent parts," since the phrase "when there is abundance in the final member" continues to apply there as well, it would likewise apply only to *bahu*. It would not apply in cases such as *aguṇaḥ* or *saguṇaḥ* (where the rule would otherwise apply after *nañ* and *su*). Therefore, the following is the purpose:

It is so that the accent which depends on the negative particle (*nañ*) even in another context may also be extended [to this case]. He demonstrates this by stating: "In the case of *nañ*, it has been stated that [the words] *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta* [take the acute accent]," and so forth.
Qualities and the like are not constituent parts. 6-2-173.

In the enumeration of qualities (*guṇa-saṃkhyāna*), [the suffix] *ac* is applied after roots beginning with *cur* and those ending in short *a*. From the root *aś*, [with the substitution of] *sara*, we have *akṣara*. That by which the meter (*chandas*) is measured is *chandomāna*. From the root *vac* preceded by *su*, the suffix *kta* is applied: *sūkta*. That from which one studies is *adhyāya*; here the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to the rule *iṅaśca*. These are the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
After a prefix, a word denoting a limb of the body that is fixed [in its position] takes the *ṣatva* substitute for the initial *s*, except after the word *praśu*.

Because there is no connection with an action (*kriyā*) toward one's own limb (*svāṅga*), the inclusion of the prefix *upa-* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). By the phrase "of whom [there is] constantly," etc., he demonstrates the immobility (*dhruvatva*) of the back. In the compound *tīrthapṛṣṭhagūḍhayūtha*, the word *pṛṣṭha* is treated as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term.

"Udvāhuḥ krośati" (he cries out with uplifted arms). Here, the state of having uplifted arms exists only at the time of crying out, not at all times; thus, there is instability (*adhruvatva*). Regarding the rule "spṛśeḥ śvaṇ-śunau pṛ ca": from the root *spṛś*, the suffixes *śvaṇ* and *śun* occur, and the root undergoes the substitution *pṛ*. Because of the mention of *bahula* (diversity), the letter *ś* does not receive the technical designation *it*. Consequently, *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* apply respectively: *pārśvam* (side) and *parśuḥ* (rib).

"Pareramitobhāvi maṇḍalam. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and so forth. When it is a *bahuvrīhi*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has its bank (*kūla*) surrounded (*paritaḥ*). In the case of a *prādisamāsa*, however, it is "the bank that has been encompassed (*parigataṃ kūlam*). Furthermore, when it is an *avyayībhāva*, it is "from around the bank (*parikūlāt*). Regarding the phrase "even in the case of the *avyayībhāva*" and so forth: even in the *avyayībhāva* construction, this very accent (*svara*) must be desired; the meaning is that the derivation is not accomplished by the accent of a general compound (*samāsasvara*). [The term] *amitobhāvī* means "that which possesses a state (*bhāva*) that is immeasurable (*amita*)."

He says "amitobhāvī" because, in worldly usage (*laukike yoge*), brevity (*lāghava*) is not universal, and thus the *bahuvrīhi* compound was not resorted to; [the suffix] *-ṇini* is applied according to the rule *supsyajātau*. And "that which has such a nature" means that which has the nature of becoming manifest on all sides (*abhitobhavana-svabhāva*).
The word *prāda* [is used] before a body part (*svāṅga*) when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). 6.2.183.
In cases such as *prakoṣṭha*, there is either a *prādisamāsa* (prepositional compound) or a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound).
And [the suffix *kan* is applied after words such as] *nirudaka* and others. 6-2-184.

"Of these," and so forth. When it is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes), the analysis (*vigraha*) is either "water has gone out" (*nirgatam udakam*) or "gone out from water" (*nirgatam udakāt*). In the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, it is "that from which water has gone out" (*nirgatam udakam asmāt*). Now, why is the inclusion of these [prefixes] not also for the purpose of forming an *avyayībhāva*? To this he says: "But in the case of an *avyayībhāva*... [The example is] *niṣkālika*. From the word *kāla*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *jānapadādi-sūtra*; then the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*); by the rule *ke'ṇaḥ*, there is shortening, resulting in *kālikā*; then a *prādi-samāsa* is formed.

"Niṣpeṣa" [is formed] by adding the suffix *ghañ* to the root *piṣ*. "Kutsitastarīyaḥ": he shows that the prefix *duḥ* is used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*). Others read "nistarīkaḥ"; the ellipsis [to be supplied] is "they read," and the word *ajina* is preceded by *ni*. That same [word] is preceded by *ud*. "Parer" and so forth: following *pari*, words beginning with *hasta* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on their final syllable. Examples include *parihasta* and so forth. (*Harikeśaḥ*: one whose hair is like that of a lion; *kapikeśaḥ*: one whose hair is like that of a monkey).
The word *abhi* takes the sixth case ending when it signifies "towards" (*mukha*). ||6-2-185||

It is established by the rule *upasargātsvāṅgaṃ dhruvam*. However, the term *mukham* as a *svāṅga* (body part) is not established, because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *na avyaya-dik-śabde*.
And [the substitution of *ap* occurs] for the word *apa*. (Pāṇini 6.2.186)

"The *avyayībhāva* compound also serves as a motivation here. Why? He says: "For even there," etc. Since in that case as well, the rule stating that the initial member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)—namely, *pari-prati-upa-apa*—has been taught, the meaning is that this [compound] also serves as a motivation. "The separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows" means that in the subsequent rule, the term *upa* alone should be carried over (*anuvṛtti*), so that it does not apply to *abhi*.
The words *sphig*, *pūta*, *vīṇā*, *añc*, *adhvan*, *kukṣi*, and *sīra* [are followed by the suffix *aṇ*] when they are names; and so too is the word *nāman*. (Pāṇini 6.2.187)

The mention of the name (*nāmagrahaṇa*) is connected with the word *sīra* alone, and not with the buttocks (*sphig*) and so forth, because the buttocks, the back, and the belly are mentioned separately.

Regarding the rule "after a prefix, [the suffix] *ṭac* is added to the word for a road" (*upasargād adhvanaḥ*), when there is a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*), and so on; he states the reason for this here: "for when that [suffix] exists," and so forth. But surely, [one might object]:

However, in the rule *caupasargādadhvanaḥ*, neither an option (*vikalpa*) is explicitly stated nor is one under discussion; so why is it said, "when the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is absent"? To this he replies: "and it is non-eternal" (*anityaśca*). If the compound-ending suffix were eternal, the mention of *adhvan* here would not have been necessary, because the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*) would already be established by the fact that the suffix *ac* is marked with the indicator *c*. Yet it has been included; therefore, it indicates that the rule for compound-endings is non-eternal.

Regarding the phrase "sphigapūtakukṣīṇām" and so forth: when these words denote one's own limbs (*svāṅga*) and are indeclinables (*dhruva*), and there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then the rule is already established by [Pāṇini 6.2.177], which states: "After a prefix, [the final vowel of] a word denoting one's own limb [is lengthened]."
The suffix *matup* is applied after a word ending in *adhi*, provided that it stands immediately before [the word ending in *adhi*]. (Pāṇini 5.2.18)

"Standing above" (*uparistha*) means "standing on top"; [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*. By the phrase "above the tooth," etc., he demonstrates its state of being situated above.

Regarding the term "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*): here, by the accentual rule for the base form of the second member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*), the vowel *ā* of the syllable *ka* is acute (*udātta*).
The word *anīyas* [is used] after *aṇu*, *pradhāna*, and *kanīya*. (Pāṇini 5.3.64)

In the example *udārahaṇe*, it shows that the meaning of the second member (*uttarapadārtha*) is not predominant; rather, this *prādi*-compound has the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapadārtha*) as its primary sense. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *kanīyaḥ* is for the sake of the predominant meaning, because in other cases the formation is already established by the mention of the non-predominant [member].
In the phrase *anugato jyeṣṭhaḥ*, he demonstrates through a specific analysis (*vigraha*) that the word *jyeṣṭha* expresses the predominant sense.
And the word *puruṣa* is also [an example] when it is subsequently specified (*anvādiṣṭa*). 6-2-190.

*Anvādiṣṭa* means taught as secondary (*apradhāna-śiṣṭa*), such as the bringing of the cow in the command, "Go for alms and bring the cow. Or it is that which is mentioned after having been previously mentioned; when something else is mentioned subsequently after something has already been said, that is *kathitānukathita*. *Anugata* means followed or come after.
The suffix *kṛt* is applied after a verbal root to form a noun denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). (Pāṇini 3.4.67)

"akṛt ca padaṃ ca = akṛtpade. Regarding "ātaḥ kārake": *svatī pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.67) [is used here], thus it is a *prādi-samāsa*. Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the rule applies] when there is elision of a verbal root (*dhātu*) after *ati*": in examples such as *aty-aṅkuśa-caitya*, within the scope of a compound (*vṛtti*), the word *ati* functions in the sense of "transcending" (*atikrānta*). Thus, because the root *kram* is not actually employed, there is indeed an elision of the verbal root. In the case of *ati-gārgya*, according to the alternative formulation (*yathānyāse*), the rule would apply here as well, because the word *gārgya* does not end in a *kṛt*-suffix. In the case of *ati-kāraka*, however, according to the alternative formulation, the rule would not apply, because the word *kāraka* does end in a *kṛt*-suffix.

Therefore, in order to avoid the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), one should remove the word *akṛt* and state instead: "after the root [is elided], there is elision of the suffix" (*ater dhātulopaḥ*).
[The rule] *ner anidhāne* (Pāṇini 6.2.192) [follows].
"Treasure that is unmanifest": it is not a non-treasure; its root has gone forth, or its root is gone forth, thus it is "rootless" (*nimūla*).

He says this for the sake of explaining the treasure; the meaning is that he speaks of its unmanifest state. To the question, "How, moreover, does the word *ni-* have this meaning? he replies: "For *pra* and the others... [as stated in the rule *prādayaḥ*].
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, words such as *prateraṃśu* and others [are placed first]. 6.2.193.

The word *aṃśu* is established as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) by the rule *mṛgayvādayaś ca*, while the word *kuśa* follows from the rule *aṃśuśabdaḥ kuś ca*. From the root *rāj* with the suffix *kanin*, we have *rājan*. From the root *uṣ* (to burn) with the suffix *ṣṭran*, we have *uṣṭraḥ*. From the root *khiṭ* with the suffix *ṇvul*, we have *kheṭakaḥ*. From the root *aj* with the suffix *kirac* (as prescribed in the rule *ajiraśiśira*), we have *ajiram*. From the root *drā* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *ātaś copasarge*; due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*), the augment *rak* is added after *āṅ*, resulting in *ārdrā*. From the root *śru* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, we have *śravaṇam*. From the roots *kṛt*, *bhid*, and *lī*, the suffix *kit* is applied; since *tikana* was previously introduced [by the rule *kṛtabhidilatibhyaḥ kit tikan*], we have *kṛttikā*.

From the root *ṛgh* with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), we have *ardha*. From the root *pur* (meaning "to go before") with the suffix *ka* (after a root with an *iṭ*-type penultimate vowel), we have *pura*. These are the words beginning with *aṃśu*.
After *uk* (u, ū), the suffix *aṇ* is applied to form the word for "white" (*gaura*) when it follows a dissyllabic stem ending in *j*, provided the resulting form is not *maragaura*. (Pāṇini 6.2.194)

From the root *gur* meaning "to exert effort," with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac) and then the suffix *aṇ* (prajñādyaṇ), we derive *gaura*. The time conjoined with the asterism Tiṣya is called *taiṣa*. Regarding *leṭ* and *loṭ*: these are derived from the roots listed in the *kaṇḍvādi* group with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), yielding *leṭ* and *loṭ*. *Jihvā* is derived from *dih* according to the *uṇādi* rules. From the root *kṛṣ* with the sense of color, the suffix *nak* is applied and *ṭāp* follows—thus *kṛṣṇā*. The word *kanyā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term, as are words such as *adhnyā*. From the root *guh* meaning "concealment" (*ghanatve*), with the suffix *ka* after a root having *i* or *u* as its penultimate vowel (*igupadhātkaḥ*), we have *gudha*. From the roots *klṛp* and *pad*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied—yielding *kalpa* and *pāda*.
The suffix *ṣvan* is applied after the root *kṣip* in the sense of "scattering. (Pāṇini 6.2.195)

In the case of *udārahaṇe*, however, there is a compound with the *karmapravacanīya* [particle] *svati* according to the rule *svatī pūjāyām*. Therefore, one should not suspect that the formation of *supratyavasite* would fail due to the accentuation rule *thāthādisvara*. If the word *su-* here functions only in the sense of "praise" (*pūjā*), how then is "censure" (*kṣepa*) understood? To this he says: "But the meaning of the sentence... He asks, "How? and replies: "Because it is expressed in such a way out of envy. For when it is said of someone who remains in a state of pleasure while misfortune has arrived, censure is understood from the very context.
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after [the word] *utpuccha*. 6.2.196.

This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases. In the first application, because it is sublated by the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the prior member, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of the compound does not apply; however, in the second case, since it would necessarily apply by the rule for *thā-tha* and so forth, [the option is established].

Regarding the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhasu bahuvrīhau*: the word *dvitribhyām* is a fifth case (*pañcamī*) characterized by its connection with a direction (*digyogalakṣaṇā*), while *pāddanmūrddhasu* is a seventh case (*satsaptamī*) [indicating the presence of the suffix]. The *bahuvrīhi* compound is that which undergoes the operation; thus he says: "by these two, *dvi* and *tri*. In the example *dvipād*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* as a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) according to the rule *saṃkhyā-supūrvasya*. In *dann*, [the suffix] *datṛ* replaces *danta* when referring to age (*vayasi*). As for *mūrddhan* and so forth, since it is impossible for these forms to occur without the application of a compound-final suffix, he says: "this very [suffix]."

If, then, the compound ending (*samāsānta*) has not yet been applied, this being the case, if the compound ending were to be applied [later], it would not apply because that would constitute a different word; therefore, he says: "Even though... Here, indeed, the *bahuvrīhi* is taken as the subject of the operation, not the word *mūrdhan*. And because it is a part of that: the meaning is "because of its being a portion, a constituent part, of that *bahuvrīhi*—the state of being such, that very fact. Thus is the sense.

Regarding the reading *tadekadeśitvāt*: that rice (*vrīhi*) is the "possessor of parts" (*ekadeśin*), that is, the whole (*avayavin*); the state of being such is *tadekadeśitva*, and [the suffix is applied] because of that. This is the very same meaning. Thus, since the *bahuvrīhi* is the object of the operation and because it possesses a single part, even when the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied, this rule still certainly takes effect.

Another says: even when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is the one subject to the grammatical operation, nevertheless, since the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) occurs first by virtue of its priority, the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied afterwards; then, once the *ṭi*-elision has taken place, the acuteness of the *ṣa*-suffix is established precisely by the accent of the disappearance of an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). Thus, in the case of *kalyāṇamūrdhā*, the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) alone remains here. The word *kalyāṇa* is acutely accented on the middle syllable according to the rule *laghāvante*.
And [the substitution of *ū* for *u* occurs] after the word *sakthi* when it is followed by a word beginning with *ā*. (Pāṇini 6.2.198)

When the compound suffix *ṣac* is applied by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac*, the word *saktha* that results is what is understood here. That which has *kra* as its final member is *krānta*; that which is other than this is *akrānta*. Thus, in *gaurasaktha*, the word *gaura* is oxytone because it ends in the suffix *aṇ* belonging to the *prajñādi* group. The word *ślakṣṇa* is oxytone by the rule *śliṣer añ copadhāyāḥ*. Regarding the phrase "because of the *cit*-designation of *ṣac*": by this he shows that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accent of a *cit* suffix, and that it is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*).
In the Vedic language, the accentuation of the first syllable and so forth occurs diversely.

Regarding the term *parādi*: here, by the word *para*, only the word *saktha* is understood, because it alone was present in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*). If this were so, the mention of *para* would be redundant, for the word *saktha* would simply carry over from the previous context. This is not the case; for if it were carried over as part of the *prakṛti* (base) of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, its initial udātta accent might be suspected [as applying here as well]. Since the term *vibhāṣā* is already in effect, the purpose of using the term *bahula* is so that there may be other purposes as well. For example: *ṛjuvāhuḥ*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

The words *vākpatiḥ* and *citpatiḥ* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In this context, regarding the domain of common speech (*bhāṣā*), because the prohibition "not after *bhū*, *vāk*, *cit*, or *didhiṣū*" applies to the rule "in the case of *pati* when denoting lordship" (*patyāvaiśvarye*), the final member of the compound retains its original accent (*samāsāntodāttatva*).

He demonstrates by means of a verse the meaning established by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways): "and beginning with *parā*, and ending with *parā*. By the words *pūrva* and *para*, the preceding and following members of a compound are understood. Since an acute accent (*udātta*) beginning with *parā* and so forth is observed in the Veda (*chandas*), for that reason, a change of accent (*svaravyatyaya*) is stated to occur *bahulam*. The meaning is that the inclusion of the term *bahulam* was made for the purpose of accounting for such changes of accent.
Thus ends the second quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the third quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī*.
In the case of *alaguttara* words, [the final vowel is lengthened]. 6-3-1.

Regarding the phrase *alugiti cetyādi*: it demonstrates the declaration (*pratijñāna*) that each [term] possesses the *svarita* accent. Its purpose is this: so that when one [element] is elided, another might not also be elided. In the expression *stokānmuktaḥ*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is applied by the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpakṛcchra-* etc., and the compound is formed by the rule *stokāntika-* etc. As for the question "Why [is the word] *uttarapade* [specified]?", since the elision (*luk*) is already established only in the context of a compound (*samāsa*), it is understood through the force of the context (*sāmarthyāt*) that the term *uttarapade* is intended.

In rules such as *nalopo nañaḥ*, the question arises: since the term "compound" (*samāsa*) is understood through its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), and because the subsequent member of the compound (*uttarapada*) is thereby obtained, the absence of the elision of *n* in *nañ*—as in *natarām* and similar forms—is established. However, in the case of *nistokaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) even after words such as *stoka* when they function as the subsequent member of a compound.

But surely, by the paribhāṣā "that which is taught by its specific definition," the ablative case prescribed after words such as *stoka*—as well as the specific compound formed with them—will undergo elision (*luk*) precisely there and only there; so why is the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) made for the purpose of excluding that? To this, he says: "For another purpose," and so forth.

The rule for *ānaṅ* is intended so that it applies when the word ending in *ṛt* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*) of a *dvandva* compound, but not to the second member itself—such as in *hotāpotārau*. Otherwise, since the substitution of *guṇa* for *ṛt* before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix would be *bahiraṅga* (external) with respect to the *dvandva* formation, *ānaṅ* would supersede that *guṇa* and apply immediately after the formation of the *dvandva*, resulting in forms such as *hotāpotṛbhyām*.

Similarly, for the sake of ensuring that rules such as *iko hrasvo’ṅyo gālavasya* apply specifically when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), and so that they do not apply to the subsequent member in cases like *grāmaṇīḥ*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the subsequent member must necessarily be established; this [heading] should be placed right here [at the beginning of the section], so that the continued application of the term "compound" (*samāsa*) does not require one to invoke the technical paribhāṣā regarding "that which is indicated by a definition versus that which is explicitly stated. When the question arises as to where these two headings end, he says: "The heading *aluk*," and so forth.

For when a stem ending in *ṛ* is followed by an immediately subsequent *uttarapada*, such as in *pitṛ-putra* and similar forms, *ānaṅ* ought to occur. If, however, there were *aluk* (non-elision) here, there would be an intervention by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Alternatively, a grammatical operation (*kārya*) that is directly prescribed, such as *ānaṅ* and the like, sets aside the *aluk* established by the context; thus, the section on *aluk* precedes the section on *ānaṅ*. Furthermore, an operation prescribed for a base (*aṅga*) occurs only where that which is called "base" (*aṅga*) actually exists. And since this [status of being a base] occurs in relation to an affix (*pratyaya*) and not in relation to an *uttarapada*, it follows by implication that the section on *uttarapada* precedes the section on *aṅga*.
The ablative case ending is used after the words *stoka* and others when they are joined with a fifth [case-ending word]. Pāṇini 2.3.31.

Since words such as *stoka* are not included in the list of nominal stems (*pratipadika-gaṇa*), he states that those read in the sūtra are what are intended: "The words *stoka*, *antika*, *dūra*, and their synonyms, as well as *kṛcchra*, are the *stoka*-group. However, in rules such as *karaṇe ca stokālpakṛcchraḥ*, the *stoka*-group is not taken [in its entirety], because of the lack of pervasiveness; rather, the majority of the items found in the rule *stokāntika...* are included by virtue of the mention of "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇāt*). "The elision (*aluk*) does not occur" means that elision (*luk*) does not take place. This refers to the case where elision of the case-ending (*sup*) would otherwise have occurred by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*.

"A prohibition is being made. This indicates that *aluk* is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). However, this section has not been commenced immediately after "not after an indeclinable" (*nāvyayībhāvāt*) in order to rely upon the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada-adhikāra*). The rule "and as a singular" (*ekavacca*) is a transfer of meaning (*arthātideśa*) that forms a supplement to the entire section on *aluk*. It must be stated that the object of whichever case-ending for which *aluk* is prescribed becomes "as if one," whether its nature be dual or plural.

[Objection: If there were also an analysis such as *stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* or *stokebhyo muktaḥ*, then in these cases—*stokābhyāṃ muktaḥ* and *stokebhyo muktaḥ*—there would likewise be the formation of a single word (*ekapadya*) and a single accent (*eka-svarya*). [Response: This is not a fault. Regarding the rule *karaṇe ca stokālpa-* (Pāṇini 2.3.33), which prescribes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) for *stoka* and so on in each specific instance, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. Furthermore, since that ablative cannot occur after words denoting non-substances (*asattvavacana*) in the dual or plural, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) for these words will not occur at all in the sense of the "starting point" (*apādāna*), as in *stokābhyām* or *stokebhyaḥ*. Thus, it will not be so.

Even so, there would be the undesirable consequence [of *aluk*] in cases such as *dūrābhyām āgataḥ* (come from two distant places) and *dūrebhya āgataḥ* (come from many distant places), for here the ablative (*pañcamī*) is prescribed by the specific rule *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*. Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of *aluk* in examples such as *antikābhyāṃ kṛtam* (done by two near ones) and *antikebhyaḥ kṛtam* (done by many near ones). Therefore, it must be stated that [the compound] is singular (*ekavad*).

Now, it may be asked: in a compound (*vṛtti*), subordinate words abandon numbers such as one and so forth and attain the number of "non-dual unity" (*abhedaikatva-saṅkhyā*). But what is this number of non-dual unity? It is the state of particulars existing without division, just like the medicinal juices in honey; for there, no distinction is seen such that "this is the juice of this plant" or "that is the juice of that," yet those very same particulars are experienced and not a general essence of "juice. Likewise here, in the case of *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), the meaning of "king" does not possess particularities such as singularity and so forth. And it has been said:

"Just as all medicinal juices, when placed in honey, exist without distinction because their potencies have been merged, they know that number to be of such a kind. Alternatively, "non-dual unity" (*abhedekatvasaṅkhyā*) is a generality (*sāmānya*) inherent in unity and so forth, wherein a specific number is not apprehended, just as the mere form (*rūpamātra*) [is perceived] in deep darkness.

It is not apprehended as "white" or "black," and likewise here too; thus, the meaning of the word *rājan* (king) possesses number (*saṅkhyāvat*), and it is not understood to be devoid of number (*niḥsaṅkhya*) like the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). And it has been said:
"Either through the abandonment of its particular differences, that [word] of such a nature consists of number itself;
or, by excluding the differences of the class-part, it functions [through its universal]."

"Because form is manifested through a concealed distinction, the specific difference of the form, such as white and so forth, is not perceived. Thus, since non-dual unity is the basis [of the cognition], there is no application at all of words ending in dual or plural suffixes; how much less so in the case of a compound? Consequently, due to the absence of a compound, *aluk* will occur. What then is the use of "acting as a single unit" (*ekavadbhāva*)? Furthermore, what is the reason? In a derivative formation (*vṛtti*), non-dual unity is understood because there is an absence of anything that expresses a specific number.

For the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is the indicator of that [number], and it ceases to exist in a compound (*vṛtti*). When it has ceased, according to the view that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) consists of the three" (gender, number, and substance), there is an absence of any indicator even for the generality of number. If, however, when "molasses" (*guḍa*) is said, number is understood through non-deviation—just as sweetness and so forth are understood—and this non-deviation belongs either to the generality of number or to an unrestricted particularity, then that itself is the number of "unitary identity" (*abheda-ekatva-saṃkhyā*).

Even in the case of *pañcaka* (the word for five), since case-endings (*vibhakti*) are required as indicators even for the comprehension of a specific number, their absence means that either a general [number] or an unspecified particular is understood; thus, that itself is the number of non-dual unity (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*). For indeed, it is only in cases where meaning, context, and so forth serve as the means of cognition for a specific [number], that there is a compound (*vṛtti*).

For example: *maudgika* (made of beans) is derived from *mudga* by the rule *aryān mudga-*, for a purchase cannot be made with a single bean; and in the expression *kārakamadhya* ("in the midst of the factors of action"), a "midst" (*madhya*) cannot belong to a single entity. Furthermore, according to the specific instruction [of Pāṇini] that this is for the sake of providing an occasion for your words, the possessive suffixes in *tāvakīna* ("your") and *māmakīna* ("my") apply here. However, in cases such as *māsajāta* ("born a month ago"), the meaning of the nominal stem itself already possesses a specified measure. In cases such as *dviputra* ("having two sons"), the number is determined by the proximity of a numeral word.
Thus, wherever there is an absence of evidence for a specific distinction, the number is one of non-differentiation (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*).

If this is so, then in the absence of *aluk*, the case-ending itself would be the authority; thus, there would certainly be a compound of words ending in the dual and plural numbers. However, when the specific [referent] is understood through context, meaning, and so forth, such that the formation (*vṛtti*) occurs for words ending in the dual and plural, then what room is there for doubt when the case-ending is already present? Furthermore, if the absence of *aluk* for the dual and plural is due to the arising of the number "one" characterized by non-difference (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*), then it would not apply to the singular either; for even in that case, the expressed meaning is pure oneness, not the number "one" characterized by non-difference.

Now, if it were argued that—in the absence of a case-ending, when there is a need for the determined particularization of a perceived general number—pure singularity is understood even in a compound (vṛtti) according to the maxim "he who assumes many assumes one," then the expression "the number of non-different unity" (*abhedaikatvasaṅkhyā*) would be untenable. Therefore, in a compound, the application of a word ending in the singular, dual, or plural occurs as desired.

Nor can it be argued that there is the number one through non-difference, and that the specific [referent] is understood through context, purpose, and so forth; for in that case, by the previously stated reasoning, the non-elision (aluk) of the dual and plural endings would result, and thus an extended application (atideśa) must be resorted to.

If this is so, then for words such as *gopucchaḥ*, *apsuyoniḥ*, and *apsavyaḥ*—which are always plural—the same contingency of using the singular would arise due to the transfer of singularity even when the elision (*luk*) occurs. In that case, the reason here is simply non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). Thus it is said: "But because there is no usage of forms ending in the dual or plural. If that were so, then the sentence (*vākya*) would also not be possible. Nor can it be argued: "There is no usage in the compound (*samāsa*), but there is in the sentence."

For the designation of "compound" (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) is not employed for the expression of meaning; rather, it is the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the case-ending (*vibhakti*) that are employed, and since all of these remain intact, what can the non-expression [of the compound] do here? To this he replies with the words "Therefore, in this case," and so forth. Since even the accent (*svara*) is useful for the expression of meaning, it is logical that a sentence accompanied by distinct accents is expressive, whereas a compound accompanied by a single uniform accent is not expressive. This is the meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with *brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ*: what, then, is being added here? Is the ablative case used in the sense of the accusative, such that *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* means "one who recites the Brāhmaṇas"? This is indeed established by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, which allows for the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. But one might object: he recites the *Śāstras*, not the *Brāhmaṇas*. This is not a fault; for the word *brāhmaṇa* should be understood as referring to those *Śāstras* which are prescribed in the *Brāhmaṇas*.

Another [teacher] says: "In this case, the meaning of the ablative (*pañcamī*) is indeed appropriate; the root *śaṃs* (to recite) occurs in the sense of reciting preceded by taking up [the text]. Thus, one who recites the hymns (*sūktas*) after having taken them from a Brāhmaṇa is a *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. If this were so, the title *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* would also apply to the Hotṛ and others; to this he replies: 'This is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) for a specific class of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Regarding the word 'of that' (*tasyāḥ*): it means of this conventional term, namely *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. Regarding the word 'existent' (*satā*):
in the case where [the term is derived as] *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*, the meaning of the ablative is not possible; however, in the other alternative, it is possible."
The third case endings [are used] after *ojas*, *sahas*, *ambhas*, and *tamas*.

In the examples [given], the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). Why does it not occur here in the case of *satatanaiśatamovṛtām*? It is said in reply: the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) draws in the preceding member (*pūrvapada*), and by that, the specific terms beginning with *ojas* are qualified as they exist in the position of the preceding members.

Regarding the rule "after *ojas* and so forth": here, the word *tamas* is not the prior member (*pūrvapada*); rather, it is the compound *satatanaiśatamas*. Where a rule is intended to apply to that which ends in such a [compound], the prior member—implied by what has been mentioned—is qualified; therefore, the rule applies both to that [prior member] and to that which ends in it: as in *iṣṭakacitam* and *pakveṣṭakacitam*.

In some cases, however, that grammatical operation applies only to what has been directly mentioned (*upātta*) when it is immediately followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*); it does not depend on the status of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*), whether of the directly mentioned word itself or of a compound ending in it. For example, in the rule *ānaṅ ṛto dvandve hotṛpotṛneṣṭodgātāraḥ*, the word *neṣṭṛ* is neither the prior member nor is there a prior member ending in it; rather, it is the word *hotṛ* [that precedes], yet its subsequent member is not immediately following. *Añcasā* means "by straightness" (*ārjavena*). He whose elder brother is male is called "younger" (*anuja*) by reason of that male elder brother. *Januṣāndhaḥ* means "blind from birth" (*jātyandhaḥ*); *janu* means "birth" (*janman*).
And [the suffix *kha* is used] after the word *ātman* in the sense of filling. 6.3.6.

This is indeed a *vārttika* recited in the form of a *sūtra*. Because the word "pūraṇa" (ordinal) is marked with the *svarita* accent, it indicates that the suffixes prescribed under that governing rule (*adhikāra*) are to be understood here, not the word-form itself; thus he says, "ending in an ordinal suffix. Although it will be taught later in the section on "subsequent members" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*)—in the rule *dṛḍhasya dṛḍha-lekhaḥ*—that when a suffix is mentioned, the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) does not apply, nevertheless, since an ordinal suffix cannot possibly follow the word *ātman*, the rule of "ending-in-that" applies here by virtue of the sense (*sāmarthya*).

Regarding the phrase *ātmānā vā kṛtaḥ*: since that which has achieved its purpose (*kṛtārtha*) is included within the compound, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, there is a compound according to the rule *tṛtīyā tatkṛtārthena* (Pāṇini 2.1.30), as in the case of *kuṅkumalohita* ("red with saffron") and similar expressions.

As for the phrase *ātmā caturtho yasya*: it is not contradictory for even a single object, when differentiated by conceptual construction (*buddhiparikalpita*), to function both as the referent of the compound itself (*vṛttipadārthatva*) and as the referent of the external member (*taddanyapadārthatva*).
In the grammatical tradition, [the term] "vaiyākaraṇa" is used for the dative case. 6.3.7.

Regarding the phrase "of the grammarians" (*vaiyākaraṇānām*) and so forth: if, however, one were to explain *vaiyākaraṇī* as "pertaining to grammar" (*vyākaraṇe bhavā*), with the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *aṇ ṛgayanādibhyaḥ*, and then derive *vaiyākaraṇākhyā* as "the name of a grammarian," then [the terms] *ātmanebhāṣa* and *parasmaibhāṣa* would not be possible, because these two are not recited in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Therefore, it has been explained exactly as previously shown.

If this were the case, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to worldly proper names such as *kuberabali*, since even grammarians employ them in their linguistic usage; therefore, he says: "by which... The intention is that a restriction is understood through the force of the qualifier. However, when grammar consists of the five components—roots, sūtras, gaṇas, uṇādi, and vārttikas—then there is no fault even in the interpretation "that which is both pertaining to grammar (*vaiyākaraṇī*) and a name (*ākhyā*). Regarding the term *ātmanepadam*: its etymological meaning has been demonstrated in the rule prescribing compound formation.
And [the rule] *parasmai ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.8).

Why is this stated so that the *aluk* (non-elision) may occur—as in *parasmaipada* and *parasmaibhāṣaḥ*? Here, the *aluk* is already established by the preceding rule; however, [the word] *ātmanaḥ* from that [previous rule] continues to apply. If it were to cease, then [the *aluk*] would also apply in the case of *taddhitāḥ*, meaning "those beneficial to them. Therefore, while *ātmanaḥ* continues there [in the previous rule], one must state [the addition of] *parasya ca* ("and of another").
In a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the locative case ending after a word ending in *hal* (a consonant) or *dant* (tooth) is elided. Pāṇini 6.3.9.

In the examples, there is a compound by the rule *saṃjñāyām*. [Examples include] *gaviṣṭhira* and so forth. Otherwise, since the elision (*luk*) is a "foreign" (*bahiraṅga*) operation that overrides even "internal" (*antaraṅga*) rules, the substitution of *ava* for *avaḥ* would not occur because the word would lack the suffix *aṅ* and end in *hal*; as in the case of *bhūmipāśa*, where the noose is on the ground. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the words *hṛddyubhyām*: this is for the purpose of avoiding [the application of] technical names (*saṃjñā*). Examples are *hṛdispṛk* (touching the heart) and *divispṛk* (touching the sky). This locative case is used in the sense of the accusative; for thus says the Bhāṣya: "This locative case should be understood as having the meaning of another [case]; 'it touches the heart' is *hṛdispṛk*, and 'it touches the sky' is *divispṛk*. Because the term *ākhyā* ("name") is used in combination [with *saṃjñā*] there, it refers to a technical name here. However, in that very same context, the term *ākhyā* should be used alone, without being combined [with *saṃjñā*].
And for the ancients, [the suffix *cha*] is applied after a word denoting the cause, provided it ends in a consonant and begins with *ha*.

The portion to be taken by the king, established by merchants, cattle-herders, and farmers, is called *kara*; *kāra* is derived from *kara* itself, with the suffix *aṇ* applied according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*.

The phrase "restrictions and alternatives" (*niyamavikalpāḥ*) means specific restrictions (*niyamaviśeṣāḥ*). He demonstrates these very [restrictions] with the words "only when called *kāra*, etc. The first restriction is: if [the suffix] occurs after a word beginning with a consonant (*halādi*) in the eastern regions (*prācām deśe*), it occurs only when [the word] is called *kāra*. However, in a region not belonging to the East, it certainly occurs even when [the word] is not called *kāra*, as in the case of *tvacisāra* and others. The second [restriction] is: if [the suffix] occurs after a word beginning with a consonant in the eastern regions, it occurs only when [the word] is called *kāra*. The third [restriction] is: if [the suffix] occurs in the eastern regions and when [the word] is called *kāra*, it occurs only when [the word] begins with a consonant.

A collection of sheep is *avikaṭam*; the suffix *kaṭac* is used in the sense of a multitude. How can three rules be obtained within a single sentence? Who, moreover, says that this is a single sentence? Since the specific [restrictions] are being grasped, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the particle *eva* with each [word], and thus there are indeed three sentences. By the mention of the technical term (*saṃjñā*), it applies even to the present case.

The mention of the term *nāman* (name) is made in order to clarify that [the rule] has a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*); otherwise, even the status of being an original injunction (*vidhyarthatā*) would be possible in the absence of a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). How so? In the case of a name such as *purasaṃjñā*, there is a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*). This itself would be the indicator (*jñāpaka*): that in the domain of common usage (*prācām*), when the first member is a word beginning with a consonant (*halādi*) and serves as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), a locative compound occurs even in the absence of a technical name. This itself would be the indicator: that in the domain of common usage, when a word beginning with a consonant is the subsequent member, a compound occurs even for those [words] that are not technical names.
Since the rule would have been established by the words "in which [there is] an operation" (*yasminvidhiḥ*) alone, the inclusion of the word *ādi* (beginning with) is for the sake of clarity.
