The suffix *kan* is not applied after a word denoting one’s own body part ending in *mūrdhan*, except when the sense is "desire. (Pāṇini 5.2.12)

In the examples and counter-examples, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). For instance, in *akṣaśauṇḍa*, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*.
And in the case of the word *bandha*, there is an option. (Pāṇini 6.3.13)

The rule "from its own member" (*svāṅgāt*) has been excluded; this is a general injunction. Here, the verbal root *bandh* itself is imitated by means of its accompaniment. Since the prohibition was stated specifically regarding the verbal root in the rule "not in *siddha*, *badhnāti*, etc.," therefore, only a *bahuvrīhi* compound is the domain of this option.

In that regard, since there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) when the member is a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*), such as in *hastabandha*, and an option when it is not a part of one's own body (*asvāṅga*), such as in *cakrabandha*, the rule results in being an "option in both cases" (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*). However, the concern arises that this [rule] might not apply at all in a *tatpuruṣa* compound; he dispels this doubt by stating that the word *bandha* is understood here as ending in the suffix *ghañ*. Consequently, its occurrence even in a *tatpuruṣa* is not contradictory, because the prohibition finds its scope of application in cases such as *bandhana* (the act of binding). This is the intended meaning. Thus, it is an "option in both cases."

He asks, "How so? and replies: "In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* [compound], when it does not refer to a body part (*asvāṅga*). As for "but in the case of a *tatpuruṣa*": although one could argue that the rule is simply unapplicable in a *bahuvrīhi* because it does not refer to a body part, nevertheless, he shows its application in a *tatpuruṣa* by stating, "and its application in a *tatpuruṣa* occurs by way of a prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). Otherwise, the *bahuvrīhi* would be its scope, while the prohibition [of the suffix] would have "binding" (*bandhana*) and the like as its scope; however, in a *tatpuruṣa* ending in a *ghañ*-affix, when both [the suffix and the prohibition] would otherwise apply, the prohibition alone would prevail due to its being subsequent in the order of rules.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the sixth case-affix is frequently retained before a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix.

Here too, there is the inclusion of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, not merely of a *kṛt* suffix itself; since a locative case (*saptamī*) cannot occur after that [suffix], why does it not apply here in the case of *parame kārake* (in the highest agent) forming *paramakāraka*? It is said: the locative case is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it is caused by the action conveyed by the *kṛt* suffix; however, in this case, the locative is caused by another action, as in "place it in the highest agent. Therefore, because it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), it is not included.

Regarding the term *kurucara*: this has been cited without relying on the governing rule (*adhikāra*) *haladantāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.9). While the option (*vibhāṣā*) is already in force, the use of the term *bahula* is for the purpose of including cases such as the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth. Consequently, in *karṇejapa* and similar forms, there is no elision (*aluk*); in *madracara* and similar forms, there is indeed elision (*luk*); and in *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and similar forms, there is non-elision even when [the suffix] is not in the locative case. Thus, the entire section concerning non-elision (*aluk-prakaraṇa*) is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of this very point.
The [suffix *ṅi*] is applied after the words *prāvṛṣ*, *śarat*, and *kāla* when they denote the day (*divā*). Pāṇini 6.3.15.
Because the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*) and autumn (*śarat*) are mentioned separately, the term "time" (*kāla*) here refers to its own essential form.
In the case of words denoting time, when used with the suffixes *gha*, *kal*, or *tana*, the sixth case ending is employed after the word expressing the time.

The term *gha* refers to the inclusion of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*; *kāla* refers to the inclusion of the word-form itself; and *tana* refers to the inclusion of the substitute for *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* together with its augment *satuṭ*.

Regarding the form *pūrvāhṇetana*: the suffix *-tana* expresses excellence in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*). Since this [excellence] does not pertain to a substance (*adravyaprakarṣa*), the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending does not occur in the alternative where there is no elision; consequently, by the rule *kimettiṅavyayaghād ām*, the suffix *ām* is added. However, in the alternative where there is elision (*luk*), because the cause for its application is absent, the suffix *ām* is also absent even when there is no excellence of a substance. The locative case is formed from the word ending in the suffix *-tarap*. In some instances, however, the locative is stated to follow the entire compound even in the case where there is no elision; in that case, the prohibition "when there is no excellence of a substance" should be explained as being intended to refer to the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) itself. As for *pūrvāhṇe*: the suffixes *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* are applied by the rule *vibhāṣā pūrvāhṇāparāhṇābhyām*, and the substitution of *an* and the augment *tuṭ* are also applied.

But how is it that the non-elision (*aluk*) is cited only when there is a suffix (*pratyaya*) as the condition? For, by the maxim regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the non-elision should be prescribed when the suffix occurs at the end of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). To this he says: "Because of the governing rule concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*). He asks: "Why? and replies: "Because of the mention of *lekha*. Since, while the mention of the suffix *aṇ* is being made in the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu*, he makes the mention of *lekha*, this indicates that when a suffix is mentioned within the governing rule concerning the subsequent member, the designation of the whole ending in that suffix (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply.

If [the word] *anaṇ* existed [as a technical term], one would not have included the mention of *lekha*, because [the desired form] would already be established by [the rule] *anaṇ*. But surely the mention of *lekha* is for the sake of the sense of the suffix *ghañ*; [we reply: no, for a form ending in *ghañ* is not intended here. [The objection continues: "In the case of *kāla*, there is no apprehension of the specific form [of the word]. [We reply: No, because of the mention of the name [itself]. In some places, *nañ* is not recited; in those cases, the meaning is that there is an apprehension of the specific form of the word [even when preceded by *nañ*].
The sixth case ending is used after words meaning ‘bed,’ ‘dwelling,’ and ‘resident’ when they do not denote time.

In this context, "atime" (improper time) expresses a censure of the meaning, as is clear from the commentary. Thus he says: "of that which denotes an improper time. Regarding "khaśayaḥ": the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule "the root √śī takes *ac* when denoting the locus. Regarding "vāsaḥ": the suffix *ghañ*. Regarding "grāmevāsī": the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "after a word ending in a case-suffix, when not denoting a genus, [the suffix *ṇini* is added to a verb]."

"Apoyoni," etc. Because sound (*śabda*) is the primary factor, there is the singular form "apah" (waters). "Yoni" means origin; that whose origin is in the waters is "apsuyoni. Regarding "apsavya": [the suffix] *ya* is applied after the word ending in *o*, and the *v* is substituted for the final *au* before a suffix beginning with *y*. Regarding "apsumantau": since the suffix *matup* cannot occur after a word ending in the locative case, those two in which the word "apsu" exists are the "apsumantau"—namely, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings in the *Kārīrī* sacrifice. For in their respective invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*), the word "apsu" occurs: "O Agni, your seat is in the waters" (*apsv agne sadhiṣṭavaḥ*) and "Soma has spoken to me in the waters" (*apsu me somo abravīt*).

If this is so, then because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there will be no elision [of the suffix], as in the case of *asyavāmīya* and others; therefore, what is the purpose of mentioning the word *matup*? However, others read the word *mati*, citing it as: "In this [verse], Soma is indeed *apsumati*"; but that is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

In the case of *nensiddhabadhnātiṣu*, the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14), which would have applied, is prohibited. Since it is impossible for a suffix (*pratyaya*) alone to follow a locative case-ending, even though the governing heading is on "the subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), he states that when a suffix is mentioned, the designation refers to that which ends with it (*tadantavidhi*): "the subsequent member ends in *in*. In *sthaṇḍilavartī*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *vrate* (Pāṇini 3.2.80). This is an *upapada* compound (*upapadasamāsa*). In *sāṅkāśayasiddhaḥ*, the compound is formed by the rule *siddhaśuṣkapakvabandhaiśca* (Pāṇini 2.1.41). In *cārabaddhaḥ*, [the same applies].

The word *baddha* ends in a *niṣṭhā* suffix. It forms a compound by means of the word *baddha*, [this being] due to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). As for the word *tat*: the form of the word is simply *bandha*. Now, why does it not end in the suffix *dhañ*? To this he says: "For if it ended in *dhañ*... Alternatively, why does this option—namely, that there is an optional application when the suffix is *pacādyac* and when the word is *bandha*—not apply? To this he says: "For if it ended in *dhañ*..."
And [the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs] before *stha* in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).
In the word *ākhareṣṭhaḥ*, [the rule] "sthaḥ ka ca" applies, and [the final *a*] becomes *ka*.
The sixth case-affix is used in the sense of "abuse" (ākrośa).

Regarding "paśyatohara" (one who steals while being watched): the genitive case is used here according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* ("the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard"), meaning "he steals while disregarding the one who watches.

Regarding "śunaḥśepa": the word *śepa* exists ending in the vowel *ā*, not only ending in the consonant *s*. [The compound] *śunaḥśepa* is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose tail (*śepa*) is like that of a dog (*śvan*). Similarly, *bahuvrīhi* compounds are also formed with *puccha* and *lāṅgūla*. These are the names of specific sages (*ṛṣi*).
The term *ṛtaḥ* [is used] in reference to connections through learning and birth. 6-3-23.

"Vidyā and yoni" form the compound *vidyāyonī*; because knowledge (*vidyā*) is more venerable, it is placed first. Those who possess a relationship established by those two are "those related by learning and birth" (*vidyāyonisambandhāḥ*); the word "established" (*kṛta*) is not explicitly used because its meaning is already implied. [The example is] "the son of the father. The meaning is: one born from a renowned father.

Regarding the rule "the inclusion of both the preceding and following words [occurs] in the case of relations through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*)," the meaning is as follows: because the *sūtra* employs the ablative case (*pañcamī*), it would follow that only the preceding words denote relations of learning or birth, and not the following words. Alternatively, if the locative case (*saptamī*) were employed, only the following words would be understood to denote such relations, and not the preceding ones. Therefore, it must be stated that this rule applies when both types of words denote those relations. Furthermore, because this term is intended to function in other grammatical formations (*anyavṛtti*), it occurs even when there is a mutual transposition of them—as in *hotuḥ putraḥ* ("the son of the Hotṛ") and *pitur antevāsī* ("the pupil of the father").
In a copulative compound (dvandva), the vowel *ṛ* of the word *ānaṅ* [is substituted for the final vowel of the first member]. 6.3.25.

In this context, if it were understood that *ānaṅ* occurs for the vowel *ṛ* when it is part of a *dvandva*, then *āṅ* would also follow after *pitṛ* and *pitāmaha*; furthermore, the rule *ṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.3.27] would be rendered useless because its application is already established by the current subject matter. Therefore, *ṛt* is a qualifier of the *dvandva*. Considering that this singular number refers to the genus (*jāti*), he says: "of those ending in the vowel *ṛ*, etc."

In this context, the instruction of the phonemes is for the sake of grammatical operations (*kārya*) or for the sake of being heard (*śravaṇa*). Now, this letter *na* is not heard anywhere; since "there is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*), elision of the *n* ought to occur everywhere. Furthermore, no grammatical operation whatsoever is prescribed for it. Therefore, there is no purpose in its [instruction], and to this he says: "The utterance of the letter *na*, etc."

If the letter *n* were not present, then by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, only an *aṇ* substitute would remain in place of *u*, and since that [substitute] would be followed by *r*, only *thaaṇ* and other such forms would remain; thus, there would be no occasion for the application of *raparatva*. Therefore, the pronunciation of the letter *n* is for the purpose of preventing *raparatva*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of making it a substitute for the final sound, according to the rule *ṅicca*.

And where a qualifier of the element undergoing the grammatical operation (*kāryin*) is specified, there the rule "substitutes apply to that which is being specified" holds; however, in this case [of *ṛtaḥ*], "after *ṛ*" is not a qualifier of the element undergoing the operation, but rather a qualifier of the *dvandva* compound. As for the statement "it follows from *putra*," it follows from the rule *putre 'nyatarasyām*.

If the term *yadyatra* (if here) were to apply [to the rule] *putre* (*in the word putra*), and if *vibhāṣā svasṛpatyoḥ* (*optionally in the case of svasṛ and pati*) were to follow as a governing rule (*anuvarteta*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of optional application even in cases such as *bhrātuṣputra* where there is no censure (*anākrośe*). If that is so, then by virtue of the explanation (*vyākhyānāt*), it is connected only with this very [rule]; for this reason it was said, "here" (*atreva*). Even so, when *putra* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *anaṅ* would apply to the preceding member alone, because the specific element undergoing the change (*kāryin*) has not been specified; since the audible form *ṛtaḥ* belongs specifically to the *dvandva* compound, he says: "and also because of *ṛtaḥ*."

The word "anuvartate" (is carried over) refers to the term "añ" from the rule "ñatovidyāyoni. The meaning is that this [term] will qualify the subject of that [rule]. Although that [term] ends in the fifth case (pañcamī), nevertheless, by virtue of the current explanation, it is here transformed into one ending in the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī).
And [the first vowel retains its accent] in a copulative compound (dvandva) of deities. 6.3.26.

The statement is for the purpose of excluding those ending in *an* or *ṛ*, and for the purpose of indicating a connection to a source that is ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the phrase "the term 'dvandva' being present," and so forth:

the mention of *dvandva* under discussion is for the sake of identifying a specific type of compound; this refers to the inclusion of a pair whose association is well-known. But why is there no inclusion [of other pairs]? To this he says: "because of extreme concomitance," and so forth.

Regarding the rule *dvandvo rahasyamaryādā*, the inclusion of the term "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) allows for the technical application (*nipātana*) of the term *dvandva* to a pair that is in absolute association; here, that [pair] is referred to by the word "deities. This is an adjective—functioning through its meaning—to qualify the *dvandva* under discussion: that is to say, a *dvandva* that denotes a pair in absolute association. He specifies this very association with the word "therein" (*tatra*). "Simultaneous pouring" (*sahavāpa*) means "pouring together," as in: "I pour what is pleasing to Agni and Soma" (*agnīṣomābhyāṃ juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), and so forth. "In both cases" means as the prior member and as the subsequent member.
The word *id* [is substituted for *kim*] when expressing increase. (Pāṇini 5.4.28)

In this context, the term "vṛddhi" refers to a compound whose final member (*uttarapada*) contains a *vṛddhi* vowel, because it is impossible for a final member itself to possess the nature of a *vṛddhi* vowel. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "Agni and Varuṇa are its deities" (*agnīvaruṇau devate asya*), and "Agni and Marut are its deities" (*agnāmarutau devate asya*). In the former case, there is the substitution of *it*; in the latter, there is *anaṅ*. The status of being a deity (*devatātva*) resides in two substrata; thus, the singular number in the word "deity" (*devatā*) is used. This is intended to override both *anaṅ* and *ītva*. For while *ītva* would apply in the case of Varuṇa, *anaṅ* would apply elsewhere.

Although the application of *anaṅ* and *ītv* occurs first in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) before the *vṛddhi*, nevertheless, because they fall under the scope of an exception (*apavāda*), they are not applied in the procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*); however, they do indeed occur in the common worldly sentence (*laukikavākya*).
Regarding *vṛddhi*, there is a prohibition concerning Viṣṇu: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu" (*āgnāvaiṣṇavam ekādaśakapālaṃ nirvapet*).
And [the word] *divasa* [is used in the masculine gender] when it refers to the earth. || 6.3.30 ||

The word *divasaḥ* ends in the nominative case. For what purpose is the vowel *a* pronounced? Since there would be no need for it, the letter *s* would not receive the technical designation *it*. To this he replies: "The pronunciation of the vowel *a*... If that [vowel] were absent, when followed by the word *pṛthivī*, the letter *s* would undergo the following modifications: substitution with *ru*, the *visarjanīya*, and, according to the rule *kupvoḥ ka-pau ca*, the letters *k* or *p*. When the vowel *a* is present, the letter *s* is actually pronounced; therefore, in usage, this very unmodified form is what is understood.

"How so? and so forth. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "in a *dvandva* [compound]," the question arises that [the substitution] would not apply at all in a sentence. "An effort must be made here" means: this usage is Vedic; since "in the Veda one follows what is observed," this is the effort required here.
*uṣāsoṣasaḥ* (6-3-31).

Regarding the phrase *uṣāsānaktā*: this is a Vedic usage. It is a *dvandva* compound meaning "Dawn and Night," with the substitution of *ḍā* for the nominative dual ending. Here, at every instance of the word-division (*padakāla*), the makers of the *pada-pāṭha* recite it with a short vowel as *uṣasānaktā*.

In a compound where a feminine word follows a word denoting the same object (samānādhikaraṇa) that has an equivalent masculine form and is not marked with the suffix ūṅ, the feminine form is treated like the masculine, except in the case of ordinal numbers and words such as *priyā* and the like. (Pāṇini 6.3.34)

In this context, three possible interpretations arise: the mention of *strī* as the feminine suffix (*strī-pratyaya*), the mention of the meaning (*artha*), or the mention of the word-form (*śabda*). If the mention of *strī* (the suffix) is intended as having an accent (*svarita*), then by virtue of that accent, the understanding arises that the vowels *ā* and *ī* are included; thus, the suffixes such as *aṣṭāp* and others prescribed under the heading of "feminine" (*stry-adhikāra*) are understood. For example, in the rule *gos-triyor upasarjanasya*, this is the resulting meaning: just as the feminine suffixes *ṭāp* and others do not occur after a word that has been mentioned in the masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), so too they do not occur when [that word] is in the position of a subsequent member (*uttarapada*).

[They] "become. Now, it might be argued that in sentences where a verbal form is not heard, the insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is observed elsewhere. To this it is replied: in the case of indications using the suffix *vat*, whatever is well-known—whether existence or non-existence—in the object of comparison (*upamāna*), that is to be extended (*atideśya*) to the object of comparison (*upameya*). For example: "In the land of the Madras, there are barley-grains, just as in the land of the Uśīnaras; [or] they do not exist. Consequently, because the feminine suffix is absent in the masculine [form], its absence is also extended to the feminine. Thus, the remainder of the sentence must be supplied as "it will not become" (*na bhaviṣyati*); for in that case, it would stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *anūṅ*.

The word *śriyaḥ* is a genitive used in the sense of the nominative; *puṃvat* is a suffix *vati* added to a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī-samartha*). In this context, since the feminine suffix has already been applied in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) prior to the compound itself, it is impossible to establish its absence before the final member (*uttarapada*)—as one might do in cases such as *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ*. Therefore, what must be established is the removal of that which was already applied, as in the rule *luk taddhitaluki*. The meaning is that the feminine suffixes applied in the analytical sentence are removed—that is, they are elided—when a subsequent member follows.

But when a substance endowed with femininity is expressed by a feminine word as being like the masculine, then there is the inclusion of the meaning; the sense is that the grammatical operation (kārya) occurs for the feminine—that is, for the feminine meaning—as it does for the masculine, i.e., for the masculine meaning. And in that case, the suffix -vati is applied after a genitive compound.

However, when a word denoting a female object is expressed by the word *strī*, then there is the mention of "the word" (*śabda*); this constitutes a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*), meaning that the form of the word for a female—that is, a word in the feminine gender—becomes like the masculine form. This is because, within the scope of a compound (*vṛtti*), there is no operation belonging to a masculine word to be transferred. Furthermore, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is precisely the form of that feminine word which, having undergone the state of masculinity (*puṃbhāva*) in another usage while denoting a male, that is transferred, and not the form of just any word whatsoever.

The nominative case in *anūṅ* is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*). In that context, when "meaning" (*artha*) is taken as the referent, the word *strī* is primary. However, since the priority or posteriority (*paurvāparya*) of the meaning with respect to the subsequent member cannot exist inherently, it must be understood as being mediated by the words themselves. In the other two views, however, the word *strī* is secondary (*gauṇa*). Since the priority and so forth are consistent [in all cases], it is not possible to adopt a specific view based on authoritative evidence; therefore, the faultless view should be adopted.

In that regard, according to the first position, from the word *eta* in the compound *etadbhāryā*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *varṇādanudāttāt*; and when the *t* is replaced by *n*, because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole, the *ī* following the word *eta*—which is of the masculine gender as previously stated—is present. Thus, even though that [masculine] form has ceased, the feminine nature of the meaning has not ceased, and consequently, the *n* would be heard.

Nor does the elision of the *nakāra* follow from the elision of the *ikāra* due to their being taught as a fixed conjunction (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*), because when there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in a preceding rule—namely, the elision of the *nakāra* resulting from the elision of the feminine suffix caused by the subsequent member—the absence of one of the two cannot be established. Furthermore, the elision of the *nakāra* does not occur through the same process of "masculine-like behavior" (*puṃvadbhāva*) as the *ikāra*, since the *nakāra* does not follow a word that has been previously mentioned with a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and because, not being a suffix (*apratyaya*), it lacks similarity to the *uṅ* vowels.

Similarly, in the case of *paṭvī-bhāryā* (whose wife is clever), *paṭubhārya*, even though the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) has been elided, the substitution of *yaṇ* would occur due to the status of the elided element as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Now, if it were argued that when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows, a feminine suffix that does not contain the vowel *ūṅ* does not occur after a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), and thus—as in the rule *na kroḍādibahvacaḥ*—the non-occurrence (*prāgabhāva*) itself must be prescribed here; and that by the force of this [prescription], the feminine suffix, though it would otherwise have been applied internally (*antaraṅga*) based on the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), is not actually formed—then, while this specific fault would be avoided, there would still be a fault regarding the rules for *lug* (elision), *aluk* (non-elision), and feminine suffixes such as *dvistri* (twice, thrice).

Regarding *luk*: the feminine descendant of Vataṇḍa is formed by the suffix *yañ* (which becomes *īn* due to its inclusion in the *śārṅgarava*-group), and according to the rule *vataṇḍācca luk striyām*, the suffix is elided in the feminine. Thus, we have *vataṇḍī*. When this is compounded with *vṛndārikā* as *vātaṇḍyavṛndārikā*, although the vowel *ikāra* is removed by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*, the femininity inherent in the meaning has not been removed; consequently, the rule *yañaśca* would require the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ*.

It might be argued: "By the elision of the vowel *ī* through the doubling (*praśleṣa*) of the word *strī* as *strī-ī*, the elision occurs when the *ī*-vowel follows [the feminine suffix]; however, in this case, because the *ī*-vowel has not arisen due to the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment), the elision will not occur. This is not so, because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). How so? The word *vataṇḍa* is listed among the *śārṅgarava*-type stems with the *yañ* suffix elided; consequently, the *ī*-vowel does not exist until the elision has occurred, and the elision cannot apply until the *ī*-vowel exists. Thus, there is a circular dependency.

In the case of *aluk*: [consider] "the female descendant of Garga" (*gargasyāpatyaṃ striyaḥ*). By the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied; then by *yañaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, resulting in *gārgyāḥ*. When these are combined with *vṛndārikāḥ* to form *gārgyavṛndārikāḥ*, even though *ṅīp* has been elided, the feminine gender (*strītva*) has not ceased to exist. Consequently, the elision (*luk*) required by the rule *yañañośca striyām* does not apply, and thus, as in the case of a full sentence, there would be no elision at all.

Regarding the category "not feminine" (*astrīviṣaya*): *kuñjasyāpatyaṃ strī gotre* ("the female descendant of Kuñja in the sense of a lineage [gotra]") takes the suffix *cphañ* by the rule *kuñjādibhyaś cphañ*. Since "lineage" (*gotra*) includes the Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), this is a genus (*jāti*), and thus the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. She is both *kauñjāyanī* and *vṛndārikā*, hence *kauñjāyanavṛndārikāḥ*. Even though *ṅīṣ* has been removed, because femininity (*strītva*) has not ceased, the condition "not feminine" (*astrīviṣaya*)—as required by the rule *vrātacphañor astriyām*—would not apply.

Regarding the case of two or three feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*): [consider] *gargasyāpatyaṃ strī* ("the female descendant of Garga"), where *yañ* is applied by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*; then *ṣpha*, a secondary suffix (*taddhita*), is added by the rule *prācāṃ ṣpha taddhitaḥ*; and finally, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the characteristic of *ṣit*. In forms such as *gārgyavṛndārikā* ("a Vṛndārikā who is a Gārgyāyaṇī"), where there are two feminine suffixes, that *ṣpha* which follows a word that has a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) does not occur before the final member (*uttarapada*), because it is separated from it by *ṅīṣ*. Furthermore, the *ṅīṣ* that occurs before the final member does not follow a word that has a masculine counterpart, because it is separated from it by *ṣpha*, and because *ṣpha* is prescribed only for feminine nouns. Consequently, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would simply not take place.

Likewise, *aiḍaviḍavṛndārikā* refers to a woman who is the daughter of *iḍaviḍa*—to which the suffix *añ* is applied because it is a word denoting a *kṣatriya* tribe—and a woman who is the daughter of *darada*, to which the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *dvyañmagadha*. By the rule *ataśca*, there is elision (*luk*) of these suffixes, resulting in *iḍaviḍ* and *darat*. When these are compounded with *vṛndārikā* as in *aiḍaviḍavṛndārikā*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not occur here, because there is no suffix prescribed by a governing rule (*adhikāra*) that would trigger such a change.

In the second alternative, however, since it is extended that when the object possesses the status of being a human goal (*pumartha*), the word denoting it functions [as such], these faults do not arise; yet, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between this shortening (*hrasvatva*)—governed by the rule *khity anavyayasya*—and the masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) is untenable because their spheres of application are distinct. Shortening applies to the vowel (*ac*), whereas masculine-like behavior applies to the meaning (*artha*). Consequently, in the case of *kālimmanyā*, where a conflict would otherwise apply the principle "the later [rule] prevails," the desired shortening is not obtained.

In the view that these are words (*śabda*), however, there is a conflict because both rules apply to the same object. There is scope for *puṃvadbhāva* (the substitution of the masculine form) where there is no suffix ending in *-khid*, such as in *dīrghanīyabhāryaḥ*; and there is scope for shortening (*hrasvatva*) where there is no *puṃvadbhāva*, such as in *kālimmanyaḥ pumān*. When both would apply—as in *kālimmanyā strī*—shortening occurs because it is subsequent in the order of rules. Nor does the application of *puṃvadbhāva* follow once shortening has been applied, on the grounds that the principle of "once [a rule] has taken effect" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*) is adopted, which precludes further application based on the recurrence of the occasion.

Furthermore, even on the view that [the suffix] denotes the meaning (*arthapakṣa*), there is no contradiction based on impossibility (*asambhava*) due to the lack of a single referent (*ekaviṣayatva*), because this very [allegation of] "impossibility" is unestablished. For although, when the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs and the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is removed, the short vowel (*hrasva*) would not apply because the word would no longer end in a long vowel, nevertheless, once the short vowel has indeed applied, the masculine form still follows because the meaning has not been removed.

Thus, because the first two [options] are defective, he states the third alternative, beginning with "by which word a male is expressed," and so forth. By taking the *bahuvrīhi* compound with "word" (*śabda*) as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—meaning "that word by which a male is expressed"—it would follow that even for a word existing in both the feminine and masculine genders whose basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) differs, [the suffix] would apply; for example, *droṇībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a wooden trough") and *pātrībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a bowl").

The word *droṇa* is masculine when denoting a measure; the word *pātra*, being part of the *ardharca* group, is masculine when denoting a measure, but feminine when referring to a specific type of vessel. Considering that even though the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) differs in all these cases, the very same word which was designated as masculine in another usage now occurs in the feminine, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would indeed apply; therefore, [the author] specifies: "when the form is the same" (*samānāyām ākṛtau*). This is a passage from the Bhāṣya; hence he explains it as: "when there is a single basis for application. That [word] is one whose masculine form has been previously mentioned (*bhāṣitapuṃska*).

"Sound" (*śabda*): this means that this is the intended meaning. He asks how this meaning is obtained by the very words of the aphorism (*sūtra*) with the words "How then does this... and so forth; the meaning is: "In what manner does this form of the meaning come to be? The answer is: "The *bahuvrīhi* compound [is used] in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*), which is characterized as the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and in the sense of the locative case."

This is what is meant: when a word is spoken as masculine with respect to a certain ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), that speaker is said to be "one who has spoken it as masculine" (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) if, while speaking of a feminine referent, he employs that same ground for its application which was associated with the masculine form.

But even so, would there not still be a fault in examples such as *droṇī-bhārya*? How so? When the word *droṇī* applies to a certain female cow (*gavādanī*), and that [cow] is also called "the meaning," then it is joined with the cause of application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) that has been expressed as masculine. And since the cause of application for the word is also present in the female cow because it is being sought after, the word *droṇī*—though residing in that [female cow] and not itself denoting that cause of application—nevertheless denotes the object which is in fact endowed with it.

This is not the case; for if it were so, the mention of "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a corresponding masculine form) would be useless, as [the condition] would be easily available everywhere. Therefore, that word which expresses its own meaning—possessed of a basis for application (pravṛttinimitta) associated with a masculine form—in that very same form and not in another form, is understood here as "bhāṣitapuṃska. The word *droṇī*, however, applies to a female cow (*gavādi*) by virtue of a form associated with the universal (*jāti*) of "droṇī-ness," and not by virtue of being something desired.

Even so, in the case of *dyubhārya* ("one whose wife is heaven"), where *dyu-* is feminine, the masculine form *svarga-* would be expected for the word *div-*; for the word *div-* denotes "heaven" by the very same form that the word *svarga-* uses. This being the case, however, because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it is understood that when the rule of "masculine-like behavior" (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prescribed, it applies only to that which is masculine in its own usage. Thus, it is that which possesses the same basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) as that which expresses the masculine in another instance of its own usage.

The meaning is that for one who currently refrains from speaking, the very form which the word *strī* (woman) possessed during the state of speaking as a male continues to exist even now. Furthermore, the use of the suffix *-vat* in the term *puṃvat* is due to a difference based on extended application (*atideśika*).

Since *anūṅ* is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), by the maxim of "that which is connected with *nañ* or *iva*," it would include items such as *ṭāp* that resemble *ūṅ*; consequently, in cases like *aiḍaviḍavṛndārikā*, because there is no feminine suffix, [the rule] would not apply. Thus, he shows that it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) by stating: "*anūṅ* means the absence of *ūṅ*. Regarding the phrase "*bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*" (from a word having a masculine form, provided it is not *ūṅ*): if this were a compound (*samāsa*), then *anūṅ* would have to be either in the nominative case or one in which the genitive case ending is elided.

In the view that this is a genitive construction (*ṣaṣṭhīpakṣa*), the meaning is as follows: "The form of the word *strī* following a word that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) occurs, but not for that which ends in *ūṅ*. Consequently, the quality of having a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃskatva*) would not serve as a qualifier for the feminine word that undergoes masculine assimilation (*puṃvadbhāva*). What would be the fault in that? It would lead to an undesirable application here: suppose there are birds named *aṅgāraka*; their females are *kālikā*. Then, from these [females], one would have to derive the form *kālikāvṛndārikāḥ*.

From this word *kālikā*, which follows a word that has been stated to have a masculine counterpart (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), there would arise the status of being a masculine form (*aṅgārakatā*) even for its feminine referent. For indeed, those [feminine entities] could be designated by the word *aṅgāraka* due to association (*sāhacarya*). Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in cases such as "the mare of the horse," "the woman of the man," "the female swan of the male swan," and "the female tortoise of the male tortoise. Furthermore, in cases such as *darśanīyabhārya* ("one who has a beautiful wife"), it would not apply; for here, the word *darśanīya* does not follow a word that has been stated to have a masculine counterpart.

In the first interpretation, however, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*, the word *striyāḥ* must be taken as an ablative; this is because no other meaning is possible for it in the genitive case. Consequently, the meaning becomes: "A suffix other than *ūṅ* following a feminine form that has a corresponding masculine form is treated like the masculine. In that case, the same fault arises as in the first position. Thus, since faults would result in the case of a compound, he states—beginning with *bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*—that one must resort to a *bahuvrīhi* with non-coreferential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*).

Regarding the statement "by means of the *nipātana* [irregular formation], the ablative case is elided": this is not a valid solution, because this [formation] is *alaukika* (non-grammatical/extraordinary) precisely due to its being a *nipātana*. Consequently, even the elision (*luk*) would not apply, for the same reason that it is *alaukika*; thus, this argument is trivial. In the expression *anūṅ*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive; therefore, the meaning established here is: "that [feminine base] in which there is an absence of *ūṅ* from itself after a word that has a corresponding masculine form. What is the meaning? It means: in that feminine word where *ūṅ* has not been applied following a word that has a corresponding masculine form. Thus it is.

Another says: in the rule *bhāṣitapuṃskāt*, the ablative case is used in the sense of the genitive; everything else is as before. That is to say, a feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form takes the same form as its masculine counterpart, but this does not apply to a word ending in *ūṅ*.

If this were accepted, then [the rule] would apply only in cases where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows immediately after a word that has been stated to have a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), such as *darśanīyabāhu*. For here, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the word *darśanīya*—which is *bhāṣitapuṃska*—is included by the mention of *bhāṣitapuṃska* because, due to the status of the preceding element as if it were its final sound (*pūrvam praty antavadbhāvāt*), it is considered a *bhāṣitapuṃska*. However, in cases such as *gārgyavṛndārikā* (where *gārgī* is both a descendant of Garga and a *vṛndārikā*), the rule would not apply; for the word *gārgya*, which is *bhāṣitapuṃska*, is not followed immediately by the subsequent member, as it is separated by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

If that [word] immediately preceding the word *gārgī* were not one that has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), then this would be so; however, it is precisely for a word that is *bhāṣitapuṃska* in another usage and is currently applied to a feminine that the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) is prescribed. We state the *puṃvadbhāva* for a word that is *bhāṣitapuṃska* at the very moment it is applied to a feminine, and it is indeed possible for a word to be *bhāṣitapuṃska* while applied to a feminine, on the grounds that it denotes a female who is connected with a *pravṛttinimitta* (basis of application) that has a corresponding masculine form.

And thus, the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs only when the feminine word itself is the internal prior member followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*); in this way, it is established in all cases. For example, in *grāmaṇidṛṣṭir asya* ("his vision is that of a village chief"), the word *grāmaṇi*, without having abandoned its own gender, stands in grammatical apposition with the word *dṛṣṭi*.
If the transformation into the masculine form were to apply here, the shortening of the neuter vowel would be precluded.

"How so? and so forth. The basis for the application of the word *garbhiṇī* (pregnant) to a woman is its connection with a fetus that is not a constituent part [of her body], whereas in the case of a man, it is the connection with a fetus that is a constituent part. Furthermore, for the words *prasūtā* and *prajātā*, the basis of application to a woman is the release of the fetus, while in the case of a man, it is the conception of the fetus. "Effort must be made here" means that the mere connection with an object existing within is the basis for the application of the word *garbhiṇī*; whether that [object] is a constituent part or not is irrelevant.

In this way, even for the words *prasūta* and *prajāta*, by excluding the meanings of "conception" (*ādhāna*) and "delivery" (*vimocana*), only the relationship with offspring (*apatya*) is adopted as the basis [for the application of the suffix]. This is the effort made here. Regarding the term *brahmabandhūbhārya*: there is no exclusion of the suffix *ūṅ*. Since the mention of *ūṅ* should have been included in the very rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.37), the fact that it is stated separately as a specific prohibition makes its distinctness known. Consequently, in the case of *brahmabandhūvṛndarikā*, even though the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prescribed by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.3.42) within the scope of the prohibition, it does not occur. And this meaning is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anūṅ* in that context.

However, this prohibition regarding "apūraṇī," "priyā," and so on, should be applied only in that specific context; for its recurrence in the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* is not desired. This is because in cases such as *mahānavamī*, *mahādvādaśī*, *akṣayatṛtīyā*, and *kṛṣṇacaturdaśī*, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is accepted even when the ordinal number (*pūraṇī*) occurs in a *karmadhāraya* compound. The statement "the mention of the principal ordinal (*pradhānapūraṇī*) must be made" means that it should be stated that the prohibition applies only to that [ordinal] which is the principal member. And this is obtained through the principle that an operation applies to the principal element (*pradhāne kāryasaṃpratyayāt*). For example: *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ*.

In this case, since the referent of the compound (*anyapadārtha*) is a "night" whose internal distinctions of parts are concealed, the ordinal number does not enter into it; therefore, there is no predominance [of the ordinal]. However, in examples such as *kalyāṇapañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("nights with a fifth that is auspicious"), the referent of the compound is "nights" whose internal distinctions of parts are manifest. In that instance, just as the nights are denoted by the compound, so too is the fifth; thus, there is predominance of the ordinal.

Now, regarding the forms *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* and *śobhanabhaktiḥ*, how is the masculine replacement (*puṃvadbhāva*) justified here, given that the word *bhakti* is listed among the words beginning with *priya* (in the rule governing feminine compounds)? To this he says: "In cases such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* and so forth. The meaning is that one must provide the following resolution to the objection: the feminine nature of the first member of the compound is not intended to be expressed; therefore, the formation of *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ* and similar forms is established.

In this context, the word *dṛḍha* (firm) is intended to signify the cessation of firmness; the point is that when the injunction is intended to signify the cessation of firmness, the employment of the feminine gender is irrelevant. Nor does this imply that the rule [of Pāṇini] is to be disregarded, for if one intended to express a specific gender, undesirable consequences such as *darśanīyabhāryaḥ* would follow.

Now, how should it be in this case—*paṭvīmṛdvyau bhārye asya*? It should be *paṭvīmṛdubhāryaḥ*, because the rule states that the transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies to that whose following word is immediately adjacent, and not to the other.
In the case of suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending with *ām*, the substitution of *su* for the final vowel and following consonant of a word occurs, except before the suffix *kṛtvasuc*.

The attainment of the state of unsurpassed reality (*anuttarapadārtha*). Regarding the phrase "then there" (*tatastatra*): because it is a case-ending (*vibhakti*) according to the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ*, it undergoes the substitution of the *tyadādi* group, the addition of the suffix *ṭāp*, and by this [rule], the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is applied.

In this regard, some [words] are listed in the *tasil*-group and so forth, where the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is not desired; others are listed elsewhere, where the masculine form is desired. Therefore, he says: "it is a complete enumeration" (*parigaṇanam*). An example of the suffixes *tra* and *tas* has been given. For *tarap* and *tamap*: *darśanīyatarā*, *darśanīyatamā*. For *caraṭ* and *jātīyar*: *paṭucarī*, *paṭujātīyā*. For *kalpap* and *deśīyar*: *darśanīyakalpā*, *darśanīyadeśīyā*. There is no listing for the suffix *deśya*.

*rupap* and *prāśa*: *darśanīyarūpā*, *paṭuprāśā*. *tham* and *thālu*: [The suffix] *thamu* is prescribed by the rule "idamasthamuḥ, kimaśca" (*Pāṇini 5.3.24*). [The suffix] *thāl* is used in the sense of "manner. By this base [it is formed] *ittham*; by which manner? *katham*; by that manner? *tathā*. *dārhil* and *o*: At that time—*tadā*, *tarhi*. *til* and *thyan*: [The rule] "vṛkajyeṣṭhābhyāṃ tiltātilau ca chandasi" (*Pāṇini 5.3.99*) [is applied]. A wolf that is excellent is *vṛkatiḥ*. There is a reading "tāti-lo-nā-siti. From *ajā* and *avi*, [the suffix] *thyan*: beneficial for a goat is *ajathyā*.

In these examples involving the suffixes *ghar* and *kalpa*, the short vowel (*hrasva*) occurs because the rule for the feminine suffix *ṅī* is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Thus: *paṭivattamā*, *paṭivakalpā*, *paṭivarupā*.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has the sense of 'many' or 'few'": the meaning is that this *śas* suffix, following words with the sense of "many" or "few," should also be understood as belonging to the group beginning with *tasil*.

Regarding the term *nāstikam*: if the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were not applied here, then after the elision of the suffix *ya* (the *yat* suffix) from the word *hastinī*, that elision would be subject to the rule *sthānivat* (treating the substitute as the original). Furthermore, because of the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*, that elision would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Consequently, the elision of the final vowel by the rule *na-staddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144) would not occur. Therefore, the substitution of the masculine form is prescribed. The substitution of the masculine form is not obtained by the rule *ṭhak-chasoś-ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.95), because that rule refers to the suffix *ṭhak* when it occurs in association with the suffix *chas*. Examples: *śyaineyaḥ* and *rohiṇeyaḥ*. These are derived by the rule *śyeta-rohitābhyāṃ varṇādanudāttāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.39).

The suffixes *ṅīp* and *nakār* [are mentioned]. Here, if the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were to apply, the forms would have to be *śyaiteyaḥ* and *rauhiteyaḥ*. As for the question "How so? and so forth: if the masculine form is prohibited in the case of the *ḍha*-suffix, then, because of the rule "In the feminine of *agni*, [the vowel] of *vṛṣākapi*, *agni*, *kusita*, and *kusida* is udātta," when the *ṅīp* is added to the word *agni*, and the *aikāra* is replaced by *āy*, one obtains *agnāyī*. Then, in the derivation of *agnerḍhak* ("*ḍhak* after *agni* when it is its deity")—that is, in the *ḍhak* suffix according to the rule "In all cases, *ḍhak* after *agni* and *kali"—since the masculine form is prohibited, one would obtain *āgnāyeya*. Therefore, how is it that *āgneya* must be formed here? This requires effort.

Some say: instead of *aḍhe*, one should state *anapatye*. By this, the following is also established: [the derivation of] *kuṇḍinyā apatyam* (the offspring of Kuṇḍinī). Here, the suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*. Since there is no *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) in this case, when the *y* is elided by the rule *yasyeti ca*, that elision is treated as a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original element) by the rule *yasyeti ca*. Consequently, the rule *na staddhite* (elision of the final vowel and its following consonant before a *taddhita* suffix) does not apply, and thus the form *kauṇḍinyaḥ* is obtained.

If, however, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) were to apply, the form would result as *kauṇḍya*. Likewise, the offspring of a *sapatnī* (a woman with a co-wife) takes the suffix *aṇ* because [the word] belongs to the *śiva*-class; since there is no masculine substitution in that case, the form becomes *sāpatna*. If the masculine substitution were applied, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the marker *n*—which are prescribed by the rule "always in the case of *sapatnī* and others"—would be eliminated, resulting in *sāpata*. Thus, by the statement "not when denoting offspring" (*anapatye*), the masculine substitution occurs even in the *ḍha* suffix when it does not denote offspring, as in *sa āgneyaḥ*; but it does not occur when denoting offspring, as in *śyaineyaḥ* and *rauhiṇeyaḥ*.

If it were said that [the rule applies] when there is no offspring (*anapatya*), then in the case of *gargasyāpatyaṃ strī* (the female offspring of Garga), namely *gārgyāyaṇī*, when the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule *gotra-striyāḥ kutsane ṇa ca* ("the suffix *ṇa* is applied after a feminine of the *gotra* class in the sense of contempt"), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would not obtain. Consequently, one would have to say *gārgyayaṇo jālmaḥ* ("this wretch is a Gārgyāyaṇī"), whereas *gārgyo jālmaḥ* ("this wretch is a Gārgya") is what is intended. Therefore, it cannot be said that [the rule applies] when there is no offspring. How then [is the form] *kauṇḍinyaḥ* established? It is established by the specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ*.

How can the word *sapatna*, which is a synonym for "enemy" (*śatru*), have the sense of "co-wife" (*sāpatna*)? This is because of the grammatical evidence in the rule *vyansapatne*. That [term] should be included among the *śārṅgarava* group; from that, the suffix *aṇ* applies according to the rule *śivādyaṇ*, and thus, under the rule *strībhyo ḍhak*, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is established—this interpretation alone is the refuge here.

Regarding the rule *ṭhak-chasoh*: because the suffix *chas* is marked with *s*, the designation *pada* is prescribed by the rule *siti ca*; since [the word] would thus lack the status of *bha*, this statement is made. Why is the mention of *ṭhak* necessary? Once the substitution of *i* has been performed, the result would be established simply by the rule *bhasyāḍhe*. [The purpose is that] it should apply specifically while in the state of *ṭhak*. What happens when this is so? The substitution of *ka* by the rule *is-us-uk-tāntāt kaḥ* becomes established. Otherwise, if the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment) were to occur after the substitution of *i* had been made, then—just as in the case of *māthitika* where the substitution of *ka* does not take place once the substitution of *i* has occurred—the same would not happen here in *bhāvatka*.
And [the suffix *ka*] is also applied after words ending in *mānin*. (Pāṇini 6.3.36)

This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in "this is hers" and "she is his. It is already established by the preceding rule alone, because since there is only one [entity], it cannot simultaneously possess the status of both object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*), and thus coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is absent.
Not [is there elision] of the penultimate vowel when the suffix *kopadha* (having *k* as its penultimate letter) follows.

*Madrikā* and *vṛjikā* are derived from *madra* and *vṛji* respectively, with the suffix *kan*. Regarding *vailepikam*: here, the application [of the feminine suffix] prescribed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānikī*)—"after *mahiṣī* and so on, when a *taddhita* beginning with *bh* or *āḍha* follows"—is prohibited. However, in the preceding cases, the application is based on the *sūtra* itself. "The mention of *taddhita* and *vu*" means it should be stated that [the prohibition applies] to the *k* of a *taddhita* and to the *k* of *vu*. In *pākabhāryā*, the word *pāka* denotes the first stage of life; consequently, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied by virtue of its being listed among the *ajādi* group, as an exception to *ṅīp*.
And [the feminine suffixes] *saṃjñā* and *pūraṇī* [are not elided]. 6.3.38.

The prohibition of the designation "feminine" (*saṃjñā-pratiṣedha*) applies to those words used in common worldly usage which are based on actions such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth, and are employed for both males and females. However, in the case of words that are designations based on a single substance or based on location, there is no possibility [of the feminine suffix] precisely because they have not been previously mentioned as masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). For example: *dattāyate*, *guptāyate*. Although there would be no difference whether this prohibition were applied or not in these instances, this example is nevertheless presented simply because it is, in fact, the proper domain of the prohibition.
And [the suffix *ṣyañ*] is not applied to a *taddhita* suffix that causes a vowel increase (*vṛddhi*), when it does not denote a colored product or a modification. 6.3.39.

The letter *ṇ* [is added] because of the term "vṛddhi. Here, the mention of "nimitta" (cause) need not be made; one should simply say "vṛddhes taddhitasya" (of the taddhita suffix following a vṛddhi). What is a taddhita suffix following a vṛddhi? It is that which is the very cause of that [vṛddhi]. Since this is already established, by including the word "nimitta," a bahuvrīhi compound with different case-roles (*vyadhikaraṇa*) is formed. Another says: it is a *darśa-ādi* suffix [added] after a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

Alternatively, the compound is formed with a word ending in the plural because it refers to the apprehension of the cause (*nimitta*): "the cause of all three *vṛddhi*s" is *vṛddhinimittam*. However, in reality, the cause belongs only to the vowel *ā*. Here, however, in the case of *sārvabhārya*—meaning "one whose wife is *sārvā* (beneficial to all)"—even though the vowel *ā* alone becomes the *vṛddhi* when the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule *sarvapuruṣābhyām*, nevertheless, that [suffix] is not the cause of *vṛddhi* in its own form; rather, it is by virtue of being marked with *Ṇ* (*ṇit-tva*). And that [quality of being *ṇit*] is the cause for all three [types of *vṛddhi*].

*Madhyamā* means "situated in the middle"; *madhyāt maḥ* [is the rule for its formation]. *Kāṇḍalāvī*: one who cuts stalks (*kāṇḍa-lāvī*); the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiṭñāṇañ*. *Tāvatī*: from the words *yat*, *tat*, and *etad*, the suffix *vatup* is applied in the sense of measure; *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of the pronoun, and *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *agitaścaṅīp*. If this were based on a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there would also be a prohibition of this [suffix]; however, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because the letter *ṇa* does not occur at the beginning, it does not apply. *Kāṣāyī*: that which is dyed with that [color], by the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (the suffix *aṇ* is applied). *Lauhī*: [formed] by the rule *prāṇirajatādibhyo'ñ*. The word *khadira* belongs to the *palāśādi* group. *Īṣā* is a specific part of a chariot.
The word *svāṅga* [is used] before *cetas* and *amānin*. (6.3.40)

Regarding the rule *svāṅgācceto 'mānini*: the term *amānini* has been inserted into the sūtra based on its appearance in the Vārttika. By the rule *svāṅgāccopasarjanāt*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, as in *dīrghakeśī*. However, by the prohibition *sahanajvidyamānapūrvācca*, the form *akeśā* is derived.
And [the suffix *taddhita* is applied] after a genus-word (*jāti*). 6.3.41.
Because *kaṭha* and *bahvṛca* denote both a lineage (*gotra*) and a Vedic school (*caraṇa*), they possess the status of a genus (*jāti*); therefore, by rule [4.1.63], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
Regarding "this," and so forth: here, the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) is the refuge for understanding.
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, and after the suffixes *jātīya* and *deśīya*, [the feminine suffix] is treated like the masculine. 6.3.42.

[Objection: But surely the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is already established for a *karmadhāraya* by the rule "the feminine [stem] is like the masculine" (*striyāḥ puṃvat*), and it is also established for the suffixes *jātīya* and *deśīya* by the rule "in the case of *tasil* and so forth. For what purpose, then, is this new rule commenced? [Response: To this he says: "This is for the sake of what has been prohibited" (*pratiṣiddhārtho'yam*). The meaning is: so that the masculine form may occur even where it has been prohibited. In the reading "this is for the sake of prohibition" (*pratiṣedhārtho'yam*), the word "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*) refers to the scope of the prohibition. Alternatively, the word *artha* means "cessation" (*nivṛtti*).

"Of the hen and so forth," etc. This statement is for the purpose of excluding the feminine meaning and for the purpose of non-co-referentiality (*asamānādhikaraṇa*). "Or not," etc.: he rejects the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). "Or it need not be stated. For what reason? Because the feminine nature of the prior member is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatva*). Here, there is no determination of femininity that must be resorted to even when the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) is being commenced; even if it were not commenced, the same would result. If, then, there will be no compound with a feminine gender [prior member]...

While it may indeed be possible to explain it thus in that case, how can it be so here in the expression *mṛgyāḥ kṣīram* (the milk of a female deer), meaning *mṛgakṣīram*? For there is no inherent connection between a male and milk. Even here, because the injunction aims at the exclusion of other species, the feminine gender is irrelevant and thus not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). However, where gender serves as a specific qualification, it is certainly intended to be expressed, as in: "It should be sprinkled with the urine of a he-goat. In this instance, the referent of the first member of the compound is the genus (*jāti*).

In the compound *kukkuṭāṇḍa* ("hen's egg"), the meaning of the first member is "genus" (*jāti*); the sense is that this is intended in a general form, devoid of specific qualities such as femininity and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in *khid* and so forth": among those, the counter-exception (*vipratiṣedha*) concerning *khid* has already been illustrated under the rule *striyāḥ pumvat*. Regarding the *gha*-affixes and so forth, the scope of the rule "the short vowel of a *nadī* [stem] occurs" is exemplified by *nartakitarā*, *nartakitamā*, *nartakirūpā*, and *nartakikalpā*; whereas the scope of the prohibition against *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) in the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* applies where the suffixes *tasil* and so forth are present. The scope of *puṃvadbhāva* applies when the stem does not end in a *ṅī* vowel—for example, *darśanīyataretyādi*.

In cases such as *paṭvitara*, where both [rules] would otherwise apply, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope of the rule "a short vowel occurs after *ke* following a *ṇi*-ending stem" (*ke'ṇo hrasvaḥ*) is exemplified by *nartakikā*. The scope of the rule for masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) is exemplified by the feminine descendant of *darada*: from *darada* with the suffix *aṇ* according to "the *aṇ* suffix follows *dvyañc* and *magadha*" (*dvyañmagadhakaliṅgasūramasādaṇ*), its elision (*luk*) by "also after a stem ending in *at*" (*ataśca*), then *ka* by "after words beginning with *prāgin*" (*prāgivāt kaḥ*), and finally, due to masculine-like behavior by "in the case of *tasil* and so forth" (*tasilādiṣu*), the word becomes *dārada*; then, by "after a suffixal *t* or *th*" (*pratyayasthāt...itvam*), the form *dāradikā* is obtained.

But surely, the suffixes beginning with *tasil* have been enumerated, and the suffix *kap* does not exist among them. If that is so, then it is inferred that the suffix *kap* is also admitted there precisely because of a conflict (vipratiṣedha); for in cases such as *paṭvikā* and *mṛdvikā*, where both [suffixes] would otherwise apply, the short vowel (*hrasva*) occurs by virtue of its being subsequent (paratva), and in all such instances, because the principle of "once only" (*sakṛt*) is adopted, there is an absence of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

He demonstrates the purpose of what was stated as "anūṅ" with the words "iha" and so forth. Regarding the suffix *tadrāja*: for those [names] consisting of two syllables, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *dvyañmagadha-*; for the remainder, the suffix *añ* is applied by the rule *janapadaśabdāt*; and *pṛthū* ends in the letter *th*.

In place of the final vowel of the words *ghara*, *upakalpa*, *cela*, *aḍba*, *bruva*, *gotra*, and *mata*, as well as of a stem consisting of more than one syllable, the substitution of a short vowel occurs before the suffix *ṅya*.

Since words such as *cela* (garment) function as terms of reproach regarding conduct, the compound is formed according to the rule "those which are reproached by means of reproaches" (*kutsitāni kutsanaiḥ*). In the case of the suffix *ṅya*, an augment would have been required—as in the rule *īyāś chandasi bahulam*—but it was not applied because the work is a *sūtra*.

Regarding the rule *dattātara-*: [An objection is raised]—"But surely, from the rule *svāṅgāccetaḥ*, the term *ītaḥ* will be carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. Even so, in the case of *prāmaṇītaraḥ*, the suffix would still apply here; for the word *striyām* ("in the feminine") is still being carried over. Even so, in the case of *pramaṇītarā*, the suffix would still apply here; for *striyām* is indeed being carried over, and the meaning of *strīyā ītaḥ* is "of that which denotes a female, the long vowel *ī* [is applied]. However, in the word *grāmaṇī*, the long vowel *ī* is meaningless [for the formation of the feminine].

In that case, the mention of *ṅīp* is for the sake of establishing the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). For when *ṅīp* is mentioned, because it is explicitly stated as "the *ṅī* [affix] of that which has more than one syllable," the remainder is understood in relation to it: "that which is not *ṅī*, namely a *nadī* (feminine stem), and that which ends in *ṅī* and has only one syllable. Even without the mention of *ṅīp*, the remainder is already established; for how so? The term *ītaḥ* (from an *ī*-ending) continues to apply, meaning: "that which is not *ī*, namely a *nadī*, and that which ends in *ī* and has only one syllable. Let this mention of *ṅī* stand for now.
The suffix *śas* is applied after the word *nadī* when it occurs at the end of a compound with another word. 6.3.44.

The phrase "not having the marker *ūṅ* after a word that has a masculine form" (*bhāṣitapuṃskādanūṅ*) has ceased to apply. Now, what is meant by "the remainder" (*śeṣa*)? If "the remainder" refers to those cases where a short vowel was not intended by the previous rule, then the shortening would undesirably apply even to words that do not have a masculine counterpart, as well as to polysyllabic *ṅī*-stem words that have a masculine form despite having a different configuration (e.g., *āmalakītarā*, *drīṇītarā*). The question here is: why would shortening apply even in these cases, since it was already prescribed by the previous rule? The answer is: "The remainder" is relative to that which was explicitly mentioned in the previous rule.

The mention of *śeṣa* (the remainder) could have been omitted. How so? The general rule (*utsarga*) is "for a nadī-stem, optionally short" (*nadyā anyatarasyām hrasvaḥ*). An exception (*apavāda*) to that is "for a stem with more than one vowel ending in *ī*, there is always shortness" (*tasyānekāca īto nityahrasvatvam*). When that constant [shortness] would otherwise apply, the optional rule "and for a stem ending in an *ugit*" (*ugitaśca*) is introduced. If this were the case, then in the rule "for a nadī-stem, optionally," the term "from a word that has already expressed the masculine gender" (*bhāṣitapuṃskāt*) would still be understood as carrying over; consequently, [the shortening] would undesirably apply even here in the case of *droṇītarā*. Therefore, the mention of *śeṣa* must be made. And when that is made, so that "remainder-ness" may be understood in relation to what is actually heard [in the sūtra], the mention of *ṅī* must also be made in the preceding rule.

Regarding the word *lakṣmī*: according to the rule *avitṛstṛtantribhya īḥ* and *lakṣermuṭ ca*, the word *lakṣmī* ends in the suffix *ī*; thus, it is a word ending in a *kṛt*-derived feminine noun (*kṛnnadī*). In that case, the prohibition [of the designation *nadī*] must be stated. It need not be stated. How so? Because the term *striyām* ("in the feminine") continues to apply; we shall therefore qualify the word *nadī* by it, [interpreting the rule as applying only to] "a feminine *nadī*. And a *kṛt*-derived feminine noun like *lakṣmī* does not denote a female being. If so, then the designation *nadī* would not apply to it either. The resolution for this has already been stated in the section on the *nadī* designation.
And [the feminine suffix ṅīp] is applied after a stem ending in an *ugit* vowel.

It has been stated that even the treatment as a masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*) should be mentioned here in this rule; however, this is not seen in the *Bhāṣya*. By the words "because of the connection with excellence" (*prakarṣayogāt*) and so forth, he rejects what was to be stated. For the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is the primary cause for the derivation of a word. And it is thought that here, since there is no intention to express femininity prior to the connection with excellence, there is no feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).
The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the word *mahat* occurs when it stands in apposition with another word or when followed by the suffix *jātīya*. (Pāṇini 6.3.46)

"Mahataḥ putraḥ" becomes "mahat-putraḥ. Now, one might argue that in this case, only the rule "ānmahataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.46) should be formulated; then a second rule, "jātīye ca," would follow. In that context, the first rule would bring to mind a compound with a subsequent word, and by the maxim "lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā," only that [compound] prescribed by the rule "sanmahatparamottamotkṛṣṭāḥ pūjyamānaiḥ" (Pāṇini 2.1.61) would be understood. Furthermore, by the maxim "samānādhikaraṇe" (Pāṇini 1.2.42), only that [compound] prescribed by "sanmahat... which functions as a coordinate construction (samānādhikaraṇa) would be grasped.

Thus, the inclusion of the term "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) in the rule is redundant; he first raises this objection with the words, "because it is stated in the definition. He refutes it with the words, "even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*. The phrase "for that purpose" means for the sake of ensuring that [the rule] applies even in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, or alternatively, for the sake of setting aside the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta* paribhāṣā.

Here, in the expression *āmahān mahān saṃpannaḥ mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*, the word *mahat* and the word *bhūta* both refer to the single object, the moon; because they are co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the substitution of *āt* (long *ā*) would consequently apply.

It might be argued as follows: the suffix * cvi* is prescribed in the sense of "the becoming of that which was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāve*). And what is this "becoming of that which was not previously so"? It is the state of a cause—which was not previously existing in the form of its modification—coming into existence in the form of that modification. In that case, the base (*prakṛti*) is the agent, not the modification (*vikṛti*). Accordingly, we observe the plural number and the first person based on the base in such examples as *brāhmaṇāḥ saṅghībhavanti* ("the Brahmins become a group") and *tantavaḥ paṭībhavanti* ("the threads become a cloth"), as well as *atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate tvadbhavati* ("he who was not you becomes you"). We do not observe the singular number and the second person based on the modification. Therefore, and consequently...

The suffix *kta* in the word *bhūta* is produced in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) of the action of "becoming" (*bhavana*), and not in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, what [is the point]? There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between *bhūta* and *āmahata*, but not with *mahata*. For even if there is identity between that which possesses states (*avasthāvat*), coreferentiality between two distinct states is not possible; for it does not occur that "he is both a child and an old man," whereas it does occur that "he is both a child and Devadatta. Thus, because of this lack of coreferentiality, the substitution of *āt* does not take place.

If this were so, then in the case of the expression *amahatī mahatī saṃpannā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brāhmaṇī woman who was not great has become great"), the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) would also not occur precisely because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Just as agency is observed in the case of the material cause (*prakṛti*), it is likewise observed in the case of the modification (*vikṛti*). And thus says the Bhāṣya in the *Paspaśā*: "A lump of gold becomes two earrings having the color of khadira-wood coals."

Likewise, regarding the rule that "the fourth case (dative) should be stated when something is being transformed" (*klṛpi sampadyamāne*), the dative prescribed for the agent of the transformation occurs with respect to the *vikāra* (the product), not the *prakṛti* (the material cause). For example, one says, "barley-gruel is suitable for urine" (*mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ*), referring to the transformation, not the source. Similarly, expressions based on transformation are observed, such as "a non-group of Brahmins becomes a group of Brahmins" (*asaṅgho brāhmaṇasaṅgho bhavati*) and "threads that were not cloth become cloth" (*apaṭas tantavaḥ paṭo bhavati*). In such cases, if the grammatical agreement (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) were established by relying on the agency of the *vikṛti* (the product), then the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would be prescribed; however, the substitution of the long vowel *ā* (*āttva*) would also [erroneously] occur.

Now, if agency belonged to the material cause (*prakṛti*), then [the substitution of] *ā* would not occur due to a difference in grammatical substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), nor would there be the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). To this it is replied: it has already been shown how, in the domain of the suffix * cvi*, both the material cause and the modification (*vikṛti*) possess agency. And this is logical, provided that the suffix is based on the agency of the modification. Furthermore, when a single entity consisting of both material cause and modification is resorted to, then the conventional usage of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) applies. As it has been said: "When [an object], relinquishing its former attribute, assumes another..."

"A substance that does not deviate from its true nature (tattva) is said to undergo transformation (pariṇāma). When, however, the distinction between one state or the other is not intended to be expressed, then there is the state of "becoming"—as in "the threads become" or "the cloth becomes. That object which, while abandoning the preceding property and assuming a subsequent one, arises as a unified entity, is called the "agent of accomplishment" (sampadyakartṛ). And because of the non-difference [of the substance] from that [unified entity], agency belongs to the preceding and succeeding states as well; therefore, this [objection] too is refuted.

If an unreal subsequent state were to arise, even a rabbit’s horn would arise; and if a real prior state were to arise, then all things such as cloth and the like would be arising at all times. How is this refuted? Does that which is existent arise, or that which is non-existent? A thing persisting through both the prior and subsequent states does not arise in any form—neither as something different nor as something non-different—from that [prior state], just as the substance of clay [does not arise] in the form of a jar.

If this is so, what wrong has the prior state committed that it does not arise again? It has committed no wrong at all; rather, how could that which is non-existent be the agent? For when that [prior state] has perished, the subsequent state arises, just as a jar arises from the state of a lump of clay. Therefore, it is logical that the primordial matter itself transforms into those various forms such as the lump and so forth. This continues down to the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). That primal nature, however, transforms into those various forms such as earth and so forth without depending on any other material cause.

Thus, it is established that the self-nature of the object, being in a state of coalescence (*sammūrchita*), is the agent of its own manifestation; and because there is no difference between it [in this state] and its prior and subsequent states, agency belongs to it even in those former and later conditions. And it has been said: "The self-nature of the object, while abandoning its prior state and touching upon a subsequent property, is designated as 'being born' (jāyamāna), as if it were in a state of coalescence."

This being the case, in a sentence expressing the sense of *cv-* (the suffix *-tva*), the agency sometimes belongs to the base (*prakṛti*) alone, because that which ends in *cv-* functions as a *gati* (preverb), and *gatis* are adverbs modifying the action; for one thing is "becoming" (*bhavana*), while another is "becoming a group" (*saṅghībhavana*). In that regard, in simple "becoming," the group (*saṅgha*) is the agent; but in "becoming a group," the Brahmin is the agent. For example, in the expression "he makes a sūtra of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya sūtraṃ karoti*), the sūtra is the object of the specific act of making; likewise, in "he grammaticalizes" (*vyākaraṇaṃ satrayati*), grammar is the object of the qualified act of making. It is the same here as well.

In that regard, in the expression *maddbhūtā candramāḥ*, this word ending in *cv-*—namely the word *mahat*—resolves into the sense of "becoming" (*bhavana*), which is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *bhūta*. However, since the word *bhūta* here refers to the moon in its own form (*svarūpe*) without being touched by greatness (*mahattvena*), there is an absence of the *ātva* substitution due to a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). In the case of *mahadbhūtā brāhmaṇī*, however, the rule is established because the feminine nature of the prior member is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*), just as in the case of *mṛgakṣīra* ("deer's milk") and similar expressions. But where femininity is indeed intended to be expressed, the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur at all—as in: *agomatī gomatī saṃpannā gomatībhūtā brāhmaṇī* ("the Brahmin woman who was not wealthy became wealthy").

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, offers a resolution based on the fact that even when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to the agency of the modification (*vikṛti*), it is secondary (*gauṇa*); for he says, "because the meaning of 'great' (*mahaḥ*) is secondary. For when there is a choice between the secondary and the primary, the understanding applies to the primary—just as in the injunctions "A cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyā*) and "A goat dedicated to Agni and Soma" (*aja agnīṣomīyaḥ*), the Vāhīka (a man from a specific region) is not the one to be sacrificed. Furthermore, in our own grammatical system, by the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) in the rule *svarūpam*, it is indicated that the meaning possessing that form is also a governing factor (*tantra*). Therefore, since the primary meaning is accepted here, the word "great" (*mahaḥ*) is understood in its primary sense.
