There is an absence of *āttva* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*) in the case of a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning. For in words ending in the suffix * cvi*, a single entity is understood to possess a dual nature by virtue of being both the original material and its modification. When it is said, "it becomes a cloth" (*paṭībhavati*), one understands that what was previously not a cloth is now transforming into the nature of a cloth. However, when it is said, "it becomes a cloth" (*paṭo bhavati*), such an understanding does not arise; rather, it is also understood as "the cloth becomes [red] in color," and so forth. In that case, the application of the word *paṭa*—which denotes only the state of modification—to both the prior state and the subsequent state of persistence is not possible without resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication).

Another says: the word *mahat* functions [to denote] even that which is not large when it is tending toward transformation by way of its magnitude. And the proof for this is as follows: in the sentence "the cloth comes into being" (*paṭo bhavati*), it is understood that it comes into being in the form of red or other qualities; however, in the case of "it becomes a cloth" (*paṭībhavati*), it is understood precisely that "what was not a cloth becomes a cloth. Since such usage would not be possible without metaphorical application (*upacāra*), one should consider that the absence of the *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*) is due to the word having a figurative meaning.

If, then, the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is prescribed without taking into account any specific distinction, it would apply even to the secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning; for the principle of primary versus secondary application (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) holds only when a specific word-form is taken into account. However, in a case such as *gomatībhūta*, one must strive to prevent the application of the masculine form.

If, then, the primary meaning is accepted in the treatises on grammar (*śāstra*), how is it that [terms such as] *vāhīka* undergo vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) and become *gaurvāhīkaḥ* or *gāṃ vāhīkam*? [The answer is: when a word is connected with another word, its figurative meaning (*gauṇārtha*) is manifested; and it is the word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*) that is connected with another word. Therefore, this rule applies only to the meaning obtained when a word is connected with another word, and not to operations concerning the nominal stem (*pratipadika*). Thus, [in the case of *vāhīka*], it remains in its own primary sense.

In the case of the word *go*, having experienced the substitution of *ā* (āttva) during its usage in reference to an object possessing a dewlap and so forth (*sāsnādimat*), the word *go* will subsequently apply to a *vāhīka*. However, in this instance, the substitution of *ā* prescribed for the word *mahat* when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) must pertain precisely to its primary meaning at that stage.

By this very logic, the designation *pragṛhya* as *ot* does not apply to that word *go* in the expression *gauḥ abhavat*; nor does the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) apply in the expression *agnisomau māṇavakau* according to the rule *agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ*; nor does the substitution of *it* (ittva) apply to *agni* in the rule *īdagneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *mahadāt-tva* and so forth: the word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), not in the sense of mere addition (*anvācaya*). Thus, wherever there is the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), there alone is the substitution of *āt*. The example *aṣṭākapālam* is as follows: "prepared on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam*) is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; this is then elided by the rule *dvigoḥ*. [Thus we get] *aṣṭakapāla*. This is a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). Due to its inclusion in the *pātrādi* group, it lacks feminine gender.

Regarding the term *aṣṭāgavena*: it is a three-membered *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which eight oxen (*go*) are yoked. Since the first two members form a *dvigu*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element according to the rule *gor ataddhitaluki*. In that case, because the long vowel [of *aṣṭā-*, derived from *aṣṭan-*] conveys the sense of being "yoked," the word *yukta* ("yoked") is elided. Alternatively, it may be a *samāhāra-dvigu*; by association (*sāhacarya*) and through metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) as non-different, it functions in the sense of "yoked."

The inclusion of *kaṣa* is for the sake of clarity; it is not intended to exclude those [words] whose vowels occur at different times, because [the rule] is not restricted to such cases (*anaṇtvāt*), nor is it intended to include those with different qualities (*guṇa*) occurring at the same time, because qualities do not constitute a difference [in the vowel itself]. Since this matter should have been stated in the very section on *ānaṅ*, the mention here as *āt* is for the purpose of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule). By this, the substitution of *āt* is established in *aṣṭākapāla* and other such instances. And thus, the substitution of *āt* occurs elsewhere even in the eleventh [case], as evidenced by the usage *prāgekādaśabhyo 'cchandasī*.
In a compound denoting a number, the word *dvi* (two) is substituted for *dvyaṣṭan* (eighteen), except when it occurs in a *bahuvrīhi* compound or before the word *aśīti* (eighty). Pāṇini 6.3.47.

In this case, there is no application of the rule for the designation of enumerated items (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*). If it were so, there would be a prohibition regarding the form *aśīti* (eighty) after the word *aṣṭan*, and thus that [prohibition] would be rendered useless. Even if the substitution of *āt* is prohibited, the long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar sounds (*savarṇadīrgha*) must still occur. In forms such as *dvādaśa* (twelve) and *dvāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-two), there is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāre dvandvaḥ*). The rule "it is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*) does not apply here, because gender is based on worldly usage (*lokāśrayatvāl liṅgasya*). Regarding *dvitrāḥ*: the compound is formed with the sense of "optionality" (*vārthe*) by the rule *saṃkhyayāvyayāsannādūrā...*, and since it is a bahuvrīhi denoting a number to be counted, the suffix *ḍac* is applied. *Dvidaśāḥ* means "two tens. This is a compound in the sense of the suffix *su*.
The word *tri* becomes *tre-* before the suffixes *trayaḥ*. (Pāṇini 6.3.48)
Because the word *trayodaśa* is listed in the *sandhivelādi* group, this substitute ending in *s* [is applied].
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, when the number forty or more is mentioned, it refers to all [the categories]. (Pāṇini 6.3.49)
"Of all [the suffixes]," and so forth. For if that were not the case, there would be an option only for the immediately preceding rule, namely *trestrayaḥ*.
In the case of *hṛdaya*, [the substitution of] *hṛd* occurs before the suffixes *hṛllekha*, *yad*, *aṇ*, and *lāsa*. 6.3.50.

"The inclusion of that which ends in *aṇ* is intended," because of the [authoritative] commentary. Here, he shows what is excluded: "But in the case of *ghañ*. And when there is the inclusion of that which ends in *aṇ*, not that which ends in *ghañ*, then the mention of *lekha* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Or [the suffix *yat* is used] after the words *śoka*, *vyasana*, and *roga*. (6.3.51)

Regarding the phrase "by the word *hṛdaya*" and so forth: they do not accept what has been stated, precisely because of the prescription of alternative forms (*vikalpa*), and because of the prescription of the *hṛd* substitute for the region [of the word] in the rule *paddannomās...hṛt*.
The substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs before the words *jyā*, *ati*, *go*, and *upahata*.

This substitute ending in the vowel *ā* is devoid of case endings (*avibhaktika*). [The rule] "from *aj* and *ati*" refers to *aja* (meaning "going, throwing, or moving") and *at* (meaning "continuous motion"). Regarding *padaga*: the suffix *ḍa* is applied because it is seen elsewhere in the section on *ḍa*-suffixes. "Only as an *apadeśa*" means that it occurs immediately after the act of compounding, even before the accent of the compound itself has been established. "It is prescribed as having the udātta accent on the final syllable": otherwise, by virtue of proximity (*āntaryata*), it would have the udātta accent on the first syllable. By the words beginning with "by that," he states the purpose of prescribing the final-udātta accent.

The point regarding the mention of "upadeśa" (original enunciation) in the rule beginning with *padāji* is as follows: If the substitution of the word *pada*—which is acutely accented on the final syllable—were to occur only after the *kṛt*-suffix accent had already been applied, then, because it would be subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*), it would supersede the *kṛt*-accent. However, if the substitution of the acutely accented final syllable occurs at the very stage of the original enunciation, then the *kṛt*-accent itself remains the subsequently prescribed one. Furthermore, the specific mention of the acutely accented form is not redundant, as it is actually heard in forms such as *padopahata*. This is the summary of the argument.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *pāda* when it does not mean "a foot. (Pāṇini 6.3.53)

Regarding the phrase *icareti*: the meaning is that the suffix *ik* occurs in the sense of "moving" (*carati*), and it is a *kṛt* suffix. Because this *vārttika* is not seen [in other recensions], in the *pārṣada* lists it is read as *pādaḥ pat* (with *pat* instead of *pad*). Regarding the term *śarīrāvayavasya* ("of a limb of the body"): here, the commentary (*vyākhyāna*) is the authority. Another says: first, there was the inclusion of "a limb of the body," because only that can function as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) in cases such as *ājya* (clarified butter); therefore, that same [term] is carried over here as well. In the rule *ṛcaḥ śe*, since a "limb of the body" is impossible in the context of a *ṛc* (verse), the term is taken to mean "a fourth part. As for the passage beginning with *tena* ("by that," etc.): *tena pādasya lopo 'ci* || 6.4.130 || By that, there is the elision of *pāda* before a vowel. The word *aci* means "before a vowel" (*acām madhye*). The word *lopaḥ* means "elision" (*lopyate*). The word *pādasya* means "of *pāda*. The word *tena* refers back to the aforementioned *vārttika*. The meaning is: by that aforementioned *vārttika*, there is the elision of the word *pāda* when it occurs before a vowel. For example: *dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two steps"), *tripadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives three steps"). *ṭaḥ puṃsi nā* || 6.1.103 || In the masculine, the nominative singular ending *ṭā* becomes *nā*. The word *ṭaḥ* means "of *ṭā*" (*ṭā-pratyayasya*). The word *puṃsi* means "in the masculine" (*puṃliṅge*). The word *nā* means "*nā* is substituted" (*nā-ādeśo bhavati*). The meaning is: in the masculine, the nominative singular ending *ṭā* is replaced by *nā*. For example: *dvipadikāṃ dadāti*, *tripadikāṃ dadāti*. *saṅkhyāsupūrvasya* || 5.4.140 || [The suffix *kan* is applied] after a compound whose first member is a numeral or the word *su*. The word *saṅkhyā* means "numeral" (*saṅkhyā-vācin*). The word *supūrvasya* means "preceded by *su*" (*su-śabda-pūrvasya*). The word *saṅkhyāsupūrvasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word *kan* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is: the suffix *kan* is applied after a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose first member is a numeral or the word *su*. For example: *dvau pādau prakṛtī asyāḥ* ("two feet are its base") → *dvipadikā*; *trayaḥ pādāḥ prakṛtī asyāḥ* ("three feet are its base") → *tripadikā*. *ṛcaḥ śe* || 5.4.74 || After the word *ṛc*, [the suffix *kan* is applied] in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe*). The word *ṛcaḥ* means "after the word *ṛc*. The word *śe* means "in the sense of a remainder" (*śeṣe*). The word *kan* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is: the suffix *kan* is applied after the word *ṛc* in the sense of a remainder. For example: *ekarcam*, *dvyrcam*, *tryrcam*. *chandaso nirmite* || 5.4.21 || After the word *chandas*, [the suffix *kan* is applied] in the sense of something constructed (*nirmite*). The word *chandasaḥ* means "after the word *chandas*. The word *nirmite* means "in the sense of something constructed" (*nirmite'rthe*). The word *kan* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is: the suffix *kan* is applied after the word *chandas* in the sense of something constructed. For example: *chandasā nirmitaḥ* ("constructed by meter") → *chāndasaḥ*. *matvarthe* || 5.2.94 || In the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). The word *matvarthe* means "in the sense of possession" (*matvarthe'rthe*). The word *kan* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is: the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of possession. For example: *gomān* ("possessing cows"). *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* || 5.3.1 || Before the words beginning with *prāgdiś* (5.3.1–27), [the suffixes taught there] are called case-endings (*vibhakti*). The word *prāgdiśaḥ* means "before the words beginning with *prāgdiś*. The word *vibhaktiḥ* means "case-endings" (*vibhakti-saṃjñā*). The meaning is: the suffixes taught from 5.3.1 onwards are designated as case-endings. For example: *prathamā*, *dvitīyā*, *tṛtīyā*. *avyayād āpsupaḥ* || 2.4.82 || After an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the feminine suffix *āp* and the case-endings (*sup*) are elided. The word *avyayāt* means "after an indeclinable. The word *āpsupaḥ* means "the suffix *āp* and the case-endings" (*āp-ca sup ca*). The word *lopaḥ* is understood from the previous rule. The meaning is: after an indeclinable, the suffix *āp* and the case-endings are elided. For example: *uccaiḥ*, *nīcaiḥ*. *na veti vibhāṣā* || 1.1.44 || The expression *na vā* ("or not") is called *vibhāṣā*. The word *na veti* means "the expression *na vā*. The word *vibhāṣā* means "it is called *vibhāṣā*" (*vibhāṣā-saṃjño bhavati*). The meaning is: the expression *na vā* is designated as *vibhāṣā*. For example: *vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau* (2.4.7). *iko guṇavṛddhī* || 1.1.3 || The terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* refer to the vowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ* (as well as their long forms) when they are designated as *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. The word *ikaḥ* means "of *i*-sounds" (*ikām*). The word *guṇavṛddhī* means "the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*" (*guṇaś ca vṛddhiś ca*). The meaning is: the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* refer to the vowels *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *lṛ* (and their long forms) when they are designated as *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*. For example: *dadhi* (where *i* is *guṇa*), *madhu* (where *u* is *gu

In the rule *paṇapādamāṣaśatāt*, because of the association with *paṇa* and the others which denote measures, it is the measure that is understood, not a limb of the body. [The example] *dvipādyam* [is formed] with the suffix *yat* in the sense of "bought with that" (*tena krītam*). Here too, it can be said: that which is qualified by *pāda*—namely, the *yat* belonging to *pāda*, and whatever *yat* is prescribed after *pāda*—whereas in *dvipādyam*, the suffix *yat* is prescribed after a *dvigu* compound ending in the word *pāda*.
And [the substitution of *s* for *visarga* occurs] before *himaka*, *āṣi*, and *hati*. (Pāṇini 6.3.54)

The cold that belongs to the foot is *paddhima* (foot-cold). Those who rub their feet are *patkāṣiṇaḥ*—that is, those who travel on foot; the suffix *ṇini* is applied here according to the rule *supsyajātau*. That which is struck by the two feet is *paddhatiḥ* (a path).
The word *ṛc* takes the suffix *śe*. (Pāṇini 6.3.55)

The term *śe* is an imitation of a portion of the suffix *śas*, because no other word *śa* is possible [in this context]. But is it not possible that this [suffix] occurs, as in *pādaśaḥ*—derived from the root *śī* with the locative sense "he lies in the foot"—by means of the suffix *ac*? This possibility does not exist, for no one indeed lies within a quarter-verse (*ṛkpāda*). And as for the suffix *śa* prescribed after words such as *loman*, that too is impossible for the very same reason: the word *pāda* is not included among the *loman*-type words.
Or [the elision of *a* occurs] in words mixed with sounds containing the phoneme *ghoṣa*. 6-3-56.
Regarding the term *pāṇniṣka*: the word *niṣka* denotes a species of gold, while the word *pāda* denotes a measure; thus, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The word *uda* is substituted for *udaka* when it forms part of a compound name. 6.3.57.

Regarding *udamegha*: this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). It is a name for a person based on similarity; because the father’s name is not well-known, he is designated by means of his son. [In the term] *udavāha*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of an object according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*, meaning "one who carries water. *Kṣīroda* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). On this point, some say: there is a word *uda* which has the same meaning as the word *udaka*, and it is thus employed even in names, as in *aprasannoda* ("of un-clear water"). This statement is intended to preclude the use of the word *udaka* in names. However, if this were so, the alternative option (*vikalpa*) to be stated hereafter would be rendered purposeless.
And [the elision of the final *i* of a verbal root occurs] before the suffixes *peṣam*, *vāsa*, *vāhana*, and *dhi*. Pāṇini 6.3.58.

This is for the sake of excluding the notion [of "ocean" as a common noun]. Regarding the term *udadhi*: the suffix *ki* is applied by the rule "after a verbal root, when the object or the locus is to be expressed. Here, *udadhi* refers to a jar or similar vessel; for if it referred to the sea, it would already be established by the preceding rule.
When filling out a word consisting of one syllable and so forth, [the augment *āṬ*] may optionally be applied. 6.3.59.

Regarding the phrase "one, without a companion": if this word *eka* were to denote a number, then the term *eka* would be redundant; for it is never possible for two or many to be the initial [subject]. Therefore, the word *eka* denotes being without a companion.

But even so, its exclusion [from being the first] is not possible; for how can speech be subject to each individual phoneme? For if there were a simultaneous utterance of multiple phonemes, then a word such as *sthālī* would consist of multiple consonants (*hal*) at the beginning; or if the phonemes, though uttered sequentially, were to persist [simultaneously], then too there would be "beginning-ness" due to the perception of two phonemes simultaneously. However, since there is neither simultaneous utterance nor simultaneous perception of the phonemes, therefore it is not the case that only one [phoneme] has the status of being the beginning.

If it is possible to exclude [something] by the mention of "one" (*eka*) alone, then, by the force of mentioning "one," a specific state of being without a companion (*asahāyatva*) is intended. What, then, is that? It is immediate succession (*ānantarya*). This is what he says: "by an immediate [element] of the same class. Because there is no established state of being without a companion when there is an intervention by something of a different class—due to its being of the same class in terms of being a *hal* (consonant), and due to differences in position and so forth—it has been stated thus.
And [the word *mantha* is used] in the sense of *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *vajra*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gādha*. (Pāṇini 6.3.60)

Barley meal mixed with a liquid substance is *mantha*; "barley meal with water" (*udakena manthaḥ*) is a compound formed by splitting the rule *tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). Alternatively, if *prathyate* is taken as a verbal noun (denoting the action), then the compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32); or by the rule *saktvaudanābhyām annena vyañjanam* (Pāṇini 2.1.34); or by the rule *binduvajravīvadhaiḥ ṣaṣṭhī* (Pāṇini 2.1.35) [as in] *bhārahāragāhaiḥ*, where the suffix *aṇ* is added in the sense of the object; or by the rule *upapadam atiṅ* (Pāṇini 2.2.19). [In this context], *vajra* refers to the "hardness of water," based on the observation that "that which is the hardness of waters" is so called.
Other compounds also occur according to possibility; for example: *udakavajraḥ*, "one who splits the heart like a thunderbolt," where *vajra* is used as the instrument of the action.
According to Gālava, a short vowel is substituted for an *ik* vowel when it is followed by a non-*yaṇ* vowel.

*Grāmaṇiputra*: [The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc., and the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *agrāgramābhyāṃ nayateḥ*. *Gārgīputra*: From the word *gārgya*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *yañaśca*, followed by the elision of the *y* by the rule *yasyeti ca*, and the elision of the semivowel by the rule *halastaddhitasya*. *Kārīṣagandhīputra*: There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *ṣyaṅ* suffix, and a long vowel is substituted by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*. *Kāṇḍībhūtam*: By the rule *ūryādijviḍāśca*, this receives the designation of a particle (*nipāta*), and thus functions as an indeclinable (*avyaya*). A male dancer who wears female attire is called a *puṃścalī-bhrūkuṃsaḥ*.

In the expression *ihālābukarkandhujambuphalam*, the word *phala* (fruit) occurs as the final member (*uttarapada*), and there is shortening of the vowel in *jambu*. In a *dvandva* compound where *jambu* is the final member, there is shortening of the vowel in *karkandhu*, but this does not apply to *alābu* because *karkandhu* is not the final member. If that is so, then the analysis (*vigraha*) should be constructed as follows: *alābuśca karkandhūśca* = *alābukarkandhavau*; *te ca jambūśca* = *alābukarkandhujambvaḥ*; and their fruit is *alābukarkandhujambuphalam*. Even so, [the rule applies] to *jambu*.

The rule for prior placement (pūrvanipāta) would apply. The same should be understood regarding the dual compound of *karkandhu* and *jambu*. The word *jambu* should be looked for among the *rājadantādi* group [of compounds].
The suffix *taddhita* is also [elided] when it is a single [syllable]. 6.3.62.

The term *eka* is an indeclinable (or a stem-form) reference; for if it were in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the form would already be established by the rule of masculine substitution for a feminine word (*puṃvadbhāva*). This [use of the indeclinable] is for the sake of a non-appositional meaning (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Regarding the term *ekatvam*: this word *eka* signifies "without companion" and so forth; however, in the case of a numeral, the masculine substitution is already established by the rule "of words denoting qualities, before the suffixes *tva* and *tal*" (*guṇavacanasya*). Why, then, is only the feminine form cited as an example, rather than the masculine or neuter forms as they are heard in the text? To this he replies: "of that which is qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭasya*).

The prescription of short vowels (*hrasva*) is meaningful only for that which possesses the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*), and not for the other, because the latter is already naturally (*svataḥ*) characterized by a short vowel at its end. Now, one might object: "Granted that the [stem] *arā* is naturally short-voweled at its end, but as for that initial *ai* (i.e., *ai-ara*), for its sake the inclusion of the 'other' is also meaningful. To this, he says: "aC" (*aci*).

This might be so, if the vowel (*ac*) introduced by the word *eka* in the rule *acaśca* were to qualify the word *eka*—that is, if it meant "the vowel belonging to the word *eka*, wherever it may be situated. However, in this case, the word *eka* being mentioned is qualified by the vowel (*ac*) that has been introduced [by the previous rule]: "the short vowel occurs for *eka*. [The question arises: of what kind of [vowel]? [The answer is: of a vowel that ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). In that case, according to the rule *alontyasya*, the final [vowel] would have to be shortened; and that [final vowel] is meaningful (*arthavat*) only for a feminine form ending in *ṭāp*, not for any other. The particle *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
In the case of technical names and in Vedic literature, the substitution of *ī* for *ni* and of *ū* for *nu* occurs diversely.

Because of the inclusion of the word *bahula* (in various cases), this [substitution] occurs even when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For example: *anugāyanti nayo gābhinyo* ("the three rivers flow along with pregnant women"). By taking it in this way, the justification for the counter-example *phālgunīpaurṇamāsī* is established; otherwise, in a *karmadhāraya* compound, the rule for masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) would apply. Regarding *ūrṇamradā*: it means "as soft as wool" (*ūrṇāvan mradīyasī*). The form *īyasī* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) variant of *īyas*. However, the Taittirīyas read it with a long vowel: *ūrṇāmradasaṃ cāstṛṇāmi* ("I spread out that which is soft as wool").
In the case of *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā*, [the final vowel is optionally shortened] before the suffixes *cita*, *tūla*, and *bhārin*.

Regarding the term *iṣṭakacitam*: it is a compound formed according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). Regarding *iṣīkatūlam*: it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding *mālabhāriṇī*: from the analysis *mālām bibharti*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *supsyajātau* (Pāṇini 3.2.78). However, the root *harati* is generally taught [in this context], yet the usage is of *bibharti*; thus we have forms such as *gāllikā mālabhāriṇyaḥ*. It should be understood that by means of the words *iṣṭaka* and so forth, there is also the inclusion of those ending in them. How this occurs has already been explained in the section on the non-elision of the case-ending (*alukprakaraṇa*).
The *khiti* suffix is indeclinable. 6.3.66.

By the term *ikah*, the word *acaḥ* (a vowel) is brought to mind [by the rule of proximity]. In that context, if the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) were qualified by the vowel—meaning "the vowel of the preceding member becomes short wherever it occurs"—then it would undesirably apply even in cases such as *vāṅmanya*. Therefore, the preceding member is qualified by the vowel: "of the preceding member ending in a vowel. Consequently, in cases such as *kālimmanyā*, even after the suffix *mum* has been applied, there would be no shortening because the preceding member no longer ends in a vowel; hence he says: "The shortening is not barred by *mum*."

Why is this so? To this he says: "Otherwise, indeed. This is stated: [the rule] "a short vowel for that which ends in *aj*" (Pāṇini 6.4.72) would be rendered meaningless if the *mum* augment were applied first. Therefore, the *mum* augment is not superseded by the shortening of the vowel.

But how is it that the sublation (*bādha*) of *mum* by the short vowel (*hrasva*) was suspected? For, since *mum* has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *stanandhaya*, it would rather be the sublation of [the long vowel] in *kālimmanyati* and similar forms by the short vowel itself that should be suspected. Therefore, this is the meaning: just as previously the short vowel was not sublated by *mum*, so the meaning of the rule (*sūtra*) must be described such that the short vowel is prescribed for a stem ending in a short *a* (*ajanta*), and not that the vowel belonging to the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) becomes short.

In that view, even if the *mum* augment has been applied, since the occurrence of the short vowel is still possible, there is no lack of scope [for the shortening rule]; therefore, once the *mum* has been applied, the short vowel would occur afterwards, whereas previously it would have been superseded by the *mum*. As for what was further stated—that the supersession of the *mum* itself by the short vowel should be suspected—the author will provide the resolution for this in the subsequent sūtra.

But how, then, is there the inclusion of that which ends in *khit* here, given that it has been established that in the context of subsequent members (*uttarapada*), when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends in that suffix? To this he says: "only this [term], *anvayasya*. Since the suffix *khit* is prescribed only after a verbal root (*dhātu*), a suffix ending in *khit* cannot occur after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Therefore, the meaning is that because of the prohibition regarding indeclinables, there is here an inclusion of that which ends in it.
The augment *mum* is added after the final vowel of a word ending in *ar*, *dviṣat*, or a word whose final member ends in *ac*, when followed by a word beginning with a vowel.

Regarding *aruntuda*: by the rule *vidhvaruṣostudaḥ*, the suffix *khaś* is applied; because it belongs to the *tud*-class, the suffix *śa* is added. When the augment *mum* is inserted before the *s*, there is elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the *s*. Regarding *dviṣantapa*: by the rule *dviṣatparayostāpe*, the suffix *khac* is applied. In the presence of *khac*, the vowel is shortened (*hrasva*), and the *mum* augment and so forth are as before. Regarding *vidvanmanya*: by the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsu*, the substitution of *d* occurs; then, by the rule *yaro'nunāsike'nunāsiko vā*, the preceding *n* may optionally become a nasalized substitute.

The mention of "the end" (*anta*) would be redundant, since the rule for "that which ends in it" (*tadantavidhi*) applies everywhere when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned; therefore, he says "the mention of the end," and so forth. The word *anta* signifies proximity; thus, "ending in a vowel" (*ajanta*) means that which is both a vowel (*ac*) and at the end (*anta*). The inversion of the qualifier [to place it after the qualified] occurs by way of a formal exception (*nipātana*).

But what is this short vowel (*hrasva*) prescribed in the preceding rule, by which there is an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to the prior member? What is meant is this: *mum* is applied to that which ends in the short vowel prescribed in the preceding rule, which is proximate to this present rule; for it is only when the shortening has been effected that *mum* occurs. By this, the following objection is also refuted: that *mum* itself would be subject to sublation by the shortening. How so? Because *mum* is caused by that [shortening]; indeed, this *mum* occurs precisely because the short vowel is its cause.

If this is so, then in cases such as *sthandila*, where a short vowel is not applied, the *mum* augment would not apply. What, then, is the reason that a short vowel is not applied here? Because there is no purpose [for it]. But there is a purpose: so that the *mum* may occur. For it was just stated: "The *mum* is caused by a short vowel."
In this [section], for a monosyllabic stem ending in /i/ or /u/, the substitution of /īy/ and /ūy/ respectively occurs as before, and it is treated like the suffix *am*.

"The augment *am* occurs. How does this [augment] possess the status of an "augment" (*āgama*)? Because it has the designation *mit*. If this is so, then the letter *m*, having the technical name *it*, would not be heard in actual usage—as in *śriyammanyaḥ* and *bhruvammanyaḥ*—for there is no hearing of this *m*; rather, it is the *mum* [augment] that is heard. But surely, since this augment is introduced when the *mum* has not yet applied, it should supersede that; it would not supersede it. For it was stated in that regard: "The mention of the 'end' (*anta*) is for the purpose of understanding that the operations pertaining to what ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) have already been performed"; therefore, it will also apply in this present case.

We, however, say this: this *m* which is designated as *it* is not [the substitute *am*], because of the prohibition "not in a case-ending (*vibhakti*) after *t* or *s*" regarding its treatment as if it were the suffix *am*. If that were so, the substitution would apply; yet it will remain subsequent [to the word] by virtue of its treatment as the suffix *am*. The designation as an "augment" (*āgama*), however, is etymological, meaning "that which comes near," just as in the rule "not after *eC* ending in *y* or *v* at the end of a word. Alternatively, the second *m* should be understood as having been elided and thus not explicitly stated due to the elision of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

If only "provided there is a suffix having a marker" (*pratyayavat*) were stated here [in Pāṇini 1.4.10], then in the case of *gāmmanyaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *auto 'mśasoḥ* would not occur, because in that rule the *am* is understood as being accompanied by *śas*. Furthermore, in the case of *strīmmanyaḥ*, the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute) by the rule *ami pūrvaḥ* would not occur, because the phrase *prathamayoḥ* is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule. And in the case of *narammanyaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ* would not occur, because when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of a general property, there is no extension of its specific instances.

For where there is an extension (*atideśa*) by means of a general term (*sāmānya-śabda*), since specific instances are not the direct meaning of that word, the grammatical operation (*kārya*) is obtained as being based solely on the general property; for example, in the injunction "one should behave toward this Kṣatriya as toward a Brāhmaṇa," the operation prompted by the category of "Brāhmaṇa" in general is extended, but not the operation prompted by specific individuals such as Māṭhara. Thinking that in the present case as well, the extension would apply only to *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, which are prompted by the suffix (*pratyaya*) in general, and not to [the vowels] beginning with *ā*, he says: "The *am* [augment] is like the suffix (*pratyayavat*) when *ec* follows."

He explains this very point with the words: "and like the second singular. Now, one might object: if the mention of the single case-ending *am* here refers to the augment (*āgama*), then the suffix (*pratyaya*) would not be specified; conversely, if the suffix were being specified, the augment would not be mentioned. To this he says: "For [the word] *am*," and so forth.

But surely, even on this view, there would be an extension (*atideśa*) only of the *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) and the *pūrvatvam* (the single-substitute operation) which are occasioned by the suffix *ām*, and not of the *guṇa* (vocalization) whose sole cause is the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, much less of the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions whose causes are the suffixes alone. This would indeed be so, if the extension applied only to that which is specifically prescribed for the case of *ām*. We, however, extend everything that is observed in the presence of *ām*, whether it be based on general conditions or specific ones.

Regarding the term *tvanmanya*: here, one would expect *tvacammanya*, according to those for whom there is only one *m* [in the suffix], on the view that this [suffix] behaves like a *pratyaya*. For those for whom there is a second [m], an *am* would follow after the vowel (*ac*). However, for those for whom the *m* is designated as having the technical name *it*, it should be considered: what fault is there even if it follows the syllable (*akṣa*)? Now, one might think: "It will not occur here simply because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of *aj*; for the separate continued application of a compound is difficult to discern. [The example is] *lekhābhrumanya*, where, as before, there is shortening and the addition of the augment *mum*.

Now, regarding the passage beginning with *athaha* and so forth: in the Bhāṣya, starting from *atheha katham*, it is established—meaning settled—that [the form] should be *śrimanyam*. Therefore, one should not suspect that there are different authors [for the two parts]. Now, an objection is raised: since the word *śrī* is feminine, how can the form *śrimanyam* be correct? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the justification with the words *taccedam*.

For some words, when functioning in a different meaning, operate by abandoning their own gender; for example, words such as *yaṣṭī* (staff), *pracarī* (carrying-pole), and *gaṇikā* (courtesan) function in the feminine due to association with a male (*puṃyoga*). Others, however, retain their own gender, as in the command: "Bring in the men who are staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ puruṣān praveśaya*). In this context, the first type is intended by the author of the Bhāṣya; thus, when the elision of *am* occurs according to the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, the form *śrīmanyam* results.

If this is so, then by extension (*atideśa*), the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* would also apply here, since that [elision] is also observed before the ending *am*. Now, if it is argued that because of the force of the prescription of *am*, there is no extension of this elision, then the elision prescribed by *svamornapuṃsakāt* would likewise not occur. To this it is replied: either by the principle *yena nāprāpte* ("that which applies when another is already applicable"), or by the principle *madhye'pavādāḥ* ("exceptions [occur] in the middle"), the prescription of the elision of *sup* by *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* prevails by virtue of its own force, and thus subverts [the elision] of *svamornapuṃsakāt*, but not that of *am*.

Even so, because they both depend on a single word (*ekapadāśrayatva*), the elision (*luk*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the augment *am* is external (*bahiraṅga*) by the opposite principle. Thus, when the internal elision must take effect, the external augment *am* simply does not exist; how then could the rule regarding external elements (*bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*) be invoked here to prevent the elision? For otherwise, even the *anusvāra* would not occur in forms such as *aruntudaḥ* and *dviṣantapaḥ*. Therefore, when the elision occurs here, the form becomes *śrimanyam*. However, for those who hold that the letter *m* in *am* is marked with the *itsaṃjñā* (and thus elided), while the *mum* augment is heard in actual usage, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the *mum* augment after the mere vowel *a* has been elided.
And [the forms] *vācaṃyama* and *purandara*. 6.3.69.

Regarding *vācaṃyama*: the suffix *khac* is applied by the rule *vāci yamo vrate*. Regarding *puraṃdara*: the suffix *khac* is applied by the rule *pūḥsarvayordārisahoḥ*, and the vowel is shortened. In both cases, the fact that the preceding member ends in the suffix *am* is established as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
The substitution of *kāra* occurs for the final vowel of *satya* and *agada* before a suffix beginning with *k*.

*Satyaṅkāraḥ*: the making of a pledge or agreement (*samayakaraṇam*). Even though there is no oath (*aśapatha*), because it refers to another [action], the suffix *ḍāc* is set aside, and only the suffix *kāra* with the augment *muṭ* occurs; thus, *taāgadaṅkāraḥ* is the preparation of a specific substance that counteracts poison (*viṣapratipakṣadravyaviṣeṣakaraṇam*). *Bhakṣaṅkāraḥ*: the performance of the consumption of substances in a particular sacrifice (*yāgaviśeṣe dravyabhakṣaṇasya karaṇam*). Alternatively, *bhakṣaṅkāraḥ* means "one who performs the eating" (*bhakṣaṅkaroti*), formed with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of an agent (*kartari*).
Regarding *dhenumbhavyā*: a cow that is yet to be (or will be) a cow is so called; here the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *bhavyageya*.
"Fill the world" (*lokam apṛṇa*). The root *pṛṇoti* has the sense of filling; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for the class beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.

"Not approaching" (*anabhyāśamitya*): by the rule *eti-stu-śāsu-* etc., the suffix *kyap* is applied—meaning that which is to be approached (*etavya*) or reached (*itya*). "Anabhyāśam" means "far away.
Thus, *anabhyāśamityaḥ* refers to one who is to be avoided from afar.

*bhrāṣṭram indhaḥ* (one who kindles a frying pan) and *agnim indhaḥ* (one who kindles fire). [The former is formed] with the suffix *aṇ* after an object [of the action], or it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*.

*Timiṅgila*: a specific kind of fish. [The form is derived] from *timiṃ gilati* ("it swallows a *timi*") as before with the suffix *ka*, and the substitution of *i* for *ī*. By the rule *aci vibhāṣā*, there is optionally the substitution of *la* for *ra*. *Timiṅgilagila*: this too is indeed a specific kind of fish.

Regarding *gilagila*: when it is derived as "one who swallows a *gila*" (*yadā gilaṃ gilati iti gilagilaḥ*), namely *timiṅgilagila*, then this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) is required. However, when it is derived as "one who swallows a *timiṅgila*" (*yadā hi timiṅgilaṃ gilati iti timiṅgilagilaḥ*), then there is no need for this. [Examples such as] *uṣṇaṅkaraṇam* and *bhadraṅkaraṇam* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Regarding *putraḍ vā*: the letter *ḍ* is for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
As for the words beginning with "some, however" (*kecittu*): according to their view, this supplementary rule need not be commenced.
By the words "for even elsewhere," etc., he confirms the very reading of the *śārṅgaravādi* group; others, however, do not accept the reading of the *śārṅgaravādi* group.
The suffix *ñya* is applied after the words *śyena* and *tila* when they signify falling (*pāta*).

Regarding the expression *śyenapāto 'syāṃ kriyāyām* ("the hawk’s swoop occurs in this [action]"): although the mention of "action" (*kriyā*) in the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam* (Pāṇini 3.3.18)—which extends the application of *ghañ*-derived forms—is a qualifier of the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) and not the meaning of the suffix itself, as evidenced by the example *śyenapātā tithiḥ* ("the lunar day on which the hawk’s swoop occurs"), nevertheless, since the feminine gender alone is the meaning of the suffix in the form *asyām*, it is not contradictory for the action also to be the meaning of the suffix. Thus, *śyainampāta*: "swooping" is *pāta*; "the swoop of a hawk" is a genitive compound with the agentive case; from that, the suffix *ñ* is applied according to *ghañarthe kavidhānam*.
The suffix *kṛt* is optionally applied after the word *rātri*.

Regarding the phrase "the *kṛt*-suffix ending is the final member (*uttarapada*)": although a *kṛt*-suffix such as *tṛc* can immediately follow the word *rātri* when it ends in the *kvip* suffix used in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*), nevertheless, because that [secondary] meaning is figurative (*gauṇa*), it is not included. Thus, by implication, even under the governing rule for the "final member," there occurs here an interpretation of the term as referring to the whole ending in that suffix (*tadantavidhi*). *rātriṣcaraḥ*: "he who wanders at night. [This is formed] with the suffix *ṭa* after the root *car* [meaning "to wander"] when preceded by *rātri*. *rātrimāṭaḥ*: "one who wanders through the night. [The analysis is: *aṭaḥ* means "one who wanders" (from the root *aṭ* with the suffix *ac*, belonging to the *pacādi* class). The compound is formed according to the rule *sādhanaṃ kṛtā*. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [the previous rule] was not otherwise applicable.

But is it not the case that this option (*vibhāṣā*) is appropriate in both instances—since [the suffix] *khid* applies in cases such as *rātrimmanyā*, where [the rule for *mum*] has already been reached, and it does not apply elsewhere? To this he says: "For when there is *khid*, *mum* necessarily occurs. The intention is that this is by way of a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).
There is elision of the *n* of the negative particle *nañ*.

The mention of *nañ* includes that which has an *anubandha*, so that [the rule] *pāmādibhyo naḥ*—as in *pāmanaputra* and so forth—does not apply. Now, even if the mention of the form with the *anubandha* were made, why would it not apply in the case of *straiṇaputra*? Because the *ṅit*-ness [of the suffix] has already served its purpose in [triggering] *vṛddhi* and accentuation, whereas the *ṅit*-ness of the *nipātana* [suffix] has not yet served its purpose. Alternatively, *nañ* is qualified by the preceding word; thus, because it is not a preceding word [in this case], it will not apply. And having done this, there is no need even to utter the *anubandha*; for precisely because it is not a preceding word, it will not apply in *pāmanaputra*.

Regarding the rule *avakṣepe tiṅi*: "avakṣepa" means censure. Although the elision [of the *na*] would be established by either the rule *naño 'śiti* or *naño 'niti*, they say that the explicit statement of the elision is for the sake of including cases where the suffix *kā* is present (*sākackārtham*).
Therefore, *nuṭ* [is inserted] before a vowel. (Pāṇini 6.3.74)

For it would indeed occur right there [in the word *nañ* itself], because of the rule stating "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*) when that [word] is specifically indicated. Furthermore, if the augment *nuṭ* were applied to *nañ*, an undesirable form would result; thus, the prescription for the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would be intended for cases other than those beginning with *nañ*. Therefore, since the mention of *nañ* exists, the ablative indication (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) takes precedence, and the operation occurs only for what follows. [Objection: But if it were to occur only there, one should have prohibited the elision of *n* by saying "not after *a*" (*nāci*). That statement, however, will apply only to the subsequent member of the compound.

Therefore, it should be stated as follows: since the augment *nuṭ* is introduced before the elision of *n* has taken effect, it would sublate that elision; however, when the mention of *at* is present, the elision of *n* becomes the very cause for the *nuṭ*.

"Why was this [the *ṅamuṭ* augment] not placed at the beginning of the rule itself? For in that case, it would belong to the negative particle (*nañ*) alone, and thus there would be no such fault. To this, he replies: "In that regard, this is also the meaning: in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau*, one should remove *tadoḥ* and instead employ the term *toḥ* as a reference to the entire class of consonants (*vargagrahaṇa*). For if it were placed at the end of the rule, as in *karoti* in the example *anena karoti*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *ṅamuṭ* augment applying even to the *n* of *nuṭ*; therefore, a reference to the entire class is impossible. To this, he says: 'If it were at the beginning of the rule, the *ṅamuṭ* would apply.'"

The intention is that the elision of *n* (by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*) does not occur here due to the force of the specific injunction [of the augment *nuṭ*]. Even in this view, the following must be stated: since the augment *nuṭ* is introduced when the elision of *n* has not yet taken effect, it should be the sublater (*bādhaka*) of that elision.
In the words *nabhrāj*, *naptṛ*, *nava*, *veda*, *anas*, *satya*, *anṛca*, *nakula*, *nakha*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *naga*, and *nāka*, the initial *a* remains as its original form (*prakṛtyā*).

Regarding *nabhrāṭ*: by the rule beginning with *bhrājabhāsa-*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; *vraścādi-* applies *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*), followed by *jaśtva*—which is the letter *ḍ*; then, according to the option provided by *vāvasāne*, [it becomes *ṭ*].

*cartvam* refers to the substitution of *ṭ* for *t*. Regarding the statement that *pāt* ends in a present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), [it is argued that] *tanūnapāt* is mentioned, and since forms such as *apānnapāt* are seen even when not neuter, and because it is stated in the rule *ubhe vanaspatyādiṣu* that the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *pā-* with the elision of the penultimate vowel (*tug*) by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), this reading [of *pāt*] is incorrect. The correct reading is that *pād* ends in *kvip*. Alternatively, after the phrase "ending in a present participle suffix," one must supply the words "it should not be considered by men. As for the statement that it is an *auṇādika* suffix *ki*, it is by the rule *igupadhātkiḥ*.
*Kam* means happiness; *akam* means suffering. That which does not have these is *nāka*, namely heaven (*svarga*).
That happiness which is not overwhelmed by suffering, nor immediately swallowed up by it,
and which is brought about by desire, has heaven as its locus.

Thus they recite. Here, since there is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) for the three beginning with the neuter, those should be accepted exactly as they are. In other cases, however, one should simply state that the negative particle (*nañ*) is applied according to the original form of the final member alone. This being established, the reading of the entire compound is for the purpose of including well-known usage. Consequently, *nāsatyau* occurs only in reference to the Aśvins; elsewhere, it is simply *anasatyau*. In other instances as well, this should be understood accordingly. *ekādiścaikasya cāduK* (Pāṇini 6.3.76).

"Ekādi" (one, etc. is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The word "ādi" (etcetera) expresses a fixed limit. Regarding the term "ekānnaviṃśati" (nineteen): first, one should form a compound of the negative particle *nañ* with "viṃśati" and the like, and subsequently, a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) should be made.

But for what purpose is this [augment] *āduṭ* applied at the beginning (*pūrvānta*)? Why not apply *rāduṭ* at the end (*parādi*) instead? [If it were so], then the instruction "of one" (*ekasya*) would not need to be stated, because the negative particle (*nañ*) itself would already be understood as the subject under discussion. To this he says: "And this is at the beginning. In the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā*, the term *padāntāt* (from the end of a word) is carried over from the preceding rule *na padāntāṭ ṭoranām*. This is so that [the substitution] does not occur in cases such as *avidhnaḥ* and *badhnāti*.

If *parād* were present, the letter *d* would not be at the end of a word, and thus the nasalization (*anunāsika*) would not occur. Alternatively, if *anuṭ* were applied, even then there would be no hearing of the letter *d* in the word *patre*. This is why it was stated: "so that the nasalization may optionally occur. For what purpose is *purād* applied? Why not simply apply *adug*? In that case, [the form] would be established by the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*). Furthermore, the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* would not occur due to the very force of the pronunciation of the vowel *ā*; if it were to occur, he would have prescribed *duk* alone.

The formation of a long vowel of the same kind (*savarṇadīrghatva*), however, will occur by virtue of the maxim: "A rule whose teaching is otherwise purposeless with respect to a particular operation [is superseded]. Nevertheless, the author of the *Vṛtti* has explained it as *ādguṇa* for the sake of brevity in comprehension.

The word *naga* [is formed] from the root *gam* with the suffix *hap*, optionally when it does not refer to living beings; this is because the rule for the suffix *hap* after *gam* is seen elsewhere as well, even outside the specific section on the suffix *ḍa*.
The word *sahasya* [is substituted] for *saha* when it occurs in a compound with a word denoting a name (*saṃjñā*). 6.3.78.

Regarding the word *sahayudhvā*: the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *yudh* by the rule *rājani yudhi kṛñaḥ sahe ca*, and the substitution of *sa* for *saha* is prescribed. It is stated that this [substitute] is prescribed as acute (*udātta*). To address the question of what would otherwise occur, he says: "For [the substitute] of that which possesses both acute and grave [accents]. In the word *saha*, since particles are acute on the first syllable, the sound *sa* is acute; by the principle of the remainder being grave (*śeṣanighāta*), the sound *ha* is grave. Thus, it possesses both acute and grave accents. If [the substitute] were to take its place, the sound *sa* would become circumflex (*svarita*) due to proximity (*āntarya*). To prevent this defect, it is prescribed as acute.

If this were so, then even in an *avyayībhāva* compound, that very [substitute] would be heard as acute; to this he says: "And that" (*sa ca*). This is the intended meaning: when the compound has been formed, both the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*) and this substitute (*ādeśa*) apply. Therein, because it is subsequent, once this substitute has been produced as acute, the accent of the compound applies again by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). And since that [compound accent] is "left over" (*satiśiṣṭa*), it alone is what is heard.

However, regarding the accentuation of the *udātta* [on the first member], it is heard only in those instances where, in a *bahuvrīhi* or *tatpuruṣa*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member—namely, in *seṣṭi* and *sapaśubandha*. When expressing the sense of "ending with," it is an *avyayībhāva* compound.
And [the elision of *n* occurs] when there is an addition at the end of a word. 6.3.79.

Regarding the word *sakala*: *kalā* refers to a specific division of time, and the literary work associated with it is also called *kalā*. The same applies to the term *samuhūrta*. Regarding *sasaṃgraha*: this was written here by mistake, for the retention of the *sa-* sound is already established by the rule to be stated later, *avyayībhāve cākāle*. [The rule applies] when the final member (*uttarapada*) denotes time.

Although words such as *kāla* refer to the texts associated with them, nevertheless, because their status as referring to the text is understood through the employment of another word, namely *adhīta*, that [textual] reference is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*). Thus, it is thought that there would be a prohibition based solely on time.

Regarding *sadroṇa*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound formed by the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge*. Since the option provided by the rule *tena vopasarjanasya* would apply here, this statement is made for the purpose of making it obligatory.
And [the same applies] to the second [person], which is indefinable. 6.3.80.

That which is subordinate is called "the second" (*dvitīya*), because in common worldly usage the word *dvitīya* is employed in that very sense; for between a master and a servant, the servant is said to be "the second" in relation to the master, and not vice versa. The explanation of the term "is recounted" (*upākhyāyate*) is: "it is perceived through direct perception" (*pratyakṣeṇopalabhyate*). [This occurs] in the sense of the suffix *-ghañ*.

Regarding the rule *kavidhānam*: here *ka* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding *sāgni*: this is a bahuvrīhi compound as before; this statement is also for the sake of establishing a permanent rule. By the phrase "fire and so forth," he demonstrates the lack of perceptible evidence (*anupākhyatva*); if a pigeon should strike the house, then fire is inferred by means of that pigeon. Furthermore, there is a report that a *rakṣas* or a *piśāca* dwells within lightning and wind.
In an *avyayībhāva* compound, [the word following] a preposition (*upasarga*) retains its original accent, provided it does not denote time.

Regarding the term *akālavācinī* ("not denoting time"): this is not a reference to the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). This is because of the inclusion of the word "text" (*grantha*) in the rule *granthāntādhike ca*; for that [inclusion] is for the purpose of ensuring the application in cases such as *samuhūrtam*. If there were a reference to the word-form here, then since there would be no prohibition regarding *muhūrta* and so on, that [rule] would be rendered useless, as the desired result would already be established by this very [present] rule. *Sacakram*: an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*). *Sapuram*: the suffix *a* (short *a*) is added at the end of the compound according to the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*. *Sahapūrvāhvam*: an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of totality (*sākalya*).
The final vowel of a word that is not a subordinate member (upasarjana) [is replaced by the *ṅīp* suffix].

If this [rule] regarding the *upasarjana* were applied to the word *saha* when it functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then it would also apply in cases such as *sahayudhvā* and *sahakṛttavā*; furthermore, the qualification would be purposeless. Moreover, since the word *saha* denotes a non-substantial entity (*asattvavācin*), a *dvandva* compound is not possible with it. In other compounds as well, *saha* is indeed the *upasarjana*. Therefore, this is understood to be a qualification of the compound itself, which is brought to mind by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Even in that case, it applies by way of its constituent parts.

Since there is no designation of "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*) for the compound as a whole, in every compound some constituent part is necessarily subordinate. When it is stated, "of the subordinate member," this is understood by way of all its constituent parts; thus it is said: "of every subordinate member. In the phrase "of that constituent part" (*tadavayavasya*), he shows that the genitive case expresses a relationship with a constituent part (*avayavayoga*). In the example *sahakṛtvapriya*, there is an optional placement of the word *priya* at the beginning according to the rule *vā priyasya*.

The meaning is as follows: "In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which is the final member (*uttarapada*)"—because of the governing rule concerning the final member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), and because the *bahuvrīhi* where all elements are subordinate (*sarvopasarjana*) is what is being relied upon—it is intended that the word *saha*, when immediately preceding such a related final member, must undergo the change to *sa*. Thus, the word *saha* does not occur in that position [immediately preceding the final member].
In the former case, it does not occur because of the intervention by the word *kṛtva*; in the latter case as well, the subsequent member is the compound *sahakṛtvā*, not the word *kṛtva*.
The genitive case is used in place of the sixth case after the words *prakṛti*, *āśis*, *śiṣya*, *go*, *vatsa*, and *hala*.

The sūtra is simply *prakṛtyā āśiṣi*; the remainder has been read as a sūtra based on the observation of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika. Although one could have said *na*, the use of the word *prakṛti* is for the sake of variety.
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *samāna* occurs for the word *saha* when it is followed by words beginning with *mūrdhan*, *prabhṛti*, or *udarka*. (Pāṇini 6.3.84)

Regarding the statement "there is a separation of the *yoga* (sūtra) for the word *samānasya*," another says: there exists a word *saha* meaning "similar" (*sadṛśa*), as in the example "one who is similar to a friend is a *sasakhi*. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose analysis is not contained within its own constituent members (*asvapadavigraha*): "that which has a common property (*samāno dharmaḥ asya*)," "that which has a common side (*samānaḥ pakṣaḥ asya*)," or "that which has a common genus (*samānā jātiḥ asya*)," whereby the substitution of *sa-* [for *samāna-*, by Pāṇini 6.3.84] occurs when it is an upasarjana. However, for the word *samāna-* itself, forms such as *samānajātīya-* and so forth arise. But if there were a separation of the *yoga*, this would not be established because that [substitution] is obligatory. Therefore, the separation of the *yoga* is not mentioned in either the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*.

In the case of words meaning light, a country, night, the navel, a name, a lineage, a form, a station, color, age, speech, or a kinsman, [the final vowel and the preceding consonant, if any, take the udātta accent]. 6.3.85.

Regarding the term *sajyotis*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has the same light" (*samānaṃ jyotirasya*). When impurity (*āśauca*) follows a person from sunset until the disappearance of that very light—whether that light be the sun or a lunar mansion—it is called *sajyotis*. The form [of the compound] is derived through the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for words of identical form. Furthermore, because of the specific mention of *sa-sthānena* in the rule *sthānāntādvibhāṣā*, this substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs even in a *bahuvrīhi*, and not only in the *tatpuruṣa* compounds explicitly mentioned in the rule *pūrvāparaprathamacaramajaghanyasamāna...*.
The suffix *caraṇa* is applied after the word *brahmacārin*. || 6 - 3 - 86 ||

The word *caraṇa* is primarily used for specific Vedic branches such as the Kaṭha and Kalāpa, and secondarily for the persons who study them. Here, the primary sense is intended—the term *sabrahmacārī* meaning "one who has the same *brahmacarya*. The meaning is that he practices or follows that [Vedic branch]. The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of a religious vow (*vrata*), thus forming the word *brahmacārī*. Having thus analyzed the word *brahmacārī*, and desiring to etymologically explain the word *sabrahmacārī*, he states the meaning of the word *samāna*: "Because it is similar to that very Brahman. The phrase "of that very" refers to what was mentioned previously.

The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the commonality (*sāmānyatva*) of those practicing the religious life (*brahmacārin*) is what is intended to be expressed, therefore this meaning of the term *sabrahmacārin* which is about to be stated follows. He demonstrates that very point with the words: "in the same *brahman*" (*samāne brahmaṇi*). "In the same" means "in common" (*sādhāraṇa*). The meaning is: those two for whom a vow has been prescribed at one time by one teacher for the purpose of studying a single branch of the Veda (*eka-śākhā*) are called *sabrahmacārin*s in relation to each other.

And this is obtained from the mention of *caraṇa* (foot); for that [mention] was made so that [the rule] might apply when the *caraṇa* is identical, but not in cases such as *ākāra* and so forth. Thus, even in the case of the expression "when the *caraṇa* is understood," the meaning should be seen as "when it is understood by way of being identical in its *caraṇa*."
In the case of [words ending in] *tīrtha*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after those [words denoting a patronymic] which [are used in the sense of a descendant]. (Pāṇini 4.1.87)

Regarding the phrase "vibhāṣodare" (optionally [substituted] for *udara*): "ending in the suffix *ya*" means that in the preceding rule, by the mention of *ye*, there is the inclusion of a suffix beginning with the letter *y*. That which has such a suffix (*ya*) at its end or in its vicinity is described as such. In that context, when the substitution of *sa-* occurs, it is *sodarādyaḥ*; but when it does not occur, it is *samānodare śayitaḥ* (one who lies in the same womb), formed with the suffix *yat*.
In the case of words ending in *dṛś* and *dṛk*, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] before the words *vat* and *uṣ*. (Pāṇini 6.3.89)
"The inclusion of the term *vat* is for the sake of what follows," because [the suffix] is impossible in the case of a word that is identical (*samānaśabda*).
Regarding "and in *dṛkṣe*," some say this is Vedic; however, since *sadṛkṣam* is not cited as an example in the Bhāṣya, on that view the suffix *ksa* also occurs only in the Veda.
The word *kimoriśkī* [is formed with the suffix *ka*] according to Pāṇini 6.3.90.

Regarding the phrase *iyān kiyān*: when the substitution of *iy* for *ghas* has been made, by the rule *yasyeti ca*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. [One might ask: "Is this [the suffix] *vatup*? [The answer is: by the rule *kim-id-ambhyo vo ghaḥ*, [the suffix] *vatup* is indeed intended here. The sense is that since the letter *v* of the non-existent *vatup* cannot be prescribed as *gh*, the prescription of *vatup* itself must also be understood through this very rule.
[The substitution of *a* occurs] for the final vowel of a pronominal stem. 6.3.91.

Therefore, the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is for the sake of the *guṇa* [substitution]; let there not be the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). However, the prescription of the vowel *a* would serve to eliminate the final [element], whereas in the case of prescribing elision (*lopa*), there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).
The suffixes *adrī* and *añcatu* are substituted for the words *viṣvak* and *deva*, respectively, when the suffix *vapra* follows.

The suffix *vap* is called the *vap*-suffix because it begins with *va*. Regarding *viṣvadryaṅ*: from the root *añc*, with the *kvip* suffix, there is elision [of the final consonant]; then, by the rule *ugidacām*, the *num* augment is added; there is the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*); and by the rule *kvinpratyayasya kuḥ*, the *kutva* change occurs—the *na* becomes *ṅa*. Regarding *adrisadhryaḥ*: since the Vārttika is general in application, the word *sadhra* is included here. [In the case of] *aśvācī*, meaning "one who goes toward horses," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *añcateścopasaṃkhyānam*; there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*; and lengthening occurs by the rule *cau*. Regarding *viṣvagyuk*: [it means] "one who joins everywhere"; the *kvip* suffix is applied by the rule *satsṛdvipa-* etc. Regarding *viṣvagañcanam*: this is the suffix *lyuṭ*.

How could there be this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) here, given that it is stated [in the rule] "when there is a subsequent member" (*uttarapade*), and in this case *añcati* is not the subsequent member, but rather ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*? Furthermore, there is no rule for extending [an operation] to what begins with that (*tadādividhi*). [The author] says "the mention of the suffix *vap*" because the extension to what begins with that occurs only when there is the mention of the letter *al*. If, upon the mention of a verbal root (*dhātu*), there were no extension to what begins with it, the mention of the suffix *vap* would be unnecessary; however, since it is mentioned, it indicates that there is such an extension. He states the purpose of this here: "by that," as in the example *apaskṛtam*.
If, however, the [suffix] were not taught for the purpose of making known [the formation], then it would apply only in cases such as *ayaskṛt* where *kṛt* alone is the final member;

for example, *viśvācī* and *dhṛtācī*. This Vedic reading has been shown, but *pṛtācī* is not cited as an example because there is no possibility of its occurrence. By means of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "in the feminine" (*striyām*), we have *nāryaḥ*; for even in the masculine, the substitution of *adri* is sometimes not observed. Therefore, [we have] *vipvañcau* and *prāthaṇāpānau*. As for *kavrīcī*: the substitution of *adri* occurs for the final syllable of the word *kim*, and as before, there is the addition of *ṅīp*, elision, lengthening, and so forth.
The word *tiras* [retains its accent] when the suffix *lyap* is elided. 6.3.95.
When its elision does not occur; however, the meaning "when there is elision of the letter *a*" does not apply, because of the [authoritative] commentary.
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *sādhā* for *saha* occurs when it is followed by a word ending in the locative case or the suffix *māda*. (Pāṇini 6.3.96)

Some say that *sadhamāda* means "glorious" (*dyumni*). In this mantra, the word *dyumnir* and so forth are adjectives qualifying the waters, and *sadhamāda* is also in grammatical apposition with them, being a nominative form derived from the root *mad* with the suffix *kvip*. In Vedic usage, the substitution of *sadh-* for *māda-* is seen frequently—for instance, in such passages as "May the great bay horses, having been harnessed, bring thee hither, O Indra, to the *sadhamāda*" (*ā tvā vṛhanto harayo yujānā arvāg indra sadhamādo vahantu*).

Another says: *mada* means intoxication; although the rule "the suffix *ghañ* occurs after *mad* when there is no prefix" applies here, the form *ghañ* is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). That which exists together with that [intoxication] is called *sadhamāda*. However, in expressions such as *revatīsthaḥ sadhamādaḥ*, *sadhamāda* refers to the sacrifice, based on the derivation: "in this [sacrifice], the gods rejoice together."
The substitution of *ī* for *ap* occurs after the words *dvi*, *antara*, and those beginning with a prefix (*upasarga*).

In the examples, the analysis [of the compound] is "in this, waters have gone twice," and so forth; the suffix *a* is applied according to the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*. Regarding the name *samāpa*: since the substitution of *ī* is prohibited, the lengthening of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*. Another says: there is the use of the word *sama* here; thus, *samāpa* means "in which waters are equal" (*samā āpo 'smin*).

Regarding the phrase "apśabdam pratītyādi": here, those particles (*prādayaḥ*) which are connected with an action possess the status of *upasargas* (prepositions); however, the word *ap* does not denote an action. Therefore, it is understood that the mention of *upasarga* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those particles whose status as *upasargas* is established elsewhere.
In the sense of "in the direction of," [the seventh case ending is used] after words meaning "ūrdhva" and "ūrdhvam. (Pāṇini 6.3.98)
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the *avagraha*": that is the *avagraha*, wherein the forms of the constituent members of a compound are displayed by the makers of the *pada-pāṭha*.

The substitution of *du* for the final vowel of a word ending in *anyat*, provided it does not stand in the sixth or third case, occurs before the words *āśis*, *āśā*, *āstha*, *sthita*, *utsuka*, *atikāra*, *kara*, *rāga*, and *cheka*. (Pāṇini 6.3.99)

In the case of *udāra* and similar words, there is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). It should be understood that in the list beginning with *gaha*, the word *anya* (other) is to be supplied; this is because those [words] have not been included in the *vṛtti*. Regarding the statement "the augment *duk* is applied without distinction," etc.: when the suffix *cha* follows, the augment *duk* must be applied generally and without distinction. In what kind of *cha*? In one accompanied by a term denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka*), meaning in a *cha* suffix that occurs after a word expressing a *kāraka*. In the reading *kārakacchayoḥ*, the latter member is placed first because the rule governing the prior placement [of the *kāraka* term] is non-obligatory. As for the other seven [suffixes], such as *āśīḥ* and so on, the sixth and third cases are not desired; the meaning is that the prohibition applies only to those [seven].

He asks, "How is this obtained? and replies: *asya ca*. Although the rule would have been established simply by saying "not standing in the sixth or third case," the repetition of the negative particle (*nañ*) is for the purpose of making known that this prohibition is not universal (*anityatva*); furthermore, this is the method of explanation. For it could indeed be said that the repetition of the negative particle is for the sake of strengthening the rule. [The rule continues: *koḥ kat tatpuruṣe 'ci* (Pāṇini 6.3.101).

In the examples [of *udāra* and *haṇa*], the compound is formed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*. Regarding *kūṣṭra*: this very mention of the *tatpuruṣa* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in this section, even a compound not explicitly prescribed [by a specific rule] is included; therefore, by the rule *jyotirjanapada*, the substitution of *sabhāva* occurs even in a *bahuvrīhi*.
As for the statement "there should be an addition regarding *trā*": it is established by the rule *katryādibhyaḥ*.
The [suffix] *ka* is applied after [the verbal roots] *path* and *akṣ*. (Pāṇini 6.3.104)

An undertaking that lacks purpose is "anīṣadartha. A contemptible path is "kāpatha"; the compound suffix is applied as in the previous case. Regarding the term "kākṣa": it is either a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the word *akṣa*, or a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *akṣi*; in the case of the *bahuvrīhi*, the suffix *ṣac* is added according to the rule "sakthyakṣṇoḥ."
The particle *īṣat* is used in the sense of "slight" or "a little. (Pāṇini 6.3.105)

Regarding "kāmadhuram": this is a compound meaning "bad state" (*kugati*). The statement that *ku* has the sense of "evil" (*pāpa*) is merely common usage. Regarding "kāmlam": [an objection is raised]—"But surely here, by the rule *koḥ kattatpuruṣe'ci*, the substitution of *kat* for *ku* should apply; however, this [rule] finds its scope in cases where the following suffix does not begin with a vowel. To this he replies: "Even when beginning with a vowel (*ajādau api*)."
The term *vibhāṣā* [is used] when referring to a person. 6.3.106.
"This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) for what has not [otherwise] been established," because the scope of the term "in the sense of slightness" (*īṣadarthe*) has ceased [to apply].

Now, if this were the case, it would be logical that this is a *vibhāṣā* applicable in both respects: since it is already established in the sense of slightness, and not yet established elsewhere. To this he says: "But in the sense of slightness... The scope of the rule *īṣadarthe ca* is, for example, *kāmadhuram*; the scope of the rule *vibhāṣā puruṣe* is, for example, *kutsitaḥ puruṣaḥ kāpuruṣaḥ*. When there is a conflict between these two—such as in the case of *īṣatpuruṣaḥ*—there is a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of the former).
The word *kavañcu* is optionally neuter. (6.3.107)

In Vedic usage, [the suffix] is seen even elsewhere—as in "na kavādibhyo na hi te pṛṇanti" (not from the Kavās, for they do not give). The word *kava* is also seen in its isolated form—as in "kavātiryag vā upatiṣṭheta," meaning "slightly obliquely."
Words such as *pṛṣodara* and others are formed according to traditional usage.

The *uṇādayo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.1] rule is stated by the grammarians (*saddhiḥ*) to establish non-compounded words established through treatises such as *Nirukta*; however, this [present work] states the derivation of compounded words such as *jīmūta*, *valāhaka*, and so forth. He shows that the word "etc. (*ādi*) here denotes a class (*prakāra*) by saying "of the *pṛṣodara* type. If the word "etc. were intended for the purpose of restriction (*vyavasthā*), then the phrase "as taught" (*yathopadiṣṭam*) would be redundant; this is the sense. He explains the "type" (*prakāra*) by saying "in which," and regarding the phrase "as taught," he says "whichever they may be" (*yāniyāni*) to indicate that this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in a distributive sense (*vīpsā*).

The root *diś* denotes the action of uttering; for having uttered the phonemes (*varṇa*), one says, "These phonemes have been taught. By whom, then, were they taught? By the cultured (*śiṣṭa*). The cultured, moreover, are those whose nature is free from desire, who know things as they truly are, who speak according to what is prescribed, and who, with some degree of excellence, have reached the further shore of certain branches of knowledge; it is concerning them that this is said:
"For those whose light has manifested and whose minds are unclouded, their knowledge of the past and future does not differ from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
"Those who perceive with the eye of the seers (*ārṣa*) entities that are beyond the senses and imperceptible—their word is not sublated by inference.

If, then, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) are the authority regarding words, what is the purpose of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*? [Reply: The *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the sake of knowing the learned. How does one who studies the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* perceive another who does not study it, and who employs those [words] which have been taught [by him]? He perceives: "Surely, this person..."

Whether it be by divine favor or by his own nature that he studies this *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, and yet employs the words prescribed therein, it is certain that he knows others as well; thus, this *Aṣṭādhyāyī* is for the purpose of knowing the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). *Jīmūta*: a cloud, being a container (*bhājana*) for the water of life (*jīvana*), just as a granary is for grain; *kha* means a hole or cavity; *piśita* means flesh; *bṛsī* is a seat made of grass. Other such examples follow. In the case of the words *kapi*, *aśva*, and *mahī* as upapadas, when the root *sthā* is preceded by a *sup*-ending word, the *s* is changed to *t*, and the vowel in the word *mahī* is shortened.

"Dakṣiṇatāram" is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*). "Vāgvāda" [is derived] with the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of an action (*karmaṇi*). "Ṣoḍan" [is formed] by substituting *datṛ* for *danta* when expressing age; the augment *num* is applied because it ends in an *ugit* vowel. "Ghāsu na" indicates that this is an optional alternative to the substitution of *u*. However, in the case where *u* is substituted, the substitution of *ṣṭu* (the change of *t* to *ṣ*) occurs invariably; here, by the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the suffix *gha* is intended. A "word" (*pada*) is so called because meaning is reached or understood through it; it is both "subsequent" (*uttara*) and a "word" (*pada*), hence "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). In "ṣaḍdha," there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṣṭu* by the rule "na padāntāṭṭoranām. [The phrase] "expressing different substrata" (*nānādhikaraṇavācin*)...

The plural number is superimposed upon the word based on the multiplicity of the meanings; thus, there is the use of the plural form in *dhāḥ*. Consequently, this refers to the suffix *dhā* as it occurs in the rule *adhikaraṇavicāle ca*. Regarding *ṣaḍdhā*: the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*, and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added. If it is argued that this [form] is not included because it is derived from a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), even so, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] to forms ending in *kvip*. Regarding *naśyate*: the root *ṇaś* meaning "disappearance" takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Regarding *dabhyate*: the root *dambh* meaning "deception. Regarding *svo rohāva*: this is the first person dual of the imperative (*loṭ*).

"Addition of a phoneme," and so forth: in the word *vṛñjara* (meaning "one who ages"), there is the addition (*āgama*) of the phoneme *na*. In the word *siṃha* (meaning "he kills"), there is a reversal (*vyatyāsa*)—that is, an inversion—of the initial and final phonemes.
