In the word *ṣoḍa*, there is the transformation (*avikāra*) of the phoneme *ṣa* into the form of the vowel *u*. In words such as *pṛṣodara*, there is the destruction (*vināśa*) of the phoneme *ta* and others. When a root has a well-known meaning, its connection with another meaning—that is, its connection with an excellence of that meaning—is [the basis for the formation of the word].
This fivefold etymology—the method of derivation—is stated by means of those very suffixes in the Sūtra; such is the meaning of the verse.

In the locative case (ṅi), the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* optionally applies when it follows a numeral or the word *viṃśati*, provided that *ahar* is not preceded by another word [in a compound]. (Pāṇini 6.3.110)

Regarding *dvyahra*: this is a compound (*samāsa*) formed according to the rule *taddhitārthe* (Pāṇini 2.1.51); [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *kālāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.11); its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88); [the suffix] *ṭac* is added by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (Pāṇini 5.4.91); and the substitution of *ahna* for *ahan* occurs by the rule *ahno 'hr etebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.88). Regarding *dvyahrī*: there is an optional elision (*allopavikalpa*) of the final vowel by the rule *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.137). Regarding *tryahra*: this is a *prādi*-compound; the remainder is as before. Regarding *sāyāhra*: this is a part-whole compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*).

But surely this [term] is not recited in the *pūrvāparādi* sūtra; how then can there be an *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) for it? To this he says: "The partitive compound," and so forth. In the rule *ahno 'hna etebhyaḥ*, the words beginning with "number" (*saṃkhyā*)—which were introduced in the sequence *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ*, *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśasaṃkhyātapuṇyācca rātreḥ*—are referred to. And if only *pūrva* and the others were to be compounded with the part-possessor (*ekadeśin*), [the rule would be unnecessary].

Consequently, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (forenoon) from that [previous rule] would be untenable here. Therefore, it is inferred that the word *sāya* (evening) forms a compound. This is established there; he demonstrates this with the words "by that" (*tena*). The word *sāya*, derived from the root *syati* meaning "to end," is formed with the suffix *ghañ* and denotes the conclusion of the day. Regarding *pūrvāhṇa*: the formation of the compound and so forth is as before; the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *ahro'dantāt*. [This refers to the rule:
"When *ḍh* or *r* is elided, the preceding vowel is lengthened, provided it is not *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 6.3.111).

The letter *ra* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). If this were a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, then the "precedence" (*pūrvatva*) of the *aṇ* would not be possible, because an elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*). Even if one were to rely on a sequence of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*) imagined by the intellect, even so, in cases such as *karaṇīya*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of lengthening the preceding vowel when the *repha* of the suffix *anīyar* is elided. Having observed this defect in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, he states that it is a *bahuvrīhi* with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*), like the expression *kaṇṭhekāla* ("one whose throat is black"), meaning: "there is an elision of the *ḍha* and the *repha*."

Regarding the phrase *yasmin*: the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here is the grammatical rule *bhavyageyapravacanīya*. Regarding *līḍham*: from the root *liha* (to taste), with the suffix *niṣṭhā*, the form is derived through the substitution of *ḍha* for *ha*, *dha* for *ḍha*, *ṣṭu* for *ṭu*, and the elision of *ḍha*. [The roots] *miha* (to sprinkle), *guha* (to conceal), and *muha* (to be confused) are also included. [Objection: The mention of *pūrva* (preceding) is redundant, since the rule "when [something] is specified by the word *tasmin*, [an operation applies] to what precedes" already establishes this. [Response: To this he says: "The mention of *pūrva*, etc."

If the inclusion of the word *pūrva* (preceding) were present, then although [the elision] might occur even when there is no *uttarapada* (subsequent member) due to the authority of the rule regarding the elision of *ḍh*, it would not occur for the elision of *r* in the absence of an *uttarapada*, since in examples such as *nīraktam*, the presence of an *uttarapada* is possible. Regarding *ātṛḍham*: from the root *tṛhū* in the sense of "injury," there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*. In some places, the reading is *ādṛḍham*; that is incorrect, because this root takes *iṭ*, and the form *dṛḍhaḥ*—meaning "thick" or "strong"—is derived through the prescribed elision of the consonant (*halopa*). Regarding *āvṛḍham*: from the root *vṛhū* in the sense of "lifting up."
The substitution of *o* for the vowel of the roots *sah* and *vah* occurs before the suffix *u*.

Regarding the word *ūḍha*: here, if the mention of the vowel *a* (in the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*) were not present, then when the form *vah-ta* is established, the substitution of *o* for the *u* would not take place because it is caused by the elision of *ḍh*. In this case, since the rules for changing *v* to *ū* (*ḍhatva*) and so on are considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) by the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the semivowel *v* undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) first due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group; once that has occurred, the substitution of *o* for the *u* would then apply. However, in the Bhāṣya, the mention of the vowel *a* has been rejected. The changes such as *ḍhatva* are "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because they depend upon individual phonemes, whereas the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon a specific suffix; furthermore, since the latter is also "unestablished," the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham* does not apply here.

Alternatively—since the elision of *ḍh* is relied upon as the cause for the application of the rules regarding *aut* (the substitution of *o*) and lengthening, the rules such as the substitution of *ḍh* are not considered *asiddha* in this context; therefore, before the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization), because it is subsequent, the substitutions of *ḍh* and so on are performed first. When the form *vaḍha* has thus been established, both *samprasāraṇa* and the substitution of *aut* (*o*) apply. Because the substitution of *aut* is subsequent, *aut* takes effect first, followed by *samprasāraṇa*. Once *pūrvarūpa* (the single substitute of the preceding vowel) has occurred, the substitution of *aut* does not recur, because it has already been applied in that very same operation. Since its absence [of *aut*] now exists, the rule for lengthening will subsequently take effect due to the presence of its cause.

"What is the purpose of mentioning the term *varṇa* (phoneme)? This is the question: "It should be stated as *odasya*. [The author replies with] "Even when it has been done," and so forth. From the root *vah* preceded by *ut*, in the *luṅ* tense, after *sic* is applied to the suffixes beginning with *tām*, there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*), followed by the elision of *s*, the substitution of *ḍha*, and so on. In that case, if the mention of *varṇa* were not present, the rule being stated for a short vowel (*mātrika*) would not apply to a long vowel. [Objection: But since "a non-*a*-vowel (*avarṇa*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)," the long vowel *ā* would also be included; to this he says: "A phoneme followed by *t* is itself [the limit], even if another [phoneme] follows it" (*tād api paraḥ taparaḥ*).

This very mention of *varṇa* (phoneme) is the indicator that, in the rule *taparas tatkālasya*, a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is also intended. Consequently, one should not raise the objection: "Why was it not formulated as *sahivahor asyait*?"
In the Vedic language (nigama), the forms *sāḍhyai*, *sāḍhvā*, and *sāḍha* [are used]. 6.3.113.

The statement that "sāḍha" is the form [of the root] in the *tṛc* suffix is a corrupt reading (*apapāṭha*). This is because in instances such as "āpāḍho 'gnir bṛhadbhāḥ," "āpāḍham ugraṃ sahamānam," "āṣāḍhaṃ yutsu pṛtanāsu," and "āṣāḍhāya sahamānāya," the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) is not observed in the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Therefore, the correct reading is that it is the form in the *niṣṭhā*. Furthermore, in the commentary on the Sūtra (*Sūtravṛtti*), one should divide the word as "sāḍha" with a short vowel at the end. If, however, the substitution of *ā* is observed even in some instances of the *tṛc* suffix, then this can be established by taking the particle "iti" in the Sūtra to have the sense of "in this manner" (*prakārārtha*).
In the *saṃhitā* [text], [the following rule applies]. (Pāṇini 6.3.114)

Grammatical operations are prescribed for the final member (*uttarapada*) by means of immediately preceding rules, and the *uttarapada* occurs within a compound (*samāsa*). In that context, there must always be *saṃhitā*, because of the rule stating that "in a single word (*ekapada*), *saṃhitā* is obligatory. Yet, even in the case of an avagraha (word division), an operation is sometimes observed and sometimes not: for instance, *ikaḥ kāśe* results in *anūkāśam* (where it is read as *anū-kaśam*), and *aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām* results in *aṣṭābandhuram* (where it is read as *aṣṭā-bandhuram*). Therefore, these [rules] do not necessarily have application in those cases.

He provides an example where an operation is prescribed with reference to an *uttarapada* (subsequent member): he will state [in Pāṇini 6.1.172], "after a word ending in two vowels, except for a *tiṅ*. For here, since a word ending in a *tiṅ* cannot form a compound, the term *uttarapada* is not connected [to that rule]. As in the example *vadmā hi tvā*: this is the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *vid*, with the first person plural suffix *mas*; or it is the present tense of the root *vid*.

In the word *karṇa*, when it follows [a word ending in] *lakṣaṇa*, *āviṣṭa*, *aṣṭa*, *pañca*, *maṇi*, *bhinnā*, *chinna*, *chidra*, *sruva*, or *svastika*, [the feminine suffix *ī* is applied]. (Pāṇini 6.3.115)

Therefore, in this context, "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) is understood; for that is the well-known meaning of the word *lakṣaṇa*, and because it excludes [objects] such as those pierced by arrows. The word *dātra* (sickle) and others function through metaphorical extension (*upamāna*) to denote a mark that possesses that shape.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *nah*, *vṛt*, *vṛṣ*, *vyadh*, *ruc*, *sañj*, and *niṣ* when followed by the suffix *kvi*.

It is called *upānat* because one binds (*upanahyate*) with it; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) due to its inclusion in the *sampadādi* group, and the *h* of *nah* is changed to *dh*. Regarding *parīṇat*: the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is no compound, provided an *upasarga* precedes. Regarding *nīvṛt*: the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as in the *nīvṛt*-class, and there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *vyadh* according to the rule for *grahijyādi* roots. Regarding *ṛtīṣāham*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule "after a preceding word ending in a vowel" (*pūrvapadāt*). Regarding *parītad*: since the elision (*lopa*) of the *anudātta* [suffix] is conditioned by *kṅit* or *jhal* affixes, and such conditions do not apply here because of the *kvip* suffix, the nasal is dropped by the rule "of *gam* and so forth" (*gamādīnām*), followed by the insertion of *tuk*.
In a compound denoting a name, the words *koṭara*, *kiśulaka*, and so forth are used in the sense of a forest and a mountain respectively. (Pāṇini 6.3.117)
Regarding the term *koṭarāvaṇam*: according to the rule *vanaṃ puragā*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.
The substitution of *v* occurs before *le*. (Pāṇini 6.3.118)

The suffix *valac* is understood here because of its association with the suffix *matup*, which will be mentioned later. Therefore, the long vowel does not occur in that nominal stem derived from the root *val* (meaning "to cover") by adding the *ac* suffix of the *pacādi* class;
it occurs only after the suffix *aṇ*—as in *bhartṛvalaḥ*.
The final vowel of words denoting a multitude, excluding those beginning with *anajira*, is optionally shortened [before the suffix *matup*].

Regarding the statement "in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), there is *vatva* [the substitution of *v* for *m*] after the suffix *mat*": although the substitution of *v* is established by the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ* in the examples cited, nevertheless, even here in the case of a technical name, it is more appropriate that the substitution of *v* occurs by this very rule due to its superior status (*paratva*). Furthermore, it is presented that even in the counter-example *vrīhimatī*, the substitution of *v* does not occur by this rule. The inclusion of words beginning with *ajira-* among those with many syllables (*abahvac*) is for the sake of including *uṣas*.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of *apīlu* occurs before the suffix *vaḥ*.
*Ṛṣīvahādayaḥ* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The word *vaha* ends in the suffix *ac*, added according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*.

Regarding the rule *upasargasya ghañi yan-ṅidbhyo bahulam*: since the suffix *ghañ* is not prescribed after a prefix (*upasarga*), even though there is a governing heading for "subsequent member" (*uttarapada-adhikāra*), it is understood here that the rule applies to words ending in *ghañ*. Thus he says: "when the subsequent member ends in *ghañ*. In the example *vimārga*, there is *vṛddhi* by the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*.

*Kṛtrima* means "produced by an instrument"; the meaning is "accomplished through human activity. *Niṣāda* is so called because "evil settles (*niṣīdati*) in this"; the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *halaś ca*.
The word *ika* [is substituted] for [the final vowel of] *kāśa*. 6.3.123.

This word *kāśa* ends in the suffix *ac*, belonging to the *pacādi* group; it does not end in the suffix *ghañ*. In that case, the desired form is already established by the preceding rule. For example, in the Vedic usage (*nigama*): "He gives two *prākāśas* to the Adhvaryu priest. In the rule *iko vahe 'pīloḥ*, it is intended that the operation applies to the first member alone; however, here [in the present context], it is stated that the operation applies to the prefix (*upasarga*) because of that [preceding rule]. Thus, it is said that there are two instances of *ik*.
The suffix *dasti* [is applied after a word ending in *as*] when expressing possession. 6-3-124.

The word *dā* is the beginning [of the rule]. Here, the compound *takārādi* is a *karmadhāraya*. Regarding the phrase "when that follows": according to the rule *yasmin vidhis tadādau* ("a grammatical operation applies when such an element follows, [meaning] at the beginning of that"), the meaning is "when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) begins with that. The intended sense is that there is lengthening when the subsequent member begins with the letter *t* which is related to this *dā*. For example: *nīttam*.

But surely, in this case, the letter *t* is not the initial [of the following word]; for the *t* that occurs by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* is applied to the final [letter] by the rule *alo'ntyasya*, and even the *t* that occurs for the *d* by the rule *khari ca* is considered *asiddha* (unestablished) when this lengthening is to be performed. Therefore, he says: "By the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ*, etc. This is stated [in the commentary] regarding the case where the subsequent word begins with *t*. If the change to *c* (*cartva*) were *asiddha*, the prescription for lengthening would be purposeless; therefore, the change to *c* is established on account of its basis.

The meaning is that, by that [rule], the letter *t* can occur as the initial of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). As for the phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*), he shows by this that nothing further needs to be said regarding the adoption of the position involving two *t*s. [The example is] *sudattam*.
In the sense of "beginning an action," the forms *avadatta*, *vidatta*, and *pradatta* are desired;
likewise, *sudatta*, *anudatta*, and *nidatta* are also intended.
Thus, by this rule, the substitution of *dad* occurs here.
And also in the Vedic language (chandas). || 126 ||

Regarding the term *aṣṭākapālam*: in the rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.46), the forms *aṣṭākapāla*—meaning "an oblation on eight potsherds"—and *aṣṭāgavaṃ śakaṭam*—"a cart drawn by eight oxen"—have already been explained; however, this present instance is for the purpose of demonstrating the alternative derivations, namely that there may be either the substitution of *āt* or the lengthening of the vowel.
The word *viśvasya* [takes the genitive ending] when it is connected with *vasu* and *rāṭ*. (Pāṇini 6.3.128)

Regarding *viśvārāṭ*: [it is derived] from *viśvam rājate* ("he shines over all"), with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule beginning with *satsūdviṣaḥ*. Regarding *yatrāsyaitat*: the meaning is "in the domain of the technical designation *pada*."
In the *ṛc*, [the substitution of] *tu*, *nu*, *gha*, *makṣu*, *taṅ*, *kṛt*, *ru*, and *uṣyāṇ* [occurs]. (Pāṇini 6.3.133)

In the rule *mantre*, the mention of the base form *ṛc* is for the purpose of identifying a specific type of mantra. The term *gha* is a mention of the actual word-form (*svarūpa*), and not of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*; for in the Veda, only the word *gha* is seen with a long vowel, as in *uta vā ghā syālāt*. Here, *syālaḥ* means "the brother of the wife" (*bhāryāyā bhrātā*); from that [word] comes the fifth case ending. Regarding *taṅ*: this is a mention of the substitute *t* for *th* when it possesses the marker *ṅ*. The meaning is that there is a mention of that substitute *t* which occurs for the *th* of the second person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*)—which, by the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule *loṭo laṅvat*, takes the place of the *laṅ*—when that [substitute *t*] has the marker *ṅ*.

Regarding the form *śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ*: by the rule *taptanaptanathanāśca*, there is the substitution of *ta* for *tha*. Here, because it is marked with *p* (as in *śru*), it does not possess the property of being marked with *ṅ* (*ṅittva*). As for the statement in the *Vṛtti* that "the term *taṅ* is a *pratyāhāra*," no such reading is seen anywhere. Furthermore, the claim made therein—that the *pratyāhāra* begins from the third person plural of the imperative (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣabahuvacana*) up to *mahiṅ* because of the letter *ṅ*—is also incorrect, since a *pratyāhāra* cannot be formed by means of a letter that is not situated [within the sequence]. [The example continues: *uruṣyā ṇaḥ*.

The root *ruṣyati* ends in the *ya*-affix of the *kaṇḍv-ādi* class and has the sense of "protecting"; it is in the imperative (*loṭ*), with *si* replaced by *hi*, which is elided by the rule *ato heḥ*; and the substitution of *ṇa* for the *na* of *naḥ* occurs according to the rule *naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ*.
The suffix *suñ* is applied in the sense of "one who is" [or "that which is"]. (Pāṇini 6.3.134)
The term *suñ* is taken as a particle (*nipāta*), and the letter *ñ* therein serves specifically for the purpose of specification. In the form *ūṣuṇa*, there is the lengthening of the vowel *u*.
A word consisting of two syllables ending in /t/ is pragṛhya when it is not a particle (tiṅ).

"Bhavata" is the second person plural of the imperative. "Vakṣi" and "yakṣī" are the second person singular forms of the subjunctive (leṭ) of the roots *vah* and *yaj*. This specific rule, however—"sibbahulaṃ leṭi"—does not apply here because of the plural ending. By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision of the suffix *śap*; there is the substitution of *ḍha* for *vaha*, and the substitution of *ṣa* for *yaj*. For both of these, by the rule "ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si," there is the substitution of *ka*. "Bring the gods and sacrifice"—this is the speech of Bharadvāja addressed to Agni.
And [the word] *niṣāda* [is also included]. 6.3.136.
The word *eva* is a particle (*nipāta*) because it is listed among the "and others" (*ādi*) group; the word *accha* [is a particle] according to the rule governing words meaning "motion toward."
It is also seen in other cases. (Pāṇini 6.3.137)

The word *mantra* is excluded [from the scope of the rule]. Regarding *keśākeśi*: here, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed by the rule *tatra tenedam...* (Pāṇini 2.2.26), and the suffix *ic* is added by the rule *ic karmavyatihāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.127). Regarding *jalāṣāḍ*: the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.63), and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.56). Regarding *pūruṣa*: there is a lengthening of the first vowel of the word *puruṣa*.

Regarding "sunodanta" and so forth: in that context, *śvadaṃṣṭra* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; elsewhere it is either a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*. They say that because the form with a short vowel (*daṃṣṭrā*) is taken [as the base], this long vowel [substitution] does not occur when the word ends in a long vowel. Others, however, reading the word as ending in a long vowel, maintain that it applies without distinction.
The substitution of *cau* [for *śnā*] occurs before the suffix *caṅ*. (Pāṇini 6.1.31)

The root *añc* is understood [here], but the *ca*-class (the palatals) is not included because of the specific explanation [of the rule]. Regarding the example *dadhyaca*: one might object that, due to its being *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *yaṇ* must occur first; however, the elision of the vowel (*akāralopa*) is prescribed for a *bha* stem, and the designation *bha* occurs only when a suffix beginning with *ya* or *ja* follows, thus it is *bahiraṅga*. Furthermore, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) depends upon that elision and is therefore also *bahiraṅga*. To this, he replies: "Even though it is *antaraṅga*..."

The [author] thinks as follows: here, by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the rule *acaśca* ("and of a vowel") applies; therein, the first member (*pūrvapada*) is qualified by the vowel—namely, "of a first member ending in a vowel. If there were a substitution of *yaṇ*, there would never be a first member ending in a vowel. Even in cases such as *prācaḥ*, there would result the application of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*) precisely at the first stage. Therefore, even an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule is set aside. And the evidence for this is the citation *pratīcaḥ*.
The substitution of *samprasāraṇa* [is applied] in place of [the semivowels]. (Pāṇini 6.1.108)

Regarding the passage beginning with *akṛta eva*: when the form *kārīṣagandhiputraḥ* is established, both the rule for shortening (*hrasvatva*) and this rule for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) apply. The scope (*avakāśa*) for the former is *grāmaṇikulam*; the scope for the latter is the alternative case where shortening does not occur. In the other case (where both rules apply), there is a conflict between the two. Although the lengthening has its scope in the alternative case where shortening does not occur, nevertheless, because it is subsequent (*paratva*), the shortening takes precedence over it. Now, one might ask: once the lengthening has been applied, why does the [shortening] not recur? To this he says: *punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñānam ca*.
Thus ends the third quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter:
"Of the member" (6.4.1).

"This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*)," because it is marked with the *svarita* accent. On this point, some hold the view that this governing rule for the *aṅga* (stem) extends only prior to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-vikāra*). For if this were so, the mention of *luk* (elision) in the rule *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ* would not need to be made; [the desired result] would be established simply by the principle of *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the application of a grammatical operation conditioned by a suffix). However, if this governing rule were to extend even to the modifications of the reduplicated syllable, then—because [the rule] is prescribed under the governing rule for the *aṅga*—the prohibition *na lumatāṅgasya* ("there is no [application of an operation] to an *aṅga* when a suffix is elided by *luk*, etc. would apply.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, maintains the following: if the scope of the *aṅga* (the stem) were prior to the modifications of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), then in the case of *vavraśca*—derived from the root *vṛśc* with the suffix *liṭ*—after the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) of the *r* by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, after the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*), and after the elision of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), the semivowel substitution would also apply to the *v*. A prohibition of this by the rule *na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam* is desired, but it would not obtain because the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* (*uratva*) is not itself a semivowel substitution (*asamprasāraṇatvāt*).

And it does not possess the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivat*), because its cause is subsequent. Up until the completion of the seventh chapter, since there is again the governing rule regarding the *aṅga*, the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* has a subsequent cause, because the *aṅga* implies the suffix that is its own cause.

As for what was said—that the mention of *luk* need not be made—that too is not correct; for there, the prohibition does not apply only to that which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*). What then? When an affix is elided by *lumat*, there is a prohibition of every grammatical operation—whether pertaining to a stem or not—belonging to that which is in fact the stem at that time. Therefore, it is logical that this governing heading of "stem" (*aṅga-adhikāra*) extends until the conclusion of the seventh chapter. In forms such as *hūta*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* group. As for *jīna*: [it is derived from *jyā* with the suffix *kta*].

By the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), and by *lvādibhyaḥ* (8.2.44), there is the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* suffix. Thus we have *niruttam* and *turuttam*. The root *ghañ* (in the sense of *tantusantāne*) belongs to the *yajādi* group; here, the lengthening of the vowel does not occur based on the consonants *h* and *l* that belong to the components *ni* and *dur*, which are not included within the verbal base (*aṅga*). [The form] *krimiṇām*: from the words *krimi* and *pāman*, the suffix *na* is added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) by the rule *pāmādibhyo naḥ*; there is elision of the *n* in *pāman*, and in the feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, followed by the second case singular ending.

In this context, because the aggregate *nām* is not a suffix (*pratyaya*), the preceding element does not possess the status of being a stem (*aṅga*) with respect to it; thus, even though [the preceding element] would be a stem with respect to the suffix *nap*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) does not occur. Furthermore, in the case of *pāmanām*, once the *n*-elision (*nalopa*) has taken place, there is the contingency of lengthening because the word ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). Nor can the elision of *n* be considered "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*), because it is not a rule concerning *sub* (inflectional endings). For at this stage, the lengthening is not a *sub*-rule. Or, even if its "as if non-existent" status were granted, there would still be the contingency of lengthening by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*.

Bhīṣma: [The examples are] *odana* (rice), *bhissadā* (food), and *didhi*. Now, in the case of *krimiṇām*, even though the suffix (*pratyaya*) has meaning, the entire complex (*samudāya*) is meaningless because its parts are not mutually connected; likewise, in *bhissā* and *bhissada*, the word *bhis* is [meaningless]. Therefore, by the rule "that which is meaningful is taken, not that which is meaningless," [the suffix will not be affected]. To this, he says: "In the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the stem (*aṅga*)," and so forth. The purpose [of the mention of the stem] is in the governing context of the stem (*aṅgasya*) regarding the following operations: *saṃprasāraṇa*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*), *etva*, *tātaṅ*, *iyaṅ*, *uvaṅ*, *anuṭ*, and shortening (*hrasvatva*).

The purpose of [preserving] the long vowel in *san* is so that [the substitution of *i* for *an*] does not occur in *dadhisā* (from *dadhi sanoti*). The purpose of the lengthening of the semivowel (*samprasāraṇa*) is so that it does not occur in *niruttam* or *duruttam*. The purpose of the substitution of *e* for *ai* before the *liṅ* suffix (when it is not *saṃyogādi*) is so that it does not occur in *niryāyāt* or *nirvāyāt*. The purpose of *tātaṅ* is so that [the substitution of *i* for *ai*] does not occur in *nipātsyaḥ*, as in *jīva tu tvam*. The purpose of *ivaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is for the sake of *śay* and *var*, so that it does not occur in *śayartham* or *vartham*. The purpose of the augment *nuṭ* (after short vowels, *nadī*, and *āp*) is so that it does not occur in *kumārī ām ityāha*.

The rule for shortening (*hrasvatvam*)—namely *ke’ṇaḥ*—should not apply in cases such as *kumārī kasmai spṛhayati*, *kumāryāḥ kaṃ sukhaṃ kumārīkam*. The rule for the substitution of *t* (*tatvam*)—namely *apo phiḥ*—should not apply in cases such as *abbhāraḥ*. For this purpose, the governing heading of "stem" (*aṅgādhikāraḥ*) must be established. Although that [heading] was formulated for other purposes, it also determines the lengthening in the rule *nāmī*; that is, it restricts the operation to the intended domain. This is by means of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the inclusion of meaningful elements (*arthavadgrahaṇa*). This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇam*); [otherwise], [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *anane muk* and *prāṇaḥ*.

The technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding "that which is taught by its specific definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) and the logic of "the negative particle and *iva*" (*nañivayuktanyāya*) need not be resorted to for the purpose of preventing [the application of] the rule "a long vowel for the *akṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes" in cases such as *dadhi yātam*.

Because of the statement "the genitive denotes the element to be replaced" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*), the term *aṅgasya* here is a genitive of the locus of substitution (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Consequently, in the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the word *ataḥ*—being in the ablative case—is not logically a qualifier in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *aṅgasya*, which is in the genitive; thus, because only the phoneme *a* is grasped, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substitution would apply even in forms such as *brāhmaṇabhisi*.

Furthermore, there would be no established basis for the "sixth case" (genitive) expressing a part-whole relationship (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth; consequently, in the rule *ūdupadhāyāṃ goho 'ṅgasya*, because the genitive expresses a "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), it would be restricted to the final letter, and thus the substitution of *ū* would apply to the final letter of *goh*, as well as to the entire penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) due to the explicit statement *upadhāyāḥ*. Anticipating such an objection regarding rules like *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* and others, he says: "The genitive in *aṅgasya* expresses a general relationship."

This is the intended meaning: this is an *adhikāra* (a governing heading), and it serves the purpose of another; likewise, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the genitive [case] takes the place of the locative" also serves the purpose of another. There is no mutual relationship between two things that serve the purpose of another, as it has been said: "Because subordinate elements (*guṇas*) serve the purpose of another, there can be no connection [between them], since they are equal [in status]. Therefore, the genitive in *aṅgasya* denotes only a general relationship prompted by its own inherent nature. This is expressed by the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*).
The meaning is that in whatever grammatical operation (*yoga*) there exists a manifestor of a particular relationship, that operation results in that very specific [relationship].

For example: in rules such as *hanter jaḥ*, the genitive case denotes the *sthāna* (substitute) relationship; in *ūdupadhāyā gohaḥ*, it denotes the *avayava* (constituent part) relationship; and in *yuvoranākau*, it denotes the relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-nimitti-sambandha*). This is like common worldly usage: for instance, when the genitive is employed in a general sense in the world—as in "Devadatta’s"—it results in various specific meanings according to the respective correlate, such as "son," "hand," or "blanket."

Now, regarding the phrase "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth: it was previously stated that even when intended for expression, the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is of a general nature; however, it is now said that the genitive is uttered merely for the sake of grammatical correctness in usage (*prayogāsādhutva*), and not with a specific intention to express its particular meaning. Furthermore, it must necessarily be indicated by some case ending or other. The adherence to the genitive, however, is due to the fact that its meaning is most frequently employed. Thus, it is transformed into whichever case is appropriate, just as occurs in common worldly usage.

For example: "High are Devadatta’s houses," "Devadatta, son of Vaidhabī, is wealthy," "Invite this Devadatta," and "What business have we with Devadatta?"—in these cases, when the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is substituted for *bhisa* in the rule *tena ato bhisa ais*, the meaning becomes "an *aṅga* [stem] ending in the vowel *a*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), rules such as *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso'ś* are included.

By the word *api* (also), he shows this: that this particular [substitution] is established not only in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), but also in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyartha*). However, in the previous position, in the rule *ato bhisa ais*, the genitive is used to express the relationship between cause and effect (*nimittanimittisambandha*): "the *bhis* which is the cause of the *aṅga*. And what is the cause of the *aṅga*? That in which the *aṅga* occurs. And in what does this occur? In an affix (*pratyaya*).
[The suffixes mentioned hereafter] are applied after a verbal root ending in a consonant (*hal*).

[Question: What is the purpose of the word "hala" [in the rule]? [Objection: By what means is the long vowel now established in these examples? [Response: It is thought thus: just as "śeṣe" functions both as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and as a governing heading (*adhikāra*), so too does "aṅgasya"; therefore, the long vowel will occur in the intended domain. [Reply: But the answer is that this leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Examples of over-extension are: *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ*. [Derivation: From the roots *vyadh* "to pierce" and *vyac* "to deceive," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with "grahijyā."

"Only *aṇ*"—this is because [the word] "aṇ" is understood from the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ*. Nor is there an interruption of that [term *aṇ*] by the mention of *ik* in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*; for since there is no contradiction there, *aṇ* itself is qualified by the mention of *ik*: namely, "*ik* which is an *aṇ*" (*iko'ṇaḥ*). Now, starting from the rule *cau*, only *aṇ* will continue to be supplied, not *ik*. Or, it is due to a formal irregularity (*nipātana*) regarding the term "third. The meaning is: even if the word *aṇ* does not continue [from the previous rule], the lengthening of a vowel that is not an *aṇ* will not occur, precisely because of this irregularity found in the expression "second, third, fourth" (*dvitīya-tṛtīya-caturtha*).

But surely, only one "limb" (aṅga) was under discussion; if that [term] were the qualifier of "consonant" (hal), then the status of being the object of the grammatical operation would not be obtained for the limb here.
Consequently, even in cases such as *viddha*, the occurrence of a long vowel would follow [by rule].
Now, it is stated: that which possesses a single purpose (*ekārtha*) cannot be a qualifier for something that is not a suffix (*ahala*).
Consequently, even in cases such as *nirukta*, lengthening would result;
moreover, it is not logical for a single [element] heard only once to serve two purposes.
Therefore, he says: "The mention of the 'limb' (aṅga), etc.
Even a single recurring factor assumes the status of a subordinate element for many, just as a vessel serves as a common support for people who do not eat together.
Not [if it is] *nāmī*. 6-4-3.

Since the form *nām* is not prescribed anywhere in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), he says—beginning with "the genitive plural *nām*"—in order to explain its nature. As for the reading *nāmī* with a long vowel, it is not standard. Regarding the term *āgatanuṭkam*: since the root *ram* has the sense of "going," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of either the object or the agent; thus, that by which the augment *nuṭ* has arrived, or that which has arrived at the augment *nuṭ*, is *āgatanuṭkam*. In forms such as *agnīnām*, the lengthening is established by the rule *supi ca* [Pāṇini 7.3.102] for a stem ending in *a*.

Regarding the phrase "of the *kartṛ* [stems]": one might object that the term *aṇaḥ* (of a vowel) continues to apply here; to this he replies: "this [term] *aṇaḥ*... The intention is that [the rule applies] because of the prohibition [contained in] *na tisṛcatasṛ*. "For the sake of the subsequent [rule]" means that the lengthening prescribed by *nopadhāyāḥ* should apply to the *ām* ending when it is accompanied by *nuṭ*, as in *pañcānām*, *saptānām*; and by the rule *ṣaṭ-catur-bhyaś-ca*, the *nuṭ* should not apply in cases such as *carmaṇām* where *nuṭ* is absent. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of ensuring the application of lengthening once *nuṭ* has been applied. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the mention of that which has already acquired *nuṭ*. Otherwise, etc. [as follows].

If the inclusion of the augment *nuṭ* for that which has arrived [before the suffix] is not made, then, when *agni-ām* is established, both lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and the subsequent *nuṭ* would apply. Lengthening is obligatory; it applies whether *nuṭ* has been applied or not. Consequently, once lengthening is performed, because the vowel is no longer short, the *nuṭ* itself would not occur. The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is that this very *nuṭ*, which is established effortlessly in the final system (*siddhānta*) by being adopted as a causal condition (*nimitta*), would simply not exist.

But has he not said that *nuṭ* is added after a stem ending in a short vowel? And since [the substitution of] the long vowel is obligatory, there is no stem ending in a short vowel anywhere once that has been applied. Therefore, we shall understand it thus: "that which formerly ended in a short vowel. But surely this [stem] now ends in a short vowel—as in *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*. This is not so; for in the case of *catasṛṇām*, the addition of *nuṭ* is already established by the rule *ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca*. As for *tisṛṇām*, the addition of *nuṭ* is also established by the fact that the word *treḥ* is carried over from the rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (which follows immediately after *trestrayaḥ*).

When, however, there is a prohibition of lengthening by the rule *na ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.7), then there is scope [for the present rule]. Furthermore, a single mention of *nṛ* does not necessitate the formulation of a new grammatical rule (*yogārambha*). If this were the only purpose, one would simply have said *nṛnadyāpo nuṭ*; however, because of the mention of the short vowel (*hrasvagrahaṇa*), it is understood that the status of having previously been so (*bhūtapūrvagati*) is intended.

If this were so, then in the case of *asthnām* and *dadhnām*, even after *anaṅ* has been applied by the rule *asthidadhisakthyakṣṇām*, the augment *nuṭ* would still apply because [the stem] was previously short-voweled; consequently, after the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāyāḥ*) and the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), the form *asthānām* would result. Alternatively, when the consideration of what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagati*) applies to the prescription of *nuṭ*, then *nuṭ* is constant while *anaṅ* is non-constant; thus, if *nuṭ* were applied first, the form *asthīnām* would result. Furthermore, in cases such as *dvipadām*, once the substitution of *lopa* for *pāda* has occurred, there would be the undesirable contingency of *nuṭ*.

In the same way, this objection should be applied even to those substitutes for words ending in a short vowel, such as in *paddannomās*. Therefore, it is not possible to understand [the rule] by means of the notion of what previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagati*). As for what was said—that because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *tri*, the augment *nuṭ* is established in the case of *tisṛṇām*—that too is without authority; for when there is no requirement for either one of two things or for both, and the particle *ca* is absent, a continued application cannot be determined with certainty. Thus, it remains established that otherwise the *nuṭ* augment would simply not occur.

Regarding the very point already stated, he recites a summary verse: *nāmidīrgha* (Pāṇini 6.4.3). The meaning is: if the rule were formulated simply as *āmī* without applying the augment *nuṭ*. "By the force of the statement" (*vacanāt*) means that by the power of the explicit statement, the understanding of a former state [of the word] is obtained; this is the intended sense. "Where that does not exist" (*yatra tannāsti*) means that in the case of *tisṛṇām*, where lengthening (*dīrghatva*) does not occur, there is the scope for that statement. "And of the penultimate vowel" (*nopadhāyāśca*): the word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction.
The forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* [do not undergo the substitution of *r̥* for *ṝ*]. 6.4.4.

In the Sūtra, there is an elision (*luk*) of the genitive dual ending, as in *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*. But how can there be the possibility of lengthening here, given that lengthening applies to a stem ending in a vowel by the rule *nāmī*, whereas here an ending in a vowel is not possible? For when *tisṛ-ām* is established, both the augment *nuṭ* and the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* would apply; and since the substitution of *r* is subsequent, it would take effect first. To this, he replies: "This very [Sūtra... etc.
In the Vedic language, both ways [are used]. (Pāṇini 6.3.5)

Regarding the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, a variation is observed without distinction: in the Taittirīya, there is the short vowel in "ayaṃ pitṛṇām agniḥ" and "dhātā dhātṛṇām," whereas in the Ṛgveda, there is the long vowel.
And not before *nṛ*. 6.4.6.

Some say "here" [refers to the Vedic language], because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*. However, those who carry forward [the previous context] carry forward the mention of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* from the preceding sūtra.
The substitution [of *u* for *v*] does not take place when the vowel *u* is the penultimate letter of the word.

The purpose of the undertaking is to exclude the nasalized vowel (*anajantārtha*). The term *na* is in the singular genitive case; its mention as such is due to its being a *sūtra*-form, and the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation. In forms such as *pañcānām*, because the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when the case-endings (*sub*) are applied, the word retains its status as ending in *n*. The inclusion of the term *upadhā* is so that [the rule] does not apply to the first vowel.

This purpose is not necessary: we shall qualify the vowel (*ac*) presented by the term *dīrgha-śruti* as being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna*, and subsequently as being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna*. In that case, according to the principle "whereby there is no intervention," the rule will apply even when there is an intervention of a single phoneme. However, for the sake of the subsequent rule—*in-han-pūṣāryamṇāṃ śau*—it will be stated that because of the restriction regarding the *upadhā* (penultimate) vowel in the prescription of lengthening, the mention of *upadhā* is required; therefore, the mention of *upadhā* [is made here].
And [the substitution of *su* for the nominative case ending] occurs before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix, except in the vocative singular.

Regarding *rājanīti*: in the alternative view (*vibhāṣā*) where the elision (*al-lopa*) of the *ṅi* and *śi* endings does not occur, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of lengthening [the vowel]. Similarly, there is also the consequence of this [lengthening] in cases such as *carmaṇām*.
Or [the substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] in the Vedic corpus (*nigama*) when preceded by *ṣ*. Pāṇini 6.4.9.

In this context, the term *upadhā* (penultimate) serves as a qualifier for the vowel (*ac*) brought forward by the long-vowel rule (*dīrgha-śruti*). The phrase *ṣapūrvasya* (preceded by *ṣ*) is also a qualifier of that very [vowel]; thus, considering that there is no contradiction with the masculine form, he says: "of a vowel preceded by *ṣ*. Regarding *ṛbhukṣaṇam*: the word *ṛbhukṣin* is a conventional formation (*nipātita*) in the *uṇādi* lists; the vowel *a* is substituted [for the final *n*] by the rule *ato 'tsarvanāmasthāne*.
[The rule applies] to a conjunction with a following *mahat* (great) that is preceded by a *sānta* (ending in *s*). 6-4-10.

The letter *a* in the word *sakāre* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). That which has this as its end is "ending in *sa*" (*sāntaḥ*). The term *sānta* is a separate word with an elided genitive case, serving as an adjective qualifying *saṃyoga* (conjunction). A conjunction characterized by that [ending in *sa*] is the qualifier of the letter *na*. The word *mahat* is also a qualifier of that very same [letter *na*]. By the term *sarvanāmasthāne*, which is supplied from the previous context, both the conjunction ending in *sa* and the word *mahat* are qualified. Consequently, there is no lengthening of the vowel in forms such as *haṃsaḥ* and *haṃsau*. Regarding the phrase *mahataśca*: the word *yaḥ* ("which") is expected to refer to the letter *na*.

Regarding the word "tasya" (of that), it refers to the letter *n*. But what is the relationship between the letter *n* and the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel)? For while it is true that in a given aggregate, that which precedes the final consonant is the *upadhā* with respect to that [consonant], here, due to the absence of such a [direct] movement, the relationship is characterized by proximity.

The meaning is that [the rule applies] to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) with respect to that very group ending in *n* which stands near the letter *n*. This usage is well-established in the *Kalpasūtras*, as for example: "The *visarjanīya* is not elided when a non-vowel (*anatvakṣara*) is the penultimate. Regarding *śreyān*: [from the root *praśasya* (to be praised), the substitute *śra-* occurs]; then by the rule *ugidacām*, the suffix *num* is added. Regarding *śreyāṃsi*: [here] *śi* replaces *jas* and *śas*; then by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, the suffix *num* is added. Regarding *mahān*: because of the statement [*bṛhanmahacchatṛvacca*], which treats *bṛhat* and *mahat* like the present participle (*śatṛ*), the suffix *num* is added by the rule *ugidacām*.
The *ṅīp* suffix is applied after the stems *aptṛ*, *nṛ*, *svasṛ*, *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.11)

Regarding the word *āpaḥ*: since the word *ap* is invariably plural, the dual and singular [number endings] are impossible. [The form] *bahvām api* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Under the heading governing the stem (*aṅga*), the rule "of that [stem] and its subsequent member" is accepted as applying to the final element of the compound. What, then, is intended here? It is not the absence of the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) obtained by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ*; thus he says: "In that case. He shows what is indeed intended: "Even though it is obligatory (*nityam api*). The augment *num* is obligatory because it applies both when the suffix has been added and when it has not.

Regarding the phrase "janāpavādān" (from public censure): because of the prohibition of the genitive case in connection with the suffix *tṛn* by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām," only the accusative case is used for the object. This [use of the accusative] is employed specifically to manifest that the word ends in *tṛn*; by this, the form "kaṭasya" (of the mat) is explained. One should consider the purpose for employing the specific mention of *tṛn* and *tṛc* as distinct, rather than using a general designation such as "tuḥ" (as in "tuḥ iṣṭhemeyassu" or "tuḥ chandasi").

Regarding the phrase "in the view that [the suffixes] are not derived" (*avyutpattipakṣe*): the sense is that the grammatical operation resulting from derivation does not necessarily occur; this is understood from the inclusion of the word *kaṃsa* in the rule *kṛkami-kaṃsa-* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), as it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Regarding the phrase "in the view that [the suffixes] are derived" (*vyutpattipakṣe*): - From the root *nam*, with the suffix *tṛc*, the *m* is changed to *p*: *naptā* (grandson). - From the root *nayati*, with the suffix *tṛn*, there is the augment *ṣuk* and *guṇa*: *neṣṭā* (the Neṣṭṛ priest). - From the root *tviṣ*, with the suffix *tṛn*, the penultimate vowel is replaced by *a*: *tvāṣṭā* (Tvaṣṭṛ). - From the root *kṣad*, with the suffix *tṛn*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ*: *kṣattā* (the Kṣattṛ attendant). - *Hotā* (the Hotṛ priest) and *potā* (the Potṛ priest) are formed with the suffix *tṛn* alone. - From the root *pra-śās*, with the suffix *tṛc*, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ*: *praśāstā* (the Praśāstṛ priest).
"Of such [words]" means: "of such [words]. This is its explanation: "of nominal words."
In the case of *in*, *hañ*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*, [the substitution of *u* for *n* occurs] before a word beginning with *ś*.

The rule *aninasmingrahaṇānyarthavatā cānarthakena ca tadantavidhiṃ prayojayanti* ("the mention of *in*, *an*, and *as* causes the application of the rule for what ends with them, whether [the suffix] is meaningful or meaningless") implies that by the mention of *in*, that which ends in *in* is understood. Since *śi* cannot occur after the others in their isolated forms, how is it that *inn* is the mention of the root *han* ending in *kvip*? The suffix *kvip* is prescribed after *han* following *brahma* and *dyu*; furthermore, the other two [suffixes] are masculine. Therefore, the application of the rule for what ends in those [suffixes] is understood to apply to all of them; thus he says: "of those ending in *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*. [The example is] *bahudaṇḍīni*.
"For the sake of avoiding irregularity, there is the mention of the first two [deities] among the many preceding ones;
and their plurality [is established] because of the difference in time, as in the case of Pūṣan and others."

An objection may be raised that here, in the cases "daṇḍīni brāhmaṇakulāni" (families of Brāhmaṇas who carry staves) and "brahmahāṇi brāhmaṇakulāni" (families of Brāhmaṇas who have killed a Brahmin), the introduction of the examples for the suffixes *in* and *han*—which are governed by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* (*in* and *han*)—is possible even without the word *bahu*. However, the answer is that the examples are introduced with *bahu* preceding them in order to avoid an inconsistency. An objection may be raised: "Vṛtrahan is Indra, and he is one; likewise for Pūṣan and Aryaman. How can 'plurality' serve as a qualifier for them? The answer is that Indras and the others differ according to the distinctions of time, such as different Manvantaras.

Alternatively, those families of Brāhmaṇas by whom Indra and the other gods have been invited to many sacrifices are so designated. Now, one might ask: since the lengthening of the vowel is already established by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne cāsambuddhau*, what is the purpose of this new rule? To this he replies: "The rule is formulated even though [the result] is already established. This means that for stems ending in *in* and so forth, the lengthening occurs only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix beginning with a *ś* (i.e., *su*). However, the reverse restriction—that the lengthening occurs only before a *ś* suffix for stems ending in *in* and so forth—does not apply, because of the specific enumeration: "The case endings *su*, *au*, and *jas* are each called *sarvanāmasthāna*. Thus, we have *vṛtrahaṇau*.

But surely, since the rule "thai" (Pāṇini 6.4.140) applies when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows that is not the vocative, why does the long vowel not occur here? Is it not the case that this [rule] is a restriction (*niyama*) for that [preceding rule], because it is neither the subject under discussion nor explicitly mentioned? True; however, by the very force of establishing a restriction, the [long vowel] is also excluded by this [present rule].

Let it be so in the case of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes]; however, in other case-endings (*vibhakti*), a long vowel characterized by nasality would apply everywhere. Therefore, he says: "the rule for the long vowel" (*dīrghavidhi*). Having restricted—that is, having made a limitation upon—that rule for the long vowel which applies here in this treatise to *in*-stems and others, [he specifies] where: in the *suṭ* [augment], that is, in the *sarvanāmasthāna*. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); by it, the substitution of *śas* is also included as *śi*. The word "iti" indicates the reason (*hetu*), and it should be seen as displaced in order, appearing at the end of the verse.

What then should one do? One should establish the rule again. The particle *eva* (only) is to be understood as displaced and placed immediately after the word *na*. This implies that because it is impossible to apply two rules simultaneously within a single *yoga*, a division of the *yoga* must be made. Thus, there is one *yoga*: *in-han-pūṣāryamṇām*; and the term *sarvanāmasthāne* also carries over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that for words ending in *in* and the others, the long vowel occurs only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix.

In this context, the inclusion of [the suffixes] other than *han* is for the sake of what follows. Therefore, the second rule is *śau*, meaning that even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is only before *śi*, not everywhere. Following that is the sūtra *sau ca*.

It is for the purpose of an injunction. And thus, when these two *yoga*s (rules) are being formulated, he shows what is thereby accomplished: "In the case of *bhrūṇahanī*, it would not be defective in that way. The word "in that way" (*tathā*) means when the two *yoga*s are present. "Of this" (*asya*) refers to the teacher. Regarding "*bhrūṇahanī*," in the singular locative case, since there is no elision (*allopābhāva*) according to the rule *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ*, the lengthening (*dīrgha*) characterized by the presence of a nasal (*anunāsika*) does not occur. The singular locative is merely illustrative, because it has already been stated that the occurrence of lengthening applies everywhere.

Having thus resolved the objection by means of a division of the *yoga*, he says "I shall teach" (*śāsmi*) in order to resolve it within a single *yoga*. "I shall teach"—that is, I shall explain that method by which there is no fault even when there is a single *yoga*. Here too, by the term *suṭ*, the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes] are indicated; having set aside the specific mention of *sarvanāmasthāna*, this is done by relying on the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) alone, without depending on the specific qualification of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*. Or, establish a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the *śi* [suffix]. Or act in this way, or follow the previously mentioned method—this is the meaning.
And thus, this restriction being applied to *ś* without regard for its specific distinction, effects the exclusion of all other suffixes that belong to the same genus by virtue of being suffixes.

If this were so, then in forms such as *vṛtrahāvācarati* and *vṛtrahāyate* (derived with the suffix *kyaṅ*), the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] prescribed by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* would not occur; therefore, he says: "Because of the rule for lengthening" (*dīrghavidheḥ*). This genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*), and the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). By the word "penultimate" (*upadhā*), what is meant is the lengthening characterized by being a penultimate vowel. The meaning is that, among the rules prescribing lengthening, there is a restriction regarding the lengthening characterized by being a penultimate vowel. And this is indicated by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*).

The meaning is that there is no fault in a rule prescribing lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*) when *han* occurs as part of *hanti* or *hantiyaḥ*. In some places, however, the particle *han* is read as being used for the purpose of addressing someone (*abhimukhīkaraṇārtha*). Here too, the mention of *yi* is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, in the case of *daṇḍībhūta*, lengthening indeed occurs by the rule *cvau ca*.

Now, he says "even when *suṭ*" (*suṭyapi*) to show that there is no fault even if there is no formal separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), provided that there is an expectancy for a *sarvanāmasthāna* [ending]. The word "also" (*api*) should be connected with the phrase "in the prohibition of the original form" (*aprakṛtipratiṣedhe*). The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative view. Here too, "*suṭ*" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *sarvanāmasthāna*; thus, this is the meaning: or rather, when *suṭ*—that is, a *sarvanāmasthāna*—is under discussion and is expected due to the context.

By this, he accepts the worldly scope [of the rule], but the scriptural scope is certainly not accepted. The term "without occasion" (*anavakāśa*) is a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). Since the restriction (*niyama*) regarding *śau* is without occasion, it therefore operates even when the prohibition and exclusion of the nasalized long vowel (*anunāsika-dīrgha*), though not the subject under discussion, must be applied.

How is there no room for this [objection]? To this he says: "For that... (*yasya hi*). There are two kinds of *sarvanāmasthāna*: *śi* and *suṭ*. Among these, *śi* belongs to the neuter, because it is prescribed for that; whereas *suṭ* belongs to both feminine and masculine, according to the rule "the *suṭ* of the non-neuter. Consequently, if a restriction is made regarding *śi*, which belongs to the neuter, then this cannot apply to the neuter when the *sarvanāmasthāna* is *suṭ*, because of the statement "not of the non-neuter" (*anapuṃsakasya*).

The word *hi* indicates the reason (*hetu*); because it is so, for that reason, since the possibility of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) exists there in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix (*suṭ*), a restriction (*niyama*) is adopted without distinction by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), setting aside [the specific application]. This is what is meant: if the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*, which is not otherwise obtained through the context, is relied upon for the sound *śi*, then its connection with the neuter gender must also be relied upon.

Alternatively, if both [conditions] are relied upon, the meaning becomes this: "Lengthening occurs for neuter words ending in /i/ and so forth only before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]. What similar class of items could such a restrictive rule (*niyama*) exclude? Since there is no other *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix following these neuter words, the very force of establishing this restriction causes both the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna*—which is obtained through the context—and the status of being neuter—which is obtained through the force of the rule—to be set aside without distinction. Consequently, lengthening is excluded from the mere suffix itself, whether it pertains to feminine or masculine.
*Viniyamyam* means "to be properly restrained.
He explains the first verse with the rule *hanteranunāsikasya*, etc.;
the first half of the second [verse] with *sarvanāmasthāne*, etc.; and the second half with *yas tu*, etc.

Now, by the words "or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth, the third verse is addressed. Regarding the phrase "even though it continues" (*anuvarttamāne 'pi*): what is intended here is its continuation in common worldly usage (*laukika*), not its continuation based on the technical property of *svarita* accentuation as used in the grammatical treatise (*śāstrīya*). For if that were the case, there would be an abandonment of the neuter gender (*napuṃsakatva*) which is obtained through contextual force (*sāmarthya*), but not of the status of being a "place for all names" (*sarvanāmasthānatva*) which is obtained through explicit rule (*vacana*). There would be an abandonment of the neuter gender obtained through contextual force, but not of the status of being a "place for all names" obtained through explicit rule.

It was stated [above] that this follows from the force of the context; he demonstrates that very point with the words "for the word *śi*... and "without distinction. The meaning is: without relying on any specific qualification, such as its neuter gender or its status as a *sarvanāmasthāna*. It was stated in the first two verses that a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—which would rely solely on the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* without first invoking its neuter gender—is not adopted here, because that would lead to undesirable consequences (*doṣaprasaṅga*).

The author of the Vṛtti, however, states that even resorting solely to the neuter gender while abandoning the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* must not be done under any circumstances, as it would lead to undesirable consequences; thus he says, "In that case, however" (*tatra tu*). The word *tu* (however) has the sense of the word *api* (even), and its position is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the word *etat*. The meaning is that when this rule is established, even the qualifier "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*) is not to be resorted to. He demonstrates what is accomplished by this being the case:

"By that [statement]" means: for if one were to rely on that, the meaning would be that neuter stems ending in *in* and so forth undergo lengthening only before the suffix *śi*; consequently, lengthening would not occur in examples such as *bhrūṇahani brāhmaṇakule*, but only in other genders. Therefore, the intention is that even the quality of being neuter (*napuṃsakatva*) need not be adopted as a qualifying condition.

But how could there be the contingency of resorting to a neuter gender that is neither inherent nor explicitly designated? To this he says: "But in the rule for [the designation of] *sarvanāmasthāna*... Here, *sarvanāmasthāna* is a peripheral indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is: "in that [rule], namely *jaśśasoḥ śi*, which prescribes this *sarvanāmasthāna*—that is, the *śi* substitute. Regarding the reading *sarvanāmasthānasaṃjñāvidhāne tu*, we do not see a correct meaning in that version of the text.

For instance: the rule *śi sarvanāmasthānam* is an injunction establishing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhāna*), and therein the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) is mentioned. Now, since the word *śi* never deviates from being neuter, the reference to the neuter is understood by implication; thus, this could have been stated right here in the same sūtra. Why, then, is it said: "But when there is the understanding of a technical name (*saṃjñā-vijñāne tu*)..."?

Now, if this very reading must necessarily be applied, they say that there is a *praśleṣa* (splitting of the word), and that [the term] is a restatement of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). "The prescription of the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*" means the non-prescription of the technical name *sarvanāmasthāna*. "Therein" refers to that very same point which we stated previously. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a reason; "it might be" (*api syāt*) expresses a possibility. The meaning is: since the prescription of *śi* occurs only after a neuter [stem], therefore the possibility arises that the restriction being made with respect to the word *śi* has the neuter as its scope.

Regarding the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ*: "In this [rule]," and so forth. Now, one might object that because it is both subsequent (*paratvāt*) and obligatory (*nityatvāt*), the augment *num* should indeed apply first; to this he replies: "If, however," and so on. Here, by the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the vowel (*ac*) is understood as the locus of substitution (*sthānin*). And that [substitution] does not occur in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), but rather is based on its status as a penultimate (*upadhā*), due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "penultimate. For this very reason, there is no lengthening for a stem ending in *a*. Therefore, in this context, the word "cause" (*nimitta*) is employed specifically with reference to that which possesses a fixed locus (*sasthānin*).

Regarding the forms *piṇḍagraḥ* and *carma-vaḥ*: the roots *grasu* and *glasu* mean "to eat," while *vas* means "to cover"; [the suffix] *kvip* is applied here. Now, one might object that since these are meaningless (*anarthaka*), the rule will not apply here; however, in the original examples, it is established because the suffix *asun* is meaningful. Therefore, he says: "even though it is meaningless. He states the reason for this very point: "because of the inclusion of *an*, *in*, and *asmin*. This very prohibition of verbal roots (*dhātu-pratiṣedha*) indicates that such a paribhāṣā exists.

This is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*); rather, this [rule] would be for the sake of [excluding] *śatru*: [the word] *śatru* [is formed] from *śatru-vas*, meaning "one who shoots enemies. Therefore, this is indeed a formal statement (*vacana*). However, when *atu* is mentioned, since there is no meaningful word *atu*, only the meaningless one is taken.

The mention of "end" (*anta*) would be redundant, since the rule is already established by the fact that there are no instances of *atva* (the substitution of *a* for *ā*) or *as* alone; therefore, he says "the mention of 'end'... and so forth. "Instruction" (*upadeśa*) refers to the rule-formulations (*lakṣaṇavākya*) and the list of word-groups (*gaṇapāṭha*). "Usage" (*prayoga*) means that which is employed; thus, "usage in instruction" (*upadeśaprayoga*) means usage within the instructional [texts]. The meaning is that this is for the purpose of including even a portion of a form—namely, that which ends in *at* or *as*—which is employed in its entirety during instruction. If the mention of "end" were not made, what would not be included? To answer this, he says: "Otherwise, however," and so forth.

The mention of *matup* is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). It would not include the rule *kumudanaḍavetasebhyo ḍamatup* either. To the question "What is the reason? he says: "In the original instruction" (*upadeśe*). "Form-grasping" (*rūpanirgrahaḥ*) means the determination of form. Although that [determination] occurs in common usage, the form joined with its *anubandhas* is determined only in the original instruction; therefore, it is said "in the original instruction. This [suffix] does not end in *at*.

Although that [term] ends in *t*, it does not end in *d*; nevertheless, the instruction is not for the sake of that [ending in *t*], and that for which the instruction is intended does not end in *t*, because it ends in *p*. Consequently, its inclusion would not occur; however, by the force of the mention of "end" (*anta*), there is the inclusion of even that much of the limit as ending in *d*.

A nasalized vowel (anunāsika) is replaced by its corresponding non-nasalized counterpart before an affix beginning with *k* or a consonant other than *y*, provided that the affix has an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*.

Because the *jhal* [consonants] are specified as qualifying the [element] implied by the *aṅga*, there is an application of the rule [of substitution] to that which begins with it. The term *kiti* (before a *k-it* suffix) qualifies only that which begins with a *jhal*, due to both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Examples such as *pratān* and so forth: from the roots *tamu* (desire), *śamu* (pacification), and *damu* (weariness), the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ*, the *m* is changed to *n*. This is stated in reference to the form ending in *yaṅ*-elision followed by *tas*; here, *ṅittva* is applied by the rule *sya sārvadhātukamapit*. This is merely a statement of fact; it does not, however, preclude the suspicion of a *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix, because the discussion begins with the words *ṅiti khalv api*.

Furthermore, the suffix iṭ must necessarily apply in the case of the niṣṭhā [kṛt-suffixes], and there is no prohibition by the rule "na codittvād yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15), because the condition "ekācaḥ" (of a one-vowel root) is understood to carry over into that context.
The augment *s* is added after a verbal root ending in a long vowel when followed by the suffixes beginning with *a*.

In this context, if the term *apadhāyāḥ* were to carry over [from the previous rule], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of lengthening for a consonant in words ending in vowels; therefore, it is excluded. If that is so, then there would be the consequence of lengthening for the final vowel of the roots *han* and *gam*; this is not the case, because of the presence of the rule *acaśca*. Nor does this lead to the same consequence for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); for when the form *han-sa* is established, since lengthening applies first due to its higher priority, the reduplication occurs again based on the principle of "reapplication" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). Or, even if lengthening were to apply to the reduplicated syllable as well, it will subsequently become short by the rule *hrasvaḥ*. Thus we have *jighāṃsati*.

And because of repetition (*abhyāsa*), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*). In the form *adhijigāṃsate*, the root *gam* is the substitute for *iṅ* by the rule *iṅaśca*. Here, there are many instances of *gam*: the root *gamlṛ* (to go); *gam* in the sense of non-cognition when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*; the substitute *iṇ* when followed by the desiderative suffix *san*; the substitute *ik* according to the statement "it should be stated that [the substitute] is like *iṇ*"; and the substitute *iṅ* by the rule *iṅaśca*. Since all of these would apply here without distinction, he says: "It should be stated that [the substitute applies] to the *gam* which is the substitute for *iṅ*. Thus, since the single substitute for *iṇ*, *ik*, and *iṅ* is indicated here, the substitute applies to the three [roots], excluding only one root.

There is inclusion [of the root *gam*]; and so he will state: "of the substitute *gam* for *aja*. In this way, even for the substitute *iṇ* for *gam*, when there is ātmanepada in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), and when the suffix *san* begins with a *jhal* consonant, the lengthening by the rule *aj-jhan-gamām sani* indeed occurs, as in *sañjigāṃsyate* and *sañjigaṃsate*.

The *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the root *gam* by the rule *gameḥ samo gamyṛcchi*. In that context, the term *akarmakāt* ("from an intransitive verb") is understood to carry over; therefore, even when the desiderative suffix *san* is added, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs only from an intransitive base according to the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ*. Consequently, the reading "mātaram" is incorrect; rather, "mātrā," ending in the instrumental case, should be read. Regarding the form *sañcigāṃsad*: this is the desiderative (*san*) of *gam* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Because it is transitive, it takes the *parasmaipada* ending. The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to its Vedic character, and the absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge'pi*. However, in the *Vṛtti*, it is generally explained as being accompanied by the augment *aṭ*.

With the words "here" (*iha*) and so forth, he refutes the statement that it should be specified as "of the substitute for *gam* [beginning with] *iṅ*" (*gamer iṅādeśasyeti vaktavyam*). But how is it that, when the rule is formulated merely as "there is lengthening in the presence of *san*" (*sani dīrghaḥ*), lengthening is obtained only for that which ends in a vowel? To this he says: "In that case, [the word] 'vowel' (*ac*)," and so forth.

When the rule *sani dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.12) is being formulated, the term *aṅgasya* (of the stem) is understood from the previous context; alternatively, by virtue of the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the term *acaḥ* (of a vowel) from Pāṇini 1.2.28 is brought into play. In this regard, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified, and because a long vowel is prescribed for the roots *han* and *gam* in subsequent rules, the stem (*aṅga*) that is being grasped is qualified by the vowel (*ac*). Thus, the stem is qualified by the qualifier, and by means of that qualifier, the rule of "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; consequently, the lengthening of the vowel at the end of the stem is established, as in the case of the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. Therefore, the explicit mention of *ac* (vowel) here [in the rule *sani dīrghaḥ*] is unnecessary.

To the question "For what purpose, then, is it performed?", he says: "It is performed for that. By means of a distinction in activity—that is, a distinction in operation—he demonstrates this very point by saying "of that which ends in an *aj* vowel. And thus, it is stated that the mention of *aj* is, by virtue of its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), understood to be repeated.
The suffix *kvip* is optionally applied after the root *tan*.
"By means of an addition" refers to the rule: "An addition [to the list] is made for the roots *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*.
And [the following is stated]: "The sequence [of the suffixes] occurs before the suffix *ktvā*. (Pāṇini 6.4.18)

This optional rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the obligatory lengthening prescribed by *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ kṅiti*. Regarding the mention of *upadhāyāḥ*: although the mention of *upadhā* has already been withdrawn [by the previous rule], it is stated thus because of the presence of the rule *acaśca*, since no other vowel (*ac*) is possible [in this context].

In the form *kramitvā*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the option provided by *udito vā*. As for the statement that the substitution of *lyap* is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), this is indicated by the inclusion of the term *lyap* in the rule *ado jagdhiḥ lyapti kiti*.
The substitution of *śū* for *ch* and *śv* occurs before a nasal sound and also before the augment *uṭ*.

If, in this context, there were the inclusion of *cha* alone, then after the substitution of *upadeśa*, once *tuk* has been applied and the suffix *kta* follows, the single letter *cha* would undergo the substitution of *śa*; subsequently, through the application of *ṣatva* and then *ṣṭutva* to the *tuk*, the undesirable form *ṣṛṣṭa* would result. Nor can it be argued that the *tuk* is withdrawn on the principle that "in the absence of the cause, the effect also ceases to exist," for this is neither an explicit rule (*vacana*) nor a logical necessity (*nyāya*). Indeed, there is no logic whatsoever for the withdrawal of what has already been produced.

How then, in the case of the form *sthātā*, does the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣṭutva) cease once the substitution of *s* (satva) has been applied? It is not that the substitution of *ṣ* which was already effected is here being revoked; rather, because [the substitution of *ṣ*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *s* occurs first. Consequently, there is no occasion for the application of the substitution of *ṣ*. Having thus observed the defect in taking the vowel *u* as having the augment *t* (vituk), he says: "of this *cha* with the augment *t*. How, then, is it known that the reference is to the *cha* with the augment *t*? It is known from the fact that the suffix *naṅ* is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ* in the rule *yajayāca-*.

For in the case of *viśna*, [if the suffix were taken] without the *t* (as *viśn*), there would be no *guṇa*; however, if the substitute *śā* is applied to the form with the *t* (*vituk*), then because the penultimate vowel is light (*laghūpadhatva*), the occurrence of *guṇa* would follow. But if the substitute *śā* is applied to the form without the *t* (*atuk*), then the *t* is the penultimate, not the *i*; and furthermore, by the rule "a syllable preceded by a conjunct consonant is heavy" (*saṃyoge guru*), it receives the technical designation of "heavy" (*gurusaṃjñā*). As for *pṛcch*, however, the *ṅit*-nature of the augment *naṅ* does not apply for the sake of *samprasāraṇa*, due to the specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*) "in the sense of questioning and regarding immediate time. Therefore, the form with the *t* (*satuk*) is what is intended. And by accepting this, the citation "in the response to what was asked" (*pṛṣṭaprativacane*) becomes logically consistent.

But surely, even if [the suffix] *satuk* (with the augment *tuk*) is included, there would still be the undesired application of the rule *alo'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52) to the final *ch* alone; for there is no rule regarding the substitution of the final letter when the element is meaningless (*anarthaka*). If, on the other hand, the member (*aṅga*) is qualified by *ch* together with the *tuk*, then there would be the undesired application of the rule to the final vowel (*al*) of that member ending in *ch*; even then, however, since "substitutes take the place of what is specifically indicated" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), it will occur together with the *tuk*.

"Because it is internal (*antaraṅgatvāt*).
