Internal status arises here due to the sequence of instruction; [the substitution of] *ś* is external (*bahiraṅga*), whereas [the designation of] the base (*aṅga*) occurs once the suffix has been produced, and the substitution of *ś* applies to that which is a base. Nor is it the case that what pertains to vowels (*vārṇa*) is stronger than what pertains to the base (*āṅga*), because they belong to different times.

Regarding the statement "the suffix *na* is [added] by the *auṇādika* [rules]": although the suffix *na* is not prescribed after the root *sivi* directly, it is applied by virtue of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). It is stated that the augment *ūṭh* is applied prior to the *guṇa* substitution [prescribed by Pāṇini 7.3.86] for roots ending in *puK* or having a light penultimate vowel. The reason for this, which will be stated later—that it is because [the former] is more internal (*antaraṅga*)—should be brought forward here as well. For the *guṇa* substitution depends on many factors and depends on a suffix that is external; however, *ūṭh* is more internal because the opposite is the case. Therefore, that [augment *ūṭh*] alone is applied first. Once that has been applied, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs because it is more internal.

The *yaṇ* substitution is *antaraṅga* because it depends on fewer factors (*alpāpekṣatva*), whereas the *guṇa* substitution is *bahiraṅga* for the same reasons as before. Furthermore, it is because they have different bases (*nānāśrayatvāt*). Where both a *vārṇa* (phoneme-based) and an *āṅga* (suffix-based) operation apply simultaneously to the same cause, the *āṅga* operation is stronger. Thus, while *vṛddhi* by the rule *aco ñṇiti* finds its scope in *gauḥ*, and *yaṇ* finds its scope in *dadhyatra*, when the sequence *kṛ-a* arises in *cakāra*, both would apply; however, although *vṛddhi* is subsequent, it is set aside by *yaṇ* due to the latter's *antaraṅga* status, and by the principle *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*, *vṛddhi* takes effect.

*Śabdaprāk*: [The suffix] *kvip* is applied after the root *praś* (to cut), with the substitution of *ṣ* by *vraścādiṣatvam*, and the substitution of *j* by *jaś* and *ja*. *Goviḍ*: [Derived from] *vicch* (to go); having analyzed the compound as "one who desires a cow" (*gāṃ vicchāyati*), there is an absence of the *āya* affix in the alternative view under the rule *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā*; thus, *kvip* is applied. *Akṣadyūḥ* and *hiraṇyaṣṭhyūḥ*: [These are formed] from the roots *div* (to play) and *ṣṭhiv* (to spit) with *kvip*; there is an absence of the *s* substitution because of the prohibition stated in the rule *subdhātuṣṭhibuṣvaṣkatītanāṃ pratiṣedhaḥ*.

But surely, since the *uṭ* augment is external (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the internal (*antaraṅga*) *yaṇ* substitution, the *yaṇ* replacement should not occur here? To this he says: "The external is non-existent with respect to the internal. [And regarding] *nājānantarye*: the meaning of this is that where either an internal or an external operation depends upon the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of vowels (*ac*), the *paribhāṣā* concerning external operations does not apply. And this has been made known by the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*. [The example is] *dyumyām*.

The scope for *dyūtaḥ* (the rule for *dyu*) is [forms like] *dyūtavān*; the scope for *utva* (the substitution of *u*) is [forms like] *aharvimaladyuḥ* and *dyubhyām*, and so on; thus, there is a conflict (*ubhayaprasaṅga*) in such cases. Therefore, the intention is that the term *kṅiti* must be carried over (*anuvartayitavyam*) from the previous rule. Regarding the phrase "some say" (*kecit*), etc.: according to their view, when *īṭ* is absent after the *yaṅ*-luṅ forms of roots such as *div*, if *ūṭh* occurs, we have *dedivīti*, *dedyoti*, *dedivīṣi*, and *dedyoṣi*. But in the former alternative, when the *val*-lopa (elision of the semivowel) occurs, we have *dedeti* and *dedevīti*.

Regarding the question, "How is it that *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* [are formed] when *ūṭh* has been applied?"—the point of the question is this: since the condition *kṅiti* does not carry over here, *ūṭh* ought to apply by virtue of its higher status (paratva), and once *ūṭh* is applied, the forms should be *dyūbhyām* and *dyūbhiḥ*. The answer begins with, "Because of the use of the *tapara* marker in *diva uṭ*" and so forth. For in this case, the *tapara* marker should not have been employed; since a consonant, which has a duration of half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), is already established as being short (*hrasva*)—having a duration of one full mora—the marker is used to ensure that a long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not occur even by another rule.
The meaning is that even after *ūṭh* has been applied, the duration of one mora (*mātrākāla*) will take effect by the rule *diva ut*.

Alternatively, the phrase "when *ūṭh* has been made" is connected with the subsequent explanatory passage. In that case, the meaning is as follows: let *ūṭh* be applied generally, both before *kṅit* suffixes and elsewhere; once it has been applied, because the modified single part is not different from the original, that very *ūṭh* will have the duration of one mora due to the presence of the *tapara* (the short *u*). [This explains] the words "of those," and so forth.

For when the mention of *kṅit* has ceased, since the rule would apply even to suffixes beginning with *tṛj* and so on by this [present] injunction, the mention of *ch* in the *vraśca*-sūtra need not be made; for everything is accomplished simply by the prescription of *ṣatva* for the letter *ś*. However, for those who maintain that the mention of *kṅit* continues [into this rule], because there is no *ṣatva* for *ś* in suffixes beginning with *tṛj*, the prescription of *ṣatva* must be made specifically for *ch*. Even in that case, the mention is of *ch* together with its *tuk* augment (*satukkasya*).

If *ūṅ* were intended to be added [after the root], then rules such as "the *ṭit* and *kit* suffixes are applied to the beginning and end [of the element]" would apply; let it be *vakāra* instead. When *vakāra* is elided by the rule for elision before *val*, forms such as *akṣadyūḥ* are established. Nor should one suspect that *ūṅ*—being introduced when the elision of *val* has not yet taken effect—would subvert that elision; for they belong to different categories: *ūṅ* is an augment (*āgama*), whereas elision is a substitute (*ādeśa*), and what belongs to a different category cannot act as a subverter.

It is true that when it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brahmins, and a blanket to Kauṇḍinya," the blanket does not exclude the curd; however, in the subsequent sūtra, because of the distinction in the manner of arrival (*āgamibheda*), there would be two instances of *ūṭh*: one before the letter *v*, and another in place of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). Therefore, thinking that the status of *ūṭh* as having the marker *ṭ* must necessarily be accepted, he states the purpose for accepting it: "The making of *ūṭh* ṭit."

By stating this, it is implied that in the rule *etyedhatyūṭhasu*, the letter *ṭ* is used as a representative of the letter *c* through the process of *cartva*. If the letter *ṭ* were not employed there, then it would not be included even in the rule prescribing *vṛddhi*; consequently, [the substitution] would apply even in cases such as *pra-ūhate* and *pohataḥ*. Furthermore, the form *ūḍ* in the rule *vāha ūṭh* is likewise [a substitute] for *ṭh*; otherwise, its inclusion in the rule for *vṛddhi* would not occur, since here too the letter *ṭ* is not heard due to the processes of *jaśtva* and *cartva*.
The penultimate vowel of the roots √jvar, √tvar, √sriv, √vyav, and √mav, as well as that of the root √mā (to measure), is lengthened before the suffix *kta*.

In the case of *jvara*, [the meaning is] fever; in *ñitvarā*, agitation; in *strivu*, going and drying up; in *ava*, protection; in *mava*, binding. "The roots beginning with *jvara* and *tvare*" and so forth: this is a statement of the actual subject matter.
There is elision of *r* [in the reduplication] before a suffix beginning with *l*.

*murcheti*: *murch* [is used] in the senses of fainting (*moha*) and rising (*samucchrāya*). *hurcheti*: *hurch* [is used] in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilya*). Now, one might object: "In the previous rule, there was the inclusion of the letter *ch* with its *tup* augment (*satuk*), whereas this [present case] is without that *tup* (*vituk*); so how can there be elision here? To this he says: "By the rule *rāllopa*," and so forth.

Now, even if it is true that a *cha* or *śa* followed by a *tuK* augment after the letter *ra* is impossible, does this mean that there is a mention of a solitary *cha*—one that is irrelevant and not present in the context? Therefore, it should be explained as follows: in the preceding rule, the mention was of a double *cha*; therein, one *cha* was accompanied by a *tuK* augment, while the other was taken as solitary. And since a *cha* accompanied by a *tuK* is impossible after *ra* (due to the rule *rāllopaḥ*), the solitary one is understood.

If the previous mention were of two *c*-sounds (dvicchakāraka), then the mention as *cchvoḥ* would not be justified; how then could there be the application of the singular number in a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*)? This is not a fault, for first a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*) will be formed of the two *ac* sounds, and subsequently a copulative compound (*itaretarayogadvandva*) will be formed with the sound *v*.

Even so, by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntātsamāhāre*, the suffix for a compound would apply; therefore, having formed a *samāhāra-dvandva* of the letters *cha* and *va*, there will then be an *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* of that [compound] together with *cha* plus its *tuk*. If, however, in the previous case [the word] were taken as being without the *tuk*, then the substitution of *ś* would apply to the root *vāñch* when it takes the *kvip* suffix; this is exactly what is intended to be included—the forms must indeed be *vāṃśau* and *vāṃśa*.
In this [section], it is treated as if unestablished.

The rule "until the mention of *bhād*" has been explained by the rule "up to *kaḍāra*. The word *siddha* means "accomplished. That which is not accomplished is *asiddha*. Furthermore, that which, though accomplished, does not perform its function, behaves in the same manner [as the unaccomplished]; thus, it is "as if non-existent" (*asiddhavat*). What, then, is that [which is treated as non-existent]? It follows that it must be the primary element, namely the grammatical operation (*kārya*), because the technical rule (*śāstra*) is subordinate since its purpose is for the sake of the operation.

If the effect were non-existent (*asiddhatva*), then only the prohibition of that which is characterized by a substitute (*ādeśa*) would be established—namely, in *āgahi* and *jahī*; however, the existence of that which is characterized by *ut* and *gal* would not be [prohibited]—as in *edhi* and *śādhī*. For if the effect were non-existent, the meaning would be this: "Even though a scriptural operation has occurred up until this point, it does not bring about its own occurrence"; consequently, there would be a prohibition only of that operation which is based upon an already occurred operation.

Furthermore, in the case of *edhi* and *śādhi*, there is no operation dependent upon the elision of *e* or the absence of *ś* that could be understood as being subject to prohibition. However, the rule (*śāstra*) pertaining to the *ābhīya* [vowels] would certainly perform its own function. Therefore, once the two rules concerning the elision of *e* and the absence of *ś* have operated—thereby effecting their respective results—the substitution of *dhi* (*dhitva*) would simply not occur, because the original bases (*sthānin*) upon which it depends no longer exist. But if the rule is considered "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*), the meaning is this: the *ābhīya* rule, even though it has been established, does not carry out its own function.

Therefore, because the rules for *etva* (the substitution of *e*) and *abhāva* (elision) have not yet operated or ceased to operate regarding their own respective effects, the cognition of the original element (*sthānin*) persists for the rule concerning *aitva* and *adhibhāva*; thus, the grammatical operation based upon that [original element] is accomplished. Consequently, due to its pervasiveness, it is precisely this rule [of *aitva*] that is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), and because it is specifically designated as the domain of the rule beginning with "ā bhāt."

If this were an independent injunction (*svatantra-vidhi*), then the mention of *ā-bhāt* would either be for the purpose of specifying its scope—meaning "in the grammatical system up to the rule *ā-bhāt*"—or for the purpose of specifying that which becomes as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*). However, the mention of *atra* (here) would then be for the sake of the scope—meaning "this [rule] becomes as if unestablished only when the rule to be applied here, within the scope beginning with *ā-bhāt*, is being performed. In that case, regarding the first alternative, since there would be no specification of what becomes as if unestablished, any operation whatsoever in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* [would be subject to it].

All of that would have to be treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) when an *ābhīya* operation is to be performed; consequently, because the rule *cadhivikṛṇvyora ca* would be *asiddha*, the elision [of the penultimate vowel] in *dhinute* and *kṛṇute* would not occur. Furthermore, the mention of *atra* (here/in this case) would be purposeless, because the meaning—that "an operation must be performed there [in the subsequent rule] as if it were incomplete"—is obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

In the second alternative, however, the distinction of having a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) would not be obtained; consequently, because the short vowel in *praśamayya* (from the root *śam* with the suffix *ktvā*, changed to *lyap*) would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *m* would not be preceded by a light vowel, and thus the substitution of *ay* in the rule *lyapi laghupūrāt* would not apply, resulting in the ungrammatical form *prabebhidayya*. Similarly, in *prastanyya* (from the root *stan* with the suffix *ṇac* following the *yaṅ*-derived stem *stan-ya*), because the elision of *y* in the rule *yasya halaḥ* would be considered non-existent, the *ṇac* suffix would not follow a light vowel, as it is separated by the letter *y*; thus, the substitution of *ay* would not occur. [This applies to] the word *stan* ending in *ad*.

Therefore, because the elision (*al-lopa*) [of the penultimate vowel] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *ṇic* follows only what is light (*laghu*), and not what is preceded by a light vowel; thus, the substitution of *ay* (for *e*) does not apply. From the root *san* in the sense "he bestows cattle" (*paśum sanoti*), the suffix *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhanām viṭ*; then, by *viḍvanor anuṇaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel; and by *sanoter anaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ś* for *s*. Thus we have *paśuṣāḥ*. Then, in the nominative plural form *paśuṣo navājān* and so on, because the substitution of *ā* is treated as non-existent, the elision of the *ā* of the verbal root (*dhātu*) by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* would not occur. Similarly, in *cākhāyita*, from the root *khan* with the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*), after reduplication, the substitution of *ā* occurs optionally by *ye vibhāṣā*; then, after reduplication, the suffix *tṛc* is added.

Because the substitution of *āt* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of *y* prescribed by the rule *yasya halaḥ* would apply [prematurely], resulting in errors such as in the form *papuṣaḥ*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the limit *ā bhāt* in this governing heading (*adhikāra*) would be redundant, since that purpose is already achieved through the governing heading itself. To explain: when the present heading is in force, the rule *śnān nalopaḥ* means that there is an elision of the *n* following a *śn*-affix, and that elision is treated as non-existent (*asiddhavat*). This applies likewise to rules such as *anudāttopadeśa* and others. Therefore, what is the use of the mention of *ā bhāt* for the purpose of indicating that these [substitutions] are treated as non-existent?

Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the term *ābhāt* is for the purpose of establishing a limit, so that [the rules] do not become *asiddha* (non-existent) for you; for if this were a governing heading (*adhikāra*), then because no limit would be specified, rules such as *yuvoranākau* would also be rendered *asiddha*. This is not the case, because the extent of a governing heading is understood even without the specification of a limit, just as in the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*.

Now, if there were no mention of *asatyābhāt* (not being separated by anything else) in this governing rule (*adhikāra*), then wherever this is governed, only that very sūtra or the operation prescribed therein would be referred to by the term *atra* (here), because of the absence of any other proximate element. Consequently, the meaning of the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* (there is elision of the *n* after *śnā*) would be: "There is elision of the *n* following *śnā*, and that [elision] is as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*) specifically here, when the elision of *n* after *śnā* is to be performed. This would apply everywhere in such cases.

Consequently, in the rule *ciṇo luk*, the desired result would be established—namely, *akāritaram*—and in cases such as *gataḥ* and *gatavān*, since one *ābhīya* [operation] does not cause another *ābhīya* operation to be considered *asiddha*, the elision (*lopa*) and so forth would indeed take place.

However, when the rule (*vidhi*) is understood by employing the mention of *ābhāt* (the limit up to *ābhīya*), then because that very proximate [term] is referred to by the mention of *ātra*, the meaning "that which is *ābhīya* is as if non-existent (*asiddhavat*) with respect to another *ābhīya*" is obtained; this is what is stated. Even though this is a governing heading (*adhikāra*), since there is no purpose in stating its non-existence specifically in rules such as *anudāttopadeśa*, this becomes as if non-existent by abandoning its specific form as a particular operation.

In this context, because there is a reference in a general form as "when this is to be performed," the state of being *asiddha* (non-existent) for one rule will also apply to another even in a different case; thus, the mention of *atra* (here/in this) is understood to serve the purpose of delimiting the scope (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, the understanding that they become *asiddha* arises from the governing heading (*adhikāra*). However, the mention of *atra* is for the sake of establishing that they share the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*). [Objection: If both rules subject to the *ābhīya* designation obtain by depending upon one and the same cause (*nimitta*), then in such a case one becomes *asiddha* with respect to the other; what then is the purpose of the mention of *atra*, since the establishment of *samānāśrayatva* is already achieved? [Response: To this he says, regarding the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*): [The mention of *atra* is] not [for that purpose]. Why? Because... [the rest of the passage follows].

For instance, when the rule *anudāttopadeśa* (P. 6.4.37) is present, the meaning is this: "There is elision (*lopa*) of [nasals] taught with an anudātta accent when followed by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant and marked with *k* or *ṅ* (*kṅit*); and that [elision] is as if non-existent (*asiddhavat*). In what respect? When something belonging to the *ābhīya* group is to be applied here. What is the meaning? It has been stated that there is elision of the nasal before a *kṅit* affix; and it means that when the cause for a *kṅit* affix is present, if something belonging to the *ābhīya* group is to be applied, then [the elision] is as if non-existent in relation to that application. This applies everywhere. And in this way, the fact of having a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) is clearly established by the very words of the text.

If this is the governing principle (*adhikāra*), then starting from the very place where its application occurs, that which follows would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) only in that specific location, but not in those preceding it; for when a speaker utters the prefix *āṅ*, the understanding of either a limit (*maryādā*) or an inclusive range (*abhividhi*) begins from that very point—just as in the expression "it has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra. And thus, the rule *dhvasoreddhau* would mean: "the substitution of *e* for *as* [of the root *as*] occurs, and if, starting from that [point], something follows, then [the former] is as if non-existent."

And consequently, in the previous case, the rule would not be treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the doubling (*dvitva*). However, if the rule is independent (*svatantra*), then at this very point in the section concerning the meaning of *āṅ*, starting from the very beginning, when a rule follows one that begins with *bhā*, it becomes *asiddha* only with respect to what must be performed at this very point—thus causing the non-existence of mutual *asiddha*-status for all the rules starting from "the elision of *n* after *śnā*" up to "ṛtvyavāsttvya. It is said in reply: there are two types of governing principles (*adhikāra*): the governing principle of words (*śabdādhikāra*) and the governing principle of meanings (*arthādhikāra*). Therefore, this fault would apply only if it were a governing principle of words.

However, within this very section concerning meaning (*arthādhikāra*), the particle *āṅ* establishes its own meaning as before; and that [meaning] remains present in what follows from the meaning already established. And being thus present, it is qualified by the mention of "here" (*atra*) which is present in each respective instance; thus, everything desired is established.

By this subtle [rule], the following meaning is established: from the sūtra beginning with *śnān nalopaḥ* up to the end of the chapter (*apādaparisamāpti*), those sūtras which have the same cause (*tulyanimitta*) are as if unestablished (*asiddhavat*) with respect to one another. All of this is to be applied in its proper place within the commentary (*vṛtti*). In the phrase "it becomes dependent on that very [cause]," the term *asiddhavat*, which is to be mentioned later, should be drawn forward [to complete the sense]. "Having different bases" (*vyāśraya*) means having different causes (*vibhinnanimitta*).

"Regarding the statement 'asiddhavacanam' and so forth: that which is abandoned—that is, set aside by a substitute—is called an *utsarga*, meaning the original element (*sthānin*). That which has this *utsarga* as its characteristic or cause is termed *utsargalakṣaṇa*; its state is its occurrence, so that it may take effect. And it has been stated that this is obtained by resorting to the fact that [the subsequent rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) within the system of grammar. In the word *āgahi*: by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix; and by the rule *anudātopadeśa...* and so forth, there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*). In the word *jahī*: by the rule *hantar jaḥ*, the substitution of *ja* occurs."

Regarding *abhājī*: there is the elision of the nasal [of the root] *bhañj* by the rule *ciṇi*. Regarding *rāga*: there is the elision of the nasal [of the root] *rañj* by the rule *ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*.

Regarding the question "What is the purpose of including the word *atra*?"—although the purpose of including *atra* was already stated previously as being for the sake of understanding that [the two elements] must have the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*), nevertheless, there remains an occasion for the question: "What is the result of understanding that they have the same locus? *Papuṣaḥ*: from the root *pā* (to drink); by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, the *ā* is elided. *Cicyuṣaḥ*: from the root *ciñ* (to gather); by the rule *eranekācaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. *Luluviṣaḥ*: from the root *lūñ* (to cut).

But how, then, is there a difference of substratum (*vyāśrayatva*) here? He says: "For [the rules regarding] *āl* and so forth... Now, even so, the [substitutions of] *āl* and so forth would not be established here, because they are *antaraṅga* (internal), since they depend upon the *samprasāraṇa* which is included within them; whereas the *samprasāraṇa* is *bahiraṅga* (external), because it depends upon the case-ending (*vibhakti*) which is external. To this he replies: "The *bahiraṅga* is not established in relation to the *antaraṅga*," and so forth. The neuter gender in the word *etat* is used in reference to the statement (*vacana*).

"Why does [the rule] not apply? To this he says: "For this... [namely], "as far as the technical rules (śāstra) extend. This is because it has been made known in the rule *vāha ūṭh*. What follows from that? He says: "In that case... [namely], by the maxim that there is no simultaneous presence of the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*), simultaneity must be admitted with the Paribhāṣā. The meaning is that when the Paribhāṣā is present, there is no coexistence of the internal and the external.

The *vasu*-samprasāraṇa is one basis for both the paribhāṣā and the elision (*āllopa*) and other operations; thus, there is also the condition of having a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*). And this has been stated without relying on the principle *nājānantarye* (there is no application of a rule when there is immediate sequence of vowels). For the elision of *ā* and other operations apply by depending upon the immediate sequence of vowels (*acorānantarya*).

Regarding the rule *vugyuṭau*: therein, it need not be stated that the status of being established (*siddhatva*) applies to *yuṭ*, because by the very force of the prescription of *yuṭ*, the *yaṇ* substitution will not occur. In this regard, the prescription of *yuṭ* is for the purpose of preventing the hearing of the letter *y*; for [otherwise], due to the prescription of doubling in the rule *yaṇo mayo dve bhavataḥ*, as well as the optional prescription of elision in the rule *halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*, the hearing of two *y*-sounds would be established in one alternative case.

It should not be said that *vuk* is established [as valid]; for how so? Since *vuk* is being introduced when *uvaṅ* has not yet been reached, *vuk* will be an exception (*apavāda*) to it. But surely, at the time when an obstructing rule (*bādhaka*) operates, that which is contradicted is removed by that obstructor and does not proceed. When *vuk* is operating—leaving no room for *uvaṅ*—it cannot be obstructed because it does not manifest itself due to its being "not established" (*asiddha*). Thus, once *vuk* has been applied, because of its non-establishment, [the substitution] would indeed occur. If this is the case, then *vuk* will not be applied; rather, [the substitution] of *bhū* [will apply].

Let there be the rule *luṅliṭoruṭ upadhāyāḥ*. In that context, the term *oḥ* will be carried over from the rule *oḥ supi*; thus, by relying on the principle that "the *ū* occurs for the *u* of the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the root *bhū*," the *ū* will arise once *uvaṅ* has been applied. If this were so, then in *babhūva* and *babhūvitha*, since *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have already taken effect and the *av* and *āv* [substitutions] have occurred, the *u* would no longer be the penultimate; consequently, *ūtva* would not apply. Even in those cases, however, because the *liṭ* suffix following the roots *indh* and *bhū* is *kit*—by the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*—there is an absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and thus *ū* will arise after *uvaṅ* has been applied. If this is the case, [then...]

Because the rule for *indh-* pertains specifically to Vedic meters (*chandoviṣayatvāt*), and because of the maxim that the substitution of *vuK* for *bhū-* is obligatory (*nityatvāt*), it follows that [the application of the *iK* augment] need not be performed. Furthermore, one must necessarily establish the form *babhūva* by relying on the obligatoriness of *vuK*; otherwise, since the term *iK* would not be present in the rule *aco ñṇiti*, the *vṛddhi* substitution—which is not characterized by *iK*—would certainly occur. If this is so, then there is no purpose for *vuK*, nor for its being marked with *k* (to indicate it is kit). In the rule *oḥ supi*, the vowel *a* is also to be understood as included; for when the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the *a* and *u* vowels, the form is indicated by the single substitute (*pūrvaikādeśena*) according to the rule *ṅasiṅasośca*.

By that [rule], once the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions have been applied and the *av* has been replaced, an *ū* will arise for the penultimate vowel *a* as well—as in *babhūvatuḥ* and so on—and an *uvaṅ* substitution having been applied, an *u* vowel will likewise arise.

If this is so, since there is also a mention of the vowel *a* in the rule *oḥ supi*, then in cases such as *kīlālapaḥ paśya*, the *yaṇ* substitution would also apply; however, the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by *āto dhātoḥ* will be the sublater because it is subsequent. The scope of that elision is a verbal root ending in *ā* preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), while the scope for the inclusion of the vowel *a* (in *oḥ supi*) is in subsequent instances—such as *babhūva* and *babhūvitha*. When both [rules] would apply in a case like *kīlālapaḥ paśya*, the elision of the *ā* occurs due to its being subsequent. For it will be taught that in the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the principle of "being as if non-existent" (*asiddhatva*) does not apply.

Even so, in the case of *kīlālapau* (the dual nominative/accusative form), since the designation *bha* does not apply to a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the elision of the long *ā* would not occur, and thus the *yaṇ* substitution [of *u* for *v*] would take place. If this is the objection, then in the rule *oḥ supi*, the term *yvoḥ* will be understood as being carried over from the preceding rule *aci śnudhātubhruvām*. Consequently, even though there is a mention of both *c* and *u* (*cakārokākamujānirdeśe*), by the force of the qualification *yvoḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution will apply only to the *u*-vowel and not to the *a*-vowel; thus, by implication, the explicit mention of the *a*-vowel in the subsequent rule serves only for the sake of what follows. This being the case, it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that, despite this rule, it is unnecessary to state that the *vuk* and *yuṭ* augmentations are already established.

However, some say that in the rule *bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ*, the term *oḥ* must be carried over [from the previous rule] so that the augment *vuk* occurs for *bhū* when it ends in an *u*-vowel—such as in *bobhāva* and *bobhavitha*—which are formed with *yaṅluk*. This is for the purpose of ensuring that [the *vuk*] does not apply to the form ending in *anu* (as in *anubhū*) after the suffixes *pit* and *liṭ*, where, according to the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*, there is no *kittva* due to the designation by *śtip*, and thus *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have already taken effect.

And so it was: even in the case of *babhūvitha*, since the *vuk* augment would not apply once the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions have been made—because [the rule for *vuk*] is non-permanent—the status of being *kit* must be prescribed by the rule *indhībhavatibhyāṃ ca*. And in that context, because the governing heading *ṅit* is in force, both *kit* and *ṅit* statuses are prescribed; thus, in *babhūva*, even a *vṛddhi* not characterized by *iṭ* does not occur. This very point reveals the intention of the Sūtra-author, who provides the *śtipā* (the *ti* suffix) indication when there is *kit* status, yet omits it when there is *vuk*. Therefore, for them, the established status of *vuk* must indeed be stated.

Furthermore, the employment of the suffix *vat* does not result in the attainment of "establishedness" (*siddhatva*) for the *vuk* augment even in its own locus, so that it might apply as such. For whether or not there is an extension (*atideśa*) by means of *vat*, there is no reversal of the operation belonging to the locus (*āśrayakārya*) when it is not contradicted by the extended rule; however, since "establishedness" and "non-establishedness" are mutually contradictory, how could the suffix *vat* bring about establishedness? Or how could a distinction of scope be obtained [in cases like] *sthānivat*? In those instances, however, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would occur even without *vat*; therefore, the employment of *vat* is explained as being for the purpose of extension while simultaneously serving to indicate the operation belonging to its own locus.

In that case, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (P. 6.4.111), which includes the vowel *t* as a marker (*taparakaraṇa*), it is inferred that [the rule] is sometimes established (*siddhatva*). For that [marker] is intended so that [the elision] does not occur in forms such as *āstām*, where the augment *āṭ* would otherwise apply. If this non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) were permanent, then because the augment *āṭ* itself would be non-established, the elision would not take place anyway; what then would be the purpose of the marker *t*? As for the use of the suffix *-vat*, it is merely for the sake of ease of understanding (*pratipattilāghava*). Furthermore, in rules such as *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (P. 6.1.86) and *goto ṇit* (P. 7.1.90), even without the suffix *-vat*, an extension (*atideśa*) is accepted simply through the use of the word "para" (subsequent) in reference to what follows. And in those cases as well, that which is inherent to its own basis (*svāśraya*) certainly remains uncontradicted.

In this context, if *āṅ* were used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), then the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of what falls under the jurisdiction of *bhā* would not occur. Nor is the mention of *āṅ* intended for the sake of the scope (*viṣaya*), for it has been stated that the understanding of its being "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*) follows from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) itself. Therefore, even when *āṅ* signifies a limit, its application within the jurisdiction of *bhā* is not obstructed.

Therefore, it must be stated as follows: [if one were to argue that] when an operation governed by the domain of *bh* (the *bhādhikārīya*) is to be performed, the fact that even the preceding *prakaraṇa* governed by *bh* is not established has not been stated—this is true; this very point is the fault. In that case, regarding the rule "sūryeṇaikadik" (sharing the same direction as the sun), when the suffix *aṇ* is applied, there is the elision of the vowel by the rule "yasyeti ca"; then the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; then again the elision of the vowel of the suffix *aṇ* by "yasyeti ca". Now, in this context, the elision of *y* is desired by the rule "sūryatiṣyāgastyamatsyānām ya upadhāyāḥ" to form "saurī balākā" (a crane belonging to the sun); however, that [elision of *y*] would not be obtained because the elision of the vowel occurs under the jurisdiction of *bh*.

Because the elision (*lopa*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the letter *y* is not a penultimate vowel (*anupadhā*). Furthermore, the rule of "acting as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is prohibited with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*. Having observed this flaw regarding the limit [of the domain], he says: "The particle *ā* in *ā bhāt* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Thus, even within the section concerning *bhā*, something is treated as if it were non-existent (*asiddhavat*). The meaning is that even within the section concerning *bhā*, that [non-existence] remains established; and when something else is to be performed there, both that and anything else is treated as if non-existent. This is how the commentary (*vṛtti*) explains it.

What, then, are the purposes of this grammatical application (*yoga*)? Here, [the word] *pāda* exists; from it, by the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*, we have *pādikaḥ*. From *udakaṃ vahati*, by the suffix *aṇ*, there is the substitution of *ud* for *udaka* when forming a name (*saṃjñāyām*); from *udavāha*, the derivative *apatyam* (offspring) is formed with *ata iñ*, yielding *audavāhiḥ*. From the words *sāraṇa* and *vāraṇa*, which end in the suffix *lyu*, the suffix *iñ* is applied, resulting in *sāraṇiḥ* and *vāraṇiḥ*. From the words *śātana* and *pātana*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because they end in *ṭi*, resulting in *śātanī* and *pātanī*. From the roots *sraṃs* and *dhvaṃs*, with the causative suffix *ṇic* followed by the suffix *yak*, we have *sraṃsyate* and *dhvaṃsyate*; here, after the elision of the *ya* by the rule *yasya ca*, and the elision of the *ṇic*, [the forms are established].

The rules for *padbhāva*, *ūṭh*, *nalopo 'naḥ* in a *taddhita* suffix, and *aniditām* would apply; however, because the elision (*lopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), they do not occur. That is not so, for these are established even by means of the status of being as if occupying the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule *acaḥ parasmin*.

In the case of *śā hau*, the word division is *śās hau*. The substitute *śās* occurs for the root *śās*; what is the purpose of this? It is for the sake of subverting the substitution of *it*. Then, by the rule *hujhalbhyaḥ*, there is the substitution of *dhi*, and by *dhi ca*, there is the elision of *s*. Thus, *śādhi* is established. It is not accepted that there is an elision of *sic* when *s* follows *dhi*; rather, it will be determined that the form must be *cakādhi* alone.

In the rule *dhvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca*, because the term *allopa* is carried over from the preceding rule *śnasorallopaḥ* for the sake of defining its scope, the substitution of *e* will apply only to the vowel *a* that is subject to *allopa*; consequently, as before, the form *edhi* is established through the shortening of the vowel and the elision of the *s*.

And here, in the case of *kuru* and *ka-uhi*, when [the suffix] *hi* is present, both the substitution of *guṇa* and the elision (*luk*) of *hi* would apply. Because the latter [rule for *guṇa*] is subsequent, once *guṇa* has been applied, both the substitution of *ut* (by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke*) and the elision of *hi* would apply. However, because the elision of *hi* is permanent (*nitya*), even after it has been performed, the substitution of *ut* is established by the force of the mention of "sārvadhātuka," even though that [suffix] did not previously exist [in its current form].

In the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ*, because the term *upadeśe* (in the original instruction) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), or by relying on the mention of two *l*s, the augment *aṭ* and *āṭ* occur in the *luṅ* and other tenses precisely while the root is still in the state of *l*. Thus, in forms such as *akāri* and *aikṣīt*, once the obligatory elision of *ciṇ* (*ciṇo luk*) has been applied, *aṭ* and *āṭ* are established. Likewise, in *āsann*, even before the elision of the *n* of *as* and *san* (*śnasorallopaḥ*), once *āṭ* has been applied, the elision does not occur due to the *tapara* designation [of the *a*]. Similarly, in *ayann*, once *āṭ* has been applied prior to the substitution of *yaṇ* for *iṇ* (*iṇo yaṇ*), the desired form is established.

If this is so, then in the case of *aijyata* and *aupyata*, since the augment *aṭ* would apply because the roots *yaj* and *vap* do not begin with a vowel at the stage of the *laṅ* suffix being replaced by *l*, the rule *āṭaśca* would not result in vṛddhi; we shall provide the resolution for this under the rule *āḍajādīnām*. Furthermore, in the rule *ato heḥ*, by carrying down (*apakarṣaṇa*) the mention of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) from the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*, there will be no elision (*luk*) of the suffix after the root *han* when it undergoes the substitution of *ja* in the form *jahī*.

Therefore, in the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), because the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) is understood from the preceding rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (6.4.37), the meaning is: "there is elision of that which ends in /a/ at the time of its original enunciation. Consequently, although the forms *gataḥ* and *gatavān* end in /a/ at the present moment after the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*) has occurred, that [elision] does not take place here [by this rule]. If that were so, then [the rule] would also not apply here: *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80), as in *dhinutaḥ*. [Objection: Is the base (*aṅga*) not connected with the mention of "original enunciation"—meaning "that base which ends in /a/ at the time of its original enunciation"? [Response: No; rather, the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is what is connected: "that which ends in /a/ at the time of the original enunciation of the *ārddhadhātuka* suffix."

This is what is meant: when an ārdhadhātuka suffix has arisen, even for a mere moment, there is no instance where it follows something that does not end in the letter *a*; therefore, by the rule "there is elision of the final [element] of that," in the case of *dhinute*, since the suffix *u* is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix *up*, the suffix *u* never arises following anything other than an *a*.

And here, because [the word] *madhumat* exists, the suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule *chandasi vanipau ca*; from this form ending in *van*, the suffix *śas* is added. By the rule *śvayuvamaghonām*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). When the form *magha-un-as* stands, the elision of the *y* (by the rule *yasyeti ca*) would have been applicable, but it does not take place because that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the vocalization. However, such non-existence cannot be admitted here, because the two operations depend on different bases: the vocalization applies to the *śas* case-ending, while the elision of *y* applies to the vocalized vowel. Therefore, the word *madhu* is a derived nominal stem (*prātipadika*); consequently, since there is no secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix, the elision does not occur.

And here [in the verse], "kaṃsvit garbhaṃ prathamaṃ dadhre āpiḥ": when the root *dhā* (to place) is in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, resulting in *dhā-ire*, the substitution of *re* for *ira* occurs by virtue of its being obligatory (*nitya*), according to the Vedic rule "the two *ira*s become *re*. Then, the *liṭ* suffix is applied; by the rule "in the Veda, even that which is an *ārdhadhātuka* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*," the *śap* augment is added; then there is *ślau* (doubling), and doubling occurs. Because of the prohibition in the rule "ī haly adhoḥ," the elision of the long *ā* of the *śnā* and *abhyasta* stems—which would otherwise apply—is established. In cases other than those beginning with *ghu*, such as *mā* and so forth, it will occur according to what is observed, due to the Vedic nature of the usage.

In this case, then, when *kurvaḥ*, *kurmaḥ*, and *kuryāt* arise—corresponding to the forms *kṛ-u-vas*, *kṛ-u-mas*, and *kṛ-u-yāt*—both the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *ye ca* and the *guṇa* substitution for the root *kṛ* would apply simultaneously. Since both are obligatory (*nitya*), the *guṇa* takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of rules. Once the *guṇa* has been applied, the *utva* (substitution of *u*) prescribed by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke* would be blocked; furthermore, because the elision of the *u* is obligatory, it would take effect first. Consequently, once the elision of the *u* has occurred, the *bhūtvam* (substitution of *bhū*) which is prescribed when an *upratyaya* follows a *sārvadhātuka* suffix would not occur. Moreover, it is not possible to apply the *utva* only when a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows.

To establish this, for if that were the case, then in forms such as *kuruta*, the substitution would not occur even when there is an intervention by a *vikaraṇa* suffix. Where, then, would it apply? It would apply where there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *vikaraṇa*, as in *kuryāt* or *kurmaḥ*. Although here too there is an intervention due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), nevertheless, on the basis of the explicit statement (*vacana*), such an intervention is accepted. Therefore, this is indeed the purpose [of the rule]. [Objection: Even if the *u* is elided, the substitution will still take place because of its status as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), or else—by the application of the rule *ata ut*—because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *mvośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.12), the change to *u* will occur. Thus, it is not a purpose.

In this case, however, [the rule] will be applied thus: because the *ciṇvad-iṭ* augment is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) takes place; otherwise, there would be a prohibition by the rule "when there is no *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*). In that context, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "*ciṇvad-iṭ ca*" serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*), meaning: "both the *iṭ* and whatever else applies. What else applies? The elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*). The elision of the *ṇi*-affix must necessarily be conjoined by the word "and" itself; otherwise, even though the *ciṇvad-iṭ* is non-existent, the perception of the root as being "possessing *iṭ*" (*seḍ-buddhi*) would arise due to the *iṭ* conditioned by the suffix beginning with a consonant and having *vaL* (any consonant except *y*, *r*, *l*, *v*) as its first letter, and thus the rule for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix would not apply in this instance, and the elision would simply not occur.

It may be argued that in the rule *ciṇo luk*, one should carry forward the mention of *kṅit* from the preceding rule *anudāttopadeśa...*, and by interpreting the ablative *ciṇaḥ* as a genitive, the elision (*luk*) of a following *kṅit* suffix after *ciṇ* is prescribed; thus, in forms such as *akāritarām*, the suffix *tarap* will not occur.

In this case, for the word *śunaḥ* (genitive singular of *śvan*), when the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) applies according to the rule *śvayuvamaghonām*, the rule *su-anaḥ-samprasāraṇapūrvatvam* would be set aside by the elision of the *a* via *allopo'naḥ*. Consequently, the accent of the case-ending would result in the *anudāttanivṛtti-svara* (the acute accent replacing a non-acute). However, once this present rule (*yoga*) is applied, because the semivowel substitution is treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of that rule, the prohibition *na saṃyogādvamantāt* prevents the elision of *a*. Thus, when the substitution of the semivowel and its subsequent replacement by the preceding vowel have occurred, the resulting single substitute is acute by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, and the word becomes acute on its first syllable.

In this case, when there is elision (*al-lopa*), there is no possibility for the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that arises upon the removal of an acute accent), because of the prohibition: "not after *go*, *śvan*, or a word ending in *s* or *au*, if followed by a vowel. This is not a prohibition of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*; rather, it is a prohibition of the third accent and those following it. And that [third accent] occurs in forms such as *śvabhyām* and *śvabhiḥ* when followed by a consonant (*hal*).

[Objection: It is already purposefully fulfilled by the absence of the loss of the acute accent (*udāttalopa*) in a case-ending (*vibhakti*). [Response: If that is so, then we do not teach a prohibition of the rule itself; rather, [we teach a prohibition] of whatever third-case (*tṛtīyā*) accent or subsequent accent might otherwise apply. [Objection: In that case, where no third-case or subsequent ending exists—as in *śunaḥ paśya*—the accent for the removal of the acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*) would necessarily apply. [Response: If that is so, then even the mention of "third-case etc. (*tṛtīyādi*) will be dispensed with; there is a prohibition of the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) in its entirety, without distinction.

Or rather, this is established by an indicator (*jñāpaka*): the fact that he recites the word *śvan-* in the *gaura*-group indicates that the *anudātta-nivṛtti-svara* does not descend [to the final vowel] here. Even so, there is a distinction: whether the elision of *al* occurs by the rule of *nivṛtti* or by the rule of *al-lopa*, since the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that in which there are many dogs" (*bahuśvan-*) would be one whose penultimate vowel is elided, it would have to take the suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *ana upadhālopinaḥ*, resulting in *bahuśunī*; whereas in the absence of that [suffix], it becomes *bahuśvā*. Furthermore, the *ṅīṣ* of the *gaura*-group also does not apply here because of the governing rule *anupasarjanāt* ("provided it is not a subordinate member").

Furthermore: [If it were not so], because of a general prohibition based on an indicator (*jñāpaka*), even in the absence of the *udātta-nivṛtti-svara*, how could the word have its initial syllable as *udātta*? For when there is elision of the case-ending (*al-lopa*), there is no accent for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa-svara*); consequently, the entire word would become *anudātta*. This is both a purpose and not a purpose; rather, by virtue of being *antaraṅga*, the "prior-ness" (*pūrvatva*) occurs. Nor is the rule that "an *āṅga* operation is stronger than one based on phonemes" (*vārṇād āṅgam balīyaḥ*) applicable here, because they depend on different factors: the elision of the case-ending (*al-lopa*) has the case-ending as its cause, whereas the "prior-ness" depends on the vowel of the word *śvan*.

In this case, because the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* is not established [at the time of application], the *guṇa* substitution would not occur [in the penultimate vowel]. [Objection: It will not occur by virtue of the force of the long-vowel pronunciation (*dīrghoccāraṇa*). [Reply: There is indeed a purpose for the long-vowel pronunciation; what is it? [It is] "by *bhūman*" (*bhūmnā*). [Objection: This is also established by means of a formal exception (*nipātana*), as in the rule "when *bhūman* is the final member" (*uttarapadabhūmni*). And in the case of *saurī balākā*, meaning "a crane in the same direction as the sun," even though the two *a*s are elided by the rule "of that which has [more than one vowel]" (*yasyeti ca*), the elision will occur by resorting to the status of having previously existed (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*) on account of the penultimate vowel, due to the force of the specific statement.
Thus, there being no purposes [for the rule], the sūtra was commenced merely to avoid the burden of comprehension (*pratipattigaurava*).
There is the elision of *n* after *śaṇ*. (Pāṇini 6.4.23)

The term *pṛthakpada* (separate word) has its genitive case ending elided; therefore, in the subsequent rule, the letter *n* is qualified by the mention of the *upadhā* (penultimate vowel). Since the *śna* suffix consists of the letter *n* with a dropped *a*, that *n* is what is understood here—because no other *śna* is possible. Examples: *anakti* (he anoints), *bhañjati* (he breaks), *hinasti* (he injures). [The roots are: *añjū* in the sense of manifestation, smearing, and movement; *bhañj* in the sense of crushing; *his* in the sense of injury. Why is there the mention of "possessing the letter *ś*" (*śakāravat*)? So that this does not apply here: *nanditā* (one who delights), *nandakaḥ* (a gladdener). [Objection: One might say this: [first state] "there is no elision of *n* for those [roots] whose *it* is not elided (*aniditām*) before *ta*," and then [state] "for a root ending in a consonant (*hal*), when *k* or *ṅ* follows, provided the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is present"—this would suffice, and the rule "for those whose *it* is not elided" (*aniditām*) need not be repeated; thus, *hinasti* would also not be affected here. [Response: [If you omit the mention of *śakāravat*,] then in the case of *nanditā* and *nandakaḥ*, the elision of *n* would indeed occur. Therefore, the mention of "possessing the letter *ś*" is necessary so that the elision of *n* does not take place in these cases. Thus, one must state: "there is no elision of *n* for those whose *it* is not elided (*aniditām*) before *ta*"; and then, "for a root ending in a consonant (*hal*), when *k* or *ṅ* follows, provided the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is present. In this way, even in the case of *hinasti*, the elision would not occur.

Regarding the rule *pāmādibhyo naḥ*: this [suffix] would indeed be included. If that is so, then the term *kṅiti* continues to apply; and this is a locative absolute (*satsaptamī*), meaning "when there is a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Therefore, in the case of *hinasti*, although the *tip* suffix is not *ṅit* because it is marked with *p*, the elision will still occur by relying on the fact that *śnam* itself is *ṅit*.

In that case, the rule would apply here as well in the word *nandamānaḥ*, because the suffix *cānaś* has the marker *ṅ*. If this is so, we shall then qualify the word *na* itself by the property of being marked with *k* and *ṅ*—that is, [the rule will read] "after a word ending in *na* which is marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Therefore, it must be stated that there is no elision of *an* after such a word. With this in mind, he asks: "Why is there a mention of the word containing the letter *ś*? [The answer is: in the word *yajñānām*. By the rule beginning with *yajayāca* etc., the suffix *naṅ* is applied; then there is the substitution of *śna* for *na*. Because that [substitution] is not yet established (*asiddha*), this is indeed the word *na*.

[Objection: Even if this *lopa* (elision) of *nā* is not subsequent to [the substitution of] *dīrgha* and so forth, the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) by the rule *supi ca* follows after this; once that has been applied, the elision will not occur simply because the designation *nā* no longer exists. To this, he says: "And when *sup* follows," etc. [The reason is] "due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. This means that even in a rule concerning what precedes, there is the status of being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Now, even if the inclusion of the form accompanied by the letter *ś* is accepted, why does [the elision] not occur in *viśnānām* and *praśnānām*? For surely, since the form *śna* is present here at the moment, the rule should apply precisely here. To this, he says: "In *viśnānām*," etc. Here is the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*):

Is this [the form] *nandita* not to be derived from the root *nand*, since [the rule] "lub-ani-ditām" applies? Indeed, there would be no application [of that rule] to the root *hiṃs* when a *kṅit* suffix follows; yet, if it were so, *nandamāna* would not be established.
If you say it is from the root *nand* because it ends in a *kṅit*, then even with effort, the plural number in the injunction [of the rule] is faulty due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.
Since it is established by the statement of each individual step as described in the characteristics [of the Viśvajit], there is no fault.
*Lopanam* means *lup*, that is, elision (*lopa*). Although the rule *rāllopaḥ* (elision after *ra*) was already established, the explicit mention of *lopa* here is for the sake of clarity.
The penultimate vowel of roots that do not have *i* as an it-marker is elided before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

Those roots whose *ik* (the vowel *i*) bears the technical designation *it* are called *idit*; others are *anidit*. The term *hal* serves as a qualifier for them. The singular number is used by way of ellipsis (*vyatyaya*). Regarding *sanīsraṃsyate*: the augment *nīg* is added to the reduplicated syllable according to the rule *nīg vañcu-*. Regarding *nānandyate*: the root *ṭuṇadi* means "to prosper"; the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied, and the long vowel occurs because the root is not marked with *kit*. Regarding *nahyate*: the letter *n* is specified by virtue of being followed by *kit*. The sense is that the principle "by which there is no intervention" (*yena nāvyavadhānam*) is understood here to allow for an intervention of a single element; however, this point is difficult to ascertain.

Regarding the forms *laṅgita* and *kampita*: the mention [of these roots] is because they are marked with the *it* indicator (*idittvāt*). Here, "affliction" (*upatāpa*) refers to the experience of hardship, not disease, since bodily deformities are already established by the rule itself.

In this context, "bodily deformity" refers to illness (*vyādhi*), not natural conditions such as obesity and the like. The forms *vilagita* and *vikapita* have the suffix *kta* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning motion that are intransitive," etc.

Because of the *mit* designation, there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatvam*). This very mention of the *mit* designation is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs for the root *rañj* even when the suffix does not have the *aṅ* augment.

Regarding the statement "there should be a supplementary rule for *rajaka* and *rajanī*": this is established by virtue of the *kit* designation. These are *auṇādika* suffixes beginning with *kit*: from the root *rañj*, with the suffix *kvun* used for both an artisan and a name, we have *rajaka*. With the suffix *ṅīṣ* due to connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), we have *rajakī*; however, in the absence of such a connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not occur at all. From the root *rañj* with the suffix *kyun*, we have *rajana*; and because of the diversity of usage (*bāhulaka*), that suffix is treated as having the marker *ṭi*, resulting in *rajanī*. From the roots *śṛ* and *rañj* with the suffix *asun* (which is also *kit*), we have *śiraḥ* and *rajaḥ*.
In the presence of the suffix *śap*, [the substitution of *na* for the final consonant] occurs in the roots *daṃś*, *sañj*, and *svañj*.
Regarding the form *pariṣvajate*: the root *ṣvañj* means "to embrace" and is anudātta; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule beginning with *upasargāt sunoti*.
And [the substitution of *a* occurs] for the vowel following the root *rañj*. (Pāṇini 6.4.26)
The separate formulation of the rule is for the sake of what follows; it is so that only the root *rañj* may be carried forward in the subsequent rules, and not roots such as *daṃś* and others.
And when the suffix *ghañ* is applied, [the long vowel is substituted] for the root vowel in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Regarding the word *rāga*: in the case of *hara*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) or locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and by the rule *cajoḥ ku dhiṇṇyatoḥ*, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) occurs for *c* and *j*.
The suffix *syad* is used in the sense of speed. (Pāṇini 6.4.28)
*Javaḥ* means speed (*vegaḥ*). Regarding *gosyada*: the meaning is speed pertaining to the movement of a cow. Regarding *tailasyanda*: the meaning is the flowing of oil.
The [substitutes] *avoda*, *edhodama*, *praśratha*, and *himaśratha* [are formed by the elision of the suffix *ghan*]. (Pāṇini 6.4.29)
*undī* means to moisten; *indhī* means to kindle or shine; *śrantha* means to release and to rejoice.
The suffix *añ* is not used after [a word ending in] *pūjā*. (Pāṇini 6.4.30)

In the example, the suffix *kta* is applied while [the action] is present, according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārtha* etc.; and by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*, the genitive case is used for the agent. Now, why was it not simply stated as *na añceḥ iṭi*? It cannot be stated thus, because in that case it would not apply here: *samañcate guruḥ* (the teacher honors) and *guruṃ samañcyāgataḥ* (having honored the teacher, he has come).

Regarding the rule for *iṭ*, the author of the *Vṛtti* will state: "Since the prohibition [of *iṭ*] applies to the past participles (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule 'for this [root], it is optional,' and since an option applies to the gerundive (*ktvā*) by the rule 'after an *udit* root, it is optional,' *iṭ* is prescribed invariably when expressing honor (*pūjā*). Therefore, *gurum aṅktvā* is indeed incorrect when expressing honor.
The substitution of *iK* occurs for the final vowel of the roots *skandi* and *syandi* when followed by a suffix beginning with *ktvā*.
The meaning is that because of the prohibition of *kittva* by the rule "na ktvā seṭ," no example of the *ktvā* suffix with the *seṭ* augment has been presented.
The substitution of *jha* for *śa* is optional when followed by *na* or *śa*.

*maktvā*, *maṅktvā*, *naṣṭvā*, *naṃṣṭvā*. The suffix *tum* [is applied] by the rule *masjinaśorjhali*. The mention of the final letter (*antagrahaṇa*) is for the sake of clarity, since the application of the rule to that which ends in those letters is obtained simply from the mention of the phonemes themselves.
The substitution of *śā* for the root *śās* occurs before the suffixes *iṭ* and *aṅ*.

Because the suffix (*pratyaya*) implied by the term *aṅga* is qualified by the condition "after a consonant" (*hal*), the rule applies to that which begins with it; thus he says: "and when a consonant-initial [suffix] beginning with *k* or *ṅ* follows. Regarding the form *śāsaḥ* [in the rule *śāsaḥ kvau*], since the suffix *kvip* is always elided, there is no [suffix] beginning with a consonant; therefore, this statement is made. However, [the desired form] is established by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the suffix being considered present for the application of grammatical operations). Yet, where an operation depends on the actual phonetic form of a suffix as its cause, it does not occur by virtue of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* because it relies on the specific phonemes themselves—as in *raikulam*, where the substitution of *āy* in *rāyaḥ kulam* would otherwise apply.

However, that which is the cause for a cognition qualified by a specific phoneme certainly does occur; for example, in *atṛṇeḍ*, the augment *im* prescribed for the root *tṛṇah* before an affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) and being a *sārvadhātuka* ending in *p* occurs. Similarly, this substitution of *it* (the short *i*), though prescribed before an affix beginning with a consonant and having *k* or *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*kṅit*), occurs even when [that consonant] has been elided. As in *āryaśīḥ*: after the *s* is changed to *r*, the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *rvor upadhāyāḥ*.

Now, as for the question: "Why does [the substitution] not occur here in *āśāste* and *āśāsyamānaḥ*? he says: "Because of [the rule concerning] the root *śās*. In the rule prescribing the suffix *aṅ*, the root *śās* is understood to be parasmaipada because of its association with the parasmaipada roots *arti* and *sarti*; here too, due to its connection with *aṅ*, the specific *śās* is understood, since association is a cause for determining a specific meaning. For example, when one says, "Let the cow be brought along with her calf," or "along with its young," the word *dhenuḥ* (cow) is understood to refer specifically to a female cow.

But surely, in this case, the vowel *a* alone is not the cause (*nimitta*), for the consonant *h* and others are also present, and those can occur even after verbs that take the *ātmanepada* endings; so how can there be a cognition of the specific [vowel] through association? This is not a fault. When there is a conjunction of both common and uncommon correlates, only that which is the uncommon correlate is grasped. For example, when it is said, "Cows are tied up among old mares and young fillies," it is understood that "mare-cows" are being tied up.

Therefore, when both [forms] ending in *aṅ* are included, only that for which *aṅ* is prescribed by the rule is to be understood; however, in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ṣ* (*śāsivasighasītanāṃ ca*), one should understand that *śās* alone is intended, as evidenced by the technical designation "the optative and imperative moods in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi liṅloṭau*).
The substitution of *ś* occurs before *h* and *au*. (Pāṇini 6.4.35)

The phrase "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) has ceased to apply. For that mention of "penultimate" was connected with [the condition] "before *k* or *ṅt*" (*kṅiti*); and since he will state here that the mention of "*kṅt*" has ceased, the mention of "penultimate" which was connected to it has also ceased. The genitive case [in *sthāni*] expresses a relationship of substitution (*sthāne-yoga*). This is obtained by resorting to the view that the governing context pertains to words (*śabdādhikāra*); for if the governing context pertained to meanings (*arthādhikāra*), then even here, because of the connection with a specific part [of the word], the operation would not apply to the whole.

The phrase "even when *kṅit* follows" has also ceased to apply, because *kṅit* is mentioned again later on. Regarding the word "thereby": otherwise, according to the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, since there would be no *ṅit*-ness in the case where it is *pit*, the substitution of *śā* would not occur. One might argue: "Let it not occur in the *pit* case; however, the observed usage is compatible even with the *apit* case. To this he says: "Even [the form] *śādhi* is accented on the first syllable. For if the substitution of *śā* did not occur before a *pit* suffix, then *śādhi* would be oxytone (accented on the final syllable) due to the accent of the suffix, which remains by the principle of "that which is taught last" (*satiśiṣṭa*). Yet it is seen to be accented on the first syllable; therefore, the substitution of *śā* must be understood to occur even before a *pit* suffix.

Here, "ā" must be stated [as a substitute] for "hau," following the rule *upadhāyāḥ* alone; the explicit mention of the vowel *ā* is for the purpose of subverting its status as an *it*. Thereafter, by the rule *huḍhalbhyo herdhiḥ*, there is the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*; and by the rule *dhi ca*, there is the elision of the *s*. However, for those who hold the view that "there is elision of the *sic* before *sakāra* when *dhi* follows," only the absence of *ś* (*śābhāva*) needs to be prescribed. Otherwise, even if the reference to *upadhāyāḥ* were removed, although the substitution of *dhi* would still be obtained because the *sakāra* would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when replaced by *ā*, one might still suspect the application of the *it*-substitution (*ittva*) to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) by the preceding rule, since there would be no contradiction.
The suffix *ja* is applied after the root *han*. (Pāṇini 6.4.36)

The mention of *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* suffixes. "In the case of roots taught with an anudātta vowel, there is the elision of the nasal before a *jhal* [consonant] ending in *k* or *ṅ*" (*anudāttepadeśāvanatitanotyādīnāmanunāsikalopo jhali kṅiti*). "Upadeśas" (teachings) are those which are taught (*upadiśyante*). "Anudāttopadeśāḥ" means those that are taught with an anudātta accent; the meaning is: those which are anudātta at the stage of being taught. "Anunāsika" is a separate word with its sixth case ending elided, acting as an adjective qualifying "anudāttopadeśānām"; by this, the rule applies to those ending in such a nasal (*tadantavidhiḥ*). Examples include *yam*, *ram*, and so forth. Regarding *yam*: the verse beginning with "among those ending in *yam*" (*yamiryamanteṣu*) will be stated later. Regarding *vanati*: the root *vana* (with *ṣaṇa*) is used in the sense of "to share in" or "to enjoy."

[The author] will state that there is ātva for the root *san* by means of the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*. [Examples are: *atata*, *atathā*; here the *sic* is elided by the rule *tanādibhyastathāsoḥ*. And [the purpose of the mention of *san*] is so that [the rule] may apply here; otherwise, because the word would be acutely accented on the first syllable (*nid-svara*) due to the suffix *ktin*, [the rule] would not apply. And [the purpose is] so that it does not apply here; otherwise, once the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) has been applied and the remainder is suppressed (*śeṣa-nighāta*), because the word would be unaccented (*anudātta*) on the first syllable, [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *śānta*.
The root *gam* [is replaced by *kvi*] when followed by the suffix *kvip*.
"Adhvagata" means "goers on the path. When the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) is elided, the *tuk* augment is applied after the short vowel.

Regarding "saṃyat": [it is derived] from the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *kvip*. Regarding "parītat": [it is derived] from the root *tan* with the suffix *kvip*; the lengthening of the first member of the compound occurs according to the rule beginning with "nahivṛtivṛdhi... and so forth.

It is stated [in the commentary]: "And by the word *ca* (and), there is also the elision of the nasal. Regarding *agregūḥ*: once the nasal has been elided, the vowel *u* replaces the *a*. In some places, the letter *ṅ* is recited [after the *ū*] in the rule *ūṅ*, but that serves no purpose. By the rule *oḥ supi*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs because it is a verbal root (*dhātu*); thus we have *agregvau* and *agregvaḥ*. Regarding *agrebhrūḥ*: having done this, the mention of *bhrū* in the rule *aci śnudhātu...* need not be made, as it is established simply by virtue of being a verbal root.
In place of an anusvāra that follows a semivowel or a consonant, *a* is substituted when it occurs before a following nasal.

"Agre-gā" and so forth. Although [the form] would be established even by the rule for *akāra* through the application of *savarṇa-dīrgha*, [the author] has instead prescribed *pararūpa* by the rule "ato guṇe"; for had he intended merely the elision of the *akāra* (*ato lopaḥ*), he would have simply formulated that. However, for the sake of those roots which do not have *akāra* as their penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), there is the pronunciation of the long vowel—such as *ghuṇa*, *ghūrṇa* (meaning "to wander"), from which the suffix *vanip* is seen to apply according to the rule "anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante": *dhvāvā*, *dhūrāvā*; *kṣiṇu*—*kṣāvā*; *ṛṇu*—*rāvā*; *oṇṛ*—*avāvā*.
The substitution of *sañjhal* occurs for the genitive (*jana-sa*) and locative (*kha-na*) case endings. || 6.4.42 ||

Here, by the term *jhal*, that which begins with *jhal* is understood, because the suffix implied by the *aṅga* (stem) is qualified by *jhal*. The mention of *kṅit* is its qualifier. However, the current mention of *jhal* is a qualifier of the *san* suffix.

"Tadiha" (in this case) introduces the statement. "Because of conflict" (*vipratiṣedhāt*): the scope for the inclusion of *san* in the recitation of the *tan*-class and so forth is for other operations belonging to the *tan*-class, such as "the suffix *u* after *tan* etc. and *kṛñ*" (*tanādikṛñbhya uḥ*) and "the substitution of *ta* and *tha* for *tathāsoḥ* after *tan* etc. (*tanādibhyastathāsoḥ*). However, here, in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā* (*āttvavidhi*), the mention of *san* has its scope; thus, in cases like *śiṣāsati*, *syataḥ*, and *sātavān*, where both rules would apply, the substitution of *ā* takes place because it is subsequent in the order of the rules (*paratvāt*).

But will it not be stated in the *Asiddhakāṇḍa* that "when [a rule] is not established (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it, there is no conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the non-existence of the subsequent [rule]"? For if indeed there is an absence of conflict when even one of two rules is *asiddha*, what need be said of the case where both are *asiddha*? To this he says: *ghumāsthāgāpājahātī-* etc. [The phrase] "there is a conflict" means that when a resolution is being made by means of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the state of being *asiddha* does not apply.

How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the purpose of the mention of *hal*? It is so that [the suffix] may apply when preceded by a *hal*, but not in cases such as *gaudaḥ* and *kambaladaḥ*. For if there were no rule of mutual exclusion (*vipratiṣedha*) here, the mention of *hal* would be redundant.

Let there be this [objection]: since that [substitution] is not established, the substitution of *iyaṅ* would apply when the elision of *āl* is absent; however, when there is a conflict (vipratiṣedha), the elision of *āl* finds its scope in cases such as *pāṇitram* and *aṅgulitram*, while the substitution of *ī* finds its scope in cases such as *dīyate*, *mīyate*, and *goda*. Without the mention of *hal*, the substitution of *ī* would prevail due to its higher status in the order of rules. Thus, the mention of *hal* is purposeful. This is not a correct argument, for this [mention of *hal*] is intended for the sake of establishing a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*).

For if that [substitution] were not present, because the substitution of *ī* would be unestablished (*asiddha*), there would be elision of *ā*; and because that elision would be unestablished, the substitution of *ī* would follow—thus a circularity (*cakraka*) and lack of finality (*avyavasthā*) would result. But there is no such contingency of circularity, for the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is not intended to produce a state of non-finality; rather, finality is established by the treatise itself. In this case, first there is the substitution of *ī*; because that is unestablished, there is elision of *ā*; and through that elision, the finality [of the form] will be secured.

Even so, how is it determined that the substitution of *ī* occurs because the elision of *ā* is not yet established (*asiddha*), whereas the elision of *ā* occurs because the substitution of *ī* is already established? Why could it not be the reverse—that first there is the elision of *ā*, and because that is not yet established, the substitution of *ī* takes place, resulting in the establishment of *ī*? If this were for the sake of establishing such a sequence, the author would not have included the mention of "hal" (consonant) [in Pāṇini 6.4.64]. Instead, he would have prescribed the substitution of *ī* without distinction, and then provided an exception (*apavāda*) for its elision before vowels (*aj-ādi*). How so? [He would have formulated it thus: "There is elision of *āt* (the long vowel *ā*) before an affix beginning with *iṭ* and before consonants," and then: "There is elision of the final vowel of roots beginning with *dhū*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, and *jahāti*."

It occurs [by the rule] "before *iṭ* and before a *kṅit* beginning with a vowel. But for what purpose does he state this *ī*-substitution? He will say: "That is for the sake of setting aside that [rule]. The *ī*-substitution applies to the roots *dhmā*, *pā*, and *sthā*; then [the rule] "before the *liṅ*"; then "optionally for another [root] beginning with a consonant cluster"; then "not before *lyap*"; then "for the root *mā*, the *ī*-substitution optionally"; then "and before *yat*"—and before *yat*, the *ī*-substitution applies to the root *ā*. Since this is established by such a concise formulation (*nyāsa*), the fact that he employs the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) in the rule for *yat* indicates that the Teacher undertakes a more laborious effort;
he thereby makes known that there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) here.

In this case, the mention of *jhal* could be omitted. How should the rule be divided? First: "In place of the nasal of the roots *jan*, *san*, and *khan*, there shall be the substitution of *ā*, when followed by a *kit* or *ṅit* suffix ending in *jhal*"; then: "And also in the case of *san*, the substitution of *ā* occurs for the nasal of *jan*, *san*, and *khan*, provided it is followed by *jhal*" alone.
The term *vibhāṣā* [is used] in the sense of "optionally. (Pāṇini 6.4.43)

Regarding the statement "it is born" (*jāyate*): the substitution of *ja* occurs invariably. Because that [substitution] has no other scope for application, by virtue of it, only *jāyate* occurs in the *śyan* [suffix], and never *janyate*.
After the root *san*, when the suffix *ktic* follows, there is optionally the elision of both the penultimate vowel and the following consonant.

The mention of *asya* (of this) is so that [the suffix] *ktic* might not apply to what immediately precedes, but rather so that it applies to the root itself, even if separated by other elements. For when that [mention of *asya*] is made, because of its status as the subject (*kāryitva*), there is a reference specifically to the root, even though it is separated. The mention of *anyatarasyām* (optionally) would be redundant, since *vibhāṣā* (optionally) is already under discussion; therefore, he says: "The mention of *anyatarasyām*... But is it not clear that what is under discussion is being carried over? To this he says: "For that which is connected..."
Before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. (Pāṇini 6.4.46)

Regarding the term *cikīrṣita*: since the suffix *tṛc* occurs after a root ending in *san*, when the elision (*lopa*) of the *a* is applied everywhere, what scope remains for the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*? [The opponent argues: "By virtue of an explicit statement (*vacana*), let there be lengthening in cases such as *pacāvaḥ*, overriding the elision. [To this we reply: In that case, the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a root with a low-pitched vowel in its original enunciation (*adupadeśāt*) are unaccented" would find its application; however, even that is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the absence of the elision of *a* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. [The opponent continues: "In that case, the fact that the scripture teaches the elision (*luk*) of *śap* after roots beginning with *ad-* indicates that there is no elision of the *a* of *śap*. To this, he replies: "The *śap* after roots beginning with *ad-*... [is taught specifically for those roots].

As for those roots beginning with *ad* and so forth that do not undergo *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*, their inclusion among the *ad*-class roots is indeed purposeless; however, there is a purpose for the jurisdiction (*adhikāra*) of "after [a root] ending in *at*" (*ataḥ lopaḥ*) in forms such as *vṛkṣatvam* and *vṛkṣatā*: namely, that in *bebhidyate*, the substitution does not occur before the *sārvadhātuka* suffix *śap*. As for the elision of the *yakāra* of the *yaṅ* suffix, it serves its purpose in the case of roots ending in consonants (e.g., *kārayati*). Furthermore, the prescription of the causative suffix *ṇic* would serve the purpose of applying the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule and for the occurrence of *iyaṅ*.
