Regarding the word *yānti*: [one might object] that the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112) will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the shortening of the long *ā* occurs only before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix when it follows a root with the affix *śnā* or an abhyasta (repeated) root. This is not so; for the restriction could even be the opposite: that the shortening occurs only before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix when it follows *śnā* or an abhyasta root. In that case, forms such as *yayatuḥ* would not be possible. Furthermore, the mention of *śnā* in the rule would then be for the sake of subsequent rules. Regarding *adātām*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense; the *sic* suffix is elided by the rule *gātisthāghupābhūbhyaḥ sicaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.77).

"If the *ciṇvad-bhāva* (the treatment as if it were the *ciṇ* suffix) occurs, there would be *vṛddhi* [vowel lengthening]. Now, one might object: "But surely, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the elision of the short *a* takes precedence over *vṛddhi* through the principle of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). For example, in the case of *cikīrṣakaḥ*, since the absence of the elision of the short *a* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is indicated by the prescription of the elision of *śap* after roots such as *ad*, *han*, and *mā*, let the elision of the short *a* not occur by its own inherent nature; however, because that elision is seen to occur in the *ciṇ* suffix due to the *ciṇvad-bhāva*, it would indeed take place here. But the author of the *Vṛtti* has stated, "There would be *vṛddhi*," by relying merely on the possibility [of the application]. The mention of *vṛddhi* is intended to indicate the fault [in general]; for even if the elision [of the short *a*] were to occur, the form would still remain unestablished.

"Then [the rule] *yuk* would apply"—but because [the vowel] is a phoneme (*vārṇa*) by the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, [the addition of] *yuk* is not obtained; however, the contingency of *iṭ* is not mentioned here because there is no distinction [in that case]. The verse summarizing the purposes has already been explained. As for the rules *bhrasjo ropadhayoramanyatarasyām* and *dīṅo yuḍaci kṅiti*, these have no purpose [for this discussion]. How so? From the root *bhṛj* (to fry), when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the *śap* affix is applied because it belongs to the *tudādi* class; therein, *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule *grahijyā-*. In the case of *dīṅ* as well, since it belongs to the *divādi* class, it must take the *śyan* affix; thus, the aforementioned purposes [of the rules] are already accounted for.

In order to prevent the status of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), substitutes (*ādeśa*) belonging to the scope of the second chapter are not prescribed here; rather, *vuk* and elision (*alopa*) are the intended purposes.
Otherwise—because the substitute *asti* for the root *bhū* would be considered asiddha, the augment *vuk* would not occur;
nor would the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) occur in forms such as *ācakhyatuḥ*, because the substitute *khyāñ* would be asiddha.
In place of the final consonant of the root *bhrasj*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel, there is optionally the substitution of *ra* for both the penultimate *r* and the final *j*.

If this *ram* were to occur in place of the vowels with *r* or *u* as penultimate (*ropadha*), its status as a *mit* (having an indicatory *m*) would be purposeless. On the other hand, if it were an augment (*āgama*) following the final vowel of the base, then the vowels with *r* or *u* as penultimate would still be heard [in their original form]. To this he says: *ram* is employed when there is occasion for [the vowels] with *r* or *u* as penultimate; the meaning is that the vowels with *r* or *u* as penultimate are not employed. And since it is being employed as *ram*, by virtue of its *mit* status, it is placed after the final vowel of the base.

However, that for which there is no prescription in another location remains in its own place (*sthānin*); for its prescription occurs in connection with that [original form], and the "occurrence" (*prasaṅga*) of the original form refers to a specific location. But here, this rule is set aside by the status of being a *mit* (a short vowel as an *it*). Nevertheless, by the force of the indication of the genitive case in the sense of "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), they—taking over the mention of "elision" (*lopa*) from the rule *sanaḥ ktici*—prescribe the elision of both the *repha* (r) and the penultimate vowel (*upadha*), as well as the augment *ram*, optionally. Thus, in *bhrajjanam*: when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, the *jaś*-substitution of the *s* results in *d*; then, by the *cutva* substitution of that *d*, it becomes *j*.

Regarding the phrase "by way of a prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedhena*): the scope for *ram* is seen in *bhraṣṭā*, *bhraṣṭum*; the scope for *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) is seen in *bhṛjjati*. Since [the latter] occurs before an affix beginning with a *sārvadhātuka*, *ram* does not apply here. However, in forms such as *bhṛṣṭaḥ* and *bhṛṣṭavān*, there is a prior prohibition [of *ram* by *samprasāraṇa*]. Now, why was it not stated in this way: "In place of *ram* related to the root *bhrasj*, there is optionally *ṛ*" (*bhrasjo rasa ṛd anyatarasyām*)? The meaning would have been: "In place of this cluster which is *ram* related to the root *bhrasj*, there is this substitute *ṛ*."

When *guṇa* is applied to that [root] before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, forms such as *bharjana* arise; however, in the alternative where there is no *ṛ*-vowel, the form is *bhrājana*. Before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, in the case of the *ṛ*-vowel, the form is *bhṛṣṭa*, whereas in the absence of that [vowel], when *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule *grahijyā...* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), that same form results. Thus, a "prior counter-exception" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) need not be stated, nor should the mention of "original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇa*) be carried over [from the previous rule], for in this alternative there is no occasion for *rī*. Even in this case, a prior counter-exception must be stated: in what context? Before the *sic* affix.

In the case of *abhārkṣīt*, otherwise the optional substitution of *ṛ* would be set aside by the rule for *vṛddhi* (P. 7.2.3) because it is subsequent, and thus *vṛddhi* would necessarily apply after a consonant-final root. However, when the substitution of *ra* (for *ṛ*) is applied, even though *vṛddhi* has already occurred due to its priority, the principle that "there is a re-application [of a rule] when there is a possibility for it again" (*punar-prasaṅga-vijñāna*) ensures the result: *abhārkṣīt*. Nor can it be argued that the substitution of *ṛ* occurs first because it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), since it will be stated later that there is no "internal" operation within the domain of the *sic* suffix.

If that were the case, then because it is permanent (*nitya*), there would be no substitution of *ṛ* [for *ṛ*]; for even when the *vṛddhi* has been applied, that [substitution] would still apply, and even when it has not been applied, because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]. Furthermore, there is no attainment of a different word (*śabdāntara-prāpti*); however, since *vṛddhi* applies when the *ṛ*-substitution has been made—resulting in the vowel *ṛ*—and it does not apply when it has not been made—resulting in the vowel *a*—there is indeed the attainment of a different word, and thus [the rule] would be non-permanent (*anitya*). Therefore, *ṛ* alone should have been prescribed; yet it was not done so. When it is stated that "the root *bhrasj* becomes *bhṛjj*," there is a fault in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of *yaṅ*). In that case, the substitution of *bhṛjj* would apply to the entire form including the reduplication (*sābhyāsa*), whereas it is intended that in that instance as well, only the *r* and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) are removed, and the substitution of *ram* occurs.

Regarding the form *barībhṛjyate*: since it is stated that "in the case of the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix], *rīg* should be prescribed for [roots] ending in *ṛ*," there arises the contingency of applying *rīk*, because that which falls within [the domain of] a term is included by the mention of that term.
Therefore, there is elision [of the final vowel]. (Pāṇini 6.4.48)

[The forms] *dhinutaḥ* and *kṛṇutaḥ*. The roots *div*, *dhiv*, and *prī* have the meaning "to please"; *kṛv* has the meanings "to injure" and "to do. [In these cases,] there is the present tense suffix (*laṭ*), which becomes *tas* in the dual. By the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*, there is the suffix *u* (*upratyaya*) and the substitution of the final vowel with *a*. Furthermore, by the rule *ato lopaḥ*, there is the elision of the *a* before that suffix *u*. In the singular, however, even without the elision of the *a*, the form is established through the *para-rūpa* (single-substitute) rule *ato guṇe*, after the *guṇa* substitution has been applied to the suffix *u*.

"Cetā," "stotā. Since the inclusion of *ta* (the *tapara* marker) will be shown to serve the purpose of excluding specific cases, this is a counter-example for the mere vowel *a* devoid of that marker. And thus, since [the rules for] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* have their application in long vowels, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision in short vowels. But surely, by virtue of being subsequent, the *guṇa* rule will take effect; therefore, an example of the undesirable consequence of elision should be cited in such cases as *kṛt* (in the sense of voiding excrement) and *dhru* (in the sense of movement and steadiness), as in *yātā*, *vātā*. Thus it is said: *taiti*.

If the letter *takāra* were not present here, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision even in this case. [One might argue: "The rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the elision of *ā* occurs only before an affix beginning with a vowel that has the marker *k* or *ṅ*, and when followed by *iṭ*, and not elsewhere. This is not so; for the restriction could be formulated in the opposite way: "The elision of *ā* occurs only before *iṭ*, and not before any other [affix]. And in that case, the form *cikīrṣitā* would not be possible.

Regarding the rule *vṛddhadīrghābhyām*: the scope of *vṛddhi* (by *aco ñṇiti*) is, for example, *nauḥ*; the scope of the elision of *at* (*ato lopaḥ*) is, for example, *cikīrṣitā*. When both would apply in the case of *cikīrṣakaḥ*, there is a *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of the former). For if *vṛddhi* were applied, with the addition of *yuk*, it would result in *cikīrṣāyakaḥ*. The scope of the lengthening (by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*) is, for example, *cīyate*; the scope of the elision of *at* is the same as before, *cikīrṣyate*. When both would apply here, there is a *pūrvavipratiṣedha*.
[The substitution of *u* for *i* occurs] in place of that *hal* (consonant) which [is followed by *ī*]. 6.4.49.

Regarding the phrase "of which" (*yasya*): if the letter *a* were adventitious, then there would be a reference to a single phoneme (*varṇa*); otherwise, however, there would be a reference to a whole word (*saṅghāta*). Since both these positions are possible, he says: "‘Of which’ refers to the whole word. The underlying intention is that there is no reason to disregard the *a* that is actually heard; therefore, [the desired result] is already established by the rule "there is elision of *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*) alone.

Let it then be a restriction (*niyama*) such that [the suffix] occurs only after a consonant and not after anything else—as in *lolūyitā* and *popūyitā*. For a restriction arises from the consideration of purpose (*kaimarthya*), on the grounds that there is nothing else to be enjoined; however, in this case, there is something to be enjoined. Since the deletion of the final letter (*antyasya lopaḥ*) is applicable, is it to be enjoined for the whole? In that regard, whether it be a novel injunction (*apūrvo vidhiḥ*) or a restriction (*niyamaḥ*), it shall be a novel injunction alone.

Even so, there is a fault regarding the optional application (*vibhāṣā*) of *kyap*: one desires fuel, *samidhyati*; the trisyllabic root *samidh* takes the suffix *iṭ*, resulting in *samidhitā*. When there is elision (*lopa*), there would be elision of the entire [stem]; when, however, there is the alternative of non-elision (*alopapakṣa*), then non-elision of the entire [stem] would result. For, when the term "group" (*saṅghāta*) is mentioned, the elision of *at* (A 6.4.48) must be superseded by the rule "of that which follows a consonant" (A 6.4.129) according to the principle of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*); likewise, the elision of *y* (A 6.1.66) would also be superseded optionally by the rule "the optional application of *kyap*" (A 3.1.119). Consequently, in some instances, only the entire group would be heard.

Since the elision of *ā* (ā-lopa) would also be optionally blocked just like the elision of *y* (yalopa), he says: "or [by] *halaḥ*" and so forth. Thus, by the rule *kyasya vibhāṣā*, there is optional elision of the *y* alone, whereas for the *a*, the elision is compulsory by the rule *ato lopaḥ*. This is established as the desired result; moreover, the elision of *a* (*ato lopaḥ*) must necessarily be accepted here. Otherwise, in forms such as *pāpacakaḥ*, there would be the *vṛddhi* substitution [of *au*] by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*; however, this does not occur because of the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Therefore, the term refers to the entire cluster (*saṅghāta*), while the elision occurs part by part (*avayavaśaḥ*); that alone is logical.

Regarding the word *mavyati*: there exists a root *mavy* ending in a consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta*), whereas in the rule beginning with *jvaratvārādi*, a form ending in the letter *v* has been cited.
The substitution of *ky* is optional. 6.4.50.

The term *kya* refers to both *kyac* and *kyaṅ* in general; however, *kyaṣ* cannot occur after a word ending in a consonant (*halanta*). [The example] "he behaves like fuel" (*samidham ivātmānam ācarati*) is a corrupt reading. For if this were so, the syntactical formulation for *kyaṅ* would not have been demonstrated, and the second formulation for *kyac* would be purposeless. If it is argued that it is not purposeless because there is a difference in the rule (*vidhi*), then the formulation "and from a locative" (*adhikaraṇācca*) should also have been demonstrated. Therefore, the correct reading is "he behaves like fuel" (*samid ivācarati*).

On this point, some maintain that the *kaṇḍvādīya* [suffix] should also be included; they claim that the intention of the rule "of the *ky*" (*kyasya*) is to include the *yakāra* of the *kya*, and thus the initial status of the letter *k* is not intended to be significant. We, however, say "no," because there is no evidence for such an intention regarding the initial status.
The augment *ṇi* is not applied when an affix marked with *ṇ* or *it* follows.

Since the entire domain [of application] is already occupied by the *iyaṅ* and other [substitutions], the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) has no scope; therefore, he states that these [latter] are sublated by the former, beginning with "iyaṅ-yaṇ... and so forth.

But surely, one will cite examples such as *pāktiḥ* from the root *pācayati* and *yāṣṭiḥ* from *yājayati*; since *yuc* would be applicable by the rule *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*, the suffix *ktin* is applied by the rule *ktinnajādibhyaḥ*. Furthermore, this [suffix *ktin*] should be understood as being optionally replaced by *kviṣ*. Therefore, how can it be said that [the present rule] has no scope? It is replied: if this were the only purpose, the word "aniṭi" (before an affix beginning with a vowel and not taking *iṭ*) need not have been stated. Since the word "aniṭi" is indeed stated, it is determined that the scope of this [rule] is restricted solely to those cases where the verbal root has a long vowel in the *dhātu* stage. Consequently, it is appropriate that it serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *iyaṅ* and other such substitutions.

The author of the Vārttika, however, has stated a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*): "By a prior counter-exception, [the operations of] *ṇi*-affixation, elision (*allop*), *iyaṅ*, *yaṇ*, *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and lengthening [take precedence]. As in the example *atatakṣat*: here, because the *caṅ* affix is marked with *ṅ* (indicating it is *ṅit*), there is no occasion for *guṇa*; and because it is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogapūrva*), there is also no occasion for *yaṇ* according to the rule *eranekācaḥ*. [This leaves room for] *iyaṅ*.

This is indeed the scope [of the rule *eranekācaḥ*]; because it is preceded by a *saṃyoga*, there is no possibility of *yaṇ* substitution either. This is specifically the scope for *iyaṅ*; since *iyaṅ* occurs here, by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), even if the elision (*lopa*) were to apply, it would affect only the final letter. As for the form *āśiśat*: here there is the possibility of *yaṇ* substitution by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. Even though *yaṇ* occurs here, the desired result is established either because [the subsequent operation] is considered *asiddha* (non-existent), or because the elision of the *ṇi*-affix occurs through the principle of re-occurrence. The same should be understood regarding the scope of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *dīrgha* substitutions.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of the substitution of *ay* for the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [vowels], because the internal (*āṅga*) operation prevails over the external (*vārṇa*) one; thus, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix occurs. Regarding the form *jñīpsati*: there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening [the vowel] by the rules *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt* and *ajjhanagamāṃ sani*. The term "before an affix marked with *ṅ* (aniṭ)" could be omitted. How then would one explain *kārayitā*? [The rule] *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): "if [the lengthening] occurs before an affix marked with *ṅ*, it occurs only before the *niṣṭhā* affixes. However, the reverse restriction—"only before the *niṣṭhā* affixes when they are marked with *ṅ*"—does not apply, because it is impossible for a *niṣṭhā* affix to be *aniṭ*. That impossibility will be explained in the subsequent sūtra.

Alternatively, in the rule *ayāmantālvāyyenviṣṇuṣu*, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) is made as *ṇeḥ*: after a *ṇi*-affix, when followed by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix marked with *iṭ*, the substitution *ay* occurs in place of the *ṇi*, serving as an exception to the elision (*lopa*).
Before an affix marked with *ṅ* or *ṣ* that carries the augment *iṭ*, [the substitution of long *ī* for the final vowel of the root occurs].

The question "What is meant by *seṭ*? arises because, since [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇa*) for roots that do not take the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), this present rule must be intended for the sake of those roots that do take *iṭ* (*seṭ*). The answer is that, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), there is an exclusion precisely of what would have been obtained from the preceding rule. Regarding the example *saṃjñāpitaḥ*: in the rule *vā dānta-śānta-pūrṇa-* (Pāṇini 7.2.27), the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) of the root *jñap* is relied upon—yielding both *jñaptaḥ* and *jñapitaḥ*. As for the phrase "Now again" (*atha punar*): this is an expression used with doubt due to a disagreement among learners (*pratipattṛ-vipratipattyā*).

"Regarding the phrase *kālāvadhāraṇārtham* (for the purpose of determining the time): when the mention of *seṭ* is made, it is understood that the elision (*lopa*) occurs only when the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] is *seṭ*, and not before; thus, a determination of time is obtained. What, then, would happen if the mention of *seṭ* were not made for this purpose? To this he says: *akṛte hi* (if it were not done). [The elision would occur] "when the *ṇi*-elision has taken place," because [the *ṇi*-elision] is obligatory (*nitya*).

For that [augment] occurs whether the *iṭ* has been applied or not; however, the *iṭ* itself is non-eternal (*anitya*), because when there is elision of the *ṇi*, the prohibition "provided it is monosyllabic" (*ekācaḥ*) applies. That whose cause is obstructed by another rule is not considered non-eternal; for when Bāli and Sugrīva were fighting and Bāli was slain by the Lord Rāma, those who pride themselves on their heroism do not consider Bāli to have been weaker than Sugrīva. Indeed, the designation of "non-eternal" is resorted to only when one intends to express the presence or absence of an effect based on its actual operation. [Otherwise], the prohibition of the *iṭ* would result as an undesirable consequence.

Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]; and this has been stated even without relying on the status of being "as if in the place of" (sthānivadbhāva) in the preceding rule as well.

In the Bhāṣya, however, this sūtra is rejected. In the seventh [chapter], the rule *ṇeradhyayane vṛttam* should be divided into three parts, and a reversal of the sequence must be adopted: first, the rule *ṇeḥ*; there, the phrase *niṣṭhāyāṃ neṭ* (from the previous sūtra) continues—meaning that after a root with the causative suffix *ṇi*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*). Then follows *vṛttam*: the form *vṛtta* is thus established as a nipātana, involving the elision of the *ṇi* suffix. For what purpose is this? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): the elision of *ṇi* occurs only here in the past participle, and not elsewhere.

Let it not be that [the suffix] is rendered ineffective or lost; for a restriction (niyama) occurs due to the purpose [of excluding other possibilities], on the grounds that there is nothing else to be enjoined. But here there *is* something to be enjoined: what is it? It is the absence of the secondary element (*guṇa*). If this is so, then by resorting to one of the principles of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*, one [form of the suffix] serves the purpose of restriction, while the other serves the purpose of prohibiting the *guṇa*. Consequently, in the case of *adhyayana*, [the form] *adhyayana* itself results from the elision of the *ṇi* suffix.
The word *śamitṛ* [is derived with the suffix *tṛc*] in the sense of "one who performs the sacrifice. (Pāṇini 6.4.54)

The statement that "in the case of the *tṛc* suffix, this [form] ends in the vocative" is intended as an illustration. In the Sūtra, however, it is in the pure nominative singular. The irregularity (*nipātana*) applies across all case endings because the nominative singular is not intended to be restrictive. Thus, at the time of explaining the meaning of the Sūtra, it was stated generally regarding the *tṛc* suffix that [the form] occurs before vowels beginning with *i*. The usage is likewise of that same nature—as in "O slaughterers (*śāmitāraḥ*), whatever merit is here," and "to the slaughterers (*śamitṛbhyaḥ*) and indeed to the restrainers (*nigṛhītṛbhyaḥ*)."

The form *śāmitram* occurs even when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is applied; furthermore, if the vocative singular ending were intended in the sūtra, it would result in the form *śamitaryajña*.
The substitution of *ū* for the final vowel of a word ending in *u*, *y*, *m*, *t*, *l*, *v*, *ai*, *yy*, *e*, *tn*, or *viṣṇu* occurs before a following vowel. || 6.4.55 ||

Regarding *gaṇḍayantaḥ*: the roots *gaḍi* (in the sense of "to sprinkle") and *maḍi* (in the sense of "to adorn") belong to the *ghaṭādi* group; from these two, the *auṇādika* suffix *jhac* is applied, with *jha* becoming *ant*. Regarding *spṛhayāluḥ*: the suffix *āluc* is applied according to the rule beginning with *spṛhi-gṛhi*. Regarding *spṛhayāyyaḥ*: the suffix *āyya* is applied according to the rule *bhṛ-dakṣi-spṛhibhya āyyaḥ*. Regarding *stanayitnuḥ*: the *auṇādika* suffix *itnuc* is applied. Regarding *pārayiṣṇavaḥ*: the suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied according to the rule *ṇeś chandasi*.

"It should be stated as *na* (negation)" means that if the prohibition of the *ṇilopa* were not in place, then once the *guṇa* had occurred, the substitution of *ay* would be established; furthermore, there would be brevity of syllables (*mātrālāghava*). "For the sake of the subsequent [rule]" refers to the rule *lyapi laghupūrvasya*. Some have taught this with a genitive ending (*laghupūrvasya*), while others have taught it with an ablative ending (*laghupūrvāt*). In the first case, in forms such as *praśamayya*, the rule would not apply to a word ending in a consonant, because here the *ṇi* is not preceded by a light vowel (*laghu*), but rather preceded by a consonant. Nor does it apply when there is no immediate intervention.

Where, then, would [the rule] apply? In cases such as *pragaṇayya* and *prastanayya*, even though once the elision of *al* (*al-lopa*) has occurred, the *ṇi* is no longer preceded by a light syllable, and because the two operations depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*), the elision is not considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), nevertheless, it would still apply here by relying on the fact that it was previously preceded by a light syllable. Similarly, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to cases like *pracikīrṣya*, for although it is now preceded by a heavy syllable, it was previously so by way of its prior state. Therefore, adopting the second alternative, he explains: "from a syllable preceded by a light [syllable]."

But even in this view, since short vowels and the like would be *asiddha* (non-existent) in forms such as *praśamayya*, the substitution of *ay* (*ay-ādeśa*) would not occur; where, then, would it apply? It would apply in cases such as *pramṛdayya gataḥ*, where, after the addition of the causative suffix *ṇic*—meaning "he causes the earth (*mṛd*) to be crushed"—the elision of the penultimate vowel (*ṭilopa*) does not take place due to the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (P. 6.4.163), which maintains the original form of a monosyllabic root. To address this, he says: "of the short vowel, the *yalopa*, and the *āllopa*."
The word *āpaḥ* optionally [retains its original form] before a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel. 6.4.57.

The root *āplṛ* is included here because it belongs to both the *curādi* group (meaning "to cause to obtain") and the *svādi* group (meaning "to pervade"). Here, one might object that since the rule *iṅ adhyayane* takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*), and because of the rule *krīṅjīnāṃ ṇau* which causes the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate vowel], and because of the rule *attihrī* etc. which adds the augment *puK*, the form *adhyāpya* would also result in the form *adhyāpita* when combined with the past participle suffix (*kta*). Since the presence of the prefix *ā-* exists in both cases, the root should be cited with its *anubandha* [the marker *ṅ*]. Therefore, it should be read as *āplṛ*. From the word *āplṛ*, by applying the suffix *ṅas*, and because the vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ* are considered homogeneous (*savarṇa*), the substitution of *u* for *at* occurs by the rule *ata ut*, and the *ṛ* is replaced by *r* by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*. Thus, the form *āpūrtaḥ* is established.

In this context, because the *rap* pratyāhāra is included [in the rule], the *l* follows; there is the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the *s*. To the objection that "then it should indeed be recited in that way," he says: "No, because of the substitution of *ṅ*."
In the sense of completion (niṣṭhā), [the suffix *kta*] is used except when it has the sense of the agent (*aṇyadartha*). Pāṇini 6.4.60.

The meaning of the *kṛtya* suffix *ṇyat* is "the state of being" (*bhāva*) and "the object" (*karman*). Although in the list beginning with *bhavya-geya-* (Pāṇini 3.4.68), the agent is also optionally denoted by the two words ending in *ṇyat*, namely *āplāvya* and *āpātya*, nevertheless, due to the proximity of the word *kṣiyaḥ*, only the meaning of *ṇyat* belonging to that [list] is excluded.

Thus, in the example *prakṣīṇam idaṃ devadattasya* ("this has been wasted by Devadatta"), the genitive case is used for the agent according to the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaś ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.68). Regarding the term *adhikaraṇe*, the phrase "the suffix *kta*" is to be supplied. The same applies to the expression *akṣitam* when it denotes the state of being (*bhāve*).
Or [the suffix *ktvā* is used] after [a verbal root] in the sense of reviling or dejection. 6.4.61.

*kṣitāyuḥ*: here, as before, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). *kṣīṇakaḥ*: here the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of compassion (*anukampāyām*). This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*). It applies only when the meaning is not that of the root itself (*aṇyadarthe*)—for example: "everything has been consumed by him" (*kṣitaṃ sarvam asya*), or "this poor man's [wealth] has been consumed" (*kṣitam asya tapasvinaḥ*).

In the case of the affixes *syas*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās* when used in the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or passive (*karman*), there is optionally the substitution of *ciṇvadiṭ* for the roots ending in *a*, those containing *han*, *grah*, and *dṛś* as taught in the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*).

*Ciṇīva ciṇvat*: here, the suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*, because the locative case is specified in the rule *syasicsīyuṭtāsiṣu* to indicate the point of comparison (*pratiyogin*). For example: "There is a palace in Pāṭaliputra as there is in Mathurā. By the phrase "in the domain of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*)," he shows that the locative case is used to indicate the scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*) according to the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

If it were understood that the rule applies to those *sy*-class suffixes (*syādayaḥ*) which occur in the sense of the passive and the impersonal (*bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*), then only the *sīyuṭ* augment would be specifically qualified, while the *syādayaḥ* themselves would not be qualified; for the substitutes of *la* (*lādeśa*) express the passive and impersonal senses, and the *sīyuṭ* is a part of them. Thus, the *syādayaḥ* would remain unqualified, and the *sīyuṭ* alone would be qualified because it is a constituent part of them.

Now, when the suffix denoting the action or the object (*bhāva* or *karman*) is itself expressed by the words *bhāva* and *karman*, then the meaning would be: "those *syādi* suffixes which occur after a suffix expressing the action or the object. In that case, the *syādi* suffixes would be specified, but the *sīyuṭ* augment would not be specified; for it is impossible for that which is a part of the suffix (*tadbhakta*) to stand in a temporal sequence of priority or posteriority with the suffix itself. Therefore, for the sake of including all cases, a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*) alone is appropriate, as in the rule: "when [the suffix] has *ciṇ* or *vat*, then the augment *iṭ* and *caṅ* occur," because the letter *c* in *caṅ* serves the purpose of indicating a simultaneous application (*sanniyoga*).

Regarding the question "Whose [is it]? (kasya): An augment (*āgama*) belongs to that which is indicated by the genitive case; whereas *syat* and the others are indicated by the locative case. Since [the rule] *aj-jhan-agraha-dṛśām* is indicated by the genitive, and the term *aṅgasya* ("of the stem") is understood from the context, the question arises from one who considers it a reversal [of the expected relationship], thinking that it is more logical for the augments to belong to the stems ending in vowels and so forth that are indicated by the genitive. [The answer is: "[It belongs] to *syat*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tāsī* alone. He asks, "How so? and replies, "For they are the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*)," meaning they are present in proximity.

[Objection: But surely the *aṅga* (stem) is also the subject under discussion and possesses the appropriate case-ending; to this he replies: "But of the *aṅga*... [The objection continues: "Because it contradicts the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*). Alternatively: In the seventh [chapter], a rule-division (*yogavibhāga*) is made: "There is *iṭ* for the *ārdhadhātuka*. This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim): whatever *iṭ*-augment there may be, all of it should be understood as belonging only to the *ārdhadhātuka*. Therefore, this *aṭ*-augment occurs only for *sy-* and the others, not for the *aṅga*.

"What, then, [is meant]?"—this is the question: is it that only what is explicitly prescribed for the *ciṇ* suffix is extended [by analogy], or rather, whatever is merely observed in the *ciṇ* suffix? In this regard, the second position is adopted, as shown by the verse: "The *vṛddhi* is like that of the *ciṇ*" (*ciṇvadbṛddhiḥ*). Just as there is *vṛddhi* in the *ciṇ* suffix, so it is desired even in the *syat*-class [optative] endings—as in *ghāniṣyate*. This is one purpose; likewise for the subsequent cases as well. The extension should be applied according to the requirements through its connection with each individual case.

Regarding the form *dāyiṣyate*: by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, the suffix *yuk* is added; this is specifically prescribed for the *ciṇ*-substitute. Furthermore, regarding the substitution of *k* (as in *aghāni*) seen in the rule *ho hanteṛṇinneṣu*, that too is a purpose [for the *ciṇvadbhāva*]. This also is specifically prescribed for the *ciṇ*-substitute: in the forms *śamiṣyate* and *śāmiṣyate*, after the root *śam* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the shortening of *mit* roots applies; then, in the future tense (*lṛṭ*) with the suffix *sya*, there is an option for lengthening due to the *ciṇvadbhāva*, and the elision of the *ṇic* occurs by the rule *taṇeraniṭi*.

Now, it is stated that [the suffix] is *aniṭ*, yet this [suffix] is *seṭ*; therefore, he says: "And the *iṭ* is as if non-existent" (*asiddha*). When the *ṇi*-elision prescribed by the rules up to the *bhā*-section is to be performed, the *iṭ* prescribed by the rules up to the *bhā*-section—as if it were *ciṇvadiṭ*—is as if non-existent. Thus, the meaning is that the *ṇi*-elision is established because [the root] begins with what is *aniṭ*. The word "me" is a statement made by the author of the Sūtras while acting as his own authority (*ātmānam sūtrakāram manyamānasya vacanam*).

But surely, the scope for this *ciṇvad-iṭ* is those [roots] which are *aniṭ* (lacking an *iṭ* augment) and for which there is no specific rule (*pratipadavidhāna*) such as "after roots ending in *ṛ* or *han*, before *sya*" and so on; whereas the scope for the rule *ārddhadhātukasya iḍ valādeḥ* is where this [former] does not apply. However, in a case that is the domain of both the *seṭ* [rule] and this sūtra, the latter—namely *ārddhadhātukasya iḍ valādeḥ*—would prevail due to its higher status (*paratva*). How then can [the former] be considered *asiddha*? To this he says: "And this is obligatory (*nitya*)."

This [augment] *iṭ* prescribed by the rule *ciṇvadiṭ* is optional (*anitya*). For even when the *iṭ* characterized by the condition of beginning with a *val* letter has been applied, it remains applicable; and even when it has not been applied, it remains applicable, because this [augment] does not depend upon the status of being preceded by a *val* letter. However, once this [first *iṭ*] has been applied, the *iṭ* characterized by the condition of beginning with a *val* letter does not apply. Therefore, the *iṭ* caused by a *val* letter is optional. [The term] *vadhātī* means "he who possesses non-application due to the absence of a cause" (*vidhāta*: non-application due to the absence of a cause; he who has that is *vadhātī*). Thus, because it is permanent (*nitya*), this very [augment] occurs even after roots that would otherwise take the *seṭ* augment; and since this [latter *iṭ*] is considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the fault of the non-elimination of the *ṇi*-suffix does not arise.

And by this very [rule], the *iṭ* must necessarily be desired even after [roots ending in] *seṭ* [vowels]; otherwise, the substitution of *ciṇvadbhāva*, which is conditioned by this *iṭ*, would not occur either. Nor can it be argued that this [substitution] is also non-eternal (*anitya*) because it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*), for in the view of the *ākṛti* (the class), there is no difference in the word-form. [The rule states] "the lengthening of the *iṭ* of the present subject," because the *iṭ* characterized by the condition of being preceded by a consonant-group (*valādi*) is the subject under discussion. [Regarding the phrase] "when the *guṇa* has been applied": this is because [the *guṇa*] is both subsequent and obligatory. [The phrase] "it occurs because of the mention of 'upadeśa'" means that although the root *kṛ* is not vowel-ending (*anajanta*) at a later stage, it is indeed vowel-ending (*ajanta*) at the time of its original enunciation (*upadeśa*).

If the *ciṇ* substitution were to apply to everything seen [prescribed] for the *ciṇ*, then the substitutes *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅi* would also result, since they too are seen there; therefore, he says: "that which is prescribed under the heading of the *aṅga*. Only that which is seen in the *ciṇ* and is prescribed by taking *aṅgasya* as the governing context (*prakṛtya*) is extended [by atideśa], because of its immediate proximity. And since the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅi* are not of such a nature, they are not extended. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The *ciṇvat* treatment applies to the *sīyuṭ* affix by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), because of the absence of *vadh*."

The scope for the substitution *vadh* is: *vadhyāt*, *vadhyāstām*, *vadhyāsuḥ*. The scope for the inclusion of the root *han* [in Pāṇini 6.4.62] for the purpose of the *ciṇvadbhāva* treatment is: *dhāniṣyate*, *adhāniṣyata*, *adhāniṣātām*, *aghāniṣata*, and *ghāniṣīṣṭa*. When both [rules] would apply here, the *ciṇvadbhāva* occurs by virtue of the "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*). Now, why does the substitution of *vadh* not occur again after the *ciṇvadbhāva* has taken effect, given the principle that "when a conflict has occurred once, what is sublated remains sublated"? [The answer is: because of the understanding that the rule applies only once.

Now, in the second chapter, regarding the rule *tatrārdhadhātuke*, is this a locative of occasion (*nimitta-saptamī*)? If so, would not the substitution of *vadh-* for *han-* be internal (*antaraṅga*)? This is not the case; because of the specific mention of *liṅ* [in the rule *liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*], it is a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). However, where there is no such specific mention—as in rules like *asterbhūḥ*—there it must be understood as a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*) for the sake of establishing forms such as *bhavya*.
The augment *yuṭ* is applied after the root *dīṅ* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

Regarding the statement "because of the mention of *dīṅ* in the ablative (pañcamī)": if this were in the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī), the suffix *yuṭ* would apply only to the beginning of *dīṅ*. However, since there is a mention in both cases—the ablative and the genitive—and the ablative mention is stronger, when the genitive is substituted for the genitive [in the rule *aci*], *yuṭ* occurs after that which begins with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). The mention in the locative (saptamī), however, is for the sake of subsequent rules and for the purpose of the rule regarding the beginning of that [following element]. And it is also because of the force of the formulation itself.

If the substitution of *yaṇ* were to occur because the augment *yuṭ* is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), then the prescription of *yuṭ* would be purposeless, since there would be no difference in form between [the forms] *upadidīye* and *upadidye*. Nor can it be argued that there is a difference due to the hearing of two *yakāra*s, because in the alternative view (*pakṣe*) where *ya* is elided by the rule "there is elision of *yama*s before *yama*" (*halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*), the elision of *ya* is prescribed. Nor is there a difference in audible phonetic realization (*śrutibheda*) in that alternative view, since this is already established by the very prescription of doubling (*dvirvacana*) in the rule "doubling occurs after a semi-vowel before a semivowel" (*yaṇo mayo dve*). Furthermore, it must be considered what kind of difference in audible realization could exist regarding a single or multiple *yakāra*s following a consonant.

Regarding the term *upādāna*: by the rule *mīnāti-minoti-dīṅāṃ lyapi ca*, there is the substitution of *ā* [for the vowel of *dī*]; the specific mention of *dīṅ* with its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is so that this substitution does not occur in the case of the elision of *yaṅ*.
The elision of the final *ā* occurs before an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k*, and also before an affix beginning with *iṭ*.

In this context, regarding the three conditions—"before a vowel," "before a suffix marked with K or Ṅ," and "before an ārdhadhātuka suffix"—since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), twelve possible positions arise due to the potential combination of the augment *iṭ* with any one of these three, whether that one has experienced the other two as qualifiers, both have been experienced as qualifiers, or none have been experienced as qualifiers.

In this regard, if first of all the conjunction of *iṭ* with [the suffix] is understood to occur prior to its connection with the qualifier—whether it be that the suffix implied by the *aṅga* is qualified, or that [it is understood as] "in a suffix beginning with *aj* when *iṭ* follows"—then the mention of *iṭ* would be for the sake of excluding those beginning with *aj*. This is because a conjunction of *iṭ* (which begins with *aj*) with a suffix beginning with *aj* is impossible. And in that case, the two qualifiers (*ṅit* and *ārdhadhātuka*) would apply only to [suffixes] beginning with *aj*, since *iṭ* cannot possess the property of being *ṅit* when it begins with a consonant (*hal*), given its status as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, and because there would be no deviation [from this rule].

Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of elision (lopa) in forms such as *dāsīya*. Now, if it is argued that there is a conjunction with the vowel (*ac*) qualified by *kṅit*—namely, "it occurs when *kṅit* follows" and "when *iṭ* follows"—then the aforementioned fault does not arise. Alternatively, if there is a conjunction with the vowel (*ac*) qualified by *kit*—namely, "it occurs when *kṅit* follows" and "when *iṭ* follows"—then the mention of *iṭ* serves both for the sake of cases where it is not *kṅit* and for the sake of cases where the suffix begins with a vowel other than *a* (an-ādi), as in *papitha* and *dāsīya*. Or, if there is a conjunction with the vowel (*ac*) qualified by *ārdhadhātuka*, then the mention of *iṭ* serves for the sake of cases where it is not *kṅit*, for the sake of cases where the suffix begins with a vowel other than *a*, and for the sake of *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes.

In *papitha*, *dāsīya*, and *vyatyare*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision (*lopa*) by the mere presence of the suffix *iṇ*. Thus, with this conjunction (*samuccaya*), there are four positions. Likewise, with *ārdhadhātuka* and with *kṅit*, there are twelve positions. In both of these cases, when qualified by the aforementioned [conditions], the same faults (*doṣa*) apply as those which we have already stated.

If there is a conjunction with an *ardhadhātuka* suffix that is not qualified by [the condition of] being *kṅit*, then the mention of *iṭ* would not be for the sake of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, the rule would apply only in cases such as *vyatyare*. If, on the other hand, there is a conjunction with an *ardhadhātuka* suffix qualified by being *kṅit*, then the mention of *iṭ* would be for the sake of [suffixes] that are neither *kṅit* nor *ardhadhātuka*—as in *papitha* and *vyatyare*. Or, if there is a conjunction with an *ardhadhātuka* suffix qualified by beginning with a vowel (*aj*), then the mention of *iṭ* would be for the sake of [suffixes] that neither begin with a vowel nor are *ardhadhātuka*—as in *dāsīya* and *vyatyare*. Or, if there is a conjunction with a *kṅit* suffix qualified by beginning with a vowel...

There is a conjunction [of the two conditions]. Therefore, the mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of [roots] beginning with *an* and for the sake of *kṅit* [affixes]—as in *dāsīya* and *papitha*. Alternatively, if there is a conjunction with *kṅit* as qualified by being an *ārdhadhātuka*, then the mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of non-*ārdhadhātuka* [affixes] and for the sake of non-*kṅit* [affixes]—as in *vyatyare* and *papitha*. Thus, these eleven positions are flawed.

The twelfth alternative remains: that there is a conjunction with *kṅit* in its unqualified sense. And in this alternative, because the two qualifiers—*aci* and *ārdhadhātuke*—apply without distinction, both *kṅit* and *iṭ* would apply; thus, the mention of *eṭ* serves the purpose of excluding *aṅit*. Consequently, in forms such as *papitha*, the elision of *ā* (by P. 6.4.64) occurs, as in *dāsīya* and *vyatyare*.

Thus, [the augment] does not occur before vowels beginning with *a* or in non-ārdhadhātuka suffixes. This is the faultless position, which he adopts: "The augment *iṭ* occurs before non-ārdhadhātuka suffixes beginning with a vowel. Regarding the rule *kṅiti ca*: the phrase "in non-ārdhadhātuka suffixes beginning with a vowel" is to be supplied as a carry-over (*anuṣaṅga*). In the example *dāsīya*, the suffix is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), in the first person singular; the augment *iṭ* is applied, and then *an* replaces *iṭ*. Here, because the *sīyuṭ* augment is a part of the *iṭ*, the *iṭ* itself is not considered to begin with a vowel (*ajāditva*).
The substitution of *ī* occurs for *yā* and *āti*. 6-4-65.
The prescription of the long vowel is for the sake of subsequent rules—as in *adhyagīṣṭa*—but here, since a *guṇa* substitute ought to occur, only the short vowel should be prescribed.
Before an affix beginning with *h*, the final vowel of the roots *dhūm*, *asthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *jā*, *hā*, and *atisā* is replaced by *ī*.

By the mention of *mā*, there is the inclusion of all [roots]: *meṅ* in the sense of "sending forth" (*praṇidāna*), *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māna*), and *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māna*). Similarly, regarding *gā* as well, there must be stated that there is the inclusion of all forms of *gā*: *gāṅ* in the sense of "going" (*gati*), *gai* in the sense of "singing" (*śabda*), *gā* in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*) in the Veda (*chandas*), *iṇ* becoming *gā* in the *luṅ* tense, and *iṇ* being treated like *ik*. This is because of the statement: "In the mentions of *gā* and *ā*, there is no distinction," which means that by the mention of *gā* and *ā*, there is the inclusion of all those forms containing *gā*. Regarding *jahateḥ*: this refers to *ohāk* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāga*). Regarding *jihāteḥ*: this refers to *ohāṅ* in the sense of "going" (*gati*). If the rule *bhṛñām it* were applied, causing the *it* substitution in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the grammatical citation *jahāti* would not be possible.

Granted that there might be the contingency of [the substitution of] *jihvā* due to the mention of *hāg*, it is nevertheless not so applied. This very point, etc., has been explained under the rule *janasanakhanām*. Regarding the substitution of *ī* (ītvam), there is a prohibition concerning the letter *v* (*vakāra-pratiṣedha*). "Prohibition concerning the letter *v*" means a prohibition based on the status of the letter *v* as a cause; the meaning is that the substitution of *ī* does not occur when *v* begins [the following element]. [Examples: *ghṛtaṃ pibanti* → *ghṛtapāvānaḥ*; *vasāṃ pibanti* → *vasāpāvānaḥ*. In the case of the suffix *kvanip*, the substitution of *ī* does not occur.

In the case of *dhīvarī* and *pīvarī*, the vowel *ī* is derived from the *uṇādi* suffix; alternatively, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the roots *dhā* and *pā*. Accordingly, in the rule *sthaḥ ka ca*, the absence of the *ī* vowel is cited as an example when the suffix *kvip* is applied.
Or [the elision of *n* occurs] after another [vowel], such as in the case of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), etc. 6.4.68.

Regarding the word *stheyāt*: if another [rule] were not included, the previous rule would find scope in other instances; furthermore, since this rule might also apply to cases such as *glāyāt* and so forth, where both rules would otherwise apply simultaneously, this very rule would prevail due to its posteriority. Therefore, the inclusion of another [term] is necessary.
Not so, even in the case of *lyap*. (Pāṇini 6.4.69)
As for what was stated: there is the substitution of *ī*, but not the subsequent substitution of *e*, because [the latter] would have no occasion to apply.

Regarding *mayateḥ id anyatarasyām*: in the form *apamitya*, the suffix *ktvā* is applied according to the rule *udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre*; once the substitution of *i* for *ā* has been made, the augment *tuk* is added.
The [vṛddhi] substitution occurs for the vowels of words beginning with *aja* and *āḍa*, as well as for those ending in *āṭ*. 6.4.72.

In forms such as *aijyata*, since the roots *yaj*, *vap*, and *vah* begin with a consonant (*hal*), the augment *āṭ* would not apply; however, once *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) has occurred, it will apply because they then begin with a vowel (*aj*). Since the augment *āṭ* must occur before the substitutes for *l* (the *lādeśas*), and subsequently the *lādeśas*, then the *yak* suffix, and finally the *samprasāraṇa*, [the author] says: "In this case... The *lādeśas* are *antaraṅga* (internal) because they depend only on the presence of the *lakāra*. The augment *āṭ*, however, is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends on both a specific *lakāra* and the verbal base (*aṅga*). Furthermore, because its application occurs whether or not the other operations have already taken place, the formation of the *yak* suffix is considered *nitya* (obligatory).

[Objection: But surely the augment *aṭ* is also permanent (*nitya*), since it applies whether the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) has been applied or not; consequently, by virtue of its priority, the augment *aṭ* alone would apply. To this he replies: "Because [the application] results in a different word-form" (*śabdāntaraprāpteḥ*). He demonstrates precisely how it results in a different word-form with the words: "For when [the suffix] has been applied" (*kṛte hi*). The augment *aṭ* belongs to the stem (*aṅga*); once the suffix has been applied, because it results in a different word-form, it is non-permanent (*anitya*). For instance, when the *aṭ* has been applied, it occurs before the root that begins with that [augment]; whereas when it has not been applied, it occurs before the root alone. Therefore he says: "Of a different word-form" (*śabdāntarasya*).

The meaning is that this *paribhāṣā* applies when an augment (*āgama*) or a substitute (*ādeśa*) is prescribed for that which is indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and not when there is an indication by the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Regarding the phrase "precisely because of its permanence" (*nityatvāt*): the particle *eva* is used for emphasis; it was stated previously that [the rule] sets aside the augment *aṭ* precisely because of its permanence, and in this case as well, that same reason applies. However, the augment *aṭ* does not apply once *saṃprasāraṇa* has taken place, because it has already been set aside by *āṭ*. The underlying intention is that the principle "that whose cause is obstructed by another rule" is not universally applicable.

This application [of the rule] could be avoided: let there simply be *aṭ* for roots beginning with vowels and so forth by the preceding rule. [Objection: How then will the *vṛddhi* substitution be obtained in the case of *āṭaśca*? [Response: I shall state it as *aṭaśca*. [Objection: In that case, it would also apply here: *akārṣīt*, because *acīti* is still in force. [Response: Even so, in the case of *asvapo hasati*—where *svap* takes *laṅ*, *sip*, *aṭ* for *sip* according to "gārgyagālavayoḥ", *rutva*, and *utva* according to "haśi ca"—there would be the undesirable consequence of *vṛddhi*. [Response: I shall state the *vṛddhi* substitution specifically when a root begins with a vowel.

In that case, it should be stated as "before a verbal root" (*dhātau*). It need not be stated; the phrase "after a prefix before a root ending in *ṛ*" (*upasargād ṛti dhātau*) is drawn back [from the previous rule] to this point. In the rule *aṭaś ca*, the word *ca* ("and") serves to conjoin that very same prescription—so that even when there is an alternative rule for *aṭ*, only the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) occurs, thereby overriding it. Consequently, in forms such as *aṭiṭat*, even though the subsequent rule *ato guṇe* (P. 6.1.97) which prescribes *pararūpa* (the single substitute of the form of the following vowel) would apply, it is overridden and *vṛddhi* alone takes place. This is just as in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), where in the rules *ausīyat auṅkarīyat* (Vārttika on P. 6.1.95), *usyapadāntāt* (P. 6.1.96), and *omāṅoś ca* (P. 6.1.95), [the *vṛddhi* prevails].

Thus, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule does not apply. Now, the mention of *āṬ* is for the sake of the subsequent rules, as it is seen even in the Vedic language—as in *suruco vena āvaḥ*. Here, the lengthening will be a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon, as in the case of *pūruṣaḥ* and *nārakaḥ*. Just so, in the case of *āsann* as well, when *āṬ* has been applied while still in the state of *l* (the substitute for *sip*), the situation is *a-as-l*. Here, both the *vṛddhi* (prescribed by *aṭaśca*) and the substitutes for *l* would be applicable; however, because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the substitution for *l* takes precedence.

The substitution of *vṛddhi* depends upon the condition that the suffix beginning with a vowel follows; however, once the substitution of *la* has been made, both *vṛddhi* and the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* would apply. In that case, because it is *antaraṅga*, *vṛddhi* takes precedence. Furthermore, since they have different bases (*nānāśrayatva*), the rule "that which pertains to vowels (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to suffixes (*āṅga*)" does not apply. Thus, once *vṛddhi* has been effected, there is no elision of the long *ā* due to the specification of the short *a* (the *tapara* marker).

And here, in the case of *āyan*—derived from the root *iṇ* in the *laṅ* tense with the augment *aṭ*, resulting in *a-i-an*—the rule *aṭaśca* would require Vṛddhi, and the rule *iṇo yaṇ* would require the substitution of *yaṇ*. In that situation, because Vṛddhi is internal (*antaraṅga*), and because "an operation pertaining to a suffix (*āṅga*) is stronger than one based on a phoneme (*cavārṇa*) when they have different bases," the desired result would not be achieved. However, by splitting the rule into two—*iṇo yaṇ* and *eḥ*—the *yaṇ* substitution is prescribed for an *iṇ* ending in an *i*-vowel; since this does not apply to the single letter *e*, the desired form is established through the substitution of *āy*. Regarding this, there are two verses: "If it is argued that [the forms] beginning with *aj* are already established by the augment *aṭ* for the purpose of Vṛddhi, then one should remember that the Vṛddhi of the augment *aṭ* applies in the case of the root *asvap* in *halati*."
The substitute *pararūpa* occurs by virtue of the *guṇa* [rule] when *om*, *āṅ*, or *u* follow; it is the same as that [substitution].
For the sake of Vedic meter (*chandas*), there is frequently a long vowel (*dīrgha*) due to the internal application (*antaraṅga*) of the rules for *iṇ* and *asti*.
Thus, [the substitution does not occur] when used with *māṅ* (prohibitive *mā*). (Pāṇini 6.1.74)

If this were a prohibition specifically of the immediately preceding *āṭ* alone, then it would have prescribed the prohibition in connection with that very element—namely, "āṭ before vowel-initial roots, except in conjunction with *māṅ*. However, because the prohibition is stated independently, it is understood as a prohibition of everything under discussion; thus he says: "that which was prescribed for the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ* does not take place. An example for the *luṅ* has not been shown there, because such a case is impossible when *māṅ* is in conjunction.

The inclusion of the word "itself" (sva) [in the definition] is for the purpose that the prohibition should not apply when the word *mā* is a substitute for *asam*, as in the rule "the second case endings [are used] after *tvam* and *mām*. Thus, there would be no prohibition in a construction such as *sukhinaṃ mā akārṣīt*. But then, how is it [to be explained] in the case of *mā bālipathamanvagāḥ*?
It is said that the sages follow their own will; they do not follow the scriptures.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the augment *aṭ* is frequently applied even when the prohibitive particle *mā* is used.

"May they not sow in your field. In your field—that is, in your wife—may the seeds of others, the virility of others, not be sown; may they not have been sown. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the passive sense of the root *vapi*; there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) to the *parasmaipada* (active voice), *jus* for *jhi*, the addition of *sic*, and the *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *vadavraja*. However, having begun with the observation that [the augment] occurs even in connection with *māṅ*, the reading *avāpsuḥ* is found; yet such a recension is nowhere observed. [The form] *abhitthāḥ* is from the root *bhid* with the suffix *thās*; the *sic* is elided by the rule *jhalo jhali*. [The form] *āvaḥ* has already been explained in the commentary on the preceding sūtra.
The word *hari* [is used] in the sense of "O! (an address). 6-4-76.

Regarding the word *daghra*: one might object that since the substitution of *rebh* would apply here by virtue of its higher status, the elision of the final vowel (*āllopa*) would not occur because the stem would no longer begin with a vowel (*an-ādi*). To this, he replies: "Because the substitution of *rebh* for the suffix *ghañ* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*)."

[Objection: Even so, once the substitution of *re* has been applied, the augment *iṭ* would still apply to that very [root]. Nor is the substitution of *re* useless, since it finds its purpose in roots such as *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, and others which lack the augment *iṭ*. To this, he says: "In this case" (*atre*). But how can there be the substitution of *re* for that word *thairai* which is derived through grammatical rules (*lākṣaṇika*), or how is it that, having first applied the augment *iṭ* to it, there is no fault of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) when it subsequently applies to itself? To this, he says: "And for the sake of that" (*tadarthe ca*). The meaning is that because of the dual-number indication, neither of the two faults occurs.

In place of the final vowel of a verbal root ending in *aci* (a vowel other than *a*), as well as in the case of the roots *śnu*, *dhātu*, and *bhru*, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are made respectively before the suffixes beginning with *y* and *v*.

*i* and *u* form *yu*; [the term] *yvoḥ* refers to those two. This is a mention of the short vowels, yet the grammatical operation applies to the long ones as well, due to the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇāt*). Since *yvoḥ* is a mention of the phonemes themselves, there is an application of the rule regarding that which ends in them (*tadantavidhi*) to roots such as *śnā*. In this context, since the substitutes apply to what is specifically indicated (*nirdiśyamāna*), the final element is already established; thus, the letter *ṅ* is for the sake of clarity. [The examples] beginning with *āpnuvanti* are illustrations where the root is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) and preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*); otherwise, in cases like *hu-śnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke* and *eranekācaḥ*, the *yaṇ* replacement would have to occur.
However, forms such as *luluvatuḥ* certainly do occur, because of the rule *oḥ supi*.

Regarding the phrase *iyaṅbhyām*: the scope for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is, for example, *cetā* and *gauḥ*; the scope for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is, for example, *cikṣiyatuḥ*, *luluvatuḥ*, *cayanam*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanam*, and *lāvakaḥ*. In cases where both would apply simultaneously, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

Regarding *tanuvam*: since it is not a stem ending in a semi-vowel (*adhātu*), the substitution *uvaṅ* does not apply [by default], and thus it is prescribed here. Regarding *tanvam*: by the rule *vā chandasi*, when the case-ending *am* is present, there is an absence of the *pūrva-rūpa* (single-substitution), and thus *yaṇ* applies. Regarding *viṣvam*: from the root *viṣ* with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *satsūdviṣa...*—here, the substitution *yaṇ* would have applied invariably by the rule *oḥ supi*.
In the *yajurveda* and similar texts, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur; in the *bahvṛca* (Ṛgveda), *yaṇ* occurs.
The doubling of a consonant occurs before a non-homogeneous vowel following an *abhyāsa* (reduplication syllable). 6-4-78.

This [sūtra] is commenced because the rule was previously prescribed for a suffix beginning with a vowel following the initial member of a compound. Regarding "iyeṣa": whatever needs to be said concerning the status of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as the original element) of the *guṇa* (vocalic strengthening) in this context has already been stated under the rule *dvirvacane'ci*.
[The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a feminine [stem]. 6.4.79.

Regarding the phrase "of this word *strī*": there is no inclusion of words ending in feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*) or words that function in the sense of a female (*stryartha*), because of the specific indications such as *āṇ nadyāḥ* (P. 7.3.112) and *kumāryā vayasi* (P. 6.2.95). [The mention of *strī*] is for the sake of the subsequent rule; thus, in what follows, only the term *striyāḥ* (of the feminine) should be carried over, so that it does not apply to verbal roots ending in *śnu*, nor to the word *bhrū*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs in place of *iṇ*. (Pāṇini 6.4.81)

In this context, following the explanation of the meaning of the Sūtra, it is stated in some places: "Since [the substitution] is established by *iko yaṇ aci* due to its being internal (*antaraṅgatvāt*), this statement is for the purpose of indicating that when both [rules] have the same basis (*samānāśraye*), that which pertains to the base (*āṅgam*) is stronger than that which pertains to the phoneme (*vārṇāt*). This is incorrect; for he will state later that "this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *iyaṅ* substitute. How then could the *yaṇ* substitution apply in the domain of *iyaṅ*? [The answer is: "This is an exception to the *iyaṅ* substitute. The meaning is that it is an exception specifically to the *iyaṅ* substitute. Why? He says: "Exceptions [occur] in the middle" (*madhye'pavādāḥ*).

This being the case, he demonstrates what is established as desired with the words "by virtue of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For if, because of its introduction before another rule has already applied, every subsequent rule were to subvert the *yaṇ* [substitution], then it would also apply in the domain of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Now, why was it not simply stated as "of *iṇ*, *na*" (P. 7.1.56)? For, in the case of the *iyaṅ* substitute...

If [the substitution of] *yaṇ* were prohibited by the rule "iko yaṇ aci," then *yaṇ* would simply not occur; oh, what a subtle observer is the Beloved of the Gods! For this too was not seen: in *īyiva*, *īyima*, and in the passive *īyire*, when *iyaṅ* is prohibited, the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of vowels (*sarvārṇadīrghaḥ*) would occur. Therefore, *yaṇ* alone must be prescribed.
In a word consisting of more than one vowel, the final vowel is replaced by *i* when it is not preceded by a conjunct consonant. (Pāṇini 6.4.82)

"By that, the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is qualified. Even though the conjunction is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to the meaning of the other word, nevertheless, it is precisely that which is qualified by the term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*), because there is no other purpose for the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of that term. [Objection: There is this purpose: "I shall qualify the *i*-vowel. [Response: This is not so; for if an *i*-vowel follows a non-root and is not preceded by a conjunction, it must necessarily undergo *yaṇ*-substitution according to the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, as in the examples *kumārthau* and *kumāryaḥ*.

[Objection: "Surely, just as in the case of *grahamaṇi*, the *yaṇ* [substitution] should not override the *pūrvasavarṇa* [dīrgha]; therefore, the vowel *i* should be qualified by the word 'root' (*dhātu*) itself. [Response: No, they say; the *yaṇ* is for the purpose of overriding *iyaṅ*. Furthermore, there is no possibility of *iyaṅ* applying to a root [in this context]. How then can the recurrence of the term 'root' (*dhātu*) be justified as being for the purpose of excluding non-roots? Therefore, it has been well said: "The conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is merely subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), is what is qualified."

[The word *aṅga*] is used as a qualifier so that [the rule] does not apply to [the whole word]. Otherwise, by virtue of the governing context (*adhikāra*), the mention of "not preceded by a consonant cluster" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) would qualify that very [word] which is proximate [to it]; consequently, the rule would undesirably apply even in cases such as *yavakriyau* and *yaṣakriyaḥ*, for in these instances, the *aṅga* is not preceded by a consonant cluster as its initial member. Now, one might object: "But *yv-oh* is the subject under discussion; if *eḥ* were not stated there, then *yaṇ* would also apply to *oḥ* in forms like *luluvatuḥ*, and thus [the mention of *eḥ*] would be intended to exclude that as well. To this, he says:

Regarding the statement *luluva-lurllavu-rit-etat-tv-iti*: since the form *luluvaḥ* is established even without explicitly stating *eḥ*, the rule *oḥ supi* serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the substitution of *v* for *u*] occurs only before a *sup* suffix. However, the reverse restriction—that it occurs only before a *sup* suffix—is not intended, because of the prohibition of *yaṇ* in the rule *na bhūsudhiyoḥ*. Consequently, since forms such as *luluvaḥ* are already established by this very restriction, the mention of *eḥ* would be redundant for the purpose of excluding *oḥ*; therefore, the previously stated purpose remains valid.

If, however, by the dual-number indication in *asaṃyogapūrvayor*, this qualification were stated as referring only to the two [consonants], then the mention of *oḥ* could have been omitted. [The objection] "it would not occur here either" means: if there were no connection with a verbal root (*dhātu*), or if [the rule] were not qualified by connection with a verbal root. In some places, the reading is "so that it may also occur here," where the meaning is that the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs because it is the subject under discussion. Regarding "by a gati or a kāraka," and so forth: this is merely a desired result (*iṣṭi*). In the case of *paramaniyau*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kartṛ*).
The substitution of *o* for the final vowel of a stem ending in *u*, before a case-ending beginning with *s* or *p*. (Pāṇini 6.4.83)
Regarding *sakṛllvau*: because it functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), *sakṛt* possesses the status of a *kāraka*.
Regarding *kaṭapruvau*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvibvacipracchi...* and so forth, and there is also lengthening of the vowel.
And [the word] *varṣābhva*. 6.4.84.
This is a statement made because the prohibition [of the *ṣat* augment] by the rule *na bhūsudhiyoḥ* would otherwise apply.
"And *punarbhū*" and so forth; thus, the formulation of the sūtra is *punarvarṣāreṣu bhuvaḥ*.
*Na bhūsudhiyoḥ* || 6.4.85 ||
By the word *bhū*, that which ends in it is understood, because the simple [root] cannot undergo *yaṇ* substitution.

Nor is there a prohibition of *uvaṅ*, because [the rule for *uvaṅ*] is interrupted [by other rules], and because of the specific introduction of the rule *varṣābhvaś ca*. Regarding *sudhiyau*: from the root *dhyai* with the suffix *kvip*; the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs due to the inclusion of the root *dṛś* [in the relevant rule].
The substitution of *u* for the root-vowel occurs before the suffixes *hu*, *śnu*, and those that are *sārvadhātuka*.

The terms *anekācaḥ* (having more than one vowel), *asaṃyogapūrvasya* (not preceded by a conjunct consonant), and *oḥ* (of *u*) carry over [from the previous rule]. Although it is an invariable fact that the suffixes *hu* and *śnu* end in a vowel (*u*), the term *asaṃyogapūrvasya* is nevertheless carried over as a qualifier for *oḥ*, so that the prohibition may apply there; it is carried over for this purpose so that it does not apply to *hu* and *śnu*. For if these were qualifiers of *hu* and *śnu*, then because of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] in cases such as *takṣṇuvanti*, it would not apply in cases such as *āpnuvanti*; in those instances, the two genitives in *asaṃyogapūrvasya oḥ* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), referring to the suffix *śnu* which ends in a vowel and is not preceded by a conjunct consonant.

The meaning is: "that which has an *u* belonging to a portion of a stem ending in the suffix *śnu*, provided that this *u* is not preceded by a conjunct consonant. The term *anekācaḥ* ("having more than one vowel") is in grammatical apposition with the stem (*aṅga*). The mention of *sārvadhātuka* ("present-system suffix") is for the sake of the root *hu-* (to sacrifice), and not for the sake of the suffix *śatṛ*, because there is no deviation [in the case of *śatṛ*]. For example: *juhvatī* (from *juhvanti*), by the rule *ad abhyastāt*. *Juhrat* (from *juhvantaḥ*), where the prohibition of *num* applies by the rule *nābhyastāc chatuḥ*. *Yoyuvati*, *roruvatī*: from the roots *yu-* and *ru-* with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*), in the present tense (*laṭ*), the preceding *jhi* is replaced by *at*.

"‘This very [rule], etc. This was stated by relying on the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *chandas* (Vedic) in the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca*. However, Ayāditya did not rely on the continued application of *chandas* there. But how is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: ‘For in the Veda... The meaning is as follows: in the Veda, the mention of *hu*, *snuk*, and *grah* would not be necessary for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅanta (the elided form of the intensive), because the suffixes following them would be *ārdhadhātuka*; thus, the substitution of *yaṇ* would not apply."

And thus, regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "If it is argued that [the rule] is for the sake of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), [we reply] it is established because [the suffix] belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* category. This might be the case: since [the rule] will apply by excluding other cases from those ending in *yaṅluk*, the mention of *hu* and *sn* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). To this he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). "Preceded by a non-conjunct" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) means "ending in a vowel preceded by a non-conjunct. Here, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of "after *o*" (*ostyi*), [the rule] will not apply in cases such as *mimate*; and because of the continued application of "having more than one vowel" (*anekācaḥ*), it will not apply in cases such as *dhuvanti*.

In *ayuvan* and *thaaruvan*, since the augment *aṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), there is indeed only one vowel (*ekāctva*). Because of the continued application of the rule "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrvasya*), it will not apply in *prorṇuvanti*; however, in *tanvanti* and similar forms, it must certainly apply as *yaṇ*. Therefore, nothing other than the *yaṅ*-luṅanta form remains to be excluded. And so it has been said: "The mention of *hu* and *nuṅ* is purposeless, because there is no other [form] to be excluded."
The substitution of *vuk* occurs for the root *bhū* before the suffixes *luṅ* and *liṭ*.

Regarding "abhūvan": by the rule *gāti-sthā-*, etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. Regarding "abhūvam": there is the absence of the substitution of *am* for *mip*. The phrase "in *luṅ* and *liṭ*" (from *luṅ-liṭoḥ*) is used [to specify the scope]; it does not apply to *bhavati* or *bhaviṣyati*, because these take the suffixes *śap* and *syap*. If it were understood that the term *kṅiti* (before a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ*) continues to apply, then it would not apply even in the case of "abhūvam. In that case, however, the term *ār* (the vowel *ā*) will continue to apply; once the *guṇa* substitution has taken place, it will not apply because the stem no longer ends in the vowel *u*. In the case of "abhūvam," the stem ends in the vowel *u* because of the prohibition of *guṇa* by the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi*.
In this case, it is not possible to carry forward the word "aḥ" (the suffix *a*); this has been explained in detail under the rule *indhībhavatibhyāṃ ca*.
The substitution of *ū* occurs for the final vowel of the word *ūdhas* when it follows the word *go*. (Pāṇini 6.4.89)

In the examples, these suffixes occur: *ṇic*, *ṇvul*, *taṇaniḥ*, *ṇamul* (in the sense of repetition), and *ghañ*. In all cases, once *guṇa* has been applied, the vowel *o* becomes *ū*. [Question: Why is the word "upadhāyāḥ" (of the penultimate) stated? [Answer: Since the term "oḥ" is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over from a previous rule), the change will apply to the vowel *o*; furthermore, that [vowel *o*] is necessarily a penultimate (*upadhā*). [Objection: But it is said "of *o*" (*oḥ*), and it is not possible for this [suffix *go*] to have a penultimate *o*. [Response: By the force of the *anuvṛtti* of "oḥ," the phrase "of *go*" (*gohaḥ*) will serve as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the specific scope, namely the rule "thai" (*thaiḥ*); however, it is not...

The purpose is to acknowledge the merit [of the author]; let there not be [the impression] that it belongs to another. There is no evidence for [the suffix *mat*] being a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the sense is that the mention of *upadhā* (the penultimate vowel) must necessarily be made even for the sake of excluding the application of the term "impossible" (*asambhāvadoṣa*).

"The mention of the modified form (*vikṛta*) is for the purpose of restricting the scope (*viṣayaniyama*). When *guha* is mentioned, it would be a reference to the verbal root (*dhātu-nirdeśa*); consequently, even in the domain of *kṅit* suffixes, the substitution of *ū* (*ūtva*) would apply based on the root's own form. Therefore, so that a specific domain for the substitution of *ū* may be indicated, the mention of the modified form—which has undergone the substitution of *guṇa*—is made. He clarifies its purpose as being for the sake of the scope with the words "where" (*yatra*). The meaning is: so that it may apply in the domain of *guṇa*. And some maintain that it is also for the purpose of prohibiting the *ayādeśa* substitution, and so forth.

It was stated that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in determining the preceding object (*pūrvaviṣayāvadhāraṇa*); and that is accomplished when [the rule] is stated as *akṅiti*. However, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), it is stated as *gaha*; and that also results in determining the time (*kālāvadhāraṇa*) by implication, namely, that the state of being *ū* occurs after the *guṇa* has taken place. Now, however, it is said that the intended meaning applies to both cases; it applies to the domain of *guṇa*, and therein also, "when the *guṇa* has been performed."

For if the substitution of *ū* were to occur prior to the *guṇa*, then when the substitute [of *ya*] is applied by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt*, that [substitution] would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and since the *hakāra* would thus be preceded by a light vowel, the substitution of *ay* would occur. However, when the *guṇa* is applied first, and the substitution of *ū* takes place in its stead, then—even though that [substitution] is non-existent—the absence of the *ay* substitution is established because the *okāra* is heavy. He refutes this with the words "because they have different bases" (*vyāśrayatvāt*). To the question "How is there a difference of bases?", he says: "The substitution of *ū* occurs in relation to *ṇi*" (*ṇāvūtvam*).
[This refers to the rule: *doṣo ṇau* (Pāṇini 6.4.90).

For what purpose is the inclusion of the modified form *duṣi* made instead of simply saying *duṣaḥ*? If it is argued that it is for the sake of specifying the scope (*viṣaya*), this is not so, because the scope is already explicitly indicated by the word *ṇau*. If it is argued that it is for the sake of prohibiting the substitution of *ay* in cases such as *pradūṣya gatāḥ*, this is also not so, because the answer has already been given: namely, that there is no status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) due to the rule relying on different bases (*vyāśrayatvāt*). Therefore, one should simply say *duṣaḥ*; hence he says: "the inclusion of the modified form. *Krama* means sequence, context, or subject matter.
Or [the substitution of *u* occurs] before the word *cittavirāga*. (Pāṇini 6.4.91)
Cittavirāgaḥ means the absence of pleasure in the mind. This is an optional rule (vibhāṣā). It applies only when the suffix ṇa is present—as in cittasya doṣaḥ.
A short vowel is substituted for a prosodically light (mita) vowel. 6.4.92.

Regarding the form *rañjayati*: by the rule "the elision of the penultimate vowel [of the root] *rañj* should be added to the list of exceptions for the causative suffix *ṇic* when meaning 'to delight like a deer'," there is the elision of the penultimate vowel.
After a root that has undergone reduplication (ciṇṇamul), the long vowel [of the reduplicated syllable] may optionally be substituted.

The meaning is that it is not intended that only the short vowel alternative (*hrasva-vikalpa*) be prescribed; for even so, in the case of the short vowel, *aśamī* is established, while in the other alternative, *aśāmī* remains as it was originally obtained, namely with the long vowel (*dīrgha*).
