Regarding the phrase "he employs one who is pacifying" (*śamayantaṃ prayuṅkte*): although in the domain of the *ciṇ* affix the object and the past tense must be indicated, nevertheless, here the intention is merely to indicate the causal operation (*hetu-vyāpāra*) for the sake of deriving the *ṇic* affix; since neither the agent nor the present tense is intended, there is no fault.

"Because of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elided *ṇi*. For if *sthānivadbhāva* were to apply, then in a case where *ṇi* is followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*, the element (*aṅga*) would not have *m* [as its penultimate] because it is separated from that *ṇi* by the preceding *ṇi*; and in a case where the element has *m* [as its penultimate], that *ṇi* would not be followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* because it is separated from them by the subsequent *ṇi*. Consequently, the optional shortening (*hrasva*) would not occur; rather, by the previous rule, the shortening would be obligatory.

[Objection: But surely, since there is substitution (*sthānivadbhāva*) even in the case of the optional long vowel (*dīrghavikalpa*), how is this established? To this he says: "But in the rule for the long vowel" (*dīrghavidhau tu*). The meaning is that because the prohibition of substitution by the rule beginning with *na padāntadvirvacane* applies, this [optional long vowel] is indeed the proper domain [of that prohibition]. Regarding the phrase "in the same way," etc.: here, the ellipsis to be supplied is "in the rule for the long vowel, however, a substitute not beginning with a vowel (*ajādeśa*) does not possess the status of the original."

The meaning is as follows: after the application of *yaṅ*, reduplication, the augment *nuk*, and the elision of *a* before the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—resulting in the form *taṃ-śami* according to the rule *yasya hala*—when the suffixes *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* are subsequently applied, the optional lengthening of the vowel is established because the substitute (*ajādeśa*) does not possess the status of being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

He clarifies this very point with the words "yo'sau" (that which... and "yaṅkāraḥ" (the suffix yaṅ). The connection is that [the suffix] *ṇi* is elided after [the root]. Thus, it has been clarified that in the rule prescribing a long vowel (*dīrghavidhi*), a substitute beginning with *a* (*ajādeśa*) does not behave as if it were the original (*na sthānivat*). Regarding what was stated—that because of the status of the elision of *ṇi* as *sthānivadbhāva*, there would be no optionality regarding the short vowel (*hrasvavikalpa*)—he establishes that point with the words "hrasvavikalpe tu. *Ṇerṇiḥ* means *ṇi-ṇi*; that which has such a suffix at its end is *ṇiṇyanta*. By this, the expression "yaṅ-ṇyante" (after a reduplicated [yaṅ] or a causative [ṇic] ending) is explained.

"It is simply non-establishment. Because of what? Because the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is the subject under discussion. By the word *eva* (only) and the particle *tu* (but), he shows this: since the rule for *vṛddhi* is prescribed by relying on the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is a possibility of the long vowel; however, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision of the *ṇi*, this option would not occur—this is the very fault. Even if this option were to occur in the case of the intensive (*yaṅ*) with a causative suffix, even so, the hearing of the long vowel in one alternative would not be established; for when *vṛddhi* is to be applied in relation to the *ta*-causative, the elision of *ataḥ* would have the status of a substitute, and thus the long vowel would not manifest.

It might be argued: "Even if there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is prescribed in this alternative, the long vowel still cannot be established here because the elision of *ṇi* and *yaṅ* is considered 'as if unestablished' (*asiddhavat*) by the rule *asiddhavadatrābhāt*. Therefore, he says: 'Because they have different bases' (*vyāśrayatvāt*). He demonstrates this very fact of having different bases with the words 'In the case of *ṇi*, etc. Furthermore, the root *heḍ* (meaning 'to cover') belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group; in the absence of the short vowel, it would be *aheḍī*, but when the long vowel is applied after the short vowel has been made, it becomes *ahīḍī*.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the long vowel alone should be subject to the option."
The substitution of *hlāda* occurs before a suffix marked with *niṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 6.4.95)

The root *hlād* is used in the sense of pleasure (*sukha*), and because it is marked with the indicator *ī*, it is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). It is sometimes taught as *hlād* [with a short vowel], and a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made so that [the form] *prahlattiḥ* may also occur even with the suffix *ktin*. However, this is not seen in the *Mahābhāṣya*.
The long vowel substitution for the final *i* of the prefix *adhi* before the root *chad* occurs when the suffix *gha* follows, provided that two prefixes precede it.

Regarding the word *uraśchada*: the root *chad* means "to cover" (*āvaraṇe*); it takes the causative suffix *ṇic* (belonging to the *curādi* class). By the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyām*, the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), resulting in the form *chada*. A compound is then formed with the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting the object (*karmaṇi*). Now, one might object: here, when the suffix *gha* follows, the base (*aṅga*) ends in the causative marker *ṇi*; its penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is the letter *a*, and that [vowel] is not subject to shortening (*hrasva*). Nor can it be argued that once the *ṇi*-elision (*ṇilopa*) has been performed—

The form *ākāra* [is derived] with a short penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) because the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is treated as if it were not yet accomplished (*asiddha*) by the rule "this is as if unestablished in this context" (*asiddhavad atrābhāt*), and also due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to the rule "when a subsequent element follows, the preceding [vowel] is like its original" (*acaḥ parasmin*). Therefore, he says: "and of the elision of the *ṇi*. Another teacher says: the word "*ṇau*" (in the presence of *ṇi*) is understood; when *ṇi* follows *dhe*, the penultimate vowel of that which is the stem (*aṅga*) undergoes shortening. The mention of *chādeḥ* is for the sake of indicating the letter *i*, and not for the sake of the *ṇic* suffix itself.

[Objection: Surely, wherever there are three or more [prefixes], two are also present there; therefore, since the rule *advyupasargasya* (of that which has not two prefixes) would already apply, what is the purpose of the instruction in this sūtra? To this he says: *uttarā hi* ("for the subsequent ones..."). He confirms this very point through common worldly usage with the words *na hi*. In the case of *is*, *man*, and *van*: the suffix *isi* is applied by the rule *ārci-śuci-husṛpi-cchardi-chardibhya isiḥ*; the suffix *manin* is applied to all roots (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ*); and the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied to all roots. Due to the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), [the suffix *isi*] occurs even after two or more prefixes—as in *samupacchadiḥ*.
There is elision of the final vowel of the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *dhas* before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*, except when the affix is *anaṅ*.

Regarding *jajñatuḥ*: the substitution of *k* for *n* occurs by the rule *abhyāsācca*. Regarding *jajñatuḥ*: the root *jan* in the sense of "birth" is *parasmaipada* and belongs to the *juhotyādi* class; the *n* undergoes the *cutva* (substitution of *c*). Regarding *jajñe*: the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" is *anudātta* and belongs to the *divādi* class. Regarding *jakṣatuḥ*: by the rule *liṭyanyatarasyām*, the substitute *ghas* is applied for the root *ad*; the *gh* undergoes *cartva* (substitution of *k*), and the *ṣ* is substituted by the rule *śāsivasighasitanāṃ ca*. Regarding *akṣan*: in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *san*, the substitute *ghasṛ* is used for *ad*; in the Vedic mantra, the *cli* is elided by the rule *mantre ghasa*.

"Before a vowel" (*aci*) [is understood] from the rule *aci śnu-dhātu-...* (P. 6.4.77). However, its application has not been demonstrated starting from the rule *tasya tu doṣo ṇau* (P. 6.1.59), because in some cases there is no deviation [from the rule], and in others it is impossible. Here, however, it is applicable; likewise, he will state this in the subsequent sūtra as *hali ca* (P. 8.2.77).
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ṣa* for *sa* occurs] in the case of the roots *tan* and *pat*. (Pāṇini 6.4.99)

Regarding *vitatnire*: by virtue of the provision for elision (*lopavidhāna*), even though [the doubling] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) do not occur under the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*. Regarding *paptima*: this is the *liṭ* suffix, *mas*, with the augment *iṭ*.
The substitution of *gh* for *j* and *bh* for *d* occurs before a consonant other than *y*, as well as before the vowel *a*.

The reading of the letter *ca* in the Sūtra is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*). Thus, the Vārttika states: "The mention of *hal* is not a general rule (*aparibhāṣya*), because it is seen elsewhere as well. The phrase "it is not done" means that if it were done, there would be no doubling (*dvirvacana*) due to the absence of a vowel (*anackatva*). Since the governing term *aci* from the preceding [sūtra] applies here, the word *hali* is stated; by its inclusion, the implication is that [doubling] would not occur before a vowel, and thus there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the letter *ca*. If *aci* were to continue to apply from the previous [sūtra] alone, the word *iha* would not be necessary; in that case, the rule *hali ca* could have been omitted, though it was stated for the sake of the subsequent [rules].
After the consonants *h*, *u*, *jha*, and *l*, the substitute *dhi* is applied in place of the imperative suffix *hi*.

Regarding the phrase *halādeḥ*: the meaning is that by the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *hu-jha-l-bhyaḥ*, a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is figuratively constructed for the locative case (*saptamī*) in *hal-i*. If this is so, then because the rule *yasmin vidhiḥ* (P. 1.1.72) would not apply, there would be no "specification of the initial" (*tadādividhi*). [Response: It will occur by virtue of the force of the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to *hal-i* and because of the absence of being a suffix beginning with a consonant (*halanta*). In *bhindhi*: there is elision of the *śn* and *as* suffixes (*śnasoralopaḥ*). In *prīṇīhi*: [the substitution of] *ī* occurs before a consonant (*hal*) except for *adhi* (*ī halyaghoḥ*). In *juhutām*: the *tas* suffix is replaced by *tām* (*loṭo laṅvat*). In *rudihi*:

since both [rules] are non-permanent (*anitya*) due to the application of a different word-form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*), the augment *iṭ* is applied first because it is subsequent; however, there is then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of reduplication occurring again.

"Regarding *iha* and so forth: the scope (*avakāśa*) of *dhi* is in non-benedictive forms such as *juhudhi*; the scope of *tātaṅ* is other than after *hu* and *jhal* sounds, such as *jīvatāt tvam*. When both would apply after *hu* and *jhal* sounds in a benediction, *tātaṅ* occurs because it is subsequent. Now, even when that [substitution] has been made, why does *dhi*-ness not occur due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)? To this he says: *tatra kṛte* (when that has been done). If one were to argue that in *bhindhaki* and *chindhaki*, *dhi*-ness would also occur by virtue of being subsequent and thus the *akac* suffix would not be applied, he says: *bhindhīki*."

Another says: the vowel *i* in both the original form (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is merely for the sake of pronunciation; thus, *dh* is the substitute for *t*, and the term *halī* need not be carried over [from the previous rule]; consequently, there is no possibility of any undesirable consequence whatsoever.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *asun* is applied after the roots *śru*, *śṛ*, *pṛ*, *kṛ*, and *vṛ*.
In the phrase *urukṛd uruṇaskṛdhi*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by the rule *naś ca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ*; and in *kaḥ karat*, the *s* replaces the *visarjanīya* by the rule *kaḥ karat*.

Regarding the statement "it is also seen in other cases," this refers to the lengthening of the vowel. It is not only in the case of *śrṛṇudhī giraḥ* that the lengthening occurs by this very rule; it also occurs in *śrudhī havam* and *apāvṛdhī*. The phrase "other than that" means in all the examples other than *śrṛṇudhī*.
And [the augment] *iṭ* [is applied] after [a root ending in] a nasal. (Pāṇini 6.4.103)

"However, there is no elision of *m*" means that there is an absence of that elision of *m* which [would otherwise occur] by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa...". "Precisely because it is not marked as having an indicatory letter *ṅ*"—the meaning of the word "precisely" (*eva*) is that this [elision] is not something to be accomplished through a specific effort. "There is elision of the *śap* suffix after the root *yam*" applies only to the Vedic language, according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi". The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.
There is elision (luk) of the *ciṇ* affix. 6.4.104.

*Ciṇ* is the fifth case (ablative), not the sixth, due to the force of the rule's formulation. Regarding the term *pratyayasya*: this is understood from the statement "the elision (*luk*, *ślu*, *lup*) of a suffix" and because it occurs within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of the stem (*aṅga*). Therefore, in the form *akāritarām*, there is simultaneous elision (*luk*) of the entire cluster consisting of the element *ta*, the suffix *tarap*, and the suffix *ām*; for although each individual member is a suffix, the cluster as a whole is not a suffix.

Now, one might object: "But this [rule] is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to this [other rule]; since the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is based on difference, how can *ciṇo luk* be unestablished only with respect to *ciṇo luk*? To this he says: "The phrase *ciṇo luk*... Alternatively, the term *kṅiti* is understood to carry over; *ciṇaḥ* is in the ablative case, which will be interpreted as a genitive. Thus, the elision (*luk*) being prescribed for a suffix beginning with *k* or *ṅ* will not apply to the *tarap* suffix.
The suffix *he* [is applied] after the root *hi*. (Pāṇini 6.4.105)

"Go! (*gaccha*). [The rule] *iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ* [applies]. "Run! (*ghāva*). [The root] *ghāvu* is used in the sense of "to go" and "to purify"; by the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*, there is the substitution of *dhāv* for the root *sṛ*. "Mow! (*lunīhi*). [The rule] *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* [applies], and *ī* [is substituted] before a consonant beginning with *hal* that is not *ghu*. Now, one might object: "In this case, because the root does not end in a vowel other than *a* (*anavarṇāntatvāt*), this [substitution] will not occur; rather, the substitution of *ī* (by *ī halyaghoḥ*) will indeed take place because it is subsequent. To this he says: "Of the substitution of *ī*. Now, even so, in the two counter-examples here, [the substitution] will not occur precisely because of the two conditions (*upādhi*) mentioned in the subsequent rule—namely, "after a vowel other than *u*" (*utaḥ*) and "before an affix" (*pratyayāt*).

And if, in the case of *lunīhi*, the substitution of *ī* occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], then there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*), since it has been stated that such [asiddhatva] does not apply in the domain of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). Therefore, *ihi* and *adhīhi* are the counter-examples for the rule *ataḥ*; while *yāhi* and *vāhi* are the counter-examples for the inclusion of the long vowel marker *tapara*.
And also [the substitution of *i* for the final vowel] occurs before a suffix that does not begin with a conjunct consonant. 6.4.106.

Furthermore, regarding the two terms "uk" and "pratyayāt," there is freedom of choice as to which functions as the qualifier and which as the qualified. In that context, because the vowel *u* is the qualified element (*viśeṣya*), there is no state of being "ending in that" (*tadantatā*) [with respect to the suffix].
And it is impossible for the vowel *u* to be a suffix ending in itself when it occurs again.
The suffix is qualified by the letter *u*, whereby its status as ending in that [letter] is established;
thus, both of those two positions regarding the suffix are possible.

In that case, according to the first alternative, the suffix *sun* would apply only in instances such as *tanu* and *kuru*, but not in cases like *cinu*. Furthermore, since the vowel *u* is not preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) when it is a suffix, the mention of "not being preceded by a cluster" (*asaṃyogapūrva*) would be understood as a qualifier of the stem (*aṅga*) in this view; consequently, it would not apply in cases such as *kṣiṇu*. For *kṣiṇu* belongs to the *tanādi* class meaning "to injure," and they say that in this instance there is no *guṇa* substitution for the root. Therefore, the vowel *u* is the qualifier, and by means of it, the rule applies to that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*).

If this is so, then [in the case of] *tanu kuru*, [the rule] would not apply here, because the suffix here is merely the phoneme *ik* and not that which ends in it. To this, [it is replied]: even here, it is that which ends in it, by virtue of the principle of "designation as if possessing" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). This being the case—if the condition "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrvatva*) is a qualifier of that which ends in *u*—then in *āpnuhi*, there would be elision (*luk*) of *hi*, whereas the prohibition [of elision] applies in *takṣṇuhi*.
Therefore, let this [term] be understood as belonging specifically to the vowel *u*.

But surely, according to the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* ("that by which a grammatical operation is prescribed applies to that which ends with it"), the designation (*saṃjñā*) refers to that which ends in the vowel *ū*; what then?
A designation is intended to convey the thing designated (*saṃjñin*), so how can there be a qualifier for it? If this is considered improper, the following resolution is stated here.
It is true that the designation applies to that which ends with the suffix; nevertheless,
because the quality of being a qualifier manifests even before the suffix is produced, the suffix itself is indeed the qualifier here— nothing at all remains hidden.

This is what was stated: "When this *ukāra* (the letter *u*) is not preceded by a conjunct consonant, [the substitution of *dh* for *hi* occurs] after a verbal root ending in that [letter]. For example: *yuhi*, *ruhi*. [Objection: But surely, because the rule for changing *hi* to *dhi* is prescribed specifically for the *hi* following the root *hu*, it will not apply to anything other than a verbal root; thus, the mention of "after a suffix" (*pratyayāt*) is unnecessary. [Response: True, yet this indicator (*jñāpaka*) would apply only to a specific domain; therefore, the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is included to ensure its universal application. Furthermore, it should be stated that "in the Vedic language (*chandas*), it is optional. By doing so, the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) in the subsequent sūtra becomes unnecessary.
And its [the final *m* of the pronoun *asmad*] is optionally elided before the case-endings *m* and *v*. (Pāṇini 6.4.107)

By the word *asya* ("of this"), the suffix ending in the vowel *u* is referred back. If *asya* were not stated, then by resorting to the genitive case in the rule *mvoḥ*, one would understand that the elision applies only to *m* and *v*. In this way, the ablative case in the rule *utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt* remains uncontradicted. Regarding the phrase "while *luk* is in force," and so forth: for if *luk* were applied only to what is currently under discussion (the specific suffix), it would apply to every suffix. We have already stated in the section on the definition of technical terms (*saṃjñāvidhi*) that *luk* and the others are substitutes for the whole (*sarvādeśa*).

If the elision (*lopa*) were applied to the entire [suffix], forms such as *sunvaḥ* and *sunuvaḥ* would not be established. Therefore, the mention of "elision" (*lopagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of eliding only the final [element]. Furthermore, in cases such as *kurvaḥ* and *kurmaḥ*, if there were a zero-substitution (*luk*), the *guṇa* substitution would not occur because of the prohibition "na lumatāṅgasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.63). However, when there is merely an elision (*lopa*), the *guṇa* does indeed take place.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* when it signifies "doing" something habitually. (Pāṇini 6.4.108)

"Of the root *kṛ* ending with the suffix *u*"—this is understood through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*. By the phrase "of the elision of *u*" and so forth, he restates the occurrence of lengthening along with its justification and then demonstrates the prohibition.
Although the result is established by the very force of the rule's formulation, the inclusion of the word *nitya* ("always") is for the sake of clarity.
Therefore, [the substitution of *u* for *ū* occurs] before an affix beginning with a vowel that has an indicatory letter *s*, provided it follows a verbal root. (Pāṇini 6.4.110)

Regarding the phrase "of the root *kṛ* ending in the suffix *u*": this is understood through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *utaśca pratyayāt*. [Question: Why include the term *sārvadhātuke*? [Answer: Even if the mention of *sārvadhātuka* were omitted, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the substitution] would apply to the final syllable of *syatāsī* (in forms like *kartārau*). However, because of the intervention (*vyavadhāna*) of *syatāsī*, it would not occur. But then, in the case of *kurute*, it would likewise not occur due to the intervention of the suffix *u*. Therefore, since the sense is possible—that [the substitution applies] to the root *kṛ* when it is part of an *aṅga* (base) followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix—one must rely on the interpretation: "of the root *kṛ* which is a constituent part of that *aṅga* which stands before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix."

And if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply even to the final [form] as well. Furthermore, the phrase "after a suffix ending in *u*" (*utaśca pratyayāt*) must necessarily be supplied; for otherwise, in the case of *karoti* ending in the suffix *up*, the subsequent *sārvadhātuka* suffix would have to be *kṅit*—this is the objection. Regarding the phrase "even when it has previously occurred" (*bhūtapūrve 'pi*): when *karu-hi* is established, both the substitution of *u* (*utvam*) and the elision of the suffix *hi* (*hiluk*) are applicable. Since the elision of *hi* (*hiluk*) is obligatory (*nitya*), once it has been performed, the *u*-substitution would not take place because of the absence of a *kṅit* suffix following it. [Objection: This is prevented by the rule "there is no application of a suffix-characteristic (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when a suffix is elided by *lumat*" (*na lumatāṅgasya*). [Response: No, because [the rule] is prohibited.

Therefore, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is made so that [the rule] may apply even when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows a previously existing form. The elision of *hil* is not established; because it is not established, the substitution of *u* will take place. Thus, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is for the sake of clarity. Just as there is no further utility for this [mention] later on, so it will be stated in various places.

In this context, although the vowel *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), nevertheless, by virtue of internal similarity (*āntarya*), it will be only the short *u* (*mātrika*) that replaces the short *a* (*mātrika*), and not the long *ū*. Therefore, there is no purpose for the letter *t* [in *ut*]. To this he replies: "The inclusion of the letter *t* (in *tapara*) is for the sake of excluding [the application of] other grammatical rules. For if that were absent, then by relying on the suffix *u*, the *guṇa* substitution characterized by a light penultimate syllable (*laghūpadhalakṣaṇa*) would apply; so that this may not occur, the letter *t* is included. Its purpose is indeed to ensure that a long vowel does not occur even by means of another rule.
The *am* of *śnas* is elided before the suffixes *ra*, *l*, and *luṅ*.

What is the purpose of the long vowel marker (taparakaraṇa)? It is so that [the substitution] does not apply to *āṭ*—as in *āstām*, *āsan*; for *āṭ* is considered *asiddha*. If this is so, then the long vowel marker is used to indicate that the *asiddha* status of what belongs to the *ābhīya* group is not universal (*anitya*). Furthermore, there is no need here for the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *sārvadhātuka*, as he says: *śn* occurs only before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, whereas for the root *as*, the substitution of *bhū* must take place even before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

[Objection: But surely, when there is an *anuprayoga* (subsequent application of the root), the change to *bhū* does not occur—[as in] *īhāmāsuḥ*. [Response: True; however, in that case, once reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the *halādiśeṣa* have been applied, by the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenānāprāptinyāya*), the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels (*ato guṇe*) is set aside, and the lengthening by *ata ādeḥ* is applied. Then, even when the *saṇ* suffix is elided, the desired form is established.
The long vowel *ā* is elided after a root ending in *ś* or a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*), when followed by the suffix *āt*.

Regarding *lunata*: [this is] the present tense (*laṭ*); by the rule *ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ*, there is the substitution of *ad* for *jha*. Regarding *lunatām*: in the imperative (*loṭ*), *ām* is substituted for *ta*. Regarding *alunata*: this is the imperfect (*laṅ*). In forms such as *mimāte*, there is the substitution of *it* by the rule *bhṛñām it*. Regarding *yānti* and *vānti*: the point is that if the mention of the *śnā* affix and the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) root were not made, then in the rule *ato guṇe*, the inclusion of the *tapara* (the short *a*) would already find its application in cases like *yānam* where an *aṅit* suffix follows; consequently, in the present case, there would be only elision (*lopa*).

Regarding the word *ālunaḥ*: since the connection with the term *kṅiti* from the preceding sūtra remains in force, this is not the domain of the substitution of *ī*. Because the terms *ik*, *aṅgāt*, and *kāraṇāt* serve as qualifiers for *abhyasta*, the elision (*lopa*) does not occur for that which ends in *ā*, as in *jāgrati*. Having considered that—either by the rule "substitutes apply to that which is specifically indicated" (*nirdiśyamānasya*) or by the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo’ntyasya*)—the elision applies only to the *ā*, [the author] has explained it thus: "of this *śnā* and of the *ā* of reduplicated forms. However, it should rather be explained as "of those ending in *ā*."

In this case as well, [the elision] occurs only before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; likewise, even when the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) ends in long *ā*, there is indeed elision in forms such as *vavatuḥ*.

The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a verbal root ending in a consonant occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel that has an indicatory *h* or *y*, provided the root does not end in *a*.

Regarding the word *lunanti*: if the mention of the term *hal* (consonant) were not made, there would be an optionality between the substitution of *ī* and elision (*lopa*), because they would share the same domain of application. Alternatively, elision would occur only in the case of those [roots] designated as *ghu*. In this case as well, as before, only a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is possible.
The suffix *id* is applied after the word *daridra*. (Pāṇini 6.4.114)

This [suffix] also occurs only in *sārvadhātuka* contexts, because its elision is prescribed elsewhere. Regarding the word *siddhaśca*: just as in the case of the prescription of an affix, it becomes established at the very time the affix is prescribed, so too must the elision be performed; the sense is that one must resort to a locative absolute construction (*saptamī*) such as "when there is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix."

Regarding the phrase "characterized by having an *ā* as its final element": since the rule *ārdhadhātuke* is a locative in the sense of "when [an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix] follows," the elision (*lopa*) must be performed with reference to the arising of that suffix. Consequently, in the case of *syād-avyaya*, the suffix *ṇa*—which is characterized by having an *ā* as its final element—would apply. Once that is applied, both this elision and the *yuk* augment would be required. In that situation, because the elision is non-permanent (*anitya*) due to the application of another word-form (*śabdāntara-prāpti*), whereas the *yuk* augment does not apply once the elision has been performed, the *yuk* augment would prevail over both of these non-permanent rules on account of its higher status (*paratva*). Furthermore, even if...

There would be elision [of the *ya*]. Even so, in the case of *adaridrata*, the accent prescribed by the rule *ackāvaśaktau* would not apply. Furthermore, in the case of *īṣaddaridram*, the suffix *yuc* prescribed by the rule *āco yuc* would apply, resulting in *daridrāyaka*.

In *daridrāṇa*, the suffix *lyuṭ* applies. In *didaridrāsati*, there is the augment *iṭ* because of the provision for the addition of *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā* under the rule *tanipatidaridrāṇām upasaṃkhyānam*; this is a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), whereby *iṭ* occurs in the case of elision, while in other instances there is an absence of *iṭ*.

Regarding the term *adyatanyām*: this is the designation for the *luṅ* [aorist] used by the ancient grammarians (*pūrvācārya*). In the example *adaridrāsīt*, [the rule] *yam-ara-mana-mā-tāṃ sak ca* applies. According to one opinion, the condition *ekācaḥ* (of a monosyllabic root) is understood as carrying over (*anuvartate*) there. In the case of the *ciṇ* suffix: *adaridri* and *adaridrāyi*. In the case of the *ṇal* suffix: *dadaridrau*. The shortening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasam*); otherwise, if the *ā* of the root were elided by the rule *āto dhātoḥ*, the citation would have been *daridra*.
After *bhī*, [the suffix *ām*] is optionally used in the feminine.

Regarding the rule *halādau kṅiti sārvadhātuke*: these [rules] have no application here, and thus no counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) have been shown. For instance, let there be [the form] *bibhyati* even when preceded by *uj* and so on; by the rule *eranekācaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitution will occur for the short vowel as well. Nor is the prescription of *it* (in P. 7.1.100) redundant, since it serves its purpose in cases where a consonant follows. Likewise, let there be [the form] *vibheti* even when not followed by *kṅ*; the *guṇa* substitution will occur. And the prescription of *it* finds its scope of application in cases where *kṅ* follows.

Likewise, because of the continued application of the phrase "of that which has been practiced" (*tathāthaabhyastasya*), [the substitution] will not occur in *ārdhadhātuka* affixes such as in *bhītaḥ*. But then it would follow that it also occurs in *kvasu*; however, *kvasu* is Vedic, and in the Veda, one follows what is actually observed.
And [the substitution of *ya* occurs] for the root *jahāti*. (Pāṇini 6.4.116)

In this case as well, the rule *na sārvadhātuke* has no application; for this very reason, no counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for it has been shown. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *abhyastasya*, [the substitution] will not occur in an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, such as the *liṭ* beginning with a consonant other than *j*.
And [the substitution of *au* for *ā* occurs] before *ca* and *ha*. (Pāṇini 6.4.117)
For it is indeed only [the suffixes] belonging to the *sārvadhātuka* category.
There is elision of *y*. (Pāṇini 6.4.118)

"Dehi," "dhehi"—these forms arise from the roots *dā* (to give) and *dhā* (to place). However, in the case of *do* (the substitute for *dā*), *dāṇ*, *dheṭ*, and others, the augment *hi* is separated by the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). The root *deṅ* takes the *ātmanepada* endings. Regarding the statement "this [suffix] has *śi*": the letter *ś* heard in the rule is not the *ś* of the case-ending that arrived through the *ścutva* substitution; rather, it is an inherent part of the word *lopa*. The intention is that, among the case-endings, there is the elision of *hal*, *ṅ*, etc. Furthermore, an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) attached to a technical term brings about its effect upon the named entity (*saṃjñin*), just as the *ṅ* in *ṅamuṭ* causes the addition of *ṭ*.
And this was stated without relying on the principle that "a grammatical operation applies to the final letter of a meaningful unit" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*).

Therefore, [the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* occurs] for a vowel situated between two single consonants that does not begin with a substitute [consonant], when the suffix *liṭ* follows. (Pāṇini 6.4.120)

The word *eka* here signifies "without a companion" (*asahāya*), not the numerical value "one," because there is no middle [between one and another]. Furthermore, the compound involves a dual-ending term, for a middle can only exist between two things. In this context, if the mention of *liṭi* were intended as a specification of the conditions for the *etva* (substitution of *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) that are being prescribed, then the substitute (*ādeśa*) would not be qualified. Consequently, there would be a prohibition even in cases such as *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*, *sehe*, *sehāte*, and *sehire*, because once the [reduplication] has ceased to exist, the base (*aṅga*) would begin with a vowel (*ādi*). However, [this is not the case, as the rule applies] when the two operations have not yet taken effect.

Therefore, he shows that this is a specification of the cause even for a substitute (*ādeśa*) that has become a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*), by stating: "when *liṭ* follows. The meaning is: when *liṭ* is situated subsequently, that which is prescribed as a substitute does not exist at the beginning of the stem (*aṅga*).

Regarding the statement "they two protected" (*rarakṣatuḥ*): this is incorrect because [the root] begins with a semivowel (*ādeśāditvāt*). In some places, however, *tatakṣuḥ* is read; that too is incorrect because, due to being a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntatvena*), the *liṭ* suffix lacks the *kit* designation. Therefore, the counter-examples are *tatsaratuḥ* and *tatsaruḥ*. [The root] *tsara* means "to move stealthily. Regarding *cakaṇatuḥ*: the root *kaṇati* is listed in the *bhūvādi* group among the verbal roots whose meaning is "sound. Regarding *jagaṇatuḥ*: [the root] *gaṇa* means "counting"; since it belongs to the *curādi* group, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would apply there.

If this is not accepted, then the roots *aś*, *nu*, and so forth would be considered non-ṇi-ant (not having the causal marker). This point will be explained under the rule *dhuṣir aviśabdane*. Although the substitution of *c* for *kṛ* and *hṛ* (*cutva*) is not explicitly prescribed for the *liṭ* (perfect) tense by the rule *kṛ-hoś cuḥ*, it nevertheless applies when there is a suffix conditioned by the absence of *ta-k* (the augment *ta*), and thus it also occurs when the *liṭ* is the cause; in any case, it takes place after the *liṭ* has been produced.

Regarding the statement "not in *anaimittika* (non-conditional) nor in *asatva* (non-substitution)": consequently, those two [the *liṭ* and the *kṅit*] must exist even prior to the production of the *liṭ*. Therefore, that which begins with the substitute for *liṭ* does not have that as its initial element if *liṭ* is used as a qualifier. If *liṭ* were to qualify the substitute, then the substitution of *etva* (the change to *e*) would occur even where there is no *liṭ*, as in *pakvaḥ* and *pakvavān*. This is not a fault; the particle *ca* here denotes conjunction (*sabhuccaya*), not mere addition (*anvācaya*). Thus, the *etva* occurs only where there is elision of the reduplication (*abhyasalopa*). In that case, it would apply here: *pipaṭhiṣati*, because of the rule *kṅiti*.

[The rule] applies. Even so, it is recited [in the *Kāśikā*]: "In this case too, [the elision] would apply; this is not a fault. For here, in the operations concerning reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the shortening of the vowel and the retention of the first consonant (*hal-ādi-śeṣa*) are general rules (*utsarga*), while others are exceptions (*apavāda*) to them. Here, both lengthening by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* and elision by this [present rule] would apply. In that regard, the scope for lengthening is, for example, *bābhāṣyate*; the scope for this present rule is, for example, *pecatuḥ*, *pecuḥ*, and *pāpacyate*. When both [rules] would apply here, by the prohibition of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between an exception and a general rule, this elision of the reduplication takes place through the force of lengthening."

It is superseded because it is taught as being conditioned by that [long vowel]; therefore, even this [shortening] will not occur. In the case of modifications involving reduplication (*abhyāsa*), there is a co-occurrence of both [operations] where all [rules] apply. But here, although there would be the occasion for both the substitution of *e* (*etva*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) even when the lengthening has been performed, and once those two have been performed there is no occasion for the lengthening—thus, there is no application of all [the rules] simultaneously.

But surely, in forms such as *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*, since the substitution of the unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) and the retroflex (*cartva*) arising from reduplication would be considered *asiddha*, and because [the root] does not begin with a substitute [consonant], there ought to be the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) and the change to *e* (*etva*). However, the prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*) would find its scope of application in cases like *jahasatuḥ* and *jahasuḥ*, where the substitution of *c* for *k* and *h* (*kutva*) is performed by the rule *kuhoścuḥ*. To this he says: "In this case... He provides the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this very point: "And thus... [He says]: "But when there is no difference in form..."—that is to say, in a case where there is no difference in form between the substitute and the original element (*sthānin*).

Regarding the phrase *śasidadyoḥ*: since the rule *abhyāse car ca* applies everywhere, when both *jaś* and *car* substitutions are applicable, this will be stated—attained through the operation of the *antaratama* (most similar) principle—that "the *car* substitutes for original *car*s, and the *jaś* substitutes for original *jaś*s. Consequently, for the letter *ś* of *śasi*, there is the letter *ś*; and for the letter *d* of *dad*, there is the letter *d*. These two also become the initial elements of the substitutes.

If an *ādeśa* (substitute) were to be accepted even when its form is identical [to the original], then since the prohibition would already be established by the very fact of being an *ādeśa*, the specific prohibition "not for *śas*, *dad*, *avādi*, *guṇa*, and *an*" would be redundant; however, its inclusion serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, in cases where the form is identical, such an *ādeśa* is not to be accepted here. If, on the other hand, it were accepted, what would happen? To this he says: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).

For those [roots] whose *prakṛti* (base form) begins with a *jaś* sound or a *carc* sound and so forth, [the substitution] would not occur; however, the statement finds its application in examples such as *reṇuḥ*. As for *ahaṃ papaca*: this is the form when the *ṇal* suffix is in the first person (*uttama*) under the view that it lacks the *ṇit* designation. Under the view that it *is* *ṇit*, however, since the *vṛddhi* replacement occurs by virtue of its higher priority, there is no possibility [of the rule applying] precisely because of the absence of the vowel *a*, due to the inclusion of the *tapara* marker.

As for *debhatur*: when the *liṭ* suffix is *kit* by the rule *śranthigranthidambhisvañjīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.25), there is the elision of *na*. Regarding the rule *naśimanyoraliṭyettvam*: the mention of *aliṭi* (not in the *liṭ* tense) is a restatement for the sake of completing the verse (*pādapūraṇārtha*), for the verse is recited thus in the Bhāṣya.

"In the Vedic language, the substitution of *et* occurs for the root *naś* and *man*, even when followed by *am* or *ip*; thus we have *aneśan* and *mene*. Furthermore, in the optative (*liṅ*), *yam* would become *yeciraṇ*."

Regarding *aneśan*: *jha* is the substitute for the final sound (*antādeśa*). Thus, *tha* becomes *aneśan* with the addition of *as* and *uṣ*. However, the reading *aneśam* is generally found; in that case, there is the substitution of *am* for *mip*. Regarding the phrase "in the *kṣipakā*-class": for in the *kṣipakā*-class, the prohibition of *it*-substitution will be stated. This was stated without relying on the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) "and in the sense of benediction (*āśis*)" under the rule *na yāsayoḥ*; because of the statement "in the Vedic language (*chandas*)," the form *menakā* would not be obtained in the common language (*bhāṣā*). If it is desired [to have it], it should be seen as belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Regarding the statement "the elision (*luk*) is not performed": [this refers to the fact that the elision of the suffix is not applied].
Because it is Vedic, or because the suffix *śap* is elided according to the rule "in the Veda [it is] manifoldly [so]," as in the form *peciran*; where one would expect *paceran*.

In some places it is recited: "For *yaj* and *vap*, [the substitute] *eś*; for *ā-yaj* and *ā-vap*, [the substitute] *āve*; and for *yaj* and *vap* in the *laṅ* [tense], [the augment] *āṭ* is seen even in the Veda, even though [the root] does not begin with a vowel. Another says: "In the *liṭ* [perfect], there is the substitution of *eś* for that [root]; because of the continued application of the rule 'or, in the Veda, when preceded by *samprasāraṇa*', there is the substitution of *yaṇ*; then [there is] the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication; and by the rule 'with a *tiṅ* having an acute accent', there is a compound with *āṅ*. And thus they divide the words (*avagṛhṇanti*): *yacchañcayośca manurāyaje pitā*, and *āyeja* as *ā-ayeje*.
The suffix *ṣaṭh* is applied after the word *sthālī*. (Pāṇini 6.4.121)

*pecitha*. Since the rule *krādiniyamāt* (Pāṇ. 1.2.13) would require the augment *iṭ*, and since the prohibition *upadeśe 'tvataḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.2.62) would apply, the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (Pāṇ. 7.2.63) results in *iṭ* optionally. Thus we have *papaktha*. According to the opinion of others, however, there is a prohibition [of *iṭ*]. The mention of *thal* is redundant; for in cases such as *peciva* and others where the suffix is *seṭ*, the suffix must necessarily be treated as *kit* by the preceding rule (*na ktvā seṭ*). Therefore, he says: "The mention of *thal* is for the sake of clarity. What is it that needs to be clarified here? He shows this: "For the sake of [suffixes] other than *kṅit*, etc. This conclusion could indeed have been reached simply by the force of the rule's very commencement.

Regarding the statement "for that purpose where [the rule] is not established by the preceding [rule]," many specific cases (*viśeṣa*) have been introduced—namely, those such as *ekahalamadhye tha* (Pāṇini 7.2.31). In that context, if the mention of *thal* were absent, there would be doubt: Is this statement intended for the sake of [roots] other than those ending in *a*, as in *dadiviva* and *rarādiva*; or is it for the sake of [roots] consisting of more than one consonant in the middle, as in *tatsariva*; or is it for the sake of a substitute (*ādeśa*), as in *babhaṇiva*; or is it for the sake of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], as in *paṭhita*; or is it for the sake of [roots] marked with *k* or *ṅ*, etc.? In this regard, the specific rules such as *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.100) continue to apply.
However, the rule *kṅiti* is excluded [from this context], which is difficult to understand without an explicit explanation; therefore, the mention of *thal* has been made for the sake of clarity.
The suffixes *tṛ*, *phal*, *bhaj*, and *trap* [are applied after a verbal root] when expressing the sense of "fearing" (*bhīta*). 6.4.122.

Regarding the forms *phala* and *niṣpatti*: both roots are included here—*ñi-phalā* in the sense of "bursting open" (*viśaraṇe*) as well as *phal* in the sense of "producing fruit" (*niṣpattau*). The phrase "for the sake of the [guṇa] substitute" means that this is intended to override the prohibition stated in the rule *na śasadadavādiguṇānām*. As for *śrethatuḥ*, the *kittva* designation and the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) apply as in the previous case.
The root *rādh* is used in the sense of injury. 6-4-123.

Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *rādh* functions here in the sense of "injury. Now, one might object: "In this case, there is no mention of the vowel *a* (*avarṇa*) that has not been previously established; and since the *mātrika* [vowel] is under discussion, its duration is restricted by the addition of the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with the following *ṛ*). Therefore, how can it be said that the substitution of *etva* occurs in place of an *avarṇa*? To this he replies: "The word *ataḥ*... The word *ataḥ* remains present due to its svarita accent; however, because a specific duration consisting of a single *mātrā*, which would be produced by the *tapara* designation, is impossible here, it discards that [temporal specification] and indicates the mere vowel *a* (*avarṇa*). Alternatively: in the previous rule, because the term *ataḥ* was used as a contradictory element, it has no connection with the word *āt*.

Regarding the phrase *ekahalmadhye ca*: here, only *ekahalmadhye* applies; therefore, neither *ataḥ* nor *ātaḥ* is carried over [from the previous rule]. The meaning is that by the recurrence of *ekahalmadhye*, the original element (*sthānin*) is obtained through the implied supply of the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat*.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the word *phaṇa* when it occurs before the number seven (*sapta*). 6.4.125.

He states "of *phaṇ* and the rest" because the sense of "beginning with" is understood from the use of the plural number. *Phaṇ* means "to go," *rājṛ* means "to shine," *ṭubhrāśṛ*, *ṭubhrājṛ*, and *ṭubhalāśṛ* mean "to shine," and *syam*, *svan*, and *dhvan* mean "sound"; these seven, excluding the last, are the *phaṇ*-class. Here, even for roots beginning with *rāj*, the substitution of *e* occurs for the vowel *a*. The reasoning for this has already been stated in the rule concerning *rādha* in the sense of "injury."
There is no [substitution] of the qualities beginning with *śa*, *sa*, *da*, and *da*. 6-126.

In this context, if the prohibition were applied to that very *akāra* which is designated as "guṇa" in reality, then because the injunction and the prohibition would share the same object, there would be an option (*vikalpa*). Consequently, the mention of *vā* in the rule *vā jabhramutrasām* (Pāṇini 6.1.175) would have to be recited at the very beginning [of the section]. Therefore, he states—by saying "and of that which is thus produced as a guṇa"—that by the mention of "guṇa," there is the inclusion of that which is designated by that term and which is destined to become it. The meaning is: the *akāra* which belongs to that [guṇa].

Its status as being related [to the root] should also be understood accordingly, based on its being the substitute for that [root] and its being a constituent part of it. Regarding *viśaśasatuḥ*: the root *śasu* means "to injure"; *dadu* means "to give" and is anudātta; *ṭuvam* means "to vomit. Regarding *viśaśaratuḥ*: the root *śṝ* means "to injure"; the guṇa substitution occurs by the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām*.

Regarding what was stated—"of that which has been produced as a *guṇa*," he shows an example of this by saying, "of that which has been produced as the word *guṇa*. In the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*, because of the statement "it is established, however, that when [a substitute] occurs, it is followed by *r*," the *guṇa* is produced already bearing the letter *r* at its head; thus, the vowel *a* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *ar* once it has been so produced. In the case of *lulavitha*, however, the substitutes *av* and others take the place of the *u* that has already been produced, and the vowel *a* is a constituent part of those [substitutes].

In some places it is recited: "By the force of the term *guṇa* here, there is the inclusion of those [sounds] conditioned by that [guṇa], because of the capacity for the inclusion of *śas* and so forth. For indeed, if only the vowel *a* were included, the inclusion of the *v*-sounds in *śasi*, *dadi*, and so on, would be purposeless; such is said to be the meaning of that [statement].
The substitution of *u* for the final vowel of *arvan* occurs before the suffix *tras*, provided it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

The letter *ṛ* is for the purpose of triggering operations associated with *ugit* stems; therefore, the augment *num* occurs before a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. And that [augment] does not occur after a negative particle (*nañ*)—this is the connection with the word "if" (*cet*). In the form *arvatī*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because it is an *ugit* stem or because it ends in *n*. In the form *ārvataṃ*, it also occurs before a *taddhita* suffix. Here, the expression "asau" (in this case) is an absolute prohibition (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), not an exclusion (*paryudāsa*); consequently, by the absence of the maxim regarding "that which is connected with *nañ* or *iva*," there is no grasping of the case-ending itself. Thus, the rule "if *su* does not follow" refers here to the nominative singular (*prathamā-ekavacana*), and not to the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*), according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
The word *maghavān* becomes *bahulam*. (Pāṇini 7.1.93)

Regarding *maghavā*: the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*). Regarding *maghonaḥ*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *śvayuvamaghonām*, followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvatvam*) and the formation of a single guṇa vowel (*ādguṇaḥ*). Now, one might object: *maghavān* is derived from "he who possesses wealth" (*magham asyāsti*), where *magha* is a name for wealth. According to the rule *chandasi vanipaś ca*, the suffix *vanip* is applied; once the vocalization has been performed, the preceding portion receives the designation *bha*, which would entail the elision of the *y* sound by the rule *yasyeti ca*. However, one need not even suspect that this elision is non-existent due to being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) because it depends on different factors (*vyāśrayatvāt*), since the vocalization occurs before the suffix *śas* [is added], whereas the elision of *y* would occur after it.

If it is argued that this [form] must therefore be something else entirely, unanalyzed, so that its usage in the common language (*bhāṣā*) might be justified; however, according to the Bhāṣya, it is not only this [word *arvan*], but even the word *arvan* itself is an incorrect usage in the common language. For it says:

"The forms *arvaṇas* and *maghonas* need not be taught [for the common language], for they are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, because the suffixes *matup* and *van* are prescribed [in the Veda], both [types of forms] are seen in the Veda."

From the root *ṛdh*, when the suffix *vanip* is applied and *guṇa* is performed, the form *arvan* is obtained. From that, by applying the suffixes *vic* and *matup*, forms such as *arvantau* and so forth are established; likewise, from the word *magha*, the two suffixes are also established, resulting in forms such as *arvaṇām*. Thus, there is no purpose for the two rules [Pāṇini 6.4.127 and 6.4.130]. However, in forms such as *maghonaḥ*, the absence of elision (*lopa*) of the *ya* (of *māghavan*) occurs precisely because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the case of *māghavanam*, the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) remains due to the suffix *an*.
The word *pāda* [is substituted for its final vowel] when followed by *pat*. 6.4.130.

The word *pāda* is understood here as having its vowel *a* elided (*luptākāra*). The author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated in the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* that even the root *pādayati* ending in *kvip* is included here. Therefore, this passage should be interpreted by supplying the word *api* (also): the word *pāda* with its vowel elided is also included, and the root *pādayati* ending in *kvip* is also included. Since it is stated under the heading governing *aṅga* (the base) that "it [the suffix] applies to that and to what ends in it," one should understand that in the rule concerning the *aṅga* ending in that [suffix], the phrase "and to that *aṅga*" must also be applied.

However, at the end of that [rule], it must be stated that "it exists" (*asti*), and thus its introduction is primarily by means of the genitive case; he shows this with the words "and that" (*sa ca*). Although the entire aggregate ending in *t* is indicated by the word *pāt*, nevertheless, since the genitive is heard even in that which is specified as a qualifier, the substitute applies to that alone, not to the aggregate that is merely understood—this is the meaning. Regarding "dvipada": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has two feet," and the final syllable is elided by the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*. Regarding "dvipadikām": [the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added].
The suffix *vun* is applied after words such as *pādaśata* (one hundred feet) and others, and there is also elision [of the final syllable]. The word *vyāghrapāt* belongs to the *gargādi* group.
The semivowel of *vasu* undergoes vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).

Regarding the word *pecuṣaḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *pac* with the suffix *kvasu*, with the substitution of *et* (i.e., *e*) and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). But how can there be the inclusion of *kvasu* which has two indicatory letters (*dvyanubandhaka*)? To this he says: "by the mention of *vasu*. And this is obtained because the letter *ū* was added as an indicatory letter to the *vasu* that is the substitute for *śatṛ*; for its sole purpose is so that there may be a general inclusion here, since the operation required by an *ugit* [suffix] is already established through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
The substitution of *ūṭ* occurs in place of *vāh*. (Pāṇini 6.4.132)

The term *vāha* refers to the root *vah* ending in the suffix *ṇvi*; since this suffix is prescribed after a word accompanied by an upapada, it follows by implication that here there is an extension of the rule to include what ends in that suffix—thus he says, "ending in *vāh*. [The phrase] "samprasāraṇa occurs" shows the continued application of the mention of *samprasāraṇa*. By this, it occurs in place of the letter *v*; otherwise, it would apply to the final letter. In the examples, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied according to the rule *chandasi sahaśca vahaśca*.

"Then," and so forth. The question is: by the mere word *vāha*, is it the previously mentioned *samprasāraṇa* alone that is to be prescribed? He states the resulting form: "when the *samprasāraṇa* has been performed. And [the rule] "when there is *guṇa*"—the word "having been performed" (*kṛte*) is to be supplied here as well. With respect to the *ṇvi* suffix, the *guṇa* occurs by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). But if this were so, in cases such as *śālīn vahati*, where the subordinate word (*upapada*) does not end in *a*, the form *śālyūha* would not be established. To this he replies: "and when it ends in something other than *a*. By the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that this also applies when the prefix (*upasarga*) ends in *a*.

Therefore, one should not raise the objection that in forms such as *prauha*, the rule *eṅi pararūpam* (P. 6.1.94) would apply [instead]. [The author states: "It serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). He asks, "How is this an indicator? and replies: "For when that [rule] exists... The quality (*guṇa*) is *antaraṅga* because it depends on the internal element *aṇ*; whereas the other is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on external suffixes such as those beginning with *ā*. Thus, the *bahiraṅga* status of the latter follows from its dependence on external suffixes beginning with *ā*.
In the absence of a taddhita suffix, the *u* of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* is replaced by *a*.

Regarding *śauvam*: there is elision of the *ṭi* (the vowel *u*) by the rule *na taddhite*. Regarding *yauvanam*: from the sense "the state of a youth" (*yūno bhāvaḥ*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo 'ṇ*; the *an* [of *yuvan*] remains as the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*). *Māghavanaḥ* means that which has Maghavā as its deity.

Since the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) includes its form qualified by gender as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *samprasāraṇa* even for the word *yuvati*. Similarly, in forms such as *maghavataḥ*, once the substitution of *tr* [for *t*] has been applied according to the rule *maghavā bahulam*, there would be the consequence [of the same substitution] because "that which is modified in one part is not different" (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*). To address this, he says: "Of *śvan* and so forth," etc. He explains how this is obtained: "For this purpose," etc. The term *anaḥ* is the remainder for both [rules], and not for the immediately preceding one alone, due to the force of the division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*).

Nor does this [rule] apply to cases such as *maghavata* and so forth, because that which is modified in one part is not considered different [from the original], since when there is an extension of a general rule, there is no extension of its specific instances.
The *ana* suffix is substituted for the *allopa* [of the final vowel] when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel.

*Aditi* is a word with its case-ending elided (*luptavibhaktika*). Therefore, in rules such as *āto dhātoḥ*, there is a connection with the word *lopa* alone. Regarding *rājakīyam*: under the governing rule *garttottarapadācchaḥ*, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *rājñaḥ ka ca*; the letter *k* is a substitute for the final [letter]. Here, because that which has undergone a partial modification is not different from the original, the application [of the rule] follows.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is also applied after words preceded by *ṣat*, *pūrvahan*, *dhṛtara*, and *rājan*.

Is this for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), or rather for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*)? And how is it for the purpose of restriction, or how is it for the purpose of an injunction? If the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-elision of the original form) applies only to the immediately preceding elision of the *ṭi*-suffix (*ṭilopa*), then—since the elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) has not been prevented by that *prakṛtibhāva*—it is already established by the previous rule; therefore, [the present rule] is for the purpose of restriction. On the other hand, if the *prakṛtibhāva* applies without distinction to both the elision of the vowel and the elision of the *ṭi*-suffix, then it is for the purpose of an injunction.

Even there, regarding the position of restriction (*niyamapakṣa*), if the restriction were such that [the suffix] *aṇ* occurs only after words beginning with *ṣatpūrva*, then it would not apply here in the cases of *sāmanaḥ* and *vaimanaḥ*; however, there would be the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) in the case of *tākṣṇya*. Alternatively, there might be a restriction of both kinds.

It might be argued that [the rule applies] only to those beginning with *ṣapūrva* when followed by *aṇ*, or only to *aṇ* following those beginning with *ṣapūrva*. Even so, in the cases of *sāmanaḥ*, *vaimanaḥ*, and *tākṣṇyaḥ*, the form *sāmanyaḥ*—meaning "one who is good at the *sāmans*"—would result here. Therefore, accepting that there is *prakṛtibhāva* (original form preservation) for both, he says this for the sake of clarity: "there is elision (*lopa*) of that vowel *a*. Thus we have *tākṣṇaḥ*. Here, *aṇ* is used in the sense of "belonging to" (*idamarthe*), whereas in the sense of "descendant" (*apatye*), the suffix *ṇya* occurs after *tākṣṇa* (as in *tākṣṇyaḥ*). Thus, neither of the two suffixes applies. Furthermore, the exclusion of the elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable) is established even by the prohibition;
however, by the statement "by its original base" (*tat-prakṛtyā*), the cessation of both [suffixes] is effected.
The substitution of *vibhāṣā* (optionally) occurs for the case endings *ṅi* and *śi*.

The term *śī* here refers to the word-form *śī* [as prescribed] by the rules *jasaḥ śī*, *auṅa āpaḥ*, and *napuṃsakācca*; it does not refer to the *śi* [substitute] for *jaś* and *sas* [prescribed by] *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ*, because that short-vowel-ending form lacks the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) required in this context.
Not so, when the suffix *vam* follows a root ending in a conjunct consonant. Pāṇini 6.4.137.

Since the conjunction is qualified by the letters *va* and *ma*, the rule of "specification of the end" (*tadantavidhi*) applies here; thus, the inclusion of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of clarity.
A vowel [is designated as a "light" syllable]. 6.4.138.

Here, the term *aca* is understood as the root *añc*, with its nasal (*n*) elided. It is not, however, a reference to a *pratyāhāra* (a grammatical abbreviation); for if it were so, the meaning would be "there is elision of a stem ending in a vowel (*ac*)," and consequently, the rule *āto dhātoḥ* ("elision of final *ā* of a verbal root") would become redundant. Furthermore, since [the author] specifies *yat* after *dyu-prāg-apāg-udak-pratīcaḥ* and states *cau*, it is known that here only the root *añc* is being referred to. By this, it is also established that the *ac* suffixes such as *pacādyac* are not included here.
The long vowel *ā* is substituted for the final short vowel of a verbal root ending in *a*.

The meaning is that [the rule] is established as such even in the usage of people like us outside of the Sūtra; however, within the Sūtra itself, it is established simply by the fact that it is a technical (sautra) designation.
In mantras, the substitution of ātman for āṅ and other such forms occurs from the beginning [of the word]. 6.4.141.
The term *āṅ* is understood as the third case singular by the method of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).

[The objection is: "Since *āṅ* is seen elsewhere as well, it should not be stated that 'it is *āṅ*'. [Response: Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *ātaḥ*, the word *ādeḥ* (beginning) can also be omitted. In the form *ātmanye*, the substitute *yā* is for the seventh case singular.
The suffix *ḍin* is applied after the word *viṃśati*. (Pāṇini 5.2.46)

What is the purpose of including the word *ti* [in the rule]? It is so that [the elision] might not apply to the final [sound]. Since the elision of the final sound is already established by the subsequent rule, this present formulation must be for the sake of a restriction (*niyama*): namely, so that it may occur only when there is a *ḍit* suffix, and not otherwise, lest the elision of *ya* (by *yasyeti ca*) should take place.

Furthermore, when both a general rule (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible, the general rule alone is superior. Even so, by the force of the initial undertaking [of the present sūtra], the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52) is set aside, and there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would indicate the elision (*lopa*) of the entire aggregate, rather than the elision of the word *ti*, which is not explicitly mentioned [as the object of the genitive]. However, when the mention of *ti* is present, by its own force, the rule *alo 'ntyasya* does not apply; thus, the elision occurs for the entire word *ti*. In forms such as *viṃśam* and *viṃśakam*, once the elision of *ti* has taken place, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) applies by virtue of the rule *ato guṇe* (P. 6.1.97). The elision of *i* prescribed by *yasyeti ca* (P. 6.4.148) does not occur here, because the elision of *ti* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
The final sound of a word ending in *ṭi* is elided. (Pāṇini 6.4.143)

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of *ḍitya*": the letter *ḍ* is not for the purpose of pronunciation (*śravaṇārtha*). First, in the rule *ḍmatup*, it is understood that this applies when the name refers to a country (*deśe tannāmni*); however, a country named after such [an object] is not understood by means of a suffix containing the letter *ḍ*. Furthermore, even in the case of *ḍa*, the letter *ḍ* is not for the purpose of pronunciation, because it is specifically prescribed in the rule *prāvṛṭ-śarat-kāla-divāṃ je*. As for the example *mandurajaḥ*, the shortening occurs according to the rule *ṅy-āpoḥ saṃjñā-chandasor bahulam*.
The [vṛddhi] substitution does not take place before a taddhita suffix. Pāṇini 6.4.144.

Regarding the word *teṣām*: the phrase "the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) is obtained" is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅga*). One who moves by means of a stool is a *pīṭhasarpī*. From the word *kalāpin*, in the sense of "taught by," the suffix *aṇ* is applied; and according to the rule *chandobrāhmaṇāni ca tadviṣayāṇi*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "one who studies that"; then, by the rule *proktālluk*, there is elision [of the feminine suffix], resulting in *kālāpāḥ*. Similarly for *kauthumāḥ*. But what is the reason for resorting to a secondary (*gauṇa*) application rather than the primary (*mukhya*) meanings, such that the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "taught by him" and so forth? To this he says: *śaiṣikeṣu*.

Some read *titali* as *tilānāṃ talam* (the base of sesame seeds), following the *pṛṣodarādi* group; that which possesses this is *titalī*. The same applies to *lāṅgalī*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he extends [the application] to all cases. In the three subsequent [examples], the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of "belonging to this" (*idamarthe*). The same applies to *āśmā*. In *cārma*, it is in the sense of a derivative (*vikāre*). In *cārmaṇa*, it is in the sense of "belonging to this" (*idamarthe*) and also in the sense of a derivative, provided it is not a vessel (*kośāt anyatra*). Regarding *śauva*: here, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "its" (*tasyedaṃ*). Since *vṛddhi* would have been required by the subsequent rule, its prohibition is applied because the word belongs to the *dvārādi* group; then, after the *aij* substitution has occurred, the *ṭi*-portion is elided.

Regarding the phrase "the other is *śauvana*": however, because [the suffix] *añ* applies to both modifications (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*) when the source is a living being, there is an absence of the *prakṛtibhāva* (preservation of the original form), and thus the form remains simply *śauva*.

"What then?"—this question arises because [the word] is not included in the list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*). The answer is that this is an "open-ended class" (*ākṛti-gaṇa*) because the word *ādi* (beginning) signifies "type" or "manner. Regarding *sāyamprātikam*: since it has been stated that [the suffix] occurs even for words denoting time in any way whatsoever, the suffix *ṭhañ* itself applies even to a collection of times; and because of the citation "and those whose opposition is eternal" (*yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāśvatikaḥ*), there is no substitution of *ka* by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*. Regarding *śāśvatam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya*.
The augment *ah* is applied before *ṛṣṭi* and *khora*. 6.4.145.

Regarding *dvyaha*: by the rule *na saṅkhyādeḥ samāhāre*, the substitution of *ah* is prohibited. Regarding *dvyahīna*: a *dvigu* compound is formed for the sake of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [followed by] the suffix *kha* after *samā*; then, by the rule *dvigor vā*, and *rātry-ahaḥ-saṃvatsarāc ca*, the suffix *kha* is applied. Regarding *āhnikam*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of *ārhīya*. He states that the employment of the particle *eva* is for the sake of clarity; however, it is not for the purpose of excluding a contrary restriction. He says "only *ahar*" because, if there were a contrary restriction, the rule *ātmādhvānau khe*—which prescribes the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*)—would become useless, as there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of the *ṭi* vowel when the suffix *kha* follows another word.
The substitution of *orguṇaḥ* [occurs]. 6.4.146.

The suffix *yañ* occurs after [patronymic] lineages such as *bābhravya*; the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of "purchased" (*prākkrītīya*) after bases beginning with *śaṅku*, as in *ugavādibhyo yat*; and the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) after bases such as *aupagava*. Rules such as "a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*)... and so forth are stated even though they were not explicitly mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*, because their usage is widespread. Regarding the category of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) itself: [the rule] "after a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) ending in *ū* or *ī*, [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied]" results in *paṭvī*.
The elision of *ḍha* occurs [after *a*] except when it is part of the word *akadrūḥ*. 6.4.147.

From the word *madrabāhu*, by the rule *bāhv-antāt saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.96), the suffix *uṅ* is applied; from the word *kadru*, likewise by the rule *kadru-kamaṇḍalvoḥ chandasi saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.71), the suffix *ūṅ* is applied. From these two [words ending in *ūṅ*], the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to form the feminine derivatives denoting offspring (*apatya*). In other cases, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied after words denoting four-footed animals. Regarding the word *kamaṇḍalu*, the *Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa* states: "one should place [it] upon. *Śṛgāla* means a jackal, and *śivā* means a female jackal. A jackal itself is called *jambū-jambuka*.
And [the genitive ending] is used after a word denoting that [to which something belongs], as in *yasya*. (Pāṇini 6.4.148)

In the compound *iśca aśca* (i-a), which is a collective dvandva, the word *aś* would normally be placed first according to the rule "in a dvandva of words ending in vowels, that beginning with a vowel other than *a* and ending in *a* takes precedence" (*dhyantādajādyadantaṃ vipratiṣedhena*). However, this does not occur here because it is a *sautra* (Vedic/Pāṇinian) usage. Furthermore, the word *ya* is not included [in the technical name *iyaṅuvaṅ*], as there is evidence for this: namely, that the author specifies the elision of the suffix *yañ* after the word *garga* and the suffix *ṅīp* after the word *kumāra* in the rules "oto gārgyasya" and "kumāryā vayasi. From this very indication, it follows that in the case of the vowel *e*, there is the inclusion of the short vowel, and by association, the same applies to the vowel *i*.

However, the long vowel [substitution] occurs even for a short [vowel] due to the inclusion of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*). For example, *dākṣī* [is derived from *dakṣi*] by the rule *ito manuṣyajāteḥ* (P. 4.1.65), and likewise *sakhī* from the word *sakhi* by the rule *sakhyaśiśvīti bhāṣāyām* (P. 4.1.62). In all such cases, the form is established through the long vowel substitution of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇadīrghatva*); what is the purpose of [the subsequent] elision (*lopa*)? To this he replies: "For, in the case of *savarṇadīrghatva*... [and so on]. Regarding *atisakheḥ*: in the *tatpuruṣa* compound *atikrāntaḥ sakhīm*, the suffix *ṭac* prescribed by *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (P. 5.4.91) does not apply because that rule is non-universal (*anityatva*).

Consequently, there would be the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*) by the rule *ekādeśasya*. Since this [shortening] is applied to that which has been formed together with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, the prohibition [contained in the rule] *asakhī* would apply. But how could a prohibition stated for the word *sakhi* result in a prohibition for the word *atisakhi*? [The answer is: because there is no extension of application (*tadantavidhi*) to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is used in a form already including that extension.

He thinks as follows: according to the view that "technical designations and rules of interpretation apply at the time they are needed," in the rule *gher ṅiti*, the designation *ghi* is present; and since there is the governing heading *aṅgasya*, there is the application of the rule regarding the inclusion of what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*)—namely, "of that [stem] and its subsequent word. Alternatively, the designation *ghi* applies to the remainder consisting solely of the phonemes *i* and *u*, and not to that which ends with them. Consequently, in the prohibition *asakhi*, the prohibition also applies to the *i*-phoneme of the word *sakhi*, and not to the word *sakhi* itself.

And since, in the case of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), this is simply the vowel *i* of the word *sakhi*, the prohibition would indeed apply even when it occurs at the end of a compound. However, when there is elision (*lopa*), although the form remains identical after the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) has been applied, the prohibition does not take effect because that [form] is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*). In *dauleya* and similar forms, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule *itaścāniñaḥ*. The words *balākā* and *sumitrā* belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group. Regarding *saurya*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tenaikadik*; and this example is cited without regard for the specific restriction in the rule *sūryāgastyayośche ca ṅyāṃ ca*.
Regarding the rule *iyaṅuvaṅbhyām*: the scope for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is, for example, *śriyau* and *bhravau*; the scope for elision (*lopa*) is, for example, *dauleyaḥ* and *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*.
[The rule] *sūryatiṣyāgastayamatsyānāṃ ya upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.149) [prescribes elision of the *y* of these words when followed by a *taddhita* suffix beginning with a vowel].

If, in this context, the sun and so forth were qualified by their status as *bha*—that is, [if the rule applied] to "those called *bha*, such as the sun and so forth"—then it would apply only where the sun and so forth themselves bear the designation *bha*, as in *sūrī* (the wife of Sūrya) or *agastī* (the wife of Agastya). However, it would not apply in cases such as *saurī balākā* ("the crane belonging to the sun"), because here the word *sūrya* is not designated as *bha*; rather, it ends in the suffix *aṇ*. Therefore, the elision (*lopa*) is connected with the mere category of *bha* without regard to its specific form; the letter *y* is qualified by the sun and so forth.

Demonstrating this, he says: "In the case of *sūrya*, *tiṣya*, *agastya*, *matsya*, etc. The meaning is that there is elision of the *yakāra* which is the penultimate (*upadhā*) of a stem designated as *bha*, provided it belongs to *sūrya* and the others. Regarding *saurī*: he shows how the stem *saurī*, being a *bha*-designated member ending in *aṇ* when followed by the suffix *ī*, has its *yakāra* as the penultimate; this is shown by the rule "elision of *ya* when *aṇ* follows" (*aṇi yasyeti ca*). Regarding "because of having different bases" (*vyāśrayatvāt*): there is a difference of basis (*vyāśrayatva*) because [the former rule] is the elision of *ya* when *aṇ* follows, while [the latter] is the elision of *ya* when *ī* follows.

Regarding the rule *īkāre tu yaḥ*: the word *lopaḥ* (elision) is understood from the context. The phrase *bhasyāṇantasya* means that for a stem designated as *bha* which ends in the vowel *a*, the *y* becomes the *upadhā* (penultimate). However, the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is prohibited for both instances of elision of *y* with respect to the rule for the elision of *y*. In the example *matsyacarī*: [the derivation is] *matsī* (fish-woman) having existed previously (*bhūtapūrva*), followed by the suffix *caran*. By the rule *tasilādiṣu*, there is *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution). Due to the *ṭi*-marker, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Here, the word *matsyacara* is designated as *bha*, and the *y* is related to *matsya*; however, this *y* is not the *upadhā* of the *bha*-designated stem, and thus there is no elision.

"The inclusion of the word *artha* is for the sake of what follows; however, in this case, since only the vowel *i* which is the penultimate (*upadhā*) of that which bears the technical name *bha*—when related to *sūrya* and so on—is intended, and not any other letter, there is no purpose [for it] here.

Regarding *saurīya*: from the word *saurya*, the suffix *cha* (yielding *-īya*) is applied by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. Similarly: *āgastīyaḥ*; *āgastyaḥ* (where *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied by the rule *apatye*). Regarding the rule *tiṣyapuṣyayor* (Pāṇini 4.3.34): since [the suffix] is already obtained for *tiṣya* by the very rule [4.3.33] concerning lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*); for *puṣya*, however, it is an original injunction (*vidhi*) because [the suffix] was not otherwise obtained. If the word *artha* were not included in the sūtra, this [application] would also follow as a possibility.

Regarding the passage beginning with *antikasya*: this is desired in the Vedic language (*chandas*). "Of a word beginning with *ka*" means of the letter *ka* and the letter *a*. "And [it becomes] udātta on the first syllable" is an exception to the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).
