Regarding *antitaḥ*: the suffix *tasi* is applied according to the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*. Regarding *kādeḥ*: this means of the word *ka*. Regarding *antiṣat*: the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *mantr̥-viṣ-...* and so forth. However, the followers of the Bahvṛca school read the text separately. Regarding *ye ca*: this is understood in connection with the word *dṛśyate*. Regarding *antiya*: the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*. Because the elision of the initial *ka* is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*), there is no elision of the *y* by the rule *yasyeti ca*.
The elision of the *taddhita* suffix occurs after a word ending in *hal*. (Pāṇini 6.4.150)

The phrase "taddhita" (secondary derivative) is understood as excluded [from this rule]. This is because the term "taddhita" is mentioned again in the subsequent sūtra; therefore, this is a rule for the suffix *īya*.
And in a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel other than *ā*, the final *i* or *u* of a patronymic (*apatya*) is elided.

Regarding "gārgaka": [the suffix] *vuñ* is applied by the rule *gotrokṣoṣṭra-* etc., and [the suffix] *ṇya* is applied by the rule *saṅkaśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*; thus, by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-ādayas-tadrājāḥ*, these are *cāturarthika* suffixes. Thereafter, the suffix *vuñ* is applied by the rule *dhanvayopadhād vuñ* in the sense of "born there" (*jāta*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the mention of *taddhita*," etc.: [in the case of] *somo devatā asya*, the suffix *ṭyaṇ* is applied after *soma*; because it has the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added. The mention of *taddhita* is made here so that the elision prescribed by the rule *halas taddhitasya* may apply even to this *ya* which is not part of a patronymic (*anapatya*). Otherwise, the previously mentioned mention of *taddhita* would have to be carried over (*anuvartate*) here; and while that is being carried over, the term *īt* connected to it would also be carried over. If both of those were carried over here, they would also have to be carried over into the preceding rule.

Furthermore, since the result would already be established by the preceding rule alone, this restriction—"in the case of a *taddhita* suffix ending in *ī*, [the *vṛddhi* substitute applies] only for a patronymic"—would have to be understood as applying specifically to *taddhita* suffixes beginning with non-*ā* vowels. Consequently, just as the *vṛddhi* does not occur for a non-patronymic in a *taddhita* suffix—as in *sāṅkaśyaka*—likewise, it would also not occur in the case of a suffix beginning with *ī*, such as in *saumī iṣṭiḥ*.

However, since the mention of *taddhita* implies that by it the mention of *taddhita* is excluded from the preceding rule, the elision of *ī* would be prescribed by the previous rule for both [words]—whether they are *apatya* (descendants) or *anapatya* (non-descendants). Thus, the elision of *y* is established even in the case of *saumī iṣṭiḥ*; therefore, the mention of *taddhita* is made.

But surely, if this restriction were to apply to both [the base and the suffix], the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless; one could simply have formulated a single rule: *hala āpatyasya taddhitasyānāti*. Then, by virtue of that split of the rule, there would be the continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of only one of the two. Even in that case, because of the statement "when not followed by *ai* or *au*," the same fault remains: the elision would apply even to a non-patronymic *taddhita* suffix. How so? If it applies to a patronymic, the restriction would be possible only when it begins with *th* and is not preceded by *ā*; thus, in cases such as *sāṅkāśyaka*, the elision would indeed occur.

The restriction that [the suffixes] are without the vowel *ā* (anākārāḥ) is possible. If it is not possible, then there is no fault whatsoever, because one relies on two restrictions: first, that [the suffixes] are applied only to the base ending in *apatya* when a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) follows; and second, that even in that case, they are applied only after a base that is without the vowel *ā*.
And [the substitution of *i* for the final vowel occurs] before the suffixes *kyac* and *vya*. (Pāṇini 6.4.152)

Regarding *gargīyati*: by the rule *kyaci ca*, there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel. Regarding *gārgīyate*: by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ*, there is lengthening; however, this is impossible in the case of *kyaṣ* because it does not denote a descendant (*apatya*). Regarding *gārgībhūta*: by the rule *asya cvau*, there is the substitution of *i* for the final vowel.
There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cha* after [the group of stems] beginning with *bilvaka*.

Since *bilvaka* and others are not included in this list of nominal stems (*prātipadika-gaṇa*), he says "in the *naḍādi* group" in order to identify them. *Bilvaka* and the rest are indeed recited among the *naḍādi* stems; there, when the suffix *kuk* is applied, the form ending in *k* is what is reproduced here. The compound is analyzed as "those for which *bilvaka* is the first. The reason it was not done [with the suffix *ka*] when applying the *jaś*-rule (the substitution of voiced stops) is that it would have resulted in the destruction of the intended form. Therefore, in the sense of the "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, [the suffix *ka* is applied] to those for which *bilvaka* is the first.

One need not suspect the inclusion of those ending in *cha*, because they do not appear in the recitation (*pāṭha*). [The questioner asks: "Why is *cha* mentioned? The question implies that nothing else can possibly follow after the addition of the augment *kuk*. [The author replies: "How then could there be the possibility of the removal of *kuk*? He says: "Otherwise... This very mention of *cha* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that this *paribhāṣā* exists. [Regarding the phrase] "of the mere *yakāra*": since the word "of the penultimate" (*upadhāyāḥ*) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), the substitution would apply only to that [the *yakāra*].
Even if that [carry-over] were removed, the undesirable result would still follow because of the rule "of the first of the following" (*ādeḥ parasya*).
In the case of the suffixes *tṛ*, *iṣṭha*, and *imaya*, [the final vowel of the preceding stem is replaced by its Guṇa substitute]. || 6 - 4 - 154 ||

In the case of *dohīyasi*, because the substitution of *gh* and so forth is considered *asiddha*, the suffix *tṛ* is first elided; subsequently, due to the absence of its cause, those substitutions (*gh*-ness, etc. do not occur. It was stated that "elision takes place," and since that would apply to the final letter, he says: "of the whole. He states the reason: "for [if it were] of the final..."

[Objection: In that case, only elision (*luk*) should be prescribed; in this way, the cessation of everything is easily obtained. To this he says: "But as for this [term] *luk*... What, then, would be the fault in its continued application? To this he says: "For thus... Nor does the *guṇa* substitution occur first, because of the rule stating that elision (*luk*), though external (*bahiraṅga*), sublates even internal (*antaraṅga*) operations.

"The mention of *imanij* is for the sake of subsequent rules; it is not for the sake of this [present] rule, because that suffix cannot occur after the word *tṛ*. Nor can this very [mention] be considered a restrictive rule (*kalpaka*), since its purpose is justified by its application to subsequent rules. [Objection: But if that were so, then even the suffixes *iṣṭhan* and *īyasun* would be impossible due to the restriction 'only after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) do [the suffixes] beginning with *aj* occur'; therefore, he says: 'But the other two...'"
The final phoneme of a word-stem (aṅga) ending in /ṭ/ is elided. Pāṇini 6.4.155.

Regarding the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavat*: the suffix *vati* is used here in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*). Since the word *ṇau* (in the locative case) is specified as the point of comparison (*pratiyogin*), the grammatical operation that applies to the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* is extended [to the causative suffix *ṇic*], but not the operation that applies to the base form of *iṣṭhan* itself. Consequently, in the example *bahayati* (he causes many to speak), the substitution of *yi* for *ṇi* occurs by the rule *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*; however, in the absence of that [substitution], the change of *bhū* [to *bhu*]—which is taught in conjunction with it—also does not occur. Some, however, cite the change to *bhū* as an example, as in *bhāvayati* (he causes to be) and *etayati* (he causes to go).

Since the removal of the *nakāra* is already established by the very extension (*atideśa*) of the elision of *ṭi*, the explicit mention of "like the masculine" (*puṃvat*) is for the purpose of indicating that the rule regarding simultaneous prescription (*sanniyogaśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By this, forms such as *śyaiveyaḥ* and *aineyaḥ* are established.

Another says: in cases such as *aiḍaviḍayati* (meaning "he calls himself Aiḍaviḍa") from *iḍaviḍa*, or *dāradayati* (meaning "he calls himself a Darada") from *darada*, the mention of "masculine-like" (*puṃvat*) is for the purpose of extending the masculine gender. But surely, the masculine-like form of words like *iḍaviḍa* is not observed in the presence of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, because *iṣṭhan* itself is impossible there. It is not the case that what is actually observed in *iṣṭhan* is extended; rather, it is what is possible [there] that is extended. Otherwise, in forms such as *atirājayati*, the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) would not occur.

The mention of the *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is an indicator for the base form (*prakṛti*) in general. Therefore, even in cases such as *droṇīm ācaṣṭe*, the elision of the *ṭi* portion occurs. There is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) here, because the word has not been previously used in the masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*). Alternatively, by the *paribhāṣā* regarding forms qualified by gender, there is the inclusion of that which ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*. For it was stated previously: "In the case of the mention of a *prātipadika*, whatever [form] may be mentioned, that which is qualified by gender is included."

In forms such as *sthāpayati*, the vowel elongation (*vṛddhi*) prescribed by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* does not occur, because of the metarule: "When an operation has already taken effect upon a stem (*aṅga*), there is no further application [of another operation] once that [stem] is finalized. The meaning of this is as follows: when some operation prescribed under the heading of "stem" (*aṅgādhikāra*) has occurred, and a subsequent operation is about to take effect, there is no application of that subsequent operation provided the stem has become "finalized"—that is, ready for usage. However, where the stem is not yet finalized, the operation certainly takes place—as in *prāpayati* and *sthāpayati*.
In examples such as *kartāram ācaṣṭe*, one must consider whether or not the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *tṛ* occurs by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu*.

In place of the [final phoneme] of *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *hrasva*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, as well as the preceding vowel, there is *guṇa* substitution when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaṇ*.

Although the word *lopa* (elision) under discussion is generally used as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), it is understood here as an object-noun (*karmasādhana*) because of its coordination with "the *yaṇ*-class sounds and so forth" in the expression "that which follows the *yaṇ*-class sounds and so forth is elided. Thus he says: "that which follows the *yaṇ*-class sounds and so forth is elided. The inclusion of the term "preceding" (*pūrva*) is for the sake of clarity; the intention is that by the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi replace *ik*," the guṇa will apply to that *ik* which remains after the elision. For this very reason, suffixes beginning with vowels occur [in place of the elided element].
However, the suffix *iman* does not occur after bases not listed among those beginning with *pṛthu*, due to lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).

In place of *praya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *urū*, *bahula*, *guru*, *vṛddha*, *tṛpra*, *dīrgha*, and *vṛndāraka*, there are substituted respectively *prastha*, *spha*, *var*, *ihar*, *gar*, *varṣ*, *itra*, *dradhi*, and *vṛnda*. (Pāṇini 6.4.157)

The words *priya*, *sthira*, *uru*, *bahula*, and *dīrgha* are recited among the *pṛthu*-group (Pāṇini 5.1.122). Therefore, since the application of the suffix *imanic* has its purpose fulfilled by these [five], this statement—that the suffix *kalpa* applies to the others—is not intended for them. Thus he says: "therefore, for the others... (*tenānyeṣām*).
The final syllable of *bahu* is elided, and *bahu* is replaced by *bhū*.

Regarding the word *bhūyān*: there is the elision (*lopa*) of the initial [element] by virtue of the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54). As for the phrase *anyathā hi*: if, on the other hand, the word *bahoḥ* were not stated, then just as there would be elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes, so too the substitution of *bhū-* would apply to those very same suffixes. One might argue that in that case, elision could optionally apply to the initial [element], while the substitution of *bhū-* could be said to apply to the whole [suffix], since the suffixes are mentioned separately [in the two rules]. Otherwise, one would have simply said *bhūlopo bahoḥ*. It is by adopting this interpretation that the mention in the rule *uttarapadabhūmni* becomes logically consistent.
In place of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, *yiṭ* is also substituted.

The introduction of the augment *yiṭ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to elision (*lopa*). This is because it is formulated when that [elision] has not yet taken effect. Regarding the word "in that" (*tasmin*): it refers to the state where elision is about to occur as an exception. However, if elision were also prescribed by being drawn over (*anukṛṣya*) from the previous rule, then the vowel *i* would not be for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
The *jya* [substitute] is applied in place of *jyā* when followed by the suffixes *īyas* or *iṣṭhan*.

Regarding the word *lopasya*: the sense is that if the elision (*lopa*) were not separated from the augment *yiṭ*, then by that very [elision] forms such as *jyāyān* would be established; thus, it would have been unnecessary to state *āt*. He asks how the establishment [of the form] occurs when there is elision, and answers with *lope hi*. The meaning is that here the term *kṅiti* does not follow [from the previous rule]. In cases such as *uruyā*, the absence of the long vowel is due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The substitution of *ra* occurs for the light vowel *ṛ* that follows a consonant and precedes a suffix beginning with *ha*.

A systematic enumeration must be made. And thus, the rule "of a light vowel following *hal*" need not be stated [separately]. Regarding the form *mātayati*: because the *uṇādi* suffixes are considered non-etymological (*avyutpanna*), the elision of the *tṛ* sound prescribed by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* does not occur; rather, in this case, the substitution of *ra* (by *raṛtoḥ*) would apply, superseding the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) due to its higher priority.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied after a verbal root beginning with a consonant by virtue of its inherent nature.

Regarding the rule "in the case of *iṣṭha*, *im*, and *yas*, [the final vowel and consonant of the stem] are replaced by [the corresponding long vowel] when followed by these," if there were no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *iṣṭha* and the others here, then in the following cases—*śriye hitam* (beneficial for prosperity), where the suffix *cha* is applied before *krīta* according to Pāṇini 5.1.1, resulting in *śrīyam*; and *jño devatāsya* (that whose deity is Jña), resulting in *jñaḥ sthālīpākaḥ*—the elision of *ya* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.148) would not occur. Consequently, in the form *śrīyam*, the substitution of *iyaṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.77) would take effect. Therefore, *iṣṭha* and the others must be understood as recurring. Thus, we have *srajiṣṭhaḥ*.

Why were *tha* and *pra* etc. overlooked? [In forms such as] *preṣṭhaḥ*, *preyān*, *stheṣṭhaḥ*, and *stheyān*, because *pra* and the others are not established [by the rule], the elision of the *ṭi* (the *i*) and the elision of *ya* (by *yasyeti ca*) will not occur. In this case, however, [in forms like] *śreṣṭhaḥ* and *śreyān*, the elision will not occur due to the force of the explicit utterance of the vowel *a*. Therefore, the possibility of this example exists only when there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup*.

If this is so, it is true that when the *ṭilopa* (elision of the feminine suffix) has not yet occurred, the rule for the elision (*luk*) of the *vin* and *matup* suffixes will indeed supersede that *ṭilopa*. For [the rule] supersedes the *ṭilopa* that applies to a stem ending in *vin* or *matup*. But as for the *ṭilopa* that would apply to the remaining portion once those two have been elided, how could that be superseded? For the elision of *vin* and *matup* is not initiated while that [remaining *ṭilopa*] is still unobtained.

This must necessarily be understood in this way: that the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) does not obstruct [the application of] what remains undifferentiated (*aviśiṣṭa*). Otherwise, even in cases where what remains consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the elision of the *ṭi* would not occur; consequently, counter-examples such as *vasiṣṭhaḥ* and *vasīyān* would be untenable. Thus, in the case of *brahmaṣṭhaḥ*—meaning "one who possesses *brahman* to a superlative degree"—the elision of the *ṭi* occurs by the rule *na-staddhite* ("there is elision of the *n* when a *taddhita* suffix follows"). Likewise, the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* states: "Therefore, one should make a Brāhmaṇa a *brahmiṣṭha*" (one most devoted to sacred knowledge). Similarly, from *payasvin* (possessing milk), we have *payiṣṭhaḥ* (most full of milk), but not *payasiṣṭhaḥ*.
Another says:
"The suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *ra* are not desired even for that which remains when it has more than one syllable;
the elision of the *ṭi* [vowel] is accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya when there is the elision (*luk*) of *vin* and *matup*."

"By nature," and so forth. *Rājanya* is the offspring (*apatya*) of a king; [the suffix] *yat* is applied after *rājan* and *śvaśura*. *Manuṣya* is the offspring of Manu; [the suffix] *añ* is applied after *manu* when denoting a genus, and the augment *puk* is added. From these two, the suffix *vuñ* is applied to form a collective, according to the rule beginning with "in the sense of a collection of cows, oxen, camels," and so on. Regarding the rule "of the offspring-suffix," etc.: this was stated by accepting that these two [suffixes, *yat* and *añ*] denote offspring. However, when the alternative view is held that in both cases the word-meaning is merely the genus (*jāti*) and there is no sense of offspring at all, then since they would not be "offspring-suffixes" (*apatyapratyaya*), the elision (*lopa*) would not even arise; thus, there would be no purpose for the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
The suffix *inaṅ* is applied [to a word ending in *ī*] when it does not denote a descendant. Pāṇini 6.4.164.

Regarding the word *sāṃkūṭinam*: the root *kūṭ* means "to burn" and has a long vowel in its penultimate syllable; the suffix *inuṇ* is applied in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*) to form an abstract noun (*bhāva*), and the suffix *amanuṇ* [is added] after such a formation.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is applied after the words *gāthika*, *vaidathika*, *aiśika*, *gaṇika*, and *paṇika*.
These [words] end in the possessive suffix *in*. The word *gāthā* belongs to the *vrīhy-ādi* group. *Vidatha* means sacrifice (*yajña*).
And [the suffixes] beginning with *saṃyoga* [are applied]. 6-4-166.
This undertaking is for the sake of offspring.
The augment *an* is applied [after the root] *gam* when followed by the suffixes *kvi*, *kvip*, or *kvun*.

The term *anapatye* (not denoting a descendant) is excluded. From *sūmanas* and *veman*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyedam*. From *suyajas*, [the suffix] *aṇ* with the *uṅarvanip* augment is applied; for a short vowel, there is the *tuk* augment—thus *sutvā*. His descendant is *sautvanaḥ*.
The word *brāhma* [is used] when not denoting a caste (*ajāti*). Pāṇini 6.4.171.

A *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) is made here. If it were not made, then the term *apatye* (in the sense of offspring) would either continue to apply or not; if it did continue, then because the preceding rule [P. 6.4.163] would prohibit *prakṛtibhāva*, the elision of the suffix *ṭi* would already be established by the rule *naṣtaddhite* [P. 6.4.144]. Consequently, this present rule would serve as a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), meaning "only in the sense of non-kinship (*ajāti*) and in the sense of offspring. In that case, the desired forms for offspring would be established: *brāhmaḥ nāradaḥ* (Nārada is a descendant of Brahmā) and *brāhmaṇajātiḥ* (the Brāhmaṇa caste).

However, in the case of non-apatya [derivatives], whether the suffix occurs after a genus (*jāti*) or a non-genus, there would never be the elision of the *ṭi* [the final vowel and following consonant]. For example: *brāhmī oṣadhiḥ* (a medicinal herb belonging to Brahman) and *brāhmaṃ haviḥ* (an oblation belonging to Brahman). But since both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are possible when a term does not recur [from a previous context], the injunction is superior. Thus, while the status of the base form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would apply by the rule "in the case of non-apatya, *an*," this present rule serves as an injunction for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* in the case of non-genuses. Consequently, forms such as *brāhmaṃ haviḥ* are established; however, *brāhmī oṣadhiḥ* is not established because of the prohibition "in the case of non-genus," which would instead result in *brāhmaṇī oṣadhiḥ*.

The meaning is that the form *brāhmaṇa* is not established when applied to offspring (*apatya*), because once the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*) has been prohibited by the preceding rule, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision of the suffixal *ṭi*. He states the purpose of the separate rule: "the word *brāhma*... [is used]. "By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*): since the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* in the sense of offspring is already established by the preceding rule, and since it is impossible to formulate a restrictive rule (*niyama*) by merely saying "*brāhma*," in that case—even for offspring—the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* occurs by this very rule alone due to its higher priority, as in *brāhmo nāradaḥ*. "Or in the sense of offspring" (*apatye vā*).

Otherwise, there would be a prohibition regarding both childlessness and the birth of a child; therefore, he states "in the case of a child born" (*apatye jātāv*) to show that this is a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
The suffix *tācchīlya* (denoting habitual action) is applied after the word *kārmast*. 6-4-172.

"If this is so" means: if, however, this is the suffix *ṇa*. [The objection is that] by the rule *na-staddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.144), the elision of the *ṭi* portion is already established; for in the case of the suffix *aṇ*, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) is indeed applicable. [The reply is: "It is for the sake of providing an indication (*jñāpana*). And thus, for the sake of brevity, the rule *chattrādibhyo 'ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.4.62) should be formulated, since there is no purpose for mentioning the suffix *ṇa*. Regarding the term "denoting habitual action" (*tācchīlika*): because the indication applies to things of a similar nature, it follows that in cases such as *tad-asyām praharaṇam* (Pāṇini 4.2.57) or *prajñā-śraddhā-arcā-* (Pāṇini 5.2.101), where the suffix *ṇa* occurs, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* does not apply.

The forms *dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *ārṣṭiṣeṇa*, *jābāli*, *audameghi*, *sauśruta*, *dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *ārṣṭiṣeṇa*, *jaimini*, *śaiśiri*, *vāśināyani*, *bhrauṇahatya*, *dhāivata*, *sāravaiṅkṣvāka*, *maitreya*, and *hiraṇmaya* [are formed with the suffix *phak*]. 6.4.174.

Regarding the phrase "by way of metaphor" (*upacārāt*): the impossibility of the primary sense is the reason for resorting to a metaphorical usage. As for the form *bhrauṇahatya*, however, there is no purpose in [positing] a *nipātana* (irregular formation), because the substitution of *t* for *h* is already established by the rule *hanasta aciṇṇaloḥ*. Nor does the rule *na-staddhite* entail the elision of the suffix *ṭi*, because between those two [rules], which are both non-obligatory, the latter alone applies due to its priority; therefore, he says: "by the rule *hanasta aciṇṇaloḥ*."

When a grammatical operation is prescribed by the rule *dhātoḥ* (P. 6.4.1) regarding the assumption of the root's own form (*dhātusvarūpagrahaṇe*), that operation is understood to apply only in that specific context; however, the suffix *ṣyañ* is not prescribed in this manner. Rather, it is prescribed by the rule *prātipadikāt* (P. 4.1.1). Therefore, in this case, the *t* is substituted [for the *d*] by means of a technical irregularity (*nipātana*). How so? By means of an irregularity (*nipātanāt*). If that were the case, one might argue that the irregularity is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *kutva*. But this is not so. For, within the section beginning with *na kvādeḥ* (P. 7.3.59), he would have stated *bhrūṇaghnaḥ ṣyañi* instead. Thus, even though the irregularity serves its own purpose, it is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the aforementioned principle].

This word *aikṣvāka* is intended to be both ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) and antodātta (accented on the last syllable). In that case, if only one of these two [accents] were recited, the elision of the vowel *u* in the other would not be established. To this, he says: "by means of the pronoun of accent" (*svarasarvanāmnā*). The state of existing without distinction among the udātta and other accents is *ekaśruti* (monotone). It is called a "pronoun" (*sarvanāma*) because it is like a pronoun. For just as in examples such as *tasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of him"), a pronoun denotes specific individuals such as Upagu and others, so too does *ekaśruti* denote specific accentual distinctions such as the udātta; thus, *ekaśruti* functions as a pronoun for accents. Regarding the phrase "an exception to the substitution of *iy*" (*iyādeśāpavāda*): the substitution of *iy* is what would have been obtained by the rule concerning *kekaya* and others.

In this context, the word *mitrayu* is mentioned four times: first, for the sake of establishing the suffix in the *gṛṣṭyādi* group; second, for the sake of elision (*luk*) in the *yaskādi* group; third, for the sake of the substitution of *itya* in the *kekayādi* rule; and this fourth time is for the sake of the elision of *yu*. With the intention that the double mention [of the word] could have been avoided, he asks: "Now, for what purpose? [The answer is: the reading for the sake of elision need not be made, since it is already established by the rule *yañañoḥ*. He refutes this, saying: "That is not so," because [otherwise] the suffix *aṇ* would apply.

If, however, "na maitreyāt" were not stated immediately after "saṅghāṅkalakṣaṇeṣu," then there would be three instances of elision (*grahaṇa*), and the *nipātana* (irregular formation) would serve no purpose. Regarding "yalopaḥ": this means the elision of the sound *yu*.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the forms *ṛtvyá*, *vāstvyá*, *vāstvyà*, *mādhvī*, and *hiraṇyayá* [are valid]. 6-4-175.

It is stated that the *m* is elided by nipātana (irregular prescription). Because that [elision] is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), there is no application of the *yasya* elision (Pāṇ. 6.4.148). Even so, the rule "lengthening occurs before non-kṛt and non-sārvadhātuka suffixes" (Pāṇ. 7.4.25) would result in lengthening; however, this will not occur because of the principle "when a grammatical operation has already taken effect upon a stem, it does not recur" (*aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttau*). In some places, however, they read "the elision of the *m*. In that case, once the *yasya* elision has been applied, the vowel *ā* of the suffix is heard.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the sixth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Oṃ. Now begins the first quarter of the seventh chapter.
In place of the *yū* (the vowels *i* and *u*) and the *vu* (the semivowels *y* and *v*), when followed by a suffix marked with *ṅ*, there are substituted respectively *an* and *ak*.

For the sake of brevity in the treatise (*śāstra*), the suffixes *yu* and *vu* have been taught; by this [rule], the substitutes *an* and *āk* are prescribed for them. For if *an* and *āk* were taught in their place in each respective instance, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in the treatise. Why does [the substitution] not occur here—[in the case of] *yu* in the sense of "begging" (*bhikṣaṇe*), as in *yutaḥ* or *yutavān*? [Answer: This is the inclusion of the two [suffixes] *yu* and *vu*. How so? Because in the case of *lyaṅ* and others, the vowel *u* is marked with the *it* designation (*itsaṃjñaka*) as being nasalized (*anunāsika*).

Even so, [the substitution] would apply here in *dyūtvā*, *dyūtaḥ*, and *dyūtavān*; however, *ūṭh* has no scope when followed by a vowel (*anu*). Or rather, there is the mention of the word *yu* as having meaning; but this [word *yu*] is meaningless [in these cases], and therefore the substitution does not occur at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*). In *bhujyuḥ*, *mṛtyuḥ*, *kaṃyuḥ*, *śaṃyuḥ*, *ūrṇāyuḥ*, and so on, because the letter *u* is not designated as an *it*, there is an absence of the substitute.

If, then, the letter *u* in *lyuṭ* and other such suffixes were designated as an *it*—as in *nandanaḥ* and *kārakaḥ*—then by the rule *ugidacām*, the augment *num* would apply; for *num* is prescribed after a stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*) that is *ugit*, and these two [suffixes] do not end in a *jhal*.

In that case, should the mention of *jhal* (the rule regarding the suffixes beginning with *jhal*) be made? No, he says. This mention of *jhal* in the rule "of the neuter [stem] ending in *jhal* or *ac*" (*napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*) will be drawn forward [to subsequent rules]. First, [it is drawn to]: "after an *ugit* [stem] and after *ad*-stems, before a *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffix], except for a verbal root" (*ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne'dhātoḥ*); then [to]: "*yuj* [takes *num*] except in a compound" (*yujerasamāse*). Then [the rule becomes]: "of the neuter [stem] ending in *jhal*" (*napuṃsakasya jhalaḥ*); then [to]: "after an *ac* [stem], of the neuter" (*acaḥ*, *napuṃsakasya*). And this mention of *jhal* must necessarily be drawn forward; otherwise, *num* would undesirably apply even to a feminine form specified by gender—such as *gomatī bhavatī*.

In that case, O Nandana, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply [to words ending in *yū*] by the rule *ugitaśca*. This is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Since the author [of the Sūtras] in certain instances applies the suffixes *yuc* and *ṣvan* as *ṣit*, and *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* as *ṭit*—as in *śilpini ṣvun* and *ṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca*—this indicates that the long vowel *ī* does not occur for *yuc* and *ṣvan*. This is not a valid indicator. The application of the marker *ṣ* is for the sake of the suffix *ṅīṣ*; the application of the marker *ṭ* is for the sake of non-derivative (*anupasarjana*) forms, because *ṅīp* occurs after a *ṭit* stem that is not a derivative, whereas for an *ugit* stem, it occurs without distinction.

Likewise, the words *śātanī* and *pātanī*, ending in the suffix *lyuṭ*, are listed in the *gaurādi* group; in that case, for the forms *śātanitarā* and *pātanitarā*, the optional shortening conditioned by the presence of an *ugit* vowel—according to the rule *nadyāḥ śeṣasyānyatarasyām ugitaśca*—would apply.

Now, one might object: "Is not the term *nadī* (feminine noun) understood there by the mention of the technical designation *ugit*, so that its inclusion [in the rule] is already established? To this he replies: "No; for in this case a fault would arise. Namely, in forms such as *bhogavatitarā* and *gaurimatitarā*—which end in the feminine suffix *ṅīp* belonging to the *śārṅgarava* class—the optional substitution of the short vowel (*hrasva*) would not occur, yet the author of the Bhāṣya intends this optional shortening even here. Therefore, it cannot be maintained that "the mention of *udīcām* and *yuvan* is intended [to include these cases]."

If it were not so, then [the rule] would also apply to cases such as *yutaḥ*, *yutvā*, *bhujyuḥ*, and *śaṃyuḥ*. To this he says: "of the *yaṇ* [substitutes] that are nasalized" (*anunāsikayaṇoḥ*). For there are indeed *yaṇ* sounds that are nasalized and those that are non-nasalized; among these, the *yakāra* and *vakāra* should be recited as nasalized in those instances where their substitution is desired. Consequently, there is no possibility of an undesired result occurring anywhere. The phrase "of the two suffixes" (*pratyayoḥ*) is merely a statement of fact; it is not intended to exclude non-suffixal occurrences, because such a nasalized *yaṇ* is impossible in a non-suffixal context.

Regarding the word *mṛtyu*: this has been cited because it is mentioned together with others in the rule *bhuji-mṛṅ-bhyaṃ yuktyukau*. For one could indeed say here: "Of the stem, which are the *yuv* and *yū*? And of what stem do the *yuv* and *yū* occur? Of which two does the stem occur?"—and [one might conclude] that these are suffixes (*pratyaya*), yet they are not suffixes. Furthermore, because they would otherwise be meaningless, once the *ṭyu* and *ṭayul* suffixes have been applied, the subsequent addition of *tuṭ* possesses both meaningfulness and the status of a suffix.

Why is it said that "nasality is not promised" (*na pratijñāyate*), rather than "it is not recited"? To this he says: *pratijñānunāsikyāḥ*. Those for whom nasality exists by virtue of a promise (*pratijñā*) are so described. Since there is no recitation [of these sounds] everywhere, or because even where there is a recitation it is confused, the meaning is that nasality is to be understood solely through a formal promise.

If [the form] *yuvor* were a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), then by the rule "a copulative compound is neuter," it would be neuter; and since there is the statement, "In the case of [the neuter suffix] *num*, it prevails over the substitution of *aut*, guna, vṛddhi, and the treatment as *tṛc*," this would block the guna substitution prescribed by *gher ṅiti*; consequently, with the application of *num* by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*, the form would have to be *yuvun*. However, if it is an associative copulative compound (*itaretarayoga-dvandva*), then after reduplication and the substitution of *yaṇ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing two *v* sounds.

Because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no elision (*lopa*) even before a consonant (*val*); therefore, he asks how this [grammatical] instruction is possible, and replies: "of *yu* and *vu*. And as for the neuter gender—this is to be connected with what will be stated later, namely, that "it does not occur. The reason is given in the middle: "gender is not to be prescribed" (*liṅgamaśiṣyam*). "The elision of a phoneme is Vedic" (*chāndaso varṇalopaḥ*): the elision of the vowel *u* occurs either before the *yaṇ*-substitution has taken place, or after it has taken place, [resulting in the elision] of one of the two, the *v*. Another says: this is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the designation of the whole is made by means of the property of its parts.

Regarding the statement "that which is the aggregate characterized by *yu* and *vu*, and that which is *vu*": since the aggregate as a whole does not exist anywhere [as a single entity], the substitutions for *an* and *āk* apply only to its constituent parts.

[The rule] *āyan-ey-īn-īy-iy-aḥ pha-ḍha-kha-cha-ghāṃ pratyayādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.2) [states: The substitutes *āyan*, *ey*, *īn*, *īy*, and *iy* take the place of the initial sounds of the suffixes *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha*.

In the case of [the suffixes] beginning with *pha*, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). At the end, there is only the consonant, because of the mention of the suffixes without vowels in the rule *phaḍhakhachaghām*. And thus, the paribhāṣā regarding "suffixes without an indicatory letter" (*niranubandhaka*) does not apply. In the example *āḍhyakulīnaḥ*: by the statement "not when preceded by another word" (*apūrvapadāt*), the suffix *kha* occurs even after a compound that has a preceding member, according to the rule *kulātkhaḥ*. In the roots *phakka* (to go low) and *ḍhokṛ*, *taukṛ* (both meaning "to go"), the acute accent on the first syllable of the suffix is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), because it is prescribed in conjunction with the formation of the technical name (*saṃjñā*).

However, these [suffixes] beginning with *āyan* are *bahiraṅga* because they are prescribed under the heading of *aṅga*; consequently, in cases where there is no *anubandha* for the sake of accent—such as in *śilāyāḥ* with the suffix *ḍha*—[the rule does not apply].

In rules such as *vṛddhāc chaḥ*, once the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) has been applied, one might object that these subsequent substitutes would have no fixed accent because it is possible to pronounce a vowel that lacks an accent. Anticipating this, he says: "The *āyan* and others," etc. The intention is as follows: since the *phak* and other markers attached to suffixes are invariably connected with the stem (*aṅga*), and since there is no further purpose [for specifying them here], the term "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is not connected [to these rules]. Therefore, these [substitutes] are also internal (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, these [substitutes] being applied first by virtue of their priority, the initial acute accent is applied afterwards.

Regarding this, he states the indicator (*jñāpaka*)—namely, "and so" (*tathā ca*). The sense is as follows: if the substitutes *āyann* and so forth were to occur after the accentuation of the suffix had been applied, then, once the vowel of the word *gha* was made udātta and the consonant *gha*—which by nature tends toward elision (*sraṃsanadharmī*)—was replaced by an anudātta substitute that likewise tends toward elision, the final udātta-accent would already be established. Consequently, the employment of the marker *c* (in *ghac*) would be purposeless. As for the term *iyaṅ*: the mention of the option (*vāvacana*) is the indicator. If these substitutes were to apply even to verbal roots and suffixes, [the author] would have said *ṛteśchaṅ*.

Nor should it be argued that when the suffix *chaṅ* is present and the augment *iṭ*—characterized by the *valādi* rule—is applied, the substitution of *iy* would not occur because [the original vowel] is no longer initial; for it has just been stated that "substitutions are internal (*antaraṅga*)."

Another says: If this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding suffixes attached to verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is also possible to state it regarding suffixes attached to nominal stems (*prātipadika*). When the Teacher prescribes the suffix *īyasun*, he indicates that these [suffixes] are not substitutes for suffixes attached to nominal stems. If they were such substitutes, he would have prescribed only the suffix *chasun*. Furthermore, there are only these two types of suffixes—those attached to verbal roots and those attached to nominal stems—and since substitutes are mentioned, they should apply everywhere by virtue of that explicit statement.

"One must assume that [the suffix] has the designation *it*. Nor can the designation *it* be set aside by the force of the statement itself," he says: "For in the case of *taddhita* suffixes... A counter-argument must be made. As for the counter-argument: in the rule *prācām avṛddhāt phin bahulam*, the addition of the marker *n* to *phin* indicates the absence of the *it*-designation. Nor is the addition of *n* in the rule *pheś cha ca* intended for the sake of a general reference to both *phin* and *phiñ*; for since the governing term "from a base ending in a *vṛddhi* vowel" (*vṛddhāt*) is in effect, only *phiñ* is understood there, not *phin*.
The letter *jha* is the final [element]. 7-1-3.

The inclusion of the word *ādi* (etcetera) has ceased [to apply]. For if that were to continue, then in the case of *śayāntaiḥ*—where *śīṅ* occurs in the *leṭ* mood and the rule *leṭo’ḍāṭau* applies—the augment *āṭ* would be added while the suffix is still in the state of *l*. Consequently, because the letter *jh* would not be initial [in the word-form], the desired result would not follow. But how can a single part of a compound-stated term continue [to apply] when the whole has ceased? This is not a fault. In the view that a mere word-form continues by virtue of its being marked with a *svarita* accent regardless of its meaning, only that which is specifically declared to possess the *svarita* accent continues.

In the view that the meaning (artha) is the governing factor (adhikāra), however, since the meaning of the compound is a single unit, its recurrence would either occur or not. Alternatively, in the previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*), the term *pratyaya* is a separate word with its case-ending elided; therefore, it alone will recur [in the subsequent rule]. As for the substitute (*ādeśa*), the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*); thus, there is no audible [nasalization] in forms such as *pacanti*.
[The suffix *aṅ*] does not occur after a reduplicated stem. 7.1.4.

Regarding "dadati" and so forth: in cases such as "jakṣati," where the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) applies immediately after the verbal root (*upadeśa*), one must necessarily anticipate the absence of the *vikaraṇa* suffix; otherwise, because [the suffix] is constant (*nitya*), once *śap* has been applied, the [substitution] would not occur due to the intervention of that [suffix]. Consequently, even in "dadati" and similar forms, when *śap* undergoes *ślau* doubling and the designation *abhyasta* is applied, the substitution of *ad* occurs. However, it is superseded by the substitution of *jus*, because the latter is without scope (*anavakāśa*). In this case too, once the substitution has been made, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the beginning of the affix (*pratyaya*) applies; this is the intention regarding the phrase "in the subsequent [rule]. But here, the accent "the beginning of *abhyasta*s" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*) applies.
In the *ātmanepada* [verbal endings], [the augment] *it* is not applied after a stem ending in short *a*.

This statement has an unstated purpose: "Let them collect" (*cinvantām*). This is the imperative (*loṭ*); the *etva* (change to *e*) occurs by the rule *ṭeretvam*, and the *ām* replaces the *ta* by the rule *āmetaḥ*. Regarding "they fall away" (*cyavante*):

[An objection is raised]—"But even here, since the substitution of *ad* would apply before the suffix *śap* due to its higher priority, and the rule *anataḥ* would have its scope in examples such as *bebhidante*, why is this stated? To this he replies: "Because it is obligatory (*nityatvāt*). [The question is asked: "What is the purpose of qualifying the letter *jh*? The question implies: what fault is there if the suffix under discussion is qualified by the *ātmanepada* endings that are actually heard? [The example given is: "they lie down" (*śayānte*).

In this case, the āṭ augment following the verbal base (aṅga) is included by the mention of that [base], because it is a part of it; however, the suffix *jhakāra* is separated from it by the *āṭ*. As for the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*), since no specific verbal base is specified, it occurs here as well.
The augment *ruṭ* is added after the root *śīṅ*.

"Of *jha*, *āt*. Now, is there not an absence of the mention of *iha* here? Even that which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is indicated by the nominative; however, the purpose here is served by what is indicated by the genitive. This fifth case [ending] in *śīṅaḥ* will cause the sixth case to be understood for the first case [ending] *at*, according to the principle "that [which is taught] after something [applies] to what follows it. Thus, in *śerate*, the substitute *āt* is for the *jha* that is a part of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix; the augment *ruṭ* is included by the mention of that [suffix].

In common usage as well, a part is observed to be a constituent of a whole, as in the expression "Devadatta’s finger. Similarly, since *ru* is a part of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* applies, and the *guṇa* substitution takes place.

What, then, is the reason that the augment *ru* is prescribed for the *at* which is the substitute for *jha*, rather than being prescribed for the letter *a* itself? For if it were so, the genitive case would not need to be employed.

Therefore, he says: "This [augment] *ruṭ* is inserted after [the final letter]. For if the preceding end were formed by attaching the letter *k*, then in the case of *śerate*, there would be no *guṇa* substitution because the stem would not end in a vowel (*anigantatvāt*). Therefore, it must be stated that it occurs at the very beginning of the following element. If it were to belong to the letter *jh* itself, then just as in *śayānte* the substitution of *āt* for *jha* does not occur because it is separated by the augment *aṭ*, so too in *śerate* it would not occur because it is separated by *ruṭ*.

But is it not logical that the augment *āṭ* would cause an intervention? For since it is a portion of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix, it should not itself intervene; however, it certainly does intervene before the letter *jha*. Furthermore, the augment *ruṭ* is a portion of the letter *jha*; how then can it be an intervener for that [suffix]? It is said in reply: let it be grasped by the mention of that [suffix]; nevertheless, according to the principle that "substitutes apply to what is explicitly mentioned," that specific form which is mentioned here as *jha* does not follow immediately [after the root], and that which is immediate—the aggregate consisting of the *repha* (the letter *r*) and the letter *jha*—is not [the object of the rule].

If it were said that [the substitute] is "specified" (*nirddiśyate*), then there would be no substitution at all. Another says: "There would be no substitution"—what does this mean? It means there would be no substitution for *jha*. For whom, then, would it apply? According to the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("of the first of what follows"), it would apply only to *ruṭ*. And the *ruṭ* would not be redundant, because its purpose is to ensure the audible pronunciation of the letter *jha*. This is to be considered: since [the substitute] has more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), it would necessarily result in a total substitution (*sarvādeśa*). If it is argued that the *ruṭ* would be redundant in the case of a total substitution, what can we do? Let there simply be no substitution.

The pronunciation of the indicatory letter *ṅ* (in the root *śīṅ*) is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elided *yaṅ* formation); thus, we have *vyatiśeśyate*. Even the *guṇa* substitution does not occur there, because of the mention of the indicatory letter.
The substitution of *vet* or *vibhāṣā*. 7.1.7.

Regarding *saṃvidrate*: the ātmanepada ending is applied by the rule *samo gamyṛcchi-ādi* (Pāṇini 1.3.29). Regarding *vitta* and so forth: the root *vida* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇa*) belongs to the *rudhādi* class and is anudātta. However, the roots meaning "existence" (*sattā*) and "acquisition" (*lābha*) are not included here precisely because they are separated by their respective *vikaraṇas*. Furthermore, the plural form (*bahuvacana*) serves as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). The presentation of the other two [roots] is for the purpose of demonstrating that this form in the plural belongs to the root meaning "investigation."

The form *vidante* occurs because the root *vid* is included in the *tud-ādi* class in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābha*). Due to its *svarita*-accented initial vowel, the *ātmanepada* ending is applied; in the singular, after the addition of the augment *num* by the rule *mucādīnām*, the form is possible. Furthermore, by the very mention of *vetteḥ* with the suffix *śtip*, the [augment] does not occur in the *yaṅluk* formation—as in *vyativevidate*.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *o* for *as*] occurs frequently.

Because of the mention of "frequently" (*bahula*), it occurs elsewhere as well. For this very purpose, the term "frequently" (*bahula*) was employed even though the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) was already in effect.
Regarding *adṛśram*: the optionality is due to the rule *irito vā*.
Therefore, *ais* is substituted for *bhisa*. (Pāṇini 7.1.9)

Regarding the term *atijarasaiḥ*: here, the substitution *ais* is applied precisely for the sake of hearing the single vowel *e*. In forms such as *vṛkṣaiḥ*, even when the *ais* substitution occurs, the form is established through *vṛddhi*. Therefore, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule governed by *ato guṇe* does not apply; for if it were to apply, [the author] would have prescribed simply *is* instead.

"Because it is subsequent. [The opponent asks: "What is the scope for *etva* (the substitution of *e*)? Its scope is in forms such as *vṛkṣeṣu*. What is the scope for *ais* (the substitution of *ais*)? Its scope is when *etva* has already occurred. If you think that when both would apply before *etva*, *etva* applies because it is subsequent, then where will *ais* occur? Once *etva* has been applied, the word no longer ends in the primary vowel *a*; this is the question. [The answer is: 'Because of its former state (*bhautapūrvyāt*) after *etva*. The state of having previously existed is *bhautapūrvyam*. The meaning is that since the current form does not exist, one resorts to the understanding of its former state. But *ais* is permanent; if that were so..."

For if this were so, the substitution *ais* would be permanent (*nitya*), because it would apply both when the change has already been made and when it has not. However, once the substitution *et* has been applied, *ais* does not apply, because the preceding sound is no longer a vowel (*ajhalāditvāt*). Nor can one resort to the principle of "having previously existed" (*bhūtapūrvagati*) in that case, since the primary condition itself is possible. This resolution of the objection should be understood as being made without relying on the relationship between a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*); for if that were relied upon, since *ais* is introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to *et* before the latter has even taken effect, the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) would be untenable.
The substitution of *na* for the genitive case-ending does not occur after the words *idam* and *adas*, except when followed by the suffix *ak*.

In the rule *idamadasoḥ*, the genitive case is used to indicate a relationship (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the suffix *bhis*. Regarding *ebhiḥ*: the substitution of *ya* for the initial of *tyad*-type stems occurs, and by the rule *hali lopaḥ*, there is elision of the portion *it*. Regarding *amībhiḥ*: when the substitution of *ais* is prohibited, the substitution of *et* occurs by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*; then, by the rule *eta īdvahuvacane*, the substitution of *īt* and *at* takes place.

The mention of *akoḥ* (of non-*k* sounds) here is purposeless; for how can this prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)—namely, "this [suffix] applies to *idam* and *adas*"—be restricted to specific forms? Since the form will simply not occur once *akac* has been applied there, he says: "the mention of *akoḥ* itself [serves a purpose]. The further utility of this indication (*jñāpana*) is that the operations of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) apply in cases such as *sarvake*.

These two prohibitions are stated [in the rule], yet both could have been omitted. For how could I have formulated it thus: "after *idam* and *adas*, when followed by *kā*" (P. 7.2.108)? That would have served as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) meaning "only after *idam* and *adas* when followed by *kā*. Consequently, forms such as *sarvakaiḥ* would not be possible, while forms such as *ebhiḥ* would indeed be possible; furthermore, the paribhāṣā concerning "the middle" (*tanmadhya*) would not have been indicated. However, in some commentaries (*vṛtti*), it is read exactly as "after *idam* and *adas*, when followed by *kā*" and not stated otherwise; for even the reverse restriction might have occurred, namely: "only after *idam* and *adas* when followed by *kā*."
The suffixes ṭā, ṅasi, ṅas, ām, ina, āt, sya, and su [are substituted for the case endings of the second case]. 7.1.12.

Regarding the passage beginning with *atijarasiṇā*: when the short vowel (*hrasva*) is applied in the compound, the substitution of *in* occurs; subsequently, because the *sannipātaparibhāṣā* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the substitution of *jaras* takes place.

Similarly, in *atijarasāt*, once the substitution of *āt* has occurred, the substitution of *jaras* follows. Now, one might object: since only the case endings *ṭā* and *ṅasi* begin with a vowel (*aj-ādi*), the substitution of *jaras* should occur prior to the substitutions of *in* and *āt*.

[One might argue that] it would attain [the form *atijara*], for that [base *jaras*] is eternal and supreme; since the substitution of *in* and *ad* would not occur there because it does not end in *at*, the forms should be *atijarasā* and *atijarasa*. This is not a fault, for in that case, the prescription of the *in*-substitution and the *ad*-substitution would be purposeless; the *in*-substitute and the *ad*-substitute would have to be prescribed, as the form is already established [by the rule *jarāyā jaras*].

In this case, regarding the form *vṛkṣeṇa*, the rule for *etva* (the substitution of *e*) will be formulated through a split of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*): first, "in the plural, when followed by a *jhal* [consonant], there is *etva*"; then, "also before *osi*"; and finally, "also before *āṅ*"—meaning that when *āṅ* follows, there is *etva* of the vowel *a*, as in *vṛkṣeṇa*. This cannot be done in this way; for if one were to apply the rule "there is elision [of the final phoneme] when followed by a *hal* [consonant]" (*hali lopaḥ*) to the form *anena*, then after the elision of the *id*-portion (*id-rap-lope*), the form would result in *enena*. To avoid this, having set aside the rule "elision when followed by a *hal*," the rule would instead be formulated as "elision when followed by a *jhal*" (*jhali lopaḥ*). In that case, because the letter *n* is not a *jhal* (it is a *hal*), there would be no elision.

It is not possible to state that there is elision [of the suffix] before a *jhal* consonant; for in this case, it would not apply: *ayāviṣṭa*, *ajanayat*. Here, in the word *ayā*, the substitution of *yā* for the dative singular of *idam* occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* etc., and the absence of the lengthening [of the vowel] in the presence of a *sup* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In that instance, because it does not begin with a *jhal* consonant, the elision of the *it*-marker would not occur.

Therefore, only elision (*lopa*) should be applied when a consonant (*hal*) follows; consequently, the form *anena* would not be established at all. If that is the case, then the citation *anāpyakaḥ* contains two *n*s. Therein, the [first] *n* connected with the substitute is elided because it is at the end of a word (*padānta*). Then, since *na* and *āp* form *nāp*, by relying on the meaning of the rule "the substitute *id* occurs in place of *it* when followed by *nāp*," the exception to the elision of the *it*-augment will apply, and the substitute *nā* will indeed occur when followed by the word *na*.

If this were so, then because the elision (*lopa*) would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by virtue of being a substitute (*ādeśa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening (*dīrgha*) in forms such as *rājā*, just as in the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.102]; however, this fault does not apply here because, once the elision of the case-ending (*sup*) has been effected by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the prohibition *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) prevents the application of that rule. In the case of *vṛkṣāt* as well, the form is established simply through the homogeneous quality (*savarṇa*) of the vowels; furthermore, by the force of the explicit utterance of the letter *a*, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) will not occur.
Thus, their intention is that first the substitutions of *in* and *āt* take place by the force of their specific prescription, and only afterwards does the substitution of *jaras* occur.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yathā tu* and so forth: in the Bhāṣya, indeed, by relying on the previously mentioned grammatical process (*prakriyā*), the substitution of *nād* and the substitution of *ad* have been established. If these two forms were intended [by Pāṇini], then the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of those two substitutions would be untenable. In that regard, some hold that because the substitution of *jaras* does not occur due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the forms *atijareṇa* and *atijarāt* are what the author of the Bhāṣya intended. Others maintain that since the substitution of *jaras* has already occurred, the forms *atijarasā* and *atijarasaḥ* are what was intended.
The suffix *ṅī* [is applied after a stem ending in] *ya*. (Pāṇini 4.1.75)

The term *ṅe* is understood as the citation of the singular dative case ending (*caturthī-ekavacana*). For its form *ṅe* is *pratipadokta* (directly stated in the rules), whereas the form of the singular locative case ending (*saptamī-ekavacana*)—which is *gher ṅiti*—is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through grammatical operation). Although *ṅeḥ* is presented as a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*), and thus both [the dative and locative forms] are *lākṣaṇika*, nevertheless, the application of the Paribhāṣā depends on the comparison between the *lākṣaṇikatva* and the *pratipadoktatva* of the portion preceding the suffix.

If this is so, then the same contingency would arise even in the rule *ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ*; therefore, the only recourse here is the [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). And there is indicative evidence (*liṅga*)—namely, the rules *tasmai prabhavati*, *tadasmai dīyate*, *tasmai hitam*, *tadasya praharaṇam*, and *krīḍāyāṃ ṇaḥ*, etc. Regarding the form *vṛkṣāya*: the lengthening is by the rule *supi ca*. But how can that which is produced by the conjunction of the letter *a* (in *vṛkṣa-a-ya*) be the cause for the removal of that very [conjunction]? To this he says: "characterized by the conjunction" (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*). Its non-eternality is understood from the citation in the rule *kaṣṭāya kramaṇe*.
The suffix *smai* is substituted for the case-ending *e* following a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).

"Let it be so. Because of the rule stating that "the pronouns beginning with *tyad* have two final vowels," there is an absence of the substitution of *at* for *tyad* and so on in other instances, resulting in a stem ending in *an*. Regarding the statement "when the substitute *aś* has been applied in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*)," [it means]: in the case of non-subsequent reference (*ananvādeśa*), however, if the form *asmai* were present, there would be the elision of the *id*-form; and if the elision of the *id*-form had not occurred, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would not apply. Nor does there arise the contingency of *guṇa* substitution by *ād-*, because it is blocked by the obligatory elision of the *id*-form. The objection "the single-substitute would apply" arises because [the elision] is obligatory. And this objection pertains to the view that the refinement of the sentence (*vākya-saṃskāra*) occurs first.

For that [substitution] is employed in common usage for the purpose of conveying meaning, and it is precisely that which is analyzed and explained in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding the phrase "because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*): its internality arises from being part of a single word (*ekapadatvāt*); whereas the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is external because it depends upon two words (*padadvayāśrayatvāt*).
The suffix *smāt* is optionally used after the nine [directional stems] beginning with *pūrva*.

Regarding the nine beginning with *pūrva*—those recited in the Sūtras and those recited in the Gaṇapāṭha—the term *sarvanāmnaḥ* (of the pronoun) is understood here as well. In that context, if the mention of "nine" (*nava*) were not made, then in the case of the *ṅasi* and *ṅi* [case endings], only those [words] from the Gaṇapāṭha which possess the technical designation *sarvanāman* would be included; therefore, the mention of "nine" is necessary. In this regard, the arrangement of the Sūtras should have been:

*jasi ṅasi ṅīnāṃ śī smāt sminaḥ pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā*, *auṅa āpaḥ*, and *śī napuṃsakācca*. In this way, three optional Sūtras for the *jas* [ending] would not have had to be composed. However, it was not done in that manner.
The *śī* [augment] follows after *jas*. 7.1.17.

The long vowel pronunciation is for the sake of subsequent rules. Here, however, because of the governing rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.90), a *guṇa* substitution would have to occur; thus, the form is established even with a short vowel. Furthermore, in the case of *na ca sarve chattriṇaḥ*, there is no possibility of the obligatory *tuṅ* augment depending on the short vowel, because of the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86), which renders the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation non-existent [for the purposes of the following rules]. For in that context, the non-existence applies only to that single-substitute which occurs between the end of a word and the beginning of a word.
The substitution of *auṅ* occurs for *āp*. (Pāṇini 7.1.18)

The mention of *auṅ*—being made as a restatement (*anuvāda*)—raises an objection: "This is [the form] *au*. What kind of method is this? This is an improper way of composing a rule; for a restatement is appropriate only for that which is already established, as in the case of *ṅeḥ yaḥ*. But this [form *au*] is not established anywhere. He refutes this by saying: "It is for the sake of another purpose. If it were stated as *autaḥ*, it would apply only to the nominative dual because it lacks an *anubandha*, and not to *auṭ*, which possesses an *anubandha*.

Although the letter *ṭ* is an adjunct (*anubandha*) to the entire group for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*, nevertheless, its status as an adjunct to the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not contradictory. Causes can serve multiple purposes; for example, "the mango trees were watered and the ancestors were gratified. If it were stated simply as *auṭ*, the [suffix] of the nominative dual would not be included. Therefore, the mention of the adjunct *ṅ* is intended to include both [the *auṭ* and the *jas*] in common.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the restatement (*anuvāda*) of something non-existent is untenable? [Response: This objection is raised; however, the statement of its purpose (*prayojana*) is irrelevant there. This fault does not apply. From this very restatement, the rule *audaṅ auṅi* will be inferred, and it is for that [inferred rule] alone that the purpose is stated. Again, he objects with the words "And of that" (*tasya ca*). If this [suffix] were understood as having the indicatory letter *ṅ* attached (*ṅakārānubandha*), then for you who speak thus, the operation of being *ṅit*—namely, the substitution of *yāṭ* in place of *āp* [as prescribed by] *yāḍāpaḥ*—would apply when the word *śī* follows.

He says "let that fault indeed attach [to us]" (*prasajatu nāma tatrāha – sa doṣa iti*). Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "fault" (*doṣa*), the pronoun "that" (*sa*) is used in the masculine gender. He provides the rebuttal: "because of the *ṅit*-ness" (*ṅittve*). What was intended was a reference to the mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*); however, for fear of breaking the meter (*vṛttabhaṅga*), the word *mākṣa* was used in place of *mātra*. Regarding the rule *yāḍāpaḥ*, the term *ṅiti* which is supplied by way of anuvṛtti is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has a *ṅ* as its initial" (*ṅ id yasya*); rather, it is a *karmadhāraya*: "the *ṅ* and that which is not a suffix" (*ṅaś cāsau avic ca*). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "whatever [suffix] would occur after a phoneme. This refers to the principle: "when a rule is stated with reference to a specific element (*algrahaṇa*), the operation applies to that which begins with that element."

This much has been said as a rebuttal by accepting that [the suffix] is *ṅit*; however, he states that it is not *ṅit* at all: "And this is a phoneme (*varṇa*). The word *ca* is read in the sense of *vā* (or). Alternatively, the reading is simply "or this is a phoneme" (*varṇo vāyam*). This [suffix] *auṅ* is taken as a phoneme, not as a suffix (*pratyaya*). The letter *ṅ*, however, is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtha*), just as the letter *d* is in the rule *ṛdorap*. Because it qualifies the suffix implied by the term "stem" (*aṅga*), the meaning is "of a suffix ending in the vowel *au*."

And when there is the apprehension of the vowel *au* by virtue of its phonetic form (*varṇarūpatā*), there is the apprehension of both *au*s, because the maxim regarding that which lacks an *anubandha* applies to the object of the suffix. As for the statement "there is no fault even if it has the marker *ṅ*," the meaning is that even the fault that would arise if *ṅittva* were present does not occur, because *ṅittva* itself is absent; or rather, this connects with the previous solution.

He states another solution: "This is a technical designation (*nirdeśa*). For the ancient teachers read both of these [suffixes] in the sūtra as *auṅ* in the dual number; this designation is based upon that, and by means of it, there is the inclusion of both. Nor does there arise the contingency of the operations belonging to a *ṅit* suffix, for operations are not performed here on the basis of the markers (*anubandha*) used by the ancient teachers.
The suffix *śi* replaces the dual endings *jas* and *śas*.

Regarding the term *kuṇḍaśaḥ*: although this is a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), when—by virtue of the context of the meaning or other factors—it refers to a single individual instance which serves as the locus for the genus, then its mode of application (*vṛtti*) is singular, and thus the suffix *śas* occurs by the rule "from a singular number" (*saṃkhyaikavacanāt*). However, in the absence of such contextual factors of meaning and so forth, the counter-example is given there: *ghaṭaṃghaṭaṃ dadāti* ("he gives pot after pot").
The substitution of *auś* occurs for the [genitive] ending *bhyas* after the eight [prātipadikas].

"The word *aṣṭan* is understood as having its vowel form already changed (*kṛtākāra*). This means that the word *aṣṭā* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form with the vowel change already applied, rather than being a form where the substitution of *ā* for *a* has been effected by the force of a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows.

"Why is it understood as having the vowel change already applied?"—this asks why one has resorted to an imitation of a form possessing the *ā*-substitution. The answer is: "So that [the rule] should apply only at the very time when the *ā*-substitution occurs."

Regarding the word "eight" (*aṣṭa*): how then is there an absence of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) here, given that an option is not present in the rule prescribing that [substitution]? To this he says: "This very [point]. Here, one ought to say "of eight" (*aṣṭanaḥ*), as in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau*. Since this is already established, the fact that the form *aṣṭābhyaḥ* is used in the rule indicates that it is an imitation of a form in which *ātva* has already been applied; this much is certain. And the purpose of this is so that [the rule] may apply only when *ātva* has occurred.

If the meaning [of the rule] has already been indicated by the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt*, whether that [mention] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) or this [present rule], what difference does it make here? This much must be stated: that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk*. The restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) "to this alone" is to be understood. He states the reason: "nāprāpte ca" (and when [the previous rule] was not yet applicable). For that [luk-elision] applies only to a compound (*samāsa*), not to a sentence (*vākya*). Thus, [the example] is *aṣṭaputraḥ*.

According to the rule "An external elision (luk) subverts even internal operations," the substitution *auś*—though applicable at the stage of the sentence (*vākya-avasthā*)—is not performed; or rather, the elision (*luk*) occurs by virtue of the status of *auś* as a *sthānin*. It is intended here that the term [ending in] "that" (*tadanta*) is included, because of the statement in the section on *aṅga*: "of that [stem] and of its subsequent member. If this were so, the [substitution] would apply even where the meaning of the word *aṣṭan* is subordinate (*upasarjana*). To this he says: "in the case of *priyāṣṭānaḥ*. How, moreover, the substitution of *āt* does not occur here will be explained in the very rule prescribing that [substitution].
There is elision [of the case-ending] after the six [cases]. 7.1.22.

Regarding the phrase *ṣaṭpradhānāt*: the meaning is "from that in which the meaning of those termed 'six' (*ṣaṭ*) is the principal element. In the example *priyaṣaṣ*, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is the principal element. Although the rule *sarvanāmasaṃkhyayor upasaṃkhyānam* would have required the numeral *ṣaṣ* to be placed first, the word *priya* is placed first instead by the rule *vā priyasya*.
The suffixes *su* and *am* are elided after a neuter stem.

The term *su* is understood here as the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*), and not as the locative plural (*saptamībahuvacana*), because of its association with the singular *am*. In the case of *tad-brāhmaṇa-kulam*, once the substitution of *tyadādyatva* (the replacement of the initial *ta-* by *a-*) has occurred, the elision (*luk*) would not apply; for it is sublated by the presence of the suffix *am* according to the rule *ato 'm*. Therefore, it must be stated that [elision occurs] "after words beginning with *tyad*" (*tyadādibhyaśca*). Hence he says: "In the case of *tad-brāhmaṇa-kulam*... He adds: "...or because of its constancy" (*nityatvāt*); the ellipsis is that the substitution of *tyadādyatva* is sublated by the elision (*luk*).

But how can *luk* (elision) be considered permanent (*nitya*), given that once the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the pronoun] has been applied, the rule *ato 'm* prescribes an exception (*apavāda*), and thus *luk* itself would be non-permanent? To this he says: "For *luk*... (*luko hi*). For if the rule *ato 'm* did not exist, even a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a* would certainly be a cause for *luk*. What follows from that? To this he says: "And of that which... (*yasya ca*). However, once *luk* has been applied, the substitution of *tyadādi* does not apply at all, because of the prohibition: "When [an affix] marked with *lu* is present, [the operation] does not affect the stem" (*na lumatāṅgasya*).

If this is so, then that too is sublated by another rule; it is not a prohibition of the absence [of doubling], but rather of what? Of the condition for the suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa); for the application [of the suffix] occurs by virtue of the condition for the suffix.
From this, "am" [is substituted]. (Pāṇini 7.1.24)

In this context, the word division is *ami*, and not *mi*; for if it were *mi*, one would have simply said *mata* for the sake of brevity. Why, then, is *am* prescribed instead of merely saying *m*? For even in the case of the second person singular [accusative], after the *m* is substituted for the initial *a* of the suffix by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the desired result is already established by the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) of the other *m*. However, there is the undesirable consequence of lengthening (*dīrghaprasaṅga*), as the rule *supi ca* would cause the vowel to become long. Nor does the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* apply to the prescription of length, because that would lead to over-extension in cases such as *vṛtrāya*. Therefore, *am* itself must be prescribed.

Another says: "By the force of the rule prescribing *am*, the substitution of *jaras* occurs in the case of *atijarasam*; however, that is to be considered doubtful, because by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the non-disturbance of a cause-effect relationship), the substitution of *jaras* would not apply. Furthermore, the prescription of *am* serves its purpose by precluding the long vowel (*dīrgha*)."
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after the five [stems] beginning with *adḍara*.

The substitute *ad* occurs. To indicate the specific form of the intended substitute, the rule of *ṣṭutva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) has not been applied. How, then, is it known that this substitute consists of the letter *ḍ*?

If *ḍin* were indeed [the augment], one would simply have said, "after the five beginning with *katara*, *at* [is the substitute]. Why, then, is the purpose stated as the prevention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) itself, rather than saying "*am*"? To this he says: "In this case, however... "If that is so," [he replies]. The sense of the objection is this: by carrying over the *am* prescribed by the previous rule and reinterpreting the ablative *ḍatarādibhyaḥ* as a genitive, the letter *da* will be prescribed as a substitute for that very *am*. Thus, in the form *he katarat*, the elision of the vocative marker (*sambuddhi-lopa*) would not occur. And this defect is common even to the previous position.

But surely, when the *sambuddhi* (vocative singular) elides, the term *apṛkta* will be carried over from the rule *halḍyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. And here, when the *ā* of *ām* is replaced by *d* according to the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the *m* would be elided due to being at the end of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Since that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), this [remaining *a*] is not an *apṛkta*; likewise, the substitute *ad* is not an *apṛkta*. If the term *apṛkta* is indeed carried over, then there would be the fault that even the *ām* in forms such as *he kāṇḍe* would not occur.

This has been stated: "Now, since the mention of *apṛkta* (non-combined) has been withdrawn, there is a fault regarding [the suffixes] *ḍatara* and so on—namely, that in forms such as *he katarat*, elision would occur. Therefore, because the substitute *ad* is prescribed with the marker *ḍit*, and because that [substitute] also bears the marker *ḍit*, there is neither elision of the vocative (*sambuddhi*) nor the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
However, if one were to follow the *am* prescribed by the previous rule and prescribe *ad* as its substitute, it would have been possible to omit the marker *ḍit*.
In the Vedic language (chandas), [the substitution of *i* for *ī*] does not occur after any other [vowel]. Pāṇini 7.1.26.

Therefore, [the word] "immediately after *am*" means that the substitution of *am* itself will be an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *adḍ*; consequently, it is not necessary to state "na" (not), which is the intended meaning.
After the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the suffix *ṅas* is replaced by *aś*.

"The utterance of *śit* is for the purpose of [indicating] a total substitution (*sarvādeśa*); otherwise, by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, it would apply only to the initial [sound]. Now, one might object: since there is no purpose in pronouncing the vowel *ā* when the vowel *ā* is already present, the application of the initial [element] is blocked; thus, by the rule *alo 'ntyasya*, the *ā* would replace the final *m*, and then by *ato guṇe*, the desired form would be established through the *para-rūpa* (single-substitute) sandhi. To this he replies: "Otherwise... The term *ādeśa-vyapadeśa* means the designation of a substitute. The meaning of the word *eva* is: "It would apply only to that substitute which you think has no purpose."

Furthermore, what is the purpose of designating [the forms] as "substitutes" (ādeśa), such that [the rule] would apply only to the initial [portion]? To this he says: *tataśca* ("and therefore"). The particle *ca* is read here in the sense of *hi* ("for"). For, because of that designation as a substitute, the substitution of *ya* (in the rule *yo'ci*) would not occur; the absence of that *ya*-substitution is the purpose of the designation as a substitute—this is the meaning. In the rule *yo'ci*, the phrase *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* ("of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when not in the state of a substitute") is understood to carry over.

But surely it will be understood there that "the case-ending itself is the substitute" (*anādeśa*); for there is no rule [Pāṇini 1.1.54] regarding "that which begins with it" (*tadādividhi*) by which one could understand "[at the beginning of] what follows an *anādeśa*. Consequently, even if the case-ending begins with a substitute (*ādeśa*), since the case-ending itself is not an *anādeśa*, the substitution of *yat* would indeed occur; thus, the prescription of *ā* for *ā* would be entirely redundant. [The author] thinks as follows: according to the maxim "all substitutes are substitutes for entire words," the substitute is prescribed for the case-ending itself by way of a modification at its initial position; therefore, the case-ending itself is the substitute.

Regarding the statement "all [substitutes] are substitutes for words" (*sarve sarvapadādeśāḥ*), the word "word" (*pada*) here does not refer to that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Rather, a "word" is so called because "by means of this, the meaning is reached" (*padyate gamyate 'nenārthaḥ*).
