Consequently, just as in the case of *pacatu*, where the word *tu* replaces the word *ti*, so too here the substitution of *aś* for *ṅas* is prescribed; thus, the case ending indeed possesses the status of being a substitute for a word.
ṅe prathamayoram || 7.1.29 || The [substitute] am is applied in place of the dual endings ṅe and prathamā.

The term *ṅe* is presented here without a case ending. He will state that the expression "of the first two" (*prathamayoḥ*) refers to the inclusion of both the first and second [cases]; the point is that if this were a compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of using the plural number. It is certain, however, that the meaning of "first" (*prathama*) here is not the technical grammatical sense defined by primacy, but rather the inclusion of the first [case] with reference to a specific arrangement.

However, it is simply impossible for *yusmad* and *asmad* to occur with the [terminations] *tiṅ* and *prathamā*; therefore, there arises a doubt as to whether the reference there is to the suffixes (*pratyaya*) or to the case-endings (*vibhakti*). If the mention were in the feminine gender, then it would refer to the case-endings; but if the mention were in the masculine gender, it would refer to the suffixes. Regarding this, he states the established conclusion: "and in the two case-endings *prathamā*. He clarifies this very point: "of the first and second [cases]. How is it that the second case is expressed by the word *prathamā*? It is through association (*sāhacarya*).

Now, one might object: "Does a word employed once function in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) or in a secondary sense (*jaghanyavṛtti*), but not in both? This is true; however, in the combination of the first and second [cases], this [word] functions only in a secondary sense, and since the aggregate has its constituent parts manifested, the dual number is used. But how is it known that there is a reference to two case-endings (*vibhakti*)? It is because of the prescription of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) in the rule "in the second case" (*dvitīyāyām ca*). For that is stated for the purpose of providing a substitute; otherwise, since the rule "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when not followed by a substitute" (*anādeśe yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*) would already suffice, such a prescription would be unnecessary.

If, moreover, there were a mention of the two case-endings (*vibhakti*) here, then its status as a substitute (*ādeśa*) would be logically established. But one might object: "Could it not be for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *y* (by P. 7.2.89, *yo 'ci*), since that would be its only purpose? If that were the sole aim, he would have specified the substitution of *y* itself, saying *yo 'cyapi*. [The answer is: *ā* is a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation), just as in the expression *anāpyakaḥ*. However, because he teaches the substitution of *ā* in the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*), it is understood from this that the two case-endings are indeed mentioned here.
The substitution of *ś* for *s* does not occur before the suffix *śas*. (Pāṇini 7.1.29)

"No," [says the author], "this is an uninflected (avibhaktika) statement; thus, this is a prohibition of what was obtained by the preceding rule"—so it was questioned in the *Bhāṣya*. But what is the fault when there is a prohibition? For even when *ami* is prohibited, when *yatva* is applied by the rule *yo 'ci*, and *ātva* is applied by the rule *dvitīyāyām*, and the single-substitute long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is applied by the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, and then *natva* is applied by the rule *tasmāc chaso naḥ puṃsi*, the form *yuṣmān* is indeed established. True, it is established in the masculine; however, it is not established in the feminine and neuter genders.
This very point has been demonstrated: *yuṣmān asmān brāhmaṇīḥ*, and so forth.

The forms *yuṣmā* and *asmā* occur in the absence of gender (*aliṅge*), because they are so listed in the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. However, in the actual example, by the rule *ādeḥ parasya*, the initial vowel [of the suffix] becomes *na*; then, by the rule of the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*), the *s* is dropped.
The substitute *bhyam* is applied in place of the case-ending *bhyas*.

"It attains *etva* (the substitution of *e*). This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the long vowel [substitution] by the rule *supi ca*. Regarding "when the operation pertains to the base" (*aṅgavṛtte*), etc., its meaning has already been explained previously. Regarding "some, however," etc.: for those [grammarians] for whom the elision of the remainder (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) means the elision of the final letter, there is the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) consisting of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) by the rule *ato guṇe*, as well as the accent (*svara*). The phrase "for the sake of preventing *etva*" also serves as an elliptical indication of the long vowel here; and because the pronunciation of the vowel *a* is meaningful through the prevention of *etva*, the long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) does not apply for them.

[The form] occurs. Regarding the phrase "but for those [who hold that]": there is a difference of opinion in the view that the final syllable is elided—namely, whether *bhyas* is replaced by *bhya* or by *abhyam*. However, in the view that the *ṭi*-portion (the suffix *as*) is elided, *abhyam* is necessarily the replacement; otherwise, the desired form would not be established. Now, an objection is raised: "In this case, there is a fault regarding the accent. How so? In the rule *anudāttasya ca yatro dāttalopaḥ*, the term *antodāttaḥ* ("having an acute accent on the final syllable") from the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ* is understood to carry over. Consequently, the acute accent would result on the final syllable of *bhyam*. To this he replies: "And [this is governed by] the accent of the disappearance of an acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*)."

The application of the term "end" (anta) does not follow there; rather, by virtue of proximity in the order of pronunciation, the meaning is that the udātta accent belongs to the first [syllable] alone.
The word *sāman* [is substituted] for *ākam*. (Pāṇini 7.1.33)

The form *sām* is understood here as the genitive plural (*ṣaṣṭhī-bahuvacana*) with the augment *suṭ* applied, because no other [form] could possibly serve as the cause for the technical designation *aṅga*.

Now, for what purpose is the *suṭ* augment, which has arrived [at the beginning], taken? Although it was the subject under discussion that "the genitive plural form with the *suṭ* augment is taken," here, however, there is a masculine designation (*puṃlliṅga*) in view of the suffix; or rather, it should have been read in the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*). The word "atha" (now) does not constitute a question primarily concerning a purpose; rather, it is primarily concerned with the impossibility of such a thing occurring after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. For this very reason he says: "For at the time of prescribing the substitutes, the *suṭ* does not exist. Regarding the rule for *suṭ*:

From the rule *ājjaserasuk*, the term *āt* (ending in *ā*) is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*). Furthermore, the state of ending in the vowel *a* for the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurs when the final letter is elided by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*. And what is this "remainder" (*śeṣa*)? It is the substitute (*ādeśa*), because the rules for changing [the stems] to *ya* and *āva* are prescribed only when there is no substitute. Moreover, the status of being a substitute exists only when the *akam* substitute has occurred. Nor does the state of ending in *a* arise through the substitution of *yat* (for the *tyad*-class stems), because of the traditional rule that "the *tyad*-class stems end with the letter *t* up to the word *dvi*. Therefore, at the time of the prescription of the substitute, the suffix *su* does not exist.

The respondent, however, says—referring to the phrase "tasyaiva tu"—that although *suṭ* is introduced at the time of prescribing the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is nevertheless a purpose for its introduction. If [the form] without *suṭ* were taken, then by the logic previously stated, by what would the subsequent *suṭ* be prevented from occurring, since it would be included within the substituendum (*sthānin*)? The sense is that this is due to the force of taking it as having the same substituendum as that [original *suṭ*]. And this is a contingent purpose.

In which case [is this necessary]? When there is elision of the suffix (*śeṣalopa*), that is, elision of the final letter; but when there is elision of *ṭi*, then even subsequently there is no possibility for *suṭ* to apply, so this is not the purpose [of the rule]. [Regarding] "the pronunciation of the long vowel" and so forth: otherwise, by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there would be the substitution of a single substitute (*pararūpatva*) [for the vowel and the following *u*]. Now, one might argue that it will not occur due to the force of the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *a*; otherwise, he would have simply prescribed *a* itself. To this he says: "But in the case of *akam*" (*akami tu*). [The sūtra: *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34).

In cases such as *papau*, when the form *pā-a* is established, three operations simultaneously present themselves: reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitution of a single long vowel for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*), and the substitution of *au* (*autva*). Regarding the sequence in which these are to be performed, the author demonstrates it with the word "here" (*atra*). He does not, however, introduce the accentuation of the *liṭ*-suffix (*litsvara*), because the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) is established regardless. He states the reason for the aforementioned sequence: "because of the single-substitute [vowel]" (*ekādeśāt*). For if the single-substitute vowel were applied first, the substitution of *au* would not occur due to the absence of distinct demarcation (*vyapavarga*); thus, that [substitution of *au*] would be without occasion (*anavakāśa*).

"Because it follows [another vowel], there is a single-substitute (ekādeśa). Here, *vṛddhi* is the single substitute; due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*). This *sthānivadbhāva* occurs by the rule "in the case of reduplication before a vowel" (*dvirvacane'ci*). For in that rule, the mention of "before a vowel" (*acīti*) is not an indication of the cause for the *sthānivadbhāva*; rather, it refers to the substitute for a vowel—namely, "that which is a substitute for a vowel when a vowel is the cause of reduplication. Therefore, even though the vowel does not currently follow [the substitute], the *sthānivadbhāva* still certainly takes effect.

Since there is no difference in terms of ease between the vowels *o* and *au*, only the vowel *au*—which is inherent in the usage (*prayogasamavāyin*)—was prescribed. Another [teacher] says: the vowel *o* is the vowel *ā* joined with *u* (*āṅ-praśliṣṭākāra*), and in its pronunciation there is ease of effort; whereas the vowel *au* is the vowel *ā* separated from *u* (*viśliṣṭākāra*), and in its pronunciation there is heaviness of effort. Thus, in the rule for the formation of *dadaridrau* from the root *daridrāti* (as in *daridrāti artham dadaridrau*), even though the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule "the elision of the vowel *ā* of the root *daridrā* should be stated before an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix," the vowel *au* is still heard.

Although, by the rule *siddhaśca pratyayavidhau*, when the *liṭ* suffix is intended, the elision of the vowel *a* occurs and thus the substitution of *au* (*autva*) does not apply; and although, by the rule *sāsyānekājgrahaṇaṃ culumpādyartham*, when the *ām* suffix is present, the *ṇal* suffix itself is impossible—nevertheless, due to the force of the prescription for *autva*, neither of these two [obstacles] takes effect.
In the sense of a benediction, the substitutes *tāt* and *aṅ* may optionally take the place of *hi* after the words *tvam* and *yūyam*.

Regarding the example *jīvatāt tvam*: here, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original), the *tātaṅ* would be included under the term *hi*; consequently, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *ato heḥ* would apply. This is not a fault. In the rule *hu-jhalbhyo herdhiḥ*, while the word *hi* is still understood from the previous context, the rule *ato heḥ* mentions *hi* again for the purpose that the substitution of *dhi* should apply only to that which is *hi* by its own nature, and not to that which becomes *hi* through *sthānivadbhāva*.

Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of the marker *ṅ*," etc.: although it has not yet been determined that the purpose of [the marker *ṅ*] prior to its becoming a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśa) is to prohibit *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, nevertheless, even if it were a substitute for the whole, the purpose of the *ṅ*-marker is possible in the case of *tāt-aṅ*; however, in the case of *anaṅ* and others, no such purpose for being a substitute for the whole is possible. Thus, since the *ṅ*-marker serves no other purpose in those cases, the rule *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53) applies immediately; but in the case of *tāt-aṅ*, because there is a possibility of another purpose [namely, prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*], a slight delay occurs.

Therefore, in this matter, the application of the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) occurs simultaneously; thus, even setting aside the exception *ṅicca* (P. 1.1.53), the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (P. 1.1.55) alone operates because it is subsequent. This has been properly demonstrated under the rule *ṅicca*. In that regard, there is a prohibition of *guṇa* in forms such as *brūtāt*, and a prohibition of *vṛddhi* in *mṛṣṭāt*; and [the reason for this is] "because of its *ṅit*-ness."

"But surely, let there be the operation of a *ṅit* [suffix]; since the status of being a *pit* is obtained through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, the operation of a *pit* [suffix] would also occur—what is the contradiction? To this, he says: "A *ṅit* does not become a *pit*. This statement is formulated by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) within the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*. In the rule *bruva īṭ*, this is merely an illustration; for instance, in the form *tṛṇḍhādbhavān*, the augment *im* after *tṛṇaha* does not occur.

The two verses beginning with "The *ṅittva* in *tātaṅ*" are recited in some places. The *ṅittva* established in *tātaṅ* should effect a transfer; "transfer" (*saṃkrama*) means the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. [The optative] *liṅ* is used in the sense of fitness (*arhārthe*). It is fit to be that which effects the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. If it is a rule concerning the final letter (*antyavidhi*), then because it is the cause of a rule concerning the final letter, the *ṅittva* is a rule concerning the final letter. Alternatively, the word "rule" (*vidhi*) has an instrumental derivation; the meaning is that the *ṅittva* is for the purpose that it should apply to the final letter.

He refutes this: "And that is not so. The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis and is connected with the negation; thus, that *ṅittva* (the property of having the marker *ṅ*) should not be applied in that manner. However, immediately after the rule *eruḥ*, the rule *tuhyostātaṅāśiṣi* should have been stated; since the desired result is already established by *eruḥ* alone, it is certain that the application of *ṅittva* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, without being a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatā*), the function of *ṅittva* as a prohibition against those [guṇa and vṛddhi] would not be logically possible.

The *tātaṅ* substitute occurs for every [form of the] imperative suffix. One might object: "Let it be a rule concerning the final letter, and let the *ṅ* marker serve to prohibit *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitution according to the maxim that 'what is prescribed with respect to a part [of a word] applies to the whole'; this is because of the force of the *ṅ* marker. Anticipating this objection, he states another solution: "The section on *hi* [is still in effect]."

Therefore, in the rule for elision *ato heḥ*, since the term *heḥ* is already present as a governing heading (*adhikāra*) from the rule *hu-jhal-bhyo her dhiḥ*, the author of the Sūtras provides this *heḥ* as a further governing heading as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For its purpose is this: that the substitution of *dhi* should apply only to that *hi* which is itself the element *hi*, and not to that which becomes *hi* by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). And that [purpose] is only possible if the substitution is a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*).

One might object: "Since the rule *heḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.79) applies specifically to that which is *hi*, let it apply to the *hi* that is modified [into *tāt*], but not to the *hi* that remains unchanged; thus, even though *tāt* is a substitute for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*), the governing rule *heḥ* remains applicable. Anticipating this objection, he states the direct solution: "By virtue of the *ṅit*-marker on *tāt*. Indeed, it might be argued that this would be a rule for a final substitution by virtue of the *ṅit*-marker; however, such a functional necessity does not exist, because there is a purpose for it even when it is a substitute for the whole word. Consequently, according to the previously mentioned method of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), *tāt* becomes a substitute for the whole word.

In cases such as *anaṅ sau* and others, it is not that *anaṅ* and the rest lack the functional force (*sāmarthya*) of being marked with the *ṅ*-sign; rather, by virtue of that [marking], they become substitutes for the final phoneme.
The substitute *vasu* is applied for the genitive case ending *śas* after the root *vid*.

Regarding the term *vida jñāne*: since the roots meaning "existence" (*sattā*) and "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) are ātmanepada, the suffix *śatṛ* is impossible for them; although the root meaning "acquisition" (*lābha*) is ubhayapada and thus *śatṛ* is possible, it is intervened by a verbal affix (*vikaraṇa*) because it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*. Therefore, the intention is that only the root meaning "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is parasmaipada and has the elided (*luk*) affix, is to be understood here.

"Also for the sake of including *kvasu* in the general rule. Otherwise, if it were stated simply as "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of *vas*," only this [root] would be included because it is without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*). Now, one might object: "Even if the indicatory letter *u* is added, since it has only one indicatory letter, only this [root] would still be included. To this he says: "In the inclusion of that which has only one indicatory letter... [The rule continues: "In a compound, when preceded by *an* or *ava*, there is *lyap* in place of *ktvā*. (Pāṇini 7.1.37)

The word *pūrva* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*). A compound in which no negative particle (*nañ*) precedes as a constituent part is called *anañpūrva*. Regarding *prakṛtya*: the suffix *ktvā* is applied according to the rule "for two actions having the same agent, [the suffix is used] for the earlier time"; then there is compounding by the rule "with *ku*, *gati*-particles, and *pra* etc."; and when *lyap* is substituted, the augment *tuk* is added after a short vowel. Regarding *pārśvataḥkṛtya*: the suffix *tasi* is added to a word ending in the locative case because it belongs to the group beginning with *ādi*; then, by the rule "after a word denoting one's own limb, when followed by the suffix *tas*, [the suffix] *ktvā* is used with the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*"; and finally, there is compounding by the rule "compounds with words beginning with the third case-ending are optional, as is the case with *ktvā*. Regarding *nānākṛtya* and *dvidhākṛtya*: the suffix *ktvā* is used in the sense of the suffix *cvi* when following words expressing "not" (*na*) or meanings related to "various" (*nānā*), and the compounding is as previously described.

"Without having done," "without having taken"—the word *hṛtvā* (having taken) is here negated; in this case, the word *kṛtvā* (having done) precedes [the negative particle] like the *nañ*, yet the entire compound does not form a *samāsa*. In the example *paramakṛtvā* (having supremely done), there is a *samāsa* according to the rule *sanmahat* etc.; the suffix *ktvā* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) because of the governing context of the *tumun* suffix. Furthermore, since supremacy (*pāramya*) is also a qualifier of the action itself, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

But how is this a counter-example, given that this compound is indeed one where the first member is not *nañ*? To this he says: "For [the word] *janañ*... This "not *nañ*" (*anañ*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). In that context, by the maxim of "that which is joined with *nañ* as if it were *iva*," an indeclinable (*avyaya*) similar to *nañ* is understood. Therefore, in the case of *parama-janañ*, since *janañ* is not an indeclinable, it does not become a non-*nañ* [compound], due to its difference from *nañ* and because it is not an indeclinable. [This applies to examples such as] *snātvā-kalaka*. Etc.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples such as *pītāsthiraka* are included. In cases where no verb is expressed in the second member of the compound, the suffix *ktvā* occurs on the basis of an implied verb. Even though there is a state of mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), the compound is formed by virtue of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). The sense is that it is not only the compound belonging to this specific context that is prescribed by exception, but rather everything for which no other rule exists. Furthermore, by virtue of this exception, the substitution of *lyap* does not take place. The meaning is that it is not merely the compound occurring in this particular section that is being prescribed by exception, but rather all such instances for which no formal rule is provided.

The locative case is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). The singular number is used because it refers to a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*), or it is a change of grammatical expression (*vacanavyatyaya*). It is the compound itself that is specified, because specification depends upon a common genus (*tulyajātīya*).

But how can a compound end in *ktvā*? For when a suffix is mentioned, there is a rule that the term refers to that which begins with the element from which the suffix is prescribed and ends with it; yet *ktvā* is not prescribed after a compound. If, on the other hand, one were to argue that by mentioning a *kṛt* suffix, even a compound preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is included and thus the compound ends in *ktvā*, even so, this would apply only to cases like *prakṛtya* or *pārśvataḥkṛtya*, but not to cases like *uccaiḥkṛtya* and the like, because [in the latter] there is neither a *gati* nor a *kāraka*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And that... (*sa ca*).

In that context, since "the substitutes occur for what is being specified," the suffix *lyap* applies only to the element ending in *ktvā*. Now, one might object: "In the domain of suffixes, the determination of *tadantavidhi* (the rule that an operation applies to that which ends with the element specified) is established by the two preceding paribhāṣās, not by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (an operation applies to that which ends with the element by which it is prescribed). To this he replies: "And so it is. He asks: "But how is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? and answers: "But [the rule] 'of that preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*...'". He asks: "How is there no such contingency? and answers: "A negative particle (*nañ*) is not a *gati*."

Regarding what was stated in the rule *ado jagdhir lyapti kiti*—"it is established in the case of *jagdhi* because it is *antaraṅga*"—that is now recalled in the context of forms such as *pradhāya* and *prasthāya*. What, then, are the *antaraṅga* operations? They are: doubling (*hitva*), substitution of *da* (*datva*), substitution of *ā* (*ātva*), substitution of *it* (*itva*), substitution of *et* (*etva*), lengthening (*dīrghatva*), and the augment *śūṭ* with the augment *iṭ*. Doubling (*hitva*): from the root *dhā*, the substitution of *hi* occurs; thus, *hitvā* and *pradhāya*. Substitution of *da* (*datva*): by the rule *do daddhoḥ*, [we have] *datvā* and *pradāya*. Substitution of *ā* (*ātva*): by the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sanjhaloḥ*, [we have] *khātvā*, *prakhāya*, and *prakhanya*. Substitution of *it* (*itva*)— [The text continues: ...*itva*— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly after "itva—", so the translation reflects the available portion.)

Regarding the suffix *ktvā* with the marker *k*: from the roots *dya*, *tiṣ*, *mā*, and *sthā*—as in *sthitvā* and *prasthāya*. Regarding the substitution of *ī*: for the roots *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, *gā*, *pā*, *jahāti*, and *sā* before a consonant (*hal*)—as in *pītvā* and *prapāya*. Regarding lengthening (*dīrghatva*): for a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) before *kvip* or a consonant (*jhal*) with the marker *k* or *ṅ*—as in *śāntvā* and *praśamya*. Regarding *śū*: for *ch* and *v* before a nasalized suffix (*anunāsika*) or *ūṭh*—as in *pṛṣṭvā* and *āpṛcchya*. Regarding *ūṭh*: as in *dyūtvā*. Regarding *iṭ*: after a root marked with *ud* optionally—as in *devitvā* and *pradīvya*. If *iṭ* were not present here, the prohibition of the *kit* status by the rule "the *ktvā* suffix is not *kit* when it has *iṭ*" would cause *guṇa* substitution to occur.

What is the purpose of including the word *pūrva*? If it were stated simply as *anañ*, it would refer to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which the negative particle (*nañ*) does not exist"—and consequently, a prohibition [of the feminine suffix] would apply even in a case such as *straiṇīkṛtya*. However, when *pūrva* is included, this fault does not arise, because that term denotes a constituent part situated in a fixed position. The inclusion of the *liṭ* marker is for the sake of the accent of the syllable preceding the affix in forms such as *pracikīrṣya*; in cases such as *prakṛtya*, however, the form is established by the accent of the verbal root itself. The inclusion of the *pit* marker is for the sake of the augment *tuk*.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *ktvā* is also [used]. 7.1.38.

Because of the word *api*, [the suffix] *lyap* also [occurs]. And that occurs both in a compound and in a non-compound, because the word *api* serves to introduce *lyap* even in cases where it would otherwise not apply; otherwise, one would have simply said "in the Veda" (*chandasi*). Accordingly, even the authors of the Kalpasūtras, who follow the rules prescribed for the Veda, employ [it], as in: "He anoints the two eyes with clarified butter" (*ājyenākṣiṇī ajyeti*), and so forth.
In place of the case-endings (sup), there may optionally occur: *suluk*, *pūrvasavarṇa*, *āc*, *śe*, *āṭ*, *āḍ*, *yāṭ*, *yāc*, and *āl*. (Pāṇini 7.1.39)

If the substitution *su* were being prescribed, other *sup* [case endings] would not be obtained; therefore, having removed the mention of *su*, one should instead employ the mention of *suṭ*. Thus he says: "of *sup*s, *sup*" and "of *tiṅ*s, *tiṅ*. And this is established by the rule "transposition occurs abundantly" (*vyatyayo bahulam*). The rule "of *sup*s, *sup*" is also an elaboration of that very same principle. However, in the case of *takṣṇvanti*, the reading *yuktaḥ* (proper) is appropriate.

Regarding the example *ādre carmann*: But surely this is already established by the rule for the homogeneous substitute (*pūrvasavarṇa*). How so? When *carman-i* is situated, the *nakāra* is the homogeneous substitute for the preceding vowel *ikāra*. Thereafter, since the designation "word" (*pada*) applies by the rule *svādiṣu*, there is elision of the preceding *nakāra*. In that case, this further purpose [of the present rule] follows: the mention of *ṅi* in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* need not be made, because the elision of the *nakāra* of the case-ending would not even arise due to the fact that it is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*); whereas the elision of the preceding *nakāra* is indeed desired.

[Objection: This is not correct; for in this case, if the *pūrvasavarṇa* [diphthong] were to occur, it would—by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*)—be a non-nasalized *dakāra* (the letter *d*) itself. [Reply: Let it be so; the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) will take place. [Objection: The elision of the final consonant of a conjunct does not apply here, because once the designation "word" (*pada*) applies by the rule *svādiṣu*, and the preceding *nakāra* has been elided, the word is no longer a conjunct (*asaṃyogāntatvāt*). For the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is established only when there is an elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

If that is the case, then the mention of *ṅi* in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* will be made; there, in the absence of the elision of *n*, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would apply. Since this [elision] is thus established otherwise, he states another example: *havirddhāne yatsunvanti*. When *yat-i* is situated [there], if the *dakāra* were a *pūrvasavarṇa* [substitute], then once the substitution of *ya* for the *tyad*-class [pronoun] has occurred, the state of *smin* would result by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. Therefore, in this case, only *luk* (elision) should be applied.

Furthermore, in the case of multiple *al* sounds such as those beginning with *bhyām*, if the final sound were replaced by a homogeneous (*pūrvasavarṇa*) vowel, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) of not hearing the preceding portion; therefore, even in those cases, elision (*luk*) alone must be applied. [Examples such as] *dhītī* and so forth: from the words *dhīti*, *mati*, and *suṣṭuti*, the third-case singular ending takes a homogeneous *i* vowel, which then undergoes lengthening due to the following *ka*-vowel. [Regarding the rule] "not after *tad* or *brāhmaṇa*": from the word *tad* and the word *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *śas* is applied; for that [suffix], *āt* is the substitute. By the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ*, the *it*-designation is prohibited. The Rigvedic reciters (*bahvṛcaḥ*) read: *yā deva vipnatāt tvā mahāntam*. As for the statement "the forms *yūyam* and *vayam* would result": [this refers to the application of the aforementioned rules].

This is a reading based on negligence; for instance, in the mantra "na yuṣme bājabandhavaḥ," the gift of two kings named Ṛkṣa and Aśvamedha is being praised. The plural number is used by way of transference (vyatyaya) for the two [kings]. "Bāja" is a name for food; they are addressed as "O Bājabandhavas," meaning "O you who are kinsmen through the giving of food. The word "yuṣme" is connected with "adhī" (in you), and it expresses the sense of the locative case.

And *ninitsuḥ*, meaning one who is habitually censuring, does not hold (*dhārayati*) nor take to heart (*avadhārayati*) blame against you; the sense is that there is an absence of blame [toward you]. In the phrase "O Indra and Bṛhaspati, [bestow] upon us," the verb is "bestow" (*dhattam*); and the root *dadhāti* here has the sense of giving. Therefore, the reading "upon you [is] ours" (*yuṣmāsu asmākam*) is appropriate. Furthermore, the rule regarding the substitution of *yūya-* for *yuṣmad-* and so forth need not be recited here. Regarding the form *anuṣṭhyā*: although *anuṣṭhamā* would have been expected, in the *adhrigu-praiṣa* we find "drive them out by means of *anuṣṭhyā*" (*tā anuṣṭhyā vyāvayātāt*). From the root *sthā* preceded by *anu*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Thus, *anuṣṭhāna* becomes *anuṣṭhā*; by that, it is *anuṣṭhyā*.

Regarding *prabāhava*: by the rule *dherṅiti*, there is *guṇa*. Now, one might object: "It has been stated that when a marker (*ṅit*) is present, one should understand it as a mere reference to the phoneme; and whatever [operation] applies to that phoneme, one should know it applies to what begins with it. This is true; however, the *guṇa* occurs here by virtue of the power of the application of the *ṅit* marker itself. Regarding *prabahunā* as the form obtained: the reading *bāhunā* would indeed be more appropriate, because the prefix *pra-* is connected with the verb. The short vowel *a* in *ayāc* is for the purpose of preventing the lengthening [of the vowel] before a case-ending (*sup*).
The *am* [case-ending] is substituted for the genitive plural ending *ām* after a word ending in *m*. (Pāṇini 7.1.40)

The substitute *mip* is understood here as *am*. This is not a reference to the second person singular ending, because in Vedic usage one follows what is observed there, and because in the rules to be stated below, verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are predominantly cited. Regarding the form *vadhīm*: it is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *han*. By the rule *luṅi ca*, the substitute *vadh* is applied. Then, *sic* is substituted for *cli*. The augment *iṭ* is added. There is the substitution of *am* for *mip*; the *m* in *maś* is for the sake of pronunciation. By the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, the augment *iṭ* is added. Then, by the rule *iṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of *sic*. Finally, there is the lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatvam*).

The utterance of *śit* is for the purpose of making [the substitute] apply to the whole [of the original]. For otherwise, by the rule *alo'ntyasya* ("a substitute replaces the final phoneme"), since there would be no purpose for pronouncing the letter *m* in place of *m*, it would follow that the substitute applies to the whole; therefore, he says "even of the letter *m*. The intention is that this is as in the case of the rule *mo rāji samaḥ kau*. However, because there is no mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the rule *ādeḥ parasya* ("a substitute replaces the initial phoneme of what follows") does not apply.

Now it is said: "This instruction will be formulated in two ways; therein, even if there is elision of the final consonant of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), forms such as *vadhīm* and so forth are established. Even so, there is no advantage in terms of brevity (*lāghava*). Furthermore, because the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the augment *īṭ* characterized by being a single phoneme (*apṛkta*) would indeed occur. If that is the case, then [the root] will be formulated with an initial *y*. Why is the *y* not heard? The *y* is indicated as being elided when followed by a strong consonant (*bali*); there is no fault here at all. Therefore, the *śit*-suffix is employed.
There is elision of the *ta* [of the suffixes] in the *ātmanepada*. (Pāṇini 7.1.41)

Regarding *aduhra*: by the rule *dūrē laṅ ātmanepadeṣv anataḥ*, there is the substitution of *ad* for *jha*; by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the augment *ruṭ* is added; upon the elision of the letter *t*, the two *a*s undergo *guṇa* substitution, resulting in the single substitute form of the subsequent one (*pararūpatva*). Regarding *śaye*: in the case of *śete*, once the *t* is elided, the substitution of *ay* occurs. Regarding *duhām*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*); the *ṭe* is replaced by *e*, *am* is substituted for *ta*, and the *t* is elided.
As for the phrase "because of the governing context of *api*": thus, the statement "in the *ātmanepada*s" is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very [rule].
The *t* of that [substitute] is elided. (Pāṇini 7.1.44)

Regarding the phrase "of the middle person plural": there is no inclusion of the first person singular, because in Vedic usage one follows what is observed [there], or because of its association with the two preceding and following plurals. As for *kṛṇutāt*: the root *kṛv* means "to injure" and "to do"; by the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*, the suffix *u* is added, the *v* is replaced by *a*, and then the *a* is elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ*.
And [the suffixes] taP, naP, taNa, and thaN [are applied after a nominal stem ending in a short vowel]. (Pāṇini 7.1.45)

Regarding *śṛṇota*: by the rule *śruvaḥ śrṛ ca*, there is the suffix *śnu* and the substitution of *śrṛ*; because the suffix is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *ṅit*), there is no *ṅittva*, and thus the *guṇa* substitution occurs. Regarding *dadhātana*: here too, due to the absence of *pittva*, there is no elision of the long *ā* by the rule *śnābhyastayoḥ*. Regarding *jujuṣṭana*: the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*); the suffix *śa* is added because the root belongs to the *tud*-class; for that [suffix], *śnu* is applied frequently in the Veda (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), followed by reduplication. Since the root *juṣ* is *anudātta-it*, the reading *juṣadhvam* would be expected, but the reading *jujuṣṭana* is appropriate due to irregularity. Regarding *yadi cchata*: this is what was expected.
The Bahvṛcas, however, read *yatiṣṭhana* in this verse, *ko vaḥ stomo maruto yatiṣṭhana*; at the time of the *padapāṭha*, they read *yatiṣṭhana*, which is the form of the root *ās*.
The vowel *i* followed by *t* becomes *mas* before a suffix beginning with *n*. (Pāṇini 7.1.46)

The term *masi* is a citation without a case ending (*avibhaktika*). The vowel *i* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). The word *anta* denotes a part; thus, that which has *it* as its final member is *idanta*. The inclusion of the long vowel marker *ā* (the *tapara* rule) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; for if it were stated simply as *yant*, a doubt might arise: "Is it one ending in *y* followed by *it*, or one ending in *ī*? In that case, if the intention were to refer to something ending in *i* by suppressing the *s*, it would have been necessary to say simply *masa itaḥ*. Therefore, the *s* remains in its original state, and the sound *i* is added to it.

And because it is included by the mention of its final element (*anta*), this [suffix] is thereby grasped; consequently, even though there is no formal marker (*liṅga*) such as *ṭit* for an augment, it follows by implication that this is indeed an augment. This is what was stated: "of *mas*, which ends in *s*" and so forth. And thus, one ought to have said *masa ik*; however, it was not stated in that way because of the risk of confusion regarding the pratyāhāra.
The suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *yak*. (Pāṇini 7.1.47)

Regarding the word *dattvāya*: [the rule] *do daddhoḥ* applies. An example found in a mantra is: *saubhāgyam asyai dattvāya, dattvāyāsmabhyam draviṇeha bhadram*. In some places, it is read as *dattvāya savitā dhiyam*; in that case, the Taittirīyakas read *tattvāya*.
[This is explained by the rule] *ktvāpi chandasi*, etc.; for in this way, the repetition of the mention of *ktvā* would not have been necessary.
The suffix *as* (in the nominative singular) is substituted for the pratyāhāra *ājjas* (the case endings from the nominative singular through the accusative plural).

The mention of *jasaḥ* is made in accordance with the tradition of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). Regarding *brāhmaṇāsaḥ*: when the augment *asuk* is applied, there is the audible retention of the *s* of *jas*, while the *s* of *asuka* becomes a *visarjanīya*.

[Examples include] *ye pūrvāsaḥ* and so forth. An objection is raised: regarding *uparāsaḥ*, the vowel *u* at the beginning of the word *apara* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly. However, if this [augment *asuk*] were treated as belonging to the end of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), such that the rule would be "after this [stem], *jasi*, *asuk*," this would not be possible; for in that case, by the rule of *pararūpa* (single-substitute replacement), the form would simply be *uparāḥ*. As for the explicit pronunciation of the vowel *a*, it is for the sake of the subsequent sūtra.

In examples such as *dadhyasyati*, [the rule] would be for the sake of being heard [as a distinct form]. The phrase "when occurring once" (*sakṛdgatau*) and so forth is the solution. Although this is already established by the optionality regarding the nominative plural (*jas*) for *pūrva* and others within the designation of pronouns (*sarvanāman*), there is the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *śī* in the case of *ubhayāsau jātavedaḥ syāma*; for here, the designation [of pronoun] occurs invariably because it is listed among the *sarvādi* group, thereby overriding the optionality prescribed by the rule "the first and the last" (*prathamacarama*). Indeed, that [designation] is internal (*antaranga*).
The [genitive case] is used for *aśva*, *kṣīra*, *vṛṣa*, and *lavaṇa* when the suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of "one's own pleasure. (Pāṇini 7.1.51)

Regarding the word *aśvasyati*: the vowel *a* in this form has already fulfilled its purpose in earlier instances such as *brāhmaṇāsaḥ*; therefore, by the rule *ato guṇe*, the substitution of a single substitute (pararūpa) occurs. Furthermore, because of the restriction *naḥ kye*, the *u*-vowel [of the suffix] is not at the end of a word. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of desire for sexual intercourse": when the desire directed toward a horse is for the purpose of mating, only then does the form *aśuṣ* occur. And because the usage is focused on the desire for sexual intercourse, the mention of the "horse and the stallion" (*aśvavṛṣa*) is not restrictive; thus, it is also employed in reference to humans and others—as in the example *rāmo vṛṣasyantīm*. Regarding the phrase "excess of thirst": [this refers to the state of intense longing].

*Abhyavajihīrṣā* means "excessive desire"; it refers to an excessive longing for milk or salt intended for consumption (*abhyavahāra*), and not for purposes such as *homa* (sacrificial oblation) and the like. Regarding the phrase *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*: this dative case ending (*caturthī*) expresses the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*), meaning "for the sake of all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadika*), which is to say, "for all nominal bases" (*sarveṣāṃ prātipadikānām*).
[The sūtra: *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.52). [This prescribes the augment *suṭ* after a pronominal stem when followed by the genitive plural suffix *ām*.]

There are many instances of this suffix *ām*: in *ṅasi-ṅasoḥ* and *ṅerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ*; in *kimettiṅavyayaghādāmvadravyaprakarṣe*; and in *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi*. Among these, which *ām* is being referred to? He says: the genitive plural form *ām* is what is intended here. For that [suffix] indeed takes precedence due to its position later in the rules.

The scope for *suṭ* and *nuṭ* is the genitive plural; whereas the scope for *āṭ* and the others is the dative singular and so forth. When both would apply—as in the case of *ṅeḥ* becoming *ām*—*āṭ* and the others take effect because they are subsequent rules. Once those have been applied, *suṭ* and *nuṭ* do not occur, by recourse to the maxim that "what has already taken effect once does not recur. As for the rule *ghādāmu*: it means exactly *kim-ettiṅ-avyaya-ghādāmu*. The particle *ca* has the sense of "and," or rather, *tu* should be read instead. Regarding *ām ca liṭi*: the meaning is that the *ām* prescribed by the rule *kāspratyayāt* occurs when *liṭ* follows.

The meaning is this: those two [the forms *sarva* and *viśva*] do not stand after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*). Therefore, for the time being, they are not included here; and since only that which is included here continues to be the subject of the rule in what follows, they are likewise not included in the prescription of the augment *nuṭ*. Furthermore, because words ending in the denominative suffix *kvip* derived from *sarva*-type stems lack the sense of "all," they lack the designation of pronominal (*sarvanāman*), and thus the suffix *ām* after a pronominal following a reduplicated perfect (*liṭ*) is impossible in their case.

However, for one who thinks: "When there is a general application [of the rule], the operation is understood according to the specific context as far as possible; consequently, the *nuṭ* augment would apply to those two [suffixes] as well," he states another solution: "Or, they are with their indicatory letters (*sānubandhaka*). For if there were a general application, then in *pacatitarām*, the *nuṭ* would occur by virtue of its higher status, overriding the elision of *ya* (*yasyeti lopa*).

But in *kārayām* and *cikīrṣīm*, since the substitution of *ay* by the rule *ay-ām-anta-* is compulsory, and once the elision of *at* has been performed, the *nuṭ* does not apply because the short vowel is no longer present.

"Regarding the phrase *uttarārtham* (for the sake of what follows): [the rule] *trestrayaḥ* [is stated] so that [the form] may remain as it is when followed by the suffix *ām*. But here, however, the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is understood through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *āt*, which is supplied from the preceding context; and by doing so, the formulation of the rule *hali sarveṣām* becomes justified."
The suffixes *tra*, *tṛc*, and *a* [are applied after verbal roots to form nouns denoting the agent]. (Pāṇini 3.1.133)
The word "trayāṇām" is in the genitive case, not the ablative, as indicated by the rule "ṇijāṃ trayāṇām."
The augment *nuṭ* is added after a short vowel, the vowels *nadi*, and the vowel *āp*.
The term *hrasvanadyāp* is in the ablative case; by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the term *nāmi*, otherwise there would be no possibility of a *nām* [vowel] having its cause in the *aṅga*.
And after [the words] *ṣaṣ* and *catur*, [the suffix *ām* is substituted for the case-ending *bhyas*]. (Pāṇini 7.1.55)

When the suffix *nuṭ* is applied, there is lengthening of the vowel by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*. Then, by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*, the final *n* is elided, resulting in *ṣaṇṇām*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo'nte*, the sibilant *ṣ* is changed to the voiced stop *ḍ*; then, by the rule *yaro'nunāsike*, the *ḍ* is changed to the nasal *ṇ*; finally, the rule *ṣṭutvam* applies.

Now, regarding the rule *ṣṇāntāḥ ṣaṭ* ("those ending in *ṣ* or *n* are called *ṣaṭ*"), why is the designation *ṣaṭ* not prescribed for a number ending in *r* by simply adding the letter *r* [to the rule]? For if that were so, the mention of "four" (*catur*) here would not be necessary, and likewise [the mention of] "six" (*ṣaṭ*) in the rule *ṣaṭ-tri-caturbhyo halādiḥ* would also be unnecessary. To this he says: "ending in *r*" (*rephāntāyāḥ*). [He adds: "because of the indication by means of the plural number."

For if the word-form (*śabda*) were predominant, there would have to be a dual ending in a *itaretara-dvanda*, whereas in a *samāhāra-dvanda* there would have to be a singular ending. However, when the meaning (*artha*) is predominant, it is justified that the plural ending occurs because those very items designated as "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñaka*) are each individually plural in meaning, as is the word *catur*. In this case, the "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) of *ām* is mediated by the word-form. In the expression *paramaṣaṇṇām*, here too, because the plurality of meanings is predominant, *ām* follows immediately after that [the word *ṣaṣ*] for that very reason.
But in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, since the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is predominant, the subsequent-ness is not in relation to the meaning of "six," and thus [the rule] does not apply.
Regarding "priyapañjām": when elision (alopa) has occurred, the substitution of *ñ* for *c* takes place. Thus, it is the letter *ñ*.
The forms *śrī* and *grāmaṇī* [are used] in the Vedic language. 7.1.56.

Regarding the statement "it is for the sake of establishing a permanent rule": otherwise, there would be an option (vikalpa) as in the case of the vernacular (bhāṣā). If it were only seen in the Vedic language (chandas), yet there exists a grammatical rule (lakṣaṇa) for it, one must consider this: what occasion for an option could there be? This point requires reflection.

And [the examples] "sūtāśca" and "te grāmaṇyaśca": this is not a sentence for a *karmadhāraya* compound; rather, it serves as the purpose for the application of the augment *nuṭ* when there is a *dvandva* in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) between two words ending in the plural. He shows that when a *samāhāra-dvandva* is formed with two words ending in the singular and then a *ekaśeṣa* is performed, the *nuṭ* is already established simply because the stem ends in a short vowel, and thus it would have no purpose [in that case]. And in this way, the word "te" need not be recited.

If, even here, only the augment *nuṭ* is observed and its justification exists, then a *dvandva* compound of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) need not be formed; thus, this rule has been rejected in the Bhāṣya.
[The substitution of *go* occurs] before the word *pādānta*. (7.1.57)

The term "in the Veda" (*chandasi*) is an governing heading (*adhikāra*); he specifies that this refers to the quarter-verse of a *ṛc*, not the quarter-verse of a *śloka*, by stating "at the end of an *ṛc*-quarter" (*ṛkpādānte*).
The augment *num* is added after a verbal root ending in *i*, *ī*, or *u*.

The roots *kuḍi* (to burn) and *huṅ* (to destroy) belong to the *aṅ* class; therefore, the augment *num* occurs before a suffix beginning with a consonant. Consequently, in forms such as *kuṇḍā*, the suffix *ktin* is used, and not the suffix *ā* prescribed for a heavy vowel (*guror halaḥ*) followed by a consonant.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "This [is the case]. He states the authority for this here: "For it is thus. But how is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*), given that according to the rule *ik-stipau dhātu-nirdeśe vaktavyau*, when the suffix *ik* is applied, the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) occurs, and consequently, by the force of the grammatical rule itself, the inclusion of those forms accompanied by the augment *num* must necessarily be made? He thinks as follows: this is not an indication by the letter *i*; rather, it is by means of an adventitious *i*-vowel, and in that case, the *num* augment would not otherwise apply.

Anticipating the objection that there is no evidence for this, he says: "And the mention of 'root' (*dhātu*). The sense is that the mention of "root" is for the purpose of indicating that only the status of being a root (*dhātutva*) is required, and not the status of being a verbal suffix (*aṅga*), and that there is no other purpose whatsoever. Now, one might argue that the mention of "root" must be for the sake of preventing the *num* augment in cases like *bhettā* and *abhaitsīt*, where the suffixes *tās* and *sic* (which have *i* as an *it*) would otherwise apply; to this he replies: "In the case of *tās* and *sic*..."

Now, one might object that in forms such as *amaṃsta*, the ātmanepada suffix is marked with the indicator *ṅ*; therefore, to prevent the elision of the final *s* of the *sic*-affix by the rule *aniditām...* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the *sic* would have to undergo the operation of having the *it*-indicator *i*. To this, he says: "In *amaṃsta* etc. Just as the prescription of the *kit* status for *han* in the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14) serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this [point], so too has it been explained in that very same place.

In that case, the inclusion of the letter *it* in [the rule for] *mant* and so forth would serve the purpose of preventing the elision of the penultimate *n* when the first-person singular *ātmanepada* ending is replaced by *ḍā* and the *ṭi*-portion is elided, resulting in the form *man-ā*. Therefore, he says: "in the case of *mant*. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "there is no elision of the *n*."

Jayāditya, however, relying on the fact that the status of being "not established" (*asiddhatva*) with respect to what is internal (*ābhīyam*) is non-eternal (*anitya*), stated that the inclusion of the marker *i* in the root *tās-* is for the purpose of prohibiting the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). In his view, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) must be made [in the rule] to exclude *tās-*, and thus a further effort must be undertaken regarding the rule *upadeśe 'j anunāsikaḥ*.

In this context, regarding roots such as *bhid* and others, the vowel *i* receives the designation *it* by the rule *aj-anunāsikaḥ kaḥ*, and the *r* also receives the designation *hal-anta*. Consequently, the augment *num* would apply because they possess the *it* designation; to this he replies: "of those marked with *ir*" (*iritām*). By the supplementary rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*) *ir-ity-upasaṅkhyānam*, the designation *it* applies to the entire group [the root plus the suffix], not to each individual element according to the sūtra. Therefore, since they do not have the *it* designation [individually], the augment *num* does not occur. This is the meaning.

"But even so, the *ātmanepada* ending conditioned by the *svarita* accent would not apply to roots such as *bhid* and others; therefore, a solution must be stated for each individual case. Thinking thus, he states the solution for each individual case: "Even part by part (*avayavaśo 'pi*). Another says: "In the rule *iditaḥ*, this is not a *bahuvrīhi* compound; what then? It is a *karmadhāraya*. Consequently, this is a mention of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*). In that case, by the rule of *tadantavidhi*, the augment *num* applies to a root ending in the vowel *i* which bears the technical name *it*."

Now, one might ask: why were these roots not taught here with the *it* markers (*it*) already attached? If that were the case, this [present rule] would not need to be composed. For, first of all, the mention of *num* must be made for the sake of subsequent rules; and since there are many roots with *it* markers, it is more concise to state this very sūtra rather than pronouncing the letter *n* individually for each one.
The substitution of *ś* occurs for the initial consonant of roots beginning with *muc* [in the context of the *liṭ* affix].

The roots beginning with *muc*—starting from *muclṛ* "to release" and extending to the end of the *tud*-class—should be understood as belonging to that group. But what are the "roots beginning with *tṛp*"? This question arises because, if the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) were taken in its restrictive sense, there would be the undesirable consequence of including even those roots that lack the nasal suffix (*anuṣaṅga*). The answer is that the word "beginning with" (*ādi*) here denotes a class (*prakāra*), and "class" means similarity; and that similarity consists in being accompanied by the suffix *n*. If the augment *num* were prescribed again for these roots which already possess the suffix *n*, then, once the subsequent *n* had been changed to an *anusvāra* and then to its homogeneous letter (*parasavarṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing both the *n* and the *m* [in the form *nnm*]. Therefore, he says: "Of these... (*teṣām*).

Now, why does the elision (*lopa*) of its *num* augment not also occur? To this he says: "And [the word] 'ca'. [The reason is] "by virtue of the force of the specific injunction" (*vidhānasāmarthyāt*). And this [injunction] applies only to the *muc*-class of roots.

[The mention of *tṛp* and others] is the reason for the absence of elision [of the nasal]. As for the roots beginning with *tṛmph*, however, the absence of elision of the preceding *n* is established precisely because the elision of the subsequent *n* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the principle of the elision of *ciṇ* (*ciṇo luk*). Now, why are *tṛp* and the others not read among the roots beginning with *muc*? To this he says: "But those which... The intention is as follows: in this system (*tantra*), there is a single enumeration of both the forms with the nasal suffix (*anuṣaṅga*) and those without it. In that case, if all were read among the *muc*-class roots, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *num* even for those without the nasal suffix. On the other hand, if they were read separately from the nasalized ones, there would be the consequence of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to having to state the meaning twice.
The substitution of *mas* for *naś* occurs before the suffix *jhal*. (Pāṇini 7.1.60)

In *ṭumasjo* [meaning] purification, the suffix *tṛc* is applied; there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekācaḥ*. The augment *num* is placed before the final letter *j*. By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca*, there is the elision of *s*; then *kutva* (the substitution of *g*) occurs, followed by *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*. Regarding *naṃṣṭā*: in the alternative view where *iṭ* is absent by the rule *radhādibhyaśca*, *num* is applied. Regarding *majjanam*: when *j* follows, although the substitution of *ścu* (i.e., *ś*) for *s* would have been applicable, because the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *j*) is considered asiddha (not yet established), the *ścu* substitution takes effect first; then, the *jaś* substitution applies to the *ś*, resulting in the letter *j*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *masjerityādi*: if [the augment] were to follow the final vowel (*ac*), then the entire collection of *na*, *sa*, and *ja* would constitute a single *saṃyoga* (conjunction); consequently, because the *s* would not be the initial member of a *saṃyoga*, its elision (*lopa*) would not occur. Alternatively, even if one were to resort to assigning the designation of *saṃyoga* separately to *sa* and *ja* so that the elision might take place, even then, because that elision would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), the *n* would not be an *upadhā* (penultimate letter), and thus its elision would not occur. Therefore, the *num* augment must be desired to be placed before the final *j*, between *sa* and *ja*.
After the roots √radh and √jabh, the augment iṭ is applied before an affix beginning with a vowel.

The roots *radh* (in the senses of injury and propitiation) and *jabh* (*jṛbhī*, in the sense of bending the limbs) provide an occasion for the application of *num*. Examples include *randhanam* and *rarandhatuḥ*. The rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), which prescribes *vṛddhi*, provides another occasion—as in *pācakaḥ*, *pāṭhakaḥ*, and *randhakaḥ*. When both [rules] would apply simultaneously, *vṛddhi* prevails due to its higher status in the order of rules; regarding this, he says: "Even though it is subsequent... Once *num* has been applied, *vṛddhi* no longer applies because the vowel *a* is no longer the penultimate (*upadhā*) letter, and thus it is considered non-eternal (*anitya*). As for *raddha*: by the rule *radhādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.45), there is optionally an absence of *iṭ*; then, by *jhapastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40), the *t* is changed to *dh*.

In this case, the formulation of the rule should have been "iha jabher aci radheliṭi ca neṭ" (here, after the root *jabh*, and after *radh* before the suffix *liṭ*, there is no *iṭ*), but it was not done in that way.
The substitution of *na* for the final consonant of the root *radh* does not occur before the affix *liṭ*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *numi kṛte* and so forth: [the opponent objects] "But surely, since [the root] *ceṭ* belongs to the *satyajādi* group, the augment *num* ought to occur; indeed, the status of *ceṭ* as having the marker *k* would apply even earlier, and thus the rule *na ca aliṭi* would be rendered useless, because it serves a purpose for the suffix *thal*. For in this way, due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term 'dhātoḥ' (from the root), the *num* occurs precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśa*). However, the term *aci* is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*)."

Regarding the word *atha*: for those who hold that the suffix *kvasu* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), this deliberation does not arise, because in the Vedas one follows whatever is observed there. [The phrase] "when the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication have been performed" is stated precisely because, in the rule *vasvekājādghasām*, only monosyllabic roots (*ekāc*) that have already undergone reduplication are included. Regarding the point "the augment *num* [is applied]"—this is because of the mention of the condition *aci* (before a vowel). As for the passage beginning with *tasya* (of that):

although, as in the case of *rarandhiva* and so on, there is no transferred (*ātideśika*) *kit*-status even for *kvasu*, nevertheless, the elision of *na* occurs by relying upon the original (*aupadeśika*) *kit*-status. This is the meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with *atha* and so forth: the sense is that this being the case, both prohibitions—namely those expressed by *neṭyaliṭi*—would not need to be stated. It might be suspected that the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) would be reversed; however, even if the particle *eva* were employed, there would be no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*).
The substitution of *rabhi* for *rabh* does not occur before the suffix *aś* nor in the *liṭ* tense.
The root *rabh* is used in the sense of rashness; it is anudātta.
And [the augment *it* is applied] after [a verbal root ending in] *labh*. (Pāṇini 7.1.64)

The root *labh* is used in the sense of "attaining" (*prāptau*), and it is marked with an anudātta accent. Since the rule "only after a prefix [the suffixes] *khal* and *ghan*" will be stated later, this [current reading] is a corrupt text (*apapāṭha*). Some maintain that the suffix *gha* occurs here because of the word *ca* in the rule *khano gha ca*, just as in the case of *bhagaḥ* and *padam*. The separation of the *yoga* (sūtra division) is for the sake of what follows; [this ensures] that the subsequent rule applies only to *labhi* and not to *rabhi*. Furthermore, it is intended to prevent a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) between *kḷp* and *śilp*.
After the prefix *āṅ*, [the substitution of] *yi* occurs in place of *yat*. (Pāṇini 7.1.65)

Since the term *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) is understood here [from a previous rule], the augment *num* must occur precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*). Therefore, he states that *yi* is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) by saying, "when a suffix beginning with *y* is the scope. By the words "prior," etc., he demonstrates the result of resorting to the locative of scope. Regarding "therein," etc.: there is no difference in form; even when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the augment *vṛddhi* should certainly not occur, because *num* is permanent and thus its cause is already established. However, in the case of the suffix *yat*, there would be the acute accent on the first syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapadādyudāttatva*).

Because [in the word] *anāvaḥ*, the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) is udātta. Regarding *ālabhya*: the suffix *yak* is applied; thus, the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal) is performed. By this, the suffixes *yak* and *kyap* are explained. Therefore, although the term *yi* was stated as a general designation, the intention is that only *ṇyat* has been illustrated here.
The suffix *upāt* is used in the sense of praise. (Pāṇini 7.1.66)

In this case, attainment (*prāpti*) alone is the meaning of the verbal root; however, praise (*praśaṃsā*), being understood by implication, serves as a qualifier. Therefore, an example occurs where either the attainment itself, or the cause from which the attainment arises, is the basis for praise; whereas the counter-example occurs in the opposite case.
After a prefix, the augment *iṭ* is not applied before the suffixes *khal* and *ghañ*.

Regarding the phrase "siddhe sati" (it being established): this is by means of the rule *labheśca*. Regarding the phrase "upasargādeva" (only after a prefix): the reverse restriction—that [the suffixes] *khal* and *ghañ* occur only after a prefix—does not apply here, because of the specific mention of the roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* in the rule *halambhane*.
Not [is the suffix *kha* used] after the two words *su-* and *dur-*, when they stand alone. (Pāṇini 5.4.70)
The word *kevala* (exclusive/only) expresses the absence of any other thing of the same class as that which is denoted by the word [itself]. For example, when it is said,
"One must enter here with these two alone," the entry of any other person is thereby prohibited.
It is not so for parrots and the like; likewise here too, these two—whether joined with one another, solitary, accompanied by a heterogeneous element, or entirely alone—are [to be understood].

Examples include *sudurlabham*, *sulabham*, *durlabham*, and *atisulabham*; as well as *sulābhaḥ* and *durlābhaḥ*. In these cases, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). However, when the sense is that of the object (*karmaṇi*), the suffix *khal* occurs. Alternatively, the prefix *su-* may signify "contempt" (*kṣepe*), as in *suṣiktam nāma* ("so-called 'well-poured'"); and *dur-* signifies "reproach" (*nindāyām*), as in *durbrāhmaṇaḥ* ("a bad Brahmin"). Consequently, because they do not possess the meanings of "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) or "ease" (*akṛcchra*), the suffix *khal* does not apply.

"Considering it as the third [case]" means that this is a counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) specifically in the case of the third case (*tṛtīyā*). Now, why is it not a counter-example in the case of the fifth case (*pañcamī*)? To this he says: "For in the fifth case... Nor is it a counter-example because it is impossible even then; for it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This usage does not exist."

Regarding the phrase "atisulabham ity atra": the intention is that because the term *upasargāt* (following a prefix) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over), the prefixes *su-* and *dur-* are what are intended here. Furthermore, by the rule *atiḥ atikramaṇe ca*, the word *ati* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya*; and by that designation, its status as an *upasarga* (prefix) is superseded, since there is a governing rule (*adhikāra*) stating that only one designation applies at a time. The phrase "even in the case of the view involving a reference to the fifth case" (*pañcamī-nirdeśa-pakṣe*) means that, since the mention of the word *kevala* (alone) must be made in every respect, and since there is no basis for the violation of the sequence [of rules], the counter-example is shown by resorting to the third case [ending] from the preceding [rule].

There is an option regarding the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel of a verbal root before the affixes *ciṇ* and *niṅ*, as well as when the suffix *kṛt* *kvasu* (which is treated as having the marker *m*) follows. (Pāṇini 7.3.69)

Therefore, his conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is unafflicted (*anupasṛṣṭa*). And so says the Vārttika: "The [suffixes] *ciṇ*, *ṇamul*, and others [are used] when there is no prefix (*anupasarga*)."

The long vowel *ā* is substituted for the final short vowel of a verbal root ending in a consonant (other than *h*) or of a root marked with the indicatory letter *ū*, when followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix. (Pāṇini 7.1.70)

Regarding the phrase *dhātu-varjitānām* (of those excluding verbal roots): this is not a demonstration of the meaning of the rule *na idam-adhātoḥ*, because that [rule] has a different purpose. Therefore, the point which will be stated later—that the mention of *añcati* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*)—is already established and demonstrated by this very [phrase]. However, in demonstrating the meaning of *adhātoḥ*, one should have shown: "The augment *num* occurs after *ugit*-ending stems and after *añcati*, provided they are not verbal roots. Thus, the mention of *añcateḥ* [in the rule] is intended to show this.

However, the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* "aj" [in the rule *aj-ād-yat*] does not apply here, because of the repeated mention of "aj" in the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*; for in that context, only the *pratyāhāra* is intended, not the root *añc*, since it ends in a *jhal* consonant. *Bhāvan*: the long vowel is applied by the rule *atvasantasya ca*. Here, a grammatical characteristic (*liṅga*) applied to a constituent part also serves as a qualifier for the whole; thus, the *aṅga* possesses the quality of being *ugit*. *Prāṅ*: [the suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā*; then *su-* (the nominative singular ending); then the elision of the *saṃyoga* [consonant cluster] according to *hal-ṅyādi-* and *saṃyogāntalopaḥ*; and finally, by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*, the *kutva* (palatalization) occurs—namely, the change of *n* to *ṅ*.

The inclusion of the term *añcati* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). For this [rule] does not serve as an injunction (*vidhi*) where [the suffix] would otherwise not apply due to the prohibition "not after a verbal root" (*na hi adhātoḥ*). Indeed, if it were so, the expression "not after a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) need not have been stated, since the desired result would be established by the restriction alone. In the case of *ukhāsrat*, the substitution of *d* occurs by the rule beginning with *vasusraṃsu*.

Regarding the question "Why [is it stated] 'not a root' (*adhātoḥ*)?": the question is raised because, due to the inclusion of the term *añcati* in the rule, by that very restriction, [the suffix] will not apply to a root. Regarding the phrase "even of that which was previously not a root": the meaning is that it should apply even to that which was observed at some time to be non-root (*adhātu*), even though it is currently a root. Regarding *gomatyaḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*; the suffix being applied is *avadyamāna-pratyaya*—that is, *apratyaya* (non-suffix)—which is again *kvip*. Then there is the elision of the final vowel (*ato lopaḥ*); then the elision of *y* according to *kyasya vibhāṣā*; and finally the addition of *num*, resulting in *gomān*.

But how can there be lengthening here, since it is stated that [the rule applies] to what ends in *at* or *as*, provided it is not a verbal root (*adhātu*)? This is not a fault; for the term *adhātuḥ* is analyzed separately, and by virtue of that, this prohibition applies specifically to what ends in *as*, not to what ends in *at*. For this very reason, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that point, only an example ending in *as* is presented as a counter-example.
The suffix *yuc* is applied after a verbal root ending in *i* or *u*, provided it does not form a compound.

*yuṅ*, *yuñjau*, *yuñjaḥ*—the suffix *kvip* and so forth are applied as before. *aśvayug*—the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc. This very statement regarding non-compounds (*asamāsa*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, within the governing heading of "stem" (*aṅga*), there is the inclusion of both the stem itself and its subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Regarding the mention of the vowel *i* in *yujeḥ*: the intention is that this is not a citation of the verbal root from the eighth chapter (*nāvamikā*), but rather an imitation of the vowel *i* found in the Dhātupāṭha. *yujam*—the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group.
The substitution of *nuṭ* occurs after a neuter stem ending in a consonant (*jhal*) or a vowel (*ac*).

Regarding the word *trapūṇi*: although the augment *num* is established here by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*, nevertheless, because the mention of the pratyāhāra *acaḥ* serves no other purpose, the *num* occurs by this very rule alone. What, then, is the difference here—whether the *num* is present by that [rule] or by this one? There is no difference at all; rather, the underlying principle (*bhāṣya*) has been demonstrated. If that is so, let the mention of the pratyāhāra not be made; let only the letter *a* be taken—namely, in the form *jhalataḥ*. But what is the advantage in such brevity?

Furthermore, it was stated that because the term *akṣa* is used as a *pratyāhāra*, the root *añc-* is what is understood in the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), and not the *pratyāhāra* itself; however, even that would be undermined.

Consider the example *bahupurī*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those who have many cities," the suffix *a* prescribed by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.74) for the final member of the compound would be applicable, yet it does not occur because the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) is not invariably obligatory (*anitya*). [The example] *vimaladivi dināni* means "days whose sky is pure."

In this context, the scope for the *num* augment characterized by the rule [Pāṇini 7.1.70] (*jhal-antāt*... is when it follows an *ugit* stem that is not neuter, as in *sarpīṃṣi* and *dhanūṃṣi*; whereas the scope for the *num* augment characterized by the rule [Pāṇini 7.1.71] (*tug-anta-ugid-acām...*) is when it follows an *ugit* stem that is neuter, as in *gomān* and *yavamān*. When both rules would apply to a neuter stem ending in a *jhal* consonant that is also *ugit*, the *num* augment occurs by this very [latter] rule due to its superior status (*paratva*).

Let it be so; however, because the rule is understood to apply again once [the substitution] has been made, the *num* augment—characterized by having a vowel (*u*) as its initial letter—would also result. But how is it possible for multiple [sounds] to be subsequent (*para*) with respect to a single final vowel? This may not be possible in actual usage (*prayoga*), but it is possible at the time of formulation (*vidhāna*). For example, in the case of *pacati*, where there is the suffix *laṭ* and the suffix *śap*, in forms such as *tudantī* and *nudantī*, after the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions have been applied to the subsequent *n*, there is no difference regarding the perception of two *n*s.

In this case, then—in forms such as *kṛṣanti* and *rupanti*, once the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* have been applied to the following *num*, the preceding [nasal] would not undergo *anusvāra* or *parasavarṇa* because it is followed by a non-nasal (*ajhal*) sound; thus, by the rule *aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi*, the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) would result. Furthermore, when there is a single *num*, both *anusvāra* and *ṇatva* would apply to it. Since *ṇatva* is considered *asiddha* (unestablished) with respect to *anusvāra*, once *anusvāra* has been made, *parasavarṇa* occurs; since that too is *asiddha*, the absence of *ṇatva* is established. Therefore, regarding that which is characterized by the *ugit* suffixes...

Anticipating the objection that a prohibition must be stated, he says: "of a [stem] ending in *ugit* and having a *jhal* [consonant]. He indicates by means of the word *eva* (only) that the maxim of "once-occurrence" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*) is to be resorted to here; [this is shown] by the phrase "by this very [rule].
"Before the final [letter]" means between the letter *r* and the letter *j*.
In any case-ending, [the final vowel of a word ending in *i* or *u* is elided]. (Pāṇini 7.1.73)

"What is the purpose of saying *ika*? [The answer is: The mention of *aj* (vowels) made previously should have been made right here—namely, "of a neuter [stem] ending in *jhal*, and of a vowel (*ac*) before a vowel (*aci*)"—and by that, it would not apply to a stem ending in a consonant (*hal*), because there is no neuter stem ending in a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*). This is the question. For this very reason, he provides a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for one ending in *a*, and not for one ending in a consonant.

[Question: Why does [the author] say "not so"? [Answer: In forms such as *trapubhyām*, even though there is a *num* suffix before a consonant (*hal*), once the designation *pada* applies by the rule *svādiṣu*, the desired result is already established by the elision of the final *n* of the nominal stem (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*). This is the question. The other [author], having understood the intention, says: "For the sake of subsequent rules. [This means: so that the substitution *anaṅ* may apply to *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi* before a vowel (*aci*), but not before a consonant (*hal*) as in *asthibhyām*. Again, he objects: "If this is so... He replies: "But here... [as in] *he trapo*.

In this case, the application [of *num*] would have occurred previously; once *num* has been applied, because the stem no longer ends in a vowel (*anigantatvāt*), there is no further application. This might be argued: "Let *num* be applied here; since the *sU* of *svamornapuṃsakāt* is elided, the word ending in a *sup* suffix receives the designation *pada*, and thus the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) will take place. To this he replies: "Not before *ṅi* or the vocative (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*). As for the words beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*), etc.: the particle *eva* is displaced in its order and, being connected with the prohibition, negates even the figurative existence of the case-ending.

The existence of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) is twofold: primary (*mukhya*) and figurative (*aupacārika*). Therein, the primary exists when the ending is actually heard; the other [the figurative] exists by means of the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when the ending is elided (*lupta*). Here, because [the ending] is elided, the primary [existence] does not exist; and since the characteristic of a suffix is prohibited, the figurative [existence] likewise does not exist at all. In that case, regarding what is stated as "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*), what occasion would there be for *num* to apply such that it would occur when the case-ending is absolutely non-existent? It would not apply at all. Therefore, there is no purpose in the mention of the vowel *a* (*aj-grahaṇa*). This is precisely what [the author] says, beginning with "this very... and so forth.

Otherwise, he would not have included the mention of *aj* (vowels); yet it has been included, which indicates that in this context, when a neuter stem ends in a vowel (*akṣara*), the prohibition regarding the application of suffixal characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply to the vocative case (*sambuddhi*). He demonstrates the purpose of this indicator (*jñāpaka*) with the words "And thus," etc. While the rule "and in the vocative" (*sambuddhau ca*) is in effect, the "guṇa of a short vowel" (*hrasvasya guṇaḥ*) prescribed in the subsequent rule constitutes the "vocative guṇa.
[The example is] *laumburavam*. [The suffix] *añ* is applied after *u* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

Regarding the rule *iko 'ci* and so forth: it is stated that the substitution occurs when an *ac* (vowel) follows; let it not apply when a consonant (*vyañjana*) begins [the following word], as in *trapubhyām* and *trapubhiḥ*.
