Let there be elision (*lopa*); let there be the augment *num*; and let there be the elision of the final *n* of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*. But how will the accent (*svara*) be? In the forms *pañcatrapubhyām* and *pañcatrapubhiḥ*, the accent prescribed for a *dvigu* compound—wherein the preceding member retains its original form (*prakṛti-svara*) when the subsequent member ends in an *ik* vowel—is not obtained because, with the presence of *num*, the word does not end in an *ik*. Even if the elision of *n* is performed, since the operation of elision is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purpose of applying an accent rule, the word still does not end in an *ik*. Thus, it remains non-*ik*-ending.

"Even when [the *nakāra*] is elided, will the accent not indeed occur?"—the word *vai* is used here in the sense of "certainly. Even when the *nakāra* is being heard, the accent occurs—as in *pañcatrapuṇe* and *pañcatrapuṇaḥ*. Why then will it not occur when it is elided? Where its occurrence is possible by virtue of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) rather than by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why would it not occur there? It will certainly occur.

What, then, is the reason that the accent occurs even when the augment *num* is heard? It is because this [augment] is dependent upon the entire complex (*saṅghātabhakta*); it is not capable of obstructing the fact that the subsequent member ends in a vowel (*agantatā*). Furthermore, if the accent is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it will take place even before the case endings (*vibhakti*) have been produced.

In this case, then—regarding the forms *atirābhyām* and *atirābhiḥ*: when *atiribhyām* has been established and the augment *num* is applied, the substitution of *ā* by the rule *rāyo hali* does not apply because of the intervention [caused by *num*]. Even if the *nalopa* (elision of *n*) is performed, since that is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) with respect to a *sub*-operation, there remains the same intervention. The *num* augment, being a part of the entire cluster, would not intervene against that [cluster] itself, but it certainly intervenes against the word *rai*.

Furthermore, even though in this context of the *aṅga* (stem) rule, by the statement "of that [stem] and its subsequent member," the status of being a stem (*aṅgatva*) is prescribed for what ends in the word *rai*, there is no intervention of the *num* augment between the stem and the suffix. Nevertheless, according to the principle that "substitutes apply to that which is explicitly mentioned" (*nirdiśyamānasyādeśā bhavanti*), there is indeed an intervention of the word *rai*. Moreover, if the substitution of *āt* applies to the stem, even so, the substitution of *āt* would apply only to the *num* itself; in that case, when the *yaṇ* replacement occurs for the preceding vowel, the form would have to be *atiryābhyām*.

Likewise, in the case of *priyatisṛbhyāṃ brāhmaṇakulābhyām*, when [the form] *priyatribhyām* is established, the substitution of *tisṛ* would not occur because of the intervention of the *num* augment. Even if the *n*-elision (*nalopa*) has been performed, the reasoning is as before.

This is not a fault; for even when there is an intervention by *num*, the substitution of *rāy* and the change to the form *tisṛ* still take place. The ablative in *vyavadhānāt* is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* (meaning "despite" or "even though"), signifying that they occur even upon reaching an intervention by *num*. The point is that the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) which exists at the stage of the prescription of the case-ending is what is relied upon there, and not the sequence at the stage of the prescription of the substitute. In the expression *numā api*, the long vowel *savarga-dīrgha* has not been applied because the *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) is not intended to be expressed. Others, however, read the word *hi* in the middle [of the sentence].

By the word *api* (also), he indicates this: that the substitution of *āt* and the change to *tisṛ* are established even by another method. How so? When the form *ka-at-ibhyām* is established, since both the *num* augment and the substitution of *āt* are optional (*anitya*), the substitution of *āt* occurs first because it is subsequent; likewise for the change to *tisṛ*. In that case, the absence of *num* is achieved by resorting to the maxim of "once [a rule] has applied" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*). Or, even if *num* were present, there would be no fault whatsoever. If that is so, then the mention of *ac* was made for the purpose of resolving the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between *num* and *nuṭ*.

The rule *hrasvanadyāpo nuṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54) has its scope in cases such as *agnīnām*, *vāyūnām*; the scope of *num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58) is in cases such as *trapuṇe*, *jatune*, *trapūṇām*, *jatūnām*. When both rules would apply simultaneously, *nuṭ* is desired by means of a "prior conflict" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), so that the lengthening prescribed by *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3) may take effect. This conflict is possible only if there is the mention of *ac* (the vowel), because both rules are equally strong as they are both non-obligatory (*anitya*). For if the mention of *ac* were absent, *num* alone would apply, since it is obligatory (*nitya*) due to its application regardless of whether the other rule has already taken effect or not.

This also refutes the stated purpose—namely, that "the augment *nuṭ* must be prescribed"—by stating: "even if the mention of *ac* (*ajgrahaṇa*) were made, *nuṭ* would still have to be prescribed there; it would have to be established by an explicit rule (*vacanenaiva*), for otherwise, due to its higher status (*paratvāt*), *num* alone would occur. Consequently, two efforts would have to be undertaken: the mention of *ac* must be made, and a prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) must be stated. The meaning is that instead of making the mention of *ac*, only a single effort for the sake of *nuṭ* need be made.

In that case, this is the purpose: by that very effort, let there not be *num* in the same place where *nuṭ* occurs—that is, in a base beginning with a non-*an* vowel (*anaj-ādi*). Let it be so; [one might argue] the elision (*lopa*) will take place, but because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the base would not end in an *an* vowel, and thus the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by the rule *nāmi* would not occur. [Objection: Let it not be so; the lengthening will occur by the rule *nopadhāyāḥ*. [Reply: In that case, consider the forms *śucīnām*. By the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "in the case of *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*, [the penultimate vowel is lengthened] before the nominative plural suffix *śas* and the nominative singular suffix *su," the lengthening would not occur here. For in that rule, the word *in* refers to the specific (pratipadokta) stem, whereas this [form *śuci*] is derived through a grammatical derivation (*lākṣaṇika*).

When the inclusion of the term *aj* has been thus rejected, he states the purpose [for its inclusion]: "But for the sake of what follows" (*uttarārthaṃ tu*). The word *tu* has the sense of "then" (*tarhi*). If its purpose lies in what follows, then it should have been placed right there; therefore, he says: "In this case, something... The substitution of *yaṇ* was not applied here because of the rule prescribing the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the sūtra *iko'savarṇe śākalyasya*. In the example *trapo*, however, because it is a vocative (*sambuddhau*), the status of being a *pragṛhya* applies by the rule *śākalyasyetāvanārṣe*, and thus there is no substitution of *ava*.

Some here maintain that there is a dual form—*he trapo* and *he trapu*—and state that this makes known the optional nature (*anityatva*) of the prohibition regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), rather than its total absence in this context. Accordingly, both *he trapu* and *he trapo* are cited as examples in the Bhāṣya. Others, however, explaining the Bhāṣya’s statement "when *he trapu* would [otherwise] occur, it becomes *he trapo*," maintain that the guṇa substitution is indeed obligatory. Thus, only the guṇa form is cited as an example in the Vṛtti.
In the case of the third case and those following, for a word that has a masculine counterpart, the feminine form may optionally take the masculine form according to Gālava. (Pāṇini 7.1.74)

The word *napuṃsakasya* (of the neuter), which was previously established as ending in the genitive case, becomes here a nominative by its connection with the term *bhāṣitapuṃskam* (having been stated as masculine). Regarding *puṃvat* (like the masculine): the meaning is "equal to the word for a male. When the expectation arises as to in what manner it is equal to the word for a male, he says: *yathā* (just as).

The absence of the *num* augment and the short vowel (*hrasva*) is observed in the word *puṃs*; by means of that [word], the similarity [to it] is extended here [to other words], because no other similarity to the word *puṃs* is possible in the third case and so forth. Consequently, this results in a prohibition of both the *num* augment and the short vowel. [Objection: Even so, since the *num* augment is the subject under discussion, it would be more appropriate to extend its absence alone, not that of the short vowel. Therefore, since the short vowel would remain present, one would have to state a prohibition for the grammatical operations dependent upon it—namely, *guṇa*, *na*, *abhāva*, *nuṭ*, and *aut*.

The *guṇa* [substitution] applies by the rule *gher ṅiti*; the substitution of *aut* occurs in *grāmaṇye kulānām* (by *aut*); and the substitution of *at* occurs in *grāmaṇyām brāhmaṇakule* (by *acca gheḥ*). There is no fault here, because of the force of the extended application (*atideśa*).

The absence of the short vowel is also extended [by this rule]; otherwise, it would have merely prescribed the prohibition for Gālava. For example: *grāmaṇīr brāhmaṇaḥ*. This is an illustration of a word that has been previously used in the masculine. In the case of *grāmaṇi brāhmaṇakulam*, the shortening occurs because of the neuter gender; therefore, it is shown by this [rule] that the absence of that [shortening] is being extended. The remaining example, *śuci brāhmaṇakulam*, is presented to avoid breaking the continuity of the discussion.
In the counter-examples, the augment *mum* and the shortening occur invariably as appropriate.

Regarding "the fruit of the *pīlu*": in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *orañ* when it denotes a fruit, provided that the general form (*ākṛti*) is the same. This is explained by the phrase "when the cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is identical. That by connection with which a word is applied to a substance is its cause of application, such as leading [cattle] to a village and so forth. Granted that this is so, what is relevant to the present case? To this he says: "But here... The meaning is that in the application of the word *pīlu* to a male [tree], the tree's form—that is, the specific sub-class of tree—is the cause of application. "The neuter [form] is based on the form of the fruit."

The phrase “of the word whose basis for application [is such-and-such]” (*pravṛttinimitta-śabdasya*) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. “Form of the fruit” (*phalākṛtiḥ*) means a subordinate genus (*avāntara-jāti*) of the fruit. In that regard, although in the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of *pīloḥ phalam* (the fruit of the *pīlu* tree), a subordinate genus of the tree is also accepted, nevertheless, that [genus of the tree] is not the basis for the application [of the name] to the fruit; rather, it is only the subordinate genus of the fruit itself. Thus, the basis for application differs. This very point has been explained under the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*; it should be understood from that [section]. Regarding *kīlālapena*: if the short vowel were removed, there would be the elision [of the final *ā*] by the rule *āto dhātoḥ*.
In the place of the words *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the substitution *anaṅ* occurs, and it is acute-accented.

The second *a* in *anaṅ* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), while the *ṅ* is for the sake of the final substitution (*antādeśārtha*). [In the case of] *asthi* and so on, the first syllable is udātta by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya*; the remainder is anudātta. In that context, since an anudātta substitute would normally apply by internal correspondence (*antaryataḥ*), the explicit statement of "udātta" is made so that, when the *a* is elided by *allopo'naḥ* in forms such as *asthnā*, the case ending becomes udātta according to the rule *anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ*.

In the alternative view where the elision (*allopa*) of the *ṅi* and *śi* endings is not applied—according to the rule *vibhāṣā ṅiśyoḥ*—the acute accent of the vowel *a* is heard, as in *asthanī*. This is seen even in the Vedic language, for example in the passage *indro dadhīco asthabhiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "by these [words] beginning with *asthi*," etc.: here, within the governing context of the *aṅga* (stem), the term refers to that which ends in those [stems], according to the principle *tasya ca taduttarapadasya ca*. Furthermore, because the word *anapuṃsakasya* (of the non-neuter) is present by way of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), it qualifies the stems beginning with *asthi* due to its proximity (*śruta*), and not the *aṅga* under discussion; therefore, it includes even those [stems] that are non-neuter.

But for what purpose are *asthi* and the others specified as neuter? [It is so] lest there be masculine arbitrary (*yadṛcchā*) words such as "Dadhi" (as a proper name), [and one might think] "by that Dadhi. This is not a valid purpose, for:

"Those words whose referents are clearly manifested, which are independent, and whose forms are well-known through elision—it is upon these that the meaning of the grammatical rule (*śāstrārtha*) must be applied, not upon the utterances of those [arbitrary] words."

In that case, the phrase "of the neuter" (*napuṃsakasya*), which is understood from the previous context, has merely been shown its connection [to the following]: "by these [words] beginning with 'bone' (*asthi*) when they are neuter."
It is also seen in the Vedic language (chandas). 7.1.76.

Since the rule is already established by the phrase "in the Veda" (*chandasi*), the addition of the words "is also seen" (*api dṛśyate*) is for the purpose of showing that [the application] deviates from all such conditions; otherwise, by the force of its formulation, one might suspect that the deviation applies only to some specific cases. This is what was stated: "Where it is prescribed, it is seen elsewhere as well. Regarding the form *asthanvantam*: once *anaṅ* has been applied, the augment *nuṭ* is added to the suffix *matup* by the rule *anonuṭ*, and there is the elision of the letter *n* of *anaṅ*.
And the vowel *ī* [is substituted for the dual ending] in the dual number.

Regarding *akṣī*: when *akṣi-au* is established, the substitution of *śī* occurs for *auṅ*; the preceding vowel becomes *ikāra* (the short *i*), and there *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* applies. Since the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* provides a permanent prohibition of that long vowel, the alternative *vā chandasi* optionally allows for the long *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel; or else, the lengthening is achieved by *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*. Now, one might object: even without this specific rule, the form would be established simply through the long *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel. [To this we reply: No, the long *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel does not apply here, because it is superseded by *num*, which is subsequent in the order of rules.

If that is the case, then the masculine form of a neuter noun must be prescribed in Vedic usage—for the sake of examples such as *madhostṛptā ivāsate* (they sit as if satisfied with honey). By means of that masculine form, since the *num* augment and the *śī* substitution do not occur, the form *akṣī* is established even through the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*). This is true; however, the accent is not established, because the word *akṣi*, being a neuter ending in *i* and falling under the rule for words beginning with *na*, is udātta on its first syllable. Furthermore, it is not desired that the masculine form should extend by prescription the absence of accent as well.
Therefore, for the sake of the accent alone, the vowel *ī* itself must be prescribed.
The nominative suffix *śas* is not replaced by *au* after a stem ending in *nābhi* when it is not a repeated (abhyasta) word.

Regarding the word *dadat*: there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*. In forms such as *jakṣat*, the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) is applied by the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ*. Now, one might ask: how can the prohibition of *num* be understood for that which is separated from [the preceding vowel] by four rules? To this he says: "The *śatṛ* [suffix] is not prescribed immediately before. An *īkāra* is not prescribed immediately after a stem ending in *śatṛ*; thus, when searching for what is prescribed in immediate succession, the process culminates in the case of *num*.
The augment *num* is inserted after the vowel of the roots *āp* ("to obtain") and *chid* ("to cut"), when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel.

"Of the *śatṛ* [suffix] following a verbal base ending in a vowel other than *a*"—this is precisely the meaning understood from the words of the sūtra, and thus it has been explained; however, this is not the definitive meaning of the sūtra, because a refutation will be stated later. Therefore, since a refutation cannot be stated without first demonstrating its scope, this [explanation] should be seen as intended to demonstrate that scope. *Yātī kule*: By the rule *napuṃsakācca*, the *auṅ* case-ending is replaced by *śī*. *Yātī brāhmaṇī*: By the rule *ugitaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. *Kariṣyati*: This is the *lṛṭ* (future) tense; by the rule *lṛṭaḥ sadvā*, the *sat* designation applies, and by the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye*, the augment *iṭ* is added.

The objection begins with "here" (*atretyādi*). Furthermore, the substitution (*ekādeśa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it depends solely upon the *śatṛ* suffix; whereas the *num* augment is external (*bahiṅga*) because it depends upon the production of the feminine suffix *śī*. "Distinction" (*vyapavarga*) means separation—specifically, the form: "this is a stem ending in the vowel *a*, this is the *śatṛ* suffix. That distinction no longer exists once the substitution has been made, like milk and water. For example, when milk and water are mixed, one cannot discern: "this is the milk" or "this is the water," nor can one say: "in this place is the milk, and in that place is the water."

It is not tenable to say that [the substitution applies] to the *śatṛ* following a verbal base ending in *a*. The meaning is that it is not tenable in the manner you previously stated. For indeed, in every case, there must be the removal of the vowel *a*: sometimes by *luk*, as in *adatī* and *dhnatī*; sometimes by *ślu*, as in *juhvatī*; sometimes by a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), as in *tudatī* and so on; and sometimes by the elision of the long *ā* according to the rule *śnābhyastayor ātaḥ*, as in *lunatī* and so on.

It might be argued: "In the case of a single substitute, the status of being 'end-like' (antavadbhāva) or 'beginning-like' (ādivadbhāva) will apply. To this, he says: "When there is a dependence on both sides" (*ubhayata āśraye*). Where both the preceding and the following elements are simultaneously depended upon, there the status of being end-like or beginning-like does not exist; for example, in *upasargād dhrasvaḥ* as in *ūhate*, *prohate*, or in *eter liṅi* as in *abhīyāt*. Here too, both the member (*aṅga*) ending in an *a*-vowel and the *śatṛ* suffix are simultaneously depended upon; therefore, the status of being end-like or beginning-like does not apply.

Now this is being stated: [the rule applies] to the *śatṛ* suffix following a stem ending in a vowel other than *a*. However, at present, such a *śatṛ* suffix is not possible anywhere; therefore, one must resort to the principle of "having existed previously" (*bhūtapūrvagati*). That is, one resorts to the principle of having existed previously in the sense that "formerly there was a *śatṛ* suffix following a stem ending in a vowel other than *a*. Regarding this, he says: "Or, by resorting to the principle of having existed previously. The term *samādhiḥ* means a resolution or a solution. [The rule refers to] "from a word ending in a vowel other than *a*."

It should be understood that [the term] "from the stem" (*aṅgāt*) is intended; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *dadati*. For here too, the letter *t* follows an *a*-sound that is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the suffix *śatṛ*. But how can there be the status of being a stem (*aṅgatva*) for that which does not end in an *a*-sound? [The answer is: because of the treatment of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) as being like the final element (*antavadbhāva*). Indeed, at this point, the quality of being a final element (*ādiṣatva*) is not intended with respect to what follows; rather, the *t* itself is a constituent part of the suffix. Thus, by means of that *t*, there is again the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) for the stem; the word "of the stem" (*aṅgasya*) is repeated here.

"But others," he says. Even in this view, both [the *anta* and *ādi* properties] are not accepted simultaneously; rather, they occur sequentially, so that the status of being "as if the end and beginning" (*antādivadbhāva*) exists. Now, one might object: in forms such as *tudanti*, let the base (*aṅga*) ending in the vowel *a* exist by virtue of the status of being "as if the end and beginning"; nevertheless, *śī* and *nadī* do not follow from that [base], because there is an intervention by the letter *t*. To this, he replies: "In that case."

Since the *num* under discussion is connected with the prohibition [of its application], when that [prohibition] is repeated here as well, it is precisely the prohibition that is optional: either *num* does not occur for *śī* and *nadī* after a stem ending in an *a*-vowel, or it does. But by what [rule] would there be the occasion [for this prohibition], such that this very [text] would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *num* exists for *śī* and *nadī*? For otherwise, in cases such as *kurvatī*, there would be a constant occasion for *num* because the stem does not end in an *a*-vowel. To prevent this from being understood [as a general rule], the mention of *num* [in the sūtra] is made.
The substitution of *śa* for the personal endings of the present (*śatṛ*) and future (*syatṛ*) suffixes is compulsory.

Regarding the phrase "of these two, [the suffix] śatṛ": the meaning is "of that which is the suffix śatṛ belonging to these two. And the relationship is one of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika-bhāva). In some places, however, the reading is "of the related elements" (sambandhin). Regarding the mention of the word "nitya" (invariable): one might object that by the very force of the rule's formulation, it will necessarily be invariable; to this he replies: "In this case... (iha).
The [substitution of] *u* for the final vowel of *anaḍuh* occurs before a case-ending beginning with a vowel. 7.1.82.

In this context, one might raise the objection that the augment *ām*—prescribed by the rule *caturanaḍuhorāmudāttaḥ* for all *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes—would have scope elsewhere than in the nominative singular (*su*), and thus be superseded by the *num* augment, which has no other scope; similarly, the *num* augment, which has scope in the nominative singular other than the vocative, would be superseded in the vocative by the specific rule *am sambuddhau*. Anticipating this, he says: "In this regard, some... and so forth.

But how is it that even when the word *āditya* is understood to follow [from the previous rule], the *num* augment occurs after the two vowels *ā* and *i*, rather than after the vowel *a* alone which is permanently present in *anaḍuh* and immediately precedes [the suffix]? It is said in reply: if that were the case, the paribhāṣā "midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ" (the augment follows after the final vowel among the vowels) would be sublated; and since an interpretation without sublation is possible, sublation is not logical. Therefore, one must explain the matter in such a way that the paribhāṣā is not sublated and the continuation of the word *āditya* remains meaningful.

If *num* were to occur after both *am* and *ām*, then neither of these two would be favored; therefore, *num* will occur only after those two [that is, after *am* and *ām*]. Thus, neither *am* nor *ām* is sublated. The meaning is that not only is *am* not sublated, but both *am* and *ām* are not sublated. *Am* is cited here as an illustration; the point is that just as *am* is not sublated, so too is *ām*. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of *am* being sublated by *num*, because *am* is prescribed as a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*), whereas *num* is sublated by *ām* and *ambhyām*.

The phrase "it is not sublated" is to be supplied by modifying the wording [of the previous statement]. Here too, the meaning is that just as the *āmā* is not sublated, so also is the *amā*. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of sublation regarding the *num*, because it is a universal (*sāmānya*). As for the passage beginning with "Others, however," they maintain [the following].

Because of this statement, some maintain that this is indeed a *bādhaka-iṣṭi* (an intended sublation). Others, however, say: "Granted that there may be a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) when two rules—a general and a specific—occur in proximity; but here, there is an intervention by multiple grammatical operations (*yoga*). For sublation occurs only when coexistence is impossible; yet here, such coexistence is possible, since both could apply, resulting in the simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the augment *num* and the long vowel. As for the example: when the doubling [of the consonant] has not yet taken effect, the rule for the long vowel is initiated.

Nevertheless, there is a co-occurrence [of both rules] due to their applicability and the distinction of their respective contexts. In the case of *bahvanaḍvāṃhi brāhmaṇakulāni*, once the *ām* suffix has been applied by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), the *num* augment occurs again by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, because of the principle that a rule applies again when there is a possibility for it to do so (*prasaṅgavijñānāt*).
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *dṛś* occurs for *sva*, *vasu*, and *svatavas*. (Pāṇini 7.1.83)

In *īdṛk* and similar forms, after the suffix *kvip* has been applied to the root *dṛś-* in the sense of "not perceiving" (as prescribed by the rule *tyadādiṣu dṛśo'nālocane kañ ca*), and the augment *num* has been added, the change to *k* (*kutva*) occurs as before.
The substitution of *au* for *div* occurs before a suffix beginning with a vowel. (Pāṇini 7.1.84)

It must be stated that the [application of the rule] is prohibited for verbal roots (*dhātu*), as in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*. Since a word modified in one part is not different from the original, once *ūṭh* is applied, this would still be the word *div*, and thus the [rule] would apply. This is established by the governing context of "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*). The term "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*) is understood [from the previous sūtra]. Where was it introduced? In [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.70]: "For *ugit*-pratyaya endings and for *aj*-stems, [the long vowel is substituted] before a nominal ending (*sarvanāmasthāna*), provided they are not verbal roots. If that were to be understood here, it would also be connected with [7.1.72]: "In the neuter, for stems ending in *jhal* or *ac*. Consequently, it would not apply in cases such as *kāṣṭhataṅkṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*.

Therefore, since it is impossible to follow that [interpretation], and consequently the prohibition must indeed be stated for the verbal root (*dhātu*), he raises this objection and says: "The word *div* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)," and so forth.
The substitution of āt occurs in place of the final vowel of the words *pathin*, *mathin*, and *ṛbhukṣan*.

Regarding the word *panthāḥ*: by the rule *itaḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*; then, by *savarṇadīrghatvam*, there is lengthening; and by *tho nthaḥ*, *tha* is replaced by *ntha*. Having raised the objection—why does the nasalized vowel *ā* not occur here due to the internal proximity (*antaryataḥ*) with the nasal *n* which is the original element (*sthānin*)?—he says: "even though the original element (*sthānin*) is nasal. He states the reason for this: "by that which is being produced (*bhāvyamānena*)."

Some read that "an *aṇ* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). For them as well, the mention of *aṇ* is intended as an indicator for any [vowel] that is a grasper (*grāhaka*); therefore, even the vowel *ā* (as in *āt*), when being taught, does not become a grasper. However, there might be a suspicion of its inclusion based on the rule *taparas tatkālasya* ("a vowel followed by *t* denotes only those of its own duration"), for it is stated therein: "This is for the purpose of an injunction regarding what is not an *aṇ*. To this one might object: "Let there be no inclusion of the homogeneous counterparts; however, since only the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel is pronounced in the sūtra, that alone would be the one [to be understood]. To this he says: "For this [vowel] is pure (*śuddha*)."

In the prescription of the vowel *a*, if [the rule] *ato guṇe* were applied, it would result in *parūpaṃ*. However, the prescription of the vowel *a* must be for the purpose of eliminating the letter *n*, because applying the rule for elision (*lopa*) would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the vowel *ā* alone is prescribed.
From this point [up to the end of the chapter], [the term] *asarvanāmasthāna* [is understood]. (Pāṇini 7.1.86)

What is the purpose of stating "advacanam" (the mention of *at*)? [Is it] so that the short vowel might be heard? This is not the case; for in this instance, first of all, the long vowel by rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*) occurs. Furthermore, it does not apply elsewhere, because in the case of a "sarvanāmasthāna" suffix, it must be a long vowel. Therefore, the vowel *ā* itself is what should be prescribed in the present context. Hence he says: "since *āt* is understood [from the previous sūtra]. The meaning is that its purpose lies where this prescribed *akāra* is preceded by a *ṣakāra*. He demonstrates that very point with the example: "in the word *ṛbhukṣaṇam*."

In the rule for the substitution of *a*, however, there would be only one form; the alternative long vowel (*dīrgha*) would be for the sake of forms such as *takṣaṇām* and *takṣāṇām*. Furthermore, the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*aḥ*) in the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.
The *tho* [augment] is placed at the end [of the word]. 7-1-87.

Regarding the rule *pathimathoḥ*: although three [stems] are under discussion, the connection is made with these two alone because the letter *th* occurs only in them. In the substitute, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). It might be argued: "Let the rule be *theran thaḥ*; let the *a* also be intended [as part of the substitute], so that *an tha* is the substitute for the word *thi*. By doing this, the rule *ito't* need not be stated. That too must be stated for the sake of the word *ṛbhukṣin*.
The elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs after a *bha* stem.

Regarding the phrase "pathy-ādīti": because each term is connected individually, the singular form *bhasya* is used. Regarding the phrase "due to contradiction" (*virodhāt*): the contradiction consists in the absence of the designation *bha* when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows. The sense is that [the designation *bha*] is not connected here [in this specific rule], yet it certainly continues to apply for the sake of subsequent rules.
The suffix *asuṅ* is applied after the word *pums*.

The letter *ṅ* in the suffix *asuṅ* is for the purpose of substitution at the end; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding the word *pumān*: because the stem *puṃs* ends in an *ugit* vowel, the augment *num* is applied, for it is derived from the root *puñ* with the suffix *ḍumasun*. The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant); the letter *u* is for the purpose of the operations prescribed for *ugit* stems—as in *bahupuṃsī*, where the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs by virtue of the *ugit* characteristic. The letter *n* is for the purpose of accentuation; in the letter *m*, the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation.

"Here," and so forth, introduces the objection. "Even before the production of the suffix" (*pratyaya*): here *pratyaya* refers to a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending. "The udātta accent at the end of the compound": this refers to the vowel *u* of the word *puṃs*. "An undesired accent": the meaning is that in place of the *sakāra*, which has the property of falling away (*sraṃsanadharman*) when following a consonant (*hal*), there would be a substitute (*ādeśa*) having that same property—an *anudātta*.

[Objection: But surely, even though the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound has been applied to the word ending in *ukār*, it will be set aside when *asuṅ* is applied because [the *ukār*] is no longer final; and since *asuṅ* is now final, it will take effect. [Reply: This is not so, because when the internal (*antaraṅga*) accent is to be applied, the external (*bahiraṅga*) *asuṅ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and furthermore, it is impossible to revoke what has already taken effect. The phrase "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) and so forth is the solution. The word *artha* here signifies "cessation"; thus, the meaning is "for the sake of the cessation of that undesirable accent. "The statement 'as if it were taught' (*upadeśivad-vacanam*)" refers to this.

"One who possesses instruction" (*upadeśī*) means one who has [grammatical] instruction; the suffix *sakāra* (the letter *s*) is present just as it was during the state of the original instruction, and so too is the *asuṅ* substitute—this is the meaning. It is thus stated that the locative case in the rule "before a *sarvanāmasthāna* ending beginning with *k*" must be understood as a locative of occasion (*viṣayasaptamī*). In that case, since the *asuṅ* substitution occurs immediately after the compound formation because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the resulting acute accent applies to the vowel of the *asuṅ* itself; thus, the desired result is established.

If this were so, then even in the absence of a compound—as in *pumān*—once the suffix *asuṅ* has been applied during the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), the accent of the nominal stem (*pratipadikasvara*) would apply specifically to *asuṅ*. To address this, he says: "But as for this word *pumān*... It has been stated that in the word *puṃs*, the suffix is marked with the indicator *n* (*nit*); by virtue of that, it possesses an acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).
The suffix *ṇit* is applied after the word *gotra*.

As many positions as there are in the *gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ sūtra*, so many are there here as well; likewise are the merits and defects, and in that very same way the position of extended application (*atideśapakṣa*) is adopted, as it says: "it becomes *ṇit*. A word for something else is employed for another thing even without the suffix *-vat*, conveying the sense of *-vat*; just as in the expression, "The boy is a lion."

Because of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *ṇit*, the locative form *sarvanāmasthāne* is transformed into the nominative. Since it is impossible for the status of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* to be the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*) by the word *ṇit*, the operation that occurs when there is a *ṇit* suffix is extended (*atidiśyate*) to what precedes the *sarvanāmasthāna*. Thus he says: "The meaning is that the operations belonging to a *ṇit* suffix take place there [in the *sarvanāmasthāna*]."

Regarding the example *citraguḥ*: in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is shortening [of the final vowel] according to the rule *gosjñiyorupasarjanasya*. Here, if the marker *t* (in *tapara*) were not present, then because the extension of the domain of the *aṅga* (the stem) is accepted as including that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*), the maxim "all [substitutes] are substitutes for the entire word" would apply; thus, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the word would end in *go*, and consequently, the status of being a *ṇit* would apply.

However, when the marker *t* is present for the purpose of specifying duration (*tatkālārtha*), this does not occur because the durations differ. It is held that since the term *aṇ* has been removed from the rule *taparastatkālasya*, the restriction to that specific duration applies even to non-*aṇ* sounds.

How so? The question is: even when the *guṇa* substitution has been applied by the rule *hrasvasya guṇo jasi ca*, the *ṇit*-character would still apply because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) and because it possesses that same temporal duration (*tatkālatva*). Furthermore, the maxim regarding "that which is taught by its own specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*) does not apply in the domain of *sthānivadbhāva*, as that would result in its becoming redundant. The resolution begins with "when the operation pertains to the stem" (*aṅgavṛtte*) and so forth; the meaning is that the *ṇit*-character does not occur, i.e., the effect of being *ṇit* does not take place.

"Let this be a solution for the case of *sambuddhi*; however, since the suffix *jas* lacks the substitution of *at*, the base (*aṅga*) remains incomplete, and thus this is not a solution for that case. Anticipating this objection, he says "Or rather" (*atha vā*). With the words beginning with "And which" (*yac ca*), he states a specific connection by way of its meaning.

However, if there were the possibility [of the application of the rule] even from the word *citragu* when the relationship is based on immediate sequence (*ānantarya-lakṣaṇa*), then—since the non-application in the case of *citragu* follows precisely from resorting to a relationship mediated by meaning—what is the purpose of the inclusion of *t* (the *tapara* marker)? To this he says: "The inclusion of *t*, however, is solely for the sake of clear indication. The meaning is that it is for the sake of a clear indication. Otherwise, if it were stated simply as *goḥ*, the indication of the word *gu* might also be suspected.

"Ke-cit" and so forth. He states the purpose of this reading: "even from the word *dyo*. As for those who do not read it thus, how can there be the status of being a *ṇit* in the word *dyo*? To this he says: "this very [sūtra] *gotaḥ* [is the basis]. But how can this be understood as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that which ends in the vowel *o*? To this he says: "In the case of the mention of a specific phoneme (*varṇa*), the use of *t* as a marker (*taparatva*) is observed; therefore, because of the inclusion of *t* here, it is understood as an indication of that which ends in the vowel *o*."
When followed by a nasal (ṇ), the final vowel of a verbal root ending in a consonant may optionally take the augment nu before the first person singular ending.

The meaning is that the operation conditioned by *ṇit* occurs there. By this, he shows that it is said "it possesses *ṇit*" because the operation conditioned by *ṇit* is absent in one alternative, and not because the designation *it* is prohibited for the letter *ṇ* in that alternative. And this is obtained from the extension (*atideśa*) of the operation in the preceding case. Regarding the word "and" (*ca*): in the alternative where there is *ṇit*-ness, there is *vṛddhi*; otherwise, its absence.
The substitution of *sakhi* for *sakhin* occurs before any case-ending other than the vocative singular.

Here too, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *ṇit*, the word *sarvanāmasthāne* ends in the nominative case. Just as the word ending in the locative case, *asambuddhau*, which is included for the sake of the subsequent rule, is construed here, so he demonstrates it: "the word *sakhi* which [occurs] when not in the vocative.
[This is followed by: *anaṅ sau* (Pāṇini 7.1.93).

Because of the context of the section on *sarvanāmasthāna* and because of the exclusion of the vocative (*sambuddhi*), the term *sau* refers to the nominative singular ending, not the locative plural. [Objection: If the vowel *ā* were prescribed [for the nominative singular], then the elision of *su* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* would not occur. [Reply: In that case, let the substitution of *ṅ* for *su* be prescribed. However, since this is already established, the fact that [the sūtra] teaches *anaṅ* indicates that there are instances where *anaṅ* itself is heard [as a substitute]. Therefore, what he will say later—that even in the vocative, *anaṅ* is desired in one alternative—becomes justified.
The suffix *matup* is applied after the words *ṛduśanas*, *purudaṃsas*, and those ending in *anehas*. (Pāṇini 5.2.130)

Regarding the statement that "even in the case of the vocative (*sambuddhi*), when *aṅ* is not present, it is desired [that the elision occurs]," he confirms this by means of authoritative scripture (*āptagama*) with the words "and so it has been said. In the sense of "in the vocative" (*sambodhane*), *sambuddhau* refers to the collection of the three forms, which is *trirūpam*; it belongs to the *pātrādi* group.

What, then, are those forms? To this he says: "sāntam" and so forth. *Sāntam* refers to the case where there is no elision of the nasal (*anaṅ-abhāva-pakṣe*); *nāntam* refers to the case where there is no elision of the *n* (*nalopa-abhāva-pakṣe*); *tadantam* refers to the case where there is elision of the *n* (*nalopa-pakṣe*). *Mādhyandiniḥ*—the descendant of *Madhyandina*—is the teacher; he "desires" (*vaṣṭi*) [this form]. We have already stated in the section on "the six beginning with *jakṣ*" that its correctness in the common language (*bhāṣā*) is to be considered.

Likewise, the meaning of the verse "guṇaṃ ṣaṣṭhī" is that [the rule applies] to the neuter gender—that is, in relation to what is neuter—as in the case of *vaiyāghrapadya*, the teacher who is the most excellent among the offspring of Vyāghrapad; and in cases such as *he trapo* (vocative singular of *trapu*), where the stem ends in an *iK* vowel.
The word *kroṣṭu* is treated like a word ending in the suffix *tṛc*.

The word *kroṣṭu* ends with the suffix *tun*. [The root] *kruś* means "to call out"; [the suffix *tun* is applied] by the rule: "The suffix *tun* is added after the roots *sita*, *ni*, *gam*, *mi*, *mas*, *saci*, *vidhā*, *dhā*, and *kuśi*. It is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), because the suffix *tun* is prescribed for the purpose of forming a name; furthermore, this is the specific name for a jackal (*jambuka*). This is a statement regarding the actual nature of the thing. Immediately following this, the word *tasya* ("of that") should be read, because in the sūtra it is indicated by the genitive case as *kroṣṭuḥ*. Regarding the expression *tṛjvadbhavati*: *tṛjvat* means "like *tṛc*. In this context, the suffix *vati* is applied to a word ending in the genitive case according to the rule *tatra tasyeva*.

All of this has been clarified in the subsequent section of the treatise: "Whatever form belongs to that which ends in *tṛc*, that same form belongs to this [word]. By means of the paribhāṣā rule concerning the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the phrase "of that which ends in *tṛc*" is obtained.

Extended application (*atideśa*) is of many kinds, having as its objects: cause (*nimitta*), designation (*vyapadeśa*), identity (*tādātmya*), scripture (*śāstra*), operation (*kārya*), and essential form (*svarūpa*). Among these, because the first three are impossible in this context, there is no extended application of them; furthermore, there is this distinction between the extended application of scripture and the extended application of operation. In the case of the extended application of scripture, the operations occur by means of that specific scripture [to which it is extended]; however, in the case of the extended application of operation, they occur by the extended-application rule itself. Thus, in the event of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between them, there is a difference in the result.

For example, in the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of a grammatical operation, if it were an extension of the technical term (*śāstrātideśa*), then the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (3.1.31) would be superseded; consequently, by relying on the agency residing in its own substrate (*svāśraya-kartṛtva*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the Parasmaipada suffixes for the remaining cases under the rule *kartari parasmaipadam*. However, if it is an extension of the effect (*kāryātideśa*), then the Ātmanepada suffix alone occurs because it is the subsequent rule.

But here, since such a distinction is not possible, the investigation in the *Mahābhāṣya* proceeds by assuming their non-difference: "Is this an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule (*śāstra*), or rather an extension of the form (*rūpa*)? In that regard, because a rule is proximate to another rule, the extension of the rule would follow; however, due to its primacy, there arises the possibility of an extension of the form, for the purpose of other extensions is for the sake of that [form].

In that regard, concerning the first position: either the rule (*śāstra*) that applies specifically to the *tṛca* is extended [by analogy], or it is extended without being restricted. If the rule is extended just as the word *tṛc* is, then that is the "restricted" (*āhatya*) position. Alternatively, if in the word *tṛc* only the vowel *ṛ* is intended to be expressed—the letter *c* being for the sake of accentuation and the letter *t* for the purpose of removing the suspicion of an unfamiliar form—then it would be stated as *ṛjvat*. If it were stated thus, one might suspect an extension based on an unfamiliar source, or one might suspect an extension of a compound suffix (*samāsānta`) conditioned by the word *ṛk*. Therefore, it ends in *t*.

The position is that a treatise or an operation enjoined by the letter *y* is extended [to the case of *tṛc*] as being "already established" (*āhṛtya*). In that regard, according to the view that it is "already established," only the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *aptṛntṛc* would be extended; the *anaṅ*, the *guṇa*, and the substitution of *rapara* would not be extended—namely, *anaṅ* (by *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasāṃ ca*), the *guṇa* (by *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ*), and the *rapara* (by *uraṇ raparaḥ*)—for these are not prescribed by means of the technical designation *tṛc*.

But surely, when "lengthening" (dīrghatva) is extended [by analogy], *anaṅ* and the other substitutes are also necessarily extended; how then can it be said that in the rule for lengthening, the term *upadhāyāḥ* ("of the penultimate") applies, and *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") also presents itself, so that it is stated that a lengthening occurs for a stem ending in *-tu* just as it does for one ending in *-tṛ*, which would mean that a lengthening occurs for the penultimate vowel of the *-tu* stem? And this is impossible as long as *anaṅ* and the others have not yet been applied, because the penultimate [vowel] of the *-tu* stem cannot exist [as such] until then.

If it is argued that [the rule] applies because both the substitution of *guṇa* and the substitution of *āv* are possible, we say no; for a single example does not justify the commencement of a grammatical rule (*yoga*). If this were the only purpose, one would have simply included the mention of *kroṣṭu* in the rule *aptṛn*. [Objection: But in that case, for the sake of the rules "also in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*) and "optionally before vowels beginning with the third case-ending" (*vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣvaci*), one would have to state again "for *kroṣṭu*, like *tṛc* and *an"* (*tṛjākavat kroṣṭuḥ*), which would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). [Response: This might be so; however, immediately after the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ*, I shall state "for *kroṣṭu* in the feminine, optionally before vowels beginning with the third case-ending" (*kroṣṭuḥ striyām vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣvaci*) for the sake of the substitution of *r*. Thus, there is no complexity.

Even so, forms such as *kroṣṭuḥ*, *kroṣṭari*, and *pañcakroṣṭubhī rathaiḥ* would not be established, nor would the accent [of the vowel] by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*. Since a word ending in the suffix *tun* is necessarily ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable), even if the lengthening [of the vowel] were extended to the *jas* case-ending, the non-acceptance of that extension would not be purposeless; thus, the establishment of *anaṅ* and other substitutes through implication (*ākṣepa*) based on the force of that [extension] is not possible. Therefore, this alternative position is indeed flawed.

Now, regarding the view that there is no direct application (*anāhatyapakṣa*): the elements such as *anaṅ* and so on are extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*), whereas length (*dīrghatva*) is not; for that [length] is not prescribed by the rule "after *ṛ*" (*na hi tad ṛta iti vidhīyate*). Alternatively, if it is intended that the entire aggregate "tṛj" is meant, and not merely the phoneme *ṛ*, and if the view of non-direct application is not resorted to, then rather than that, whatever basis is observed in the suffix *tṛc*—whatever it may be—is all of that extended by analogy. Even so, because of the context of the *aṅga* (stem), only that rule or operation which is prescribed within the domain of *aṅga* operations is extended, and not something remote that does not pertain to the *aṅga*.

Just as by virtue of its own form (*yathāsvam*), only the operations of *vṛddhi* and so forth occur, and not the substitution of *ha*, *ni*, or *ṅi*; consequently, the status of having *r* as a subsequent element (*raparatva*) would not be extended [to the substitute]. Now, *raparatva* is also a property of the *āṅga* (the base undergoing modification); and since the technical rules (*saṃjñā-paribhāṣā*) apply at the time of the operation (*kāryakālam*), when the rule "guṇa occurs for *ṛ* before the endings *ṅi* and *sarvanāmasthāna*" is applied, this [other rule]—"in place of *ṛ*, *ra* is the subsequent element" (*uraṇ raparaḥ*)—is present. If that is the case, then in the word *kroṣṭrī* under the rule "and in the feminine" (*striyāṃ ca*), there would be no extension (*atideśa*) of the long *ī* and the semivowel *yaṇ* because they are not part of the *āṅga*. [Response: It will occur by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacanāt*). However, in the feminine, there is nothing belonging to the *āṅga* that ends in *tṛc*.

There is also a certain point regarding the feminine gender: a chariot purchased for five makers is called *pañcakartṛ* (a five-maker chariot). In the feminine forms *he pañcakartṛ* and *pañcakartṛi*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the guna-vowel seen in the vocative singular of the masculine word *kartṛ*, according to the rule *striyāṃ ca*. For this cannot be established by the rule *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ* in the vocative; since that rule is governed by the heading *asambuddhau* ("except in the vocative"), it would not apply here. Furthermore, in the locative singular, the rule *vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣvac-i* would result in an optional form.

It might be argued as follows: in the rule *striyāṃ ca*, no specific cause (*nimitta*) is mentioned; therefore, even prior to the production of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), there is an extended application (*atideśa*) based on the observation that [the suffix] occurs in the feminine when ending in *-tṛc*. Since at that time the base (*aṅga*) cannot exist, this would be an extended application even for what is not a base. Even so, in the case of *pañcakroṣṭṛbhir rathaiḥ* ("by five carts bought with five *kroṣṭṛ*s"), the appearance of the suffix *-tṛc* could not possibly occur in any way.

Likewise, in the *Vibhāṣā* regarding the rule "in vowels beginning with the third case-ending" (*aci*), since the possibility exists for the extension (*atideśa*) of the *guṇa* substitution belonging to the base (*āṅga*) as in the form *kroṣṭari*, the rule for *yaṇ* substitution and the rule for the substitution of *ut* in *kroṣṭrā* and *kroṣṭuḥ*—which do not belong to the base—are not extended, nor is the accent (*svara*).

[Objection: But surely, even in that case, by the force of the mention of "the third case-ending and so forth" (*tṛtīyādi*), even the absence of the *aṅga* status would be extended; otherwise, one would simply say "optionally before the locative ending *ṅi*" (*vibhāṣā ṅau*). [Response: This is not so. The mention of "the third case-ending and so forth" would be for the purpose of extending the absence [of grammatical operations]; for in the case of rules employing the suffix *-vat*, the extension of absence is also observed, as in: "There is water in this village as in the desert" (*marubhūmivad asmin grāme jalam*). In the grammar as well, in the rule "before the third case-endings and so forth, that which has been mentioned as masculine" (*tṛtīyādiṣu bhāṣitapuṃskam*), the absence of the *num* augment and the short vowel is extended.

For when it is established that, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), only the *aṅga* (the stem) is to be extended (*atideśya*), then an extension of the operation (*bhāva*) is not possible across all instances beginning with the third case-ending. Consequently, the operation of whatever rule is observed in a form ending in *-tṛc* is extended to a form ending in *-tuN*; however, whatever is absent in the former would also have to be extended as an absence in the latter. Thus, because this extension of rules (*śāstrātideśa*) is full of flaws, one must resort to an extension of form (*rūpātideśa*) alone. Therefore, he says: "This is an extension of form."

If this were so, then the form of any *tṛc*-stem would be extended [to others], such as *paktā* and *vaktā*; to this he replies: "due to proximity" (*pratyāsatter*). Now, regarding this extension of form, the forms actually occurring in usage are as follows: *kroṣṭā*, *kroṣṭārau*; in the instrumental plural, *pañcakroṣṭṛbhiḥ rathaiḥ*; in the singular, *kroṣṭrā*, *kroṣṭuḥ*, *kroṣṭari*; likewise, in the dual and so on, it ends in *-ā*; in the feminine, it sometimes ends in *-r* and sometimes in *-ā*; and from the third case onwards, it ends in *-r*, while in the genitive singular (*ṅasi*) and locative singular (*ṅasi*), it ends in *-u*.

Is it that which is heard in the word *āvaranta* which is extended [by analogy], or rather is it that form which is taught in the grammatical system—namely, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc*, as heard in both the instructional rule (*upadeśavākya*) and the rule of extension (*atideśavākya*), such as *tṛjvat kroṣṭuḥ*—that is being extended? Regarding these two positions, in the first case, the accent prescribed by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* would not be established; for in forms such as *kroṣṭre*, the state of the vowel *ṛ* is never observed, such that this [suffix] could be an *udāttayaṇ*. Therefore, the second position must be adopted. Thus he says: "And that is the word *kroṣṭṛ* itself."

"But even in this view, since the word *tri* is not pronounced with an acute accent (*udātta*) in either the original injunction (*upadeśavākya*) or the extended application (*atideśavākya*), or because the accents of what is already pronounced do not differentiate [the form] and are thus irrelevant, there would be no transfer of accent. True; however, by the force of including the letter *ca*, its transfer will also occur. Thus he says: "even that which is oxytone (*antodātta*)."

Alternatively—let there be no extension (*atideśa*) of the accent; when the form ending in *tṛc* is extended, just as lengthening and other properties occur by their respective rules through the cognition of *tṛc*, the accent will likewise occur in this very manner. Furthermore, this extension is resorted to because of the use of the suffix *-vat*. If, instead of using the suffix *-vat*, one were to resort solely to the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*), nothing undesirable would result; however, it was not done in that way.
And [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a feminine [base]. 7.1.96.

The statement that "the word *kroṣṭu* becomes like *tṛj*" is merely an explanatory gloss (*arthakathana*). It would, however, be more appropriate to read it as ending in the genitive case (*kroṣṭoḥ*). Others, on the other hand, considering this to be a case of eliding the case-ending (*paryālopa*) within the compound, believe that even in the preceding rule, *kroṣṭaḥ* ends in the nominative. However, the substitution of *tṛj* was not applied [here] because it would have resulted in the destruction of the form being imitated (*anukriyamāṇa*). The suffix *-vat* also [occurs] only when the third case is the governing term (*samartha*). Since it "behaves similarly" (*tulyaṃ vartate*) to that which ends in *tṛj*, its similarity consists in sharing that form; thus, it is a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*).

And thus, in the previous *sūtra* as well, in the original text, one should not read "of that" (*tasya*). [Rather, it should be understood as: "whatever form belongs to that which ends in the suffix *tṛc*, that same form comes to belong to this. This is an explanation of the meaning. If the term "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) were to carry over here, then in a *bahuvrīhi* compound such as *kroṣṭrī-bhaktir asya* ("one whose devotion is feminine"), because the word *bhakti* is listed among the *priyādi* group, there would be an absence of the masculine-like treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*). Consequently, the form *kroṣṭrī-bhaktiḥ* would not be established, because the case-ending belonging to the object of the compound has been elided by *lup*.

Alternatively, the substitution of *tṛjvat* will occur precisely at the stage of the sentence (*vākya-avasthā*), for a rule that is external (*bahiraṅga*)—namely, elision (*luk*)—subverts even internal rules (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) cannot here be resorted to as the cause; what then is the cause? He says: "Some," and so forth. But how can the suffix *ṅīṣ* be the cause when it is recited among the *gaura*-class [of words]? It is not understood in this way: "in the sense of feminine. Rather, it is understood as "in the feminine gender."

How then [is it explained] regarding the word *striyām* (in the feminine)? It means: "in that case where the vowel *ī* is the indicator (*dyotaka*) of femininity. Having superimposed the femininity residing in the meaning onto the vowel *ī*, the technical terms *nadī* and the suffixes *ām* and *āṭ* are applied by the rule *striyām*. To state the undesirable consequence for those who hold such a view, he says: "For them... [The example is] *pañcakroṣṭṛbhiḥ*. This is a compound in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the rule *adhyardhapūrva-* [Pāṇini 5.1.28], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṭhak* used in the sense of price (*ārhīya*). Then, by the rule *luktaddhitaluki* [Pāṇini 1.2.49], there is also elision of the feminine suffix. In that context, the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.63] applies.

Because of this prohibition, the substitution of *tṛjvat* (the form of the agentive suffix *-tṛ*) conditioned by the long vowel *ī* is not established. Furthermore, since internal operations (*antaraṅga*) are superseded by elision (*luk*), the *tṛjvat* substitution cannot be obtained prior [to that elision]. In that regard, it has been stated that while the *tṛjvat* substitution is established by the preceding rule (*pūrveṇa*) in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* (nominal stem ending), it is unestablished in the case of the third case and so forth; likewise, even in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna*, it is unestablished in the vocative (*sambuddhi*), as in the example: "he pañcakroṣṭar."

Likewise, in the case of *śasi* (the accusative plural ending), there would be five *kroṣṭṝn*; and likewise, in the case of feminine stems beginning with vowels such as the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth, an option would also apply by the subsequent rule—resulting in *pañcakroṣṭrā* or *pañcakroṣṭre*. Now, even if this [present] rule were commenced, would not the option still prevail due to its being a subsequent rule? No; because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), this very rule is obligatory (*nitya*). In that regard, a counter-argument must be provided. In this matter, the explicit statement of the rule itself is the refuge.

As for those who do not read [the word *strī*] among *gaura* and the others, what is their reason? He says: "But as for... and so forth. The word *ca* ("and") is included in accordance with the literal wording of the sūtra. Now, even if no specific cause is resorted to by the word itself, the term *aṅgasya* ("of the base") is indeed resorted to; and when the base (*aṅga*) is resorted to, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is also necessarily resorted to. As it has been said: regarding the rule *aṅgasya*, for the sake of establishing [the forms] *vavraśca* and so on, it is true that technical definitions (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) apply at the time the operation is to be performed (*kāryakālam*). This has been stated.

For in that [the *yathoddeśa*] view, the rule defining the technical term *aṅga* applies to the rule *urat*; consequently, the suffix [in *uraḥ*] possesses the status of a cause (*nimitta*) both for the designation *aṅga* and for the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, because its proximity is not distinguished [from the other]. However, here the *yathoddeśa* view is adopted; therefore, in reality, the substitution of *tṛjvat* is prescribed for the word *kroṣṭu* when it functions as an *aṅga* in the feminine, and no subsequent cause (*paranimitta*) is relied upon. Furthermore, the designation *aṅga* will occur by means of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

Because of the mention of the word *aṅgasya*, that which is an operation characterized by an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) belonging to that which has received the designation *aṅga* is alone prohibited; however, the designation *aṅga* itself is not an operation of the *aṅga*. Thus, the word *kroṣṭrī* remains oxytone (*antodātta*). It is oxytone because it is listed among the *gaurādi* group, whereby it takes the affix *ṅīṣ*, and by the accent of that affix it becomes oxytone. Even in this view, the meaning of the word *eva* (only) is that the suffix *tha* [in *kroṣṭrī-tha*] is likewise oxytone according to the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*.

However, some say that even for the suffix *ṅīp*, the acute accent occurs by the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ" itself; otherwise, if *tṛjvadbhāva* were applied after *ṅīṣ*, the *citsvara* would be more established (*satiśiṣṭa*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of *ṅīṣ* being unaccented.
The third case-affix and those that follow it are optionally used in place of the seventh case-affix when followed by a vowel.

This is an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an option where [the rule] was not otherwise applicable). The word *striyām* ("in the feminine") does not carry over [from the previous rule]. We have already stated that in forms such as *pañcakroṣṭṛ*, the substitution of *tṛjvat* (treating the stem like one ending in *tṛc*) occurs invariably by the preceding rule due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal); therefore, even the *ubhayatra-vibhāṣā* (option for both cases) does not apply here. Regarding the phrase "by way of *pūrvavipratiṣedha*" (priority of application): the scope of the *tṛjvat*-substitution is, for example, *kroṣṭre*; the scope of *num* and *nuṭ* is, for example, *trapuṇe*, *jatune*, *agnīnām*, *vāyūnām*, and *priyakroṣṭunaḥ*. When both would apply simultaneously, the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (the former prevails) takes effect.

Now, for what purpose is the substitution of *tṛjvat* prescribed? For even by means of the suffix *tṛc* itself, forms such as *kroṣṭre* would be established; [the rule is stated] so that the usage of the form ending in *tun* might not occur in the vocative, in the case of a *sarvanāmasthāna* (nominal stem ending), or in the feminine, whereas it should occur only for the form ending in *tṛc*.

In that case, what is the purpose of the *Vibhāṣā* rule "in the case of vowels beginning with the third case-ending" (*vibhāṣā tṛtīyādiṣv aci*)? For [without it], forms such as *kroṣṭre* would be established only for the stem ending in *-tṛ*, while forms such as *kroṣṭunā* would apply only to the stem ending in *-tu*. Thus, just as both forms occur before vowel-initial endings, they would likewise occur before consonant-initial endings. However, in the case of the suffix *-śas* as well, only the form ending in *-tu* is desired there. Therefore, this rule is also for the sake of restriction: "both forms occur only from the third case-ending onwards," and even then, "only before vowel-initial endings."

But for one who thinks that the application of the suffixes *tumun* and *tṛc* has a fixed scope solely by virtue of their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), even these three sūtras could have been omitted.
In the word *catura*, the vowel *ā* is acute-accented when followed by the suffix *anaḍuha*.

Here, the term *sarvanāmasthāna* is emphasized (svarita), not the phrase "in the third case and so on. The explicit mention of "acute" (*udātta*) is for the purpose of setting aside the rule that suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*). In this context, the rule of inclusion of what ends with that (*tadanta-vidhi*) is intended, because of the statement in the section on *aṅga*: "and of that [stem] and its subsequent word. Regarding *prayacatvā*: although the word *catur* would normally be placed first in a *bahuvrīhi* compound according to the rule "there is an addition [to the list of words] for pronouns and numerals," the word *priya* is placed first instead, by the rule "optionally for *priya*."
When [the word] *aṃsa* is a member of a compound, [the final vowel of the preceding word takes its *udātta* accent]. (Pāṇini 6.2.105)

Since the word *catuḥ* alone lacks a vocative case ending, this is an example of it occurring in composition. However, the example of the form ending in *-anaḍuh-* is given both to avoid breaking the continuity of the grammatical procedure (*prakrama*) and to demonstrate that here the rule of "extension to what ends with [the stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) is intended to apply.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ṛt*.

Regarding *kirati*: the roots *kṝ* (to scatter) and *gṝ* (to swallow) belong to the *tudādi* class. Regarding *āstīrṇam* and *viśīrṇam*: the root *stṝñ* (to cover) and *śṝ* (to injure); the lengthening occurs by the rule *hali ca*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant of the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs by the rule *radābhyām*. Regarding *mātṝṇām*: one might argue that even though the lengthening has been applied, the rule will not apply here because [the form] is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical rule). To this he says: "even of that which is *lākṣaṇika*. He asks: "What is the purpose? and answers with *cikīrṣati*, etc. Thus, the intention is that the mention of the word *dhātu* (root) is for that very purpose. In some versions, however, this is read in the *vṛtti* itself as *upadhāyāśca* (7.1.101).

In the preceding rule, the substitution of *i* for the final *ṛ* of a verbal root was stated; this present rule is commenced so that the same substitution may also occur when the *ṛ* is in the penultimate position (*upadhā*). Objection: In the previous rule, we shall qualify the *ṛ* by means of the word "root" (dhātu)—that is, we will mean "the *ṛ* which belongs to a root wherever it occurs. If so, then the substitution would apply here as well: *ṛkārīyati*, meaning "he desires the sound *ṛ*. Response: Even so, the desired result is established by the rule *kṛt-i* alone. Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṛtaḥ* from the previous rule, the substitution will not occur for the final letter. However, the rule was not formulated in that way [for the sake of brevity]. The form *kīrttayati* is derived from the root *kṛt* (meaning "to mention" or "to proclaim"), belonging to the *cur*-class (the tenth class).
[The substitution of *ū* for *v* occurs] when the preceding [syllable] begins with an *u*-sound or a labial.

Regarding *pūttī*: from the root *pṝ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling. There is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final consonant in the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule *na dhyākhyāpṝmurcchimadām*. Regarding *mumūrṣati*: from the root *mṛṅ* in the sense of "giving up life. Regarding *susmūrṣati*: from the root *smṛ* in the sense of "thinking. Regarding the reading *susvūrṣati*, this is the form when there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *sanīvantardha* etc., [derived] from the root *svṝ* in the senses of "sound" and "affliction. However, the former reading alone is correct, because a separate example will be given later.

"Even when preceded by a dental-labial," and so forth. The intention is that only the quality of being labial (*auṣṭhyatva*) is intended to be expressed, not the exclusion of other [sounds]. Regarding "the labial here," and so forth: just as in the rule *halaḥ* (P. 6.4.2), the base (*aṅga*) is qualified by the consonant (*hal*), whereby there is *samprasāraṇa*, and by that [consonant] again the base is [qualified], so too here: it refers to a base whose final member is that which has a labial sound preceding it as a constituent part (*avayava*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *ittvottvābhyām*: the examples shown for *ittva* (shortening to *i*) and *uttva* (shortening to *u*) constitute their scope (*avakāśa*). The scope for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is, for instance, *cayanaṃ* and *cāyakaḥ*. When both [rules] would apply simultaneously, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). As for *āstaraṇam*, here the *guṇa* substitution is not absolute (*nitya*), because the defining conditions (*lakṣaṇa*) differ. For previously, a *guṇa* conditioned by the root ending in a short vowel (*iganta*) applies; whereas once *ittva* and *uttva* have been applied, a *guṇa* conditioned by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) applies.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of the genitive ending] is frequent.

Regarding *taturi* and *jaguri*: from the roots *tṝ* and *gṝ*, the suffix *kin* is applied by the rule *ādṛgamahanajanaḥ*. There is the substitution of *u* (the *utva*), and because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *tasya dvirvacane'ci*, there is reduplication of the sequence *tṝ-gṝ*. Regarding *papritamam*: from the root *pṝ*, *kin* is applied as before; due to the absence of the substitutions of *it* and *ut*, there is the *yaṇ* replacement, and because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, there is reduplication. The suffix *tamap* is used in the sense of superlative degree (*atiśāyane*).
Thus ends the first quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the second quarter of the seventh chapter:
"Vṛddhi [substitution] occurs in place of the vowel of the root before the *sic* affix when followed by Parasmaipada endings. (Pāṇini 7.2.1)

In this context, both [the terms] *sici* and *parasmaipadeṣu* are locatives in the sense of "after" (*parasaptamī*). Therein, the "subsequent-ness" (*paratva*) of *sic* is with respect to the *aṅga*, while that of the *parasmaipada*s is with respect to *sic*. Because of the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, the term *ik* is understood [as the subject]; since it qualifies the *aṅga*, there occurs an extension of the designation (*tadantavidhi*) to that which ends in an *ik*. Thus he says: "of an *aṅga* ending in an *ik*. In the examples, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, and its elision occurs by the rule *seṭaḥ sica iṭ īṭi*.

Now, one might object: since the *guṇa* substitution depends only on the *siC* affix which is internal (*antarbhūta*), it is *antaraṅga*; whereas the *vṛddhi* substitution depends on the external *parasmaipada* and the *siC*, it is *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, if *guṇa* were applied first, the rule "of a stem ending in an *iK*" would no longer apply. To this, he says: "even though it is *antaraṅga*."

"In that case, just as it would subvert the *guṇa* substitute, it would likewise subvert the *uvaṅ* substitute as well. To this he replies: "In the cases of *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*. The roots *ṇū* (in the sense of praising) and *dhūñ* (in the sense of shaking) belong to the *kuṭādi* class. For where *vṛddhi* applies, there it might subvert what is *antaraṅga*; but here, since [the *vṛddhi*] does not apply due to the prohibition, it is unable to subvert [the *uvaṅ*].

But surely, just as the *guṇa* substitution is sublated, so too should this prohibition be sublated; for a rule that is commenced when another has not yet taken effect becomes a sublater of that other. Now, the *vṛddhi* substitution is commenced when the *guṇa* has not yet taken effect, whereas the prohibition is commenced both when it has taken effect and when it has not.

Now, why is it not postulated as follows: since the internal factor (*antaraṅga*) takes precedence, once the *guṇa* substitution has occurred, by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), the *vṛddhi* substitution also occurs even for roots ending in *ṇi*, just as in *acaṣīt* and so on for the root *ci*, and in *ahauṣīt* and so on for the root *hu*. In that case, the meaning would be this: in the rule *hmyantakṣaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.5), the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* need not be made; for how [could there be a problem], since in forms such as *aunayīt* and *aśvayīt*, once the *guṇa* and *āyādeśa* substitutions have been applied due to their being internal factors, the prohibition "of those ending in *y*" under the rule *hmyantaḥ* is already established? It cannot be done in this way.

To assume [this], for if it were assumed in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of vowel-vṛddhi even for a consonant in cases such as *abhaitsīt*. [Objection: The rule *vadavrajahalantasyācaḥ* will block the vowel-vṛddhi of a consonant. [Response: No, because that [rule] is formulated when that [consonantal vṛddhi] has not yet applied.

In that case, where that [vṛddhi] is prohibited—as in *anandīt*, *adevīt*, and so forth—there the vṛddhi of the consonant before the suffix *sic* would apply. This is not a fault; for by the rule *neṭi*, whatever vṛddhi applies to a stem ending in a consonant—whether by the rule *vadavrajaḥ* or by the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ*—all of it is prohibited.

In this case, then, regarding the form *āgavīt*—where the word *go-* has the *kvip* suffix denoting habitual action (*ācārakvibanta*)—the rule for *vṛddhi* would apply before the *sic* suffix. However, because it is *antaraṅga*, the substitution of *av* occurs first; once that is done, the prohibition "there is no [vṛddhi] when *iṭ* follows" (*neṭi*) blocks the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise be conditioned by the final consonant (*halantalakṣaṇā*). Consequently, the optional rule "of a light penultimate vowel following a consonant" (*ato halāder laghoḥ*) applies, even though the *vṛddhi* here is characterized by the vowel *i*.

In this case, then, regarding *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *kṅiti ca* would not apply, because it is not characterized by *it*. Let there be no such prohibition; rather, the substitution of *uvaṅ* will take place due to its being an *antaraṅga* operation. And here, in the case of *akārṣīt*, once *guṇa* and the replacement by *ra* have been applied, the *vṛddhi* conditioned by a final consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) occurs—even where that [vṛddhi] is prohibited, as in *atārīt* and *astārīt*, there too the *vṛddhi* is established by the rule *ato lrāntasya*.

In that case, regarding *alāvīt* and *ayāvīt*, since the substitutions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would apply first due to their being internal (*antaraṅga*), the prohibition by the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4) would apply because the root ends in a consonant (*halanta*). Consequently, the option provided by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) would arise. Therefore, the letter *v* is also included within the term *ato lrāntasya*. Why is the *v* not heard? Because the *v* has been indicated as elided (*luptanirdiṣṭa*). If so, then [the option] would also apply here in the cases *mā bhavānavīt* and *amavīt*. It has already been stated that in this view, the mention of the roots *ṇi* and *śvi* need not be made; I shall simply insert *avi* and *mavi* in place of those two.

As for the simplicity shown in this alternative view—that the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* need not be made—that very point is lost if this [other] view is accepted. Furthermore, in the case of *agavīt*, the optional rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* would be set aside, and by the inclusion of the letter *v* (in the rule), obligatory *vṛddhi* would result. Likewise, in forms such as *acecāyīt* from the roots *ci* etc. in their *yaṅ*-luṅ (*yaṅluk*) form, after *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* have been applied, the prohibition *na yvābhyām* would apply because the root ends in *y*. Similarly, in the case of *ciriṇoti* and *ciriṇoti*...

[The forms] *acirāyiṣṭa* and *ajirāyiṣṭa* [are derived thus]. Therefore, it is correct that this *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) overrides even the *guṇa* (vowel shortening) which is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), on account of the explicit statement (*vacana*). It is not, however, the case that one first admits the operation of the *antaraṅga* rule and then, by virtue of the statement, allows the *aniṭ* (absence of *iṭ*) augment to occur. What, then, is the reason for adopting this very interpretation? Because of the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi*; otherwise, as was stated immediately prior, the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* would not be necessary.
Therefore, [the rule] "of that which ends in lṛ" [applies]. (Pāṇini 7.2.2)

This word *anta* has two meanings: it denotes a "part," as in *vastrāntaḥ* (the edge of a garment) or *vasanāntaḥ* (the hem of a cloth); and it denotes "proximity," as in *udakāntaṃ gataḥ* (gone to the water's edge).
