Regarding the first alternative, in the term *lṛntasya*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the "limb" (*aṅga*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*), because no other meaning is possible. In that context, whenever there is a mention of a phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), it is always a *bahuvrīhi* where the "limb" is the external referent, since no other meaning is possible.

In that regard, since the rule of "specification by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) would already suffice for the inclusion of all vowels (*varṇagrahaṇa*), the explicit mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is redundant. Therefore, the word *anta* here signifies "proximity. Even so, if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*)—meaning "vṛddhi occurs for the vowel *a* that is proximate to the *repha* (r) or *lakāra* (l)"—then [the rule] would apply only to cases such as *laṣiraṇi*.

If the word *anta* signifies "proximity to another," then while it would succeed in the desired case, it would also apply to an undesired case; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] even in a case such as *akhallīt*. Therefore, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, and the qualifier is placed last by virtue of an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). By the term *lrānta*, the *repha* and *lakāra* which have become proximate [to the vowel] are meant.

These two [the letter *r* and the letter *l*] are intended to be expressed. When the expectation arises as to "in proximity to what?", there is a connection with the word "ataḥ" (from this). Thus, because the base (*aṅga*) is qualified by the *r* and *l* thus specified, the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Therefore, the meaning is: "of that base which ends in an *r* or *l* occurring in proximity to 'this' (*ataḥ*)."

If this is so, then because the word *ataḥ* (from this) is identical [to the initial *a*], and because that [word] is exhausted merely as a qualifier for the *repha* and *la-kāra*, the vowel (*ai*) would not be indicated as undergoing the *vṛddhi* [substitution]. However, there is no such fault; since the vowel *a* is explicitly heard as the qualifier, the *vṛddhi* occurs only for that. This is what was stated: "As far as the *repha* and *la-kāra* are proximate," and so forth.

We, however, say: the operation of the syllables is simply this—that *vṛddhi* occurs in place of the *at* (the short *a*) of a stem (*aṅga*) that has *r* and *l* in proximity. In that regard, when there is an expectation as to what [elements] are in proximity, it is understood from the context (*sannidhāna*) that they are in proximity to the *at*. Another says: *ra* and *la* form *lr*; the vowel *a* is adventitious (*āgantuka*); the mention is by means of the elision of the genitive case; here, because the stem is qualified by *lr*, the rule of "specification by the final" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, and thus *vṛddhi* occurs in place of that *akāra* which belongs to a stem ending in *lr*.

Of what kind [of root] is it that has become proximate? Because of proximity, it refers to that which has become proximate to *lṛ*. Furthermore, the word "other" (*anya*) denotes mere proximity and does not denote extreme proximity.
Regarding the examples: *kṣara* (to move), *tsara* (to go stealthily), *jvala* (to blaze), *hvala* (to move).

[The forms] *nyakhorīt* and *nyamīlīt* [are derived from] *khura* (to cut) and *mīla* (to close the eyes). [In the phrase] *mā bhavān* etc., the use of *māṅ* is for the purpose of preventing the addition of the augment *aṭ* [in the case of] *aṭa* (to wander) and *aśa* (to eat).

[The examples] are *avamrīt* and *akhallīt*. The root *vabhri* means "to go," and *khalli* means "to go quickly. Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of the "end" (*anta*)? One might ask: why not simply say "after *l* and *r*" (*lrāt*), since [the rule] would apply here as well—namely, *avamrīt* and *akhallīt*? We shall qualify the vowel *a* itself by its position immediately following the suffix *sic*: "there is *vṛddhi* for that *a* which belongs to a stem ending in *l* or *r*, when *sic* follows immediately."

Furthermore, since it is impossible for an *akāra* belonging to a stem ending in *repha* (*r*) or *lakāra* (*l*) to be immediately followed by *sic*, it follows by implication that "where there is no intervention, [the rule applies]; where there is intervention, it applies nonetheless due to the authority of the statement. Thus, an intervention by only a single phoneme will be accepted. Alternatively, this sūtra should be placed immediately after *ato halāderlaghoḥ*; in that case, the word *ataḥ* need not even be mentioned there, because the term *laghoḥ* would carry over from that context, and consequently, the rule would not apply to forms such as *akhallīt*.

Even so, when the suffix *kvip* follows the word *catuḥ*, and the *luṅ* tense with the *sic* affix is applied, the [vṛddhi] would apply to the letter *ca* as well. To that we shall reply: there too, we will qualify [the condition] by immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with respect to the *sic*. Just as in the case of *acakāsīt*, where the vṛddhi of the vowel *a* of the syllable beginning with *ha* (i.e., *kā*) after a light vowel does not occur by the rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ*, for what reason? Because the condition of immediate succession with the *sic* is qualified. In the same way, it will not occur in the word *catuḥ* either. And having done this, even the mention of "light" (*laghoḥ*) need not be stated; however, it was not done in that manner.
In the case of a vowel following *v*, *d*, a conjunct consonant (*vr̥j*), or a *hal* (consonant), [the substitution of the single substitute for both is applied].

"Regarding the phrase *vikalpabādhanārtham* (for the purpose of setting aside the optionality): therefore, the optionality [of the rule] *ato halāder laghoḥ* will be stated later. It was not said that "the prohibition by *neṭi* having been reached," because in reality, only the optionality itself is what is reached. Regarding *atretyādi*: *vadavrajoḥ* is one rule (*yoga*), and *acaḥ* is the second; there, the stem (*aṅga*) is qualified by the vowel (*ac*)—meaning "of that vowel which stands wherever it may be within the stem. By this, the meaning is that the *vṛddhi* substitution is established for a stem ending in a consonant (*halanta*)."

What, then, is the reason that [the rule] is qualified by the member *aṅga* rather than [qualified by] "of the member" (*aṅgasya*)? Because [such a qualification] is impossible. In forms such as *acikīrṣīt*, first of all, the prohibition "there is no *iṭ* after a [stem] ending in *at*" (*neṭi*) applies to what ends in *at*. However, a stem ending in long *ā* cannot occur with the suffix *sic*, because the rule "after the roots *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, and those ending in *ā*, there is *sag*" (*yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca*) prescribes the addition of *sak*. Even if such a case were possible, there would be no difference whether the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs or not. As for a stem ending in an *iṅ* vowel, the *vṛddhi* is already established by the rule "there is *vṛddhi* in place of an *iṅ* vowel before *sic*" (*igantasya tu sici vṛddhiḥ*). Furthermore, a stem ending in *ej* (long *e* or *o*) is also impossible, because [in such cases] the substitution of *ā* is prescribed.

In the case of *agavīt*, however, there is the prohibition by the rule *neṭi*. Thus, it is a statement made with insight that the vowel (*aj*) is qualified by the suffix (*aṅga*). When the mention of *hal* has been thus refuted, he states the purpose [for its inclusion]: "tadetad... [and so on]. But what is the reason that, without the mention of *hal*, the inclusion of the *hal*-group as a whole is not established? Therefore, he says: "anyathā hi... [and so on]. And this should be understood to apply when the *aj* which undergoes *vṛddhi* is itself qualified by its status as being followed by *sic*.

When the *aṅga* (the stem) is qualified [by the condition of having more than one vowel], the rule is established in all cases. However, in the case of forms such as *acakāsīt*, which have more than one vowel (*anekāc*), there would not be the undesired application of *vṛddhi* even to the preceding vowel, because of the prohibition by the rule *neṭi*. Furthermore, there is no root *niṭ* that has more than one vowel. Nor is there the possibility of *vṛddhi* applying to the augment *aṭ* in forms such as *apākṣīt*; for what reason? Because in the *luṅ* tense, the *aṅga* is that which ends in *sic*, and the augment *aṭ* is included within that very *aṅga* by virtue of being part of it; it is not included by virtue of being part of the *aṅga* that exists when *sic* is present. Even in cases where the elision (*luk*) of *sic* occurs—as in *adāt* and *adhāt*—there is no possibility of *vṛddhi* because *sic* does not follow [the vowel].

Regarding the form *udavoḍhām*: from the root *vah* in the *luṅ* tense, with *tām* as the suffix and *sic*, we have the intermediate stage *vaha-stām*. At this point, both the rule for *vṛddhi* (Pāṇini 7.2.1) and the rules for *ḍhatva* and so forth apply. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is included the elision of *sic* by *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26), the substitution of *dha* for *tha* by *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ* (8.2.40), the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭa*, and the elision of *ḍh*. Since the rules for *ḍhatva* and the others are considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of the preceding operation, *vṛddhi* is applied first; subsequently, the elision of *ḍh* takes place due to the presence of the *ot* augment.

Now, as to why there is no further *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) for that [element], he says: "In that case, it is already formed" (*kṛta*). The meaning is: although the *vṛddhi* has not been applied to the single vowel *e*, nevertheless, in this specific usage, it is considered "already formed. As for the phrase "but where": the absence of *vṛddhi* is not based on the fact of being a single vowel (*okāratva*), but rather is based on the fact of being already formed (*kṛtatva*). One who has withstood or overcome enemies is called *soḍhāmitra*.
Not so, [it is] not thus. 7.2.4.

In the examples—the roots *div* (in the sense of playing, etc.), *siv* (in the sense of weaving), *kuṣ* (in the sense of pulling out), and *muṣ* (in the sense of stealing)—the following objection is raised: "But surely... and so forth. The rebuttal begins with: "This is not so," and so forth. Both of these points have been explained under the rule regarding the *vṛddhi* substitution for *sic*.
The substitution of *h* for *ha* occurs before the suffixes *am*, *anta*, *kṣaṇa*, *śvas*, *jāgṛ*, *niś*, *vi*, and *edhita*. || 7.2.5 ||

In the examples, the verbal roots are: *graha* (to seize), *syamu* and *svana* (in the sense of sound), *ṭuvama* (in the sense of vomiting), *vyaya* (in the sense of spending money), *kṣaṇu* (in the sense of injury), *śvasa* (in the sense of breathing), *jagṛ* (in the sense of the cessation of sleep), *ūna* (in the sense of diminution), *ila* (in the sense of instigation) belonging to the *cur*-class, *ṭuośvi* (in the senses of motion and growth), *rage*, *lage*, *sage* (in the sense of attachment), and *kakhe*, *khage*, *kage* (in the sense of laughing). Regarding the forms *ūnayati* and *elayati*, there is a prohibition of the *caṅ* affix [for the reduplication] in the case of *nonayati* and *dhvanayati*.

"And if the *guṇa* were to occur first," and so forth. This too has been explained in the very sūtra concerning *vṛddhi* after *sic*. Now, as for the question "What is the purpose of including *jāgṛ*?"—the one who asked this shows exactly how it need not be done by stating: "In place of *jāgṛ*, [vṛddhi occurs] before *vi*, *ciṇ*, and *liṭ*. [The phrase] "when the *guṇa* has already occurred," and so forth, does not rely on the principle that "there is no further application of a rule once a grammatical operation on a stem has taken effect," because it is difficult to determine what constitutes a "completed" state (*niṣṭhitatva*). "But if," and so forth.

The sense is that otherwise, the prescription of *guṇa* with respect to the domain of *vṛddhi* would be purposeless. Regarding the phrase "and likewise": by means of the prohibition concerning *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, it is indicated in a general sense that not merely the *vṛddhi* occurring at a subsequent time takes place; the sense is that it is not indicated in a specific sense that the *vṛddhi* characterized by the *upadhā* does not take place.

When the root *jāgṛ* is included, this is the sequence of application of the rules: once *jāgṛ-is-īt* is established, the *yaṇ* substitution is first applicable; however, because it is an exception (*apavāda*), the *guṇa* rule (*sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ*) subverts it. That *guṇa* is further subverted by the *vṛddhi* rule for *sic*. That *vṛddhi* is also subverted by the *guṇa* of *jāgarti*. When that has been applied, the *vṛddhi* prescribed for roots ending in a consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) applies. That is prohibited by the rule *neṭi*. Then, the optional rule *ato halāderlaghoḥ* applies. After that, the obligatory *vṛddhi* of the rule *ato lrāntasya* applies. Finally, this [present] prohibition (*thaiti*) applies. And so it is said:
Guṇa, vṛddhi, guṇa, vṛddhi, prohibition, option,
again vṛddhi, prohibition— thus there are nine applications resulting from the rule *yaṇaḥ pūrvaḥ*.
Therefore, [the rule] "of a light [vowel] following *h* and so forth" (Pāṇini 7.2.7).

*nyukuṭīt*, *nyapuṭīd iti*. [The roots] *kuṭa* (to bend) and *puṭa* (to join) [are used here]. Now, one might object: "Since these belong to the *kuṭādi* group, they possess the *ṅit* designation; and because of the prohibition [of *guṇa*] before a *khit* suffix, *vṛddhi* will not occur anyway. What is the purpose of the mention of 'from *at*' (*ataḥ*) here? To this he replies: "If this [condition] 'from *at*' (*ataḥ*) were absent... [Examples: *atakṣīt*, *arakṣīd iti*. [The roots] *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin," and *rakṣa* means "to protect. Since the *aṅga* (stem) is qualified by its being followed by *sic*, there is an occasion for [the application of the rule] here.

Now, why does this not occur here? If the *aṅga* (the stem) is qualified by its having *sic* following it, then the objection is that the rule would still apply here as well. The answer is based on the assumption that the *ak* (the vowel *a*) is qualified by its having *sic* following it, according to the authority of the statement "that by which there is no intervention" (*yena nāvyavadhānam*). In forms such as *apipaṭhiṣīt*, the *a* of the immediately preceding element ought to be elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ*.

But surely, since both [the suffixes] are equally subsequent, *vṛddhi* should take effect? Let *vṛddhi* occur; however, by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, the elision of the vowel *ā* will occur. It will not occur, for because they are subsequent, *sārvadhātuka* and *iṭ* would indeed prevail. In that case, by the rule *ṇyallopāviyaṅuvaṅyaṇguṇavṛddhidīrghabhyaḥ pūrvavipratiṣiddhau*, the elision (*lopa*) will take place, as in the example *cikīrṣakaḥ*.

In that case, the rule *aco ñṇiti* (P. 7.2.115) [prescribing] *vṛddhi* has its scope elsewhere; however, this [rule prescribing *vṛddhi*] being enjoined for a different *āt* in the *sic* suffix would be without scope (*niravakāśā*). Therefore, by the force of the fact that the word "of a consonant-ending" (*hal-antasya*) is understood [from a previous rule], an immediately preceding *a*-vowel is not possible; this is the implication. As for the phrase "but if" (*atha tu*): since it remains established that there must be an intervention, if one assumes that the intervention is by a consonant (*hal*), then the mention of "light" (*laghu*) must be made; however, if one assumes that the intervention is by a single phoneme (*varṇa*), then it need not be made—this is the meaning.
In the case of *neḍ*, there is no substitution for the following *kṛt* suffix. || 7.1.8 ||

The mention of *vaśi* in the locative case (*vaśi kṛti*) is for the purpose of the rule *tadādividhi* (the application of a grammatical operation to that which begins with the specified element). We shall explain the purpose of placing it before [the suffix] in the rule concerning the *krī*-class. The citation of *īśitṛ* and so forth is intended to demonstrate that the prohibition based on the verbal root (*prakṛtyāśraya-pratiṣedha*) would not otherwise be established. In *īśvara*, the suffix *varac* is applied by the rule *stheśabhāsa-*. In *dīpra*, the suffix *ra* is applied by the rule *namikampi-*. In *bhasman*, the suffix *manin* is applied by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*. Alternatively, it is also established by resorting to the view of non-etymological derivation (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*) within the *uṇādi* group. In *yācñā*, the suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule *yajayāca-*.

"Showing the possible examples" means that this is for the purpose of demonstrating how many such examples are possible. [The forms] *rudiṃva* and *rudima*: if the mention of the *kṛt* suffix were not present [in the rule], then by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*, there would be a prohibition of *iṭ* here [in the imperfect]; however, its scope (*avakāśa*) is [the present tense], as in *roditī*. In some places, *rurudiva* and *rurudima* are cited for the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), but that is incorrect, because the *iṭ* is already established by the restriction of the *krādi* group.
And [the substitution of *e* for *i*] occurs before *ti*, *tu*, *tra*, *ta*, *tha*, *si*, *su*, *sa*, *ra*, *ka*, and *se*. (Pāṇini 7.2.9)

There is a general inclusion of both *ktin* and *kṛt*. In the case of *roditī*, there is no inclusion of the *tip* suffix, even though it is a singular ending, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *kṛti*.
Regarding "dīpti": the suffix *ktin* is applied by the rule *ktin nabādibhyaścaḥ*. The phrase "only that which is *auṇādika*" is understood through its association with numerous *auṇādika* forms.

"In *tatutreṣu*": the meaning is "in this sūtra. "Of *agrahādīnām*": the meaning is that there is a prohibition regarding the *titutrá*-suffixes and others associated with verbal roots other than *grah*. He says that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) indicates a type; thus he says, "types of *grah*. But what is the type? He says: "those for which... *Nikucitī*: from the root *kuñc*, the suffix *ktin* is applied as before, with the elision of the penultimate vowel; or else, it is derived from *kuc* (meaning "to make a sound") with the suffix *ktin*.
A verbal root that has a single vowel in its original enunciation (upadeśa) and is anudātta (unaccented) [does not take iṭ in the formation of the ārdhadhātuka affixes].

*Anudāttāt* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: that in which no acute (*udātta*) accent exists is "anudātta. If it were taken in its technical sense as a single *anudātta* vowel, only vowels such as *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* (the *iṇ* group) would be understood, and not words like *pac* which consist of a collection of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*). Consequently, their being taught with an *anudātta* accent would be purposeless. Alternatively, because the entire word possesses an *anudātta* marker (*c*), the whole collection itself is called "anudātta," just as in the rule "an *anudātta* word [is treated as having a single accent]. *Upadeśa* refers to the recitation of the verbal roots (*prakṛti-pāṭha*). And thus: "anudātta-... [and so forth].

The word "in the case of an instruction" (*upadeśe*) is required [as a governing condition]. This is intended as a qualifier for both [the root and the suffix]. However, if it were understood as a qualifier for only one of them—namely, "if the root is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) and currently unaccented (*sampraty-anudātta*) in the instruction"—then the same rule would undesirably apply here as well in cases such as *laviṣyati* and *paviṣyati*, because this [root] is currently unaccented due to the *śeṣanighāta* (the non-accentuation of the remainder) when the suffix is accented. Furthermore, in cases such as *karttā* and *karttum*, the rule would not apply, because in the *prakṛti-pāṭha* (the list of verbal roots), it is currently accented due to the *nit-svara* (the accent on the *nit* augment).

Otherwise, the teaching that these [roots] are *anudātta* in their original enunciation (*upadeśa*) would be purposeless. Furthermore, if it were understood as "from a root that is *anudātta* in its original enunciation and consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*) when actually heard," then the restriction in the rule for the *krādi*-group would not be tenable; in cases such as *cakṛva* and *cakṛma*, because the form as it is heard consists of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), the rule would apply as a general injunction (*vidhi*). What would be the fault in that? [The fault is that] in forms such as *bibhidiva* and *bibhidima*, the augment *iṭ* would not occur.

But surely, since there are now multiple vowels (*anekāctva*), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] does not apply here, and thus *iṭ* will indeed occur. In that case, however, in forms such as *peciva* and *pecima*, once the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) have taken place, the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply because the root is now perceived as having a single vowel (*ekāc*). [Objection: Since *iṭ* is subsequent, it will occur first, and only then will the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication take place. [Response: No; the substitution of *et* and the elision of the reduplication are permanent (*nitya*), for they apply whether *iṭ* has occurred or not. On the other hand, *iṭ* is non-permanent (*anitya*), because once those two operations have occurred, the root is perceived as having a single vowel, and thus the prohibition applies.

If that is so, then in the rule *thal-i ca seṭ-i*, the mention of *seṭ* will be for the purpose of restricting the time [of application]; why then should the mention of *thal* not be made there? It is established by the mere mention of *seṭ*; therefore, everything beginning with *ekahalmadhye* continues to apply, while the single mention of *kit* is removed, and no other *seṭ* suffix besides *thal* can possibly be *kit*.

Since this [rule] is already established, the purpose of including the mention of *thal* here is for the sake of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the *kit*: that is, so that "when there is a *seṭ* suffix, both *thali* and when there is a *kit*, the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) occur. In that regard, since [the rule] regarding the *kit* is already established by the preceding rule, this statement is made for the purpose of determining the time [of application], so that the substitution of *e* and the elision of the reduplication may occur when [the suffix] is applied, and not when it is not applied—just as in the case of the rule "when there is a *seṭ* suffix in the *niṣṭhā*."

Even so, in the case of *vidhitsati* and *cicchitsati*, once reduplication has occurred because of the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.1], the prohibition [of reduplication] based on the condition "from a monosyllabic root (*ekācaḥ*) that is actually heard" would not apply. Therefore, the mention of "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) qualifies both [the root and the monosyllabic condition]; for this very reason, it is placed in the middle [of the sūtra]. If it qualifies both, then [the prohibition] would also apply here in *bebhiditā* and *cecchiditā*; however, it will not apply there because of the status of being "as if in its original state" (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the elision of the *al* (the *i* of the suffix) even when a rule precedes it.

In that case, the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) forms would also be included—such as *bebhiditā* and *cecchiditā*. [Objection: Where there is the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj-grahaṇa*), these five [roots] will not apply because of the statement, "not in the *yaṅ*-luṅ. [Question: Which ones, then? [Answer: The question arises because of the possibility of confusion in the recitation (*pāṭha*). The answer is that they should be recited without confusion. "Distinctly" (*pravibhaktāḥ*) means according to the distinction between vowels, consonants ending in a vowel, and consonants beginning with *k*, etc. In the verses, the mention of "non-*iṭ*" (*aniṭ*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those roots that are unaccented (*anudātta*).

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and locative (*saptamī*) cases here should be understood as used for the purpose of specifying the domain of the verbal roots (*dhātu-viṣaya-nirdhāraṇe*). In the expression *śvi-ḍī-ḍ*, it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) ending in the accusative case.

The phrase "situated in the list" (*gaṇastham*) is for the sake of completing the verse; it is merely a statement of the inherent nature [of the term]. "Learn from me" (*mat mattaḥ nibodhata*) means "understand. This is an explanation of the two verses beginning with *dvy*. The phrase "ending in vowels" (*iti svarāntāḥ*)—its repetition should be seen as intended to show that it is self-evident (*nigada-vyākhyānatām*). Others, however, do not recite this earlier.

Regarding "yamiryamanteṣu": it is recited in the *śyan* [section]; the meaning is that it is recited in the *divādi* [class]. Regarding "of those expressing a prohibition": this means according to the opinion of the teachers who establish the prohibition of *iṭ*. Regarding "dihir duhiḥ": those subjects regarding which there is no doubt for people are "free from doubt. "Another system" (*tantrāntaram*) means another grammar (*vyākaraṇāntaram*), such as that of Āpiśali and others. Regarding "the option for *sah*" (to endure): this is by the rule *tīṣasaha*, etc. "Possessing an option" (*savikalpau*).
"Conceptualization has that as its object" means that doubt is its domain. "They are doubtful in their very nature" means that even the doubt as to whether those two exist or not is present therein.

Regarding "the gaze upon the direction": those who study the ancient grammar are called *puraṇagāḥ*. [The rule applies] to the recitations, such as the list of roots (*dhātu*) and so forth. By the rule beginning with "of those having *ṛ* in the penult," etc., he adds another purpose for those [roots] taught as unaccented (*anudātta*).
Thus, it is certain that in the verses, the term "non-iṭ" (*aniṭ*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of being unaccented.

"Rudhiḥ sarādhiriti" (the root *rudh* and *sādh*); "nyāyyavikaraṇayoriti" (of the two [roots] having the regular *śap* conjugational sign). "Nyāyyaḥ" means the general rule (*utsarga*), that is to say, those having the *śap* conjugational sign. However, in some places there is the reading exactly as it stands; some read the root *sidh* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class as being marked with an *udit* vowel—namely, "ṣidhu gatyām" (to go)—and therefore, because the *it* augment is optional for its *ktvā* suffix, there ought to be a prohibition of the *niṣṭhā* suffix by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā."

Likewise, there is no difference in meaning or form between *budh* belonging to the *divādi* class and that belonging to the *bhūvādi* class; therefore, this *budh* is indeed one and the same. Its inclusion in two classes is for the sake of the two different *vikaraṇas*. Furthermore, since both the addition of *iṭ*—characterized by the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes—and its prohibition have been stated for it, it possesses optional *iṭ* (*vibhāṣiteṭ*) because they share the same domain. Consequently, thinking that there ought to be a prohibition of *iṭ* even in the case of the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix, he says in response: "even in the *niṣṭhā*."

The fact that the roots *sād* and *rud* have an indicatory *iṭ* (i.e., are marked with *it*) is for no other purpose [than to indicate their specific properties]. Furthermore, the presence or absence of *iṭ* in the case of a root ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix is not a condition for the prohibition [of *guṇa*] in an arbitrary manner; rather, the meaning is that the presence of *iṭ* is optional (*vikalpita*), as indicated by the word *vibhāṣā*, which expresses optionality. Regarding the phrase *tapi tipimiti*: the reading is *tipikṣapī*. Understand that those [roots] read with a low tone—that is, with an *anudātta* accent—are to be known [as having optional *iṭ*]. The reading *prastāvātapratīteti* is preferred, whereas in the reading *pratīhīti*, it follows the subsequent [text]: "Know those [roots] that lack *iṭ* and are *anudātta*."

*tepteti*: *tipṛ*, *tepṛ*, *ṣṭipṛ*, *ṣṭepṛ* [mean] "to flow. *chopteti*: *chup* [means] "to touch. *paci-vacimiti*: *sṛj* and *mṛj* [form] a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). Those whose cause for being *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) is their accent are called *aniṭ-svarāḥ*.

Therefore, it must be understood that this [root] is accompanied by the augment *vikalpa* (an optional suffix). Consequently, the reading as *anudātta* (unaccented) does not serve the purpose of indicating the absence of the augment *iṭ*. Likewise, the augment *am* also [does not apply]. Therefore, the reading as *udātta* (accented) does not serve that purpose either. To the question, "Why then is it recited here among the *aniṭ-kārikās*? he says: "Some," and so forth. And this is logical, as he states: "For in the case of *nij* and others," etc. The roots beginning with *nij* are those recited in the rule *ṇijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ ślau*. In this very context, he shows the agreement of other grammatical systems, saying: "And likewise," and so forth.

"He killed," it is said. But why is this taught as unaccented (*anudātta*) in its instruction? He says: "In *om*. Where, then, is its instruction? [It is given] in the rule *hano vadha liṅi*. Why is it taught as unaccented so that I might not have to exclude the mention of "having a single vowel" (*ekāj*)? For there is no other purpose for its being unaccented. We do not say that it is unaccented in this very instruction; rather, the root *han* is unaccented, and when it occurs in place of that [root], it becomes unaccented by virtue of the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

If it is argued that even when the term *ekāj* (monophthongic) is included, since there is the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), why is this [the prohibition] not applied? Well then, in the case of the designation *anudātta* (unaccented) as well, since it depends on the original vowel (*sthānyal*), how could it possibly apply here? This is not so; there is no application here by way of the status of being a substitute, but rather by virtue of the mention of *upadeśa* (original instruction), as in cases such as *kartā* and *kartum*, where there is a difference in form and a difference in accent.

For what reason? Because that which was unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original instruction (*upadeśa*) has reached this very state; it is not so because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Likewise here, since the term "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) is employed, the same contingency applies: that which is the root *han* unaccented in its original instruction is precisely this [form]. Thus, there is an undesired application (*prasaṅga*).

Even if the mention of "single-vowel" (*ekāj*) is made, how can there be an exclusion of this [root *han*], since the mention of "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) is connected with both [the conditions]? For it would follow that "that which is single-voweled in the original enunciation is precisely this [root *han*]," and thus the undesired application (*prasaṅga*) would indeed occur. Therefore, the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) must be specifically prescribed for *vadhi*. By virtue of that [prescription], the prohibition—though based on the fact that the root *han* is unaccented in its original enunciation—does not apply. For this initial acute accent is not inherent in the actual usage (*prayoga*), as it is superseded by the accent of the suffix; such is the explanation to be stated here. The mention of "single-vowel" is for the sake of what follows.
A long vowel is substituted for the final *i* or *u* of a verbal root ending in *śri*, *yu*, or *ru* before an affix beginning with a *k*-letter or marked with *k*.

Since there is no prohibition for a word ending in *yoṣ* by its very nature, this [rule] is for that purpose: *śritaḥ*, *śritavān*, *yutaḥ*, *yutavān*. Because the suffix *iṭ* is optional by the rule *sanīvantardhaḥ*, the prohibition established by *yasya vibhāṣā* is already accomplished.

"Ke-cid-ityādi" and so forth. As it was stated in the rule *glājisthaśca ksnuḥ*: "Because *ksnu* has the marker *g*, there is no substitution of *ī* for [the vowel of] *stha*, etc. If the letter *ga* were included [in the root *stha*], then the grammatical reference (*nirdeśa*) *śrayukaḥ kiti* would not be tenable; for after the letter *ga*, by the rule *haśi ca*, the substitution of *ū* (utvam) would apply, and once *carv* (the change of *t* to *c*) had been performed, the rule *kupvoḥ ka pau ca* would apply. Since *carv* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), only the substitution of *ū* would result; therefore, he says: "Because it is a Vedic/Sutra usage (*sautratvāt*)."

In this work as well, the phrase "they describe" is connected [to the preceding]. He refutes this [view] with the words: "In the rule *glājisthaśca snuḥ*. If there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā*, the meaning becomes "from the root *sthā* ending in *ā*"; and since *sthā* indeed ends in *ā*, the qualification is understood for the purpose of excluding the *i* that occurs at a later stage. Consequently, the objection—"How can this *ā* be the prescribed element (*vidheya*) when it is heard in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) following the mention of the verbal root (*prakṛti*)?"—is thereby dispelled.

Regarding *sthāsnoḥ*: this refers to the word *sthāsnū*. "This is nothing" means that this description involving the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *ga* is untenable. For the elision of *ga* would be appropriate only if the suffix *gasnu* were marked with the marker *g* (indicating it is *seṭ*); however, even if it were marked with *k* (indicating it is *kit*), the substitution of *ī* for the root *sthā-* is precluded by the reason already stated.

[The author says: "So that [the rule] may apply here as well in the case of *tīrṇa*. But in this case, forms such as *tīrtvā* and *pūrtvā* are established by the sequential order [of rules]. However, when *tatvā* and *patvā* are present, as long as the prohibition of *iṭ* has not yet commenced, *itva* and *utva* would apply. What is the reason? It is because it is stated [in Pāṇini 1.2.5] "before an affix marked with K or Ṅ" (*kṅiti*). And the affix *ktvā* does not become marked with K until the prohibition of *iṭ* has been effected, because of the prohibition [stated in 1.2.18]: "The affix *ktvā* is not [marked with K] when it has *iṭ*" (*na ktvā seṭ*). Furthermore, O venerable one, *itva* and *utva* are prescribed before an affix marked with K; they are not prescribed for an affix marked with K, but rather they are understood to apply when [the root] is followed by an affix marked with K.

How do the substitutions *it* and *ut* occur by way of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) with the [application of] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*? Therefore, since the prohibition of *iṭ* has already taken effect by relying on the fact that *kit*-ness is present beforehand, the substitutions *it* and *ut* occur. [Objection: Once those two have been applied, the status of having a stem ending in *u*—which is the cause for the prohibition of *iṭ*—is lost; consequently, there would be a recurrence of *iṭ*. And if that were the case, because of the prohibition of *kit*-ness in the rule "ktvā is not *seṭ*" (*na ktvā seṭ*), *guṇa* would apply, resulting in the undesired forms *teritvā* and *poritvā*. [Reply: This is not so, because once something has been set aside by a prohibition at the stage of its potential application, it is impossible for it to recur when its opportunity has been lost.

And here, in the cases *titīrṣati* and *mumūrṣati*, since the prohibition of *iṭ* has not yet occurred, the *san* suffix would not be *kit* because it does not begin with a vowel (*ajhal-ādi*). And if it were not *kit*, this would be a domain for *guṇa*; thus, there would be no occasion for the substitution of *it* and *ut*. Therefore, [the desired forms] are established precisely through this sequence of operations.

Alternatively, when *tṝ* + *sa* is established, because there is no other occasion [for its application], the optional rule *iṭ sani vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.41)—which prescribes the optional *iṭ* augment conditioned by a root ending in *ṛ*—comes into operation. In that case, in the alternative where *iṭ* is absent, the *guṇa* substitution is prohibited due to the *kit* designation; even though *itva* and *utva* have been applied, since the occasion for the rule prescribing *iṭ* has already been lost (*bhraṣṭāvasara*), it cannot apply again. Thus, the desired form is established. Therefore, the utility of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśe*) is seen in the derivation of *tīrṇa*.

"Why, then, would this not apply here even though there is no governing rule (*adhikāra*) for *upadeśa*? To this he says: "Because *it* has already been applied. But what is the reason that *it* alone occurs? Because it is permanent (*nitya*). "Let it not be so," says the objector (*codaka*). "Of what [would it not be]? asks the other. "Of *ṛ*," etc., says the objector. "If that is so," etc., says the other. "Due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*," says the objector. "In a rule where *al* is not prescribed" (*an-ālvidhau*), etc., says the other. Furthermore, the fact that it is a rule concerning *al* follows from the inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* "uG."

[Objection: "But surely, once the substitutions of *it* and *ut* have been made, even though the vowel *ṛ* is no longer present, that same root remains because 'that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original]'. Therefore, since the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) was prescribed for that root, the prohibition of *iṭ* will apply. [Response: This is not so. By means of a formal split (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *āditaśca*, it will be signaled that "the prohibition applies to that very same condition under which the optionality was prescribed. Consequently, since the state of ending in the vowel *ṛ* is the condition for the optionality of *aṭ*, and that condition no longer exists once the substitution of *it* has been made, how could the prohibition apply? Therefore, [the author says] "tasmāt" and so forth.

Since, in this way, if the mention of *upadeśa* (the original form) were not present, the prohibition regarding the term *tīrṇaḥ* would not be established, therefore the word *upadeśe* must be understood as carrying over [from the previous rule]. And thus, "when that is the case" (*satīti*) means when the word *upadeśe* is being carried over. Here too, [the prohibition] would apply; for in the state of its original form (*upadeśāvasthā*), the root *jagṛ* ends in the vowel *u*. For that purpose—that is, for the sake of establishing forms such as *jagarita*—or rather, for the sake of removing the prohibition of *iṭ* in cases such as *jagarita*.

And so says the *Vārttika*: "The mention of 'ekāj' (single-vowel) is for the sake of *jagṛhuḥ*"; the meaning is that since it was of no use in the preceding rule, the mention of 'ekāj' is for this purpose.

But the author of the *Bhāṣya* says: "That root is resorted to in which an optional *iṭ* is observed somewhere—namely, one for which [the rule] 'vibhāṣā' applies—but not the cause of the optionality residing within it, such as the vowel 'a'. Since when the substitution of *it* and *ut* has been made, this too is that very same root, the prohibition is established in cases such as *tīrṇaḥ*."

If this were so, then by the rule *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām* (Pāṇini 7.2.68), because of the association with the root *viś*, there would result a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* for the root *vid* belonging to the fourth class (*divādi*) in the *niṣṭhā* suffix as well—just as it is optionally applied to the root *vid* of the sixth class (*tudādi*) in the *kvasu* suffix—resulting in forms such as *viditaḥ* and *viditavān*. This is not the case, however, because of the difference between the roots (*dhātubheda*). How is there a difference between the roots? Through a difference in meaning, a difference in indicatory letters (*anubandha*), and a difference in verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Therefore, the purpose [of the rule] is neither through the governing context of "instruction" (*upadeśa*), nor through the continued application of the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*).

For what purpose, then, is the mention of "a single vowel" (*ekāj*) in the previous sūtra? It is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix). But surely, even if the mention of "a single vowel" were made, the prohibition would still apply to the *yaṅ*-luṅ form, because the mention of "original instruction" (*upadeśa*) qualifies both [the root and the single vowel], as in the case of *bibhitsati*. To this, one might say: when the mention of "a single vowel" is made, it does not apply to the *yaṅ*-luṅ form because of the statement "wherever there is a mention of 'a single vowel'. But that is untenable, for even if the mention of "a single vowel" were not made, [the prohibition would still follow].

An alternative solution may be adopted by relying on another statement: let that very rule be read as "tropadeśāgrahaṇam" (the mention of "upadeśa" [is not required]). [Objection: In that case, the elision of the nasal (anunāsikalopa) characterized by being taught with an anudātta accent would also not occur for roots ending in *yaṅ* when followed by suffixes such as *tas* and so on; likewise, the optional application of *iṅ* (the augment *iṭ*) would apply even to roots like *div* ending in *ap*, when they are in the *yaṅ*-lopped state (*yaṅluk*). [Response: However, when the mention of "one-syllable" (*ekāj*) is made, it does not occur, because the term "that which consists of one syllable" (*ta ekācaḥ*) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that context.

If this is not accepted, I shall state it thus: "In the case of *yaṅluk*, [the suffix] *kit* following an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel is not [subject to the rule]. This is an *adhikāra* (governing heading); wherever the operation of *yaṅluk* is desired by means of the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj-grahaṇa*), this heading applies there. Even so, the root *vṛt* in the sense of "hindering" (*varaṇe*) is listed in the Divādi class as having multiple vowels (*anekāc*) and being unaccented (*anudātta*). Accordingly, there is the usage in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "Then, turning back (*vāvṛtyamānā*), she entered Rāma’s hut."

In that case, for a root ending in *vibhāṣā* (P. 7.2.15), which is desired to have an inserted *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] would apply. However, when the term "having one vowel" (*ekāj*) is included, this does not occur, because the word "having one vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) there as well. And thus, regarding P. 6.4.52 (*niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*), the author of the Vṛtti has also stated: "Furthermore, the word 'having one vowel' (*ekāc*) carries over there," and so forth.

Others, however, say that this [application] is not desired because the author of the Bhāṣya has rejected the inclusion of the term *ekāj*. And likewise, the author of the Vṛtti has also stated it as being merely optional: "If, on the other hand, the word *ekāj* follows there [from the previous rule]. Enough with this excessive elaboration.
And [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel] occurs before the suffixes *san*, *grah*, and *guha*. (Pāṇini 7.2.12)

The letter *u* is for the purpose of including [the root *ug*]. Nor can it be argued that because the suffix *san* is marked with the *kittva* (indicatory *k*) by the rule *iko jhal*, the forms derived from roots ending in *ug* are already established by the preceding rule; for what reason? Because the *kittva* of *san* applies when it begins with a *jhal* consonant, and *san* does not begin with a *jhal* unless there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Therefore, in cases where there is no prohibition of *iṭ* based on the root itself, once *iṭ* has been prohibited by this very [present] rule, the *kittva* of *san* follows from its beginning with a *jhal* or a vowel (*ac*). Thus is the sequence. [Example: *jidhṛkṣati*.

By the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* [Pāṇini 1.2.8], there is the *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*) of the suffix *san*; by the rule *grahijyāvayivyadhivaṣṭivicativṛścatipṛcchatibhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti ca* [Pāṇini 6.1.16], there is the *prasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) of that [root]; *ho ḍhaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.31] changes *h* to *ḍh*; *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si* [Pāṇini 8.2.41] changes *ḍh* to *k* before *s*; and *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* [Pāṇini 8.2.37] changes the *baś* (stop) to *bhaṣ* (aspirated stop). Thus we have *jughukṣati*. The root *guhū* (to conceal) is *svarita*-accented; by the rule *halantācca* [Pāṇini 1.2.10], there is the *kittva* of *san*. Now, why is *śri* not also drawn along by the word *ca* (and) from the rule *ugidacāṃ sarvanāmasthāne 'dhātoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.70], just as *div* is? To this he says: *śrisvṛyūrṇvityādi*.
In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, the roots *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *mṛ*, *vṛ*, *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *vu* take the substitute *saṃprasāraṇa*.

"Only *krādi* roots are *aniṭ* (lacking an *iṭ* augment) in the *liṭ* [perfect tense]. However, the reverse restriction—that "only in the *liṭ* are *krādi* roots *aniṭ*"—does not hold here, because of the force of the fact that *krādi* roots are taught with an *anudātta* (low-pitched) accent. This is also evident from such grammatical indications as: *kṛta-labdha-krīta-kuśalāḥ*, *tam adhīṣṭo bhṛto bhūtaḥ*, and *parivṛto rathaḥ stutastomayoḥ*.

But by what means is the prohibition of *iṭ* for these [roots] established, such that this present rule is commenced for the sake of restriction? To this he says: "Of those taught with an anudātta accent," and so forth. For roots other than *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, which are taught with an anudātta accent, the prohibition of *iṭ* is established by the rule "ekāca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), which depends on the root (*prakṛti*). But for *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, the prohibition depends on the suffix (*pratyaya*), according to the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11). Therefore, [the prohibition] applies to both: that which depends on the root and that which depends on the suffix.

But how is this restriction regarding the basis of the suffix established, given that the mention of *vṛñ* could serve as an injunction for *thali* after *vṛñ*, since in that case there is no prohibition based on the root—because *vṛñ* is udātta—and no prohibition based on the suffix either, because *thali* lacks *kittva*; and if the restriction based on the suffix did not exist, the *iṭ* augment would not occur in forms such as *luluvitha*? To this he says: "For *vṛñ*... (*vṛño hi*). *Vyavasthā* means restriction (*niyama*).

In cases such as *tuṣṭotha*, the augment *iṭ* would apply by virtue of the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.63), just as in *yayitha*, *papitha*, and so forth. For instance, in *yayitha* and *papitha*, the *iṭ* prescribed by *ārdhadhātukasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.35) is prohibited by *ekāca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.10); then, it is again applied by the restriction of the *krādi* group (*krādiniyamāt*), and subsequently prohibited by *acastāsvatthali* (Pāṇini 7.2.61). Thereafter, by the restrictive rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya thali pratiṣedho nānyebhyaḥ*, the *iṭ* occurs optionally. The same would apply here as well.

How indeed does the restriction of Bhāradvāja—which sets aside the prohibition *acaḥ tāsvat* while setting aside the restriction of Krādiniyama—not set aside the prohibition of the *krādi* group? This is the aforementioned fault regarding the roots *kṛ*, *bhṛ*, and *vṛ*; for since these end in ṛ, even according to the view of Bhāradvāja, the *iṭ* augment is prohibited.

In that case, the mention of the roots *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru* will be for the purpose of a rule (*vidhi*), because a restriction (*niyama*) occurs only when there is something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and here there is indeed something to be enjoined. What is it? It is the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* which would otherwise be applicable by the restriction of Bhāradvāja in the case of the suffix *thali*; however, the mention of the other roots, beginning with *kṛ*, will be for the purpose of a restriction. Thus, there is no fault even in forms such as *bibhidiva* and *luluviva*.

But how is it that we praise [the root *stu*]? For here, by the rule of Krādi, the augment *iṭ* would apply; this is not a fault. The mention of *studrusruśru* is for the purpose of prohibiting both [types of *iṭ*]. The meaning is: both that *iṭ* which is obtained by the rule of Krādi and that which is obtained by the rule of Bhāradvāja.

If this were so, one might object: "By the principle of *aprāptinyāya* (the rule of what was not previously obtained), the prohibition regarding *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru* would sublate only the restriction concerning *krī* and the others, but not the restriction of Bhāradvāja which is obtained optionally; therefore, that [restriction] would indeed still apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says: Because the prohibition comes later, the section on positive injunctions must be recited first—beginning with *ārdhadhātukasya* and ending with *īḍaḍajanordhve ca*—and only afterwards the section on prohibitions, as is also seen elsewhere, for example, in the case of the agent (*kartari*).

Regarding the rule *karmavyatihāre*, [it is stated] *na gatihiṃsārthebhyaḥ*. In that context, the meaning is this: it would not be necessary to mention the word *iṭ* twice, as the previously mentioned [rule] continues to apply.

[Objection: But in that case, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* in the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* would indeed be severed from the rule *liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya*. [Response: If that is so, then it should be read precisely in the rule *na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ*; for in this way, the prohibition is made immediately after the injunction, the mention of *dvis* (twice) need not be made, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is not severed from the rule regarding the elision of *s*, and furthermore, the double prohibition need not be made.

Since this [rule] is thus established, the purpose for which he places the section of prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) before it is this: lest the mere presence of *iṭ* (the augment *it*), without regard for the specific injunctions, be sublated by a prohibition taught as a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*). For if this section were placed after the restriction of Bhāradvāja, then—by the maxim of the intermediate exception (*madhye’pavādanyāya*)—the restriction of Bhāradvāja would sublate only the prohibition "acastāsvat" and not the prohibition regarding the *krādi* group; therefore, there is no fault in placing the prohibitions at the beginning.

Another says: Let the formulation of the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) occur wherever it may; however, the *Bhāradvāja-niyama*—namely, the two rules *acaḥ* and *tāsau nityam*—is a restrictor (*niyāmaka*) precisely of that prohibition which would otherwise apply to the suffix *thali* by the rule *krādiniyamāt*. This is based on the principle that "a rule or a prohibition applies only to what is immediately preceding. Consequently, in the case of the roots *stu*, *dru*, *sru*, and *śru* as well, it is only the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the *Bhāradvāja-niyama*—specifically by the rule *acaḥ* and *tāsau nityam*—that is set aside, and not the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the *krādiniyama*. We shall demonstrate later the purpose of formulating the prohibition earlier in that view.

It should be stated that [the rule] applies to *kṛ* when it is not preceded by *suṭ*. Even when *suṭ* is applied, the form *karoti* still occurs; thus, there arises the contingency of the prohibition [of *iṭ*].
[The sūtra] *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.14) [addresses this].

What is the purpose of including *śvi* [in the rule]? It might be argued that once *samprasāraṇa* has occurred and the subsequent vowel has been replaced by the preceding one, such that the root ends in *u*, the result would be established by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* alone. This is not established; for when the form *śvi-ta* stands, *iṭ* would apply because it is a subsequent rule. Even if *samprasāraṇa* occurs first, since the word *upadeśe* (in the original enunciation) is understood to carry over to the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*, and since the other [root *śvi*] does not end in *i* in its original enunciation, the desired form is still not established.

"Ḍīṅ," etc. This root *ḍīṅ* is recited among the *svādi* group, and these are *odit* (marked with the indicatory letter *o*), according to the rule "the *svādi* roots are *odit*. To the question, "How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? he says: "For that... [meaning] "from the *niṣṭhā*"—that is, from the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix. "An immediate [operation] is prescribed": if the augment *iṭ* were present, the state of being immediate would be obstructed. And this being the case, it would be possible not even to include *śvi* here; for by the very same reasoning already stated, the absence of *iṭ* is established for *olasjī* and the others as well.
That for which there is an option (vibhāṣā). Pāṇini 7.2.15.

The phrase *yasya vibhāṣā* is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Here, the ellipsis (*vākyaśeṣa*) is "for which *iṭ* has been prescribed. Because of the constant connection between *yat* and *tat*, this results in the prohibitive statement: "for that [root], *iṭ* does not occur in the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes]. [Objection: "But the augment *iṭ* occurs by virtue of being a nipāta. Another says: "This prohibition is non-permanent (*anitya*), because of the force of the *idit* designation in the root *kṛtī* (meaning 'cutting').

For if this rule were permanent, since *iṭ* would be optional by the rule *se'sici* (Pāṇini 7.2.57), the prohibition would already be established by this very [present] rule, and thus the *idit* designation would be purposeless."
And [the augment] is placed at the beginning. 7.2.16.

"Recovered" (*āśvasta*) and "vomited" (*vānta*). Although not explicitly stated in the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*, it is mentioned here because of its frequent usage. As for the question, "What is the purpose of making this separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*)?", the very act of separating the rules is indeed a fault. Furthermore, if there were a single rule (*ekayoga*), the particle *ca* would not need to be employed; such is the question. Consequently, the particle *ca* should not be recited in the subsequent text. However, since it is being recited, it must be explained as having the sense of an "inclusion of what was not mentioned" (*anuktasamuccaya*).

But how is the prohibition established elsewhere than in the cases of *bhāva* (intransitive action) and *ādikarman* (beginning of an action), given that there is only one rule? To this he says: "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*). Regarding the phrase "from *guṇa* and so forth": an *upādhi* (conditioning factor) is a differentiator, such as the meaning to be expressed and so on. If these conditioning factors were not differentiators, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would be purposeless. However, since they are differentiators, because an option (*vikalpa*) is prescribed for *bhāva* and *ādikarman*, there would otherwise be no prohibition regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*); therefore, the division of the rule must be made for that purpose.

What is the purpose of making this known? To this he says: "by that" (*tena*). Regarding the rule *lābhārthasya vibhāṣā* ("there is an option for roots meaning 'to obtain'"), the reason will be stated hereafter. If, then, an adjunct (*upādhi*) is a differentiator, then by the rule *udito vā* ("for a root marked with *u*, there is an option"), since the suffix *ktvā* denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*), the prohibition would apply to the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) only when it likewise denotes the abstract action, and not in other meanings. For an adjunct is a differentiator only when it is explicitly relied upon by the word. And in the rule *udito vā*, the state of denoting the abstract action is not explicitly relied upon by the word.

Thus, there is the justification for such forms as *tena nirvṛttam* ("completed by that") and *nirvṛtte 'kṣadyūtādibhyaḥ* ("the suffix *kta* occurs after words like *akṣadyūta* when they denote what has been completed").
The suffix *kta* is optionally used after a verbal root in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*). (Pāṇini 7.2.17)

"In *meditamanena*": because of the prohibition of *kittva* by the rule *niṣṭhā śīṅ*, there is *guṇa*. In *praminna*: the *kta* suffix is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ kartari ca*.

"The followers of Sunāga" (*saunāgāḥ*): the disciples of the teacher Sunāga are the *saunāgāḥ*. Regarding "the jar is capable of being made": although the root *śaki* is intransitive when used alone, it nevertheless becomes transitive by virtue of being qualified by the action expressed by the suffix *tumun*. Accordingly, verbal suffixes such as *lādi* are seen used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), as in: "this grammatical rule is capable of being stated," or "this meaning can be stated."

The words *kṣubdha*, *svānta*, *dhvānta*, *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, *viribdhi*, *phāṇṭa*, and *bāḍha* are used in the senses of "agitated," "mind," "darkness," "clung," "indistinct," "sound," "unstrained [liquid]," and "excessive" respectively. (Pāṇini 7.2.18)

"If it is called 'churning' (mantha)" means that if the churning is denoted by the aggregate as a whole. By this, [it is shown that] the churning and so forth [are designated] by virtue of being the objects denoted by the aggregates.

He shows that [these terms] are included here. However, if they were to be accepted as being conditioned by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—that is, if *kṣubdha* and so forth were treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*) when the meaning of the root is the instrument such as churning (*mantha*)—then [the form] would also apply in cases such as *kṣubhitaṃ manthena* ("churned by means of churning"). For we see [the usage]: "barley meal mixed with liquid substances is *mantha*; [he makes] *dadhimantha*s and *madhumantha*s. Others, however, say that *mantha* refers to the churning-stick (*mathanadaṇḍa*), the handle, because "it is churned by this."

In cases such as *mantha* ("churning"), the connection of words like *kṣubdha* ("agitated") with actions such as "moving" should be understood according to their respective possibilities. Regarding the phrase "from comparison" (*upamānāt*): comparison means similarity, and that should be understood according to its respective possibilities.

By the word *svānta*, the mind that is undistracted and unperturbed regarding sense objects is expressed. *Svanitam* means "made to sound. In the expression *manasā*, the instrumental case is used either in the sense of the agent or the instrument. The same applies to the expression *dhvanitaṃ tamasā*. Regarding *lagnim*: the roots *rañj*, *lag*, and *ṣṭag* mean "to cover," and here the substitution of *na* for *ta* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is also prescribed by grammatical rule.

Regarding the word *gliṣṭam*: the root *mlecch* means "inarticulate sound. *Mlecchitam* means "spoken incorrectly" (*apabhāṣitam*). Here, because the meaning is unclear, the sound is also indistinct; for even though the forms of corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are manifest, their meaning is not. In the examples, there is a lack of manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇa*), which is the lack of clarity. As for *phāṇḍam* and so forth—what kind of "effortlessness" (*anāyāsa*) is intended here? To this he says: "When [the word] is not heard," and so on.

For whatever disease there is a specific medicine produced, its preparation is fivefold: *rasa*, *kalka*, *śr̥ta*, *śīta*, and *phāṇṭa*. *Rasa* is the fresh juice (*svarasa*). *Kalka* is the paste (*piṣṭa*). *Śr̥ta* is the decoction (*kvātha*). *Śīta* is when the prepared medicinal substance is placed in water and left to steep overnight; this water is drunk in the morning. *Phāṇṭa* is when that same substance is placed in hot water, immediately strained, filtered, and drunk.

As Vāgbhaṭa said: "That which is strained immediately after being pressed is *phāṇṭa*. These are the five types of decoctions (*kaṣāya*). Among them, the term "unboiled" (*aśṛta*) excludes the *kvātha*; "unpounded" (*apiṣṭa*) excludes the *kalka*; "by contact with water" excludes the *svarasa*; "slightly warm" (*īṣaduṣṇa*) excludes the *śīta*; and the word "measure" (*mātra*) is a restatement of its natural state. "Having distinct flavors" (*vibhaktarasa*) means having differentiated tastes at the initial stage. The meaning is that a decoction which is thus characterized is a *phāṇṭa*. The word *kaṣāya* is of both genders. How, then, is this expressed by the word "without effort"? By way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as he says: "without effort" (*anāyāsena*).
The roots *ghṛṣ* and *śas* are used in the sense of impudence (*vaiyātya*). 7-2-19.

The root *dhṛṣ* is used in the sense of boldness (*prāgalbhya*), and *śas* in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*). The nominative case is used here in the sense of the genitive. "Virūpa-yātam" means a distorted or improper course; he whose conduct (*gamanam*) or behavior (*ceṣṭatam*) is thus is called *viyātaḥ*, meaning ill-behaved (*avinītaḥ*).

In the passage beginning with *śaser api*, the phrase "the prohibition of *iṭ* is established" is to be supplied as a continuation. Now, one might ask: why is the mention [of the root] not intended to provide for the compulsory application of the rule where an option (*vibhāṣā*) would otherwise apply—namely, by the rule *dhṛṣer vibhāṣā bhāvādikarmaṇoḥ*? To this he replies: "even in the case of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the passive/objective (*ādikarman*. Thus, the purpose of its being listed at the beginning [of the *adādi* class] must be considered. *Dharṣitaḥ* means "overpowered"; as before, there is no *ak* suffix. *Viśasitaḥ* means "mutilated."
The word *dṛḍha* [is used] in the sense of "firm" (*sthūla*) and "strong" (*balavat*). 7-2-20.

*Sthūlaḥ* means "fleshy" (*māṃsala*), even if [otherwise] weak. *Balaḥ* means one who is strong even though not fleshy. Regarding the rule *balavati ca*, the author shows that the word *bala* ends in the suffix *ac* belonging to the *arśa-ādi* group. Regarding the root *dṛh*: the reading is simply *dṛhi vṛddhau*—this is the view of the author of the Vārttika; whereas for the author of the Bhāṣya, it is *dṛha dṛhi vṛddhau*.

Now, for what purpose is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ha* prescribed as a technical anomaly (*nipātana*), rather than simply prescribing the substitution of *ḍha*? [One might argue: "Let there be the substitution of *ḍha* for the following [letter], let there be the substitution of *ṣṭu* for that [following *ta*], and by the rule 'elision of *ḍha* before *ḍha*' (*ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*), the form *dṛḍha* would be established. To this, he says: "The prescription of the elision of the letter *ha*... [is for the sake of ensuring] that the letter *ra* does not occur. In the rule *rādiphaḥ*, the word *varṇāt* is not required; therefore, the meaning is that the sound *ra* would not occur [in its place].

The meaning is that, because the elision of *ḍh* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the designation *guru*—which arises from the rule "a syllable with a conjunct consonant is heavy" (*saṃyoge guru*)—supersedes the designation *laghu*; consequently, the grammatical operation dependent upon that [lightness] does not occur. Regarding the phrase "and here": the meaning is that there would be the occurrence of a grammatical operation dependent upon the designation *guru*. The word *dṛṃhitam* is a counter-example for the root *dṛṃh*; *dṛhitam* is from the root *dṛh*. And in this context, by means of its long vowel and so forth, it is called "increased" (*vṛddha*).
The word *parivṛḍha* [is used] in the sense of "lord" (*prabhu*). || 7 - 2 - 21 ||

"It is the same as the preceding" means that it is identical to the preceding case because the absence of the *iḍ* augment and so forth is equal [in both]. "Of *vṛhi*" refers to the view of the author of the Vārttika, according to whom there is the root *vṛhi* in the sense of "growth. According to the author of the Bhāṣya, however, it is *bṛhi* in the sense of "growth. "And if *vṛhi* is a separate verbal root"—the meaning is that if such a root exists, then it too must be treated as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). "That itself is the purpose" means the absence of the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

Regarding the phrase *athem kathaṃ parivṛḍhayyeti atra lyabādeśaḥ*: since the analysis (*vigraha*) is "he describes one who is powerful" (*parivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) should be applied directly from that [root *vṛdh*], and because the entire complex is a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffix *ktvā* should also be applied from that same source. Consequently, because the prefix *pari-* is included within the element ending in *ktvā*, this would not be a compound; furthermore, in the case of *parivṛḍhayati*, since the word *pari* is included within the element ending in a personal suffix (*tiṅanta*), the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) for the elision [of the preceding *tiṅ*] would not apply. To address this, he says: *parivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*.

Regarding the word *vigṛhya*: since the suffix *ṇic* arises [here], the root must be cited with the *ṇic* affix (*ṇyanta*). However, if it were cited without the *ṇic* affix (*aṇyantapāṭha*), the suffix *ktvā* in *vigṛhya* would not be possible, because the agents of the two actions would not be the same. As for the rule "only from the root *grāmayati* when preceded by a prefix," whatever needs to be said about that has already been stated under the rule *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacveḥ*. Regarding the statement "the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) occurs": this is an elliptical expression that includes *aṭ* and reduplication as well—for example, *paryavraḍhayat* and *parivivraḍhayiṣati*. *Parivṛṃhitam* is a counter-example for the root *vṛṃhi*; *parivṛhitam* is a counter-example for the root *vṛhi*.
The root *kaṣ* takes the affix *khal* when meaning "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) or "thicket" (*gahana*).

The root *kaṣ* has the meaning of "to harm" (*hiṃsā*). Thus, "fire is *kaṣṭa*" means that the fire being piled up is intended here by the word "fire," and it is *kaṣṭa* because the method of piling it is difficult to understand. Grammar is *kaṣṭa* because the systematic arrangement of the augment *iṭ* and so forth is difficult to understand. Sāman is *kaṣṭa* because the specific tones of the bull-like [chant], the *stoma*, and so forth are difficult to understand. It is also [called *kaṣṭa*] in the sense of a cause, either through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or by etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) from the root *kṛcchra*.
The root *dhuṣ* is used in the sense of "not making a sound. (Pāṇini 7.2.23)

*Ghuṣṭā* means *aviśabditā* (not proclaimed). *Avadhuṣitam* means *viśabditam*, that is to say, one whose intention has been made manifest. This is also the usage of the root belonging to the *curādika* (caurādika) class, for it is that very root which occurs in this sense. "Both" means that the form *ghuṣi* included in the rule is common to both [roots]. [Objection: How can there be a general inclusion, since there ought to be a *ṇic* affix in the sense of proclaiming (*viśabdane*), yet here only the simple root *ghuṣi* is mentioned? To this he says: "And there is a prohibition of [the sense of] proclaiming."

Regarding the statement that [the root] *viśabda* has the meaning "to speak," others say that the general rule "the roots *cana*, etc., are optionally non-causative" (*anitya-ṇyantāś-cana-rādayaḥ*) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Another says:
"The fact that the root *cit* is marked with the *it*-sign in the sense of 'memory' (*citi smṛtau*) is the indicator here;
for its purpose is so that the elision of the penultimate vowel does not occur in forms such as *cintita*."
And since the *ṇic* suffix is permanent, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would not apply here;
therefore, it should be read simply as "cinta smṛtyām."
Regarding the phrase "this too": although he stated an unrefined expression—namely, *ity etat*—nevertheless, the usage *jughuṣuḥ* is also justified; such is the meaning.
And [the suffix *ṅasi*] becomes *abhi* when it is not far from [the point of reference]. 7.2.25.

"Far" (*dūra*) means "distinctly distant" (*viśeṣeṇa dūraṃ*); that which is other than this is [called] *avidūra*. Furthermore, it should be understood that when something is near (*āsanna*) or not remote (*aviprakṛṣṭa*), it is [termed] *avidūra*. The state of being that is *āvidūrya*. Because the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied. Now, one might object that the prohibition "not from a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by *na*" would apply here; to this he says: "Precisely for this reason. The rule "not from one preceded by *na*" is a governing heading (*adhikāra*); therefore, it is stated "of the subsequent" because the prohibition therein applies to the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) that follows that specific sūtra.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the root *adhi-i* (to study) when the sense is "having studied" (*vṛtta*). 7-2-26.

The word *adhīyata* [is derived as follows]: the term *adhyayana* (study) is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. This is a qualification of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*)—namely, "in the case of a past participle denoting study. Regarding the phrase "with the elision of the causative marker (*ṇiluk*)" (*ṇiluk ca*): the elision of the causative marker (*ṇerluk*) is prescribed so that the *guṇa* substitution does not occur by virtue of the presence of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*); for if there were merely an elision (*lopa*) of the marker, the *guṇa* would indeed take place. In the example "the *guṇa* was performed by Devadatta" (*vṛtto guṇo devadattena*), *guṇa* means recitation—a specific type of study consisting of the *pada*, *krama*, and *saṃhitā* methods; "it was performed" (*vṛttaḥ*) means it was accomplished.

With the words "vṛtirayam" and so forth, he raises the objection that this sūtra need not have been commenced. The word *akarmaka* (intransitive) is understood from the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.52], which concerns the suffix *suṅ*. This statement was made for the purpose of employing the past passive participle (*kta*) in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). For when a root is intransitive, the *niṣṭhā* suffix occurs in the sense of an abstract action, because of the continued application of the rule "and in the case of intransitives, [the *niṣṭhā*] is used in the sense of an abstract action" (*tayoreva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*, with the anuvṛtti of *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*). Even the *kta* suffix used in the neuter sense of an abstract action does not occur after transitive roots, because in the rule "tayoreva," only the *kta* suffix in general is mentioned [without restriction].

Otherwise, if the *kta* suffix were prescribed after a verb with a transitive sense, the accusative case would be required for the object—as in "the village was gone to" (*grāmaṃ gatam*) or "the rice was eaten" (*odanaṃ bhuktam*). If, then, it is intransitive, how [is this so]?

Fearing that the term *vṛtta* might be interpreted as a *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) in the sense of the object (*karman*), he says: "when it occurs in the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*). Alternatively, this entire passage—"this root *vṛt* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), yet when occurring in the sense of the causative"—is a single syntactic unit. Even intransitive roots become transitive (*sakarmaka*) through an internalized causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) by means of an implied object (*prayojya-karman*), just as in the case of *rājā yudhyati* ("the king fights [for himself]"). Furthermore, since the usage of *vṛt* with an internalized causative sense is observed, he says: "for by that, [it signifies] accomplishment (*nirvṛtti*)."

Nor does the verb become transitive here by virtue of the prefix (*upasarga*), because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is understood; that is to say, the meaning [of the root] is apprehended even in such examples as *nivartyate yair niyamābhiṣekaḥ* ("by which the ritual consecration is brought about"). Therefore, the phrase "from the verbal base itself" (*vṛtter eva*) means "from the very root. Regarding the expression "the quality has ceased" (*vṛtto guṇaḥ*): since the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* according to the rule *udito vā*, the prohibition of *iṭ* is established by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*. Thus, the objection is simply this: the technical designation (*nipātana*) is purposeless.

He refutes this, saying: "it is performed for that purpose. The meaning is that even if the desired result is established otherwise, the rule is prescribed for the sake of avoiding an undesired result. Regarding the phrase "but others": according to their view, there is no purpose served by this rule in the Sūtra.
Or [the final vowel] of *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *channa*, and *jñapta* [is elided]. (7.2.27)

"Dāntaḥ" (tamed) and "śāntaḥ" (calmed). The roots *dam* and *śam* mean "to pacify. [In the formation of these words,] there is lengthening according to the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*, due to the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇaluk*) and the prohibition of the *iṭ* augment. Furthermore, because the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇiluk*) is not caused by any subsequent factor, and because there is a prohibition against applying the rule for lengthening, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply here. "Pūrṇaḥ" (full): the root *pūrī* meaning "to swell" belongs to both the *divādi* and *curādi* classes. "Dastaḥ" (wasted): from the roots *tasu* meaning "to perish" and *damu*. Here, shortening (*hrasvatvam*) is also prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity). "Spaṣṭaḥ" (clear) and "channaḥ" (covered).

The roots *spaś* (in the senses of "observing" and "touching") and *chad* (in the sense of "covering") also undergo shortening [of their vowel] by way of nipātana (irregular derivation). Regarding the form *jñapta*: the root *jñap* belongs to the *curādi* (Tenth) class and is marked with the mute letter *m*. It is stated that the prohibition of *iṭ* and the elision (*luk*) of the causative suffix (*ṇi*) are established here by nipātana. Furthermore, due to the word "and" (*ca*), there is sometimes shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*). In some places, it is recited as follows: because the rule "for *jñap*, *bhram*, *jñapi*, and *san*" prescribes an optional application, and since the prohibition of *iṭ* would otherwise apply under the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," this nipātana is for the purpose of providing an option. The intention is that the mention of "a single syllable" (*ekāj-grahaṇa*) does not carry over into the rule "yasya vibhāṣā."

In this context, the inclusion of the first four [roots] could have been omitted. How so? Because for roots that inherently include the causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇyartha*), forms such as *dānta* and others belong to the base form (*prakṛti*), whereas elsewhere, for those with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), forms such as *damita* and others occur.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the words *ruṣ*, *amatra*, *saṃghuṣa*, and *svana*.

Regarding *abhyānta*: the root *am* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth; the lengthening of the vowel is as before. Regarding *tṛṇṇa*: from the root *ñitvarā* in the sense of "agitation," the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule *jvaratvara-* etc. [Pāṇini 6.4.20]. Regarding the statement "since the prohibition of *iṭ* would apply by the rule *āditaśca*": if the root were marked with *ādi* (indicating that *iṭ* is prohibited), its purpose must be sought elsewhere—for instance, some [scholar] suggests an *anubandha* letter *th* should be attached for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings. However, someone else says: "The *ādi* designation is for the sake of the *yaṅluganta* form"; for in that case, this option [of applying *iṭ*] does not exist, because the term *ekācaḥ* ("having a single vowel") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

By virtue of the rule *āditaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.16), even for a root with an initial augment (*anubandha*), the prohibition of *iṭ* applies when the *yaṅ-luk* occurs, according to the rule *āditaśca*. Regarding the phrase "of *ghuṣ* preceded by *sam*": the root *ghuṣ* in the sense of "not making a sound" (*aviśabdane*) provides the scope for the rule when not preceded by *sam*—as in *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope is sounded"). The scope for this optional alternative (*vikalpa*) is when it is preceded by *sam* and used in the sense of "making a sound"—as in *saṃghuṣṭaṃ vākyamāha* ("he spoke a resonant sentence"). Thus, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) regarding the root preceded by *sam* when not used in the sense of "making a sound. The phrase "preceded by *āṅ*" and so forth follows.

The scope for the irregular formation (*nipātana*) *kṣubdhasvānta* is when it denotes "mind" (*manas*) and is not preceded by the prefix *ā*. The scope for this alternative rule is when it is preceded by the prefix *ā* and does not denote "mind. When it is preceded by *ā* and does denote "mind," there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
The suffix *kta* is used after the root *hṛṣ* when referring to body hair (*loman*).

"Hṛṣṭāni" means "fully grown. "Mūrdhajāḥ" refers to the hair of the head. "Lomāni" (body hairs) are those growing on other parts of the body; this is well-established in the *Nighaṇṭu*. There are also usages consistent with that among the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*, such as: "They cause the hair of the head (*keśa*), the beard (*śmaśru*), the body hair (*loman*), and the nails (*nakha*) to be shaved. However, since the hair of the head is also included here, he says: "the hair of the head and the hair of the body. The specific referent (*viśeṣya*) here must be sought [in the context]. He states "as follows" (*yathā*) to show where they are taken in a general sense.

Now, one might ask: how can a verbal root, which denotes action, function with respect to body hair (*loman*), which consists of substance? To this he says: "And with regard to that object. The meaning is: they are "struck down" by being bitten by a hard substance, or "stricken" by the cold wind.
And [the word] *apacita*. 7-2-30.
