"He has honored his teacher" (*apacito 'nena guruḥ*). The root *cāyṛ* is used in the senses of "honoring" (*pūjā*) and "perceiving" (*niśāmana*). This usage refers to the sense of perceiving; however, in the sense of honoring, since the suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "thought," "intellect," or "honor" (by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*), there would have to be a genitive case by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. [But this is not the case here because the form is *apaciti*, derived from] *ktin*. By the rule *ktinn ābādibhyaḥ*, the suffix *ktin* is applied. Otherwise, by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, the long vowel *ā* would have occurred.
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *hrū* for *hvar* occurs before a case-ending. (Pāṇini 7.2.31)
The root is *hvar* (as in *hvarati*). The meaning is "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*). The inclusion of the letter *i* is for the sake of indicating the presence of the *guṇa* vowel.
And [the suffixes] *aparihvṛta* and *aś* [are applied]. 7-2-32.

"Regarding the absence of the substitute": this refers to that which was obtained by the preceding rule. The use of the plural number is because its employment is observed only in Vedic (chandas) usage.
The substitution of *h* occurs for the sound *hv* [at the beginning of a word]. 7-2-33.
The augment *iḍ* and the *guṇa* [substitution]; by the word "and" (*ca*), the absence of the substitute is also included.

And [the following roots] end in *ca*: *gras*, *skam*, *stabh*, *ut-stabh*, *catt*, *vi-śas*, *śas*, *śās*, *tarutṛ*, *tarutṛ*, *varutṛ*, *varutṛ*, *varutrī*, *ujjvaliti*, *kṣariti*, *kṣamiti*, *vamiti*, and *amiti*.

*gras* in the sense of devouring; *skambh* and *stumbh*, two roots belonging to the Sūtra (Dhātupāṭha) in the sense of obstructing; *cat* in the sense of begging; *kas* in the sense of moving; *śas* in the sense of harming; *śaṃs* in the sense of praising; *śās* in the sense of instructing; *tṝ* in the senses of floating and crossing over; *vṛṅ* in the sense of choosing; *jval* in the sense of flaming; *kṣar* in the sense of moving; *kṣamūṣ* in the sense of enduring; *duvama* in the sense of vomiting; *am* in the senses of moving and so forth. Regarding the form *uttābhitā*: by the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya*, there is a homogeneous substitute for the preceding [vowel], and the *s* is replaced by *t*.

The word *stabhita* does not occur preceded by any other prefix (*upasarga*). If it did, the mention of *uttabhita* would be redundant. [The phrase] "with regard to the multiplicity of irregular formations" (*nipātanabahutvāpekṣam*) means that, because of this, a Vedic usage ending in the singular number has also been cited; such is the intended meaning. The particle *iti* is for the purpose of illustration, since it signifies a type or manner (*prakāra*).
The long vowel substitution occurs for the penultimate short *i* or *u* of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix that begins with a consonant other than *y*.

"It remains," "it dwells"—[these forms are derived]. But surely, the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke* ("after *rud* and the others, [the augment *iṭ* is added] before a sārvadhātuka suffix") will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the augment occurs only after *rud* and the others when followed by a sārvadhātuka suffix?

To this he replies: regarding the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*, it is said that "in that case" (*tatra*). If this restriction were understood, a contrary restriction might also be possible: namely, that the augment occurs only before a sārvadhātuka suffix after *rud* and the others. And in that regard, it must be stated that it will not apply [here], because the *kittva* (the status of being marked with *k*) is prescribed for the suffixes *ktvā* and *san* in the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* [Pāṇini 1.2.7]; for [the augment] would already be established by the rule *ta-an-iṭaḥ sano jhalāder halantācca* [Pāṇini 1.2.9].

[The opponent argues: "Even for the suffix *ktvā*, since the *kit*-status is present by its original instruction (*aupadeśika*), there would consequently be a burden of understanding [the rule]. [The proponent replies: But surely, even if the mention of *ārdhadhātuka* were absent, the augment *iṭ* would apply only to that [root] because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "of the *aṅga*. This is established by the following indicator (*jñāpaka*): namely, that the author teaches the prohibition of the *iṭ* of the suffix in the rule "ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt" (P. 7.2.10), and that he says "niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi" (P. 7.2.47) and "na ktvā seṭ" (P. 1.2.18). These [statements] indicate that this *iṭ* belongs only to the suffix.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of the application of the nominal suffix in cases such as *vṛkṣatvam*, because of the governing rule *ṛtaḥ taddhitasya*. Even so, there would be an undesired application in forms such as *jugupsate*, *lūbhyām*, and *lūbhiḥ*; however, from the rule *idito num dhātoḥ*, the term *dhātu* (root) will be understood as recurring for a second time. Of these, one refers to the word-form itself (*svarūpa*). Consequently, since the augment *iṭ* is prescribed after a root that is connected to the designation "root" by the rule *dhātoḥ*, no undesirable form can arise anywhere.
Thus, because there are so many things that must be addressed, the term *ārdhadhātukasya* was stated in order to avoid the burden of detailed exposition.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of removing the prohibition": by what, then, is the possibility of a prohibition being applied suspected? This very statement would serve as the basis for the assumption: "There is an augment *iṭ* for the *ārdhadhātuka* in general, from which it is prohibited [only] after [roots ending in] *val* and so forth. In that case, prohibitions such as *neṅvaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8) would be for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).
The substitution of *iṭ* occurs after the roots *snū* and *kram*, provided that the following cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is absent.

Since the augment *iṭ* is already established for the roots *snuk* and *kram* due to their being udātta, this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*): that [the augment] should occur only when there is a cause for the non-middle voice (*anātmanepada*), and not otherwise. Now, as for the forms *prasnutaḥ*, *prasnutavān*, *prasusnūṣati*, *krāntaḥ*, and *krāntavān*—since the prohibitions [of *iṭ*] apply here by the rules "after a root ending in *śrī*, *y*, or *u*" (*śryukaḥ kiti*), "in the case of *san* after *grah* and *guh*" (*sani grahaguhośca*), and "optionally after a root ending in *ya*" (*yasya vibhāṣā*)—why is this [present rule] not taken as an injunction (*vidhyartha*) rather than a restriction? [The answer is: because the section containing prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) was composed earlier [in the Aṣṭādhyāyī].

For its purpose is this: so that there may be a negation of the mere root *iṇ* alone, without regard for any specific rule [prescribing] the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). If it were a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*)—meaning "if the cause for the middle voice is present, then *iṇ* does not occur"—then this would have to be read within the very section on negations. In that case, the inclusion of the negative particle *nañ* would not be necessary; however, it was not done in that way.

In this context, if one were first to form a compound of *nañ* with the word *ātmanepada*, and subsequently form a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound with the word *nimitta*—meaning that "non-ātmanepada" (i.e., *parasmaipada*) is the cause [of the substitution]—then the meaning would be that the augment *iṭ* occurs only where *snu* and *kram* have *parasmaipada* as their cause, as in *cakramitha*, *cakramiva*, *cakramima*, *prāsnāvīt*, *prasusnuviva*, and so on; consequently, it would not occur before a *kṛt* suffix, as in *prasnavitā*.

[If it were not so,] one could not derive forms such as *prastravitum*, *prasnavitavyam*, *prakramitā*, *prakramitum*, *prakramitavyam*, nor even *cikramiṣati*; for the *parasmaipada* suffix arising from a desiderative (*san*) does not have the root *kram* as its cause. Furthermore, one would have to state the rule simply as "the *parasmaipada* [is used after *kram*]. Therefore, one should first form a compound of the word *ātmanepada* with the word *nimitta* (cause), and subsequently form a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) with that.

However, if this were an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), this very position would fail to arise at all. In that case, if there were a locative singular [in the rule] stating "when there is a cause for the middle voice," the meaning would be: "it does not occur when that which is the cause of the middle voice—such as the marker *ṅ*—is present. Consequently, a prohibition would also apply to forms such as *prasnavitrīyate*, because here too the cause of the middle voice exists, namely the *ṅ* of the suffix *kyaṅ*.

He shows that the dual ending of the nominative (*prathamādvivacanāntam*) qualifies *snukramoḥ* by stating: "and if *snukramau* are not the cause (*nimitta*) for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The singular number [in the commentary] is used in the manner of the expression "the Vedas are the authority" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*). However, in the Sūtra, the dual number is used because the status of being a cause is intended to apply to each one individually. This word *nimitta* (cause) exists in the sense of mere suitability; even regarding seeds remaining in a granary, speakers say, "these are the causes of sprouts. It also exists in the sense of something currently producing its effect (*kurvadrūpa*).

In that regard, under the first position, there would also be a prohibition of the *kṛtya* suffixes—for instance, *prasnavitā*, *prasnavitum*, *prasnavitavyam*, *prakramitā*, *prakramitum*, and *prakramitavyam*. For here, according to the circumstances, there exists a fitness for the *ātmanepada* because they fall within the scope of the states (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), or the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, he asks: "And what, then, is the cause for the *ātmanepada*? The other [the opponent] replies by resorting to the view that [the suffix] functions as the actual producer: "Where... and so forth.

In this regard, it should be explained as follows: that upon which the *ātmanepada* is based is precisely what constitutes the cause (*nimitta*) for the *ātmanepada*. But what is it upon which that *ātmanepada* is based? To answer this, he says "bhāvakarma" and so forth. For in this context, the *ātmanepada* is heard [prescribed] after the roots *snu* and *kram*; thus, the word "cause" is used in its primary sense when it is actually producing the effect, whereas it is used figuratively when there is merely the potentiality [for it to do so]. This is the intended meaning.

But surely, it is those very meanings—namely, the state [bhāva], the object [karman], and so forth—that are the conditions for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the case of roots such as *snū* and *kram*. Where, then, would the prohibition apply? It would apply where the mere root itself is the condition, or in the case of "provided it is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*), as in *kraṃsyate*. This is not a fault; for the state, the object, the agent, and [the meanings] such as "movement" (*vṛtti*) are all qualifiers of the verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of being its domain. However, the verbal root alone is the direct condition for the middle voice—meaning that the middle voice occurs after a verbal root whose domain is the state and so forth. Therefore, etc. Since...
The meaning is that in this context, the very form of the word as it functions (*kurvadrūpa*) is the cause; therefore, this prohibition applies even when the *ātmanepada* endings are present.

Why is it called a "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*), given that it was explained in the introduction by relying on the principle of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? To this he replies: "And this sūtra has the result of being a prohibition. This is true; however, even in the case of exclusion, because it serves the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and because a restrictive rule has the effect of excluding other possibilities, it is described in this way.

"Prasnoṣīṣṭa": here the *liṅ* suffix is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), and the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule "bhāvakarmaṇoḥ. "Prakaṃsīṣṭa": here, however, the *ātmanepada* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule "propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām. With the words "In all cases," etc., he demonstrates the meaning of the sūtra through examples. Now, one might object that for the *ātmanepada* prescribed after a desiderative (*sananta*) root, that very desiderative suffix is the cause [of the application], and not the roots *snū* or *kram*; to this he replies: "Even after a desiderative. The sense is that, because of the statement "as before" (*pūrvavat*), the cause residing in the original base (*prakṛti*) remains the cause even when the desiderative suffix is present.

If, then, the *ātmanepada* occurs after a root ending in *san* (the desiderative suffix) when expressing the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), the prohibition [of the *parasmaipada*] would not apply; for in that case, the condition residing in the original root (*prakṛti*) is not required, but rather the form ending in *san* itself is the independent condition, as in the case of *putrīyati* and so forth. If this is so, then even when expressing the sense of the action or the object after a root ending in *san*, the *ātmanepada* will occur by the rule "as before, after *san*" (*pūrvavat sanaḥ*), because the *ātmanepada* was observed in the original root (*prakṛti*) in those two senses.

In this regard, although a causative form (*sananta*) itself may also function as its own cause, nevertheless, there is scope for the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13)—as in *bhūyate* and *pacyate*; and there is scope for the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62)—as in *śiśayiṣate*. When both [rules] apply to a causative form (*sananta*) regarding the sense of the action or the object, the latter will prevail by virtue of its superior status (*paratvāt*). If it is argued that there is no distinction [between them], that too is not correct, because a distinction is indeed possible in this very case.

Even so, this is not established; for in the rule *pūrvavat sanaḥ*, the term *kartari* (in the sense of the agent) is understood from the preceding rule *karmavyatihāre*. Indeed, in that context, the word *kartari* is connected with *sarvaiva* (the suffix *san* itself). Even if it were not so connected, even then, when the suffix *ṇic* is added after a stem ending in *san*, the ātmanepada would occur by the rules *ṇicaśca* or *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*; consequently, the prohibition [of the ātmanepada] would not be established in forms such as *cikraṃsyate* and *cikraṃsyate*.

Furthermore—oh, even then a prohibition is desired; indeed, it is desired. As the author of the Vārttika said: "But [the augment] *iṭ* is established as prohibited when [the root] *snū* is in the same word with the ātmanepada suffix, because of the rule regarding *krami*. Thus, since the author of the Vārttika establishes a prohibition when [the root] is in the same word with the ātmanepada suffix, it is evident that he intends a prohibition in such cases. However, as explained by the author of the Vṛtti, it would not apply; therefore, an effort must be made here [to resolve this].

If the prohibition applies when the *ātmanepada* endings are present, let there be no mention of the "condition" (*nimitta*), and let it simply be stated: "in the case of non-*ātmanepada*. This would be understood as a locative absolute (*satisaptamī*), meaning "it does not occur when the *ātmanepada* is present. If this were obtainable, it would be well; however, it is not obtainable, because of the rule that all locatives in the grammatical treatise are locatives of sequence (*parasaptamī*). But if, under the *parasaptamī*, the two roots *snū* and *kram* are qualified such that [the prohibition applies] "when the *ātmanepada* follows immediately after *snū* and *kram*," then the forms *prasnoṣīṣṭa* and *prakrasīṣṭa* are established.

[The rule] "prasnoṣyate" and "prakraṃsyate" would not apply here because [the affix] is separated by *sy*. [If it is argued that] the term "ārddhadhātuka" is a qualifier [of the following element]: "when an *ātmanepada* *ārddhadhātuka* follows immediately after *snū* and *krami*," then the forms "prasnoṣyate," "prakraṃsyate," "prasnoṣīṣṭa," and "prakraṃsīṣṭa" would still not be established, because the augment *sīyuṭ* is a part of the *ātmanepada* [suffix].

In both ways, [the rule] will be intended to apply; however, it does not apply here, for in this case, there is no *ātmanepada* suffix immediately following a *sārvadhātuka* that has that as its antecedent. Therefore, the mention of the "cause" (*nimitta*) must be made. Thus he says: "The mention of the cause," and so forth. That which has the *ātmanepada* as its subsequent element is "that-para" (*tatpara*). In forms such as *pracikrasiṣyate*, the suffix *syat* is that which has it as its subsequent element; that is "that-para," namely, the *san* suffix. As for "but here," and so forth, it has already been explained previously.

Regarding the form *prasnaviṣyate*: the rule *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.27] applies. Even according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, there is no prohibition here; why? Because of the statement "when situated within the same word" (*samānapadasthasya*). The status of being a word (*padatva*) must be considered in relation to the addition of the augment *iṭ*. In that case, although the status of being a word is obtained once the suffix *tṛc* has arisen and the case-ending has been produced, the augment *iṭ* still operates because the *ātmanepada* endings are not yet present. However, in the form *pratikraṃsiṣyate*, because the *ātmanepada* endings are present at the stage when the word is formed, the prohibition takes effect.

"From that which is the domain of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). This means "from that which is suitable for it. Since it has been stated that the prohibition applies when the middle voice occurs, this [sūtra] is commenced. Regarding the forms *krantā* and *kramitā* from the root *kram-* without a prefix (*anupasarga*), some say that both are possible because of the option provided by the rule *anupasargādvā*; they argue that since the middle voice is the cause [for the application of the suffix], the prohibition applies. Others, however, explain the word "domain" (*viṣaya*) as meaning "exclusive occurrence," and thus maintain that only *kramitā* should occur.

Regarding the rule *sni-sani-kiti ca*: this is an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*). One should also consider the rule *kramaśca niṣṭhāyām yasya vibhāṣā*. As for the statement "the prohibition occurs," the reason for this has already been stated previously.
In the *aliṭ* (non-aorist) [tense], there is lengthening of the vowel of the root *grah*.

Regarding the rule *graha-uttarasyeṭaḥ*: how, then, is the lengthening of the augment *iṭ* obtained? Since the term *iṭ* which is under discussion (*prakṛta*) is indicated in the nominative case (*prathamā-nirdiṣṭa*), whereas here [in the sūtra] the requirement is for something indicated in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdiṣṭa*). If that is the case, I shall place the word ending in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) immediately before [the word *iṭaḥ*]. Even so, there is a fault: if one says *iṭaḥ* without regard for the *iṭ* under discussion, then by virtue of there being no distinction, the lengthening would undesirably apply even to the *iṭ* of the *ciṇvadiṭ* type. In that case, let it be exactly as it was stated in the nominative (*praśamāntam*).

In this context, when there is a grammatical coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that "the long [vowel] becomes *iṭ*," it results by implication in a rule for the introduction of the augment *iṭ*. If one were to say "the *iṭ* is long," it would be a contradiction: if it is *iṭ*, it is not long; if it is long, it is not *iṭ*; thus, "the *iṭ* is long" would be contradictory. This might be argued: when it is stated that "the long [vowel] becomes *iṭ*," by implication the reference to individual instances (*vyakti*) is abandoned and the universal (*jāti*) of the phoneme /i/ is resorted to; and because of the mention of "long," that universal as inherent in those individual instances is what is prescribed.

Even so, there would be this fault: in the case of *vivariṣate*, when the suffix *san* is applied, the rule *vṛto vā* would optionally apply a long vowel, and since *iṭ* is also applicable, both [the long vowel and *iṭ*] would be prohibited by the rule *sani grahaguhośca*. Consequently, although *iṭ* is prescribed optionally by the rule *iṭ sani vā*, because there is no further prescription of *iṭ* in that context, the long vowel *ī* would not be heard in its optional form. This is not a fault, because in the rule *iṭ sani vā*, the terms "long" (*dīrgha*) and "*iṭ*" from the preceding rule, as well as *vṛtaḥ*, will carry over (*anuvartisyate*).

In that case, however, a rule that prescribes *iṭ* after prohibiting it for a root situated elsewhere would not be established. For instance, regarding the rule *jṝvraścoḥ ktvi*, in the forms *jaritvā* and *jarītvā*, *iṭ* is first obtained because the root is udātta; then, by the rule *vṝto vā*, the long *iṭ* is optionally applied. Subsequently, since both are prohibited by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti ca*, *iṭ* is prescribed once again. Yet, in that context, there is no possibility of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) being carried over [from the previous rule].

But surely, in the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*, because of the governing authority of *neḍvaśi* and because of the adoption of the view that [the suffix] is a specific individual (*vyaktipakṣa*), there is a prohibition of only the short *iṭ* and not of the long *iṭ*; therefore, the long *iṭ* prescribed by *vṝto vā* remains as it was, and since it is reintroduced by *jṛvraścoḥ ktvi*, forms such as *jaritvā* and *carītveti* would be established even for the long vowel. This would indeed be the case if another *iṭ* were taught as a separate augment; however, here, because of the statement "the *iṭ* is long," its function is also that of the *iṭ*.

It is indeed so. Otherwise, in the case of *agrahīt*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *hrm-y-anta-kṣaṇaḥ* would not apply; the elision of the *sic* suffix by the rule *iṭa īṭi*; the optional substitution of the retroflex *ḍha* by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* in forms such as *agrahīḍhvam* or *agrahīdhvam*; and the prohibition of *kit*-treatment by the rule *na ktvā seṭ* in the form *jarītvā*—none of these grammatical operations would be established.

Therefore, it must be admitted that even for this [root], *iṭ* becomes *iṭ*-less (*aniṭ*). Consequently, when there is a prohibition and then a subsequent prescription regarding that which resides in another location, the same fault would persist; thus, a long vowel cannot be prescribed as *iṭ*. If that is so, then the term "of the *ārdhadhātuka*" (P. 7.2.35) continues to apply, meaning that a long vowel occurs for the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix following the root *grah*. In that case, it would follow here as well: [the form] *grahaṇīyam* [would require lengthening]. [To this we reply: the phrase "beginning with *val*" (P. 7.2.36) continues to apply.

In that case, it would not apply here either—to [the forms] *grahītā* and *grahītum*. One must understand this as referring to what occurred in the past (i.e., the root *grah*). But then it would apply here too—to *grāhaka*. Let it be then that the augment *iṭ* applies simply [to the root]. But was it not already stated that the meaning here is indicated by the genitive case? [If so, how do we get *graha*? The word *grahaḥ* is in the fifth case; it will cause the first case (*iṭ*) to be understood as a genitive, according to the rule: "That which follows [is affected] because of the word 'tasmāt'."

Regarding the phrase "of the subject under discussion": this refers to that which is prescribed immediately after [the rule] *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ*. [The objection is: "The *iṭ* of *ciṇvadiṭ* does not occur. However, in the case of *jaritvā*, this very *iṭ* prescribed by *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ* is prohibited and then restated (as an exception), so the lengthening indeed takes place.

In the case of *jarīgṛhīta*, after the suffix *yaṅ* has been applied, and after the elision of *ṛ* and the elision of *y* have taken place, there is reduplication according to the rule "the doubling of the application" (*dvirvacanam*). Since this very root *grah* is present, the long vowel [of the reduplicated syllable] would apply by the rule "a long vowel occurs for *grah*" (*graher dīrghaḥ*). However, that status of being "as if occupying the original place" (*sthānivadbhāvaḥ*) which applies when a rule is prescribed based on what precedes, is also prohibited in the case of a rule prescribing a long vowel. Therefore, one must here resort to a qualification of what is prescribed: "The long vowel occurs for that *iṭ* augment which is prescribed for that *ārddhadhātuka* suffix which is prescribed for *grah*. *vṛto vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.38).

In this context, if the term *vṛ* were intended as a reference to the root *vṛ* (in the sense of "choosing") by means of the suffix *tasil*, it would have been specified simply as *vraḥ*, just as in the rule *gro yaṅi*. Alternatively, if there were an inclusion of both that [root] and those ending in *ṛ*, even so, its separate mention would be purposeless, because it already ends in *ṛ*. Furthermore, if there were an inclusion of that [root] and those ending in *ṛ*...

And that being the case, in the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ*, the mention of *ṛtaḥ* need not be stated, because this very [term] is carried over [from the previous rule]. Alternatively, even if [the rule were applied to] *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* as well as those ending in *ṛ*, the inclusion of *vṛ* would still be useless, since they end in *ṛ*. Therefore, only those [roots] pointed out by the author of the Vṛtti are to be understood. As for the question "Why say *vṛtaḥ*?", he thinks that one should rather say *uḥ*.
Not in the case of the optative suffix (liṅ). Pāṇini 7.2.39.
"May it spread extensively"—the middle voice (ātmanepada) is used here because the word refers to the object (*karman*).
And before the suffix *sic* in the *parasmaipada* [voices]. Pāṇini 7.2.40.
*Atāriṣṭām*: the root *tṛ* is used in the senses of leaping and crossing over. *Astāriṣṭam*: the root *stañ* means to cover; it takes both voices (*ubhayapadī*) due to the suffix *ñit*.
Before the suffix *san*, [the substitution of *iṭ*] is optional. (Pāṇini 7.2.41)
In this context, the reading *atistīrṣati* in the *parasmaipada* is not appropriate.
The substitution of *iṭ* occurs after the suffixes *liṅ* and *sic* when they belong to the *ātmanepada*.

Regarding the phrase "when an *ātmanepada* [suffix] follows": this is a qualification of *sic* alone, not of *liṅ*, because [the latter] is impossible [in that context]. Nor does this lead to the undesired application [of the rule] even when *parasmaipada* [suffixes] follow, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "after [a suffix] beginning with *val*" (*valādeḥ*). In forms such as *prāvṛṣīṣṭa*, there is *kittva* by the rule "and after *u*" (*uśca*).
And a single substitute for a consonant cluster beginning with *ṛ* is a *guṇa*. (Pāṇini 7.2.43)
In the examples provided, the *ātmanepada* ending is used for both the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*).

In the form *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*, the substitution of *s* [for the initial *k*] occurs by virtue of the rule *samaḥ suṭi*, which states that for the words *sam*, *pum*, and *kān*, *s* should be stated [as the substitute]. Thus, there is the change to *s*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta/ktavatu) following the roots *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*, *dhūñ*, and those ending in an *ūdit* vowel optionally takes the augment *iṭ*.

In this case, since the root *svarati* is *anudātta*, the rule would not apply [to it] by default; however, for the followers of the Taittirīya school, it does apply, hence the option (*vibhāṣā*). This is because the word "optionally" (*veti*) is present, following from the rule *iṭ sani vā*. The phrase "for the sake of excluding *liṅ* and *sic*" means that otherwise, those two suffixes (*liṅ* and *sic*)—which are connected with the mention of "optionally"—would also continue to apply. The phrase "for the sake of excluding *pū* meaning 'impelling'" means that otherwise, because it lacks an *anubandha*, only that specific root (*pū*) would be understood.

If that is the case, then one should simply state "sūṅ. Even so, according to the principle that when there is a choice between a root with a *luk*-vikaraṇa and one with an *aluk*-vikaraṇa, only the one with the *aluk*-vikaraṇa is to be understood, there would be the inclusion of *sūyati* alone, and not *sūti*. The existence of this paribhāṣā is indicated by this very mention of the vikaraṇa. [The mention of the vikaraṇa] is for the purpose of excluding the root *dhū* meaning "shaking" (*dhūvidhūnane*). Otherwise, as before, there would be the inclusion of that [root *dhū*] alone. As in *dhuvita*: due to its being a member of the *kuṭādi* class, it has the *ṅit* designation.

Regarding the rule *svarateḥ*: the scope for this optional alternative (*vikalpa*) is [the forms] *svarttā* and *svaritā*; the scope for the rule *ṛddhanoḥ sye* is *kariṣyati*. When both rules would apply to the suffix *sye* after the root *svar*, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). However, in the case of a *kit* suffix, the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* applies. Now, one might object: "Just as this optional alternative sets aside the prohibition characterized by having a single vowel (*ekāj-lakṣaṇa*) in the case of *tṛc* and other suffixes, would it not likewise set aside the prohibition characterized by a *kit* suffix? It does not set it aside. Why? Because a rule sets aside another only when the latter would necessarily have applied without the former.

Therefore, the status of being an exception (*apavādatā*) belongs to this [rule] only with respect to a prohibition characterized by a single *aṅga*; however, when both [the general rule and the exception] are applicable, the prohibition alone prevails because the section on prohibitions (*pratiṣedhakāṇḍa*) is placed first. This is also indicated by the evidence (*liṅga*): namely, that [Pāṇini] teaches an option (*vikalpa*) in the rule "svṛ-yūṝ-ṇu-bhara-jña-pi-sanām" (A 6.1.194). Otherwise, since the option would already be established by this very [preceding rule], he would not enjoin it again.
In the *Vṛtti*, however, even by the word "conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*), it is intended that the section on prohibitions is indeed placed first, because the result is the same.
And [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *rādhā* and others. 7.2.45.
*radh*, *naś*, *tṛp*, *dṛp*, *duh*, *muha*, *ṣṇuh*, and *ṣṇih*—
these roots beginning with *radh* are recited by the eight groups of scholars among the *divādi* (fourth class) verbs.

Regarding *neṣṭā*: the augment *num* is applied by the rule *masjinaśorjhali*. Regarding *tṛp* and *dṛp*: the augment *am* is optionally applied by the rule *anudāttasya cardupadhasya*. In forms such as *droḍhā*, the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha* occurs by the rule *vā druhamuhaṣṇuhaṣṇihām*.

"Because of the rule regarding *krādīni*. [Objection: But surely this is a restriction (*niyama*) concerning the prohibition; and in the case of roots beginning with *radh*, no prohibition—whether dependent on an affix or dependent on the root-base—applies. Even for those two, *tṛp* and *dṛp*, for which a prohibition would otherwise apply, even if that prohibition is set aside by this [rule] regarding the *liṭ* suffix, this option (*vikalpa*) would still certainly occur, because an option is not fixed. Thus he thinks: whatever absence of *iṭ* there may be, whether based on a prohibition or based on an option, of all that...

"By the rule [beginning with] *kr-ādi*, there is a restriction (*niyama*). And thus, in the subsequent text, the phrase "of the restriction of the prohibition" (*pratiṣedhaniyamasya*) should be understood to mean "of the restriction regarding non-existence" (*abhāvaniyamasya*). As for the word "another" (*apara*): [an objection]—but let it be that the prohibition is stronger; what follows from that? Since the restriction has the prohibition as its object, the restriction is also stronger, so there is no fault. [Therefore,] there must always be the augment *iṭ*.

Since the rule is understood as a restriction—namely, that by virtue of the section on prohibitions, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the roots beginning with *kṛ* alone when the *liṭ* affix follows—it might be thought: "Let there be no prohibition whatsoever for other verbal roots; why, then, should there not be an option?"
The *kuṣ* [substitute] follows *nir*. 7.2.46.

Regarding *niṣkoṣṭā*: the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is by the rule *idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya*. As for the statement "it should be stated as *nisa*": the reason is that *nisa* is recited among the *pra*-type prefixes, and thus there is the specific mention *nirastapati* when *ti* follows; this is the intended meaning. To the question "What is the purpose of this indication?", he says: "of that" (*tasya*). Now, one might object: "Once *ru* has been applied permanently, the *la* substitution will occur [automatically]. To this he replies: "For *nisa*... (*niso hi*).
In place of the genitive case ending *iṇ*, [the suffix] *ṣaṣṭhī* is substituted. (Pāṇini 7.2.47)

Since *iṭ* is already understood from the current context, for what purpose is *iṭ* mentioned again? To this he says: "The mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of making it obligatory (*nitya*). But surely, by the very force of its initial introduction, *iṭ* will be obligatory, since the optionality was already established by the preceding rule? To this he says: "For the introduction... If, then, the mention of *iṭ* is made for the sake of obligatoriness, would not the rule in the subsequent [sūtra] also be obligatory? To this he says: "Only here..."
The augment iṭ is applied after the roots tīṣa, saha, lubh, ruṣ, and riṣ.

Regarding the statement "of the root *iṣ* in the sense of 'desire'": this refers to the root belonging to the *tudādi* class. Regarding "preṣitā": [this is formed] by the rule *eṅi pararūpam*. Regarding "they recite it as having the marker *u* (*uditam*)": the meaning is that, having recited the root in the sense of desire as marked with *u* in the *dhātupāṭha*, they explain that its very inclusion here [in the present rule] is for the purpose of including that same [root]. This indeed is the purpose of the marker *u*, because the optionality of the augment *iṭ* after the suffix *ktvā* is already established by this very rule. Those, however, who do not recite it as marked with *u*, say that the root in the sense of desire is understood here by virtue of its association (*sāhacarya*) with the other [root] marked with *u*.

In both cases, the mere letter *a* is the cause of modification (*vikāraka*). However, according to the *Vārttika*, the inclusion of the root belonging to the *krīyādi* class is also intended here; as it says: "There is a prohibition [of the substitution] when the suffix *śyan* follows the root *iṣ* with the letter *t*. According to that view, all three [roots] are likewise without an indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*).
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots *san*, *iṇ*, *vañc*, *tṛd*, *bhraṃś*, *dambh*, *śri*, *svṛ*, *ūrṇu*, *bhṛ*, *jñapi*, and *san* occurs before the suffix *ni*. (Pāṇini 7.2.49)

Regarding the rule *bhrasjeḥ ekācaḥ*: a prohibition is obtained by the rules *śrayateḥ*, *ugantānāṃ ca sani*, and *grahaguhośca*; however, for the others, the augment *iṭ* is invariably obtained. Thus, this [sūtra] is commenced for forms such as *ardidhiṣati*. In the case of *laghūpadhalakṣaṇe guṇe*, by the rule *ajāder dvitīyasya*, the portion *dhiṣ* undergoes reduplication; however, the letter *r* is excluded by the prohibition *na ndrāḥ*. Regarding *īrtsati*: by the rule *āpjñapyṛdhāmīt*, the vowel *ī*—with *r* following it (*rapara*)—is substituted for the *ṛ*-vowel; then, by the rule *śabdasya dvirvacanam*, the portion ending in *dh* is reduplicated, and here there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*lopo'bhyāsasya*).

*bibhrajiṣati*: [This is derived from the root] *bhrasj*. By the rule *bhrasjo ropadhayo ram anyatarasyām*, the substitute *ram* is optionally applied. *vibhraṣkṣati*: Here, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *vraścabhrasj...* (*vraścādinā ṣatvam*), and the substitution of *k* for *ṣ* and *ḍh* occurs before *si* by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*. *dhīpsati*: By the rule *dambha ic ca*, there is both the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel and the augment *i*. Since the root ends in a consonant (*halantāt*), the suffix is marked with *k* (*kitve*), resulting in the elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*). As in the previous case, there is the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopaḥ*). *yiyaviṣati*: By the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*, the substitution of *i* occurs for the vowel of the reduplicated syllable.

Regarding the root *bhṝñ*: this [root] ends in a long vowel. Thus, in the form *bharaḥ*, the substitution of *ap* occurs. Regarding *sisaniṣati*: due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only after the roots *stu* and *ṇī*," there is an absence of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) here. Regarding *siṣāsati*: because the suffix *san* has undergone *ṣatva*, the *ṣatva* [of the following *s*] occurs here by virtue of that same restrictive rule.

Some [grammarians] hold this view here. However, those who do not read this [sūtra] begin a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Regarding *titāṃsati*: in the alternative view that there is optional lengthening for the root *tan*, there is lengthening. Regarding *pitsati*: by the rule *sani mīmādhu* etc., there is *is*-substitution for the vowel; by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, there is elision of *s*; and as before, there is elision of the reduplication. Regarding *didaridrāsati*—some say—and *didaridriṣati*: in the alternative view where *iṭ* is present, there is elision of the vowel *ā* of the root *daridrāti*.
The substitution of *li* for the root *kliś* occurs before the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 7.2.50)

Regarding the word *kliśitvā*: the suffix *k* is applied by the rule *mṛḍamṛda-*, etc. Since the option [for the *k* suffix] is already established by the rule *udittvāt svaratyādi-*, for what purpose then is the mention of *ktvā*? To this he says: "of the root *kliś* in the sense of 'affliction' (*upatāpe*)."
The affix *iṭ* is applied after the verbal roots *vas* (to dwell) and *kṣudh* (to hunger).

Regarding *uṣitvā*: the *kit* designation is as before; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) because the root belongs to the *yajādi* class; and the *ṣ* substitution occurs by the rule *śāsivasi-* etc. Regarding *vastitvā*: although the citation with the *śap* suffix is intended to exclude the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) form, even in that case, the augment *iṭ* occurs by the general rule for the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*—thus: *vāvasitaḥ*, *vāvasitavān*, *vāvasitvā*. Because [the root] depends on its specific *gaṇa* (class), there is no vocalization.
The substitution of *añc* occurs for the root *añc* when it signifies worship. (Pāṇini 7.2.53)

"Her eyebrows are arched" (*añcitā asya*): the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca*; by the rule *na añceḥ pūjāyām*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is prohibited; and by the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent.
The root *lubh* is used in the sense of "deluding. (Pāṇini 7.2.54)
*Lubhitvā* and *lobhitvā*: there is an option for the *kittva* (the absence of guṇa) by the rule beginning with *ralo vyupadhāt*.
The suffix *as* is applied after a verbal root ending in *i*, as well as after roots ending in *kṛ*, *cṛ*, *chṝ*, *tṛd*, and *nṛt*. (Pāṇini 7.2.57)

The letter *i* here is for the sake of pronunciation, because of the prohibition [of the augment] in the rule *ta-asi-ci*. Therefore, this option applies even to the suffix *sya*. Both *kṛtī* in the sense of cutting—belonging to the *muc*-class—and *kṛtī* in the sense of cutting—belonging to the *rudh*-class—are included. The purpose of the *it*-marker has already been stated. [The roots] *cṛtī* in the sense of harming and tying; *ūcchṛdir* in the sense of shining and playing; *taūtṛdir* in the sense of harming and disrespect; and *nṛtī* in the sense of moving the limbs—the *īt*-marker in these cases functions as before.
The affix *iṭ* is applied after a verbal root ending in *m* when followed by a *parasmaipada* suffix.

Regarding the form *saṃgaṃsyate*: the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule *samo gamyṛcchi*. [The phrase] "of the substitute *iṅ* for *gam*" means that, for this reason, the suffix does not occur in *sañjigaṃsate*; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "belonging to the same word (*samānapadastha*) as the *ātmanepada*": here, however, in forms such as *jigamiṣitevācarati* or *jigamiṣitrīyate*, because the *ātmanepada* is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*), there is no prohibition. And this has been explained by the author of the Vārttika in the case of *prasnavitrīyate*. [The statement] "it is desired everywhere else" is justified by a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*). But how, even when it is desired, is it obtained? [It is obtained] through the split of the rule.

One rule states that the augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *gam* when followed by an affix beginning with *s*. A second rule, "in the *parasmaipada* endings," is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Some say that because a restriction depends on what is of the same class, *iṭ* is excluded from the domain of the *ātmanepada*.

Others, however, think that because of the locative indication in "in the *parasmaipada* endings" (*parasmaipadeṣu*), this meaning results from taking immediate succession (*ānantarya*): if *iṭ* occurs after *gam* before an *ārdhadhātuka* affix beginning with *s* that follows immediately within *tiṅ* endings, it occurs only in the *parasmaipada*; consequently, the exclusion applies only in cases such as *saṅgaṃsyate*.

It might be argued that [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *saṅgaṃsīṣṭa*, nor in *saṃjigāṃta* and so forth, because of the intervention by the suffix *śap*. However, there is no intervention in the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), for a single-substitute is treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) with respect to a preceding operation; thus, even through *sthānivadbhāva*, there is indeed an intervention. Furthermore, in cases such as *saṃjigaṃsiṣyate*, [the rule] would simply not apply at all. Therefore, this must be regarded as a desired result (*iṣṭi*). Hence it was said, "it is desired in this very way. *Padaśeṣa* is the name of a specific type of treatise. Regarding the phrase "by that" (*tena*) and so forth...

This is a refutation of what was just stated; this position has not been established, because it contradicts the *Vārttika*. As it says: "It is established that [the augment] *iṭ* is prohibited for the root *gam* when it occurs within the same word as the *ātmanepada* ending."
The substitution of *iṭ* does not occur after the four roots beginning with *vṛ*.
Because of the use of the plural number and because of the explicit mention of "four," it is understood that the meaning refers to the first [set].
These four, beginning with *vṛt*—namely *vṛtti*, *vṛdhi*, *śṛdhi*, and *syandi*—are the roots starting with *vṛt*.
The root *śṛdhu* is used in the sense of contemptuous sound; the others are well-known. In the examples provided, the Atmanepada is replaced by Parasmaipada according to the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ*.

"It need not be stated that [the rule applies] 'after four'. For what reason? To this he says: "For the mention of *vṛt*," etc. If [the mention of *vṛt*] is for the sake of completing the list beginning with *dyut*, then what follows from the completion of the list beginning with *vṛt*? To this he says: "That very same [reason]," etc. The sense is that there is no distinction between them being mentioned. "Even though it is internal" (*antaraṅga*): the option is internal because it depends solely upon the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes.

But this prohibition is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), because it depends upon specific [letters] such as *s* and others, and because it depends upon the external parasmaipada [suffixes]. Now, one might object: even in other cases such as *vṛt* and so on, the *iṭ* augment characterized by the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes is indeed intrinsic (*antaraṅga*); if you say that its prohibition occurs here by virtue of the force of the explicit statement, then the same would apply to the optional [prohibition]. This is not so; for a rule sublates another only when the latter would necessarily apply (*nāprāpte*). And while the rule "the *iṭ* augment follows an *ārdhadhātuka*" would necessarily apply, the rule characterized by *udic* (i.e., the option) would not.

At most, one might argue that because it is subsequent (*paratva*), the prohibition would override even the *iṭ* characterized by the presence of *ud*. But even that is not so, because a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the internal (*antaraṅga*) and the external (*bahiraṅga*) is impossible. If this is so, how is there a prohibition of that [prohibition] even when the mention of "four" (*caturgrahaṇa*) exists? To this he says: "For when there is the mention of 'four'... When that [mention] exists, there arises the understanding that the prohibition must apply to the dative case (*caturthī*). Otherwise, in the absence of a word denoting a number, there would be no specific restriction even if the prohibition applied to only one [case], and thus nothing would be established.

"Only in the case of *parasmaipada* endings. If this were so, the rule would apply only where a *parasmaipada* ending immediately follows an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix after roots such as *vṛt*—as in *vartsyati* and the like—but it would not apply in cases such as *vivṛtsati*, because of the intervention of the *śap* affix.

Even when a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is indeed an intervention due to the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*); in cases such as *vivṛtsiṣyati* and *vivṛtsayati*, the intervention is directly perceptible. Furthermore, when there is a *kṛt* suffix and the elision of the *parasmaipada* ending, there is not even a trace of the *parasmaipada* character remaining; thus, [the desired result] would simply not occur in those instances. To this he says: "In this case too... This is merely an accepted position (*iṣṭi*). And in cases such as *vivṛtsitriyate*, the solution has already been stated.
And [the substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs] before these [vowels], as well as before *klṛp*. (Pāṇini 7.2.60)

In the examples, the *parasmaipada* ending is applied by the rule *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "even from *klṛp*" and so forth: the intention is that otherwise [the prohibition] would apply only in cases such as *kalpsyati*, but not in cases such as *ciklṛpsitā* or *ciklṛpsa tvam*.

However, in this context, it should rather have been stated as *na vṛdbhyaḥ pañcabhyastāsi ca*; the mention of *klṛp* could indeed have been omitted. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the [prohibition] applying to *tās* after roots like *vṛt* and the rest, because they do not take the *parasmaipada* endings and because [the *tās*] resides in the same word (*samānapada*) as the *ātmanepada*.

In the case of roots that do not take *iṭ*, the suffix *kta* is always *seṭ* (provided with the augment *iṭ*) when it follows a root ending in a long vowel, provided the root is not one of those listed as having an indicatory *ṭ*.
The augment *iṭ*, which would have been required by the rule *krādiniyama*, is prohibited;
this is the derivation of the suffix *ṅīp* starting from the fifth sūtra up to that [point].
Even the acceptance of the instruction mentioned here is set aside;
for even if the suffix *guṇa* were made permanent, how could this [suffix] apply when [the root] ends in *ṛt*?

When the question arises as to where [the rule] "always aniṭ" applies, it is understood that it applies specifically there because of the proximity of *tās*. Alternatively, the word *tāsi* (from the previous sūtra) is understood to carry over. The form *yātā* is introduced for the purpose of demonstrating that [the root] is *aniṭ* in the *tās* suffix.

Regarding the word *lūtvā*: if the term *tāsvat* were not stated, the prohibition would apply to *sthali* (the suffix of the perfect tense) after any root that is invariably *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*). Now, this root *lū* is invariably *aniṭ* before a *kit* suffix because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.2.11] *śryukaḥ kiti*. [Examples of forms with *iṭ* are: *yayiva*, *yayima*. [The rule] *āto lopa iṭi ca* [applies]. The mention of *aniṭ* is for the purpose of qualifying [the word] *nityam* (invariably). If the mention of *aniṭ* were absent, the word *nityam* would qualify only the prohibition itself—[meaning] "it is invariably not present" (*nityam aṅ na bhavati*).

Although this alternative view is not the subject under discussion here, nevertheless, this very mention of *nitya* (obligatory) would indicate that the preceding rule is non-obligatory (*anitya*). However, the mention of *aniṭ* (unaccented) is not for the purpose of excluding [roots] with a *seṭ* augment; how so? It is stated as "like *tāsi*," meaning that just as it does not occur in *tāsi*, so too it does not occur in *thali*. Furthermore, the prohibition in *thali* applies to that which was *seṭ* in *tāsi*, and thus it is made contingent upon *tāsi*. For example: *vidhotā*, *vidhavita*. By the rule beginning with *svarati-*, the *iṭ* augment is optional in *tāsi*.

According to Pāṇini as well, the form *cakramitha* must be admitted; for that root *kram* is not invariably without the augment *iṭ*, since it lacks *iṭ* in the ātmanepada but possesses it in the parasmaipada. The sense of this position is that, according to the rule "in the *thala* suffix, there is invariably the augment *iṭ* after a root that optionally takes *iṭ*," whatever absence of *iṭ* exists—whether based on a prohibition or based on an option—is all regulated by the sūtra governing the *krādi* group. This is the intended meaning.

However, according to the view that—by virtue of the governing rule of prohibition (*pratiṣedhādhikāra*) and the restriction that "the augment *iṭ* does not occur after roots beginning with *kṛ*"—the entire prohibition is indeed set aside, while the optional rule (*vikalpa*) characterized by the *svarati*-group still remains in effect; then both forms, *vidudhotha* and *vidudhavitha*, are possible.

If this is so, it need not be stated that "the root *as* is always without the augment *iṭ*," for even in the case where *as* is optionally *iṭ*-less, this prohibition would still apply; and by the restrictive rule "for Bhāradvāja, after *ṛ*," the option would remain established. This cannot be maintained, because there would be a fault regarding the vowel *svarita*. For even on the side of Bhāradvāja’s view, since that [augment] is prohibited, the form would have to be only *sasvartha*. However, when this prohibition does not apply to the optional *iṭ* in the suffix *thali*, then both forms—*sasvartha* and *sasvaritha*—occur.

Regarding the phrase "tāsvaditi vatinirdeśaḥ": the meaning is that this is an indication by means of the suffix *vat* (the sense of "like that"). If "tāsvat" were not stated, then even if there were a continuation (*anuvṛtti*) of the previously mentioned term "tāsī," only this much would be obtained: "In the case of *tās*, [the augment] *iṭ* does not occur after a root that is invariably without *iṭ*. Consequently, this would undesirably apply even to that *tās* which ends in *-as*, since such a form is inherently without *iṭ*. However, when "tāsvat" is stated, because the suffix *vat* has similarity as its scope, the rule means: "Just as there is no *iṭ* in *tās* for a root of such a nature, so too there is none in *thali*."
The objection that "it ought not to be desired" does not apply at all.

For when the prohibition of the root *tās* (the desiderative suffix) is prescribed in the case of the *thali* suffix, the resulting absence would not be similar [to the original]; rather, it would be the absence of *tās* in the context of *thali*.

Regarding *adhasitha*: they say that because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), this form is already established by the rule *iḍattyartivyayatīnām*. Regarding "also in the subsequent sūtra": by this, he shows that the word *tāsvat* is stated for the sake of the subsequent [sūtras]. As for "for the substitute of *ad*" (*adādeśa*): [an objection] might be raised, "But surely its original locus (*sthānin*) exists in the state of *tās*, and since it possesses the property of having no augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), then by the status of being a substitute, the substitute itself would also possess both existence (*sattva*) and the property of having no *iṭ* (*aniṭ*). This is not so; the status of being a substitute operates only with respect to grammatical operations (*śāstrīya*). And "existence" (*sattva*) is not a grammatical operation.
In the case of an upadeśa [root] containing the vowel *at*, [the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel occurs before the suffix *ya*]. 7.2.62.

The present undertaking is for the sake of those who do not know [the rules]. Regarding *iyaṣṭa*: by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication; by the rule *vraścādiṣṭutvam*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Regarding *cakarṣitha*: the root *kṛṣ* means "to scratch. This root now possesses the vowel *a* once the *guṇa* has been applied, but it does not possess it in its original form (*upadeśa*). Regarding *jigrahitha*: because of the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *sani grahaguhośca*, this root is invariably without *iṭ* in the *san* [desiderative], but not in the *tās* [aorist].
Regarding *ānañcitha*: by the rule *ata ādeḥ* and *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*, the augment *nuṭ* is added; furthermore, by the rule *svaratyādi-sūtra*, *iṭ* is optionally added in the *tās*.
The [substitution] of *ṛ* occurs for [the vowel] of Bhāradvāja. 7.2.63.

Regarding *sasmartha*: the root *smṛ* means "to remember. Regarding *dadhvartha*: the root *dhvṛ* means "to perish. As for the phrase "since [the forms] are already established," etc.: among roots ending in short *a*, *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* are udātta. Even there, *vṛṅ* cannot occur [in this context], because it is ātmanepada. As for *vṛñ*, however, due to its specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*), the augment *iṭ* must occur in the common language (*bhāṣā*) in forms such as *vavartha*. Therefore, this [sūtra] is not applicable for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* for those two. As for other roots ending in short *a* that are invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭaḥ*) in the *tās-* [futures], the prohibition is already established by the rule *acaḥ tāsvat*.

But surely, since the substitution of *guṇa* takes precedence, and once *rapara* has been applied, the form fails to end in *an*, so it would not be established; furthermore, it would not be established by the previous rule either, for there are no words ending in *a* that are taught (*upadeśe*) as having *at* [as their penultimate]. Therefore, the restriction is untenable. Let it then be for the sake of an injunction in cases such as *dadhvartha*.

If this were the case, then in forms such as *sthāyāpaci* and others, there would always be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the two preceding rules; furthermore, in cases such as *jahartha*, there would be the undesirable consequence of an optionality based on the statement "according to Bhāradvāja. In that event, the mention of Bhāradvāja would be made only in the rule *acaḥ tāsvat* (P. 7.2.61), and that very same mention would carry over into the immediately following rule (*na ktvā seṇaḥ*), but would be withdrawn here [in P. 7.2.63]. This is true; however, this Bhāradvāja would then be forced to deviate from his own opinion.

His opinion is as follows: elsewhere than after a root ending in *ṛ*, the augment *iṭ* occurs in forms such as *yayitha* and *pecitha*, but not after a root ending in *a*. However, in the grammatical formulation (*nyāsa*) you have proposed, the opposite of this opinion would be established. If that is the case, then he considers the prohibition to be already established because of the inclusion of the term "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*)—which is drawn back [from a previous rule] into the rule *acaḥ tāsvat*—since [the roots in question] end in a vowel (*ajanta*) in their original enunciation. The restriction is precisely "only after *ṛ*" according to Bhāradvāja; however, the reverse restriction—that it applies only for Bhāradvāja—is not intended.

If it were [the case that the rule applied universally], the recourse to a restrictive rule (*niyamāśrayaṇa*) would be purposeless; rather, on the grounds previously stated, one must resort to its being for the sake of an injunction (*vidhyarthatva*). Regarding the phrase "of the two preceding rules": first of all, the principle that "an operation applies to what follows immediately" is impossible in the case of those roots ending in *ṛ*. As for that which is applicable—namely, the rule *acaḥ tāsvat*—it is only for that that a restriction (*niyama*) would be appropriate. How then can there be an option (*vikalpa*) for both of the two preceding rules? It is thought thus: because this [new] rule is commenced immediately after both [the previous ones], it is understood that, according to Bhāradvāja, among those roots that are invariably non-ṅit (*aniṭ*), the [substitution of *iṭ*] occurs only after a root ending in *ṛ*.

"Not for others"—thus, a restriction (*niyama*) must be adopted in this general form. For if that were not the case: if the *tapara* (the *ṛ*) were not employed, there would be the inclusion of even those nouns ending in *ṛ*; and since those [nouns] are established as *tāsu* (in the locative plural), the rule *tāsvat* would not apply, and consequently, this present rule would serve only as an original injunction (*vidhi*), rather than as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) by virtue of the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*). This is because, when both an injunction and a restriction are possible, the injunction alone is superior—this is the meaning.
The suffix *ap* is optionally applied after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*. (Pāṇini 3.3.16)

*Sasnaṣṭha*, *dadraṣṭa*: by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhalyamakiti*, the augment *am* is added before a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant when it is not marked with *k* or *it*; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is as previously described.
The substitution of *iṭ* occurs for the roots *ṛ*, *dṛ*, *vyay*, and *at*. 7.2.66.

In this context, the mention of *iṭ* is for the sake of clarity. Now, since an option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise apply, why is it not for the purpose of making [the rule] obligatory? To this he says: "For, in the case of prescribing an option... Even so, a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is the subject under discussion; therefore, the mention of *iṭ* might be intended to suspend that [prohibition]. To this he says: "In the case of prescribing a prohibition... [The sūtra: *vasvekājādghasām* (Pāṇini 7.2.67).

*Vasu* is a mention without a case-ending; it means *vasoḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of those that have undergone reduplication": how, then, is this specific restriction obtained when no distinction was stated? It is obtained by the force of the inclusion of *ekāj* (a single-vowel root). For there exists no *ekāj* root that has not already undergone reduplication such that the inclusion of *ekāj* would be for the purpose of excluding it. [Objection: Since the rule *ciri-jiri-cakāśibhyaḥ kāsyanekāj-grahaṇam culumpādy-artham* implies that the suffix *ām* must occur [after these roots], there is no possibility of *vasu* [ending] occurring after them. [Response: However, in the case of *ūrṇoti*, because of its treatment as having the form of *ṇu*, the inclusion of *ekāj* does not exclude it.

But surely, the form *jāgarti* exists, because the suffix *ām* is optional by the rule *uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām*; and even in the Veda, in the passage *jāgṛvāṃso anugman*, there is an absence of reduplication because of the statement "in the Chandas [Vedic language], it should be stated that [reduplication] is optional" (*chandasi vā vaktavyam*) within the section on reduplication. Thus, a single example does not necessitate the inclusion of the term "single vowel" (*ekāj*) [in the rule]. If this were the only purpose, one should have simply said *jāgaternna*, for the comprehension of a direct prohibition is more concise. Or rather, this point is established by logic.

For instance, there is scope for reduplication (dvirvacana) in *paṃpāca*; there is scope for the augment *iṭ* where, once reduplication has occurred, the root is monosyllabic—as in *pecivān*, *ādivān*, *bibhidvān*, and so on. However, when both would apply, reduplication takes precedence due to its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Regarding the phrase "obtained by the rule [beginning with] *ka-*": since the prohibition based on the affix—namely, *neḍvaśi kṛti*—is present everywhere, the augment *iṭ* of *vas* is obtained everywhere solely by the restriction of the rule beginning with *ka-*.

"The inclusion of the term *āt* (long *ā*) is for the sake of [roots] consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*). But surely, when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*), even after the elision of the long *ā*, they would still consist of only one vowel (*ekāc*), so how is this established? To this he says: "For in the case of reduplication... The elision of the long *ā* is conditioned by the presence of the suffix *iṇ*; it does not occur in its absence. Consequently, there is the state of having more than one vowel (*anekāctva*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "even if *ām* is not applied": since the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34) ought to have prescribed the phoneme *au*, the prescription of the phoneme *au* instead indicates that the *ām* augment is not invariably applied to the root *daridrā*. Therefore, this is accepted: *dadaridravān*; in this case, the prohibition *neḍvaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8) indeed applies.

Now, what is the purpose of including *ghasi*? Since, once reduplication has occurred, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) would take place by the rule *ghasibhasor hali ca*, and because the root would then consist of only one syllable (*ekāc*), the desired form would be established even without the mention of *ghasi*. To this he says: "Even of *ghasi*. The phrase "because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*) should also be understood as implying "and because it is obligatory" (*nityatvāt*), since that [elision] is prescribed even when a consonant (*hal*) follows. Regarding the phrase "because it is not a substitute" (*anaṅkatvāt*): even the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply here, because the elision of the penultimate vowel is caused by a consonant (*hal*). However, when the mention of *ghasi* is made, this fault does not arise; thus he says: "But when it is made," etc.
The substitution of *i* occurs for the final vowel of the roots *gam*, *han*, *vid*, and *viś* before the suffix *bhaviṣya*.

*Jaghnavān*, *jaghanvān*. [The rule] "ho hantoḥ ñṇinneṣu" [applies]. By the rule "abhyāsācca," there is the substitution of *k* (the *kutva* change). Regarding "by the root *viś* belonging to the *tudādigaṇa": although there is association (*sāhacarya*) with the root *han* belonging to the *adādigaṇa*, nevertheless, according to the principle of "the subsequent word taking precedence" (*śabdaparavipratiṣedha*), the meaning is that association with *viś* alone is the determining factor. Regarding "of the root meaning 'to know' (*jñāna*)": the meaning is that since the roots meaning "existence" (*sattā*) and "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*) are *ātmanepada*, the suffix *kvasu* is simply impossible for them. *Vividvān*: here, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies to the root *vid* preceded by *vi*. *Sanisasanivāṃsam* || 7.2.69 ||
Because *kvasu* is Vedic, and because the specific sequence [of sounds] is intended to be expressed, this is a formal derivation (*nipātana*) occurring only in the Veda.
The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of a root ending in *ṛ* or *ṝ* occurs before the affix *sya*.

He recalls what was stated in the *svarati-ādi* sūtra—"from this root *svarati*, there is an option," and so forth—by saying, "because of the *veṭ*-ness of *svarati*. That which has an optionally applied (*vā-vikalpita*) augment *iṭ* is called *veṭ*; its state is *veṭ-tvam*, which is to say, its connection with an optional *iṭ*.
The suffix *sakta* is applied after the verbal roots *yam*, *ram*, and *mā*. || 7.2.73 ||
Regarding the form *vyaraṃsīt*: the substitution for the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the rule *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*.

It is appropriate here to provide examples in the dual and plural numbers, for in those cases there is a distinction when the augment *iṭ* is present; however, it was not mentioned in the singular because there is no such distinction there. To this he says: "of *yama* and the others. In the rule *hrmyantakṣaṇa*, the word *iṭ* also continues to apply. As for the example *apāsīt*, it was cited merely to avoid breaking the continuity of the discussion, but there is no actual distinction [between the presence or absence of *iṭ*] in this case.

But surely there is a difference in accent here—namely, that [the form] *mā hi māsīt* should not occur? For if the augment *iṭ* were absent, the word would be acute on the first syllable; but when it is present, because it belongs to the suffix *sic*, it becomes acute by the *cit*-accent, and by the rule "a single substitute for an acute and a non-acute is acute," the word becomes acute on the final syllable. In that case, by the rule "the initial of *sic* is optionally [acute]," there would be acute on the first syllable in one alternative and acute on the final syllable in the other. This difference does not exist, because of the statement "there is an addition [to the rule] regarding the *sic* of roots that lack *iṭ*," so that in forms like *mā hi kārṣam*, as in the alternative case...

Just as there is both initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) and, optionally, final acute accent (*antodāttatva*), so it will be here as well. Regarding *āyaṃsta*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *samudāṅbhyo yamo’granthe*. Regarding *anaṃsta*, since it refers to the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*), the suffix *ciṇ* is prohibited by the rule *na duhastanūnamāṃ yakciṇau*.
The augment *iṭ* is added after the roots √smi, √pūṅ, √rañj, and √vaś when followed by the suffix *san*.

The term *ṛ* is used here to denote the verbal root, not words ending in the vowel *ṛ*, because the suffix *iṭ* is prescribed for *kir* and other such roots later on. Regarding *pipaviṣate*: by the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Regarding *añjijiṣati*: by the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya*, the element *ji* is reduplicated; however, the letter *n* is not reduplicated due to the prohibition in the rule *na ndrāḥ*.
And [the suffix *kyaP*] is applied after [a verbal root ending in] *kira*, following the five [roots]. (Pāṇini 3.1.75)

*Kiraḥ* is a singular form used by way of transference (*vyatyayena*). From the plural *pañcabhyaḥ*, the meaning "and so forth" (*ādi*) is understood. *Kṛ*, *gṛ*, *dṛṅ*, *dhṛṅ*, and *pracchati*—these beginning with *kṛ* are the *kirādayaḥ* among the *tudādi* class. In *pipṛcchiṣati*, there is *kittva* for the suffix *san* by the rule *rudavidamuṣagrahi...* [Pāṇini 1.2.8]. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyā...* [Pāṇini 6.1.16]. Regarding *kira-ti-giri-ty-eri*: however, because the remaining roots are *anudātta*, there is a prohibition [of the long vowel]. As for the statement "they do not desire the lengthening," this is merely an established opinion (*iṣṭi*).
The augment *ruṭ* is added before an affix beginning with a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that starts with a consonant.

In rules such as *rudisvapśvasanijakṣiradādiṣu rudādayaḥ*, when there is a mention of both [the base and the suffix], the ablative (pañcamī) mention is stronger; thus, by the ablative *rudādibhyaḥ*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) of the locative *sārvadhātuke* is substituted. However, the locative mention will serve a purpose later on. [The example] *prāṇiti*: here, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *aniteḥ*. [The example] *svaptā*: but in other cases, the augment *iṭ* must occur after the *ardhadhātuka* suffix.
The word *īśa* [is substituted] for *se*. (Pāṇini 7.2.77)

The root *īś* (to rule), belonging to the first class (*ādādika*), is used here. The form *se* is a citation without case endings. From the form *īśiṣva*, by the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau*, [the substitution of] *v* occurs; because a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the word, this remains simply the word *se*.
And [the substitution of *īṭ*] occurs after the roots *iḍ*, *jan*, and those ending in a vowel, when followed by an affix beginning with a consonant.

The root *īḍ* (meaning "to praise") belongs to the *adādi* class. Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śyan* suffix. However, in the common language (*bhāṣā*), as in the form *jāyase*, because the *śyan* suffix is obligatory, its presence creates an intervention [between the root and the personal ending], and thus the augment *iṭ* does not occur. [This rule applies] also to the root *jan* (meaning "to be born"). Now, one might object: "But that [root *jan*] is parasmaipada; how then can this [ātmanepada form] apply? To this he replies: "In the sense of reciprocal action (*kamavyatihāra*). If, then, the ātmanepada is possible for that [root *jan*] as well, it would follow that only that [root *jan*] is intended to be included, since it lacks an indicatory marker (*anubandha*). [To this we reply: Because of its association with *īḍ*, which also possesses an indicatory marker, the inclusion will be of the ātmanepada [form of *jan*] as well.

Regarding the phrase "some [read] for that purpose": those who do not read it thus, they cause the entire preceding sūtra to be supplied by means of the particle *ca*. Regarding the term "beginning with *sa*": because the letter *s* is indicated with the elision of the locative case (*s* [in place of *si*]), the rule applies to what begins with that.

If, then, *iṭ* is added even to the root *īś* when followed by *dhve*, the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) need not be performed; one should simply state: "After *īś*, *iḍ*, and *jan*, [the augment *iṭ* occurs] before *sedh* and *dhvam*. For in this way, a separate case-ending would not have to be uttered, and the letter *ca* (meaning "and") would not be necessary. To this he replies: "After *īś*, *iḍ*, and *jan*, [before] *sedh* and *dhvam*. This means that it does not occur in the case of *dhvam* in the *laṅ*. But then it would not apply to *dhvam* in the *loṭ* either; to this he replies: "But in the *loṭ*..."
In the case of the optative suffix (liṅ), there is the elision of the *s* of the non-final [augment] *jhi*.

Regarding the rule *sārvadhātuke yo liṅ* ("the *liṅ* that occurs in a *sārvadhātuka* [suffix]"): this is not a locative case in the sense of "following" (*parasaptamī*), because a *liṅ* suffix following a *sārvadhātuka* suffix is impossible. Therefore, it is a locative used for selection (*nirdhāraṇe saptamī*). The singular number is used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*); the meaning is: "among the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes, that which is a *liṅ* and bears the technical designation *sārvadhātuka*. In the form *kuryāt*: by the rule *ata utsārvadhātuke*, the vowel *u* is substituted [for the *ṛ* of the root *kṛ*]; then by the rule *ye ca*, the *u* is elided. Here, there is the elision of the *s* of both *yāsuṭ* and *suṭ*. In the form *kuryuḥ*: [the same process applies].

*jherjum*: [In *kurvanti*] there is the elision of the *s* of *yāsuṭ*; by the rule *usyapadāntāt*, there is the substitution of *ru*. *Kurvīta*: [In this case] there is the elision of the *s* of both *sīyuṭ* and *suṭ*. *Kurvīran*: [Here] *jha* is replaced by *ran*; in this instance, there is the elision of *sīyuṭ* alone.
Therefore, [the suffix] *yat* is applied [to denote the material cause]. (Pāṇini 5.2.80)

The term *sārvadhātuke* (in a sārvadhātuka affix) is understood from the context as being in the genitive case; thus he says: "of the sārvadhātuka [affix] following an aṅga ending in the vowel *a*. This genitive denotes a relationship of part to whole, meaning "of the *ya*-sound which is a constituent part of the sārvadhātuka [affix]. As for the form *iy*: in the sūtra, however, the vowel *ā* is for the sake of pronunciation. In the example *pacet*, once the substitution of *iy* has been made, there is *guṇa* [substitution] with the *śap* suffix, and since it begins with a *val* letter, there is elision of the *val*.

And there is the hearing of the letter *ya*, as in *paceyuḥ*, *paceyam*, and so forth; and in the case of *paceyuḥ* etc. [the following applies]: the scope for the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule is seen in forms such as *cinuyuḥ* and *sunuyuḥ*, whereas the scope for the *iyādeśa* (substitution of *iya*) is seen in forms such as *paced*. However, when both rules would apply simultaneously in a form like *paceyuḥ*, the *iyādeśa* takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratvāt*). If the *pararūpa* were to occur first, the *iyādeśa* would not occur because the sound *yā* would no longer exist. In this way, it would also act as an obstruction to the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a*. This has been stated without relying on the maxim that "exceptions [apply] in the middle" (*madhye'pavādāḥ*).

If one were to resort to that [interpretation], however, it would only be an exception (*bādhaka*) to the elision (*lopa*) of *ataḥ*; the long vowel (*dīrgha*), on the other hand, would certainly occur due to its higher status (*paratva*). [The author] says: "This might be so," and so forth. In the rule for the prescription of the long vowel, the governing context (*prakṛta*) is *turustuśamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke* and *mūsuvostiṅi*. As for the expression *yo yaḥ*, it is a mention without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). The meaning is that within the aggregate *yeyaḥ*, the word *yā* is mentioned without a case-ending. Or, as for *ya iti*: this is the genitive case from the word *yā*, with the elision of the final *ā* by the rule *āto dhātoḥ*. Some, however, read it as *ato yās*, taking it as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in *s*.
A substitute for a *ṅit* suffix following a verbal root ending in /ā/ is long /ā/.

Since a mere *ākāra* (the vowel 'ā') cannot be *ṅit*, the two genitive cases in the rule *ātaḥ ṅitaḥ* are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "of that which has *ā* as its initial part, provided it is *ṅit*. In the examples, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because of the *svarita* accent. Now, it was argued that in the *gāṅ-kuṭādi-sūtra*, because the word *para* is used in a subsequent rule, the term *vat* must be supplied from a locative construction—namely, "like one that is *ṅit* when [the suffix] follows"—otherwise, in forms such as *cukuṭiṣati*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the middle voice due to the *ṅit*-ness of the suffix *san*.

In the rule *sārvadhātukamapit*, that very same [term *ṅit*] is also understood to follow; consequently, the *ṅit*-ness of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix applies only with respect to the operation of what precedes it, and not with respect to its own operation. Therefore, examples such as *apacetām* and *akariṣyetām* (from *laṅ* and *luṅ*) are inappropriate; rather, one should cite appropriate examples such as *mamāte* and *mimāthe*. For even in these cases, there is *ṅit*-ness by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). Thus he says: "In the rule *sārvadhātukamapit*," and so forth. If the marker *t* were not present in *tapara*, then because of the rule *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* (P. 6.4.112), this very rule [of *mimāthe*] would apply later than the elision of the *ā* vowel.
The substitution of *muk* occurs after the verbal root *āp*. (Pāṇini 7.2.82)

In this context, the locative case in *āne* is not purposeful [as a primary referent], whereas the ablative *ataḥ*, having already served its purpose in the preceding rule, is transformed into a genitive by the principle: "When [an element] is specified by the locative, [the operation applies] to what precedes it. Since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), the intention is that the *aṅga* (stem) is qualified by the vowel *a*, and not that the vowel *a* is qualified by the *aṅga*. With this in mind, he says: "This [augment *muk*] is attached solely to the vowel *a*. The meaning is: "*muk* is [the augment] of that *a* which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the *aṅga*. He asks: "What follows from this? and answers: "By not including [stems] taught with a low-pitched vowel (*adupadeśa*)."

In the rule *upadeśe 'j-at-*, [the term *at*] refers to that which is taught [as such] in the original instruction (*upadeśa*). If, however, it were a part belonging to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in *a*, then it would not intervene between that [stem] and its suffix; yet it certainly does intervene with respect to the letter *a* which is a constituent part of that [stem]. Consequently, the correct accentuation would not occur. Furthermore, in the application of accentual rules, a consonant is treated as non-existent. Why? Because the author of the Bhāṣya has taught the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "in the event of the occurrence of a vowel following a *hal* (consonant), the consonant is treated as non-existent. Otherwise, in forms such as *agnicitvān*, there would result the accentuation prescribed by the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*.

If, however, this augment *muk* were inserted in the middle as a non-initial element (*abhakta*) like other suffixal modifications (*vikaraṇa*), then in the absence of an initial element (*abhakte muki*), the vowel would not be subject to accentuation. If, on the other hand, this were treated as an initial element (*parādi*)—that is, as the *muṭ* augment of the suffix *āna*—then in the case of its being an initial element, there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening (*dīrghatvaprasaṅga*).
