For instance, in the form *pacamāna*, the rule "lengthening occurs before a suffix with the marker *ya*" (*ato dīrgho yañi*) would result in the lengthening of the vowel; yet this fault is merely occasional (*pākṣika*). In which case? If [the suffix] is indeed designated as *sārvadhātuka*, then that fault applies. But if it is designated simply by the marker *ṅī*, then there is no fault.

Therefore, this [element] is a partial (*bhakta*) portion of that [vowel], and even there, it is established as *muk* for the vowel *a*. "If it is thus" means: if, because it is a partial portion of the vowel *a*, it is included by the mention of that [vowel]. "One and a half measures" (*adhyardhamātra*): that which has an additional half is "one and a half" (*adhyardhā*); that which has one and a half measures is "one and a half measures. In that case, the rule for the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent of the *l*-suffixes (*lasārvadhātuka*) would also not apply, because in the rule prescribing that [accent] as well, the term is specified with a *tapara* (a vowel followed by *r*).

Regarding this, he says: "The taking of the instruction is performed here. And likewise: "When it occurs even when there are two morae, what doubt could there be regarding the case of one and a half morae?
This is the intended meaning.
The substitution of *īd* occurs for the final vowel of a word ending in *as*. (Pāṇini 7.2.83)

The ablative case ending *āsaḥ* (of the fifth case), whose purpose has already been fulfilled there, effects a transformation of the locative case ending *āne* (of the seventh case) into a genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the preceding rule.
The substitution of *aṣṭan* for *aṣṭā* occurs before all case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Because the instruction is based on the Sūtra, the elision (*allopa*) has not been applied. This is an indication of a specific individual (*vyakti-nirdeśa*); the meaning is that the specific individual *ā* sound, as heard with its non-nasal quality (*niranunāsika*), is being indicated. He states that an indication of a genus (*jāti-nirdeśa*) is faulty: "But [this is] an indication of a form (*ākṛti-nirdeśa*)," for *ākṛti* here means genus (*jāti*), not physical configuration. For when there is an indication of a genus, since the pure genus cannot be taught by itself, the individuals that serve as its substrata are what are prescribed.

In this regard, although there is no possibility of short (*hrasva*) or protracted (*pluta*) manifestations due to the force of the long (*dīrgha*) pronunciation, all long manifestations would nonetheless be applicable. Among those, by virtue of proximity (*antarya*), only the nasalized (*anunāsika*) manifestation would occur; consequently, the long vowel resulting from its coalescence with the preceding [nasal] would also be nasalized. Furthermore, the phrase "optionally" (*vikalpena*) and so forth is explained in that very same place [in the commentary], where it is shown how the mention of the long vowel and the reference to the form with the *āt* substitution serve as indicative marks (*liṅga*) for this meaning. Moreover, the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*) is intended here.

Because of the rule stating, "In the section on *aṅga* (bases), [the substitution applies] to that [stem] and its following member," and because of the use of the singular number [in the sūtra], the formal word-form (*svarūpa*) is intended to be grasped, not the meaning; therefore, the substitution occurs even when *aṣṭan* is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). Since there too the substitution is optional, one also finds forms such as *priyāṣṭā*, *priyāṣṭānau*, and *priyāṣṭānaḥ*. Furthermore, in the domain of the technical designation *bha*, if the substitution of *ā* (for the final vowel) takes place, they accept the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140), resulting in forms such as *priyāṣṭaḥ paśya*; however, in the alternative case where the substitution of *ā* does not occur, there is elision of the *a* and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for *ṣṭu* (by Pāṇini 8.4.41), resulting in forms such as *priyāṣṭnaḥ*.
The substitution of *hal* occurs in place of *rāy-* before a case-ending beginning with a consonant.
The section governing case endings (*vibhakti-adhikāra*) extends prior to the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114). This textual portion should be read at the end of the preceding sūtra:
*yuṣmadasmador anādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86).

Regarding *yuṣmadasmad*: in the fifth case (*pañcamī*), the rule *at* (Pāṇini 7.1.29) prescribes the substitution of *at* for *bhyas*. One might object that this substitution should not occur here because of the governing context of the rule *halī* (Pāṇini 7.3.103), which restricts operations to contexts where a consonant follows. However, there is no substitute for *bhyas* that begins with a consonant; rather, this is the substitute *abhyam*. The phrase "in the subsequent [rule]" means that the substitution of *yat* (the replacement of *d* by *y*) by the rule *yo'ci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89) should not apply to the substitutes [of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] in forms such as *tvam* and *aham*. Furthermore, it is for the sake of establishing the status of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) according to the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90). Therefore, it is performed right here, as there is no difference in terms of brevity (*laghu*).
And [the suffix] *dvitīyā* [is applied] in the second case. || 7.2.87 ||
In the examples, the substitution of *am* for the case endings *ṅe* and *prathamayoḥ* occurs according to the rule *am*.
And [the substitution of *au* for *as*] occurs in the first case dual in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "of you two" (*yuvayoḥ*): [one might object] that the substitution of *y* (by the rule *yo'ci*) will be the sublater here, even though it occurs in the first dual case. In that case, however, the elision of the final syllable (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) would be the sublater. If, on the other hand, the elision is sublated by a specific rule (*vacanāt*), then the substitution of *y* should also be sublated. Or else, according to the maxim of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāyena*), there would be a sublation of the substitution of *y* alone.
That which ends in a vowel [is called a pada]. 7.2.89.

"It is possible that this [substitution] could not be performed. How so? The substitution of *ya* prescribed when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) has not been specifically indicated is the general rule (*utsarga*); in that very context, the substitution of *ā* before a consonant-initial ending is the exception (*apavāda*). For example: *tvat*, *mat*. And by the rule "and of the singular," there is the substitution of *ad* for *ṅasi*.
There is elision of the remaining [suffix]. (Pāṇini 7.2.90)

The *śeṣa* (remainder) is that which is other than what has been employed [in the preceding rules]. There is a summary verse for this: "Of the fifth," and so forth. Those dual endings (*advivacana*) belonging to the fifth case and the others—this is the *śeṣa*; in that *śeṣa*, elision (*lopa*) is prescribed. The term "dual endings" should be understood as being relative to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*). However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), even the dual—as in "yuvaṃ vastrāṇi"—is indeed *śeṣa*.

The inclusion of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is for the sake of clarity. How so? [Without it,] there would be elision (*lopa*) in every case of a case-ending (*vibhakti*). That [elision] would be an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ya* and *va* when no specific case-ending has been prescribed. Furthermore, the substitution of *ā* before a consonant beginning with a *hal* would also be an exception to this [elision]. Thus, the substitution of *āt*, the substitution of *ya*, and elision would be established without confusion. However, even if the mention of "remainder" were not made, the mention of the vowel (*aj-grahaṇa*) must indeed be performed for the purpose of distinguishing the respective domains of the substitution of *ya* and elision. Regarding the phrase "characterized by conjunction" (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*): the fact that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in the vowel *a* is brought about by the conjunction of the case-endings.

If, therefore, *ṭop* were the cause, it would obstruct their conjunction. This was stated while accepting that [the word *ṭop*] possesses feminine gender like words such as *tyad* and so on; now, however, he says "or in the absence of gender" (*jaliṅge vā*), meaning that gender itself does not exist [in this case].

"But some," etc. They maintain this [position] precisely for the sake of excluding the *ṭāp* suffix. How so? The question is: where neither the vowel *ā* nor the semivowel *y* has been prescribed, that is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*); in that case, the elision (*lopa*) being prescribed would logically apply only to the final [element], according to the rule *alo 'ntyasya*. Keeping in mind the previously mentioned redundancy of the term "remainder," he says: "to be stated later," etc. That for which the substitutes (*ādeśāḥ*) are to be stated later is "that for which the substitutes are to be stated later. He asks: "But what is that? and answers: "And those," etc.

That which is other than those ending in *map* is called *śeṣa*, and that [term] refers only to *ṭi*. In this context, the locative case in the rule "there is elision (*lopa*) here" is intended to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the substituendum (*sthānin*). Why, then, is "elision" (*lopa*) stated again, since this would already be established by the designation of *tyadādi*? It is not established; for there is a rule stating, "the *tyadādi* stems end in *dvi*. Furthermore, when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are used as secondary members (*upasarjana*), the substitution of *tyadādi* is not established. However, in the view that the elision of *ṭi* applies, the rule must certainly be commenced.
[The substitution of *ṇatva* applies] up to the end of the word. (Pāṇini 8.4.1)

Because the term *maparyantam* is specified as the substitute for a constituent part (*avayava*), it is understood that the genitive case in *yuṣmadasmadoḥ* denotes a relationship between a whole and its parts (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). That which has *m* as its final limit or boundary is *maparyanta*. Although both [words] have two such limits ending in *m*, the singular number is used here with the intention of not making a distinction between them.

"What does 'to the end of the map' mean? This question arises because if the substitution were applied to the two composite wholes (*samudāya*), there would be no fault, since the substitutes themselves would also end in *a*. [The answer is: "It should not apply to that which has the augment *akac*. Since that which falls in the middle of a form is included by the mention of that form, there is the possibility of the rule applying. [Furthermore,] "It should not apply to the whole. Why was it not stated as "it should not apply to that which has *akac*"? Because it was stated in the rule for the introduction of *akac* that in forms such as *tvayā*, *mayā*, *tvayi*, and *mayi*, the augment *akac* is added to the *subanta* (inflected nominal) before the final vowel. [Otherwise] an undesirable form would result; namely, the undesirable forms *tvyā* and *myā*.

Now, for what purpose is the inclusion [of the word *parigrahaṇa*]? One might simply say "of that which ends in *m*" (*māntasya*), meaning "of that portion of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* which ends in *m*. To this he replies: "Since it is already established by the rule 'of that which ends in *m*,' [the mention of] 'in this' (*asmin*) [is for a specific purpose]. This means that in the absence of substitution for the form with the *kac* suffix (*sākacka*), there would otherwise be the forms *yuvakām* or *avakām*. [The phrase] "for the sake of indicating the limit" (*avadhidyotanārtham*) means: "I indicate the limit by means of the word 'paryanta' (end/boundary)."

Otherwise, if it were stated as *māntasya* ("of that which ends in -m"), it would be possible to assume that *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are qualifiers in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, because of the connection with each [word] individually, the singular number would apply; consequently, the substitutes would occur only where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in -m. Even if a lack of apposition (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) were intended, nevertheless, since there is no distinction in the case where they end in -m, the substitutes would not occur. Moreover, the treatment of a word as if it possessed its own designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is prohibited by the rule concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*).

However, when the word *paryanta* (limit) serves to indicate a boundary (*avadhi*), by the very power of its inclusion, the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are understood to apply even to the parts [of the compounds] containing *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; thus, the substitution is established everywhere. Alternatively, if the relationship is construed through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then by the force of the inclusion of the word *pari*, the rule "that which is treated like that which has a designation does not [apply] to what is not a nominal stem" (*apratipadikena*) does not take effect, and consequently, the substitutions are established even for those forms ending in *-m*.

Another says: the word "paryanta" (limit/end) implies that something remains; therefore, because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, the connection occurs only through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *-m*, the substitutes do not occur at all; this is what is meant by the statement, "lest [the substitutes] occur when [the stems] end in *-m*. The meaning is: "lest they occur precisely when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *-m*, or even in that case, let them not occur. But where do *yuṣmad* and *asmad* end in *-m*? He says: "in the case of the two [stems] ending in the causative suffix *ṇi*."

He speaks of you: *yuṣmayati*; he speaks of us: *asmayati*. When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) undergoes the treatment of the suffix *-iṣṭhan*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant). Regarding the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, because this occurs under the heading of the singular number, the substitutes *tvam* and *aham* do not apply. When the *kvip* suffix is applied, there is elision of the *ṇic*. Now, one might object: "The substitutes [for *tvam* and *aham*] must occur before case-endings (*vibhakti*), but here there is an intervention caused by the status of the elided element (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *ṇic*. To this he says: "And regarding the status of being a substitute... The author of the *Bhāṣya* maintains that because the *ṇic* has been elided by the *kvip* suffix, its elision does not function as a substitute (*sthānivat*) in this context.

In this regard, for one who maintains that the substitutes also apply when [the suffixes] are present at the end of a word (*mānta*), these are the examples according to that view. Because they are *kṛdanta* (words ending in primary suffixes), they take case endings; and since a form modified by a partial change is not considered different from the original, the substitutes for the case endings dependent on *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, as well as the substitutes for the stems such as *tvad* and *mad*, occur there in instances governed by rules such as "tvāhau sau" (Pāṇini 7.2.94).

Elsewhere, there is elision (*lopa*) except before case-endings that are substitutes; *yatva* occurs before vowels beginning with *aj*, and *ātva* before consonants beginning with *hal*. Thus: *tvam*, *yuṣām*, *yūyam*, *yuṣām*, *yuṣām*, *yuṣān*, *yuṣyā*, *yuṣābhāyam*, *yuṣābhiḥ*, *tubhyam*, *yuṣābhyām*, *yuṣabhyam*, *yuṣat*, *yuṣābhyām*, *yuṣat*, *tava*, *yuṣyoḥ*, *yuṣākam*, *yuṣyi*, *yuṣyoḥ*, *yuṣāsu*. The same should be understood for *asmad* as well. However, when the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is adopted with respect to the limit of *map* (i.e., the *map*-ending forms), because there is nothing following *ma*, there is no elision, and thus forms such as *yuṣmabhāyam* and *yuṣmad* arise.

But when *tvām* and *mām* are derived by analyzing them as *tvām ācaṣṭe* and *mām ācaṣṭe* and applying the suffix *kvip*, then—after the application of the rules *pratyayottarapadayoś ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98) which change *tvam* and *mam* to *tvad* and *mad*, and *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163) which maintains the original stem form—the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel) does not occur. Consequently, by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), a *vṛddhi* strengthening takes place. If the base (*aṅga*) were already established [before the suffix], then there would be no substitution of *vad*. Thus, having reached the forms *tvad* and *mad* (from *tvāds* and *māds*), since the condition "ending in *maparyanta*" (*maparyantābhāvāt*) is absent, the rule *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94) and others do not apply; therefore, in the case of *vṛddhi*, the forms become *tvām* and *mām*.

In the alternative view, however, [the forms] are *tvam* [in the nominative singular]. In the dual, [they are] *tvām* [in the accusative], and *tvam* [in the nominative]. In the second case (accusative) and those that follow, however, [the forms are]: *tvām*, *tvām*, *tvān*; *tvayā*, *tvābhyām*, *tvābhiḥ*; *tubhyam*, *tvābhyām*, *tvabhyam*; *tvat*, *tvābhyām*, *tvat*; *tva*, *tvayoḥ*, *tvākam*; *tvayi*, *tvayoḥ*, *tvāsu*. The same applies to *asmad* as well.

When, however, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to forms ending in the dual number, then too one says *yuṣmayati* or *asmayati*; because the case endings are absent, the substitutions *yuv-* and *āv-* do not occur. Since there is no single referent (*ekārthatva*), the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* also does not apply. But when a case ending is present, the substitutes *yuv-* and *āv-* do occur. In instances such as *tvam* and *aham* with the nominative singular (*su*), those very forms remain. For those who do not accept the substitutes for the forms ending in *-m*, according to the view that there is elision of the remainder (*śeṣalopa*) in the nominative singular, the forms become *yuṣam* and *asam*.

In the alternative case, however, [the forms] are *yuṣmām* and *asmām*. This should be understood similarly elsewhere as well. This logic of the grammatical procedure is profound; therefore, we desist.
The substitutes *yuvām* and *āvām* are used for the first and second person dual endings.

Regarding the statement "the term *dvivacana* refers to the meaning": the word *vacana* means "that which expresses" (*vakti*), with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Thus, *dvivacana* means "in the expression of two meanings. This word ends in the nominative dual; hence he says: "in the dual [expression] of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. But what are these? He says: "in the domain of the denotation of two objects. And this is understood from the inclusion of the term *vacana*. Why is it not stated simply as "in duality"? Because the rule already specifies "in an inflectional ending" (*vibhaktau*); the meaning is: "in that inflectional ending which occurs when there is duality."

He demonstrates what is achieved when the term *artha* (meaning) is included, using the words "when" (*yadā*). The sense is that if the technical dual number were taken [as the basis for the rule], then because it would be absent in this particular context, the substitutes *yu* and *vau* would not apply, resulting in an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) of the rule. The phrase "they are not superseded by other substitutes" means that the sublation (*bādha*) will be explained precisely in the section concerning "sublation due to posteriority" (*paratvāt*). An example of such sublation by another substitute occurs in the forms *atikrāntau yuvām* (having surpassed you two) in the nominative singular (*sau*) and nominative dual (*jasi*), where the rule is superseded by other specific substitutes.

Even if the technical term *dvivacana* (dual) were accepted [in the previous rule], the desired result would still be established; thus, there is a departure from the primary [meaning]. Furthermore, even if the technical term were accepted in the subsequent [rule], the result would still be established; thus, there is a departure from the primary [meaning]. Moreover, this same reason applies to the departure from the dual in what follows as well. In that context, one should observe the various substitutions for case-endings (*vibhaktyādeśa*) as appropriate, such as: the substitution of *āt* before endings beginning with a consonant (*hal*) when no other substitute has been prescribed; the substitution of *yat* before endings beginning with a vowel (*aj*); elision (*lopa*) in the remaining cases; and the substitution of *am* for the endings *ṅe* and *prathamā*, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because of posteriority": the scope of *tvāhādi* (the forms *tvam*, *aham*, etc. is when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* refer to a plurality of objects—as in *atikrānto yuṣmān* ("one who has surpassed you all") or *atitvam*, *atyaham*. The scope of *yuvā* and *āvā* is when there is a dual sense—as in *yuvām* ("you two") or *āvām* ("we two"). When both [sets of rules] apply simultaneously, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *yadā tu*: the sense is that if the technical (pāribhāṣika) definition were accepted, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as that [definition] would also apply in those cases. For example, in *atikrāntau tvām* and *atitvām*, the substitution of *ā* occurs by the rule *prathamāyāśca dvivacane bhāṣāyām*. This example is cited assuming that the technical definition is intended here. However, even if the meaning (*artha*) were accepted there, there would still be an over-extension in the case of multiple referents; thus he says: *atikrāntau yuṣmān*. Here, the substitution of *ā* is as before. It should be understood in this way: *atiyuṣmām*, *atiyuṣmābhyām*, *atiyuṣmayoḥ*. The same applies to *asmad*.
The substitutes *yūyam* and *vayam* are applied in place of the second-person and first-person plural pronouns before the suffix *jas*.

Regarding the term *paramayuṣmabhyam*: here, the application of the suffix *pāramya* (the state of being supreme) should be understood according to what is possible. The rule of "finality" (*tadantavidhi*) applies here, because of the statement in the section on *aṅga* (bases): "and of that [base] and its subsequent member. Even when it refers to that which ends in [the base], it does not apply to everything, because of the governing rule: "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, up to the end of the stem" (*maparyantasya*).
The forms *tvā*, *vām*, and *vaḥ* [are substituted for the second person pronoun] when followed by *au*, *sāu*, and *sau*.

Regarding the word *tvam*: although the substitution of *tvā* is established here by the rule *tvamāv ekavacane*, nevertheless, the substitution of *ah* must first be prescribed. In that case, if it were stated as *ahaḥ sau*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it applying to *yuṣmad* as well; whereas if it were stated as *asmado 'haḥ sau*, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, even in this instance, the substitution of *tvā* alone should be prescribed. Furthermore, in the case of *atitvam*—meaning "one who has surpassed you two" or "one who has surpassed you all"—there is not even a suspicion of the application of the *tvā* substitution.
The substitution of *tvam* occurs for *yuṣmad* in the singular number.
The phrase "the singular number" is an indication of the meaning, and so forth; this is to be construed in accordance with the statement that "the dual number" is an indication of the meaning.

He demonstrates what is intended regarding the apprehension of the meaning with the words "then" (*tadā*). However, if only the technical singular number were apprehended here, there would be no [application], resulting in an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). But in the case of *atitvām*, even then, this serves as an example for the rule that "the forms *tvam* and *mām* occur. Thus, *atitvām*; the substitution of *ā* (for *tva*) is as before. In the same way, other examples should be cited. This [rule] also connects with *atitvam* and *ati-aham*. Likewise: *atiyūyam*, *atitubhyam*, *atitava*. The same applies to the stem *asmad*.

The connection with the form *atitvām* is indeed clear: *atitvām*, *atitvān*, *atitvābhyām*, *atitvābhiḥ*, *atitvābhyaḥ*. *atitvām*, *atitvayoḥ*, *atitvākam*. *atitvayi*, *atitvayoḥ*, *atitvāsu*. The same applies to the stem *asmad*.

Immediately following this, when the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad* refer to duality or plurality while the meaning of the compound is singular, then the suffixes *tvam* and *au* do not occur. For example: *atiyuvām* (one who has surpassed you two) and *atyāvām* (one who has surpassed us two); *atiyuṣmān* (one who has surpassed you all) and *atyasmān* (one who has surpassed us all). This should be understood in the same manner; however, it is not explicitly stated here because it is already implied by what precedes it.
And [the substitution of *na* for the final letter of the root] occurs before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*, and before a word that follows as a secondary member (*uttarapada*).

"Regarding those two occurring in the singular number" means regarding those whose domain is the expression of a single object (*ekārthābhidhāna*). This is a statement concerning the actual state of affairs (*vastu*), not a statement concerning the literal meaning of the word; for the term *ekavacane* [in the rule] ends in the nominative dual. In the case of *tvadīya*, the designation *vṛddha* applies by the rule *tyadādīni ca*; from a *vṛddha* [base], the suffix *cha* is added. In the case of *tvattara*, there is a connection with the sense of "being preeminent" (*pāramya*) or "excellence" (*prakarṣa*).

"Because of the governing rule (adhikāra) 'in a case-ending' (vibhaktau). Now, one might object: "In the preceding sūtra, 'in a case-ending' was not intended; how then could that which continues from [the previous rule] up to the end of the section on *vṛddhi* not be connected? Even so, the division of the yoga (yogavibhāga) need not be made. One should simply make a single yoga: "tvam and *mā* in the singular, [and these replacements occur] in a suffix or a subsequent member of a compound" (*pratyayottarapadayoḥ*). For in this way, the particle *ca* would not need to be used. But this cannot be done; for if it were stated thus, a correspondence according to order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) would result: [the replacement of] *yuṣmad* in a suffix, and [the replacement of] *asmad* in a subsequent member.

Thus [it is argued]. Now, even if the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) were to be made, since there is equality between the two causes, why would the correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*) not occur? No, this is not a fault; for the particle *ca* (and) is employed here, and it will conjoin both causes with respect to both [rules].

"Now, if [it is argued]..."—this is the challenger (*codaka*). [He explains: "That which occurs between the base and the suffix, or between the preceding and following words, is the 'intervening' (*antarvartin*) case-ending. He refutes this, saying: "This cannot be so"—the word "to obtain" (*labdhum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He asks: "For what reason? and replies: "Because that [case-ending] must undergo elision (*luk*). Elision occurs by the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ*. [The phrase] "They are internal" (*antaraṅgau*), etc., is the challenger's statement.

Because it depends solely on the case-ending (*vibhakti*), [the substitution of *ś* for *s*] is *antaraṅga*; however, the elision (*luk*) is *bahiraṅga*, as it occurs later, depending on the suffix, the subsequent member of the compound (*uttarapada*), and the verbal root (*dhātu*), once the status of being a verbal root and a nominal stem (*pratipadika*) have already arisen. Even though this [elision] is obligatory (*nitya*), nevertheless, between an obligatory rule and an *antaraṅga* rule, the *antaraṅga* alone is stronger. As it has been said: "When opposing rules—namely, those that are subsequent (*para*), obligatory (*nitya*), *antaraṅga*, or directly stated (*pratipada*)—occur together, among them, the subsequent one is stronger. This is what is meant by the phrase "this very [rule]," and so forth.

The rebuttal: He states "by that" (*tena*) to show the purpose of this teaching. By the first word "etc. (*ādi*), forms such as *gomatyati* are included; by the second, the elision of long vowels and the elision of *hal-ṅy-ādi* suffixes are included. For if there were elision of *hal-ṅy-ādi*, then by the rule of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), *num* and so forth would indeed occur. However, in the case of *luk*-elision, because of the prohibition of "characterization by the suffix" by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, it does not occur. He states another purpose of this teaching: "And thus... (*evaṃ ca*).

He raises an objection again with the word "atha" (now): for something serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only when there is no other purpose; yet here there is a purpose—namely, the sublation (*bādhana*) of these very substitutes such as *tvāhā* and so on. Since this purpose exists, an indication (*jñāpana*) is not tenable. He provides the reply: "by way of the persistence or non-persistence of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*)."

Expressions such as *gomatpriya* are established in the world as correct forms (*sādhubhāva*). If this [rule] were understood as being for the purpose of subverting other substitutes (*ādeśāntara*), those forms would not be included; yet they must be included, since grammar is rooted in actual usage. Therefore, with respect to them, it is not appropriate to understand this rule as being for the purpose of subverting other substitutes.

Another says: If this [rule] were intended for the purpose of subverting other subsequent rules (*ādeśāntara*), then the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "ending in *map*" would be meaningless. Why? Because exceptions (*apavāda*) occupy the same location as their general rules (*utsarga*), as is observed in the case of *śyan* and others. This is not a fixed rule—that exceptions occupy the same location as their general rules—because there are counter-examples in the case of *śnam* and others. For indeed, *śna*, *bahuc*, and *kac* do not occupy the same location as *śap* and the others.

Therefore, if it must necessarily be stated that [the suffix] *upapatti* occurs, it should be stated thus: "In this case, however, *tvāhādi* also recurs up to the end of *map*" (*maparyanta*). Since the exclusion of those [suffixes] is already established by the recurrence of *tvāhādi* alone, the recurrence of the phrase "up to the end of *map*" serves to bring about what has not yet been obtained; thus, it is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned point.

We, however, say: one must continue to supply the phrase "of that which ends in *map*" (*maparyantasya*) and thereby enjoin the substitutes for it. For if these substitutes were *antaraṅga* (internal), then since a word ending in *map* could never occur after a suffix or a second member of a compound, the prescription of those substitutes would be untenable; thus, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the stated meaning.
In the feminine gender, the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* replace *tri* and *catur*.

"The qualification [applies] only to the three and four," because that is what is heard in the scripture (*śrutatvāt*). "Not for the member (*aṅga*)," because of the opposite case (*viparyayāt*). He asks, "What is established by this? and says: "By this... [The forms] *priyatisā*, *priyatisrau*, and *priyatisraḥ*. In *priyatisā*, there is no *anaṅ* [substitution], because of the rule *ṛduśanaspurudaṃso'nehasāṃ ca*. In *priyatisnau*, although the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ* [prescribes] *guṇa*, the substitution of *r* (by the subsequent rule) overrides even that *guṇa*. [The form] *priyatisṛ*.

By the inclusion of the term *it* in the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*, it is indicated that even when a suffix is elided by *lumat* (P. 1.1.63), the suffix-stipulation (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) sometimes still applies. Consequently, although the elision of the case-endings *su* and *am* from a neuter noun is compulsory by *svamornapuṃsakāt* (P. 7.1.23), the substitution of *tisṛ* takes place [before the elision]. Thus we have *priyatisṛṇī*. Regarding the reading found in some texts—"the augment *num* occurs by prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) before the substitution of *ra*"—it means that the suffix *ka* prescribed by *nadyṛtaśca* (P. 5.4.153) does not apply; the intention is that in that rule, the word *ṛtaḥ* refers to a stem ending in *ṛ* at the stage when it is being compounded.

The reason for the absence [of the suffix] is stated as "because it is the substratum of a case-ending," and so forth. Thus, first of all, by qualifying *tricaturaḥ* with the word *striyām*, the demonstration of the avoidance of under-extension (*avyāpti*) has been shown.

He states that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is also avoided with the words "And when... (*yadā ca*). Regarding *tisṛkā*: the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), denoting smallness, contempt, or as a proper name (*saṃjñā*). In that case, since the case-ending would be elided, the substitution of *tisṛ* (for *traya*) which is prescribed there would not occur; hence this statement [of the rule]. On this point, some hold that because it ends in a primary derivative suffix (*svārthika-pratyaya*), the word *tisṛkā* is a proper name (*saṃjñā*) ending in the plural. Others hold that this is a conventional name (*rūḍhi*) for a certain village, and thus there is no occasion for the plural.

Regarding *catasraḥ*: just as in the case of *priyatisrau*, where the substitution of *r* occurs by overriding the *guṇa* [substitution] prescribed for the *savanāmasthāna* [cases], so too would it apply in the *ṅi* [locative singular] case; and accordingly, the author will cite *priyatisrī* as an example of the *r* substitution even in the *ṅi* case in the subsequent sūtra, and will also state a prior prohibition (*pūrvapratiṣedha*) there. On this point, they say: "From this very indication, the substitution occurs only when the meaning is predominant; however, here, because the phonetic form itself is predominant, the *guṇa* applies in its absence. Thus: *catasraḥ*.

In this case, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), when the final syllable is acute by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*, there would follow the acute nature of the suffix *śas* by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*; however, that is set aside by the accent of the irregular formation (*nipātanasvara*). Just as the accent of the irregular formation sets aside the accent of *śas*, so too [it sets aside] the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*.

He states that [the rule] would even override the accent of the case-ending (*vibhaktisvara*) there, saying: "But in the case of *catasṛṇām*," etc. He states the reason for this: "By virtue of the inclusion of the term 'beginning with a consonant' (*halādi*). In that context, the sole purpose of including the term 'beginning with a consonant' is to exclude the form *catasraḥ paśya*; nothing else. And this has been demonstrated in that very place.

If the accent of an *nipātana* (irregular formation) were also to supersede the accent of a case-ending (*vibhakti*), then even without the mention of *hal*, the accent of the case-ending would not occur; what, then, is the purpose of including the mention of *hal-ādi*? Its inclusion serves to indicate that the accent of the case-ending supersedes the accent of the *nipātana*. Others, however, say that from the very mention of *hal-ādi*, it is understood that in forms such as *catasraḥ* and *paśya*, the rule *caturaḥ śasi* does not apply.

If [the word *catasṛ*] were [already] acute-accented, then by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*, the case-ending would necessarily be acute; therefore, the mention of "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*) would be useless for the purpose of excluding that [application]. Consequently, the substitution of the initial acute accent [for *catur*] need not even be prescribed. In that case, since the word *catur* is [already] initial-acute, when the substitution of *catasṛ* occurs [by *caturanaḍuhorāmudāttaḥ*], the case-ending in *catasṛṇām* becomes acute by the rule *ṣatricaturbhyo halādiḥ*.
The substitution of *ṛ* occurs for *aci* (a vowel) following *ṛt* (the phoneme *ṛ*). || 7.2.100 ||

"By *pūrvasavarṇa*, *utva*, and so forth": in the case of *tisraḥ paśya*, this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*. In the case of *priyatisnaḥ svam*, it is an exception to the rule *ṛta ut*. In the case of *priyatisni*, *priyatisnau*, and *priyatisnaḥ tiṣṭhanti*, it is an exception to the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ* regarding *guṇa*.

Now, one might object: "In cases where another rule does not apply—such as *priyatisnā*, *priyatisne*, and *priyatisnoḥ*—the form is already established by the rule *iko yaṇ aci* alone; therefore, this [new] rule is commenced for the domain of that other rule. In that case, it is correct to say that 'intermediate exceptions set aside preceding rules,' and thus it sets aside both the substitution of *u* (*utva*) and the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*). However, regarding the domain of *guṇa*, because it is subsequent, *guṇa* itself would occur. To this, he says: "For even though it is subsequent... and so forth.

"What is the purpose of [specifying] *ṛtaḥ*? This question arises because, since *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are understood to carry over [from the previous rule], the desired result would be established by the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) alone. [The answer is: "It is for the sake of ensuring the application (*pratipatti*) of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*. The meaning is that the substitution of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* should occur even before vowel-initial case-endings. For otherwise—if *ṛtaḥ* were not stated—this substitution would apply only to *tri* and *catur*, as they are specified in the genitive case; and since this [substitution] is prescribed where *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* themselves do not yet apply, it would consequently become an exception (*apavāda*) to those two.
In place of *jarā*, the substitute *jaras* may optionally be applied.

Regarding the example *atijarām̐si*: when the form *atijara-i* is established, if the augment *num* were to occur first, it—being an integral part of the stem (*aṅgabhakta*)—would not intervene between the stem and the suffix. However, it would indeed intervene after the word *jarā*, which is a constituent part of that stem. Consequently, even though the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies, the substitution of *jaras* for the word *jarā* would not take effect; for according to the principle that "substitutes apply to what is explicitly mentioned," the substitute *jaras* is prescribed to replace the word *jarā* which is a constituent of the stem ending in *jara*, immediately preceding the case-ending. Thus, the desired result would not be obtained.

Even so, there would still be the audible presence of *num* after the letter *s*. Therefore, because it is subsequent, the substitution of *jaras* must be desired first. Once that has been applied, *num* occurs by virtue of the word ending in a *jhal* consonant. In the case of *atijarasam paśya*, where *atijara-am* is the state of the form, since a modification of one part does not alter the identity of the whole, the substitution of *jaras* for the word *jara* is effected; subsequently, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* would apply. Nor is there any occasion for the substitution of *am* at that time, because the word no longer ends in *a*.

[Objection: But surely, since the word *atijaras* ends in an *a*-vowel, it would not be correct for the elision (*luk*)—which had been superseded in that state by the substitution of *am*—to apply again, because its opportunity has passed (*bhraṣṭāvasaratvāt*). [Response: This is not so; here the substitution of *am* does not actually take effect, as it is superseded by the substitution of *jaras* due to the latter's higher status and its obligatory nature (*nityatva*). Once that [substitution of *jaras*] has occurred, there arises the possibility of elision. [Objection: In that case, the elision will not occur by virtue of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the non-disturbance of the cause of a grammatical operation).

The substitute *jaras* produced by the co-occurrence (*sannipāta*) with [the suffixes] beginning with *aj* is not capable of being the cause for its own elision (*luk*). If this were so, forms such as *atijarasaṃ brāhmaṇakulaṃ tiṣṭhati* and *atijarasaiḥ* would not be established; for how could the substitute *jaras*, which was applied by the co-occurrence of the suffix *su* or *bhis* with a stem ending in *a*, not be the cause for that very substitution of *jaras* which prevents the stem from ending in *a*? This point is indeed intended to be included [in the rule].

It should be *atijaramatijaraiḥ*; this is the position of Gonardīya. This is what is stated: "In this case," and so forth. "In this case" (*iha*) introduces the statement. The view of Gonardīya extends from "the Brāhmaṇa family is *atijarasam*" up to "it should be so. As for what was said—that the rule for elision (*luk*) does not apply—and as for what was further stated—"the Brāhmaṇa family is *atijaram*" and so on—the reason for both of these cases is the principle: "that which is characterized by its occurrence in conjunction" (*sannipātalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "na punarlukśāstram," the meaning of the word *punaḥ* (*again*) is as follows: previously, the occurrence of elision (*luk*) was set aside by the possibility [of other operations]; however, that occurrence which would otherwise take place once the substitution of *jaras* has been applied is likewise prevented by the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*.
As for the passage beginning with "anye tu" (*others, however*), this has already been explained under the rules *ṭāṅasiṅasāminātsyāḥ* and *ato bhisa ais*.
[The substitution of *a* for the case endings of] *tyad* and the other [pronouns]. 7.2.102.

"Ending in *dvi*, etc. and so forth—this is merely an *iṣṭi* (an intended application). As for what is said—that the mention of "elision in the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of the exclusion of technical names and secondary members]—that is incorrect, because it serves the purpose of [excluding] secondary members (*upasarjana*), as in the cases of *atiyūyam* and *ativayam*. However, when the elision in the remainder is indeed the elision of the *ṭi*-suffix, then it is all the more not an indicator. For they are excluded by the very recitation [of the list]. And thus, there is a Vārttika on the *sarvādi* sūtra: "The prohibition of technical names and secondary members; their exclusion is by virtue of their recitation [in the list]."

Therefore, by virtue of this reliance on the recited list (*pāṭha*), this [rule] also does not apply to those [words] that have become subordinate (*upasarjana*) as technical designations (*saṃjñā*). "In the case of *tyad* and so forth" means: in a compound where the meaning of *tyad* and so forth is the primary element (*pradhāna*). For they are not excluded from the recited list.
The substitute *ka* is applied in place of the interrogative pronoun *kim*.

Therefore, why is it that *im* alone is not prescribed with the vowel *a*? But how, if *a* is prescribed, is the form *kaḥ* and so forth established, given that [the rule] would apply to the final letter, and the final letter is not established by the preceding [rule], since it has been stated that "the *tyad*-group [of pronouns] ends in two"? Others, however, out of fear of this objection, read it thus: "Therefore, *im* alone is not prescribed with the vowel *a*."

This is the meaning: let the sūtra simply be *imaḥ*. By the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ*, the vowel *a* belonging to those words beginning with *tyad* (the pronominal series) becomes [the substitute for the final phoneme]. In that case, according to the principle *nānarthake 'l-antya-vidhiḥ* ("there is no substitution of the final phoneme when the element is meaningless"), the vowel *a* would apply to the whole word *imaḥ*. For those who read [the sūtra] in this way, the mention of *kimaḥ* later on must be made; or rather, it need not be made, for I shall state [the rule] as *hoḥ*—that is, *imaḥ* alone—and then [add] *vā ti*, meaning *imaḥ* alone, so that the substitution of *va* occurs for *imaḥ*. Therefore, the substitution of *ka* was prescribed specifically for the sake of including the form with the suffix *sākac* (i.e., *kim*).
The substitution of *ku* occurs before *ti* and *hoḥ*. || 7.2.104 ||

Since the word *ti* lacks a case-ending (*vibhakti*), the vowel *i* in the syllable *takāra* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding *kuha*: the suffix *hapratyaya* is applied according to the rule *vā ha ca chandasi*.
kvāti || 7 - 2 - 105 || [The suffix *kvip* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā*, when followed by the particle *ati*.]
"Where?"—from the word *kva*, the suffix *at* is applied according to the rule *kimot*.

Now, for what purpose is the prescription of a different substitute (*ādeśāntara*)? Why not simply prescribe the original *ku* sound itself? If this were done, even the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) would not need to be made; let it simply be "after *ku*, [the suffix] *it*. How is the form established? Once the *yaṇ*-substitution has been applied, the form *kvā* is established. As for the *guṇa* substitution of *o*, it will not occur because of the maxim: "When an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅga*), it does not recur" (*aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ*). However, the *yaṇ*-substitution does indeed occur because it is not part of the stem itself. To this, he replies: "The prescription of a different substitute is for the purpose of preventing the *guṇa* of *o*."

The sense is that the established reality (*niṣṭhitatattva*) is difficult to know. If that is so, then instead of saying *kimo't*, one should say *kimoḍvat*; for once the *ṭi*-elision has been applied, the form *kvā* would be established. To this he says: "and [the rule] *kimoḍvat*. But how is the formation of the form accomplished through another suffix, given that the *jaś*-substitution would apply to the letter *k*? For the *ṭi*-elision will indeed be a *ḍit*-suffix. How can there be the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*)? [It is because] "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)."

For the elision of *ṭi* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends upon a *ḍit* suffix, whereas the change to *jaś* is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) because it does not depend upon that. [The author says: "It is for the sake of [the form] with *sakac*. For if another suffix containing *kak* were prescribed, [the result] would be *kakvet*; however, according to the present formulation, even in that case, it becomes simply *kvā*.
In place of *tad* and *doṣ*, *saḥ* and *sā* are substituted respectively when they are final members of a compound.

The term *sau* refers to the nominative singular (*prathamaikavacana*), not the locative plural (*saptamībahuvacana*), because of such grammatical indications as *syaś chandasi*, *so 'ci lope cet*, and others. Nor does it refer to both cases; for if that were the case, he would have simply said *si*, meaning "in a case-ending beginning with *s*."

The question "Why [specify] 'of the two non-final [sounds]'? arises because, since there is freedom in choosing between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāve kāmacārāt*), and because a *t* ending [word] cannot occur among the *tyadādi* group [if it were the qualifier], the *t* and *d* of *tyadādi* words are qualified by the *tyadādi* group itself; thus, the forms *tāu* and *tāu* are established for the two non-final sounds, while the substitution of *at* for the final sound will apply to the final one. The answer is that because the rule for *at* substitution after *su* (the nominative singular suffix) has its own scope elsewhere, this very rule [for *at*] would apply by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*). In that regard, since there is no distinction in the masculine when *su* alone is present, examples are provided for the vocative (*sambuddhau*) and for the feminine.

Why, then, is it stated as *tadoḥ*? One might simply say *taḥ*, [meaning] "for *ta*. If one were to formulate it as *taḥ saḥ sāvanantyasya*, then the substitution would apply to the letter *n* as well, resulting in forms such as *aneṣaḥ*, *taanayam*, and *anasau*. [To prevent this, it is stated as *tadoḥ*. Since *nuṭ* is a prefix (*parādi*), it is included by the mention of that [initial *na*].
The *au* of *adas* [is replaced by *am*,] and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *s*.

Regarding the form *asuka*: when *adas* is followed by *su*, the substitution of *au* is prohibited; consequently, the *tyadādi* substitution (*atva*) applies, the *d* is changed to *s*, and the *u* is substituted for the vowel following that *s* within the *akac* suffix.

Regarding the phrase "of those that have become the final members of a compound," and so forth: when a case ending (*vibhakti*) arises after a compound, the substitute (*ādeśa*) is considered external (*bahir-aṅga*) because it depends upon that [compound]. Consequently, once the internal (*antaraṅga*) single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, since that [result] is treated as if it were the initial element (*ādivadbhāva*), an undesirable consequence would arise—such as *paramayam* or *paramaham*—when the substitutes are being applied. Therefore, these substitutes must be stated as applying only to those [words] for which the sandhi operations have not yet taken effect. And this will be made known in the rule *nendrasya parasya*.

Regarding the statement "for *adas*, *s* [the nominative singular ending] would become [au]," and so forth: let the rule simply be "for *adas*, [when followed by] *au*. Here, *sau* is the ablative case (*pañcamī*) of *su*, while *adasaḥ* is the ablative case (*pañcamī*). Since the former [ablative] has already served its purpose in the preceding rule, it is here interpreted as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, the meaning is: "for *adas*, the substitution of *au* occurs for the following *su*. In that case, once the substitution of *ya* for the *tyad*-class stems has been applied, the form *asau* is established; why then is the elision of *su* prescribed? [Otherwise], the vocative suffix would be elided after a short vowel.

If the substitution of *au* were prescribed [for the vocative ending], then in the case of *asau*, where the *tyadādi* replacement has occurred, there would be elision of the *au* of the vocative following a short vowel; however, this fault does not apply because the elision is prescribed specifically after a consonant (*hal*) in the rule *halaḥ*.

If this is so, then the mention of *hal* (consonant) should be made there; no, he says, for that [term] is the subject under discussion in the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt*. But surely this [term *dīrghāt*] is indicated in the nominative case; it will therefore bring about a genitive interpretation according to the principle *tasmād ity uttarasya* ("from that, of what follows"). Or else, as in the previous sūtra, there will be some way to manage it through the nominative itself. In that case, the substitution of *e* would apply to *āp*.

In this case, then, regarding the vocative singular of a feminine stem ending in *ā*, [the rule] *as-áu-āṅi cāpaḥ* (P. 7.3.105) and *sambuddhau ca tha* (P. 7.3.106) would apply; however, since the substitution of *au* (*auttvam*) applies to the base itself (*prakṛteḥ*), the *ṭāp* suffix is absent, and thus the substitution of *e* (*ettvam*) does not occur. No, there is no such fault, because the word *jhal* is carried over [from the previous rule]. From the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* (P. 7.3.103), the word *jhal* is understood there [in P. 7.3.106] to mean "in a vocative beginning with a *jhal* [consonant]. Once the substitution of *au* has been applied, [the condition of] beginning with a *jhal* is no longer met, so [the substitution of *e*] will not take place. Furthermore, by the rule *pratyayasthācca kāditvam* (P. 7.3.44), the *kādi* status [is established].

In this case, when *asakā-au* is present for a feminine noun with the suffix *akac*, the substitution of *ī* (by Pāṇini 7.3.103) would apply to the vowel preceding the *k* of the affix. However, since the long *ā* (*au*) belongs to the base itself, the suffix *ṭāp* does not occur, and thus the substitution of *ī* does not take place. Furthermore, the substitution of *śī* (for the dual ending *au*) would also follow. And here, when *asā-au* is present for a feminine noun, the substitution of *śī* (by Pāṇini 7.1.18) would apply because of the rule *auha āpaḥ*. But the prescription of the substitution of *au* (by Pāṇini 7.3.118) serves its purpose in the masculine. This fault is only occasional; it does not exist when the earlier teachers’ formulation *auṅa āpaḥ* is followed, but it does exist in the other two positions.
That which is *sau* [is called *padam*]. (Pāṇini 1.4.14)

In the feminine, this [base] has the letter *ya*. However, in the neuter, because the suffix *su* is elided by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, the absence of *su* occurs due to that elision (*lumatā luptatvāt*).
There is elision of the *hal* (consonant) [of the suffix *śnā*]. (Pāṇini 7.2.113)

The term "non-inclusion" (agrahaṇa) continues [from the previous rule]. Although that [term] ends in the nominative case, nevertheless, by means of the locative "in a consonant" (halī), its status as a genitive is established.
In place of the vowel of the root *mṛj*, there is vṛddhi [before an affix having an indicatory *k* or *ṅ*].

Regarding the phrase "and the operation [kārya] being stated for a root (dhātu)": in reality, that which is stated as an operation of a root is intended here by the expression "stated for a root. Whether that root is taken in its own form or not, when it is grasped, this augment *am*—by the rule *anudāttasya cardupadhasyānyatarasyām*—becomes an augment of the root and the affix (*dhātupratyaya*) itself, and not [an augment] in cases such as *pramṛḍbhyām*. Regarding the term *tatpratyaya*: it refers to what is prescribed by the word *dhātoḥ*. In the case of *kaṃsaparimṛḍbhyām*, there would be an undesired application (*prasaṅga*) due to the rule of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*).
The final vowel of a word ending in *a* is lengthened before an affix marked with the technical markers *ñ* or *ṇ*.
In examples such as *taṇḍulaniścāya*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after all roots when the sense is that of a measure (*parimāṇa*).

*gauḥ*, *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*. Here, *gauḥ* is the direct example; in the other cases, once the substitution of *āv* has been made, the form is established by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*. *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*. Here too, *sakhāyau* is the example; but in the case of the nominative plural (*jasi*), once the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement by *ay* have been made by the rule *jasi ca*, it is established as before. *cyautnam* is a name for strength (*bala*); it is Vedic—as in: *tamiccyautnairāryanti*.

But for what purpose is this stated? For, in the absence of the words *jetṛ* and *yotṛ*, [the forms] *jaitram* and *yautram* are established through the suffix *aṇ* added to *prajña*. As for *cyautna*, these are underived nominal bases (*avyutpanna-prātipadika*) belonging to the *uṇādi* class. Regarding [the rule] *taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ ścāvakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*, etc., [one might ask]: since there is the rule *goto ṇit*, should it not be stated as *gota aut*—that is, "there is the substitution of *au* for *go* when a *sarvanāmasthāna* follows"? [The answer is: It is stated thus so that [the rule] may apply even when the word *go* is used in its uninflected form (*avyayībhāva*), such as in *gaviṣṭhaḥ*. Otherwise, if it were stated as *gota*, it would not apply here because the condition of being a *sarvanāmasthāna* following a stem ending in *go* would not be met. Furthermore, it is stated so that the substitution of *au* occurs even when the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes are elided (*luk*), as in *gauḥ* (where the nominative singular suffix *su* is elided). If it were stated as *gota*, the substitution would not occur in the case of *gaviṣṭhaḥ* or *gauḥ* because the condition of a *sarvanāmasthāna* following [the stem] would be absent. Therefore, it is stated as *gota aut* to ensure the correct formation of these forms.

"How [should one explain] *sakhāyau* and *sakhāyaḥ*? I shall state that this [substitution] applies to *sakhi-* except in the vocative singular (*asambuddhau*). To this it is replied: first, the rule *ñṇiti* must be stated for the sake of subsequent rules. Furthermore, in forms such as *prāpayati* (from *priyam ācaṣṭe*), there would be no *vṛddhi* substitution for the initial vowels (*prādi*) [if the rule were not applied]. Moreover, if those [forms] were prescribed with long final vowels, it would be excessively cumbersome; therefore, let it remain exactly as it is in the original arrangement (*yathānyāsam*).
In the case of taddhita suffixes, [the first vowel] among the vowels (acām) [is strengthened]. (Pāṇini 7.2.117)

"Vṛddhi is substituted for the *ac* that follows *aja* and so on. Now, an objection is raised: since the *ik-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the substitution of *ik*) is present, it must be an *ik* vowel that functions as the substitute; even though there is a selection from among similar classes—just as when it is said, "Among cows, the black one has the most milk," only a cow is understood—nevertheless, in this case too, because there is no explicit mention of "of the *ac*s" (*acām*), the *ik-paribhāṣā* would indeed apply, meaning "an *ac* consisting of an *ik*. Therefore, it must be stated that "for the *ac*" is mentioned in order to specify the substitute; but that is not correct.

The subject under discussion must be stated: *aco ñṇiti* (P. 7.2.115). In that context, because the rule specifies a particular locus (*nirdiṣṭasthānikatva*), the *ādiparibhāṣā* (the maxim concerning the initial letter) has no application.

Now, regarding *tvāṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*: when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the words *tvaṣṭṛ* and *jagat* by the rule *tasyedam* (P. 4.3.120), why does the *vṛddhi* not occur respectively by *aco ñṇiti* and *ata upadhāyāḥ* (P. 7.2.116; 7.2.117)? To this he replies: "In the case of *tvāṣṭraḥ* and *jāgataḥ*, [the former] subverts the *vṛddhi* characterized by the final and penultimate letters. The intention is that this is due to its being a subsequent rule (*paratvāt*).

The scope for the *vṛddhi* [substitution] characterized by the final vowel and the penultimate vowel (*antyopadhālakṣaṇā*) is, for example, in *gauḥ* and *yācakaḥ*; the scope for this [present rule] is, for example, in *suśrut* > *sauśrutaḥ*, *tvāṣṭraḥ*, and *jagataḥ*. Where both would apply simultaneously, the initial *vṛddhi* (*ādivṛddhi*) occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Furthermore, the principle that "what has been once applied does not recur" (*sakṛdgatinyāya*) is adopted, rather than a cognition of repeated application (*punaḥprasaṅga*). And having established this, the inclusion of the word *puṣkarasat* in the *anuśatikādi* group becomes meaningful.

If, however, the penultimate vowel were to undergo *vṛddhi* in a case where the initial vowel is already subject to *vṛddhi*, then the form *pauṣkarasādi* would be established by that very *vṛddhi* conditioned by the penultimate vowel; consequently, it would not need to be listed among the *anuśatikādi* group. Its inclusion there would be for the sake of the suffix *ṭhak*.

[Pauṣkarasādi says: "In this case, the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] conditioned by the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) does not apply, because [the suffix] is not *añ* or *ṇit*. This is not so; for the suffix *ṭhak* is not produced after this [base] in the sense of "one who moves" (*caratī-arthe*), due to the lack of such an expression (*anabhidhānāt*). Alternatively, the rule that "in the case of *iñ* prescribed by the specific rule [Pāṇini 4.1.95], there is *vṛddhi* of both members [of the compound]" applies only where [the suffix] is prescribed as a specific rule (*apratipadavihita*)—such as in the case of *iñ* following bases like *bāhu*; it does not apply elsewhere. Thus, the reading [of Pauṣkarasādi] is not intended for the sake of *ṭhak*. However, where initial *vṛddhi* is prohibited, there the *vṛddhi* conditioned by the final or penultimate vowel does take place.

Why does it not occur? [Because] from *vyasuri* one would derive *vaiyasavaḥ* by the rule *igantācca laghupūrvāt*, and from *vyāpad* one would derive *vaiyāpadaṃ bhāṣam*; in those cases as well, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (by the rule *aij āgamaḥ*) would prevail and thus override [the suffix *aṇ*]. This is established.
And [the substitution of *i* occurs] before the suffix *kit*. (Pāṇini 7.2.117)

*Nāḍāyanaḥ*, *cārāyaṇaḥ*: [these are formed] by the suffix *phak* after [stems] beginning with *naḍa*. *Ākṣikaḥ*, *śālākikaḥ*: [these are formed] by the suffix *ṭhak* in the sense of "playing with" (*dīvyati*).
Thus ends the second quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Padamañjarī*, composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra; [this concludes] the *Kāśikāvṛtti*—6.
Now begins the third quarter of the seventh chapter.
The suffix *cha* (i.e., *īya*) is applied after the words *devikā*, *śiṃśapā*, *adityavāṭ*, *dīrghasattra*, and *śreyas*, [to form patronymics]. 7.3.1.

In this matter, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the *aṅga* may be qualified by the *devikā*-type words, or those [words] may be qualified by it; and even in that case, it may be through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Thus, there are four positions. Among these, if the *aṅga* is qualified by the *devikā*-type words through coreferentiality, then because the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) is possible, the meaning would be: "the vowel *ā* occurs in place of the initial vowel of a stem ending in *devikā* etc. In that case, it would not apply to the simple [stems], for a thing cannot be its own ending.

The principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is also prohibited by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, if that prohibition applies only to the domain of suffix-vidhi (rules for the application of suffixes), then let it hold for isolated stems; it would not, however, apply to those beginning with such a stem—such as *dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing on the banks of the Devikā river"). Furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding those ending in such a stem—such as *saudevikam* ("produced from Sudevika"); in this case, the vowel *a* would replace the *u* of *su*.

Now, as for the qualification by means of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—namely, "that which is a member (*aṅga*) of the *devikā*-type [suffixes]"—it refers to something that is a member of the *devikā*-type suffixes and wherein they exist as constituent parts (*avayava*). Consequently, it would not apply to the suffixes alone; for a thing cannot be its own constituent part. Furthermore, the treatment of a word as if it were distinct (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is prohibited with respect to nominal stems (*prātipadika*). If, however, that prohibition applies only to the domain of suffixes, then let it apply to the suffixes alone; yet in the case of those ending in them, there would be the same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) as before.

In this view, only the non-application [of the rule] to those beginning with *tad* has been avoided. Now, if "member" (*aṅga*) is defined as a coreferential qualifier—as in "those members which are *devikā* and so forth"—then while the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to those ending in such terms is avoided, the non-application to those beginning with them would certainly still occur.

In that case, would the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) then be one with a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*)—namely, "the *ā* of the initial vowel (*ac*) of those [words] such as *devikā* which constitute parts of the *aṅga*"? If so, there would be no fault in the case of a simple [word] or one beginning with that [suffix], but there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *ā* substitution even for those [words] that have become subsequent members (*parapada*). In that regard, in cases such as *pūrvā śāṃśapā prāggrāmāt*, the *ā* is indeed desired; however, in cases such as *sudevika* when it is not a prior member (*agra*), there is the occurrence of an undesired result. Thus, all four of these positions are flawed.

Now, there is another view: the term *devikā* and others are qualified by *ācām* and so forth—meaning that the form *ā* occurs for *ācām* and the rest, provided it belongs to *devikā* and the others. In this view, there is no fault regarding the simple [forms] or when the suffix *taddhita* follows; nor does the undesirable consequence arise that the first or the second member of the compound would be [the one affected] in the case of *saudevikam*. However, [one might object]: in cases such as *prāggrāme pūrvaśāṃśapaḥ*, the *ā* substitution would not occur for *devikā* and others because they function as the second members of the compound? This is not a fault; [for the rule applies regardless].

The phrase "of the villages and cities of the Easterners" (*prācāṃ grāmanagarāṇām*) will follow here, and its connection there is through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*): [the rule] "there is *vṛddhi* for the first vowel among the vowels of the second member (*uttarapada*) of the villages and cities of the Easterners," and [the rule] "for the second members beginning with *devika*, etc., there is *ākāra* for the first vowel among the vowels. This too is not the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*; for if this were his view, he would have stated simply that "this follows even in the case of the *vṛddhi* of the second member. What then is the view of the author of the *Vṛtti* being expressed? This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) that sets aside the *paribhāṣā* concerning "nearness" (*āntarya*).
"Where an increase (*vṛddhi*) of vowels beginning with *ā* is applicable in the case of *devikā* and others, there [the rule] applies; by this, everything desired is accomplished. Thus it is said.

If this [rule] were not stated, then when the vṛddhi substitution occurs for the first vowel of *devikā* and so forth, the vowel *ai* would result by virtue of the rule concerning the "most similar" (*sthāne 'ntaratama*). That is set aside by the vowel *ā*, which is obtained as its exception. In that case, let the *aṅga* (stem) be either the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) or the following member (*uttarapada*); in any event, it is established as a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) that wherever there is the contingency of vṛddhi for the first vowel among the vowels of *devikā* and so forth, there the vowel *ā* occurs. But is it not the case that the term "*aṅgasya*" (of the stem) is still in force? True.

The connection is not as follows: "An *ā* occurs in place of the initial vowel of a stem if that stem belongs to the *devika*-class and so forth. What then? "An *ā* occurs in place of the initial vowel of the *devika*-class and so forth if that [vowel] belongs to a stem. Now, if the connection is made in this way, what is being excluded? Nothing at all; rather, it is merely necessary to state the connection with the term that is being carried over (*anuvṛtta*). That [connection] also results in the substitution of *ā*. The reason for this has already been stated.

Regarding the term *vaihīnari*: that which possesses the power of carrying (*vaha*) is *vahī*; it is both *vahī* and a man (*nara*), hence *vahīnara*. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. As for *vaihīnari*, here the increase (*vṛddhi*) of the vowel *a* would have been applicable, but it is superseded by the vowel *i*. However, the increase of *ai* does indeed occur for that [root *vahi*], because the vowel *i* is not prescribed until that [increase of *a*] has already become applicable. If this were the case, then in the sūtra itself, only the vowel *a* should have been prescribed; for when the increase of *a* applies, the desired form is established. Yet, it was not done in that way. Thus [the point is made].
Regarding the phrase "some, however": *vihīna* means one who has been deprived; in the word *vihīnara*, the syllable *na* is elided according to the rule governing the *pṛṣodarādi* group of words.
In the words *kekaya*, *mitraku*, and *pralaya*, the vowel following the initial consonant (*yādi*) is replaced by *iy*.

For in that context, the worldly (*laukika*) lineage (*gotra*) is intended. When the word *mitrayu*—by means of a metaphorical application of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*)—refers not merely to its original form (*prakṛti*) but to the lineage of its descendants, then this [rule] is stated. However, when the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after words such as *gṛṣṭi* and others, and its elision (*luk*) occurs in the plural due to their inclusion in the *yaskādi* group, then there is no fault even if [the term *gotra*] is used in its technical (*pāribhāṣika*) sense. In this regard, although this substitution is prescribed when there is the contingency of *vṛddhi*, nevertheless, *vṛddhi* is not sublated;

for the domains (*viṣaya*) are distinct: *vṛddhi* applies to the first vowel (*acāmādi*), while the substitution of *iy* applies to the *ya*-class of sounds. The stem (*aṅga*) is the qualifier for both, but it is not the object of the operation (*kāryin*).

The vowels *ai* and *au* do not undergo [the substitution of *ay* and *av*] when they follow those two [consonants] which stand at the end of a word; however, they do undergo it when preceded by those two.

In this case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the prescription of two distinct meanings; however, the word *tu* serves to indicate that very [intended meaning]. Since [the term] "the two preceding" (*pūrvau*) is connected [to the rule], one might expect the dual form *aicau*; yet the singular form is used here as a Vedic usage (*sautra*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, the singular is used because it functions as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). [The phrase] "preceding those two" means that the augment *aij* occurs. Although it lacks the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of an augment—namely, the marker *ṭi*—it is called an "augment" (*āgama*) because it occurs in a specific location relative to the word "preceding" (*pūrva*); for it is said that "that which comes (*āgacchati*) is an augment (*āgama*). [The example given is] *vaiyasanam*.

We have already explained that the rule "there is compounding of *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* prior to the arising of the case-ending" pertains to the final member of the compound; by this, the letters *y* and *v* in words such as *vaiyasanā-* possess the status of being word-final (*padānta*). The word *svaśva-* belongs to the *śiva-* group (of nominal stems).

Regarding the term *yāṣṭīka*: [it is derived] by the rule *śaktiyaṣṭyorīkak*. Now, one might object: "In this case, [the substitution] will not occur simply because we rely on the rule that [the substitution applies] when *y* or *v* take the place of vowels (*ac*) at the beginning of a word. To this, he says: "Because these... The form *imaḥ* is derived from the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") with the present tense suffix *laṭ*, which is replaced by *śatṛ*; there is elision of *śap*, and then *iṇo yaṇ* applies. Here, even if the prohibition were absent, in a form such as *vaiyasanam*, where *vyasana-a* is established, both the *vṛddhi* substitution and the augment *aij* would apply. Among these, the *vṛddhi* is non-permanent (*anitya*), because it is superseded by the application of another rule.

For once *ai* has been applied, that very [substitute] is obtained, because what falls in the middle of it is included by the mention of it. Since the substitution of *ai* is obligatory, that indeed occurs first. Once that has been done, even if *vṛddhi* were to apply again—on the basis of the principle of "re-application" (*punah-prasaṅga*)—nevertheless, due to internal proximity (*āntarya*), an *ai* replaces an *ai*, and an *au* replaces an *au*; thus there is no fault whatsoever, so what is the use of a prohibition?

[Objection: But if that [suffix] were absent, in the case of *vaiyākaraṇī bhāryā asya* (his wife is a female grammarian), there would be a prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) by the rule "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" (*vṛddhinimittasya*). However, when [the suffix] is present, the prohibition does not apply. How is it that it does not apply, given that the term *vṛddhinimitta* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in which the cause of *vṛddhi*—namely, the letters *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*—is found," and the letter *ṇ* is indeed found here? [Reply: True, it is found, but it is not the cause. It has been stated: "The word 'cause' (*nimitta*) is used in its primary sense for that which is currently producing the effect."

[Objection: But surely, let it be granted that the *ṇit* suffix is not the cause for the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "in *taddhita*s, [the vowel] at the beginning of the *ac* group" (*taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*). However, since the *aij* substitution is prescribed for that very *taddhita* which is marked with *ṇit*, the letter *ṇ* would indeed be the cause for that which bears the technical name *vṛddhi*; thus, the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like behavior) should certainly apply. [Reply: It is said in response: The prohibition does not apply to something that possesses a cause such as the letter *ṇ* for that *vṛddhi* which exists in reality. Rather, it applies to the cause of that which is prescribed as *vṛddhi* itself.

Therefore, must a prohibition of *vṛddhi* be stated specifically in order to prevent the application of the prohibition against *puṃvadbhāva*? It need not be stated; for within a single stem (*aṅga*), the specifically prescribed *ai* and *au* will override the generally prescribed *vṛddhi*, according to the maxim that "an override occurs even when there is a possibility [of both rules applying]."

Furthermore, since the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) would not apply here as in the previous case, one might ask: "Let it simply be 'yvābhyāṃ pūrvamaic'; what is the purpose of the prohibition? To this he replies: "The statement of the prohibition. When the prohibition is stated, the meaning becomes that the *aic* vowels (*ai*, *au*) occur only before those same *y* and *v* sounds for which the substitution of *vṛddhi* had been previously applicable and is now prohibited; for if that [prohibition] were absent, any *y* or *v* whatsoever might be taken.

Therefore, the meaning is that this prohibitive statement is made so that a distinct domain for *ai* and *au* may be established; [for example] *dādhyaśviḥ* and *mādhvaśviḥ*. One whose horse (*aśva*) is fond of curds (*dadhi*) is *dadhyaśva*; likewise, one whose horse is fond of honey (*madhu*) is *madhvaśva*. From these two, by the rule *ata iñ*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied].

But surely we shall qualify *yv* by the rule *acāmādeḥ*—that is, "the *yv* that stand in place of an *ac* which is the initial of the vowels"? Even so, [the rule] would apply in the case of *dvy-aśītikaḥ*: [the derivation is as follows: *dve aśītī adhīṣṭaḥ* ("he was commissioned for eighty-two"), then the compound *taddhitārtha*, then [from *tam adhīṣṭaḥ*] the suffix *ṭhak* by the rule *prāgvateṣṭhak*. However, when the prohibition exists, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ*, it is understood that the prohibition applies to those two [suffixes] after which the *vṛddhi* prescribed by *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* would otherwise have occurred.

In this case, however, since the rule "of a numeral and a word denoting a number of years" prescribes a vṛddhi substitute for the final vowel of the second member, the absence of the ai-substitution (aijāgama) is established because there is no prohibition of that [vṛddhi].

It might be argued as follows: "The term *acāmādeḥ*, which is carried over [from a previous rule], being taken in its own form (*svarūpapara*), serves as a qualifier for *vṛddhi*. The meaning would be: 'In the event of that *vṛddhi* which occurs by virtue of the rule *acāmādeḥ*, the two vowels *ai* and *au* take the place of the preceding *aic* (i.e., *ai* and *au*) as exceptions to it. However, since there is no such occasion for *vṛddhi* here, the *aic* vowels will not occur. Even so, the *y* and *v* would remain unqualified; consequently, the rule would apply in cases such as *dādhyaśva*.

Furthermore, the phrase "not after *acāmādi*" cannot qualify both [the *ai* and *au*] simultaneously, such that *y* and *v* would replace *acāmādi*, and the diphthongs (*aic*) preceding them would become the substitutes; for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *vṛddhi* applying by virtue of the rule "after *acāmādi*. Since no authority exists for resorting to any one of the methods—tantra, repetition (*āvṛtti*), or single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*)—it is well said: "The statement of the prohibition is for the purpose of establishing the scope (*viṣayapratipattyartha*) of the two diphthongs (*aic*)."

"Even for the *vṛddhi* of the final member (*uttarapada*)"—this is understood from the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning *alasa* in that context. "But where..."—this too is understood by qualifying the *y* and *v* with the final member: the *vṛddhi* does not occur after those *y* and *v* which belong to the final member, and instead, there is the augment *aij* before them.

In this context—*ai* and *aja* form *yajau*; *u* and *aja* form *vajau*. Of these two, there are the forms *aiyajam* and *auvajam*. Because *ai* and *au* are not *bhakta* (integral parts of the suffix), and because they fall in between [the base and the suffix], they are not included by the term "aṅga" (base). Consequently, in forms such as *aiyajīya* and *auvajīya*, the *śeṣanighāta* (the low-pitched accent for the remaining syllables) would not occur, and if one intended to express them as "remainder" (*śeṣa*), the suffix *cha* after a "vṛddha" (vṛddhi-vowel-initial) nominal stem would not apply, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) would not be "vṛddha. It is replied: [This is not so].
