If such an expression exists, then the word *pūrva* must be repeated; therein, one [instance of] *pūrva* expresses a constituent part (*avayava*), while the other expresses a fixed position (*vyavasthā*)—meaning that those two by which the *aic* vowels are substituted are the constituents of the base (*aṅga*).
On this point, there are two summary verses:
"For since the substitution of *vṛddhi* has not yet [otherwise] obtained, the specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) for *aij* would sublate it; what then is the purpose of the negative particle (*nañ*)?"

By means of those two *y* and *v*, the subsequent *ai* is applied; therefore, this [substitution] should occur as something preceding them, lest it happen in cases such as *dādhyaśva*. If it is argued that "since *y* and *v* are prescribed to take the place of the initial vowel, such a thing does not occur here," [the answer is: you have been instructed in two sets of eighty [rules].

If [the term] *aij* were applied to the *ac* (vowels) prescribed in the eighty-second [sūtra], *aṅgādyacaḥ*, then since *aic* would follow as a consequence, *y* and *v* would not be specifically distinguished; moreover, even if heard, it is not possible for a single [term] to differentiate both.
This [term *aij*] would also have jurisdiction over what follows, and here, regarding the subsequent word containing *y* or *v*—
If there were *vaṃ* in the previous *traiyaliṇda*, then two *aśītis* would not have been taught.
And [the suffix *ya* is applied] after *dvāra* and so forth. 7.3.4.

Regarding the term *dauvārika*: [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "appointed to that," as in *dvārapālasyedam* ("belonging to the gatekeeper"), resulting in *dauvārapālam*. [One might ask: why does the *vṛddhi* characteristic not apply here, given the rule "a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory"? [The answer is: because in the rule *kalāpino 'ṇ*, the explicit mention of the suffix *aṇ* is intended to provide an additional prescription. But how can this rule apply to the word *dvārapāla* when the word *dvāra* alone is listed [in the *gaṇapāṭha*]? To this he says: "In this case, the rule of extension (*tadādividhi*) also applies."

And the reason for this has already been stated in the *Devikā* and other sūtras; furthermore, he will provide an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for it here. [The term] "sauvara" refers to the chapter [beginning with] "phiṣ". Moreover, that [chapter] was composed by Śantanu, starting with "phiṣ". Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "The locatives in 'sauvara' are locatives of that which ends in it," [it means]: a beautiful chapter is a *svādhyāya*. Here, the prefix *āṅ* should be inserted in the middle, or else the lengthening of the initial vowel of the second member occurs according to the rule "it is seen in others as well. [The commentary continues with] "even so," and so forth.

If the word *sva* (self) is recited here [in the rule], what follows from the word *svādhyāya* (one's own Veda)? To this he says: "For even at the beginning of that... Words such as *svārthika* and *svābhāvika* are correct by virtue of their usage in the Bhāṣya. In *sphaiyakṛtaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied because he is a seer (*ṛṣi*). Regarding *śauvādaṃṣṭro maṇiḥ*: there is lengthening according to the rule "the *danta* and *daṃṣṭrā* of *śvan*," and the suffix *aṇ* is applied as before.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *nyagrodha* when it occurs alone. 7.3.5.
Regarding *naiyagrodha*: the meaning is that it grows by means of downward-growing shoots (*praroha*).

However, according to the view that [the suffix] is not derived (*avyutpatti*), it is for the sake of a specific injunction (*vidhi*) because the letter *y* is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). Now, even in this view, what is the purpose of using the term "alone" (*kevala*), since it is stated as "of *nyagrodha*"? What possibility is there that it would occur at the beginning of that [word]? It is, however, for the sake of providing technical knowledge (*jñāpana*). This makes known: in this section, those terms which are employed serve as qualifiers for the vowels (*ac*) that undergo vṛddhi, specifically those vowels that stand at the beginning of such words.
Not in the case of the exchange of actions. 7.3.6.
"Regarding what was stated concerning the exchange of actions": the meaning is that whatever has been stated in this section does not apply to the exchange of actions.
And [the suffix -matup is applied] after words such as *svāgata*. 7.3.7.

In examples such as *vyāvakrośī*, the verbal root preceded by the prefix *vi-ava-* is seen to function in the sense of "mutual exchange of action" (*karmavyatihāra*); thus, the word *vyavahāra* also occurs in that sense. Consequently, one might suspect that since this is already established by the preceding rule, its inclusion here is redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "This word *vyavahāra*... Because the word *sva* is listed among the *dvārādi* group, there is an occasion for its application here. It has already been stated that "in that [list], the inclusion of words beginning with *tat* also takes place."
The substitution of *śvan* for *śva* occurs before the suffix *iñ*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *tatra ca* and so forth: if the rule for "that which begins with that" (*tadādividhi*) were not applicable there, this statement would be purposeless. Why? Because the word *śvan* alone is listed among [the group] beginning with *dvāra*; what occasion would there be for it to be something that "begins with that"? Thus, the meaning is that the statement "the rule for 'that which begins with that' applies" serves as an *jñāpaka* (indicative proof) for the point that what is stated in this section is a qualifier of the vowels (*ac*) that undergo *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "beginning with *ik*" and so forth, the meaning is that one should state "of *śvan* and the rest" (*śvādeḥ*).

In this context, because of the mention of the locative case (*saptamī*) in the rule for the apprehension of the *varṇa* (the phoneme *i*), the rule applies to that which begins with it (*tadādividhi*). For example, in *śvāgaṇika*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *śvagaṇāṭṭhañ*. Regarding the phrase "of that which ends in it" (*tadantasya*): it refers to that which ends in *iñ*. In *śvābhastra*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *iñaśca*. Since the prohibition of *vṛddhi* caused by that [suffix] and the introduction of the augment *aij* belong to different levels of grammatical operation, they cannot be prevented by a prohibition based on *iñ*; therefore, this new statement is commenced.
Of the final member [of a compound]. 7.3.10.

Since the phrase "of the vowels beginning with [the first]" (acāmādeḥ) is understood to carry over to what follows, it should be understood that the vṛddhi substitution applies to the initial vowel of the subsequent member (uttarapada).

But surely, in rules such as *avayavād ṛtoḥ*, the word *avayavāt* and so forth is in the ablative case; therefore, even without the mention of the term "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the rule will apply to the subsequent member alone? To this he replies: "In which [rules]... By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the following rules: *hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca*, *anuśatikādīnāṃ ca*, and *devatādvandve ca*. In these grammatical operations, because there is no mention of the ablative case, if this governing heading (*adhikāra*) did not exist, the *vṛddhi* substitution would apply to the first vowel of the entire *aṅga* (the whole base), and not to the subsequent member.

The explicit statement (*vacana*), however, must serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): either that [the suffix *cha*] occurs only after the word *proṣṭhapadā*, and not elsewhere; or that it occurs only after *proṣṭhapadā* when followed by the sound *j*. Alternatively, by the force of the explicit statement, it may be intended to prescribe the *vṛddhi* strengthening of only the first member of the compound when its initial vowel is not the first of the entire word. Therefore, this governing heading (*adhikāra*) must indeed be formulated for this very purpose.

Is there now only this inquiry regarding the mention of the fifth case? No, he says: "even in the mentions of the fifth case. [The phrase] "and for the sake of the designation of *vṛddhi*" means that it is for the purpose of ensuring that there be the designation "the *vṛddhi* prescribed in the section concerning the final member (*uttarapada*). But what is the need for such a designation? To this he says: "in the case of *vṛddhi* of the final member, and in the rule *sarvaṃ ca*," etc.
It was adopted in that very context so that [the designation would not apply] in cases such as *sarvabhāsaḥ* and *sarvakāraḥ*.
[The suffix *ka* is applied] after a word denoting a part of a whole, when it is accompanied by the word *adṛś*. (Pāṇini 5.2.37)

Regarding the rule *ṛtor vṛddhimadvidhau* and so forth: in the case of a suffix prescribed when there is an occasion for *vṛddhi* (the substitution of *vṛddhi*-vowels) after a word denoting a season (*ṛtu*), the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies; the meaning is that the suffix occurs even after a compound ending in a word for a season. Does this apply everywhere? No; therefore it says *avayavāt*. This means: when a word denoting a season follows a word expressing a part [of that season]. Those who read the text as *avayavānām*, using the genitive plural, do not provide a correct interpretation.

And thus, it was indicated by the ablative case in the rule *susarvārdhadikśabdebhyaḥ*. [The example is: "born in the eastern rains" (*pūrvāsu varṣāsu bhavaḥ*). This is a compound formed under the rule *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51). Others, however, consider this a specific type of compound because the word is not a directional term (*adikśabda*). Now, why does the suffix *ṭhañ* not apply here as well—by the principle of extension to what ends in that (*tadantavidhi*)—from the word *varṣā* itself? To this he says: "For only when preceded by a constituent part... and so forth.
The suffix *cha* is applied after a word denoting a country that ends in *su*, *sarva*, or *ardha*. 7.3.12.

Regarding the phrase "denoting a country" (*janapadavācinaḥ*): this is not a reference to the actual form of the word itself, because the subsequent sūtra prohibits [the application of the suffix] to *madra*. Regarding the rule beginning with *su-sarvārdha-* and so on: when a suffix is prescribed after a word denoting a country, that which ends in such a word is also included, provided that it can occur after words such as *su* and the others. This is the meaning.
The word *diś* [is substituted] for the [final vowel of the first member] of *amadrāṇām*. 7.3.13.

Regarding "pūrvapāñcālaka": this is a compound (samāsa) in the sense of a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita). In "paurvapañcālaka," the word *pūrva* denotes a part; from this *ekadeśi* compound, the suffix *vuñ* is applied. Because it belongs to the class of words beginning with *adi*, only the initial vowel undergoes vṛddhi strengthening.

If this is so, should the suffix *vuñ* also not apply, precisely because [words like] *pūrvā* and others are directional terms (*dikśabda*)? There is a distinction here: in the rule *susarvārddhāddikśabdebhyaḥ*, the inclusion of the word "term" (*śabda*) in the compound is made for the sake of the rule of "inclusion of that which ends with [the preceding member]" (*tadantavidhi*), so that it may be understood that a "directional term" is a term observed to denote a direction. However, in the rule prescribing the *vṛddhi* vowel, only the word *diś* is mentioned. Consequently, they cite as a counter-example only that which ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [words denoting] villages and cities of the eastern regions. 7.3.14.

The term "of the Easterners" (*prācām*) is not a designation for specific teachers, because it is used in association with regions such as *janapada*. For example, in the case of *pūrva-eṣukāmaśamī*: since it is both "eastern" (*pūrvā*) and "Eṣukāmaśamī," it forms a compound according to the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. Subsequently, to express the sense of "originating therefrom," the suffix *ñ* is applied according to the rule *dikpūrvapadādasaṃjñāyāṃ ñaḥ*.

Regarding the term *pūrvapāṭaliputraka*: the compound is formed as previously described, and the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule *ropadhetoḥ prācām*. Although there is only one Pāṭaliputra, nevertheless, because the word "Pāṭaliputra" is used to denote a specific part of that city, the qualification "eastern" (*pūrva*) is entirely appropriate.

Where people reside, that is a village; therefore, even a city is a village. For those rules which are intended to apply to a village are applied even more strictly in a city. For example: "The village cock is not to be eaten"—by this, the city cock is certainly not eaten either. "One should not study in the village"—by this, one studies even less in the city.

In the *Śāstra* as well—it is stated: "From a northern village name that has many syllables and is oxytone," "And from Vāhīka villages," and "Directional words [are used] for names of villages, districts, and [places] other than Cānarāṭa"—the word *nagara* (city) is also included therein; therefore, is there no need for the inclusion of the word *nagara* here? To this he says: "Precisely because it is a village (*grāmatvāt*). [The inclusion of *nagara* is] for the purpose of conveying a distinction in the relationship.

The term *aṅgasya* is understood from the context, as is the term *uttarapadasya*. Therein, the word *grāmāṇām* is connected with *aṅgasya*, meaning "of those members (*aṅga*) which denote villages. The word *nagarāṇām* is connected with *uttarapadasya*, meaning "of those final members (*uttarapada*) which denote cities. This distinction in connection would not be possible if the word *grāma* were mentioned only once; therefore, the mention of *nagara* is made.

In that context, by the phrase "because the first member is a direction" (*dikpūrvapado hi*), the reason is shown for why a distinction between relations must be resorted to. By the phrase "in that case" (*tatra*) and so forth, however, that very distinction between relations is [further] explained. Here, in the formation of *pūrva-eṣukāmaśamī*, after the act of compounding, the *guṇa* substitution—which applies to both the prior and the subsequent members—is *antaraṅga* (internal), whereas the *vṛddhi* of the subsequent member is *bahiraṅga* (external) because it depends upon the subsequent application of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). Once the *guṇa* has been applied, since there is no longer a distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) between the prior and subsequent members, the *vṛddhi* would not apply.

The treatment of [the final of] the former and [the initial of] the latter as being like the whole (antādivadbhāva) is also prohibited when both are simultaneously relied upon. For here, the prior member denoting a *dig* (direction) and the subsequent member are relied upon at once; regarding this, he says: "in cases such as *pūrveṣukāmaśamaḥ*," and so forth. Just as the rule *nendrasya parasya* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), we shall explain that point in its proper place.
[The elision of the case-ending] occurs after a numeral and after a word denoting a number of years. (Pāṇini 6.3.15)

*Saṃvatsara* (year) and *saṃkhyā* (number) form the compound *saṃvatsarasaṃkhyam*, which is a collective dvandva. Regarding *dvisāṃvatsarika*: by the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; however, its elision (*luk*) does not occur by the rule *adhyardhapūrva*, because [the word *dvi-*, being a number,] is not an *anārhīya* (not denoting a price).

Regarding *dviṣāṣṭika*: one might object that in the rule *tam adhīṣṭo bhṛto* (P. 5.1.79), the term *kālāt* ("from a word denoting time") is understood [as a governing condition]; how then can the suffix be applied after words such as *dviṣaṣṭi*? To this he says: "the word *dviṣaṣṭyādi*. The intention is that a word functioning to denote time is what is intended there, and not specifically [subordinate units] like months and so forth.

But surely, in the rule "paramāṇvantasyāsaṃjñāśāṇayoḥ," only the state of being a cause of measurement (*paricchedahetutvamātra*) is intended, and not specifically that which measures by ascending or expanding, such as a *prastha* or similar vessel; otherwise, the prohibition of *śāṇa* would be meaningless. Furthermore, time (*kāla*) is indeed a cause of measurement, and consequently, the mention of "year" (*saṃvatsara*) would be redundant, since the term "end of a measure" (*parimāṇāntasya*) would already suffice. To this he says: "The mention of 'year'... [and] "lasting two years" (*dvaisamika*).
In the case of words like *adhīṣṭa*, the suffix *kha* is applied by the rule "samāyāḥ khaḥ," while in the alternative view, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "dvigorvā."

The indicator [of the rule] does not apply only to the domain of increase (*vṛddhi*); rather, it is universal. Thus he says: *dvivarṣā māṇavikā*. [The analysis is: "she who has become two years old. As before, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied; then, by the rule *varṣāl luk*, there is elision (*luk*), and by the rule *cittavati nityam*, that elision is obligatory. [This means] the exception (*paryudāsa*) does not occur—that is, the prohibition [of the elision]. Therefore, the prohibition itself takes effect.

Now, what is the purpose of including the mention of "number" (*saṃkhyā*), since a thing is also delimited by number? In that case, would it not be established simply by the rule "of that which ends in a measure-word" (*parimāṇāntasya*)? Some say: the mention of "number" is also for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*), namely, that number is not included by the mention of "measure-word. And thus it is stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *aparimāṇabistācita-*: "Time and number are not measures; [examples are] *dvivarṣā*, *trivarṣā*, *dviśatā*, *triśatā*."

Another says: "The number is mentioned here separately from dimension so that the state of being an effect, which was inferred by the Teacher himself through its status as a cause, may not be sublated."
It will be [the name] of the year. || 7.3.16 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *yasya* and so forth: the meaning is that he who intends to sacrifice (*yiyakṣuḥ*) and for whom grain will be available for three years starting from the year of the sacrifice—sufficient for his livelihood during that time—is qualified for the *Soma* sacrifice, but not one who has less. As for the phrase *gamyate hi*: the meaning is that in that context, the future tense (*bhaviṣyattā*) pertains to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), not to the word-meaning (*padārtha*). Regarding the example *dvivarṣo manuṣyaḥ*: by the rule *varṣāl luk*, the suffix is elided; however, by the rule *cittavati nityam*, the elision does not necessarily occur [in all cases], for that [suffix] is intended only in the sense of the past (*bhūtārtha*), whereas in other instances, even when referring to a sentient being (*cittavat*), the elision is merely optional.
The final vowel of a word denoting measure is elided before a taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel, except when the suffix is *asaṃjñā* (not a name) or follows *śāṇa*.

Regarding *dvikauḍavika*: in the derivation of *kuḍava* from the root *kuḍ* with the suffix *av*, the *Uṇādi-sūtras* explain it as "a fourth part of a *prastha*. However, *kuḍava* should be regarded as a distinct, non-etymological (avyutpanna) word. From that [base], the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule *prāgvateṣṭañ*; because it does not denote something "worth" (*anārhīya*), there is no elision [of the final vowel]. Regarding "by two *suvarṇas*": since there is a prohibition against using [weights] like the *śāṇa*, "measure" (*parimāṇa*) here refers to the means of delimitation; thus, it applies even to weight (*unmāna*). A *lohinī* is a *guñjā* seed; gold characterized by a specific shape and measured by five of those is called *pāñcalohitika*. A *kalāpa* is a certain specific measure.

"Because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). This is stated because in the preceding rules, "that which is its measure, [derived] from a numeral, is a name" was taught as a single rule (*ekayoga*), yet the *Bhāṣya* mentions a division of that rule; therefore, this was said. And "this ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). As for the Vārttika regarding the rule "after *adhyardha* and a *dvigu*," we have already explained in that very place that it is a name when there is the elision of the secondary suffix (*taddhitaluk*). Regarding *dvaiśāṇa*: if the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) were to occur here in the final member, it would not occur in the prior member. *Kulija* is a measure of grain. The inclusion of the word "final" (*anta*) has a purpose that is to be considered.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *proṣṭhapadā*. (Pāṇini 5.4.120)

The word *ja* is indicated as having the meaning "born" (*jāta*). In examples such as *upasaraja*, there is the usage of a single part of a word (*padaikadeśa*) as seen [in the tradition], just as *Bhīmasena* is referred to as *Bhīma*.

Regarding the mention of the plural number: although the word *proṣṭhapadāḥ* ends in the plural because the stars (*jyotiṣ*) are many, nevertheless, with respect to the form of the word itself, the singular is considered more appropriate.
The final vowel of the first member [of a compound] becomes long before *hṛd*, *bhaga*, and *sindhu*. (Pāṇini 6.3.19)

Regarding the word *suhṛd*: the term *suhṛt* is established as an irregular form (*nipātita*) by the rule "the words *suhṛt* and *durhṛt* [denote] friend and enemy. However, when the reading is *suhṛdayasyedaṃ* ("this belongs to one with a good heart"), then the substitution of *hṛt* for *hṛdaya* occurs according to the rule "for *hṛdaya*, [the substitute] *hṛt*" and so forth. Regarding *sauhārdyam*: the substitution of *hṛt* for *hṛdaya* occurs by the rule "optionally [the substitution of *hṛt* for *hṛdaya* applies] before the suffixes *śas*, *añ*, and in the case of diseases. *Sindhavaḥ* refers to a region (*janapada*); it includes both the sense of "river" and the sense of "ocean."
And [the suffix yañ is applied] after the group beginning with *anuśatika*. (Pāṇini 7.3.20)

Regarding *ānuśātikam*: that which is bought for a hundred is *śatikam*; [the suffix] *ṭhan* is applied by the rule "after *śata*, [the suffixes] *ṭhan* and *yat* occur when it is not one hundred. That which follows the hundred is *anuśatikaḥ*; from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*). Regarding *ānuhauḍikam*: the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "he goes [there]. Regarding *ānusāṃvaraṇam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "and what is given there, or what is to be done there, takes the suffix *aṇ* as in the case of *bhava*. Regarding *ānusāṃvatsarikam*: the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by the rule "after a word with many vowels that is oxytone. The word *kurukata* belongs to the *garga*-class.

Regarding *sārvalaukika*: [the suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after the words *loka* and *sarvaloka*. Regarding *sārvabhauma*: the suffixes *aṇ* and *añ* are applied after the words *sarvabhūmi* and *pṛthivī*. The terms *adhideva*, *adhibhūta*, and so forth, belong to the group beginning with *adhyātma*. Regarding the rule "or after *kulaṭā*, the suffix *inaṅ*": this is a corrupt reading; for in that context, there is a mention of the word-form itself (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). Since the word *parastrī* is listed among the *kalyāṇī*-type words, the correct reading is "the suffix *inaṅ* after the *kalyāṇī*-type words. Regarding *cāturvaidya*: the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) because it belongs to the *cāturvarṇya*-type group. Furthermore, those four sciences (*vidyā*) are the four Vedas.
And [the first vowel of the second member] is optionally substituted for both vowels when two deities are expressed in a copulative compound. 7.3.21.

That which has Agni and Varuṇa as its deities is *āgnivāruṇa*; that which has Agni and Marut as its deities is *āgnimāruta*. In the word *agni*, the substitution of *it* (short *i*) occurs by the rule *id vṛddhau*. Regarding the phrase "that which is a dual compound of deities" and so forth: that which a hymn (*sūkta*) pertains to by way of being its object of praise is "connected with the hymn" (*sūktasaṃbandhī*); that for whom an oblation (*havis*) is offered is "connected with the oblation" (*havissaṃbandhī*). This qualification of the dual compound is mediated through the meaning [of the deities]. Thus, *skāndaviśākha*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sāsya devatā*. *Brāhmaprajāpatyam*: the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule *patyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ*.

Now, an objection is raised: in the rule *sāsya devatā* ("that is its deity"), the word *devatā* does not denote a genus (*jāti*); what then? That for which the oblation is prepared, or that which is praised by a mantra, is understood as "its deity. And such is not the meaning of the compound here [in *indrāgnī*]. Or, if it were so, would this injunction not also apply just as the secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) do? To this they reply: the secondary suffix occurs even elsewhere—e.g., *jñaḥ* (from *jñā devatāsya*), and *sthālīpākaḥ*—for this is seen in the Bhāṣya.
Not [the substitution of *na* for *ni*] occurs before *indra* or another [word]. 7.3.22.

Regarding *āgnendra* and *saumendra*: the word *indra* does not undergo prior placement [in the compound] according to the rule *ajādyadantam*, because that rule is merely conventional (*prāyikatvāt*).

As for the phrase "the word *indra*" and so forth: in a *dvandva* compound with a word ending in a consonant, such as in *indraśca marut ca*, the word *indra* ought to be placed first, as in the example: *aindrāmārutīṃ bhedakāmālabheta*. The point is that a *dvandva* such as *vāyvindrāv* and the like does not relate to a *sūkta* (hymn) or an oblation (*havis*).
And after [the word] *varuṇa* when it is long [in its final vowel]. 7.3.23.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atra hi" and so forth: in the examples, once the substitution of *ānaṅ* has been applied by the rule "devatādvandve ca," the word *varuṇa* follows a long vowel.
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [a word ending in *prāc*] at the end of a city name. 7.3.24.
Regarding the phrase "in the eastern region": the mention of the teacher (ācārya) does not apply here, because of the statement "optionally" (*vibhāṣitam*) in the subsequent sūtra.
The suffix *uttara* is optionally applied after [the words] *jaṅgala*, *dhenu*, and *valaja*. (Pāṇini 5.4.138)

*Jaṅgala* is a region consisting mostly of forest; *kurujaṅgala* is the *jaṅgala* among the Kurus. *Dhenu* means a cow that has recently calved; *viśvadhenu* is the cow of all. *Valaja* is a product of gold; *sauvarṇavalaja* is a golden product. By the word "subsequent" (*uttara*), the final member of the compound is indicated, because it is always in close proximity [to the preceding element]. Since it is not possible for the term itself to be designated as "optional" (*vibhāṣita*) by its own form, the statement that it is "optional" (*vibhāṣita*) refers to its having an optional increase of the vowel grade (*vṛddhi*); thus, it is a figurative expression.
The suffix *kan* is optionally applied after a word denoting a measure that ends in *ardha*, provided it refers to something prior [in time].

Regarding the term *ardhadrauṇikam*: the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied here according to the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ*. The inclusion of the word *vā* (optionally) is redundant, because the term *vibhāṣitam* (optionally) continues to apply from the previous context; therefore, it should have been stated there as "but previously" (*pūrvaṃ tu*). However, it was not done in that way.
Not for anything subsequent to this. 7.3.27.

"Ārdhaprasthikam" and "ārdhakaṃsikam": here, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied as before. However, the suffix *ṭiṭhan* does not apply after the word *kaṃsa*, because there is no rule for extension (*tadantavidhi*) to that [specific] ending. Extension to the end of a compound applies to those preceded by numerals prior to the suffix *vat*, but the word *ardha* is not a numeral.

Furthermore, what would be the consequence? [The opponent] thinks that the form is simply *vṛddhi*, and thus there is no difference whether the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies or not. But what is the reason why the prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) would not apply? To this he says: "For where... As it has been stated: "The word *nimitta* (cause/condition) is used in its primary sense for that which is currently producing an effect."

What is the purpose of specifying "of the subsequent" (*parasya*)? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to the preceding. Since the inclusion of the qualification "from *ataḥ*" (from *a*), it will not apply to the preceding; for in the preceding word *adhas*, there is no element other than the vowel *a* that undergoes *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, if there were a prohibition regarding the preceding, the rule "but optionally for the preceding" (*pūrvasya tu vā*) would be rendered meaningless. Then what is the purpose? It is so that the rule of extension to that which ends in such (*tadantavidhi*) does not occur; otherwise, it would be understood as applying only to a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ending in the vowel *a*.

What fault is there in that? There would be a prohibition in this case: *ardhadrauṇikam* (half-a-droṇa), *ardhakauḍavikam* (half-a-kauḍava). However, the previous rule [P. 5.1.26] has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *ardhamauṣṭikaḥ* (bought for half a handful) and so forth. Therefore, the word "of the subsequent" (*parasya*) is stated in order to exclude the application of the rule regarding that which ends in [the aforementioned suffixes].
The suffix *ḍha* is applied after *pravāhaṇa*.

In the rule regarding the word *pravāhaṇa* when followed by the suffix *ḍha*, the two genitive cases (*ṣaṣṭhyau*) are in a non-co-referential relationship (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "of that which is the *uttarapada* (final member) constituting a part of the word *pravāhaṇa*. Now, one might ask: since the *uttarapada* here is already inherently possessed of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening), for what purpose is its *vṛddhi* prescribed once again? It is said in reply:

When there is no *vṛddhi* in the first member (*pūrvapada*), if there were likewise no *vṛddhi* in the second member (*uttarapada*), then the prohibition of the *puṃvadbhāva* by the rule "of that which has *vṛddhi* as its cause" would not apply—as in the case of *pravāhaṇeyībhārya*. Let it not be so; [one might argue] that it will be governed by the rule "and of a genus (*jāti*)," since "a *gotra* together with a *caraṇa*" constitutes a genus. If this is the case, then this [usage] indicates that this prohibition is not eternal (*anitya*).

In the case of *hāstikaṃ* (a herd of female elephants), derived from *hastinīnāṃ samūhaḥ*, there is no prohibition of the optional *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) that would otherwise apply by either the rule *bhasyāḍhe* or the rule *ṭhakchasośca*. [The word] *pravāhaṇaḥ* means "one who causes to flow"; it is formed from the root *vah-* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *lyuṅ* according to the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *ṇervibhāṣā*. And [the same applies] to the suffix *tat*. (Pāṇini 7.3.29).

*Pravāhaṇeya* is formed by the suffix *iñ* [Pāṇini 4.1.95] after *yuvan* (a young descendant). *Pravāhaṇeyaka* is formed by the suffix *vuñ* [Pāṇini 4.3.126] after a *gotra* (lineage) or *caraṇa* (school).

For what purpose is this stated? An option was previously prescribed for when *ḍha* follows; [this rule is stated] so that there might not be obligatory *vṛddhi* in the case of a stem ending in *ṭha* before an affix beginning with *iñ*. But this is not a valid purpose, because even for a *vṛddhi* caused by *iñ* and other such affixes, the option conditioned by *ḍha* itself will serve as a sublater. For "after *ḍha*" (*ḍhe*) is a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*), not a locative of cause (*nimittasaptamī*); therefore, a prohibition of *vṛddhi* even for that which has another cause is indeed obtained when *ḍha* follows. To this he replies: "caused by a *brāhmaṇa*-derived *taddhita*."

This is the intended meaning: when the two [suffixes] have arisen, the optional alternative (*vikalpa*) first operates, subverting the *vṛddhi* that would otherwise depend on them; subsequently, the suffixes *iñ* and so forth arise, and the *vṛddhi* conditioned by them is obtained. However, at this point, the optional alternative conditioned by the suffix *ḍa* does not apply, because it has already operated previously and cannot operate again.
The negative particle *nañ* [is compounded] with *śuci*, *īśvara*, *kṣetrajña*, *kuśala*, and *nipuṇa*. (Pāṇini 2.2.60)

"It is prescribed as something not yet obtained. He demonstrates this very non-obtainment with the words: "not from that which is preceded by *nañ*. "The subsequent suffix denoting a state" means that the suffixes beginning with *ṣyañ*, which follow the suffixes *tva* and *tal*, and thus the subsequent suffix denoting a state, must be prescribed first from words such as *śuci* even before the *nañ*-compound is formed; only afterwards does the *nañ*-compound occur. Since the negative particle (*nañ*) is not included within the base of the word, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is prescribed for what was previously unobtained.

Regarding the phrase "tadapare" and so forth: if there were no object [for the suffix], the application of the *aṅ* suffix would have to be set aside; however, such an object does exist. What, then, is it? It is the suffix prescribed for [denoting] offspring and the like, which is distinct from that which expresses an action (*bhāvavacana*). Even if there is confidence in the expression of an action, that too can indeed be demonstrated; thus he says: "and of the *bahuvrīhi*."

He states that even the claim "the suffix denoting state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is prohibited in the subsequent [term]" is not universally applicable here, by saying "not pertaining to the knower of the field" (*akṣetrajña*). Thus, it is established that the governing rule for secondary members (*aṅga-adhikāra*) is not to be set aside. And in this way, the formation of expressions such as "impurity resulting from contact with that" (*tadupasparśādaśaucam*) is justified. However, in cases such as "impurity due to death lasts ten days" (*daśāhaṃ śāvamāśaucam*), the suffix *aṇ* should be understood in its primary sense (*idamartha*).
The suffix *thāl* is used after the words *yathātatha* and *yathāpura* in the sense of "alternately" (*paryāyeṇa*).

These two are to be understood as negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) in the case of *abrāhmaṇa* and so forth. Therefore, the intention is that the prohibition of the suffix *ṣyañ* by the rule "not after [a word] preceded by *nañ*" does not apply. For example, *yathāsādṛśye* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva-samāsa*). In the sense of "not exceeding the meaning of the word" (*padārthānativṛtti*), *yathātatham*—meaning "truth"—is said to be that which has not exceeded its state of being; and *yathāpuram* is said to be that thing which, having existed in a certain way previously, has not even now exceeded that state of being.

What, then, is the proof for its being an *avyayībhāva* compound? To this he says: "For thus... [and] "In the Bhāṣya, however... For indeed, without first applying the shortening of the vowel (*hrasvatva*), the demonstration of the analysis (*vigraha*) of the *avyayībhāva* would not be possible.

This derivation can be explained. How so? When there is *vṛddhi* of the first member (*pūrvapada*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied after the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*). But when there is *vṛddhi* of the second member (*uttarapada*), then the negative compound is formed with a word ending in the suffix *ṣyañ*. There is also no difference in accent; for in both cases, the initial syllable is acute (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the first member. Furthermore, no other suffix occurs after these two, because such a formation is not sanctioned by usage (*anabhidhānāt*).
The substitution of *ha* for the final consonant of a root ending in *h* occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel, except when the affix is *ciṇ* or *ṇal*.

The phrase "in the case of *taddhita* suffixes" has ceased to apply. This is because when a verbal root is mentioned by its own form (*svarūpa*), the operation is understood to apply to a suffix attached to it. The phrase "before a *kit* suffix," which is connected to that [previous rule], is also understood to have ceased to apply. However, the mention of *ñṇit* is connected only with the suffix itself; therefore, even though "in the case of *taddhita* suffixes" has ceased, that [mention of *ñṇit*] continues to apply. In these examples, the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) occurs according to the rule "the *h* of *han* [is replaced by *k*] before *ñṇit* suffixes."
The augment *yuk* is added after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, except when followed by the affix *ciṇ* or *kṛt*.

The mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of excluding *kṛt* suffixes, as in *dadau* and *dadhau*. [Objection: But surely the substitution of *au* by the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* will be the sublater here; for rules that have no other occasion (*anavakāśa*) are sublaters, whereas the substitution of *au* has its own occasion. What is its occasion? It is when there is the absence of the *ṇit*-characteristic in the *ṇal* of the first person singular. [Response: In that case, the phrase *aciṇ-ṇaloḥ* will be carried over [from the previous rule]; however, in the case of *ciṇ*, it will occur by virtue of the explicit statement. To this, he says: *cauḍiḥ*, *bālākiḥ*. [These are formed] with the suffix *iñ* because they belong to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

In this case, since the elision of *y* (yasyeti-lopa) has already fulfilled its purpose regarding [the suffixes] such as *dakṣya*, the augment *yuk* would apply by virtue of being subsequent [in the order of rules], thereby subverting that elision. Would it not fail to apply because of the continued reference (*anuvṛtti*) to "of the vowels" (*acām*) and "of the first" (*ādeḥ*)? To this he says: "He whose deity is *jñā*" (*jñā devatā asya*). Here, there is the possibility [of *yuk* applying] due to the treatment of the whole as if it were the first member (*ādivadbhāva*). Furthermore, if "of the vowels" (*acām*) and "of the first" (*ādeḥ*) were continued [from the previous rule], then [the form] *daridrāyaka* would not be possible.

The final *m* of a verbal root that is not taught with an acute accent on its first syllable, provided it does not end in *m*, is not elided before an affix beginning with *y* or *v*, except for the root *ā-cam*.

"Upadeśe udātta" means "having an acute accent in its original enunciation. This form is correct precisely because of this specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). As for the question "What has been stated?": since nothing proximate [to the rule] is applicable, the question is asked. [The answer is: "By the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*, there is *vṛddhi*. However, this [rule] was not commenced immediately after that [previous rule], for the purpose of depending upon both the *ciṇ* and the *kṛt* suffixes.

It should be understood as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). However, for those who hold the view that "the assignment of meanings in the *dhātupāṭha* is not by Pāṇini," there is an absence of *vṛddhi* here on the basis of the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not obligatory. Thus we have *śamī* and *tamī*. In the case of *śamityaṣṭābhyo ghinuṇ*, once the accent of the suffix has been applied, the root is now unaccented (*anudātta*). In *yāmakaḥ* and *rāmakaḥ*, once the accent of the *liṭ*-suffixes has been applied, this [word] is now acutely accented (*udātta*).

Is it not too little that only "anācameḥ" is stated? To this he says: "It should be stated as 'anācamikamivamīnām'. [The roots are: *ṭuvam* (to vomit), *kam* (desire), and *cam* (eating). In that rule (*sūtra*), there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the root preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, whereas in the explanatory sentence (*vākya*), it refers to the simple root alone. However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), an example from the sentence is shown only for the root preceded by *āṅ*; this was not determined by the authoritative teachers (*āpta*). Regarding *kāma*: from the root *kam*, in the absence of the suffix *ṇiṅ* according to the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā," the suffix *ghañ* is applied, resulting in the *vṛddhi* vowel.

"In the case of the causative (*ṇic*), when there is *vṛddhi*, [the form] is *satyam*. For in that case, this prohibition does not apply; because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not a *kṛt* suffix. [Objection: "But even if there is *vṛddhi*, since the roots *jan*, *jṝ*, *ṣṇas*, and *rañj* are designated as having the marker *m* (by the rule *janījṝṣknasurañjaumantāśca*), there ought to be a shortening by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*? To this he says: "In that case, however... [The meaning is: "Others are not *mit* when not preceded by a cause" (*nānye mito'hetāviti*). This means that among those enumerated in the *curādigaṇa*, other than those preceded by a cause (*ahetau*), the roots ending in *-am* and so forth are not designated as *mit*. "They consider it improper" means exactly that.
The meaning is that it should be read as "viśrāntibhūmiḥ" (the ground of rest). By this, the phrase "let this bow of ours obtain rest, with its string-bands loosened" is explained.
And [the substitution of *j* for *y* occurs] before the roots *jan* and *vadhi*. (Pāṇini 7.3.35)

The root *vadhi* is a distinct verbal base (*prakṛtyantara*), because it is listed in the *bhūvādi* class [of roots] as "√*vadha* in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyām*). Regarding the phrase "if he is an eater": this is intended to demonstrate that even for one who purchases meat and eats it, there is an inherent connection to the act of injury (*hiṃsā*). As Manu says (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 5.51):
"The consenter, the butcher, the killer, the buyer and seller, the preparer, the server, and the eater—all these are slayers."*

Regarding "of the substitute *han*": this refers to the rule where *dasyuḥ* is the limit (*avadhi*). In the phrase "he generated the embryo" (*jajāna garbham*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*); because the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is implied, it possesses an object (*sakarmakatva*).
The suffix *puṅ* is applied after the verbal roots *arti*, *hrī*, *vrī*, *knūyī*, *kṣmāyī*, and *ātaḥ* when followed by the causal suffix *ṇi*.

The roots *vlīṅ* in the sense of "covering," *knūyī* in the sense of "sound," and *kṣmāyī* in the sense of "shaking" [are included]. In the examples, the *guṇa* substitution characterized by the presence of a *puk* augment applies. The inclusion of both [roots] is because no specific distinction is stated.
As for the mention of *rī* as well: although that root meaning "flowing" possesses an *anubandha*, the point is that its inclusion is also traditionally recorded by the Teachers (*ācāryas*).

The insertion of *puṭ* at the beginning is not arbitrary; rather, it is intended. Thus he says: "The insertion of *puṭ* is for the sake of the initial limit (*pūrvāntakaraṇam*). Consider the form *adīdapat*. If, however, *puṭ* were inserted after the *ṇi*, then because that [newly formed element] would be included by the term *ṇi*, the rule stating that "the vowel *a* of the base (*aṅga*) preceding *ṇi* is short when it is an *upadhā*" would not apply, and thus the shortening would not occur. This is merely an illustration of a fault; for in forms such as *dāpyate*, since the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "*ṇer aniṭi*" [Pāṇini 6.4.51], the letter *p* would not be heard. This is not a fault.

For a deletion does not remove everything; rather, by the rule *alo’ntyasya*, the deletion applies only to the final [element]. In that case, however, in the form *knopayati*, the augment *iṭ* would result. Furthermore, no benefit whatsoever is seen here from the presence of the suffix beginning with *par* (the *yaṅ*); for otherwise, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed for a stem ending in *puK* would have to be stated as a *vṛddhi*.

As for what is said—that when *guṇa* is prescribed after a *puṭ* augment, the mention of *puganta* need not be made, because it is already established by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ"—that too is mere empty hope; for even in the case of *parasmaipada* endings, *guṇa* must necessarily be prescribed after a *puṭ* augment, otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *vṛddhi* by the rule "aco ñṇiti."
The suffix *yuk* is applied after the verbal roots √śās, √sā, √hve, √vyā, and √vep.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of *pā*," and so forth: this is merely a desired interpretation (*iṣṭi*), because the form *pā* is derived through secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇika*).

As for the statement "the augment *luk* [is applied]": although the form *pālayati* is established from the root *pāl* (meaning "to protect") belonging to the *curādigaṇa*, which is already transitive (*ṇijanta*), and which is further followed by a causative *ṇic*, nevertheless, the rule prescribing *luk* is stated so that there may not be the forms *pāpayati* (from *pā* with the suffix *puK*) or *pāyayati* (from *pā* with the suffix *yuK*).

Regarding the roots *dhūñ* and *prīñ*: *dhūñ* means "to shake" and *prīñ* means "to satisfy"; these are cited as ending in *ñ* (i.e., *dhūñ* and *prīñ*), and therefore the augment *nuk* does not apply to the root *dhū* belonging to the *divādigaṇa*.

"These also" means these [roots] beginning with *yuj*, as well as those beginning with *yu* that will be mentioned later. "The inclusion of those whose final vowel has been changed to *ā*" means that after prescribing the augment *yuk* for roots ending in *ā*, when those ending in *ā* are subsequently included, the application of *yuk* is thereby explained; this is the intended sense. "And so forth"—by the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of examples such as *krāpayati*, *nijāpayati*, *vilāpayate*, *muṇḍo vismāpayate*, and *priyam ācaṣṭe* (expressing as dear) which becomes *prāpayati*.
The suffix *ju* is applied after the root *dhū* in the sense of "shaking. (Pāṇini 7.3.38)

The very mention of *vidhūnane* (in the sense of "shaking") is the indicator that the augment *nuṭ* occurs after the root *dhūñ* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇi*. Regarding the word *vā*: this refers to the root *vā* meaning "motion" and "smelling. Since the form *vājayati* is already established from the root *vaja* or *vraja* meaning "motion" when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, the specific prescription of *juk* is for the purpose of excluding the *puk* augment from the root *vāti*.
The suffixes *lī*, *lū*, *nuk*, and *luk* are optionally applied after a verbal root [ending in a consonant] when expressing the act of pouring out oil or fat. 7.3.39.

*Snēha* (oil/fat) refers to ghee and the like; its *vipātana* is the operation that causes it to lose its state, namely, to abandon its hardness. The meaning of *snēhavipātana* is the induction of fluidity through roasting in fire and so forth in the case of that which has attained hardness. It does not, however, apply to that which has already been liquefied. For there is the contingency [of the rule applying] because a form modified in one part is not considered different from the original. In the example *jaṭābhir ālāpayate*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule: "The root *li* takes the middle voice when meaning 'honoring' or 'making someone humble'."

The mention of *lī* includes both *lī* (the root meaning "to dissolve") and *līṅ* (the root meaning "to cling"). These belong to the *kryādika* and *daivādika* classes [of roots], respectively. The paribhāṣā rule regarding "that which lacks an indicatory letter" (*niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*) is not intended here. Furthermore, the mention of *līyati* refers to the form that has undergone the change to *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*). The word "mention" (*grahaṇam*) is to be supplied [as the object of these statements].
The suffix *ṣuk* is applied after the word *bhī* when it means "fear of a cause. (Pāṇini 7.3.40)

The word *hetu* is technical (*pāribhāṣika*). *Bhī-* means fear (*bhayam*); thus, *hetubhayam* is "fear caused by a [specific] cause. [The suffix *ṇic* is applied] to that which exists therein. Regarding *bhīṣayate*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule "after the roots *bhī* and *smi*, when there is fear caused by a [specific] cause. Regarding *bhāpayate*: the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) occurs by the rule "after *bhī*, when there is fear caused by a [specific] cause."
The substitute *pu* optionally takes the place of the final vowel of the word *ruha*.

This grammatical application (*yoga*) is capable of being explained. How so? The root *ruh* is listed in the *divādi* class with the meaning "to delude" (*vimohana*); that same root, when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), will be used here in the sense of "birth. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, [the form] *ropayati* is derived from that [causative root]. However, from the root *ruh* [in its primary sense], one forms *ārohayati*. [The rule: *pratyayasthātkātpūrvasyāt idāpyasupaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.44).
[This rule prescribes the substitution of *i* for the vowel preceding a *k* that stands before a suffixal *t*, provided that the suffix does not end in a case-ending (*sup*).]

In this context, if the vowel *a* were intended [in the rule *kādi*], then the substitution of *it* would not occur in the example *etikāś caranti*. This form is derived from *etad-* with the addition of *akac*, the replacement of *t* by *at* (the *tyadādyatva* rule), and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. For in the case of *akac*, the final *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*) and not for the sake of being heard (*śravaṇārtha*); otherwise, forms such as *bhindhiki* and *rundhaki* would result in grammatical failure. Consequently, because the word *ka* would be absent, the form *etikā* could not be established at all. Furthermore, the prohibition "not after *yā* or *as*" (*na yāsayoḥ*) would be rendered meaningless if it were understood as referring to a combination of sounds (*saṅghātagrahaṇa*).

Therefore, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; he says that only the phoneme itself is intended: "from the *k* of a suffix" (*pratyayasthātkakārāt*). As for the phrase "if that": the meaning is that if it does not follow an *āp* which is itself after a *sup*, then this substitution of *it* occurs. By the technical rule regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), it should be understood as "following a word ending in a *sup*. Examples: *jaṭilikā*, *muṇḍikā*. From the two words ending in *ṭāp*, when the sense is "unknown" and so forth, there is the suffix *ka* by the rule "after *prāgdiva*, *ka*" (*prāgivātkaḥ*); then, by the rule "shortening of *eṇaḥ*" (*ke'ṇaḥ*), there is shortening; then *ṭāp*; then the substitution of *it*. Although this *a* is a derivative (lākṣaṇika) form, nevertheless, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule "of the northerners, in place of *āt*" (*udīcāmātaḥ sthāne*), it also occurs here.

It takes only the letter *ka*. This has already been stated: "In the expression 'from *kā*,' it is intended as the mere phoneme (*varṇa*). There is no suffix consisting of the letter *ka* alone; therefore, even when it is said "from the suffix *kā*," the word "suffix" will apply to a part of that suffix. Thus, what is the purpose of including the term *sthā*? This is the meaning.

*paṭukā*, *mṛduketi*. When the suffix *ka* is applied to the words *paṭu* and *mṛdu*—which here function in the feminine sense—the suffix *ṭāp* follows. If the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrvagrahaṇa*) were not present, then by the rule "from that [the preceding], the subsequent [is affected]" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*), the substitution of *it* would apply only to the vowel following the *ka*, thereby overriding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) on the grounds that "an operation concerning a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a grammatical element (*āṅga*). Although this undesirable consequence could have been shown in examples such as *jaṭilikā* and *muṇḍikā*, nevertheless, another example has been presented for the sake of clarity. *rākā*, *dhāketi*. [These are derived] from the rule: "The suffix *ka* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kal*."

Regarding the question, "What is qualified by the word *atha api*?"—the question arises from the doubt as to whether it is the letter *ka* or the suffix (*pratyaya*) that is being qualified. [The opponent suggests: "It is the letter *ka*. [The author replies: If the suffix were being qualified, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to words such as *rathakaṭyā*. Although the suffix is also heard in the text, nevertheless, because it is subordinate (*upasarjana*), it is the letter *ka* alone that is qualified. [The opponent objects: "In the case of *kārikā*, [the suffix] would not [apply] either. The meaning of the word *api* (also/even) is: "Let the over-extension stand for a moment; even what is desired is not established."

If it were understood that "the *ka* which follows [the *i*]," then even the form *kārikā* would not be possible, because of the intervention by the second *a* resulting from the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). [The objection is answered: "Such an intervention is accepted on account of the explicit statement. This connects with what is to be said later. He explains the phrase "such" as "produced by the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). The mention of "by one phoneme" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); the intended meaning lies simply in the fact that it is produced by the status of being like the original.

Otherwise, in the case of *etikā*, the substitution of *it* would not occur because of the intervention of two *a*-vowels. One [a-vowel] belongs to *etad-*, and the second is the *a* prescribed by the rule *tyadādīnām aḥ*; in that context, there is both the single-substitute *pararūpa* of the two *a*-vowels and the long vowel (*dīrgha*) with the *ṭāp* suffix—*sthānivadbhāva* applies to both of these. Others, however, say: even here, *sthānivadbhāva* applies only to that single substitute which occurs together with the *ṭāp*, but not to the *pararūpa* formed between the two *a*-vowels.

Because the purpose of the technical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is fulfilled by a single application, there is an intervention by only one [element] here as well. While it could have been stated that "it will occur even with an intervention based on the explicit statement," he shows what is excluded by the phrase "in *rathakaṭyā* and so forth. A collection of chariots is *rathakaṭyā*, according to the rule *initrakaṭyacaśca*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), forms such as *gargakāmyā* are included. From the sense "one who desires the Gargas for himself," the suffix *kāmyac* is applied; from that, the suffix *apratyaya* is added, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.

This is what is meant: that which is expressed by the immediate succession (ānantarya) conveyed by the locative case in the word "āpi" is not abandoned entirely; rather, it is resorted to as long as possible.

"This [word] ends in a *su*-affix following the word *parivrājaka*. Its status as ending in a *su*-affix (*subantatva*) is established by means of the technical definition (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "for in the case of exclusion" (*paryudāse hi*): the meaning is that it is something other than a *sup* (i.e., *asu*), and this is assumed when it is followed by an *āp* vowel. "Because it does not end in a *su*-affix with respect to the whole" (*samudāyādasubantāt*): the *su*-affix is produced after the constituent part, the word *parivrājaka*, and not after the whole; therefore, the whole does not end in a *su*-affix. "Even so, it is not accepted": the meaning is that even a *bahuvrīhi* compound is not accepted here. Why? To this he says: "For thus... (*tathā hi*).

Regarding *bahucarmikā*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has many hides" (*bahūni carmāṇy asyām iti*). The suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. However, if this were a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would not follow the final stem-ending vowel here, because it is separated [from that vowel] by the suffix *kap*. Regarding *māmikā*: it means "this belongs to me" (*mama iyam*). The suffix *aṇ* is applied, and the substitution of *mamaka* for *mama* occurs by the rule *tavakamamakāvekavacane*. Regarding *dākṣiṇātyikā*: [the word] *dakṣiṇā* is derived from *dakṣiṇā* with the suffix *āc*. Then, for the sense of "originating there" (*bhava*) and so forth, the suffix *tyak* is applied by the rule *dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak*. Regarding *ihatyikā*: the suffix *tyap* is applied after an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the rule *avyayāttyap*.
Not [the suffix *yat*] after the words *yāsa*. (Pāṇini 7.3.45)

This prohibition is stated because the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.109] prescribing the constant substitution of *it* (the long vowel *ī*) would otherwise apply by virtue of what precedes it; for a prohibition presupposes a prior application. When the suffix *akac* is applied to *yat* and *tat*, then the prohibition applies—as in *yakā* and *sakā*. Since *yat* and *tat* take *akac*, and then *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *a* for the initial) followed by *ṭāp* occurs before the nominative singular (*sau*), one might think that because the forms *yā* and *sā* are cited in the nominative singular, the prohibition would not apply to other case endings. To this, he says: "The mention of *yā sā* is not restrictive"; that is, it is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *yat* and *tat*.

If this is so, should one not simply say *yat-tadoḥ*? True; however, it was not done that way—what can we do? [As in the examples: *yakāṃ yakāmadhīmahi*, meaning "the ṛc and the gāthā"; and *takāṃ takāmpacāmahe*, meaning "the herb and the vegetable. These are two such usages. Regarding *upatyakā*: [it is formed] by the rule *upādhibhyāṃ tyakannāsannārūḍhayoḥ*. Here someone says: "This suffix *tyakan* ending in a feminine object; therefore, although one could have said *tyikan* for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation, the absence of the *it* augment (the short *i*) is due to the power of the vocalization of the letter *a* in *tyakan*. That is incorrect.

In examples such as *pañcopatyakaḥ* ("purchased for five valleys"), where the suffix *ṭhak* (which forms adjectival derivatives) is elided by the rule *adhyardhapūrva*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is also elided by the rule *luk taddhitaluki*. Consequently, because the cause [for the application of the suffix] has disappeared, the substitution of *it* (the replacement of the final vowel with its short counterpart) would not occur. Therefore, this [rule regarding the preservation of the suffix] must exist for the purpose of preventing the elision of the *taddhita* suffix. Furthermore, elision (*luk*) is a "foreign" (*bahiraṅga*) operation, and "a foreign elision subverts even internal rules. Now, one might object: "Does this not concern the domain of the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (which prescribes the elision of case-endings after verbal roots and nominal stems)? He says: "No."

Whatever *tug* augment there may be, it subverts all internal (*antaraṅga*) rules. For example, in forms such as *sanīsraṃsa*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) does not occur. In forms such as *pañcakhaṭva*, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *ṭāp* does not occur; for if it did, then due to the status of being like the initial (*ādivadbhāva*), the *ā* would be included by the mention of *ā* [in the rule for elision], and upon that elision, the vowel *a* would not be heard here.

Regarding *pāvakāḥ*: they purify (*punanti*) or cause to purify (*pāvayanti*), thus they are *pāvakāḥ*. Regarding *alomakāḥ*: this is the suffix *kap* after a *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding *jīvakā*: the suffix *vun* is applied by the rule "also in the sense of benediction" (*āśiṣi ca*).

*Devaka*: From the word *devadatta*, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). According to the rule "and when [the suffix] begins with a vowel other than *a*, the elision [of the final part] is optionally to be stated," there is the elision of the word *datta*.

*Kṣipakā*: From the root *kṣip*, the suffix *ka* is applied because it has an *i* as its penultimate letter (*igupadha*). For the root *dhru* (meaning "motion" and "stability"), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the *pacādi* group; due to its inclusion in the *kuṭādi* group, there is no *guṇa* substitution, and thus *uvaṅ* is applied. From both of these, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of "unknown" (*ajñāta*) and so forth, according to the rule "after words beginning with *prāg* [i.e., *prāk*], *ka*."

From the root *tṛ* with the suffix *ṇvul*: *tārakā*. That which describes qualities such as greatness is a *vaṇaka*, a type of cloak; *tāntava* is a derivative of threads, formed with the suffix *orañ*. Regarding *vaṇikā*: this is the *bhāgurī*, a specific commentary (*ṭīkā*). From the causative form of the root *vṛt* with the suffix *ṇvul*: *varttikā*.

Regarding *aṣṭakā*: it is called *aṣṭakā* because "Brahmins eat rice (*odana*) on this [day]," derived with the suffix *takan* according to the rule *iṣyaśibhyāṃ takan*. Regarding *pitṛdaivatyam*: the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities (*devatāḥ*), hence *pitṛdevatāḥ*; the rite for their sake is *pitṛdaivatyam*, derived with the suffix *yat* according to the rule *devatāntāttādarthye yat*. Regarding *aṣṭikā*: its measure (*parimāṇam*) is eight, derived with the suffix *kan* according to the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan*.

Regarding *sūtaka*: the suffix *kan* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*), as indicated by the prohibition in the rule "not when expressing a part" (*na sāmivacane*). Regarding *putrikā*: after the feminine suffix *ṅīn* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *śārṅgarava*-class, the possessive suffix *kan* is added; by the rule "when *ka* follows, [the vowel] of *aṇ* is short," the vowel *i* becomes short, and in one alternative, the substitution of *a* for that [short *i*] is prescribed. Regarding *vṛndārikā*: the suffix *ārakan* is prescribed by the rule "after *śṛṅga* and *vṛnda*, *ārakan* should be stated."
According to the usage of the northern grammarians, [the substitution of *ya*] occurs in place of the long vowel *ā* when it is preceded by *ya*.

That which has *yak* preceded by something is called *yakapūrvā*; what is the referent of the other word? It is the vowel *ā*. The feminine gender, though residing in the meaning, is superimposed upon the word for the sake of grammatical designation as feminine. The word *pūrva* expresses "preceding" in a fixed order. Regarding *ibhyikā*: it is derived from *ibha* (elephant) with the suffix *yaḥ* according to the rule *daṇḍādibhyo yaḥ*, forming *ibhya* (wealthy); then the suffix *pūrvakaḥ* is applied, and the vowel is shortened. Regarding *caṭakā* and *mūṣakā*: the suffix *ṭāp* is added because these words belong to the *ajādi* group. Regarding *sāṅkāśyikā*: that which is produced from the *saṅkāśas* is *sāṅkāśyam*, formed by the suffix *ṇyaḥ* according to the rule *saṅkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ*. Then, to express the sense of "belonging to that place," the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule *dhanvayopadhādvuñ*.

Is the inclusion of the term *sthāna* (place) redundant, since it is already established by the rule "the genitive [case ending] denotes a relation of substitution" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*)? To this he replies with the words beginning "The inclusion of *sthāna*... The intention is that because a *paribhāṣā* (technical metarule) is supplementary to a specific injunction (*vidhi*), it would not apply in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). He clarifies its status as a restatement with the words "For by the word *ātaḥ*... The meaning is that in the formulation of the statement "the *it*-ness (the substitution of *i*) occurs for that which is the letter *a*," there is no contact whatsoever with an injunction regarding the letter *a*.

"Regarding the phrase *strīpratyayasya pratipattyartham*: the meaning is that this is for the sake of ensuring the recognition (*pratipatti*) of that which is a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), namely, the *ṭāp* and other such suffixes prescribed under the governing rule (*adhikṛta*) "in the feminine" (*striyām*). For if the feminine gender were not specified, any vowel whatsoever might be taken; thus [one might derive] *śubhaṃ yāti*, *bhadraṃ yāti* (he goes auspiciously, he goes favorably). Here, the suffix *kvip* is applied. The forms *śubham* and *bhadram* are established as ending in *m* by nipātana (irregular derivation), followed by the addition of *ka* as before, and the shortening of the vowel.

Regarding the term "prohibition" (pratiṣedha): by that [prohibition], it becomes a positive injunction (vidhi) itself. Thus, *sunayikā* and *suśayikā*. From the roots *nī* and *śī*, the suffix *ac* is applied (*erac*), and a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the word *su-*; the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and so forth are as before. *Supākikā* and *suśokikā*. From the roots *pac* and *śuc*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied; the substitution of *ku* occurs according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*. The remainder is as before.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the word *bhastrā*, as well as after *aca*, *ajā*, and *dvyaṅgava*, even when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.50)

The word *svā* is the nominative case used in place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). The mention of *eṣā*, with the substitution of *s* for *ṣ* already effected, serves as the governing rule (*tantra*). Thus, it is illustrated that in the case of the suffix *jas*, the substitution of *i* for *e* is obligatory, as in the example *etikāś caranti*.
In this context, the word *sthāne* (in place) is an adjective qualifying the word *sva* (its own);
for both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*) exist there in the case of the suffixes *kak* and *cak*.
The occurrence of these two [suffixes] does not exist after the words *dvi* and *eta*; nor is there any deviation elsewhere.
Therefore, this rule would not apply to a pronoun that is its own word (*svaśabda*).

Regarding the word *dvake*: from the word *dvaki*, when the dual number is applied, the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems occurs, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; then, because of the presence of that [suffix], the substitution of *śī* for *auṅ* takes place. However, the substitution of *yat* for the *tyad*-class stems does not occur for the case-ending that follows the meaning of the compound, according to the rule: "An external operation (*bahiraṅga*) subverts even internal operations (*antaraṅga*). Thus, it is "after a *subanta* (word ending in a case-suffix)" because of the case-ending situated within [the compound] itself, by means of the technical designation (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) of being a *subanta*.

In that case, by this same reasoning, one might argue that the word *sva* itself, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, should not be employed [as a cause for the suffix *ka*]. To this he says: "But the word *sva*... For, according to the rule "The word *sva* [is used] except when denoting kinsmen or wealth," it is not designated as a pronoun (*asarvanāman*) when referring to kinsmen or wealth; therefore, the suffix *ka* must be applied to it, and not *akac*. In that context, when the suffix *ka* is added in a *nañ*-compound and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added after that [form ending in *ka*], the [suffix *ṭāp*] does not follow immediately after a case-ending (*sup*), because it is separated [from the case-ending] by the [suffix *ka*]. Consequently, the word *sva*, even when preceded by *nañ*, remains indeed a prompter [of the suffix *ka*] as long as it is not designated as a pronoun.

*Abhastrakaḥ*, *abhastrikaḥ*. [The suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule "after words meaning 'small,' [the suffix] *ka* follows those beginning with *prāgdiv*" (Pāṇini 5.3.71). He demonstrates how it would not be established if the mention of *bhastrā* were absent, saying: "in this case. The *bahuvrīhi* compound also occurs in the masculine—as in *abhastraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("a man who is not a bhastrā"). By the mention of "prescribed" (*vihita*), he shows this: even though the word *bhastrā* is one whose masculine form has not been stated (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), and the suffix *ka* follows it, nevertheless, that suffix is not prescribed after that [specific feminine form].

Furthermore, the mention of "bhāṣitapuṃska" (having a corresponding masculine form) applies to the subsequent rules as well; otherwise, there would be an over-extension even in cases such as *akhaṭvikā*—derived from *akhaṭvā*, meaning "one for whom no bed exists"—and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that by the inclusion of the word *api* (also), there is a conjunction only of [words] beginning with *bhastrā* and so on, and not of those preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*), he says: "even those preceded by *nañ*, because of the word *api*. By saying "it is desired," he shows that this is not an application obtained through its own inherent power (*svataḥ*). If it were indeed desired in all cases, then one need not say "even those preceded by *nañ*"; for in every case it would apply simply by the rule "in the governing context of *aṅga*, of that [stem] and of its subsequent member. To this he replies: "In that case..."
And [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after a word that does not have a corresponding masculine form.

He states that "abhāṣitapuṃskāt" is a qualification of what is prescribed, saying: "prescribed after [a stem] that does not denote the masculine. Thinking that the word *khaṭvā* is restricted to the feminine alone and is therefore *abhāṣitapuṃska*, whereas a *bahuvrīhi*—because its gender follows the gender of the object denoted (*abhidheya-liṅga*)—lacks the status of being *abhāṣitapuṃska* and thus this optional rule should not apply to it, he says: "in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*. To the question "How does it occur? he replies: "even there. The particle *iti* indicates the reason.

Regarding the phrase *yadā tu*: this refers to the alternative view where the suffix *ka* is absent. When *akhaṭvā* is established, there is shortening of the feminine prefix (*upasarjana-hrasvatvam*), then the addition of the suffix *ṭāp*, and again shortening by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ*. Since that [shortening] occurs after a *ṭāp* produced from a compound that has been stated as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃsaka*), this optional rule does not apply. If it were understood as "of the *at* following a word that has not been stated as masculine" (*abhāṣitapuṃskāt*), then this option would indeed apply here. In the case of *atikhaṭvikā*, here too the *ṭāp* is produced from a compound that has been stated as masculine.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after the word *ācārya*] in the sense of "from" (ablative). 7.3.49.

This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to *yogavibhāga*. It is also an exception to the short vowel [prescribed] by the rule *ke’ṇaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "of the teachers" (*ācāryāṇām*): since it was previously stated "of the Northerners" (*udīcām*), the meaning here is "of other teachers. Another says: the teacher referred to here is the teacher of the teacher Pāṇini; the plural number is used because of his status as a venerable authority (*guru*). In any case, for words that do not undergo masculine inflection (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), there are three forms: *akhaṭvakā*, *akhaṭvikā*, and *akhaṭvākā*.
The substitute *ika* is applied in place of *ṭha*.

In this regard, there are two views: one view is that only the consonant *ṭha* is specified as the substituendum (*sthānin*), while the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation; this applies likewise to suffixes such as *ḍhak* and others. The second view is that the entire suffix is the substitute, and the substituendum here is also that same [entire suffix]. In the first view, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying [the suffix] even to the end of verbal roots (*dhātu*), as in *paṭhitā* and *paṭhitum*. In the second view, however, it would also apply in cases such as *karmaṭha*, where the suffix is *aṭhac*.

Demonstrating how there is no fault in either of the two positions, he says: "The suffix *yaṣṭha* is the cause (*nimitta*) of the *aṅga*. In this context, the relationship is not characterized by that of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *paṭhita*. What then? It is characterized by the relationship of cause and effect (*nimitta-naimittika-bhāva*). When it is said "belonging to the *aṅga*," only that which is related to its form is understood; and the suffix is related to its form, since the designation "aṅga" depends upon it.

Thus, because the suffix is understood as being designated by its member (the *aṅga*), there is no fault in either of the two positions. Furthermore, in the view that [the word] is a composite (*saṅghāta*), since the word ending in *ṭhaC* is understood as being meaningful (*arthavat*), the undesired application [of the rule] does not occur in the case of *karmaṭhaḥ*. However, when [the rule] refers to individual phonemes (*varṇa*), the maxim "that which is meaningful" (*arthavat-paribhāṣā*) does not apply. Having raised another objection regarding the composite view, he refutes it with the words "In that case. Again, he raises a further objection against that very same position with the words "His merchandise is *mathita*."

However, if there were the mention of *varṇa* (the phoneme), then by the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* according to the rule "analvidhau," the substitution of *kā* would not apply. [The objection is: "The substitution of *kā* would follow. [To this it is replied: "But it is stated that [the substitution applies] after an *aṅga* ending in *t*; and here the *aṅga* does not end in *t*, because the suffix is not prescribed after it. This is not so; for that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original], and thus it remains an *aṅga* and ends in *t*.

And so, just as in the case of *anukampito bhānudattaḥ*, where by [the application of] the suffix *ṭhak* (which becomes *ac*), there is elision of everything after the second vowel, resulting in the substitution of *kā*—yielding *bhānukaḥ*—would such an application not also occur here? He provides the rebuttal: "by the rule *sannipāta*... Since the state of ending in *t* arises through the conjunction (*sannipāta*) with a vowel-initial [suffix], that which causes the destruction of that very conjunction cannot logically be its cause. He states another rebuttal: "of the elision of *yasya*... However, the status of being as good as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established by the rule: "In a subsequent operation concerning a vowel, [the substitute] is like the original."

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not said that [the rule] applies to the preceding [element], while this [rule] applies to the subsequent? To this he replies: "For even from the preceding... The meaning is that a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is also resorted to there. Others, however, say: "Since the designation of that which ends in [the suffix] is already established by the very mention of the *varṇa* (phoneme), the inclusion of the word 'end' (*anta*) is for the purpose of understanding that which ends in *ta* at the time of the instruction of the suffix."
The suffix *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṣ*, and after a root ending in a long vowel (*kta*).

*Sārpiṣka*: [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "that which is his merchandise" (*tadasya paṇyam*); the substitution of *ṣ* for the visarga is by the rule "for [the final of] *iṇ*, *ṣ*" (*iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*). *Dhānuṣka*: [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by the rule "a weapon" (*praharaṇam*). *Yājuṣka*: [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he plays with" (*dīvyati*). *Naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*, *śābarajambukaḥ*: [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "originating from" (*bhavādau*) by the rule "after *u*, when denoting a place" (*ordeśe ṭhañ*); once the substitution of *ka* for *ṭha* has been made, the shortening of the vowel is by the rule "when *ka* follows, [the vowel of] *aṇ*" (*ke'ṇaḥ*). *Mātṛkam*, *paitṛkam*: [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied after *ṛt* by the rule "after *ṛt*, *ṭhañ*" (*ṛtaṣṭhañ*) in the sense of "come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*). *Audaśvitka*: [The suffix] *ṭhak*.

In the examples *saṃskṛtabhakṣāḥ*, *dadhnasṭhak*, and *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the locative case. Thus we have *śākṛtkaḥ*, *yākṛtkaḥ*, and *yākṛtkaḥ*. In the rule *saṃsṛṣṭe*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is used. Regarding *āśīḥ*: from the root *āṅ-śās* in the sense of "desire," the word *āśīḥ* (blessing) is formed by adding the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group; the substitution of *ī* for *ā* occurs by the rule *āśāsaḥ kvāv upasaṃkhyānam*. Regarding *uṣā*: from the root *vas*, the suffix *kvip* is added; the form is technical (*lākṣaṇika*) due to the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurring because the root belongs to the *yajādi* group.

In the case of *sarpiḥ* and so forth, however, the forms *iṣ* and *us* are those prescribed by specific rules: namely, *arciśucihūsṛpicchādibhya iṣiḥ*, *janerusiḥ*, and *artivapiyajitrāpidhanibhyo niṭ*.

Regarding the statement "there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *doṣa*": since parts of letters are not grasped by the mention of the whole letter, the *u* within the *o* (of *doṣaḥ*) is not grasped by the mention of the *u*; therefore, an addition is required.
The substitution of *ku* occurs for *ca* and *ja* before an affix marked with the *ṅiṭ* or *ṇiṭ* indicatory letters, except when the affix is *ghin* or *nyat*.

In *pāka* and similar forms, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). In *pākyam* and similar forms, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
