Here, there is no correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhya*)—namely, that the *ca* in *ghit* corresponds to the *ja* in *ṇyat*—based on such indicative marks (*liṅga*) as "the words *bhuj* and *nyubj* [are used] in the senses of 'hand' and 'affliction'," "the words *prayāja* and *anuyāja* [are used] in the sense of 'limbs of a sacrifice,'" and "the word *vac* [is used] except when it is a technical grammatical term.
However, in some places it is stated: "Correspondence in order is not intended here, because of the indicative mark in the rule *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (A 4.2.1)."
And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after *nyaṅkva* and others. 7.3.53.

Regarding the phrase "of *nyaṅku* and so forth," the word "for the sake of establishing" (*siddhaye*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis, because these words are recited in the list [of roots] precisely with the *kutva* substitution already applied. Why, then, is this rule necessary? For one might argue that just as other operations such as *ghatva*, vowel strengthening (*guṇa*), or lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occur by virtue of specific technical injunctions (*nipātana*), so too will the *kutva* substitution occur. This is true; however, if that rule did not exist, then since the list would serve no purpose whatsoever in the context of a restatement (*anuvāda*), one might suspect it was an erroneous recitation. As for the mention of "the *ac*-affix beginning with *pac*" (*pacādyaci*), this is because the *kutva* substitution is not established when the suffix *ghañ* is present.

Regarding "megha" and so forth in the section on *saṃjñā* (names): *megha* means a cloud; *nidāgha* means heat or the summer season; *avadāgha* is also that same thing. *Argha* refers to the quantity of grain and such being sold; others say it means price. Regarding *vīrudh*: the lengthening of the vowel in the prefix occurs by way of an irregular grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
The substitution of *ha* occurs for [the final consonant] of the root *han* before suffixes beginning with *ṇ*, *n*, or *ṅ*. || 7.3.54 ||

*Ñ* and *ṇ* are *ñṇau*; those two, when they are the *it* (indicatory letter) of something, are *ñṇit*. Those, together with *n*, are *ñṇinnāḥ*; [the rule applies] in those cases where there is *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *n*. In the case of the letter *n*, the vowel *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation; therefore, it also occurs in forms such as *vṛtraghni* and *vṛtraghnau*. In forms such as *ghnantī*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule "gamahana" (*Pāṇini 6.4.98*).

Is this mention of "ñṇit" a qualifier of the root *han*—meaning "the *h* which follows what is preceded by *ñ* or *ṇit"? Or is it a qualifier of the letter *h*—meaning "if that *h*, followed by what is preceded by *ñ* or *ṇit*, belongs to the root *han*"? In the first case, there is a failure [of the rule] here: *ghnanti*, *ghnantu*; for a part of itself cannot be posterior to itself.

In the second view, however, it would never occur; for the condition of having *ñ*, *ṇ*, *n*, or *k* following the *h* is impossible anywhere—firstly, in forms such as *ghātayati*, there is an intervention by the letter *a* and the letter *t*; and in forms such as *ghnantī*, there is likewise an intervention due to the status of the elided penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). If it is argued that [the rule] will apply despite the intervention on account of a specific statement (*vacana*), then it would follow here as well: from *hatīyati* (derived from *hataṃ icchati*), with the suffix *ṇvul*, we get *hatāyaka*; and even with the letter *n*, there would be the undesired application in *hantā*, *hananam*, and so forth.

Now, what would be the purpose of including the letter *na*? It is so that [the rule] may apply where the letter *na* is heard, but not here in cases such as *hataḥ* and *hathaḥ*. Having thus observed the defect in both positions, he presents another alternative: "a suffix marked with *ṇ* or *ṇit*," and so forth. Although it is logical that those items specified in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) share a single status regarding their application and non-application, nevertheless, since possibility and deviation are the prerequisites for the relationship between qualifier and qualified, this very method is adopted.

But was it not already stated that "due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of the letter *n* is not possible"? To this he says: "And that... [meaning] "produced by conjunction" (*sannipātakṛtam*). This means "produced by direct audition" (*śrutikṛtam*). Alternatively, let the second position stand; even there, the fault is easily countered? To this he says: "Even when... Since the intervention by the letter *n*, which is a constituent of the verbal root (*dhātu*), is invariable, that alone is relied upon, and not another word; this is the resolution regarding the rule *ñṇiti*. As for the letter *n*, the solution has already been stated.
And because of practice. 7.3.55.

"ahaṃ jaghana" is an example [of a case] where there is an absence of the *ṇit* designation. In the alternative view that it does have the *ṇit* designation, the form is already established by the preceding rule. Similarly, "jaghanitha," "jaghantha," and "jaghanvān" are examples. [The phrase] "the suffix is caused by the reduplication" and so forth—this meaning is obtained because the suffix is implied by the section on *aṅga* (bases) and by the mention of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). Regarding "jihananīyiṣati": here, the base *han* is not the cause of the reduplication when the suffix is *lyuṭ*; and that which is the cause of the reduplication, namely the desiderative suffix *san*, is not the base for *han*.
The substitution of *chaṅ* for *liṅ* occurs after the verbal root *hṛ*. (Pāṇini 7.3.56)

Regarding the form *prājīhayat*: it is derived from the root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the aorist marker (*luṅ*), the reduplication marker (*caṅ*), and the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*). There is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāhrasvatva*), reduplication according to the rule "in the presence of *caṅ*" (*caṅi*), the substitution of *c* for *k* and *h* according to the rule "for *ku* and *hu*, there is *cu*" (*kuhoścuḥ*), and finally, lengthening of the light vowel according to the rule "lengthening of the light [vowel]" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).

He refutes the inclusion of the term *acaṅ* by stating: "The mention of *acaṅ* can be omitted. Why? To this he says: "In the case of *caṅ* and the reduplication (*abhyāsa*). The meaning is that just as [the rule] does not apply in the previous example *jihananīyiṣati*, it will likewise not apply in *prājīhayat*; so what is the purpose of the phrase *acaṅi*? The response begins with "That is done," and so forth. What is the purpose of this indication? To this he says: "By that..."
The suffix *san* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ṛ*, as well as after *liṭ* and *ūrja*.

Regarding the rule *jyā vayohānau*: when the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) is applied by the rule *grahijyādi* before a *kit* suffix, and the subsequent *pūrvarūpa* (the merging of the preceding vowel with the semivowel) has occurred, the form *ji* arises; consequently, the rule *halaḥ* (which would otherwise cause lengthening) is superseded, and the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *j* becoming *g*) would apply. Alternatively, even if the lengthening were applied, because that which undergoes a partial modification remains essentially the same (*ananyatvāt*), the application of *kutva* would still follow—as in the case of *jigīṣati*. Therefore, he says: "of the root *jināti*" and so forth. [In this context,] the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs according to the rule *eranekācaḥ*.
The substitution of *na* does not occur for the initial sound of *kvā* and so forth. Pāṇini 7.3.59.

*Kūja* and so forth. *Kūja* means "inarticulate sound," *kharja* means "affliction," and *garja* means "sound. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "There is no prohibition for roots beginning with *kvā*, *aja*, *vraj*, *yā*, *ci*, and *ruc*, because the substitution of *k* [for *j*] is prescribed in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes when they are not *iṭ*-taking. The meaning of this is as follows: the rule should be formulated as "the substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs before *ghi*, *ṇya*, and *tṛc*, provided the root does not take *iṭ* in the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Since by that very rule the prevention of the *k*-substitution for roots such as *kvā* and *aja* is already established, there is no need for a separate statement of prohibition.

But surely, in this case, since *pruc*, *gluc*, *juj*, and *khuj* are *aniṭ* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), they would undergo the change of *j* to *g* (*kutva*). Likewise, since *aji*, *saji*, and *tarji* are *seṭ* in the past participle, there would be no occasion for *kutva*. Is it not the reverse of what the Sūtra implies? It is replied: according to the Vārttika—"The authority of the sages increases in descending order"—the presence or absence of *kutva* must be determined accordingly. But if there is no prohibition for the root *aj*, then in the word *nivīta*, since the past participle is *aniṭ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *kutva* in *samāja*. This is not so; [for the rule applies only when the suffix *kta* follows immediately after the root].

The designation [of *aj* as *aniṭ*] applies to the *niṣṭhā* suffixes, but not to *aj* itself; however, that [root *aj*] is desired to be optionally [seṭ] before a *valādi* ārdhadhātuka suffix. Thus, in the alternative where there is no substitution of *vī*, *ajita* is indeed *seṭ*. How then are *śokaḥ* and *samudgaḥ* formed, given that *śuci* and *ubji* are *seṭ* in the *niṣṭhā*? If this is so, I shall state: "In the case of *śuci* and *ubji* when *ghan* follows. And this must be stated even according to the established rule (*yathānyāsa*)—to ensure it occurs only with *ghan* and not with *ṇyat*, as in the example: *aśocyānanvaśocastvam*. That very point will serve as a prescriptive rule (*vidhyartha*) in the view of the author of the Vārttika.
And [the substitution of *a* for the final vowel] occurs before the words *ajinam* and *vrīhi*. 7.3.60.

The forms are *samājaḥ* and *udājaḥ*. In meanings other than "animals," the suffix *ghañ* is applied by the rule *halaśca*; however, when referring to animals, the suffix *ap* is used by the rule *samudorajaḥ paśuṣu*.
The words *bhujanyubja* are used in the sense of causing pain to the arms and the hands, respectively. || 7.3.61 ||

By the word *pāṇi* (hand), the arm possessing it is indicated, and not the region of the five fingers below the wrist. Even in common usage, the word *bhuja* is a synonym for the arm; [it is so called] because "one enjoys" (*bhujyate*) with it. [The root] *bhuja* [is used] in the senses of "protecting" and "eating. Regarding the term *nyubjitāḥ*: they are face-downward and motionless. This is merely a statement of the fact; however, the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) should be shown as "that in which they lie face-downward" (*nyubjanti asmin*).

The inclusion of *nyubja* (prone) [in the rule] could have been omitted. How so? In whatever disease one lies prone (*nyubjitāḥ*), he causes them to lie prone; in that case, the form *nyubja* is established by adding the suffix *ac* (after a root ending in a causative marker *ṇi*). Nor is there any difference in accent between the suffixes *ghañ* and *ac* here, because by the rule *thāthādi-sūtra*, even with *ghañ* the final syllable is prescribed to be udātta. However, the word *bhuja* is ādyudātta when formed with *ghañ*, whereas it is antodātta when formed with the suffix *ka* according to the rule *igupadhala-kṣaṇa*.
[The rule] *prayājānuyājau yajñāṅge* (Pāṇini 7.3.62) [is stated].

Regarding the statement "there are five after-offerings" (*pañcānuyājāḥ*): in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) there are three after-offerings; in the Four-Monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) there are nine; and in the Animal sacrifice (*paśu*) there are eleven. Since the number five is not observed anywhere, the reading should therefore be "three after-offerings" (*trayo 'nuyājāḥ*).

The phrase "for the sake of illustration" is understood from the mention of *yajña* (sacrifice). For the fact that these two refer to parts of a sacrifice is established by the very rule of grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), since the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *ṛtuyājas* are constituent parts (*avayava*) with respect to the aggregate of the sacrifice (*yajñasamudāya*). Indeed, these are primary sacrifices (*pradhānayāga*); as for the others, their status as subordinate members (*aṅga*) follows the principle that "that which is fruitless in proximity to that which possesses fruit is its member."
The root *vañc* [takes the suffix *aṅ*] in the sense of "going. (Pāṇini 7.3.63)

"Deceiving those who are to be deceived" means "going where it is to be gone. Regarding the word *vaṅka*: this is a term for a quality (*guṇa-śabda*) formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state; through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), it functions to denote the possessor of that quality (*guṇin*).
The substitution of *u* for *o* occurs before *uc* and *ke*. 7.3.64.

Regarding the root *uc* in the sense of "to assemble": *nyokaḥ* means "a bird," because it assembles or gathers at its nest and so forth; *nyokaḥ* also means "a house," because people assemble, gather, and dwell therein. As for the suffix *asun*, this very form is more commonly employed in the world.
The suffix *ṇya* is used in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).

In the examples, the suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule "āvaśyakādhamarṇyayorṇiniḥ," and the suffix *ṇyat* by the rule "kṛtyāśca"; there is a compound according to the group beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*, and the elision of the *ma* in *avaśyam* occurs by the rule "lumpedavaśyamaḥ kṛtye."
The suffix *ya* is applied after the verbal roots √yaj, √car, √ruc, √pru, and √arc.

Regarding the word *ārṣyam*: [it is derived from] the root *ṛc* in the sense of "praising. Regarding the phrase "to be proclaimed by name" (*pravācya*): it is called "to be proclaimed" (*pravācya*) because it is spoken forth (*prakarṣeṇocyate*); it refers to a specific work characterized by a particular recensional text (*pāṭha*). As for the phrase "others, however": they hold the view that the root *vac* preceded by the prefix *pra* functions only in the sense of a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*); since no thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is possible in that context, it constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

"And this" refers to the word-form *avivākyam*. What, then, is this specific meaning? To this he says: "of the ten-night [sacrifice]. In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is a two-night period at both ends and a ten-night period in the middle; the tenth day of that ten-night period is the *avivākyam*. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": thus, on this day nothing is to be spoken by anyone to anyone; they call this the *avivākyam* (the non-discussable).

Regarding the doubt as to whether the recitation (*svādhyāya*) takes place outside the sacrificial altar (*bahirvedi*) or within it (*antarvedi*), some hold that the substitution of *k* for *p* occurs on specific days (*aharviśeṣe*), while its absence occurs elsewhere; this is how it was applied by Āśvalāyana. Likewise, even when preceded by other prefixes, only a prohibition is intended, not a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

And having established this, the mention of the root *pravaci* could have been omitted; for it is thus established as desired: the substitution of *k* occurs on specific days due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, while a prohibition applies elsewhere. Otherwise, if there were a restrictive rule, much would have to be provided as an exception.
The suffixes *ṇic* and *ṇīy* are applied in the sense of what is possible (*śakya-artha*).

In this context, it should have been stated that "the suffixes *ni* and *yu* are used in the sense of capability" (*prayuñjanīyujaḥ śakyārthe*). Since the desired form would be established by simply saying "after [the root] *ṇi*" (*ṇye*), the recourse to this irregular derivation (*nipātana*) is for the sake of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*): so that the use of these two words occurs only in a subordinate sense (*guṇabhūta*), as in "a servant who is to be employed" (*prayonyaḥ bhṛtyaḥ*) or "a slave who is to be directed" (*niyojyaḥ dāsaḥ*). The words *prayojya* and *niyojya* do not apply to a master.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the root *bhuja-* when it means "to eat" (*bhakṣye*).

"Yavāgū is to be eaten (*bhojyā*). Now, one might object: "Was it not stated in the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* that this root *bhakṣ* refers to solid food (*kharaviśada*) that is consumed? How then can it apply to a liquid substance? To this he says: "In this case... He thinks as follows: here the root *bhakṣ* does not refer exclusively to solid food, because it is also seen in such expressions as *abbhakṣaḥ* ("one who subsists on water") and *vāyubhakṣaḥ* ("one who subsists on air"). This is so by the force of the proximity of other words.

"The root *bhakṣ* (to eat) exists in its own nature as being [restricted] to solid food (*khara-viśada*) alone"—this is the position of the author of the Vārttika, as he says: "It should be stated that 'the object of eating (*bhojya*) is that which is to be swallowed (*abhyavahārya*)."
Or *ghorlopa* occurs in the *leṭ* [mood]. 7.3.70.

Regarding the word *dadhāt*: this is the *leṭ* (subjunctive) form of the root *dhā* (to give), with the suffix *tip*. By the rule "the *it* [augment] is elided after [roots ending in] *i* in the *parasmaipada*," the *ikāra* (*i*) is elided. The meaning is: "he should give" (*dadyāt*) "gifts" (*satnāni*) "to the donor" (*dāśuṣe*), that is, to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Others, however, say: this [form] *dadhāt* contains the present participle suffix *śatṛ*; thus *dadhāt* is the form of the root *dā* (to give). Wishing to refute the mention of the alternative option (*vāvacana*), he says: "if there is the augment *āṭ*. The meaning is: let there be elision here [of the *i*]; nevertheless, the hearing of the *āṭ* will occur.

For what purpose, then, is the mention of the word *vā*? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). What is to be made clear here? To this he says: "For this... Others, however, say: the mention of *vā* is for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*); it indicates that the teaching regarding augments (*āgama-śāsana*) is not eternal (*anitya*). If it were not eternal, then in the absence of the augment *āṭ*, the form *dadāti* would not occur; therefore, the mention of *vā* must be made for the sake of establishing that form.
The substitution of *ota* occurs before the suffix *śyan*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *śyatīti* and so forth: [the roots] *śo* (in the sense of thinning), *cho* (in the sense of cutting), *do* (in the sense of breaking), and *ṣo* (in the sense of finishing). Here, it should have been stated as *otaḥ śiti* ("for a root ending in *o*, [the substitution of *śn* occurs] before a *śit* suffix"); for there is no other *śit* suffix possible for roots ending in *o* besides *śyan*, and by doing so, there is brevity by one half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). In that case, this further purpose is served: the mention of *śit* in the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* need not be made, as this very [rule regarding *otaḥ*] will be carried over [there]. [Objection: But the mention of *śyan* must be made for the sake of subsequent rules—namely, *śamāmaṣṭānām*? [Response: In that case too, let it simply be *śiti*.

If it is said that [the rule applies] when *śit* is used, then in the alternative where *bhrāśa* is substituted for *bhram*, as in *śap* [is added to] *bhramati*, would this not also apply here? We shall qualify *śit* by means of *śam* and the others—namely, that *śit* which is prescribed after *śam* and the rest. And since *śyan* alone is prescribed after all of *śam* and the rest, even so, because *śam* and the others are employed as qualifiers of *śit*, there is an absence of a specific mention of the operation [to be applied]; thus, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as *naśyati*? This is not a fault;
by the word "of eight" (*aṣṭānām*), the things to be numbered—the subjects of the operation—are indicated, and they shall be understood from their proximity to be none other than *śam* and the rest.
[The substitution of] *ī* for [the final vowel of] a stem ending in *kṣa*, before a vowel. || 7.3.72 ||

Regarding *adhukṣātām*: since the root *duh* is marked with a circumflex (*svarita*), it takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The suffix *ātām* follows; here, in the absence of the elision [of the *k*], the substitution of *iy* would apply by the rule *āto ṅitaḥ*. Regarding *adhukṣi*: there is elision when the augment *iṭ* is present.
Because the word *sa-* is taken here as being accompanied by the letter *k*, this [elision] does not occur in the following cases: *vatsau*; and *tṛṇādibhyaḥ saḥ*, as in *tṛṇasau* and *tṛṇasaḥ*.
The substitution of *u* for the vowel of the roots *duh*, *dih*, *lih*, and *guh* occurs before a dental consonant when the Ātmanepada affixes follow.
"Of these *aṅga*s, [the substitute occurs] for that which is *ksa*": the meaning is "of that *ksa* which belongs to these [roots] by virtue of being their cause.

"For the sake of a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*)" means that it was stated in the rule prescribing the technical name (*saṃjñā*) that "elision (*luk*) effects the removal of everything. "For the sake of the *vah* [suffix]" means "for the sake of the dual number of the first person. Why then does it not serve another purpose? To this he says: "Elsewhere," namely, by the rule "of the final [alophon]. But the rule "of the subsequent [element], the initial [is replaced]" does not apply here, because there is no mention of a fifth case (*pañcamī*). "By elision according to *jhalo jhalī*" means that the rule "there is elision of *sic* before *dh* and *s*" is not resorted to.

The intention is that the mention of *sij* there is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the substitution of *cli*. "Of the vowel *a*" means "of the elision of the vowel *a*"; or rather, that is the very reading [in the text].

But surely, even if the mention of *luk* (elision) were made, there should still be no elision by *luk* in the case of *vah*, because it ends in a vowel; for is it not a dental-labial (*dantyauṣṭhya*)? To this he says: "Even though it is a dental-labial," and so forth. The intention here is that the connection with the teeth (*dantānvaya*) is what is intended to be expressed, not the exclusion of other [articulations]. Thus, although the matter is established by logic, he also demonstrates the force of the explicit statement (*vacanasāmarthya*) with the words "And if... and so on. "Those two" means those beginning with the *tavarga* (the dental class). For all other *ātmanepada* endings of *vah* that begin with dentals and so forth belong to the *tavarga*.
In the *śyan* [present] tense, the long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of the eight roots beginning with *śam*.
*śamu*, *stamu*, *śramu*, *dam*, *bhramu*, *kṣamumadalkama*:
these roots beginning with *śam* are recited by the eight groups of scholars among the *divādi* (fourth) class.
The suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the roots *ṣṭhiv* (to spit), *klam* (to be weary), and *ācam* (to sip water).

Regarding the form *klamati*: the suffix *śap* is applied by the rule *vā bhrāśa-bhlāśa-bhramu-krama-klamu-trasi-truti-śvitām*. The inclusion of the root *klam* [in the rule] is for the sake of the *śap* affix, because [the form] would already be established by the preceding rule (*śyan*) alone. Its reading among the roots beginning with *śam* (in Dhp. 3.2) has a purpose that requires consideration, since even in the case of *śyan*, the form is established by this very [rule]. In that regard, should there not simply be the mention of the seven [roots]? Is the mention of *āṅ-pūrva-cami* (the root *cam* preceded by *āṅ*) intended as a restrictive rule (*tantra*), rather than being non-intended (*avivakṣita*)—as is the case with forms like *upeyivān*? To this he says: "of *cam* preceded by *āṅ*. This is precisely the meaning of the Vārttika: *dīrghatvam āṅi camaḥ* ("lengthening occurs when *āṅ* follows *cam*").
The *krama* [substitution] occurs before the *parasmaipada* endings. || 7.3.76 ||

"Here," and so forth, introduces the objection (*codya*). "When *hi* has been elided by [the rule] *ato heḥ*" refers to that very rule. "This is not a fault," and so forth, introduces the resolution (*parihāra*). For in the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, this meaning was established on account of its immediate proximity: when a suffix is elided by a marker containing *lu*, the grammatical operation dependent upon that stem (*aṅga*) does not take place. What follows from this? To this he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The substitute *cha* is applied in place of the final phoneme of the roots √iṣ, √gam, √yā, and √mā [before an affix beginning with a vowel].

Regarding *icchatīti*: the suffix *cha* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *tudadi* class. Regarding *iṣyatīti*: from the root *iṣ* in the sense of "going. Regarding *iṣṇātīti*: from the root *iṣ* in the sense of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*). As for those who say that the root *iṣ* with the *udittva* marker is not studied in the *Dhātupāṭha*, they maintain that the word *aci* is carried over (*anuvarttate*) into this rule from the rule *ksasyāci*. Now, even if *aci* is carried over, would there not still be the substitution of *cha* in *iṣāṇa*—where the substitute *śnā* becomes *śānac* by the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau*—because it begins with a vowel (*ajādittvāt*)? To this he says: *tatra*.

This might be so if *aci* were the qualifier of *śit*—that is, [the rule] "there is *cha* when *śit* occurs"—[were to mean] "in what kind of [context]? When *ac* [follows]," meaning "when preceded by *ac*; but here, *ac* is the qualifier of *śit*—"there is *cha* when *ac* occurs"—"in what kind of [context]? When *śit* [occurs]. Therefore, the rule of "specification of that which begins with [the element]" (*tadādividhi*) does not apply. What is the reason? To this he says: "In whatever [element] there is a prescription" (*yasmin vidhiḥ*). The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that the requirement for being a qualifier is not only in the case of specification of that which ends with [the element] (*tadantavidhi*), but also in the case of specification of that which begins with [the element] (*tadādividhi*). Thus, [the rule applies] even in the case of *iṣāṇa*.

The meaning of the word "also" (api) is that [the rule] applies not only to the case of *iṣyati*—namely, that this [root] is not merely *aj*. The meaning is that the status of being a *śit* does not belong to every *aj* here. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

In place of the verbal roots *prā*, *ghrā*, *sthā*, *mnā*, *dāṇ*, *dṛśi*, *ṛti*, *sṛti*, *śad*, and *sad*, [the substitutes] *piba*, *jighra*, *tiṣṭha*, *manya*, *yaccha*, *paśya*, *ṛccha*, *dhau*, *śīya*, and *sīda* are substituted [respectively] before the suffix *ātmanepada*. (Pāṇini 7.3.78)

The root *pā* is [the one] in the sense of "drinking" (*pāne*). However, there is no inclusion of the root *pā* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*), because it belongs to the *lug-vikaraṇa* class and because the suffix *śit* is impossible for it. *Ghrā* is "taking up odor" (*gandhopādāne*); *dhmā* is "sound and contact with fire" (*śabdāgnisaṃyogayoḥ*); *ṣṭhā* is "cessation of motion" (*gatinivṛttau*); *mnā* is "repetition" (*abhyāse*); *dāṇ* is "giving" (*dāne*); *dṛśir* is "seeing" (*prekṣaṇe*); *ṛ* is "motion and reaching" (*gatiprāpaṇayoḥ*); and *sṛ* is "motion" (*gatau*); these belong to the Bhūvādigaṇa. However, there is no inclusion of the two roots *ṛ* and *sṛ* belonging to the Juhotyādigaṇa (meaning "motion"), because the suffix *śit* is impossible for them.

If it is argued that this [form] is possible, it has been stated here: "Whatever [suffix] occurs after a root-vowel (varṇa), one should know that it [occurs] at the beginning. For *śiti* is a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, that which is both *śa* and *it*. [The roots are: *śadlṛ* in the sense of "falling," belonging to the *bhūvādi* class; *śadlṛ* in the sense of "perishing," belonging to the *tudādi* class; and *ṣadlṛ* in the senses of "perishing, going, and sinking. It is prescribed as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). If it were not so prescribed, then, since the rule "the suffix of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) would result in an acute accent on the final syllable, and once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *śap* had been made, the word *pibati* would become acute-accented on the middle syllable by the rule "a single substitute for [an acute and another vowel] is acute"; however, it is desired to have the acute accent on the first syllable.

Regarding the term *vegitāyām*: it means "in one who has acquired speed. Alternatively, *vegitā* is the state (*bhāva*) of being swift (*vegin*); and the meaning is "of one who is engaged in motion while that state exists."
The substitution of *jā* occurs for the roots *jñā* and *jan*.

The root *grah* belonging to the *divādi* class is intended here, not that belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, because [the suffix] *śit* is impossible in the latter case. The purpose of the long vowel pronunciation will be explained in the subsequent sūtra.
The short vowel replaces [the final element] of words beginning with *pu* and so forth. 7.3.80.

The roots beginning with *pvā* are recited in the *kryādi* class. Those, however, which are recited in the *bhūvādi* class—such as *pūñ* "to purify" and so on—are not included here; for among those [in the *bhūvādi*], some possess short vowels, and even for them, there ought to be *guṇa* substitution when the suffix *śap* follows. Furthermore, the long vowel was pronounced in the preceding rule (*pūṅaḥ ktvā*) for the purpose of preventing the shortening of the *jānāti* belonging to the *kryādi* class; that too is proof that the *kryādi* roots are intended to be included.

"Regarding the passage beginning with *vṛtkaraṇam* etc.: the sense is that there is no burden whatsoever in the *vṛtkaraṇa* (the formation of a group) when it serves both purposes. Regarding the phrase *apare tu*: the sense is that because [the roots] beginning with *lū* follow immediately after. Likewise, even for these two—*da* in the sense of 'filling' (*pūraṇe*) and *da* in the sense of 'fear' (*bhaye*)—which are recited after the *vṛtkaraṇa*, the short vowel occurs: as in *yaḥ pṛṇāti sa ha deveṣu gacchati*, *pṛṇīyādinnādhamānāya*, *pṛṇantaṃ ca papuriṃ śrasyava*, and *ādṛṇāti*. In the former view, they read these two with a short final vowel."

He raises an objection with the words "of those who... (*yeṣām*). [The term] *agaṇāntāḥ* means those who have come to the end of a group (*gaṇa*). He refutes this with "the roots *jñā*, *jan*, and *jī*. If there were shortening in the case of *jānāti*, he would have prescribed a substitute ending in a short vowel. [Objection: But surely the prescription of a substitute ending in a long vowel must be for the sake of another purpose; for otherwise, the form *jāyate* could not be established? To this he replies: "and also *ja*."

Even when the substitution of a short vowel is prescribed, the form *jāyate* is established by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*; for in that rule, the term *sārvadhātuke* is understood from the preceding rule *turustuśamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke*, and not the term *taṅi*. For this very reason, in the rule *āne muk*, the augment *muk* is made a prior element (*pūrvānta*) and not a subsequent one (*parādi*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of lengthening the vowel.

As for those who explain the formation of *vṛt* as being for the purpose of excluding both [the short and long vowels], for them, what is the purpose of the long-vowel pronunciation? [They might say: "It is so that the long vowel occurs in *jānāti*; otherwise, by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi*, the long vowel would not occur. This is not established; for there is the principle: "When an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅga*), a subsequent operation does not apply to that which is already finalized. A stem is not considered finalized merely by the substitution of *ja*. In this regard, the very pronunciation of the long vowel is the indicator that the group beginning with *ṣu* extends up to the end of the *gaṇa*.
The quality [of being] "mider" (soft). 7.3.82.
"Medyati" [is formed] with the suffix *śyan*; "midyate" [is formed] with the suffix *yak* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).
And likewise, *jusi*. 7.3.83.

In the examples, for the *laṅ* [suffix], there is *ślu*-elision of *śap*, reduplication, the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*), and by the rule "after *sic*, after reduplicated stems, and after those prescribed by rule," there is *jus* in place of *jhi*.

"Then," and so forth. There is the possibility [of the rule applying] because *yāsuṭ*, which is a portion of *juhotyādibhyaḥ*, is included by that [term's] mention. "Based on the *ṅit*-ness which has a *sārvadhātuka* as its locus": that whose locus is a *sārvadhātuka* is "having a *sārvadhātuka* as its locus"; that prohibition for which such *ṅit*-ness is the cause is described in that way. By this, the phrase "based on the *ṅit*-ness which has *yāsuṭ* as its locus" is explained. In that regard, it applies "both when [the condition] is present and when it is absent": in cases such as *cinuyuḥ*, it is present; in cases such as *ajuhavuḥ*, it is absent.

The phrase "of *kṣa*, *āc* [is] understood" continues [from the previous rule]. This is another solution: however, the pronunciation of the letter *j* is for the purpose that [the suffix] not apply in cases such as *cakruḥ* where the *liṭ* [suffix] occurs.
[The substitution of guṇa occurs] in place of [the final vowel of a verbal root] before both sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka affixes. Pāṇini 7.3.84.

[Question: Why [is the rule] stated as "before a sārvadhātuka or ārdhadhātuka suffix"? [Objection: One might think that it should simply be stated "before a suffix" (*pratyaye*), for even so, the desired result would be established in the relevant cases. [Explanation: *saṅ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated term); it begins with the letter *s* of *san* and ends with the *ṅ* of *mahiṅ*. [Example: *agnitvam*. If it were stated "before a suffix," this [suffix *tva*] would also be subject to the rule. [Example: *agnikāmyati*. If it were stated "*saṅi*," this [suffix *kāmyac*] would also be subject to the rule.
The substitution of *guṇa* for the final vowel of the root *jāgṛ* occurs before the affixes *a*, *vic*, *ṇi*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ*.

"Except after *vici*, *ṇal*, and *ṅit* suffixes" means: when other suffixes follow those that are not *vici*, *ṇal*, or *ṅit*. "Jāgārayati" and similar forms are examples in the domain of *vṛddhi*; "jāgaritaḥ" and "jāgaritavān" are examples in the domain of the prohibition [of *vṛddhi*].

But what is the reason that examples are presented only for the domain of the prohibition of *vṛddhi*? To this he says: "In the domain of *vṛddhi* and in the domain of prohibition. Since elsewhere the substitution of *guṇa* is already established by the preceding rule, this *guṇa* applies only in this specific domain; moreover, it applies to both domains. How so? Because of the prohibition regarding *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, it occurs first in the domain of *vṛddhi*; and because of the prohibition regarding *ṅit* suffixes, it also occurs in the domain of prohibition. Thus: "when that has been applied."

This is stated without relying on the principle that "when a grammatical operation has already applied to a constituent part [of a word], it does not apply again to the whole. Why? He says: "For if... Even though the rule for *guṇa* substitution has fulfilled its purpose in cases such as *jāgaritaḥ* and *jagaritavān*, it has nevertheless been stated that this rule applies even in the domain of *vṛddhi*; therein, its lack of purpose (*anarthakya*) is asserted. Furthermore, he says: "And in the case of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*... If the *vṛddhi* were to occur by the rule "the penultimate vowel is lengthened" (*ata upadhāyāḥ*) after the *guṇa* had already taken effect, then the prohibition of *guṇa* in the rules for *ciṇ* and *ṇal* would be rendered useless.
Let there be a benefit even in that case: when there is *vṛddhi*, the forms *ajāgāri* and *jajāgāra* are established.

As for *jāgṛtaḥ*: this is the present tense (*laṭ*), the suffix *tas*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; and by the rule "that which is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix not marked with *p* is treated as having the *ṅit* designation," it acquires the *ṅit* quality.

Regarding this, some say: "In the rule *aviciṇṇalṅitsu*, they describe the vowel *i* that follows the letter *v* as being for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*); in that case, by the principle *yasmin vidhiḥ* (an operation applies to that which contains the element), there would be a prohibition against [the augment] when *v* begins the suffix. But why do they describe it in this way? To this he says: "Also in the case of *kvasu*," etc. In the form *jajāgṛvān*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *neḍvaśi kṛti*. In that situation, although *iṭ* would have been required by the restriction of the *krādi* group, it does not occur due to the restriction *vasvekājādghasām*.

However, for those who do not accept the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) because of the elision of *kvip* and because of the prohibition of applying the rule of suffix-characteristics (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) when depending on a phoneme (*varṇa*), the guna substitution indeed occurs in *jāgariti*. Others, however, say: just as in *atṛṇeḍ* the augment *iṭ* occurs by the rule of suffix-characteristics—since the phoneme is a qualifier of the suffix—so too there is an exclusion of *kvip*; consequently, the form becomes *jāgṛd*.

He objects: "How can they not be non-waking? He thinks as follows: this is a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) [of the suffix *liṭ*], and thus there would be a prohibition of the *guṇa* even by the rule "jusi ca"; furthermore, in the case of the first person plural ending *ṇal*, where the *ṇit*-character is absent, a *guṇa* is desired by the rule "sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ," yet a prohibition of that too would consequently follow. He refutes this: "No, because it is not a prohibition. This fault does not arise; why? Because it is not a prohibition.

This is not a non-prescriptive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); what then is it? He says: "In the case of *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and *liṅ*," this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For in an exclusion, there is neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition regarding *vi*, *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, and *liṅ*; rather, there is an injunction for other cases. Consequently, the *guṇa* substitution, which is obtained by another rule in the case of *jusi* and *ṇal*, indeed takes place.

He speaks also regarding the absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) with the words "or else" (*atha vā*). The intention is that "either a rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes. Some explain the word *darvi* as having the *vic* suffix derived from the *uṇādi* group because they observe a *guṇa* [substitution] therein; for them, a *guṇa* would result in the case of *jāgṛvi*. Nor is the prohibition after *vi* redundant, since it serves its purpose in the case of the *kvip* and *kvasu* suffixes. Therefore, it must be stated that the suffix [after the root] *jāgarti* is *kit*.
And [the substitution of *gh* occurs] for the final light consonant of a word ending in *upadha*. (Pāṇini 7.3.86)

[The opponent asks: "But how can there be *guṇa* substitution here, since, given the immediate succession of two *hal* sounds—one at the end of the verbal root and the other being the initial sound of the suffix—the designation *guru* (by the rule *saṃyoge guru*) would subvert the designation *laghu*, and thus *guṇa* would not apply? For *guṇa* finds its scope in cases such as *bhedanam*. To this he replies: "Because [the rule] specifies 'of the suffix-initial' (*pratyayādeḥ*). [He explains further: "By the fact that *kn* and *san* are marked with the *k*-diacritic (*kit*). The purpose of marking *kn* with the *k*-diacritic in the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* is so that *guṇa* does not occur in forms such as *gṛdhnur*.

And if, in such a case, there were no guna substitution because [the suffix] is treated as having a guru (heavy) penultimate vowel, then the marking of *knū* as *kit* would be purposeless. Likewise, the purpose of prescribing the *kit* status for the suffix *san* by the rule "halantācca" is so that there may be no guna substitution in forms such as *pipatsati*; that too is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned point. However, this particular indicator is not tenable.

In forms such as *sisṛkṣati* and *didṛkṣate*, this [the *kit* designation] would serve the purpose of preventing the augment *am* prescribed by the rule *sṛjidṛśoḥ*; likewise, in *dhitsati*, it would serve to prevent the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*). Therefore, the *kit* designation of the suffix *knō* itself is the indicator (jñāpaka). In *bhinatti* and *chinatti*, the base has a light penultimate vowel due to the *am* suffix; in that case, *guṇa* would apply to the *i* of the root. To this he says: "with respect to the penultimate" (*upadhāttra*). For here, no arbitrary penultimate is taken; rather, because of the presence of the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*, it is the *iK* itself that is proximate as the substituendum (*sthānin*).

"But others," however, [is] connected with "they explain. Regarding "puki anta" (a *pu*-affix and what ends in *ant*): the word *anta* signifies proximity. Although there is no fault even if "puganta" is analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi*, nevertheless, for the sake of uniformity in the qualification, this is also explained specifically as a *tatpuruṣa*. "A light *upadhā*" is a *karmadhāraya*. In this view, the connection of the *ik* vowel with the *upadhā* is purely grammatical—that is, "the *ik* of a light *upadhā*. "Pug-anta-laghūpadham" is a collective *dvandva*.

In some places, prior to the passage beginning with *upadhātra*, the three verses beginning with *saṃyoge gurusaṃjñāyām* are recited. [The objection is: "If the designation *guru* applies when there is immediate succession between a *hal* at the end of a root and a *hal* that is the beginning of an affix, then the *guṇa* substitution for the word *bhettṛ* (the agent of breaking) would not be established. He resolves this: "It depends on the specific rule (*vidhyapekṣam*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "this is the injunction. The meaning is: when a *sārvadhātuka* or *ārdhadhātuka* affix is prescribed after a stem having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), then there is *guṇa* of that stem.

Objection: Since there is no ablative case (pañcamī), how can the prescription be justified? Response: It is said: even in the view that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is used, if it is argued that [the suffix] is qualified [by the word "laghu"], what fault is there? [The meaning would be: "those [suffixes] which are sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka after a root having a light penultimate vowel. And which are those? They are those prescribed after such a root; thus it is justified. Furthermore, in the reading "laghoścāsau," the meaning is: "and this [suffix] is prescribed as tṛc after a root having a light penultimate vowel. The word *upadhā* (penultimate) was not employed [in the verse] for fear of breaking the meter. How then is the form *kuṇḍiḥ* derived?

Since the addition of *num* is prescribed under the heading of "stems" (*aṅga*), the suffix is prescribed as having a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) even before *num* has been applied. In that case, when the cause [for the application of the suffix] is present—as in *kuṇḍitā* and so on—the *guṇa* substitution would result, provided that the prescription is qualified [by the condition of being a stem]. He refutes this by stating: "The *num* of the root. This is an ablative in the sense of cause; the meaning is: because there is *num* of the root-stem in that context, therefore [the *guṇa* does not apply].

For it has been stated there: "The purpose of mentioning the verbal root (*dhātu*) is so that *num* may occur precisely at the stage of the instruction of the root. Consequently, *num* occurs first, and the suffix follows later; thus, this [suffix] is not prescribed for one whose penultimate vowel is light (*laghūpadha*). How then [could it apply] to the root *rañj*? If the prescription were restricted even when the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for reference, then there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) elsewhere as well; consequently, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (P. 7.2.116) for a suffix prescribed after a root having *a* as its penultimate vowel would not apply to *rañj*.

Prior to the arising of the suffix, because it has *nakāra* as its penultimate (*upadhā*)—as in *rāga*, there is the elision of *nakāra* by the rule "ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ. Although the rule prescribes the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the penultimate vowel *a*, and the prescription of the suffix cannot occur from that [strengthened form], nevertheless, the very prescription of the suffix after that which has *a* as its penultimate is considered to be the prescription for the penultimate itself. [This applies to] the roots *syandi* and *śranthi*.

When [the author] prescribes the absence of *vṛddhi* for the roots *syand* and *śranth* in the rules "asyado jave" and "avodaidhodmapraśrathahihaśrathāḥ," he thereby indicates that *vṛddhi* indeed occurs for such classes of words. For in those cases, the recourse to *nipātana* (irregular prescription) must be adopted both for the purpose of eliding the nasal (*nalopa*) and for the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi*. If the application were restricted to cases where *vṛddhi* would otherwise apply, then, since there would be no occasion for *vṛddhi* to arise, the recourse to *nipātana* would be rendered meaningless.

For the establishment of the elision of *nal*, a formal rule (*vidhi*) alone must be resorted to, for it is by resorting to a formal rule that multiple purposes are accomplished. Regarding the term *anallope*: the elision of *al* belonging to a stem ending in *an* is "the elision of *al*" (*anallopa*). There is the lengthening [of the vowel] before the case-ending *śas* (which is a *śit* suffix), and there is the lengthening [of the vowel] before a *śit* suffix; these two form a copulative compound (*dvandva*). The elision of *al* and the lengthening before a *śit* suffix would not be established if they were dependent upon a formal rule (*vidhi*). Furthermore, if even in the case of a genitive reference (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*) the operation were restricted to a specific context, then [the rule] would apply only in instances such as *allopo rājñaḥ* ("elision of *al* in *rājan*").

[Otherwise], [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *asthnā*, *asthne*, *dadhnā*, *dadhne*, and so on. Furthermore, the lengthening [of the vowel] before the nominative plural suffix *śas* would occur only in cases like *sāmāni*, but not in cases like *kuṇḍāni*. Therefore, since there is the risk of error if one takes "that which is prescribed" (*vihita*) as the qualifier when the genitive case is used [in the rule], the guna substitution for the root *bhī* would not be established. If this is so, then the desired result is established by means of an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark). Namely, that the author employs the mention of *ac* in the rule *nābhyastasyāci* ("there is no guna for a reduplicated stem before a vowel") serves to indicate that guna substitution indeed occurs in such instances.

For its purpose is this: [the mention of *aj*] so that in forms such as *nenakti*, there may not be a prohibition of *guṇa* before a consonant-initial [suffix]. If *guṇa* would not occur before a consonant-initial [suffix] because the penultimate vowel is not light (*alaghūpadha*), then, since there would be no possibility for *guṇa* to apply, what would be the use of the mention of *aj* for the sake of excluding it? This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*); for that which he stated regarding the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) with respect to a vowel-initial [suffix] in the sense of the *laṅ* tense would have been rendered superfluous.

The statement that [the rule] prohibits [the substitution of *guṇa*] for a root beginning with a vowel when preceded by an augment (*abhyasta*) would have been made for the sake of the *laṅ* [tense], where a consonant-initial suffix is elided—namely, by the rule "an-ineg" (Pāṇini 1.1.5). Therefore, it is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*). If that is so, then the fact that the *kit* designation is applied to the suffixes *knus* and *nu* must be the indicator for the absence of *guṇa* in a light syllable; this has already been explained.
The substitution of *guṇa* does not take place for a reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel that has the marker *p*.

*nenijāni*, etc. [is formed as follows]: the *loṭ* [imperative] mood; by the rules *merniḥ* [Pāṇini 7.1.34] and *āḍuttamasya picca* [7.3.96], the *śap* [present tense marker] is replaced by *ślu*; there is reduplication; and by the rule *ṇijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ ślau* [7.4.75], the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the three *ṇi*-roots. *anenijam*, etc., is the *laṅ* [imperfect] mood; here, the *mip* ending is replaced by *am*.

"Vedāni" [is derived from] the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing. The *loṭ* (imperative) and other suffixes are applied as appropriate, as before; there is elision (*luk*) of *śap*. "Nenakti" [is derived from] the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the suffix *tip*, and the substitution of *k* for *n* (*kutva*). It is said that "the mention of *pit* is for the sake of subsequent rules," so that the augment *im* may occur after *tṛṇaha* when followed by a *pit* suffix. However, in this case, even where there is no *pit* suffix, a prohibition must certainly apply because of the *ṅit*-character, according to the rule "a *sārvadhātuka* suffix not having *pit* is *ṅit*. "Nineja" [is derived from] the suffix *ṇal*, which, by the rule "and *liṭ* is also [an *ārddhadhātuka*]," receives the designation of *ārddhadhātuka*.

Regarding *jujoṣat*: the root *juṣ* means "to please" and "to serve. This is in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*), and the suffix is *tip*. By the rule *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*, the *i* is elided; by *leṭo’ḍāṭau*, the augment *aṭ* is added; and by transposition, there is *ślu* (reduplication substitute) for *śap* (the present marker), followed by reduplication (*dvirvacana*). If a prohibition of *guṇa* were intended here, then [in forms like] *paspaśāte* and others, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatvam*) would not be obtained even if it were intended. Therefore, for reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*), only the shortening of the penultimate vowel should be prescribed, not the prohibition of *guṇa*.

Regarding the question "How is *nenijāni* formed? and so forth: once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, would not the desired form be established by the rule "for *ec*, there is the substitution of *it* when a short vowel follows"? To this, he says: "*paspaśāte*" and so forth. The root *spaś* is a verbal root, even though it is not listed [in the standard Dhātupāṭha], according to the statement of the author of the Vārttika. From that root, the suffix *leṭ* is applied; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*); the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* occurs; the augment *āṭ* is added by the rule "the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* are added to *leṭ*"; the elision of the *śap* suffix occurs by the rule "it is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*); and reduplication follows. Alternatively, in the case of the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*), the shortening of the reduplicated syllable is a Vedic anomaly. Thus is formed *cākaśīti*.

The root *vāśrṛ* means "to shine. From this, with the *yaṅ*-loop (*yaṅ-luk*), the present tense marker (*laṭ*), and the third person singular suffix (*tip*), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied by the rule *yaṅo vā*. Thus we have *vāvaśīti*. Alternatively, from the same root *vāśrṛ* meaning "to shine," with the *yaṅ*-loop, the present tense marker, the substitution of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, and the nominative plural suffix *śas*, we obtain *vāvaśīḥ*. The shortening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). If, however, one were to reject the prohibition of *guṇa* and instead state that there is shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*), then in forms such as *narnṛtīti*, where the penultimate vowel is *ṛ*, once *guṇa* is applied—resulting in *ar*—there would be no short-vowel penultimate to undergo shortening, and thus the desired form would not be established.

Therefore, the intention is that the short vowel must be accepted as being Vedic (*chāndasa*) alone. Regarding the phrase "only other roots": [these are] *spaśa* in the sense of "afflicting" and "touching," *kaśa* in the sense of "motion" and "instructing," and *vaśa* in the sense of "desire."
The substitution of *bhū* for *as* occurs before a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).

*abhūt*: [This is] the *luṅ* [aorist]; by the rule "gātisthā" etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*. *suvai*, *suvāvahai*, *suvāmahai*: from the root *ṣūṅ* "to release the embryo of a living being," in the *loṭ* [imperative], there is the substitution of *er* for the suffix, "eta ai," "āṭ uttamasya pi ca," elision of *śap*, and the substitution of *uvaṅ*. Regarding "of *suvati* and *sūyati*": *ṣū* "to impel" belongs to the *tudādi* class; *ṣūṅ* "to give birth to a living being" belongs to the *divādi* class. *bhavati*: with *śap*, there is *guṇa*. *vyatibhaviṣīṣṭa*: in the sense of benediction (*āśis*), the *liṅ*; by the rule "liṅāśiṣi," it receives the designation of *ārdhadhātuka*; by the rule "kartari karmavyatihāre," the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] is applied.

Regarding the word "atha": since the mention of a root-form includes its *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) form as well, an undesirable application [of the rule] would arise. Regarding the phrase "due to an indicator" (*jñāpakāt*): because there is no specific irregularity (*nipātana*) for the root *sū*, the prohibition of *guṇa* certainly applies to it—as in *soṣuvīti*.
Moreover, there is vṛddhi substitution for the penultimate vowel before a consonant beginning with *h* when the suffix *luK* is elided.
Regarding the word *yavānī*: this is the first person singular of the imperative (*loṭ*).

In the phrase *api stuyāt*, the particle *api* is used in the sense of "possibility" (*sambhāvane*) as a *karmapravacanīya*; therefore, by the rule *upasargātsunoti* etc., the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. As for the statement "*ṅicca pinna bhavati*" (the marker *ṅit* does not become *pit*): the *ṅittva* of the *sārvadhātuka* affixes beginning with *yāsuṭ* is directly prescribed and thus has no other scope; whereas the *pittva* of *tiP* and so forth has scope in other *lakāra*s. Consequently, even though both rules—"*ṅicca pinna bhavati*" and "*picca ṅinna bhavati*"—exist, the intention here is that only the rule "*ṅicca pinna bhavati*" applies.

The prohibition [stated] in the rule *kṅiti ca* does not apply here. Why? Because that prohibition applies to the *vṛddhi* that occurs by means of the technical designation *ik*; however, in this case, because the locus is specified as "after *ut*" (*uttaḥ*), the *ik-paribhāṣā* does not come into operation.
The augment *guṇa* is applied when [the suffix] is not separated [by another element].

But surely, since "in a consonant" (hali) and "before a suffix beginning with p" (piti) are both understood [from previous rules], and a suffix is brought forward by the term "aṅga" (the base), then the guṇa substitution prescribed before a suffix beginning with p that consists of a consonant will necessarily apply only to a single-consonant (apṛkta) suffix; thus, there is no purpose in the mention of "apṛkta. To this he says: "while 'in a consonant' (hali) is understood... [and so forth].

Indeed, the inclusion of the term *apṛkta* (uncombined) is made for this purpose: so that [the substitution] does not occur before a consonant (*hal*). If this *paribhāṣā* were not in existence, one would not have included the term *apṛkta*; yet it has been included, and thus it indicates that this *paribhāṣā* exists. However, this must be addressed here: why is the inclusion of *apṛkta* not intended to exclude the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*)? For if there were such specification by the final letter, the [substitution] would undesirably apply even when *mip* becomes *am* in the *laṅ* tense.

Is it not the case that there is indeed a benefit [in this rule]? How so? Because even in the preceding rule prescribing *vṛddhi*, the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) applies. One must consider how this mention of *apṛkta* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule of *tadādividhi* (extension to what begins with that). If it were stated simply as "not before an *apṛkta*," there would be a prohibition of the immediately preceding optional *vṛddhi*, whereas the obligatory *vṛddhi* would still certainly take place. Therefore, the mention of *guṇa* [is necessary].
The suffix *im* is added after the root *tṛh*.

Regarding *tṛṇeḍhi*: when *śnam* is applied, [the sequence is] *tṛn-ś-n-a-d-h-i*. By the rule *ād guṇaḥ*, the *a* of *śnam* combines with the preceding vowel to form *e*; by *ho ḍhaḥ*, *h* becomes *ḍh*; by *jhaṣas tathordho 'dhaḥ*, *d* becomes *dh*; by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, *ṇ* and *ḍh* become *ṇ* and *ṭ*; and by *ḍhalopaḥ*, the *ḍh* is elided. Thus: *tṛṇekṣi*. [In *tṛṇekṣi*,] by *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, *ḍh* becomes *k*. Regarding *atṛṇeḍ*: [this is formed from] the *laṅ* [augment], either *tip* or *sip*, the elision of *halṅyādi* [suffixes], and the application of *ḍhatva*, *jaśtva*, and *cartva*.

But surely it is stated that [the rule applies] "when preceded by a consonant" (*halādau*), and we do not see a consonant at the beginning here? [The answer is: by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the consideration of the suffix as present). Is there no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when the basis is a phoneme (*varṇa*)? Therefore he says: "even when the basis is a phoneme, here [it applies]. That for which a mere phoneme alone is the cause is "based on a phoneme" (*varṇāśraya*); for example, in *go-hitam* ("beneficial to a cow"), where the substitution of *ava* [for *go*] occurs.

But here, in the rule *piti sārvadhātuke*, the suffix (*pratyaya*) itself is the cause (*nimitta*), while *hal* is its qualifier; therefore, because it has a suffix as its cause, [the substitution] certainly takes place—this is the meaning. Regarding *tṛṇaha*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*), with the suffix *meni*. Regarding *tṛṇaḍḍhi*: the substitution of *ḍh* and so forth is as before, followed by the elision of the vowel after *śna* and *as* (*śnasorallopaḥ*), and then the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions.

Now, for what purpose is *tṛh* (from the root *tṛh*) included here? It is so that the root *tṛha* belonging to the *raudhādika* class—meaning "to injure"—may be understood, and not the root *tṛhi* belonging to the *taudādika* class, meaning "to injure. For [the suffix] *pi*, *id*, *l* etc., which are *sārvadhātuka* affixes, cannot occur immediately after this [root], because they are separated by the *vikaraṇa* affix.

[Objection: But surely this [root *tṛh*] can also occur in its *yaṅ*-luṅ form; if that is so, then because it possesses an *anubandha*, it will not be included [in the rule]. To this he says: "Regarding *tṛṇaha*," and so forth. If the root with the suffix *śnam* were not included, then the augment *im*, being introduced when *śnam* was not yet applicable, would be an exception (*bādhaka*) to it. Even if it were not an exception, nevertheless, once *śnam* has been applied, the desired restriction regarding *im* would not hold. There would even be a reversal: first the addition of *im*, and afterwards *śnam*.

However, in the mention [of the root] together with *śnam* and *kan*, there is no cessation of *śnam*, and the desired grammatical arrangement is established—namely, that *śnam* occurs first and *it* (the augment) afterwards. Therefore, *śnam* is understood as it has arrived for that purpose. Furthermore, the inclusion of even the *rudhādi* class when it is in the *yaṅ-luk* form occurs precisely because of this mention together with *śnam* and *kan*.
The augment *īṭ* is added after the root *brū*.

The word *bruvaḥ* is in the ablative case (pañcamī), not the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī); this is because of the [authoritative] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Since that [ablative] has already served its purpose there, the locative case *sārvadhātuke* (occurring in the preceding rule) is converted into a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the sake of the current application. Thus he says: "after this [root] *bruva*. Here, in the form *brūtāt* bhavān, the *pittva* (the property of being followed by a *pit* suffix) caused by *sthānivadbhāva* is set aside by the original (*aupadeśika*) *ṅittva* of the substitute *tātaṅ*; according to the principle "a *ṅit* [substitute] does not possess *pit*-ness," the augment *iṭ* does not occur.
Or [the substitution of *ya* occurs] for *yaṅ*. 7.3.94.

*Lālapītī* and so forth: from the roots *lap*, *vad*, and *ru*, there is the elision of the *yaṅ* affix (*yaṅ-luk*), followed by reduplication. For the root *ru*, there is *guṇa* in the reduplicated syllable; for the other two, there is lengthening. *Vavarti*: this is the form of the root *vṛt*; by the rule "and *ruk* and *rik* [are substituted] when there is elision," *ruk* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable. But what is the reason that only the forms with the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅ-luk*) are cited as examples, and not those with the suffix *yaṅ* itself? To this he says: "of that which begins with a consonant" (*hal-ādeḥ*). For in the case of a suffix ending in *yaṅ*, the *śap* augment must occur, and that [suffix] does not begin with a consonant.
The *tur*, *u*, *tuś*, and *yam* [substitutes] occur before an *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

The word *tu* is a verbal root (dhātu) according to the Sūtra; it signifies "increase," while others say it means "motion" and still others say it means "injury. Regarding *uttavīti*: the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Regarding *śamīdhvam*: from the root *śam*, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, there is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of a command; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*), followed by the suffix *śap*, which is elided by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

"Āpiśalāḥ" means the disciples of Āpiśali. Regarding "in sārvadhātuka [affixes]," this refers to the feminine form ending in *ṭā*. In that context, the mention of "sārvadhātuka" as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would be redundant, since [the term] is understood by way of its recurrence from the preceding sūtras such as "not [before] a reduplicated stem" (*nābhyastasya*). Therefore, he says: "the word 'sārvadhātuke' is understood [from the previous rule]."

For that mention of *sārvadhātuka* is connected with [the rule] *pitī*; therefore, if that were to recur, that [mention of *sārvadhātuka*] would also recur. To prevent its recurrence, the mention of *sārvadhātuka* is repeated. However, the term *hali* does indeed recur, for it is not connected with the mention of *sārvadhātuka*.
The suffix *asti* is treated as if it were not present (*apṛkta*) when it follows a verbal root ending in *s*.

In the rule *apṛkte*, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive; therefore, this augment belongs only to an *apṛkta* [suffix]. Regarding *āsīt*: from the root *as* "to be," there is the elision of *śap* (the present marker), and *īṭ* is added to *tip*. Regarding *alāvīt*: this is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense; by the rule *iṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of *sic*.

"Regarding the prohibition of *īṭ* for *āh* and *bhū*, etc. This is a *vārttika* on the *sthānivat* rule. The meaning is that a prohibition of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) must be stated for *āh* and *bhū*, and the purpose is the prohibition of *īṭ*. In the case of *āttha*: by the rule "for *brū*, there is the substitution of five [sounds]" (*bruvaḥ pañcānām*), the suffix *sip* is replaced; *brū* is replaced by *āh*; by the rule "for *āh*, there is *th*" (*āhasthaḥ*), the *h* is changed to *th*; and by the rule "before a *khari* [stop]," this *th* undergoes *cartva* (substitution by a voiceless unaspirated stop), becoming *t*. In the case of *abhūt*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist); *as-* is replaced by *bhū* by the rule "for *as*, there is *bhū*" (*asterbhūḥ*); and by the rule "for *gāti-sthā*, etc.," there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*.

In this case, because the status of being a *sthānin* (original element) is prohibited, the augment *īṭ* does not occur by virtue of depending on the root *as*. Nor does it occur by depending on the *sic* suffix, due to the force of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*. Let it be so regarding the substitute *bhū* for *as*; however, in the case of the pure root *bhū*, the *īṭ* depending on *sic* would apply; therefore, it is precisely *īṭ* that must be prohibited here. Regarding the domain of the root *ah*, another solution is established through a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), namely that the substitution of *th* in the rule "āhasthaḥ" is taught within the section concerning suffixes beginning with *jhal*.

But is it not the case that this [rule] is for the sake of including those [suffixes] which were previously *jhal*-initial? This is not so; for in that case, since all five [suffixes], beginning with *tiP*, would have been *jhal*-initial in the past, the substitution of *tha* would result everywhere, and therefore one should simply have prescribed *tha* itself.
In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *u* for *ū*] occurs frequently.

Regarding "ā": this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) of the root *as*, with *tip* (the third-person singular suffix), the elision of *śap* (the class marker), and the application of *rutva* and *visarjanīya* [resulting in *akṣāḥ*]. Regarding "atsā": from the roots *kṣara* (to move) and *tsara* (to go by stealth), in the *luṅ* (aorist), there is the elision of *tip* according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Then, by the rule *rātsasya*, there is the elision of the *sic* (augment). The *visarjanīya* arises from the *repha* (the letter *r*) of the root. As for the phrase "because of its being Vedic" (*chāndasatvāt*): the meaning is that by the rule "in the Veda, [the augment] is diverse even when combined with *māṅ*," not only is the absence of *aṭ* and *āṭ* established when *māṅ* is not present, but rather, their presence is also permitted when *māṅ* is present. And regarding the absence of the *iṭ* augment after *sic*: this too depends on the phrase "because of its being Vedic."
And *rud* [takes *aṅ*] after the five [roots]. 7.3.98.

*rud*, *svap*, *śvas*, *an*, and *jakṣ*—these five are the roots beginning with *rud*. The singular form *rudah* is used in place of the plural; the understanding that it signifies "the first" (of the group) is derived from the mention of *pañcabhyaḥ* ("from the five").
The substitution of *aṭ* occurs for [the augment] of Gārgya and Gālava. 7.3.99.

The mention of Gārgya and Gālava is for the sake of honor, not for the sake of providing an option; for the optionality of *aṭ* and *iṭ* is already established by the force of the rule itself. The mention of multiple teachers is likewise for this very reason.
That [suffix] is used for all [cases]. 7.3.100.
The inclusion of all [names] is for the sake of making it obligatory; otherwise, the mention of Gārgya and Gālava here might be suspected of being intended as an option.
Therefore, [the vowel] is long before the suffix *yañ*. (Pāṇini 7.3.101)

Some maintain that *tiṅ* is carried over here from the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi*. Thus, in *bhavān*, the suffix *kvasu* is added to the root *bhū*; because [the suffix] is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the *śap* augment is applied. Since the word *dhātu* is explicitly mentioned in the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ*, there is no reduplication of the stem ending in *śap*. For those, however, who carry over only *sārvadhātuke*, there is an absence of the long vowel due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Now, why is the augment *aṭ* not simply prescribed [by the rule] "ato yañi" (*Pāṇini 7.3.101*)—meaning, "the augment *aṭ* occurs before a verbal suffix beginning with *yañ* that follows an *aṅga* ending in *a*, as in *pac* + *avas*; and once *savarṇadīrgha* has applied, *pacāvaḥ* is established? Furthermore, by the force of the specific prescription, the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pararūpa*) by "ato guṇe" (*Pāṇini 6.1.97*) will not occur? It cannot be done in this way; for in cases such as *adhukṣāvahi* and *adhukṣāmahi*, the elision [of the *ks*] by "ksasyāci" (*Pāṇini 8.2.26*) would undesirably apply. And here, in *atijarābhyām*, the substitution of *jaras* would [undesirably] apply.

Even so, the mention of *dīrgha* (long) would be purposeless, as only the form of the sun (*ādityākāra*) should be prescribed. In that case, its purpose here is this: [in the example] *apākṣīd rodanaṃ devadattaḥ*, [the long vowel is required]. But surely, in [the example] *pacāmi bhoḥ*, the *pluta* (protracted) vowel would also apply by the rule "also for a non-final [vowel] in questions and narrations"? The mention of *dīrgha* is so that this [pluta] does not occur, but rather that there may be only a long vowel.

The addition of *ta* in *ataḥ* (from *at*) is for the sake of what follows, so that the substitution of *et* in the rule "when *jhali* follows, *et* replaces [the final vowel] in the plural" does not occur in [the example] *khaṭvābhiḥ*.
And [the substitution of *śu* for the root *svap* occurs] before the suffix *suP*. (Pāṇini 7.3.102)

Regarding the form *vṛkṣāya*: here, lengthening occurs because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning the non-disturbance of phonetic combinations) is not universally obligatory. Its non-obligatoriness is established by the specific grammatical citation *kaṣṭāya*.
In the case of a plural ending beginning with a *jhal* consonant, *e* is substituted for the final vowel of a word ending in *as*.

Regarding the phrase "of trees" (*vṛkṣāṇām*): the point is that if the condition "before a consonant" (*jhal*) were not stated, then the rule *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3), which finds its scope in forms such as *agnīnām*, would be superseded by this present rule [for *etva*], and consequently, the substitution of *e* would occur even for words ending in *a*.
And [the substitution of] *ā* for *apaḥ* occurs before the prefix *āṅ*.

*khaṭvayā*, *khaṭvayoḥ*, and so forth are the examples for *ṭāp*, *ḍāp*, and *cāp* respectively. Regarding *kīlālapā*: [the word is derived from] *kīlālaṃ pibati* ("he drinks the sweet drink") with the suffix *vic* by the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*; in the third case singular (*tṛtīyaikavacane*), there is elision of *ā* by the rule *āto dhātoḥ*. However, if the term were not qualified by the presence of the suffix *pi* (the drinking agent), then in forms such as *kīlālapaḥ paśya* ("look at the drinker of sweet drink"), this very substitution of *etva* (change to *e*) would apply by virtue of being subsequent (*paratvāt*), thereby overriding the elision which has its scope in cases like *kīlālapaḥ* [as a base].

Regarding the statement "because when *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, short vowels are not included": wherever *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, it is the long vowels that are intended, not the short ones. However, there would be the contingency [of applying the rule] by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*). In that regard, in the context of the sūtra prohibiting the status of being a substitute, there is a Vārttika: "When *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, [the substitute] is not long. This means that when *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, a long substitute is not treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*). By implication, this implies that when *ṅī* and *āp* are mentioned, it is the long vowels that are intended; this has been demonstrated by the author of the Vṛtti.
The final vowel of words ending in *ambā*, those having the sense of *artha*, and those ending in *nadī* becomes short [before a case-ending beginning with a consonant].
The term *ambārthāḥ* means "words having the sense of 'mother' (*mātṛ*)".

Regarding the expression *ḍalakavatīnām*: words having the sense of "mother" are indicated by virtue of the femininity residing in their meaning, or the feminine gender indication is based on the phonetic form itself—meaning "of those phonetic forms (*śrutīnām*) possessing the sounds *ḍ*, *l*, and *k*. Furthermore, the *ḍ*, *l*, and *k* sounds are understood when not joined with other consonants; therefore, in *akka* and *alla*, the short vowel indeed occurs. In the case of *devate bhaktiḥ*, once the shortening has been applied, because of the prohibition against treating the substitute as the original (*sthānivadbhāva-pratiṣedha*) in the rule "when there is the mention of *ṅī* or *āp* [the operation does not apply] to what is long," neither the augment *yāṭ* nor the replacement of *ṅe* with *ām* takes place.

Regarding the word *mātṝṇām*: because there are many instances of the word *mātṛ* due to the variation of preceding words, the plural number is used. Regarding *putrārtham*: the meaning is that the word *mātṛ* which is employed to denote a son [is the subject]. Furthermore, since in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is expressed by the constituent members (*varttipada*), this substitution occurs precisely therein. As for the question "for what kind of son?": although the son is subordinated within the compound, he is pointed out by mentally isolating him, just as in the case of: "Now begins the instruction on words; of which words? [where "words" is mentally extracted from the compound].

"Deserving designation by his mother" means that the son, because of his praiseworthy qualities, deserves to be designated by his mother who is born of a noble lineage. However, where the designation by the mother occurs due to the father's lack of recognition, [the suffix] does not apply; this is obtained because the rule for the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present participle (*laṭ*) is prescribed in the sense of praise, as in the word *arhat*. This is an exception to the rules governing compound endings (*samāsānta*), because this [new rule] is commenced even though that [general rule] has not yet been reached.
A short vowel is replaced by its corresponding guṇa. (Pāṇini 7.3.108)

"By virtue of the power of the prescription of the short vowel. Now, one might object: "The prescription of the short vowel would be solely for the purpose of prescribing the *guṇa* [substitution], because otherwise, in the absence of shortness, the *guṇa* would not occur. To this he says: "If... The meaning is that if the *guṇa* were prescribed after first prescribing the short vowel, there would be prolixity (*prakriyā-gaurava*) in the process; therefore, for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), one should prescribe the *guṇa* directly.

Objection: If it were stated that "there is guna for *nadī* and short vowels," would not the term *nadī* also carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into the rule "and before *jas*" (*jasi ca*), since they are both mentioned within the same compound? Response: This is not a fault. Even when two elements are mentioned in a single compound, only one part may carry over. For example, in the rules "the suffix *ṅīp* follows numerals and indeclinables" (*saṃkhyāvyayāder ṅīp*) and "also after those ending in *dāman* and *hāyana*" (*dāmahāyanāntācca*), the mention of "numerals" (*saṃkhyā*) carries over, but the mention of "indeclinables" (*avyaya*) does not.
And before the suffix *jasi*. (Pāṇini 7.3.109)

Regarding the phrase *jasādiṣu*: the word *ādi* (etcetera) denotes a class or type; therefore, it includes those [words] mentioned in the preceding rule as well. Regarding *darvī*: this was stated without regard for the optional application of the suffix *ṅīṣ* by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*; however, both forms are established by that very rule. Regarding *śatakratvaḥ*: in the alternative where there is no *guṇa* substitution by the rule *jasi ca*, the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of the same quality as the preceding) prescribed by *prathamayoḥ* also does not occur due to the statement *vā chandasi*; thus, the *yaṇ* substitution takes effect. Regarding *kikidīvyā*.

The substitution of *nā* [for *na*] by the rule "āṅo nāstriyām" does not occur here. The word *kikidīvi* is established as an irregular form (*nipātita*) among the *uṇādi* suffixes in the rule "kṛvidhṛṣvi."
The substitution of *ṛ* for the final vowel of the word *ṛtu* occurs before case endings beginning with *ṅ* and before the strong case endings (*sarvanāmasthāna*).

The inclusion of the long vowel *ā* (in the term *tapara*) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*), because a stem ending in a long vowel cannot occur before the case endings *ṅi* or the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes. Nor is it possible for this to be an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root (*dhātu*), because the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" prescribes the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* within a root. Furthermore, in forms such as *kartṛṇī*, the addition of *num* would be impossible due to its being treated as a *pūrvānta* (an integral part of the preceding element).
Before an affix beginning with *gh*, *ṅ*, or *it*. (Pāṇini 7.3.111)

Regarding the phrase "of the final member [ending in] *ghi*": this was stated on the assumption that the designation *ghi* applies to the phoneme alone. However, in the alternative view that the designation applies to that which ends in such a phoneme, the word *ghi* should be understood as referring to the phoneme that constitutes a portion of the *ghi*-ending element. By this, the rule concerning endings in *nadī* is also explained.

"Only when *sup* follows," [is said] because of the rule *supi ca*. "Paṭvī" is derived from the rule *vāto guṇavacanāt*. "Kurutaḥ": whatever does not have the designation *nadī* is entirely designated as *ghi*, and not merely according to its gender. The word *kuru* has the designation *ghi*; therefore, when *tasi* follows—which is a *ṅit* suffix—there is no *guṇa* substitution.
