And this is stated by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* interpretation of the term *ṅit*.

If, however, *ṅiccāsāv icca* is analyzed as a *karmadhāraya*, then there is no such contingency here at all; for by the rule *sārvadhātukam apit*, that which is an operation of a *ṅit* element is extended [by way of *atideśa*] when there is a *bahuvrīhi*, and by this much alone, the letter *ṅ* does not become the initial [element] of *tas*.
[The suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *ān* to form a feminine derivative, provided that the word is not *ānaddhā*. 7.3.112.

The ablative case in *nadyāḥ* (from "nadī") has its purpose already fulfilled; therefore, it brings about a sixth-case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) interpretation for the locative *ṅiti*. Consequently, he states that this augment is understood to follow only after that which ends in *ṅit*: "after an *aṅga* ending in *nadī*. For example, in *kumāryāḥ*, there is the *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *āṭaśca*. Now, what is the purpose of pronouncing the long vowel [in the sūtra]? Could one not simply say *aṭ*? Would not the forms *kumāryai* and *kumāryāḥ* be established through the *vṛddhi* rule *vṛddhireci* and the long-vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) rule? They would not be established; by the rule *ato guṇe*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) would apply.

Will [the accentuation] not occur by the force of the explicit mention of *aṭ*? There is a purpose for the mention of *aṭ*. What is it? In the forms *śriyai* and *śriyāḥ*, let there not be the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*; rather, let there be the grave accent (*anudātta*) of the augment (*āgama*), especially here because of the force of the explicit mention of *aṭ*. For the grave accent of the augment indeed overrides both the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*) and the accent of the case-ending (*vibhakti-svara*).
The word *yā* [is substituted for *yat*] before the suffix *āpa*. 7.3.113.

What is the purpose of the long vowel [in *khaṭvāyām*], for could one not simply say *yaṅ*? Once the *vṛddhi* has been applied and the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel substitution) has occurred, would forms such as *khaṭvāyai* and *khaṭvāyāḥ* not be established? They are not so established; by the rule *ato guṇe*, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) would apply. [Objection: It will not occur because of the force of the explicit utterance of the short *a*. [Response: There is another purpose for the utterance of the short *a*: that in forms such as *jñāye* and *jñāyāḥ*, the acute accent (*udātta*) prescribed by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* should not occur, but rather the grave accent (*anudātta*) of the augment (*āgama*) should take effect.

Furthermore, it might be suspected that the letter *a* [in the rule] is intended for the purpose of pronunciation; for in this case, in a *prādi*-compound such as *atikhaṭvām* (having transcended the bed), after the shortening has occurred, because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *yāṭ* augment would apply by this [rule], overriding the substitution of *ya* for the fourth-case singular ending according to the rule *ṅeryaḥ*. Once that is applied and the lengthening occurs, there would arise the undesirable result [*prasaṅga*] of *atikhaṭvāyai devadattāya*. To this, he says: "In the case of *ātaḥ khaṭvāyāḥ* etc. [He adds: "When the lengthening has not yet occurred"; this was stated in the state prior to the substitution of *ya*.

If that substitution of *y* and the lengthening have already taken place, then since this [suffix] was previously characterized by the marker *ṅ*, would it not follow that the augment *yāṭ* applies? To this he says: "And because it has been produced by a rule (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*)."
After a pronominal base, the suffix *syāṭ* is added [before the case endings beginning with vowels], and the final vowel of the base is shortened.

The long vowel *ā* is pronounced in the rule *sarvasyāḥ* so that *vṛddhi* may occur there; otherwise, by the rule *ato guṇe*, there would be *pararūpa* (single-substitution of the following vowel). However, the short *a* is pronounced so that in the form *asyāḥ*, the rule *ūḍidampadādi* does not apply and cause the initial accentuation (*ādyudāttatva*) of the case-ending; rather, it ensures that the augment remains unaccented (*anudātta*). Furthermore, the short *a* might also be suspected of being merely for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*).
The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies after the second and third [case endings]. Pāṇini 7.3.115.

This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) that has not yet been reached [by the previous rule], because [the word *dvitīya*] is not a pronoun (*asarvanāman*). But is it not the case that this is already established by the rule "there is an addition [to the rule for *ṭā*] for the second [ordinal] when followed by a *ṅit* suffix," so that there is no purpose for this [present rule]? And that [rule] must necessarily be stated so that the forms *smāi* and so on may optionally occur even for other genders. This is not correctly stated; for what is not established by a *sūtra* must be accomplished by an *upasaṃkhyāna* (supplementary addition), but it is not proper to reject a *sūtra* by resorting to an *upasaṃkhyāna*.

If, however, one were to adopt the inclusion of the short vowels here, set aside the mention of *syāt*, and instead maintain the extension (*atideśa*) by carrying forward only the term "of a pronoun" (*sarvanāmnaḥ*)—that is, [interpreting the rule as]: "Whatever has been stated regarding a pronoun applies optionally to the second and third cases"—then this supplementary addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) could be dispensed with.
[The suffix *ṅi* is substituted for the case endings] after words ending in *ṅa*, *rā*, *nadi*, and *āp*.

The term *ṅeḥ* is taken as the singular locative case ending; this is because of the specific indications such as "in the sense of desire" (*icchāyām*) and "in the feminine" (*striyām*). Regarding the form *grāmaṇyām*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *satsūdviṣa-* etc.; the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *agragrāmābhyām*; and the *yaṇ* replacement [of the semivowel] occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*.
[The suffix *ṅasi*] is replaced by *āt* after [stems ending in] the vowels *i* and *u*. (Pāṇini 7.3.117)

The term "nadī" (feminine noun) is understood here by way of anuvṛtti [from the previous rule]. If this is so, then this [present rule] is redundant, since it is already established by the preceding one; therefore, one might argue that the single rule "idudbhyām aut" should have been formulated. This cannot be done; for then the vowel *au* would apply [in all cases], whereas the scope for the suffix *ām* characterized as a "nadī" is in forms such as *kumāryām*, and the scope for *aut* is in forms such as *patyau* and *sakhyau*. However, in the case of *kṛtyām*, when the designation "nadī" applies, then by the principle of priority (*paratva*), *aut* would take effect.
Or [the substitution of *au* occurs] in place of [the dual endings *au* and *bhyām*]. Pāṇini 7.3.118.

Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is not termed *nadī*," etc.: the [substitution] was prescribed by the preceding rule for that which is termed *nadī*, while for that which is termed *ghi*, the author will later state that *aut* replaces [the final vowel] when it is joined with *at*. Therefore, the examples for these two rules are distinct. In that regard, in the former case it was stated, "from that which ends in a *ghi* or a *nadī*," whereas here it is stated, "ending in *i* or *u*. Furthermore, regarding the prescription of technical terms (*saṃjñā*), two alternatives have been shown: that the term applies to the mere phoneme itself, or to that which ends in it. Consequently, there is no contradiction.
The substitution of *gh* occurs in place of *ghu* when followed by the suffix *ac*.

In the forms *kṛtau* and *dhenau*: now, once the substitution of *au* (*autva*) has been applied here, why does the suffix *ṭāp* not apply by the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*? Let it be so; what is the harm? [If it were applied,] the two rules *ḍerāmnadyāmnībhyaḥ* and *yāḍāpaḥ* would become applicable. But the prescription of the substitution of *au* (*autva*) serves its purpose in the masculine. Therefore, he says: "The inclusion of the marker *t* (in *autoḥ*) is for the purpose of excluding *āp* in the feminine."

For here, because the substituend (*sthānin*) is a *mātrika* (one-mora) vowel and is being operated upon (*bhāvyamāna*), there is no possibility for a long vowel to replace the short vowel *a*; therefore, the addition of the *t* in *tapara* (as in *ataḥ*) would not be required for the purpose of excluding such a long vowel. Consequently, the *tapara* is employed so that even by another rule a long vowel might not occur; and this has been stated without relying on the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. For the substitution of *at* (short *a*) produced by the conjunction [of *a* and *ṭā*] does not become the cause for the *ṭā* suffix which destroys that very conjunction.

Regarding the phrase "audacca gheriti yeṣām" and so forth: here, some students study the rule *audacca gheḥ* as a single, unified injunction (*ekayoga*). In that case, if the word *ca* were intended as a conjunction (*samuccaya*), then the substitution of *au* would apply only where the substitution of *ā* applies—namely, in the form *dhenau*; and since the substitution of *ā* would also apply to the stem *ghi*, the substitution of *au* would not occur in forms such as *asakhyau* and *apatyau*. To avoid this fault, they explain that the substitution of *au* is the primary enjoined element (*pradhānaśiṣṭa*), while the substitution of *ā* is merely a secondary or incidental injunction (*anvācayaśiṣṭa*).

In this regard, just as in the rule "kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca" (Pāṇini 3.1.11), the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs in forms such as *śyenāyate* even in the absence of the elision of *s*, which is taught as an optional alternative (*anvācayaśiṣṭa*), so too here, the substitution of *au* occurs in *sakhyau* and *patyau* even in the absence of the substitution of *at*. This is the meaning.
After the prefix *āṅ*, [the substitute] *nā* is used for [the root *nam*,] except in the feminine.

Because of the mention of another substitute in the word *āṅaḥ*, he says that the genitive case in *gher* is converted into the ablative, namely: "of what follows after *ghi*. Now, for what purpose is the phrase *astriyām* (in the non-feminine) stated? Could one not simply say *āṅo nā puṃsi* (after *āṅ*, *nā* replaces [the final vowel] in the masculine)? For in this way there would be brevity (*mātrā-lāghava*), and the desired result would be achieved. If it were stated thus, however, [the rule] would not apply in the neuter in cases such as *trapuṇā* and *jatunā*.

"Let there not be [the absence of] *nā*. [Objection: Once *num* is applied by the rule "ikoci vibhaktau," the desired form is established. To this, he says: "It is not stated that [the word applies] in the masculine," and so forth. In the example *amunā brāhmaṇakulena*, if it were stated that [the word applies] "in the masculine," *nā* would not occur. Furthermore, *num*—which is conditioned by a vowel (*iglakṣaṇa*)—would also not occur, because the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). If it were stated that [the word applies] "not in the feminine," then *nā* would also occur in the neuter. When *nā* is to be applied, the non-existence of *mutva* does not hold.

Because of the prohibition "not in the case of *muni*," the desired form is not established even when the rule "in the neuter" (*napuṃsake*) is stated; therefore, one must simply say "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*).
Thus ends the third quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra. [End of] the *Kāśikāvṛtti*—6.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the seventh chapter.
Before the affix *ṇau* (the causative suffix) and before the augment *caṅ* (the reduplication of the aorist), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is shortened.

In the rule "ṇau," the locative case is used in reference to the *aṅga* (the stem), while in "caṅi," it is used in reference to the *ṇi*. In the examples, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the roots *kṛ*, *hṛ*, *lū*, and *pū*; then follows the aorist marker (*luṅ*), the reduplication marker (*caṅ*), the elision of *ṇi*, the shortening of the vowel, and reduplication. In that process, because what is performed upon the *ṇi* is treated as if it were in its original position (*sthānivadbhavati*), the verbal forms *kṛ* and so forth are reduplicated. For the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*, the substitution of *ur* for the final vowel occurs; for these two, the substitution of *it* occurs due to the application of the rule "sanvallaghuni" (treating them like the *sa*-present). For the other two as well, the substitution of *it* occurs by the rule "oḥ puyaṇjyapare. In all cases, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "dīrgho laghoḥ."

Regarding this: "in the examples cited immediately above. As for the phrase "because of its priority": *caṅ* (the *aṅ* suffix with *ṇiṅ*) provides scope for reduplication in forms such as *ā-śiśriyat*; however, the short vowel (*hrasva*) provides scope when reduplication has already occurred. But when reduplication has not yet occurred, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). In that case, reduplication takes place first. Consequently, when the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*) is to be applied, the shortening of the vowel does not behave as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) precedes the vowel from which the desired grammatical operation is to start. This is the intended meaning. He raises an objection: "But here... [meaning] that the augment *āṭ* should not occur in the usage of *māṅ*.

"Because of its permanence" (*nityatvāt*). For the doubling (*dvirvacana*) would apply whether the shortening (*hrasvatva*) has been performed or not; and since that [doubling] would thus remain, what fault is there? To this he says: "If that were so... He refutes this, saying: "This is not a fault. Regarding *oṇeḥ*: the purpose of marking the root *oṇṛ* ("to remove") with the marker *ṛ* is so that the prohibition "not after one marked with *ṛ*" (*ṛdito na*) may apply.

If there were reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in this case, the marking of the root as having an *ṛt* vowel would be purposeless; for once reduplication has occurred, shortening (*hrasvatva*) would not take place simply because [the original vowel] is separated by the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). However, the Teacher perceives that shortening is stronger than reduplication, and therefore he marks the root *oṇ* with an *ṛt* vowel. Why [is it said] "when followed by *ṇi*"? Because, due to the mention of the short vowel, the technical rule concerning vowels (*ac-paribhāṣā*) is brought into play, and thus the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of a vowel must be shortened.

Furthermore, for roots ending in a nasal (aṇ), a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) capable of becoming short cannot occur under the *caṅ* [affix], because the roots *śri*, *dru*, *nu*, *dheṭ*, and *śvi* do not have a penultimate vowel. However, for the roots *kam* and *gup*, the penultimate vowel is indeed short; consequently, when there is an affix following *caṅ*, the penultimate vowel becomes short, and that [affix] is precisely *ṇi*. In that case, since the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) takes precedence, once the *vṛddhi* and other substitutions have been applied, the rule "the penultimate vowel becomes short" is established as desired—this is the question.

The other [author] says—thinking that since the connection [of the rule] is possible exactly as heard, the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) "the suffix which follows *caṅ*" is not appropriate, and thus [the rule] would override even internal operations such as *vṛddhi* by virtue of the stated injunction—he says: "when *caṅ* follows, the penultimate vowel... [meaning] "it should become short. Now, one might object: "Surely there is a shortening of the vowel *ū*; once that is performed, let there be no *vṛddhi* because it has been overridden. But *guṇa* will certainly occur, as it has not been overridden by anything; then, through the substitution of *av*, the form *alīlavat* is established. This is not so.

Because the [substitution of] *guṇa* is superseded by the [substitution of] *vṛddhi*, and because that *vṛddhi* is in turn superseded by the [substitution of] *hrasva*, the *guṇa* has lost its opportunity; how then could it apply again, such that *uvaṅ* would result? Or, even if *guṇa* were to apply there, he states another fault: "in the case of *adīdapat*."

However, when the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies to *caṅ*-substitution (*caṅparanirhrāse*), then—after the *vṛddhi* and *ā* substitutions have been made and *puK* has been added—the *ṇi*-elision lacks *sthānivadbhāva*. Consequently, since only that which is the *aṅga* during the *caṅ* stage can possibly have a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) subject to shortening, the word "in the presence of *ṇi*" (*ṇau*) need not be stated [in the rule]. It was stated as "in the presence of *ṇi*" because the author of the Sūtras did not provide the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*.

"What is the purpose of [specifying] *caṅ*?"—this question arises because, since the rule for shortening (*hrasva*) applies to the roots designated as *mit*, there would be no shortening at all in the case of the causative suffix *ṇi* by this [present rule]; furthermore, one might assume that the desired distribution is established based on observed usage (*prayoga*). The other [the author] replies—"He causes to do" (*kārayati*), "he causes to take away" (*hārayati*)—thinking that the distinction between what is desired and what is not is easily understood without an explicit statement. Moreover, the mention of shortening for *mit* roots would be for the sake of the rule "it is treated as non-existent (*asiddhavat*) here, prior to the end of the following *āṅ*" (*asiddhavadatrābhāt*). "What is the purpose of [specifying] *upadhāyaḥ* (of the penultimate vowel)?"—this is the question.

By virtue of the short vowel pronunciation (*hrasva-śruti*), the term *acaḥ* (of a vowel) is understood [from the previous rule]. In that context, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified, the vowel is qualified by the *aṅga* (the stem); thus, wherever a vowel belonging to an *aṅga* occurs, it becomes short. Consequently, the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is already established—this is the question. The other [the opponent] also cites an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) as an example: *acakāṅkṣat*.

[Objection: But surely we shall qualify *ac* by means of the word "in *ṇau*"—that is, [we will interpret] "of the *aṅga* which has an *ac* when *ṇau* follows. There, by virtue of the requirement (*sāmarthyāt*), a single-vowel intervention must necessarily be resorted to because it is inevitable. To this he says: "This very thing... [He says] "for the sake of the subsequent rule. [That is to say: in the rule "there is elision of *pibati* and *ī* for the reduplication," the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) must certainly be employed so that [the substitution] applies to the penultimate vowel and not to the final one. If the term "penultimate" is for the sake of the subsequent rule, then it should be formulated in that very place.

If this is so, why not apply it in that very place? To this he says: "The same applies here as well. [Regarding the rule] *āllopaḥ pibateḥ*: if it were stated thus, the elision of the vowel *ā* (*āllopa*)—despite being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*)—would supersede the *yuk* augment because it lacks any other scope (*anavakāśatva*). However, when the term "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is included, the *yuk* is applied first due to its being an internal operation; subsequently, the elision of the penultimate *ā* occurs, and thus there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "penultimate" is for the sake of subsequent rules.

Another says: The mention of *upadhā* (penultimate vowel) is for the sake of this very point as well; otherwise, when the suffix *ṇic* follows, a short vowel being prescribed for the immediately preceding element would—despite being an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation—subvert operations such as *vṛddhi*, and once the form *lū-i-at* is established, the substitution [of a short vowel] would apply to the letter *u*. This is not a fault; for the fact that he teaches the prohibition in the rule "not for those whose penultimate vowel is elided (*aglopi*), nor for *śā*, nor for reduplicated roots (*ṛdit*)" indicates that the shortening does not apply to the final letter alone.

"An addition [to the rule] regarding *ṇau* and *ṇic*": this means when *ṇi* follows *ṇau*. In the reading *ṇeṇici*, the meaning is "prescribed after a *ṇi*-affixed root when followed by *ṇic*". "He caused him who had played [an instrument] to act": because the *luṅ* suffix denotes past time, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with the past tense "he caused to act."

But how is it in the case of *vāditavantam*? If he has already sounded [the instrument], how can there be an instigation (*prayukti*)? For instigation belongs to one who is currently acting or about to act, not to one who has already acted. We do not say that the past tense here is used in reference to the time of the instigation; rather, it is in reference to the time of the use of the word itself. In the expression *prayojitavān*, the past tense applies precisely in reference to that [time of the word's use], and thus it applies to the operation of the one being instigated as well. As for *avīvadat*: from the root *vad*, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added after the denominative suffix *ṇi*, followed by the aorist (*luṅ*) and so forth.

But what is the reason that [the rule] is not established? To this he says: "That which... For if there were the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva), then in a case where a *ṇi* follows *caṅ*, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) would not be subject to shortening; and in a case where the penultimate vowel is subject to shortening, that [root] would not have a *ṇi* following *caṅ*, because it is separated by a second *ṇic*. "By that" means by the elision of the *ṇic*. "Because of the absence of the [original] vowel" (*aglopitvāt*).

But surely, when a *ṇic* is applied after a root already ending in *ṇi*, both the elision of the *ṇi* and the *vṛddhi* (by the rule *aco ñṇiti*) would apply. In that case, the elision is *anitya* (non-permanent) because it applies only when there is a change of word-form (*śabdāntara*), whereas the *vṛddhi* is absolutely non-applicable once the elision has occurred. Since both are *anitya*, the *vṛddhi* takes precedence due to its subsequent position in the rules, and once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, the elision of the *ai* vowel occurs; thus, the base (*aṅga*) does not become one whose penultimate vowel is elided (*aglopi*). If this is so, then the fact that the author teaches the prohibition "not for those whose [penultimate] vowel is elided" (*yad aglopināṃ na*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the elision is stronger than the *vṛddhi*.

Otherwise, when *vṛddhi* has been applied everywhere, there would be the elision (*lopa*) of *ai* and *au*, but not of *ak*. This is not a valid indicator (*jñāpaka*); for this rule might be intended for cases where even after *vṛddhi* has been applied, only *ag* is elided—such as in *atyararājat*, meaning "he surpassed the king. But why then does [the author] employ the mention of the *pratyāhāra* (*ak*)? Otherwise, he would simply have said "not for those that elide *al*. Even this is not a valid indicator.

"He said 'asva' [meaning] 'there were no horses'; he said 'gomuca' [meaning] 'he did not release the cows'; he said 'prāvṛṣ' [meaning] 'the rains did not come'; he said 'yādṛśa' [meaning] 'it was as it was'—this [use of the suffix] would be for such purposes as these. Regarding this, they say: "The causative suffix (ṇic) is not present here; because it is not so expressed! And this is understood from the fact that the author of the Bhāṣya established it as a *jñāpaka* (an indicator)."

In that case, where the suffix *vin* is accepted, this would be the example for the rule "the elision of *vin* and *matup*": did he describe one who possesses light as *ababhāsat*? This is not the purpose of including the pratyāhāra [in the sūtra], for here it is simply the vowel *a* of the *matup* suffix that is elided. But where there is the elision of *vin*—as in *asasrajat*, describing one who wears a garland (*sragvin*)? Here too, the penultimate vowel does not become short. Therefore, it is established that the inclusion of the pratyāhāra is an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Even so, what was stated—that the substitution of *at* [for *i*] in *harati* and *kalayati* is for the purpose of prohibiting the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*)—is contradicted by this. For, even if the substitution of *at* were not applied, once the *vṛddhi* is superseded and the *ik* is elided, there would be no occasion at all for the application of the *sanvadbhāva*. Therefore, the argument "because it is *aglopi*" is not his own position; rather, it should be understood as stated from the perspective of another school.
Let the wise observe that the interpretation of the Bhāṣya here is likewise consistent;
however, when the opposite view is asserted, no supporting reasoning whatsoever is seen.
And thus, according to what Paṭu stated, one would have *apīpaṭat* and *abībalat*; however, according to the Bhāṣya on this point, it becomes *apapaṭat* and *ababalat*. Enough of this.

He rejects the proposed addition [to the rule], stating: "It is established by the indication of the class (*ākṛti*) of *ṇi*. Here, "class" (*ākṛti*) refers to the genus (*jāti*). That is to say: "In that case where there is the genus of *ṇi* which is followed by *caṅ*. Consequently, even though the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies, because it is the very class of *ṇi* that is followed by *caṅ*, that same *ṇi* which is followed by *caṅ* is indeed the one that precedes [the root], and that same [root] which precedes is indeed the one followed by *caṅ*; thus, the shortening is established. As for what was also said—"because of its being a non-eliding element (*aglopin*)"—that too is not correct.

For when the general form (*ākṛti*) is specified, the short vowel is not relied upon as being the cause for that general form of *ṇi*. In that case, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the elision of any other vowel [than the short one] belonging to that general form of *ṇi* is understood as the object of the prohibition; thus, everything is clear.
The substitution of *iK* for the final vowel of a verbal root does not occur when the root ends in a nasal, or when it belongs to the *śāsu* group, or when its penultimate vowel is marked with *ṛt*.

In this context, that which undergoes elision of the penultimate vowel (*aglopa*) when followed by the causal suffix *ṇi* is what is understood as *aglopin*. This prohibition does not apply to roots such as *div*, because of the inclusion of the term *śāsvṛd* in the rule.
It is possible that the root *śās* (to command) is not included [in the list], for this [root] will be read as *ṛd*.
Some authorities declare that *ṛśāsū* means "instruction."
Others, however, maintain that in this sūtra the root *śās* is read without an anubandha,
so that the prohibition [of the substitution of *śāsaḥ* for *śāsti*] would apply even in the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ.

In this regard, it is established even by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original). For when *sthānivadbhāva* applies, a short vowel cannot occur as the penultimate (*upadhā*). However, in the case of a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a consonant (*hal*), it is not established. Just as in the rule *sudhātur akaṅ ca*, when the entire complex is a substitute, the individual part is not a substitute; consequently, the substitution of *rapara* for the vowel *a* does not occur—resulting in *saudhātakir*—so too, when the whole is the original (*sthānin*), the part is not the original, and thus, due to the absence of being a substitute for a vowel (*aj-ādeśa*), there is no *sthānivadbhāva*.
But here, by the force of the mention of *aglopi*, even the elision of the whole complex is accepted as "elision of a vowel" (*aglopa*).
The augment *nuṭ* is optionally inserted before the suffix *kvip* after the verbal roots *bhrāj*, *bhās*, *bhāṣ*, *dīp*, *jīv*, *mīl*, and *pīj*.

*bhrāja* (to shine), *bhāsṛ* (to shine), and *bhāṣa* (in the sense of distinct speech) belong to the *bhūvādigaṇa*; *dīpi* (to shine) belongs to the *divādigaṇa*; all of these are *anudātta-it* roots; *jīva* (to sustain life) belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*; and *mīla* (in the sense of closing the eyes) and *pīḍa* (in the sense of afflicting) belong to the *curādigaṇa*.

Regarding the rule *bhrājabhās-* and so forth: an anudātta indicatory letter (*it*) must necessarily be attached to these two roots; however, it is said that following the presence of the vowel *ṛ* [as the indicatory letter] is un-Pāṇinian. This is because [the suffix *kvip*] would be optional (*vibhāṣā*) when the *ṛ*-indicatory letter is present, whereas it would be optional when another vowel is present. Since there is no specific result in favoring the vowel *ṛ*, its adoption is considered un-Pāṇinian. Regarding "of *kāṇi* etc.": *kāṇi*, *vāṇi*, *rāṇi*, *heṭhi*, *lopi*, and so on, are the *kāṇyādayaḥ*. The word "etc. (*ādi*) denotes a class or type (*prakāra*).
There is elision of the root *pā-* [in the reduplicated portion], and the augment *ī* is substituted for the reduplicative syllable. (Pāṇini 7.4.4)

Regarding the form *apīpyat*: one might object that since the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) occurs first—due to its higher status and its obligatory nature—the reduplication would not apply because the root would then lack a syllable. To this, he says: "when the elision of the penultimate vowel has occurred. The mention of the "reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*) is intended to prevent the substitution of *it* from occurring alternatively for the penultimate vowel itself. Because the stem (*aṅga*) becomes "one whose final vowel is elided" (*aglopi*) through the elision of the letter *ā*, and because there is no possibility of a light syllable following [the reduplication], the rules for *it* and lengthening—namely, *san-vallaghuni*—do not apply; thus, this rule for *it* is established. The mention of the suffix *tip* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix).
The suffix *it* follows the root *sthā*. (Pāṇini 7.4.5)

Regarding *atiṣṭhipat*: because the substitution of *i* (itva) made in the causative (*ṇic*) is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*), there is reduplication of the root *sthā*. Due to the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule, the penultimate vowel of the reduplicated syllable receives the substitution of *i* (ittva). The mention of the suffix *tip* is as in the previous case.
The substitution of *ur* occurs [in place of *ṛ*] before a suffix beginning with a vowel. 7.4.7.

Regarding the rule *upadhāyā ṛvarṇasya*: why is there not a reference here to the root *ṛt* (as in *ṛt-*) so that forms such as *mā bhavān arpipat* might occur? It is because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*). For that ensures that even when the substitute is long, it remains short. [The statement] "it is an exception to *har*, *rar*, and *ār*" means: for the root *kṛt* (in the sense of 'utterance'), the substitution of *it* prescribed by *ṛta iddhātoḥ* would apply; for roots such as *vṛt* (in the sense of 'turning'), *guṇa* would apply; and for *mṛj*, *vṛddhi* would apply—these being followed by *rapara*, they become *har*, *rar*, and *ār*.

Regarding the form *acikīrtat*: even though the substitution of *it* (the *it*-augment) has been applied within the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it does not behave as a *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original element). Where there is reduplication, the rule of *sthānivattva* applies only to the first vowel (*ajvarṇa*) of the subsequent portion. Thus, the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) in the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* is of this very nature. Now, one might object: "The substitutions of *ir*, *ar*, and *ar* are *antaraṅga* (internal), because they depend only on the causative suffix (*ṇic*); whereas the substitution of *ṛ* is *bahiraṅga* (external), for it depends on the subsequent *caṅ* (the aorist marker). Therefore, how can these [rules for *ir*, *ar*, and *ar*] be superseded by that [rule for *ṛ*]? To this he replies: "By the force of the explicit statement. If *ir*, *ar*, and *ar* were to occur here by virtue of being *antaraṅga*, this specific rule would be entirely redundant.

Regarding the phrase "the addition of *tapara*," etc.: if that [mark] were not present, then in a case where the substitute (*sthānin*) is long, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratamya*), only a long vowel would result. Now, one might object: "An *aṇ* vowel being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*); so how could there be any possibility of a long vowel? To this he says: "And this is not [the case]. The meaning is: "if the addition of *tapara* were not present. How is it not being taught? To this he says: "by another substitute," etc.

The intended meaning is as follows: it is a general principle that when a prohibition of what has already been established can be accounted for by a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*), it is not proper to formulate a new injunction (*apūrva-vidhāna*). Consequently, if the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with the *p*) were not employed, then for the sake of excluding other substitutes such as *ir*, *īr*, and *ār*, the very nature of the *ṛ*-vowel as it exists would be permitted. The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility; and this possibility of permitting the actual form occurs only when there is the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*).

In that context, if one were to allow only the word's own form (*svarūpa*) [to be understood], there would be the inclusion of the vowel with its own phonetic quality (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). However, when the marker *t* (the *tapara*) is employed, the allowance of the own form is not possible; therefore, the *tapara* is used to ensure the status of being "that which is being taught" (*bhāvyamānatva*). Generally, however, the reading *abhyanujñāyate* ending in the suffix *uṅ* is found, but that does not yield a correct meaning; for the present tense (*laṭ*) occurs only in reference to an action currently being performed. Others, however, explain it thus: "The own form is allowed so as to exclude other substitutes"—it would result in this [interpretation].
The substitution of *di* for the root *dayati* occurs before the *liṭ* suffix.
Regarding the word *avadigya*: from the root *diṅ* "to protect," the *ātmanepada* ending is applied because it is marked with the *ṅit* suffix; the *yaṇ* substitution occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*.
However, this does not apply to the root *day*, which is listed as *daya* "giving, going, protecting. For that [root], the *ām* augment is prescribed in the *liṭ* tense by the rule *dayāyāsasaśca*.

It is intended that the substitution of *digy-* should supersede reduplication, because this [substitution] is commenced even though reduplication has not yet applied. Now, one might object: let the reduplication applicable to the root *day-* be superseded, but as for the substitution of *digy-*, reduplication applies to it by virtue of its being treated as the original (sthānivadbhāva); how then can it be superseded? For it is not the case that the commencement of this [substitution] occurs when reduplication has not already applied. It is replied: regarding the relationship between the sublated and the sublater, there are two possibilities—either the target (*lakṣya*) is superseded by the rule (*lakṣaṇa*), or the rule is superseded by it.

In that regard, this objection would apply to the first alternative, because the rule for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) remains uncontradicted; however, in the second alternative, the very rule for reduplication is contradicted in this context by the rule for the substitution of *di* (and so on). Thus, even when the substitution of *di* has been applied, there is no occasion for reduplication. If this were so, then in the case of *aster bhūḥ*—as in *babhūva*—there would be no reduplication; for rules that have no other scope (*anavakāśa*) are subverting (*bādhaka*), yet this [rule for *di*] does have scope. What is its scope? It is *bhavitā* and *bhavitum*.

If, then, [the substitution] is prescribed only for the *liṭ* [perfect tense]—as in the rules "for *cakṣiṅ*, *khyāñ*" and "optionally in the *liṭ*"—then reduplication would not apply there, as in *ācakhyau*. This is not a fault; for in the rule "in the *liṭ* of the *ārdhadhātuka*," the locative case denotes the scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Consequently, the substitution of *khyāñ* occurs even before the production of the *liṭ* that is the cause of reduplication; subsequently, when the *liṭ* follows, reduplication takes place. However, in this present case, because the locative case is taken in the sense of "when following" (*parasaptamī*), the substitute *khyāñ* is introduced while reduplication has not yet applied, and thus it supersedes it.

Likewise in other cases as well, wherever sublation (bādha) is not intended, there the sublation of the *lakṣya* must be stated, or else the locative of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*) should be resorted to.
And a vowel following *ṛ* or a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) is subject to the rules for *guṇa*. (Pāṇini 7.4.10)

Regarding *sasvaratuḥ* and so forth: the roots are *svṛ* in the sense of "sound and affliction," *dhvṛ* in the sense of "fainting," and *smṛ* in the sense of "thinking. Here, because the rule for *guṇa* (vocalization) applies later, it is applied first, and subsequently the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs; thus, at the time of prescribing the *guṇa*, the stem (*aṅga*) begins with a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). Alternatively, once the reduplication has occurred and the *halādi-śeṣa* (retention of the initial consonant) has been performed, since a [present] cluster is impossible, the *guṇa* is applied by relying on the fact that it was formerly preceded by a cluster.

Regarding the phrase "the object of prohibition": in the case of *thali*, in the first person singular (*uttama*), and in the case of *ṇal* when the *ṇit*-designation is absent, the general rule for *guṇa* is not established at all—[as in] *sasvartha* and *ahaṃ kila sasvara*. In that case, would this very *guṇa* apply by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*) in the domain of *vṛddhi*? To this he says: "But in the domain of *vṛddhi*" and so forth. The scope of *guṇa* is [seen in] *sasvaratuḥ*; the scope of *vṛddhi* in the presence of a *ṇit* affix is [seen in] *kārakaḥ*, *hārakaḥ*. In cases such as *sasvāra*, where both rules apply to the domain of *vṛddhi*, there is a prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

But surely, even if that [guṇa] were applied first because it is subsequent, the form would be established by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ*? True; however, this other solution should be considered: the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of specific reference (*nirdeśārtha*). As for a long vowel, in forms such as *ātastaḥ* and *taruḥ*, the guṇa indeed occurs by the subsequent rule. Nor can one argue that the application of that [long-vowel rule] is also excluded from words beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) by virtue of the power of the marker *t*; for its validity is established by its being intended for specific reference.

"From [roots] beginning with *saṃyoga*, etc. This statement is made because the root *kṛ* (in forms such as *saṃskṛ*) is not preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). The mention of "penultimate" (*upadhā*) is an indicator of a specific position, since the technical designation "penultimate" (*upadhā-saṃjñā*) is prescribed for an *al*-element (a vowel) alone, and it is impossible for a consonant cluster to be a penultimate. Alternatively, the word "cluster" (*saṃyoga*) may refer to a member of the cluster, whereas its status as a "penultimate" is primary. In the form *sañcaskaratuḥ*: the augment *suṭ* is applied according to the rules "after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*, when *kṛ* means 'adornment'" and "even when there is intervention by *aṭ* or the reduplicated syllable."

If the inclusion of "having a conjunct as a penultimate" (*saṃyogopadha*) is made, there is no purpose in including "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādi*); for here too, in *sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*, it would be established by the rule "of that which has a conjunct as its penultimate" alone? It would indeed be established—*sasvaratuḥ* and *sasvaruḥ*—but this is not established: *sañcaskaratuḥ* and *sañcaskaruḥ*. What is the reason? Because of being characterized as extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). The augment *suṭ* is extrinsic, while the *guṇa* [vowel substitution] is intrinsic. How is *suṭ* extrinsic? To this he says: "For here... (*atra hi*).

In this view, the *liṭ* suffix first expresses the sense of the verbal root; since the cause [for the application of a rule] exists at that very stage, *guṇa* substitution would apply. However, *suṭ* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon the prefix (*upasarga*) which arrives later; therefore, since *suṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when *guṇa* is to be performed, there would be no *guṇa* due to the word not having a consonant cluster as its penultimate element (*asaṃyogopadhatvāt*). Furthermore, the rule finds its scope of application in cases such as *sasvaratuḥ*.

But when the inclusion of "saṃyoga" and so forth is made, since the inclusion of "saṃyogopadha" serves no other purpose, its status as *asiddha* (not yet established) is set aside; thus, the *guṇa* [substitution] is established. Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that *suṭ* is *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic); hence he says, "and having done so. Regarding the statement in the rule *suṭkātpūrvaḥ*—"the mention of 'before the *k*" is for the purpose of indicating that *suṭ* is not a part (*abhakta*) [of the word]"—here, however, a resolution is given even if it is a part (*bhakta*), by resorting to the position of the Bhāṣyakāra; therefore, there is no contradiction.
The root *ṛch* takes the augment *ṝt* [before the suffix *ām*]. || 7.4.11 ||

The root *ṛcch* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth. Here, the root *ṛt* is also included by elision (praśleṣa), as he says: "of this [root] *ṛ*. This is understood from the mention of the plural number (*bahuvacana*). However, there is no inclusion of the vowel *ṛ* (the phoneme *ṛ-varṇa*); for otherwise, roots ending in the vowel *ṛ* would have been included. But why is *ṛt* included? So that forms such as *āratuḥ* and *ārur* may be produced. Otherwise, when *ṛ* + *atus* and *ṛ* + *us* are situated, the doubling (*dvirvacana*) and the substitution of *uratva* would set aside the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrghatva*), because the former is based on the phoneme (*vārṇatva*).

In this regard, if [the root] were included by the mention of "repetition" (*abhyāsa*), then after the substitution of *u* for *ṛ*, the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ*, the lengthening by "ata ādeḥ," and the elision of *ā* by "āto lopa iṭi ca," only the form *atur-ur* would be heard. Alternatively, if it were included by the mention of "dhātu" (root), then because it ends in *ṛ*, when *guṇa* is applied, the forms *aratuḥ* and *aruḥ* would result. Similarly, in the case of the suffix *kvasu*, after *guṇa* is applied, there is reduplication of *ari*, *halādiśeṣaḥ*, lengthening by "ata ādeḥ," and the addition of *iṭ* by "vasvekājādghasām"; thus, the form *ārivān* is obtained.

[The objection is raised: "Because the root *ṛcch* has a non-light (*alaghu*) penultimate vowel, there would be *guṇa* substitution. [The answer is: Because it is *antaraṅga*, once the *tuk* augment is applied by the rule "che ca," the vowel *ṛ* becomes heavy by the rule "saṃyoge guru"; it is neither light nor a penultimate vowel. As for the phrase "but in the case of roots ending in *ṛ*": here too, as in the preceding sūtra, the root *ṛt* (from *ṛtīyate*) is to be understood by ellipsis. As for the phrase "but in the domain of *vṛddhi*": even if *guṇa* were to apply because it is subsequent, the form is nonetheless established by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ"—this is another solution.
In place of the final vowel of the roots √śrī, √dṛ, and √prā, a short vowel is optionally substituted [before the suffix kta].

The roots *śṝ* (in the sense of injury), *dṛ* (in the sense of tearing), and *pṝ* (in the senses of protecting and filling) [are examples]. In forms such as *viśaśaratuḥ*, etc., there is a prohibition of the substitution of *et* (the short *e*) and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) by the rule "not for *śaś*, *dad*, *vā*, and so forth.

Now, for what purpose is the short vowel prescribed as an option? Why not simply opt for the *guṇa* substitution that is under discussion; for in the alternative case where *guṇa* does not occur, the form *viśaśratuḥ*, etc., would be established through the *yaṇ* substitution? To this he says: "The mention of the short vowel is for the purpose of preventing the *it* [substitution]. Otherwise, by the principle "that which depends on the phoneme (*varṇa*) is stronger than that which depends on the grammatical element (*aṅga*)," the *it* substitution would apply, overriding even the *yaṇ* substitution—which, though *antaraṅga* (internal), depends on a phoneme.

"Ke-cit" and so forth. But how is the formation of the word *viśaśratuḥ* and others established if this [rule] is rejected? To this he says: "śrā pāke," etc. [An objection: But is there not a difference in meaning? [He replies: No; he says, "they have multiple meanings. Likewise, by means of the words "satti," etc., he refutes the rejection [of the rule]. In that context, from the root *śrṛṇāti* with the suffix *kvasu*, we have *viśaśarvān*; but from *śrāti*, we have *viśaśrivān*. Therefore, the meaning is that only the short vowel (*i*) is to be optionally applied.
[The substitution of] *ke* [takes place] for *aṅ* [before the suffixes beginning with *ṇ*]. || 7.4.13 ||

Regarding *jñaka*: there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it* by the rule *bhastraiṣājājñā*. Regarding *goka*: it was explained in the rule *laṇ* that the pratyāhāra [of vowels] is formed with the preceding *ṇakāra*. Regarding *rākā* and *dhākā*: [the suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *kṛdādhārācikalibhyaḥ kaḥ*. "Also of *kan*" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for [the suffixes] with indicatory marks (*sānubandhaka*), such as *ṭhañ* in the sense of a place by the rule *ordeśe ṭhañ*, as in *naiṣādakarṣukaḥ*.
Not after *kapi*. 7.4.14.

In examples such as *bahukumārīka*, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule *nadyṛtaśca*. Now, if this [application of *kap*] is prohibited, why does the shortening of the *upasarjana* (the preceding feminine noun) not occur? Precisely because of this prohibition. This is not a prohibition of the shortening itself; what then? It is a prohibition of the immediately preceding rule, *ke'ṇaḥ*. Why is this so? Because of the principle: "A rule or a prohibition applies only to that which is immediately contiguous. If that is the case, he says: "This shortening does not take place when *kap* follows. For if the shortening of the *upasarjana* were to occur, this specific statement would be rendered meaningless.

Therefore, by the force of this statement, there will be a prohibition of both whatever [shortening] and however much shortening exists. There is scope for this statement where the shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not apply, namely in the case of non-feminine suffixes—as in *bahuyavāgūkaḥ* and *bahulakṣmīkaḥ*. However, in the case of a feminine suffix, the shortening of the subordinate member would certainly still occur. To this, he says: "This rule, *go-striyoḥ upasarjanasya*, also [applies]. Why? To this he says: "For the sake of the compound," and so forth.

In the rule *samāsāntāḥ*, the word *anta* signifies a "constituent part. And how does something become a constituent part of a compound? If it forms a compound with that [word]. And how does it form a compound with that? If, while the compound itself is not yet formed, the suffix *ka* arises from the final member (*uttarapada*) expressing that meaning, and subsequently the compound is formed with that which ends in *ka*.

But surely, *kapa* is first [added] to that which ends in a *sup* (case-ending); how then can there be a compound with that which ends in *kap*? [Answer: Because of an explicit rule (*vacana*), there is a compound even with that which does not end in a *sup* in the case of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*). Another says: "The compound-final suffix is like an inflectional affix (*vikaraṇa*) between the case-ending of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and its base (*prakṛti*); since what falls between them is included by the mention of those two, there is a compound with that which ends in a *sup*. There is a fault in one who speaks thus: in examples such as *bahucarmikā*, the substitution of *i* by the rule *pratyayasthāt* would not occur.

What is the reason? [It is because] the *sup* suffix follows *ka*, and after that, the *ṭāp* suffix [is applied], as in the example: *bahuparivrājakā mathurā*. If the compound were formed subsequently after *kap* had been added, what would follow? To this he says: "A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that is a compound ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) does not [occur]."

In the rule "gostriyoḥ," the term "of the nominal stem" (prātipadikasya) is understood to carry over; furthermore, a nominal stem status (prātipadikatva) belongs to that which ends in a feminine suffix only when it occurs in a compound (samāsa). However, in the manner described here, the preceding portion ending in the suffix *kap* possesses neither the status of a compound nor the status of a nominal stem. Therefore, there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel for the subordinate member (*upasarjana*).
In place of the vowel *ṛ* (and its long counterpart *ṝ*), there is *guṇa* substitution before the suffix *aṅ*.

The term *ṛ* is used here to denote the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*), because of the [authoritative] commentary. In forms such as *akarata*, the substitution of *aṅ* for *cl* occurs by the rule *kṛmṛdṝruhibhyaśchandasi*. In *asarat*, the substitution of *aṅ* occurs by the rule *sartiśāstyarttibhyaśca*. In *adarśat*, the substitution of *aṅ* occurs by the rule *irito vā*. Why is there the mention of "guṇa" (vowel strengthening)? Could one not simply say *ṛdṛśoṅyaḥ*? It is not possible; otherwise, the final letter of the root *dṛś* would undergo the substitution [of *ṛ*], but because of the mention of "guṇa," the *ik* vowel [the radical *ṛ*] is strengthened. If the word *aṇ* were understood from the previous rule, the mention of "guṇa" could have been omitted. However, it was not done in that way.
The suffix *thuk* is added after the root *as* when followed by the suffix *te*.
"He sat down" (āsthat). [This is formed] by the rule: "The suffix *aṅ* is applied after the roots *as*, *vac*, and *khyā*."
The suffix *ara* is applied after the root *śvi*.
The form *aśvadit* is derived by the application of the suffix *aṅ* according to the rule beginning with "jṝstambhu."
The substitute *pu* replaces [the final consonant] of the word *pataḥ*. 7.4.19.
"Apaptat"—this form is derived from the root *pat* with the suffix *aṅ*, due to its being listed in the *lṛdita* group.
There is *guṇa* substitution for the root *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

The mention of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter) is intended so that [the rule] does not apply when there is *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix), as in *śeśītaḥ* and *śeśyati*. If it were stated simply as "of *śīṅ*, *e*" (*śīṅa eḥ*), then the genitive case would be uttered with respect to a form possessing an *anubandha*; and since an *anubandha* is by nature subject to cessation, once its cessation is achieved through elision (*lopa*), another interpretation might be understood: that the *ekāra* (the vowel *e*) is not the cause of its cessation, but rather that the *ekāra* itself is what is being referred to. However, the mention of the *guṇa* (the vowel *e* as a *guṇa* substitute) excludes the single substitute (*ik*). As for the letter *ṅ*, it ceases by its very sound. Therefore, the mention of the *guṇa* is necessary.
In this [section], when followed by a consonant (kṅit), [the substitution of long ī for the short i of the suffix *iṭ* does not take place]. Pāṇini 7.4.22.

Regarding *śayyata*: [the suffix] *yak*. Regarding *śāśayyata*: [the suffix] *yaṅ*; because it is both subsequent (*paratva*) and obligatory (*nitya*), the substitution of *ayaṅ* is performed first, and then reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Regarding *praśayya*: [the suffix] *lyap*.
A short vowel is substituted for the initial vowel of the root √ūh when it follows a prefix. Pāṇini 7.4.23.

An example has not been shown because [the application] is impossible. First, the *yaṅ* [intensive suffix] is impossible because [the root] begins with *a*. Furthermore, even for *yāsuṭ*, there is an intervention by *śap*. However, in the benedictive (*āśis*), *yāsuṭ* is indeed *kit*. Thus, this rule is stated for the purpose of precluding the long-vowel usage in *ūhati*. As for forms such as *samuhyate*, they are established simply by applying *saṃprasāraṇa* to the root *vah*. Since roots have multiple meanings, a difference in meaning is also irrelevant. [The form is] *ā ūhyate*.

This is not a worldly sentence fit for usage, for in such a case there is no *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) between the verbal root and the prefix, according to the traditional rule: "The *saṃhitā* is obligatory within a single word, and obligatory between a verbal root and a prefix. Therefore, the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the augment *aṅ* is demonstrated by means of an unworldly analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), and thus the shortening [of the vowel] is not performed; this is because the science [of grammar] is intent upon producing correct worldly usage. Others, however, read the shortening even here [in this context], as in the form *ohyate*.

In this case, once the single-substitute (ekādeśa) has been applied, because there is no longer a distinct separation (*vyapavarga*) between the two sounds, the short vowel (*hrasva*) does not occur. Furthermore, by the rule *upasargād ūhateḥ*, since the substitution depends on both sides [the prefix and the root], there is also no treatment as being like the end or the beginning (*antādivadbhāva*). Regarding the form *samūhyate*: here, because the single substitute is treated as the beginning of the following element, there is the contingency of shortening the vowel following *samaḥ*. However, this does not happen because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *aṇaḥ*; the pratyāhāra is formed with the preceding *ṇ* alone. Thus, since this rule is dependent upon a specific phonetic form (*rūpāśraya*), and that particular form is not extended [to the substitute], the short vowel does not occur.
The suffix liṅ is used in the sense of "eternal" (nitya). || 7.4.24 ||

By the rule *āśiṣi liṅ* and so forth, he shows the scope of the sūtra. For when the *liṅ* affix follows a verbal root (*sārvadhātuka*), lengthening of the vowel *i* is not possible. But surely, if there were *savārṇa-dīrgha* (lengthening by homogeneity), it would be possible—as in *abhīyāt*, *pratīyāt*, and *parīyāt*; here, it should not be short. What is the reason? Because, due to the application of both [rules]—namely, *upasargādeteḥ*—there is an absence of the treatment as either the final or the initial (*antādivadbhāva*). Thus, *ā-īyāt* and so forth. This has been explained by the example *ā-ūhyate* and so forth.
There is lengthening of the vowel before both the *akṛt* suffixes and the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes.

Regarding the phrase *akṛdyakāre*: since a suffix consisting of the letter *y* alone is impossible, the meaning is "in an *asārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with *y*, other than one belonging to the *kṛt* class. *Bhṛśāyata*: [This is formed] by the *ky-aṅ* suffix according to the rule *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacveḥ*. *Sukhāyata*: [This is formed] by the suffix [according to the rule] *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām*. *Cīyate*: [The suffix] *yak*. *Cecīyate*: [The suffix] *yaṅ*. *Toṣṭūyate*: [In this form, the rule applies] *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*. *Cīyāt*: [This is] the *liṅ* (optative) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

"Having ascertained," "having commenced"—these [forms] contain the suffix *lyap*, which bears the technical designation *kṛt*. Now, one might object: "A long vowel (*dīrgha*) is prescribed for a stem ending in a vowel (*ac*), but here, once the augment *tuk* is applied, the stem no longer ends in a vowel (*anajanta*); therefore, the long vowel will not occur. To this, he says: "Because it is subsequent" (*paratvāt*). The scope of *tuk* is, for example, *ganicit* and *somasut*; the scope of the long vowel is, for example, *cīyate* and *stūyate*. In the case of *niścitya* and *prastutya*, because the rule for *tuk* is subsequent, it is superseded by the rule for the long vowel.

Generally, however, the reading is *prahṛtya* (not *prakṛtya*). In that case, because of the subsequent rule, there would be an occasion for the substitution of *rīṅ*, which would result in a long vowel (*dīrghatva*) and thereby subvert the application of *tuk*; thus, [the reading *prakṛtya*] would be incorrect. Alternatively, it may be explained with the intention of referring to the first possible application. As for *cinuyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), etc. In *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, the substitution of *yā* occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* and so forth.
The substitution of *ri* for *ṛt* occurs [before a following vowel]. 7.4.27.
Regarding the word *piyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *pituryacca*; once the substitution of *rīṅ* has been made, there is the elision of the *sy-* portion [of the suffix].

But how is it that the substitution of *rīṅ* occurs here when the condition "before an affix marked with K or Ṅ" (*kṅiti*) is still in force? To this he says: "In this case, the requirement 'before an affix marked with K or Ṅ' is no longer operative."

Regarding *cekīryate*: from the root *kṝ* "to scatter," with the intensive suffix *yaṅ*, there is lengthening by the rules "ṛta iddhātoḥ" and "hali ca. Regarding *jegilyate*: here, although the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs by the rule "gro yaṅi," because the *r* is absent, there is no lengthening. Now, for what purpose is it stated as *rīṅ*? Why not simply say *riṅ*, since the lengthening will occur by the rules "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ" and "cvau ca"? In that case, this is also the purpose: the mention of *riṅ* need not be made subsequently.

In that case, the mention of *ya* and *liṅ* would also not need to be made; one could simply say "and before *śe*," and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), [the rule] would apply before the *yak* of both *akṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. If this were so, then just as the long vowel occurs in forms such as *mātrīyati*, it would likewise occur before *ya* and *liṅ*—as in *kriyate* and *kriyāt*. If it is argued that in those cases, since the substitution of *riṅ* is prescribed when the [application of the] long vowel has not yet taken effect, it therefore subverts the lengthening; then it would follow that it would also subvert [the application of the long vowel] in the case of *kyac* and other such suffixes.

Now, it might be argued: "Let the lengthening of the vowel *ṛ* be set aside for now; but how is the substitution of *riṅ* set aside? For that [substitution of *riṅ*] is not introduced when the lengthening has not yet taken effect. [The reply is: In that case, the substitution would not be set aside even in the case of the *yaṅ* and *liṅ* suffixes. Therefore, two distinct substitutes must be stated so that the lengthened form may be heard in the case of *kyaj* and others, while the short form may be heard in the case of *yaṅ* and *liṅ*.
Before *riṅ*, *śaya*, and *liṅ*, [the suffix *k* is applied]. (7.4.28)

The mention of *liṅ* and the continued application of the rule regarding *akṛt-sārvadhātuka* suffixes qualify *liṅ* alone—based on the principles of possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—and not *śa* or *yak*. [Examples: *ādriyate*, *ādhriyate*. [Derivation: From the roots *dṛṅ* in the sense of "respect" and *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining," the suffix *śa* is applied because they belong to the *tudādi* class; when *riṅ* is substituted, the *iyaṅ* replacement occurs. The mention of *riṅ* is for the purpose of preventing lengthening (*dīrgha*). Once *riṅ* has been applied, lengthening would apply by the rule "*akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*"; the point is that this rule is intended to prevent even that lengthening.
The suffix *guṇa* is applied after the roots *ṛ* and *si*, when they are joined with a prefix (*upasarga*). 7.4.29.

The root *ṛ* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class in the sense of "going" and "attaining," while *ṛ* and *sṛ* belong to the *jauhotyādi* class in the sense of "going"—in both cases, this is indicated by the elision (*luk*) due to their Vedic character. If the form were specified as *ṛcchati*, it would not apply to *iyarti*; if specified as *iyarti*, it would not apply to *ṛcchati*. However, the simple mention of *ṛ* alone was not made for the sake of variety. Nor does this give rise to the suspicion that a mere phoneme (*varṇa*) is being referred to, because the term *ṛtaḥ* (of *ṛ*) is understood from the previous rule. Furthermore, the word *śa* is excluded here because it is impossible [for such a case to occur], for neither the root *ṛ* nor any root beginning with a conjunct consonant is listed among the *tudādi* roots.

In the case of *saṃskriyate* and *saṃskriyāt*, once the augment *suṭ* has been applied, there arises the contingency of *guṇa* substitution because [the root] is now a stem (*aṅga*) beginning with a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). To this, he says: "In this case" (*iha*). The *suṭ* is considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on two words; however, this statement is made on the basis of the principle that "first the verbal root is joined with its grammatical operation" (*sādhana*). He also states, regarding another alternative view: "Or because it is not a part" (*abhaktatvāt*). As for *iyṛyāt*: this is the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of injunction (*vidhi*), etc.; there is *ślu* (elision) of the suffix *śap*; reduplication; the substitution of *it* for the reduplicated syllable by the rule *artipipartyośca*; and the substitution of *iyaṅ* for the reduplicated syllable by the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*.
Since the mere vowel *a* would have sufficed to state the result, the explicit mention of *guṇa* here is of questionable utility.
And [the suffix] *yaṅ* [is applied after a verbal root]. 7.4.30.

Regarding the term *ghnībhāva*: the pronunciation of the letter *gh* is for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), because if the substitution of *hrī* were prescribed, there would be the undesirable consequence of increased complexity (*gaurava*) due to the application of the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini 7.3.55) to cause the substitution of *k*. In the form *jeghnīyate*, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is not sublated by the substitution of *ghnī*, because their spheres of application (*viṣaya*) differ: the reduplication applies to the entire *yaṅ*-stem, whereas the substitution of *ghnī* applies only to the verbal root (*prakṛti*). In the form *jaṅghanyate*, this [root] has the meaning of "going. [The sūtra: *ī ghrādhmoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.31).
Even in the rule prescribing the substitution of *i*, there is the [sūtra]: "There is lengthening for the *a* of a kṛt or sārvadhātuka suffix" (Pāṇini 7.4.25).
And: "The *a* [is replaced by *i*] before the suffix *cv-*" (Pāṇini 7.4.32).

Since the long vowel would have been established by the rule *cvau ca*, the specific prescription of the vowel *ī* is for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*). [Pāṇini 7.4.33: *kyaci ca*.

The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of subsequent purposes; that is, [the substitution] should apply only in the case of *kyac*, as in "not in *chandas* or when not meaning 'son'," etc., but should not apply in the case of *cvī*.

**Pāṇini 7.4.34**: *aśanāyodanyadhanāyā bubhukṣāpipāsāgardheṣu* (The forms *aśanāyā*, *udanyā*, and *dhanāyā* are substituted for the denominative roots *aśanāyati*, *udanyati*, and *dhanāyati* when they mean hunger, thirst, and longing, respectively).

"In these meanings" means when they are being understood. An example here is one who, being hungry at that very moment, desires food. A counter-example here is one who, already having eaten his fill, desires food for a subsequent purpose.

"Udakīyati" means he desires water for the sake of bathing and so forth. "Dhanāyati" means an excess of longing—*gardha*; it means that even while possessing wealth, he desires further wealth. "Dhanīyati" means that being poor, he desires wealth. [The rule] "not after *na* or *chandas*" [applies]. (Pāṇini 7.4.35)

In this context, by proximity, only the prohibition of *ītva* (the substitution of *ī*) would apply. Consequently, once that exception (*apavāda*) is removed, the general rule (*utsarga*), namely "lengthening occurs before non-*kṛt* and *sārvadhātuka* suffixes" (*akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*), would apply. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which was stated regarding *kyac* does not take place. What, then, is that? To this he replies: "Lengthening and *ītva*. He thinks as follows: since the author teaches the substitution of *āt* in the rule "for *aśva* and *agha*, *āt*" (*aśvāghasyāt*), he thereby indicates that this prohibition applies even to lengthening.

Otherwise, since [the desired forms] would already be established by the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*), the statement regarding *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) would be purposeless. In examples such as *mitrayu*, the suffix *u* is applied according to the rule *kyācchandasī*. In *putrīyantaḥ* ("desiring sons"), they desire sons; in *janīyantaḥ* ("desiring people"), they desire people. Here, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is replaced by the suffix *śatṛ*, and the augment *num* is added according to the rule *ugidacām*. However, others say: *janīyantaḥ* means "those desiring a wife," for the word *janī* denotes a bride. In that case, another purpose for the inclusion of the term "beginning with" (*ādi*) must be sought.
Desiring to harm, desiring wealth, he strives for virility; he seeks to cause injury. 7.4.36.

Regarding the phrase "duṣṭīyitā" being obtained: in the context of common speech (*bhāṣā*), "obtained" (*prāpti*) is intended; since the suffix *u* is absent there, the suffix *tṛc* is employed as having the same meaning. However, it is usually recited with the present indicative ending (*laṭ*); in that case, the intention lies solely in the verbal root (*prakṛti*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the name Aśvaghoṣa [to form patronymics]. 7.4.37.
"Etadeva" and so forth; this has already been explained previously.
In the Kāṭhaka Yajurveda, the substitution of *deva-sumna* occurs. (Pāṇini 7.4.38)

In this context, the word *yajus* refers to the Veda, not to a mantra. *Kāṭhakam* means "this belongs to the Kaṭhas," according to the rule *gotracaraṇād vuñ*. Thus, it means "in the *yajus* of the Kaṭhas," that is, in the Kaṭha branch (*śākhā*). And this being the case, the substitution of *ā* occurs in a mantra consisting of *ṛc*s within the *yajus* of the Kaṭha branch; likewise, it also occurs in the *Ṛgveda* if that mantra is seen in the *Kāṭhaka*. For example: *devān jigāti sumnayur iti*. Since the Kaṭha branch also exists among the followers of the *Bahvṛca* (the *Ṛgveda*), there is consequently a counter-example. Indeed, the Vedas are infinite.

Regarding the rule *dyatisyatimāsthāmitti kiti*: the roots *do* (in the sense of "cutting") and *ṣo* (in the sense of "concluding"), as well as *mā* (in the sense of "measure"), *māṅ* (in the sense of "measure"), and *meṅ* (in the sense of "giving"—all three are included here because there is no distinction made in rules concerning the inclusion of *gā*, *mā*, and *hā*). In *avadāya*, the suffix *lyap* is applied. In *avadātā*, the suffix *tṛc* is applied. In the expression *dyatisyati*, the citation with the marker *śtip* is for the purpose of specifying particular verbal roots.
The substitution of *śa* or *cha* for the final letter of a verbal root ending in *ś* or *ch* may optionally take place before an affix beginning with a vowel.

The root *śo* means "to thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*), and *cho* means "to cut" (*chedane*). Regarding the word *śyateḥ*: the domain specified is "vow" (*vrata*), not the subsequent word [of the compound]. Therefore, even in the case of *saṃśito brāhmaṇaḥ*, the substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs invariably. In the word *saṃśita*, one who is diligent regarding a vow is expressed. In the term *saṃśitavrata*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose vow has been perfectly accomplished. Although the substitution of *i* occurs elsewhere than in the context of a vow, it is mandatory when the vow is involved; thus, because the word *saṃśita* is a general term, its usage alongside the word *vrata* is not contradictory.

It is established through the understanding of the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option). In some cases there is constant application, in some cases by way of an alternative, and in some cases there is no application at all—such is the variously established option known as *vyavasthitavibhāṣā*.

He shows a mere indication of the established *vibhāṣā* rules by means of a verse, beginning with "Devatrāta. The suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām*. By the rule *nudavidondatrā*, the substitution of *na* does not occur when a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is involved. Since the mention of "deva" is illustrative, the absence of *na*-substitution also applies in cases such as "Bhavatrāta" and others when they are proper names. However, when used as a verbal derivative (*kriyāśabda*), both forms—*trātam* and *trāṇam*—are possible. Regarding "gala": [the same principle applies].

Regarding the rule *aci vibhāṣā*, the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs optionally; however, when referring to a limb of a living being, it occurs invariably. Thus, that which swallows food (*girati annam*) is called the *gala* (throat). But in the case of poison (*viṣa*), it does not occur at all; thus, that which is swallowed by those seeking an oath (*gīryate śapathārthibhiḥ*) is called *gara*. However, when the word is used as a verb (denoting an action), both forms occur: *gara* and *gala*. As for *grāha*: according to the rule *vibhāṣā grahaḥ*, when referring to the sun and so forth, only the suffix *ac* (from the *pacādi* group) is applied. But when it is a verb (denoting the action of seizing), it is as before. Regarding *itihāsa*: [the same applies].

In expressions such as *hantīti palāyate* ("he flees because he is being struck") or *varṣatīti dhāvati* ("he runs because it is raining"), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* do not occur [after the verb] when used with *iti*, according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*. As for the word *mithas*: they are not optional alternatives within a single domain, but rather with respect to different domains.

This is logical on the view that the word denotes the *ākṛti* (form/class), for in that case, having simultaneously perceived the entire range of things to be characterized (*lakṣyajāta*), two categories are taught: existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*). Although these two operate with respect to distinct objects, they both apply to the aggregate. Their non-confusion, however, is to be understood from the force of usage. For example, in the case of *gavākṣa*: when it means "window" (*vātāyana*), the substitution of *avaṅ* by the rule *avaṅ sphoṭāyanasya* occurs invariably; but when it refers to a "limb of a living being," as in *go'kṣam*, it does not occur. In other instances, there is an option: *gavāgram* or *go'gram*. [The rule] *dadhāter hiḥ* [is stated]. 7.4.42.

Although forms such as *hita* from the root *hi* (to impel) are established by other rules, this sūtra is commenced to prevent forms such as *dhīta* from the root *dhā* (to place). The mention of the suffix *śtip* is so that the root *dheṭ* (to suck) is not included. If it were simply stated as *dha*, it might be suspected that *dheṭ* is also being cited—as occurs in the rule *dādhā ghu adāp*. However, in the case of *yaṅ*-luk, when the augment *iṭ* is applied, the form becomes *dādhita*.
And [the substitution of *i* for *ya* occurs] after the root *jahāti* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*.

This statement, "lest there be [the form] *jahitvī*," is also [intended to prevent that]. However, the purpose of the technical designation *śtip* has already been demonstrated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) itself: namely, that when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), the form becomes *jāhitvī*.
In the Vedic language, there is an option [regarding the application of grammatical rules].

This [sūtra] is commenced because of the commencement of the preceding sūtra; otherwise, the two forms of the roots *hi* (to impel) and *hā* (to abandon) would already be established. [The form] *hātveti*: due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is an absence of the substitution of *ī*.

The suffix *kvi* is applied after the verbal roots √sudh, √vasu, √dhā (in the sense of *nemi*), and √dhiṣ, and it is also applied after the root √dhiṣ with the addition of the augment *i*. (Pāṇini 7.4.45)

Regarding "the augment *iṭ* optionally": when the augment *iṭ* is present, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "there is elision of *ā* before *iṭ* and [before suffixes beginning with *ya*]. In the word *vasudhitam*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound. It is also seen in the case of the suffix *ktin*—as in "or indeed this *vasudhiti* in its entirety. In *nemadhitam*, this too is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

In *dhatsva*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "of the *ā* of *śnā* and reduplicated stems," and the substitution of *bhaṣ* (the voiced unaspirated stop) by the rule "of *dadh-* before *t* and *th*."
The substitution of *d* for *da* occurs before *ghu*. (Pāṇini 7.4.46)

Regarding the word *dhītā*: the substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule *ghumāsthāgāpājahātisām iti*. [The opponent says: "This form belongs to the root *gheṭ*. But for the root *dadhāti*, the substitute *hi* occurs by the rule *dadhāter hiḥ*. Regarding *dātam*: this is from the root *dāp* in the sense of "cutting"; the meaning is "cut. Regarding *avadātam*: this is from the root *daip* in the sense of "purifying. [The opponent asks: "Why is this desired as having a final *t*? He replies: "For it has been stated thus."

Although the letter *da* is heard [in the traditional recitation], nevertheless, since this form is possible even when the letters beginning with *ta* undergo the *jaś*-substitution (*jaśtvam*) within the *saṃhitā*, all four alternatives are possible. If this substitute were to end in *ta*, then in the word *sudattam*, there would be lengthening by the rule *dasti*; for the meaning of that rule is "when there is a *t* belonging to the element *dā*. On the other hand, if it were to end in *da*, the substitution of *na* by the rule *radābhyām* would necessarily follow.

Now, regarding the form ending in *dh*: by the rule "after *jhaṣ*, *t* and *th* become *dh*" (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), it would undergo the substitution of *dh*. [Objection: There is no fault in the case of a form ending in *th*. [Response: Here, the negative particle *nañ* is to be supplied; this is because the concluding statement is "therefore, [the fault does not apply] to that which ends in *th*. [Objection: But what if...? In the rule "before *da*" (*dasti*), there are two alternatives: either the substitute for *dā-* is one that ends in *t*, or it begins with *t*. In the second alternative, this fault does not arise. Regarding the forms ending in *d* and *dh*: the substitution of *d* (*dadbhāvaḥ*) which occurs due to the proximity of an affix beginning with *t* does not become the cause for the destruction of that very [proximity].

Regarding "avadattam" and so forth: the term "in the sense of an initial action" (*ādikarmaṇi*) is a qualification of "pradatta" (bestowed), not of the others, because [the application] of those others is impossible. By the phrase "and it is so intended," the word "ca" implies "and as it has been previously established"; therefore, forms such as *avattam*, *vittam*, and *prattam* also occur.

"Or rather, these [prefixes] are not *upasargas*. How is there the status of being non-*upasargas*? To this he says: "They have other actions as their object. There is a connection between the root *gam* (to go) and others such as *ava*; therefore, according to the rule "those particles beginning with *pra* which are connected with an action receive the designation of *gati* or *upasarga* with respect to that [action]," they do not function as *upasargas* with respect to the root *dā* (to give).
In this context, after a prefix, the suffix *ta* [receives the augment *iṭ*]. (Pāṇini 7.4.47)

Regarding "ta ity ayam": the letter *a* in *takāra* is for the sake of pronunciation. Regarding "prattam": here, the vowel *a* [of *pra*] is replaced by *t*, and the *d* [of *tta*] undergoes *cartya* (substitution with *t*). Regarding "nīttam": the lengthening occurs according to the rule "dasti" (Pāṇini 6.1.71).

[The substitution] of *al* would apply to the beginning [of the following element], because of the rule "of the subsequent, that which belongs to the beginning" (*ādeḥ parasya*). [Objection: The term *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is repeated [in the sūtra]. Or rather, the word *asya* ("of this") is understood from the context; where was it introduced? In the rule "*asyacvau*" (P. 7.4.32). [Consequence: Then even this substitution of *dadbhāva* (the change to *dad*) in the rule "*dodadghoḥ*" (P. 7.4.46) would apply to the vowel (*avarṇa*), and consequently, in the word *dattam*, the initial of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) would be heard [as *da*]. If that is so, then I shall state it thus: "*do'dghoḥ*," meaning that for the letter *ā* which follows *do*, there is *at*. [Question: Why is there a double *t* [in *dattam*]? [Note: The double *t* arises because the substitute *at* is a single phoneme (*ekāl*), and according to P. 1.1.55, a single-phoneme substitute takes the place of the final phoneme of the original.
