Since the original *ā* is not at the end of the stem *do*, the entire stem undergoes the substitution, resulting in *dat-t-am*. The first *t* is part of the substitute, and the second is the original final *t* of *do*.]*

There are two exceptions (*apavāda*) to the rule *alo’ntyasya*: namely, *ādeḥ parasya* and *anekālśitsarvasya*. In the event of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between these two, the latter prevails. [Objection: In that case, would there not also be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) in the rule *apo bhi*? To this he replies: "In the case of *apo bhi*, etc. Here, of the two *t* sounds, the final one undergoes elision due to being at the end of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*), while the preceding one undergoes the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*).

On this point, some say: "The word *aca* must necessarily be carried over (*anuvartya*) here; otherwise, [the suffix] *ap* prescribed by *ṛdorap* would also apply in cases such as *lavābhyām* from the root *lūñ*. But that is not so; since the letter *p* has been elided, the word *ap* does not exist there, and therefore [the rule] will not apply in this case."
The movement of what has previously existed is logical, but its occurrence in the present is not;
nor is there any possibility here for that which is neither a condition nor a non-condition.
Because the two [suffixes] are not of equal status, the suffix *ap* is indeed not heard in the case of *pratyaya*;
[this is stated as] *apo bhi* (Pāṇini 7.4.48).

Regarding *svavabhiḥ*: from the root *ava*, the suffix *asun* is applied; those who possess excellent protection (*ava*) are *svavasaḥ*. Regarding *tu*: this is a verbal root found in the *sūtra*; those who possess good strength (*tavas*) are *svatavasaḥ*. Regarding *mādbhiḥ*: by the rule *paddannomās*, the word *māsa* undergoes the substitution *mās*. Regarding *uṣadbhiḥ*: the suffix *asi* is applied according to the rules *mithune'siḥ* and *vaseḥ kiñca*.
That [suffix] is called *ardhadhātuka* when it follows a verbal root (*dhātu*).

Regarding "he will dwell" (*vatsyati*), and so forth: the root *vas* [is used] in the sense of "dwelling," with the suffix *laṭ*. Regarding "he wishes to eat" (*jighatsati*): [this is derived from] *ghas* [with] *luṅ* and *san*. Regarding "you sit" (*āsse*) and "you wear" (*vasse*): *ās* is used in the sense of "sitting," and *vaś* in the sense of "covering"—both belong to the *adādi* class and are *anudātta-it*. If it were stated [in the rule] "when *taṅ* [the ātmanepada endings] does not follow," then [the substitution] would not occur even in the case of *vyativatsīṣṭa*.
There is elision of the [final] *t* and *s* of the verbal roots √as and √sas.

Regarding the form *vyatiṣe*: the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *kartari karmavyatihāre*; there is elision of the *śap* affix; and the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*. The point is that this word consists of the suffix alone; therefore, by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, the prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* applies.
And [the substitution of *ri* occurs] before *ca*. (Pāṇini 7.4.51)
No example has been shown for [the suffix] *aster*, because it is impossible for it to begin with the letter *r*.
ha eti || 7.4.52 || [The substitution of *ha* occurs before *eti*.]

This *hakāra* does not occur [in the form] *edhāmāse*. What is the reason? Because the *ekāra* that occurs after *tās-* occurs there [after *ās-*] as well. And what occurs after *tās-*? The first person singular. Another says: [it is] the first person singular and it is a *sārvadhātuka*; therefore, in "I slept while watching you" (*supto'haṃ tvāṃ prekṣāmāse*), it does not occur even when it is in the first person and an *ārdhadhātuka*.
The reduplication of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, which consist of a single vowel, [is treated as having a long vowel]. Pāṇini 7.4.53.

In the syllable *yak*, the letter *i* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). [The rule] "there is elision" (*lopo bhavati*) applies. However, the letter *h*, even though it is immediately preceding, does not carry over (*anuvartate*) because it is not marked with the *svarita* accent. *Ādīdhyeti*: [the suffix] *lyap*. *Ādīdhyaka*: [the suffix] *yak*. *Ādīdhitā*: [the suffix] *tṛc* and *iṭ*. *Ādīdhyanaṃ*: [the suffix] *lyuṭ*; here there is a prohibition of *guṇa* substitution by the rule "*dīdhīvevīṭām*". In this case, regarding the suffix *vuñ* after the root *ādīdhaya-*—as in *ādīdhyaka*—the suffix *ṇvul* occurs while the causative marker (*ṇi*) is still being heard (*śrūyamāṇa*). Although the elision would have applied even prior to the production of the suffix, it does not take place because of the mention of the specific phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇāt*). [Question: Why is the mention of the phoneme superfluous, such that [elision] does not occur? [Answer: No, he says.

This is the literal meaning; how so? The root *varṇ* belongs to the *curādi* class, meaning "to describe" or "to perceive"; thus, that which is described or perceived is a *varṇa*. In the compound *varṇa-aviśaḥ*, where *aviśa* is a qualifier, the inversion of the order [placing the qualifier last] occurs due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
The augment *iṭ* is applied after the roots √mā, √mī, √ghu, √rabh, √labh, √śak, √pat, and √pad when followed by the suffix *san*.

The term *sī* (ending in *ī*) which recurs here is a qualifier for *san*. Regarding the rule *mīnātiminotyoḥ*: this refers to both *mīñ* "to injure" and *ḍu-mīñ* "to cast"; both are included because the form *mī* is possible even for *minoti* once the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by *aj-jhan-gamāṃ sani* has been applied. One might object: "But that [form] is derived through a grammatical rule (*lākṣaṇika*)? True; this is indeed an intended extension (*iṣṭi*), as he says: "it is desired. The three roots *mā* "to measure," *māṅ* "to measure," and *meṅ* "to give" are all included.

Regarding *mīnāti* and *minoti*: since the suffix *san* is *kit*, these roots do not fall under the scope of *anej* (roots beginning with a vowel), and thus the form *mā* is impossible; therefore, they are mentioned separately. Regarding *ghu*: the roots designated as *ghu*—namely *dā* and *dhā*—are understood here. [Also included are] *rabha* in the sense of "rashness," *ḍulabhaṣ* in the sense of "attainment," *śaklṛ* in the sense of "ability," and *pallṛ* in the sense of "motion. In *mitsati*, the *s* is changed to *t* by the rule *sa syārdhadhātuke*, and the *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is elided by *atra lopo'bhyāsasya*. In the *ātmanepada* forms, the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* applies. In *āripsate* and similar forms, the *s* is elided by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*.
The substitution of *ī* occurs for the final vowel of the roots *āp*, *jñap*, and *ṛdh*.

The root *āp* means "to pervade," and *jñā* means "to understand. When the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is added, the augment *puK* is inserted; furthermore, according to the rule "for *jñā* in the senses of killing, pleasing, and perceiving," it receives the designation *mit*. By the rule "the short vowel for *mit* roots," [the penultimate vowel is shortened]. The root *ṛdh* means "to increase. Regarding the form *īrtsati*: the vowel *ī* has *r* as its subsequent element (*rapara*), and there is the substitution of *c* for the dental *dh* (by the rule of *cartva*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *jñapi*: here, the term *acaḥ* (of a vowel) is understood from a previous rule. Since *jñapi* is being qualified by that [term], the substitution of *it* prescribed for the vowel-final *jñapi* would, according to the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52), apply only to the final [vowel]. Furthermore, the qualification "of a vowel-final" (*ajantasya*) would be redundant, as there is no possibility of deviation [from this condition]. Therefore, *jñapi* is qualified by the vowel: [the meaning is] "of the vowel of *jñapi*, wherever it may occur," as in the examples *ābṛdhibhyām*.

And thus, there is a single type of relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). In that regard, since the substitution of *ī* (īttva) has scope when the vowel is not final, the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*)—by means of the "prior prohibition" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*)—sublates it when the vowel is final. This is what was stated: "the elision of *ṇi*" (*ṇerlopaḥ*). "But as for the other," [referring to] another who says: "Let there be the substitution of *ī* even for *ṇi*; because of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the elision of *ṇi* will occur. However, the explicit mention of the substitution of *ī* is for the purpose of its being heard [as such] when the vowel is not final. Regarding the form *ardidhiṣati*: after the suffix *san* is added, the augment *iṭ* is applied, the penultimate *guṇa* is substituted, and *ra* is inserted as a subsequent element (*rapara*). Then, due to the prohibition "not *n*, *d*, or *r*" (*na ndrāḥ*), there is reduplication of the second monosyllable (*ekāc*) excluding the *repha*.
The suffix *icca* is applied after the word *dambha*. 7.4.56.

Regarding *dhipsati* and *dhīpsati*: because the suffix *san* is marked with *k* by the rule *halantācca*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), and the change of *bh* to *p* occurs by the rule of *cartyam*. It would have been possible to omit the rule for *ittvam*; one could instead have stated: "In the case of roots beginning with *mī*, *mā*, and others, the vowel *a* is replaced by *i* when followed by *san*, and for the root *dambh*, *i* is substituted [for the penultimate]; and by the inclusion of the letter *c* [in that rule], the substitution of *is* [for the final consonant] would also follow. Thus, one could simply have said: "*āpjñapyṛdhāmīt*."
For the root *muc* when it is intransitive, there is optionally the substitution of *guṇa*.

Regarding the form *mumukṣate*: according to the rule "the roots *bhūṣ*, those taking an object (*karmaka*), *kira* etc., and *san* [take the *ātmanepada*] except when there is a reflexive (*ātmanepada*) sense," there is an absence of the *ya*-affix in the case of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Since the reflexive status is not removed by extension (*atideśa*), the *śap* affix occurs in the sense of the agent, as in: "the staff bends by itself. Alternatively, it is because the specific nature of the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatvāt*). For it has been said:
"An action is intransitive (*akarmika*) due to common usage or because the object is not intended to be expressed."
In this context, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable (abhyāsa). Pāṇini 7.4.58.

He shows the meaning of the word *atra* (here) with the words "that which is this... Now, what is the purpose of including the term *atra*? It is so that [the rule] may apply within this specific context, such as in the section beginning with *sanimīmā*, and not in cases like *dadau* or *dadāti*. This is not a necessary purpose, for one could have stated it thus: "*sani mīmāghurabhalabhaśakapatapadāmaca is abhyāsalopaśca*"—and likewise in the subsequent rule, simply "*abhyāsalopaśca*"? To this he replies: "*sani mīmādhvityādi*. This refers to the determination of scope—the restriction of the domain.

What, then, is this? To this he says: "In this very [context]," and so forth. He shows what is excluded by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)—namely, that [the rule] does not apply in the domain of *saṇvadbhāva* (the treatment as if having the suffix *san*). [The example is] *amīmapat*. [Derivation: from the root *miñ*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is the substitution of *ā* by the rule "for *mī*, *mināti*, *minoti*" (*mīnātiminoti...*), then the augment *puk*, the suffix *luṅ*, and reduplication (*dvirvacana*) before *caṅ*; then, due to *saṇvadbhāva*, the substitution of *it*, and finally the lengthening of the short vowel (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).

But how is there an occasion for the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) here when it is said to behave like *san*? To this he says: "as in *sanvadbhāva* when [the penultimate] is light" (*sanvallaghuni*). For just as the substitution of *it* occurs by virtue of behaving like *san*, so too would the elision of the reduplicated syllable occur; in response to the doubt that the elision should apply to the final letter according to the rule *alo 'ntyasya*, he says: "of the whole" (*sarvasya*). But how is it obtained that it applies to the whole? To this he says: "for that very purpose. The suffix *tral* is added to the word ending in the genitive case according to the rule *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante*.

The meaning is that this well-known repetition (*abhyāsa*) is subject to elision (*lopa*), but not that which ends with it. Furthermore, the restriction of the scope [of the rule] is established even otherwise. It is not the operation (*kārya*) "like *san*" (*sannvat*) that is extended by analogy (*atideśa*); rather, it is the form (*rūpa*). And since this elision is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), it is not a form and thus is not extended by analogy. Others hold that because of the principle "the rule for the final letter does not apply to what is meaningless" (*nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ*), they effect the elision of the whole [stem]. However, the prohibition "in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable" (*anabhyāsavikāreṣu*) does not apply here, because elision is not a modification.

And likewise, in the *Paspaśā* [section], there is a separate mention of "one who knows elision, augmentation, and the modification of phonemes," and in the *pṛṣodarādi* rule, there is the statement: "and two others, namely the modification and destruction of phonemes. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), meaningfulness is determined; however, since no meaning whatsoever is perceived when an *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is produced, the *abhyāsa* is devoid of meaning.
The short [vowel] [is substituted]. 7.4.59.

It is not the case that the *halādiśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant) does not occur here. Nor should it be argued that the absence of *halādiśeṣa* is due to the force of the rule prescribing the augment (*āgama*), for otherwise [the sūtra] would have prescribed the substitute *ā* itself. Even if *halādiśeṣa* were to apply, the vowel *ā* is intended to ensure the distinct hearing of the individual components—as in the analysis *cala-acalam*.

For in a *karmadhāraya* compound, because the word "ādi" (beginning) functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), its placement before [the head noun] would be required. In a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*, however, the status of being the "beginning" of a consonant (*hal*) would depend on the intervening consonant (*halantara*) and not on the reduplication (*abhyāsa*); consequently, there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even to cases like *ajādi*. In the form *ānakṣa*—derived from the root *akṣu* in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*) with the perfect suffix (*liṭ*)—the elision of the *kakāra* would be required. Furthermore, in forms such as *āṭatuḥ*, there would be an over-extension due to the treatment of the preceding element as the beginning (*ādivadbhāva*). However, in both the *karmadhāraya* and *asamāsa* (non-compound) interpretations, the status of being the "beginning" depends on the reduplication; thus, this fault does not apply. Therefore, it is said: "that which is not at the beginning is elided."

A consonant (*hal*) is required; by this, the view that there is no compound (*asamāsa-pakṣa*) is shown. For in a compound, since it is impossible for that which is compounded (*upasamasta*) to have a requirement [for another], one would have to perform the mention of "consonant" (*hal*) again, stating "the initial consonant is without beginning" (*anādir hal*).

Now, an objection might be raised: "But the status of being a remainder (*śeṣa*) is already established for the initial [element] (*tattvādi*); so what is the purpose of this? To this he says: "This is caused by the remainder of the initial. True, "when something is already established, a new rule is begun for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, only the initial is retained, and not that which is not initial. Therefore, the meaning is that this elision (*lopa*) of the non-initial is prescribed as being caused by the retention of the initial; thus, this [rule] is not purposeless.

If the remainder of the initial [element] were the cause for the non-deletion of the beginning, then in forms such as *papāca*, where a consonant (*hal*) follows the initial, the deletion of the other would occur only there; however, it would not occur in cases such as *āṭatuḥ*. Therefore, he says: "In that case. Under the view that the category (*jāti*) is the basis, the presence of the initial element is required only within the class of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-jāti*), and not with respect to every individual instance (*prativyakti*); thus, there is no fault.

"But others," however, [hold as follows]. In the previous position (*pakṣa*), the meaning of the word is simply "remaining" (*avasthāna*); through the recourse to a restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is the exclusion of others. But in this position, even "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) is expressed by the very word *śeṣa* (remainder), which functions as a subordinate element. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That remaining," and so forth. "By way of statement" (*uktitaḥ*) means by way of the operation of the word (*śabdavyāpārataḥ*). "But because it is not something to be enjoined" (*avidheyatvāt*) shows its lack of primacy in terms of its actual sense (*ārtham*). He states that cessation is the opposite: "But cessation itself... and so forth.

Even in common worldly usage, as in the expression, "While walking, study; while muttering, perform the circumambulation," a distinction in words is perceived even though there is no difference in meaning. What follows from this? To this he says: "In that case. Because it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), cessation (*nivṛtti*) is subordinate (*pradānabhūtā*). How could it expect [the performance of] "what" and so forth, which are not themselves ceased? Of what nature is it? It is that which is not to be enjoined (*avidheyā*). The meaning is that because it is not to be enjoined, it is not primary (*apradhānabhūtā*).
A primary element does not follow after a subordinate one; therefore, there is no need for such an expectation.

In the Bhāṣya, another solution is offered: "hal" is one rule (yoga), and "atra lopaḥ" (elision here) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Furthermore, that [elision] is derived as the object of the action (*karmasādhana*), as in the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt," where the *hal* of the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is elided, and then the first [remaining consonant] is retained as the remainder (*ādiḥ śeṣaḥ*). Alternatively, the *saṃhitā* reading itself is "hrasvohalādiḥ śeṣaḥ"; in this case, the word division is "a-hal"—the reduplication becomes non-*hal*, meaning it becomes one in which no *hal* exists, and then the first [consonant] is the remainder.
When preceded by a sibilant (śar), the consonants k, kh, g, gh, ṅ (khayaḥ) [are doubled].

When the rule regarding the remainder (*śeṣa*) from the preceding [section] would have applied, the remainder is here prescribed by you (*khayā*). In this case, the remainder of the suffix (*ādiśeṣa*) is not sublated by the remainder of the single repetition (*ekābhyāsaviṣaya-anādiśeṣa*); for according to the maxim, "sublation occurs even when coexistence is possible. Furthermore, impossibility can also be asserted here. How so? This word *śeṣa* denotes a state characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*), and a state qualified by cessation cannot possibly exist when both [the original and the substitute] persist simultaneously. As in the examples *cuścyotiṣati*—where *ścyutir* means "to flow"—and *pispandiṣate*.

The root *spadi* is marked with an *anudātta* accent, meaning "to move slightly. Regarding *sasnau*: this is from the root *ṣṇā*, meaning "to cleanse. Regarding the phrase "preceded by *khar*" (*kharpūrvā*): the meaning is that in the rule, the mention of *śar* should be removed and replaced by the mention of *khar*. Regarding *ucicchiṣati*: this is from the root *ucchī*, meaning "to loosen. Regarding "because it is *antaraṅga*": since it applies immediately after the original instruction (*upadeśa*), the *tuk* augment is applied first due to its *antaraṅga* status; then, the reduplication occurs. And because that [reduplication] is "not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*)—meaning the substitution of *ch* for *c* is not yet established—it occurs precisely with the *tuk* still present. If, after that has been done, the *halādiśeṣa* (elision of all consonants except the first) were to apply here, the letter *t* would be heard in the reduplicated syllable.

And this has been stated without relying on the rule "that which is not established in what precedes does not apply when there is reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane*). However, if that rule were relied upon, then once the substitution of *c* for *ch* (*cutva*) had been applied, because that [substitution] would be considered established (*siddha*), the reduplication of the word *cchis* would result in the correct form through the remaining *c* alone. Nor is there a principle such as "in the absence of the cause, the effect also ceases to exist," by which the substitution of *c* (*cutva*) would be nullified.
The suffix *cu* is applied after the root *kuh*. (Pāṇini 7.4.62)

Regarding *cakhāna*: the letter *kh* becomes *ch*, and by the rule "in reduplication, *c* and *t* [become *k* and *t* respectively]," that *ch* becomes *c*. Regarding *jaghāsa*: the letter *gh* becomes *jh*, and by the rule of *jaś*-ness, that *jh* becomes *j*. Regarding *jihīrṣati*: by the rule "the suffix *san* is *kit* after an *ik*" (*iko jhal*), the *san* is *kit*; thus the *h* also becomes *jh*, and by the rule of *jaś*-ness, that *jh* becomes *j*.
The substitution [of *ku* for *kavatari*] does not occur before the suffix *yaṅ*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *kavateḥ*: the root *kūṅ* (meaning "to sound") belongs to the *tudādi* class; *ku* (meaning "to sound") belongs to the *adādi* class; and *kuṅ* and *khuṅ* belong to the *bhūvādi* class—all of which have "sound" as their meaning. In this context, if the specific *vikaraṇa* were not indicated and one simply said *koḥ*, all three roots would be included. If, on the other hand, the *tudādi* root ending in a long vowel (*kū*) were intended, even then only two roots would be included. Nor can it be argued that only the *adādi* root is meant because it lacks an *anubandha*; for that root has a *luk*-type *vikaraṇa*. Therefore, the *vikaraṇa* is specified so that only the *bhūvādi* root may be understood.

The forms *dādharti*, *dardharti*, *dardharṣi*, *bobhūtu*, *tetikte*, *alarṣi*, *apanīphaṇat*, *saṃsaniṣyadat*, *karikrat*, *kanikradat*, *bharibhrat*, *davidhyat*, *davidyutat*, *taritrataḥ*, *sarīsṛpatam*, *varīvṛjat*, *marmṛjya*, and *aganīgan* are also [formed with reduplication]. 7.4.65.

Regarding "from *dhārayati*": the root *ghṛṅ* meaning "to stand" is used here with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*). Regarding "or from *dhṛṅ*": this is simply another verbal base (*prakṛtyantara*). Regarding "in the case of *ślu* and *yaṅ-luk*": the term "*ślau*" is connected to both "from *dhārayati*" and "or from *dhṛṅ*"; however, the phrase "*and in the case of *yaṅ-luk*" is connected only with "or from *dhṛṅ*". Thus, the meaning is as follows: in the form *dādharti*, the suffix *ṇi* is elided and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is prescribed for *dhārayati* when *ślu* occurs; or, for *dhṛṅ*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable when *ślu* occurs.

In this context, the *parasmaipada* ending is also treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*), or rather, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is treated as an irregularity when there is the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*). In the form *dardharti*, however, there is the elision of *yaṅ*. In the alternative case, it is *dādharti*. By means of this irregularity, the absence of the lengthening that would otherwise be obtained is established; for the augment *ruk* is already established by the rule "and *ruk* and *rik* [are added] when there is elision" (*rug-rikau ca luki*). But in the case of the elision of *ślu*, even *ruk* must be treated as an irregularity. In *dardharṣi*, there is the elision of *yaṅ*; in the alternative case, nothing is treated as an irregularity. *Bobhūtu*: the imperative (*loṭ*) from the stem with the elision of *yaṅ*. *Bobhavīti*: the present indicative (*laṭ*); in the alternative case, the augment *īṭ* is applied according to the rule "or *īṭ* after *yaṅ*" (*yaṅo vā*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the characteristic of the suffix": although the *ātmanepada* [voice] caused by the *ṅit* status [of a root] according to the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* is not caused by the suffix itself, nevertheless, in forms such as *lolūyate*, the *ātmanepada* occurs after a *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅanta*) because that suffix possesses the *ṅit* status; thus, the principle of "characteristic of the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) certainly applies here. Consequently, in the case of the *carkarīta* [reduplicated present], the mention of *parasmaipada* [in the rule *carkarītaṃ parasmaipadam*] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Since this *ātmanepada* is restricted only to the agent (*kartṛ*), the *ātmanepada* indeed occurs after a *yaṅluk* [intensive without the *yaṅ* suffix] in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

Regarding *karikraditi*: here, only the absence of *cut* (the elision of the final vowel) is prescribed as a *nipātana* (irregularity); however, the augment *rik* is already established by the rule "*rugrikau ca*". And so, "of this" (*tathā cāsyeti*) refers to the explanation in the Brāhmaṇa of this mantra-word which was not [previously] connected.

Regarding *bharibhraditi*: here too, only the absence of *jaśtva* (the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop) is prescribed as a *nipātana*. Regarding the form in the nominative plural (*jasi*): there is a prohibition of the *num* augment by the rule "*nābhyastācchatuḥ*" ("there is no *num* after a reduplicated stem followed by *śatṛ*").
The substitution of *urat* occurs [in place of the final vowel and following consonant of a verbal root ending in *ṛ*, before an affix beginning with a vowel]. 7.4.66.

In forms such as *vavṛte*, once *halādiśeṣaḥ* has been applied, the state of having an *ṛ*-vowel at the end arises, and then the substitution of *at* (by *ata ādeḥ*) occurs; then, when *raparatvam* (the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*) takes place, *halādiśeṣaḥ* applies again.

Regarding forms such as *narnarti*, one might suspect that since the state of having an *ṛ*-vowel at the end no longer exists once the *rugādi* substitutions have been applied, the substitution of *at* would not occur; anticipating this objection, he says: "In *narnarti* etc. He will explain later, under the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*, how obstructive operations do not obstruct the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
There is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) for the roots *dyuti* and *svāpi*.

Regarding *vididyute*: the root *dyut* in the sense of "shining" is anudātta. Regarding *vyadidyutat*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) from the causative (*ṇyanta*), with reduplication (*dvirvacana*) due to the *caṅ* suffix. Regarding *vididyotiṣate* and *vididyutiṣate*: there is an option for the *san* suffix to be *kit* by the rule *ralo vyupadhāt*.

"The root *svāpi* is understood as that which ends in *ṇi*. This means there is a reference to that which ends in the *ṇic* affix added to the root *svap*. Consequently, this does not apply to the root *svāpi* that results when *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he causes sleep" (*svāpaṃ karoti*). Furthermore, this is understood because when "svāpi" is stated, it is that very [root with *ṇic*] that is first perceived. By this very rule, the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is established for the reduplication of the root itself when it is not ending in *ṇic*.

For instance: in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, when it is *kit*, reduplication occurs of that which has already undergone *samprasāraṇa* according to the rule "of *vac*, *svap*, *yaj*, and so on, before a *kit*"; even when not *kit*, there is *samprasāraṇa* of the reduplicated syllable according to the rule "of both classes of roots before the *liṭ*"; in the case of the desiderative (*san*), it is only *kit* according to the rule "of *rud*, *vid*, *mush*, *grah*, and *svap*"; and in the case of the intensive (*yaṅ*), reduplication occurs of that which has already undergone *samprasāraṇa* according to the rule "of *svap*, *śyas*, and *vyen* before the *yaṅ*."

Furthermore, although the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is not obtained by any [rule] when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), nevertheless, the form *svāpeḥ* is used precisely because of that specific mention, which indicates the inclusion of the causative (*ṇyanta*) stem. Regarding the phrase "of that," etc.: here, by means of the reduplicated syllable, the affix (*pratyaya*) which is its own cause is brought into proximity; by that, the base (*aṅga*) is qualified as follows: "that which is the base of *svāpi* when there is an affix caused by the reduplication."

In the case of *sisvāpayiṣati*, the suffix *san* which is the cause of reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is not an *aṅga* (stem) for the root *svāpi*; and that suffix (*ṇvul*) for which *svāpi* is an *aṅga* is not the cause of the reduplication. But as for *dyuti*—in *vyadidyutat*, although the *caṅ* which is the cause of the reduplication is separated from it by the *ṇic*, nevertheless, *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) is desired.
How is this discrepancy between the two [roots] mentioned in the *dvandva* compound obtained?
Therefore, we consider that this must indeed be explicitly stated.
It must be considered whether or not there is vocalization (prasāraṇa) of the reduplication in the desiderative (*sani*) of the root *dyut*.
[The rule] *vyatho liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.4.68) [applies].

Regarding the form *vivyathe*: the root *vyatha* (meaning "fear" and "trembling") is *anudātta*. Here, one might raise the objection that once the *yakāra* has been eliminated by the rule *halādiśeṣaḥ*, there would be the contingency of *prasāraṇa* for the *vakāra*; anticipating this, he says: "of the *yakāra*.
In this context, the word *vyathaḥ* should have been stated immediately after [the rule] *liṭy abhyāsasyobhayeṣām*; however, it was not done in that manner.
The long vowel [is substituted] for the root √i before an affix beginning with a kit suffix.

Regarding the statement "when the substitution of *yaṇ* has been made": this is because [the rule for] *sthānivadbhāva* (treating the substitute as the original) takes precedence. The *sthānivadbhāva* is governed by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* ("in the case of reduplication, when followed by a vowel"). Thus, in the forms *iyāya* and *iyayitha*, once the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions have been applied in the suffixes *ṇal* and *thal*, reduplication occurs due to *sthānivadbhāva*, and the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs according to the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*.
7.4.70. From this point [onward, the following rule applies].

Because of the mention of *ādeḥ* ("of the first [sound]"), the rule of "specification by the final letter" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply here; *liṭi* ("in the *liṭ* [perfect]") is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*), but the mention of *kit* ("before a *kit* suffix") has ceased. When *pararūpa* ("substitution of the subsequent form") would apply by the rule *ato guṇe*, this [rule for] lengthening is commenced. Why is the *tapara* (the *ṛ* with a following *p*) used? So that it does not apply to a long vowel—for example, from the root *ā-chi* in the sense of "stretching": *āccha*, *āñchatuḥ*, *āñchuḥ*. Furthermore, what would happen if there were lengthening here? The augment *nuṭ* would be improperly applied by the rule *tasmānnuḍ dvihalaḥ*.

Even though *ad* would still result here even if shortening were applied, nevertheless, by virtue of the inclusion of the *t* in *tapara*, it is understood as "that which is *at* [the vowel *a*] followed by *e*," whereby the naturally occurring single-mora (*mātrika*) vowel is accepted.
Therefore, *nuṭ* is inserted after a word ending in two consonants. (Pāṇini 7.4.71)

Regarding *ānaṅga*: the roots *agi*, *ragi*, and *lagi* have the meaning "to go. Regarding *ānañja*: the root *āñjū* has the meanings "manifestation," "smearing," "beauty," and "going. The mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihal*) is an indicator for "having more than one consonant"; therefore, in the case of *anarcha*, even though there are three consonants once the *guṇa* substitution and the insertion of *r* (*rapara*) have been applied, the rule still holds. In the rule *ai-au-c*, it was stated that "among phonemes, those which are parts of a phoneme and have the same form as other phonemes do not undergo that [specific] grammatical operation," and it was further stated that "in the case of the prescription of the augment *nuṭ*, the substitution of *l* (*lādeśa*), and *vināma*, an exception must be made regarding the phoneme *ṛ*. Now, having reached that occasion, he provides an exception regarding the prescription of *nuṭ*: "a part of the phoneme *ṛ*" and so forth.

In this context, the mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihal*) need not be made; let it simply be "after that, *nuṭ* [is added]. If this were stated, would it not also apply to *āṭatuḥ* and *āṭuḥ*? The rule "*aśnoteśca*" (and after *aś*) will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), meaning: "if [the root] has two consonants, then only after *aś* [does *nuṭ* apply]. To exclude *aśnāti*, one might instead have said "not after *aśna*. Since the desired result is established even without the mention of "having two consonants," the very reason he includes the mention of "having two consonants" is this: so that it may also apply to those forms that merely resemble having two consonants.
The affix *ara* is applied after the root *bhū*.

This [rule] is not stated immediately after "urat" for the sake of depending upon [the condition] "liṭi" (in the case of the *liṭ* suffix). If, however, that were stated right here [after "urat"], it would not be possible; for it would apply only to *liṭ*. The mention by means of "śtip" is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of *yaṅ*).
The word *sasūva* is used in the Vedic scriptures (*nigama*). 7.4.74.
This should be recited only among the words beginning with *dādharti*.
The reduplication of the three roots ending in *ṇi* takes the augment *guṇa* when the suffix *ślau* follows.
*Nijir*, *vijir*, and *viṣlṛ*—these three [roots] belong to the *juhotyādi* class in the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*).

The mention of these three is for the sake of what follows. [This is so that] by the rule "the *it* [augment] is applied to the roots *bhṛ*, etc. (*bhṛñām it*), the *it*-strengthening may apply to these three alone. Now, why does it not also apply here [to the present context]? To this he says: "For of these... (*eṣāṃ hi*). If, then, the mention of the triad must be made for the sake of what follows, let that be so; but could the formation of the *vṛt* (section) be omitted at the end of *nijir*? True; yet it has indeed been done.

The mention of *guṇa* is for the purpose of bringing the *ik-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the substitution of *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*) into effect; therefore, once *halādi-śeṣa* has been applied, the *guṇa* substitution takes place. Otherwise, as an exception (*apavāda*) to that, only the vowel *e* would result from *hal*. Now, if one were to rely on the principle that "in the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), an exception does not supersede a general rule (*utsarga*)," then the mention of *guṇa* is for the sake of clarity.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the roots belonging to the *bhṛñ* class [is applied before the affix *liṭ*].
These roots—*bhṛñ*, *māṅ*, *ohāṅ*—beginning with *bhṛñ*, are also [included] in the context of *juhuyāt* and so forth. Regarding *mimīte*: [the substitution of] *ī* occurs by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*.
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots *ṛ*, *pṛ*, and *pṛ*. (Pāṇini 7.4.77)

Regarding the word *iyarti*: from the roots *ṛ* (to go) and *pṛ* (to protect or fill), the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs for the reduplicated syllable when followed by a vowel that is not homogenous (*asavarṇa*). This rule is intended for non-Vedic purposes (*achandaḥ*), because in Vedic literature (*chandas*), the desired form is already established by the subsequent rule.
The suffix *yat* is applied [after a word ending in *saṃ*] to form a possessive compound. || 7.4.79 ||

Regarding *yiyakṣati*: the substitution of *ṣ* for the root *yaj* occurs by the rule *braśca-ādinā ṣatvam*, and [the substitution of *k*] by *paḍhoḥ kaḥ si*. What is the purpose of the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *san-t*)? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in the case of *pāpacyateḥ san*, resulting in *pāpaciṣate*. But what is the reason that the short vowel (*hrasva*) does not occur here? Because of the force of the prescription of the long vowel (*dīrgha*). However, if it were understood as "the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) which occurs in *san*," then, since there would be no difference in terms of brevity (*lāghava*), the inclusion of the marker *t* would be superfluous.
The vowel *o* [is substituted for the final *a* of a verbal root] before a suffix beginning with *p*, *y*, *ṇ*, *j*, or *y*, provided that these letters are followed by a consonant (*apara*).

The term *puyaṇjakārāṇām* is a singular locative (*saptamyekavacana*) formed from a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). The suffix added to the compound—by the rule "after a copulative compound ending in *cu*, *ṭu*, *ṣu*, or *ha*, when it denotes a collection" (*dvandvāccudaṣahāntātsamāhāre*)—does not occur here because that rule is not mandatory (*anityatvāt*). The word *aparam* means "that after which *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, or *j* follows," i.e., "followed by a vowel" (*avarṇaparam*). Regarding the form *pipaviṣate*: the root is *pṛṅ* (meaning "to purify"). By the rule "for *smi*, *pūṅ*, *rañj*, and *vaś* before the desiderative suffix *san*" (*smipūṅrañjaśāṃ sani*), the *īṭ* augment and the substitution of *guṇa* occur. Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) according to the rule "in reduplication, [the substitute] is like the original when followed by a vowel" (*dvirvacane'ci*), the form *pū* is reduplicated. Regarding *pipāvayiṣati*: [this is derived from the causative of the same root].

From that very same [root] with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the desiderative suffix *san* is applied: *vibhāvayiṣati*. This is the desiderative *san* added to the root *bhū* with *ṇic*. *Yiyaviṣati*: from the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing," the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *sanīvantardhe*. *Yiyāvayiṣati*: the desiderative *san* is added to that very same [root] with *ṇic*. *Rirāvayiṣati*, *lilāvayiṣati*: the desiderative *san* is added to the roots *ru* and *lū* after they have been made causative (*ṇic*). *Jijāvayiṣati*: the root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root mentioned in rules such as *jucaṅkramya*.

But how [is this rule] applied to causative verbs (*ṇyantāni*), given that the reduplication of the penultimate syllable applies only when it ends in *sa*, *n*, or *y*? For once the *vṛddhi* and *āv* substitution have been performed in the causative (*ṇau*), the reduplication must apply to a stem ending in *ā*; yet no rule has been established for the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original place) of what is done in the causative, because the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is not the cause of reduplication. To this, he says: "This very [rule applies]. For without the *sthānivadbhāva* of what is done in the causative, it is impossible for *p*, *u*, *ṇ*, or *j* to be followed by a vowel (*avarṇa*).

If it is argued that [the forms] *pipakṣati* and *yiyaviṣate* are possible [by this rule], what follows from that? The inclusion of the entire class (*varga*), the inclusion of the technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*), and the inclusion of the letter *j* become meaningful. Therefore, this very statement is the proof for the aforementioned point. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated under the rule *dvirvacane 'ci*; it should be understood from that source.

Regarding *pāpaciṣate*: this counter-example is given without relying on the rule "the reduplication that occurs before *san*" (*sani yo'bhyāsaḥ*). However, if one does rely on that rule, another counter-example must be sought, if possible, such as *avatutāvayiṣati*. Here, *tu* is a verbal root (dhātu) mentioned in the sūtra *turustuśamyamaḥ*. *Juhāvayiṣati* is derived from the causative (*ṇic*) form of the root *hu* with the addition of *san*.
Or [the suffix -na] is applied after the roots *sravati*, *śṛṇoti*, *dravati*, *pravati*, *plavati*, and *cyavati*.

The root *śru* means "to hear"; others [of the same class] mean "to go. In the examples, the desiderative suffix *san* is applied after the causative (*ṇic*) forms. But how can the shortening of the vowel (*ittva*), which is prescribed when the causative suffix *ṇi* follows, occur when there is an intervention by the consonant *s*? To this he replies: "By the force of the statement" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*). By the words "in the previous rule," etc., he shows that this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) for a case where [the shortening] would otherwise not have applied.
The *guṇa* substitution occurs before the *yaṅ* affix and its elision (*yaṅluk*).

By the word *luk* here, only *yaṅ-luk* is understood, because of its proximity. Furthermore, this *guṇa* (vocalization) is prescribed for the reduplicated stem (*abhyāsa*), and a reduplication cannot occur in other types of *luk*. [The example is] *cokruśīt*. From the root *kruś* with *yaṅ-luk*, the suffix *tip* is added; by the rule *yaṅo vā*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied; and by the rule *nābhyastasyāci piti*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*).
The long vowel [is substituted] for the kit-affixes. 7.4.83.

Regarding the phrase "because it is an exception" (*apavādatvāt*): since the suffix *nuk* is introduced when the long vowel has not yet applied, it functions as an exception. Regarding the phrase "precisely because it does not end in a vowel": the intention is that, by the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) and the application of the rule *acaśca*, a long vowel is prescribed for an abhyāsa (reduplicated syllable) that ends in a vowel, as the vowel serves as a qualifier of the abhyāsa. Regarding the phrase "in the case of modifications of the abhyāsa," and so forth: the mention of "exception" (*apavāda*) is an indicator for any sublater (*bādhaka*) in general, and the mention of "general rule" (*utsarga*) is likewise an indicator for anything that is sublated (*bādhyamāna*).

In this regard, the scope for shortening (*hrasvatva*) is seen in forms such as *yayau*; the scope for lengthening (*dīrghatva*) is seen in forms such as *pāpacyate*. In cases like *ḍoḍhaukyate*, where both would apply, lengthening prevails due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratva*), not because it is an exception (*apavāda*). Similarly, the scope for the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*) is seen in forms such as *acikṣaṇat*; the scope for lengthening is seen in forms such as *adīdipat*. In cases like *acīkarat*, where both would apply, lengthening prevails due to its higher status in the order of rules.

In the case of *mīmāṃsate*, there is the contingency of lengthening (*dīrghatva*) because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) due to its being non-conditional (*anaimittika*); however, the substitution of *it* (*ittva*) is external (*bahiraṅga*), since it is prescribed for a reduplicated stem ending in *ā* when the suffix *san* follows, within the governing context of the "stem" (*aṅga*). But in the case of *ajīgaṇat*, by the maxim of "that which does not apply when another [rule] applies" (*yenanāprāptinyāya*), the substitution of *it* would prevail as an exception (*apavāda*) over the *halādiśeṣa* rule.

But here, in forms such as *apacacchatuḥ*, *apacacchuḥ*, *cacchadatuḥ*, *cacchaduḥ*, *cicchādayiṣati*, *cicchardayiṣati*, and *ceccchidyate*, because the rules for shortening (*hrasvatva*), *it*-insertion (*ittva*), and *guṇa* are of higher priority, they are applied first, and only afterwards is the augment *tuk* inserted. Therefore, one should not raise the objection that "once *tuk* has been applied, these rules do not apply. Furthermore, there is no prohibition regarding the root *ohāk* (meaning 'to abandon'), for this root is *kit* (marked with *k*), but the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is not. The letter *k* in the rule *haśca vrīhikālayoḥ* is intended to include both *hāṅ* and *hāk* in a general sense.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the verbal roots *nīj*, *vañc*, *sras*, *dhvas*, *bhraṃs*, *kas*, *pat*, *pad*, and *skand*. (Pāṇini 7.4.84)

The roots *vañc*, *kṣip*, and *pat* have the sense of "going. *Skand* has the sense of "drying," while the others have the sense of "falling away. In forms such as *vanīvacyate*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) according to the rule *aniditām*. In forms such as *vanīvañcīti*, this does not occur because the *yaṅ* suffix is elided by *lumatā lupta*; furthermore, due to the force of the explicit utterance of the long *ī* (in *vanīvacyate*), when the *nīk* augment is applied, neither *guṇa* nor *hrasva* substitution takes place.
The *nugata* augment is applied to a word ending in a nasal consonant [before the suffix *matup*].

Regarding the phrase "nug ity etad" and so forth: by what relationship is it an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicator)? To this he says: "by the *sthānin*" (the original element). What is established by its being an *upalakṣaṇa*? To this he says: "by that. [The phrase] "even when followed by a non-*jhal*" means that in cases such as *tantanyate*, when followed by a *jhal*, the *anusvāra* is already established by the rule "naścāpadāntasya jhali."

By the rule *anusvārasya yayi parasavarṇaḥ*, a *parasavarṇa* substitution would necessarily apply; however, it is desired that in some cases the *anusvāra* be heard [unchanged]. Therefore, he says: *padāntavat ca*. How is this obtained? Here, the mention of *anta* (end) need not be made, as it is established through the rule of "that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*). It is nevertheless included so that whatever property belongs to an *anusvāra* at the end of a word may also belong to this one. And thus, *anunāsikāntasya* is a separate word, while *anunāsika* has its genitive case-ending elided. As for *tetimyata iti*: the root *tim* means "to become moist."

"What is the purpose of including the *ta* (the long vowel marker)? This question arises because, since *hrasva* (short vowel) occurs everywhere [in this context], there is nothing for it to exclude. "Even of that which previously existed" (*bhūtapūrvasya api*): the sense is that otherwise, the inclusion of the *ta* would be purposeless. "It is agitated" (*bābhyasyate*): [from the root] *bhāma* in the sense of anger.
The substitution of *a* occurs for the final vowel of the verbal roots *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, *daś*, *bhañj*, *paś*, and *śam*. (Pāṇini 7.4.86)

The root *jap* (to mutter) is used in the sense of distinct speech; *jabh* and *jṛbh* (in the sense of bending the limbs); *dah* (in the sense of reducing to ashes); *daṃś* (in the sense of biting); *bhañj* (in the sense of crushing); and *paś* is a root belonging to the *sūtra* (Dhātupāṭha). In the four forms beginning with *jañjapyate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to the rule "after *lup*, *sad*, etc."; in the other case, it is applied by the general rule.
And [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after *cara* and *phala*. 7.4.87.

The root *car* has the meaning of "eating. Regarding the two roots *phal*—namely, *ñi-phalā* in the sense of "falling apart" (*viśaraṇe*) and *phal* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*niṣpattau*)—both are intended to be included. In the form *cañcūryate*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *lupa-sada*. By the subsequent sūtra, the vowel *a* is changed to *u*, and by the rule *hali ca*, lengthening occurs. The division of the yoga (the separation of rules) is for the sake of what follows.
After the letter *a*, when followed by another vowel, [the augment *ut* is inserted]. 7.4.88.

[The rule] "of the repetition" (abhyāsasya) is stated so that [the operation] does not apply to it; otherwise, by virtue of the context, there would be the contingency of applying [the rule] to that very [repetition]. [The rule] "of the final" (antyasya) is stated so that [the operation] does not apply to it. However, there is no contingency for the rule "of the substitute of what follows" (ādeḥ parasya), because there is no mention of the ablative case (pañcamī).

"Why is the *tapara* (the marker *ṛ*) used? Even though the vowel *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), the question is raised because, by virtue of internal similarity (*āntarya*), it would follow that a short [vowel] would result only for a short [vowel]. "The purpose is to prevent the *guṇa* substitution of a light penultimate syllable (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). The meaning is this: since a long vowel is not subject to this particular rule, even when another rule would apply, the resulting modification is blocked by the force of using the *tapara* marker. [Objection: "If the *guṇa* is thus prevented, would not the lengthening [prescribed] by the rule 'also before a consonant' (*hali ca*) likewise be prevented? To this he replies: "For in the case of lengthening... [and so on].
And [the suffix] *ti* [is applied after a verbal root ending in a vowel]. 7.4.89.
"By the force of the statement," because [the desired form] is already established by the preceding rule even when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*).
And [the substitution of *guṇa* for the final vowel] occurs before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *r* or *l*, provided that the root has *ṛ* or *ḷ* as its penultimate letter.

Regarding the term *ṛtvataḥ*: that which contains the vowel *ṛ* is understood only when followed by *yiṅ*, not when it possesses *ṛ* in its original instruction (*upadeśa*). Consequently, in forms such as *parīpṛcchyate*, the substitution occurs even after the semivowel *ṛ* has been changed to a vowel (*samprasāraṇa*).
And [the substitution of] *rug* and *rik* occurs when there is elision (*luk*). 7.4.91.
Regarding the statement "marmṛjyate": since the *ruk* augment prescribed for the case of elision (*luk*) would not apply when the suffix *yaṅ* is present, this rule is stated.
And after *ṛta*. 7.4.92.

"Kiratim" (the root *kṛ*): this is an elliptical expression for roots ending in the vowel *ṛ*. "Carkarītam" is the designation used by ancient grammarians for the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*). "Pacati" (he cooks): this is an elliptical expression for the present tense marker (*laṭ*); by this, forms such as "pacanti" and so on are included. The meaning is: one who would lead the root *kṛ* [into the same category] as *pacati*. Alternatively, the meaning here is: one who would lead *kirati*—that is, one who would lead it into forms identical in shape to *pacati*, leading it as if it were like *pacati* without applying the *rug*-augment and so forth. "Prāptijñaḥ" (one who knows what is applicable).

One who knows the attainment (*prāpti*) of *rug* and the other [words] according to the distinction of their respective objects is called "one who knows attainment" (*prāptijña*). Regarding the term "commenced" (*prārabdha*): "collection" (*saṃgraha*) means the act of collecting; it refers to the collection of correct words (*sādhuśabda*). He is praised by this because he has commenced [the work], thereby manifesting an excellence of fitness (*yogyatātiśaya*).

In that context, regarding the term *prāp-ti-jñam*, he explains *prāpti* as follows: "In this case, this is the *prāpti*. [He says] "by the force of the inclusion of *ta*" (*taparakaraṇasāmarthyāt*). However, if *abhyāsa* (the reduplicated syllable) were the qualifier, then the inclusion of *ta* should be explained as being for the purpose of excluding a long vowel that existed previously (*bhūtapūrva-dīrgha*). For when the primary object of exclusion is possible, it is not logical to resort to a secondary interpretation; thus, the meaning is that *ṛtaḥ* is adopted as the qualifier of the *aṅga* (the base).
A reduplicated syllable ending in a *laghu* vowel is treated as if it were heavy (*sanvat*), when followed by the suffix *caṅ*, provided that no *a*-vowel is elided.

In the rule "laghuni caṅpare," the two locative endings are in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇe*), not in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇe*); for it is impossible for a light vowel to follow immediately after a *caṅ*. [The phrase means] "when a *ṇi*-affix follows that which has a *caṅ*. But how is it understood that it refers to a *ṇi*-affix? Because nothing else can possibly follow a *caṅ*. [Objection: But surely there is the letter *m* in the word *ācacakamata*.

[Question: Is there a *v* in forms such as *asambhavat*, *adudruvat*, and *asusravat*? [Answer: In that case, the term "followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*) is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (stem)—meaning that when there is a stem followed by *caṅ*, the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of that stem undergoes the operations of *san*-lengthening (*sanvat-kārya*). Regarding the rule "when a light [vowel] is the phoneme of the root" (*laghuni dhātvakṣare*), the meaning is: "that which is light and belongs to the stem which is related to the *ṇi* (causative suffix) followed by *caṅ*. By implication, this refers to the stem ending in *ṇi*. The meaning is that the stem situated immediately after the *ṇi* is what is being referred to.

Or, it may mean that there is the inclusion of that *aṅga* which constitutes a part of the causative (*ṇyanta*) [stem]. Regarding the term *anaglopa*: it is called *anaglopa* because in it (*asmin*) no elision of *a* (*ag-lopa*) occurs. And this [term] is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the expression *caṅpare*. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: when the *caṅ* suffix follows, provided that there is no elision of *a* (*ak-lopa*) in the causative (*ṇau*). In the case of *atatakṣat*, the designation "heavy" (*guru-saṃjñā*)—due to being followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*)—sublates the designation "light" (*laghu-saṃjñā*). In the case of *ajajāgarat*, the vowel *ā* is [the heavy one]. It is "following" (*paraḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "some here" (*atra kecit*) and so forth: [the opponent objects] "But is not the letter *ga* separated from the word *jā*? To this he replies: "In all cases indeed. The meaning is that even in forms such as *acīkarat*, because there is an intervention by the letter *ka* and others, there is no immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of the light syllable; therefore, according to the authority of the rule, the *sanvadbhāva* (treatment like *san*) must occur precisely when there is such an intervention—this is their intention. He refutes this: "That is incorrect."

If, then, one does not rely on the intervention of a cluster of vowels (*varṇasaṅghāta*), [the opponent], thinking that it would likewise not be established even when there is intervention by a cluster of consonants (*vyañjanasaṅghāta*), asks: "How so? [The author replies: "Of such a kind," meaning those that are intervened by a conjunction [of consonants].

Regarding *acakamata*: by the rule "there is an addition [to the root] for the root *kam*," the substitute *caṅ* is applied to the suffix *cli*. Regarding *acakathat*: the root *katha* (meaning "in the composition of speech") belongs to the *cur*-class and ends in a short *a*; thus, by the rule "elision of *a*," the final vowel is dropped. Here, since the elision of the *a* would be considered as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), there would be no intervention [between the cause and the effect], and thus the rule would not apply; therefore, another counter-example is presented. Regarding *adadṛṣat*: by the rule "he describes that" (*tadācaṣṭe*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added, and by the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) is elided. Here, the elision concerns both a vowel (*ac*) and a consonant (*hal*), and since the rule does not apply to the elision of a mere vowel (*aca*) alone, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*.

And for this purpose, the mention of the rule "anaglope" is made [in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*] because its application prevents the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if preceded by a *san* suffix) in the form *acakathat*.

If the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were *san*) is prescribed for the reduplication when there is a light vowel following that which is the base (*aṅga*) of the *ṇi* that follows *caṅ*, then it would not apply even in the case of *avīvadat*—meaning "he caused [him] to play" (*vāditavantam prayojitavān*). Why? Because the *ṇi* that follows *caṅ* is not followed by a light vowel; it is separated from it by the preceding *ṇic*. [Objection: Once the elision (*lopa*) has been performed, there is no separation. [Response: Due to the rule that "a substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānin*) with respect to an operation concerning what precedes it" (*ajādeśaḥ pūrvavidhau sthānivadbhavati*), there is indeed still a separation because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*.

Although the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if occupying the original position) is prohibited with respect to the rule for lengthening (*dīrghavidhi*), it would nevertheless apply in the case of the *sanvadbhāva* (the treatment as if followed by *sa*). Furthermore, that *ṇi* in which the vowel is light is not "preceded by *caṅ*" (*caṅpara*), because it is separated by a second *ṇic*. Or, even if the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* were to apply, [the rule] would not apply because the stem (*aṅga*) lacks the elided portion (*aglopitvāt*). When the *vṛddhi* has been applied, there is the elision of the *ṇi*; thus, that stem does not become one lacking an elided portion (*aglopi*). Or, let it be that it lacks an elided portion (*aglopi*); for the elision of the *ṇi* occurs even before the *vṛddhi*? To this, he states the resolution: "That elision of the *ṇi* in the *ṇi*," and so forth.

The phrase "tato 'nyo 'glopaḥ" (other than that, there is no elision of *a*) means that another form [of elision] is stated as being different. For, when resorting to the general category (*jāti*), according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), since the general category of *ṇiC* has been accepted as the cause, the elision of an *a* belonging to something other than that is taken as the object of the prohibition, but not the elision of that very category of *ṇiC*. Consequently, because this elision is not based on the quality of being an "elision of *a*" (*aglopa*), the base (*aṅga*) does not become "one whose *a* is elided" (*aglopī*); thus, the treatment as if having a *san* suffix (*sannvadbhāva*) certainly occurs here. This is because roots such as *mīmā* are included here.

For in that context, since the result would already be established by the rule "acaḥ" (P. 7.4.60) followed by "abhyāsalopaśca" (P. 7.4.58), the inclusion of the word *atra* is for the purpose of delimiting the scope: [it indicates] that this [substitution] occurs only when there is a primary *san*, and not in cases where the *sanvadbhāva* applies.

"Furthermore," and so forth. By this he says the following: it is not merely the formal adoption of *san* that is the cause here; what then? Even the absence of *s* (*asbhāva*) is indicated as the object [of the rule]. And in this case, because the root undergoes the treatment of *san* (*sanvadbhāva*), the absence of *s* (*isbhāva*) does not occur; consequently, the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) also does not occur. Alternatively, the elision of the reduplicated syllable is prescribed when *san* begins with the letter *s*, not for *san* in general; therefore, since a specific [rule] is not extended by a general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*), there is an absence of elision.
A long vowel [is substituted] for a short vowel [in the case of a suffix beginning with a vowel]. Pāṇini 7.4.94.
Regarding "abribhrajat": by the rule beginning with "bhrājabhāsa-", the shortening of the penultimate vowel is optionally prohibited.
The substitution of *u* occurs for the final vowel of the roots *ut*, *smṛ*, *dṛ*, *tvar*, *prath*, *mrad*, *stṝ*, and *spaś*.

Regarding the phrase "due to the purpose of the *tapara* marker": since the substituend (*sthānin*) is short, and because a vowel being taught as a rule (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), there is no occasion for a long vowel by this [rule]. Therefore, the lengthening that would otherwise result from another grammatical rule is precluded by the inclusion of the *tapara* marker.
The vowel *ī* is also [the substitute] for a *gaṇa*. (Pāṇini 7.4.97)

The root *gaṇ* (meaning "to count") belongs to the *curādi* class and ends in a long vowel (*ā*). Because of this, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *anaglope* applies; therefore, this specific statement is made. Once the elision of the penultimate consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) and the lengthening of the vowel have been applied, the substitution of *ī* and *ā* is prescribed.

Should it not be stated here that "the elision of *pibati*" as "there is elision of the *ā* of *pibati*," with the word "and" (*ca*) implying that there is also *ī* for the reduplication? True; however, one might suspect that the term *vibhāṣā* ("optionally") would then continue to apply [to this case as well].
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the seventh chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra;
[this is] the Kāśikāvṛtti: 6.2.1 *sarvasya dve*.

Because rules such as *nityavīpsayoḥ* are expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*)—since they do not specify either the operation to be performed (*vidheya*) or the subject of that operation—and because they are marked with the svarita accent, this [section] constitutes a governing heading (*adhikāra*). Thus he says: "of the whole" (*sarvasya*) and "two" (*dve*). The meaning is: the nature of the matter consists of what is understood when "of the whole" is stated, and what is understood when "two" is stated.

Although it would be logical to take the own-form (*svarūpa*) of both [the base and the suffix] based on the rule *svaṃ rūpam*, nevertheless, because grammatical operations are prescribed with respect to the existence of the word *ac* within a reduplicated form—by the rules *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* and *nityamāmreḍite ḍāci*—that [taking the own-form] does not occur. For if one were to take the own-form of either one or both, the word *ac* could not possibly exist within a reduplicated form; likewise, the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam* would be untenable due to the absence of a "prior" and "subsequent" element.

Therefore, the term "object" (*artha*) is included. This word "all" (*sarva*) functions with respect to the entirety of a substance (*dravya*), a type (*prakāra*), or a part (*avayava*). Regarding the entirety of a substance, as in: "He gives his all" (*sarvasvaṃ dadāti*); it is understood that he gives whatever property he possesses, both what it is and how much there is. Regarding the entirety of a type, as in: "The mendicant eats all kinds of food" (*sarvānnīno bhikṣuḥ*); it is understood that he consumes food of every variety. Regarding the entirety of parts, as in: "The cloth is all burnt" (*sarvaḥ paṭo dagdhaḥ*); it is understood that the cloth is burnt in all its constituent parts.

In this case, however, because words with specific meanings such as *pary-*, etc., are employed, the [meanings of] "substance" (*dravya*) and "totality" (*kārtsnya*) are impossible. Even where something is not specifically employed, as in the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, there too the application of the entire word is established precisely because no particular [part] is excluded. Therefore, the occurrence of "totality" is understood here as referring to the totality of the parts. The meaning is that for the prefix *pari-*, two forms of the entire word occur, and no part whatsoever is excluded by the reduplication.

In this context, since "numbers up to ten denote the numbered object," and because the term *dve* (two) requires a numbered object, and given that the subject under discussion is the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the numbered object here is the form of the word. Consequently, by the rule "the genitive denotes the element in place of which [something else is substituted]," the genitive in *sarvasya* is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). The meaning is that two word-forms take the place of the entire *paryādi* [root]. This is just as in the rule *asterbhūḥ*. Thus, the view that "doubling occurs in place [of the original]" (*sthāne dvirvacanam*) is established.

However, when the utterance (*uccāraṇa*) is related to the word (*śabda*), the relationship of original and substitute (*sthānyādeśabhāva*) is not possible regarding the thing to be numbered; for if the original (*sthānin*) were a word characterized by cessation, once it has ceased, of what would there be an utterance? Therefore, with reference to the word "utterance" supplied [by implication], the genitive case in *sarvasya* is used in the sense of the object according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*; thus, two utterances of the whole, beginning with *pari*, occur—the meaning being that the whole, beginning with *pari*, is to be uttered twice. In that case, this is the position: "Reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is the double usage (*dvih-prayoga*)."

Therein, he presents the first position: "In place of every [element], two [sounds] occur. [The question is: "Which two? Since no specific distinction is mentioned, the question implies that any two whatsoever would apply. The other [proponent], relying on the *paribhāṣā* (metarule) regarding the "nearest" (*antaratama*), says: "By virtue of the word-form (*śabda*) and so forth. For words such as *akṣa* which denote the *bibhītaka* tree and the like, the proximity is by virtue of the word-form alone; for [words like] *taru*, *pādapa*, etc., it is by virtue of the meaning alone; but for the two instances of the word *pacati*, the proximity is both ways.

In that context, the mention of "both" is so that those two [the *sthānin* and the *ādeśa*] may indeed be as they are; he shows that those very two are the closest in both ways with the words "of one."

But surely, in this view, in cases such as *rājārāja*, *vāgvāk*, *liṭliṭ*, *godhuggodhuk*, *śabdaprāṭśabdaprāṭ*, *upānadupānat*, and *gaurgauḥ*, since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), *k*-substitution (*kutva*), *ḍha*-substitution (*ḍhatva*), *gha*-substitution (*ghatva*), *ṣa*-substitution (*ṣatva*), *dha*-substitution (*dhatva*), and lengthening (*dīrghatva*) [or *vṛddhi*] would be considered *asiddha*, these operations would not apply before the reduplication is performed. Since the entire complex is prescribed in place of the word (*pada*), by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, that complex alone would possess the status of a *pada*, and not its individual components; thus, the elision of *n* and so forth would not occur in the preceding part. However, in the subsequent part...

Is it not also established by virtue of being a word in a compound? But surely, elision of *n* (*nalopa*) and the like are *antaranga* (internal) operations because they depend solely on the status of being a word (*padatva*), whereas reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is *bahiranga* (external) because it depends on meanings such as distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Therefore, once those [operations] have been performed, reduplication will take place. Even so, since those [operations] remain *asiddha* (non-existent) when reduplication is to be carried out, the reduplication would apply to that which still possesses the letter *n* and so forth; consequently, due to the absence of the cause [the *n*] in the preceding member, those operations would simply not occur again, just as in the case of *aujaḍhat*, where even though the augment *āṭ* has already been applied...

Since the sounds beginning with *ḍha* are not established (*asiddha*), would there not be the hearing of only the letter *ha* in the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) of the word *hata*? This is not a fault; for he will state that "that which is *asiddha* in respect to what precedes does not apply to reduplication. Consequently, because they are either subsequent or internal (*antaraṅga*), once the elision of *na* (*nalopa*) and other operations have been performed, the reduplication will occur of that very form thus modified.

In that case, those word-level operations (*padakārya*) which do not apply before reduplication would not occur; for example: in *kiṃ-kiṃ*, there would be no optional substitution of the same following sound (*parasavarṇa*) according to the rule *vā padāntasya*; in *apacan-apacan*, there would be no insertion of *ṅamuṭ*; in *agnā-agnau*, there would be no elision of *v* (*valopa*); in *chāyā-chāyā*, there would be no optional insertion of *tug*; in *vṛkṣa-vṛkṣān*, there would be no prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *padāntasya*; and in *aje-aje*, there would be no formation of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*) according to the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati*.

Furthermore, in this case, the rule "svarito vānudātte padādau" would not apply, because the latter part [of the compound] would not be a word (*apada*); likewise, due to its status as a non-word, grammatical operations dependent upon that status would arise—such as, for example, in *aṅganā-aṅganā*, there would be the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) by the rule for *guṇa*, and in *payaḥ-payaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *s* by the rule "so 'padādau. This is the general direction of the argument. Therefore, both parts must be accepted as separate words.

This is explained as follows: if the single substitute (*ādeśa*) were such that the distinction between its parts had completely vanished, then the dual number "two" (*dve*) would be untenable. Therefore, by virtue of the expression "two," two words combined are prescribed simultaneously as the substitute in place of one word. In that case, the status of being a word (*padatva*) belongs to the aggregate both by virtue of the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) and inherently; likewise, it belongs to the individual parts as well. Thus, the grammatical operations pertaining to words will apply to both the aggregate and the individual parts.

Even so, in the case of *visaṃvisam* and *musalamusalam*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. This is not a fault; for it is not understood thus: "the *s* of the substitute. How then? It is understood as: "that which is the *s* belonging to the substitute. And here, since the substitute is the entire cluster [of sounds], and not merely the letter *s* for the letter *s*, the rule will not apply. In this case, however, in *nṛbhiḥ-nṛbhiḥ*, because the entire cluster constitutes a word (*pada*), the *ṇ* would undesirably follow for the *r* and *n* due to their being situated within the same word by the rule *raṣābhyām*. This too is not a fault; [because...]

In that case, the mention of *samāna* (identical) need not be made; let there simply be the word *pade* (in a word). Since it is impossible for a cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*nimittin*) to reside in different words, the mention of *pada* is intended solely to express singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*), whereby the status of residing in the same word (*samānapadasthatva*) is established. Consequently, by virtue of the mention of *samāna*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs only where there is indeed residence in the same word. However, in the present instance, although there is the status of being a single word (*ekapadatva*) due to the principle of "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), in reality the substitute consists of two words and thus resides in separate words; therefore, there is no substitution of *ṇ*. Thus, the position that "doubling occurs in place [of the original]" (*sthāne dvirvacana*) is free from fault.

Now he shows the second position with the words "But when... (*yadā tu*). Regarding the phrase "it occurs twice" (*dvirāvartate*): here, "occurrence" (*āvṛtti*) refers to the operation of a word being uttered, namely the act of pronunciation; the meaning is that it is pronounced twice. "There are two occurrences" means there are two acts of pronunciation. It does not mean that there are two primary occurrences themselves, for if that were the case, it would follow that there must be a triple utterance.

Now, in this view, in the case of *āṃ pacasi pacasi devadatta*, because the singularity of its own substratum (*svāśraya*) is set aside by the number two based on the distinction of repetitions, there would be an absence of "single-interval" (*ekāntara*) status; consequently, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *āma ekāntaram* would not apply. This is just as in examples such as *kiriṇā*, where, although the status of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) of its own substratum is set aside by the state of having two syllables (*dvyactva*) based on the distinction of repetitions, the acute accent on the first syllable of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* does not occur. It is exactly like that.

In the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*), however, because the entire reduplicated form also possesses the status of a word (*padatva*) by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva*, the desired result is established; likewise, in the word *paunaḥpunyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) to the word *punaḥpunaḥ*, which denotes that which occurs repeatedly.

The forms *paunarbhavaḥ* and *paunaḥpunikaḥ* are derived from the word *punaḥ-punaḥ* with the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the rule *kālāt ṭhañ*. In this case, since the repetition of the word is understood as applying to the entire compound (*samudāya*), the compound possesses meaning by virtue of its function as a distributive (*vīpsā*) expression. Nevertheless, because the rule "the mention of compounds [in grammatical rules] refers to meaningful compounds" is a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), these are not considered nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Consequently, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix does not arise. Even under the view that suffixes are produced after words ending in case-terminations (*sup*), the suffix would still not apply because the entire compound does not end in a case-termination. However, under the alternative view (that suffixes are added to the base), both conditions are met through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), and thus the formation is established.

Even though its locus (*sthānin*) is a word ending in a *sup* suffix, nevertheless, once the *sup*-elision (*luk*) has occurred, the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) remains unprecluded. This is because, by virtue of the prohibition "not [before] *ṅi* or the vocative" (*na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), there is no application of the rule "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*) through the principle of treating the elided suffix as present (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, the following solution is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: since the meanings and forms of *pacasi* and *pacati* are identical, it is the same word *pac-* that is involved; and it is the same *tiṅ* suffix that follows. Consequently, what is prescribed after the former is also prescribed after the latter, and what is prescribed after the latter is also prescribed after the former.

And the inclusion of the word "beginning with that" (tad-ādi) continues to apply in the definition of a *pada*. In that case, although both the whole and its parts possess the status of being *tiṅ*-ending, the designation of *pada* will apply to the whole alone, just as in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*). For example, in the form *papāca*, although the whole and its parts equally consist of a single vowel (*ekāc*), reduplication occurs for the whole alone, not for the parts.

For what reason? Because it would result in the abandonment of the grammatical rule (*śāstrahāni*). For if there were a doubling of individual components, the rule would be abandoned with respect to other components as well as with respect to the whole (*samudāya*); likewise, the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) will also belong only to the whole, and thus the requirement of being separated by one intervening syllable (*ekāntaratā*) is justified. In cases such as *paunaḥpunyam*, even the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is established by the aforementioned principle, because the whole possesses the status of a "form ending in a case-suffix" (*subanta*) and the status of a "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*).

In this regard, they raise the following objection: Since the designation *pada* was already applied to the form *pacasi* prior to the doubling [of the suffix], why does it apply again even after the doubling has been performed? Or, if it does apply, why does it apply only to the entire aggregate and not to each of the two constituent parts individually? For such is not the scope of the rule regarding doubling, as stated in the discussion on the designation *saṃyoga*; for in cases such as *nirgleya*, the designation *saṃyoga* is accepted for two consonants even when three are present.

Furthermore, in cases such as *apacannapacan* and the like, where the status of being a "word" (*pada*) belongs to the aggregate alone, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the word-operations (*padakārya*) do not apply to the individual components.

Another [scholar] says: here it is only the act of utterance (*uccāraṇakriyā*) that differs; however, due to that difference, the distinction between words is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). In reality, there is only one single word, and thus the requirement of a single interval (*ekāntaratā*) is appropriate. Moreover, because the aggregate also possesses meaning through its sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) characterized by distributive iteration (*vīpsā*), it qualifies as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Nor does the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) preclude this, because they belong to different classes (*atulyajātīyatva*).
