For when there are distinct meanings that possess only a mutual relationship as an additional factor, the exclusion [of the meaning] occurs by means of that very collection of similar types. However, neither of these two conditions exists here. Indeed, the meaning of two words is not distinct, nor is their mutual relationship additional to their collection; rather, what is it? It is something entirely different, consisting of the nature of *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution).

If this is so, then in cases such as *kiriṇā*, would there not be the accent of the case-ending according to the rule *sāvekācastṛtīyādiḥ*? For even there, it is only the act of pronunciation that differs; in reality, however, the vowel *i* is one and the same. Furthermore, since for eternal and all-pervading phonemes (*varṇas*) and for words (*padās*) consisting of them, neither separation nor non-separation is possible in their own nature, one must rely on these properties as residing solely in the cognition [of them].

In that case, just as there is a difference in apprehension even when there is a difference in words, so too would it be when there is no such difference; how then could there be absolute distinctness? Furthermore, if—according to the principle stated in the passage beginning with "paunaḥ-punyam"—the entire aggregate were also to possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then alas, in cases such as *grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ*, since the aggregate would likewise possess the status of a nominal stem, there would result the elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*). Therefore, we prefer the view that here there is merely reduplication in place (*sthāne dvirvacanam*).
For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti first demonstrated "reduplication in place," and subsequently showed "double usage" (*dviḥ prayogaḥ*) merely as a possibility.

In this context, the mention of the word *sarvasya* (of all) may be intended either to exclude the final [phoneme] or to establish the sense of the genitive case. Now, regarding the view that there is substitution (*sthāna*) by doubling (*dvirvacana*), there must be two substitutes that are most similar (*antaratama*) both phonetically and semantically. And those elements of such a nature are necessarily of a multi-phonemic (*anekāl*) character; thus, even without the inclusion of the word *sarva*, the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* will ensure that the operation applies to the whole.

The sense of the genitive case is established in instances such as "parervarjane," where the genitive is explicitly uttered. Even in cases where the genitive is not present—such as in the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ"—it is obtained through the force of the context: that is, "of the word which [expresses] frequency or distributive repetition, there is a doubling. In the view that there is a double utterance, however, there is no possibility at all of applying the rule regarding the final letter (Pāṇini 1.1.52); for there is no genitive denoting the "place" (sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī). Furthermore, the sense of the genitive is indeed obtained, because the act of utterance is a property of the word.

Therefore, with the intention that [the rule] applies by means of the inclusion of "all," the Master asks: "What is the purpose of 'of all'? He says: "For the sake of clarity. The meaning is: for the sake of easy comprehension for one who is unable to understand it in this way, the word "of all" is stated. Regarding "Now," etc.: he thinks as follows—[the word] "of a word" (*padasya*) must necessarily be stated in order to exclude compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and sentences.

First, regarding the purpose of excluding compounds: in the case of *saptaparṇaḥ* and *aṣṭāpadam*, it is the seven leaves (*sapta-saṃkhyāni parṇāni*) that are distributed [over the parts], and not the tree possessing them. Since unity is not included within distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there would have been the undesirable consequence of the dual number even before the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is applied. However, this does not occur because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning "words" (*pada*).

Regarding *taddhita* [derivatives]: in the example *dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two paces"), the object associated with the number two is intended to be distributive (*vīpsā*). Since the gender (femininity) and number (singularity) are not included within the [meaning of the] *taddhita* suffix itself, reduplication—which would otherwise apply once the compound has been formed prior to the arising of the *taddhita*—does not occur because the resulting form lacks the status of being a "word" (*pada*). Regarding a sentence: in *grāmegrāme pānīyam* ("water in every village"), reduplication does not occur because a sentence is not a word, as in the case of *grāme pānīyam*. Furthermore, it need not be stated later that [the rule applies to] a "word" (*pada*).

Regarding the phrase "from the word *pada*," this refers to its very recurrence [in the rule]. It cannot be maintained that way. His intention here is as follows: even if the term "*pada*" were stated, in examples such as *saptaparṇābhyām*, there would be the undesirable consequence of doubling because the preceding element would possess the status of a *pada* due to the suffixes beginning with *su*; therefore, the resolution must be stated in this way: that which is joined with repetition (*vīpsā*) is not employed in this context.

What, then, is that [example]? It is "saptaparṇo vṛkṣaḥ" (the seven-leaved tree), where the word *parṇa* occurs in the sense that "it has seven leaves on every joint (*parvaṇi-parvaṇi*). And that which is employed there is not connected with repetition (*vīpsā*)—namely, the word *parṇa* in the expression "it has seven leaves. However, in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), there is no doubling because the meaning is already expressed by the derivative suffix itself; for that suffix is prescribed "in the sense of repetition. Furthermore, doubling of a sentence does not occur either, because repetition is already expressed by the doubling of the individual words. Therefore, the governing rule for "word" (*pada-adhikāra*) need not be established for the purpose of excluding compounds and the like.

On the contrary, he states that if the status of being a *pada* (word) were applied [to the whole], there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), saying: "In this case, it would not occur," namely, in the form *prapacati*. Here, the combination of root and prefix (*dhātūpasarga-samudāya*) expresses a specific action. However, the separate conceptualization of the root and the prefix is for the sake of establishing the application of the augment *aṭ* and other such elements; consequently, since the property of permanence (*nityatā*) belongs to the action as a whole, reduplication applies to that very whole. Regarding the phrase "in this case" (*ihetyādi*): when the suffix *tṛc* is prescribed after the root *druh*, both the substitution of *gh* for *h* and the substitution of *ḍh* for *h*—according to the rule *vā druhamuhaḥ*—as well as reduplication, would apply.

In that case, since both *ghatva* (the substitution of *gh*) and *ḍhatva* (the substitution of *ḍh*) are not established [simultaneously], the doubling (*dvirvacana*) would first apply. Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). When the optional rule (*vikalpa*) subsequently operates, if *ḍhatva* occurs in the latter instance, then by the absence of a restrictive rule (*niyamābhāvāt*), *ghatva* might also occasionally occur in the former instance. The same should be understood regarding *ghatva*: that *ghatva* occurs in the latter instance while *ḍhatva* occurs in the former.

And this statement—that the usage established for one *ākṛti* does not apply to a second or a third—should be understood as being made without relying on this underlying principle (*nyāya*). Furthermore, this principle has been explained specifically in the context of the rule: "The root *kṛ* is employed after [a verb] when the periphrastic perfect suffix *liṭ* follows."

Regarding the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*: that grammatical operation such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) which occurs within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "that which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) is called *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*; that [operation] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to anything other than reduplication (*dvirvacana*). Alternatively—*pūrvatrāsiddham* refers to the elision of *n* and so forth, which are non-established within the first seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*); the state of being non-established (*asiddhatva*) residing therein is *pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*. That [state] does not apply when reduplication is to be performed; consequently, once the substitution of *gh* or *ḍh* has taken effect, the reduplication applies only to that which is already endowed with those [substitutes], and thus there is no fault.

"Of all," and so forth. Previously, *droḍhā* and *droḍhā* were established by relying on the rule "that which is not established in what precedes does not [cause] reduplication. Now, they are established by this [rule] "of all"; thus, regarding a single thing to be accomplished, there is an option between two reasons. But how is the understanding of all operations (*kārya*) obtained through the word "all" (*sarva*)? This word *sarva* ends in the suffix *ac* (the *aṇ* suffix) according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. That in which all operations exist is "all" (*sarva*); of that, there are two [occurrences]. The meaning is: when all operations have been performed, there is reduplication.
Its repetition is called *paramāmreḍita*. (Pāṇini 8.1.2)

In the expression *tasya*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a part-whole relationship (*avayavayoga*), and the word *para* denotes a part. Although in the rule *dikśabdāñcūttarapada* ("after words denoting direction, when followed by *añcu* as the final member of a compound"), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is prescribed because a "direction-word" (*dikśabda*) is defined as "a word seen to denote a direction"—and thus [the word *para*] is not currently a direction-word—the present grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) itself establishes that the genitive case occurs in connection with words denoting parts. In this way, forms such as *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body") are established. In the example provided, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied according to the rule *āmreḍitaṃ bhartsane* ("the reduplicated form is used in the sense of reproach").

Its mention is for the purpose of defining the scope: "of this very one just mentioned, which has been stated twice. Therefore, this technical designation does not apply to the sixth [type of] reduplication. Now, it may be objected that the word *āmreḍita* is well-known in the *nighaṇṭus* in the sense that "that which is repeated twice or thrice is called *āmreḍita*. True, it is well-known in that sense; however, here it is being defined as a technical term (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the word itself.
This creation of a major technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is in accordance with the tradition of the ancient teachers.
And [the final vowel] is also unaccented (anudātta). 8.1.3.

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "param" (other), and because that [word] consists of a collection of vowels and consonants (*ajjhal-samudāya*), the term "anudātta" here has the sense of "other"—that is, "anudātta" means that in which an acute accent (*udātta*) does not exist. Since an circumflex accent (*svarita*) also contains an acute accent, it too is excluded. Even so, it is not known by which accent the *āmreḍita* (the repeated portion) should be uttered. It is said in reply: since the acute and circumflex accents have been prohibited, and the utterance of a vowel (*ac*) without any accent is impossible, then by the principle of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), it must necessarily be anudātta.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "that which has an anudātta vowel is anudātta"; that is, the vowels of the *āmreḍita* (reduplicated) portion become anudātta. In the example *bhuṅkta-bhuṅkta*: the form *bhuṅkte* is derived from the root *bhuj* with the Ātmanepada suffix due to the rule *bhujo'navane*. Its [the *te* suffix's] anudātta nature follows from the rule *tāsyanudāttet*. The *śna* augment takes the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). When the *a* of *śna* and *as* is elided by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, the resulting word *bhuṅkte* becomes oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule *udāttanivṛttisvara*. Through reduplication, the subsequent [portion] becomes anudātta. The word *paśu* ends in the *ku*-suffix and is thus oxytone.
The double application [of a word] occurs in the sense of continuity and distributive repetition. Pāṇini 8.1.4.

"Regarding that which occurs in the sense of the eternal (*nitya*) and in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). By this, he shows that the locative case here is for the purpose of indicating the meaning [of the suffix]. Repetition is a property of the speaker, and it is not denoted by words such as "village" (*grāma*). Even in the case of *pacati-pacati* ("he cooks repeatedly"), that which is eternal in reality is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); rather, eternality is manifested by the reduplication (*dvirvacana*).

Therefore, this is the meaning here: [the rule applies] when *nityatva* (permanence) is the object as that which is to be indicated (*dyotya*), or when *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) is the object as that which is to be indicated. And this alone is the function (*vṛtti*) in that case: that the word has as its domain that which possesses the quality (*vattā*). If, however, this were a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the rule would apply to all forms (*sarvarūpavidhi*), and consequently, the grammatical indications such as "always in the sense of play and livelihood" (*nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ*) and "of a hundred or a number, etc., in the sense of repetition" (*pādaśatasya saṃkhyādervīpsāyām*) would not be tenable.

If, however, it were said that "the word whose object is an eternal thing is eternal," and that "the distributive [word] is that whose object is a distributive sense," then there would be no fault even with the genitive case. Yet, because this would entail a figurative usage, that [interpretation] is not accepted. This word "eternal" (*nitya*) is seen to be applied even to those things such as the Self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*), which persist for all time and whose production and destruction are not perceived by speakers—for example: "the Self is eternal," "space is eternal," and "the sky is eternal."

Even in the case of frequency—as in "constantly laughing" (*nityaṃ prahasitaḥ*) or "constantly talking" (*nityaṃ prajalpitaḥ*)—since there is no distinction [in the rule] and both meanings would be included, one might think that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubling even words such as *ākāśa* (ether) and so forth; thinking thus, he asks: "In which cases does 'permanence' (*nityatā*) apply?"

Alternatively—the primary meaning of the word *nitya* is precisely that which is characterized by being unchanging (*kūṭastha*), because it does not depend on the proximity of other words; whereas frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is a secondary meaning, to be understood through the employment of a verbal form, since that term is used there by relying on the commonality of uninterrupted perception. Therefore, considering that "between the primary and the secondary meanings, the understanding [of the word] applies to the primary one," and thus concluding that only those words denoting the unchanging would undergo reduplication, he asks: "In what things is there permanence?"

The other, having understood the intention, says: "In the case of *tiṅ* [verbal endings]. Thinking that there is no distinction [between the two cases], he asks: "Why? [The answer is: "Because here [in this context] there is repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*). The intention is as follows: if the term were taken to mean "unchanging" (*kūṭastha*), then verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) would not be included; however, if "permanence" (*nityatva*) characterized by repetition is accepted, then the doubling (*dvirvacana*) characterized by that [repetition] applies to verbal endings, while the doubling characterized by pervasion (*vīpsā*) applies to nominal endings (*subanta*), and thus both are accommodated.

Even a secondary (gauṇa) meaning is resorted to here on the strength of observing the intended sense—as in examples such as *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi* ("acting despite cold and heat") and *pārśvenānvicchatī* ("searching by the side"). If both types of "constancy" (*nityatva*) were accepted, then the reduplication of nouns ending in case-suffixes expressing those meanings would apply only to their own primary sense; yet such usage does not exist in common worldly practice—for instance, one does not say *ātmātmeti*. For when that is said, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is understood, not the primary sense itself. Therefore, only "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is to be understood; thus, in this context, constancy is frequency.

And that [frequency] occurs in the case of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), and primary derivatives (*kṛt*). From what is this true? He says: "Frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is a property of action (*kriyā*). Repetition is frequency. And that is possible only for an action whose nature is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); however, the repeated performance of things of that same class is also possible in the case of jars and the like. Nevertheless, the cognition is that "it is performed again" only with respect to an action.

Furthermore, words such as *ābhīkṣṇya* (repetition), *nitya* (constancy), and so forth, which denote those [states] repeatedly, are like words such as *yugapat* (simultaneously) and *pṛthak* (separately), which have action as their object. And while action is expressed by verbal suffixes (*taṅ*) and primary suffixes (*kṛt*), in words such as *pācaka* (cook), the means (*sādhana*) is predominant. Even in cases such as *pāka* (cooking), it is the state of being accomplished (*siddhatā*) that is predominant, not the action.

What, then, is that action whose property is frequency? He says: "the action which... and "that is constant. Because the word *nitya* is neuter, the pronoun *tat* referring to it is also neuter, just as in the rule *aṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartā*, where [the gender] is masculine. [Examples: *lunīhi-lunīhi* ("cut—cut!"). [This is] the imperative (*loṭ*) used for the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*).

Although an example for a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) has already been shown, this is introduced again because there is something further to be said; he demonstrates this with the words: "of *ktvā*, *ṇamul*, and the imperative (*loṭ*). Since *ktvā* and *ṇamul* are prescribed even in other senses by rules such as "when two actions have the same agent" (*samānakartṛkayoḥ*), and the imperative (*loṭ*) is also prescribed in other senses such as injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth, these suffixes—being general terms—reveal repetition only when they depend on reduplication. However, the *yaṅ* suffix does not depend on that [reduplication].

For that [intensive suffix *yaṅ*] never deviates from the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*); so why should it depend on reduplication (*dvirvacana*) to indicate that? But surely, reduplication is also sometimes desired for forms ending in *yaṅ*; how is that so? To this he says: "But when... For the repetition of an action is of two kinds: frequency (*paunaḥpunyam*) and intensity (*bhṛśārtha*).

In this context, when there is reduplication, it occurs through the suffix *yaṅ* in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*). The meaning is that the reduplication serves to indicate the repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) of that very action, because that repetition has not already been indicated by the *yaṅ*. Furthermore, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), even though the word *kriyāsamabhihāra* is a general term, its application (*vṛtti*) should be understood as referring specifically to "intensity" (*bhṛśārtha*) characterized as the repetition of action. As for the example *pāpacyate*: the meaning is that he cooks again and again, performing all the constituent actions of cooking by himself.

The imperative (*loṭ*) also occurs—as in "pāpacyasva pāpacyasva" (boil, boil!), which results in "pāpacyate" (he boils repeatedly). Now, if reduplication were prescribed for the state of being eternal (*nityatā*), why does it not apply to the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone, since that indeed expresses action? It is said in reply: action becomes useful for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) only when its means (*sādhana*) are grasped; therefore, because it denotes that [action], reduplication does not occur for the mere root. Alternatively, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the word (*pada*) must be relied upon.

With this very intention, it was previously stated: "Why is it not simply said, 'of the word' (*padasya*)? On this view, reduplication must indeed be prescribed for that which includes the prefix (*sagatika*). By this, the following argument is also refuted: "The *yaṅ* affix, which has scope in the sense of intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), is superseded by the subsequent reduplication [of the word] in the sense of repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). How is this refuted? It has been explained that while the reduplication of the word applies to the entire base, the *yaṅ* affix applies to the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, it is not proper for the internal (*antaraṅga*) [element, the *yaṅ*] to be superseded.

Intending to explain *nitya* (perpetual) as *vīpsā* (repetition), he first asks about its scope with the word "atha" (now). [He says] "in the case of *sup* suffixes, there is repetition," because only those *sup* suffixes are capable of manifesting it. Having thus stated the scope, he asks about its essential nature: "What, then, is it? If repetition were simply the desire to pervade in a general sense, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubling in cases such as *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do"), because the desire to pervade the mat and other objects by means of actions such as "doing" is manifold.

With the intention that "the other [term] is a word with both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*) and denotes repetition (*vīpsā*)," he says: "having as its object a specific pervasion (*vyāptiviśeṣaviṣaya*). Regarding the phrase "by the speaker's intention": by this, it is shown that repetition is not taken here as the denoted meaning—namely, that "there are two forms of a word expressive of repetition"—but rather it is a property of the speaker, like the [intentional] affliction. When one says "gone-gone" (*gatagata*), it is understood that the speaker utters the sentence because they are distressed by the long absence of a loved one; thus, he demonstrates that reduplication occurs in cases such as *cikīrṣati*.

It was stated that [the repetition] has as its object a specific pervasion (*vyāpti-viśeṣa*), but since that specific [pervasion] has not yet been explained, he asks again: "What, then, is this? [The author replies with the verse beginning] "Of words denoting various things," and so forth. The definition of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) was recited previously; he now explains it: "Of those denoting various entities" (*nānābhūtārthavācinām*). Because of the expression "denoting various things" (*nānāvācinām*) therein, there is no doubling for words denoting a genus (*jāti*); for example, *brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ* ("A Brahmin must not be killed") and *sampanno vrīhiḥ* ("The rice is abundant"). For words denoting a genus do not denote various distinct entities, because a genus is a single entity.

Because they are apprehended simultaneously, there is no doubling [of a word] when a sequential intention is intended. For example, in the case of sequentially establishing the beauty [of trees] by saying, "In this forest, this tree is beautiful, this tree is beautiful," even though many words are employed, a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) does not occur—such as "In this forest, the trees are beautiful"—because there is an absence of expressing multiple distinct referents. Indeed, expressing multiple distinct referents consists in having separate terminations for individual meanings, and that is not present in the case of *ekaśeṣa*.

For this very reason, in that case, a connection with the thing to be enjoined is not necessarily perceived for each individual. For when it is said, "A hundred should be given to the Brahmins," it does not follow as a rule that a hundred must be given to each one. However, when it is said, "A hundred should be given to every Brahmin," a hundred is given to each; why is that? Because, since the meaning terminates separately for each, there is a connection with a separate gift for each.

And when there is a determination of distinct meanings, then as many words as there are meanings intended to be expressed, that many words would each individually result in a separate meaning; this [rule] effects their exclusion—namely, that in the case of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), only two should be employed, and not many. But how is the meaning of those [words] excluded understood, since if there were a determination of individual meanings, there would be comprehension of only two? It is said:
just as in the case of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one), the meaning of the others is understood through the retained one.
Similarly, here too, even though there is a distinction, the cognition of the other meaning arises from the two remaining [words].

For just as in the case of the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation "tree" from "tree and tree," the single remaining word expresses the meaning even of those [words] that have ceased [to be uttered], so too here, the two words being retained will express the intended meanings. Nor does there follow the contingency of a plural number, because many things whose singularity has been grasped are being denoted.

Otherwise, because a separate relationship is not perceived, even if plurality is understood after the dual ending has occurred, there would be an absence of the plural suffix due to the lack of *prātipadika* status; just as in the expression "Look, the deer runs," although there is an objecthood (*karmatva*) relative to the act of seeing, the accusative case does not occur.

In the case of *ekaikam*, however, although it possesses the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) due to the application of the rule for treating it as a *bahuvrīhi*, the singular number occurs rather than the plural; this is because the single referent (*ekārtha*) whose unity has been grasped cannot be connected with distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), and thus the singular is more internal (*antaraṅga*). The plural is excluded because the cognition of plurality is external (*bahiraṅga*). The indication (*liṅga*) for this very point is the grammatical rule: *ekaikasya prācām*. Enough of this.

This is the meaning here: *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) is the desire to pervade, by means of either an action (*kriyā*) or a quality (*guṇa*), each of those substrates (*adhikaraṇa*) denoted by words expressing various distinct objects, which are intended to be expressed together and are associated with their respective individual numbers. The mention of "action" and "quality" is also an indication for "substance" (*dravya*). Examples: *grāme grāme pānīyam* ("water in every village")—this is an example of the pervasion of a substance. *puruṣaḥ puruṣo nidhanam upaiti* ("every man meets his end")—here *nidhana* means death; the sense is that for one who is born, death is certain.

Another says: "The specific division (*bhakti*) of the *sāman* chants is the *nidhana*; the meaning is that all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) arrive at the *nidhana*. Regarding the phrase "that which ends in a verbal suffix" (*tiṅanta*), and so forth: here, the reason is a conflict of rules (*vipratiṣedha*). The scope for reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is where constant repetition (*nityatā*) is intended to be expressed, not intensity (*prakarṣa*)—as in *pacati-pacati*. The scope for the suffix of intensity (*prakarṣapratyaya*) is where only intensity is intended to be expressed, not constant repetition—as in *pacatitarām*. When both are intended and both [rules] would apply, reduplication occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Then, by the principle of "re-occurrence" (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*), the suffix of intensity is applied.

Alternatively—excellence (*prakarpa*) which depends on a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is "external" (*bahiraṅga*), whereas repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) is "internal" (*antaraṅga*); thus, the doubling [of the suffix] occurs first. As for the passage beginning with "But here," etc., this is simply a desired conclusion (*iṣṭi*). Or rather—since only those who are rich and so forth when endowed with excellence are employed in the act of bringing, it is only those possessing light (or slight) excellence that are intended to be repeated. Furthermore, if the suffix *tarap* were applied after the doubling has occurred, the form would have to be *āḍhyātara*, and in that case, the sense of excellence would be understood, not repetition; therefore, the connection with excellence occurs first.
In the case of excluding a person, [the suffix *niṣ* is used]. 8.1.5.

Regarding *pari trigartebhyaḥ*: by the rule *apaparī varjane*, *pari* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya*, and by the rule *pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed. Regarding *pariṣiñcati*: here *pari* signifies "on all sides" (*sarvato bhāve*), and the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti* and so forth. Regarding *parervarjane* and so on: in the rule *parervarjane*, it should be stated that this applies when there is no compound (*asamāse*), and it should also be stated that it is optional (*vā*). Consequently, it occurs only when there is no compound, and even then, only when [the word] follows immediately (*visaplena*).

But in other cases, it does not occur at all; thus he says: "But in a compound," etc. [The reason is] "because it has already been expressed by that. Now, one might object: in a sentence (*vākya*), the exclusion is indeed indicated by the prefix *pari-* alone, and in a compound (*samāsa*) as well, *pari-* is present; so why should the power to express exclusion be attributed to the compound itself? To this they reply: according to the view that "the compound operates by abandoning its own meaning" (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), it is the compound itself that functions in the sense of exclusion, with the excluded element as its subordinate member (*upasarjana*), while the two constituent parts (*avayava*) are themselves devoid of meaning.

However, when the position is that "the compound formation does not abandon its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), then in the case of a simple sentence, the prefix *pari* occurs in the sense of exclusion; therefore, reduplication takes place only there. In a compound, however, because *pari* encompasses the meaning of the object being excluded, it does not denote exclusion alone; thus, there is an absence of reduplication.
The particle *prasamupodaḥ* is used for the purpose of completing the meter. || 8.1.6 ||

The term *prādīnām* is a collective *dvandva* compound; however, the suffix prescribed by the rule *dvandvāccudaṣahāntātsamāhāre* does not apply here, because the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not invariably obligatory. As for the example cited in some places, *udittham jātavedasam*, that is incorrect; for there is no second word *ut* here, but rather the word *u*.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini 8.1.7: *uparyadhyadhasaḥ sāmīpye*.

The doubling [of words] such as *upari* serves to indicate proximity (*sāmīpya*) to that which is their meaning. Proximity means nearness; and that is either spatial or temporal. *Uparyupari duḥkham* ("above, above suffering") is an example of the temporal kind. The meaning is "above," in the sense of being proximate to suffering. The accusative case is used by virtue of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "for *ubha* and *sarvatas*. *Uparyupari grāmam* ("above, above the village") means a location above, in the vicinity of the village. *Adhyadhi grāmam* ("upon, upon the village").

The term *adhi* denotes the sense of "above" (*uparibhāve*), as in: "Having brought the fuel and the ladle over and over the *gārhapatya* fire. It also denotes "below" (*adhas*), as in "below the village" (*adho'dho grāmam*). This means a place situated beneath the village in its vicinity; for example: "Beholding the ever-new, vast breasts below [the clouds]. "Everyone becomes impoverished while looking upward; whose majesty does not arise when looking downward?"

The doubling [of the word] here is for the sake of repetition (*vīpsā*). Regarding "the moon is above" (*upari candramāḥ*): in this case, there is no proximity of the state of being "above" relative to something situated on the earth. Regarding "above the head" (*upari śirasaḥ*) and so forth: the actual existence of an object is not the primary cause for the production of such a word; what then? It is the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), and that is not present here. For what is intended here is that "he holds a pot above the head, not below"; whereas proximity, however, is possible in terms of the actual object.
The first word of a sentence that is an address (āmantrita) retains its original accent when expressing envy, approval, anger, contempt, or threat. Pāṇini 8.1.8.

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words having a single meaning. As the venerable Jaimini stated: "Because of the unity of purpose, there is a single sentence, provided that if it were divided, the parts would remain syntactically expectant. In some places, however, it is read as: "A sentence is a collection of words containing a single finite verb (*tiṅ*)," where *ekatiṅ* means that in which there is one finite verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*). In other instances, no definition of a sentence is given at all; rather, it is said: "If it [the collection of words] occurs in cases of envy, salutation, anger, censure, or threat, it constitutes a sentence."

Although the word "vākya" (sentence) is subordinate within the compound *vākyādeḥ*, nevertheless, the connection with envy (*asūyā*) and the others is established through that very term—as in "the sentence and so forth which [occur] in envy and the rest"—and not by means of the principal element, the vocative (*āmantrita*). For envy and the like are attributes of the speaker (*prayoktṛdharma*), not attributes of the signified object (*abhidheyadharma*); and these are manifested by the sentence itself, not by the vocative. In the examples, the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of "consent" (*sammati*) and "pity" (*anukampā*), while elsewhere, in the sense of "contempt" (*kutsita*), the suffix *ka* is used. "Rikta" means empty; its meaning is "mean" (*kṣudra*).

The suffix *ka* is applied after the words *śakti* and *yaṣṭi* when they refer to women possessing those objects, provided they are used in a derogatory sense (*kutsita*). For in this way, both the expression of contempt and the address become appropriate. Regarding the phrase "but in the case of reproach" (*bhartsane tu*), etc.: although by the rule "in the alternative to reproach" (*bhartsane paryāyeṇa*), the [suffix] prescribed for the preceding [word] is established there even for reproach and contempt—since anger and envy exist there as well due to being the cause of it—is there not, therefore, no purpose in mentioning both "contempt" (*kutsana*) and "reproach" (*bhartsana*)?
This is not so; for teachers, because they desire one's welfare, may engage in reproach even when they are not angry.
But when they are being reviled, they respond with anger toward those who provoke them.
The author of the Sūtras, who perceives with subtle insight, has provided a separate enumeration of these two, because they bring about contempt even without the presence of envy.
Teachers strike with hands moistened by nectar, not with those sprinkled with poison;
faults reside in indulgence, while virtues reside in discipline.
The meaning is that when the intention is corrupt, faults arise even from pampering; conversely, however, virtues arise even from striking.
In this way, it is like a bahuvrīhi compound. 8.1.9.

In this context, if a simple *bahuvrīhivadbhāva* (the treatment as if being a *bahuvrīhi*) were prescribed by this rule without a specified scope, then it would apply here as well—in the case of *eka*. Consequently, there would be the elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sub*). One might argue: "Let it be; another *su*-suffix will arise from the *bahuvrīhivadbhāva*. But that is not so; for the elision of the nominal suffix does not apply here, because *eka* is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*) since it ends in a suffix.

In the rule *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*, the mention of *samāsa* (compound) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), not for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*); therefore, by that [rule], there is no status as a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*). If so, would the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) not apply here in the case of *ekā*? It would indeed apply; however, because of the governing context of the word *dve* ("two"), the treatment as a bahuvrīhi compound—which is prescribed in conjunction with the doubling of the word—is absent here, and thus it does not occur.

Now, why does that same reduplication (*dvirvacana*), being prescribed by that [rule], not occur here? Therefore, its scope must be stated. To this he says: "The word-form *eka* is reduplicated. True; the term *dve* (two) is understood from the previous rule, but the reduplication is not prescribed by that [term]. What then? Having referred to the reduplication as already prescribed by another [rule], the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi*-compound (*bahuvrīhivadbhāva*) is prescribed therein. And where has the reduplication been prescribed by another? In the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).

If, however, one were to follow the mention of *vīpsā* (repetition) and thereby enjoin the application of the rule for *bahuvrīhi*-like behavior (*bahuvrīhivad-bhāva*) in that context, this would not be possible; for by the application of *bahuvrīhi*-like behavior, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is sublated. Now, if both [the mention of *vīpsā* and the word *dve*] were followed—namely, "two" (*dve*) in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*)—such that both reduplication and *bahuvrīhi*-like behavior are enjoined by this [rule], then there would be no fault. However, the author of the *Vṛtti*, asking what is the use of following the mention of *vīpsā*, has simply followed the word "two" (*dve*) alone.

Regarding "elision of the case-ending (*sublopa*) and the *puṃvadbhāva*": although these two are not explicitly stated [in the rule] as applying to a *bahuvrīhi*, nevertheless, by the principle of extension (*atideśa*), they apply here because they were observed in that context. In some places, however, this very meaning is recited directly within the rule itself. As for *ekaikam*: when the word *eka* is reduplicated, both case-endings (*sup*) are elided; then, by virtue of the *bahuvrīhi*-like treatment (*bahuvrīhivad-bhāva*), a new case-ending is introduced. As for *ekaikayā*: the third case ending is applied to a stem ending in *ṭā*; that entire form is then reduplicated. Upon the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), the *ṭāp* suffix in the first member is removed through the process of *puṃvadbhāva*.

But what is the difference here, whether the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is removed or not? There is a difference in the *avagraha*: [in the case of] *aikaikayā*, it becomes *eka-ekayā*; and later, in examples such as *gatagata*, there is the purpose of applying the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*).

Now, if every operation seen in a *bahuvrīhi* compound is extended [to the *tatpuruṣa*], then would not these rules—the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman*, accentuation, and the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*)—apply? To this he says: "the prohibition of the designation *sarvanāman*, accentuation, and the compound-final suffix. This means that the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.29], "not in a *bahuvrīhi*," does not apply here.

For in that context, while the term "in a *bahuvrīhi*" (*bahuvrīhau*) is already being carried over from the rule "optionally in a *dik-samāsa* [and] a *bahuvrīhi*" (*vibhāṣā diksamāse bahuvrīhau*), the mention of "*bahuvrīhi*" once again is intended so that the rule may apply only to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* by its very nature, and not to that which is a *bahuvrīhi* only through the application of the *bahuvrīhi*-treatment. By this, the prohibition of the technical name (*saṃjñā-pratiṣedha*) is understood to apply specifically to a *bahuvrīhi* within the governing heading on compounds (*samāsādhikāra*). Examples are *nanu* and *susu*. In these cases, the doubling [of the word] occurs by the rule "also in the sense of affliction" (*ābādhe ca*).

A portion of the statement beginning with "nana karoti" and "susu jāgarti" has been cited [as an example]. [In these cases], the rule for final acute accentuation (*antodāttatva*) by means of the suffix *nañ* or a *su*-stem does not apply. For in that context, the word "in a compound" (*samāse*) from the rule "vanaṃ samāse" is connected [to the present rule] according to the maxim of the lion’s backward glance (*siṃhāvalokita-nyāya*), as well as the word "in a bahuvrīhi" (*bahuvrīhau*) from the rule "bahuvrīhāvidametattadbhyaḥ. Since a bahuvrīhi is never anything other than a compound, the further qualification "in a compound" (*samāsa*) is intended to include only those bahuvrīhis prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "compound" (*samāsa*).

Now, in this case, when the final acute accent (*antodātta*) applies by the rule *nañsubhyām*, what accent prevails? For here four accents would otherwise apply: the final acute of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatva*), the acute of the *nañ* and *su* [by *nañsubhyām*], the grave of the *āmreḍita* [by *āmreḍitam anudāttam*], and the acute of the *bahuvrīhi*. Regarding that, it has already been stated that the accent [prescribed] by *nañsubhyām* does not apply here. Nor does the grave accent of the *āmreḍita* apply. Why? In the case of the transfer of an operation (*kāryātideśa*), since this very [rule, *nañsubhyām*] is the prescriber of the operations, the grave accent of the *āmreḍita* is superseded by the *bahuvrīhi* accent on account of its posteriority.

Even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of a rule from a treatise (*śāstra*), because that which is contradictory is removed by the extension of its own substratum (*svāśraya*), the non-udātta nature of the *āmreḍita* (the repeated word) does not occur. Furthermore, in the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the first member retains] its original accent" (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā*), the term "compound" (*samāsa*) does not continue to apply; therefore, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), arising through the treatment of the *bahuvrīhi* as if it were the actual compound itself, subverts the final udātta accent of the compound. In the example *ṛgṛk*, the reduplication is according to the rule "also in the sense of intensity or distress" (*ābādhe ca*). And thus, the suffix *a* prescribed for compounds ending in *ṛc*, *pūḥ*, etc., does not apply here.

For in that context, while the word "from a compound" (*samāsāt*) is being carried over from the rule "and from a compound referring to that" (*samāsācca tadviṣayāt*), the repeated mention of "compound" (*samāsagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of including only that compound which is prescribed within the governing heading on compounds (*samāsādhikāra*). Consequently, a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) does not occur in a compound that is merely extended by analogy (*atideśika*). Thus, these [rules], beginning with the prohibition of technical names (*saṃjñā-pratiṣedha*), are understood to apply specifically to the *bahuvrīhi* prescribed under the governing heading on compounds.

The author of the Vārttika, however, considers all of this to be based solely on explicit scriptural injunction (vācanika), as he says: "There is a fault regarding pronouns, accents, and the suffixes of compounds. Now, one might ask: why does the elision of *n* not occur in the word *nanu* due to its treatment as a bahuvrīhi compound? It is replied:

The term "in the following word" (*uttarapade*) continues [from the previous rule], and *nañ* is specified as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*). In that case, the status of *nañ* as a cause (*nimitta*) is set aside by its being directly taught as the subject of the operation; just as in the example *madrahradaḥ* / *bhadrahradaḥ*, where the doubling of the *r* sound would otherwise apply according to the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve*, it is stated: "These two *r*s are not the subjects of the operation; rather, these two are the cause for the doubling. This resolution should be understood to apply to the preceding rules as well, as far as possible.
And [the suffix *khañ* is applied] after [a word denoting] a disease (*ābādha*). 8.1.10.

"Affliction (*ābādha*) means the act of afflicting. This is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). [This is] a property of the speaker (*prayoktṛdharma*), not a property of the denoted object (*abhidheyadharma*). For if it were a property of the denoted object, the reduplication would apply only to words such as *bādhita* ("afflicted") and *pīḍita* ("tormented"), but not to words such as *gata* ("gone"); however, since it is a property of the speaker, it applies to those [words] as well—thus there is pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "of that which exists therein": when reduplication occurs, because affliction is understood [from the reduplicated form], words such as *gata* function in that context, but not because they denote it [directly].
"Due to the long absence of the beloved, etc."—this shows that affliction is a property of the speaker. By the word "etc.," destruction and so forth are included.
In the subsequent [rules], it is like a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Because there is also the treatment as a *karmadhāraya* for that which has a penultimate *kup* vowel, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs. Therefore, while the treatment as a *bahuvrīhi* would otherwise be applicable, the treatment as a *karmadhāraya* is specifically prescribed; this is the intended meaning. By this [rule], the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound is prescribed. This was stated according to the view that the extension applies to the grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*). However, in the case of the extension of the rule itself (*śāstrātideśa*), although the lack of accent on the *āmreḍita* (repeated word) is indeed the primary result, it nevertheless does not occur here; for the rule being extended precludes its own inherent opposite.
The suffix *am* is applied after a word denoting a quality when it expresses a manner [of action]. (Pāṇini 5.4.11)

"Mode" (*prakāra*) means either "difference" (*bheda*) or "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), since the word *prakāra* is observed to be used in both senses. First, regarding difference: in the expression "he eats in many modes," it is understood as "in many differences" or "in many particulars. Regarding similarity: in the expression "this boy is of the mode of a Brāhmaṇa," it is understood as "similar to a Brāhmaṇa. As for the phrase "tadiha": the word *tat* is used to introduce a statement (*vākyopanyāse*). Alternatively, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) functioning in the sense of the locative case, meaning "therein" (*tatra*). Thus, "mode" is taken here in the sense of similarity.

Because that very [meaning] is understood from the reduplication; and here, the inherent nature of the expression is the reason. Regarding the phrase "of that which exists in the manner": its occurrence there is due to the manifestation of that [manner] by means of the application of reduplication. The meaning is "one whose quality is incomplete. How is this so? He says: "by one whose quality is complete.

When one who possesses full proficiency—that is, one who performs tasks with skill—is compared to someone of deficient proficiency, then the usage *puṭupaṭuḥ* occurs; thus, by implication, the meaning becomes "one whose quality is incomplete."

It is not intended that the suffix *jātīyar* should be superseded by this double application (*dvirvacana*). Therefore, it is considered that both types [of meanings] are included in its rule. Jayāditya, however, says therein: "A *prakāra* (mode/type) is a particular that differentiates a general category. This is indeed the accepted view; otherwise, in cases such as *brāhmaṇajātīyaḥ* ("belonging to the Brāhmaṇa class"), where the word is not a quality-term (*aguṇavacana*), and in cases such as *paṭujātīyaḥ* ("of a clever type"), where it is a quality-term (*guṇavacana*), the suffix *jātīyar*—which has already fulfilled its function elsewhere in denoting difference from similarity—would be barred from expressing similarity when applied to quality-terms.

Regarding the example "Devadatta is clever" (*paṭur devadattaḥ*): here the word *paṭu* (clever) functions as a term for one whose qualities are complete, not for one with deficient qualities due to similarity to that [quality].

Regarding "The boy is fire" (*agnir māṇavakaḥ*): the word *agni* (fire) is established in its primary sense as fire; it is applied to the boy through a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) based on extreme similarity. Thus, although it previously denoted a substance, it now also denotes a substance and is therefore not a word for a quality (*guṇavacana*). Similarly, in the case of "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), the word *go* (cow), having functioned in reference to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, is now applied to the Vāhīka.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the word *agni* (fire) is indeed a term expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), since it is employed to convey the sharpness residing in fire when applied to a young boy (*māṇavaka*)? Likewise, is the word *go* (cow) also a term expressing a quality, since it is employed for a Vāhīka person to convey the dullness residing in one who possesses a dewlap and so forth? To this, he says: "Even though here the word *agni*... and so on.

The word "fire" (agni), when applied to a boy, conveys that specific sharpness of fire which is distinct from axes and the like, and not sharpness in general; likewise, the word "cow" (go) conveys that specific dullness of cows which is distinct from humans. For sharpness, dullness, and so forth, are differentiated by their connection to a particular substratum. Thus it is said: "Sharpness, dullness, and the like, have their distinctions determined through their connection with the primary referent."

The meaning that is understood from the mere hearing of a word, without the proximity of another word, is the primary (mukhya) meaning; the opposite is the secondary (gauṇa). "With its difference ascertained" means with its distinction determined. By the word "etc. (ādi), qualities such as tawny color (paiṅgalya) and the carrying of a load are included. "In another sense" refers to the secondary sense, namely, in the case of a young Brahmin boy (māṇavaka) or a Vāhīka person. It is not stated twice because it does not always denote a quality.

Since the status of being a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) is already established by the phrase "of that which exists in the sense of a manner" (*prakāre varttamānasya*), the explicit mention of "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) once again indicates that we must understand the term as referring to something that is *always* a quality-word. However, this [word] is not always a quality-word; for prior to its application in the sense of a manner, it denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*).

In this regard, some maintain that the term *guṇavacana* means "that which expresses a quality" (*guṇamuktavān*), and thus they desire reduplication for that which expresses a substance qualified by a quality (*guṇopasarjanadravyavacana*). Others, however, desire it without distinction for both that which expresses a quality and that which expresses the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*), as in: *śuklaśuklaṃ rūpam* ("a white-white color") and *śuklaśuklaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a white-white cloth"). In the expression *navaṃnavaṃ prītiraho karoti*, the reduplication occurs due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); however, if this [general rule] were applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the elision of the case-ending (*sublopaprasaṅga*), as in: *navanavāvanavāyubhirādedhe*. [Examples include: *mūlemūle*.

For a single object, such as a bamboo stalk (*veṇudala*), there is only one primary top and one root; however, for the other parts, the designations "root" and "top" are merely relative. Furthermore, thickness and thinness are not uniform; rather, thickness increases toward the root and thinness toward the tip. Thus, a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is impossible here. In this context, in the phrase "at every root along the path of the trees," the doubling [of the word] occurs precisely because of distributive repetition.

Regarding the term *svārthe* (in its own sense): this is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the absence of any other meaning. Regarding the expression *asmārtkārṣāṇāt*: a *kārṣāpaṇa* is a collection of many *māṣa*s. In that case, not all the *māṣa*s are pervaded by the act of giving; rather, it is only two. Thus, there is an absence of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Now, one might object: just as when two specific *māṣa*s are identified and pervaded by the act of giving, then the doubling [of the word] occurs in distributive repetition—as in "give a *māṣa*, a *māṣa*" (*māṣaṃ māṣaṃ dehi*)—[so too should it be here].

In this way, even from a collection of many *māṣa* coins that constitutes a *kārṣāpaṇa*, does the operation of giving pervade only two [coins]? Not so; for in that case, there is no exclusion of any part of the object present there, whereas here there is exclusion, since after he has given one *māṣa* after another, he asks about the remainder: "What shall be done with this? This is what was stated: "For in this case... [namely], "Give a *māṣa*, give two *māṣas*, give three *māṣas*."

By this [rule], he shows the absence of restriction with the intention of saying "give as much as you wish. "Fickleness" (*cāpala*) is a quality of the speaker; when that is to be indicated, reduplication of every word within the sentence—whether it ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)—is not mandatory. Therefore, this is not a reduplication prescribed by the grammatical system (*śāstra*); what then? It means the employment of multiple independent words for the purpose of communicating to another.
And since this is the case, because there is no lack of accentuation for the *āmreḍita* (the repeated word), the accent remains as it naturally occurs.

Regarding the term *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition of an action): this reduplication applies only to forms ending in the imperative (*loṭ*), not to those ending in the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*). This is because the imperative is prescribed even for the purpose of expressing a combination of actions (*samuccaya*); thus, it lacks the inherent capacity to manifest *kriyāsamabhihāra* on its own. The *yaṅ*, however, has *kriyāsamabhihāra* as its very domain, and therefore, by its own inherent capacity to indicate that meaning, it does not require reduplication.

Regarding the term *ābhīkṣṇya* (frequency): this statement is presented in response to one who might suspect that, according to the preceding rule, reduplication applies only to that which is prescribed by the designation *kriyāsamabhihāra* (intensive repetition). It was stated there [in the commentary] that "it is established simply by [the word] *nitya*. For in the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, it was said: "The capacity to manifest frequency belongs only to those forms that require reduplication, namely the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul*, as well as the imperative (*loṭ*). Others, however, say: "*Ābhīkṣṇya* is the repeated production of an action."

For instance: when it is said, "having eaten, having eaten, he goes," even though there is an interruption of the action, one understands a repetition of the action—namely, that he eats again and again and goes again and again. Permanence (*nityatā*), however, is the non-interruption of the action; as when it is said, "he lives, he lives," one understands that "this person indeed lives," and not that "having lived he dies, and having died he lives. Rather, it is life itself that is understood as uninterrupted. Therefore, "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) and "permanence" (*nitya*) are two distinct meanings.

Another says: this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), so that when *dvirvacana* (reduplication) is applicable to both forms ending in *ktvā*, *ṇamul*, and those ending in *tiṅ*—as in examples such as *bhuktvā vrajati*—it may apply to that which is prescribed by the specific mention of *ābhīkṣṇya* (repetition), but not to that which ends in *tiṅ*.

Regarding the term *ḍāci*: this is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*); therefore, reduplication occurs for forms such as *paṭat* even before the elision of the *ṭi* suffix has taken place when *ḍāc* is introduced. Subsequently, the elision of the *ṭi* occurs by the rule *avyaktānukaraṇāt*, and the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) occurs by the rule *nityamāmreḍite ḍāci*. Another [scholar] says: "This very prescription of the single subsequent form for the sound *ac* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that reduplication takes place even before the elision of the *ṭi*, despite the locative case *ḍāci* being a locative of sequence (*parasaptamī*). That is incorrect.

In examples such as *patat*, since the word *ac* is possible even after the elision of the *ṭi* suffix, [the rule] "the second [syllable] of *karoti*" applies, resulting in *ḍāc* by the rule "after the root *kṛ*, [the affix] *ḍāc* follows when a word ending in the second case is used. Should one then state that there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) in the case of *ḍāc*? It need not be stated; the activity of the Teacher indicates that "reduplication occurs for an unexpressed imitation (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) when *ḍāc* follows," since he teaches the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) in the rule "when *ḍāc* follows an iterated (*āmreḍita*) word, [the substitution is] obligatory."

Regarding the rule *pūrvaprathamayoḥ*: the reduplication of these two words, *pūrva* and *prathama*, occurs where? When there is a desire to express an excellence of meaning—that is, when the excellence of their respective meanings is intended to be expressed. [The statement] "the suffixes expressing excellence (*ātiśāyika*) are also seen" is a formal rule (*vacana*) provided because the reduplication would otherwise have sublated them. The word *atiśaya* (excellence) should be understood as belonging to the *anuśatikādi* group [of nominal stems]. However, some maintain that because the meanings are distinct, the suffixes expressing excellence are not sublated by the reduplication.

For instance: when it is said, "He eats earlier," a doubt arises as to whether the priority of the eating is in relation to another action accomplished by himself, or in relation to an act of eating accomplished by another eater. Similarly, when it is said, "It flowers earlier," this meaning is understood: that it has not yet put forth sprouts so long as it flowers. From the expression "it flowers earlier than others," however, the sense perceived is that it flowers with greater priority than other flowering plants.

Regarding the rule *ḍataraḍatamayor iti*: words ending in the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* become double [in form] when there is a comparative deliberation (*sampradhāraṇā*) based on a common attribute such as wealth and so forth. Regarding the phrase *strīnigade bhāva iti*: *bhāvaḥ* means existence (*bhūtiḥ*), that is, prosperity or wealth (*sampad*, *āḍhyatā*). It is called *nigada* because it is expressed; the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object according to the rule *nau gada* etc. By the word *strī*, a word in the feminine gender is designated. "The expression of a woman" (*striyā nigadaḥ*) is a compound formed with a genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

The meaning is: "of that which exists as a being denoted by a word in the feminine gender. The question "katarā-katarā anayor āḍhyatā? (Which of these two is wealthier? asks whether it is produced by a perfection of means or produced by fortune.

Regarding the term *karmavyatihāra*: this means "in the reciprocal exchange of actions. In that context, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) is compulsory, whereas the treatment as a compound (*samāsavadbhāva*) is optional (*bahulam*). In the word *anyonya*, because the treatment as a compound does not apply, there is no elision of the case-ending (*subluk*), nor does the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) of a compound occur; rather, the enclitic grave accent (*āmreḍitānudāttatva*) applies. In the word *itaretara*, however, the treatment as a compound is compulsory; thus, both the elision of the case-ending and the accent of the compound occur. In the form *anyonyam*, there is reduplication of the word ending in the singular accusative case.

Regarding the phrase *anyo'nyasya*: this is the genitive singular form. It means "the sons and so forth who are related to one another. Regarding the phrase *strīnapuṃsakayoḥ*: there is the substitution of *ām* for the case-ending situated at the end of the second member (*uttarapada*); otherwise, because it would consist of more than one phoneme (*anekāltvāt*), it would replace the entire second member. In that context, since the rule "in all compound formations (*vṛtti*), a pronoun takes the masculine form" applies, once the masculine form has been applied to both the first and second members, the prescription of *ām* occurs optionally.

However, when the word *anyā* undergoes reduplication, because the application of the rules governing compounds (*samāsavadbhāva*) is not mandatory due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is elided. In the neuter gender as well, the substitution of *adḍ* [for the final syllable] prescribed by the rule "adḍutarādibhyaḥ" is elided. Since the phrase "as in a *karmadhāraya*" (*karmadhārayavat*) is not connected to the *vārttikas*, there is no elision of case endings (*subluk*) and so forth.
In the sense of "not with difficulty," the suffix *khal* may optionally replace *tṛn* after the words *priya* and *sukha*.

In the expression *priyapriyeṇa*, when the word ending in the third case singular is doubled, the *karmadhārayavadbhāva* (the treatment as a *karmadhāraya* compound) applies; consequently, after the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending, that same case-ending reappears. The meaning is that one gives even an extremely beloved object without effort.
The suffix *tham* is applied after the word *yathā* when it means "according to one's own" (*yathāsve*).

In the expression *yathāsve*, the compound is an *avyayībhāva* formed with the distributive particle (*vīpsā*) according to the rule *yathā’sādṛśye*. He shows that the word *sva* denotes either the self (*ātman*) or what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), as in the phrase "whichever is the self. However, there is no inclusion of the meanings "kinsman" or "wealth," because the distributive repetition (*dvirvacana*) is incapable of functioning in those senses.
The term *dvandva* [is used] in the senses of secrecy, a boundary, transgression, the employment of sacrificial vessels, and manifestation. 8.1.15.

Regarding the term *pūpavat* (like *pūpa*): when *dvi-au* and *dvi* are present, by virtue of the application of the *karmadhāraya*-treatment, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided (*luk*). Then, the substitution of *ām* for the vowel *i* that constitutes part of the first member (*pūrva-pada*) and the substitution of *a* for the vowel that constitutes part of the second member (*uttara-pada*) are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). By the force of the word "and" (*ca*), neuter gender is also prescribed, as is the singular collective form (*ekavad-bhāva*) in some instances. As for the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound, it occurs because of the application of the *karmadhāraya*-treatment. In this context, the secret (*rahasya*) is what is denoted by the word *dvandva*. The meaning is that this is a *yogarūḍhi* [compound]—an etymological-lexical formation—referring to a secret established through two [means].

"Consulting in pairs" means that they consult having become two by twos; for in this way, that [consultation] remains secret. Regarding "up to four": the prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). The word *catuḥ* should be understood as signifying the completion of four; thus, the meaning is "up to the fourth. "Coupling in pairs": by the word *mithuna*, its activity—sexual intercourse—is indicated. From the desire for that, the suffix *kyac* is applied. Generally, however, the form ending in *kyac* is read as *mithunāyante*; in that case, the basis of the comparison must be sought.

With the words "The mother by the son," etc., he clarifies the statement regarding the boundary (*maryādā*). "By his son as well" means that such is the full extent of the life of domestic animals. "Having gone beyond in pairs" means having become two wings and remaining separately. The doubling of the word and its treatment as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) are for the sake of the primary meaning itself. "In pairs, he employs the vessels face-down"—that is, he sets them down; "face-down" means turned downwards, with their openings facing downward. "In pairs, the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the potsherds (*kapālāni*)" means two of each.

In this instance, there is reduplication due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), as well as the substitution of *ambh-* and so forth, and the treatment as a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*). The meaning is that the two [words] are manifested through association. Here, the reduplication for its own sake (*svārthe dvirvacana*), the singular collective form, and all such rules are prescribed as irregular formations (*nipātana*).

"Dvandva means battle. Here too, there is reduplication for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). "They endure the *dvandvas*": cold and heat constitute one *dvandva*, pleasure and pain another, and hunger and thirst yet another. Here too, there is reduplication for the sake of the base meaning (*svārthe*), as well as the treatment as a singular collective (*ekavadbhāva*) and so forth; therein, plurality arises by virtue of the rule of single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). "A *dvandva* occurs in the sense of conjunction (*cārtha*). When two words denoting objects connected by "and" (*ca*) are compounded, it is a *dvandva*. Here too, there is reduplication for the sake of the base meaning and so forth, as well as the masculine gender.
[The substitution of *ṣat* for *pad* occurs] when it is a word-form (*pada*). || 8.1.16 ||

"Prior to the governing rule [beginning with] *apadānta*": however, in the section beginning with *apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*, because of the mention of a contradictory element, this [prohibition] is not applied. Thus, in *pacantau* and *yajantau*, there is no elision even though they end in a *saṃyoga*. Likewise, in *rājānau*, there is no elision of the *n*; and in *praśāmāu* and similar forms, the substitution of *na* by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ* does not occur.

In the subsequent rules, since operations are prescribed only for words consisting of a nominal stem (subanta) beginning with an item such as an āmantrita, or for a verbal form (tiṅanta), those [rules] are bypassed. Furthermore, there is no need for the application of the *samartha-paribhāṣā* in those cases, because even without it, the result is established simply by the fact that these are operations on words (*pada*) in relation to what immediately precedes them. Moreover, it will be stated later: "In a single sentence, the *nighāta* accent, the substitutes *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and so forth [apply]."

However, in the case of *kutv* and other such changes, even though the constituent part (*avayava*) bears the designation *bha*, they are indeed desired on the basis of the entire word (*samudāya*) having the designation *pada*—as in *vaktari* and *dogdharī*. Therefore, the exclusion of those items designated as *bha* is not a purpose [of the rule].

Because of the rule "the genitive [case ending] denotes the relation of 'in place of'," the term *padasya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Consequently, the meaning of the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ svarito'nudāttasya* becomes this: when there is a *yaṇ*-substitute for an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, that which follows it—an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel—at the end of the word (*padasya*) becomes circumflex (*svarita*), according to the principle that "the substitution applies to the final [element] of the remainder. Therefore, this would apply only in a case such as *kumāryau*.

In the case of *kumāryaḥ*, [the rule] would not apply, for here the *s* is at the end of a word (*padānta*), and when a vowel accent is to be applied, a consonant is treated as if it were non-existent. Likewise, in the rule "a single substitute for [an udātta and an anudātta] is udātta," this is the meaning: the substitute occurs for the final letter of the word that ends in that single substitute which results from the combination of an udātta and an anudātta. And thus, it would apply only in this instance: *vṛkṣau*.

One might object: "In the case of *vṛkṣān*, [the rule] should not apply, for here the letter *n* is the final of a word (*padāntya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "with reference to the statement to be stated later. The intention is as follows: this heading (*adhikāra*) is for the sake of another, and a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) is also for the sake of another; therefore, by the maxim "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no connection [between them] due to their equality," the technical definition regarding the application of a substitute (*sthāneyoga-paribhāṣā*) does not apply here.

However, where this [term *pada*] has jurisdiction over the sentences to be stated hereafter, its application is restricted to those very cases. In that context, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified, the term *padaḥ*, which recurs from the previous rule, serves as a qualifier for the *kāryin* (the element undergoing the operation) and not for the purpose of indicating the *kārya* (the operation itself). Consequently, because the accentuation is prescribed for the two elements that are parts of a word (*padāvayava*)—namely, the *anudātta* and the *ekādeśa*—it applies even to those that are not final (*anantya*).

However, in cases such as the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), because the word (*pada*) is qualified by the initial member of the conjunct, the genitive case denotes the *sthāna* (the position to be replaced). Therefore, having reflected upon and considered the sentences to be stated hereafter, the meaning of the genitive "of the word" (*padasya*) must be established; it is not, however, established merely by reflecting upon this present sūtra. He demonstrates that very establishment [with the words] "in some cases. If this were exclusively a *sthāna*-genitive, then the mention of the word "final" (*anta*) in the rule "there is no elision of the final of a nominal stem" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*) would be purposeless.

For this [term *anta*] is indeed for the purpose that [the operation] should apply to the end of a word (*padānta*), and not to a part of a word (*padāvayava*). If, however, the genitive were one denoting "place" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then because the rule "of the final [element]" (*alontyasya*) would already be established, the inclusion of the term *anta* would be redundant. Therefore, by virtue of the inclusion of the term *anta*, it is understood that in some instances the genitive denotes a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
After the word *pad* [the suffix *ṅasi* becomes *āt*]. 8.1.17.

[The rule applies] from the point where "prāk kutsane ca supyagotrādau" occurs. However, if the term *padāt* were to be carried over (anuvarteta) here, then the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would apply only to the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) in "yat pacati pūti," and not in "pacati pūti."
Everything [in a compound] is unaccented, except when it occurs at the beginning of a metrical foot (pāda).

Regarding the passage beginning with *yatte niyatam* and so forth: here, there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the word *mṛtyo* at the beginning of the quarter-verse (*pāda*). Examples include the single quarter-verse *yadaṅgadāśuṣe tvam*, another quarter-verse beginning with *agne*, and others such as *agne bhadraṃ kariṣyati*.
Regarding the passage beginning with *rudro viśveśvaraḥ* and so forth: here, there is an absence of the substitutes *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*.

"A quarter of a *ṛc* and a quarter of a *śloka* are included," because no specific distinction is mentioned. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of "all" (*sarva*), given that by the rule "in a word, all syllables except one are *anudātta*," only one *udātta* or *svarita* can occur in a single word? As for those words that have two *udāttas*—such as "both [members] simultaneously in the case of *vanaspati* and so forth"—it is not the case that *anudātta* status is prescribed for them anywhere in this section; rather, when they function as vocatives (*āmantrita*), they possess exactly two *udāttas*.

This, then, is the purpose: so that even an original (anādi) udātta may become anudātta. Otherwise, because of the governing rule *padīd* and the principle *ādeḥ parasya*, it would apply only to the beginning [of the following element]; consequently, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would apply only here—namely, in *devadattaḥ pacati*, for here the suffixes *śap* and *tip* are anudātta and the accent belongs to the root. But in this case, *devadattaḥ karoti*, it would not apply, because this word is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) due to the accent of the *vikaraṇa*.

If, however, the term *sarva* (all) is included [in the rule], the meaning results that every constituent part (*avayava*) of the word becomes unaccented (*anudātta*). This is established by the prohibition regarding the *luṭ* suffix; for when the author teaches the prohibition "not in *luṭ*" (*na luṭ*), he indicates that "the principle *na ādeḥ parasya* (P. 1.1.54) does not apply here. Indeed, there is no form ending in *luṭ* that has its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).

Even so, when an exception (*apavāda*) is set aside by an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding the initial rule (*ādividhi*), would [the accent] not apply only to the final letter (*alo'ntyasya*)—as in *ubho kurutaḥ* and similar cases? Here, the final syllable of the *asārvadhātuka* suffix is acute due to the accent of the suffix itself (*pratyayasvara*), while the *vikaraṇa* receives the *nighāta* (elision of accent). However, the accent of the *vikaraṇa*, even though it is "later remaining" (*satiśiṣṭa*), does not override the accent of the *sārvadhātuka*; for this is indicated by the rule prescribing the anudātta (unaccented) nature of the *tās* suffix when it follows a *lasārvadhātuka*.

In that case, the rule is established by the prohibition regarding the *lṛṭ* [future] tense. Since this [sūtra], "When there is a *loṭ* [imperative] expressing motion, the *lṛṭ* is not used," teaches a prohibition of the *lṛṭ*-ending form, it indicates that the rule "of the final [alphon]" (*alo'ntyasya*) does not apply here. For indeed, there is no *lṛṭ*-ending form that is oxytone (having the acute accent on the final syllable); rather, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix following an *adupadeśa* [root beginning with a vowel] is unaccented. This is not so; this [prohibition] must be an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the sake of the augment *iṭ*, as in the example *bhokṣye*. For this [form *bhokṣye*] is oxytone due to the accent of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

If that is so, then this has already been stated: that in some cases the genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs for the word *pada*, and not only the genitive of position (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). What follows from this? In the rule prescribing the anudātta accent, the genitive of qualification will be resorted to; by virtue of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the nominative in *tiṅ* functions in the sense of the genitive. Thus, the meaning is: "The vowel (*ac*) which is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word (*pada*) ending in a *tiṅ* becomes anudātta. Since there is no genitive of position here, the rule *alo'ntyasya* ("of the final [al]") does not apply. Therefore, what is the purpose of including the word *sarva* [in the sūtra]? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "The inclusion of the word 'all' (*sarva*), etc. If the term "all" were not present, then the rule for being unaccented (*anudāttatva*) would be prescribed only in cases such as *āmantritasya* where there is no other element to be enjoined (*vidheya*). For in those instances, the vocative (*āmantrita*) and so forth are restated (*anūdya*) precisely for the purpose of enjoining this [unaccented quality]. However, when another element to be enjoined exists, the unaccented quality would not be prescribed for that [vocative], because it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). To explain: a further property (*dharmāntara*) can be enjoined for an entity that is already established, but not for one that is not yet established; for there is no painting on a wall that does not exist.

Furthermore, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because the *vaṣaṭ* and other elements would have to be enjoined by one sentence, while their low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) would be enjoined by another. Even in the case of an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), a syntactical split characterized by the excessive burden of enjoining multiple matters (*vidhigaurava*) would certainly occur. Since a syntactical split is not desired when a single sentence is possible, [the author] says "by that" (*tena*) to address the question: "But if the word 'all' (*sarva*) is present, is the syntactical split tolerated due to its inherent power? Thus he says: "By that."
