He states another purpose: "So that the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* may apply to every inflected word (*subanta*). Otherwise, they would apply only to the bare stems *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. In the case of the singular genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacana*), although there is no fault because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the preceding vowel occurs via the rule *ṅasiṅasośca*, there would still be the risk of a fault in other cases. However, by including the term *sarva* ("all"), a word (*pada*) having *yuṣmad* and *asmad* as its constituents is indicated; thus, the substitutes *vām*, *nau*, and so forth, apply to the entire word.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the phrase "not of a word" (*na padasya*) continues [from a previous rule], and since a word (*pada*) is that which ends in an inflection (*vibhaktyanta*), then even without the mention of *sarva* ("all"), the substitution will apply to that which ends in an inflection? [Response: To this he says, "Even where... The point is this: this would indeed be so where a word ends in an inflection; however, where a word occurs within an inflection, there is the contingency of applying the rules only to *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. For example, in the expression *grāmo vāṃ dīyate* ("the village is given to you two"), in the dual dative, the preceding element becomes a word (*pada*) by the rule *svādiṣu*.
And [the substitution of *e* for *o* occurs] for a vocative case ending. 8.1.19.

"Everything becomes unaccented" means that all vowels (*ac*) connected with the vocative (*āmantrita*) become unaccented (*anudātta*). This merely demonstrates the application of the word "all" (*sarva*) which has been carried over [from the previous rule], but it has no further utility here.

"Within the same sentence," and so forth. While having a single purpose (*arthaikatva*) and the like is the definition of a sentence according to common usage (*laukika*), here, however, the sentence is technical (*pāribhāṣika*). A sentence is "a verb (*ākhyāta*) together with its indeclinables, cases, and qualifiers. By the term "verb," singularity is intended. It must be stated that when the cause and the effect (*nimitta-nimittin*) reside in the same single sentence as their substratum (*ādhāra*), then the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) and other such operations occur. He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "In this [context]. The two phrases, "Bhavatīha viṣṇumitraḥ" and "Devadattāgaccha," constitute two distinct sentences.

Because of the connection with two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the vocative "Devadatta" here. Now, one might object: this is a rule concerning word-formation (*padavidhi*), and therefore it will not apply here simply because of a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*). However, there is indeed syntactic capacity here; this is said in reference to Devadatta who, having searched for Viṣṇumitra, is going elsewhere. Thus, Viṣṇumitra’s arrival is stated here as the cause for Devadatta’s departure, and so there is a mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). In some places, this example is not recited.

In the phrase "ayaṃ daṇḍaḥ" (this stick), because it is understood that [the stick] exists, this much constitutes a single sentence. Here too, since the stick—which is referred to by the pronoun *anena*—functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is semantic competency; thus, there arises the contingency of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) for the finite verb ending. For example: "odanaṃ paceti" (cook the rice).

Since there is an expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) between the act of cooking and the referents of the second-person and first-person pronouns—such that the rice will have you as its agent and thus be "yours," while it will also have me as its agent and thus be "mine"—there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the substitutes [for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*]. Thus, it was stated that the purpose [of the rule] is to avoid such over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, he states that avoiding under-extension (*avyāpti*) is also a purpose: "And here... and so forth.

But what is the reason that the *nighāta* (elision of accent) and other such operations do not occur in these examples? To this he says: "The end of an *āmantrita*," and so forth. Here, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is with "the mother standing here" (*mātā sthitā*), and not with "Devadatta" (*devadatta*); the connection is with "the bank of the river" (*nadyāḥ kūlam*), and not with "she stands by the river" (*nadyāḥ tiṣṭhati*); the connection is with "rice-gruel of rice" (*śālīnām odanam*), and not with "of those rice-grains yours" (*śālīnām te*). Therefore, the meaning is that because there is a lack of semantic expectancy (*asāmarthya*), these operations would not occur.
In place of the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* standing in the sixth, fourth, or second case, *vām* and *nau* are optionally substituted.

"Only for those ending in the dual number. The sense is that this has been illustrated by means of another grammatical number. [Objection: Is the mention of *stha* (the suffix *-stha*) redundant? For since substitutes (*ādeśa*) are prescribed for the genitive and other cases, their "being located therein" (*tātsthya*) is already established. To this he replies: "The mention of *stha*... The meaning is: so that the substitutes may apply only when the case-endings are actually heard (*śrūyamāṇa*), and not when they have been elided (*lupta*). For "being located therein" occurs only when the case-ending is heard, and not when it is elided. Furthermore, it is either an operation (*kārya*) or a rule (*śāstra*) that is extended by means of the technical designation of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), but not its "being located therein."

Alternatively, the root *sthā* is also seen in the sense of "not abandoning," as in the example: *samaye tiṣṭha sugrīva*, which means "do not abandon the agreement. Therefore, the meaning is this: the substitutes [tvam, aham, te, me, etc. occur for the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they do not abandon their case-endings, namely the sixth (genitive), fourth (dative), and second (accusative). Thus, in the phrase *iti yuṣmat-putraḥ*, because the words follow immediately after the word *iti*, the substitutes *va* and *na* do not occur for the genitive forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* by virtue of the rule regarding the treatment of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*).
The particle *na* does not take the acute accent when joined with *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, or *eva*. Pāṇini 8.1.24.

*ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*), *vā* for option (*vikalpa*), *ha* and *aha* for wonder (*adbhuta*), *ha* also for distress (*kheda*), and *eva* for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). "When joined with these" means when there is a connection with these; or alternatively, it means when the referents of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are joined with these. [An objection: Is the inclusion of the word *yukta* (joined) redundant? For it is already established by the use of the instrumental case ending, as in the rule *tulyārthairatulopamābhyām*. To this, he replies: "The inclusion of the word *yukta*... [is for the following purpose].

When particles such as *ca* and others indicate conjunctions and so forth that pertain to the meanings of the pronouns *yuṣmad* (you) and *asmad* (we), then there is a direct connection between those particles and the two [pronouns]. It is for the purpose of ensuring that this prohibition applies only in that specific case—that it should not apply to what is connected with what is connected—that the term "connected" (*yukta*) is included. This very inclusion of the term "connected" serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) that within this section, even that which is connected with what is connected is to be understood; therefore, the subsequent prohibition applies to cases involving what is connected with what is connected.
And [the suffix *kvi* is used] after the root *paś* when it does not denote the act of looking at objects. 8.1.25.

*Darśana* means "seeing. By this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *śa* is applied in the sense of an action (*bhāva*), and by the rule *pāghrā-dhmo-dheṭ-dṛśaḥ śaḥ*, the root *dṛś* is replaced by *paśya*. Those whose meaning is seeing are "those whose meaning is seeing" (*paśyārthāḥ*). Thus he says: "those whose meaning is seeing are those whose meaning is perceiving (*darśana*). If, however, the suffix *śa* were applied in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule *pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ*, then the meaning would be "those whose purpose is the seer," and in that case, the exclusion of "mere observation" (*ālocana*) would be redundant; for meanings of mere observation do not have the seer as their purpose.

"Vision is knowledge. Although the root *dṛś* is well-known in the sense of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), nevertheless, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the meaning here is that the root *dṛś* applies to knowledge in general. "Village" means a collection of people. "Having observed" means having examined with the mind.
Optionally [the substitution of *a* for *e*] occurs after a first case ending that is preceded by another word. Pāṇini 8.1.26.

Regarding the phrase *vidyamānapūrvāt*: in the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge*, because the condition *tulyayoge* (when there is equality of connection) is merely occasional (*prāyikatvāt*), the word *saha*—even when it signifies "being present" (*vidyamāna*)—forms a compound. The substitution of *sa-* for *sa-* occurs by the rule *vopasarjanasya*. Regarding the statement *yuṣmadasmador vibhāṣā 'nanvādeśe*: this optional application (*vibhāṣā*) of substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* applies only when there is no subsequent reference (*ananvādeśe*); however, in the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśe*), the rule for the mandatory substitutes applies. This is the meaning.

"Another says" (*apara āha*) means another interpretation of the same preceding statement. Previously, it was stated that "the scope is restricted" by way of restating the option (*vibhāṣā*); now, however, it is said that "an option is prescribed specifically for a particular scope. The meaning is that not only are those [operations] which have arisen in the scope mentioned in the sūtra subject to option, but rather all [operations] across all scopes.

"Not then," [he says]. The intention is that [the rule] is established by the very fact of being stated. Regarding "for the sake of *anvādeśa*": one might object, "Previously it was said that the sūtra does not operate in the case of *anvādeśa*, but now it is said that it does operate therein; what then is the final decision here? To this he replies: "Therefore, this... The word *tat* has the sense of *tatra* (therein), or it is used to introduce the statement. The meaning is that the previous explanation is set aside.
The suffixes *tiṅ* and those beginning with *gotra* are used in the sense of censure (*kutsana*) and repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).

"Pacati gotram" (he cooks his lineage). The root *pac* here signifies "becoming manifest," as in the expression *lokapakti* (the ripening of the world). The meaning is that he makes his lineage known for the sake of food and so forth; thus, there is indeed a sense of reproach (*kutsā*). "Pacatipacati gotram" (he repeatedly cooks his lineage). This means that in matters such as marriage and the like, he makes his lineage known again and again. Since there is no reproach in this case, the mention of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) applies. The doubling [of the verb] occurs by the rule "*nityavīpsayoḥ*" (Pāṇini 8.1.4).

The word *bruva* signifies something contemptible; for this very reason, a separate example is provided for its frequent repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*). In examples such as *pacati pravacanam*, there is contempt expressed through self-praise. *Pravacanam* means teaching. He explains the *gaṇa*-sūtra "vā nāma" with the words "the word *nāma*. In the example *pacati pāpam*, *pāpam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) of the action. In *khanati gotraṃ sametya kūpam*, the meaning is: having come together as a clan (*gotram* = *kulam*), he digs a well.

Is this mention of "contempt" (*kutsanā*) and "frequency" (*ābhīkṣṇya*) a qualification of the *pāṭha* (recitation) of *gotra* and the others—meaning that *gotra* and the rest occur in these two senses and, when following a finite verb (*tiṅ*), they become unaccented (*anudātta*)? Or is it a qualification of the "unaccented" (*anudātta*) itself—meaning that *gotra* and the others, when following a finite verb, become unaccented in these two senses? Regarding this dispute, he states the resolution: "And the mention of contempt and frequency. *Pāṭha* means that which is recited; it refers to a specific arrangement [of words].

Its qualification should be understood [as follows]. And this meaning is obtained through the division of the *yoga* (sūtra-splitting): one *yoga*, "after a finite verb (*tiṅ*), [the words] *gotra* and so forth," is for the purpose of prescribing the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*); the second *yoga* is "in the sense of contempt (*kutsana*) and frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)," with "the words *gotra* and so forth" being carried over from the previous rule. This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule): in this grammar, the words *gotra* and so forth are to be understood as referring exclusively to the domains of contempt and frequency. What is established by this? To this he says: "by that. "Elsewhere also" refers to the rules "in the presence of *cana*, *cit*, *iva*, [words beginning with] *gotra*, taddhita suffixes, and reduplication, when not expressing motion" (*Pāṇini 8.1.57*) and "also in the case of contempt, when [the word] begins with *gotra*" (*Pāṇini 8.1.69*).
The augment *tiṅ* is added before *atiṅ*. 8.1.28.

"It becomes" means "it cooks"; the meaning is that the action of cooking comes into being. In that case, because there is a connection between two actions by way of the relationship of the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). As it has been said: "The actions such as 'cooking' become the agents of the action of 'becoming'. In this context, although the cooking is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with respect to its own instruments, it possesses the quality of being established (*siddhatva*) with respect to the process of coming into being. As Bhartṛhari stated: "In that regard, an action is [an action] with respect to that for which its state of being a goal is not yet established."
"But that which has already been established cannot again be the object of proof for that very same [person].

Is this so? What then? The mention of *atiṅ* (not ending in a verbal suffix) is redundant; because of the governing rule of "in a single sentence" (*samānavākya*), the phrase "in a single sentence" continues to apply, and there are not two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) in one sentence, as was stated previously. However, since the author of the Sūtras did not establish the governing rule of "in a single sentence," he included the mention of *atiṅ*.
The *luṭ* [suffix] does not [occur]. 8.1.29.
Regarding "śvaḥ karttā" and so forth: if one asks, "Now that the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) has been prohibited here, what single accent is heard? he replies: "of that which follows *tās-*."
The particles *yadi*, *yadā*, *cet*, *yadi*, *uta*, *kuvid*, *neca*, *caṇ*, *kaccit*, and *yat* are used when joined with *yatra*. (8.1.30)

*Yadi* is used in the senses of "if," "wherefore," "in the case of," and "when"; *cet* is used in the sense of "if" and "wish"; *hanta* is used in the senses of joy, compassion, the commencement of a sentence, and dejection.
*Kaccit* is used in a question; *na* in negation; *kuvit* is recorded as being used in praise. Where there is the status of a particle (*nipāta*), it serves as a qualifier for words such as *yad*.
In a compound, there is indeed no other way for those elements that have become subordinate members;
nor is the compound itself dissolved by becoming a nominal stem (*su*) or an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

In this regard, the Bahvṛcas study the collection of particles beginning with "necca": "The gods did not yoke [the chariot] here in this manner, if another does not approach. Here, the word *ced* functions in the sense of "if" (*iti cet*). The very particle *ca*, which is observed in the sense of conjunction and so forth, is the same one that functions in the sense of "if"; however, the letter *ṇ* is the marker for its functioning in that sense. Thus, according to the rule "the *ca*-group [of particles] is unaccented," this sense of "if" is also unaccented, as in: "May Indra also be gracious to us" (*indraśca mṛḍayāti naḥ*).

Thereafter, sin shall perish; that is, if Indra would have mercy upon us, he would make us happy. And you, O Soma, if you desire our life—that is, O Soma, if you should wish or desire for us to live—then we shall not die.

Regarding the phrase "and the word *ca* in [the sense of] conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth": the meaning is that [the rule] does not apply in these senses. In the examples, the word *karoti* has its middle syllable acute (udātta) by virtue of the accent of the *vikaraṇa* suffix. In *bhuṅkte*, it has the final syllable acute by virtue of the accent of the cessation of the acute (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*). In *adhīte*, it has the final syllable acute because the prohibition of the anudātta nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix applies by the rule *ahan viṅoḥ*. As for the form [of the word] in the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *iṇ*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *iṇo yaṇ*.

[Objection: But surely, because it is mentioned by its specific form (*pratipadokta*) and because of its association with *yad* and so forth, only the particle (*nipāta*) will be understood? [Reply: If that is so, then this teaches that in this section, neither of these two [criteria] is determinative.

Therefore, in the rule *yāvadyathābhyām*, there is the inclusion of the word *yāvat* even when it is a non-particle (*anipāta*) derived etymologically from *yad-tad-etad* with the suffix *vatup* in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*), as in: *tāvaduṣo rādho asmabhyam, rāsva yāvatstotṛbhyo arado gṛṇānaḥ* ("O Dawn, grant us wealth as much as you have given to those who praise you") and *yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt* ("as many horses as one might receive").

Regarding the phrase *yatra kvaca*: here, the word *yatra* is directly connected with the word *uttaram*. Regarding *dadhasaḥ*: the root *dhā* (in the form *dadh*) meaning "to hold" is anudātta. Here—[in the verse] *hantāham imāṃ pṛthivīm nidadhānīha veha vā | hanto nu kim āsa se prathamaṃ no rathaṃ kṛdhi*—the lack of *nighāta* (anudātta accent) occurs because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The substitution of *na* occurs for *pra* before the root *ārabh*. (Pāṇini 8.1.31)

The compound *na-hi* is a collection of particles used in the sense of negation. *Pratyārambhaḥ* means a renewed undertaking (*punar-ārambhaḥ*). He states its scope with the words "of that which has been enjoined" (*coditasya*). When there is disregard—that is, contempt—for something such as eating or studying that has been enjoined and presented as something to be performed (e.g., "Eat!", "Study!"), then, out of a desire to reproach (*upālipsayā*) that person who disregarded it, a connection is made through the prohibition of that very same act; this is *pratyārambhaḥ*, meaning a renewed presentation is made. This is what is meant.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied [after a verbal root] when it does not involve a reversal of the natural order of body parts. 8.1.33.

*Prātilomya* is the state of acting contrarily; *aprātilomya* is the opposite of that, namely, acting in accordance with one's desire. Thus, it should be called *ānulomya*. The word *aṅga* is used in the sense of an example (*udāharaṇa*) or permission (*anu-jñā*); however, in a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), it expresses indignation (*amarṣa*).
And [the substitution of *hi* occurs] before *ca*. 8.1.34.
The word *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or as a reason (*hetu*); furthermore, it is used in a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) or to express indignation (*tvarṣa*).
In Vedic (chandas), even multiple [words] may [be compounded] if they require further syntactic connection. 8.1.35.

In this context, the particle *hi* indicates the relationship between cause and effect; thus, even multiple finite verbs may be joined with *hi*. Since the preceding rule would otherwise result in the prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for all such verbs, this [new] rule is stated so that it might apply to multiple verbs in some cases and to a single verb in others. He states this with the words "sometimes. In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the arrangement follows what is observed in usage. In the phrase "for [he speaks] untruth" (*anṛtaṃ hi*), "sin" (*pāpmā*) refers to intoxication. The meaning is: because he, being intoxicated, speaks untruth, he is therefore joined with the fault of speaking untruth.

Regarding the phrase "udajayat ity ādyudāttam," the meaning here is that *ajayat* (he conquered) is accented on its first syllable. In the expression *ajanista garbham* (he brought forth the embryo), the verb *jan* (to be born) is transitive because it carries an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).
The suffixes *yāvat* and *yathā* [are used with the indeclinable *am*]. || 8.1.36 ||

The usage of *yāvat* and *yathā* even when they follow [another word] has been cited in order to demonstrate that the third case suffix applies in the sense of "entirety" (*sākalya*) or "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), as in the examples *yathā-yogyatādiṣu*. Therefore, this objection should not be raised: that the prohibition is already established for words ending in the suffix *vatu*—namely *yathā* and *yāvat*—by the rule *yadvṛttānnityam* alone.
In the case of *pūjā*, there is no difference [in the application of the rule]. 8.1.37.

He says that two negations convey the intended meaning: "What then? That which is unaccented (*anudātta*)," as far as the word *devadatta*. But surely a restriction will be understood from what follows: "If [the substitution] occurs when there is an intervention, it must be by an *upasarga* alone"? If this is so, then its purpose in the subsequent rule is this: let there be no other word between the *upasarga*-separated [verb] and the words *yāvat* or *yathā*. However, if the non-application [of the rule] in those cases follows simply from the restriction "if it occurs when there is an intervention, it must be by an *upasarga* alone," then the mention of *anantara* (immediate) could have been omitted.
And [the augment *aṭ* is inserted] even when separated by a preverb (*upasarga*). 8.1.38.

*Vyavāya* means intervention (*vyavadhāna*). Regarding the phrase "only immediately following": that immediacy refers to [the word] together with its prefix (*sopasarga*), not to the verbal root alone (*tiṅanta-mātra*).
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the roots *tup*, *paśya*, and *paśyat* when used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*).

Words such as *tu* (but) and so forth serve as objects of honor. In the phrase "But the boy eats," the word *tu* expresses wonder, whereby the eating is understood as an act of honor; likewise in other cases—as in "Look, the deer runs!"—this is a statement of reality.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "in the case of honor (*pūjā*), [the rule] does not apply immediately after" (P. 8.1.59) still carries over from that point? So what is the purpose of the word "in the case of honor" (*pūjāyām*) here? [Response: To this he says: "The word 'in the case of honor' being present... (*pūjāyāmiti vartamānaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "for that": if that [word *pūjāyām*] were to carry over, then even in this context—such as the domain of P. 8.1.29 (*na luṭ*) and so on—there would be a prohibition of the prohibition itself. This should not be so. The meaning is that the mention of "honor" (*pūjā*) is for the sake of ensuring that there is a prohibition specifically of the *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent).
Furthermore, in the previous rule it was "immediately after," but here it is intended without such a restriction.
And *aho* [is used as a particle of surprise] || 8.1.40 ||
The formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows; that is, so that the subsequent rule applies only in connection with *ahar*, and not in connection with *tu* and the others.
In the remaining cases, there is an option. (Pāṇini 8.1.41)
"This statement is not one of censure (*aśūyāvacana*). The meaning is that one who censures a thing that is actually not marvelous represents it as if it were marvelous.

[Objection: What is the purpose of stating the remainder (*śeṣavacana*), since it is already understood that by the power of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) alone, nothing from the preceding operations continues [into this rule], and because it has been drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*), the term "in honor" (*pūjāyām*) will be excluded? To this he says: "of the [term] 'in honor' (*pūjāyām*)."
And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] in the sense of wishing to obtain in the past. (Pāṇini 8.1.42)

The word *purā* here indicates the proximity of a future event. It indicates that the lightning and so forth—which constitute an obstacle to study—will occur before long; by this, a sense of urgency is understood. The meaning is that since study is prohibited during lightning and such events in the Dharmaśāstra, the mention of them implies: "Study quickly. In the example, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the future according to the rule *yāvatpurānipātayoḥ*; in the counter-example, it is according to the rule *laṭ sme*.

Regarding the phrase "here, the remoteness of past time": this indicates that the study, being a past action, has been ongoing for a long duration. The sense is that, by means of this, no sense of haste is to be understood here.
The particle *nanu* is used in the sense of seeking permission. 8.1.43.

*Anujñā* (permission) is an acceptance in the form "let it be done thus" toward one who is already personally intent on performing a certain action. He demonstrates the meaning of the *sūtra* by means of an example: "with reference to the instrument" (*karaṇaṃ prati*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), meaning "with reference to the movement of the instrument. In the example, the suffix *laṭ* is used for the present tense. In the counter-example, however, it is used for the past tense by the rule "when there is a reply to a question, with the particle *nañ*" (*nanau pṛṣṭaprativacane*). Like [the rule] "*aṅgāpratilomye*" and others, since the form is already established, the purpose of the particle *iti* is to show that this is a single indeclinable (*nipāta*); otherwise, one might suspect that both particles are being included.
In a question concerning an action, [the particle] *kim* is used with a verbal root that is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*) and is not prohibited [by other rules]. (Pāṇini 8.1.44)

"Unprohibited" (*apratiṣiddham*) means "for the sake of what is not prohibited. Why was the former [example] cited? Because the word *kim* is heard in proximity to it. Why, however, was the latter not cited? Because of the reverse. Regarding the words "others," etc.: it is not the fact of being heard in proximity that is the reason for the connection with the word *kim*, but rather the state of being an object of doubt. And since that [state of being an object of doubt] exists for the second [word] as well, it is connected with that [word *kim*] too; thus, the prohibition applies in both cases—this is the meaning.

As for those who say, "What was previously joined [to the particle *kim*]? they think as follows: "Let both [the preceding word and the verb] be objects of doubt; however, by the word *kim*, a question regarding the very action heard in proximity is indicated, whereas a question regarding another action is indicated by *āho-svit*. This is called a 'question concerning an action' (*kriyā-praśna*), and therefore, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies to that alone."
In the case of elision, there is an option. (Pāṇini 8.1.45)
Since *kim* is the subject under discussion, one might wonder why its elision is understood; therefore, he says: "the elision of *kim*."

Regarding the phrase *kva cāsya* ("And where is this [particle *kim*]"): the question arises because nowhere in the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is the elision (*lopa*) of *kim* prescribed. The answer is that the technical designation "elision" (*lopasaṃjñā*) does not apply only to non-appearance (*adarśana*) as defined by the treatise; rather, it applies to non-appearance in general. Regarding the phrase *yatra* ("where"): it means "it is not employed," because its meaning is understood through context, the subject matter, and so forth. In the example, the word *āho-svit* is used in a question concerning an alternative position, and since that cannot occur without a preceding question, the sense of *kim* is understood from the previous context. Thus he says: "even without *kim*."

"This is an *aprāptavibhāṣā* (an option where [the rule] was not previously established). But how is it an *aprāpti* (non-establishment), given that the preceding rule is connected with the word *kim*? To this he says: "For what purpose? The counter-examples are as before; the meaning is that they are exactly those same examples, but without the word *kim*.
The suffix *lṛṭ* is used after the particle *ehi* when it expresses consent or derision.

Regarding the phrase "by means of *ehi manye*": the singular number is used with the intention of referring to the entire group [of words]. Otherwise, since there would be two verbs (*ākhyāte*) and another word beginning with *āṅ*, the use of the plural number would have resulted. In the example, the change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*) occurs by the rule "and when *manya-* is the accompanying word in jest" (*prahāse ca manyopapade*), etc.
In the phrase "you think well," he expresses the absence of jest by showing that the matter is a reality; for this very reason, no change of person has been made.

[The objection: "Since this is already established by the rule *gatyardhaloṭā luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.13), [the present rule is redundant]. [The reply: It is for the sake of ensuring that [the *luṅ* suffix] does not apply elsewhere. Where else might it not apply? It would apply in cases such as those cited as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) by the author of the Vṛtti, namely: *ehi manyase*, etc. [In these cases, the *luṅ* would incorrectly follow the imperative *loṭ*]. [Explanation: The *loṭ* suffix follows the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*. The second person singular ending *sip* is replaced by *hi*. [The rule is necessary] so that [the *luṅ* prescribed for the future tense] does not occur in other instances. Where else might it not occur? It would occur in those cases which the author of the Vṛtti has cited as counter-examples—such as *ehi manyase* and so forth. In those instances, [if the rule were not stated, the *luṅ* would erroneously apply].

But how is it that by the formulation of the restriction "ehimanye" (in the case of *ehi* with *manye*), the application [of the rule] is excluded in the case of "ehi manyase"? To this he says: "The mention of the highest person (*uttama*) is not a restrictive condition. He states the reason for its being non-restrictive: "For [the word *manye*] occurs only in jest (*prahāsa*). The meaning is that if it were a restrictive condition, there would be no instance to exclude from the rule. In the Bhāṣya, however, the highest person is employed even in the counter-example; the meaning there is: "I think thus: 'Come, you shall go by chariot.'"
The word *jātu* is used with the indeclinable *apūrva*. (Pāṇini 8.1.47)

Regarding the phrase "the word *jātu* [expresses] something unprecedented (*apūrva*)," one might ask: why is "unprecedented-ness" not a qualifier of the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)? This would indeed be appropriate, for when a thing capable of being connected with a qualifier exists as the basis (*nimittin*), it is not proper to apply a qualifier to that which is merely the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) and subordinate. It is replied: because the author employs the term "immediately following" (*anantara*) in the rule "*āho utāho cānantaram*," it is known from this that "unprecedented-ness" is a qualifier of the occasioning cause itself.

Otherwise, since the term "apūrvam" (not preceded) continues to apply there as well, the condition of being immediately followed by a finite verb ending (*tiṅanta*) would be obtained solely from that [continuation]; so what is the use of that [new rule]? But surely it must exist for the purpose of establishing the "remainder" (*śeṣa*): namely, "optionally in the remainder" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*). And what is the remainder? Is the remainder that which is separated by an interval (*sāntara*)? Even without the mention of "immediately following," the remainder is already established. How so? "Not preceded" (*apūrva*) is the subject under discussion; therefore, that which is "preceded" (*sapūrva*) is the remainder.
And the *kivṛtta* is followed by *ciduttara*. || 8.1.48 ||

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*), as in "the occurrence of what" (*kimo vṛttam* = *kiṃvṛttam*). According to the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaśca*, the genitive case is employed in the sense of the agent; however, although the formation of a compound would normally be prohibited by the rule *adhikaraṇavācinā ca*, the compound is nevertheless formed due to this very specific exception (*nipātana*). Considering that if the term *kiṃvṛtta* were taken to include everything where the word *kim* occurs, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including forms such as *kimīyaḥ*, *kaimāyaniḥ*, and *kiṃtarām*, the author provides a restrictive definition by stating: "by the mention of *kiṃvṛtta*... [meaning it refers only to those forms derived from *kim* with the suffixes *vatu* and *kalpap*].

The term *ciduttaram* is an adjective qualifying the interrogative pronoun (*kiṃvṛtta*), not the finite verb (*tiṅanta*); this is known from the previously mentioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) which refers to the general rule.
The particles *āho* and *utāho*, when used immediately after [a preceding word], [take the acute accent on their first syllable]. 8.1.49.
"It is precisely *apūrvi*. For this very reason, there is the mention of *uta*; since the word *āho* is preceded by the word *uta*.
The remaining cases are optional. 8.1.50.

And what is the remainder? Since many [elements] have been introduced as the subject matter, this question is asked. Regarding the phrase "whatever else besides the immediate": the term *uta-āho* must necessarily be supplied to provide the basis for the negation; furthermore, because of the mention of *uta-āho*, the phrase "and something not previously mentioned" (*apūrvam*) is also supplied. In that case, the sense is that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the remainder refers specifically to that which follows immediately.

When an imperative verb (*loṭ*) expressing motion is used with a verb in the *lṛṭ* (future) tense, the *lṛṭ* does not express a different agent (*kāraka*), provided that all other factors remain the same. *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 8.1.51.

"Those whose meaning is 'going' (gati) have the same meaning as the word *gam*. This is an illustration of the meaning; the analytical breakdown (*vigraha*) is "those for whom going is the meaning. The rule (*yoga*) is "joined with an imperative (*loṭ*) having the sense of going. Furthermore, there is a relationship of cause and effect mediated by the meaning: for the meaning expressed by the imperative is the cause (*nimitta*) of that which is expressed by the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*). "If not every other factor becomes a *kāraka*. The intention is that if every other factor were a *kāraka*, then the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent would not apply. In this regard: "Whatever *kāraka* there may be, whether in an imperative or in a periphrastic future..."
When all that is grasped through the discrimination between what should and should not be spoken.
In that case, would this not then apply here as well: "O Brāhmaṇa, carry the rice; O father, eat these"?
For it is precisely where everything is distinct that [the rule] should not apply, as in the two counter-examples presented in the commentary.

And in this case, everything is not distinct because of the non-difference of the object (*śālī-karman*). Now, if the meaning were this—that the prohibition against striking applies when every factor (*kāraka*) is non-distinct, but not when it is distinct in any respect at all—then that would not apply here either: [in the sentence] "Come, Devadatta, to the village; you shall eat rice. For here the object is indeed distinct; therefore, this must be explained. To that he says: "In whichever [case] alone" (*yatraiva*). By the particle *eva*, there is the exclusion of anything other than the expressed [object], but the intention is not to imply the non-distinctness of everything; this has been made clear by the words "only the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmanī eva*).

And this [distinction] is obtained through proximity (*pratyāsatti*); for that which is expressed by that very [verb] is proximate to it. In the examples, in the first and third cases, everything is identical. However, the contingency of *nighāta* (elision of accent) for the word *drakṣyasi* must be considered; because they constitute separate sentences, there is no elision. In the second and fourth cases, the mere denotation of the root *vah* has the sense of "going" (*gatyarthatva*) insofar as it intends the subordinate act of going, whereas its actual meaning here is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). And thus it is said: "The roots *nī*, *vah*, and *hṛ*, as well as those whose meaning is 'going'..."

Thus, the enumeration has been made by way of distinction. Now, one might object: "Power (*śakti*) is the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), and since that power varies with each action, how can the factor here be considered non-different? There is no fault, because the distinction between power and the possessor of power (*śaktimant*) is not intended to be expressed here. The form *āgaccheḥ* contains the suffix *liṅ*, not *leṭ*. In *paśyati*, the suffix is *laṭ*, not *lṛṭ*; in both counter-examples, everything else remains the same. Furthermore, in the Sūtra, it is the individual instance (*vyakti*) of the factor that is understood by the word *kāraka*. Therefore, even though the status of being agent (*kartṛ*) or object (*karman*) is non-different, there is a distinction between factors due to the difference in their individual instances—as in the case of "you and I shall see."

If the term *sarva* ("all") were not employed, the [prohibition of] *nighāta* (non-accentuation) would have to apply only in cases where the expressed meaning does not differ; however, here the expressed meaning does differ—being "one" in one instance and "two" in another—and thus the prohibition of *nighāta* would not occur. But when the term *sarva* is employed, he demonstrates how it is successfully established: "for when the expressed meaning is that ending in *lṛṭ*... and so forth.
And the imperative (loṭ) [is used for the future]. 8.1.52.

"Śādhi": this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *śās*. With the suffix *sip*, *sip* is replaced by *hi*; then, by the rule "śā hau," *śā* is substituted [for *śās*]. Because that substitution is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), the substitution of *dhi* applies by the condition of being a *jhal* sound. The reading "praśādhi" is common, but it is not correct; because it contains a prefix (*upasarga*), it would fall under the scope of the subsequent rule.

The separate formulation of the yoga (sūtra) is for the sake of what follows, so that the option [of the next rule] may apply only to the imperative (*loṭ*) and not to the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*).
And *hanta* [is used] in the sense of encouragement. (Pāṇini 8.1.54)

"Hanta prabhuñjāvahai" (Come, let us both eat). This is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *bhuj*; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "bhujo 'navane" (the root *bhuj* takes the middle voice except in the sense of protecting); then the suffix *vah* is added; the substitution of *e* for *ṭi* occurs; the augment *āṭ* is added to the first person plural (*uttama*) because it is marked with *p*; *e* is substituted for *ai*; and due to its being unaccented (*anudātta*), the *lasārvadhātuka* affix is also unaccented, leaving the accent of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇasvara*).
[The following rule applies: "An *ām* [particle] is separated from a vocative (*āmantrita*) by one word when it is not near. (Pāṇini 8.1.55)

It obstructs, thus it is an *antara*—that which causes an intervention. That which has one *antara* (interval) is *ekāntara*. In the example, since the *nighāta* (elision of accent) is prohibited, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) prescribed by the sixth [chapter] applies; furthermore, there is the *pluta* (protracted vowel) by the rule "and in calling from afar" (*dūrāddhūte ca*). In the word *bhavat*, the substitution of *r* occurs by the rule "optionally for *bhavat*, *bhagavat*, and *aghavat*" (*vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām*); and for the word *ava*, the substitution of *o* occurs. Then, by the rule beginning with "for *bho*, *bhago*, etc. (*bhobhago*), the substitution of *y* occurs, and that *y* is elided by the rule "in the presence of a consonant, all [agree]" (*hali sarveṣām*).

But surely, because of the rule "an addressed word preceding [another] is as if non-existent," the word *bhoḥ* being non-existent, the state of having a single interval (*ekāntaratā*) would not be possible? To this he says: "The word *bho*...

By this [rule], both of those [conditions] are effected. But how can a prohibition of the *ekaśruti* accent be understood when it is neither under discussion nor explicitly mentioned? It is said in reply:

The negative particle *nañ* here expresses the opposite (*vipakṣa*), as in the case of *adharmānṛtādi*. "Non-proximate" (*anantika*) means that which is opposed to proximity; the meaning is "distant. And in that context, the single accent (*ekaśruti*) is prescribed. Consequently, in examples such as "O Devadatta, you cook" (*pacasi devadatta*), the single accent would prevail by setting aside the low-pitched vocative accent (*āmantrita-nighāta*), which finds its scope in cases of proximity. First, that [single accent] is prohibited. Then, when the exception (the single accent) is prohibited, the general rule—the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*)—would apply. That too is prohibited. For if only the single accent were prohibited there, this [rule] would apply in that very instance.

One might say: "The name [of a vocative] is separated by one interval. For if this were so, it would not be necessary to state the rule "a vocative that is not nearby" (*āmantritamanantike*). Since the author states this very point within the section on *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent) even though it is already established, we understand from this that the *nighāta* is also prohibited. Since a prohibition of the *nighāta* alone—which would otherwise be sublated by the single-accentuation (*ekaśruti*)—would be purposeless, the force of the context implies a prohibition of both.

But surely, even the *ekaśruti* (monotone) has its scope in cases such as *devadattā3 āgaccha*, so how can it override the *nighāta* (accentual depression) in cases like *āṃ bho devadatta*, especially since, on the contrary, due to its posteriority, the *nighāta* itself should override the *ekaśruti*, and thus the application of that [rule for *nighāta*] alone would arise here; therefore, the prohibition should logically apply to that [the *nighāta*], and when that is prohibited, the *ekaśruti* would certainly occur? To this they reply: because it depends upon only two words, the *nighāta* is *antaraṅga* (internal) and operates first; thereafter—

Since the single *śruti* (monotone) requires a specific cause—namely, a distant address—it would otherwise follow immediately [after the preceding rule]; however, by the logic previously stated, it sets aside that [single *śruti*] as well as the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). Thus it is well said: "Both of these are effected by this [rule]."

"In that case, just as the single syllable (*ekaśruti*) is set aside, would the protracted acute (*plutodātta*) also be set aside? To this he says: "But the protracted acute... [and] "of others. They think: here the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses similarity, not exclusion; otherwise, one would simply say "at a distance" (*dūre*), and thus there would be no occasion [for the rule], because there is no distance. How then is the protracted vowel cited as an example? To this he says: "The protracted also..."
In the Vedic language, when followed by *yat*, *hit* [is substituted for *dadhāti*].

In the mantra *jāye svo rohāvaihīti*, the verb *ruh* takes the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffix *vas*, and the *śap* augment; by the rule *āḍuttamasya picca*, the *āṭ* augment is added, and because the rule *loṭo laṅvat* causes the imperative to behave like the imperfect (*laṅ*), the elision of the *s* is applied by the rule *nityaṃ ṅitaḥ*. The verb *i* (in *ehi*) takes the imperative with the prefix *ā*. Since the suffix *sip* becomes *hi*, and because the phrase *rohāva* is joined by the subsequent word *ehi*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent—which would otherwise apply by the rule *loṭ ca*—is specifically set aside. Consequently, the *nighāta* accent dependent on the word *sva* does indeed occur.

Now, one might object: since there is the rule "also in the Veda" (*chandasi*), the word *svaḥ* behaves like a prior member [of a compound], and thus *jāye svare* is a vocative (*āmantrita*). Consequently, because of the rule "a preceding vocative is as if non-existent" (*āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat*), the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) would not apply, for its non-existence is prohibited here by the rule "there is a prohibition for indeclinables" (*avyayānāṃ pratiṣedhaḥ*) regarding the behavior like a prior member. This is not so. Here, the behavior like a prior member does indeed apply; for it has been stated in that context: "the mention of the sixth case [is for the sake of] the vocative and the kāraka," and "there is also the inclusion of that which is caused by it."

For the word *svaḥ* ending in the genitive case is not the vocative (*āmantrita*) agent nor its cause; therefore, while it undergoes the treatment of being a member (*aṅgavadbhāva*) with respect to accentuation, it does not become as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*). Consequently, the elision of *r* by the rule *ro ri* does not occur for the word *svaḥ*, and the change to *u* (*utva*) does take place; this is due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*).

Now, why is there not a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the word *ehi* when it is joined with *roha*, by the rule "and the imperative (*loṭ*) [is unaccented]"; for *ruh* is not a verb meaning "to go," since it is mentioned separately in the rule "verbs meaning 'to go,' intransitives, etc."? If it does not mean "to go," then in the cases "men mount the elephant" (*ārohanti hastinaṃ manuṣyāḥ*) and "the elephant makes men mount" (*ārohayati hastī manuṣyān*), the designation of "object" (*karman*) would not apply under the rule "verbs meaning motion, cognition, or eating [make their objects *saṃpradāna* or *karman*]. Therefore, the meaning of *ruh* is the activity consisting of ascending upwards.

And in the rule "gatyarthākarmaka," the inclusion of the term *ruhi* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). However, there is no prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the word *ehi*, because of the statement: "The verb [ending in a personal suffix], when accompanied by a prefix, is optionally [unaccented], except for the last person."
The substitution of *canaci*, *iva*, *gotra* and so forth, taddhita suffixes, and reduplicated forms [for the word *ati*] does not occur when the sense of "not" (*a-*) is understood. (Pāṇini 8.1.57)

Regarding the phrase "here too" (*ihāpi*): the meaning of the word "too" (*api*) is that it is not only in the rule concerning *gotra* and so forth after a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) that this applies. The reason for this has already been established in that very place. As for the example *śuklīkaroti ca*: because there is no prohibition due to the absence of movement (*agati*), the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of accent) indeed occurs here. In the case of *yatkāṣṭham*, the *nighāta* does not apply to the word *śuklī*.
And [the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs] after the particles beginning with *ca*. (Pāṇini 8.1.58)

"These are taken here" because of proximity. Those which are included in the rule *cādayo 'satve* (Pāṇini 1.4.57) are remote. Since he will state in the subsequent sūtra that "conjunction (*samuccaya*) and option (*vikalpa*) are properties of multiple things," the example *khādati ca* ("and he eats") is introduced. However, there is no possibility of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) for this [particle *ca*], because they constitute separate sentences (*nānāvākya*). As for the introduction of *khādati ha* and so forth, it is for the sake of avoiding a break in the continuity of the discourse (*prakrama*). Nevertheless, it is indeed elided (*nihanyate*), because it follows a word within the same sentence that begins with the prefix *pra*.
The nominative case is used in connection with the word *cava*. 8.1.59.

Regarding the phrase "because of non-occurrence" (*agater iti*), [the author] refers to the previous sūtra and so forth. For this very reason, it was stated during the occasion of the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) in the previous sūtra: "In this case, regarding the first finite verb (*tiṅanta*) used with *ca* or *vā*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule 'the first' (*prathamā*) is indeed maintained. He provides the justification for the feminine form of the word "first" (*prathamā*) by stating: "The first [is] the finite verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*).
He states the possibility of the second [case-ending] and others—which are excluded by the mention of "the first"—by saying: "For the connection with *ca* or *vā*..."
The particle *ha* is used in the sense of reproach (*kṣiyā*). 8.1.60.

Transgression of conduct (*ācārabheda*)—this is the violation of established custom. For example: when the preceptor is traveling on foot, it is forbidden for the disciple to travel by chariot—such is transgression of conduct.
The suffix *a* is applied after the root *ah*, in the sense of distribution (*viniyoga*).

"Having various purposes" means that an injunction (*niyoga*)—that is, a command (*preṣaṇa*)—has multiple purposes. And "protracted" (*pluta*): furthermore, that [protraction] is caused by a reproach (*kṣiyā*) in the case of a reproach, and caused by a command (*praiṣa*) in the case of an assignment (*viniyoga*).
The restriction is that there is elision only of *ca* and *ha*. 8.1.62.

In the example, he demonstrates the elision (*lopa*) of *ca*—namely, "and the village. The same should be understood regarding the elision of *aha*. In that regard, in the first case, since Devadatta alone is the agent of both the action having the village as its object and the action having the forest as its object, there is "identity of agent" (*samānakartṛkatva*). In the second case, however, due to the reversal [of the objects], one should observe a "difference of agents" (*nānākartṛkatā*). "Impossibility" (*anavaklṛpti*) means non-occurrence. For one who does not conceive of Devadatta's eating as possible under any circumstances uses the expression: "How indeed will you eat? (*kveva bhokṣyase*).
In the rule "eve cāniyoge," there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*); however, in some versions of the *vṛtti*, this very point is stated therein.
In the case of the words *ca* and so forth, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*).
The preceding rule itself serves the purpose of making the application of the word "eva" (only) mandatory.
And *vaivāva* [is substituted for *vī*] in the Vedic language. 8.1.64.

*vai* is used in the sense of "clearly" (*sphuṭārtha*) and in the sense of "patience" (*kṣamā*). *vāva* is used in the sense of "well-known" (*prasiddhi*) and in the sense of "clearly" (*sphuṭārtha*). [The particle *eva* is used] after the words *eka* and *anya* when they are semantically connected. (Pāṇini 8.1.65)

Those two words whose meanings (*artha*) are equal or identical are *samartha*. The substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs because it is observed in the *śakandhvādi* group, or else there is elision of the final vowel by means of a formal rule (*nipātana*). There is no mutual identity of meaning [between a noun and] a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*), because such a thing is impossible. Furthermore, the sense "conjoined with a verbal suffix" does not apply here, because this very meaning is already established by the continued application of the word "conjunction" (*yoga*) from the rule "the first [word retains its accent] when joined with *ca*, *vā*, or *ha*. Regarding *jinvati*: the root *jivi* has the meaning "to please"; *num* is added because it is marked with the indicatory letter *it*; then there is the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the third person singular ending (*tip*), and the class marker *śap*. Regarding *cākaśīti*: [this is derived from the root *kāś*].

It has been stated that *kaśi* is a different root (*prakṛtyantara*) having the same meaning as *kāśin*; this is its form when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided. Furthermore, [the mention of] the word *eka* is for the sake of establishing the rule. Therefore, the counter-example shown is of that very [root], not of another word; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "because of its deviation": for the word *eka* deviates from its primary sense to mean "other. Indeed, it has been demonstrated in the rule *eko gotre* that this word has multiple meanings. In that context, if the term *samartha* (having the same referent) were not included, there would be the undesirable consequence of including even words with a different meaning, such as *anya* ("other").
Furthermore, we have stated in the rule "nipātairyadyadihanta" that concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is not the determining factor in this context.
The suffix *nityam* [is applied] after the word *vṛtta*. (Pāṇini 8.1.66)

In the verse beginning "What is the derivation of *kiṃvṛtta* and *ciduttara*?", the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of the word *kiṃvṛtta* shown there should be understood here as well. [The author] says, "if this were not accepted. For if that [analysis] were accepted, then [the rule for accentuation] would not apply to forms such as *yadryañ*, *yadīyam*, and *yādāyani*. Regarding *juhumaḥ*: this is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), because the conditions "for reduplicated stems" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*) and "for *bhī*, *hrī*, *bhṛ*, *hu*, *mad*" both contain the term *aci* (before a vowel). Regarding *yadryañ*: from *yad añcati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule "and in the case of *viṣvak* and *deva*," the *ṭi* portion [of *yat*] is replaced by *adrya*.

But how, when there is an instruction by means of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), does [the rule] apply even when there is an intervention—as in *yatkāmās te*, *yadryaṅ*, *vāyuḥ*, and so on? To this he says: "Even here, despite the instruction by the fifth case. This will be made known in the subsequent sūtra. Regarding the phrase *yāthākāmye vā*: *yāthākāmya* is acting according to one's own desire, i.e., independence from place and time; when that is understood, there is an option for the prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent), as in *yatra kvacana yajate*.
The word *pūjita* following *pūjā* is unaccented when it follows words such as *kāṣṭha*. (Pāṇini 8.1.67)

Because the phrase "from *kāṣṭha*, etc. (*kāṣṭhādibhyaḥ*) is seen in the *Vārttika* and is read as a part of the *sūtra*, he explains—in accordance with that—the singular form *pūjanāt* as standing in place of the plural, saying: "from *kāṣṭha*, etc., [used] in the sense of honoring" (*pūjanebhyaḥ kāṣṭhādibhyaḥ*). Regarding the term "the subsequent word" (*uttarapadam*): since the following *sūtra* contains the mention of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and since this present *sūtra* concerns compounds (*samāsa*), it should be understood that [the word] ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*).

Furthermore, these words such as *kāṣṭha* (woodenly) and others are synonyms for "extraordinary" (*adbhuta*) and function as expressions of worship. In that regard, for those [compounds] where the status of being a synonym for "extraordinary" applies only within the scope of their usage—as in the case of *amātāputra* ("not having mother or son") and so on—the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed with another word. In the example *kāṣṭhādhyāpaka* ("one who teaches woodenly"), it is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The word *kāṣṭha* ending in the accusative case is compounded. However, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection to a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) does not occur with adverbial modifiers; the genitive occurs only with respect to that which is the object (*karman*) of the verbal root, because of its association with the term "agent" (*kartṛ*).

For when something is the agent with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies there; by association with that, the object (*karman*) is also understood in exactly the same way. However, an adverbial qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because it stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the meaning of the verbal root, is not an object with respect to it. In every respect, the genitive does not occur after an adverbial qualifier; for this very reason, it will be stated that "the *m* is elided" (*malopa*). If the genitive were present, this [elision] would be untenable due to the absence of the letter *m*.

But how, again, can there be a connection with a qualifier for an action that has become subordinate within a *kṛt*-derived form where the agent is the predominant factor? This is established just like the connection with an instrument (*sādhana*); for example, in expressions such as "gone to the village" (*grāmaṃ gataḥ*), even though the action is subordinate, its connection with the instrument is possible, and likewise its connection with a qualifier is not untenable. In the case of *kāṣṭhābhirūpakaḥ*, since "handsomeness" (*ābhirūpyam*) is qualified by "wood" (*kāṣṭhena*), there is a compound of a neuter word in the nominative singular.

Thus, because wood and other such things are connected only by way of their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) and not by way of denoting substances, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting substances; therefore, the status of being included in the *mayūravyaṃsaka*-class has been resorted to.

Regarding the phrase "and in a compound" (*samāse ca*), etc.: the particle *ca* is used for emphasis. If this [rule] were intended to apply only in a compound, how would one explain the statement made by the author of the Vārttika: "When there is the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) of that which is honored, there is the mention of *kāṣṭha*-etc., and the elision of *m*"? For in a compound, the final *m* of those words cannot occur, because the case-ending has been elided? To this he says: "also by the rule 'and the elision of *m*'. How is the scope of this indicated? To this he says: "wherever... (*yatra*).

For in a compound (*samāsa*), because of the absence of case-endings (*vibhakti*), the letter *m* is not heard; this very [absence] is what is called "elision" (*lopa*). But what is the reason for explaining the Vārttika in this way, by resorting to such a precarious support as a blade of *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass? To this he says: "For in a non-compound" (*asamāse hi*). Others, however, say: if this were intended to apply only to compounds, he would have simply said "in a compound" (*samāse*); but because of the mention of the elision of *m*, this refers specifically to the domain of the sentence (*vākya*). As for forms such as *dāruṇamadhyāpakaḥ*, if such a form is desired, then the elision of *m* must be stated as an optional alternative.

The sense is that [the rule] is established as "from the act of worship" (*pūjanāt*) itself for the purpose of including that which has been worshipped; this is because the act of worship (*pūjana*) is dependent upon that which is to be worshipped (*pūjya*). The intention is that, in order to ensure the understanding of what was worshipped immediately preceding, the general proximity (*ānantarya*) found in the rule *pūjanāt pūjitam* is understood to apply specifically to the particular instances. But how can there be the possibility of something separated [by other words] when the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is specified? To this he says: "This very [point]. He states the purpose of the indication: "And thus... (*tathā ca*).

The phrase "the term *anudātta* being understood" (*anudātta iti vartamāna*) and so forth [is explained as follows]: The mention of *anudātta* under discussion is indeed connected with the prohibition [stated] in the rule *na luṭ* and others; therefore, when that [term] is carried over [into the present rule], the prohibition would also carry over. Although, because this present rule concerns compounds (*samāsa*), such a case does not actually exist where the *nighāta* (elision of accent) in vocatives and the like is prohibited; nevertheless, in subsequent rules such as *kutsane ca supi*, there would only be a prohibition. Therefore, the mention of *anudātta* is repeated in order to exclude that [prohibition].
A verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is also [called *pada*] when it has a preceding member (*sagati*). Pāṇini 8.1.68.

Regarding the example "yatkāṣṭhaṃ pacati" (that which cooks the wood): even those who claim that the elision of *m* occurs by means of the rule "malopaśca," they likewise do not desire such elision when a *tiṅ* suffix follows. [They argue] that because of the inclusion of the term "with its prefix" (*sagatigrahaṇāt*), the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself is also suppressed.

How so? Here, the word *saha* is used in the sense of "simultaneous action" (*tulyayoga*). Wherever the word *saha* occurs in the sense of simultaneous action, there the connection with the action applies to both [elements]; for example, when it is said, "Let him eat together with his son" (*saputro bhojyatām*), the son is also made to eat. The inclusion of the particle *api* is so that [the rule] may apply even to a simple verbal form (*tiṅanta*) where no motion (*gati*) is employed; however, when a motion is employed, it applies to both simultaneously. Because of the mention of *tiṅ*, the preceding rule is understood to concern only nominal stems (*subanta*).

And [the substitution of *ṣat* for *śat*] occurs after a word ending in a *su*-affix when used in the sense of reproach, provided that the following word is not a *gotra* name or similar. (Pāṇini 8.1.69)

"He cooks" (*pacati*) and "he defiles" (*kliśnāti*). One must consider how, in this case, there can be both syntactic unity (*samānavākyatva*) and semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). Let it not be that the censure applies to the agent—as in *pacati pūti* ("he cooks badly")—where the agency itself is censured, meaning "this [action] of his is improper. Rather, the action is indeed excellent; however, the quality of being "bad" (*pūtitva*) is an attribute of the agency and is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the agent. Therefore, as in the case of *dāruṇam abhirūpakam* ("the handsome one is fierce"), the neuter gender is used. In this way, even for two or many agents, only the singular occurs: *pacataḥ pūti* ("the two cook badly") and *pacanti pūtī* ("they cook badly"). Generally, the word *pūti* is recorded as masculine.
Now, one might object: since this verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning, how can the means (*sādhana*), being subordinate, be connected with an adjective? It is replied:
when that which is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in a compound (*vṛtti*) has attained a state of semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*), its connection with an adjective is simply not possible.

For it does not occur that one says "the king’s man who is prosperous" (*ṛddhasya rājapuruṣaḥ*). However, for that [compound] in which there is no unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), even though the [subordinate member] is non-primary, it is connected with a qualifier, as in "the king’s prosperous man" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Likewise, although the means (*sādhana*) is subordinate with respect to the action, it is connected with a qualifier due to unification of meaning, as in "one who studies intensely" (*dāruṇamadhyāyakaḥ*); similarly, in *kṛt*-derived forms where the means is primary, the action, though subordinate, is connected with a qualifier, as in "one who studies intensely."

If it is indeed the case that the means (*sādhana*) is connected with a qualification, then by the same logic, it would also follow that it is connected with another action—just as in the cases: "he cooks and reads," "he cooks and sees," "the cook reads," or "the cook sees"? What can we do? For such things are not observed. This must be understood in this way:
just as a wife does not tolerate her husband's connection with another woman, she nevertheless consents to purificatory rites such as bathing for his own sake.

Likewise, action also—by means of its qualification, it consents to a connection with its own agent; however, it does not allow the agent, who is devoted to it, to go over to another action. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the word *pūti*: the word *pūti* ending in a *tiṅ* suffix is udātta on its first syllable, according to the rule *vasestiṅ*. The suffix *tiṅ* occurs after the root *pū* as well due to the irregularity (*bāhulaka*) [of the rule], and by that same irregularity there is an absence of *guṇa*. The designation *cit* is added [to the suffix] so that it may have an udātta on its final syllable, which is the cause for its suppression (*nighāta*). Regarding the term *vibhāṣitam*: a *tiṅ*-ending word with many meanings is optionally suppressed; when it is suppressed, then *pūti* has the udātta on its final syllable.

Regarding what was stated beginning with "kriyākutsane" (in the case of censuring an action), he recites the Āryā verse cited in the Bhāṣya as an authoritative source: "supi kutsane" (when a *kutsana* [censure] follows a *sup* suffix) and "malopa iṣṭo 'tiṅi coktārtham" (the elision of the suffix *m* is desired when not followed by a *tiṅ* suffix, and this is for the sake of expressing the meaning already stated). This is the sense in the Bhāṣya: when the author of the Vārttika stated "and the elision of *m*," the elision of *m* is not desired after a *tiṅ* suffix—as in "dāruṇaṃ pacati" (he cooks harshly). Thus, the statement "and the elision of *m*" was declared by the Teacher to have its purpose already explained. However, in the Vṛtti, this quarter-verse is recited because it occurs within a verse (*śloka*), yet it has no application here; for it has been stated that "this non-accentuation is desired in the case of a compound."
The word *gati* [is compounded] with a word ending in the locative case [to form a tatpuruṣa compound]. || 8.1.70 ||

Regarding the term *abhyuddharati*: the act of taking away (*haraṇa*) is understood as common to all prefixes (*upasarga*). One specifies that by saying *uddharati*; from *ut* alone, "upwardness" (*ūrdhvatā*) is understood as qualified [by that act]. One further specifies that by saying *abhyuddharati*. In this regard:

"Although there is no status as 'motion' (*gati*) between the two [prefixes] in relation to one another, nevertheless, because they are motions in relation to the action, *abhi* is designated as the motion within the motion."
Regarding "samudānayati," there is elision (nighāta) of both *sam* and *ud*. Regarding "abhisamparyāharati," there is elision of all three.

Why is it specified "when [the prefix] has occurred"? A prefix occurs in relation to an action (*kriyā*), and action is expressed by a verbal root (*dhātu*). Verbal roots are of two kinds: those accompanied by a prefix (*sagati*) and those without a prefix (*agati*). Suffixes (*pratyaya*) also occur after the verbal root in two ways: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. In that regard, when a word ends in a *kṛt* suffix, whether the prefix is present or absent, once the accent of the *kṛt* suffix or the accent of the *tha-thādi* group has been applied, the prefix is indeed suppressed by the rule of residual low-pitch (*śeṣanighāta*).

Even in the case of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) that possesses an acute accent (*udāttavat*), the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) certainly occurs by the subsequent rule; however, in the case of one that is grave (*anudātta*), it will not occur because of the reliance on a restrictive rule (*niyama*). [The question is: "If it occurs in a finite verb, it occurs only when it possesses an acute accent; therefore, only a finite verb accompanied by a prefix (*sagati*) remains. [The example is] *āmandraiḥ*. Now, a word becomes a prefix (*gati*) only when it is connected with an action (*kriyāyoga*); yet here there is no connection of the prefix *āṅ* with an action, because the word *mandra* does not denote an action? To this he says: "One understands [the meaning] as 'go' (*yāhi*)."

The rule "they [gatis] precede the verbal root" (*te prāgdhātoḥ*) is a restriction regarding usage (*prayoga*), not a restriction regarding technical designation (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that even when there is an intervention [by other words], the status of being a *gati* still exists. Objection: Since the prefixes (*pra* etc. receive the designations of *gati* or *upasarga* only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) they are connected to, then—just as *mandram* is not a *gati* with respect to the word *yāhi*, and thus the designation does not apply—the same would not apply here either in the case of *abhyuddharati*, because *udam* is not a *gati* with respect to [the action denoted by] *abhi*. Response: Let it be that it is not a *gati* with respect to *udam*; however, [it is a *gati*] with respect to the entire complex (*samudāya*).

The prefix *prati* becomes a *gati* [prefix]. Indeed, a specific action is qualified by the prefix *abhi*. In the case of *ā mandraiḥ*, too, the act of coming (*āyāna*)—which has Indra as its agent and the soft-sounding [horses] (*mandra*) as its instrument—is qualified by the prefix *ā*; thus, since *ā* is a *gati* with respect to the whole which denotes a specific action, does it not follow that the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) should apply? It does not so apply; for the verbal root is first joined with the prefix, and only afterwards with the grammatical factor (*sādhana*). For the soft-sounding [horses] function as the instrument (*sādhana*) in the act of coming—as in "Come with the soft-sounding bay horses" (*mandrair haribhir āyāhi*)—but not in the act of going.

Consequently, since the prefix *pra-* does not function as a "gati" (preverb) with respect to the whole compound, there is no such contingency here at all. To this, he replies: "of that" (*tasya*). For if the subsequent cause were not taken into account, one could not understand [the rule] as "those particles like *pra-* which are joined with an action, with respect to that [action]. And thus, he considers that the elision of accent (*nighāta*) would result based on the actual status of being a *gati*.

If, however, by virtue of the governing rule "of a word" (*padasya*) and the application of the technical paribhāṣā regarding semantic competency (*samartha*), it is understood that "the [suffix] is applied with respect to that which possesses semantic competency with the motion," then it would be possible to omit the mention of "in the case of motion" (*gateḥ*). As he says: "If the [verbal suffixes] were non-udātta by virtue of being a motion, the mention of 'motion' would be redundant; if it is argued that it is for the sake of the Vedic language because of the restriction to finite verbs (*tiṅ*), we say no, because it is not a motion."
And [the augment *naṭ* is applied] before a finite verb ending (*tiṅ*) that bears an acute accent (*udātta*).

In the example, because of the prohibition of *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule "not [after] particles such as *yat*, *yadi*, etc.," the *tiṅ*-ending word retains its acute (*udātta*) accent. What is the purpose of mentioning *tiṅ*? It is so that it may apply to a form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix, but not to the word *mandra*—as in: *ā mandrair indra haribhir yāhi*. The word *mandra* ends in the suffix *rak* and is oxytone (acute on the final syllable).

One might object: "Since the rule *yatkriyāyuktāḥ* states that [words] connected with an action [denote the agent], the word *gati*—being a relative term like the words *pitṛ* ('father') and so on—necessarily implies its own correlative. Thus, even when accented, it will denote the action itself; furthermore, the absence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding forms ending in *kṛt* suffixes has already been stated in the preceding rule. Therefore, there is no purpose in including the mention of *tiṅ*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*tiṅgrahaṇam*" (the mention of *tiṅ*). "Measure" (*parimāṇa*) means "limitation" (*iyattā*). He clarifies precisely what is meant by "having the sense of measure"—namely, "otherwise, indeed... and so forth.

If the mention of *tiṅ* (the verbal suffix) were not made, since only the verbal root (*dhātu*) expresses action, it would be the cause for the designation *gati*; consequently, the *nighāta* (elision of accent) would occur only before that which possesses the acute accent within the root itself, and not before the suffix. However, because of the mention of *tiṅ*, even though the suffix has the acute accent, the *gati* designation applies to the entire *tiṅ*-ending form as a whole with respect to the stem portion. Thus, the *gati* designation is with respect to the root alone. The compound *yasya kriyā yatkriyā* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the meaning is "with respect to that whose expressed action [it is]. And since that action is expressed by the root alone, the status of being a *gati* is with respect to that [root] alone.

[Objection: In that case, it would not apply to forms ending in *ām*. [Reply: But surely, even if the mention of *tiṅ* were not made, it would still not apply to forms ending in *ām*; for it has already been established that since a suffix is inherently acute (*udātta*), it would not apply even to forms ending in *tiṅ* when they possess an acute accent—so what need be said of forms ending in *ām*? Why, then, is it said, "In that case, [it does not apply] to forms ending in *ām*"? [Response: In this regard, the meaning is as follows: if [the rule] applies to *prakurute* and so forth by virtue of the effort made in mentioning *tiṅ*, then it would not apply to its [corresponding] form ending in *ām*, because that [form] lacks the *tiṅ* element.

Therefore, one must resort to the *karmadhāraya* compound "that action which is an action" (*yā kriyā yatkriyā*). For in this way, [the word] has the status of a "motion" (*gati*) with respect to the meaning characterized as action; since an operation cannot apply to that [abstract] meaning, when an operation is understood to apply to what expresses it, it is established everywhere in cases where action is predominant. To settle the objection just mentioned within a specific position, he says: "In this regard, some... (*atra kecit*).

In this view, the meaning of the rule *gatikārakopapadānām* is as follows: compounds of *gati*-elements, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s occur without distinction; however, in the case of *kṛt*-derivatives, they occur prior to the production of the nominal suffix (*sub*). Regarding the phrase "when there is the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) in the case of an indeclinable (*avyaya*)": since the mention of *kṛt* in the rule *gatikārakopapadāt* remains established for the sake of forms such as *prapacati* and the like, and has not been rejected, he considers that only the original accent of the first member is applicable here. This is stated even though the mention of *tiṅ* [in the rule] is not being made.

Or rather, it has just been stated how, when the mention of *tiṅ* is made, the *nighāta* (elision of accent) is established provided that [the preceding word] possesses an acute accent (*udātta*). Now, regarding the phrase "of that which ends in *tarap*": how this alternative is possible and what the defect in this alternative is—all of that has already been explained under the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yeṣāṃ tu* and so forth: the meaning is that for words such as *kugatī* and others, [the compound] occurs only with a *kṛdanta* [word], and even in that case, prior to the production of the nominal suffix (*sup*). Therefore, an effort must be made [to justify this]. In this regard, the effort is as follows: the mention of *tiṅ* (verbal suffix) will not be made; rather, it will be understood as "whatever action" (*yā kriyā*) or "whose action" (*yatkriyā*).
*Āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat* || 8.1.72 || [An] *āmantrita* (vocative) that precedes [another word] is treated as if it were non-existent.

In what sense is this "as if non-existent"? He says: "When that [is present]," and so forth. Regarding the point that when that is present, the effect does not occur, he provides an example: "The non-application of the *anudātta* accent to a vocative (*āmantrita*) and a finite verb (*tiṅ*). Regarding the point that when that is absent, the effect does occur, he provides an example: "In the case of honor," and so forth. [This refers to] when the acute accent (*udātta*) is to be applied to the vocative.

If the mention of "pūrva" (preceding) were not present, then when it is stated that "an *āmantrita* is as if non-existent," even though its own initial syllable is udātta, it would be treated as non-existent when a rule belonging to the sixth [chapter] (*ṣāṣṭhika*) is to be applied. What, then, would be its scope? Its scope would be where the status of being "as if non-existent" is either prohibited or made optional; likewise, because of the governing heading "not at the beginning of a *pāda*," the beginning of a *pāda* is also its scope—as in *uṣo no adhaṣu havā vyucchan*, for here the change of *naṣ* to *nas* occurs precisely because of the status of being "as if non-existent."

In the case of *indra tvā vṛṣabham vayam*, there is the injunction *tvādeśaḥ*.
