But then, in such instances as *indra piba tulyaṃ suto madāya*, *indra piba vṛṣabhūtasya vṛṣṇaḥ*, *agne yāhi śastribhiḥ*, and *vāyo yāhi śivādiva*, would not the suppression of the accent (*tiṅ-nighāta*) apply? An effort must be made here [to prevent this], for it was stated previously: "The governing rule *apādādau* (not at the beginning of a quarter-verse) extends until the end of the chapter."

If [the rule] "an *āmantrita* preceding [another word] is as if non-existent" were applied, then in the example *devadatta pacasi*, because the word *devadatta* precedes that which depends on *pacasi*, it would be as if non-existent; consequently, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the vocative would not occur. To address this, he says: "And as for 'preceding-ness'. Since the word "preceding" is a relative term, the status of being non-existent applies only with respect to the grammatical operation [of the subsequent element] for which it is preceding, and not with respect to its own operation; thus, there is no such fault. This is the meaning.

By the word "kārya" (the operation), he shows this: here, the operation is extended as if it were non-existent. In that context, because the preceding term is a relative term, one relies merely on the fact that [the operation] is to be performed upon the subsequent element; however, it does not mean that [the preceding element] is non-existent with respect to the subsequent element, but rather that it is existent with respect to the preceding element. This is the meaning.

In the phrase *imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati*, the word *gaṅge* is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) only with respect to the word *yamune*, but not with respect to the word *me*. Due to this intervention, the word *me* would not be the cause for the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) of the word *yamune*. However, according to the meaning as demonstrated here—namely, that "when an operation is to be performed on a subsequent element"—there is no distinction as to whether that operation is caused by itself or by something else. Consequently, even when the *nighāta* depends upon the word *me*, the status of *gaṅge* as being non-existent is established. This very point was indicated in the rule: "whether [the cause] is its own cause or another's cause."

He demonstrates what has been stated in this way with the words "here," and so forth. The meaning is that the word *gaṅgā* does not itself function as the cause [of denotation] because it is as if non-existent; however, it does not obstruct the status of the word *me* as a cause. For such would indeed be the case if one were to maintain that [the word *gaṅgā*] is as if non-existent in relation to another.

But surely, even without the use of the suffix *-vat*, an extension (*atideśa*) is observed in rules such as *goto ṇit*; so what is the purpose of the suffix *-vat* here? [Objection: If the suffix *-vat* were not present, when it is stated that "the preceding vocative is as if non-existent," would there not be the cessation of the preceding vocative? [Response: This is not a fault; since a word is employed for the sake of conveying meaning, as long as the meaning has not ceased, there can be no cessation of the word.

Furthermore, could it be intended that the subsequent application (*paraprayoga*) should occur, while the prior application (*pūrvaprayoga*) should not? Even so, one would have to state "or [the word] following the vocative in the *rājadantādi* group," meaning that only the subsequent word becomes the vocative, not the preceding one. Thus, even without the suffix *-vat*, the extension (*atideśa*) is established. What, then, is the purpose [of the suffix]? It is so that the operation may also apply to its own original locus (*svāśraya*): for instance, in "Āṃ bho Devadatta," the status of being separated by one intervening word (*ekāntara*)—as prescribed by the rule "The vocative separated by one word from *āṃ* is [treated as such] when not near"—is maintained.

For the scope of the subsequent sūtra is indeed that which ends in the singular number; however, in the case of a plural ending, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *nighāta* (elision of the accent) under the alternative view: "the plural is optionally [unaccented] when expressing a specific distinction. Even though, in the case of an extended application (*atideśa*), the inherent property of the original base (*svāśraya*) occurs provided it does not conflict with the operation of the extension—even without the use of the suffix *-vat*—nevertheless, here, due to the deliberate employment of the suffix *-vat*, even something conflicting is occasionally obtained. For being separated by one intervening syllable (*ekāntaratā*) is indeed opposed to the state of being as if non-existent (*avidyamānavattva*). And because of the authoritative explanation (*vyākhyāna*), an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) should not be raised.
When not addressed, a word denoting a general category [is compounded] with a word in grammatical apposition. 8.1.73.

He states that two negatives indicate the original meaning: "What then? It is as if they were present. For example: *māṇavaka jaṭilakādhyāpaka* ("O boy, you who have matted hair, teacher!"). Here, the word *jaṭila* (one with matted hair) is a specific term in relation to the word *māṇavaka* (boy), but a general term in relation to the word *adhyāpaka* (teacher). Thus, for both [the first and the second], there is no state of being non-existent. By the words "of the former," etc., he demonstrates the purpose of the prohibition. For example: *devadattayajñadatta*.

The author will state in the subsequent sūtra that "a general term depends upon a specific term. Consequently, just as the word *yajñadatta* does not function as a term of common reference (*samānādhikaraṇa*), so too the word *devadatta*—even though it expresses a specific form belonging to the meaning of the preceding vocative—does not become a general term. Therefore, because it lacks two constituent factors, this [interpretation] is to be reconsidered. For it has been stated thus:

In the *Taittirīyaka Brāhmaṇa*, with reference to the thousandth [cow], it says: "O *iḍā*, O *rantī*, O *aditi*, O *sarasvatī*, O beloved, O most dear, O great, O renowned—these, O inviolable one, are your names. However, the reading in the *Vṛtti* is different and should be seen in another recension (*śākhā*).
The term *vibhāṣita* is used in the sense of "optional" (*viśeṣavacana*). (Pāṇini 8.1.74)

The inclusion of the word "bahuvacanam" (plural) is an interpolation, as it is not seen in the Vārttika. "Refuge" (*śaraṇa*) is the attainment [of safety] by way of seeking protection; those who are fit for that are "refuge-worthy" (*śaraṇya*). For the word *śaraṇa* is indeed seen to be used in the sense of one who provides refuge—as in the phrase, "You are our refuge, O protector from arrows. In the reading *śarmaṇyāḥ*, those who are fit for happiness (*śarman*) are "happiness-worthy" (*śarmaṇyāḥ*). [The objection is raised: "Precisely because of the governing rule concerning words denoting generalities (*sāmānyavacana*). Since a generality depends upon particulars, that toward which something is a generality must be a word denoting a particular (*viśeṣavacana*); therefore, [the suffix] will apply only in that case.
Thus ends the first quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra; [this concludes] the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
Now begins the second quarter of the eighth chapter.
That which was previously established is not considered valid for the purpose of subsequent operations. (Pāṇini 8.2.1)

The rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (VI. 4. 22) is an *adhikāra* (governing heading). If, however, it were an independent injunction (*vidhi*), then it would mean that the aforementioned collection characterized by the "three feet" (*tripādī*) is declared to be non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the preceding collection characterized by the "seven chapters plus one quarter" (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*); it would not, however, establish the non-existence of what follows with respect to what precedes within the three feet themselves. Consequently, in forms such as *guḍaliṇmān* and *godhuṅmān*, since the substitution of *ḍha* and *gha* would not be considered non-existent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *va* for *matup* according to the rule *jhayaḥ*.

Therefore, it is not an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, if it were a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), then because throughout the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* a subsequent rule is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to a preceding one, in cases such as *tena*, *taiḥ*, and *tasya*, when suffixes beginning with *in-* (i.e., *ina*, *inas*, *inaḥ*) are to be applied, the substitution of *yatva* for the pronouns *tyad-* etc. would be non-existent; consequently, the suffixes beginning with *in-*—which are conditioned by a stem ending in *a*—would not occur. Therefore, it is an governing heading (*adhikāra*). This being the case, he shows what is accomplished by this [heading] with the words "therein" (*tatra*). "Therein" means when that governing heading is present.

For if this were an *adhikāra* (heading), then the rules contained in the three chapters [the *tripādī*] would, without distinction, be considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to those in the first seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*), and the rules of the *tripādī* would likewise be established as *asiddha* with respect to what precedes them. However, in the case of a *vidhi* (injunction), it is not possible to achieve this much, because the status of being *asiddha* for what follows with respect to what precedes cannot be applied within the *tripādī* itself. Furthermore, in the case of a *paribhāṣā* (interpretive rule), it does not conclude at this point, as it would apply everywhere indiscriminately. Therefore, because it is an *adhikāra*, it achieves precisely this much.

The meaning is that this much alone is accomplished. Furthermore, one should not be confused here by thinking: "By the statement 'this seven-chapter section with its supplement has been enumerated,' an application (*pravṛtti*) in the form of a rule (*vidhi*) is shown; whereas by 'from here onwards' and so forth, an application in the form of a governing heading (*adhikāra*) is shown; therefore, as in the case of [the term] *śeṣa*, there is both a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and a governing heading (*adhikāra*). This is because such a distinction would be purposeless, and because it has already been stated that "this is a governing heading."

For what indeed is not established by this very governing rule (*adhikāra*), for the sake of which a formal injunction (*vidhi*) would have to be resorted to? The term *saptādhyāyī* is a compound meaning "the collection of seven chapters," and *sapādā-saptādhyāyī* is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound meaning "the seven-chapter work together with its quarter. However, in the reading where *sapādā* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, it is not a compound. The reading *uttarottaro yogaḥ* [is adopted] because reduplication (*dvirvacana*) cannot occur in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*) when the case-ending elision (*subluk*) is impossible. Here, by the mention of "chapters" (*adhyāya*) and "junctions" (*yoga*), he demonstrates that the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) within the treatise is being relied upon.

And this is understood from the statement "as before" (*pūrvavat*). For the *śāstra* possesses primacy due to its specific structural arrangement; however, the primacy of the *kārya* (the grammatical operation) is merely figurative, being mediated by the *śāstra*. Indeed, when the primary sense is possible, it is not proper to adopt a secondary one. But how can it be said that the *śāstra*, having been uttered, is unestablished (*asiddha*)? For even by a hundred utterances, that which is established cannot become unestablished. To this he says: the meaning is that it does not produce an established form (*siddhakāya*).

The meaning is that an extension (*atideśa*) is resorted to on the basis of an explicit statement (*vacana*). It has been shown that the non-establishment (*asiddhatva*) of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) is resorted to, not that of the operation (*kārya*).

Regarding this, he states the purpose: "This very [point]," meaning that which is the statement of non-establishment (*asiddhavacana*) concerning the subject matter of the treatise. It is for the sake of prohibiting an operation (*kārya*) for which an *ādeśa* (substitute), *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic), or *nimitta* (cause) exists; it is called an *utsarga* because it is set aside (*utsṛjyate*) or removed by the *ādeśa*. Furthermore, the statement of non-establishment is for the purpose that the state or occurrence (*bhāva*)—that is, the application (*pravṛtti*)—of that for which the *sthānin* (the original element) is the *lakṣaṇa* or *nimitta* should take place. However, if the operation itself were non-established, the occurrence of that which has the *sthānin* as its characteristic would not be established.

In this regard, he provides an example of the prohibition based on the characteristic of a substitute (*ādeśa-lakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*): "asmā uddhara," and so forth. When *āya* and *āv* have been applied, there is elision (*lopa*) according to the rule "lopaḥ śākalyasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.19). [The phrase] "because the elision of *v* is not established" (*vyalopasyāsiddhatvāt*) means that the non-establishment of the elision of *v* is mediated by the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). For when a subsequent rule is not established in the presence of a preceding rule, then the operation prescribed by that [subsequent rule] is all the more not established. He provides an example of the existence based on the characteristic of the original form (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*): "amuṣmai."

If this [the substitution of *ma* for *da*] were not treated as *asiddha*, then because it would be subsequent, the rule "for *adas-* with *as-* ending in *ā*, *dāt* becomes *dau* and *ma*" would apply; once *utva* had occurred, the forms *smāy-* and so on would not be possible. However, if it is treated as *asiddha*, then first the forms *smā-* and so on arise, and afterwards *utva* occurs; thus the desired result is established. The phrase "of *utva*" means "of the grammatical rule (*śāstra*) concerning *utva*.

The verse beginning with *śuṣkikā* is an illustration (*nidarśana*). Here, the term "illustration" is connected to each [example]. The meaning is that an "illustration" refers to the direction of examples. When the substitution of *vat* for the suffix *mat* is to be applied, if the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops) by the rule "at the end of a word, *jhal* sounds become *jaś*" were *asiddha*, then the form *guḍaliṇmān* would be observed.

The prohibition of *puṃvadbhāva* (the treatment as a masculine) by the rule *na kopadhāyāḥ* does not apply here. This purpose was stated without relying on the principle that "in the prohibition regarding words ending in *ka*, the term *taddhita* must be understood [to include *vu*-affixes]. Thus, we have *kṣāmimān*: the change of the *ta* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix to *ma* occurs by the rule *kṣāyo maḥ*; from that form ending in *iñ* (by the rule *ata iñ*), the affix *in* is added by the rule *ata iniṭhanau*, or else the possessive suffix *matup* is added to that form ending in *in*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *vaha*: from the root *vah* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇe*), there is the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix -ta). Then, by the rule for *samprasāraṇa*, the *va* becomes *u*. By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ*, the *h* becomes *ḍh*. By the rule *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*, the *t* becomes *dh*. By the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, the *dh* becomes *ṣṭ*. By the rule *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ*, the first *ḍh* is elided. By the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho'ṇaḥ*, the preceding vowel is lengthened, resulting in the form *ūḍha*. Once this is established, when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, the *ṭi* portion is elided. Then follows the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, and by the rule *che caṅ*, the reduplication occurs. Thus, the element *hata* is reduplicated.

Because of the rule "of a second [root] beginning with a vowel" (*ajāder dvitīyasya*), and from that, by the rules "the remaining is the first consonant" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*) and "c becomes cu for ku and hu" (*kuhoś cuḥ*), there is the substitution of *cu*—namely, *jha* for *ha*; and for that, by the rule "in reduplication, *ca* and *ja* [are substituted]" (*abhyāse car ca*), there is the substitution of *ja* (the *jaś*-substitution), resulting in *jāj*. Now, why does the substitution of *i* (as in *sanvalliṭor dīrgho 'nyatarasyām*) not occur here by the rule "like *san*" (*sanvallaghuni*)? To this he says: because of the statement "when there is no elision of *a*" (*anaglope*). But how then does *aujiḍhat* come to be? To this he says: because of the statement "when there is no elision of *a*."

But how does [the form] *aujiḍhat* come about? To this he says: "As for this *aujiḍhat*, however... Here, the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane* (P. 8.2.1) applies; because [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*] is not obligatory (*anitya*). Its non-obligatoriness is understood from the statement *ubhau sābhyāsasya* (P. 8.4.21); otherwise, once the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in *aniti* has been effected, that [substitution] would be established, and when doubling occurs together with the *ṇ*, the form *prāṇiṇivat* would be correctly formed.

Regarding the form *guḍaliṇmān*: [the derivation is as follows: from *guḍam leḍhi*, the suffix *kvip* is applied; then the possessive suffix *matup* is added to that form. After the application of the rules for changing *ḍha* to *ja* (i.e., *ḍa* to *la*), the letter *ṇa* is substituted by the rule: "In the case of a *taddhita* suffix, there is an obligatory statement regarding the nasalization of a *yara* sound in the common language (*bhāṣā*). Thus, the form is *guḍaliṇmān*.

Regarding the "indications by the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśāḥ*), such as *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* ("there is elision of [a consonant] at the end of a conjunct"), the "indications by the fifth case" (*pañcamīnirdeśāḥ*), such as *hrasvādaṅgāt* ("after a short vowel, when it is part of a stem"), and the "indications by the seventh case" (*saptamīnirdeśāḥ*), such as *jhalo jhali* ("when a *jh* sound follows a *jh* sound"), there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatva*). If that were the case, then in the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*, because the principle *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* ("the sixth case indicates the element to be replaced") would be absent, its corollary *alo 'ntyasya* ("the final [element] of what precedes") would not apply; consequently, the undesirable result would follow that the entire word would be subject to elision.

In the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt* as well, because the directional terms (*dikśabda*) are supplied without restriction, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of elision for both what precedes and what follows. In the rule *jhalo jhali*, if the locative case were understood as denoting a locus of proximity (*aupaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*), there would again be an application without distinction between what precedes and what follows. However, if it is understood as a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*), then there would be an application even for what is separated [by other elements]. But how is it that those [rules] do not remain "unestablished" (*asiddha*) when the preceding *paribhāṣās* (metarules) are to be applied? To this he says: "For [the rules] are of the time of the operation (*kāryakālam*). The compound *saṃjñāparibhāṣam* is a collective copulative (*samāhāra-dvandva*). This is the intended meaning: [The *paribhāṣās* are brought forward to the place where the operations are to take effect. Because they are brought forward to the place where the operations are to take effect, they are not considered unestablished with respect to those [operations]. For it is a settled principle that when a rule is brought forward to another location, it does not become unestablished with respect to that location. Therefore, since these [rules] are brought forward to the place where the operations are to take effect, they are not unestablished with respect to those operations. Thus, the objection is refuted. Designations are for the sake of others, and technical definitions are likewise;
they do not function independently, and therefore they are not the causes for the comprehension of the actual effect.
Thinking, "Let these be subordinate to many principal [elements]," the Teacher taught these separately in different locations.
"By means of injunctive sentences, even when combined and situated here and there,
these subsequent [sentences] do not have a single preceding [sentence] as their basis, for they bring about their own respective effects."

If the technical rules (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*) were to apply at the time of the operation, then this rule—"In case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]" (*vipratiṣedhe param*)—would also apply here. Consequently, in forms such as *visphoryam* and *avagoryam*, the lengthening by the rule "also before a consonant" (*hali ca*) would occur, superseding the *guṇa* substitution due to its subsequent position. To this, he says: "But this [rule], 'In case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]...'"; the connection is that "this, however, does not operate. The reason for this is stated with the word "because" (*yena*); for conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is indeed the cause for the application of that [rule].

And what is this contradiction? It is the contingency of both [rules], being of equal strength, operating upon the same object simultaneously—like "you" and "I. But this is not possible here; therefore, the meaning is that because the cause (the necessary condition) is absent, [the rule] does not operate. If this is so, would not even a subsequent exception (*apavāda*) fail to sublate a preceding general rule (*utsarga*)? To this he says: "of the exception" (*apavādasya*). For if the exception were unestablished, the general rule alone would prevail, and the formulation of the exception would be useless.

The elision of *n* [of the suffix *ni*] does not take place before a case-ending (*sup*), a word accent (*svara*), a technical name (*saṃjñā*), or a rule concerning the augment *tuṭ*, provided that a *kṛt* suffix follows.

In this sūtra and in the subsequent sūtra, because the effect is mentioned as the basis for the operation (*upādāna*), it is stated that an effect is not established with respect to another effect. However, the term *kṛti* is connected only with the rule for the augment *tuṅ*, due to both possibility and non-deviation. The word *vidhi* functions as both an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and an action noun (*karmasādhana*); here, there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the three abstract nouns and the one action noun, because a single remainder is prescribed even for words of different meanings provided they are homophonous.

*Vidhi*, *vidhi*, and *vidhi* constitute *vidhayaḥ*; thus, there is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) of the word *vidhi* in the plural form with the *dvandva* compound consisting of *su* and the others. In all cases, the genitive is used in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Among these, in the rule concerning *su*-suffixes (*subvidhi*), the "remainder" is indeed the remainder itself; however, in the other rules, the object (*karman*) is intended as the "remainder. This is what was stated: "This word *vidhi*," and so forth. "With that which ends in a genitive expressing a general relation" means that a general relation is expressed by the genitive case, and [the compound is formed] with that which ends in such a genitive.

By means of the general term [“sup”], there is an exclusion of connection with a specific place. But how is it that the status of being a general term is obtained when the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) “the genitive [case ending] denotes connection with a place” (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*) exists? It is said in reply: here nothing is prescribed in place of *sup*; rather, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*)—namely, "wherever there is a rule for *sup*, therein [this applies]. And a technical rule does not operate upon a restatement; this is indicated by the inclusion of the word "place" (*sthāna*) in the rule "in place of *āt* according to the Northern Grammarians" (*udīcām ātaḥ sthāne*).

Regarding what was stated—that [the rule] applies with a genitive case ending expressing a general relationship—he states the purpose there as follows: "In place of *sup*," and so forth. "All this is a rule concerning *sup*" means that because everything here is related to *sup*, this mention of "rule" (*vidhi*) is made specifically for the sake of *sup*. However, there is no purpose in the case of the *svarādi* group; therefore, just as in the rule *na mu ne*, the meaning becomes "when the substitution of *nā* is to be performed," so too in the case of the *svarādi* group, the meaning will be "when [the operations] belonging to the *svarādi* group are to be performed."

However, since a connection with each member [of a *dvandva*] following a *dvandva* compound would be unavoidable, the interpretation as a noun-based derivation (*bhāvasādhana*) has been accepted. But when it is stated, "In the case of suffix rules, accent rules, technical names (*saṃjñā*), and the *tu*-augment," nothing remains to be accomplished through effort.

Regarding *rājavatī*: from the word ending in the *matup* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*. Since the word *rājan* ends in the suffix *kanin*, it is acutely accented on its first syllable. Regarding *pañcārma*: this is a compound formed by the rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. When the *n* is elided there, the preceding member ends in the vowel *a*, and thus an accent would have been required; however, because [the elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), that does not occur, and the compound accent alone prevails.

Regarding *pañcadaṇḍī*: this is a collective dvigu compound. Because the elision of the *n* (nalopa) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the designation "six" (*ṣaṭ*) applies according to the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*. This should be understood as stated without relying on what was said there—namely, that "the mention of *astan* is for the sake of understanding the original form (*aupadeśika*)"—for in this case, the prohibition of the suffix *ṭāp* by the rule *na ṣaṭsvastrādibhyaḥ* occurs. For here, although *ṭāp* would have been applicable due to the ending in *n*, it is also prohibited.

"Because there is a general injunction of prohibition stating, 'That which was stated regarding the feminine does not apply,' how then does this purpose come about? This question is intended to show that the purpose is only occasional (pākṣikatva)."

The view of some is as follows: first, a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is assigned without reference to any specific operation; subsequently, in whatever state a particular operation is applicable, that operation is performed, just as in common worldly practice. For example, in the world, when the tenth day has arrived, one gives a name to a son; once the name has been given, all subsequent operations are carried out by means of that single name, rather than assigning a new name for each individual operation. This is the position known as *yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam* ("the technical names and rules [apply] according to their enunciation").

In the view that the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is applied at the time of each specific grammatical operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), however, the technical name is established by the definition-sūtra (*saṃjñāsūtra*) which has entered into syntactic unity with each respective prescriptive rule (*vidhivākya*); thus, the application of the technical name occurs for every individual operation. Regarding this, in the first view, since the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is already accomplished by that very same technical name which serves to effect the elision (*luk*) of the nominative and accusative plural endings (*jaś-śas*), this [prohibition] is not a purpose [of the definition]. But in the second position, it does serve as a purpose; thus he says: "If for every operation... He asks: "How then is it a purpose? and replies: "For that which..."

"Regarding the phrase *jaśśasorlugarthā*: this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood as being for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṅīp*. Regarding the phrase *strīpratyayasya*: the meaning is "of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. Now, in the first alternative (*pakṣa*), the mention of the technical term (*saṃjñā*) need not be made. For here—in the case of *daṇḍiguptau* and *guptadaṇḍinau*—once the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) has occurred, the designation *ghisamjñā* would apply to the word *daṇḍi*; consequently, that very word would necessarily be placed first. However, because the elision of *n* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the designation [of *ghisamjñā*] does not occur, and thus there is no fixed rule regarding which word should be placed first."

Regarding the passage beginning with "atra kecid" and so forth: the elision of the *n* (nalopa) occurs through the immediate proximity (*sannipāta*) of the case-ending (*sup*). If that [elision] were to trigger the addition of the augment *tuk*, it would destroy that very proximity. But how could there be a destruction of the proximity, given that the *tuk* is an internal element (*pūrvānta*) and is included by the mention of *tuk* itself? True; this was said on the assumption that the *tuk* is a mere part of the short vowel. Or, it is because of its being characterized as "external" (*bahiraṅga*). The meaning is that the elision of *n*, which depends upon the external case-ending, is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) in relation to the *tuk*, which depends upon the internal *kvip* suffix.

The purpose of stating both *paribhāṣās* is to indicate their non-universality (*anityatva*). In that regard, because of the non-universality of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule "supi ca" occurs in forms such as *vṛkṣāya*. However, because of the non-universality of the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*, in the case of *eṣā dve*, the substitution of *yat* for the pronoun stem (*tyadādyatva*)—which depends on the case ending (*vibhakti*) and is thus *bahiraṅga*—is not established even when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* depends on the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Regarding *vṛtrahacchatram*: here, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is not conditioned by a *sannipāta* (the immediate proximity of causes), nor is the elision of *n* considered *bahiraṅga*; for the augment *tuK* also depends upon the letter *ch*. Regarding *rājīyati*: the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *kyaci ca*. Regarding *rājāyate*: the lengthening occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ*. Regarding *rājāśvaḥ*: the long vowel occurs by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*.
na mu ne || 8.2.3 || [The substitution of *u* for *m* does not take place before the particle *nu*.]

The term *mu* is an indeclinable (uninflected) designation. The sense is that the substitution of *na* conditioned by a *ghi*-stem would not occur; the ellipsis to be supplied is "if this [sūtra] were not commenced. By this, the purpose for the commencement of the sūtra has been stated. However, once the substitution of *na* has taken place, and so forth—the idea is as follows: if there were lengthening (*dīrghatva*) here, then even though the vowel *u* is being taught as a short one, it would include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), just as in forms like *amūbhyām* where a long *ū* becomes the substitute for a long *ū* in the original base (*sthānin*). In the same way, a long *ū* would also become the substitute for the *ā* here; consequently, it would subvert the substitution of *na*, which was caused by the presence of a short vowel.

Regarding this, they raise an objection: since the substitution of *mu* is already established, the occurrence of a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is indeed being questioned. But does the rule for the long vowel (*dīrgha-śāstra*), which applies when a *ghi*-stem follows, fail to perceive the absence of that *mu* simply because it did not perceive its presence? For this rule for the long vowel stands in the same relation to the word *vṛkṣa* and others as the rule for the *ghi* designation does; therefore, since the suffixes beginning with *yañ* are absent, how can there be the occurrence of a long vowel here? To this, they reply: In actual usage (*prayoga*), the absence [of the suffix] is certainly not heard. Furthermore, the rule for that [substitution of *mu*] is recited in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*. It is only that its cause—the suffix—is not present.
One does not perceive the long vowel as being merely non-existence; let it not be seen as such, for as long as one does not perceive its non-existence, one can still bring about its length.

Or rather (*atha vā*): just as someone of sharp intellect, when asked by one or more people, "What kind of animal is running? or "What color is it running?", answers with a single statement, "A white [animal] is running"; so too here, there are two applications (*yoga*) of this rule. Among them, one prohibits the non-attainment of *mutva* (the substitution of *m* for *n*) when *na* is to be applied, while the other applies to that which is obtained when *na* follows. This is what was meant by saying, "for both purposes. As for "by means of a common application" (*tantraṇā*):

a common application occurs when something is shared in common, such as a lamp between two people of equal status eating together; but here, the common effort itself constitutes the common application (*tantra*).

Now, he demonstrates how both [meanings] are established within a single *yoga* by saying "or else" (*atha vā*). The phrase "implied by the sense" (*arthāt saṃgṛhītam*) is like the statement of the old maiden. For example: Indra said to an old maiden, "Choose a boon," and she chose this boon: "May my sons eat food with plenty of milk and ghee from a bronze vessel. Yet, she did not even have a husband; so where were there sons, where cows, or where grain? Indeed, by this very single sentence, [the husband is also implied].

Just as [in the rule] "putrāḥ gāvo dhānyam," everything is encompassed; so too here, by stating a prohibition against the non-application of the *asiddhatva* (non-validity) of the *mubhāva* when that subsequent operation is to be performed, the *asiddhatva* of the *mubhāva* is effectively prohibited even when the *nābhāva* (the substitution of *na*) is to be performed.

Regarding the statement "the single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*)," there are four views concerning the single-substitute vowel: The first view is that when a single substitute arises for both an acute (*udātta*) and a grave (*anudātta*) vowel through their mutual proximity (*āntarya*), the rule "a single substitute [for an acute and a grave] is acute" (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*) prescribes the substitution of the acute quality (*guṇa*) in place of the already established single substitute. The second view is that once the single substitute vowel has been established, the rule prescribes the mere acute quality (*udāttamātra*) in place of the mere svarita quality (*svaritaguṇamātra*) of that single substitute.

The third view, however, is that the *paribhāṣā* "an *ekādeśa* [is] acute when [the substitute] is acute" applies to all rules prescribing *ekādeśa*. In that case, the meaning is as follows: an *ād-guṇa* occurs, and when the *ād-guṇa* of an acute and an unacute vowel occurs, it is acute; thus, the *ekādeśa* becomes acute even while it is being prescribed. The fourth view is that the *ekādeśa* of an acute and an unacute vowel, which would otherwise result in the quality of a *svarita*, becomes acute.

In this regard, by the principle of "non-attainment" (*anāprāpti*), the rule for the acute accent (*udātta*) becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for the circumflex accent (*svarita*). Under the view that this is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule), the acute accent is established in the case of *ay*-substitutions and so forth. However, under the other views, since [the substitution] would otherwise be considered unestablished (*asiddha*), its establishment is explicitly stated so that, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), the *ay*-substitution may be acute; otherwise, it would be circumflex.

Regarding the form *kumāryai*: the word *kumāra* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of its nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). From it, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule "in the first age" (*vayasi prathame*); the elision of the *i* occurs by the rule "and that which belongs to *yasya*" (*yasyeti ca*); and the *ṅīp* becomes acute by the rule "and where there is the elision of an acute [vowel], the following [vowel] becomes acute" (*anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ*). When the form *kumārī-e* stands, the augment *āṭ* is added by the rule "āṭ for nadī-stems" (*āṇnadyāḥ*), followed by the *yaṇ*-substitution. The *āṭ* becomes acute by the rule "after a vowel that is the result of an acute *yaṇ* and preceded by a consonant" (*udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*). Then, by the rule "and after *āṭ*" (*āṭaśca*), a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is formed through *vṛddhi*. That [resulting vowel] would have been expected to be a circumflex (*svarita*) by virtue of its internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*).

By the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ" (P. 8.2.5), an acute accent (*udātta*) is produced; its established status (*siddhatva*) must be stated so that the substitute *ay* may likewise be acute. Regarding the phrase "yadi" and so forth: first the acute accent is applied, and afterwards the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). The meaning is that this purpose is achieved when [the process] occurs as just demonstrated. Now, regarding the phrase "atha tu" and so forth: when *kumāryāḥ* + *e* is situated, both the *vṛddhi* by the rule "āṭaśca" (P. 6.1.90) and the accent of the *āṭ* by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" (P. 6.1.174) would apply; both of these are non-permanent (*anitya*).

The accent (*svara*) is non-eternal because it results from the attainment of another sound; for it first applies to the form *ākāra*, and once the *vṛddhi* substitution has occurred, it applies to *aikāra*. Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* rule is also non-eternal because, due to the posteriority of the accent rule regarding two unaccented vowels, it would apply after the accent has been applied to *āṬ*. When the accent has been applied, the rule concerning the replacement by a different accent for the high-pitched (*udātta*) and low-pitched (*anudātta*) vowels becomes non-eternal. Between these two non-eternal rules, the accent would apply by virtue of its posteriority; however, since *vṛddhi* depends on the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the accent, being prescribed for the case-ending (*vibhakti*), depends on the word (*pada*) and is thus external (*bahiraṅga*).

Regarding the example *gāṅge'nūpa*: [the word] *gāṅga* is derived from *gaṅgāyā idam* with the suffix *aṇ*; by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is oxytone (udātta on the final syllable). From that, the case ending *ṅi* is added; being a *sup*-suffix, it is anudātta. The single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for these two is udātta. [The word] *anūpam* means "that which has water following it" (*āpo'nugatam*); this is a *prādi*-compound. When the rule for the original accent of the indeclinable preceding member (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) would apply, the rule *anorapradhānakanīyasī* prescribes that the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is udātta, while the rest is anudātta (*śeṣanighāta*). Because that [rule] is established, etc. [as previously stated].

When the substitution of a single substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is considered established (*siddha*), this single substitute (*ekādeśa*) occurs together with an acute accent (*udātta*) according to the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati*. Consequently, by the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau*, there is optionally a circumflex (*svarita*) when the following word begins with an unaccented syllable, and otherwise an acute accent. However, if that [substitution] were not established (*asiddha*), then that *e*-vowel—by virtue of occupying the place of both an acute and an unaccented vowel—would necessarily be circumflex due to its internal proximity (*āntaryataḥ*).

And this being the case, for that [substitute], the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" would not apply with an acute (*udātta*) vowel; rather, according to the alternative view that it applies with a circumflex (*svarita*), the circumflex would not occur. Instead, since it occurs in place of both the circumflex and the grave (*anudātta*), it would necessarily always be circumflex due to proximity (*āntarya*). The reading is "sa udāttenetyataḥ," which means: "for this reason, namely, because that single substitute is together with an acute vowel."

Regarding the term *śatṛsvara* (the accent of the present participle suffix *śatṛ*): the suffix *laṭ* is applied after the roots *tud*, *nud*, and *nad*; for that [suffix], there is the accent of the feminine suffix *nadi* and those beginning with *aj*. This refers to the rule *śaturanumo nadyajādī*, where from the phrase *antodāttād uttarapadāt* (from a final acute [compound] having a second member), the portion *antodāttād uttarapadāt* is understood to carry over. Thus, *tudatī* and *nudatī*: the suffix *laṭ* is applied after the roots *tud* and *nud*, followed by the substitute *śatṛ*; then, by the rule *tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*, the suffix *śa* is applied, which is acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). The prohibition regarding the term *anuma* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

The sense is that, for this reason, its status as *siddha* (established) need not be explicitly stated. How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "By the rule *nadī*. The purpose of the prohibition [of *num*] by the rule *anumaḥ* is so that when *num* occurs in the form *nudanti* by the rule *ācchīnadyornum*, it should not take effect. Since the *śatṛ* suffix would not occur anyway—because the word lacks an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*) if the *num* were *asiddha*—what would be the use of the prohibition *anumaḥ*? It is from this very prohibition that its *siddha* status is inferred.

Is it not the case that this prohibition would apply where there is no cause for the *lasārvadhātuka* accent to be unaccented? For in forms such as *yāntī* and *vāntī*, since both the root and the suffix are acute (*udātta*), the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from their proximity is also acute, and that [substitute] is already established by the accent of the *śatṛ* suffix. Here too, once the suffix-accent has occurred, immediately thereafter the remainder of the root becomes unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*). Consequently, even here, without the accent of the single substitute, the final syllable would not become acute.

Regarding the term *ekānudāttatvam*: having thus excluded [one syllable], the fact that the remainder is unaccented (*anudātta*) constitutes "the state of having one unaccented [syllable]. In the Bhāṣya, however, the reading is *ekānanudāttam*; even there, the intended accent is precisely this: "a word has one [syllable] excepted as unaccented" (*anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*). For in that context, it is stated: "only one [syllable] is unaccented, while all the rest are accented. And so it is said therein: "But it is established because of the state of having one [syllable] unaccented" (*siddhaṃ tvekānanudāttatvāt*). [The example is] *tudanti*.

The affix (*śavikaraṇa*) is acute (*udātta*), while the *l*-sārvadhātuka suffix is grave (*anudātta*); there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) for these two. By this—namely, by the established accent of the single substitute—the sense of the rule "a word is grave except for one [acute]" (*anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*) is indicated. For if there were non-validity (*asiddhatva*) [of the single substitute], then in the absence of that exclusion (*varjyamānatā*), there would be the hearing of two acutes.

[Objection: But surely, even if the acute accent (*udātta*) is not established [as a separate entity], that circumflex (*svarita*) which is produced from the single substitution (*ekādeśa*) of the acute and grave accents by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), will serve as the basis for the exclusion (*varjyamānatā*). [Response: True; this is established when the position is held that the acute accent becomes the circumflex. However, when the acute accent is prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the circumflex, then—because that [acute] is not established and because the original element (*sthānin*) lacks any other vowel tone—by what means could there be an exclusion? Therefore, its establishment (*siddhatva*) is stated.

Nor can it be maintained that this paribhāṣā, like other paribhāṣās, applies within the Tripādī on the basis of the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that a rule operates at the time its effect is to be produced); for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, there would result the undesired suppression of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*) even in the rules "The *yaṇ* substitute for an acute or circumflex vowel is circumflex if followed by an unaccented vowel" and "An unaccented vowel following an acute becomes circumflex. However, they say that just as in the case of *yānti*, where the suppression of the remaining syllables occurs prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), so it is here as well, and thus [this paribhāṣā] serves no purpose.

Regarding the statement "the Brāhmaṇas laugh": here too, according to the view that the acute (udātta) accent serves as an exception to the circumflex (svarita), its established status (*siddhatva*) is asserted; otherwise, since there is no absence of the grave (anudātta) for what is acute, the acute would be heard in actual usage. Thus, the external (*bahiraṅga*) remains non-established (*asiddha*), by the rule: "The external is non-established with respect to the internal. In the word *pacati*, the particle *iti* is acute on its first syllable because it is a nipāta.

In this case, because the single-substitute (ekādeśa) depends upon an external element (*bāhyapada*), it is considered extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*); consequently, its accent is also extrinsic. Since that [accent] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), there is no exclusion by it. In *prapacati*, likewise, the suppression of the accent of the prefix (*gatinighāta*)—by the rule "and when a *tiṅ* ending is udātta"—does not occur. In both instances, there would have been an occasion for such an application because of the treatment of the preceding element as if it were the final member of a compound (*antavadbhāva*). In *harivaḥ*, when the suffix *vanip* is applied according to "in the Veda, *vanip* and *u" and the augment *matup* is added, and then the substitution of *ru* occurs for that [suffix], then there is no purpose for the statement regarding what is already established (*siddhavacana*).

Regarding the form *alāvīt*: this is the *luṅ* [aorist] tense. From the root *lū*, there is *sic* for the *cli* suffix, followed by *iṭ*. By the rule *astisico 'pṛkte*, *iṭ* is added after *as* and *sic*; then, by the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ*, there is vṛddhi [of the vowel]. Now, an objection is raised: in the rule *iṭa īṭi*, the word *iṭaḥ* should be understood as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), not as an ablative (*pañcamī*). Since the word *saḥ* is supplied from the previous context, the elision of the *s* of that which begins with *iṭ*—being prescribed when an *īṭ* follows—will apply to the *iṭ* itself. Thus, the form *alāvīt* is established? True, the form is indeed established; however, [the point remains].

However, there would be a fault regarding the accent: if the letter *i* were removed by elision (*lopa*), the hearing of the unaccented *īṭ* would result, because the elision would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) for the sake of the accent that replaces an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). But when there is lengthening by homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) upon the elision of the mere letter *s*, then, because the suffix *sic* is marked with the *cit* indicator, the single-substitute accent (*ekādeśasvara*) applies according to the rule "the augment *iṭ* is acute" (*iḍudāttaḥ*).

Regarding the word *vṛkṇa*: by the rule *oditaśca*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant in the *niṣṭhā* suffix. He shows what is excluded by the rule *ṣatvasvarapratyayeḍvidhiṣu* with the words "but *kutva* [is seen] in *pratī*. As for the statement that "only the word *kṣība* is cited as an example," he asks: "But how can one and the same word serve as an example in all three rules? To this he says: "For in that case... In some cases, he states that a certain purpose serves as a counter-example: "when..."

The mention of "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is because [the word] "in a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is carried over from the rule "there, in a name, [the first member is] a comparison" (*tatra saṃjñāyām upamānam*). "This accent" refers to the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*). "Kṣībika" is formed by the suffix *ṣṭhan* according to the rule "after *nau* and a dissyllabic word, [the suffix] *ṣṭhan*. A modification accompanied by a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is called a "protracted modification" (*plutavikāra*). Examples are *agnā3i* and *paṭā3u*. When the *guṇa* substitution for the vocative case has been applied to the words *agni* and *paṭu*, the first half-vowel (*ardhamātrā*) becomes a protracted *ā* according to the rule "of an *ec* vowel that is not a *pragṛhya*," while the latter half becomes *i* and *u* respectively. [Objection: "A compulsory *tuṅ* [nasalization] would result. [Response: There would be an option characterized by lengthening according to the rule "optionally after a word-final [vowel]."

What is the purpose of the word "cha" (six)? It is so that the *pluta* modification [of the vowel] might remain asiddha (non-existent) in other cases—for example, in the case of *khalapubrāhmaṇakulam*. Here, by the rule "in the vocative, when there is something following," a *guṇa* substitution occurs, resulting in the form *khalapā-u*. In this state, the *tuk* augment [prescribed] by the rule "after a short vowel, before a suffix beginning with *p* and having *kṛt*" does not take place. Furthermore, there are two kinds of *asiddhatva* (non-validity) here: that based on being *bahiraṅga* (external), and that based on the principle "what precedes is asiddha.
But for what purpose [is this asked]? The question arises because the sound *s* is never heard [in such instances].

Regarding *ucicchiti*: from the root *ucchī* (meaning "to dwell apart"), there is the suffix *tuk*, then the desiderative suffix *san*, and the augment *iṭ*. By the rule "of that which begins with a vowel, the second [syllable] is reduplicated," the syllable *chi* is reduplicated. By the rule "the *khaya* letters preceded by a *śar* are the remainder," the *khaya* letters are retained as the remainder. By the rule "in the reduplication, *ca* and *ja* are substituted for [the following sounds]," the letter *c* is substituted for *ch*. In forms such as *saṃyyanta*, the rule "a final *m* becomes *anusvāra*" applies; then, by the rule "for *anusvāra* before a *yay* sound, the homogeneous substitute (*parasavarṇa*) is applied."

"If there is the requirement of 'pada' (word)," means: if the term *pada* is required in the rules for *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) and so forth, then *latva* and the like are on the same footing as reduplication (*dvirvacana*). However, if it is not required, then reduplication—which is *bahiraṅga* (external)—is considered *asiddha* (unestablished) with respect to the *antaraṅga* (internal) operations such as *latva*. Consequently, the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* ("what precedes is unestablished") does not apply; thus, once *latva* and the like have been performed, reduplication follows, and the desired result is established. In the example *galogala*, the *latva* is applied by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*. In *dogdha*, [the same applies].

In *vā druha*, there is the substitution of *gh* [for *h*], or in its absence, *ho ḍhaḥ*. In *nunna*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix by *nudavida*. In *abhina*, there is the augment *āṭ*; [the form arises from] the root *bhid* with *laṅ*, *sip*, and *śnam*, followed by the elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* [suffix]; then, either *sipi dhāto rurvā* or *daśca* provides the substitution of *r*, which becomes *ṇ* via *ṛtvot*. In *mātuḥ svasā*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* by *mātuḥ piturbhyāmanantarasyām*. In *māṣavāpāṇi*, there is the substitution of *ṇ* by *prātipadikānta*. In *vāṅnayanam*, [there is the substitution of *ṇ*].

By the rule "a non-nasal [stop] becomes a nasal before a nasal," the *g* may optionally become *ṅ*, resulting in *vākśayanam*. By the rule "ś becomes ch before a non-ṭ [consonant]," the *ś* may optionally become *ch*. With the phrase "of the *l*-ness, etc.," he demonstrates the fault that would arise if the *l*-ness and so on were considered asiddha: namely, that an undesirable option (*vikalpa*) would occur. This undesirable option consists in the application of a rule to one of two adjacent words while it fails to apply to the other. The phrase "all this," etc., refers to this.

The recourse to this prohibition is precisely for the sake of a *yogavibhāga* (division of rules); otherwise, for the sake of brevity, one would have to resort to the formation of the word *amunā* as a *nipātana* (irregular form). Following that, there would be a second rule: *mu ne*. For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of indicating that the preceding rule does not apply universally; thus, an objection regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) should not be raised.
When a non-acute vowel follows a semi-vowel that has arisen from an acute or a circumflex vowel, that non-acute vowel becomes circumflex.

Even though this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule "udāttasvaritayoḥ," it is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the explanation. Therefore, when a *yaṇ* vowel stands in proximity to an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, the subsequent grave (*anudātta*) vowel does not become circumflex. For example: *sakṛllvyāśā*, *khalapvyāśā*. Why is this so? To answer this, he says: "by the [term] 'udāttayaṇ'"; that is to say, by that which constitutes the first part of this sūtra.

The acute accent (*udāttatva*) [prescribed] by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" does not occur here, because of the prohibition in the rule "noṅdātvoḥ. Since the word *āśā* has its final syllable acute according to the rule "āśāyā adigākhyā cet," it begins with an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel. Therefore, how could this [substitute] be a *svarita-yaṇ*? It cannot be so in any way; for this [substitute] does not arise in place of that [original] after having removed the *svarita*. Indeed, a preceding grammatical rule does not operate upon the substitute with the notion that it is the original element (*sthānin*); rather, it operates upon the original element itself.

As it has been stated: "The word *hata* is uttered twice," but it is not the case that the sound *ḍha* is uttered twice by virtue of that cognition. Regarding the phrase "by reason of its basis" (*āśrayāt*): this [author] says—"In the rule *svaritayaṇaḥ*, there is no established *svarita* vowel; in that case, its status as established will arise by reason of its basis."

While this is being stated, [the author] points out an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words "if it were so": *dadhyāśa*. The word *dadhi* is acute on its first syllable by the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya*; the rest is unaccented (*seṣanighāta*). By the rule *udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*, that [first syllable] becomes a circumflex (*svarita*). If its status as established were dependent on its substratum, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the unaccented vowel following the *yaṇ*-substitute for that [circumflex] would also become circumflex. Therefore, etc.

Since there is a fault in establishing [the rule] based on this substratum (*āśraya*), therefore it must be stated in such a way that this very *yaṇ-svara* becomes established. How so? A split of the *yoga* (division of the rule) will be made: first, "of a high-pitched *yaṇ*" (*udāttayaṇaḥ*); a low-pitched vowel following a high-pitched *yaṇ* becomes circumflex (*svarita*). Then, "of a circumflex *yaṇ*" (*svaritayaṇaḥ*); and a low-pitched vowel following a circumflex *yaṇ* also becomes circumflex, provided it follows a high-pitched *yaṇ*.

The meaning is that when a svarita vowel is produced by the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*, that svarita causes the following anudātta vowel to become svarita. Therefore, by virtue of this very svarita being established [as the cause], the desired result will be accomplished.

With the words "If this were so," etc., he refutes the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that was raised, according to the opinion of some, by saying "But some [hold]... regarding the rule *udāttātsvaritayaṇaḥ*. The meaning is: even from that *yaṇ* which follows an *udātta*—namely, the *yaṇ* prescribed by the rule *udāttādanudāttasya* for an *anudātta* following an *udātta*—the [circumflex accent] applies to what follows it. Regarding the term *taittirīyaka*: those who study what was proclaimed by Tittiri are the *Taittirīyas*; their sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is the *Taittirīyaka*, formed with the suffix *vuñ* denoting a Vedic school (*caraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in another recension" (*śākhāntare*).

The status of being a "different branch" (*śākhāntara*) is relative to whichever branch is situated in the region of the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*). For there are indeed one hundred and one branches of the Adhvaryu; or rather, the word *antara* (other/different) denotes a specific distinction. Regarding the phrase *yāste viśvā*: by the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for the word *santi*; the word *agne* receives the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the low-pitched accent for a vocative). Regarding the word *brāhmaṇa*: in that very same Taittirīya [text], the word *dadhi* has its prescribed accent, while *āśayati* receives the *tiṅ-nighāta* (the low-pitched accent for a finite verb).

But surely, in both these cases, once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, the circumflex (*svarita*) arises by the rule "the circumflex follows an unaccented vowel after an acute" (*udāttādanudāttasya svaritaḥ*). And thus, where that [circumflex] is prohibited by the rule "not [after an acute] when followed by an acute or a circumflex" (*nodāttasvaritodayam*), the circumflex is not observed—as in *svasmabhyam ābhara* and *praty agniḥ upasām agram akhyāt*. Yet this circumflex occurs even when followed by an acute or a circumflex—as in *daha aśaso rakṣasaḥ pāhi asmān*.

And likewise, in the Bhāṣya as well, the contingency that [the rule] applies only when followed by an udātta vowel was raised in the example *dadhyāśa*. Therefore, this is not a counter-example (*vyabhicāra*) to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) mentioned previously; this point requires reflection. Or, because it will be refuted later, he shows that one should not insist too much on this matter, saying: "But as... Here is the Vārttika: "It should be stated that the accent of the *yaṇ* substitute is established when the *yaṇ* substitution occurs"; and: "If it is argued that the *svarita* of the *yaṇ* is for the sake of the *svarita* [of the following vowel] and is established by virtue of its substratum, then there is a fault in the case of a *svarita* following an udātta."

Furthermore, if the intention were that the circumflex (*svarita*) resulting from the rule "after an acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*) becomes circumflex" should itself cause the subsequent grave syllable to become circumflex, then the statement [of the objection] regarding the fault would be untenable. However, he demonstrates how this matter is established in the *Bhāṣya* with the words "And thus... (*tathā ca*). The *Bhāṣya* on this point says: "Or rather, the mention of 'circumflex' (*svarita*) need not be made."

If this [rule] were not formulated, by what means would the circumflex (*svarita*) nature of an unaccented vowel following a circumflex *yaṇ* (semivowel) be established? It would follow from the rule "after an accented *yaṇ*" (*udāttayaṇaḥ*) alone; however, because it is separated by a circumflex *yaṇ*, it would not apply. [The opponent argues: "In a rule prescribing accent, a consonant is as if non-existent," and thus there is no separation. If, moreover, the circumflex nature of an unaccented vowel following a circumflex *yaṇ* after an acute (*udātta*) vowel were intended, then the rejection [of the rule] would not be appropriate.

If [the substitution] is indeed a rejection (*pratyākhyāna*), then for what purpose is the mention of *svaritayaṇ* made? To this he says: "That [mention] is made... because there is an intervention due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*)—that is, by the *i* which takes the place of the *yaṇ*. For while a consonant is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), a vowel is not. But is it not the case that the status of being a substitute is prohibited in rules concerning accent (*svara*) by the rule "not at the end of a word or in reduplication" (*na padāntadvirvacana*)? To this he says: "In rules regarding accent, lengthening, etc. As in *baidyāśa*.

The feminine form of the descendant of Bidu is *baidī*, derived by the rules "from *bidu* and others, after a non-seer [name], the suffix *añ* is applied" (*anṛṣyānantarye bidādibhyo 'ñ*) and "after *śārṅgarava* and others, the suffix *añ* takes the augment *ṅīn*" (*śārṅgaravādyaño ṅīn*). By the accentuation rule for *nit* suffixes, the word *baidī* has its first syllable udātta.
When a single substitute takes the place of both [an udātta and a non-udātta vowel], that substitute is udātta.

The term "of an anudātta" (anudāttasya) is understood [from the previous rule]. Words such as *agni* are udātta at the end by virtue of the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), while the case-ending is anudātta.

In the form *pacanti*, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent of the letter *śa*—which arises according to the rule "the anudātta following an udātta becomes svarita"—is considered asiddha; therefore, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) for the two anudātta vowels [the final vowel of the stem and the case-ending] is itself anudātta.
Or, when followed by an unaccented word beginning with a syllable that is not at the beginning of a sentence, it becomes circumflex (svarita).

Because [the word] begins with a prefix (*pra*), the compound is formed. Regarding the rule "there is a prohibition of *karmapravacanīya*s when a prefix is involved," a specific prohibition was made for that very case by the rule "the *svati* [prefixes] are used in the sense of praise. However, a *gati*-compound is not applied here, because that would entail the application of the rule "a *gati* [is elided] before another *gati*. The word *vasuka* has its final syllable accented acute (*antodātta*), as in the previous case.

"The mention of the *svarita* is for the sake of clarity. How so? He says: "For if it were acute (*udātta*)," etc. [The argument is: "By virtue of proximity (*āntarya*) alone, the *svarita* will occur. If this were the case, then because that [acute] is established, there would be the elision of the remainder (*śeṣanighāta*)—as in *gāṅge'nūpe*. Since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the beginning of the subsequent element, the word *anūpa* would result in being unaccented (*anudātta*). But when the term *svarita* is included, because that [acute] is not established, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

Now, even if the mention of *svarita* (the circumflex accent) is made, why does the exclusion [of that which is already established] not apply to the *svarita* that is already established—as in the case of *kanyānūpa*? The word *kanyā* has its final syllable *svarita* by the rule “*kanyārājanyamanuṣyāṇāmantaḥ*” [P. 6.1.155]. Thence, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the combination of the *svarita* and the *anudātta* is a *svarita* by virtue of proximity (*āntaryataḥ*). Since that [substitute] is established, would it not follow that there is an exclusion based on it? If so, then whatever solution applies here will also apply to the case of *gāṅge'nūpa*.

What, then, is this? Because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) depends upon two words, it is *bahiraṅga*; therefore, its accent (*svara*) is also *bahiraṅga*. However, the *śeṣanighāta* (the non-accentuation of the remaining syllables) depends upon a single word, so its accent is also *antaraṅga*. What follows from this? "That which is *bahiraṅga* is considered as not having taken effect (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*."
There is elision of the *n* at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).
The word *anta* in the rule *viśeṣyasyāntasya* is without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*),
and likewise, the word *prātipadika* is a qualifier of the term *pada*.

The two genitive endings in *prātipadikasya* and *padasya* are in apposition. Regarding *ahann*: this is the root *han* with the suffix *laṅ* and the *tip* ending; there is elision according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]. [Question: Why is the mention of *anta-* (final) necessary? [Answer: Let it simply be "the elision of the *n* of a *prātipadika*" (*nalopaḥ prātipadikasya*). The term *padasya* is understood [from the previous rule]; there, when the *pada* is qualified by the letter *n*, the elision prescribed for a *pada* ending in *n* will—by the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*)—occur only for the final [letter], according to the rule *alo'ntyasya* [Pāṇini 1.1.52]. This is the question. [Example: *rājānau*.

The meaning would be that if the restriction to "extreme" (anta) were not present, there would be elision of the letter *n* belonging to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or a word (*pada*), wherever that *n* might occur as a constituent; the point is that, consequently, this [elision] would apply even here [in the case of *narāṇām*, etc.]. In this way, one should also demonstrate the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) in cases such as *narābhyām*.

But surely, even if the inclusion of the term *anta* (end) were made, it would be taken as a whole with the mention of *prātipadika* (nominal stem); consequently, the meaning would be "of the letter *n* which is at the end of a nominal stem that is a constituent part of a word," and not "at the end of a word. If that were so, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *narābhyām*, whereas it would certainly apply in cases such as *rājānau*. To this, he says: "The mention of *prātipadika*..."

Regarding *ahar*: by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*, there is elision (*luk*) of the nominative-accusative suffixes (*su* and *am*). Due to the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*, the condition of being followed by a case-ending (*sup*) is absent; consequently, by the rule *ro'supi*, the substitution of *r* occurs [for the final *s*]. Regarding *ahobhyām*: by the rule *ahān*, the substitution of *r* occurs [for the final *t*].

Now, one might object: "Since the *n* has already been replaced by *r* and *ṛ*, there will be no elision of the *n* simply because the *n* no longer exists; therefore, [the author] says: 'Because the substitution of *r* and *ṛ* is not established (*asiddha*) [for the purposes of this rule]. But surely, since they are without scope (*anavakāśa*), the substitutions of *r* and *ṛ* must indeed take place; for it has been stated that an exception (*apavāda*), even if subsequent, does not become *asiddha* due to the authority of the specific rule (*vacanaprāmāṇya*)? To this he replies: 'Both of those [substitutions] do indeed have their scope. For in the vocative singular, the elision of *n* is prohibited by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8), as in the example *he ahar*."

In the alternative view that "the elision [of *n*] does not occur for neuter nouns," there is a prohibition against the elision of *n*. Here, the substitution of *r* (ratva) finds its scope of application, as in: "O Dīrghāho Nidāgha! This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a masculine word as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*); the vocative ending is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* The employment of the word *nidāgha* following [the compound] is for the sake of providing a qualifier; by the rule *haśi ca*, the substitution of *u* (utva) occurs.

Now, regarding the forms *ahaḥ*, *ahobhyām*, and so forth: even though the *n* has been elided, since that which undergoes partial modification is not considered different from the original, the word *ahar* remains the same. Why, then, is it not stated that the final vowel *a* of the remaining form is the "avakāśa" (the substitute)? The author thinks as follows: because the term *ahan* is used without discarding the letter *n*, only that which ends in *n* possesses the status of the *sthānin* (the element to be replaced); otherwise, he would have simply said *hasya*. Thus, *ahan* is [understood] as ending in the nominative singular.

When only a substitute is intended to be prescribed, [the author] would have made the reference "ahnaḥ" using the genitive case of the word ending in *n* as the nominative singular; the purpose of making the reference in the nominative case is that it serves solely to provide the formal derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of this specific form—this is the underlying intention.
The substitution of *na* does not occur before a word ending in the suffix *sambuddhi*.

Regarding the form *ārdre carmann*: the suffix *ṅi* is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc. Now, one might object: since both the *ṅi* and the vocative (*sambuddhi*) have been elided, the preceding element no longer possesses the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), because of the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) which applies by means of the technical characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, in the case of the locative (*ṅi*), the designation of a word (*pada*) does not exist either, because it is sublated by the designation of a base (*bha*), which operates precisely through the characteristic of a suffix. Therefore, how can there be the possibility of the elision of the *n* here? To this he replies: "Precisely for this reason."

But surely this [sūtra] must be for the sake of forms such as *surājñi* (O good king), for here the designation *prātipadika* applies by the rule "kṛt-taddhita-samāsāś-ca," and there is no prohibition of that [designation] by the rule "apratyayaḥ" (not a suffix), because [the word *surājñi*] is included within the sūtra itself? If that is so, then here too the term "apratyayaḥ" is understood to carry over; otherwise, since it would be possible for the sūtra to serve as an original injunction (*vidhi*) for *surājñi* and the like, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) would not function as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Therefore, its status as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is indeed established.

And this is stated on the basis of the position that "the application of technical names [occurs] after the operation has been performed," for in that case, because the name *prātipadika* would have arisen for the sake of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the elision of the *n* would not apply; furthermore, the name *bha* would also not occur. Here too, the phrase "it is made known by this very statement of prohibition through the characteristic of the suffix" is to be connected. He states the purpose of this making known: "and so," meaning that the elision of the *n* does occur, because of its status as a *prātipadika*.

"And *allopa* does not occur because of the absence of the designation *bha*. Another says: "This meaning—that the *bha* designation does not occur—is not to be established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Why? Because it is stated [in Pāṇini's rule] 'before *yac* etc. (*yaci*), and we do not see here [the suffix] *yaj* etc.; [could it be] by means of the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)? No, because there is a prohibition by the rule 'not when a suffix is elided by *lumat*' (*na lumatāṅgasya*). For in that case, when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, whatever operation pertains to the stem (*aṅga*)—whether it be an operation of the stem itself or not—all of that is prohibited."

Regarding the term *carmatila*: even though there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because it conveys the intended meaning. Now, this [rule] is stated too narrowly; for even when the suffix *ṅi* (the vocative case) is the final member of the compound, a prohibition must be stated. Otherwise, in the analysis *he rājan vṛndāraka*, when the two words ending in the vocative are compounded according to the rule "one who is honored by *vṛndāraka*, *nāga*, and *kuñjara*," the elision [of the final vowel] would not take place. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "In the case of the *ṅi* and the vocative (*sambuddhi*), provided they are not the final members of a compound."

Therefore, he says: "But in the case of *he rājavṛndāraka*," etc. Therein, there is no address (*saṃbodhana*) of the meaning of the prior member. For when two distinct meanings of the constituent parts are being addressed, a mutual unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is not possible. Furthermore, it is stated [in Pāṇini’s rule] that [the substitution occurs] "in the case of the vocative" (*saṃbuddhau*), yet we do not perceive a vocative here. Is it by virtue of the "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)? No, because of the prohibition: "there is no [application of an operation] to a stem (*aṅga*) when [an affix] marked with *l* has been elided" (*na lumatāṅgasya*).

The statement beginning with "O King" (*he rājan*) is effective only in cases where the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) is elided by the term *lopa*; however, this solution is not possible in the case of the locative singular ending *ṅi*, because [the suffix] is elided by *lumat* in all instances. Regarding the rule *vā napuṃsakānām*: this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applied where there was no prior application [of another rule]. This is because the vocative suffix has already been elided by *lumat*. [Then follows: *mādupadhāyāśca matorvo'yavādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.9).

In this context, due to the particle *ca*, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*); *ma* and *a* form a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*). Therefore, for the suffix *matup* following *mā*, *va* is substituted. Regarding the rule "and [for the penultimate vowel] (*upadhāyāśca*)," it refers specifically to *mā*; thus, *va* is substituted for the penultimate vowel of *mā* as well as for that which follows *mā*. This rule is commenced so that what was prescribed by the preceding rule for immediate succession (*ānantarya*) may also apply when there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*). Since this is how it must be explained, the intention behind the statement that "here, *matup* is the recipient of the operation" (*kāryitvena*), etc., must be sought.

Someone says: "In the assemblies of grammarians, it is taught that [the substitution of *v* occurs] after a word ending in *m*, after one whose penultimate (*upadhā*) letter is *m*, and after one whose penultimate letter is *a*; this is its justification. Even in that case, no justification is seen for the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compounds "having *m* as its penultimate" and "having *a* as its penultimate. [The rule states: "this substitute *v* occurs. Here, the word *iti* should be supplied, because the discussion begins with "this is the meaning"; thus, in the context of the prohibition regarding *yava* and others, the word *ādi* refers to the manner [of formation]. For example, *payasvān*. Because of the designation *bha* by the rule "tasau matvarthe," there is an absence of the *ru*-substitution.

One might ask: "In the case of *nṛmān* (meaning 'one who has men'), the term *nārmatam* is derived from it; once the *vṛddhi* [vowel substitution] has been applied, the rule 'from that which has *a* as its penultimate letter' (*avarṇopadhāt*) would require the substitution of *v* for *m*. Should not a prohibition of this be stated? To this, he says: "In this case" (*iha*). The meaning is that because it depends upon a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) situated outside the word, the *vṛddhi* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*); therefore, it is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *v*, which depends on the internal *matup* suffix.
The suffix *jha* [is applied after a verbal root ending in a vowel] to form the present participle. || 8.2.10 ||
Regarding "agnicitvān": as before, because it is a *bh* sound, there is no substitution of *j*.
In the case of *saṃjñā* (a name), [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs]. 8.2.11.
In words such as *ahīvatī*, the suffix *matup* is applied in the four senses (*cāturarthika*) when [the base] denotes a river (*nadī*).
The words *āsandīvat*, *aṣṭhīvat*, *cakrīvat*, *kakṣīvat*, *rumaṇvat*, and *carmaṇvatī* [are formed with the suffix -vat]. (Pāṇini 8.2.12)
"Āsandīvat, Ahisthala"— these are names of specific regions, concerning which it is said: "At Āsandīvat,
Janamejaya bound for the gods a dappled horse that ate grain, was adorned with gold, and wore a green garland."

And so it has been said in the *Prayoga-śāstras*: "The royal throne (*rājāsandi*) is the seat of King Soma. If [the form] is already established by the substitution of *vat* in the sense of "belonging to that very thing" (as in *rājña eva saṃjñāyām*), then for what purpose is this specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*) of *āsandī-vat*? To this he replies: "It is recited here, however, for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). The word "here" (*atra*) should be supplied, because the passage begins with "others say. "[Of a part of the body]" refers to the joint of the two knees. "The *sadas* and the *havirdhāna* sheds are provided with wheels (*cakrīvanti*)."

In the *Sārasvata* sacrificial session (*sattra*), the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds are mobile; they do not remain in one place, but are equipped with wheels for being drawn here and there. Regarding the word *kakṣīvān*: the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*). There is another base, *ruman*; thus [it is said]: "and *rumā* is a salt-mine.
