And regarding the purpose of the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*): because of the potential application of the prohibition "at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*). Or, it is for the sake of the augment *nuṭ* after the suffix *matup*;
in this view, there is the elision of the preceding *n*, and the *ṇatva* is also established by the rule "after *ra* and *ṣ*" (*raṣābhyām*) alone.
The word *udanvat* [is substituted for *udaka-vat*] before the word *udadhi*.

"Udanvān" is the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*). And [it refers to] that from which rain falls according to one's desire—namely, that in which water is held, such as a tank and so forth. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "after a verbal root, when the object or the locus is expressed. By the rule "in the case of *peṣam*, *vāsa*, *vāhana*, and *dhi*, [the elision of the final vowel of *udaka* occurs]," there is the substitution of *udbhāva* for *udaka*. Thus, it signifies the general property of the existence of water. Furthermore, this [general property] is also possible in the case of Devadatta and others. Or, the mention of "udadhi" (ocean) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the term] to proper names (*asaṃjñā*).
The suffix *matup* is applied after the word *rājan* when it signifies good governance (*saurājya*).

A "good king" (*śobhana-rāja*)—the state of being that is *saurājyam* (good kingship)—is formed with the suffix *ṣyañ* according to the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, followed by the elision of the *ṭi* portion. Furthermore, this refers to the relationship of the country with a good king. It is stated [by Patañjali] that "in compounds, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), the relation is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). And this is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term *rājanvān* (possessing a good king), while the actual denotation (*abhidheya*) is the country itself; as he says: "when good kingship is implied. Thus, in *rājanvān*, the possessive suffix *matup* is used in the sense of praise, and the absence of the elision of the final *n* is a formal irregularity (*nipātana*).
The [author] shows that the masculine gender in the sūtra is not intended to be significant by stating: "the earth possesses a king" (*rājanvatī pṛthivī*).
The augment *anuṭ* [is inserted] after [the root] *nu*. 8.2.16.

Regarding *akṣaṇvantaḥ*: in the word *akṣan*, the substitute *anaṅ* is applied to the stem *akṣi* before the suffix *matup* by the rule "it is also seen in the Veda. Because the augment *nuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the *n* is elided first; subsequently, *nuṭ* is inserted by way of reference to what previously existed, and its *ṇ*-substitution follows. Regarding *śīrṣaṇvatī*: by the rule "in the Veda [the form] *śīrṣan*," the substitute *śīrṣan* is applied for the word *śiras*. Alternatively, there is a separate base synonymous with the word *śiras*; *śīrṣan* is thus prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*) in the Veda.

If this *nuṭ* augment were made part of the subsequent element (*parādi*), it would be included by the mention of the suffix *matup*, and consequently, the substitution of *v* [for *m*] would apply according to the rule "mādupadhāyāḥ. However, the substitution of *v* would not apply to the *m* itself, because of the intervention of the *nuṭ* augment. But if, on the other hand, this *nuṭ* were made part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), this could not be done; for then, in forms such as *akṣaṇvatā* and *śīrṣaṇvatā*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would not occur.

And here, regarding *supathintaraḥ*: when the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the subsequent rule, because it stands at the end of a word (*padāntatvāt*), the substitution of *r* [for *n*] would apply by the rule *naśchavyapraśān*. Therefore, the augment must necessarily be placed after the final letter (*parādiḥ*), and in that case, the aforementioned fault occurs. Hence he says: "Because *nuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddhatvāt*). [Objection: Even so, a fault arises in the *avagraha* (word-separation). In the case of *akṣaṇvantaḥ*, one would have to separate it as *akṣaṇ-vante*, ending in *ṇ*; but that is not what occurs. [Response: No; grammarians (*lakṣaṇena*) are not to be followed by those who compose the *pada-pāṭha* (*padakāraiḥ*). Indeed, the *pada-kāras* are not to be made to follow the grammatical rules.
The substitution of *n* for *gh* occurs before a vowel. 8.2.17.
In *bhūridāvattara*, the suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*.

In *rathītara*, the suffix *ini* is added to the word *ratha* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), and from that form, the suffix *taraP* is added; once the *nakāra* has been elided, the vowel *ī* is substituted for the *dakāra*. However, if the substitution of *ī* were prescribed in place of the *nakāra* as an exception (*apavāda*) to its elision, then because that [substitution] would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [with respect to the elision], the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) operation would not take place.
The *ṛ* sound becomes *l* when followed by *r*.

The reading is *kṛpo dhātoḥ*. This is because it is read as *kṛpo ro laḥ* in the Bhāṣya. It has been stated that "one must provide a remedy regarding the augment *nuṭ*, the substitution of *l* for *r*, and the change of *ṛ* [in the case of] *ṝ*"; having reached that point, he provides a remedy regarding the substitution of *l*—thus [it is said to be] general.

Setting aside the distinctions created by being a phoneme (*varṇa*) or not being a phoneme (*avarṇa*), that universal (*sāmānya*) which subsists in the individual manifestation of the sound *ra*—whether it consists of a phoneme or does not consist of a phoneme—is what is taken into account, because from that [universal] there arise for both of them the identical designation and cognition "ra. The meaning is not that only the individual manifestation of the sound *ra* which consists of a phoneme is taken into account. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "By that," and "this universal as well. The word "is taken into account" is understood to complete the sense.

In this case as well, one should have read: "By that [rule], there is the inclusion of both the solitary *l* and that which resides in *ḷ*"; however, it was not explicitly stated because it is understood by following the previous [principle]. If there is inclusion of both, what follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore, this... [referring to] the solitary—that is, the pure—*l* is the substitute. Here too, "solitary" (*kevala*) should be understood [to apply]. And for *ṛ* as well, there is *ḷ*, due to proximity (*āntaratamya*).

Now, one might object: even if there is a perception of both [the *ṛ* and *lṛ* sounds], let the letter *la* residing in the *lṛ*-sound be the substitute for the letter *ra* residing in the *ṛ*-sound; however, how is it that the entire phoneme is obtained as the substitute for the entire phoneme? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "by way of a single part" (*ekadeśadvāreṇa*). The letter *ra* resides in a modification of a single part; its modification is a "modification of a single part" (*ekadeśavikāra*). Alternatively, here the letter *la* residing in the *lṛ*-sound is itself the "modification of a single part," and [the substitution occurs] by way of that.

Therefore, this is what is meant: since it is impossible to extract the *repha* and the letter *la* from when they are encapsulated by the vowel *a*, the substitute must be for the whole [cluster] as a whole. If their extraction is impossible, let there be no mention of them; however, does this mean that there can be no relationship of original (*sthānin*) and substitute (*ādeśa*) between two clusters that are not explicitly mentioned in the rule? To this he says: "And thus," etc.; "and so forth."

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of rules such as *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ*, *ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ*, and *anavaklṛptyavamarṣayoḥ*. Regarding *kalptā*: because the root is marked with *ū* (as in *ūdita*), there is optionally the absence of the augment *iṭ*. Here, because the substitution of *l* for *r* (*latva*) is considered asiddha (not yet established), the absence of *iṭ* occurs first according to *tāsi ca klapaḥ* when the suffix is parasmaipada; otherwise, however, once the guṇa has been applied, the *r* becomes *l*. Regarding *ciklṛpsati*: the suffix *san* is treated as having the *kittva* (indicating that the preceding vowel does not undergo guṇa) by the rule *halantācca*.

Regarding the word *kraper*: [the root] *krapa* is used in the sense of "compassion" (*kṛpāyām*). Granted that the form [is derived from *krap*] once the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) has been applied, nevertheless, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its inclusion [in the rule] due to the similarity of form? Therefore, he says: "For of that... It should be understood as referring to *krap* alone. [In the rule] *rañje kyun*, because of the statement "in various cases" (*bahulavacanāt*), it occurs for *krap* as well; likewise, in [the rule] *kṛkṛpibhyāṃ kīṭan*, *krap* itself should be read. [In the rule] *kharjipiñjādibhya ūrolacau*, let it also apply to *krap*; in all these instances, the vocalization occurs by virtue of the statement "in various cases."

Regarding the phrase "camphor and so forth" (*karpūrādayaḥ*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sword (*kṛpāṇa*) is included. According to the rule *yudhibudhidṛśeḥ kicca*, the suffix *ānac* is applied to the root *kṛp* as well due to its inclusion in the category of "various instances" (*bāhulakāt*). If one must necessarily resort to the principle of "various instances," then there is no fault even in applying it to *kṛp*. To this he says: "the *uṇādi* [suffixes]."

Regarding *bāla*: from the root *bal* in the sense of "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*), one who is covered is a *bāla*. Regarding *mūla*: from the root *mūl* in the sense of "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhāyām*), the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots with a penultimate *i*. The word *laghu* ends in the suffix *ku*, according to the rule "*laṅghivaṃhyornalopaśca*". *Alam* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). *Aṅgula* is derived from *aṅg* with the suffix *kuli*. The alternative derivation from *am* with the suffix *gur* and the substitution of *ra* for *la* was not adopted.

In the case of *kapilaka* and others, there is the suffix *la*. Regarding *romāṇi*: the suffix *manin* is applied to the root *ru*, yet in the rule "the forms *roman*, *nāman*, *sīman*, *stoman*, *homan*, *soman*, *loman*, *vyoman*, *vidharman*, *pāpman*, and *dhāman* [are established]," the specific formation of *loman* was not accepted as a formal derivation. Regarding *pāṃsuram*: the suffix *ra* is applied because "dust (*pāṃsu*) exists in this," according to the rule "after *naga*, *pāṃsu*, and *pāṇḍu*. Regarding *karma* from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *manin*: the specific formation of *śukra* and *śukla*—according to which the suffix *ra* is applied after *ṛjra* and others—was not accepted as a formal derivation.

Now, why was it not simply taught that *klṛp* means "capacity" (*sāmarthye*)? For in that case, the substitution of *l* (*latva*) would not need to be prescribed. This is not so; for otherwise, forms such as *acīklṛpat* would not be established. If, according to the rule "there is a mutual designation of homogeneous sounds between *ṛ* and *l*" (*ṛkāralṛkārayoḥ savarṇavidhiḥ*), the *ṛ* were replaced by *a* via the rule *urat*, the result would be *acīkṛpat*. However, when the substitution of *l* is prescribed, since that [substitution of *a*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) at that stage, the *ṛ* remains first, and then the substitution of *l* occurs; thus the desired form is established. Likewise, in *calīklṛpyate*, the substitution of *l* is also established for the *rī* sound.
[The augment *ṭi* is applied] after a prefix when [the following verbal root] ends in a long vowel. 8.2.19.

Regarding the rule *ayatau paraḥ*: here there are two possible interpretations. First, the mention of *ayati* is a qualifier of the letter *r*—meaning "of the *r* that follows *ayati*, provided it belongs to a prefix. Second, it is a qualifier of the prefix—meaning "of the *r* belonging to that prefix which follows *ayati*. In the first case, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "of that *r* which follows *ayati* and is connected with a prefix. In the second case, however, it is: "of that *r* which belongs to the prefix following *ayati*. The example is *plāyate*. Here, *ayati* is unaccented (*anudātta*).

How then is there the *parasmaipada* ending in the verse "udayati vitatordhvaraśmirajjau"? What is the use of this cleansing of a wild elephant? Or rather—[it may be explained as] the present tense (*laṭ*) with the elided *kvip* suffix after the word *udaya*, which is derived from the root *i* (to go) with the addition of the *ac* suffix (as in *pac-ādi*). Some, however, read the root *i* itself as *iṭ* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*). He demonstrates, in due order, how no fault arises in either of these two views thus presented: "In this case," [and] "because of the status of having a locus" (*sthānavadbhāvāt*).

The rule "that which is not established in what precedes is not like the original" (P. 1.1.58) does not apply here, because of the traditional exception: "there is a fault [in that rule] regarding the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga*, the substitution of *l* for *r*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. If the mention of *yati* is a qualifier of the *repha* (the sound *r*), this is because the *repha* is the primary element as the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*). Regarding the phrase "by a single phoneme": the inclusion of the word "single" (*eka*) is intended to demonstrate that the operation does not take place when there is an intervention by a cluster (*saṅghāta*), as in the case of the suffix *-ya*. "And thus" means: having done so. "In *palyayate* also" refers to the same principle.

It also operates where there is worldly intervention (*vyavadhāna*) by even a single audible phoneme (*varṇa*). The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it does not apply only in cases such as *plāyate*, where the operation is scriptural (*śāstrīya*) by way of the status of the substituendum (*sthānin*); rather, it applies elsewhere too. This separate presentation is intended to demonstrate this very distinction.

But surely, because of the indications in the rules *niraḥ kuṣaḥ* and *suduroradhikaraṇe*, there are two general rules (*utsarga*) that apply even when there is an intervening [element], and these provide scope for the specific statement [of the sūtra]. So how can [the rule] apply when there is an intervention? It is said in reply: if this were the only purpose, he would have simply said *durorayatau*; however, because of the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*), it will apply even when there is an intervention. And since this is established even by an intervention of a single phoneme (*varṇa*), there is no occasion for the application of the rule in the case of *pratyayata*. [This refers to the phrase] "if [the word] *upasarga* is a qualifier... and so forth.

The intended meaning is "because it is so stated [in the scriptures]. This is indeed established for all. The meaning of the word *eva* is that "there is no effort whatsoever required in this position regarding the rule 'that by which there is no intervention,' and so forth. As for the word *tu*, it indicates that [the result] does indeed apply. In the previous position, because of the intervention by a composite (*saṅghāta*), it did not apply; however, here it does apply—this distinction is what the word *tu* highlights. The phrase "those who are intent on the view of the first position" refers to those adhering to the former alternative.

Regarding the first position (*pakṣa*), "those who are intent on its exposition to others" means those who are devoted to it—that is, those for whom it is their ultimate resort. As for the phrase "others, however" (*apare tu*) and so forth: the word *pratyayita* is a synonym for *āpta* (trustworthy), ending in the suffix *-ita*. Thus, "those in whom trust has arisen" are *pratyayitāḥ*. Regarding the words *niḥ* and *duḥ*: this textual passage concerns cases where [the suffix] ends in *s*; however, in the case of those ending in *r*, there must necessarily be *l*-substitution (*latva*).
The suffix *yaṅ* [is applied] after a verb stem ending in *a*. 8.2.20.

In the example, there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel by *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, followed by the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*. Since the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by *hali ca* is considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *la* occurs first by this rule (*aci vibhāṣā*). Subsequently, because the cause [for the lengthening] has been removed, the long vowel does not occur. [The roots mentioned are] *girati* and *gṛṇāti*; that is, those having the sense of "swallowing" and "uttering sound," respectively. The word "generally" (*sāmānyena*) is used because no specific distinction is made. However, others maintain that only *girati* is intended to be included—this is the implication (*anuṣaṅga*). What, then, is the reason for this? To this he says: "But as for *gṛṇāti*... The particle *tu* has the sense of *hi* (because). [The form] *nigīryate* is derived with the suffix *yak*.
Before *aci*, there is optionally [the substitution of *u* for *v*]. (Pāṇini 8.2.21)

When the root's own form (*svarūpa*) is being grasped, because the operation is understood to apply to its suffix, the suffix is brought into proximity; and since there is no distinction made regarding that [suffix], the rule "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) is understood, as it says: "in a suffix beginning with *a* or *ā*. In the case of *nigirati*, the suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tud*-class; because that suffix has the marker *ṅ*, there is no *guṇa* substitution, and thus the short *i* remains. This is due to the status of the elision of the *ṇi* as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).

The intention is that because the substitution of *l* for *d* is prescribed for the entire word (*pada*), it lacks the status of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*); furthermore, since the substitution of *l* is considered "not established" (*asiddha*) by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the elision of the suffix *ṇi* occurs first. Moreover, one can argue here that the definition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) applies; nor is there a dependence on individual phonemes (*varṇāśrayatva*), because it has been stated [in the rule] "when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows."

But how can there be the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), given that it is stated: "When [an operation] is not established in what precedes, [the substitute] is not as if the original"? To this he says: "In the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe*. What, then, is the exception to this? To this he says: "The fault of that [rule]. Or, "because it is internal" (*antaraṅgatvāt*). Since the governing heading is *padasya* ("of a word"), although there is no internal-external relationship in terms of time, the substitution of *la* is internal because it depends on the presence of *ā* and other vowels which are included within the word; whereas the elision of *ṇi* is external because it depends on the suffix *ya*, which is outside the word. This is the intended meaning. The forms *girau* and *giraḥ* are for the sake of clarity.
And [the substitution of *gh*] occurs for *jha* and *ṅ*, when followed by another consonant (*para*).

Regarding *parigha*: by the rule *parau ghaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is applied, there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion of the root *han*, and the substitution of *gh*. Regarding *paryaṅka*: [the root] *aki* in the sense of "marking" takes *pacādyac*; alternatively, *ghan* is applied by the rule *halaśca*, and by the word *ca* ("and"), *gha* is also included.
Here, the mention of *gha* is intended as a reference to its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*). This is indeed a desired interpretation (*iṣṭi*). Examples: *pariyogaḥ*, *paryanuyogaḥ*.
There is elision of a final consonant cluster. (Pāṇini 8.2.23)

One might raise the objection: "In this case, in words such as *śreyān* and *bhūyān*, the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not apply, because it is superseded by the substitution of *r* (*rutva*), which is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Anticipating this, he says: "In this case... If, then, the substitution of *r* does not supersede the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct because it is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), then the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) would likewise not supersede it. Consequently, in forms such as *payaḥ* and *yaśaḥ*, only *jaśtva* would occur. To address this, he says: "But regarding *jaśtva*... For the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) is initiated whether the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct has already applied or has not yet applied—applied in cases like *śreyān* and the like, but not yet applied in cases like *payaḥ*. However, in the case of *jaśtva*, it applies only when [the elision] has already occurred in all instances.

Therefore, by the principle of "non-attainment" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), only *jaś*-ness is sublated, not the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). For example, in *dadhyatra* and so forth. Indeed, the substitution of *yaṇ* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends on two words, whereas the elision of the end of a cluster is *antaraṅga* because it depends on a single word. The mention of the word "end" (*anta*) could have been omitted; for the term "of a word" (*padasya*) is understood [from the previous rule], and when a word is qualified by a "cluster," the expression "of that which ends in a cluster" (*saṃyogāntasya*) is obtained precisely through the rule of "specification by what follows" (*tadantavidhi*).
[The substitution of *ṣ* occurs] for [the dental *s*] of the word *rātra*. 8.2.24.

"Of a word ending in a conjunct consonant," and so forth. This means that when there is a *repha* (the sound *r*) which is a constituent part of a word ending in a conjunct consonant, the *sakāra* (*s*) following it is elided; that is, the *s* is elided as the final member of that very word. Examples are *akṣāḥ* and *atsāḥ*. [The roots] *kṣara* (in the sense of "moving") and *tsara* (in the sense of "going by guile"). Regarding the rule "only after *r*" (*rātsasyaiva*): the elision of *s* occurs only after *r*, not after anything else—as in *śreyān* and similar forms. However, such a restriction does not apply here, because in the list of words beginning with *uraḥ* (the *uraḥprabhṛti* group), the form *pumān* is read with the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct already applied.

*Ūrgiti*: From the root *ūrj* in the sense of "strengthening" or "nourishing," the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *bhrājabhās...* etc. Here, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is no elision of the letter *j*; instead, by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, *k*-substitution occurs, resulting in *g*. Then, by the rule *vāvasāne*, the *c*-substitution (the retroflex *ṭ*) may optionally occur. *Nyamāḍiti*: From the root *mṛj* in the sense of "cleansing," belonging to the *adādi* class. The suffix *tip* is elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* etc. There is *vṛddhi* substitution for *mṛj* by the rule *mṛjervṛddhiḥ*. By the rule *vraścādinā*, there is *ṣ*-substitution, followed by *jaśtva* and *cartva*. *Dhi ca* || 8.2.25 || [The rule continues: "And before the suffix *dhi*."

He will state later, "From this point on, there is the elision of the *s* of *sic*. Consequently, the suffix *sic* is implied; because it is qualified by the letter *dh*, the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādividhi*) is understood, and thus he says: "in a suffix beginning with *dh*. According to the view of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, it should be understood as "when *dh* follows. [The example is] *alavidhvam*. This is the *luṅ* tense; *sic* replaces *cli*; *iṭ* is added; there is the elision of *sic*; and optionally, by the rule "optionally for *iṭ*" (*vibhāṣeṭaḥ*), the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) is substituted. [Thus, one might think that] the letter *dh* would not be heard.

Once the substitution of *ṣṭu* has been applied, [the form] would simply be *alaviṣṭam*. However, the inclusion of the term *vibhāṣā* (optionally) there is for the sake of the *sīdhvam* suffix and for the sake of the *liṅ* (optative) suffix. Regarding the phrase "from here onwards," etc.: they state that the rule "of *sthā* and *stambh* following *udaḥ*, the preceding [vowel takes its place]" (*udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ pūrvasya*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, when *ut-sthā* is established, since the *s* following the *t* would be elided by the rule "after a *jhāl* [consonant], before a *jhāl*" (*jhalo jhali*), forms such as *utthānam* would already be established; thus, that rule would be purposeless. Furthermore, this is an indicator with respect to the general category—that in this section, whatever elision occurs, it belongs to *sic*. As for "he laughed" (*cakhāda*).

"He *cakāddhi* the gray hair on his head"—the meaning is "shine forth. The root *cakāsṛ* (meaning "to shine") belongs to the *adādi* class; it is in the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), which becomes *hi*, and *hi* becomes *dhi*. By the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the *s* is changed to *d*. Regarding *payo dhāvati*: by the rule *haśi ca*, the *r* of *ror* is changed to *u*. [Objection: If the elision of *sic* is desired, then in forms such as *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, would there not be no elision by the rule *jhalo jhali*? To this, he says: "In *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*... [The elision occurs because the rule *jhalo jhali* applies here despite the presence of *sic* due to specific exceptions.]

From the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *ktin*, there is the substitution of *ghas* according to the rule "variously in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). There is elision of the penultimate vowel by the rule "of *ghas* and *bhas* before a consonant" (*ghasibhasor hali ca*). There is elision of the *s* by the rule "variously in the Veda. By the rule "for *t* and *th* after a *jhaṣ* [consonant], *dha* [is substituted], except for *adhaḥ*," the *gh* becomes *g* through the rule for *jaś*-substitution. Thus, *samānā gdhiḥ* becomes *sagdhiḥ* by the rule "the karmadhāraya compound beginning with *pūrva-apara-prathama*," and the change of *samāna* to *sa* occurs by the rule "of *samāna* in the Veda. [The form] *babdhām* is likewise derived.

The root *bhās* belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, meaning "to reproach" and "to shine. In the imperative (*loṭ*), the third person plural ending *tas* becomes *tām*. Due to the doubling of the root (*ślau dvirvacanam*), the penultimate vowel is elided as before, and the *s* is also elided. The *t* is changed to *dh*, and the *p* undergoes *jaś*-substitution to become *b*. This applies even in cases such as *payo dhāvati* ("he washes the milk"), for otherwise, because the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) would be established first, the elision of the *s* would occur earlier.

But the author of the Bhāṣya says this: previously, however, the opinion of the author of the Ślokavārttika was presented. [He argued that] another effort must be undertaken. Since *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) depends on a single word, it is *antaraṅga* (internal); since the elision of *s* (*salopa*) depends on two words, it is *bahiraṅga* (external). In that case, because the elision of *s* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the visarga—which was specified as being "prior" [to the rule for *rutva*]—does not exist; thus, due to the absence of that [visarga], there is no non-existence of the non-*asiddha* status [for *rutva*], and so *utva* (the substitution of *u*) indeed proceeds first. Furthermore, because it is a rule concerning a phoneme (*alvidhi*), there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment as the original), and thus there is no elision of the *o*.

Regarding the phrase *dhi sakāre*: although the substitute (*sthānin*) is intended as the object of reference, the locative case is used in the expression *sakāre* (in the letter *s*) to indicate that it is the domain of the rule. In the form *āśādhvam*, the root *āṅ-pūrva-śās* meaning "to desire" belongs to the *adādi* class and is *anudātta-it*. Regarding the term *jaśtvam* (the substitution of *jaś* sounds): this occurs by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*. As for the statement *sarvamevam* (all would be thus): if the form *āśādhvam* were established through the substitution of *jaś* for the letter *s*, then the entire range of linguistic examples (*lakṣyajāta*) would be established by *jaś*-substitution alone; consequently, this very sūtra would not need to be composed at all.

"And the *śruti* (auditory perception) is not divided either. This means that whether a single consonant follows or multiple consonants follow, the [preceding] *hal* (consonant) is not perceived as distinct. "And also because of the *luṅ*"—this is another advantage when *jaś*-substitution occurs: in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*, the mention of *luṅ* need not be made; for in forms such as *avyoḍhvam* and *aloḍhvam*, the desired form is established by the sequence of *ṣatva*, *jaśtva*, and *ṣṭutva* alone. [Otherwise], if there were elision of *sic* according to the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, how could *akṛḍhvam* be formed?
However, this has not been well-explained, as other defects have been pointed out.

He demonstrates this by stating: "it is corrupted before *seṭ*. And this was already stated at the very outset: "if there were no elision of the *s* here. Therefore, the rule *tasmāddhi ca* must be applied, and *luṅ* must be included in the [rule for] the cerebral (*mūrdhanya*). However, the rule "there is elision of *sic* before *dhi* and *sakāra*" remains established. In that regard, he points out another defect with the words "of *ghas* and *bhas*": the meaning is that because it would result in the non-formation of *sagdhiḥ* and *babdhām*, the elision of *sic* cannot be understood [as applying here].

He offers a rebuttal: "Or there is a Vedic elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*). The word *vā* (or) sets aside the previous position; rather, this is an elision of the suffix *sic*, whereas the elision of phonemes in the case of *ghas* and *bhas* is Vedic. To the question "Where is this as [an example]? he says: "As follows. Because it is an imitation of a portion of the phrase *iṣkarttāram adhvarasya*, the locative case is used after the word *adhvara* from [the compound] *iṣkarttāram adhvara*. In that regard, the Bahvṛcas read *iṣkarttāram*, while the Taittirīyas read *niṣkarttāram*.
A *jhal* [consonant] is elided before a *jhal* [consonant].

The roots *bhid* and *chid* are marked with the svarita accent, while *man* and *han* are marked with the anudātta accent. This [elision] also applies only to the *s* of *sic*. Alternatively, if the term "pada" (word) is understood to carry over [from a previous rule], then by virtue of proximity, this rule would apply as a single connected operation to the three specified elements—namely, the *jhal* [consonant] before a *jhal*, and the *s* [of *sic*]. Consequently, it will not occur in cases such as *somasut* or *stota*. Nor does it occur in a compound, as in *somasutsthitih*. Why? Because the *t* is not a constituent part (*avayava*) of that word which was initiated by the *s* and the *th*.
[The substitution of *u* for *ū* occurs] after a short vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant. 8.2.27.

Regarding *acyoṣṭa*: because the elision (*salopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the guṇa substitution occurs first; subsequently, because the cause [for the elision] has been removed, the elision does not take place. Regarding *ayamapi*: here, the previously mentioned *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) from the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* is the sole refuge. Regarding *dviṣṭamām*: the sibilant (*ṣatva*) is applied by the rule *hrasvāttādau taddhite*.
An *iṭ* augment is not added before an affix that itself has an *iṭ* augment. || 8.2.28 ||
In this case, there is the possibility of the suffix *sica* alone.
A *sko* (the letters *s*, *k*, or *v*) that occurs at the beginning of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) is elided before a vowel, and also when it stands at the end of a word.
Although conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), it is qualified by the two [sounds] ending in *jhal*;
for there is no possibility of a *sakāra* occurring at the end of a word that begins with a *saṃyoga*.

Thinking thus, he says: "at the end of a word" (*padasyānte*) and "when followed by a *jhal* consonant" (*jhali ca parataḥ*). This refers to the requirement that [the rule applies] to a *saṃyoga* (conjunction) that belongs to a word. In the example *lagnaḥ*: from the root *olajjī* in the sense of "embarrassment," the *niṣṭhā* suffix (*kta*) is added; because it is marked with *īt*, there is a prohibition against the augment *iṭ*. Here, when the *jhal* consonant *t* follows, the *saṃyoga* consisting of *s* and *j* is present; the *sakāra* is the beginning of that *saṃyoga*. By the rule "and after roots marked with *odit*," the *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *naṭ* (nasal). Because that [substitution] is treated as *asiddha*, the *kutva* (change to *g*) occurs. In *sādhulag*: [it means] "one who is properly embarrassed," formed with the *kvip* suffix. In *magnaḥ*: [from the root *majj*].

The augment *num* is applied by the rule "masjinaśorjhali" (Pāṇini 7.1.60), and it occurs before the letter *j*, because of the statement: "They desire the *num* to be placed before the final letter of the root *masj*. Consequently, the elision of the nasal is effected by the rule "aniditām" (Pāṇini 6.4.24), and the elision of *s* and so forth is as previously described. Regarding the form *taṣṭa*: the root is *takṣū* (meaning "to make thin"), which has an indicatory *ū* (*ūdittvāt*) and thus optionally takes the augment *iṭ*. The prohibition of *iṭ* is applied by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15). As for the statement "it should be stated that [the elision of *s* occurs] when followed by a *jhal* consonant and the suffix *saṅ*": this term *saṅ* is a supplementary rule to the present section. What is the purpose? [Examples follow: *giraḥ*, *abdhīḥ*, *dviṣṭarām*, *dṛṣatsthaḥ*, *kāṣṭhaśaksthiraḥ*.
"Let there be no such things as 'essence' (sattva) and so forth in these [elements], thinking: 'The crane is the leader.'"

Regarding *giraḥ*: here, by the rule *aci vibhāṣā*, the substitution of *l* should not occur. Regarding *abdhīḥ*: by the rule *dhi ca*, the elision of *s* does not take place. Regarding *dviṣṭarām*: by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, [the elision of *n*] does not occur. Regarding *dṛṣatsthaḥ*: by the rule *jhalo jhali*, [the elision of *t*] does not occur. Regarding *kāṣṭhaśaksthiraḥ*: by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, [the elision of *k*] does not occur. Regarding *kruñcā*: by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, the substitution of *k* (kutva) does not occur.

Regarding the form *dhurya* (meaning "one who bears the yoke"), the lengthening [of the vowel] does not occur by the rule *hali ca*. Thus, there is a Vārttika: "In the case of *saṅ*, there is the substitution of *l*, elision, the elision of the initial of a conjunct, the *kutva* change, and lengthening. The meaning is that, having introduced the term *saṅ*, the rules for the substitution of *l* and so forth must be stated. Therefore, even according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika, the form must be *cakādhī* alone; this is because of the mention of *saṅ*. The phrase "beginning with the suffix *san*" means that both roots and suffixes are included.

In this context, he rejects the utility of the elision of the initial consonant of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster), stating: "That" (*tat*). The word "that" (*tat*) is used here to introduce the statement. Regarding the term "of *śaki*" (*śakeḥ*): this is an elliptical indication for [roots] ending in *k*, by which there is likewise no usage of the *kvip*-derived forms of roots such as *kaka* (in the sense of longing) or *kuka* and *vṛka* (in the sense of seizing). Regarding the phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*): this refers to the authors of the *Bhāṣya* and others. In that regard, he first cites the *Bhāṣya*: "Just like *kāṣṭhaśak*" (*kāṣṭhaśageva*).

In the expression "the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtham*), it might be argued that the status of being a *sthānivat* (as if occupying the original position) could also be asserted, because it has been stated: "The fault therein is the elision of the initial of a *saṃyoga*."
The *cu* (the letter *c* and the group beginning with it) becomes *ku* (the letter *k* and the group beginning with it).

Regarding the phrase "or with *na* as the penultimate letter": previously, this was stated on the basis of the original presence of *ña* as the penultimate letter; however, here it is said that the *ña* has arrived [there] through the substitution of *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* for the *na*. As for the phrase "for when there is the elision of *na*": likewise, among the purposes of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, it is recited: "in the case of *nikucita*, due to the state of having *u* as the penultimate letter."

Regarding the word *kucita*, the fact that it has a light vowel as its penultimate (*udupadhatva*)—which was produced by the presence of the *kittva* suffix—does not serve as a cause for that *kittva*, according to the rule *udupadhādbhāvādikarmaṇoranyatarasyām*. Now, one might object: "Let it be that it does not have a penultimate vowel; nevertheless, once the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* have been applied, there would still be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *nakāra* becoming a *kutva* sound. To this he says: "In that case... There is no possibility here of the *cutva* substitution [of *c* for *k*], because with respect to the *anusvāra*, that [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).
*ho ḍhaḥ* || 8.2.31 || [The substitute *ḍha* is applied in place of *ha* when followed by a sibilant.]

Regarding *soḍhā*: there is an optional insertion of *iṭ* by the rule *tīṣasaha*. Regarding *turāṣāṭ*: the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ*; the lengthening of the first member of the compound occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*; and the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*. Regarding *praṣṭhavāṭ*: the suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *vahaś ca*.
The letter *gh* replaces the initial consonant of a verbal root beginning with *d* or *dh*.

What, then, is that qualification? Although this does not serve as the direct opposite of the statement "it is not in grammatical apposition" (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), since even that which is in apposition can function as a qualifier, nevertheless, in the view that there is apposition, the word "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is the qualificand; however, in this present view, it is precisely the opposite of [the claim that it is] a qualifier. "Ending in a genitive denoting a part" means: that which ends in a genitive case used in the sense of a relationship with a part.

In this case, the state of being a counter-example is quite clear: "that which is a word beginning with *d*, being a part of a verbal root (*dhātu*). And thus, even at the outset, in the phrase "that [word] beginning with *d* of the verbal root," the two genitive cases are in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*). What is accomplished by this? The meaning is: what desired result is established? "Even in the case of *adhoṅ*"—if there were grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then because the status of beginning with *d* would have been prescribed by the augment *aṭ*, [the rule] would not apply. Why? This is the question: "Is this [word] itself a verbal root, rather than a part of a verbal root? Or else...

In this view, even at the beginning [of the rule], the phrase "of a root beginning with d" (*dāder dhātoḥ*) is taken exactly as it is heard in the text. Regarding the expression "in the teaching of roots" (*dhātūpadeśe*): this is understood from the inclusion of the term "root" (*dhātu*). For it is impossible for there to exist a non-root that begins with *d* and ends in *h*.
This is because in forms such as *devān* and *anaḍudbhyām*, the substitution of *ḍh* for *dh* operates.
This statement is incorrect and falls short of careful consideration,
because words such as *dāmaliṭ* and others can occur even when they are not verbal roots (*adhātu*).

Therefore, the mention of "dhātu" (root) must be repeated. Therein, one [repetition] indicates the time of formal instruction (*upadeśakāla*). And so it is said: "tathā ca. However, in the previous alternative (*pakṣa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even in the case of *dāmaliṭ*, the rule would apply by virtue of the treatment as if possessing a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).
Or [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel] occurs before the roots *druha*, *muha*, *uṣṇuha*, and *uṣṇiha*. || 8.2.33 ||

These roots, beginning with *druh*, are recited in the *divādi* class in this very order; because they belong to the *radhādi* group, the augment *iṭ* is optional. In that regard, although it would have been sufficient to state "optionally for *druh* and the others," the explicit mention (*pratipadapāṭha*) is provided so that the rule applies even in the *yaṅluk* formation—such as *dodhruk* and *dodhruṭ*; otherwise, the principle "that which is specified by its own form and by a class" would not apply.
The substitution of *dh* occurs in place of *n*, except after *ho*. 8.2.34.

Regarding the word *parīṇat*: the suffix *kvip* is applied because it belongs to the *sampadādi* group; the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *nahivṛti*; and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *upasargādasamāse’pi*. Although for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*) only the letter *d* should have been prescribed, the prescription of *dh* is intended so that the substitution of *dh* may take place by the rule *jhaṣastathordho’dhaḥ*, and so that in the case of *naddham*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* after *r* and *d* (by the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhānatvam*) might not occur. [The sūtra] *āhasthaḥ* [is now discussed]. 8.2.35.

Now, why is not the original *dhakāra* itself prescribed? For even that would be established as *āttha* through the substitution of *cakāra* (i.e., *th* for *dh*). And since *thakāra* must also undergo the substitution of *cakāra*, one could simply have formulated a single rule: *āhanahordhaḥ*. To this he replies: "Because another substitute is made. Even so, only *takāra* should have been used [in the rule *hṛgrahorhaḥ*]. The mention of *hakāra* in the rule *hṛgrahorhaḥ* is for the sake of the root *hṛ* ("to take"). As for the word *nigrābham*: in the rule *udi grahaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is desired after the prefix *ni-* as well, in the Vedic language, when referring to the lifting up and lowering down of the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*).
In place of the final consonants of the roots *vraśc*, *bhrasj*, *sṛj*, *mṛj*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *bhrāj*, and of the suffixes *ch* and *ś*, there is substituted *ṣ*.

In this context, while *jaś*-ness would apply to the word ending in *ś*, the rule for *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) is prescribed as an exception to the *kutva* (substitution of *k*) that applies to the others. Thus we have *mūlavṛṭ* and *dhānāmṛḍ*. [The derivation is as follows: there is *samprasāraṇa* by the rule *grahijyā-*, the elision of *s* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, *jaś*-ness of the letter *ṣ* resulting in *ḍ*, and optionally *ṭ* by the rule *vāvasāne*.

"Beginning with *jhal* after *ā*," and so forth. "Is obstructed" (*paryavapadyate*) means it is intervened by [something]. In the words *rāṣṭriḥ* and *bhrāṣṭriḥ*, although the suffix *ac* would have applied by the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, the suffix *ktin* applies by the rule *ktinnābādibhyaḥ*; and the prohibition of the augment *iṭ* follows from the rule *titutratatha* etc.

In the word *śabdaprāṭ*, the suffix *kvip* applies by the rule *kvibvaci* etc., followed by lengthening and the absence of *samprasāraṇa*. [Objection: The mention of *ch* is useless; for once *ch* has been changed to *ś* by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* etc., the substitution of *ṣ* is already established for those words ending in *ś*. To this he replies: "By the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* etc. and so forth.
In the presence of the suffixes *s* and *dhv*, a single-consonant *baś* sound at the end of a word that ends in a *jhaṣ* sound becomes a *bhaṣ* sound.

If the term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is carried over here, it is in a different grammatical relation (vyadhikaraṇa), ending in a genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), and serves as a qualifier for "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*). The term "ending in *jhaṣ*" (*jhaṣantasya*) is also a qualifier of that same [root] in a coreferential relation (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Thus qualified, however, "having a single vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) becomes a qualifier ending in a genitive of part. He states this with the words: "a part of the root," and so forth. By saying "the letter *s* after a *jhali*," he shows that the letter *s* is a qualifier of the *jhali* being carried over.

Why, then, does the term *jhal* continue to apply here? It is so that the term *anta* may also continue to apply; otherwise, if *jhal* were discontinued, *anta*—which is connected to it—would also be discontinued. [Objection:
There are four substitutes (*bhaṣ*) but only three original bases (*sthānin*) of the *baś* class;
as for the letter *ḍ*, there is no possibility whatsoever for its occurrence.
And thus, due to this inequality, would the rule of "correspondence according to number" (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) not apply? To this he says: "There are four substituents," and so forth;
for at the time of the comprehension of the grammatical treatise, an equality of numbers is possible.
It proceeds according to their respective order, but in actual practice, such a sequence is impossible.

This is the meaning. However, this passage is not recited in some versions. Regarding *bhotsyante*: the root *budh* is anudātta; with the suffix *lṛṭ*, the augment *sya* is added. Therein, by virtue of the principle of "possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśavadbhāva*), the single vowel is considered a constituent part of the verbal root. Regarding *abhugdhvam*: there is the elision of *sic* by the rule *dhi ca*. The roots *guh* and *duh* are svarita-accented. Regarding *ajardhāḥ*: in the case of the intensive (*yaṅluk*) of the root *gṛdh*, after reduplication, the single vowel is a constituent part of the root. By the rule *rugrikau ca luki*, the augment *ruk* is applied; thus, with *jargṛdh* established, the suffixes such as *laṅ* are applied.

Regarding the term *gardabhayate*: from "he expresses himself as a donkey" (*gardabham ācaṣṭe*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied. The suffix *kvip* is a suffix that is not a suffix (*apratyaya*). [The commentary states: "If the mention of 'single-vowel' (*ekāj*) were not made," and so forth. If the mention of "single-vowel" were not made, then, since nothing else is heard here [in the rule], the word *dhātoḥ* ("of the root") would be qualified by *baśa eva* ("only *baś*"). Since it is impossible for a *baś* sound to end in a *jhaṣ* consonant, the word *dhātuḥ* would also be qualified by *jhaṣantasya* ("ending in *jhaṣ*"). Consequently, the meaning would be: "In place of a *baś* which is a part of a root ending in *jhaṣ*, there is *bhaṣ*. As a result, this would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in the case of *dāmaliṭ*.

However, since the meaning demonstrated by the author of the *Vṛtti* holds true when the rule "ekācaḥ" is present, that same contingency applies there as well. For here, in the case of *liṭ*, that which ends in a *jhaṣ* and is monosyllabic (*ekāc*) does not have the letter *d* as its constituent part (as in *braśca*), nor does that which has *d* as its constituent part (as in *dā*) end in a *jhaṣ*. Thus, in the form *krotsyati*, the letter *gh* does not replace the letter *k*.
The same [substitution] occurs for *dadh-* and *uś-*. (Pāṇini 8.2.38)
It is stated that the root *dadhāti* is being indicated. This does not refer to the root *dadha* in the sense of "holding," because those two [the *śap* affix and the *yaṅ*] intervene between them.

An objection might be raised: "In the case of *yaṅ*-luṅ (elision of *yaṅ*), there is no intervention; therefore, there would be the undesirable consequence of referring to that very [root *dadha*]. Consequently, one need not rely on what will be said later, namely 'by the force of the statement'? Therefore, in this matter, the explanation itself is the only refuge.

"By the force of the statement" (*vacanasāmarthyāt*). For the root *dadhāti* does not become one ending in *jhaṣ* without the elision of the vowel *ā*. And this has been stated without relying on the rule "that which is not established in what precedes is not treated as a substitute" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*). Regarding the fact that the *jaś*-substitution for the reduplication is also "not established" (*asiddhatva*), [the phrase] "by the force of the statement it does not occur" is to be supplied. For without the *jaś*-substitution of the reduplication, the substitution of *baś* for *dadhāti* is never possible.

[Question: Why is it stated "of *ta* and *tha*" (*tathoḥ*)? [Answer: The term "in the presence of a *jhal*" (*jhalīti*) is understood [from the previous rule], as is the phrase "of that which ends in a *jhaṣ*" (*jhaṣantasya*). Since there is no *jhal* consonant other than *ta* and *tha* following a root ending in *d*, the case of *s* and *dhv* is already established by the desired result. Therefore, it need not be said "of *ta* and *tha*. Furthermore, if this were the case, even the letter *ca* (the conjunction) should not be employed, as the result would be established everywhere simply by the condition "in the presence of a *jhal*. This is the question. [The answer is: "Because of immediate proximity" (*ānantaryāt*). [Objection: But is it not already established for *s* and *dhv* by the preceding rule? [Reply: It is not established; because when the elision of *ā* (*āllopaḥ*) is treated as non-existent (*sthānivadbhāvaḥ*), the root does not end in a *jhaṣ*.

But is it not the case that there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when what precedes is *asiddha*? Even so, because the *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*) produced by the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is *asiddha*, [the desired result] is not established.

If, however, in the rule "The substitution of *śatva*, *cartva*, *etva*, and *tuk* should be declared as established [with respect to one another]" (*abhyāsajaśtvacartvametvatukoḥ siddhaṃ vaktavyam*), the phrase "*etvatukoḥ*" were removed and establishment were stated without qualification, or if the mention of *phali* and *bhaji* were relied upon as a general indicator (*jñāpaka*) rather than as being restricted solely to the domain of *etva*, then the rule "*tathośca*" could be omitted. How so? Because the cases of *s* and *dh* would already be established by the preceding rule; this present rule, however, would serve the purpose of ensuring that the substitution occurs when a *jhal* consonant other than those two follows.
In the final position, *jaś* sounds replace *jhal* sounds.

"Of those occurring at the end of a word" (*padasyānte varttamānānām*) means of those occurring at the conclusion of a word (*padāvasāne*). The word *anta* signifies "conclusion" (*avasāna*), not "part" (*avayava*). For example, in *śvaliḍ*: here, although the substitution of the *jaś*-class sound would apply to the letter *h*, because that [substitution] is considered as if non-existent (*asiddhatvāt*), the substitution of *ḍha* occurs first; then the *jaś*-class substitution applies to the letter *ḍha*—resulting in the letter *ḍ*. Pāṇini 8.2.40: *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* ("After a *jhaṣ* [consonant], when *t* or *th* follow, *dha* is substituted, except after *dh* itself").

"Excluding *dadhāti*": by this, he indicates the prohibition of the verbal root [ending in] *dh*. If there were a prohibition of the letter *dh*—meaning that [the substitution] does not occur after the letter *dh*—then then such grammatical references as "gati-buddhi... would be untenable. For example: *alabdha*, *alabdhā* (in the *luṅ* [aorist], with the suffixes *ta* and *thās*); likewise, *alīḍha*, *alīḍhā*; *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*. When the substitution of *dh* is prohibited, there is the change of *dh* to *t* (*cartva*).

It cannot be said that [the term] "below" (adhas) [is not included]. Why then do we not have *dhattaḥ* and *dhattha* here? A split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made: first, "of *dadha*, and of *ta* and *tha*" (*dadhastathośca*); then, "the *jaś* substitutes for *jhal*s" (*jhalāṃ jaśaḥ*)—meaning that the *jaś* substitutes occur for *jhal*s when they follow *dadha* and *ta* or *tha*; then, "and at the end" (*ante*)—meaning that the *jaś* substitutes also occur for *jhal*s at the end of a word. In that case, because the *jaś*-substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the principle "what precedes is as if non-existent" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*) with respect to the *bhaṣ*-substitution, there is the state of ending in a *jhaṣ*.

Since the *jaś*-substitution is established as existing with respect to the subsequent *dha*-substitution, there is no state of ending in a *jhaṣ*, and thus the absence of the *dha*-substitution is established; hence the desired result is achieved.
After the two sounds *r* and *d*, the *t* of a *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *n*, as is the preceding *d*.

The term *niṣṭhātaḥ* is a compound designation. In this context, the letter *t*, which is the principal element, is qualified by the rule *radābhyām*, and not the subordinate element *niṣṭhā*; thus he says: "following [the letters] *r* and *d*. Consequently, in *caritam* and *muditam*, although the *niṣṭhā* suffix is not separated [from the root], the substitution of *n* for *t* does not occur because it is separated from the preceding letters by the augment *iṭ*. Regarding *avagūrṇam*: the root *gurī* means "to raise"; there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*, while in the previous examples [it was prohibited] by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*.

"Bhinnaḥ" (split) and "bhinnavān" (he split). In the substitute [form], the vowel *a* in "na" is for the sake of pronunciation; therefore, in place of the letter *d*, there occurs a pure *n*. [Examples: "kṛtaḥ" (done) and "kṛtavān" (he did).

[Objection: But surely, just as by the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* the letter *l* replaces the *r* of the vowel *ṛ*, so too here, by relying on the *r* of the vowel *ṛ*, the substitution of *n* would apply? To this he says: "In the case of [the word] *raḥ*. That is correct there because of the employment of a general term; but here, no general term is employed—what then? A consonant. Of what nature is it? It consists of half a mora (*mātrā*), whereas the vowel *ṛ* consists of a fourth part of a mora.

Or, even if there were a general designation [of the vowel], there would still be no fault; thus he says: "And even in the case of a general designation. For in the sound *ṛ*, there is a portion of a vowel (*ajbhakti*) on both sides and a portion of the letter *r* (*rephabhakti*) in the middle; consequently, because of the intervention by the subsequent vowel-portion, there is no occasion for the application of the rule for *natva*.

"Caritam," "muditam. If the word "pūrva" (preceding) were not stated, since the augment *iṭ* is a part of the *niṣṭhā*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being changed to *n*. [The rule says] "let it not happen for the subsequent one"; the meaning is: "let it not happen for the subsequent one alone. If the mention of "pūrva" were absent, then because of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the *niṣṭhā* is proximate; thus, only the *d* of that [suffix] would have to be changed to *n*. Therefore, this objection also should not be raised: "It will not occur because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) and because it is defined by a technical term (*lākṣaṇika*)."

Furthermore, because of the governing rule *padasya* ("of a word"), the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed only in the state of being a word (*padāvasthā*); thus, there is no lack of "externality" (*bahiraṅgatva*) [for the rule]. Since a solitary phoneme (*varṇa*) is not taught [as a base], there is also no status of being "expressed by its own form" (*pratipadoktatva*). Even if proximity (*pratyāsatti*) were not required, nevertheless, due to the mention of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), the application would occur only for what follows. In the case of *kārtiḥ*, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is external because it depends on the external *taddhita* suffix. And that which is the cause of the *vṛddhi* is the very same cause for the *repha* (the letter *r*); for the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rule prescribing *vṛddhi*.
The long vowel *ā* of a verbal root that begins with a conjunct consonant and contains the semivowel *y* or *v* [is replaced by *ī* when followed by the suffix *ya*].

Regarding *pradrāṇa*: the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ*. Regarding *niryāta*: that which is the root (*dhātu*) here is not the initial member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādi*), and that which is the initial member of a conjunct is not the root. Furthermore, the status of being the initial member of a conjunct does not possess the quality of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*). Why? Because first the root is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*), and consequently, the conjunct is already present even prior to the arising of the *niṣṭhā* suffix. This same principle applies in cases such as *pradrāṇa* and others as well.
[The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied] after words beginning with *lū*. (Pāṇini 5.1.2)

Regarding *jīna*: [the root] *jyā* is used in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*); the semivowel is replaced by a vowel (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyādi*. Regarding "like a *niṣṭhā*": because of the specific statement made in proximity to the rule for the substitution of *n*, that very [rule] is extended [here]; therefore, in the case of *pūnaḥ* (from *pū*), the optional insertion of *iṭ*—which would otherwise apply by the rules *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* and *pūṅaśca*—does not occur. Regarding *dugvoḥ*: the term *doḥ* refers only to the root *du* in the sense of "going" (*gatau*), and not to *ṭudu* in the sense of "affliction" (*upatāpe*), because the latter possesses an indicatory letter (*sānubandhaka*). Thus, it is employed by Māgha: *mṛdutayā dutayā*. Regarding *gu* in the sense of "voiding excrement" (*purīṣotsarge*):
in the word *pūnāḥ*, since roots have multiple meanings, the root *pūñ* here has the sense of "destruction."

Regarding the word *sina* (eaten): the root *ṣiñ* means "to bind. When a morsel (*grāsa*) being bound—that is, being made into a ball—is rendered compliant through the influence of a condiment such as curd, then this usage occurs when there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the object (*karman*). In the phrase *sitā pāśena* ("bound by a snare"), the suffix *kta* is used in its pure sense as an object; this is a collective counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Now he shows the individual counter-examples: "the morsel also," etc. [This refers to the rule] *oditaśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.45).

Regarding the word *āpīna*: the substitution of *pī* for *pyāya* is according to the rule "pyāyaḥ pī. The roots beginning with *ṣūṅ* (in the sense of "to bring forth life") and ending with *brīṅ* (in the sense of "to cover") are listed in the *divādi* class.
The [augment] *kṣi* is applied after a long vowel. 8.2.46.

The roots *kṣi* in the sense of "destruction" (*kṣaye*) and *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling or going" (*nivāsagatyoḥ*)—both are included here. Regarding the form *kṣīṇāḥ*: since these roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule "in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, when it does not have the sense of the past passive participle" (*niṣṭhāyām aṇyadarthe*). In the example *kṣīṇas tapasvī*, the same applies by the rule "optionally [the vowel is lengthened] in the sense of abuse or dejection" (*vā ākrośadainyayoḥ*).

It cannot be said that [the word] "dīrghāt" (from a long vowel) is stated [in the rule], because the inclusion of the long vowel is understood from the very mention of "kṣiyaḥ. For if there were an inclusion of the short vowel, then—since the substitution of *iyaṅ* would be superseded by the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule "ghir ṅiti"—one would have had to state "kṣer" [instead]. Therefore, he says: "even of that which ends in a short vowel. It is proper to refer back (*anukartum*) to the very form for which the lengthening is to be prescribed; and since the lengthening of that which ends in a short vowel is what is to be prescribed, it is that very form which is referred back in the prescription of the long vowel.

Moreover, this substitution of *iyaṅ* is observed there; therefore, the meaning is that the substitution of *iyaṅ* is not an authority for [the application of] the mention of a long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*).

If, then, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs even for a verbal root substitute (*dhātvanukaraṇa*) ending in a short vowel, would there not be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) even in cases such as "after *vi* and *parā*, [the root] *ji*" (*viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*)? To this he says: "But in cases such as 'after *vi* and *parā*, [the root] *ji*'... The reading is *avivakṣitveti*.

For in that case, the "root-ness" (dhātutva) residing in the object of imitation—which is characterized by the denotation of action—is not intended to be expressed; that is, without making such an intention, there is an imitation of the common form—such as the shared forms *vijitam* and *kūjitam*. Consequently, since an operation based on a specific [action] does not apply to the general [form], and because it was not observed in the original [root], it likewise does not apply in the imitation; this is the meaning.

But when a specific [form] is being imitated, then the grammatical operation based on that specific form applies to the imitation, just as the substitution of *atreyaṅ* [occurs]. If this is so, the production of case-endings would not be obtained, because the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) is absent due to the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*)? This is not a fault; for this "not a verbal root" is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), not a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

What follows from this? Since there is an absence of any extended (ātideśika) grammatical operation [that would block it], and because it is distinct from the verbal root (dhātu), the designation "nominal stem" (prātipadika-saṃjñā) applies by virtue of its own basis. However, the substitution of *iyaṅ* is an extended operation, as it is prescribed for the verbal root.
The suffix *śya* is applied after a verbal root denoting a non-tangible object.
Regarding the word *śīnam*: from the root *śyaiṅ* meaning "to go," and by the rule *dravamūrttisparśayoḥ śyaḥ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).

It is said that "touch (*sparśa*) is also [included] as a quality (*guṇa*). This is obtained from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*), for this word *sparśa* has two senses: it is a term for a quality, derived from the root *spṛś* meaning "to touch" with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*)—thus *sparśa* is the quality perceivable by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*); it is also a term for a disease, derived from *spṛś* meaning "affliction" with the suffix *ghañ*—thus *sparśa* [as fever]. Since no distinction is made here, both are understood.

Furthermore, would not the form *praśīna* fail to be established because [the rule] prohibits [the substitution] even in the case of disease? To this he says: "and when it is a quality" (*guṇe ca*). The meaning is: "only when it is a quality. He thinks as follows: since, after prescribing the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) for the word *sparśa* in the rule "for *śyaiṅ*, [there is vocalization] in the sense of fluidity and form," he then further states "also after *prati*," that indicates that when the root *śyaiṅ* is mentioned, the word *sparśa* does not signify disease. If it did signify it, he would not have prescribed it again; for the root *śyaiṅ* preceded by *prati* occurs only in the sense of disease.
The word *añcu* [retains its final vowel length] except when used with an *apādāna* (ablative) case.

"If there is no *apādāna* (ablative) in that case" means: in this context, regarding the sense of the root √*añc*, if there is no *apādāna*, [then the rule applies]. "In conjunction" (*samakau*) means "united. There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," and the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) occurs by the rule "aniditām.

"Udaktam" means "drawn up" (*uddhṛtam*). Regarding the word "vyaktam": this is a form of the root √*añj*—meaning "to manifest, to smear, to shine, or to go"—and not of √*añc*; therefore, the change to *n* (nasalization) does not occur here. This is the intended meaning.
[The suffix *kha* is applied after the word *div*] when the sense is "not desiring to win [something from] heaven. (Pāṇini 8.2.49)

Regarding the word *ādyūna*: by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*, [the form] *ādyūnaḥ* is derived, meaning "one who is gluttonous" (*audarikaḥ*). *Paridyūnaḥ* means "wasted away" (*kṣīṇaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "gambling takes place": one might object that here what is perceived is a game characterized by the falling of dice and such, not the desire for victory (*vijigīṣā*). To this he says: "for it is by the desire for victory... [and so forth].
The word *nirvāṇa* [is used] in the sense of "in a place free from wind. (Pāṇini 8.2.50)

Regarding the phrase *vātādhikaraṇa*: the meaning is "having the wind as its agent" (*vātakartṛka*). If the meaning were "if the wind is not the expressed object," then the prohibition would apply only in cases where the suffix *kta* denotes the agent, such as in *nirvāto vātaḥ* ("the wind has ceased blowing"); however, it would not apply in cases where the suffix denotes the action (*bhāve*), such as *nirvātaṃ vātena* ("the ceasing of the wind by the wind").

"Nirvāṇa" means fire; the meaning is "extinguished. "The monk is *nirvāṇa*" means "he has ceased [from worldly activity]. Regarding the phrase "but the wind is the instrument," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) should be understood as signifying either the instrument or the cause, according to what is appropriate. However, according to the Vārttika, the prohibition does not apply in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); thus, one says simply, "the extinguishing by the wind" (*nirvāṇaṃ vātena*).
The substitution of *pra* for *prati* is optional.
Regarding the form *prastīma*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "of *stya* preceded by *pra*."
The words *phulla*, *kṣība*, *kṛśa*, and *ullāgha* are formed [with the suffix *ka*] when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Pāṇini 8.2.55.

Regarding the word *phulla*: there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *āditaśca*; the substitution of *u* for the following *at* occurs by the rules *utparasyātaḥ* and *ti ca*. It is intended that this same substitution of *u* applies even to the form ending in *ktavatu*. The meaning is that the form ending in the suffix *niṣṭhā* with the sound *ta*—namely *phullaḥ*—is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*). However, this is not intended to apply to words such as *kṣība*, etc.

Regarding the phrase "the absence of *iṭ*": otherwise, because the elision of *tal* (the suffix *ta*) would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the augment *iṭ* would be improperly applied due to the following consonant being a semi-vowel (*val*). Or, once *iṭ* has been applied, there is the elision of the word *iccha*; this is understood from the context that [the form] is treated as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding the phrase "other than *ud* after *lāghi*": the prohibition does not apply to *ud*, because of the specific force of the grammatical indication (*nirdeśasāmarthyāt*). Regarding the phrase "only when *kṛś* is without a prefix": this is because of the rule stating, "Prepositions (*prādayaḥ*) are connected with that [verb] with which they are joined in action. He demonstrates the connection with a different action by saying, "surrounded by emaciation" (*parigataḥ kṛśaḥ*).

The meaning is "overcome by emaciation. Although words such as *phulla* and others could be derived from the suffix *ac* (pacādyac) or from the suffix *ka* (by the rule *igupadhāt kaḥ*), they are nevertheless treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*) for the sake of establishing grammatical operations such as those prescribed by the rule *niṣṭhā ca dvyajanāt*, and to prevent undesirable forms such as *kṣībita*. In the case of the word *phulla*, however, it is also for the purpose of [establishing] the form *phullāvaḥ*.
After the words *nuda*, *vida*, *unda*, *trā*, *ghrā*, and *hrī*, the suffix *khaś* is optionally applied.

Since it is impossible to prescribe the immediately preceding substitution here, it is established that the separated [substitution] is what must be prescribed. Thus, even though it is separated by other substitutes such as those in the rule *śuṣaḥ kaḥ*, it is precisely the substitution of *natva* (the change to *n*) that is prescribed. How so? First, that very [substitution] is prohibited in the subsequent sūtra, because a prohibition presupposes a prior application. Therefore, that very [substitution], which remains present in the mind, is optionally applied here as well. In the form *samunnaḥ*:

from the root *undī* in the sense of "moistening," the augment *iṭ* is prohibited because it is marked with the indicator *ī*; then, by the rule *aniditām*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
He states that this is an option (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases: "of *hrī*," meaning of the root *hrī*;

and "of *vid*," meaning of the root *vid* in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇa*), specifically the one belonging to the *raudhādika* class, because of its association with *und*, which also belongs to the *raudhādika* class. Although there is also an association with *nud*, which belongs to the *tudādika* class, nevertheless, association with the subsequent [root] alone is the determining factor, since the rule "in case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]" (*vipratiṣedhe param*) is applicable even in such instances.

He confirms that the term "vicāraṇārtha" (meaning deliberation) is to be understood by means of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), stating: "For it has been said thus. The form *vidita* is accepted as being derived from the verbal root *vit* (to know) ending in the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix -ta), because that root is *seṭ* (possessing the augment *iṭ*). However, in this context, the form *vitta* is accepted as being derived from the root *vid* meaning "existence" (to exist), because that root is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) and because [the former root] is not what is intended here. Regarding the word *vinter*: the genitive case is used because it is an imitation of a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*). As for the example *bhogavitta* (wealth consisting of enjoyments): *(Note: The commentary explains the distinction between two roots, *vit* and *vid*, based on grammatical rules regarding the suffix *niṣṭhā*. It clarifies that while *vidita* comes from the root *vit* which takes the augment *iṭ*, the term *vitta* in this specific context refers to the root *vid* meaning 'to exist', which does not take the augment and is therefore the one intended here.)*

Even in the absence of *ekārthībhāva* (the formation of a single integrated meaning), a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) is formed due to the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) by the author of the Bhāṣya. The mention of "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the two meanings of "enjoyment" and "conviction," the form *vitta* is desired for the root *vid* belonging to the Tudādi class; elsewhere, however, the form is *vinna*, where only the substitution of *n* occurs. This is not an optional alternative (*vikalpa*); this is the meaning. The reason for this has been stated.
The suffix *kta* does not take the augment *iṭ* after the roots *dhyai*, *khyā*, *mūrchi*, and *mad*.

Regarding *mūrta*: there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "āditaśca," and the elision of the suffix *ch* occurs by the rule "rāllopaḥ. Regarding *matta*: there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* because it is marked with the indicator *ī*.
The word *vitta* [is substituted for *vidita*] before the words *bhoga* and *pratyaya*. 8.2.58.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of gain" (*lābhārthāt*): the suffix *iṭ* must be applied for the sake of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth. The sense is that even for the two meanings of "existence" (*sattā*) and "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*), the occurrence of the suffixes *bhoga* and *pratyaya* is not possible. But how is it that the word *vitta*, when derived as a nipātana (irregular formation) in the sense of "enjoyment" (*bhoga*), comes to mean "wealth" (*dhana*)? To this he says: "For wealth... The meaning is that in the Sūtra, the word *bhoga* has the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*). By this, the term "*pratyaya*" is also explained. Regarding *vinna*: because the root *vid* belonging to the Taudādika class optionally takes the suffix *iṭ* in the *kvasu* participle according to the rule "optionally [after *gam*, *han*, *vid*, and *viś*]," there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) by the rule "there is a prohibition of *iṭ* where there is an option."
*bhitta* means a fragment. 8.2.59.
"This is a synonym for *śakala*. The meaning is that just as the word *śakala* is a generic term (*jātiśabda*) and not a term denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*), so too is the word *bhitta*.

Now, this word *bhida*, being derived from the verbal root *bhid*, is a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*); how then can it be a synonym for a word denoting a universal (*jātiśabda*)? To this he says: "In this case" (*atre*). For there exist those words in which the action is merely useful for the purpose of etymological derivation, whereas the universal alone is the meaning of the word by virtue of the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) of its parts; for example, one who "drinks oil" is called a *tailapāyika*. But why is this [method] adopted? To this he says: "For when the action of splitting is intended to be expressed," and so on. The inclusion of the term *śakala* (fragment) is for the sake of establishing a point of similarity.

The meaning is that just as when there is a desire to express the act of splitting, the form *bhinnaṃ śakalam* ("a split fragment") occurs, so too the usage *bhittam* (as a synonym for *bhinna*) arises. However, if [the word] were a verb (*kriyāśabda*), since the action would already be conveyed by the word *bhinna* itself, the usage *bhinnaṃ bhittam* would not occur.

Others, however, say: "Just as a fragment is produced by the act of splitting, the word *bhinna* indeed acknowledges that [act]; but when there is a splitting of that which already exists as a fragment, then for the sake of expressing that, the usage *bhinnaṃ bhittam* occurs."
The word *ṛṇa* takes the sixth case ending when it signifies a debt owed.

Regarding the word *ṛ*: it is derived either from the root *sṛ* meaning "to go," or from the root *ṛ* meaning "to go" and "to cause to reach. The phrase "from this very [root]" implies that, apart from the *śauṇḍādi* group, one must seek a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) where the final member ends in the locative case; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "at another time" (*kālāntara*), etc.: "another time" refers to a time distinct from the time of taking a loan; that which is to be paid at such a time is "to be paid at another time" (*kālāntaradeya*). The mention of "debt-relationship" (*ādhamarṇya*) is for the purpose of indicating the exchange or reversal involved therein, and not for the purpose of conveying its own specific lexical meaning.

But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? To this he says: "For even [the word] 'creditor' (uttamarṇa)... This is understood from the grammatical rule: *dhāreruttamarṇaḥ* ("after the root *dhṛ*, the creditor is the agent").
In Vedic usage, the forms *nasatta*, *niṣātta*, *anutta*, *pratūrta*, *sūrta*, and *gūrta* [are used]. 8.2.61.

The term *nasatta* and so forth is a *dvandva* compound of imitative words (*anukaraṇapada*). Regarding *niṣattam*: the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by the rule *sadiraprateḥ*. Regarding *anunnam* "in the common language" (*bhāṣāyām*): they say that the optional alternative provided by the rule *nudavidondatrā* does not apply here, because of the force of the introduction of this specific nipāta (irregular form). Regarding *pratūrtam*: when derived from the root *tvar*, then *ūṭh* is substituted according to the rule *jvaratvara* etc.; but when derived from *tud*, as in *turvī hiṃsāyām*, then there is elision of the *r* by the rule *rāllopaḥ*. Regarding the substitution of *u*: the replacement of *r* by *r* (raparatva) is already established by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*; for subsequent rules (*parabhāṣā*) operate even within the section concerning what is considered "not yet established" (*asiddha*).
A *k* is substituted for the final consonant of a word ending in a feminine suffix (*kvin*).

The meaning is that although one should have stated "kvinaḥ ku," this is because the status of being a *kvin* suffix does not deviate [from its application]. Nor should it be suspected that, if this were stated, the substitution of *gh* for the *v* of the *kvin* suffix itself would apply—bypassing the elision (*lopa*) prescribed by the rule "verapṛktasya"—and thus result in the form *dhaka*.

Similarly, when the suffix *kvip* is understood as including that which ends in it by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the mention of a suffix, and when the elision of the letter *v* of *kvip* is to be applied, the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutva*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*); consequently, only the elision prescribed by "the elision of *ra* and *l*" (*rāllopa*) takes place. Once that has occurred, the subsequent substitution of *k* will apply only to the remaining portion of the verbal root. It might be argued: "The substitution of *k* (*kutva*), being specifically prescribed, would set aside the elision—which finds its scope in *kvip* and other suffixes—on the basis of the maxim that 'a specific rule sets aside a general one due to the authority of the statement'? This is not so.
