For in this way, the mention of the *varga* (consonant class) would be purposeless. Indeed, the mention of the *varga* is for the sake of establishing multiple substitutes for a single original element (*sthānin*); however, if only the phoneme *va* were the original element, only the phoneme *gha* would have been specified. This is because the *Śikṣā* establishes an equality of quality between *va* and *gha in the rule "the third and fourth [phonemes] of the *vargas*. Therefore, one should simply say "kvinaḥ kuḥ. [The phrase] "for the sake of understanding it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound" means: for the sake of understanding it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound can also function as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), as in the example "Let the owner of brindled cows be brought"; even in the absence of the actual cows, there is the bringing of that person who is indicated by the brindled cows. Similarly here, even though the suffix *kvip* is absent, the operation applies to the verbal root (*dhātu*) as indicated by *kvin*. Thus: *asrāk*, *adrāk*. From the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*, with *luṅ* by the rule *māṅi luṅ*; *tip*; *sic* for the *cli*; elision by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]; and *vṛddhi* by the rule *vada-vraja-hala-anta-laghūnām ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.3].

In this case, when the substitution of *ṣ* (by Pāṇini 8.2.36) would have applied, the substitution of *k* (kutva) occurs: *j* becomes *g*, *ś* becomes *kh*, and for that [kh] as well, the substitution of *jaś* (8.4.53) applies, followed by the substitution of *c* (cartva) by "vāvasāne" (8.4.56), resulting in the letter *k*. The rule "pūrvatrāsiddham" (6.1.86)—which renders a preceding operation as if non-existent—does not apply here to the substitution of *ṣ* with respect to the substitution of *k*; for the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) in the rule has the force of making the substitution of *k* an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *ṣ*. The phrase "even of that ending in *kvip*" means that in forms such as *draṣṭṛ* and the like, the substitution does not occur because they are not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). And so it is with the passage beginning "this being the case," etc.; it is exactly like that. The substitution of *k* is illustrated in the form *dṛgbhyām*.
"It must be countered" means that a counter-argument must be made; a counter-argument is indeed a statement.
Or [the substitution of *naś*] for *naś*. 8.2.63.

Because it is the cause of the destruction of life, the oblation (āhuti) is called "jīvana" [life-destroyer]; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule beginning with "sampadādi."
The suffix *ma* is applied after the verbal root *dhā*. (Pāṇini 8.2.64)
He considers that while the elision of *n* does not occur, the substitution of *na* must indeed exist for the sake of that very elision.
The substitute *ru* is applied in place of the final consonant of a word ending in *s*, as well as of the word *sasajuṣ*.

Regarding *sajūḥ*: as before, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of state (*bhāve*); once *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) has been made, there is lengthening according to the rule *rvor upadhāyāḥ*; and in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*. The meaning is "possessing joy" (*saprītiḥ*).
The words *avayāḥ*, *śvetavāḥ*, and *puroḍāḥ* [retain their final visarga before a vowel]. 8.2.67.

Regarding the phrase *ṇvini kṛte*: the meaning is "when [the suffix] *ṇvin* has been applied. The sense there is that where *śvetavāh* and others possess the status of a word (*padatva*), the suffix *ḍas* must be stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to *ṇvin*; it does not mean that *ḍas* is to be stated when words ending in *ṇvin* have the status of a word. [Objection: But surely *ḍas* must necessarily be stated for the sake of forms such as *śvetavobhyām*; if it is so stated, this [rule regarding *ṇvin*] is unnecessary, because since the word ends in *s*, the substitution of *ru* is already established by the previous rule, and its lengthening is already established by the rule *atvasantasya*. To this, he replies: "For the sake of lengthening in the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*)."
The substitution of *ah* occurs [in place of the genitive case ending] after a word ending in *ahan*. 8.2.68.

Regarding "ahobhyām": the substitution of *u* occurs by the rule *haśi ca*. As for the phrase "without performing the elision of *n*" and so forth, this has already been explained in the section on the rule for the elision of *n*.
The reason given is "because it is merely occasional (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*)," since the form *ahan* is obtained through the addition of the augment *aṭ*.

Regarding the rule *hrasvavidhau*: since the elision (*lup*) by means of the suffix *lumat* occurs in a compound, the substitution of *r* would apply [to the final vowel]; therefore, the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is stated for the sake of that *r*-substitution. In the example *ahorūpam*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the example *gatamahorūpaṃ paśya*, it is not a compound. In the example *ahorātraḥ*, the compound-ending suffix *ac* is applied by the rule *ahassarvaikadeśa-* etc.; even though the vowel *i* has been elided, because that which is modified in one part remains essentially the same (*ananyatvāt*), the substitution of *u* (*utva*) takes place. However, the word *rātra* was not included [in the rule] because the substitution of *r* is required even in a non-compound such as *gatamahorātrirāgatā*.
Also before the suffix *ru*. 8.2.69.

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. In the word *ra*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). In the example *adardar dadāti*, the accusative case is used to denote continuous contact (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Regarding the rule for the substitution of *ru* for *ahar*: how this is established by that very sūtra has already been explained under the rule *na lumatāṅgasya*. In the example *dīrghāho nidāghaḥ*, the prohibition [of *ru*] is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) based on the condition *asupi*. If, however, it were an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), then since there exists a suffix similar to *sup* (namely, the *hal* following the *aṅga*), the substitution of *repha* would indeed occur here.

But in the case of a prasajya-pratiṣedha (absolute negation), since the negation applies by virtue of the technical definition of a suffix (pratyayalakṣaṇa), only *ru* remains; and consequently, the substitution of *ya* and *uva* occurs based upon that.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the words *am*, *na*, *rūdhara*, and *vāri* [are optionally treated as having a long vowel] in both ways.

Since the substitution of *ru* would have applied permanently, this rule is commenced so that the substitution of *ra* may also optionally occur. The word *amnas* is used in the sense of "slightly," as in the example *amnar astamitaḥ* ("the sun has slightly set"). *Avaḥ* means "protection. In *pracetā rājan*, the *s* is replaced by *r*; that *r* is then elided by the rule *ro ri*; and the preceding vowel is lengthened by the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *aharādīnām* and so forth, the word *ādi* (etcetera) in both instances indicates a class or category. This [substitution] applies both in the Vedic language (*chandas*) and in the common language (*bhāṣā*).
And [the word] *bhuvaḥ* [is used] for the *mahāvyāhṛti*. 8.2.71.

The three *mahāvyāhṛtis* are the designations for the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven; however, here it is the middle one that is intended: *bhuvo viśveṣu savaneṣu*. This is a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). From the root *bhū*, the suffix *laṅ* is applied because of the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used for all tenses]," followed by the suffix *sip*. The absence of *guṇa* in the presence of *śap* is due to Vedic usage, and the absence of *aṭ* is due to the rule "in the Veda, [the augment] is often absent even when not joined with *māṅ*. Since this form would already be excluded from the application of the rule due to its being a technical derivative (*lākṣaṇika*), the explicit mention of it as a *mahāvyāhṛti* is for the purpose of indicating that this *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). By means of this, the augment *puK* is successfully established in forms such as *krāpayati*.
The substitute *da* is applied in place of the final consonant of the words *vasu*, *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *anaḍuh*.

The word *saḥ* (he) is understood [from the previous rule]. If it were not carried over (*ananuvṛtti*), then in forms such as *vidvān*, the substitution of *d* for the *n* would apply, but not in cases such as *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*. The connection is made through the modification [of the gender] of the words *viśeṣyete* (they are qualified). And because it is impossible [for the rule to apply], the word *anaḍuh* is not qualified; this is the connection. One might ask: "Just as this substitution of *d* for *vas* (in *vidvad-das*), being introduced when another rule has not yet taken effect, subverts the substitution of *r* (ru-tva) in cases like *vidvadbhyām*, would it likewise subvert the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) in cases like *vidvān*? To this, he says: "When the substitution of *r* has not yet taken effect."

Now, why does the substitution of *d* not occur for the *n* of *num* in the word *anaḍvān*? To this he says: "But [the rule] regarding *num*... If the substitution of *d* were to apply to the *n*, then the prescription of *num* would be purposeless; for even with the substitution of *d* for the *h* [of *han*], the form *anaḍvād* is established.

If, then, by the very force of the prescription of *num*, the substitution of *dat* does not occur, then in cases such as *anaṅ vān atra*, would the substitution of *ru*—by the rule "after a long vowel, before a vowel (*aṭ*), within the same *pāda*"—also not apply? [The answer is: "That rule for which the instruction [of a preceding element] is rendered purposeless is sublated; however, that for which it is merely the cause is not sublated. And while the substitution of *dat* is purposeless with respect to the application of *num*, the substitution of *ru* is indeed its cause.
The *ru* substitute optionally occurs for the *sip* affix after a verbal root.

"The mention of *dhātu* (root) is for the sake of what follows. However, in this case, since *sip* follows, there is no possibility of anything other than a verbal root (*dhatu*). "And the mention of *ru*"—the phrase "for the sake of what follows" is to be supplied here as well; however, in this case, when the substitution of *da* is optional, because [the stem] ends in *s* in one alternative, *ru* is established.
And [the substitution of *u* for the final vowel] occurs before the suffix *da*. (Pāṇini 8.2.75)

Regarding the word *abhinat*: because the augment *śna* (which falls within that [root] or is a part of it) is included by the mention of that [root], the element here possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*).
A long vowel is substituted for an *ik* (i, u, ṛ, ḷ) that precedes a consonant (*rvauḥ*) when it is followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel.

Both "of the root" (dhātoḥ) and "of the word" (padasya) are in apposition and are qualified by the letters *r* and *v*; and since a rule involving a suffix applies to that which ends in the qualifier, he says: "ending in *r* or *v*. The mention of *v* is for the sake of what follows; however, in this context, it is impossible for a word ending in *v* to be both a word (*pada*) and a root (*dhātu*). [The mention of *v* is also] so that the shortening of the vowel *i* in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) does not occur. If it were to occur, then because that [shortening] would be considered asiddha, the shortening prescribed by the rule "hrasvaḥ" would not take place.
And [the substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] before the suffix *upadhāya*.

The entire rule beginning with "rvor upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.89) is understood to carry over here. This mention of *upadhā* (penultimate letter) is a qualifier for *ru* and *v*. The singular locative case (*saptamyekavacana*) is used in place of the dual genitive (*ṣaṣṭhīdvivacana*). The previously mentioned mention of *upadhā* is a qualifier for *iK* (the short vowels i, u, ṛ); and that [mention] indicates a state of being prior (*pūrvatva*) in relation to *ru* and *v*. Thus, the meaning of the sūtra as presented by the author of the Vṛtti is established. [Examples include] *hūrchita* and so forth.

In the case of *hurchā*, meaning "crookedness," and *murchā*, meaning "delusion" or "increase," because the doubling [of the consonant] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) according to the rule *aco rahābhyām*, the letter *r* remains as the penultimate (*upadhā*), and thus the lengthening occurs as before. *Ciri* and *jiri* both have the sense of "injury."

In the forms *ririyatuḥ* and *vivyatuḥ*, derived from the roots *ri* (meaning "to go") and *vī* (meaning "to go" and so forth) with the suffix *liṭ* and the ending *atus*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. Here, there arises the contingency of lengthening the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Consequently, because that [lengthening] would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the short vowel [of the reduplication] would not occur. To this, he says: *ririyatuḥ* etc., [explaining it is] "due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the *yaṇ* substitution. Nor is there a prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the prescription of lengthening, because [the *yaṇ* substitution] is not a substitute for a vowel (*alopa-aj-ādeśatvāt*).

Even so, having raised the objection that "in the absence of what is not yet established (*asiddha*), [an operation] is not as if it were the original substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*"), he states another solution: "But because of its being *asiddha*... Since the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed under the heading of the *aṅga* (the stem), it depends upon the suffix and is therefore *bahiraṅga* (external); the long vowel (*dīrgha*), however, does not depend on that and is therefore *antaraṅga* (internal).

Here, from the word *caturyita*, which ends in *kyac*, the suffix *tṛc* is added; then, after the elision of the *iṭ* augment, when the elision of the *kyac* suffix does not occur—by virtue of the rule "the elision of *kyac* is optional" (*kyasya vibhāṣā*)—there arises the contingency of lengthening because the *repha* (the letter *r*), being the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the verbal root, is followed by a consonant (*hal*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "In *caturyita* also... Here too, as before, the distinction between internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*) operations applies.

In this context, regarding the form *pratidīvne*—derived from the root *div* preceded by *prati*, ending in the suffix *kanin* according to the rule *kaninyuvṛṣitakṣi*, and then placed in the third case singular where the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *allopo'naḥ*—lengthening is desired. However, that [lengthening] does not apply because the letter *v* is not a penultimate (*anupadha*) with respect to the verbal root. Therefore, he says: "In the form *pratidīvne*... and so forth.

But how can there be lengthening by the rule *hali ca*, given that when the substitution of *al* (the elision of *y*) is treated as *sthānivat*, the letter *v* is no longer followed by a *hal*? To this he says: "In the prescription of lengthening. Now, one might object: let there be no *sthānivat* status; since the elision of *al* depends on the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it is *bahiraṅga*, and because it is considered *asiddha*, [the *v*] is not followed by a *hal*. To this he says: "As for the principle that 'what is *bahiraṅga* is *asiddha* with respect to what is *antaraṅga*,' [that does not apply here]."

However, this [rule] is not applied because of the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this *paribhāṣā*. And its non-universality is indicated by the inclusion of the term "tug" in the rule *nalopaḥ supsvara...* (Pāṇini 6.3.71). Here, from the root *jṛ* we have *jivriḥ* [formed with the suffix *krin* and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ*]; from the roots *kṛ* and *gṛ*, the suffix *kip*; thus *kiriḥ* and *giriḥ*. From these two, with the addition of *os* and the application of *yaṇ* substitution, we get *kiryos* and *giryos*. In this case, would not lengthening (*dīrghatva*) apply by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.69)? To this he replies: "The *uṇādi* derivatives are also already produced. (That is, they are considered ready-made forms, so further operations like lengthening do not apply.)

The meaning is that in the *uṇādi* suffixes, the grammatical operations resulting from etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) do not necessarily apply. This is indicated by the inclusion of the term *kaṃsa-* in the rule *ataḥ kṛkamikaṃsa-*, even though the desired form would have been established by the inclusion of *kami-* alone; namely, that in some instances the operations of derivation do indeed occur, as in *pratidīvne*. This resolution was stated in the commentary on *kiryoḥ* without relying on the view that the *yaṇ*-substitution is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*).
The substitution of *bhakuchurām* does not take place [after a reduplicated stem]. 8.2.79.
Regarding the word *churyāt*: it is derived from the root *chur* in the sense of "cutting," used here in the optative (*liṅ*) mood to express a benediction.
Regarding *pratidīvnā*: that which ends in *v* here does not bear the technical designation *bha*; and that which bears the designation *bha* does not end in *v*. What then? It ends in *n*.
In place of the *as* of *adas*, *dā* is substituted; for *dā*, *du* is substituted; and for *da*, *ma* is substituted.

In the word *aseḥ*, the vowel *i* in *sakāre* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). Regarding *amūbhyām*: here, once the substitution of *tyadādi* [for the pronoun] has been applied, the lengthening occurs by the rule *supi ca*; thereafter, by proximity (*āntaratamya*), the long *ū* replaces the long *ā*. Now, one might object: "The short vowel is specified in the sūtra, and because it is being produced (*bhāvyamāna*), there is no inclusion of its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrahaṇa*); so how is the long *ū* obtained? To this he says: "Even by that which is being produced... This is indicated by the addition of the *t* in *tapara* in the rule *diva ut*.

Some read the letter *u* here followed by *d*, as in "uddomaḥ"; for them, this *d* is inherent (*autpattika*) for the sake of ease of pronunciation, and it is not the result of the substitution of *j* for *t*. For if that were the case, the inclusion of homogeneous letters (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) would not occur. However, the reading with *ad* is preferable. [The author asks: "But [the rule] continues with the word 'of a word' (*padasya*), and this is not a word."

Is it because of the restriction "naḥ kye"? If so, then this very [sūtra] indicates that this *mutva* (the substitution of *m*) occurs for *adas* even when it is a word (*pada*): as in *amum* and *amuyā*. Otherwise, it would only occur where it is a word in the *svādi* group, such as in *amuṣyai* and *amūbhyām*.

Regarding *ano'sra*: the meaning is "that which does not possess the phonemes *o*, *s*, or *r*. In the example *adaḥ kulam*, this [word] ends in *r* because the *visarjanīya* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Regarding the phrase "for that purpose": it is for the sake of prohibiting [the substitution] of the vowel *o* and the letter *r* as well. As for the expression "of that which has *i* in place of *a*" (*aḥ seryasya*), what is its meaning? To this he says: "where. What is established by that? To this he says: "by that. How is there the substitution of *adri*? This is a question implying that something must be stated regarding this subject; to that he says: "of *adas*, when *adri* [follows]. He explains the first half of the verse with the words beginning "by whom" (*yair*). He explains the third quarter-verse with the words beginning "but those who" (*ye tu*). He explains the fourth quarter-verse with the words beginning "but for those who" (*yeṣām tu*). [The form is] *amumuyaṅ*.

From the root *añc* with the prefix *adaḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā*. By the rule *viṣvag-devayoś-ca*, the substitute *adri* is applied for the word *adas* before the suffixes beginning with *adri*. When the form *adadryañc* is established, the substitution of *m* occurs for the *d* and *r* of the word *adas* which is connected to the *adri* substitute. In the nominative singular (*sau*), the *num* augment is added by the rule *ugidacām*; then, the elision of the final consonant (*hal*) and the elision of the *y* (from *añc*) occur by the rules *hal-ṅy-ādi-* and *saṃyogānta-lopaḥ*. Finally, the substitution of *ṅ* for *n* occurs by the rule *kvin-pratyayasya kuḥ*. Thus, we have *amuyā* and *amuyor*. Here, there arises the contingency of the substitution of *u* for the *y*.
In this [section], the plural number is used for the word *etad*. 8.2.81.

"This is an indication of the meaning," because of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*). But what is the reason for explaining it in this way? To this he says: "In the technical sense" (*pāribhāṣike*). For in that case, by the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—"When [something] is indicated as 'in that' (*tasmin*), [an operation applies] to the preceding"—the *ekāra* would have to become *it* before a plural ending (*bahuvacana*), yet here there is no plural ending following.
The final syllable (ṭi) of a sentence is protracted (pluta) and acute (udātta).

An introductory heading (adhikāra) serves to exclude other headings; thus, one might raise the objection that by the heading pertaining to sentences (*vākya-adhikāra*), the heading pertaining to words (*pada-adhikāra*) would be superseded. Consequently, in cases such as *bhavantau*, even for a *n* that is not at the end of a word, the substitution of *r* by the rule *naśchavyapraśān* would undesirably apply. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The heading pertaining to words indeed continues. For the mention of "sentence" cannot possibly set aside the heading pertaining to words; for that which is the *ṭi* of a sentence is necessarily also the *ṭi* of a word by virtue of their co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "sentence" (*vākya*)? For is it not the case that a word is employed only when situated within a sentence, and never in isolation? To this he replies: "The mention of 'sentence'... When it is stated "of the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of a word," the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply to the final phoneme of every single word within that sentence; however, it is desired that it should apply only to that which is the final phoneme of the [final] word of the sentence.

Regarding the mention of *ṭi* and so forth: if the mention of *ṭi* were absent, then by the force of the rule for the protracted vowel (*pluta*), the technical definition of a vowel (*ac-paribhāṣā*) would apply, and since the rule for "specification of that which ends in it" (*tadanta-vidhi*) would apply to a vowel, the protraction would occur only at the final letter of a sentence ending in a vowel—just as the shortening of the neuter occurs in cases such as *grāmaṇi kulam*, but not in cases such as *suvāk*; it would be exactly like that. However, when *ṭi* is mentioned, by the power of its inclusion, the vowel (*ac*) is qualified by *ṭi*, rather than *ṭi* being qualified by the vowel; thus, the protraction is established even for a word ending in a consonant.
In returning a greeting, [the vowel *a* is substituted for the final phoneme] except when addressing a Śūdra.

Regarding the phrase "pratyabhivādo nāma" and so forth: the term "guru" (teacher) is used as an illustration. One who has been a *śrotriya* for three years is worthy of being saluted (*abhivāda*). When being saluted—that is, when having a blessing (*āśis*) pronounced upon him—the guru pronounces a blessing; this is what is meant by "pratyabhivāda," not merely a verbal response, because it is so well-known in common usage. As it is said: "Those ignorant ones who do not know the prolation (*pluti*) of the name in a return-salutation (*pratyabhivāda*). Regarding the word "tatra": it refers to the context of pronouncing a blessing. Of what kind [of context]? It refers to a context where one is not a *śūdra*.

One whose domain (*viṣaya*) is not a Śūdra is described as such; that is to say, when there is a salutation (*abhivādana*), there must be a return-salutation (*pratyabhivāda*). He first illustrates this with the words "abhivādaye" (I salute). The meaning is: "I cause [you] to utter a blessing preceded by a prostration. Thus addressed, the teacher returns the salutation with "āyuṣmān" (may you be long-lived). Because being long-lived is the predicate (*vidheya*), the vocative case-ending is absent. [He says] "edhi. This is the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *as* (to be), with the suffix *sip* changed to *hi*. The meaning is "be" (*bhava*).

Regarding the rule in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], "A Brahmin should be addressed with 'May you be long-lived, O gentle one! at the time of salutation," the inclusion of the word *bhava* (be) is for the sake of its meaning; therefore, the salutation also occurs through synonyms. Now, an objection is raised: since it was stated there that "the letter *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced, with the preceding vowel protracted (*pluta*)," why is this not prescribed here as well? It is replied: only that which is useful for expressing meaning needs to be taught in grammar;
the letter *a*, however, is employed solely for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and it possesses no semantic content whatsoever.

Others, however, explain the rule of Manu differently: at the end—that is, at the conclusion—of the name of this person who offers salutation, the letter *a* should be pronounced as a protracted (*pluta*) vowel; the mention of the letter *a* is illustrative (and includes other vowels), and the preceding syllable should also be pronounced as a protracted vowel. This applies to cases ending in a consonant; by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*), he means a vowel (*ac*). Thus, in the case of words ending in consonants, the vowel preceding the final consonant should be pronounced as a protracted vowel. By the phrase "by both," it is stated that the protraction of the *ṭi* (the final portion of the word) occurs through those two [the final vowel and the preceding syllable].

We, however, say that the syllable *a* must be used separately; why? Because this is the literal meaning of the words. Furthermore, in the *Bharata-śāstra*, while describing the manner of returning a greeting in the relevant context, the separate use of the syllable *a* is shown. Therefore, the formula for returning a greeting here is as follows: "May you be long-lived, O gentle Devadatta-a," or "O Agnicit-a."

However, when these [names] undergo phonetic modification (*ejanta*), in the presence of the suffix *-satya*, the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasyādhāmanepadeṣu* applies; furthermore, by the rule *tayor yvāv aci saṃhitāyām*, the *yaṇ* substitution also occurs, as in *pinākapāṇāya*, *harāya*, *śambhave*, and *viṣṇave*. Regarding the formal greeting in return (*pratyabhivāda*), they do not accept the use of the words *śarman* and *varman*. By the rule "the name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in *śarman*, while that of a Kṣatriya should end in *varman*," the use of those two is prescribed only when they are not already included within the name itself; their inclusion within the name is not intended.
Regarding the term *tuṣajaka*: the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of contempt; thus, according to the statement "the name of a Śūdra is [to be] despised," this is a name for a Śūdra.

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a woman": the meaning is that it should be stated as "except for a woman and a Śūdra. Some say: "A woman does not perform a formal salutation (*abhivādana*); she merely performs the clasping of the feet and so forth. Others, however, say: "She does perform a salutation, but she does not utter her own name or *gotra*. In either of these two views, a prohibition regarding women need not be enjoined. However, this prohibition is intended according to the opinion of those who maintain that even for women there is both salutation and the return-salutation (*pratyabhivāda*) by means of name and *gotra*.

"One who envies is an *asūyaka*—that is, one who is ill-mannered. With the words "But in his case," etc., [the author] refutes the prohibition regarding such an envious person. The meaning shown in the Bhāṣya is stated as follows: "For it has been said thus"—[namely,] as long as he is not known to be envious, one certainly performs the protracted vowel (*pluta*) [in the salutation]; however, when one knows, "This man is envious and intends to mock me," then one does not employ a return-salutation in the form of a blessing, but rather, on the contrary, bestows a curse. Thus it is demonstrated in the Bhāṣya.

The teacher, thinking that *sthālī* was a proper name (*saṃjñā*), used it with a protracted vowel (*pluta*). The resentful student said, "This is not my name; rather, I intended the logic of the 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍin*)—that is, one who possesses a bowl (*sthāla*) is called 'bowl-possessor' (*sthālī*). The teacher, however, taking even that to be the actual fact, again performed the return-greeting without the protracted vowel: "May you be long-lived, O *sthālin*! Again the resentful student said, "I did not intend the logic of the 'staff-bearer'; this is indeed my name."

Then, having recognized his malice, the Guru, becoming angry, said: "You are a malicious person," and so forth. Regarding the word *bhidyasva*, it is used in the reflexive passive (*karmakartṛ*) construction. The reading is *sthālin* (O pot), and not *sthālīvat* (like a pot).

Regarding the phrase "that which is proclaimed in the formula of salutation": that sentence by which one is saluted is the "formula of salutation" (*abhivādana-vākya*). "Name" (*nāma*) refers to a designation; "clan" (*gotra*) refers to a word ending in a patronymic suffix. This was stated because the rule for prolation (*pluti*) applies to the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence. In this context, prolation is desired. Some maintain that this is merely a specific injunction (*iṣṭi*). Others, however, say: "Salutation is performed by means of name and clan"—this is established by traditional practice (*samācāra*).

This *pluta* [protracted vowel] occurs only for that very word which stands at the end of the sentence, because it is understood as the primary element; and the primacy of a word is determined by way of its meaning. The primary meaning here is the one who offers the salutation (*abhivādayitṛ*), since the response to the salutation (*pratyabhivāda*) is intended to favor that person. Attributes such as well-being (*kuśalatva*), however, serve merely as embellishments (*saṃskāraka*) for that very person. Similarly, although the action denoted by the verb "may you prosper" (*edhi*) is primary insofar as it takes the form of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is nonetheless non-primary because it is intended only as an embellishment.

Therefore, the prolated vowel (*pluta*) occurs for that word which brings about the person who is saluting, provided that word is the primary element. And that [word] is either a personal name (*nāman*) or a family name (*gotra*). Regarding the rule "for *bhoḥ*, for Kṣatriyas, and for Vaiśyas, optionally": the term *bhoḥ* is taken as its own form (*svarūpa*), whereas for the other two, they are taken by their respective names. In that context, for the word *bhoḥ*, since it is neither a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) nor a family name (*gotra*), the option is applied where [the prolation] was not otherwise established; for the other two, since they are designatory words (*saṃjñāśabda*), the option applies where [the prolation] was already established.
And [the substitution of *o* for *au* occurs] when the vocative follows from a distance. 8.2.84.

Regarding the word *dūrāt*: the ablative case is used here according to the rule "the second case may optionally be used after words meaning 'far' or 'near'" (*dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*). *Hūtam* means "calling" (*hvānam*); the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). It is said to be "from afar," yet "far" is not fixed; for that very same thing is "very far" with respect to one person, while it is "near" with respect to another. Thus, for example, someone says to another: "Bring that water-pot which is over there"; he replies: "Stand up and take it; I am unable to go so far."

Another says: "Pāṭaliputra is far from Mathurā. He replies: "It is not far; it is near. Thus, because "far" is not fixed, it is not known in what state one ought to perform the *pluti*. Therefore, he says: "Far," and so forth. *Hvānam* means "called" (*hūtam*); that which is far in relation to that [calling] is what is intended here, because of the connection [in the phrase] "called from afar" (*dūrād dhūtam*). The particle *iti* indicates a cause, meaning that "far" does not become far in relation to another place by depending on location.

What is this "distance" in relation to calling (*hūta*)? To this he says: "where. Where there is a call, [it is] from that which is natural and established by its own nature. The sense is that in such a call, there exists distance even in relation to the call mediated by space. And as for the mention of "calling" (*hūta*): that by which another is enjoined to come is a "call," and that cannot occur without an address (*sambodhana*). For a person who has been addressed is then enjoined to come or to drink and so forth; therefore, because it is invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyakatvāt*), the mere address is indicated by the term "call. He states the purpose of this indication: "by that... [as follows].

Here, this *pluta* vowel is prescribed for addressing someone from a distance, and the *ekaśruti* (monotone) is also prescribed for that very same context—according to the rule: "The *ekaśruti* occurs when addressing someone from a distance. Since these two apply to the same domain, there must be one of three possibilities: sublation (*bādha*), option (*vikalpa*), or combination (*samuccaya*). To the question, "Which of these applies here? he says: "And of this... Sublation occurs only when there is a difference in scope, as in the case of *kāṇ* and *aṇ*; for in that instance, the specific [vowel length] is the scope of *kāṇ*, whereas *aṇ* has the general category of verbal roots as its scope. But here, there is no such difference in scope.

Optionality (*vikalpa*) also occurs between two rules that apply simultaneously, as in the case of the suffixes *tavyat* and others. However, here, since the application of *ekaśruti* (monotone) is to be performed, there is no simultaneous application because the *pluta* (protracted vowel) is not yet established; therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there is indeed a coexistence (*samāveśa*). This linguistic expression "coexistence" merely means the simultaneous operation of both [rules] within a single sentence; in reality, however, since the *pluta* is prescribed for the final syllable (*ṭi*) of the sentence, while *ekaśruti* applies to the remainder, it is actually a case of sublation (*bādha*).
In the case of the employment of *hai* and *he*, [the substitution of *hai* and *he* occurs] for *hai* and *he*. (Pāṇini 8.2.85)

Since the rule for *pluta* (protracted vowel) is prescribed for the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence whose meaning concerns an offering (*hūyamānārtha*), this [rule] is stated so that it does not apply to the two particles *hai* and *hai*, which do not have that meaning. Regarding the phrase "only to *hai* and *hai*": the particle *eva* is used for emphasis—meaning that when *hai* and *hai* are employed, it applies only to those two *hai*s. Others, however, explain it as follows: it occurs only with *hai* and *hai*, and not with the final syllable of a sentence whose meaning concerns an offering. How is this obtained? By virtue of its being prescribed through extraction (*apakṛṣya*).

When a *pluta* (protracted) vowel would otherwise apply to a word being addressed (*hūyamānārtha*), that *pluta* which is prescribed for those two vowels [the *ai* and *au*] that do not have that meaning overrides it, according to the maxim: "An override occurs even when there is a possibility [of both rules applying]. Nor is this [protracted form] unestablished, because it has been stated that "an exception [apavāda] prevails by virtue of the authority of the explicit rule. Thus: *hai3*. By the rule "In a *pluta*, the *aic* [diphthongs] become *i* and *u*," the *i*-portion becomes protracted. Thus: *he3*. By the rule "Of an *ec* [diphthong] that is not a *pragṛhya*," the modification to a *pluta* does not occur; because [the address] is from a distance (*dūrāddhūta*).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the case of *hai* and *haiḥ*"? It is so that the protracted (*pluta*) vowel may occur for *hai* and *haiḥ*; otherwise, by virtue of the very fact of this rule's formulation, it would apply only to a non-final [vocative] expressing one who is being called, as in "Devadatta, *hai*! and so forth. If that is the case, then let there simply be "in the case of *hai* and *haiḥ*"; what is the need for "when used" (*haihe-prayoge*), for a rule prescribing protraction is not possible when [the words] are not being used? It is said in reply: the word "when used" must indeed be stated so that [the protraction] occurs even in mere usage.

What is established? The inclusion of even those [particles] that are meaningless (*anarthaka*) is established. And where, then, are they meaningless? Where the word of address (*sambodhana-vacana*) is employed first, there, because the state of being oriented toward [the listener] (*ābhimukhya*) has already been indicated by that very word, there is nothing further to be indicated by *hai* and *he*; thus, they are meaningless. But where the employment of *hai* and *he* comes first, there the state of being oriented toward [the listener] is to be indicated by these two; thus, they possess meaning.

Even so, let it simply be "in usage, [the prolated vowel] occurs in place of *hai* and *hai*"; since it is explicitly stated [in the sūtra], "in usage, the prolation occurs in place of *hai* and *hai*," for what else [could it be]? Therefore, the purpose of the repeated mention of *hai* must be stated. To that he says: "again" (*punaḥ*).

If, however, it is argued that by the very mention of "in usage," the rule will apply even to non-final [vocatives], just as it does to meaningless ones, then the repeated mention of *hai* could indeed be omitted.

According to the Eastern grammarians, the word *gurōḥ* (of a heavy syllable) [is used] even when it does not end in a long vowel (*anantyasya*), provided that each individual [heavy syllable] is preceded by a consonant.

Regarding the phrase "also of a non-final [syllable]": by this word "also" (api), he shows that the previously mentioned *ṭi* is being conjoined. However, if—due to the proximity of the word *guru*—only that which is final were conjoined, such that it meant "of a *guru* that is non-final as well as final," then there would be an option only in cases where the final syllable is a *guru*. But in the case of a light (*laghu*) final syllable, the former rule would apply to it, while this present rule would apply to a non-final *guru*; thus, one would result in hearing two protracted vowels (*pluta*) simultaneously.

Because of the rule "A word is unaccented except for one [syllable]," there is no possibility of simultaneity. [Objection: The protracted vowel (*pluta*) is not established; since it is not established, does the restriction not fail to apply? [Response: This is not so. According to the principle "Technical rules and paribhāṣās are present at the time of the operation," they apply wherever the operation occurs—such as "the final syllable of a sentence is protracted and acute" and "the protracted vowel of a heavy syllable, excepting *ṛ*, is acute. At that point, this rule—"A word is unaccented except for one"—also becomes present. Therefore, there is no possibility of simultaneity.

In that case, since there is an unaccented (*anudātta*) protracted vowel (*pluta*), its simultaneous occurrence with this [other accent] would result in a conflict: when a word is used in honor or at a distance, it becomes protracted; and by the rule "in questions, at the end of a sentence, and in honor," the final syllable (*ṭi*) becomes unaccented—as in "śobhanaḥ khalvasi devadatta" (Truly, you are excellent, Devadatta!). In that situation, by that [rule], the protracted vowel of the heavy syllable (*guru*) would be udātta; therefore, only the *ṭi* should be combined [with the protraction]. For in that case, because of the expression "of each one" (*ekaikasya*), just as this alternation applies to a non-final syllable, so too it applies to the final *ṭi*; thus, there is no possibility of simultaneity.

The mention of "each one" (*ekaika*) is for the sake of providing an alternative (*paryāya*). Otherwise, there would be a simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) of both the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*anudātta*) accents in the protracted vowels (*pluta*), according to the manner just described.

It is recited in some places that this specifies the locus (*sthānin*) for that very protracted vowel which is prescribed by the rule beginning with "in response to a greeting" (*pratyabhivāde*). Its meaning is as follows: this is not an independent prescription for protraction; rather, the protraction prescribed in the cases of "response to a greeting" and "calling from a distance" occurs even for a non-final syllable (*aguror anantyasya*) of the word, and optionally (*paryāyeṇa*) for the final syllable (*antasya*) as well.

It should be understood that this rule for protracted vowels (*pluta*) applies to a word used in response to a greeting or one being offered as an oblation, and not to a teacher standing anywhere at random.

The mention of "the ancients" (*prācām*) is for the sake of providing an option; thus, in one alternative, no protracted vowel occurs for anyone. As for the phrase "therefore, by this," etc.: the word *tat* is used to introduce the statement. The meaning is that what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the rule "in the case of a command to the *Āgnīdhra* priest and for another person"—namely, that "every [vowel] is indeed protracted"—is thereby rendered consistent.

[Objection: Surely, only that *pluta* for which the mention of "the Easterners" (*prācām*) exists should be optional; how can there be an option for all *plutas*? [Response: In that case, the mention of "the Easterners" must be connected to every rule prescribing a *pluta*. To abandon the authority of the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is reckless! Therefore, the meaning is that even by one who does not abandon the treatise, every *pluta* must be prescribed as optional (*vibhāṣā*), on the basis of the traditional recollection of those learned in the tradition (*abhiyukta*).
The [substitution of *pra*] occurs in the sense of "beginning" (*abhyādāna*). (Pāṇini 8.2.87)

Because the technical rule regarding vowels (*ac-paribhāṣā*) is brought into play by the mention of the protracted vowel (*pluta-śruti*), only a vowel is protracted; since the letter *m* consists of half a mora (*ardha-mātrā*), the aggregate results in three and a half moras (*ardha-caturtha-mātra*).
[The suffix *cha* is applied] after [a word denoting a deity] in relation to the sacrificial act (*yajñakarman*). || 8.2.88 ||

It is held that this protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs only in the case of "ye yajāmahe"; however, it also occurs in the *pitryā* [offering] at "ye svadhā," because that [latter] takes the place of the former.
The substitution of *praṇava* occurs before the word *iṣṭi*. 8.2.89.

"What is this called *praṇava*?"—this question is raised because it has not been defined in this treatise (*śāstra*). Regarding the term "of the foot" (*pādasya*), that which is well-known from other treatises is adopted; just as in the case of a deity, the meaning is: "having taken the final vowel (*ac*) of the syllable. Regarding the phrase "of the remainder of the initial syllable" (*tad-ādy-akṣara-śeṣasya*): a consonant (*hal*) is the "remainder of the syllable" (*akṣara-śeṣa*); that which has that [consonant] as its final vowel is "that-initial" (*tad-ādi*); and that which is both "that-initial" and the "remainder of the syllable" is "the remainder of the initial syllable" (*tad-ādy-akṣara-śeṣa*); [the rule applies] to the final phoneme (*ṭi*) of that. Regarding "three morae" (*trimātra*): [it refers to the *praṇava*].

Some desire the [syllable] to have three morae (*mātrā*) together with the letter *m*, while others [desire] only the *bhāga*. In that regard, the rule for the *oṃ* syllable is well known in the context of the *sāmidhenī* verses and others: "Having made the *oṃ* syllable at the beginning of the *ṛc* up to its end three-moraed and ending in *m*, one should pause at the middle of the following [verse]. However, the rule for the *oṃ* syllable in the *nirṇada* is: "The *oṃ* syllable at the beginning and at the end is four-times-chanted (*caturnninarda*). But the followers of the Atharvaveda desire an option between these two everywhere; it is precisely for them that this *sūtra* is recited: *jinva-to3m*. The root *jivi* has the meaning "to please"; [the form is] the present tense (*laṭ*), third person singular (*tip*).

Regarding the phrase "the suffix *ṭi* being present," and so forth: if the mention of *ṭi* were not made, then by the rule "of the final [alphonetic element]," the *u*-vowel would apply to that which is the final [element] of the *ṭi*. For it is because there is no ambiguity that the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) is qualified as being protracted (*pluta*). Furthermore, when a designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed, the technical paribhāṣā rule applies; however, this is not the case when the prescription is for something consisting of three morae (*trimātra*) in its actual substance. Therefore, [if *ṭi* were not mentioned], the [protraction] would apply only to a consonant (*hal*).

Now, might the *praṇava* be qualified as being protracted (*pluta*) precisely for the purpose of bringing the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) into effect? Even so, it would apply only to that vowel (*ac*) which is at the end of the word (*ṭi*), and not to every final syllable (*ṭi*). However, since the *oṃkāra* is a collection of both vowels and consonants (*ajhal-samudāya*), it cannot be protracted; thus, by virtue of the governing rule "of the final syllable of a sentence" (*vākyasya ṭeḥ*), it is established that it applies to every final syllable. True; however, since the *praṇava* is designated as such only when it occupies the position of the *ṭi*, one must consider how there could be any possibility of its application to the final vowel alone.
The end of the *yājyā* [is the point of completion]. || 8.2.90 ||

Regarding the phrase *yājyākāṇḍe*: this refers to the section known as the *yājyānuvākyākāṇḍa*. Regarding the word *teṣām*: it refers to those mantras. Regarding the reading *tāsām*: it means "at the end of those *yājyās*. Regarding the word *plavate*: the meaning is that it increases by becoming three morae (*trimātra*). In the example *agnaye3*, the protracted modification (*pluta*) occurs for the word *agnaye* ending in the dative singular, according to the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasya*. Here, the mention of *antam* (the end) may either set aside the rule concerning *ṭeḥ* (the final phoneme), or serve as a qualifier for it.

In the previous [interpretation], because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the protracted vowel (*pluta-śruti*) would apply, the protraction would occur only at the end of a *yājyā* that ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). However, in the alternative view, the mention of "end" (*anta*) would be purposeless, since the final syllable (*ṭi*) is never anything other than the end. With this intention, he asks: "What is the purpose of mentioning 'end'? The other, having understood his intention, replies: "As for what is called a *yājyā*..."
The substitution of *brūhi* for *brūhi*, *preṣya* for *preṣya*, *śrauṣaṭ* for *śrauṣaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ* for *vauṣaṭ* occurs in place of the initial [portion] of the word *āvaha*.

In the case of the precept "pitryāyām anusvadha" (at the ancestral rite, [say] *anusvadha*), there is also a protracted (*pluta*) vowel in *anu-sva-dhe-ti*; this is because the word *svadhā* has taken the place of the word *brūhi*. Likewise, in the response "astu svadhā," there is also a protracted vowel; this is because it has taken the place of the word *śrauṣaṭ*. Furthermore, some authorities transmit the *vaṣaṭ*-call as sixfold—namely, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vāṣaṭ*, *vaukṣaṭ*, *vākṣaṭ*, and *vakṣāṭ*—and in all these cases, there is a protracted vowel;
for the word *vauṣaṭ* serves as an illustration for the entire category of *vaṣaṭ*-calls.

"In [mantras] such as 'Bring the gods for the sacrificer' (āvaha devān yajamānāya)," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of [mantras] such as "O Jātavedas, bring them" (āvaha jātavedaḥ) and "Sacrifice with a good sacrifice" (suyajā yaja).
In the case of the *agnītpreṣaṇa* formulas and those that follow, [the *āmantrita* accent is applied]. 8.2.92.

In this very case, this protracted vowel (*pluta*) is desired; however, in the instance of the hearing of "o svadhe" and so forth, it occurs because [the latter] takes the place of the former, as in "ā3svadhe. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "The protracted vowels are obligatory," as in "uddhara3 uddhara. The doubling [of the word] occurs in the sense of haste (*cāpala*).
The substitution of *hi* for the imperative suffix *loṭ* occurs when it expresses an answer to a question. Pāṇini 8.2.93.

This word *prativacana* also occurs in the sense of an opposing statement, since the prefix *prati* is well-known in the sense of opposition—as in *pratimalla* (a rival wrestler) or *pratikuñjara* (a rival elephant). It also exists in the sense of a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) within an *avyayībhāva* compound, as in *vacanaṃ vacanaṃ prati* = *prativacanam*. Furthermore, it exists in the sense of a resolution or response, as in "I have provided a *prativacana* for that which was stated by him. It also occurs in the sense of a reply to what has been asked. In this context, were the term "asked" (*pṛṣṭa*) not included, the intended kind of *prativacana* would not be understood.
In the example, the particle *hi* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
And [the suffix *kha* is used] after a verb meaning "to reproach" when followed by the word *anuyoga*. (Pāṇini 5.4.94)

"Having refuted" (*nigṛhya*) is a gerund (*lyabantam*). "From his own position" (*svamatāt*) means from his own thesis (*svapakṣāt*). "Causing to fall away" (*pracyāvanam*) means removal (*apanayaḥ*). "Of that very [position]" (*tasyaiva*) means the disclosure—i.e., the verbal manifestation—of that very thesis from which he has been caused to fall away, as in: "Indeed, you have stated this without any logical justification. Demonstrating the meaning of the aphorism through an example, he provides the illustration: "It has been proposed by someone that 'sound is impermanent.'"

Desiring to find fault with and reproach one who speaks thus, [the opponent] seizes him, causes him to deviate from his own position, and, displaying his own view with envy and indignation, questions him. In some versions this passage is not read, but it is read at the end; [it means that] one who asserts "today is the new moon" is made to deviate from his own position and is questioned in this manner.
A reduplicated word [is used] in the sense of reproaching. (Pāṇini 8.1.95)

In the examples, reduplication occurs by the rule "of an address at the beginning of a sentence" (*vākyāder āmantritasya*), and so forth. Although there is the governing rule "of the final phoneme of a sentence" (*vākyasya ṭeḥ*), here it applies even to a non-final [phoneme], because reduplication is prescribed specifically for a word that is at the beginning of a sentence when used in reproach.

"Regarding the phrase *tadartham* (for that purpose): it is for the sake of ensuring that the protracted vowel (*pluta*) occurs in turn in both the preceding and following parts. Regarding the phrase *dviruktopalakṣaṇārtham* (for the purpose of indicating the two parts of the reduplicated whole): the meaning is that it serves to indicate the two constituent parts within the reduplicated aggregate. This [indication] is understood because the function [of protraction] is impossible for the mere *āmreḍita* (the repeated word) alone when used in the sense of scolding; however, the application to each individual part is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "each one" (*ekaikasya*)."
That which is connected with a subordinate element (aṅga) and requires a finite verb ending (tiṅ). 8.2.96.

*Ākāṅkṣati* means "desiring" (*ākāṅkṣam*), derived with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. "Now you shall know, you wretch!"—this is the remainder for both examples. The meaning is: "In this very moment, you shall know the fruit of your chirping or the fruit of your speech. The word *aṅga* is used here in the sense of indignation (*amarṣe*), whereas in the counter-example it is used in the sense of conciliation (*anunaye*).
"O Devadatta!"—this much constitutes one sentence; and this sentence requires the [implicit] connection: "you are speaking falsely."
[The substitution of *śatṛ* for *laṭ*] occurs when [the action] is being deliberated upon. Pāṇini 3.2.124.
The cognition of the two extremes is called "investigation" (vicāra);
that which is being investigated is said to be the object of that cognition.

In this context, however, the sentences under consideration have as their object a matter that is being deliberated upon. Regarding the word *gṛhī*: the substitution of the protracted vowel (*pluta*) for the word *gṛhe* is as explained previously. Regarding *anupraharet*: "laying down" (*anuprahāraḥ*) means "causing to lie down"; the agentive suffix is used for the object by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), meaning "one should cause [it] to lie down. Alternatively, in the phrase *anupraharet*, the words *yajamāno yūpam* are to be supplied; thus, the purpose of the deliberation is: "Should the sacrificer cause the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) to lie down?"
But previously, in the case of speech (bhāṣā). 8.2.98.

Since this is already established by the preceding rule, this present one is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*). The word *tu* (but/however) serves to restrict according to the speaker's intention; it is so that it should be understood as "only in the case of the preceding [element] in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*)," and not that it should be understood as "only in the preceding [element] in the vernacular. Furthermore, the state of being "preceding" is relative to usage. In the example, the particle *nu* expresses deliberation (*vitarka*). *Loṣṭaḥ* means a lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍaḥ*).
And [the suffix *kha* is used] after a word meaning "a promise. (Pāṇini 5.1.99)

*Pratiśravaṇam* means acceptance; it is an agreement (*aṅgīkāra*). *Pratijñānam* means a promise to give what has been requested. In both these cases, there is a *gatisamāsa* compound, as the root *śru* preceded by *prati* is well-known in these two senses. *Śravaṇābhimukhyam* (being oriented toward hearing): here, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule "with *lakṣaṇa*, *abhi*, and *prati* [are compounded] when indicating orientation. The examples, however, have been given out of order. *Kimāttha?*—he asks this, meaning "What do you say? (i.e., *kiṃ brūṣe*).

And here, the inclination toward listening is understood [from the phrase] "Well then, I shall give it to you. Here, the response to what was requested is understood. "O Devadatta! is an address; he, for whose sake he is addressed, asks for the purpose of hearing: "What do you say? "Give me a cow, sir! Sound ought to be eternal. In that third example, one's own acceptance is understood.
An unaccented vowel [is used] at the end of a question or in expressions of respect. (Pāṇini 8.2.100)

That which is employed last in an interrogative sentence is the "end of the question" (*praśnānta*). It is stated in some places: "The *pluta* (protracted vowel) is not prescribed by this rule; rather, it prescribes merely the quality of being *anudātta* (unaccented) for that *svarita-pluta* which is already prescribed for cases such as calling from a distance, by the rule 'in questions and narrations, even a non-final [vowel] may be protracted'. In that context, the formulation of the statement is as follows: "In the end of a question and in respectful address, that which is a *pluta* becomes *anudātta*. Among these, in the case of respectful address, the *pluta* is prescribed by the rule "also in calling from a distance" (*dūrāddhūte ca*).

But in other cases, according to the rule "also for the final [vowel] in questions and narrations," as in *agamaḥ pūrvān grāmān*, the svarita vowel becomes a protracted (*pluta*) one. In examples such as *agnibhūte* or *paṭo*, the completion of the sentence occurs with either [the preceding or the following word]. In that case, when the completion of the sentence occurs by means of a particular word, then by this [rule], its [final vowel] becomes a protracted grave (*anudātta*) vowel, and that belongs to the preceding part; however, for the subsequent part, the vowels *i* and *u* become acute (*udātta*).
And the word *cit* is used in the sense of comparison [with the preceding word]. (Pāṇini 8.2.101)

What is the purpose of the particle *iti*? If it were not employed, when some word used in the sense of a comparison (*upamāna*) is applied, it might be understood that the word *cit* itself is protracted (*pluta*). But when the particle *iti* is present, the phrase "when [a word] is being employed" becomes an adjective qualifying the word *cit*, whereas the protraction occurs only for that [word] which is the final element (*ṭi*) of the sentence, according to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "of the final element of the sentence."

Regarding the term *kathañcit*: here the word *cit* is used in the sense of difficulty (*kaṣṭe*). In the example *agnirmāṇavako bhāyāt*, the meaning is "the young boy should shine like fire. Since the sense of comparison is understood here, there is the perception (*pratīti*) of the word *cit*; however, its actual usage (*prayoga*) does not occur. Even though other words expressing comparison, such as *iva* and so forth, also have such a perception, nevertheless, since the perception of the word *cit* also exists [in this context], the protracted vowel (*pluta*) should indeed occur. The particle *ca* serves to include this [word *cit*] in the collection of cases for the protracted vowel.

And since a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is based on a distinction (*bheda*), this is explained as being precisely a case of a protracted vowel (*pluta*); otherwise, as in the preceding rule, it would be understood that only the quality of being unaccented (*anudātta*) is prescribed for the aforementioned protracted causes. And this itself is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in the preceding rule only the quality is prescribed—as in the example *uparisvidāsīt*. (Pāṇini 8.2.102)
Here too, the mere quality (*guṇamātra*) is prescribed for the protracted vowel (*pluta*) that was enjoined by the rule "of those being deliberated upon" (*vicāryamāṇānām*).
When a word is repeated (āmreḍita), the first syllable is circumflexly accented (svarita) in cases of envy, approval, anger, and reproach. Pāṇini 8.2.103.

"The word 'or' (vā) must be supplied," [says the author]. The Vārttikakāra first cited this as "the statement that every protracted vowel (pluta) [is so]" being a remark belonging to another; the Vṛttikāra likewise cited that very same thing.
In the case of *kṣiya* and *śī*, when used in *praiṣa* (injunctions), there is expectancy for a finite verb (*tiṅ*).

*Kṣiyā* is the violation of etiquette, that is, the transgression of established conduct. *Iṣṭāśaṃsana* is a benediction (*āśīḥ*). *Vyāpāraṇa* by means of speech is an injunction (*praiṣa*). This text is also read in some recensions of the *Vṛtti*:

"May there be long life for you" (*dīrghaṃ te āyur astu*), and "Distribute the fires" (*agnīn vihara*). However, no example is given for *kṣiyā*; this is because it is inherently expectant [of a further statement]. For when only this much is said—"He himself goes by chariot"—the violation of etiquette is not understood; rather, it is understood only when it is said, "He causes his teacher to go on foot."

In this context, immediately after the rule "uparisvidāsīditi ca," one should have stated "aṅgayuktaṃ tiṅākāṅkṣam"; after that, "kṣiyāśīḥpraiṣeṣu svaritaḥ"; and after that, "āmreḍite'sūyāsammatikopakutsaneṣu. For in this way, the mention of *tiṅākāṅkṣa* would not need to be made twice. However, it was not done in that manner.
The same [substitution] also occurs for the word *anantya* when it is used in the sense of "question" (*praśna*) or "explanation" (*ākhyāna*). Pāṇini 8.2.105.

"Of all words indeed. Now, one might object: since the final [word] is prescribed as *anudātta* (unaccented) by the rule "in questions and in expressions of praise," there ought to be an *anudātta* protracted vowel (*pluta*); so how can this be a *svarita* (circumflex) protracted vowel? To this he replies: "of the non-final. Although an option (*vikalpa*) is not explicitly heard here, nevertheless, by means of this word *api* ("also"), this *svarita* protracted vowel applies to the final word as well; thus, the sense is that the *anudātta* protracted vowel becomes an optional alternative.

But surely the word *api* has its purpose fulfilled by being used as a final conjunction in a statement (*ākhyāna*). What follows from that? [One might argue that] in the case of a question (*praśna*), a compulsory protracted vowel (*pluta*) would apply to the final syllable, which is unaccented (*anudātta*); since there would be no optionality in that case, this is not a fault. For even in a question, the intended meaning of the word *api* is understood because it is mentioned together [with the particle *ca*]; consequently, at the end of a question, there will be an optionality between the two protracted vowels—the circumflex (*svarita*) and the unaccented (*anudātta*).
The vowels *i* and *u*, when protracted (*pluta*), [are called *pragṛhya*]. || 8.2.106 ||

Since the prolation (*pluta*) of *ai* and *au* would follow from another rule [P. 8.2.107], this statement is made for the purpose of ensuring the prolation of their constituent parts, *i* and *u*. By the force of the statement, even though they are only partial elements of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*), *i* and *u* are included by the mention of *it* and *ut*. Regarding the phrase "when there is the occasion for the prolation of *ai* and *au*": some say, "In the sūtra, the locative case in *plutau* is used because of the word *pluti*; thus it is shown that [the rule applies] when the prolation of *ai* and *au* is about to occur. This, however, is incorrect.

For this designation "pluta" (protracted) is based on the action [of protraction]—since it will be explained as being in the form of the nominative dual ending (*plutau*). Therefore, that was stated for the purpose of introducing the context. In the example, regarding a call from afar, the protraction occurs only by the rule "guroranṛtaḥ. If the protraction were applied to the *it* and *ut* which are constituent parts of the vowels *ai* and *au*, then the whole [diphthong] would result in having either four morae (*caturmātratā*) or three and a half morae (*ardhacaturthamātratā*). How so? These two diphthongs (*aic*), namely *ai* and *au*, are composite phonemes (*samāhāravarṇa*).

Regarding the phrase *mātrā'varṇasya*, [the options are] *mātrevarṇovarṇayoḥ*; others, however, say: "One half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) for a vowel (*avarṇa*), and one and a half moras (*adhyardhamātrā*) for the vowels *i* and *u*. In that regard, according to the first alternative, when *i* and *u* are made protracted (*pluta*) by this rule, they would each have three moras, and since the vowel *a* has one mora, the aggregate would result in four moras; whereas according to the other view, it would result in three and a half moras. Therefore, he says: "In this case" (*atre*).

But surely, the designation *pluta* has been assigned only to a vowel of three morae (*trimātra*); how then can two-mora vowels (*dvimātra*) such as *i* and *u* be made [into *plutas*] by this rule? To this he says: "For [the word] *plutau*... By this, he shows that *plutau* is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the agent (meaning "those which have become *plutas*"), and not a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*). The meaning is "those which undergo increase" (*vṛddhiṃ gacchataḥ*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *plu* also functions in the sense of "increasing. But even so, it is not understood what kind of increase this is. To this he says: "And that much... [referring to the duration].

He thinks as follows: the term *pluta*, which was introduced in the current context, is also connected here; consequently, the meaning becomes this: the *i* and *u* that are parts of the *ai* and *au* increase in such a way that the *ai* and *au* themselves become *pluta*. Therefore, there is no occurrence of the undesired type of *vṛddhi*.

"Having two and a half morae (*mātrā*)": those two whose third mora is in the form of a half are so described. It is accepted that the *pluta* [vowel] has four morae; the meaning is that its increase is accepted by virtue of having four morae. In this view, the vowel-nature (*actva*) of the four-moraic [vowel] also occurs. Consequently, in the case of *pratyaṅ aitikāyanaḥ*, the augment *ṅamuṭ* occurs; and in *glau trāta*, the doubling of the letter *t* occurs by the rule "also before a non-consonant" (*anaci ca*).
When a non-*pragṛhya* vowel is not uttered from afar, *i* and *u* are substituted for the final half-mora of the preceding syllable and the first half-mora of the following syllable respectively.

It must be performed as a determination of the scope of the subject matter. He explains this as follows: "at the end of a question," etc. "According to the subject matter" means that at the end of a question, [the final vowel] is either *anudātta* or *svarita*, while the remainder is *udātta*. However, *i* and *u* (when they are *pragṛhya*) are always *udātta*, because of the connection with the term "*udātta*" which is carried over from the previous rule.

Regarding the phrase *viṣṇubhūte*: how, then, can this be an example of the enumeration (*parigaṇana*), given that the rule states "when calling from a distance" (*adūrāddhūte*)? To this he says: "and the enumeration. Since the matter would be established by that very enumeration when it must necessarily be performed for another purpose, the expression "when calling from a distance" need not have been stated; therefore, this too is appropriately an counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) of the enumeration. [The word] *gaur*.

Due to the prohibition "not before a non-sarvanāmasthāna [suffix]," the preceding element does not become a *pada* when *su* follows. Now, if one adopts the position that even *su* is a *pada*, why does it not [become so]? This has already been stated: "of the final [element] of a sentence or a word," and here the term *visarjanīya* refers to the end of a sentence.

But surely, in the rule regarding the mention of "the end of a word" (*padāntagrahaṇam*), the word *pada* refers to a sentence (*vākya*) because it is understood according to its etymological meaning—that by which a meaning is reached or understood? And this is obtained through the recurrence of the mention of "end" (*anta*) from the rule "at the end of a *yājyā*" (*yājyāntaḥ*). [The example is] *agnibhūtā3*. This is the form of the word *agnibhūti* in the vocative case. Regarding the term "vocative" (*āmantrita*): this is a statement made even though the prolation (*pluta*) was not otherwise required.
In the *saṃhitā* [of these two], when there is *yavāva* [substitution]. (8.2.108)

For what purpose is this stated? Is it not already established by the rule *iko yaṇ aci*? To this he replies: "Because *idut* [the long vowels *ī* and *ū*] are not established [as having undergone the substitution]. But is it not indeed established? Pluta [vowels] are established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*). How is this known? Because of the prescription of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for pluta vowels in the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci*. For the original form must be prescribed for that which would otherwise undergo a modification; and if the pluta were not established, then no modification known as a vowel-sandhi would apply to it.

"Let it be granted that the *pluta* vowel is established [as existing]; what follows for the *it* and *ut* vowels? It is replied: In the section on *pluta*, the rule "that which is taught in the *kāya* [section] is established in vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*)" will be relied upon as a general indicator (*jñāpaka*). Consequently, since the *it* and *ut* vowels are also established, the substitution of *yaṇ* is indeed established. Therefore, he says: "Even if somehow... He uses the word "somehow" because the meaning of this indicator—namely, that it is dependent on a general rule—is difficult to ascertain.

If this were not stated, then in cases such as *agnā3i indram* and *paṭā3u udakam*, the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrghatva*) would apply, overriding the substitution of *yaṇ* prescribed by the sixth [chapter]; furthermore, in cases such as *aganā3yāśa*, there would be the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *iko'savarṇe śākalyasya*. Therefore, this must indeed be stated in order to override those rules.

But surely there is another effort made to prevent that; what is it? It was stated under the rule *iko yaṇ aci*: "The substitution of *yaṇ* must be prescribed for an *ik* preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel," as in the case of *bho3y indraṃ gāyati*. Here, the word *bhoḥ* has a Vedic protraction (*pluta*). Since the following vowel *i* is a particle (*nipāta*), the rule of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) would have applied; however, the *yaṇ* substitution overrides that. Thus, because this [rule] must necessarily be applied, the *yaṇ* is established by that very [prescription]. Therefore—

He says: "Even so" (*athāpi*). "For the sake of precluding a vowel dependent on *yaṇ*" (*yaṇsvaranivṛttyartham*): a vowel that has *yaṇ* as its basis is a "vowel dependent on *yaṇ*" (*yaṇsvara*). He explains this very point by saying: "of the substitute *yaṇ*" (*yaṇādeśasya*).

He summarizes the very point already stated in two verses with the words "But what... (*kiṃ tv iti*). What form is not already established by the substitution of *yaṇ* for *ik*, such that this Teacher prescribes *y* and *v* for *i* and *u*? If those two vowels (*u* and *i*) are established in the rules for vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), then [the objection stands]. The word "mine" (*mama*) is the statement of one who has become unified with the author of the Sūtras. When thus challenged, he replies: "But in the rule for the long vowel of Śākala, they are to be set aside. This [work] belongs to Śākalya, hence it is called *Śākalam*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "from Kaṇva and others, in the sense of a lineage" (*gotra*). Again, he challenges: "And *ik* is followed by a consonant" (*ik ca paraḥ*).

The author of the Vārttika also prescribes *yaṇ* for an *ik* preceded by a protracted (*pluta*) vowel; and this [prescription] is an exception (*apavāda*) not only to the rule of original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), but also to the rules regarding the Śākala and lengthening (*dīrgha*). Consequently, by that very *yaṇ*, the Śākala and lengthening will not occur even for these two [vowels], *i* and *u*. [The opponent asks: "Is there no need for this [sūtra]? He answers: "Because of *yaṇ* and accent" (*yaṇ-svara*). The reason for the commencement of the sūtra is precisely to block the *yaṇ* and the accent.
Thus ends the second quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra; [this concludes] the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.
Now begins the third quarter of the eighth chapter.
In the Vedic language, the form *matuvas* is substituted for *ru* in the vocative case.

The mention of *matu* and *vas* [in the rule *matuvasoru*] is like the mention of *yu* and *vu* [in *yuvoranākau*], made by omitting their *anubandhas*; or else, it is the inclusion of *vas* ending in *s*. Furthermore, due to *nipātana*, the word with fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) is placed last. The form *ru-* is a mention without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*). Regarding *marutva*: the substitution of *v* occurs by the rule *jhayaḥ*; the designation *bha* applies by the rule *tasau matvarthe*. Regarding *harivo medinam*: the substitution of *v* occurs by the rule *chandasyuraḥ*; and because of the statement "the elision of a final *saṃyoga* is established when *r* undergoes the substitution of *ru*," the substitution of *u* (by *haśi ca*) takes place.

Regarding the word *vana*: there is a general inclusion of both the suffixes *kvanip* and *vanip*, because since no specific indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned here, the paribhāṣā concerning "that which possesses such an indicatory letter" does not apply, and thus *kvanip* is also included. In the example *prātaritvaḥ*: from the root *i-* (to go) with the prefix *prātaḥ*, the suffix *kvanip* is applied by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*; the augment *tuk* is added after the short vowel. Regarding the phrase "and of the word *ava*": it should be understood as "of all [such words]"; for when a suffix is meaningless (*anarthaka*), the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. He rejects the need for a supplementary statement (*upasaṃkhyāna*) by saying: "or rather, through the understanding that it is a particle (*nipāta*)."

He explains this very point with the words "or rather" (atha vā). He states that this must necessarily be understood as being merely a particle (nipāta) with the words "for even when not in the vocative" (asambuddhāv api hi).

Regarding the phrase "in the feminine" (*striyām*): [as in] "O Brāhmaṇī! It has been stated that "the technical rule concerning the inclusion of the gender-distinct form (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) does not apply to grammatical operations conditioned by case-endings (*vibhakti-nimitta*)," namely: "Or rather, it is not so, because the gender-distinct form is not grasped when a case-ending follows. Therefore, the *rutva* (substitution of *r*) and *autva* (substitution of *au*) would not occur for the word *bhavatī*. Even if they were to occur, then upon the substitution of *r* for the vowel *ī*, the form of the word *ava* followed by *au* would not be established. Consequently, since these forms are observed in the feminine and outside the vocative singular (*asambuddhi*), they should be understood as being merely particles (*nipāta*).

And their status as particles (*nipāta*) is due to their being substitutes for case-endings and accents. Now, one might object: "If this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) were not present, there would be no word such as *bho* that ends in a case-ending, of which these [words] could be substitutes? Therefore, these are particles mentioned in the Sūtras—specifically indicated in the Sūtra *bho-bhago-aghobhyaḥ*—or they should be included among the *ca*-group (the list of particles). Thus, the supplementary rule has been rejected.

Others, however, say: "The suffixes *tasil* and others, which are prescribed by the rule *itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 5.3.14) for use with words such as *bhavat*, are intended so that they may also occur after [vocatives] like *bho*; thus, the *vārttika* is commenced.
Still others, however, think: "Since words such as *bhavat* are not included in the formal list [of pronouns], vocatives such as *bho* will simply function as indeclinables (*nipāta*)."
In this case, the nasalization (anunāsika) optionally applies to the preceding [vowel].

This "prior-ness" (*pūrvatva*) is relative, and the *ru* [substitute] is proximate. However, prior-ness cannot be established in relation to that [proximate *ru*], because the *ru* and the nasalized [substitute] are prescribed together. Therefore, he says, "of that which is the locus," meaning that prior-ness is understood only in relation to that for which the *ru* is prescribed.

Now, what is the purpose of including the word *atra* here? It is so that [the rule] may apply within this section on *r* (*ruprakaraṇa*). But is this not already established by the governing context (*adhikāra*)? For when there is a governing context, since *ru* and the nasalization (*anunāsika*) are prescribed together, there would be no application elsewhere. To this he says: "The inclusion of *atra*. Here, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood: namely, that it is only with *ru* that [the nasalization occurs]. But was it not already stated that this is established by the governing context? To this he says: "By the governing context..."

If the mention of "asatya" (non-existent) were not there, the extent of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) would not be known—that is, it would not be known that its operation applies to only so many rules; consequently, one might suspect that this governing rule extends even beyond the section on *ru*. The word "tu" (but) serves to highlight the distinction between the preceding [element] and the subsequent object of the operation: for the subsequent element, the substitution of *ru* is obligatory, whereas for the preceding element, the nasalization is optional.

The mention of the word *vā* (or) is redundant, for it is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because, in a subsequent rule, the author teaches that an *anusvāra* follows the *ru* after that [consonant] for which an *anunāsika* has not been prescribed. From this, it is known that this [substitution] occurs optionally. For if this rule were mandatory, it would be impossible for that *ru* to precede a consonant for which an *anunāsika* has been prescribed.
Before a vowel beginning with *a*, [the substitution of *anusvāra* for a preceding *n*] is obligatory. (Pāṇini 8.3.3)

"Some" refers to the Taittirīyas. They recite [the word] with an *anusvāra*. [The rule states: "A pure *ā* [is substituted] after [the vowel *a*]. Is the mention of "always" (*nitya*) redundant?
