For the rule would be established as permanent simply by the force of its enunciation. There is indeed a purpose for its enunciation: so that it may be a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—that [substitution] occurs only after *āt*, and not after others. Why does a restriction arise? It is because there is nothing else to be prescribed; but here there is something to be prescribed. What is it? That the nasalized [substitute] is always [to be applied].
An *anusvāra* follows a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*).

The word *anya* (other) must be supplied here. If it were not supplied, then because the word *para* (subsequent) is explicitly heard [in the sūtra], this ablative case ending in *anunāsikāt* would have to be understood in relation to that [word *para*]—that is, the word *para* would function in the sense of direction (*digvṛtti*), or in the sense of "other" (*anyārthavṛtti*), or in the sense of "prior" (*pūrvavṛtti*). In the first alternative, the anusvāra would be understood as being subsequent only to that nasal which is prior to the *ru*, and yet it is not desired to be subsequent to that.

In the other case, however, the meaning is that "the *anusvāra* is [that which is] other than the nasal (*anunāsika*). In that context, the mention of the word "other" (*para*) would be purposeless, for the *anusvāra* never deviates from being distinct with respect to the nasal. Therefore, the word "other" (*anya*) must be supplied [as an ellipsis]. And that [word] should be supplied in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*) in relation to the word "subsequent" (*para*). Furthermore, the term "of the preceding" (*pūrvasya*), which is also understood here by way of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), is transformed into the ablative case through its connection with the word "subsequent."

This being the case, he shows the meaning that results: "other than [a vowel] having an *anunāsika*. What, then, is this? He says: "that for which an *anunāsika* has not been applied. Thus, an *anusvāra* becomes an augment (*āgama*). Even though there is no formal marker (*liṅga*) of an augment such as the *ṭi*-designation, the *anusvāra* possesses the status of an augment because its specific position is established by the word "subsequent" (*para*), just as in the rule: "The diphthongs *ai* and *au* do not precede *y* or *v*" (*na yvābhyāṃ pūrvāvaic*).
The *sama* [is substituted for *samāna*] before a suffix beginning with *su*.

The statement "mo'nusvāraḥ" [Pāṇini 8.3.23] would otherwise have required an *anusvāra*; this rule [provides for the *sakāra*]. Regarding the form *saṃskarttā*: the suffix *suṭ* is applied by the rule "samparyupayebhyaḥ karotau bhūṣaṇe" [Pāṇini 6.1.137]; the *makāra* of *sam-* becomes *ru* (by 8.2.66), which becomes a *visarjanīya* (by 8.3.15); then, regarding that *visarjanīya*, the rule "vā śari" [8.3.36] provides an option; it has been shown how the *sakāra* necessarily occurs in such cases.

But how, then, is the *sakāra* (the letter *s*) indicated in this sūtra? To this he says: "The indication *samaḥ ssuṭi* contains two *sakāras*. And that [doubled form] consists of two *sakāras* because there is no possibility of confusion with the *sakāra* of the augment *suṭ*; apart from that, however, there are actually three *sakāras*: one belonging to the case-ending (*vibhakti*), the second being the substitute (*ādeśa*), and the third belonging to the *ru*. If, then, the substitute is prescribed for the *sakāra*, the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form would not be obtained.

If it is asked: "Is it not stated here that the mention of *ru* is for the purpose of establishing its obligatory association (*sanniyoga*) with *saṃhitā*?"—this is not a fault. In this context, the mention of *ru* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for whatever is prescribed within this section on *ru*. By this, the rule regarding "the preceding [element] of *ru*" in the previous sūtra has also been explained.

In this regard, when *satva* (the substitution of *s*) has been applied, if the preceding [nasal] is a nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*), then because *satva* is considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *ru* does not occur; consequently, by the rule "also after *na*" (*anaci ca*), doubling takes place, and by the rule "a *jhara* [consonant] is optionally elided before a *jhara*" (*jharo jhari*), there results either a form with two *s*s or one with three *s*s. However, when an *anusvāra* occurs, then—because the *ayogavāha*s are included in the *aṭ* pratyāhāra due to their being taught [in that group], and because it is a *hal* (consonant)—there is optionally an elision by the rule "a *jhara* before a *jhara*," resulting in a form with two *s*s or one with a single *s*.

However, when it is maintained that the *anusvāra* possesses not only the status of a consonant (*hal*) but also the status of a vowel (*ac*), then, according to the view that [the following consonant] is doubled, there are even three *s*-sounds after it. Thus, there are five forms: two or three *s*-sounds in the case of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) [anusvāra], and two, one, or three [s-sounds] in the case of the *anusvāra*. When the doubling of the *k* is performed by the rule "of *śar*, the *khaya*s" (*śaraḥ khayaḥ*) across all five of these options, ten forms arise. Some maintain the option of elision for the *sam-* [prefix].

Some teachers maintain that there is an optional elision (*lopa*) by way of alternative forms; in this case as well, both the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*) and the *anusvāra* occur. Since that [elision] is also prescribed in the section on *ru*, when the nasalized vowel option applies, there is doubling of the *s* according to the rule "anaci ca," and since elision is also optional, there occasionally arises a form with only a single *s*. In that instance too, there is optionally a doubling of the *k*; thus, twelve forms result.
A final *p* is changed to *kh* before a following *kha*, when that *kha* is followed by a vowel or a semivowel.

This is the designation for that portion remaining after the *sakāra* of the word *puṃsaḥ*; for once the final consonant of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) has been applied to the *sakāra*, it is precisely that [remaining portion] which is what is intended. The term *am* refers to the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated series), not to the second singular case ending, because of its association with the *pratyāhāra* *khay*. The example *puṃścalī* is formed by adding the feminine suffix *ṅīp* based on the inclusion of *calaṭ* in the list beginning with *pac-*. The compound *puṃścalī* is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compound. The example *puṃskāmā* is derived from the sense "she who desires a man" (*pumāṃsaṃ kāmayate*), with the suffix *ṇa* according to the rule *śīlikāmibhikṣācaribhyo ṇaḥ*.
Therefore, in this case, it must be stated that the substitute is indeed the letter *s*. This should be stated under the rule *kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca*.

As for the phrase "in the view of the double *s* notation": this means when the position is taken in the preceding rule that the notation contains two *s*s. The word *saḥ* (he/it) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

But surely *ru* is also under discussion, and thus it too would be subject [to the rule]; to this he says: "But *rutvaṃ*... He states the reason for its non-connection: "The persistence of its connection (*sambandhānuvṛttiḥ tasya*). The particle *iti* indicates a cause; the meaning is: because that [element] persists—that is, does not abandon—the connection it has with its own correlate, therefore [it is not connected]. Alternatively, "connected" (*sambandha*) means that which is connected; the meaning is: because here only that which is connected to itself persists, therefore [it is not connected].

Although the term *rutvam* (the substitution of *ru*) is indeed carried over here [from the previous rule], it is carried over only as connected with its own specific correlate by the rule *matuvaso ru sambuddhau*. Its purpose is to ensure that the *ru* is not connected with any other correlate. Terms such as *puṃdāsaḥ* and others are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). In the case of *puṃgavaḥ*, the compound suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule *gorataddhitaluki*. If the mention of *para* (in the sense of "following") were not made, one might understand the rule to mean: "when *am* follows *khay*. Consequently, the rule would apply only in cases such as *pumakṣaḥ* and *pumācāraḥ*; therefore, the mention of *para* is necessary.
The *cha* and *praśān* [substitutes] do not undergo the substitution of *ṣa* for *cha*.

Regarding the phrase *praśānvarjitasya*: in the sūtra, however, *apraśān* is the nominative case used in the sense of the genitive. The root *ṭīk* means "to go" and is anudātta (unaccented). *Tsaruḥ* refers to the hilt of a sword; one who is skilled in that is called *tsarukaḥ*, according to the rule *ākarṣādibhyaḥ kan*.
The augment *dīrghāt* is applied before *aṭ* when the following foot is identical.

One type of synonymous word is called *samānapāda* (having the same word within the same metrical foot); in that regard, this [usage] would not be established: *yajāmahe yajñiyān hanta devān ilāmaha iti*. It will be so because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [The rule] *nṝn pe* (Pāṇini 8.3.10) [applies].

In the word *nṝn*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive; likewise in the subsequent cases as well. In the term *pe*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), while the letter *p* alone is the grammatical cause (*nimitta*).
The [substitute] *svatavas* occurs in place of *pāyu*. (Pāṇini 8.3.11)

The root *vṛdh* (in the sense of "to increase") is a Vedic (sautra) root; from it, the suffix *asun* is added—thus, he whose own power (*tavas*) is his own is *svatavān*; the nasal augment (*num*) is applied according to the rule "the [augment] *num* is inserted after *dṛś*, *svavaḥ*, and *svatas* in the Veda."
The [first] *kān* [ending] remains when it is repeated. (Pāṇini 8.3.12)

Regarding the mention of *āmreḍita* (reduplication) when one could simply say "kān kān": this is so that [the rule] applies only where there is reduplication, and not here in the case of *kān kān paśyati*, where one *kiṃ* word is used in the sense of inquiry (*praśna*) and the second is used in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*).

[One might object: "Since the word *vā* is understood from the rule *samaḥ suṭi* [Pāṇini 8.3.5], would that same [optionality] apply even to the preceding rules? To this he says: "In the preceding rules...
[The sūtra follows: *ḍho ḍhe lopaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.3.13].

The vowel *ā* is for the sake of pronunciation; the mere presence of the letter *ḍh* is the cause [of the grammatical operation]. Therefore, it also occurs in forms such as *leḍhā* and *leḍhī*. In forms such as *līḍham*, there is first the substitution of *ḍh* for *h* by the rule *ho ḍhaḥ*; then, by *jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.40) and *jhaṣastathordho'dhaṛ* (Pāṇini 8.2.41), the substitution of *dh* for *t* occurs; then by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.41), the substitution of *ṣṭ* for *ṣ* and *t* occurs; and finally, by this [present rule], there is the elision of *ḍh*. Now, one might object: "But the substitution of *ṣṭ* is not yet established (*asiddha*); how then can there be elision here? To this he says: "Of the substitution of *ṣṭ*" (*ṣṭutvasya*). This is what is being stated: "When *ḍh* follows, there is elision of *ḍh*. In that case, if the substitution of *ṣṭ* were unestablished, this [rule] would be without scope (*nirviṣaya*).

But surely, where there is an original *ḍha*—as in *śvaliḍ ḍhaukate* and so on—the rule would find its scope; therefore he says: "in the case of *śvaliḍ ḍhaukate*. [He explains: "when *jaś*-ness has been applied. Because it depends on a single word (*ekapadāśrayatva*), it is *antaraṅga* (internal), or because the elision (*lopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "what precedes is as if not to have taken effect" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), *jaś*-ness occurs first. But surely, since it would otherwise have no scope, the elision of *ḍha* (*ḍhalopa*) would subvert *jaś*-ness? No, he says: "and not so. Why? He says: "for of that..."

But how can there be scope for [the application of] *līḍha* and so on, given that just as in the case of *śvaliḍ ḍhaukate*, once the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) has been applied, the cause [for further change] ceases to exist, so too in *līḍha* and so on, because the substitution of *ṣṭu* is not established, the cause [for the application of *ṣṭu*] would likewise cease to exist? If it is argued that in that case the non-establishment of *ṣṭu* is set aside by the force of the specific rule, then here too the substitution of *jaś* should be set aside; or else, some distinction must be stated. To this he says: "For in that case... (*tatra hi*).

The intended meaning is as follows: by way of the rule of non-validity (*asiddhatva*) due to elision (*lopa*), that non-validity must necessarily be set aside. In cases such as *līḍham*, there is only one instance of non-validity—namely, that "what precedes is non-valid"—and therefore that alone is set aside. However, in the case of *śvaliḍ ḍhaukate*, because the elision of *ḍ* is both external (*bahiraṅga*) and subsequent (*para*) with respect to the substitution of *jaś* (the change of *ḍ* to *d*), it possesses a twofold non-validity; thus, it is not set aside. Consequently, once the *jaś*-substitution has been applied, there is neither proximity (*ānantarya*) created by the audible phonetic form (*śruti*), nor proximity created by the grammatical rule (*śāstra*), because the *jaś*-substitution lacks non-validity. Therefore, this [case of *śvaliḍ ḍhaukate*] is not within the scope of the rule regarding the elision of *ḍ*.

What is this? Is it the mention of *ru* with its *anubandha*, or rather the mention of the letter *ra*? Whence arises this doubt? Because here the phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*) is identical: both *roḥ ri* and *raḥ rī* are the same. And what follows from this? If there is a mention of *ru* with its *anubandha*, then forms such as *indūrathaḥ* and *agnīrathaḥ* are established; however, these would not be established: *nīraktaṃ* and *dūraktam*. On the other hand, if there is a mention of the letter *ra*, then *nīraktaṃ* and *dūraktam* are established.

But this [derivation] is not established: *agnīrathaḥ* and *indūrathaḥ*, on the grounds that "when there is a mention of a [stem] without an *anubandha*, it does not include one with an *anubandha*"? This is not a fault, for this paribhāṣā does not apply in cases where individual phonemes (*varṇa*) are being mentioned.

In the rule *padasya*, the genitive case is used as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This has already been explained under the rules *padasya* and *padāt*. What is established by this? He says: "By that. However, if [the genitive] were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then because the word *pada* would be qualified by *repha* (the letter *r*), the elision would have to apply to a *pada* ending in *r*. For example, in *ajarghāḥ*, this was explained under the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ*. As for *apāspāḥ*: *ekāco baśo bhaṣ jhaṣantasya sdhvoḥ* || P. 8.2.37 || When the suffixes *s* or *dhv* follow, *bhaṣ* is substituted for a single-consonant (*ekāc*) verbal root ending in a *jhaṣ* sound (i.e., *ba*, *ga*, *gha*, *da*, *dha*, *ja*, *g*, *j*, *ḍ*, *ḍh*, *ṇ*) provided that the *bhaṣ* sound is preceded by a vowel. Here, the root *ghr̥* (to eat) ends in *r*, which is a *jhaṣ* sound. Since it is followed by the suffix *s* (which is a *jhal* sound), *bhaṣ* is substituted for *gh*. The *bhaṣ* sounds are *ba*, *ga*, *gha*, *da*, *dha*, *ja*, *g*, *j*, *ḍ*, *ḍh*, and *ṇ*. Among these, *gh* is the one substituted here. Subsequently, by the rule *khari ca*, the *gh* is changed to the unaspirated voiceless stop *k*. Then, by the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe*, the *k* is dropped. Thus, *aghats* becomes *aghat*s. Next, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the *t* is changed to *d*. Finally, by the rule *vāvasāne*, the *d* is changed to the voiceless *t*. Thus, *aghatt-s* becomes *aghatt*. By the rule *ṛdhaścurādiṇyantāt parokṣāyām am*, the suffix *am* is added after the root *ṛdh* when it belongs to the curādi class and is followed by the periphrastic perfect (*parokṣā*). The *am* causes reduplication, and the *m* of *am* is elided by the rule *ato lopaḥ*. The reduplicated form is *a-jardh-a*. Then, by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye 'nādeśāder liṭi*, the *a* is lengthened. Thus, *ajardhā* is formed. Regarding *apāspāḥ*: the root *spas* (to see) is reduplicated with *apa* prefixed. By the rule *liṭy abhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, the *s* of the reduplicated syllable is changed to *p*. By the rule *abhyāse car ca*, the *p* is changed to *ch*. By the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ*, the *ch* is changed to *ś*. Thus, *apaśpas* becomes *apāspas*. Then, by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the *s* is changed to *d*. By the rule *vāvasāne*, the *d* is changed to *t*. Thus, *apāspat* is formed. By the rule *ātaḥ*, the suffix *āṬ* is added after a monosyllabic *ārdhadhātuka* beginning with a consonant. The *ā* of *āṬ* is elided by the rule *āṬaḥ*. By the rule *uñi ca pade*, the *t* is changed to *s*. Thus, *apāspās* becomes *apāspāḥ*. The *ṣaṣṭhī* in *padasya* is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*). This has already been explained under the rules *padasya* and *padāt*. What is established by this? He says: "By that. If, however, it were a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), then because the word *pada* would be qualified by *repha*, the elision would have to apply to a *pada* ending in *r*. For example, in *ajarghāḥ*, this was explained under the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ*. As for *apāspāḥ*: *ātaḥ* || P. 6.4.140 || The suffix *āṬ* is added after a monosyllabic *ārdhadhātuka* beginning with a consonant. The *ā* of *āṬ* is elided by the rule *āṬaḥ*. By the rule *uñi ca pade*, the *t* is changed to *s*. Thus, *apāspās* becomes *apāspāḥ*. *lopaḥ śākalyasya* || P. 8.3.19 || The *y* or *v* at the end of a word is optionally elided before a following vowel, according to Śākalya. Thus, *apāspāḥ* becomes *apāspā*. *naśchavyapraśān* || P. 8.3.7 || The *r* at the end of a word is changed to *ūṣman* (a spirant) before a *chav* sound (any consonant except *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*, *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*), provided it is not the word *praśān*. Thus, *apāspāḥ* becomes *apāspāḥ*. *ro ri* || P. 8.3.14 || An *r* is elided when followed by another *r*. Thus, *apāspār* becomes *apāspā*. *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* || P. 6.3.111 || When an *ūṣman* is elided, the preceding *aṇ* (a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ) is lengthened. Thus, *apāspā* becomes *apāspāḥ*. *lopaḥ śākalyasya* || P. 8.3.19 || The *y* or *v* at the end of a word is optionally elided before a following vowel, according to Śākalya. Thus, *apāspāḥ* becomes *apāspā*. *naśchavyapraśān* || P. 8.3.7 || The *r* at the end of a word is changed to *ūṣman* before a *chav* sound, provided it is not *praśān*. Thus, *apāspāḥ* becomes *apāspāḥ*. *ro ri* || P. 8.3.14 || An *r* is elided when followed by another *r*. Thus, *apāspār* becomes *apāspā*. *ṭhūlope pūrvasya dīrgho 'ṇaḥ* || P. 6.3.111 || When an *ūṣman* is elided, the preceding *aṇ* is lengthened. Thus, *apāspā* becomes *apāspāḥ*. *lopaḥ śākalyasya* || P. 8.3.19 || The *y* or *v* at the end of a word is optionally elided before a following vowel, according to Śākalya. Thus, *apāspāḥ* becomes *apāspā*. *naśchavyapraśān*

In the word *sparddhā*, [the root] *spr̥dh* means "to contend" (*saṅgharṣe*). Due to the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, there is lengthening according to the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*. In the *laṅ* tense with the ending *sip*, there is the elision of *śap*; then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal*, there is the elision of *sip*. There is the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *d* for *t*), and then by the rule *daś ca*, there is the substitution of *ru* (i.e., *r* for *d*).
The *visarjanīya* [is substituted] for [the final *r*] before a *kha* or a *ra* vowel.

If, even here, the genitive case were a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*)—as in [the rule] *padasya*—then in cases such as *cakarṣa* and *karkaśaḥ*, the *visarjanīya* would occur for the letter *r* even when it is not at the end of a word (*apadāntasya*). However, thinking that there is no fault whatsoever if the genitive is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), whereby the word is qualified by *repha* (the letter *r*) and the *visarjanīya* is prescribed for the final letter of the word ending in *r*, he says: "of a word ending in *repha*" (*rephāntasya padasya*). Regarding the phrase "when *khari* follows or at the end" (*khari parato 'vasāne ca*), the word "following" (*parataḥ*) is connected only with *khari*, not with "at the end" (*avasānena*).

Because [the latter] is impossible: that very phoneme by which one ceases [speaking] would have to be the *avasāna* (pause). *Virati* is the non-utterance of a phoneme. In that case, regarding a *repha* at the end of a word (*padānta*), there cannot possibly exist a subsequent phoneme by which one might cease. Furthermore, the other kind of *avasāna* is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), and priority or posteriority (*paurvāparya*) is not possible with respect to non-existence. Therefore, although the locative case in "before a *khaR* or at a pause" (*kharavasānayoḥ*) is a single locative, it is divided according to the difference in its scope: it is a locative of proximity (*parasaptamī*) before a *khaR*, and a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*) at a pause.

Another says: even in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), which perish as soon as they are uttered, there exists a sequence constructed by the intellect (*buddhi-viracita*); this is possible even in terms of their actual nature (*tattva-bhāvena*). Therefore, in both cases, the locative case is used in the sense of "after" (*parasaptamī*). In the examples, there is the substitution of *s* for *visarjanīya* before a *khari* sound, the substitution of *ś* before the *cavarga*, and the substitution of *ṣ* before the *ṭavarga*.

Regarding the example *nārpatya*: [the suffix] *ṇya* is applied after a word ending in *pati*. As for the statement "because the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is characterized as being *bahiraṅga*": the *vṛddhi* is *bahiraṅga* because it depends upon a *taddhita* suffix which is external [to the base]. Regarding the phrase "of the *repha* (the letter *r*) which is based on that": its being based on that is due to its being prescribed together with it. For the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* prescribes the status of having *rapara* (having *r* as a subsequent element) by bringing it into a single operation with the rules prescribing *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; therefore, whatever is the cause for the *vṛddhi* is also the cause for the *repha*. Consequently, the *repha* is also *bahiraṅga*.

The *visarjanīya*, however, being internal (*antaraṅga*) because it arises based merely upon the *khara* (voiceless consonant), [is subject to the following objection]: But surely the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* is indicated in the rule *vāha ūṭh*, and therefore it resides in that location. What follows from this? When that [rule] is to be applied, the *visarjanīya* is "as if non-existent" (*asiddha*) by the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham*; how then can that [rule], not perceiving the *antaraṅga* [element], bring about the "as-if-non-existent" status of the *bahiraṅga*? This is not a fault; for there is the principle *kāryakālaṃ saṃjñāparibhāṣam*. Consequently, just like other *paribhāṣās*, the application of the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* in this context is not contradictory.
The substitution of *ru* for [the final vowel of a stem] occurs before a *sup* suffix.

Regarding *payaḥ su*: where two *s* sounds are recited, there the *s* replaces the *visarga* optionally by the rule *vā śari*. Regarding *sarpiḥ ṣu*: where the *visarga* is recited, there the *ṣ* replaces the *s* of the suffix by the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi*. However, when two *ṣ* sounds are recited, as before, the *visarga* becomes *s*, and for the following [suffix], as before, it becomes *ṣ*; then, by the rule *ṣṭunā ṣṭu*, the preceding [s] becomes *ṣ*. It is the locative plural that is understood here; it is not a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation).

Because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *khar*, there is no *sup* suffix beginning with a *kha* sound other than the locative plural (*saptamī-bahuvacana*). Therefore, in cases such as *payobhyām*, this [rule] does not serve as an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather as a restriction (*niyama*). As it has been said: "When something is already established, its restatement is for the purpose of restriction. Thus, the restriction is "only after *r* when followed by a *sup* suffix," and not the reverse restriction—"only after *r* when followed by a *sup* suffix"—because of the grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) such as "consonants that follow one another without an intervening vowel constitute a *saṃyoga*."
The *y* [substituted for the visarga] after *bho*, *bhago*, *agho*, and *a* when preceded by a vowel, before a vowel or a semivowel (*aś*).

If it is argued that the mention of *ru* is redundant because [the rule] does not apply elsewhere—since a consonant other than *ru* becomes *khar*, and in that case, because the substitution of *y* is "not established" (*asiddha*) by the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham*, there ought to be a *visarjanīya*; and once the *visarjanīya* has been produced, since it would be included in the term *ru* due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow? No; because it does not have *al* (a vowel) as its original locus (*sthānin*). For here, the original locus of the *visarjanīya* is the *repha* (the sound *r*) belonging to *ru*, and not *ru* itself.

Furthermore—since for this *ru* as well, that which is the substitute is the *repha* itself, and not the *ru* itself, there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule even because it is not a rule concerning vowels (*al-vidhi*). Moreover, because of the governing heading of *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ya* will not occur at the end of a word (*avasāna*); therefore, is the mention of *aś* useless? To this he says: "The mention of *aś* is for the sake of what follows. He clarifies this very point with the rule: *hali sarveṣām*. [In the example] *vṛkṣavayateḥ apratyayaḥ*, the suffix is *vic*, not *kvip*.

For in the case of the *kvip* suffix, because that which undergoes partial modification is not considered different from the original, the *v* would be included by the inclusion of the whole, and thus the *samprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the *v* would occur; then, by the rule "there is elision of *v* and *y* before a *val* [consonant]," there would be elision of the *v*. Furthermore, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original) does not apply here to the *ṇi*, because the *ṇi* has been elided in the *kvip* formation. However, in the case of the *vic* suffix, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the *ṇi*, there is no elision of the *v*; yet, in that case, the *samprasāraṇa* simply does not present itself at all.

However, regarding the rule *hali sarveṣām*, when an elision (*lopa*) is to be performed, the elision of the *v*-sound would occur because the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivat*. Therefore, [the term] is specified [as *vali*]. Now, why does the elision of the *v*-sound not occur by the rule *lopo vyoḥ* when a *k*-sound follows, since there is no *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of the *ṇi*-affix due to the prohibition against operations concerning the end of a word (*padāntavidhi*), as the *v*-sound is at the end of a word? This is not a fault; [The answer follows:]... [text continues] ...therefore, this is not a fault.

In this context, however, the word *vidhi* (rule) has an abstract sense (*bhāvasādhana*); consequently, the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* applies when a rule is being enjoined at the end of a word (*padānte*). Furthermore, elision (*lopa*) is not "at the end of a word," because it is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Regarding the word *atha*: if the purpose of the mention of *aś* in the rule *hali sarveṣām* is as stated, then it should have been formulated there simply as *haśi*. Therefore, the meaning of the question is: why, having used the term *hal*, is that [term] further qualified by the mention of *aś*? The particle *eva* is placed out of its logical order; the sense is: "Why was the mention of *haś* alone not made there? [The answer is: "For the sake of the subsequent rule. If the mention of *haś* were made there, then the mention of *hal* would have to be repeated again in the rule *mo'nusvāraḥ*.

The phrase "so that it might be merely a vowel" (halmātre yathā syāt) implies the sense that we are not liberated from both types of *grahaṇa* in every respect. Nevertheless, one must state the purpose for following the *grahaṇa* of *aś* here; thus he says: "of *v* and *y*, with greater ease of articulation" (*vyor laghuprayatnatara*).
According to Śākaṭāyana, the *v* and *y* [substitutes] are produced with less articulatory effort when they follow a light syllable.

"Exceedingly light in effort" means *laghuprayatnatara*. "Effort" (*prayatna*) is a quality of the self (*ātman*) which is the cause for the utterance of phonemes. In the examples, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a *va* is substituted for a *va*, and a *ya* for a *ya*. But what is this state of being "exceedingly light in effort"? To this he says: "the state of being exceedingly light in effort. Regarding the place (*sthāna*)—the palate and so forth—and the articulators (*karaṇa*)—the tip, the middle, the root, and the upper part of the tongue—when there is lightness of effort, these [articulators] become slack, that is, light.
There is elision [of *y*] according to Śākalya. 8.3.19.

Regarding the phrase "preceded by *a* or *ava*": as for that which is preceded by *o*, its obligatory elision (*lopa*) will be prescribed by the subsequent rule. [The opponent asks: "But since elision is also mentioned, and even the form with greater ease of articulation (*laghuprayatnatara*), both of these will occur by virtue of the explicit statement [of the rule]; so what is the purpose of including Śākalya’s name for the sake of an option (*vikalpa*)? To this, he replies: "By that... (i.e., by that mention of Śākalya).
This [suffix] belongs to Gārgya. 8.3.20.

"Of the *yakāra* following a vowel-form (*ākāra*). However, a *vakāra* is not possible in this context. This rule is commenced for the sake of making [the substitution] obligatory (*nitya*), because the option (*vikalpa*) is already established by the preceding rule.

Why, then, is the mention of Gārgya included? He says: "The mention of Gārgya is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*). In this section, both a [substitution] with even lighter effort than the *vy-oriha* rule and even elision (*lopa*) are prescribed; therefore, to which of these does this obligatory elision apply as a sublater (*bādhaka*)—to the optional elision of *la* due to immediate sequence (*ānantarya*)? He says: "This which... [referring to the obligatory elision].

"But some," however, hold this view: that in this section, the effect of *vyoḥ* is expected as a collective whole, and not merely the optional elision (*lopa*) that follows immediately; such is their intention.
And [the substitution of *u*] occurs for *ūṅ* before a word [beginning with a vowel]. || 8.3.21 ||

"By means of a previously existing *ñ*": even in the case of the example for *bhū*, the understanding is that *uñ* [is formed] by means of a previously existing *ñ*; because the *anubandha* does not participate in actual usage. "For the sake of the subsequent rule": this is so that the rule "after a short vowel, *ṅam* followed by *ṅmuṇ* is always [added] before a vowel-initial word" (*ṅamo hrasvādachi ṅamuṇnityam*) applies to words beginning with a vowel, but not here—as in *daṇḍinā*. This is not a valid purpose, because the term "of a word" (*padasya*) is understood to carry over.

In that case, does the status of being a *pada* exist here for [the compound] *paramadaṇḍin*, since this is a compound of a nominal base (*subanta*)? It does not; for it has been stated: "And when there is the status of being a final member (*uttarapadatva*), the rule regarding what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādividhi*) applies. Let this mention of *pada* stand aside for now; this rule (*yoga*) is also for the sake of making [the application] obligatory (*nityārtha*).
The [suffix] *hal* is applied after all [roots]. 8.3.22.

[The rule applies] to the *yakāra* at the end of a word (*padānta*). However, a *vakāra* preceded by *bho*, *bhago*, or *agho* is not possible; whereas one preceded by an *avarṇa* (a vowel) is possible, as in *vṛkṣav karoti*. Yet, its elision (*lopa*) does not occur, because it has been stated that there is a specific restriction [in the rule] "when followed by a non-*śit* consonant" (*aśi halīti*). Therefore, it was said [in the rule] "of the *yakāra*. Now, is it not possible in cases such as *vṛkṣav hasati*? It is not possible; because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*), for no such expression exists.

And likewise, regarding the rule *laṇ*, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "There are no hal consonants at the end of a word that are not *aṇ*. Thus, even this usage *vṛkṣav karoti* is to be considered problematic.
The *mo* [is the name] for the *anusvāra*. 8.3.23.

In this context, the term *padasya* is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*). Since the word *pada* is qualified by the letter *m*, it is understood that the *anusvāra* replaces the final letter of a word ending in *n*. Thus he says: "of the *m* at the end of a word."
A *n* that is not at the end of a word [is replaced by *anusvāra*] before a *jhal* consonant.
"He will step upon" (*ākraṃsyate*): [this is] the *lṛṭ* suffix after the root *kram*, with the *ātmanepada* ending by the rule "after *āṅ*, [the verb takes the *ātmanepada*] in the sense of rising."
The substitution of *mo* for *m* occurs before *rāji*, *samaḥ*, *kvau*. 8.3.25.

*Samrāj*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "satsūdviṣa... etc., and the change to *ṣ* occurs by the rule "vraścādi...". *Sāmrājyam*: from the word ending in *kvip*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class. Even though there is an additional [element], the root *rāj-* exists as one ending in *kvip*; thus the suffix occurs here as well, or rather, the change to *m* occurs while it is still in the state of ending in *kvip*, prior even to the production of *ṣyañ*. *Saṃyat*: in the rule "gamaḥ kvau," the elision occurs because of the statement "of *gam-* and others," and the augment *tuk* is added for the short vowel. *Kirāṭ*: this is a compound according to the rule "kiṃ kṣepe" (when *kim* expresses censure).
Or [the augment] ma is substituted for [the initial consonant of] another [word]. 8.3.26.

Regarding *hmalayati*: the root *hmal* means "to move" (*calane*). With the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the rule "in the case of *jval*, *hval*, *hmal*, and *nam*, when preceded by no prefix, it is optionally designated as *mit*" applies; thus, in one alternative, it receives the *mit* designation. By the rule "the short vowel of *mit* roots," the penultimate vowel is shortened.

Regarding "followed by *y*, *v*, or *l*": that *va* from which *y*, *v*, or *l* follow is so described. Since these [substitutes] are *y*, *v*, or *l*, they become nasalized (*ānunāsika*) due to internal similarity (*āntaratamya*). Because of the mention of the option (*vā*), in the alternative case, *anusvāra* also occurs.

The mention of *para* (subsequent) need not be made, since that meaning is already obtained by the locative case itself—namely, "in that which follows the letter *m*. However, the reverse is not possible, because it is impossible; for a letter *h* never occurs subsequent to a letter *m*.
After the vowels *ṅ* and *ṇ*, the augment *k* or *ṭuk* is added before a *śar* consonant.

In the examples, according to the view of Pauṣkarasādi that "the second [consonants] of *khay* [are substituted] before *śar*," the *k* is replaced by *kh*, and the *ṭ* by *ṭh*. Regarding the statement "by making it a final element of the preceding [word]," etc.: what, then, is the reason that the substitution of *ch* is not established at the beginning of a word? To this he says: "In the rule *śaś cho 'ṭi*. As for *virapśin*: this is a name for "great" (*mahat*); it is derived from the root *rap* preceded by *vi*, with the *auṇādika* suffix *śini* in the sense of the object. Alternatively, *virapa* means "proclaiming"; one who possesses that is *virapśaḥ*—that is, one who is "made known," meaning "one who is celebrated."

"For the purpose of prohibiting *ṣatva*": otherwise, when [the suffix] begins with *par*, the *s* would not be at the beginning of a word. "For the purpose of prohibiting *ṣṭutva*": otherwise, when [the suffix] begins with *par*, the *ṭ* would not be at the end of a word.
ṅa, si, and dhuṭ [are kṛt-pratyayas]. 8.3.29.

Thinking that "when both [case endings] are specified, the specification by the ablative is more powerful," and thus considering that the sixth case is substituted for the seventh case *sī* by means of the fifth case *ḍaḥ*, he says: "from that which ends in the letter ḍ. The use of the locative case (*saptamī*), however, is for the sake of brevity. In the examples, once the *dhuṭ* augment has been applied, there is the substitution of *c* (the *cartva* rule), resulting in the letter *t*; and according to the previous alternative, that *t* becomes the letter *th*.

Now, for what purpose is *dhuṭ* made an initial element (*parādi*)? Why not simply make *dhuk* itself a final element (*pūrvānta*)? For if that were done, the mention of *tuk* in the rule *śituk* would not need to be made, as this *dhuk* could be carried over (*anuvarttiṣyate*) there. To this he replies: "The reason for making it an initial element is [as follows]. However, although one could have simply said *tuṭ* for the sake of brevity in the process of derivation (*prakriyālāghava*), the mention of *dhuṭ* is for the sake of subsequent rules—so that *dhuṭ* may apply in the rule *naśca*, and not merely *tuṇ*.

Furthermore, what would happen in the case of *bhavānsāya*? Here, the substitution of *r* [for *s*] by the rule *naśchavyapraśān* would undesirably apply. This is not so; for the condition *ampare* (when followed by a vowel) is understood to carry over there from the previous rule. Moreover, because the augment *tuṭ* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the occurrence of *r* is also precluded. Therefore, only the augment *tuṭ* should be prescribed.
And [the substitution of *na* occurs] for *n*. 8.3.30.
Here too, because it begins with a *para* (subsequent element), in forms such as *kurvan* and *sīdati*, the prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *padāntasya* applies.

This is because the *cartva* (the substitution of *c* or *t*) for *dhuṭ* is *asiddha*. The meaning is that the *cartva* which belongs to *dhuṭ* is *asiddha*. Even though *dhuṭ* itself is also *asiddha*, it is not mentioned [here]; for even if *dhuṭ* were established, the substitution of *ru* would not apply in the absence of *cartva*. [Objection: Let the *cartva* be *asiddha*; nevertheless, *ru* still does not apply, because it is not followed by *an* (*anamparatvāt*). [Reply: True; however, this was stated by accepting that there is the status of being followed by *an* (*amparatva*) on account of that *u* of *dhuṭ*, even though it existed previously (*bhūtapūrveṇa*).
Others, however, do not read this text.
śi is substituted for tuK [before the suffixes beginning with a vowel]. 8.3.31.

The locative case ending in the word "śi" here, having not yet fulfilled its purpose, effects a change of the ablative case ending in the preceding rule—which had already fulfilled its purpose—into a genitive; thus he says: "of the letter n."

Now, for what purpose is a new *tuk* inserted at the end of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*), rather than simply prescribing the existing *dhuṭ* as beginning with the subsequent element (*parādi*)? For even in that case, the result would be established through the substitution of *c* for *t*. To this he replies: "The insertion at the end of the preceding element. This means the insertion of a new *tuk* at the end of the preceding element. [He says: "Because the *n* is not at the end of a word (*apadānta*). This is because the status of being at the end of a word is obstructed by the *tuk*. If it were at the beginning of the subsequent element, there would be no fault, because of the prohibition [in Pāṇini 8.2.24] stating "of that which is at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*). Regarding the phrase "there," etc.: in that case, the substitution of *c* for *t* (*cutva*) is established by virtue of its dependence on the *tuk*.
ṅam follows a short vowel before a vowel, and it is always applied. (Pāṇini 8.3.32)

In both instances, *ṅamaḥ* and *ṅamuṭ*, there is the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term). The element *uṭ* is connected individually with each of the letters beginning with *ṅ*. For when a marker (*liṅga*) is applied to a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it pertains to those things designated by that name (*saṃjñin*). The term *hrasvāt* is a qualifier of *ṅam*, and that [i.e., *ṅam*] in turn is a qualifier of the word (*padam*); and by means of a qualifier, the rule of "ending-in-that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Although the word *padasya* under discussion is in the genitive case, it is nevertheless transformed into the ablative case because of its connection with the word *ṅamaḥ*.

Regarding the rule "when both [case endings] are specified, the specification by the ablative is stronger," the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is substituted for the seventh case (*saptamī*) "aci" by the fifth case (*pañcamī*) "ṅamaḥ. However, the use of the seventh case is for the sake of brevity and for the benefit of subsequent rules. Having kept all this in mind, he says: "following a short vowel. Furthermore, a numerical correspondence (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) must be understood here, because the number of augments (*āgama*) and the number of those to which they are added (*āgamī*) are equal.

In examples such as *paramadaṇḍin*, there is a compound (*samāsa*) of two words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). One might raise the objection that even though the case-suffix expressing the meaning of the compound has been elided, the status of *daṇḍin* as a "word" (*pada*) still exists by virtue of the rule regarding the "characteristic of an affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and thus the augment *ṅamuṭ* would apply. Anticipating this, he says: "In this case" (*iha*). When the status of a word is to be assigned to the latter member of a compound, the characteristic of an affix does not apply—provided it is a rule concerning what is not at the beginning of a word (*apadādividhi*), meaning with the exception of rules concerning the beginning of a word. The point is that in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*, the characteristic of an affix certainly does apply because it is a rule concerning the beginning of a word. This is stated according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika.
He states this also according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras: "Or rather... (atha vā).
After *maya* (a vowel other than *a*), *uṅ* (the short vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*) is optionally replaced by *va*.

One might raise the objection: "Since this is already established by the rule *iko yaṇaci* itself, there is no need for this [new rule]"—anticipating this, he says: "Because of its status as a *pragṛhya*. And its status as a *pragṛhya* is due to the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*. Even so, one might suggest that instead of *iko yaṇaci*, one should state immediately after it: *maya uño vā*; for in that case, the mention of *v* would not have to be made. To this he replies: "Because that [substitution] is not yet established (*asiddha*)."

But when *uñ* follows immediately after [the word] *iti* and *mayaḥ* follows, then there is an option regarding the designation *pragṛhya* for *uñ*, as well as the substitution of *ūm*. In that case, when the *pragṛhya* designation does not apply, this rule provides both the substitution of *v* and the substitution of *yaṇ*; since this substitution of *v* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the substitution of *yaṇ*, the *anusvāra* also occurs once the *yaṇ* has been applied—resulting in *kiṃviti*. However, in the alternative where the *pragṛhya* designation applies, the substitution of *v* optionally occurs by this rule, resulting in *kivviti* or *kimu iti*.

By virtue of the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the substitution of *ūm̐* also results in the letter *v* in one alternative; and because it is the closest match (*antaratama*), that *v* is nasalized—this is the fourth form. In the alternative where there is no substitution of *v* for the very same *ūm̐*, it is heard [as *ūm̐*]—this is the fifth form.
The visarga is replaced by *s* [before a voiceless consonant]. (Pāṇini 8.3.34)

In this context, it has been stated that the *visarjanīya* replaces the *repha* (*r*) before both *khari* (voiceless consonants) and at the end of a word (*avasāna*). Since no specific condition (*nimitta-viśeṣa*) is mentioned here, would it not follow that *satva* (the substitution of *s*) applies both before *khari* and at the end of a word—as in *vṛkṣaḥ* and *plakṣaḥ*? [The answer is: the term "in *saṃhitā*" (*sahitāyām*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], and there is no *saṃhitā* at the end of a word, because of the absence of a following element.

Let it be that there is no subsequent [element]; rather, the *sattva* (substitution) applies based on the conjunction (*saṃhitā*) with the preceding element. However, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, since both the subject of the operation (*kāryin*) and the cause (*nimitta*) are explicitly mentioned, the conjunction between those two alone is relied upon. Thus, in the case of *dadhi-atra*, even though there is a conjunction between the *ik* (*i*) and the *ac* (*a*) of the preceding and following elements, the grammatical operation does not take place, because they are not in mutual conjunction (*parasparam asaṃhitatvāt*). This might be argued: the technical term *saṃhitā* is prescribed generally, whereas the term *avasāna* (pause) is prescribed specifically.

Because the two operations have the same phoneme as their object and because technical designations (*saṃjñā*) exist for the sake of operations, there is a relationship of sublation and sublated between the two designations themselves, since they also share the same object. Alternatively, although the definition would be established by the rule "proximity (*saṃnikarṣaḥ*) is *saṃhitā*" alone, the inclusion of the word *para* ("subsequent") is for the purpose of conveying a specific excellence—that is, that proximity which is most excellent. And what is most excellent? That which exists between both the preceding and the following [sounds]. Due to the absence of that [proximity], there is an absence of the designation *saṃhitā* for the pause (*avasāna*).

If this is so, there is a fault regarding the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsike* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), for in that context the phrase *vāvasāne* (Pāṇini 8.4.56) still applies. Furthermore, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning *saṃhitā* must necessarily be carried over for subsequent purposes—so that in the rule *toli* (Pāṇini 6.1.103), the *parasavarṇa* substitution does not occur in non-*saṃhitā* contexts, as in *agnicit lunāti*. Consequently, in cases such as *dadhi*, where the nasalization depends on both *saṃhitā* and *avasāna*, the nasalization would not occur; thus, one must admit the coexistence (*samāveśa*) of the technical designations *saṃhitā* and *avasāna*, and from that, the undesired consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *satva* [substitution of s] would follow even at the end of a word (*avasāna*). Therefore...

He says: "The term *khari* is understood to carry over. That carry-over is to be understood either by the maxim of the frog's leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*) or by the continuity of the connection; for otherwise, the grammatical operation would be understood as applying to *khari* even in the preceding rule.

What, then, is the proof here that the term *khari* continues [from the previous rule]? It is the statement *śarpare* in the subsequent rule. For that is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; regarding its external referent (*anyapadārtha*), that which can possibly follow the *visarjanīya* is precisely what constitutes that external referent, and that is only a *khaḥ* (a sibilant). This is because it is impossible for the *avasāna* (the pause at the end of a sentence) to be followed by a *śar* (a sibilant). Alternatively, if the substitution of *sa* were to apply to both *khaḥ* and *avasāna*, the prescription of the *visarjanīya* would be purposeless; one would simply have to say, "In place of [the *visarjanīya*] there is *sa* when followed by a *khaḥ* or at the *avasāna*."

In this way, indeed, the rule "of the *visarjanīya*" need not be stated. Must "of the *visarjanīya*" necessarily be stated for the purpose of specifying the substituend in the rule "the *visarjanīya* remains when followed by a *śar*"? No, it need not be stated.

This is also established by anticipation (*apakarṣa*); I shall state it thus: "When *r* [follows], [it becomes] *s* before a consonant (*kha*) or at a pause (*avasa-āna*); when *r* [follows], [it becomes] *visarjanīya* before a *sup* suffix followed by a *śar* sound. In the rule "before a *śar* sound" (*śarpare*), the term "*r*" is understood to carry over, but not the term "*roḥ*"; therefore, it applies in all such cases as *sugīḥ tsarukaḥ* and *puruṣaḥ tsarukaḥ*. Now, where will you place the rule beginning with "bho-bhago-agho-..."? Immediately after "the *visarjanīya* [is substituted for *r*] before a *śar* sound."

If this is so, then since the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *yatva* would also arise in cases such as *svaratra* and *svarnayati*, must the term *ru* be mentioned again? If that is the case, then after the rule *roḥ supi*, one should first recite *bho-bhago-* etc. for the purpose of prescribing substitutes in place of *ru*, and subsequently recite *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* and so forth. Even so, the mention of *ru* must still be made.

Is it because *ru* is interrupted? Even so, if the rule remains as originally stated, there are three mentions: two mentions of *visarjanīya* and a third mention of *sa*; whereas under an alternative arrangement, there would be two mentions of *sa* and one mention of *ru*. Thus, since the desired result is established by the more concise formulation, *satva* (the substitution of *s*) will not occur everywhere due to the specific force (*sāmarthya*) of the prescription for *visarjanīya*.

Even so, how is it known that this [substitution] occurs before *kha* (the velar stop), and not before *ava-khāna*? It is known from an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This is because the rule prescribes the substitution of *visarjanīya* for *s* when followed by *śar* or *khar*. This indicates that the substitution of *satva* (the change to *s*) indeed occurs before *khar*. For if the opposite were true—as in *puruṣaḥ tsarukaḥ* and similar cases where *satva* would be absent—the *visarjanīya* would already exist, and thus the prescription of its substitution would be purposeless. But this is not a valid indicator.

There is indeed a purpose for this formulation: [is it] so that in examples such as *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*, the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya sounds do not occur? This is not the case; if this were the only purpose, he would have simply said, "after *ku* and *tu*, *ka* and *pa* optionally [occur] before a sibilant (*śari*). Therefore, by the force of this specific rule, this prescription applies only when a *khar* (voiceless consonant) follows. And it is with this very intention that it was stated: "the term *khari* is understood to carry over."
Before a sibilant (śa), the visarjanīya [is substituted for *r*].

The term *śarpara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that after which there is a *śar*. If the mention of *para* (after) were not made, it would be understood that only the *śar* itself is the cause [of the doubling], because the word *khar* is understood from the previous rule and because of the statement "optionally before a *śar*" (*vā śari*). Otherwise, the opposite understanding might arise—that the doubling occurs when a *śar* follows a *kharp*—which would imply that the *sphoṭa* is eternal and that the person remains constant. Therefore, the mention of *para* is necessary.

Now, for what purpose is "visarjanīya" stated, rather than simply saying "not"? For if the substitution of *s* were prohibited, the *visarjanīya* would remain in its own form. To this he replies: "of the *visarjanīya*. This is true; in cases such as *puruṣas-tsarukaḥ*, it is indeed established even by the prohibition of *s*. However, in cases where *k* and *p* follow a vowel—such as *vāsaḥ-kṣaumam* and *addhiḥ-psātam*—the modification of that *visarjanīya*, namely the *jihvāmūlīya* and so forth, would otherwise occur.

But when there is the inclusion of the *visarjanīya*, it remains as the *visarjanīya* itself; even the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* do not occur. The meaning of the word "only" (*kevalam*) is that it is simply the letter *s*.
Or [the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*] before a *śar* [consonant]. (Pāṇini 8.3.36)
In the case of "vṛkṣāḥ sthātāraḥ," there is either a *visarjanīya* or *satva* (the substitution of *s*) when the elision (*lopa*) does not take place.
Before *k* and *p*, as well as before *ḥ* (visarga), *ka* and *pa* [are substituted for *ś* and *ṣ*].

"And *visarjanīya*. By this, he shows that the letter *ca* (the "and") is for the purpose of drawing in (*anukarṣaṇa*) the term *visarjanīya*. Alternatively, one might ask: why not simply carry forward the word "optionally" (*vā*) and include the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* [in the rule], so that the letter *ca* would not have to be used? This cannot be done; for if those two were mentioned [there], then by the rule "of *visarjanīya*, *sa*" (*visarjanīyasya saḥ*), there would result only the substitution of *sa*. Therefore, the *visarjanīya* must be enjoined by being drawn in precisely by the letter *ca*, and the word "optionally" (*vā*) should not be carried forward. For if it were carried forward, then even in the primary case, the substitution of *sa* would undesirably follow from all three [rules].

Anticipating the objection that since the jihvāmūlīya and upadhmānīya are pronounced together with the letters *k* and *p* in the Sūtra, they must therefore be the actual substitutes for the *visarjanīya*, he replies: "The *k* and *p* are for the sake of pronunciation. The sense is that without those [consonants], it would be impossible to pronounce them. He then asks, "What kind of substitutes are they? and answers: "They are the jihvāmūlīya... and so forth.

In this context, three substitutes are prescribed in place of the *visarjanīya*; consequently, [the rule] would apply only when *k* or *p* followed by a *śar* sound follows—such as in *vāsaḥ kṣaumam* and *adbhiḥ psātam*. For here, the *visarjanīya* exists by virtue of the rule "the *visarjanīya* remains when followed by a *śar*," and its existence is not purposeless; for where there is a *khar* sound other than *k* or *p* followed by a *śar*, such as in *tipuruṣaḥ* or *tsarukaḥ*, that [rule] finds its scope of application.

However, in the case of *aśarpara* (not followed by *r*), there would be no [substitution] for *k* or *p*, because for that [word-final sound], there is no *visarjanīya*; rather, it has been replaced by *s* according to the rule "the *visarjanīya* becomes *s*" (*visarjanīyasya saḥ*). What, then, is the reason that the substitution by *s* occurs first? Because when that [subsequent operation] is to be performed, the present rule is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Therefore, in this context, the substitute *s*—that which is prescribed by "the *visarjanīya* becomes *s*"—must be indicated as the original element (*sthānin*); thus, in place of that *s*, the three substitutions occur before *k* and *p*.

For in this way, the *visarjanīya* would be prescribed as an exception (*apavāda*) to the *s* of the [rule] concerning *kupvoḥ śar*, and thus, due to the absence of the *s*, the substitution would not apply; however, for the two [consonants *k* and *p*] alone, the substitution would indeed apply. Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] "to *s*" (*sasya*). As the author of the Vārttika said: "The *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya* are substitutes for *s* before *k* and *p*; for if the *visarjanīya* were the substitute, the substitution would apply only when followed by *śar*. To this, he states the resolution: "In this regard, [it refers] to the *s* of the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ*."

The intended meaning is as follows: In the rule "visarjanīyasya saḥ," the substitute *sa* has been prescribed for the *visarjanīya* as its locus (*sthānin*). That *visarjanīya* can be of two kinds: characterized by being followed by a *śar* sound, and characterized by occurring at the end of a pause (*kharavasāna*). Among these, because that which is characterized by being followed by a *śar* is unestablished (*asiddha*), the other [the *visarjanīya* at the end of a pause] is the locus for the *sakāra*; it is precisely this that is carried over here. Consequently, this rule is commenced before the substitution of *satva* (of *s*) has even occurred, because the entire domain is pervaded by that [rule].

The rule "śarpare visarjanīyaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.35) applies when *k* or *p* followed by a *śar* sound follow; however, it does not apply when *k* or *p* stand alone. Thus, this [subsequent] rule does not possess the character of an exception (*bādhaka*) with respect to that [preceding rule]. One might argue: "Granted that it is not an exception, yet because it is subsequent, this very rule would still apply even when *k* or *p* are followed by a *śar* sound. To this, he says: "In what is not established for what precedes it" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*).

He states another solution: "But some say... (*kecittu*). The rule *kupvoḥ* is one [independent] rule; here, the phrase *śarpare visarjanīyaḥ* continues to apply. Thus, when *k* or *p* followed by a sibilant (*śarpara*) occurs, only the *visarjanīya* remains, and not *ḥ* or *ḥk*. Furthermore, it was stated previously that since it could have been said simply "not" (*na*) in the preceding rule, the specific prescription of the *visarjanīya* is for the purpose of precluding its modification. Consequently, this rule does not even apply when *k* or *p* are followed by a sibilant.
That [suffix] occurs after the word *apavāda* and others. 8.3.38.

The phrase "apadādau" (not at the beginning of a word) is an adjective qualifying *ku* and *pu*; the singular number is used by way of transference (*vyatyaya*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. Regarding the expression "in the case of *pāśa*, *kalpa*, *ka*, and *kāmya*": this is an illustration of possibilities, not an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*), because no other [suffixes] are possible. In the example "prātaḥkalpam," although the word *prātaḥ* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti-pradhāna*), it denotes the possessor of that capacity (*śaktimat*) in the context of a compound formation (*vṛtti-viṣaye*); thus, there is a connection with "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*). This is just as in the cases "the day became night" (*doṣābhūtam ahaḥ*) and "the night became day" (*divābhūtā rātriḥ*), where there is a connection with the transformation of one state into another (*abhūtatadbhāva-yoga*).

"Regarding the rule *roḥ kāmye*, [the word] 'for the sake of restriction' (*niyamārtham*) is used. He explains this very point with the words *roreva* (only after *r*). For example: *gīḥ kāmyati*. By the subsequent sūtra, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. But what if this were stated in that very [subsequent] sūtra? It cannot be done thus; for even if there were a prohibition of *ṣ* alone, by this [present rule], the substitution of *s* would still apply. Regarding the phrase *upadhmanīyasya ca*: this is its explanation—namely, *when followed by a velar consonant* (*kavarge parataḥ*). As for the statement *ubjirayam* and so forth, how this root should be understood as having *d* as its penultimate letter has already been explained in the section on *hayaraṭ*.
The *ṣ* [substituted for the final letter] of the root *iṇ*.

Since *satva* was previously established, this rule prescribes *ṣatva* as an exception (*apavāda*) to it. On this point, some say: "That same *sakāra* which occurs in the rule *so 'padādau* is prescribed throughout the subsequent section concerning *ku* and *pu*; by this [present rule], *ṣatva* is prescribed for that very *sakāra* when followed by an *iṇ* vowel, and not for the *visarjanīya*. Furthermore, the phrase *apadādau* is not connected here. If that is so, must that *sakāra* be specified as the substitute (*sthānin*)? He says: no.

The original [rule] continues: "so 'padādau" (8.3.114). For that, the genitive case is substituted for the ablative "iṇaḥ" (8.3.57). Even so, one might object: "Does not the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* prescribed by the rules to be stated hereafter fail to apply, because those rules are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when this [present rule] is to be performed? This is not a fault; the activity of the Teacher indicates that it is not the case that one rule is non-existent with respect to another rule; rather, it is the case that within a given section (*prakaraṇa*), the subsequent is non-existent with respect to the preceding. This is shown by the fact that he includes the phrase "even in a non-compound" (*asamāse 'pi*) in the rule "after a preposition, even in a non-compound" (8.3.109).

How does this serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? Even without the inclusion of the term *asamāse* ("in a non-compound"), the substitution of *ṇ* will occur for both compounds and non-compounds because no specific distinction is made; nor does the rule "after a preceding member, when a name is formed, except after *g*" cause the cessation of the *ṇ*-substitution in a compound, because when a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is to be applied, the *ṇ*-substitution [prescribed] by the rule "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) is not yet established (*asiddha*).

The Teacher perceives that each section (*prakaraṇa*) is established independently of the others; therefore, he includes the mention of "even in a compound" (*asamāse 'pi*). For if that were not the case, since the entire section on *ṇatva* would be a single unit under a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the restriction would exclude the application of *ṇatva* after a prefix—which is already established by the rule *upasargāt*—and thus the inclusion of "even in a compound" would be necessary. Consequently, in this way, the substitution of *ṣ* is prescribed for the letter *s*, not for the *visarjanīya*;
and in what follows, only the substitution of *s* is carried forward, not the substitution of *ṣ*.

This position, too, is indeed faultless; however, because it would entail the complication of conceptualizing a sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and relying on an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence), the author of the *Vṛtti* did not adopt it. What, then, is his position? Both [the *s* and the *ṣ*] continue to apply in what follows—the letter *s* and the letter *ṣ*. If this were so, both would apply everywhere; for instance, if the letter *s* continued to apply in rules such as *idudupadhasya ca*, where a *visarjanīya* follows a *niṣ* (a word ending in *n*), there too the letter *s* alone would result.

Now, does the letter *ṣ* continue to apply in rules such as "namaspurasorgatyoḥ," whereby even where a visarga follows a non-*iṇ* [vowel], the substitution of *ṣ* would still result? This is not a fault; for it is declared that the entire group "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ" possesses the svarita accent. As it is said: "The phrase 'iṇaḥ ṣaḥ' continues. Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* will certainly not occur in cases where there is no *iṇ*. Even so, might the substitution of *s* also apply in the domain of the *ṣ*-substitution? No; because that [substitution of *s*] is superseded by the presence of the letter *ṣ*, and because the letter *c* was not employed [in the rule].

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence follows because of the capacity for subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*), that too is not correct, since subsequent application is possible even for the sake of the subsequent rule. This is what was stated: "The substitute *ṣ* occurs for the *visarjanīya* that follows *iṇ*; however, for any other [following *k* or *kh*], the substitute *s* occurs. But why is this [rule] commenced at all, when it could simply be prescribed that *satva* (the substitution of *s*) alone applies in this section? For since that [substitution of *s*] has the letter *s* as its substitute, the substitution of *ṣ* will occur by the rule *iṇkoḥ*. [Response: It is indeed established; however, the phrase "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*) is understood to apply there [in the previous rule]. This present commencement is for the purpose of [covering cases where the *visarjanīya*] is at the end of a word.
The substitution of *naś* for *nas* occurs before the suffixes *pur* and *as*, when they denote direction.

From this point onward, the restriction "not at the beginning of a word" (*apadādau*) is no longer applicable. However, for the word *namaḥ*, the rule *puro'vyayam* applies. Thus we have *puraḥ paśya*. [The root] *pṝ* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "filling. By the rule *bhrājabhāsa-* etc., the suffix *kvip* is added; from that [form ending in *kvip*], the suffix *śas* is applied. To demonstrate its ending in that [suffix], the pair *pūḥ* and *purau* is introduced.
And [the substitution of ṣ for s] occurs for a consonant that follows *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* (idut), provided it is not part of an affix (*apratyaya*).

That which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate vowel is "that whose penultimate is *i* or *u*" (*idudupadha*), referring to a composite whole; the connection with "its *visarjanīya*" is one of different grammatical cases (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). The term "not being a suffix" (*apratyayasya*) is likewise a case of different grammatical cases. Regarding the list "ni, dur, bahir, āvi, catuṣ, prāduḥ": since a prohibition for other possible [words] will be stated later, this is not an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*); rather, it is a demonstration of what is possible. As in the example "catuṣkapālam."

The *dvigu* compound occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In the case of the suffix *aṇ* [prescribed by the rule] "saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ," there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "dvigor lug-anapatye. Regarding the term *catuṣkaṇṭakam*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. As for the objection concerning "mātuḥ karoti" and so forth: here, when the form *mātṛ-as* is established, the substitution of *u* by the rule "ṛta ut" becomes *rapara* (followed by *r*) according to the maxim "that which takes the place of both [elements] is followed by [the letter of] the second element. Consequently, when the *s* of the suffix is elided by the rule "rātsasya," the *repha* (*r*) undergoes *visarjanīya*. He provides the rebuttal: "in the case of *karakā* and others. This is because of the cause of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*).

The term *karmadhārayaḥ* means "due to the cause of the single-substitute form (*ekādeśarūpa*)," or rather, it means "due to that *ukāra* for which the rule of single substitution (*ekādeśa-śāstra*) is the cause.

Regarding the phrase *pummuhusor*: since these two words are not derived through grammatical derivation (*avyutpanna*), the prohibition is stated. In that context, there is no need for a prohibition regarding the word *puṃs*, because why would *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) not occur? It does not occur because of the absence of the *visarjanīya*. For it has been stated: "There is *satva* (substitution of *s*) for *sam*, *pum*, and *kān*. Since *satva* is not considered non-established (*asiddha*) in that case, there is an absence of the *visarjanīya*.

And that [substitution] must necessarily be stated as *satva* (the substitution of *s*). Even though the substitution of *visarjanīya* is prohibited by the rule for *ṣatva*, the rule "kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca" would still apply—e.g., in the case of *muhuḥ-kāmā* ("she whose desire is constant"), where only the rule "kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca" occurs. However, in some places, *muhus-kāmā* is read with *satva*; that is a corrupt reading, for here the possibility of *satva* does not exist, as it is not established in either the *sūtra* or the *vārttika*. As for *naiṣkulyam*: the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa-ādi* group.

In the examples *niṣkulam* and *duṣkulam*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86). Regarding the phrase "of the two characterized as external" (*bahiraṅgalakṣaṇayoḥ*): the compound (*dvandva*) is external because it depends on the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that stands outside [the constituent members]; the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is also external because it requires an object such as calling from a distance (*dūrāddhūta*) and the sentence itself.
The suffix *ṣat* is optionally applied after *tiras*.
Regarding the rule "tiro 'ntardhau," the word *tiras* is designated as a *gati*.
In the expression *tiraḥ kṛtvā*, because concealment (*antardhi*) is not intended to be expressed, it lacks the status of a *gati*.
The words *dvis*, *tris*, and *catur* are used in the sense of "times" (*kṛtvas*). 8.3.43.

This is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) applicable in both cases: because the word "catur" has a *visarjanīya* that is not a *pratyaya*, the rule "idudupadhasya ca" would apply; however, for the other two [suffixes], it would not apply. One should not suspect that the rule "isusoḥ sāmarthye" provides the derivation here, because in that rule, the suffix *isa* is what is intended to be included.

"What is the purpose of including *kṛtvo'rthe*?"—this is the question, implying that words ending in *su* do not deviate from the sense of "times" (*kṛtvo'rtha*). The answer is that there is no evidence for the word *catuḥ* being a word ending in *su*. If, however, association (*sāhacarya*) were the determining factor, then the inclusion of the term *kṛtvo'rtha* would not even be necessary for its sake; yet it is included. This is for the purpose of providing a technical indicator (*jñāpaka*), which indicates that association is not a determining factor in all cases. What is established by this? It establishes that in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, the augment *iṭ* is also understood through association with verbal roots (*dhātu*).

What is the purpose of specifying "twice, thrice, four times" (*dvistriścatur*)? [It is so that] in the case of *pañcakṛtvaḥ karoti* ("he does five times"), the substitution of *s* should not occur. He says this is not a necessary requirement, adding: "provided that the rule *idudupadhasya...* (Pāṇini 8.3.41) continues to apply," and so forth. This means: that whose scope is the sense of the suffix *kṛtvas*. The meaning is that the word which occurs in the sense of *kṛtvas*—of its *visarjanīya*, [the substitution of *s* occurs]. For if the *visarjanīya* were qualified by the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas*, then [the substitution] would not apply to *caturaḥ*. This he will clarify in the verses.

Thus, according to the opinion of the author of the *Ślokavārttika*, the mention of the suffixes *dvis*, *tris*, and *catur* has been rejected. He cites those very verses beginning with "in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*. For what reason does he state that there is the substitution of *ṣ* in the sense of *kṛtvasuc*; that is to say, what is the purpose of including the mention of the sense of *kṛtvas*? And here, the intention is that which will be stated later. He states the purpose: "in the case of *catuṣkapāla*. The objector reveals his own intention: "But [the form] is established. The word "but" (*nanu*) is used here in the sense of an admission.

Let there be an option (*vibhāṣā*) even in the case of *catuṣkapāla*; nevertheless, the substitution of *ṣ* is established as obligatory. How? When this [rule] is set aside, the substitution of *ṣ* will occur by the rule "and for that which has *i* or *u* as its penultimate" (*idudupadhasya ca*). He provides the answer: "For when this is established" (*siddhe hyayam iti*). The meaning is: "when [the substitution] is already obtained. How is it obtained? He says: "when [the suffix] is elided" (*lupte iti*). When *caturaḥ* is established, the suffix *suc* is elided by the rule "of *s* after *r*" (*rāt sasya*), and the *repha* (visarga) replaces the *r*.

This [final *s*] becomes a *visarjanīya* that is not preceded by a vowel (*apratyaya-visarjanīya*). If the *suC* suffix undergoes *rutva* (the substitution of *r*), and the preceding *r* is elided by the rule "rori" (P. 8.3.14), then the *visarjanīya* of *ru* would result; however, the rule "ḍhralope dīrgho'naḥ" (P. 6.3.111) would require lengthening because the *rutva* is considered asiddha (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule). Furthermore, the elision should have occurred first. Thus, it has been stated that the mention of the sense of "times" (*kṛtvo'rtha*) must be made. Now, relying on that [point], he rejects the inclusion of the words "two," "three," and "four"—saying, "this being so. He asks, "What is to be done? meaning, "nothing at all. How so? He says: "For another... (*anyo hi*).

The author demonstrates the fault that would arise if the mention of "two" (*dvi*) and so forth were omitted: "If [this] were not done," etc. The sense is that the *visarjanīya* would be the qualified element (*viśeṣya*), because of its predominance as the subject of the operation (*kāryin*). The optative (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). [An objection is raised: "Let the *visarjanīya* be the qualified element; what is the harm? To this he replies: "In the case of *caturaḥ*. That is to say: in the manner of qualification just mentioned, the form *caturaḥ* would not be established. Why? He says: "Because of the *repha* (the letter *r*)," etc.

However, if the mention of "twice" (*dvis*) and so forth were made, this fault would not arise; thus he says: "But in that case... Since there is no distinction between the other two [cases], it was stated that the qualifier "four times" (*catur*) is appropriate. The proponent of the rejection (*pratyākhyānavādī*) says: "The word under discussion [is the one intended]. As for what was said—that "the *visarjanīya* is the primary element by virtue of being the recipient of the operation"—that is not correct.

That [rule] also [applies] to the substitution of *ṣ* for the final letter of the word under discussion; however, by implication, it occurs for the *visarga* according to the rule "of the final [letter]" (*alo'ntyasya*). Thus, the word itself is the subject of the operation; this is what is meant by the expression "that which ends in that" (*tadantam*). Regarding the phrase "of that too" (*tasyāpi*), the word *api* is used for emphasis, meaning "of that alone."

When the author of the *Ślokavārttika* has thus rejected the inclusion of the words "twice" (*dvi*) and so forth, the author of the *Vṛtti* says "thus" (*evam*) in order to establish [the necessity of those terms]. He says "by the preceding rule," meaning by the rule "*idudupadhasya ca*" (Pāṇini 8.3.41). [He says] "there would be constant *ṣatva*," for the words *dvis* and *tris* are the scope of this [present rule]. And he says—referring to the principle that "what is taught earlier is not established [for what follows]" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*)—that this very rule does not succeed simply because it is subsequent.

The intention of the author of the *Ślokavārttika*, however, is this: in the context of a specific grammatical topic (*prakaraṇa*), that topic is not established; it is not the case that every individual rule (*yoga*) within it is individually established. Therefore, its lack of establishment follows from that. Alternatively: because the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.41] is introduced as an exception (*apavāda*) to the obligatory substitution of *ṣ*—which would otherwise apply by default to a word ending in *i* or *u* followed by a suffix meaning "times" (*kṛtvas-artha*)—its status as established (*siddhatva*) follows precisely from its being an exception, or else from the authority of the explicit statement itself.

Now, why was it not simply stated as "of *suc*"? What is the purpose of this extensive formulation? If it were stated in that way, the *visarjanīya* would be qualified by *suc*—meaning "the *visarjanīya* which belongs to *suc*"—and consequently, the rule would not apply to the form *catuḥ*. If that is so, then one should say "of that which ends in *suc*"—meaning "the *visarjanīya* of that which ends in *suc*"? Even so, because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word "of a word" (*padasya*), the rule would apply only where a word ending in *suc* occurs—as in *dviṣ karoti*—but it would not apply here in *paramadviṣ karoti*.

That which is a *pada* is not a form ending in *suj*; therefore, because *suc* is not prescribed [as part of it], it is not a *pada*. And that which ends in *suj*, such as *dvir*, is not a *pada*; for, by the rule "and when there is an *uttarapada*, the designation *pada* is prohibited in rules concerning what begins with a *pada*," the technical term *pada* is barred. [This concludes the discussion of] *is* and *us* when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*). (Pāṇini 8.3.44)

"Let it stand," and so forth. Here, the word *sapari* is connected with *tiṣṭhatu*, whereas *piba* is connected with *udakam*; thus, because there is no mutual expectancy (*parasparākāṅkṣā*) between them, there is a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). In this context, "capacity" refers to mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). One should understand that restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is intended here—namely, that it is *only* mutual expectancy [that constitutes capacity]. The purpose [of this distinction] will be explained later. It is not, however, the state of becoming a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*).

In this case as well, a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be understood: that which is grasped is *ekārthībhāva* alone; the meaning is that it is not merely *vyapekṣā*. Now, the word *sāmarthya* is a general term, and a general term does not settle upon a specific instance without [contextual factors] such as the topic (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, how is it said that *sāmarthya* is taken to be *vyapekṣā* alone, and not *ekārthībhāva*; why is both not accepted? To this he says: "Or both. It is certainly not so.

The meaning of "that both are also taken" is that it is certainly not so.
