The underlying intention is as follows: since the technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding semantic competency (*samartha*) is brought to bear precisely because this is a rule governing words (*pada-vidhi*), once semantic competency has already been established, the explicit mention of "semantic competency" again serves to include only that specific kind of competency characterized by mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*); it does not include the other kind, nor both together.
The word *nityam* [is substituted] for [the final *m* of] a word ending in *m* when it occurs in a compound where it does not stand as the final member. 8.3.45.

Regarding the term *parasamarpiṣkuṇḍikā*: one might object that words such as *sarpiḥ* and *yajus* are derived by the rules *arciśucihusṛpicchadicchādibhya isiḥ*, *janerusiḥ*, and *atipayajitanidhanivapibhyo nit*, whereby they are established as ending in the suffixes *is* and *us*. Consequently, by the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the status of ending in *is* or *us* would apply only to *sarpiḥ* and so on themselves, and not to compounds like *paramasarpiḥ*; how then can there be any occasion for this [application of the rule] here? Furthermore, one must necessarily resort to the view that even the *uṇādi* derivatives are derived through grammatical derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*).

For if the position that [the suffix] is non-productive (*avyutpatti*) were adopted, then in cases such as *sarpiṣā* and *yajuṣā*, the change to *ṣ* would not be established, because the *s* is not part of an affix (*apratyaya-sakāratvāt*). Therefore, is the mention of "not being a subsequent word" (*anuttarapada*) useless? To this he says: "This very [is the purpose]," and so forth. He states the purpose of the indication (*jñāpana*) with the words: "By that," etc. Now, why does the option (*vikalpa*) not also apply to a compound (*samāsa*) by means of the preceding rule? To this he says: "And when there is mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*)," etc.

However, some, asserting that there is one rule, *nityaṃ samāse*, and a second rule, *anuttarapadasthasya*, and thus that by means of this division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), all instances of the substitution of *ṣ* in a compound are prohibited when [the word] stands at the end of the second member (*uttarapada*), state that there is no fault even if both types of semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) are resorted to in the preceding case.
Therefore, [the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after the words *kṛ*, *kami*, *kaṃsa*, *kumbha*, *pātra*, *kuśā*, and *karṇī*, when they do not function as indeclinables (*anavyaya*). Pāṇini 8.3.46.

The mention of the verbal roots *kṛ* and *kam* is for the purpose of including the roots themselves; the others are mentioned by their own forms. In the case of *ayaskāra*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. In *ayaskāma*, the suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule *śīlikāmibhakṣyācaribhyo ṇaḥ*; *ayaskaṃsa* and the others are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

The inclusion of *kaṃsa* is redundant, since it is already established by the inclusion of *kami* alone; for the word *kaṃsa* is derived from *kameḥ* itself according to the rule "from *vṛ*, *tṝ*, *vad*, *hani*, and *kami*, [the suffix] *sa*. However, it is for the purpose of providing an indication (*jñāpana*); it indicates that in the *uṇādi* list, the application of grammatical operations based on etymological derivation is not necessarily mandatory. Regarding *ayaskumbhī*: the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *kumbha* by virtue of its denoting a genus (*jāti*). Regarding *ayaspātrī*: the word *pātra* ends in the suffix *ṣṭran*; because it has the marker *ṣit*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. Regarding *ayaskuśā*.

An iron modification (*ayovikāra*) is not intended here; therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.42] *jānapada*. Regarding *ayaskarṇī*: she whose ears are like iron (*aya*) is *ayaskarṇī*; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied here by the rule [Pāṇini 4.1.55] *nāsikodara-*, etc. As for the case of *śunaskarṇa*, however, because the word *karṇī* ending in long *ī* is specified in the sūtra, there is no application of that rule here.

"Bhāḥ-karaṇam" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Regarding "bhāskara," however, the suffix *ṭa* is applied according to the rule beginning with "divāvibhā-. Jayāditya, moreover, stated in that very sūtra: "The substitution of *s* for *k* is prescribed by way of a *nipātana* (irregularity) in connection with the application of the suffix [after the word] 'bhās'. "Śvaḥkāraḥ" and "punaḥkāmaḥ" are compounds formed with words ending in the suffix *dhañ*, according to the class beginning with "mayūravyaṃsaka."
The word *adhas* is substituted for *śiras* when followed by *pade*.

Regarding the phrase "of these two": in the sūtra, however, the nominative case is used in place of the genitive. The term *pada* refers to its own form (*svarūpa*), not to that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); for the latter is already established by the governing rule concerning compounds (*samāsa*). Thus he says: "when the word *pada* follows. It is a compound because it belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. However, in the case of *adhaspada*, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
And [the substitution of *e* for *ai* occurs] in the case of the words beginning with *kaska*. (Pāṇini 8.3.48)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *kupvoḥ ḥkaḥpau ca*. Regarding the phrase "as appropriate" (*yathāyogam*): the meaning of "as appropriate" is that *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) applies to what follows *iṇ*, while *satva* (the substitution of *s*) applies to anything else. In the case of *kaskaḥ*: there is reduplication (*dvirvacanam*) of the stem *kim* when used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). In the case of *kautaskutaḥ*: there is reduplication of the word *kutaḥ* as before; from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tata āgataḥ*; and by the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre ṭilopaḥ*, the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) is elided. In the case of *bhrātuṣputraḥ*: the elision of the *ṣatva* substitute is prevented by the rule *ṛto vidyāyonisambandhebhyaḥ*.

Regarding *śunaskarṇa*: the elision [of the genitive case-ending] is not applied by the rule "the genitive is not elided when expressing an insult" (*ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*). Those who play or deal with the *pārāyaṇa* are called *pārāyaṇikāḥ*. The *pārāyaṇa* is of two kinds: the *dhātupārāyaṇa* (the complete list of verbal roots) and the *nāmapārāyaṇa* (the complete list of nouns). In the Bhāṣya, by the words "in the *vṛtti*" and so forth, he refutes the point just mentioned. By the words "where the technical definition has not been prescribed," etc., he shows that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of examples). The term *upacāra* is a designation for the *s* and *ṣ* sounds that take the place of the *visarjanīya*.
In the Vedic language (chandasi), [the substitution of *ru* for *r*] does not occur before a doubled word (*aprāmreḍitayoḥ*).

Regarding the term *ayaspātram*: this is not a compound. For if it were a compound, the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* and so forth would necessitate the obligatory substitution of *s* [for *t*]; since this optional rule is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to that [obligatory rule], and because this option finds its scope of application only in non-compounds. Alternatively, according to the view that "within a section, a preceding section is *asiddha*," it could serve as an example even for a compound; however, when this [optional rule] is set aside, the obligatory rule applies by force of that [obligatory rule]. Therefore, this is indeed a non-compound. If, however, an option is observed in the case of a compound, that must be explained as being Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Regarding *viśvataspātram*: because this is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* does not apply here. Regarding *uruṇaskāraḥ*: there is the substitution of *nas* for *asmad*, and the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ*. The word *kāra* ends in the suffix *ghañ*; since this is not a compound (*asamāsa*), the [rule concerning *kṛt* suffixes] does not apply here.

In the case of *agniḥ pravidvān*, there is the contingency of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*). However, in the dual sequence (*ubhayakrama*), the mention of the substitute *sakāra* is merely illustrative. As for *paruṣaḥ paruṣaḥ*, this is a reduplication (*dvirvacana*) used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). Forms such as *aṅgamaṅgaṃ paruṣyaru*, *catuṣpaṣpā viśaste*, and others are to be understood from the *kaskādi* group [of words]. We do not see the utility of examples such as *harikeśaḥ purastāt* in this context.

How is it that in this very rule, by the inclusion of the word *vā* ("or"), the presence and absence of both *satva* and *ṣatva* are established? What is the reason for this? It is by the principle: "All grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*)."
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after the verbs *kṛ*, *karati*, *kṛdhi*, and *kṛta*, provided that they do not follow the word *anaditi*.

*kariti*: This is the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *kṛ*. By the rule "in mantras, [the suffix] *cli* is elided after *ghas*" and so forth, there is elision of *cli*; by the rule "elision of *tip* when preceded by *hal* or *aṅ*," there is elision of *tip*; and by the rule "in the Veda, [the augment] *aṭ* is often absent even when not joined with *māṅ*," there is absence of *aṭ*. *karaditi*: This is also the *luṅ* of the root *kṛ*. By the rule "after *kṛ*, *mṛ*, and *dṛh* in the Veda," there is the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli*. *karatīti*: This is the *laṭ* (present). There is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the *śap* suffix. *kṛdhīti*: This is the *loṭ* (imperative) of the root *kṛ*. *Sip* is replaced by *hi*; by the rule "in the Veda, [the suffix] *śap* is often elided," there is elision of *śap*; and by the rule "after *śru*, *śṛ*, *pṝ*, *kṛ*, and *vṛ* in the Veda," there is the substitution of *dhi* for *hi*. *kṛtamiti*: [This is the past passive participle.]

The suffix *kta* is applied only to the root *kṛ*. The mention of the substitution of *s* is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the substitution of *ṣ*. In the case of *viśvataḥ-kara*, because it is not a compound (*avyayatvāt*) and not a *samāsa*, the rule "after *ataḥ* [before] *kṛ*, *ka*, *kami*, etc. does not apply. In the other cases as well, there is no application because they are not compounds. In expressions such as *śannaḥ karat* and *yathā naḥ śreyasaḥ karat*, the absence of the substitution of *s* is due to their being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*).

Likewise, in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], the change to *s* does not occur when the words *sakāra*, *ghakāra*, or *ka* follow [the word *kṛdhi*]: "tanma āmanasaḥ kṛdhi svāhā," "urukṣayāya naḥ kṛdhi ghṛtamanyāsai," and "śaṃ ca naḥ kṛdhi kratve."
The ablative case ending is used after a word in the sense of "beyond" (parāvat) when it denotes a limit.

Regarding the word *adhyarthe*: this is a qualifier used by others [in the sense of "above"]. *Himavataḥ pari* means "above the Himavat"; here, by transposition (*vyatyaya*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*).
In the phrase *paryoja udbhūtam*, the prefix *pari* functions in the sense of "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāve*).
And [the substitution of] *p* for *t* occurs diversely.
In some places it is read that "pātāv" is a citation of the verbal root; others, however, considering the context of the examples, believe it to be an imitation of an imperative form.

In the case of the word *vācaspati* following the genitive [case ending], [the elision of the case-ending] does not occur before *pati*, *putra*, *pṛṣṭha*, *parāpada*, *payas*, and *poṣa*. Thus, [we have] *vācaspatiḥ*; the absence of elision is according to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the suffix *kṛt* is frequently [retained]."
A retroflex (mūrdhanya) substitute occurs for [the dental *s*] at the end of a word (*apada*) when followed by a retroflex sound.

The mention of "mūrdhanya" (the retroflex nasal) is redundant, as the desired form would be established by simply stating "ṣa. To this, he replies: "Even though it is established by [stating] 'ṣa' alone... If only "ṣa" were stated, then the substitution of ṣ would undesirably apply even in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*, whereas the substitution of ḍ is intended there. If, on the other hand, the mention of "mūrdhanya" were made only here [in this rule], then the mention of "ṣa" would have to be repeated in all subsequent rules. However, when the mention of "mūrdhanya" is employed [here], no such fault arises.
For the root *sah*, when it contains the sound *ṣaḍ* (i.e., the sibilant), the substitute *sa* is applied [to the final consonant].

Regarding the term *sāḍrūpasya*: the meaning is "of that which has attained the form *sāṭ*. In the word *jalāṣāṭ*, [the suffix] *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *bhajo ṇviḥ*; the vowel *sa* [in *saha*] is used because of the rule *chandasi sahaḥ*; there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel; the substitution of *ḍha*; the substitutions of *jaśtva* and *cartva*; the lengthening of the preceding member by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*; and the replacement of the *s* by a retroflex *ṣ* (*mūrdhanya*) as the most similar sound.

"What is meant by 'with *sa-*' (*saheti*)? This is a question posed by one who considers the occurrence of the word *sāḍ* impossible elsewhere. "With *ḍa*" (*ḍena*): *aḍa* means "one whose limbs are long" (*vṛścira-kalāṅgala*); his offspring is *sāḍi*. However, regarding the word *sāḍ* [in the rule], since the word *sāḍ* is meaningless there, [the author] considered that [the application of the rule] would not arise and provided a counter-example ending in a *taddhita* suffix. For in that case, once the elision of *yasya* (*yasyetilopaḥ*) has been applied, the word *sāḍ* becomes meaningful. And there is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva* for the elision of *yasya*.

Because of the rule stating, "In regard to what is not established in the preceding [portion], there is no substitution of the original place" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na sthānivata*). Even so, because the substitution of *a* is considered non-established (*asiddha*) by the rule "the rules for *ṣatva* and *tuṅ* are non-established," the form *sāḍ* would not exist. Therefore, the reading should be *saḍ*, meaning "one who exists together with *ḍa*" (*saha ḍena vartate saḍ*). One whose name contains the word *ḍa* is *saḍ*; for example, *mṛḍ*. His descendant is *sāḍi*. [Objection: But even here, since it depends on a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) that is external, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is an external operation (*bahiraṅga*). Where, then, would it apply? [Answer: It applies in the case of *jalāṣāḍ*.

But surely, even here, the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is *bahiraṅga* with respect to the external *ṇvi* suffix? If it occurs there by virtue of a specific rule, it would also apply here—as in *turāsāham*? However, in cases such as *turāsāhaṃ purodhāya*, the suffix *ṇvi* itself is difficult to obtain, let alone the *ṣatva* [substitution].

[The rule] "let it not apply to the letter *ā*" was stated; however, it was not said "let it not apply to the final [letter]," because there is no purpose in pronouncing the letter *ḍ* for the sake of the letter *ḍ*. Now, might this statement be intended to ensure that the substitute is the closest non-palatal (*anantaratama*) retroflex? Even so, by the rule "not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya*), it will not apply to the final [letter]. But even if that is the case, once the rule "of the final [element]" (*alo'ntyasya*) is set aside, would it not follow that the retroflex substitute applies as a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*)? Why, then, was it said "let it not apply to the letter *ā*"? It is replied: by the principle "when there is a modification of a non-final element, [the substitute] takes the place of what stands nearest to the final," the retroflex substitute would apply to the letter *ā*.
[The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] after the verbal root *iṇ* (√i) and after a word ending in *ku*.

The term *iṇ* is a *pratyāhāra* formed with the subsequent *ṇakāra*; *ku* denotes the inclusion of the *kavarga*. In the compound of these two as a collective (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the singular number is used. As for the augment *num*, although the word is neuter, it is not applied, on the principle that "the rules concerning augments are not always mandatory" (*anityam āgama-śāstram*). In the form *vākṣu*, once the substitution of *ku* for *cu* (by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*) has been made, the *sakāra* follows the *kavarga*. The inclusion of the term *varga* [in the rule *coḥ kuḥ*] is for the purpose of including the letter *gha* as well in the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*, as in the form *jakṣatuḥ*.

Otherwise, because the substitution of *car* would be unestablished (*asiddha*), [the desired result] would not occur. Now, if it were argued that the establishment of the *car* substitution is relied upon by virtue of the force of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), then the purpose of including the term "class" (*varga*) must be considered. As in the example: *dāsyati*.

But has it not been stated more than once that in the rule *nājjhalau*, vowels (*ac*) are understood as not including those with which they share the same phonetic quality (*savarṇa*)? Consequently, just as in the case of *kumārī śete*, the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *i* and the sibilant *ś* is not prohibited—and just as this homogeneity is not prohibited there—so too it would be between the vowel *ā* and the sibilant *h*. What follows from this? Since the vowel *ā* would be included by the sibilant *h*, would there not be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]? This is not a fault.

The sound *ha* is open (*vivṛta*), while the sound *ā* is more open (*vivṛtatara*). For thus they recite: "The vowels have an open articulation; among them, *e* and *o* are more open; *ai* and *au* are more open than those; and the sound *ā* is even more open than those, while the sound *u* is closed (*saṃvṛta*). And by adopting this view, the grammatical indications such as in *iṣṭakāsu* and *vayasyāsu* become justified. As for the form *asau*: this is the substituted *s* [from the rules] *adasa au sulopaśca* and *tadoḥ saḥ sau*; it is not, however, followed by the sounds *i* or *ṅ*.
[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs even when there is an intervention by *n*, *visarjanīya*, *ś*, or *r*. 8.3.58.

Because of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the rule *iṇkoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not apply when there is an intervening element; thus, this [new] rule is commenced. The mention of *num* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*, because an intervention by *num* is impossible, given that the *anusvāra* is prescribed by the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali*. However, the term *anusvāra* itself was not used [in the rule], so that the substitution should occur only when there is an intervention by an *anusvāra* standing in the place of *num*, and not in cases such as *puṃsu*; for after the word *pum̐s* followed by the suffix *sup*, the elision of the final consonant cluster (*sayogāntasya lopaḥ*) applies, and the *m* becomes an *anusvāra*. [The example is] *sarpīṣi*.

The augment *num* is applied by the rule "the *jhal* [consonants] of a neuter [stem] take *num*," and the lengthening occurs by the rule "there is lengthening of a final *s* that is part of a *saṃyoga* [consonant cluster] following *mahat*. Regarding *sarpiḥ sva*: in one alternative (*pakṣe*), the visarga is substituted by the rule "optionally before a *śar* [consonant]. Regarding *sarpiṣṣu*: in one alternative, there is the substitution of *s* (by *sasajuṣo ruḥ*); then, because of that very intervention, there is the substitution of *ṣ* (by *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*), and the substitution of *ṣṭu* for the *s*. Since the mention of the letter *s* itself would have sufficed, the use of the *pratyāhāra* term *śar* in the rule is of questionable utility.

In this context, just as when an injunction such as "one must not enter by means of Śūdras" is intended to exclude Śūdras, neither entry individually nor collectively is permitted; likewise, when an injunction is intended to establish that *num* and so forth are causes for the prevention of *ṣatva*, would *ṣatva* apply when there is an intervention either individually or by a group? Since an intervention by all [the letters] is impossible in some cases, while in other cases it occurs individually, and in yet others by two [letters], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṣatva* occurring even when there is an intervention by two [letters]. To address this, he says: "by *num* and so forth."

"Separation by each [element]" (*pratyekaṃ vyavāya*). He thinks as follows: the word *vyavāya* (separation) is connected with each [term], namely, "separated by *num*," "separated by *visarjanīya*," and "separated by *śar*. As was shown at the outset, since the rule *iṇkoḥ* employs an ablative indication (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*) to establish *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) when there is immediate proximity, and since these three sentences permit *ṣatva* only when there is separation by a single element, the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam* (that which cannot be separated by anything else) implies that *ṣatva* does not occur when there is greater separation. Thus, in the example *niṃssaḥ*.

In the case of *niṣi* as a form of *cumbana* (kissing), it belongs to the *adādi* class and is anudātta. *Niḥsva* is [the imperative] *loṭ*; [here] *vām* is substituted for *sva* by the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau*.
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the letter *s* when it follows either a substitute (*ādeśa*) or an affix (*pratyaya*). Pāṇini 8.3.58.

Is this genitive case used in a partitive sense—as in "the *s* which belongs to the substitute" and "the *s* which belongs to the suffix"? Or is it used in apposition—as in "the substitute which is *s*" and "the suffix which is *s*"? Regarding these two views, in the first case, no modification of the number (gender/number) is required for the word *saḥ* as it is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) here; however, there would be no direct connection between the operation and the substitute and the suffix, both of which are explicitly heard [in the rule], because [the genitive] would be serving as a qualifier of the *s*.

In the second [interpretation], however, the dual number in the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ sakārayoḥ* must be modified. Since the connection with the grammatical operation (*kārya*) belongs directly to those two [sounds] as they are heard in the text, there is no logical basis for determining one specific alternative over the other, as both are equally subject to the fault of the wording. In that regard, if it were a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), there would be a fault in the case of reduplication (*dvirvacana*): namely, *visaṃbisam* and *musalammusalam*. If it were a partitive genitive, there would be a fault in the case of reduplication: namely, *visaṃbisam* and *musalammusalam*.

For in the case of the eighth [rule concerning] reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the alternative view that [the reduplication] occurs in place of [the original element] has also been established. Consequently, when the substitute *bisaṃbisam* is applied in place of the single word *visam* by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, there arises the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *ṣatva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*) because the *s* would be considered a part (*avayava*) of that [substitute]. If, on the other hand, the second alternative were adopted, then [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *kariṣyati* and *hariṣyati*; for in these instances, the suffix (*pratyaya*) is the entire complex [ending in *iṣya-*], and not the mere *s*.

Where, then, would it apply? Where there is only the suffix *sakāra*—as in *indro mā vakṣat* and *sa devānyakṣat*. Here, from the roots *vac* and *yaj*, the suffix *leṭ* is applied; then *tip*; then the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*; then the augment *aṭ* by the rule *leṭo’ḍāṭau*; then the suffix *sip* by the rule *sibbahulaṃ leṭi*; then the substitution of *k* for *c* in *vac*, and the substitutions of *ṣ* and *k* for *j* in *yaj*. Now, there are two other alternatives: [the rule applies] either to the *sakāra* which is the substitute (*ādeśa*), or to the *sakāra* which is the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Or is there a reversal—namely, that [the rule applies] to the *sakāra* which is a substitute (*ādeśa*), and to the *sakāra* which is part of an affix (*pratyaya*)? In the first case, those same two faults previously mentioned would apply: the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) in examples such as *bisabisam*, and the lack of application (*aprasaṅga*) in examples such as *kariṣyati*. Therefore, the latter position is adopted; thus he says: "In the expression *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, the genitive case is connected with distinct referents," and so forth.

And here, the proof is that since the author employs the mention of *ghas* in the subsequent rule, it indicates that the genitive case [used for the substitute] is one of coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇā*), not one of different referents (*vyadhikaraṇā*). Otherwise, because *ghas* is already a substitute, the sibilant of that [substitute] would be established as a *ṣ* by this very rule, and its mention would be purposeless. Furthermore, the fact that he teaches the prohibition of *s* in the rule "after *sat*, and at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*) indicates that the genitive case [used for the suffix] is one of part-whole relation (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), not one of coreferentiality.

Otherwise, since a suffix (*pratyaya*) that possesses an *āt* augment would not be a condition for the application of the rule, the substitution of *ṣ* would not occur, and thus the rule would be rendered meaningless. Objection: Is it not the case that in the term *ādeśasya*, the genitive is a "genitive of position" (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the substitution of *ṣ*, whereas in *pratyayasya*, it is a "genitive of part" (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the *s*? Since there is no intention to express them together (*sahavivakṣā*), a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is untenable. Reply: This is not a fault; because of the two previously mentioned indicators (*jñāpaka*), a copulative compound will indeed occur even in the absence of an intention to express them together.

If it is stated that the substitution of *ṣ* applies to a portion of an affix (*pratyayāvayava*), then in cases such as *indro mā vakṣat* and *sa devānyakṣat*, the substitution of *ṣ* would not apply; for here the *s* is the affix itself, and not a portion of an affix? To this, he says: *indro mā vakṣat*, etc. Here, in the case of *aśeḥ saran*—as in *akṣaram*—the substitution of *ṣ* does occur; however, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for that very same [suffix] when prescribed by the rule *kṛdhūmādibhyaḥ kit* (Pāṇini 3.2.161), as in *kṛsaram* and *dhūsaram*.

Likewise, by the rule beginning with "vṛtṝvadī," the [suffix] prescribed occurs in *kakṣam*, but does not occur in *varṣam*; this is because, due to the statement "bahulam" (in various ways), there is an absence of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a suffix (*pratyaya*).
And [the substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs] in the case of the roots *śās*, *vas*, *ghas*, and *sis*. (Pāṇini 8.3.60)

Regarding *anviśiṣat*: by the rule *sartiśāstyartibhyaśca*, *cl* is replaced by *aṅ*; by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*, there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel. Regarding *uṣita*: because the root belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is *samprasāraṇa*; by the rule *vasatikṣudhor iṭ*, the augment *iṭ* is added. Regarding *jakṣatuḥ* and *jakṣuḥ*: by the rule *liṭy anyatarasyām*, the substitute *ghas* is applied to the root *ad*; by the rule *gamahana*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). Regarding *akṣan*: this is the *luṅ* (aorist) of *ad*; by the rule *luṅsanorghaslṛ*, *ghaslṛ* is substituted; and by the rule *mantra ghasa*, etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of *cl*.

In this regard, it is appropriate to state a rule for the sake of providing an alternative form (*anādeśa*) for the roots *śās* and *vas*, but it is inappropriate for *ghas* because it is already an alternative form (*ādeśa*). To this he says: "Even though *ghas* is an alternative form. The meaning of "alternative form" (*ādeśa*) here is that the rule applies to the *s* sound situated within that which is an alternative form. However, the root *ghas* which is not an alternative form is not included here; this is because its usage is rare.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs after a reduplicated syllable only when followed by the roots *stu* or *ṇī*.

"Having become *ṣ*": this means having attained the state of *ṣ*, i.e., when *ṣ*-hood has been effected. "Of the substitute *s*" (*ādeśasakārasya*): the *s* of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not connected [to the rule] because it is impossible [for it to be the subject]. In *suṣvāpayiṣati*: there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule "of *dyuti* and *svāpi*" (*dyutisvāpyoḥ*). In *sisikṣati*: from the root *sic* in the sense of "flowing" (*kṣaraṇe*). In *susūṣate*: from the root *ṣūṅ* in the sense of "the birth of living beings" (*prāṇiprasave*). However, in the reading that prescribes the *parasmaipada* (active voice), it is a form of the root *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*).

If the commencement [of a rule] when something is already established is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), then for what purpose is the particle *eva* used? To this he says: "The employment of the particle *eva*... Now, what is the fault if the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is applied in the reverse manner? To this he says: "In the case of *stauti* and *ṇi*, [the rule *stautiṇyor eva ṣaṇi* would mean that] ṣatva occurs only before *ṣaṇ*; and here [in the rule *syād eva*], [it would mean that ṣatva] occurs only before *syāt*. For by the restriction "only before *ṣaṇ*" (*ṣaṇy eva*), the occurrence of ṣatva for *stauti* and *ṇi* is excluded before other suffixes, but not the occurrence of ṣatva for other roots before *ṣaṇ*. Consequently, the two faults previously mentioned would result.

Regarding the word *siṣeca*: if the term *ṣaṇi* were not stated, the restriction would apply to the suffix alone—namely, that if there is a *ṣ*-sound after the reduplication, it occurs only for the roots *stu* and *ṇī*. Consequently, [the rule] would not apply in cases such as *siṣeca*.

"What is the purpose (*anurodha*) in [mentioning] *vinata*?"—the term *vinata* is well-known in the *Prātiśākhyas* as referring to the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) and *ṇatva* (the change to *ṇ*), as in the rule: "In *vinata*, [there is] *su* and *smi*, provided that *na* does not follow," for example. *Anurodha* means that which is obtained through conformity; it refers to the purpose (*prayojana*). The meaning is: what is the purpose in mentioning [the root] with the *ṣatva* already applied? [The example is] *suṣupsati*. By the rule beginning with *rudavid*, there is the *kittva* of the suffix *san*; by the rule beginning with *vacisvapi*, there is *samprasāraṇa*.

If it were stated simply as *san*, the restriction would apply to the mere root *san*; consequently, just as the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur for another root ending in *s* when it has already become *ṣ*, so too it would not occur here even when it has not yet become *ṣ*. What is the purpose of including the *anubandha* (indicatory letter)? The meaning is: what is the purpose of taking the form that possesses the *anubandha* *n*? He does not ask about the purpose of the substitution of *ṇ*, because that is established by the grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*). [The example is: *suṣupiṣa indram*.

The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix is used for the sense of the root *svap* (to sleep). Because this is Vedic, by the rule "there is extensive transposition" (*vyatyayo bahulam*), the *thās* suffix is substituted; then *se* replaces *thās* by the rule *thāsaḥ seḥ*. Since the *liṭ* suffixes are *kit* by the rule *asaṃyogālliṭ kit*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) as before, followed by reduplication. By the rule governing roots beginning with *krī* (*krādiniyamāt*), the augment *iṭ* is added. When the word *indra* follows, *yā* is substituted [for the *i* of *svapiya*], and the *y* is elided by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya*. In this case, because there is no restrictive rule, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs after the reduplicated syllable. If, however, it were simply stated "ṣ," then the restriction would apply to every instance of the sound *ṣ* whatsoever; therefore, the term is taken together with its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) to specify the particular form.

"What is meant by 'due to repetition' (abhyāsāt)? It means that there should be a restriction regarding the occurrence [of the doubling] due to repetition, so that there might not be a restriction regarding the occurrence [of doubling] due to a prefix (upasarga). As for the example *abhiṣiṣikṣati*, it is irrelevant; why? Because the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* after a prefix is not established (*asiddha*), and because it is not established, the restriction will not apply."

It might be argued: "Just as in the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*, the substitute [of the root] is qualified by the [suffix] *liṭ*, so here too the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) is qualified by the [suffix] *san*; that is, 'only after the reduplication that occurs before *san* [does the substitution apply] to the roots *stu* and *ṇī*. Consequently, even for a different root, the substitution of *ṣ* would occur after the reduplication in the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix—as in *svap*, where the semivowel is vocalized by the rule *svapisyamivyeñāṃ yaṅi*—and then the desiderative *san* is added to *soṣupy* with the augment *iṭ*, followed by the elision of the *a* by *ato lopaḥ* and the elision of the *y* by *yasya halaḥ*, resulting in *soṣupiṣate*. This, then, is the purpose [of the qualification]. This is not correct.

The question is: here, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the restriction (*niyama*) is external (*bahiraṅga*); therefore, the mention of the "reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsa*) is useless. He answers with the example *pratiṣiṣati*. Since the root *iṇ* has the meaning of "informing," there is no substitution of *gam* for it by the rule *ajādeḥ*; thus, the word *si* undergoes reduplication, and by the rule *sanyataḥ*, the vowel *i* is changed to *i*. In that case, once the substitution of *ṣ* for the affix has been applied based on the reduplicated syllable, this restriction [of the rule *sani grahaguhośca*] does not apply, and so the substitution of *ṣ* based on the verbal root (*dhātu*) proceeds for the reduplicated syllable as well.

Now, [one might argue: "The term *ṣaṇi* is a locative denoting what follows (*parasaptamī*); therefore, the restriction that 'the substitution of *ṣ* occurs only before *ṣaṇ* following *stu* and *ṇy*-roots,' being established, excludes the substitution of *ṣ* for the *ṣaṇ* of similar types such as in *sisikṣati*. However, in *pratīṣiṣati*, since the reduplication occurs only within the *san* itself, this restriction will not apply because there is no *ṣaṇ* following it. [If this were so,] then the substitution of *i* by the rule *sanyataḥ* would also fail to apply, because the entire unit has the form of *san* and thus lacks the status of being followed by *san*.

Therefore, in the rules concerning *san*, the locative case (*saptamī*) should be understood as denoting the presence of the suffix; consequently, just as the substitution of *it* takes place, so too would the restriction of *ṣatva* apply—hence the inclusion of the term "repetition" (*abhyāsa*).
The suffix *sa* is applied after the roots *svad*, *iṣ*, and *hi*.

The term *sa* is an indeclinable (without case endings). Regarding the phrase "of those ending in *ṇi*": since the substitution of *s* would otherwise result in the application of *ṣ*, the substitution of *s* is prescribed; and that this applies to those ending in *ṇi* is understood through the force of the context. But for what purpose is the letter *s* stated for the letter *s*? To this he says: "of the letter *s*. Although a simple prohibition (*na*) could have been stated, the mention of the letter *s* is used because there is no difference in brevity [between the two formulations].
Before the suffix *sita*, [the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś*] occurs even when there is an intervention by the augment *aṭ*.

Because of the mention of the ablative case in the rule *iṇkoḥ*, [the augment] would not apply when there is an intervention; hence this statement [is made]. The term *aṭ* refers to the augment (*āgama*), not to the *pratyāhāra*. This has been established under the rule *hayavaraṭ*. Regarding the phrase "prior to the mention of *sita*": this means prior to the rule *parinivibhyaḥ sevasita*. Why is the word *api* included? So that [the augment] may occur even when there is no intervention; otherwise, due to the specific statement [of intervention], it would occur only when there is an intervention. For example: *abhyaṣuṇot*.

In the form *ṣuṇabhiṣeve*, it is the imperfect (*laṅ*); by the rule *svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ*, the suffix *śnu* is applied; the augment *aṭ* is added; and the change to *ṣ* occurs either before the substitution of *yaṇ* or, once the *yaṇ* substitution has been made, by depending on the letter *y* itself as the basis for the change to *ṣ*.
And [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] by practice (*abhyāsa*) in the case of the reduplicated syllables (*sthādi*) of the root *as*. 8.3.64.

These are two statements: (1) "In the case of *sthā* and the others, when there is an intervention by an abhyāsa [element], *tvaṃ* occurs"; and (2) "And the *ṣatva* of the abhyāsa occurs in those very cases, namely *sthā* and the others. Of these, the first is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*), while the second is for the purpose of a restriction (*niyama*). The phrase "for the sake of those not taught with an initial *ṣ*" (*aṣopadeśārtham*) means that if it were taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), then in forms such as *paritiṣṭhāsatī*, the result would be established by the general rule alone. As for *abhiṣiṣeṇayiṣati*: [this is explained accordingly].

In the phrase *senayābhiyātum icchati*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied by the rule *satyāpapāśa-* etc., followed by the elision of the *ṭi* (the long vowel). From that, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added, resulting in reduplication and the shortening of the vowel. Regarding the substitution of *ec* for *ig* in the case of a short vowel substitute, the word *senā* is irregularly derived (*avyutpanna*). Alternatively, *senā* is derived from the root *sah* with the suffix *a*, where the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs by the rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām*. However, when it is derived from the root *si* with the suffix *na*, as in *senā*, then it indeed possesses the status of being a location of the prefix *abhi*. [This explains] the form *abhitaṣṭhau*.

The substitution of *ṣ* for this *s*, which is a substitute [for *ś*], is also not established, because it is neither preceded by *iṇ* nor followed by *ak*. As in *abhiṣiṣikṣati*: although this substitute *s* is indeed preceded by *iṇ*, nevertheless, with respect to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the substitution of *ṣ* is not established, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "only in the case of *stauti* and *ṇi* before the suffix *ṣaṇ*. Therefore, even that substitution of *ṣ* which was prohibited and excluded by the restriction is nonetheless effected by relying upon the prefix (*upasarga*).

Now, for what purpose is the mention of "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*), since in the rule *abhyāsena*, when there is a requirement for an action, the word "separation" (*vyavāya*) is connected by virtue of the context; and since that [separation] is precisely the subject at hand due to its proximity to the word *api*, the substitution of *ṣ* will occur even in the absence of separation, just as in the preceding rule? To this he says: "The statement 'of the reduplication' is for the sake of restriction. He shows the nature of that restriction: "only in the case of [roots beginning with] *sthā* and so on."

The restriction, however, is not reversed—that is, it does not mean "only in the case of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in roots such as *sthā*. If that were the case, the prescription of the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable would be untenable, as in the form *abhisusūṣati*. In *abhisusūṣati*: the root is *ṣū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*); the suffix *san* is added; and by the rule "in *san*, [the augment] *iṭ* is prohibited after *grah* and *guh*" (*sani grahaguhośca*), the augment *iṭ* is barred. Here, the *s* of the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not undergo the substitution of *ṣ* because of the restriction "only after the roots *stu* and *ṇy*" (*stautiṇyoreva*). However, for the *s* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), there is an absence of the substitution of *ṣ* due to this very restriction.

After a prefix, the *ṣ* of the roots *su* (to press), *sū* (to bring forth), *syā* (to lie down), *stu* (to praise), *stobha* (to chant), *sthā* (to stand), *senaya* (denominative from *senā*), *sraṃsa* (to fall), *sras* (to fall), *snañja* (to embrace), and *svañja* (to embrace) is changed to *ṣ*.

*ṣuñ* (in the sense of *abhiṣava*, "pressing") belongs to the *svādi* group; *ṣu* (in the sense of *preraṇa*, "impelling") belongs to the *tudādi* group; *ṣo* (in the sense of *antakarma*, "ending") belongs to the *dvirādi* group—the elision [of the *u*] occurs by the rule *otaḥ śyani*; *ṣṭuñ* (in the sense of *stuti*, "praise") belongs to the *adādi* group; [the *u*] undergoes *vṛddhi* by the rule *uto vṛddhir luki hali*; *ṣṭubh* (in the sense of *stambha*, "obstructing") is *anudātta*. The mention of these roots with the suffix *śtip* is for the purpose of excluding their *yaṅ*-lopa forms—such as *abhisoṣavati* and so forth. [The root] *ṣṭhā* (in the sense of *gatinivṛtti*, "cessation of motion") [is used here]; *senayati* ends in the causative suffix (*ṇic*). There is no need for the mention with the suffix *śap*, because the formation of a *yaṅ* derivative is impossible [for this root].

The roots *ṣidha* in the sense of "motion" (*gatyām*) and *ṣidhū* in the senses of "scriptural authority" (*śāstre*) and "auspiciousness" (*māṅgalye*) belong to the *bhauvādika* (first) class. In that regard, because of the prohibition "the root *sedhati* [does not take ṣatva] when meaning motion," the substitution of *ṣ* occurs elsewhere. The mention with the suffix *śap* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ form, and the mention of "*ṣidhū* in the sense of 'contention' (*saṃrāddhau*)" is for the purpose of excluding the *daivādika* (fourth) class.

The root *ṣic* (meaning "to sprinkle") belongs to the *tudādi* and *mucādi* groups; *ṣañj* (meaning "to attach"); and *ṣvanj* (meaning "to embrace"), which is *anudātta*. By the rule "there is elision of the *n* in *daṃś*, *sañj*, and *svañj* before the suffix *śap*," the *n* is dropped. This [substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs even in the *yaṅ-luk* formation of roots beginning with *ṣiv*, as in *abhiṣeṣicyate*, and so forth. For these roots, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs when there is an intervention by the augment *aṭ*, and also when there is an intervention by the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), as far as possible.

The phrase "of *iṇ* and *ku*" (*iṇkoḥ*) is understood [from the previous rule]. Since the guttural class (*kavarga*) is impossible there, it is connected with *iṇ*. In that context, if *iṇ* were to qualify the prefix (*upasarga*)—that is, if it were interpreted as "after a prefix ending in *iṇ*"—then it would not apply here in cases such as *niṣṣuṇoti* and *duṣṣuṇoti*. Therefore, the prefix must be qualified by *iṇ*: namely, "the *iṇ* of a prefix."

Now, since the word *upasargāt* [in Pāṇini’s rule] is in the ablative case, how can it qualify *iṇ*? We do not say that it qualifies it through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). What then? It is a designation based on location (*tātsthāt tacchabdya*): "the *iṇ* following an *upasarga*," meaning "the *iṇ* situated in an *upasarga*. In that context, because the intervention of a *śar* letter has been accepted, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the following [letter] even after *nis*. This is what was stated: "from a cause situated in an *upasarga*.
In the example *dadhi siñcati*, the prohibition "after *sa-* and at the beginning of a word" (*sātpadādyoḥ*) applies here, for this [rule regarding *upasargas*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that.

Regarding the term *niḥ-secaka*: *nir* is indeed a prefix (*upasarga*). How then can this be a counter-example? To this he says: "In the case of *tāya*, *si* is a prefix. Those particles (*prādayaḥ*) which are connected with an action receive the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) in relation to that [action]. In the case of *abhisāvakīyati*, the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the word *sāvaka*, and then *kyac* is added; its connection is with *abhi*. However, when there is a connection with the root *su* (to press), it certainly does occur: *abhiṣāvakamicchati* becomes *abhiṣāvakīyati*.

In that case, even when the suffix *ṇic* is present, the prefix would not be connected with the meaning of the root (*prakṛti*) but rather with the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij*), such as the act of commanding (*praiṣa*), and thus the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* would not apply. To this he says: "In the case of *abhiṣāvayati*. The meaning is that the application (*prayukti*) has *abhiṣava* (the act of pressing) as its object, and not that the application itself is joined with *abhi*. However, when the application is indeed joined with *abhi*, then the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur at all. But one must consider what kind of connection there could be between *abhi* and a mere application that is not already integrated with the meaning of the root. *Sadir aprateḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.66).

In the word *sadiḥ*, the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*). Regarding *niṣasāda*: because of the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 8.3.116] that "in the case of the *liṭ* [perfect], [the substitution of *ṣa* for *sa*] does not occur after the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of the roots *sad* and *svañj*," the substitution does not take place here.
The substitution of *sta* for the root *stambh* [is applied before the suffix *kta*]. 8.3.67.

*Stanbhi* is a root belonging to the *sautra* class. [The form] *abhiṣṭabhnāti* is derived by adding the *śnā* suffix according to the rule *stunbhu-stunbhu-skanbhu-skunbhu-skuñbhyaḥ śnuś-ca*, and the elision of the nasal [of the root] occurs according to the rule *aniditām*.

The phrase "not after *pra*" does not carry over here. If it were to carry over, one would have included the mention of *stambhi* in the preceding rule itself; what would be the purpose of this separate rule (*yogavibhāga*)? There is a purpose. What is it? He will state later, "after *ava*, when meaning 'support' (*ālambana*) or 'proximity' (*avidūrya*). This is so that [the suffix] may apply to *stambhi*, but not to *sadi*. But this is not the case; even within a single rule, only that which possesses both 'support' and 'proximity' will carry over, and these two conditions are possible only for *stambhi*.
The suffix *ava* is used in the sense of "not speaking" (*avāk*) and "not being distant from an object" (*ālambanāvidūrya*).

*Ālambana* means support. *Vidūra* means distant; that which is other than that is *avidūra*. The state of being that is *āvidūrya*; for this very reason, by virtue of a grammatical exception (*nipātana*), the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is applied even after a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. *Avavaṣṭabhya* means having supported oneself with something such as a staff. *Avaṣṭabdha* means nearby. *Avastabdha* means ignited or set ablaze.
The suffix *kha* is applied after the word *veśa* when it means "eating."

In the examples, [the author] dispels the doubt that one might finish eating merely for the sake of food by abandoning one's own purpose, stating: "it is a specific act of consumption. He demonstrates that very specificity with the words: "wherein," and "gorging. The meaning is that he eats noisily.
The suffix *ṣat* is applied after the roots *sev*, *sit*, *say*, *si*, *vusa*, *saha*, *stu*, and *svañj* when preceded by the prefixes *pari*, *ni*, or *vi*.

The root *sevati* belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and is anudātta (unaccented). *Sita* is the past passive participle (*ktānta*) of the root *ṣiñ* "to bind. *Saya* is the same [root] ending in *ai*; it is derived from *ṣivu* "to weave" belonging to the *divādi* class, or from *ṣaha* "to endure," which is anudātta.

*Suṭ* refers to the inclusion of the rule "the augment *suṭ* comes before the *k*-suffix. The meanings of *stu* and *svañj* have already been stated; since their forms are established by the rule "after a prefix, in *sunoti*, etc.," the present statement is for the purpose of providing an option when preceded by *pari*, etc., in cases where there is no intervention by the vowel *a*, according to the subsequent rule.
Or [the substitution of *ś* for *s*] occurs for the sounds beginning with *śiv*, even when there is an intervening vowel. 8.3.71.

Śiva and the others are understood from the preceding sūtra due to proximity. This is an option (*vibhāṣā*) not previously established: it applies where *stu* and *svañj* would [otherwise] be governed by the rule "before *sit*" (*prāk sitāt*), while for the others, it applies where [the suffix] was not previously applicable.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the root *syand* following the prefixes *anu*, *vi*, *pari*, and *abhi*, when the object is not a living being.

The root *syandū* (to flow) is marked with the anudātta accent. Thus we have *matsyodake anusyandete* ("the fish and the water flow together"). According to the rule *jātir aprāṇinām*, where all constituent words denote non-living beings, there is a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). However, here, because the word *matsya* denotes a living being, the singular collective form does not apply. In this context, the term "non-living beings" (*aprāṇiṣu*) is a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); therefore, even in a collection of both living and non-living things, since a living being is present, the prohibition applies.
Others, however, considering it an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), maintain that the ṣatva substitution must indeed take place here.

In this case, the inclusion of the term *paryādi* could have been omitted; one could have simply stated: "and after *anu* and *abhi*," with the word *ca* ("and") implying "after *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*" as well.
And [the substitution of *ā* for *e* occurs] when followed by another vowel. 8.3.74.

"By virtue of the power of making a separate rule [in the following sūtra]: otherwise, he would have simply said, 'After the roots *skand* preceded by *vi* or *pari*, when followed by a non-*niṣṭhā* suffix'."
The suffix *ni* is always applied after the root *skabh* when preceded by the prefix *vi*.
*Skambhi* is a verbal root belonging to the *sūtra* (or *dhātupāṭha*) class.

*Inaḥ ṣīdhvaṃluṅliṭāṃ dho’ṅgāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.78). By the rule beginning with *iṇantādaṅgāduttareṣām*, it is shown that the *iṇ*-ending stem (*aṅga*) is the qualifier for *ṣīdhvam* and the others, and those [suffixes] in turn are qualifiers for the letter *dh*. However, the *iṇ*-ending stem is not a qualifier for the letter *dh* itself—[the meaning being] "of the *dh* that follows an *iṇ*-ending stem, provided that it belongs to *ṣīdhvam* and so forth. For if that were the case, in forms such as *yoṣiḍhvam*, one would have to resort to the intervention of the word *ṣī* by force of the statement [since the *dh* is not directly after the *iṇ*-stem]. In *acyoḍhvam*, there is the elision of *s* by the rule *dhi ca*.

The inclusion of the term *iṇ* is for the purpose of excluding the *ka*-group (*kavarga*). For the term *iṇ* under discussion is connected with the *ka*-group; thus, when it is carried over [into subsequent rules], that group would also be carried over. In the case of *pakṣīdhvam*, once the substitution of *ku* for *c* (by the rule *co kuḥ*) has been applied, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ḍha*. In the case of *yakṣīdhvam*, once the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule beginning with *vraśca-* has been applied, the substitution of *ka* occurs by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*.

*studhve*: here, *e* replaces *et*. *astudhvam*: this is the *laṅ* [aorist]. *pariveviṣīdhvam*: from the root *viṣlṛ* in the sense of "pervasion," belonging to the *juhotyādi* class and marked with the *svarita* accent; the vowel of the reduplicated syllable undergoes *guṇa* by the rule "there is *guṇa* for the three roots beginning with *ṇi* when there is *ślū*" (Pāṇini 7.4.75); the *sakāra* of the *sīyuṭ* suffix is elided by the rule "the *sakāra* of the *liṅ* is elided, except for the final one" (Pāṇini 6.4.102). Here, the word *ṣīdhvam* consists of the collection of the dental *ṣ* of the verbal root and the word *īdhvam*; however, this [collection] does not follow immediately after the *aṅga* (stem). For in this case, the *aṅga* ends in the dental *ṣ*, and it is not merely the portion *vevī*.

He objects: "Because of the inclusion of that which possesses meaning. He replies: "But this... This inclusion of that which possesses meaning is not relied upon here. What is the reason? For nothing at all; it simply is not relied upon.
The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the root *iṭ* occurs optionally before an affix marked with *ṅ*.

The mention of *iṇ* here is a qualifier for *iṭ*; that [iṭ] is also a qualifier for *ṣīdhvam* and the others, and those [suffixes] are qualifiers for the letter *dh*. Showing this, he says: "after an *iṇ*-ending [root], when *iṭ* follows," and so forth. In that regard, there is a proximity (*ānantarya*) based on direct audition (*śruti*) between *ṣīdhvam* and the *liṭ* [affix], but such proximity created by the technical rules of grammar (*śāstra*) is not possible, because *iṭ* is a part of those [suffixes] and is therefore included by their mention. For this very reason, this is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*) regarding these two.

Similarly, in the case of *luṅ* as well, when *dhi* has been elided in forms such as *alavidhvam*, and the *s* of *sic* remains, the stem (*aṅga*) becomes one ending in *iṇ* before the suffix *dhvam*; thus, there arises the possibility of the application of the preceding obligatory rule.

And thus, when the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not end in *iṇ*, there is the obligatory substitution of *ḍha* in forms such as *aidhiḍhvam* and so on; however, if the substitution of *ḍha* were prescribed for what is formed after a root ending in *iṇ*, then in that case, *adhiḍhvam* would not occur.

Likewise— although the rules for changing *ḍha* to *ḍha*, *gha* to *gha*, and *dha* to *dha* apply to the forms *lihidhvam*, *dogdhvam*, and *hāḍhvam*, the substitution of *ḍha* would still undesirably follow because [the suffix] *sīdhvam* is prescribed after a root ending in *iṇ*.
Likewise, when the substitution of *ga* for *iṇ* is applied in the *luṅ* [aorist] with the suffix *dhvam* in the passive voice—
as in *agādhvam yūyam etena*— the substitution of *ḍha* would undesirably follow.
Likewise, regarding the rule "the root *brū* becomes *vac*", [one might argue] that forms such as *vakṣīdhvam* are desired;
if it is claimed that all this is indeed accepted [as correct], we say no, for there is no authoritative statement here [to support it].
Therefore, it is established that this is everywhere merely an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) based on the authority of the tradition.

And likewise, in the *Taittirīyaka*, the substitution of *ḍha* is employed: "tān rudrā abruvan prayūyam ajaniḍhvam" (the Rudras said to them, "you were born forth"). [Examples include] *laviṣīḍhvam* and *laviṣīdhvam*. However, others—arguing that since the optional application of *iṭ* will be stated later, the term "aṅga" here refers to a stem other than that ending in *iṭ* according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull"—do not accept the substitution of *ḍha* in forms such as *edhidhvam*. For them, the substitution of *ḍha* occurs in *adhiḍhvam*, but it does not occur in *natsīdhvam* and similar forms.

"Āsiṣīdhvam. [The root] *ās* means "to sit. The question is: how should it be? Does this optional rule (*vikalpa*) apply here, or not? This is the meaning of the inquiry. [The form is] *upadidīyadhve*. [The root] *dīṅ* means "to perish"; [the suffix] *liṭ*; [the suffix] *dhvam*; by the rule "krādiniyama," there is *iṭ*; and by the rule "dīṅo yuḍ aci kṅiti," there is *yuṭ*. [The objection: "Because it is separated by *yuṭ*. For *yuṭ*, being a part of the whole [stem], would not separate that very [whole], but it certainly does separate *iṭ*. [The reply: "There should not be *ḍha*-ness."
The meaning is: "by this option. However, by the preceding [rule], it would always apply. Regarding the phrase "of others": in this view, there is indeed an option.
In a compound, the word *aṅguli* undergoes the substitution *saṅgu*. (Pāṇini 8.3.80)

The word *saṅga* is in the nominative case in place of the genitive. The same applies to the subsequent grammatical rules (*yoga*s). *Saṅjana* means "attachment" (*saṅga*), derived with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). That which has attachment to the fingers is *aṅgulisaṅgā*. [This is formed from] *aṅguleḥ saṅgaḥ*. Here, the rule *śarvyavāye* (Pāṇini 8.3.36) provides the occasion for the application. Others, however, cite *aṅgule saṅgaḥ* as an example, treating it as a vocative form.
The word *bhīru* takes the locative case ending [when used as the first member of a compound]. 8.3.81.
"Bhīroḥ sthānam" (the standing place of the timid one). As before, this is either in the vocative case or in the genitive case.

When it is stated that [the suffix *ka*] is applied after "aṅguli" and "bhīru" in the sense of "contact" (*saṅga*) and "standing place" (*sthāna*) within a compound, the addition of the dual ending *bhyām* would result; therefore, there must be a separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*).
The words *agni*, *stut*, *stoma*, and *soma* [are compounded with the word following them]. 8.3.82.

Regarding *agniṣṭut*: the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *sampad*. Thus, that sacrifice in which Agni is praised is the specific rite called *agniṣṭut*. In this regard, it is stated: "Or rather, among all the words for deities, one should join [the name] specifically to Agni. Regarding *agniṣṭoma*: there are seven terminuses (*saṃsthā*) of the Soma sacrifice; here, the first terminus is being discussed. Regarding "after a long [vowel] of *agni*": the meaning is that the *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣ*) occurs in a *devatā-dvandva* (compound of deity names), since the rule for the long vowel is prescribed only in that context.

Regarding the phrase "Agni and Soma, the two boys" (*agnisomau māṇavakau*), here there is an absence of the long *ṣatva* (the retroflex sibilant) because the word *māṇavaka* is employed as a proper name (*saṃjñā*). However, in the case of "Agni and Soma stand" (*agnisomau tiṣṭhataḥ*), Āśvalāyana nevertheless applied the long *ṣatva*, stating: "I shall lead forward Agni and Soma" (*agnīṣomau praṇeṣyāmi*).
The *jyotis*, *āyus*, and *stoma* [are used in the sense of "consisting of" or "characterized by"]. 8.3.83.
In the word *jyotiṣṭoma*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because of the governing rule *śarvyavāye*. The same applies to *āyuṣṭoma* as well.
The suffix *cha* (forming *īya*) is optionally applied after the words *mātṛ* and *pitṛ* when they are followed by the word *anya*.

Because that which is modified in one part is not considered different [from the original], and because the governing rule "when there is an intervention by *visarjanīya* or a sibilant (*śar*)" applies, the [substitution] would be obligatory by the preceding rule; therefore, this is an optional rule. Thus, in the case of *mātuḥ svasā*, the sixth-case elision (*aluk*) does not occur due to the rule "optionally so in the case of *svasṛ* and *pati*."

"This refers to the two [words] ending in *repha*. That is clear in the case of the *uttarapada*; by association with that, the *pūrvapada* must also end in *repha*. If this were so, then when the *visarjanīya* is substituted for the *repha*, and the optional *satva* (substitution of *s*) is applied by the rule "vā śari," the suffix would not apply because it no longer ends in *repha*. To this he says: "Because that which has undergone a partial modification is not different [from the original]. However, if the inclusion were made of those ending in *sakāra*, it would not apply to those ending in *visarjanīya*.
But if the inclusion were made of those ending in *visarjanīya*, the mention of the form following *bhyām* would be difficult to justify.
The suffix *naṅ* is applied after the root *ni-ṣad-* when followed by the word *śabda*.

"Because [the word] *abhinis* is derived from this [root]"—by this he shows that the aggregate is the cause, not each individual part. "The *visarjanīya* is called *abhiniṣṭāna*. And so Āpastamba says: "A name consisting of two or four syllables, with a verb as the latter member, ending in a long vowel or in *abhiniṣṭhāna*, beginning with a sonant consonant, and having a semivowel in the middle."

A name consisting of two or four syllables should be given. Of what kind? It should have a noun as its first member—that is, a nominal stem expressing a non-verbal concept as the prior member—and a verb as its latter member—that is, a verbal form expressing an action as the subsequent member. According to others, it should end in a long vowel or a *visarjanīya* (the *abhiniṣṭāna* following a long vowel). Furthermore, it should be such that a sonant consonant (*goṣavat*) begins it—meaning it has a voiced consonant at the start—and it should have a semivowel (*antarastha*, i.e., *y*, *r*, *l*, or *v*) in its middle; a name of this description should be made. Examples include *Draviṇodā* and *Varivodā*.
After the prepositions *upa* and *prādur*, as well as after *asti*, the suffix *ac* is applied [to form a noun] when followed by *ari*.

And those two [roots] *yac* and *añc*, when they follow after something, that is "yacpara" (followed by *yac*). Although the rule is established simply by the mention of the locative case in "after *yac*" (*yacoḥ*), the inclusion of the word "following" (*para*) has a purpose that requires consideration. [The example is] *abhiṣanti*. Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision of *śap*; [then] by the rule "elision of *a* in *śn* and *as*" (*śnasorallopaḥ*), the *a* is elided.

Regarding the word *anusṛtam*: how, then, is there a point of contention here, given that since the letter *s* is the subject under discussion, the status of being a prefix (*upasarga*) will be applied to it alone? Yet, the status of being a prefix does not apply to the letter *s* here, because that much alone does not denote an action (*akriyāvacanatvāt*); so what is the purpose of including the mention of the root *as*? Nor was the mention of *as* made for the sake of the word *prāduḥ*, because its application is restricted to the domain of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. Thus, he raises this very doubt with the words *tathāpi*.

The word *anu* belongs to the *śubhra*-class; others say it denotes "that which has four feet. From that [base], either the suffix *ṭhak* or *ṭhañ* is applied. Since the vowel *u* is elided by the rule "*ḍhe lopo 'kadr̥vāḥ*," there arises the contingency of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*, because only the letter *s* remains as the expressive element of the action.
The suffixes *su*, *vin*, *ni*, and *dur* are applied after verbal roots ending in *sū* and *sūti*. (Pāṇini 8.3.88)

The *i* in *supi* is an adventitious (*āgantuka*) element; it is not, however, the actual letter *i* that is being indicated. In that case, by the rule *vacisvapi...* which prescribes *samprasāraṇa*, this would have to be an indication of the verbal root itself after *samprasāraṇa* has occurred. Consequently, the meaning—that the substitution of *ṣ* applies wherever this specific form exists—would not be obtained. Therefore, the form used here is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form found in actual usage where *samprasāraṇa* has already taken place, by means of an adventitious *i*. Thus he says: "In *supi*, the root *svap* is understood as having undergone *samprasāraṇa*."
And this is obtained precisely from the instruction "supi"; otherwise, he would have instructed it as "vacisvapi," for example.

Regarding the phrase "sūtī," it is a reference to the word-form itself; the meaning is that there is a reference to the root *sū* ending in the suffix *ktin*. Likewise, "sameti" is also a reference to the word-form itself, not a reference to the verbal root "ṣama ṣṭama vaiklavye," because [that root] lacks either the suffix *ik* or *śit*.

Now, why is it that the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *svap* is prescribed when it follows the prefix *su-*? [The purpose is: let the *ṣ*-substitution apply to *sup-* (the desiderative form), but not to *svap* (the simple root). Since the *ṣ*-substitution is prescribed for *sup-*, let it not apply to *svap*—as in *visvapnaḥ* and *visvapnam*. [And likewise: *visuṣvāpa*.

Now, even though the term *vikṛta* (modified) is employed [in the rule], for what reason does the substitution of *ṣ* not occur for the reduplication in *visuṣvāpa*, as in the question "by what did he cause to sleep"? Since the semivowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is effected by the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām*, the form *supi* exists prior to the application of *halādiśeṣa*; or, even if that [substitution] has already occurred, because a modified part is not distinct from the original, the contingency [for the rule] remains. [However,] due to *halādiśeṣa*, it is no longer *supi*.

When reduplication has been performed, because it is subsequent, the *yakāra* is eliminated by the rule "the remainder is the first consonant" (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*); thereafter, the *vakāra* undergoes *samprasāraṇa*. Consequently, since the form *supi* never occurs at all, there is an absence of *ṣatva*. Thus, the *samprasāraṇa* is desired to take place first.

The purpose of including both [the *samprasāraṇa* and the *halādiśeṣa*] therein has been stated: so that even by overriding the subsequent *halādiśeṣa*, the *samprasāraṇa* of both may indeed take place; therefore, the *samprasāraṇa* alone is intended to occur first, and this is especially intended here. Otherwise, just as the letter *ṣ* would be eliminated, the letter *v* would also be eliminated. For there is no reason here why the *ṣ* should be eliminated while the *v* remains.

If that is the case, would not the substitution of *ṣ* not occur here simply because of the restriction "the substitution of *ṣ* for the reduplication occurs only in the case of *sthā* and so on"? The restriction regarding *sthā* and so on does not apply here. What is the reason? [Because] it follows after *su-pi*. The term "prior to *sita*" (*prāk-sitāt*) is understood there; therefore, by the restriction "the substitution of *ṣ* for the reduplication occurs only in the case of *sthā* and so on" among those roots prior to *sita*, only *sunoti*, *suvati*, *syati*, and *stobhati* are excluded. However, this [root *sup*] follows after that limit (*avadhi*).

In that case, the rule "when there is the mention of a meaningful element, that which is meaningless [is not included]" would not apply here. For while the whole is meaningful by virtue of reduplication in place [of the original], the two constituent parts are meaningless. Since the communication of meaning does not repeat itself when there is a double application, the meaning is conveyed by both [parts together]; thus, one part is indeed meaningless. To this he says: "In the case of the meaningless, as in *viṣuṣupuḥ*. If there were no mention of the meaningless, forms such as *viṣuṣupuḥ* would not be established? This is not a fault.

The word *suṣi* is stated twice. This is the intended meaning: first the verbal root is joined with the prefix; there, because it is subsequent, the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs, and for that very reason of being subsequent, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs; and it is only after the substitution of *ṣ* has been effected that the reduplication takes place. But surely, since the substitution of *ṣ* is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*), the reduplication should apply first? To this he says: "That which is unestablished in what precedes does not [apply] to reduplication."
The suffix *kha* is added after the roots *snā* (to bathe) following the words *ni* and *nadī*, when skillfulness is meant.

"Skilled in making bracelets"—in this context, the meaning is "proficient. "River-skilled" (*nadīṣṇa*) means "proficient in bathing in the river. Poets, however, employ the term in the sense of proficiency in general. "Bathed in the river" (*nadīsnāta*): the compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) regarding the locative case (*saptamī*).
The word *sūtra* takes the suffix *niṣṭhā*. (Pāṇini 8.3.90)
Although it could have been stated as "sūtraṃ prateḥ," the recourse to a technical irregularity (nipātana) is made so that [the suffix] does not occur with other suffixes.
*Kāpiṣṭhala* [is used] in the sense of a lineage (*gotra*). 8.3.91.

In this context, "gotra" is understood as that which is recited in the *Pravarādhyāya*; therein, the first male ancestor who serves as the cause for the designation of one's own lineage is called "gotra. If, however, it were taken in its technical (paribhāṣika) sense, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *kāpiṣṭhali*, where there is an affix denoting a gotra.

But if "gotra" is not indicated by the scope of the rule regarding the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*), what then? It means that the word *kapiṣṭhala* which is seen in the gotra according to the usage (*darśana*) is correct; where? It is accepted that it is wherever [it occurs]. Thus, there is no fault even if it is taken in the technical sense of gotra.
The word *praṣṭha* is used in the sense of "one who goes at the front. (Pāṇini 8.3.92)

Regarding the phrase "on the plateau of the Himalayas": the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the locative case by virtue of the governing rule "the application of *ka* in the sense of the *ghañ*-suffix."
The word *viṣṭara* is used for a tree and for a seat. || 8.3.93 ||

It is called *viṣṭara* because it is spread out (*vistīryate*). Although the suffix *ghañ* would have been expected by the rule "the suffix *ghañ* occurs after [roots] ending in *ava* when the sense is 'spreading out'," the form is derived with the suffix *ap* due to this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or alternatively, by deriving it from the root *pac* etc. with the suffix *ac*, since it is a conventional term (*ruḍhi-śabda*). A commentary composed by Ulapa is the *Aulapī*; that is the expansion (*vistara*) of the sentence, because of the prohibition [of the suffix *ghañ*] by the rule "not when the word ends in *aśabda*."
And [the substitution of *ṣa* for *sa* occurs] when the word *chandas* follows. (Pāṇini 8.3.94)

"It is *viṣṭāra* that is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*). But surely *viṣṭara* was the subject under discussion; so how can *viṣṭāra* be prescribed? To this he says: "from [the root] preceded by *vi-*. If, however, the substitution of *ā* for *i* were made here to form *viṣṭāra* as the name of a meter (*chandas*), then the rule "and in the name of a meter" (*chandonāmni ca*) could have been omitted from the prescription of the suffix *ghañ*; or else, one might say "viṣṭāra" here, or "in the name of a meter" there—what indeed would be the difference? Another says: the phrase "or in the case of *ghañ*" (*ghañi vā*) does not carry over [into this context]; therefore, forms such as *prastārapaṅktiḥ* and *saṃstārapaṅktiḥ* also occur."
The word *sthira* [is compounded] with *go* and *yudhi*. Pāṇini 2.1.59.

*Gaviṣṭhiraḥ*, *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*: this is a locative compound (*saptamīsamāsa*) by the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*). [The suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied] after the word *go*, even though it ends in a consonant. Although it becomes consonant-ending once the substitution of *ava* for *avaḥ* has been made, nevertheless, because it does not end in a consonant at the time of its formation, the use of a nipātana (irregularity) is resorted to.
After the prefixes vi, ku, śami, and pari, [the suffix ka is applied] to the word sthala.

The words *vi*, *ku*, and *pari* form a compound with [the following word] according to the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*; however, the word *śamīśa* forms a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasorbahulam*. By the explicit mention of the short vowel in the sūtra, the substitution of *ṣ* (ṣatva) is intended to apply only in the case of the short vowel. Consequently, in actual usage, when the shortening does not occur due to the force of the term *bahulam*, the substitution of *ṣ* likewise does not occur.

The suffix *stha* is applied after the words *ambā*, *amba*, *go*, *bhūmi*, *savya*, *ap*, *dvi*, *tri*, *kusa*, *kuśa*, *ṅu*, *vaṅgu*, *mañji*, *puñji*, *parame-barhis*, *divi*, and *agni*. (Pāṇini 8.3.97)

Regarding the phrase "of the *s* of the word *stha*": by this, he shows that in the rule *stha*, the term is taken as its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*) and ends in the nominative case. However, if there were a reference in the genitive case after applying the elision of the vowel *ā* from the root *tiṣṭhati* according to the rule *āto dhātoḥ*, then the substitution of *ṣ* would undesirably occur even in cases such as *gosthānam* and *bhūmisthānam*. [The example] *ambaṣṭhaḥ* means "one who stands near his mother" (*ambe tiṣṭhati*). The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*, and the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ*. Thus, it is *āmbaṣṭhaḥ*.

This is a conventional name for a particular region. Regarding *goṣṭha*: the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the locative (*ghañ-artha*) according to the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*. In *bhūmiṣṭha* and similar forms, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ*. Regarding *savyeṣṭha*: the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending occurs according to the rule *haladantāt saptamyāḥ*.

If the term *sthaḥ* were taken as the citation of its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*), it would not apply to *sthā*, *sthin*, and *sthaṇ*. Therefore, he says: *sthā-sthin-*. The word *sthā* ends in the *kvip* suffix. In the case of *savyeṣṭhā*, the substitution of *ī* (by Pāṇini 6.4.19) does not occur by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule, because of the statement: "There is a prohibition of the [substitution of] *v* when *ī* is substituted. While the rule *gameḥ iniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.168) is in effect, the suffix *ini* is added with the *kit* designation by the rule *parame sthaḥ kicca* (Pāṇini 3.2.175); thus the word *parameṣṭhī* ends in the suffix *i*. Due to the diversity of grammatical usage (*bāhulaka*), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. He who stands on the left (*savye tiṣṭhati*) is the *savyeṣṭhā*, the charioteer.
And [the substitution of *su* for *su-*, as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.3.107, does not occur] in the group of words beginning with *suṣāmā*. (8.3.98)

In some cases, where the prohibition "sātpadādyoḥ" would otherwise apply, and in other cases where the substitution of *ṣ* would not apply at all from the outset, the cerebral (*mūrdhanya*) is prescribed for the group beginning with *su-śāman* (the *suṣāmādi* class). For example, in *duṣṣāma*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs because of the governing rule "even when there is intervention by a *visarjanīya* or a sibilant. Regarding the phrase "of the word *su*" and so forth, the connection here is as follows: since the words *su* and *duḥ* refer to specific actions and thus do not function as prepositions (*upasarga*), the prohibition [of the cerebral] applies; this reading, therefore, is *duḥṣedha*.

In that context, the term *su* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule "suḥ pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 1.4.94), and this designation supersedes the designation of *upasarga*, because of the governing authority extending up to the end of the section on *ākaḍāra*. Similarly, *niḥ* and *dur* also lack the status of *upasarga*, as they relate to different actions—namely, *niḥ* in the sense of "gone out from" as in *niḥṣedhaḥ* ("one who has gone out from a prohibition"), and *dur* in the sense of "difficult to go toward" as in *duṣṣedhaḥ* ("difficult to prohibit"). Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not apply to these cases under rules such as "upasargāt sunoti... (Pāṇini 8.3.65).

Thus far, it has been stated on the assumption that the form *sedha* is derived from the root *ṣidhū* (meaning "to injure" and "to accomplish") with the suffix *ghañ*. However, when it is the form of the root *ṣidha* (meaning "to go") ending in *ghañ*, he says [the following]: "And for the purpose of subverting the prohibition regarding *seghati* in the sense of 'going'. In words such as *suṣandhi*, the suffix *ki* is applied by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*, and the change to *ṣ* occurs for *sam*. Regarding these two [words] among the *uṇādi* derivatives: while the rule *pṝbhidivyadhidhṛṣibhyaḥ kuḥ* is in effect, the suffix *ku* is applied by the rule *apaduḥsupusthaḥ*.

*Gauriṣaktha*: [The suffix] *ṣac* is applied by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, after *sakthi* and *akṣi*. *Pratiṣṇākā*: From the root *snā-* preceded by *prati-*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "Also after [a root ending in] *ā* when a prefix is present"; from that [stem ending in *aṅ*], the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added; then, in the sense of "unknown" and so forth, the suffix *ka* is applied; by the rule "When *ka* follows, there is shortening," the vowel is shortened; and by the rule "From a letter standing before a suffix," the *ā* is changed to *ī*. *Nauṣecanam*: [The suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied to the root *sic-*. *Dundubhiṣevaṇam*: [The suffix] *lyuṭ* is applied to either the root *sev-* or *sīv-*.

The *gaṇasūtra* states: "In this [list of] names, [the suffix -a] is applied after [a word ending in -i]. He explains it thus: "after that which follows the vowel *e*.
