For example: *hariṣeṇaḥ*, meaning "one whose army consists of monkeys" (*harayaḥ senā asya*). *Pariṣeṇaḥ*, meaning "one who has an army all around" (*paritaḥ senā asya*). *Pṛthvīsenāḥ*, meaning "one whose army is vast" (*pṛthvī senā yasya*). In these cases, the first member of the compound undergoes the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) according to the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat*.

Regarding the phrase "or after *nakṣatra*": since the previous rule would have made the application obligatory, this provides an option. The particle *ca* serves to include other unmentioned items and indicates that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words). Thus he says: "where no specific grammatical rule has been prescribed."
Before a taddhita suffix beginning with *t* and preceded by a short vowel, [the final *s* of a word ending in *as* or *is* is replaced by *r*]. Pāṇini 8.3.99.

Since the rule *apadāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.59) governs the present context, the state of being a *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) is not otherwise obtained and is therefore prescribed here. He states *taraptamap* because these are precisely the *taddhita* suffixes that are possible [in this context]. In *sarpiṣṭaram*: although there is no excellence (*prakarṣa*) in the genus (*jāti*) "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*), the suffix is applied to the excellence of its concomitant quality (*guṇa*), such as its fragrance. In *catuṣṭaye*: [this is derived from *catur*] by the rule *jasaḥ śī*. In *sarpiṣṭaḥ*: the suffix *tasi* is used after the ablative case in each instance of usage. In *āviṣṭya*:
in the rule *avyayāttyap*, the suffix *tyap* is applied after the word *āvis* because of the specific mention of the Vedic language (*chandasi*).

"‘Sarpis-sāt’—[this is an example of] ‘vibhāṣā sātiḥ kārtsnye’. Now, one might object: since there is a prohibition by the rule ‘sātpadādyoḥ’, the substitution of *ṣ* will not occur here anyway? To this he says: ‘of the *s* of an affix. [Examples: *bhindyustarām*, *chandyustarām*. From the roots *bhid* and *chid*, there is the *liṅ* suffix; for the *jhi* ending, there is *jus*; then *yāsuṭ*; then by ‘tiṅaśca’, the suffix *tarap*; and finally, by ‘kimettiṅavyayaghāt’, the suffix *ām*. The mention of ‘ādi’ (beginning) could have been omitted; for by simply saying ‘ti’, [the rule] ‘yasminvidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe’ would suffice. [Counter-examples: *puṃsaḥ* (prohibition), *puṃstvam*, *puṃstā*.
The suffix *kta* is used after the roots *ni-sad* and *tapa* when they do not denote habitual action.

"‘The *rakṣas* is scorched; the enemies are scorched’—this is the [objection] here. Even so, a resolution is stated based on finding a reading in a certain recensional branch (*śākhā*). However, the Taittirīyakas read only the *ṣatva* [substitution].
The *t* of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* becomes *ṭ* when followed by *tat*, provided it occurs within a word (*pāda*). 8.3.101.

In *tatakṣuḥ* (RV 7.56.20), the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* following the imitation of the word ending in *ṣ* (*svit*) occurs by the rule *num-visarjanīya-śar-vyavāye 'pi*. Regarding the phrase "in words beginning with *t*": this is a qualification of *yuṣmad* alone, because [the rules] do not deviate from it in the case of the other two [pronouns]. Examples such as *tvam*, *tvā*, and so forth, mean that these alone are possible [cases].

As for "Agni said that again," the word *agniḥ* is at the end of the preceding quarter-verse—[namely] in *yan ma ātmano mindābhūd agniḥ* (RV 10.164.3); therefore, this *s* is at the end of a quarter-verse, not in the middle of a quarter-verse.
In the Vedic language, the substitution of *ṣṭun* for *stut* and *stoma* occurs [before a word beginning with a vowel]. Pāṇini 8.3.103.

The point is that [the rule] is already established by the phrase *pūrvapadāt* alone; for there, the term *pūrvapada* is understood in its general sense and not merely as a constituent of a compound. Thus, the substitution of *ṣ* is established by that very rule even in a sentence. Consequently, the mention of *stuta-stoma* is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtha*). However, the mention of *chandas* must certainly be made for the sake of what follows.
[The suffix *ṣat* is applied] after a word ending in a *pūrva-pada*. (Pāṇini 8.3.104)
Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of a compound": this is understood precisely from the recitation of forms such as *savane-savane* in the *Savanādi* list.
[The suffix *śūna* is applied] after [the verbal root √śvi]. 8.3.105.

Regarding the word *abhīṣuṇa*: there is lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *ikaḥ suñiḥ*, and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by the rule *naśca dhātusthoruṣubhyaḥ*. However, this is sometimes read directly within the commentary (*vṛtti*) itself.
The suffix *an* is applied after the root *san*. (Pāṇini 8.3.106)

Regarding *goṣā*: [the suffix] *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhanakramagamo viṭ*; then [the vowel is changed] by *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*. However, this [suffix] is also found in some instances in the *Vṛtti* itself. Regarding *gosanim*: the suffix *in* is applied by the rule *chandasi vanasanarakṣimathām*. Regarding *sisānayiṣati*: although the root ending in *aṇ* (*san*) is mentioned in the sūtra, nevertheless, since there is no purpose in stating a prohibition for that which ends in *aṇ*, it is understood as having the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*). But here, in the case of *sisanīyati*, there is no occurrence of *ṣatva* because of the restriction [contained in the rule] *stautiṇyoreva ṣaṇi*. Regarding *sisanīḥ*.

When *kvip* is elided, then *su* is added; following the rule *halṅyādi-lopaḥ*, the *s* of *san* undergoes both *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) and *rutva* (the substitution of *r*). Since *ṣatva* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) for the purposes of *rutva*, the *rutva* occurs first. Then, by the rule *rvor upadhāyā dīrghaḥ*, lengthening of the penultimate vowel takes place. In this case, since *san* has not yet become *ṣatva*-substituted, it does not fall within the scope of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) *stautiṇyoreva*; thus, *ṣatva* would have been applicable, but it does not occur due to this restriction. However, when this purpose [of the restriction] is present, because there is a lack of capacity [for the restriction to apply] to the causative form (*ṇyanta*), as there is no restriction on the causative, *ṣatva* certainly occurs, as in *siṣāṇayiṣati*.
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *sah* when preceded by *pṛtanā* or *ṛta*.

Regarding the phrase "the division of the rule" (*yogavibhāgam*): therein, the second rule (*yoga*) is for the purpose of making known that the preceding rule does not have universal application (*asarvaviṣayatva*). As for the phrase "only in *saṃhitā*": since the heading governing *saṃhitā* applies to both [rules], this specific qualification is obtained; thus, by the rule beginning with *na-hi-vṛti-vṛṣa*, lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occurs.
[Now follows: *Na rapara-sṛpi-sṛji-spṛśi-spṛhi-savana-ādīnām* (Pāṇini 8.3.108).

Regarding *visraṃsikāyāḥ*: the suffix *ṇvul* is applied by the rule *rogākhyāyām*. Regarding *visrabdham*: the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *sṛmbhu* (meaning "to trust") by the rule *sṛmbhu viśvāse*; the prohibition of *iṭ* is by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, and the elision of the nasal (*n*) is by the rule *aniditām*. Regarding *visṛpa*: the suffix *kasun* is applied to the roots *sṛp* and *tṛd*. In expressions such as *savane-savane*, there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) to indicate repetition (*vīpsā*). As for *kiṃsa*: since there is a rule stating that "for the *ayogavāha* sounds, when followed by vowels (*aṭ*), there is the status of *suṇ*; and among the *śar* sounds, there is the substitution of *jaś* and *ṣatva*," there arises the contingency of *ṣatva* because of the intervention of a *śar* sound. However, it has been explained in the section on *hayavaraṭ* how the teaching of *śa* and *ṣa* need not be performed [in this context].

Is the inclusion of the term *aśvasani* useless because it does not end in the suffix *ṇic*? To this he says: "The inclusion of *aśvasani*. He states the purpose of this indication: namely, the form *jalāṣāham*.
The substitution of *s* for *ś* occurs before a word-initial *t* or *th*, as well as before the suffixes *sat* and *pad*.

The inclusion of the word "ādi" (beginning) need not be made; rather, the ablative designation "padāt" (from a word) should be formulated as follows: "the [substitution] of *s* following a word is not [to be applied]. If this were so, then it would not apply here either: in *agniṣu*, *vāyuṣu*, and *tvakṣu*. However, the prohibition regarding the suffix *su* makes it known that the prohibition does not apply to a word that begins with *su*. In that case, this further purpose is achieved: the prohibition is established in examples such as *dadhisik* and *madhusig*, for this *s* is not the beginning of a word.

According to the rule, "There is a statement regarding the compounding of roots with *gati*, *kāraka*, and *upapada* [elements] prior to the arising of case-endings (*sup*)," [the suffix] occurs after the word; even so, it is because the preceding member ends in a case-ending (*subanta*). However, there is a prohibition for *bahuc*. A prohibition must be stated for *bahuc* when it follows [another element]: as in *bahusektā*; for here, the *sakāra* is not after a word [ending in a case-ending].
The suffix *ya* is also applied after [a verbal root ending in] *sic*. (Pāṇini 8.3.110)

Regarding the form *pariseṣicyate*: here, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the reduplicative syllable is obtained by the rule *upasargātsunoti* etc., while the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root is obtained because it is a substitute *s*, by the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena ca*. Now, one might object: since the substitution of *ṣ* after a prefix is introduced precisely in cases where [the general rule] is prohibited, just as it sets aside the prohibition regarding word-initial *s*, would it not likewise set aside the rule *sico yaṅi*? To this he says: "The application [of the rule] that arises from a prefix... [and so on].

In that case, there is no sublation of what has not yet arrived; for while the prohibition characterized by "beginning with a word" (*padādi*) has not yet arrived, the rule for the substitution of *ṣ* after a prefix (*upasarga*) is initiated, whereas the rule "after *sic* before *yaṅ*" applies both when [the prohibition] has arrived and when it has not yet arrived. Alternatively, according to the principle: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) stated earlier sublate only those rules immediately following them, not those further ahead."

By this, the following objection is also refuted: "Just as in the case of *abhiṣiṣikṣati*, where the rule *stautiṇyoreva* (Pāṇini 8.3.61) is set aside by the rule *sthādiṣvabhyāsena ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.64) so that the substitution of *ṣ* occurs, likewise, this prohibition [of *ṣ*] would be set aside, resulting in the occurrence of *ṣ* for the *s* of the verbal root (*dhātu*)."
The suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *sidh* when it means "motion."
The application [of the rule] resulting from the phrase "after a prefix" (upasargāt) is prohibited.
And [the suffix -ta is applied] to the roots *prati-stambh* and *ni-stambh*. (Pāṇini 8.3.112)
The [grammatical] acquisition resulting from the rule "stanbheḥ" is hereby prohibited.
The [suffix] *soḍha* [is applied after a verbal root denoting a day of the week]. || 8.3.113 ||

"It is grasped as having arisen" (soḍbhūtaḥ) removes the suspicion that the word ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix is being indicated by the nominative case. "Completely dried up" (pariśoṣa) is a prohibition [of the *ṣatva*] which would otherwise apply according to the rule "after *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*."
The substitution of *śnā* for the root-vowel occurs before the suffix *caṅ* after the roots *stambh*, *siv*, and *sah*.

In this context, the application of *stambheḥ* occurs for the first [verb], while for the other two, it is by the rule *parinivibhyaḥ sevasita*. Regarding *abhyatastambhat*, the application is by the rules *prāksitādaḍvyavāye’pi* and *sthādiṣvabhyāsena ca*. Regarding *paryasīṣivat*, here too the application is by the rule *sivādīnāṃ vāḍvyavāye’pi*.
"It should be stated that [the rule applies] after a prefix. For what purpose? He says: "The attainment [of the suffix] which occurs after a prefix."
The augment *iṭ* is not applied after the root *śru* when followed by the suffixes *syat* (the future marker) or *san* (the desiderative marker).

Regarding the passage beginning with *atretyādi*: the particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetau*). Because of the restriction that [the substitution of *ṣ*] applies only to the roots *stu* and *ṇi*, there is no application [of the rule] after an *abhyāsa* (reduplication); and because of the restriction that [the substitution of *ṣ*] applies only to [roots] such as *rath*, there is no application even after a prefix (*upasarga*). Therefore, they cite *abhisusūḥ* as an example. Alternatively, how could there be the contingency of the substitution of *ṣ*? To this he says: *atra hi*. This is just as explained here regarding *sanṣa-* etc. [The phrase] "attainment from the *abhyāsa*" refers to the following.

The inclusion of the term *abhyāsa* (reduplication) is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of [the rule] applying to a prefix (*upasarga*), since such an occurrence is impossible. Consequently, there is no possibility of the application of the rule to the *s* of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when it is separated by the reduplication, nor to the *s* of the reduplication itself, because that has already been excluded by the restriction regarding roots beginning with *sthā*. Thus, in this context, the mention of *abhi* is not essential; one should have cited *susū* as the example.
The substitution of *sa* for the final consonant of the roots *sad* and *svañj* occurs before the *liṭ* suffix.

When reduplication (*dvirvacana*) has occurred in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, there are two *s* sounds. In that case, because of the rule "in the case of *sthā* and others, as well as with the reduplicated syllable" (*sthādiṣv abhyāsena ca*), there arises the contingency of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) by the rule "after *saḍ*, except after *prati*" (*sadir aprateḥ*). The same applies to *svañj*, by the rule beginning with "after a prefix, before *sunoti*" (*upasargāt sunoti*). Thus we have *pariṣasvaje*. But how is there elision of *n* (*nalopa*) here, given that the *liṭ* suffix does not possess the *kittva* (the property of causing elision) because the word ends in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogānta*)? To this he says: "of *svañj*."

And this has been explained under the rule *indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca*; furthermore, the inclusion of the root *svañj* was interpolated into the sūtra because it is seen in the Vārttika, as it says: "When there is a prohibition regarding the *liṭ* [perfect] for the root *sad*, the addition of *svañj* must be stated."
In the Vedic language, the augment *aṭ* may optionally be inserted after the prefixes *ni*, *vi*, and *abhi* when they are not separated from the following verbal root by any intervening sound.

In this context, there is a prohibition of the mere existence [of the vowel] that would otherwise apply. Regarding the example *nyaṣṭaut*: the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs by the rule "lengthening occurs for *u* before a consonant when *luk* follows"; *abhyasthād viṣaḥ pṛtanā arātīḥ* is also an example.
Thus ends the third quarter of the eighth chapter in the *Padamañjarī* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra. [The Kāśikāvṛtti—
6] Now begins the fourth quarter of the eighth chapter.
After *ra* and *ṣa*, *ṇa* is substituted for *na* within the same word (*samānapada*).

In the substitution of the two *nimitta*s (causes), the letter *c* is for the sake of pronunciation. "The same word" (*samānapada*) means that which is common to both; this is a designation of the locus for both the cause (*nimitta*) and the thing caused (*nimittin*). Thus he says: "if they reside in the same word. The word "same" (*samāna*) is a synonym for "one" (*eka*). The *nimitta* is the letters *r* or *ṣ*, and the *nimittin* is the letter *n*. Although the latter has its own established form even prior [to the rule], nevertheless, there is indeed a connection between it and that which serves as the cause for the letter *ṇ* occurring in its place. Alternatively, the letter *ṇ* itself is the *nimittin*, but its status of residing in the same word occurs subsequent to its prescription.

"The mention of *ṣ* is for the sake of what follows. He will state that there is *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so forth; [this mention of *ṣ*] is so that this rule may apply even in such cases. Now, why does it not also serve the purpose of the present case? To this he says: "This is already established by the rule regarding *ṣṭu*."

"It should be stated that [the rule applies] after a vowel containing *ṛ* (*ṛvarṇa*). Since the substitution of *ṇ* is prescribed after *ra* and *ṣa*, it would not apply after the vowel *ṛ*. Nor can it be argued that it will occur from the *repha* (the sound *r*) situated within the *ṛ*-vowel; for in this sūtra, what is taken up is the phoneme (*varṇa*) *repha*, due to its association with *ṣa*. Furthermore, parts of a phoneme are not grasped by the mention of the whole phoneme. As in the case of *tisṛṇām*: because of the prohibition "not in *tisṛ* or *catasṛ*" (*na tisṛcatasṛ*), there is an absence of lengthening by the rule "before *nām*" (*nāmi*).

If so, then that must be stated? No, he says: "It is established by the mention of the commonality of the *ra*-sound. *Ra*-sound is the auditory perception—that is, apprehension by the sense of hearing—of which two; those two are the individual instances (*vyakti*) consisting of the phoneme *ra* and the instance not consisting of a phoneme. That which is their commonality (*sāmānya*) is what is being indicated; the meaning is that it is not only the instance consisting of the phoneme that is intended.

But even so, in the case of the phoneme *ṛ*, there are three parts: vowel-portions (*aj-bhakti*) on both sides and a *repha*-portion in the middle consisting of one-quarter of a *mātrā*. Consequently, because of the intervention by the subsequent vowel-portion, [the rule] would not apply? It will apply by virtue of the expression "even when there is an intervening *aṭ*. The subsequent vowel-portion is not included within the *aṭ* category; for that [subsequent portion] is half a *mātrā* and consists of one-quarter of a *mātrā*, being a portion of the *ṛ*-phoneme. Furthermore, it is not grasped either by the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) nor by the inclusion of *aṭ* sounds.

Because it is not of the same class (*asavarṇatvāt*); for it has neither a distinct place of articulation nor a distinct effort. Therefore, even though there is a general reference [to the *ṇatva* rule], the substitution of *ṇ* is not established; hence he says: "and because of its being a portion of the phoneme" (*varṇabhaktyācca*). This means: by that subsequent portion which constitutes a part of the aggregate phoneme. Now, one might object: "The mention of *nṛnamana* would be for the sake of *vṛddhi*—[as in] 'the descendant of *nṛnamana* is *nārnamaniḥ'*"? This is not so; for *vṛddhi* is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), whereas *ṇatva* is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), according to the principle: "That which is extrinsic is considered non-existent with respect to that which is intrinsic."

The phrase "or rather" (*atha vā*) means that there is a fault even if the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is specified. Another way [to resolve this] is as follows: the two *aj-bhaktis* on either side consist of four parts (*catur-bhāga*), while the pure *repha* in the middle consists of half a measure (*ardha-mātrā*). Therefore, the meaning is that there is no fault even if the individual phoneme is specified. [Objection: But is there not an intervention by the subsequent *aj-bhakti*? [Response: In that case, a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) will be made in the following sūtra: “even when there is an intervention” (*vyavāye 'pi*). Thus, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even when there is an intervention; thereafter, the rule “by *aṭ*, *ku*, *pu*, *āṅ*, and *num*” (*aṭ-kupvāṅ-numbhiḥ*) applies.

What is the purpose of this [rule] now? It is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*): namely, that if the substitution occurs when there is an intervention by phonemes (*varṇa*), it occurs only when the intervention is by *aṭ* and so forth. Since the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "the retroflex [substitute] for what is not at the end of a word" (*apadāntasya mūrdhanyaḥ*) applies here, the mention of *ṇ* could have been omitted; furthermore, in the subsequent rule, there is a prohibition regarding "that which is at the end of a word" (*padāntasya*).
Even when there is an intervention by the letters *a*, *ṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, or *num*, [the substitution of *anusvāra* for *n* occurs]. Pāṇini 8.4.2.

Because of the mention of the ablative case in the rule *raṣābhyām*, [the substitution] would not apply when there is an intervention; therefore, this [sūtra] is commenced. Regarding *paryāṇaddham*: the root *ṇaha* means "to bind"; with *pari* and *āṅ* as prefixes, it takes the suffix *niṣṭhā*; and by the rule *naho dhaḥ*, the *h* is replaced by *dh*.

But surely, since the substitution of *ṇ* is already established here by the rule "aḍ-vyavāye" (Pāṇini 8.4.2), for what purpose is the mention of *āṅ*? To this he says: "It is already established by 'aḍ-vyavāye' alone. However, in some places, it is stated that the mention of *āṅ* is for the purpose of overriding the rule "padavyavāye'pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.37). Regarding the word *bṛṃhaṇam*: from the root *bṛhi* in the sense of "growth," the augment *num* is applied because it is marked with *i* (by Pāṇini 7.1.58), and the anusvāra is applied by the rule "naścāpadāntasya jhali" (Pāṇini 8.3.24).

If this is so, why is there not an intervention here by the *anusvāra* rather than by the *num*? To this he says: "The mention of *num* is for the purpose of indicating (*upalakṣaṇa*) the *anusvāra*. Because the *anusvāra* is prescribed in place of the *num* that follows a *jhal* consonant, the *anusvāra* is indicated by its original form (*sthānin*), the *num*. Even so, the rule would not apply in the case of an intervention by an *anusvāra* that is not in the place of *num*, as in *tṛṃhaṇam* from the roots *tṛṃha* and *stṛṃha*, which mean "to injure"? To this he says: "By that" (*tena*).

In this case, the *anusvāra* that stands in the place of *num* is not what is intended; rather, it is *anusvāra* in general. Therefore, the meaning is that the rule applies here as well. One might ask: "In cases where there is the actual hearing of *num* itself and not of *anusvāra*, does the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) occur or not? To this, he says: "Even though... (*satyapi ca*).

Just as in the injunction, "Having seen a star, one should release speech," which aims to indicate a specific time, speech is not released even when stars are seen during the day because the time indicated by them is absent; yet it is released at night even when no stars are seen because that time is present—so too should it be understood here. Regarding the word *prenvana*: since the root *ivi* means "to please" (*prīṇana*), the rule *idito num* applies, and here there arises the contingency of *ṇatva* by the rule *ijādeḥ sanumaḥ*.

In this context, the completion of a sentence is observed to occur with respect to a collective group, as in: "The Gargas shall be fined one hundred [pieces of gold]. Kings, being desirous of wealth, do not fine each individual member of the group separately. Conversely, completion is also observed with respect to each individual, as in: "The designations *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* apply to each [of the vowels] individually. In this matter, if the first alternative (the collective sense) were adopted, the rule would never apply, for an intervention by all the letters beginning with *aḍ* is nowhere possible. However, in the second case (the distributive sense), it would not apply in instances such as *arheṇa*.

[This occurs] also because of intervention by the *ka*-class consonants. Therefore, he says: "because [the mention of *aṭ*] is for the purpose of indicating intervention (*vyavāya-upalakṣaṇārthatvāt*). In this context, when certain things are employed as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), that which is indicated by one, two, or even many of them is included. For example, when it is said, "One should not eat with the Gargas," one does not eat with them individually, nor with them collectively; likewise here, since *aṭ* and the others are capable of indicating intervention whether combined or separate, the rule applies in all cases.

Regarding the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so forth, there is a prohibition when there is an intervention by anything else—e.g., in *ādarśena* and *sparśena*. Even though here there is also an intervention by something other than *aṭ*, since there is an intervention by *aṭ*, the *ṇatva* based on that would apply. But in cases where the intervention is by those [letters] not specifically mentioned, it would not occur—such as in *kṛtsnam* and *mṛdhnoti*? This is not a fault; [The reason is: The intervention by *aṭ* and so forth is intended to be a condition (*nimitta*) for the application of *ṇatva*; therefore, even if there is an intervention by others, the *ṇatva* still takes place because the intervention by *aṭ* exists. However, in cases like *kṛtsnam* and *mṛdhnoti*, where the intervention is by letters not specified [in the rule], the *ṇatva* does not occur. Thus, there is no inconsistency.

In the rule *raṣābhyām*, because the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) *tasmāt* presents itself, there would be no occurrence of *ṇatva* when there is an intervention [of other sounds]. Therefore, this sūtra, being commenced, permits *ṇatva* only when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and so forth, and not by any other intervention; for that [possibility] has been set aside by the mention of *nirdiṣṭa*. Moreover, if *ṇatva* were to occur even when there is an intervention by sounds other than those specifically mentioned (*nirdiṣṭa*), then the mention of *num* would be purposeless; since an intervention by *num* alone is impossible.

A guttural (ga) following a word-final consonant at the end of a prior member [of a compound] becomes a velar (ka) before a following *saṃjñā* (proper name), except when the following word is *go*. Pāṇini 8.4.3.

The phrase "after *ra* and *ṣ*" (from Pāṇini 8.3.15) continues [in this rule]. Since it is impossible for those two (*ra* and *ṣ*) themselves to be the prior member of a compound, by implication the meaning is understood as "following a cause situated in the prior member"; thus he says: "situated in the prior member. This does not mean "from a prior member ending in *repha* (*ra*) or *ṣakāra* (*ṣa*)," because that is not the intended interpretation according to the commentary. Regarding *drauṇasa*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose nose is like a tree" (*drur-iva nāsikā yasya*). By the rule "for *nāsikā* [the suffix] *añ* [is applied]" (Pāṇini 5.4.118), the suffix *añ* is added and *naś* is substituted [for *nāsikā*]. Regarding *vārdhrīṇasa*.

The word *vārdhrī* is a derivative meaning "made from the hide of a castrated goat" (*vadhrī*), thus referring to a rope. A *vārdhrīṇasa* is a specific kind of deer whose nose is like that rope. In this compound, because the first member resides in the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it is in a different grammatical case (*vyadhikaraṇa*); therefore, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Alternatively, the word *nas* should be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *priya*. Regarding the form *śūrpaṇakhā*, there is a prohibition [of the masculine substitution] by the rule: "In the case of a proper name (*saṃjñā*), [the masculine is not substituted] after words ending in *nakha* or *mukha*. However, when the actual connection [of the parts] is intended rather than a proper name—meaning "she whose nails are shaped like winnowing baskets" (*śūrpākārāṇi nakhāni yasyāḥ*)—[the masculine substitution does apply].

In that case, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs, but the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not—thus we have *śūrpanakhī*. Consequently, the substitution of *ṇ* and the suffix *ṅīṣ* do not apply simultaneously—as in the phrase "from that speech of Śūrpanakhī. It might be argued that the word "agaḥ" (not a mountain) could be omitted [from the rule]. Why does it not occur in the case of *ṛgayanam*, meaning "the study (*ayana*) of the *ṛc*s"? This is established by an irregular derivation (*nipātana*), according to the rule "after words other than *ṛgayanam* and so forth. As it has been stated elsewhere: "In the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of 'pronominal' (*sarvanāman*), the absence of the substitution of *ṇ* is due to irregular derivation."

The rule "only when [the word] follows a preceding member [of a compound] and [the whole] is a name" means that the restriction is not the reverse—namely, that it applies only when following a preceding member and only when it is a name—because the word *suṣeṇa* is listed among the *śiva*-group. Since a rule is formulated even when [the desired form] is already established in order to establish a restriction, [the author] asks: "How is this established here? and replies: "For even within a single word... and so forth.

Although there is indeed the condition of being situated in different words—since the cause (*nimitta*) resides in the prior member (*pūrvapada*) while the effect (*nimittin*) resides in the subsequent member (*uttarapada*)—nevertheless, once the compound (*samāsa*) has been formed, a case-ending (*vibhakti*) arises from it; when, by that [ending], the designation "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) is applied to the whole aggregate, then even though they are in the same word, the application [of the rule] occurs because of its presence therein. For in that case, "being in the same word" (*samānapadatva*) is what is relied upon, not the prohibition of "being in different words. Therefore, its status as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*) is established.

If this is so, just as the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* situated in a subsequent word is invariably excluded—as in *carmanāsika*—so too would it be excluded when situated in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) that serves as a prior member: for example, the descendant of *Kharapa* [is formed] by the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* as *Khārapāyaṇa*; that which is beneficial for *Mātṛbhoga* [is formed] by the rule *bhogottarapadātkhaḥ* as *Mātṛbhogīṇa*; and one for whom an instrument (*karaṇa*) is dear is *Karaṇapriya*. To this, he says: "And that... (*sa ca*).

A relative term necessarily brings to mind its correlative; for example, in the injunctions "one should behave properly toward one's mother" and "one should serve one's father," it is not explicitly stated, "toward one's own mother" or "toward one's own father. Nevertheless, by virtue of the relationship, this is understood: that [behavior] is toward whoever is one's mother, and service is toward whoever is one's father.

The terms *pūrvapada* (prior member) and *uttarapada* (subsequent member) are relative terms: the subsequent member exists in relation to the prior member, and the prior member exists in relation to the subsequent member. From this relationship, it must be understood that the rule applies to that which stands in the position of the [term] toward which something is called the "prior member. And toward what does this [designation] occur? Toward the subsequent member.

In that case, this would be the fault: the prohibition of the very restriction (*niyama*) "not after *g*" (*agaḥ*) would result, because [the word *agaḥ*] forms a single syntactical unit with it, rather than a prohibition of *ṇatva* itself. Consequently, *ṇatva* would still apply in a name (*saṃjñā*) where there is another *g*. To this he says: "not after *g*" (*aga iti*). This prohibition "not after *g*" (*agaḥ*) pertains to *ṇatva*, not to the restriction. The reason for this is: "by means of a split of the rule" (*yogavibhāgena*). "After a preceding member, when it is a name" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*) is one rule, and "not after *g*" (*agaḥ*) is the second.
By this [second rule], whatever application of *ṇatva* might occur—whether by way of the first rule or otherwise—is entirely prohibited, due to the force of the split of the rule.

"But others," and so forth. How, then, is the restrictive sense "only" (*evā*) obtained in the phrase "only the same"? To this he says: "Because of the mention of 'the same' (*samāna*). It would have sufficed simply to say "in a word" (*pade*); however, since it is impossible for a cause and its effect to reside in two separate words, the mention of "word" is understood to intend singularity. This being already established, the purpose of explicitly stating "the same" is so that it may be understood: "that which is a word, and only the same [word]."

To those who speak thus, he says "of them" (*teṣām*) to indicate that this is understood for the purpose of a rule (*vidhyartha*). He establishes that very fact of being for the purpose of a rule with the words "for in a compound" (*samāse hi*). Now, in this view, how is there *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in the word *khārapāyaṇa*, given that in the word *kharapa*, the word *khara* also possesses the status of a *pada*, and because of its location therein, the *repha* (the letter *r*) does not reside in the same *pada*? This is not a fault.

Where both the cause (nimitta) and the effect (nimittin) deviate from being situated in the same word, there is an absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*; however, in this case, although the *r* deviates, the substitution of *ṇ* still takes place because the *n* does not deviate from being situated in the same word.
The word *vana* ("forest") is substituted for *puragā*, *miśrakā*, *asidhrakā*, *śārikā*, *koṭara*, and *agra*. (Pāṇini 8.4.4)

In the word *vanam*, the nominative case is used in place of the genitive. In the example, the lengthening of the first member of the compound is governed by the rule *vanagiryoḥ saṃjñāyām*. Thus we have *agrevaṇam*. In this genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the word *vana* is placed last according to the group beginning with *rājadanta* (Pāṇini 2.2.31); furthermore, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending because of the rule *haladantāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.9). Alternatively, if it is not a proper name (*saṃjñā*), then the absence of elision is due to its inclusion in the *rājadantādi* group.

Regarding the phrase "siddhe sati" and so forth: this [rule] is stated for the sake of *puragā* and the others; however, they say that in the case of the word *agra*, it is for the purpose of prescribing [the substitution] when it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). The rule "from these [words] alone, [there is substitution] of the letter *n* in *vana*" does not mean "only from these [words] is there substitution of the *n* in *vana*"; for this is because of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the recitation. For that long vowel would serve as a restriction [implying] that this rule applies only to those ending in a long vowel. And since it is impossible for these words to end in a long vowel in any other *uttarapada* (subsequent member) than *vana*—wherein their *ṇatva* (nasalization) might otherwise be excluded—it follows that the long vowel serves to restrict the scope of the rule.
The suffix *añ* is applied after the words *śara*, *ikṣu*, *plakṣa*, *āmra*, *kārsmarya*, *khadira*, and *pīyūkṣā*, even when not forming a proper name (*asaṃjñāyām api*). || 8.4.5 ||

In this context, the rule for the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is prescribed where it would otherwise not have applied in the first three cases—namely, regarding both names (*saṃjñā*) and non-names (*asaṃjñā*). How so? First, with regard to names: although the rule "after a preceding member [ending in a vowel], when a name follows" (*pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), it may also serve as an injunctive rule (*vidhyartha*). In either case, the rule "the *n* of *vana*, *puragā*, etc. (*vanaṃ puragā-*) must necessarily be a restrictive rule, meaning that the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *vana* occurs only after words such as *puragā*. Consequently, there is no application of the rule in the case of prefixes (*prādi*). Furthermore, even regarding non-names, there is no application under a restrictive interpretation; for the restriction is that the substitution occurs only when a name follows.

Even in the case of the suffix *vidha*, since it is prescribed only for the purpose of forming a name (*saṃjñā*), there is no application of it elsewhere. However, in the case of words such as *śara* and others—which denote medicinal herbs or trees—the present rule sets aside the optional alternative that would otherwise apply by the subsequent sūtra, whether the word is a name or not. If the phrase "even when not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām api*) were not stated, then because of the governing heading "when it is a name" (*saṃjñāyām*), the suffix would apply only in that context. Would the heading "when it is a name" then be discontinued? If it were discontinued, the suffix would not apply to names at all; for there is a restrictive rule stating that the substitution of *van* for the syllable *na* occurs only after words beginning with *puraga*.

But this rule has scope when it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). Even in the case of a technical name, because this rule is subsequent, it will prevail; for "when a preceding operation is not established, there is no conflict" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe nāsti vipratiṣedhaḥ*). Therefore, it must be stated that [the rule applies] even when it is not a technical name: *pravaṇam*, *nirvaṇam*—these are *prādi*-compounds (*prādisamāsa*). *Antarvaṇam* is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) in the sense of a case ending. *Śaravaṇa* and others are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The suffix *vibhāṣā* is applied after the words *oṣadhi* and *vanaspati*.

The phrase "even in the case of asaṃjñā" (asaṃjñāyām api) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]; therefore, this option applies to both *saṃjñā* and *asaṃjñā*. Others, however, do not accept that as a governing heading (*adhikāra*) because it is not explicitly stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*); according to them, in the domain of *saṃjñā*, the rule "from *puraga* and so forth" (*puragādibhyaḥ*) must function as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). If, on the other hand, this [option] is desired, another effort [to establish its governing status] must be undertaken.

In this context, those which both flower and bear fruit are called *vānaspatya*; those which bear fruit but do not flower are called *vanaspati*; and those that are both are designated as *vṛkṣa* by those who know the terminology. Consequently, if the substitution of *ṇ* were made optionally based on the employment of the word *vanaspati*, it would apply only in cases such as *śirīṣavaṇam*, for *śirīṣa* and similar trees both flower and bear fruit. Therefore, the term *vṛkṣa* must be included; this is the objection being raised.

"Phalī vanaspatiḥ," and so forth. A *vanaspati* is that which bears fruit but not flowers, such as the *udumbara* tree; those that bear flowers are *vetasa* and others; those that bear fruit are *udumbara* and others; and trees like the mango (*āmra*) are those that bear both. The suffix *ḍa* is applied here because of the rule in the *Antātyantādi-sūtra*: "The suffix *ḍa* is seen elsewhere as well."

Those plants (*oṣadhi*) which perish through the ripening of their fruit—such as *śāli* rice and others; those possessing spreading creepers (*latā-pratānavat*), such as jasmine (*mālatī*) and others; shrubs (*gulma*), which are trees with short trunks; and climbing plants (*vīrudh*), which have many stems and leaves—even though a distinction between a tree (*vṛkṣa*) and a forest-tree (*vanaspati*) is recorded in traditional law (*smṛti*), he removes this doubt by stating that here they should be understood without such a distinction. And in this regard, the statement of the author of the *Bhāṣya* concerning the rule "in the case of elision [of a suffix], the gender and number are like those of what is joined" (*lupi yuktavad-vyaktivacane*) serves as the authority.

For it is said there: "What is meant by 'denoting an individual' (*vyaktivacana*)? [Consider] a village located near *śirīṣa* trees called *śirīṣāḥ*; its forest is *śirīṣavanam*. In this case, the status of being a *vanaspati* (tree) is not extended [to the forest]. If it were so extended, then by the rule *vibhāṣauṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ*, the application of the *ṇatva* suffix would result. And if the aforementioned distinction were adopted here, then because the *śirīṣa* trees themselves are not *vanaspatis*, the resulting application of both the status of being a *vanaspati* and the *ṇatva* suffix would be untenable.
The suffix *ṭu* is applied after the word *ahan*, provided it ends in a short vowel.

Regarding *pūrvāhṇa*: the compound is formed by the rule *pūrvāparā-* etc., meaning "the former part of the day" (*ahnaḥ pūrvo bhāgaḥ*). By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac*, the suffix *ṭac* is applied, and by the rule *ahno'hna etebhyaḥ*, the substitute *ahn* is substituted for *ahan*. Regarding *nirahna*: this is a *prādi*-compound meaning "gone out of the day" (*nirgato'hnaḥ*); the remainder is as before. Regarding *dīrghāhnī śarat*: this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, therefore the suffix *ṭac* does not occur; for the application of *ṭac* is governed by the heading on *tatpuruṣa* compounds. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ana upadhālopino'nyatarasyām*, and [the final *a*] is elided by *allopo'naḥ*.

Because [the word] ending in *akāra* is what is being referred to here, the substitution of *ṇa* does not occur. However, if this were a genitive indication (*ṣaṣṭhī-nirdeśa*) of the letter *na*, then the substitution of *ṇa* would occur here as well. But that it refers to what ends in *akāra* is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*). In every such context, the original base (*sthānin*) is indicated by the nominative case—as in *vanaṃ*, *vāhanaṃ*, and *yānaṃ*. Alternatively, its lack of the *ṇa*-substitution follows from its inclusion among the *yuvan*-class words. Furthermore, its inclusion in the *yuvan*-class must necessarily be performed.

The mention of "the end" (*anta*) [in the rule *prātipadikānta*] is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that in this section, the designation of being "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply even to a single phoneme (*varṇa*) without a specific effort. Consequently, in the rule *raṣābhyām*, the designation of being "ending in that" does not occur.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after a word denoting a vehicle when it expresses the act of placing [something] upon it. || 8.4.8 ||

*Vāhana* means "that by which something is carried," such as a cart and the like; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate syllable occurs due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*). That which is placed or loaded upon is called *āhita*. When [the object] is external and not actually loaded, but merely present nearby, the rule would not apply; however, it is desired even in that case. As it has been said: "It should be stated that [the term applies] to both 'placed' (*āhita*) and 'present' (*upasthita*)."

Or rather, it is not so, because the past tense is not intended to be expressed. Since the injunction is focused on the cessation of the relationship of ownership (*svāmibhāvanivṛtti*), the past tense in the word *āhitam* is not intended; therefore, [the form] will apply both to one who has already established the fire (*āhitāt*) and to one who is about to establish it (*ādhāyiṣyamāṇāt*). It occurs only when there is no intention to express the relationship of owner and owned, as stated in the counter-example: "the meaning is 'owned by Dākṣi'. Even in the case of [patronymics] such as *Dākṣya*, when they are intended to be expressed as external objects (*bāhyatvena*) and not as owners, the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* certainly takes place.
The suffix *pāna* is used in the sense of "place" [to form a name]. 8.4.9.

"Those for whom milk is the drink"—here the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Words such as *Uśīnara* and others denote persons by way of their [native] region; thus, they are designations of regions.
In the expression "the drink of the Dākṣiṇātyas," the word *pāna* likewise functions solely as a passive derivative (*karmasādhana*).
Or [the suffix *kṛt*] is used in the sense of the agent (*bhāvaka*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*). Pāṇini 8.4.10.

Regarding the phrase "of mountain rivers and so forth": they say that this is a *vibhāṣā* (optional rule) applicable in both cases—since [the suffix] would apply when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), but would not apply when it is not a proper name.
And [the substitution of *n* for *m* occurs] before the final vowel of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), before the suffix *num*, and before case endings (*vibhakti*).

Regarding "māṣavāpiṇau": the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "bahulam ābhīkṣṇye" (Pāṇini 3.2.81). Regarding "māṣavāpāṇi": [the derivation is as follows: from "māṣān vapanti," the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "karmaṇy aṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1); then "jaśśasoḥ śi" (Pāṇini 7.1.20) applies; and finally, the augment *num* is added by the rule "napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.72).

Why does this not occur here: *gargāṇāṃ bhaginī* (the sister of the Gargas), resulting in *gargabhaginī*? Is there not the application [of the rule], since the final sound of the nominal stem *bhaginī* is the letter *n*? To this he says: "Because of the governing heading of *pūrvapada*" (the preceding word). This has already been explained under the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām*. Does it therefore never occur as *gargabhagiṇī*? It occurs when there is a different intention, according to another grammatical system (*śāstra*), but not according to this one. To this he says: "But when... [and] "like *mātṛbhogīṇa*. This too has been explained in that very same place.

If "uttarapada" (the final member) is understood as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then in the case of *māṣavāpiṇī*, the substitution of *ṇ* would not apply; for the word *vāpinī*, which is the final member, does not end in *n*, and that which ends in *n*, namely *vāpin*, is not the final member. Therefore, he says: "*māṣavāpiṇī*" and so forth. This has already been explained under the rule "upapadam atiṅ. To provide the justification for the statement "the nominal stem that constitutes the final member is taken," he says: "and likewise."

How is this an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? He says: "For that... (*sa hi*). The *num* augment is prescribed for the *aṅga* (the base); consequently, the *num* which is subordinate to it (*tadbhakta*) is included by the mention of that [base] itself, and not by the mention of the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*). If any nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whatsoever were to be understood rather than specifically the subsequent member, then the mention of *num* would be entirely unnecessary; for [the desired form] would already be established by the rule "at the end of a compound nominal stem" (*samāsaprātipadikānta*).

Regarding *āryayūnā*: this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan* when a non-taddhita suffix follows. Regarding *prapakvāni*: this is a compound with a prefix (*gatisamāsa*). Here, the rule "also after a word ending in *ku*" would invariably require the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Regarding *dīrghāhnī śarad*: it has been stated that this too should be understood as belonging among the *yuvan* and other such words.
When the subsequent member consists of a single syllable, the suffix *ṇa* is applied [to form a denominative verb]. Pāṇini 8.4.12.

This is for the purpose of making it clear that the scope of the alternative options has ceased; otherwise, although a permanent injunction could be understood here by the force of its commencement, its recurrence might be suspected in what follows.
And [the suffix *matup* is applied after a stem ending in] *ku*. 8.4.13.

This undertaking involves multiple subsequent word-meanings. Regarding the example *vastrayugiṇau* ("two who possess a pair of garments"): after the suffix *ini* is applied to the word *yuga*, the compound must subsequently be formed with that form ending in *in*. If this were so, then the final *n* of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which serves as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) would become *ṇ*; otherwise, as in the case of *mātṛbhogīṇa*, the change to *ṇ* would be established by another rule alone. Even if it were stated "after *ku*," since a subsequent member consisting solely of the *ka*-group (the gutturals) is impossible, the sense of the possessive suffix *matup* is obtained. Is there no need for *matup*? True; if it were stated "after *ku*," it would be understood as a rule governing the initial element—that is, when the subsequent member begins with the *ka*-group.
The substitution of *ṇ* for the initial consonant of a root taught with an initial *n* occurs after a prefix, even when no compound is formed.

That which has *ṇ* as its initial element in the upadeśa is called *ṇopadeśa*. In the example "pra-nāyakaḥ deśaḥ," the status of *pra* as a prefix (*upasarga*) applies solely with respect to its connection with the action of going (*gati*), and not with respect to the root *nam*.

Regarding the question "What is the purpose of [the phrase] 'even in the absence of a compound' (*asamāse’pi*)?": the question arises because, since no specific distinction is mentioned, the rule would apply to both compounds and non-compounds alike. [The response is: "Because of the governing context of the *pūrvapada* (the preceding member). In this entire section, the term "*pūrvapadāt*" (from the preceding member) is understood to carry over; however, a *pūrvapada* exists only within a compound. Therefore, [the rule] would apply only to compounds. [The phrase "even in the absence of a compound"] is intended to indicate the cessation of that governing context. It is not that the inclusion of the word "even" (*api*) is used for the sake of clarity.

For instance: although the rule *pūrvapadāt* is excluded because it lacks the *svarita* accent, nevertheless the inclusion of the word *api* (even) must be made in the case of non-compounds (*asamāsa*); otherwise, [the suffix] would not apply in a compound when it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñā*), due to the restriction that [the suffix occurs] only after a prior member (*pūrvapada*) when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and because this specific rule finds its application in non-compounds. Therefore, the purpose of the inclusion of *api* in *asamāse* should be understood as follows: by way of indicating the cessation of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *pūrvapada*, so that [the suffix] may apply in both cases—both compounds and non-compounds.

[Objection: But is not the status of the prefix (*upasarga*) unestablished? Since that is unestablished, the restriction will not apply; therefore, when [the condition] "from a preceding word" (*pūrvapadāt*) has ceased to apply, should the mention of "even in a non-compound" (*asamāse 'pi*) not be made? [Response: In that case, this teaches the following: it is not the case that every individual rule (*yoga*) is unestablished, but rather that within a given section (*prakaraṇa*), the section is unestablished. This is said under the view that the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). However, when it is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*), this [objection] does not hold.
The suffixes *hin* and *mīnā*. 8.4.15.
The root *hi* meaning "to go" belongs to the *svādi* group, while *mīñ* meaning "to injure" belongs to the *kryādi* group and ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*).

Regarding the rule for the substitution of *ṇa*, there is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the forms *hinu* and *mīna* so that it may apply here as well—as in *prahiṇoti* and *pramiṇītaḥ*. Alternatively, this is already established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original). Since the properties of *ītv* (long *ī*) and *guṇa* are present in the substitute by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*, the very form that was originally intended is maintained, and thus the substitution of *ṇa* will occur. Objection: But is it not the case that "when a preceding operation is *asiddha*, [the subsequent operation] is not subject to *sthānivadbhāva*"? Reply: This is indeed a flaw in this Paribhāṣā, which is remedied by the statement: "This is its exception (*doṣa*) in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *la* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇa* (*ṇatva*). [Now begins the rule: **Āni loṭ** (Pāṇini 8.4.16).

Regarding *pravapāṇi*: it is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *vapi*, with the substitution of *ni* for *m* by the rule *merniḥ*. By the rule *āḍuttamasya pi ca*, *prayāṇi* is the form of the root *yā*. [Regarding] *pravapāṇi*: those things in which there is an excellent (*pra*) omentum (*vapā*) are *pravapāni*. The mention of *āni* [in the rule] is purposeless; because of the requirement that what is mentioned must be meaningful (*arthavat*), the word *āni* is understood only when it is meaningful, and this [form] is not meaningful. Alternatively, it is because of the condition "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*). For prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) receive the designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) only in relation to that [verb] with which they are connected in action; however, there is no connection with action in relation to this word *āni*, though such a connection exists in relation to that which ends in it.

How is it that this is not understood as "the action of which is *yatkriyā*, [meaning] that which is joined with the action of which"? Rather, how is it understood as "that action which is *yatkriyā*, [meaning] that which is joined with the action of which"? Furthermore, since an action within the scope of usage is never found unconnected [to its object], the connection with the action is taken in reference to the entire complex (*samudāya*). Thus, the connection with the action pertains to the entire complex ending in the suffix *āni*. In this regard, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of that part which is the word *āni* following an upasarga. In this way, the mention of *loṭ* (the imperative suffix) has been refuted.

And [the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] after the verbal roots *nargad*, *nad*, *pat*, *pad*, *ghumā*, *asyati*, *hanti*, *yāti*, *vāti*, *drāti*, *psāti*, *vap*, *vah*, *śam*, *ci*, and *dih*. (Pāṇini 3.1.17)

One might raise the objection: "Since there is the rule *gāmādāgrahaṇeṣv aviśeṣaḥ* (in the case of the mention of *gā*, *mā*, and *dā*, there is no distinction), when the substitution of *ā* is applied by the rule *mīnātiminotidīṅām ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.65), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including those forms that have the shape *mā*—namely both the root *mā* meaning 'to measure' (*mā māne*) and the root *mī*. Anticipating this, he says: "The inclusion of *māṅ* and *meṅ* is intended. This is simply an accepted convention (*iṣṭi*). [Thus we have] *praṇiṣyati*. The substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rules *otaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.71) and *upasargātsunoti-suvati-syati-stauti-stobhati-sthatisthā-senayasyañjām upasargasthasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.65). The roots beginning with *han* and ending with *psā* belong to the *adādi* class; *mā* meaning 'to measure' (*māne*) also belongs here. [In the form] *praṇiśāmyati*, the lengthening is applied by the rule *śamāmaṣṭānāṃ dīrghaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.74).

The mention of *tip* in [Pāṇini 8.4.17] *syasicsīyuṭ...* is for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix). Regarding the rule *aḍvyavāye’pi*: otherwise, since the augment *aṭ* is prescribed for the *aṅga*, and the *aṅga* consists of the stem plus the suffix (*vikaraṇa*), that *aṭ* would be part of the entire complex (*saṅghāta*) and could not be grasped by the mention of the root *gad* and others; thus, the rule would not apply. It should be stated that it applies even when preceded by *āṅ*—as in *praṇyāgadad*. Should that then be stated? No, it need not be stated. The phrase "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*, *k*, *p*, *v*, *āṅ*, *num*" (*aṭakupvāṅnumvyavāye*) continues [from the previous sūtra]. By this, the rule will apply both when there is an intervention by *aṭ* and when *ner* (the *ni* of *nininda*, etc. occurs before roots like *gad*. However, in cases such as *pranyupagadati*, there is no over-extension because of the prohibition in [Pāṇini 8.4.38] *padavyavāye’pi*.

In the remaining cases, there is optionally [the substitution of *u* for *v*] before a consonant beginning with *ka*, *kha*, or *pa*, provided that the word is not ending in *aṣ* in its original form (*upadeśa*).

He states that "akakhādāvaṣānte" is a qualifier of the verbal root (dhātu) brought into proximity by the prefix (*upasarga*): "the verbal root which, in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), begins with something other than *ka*, *kha*, etc., and ends with *ṣ*. The mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) could have been omitted; it would have sufficed to say "akakhe," because of the rule: "In a rule where a designation is prescribed for a certain element, that designation applies to what begins with that element. However, the mention of "ending" (*anta*) must be included; for if it were absent, it would not be known by what the rule applies to what begins with that element, nor by what it applies to what ends with that element.

Why is the term *śeṣa* (remainder) mentioned? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to *gadā* and others. If it were to apply to those as well, the preceding rule (*pūrvayoga*) would become purposeless; therefore, it is possible to say "in the remainder. In *praṇipekṣyati*: when *katva* is applied by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*, it then becomes a word ending in *ṣ*. In *pranicakāra*: when *cutva* is applied to the reduplicated syllable by the rule *kuhoścuḥ*, it then does not begin with *ka*. In *praṇiveṣṭa*: when *ṣatva* is applied to the root by the rule *vraśca* etc., it then ends in *ṣ*; however, because it does not end in *ṣ* at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśa*), *ṇatva* occurs.
[The substitution of *i* for the final vowel of a verbal root] does not occur after the root *an*. (Pāṇini 8.4.19)
Regarding *prāṇiti*: [the root] *śvas* is used in the sense of "breathing," and [the root] *an* as well; [the augment] *iṭ* is applied by the rule *rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*.
The word *antaḥ* [is used as a karmapravacanīya]. 8.4.20.

Regarding the phrase *aniterantaśca*: the meaning is "of the letter *n* which belongs to the root *ani* and stands at the end of a word. In the example *he prāṇ*, the vocative suffix is added to the form ending in the *kvip* suffix; the prohibition of the elision of *n* is applied by the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ*. However, in other cases, the *n* at the end of a word must undergo elision; thus, the vocative form has been cited as an illustration. Furthermore, "end" (*anta*) is understood here in relation to a word (*pada*), and not in relation to the [root] *ni*, because there is no possibility of such a deviation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "some, however" (*kecittu*): the meaning is that they recite only a single rule, *aniterantaḥ*, and they rely on the word *antaḥ* as signifying "proximity. For what purpose? He says: "of that which is proximate to the cause" (*nimittasamīpasya*).

But is it not the case that there is no such object where the letter *n* of the root *ani* is situated immediately adjacent to the cause [of the substitution], since in forms such as *prāṇiti*, after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is an intervention by the vowel *ā*; and in *niraṇiti*, there is an intervention by the vowel *ā*. So how can it be said that [the rule applies] to that which stands immediately next to the cause? To this he says: "separated by one phoneme" (*ekavarṇavyavahitasya*). The meaning is that, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), an intervention by exactly one phoneme is intended.

Furthermore, in the case of *prāṇiti*, one should not suspect that there is an intervention by two phonemes due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) when a rule is prescribed based on what precedes it; for the status of being a substitute is prohibited where a preceding operation is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, was it not said: "That is a defect in the cases of the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*), the substitution of *l* (*latva*), and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*)"? If so, then the status of being a substitute for what precedes is non-eternal (*anitya*); this is because of the mention of *seṭ* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi*, and this has already been explained in the very section concerning the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva-prakaraṇa*). [The examples] beginning with *taiḥ* and so forth...

For there is only one mention of "end" (*anta*), and that serves the purpose of proximity, having fulfilled its function by excluding *ṇatva* in the case of *paryaniti*; consequently, in the case of *he prāṇi*, the prohibition based on the rule "of a word-final [consonant]" (*padāntasya*) would apply. Therefore, that second mention of "end" must be resorted to either by repetition (*āvṛtti*) or by the principle of simultaneous application (*tantra*).

Now, even for those who perform a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) and rely on the word *anta* as denoting a "part," the word *anta* must still be read in the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) as signifying "proximity"; otherwise, the rule would apply even in cases such as *paryaniti*. Therefore, he says: "But for those... The meaning is that they indeed desire *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) even when [the letter *n*] is separated by only one phoneme; therefore, there is no purpose for them in including the term *anta* in the preceding rule.
Both [the *ā* and the *i*] are substituted for the *ā* of *sābhyāsa* (a reduplicated stem). 8.4.21.

Regarding *prāṇiṇiṣati*: with the suffix *san*, by the rule "the second [syllable] of that which begins with a vowel," there is reduplication of the syllable *ni*. Regarding *prāṇiṇat*: from the causative (*ṇic*), there is the *luṅ* suffix; for the *cli* suffix, there is *caṅ*; there is the elision of *ṇi*; and because of the status as a *sthānivat* by the rule "in the case of reduplication, when followed by a vowel," there is reduplication of the syllable *ni*.

Regarding the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* and so forth: if the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham advirvacane* did not exist, then in the case of the form *prāṇiṇiṣati*, once the state [of the root] is established, both reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) would apply simultaneously. Since the substitution of *ṇ* would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*) at that time, if reduplication were performed first, the *ṇ*-substitution for the *n* of the verbal root would not take place because it would be separated by the nasal *ṇ* of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). However, since this rule exists, the substitution of *ṇ* takes place first because it is subsequent (*paratva*). Once the *ṇ*-substitution has been applied, reduplication occurs; thus, even without this specific statement, forms such as *prāṇiṇiṣati* are established.

If this is so, for what purpose is this [treatise] commenced? To this he says: "But this... (*etattu*). The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the sense of possibility; the particle *iti* indicates cause; the word *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). Since this statement of exceptions (*apavāda*) cannot possibly be relied upon for this very purpose, therefore it is commenced. This is the intention: this [treatise] is commenced in order to make known the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of this rule. By that, the following becomes justified: "In the case of *aujaḍhat*, because the substitution of *ḍha* and so forth are not established (*asiddha*), the element *hat* is reduplicated twice."

Now, for what purpose is the word "both" (*ubhau*) used, given that the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the suffix (*abhyāsana*) is already established by the preceding rule? One might argue that by the force of its specific formulation, this [present rule] will apply to the *n* of the root even when there is an intervening element (*vyavāya*). True; it would indeed be established for the separated case, but for the immediately following case, it would not occur due to the maxim of "the curd for the Kauṇḍinya" (*takrakauḍinyanyāya*). Therefore, the word "both" is stated.
The substitution of *ha* occurs for the initial consonant of the root *han*.

The genitive case in *hanter* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*). In the bahuvrīhi compound *atpūrvaḥ*, the letter *na* is the referent of the other member (*anyapadārtha*). Although the qualifiers of the letter *na*—namely *antaḥ* and *ubhau*—are indicated by the nominative case, they are nevertheless indicated here by the genitive. For this is the logical course; the deviation [from the usual order] is minimal. In *praghnanti*: the suffix *laṭ* is used either in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) or the object (*karmaṇi*). By the rule *gamahana*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*), and by *ho hanteḥ*, there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *gh*). Here, the application of the rule *kuvyavāye* arises. In *prāghāni*: the suffix *ciṇ* is applied by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*.

The mention of *śtip* is solely for the purpose of indicating the verbal root (*dhātu*), not for the purpose of excluding the *yaṅ*-luṅ (the elision of *yaṅ*); [as in] *prajaṅghanīti*. For here, once *cutva* has been applied, [the substitution will] not take place precisely because of the intervention of the letter *j*.
Or [the substitution of] *va* for *vam*. 8.4.23.
Since the former [rule] applies as a permanent rule, this is an optional alternative.
In the case of *antaradeśa*. (Pāṇini 8.4.24)

Because the designation *upasarga* (prefix) applies to the word *antar* by the rule "There is an addition [to the definition of prefix] regarding the application of the suffixes *aṅ*, *ki*, the rules for *ṇatva*, and so forth," the form is already established by the rule "The substitution of *at* occurs after *han* when no other vowel precedes it. Therefore, this statement is intended to provide a prohibition regarding location (*deśapratiṣedha*). Thus, *antarhanana* means "a place of killing" (*deśa*), with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
And [the suffix] *ayana*. 8.4.25.

Regarding the term *antarayaṇam*: it is a form derived from the roots *ay* or *iṇ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*. Although this is already established by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ*, this statement is also intended to prohibit [the application of] the [suffix] to that region.
In the Vedic language (chandas), [the augment *t* is added] after a word ending in *ṛ* when followed by a pause (*avagraha*).

*Avagraha* means that which is read by being separated [from the following word]; thus, it is both a *ṛc* (verse) and an *avagraha*, hence *ṛdavagraha*. The three ablative cases—*ṛkārāt*, *avagrahāt*, and *pūrvapadāt*—are all in apposition. Since a *pūrvapada* consisting solely of the vowel *ṛ* is impossible, there is an extension of the rule (*tadantavidhi*) to include that which ends in *ṛ*: namely, "from that which ends in the *ṛ* sound which constitutes an *avagraha*. Furthermore, because this occurs under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* takes place during the time of *saṃhitā* recitation.

The *avagraha* (separation mark) is applied at the time of forming the word; therefore, because it is associated with the *avagraha*, the letter *ṛ* is called "the *avagraha*," but not because it has actually entered that state. Thus, when demonstrating the *avagraha*, the substitution of *ṇ* was not employed. The phrase "from what is not being *avagṛhīta*" (*anavagṛhyamāṇāt*) means "from that which is unfit for *avagraha*. The phrase "not from the end of a word" (*apadāt*) is used to show that while *avagraha* is applied within a word, here the word itself is being divided.
And [the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs] after a *dhātu* (verbal root), *stha*, *uru*, and *ṣu*. (Pāṇini 8.4.27)

"Dhātustha" means the letter *repha* (r) and the letter *ṣakāra* (ṣ) situated within a verbal root (*dhātu*). "Ūru" is a mention of the word-form itself. "Ṣu" is a mention of the form of the root *suñ* after the substitution of *ṣ* has occurred, and not the locative plural ending (*supsu*). Therefore, [the rule] does not apply in the example *indro dhatā gṛheṣu naḥ*. "Nas" is a general mention of both the substitute for the nose (*nāsikādeśa*) and the substitute for the pronoun *asmad*. Consequently, in this instance, only the substitute for *asmad* is the subject of the operation (*kāryin*), because it alone can occur following what is situated in a root and so forth; however, in the subsequent sūtra, both are subjects of the operation.

*Rakṣā na*: *rakṣa* is the second person singular imperative (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣaikavacanāntam*); the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *dvyaco 'tastiṅaḥ*. *Śikṣā na*: in the Veda, the root *śikṣ* has the meaning "to give. *Uruṇaskṛdhi*: this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *kṛ*; *ser hiḥ* [the substitution of *hi* for *si*]; the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs by the rule *śruśṛṇupṝkṛvṛbhyaś chandasi*; the change of the visarga to *r* occurs by the rule *kaḥ karat*, etc. *Abhīṣu na*: the lengthening occurs by the rule *ikaḥ suñi*. The same applies in the case of *ūṣu na*.
After a prefix, [the substitution of *v* for *va*] occurs diversely. Pāṇini 8.4.28.

The inclusion of the term *upasarga* (prefix) here is not intended as an illustration of the initial [letter], because at present there is an absence of the application of grammatical operation (*kriyāyoga*). In the word *praṇa*, the form *naḥ* is the substitute for the pronoun *asmad*; *praṇasaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the suffix *ac* is added as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *upasargācca*; and the substitution of *nas* for *nāsikā* occurs. There is an alternative reading: *upasargādanotparaḥ*. This means that the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *nas* occurs when it follows a prefix, provided it is not followed by an *o*-vowel; however, it does not occur when the *n* is followed by an *o*-vowel or when the preceding vowel is *o*. Since both readings are subject to the possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) or under-extension (*avyāpti*), the commentator has adopted the very reading already explained.
A *kṛt* suffix that ends in a consonant [is called a *sarvanāmasthāna*]. 8.4.29.

By the rule "the *nakāra* which is part of a *kṛt*-suffix when followed by a vowel," he shows that "vowel" (*ac*) is an adjective qualifying the *nakāra*, and not the *kṛt*-suffix itself. For if this were an adjective qualifying the *kṛt*-suffix, then [the substitution would] not occur in cases such as *prāpaṇa*; furthermore, the prohibition of *kam* and the others in the rule "not for *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kam*, *gam*, *iṣ*, *āyi*, *vep*" would be redundant. The examples beginning with *anamāna* are intended merely to show possible instances, not an exhaustive enumeration, since no other [instances] are possible. In *ana*, there is the substitution of *an* for *ya*.

In *māna*, the suffix *u* is applied by [Pāṇini 3.2.175], followed by the *śānac* and others. The suffix *anīya* is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *tavyat* (3.1.96). In *ākrośe nañyaniḥ* (3.3.112), the suffix *yani* is used; in *supyajātau ṇiniḥ* (3.2.78), the suffix *ṇini* is used; and in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*), the suffix *ṇini* is used. The substitution for the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) ending is prescribed by *radābhyām* (8.2.42). Thus, we have *prahīṇa*. The change to *ī* is according to *ghumāsthā* (6.4.66) and so forth. In *pramagna* and *prabhugna*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the *niṣṭhā* ending is according to *oditaśca* (8.2.45). Regarding *nirviṇṇasya*: there is a rule stating that the *nakāra* situated in a *kṛt* suffix does not follow an *ac* (vowel). In that case, the subsequent *n* undergoes the change to *ṇ*, while the preceding one undergoes the change to *ṣṭu* (i.e., *ṇ*).
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is optional [before a suffix beginning with *jhal*]. Pāṇini 8.4.30.

"From that which is prescribed after a *ṇi*-affix. By this, he shows that the word "prescribed" (*vihita*) is a qualifier of "from a *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*); the purpose for this will be stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) itself. There is another method: the phrase "even when there is an intervention by *aṭ*" (*aḍ-vyavāye*) is understood [from a previous rule]. Therefore, since the substitution of *ṇ* is permitted even when there is an intervention by *aṭ* after a root ending in *ṇi*, the substitution of *ṇ* is established in forms such as *prayāpyamāṇa*, even when there is an intervention by the letter *y*, provided that one assumes the rule means "after a *kṛt* suffix following a root ending in *ṇi*."
And [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs after a root ending in *h*, provided that *i* or *u* precedes the final consonant.

Regarding *prakopaṇam*: [the root] *kupa* is used in the sense of "anger. Regarding *prehaṇam*, *prohaṇam*: [the roots] *īha* is used in the sense of "exertion," and *ūha* in the sense of "reflection. In these cases, the substitution of *ṇ* by the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* occurs invariably. But how is it understood that [the root] begins with a consonant (*halādi*) when there is no mention of the word *ādi*? To this he says: "of that which has *ij* as its penultimate. Since that which has *ij* as its penultimate never fails to end in a consonant, the meaning is that, by implication, the mention of *hal* (consonant) serves as a qualifier for the beginning [of the root].
The augment *iṭ* is applied after the root *yaj* when it is followed by a nasal (*nu*) and a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*.

The term *hal* (consonant) is understood [from the previous rule]. He will state the purpose later. Now, one might object: "In that [previous] case, the mention of *hal* was a qualifier of the initial [element], whereas here the purpose is served by it as a qualifier of the final [element]. To this he says: "By that" (*tena*). Since it is impossible for a root beginning with *ij-* to begin with a consonant, the [mention of *hal*] is based on logical necessity (*sāmarthya*). Regarding *praṅkhaṇam*: the root *ikhi* means "to go"; because it is marked with the *it*-augment, the augment *num* is applied.

But surely, once the *anusvāra* has been substituted here, this [word] no longer possesses the *num*; while it may be established by the principle of "as if being the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) in cases such as *prambhaṇam*, it is not established in the present case where *num* occurs from the very beginning, for there the letter *n* is innate (*autpattika*). Furthermore, it would undesirably apply in cases like *prenvanam*, where *num* alone is heard without modification. Therefore, even here, the mention of *num* must be explained as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *anusvāra*.

Just as in the case of observing the stars, [the rule] will apply everywhere regarding a desired object and not apply regarding an undesired one; and by doing so, its status as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) is established. Otherwise, in the case of *prenvanam*, its status as an injunctive rule (*vidhyartha*) might be suspected. Nor is the formation accomplished by the rule *aṭ-kupvāṅ-num-vyavāye 'pi* (P. 8.4.2), because even there, the mention of *num* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the anusvāra. Now, one might ask: since this is already accomplished by the rule *kṛty-acaḥ* (P. 8.4.29), what is the purpose of this [present rule]? To this he says: "Since it is already accomplished... and so forth.

Regarding the term *pramaṅganam*: the root *mañj* also has the meaning of "going. In the reading *pramaṇḍanam*, it means "adorning. Now, one might object: a restriction (*niyama*) occurs when there is no other purpose, on the grounds that there is nothing else to be enjoined (*vidheya*). But here there is something to be enjoined; what is it? Since the substitution of *ṇatva* is optionally obtained after a causative suffix (*ṇic*), is it not the case that the *ṇatva* must be enjoined as obligatory? To this he replies: "Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *hal*. But surely, once the *ṇi*-suffix is elided, even a causative form ends in a consonant (*hal*); what follows from that? Even though the governing rule of *hal* applies, could it not still serve as an injunction (*vidhi*)? This is not so; for we rely on a qualification of what has been prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*).
Indeed, with this very intention, the author of the Vṛtti stated: "that which is prescribed after a verbal root ending in a consonant."
Or [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots *niṃsa*, *nikṣa*, and *nind*. (Pāṇini 8.4.33)

In the case of *ṇisi* in the sense of kissing, *ṇikṣa* in the sense of planting, and *ṇidi* in the sense of censuring, since these have *ṇ* as their upadeśa (original form), the substitution of *ṇ* would be mandatory; therefore, this rule provides for an option.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* does not take the augment *iṭ* after the roots *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kram*, *gam*, *iṇ*, *pyāyī*, and *vep*.

"By the mention of *pū*, the inclusion of *pūṅ* must be intended. This is indeed a desired conclusion (*iṣṭi*). Regarding the phrase "and of those ending in *ṇi*": this is a statement because [the rule] would not otherwise apply, since that which ends in *ṇi* is a different verbal root (*adhātu*). Furthermore, if this were to apply to forms ending in *ṇi*, there would be the fault of tautology (*anuvādadoṣa*) in certain instances; for in those cases, the exclusion [of the rule] is already established by the very option provided in the rule "*ṇer vibhāṣā*" (Pāṇini 6.4.51).
[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur] after a word-final [consonant]. 8.4.35.
