*niṣpānam*, *duṣpānam*: by the rule "idudupadhasya ca," the visarga is changed to *ṣ*; here, there is the potential application of the rule "kṛtyacaḥ. *sarpiṣpānam*: this is a compound with a genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*). *yajuṣpānam*: this is a compound according to the rule "kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam. In both cases, the change to *ṣ* occurs by the rule "nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya"; here, there is the possibility of application by the rules "pānaṃ deśe" and "vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ."

Regarding the phrase *pade 'nte*: the compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) [of Pāṇini 2.1.40], namely, "the locative case. In the example *susarpiṣkeṇa*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* meaning "that which has beautiful ghee (*sarpiḥ*)," followed by the suffix *kap*; the change to *ṣ* is by the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*. This [final element] does not become the end of what precedes it when a word (*pada*) follows; rather, it becomes the end of the word itself, because the technical designation *pada* is prescribed by the rule *svādiṣu*. Consequently, in this case as well, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would result. How, then, is it known that this is a locative compound? By the inclusion of the term "end" (*anta*).

Otherwise, if the term *varṇa* were not employed, the rule "in all cases there is the designation of that which ends with it" would result in the interpretation that [the operation applies] only after a word ending in the letter *ṣ*.
The substitution of *naś* ending in *ṣ* [is applied] before the suffixes beginning with *iṭ*.

Regarding the word *pranaṣṭa*: after the augment *num* has been applied by the rule *maśjinaśorjhali*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditām*. Then, by the rule *vraścādiṣatvam*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. [Objection: It should be stated that the rule applies to the root *naś* ending in the letter *a*, and not to one ending in *ṣ*, so that [the form] *praṇaṅkṣyati* may also be obtained here; for in this case, the substitution of *k* occurs by the rule *ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si*. Should it then be stated in that way? [Response: No, he says: "the mention of the final letter (*antagrahaṇam*)."

Because the root *naś* is qualified by the letter *ṣ*, the condition "ending in *ṣ*" (*ṣ-anta*) is already established; however, by the force of the repeated mention of the word "end" (*anta*), the prohibition applies to that which currently ends in *ṣ* as well as to that which previously ended in *ṣ*.
[The substitution of *anusvāra* occurs] for a final consonant at the end of a word. || 8.4.37 ||
"He shall act," and so forth, is also an example.
Also when there is an intervention by a word. 8.4.38.

Regarding the expression *māṣakumbhavāpena*, some say: when the analysis is "the sowing (*vāpa*) of a jar (*kumbha*) of beans (*māṣa*)," then, because the rule "when there is the status of being a subsequent member (*uttarapadatve*), the prohibition of the designation 'word' (*apadādividhau*) applies" prohibits the application of the technical designation "word" (*padatva*) by means of the condition of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the prohibition [of *ṇatva*] does not take effect due to the absence of word-status; therefore, *ṇatva* must indeed occur. Consequently, they hold that the example is based on the following analysis: "the sowing of a jar is *kumbhavāpaḥ*; the sowing of a jar of beans is *māṣakumbhavāpaḥ*. In this case, the application of the rule is provided by "and when *ku* follows" (*kumati ca*).

Regarding *prāvanaddham*: although there is an intervention by the word *ava*, the rule *aḍvyavāye* applies because of the rule *upasargādasamāse'pi*. Regarding *pragānnayāma*: this is an instance of separated usage (*vyavahita*) in Vedic literature (*chandas*). There is an intervention by the word *gām*, which ends in the second case (*dvitīyānta*). Regarding the rule *padavyavāye'taddhite*: the meaning is that this prohibition concerning intervention by a word (*padavyavāya*) must be stated as not applying when the word [intervening] is a *taddhita* suffix; that is, it does not occur in the case of a word that is a *taddhita*. Regarding *ādragomayeṇa*: the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *gośca puruṣe*; in that context, the word *go-* is a "word" (*padam*) according to the rule *svādiṣu*.
And [the rule regarding the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*] applies in the case of the roots beginning with *kṣubh*. (Pāṇini 8.4.39)

The mention of *kṣubhnā-* is for the purpose of grasping the specific word-form (*svarūpa*), not for grasping the verbal root (*dhātu*); therefore, in forms such as *kṣobhaṇam*, the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) certainly occurs. [Examples include] *kṣubhnītaḥ* and *kṣubhnanti*. However, in these cases, because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision of the suffix *-ā* and the nasal (*al-lopayoḥ*), or because that which is modified in one part is not different from the original (*ekadeśavikṛtasyānanyatvāt*), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur. *Nṛnamaḥ* means "one who causes men to bow" (*nṝn namayati*). *Harinandī* contains the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). *Harinandanaḥ* and *girinagaram* are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Regarding *narīnṛtyate*: [this is derived by applying] the rule *rīgṛdupadhasya ca*.

Regarding *tṛpnoti*: the suffix *śnu* occurs here by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) according to Vedic usage. *Parinarttanam* and *parigahanam* are *prādi*-compounds (*prādisamāsa*). *Parinandanam* is a *gati*-compound (*gatisamāsa*). *Śaraniveśa* and so forth, ending with *darbhānūpa*, are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding *ācāryabhogīna* and *ācāryānī*: in these very cases there is this prohibition; however, in forms such as *ācāryeṇa* and *ācāryāṇām*, it certainly does occur. The *kṣubhna*-group is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). The letter *ca* serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, and thus indicates this very purpose.
When a *ścu* sound (ś, ṣ, s) follows a *stoḥ* sound (t, th, d, dh, n), it replaces the *stoḥ* sound with a *ścu* sound.

In this context, the word *saṃnipāta* (conjunction) is to be supplied. In the example *vṛkṣaḥ śete*, the substitution of *s* for the *visarga* occurs optionally by the rule *vā śari*. In the example *majjati*, once the substitution of *d* for the *s* has been made by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the substitution of *c* for that *d* results in the letter *j*. However, the substitution of *jaś* is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purpose of subsequent operations); this is because of the separation of the rule *na mu ne* into two parts (*na* and *mu ne*). Thus, the grammatical indication in the form *bhṛjjatīnāṃ ṅiti* is justified.

One might raise the objection: "In this case, there are two elements subject to modification—the letter *ś* and the *tavarga* (the retroflex stops)—and there are likewise two causes—the letter *ś* and the *cavarga* (the palatals). Therefore, because of this numerical equality, would not a correspondence of position (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) follow? Anticipating this, he says: "The prohibition [applies] by the rule *śād*. The use of the instrumental case in *ścunā* is intended so that the operation may apply even when joined with what precedes—as in *yajñaḥ* and *yācñā*. If the locative case were used, however, according to the rule "when [an element] is specified in the locative, it refers to what precedes," the operation would apply only when joined with what follows.
When a *ṣṭu*-class sound follows, a *ṣṭu*-class sound is substituted [in its place]. Pāṇini 8.4.41.

Regarding *aṭṭati* and so forth: the roots *aṭṭa* (meaning "to overcome" and "to injure") and *aḍḍa* (meaning "to attack") are listed in the *gaṇa*-list with *t* and *ḍ* as their internal vowels (*upadhā*). When these two, ending in *kvip*, undergo the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the retention of the sounds *t* and *ḍ* is for the purpose of their audible pronunciation. Furthermore, the prohibition "the first members of a cluster are not doubled" (*na ndrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ*) applies to *aḍḍati* as well. Here too, the mention of the third case (*tṛtīyānirdeśaḥ*) is so that the substitution of *ṣṭu* may occur even when joined with what precedes it, as in *droḍhā*. In this case as well, due to the prohibition "of *t* before *ṣ*" (*toḥ ṣi*), there is no correspondence of number between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*nimittin*).
The substitution of *ṣ* for *ṣṭu* does not occur when *ṣṭu* follows a word-final *ṭ* or *ṭh*, except after the word *anām*.

The prohibition [of the *nuṭ* augment] applies to the genitive plural form *anām*, when it has not yet received the *nuṭ* augment. In the case of *śvaliṭ-sāya*, if the *dhuṭ* augment is absent, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (by P. 8.3.59) would apply to the *s*. However, if the *dhuṭ* augment is present, because the substitution of *c* for *t* (by P. 8.4.40) is considered *asiddha*, the rule applies to that very *dh* [which results from the *dhuṭ*]. In the case of *īṭṭe*: the root *īḍ* meaning "to praise" belongs to the second class (*adādi*) and is *anudātta*. "Ninety plus six" is *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ*. "A collection of six cities" is *ṣaṇṇagarī*.
The substitution of *ṣ* occurs in place of *t* [before a sibilant]. || 8.4.43 ||
Because of the indication by the locative case in the word "ṣi," this [substitution] occurs even when there is contact with a preceding element, as in *loṣṭā* and *peṣṭā*.
[The substitution of] *ś* [occurs] for [the final consonant of a verbal root ending in] *s*. 8.4.44.

The forms are *praśnaḥ* and *viśnaḥ*. The suffix *naṅ* is applied according to the rule *yajayāca-* etc., and the letter *ch* is replaced by *ś* according to the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*. According to the principle that "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante*), this prohibition does not apply in the Taittirīyaka: *ayo'śñāti*. Even there, however, it does indeed occur in the Kāṭhaka: *brahmacāriṇe praśnān procya prajighāya*. And since it occurs in the Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa as well, one attains all prosperity (*sakalaṃ bhadramaśnute*).
A *yara* (the consonants *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*) followed by a nasal (*anunāsika*) may optionally become a nasal.

The phrase "padāntāt" (from the end of a word), which is understood from the previous rule, is transformed here into a genitive case ending. Regarding the form *vāṅmayam*: the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule "nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.144).
After the vowels *a* and *r*, [the following consonant] is doubled. 8.4.46.

From the root *arca*, with the suffix *ghañ* and the substitution of *k* for *c*, we have *arkka*. *Marci* is a Vedic (sautra) root; from it, by the rule "after *iṇ*, *bhī*, *kā*, *pā*, *śal*, *yat*, and *arci*, the suffix *kan* is applied," and by the rule "the substitute *k* replaces *c*," we have *markka*. Here, the letter *r* follows immediately after the vowel *a*, and the letter *k* follows that as well. This should be understood in the same way for the subsequent examples as well.
And [the doubling does not occur] when followed by a vowel or a consonant-group (anac). Pāṇini 8.4.47.

Regarding the term *anacpara*: that which is other than a vowel (*ac*) is *anac*; that which has such an *anac* as its subsequent element is *anacpara*. By this, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is indicated. What is the purpose? None at all; on the contrary, it would result in a fault, for it would not apply to word-final positions (*avasāna*), since there is no other phoneme (*varṇāntara*) similar to a vowel (*ac*). The exclusion was adopted because it would otherwise entail the burden of a complex understanding (*pratipattigaurava*). For in the alternative view (where it is a prohibition, *pratiṣedha*), the general rule would have to be inferred from the specific prohibition, which is cumbersome. Examples are *ulkā* and *valmīka*. Here, the letter *l* is a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*), while the letters *k* and *m* are nasal stops (*yam*).
In *stthālī*, the letter *s* is *śar*, and the letter *th* is *khay*. In words such as *vatssa*, the letters *t*, *k*, and *p* are *khayaḥ*, while the letters *s* and *ṣ* are *śarau*.

Regarding the phrase "at the end" (*avasāne*): this rule was commenced by resorting to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). However, in the case of a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), since the subsequent cause is not relied upon, the desired result is established by virtue of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "optionally" (*vā*).
The suffix *ni* is applied after the word *nādin* when it denotes the reproach of a son.

Regarding the term *putrādinī*: the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*). As for the phrase "and when followed by that" (*tatpare ca*), it means that even when the word *ādinī* follows, the doubling of the word *putra* does not occur in that subsequent position—for example, *putrāś ca pautrāś ca* = *putrapautrāḥ*; she whose habit is to eat them is *putrapautrādinī*. Others, however, explaining it as "when the word *putra* follows that," cite *putraputrādinī* as an example; in that case, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "she eats the son of a son."

Regarding the term *hatajagdhapara*: it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of *hatajagdham* (that which is eaten after being killed) and *param* (subsequent), with the word *para* placed last according to the rule beginning with *rājadanta*. Regarding *putrahatī*: this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) meaning "one by whom a son has been killed," with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* applied according to the rule *asvāṅgapūrvapadādvā*.
Regarding *khayo dvitīyāḥ*: *khayaḥ* is in the genitive case; *dvitīyāḥ* refers to the second letters in each of the consonant groups (*varga*), namely those beginning with *kha*.
A final *ś* is elided before a vowel (*ac*).

Regarding the word *ādarśa*: it is formed by adding the suffix *ghañ* to the root *dṛś* (to see) in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Regarding the word *darśa*: here too, *ghañ* is added in the sense of a locus. This is an instance of indirect indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*), for the term *darśa* [etymologically] means "that in which the moon is not seen."
According to Śākaṭāyana, [the rule applies] when three or more [words] are involved. 8.4.50.

In *indra* and similar forms, there is no doubling of the *n* and *d*. Regarding *bhrāṣṭram*, this is because the rule *dīrghād ācāryāṇām* is considered asiddha (not yet established). It is understood that this very prohibition applies only when three or more consonants follow.
In all cases, according to Śākalya. 8.4.51.
This undertaking is for the sake of Atri and others.
According to the teachers, [the substitution of *ai* and *au* for *e* and *o*] occurs when the preceding vowel is long. Pāṇini 8.4.52.
In examples such as *dātram*, there is the application of the rule *anaci ca*.
In the presence of a *jhaś* sound, a *jhal* sound is replaced by a *jaś* sound.
In examples, *bha*, *gha*, and *dha* become *ba*, *ga*, and *da*.
The suffix *carc* is applied after a verb in the sense of repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding *cikhaniṣati*: from the root *khan*, the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added; there is reduplication; by the rule "of *ku* and *hu*, *ca*" (*kuhoścaḥ*), the change to *c* occurs—yielding *cha*; then its change to *ca* occurs—yielding *ca*. Regarding *ṭiṭhakārayiṣati*: the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "he causes the letter *ṭha* to be expressed" (*ṭhakāram ācaṣṭe*); the *ṭi*-portion is elided; then the desiderative suffix (*san*) is added; the *ṭha* becomes *ṭ*. Regarding *tiṣṭhāsati*: by the rule "the *khaya* [consonants] following *śū* [are elided]" (*śūpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*), the *tha* is the remainder; its change to *ta* occurs.

"And *prakṛtiśca* [is] *prakṛticaraḥ*. The meaning is that, for the purpose of overriding the *jaś*-rule, by the operation of a grammatical rule like Parjanya (which applies regardless of other conditions), the *prakṛti*-forms become non-different in form from their substituends (*sthānin*). This is obtained through the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the most similar substitute). "The *prakṛti*-substitutes for *jaś*-sounds are *prakṛti*-substitutes" has been explained. Regarding *ḍiḍya*: after reduplication in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *ḍīṅ*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to the rule *eranekācaḥ*.
And [the substitution of] *khari* [occurs]. 8.4.55.

Regarding *yuyutsate*: from the root *yudh* with the suffix *san*, the letter *dh* becomes *t*. Regarding *āripsate* and *ālipsate*: from the roots *rabh* and *labh*, by the rule "in the presence of *san*, [the roots] *mī*, *mā*, *ghu*, etc.," the vowel *a* is replaced by *i*; then, by the rule "of *sk* and *k*, when they are the first members of a conjunct," there is the elision of *s*, and the letter *bh* becomes *p*.
In the case of *vāvasāne*. (Pāṇini 8.4.56)

Since the substitution of *jaś* is obligatory by the rule "jhalāṃ jaśo 'nte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39), the substitution of *car* is prescribed; however, because of the mention of the option (*vā*), that [substitution of *car*] also occurs in one alternative case.
An *aṇ* vowel that is not a *pragṛhya* becomes nasalized [before a following vowel]. Pāṇini 8.4.57.
The term *aṇ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviation) formed with the preceding letter *ṇ*. [Examples: *agnī*, *vāyū*. By the rule *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam*, these receive the designation *pragṛhya*.
An *anusvāra* is replaced by a homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) when followed by a *yay* (any consonant except *h*, *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*).

Regarding the passage beginning with *śaṅkitā*: [the roots] *śaki* (in the sense of doubt), *uchi* (in the sense of gathering), *kuḍi* (in the sense of burning), *ṭunadi* (in the sense of prosperity), and *kapi* (in the sense of moving) take the suffix *it*, which triggers the augment *num*. By the rule *naścāpadāntasya jhali*, an *anusvāra* is substituted for the final *n*. When followed by the consonants beginning with *ka*, this *anusvāra* is replaced by the fifth letters of their respective classes (*varga*), such as *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*, according to the order of the following consonants.

In the forms *kurvanti* and *kṛṣanti*, when the suffix *jhi* is replaced by *anti*, the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* would apply; why, then, does this not occur? To this he says: "In this case" (*iha*). The substitution of *ṇ* does not occur before the *anusvāra*, because since the substitution of *ṇ* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) [for the purposes of the preceding rule], the *anusvāra* itself is produced first; nor does it occur afterwards, because this *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous substitute) which takes the place of the *anusvāra* is also *asiddha* when the substitution of *ṇ* is to be applied. "By means of the *parasavarṇa*" means: by means of the grammatical rule intended for the purpose of the *parasavarṇa*. "In this way," and so forth.
The meaning is that what was stated in the Bhāṣya—that having become an *anusvāra*, it transcends the substitution of *ṇa*—is so according to the manner just described.
Or [the substitution of *anusvāra* occurs] for a final *m* at the end of a word. Pāṇini 8.4.59.
Regarding the phrase "taṅktha" and so forth: after the letters beginning with *ka*, the letters beginning with *ṅa* occur in their respective order.
The suffix *tor* is applied after the word *li*. (Pāṇini 8.4.60)
In this case, the *t* sound is replaced by a pure *l*, and the *n* sound is replaced by a nasalized *l*.
After the word *ud*, the substitution of the preceding [element] occurs in place of the roots √sthā and √stambh.

The term *parasavarṇa* (homogeneous with the following) is connected here by extracting the word *savarṇa* (homogeneous), even though it was part of a compound. In the example *utthātā*, the letter *t* is the homogeneous substitute for the preceding *s*. Others, however, desire the letter *th* because of the similarity in external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*). In that case, there would be the hearing of two *t*s. Nor does the *cartya* (substitution of *t*) apply to the preceding [letter]; for when that [substitution] is to be performed, this *parasavarṇa* substitute is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*).
Regarding the statement "it should be stated [the rule applies] also in the case of *roga*," this applies without distinction to both Vedic (*chandas*) and common (*bhāṣā*) usage.
A *jh* consonant [is optionally changed to *gh*, *jha*, or *dha*] before *ha*, optionally.
In these examples, for the aspirated, voiced, and sonant letter *ha*, there are corresponding fourth letters such as *gha* and so forth.
The substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs before a consonant other than a sibilant (*aṭ*).

Regarding the rule *śaścho’mi*: the meaning is that the word *aṭ* should be removed and *ami* should be stated instead. Thus, in the examples *tacchlokena* and *tacchmaśruṇā*, the substitution of *cha* occurs for the letter *śa* even when it is followed by the letters *la* and *ma*.
There is elision of the *m* of *yam* when followed by *yam*. 8.4.64.

"Two *y* sounds": one belongs to the *kyap* suffix prescribed by the rule "in the sense of a name, from *samaja*, etc."; the second belongs to the *ayaṅ* substitute prescribed by the rule "for *i* before a *kṅit* suffix. "The third is produced by succession" (*kramaja*): "succession" means sequence; that which is born from that is "produced by succession," and it is further brought about by the doubling [of the consonant] according to the rule "also before a non-*ac* vowel. "One *y* sound after the *t*": this belongs to the *ṇya* suffix prescribed by the rule "from *ditya*, *aditya*, *āditya*, etc. "Two *y* sounds": one belongs to the *ṇya* suffix following the word *aditi*; the second belongs to the suffix following the word *āditya*.

Regarding the word *annam*: here the letter *m* is a *yam*, and it is followed by a *yam* (the *n*), but it is not followed by a consonant (*hal*). Regarding *arghyam*: the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*) according to the rule *pādārghābhyāṃ ca*; here the letter *gh* is followed by a consonant (*repha*), and this [consonant] is followed by a *yam* (the *y*), but the *gh* itself is not followed by a *yam*. Regarding *śārṅgam*: the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "a modification of" (*vikāra*) according to the rule *śṛṅgasya vikāraḥ*; there is a vṛddhi substitution for the vowel *ṛ*, with *r* as the subsequent element (*rapara*); here the letter *ṅ* is a *yam* and is followed by a consonant (*hal*), but it is not followed by a *yam*.

But is not the *vṛddhi* substitution extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*)? What follows from that? [Does it mean] that it does not follow after a consonant (*hal*)? The elision (*lopa*) is also extrinsic, because it depends upon multiple causes.
[This is stated in the rule: *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65).

Regarding the statement "there are three *t* sounds": by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ*, the *ā* of *ātapati* becomes *t*; furthermore, the *c* of that *t* becomes *t* through the substitution of *car*. One [t] is connected to the suffix (*pratyaya*), a second arises from the doubling (*dvirvacana*) according to the rule *anaci ca*, and the fourth is produced sequentially [from the doubling]. Thus, there are four *t* sounds. Regarding the statement "there are four *t* sounds": there are the three previously mentioned, the fourth is connected to the word *marut*, and the fifth is produced by doubling. This is because of the force of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *marut*; this has been explained precisely in the section concerning the "supplementary rule for the word *marut*."

Regarding "śārṅgin": this *ṅ* sound follows a consonant (*hal*) and occurs before a homogeneous *jh* sound (*jhar*), yet because it is not itself a *jh* sound, it is not elided. In "priyayañcñā": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose five faces are dear" (*priyāḥ pañca asya*). By the rule "optionally for *priya*," the word *priya* is placed first; then the third-case singular ending is applied, the vowel *a* is elided (*allopaḥ*), and the *n* undergoes the *ścutva* change to become *ñ*. This *c* sound follows a consonant and is itself a *jh* sound occurring before a homogeneous sound, yet because the *ñ* is not a *jh* sound, it is not elided.

But surely, because of the status of the elision (*al-lopa*) as *sthānivat*, the following sound would not be a homogeneous (*savarṇa*) one; so what is the purpose of this [rule] "in the case of *jhar*" (*jhari*)? To this he says: "of the elision of *a*" (*allopasya*).

Regarding *tarptā*: the root *tṛp* means "to satisfy. The substitution of *t* for *p* does not constitute a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) replacement because their points of articulation (*sthāna*) differ. Now, one might object: since the causes (*nimitta*) and the effects (*kāryin*) here correspond in number, when there is a designation according to numerical order (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*), the elision (*lopa*) would not apply in the case of *taptā*; so what is the purpose of including the term *savarṇa* to exclude that? To this he replies: "By the force of the inclusion of the term *savarṇa*. For in a designation according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), there is no *jhar* that is non-*savarṇa*, such that the inclusion of *savarṇa* would be intended to exclude it.

*Śiṇḍhi*, *piṇḍhi*. [The roots] *śiṣlṛ* (in the sense of distinguishing) and *piṣlṛ* (in the sense of crushing) belong to the *rudhādi* class. [From these, we derive] the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), which becomes *hi*; by the rule *śnasorallopaḥ*, the *a* is elided; *hi* becomes *dhi* by *herdhiḥ*; by *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi*, the *ṣ* becomes *ḍ*; by *naścāpadāntasya jhali*, an *anusvāra* is inserted after the *n*; its *parasavarṇa* substitute is *ṇ*; by *ṣṭunā ṣṭuḥ*, the *dh* becomes *ḍh*; and by this [rule], there is the elision of the preceding *ḍ* when followed by *ḍh*.
After an acute (udātta) vowel, an acute-less (anudātta) vowel becomes circumflex (svarita).

"Gārgyaḥ," "Vātsyaḥ": [the suffix] *yañ* is applied according to the rule *gargādibhyo yañ*; because of the marker *ñ*, the first syllable is udātta, the remainder is *nighāta* (unaccented), and that [first syllable] becomes *svarita*. "Pacati," "Paṭhati": the personal endings *śap* and *tip* are unaccented; the accent belongs to the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), and the letter *śa* becomes *svarita*.

This [rule] should have been stated immediately after "titsvaritam"; for in that case, the mention of *svarita* would not be necessary. To this he replies: "of this" (*asya*). If it were placed there, the rule "a word is unaccented except for one [syllable]" (*anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam*) would apply. But because it is placed here, that rule does not apply; for the *svarita* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Consequently, both the acute (*udātta*) and the circumflex (*svarita*) are heard.
According to Gārgya, Kāśyapa, and Gālava, [the *pluta* vowel] does not occur before a following acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent. Pāṇini 8.4.67.

The term *udāttasvaritāvudayau* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that from which the acute (*udātta*) and circumflex (*svarita*) [accents] arise. The word *udaya* is connected with each [of the two preceding terms], as he states: "of that which has an acute [accent] as its *udaya*" (*udāttodayasya*). In the *Prātiśākhyas*, the word *udaya* is well known to be synonymous with the word *para*. In this context, the word *tatra* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the *lit-svara* rule; the word *kva* ends in the suffix *at* according to the rule *kimo't*, and thus it is circumflexly accented (*svarita*) by the *tit-svara* rule.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated that [the substitution occurs] when followed by an acute (udātta) or circumflex (svarita) vowel": this too is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); one should simply state "of the acute and circumflex vowels," since the meaning of the word *para* ("following") is obtained from this very [rule]. As for the phrase "for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalārtham*): the mere utterance of the word *udaya* is itself auspicious. For treatises that begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, become renowned; they possess heroic men and long-lived men. Here, the word *vṛddhi* occurs at the beginning, the word *śiva* occurs in the middle—as in "the maker of welfare, peace, and prosperity" (*śiva-śam-ariṣṭasya kare*)—and this word *udaya* occurs at the end.

In this case, one [sound] is open (vivṛta) and the other is closed (saṃvṛta); both are without case-endings. That which is open is the original element (sthānin), and that which is closed is the substitute (ādeśa).

For what purpose is the substitution of *ā* for *a* prescribed? To this he says: "In this [system]," meaning "for the sake of grammatical operation" (*kāryārtham*). That operation, moreover, is the designation of *a* as being homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels; otherwise, due to the difference in their articulatory effort (*prayatna*), it would not occur. Consequently, if the short *a* were not included [in the homogeneous set], it would not include the long and protracted vowels. And in that case, there would be a fault: the rule "a long vowel replaces a simple vowel followed by a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*) would apply only here—*aindrāgnam*—and would not apply here—*daṇḍāḍhakam*.

Therefore, for the sake of such results as these, the vowel *a* is explained and its restoration (*pratyāpatti*) is promised in this treatise; for if this restoration were not performed, then that [vowel] would appear in its original form in usage, and so that it may not be so, restoration is effected here.

In this context, since the *sthānin* (the original element) *a* is *vivṛta* (open), it includes by virtue of being an *aṇ* all its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sounds; thus, it follows that even the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels would take the place of the *saṃvṛta* (closed) *a*. However, the substitute (*ādeśa*) *a* is *saṃvṛta* and is not an *aṇ*, so it does not follow that it includes its homogeneous sounds, because it is being taught as something new (*bhāvyamāna*). Consequently, one might object: "Would not the *saṃvṛta* quality with which it is uttered apply only to that specific quality, and not to the entire *avarṇa* class divided into eighteen varieties? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And [the rule applies] to the long and protracted vowels. This is simply an accepted position (*iṣṭi*).

Alternatively, this is established by the mention of the *tapara* (the *t* as a marker). The rule should be formulated as "ada. In that case, the first vowel *a* is *tapara* because the *t* follows it (*taḥ paro yasmāt*), and the second is *tapara* because the *t* is after it (*tātparaḥ*). Consequently, the substitute *a* will not include the long and protracted vowels, whereas the original (*sthānin*) *a*, even though it is not an *aṇ*, will include those of the same duration (*tatkālān*) that possess other qualities (*guṇāntarayuktān*). Or rather, this should be understood as an indication using the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical items).

In this context, six *mātrika* vowels beginning with *a* are indicated as the substituends (*sthānin*), and there are likewise exactly six substitutes (*ādeśa*). Therefore, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed for both groups. Among them, by virtue of the power of indicating the six substituends, the long and protracted vowels—which possess different durations—are not included by the substituends. Consequently, the six substitutes, which are *saṃvṛta*, take the place of the six substituends according to their respective order; thus, all desired results are established. May there be peace.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the eighth chapter in the Padamañjarī composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Haradatta Miśra.
